## Volume front matter

## Series title page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost diligence; continually illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all the works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the material treated; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, by which it may readily be discovered which Fathers, and in what places of their works, commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture.**

**The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the works reprinted, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.**

**First series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church, from Tertullian to Gregory the Great.** Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or Complete Courses in the various branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# Notice concerning the new reprinting of this Benedictine edition

[Note: [Col. 0007] N.B. 1. We have occasionally interwoven into the text the variant readings that had initially escaped the Benedictine Fathers, as they themselves recommend; their earlier reading is marked by these brackets: [ ].]

[Note: [Col. 0007] N.B. 2. Whenever it seemed appropriate to modify somewhat the text as arranged by the Benedictine Fathers, their own reading is given in the notes, distinguished by the sign “In B.”, M. [ [Col. 0007] Whatever we have added to the edition of the Benedictine Fathers will be distinguished by this sign, M.]]

It would certainly be presumptuous to claim for ourselves the immortal glory of the Benedictine Fathers. It is by no means impossible, however, to improve their labors by introducing a few alterations which they themselves, had they lived in our age, would have judged necessary. Moreover, it is now agreed among the most learned men, especially outside France, that the Benedictine edition, although deserving of every esteem and far superior to all those that preceded it, nevertheless bears certain marks of negligence—whether because the editors were unable to sustain with unremitting attention a labor prolonged over twenty full years, or because a task distributed among so many collaborators did not permit unity. Thus they sometimes seem to have neglected the collation of earlier editions. Thus, too, by placing variant readings now in either margin, now at the end of the volume, they pursue an exact recension of the texts at the expense of uniformity. Finally, in order to repair omissions or correct in whatever manner the many defective readings and citations that had been imprudently introduced, they burdened the individual volumes with additions and corrections.

We therefore devoted our principal attention to two matters: first, that nothing previously published should be omitted from our edition; and second, that each item should be arranged in the most suitable order. In addition to manuscript codices, we compared most editions, both old and recent, with such diligence that our edition necessarily had to emerge richer, and we may rightly assert that nothing has hitherto been published that is not more fully represented in it. Yet it would have been useless to gather so many riches unless they were properly arranged; nor do we intend to explain in detail everything we have done in this respect. We shall give only a few examples.

**1.** Nothing was more important to us than restoring the proper clarity of the text in the places indicated by the Reverend Fathers themselves. Whenever they seemed to have fallen inadvertently into an error, and their guidance was lacking, we established the genuine reading on the authority both of manuscripts and of books.

**2.** Apart from the clarity of the text—by which, whatever its quality, the Benedictine edition greatly surpasses all others—it possesses above all the advantage of being enriched by excellent prefaces and a great abundance of notes and variant readings. We have carefully preserved all these materials, indeed we have increased the variant readings; but we have not admitted every reading that came to us from every quarter. We readily confess that we are not inflamed by that philological enthusiasm which measures the excellence of an edition by the number of its variant readings. On the contrary, such readings will generally be of doubtful usefulness if one considers how slight their importance is, how much they interrupt the sequence of the discourse, and how much the authority of books is weakened among many readers by them; for truth does not tolerate a double reading. In our judgment, therefore, amid so many variations of manuscripts and books, it is preferable not to shake them all out with an indiscriminate hand, but not to scrutinize every one of them exhaustively, to pass over some with judicious neglect, and to admit only those that contribute, even slightly, to a correct understanding of the author.

Let the same be said of spurious works as has been said of variant readings.

It has commonly happened to the most distinguished writers of antiquity that, through the obscurity of the times, the greed of booksellers, and other causes, their genuine offspring were surrounded by an unworthy crowd of spurious works. It would certainly not have been difficult to double or triple the size of the Augustinian edition at will by adding the spurious works circulated under the name of the great Doctor. There is scarcely a library that does not boast treasures of this kind. But what then? Is it not clear that the weeds weaken the wheat, and that the reputation of true gems declines if they are mixed with counterfeits? Nevertheless, so that nothing should be lacking in our edition, we decided to omit none of the spurious or doubtful works that the Benedictine Fathers had made public. Indeed, we added several recently discovered works to their recension, all of which belong to the collection of Sermons. We used this license of enlargement sparingly, however, remembering that the Benedictine Fathers, according to the counsel and resources available to them, had certainly recognized most of those deceptive riches which some of their contemporaries claim to have unearthed, and that whatever men so commendable for learning and judgment rejected deservedly incurs suspicion and disgrace.

[Col. 0007]

**3.** It is a matter of the greatest importance, and especially suited to the easy comparison of texts, that the variant readings which the Maurist Fathers distributed in no uniform manner should always be placed, in the manner of notes, immediately beneath the text. The most recent Parisian editions gather all the variants far from the text, at the end of each volume, without following either this practice or that of the Maurist Fathers; or else they omit them with insufficient care. Having experienced more than once the inconvenience and loss of time thereby produced, we hope that our method will prove preferable both for convenience and for usefulness.

**4.** As regards the chronological sequence of Augustine’s works, we have departed slightly from the order of the Maurist Fathers in order to follow the order suggested by the analogy of the subject matter and therefore by reason itself. Thus, in this first volume, the two books of the Soliloquies, which in the Benedictine edition immediately follow the books On Order, have been placed directly after the Confessions, with which they agree especially well because of the evident similarity of their subject. The two books On Genesis against the Manichaeans have likewise been transferred from the first volume to the third, namely to the place where another twofold work on Genesis is arranged. We have also moved the book On True Religion, which in the Benedictine edition follows the book On the Morals of the Manichaeans, to the third volume, specifically after the work On Christian Doctrine, of which it will plainly appear to every reader to be a complement. Finally, various minor works, such as Letters, Sermons, and so forth, which the Maurist Fathers and, after them, the other editors scattered everywhere by adhering too closely to them, have been carefully restored to their original class, as the subject required.

**5.** The two prefaces that follow Mabillon’s dedicatory Letter a little below begin the eleventh and final volume of the Benedictine edition. This is not surprising, since the venerable editors, when embarking upon so long a course, could not have foreseen from the outset everything that would have to be done throughout its entire progress. Since we are reprinting their work and have no reason to tolerate such an anomaly, we have placed both prefaces in their natural position, namely at the beginning of the work, in the first volume. Nearly the same consideration moved us to transfer to the first volume the two Lives of Saint Augustine, the former of which the Benedictine Fathers relegated to the end of the tenth volume, while the latter was postponed until the eleventh. No one will deny that these narratives of the writer’s life are a kind of preface, composed with the intention that, through an advance disclosure of various circumstances, readers might already be initiated into the innermost and, so to speak, generative meanings of the work.

The Benedictine Fathers themselves thought no differently, as is shown by the opening words of the Admonition prefixed to the books of the Confessions:

> “The same reason,” they say, “that caused the Life of each writer to be customarily prefixed when his books were published moved, without doubt, the first editors of Saint Augustine’s works to place his Confessions immediately after the books of the Retractations … in the first volume. For it is of the greatest importance that one who resolves to read an author’s writings with pleasure and profit should have learned his character, studies, morals, integrity, faith, and other qualities.”

After such a declaration, we find it difficult to understand why the Benedictine Fathers did not prefix the Life of the holy Doctor to their own edition, especially since it was composed from all his writings. We therefore do not think anyone will take offense if, in this and in a few other matters of the same kind, about which we shall give incidental notice, we have departed from those illustrious leaders whose footsteps, in all other respects, we glory to have followed with reverence.

[Col. 0009]

# To the Most Christian King, Louis the Great, Victor, Triumphant, Peace-Bringing

Most Christian King, we present to you Augustine, the light and oracle of the Church, once the delight of Charlemagne, adorned with a new presentation and new type, to be granted a second immortality under the protection of your immortal name. Germany once welcomed him as though he were being reborn at Basel; Belgium received and cultivated him after his revision at Louvain; and now at last we present him restored, as far as we could accomplish it, to his genuine integrity. Thus, as though joining right hands and services, the Belgians with the Germans, and the French with both, seem to have combined to complete a work worthy of Louis the Great. It was fitting that such a common monument of pacified peoples should belong to a victor and triumphant king; and it was wholly appropriate that we should dedicate Augustine, complete, pure, and polished—the greatest teacher of the Church and the perpetual scourge of heretics—to the most august, greatest, invincible, and most religious of kings.

Nor may we doubt your Majesty’s favor, Most August King, since that most ample privilege was granted, sealed, and confirmed by you yourself; since written codices were supplied abundantly from the Royal Library at your command; since letters were sent to foreigners in your name for our benefit; and since Augustine’s merit, reputation, and authority inspire us with the most certain hope that you will be the supporter, patron, and defender of this edition.

Indeed, who is more worthy of the zeal and esteem of a Most Christian Prince than Augustine, whom Jerome and the Catholics of his age regarded as a renewed founder of the ancient faith? He is the light of the Doctors: a disciple of the earlier Fathers in humility and religion, easily first among his contemporaries in learning, and the guide and teacher of those who followed. While he lived, the African Fathers followed him as an interpreter of the Holy Spirit in establishing the Church’s holier regulations; among the supreme pontiffs he was revered by Innocent I; the emperors Honorius and Theodosius honored him with letters; and after his death his teaching was praised in the most distinguished terms by councils, by the holiest pontiffs and bishops, and above all by Pope Celestine and Gregory the Great.

It would be wrong at this point to pass over the Most Christian Kings of the Franks, your predecessors, Most Excellent Prince, whose respect for so great a man was no less than your own. Thus, when Engelbert, Abbot of Corbie, sought a gift not unworthy of royal majesty, he judged that nothing would be more welcome to King Louis than Augustine’s books On Christian Doctrine. And Charles V, surnamed the Wise, received with exceptional favor the books On the City of God, translated into French and dedicated to him.

But this above all deserves mention: the holy Doctor’s reading was recommended to King Robert by Adalbero, Bishop of Laon; and it was cherished by one man who ought to stand for many—Charles, truly the Great. For, as Einhard testifies, he delighted in the books of Saint Augustine, especially those entitled On the City of God. The wisest Prince understood that Empire with priesthood, majesty with religion, war with peace, and greatness of spirit with moderation could be reconciled by no author after the sacred Scriptures better than by Augustine. He was convinced that through Augustine’s reading and practical use, both private and royal virtues—religion, courage, prudence, and the other virtues—could be acquired, or at least perfected and adorned.

God has poured these qualities, so greatly desired by kings but so rarely united in one person, into you, Most Great of Kings, by a singular favor, so that under no other guide and teacher have you reached the summit of those virtues that won for your Majesty the illustrious surname “the Great.” Other kings, even those commonly regarded as preeminent, have been content to excel in individual qualities—to be religious, warlike, or lovers of public peace. In you all these virtues are so joined with the others that they make you outstanding in religion, justice, moderation, and wisdom, in war as well as in peace.

Many princes, while striving to celebrate their name by arms, cast aside the care of establishing the kingdom and entrust it to others; some, intent upon the pursuit of peace alone, hold military affairs in contempt. You meditate upon the arts of war amid the pursuits of peace, and amid the smiling successes of war you contemplate peace. Yet—and this happens to very few kings—although you are experienced in both peace and war, no adversity has ever disturbed the prosperity of your kingdom, so that all readily acknowledge that, crowned with the highest virtues, you are made fortunate by providence and are everywhere Great.

As soon as your Majesty took hold of the reins of the kingdom, Best of Kings, you regarded religion as the governing principle by which to rule yourself and your people, and you diligently considered the ordering of your subjects’ morals and discipline. Hence you began to rescue and protect Christians oppressed by the most hostile enemies by sending them aid; then you turned your mind to ending divisions within the Church and extending its boundaries; to restoring repealed laws and enacting new ones; to providing easy access for petitioners; to administering justice in your own voice; to renewing the arts and sciences; and to assigning rewards to the good and punishments to the wicked.

Nor were your legal decrees unstable or merely temporary, as often happens; in them the same constancy and religious seriousness prevail as in your words and promises. In former times, how many terrifying threats were devised against mad and utterly depraved men who, by an expressly agreed duel, rushed everywhere into mutual slaughter? Yet this variety of laws did not suppress the spreading evil, because easy indulgence toward the accused and the shameful name of empty glory rendered them ineffective. What had been lacking was your constancy, Most Just Prince, by which you order such gladiators to receive a punishment fully deserving of them, together with an eternal mark of disgrace, and you command it inexorably.

Thus, more effectively than Trajan once did, you not only remove the evils but also ensure that they cannot recur; and whatever benefits you confer, you make lasting rather than fleeting. How wisely, moreover, you have always observed in your judgments that Augustinian principle: “Let nothing be done savagely, let nothing be done inhumanely!” For the guilty feel the gravity of your justice in such a way that they cannot accuse it of harshness, and even in their punishments they recognize your equity and mercy. In these pursuits of peace, Most Prudent King, you anticipated wars in your mind and silently accomplished a great task, so that when the need for war arose, no commander other than yourself would be required.

Now, astonished, we approach those memorable deeds in which you have exposed that head, revered by the whole world, to so many dangers; distracted your mind with so many cares; and held Europe spellbound by so many prodigies. Who could grasp them even in thought, much less explain them in speech? As soon as the opportunity and occasion for war arose, you first deal amicably, so that you may not strike; you threaten, so that you may terrify; you terrify and warn, so that you may not find your enemies unprepared.

Then you advance with a distinguished selection of soldiers. Soon the Rhine gives way before your Majesty, Most Invincible King; the most strongly fortified citadels and cities, struck with terror by your presence and reputation, come in companies to surrender. Finally, nearly all Europe, conspiring against you, heaps upon your valor nothing but victories and palms.

Amid all this, after overcoming the stratagems, machines, and forces of your opponents, while everything proceeds according to your wishes and entire provinces stand ready to surrender, your moderation is so great that, in accordance with Augustine’s judgment, you prefer modest peace to glorious war. You bring the allied enemies, who are disputing conditions, to agreement; and you who had given the laws of war give the laws of peace as well.

Who, amid the trophies of so many and such great victories, would not think that a thousand triumphs had been paid to Louis the Great? Yet your mind, King Victorious everywhere, is far different from that of the ancient commanders, who, after lightly touching their enemies with arms, exhausted their subjects with triumphs and the expenses of triumphs. Your journey from war, indeed from victories, is peaceful and modest, as though you were plainly returning from peace; so that you seem to triumph over the ferocity and pride of your enemies, and over the pomp of triumphs themselves, rather than over the endurance of your subjects.

We recognize you as victorious, Most Christian King, for this one reason: amid the assaults of wars roaring everywhere, we remain tranquil and secure; and you summon the festive harmonies of all the Churches, the tongues and voices of the priests, to celebrate the divine power to which you command the glory of your victories to be ascribed.

Future generations will doubtless marvel, Most Great King, that such prosperity was joined to such moderation, so that no disorderly speech or action by anyone, however impatient in spirit, ever shook you from your composure. They will certainly marvel and demand from us the explanation of so great a prosperity.

But if we believe Ausonius, no one can give an account of good fortune. Indeed, it is easy to do so—not, perhaps, of the fortune of other princes, but certainly of yours, Most Fortunate Prince. Your happiness is not governed by uncertain accidents and events, nor by blind fortune, but by the most certain and unshakable reason.

If we consult your religion, you attribute all this happiness to the singular providence of God, by whose will empires and the condition of rulers depend. If we consult Augustine, you will also attribute it to your justice, since he calls Christian emperors happy if they rule justly and make their power the servant of God’s majesty, especially by extending the worship of God as widely as possible.

Finally, if we ask ourselves, we shall ascribe this happiness also to the incomparable genius granted to you from heaven. Its power and greatness are such that you direct the causes of uncertain events toward their appointed end, anticipate the events themselves, and close the way to obstacles that are about to arise. This is the power by which you comprehend, without difficulty and as though at leisure, matters almost infinite in number, widely different, and intricate. By it you discern the merits of distinguished men whom you place over public affairs with such discrimination. By it you are present in every place and in the deeds of all. You suffuse everything at once, as the sun is spread abroad not in some one part but wholly at once, and not for one or another person but for all in common.

From this arise the perfectly correct judgments of your mind concerning everything, that majesty of expression, those weighty decisions, and those sayings produced ex tempore, yet always polished on the whetstone of right reason—sayings that the carefully meditated speech of the wise could scarcely equal.

Yet this adds the crowning touch to your happiness and ours, Most August King: that you are educating a Son like yourself. That you fathered such a son belongs to nature; that you make him like yourself belongs to your wisdom. For you form the Most Serene Dauphin for good rule not only through the constant instruction of the choicest men, but especially through paternal admonitions and examples. By causing the distinguished deeds of all heroes to live again in your own person, you openly demonstrate that nothing more glorious can befall the son of Louis the Great than to obey his father and approach him as closely as possible through imitation.

Finally, Peace-Bringing King, we ascribe to the prosperity of your empire the fact that we are permitted to devote ourselves to correcting, restoring, and illuminating the works of Saint Augustine. These studies and labors are the leisure secured for us by you amid the very midst of wars. We would not have had leisure to spend our efforts on such arduous studies amid the clash of arms, nor would all the arts have flourished again, unless they could have existed safely under your rule.

Now, what may not be hoped for Augustine, for good letters, and for everyone from a common peace? One simple and modest prayer remains for us: that Almighty God may continue to bless your Majesty for a very long time with uninterrupted success in all things, which may at last be crowned by blessed immortality. Meanwhile, trusting in your goodness, we earnestly request that the protection of the royal guardianship—which we have experienced so often from the very beginning of your reign—may continue to be extended to us in the future. Whatever we possess, whatever we ourselves may be, we shall regard it all as belonging to you.

Your Sacred Majesty’s most devoted and faithful clients and subjects,

**The Benedictine Monks of the Congregation of Saint Maur**

Paris, from the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, on the Kalends of January, 1679.

[Col. 0013]

# General Preface to the newest edition of the works of Saint Augustine

When the superiors of our Congregation first decided to apply our brothers to literary studies, they selected chiefly those studies that offered more usefulness than display and were more suitable to religious solitude and community life. Nothing seemed more fitting or timely for them in this field than the revision and new publication of the holy Fathers, both Latin and Greek. The work itself would be especially beneficial for practicing the reading and meditation of their writings, in which the true and sincere doctrine and piety of the Church are contained; and we also possessed no small number of resources for undertaking and completing it.

In order that our brothers might gradually become suitable and prepared for this labor, certainly more arduous and difficult than splendid, as though by successive steps, the beginning was made with certain elementary exercises: namely, an edition of selected minor works of the holy Fathers. Then came the complete writings of others, until at last we reached the works of the most holy Doctor Augustine. Several illustrious prelates of the Church, as well as prominent laymen, encouraged and urged us to devote ourselves to correcting and revising these works.

Among the former was the illustrious François Harlay, recently Archbishop of Paris, who always showed himself the patron and supporter of this undertaking. Among the latter was Guillaume Lamoignon, formerly first president of the Parliament of Paris, who, because of his benevolence toward literature and learned men, wished to obtain and arrange from the King a printing establishment for us within our own house, so that this edition might be produced more conveniently and easily in private quarters. Although this condition, however opportune it might appear, was for various reasons—which it is useless to recount—not accepted, the illustrious President nevertheless persisted, as did many other highly distinguished men of various Orders, in urging us not to shrink from undertaking a work of such magnitude.

Moved by these incentives, our superiors could nevertheless scarcely be brought to undertake so vast a labor. They were perceptive men and judged—as the outcome proved—that the undertaking was full of risk and difficulty: if it did not succeed, its rash and imprudent conception would bring disgrace upon us; if it succeeded, envy might perhaps fall upon us. Moreover, according to the most learned Louvain theologians, who had deserved so well of Augustine and of the entire Christian commonwealth, it seemed rash to contemplate a new edition of the works of the holy Doctor, since it could scarcely be hoped that we would equal their diligence, much less surpass it.

They also recalled the ancient controversies and quarrels that had repeatedly arisen in the Church from the writings and teaching of the holy Doctor. They feared that, while wishing to serve the Church through the labor of their brothers, they might thereby give rise to seeds of new disputes, as experience had more than once shown. The teaching of so great a man is difficult for human understanding to grasp and offers little favor or acceptance to the desires and pride of mortals.

But these and other difficulties were entirely dispelled and removed by the supreme favor of Louis the Great, who permitted this new edition to be honored by his most august name and protected by royal patronage.

There was added, moreover, the King’s most ample privilege in favor of the new edition, confirmed by the authority of the illustrious Chancellor of France, Michel Tellier, and by a royal edict. Certain booksellers, secretly urged by hidden opponents to divert the undertaking of the new edition, protested and resisted in vain. Supported by such powerful defenses, we judged that no obstacle was insurmountable and that no envy need be feared.

Furthermore, lest this plan should seem excessively bold and rash, it had been preceded by the example of Pietro Morini, prefect of the Vatican printing house, and of other learned men of the venerable City—Abbot Adrian, Doctor Obrius of Paris, and others—who, first under Sixtus V and then under Clement VIII, the supreme pontiffs, had undertaken a new edition of Saint Augustine’s writings after the Louvain edition.

They judged that the Vatican books, which the Louvain scholars had not consulted, were excellent; that they were very numerous, so that variant readings could be extracted from them; and that many things lacking in the Louvain books, however accurate those might be, could be supplied from them. Thus, as Pietro Morini writes in his fifteenth letter to Cardinal Cajetan, who strongly supported the proposal, this edition would bring the light of Christian doctrine.

The undertaking was carried out: the Louvain books were compared with the Vatican codices with the utmost accuracy, and variant readings were placed in the margin for the preparation of the edition, over which the Cardinal of Verona, head of the Sacred College, presided. But since the project came to nothing, all those variations were communicated to us, by order of Pope Clement X, by the late Cardinal Bona, so that we might use them in our new edition.

Having therefore gathered for this purpose these and other resources from ancient codices everywhere, both from our own libraries and from those of others, we immediately set our hands to the work. Several of our fellow religious were employed in collating the codices, not only at Saint-Germain in Paris but also in other monasteries of our Congregation in different provinces. Finally, within a period of approximately twenty years, after many expenses and cares, and certainly with the greatest labor, this entire edition was, by God’s favor, fully completed and received by all who were free from prejudice with a degree of applause and success that we could scarcely have hoped for.

In order to fulfill our task and respond, according to our ability, to the public expectation of us, we attempted to provide four principal qualities in our edition: that it should be accurate, convenient, properly illustrated, and attached to no partisan interests.

To make it as accurate as possible, three conditions seemed necessary to us: that the genuine integrity of the text be restored from ancient codices and more trustworthy editions; that the authentic and genuine works of the holy Doctor be separated from the doubtful and spurious; and that the edition itself be issued, as far as lay within our power, cleansed of typographical errors.

To make it highly convenient, we chiefly attended to four things: the order of the works, sections, summaries, and indexes.

The order was arranged according to the time at which each work was written by Augustine. In this way the reader advances and progresses gradually with Augustine himself, and knowledge of the earlier works sheds light upon the understanding of the later ones. We shall say more about this order below.

The sections were arranged so that not only would the text and body of each work be divided by the chapters of the older editions, which were sometimes excessively long, but the chapters themselves would also be divided into smaller sections distinguished by numerical markings. This was done so that, when the section of a work was indicated, the cited passage could be found more easily, and also so that, in reading, the reader’s labor and attention might be relieved by intervals and pauses of this kind.

The summaries are likewise helpful—not only those placed here and there in the margin beside individual sections of the text, briefly displaying the substance of the subject under discussion, but also those prefixed to all the books and to most of the chapters, briefly explaining the subject of each book and chapter. As far as possible, we expressed the marginal summaries in the very words of the text, or retained the summaries of the Louvain scholars themselves.

As for the indexes, whose advantages and usefulness everyone knows, we have taken care not only to append individual and very full indexes to each volume, but also to compile general, or universal, indexes in this later volume, so that Augustine’s entire teaching on any subject may more easily be investigated at a single glance.

As for the order established by us in this edition, it will not be very laborious to explain its rationale. For the whole character of that order appears so natural and genuine that a bare exposition of it will suffice to justify it.

In the first volume, after the two books of the *Retractations* and the thirteen books of the *Confessions*, which are, as it were, preludes to the works that follow, come those shorter works which the most holy Doctor composed while still a catechumen or not yet a priest.

The second volume follows with 270 letters, arranged, insofar as possible, according to their chronological order and distributed into four classes. The first contains those letters which Augustine wrote before becoming a bishop; the second, those which he composed as bishop, before the Conference of Carthage and before the Pelagian heresy had been detected in Africa; the third, those written from that time until his death; and finally the fourth, those whose date is less certain. The special Preface to that volume explains why we have altered the received order of the Letters and what we have done here for the readers’ convenience.

The third volume contains the exegetical works, arranged according to the order of the Scriptures. At the beginning of the volume are prefixed the four books *On Christian Doctrine*, which everyone knows to be the foundation of the works that follow.

The *Expositions on the Psalms* have been assigned to the fourth volume.

The fifth volume contains the Sermons to the People, divided into four classes, namely, Sermons on the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, Sermons on the Seasons, on the Saints, and on Various Subjects; to these, in a fifth class, are added the doubtful Sermons.

The sixth volume comprises the moral works, together with several books of Questions.

[Col. 0017] From this point begin the polemical works, foremost among which, in the seventh volume, are the twenty-two books *On the City of God*, against the Pagans.

The eighth volume, with the book *On Heresies* prefixed at its beginning, presents the polemical works against the Jews, Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and Arians. To these works are added the fifteen books *On the Trinity*.

The ninth volume contains the polemical works against the Donatists.

Finally, the tenth volume likewise contains the polemical works against the Pelagians. To these writings are appended various materials that may contribute to their elucidation. So much concerning the order.

We also judged it necessary to prefix Prefaces to the individual volumes for the elucidation of the works of the most holy Father. In them we have endeavored to explain matters that are historical rather than dogmatic, in order to assist the readers’ diligence. In addition, we have prefixed Admonitions to most of the shorter works, explaining their subject matter. We have further added from time to time brief notes in the lower margin, either to indicate variant readings or to explain obscure passages, chiefly by comparison with other passages.

Throughout all this, one conviction was deeply fixed in our minds and impressed upon us by our Superiors: that we must carefully avoid partisan interests in explaining Augustine’s doctrine. For this reason we have refrained from more extensive commentaries and observations, lest we give anyone even the slightest cause for offense or prejudge the position of any Catholic theologian.

Yet, however much we attended to this, and however much our Superiors instructed us to attend to it, it was nevertheless difficult, in so vast a work, to prevent something from inadvertently slipping in; or, given the varying dispositions of human minds, to prevent some people from interpreting something contrary to our intention in a less favorable sense. And in fact this is what happened.

For although almost everyone judged our edition accurate, convenient, and sufficiently elucidated, and finally entirely consonant with Augustinian doctrine, and approved it by their support on these grounds, certain anonymous critics nevertheless rose against it nearly ten years after the publication of the last volume. Through clandestine writings they attempted to discredit this edition and to cast suspicion—almost—upon our good faith.

When such little writings had been scattered among the public, the nearly unanimous judgment of prudent men was that we should disdain pamphlets of this kind as insignificant: it was unbecoming, they said, for us to wrestle with ghosts and shadows, lest by replying we lend weight and authority to those clandestine pamphlets, or disturb the peace of the Church through publications issued, as is customary, back and forth. Our Superiors approved this advice with unanimous consent. Nevertheless, this did not prevent some among us, without consulting them, from undertaking as best they could to defend and protect the new edition of Saint Augustine. One of them, who was then residing in Rome, published in that holy city, under the authority of the Master of the Sacred Palace and with the approval of the Romans, a defense of this edition.

By then matters had reached the point at which those clandestine skirmishes between the two sides were almost breaking out into open war. At that moment our Superiors, finally changing their advice in accordance with the circumstances, judged that the same edition should be publicly defended against its hidden adversaries by an official writing approved by them and issued in the name of our Congregation. This writing, which would altogether vindicate both the edition and our good faith from unjust suspicion and accusation—although certain individuals among us had already done enough in this regard—was then nearly finished and ready for the press.

But while we were considering the matter, the authority of Louis the Great intervened in these quarrels. As he always watches over the peace of the Church, which he has brought about, with unremitting care, so he put an end to the dissension that was daily increasing by imposing silence upon both parties. Thus, by the authority of so great a Prince, that fierce controversy was restrained, although it seemed about to rekindle fires long since smothered. To revive it is not only far from our character; it is forbidden above all by our profound respect for the King and obedience to his royal commands; next, by our deeply rooted concern for the peace of the Church; and finally, by charity toward all those whom we would feel bound in conscience not to offend through such turbulent controversies.

Accordingly, after suppressing the treatises prepared for the defense of ourselves and our edition, we refrained from replying to the accusations of our adversaries, lest by replying we seem to be sowing new disputes contrary to the royal commands.

Yet, lest the unjust accusations of our adversaries should perhaps have implanted certain scruples in the minds of some pious and even benevolent men, we resolved to address these scruples in a few words, judging that this would be contrary neither to the royal command nor to the peace of the Church, but entirely consistent with both. For although everything we have said has been said in a Catholic manner, and certainly with a Catholic spirit, we nevertheless prefer to make some concession to their tender and pious concern for the faith rather than, through proud disdain, to disregard their scruples. As for others, if any should continue, in a contentious spirit, to revive these quarrels, we shall henceforth pass over their sayings and quibbles and regard them as nothing.

Above all, the profession repeatedly made by all of us, individually and collectively, by which we have publicly declared that we sincerely and wholeheartedly adhere to the Constitutions of the Supreme Pontiffs Innocent X and Alexander VII, ought to remove us entirely from every suspicion concerning our belief regarding the famous Five Propositions. For if a faith supported by so many arguments is not secure, none will be free from suspicion; and if such a sincere profession is insufficient for anyone, no other profession, however sworn or however explicit, would suffice. For our Superiors accepted these Constitutions among the first acts of their general assemblies, with due reverence and submission, and ordered them to be subscribed by each and every person who was to be admitted into our community.

[Col. 0019] Furthermore, we freely profess that we sincerely adhere to the ecclesiastical Instructions on Grace recently published by the most illustrious Archbishops Charles Maurice Le Tellier of Rheims and Louis Antoine de Noailles of Paris. Just as we venerate their dignity and authority, so we openly acknowledge and glory in following their doctrine.

While we thus obey with submissive minds the Roman Pontiffs and the other prelates of the Church, whom Christ the Lord has appointed arbiters and judges of doctrine, no one ought to doubt that we utterly abhor every kind of partisan interest and that, in publishing Augustine, we directed our minds toward his doctrine in such a way as to represent his words and judgments sincerely and genuinely.

To come to particulars: in composing the marginal summaries, we took care to use, wherever possible, Augustine’s very own words, and to use them in an Augustinian sense.

This is why, whenever we have used the word “Grace” in those summaries, we intend it to be understood according to the sense of the context and of Augustine, who usually designates by the name of the Grace of Christ, and of Grace properly so called—especially after the rise of the Pelagian error—the true and interior grace which Pelagius denied, and above all that grace which is victorious and efficacious. This is clear from nearly all the books he wrote against the Pelagians, such as the books *On the Grace of Christ*, *On Correction and Grace*, and, to omit the others, the four books *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*. In the fifth chapter of the last of these, the holy Doctor interprets the term “grace,” which is properly grace, as the inspiration of love, so that we may do what we have come to know through holy love.

There it is clear that by the expressions “grace which is properly grace” or “which is proper grace” (for the manuscript copies vary in this way), the interior grace is being defended. The new enemies of grace were attempting, by an evil and covert design, to overthrow this grace while reducing it either to the law or to weaker and external aids. That this was the mind of the Bishop of Hippo is plainly shown by the very passage to which we have referred. In the same chapter he observes that nowhere do these enemies of grace contrive more hidden snares for attacking grace more vehemently than where they praise the law, [lacuna], for throughout all their discussions they wish the law, under various expressions and a diversity of words, to be understood as grace, namely, so that we may receive from the Lord God the assistance of knowledge.

We have recalled these matters at somewhat greater length so that the mind of the holy Doctor might be more clearly established, and so that the many passages which the editors judged worth noting in the margin might be measured by that standard.

Accordingly, to make this whole matter easier to explain, it will be useful to note briefly two points of great importance for freeing our faith from every suspicion.

The first is what we were already suggesting from Augustine: among the other elements of Christian piety which he undertook to defend, he labored diligently to establish that all Christians must acknowledge a true, interior grace proper to the Christian law, distinct from the law, doctrine, and illumination—the only kind of grace with which Pelagius wanted us to be satisfied. That this was his purpose throughout his long struggle against the Pelagians is stated by nearly all the books published against them, as we have already noted; above all, by the book *On the Grace of Christ*, and then by the text cited above from chapter five of book four *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*.

To this first observation another must be added: the holy Bishop devoted himself to proving interior grace in general, yet he very frequently mentioned that form of grace which is considered more perfect and more vigorous, and which is called efficacious because of its superior power and the effect which, by its nature, it certainly produces. The holy herald of divine aids had true and weighty reasons for doing so.

First, he was disputing against men who, while saying that only possibility was assisted by God, denied that the will and action were likewise assisted by him. What could be more suitable for refuting this error than to bring forward that kind of aid by which the action itself is brought about? Second, since the dispute chiefly concerned works of Christian piety, and works necessary for salvation, was it not fitting to bring forward those graces from which Christian piety and the fruit of good works themselves spring? Finally, as the most learned Petavius, a man more expert in Augustinian doctrine than tenacious of it, observed long ago, the ancients—but especially Saint Augustine—when speaking of grace, often speak of that which is full, perfect, and in its own kind most perfect (*Dogmatic Theology*, vol. 1, p. 749), and so on. The learned man supports this at various points with arguments and comparisons. How much more, then, should one who deliberately disputes the aids of divine grace against those who diminish their power bring forward graces that are efficacious for his purpose?

If the impartial reader pays attention to these matters, he will readily approve our faithfulness and diligence, both in the aforementioned summary to book four *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians* and in most of the other marginal notes. To say something about the former, we noted that Augustine calls grace the inspiration of love. Who could deny that this is so, since every grace tends toward love? Moreover, inspiration may be either efficacious or inefficacious. Using the holy Doctor’s own words in general terms, we said that grace is the inspiration of love. Where is the offense? Where is the ill intention? If our author speaks of inspiration in general, so do we; if, as is much more credible, he speaks of efficacious inspiration, then we likewise speak of that. Just as we observed, in that very chapter, that the Pelagians understand the law itself as the grace of God, so also we observed that Augustine, its holy defender, understands grace as the inspiration of love—so that interior aid might be opposed to external aid, the only kind which the Pelagians seemed to admit. For this very reason Augustine calls it “grace properly so called” or “true grace,” since the grace which the inflaters of free choice confined to the law or to external assistance was neither true nor proper grace.

[Col. 0021] Nevertheless, it would be false to infer from this that, by these expressions—“grace which is properly grace”—and similar ones, Augustine designated in this passage and elsewhere only victorious and active grace, leaving no place for other aids, such as inefficacious aids and those which, in the sense of the Thomists, are sufficient. The holy Bishop undoubtedly acknowledges graces of this kind, and we, together with him, profess them to be true and properly so called. It does not matter that he mentions these latter graces less often, or that he usually calls them by other names: sometimes a small will, sometimes a small love, a lesser, weak, or imperfect love. The terms take nothing away from the reality itself. Certainly, in the seventeenth chapter of *On Grace and Free Choice*, he consistently calls the small and imperfect love of Peter, who was presuming upon himself, a gift of God. I leave aside for the moment that, for the holy Doctor, no good will can exist without grace—a point which we also did not fail to note in the margin whenever occasion arose.

Nor is there better reason for bringing a lawsuit against us because we stated that the entire economy of divine grace is set before our eyes in the book *On Correction and Grace*. First, we borrowed this from the most illustrious and learned vindicator and interpreter of Augustinian doctrine, [Note: [Col. 0021] The most eminent Cardinal Noris, *Pelagian History*, book 1, p. 143, Padua edition of the year 1673.], whose words and meaning we reproduced. Second, in no other work did the Bishop of Hippo explain more clearly the distinctions between a person standing in innocence and a person fallen and guilty. Third, nowhere did he express more carefully the causes of persevering or not persevering in either state. Finally, in that book he wove together, with admirable concision, the unshaken doctrine of eternal predestination concerning the elect. Why, then, should it be considered a fault or a crime to say that this book embraces the entire economy of grace?

Here we also state in passing that an analytical synopsis of the same work was published without the knowledge of our Superiors. One of our number thought he could comply with the wishes of certain persons who were demanding it, although neither they nor we had intended to prefix this section to the work as a whole. We readily acknowledge that it was foreign to the purpose of the work and wholly irrelevant to what was being undertaken. For it was not our intention to publish commentaries or analytical summaries of the works of the holy Doctor. As for the usefulness, value, and reliability of the aforementioned analysis, which once appeared with authority, it is not for us to speak, since judgment concerning such matters ought to belong to prelates, not to private individuals such as ourselves.

After what we have said, no one ought to be troubled either because, in the book *On Correction and Grace*, in the margin of chapter two, we seem to have attributed the name “Grace of Christ” in a particularly significant way to efficacious grace; or because, in the book *On the Grace of Christ*, we suggested that the definition of the Grace of Christ is the one which Saint Augustine gives there, namely, “the inspiration of the most luminous and ardent love”; or finally because, in chapter thirteen of the same book, we noted: “Whoever has learned through grace does everything that he has learned must be done”; and, “Whoever has learned through grace comes; whoever does not come has not learned.” These and similar statements, which are especially appropriate to efficacious grace, were made without detriment to another true and interior grace that lacks its effect, such as the school of the Thomists, after Saint Augustine, defends.

Thus, in the second book *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, where the holy Doctor asks why God does not give victorious delight to all the saints, or not always give it to them, we intended to signify only the absence or withdrawal of victorious and supreme grace. We perhaps expressed the thought more briefly in the margin as follows: “Why grace is not given to all, or not always to the saints.” We should have wished every occasion of offense removed by adding the word “victorious,” although, in Augustine’s sense—which is by no means ambiguous—we used the word “grace” simply for efficacious grace, since, with the holy Bishop, we admit among both saints and sinners lesser graces, which in the Thomist sense are sufficient.

Indeed, graces of this kind are frequently experienced even by sinners, especially in their own conversion; still less does God deny them to the just, since he does not abandon the just unless they first abandon him. Augustine establishes this distinction between God who justifies and a physician who heals: when a human physician has healed a person, he leaves that person to God thereafter to be sustained by bodily elements and nourishment, so that the same health may grow strong through suitable support. But God, after justifying the ungodly, does not abandon him if he is not abandoned, so that he may always live piously and justly, as the holy Doctor says in chapter twenty-six of *On Nature and Grace*.

With these aids, therefore, the just person would persevere if he wished to do so. If he does not wish to do so, the fault is his, although he will never wish fully and efficaciously unless he is supported by a greater and stronger aid of grace.

From this it is easily understood that God sincerely wills the salvation of all human beings. Although Augustine sometimes appears to restrict this will to the elect, or to classes of individuals, in order to counter certain distorted Pelagian views on this point, he does not thereby reject the explanation of this will in any other sense, provided, he says, that we are not forced to believe that the omnipotent God wished something to happen by an absolute will and that it did not happen (*Enchiridion*, chap. 103).

Elsewhere, therefore, he plainly suggests a certain general will of God concerning the salvation of all human beings, when he teaches:

“God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, yet in such a way that he does not take away from them free choice, by which, using it well or badly, they are judged most justly. When this happens, unbelievers act against God’s will when they do not believe his Gospel; yet they do not overcome that will. Rather, they deprive themselves of a great and supreme good and entangle themselves in punitive evils, destined to experience in punishments the power of him whose mercy in his gifts they despised” (*On the Spirit and the Letter*, chap. 33).

There are so many and such clear testimonies of Saint Augustine concerning the possibility of fulfilling the commandments that it would be idle to cite them here. Nevertheless, he denies that they are possible in the sense intended by the Pelagians, who maintained that they were possible through the powers of nature alone, without the aid of interior [Col. 0023] grace. Hence it is evident to every sincere and impartial reader in what sense we said, in the seventh section of the Preface to the seventh volume, that Bede had exposed the hidden poison in the passages of the Pelagian letter to Demetrias—among others, in these words of his: “God, who is just, could not have commanded anything impossible; nor will he, who is merciful, condemn a person for what he cannot avoid.”

In that passage, whose meaning had already been sufficiently established from other sources, we did not think it necessary to apply an antidote in order to prevent abuse of that statement, which is undoubtedly true and Catholic both in blessed Augustine and among all adherents of the Catholic faith. Indeed, in the Appendix to the same volume we reproduced the entire passage from Bede, which explicitly sets forth the twofold meaning of his statement. We only wish that both meanings had been represented in the Preface itself, so that we might have removed even the slightest occasion of offense.

We too, as Catholics ought to do, unhesitatingly acknowledge free choice in fallen humanity. Following Augustine, the defender of this Catholic truth, we think with him and with all Catholics that the human will is sufficient for evil, but not for good without grace. The Pelagians, by contrast, asserted that freedom, undiminished and uncorrupted by the first human sin, was equally balanced toward good and evil. Hence, with the holy Bishop, we were pleased to note and reject the definitions of freedom brought forward by Julian to the prejudice of grace, by which an equal facility toward good and evil is posited. Nevertheless, we frankly profess that, if free choice is considered in itself, there may have been little or no dispute between Catholics and Pelagians.

With a similar caution, we rejected, together with the blessed Bishop, Julian’s definitions of sin, because they were advanced with an evil intention: to damage the grace necessary for avoiding sins and to enlarge the power of free choice. Julian said, namely, that sin is something from which it is free to abstain, by that liberty which lacks nothing in itself for avoiding sin. If this definition had been proposed by someone other than a deceitful heresiarch, there would not have been such extensive dispute about it.

However Hippo’s Bishop may have argued with Julian concerning the definitions of freedom and sin, this is entirely certain to us: active indifference—that is, the liberty which they call freedom of contradiction, to act or not to act, and also to merit or demerit—was consistently acknowledged and approved by the holy Bishop in fallen humanity, whether the will is carried toward good by victorious grace or toward evil by itself and its own defect. The renowned defender of grace professed this dogma of the Catholic faith equally both before and after the rise of the Pelagian heresy.

Indeed, speaking of sin in book three of *On Free Choice*, chapter eighteen, he says:

“Whatever that cause of the will may be”—that is, of the evil will—“if it cannot be resisted, one yields to it without sin; but if it can, one ought not to yield to it, and there will be no sin. Or does it deceive the unwary? Then let him beware lest he be deceived. Is the deception so great that it cannot possibly be avoided? If so, there are no sins. For who sins in what cannot in any way be avoided?”

We know that this book was written by the holy Doctor before the controversy against the Pelagians concerning grace had been aired. But when Pelagius himself brought this passage against him, Augustine acknowledged his words and did not retract them, provided that sin is understood to be avoidable with the grace of God, and that things which are sins and at the same time punishments for sin are not judged to be under precisely the same condition (*On Nature and Grace*, no. 80). For although such things are committed freely, they are not committed with the same liberty as other acts that could have been committed before any sin.

With this qualification, therefore, Saint Augustine admits, in the very act of sinning, a genuine power not to sin—that is, active indifference of the sort he admitted in good acts performed through grace.

The holy Bishop did not depart from this doctrine, either in his earliest or in his latest works against the Pelagians; while contending with Pelagius and Julian, he most openly defended it. Nor is it necessary to compile an index of passages on this matter, since others have already done so. We shall observe only that Augustine sometimes uses “free” in a broader and more general sense for what is voluntary even when necessary. In this sense he said that the love of justice in God, and the innate human desire for blessedness in general, are free—that is, voluntary.

Accordingly, in *On Nature and Grace*, after citing this statement of Pelagius, “Whatever is constrained by natural necessity is deprived of the judgment and deliberation of the will,” Saint Augustine does not entirely approve it when he adds, “And here there is some question.” In this passage he indicates that Pelagius had spoken too diffusely and indistinctly, indeed even inconsiderately, and that something still remained to be questioned in his statement, since not everything deprived of the judgment and deliberation of the will is subject to natural necessity. He proves this by the example of the innate desire for blessedness in us and of the will of justice in God: both are necessary, yet in such a way that they may seem, in their own manner, to belong to the choice of the will, at least with regard to the way in which that choice is exercised.

Therefore, adhering to the words of the context itself, we placed this summary in the margin at that point: “Necessity does not conflict with the choice of the will.” This might seem somewhat harshly expressed to some, unless the context itself made it sufficiently clear that “the choice of the will,” if one attends to the matter itself, is being taken for the will itself, or for what is voluntary.

It could nevertheless be said that, since Augustine here does not wish free choice in humanity to be destroyed by every kind of necessity—which was what Pelagius wanted—a more cautious summary might have been made by adding a single word, in this form: “Not every necessity conflicts with the choice of the will.”

Indeed, the necessity of infallibility is not opposed to true liberty, as Saint Augustine explained in many passages. He also often used the word “necessity” for a certain strong inclination arising from the defect of nature. In this sense he does not hesitate to acknowledge in fallen humanity a harsh necessity of sinning, though it is only general: in the present condition, a person cannot avoid all and each of his sins, even the slightest, because of the weakness of nature. Or it may be merely moral, and almost similar to the necessity produced by bad habit through repeated acts. Saint Augustine and Julian did not think that this habit imposed a simple and absolute necessity, as could readily be shown from the arguments of both.

On the occasion of the passage cited above, it will not be out of place to observe that we corrected, on the basis of the manuscript copies, the commonly printed statement of Augustine from chapter eleven of *On Correction and Grace* as follows: “Free choice is sufficient for evil, but for good it is insufficient unless it is aided by the omnipotent Good.” The earlier Louvain editions have “is nothing” in place of “is insufficient.” Although Augustine has “is of no avail” in Letter 186 to Paulinus, no. 34, where he says that without grace free choice of the will is of no avail for not sinning, in the earlier passage, taken from *On Correction and Grace*, “insufficient” fits better than “nothing.”

For that passage concerns the first innocent human being, whom God did not wish to be without grace but entrusted to his free choice. “For free choice,” says the holy Doctor, “is sufficient for evil, but for good it is insufficient unless it is aided by the omnipotent Good.” Certainly, although one may say of fallen humanity’s free choice that, by itself and without grace, it is nothing for doing good, it seems less fitting to say this of an innocent person, whose free choice, being sound, could be directed toward good without any impediment.

We have pursued these finer points in order to remove disputes about words (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 11). Yet the condition of those who labor to edit the works of the ancient Fathers would be pitiable indeed if every unjust critic were permitted to attack with impunity even their marginal notes, as has been done against us in this edition, and to weigh every syllable of them on the harsh scales of merciless criticism. For who is there who, in a matter so slippery and difficult, does not occasionally stumble even slightly; who always reaches the author’s meaning to the utmost precision or renders it perfectly; who, finally, can at times explain an entire page exactly by so brief a compendium of words?

However unjust the criticism of certain men against us may prove to be, we shall nevertheless, God willing, continue steadfastly in our undertaking. And if they persist in troubling us, it will console us that the same fate once befell the true disciples of Augustine, especially Caesarius, Bishop of Arles, whose faith was defamed by certain detractors on account of the doctrine preached by that most holy man.

Hence the synod of bishops was assembled at Valence, before which Caesarius approved his faith. Moreover, Pope Boniface, disregarding the malicious intention of the quarrelers, confirmed the defense of Saint Caesarius by apostolic authority, as Cyprian, Bishop of Toulon, relates in his *Life*.

Perhaps, however, we should hope more confidently for human fairness. For perhaps, to use Augustine’s words, if some have thought otherwise, once they have reflected briefly with themselves, without any desire to contend, on how absurd and unworthy of discussion what they say is, they will immediately change their judgment. And if they are unwilling to do so, we should not despair so entirely of human understanding that we fear they could persuade anyone of this (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, no. 22).

What else now remains for us, after the desired completion of a long and laborious work, than to ask, with a submissive yet cheerful spirit, for the protection and support of the most illustrious prelates of Gaul?

It has come about, clearly, through the admirable plan of divine Providence, that we have laid the final hand upon a new edition of the works of the most holy Doctor of the Church, Augustine, precisely when they were assembling in one place at the shrine of Saint-Germain for a General Assembly from all parts of the Kingdom. Nothing more opportune or fortunate could have happened to us than that we should appeal to them as judges and arbiters, of whatever quality, of our labor—men whom God has established by their dignity as shepherds to govern the Church and to guard, with vigilant care and apostolic authority, the most sacred deposit of Catholic doctrine.

For this principal reason, most illustrious Princes of the Church, we bring Augustine before you: the whole of him, as it were, is set before your eyes to be contemplated under the view of a single panel. Nor can the most ardent defender of the ancient and ancestral faith fear your scrutiny, since he knows that the cause of the Church, which he so often defended, was so often supported by the protection of your forefathers. He hopes that you, who willingly follow in their footsteps, will today defend that cause with a similar spirit and zeal.

Hence there arises in us a firm hope that you will look favorably upon the recently completed edition of the Augustinian works, and that you will not withhold your patronage from the labors of that man whom all of you, together with blessed Prosper, unhesitatingly acknowledge as a special patron of the faith (Saint Prosper, *Letter to Augustine*, no. 1).

There is no need for us here to recall how great was once the agreement between the Gallican and Roman prelates in commending the works of the holy man. There remain written records both of the Pontiffs of the Apostolic See—Innocent, Celestine, and others—and of the Gallican councils of Orange, Valence, and others. In them the Bishop of Hippo is numbered among the finest teachers of the Church and, by the common voice and judgment of all, is declared an entirely faithful guardian of the ancient faith.

These most equitable judgments of the ancient Church concerning the doctrine and faith of the holy Bishop both gave us courage to undertake the burden of an immense labor and led us to approach the writings of so learned a Bishop with the reverence they deserved. We judged, namely, that pious diligence and religious caution were required so that the works which had first proceeded from the mouth and hand of the most holy Doctor with a particular mind, purpose, and faith might be published anew by us with equal faith, mind, and purpose, for the honor, advantage, and protection of the universal Church.

What success our efforts have achieved in so arduous an undertaking, modesty forbids us to proclaim publicly; yet so do the most gracious judgments concerning it pronounced by nearly every order within the Church, and above all by all of you. In them we have experienced the greatest reward for our labor—a reward far greater than our expectation or our merit—with a silent expression of grateful and submissive spirit.

Relying and trusting on these proofs of your good will, we were easily able to disregard the complaints of certain detractors. For we were firmly convinced that the work undertaken by us in illustrating Augustine would be approved by the votes of all, since it had pleased those in whose hands, as everyone acknowledges, the judgment and decision in these matters lie.

Nor did this expectation deceive us. Behold, a new and powerful support has come to our work from the recent condemnation by the Apostolic See of the pamphlets with which men who were unfair judges of our labors and fidelity sought to burden us with odium. The authority and support of your most august assembly will provide the chief reinforcement for our defense against them. We ask for this indication of your common judgment and opinion all the more earnestly and freely because we have brought the whole work of our vigils into the public light under the auspices of Louis the Great and have marked it with the royal name.

If you add the weight of your commendation to the religious Prince’s kindness and generosity in examining this undertaking, the work will be fortified with every kind of protection. No age will destroy it, and no hand or insolence will dare assail it in the future. For this distinguished favor and benefaction, most illustrious bishops of the holy Religion, we shall give and render immortal thanks both to each of you individually and to your entire Sacred Order.

[Col. 0027]

## Brief Preface to the Augustinian Appendices and Other Matters Contained in This Volume

Since those spurious little works that were attributed to Saint Augustine at various times have been set aside and relegated to a corner, it seemed appropriate to follow the same method and order here, and therefore to assign such writings a special Preface, separate from the general one, containing an account of the work we have devoted to this part as well. This is both so that no one might perhaps suspect that we had neglected them and so that the reader may be prepared for their reading and warned about the other matters contained in this final volume.

To come to the point: Appendices are placed after each of Augustine’s individual volumes. They contain the short writings that imitation of style, affinity of subject, accident, ignorance of dates, or finally the fraud of authors or booksellers attached to Augustine. We think that the imitation of style led to the attribution of many sermons by Caesarius, bishop of Arles, to Augustine. As for the fact that Pelagius’ letter to Demetrias and Fastidius’ book *On the Christian Widow*, addressed to the widow Fatalis, were attributed to the holy Doctor, I do not know whether this happened through similarity of subject or through the deceit of authors who, either to procure authority or value for their writing, or because they distrusted their own name, substituted the title of so great a name. Certainly there was no other reason why editors and booksellers prefixed the same name to those spurious writings: namely, so that they might be regarded as more valuable and those counterfeit wares sold at a higher price.

Yet it must be admitted that such booklets were generally adorned with this impressive title through the accident or recklessness of copyists and editors. For it often happened that, when booksellers had copied some of Augustine’s books and did not have enough material from the holy Doctor to make up a proper volume, they supplied what was lacking from any anonymous work that happened to be at hand. This in turn gave both copyists and careless editors an opportunity to attribute these later works to the same author whose name the earlier ones bore. The matter proceeded so far that scarcely any century passed without some such adulterine writings being added to Augustine’s genuine works.

From this arose a threefold disadvantage. The first was that the dignity and attractiveness of reading his genuine works were somewhat diminished by this mixture. The second was that the truth of tradition was in a certain way obscured, since writings from later periods were thought to belong to an earlier age. The third was that these falsely attributed offspring led unwary readers to follow misguided opinions that they found concealed beneath Augustine’s illustrious name. It was therefore of the greatest importance, in order to avert these disadvantages, to separate such spurious writings from Augustine’s genuine and authentic works and relegate them to a certain corner.

This task, first begun by several learned men, then greatly advanced and largely completed by the Louvain scholars, and afterward by John Verlin and Bernard Winding, Augustinians, did not yet appear to have been entirely finished and seemed still to require some labor. We have omitted nothing in order to satisfy that need. For this purpose we consulted as many ancient manuscripts as possible, in which each work is assigned to its proper author; we consulted learned men who, through familiar and frequent use of the holy Doctor’s writings, had become accustomed to recognize his style and character; and we ourselves carefully compared the doubtful and less certain works with Augustine’s unquestioned writings. Having compared their style, opinions, teaching, scriptural citations, and manner of explanation, we believe that we have brought the matter to the point where scarcely any work remains among Augustine’s writings that ought to be rejected but has not been rejected, and scarcely any rejected work that would not seem rejectable to impartial critics.

Yet it was not enough to distinguish these illegitimate works unless their true authors were also identified. We have therefore attempted to do this as far as we could, judging that writings whose authors are unknown are scarcely valued by readers. Nor have we regretted our labor. We were able to identify a great many authors, whose sequence we shall present below. In many other cases we observed fragments of earlier authors, which we marked either with asterisks or with brackets, indicating the places from which they had been transferred and borrowed. Thus it can easily be determined when each of these works was written. From this the careful investigator of ecclesiastical tradition will see that the books *On the Spirit and the Soul*, *On Loving God*, and the *Manual* are not earlier than the twelfth century, much less assignable to Augustine’s time, once he notices in them fragments from Anselm, Bernard, and Hugh of Saint Victor.

Moreover, lest Augustine’s teaching should in some way be contaminated by such spurious booklets if we were to mix the subjects treated in them into the same index, we have placed the general index relating to the Appendices in this final volume, which must now be discussed.

After this Preface, the final volume contains a Life of Saint Augustine, compiled by us from his own writings. In this undertaking we found the commentaries of Sebastian Le Nain de Tillemont, of blessed memory, greatly useful; he generously shared with us his commentaries on this Life, with no other motive than to serve the Church of God, to which he devoted all his labors—truly great and useful—being more than ordinarily free from the vain little glory of an empty name. This Life will serve as a kind of Annals of Augustine and indeed of the ecclesiastical figures of his time, in which the holy Doctor played a major part. His deeds will be assigned, as far as the remoteness of ancient events permits, to the individual years marked in the margin. You have another, shorter Life composed by Possidius at the end of the tenth volume.

That longer Life will be followed by three indexes of Saint Augustine’s works. The first presents the sequence and order of the individual volumes of his works, compared with the Louvain edition, with which the Erasmian edition largely agrees. The second compares the ancient order with the new. In the third, the individual short works are listed alphabetically. With the help of these indexes, those accustomed to the older editions will easily find each work.

[Note: [Col. 0029] Both Benedictine Prefaces have been transferred here; nevertheless, the three indexes mentioned are to be found in the final volume. M.]

This triple index will be followed by a universal index, the fullest of all, of every subject contained in the ten volumes of Augustine’s works; and likewise by a general index of all the passages of Sacred Scripture that are explained here and there in those works. In compiling the former index, we consulted not only the indexes of the individual volumes but also applied new diligence to supply anything that might be lacking in those particular indexes.

For a long time we were uncertain what method to follow in preparing this general index. At first we thought of composing a kind of *Summa of Augustinian teaching*, or a theological corpus according to the mind of the holy Doctor, constructed from his selected and more extensive statements according to the method of Saint Thomas or of the Master of the Sentences. In the end, however, it seemed more advisable to prepare, as is customary, a general subject index in alphabetical order. From it it will not be difficult to compile the aforementioned *Summa*, should it later seem useful to the common good; it could then be published separately.

Finally, the last place will be occupied by another general index of all the spurious short works contained in the Appendices attached to each volume. This index seemed altogether necessary to lighten the labor of readers who, accustomed to reading Augustine’s writings, could scarcely endure spending time and leisure on such alien booklets, among which there is much refuse. Nevertheless, a considerable number of writings by certain distinguished ancient authors are found among them and are by no means unworthy of readers’ attention: for example, the works of John Chrysostom, Ambrose, Maximus of Turin, Fulgentius of Ruspe, and others of this kind, as well as the sermons of Caesarius, bishop of Arles. These writings may attract readers by the names of their authors alone.
