We therefore thought it worthwhile to compile a general index of all these authors and of others, however obscure or unknown, separate from the Augustinian index, so that by means of this summary readers may, without great expenditure of time, discern whatever in those booklets is worthy of reading or knowing. In so great and varied a collection of different authors and writings, it was impossible that differing and conflicting opinions on the same subject should not sometimes occur—indeed, even errors and unusual opinions. Anyone who takes this amiss will plainly be fighting against the laws of sound reason. He will depart somewhat less from fairness if he makes us approvers or guarantors of the marginal notes. For in these our only duty is to indicate and present what is not ours but belongs to others. We do not undertake to reproduce the context exactly, but to place certain notes and signs outside the lines, [Col. 0031] so that they may remind the hurried reader, who has no leisure to read the entire booklets at length, of the subject under discussion and invite him to examine more closely whatever he understands to be relevant to him.

When these matters have been completed, only three things seem still capable of being desired from us: namely, an indication of the various editions of Saint Augustine that have been produced since the invention of the art of printing; then, a commemoration of distinguished men of every rank who contributed the assistance of ancient manuscripts toward preparing this edition; and finally, a collection of testimonies from at least ancient authors who adorned the holy Doctor and his writings with praise.

As for the first, it would be almost an endless task to mention all the editions of Augustine’s works, whether complete or individual. After the books *On the City of God*, which were among the first works to receive the honors and light of the newly invented art of printing, John Amerbach published other works of the holy Doctor from time to time. He eventually began to bring them all into a single body in 1504 and completed it within two years, divided into eleven parts. Meanwhile, Jodocus Badius Ascensius had certain of the holy Doctor’s short works printed in various years, both at Paris and at Lyon. Desiderius Erasmus published a larger collection in ten volumes at Basel in 1529. Many other editions followed in various places until 1577, when the Doctors of Louvain published at Antwerp an enlarged and far more accurate edition.

If anyone wished to enumerate how often this Louvain edition has been reprinted, the matter would become lengthy and perhaps would not be worth the effort. Who, moreover, could list the individual editions of every short work? Among these, John Ulimmer published in 1564 a new volume entitled *On Various Matters*, consisting of one hundred and thirty-two sermons, partly previously unpublished and partly corrected by him, together with the Life of Augustine written by Possidius and an index of his works. In our own time Jacob Sirmond and Jerome Vignier brought other sermons out of darkness; the latter was the first to publish the unfinished work *Against Julian*.

These were the principal aids we had in preparing our edition. To them were added almost countless ancient manuscripts drawn from many libraries, which we have mentioned in their proper places, where we recorded the collations of the individual works with ancient manuscripts. We should like to list the names of the individual men who supplied us with such assistance. At this point, however, we have decided to refrain from doing so, lest we pass over anyone without praise, mention someone out of order, or deprive anyone of the commendation owed to him. We hope that grateful readers will acknowledge all of them individually when they see their libraries mentioned in the appropriate places.

Yet we cannot remain silent, without fault of ingratitude, about how much gratitude we owe both to the most eminent prince of the Church, Antonio Ludovico de Noailles, archbishop of Paris—whom the most holy Pope Innocent XII, recognizing and approving his piety and learning, honored with the sacred purple while we were completing this work, to the joy of his heart and amid universal applause—and to the most illustrious Charles Maurice Le Tellier, archbishop and duke of Rheims. Both of them, because of their exceptional devotion to Augustine, deigned to place this new edition under their patronage and strengthened it by their authority. The most illustrious bishop of Meaux, Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet, likewise came forward with no less devoted a spirit toward the holy Doctor.

Finally, it would scarcely be worthwhile to gather testimonies from the ancients about Augustine, since his more illustrious praises are available elsewhere to every learned reader, and no others seem necessary to commend so great a man—one whom the whole Church acknowledges as a most distinguished and wholly upright Doctor in explaining the dogmas of the faith and expounding Christian moral teaching, and as one who adhered most closely to the purer teaching of Christ.

[Col. 0031]

## The Life of Possidius

Possidius, elected bishop of Calama in Numidia in the year 397, was a disciple of Saint Augustine, with whom, as he himself relates, he lived in close familiarity for nearly forty years. He received the final breath of his teacher and wrote the Life that we present below. It is precious not for the splendor of its style but for a certain gracious simplicity and the truth of its events. He added to it an index of the books, treatises, and letters of Saint Augustine.

[Note: [Col. 0031] The index in question will appropriately appear in the final volume.]

Among the various editions of this Life that have appeared, two easily hold the first place because of the excellence of their annotations: those published by the Benedictine Fathers in their collection of the holy Doctor’s works, and, separately, that published by John Salinas of Naples, a Lateran canon regular. This latter edition was issued at Rome in 1731. We consulted both. M.

[Col. 0033]

# Life of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, by Possidius, Bishop of Calama (C)

[Col. 0033]

## Note

To the various readings extracted by the Maurist Fathers from six manuscripts—namely, two from Fleury, and the Germanensis, Saint-Vaast, Fossat, and Cîteaux codices—we have added several others drawn from John Salinas, mentioned above in the Life of Possidius. That learned man, to whom several studies of the same kind are owed, especially the outstanding edition of the *Commonitorium* of Lérins, as the readers of our *Complete Course of Theology* know well, published at Rome in 1731 the Life of Saint Augustine by Possidius.

These are the sources from which he derived his distinctive variants: two codices in the Library of the Queen of Sweden, numbered 541 and 1025, and three other codices in the Vatican Library, numbered 1188, 1190, and 1191. M.

[Col. 0033]

## Explanation of the Principal Abbreviations

[Col. 0033]

Cd. — Codex, manuscript volume.  
Cdd. — Codices, manuscript volumes.  
Ms. — Manuscriptus, manuscript.  
[Col. 0034] Mss. — Manuscripti, manuscripts.  
Edd. — Editi, printed editions.  
Vatic. — Vatican codex. M.

## Preface

[Col. 0033]

With God, the Maker and Governor of all things, inspiring me, and mindful of my purpose—to serve, through the grace of the Savior, the almighty and divine Trinity by faith—I have resolved, both earlier in the life of the laity and now in the office of bishops, to benefit the edification of the holy and true Catholic Church of Christ the Lord by whatever ability and speech I have received. I must not remain silent about the life and character of the excellent priest Augustine, predestined and presented in his own time, as I saw them in him and heard them from him.

For we have read and learned that before us this was also done by deeply religious men of the holy mother Catholic Church. Inspired by the divine Spirit, they brought similar men, through their own speech and writing, to the knowledge of those eager to learn, telling and writing for the ears and eyes of those who wished to know what kind and how great were the men whom the common grace of the Lord enabled to live amid human affairs and persevere until the end of death.

Therefore I too, the least of all stewards, with sincere faith—the faith by which the faithful must serve and please the Lord of lords and all good things—have undertaken to explain what I learned and experienced concerning the origin, progress, and appointed end of the venerable man mentioned above, to whose love I clung for so many years, if the Lord should grant me the ability.

But I ask the highest Majesty that I may conduct and complete the task I have undertaken in such a way that I neither offend the truth of the Father of lights nor appear in any respect to defraud the good sons of the Church of their charity. I shall not attempt to relate everything that the most blessed Augustine himself set out in his books of *Confessions* concerning what he was before receiving grace and how he lived after receiving it. For, as the Apostle says, he wished no one to think or believe of him more than he knew himself to be, or than had been heard about him (II Cor. XII, 6). He followed the practice of holy humility, deceiving no one, but seeking not his own praise, rather that of his Lord, in recounting his own deliverance and gift, on the basis of what he had already received; and asking his brothers’ prayers for what he desired to receive.

“Therefore, to conceal the king’s secret, as it is declared by angelic authority, is good; but to reveal and confess the works of the Lord is honorable” (Tobit XII, 7).

## Chapter One — Augustine’s Birth, Conversion, and Baptism. Ambrose’s Teaching Recalls Him from the Error of the Manichaeans. He Is Baptized by Ambrose

He was born, therefore, in the African province, [Note: [Col. 0034] Salinas: I would more readily read, “He was born in the province of Africa,” as the three Vatican manuscript codices have it; especially since, when “the African province” is named without qualification, the proconsular province is understood, as in the Council of Carthage held under Cyprian concerning the repetition of baptism: “When very many bishops had assembled at Carthage from the province of Africa” (or “African,” to designate the proconsular province), “Numidia, and Mauretania.” Since Augustine was not born in the proconsular province but in Numidia, whose prosperous and distinguished town was Tagaste, it would therefore be more correct to say that he was born in the province of Africa. Here “Africa” is understood in the sense in which it was formerly divided by Pomponius Mela, Ptolemy, and ancient ecclesiastical usage into three parts: Mauretania, Numidia, and Africa in the strict sense, which was the proconsular province. Yet respect for Isidore of Seville prevented us from inserting our conjecture into the text, since in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 8, he calls Possidius a bishop of the African province, although the city of Calama was situated in Numidia. M.]

in the city of Tagaste, of respectable and Christian parents belonging to the curial class. He was brought up and nourished under their care, diligence, and expense, and was thoroughly educated in secular letters, being instructed in all the disciplines called liberal.

[Note: [Col. 0035] Salinas, from two Vatican codices: “He was brought up and nourished under their care and diligence, and was educated with greater expense in secular letters, thoroughly instructed in all the disciplines called liberal.” For although his parents helped him with whatever expense they could afford, it is nevertheless clear from the holy Doctor himself, *Against the Academics*, book 2, no. 3, that he advanced in his studies at the expense of Romanianus, the leading man in his city. In these words he gratefully testifies: “You received me, a poor young man setting out for foreign studies, with a home, with financial support, and, what is more, with your good will.” M.]

For he first taught grammar in his own city, and afterward rhetoric in Carthage, the capital of Africa. At a later time he also taught across the sea, in the city of Rome and at Milan, where the court of the younger Emperor Valentinian had then been established. At that time the episcopate of that city was administered by Ambrose, a priest most acceptable to God and most illustrious among good men.

Meanwhile Augustine stood among the people at the frequent discussions of this preacher of God’s word in the church, listening attentively and absorbed. But when he was a young man at Carthage, he had been seduced by the error of the Manichaeans. For that reason he attended more intently than the others, lest anything be said either for or against that heresy. And the mercy of God the Deliverer anticipated him, touching the heart of his priest so that the questions arising from the Law might be resolved against that error. Thus instructed, little by little and gradually, that heresy was driven from his mind by divine mercy. At once he himself was confirmed in the Catholic faith, and a fervent love for progress in religion was kindled in him, so that as the holy days of Easter approached he might receive the water of salvation.

And, by divine assistance, it came to pass that through such a great bishop as Ambrose he received both the saving teaching of the Catholic Church and the divine Sacraments.

[Note: [Col. 0035] Salinas, from Codex Reg. 1025: “And that he received the divine Sacrament.” M.]

## Chapter Two — Having Abandoned Everything, He Embraces the Purpose of Serving God, Being Already More Than Thirty Years Old

Soon, from the innermost marrow of his heart, he abandoned every hope he had placed in the world. He no longer sought a wife, children of the flesh, riches, or worldly honors, but resolved to serve God with His people and to strive to belong to that little flock to which the Lord says:

“Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom. Sell what you possess and give alms; make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven” (Luke XII, 32), and so forth.

And wishing also to do what the Lord says elsewhere, that holy man desired to fulfill this command:

“If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew XIX, 21).

And desiring to build upon the foundation of faith [Note: [Col. 0036] Salinas, from the Queen’s Codex: “And desiring to build upon the foundations of faith.” Another Queen’s Codex has “he desired.” M.] not wood, hay, and straw, but gold, silver, and precious stones, he was then more than thirty years old. His mother alone survived, [Note: [Col. 0036] According to Salinas, certain codices add the name of his mother, Monica, and shortly afterward the name of his father, Patricius. M.] remaining attached to him and rejoicing more in his purpose of serving God than in grandchildren of the flesh. For his father had already died.

He also dismissed the students to whom he had been teaching rhetoric, telling them to find another teacher for themselves, since he had resolved to serve God.

## Chapter Three — Augustine’s Withdrawal. A Certain Man Converted by Augustine

And when he had received grace, [Note: [Col. 0036] Printed editions: “having received the grace of baptism”; but the manuscripts do not contain the word “baptism.” M.] it pleased him to return to Africa and to his own home and estates with certain fellow citizens and friends who likewise served God. Having gone to them and settled among them, he lived for nearly three years with those who adhered to him, now having detached himself from secular concerns, [Note: [Col. 0036] All the manuscripts omit “secular concerns,” and one of the Fleury manuscripts has *alienatus* (“detached”) instead of *alienatis*. Salinas, from two codices, retains “secular concerns”; from Queen’s Codex 1025 he reads “having detached himself from former vices”; from one Vatican codex, which omits “secular concerns,” he reads *alienatus*. M.] living for God through fasts, prayers, and good works, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord.

What God made intelligible and revealed to him as he pondered and prayed, he taught both those present and those absent through sermons and books. It happened by chance at that time that a certain man belonging to those whom they call *Agentes in rebus*, stationed at Hippo Regius, a good Christian who feared God, learned of his excellent reputation and teaching. He longed and desired to see him, promising that he could despise all the desires and enticements of this world if he should at some time be worthy to hear the word of God from his mouth.

When this report was faithfully brought to him, Augustine desired to free the man’s soul from the dangers of this life and eternal death. He therefore came willingly and immediately to the aforementioned city, and, after seeing and addressing the man repeatedly, exhorted him, as far as God granted, to repay what he had vowed to God.

The man promised that he would do so from day to day, but he did not fulfill it then in Augustine’s presence. Nevertheless, what divine providence accomplished everywhere through such a pure vessel, honorable and useful to the Lord, prepared for every good work (II Timothy II, 21), could not be empty or fruitless.

[Note: [Col. 0036] Salinas, from two Vatican codices, reads *liberari* (“to be freed”). M.]

[Note: [Col. 0036] The Lyon edition has *haec* (“this”). M.]

[Note: [Col. 0036] Printed editions: “But certainly it was vain.” The same Salinas, from one Queen’s Codex, has the present reading. M.]

## Chapter Four — He Is Seized for the Rank of the Priesthood

At that same time the holy Valerius was bishop of the Catholic Church at Hippo. When, because ecclesiastical necessity demanded it, he was addressing and exhorting the people of God concerning the provision and ordination of a priest for the city, [Col. 0037] the Catholics, already aware of Saint Augustine’s purpose and teaching, laid hands on him. For he himself was standing among the people unsuspecting and unaware of what was about to happen. He used to say that, while still a layman, he avoided attending churches that did not have bishops.

They therefore seized him and, as is customary in such circumstances, brought him forward to be ordained by the bishop. Everyone requested with one accord and desire that this be carried out and accomplished, demanding it with great zeal and shouting, while he wept profusely. Some, as he himself later told us, arrogantly interpreted his tears and, as though consoling him, said that although the place of the priesthood was approaching the episcopate, he himself was worthy of a higher dignity.

But that man of God, as he related to us, understood and lamented with greater consideration how many and how great dangers to his life he already foresaw impending and arising from the administration and governance of the Church, [Note: [Col. 0037] The manuscript codices have *speraret* (“he hoped”).] and therefore he wept. Their desire was fulfilled as they wished.

[Note: [Col. 0037] Salinas, from Vatican Codex 1190: “And as custom is in such circumstances.” M.]

## Chapter Five — He Establishes a Monastery. Bishop Valerius Grants Augustine the Authority to Preach the Word of God in His Presence

Having therefore become a priest, he immediately established a monastery within the church and began to live with the servants of God according to the manner and rule established under the holy Apostles (Acts IV, 32): above all, so that no one in that community might possess anything as his own, but that everything should be held in common and distributed to each as there was need. He himself had already done this when he returned from overseas to his own country.

[Note: [Col. 0037] Salinas, from Vatican Codex 1190: “Which he himself had done earlier.” M.]

The holy Valerius, who had ordained him, was a pious and God-fearing man. He rejoiced and gave thanks to God that his prayers had been heard—prayers that, as he related, he had very frequently poured out, asking that a man might be granted to him by divine providence who could build up the Lord’s Church by the word of God and sound teaching. For, being Greek by birth and less well instructed in the Latin language and literature, he saw himself as less useful for this task.

He therefore gave that priest permission to preach the Gospel in the church in his presence and to expound it frequently. This was contrary to the custom and practice of the African Churches, and for this reason some bishops even disparaged him. But that venerable and prudent man knew and was certain that this was customarily done in the Eastern Churches, [Note: [Col. 0037] We have added “and was certain” from the manuscripts.] and, concerned for the usefulness of the Church, paid no attention to the tongues of his detractors, provided that the priest did what he, as bishop, clearly saw he could not accomplish.

Thus the lamp, kindled and burning and raised upon a lampstand, gave light to everyone in the house (Matthew V, 15). Later, when this kind of reputation had spread far and wide and a good example had gone before, several priests, with permission received from the bishops, began to expound the word of God to the people in the presence of the bishops.

## Chapter Six — Augustine’s Conflict with Fortunatus the Manichaean
Certainly, in that city of Hippo at that time the plague of the Manichaeans had infected and penetrated very many inhabitants and strangers alike [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions, however, have: “It had infected very many citizens and strangers.”], through the seduction and deception of a certain presbyter of that heresy named Fortunatus, who lived and remained there.

Meanwhile the Christian inhabitants and strangers of Hippo, both Catholics and Donatists, approached the presbyter [Note: Salinas, from the Vatican manuscripts, reads “or,” but nevertheless adopted “and,” explaining: “We changed nothing in the text, following the Paris edition, although ‘or’ may reasonably be read, as these two codices have it, supported by the passage a little earlier.”] [Note: The printed editions have: “They approached Augustine the presbyter.” “Augustine” is absent from the manuscripts.] and begged him to meet that Manichaean presbyter, whom they believed to be learned, and to discuss the Law with him. He, as it is written, “ready always to give an answer to everyone who asks him for a reason concerning the faith and hope that is in God” (1 Peter 3:15), and “able both to exhort in sound doctrine and to refute those who contradict it” (Titus 1:9), did not refuse at all. But he asked whether the other man too was willing that this should take place.

They immediately conveyed the matter to Fortunatus himself, asking, exhorting, and entreating him not to refuse it. Fortunatus, however, already knew at Carthage that Augustine was still established with him in the same error, and he was afraid to engage with him. Nevertheless, compelled and embarrassed chiefly by the insistence of his own people, he promised that he would come face to face and undertake the contest of debate.

Accordingly, on the appointed day and at the appointed place they gathered together, with very many interested people and curious crowds assembling; and, when the notaries’ tablets had been opened [Note: The manuscripts have: “And when the notary’s tablets had been opened.”], the debate began and was concluded on the second day. In it that Manichaean teacher, as the reliable record of the proceedings shows, was able neither to invalidate the Catholic assertion nor to prove that the Manichaean sect was supported by truth. But, failing in his answer [Note: Salinas has: “But, failing in his final answer, he said that he would confer, and so forth.” He adds this note: “Four manuscripts read this way, and correctly. Other editions have: ‘But, failing in his answer, he said that finally he would confer, and so forth.’ One manuscript has: ‘He said that finally he would confer, and so forth.’”], he finally said that he would discuss with his superiors the matters he had been unable to refute; and, if they perhaps did not provide him with an adequate answer, he would take thought for his own soul.

Thus, by all those among whom he had appeared great and learned, he was judged to have accomplished nothing in defending his sect. Overwhelmed by this humiliation, he departed from the city of Hippo shortly afterward and never returned to it. And so, through the aforementioned man of God, that error was removed from the hearts of all—both those who had been present and those who had learned, while absent, what had taken place—and the sincere Catholic religion was proclaimed and retained.

## CHAPTER VII — Augustine’s books and treatises against the enemies of the faith eagerly received even by the heretics themselves

He taught and preached, both privately and publicly, in the house and in the church, the word of salvation with complete confidence against the African heresies, and especially against the Donatists, Manichaeans, and pagans [Note: The printed editions add “and Pelagians,” contrary to the manuscripts, and rightly so: the Pelagians had not yet arisen in the time of Augustine the presbyter.], through written books and spontaneous discourses [Note: The printed editions have “and repeated discourses.” The manuscripts read “and spontaneous discourses,” that is, extemporaneous ones.]. Christians marveled beyond expression and rejoiced [Note: The manuscripts have “and praising together.”], and wherever they could, they did not keep this to themselves but spread the report.

And so, with the Lord’s help [Note: The manuscript reading is “spreading the report.” “And by God’s gift, to raise,” and so forth.], the Catholic Church in Africa began to lift up its head [Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, has: “And so, by God’s gift, peace arose in the African Church, which for a long time had lain,” and so forth.], after having lain seduced and oppressed for a long time, while the heretics there were growing stronger—especially the party of Donatus, which rebaptized and had seduced the greater part of the African population [Note: The manuscripts have “among them” rather than “there.”] [Note: Salinas, from Vatican Manuscript 1188, has: “And oppressed, it remained silent.”].

Even the heretics themselves, gathering with the Catholics, listened with great eagerness to these books or treatises of his, which by the marvelous grace of God were issuing and flowing forth, furnished with an abundance of reasoning and with the authority of the Holy Scriptures. Whoever wished and was able employed notaries, and even wrote down what was said as it was recorded. From there, throughout the whole body of Africa, the renowned teaching and the sweetest fragrance of Christ were disseminated and made manifest; and, when the overseas Church of God learned of it, it too rejoiced. For just as “when one member suffers, all the members suffer with it,” so also “when one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26).

[Note: The printed editions add: “At this same time, before the bishops who ordered him to do so—the bishops who were holding at Hippo the plenary council of all Africa—Augustine, while still a presbyter, debated concerning the faith and the Creed.” These words have been rashly transferred here from the first book of the *Retractations*, chapter 17; they are entirely absent from the manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER VIII — He is designated bishop while Valerius is alive and ordained by Megalius the primate

That blessed old man Valerius, rejoicing even more than the others at this and giving thanks to God for the special favor granted him, began—as is natural to human beings—to fear that Augustine might be sought for the episcopate by another church deprived of its priest and thus be taken away from him. Indeed, this would have happened had not the bishop, having learned of the matter, arranged for him to move to a secluded place and caused him to remain hidden, so that those searching for him could not find him [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript, has: “Had he not arranged to send him away.”].

Therefore, fearing still more, the venerable old man, and knowing that he was extremely weak in body and advanced in age, acted through secret letters with the primate of the bishops of Carthage [Note: Two manuscripts have: “With the primate bishop of Carthage.”]. He pleaded the weakness of his body and the burden of his age, and begged that a bishop be ordained for the Church of Hippo, so that Augustine would not so much succeed to his chair as join him as a fellow priest.

Having diligently pursued and requested what he desired, he obtained it by letter. Later, after a request had been made for his visitation and he had come [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “After the request for a visitation had been made, when he came.”] to the Church of Hippo, Megalius, bishop of Calama and then primate of Numidia [Col. 0040], Valerius the bishop unexpectedly disclosed his intention to Megalius, to whatever bishops happened to be present at the time, to all the clergy of Hippo, and to the whole people. While all listened, rejoiced, and loudly demanded with great eagerness that this be carried out and completed, the presbyter refused to accept the episcopate while his own bishop was alive, contrary to the custom of the Church [Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, has: “The devout presbyter refused.”].

When everyone urged that this was regularly done, and when the practice was demonstrated to him by examples from the overseas and African Churches, he was compelled and forced to yield, and accepted both the administration of the episcopate and ordination to the higher office [Note: The ancient manuscripts omit “and accepted the administration of the episcopate.”].

Later he both said and wrote that this should not have been done to him—that he had been ordained while his bishop was alive—because of the prohibition of a universal council [Note: The Council of Nicaea.], which he learned about only after he had already been ordained. Nor did he wish what he regretted having suffered himself to be done to others. Hence he also worked diligently [Note: At the third Council of Carthage, in the year 397, canon 3.] to have it established by councils that the ordinances of all the priests should be brought to the knowledge of those being ordained, or of those already ordained, by the ordainers.

## CHAPTER IX — He contends with the Donatists

And so it happened that, as bishop, with much greater urgency and fervor and with greater authority, he preached the word of eternal salvation eagerly and diligently—not merely in one region, but wherever he was invited to come—while the Church of the Lord was budding and growing [Note: The editions have “budding sweetly.” Salinas reports the same reading from one manuscript; another omits “diligently budding.”].

He was always ready to give those who asked him a reason concerning the faith and hope that is in God. His sayings, recorded in writing, the Donatists especially—those living in that same city of Hippo or nearby [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript, has: “In that same Church of Hippo, or nearby,” and so forth.]—carried to their bishops. When the bishops heard them and perhaps said something in opposition, they were either refuted by their own people, or the same answers were brought back to Augustine. Once he had learned of them, he patiently and gently, and, as it is written, “with fear and trembling,” worked for the salvation of all [Note: One Florentine manuscript has “of human beings.” The same reading appears in one Vatican manuscript cited by Salinas.] (Philippians 2:12), showing how completely they had wished and been able to refute nothing, and how true and evident was what the faith of the Church of God holds and teaches.

These matters were constantly carried on by him day and night. He also sent private letters to various bishops of the same error and to prominent laymen [Note: Salinas, from four manuscripts, has: “He also sent private letters to various bishops of the same error, prominent men, and laymen.”], offering a reasoned admonition and exhortation that they should either correct themselves from that perversity or at least come to a debate. But they, from distrust of their case [Note: Here we follow John Salinas. After reporting the reading of the Paris edition, namely “But they, because of distrust,” he adds: “Our reading nevertheless appears more correct, since shortly afterward Possidius adds, according to the Paris edition: ‘And he labored so that the distrustfulness of their case might become known to everyone’; there the Fathers of Saint-Maur correct the Louvain edition, which reads: ‘The cause of distrust.’ The Vatican Manuscript 1190 supports our reading.”], did not even once wish to reply [Col. 0041], but, enraged, spoke madly [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript, has: “They wished to reply to nothing, but, enraged, spoke furiously.”]. They loudly proclaimed, both privately and publicly, that Augustine was a seducer and deceiver of souls; they said and argued that, like a wolf, he ought to be killed in defense of their flock; and they maintained that one could undoubtedly believe that all sins were capable of being forgiven by God for those who could do and accomplish this, fearing neither God nor blushing before human beings [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript, has: “Nor respecting human beings.”].

He therefore labored so that the distrustfulness of their case might become known to everyone [Note: The Louvain edition has: “The cause of their distrust.”]. When they were summoned by official public records, they did not dare to enter into a debate.

## CHAPTER X — The fury of the Circumcellions

Those same Donatists also had, in nearly all their churches, an unheard-of kind of perverse and violent men, who went about as though under a profession of continence [Note: Salinas, from Vatican Manuscript 1190, has: “As though under a profession of continence.”]. They were called Circumcellions [Note: Several manuscripts have: “They were called Circellions.”]. They existed in enormous numbers and in mobs throughout nearly all the regions of Africa. Trained by evil teachers, with proud audacity and unlawful recklessness, they sometimes spared neither their own people nor others, and against law and right forbade unwary men [Note: The ancient manuscripts have: “Against law and right, forbidding men in lawsuits”; some of those manuscripts instead read “interceding” or “cutting off” where they read “forbidding.” Salinas gives: “Against law and right, forbidding men in lawsuits,” and adds this note:

“Manuscripts of the Queen’s Library and two Vatican manuscripts have: ‘Against law and right, in lawsuits, forbidding men’; the ancient manuscripts agree, as the Fathers of Saint-Maur testify, although in some of those manuscripts ‘interceding’ appears instead of ‘forbidding,’ and in others ‘cutting off.’ Nevertheless, the learned Fathers wished to restore to the text: ‘Against law and right, forbidding unwary men.’ Our reading appears better if the following words of Optatus of Milevis are considered. Explaining what the Circumcellions did against law and right, he says in the third book of *On the Donatist Schism*, section 4:

‘The acknowledgments of debt had lost their force; at that time no creditor had the liberty to demand anything. Everyone was terrified by the letters of those who boasted that they had been leaders of the Saints; and if there was delay in obeying their commands, a mad crowd suddenly rushed in, and, with terror preceding them, surrounded the creditors with dangers, so that those who ought to have been asked for what they had given were driven by fear of death to plead humbly. Everyone hastened to lose even the greatest debts, and it was counted as profit to have escaped their violence.’

This, then, was what the Circumcellions did against law and right: they prevented the cases of people who had given their property from being examined. For this reason Possidius notes their cruelty and injustice, since in lawsuits they forbade people to reclaim their rights. I suspect that Possidius had this passage of Optatus in mind; for what he adds here—‘And unless they obeyed, they were afflicted with the gravest losses and killings’—is altogether similar to Optatus’s words: ‘And if there was delay in obeying their commands, a mad crowd suddenly rushed in,’ and so forth.”]

Unless the men obeyed, the Circumcellions inflicted the gravest losses and killings upon them [Note: Salinas has “they were afflicted,” and adds: “Both Royal manuscripts and the two Vatican manuscripts read this way; they correspond to Optatus’s words: ‘They surrounded the creditors with dangers.’”]. Armed with various weapons, raging through fields and estates, they did not fear advancing even to the shedding of blood [Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 1025, has: “They did not fear even the shedding of the blood of the Church.” The words “advancing to” are omitted.].

But while the word of God was being diligently preached and a policy of peace was being pursued even with those who hated peace, they attacked the speaker without cause [Note: One manuscript cited by Salinas reads: “They attacked those who were speaking freely.”]. As the truth concerning their doctrine became known, those who wished and were able either rescued themselves from it or withdrew from it, and adhered with those they could to the peace and unity of the Church.

Therefore, seeing that the gatherings of their error were diminishing and envying the growth of the Church, they were inflamed and burned with the most violent anger, and, acting in concert against the unity of the Church, they carried out intolerable persecutions [Note: Most manuscripts have: “Most violent and intolerable persecutions.”] against it [Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, has: “With compacts.”]. They also made attacks by day and by night [Note: Salinas, from Vatican Manuscript 1190, has: “Just and Catholic priests.”] upon Catholic priests and ministers, and inflicted plunderings of every kind [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript, has: “Various plunderings.”].

For they weakened many servants of God by beatings. They even threw lime mixed with vinegar into the eyes of some, and killed others. Consequently, those same Donatists, the rebaptizers, also became hated by their own people.

## CHAPTER XI — The Church’s progress through Augustine; monasteries founded by his pupils

As divine teaching advanced, clerics began to be ordained for the Church of Hippo from among those serving God in the monastery under the holy Augustine and with him [Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 1025, has: “As divine teaching advanced, those serving God under the holy Augustine and with the holy Augustine in the monastery, and serving the Church of Hippo, began to be ordained clerics.” Vatican Manuscript 1190 likewise has this reading, except that it adds “in divine teaching.”].

Then, as the truth of the Catholic Church’s preaching became known and shone more brightly from day to day [Note: A Cistercian manuscript has: “The Catholic Church’s truth of preaching.” The word “preaching” is absent from one of the Florentine manuscripts. It is also omitted in Vatican Manuscript 1191, according to Salinas.], and as the purpose, continence, and profound poverty of the holy servants of God became known [Note: Two manuscripts have: “The purpose of continence and profound poverty.” A Cistercian manuscript has: “The purpose that contains profound poverty.”], peace and unity began, and afterward continued, to seek and receive bishops and clerics from the monastery that had begun both to exist and to grow through that memorable man.

For nearly ten holy and venerable men whom I myself knew—continent and most learned [Note: Salinas, from two manuscripts, has: “And learned.”]—the blessed [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript, has: “Most blessed.”] Augustine, when requested [Note: One manuscript cited by Salinas does not have the word “when requested.”], gave to various churches, including some of greater importance. Likewise, they themselves, coming from that holy way of life [Note: Salinas, from two Vatican manuscripts, has “from his holy way of life.”], propagated the Churches of the Lord and founded monasteries. As their zeal for building up the word of God increased, they supplied brothers who had been advanced in the other churches to undertake the priesthood.

Thus, as the saving doctrine of the Church’s faith, hope, and charity became known through many people and in many places—not only throughout all the regions of Africa but also overseas—and through books published and translated into the Greek language, many things came to be known, by God’s favor, from that one man and through him to many others.

And from this, as it is written, “the sinner saw and was angry; he gnashed his teeth and wasted away” [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript, has “and growled.”] (Psalm 111:10). But the servants of God [Note: Salinas, from two manuscripts, has: “But your servants, as it is said,” and so forth.], as it was said [Col. 0043], “were peaceful with those who hated peace; and when they spoke, they were attacked by them without cause” (Psalm 120:7).

## CHAPTER XII — Augustine avoids the ambushes prepared for him through the error of his guide; many gold fines imposed on the heretics

On several occasions those same Circumcellions, armed, even blocked the roads against God’s servant Augustine when he happened to be traveling, at their request, to visit, instruct, and exhort Catholic communities; for he did this very frequently. On one occasion it happened that those men, lying in wait for him, lost the opportunity to seize him. For by God’s providence, but through the error of the guide [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions have “of the guide.” Salinas adopted the former reading from Royal Manuscript 541 and Vatican Manuscript 1188.]—a human error—it happened that the priest arrived with his companions by another road, where he was headed [Note: Salinas, from Vatican Manuscript 1188, has: “With his guides or companions.”], and that, through this error, which he recognized only afterward, he escaped their impious hands.

And although he had given thanks to God his liberator for everything, they nevertheless, entirely in their usual manner, spared neither laymen nor clerics when they were enraged [Note: Salinas adds “when they were enraged,” and notes: “We have inserted the word ‘enraged’ on the authority of Royal Manuscript 541; it is consistent with Possidius’s style, since in chapter 9 he says: ‘Enraged, they spoke madly.’”], as the public records testify [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript, has: “As the public records contain.”].

Nor should we remain silent about what was accomplished and brought to completion, for the praise of God, through the zeal of that man so outstanding in the Church and through his zeal for the house of God against the aforementioned Donatist rebaptizers.

When one of those whom he had promoted from his monastery and clergy to be bishops of the Church was visiting the diocese of the Church of Calama entrusted to his care, and was preaching what he had learned for the peace of the Church against that heresy, it happened that he fell into their ambush in the middle of his journey. They overran him and all who accompanied him, took away their animals and belongings, and subjected him to the gravest insults and beatings.

To prevent the progress of the Church’s peace from being impeded any further, the Church’s defender did not remain silent before the laws. Crispinus, who was bishop of those same Donatists in the city and region of Calama, a prominent man of long standing and learning, was summoned and ordered to be held liable for the gold fine established by public laws against heretics. He resisted, was brought before the authorities, and denied that he was a heretic. It therefore became necessary, when the Church’s defender withdrew, for a Catholic bishop to resist him [Note: That Catholic bishop was Possidius himself, who recounts the affair, concealing his name out of modesty but revealed by Augustine in Letter 105, section 4, and in the third book against Cresconius, chapters 46–47], and to prove that he was what he had denied himself to be. For if the Catholic bishop had concealed the matter, the uninformed might perhaps have believed him to be a heretic, since the other man denied what he was; and thus neglect would have given rise to scandal among the weak.

With the venerable bishop Augustine pressing the matter in every way, the two Calamian bishops came to the controversy and engaged in a third contest with one another concerning that very difference of communion. A great multitude of Christian people, both at Carthage and throughout Africa [Col. 0044], awaited the outcome of the case. Crispinus was declared a heretic by the proconsular and written judgment.

The Catholic bishop interceded for him before the judge, so that the gold fine would not be exacted, and this favor was obtained for him. But when, ungrateful, he appealed to the most devout Prince [Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, has: “To the most devout judge.”], the Emperor’s due response was given to the report, and an order followed [Note: Salinas, from three manuscripts, has: “And consequently an order followed”; another has: “And an order also followed.”] that Donatist heretics were to have no standing anywhere whatsoever and were to be held everywhere subject to all the force of the laws enacted against heretics [Note: Salinas, from one Royal manuscript, has: “And there.”].

As a result, the judge, the officials [Note: Here *officium* means the personnel administering judicial affairs, such as the recorders who assist the judge, as in book 3 against Cresconius, chapter 29; the *Brief Account of the Conference*, day 1, chapter 8; day 3, chapters 1 and 17, section 32; the book *After the Conference*, chapter 24, sections 41–42; the book *On the Unity of the Church*, section 54; and frequently in the Acts of the Carthaginian Conference. The Louvain editors therefore incorrectly altered the passage to: “As a result, the judge, on account of the office.” Ulimmerius altered it even worse: “As a result, Crispinus himself and the other heretics like him were ordered to pay ten,” and so forth.], and Crispinus himself, since the fine had not at all been exacted, were ordered to pay ten pounds of gold into the treasury.

But immediately the Catholic bishops, especially Augustine of blessed memory, took action so that the condemnation of all of them might be remitted by the ruler’s clemency; and, with the Lord’s help, this was accomplished. Through this diligence and holy zeal the Church grew greatly.

## CHAPTER XIII — Peace for the Church through Augustine

For all these deeds carried out for the peace of the Church, the Lord granted Augustine the palm of victory here and reserved for him with Himself the crown of righteousness. With Christ’s help, the unity of peace and the brotherhood of the Church of God increased and multiplied more and more from day to day.

This happened especially after the conference [Note: The Louvain edition has “through the conference.” Later it substitutes “with his assistance” for “at his command.”] subsequently held at Carthage by all the Catholic bishops with those same Donatist bishops, at the command of the most glorious and devout Emperor Honorius. To bring it to completion, he had also sent from his court to Africa the tribune and notary Marcellinus as judge.

In that controversy the Donatists were thoroughly refuted and convicted by the Catholics of error, and were censured by the judge’s decision. After their appeal, they were justly condemned among the heretics by the reply of the most devout ruler [Note: The manuscripts have: “By the reply of the most devout ruler, they were unjustly condemned among the heretics.”].

As a result, more of their bishops than usual [Note: Salinas, from Vatican Manuscript 1188, has “their bishops.” Erasmus’s 1529 edition likewise reads: “As a result they were censured, more than usual, those of their bishops who did not communicate with their own clergy and people, and who, holding to Catholic peace,” and so forth.] communicated with their clergy and people. While maintaining Catholic peace, they endured many persecutions from their own people, even to the amputation of limbs and death.

And all that good, as I have said, was begun and completed through that holy man, with our bishops consenting and laboring together with him.

## CHAPTER XIV — The Donatist bishop Emeritus is defeated

After the conference held with the Donatists, some people said that those same bishops had not been permitted before the authority that heard the case to say everything on behalf of their party, because the judge belonging to the Catholic communion favored his own Church. The defeated and vanquished made this claim as an excuse, although before the controversy those same heretics knew that he belonged to the Catholic communion; and when they were summoned by him through public records to attend the conference, they declared that they would do so. If they regarded him with suspicion, they could certainly have refused the encounter.

Nevertheless, the almighty God provided assistance. Later, when Augustine of venerable memory was staying in the city of Caesarea in Mauritania—where letters from the Apostolic See [Note: Letters of Pope Zosimus. See Augustine, Letter 190, section 1, and Letter 193, section 1.] had compelled him to come with his fellow bishops, in order to settle certain other necessities of the Church—this opportunity arose for him to meet Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of that place, whom they had regarded as the principal defender of their sect at the conference.

Augustine debated publicly with him in the church, with the people of the differing communion standing by, and challenged him through the ecclesiastical records. If Emeritus had perhaps been able, as they claimed, to pursue his case at the conference but had not been permitted to do so, Augustine urged him not to hesitate now to say it freely, without any prohibition or coercive power from an authority, and not to refuse confidently to defend his own communion in his own city, with all his fellow citizens present.

Emeritus would not do this, neither in response to this exhortation nor at the urgent request of his relatives and fellow citizens. They promised him that they would return to his communion, even at the risk of their property and their temporal safety, if only he could overcome the Catholic assertion.

But he would neither say nor was he able to say anything more in the records, except this: “The records already made at Carthage among the bishops contain whether we were victorious or defeated.”

Elsewhere, when a notary urged him to answer and he remained silent [Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, has: “When a notary urged him to answer, he was silent; and when he remained silent,” and so forth. Royal Manuscript 1025 has: “When a notary urged him to answer, he said nothing. And when he remained silent,” and so forth.], his complete lack of confidence was made evident to everyone, and the growth and strengthening of the Church of God resulted.

Whoever therefore wishes to know more fully the diligence and work of Augustine of most blessed memory on behalf of the state of the Church of God should also read through those proceedings [Note: The proceedings with Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of Caesarea, in volume 9]. He will find what he said and of what kind it was: how he challenged that learned, eloquent, and celebrated man, urging him to state whatever he wished in defense of his party. He will recognize that Emeritus was defeated.

## CHAPTER XV — The merchant Firmus converted by a digression in the preacher’s sermon

I know that not only he himself but also other brothers and fellow servants, who at that time lived with us inside the Church of Hippo with that holy man, heard him say while we were all seated together at table:

“Did you notice today in the church that my sermon proceeded, in its beginning and its end, contrary to my custom? For I did not explain the matter I had intended to bring to an end, but left it unfinished?”

We replied that we knew and recognized that at the time we had indeed been astonished by it.

He said: “I believe that perhaps the Lord wished, through our forgetfulness and error, to teach and heal someone in the congregation who was wandering; and in His hand are both we and our sermons. For while I was examining the hidden aspects of the question I had proposed [Note: The manuscripts have “the sides.” Salinas, from Vatican Manuscript 1188, has “the hidden part.”], I proceeded in a digression into another subject. Thus, without concluding or explaining the question, I ended the discussion, speaking more against the error of the Manichaeans—although I had decided to say nothing about it—than about the matters I had intended to assert.”

After this, if I am not mistaken, behold, on another day or two days later, a certain merchant named Firmus came. While the holy Augustine was seated inside the monastery, in our presence, Firmus threw himself on his knees at his feet, weeping, and begged the priest to pray to the Lord with the saints for his sins [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “With his own people.”].

He confessed that he had followed the sect of the Manichaeans and had lived in it for very many years, and that for this reason he had spent a great deal of money uselessly on the Manichaeans, or on those whom they call the Elect. He also confessed that, by God’s mercy, he had recently been corrected in the church by Augustine’s treatises and had become a Catholic.

The venerable Augustine himself and we who were present carefully asked him what in particular in that discourse had satisfied him. When he reported it, and all of us recognized the sequence of the sermon, we marveled and were astonished at the profound plan of God for the salvation of souls. We glorified and blessed His holy name: when He wishes, from wherever He wishes, and in whatever way He wishes, He works the salvation of souls through those who know and through those who do not know.

From that time, the man adhered to the way of life of God’s servants, abandoned the business of a merchant, and, progressing among the members of the Church, was requested and compelled by God’s will in another region to undertake the office of the priesthood. He maintained and guarded the sanctity of his way of life, and perhaps he is still alive among human beings, established overseas.

## CHAPTER XVI — The detestable obscenities of the Manichaeans exposed; the Manichaean Felix converted

At Carthage also, when a certain procurator of the imperial household named Ursus, a man of Catholic faith, gained access to some Manichaeans whom they call Elect or Elect Women, and led and escorted them to the church, they were examined by the bishops before the tablets [Note: “Before the tablets” means that notaries recorded the questions and answers, entering them onto tablets. Thus, through the work of the notaries, those proceedings were compiled which are called ecclesiastical here and in the book *On Heresies*, heresy 46, where they are called episcopal proceedings.].

Among them was Augustine of blessed memory, who knew that detestable sect better than the others. Exposing such condemnable blasphemies from passages in the books that those Manichaeans accept, he brought them to the confession of those same blasphemies. Through the disclosures of those women whom they call Elect, it was made clear in those ecclesiastical proceedings what disgraceful and shameful things they had been accustomed, according to their evil custom, to do among themselves [Col. 0047].

Thus, through the diligence of the shepherds, both growth was added to the Lord’s flock and a suitable defense against thieves and robbers was secured.

He also debated publicly with a certain Felix, one of those whom the Manichaeans call Elect [Note: The printed editions add: “For he had come to Hippo to sow the same error.” These words are Augustine’s, from the second book of the *Retractations*, chapter 8.], in the church of Hippo, with the notaries recording and the people standing by. After the second or third conference, that Manichaean, his sect’s vanity and error having been frustrated, converted to our faith and Church, as the written record itself can demonstrate when read again [Note: The proceedings with Felix the Manichaean, in volume 8.]

## CHAPTER XVII — The Arian count Pascentius is defeated in debate; debate with Maximinus, an Arian bishop
Moreover, when challenged by a certain Pascentius, an Arian count of the imperial household, who by virtue of his position was an exceedingly zealous collector of the treasury’s revenues, fiercely and continually attacked the Catholic faith, and harassed and disturbed very many priests of God who lived by a simpler faith, with his sharp tongue and authority, Augustine held a public disputation with him at Carthage, with respected and noble men acting as intermediaries [Note: The printed editions add: “with them present”].

But that same heretic absolutely refused to have tablets and a stylus present—something our teacher [Note: Two Floriacensian manuscripts read: “because our teacher preferred it even more”] most insistently wanted both before and during the encounter. When he continued to refuse, saying that he did not wish written tablets to place him in danger through fear of the public laws, and when Bishop Augustine, together with the fellow priests who were present, saw that the proposal pleased the intermediaries—that they should debate privately without any writing—he accepted the conference. He predicted what subsequently happened: that, after the gathering had been dissolved, anyone might freely say, since there was no written record, that he had said something which he had perhaps not said, or that he had not said something which he had said. [Note: The Louvain edition adds: “at his discretion.”]

He entered into discussion with him, stated what he believed, heard from him what he held, and taught what had been established by sound reasoning and the authority of the Scriptures [Note: Most manuscripts read: “taught what had been brought forward”], and displayed the foundations of our faith. He showed and refuted the assertions of the other side as supported by no truth and no authority of the Holy Scriptures. When the parties had departed from one another, the other man, increasingly angry and raging, hurled many lies in support of his false faith, loudly proclaiming that he himself had defeated Augustine, whom many voices had praised.

Since this did not escape notice [Note: The printed editions add: “of that venerable man”], he was compelled to write to Pascentius himself, omitting the names of the disputants out of fear of him; and in that letter he faithfully reported everything that had been said or done between the parties. To prove it, if it were denied, he had a large number of witnesses—namely, the highly distinguished and honorable men who had then been present. The other man scarcely returned a reply to the two writings addressed to him—only one response [Note: Salinas, from Codex Regius 541: “When the heretic heard this, he returned one written book in response to the two writings addressed to him”—manuscript variant]—in which he was more capable of inflicting an insult than of making clear the case for his sect [Col. 0048]. This is confirmed by those who are willing and able to read it.

He also held a disputation at Hippo with a certain Maximinus, one of the bishops of the Arians, who had come to Africa with the Goths, when very many people wished and requested it, with distinguished men acting as intermediaries. What each side asserted was written down. If diligent students take care to read it carefully, they will undoubtedly discover [Note: Salinas: “We have preserved in the text the reading of the Paris manuscript; the Regius Codex 1025, however, reads: ‘they will judge’] either what that crafty and irrational heresy professes in order to seduce and deceive, or what the Catholic Church holds and proclaims concerning the divine Trinity.

But because that heretic, returning from Hippo to Carthage, boasted that he had departed from the disputation as its victor because of his abundant loquacity during the conference—and he lied; because these matters could not easily be examined and judged by those ignorant of divine law—the venerable Augustine later made a recapitulation in writing of the entire conference, dealing with each objection and response. He also demonstrated that the other man had been able to make no adequate reply to the objections, adding supplements that, because of the limited time available for the conference, could not all be introduced and written down then. The man’s wickedness had arranged matters so that, in his final speech, which was much the longest, he occupied all the time that remained in the day.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The new heretics, the Pelagianists, are defeated and condemned. How greatly Augustine’s labors benefited the Catholic Church. Heretics and pagans decline. The immense quantity of Augustine’s works.

Against the new heretics and clever disputants of his own times, the Pelagianists, who wrote with a craft that was more subtle and harmful [Note: The particle “and” has been restored from the manuscripts] and who spoke publicly and in private houses wherever they could, he labored for nearly ten years [Note: Salinas, from Codex Regius 1025: “he was laboring”] [Note: He reckons the years from the rise of the Pelagian error to its condemnation by Zosimus. Otherwise, the holy Doctor disputed and wrote against that error from approximately the year of Christ 411 or 412— in 412 he completed the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, after having earlier attacked the same error in sermons—until the year 430, when death overtook him as he was writing his final work against Julian. Hence Prosper, in book 1 of the work he published against Cassian in 433, chapter 1, no. 2, in the appendix to volume ten of our edition, says: “It is more than twenty years since the Catholic army, under the leadership of this man, has fought against and conquered the enemies of God’s grace.”] producing and publishing many books, and very frequently disputing in church before the people against that error.

And since those perverse men, through their ambition, were attempting to persuade the Apostolic See to accept the same perfidy, the holy bishops of the African councils also acted with the greatest urgency, so that first the holy Pope of the City [Note: The printed editions add: “of Rome”], the venerable Innocent [Note: In Salinas, the word “venerable” is absent from one manuscript; in another, the word “pious” is added to it.], and afterward holy Zosimus, his successor, might be persuaded how detestable and condemnable that sect was in relation to the Catholic faith.

Those bishops of that great see, condemning the same men at their respective times and cutting them off from the members of the Church, decided by letters addressed both to the African Churches of the West and to the Churches of the Eastern regions [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions instead have: “By letters addressed to the African Churches of the East and West,” corruptly. A little later, the Lyons edition and Salinas, from two manuscripts, read “to be anathematized” rather than “to be condemned to anathema.”] that all Catholics should anathematize and avoid them. And the most pious emperor Honorius, hearing and following this judgment pronounced by the Catholic Church of God concerning them, decreed that they had been condemned by his laws and were to be regarded as heretics. Consequently, some of them returned to the bosom of holy Mother Church, from which they had recoiled, and others are still returning, as the truth of the right faith against that detestable error becomes known and prevails.

That memorable man, a foremost member of the Lord’s body, was always watchful and deeply concerned for the welfare of the universal Church. It was granted to him by God that he should rejoice even in this life in the fruit of his labors. First, he saw perfect unity and peace in the Church and region of Hippo [Note: The Carnutensian manuscript reads: “in the region of the Church of Hippo”], over which he chiefly presided. Then, in other parts of Africa, whether through himself or through others—and through the priests whom he himself had appointed—he saw the Church of the Lord springing up and multiplying. He rejoiced to see that the Manichaeans, Donatists, Pelagianists, and pagans had for the most part declined and had joined themselves to the Church of God.

He also favored and celebrated the progress and zeal of all good people, patiently and piously tolerating the lack of discipline of his brothers, and groaning over the iniquities of the wicked, whether of those within the Church or of those established outside the Church. As I have said, he always rejoiced in the Lord’s gains and grieved over its losses.

So much was dictated and published by him, so much was debated, received, and corrected in the Church, so much was written against heretics or expounded from the canonical Books for the edification of the holy children of the Church, that scarcely any diligent reader could read and know it all. Nevertheless, so that we may not seem in any way to defraud those most eager for the word of truth [Note: In the Louvain and Lyons editions, “of the word” is omitted. Ulimmerius instead reads: “of the truth and word of God.” Salinas, from Codex Regius 1025: “of the truth of the word”], I have decided, with God’s help, to append at the end of this little work a catalogue of those books, treatises, and letters as well.

When they have read it, those who love God’s truth more than temporal riches may each choose what they wish to read and learn. They may request it for copying either from the library of the Church of Hippo, where more accurate copies may perhaps be found, or seek it wherever they can; and, once they have found and copied it, they may keep it and, without jealousy, themselves provide it for copying to anyone who requests it.

## CHAPTER XIX — How Augustine conducted himself in hearing cases. When opportunity arose, he taught the parties what concerns eternal life. The reward of judicial labor.

In accordance also with the Apostle’s statement:

“Does any one of you, when he has a case against another, dare to be judged by the unjust and not by the saints? Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy of the smallest judgments? Do you not know that we shall judge angels, to say nothing of secular matters? If, then, you have secular cases among you, appoint as judges those who are contemptible in the Church” [Note: The Fossatensian manuscript reads: “in the judgment of the lesser matters.” Salinas, from Codex Regius 541: “in the judgment of the least matters,” followed by: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more secular matters?”].

“I speak to your shame: is there no wise man among you who can decide between his brothers? But brother goes to judgment against brother, and that before unbelievers” (1 Corinthians 6:1–6).

When Christians or people of any sect appealed to him, he carefully and piously heard their cases, keeping before his eyes the judgment of a certain man who said that he preferred to hear cases between strangers rather than between friends. For, when judging strangers according to the equity that he considered right, he might gain a friend; whereas, among friends, he would lose one of the two when he pronounced judgment against him.

Sometimes he heard and settled these cases until the hour of the meal, and sometimes he fasted the entire day [Note: Salinas, from Codex Regius 541, omits “sometimes” and reads simply: “And he heard them until the hour of the meal”]. In all cases, however, he discerned the condition of the Christians’ souls: how much each was progressing in faith and good conduct, or falling away from them [Note: The printed editions read: “good works”; the manuscripts: “good conduct”]. When he had discovered the circumstances that provided an opportunity, he taught the parties the truth of divine law [Note: The editor of the Lyons edition and Salinas, from Codex Regius 541, read: “with the truth”], impressed it upon them, and instructed and admonished them how they might attain it and obtain eternal life.

From those to whom he devoted his time he sought nothing else but obedience and Christian devotion, which are owed both to God and to human beings. He rebuked sinners in the presence of all, so that the others might be afraid (1 Timothy 5:20). He did this as a watchman appointed by the Lord over the house of Israel, proclaiming the word and insisting upon it in season and out of season, reproving, exhorting, and rebuking, with complete patience and instruction (2 Timothy 4:2). Above all, he took care to instruct those who were capable of teaching others (ibid.).

When some people also asked him to assist them in their temporal affairs, he wrote letters to various persons. But he considered this occupation, which took him away from better things, a kind of forced service. He always found sweet either conversation or familiar fellowship with his brothers and household companions concerning the things of God.

## CHAPTER XX — How he interceded for defendants.

We know that, when his dearest friends asked him by letter to intercede with the powers of the world, he did not do so, saying that the judgment of a certain wise man ought to be observed, a man of whom it was written that, out of regard for his reputation, he had refused many requests from his friends. He added this maxim of his own: “Often the power that grants a request oppresses” [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript: “The power that demands a request oppresses”; from another: “The power that is solicited oppresses.” The Louvain edition has the latter reading in the margin].

But whenever he saw that intercession was necessary and was asked to undertake it, he did so with such propriety and moderation that he appeared not only neither burdensome nor troublesome, but even remarkable. On one occasion, when necessity had arisen, he followed his custom and interceded with a certain African vicarius named Macedonius by means of a petitioning letter. When Macedonius had complied, he sent this reply:

“I am affected in a wonderful way by your wisdom, both in what you have published and in what, when interceding for those in distress [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions: “for defendants.” In volume 2, at the beginning of Macedonius’s letter (154), the manuscripts are said to read: “for criminals.”], you do not consider it burdensome to send. For the former possess such acumen, knowledge [Note: Salinas, from one manuscript: “They possess such acuteness of knowledge”], and holiness that nothing could surpass them; and the latter possess such modesty that, if I do not do what you command, I judge that the fault remains with me, not with the case—most deservedly venerable lord and father worthy of respect [Note: In volume 2, Macedonius’s letter (154) is printed: “truly venerable father worthy of respect.”].

“For you do not press me—as most people in this place do—to extort whatever an anxious petitioner [Note: Some older manuscripts omit “petitioner.” Most read, instead of “anxious,” “more anxiously”] may wish; rather, you bring to my attention what appears petitionable to you from a judge burdened by so many cares [Note: The printed editions add: “and you ask”], with the assistance of that modesty which among good men is the most effective means of accomplishing difficult things.”

“Therefore, I immediately granted the fulfillment of the desire you commended. For I had already opened the way for hope” (Macedonius, in the collection of letters among Augustine’s letters, 154, no. 1).

## CHAPTER XXI — With what disposition he used to attend councils. In ordaining priests, greater agreement and the custom of the Church must be sought.

Whenever he could, he attended the councils of holy priests held throughout the various provinces—not seeking his own interests in them, but those of Jesus Christ—so that either the faith of the holy Catholic Church might remain inviolate, or certain priests and clerics who had been excommunicated, whether lawfully or unlawfully, might either be absolved or expelled.

In ordaining priests and clerics, he judged that the greater consensus of Christians [Note: Three manuscripts—the Fossatensian, Vedastine, and Cistercian—read “the consensus of the elders.” The Louvain edition has this reading in the margin; Salinas, from Vatican Codex 1190, reads: “He considered that the consensus of the greater Christians, according to the custom of the Church, should be followed.”] and the custom of the Church should be followed.

[Note: Concerning the ordination of priests, Cyprian says in his letter to the clergy and people of Spain, numbered 67 in the new edition: “Let the ordination be just and legitimate, having been examined by the vote and judgment of all.” In the same place he praises the ordination of Bishop Sabinus as having been made “with the vote of the entire brotherhood.”]

## CHAPTER XXII — What kind of person Augustine was in dress and food.

His clothing, footwear, and bedding were of moderate and appropriate quality—not excessively elegant, nor excessively shabby. For in these matters people generally either customarily display themselves arrogantly or debase themselves; in both cases they seek not the things of Jesus Christ, but their own interests. Augustine, as I have said, kept to the middle course, turning neither to the right nor to the left.

His table was simple and frugal. It had vegetables and legumes, and sometimes meat for guests or for those who were weaker; it always had wine [Col. 0052]. For he knew [Note: Joannes Ulimmerius, a canon of Louvain in the Augustinian order, printed this passage as follows: “For guests or for those who were weaker he provided it. He always drank wine, though moderately and temperately, because he knew,” and so on. The Louvain theologians corrected him in this form: “For guests or for those who were weaker he kept it. He always had wine, because he knew,” and so on. Nevertheless, all our manuscripts lack the word “kept,” with the possible exception of the Vedastine, which later reads “he drank wine” in place of “he had wine.” Salinas gives the same text from Codex Regius 1025; from Codex 541, however: “For guests or for those who were weaker he carried it. He always used wine, because he knew,” and so on].

He knew and taught, as the Apostle says, that every creature of God is good and that nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving; for it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4:4–5). And, as the same holy Augustine wrote in his books of the *Confessions*:

“I do not fear the uncleanness of food, but the uncleanness of desire. I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh that could serve as food; that he was refreshed even by the food of flesh; and that John, endowed with marvelous abstinence, was not defiled by animals—namely, locusts—being used as food. I know also that Esau was deceived by his desire for lentils, and that David was reproved by himself because of his thirst for water, and that our King was tempted not by meat but by bread” [Note: Salinas, from two manuscripts: “but was tempted only by bread.”].

“And therefore the people in the wilderness deserved condemnation, not because they desired meat, but because, from their desire for food, they murmured against God” (*Confessions*, book 10, chapter 31, no. 46).

Concerning the use of wine, there is also the Apostle’s statement in his letter to Timothy:

“Do not continue drinking only water, but use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses” (1 Timothy 5:23).

He used silver spoons only. The other vessels in which food was brought to the table were earthenware, wooden, or marble—not from financial necessity, but by deliberate choice.

He always practiced hospitality. At table he preferred reading or discussion to eating and drinking. And as a safeguard against the plague of human custom, he had this written there:

> Whoever delights in gnawing at the lives of the absent  
> Must know that this table is unworthy of him.

[Note: Three manuscripts give the verse as follows: “At this table he must know that his own conduct is unworthy.” Ulimmerius printed: “He must know that this table is forbidden to him.” Salinas, from Codex Regius 541: “He must know that this table is unworthy of him.”]

For this reason he admonished every guest to abstain from superfluous and harmful conversation and from slander [Note: The words “and from slander” are absent from the manuscripts]. On one occasion, when some of his closest fellow bishops had forgotten that inscription and were speaking against it, he rebuked them so severely, being moved to say either that those verses must be erased from the table or that he would rise from the middle of the meal and go to his room. I and the others who attended that table experienced this ourselves.

## CHAPTER XXIII — What he was like in the use of the Church’s revenues.

He always remembered his fellow poor [Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions: “the poor.” Salinas, from one Vatican manuscript, likewise: “the poor”], and distributed to them from the same resources from which he and all those living with him received support [Note: The printed editions add: “was distributed to him and his household”]—that is, either from the revenues of the Church’s properties [Col. 0053] or from the offerings of the faithful.

When, as sometimes happens, jealousy arose among the clergy concerning those very properties, he addressed the people of God, saying that he would rather live from the contributions of God’s people than endure the care or administration of those properties. He declared himself ready to surrender them to the people, so that all God’s servants and ministers might live in the manner in which those serving at the altar are said to have lived in the Old Testament—sharing in what came from the altar (Deuteronomy 18:1) [Note: The manuscripts read: “to share in it.”]

But the laypeople never agreed to accept this.

## CHAPTER XXIV — What he was like in domestic affairs. What donations and bequests to the Church he accepted or refused. He always wished to keep his mind free from the cares of temporal things.

He entrusted and delegated all care of the Church’s household and property to the stronger clerics. He never kept a key or ring in his own hand.
