Rather, the household superiors recorded everything that was received and distributed. At the end of each year, they reported it to him [Note: Salinas, from Codex 1188: “in the presence of the same man”], so that it might be known how much had been received, how much had been distributed, and what remained to be distributed [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions instead have: “or whatever remained undistributed or still to be distributed.” Salinas, from one manuscript, has the same reading]. In many matters he relied more on the fidelity of the household superior than on what he had learned by verification and disclosure [Note: Salinas, from two manuscripts: “whom he regarded as proved and trustworthy.”].

He never wished to purchase a house, field, or estate. But if anyone voluntarily donated or left such a thing to the Church by way of bequest, he did not reject it, but ordered that it be accepted. We know that he refused certain inheritances—not because they could have been of no use to the poor, but because he saw that it was just and equitable that they should belong rather to the children, parents, or relatives of the deceased, to whom those people, when dying, had been unwilling to leave them.

A certain distinguished man of Hippo, living at Carthage, wished to donate a property to the Church of Hippo. He voluntarily sent the completed documents to the blessed Augustine, while retaining the usufruct for himself. Augustine gladly accepted the offering and congratulated him on remembering his eternal salvation.

But several years later, when we happened to be present with the same man face to face, the donor sent a letter through his son, requesting that the documents of donation be returned to his son. He directed that one hundred solidi be distributed to the poor. When the holy man learned of this, he groaned that the man had either pretended to make the donation or had repented of his good work. With as much grief of heart as God inspired in him [Note: The printed editions read: “with a grieving heart”], he spoke against this reversal, rebuking and correcting him. He immediately returned the documents that the man had voluntarily sent, although they had neither been requested nor demanded, and rejected the money. In his reply he reproved and rebuked the man as was appropriate, admonishing him to make satisfaction to God, with the humility of repentance, for his deception [Col. 0054] or iniquity, lest he depart from this world with so serious a sin.

He also frequently said that the Church ought more securely and safely to accept bequests left by the dead [Note: Salinas: “In Vatican Codex 1190, ‘left by the dead’ is absent. Codex Regius 541 reads: ‘The Church ought to accept bequests previously left by the deceased rather than inheritances that might be troublesome and diminished.’”] than inheritances that might prove troublesome and harmful; and that such bequests should be offered rather than demanded.

He himself did not accept entrusted funds, but he did not prevent clerics who wished to accept them from doing so. Nor was he absorbed or entangled by love or attachment to what the Church possessed [Note: The printed editions add “or desire,” but the manuscripts lack it]. Rather, suspended from and clinging to greater and spiritual things, he scarcely ever relaxed and lowered himself from contemplation of eternal matters to those temporal concerns.

Once he had arranged and ordered these matters, he returned from things biting and troublesome to the inner and higher regions of his mind. There he would either think about discovering divine truths, dictate something concerning truths already discovered, or certainly correct something already dictated and transcribed. He did this by laboring during the day and keeping vigil at night.

He was like that most religious Mary, who represents the heavenly Church, of whom it is written that she sat at the Lord’s feet, listening attentively to his word. When her sister complained that she was not being helped by her, because she was occupied with much service, she heard:

“Martha, Martha, Mary has chosen the better part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:39–41).

He never desired to undertake new construction, avoiding the entanglement of his mind in such matters; he always wanted to keep it free from every temporal burden. Nevertheless, he did not prevent those who wished to build from doing so, except when their projects were excessive.

Meanwhile, whenever the Church’s money ran short, he announced this very fact to the Christian people, saying that he had nothing to distribute to those in need. He even ordered that sacred vessels be broken and melted down on behalf of captives and very many needy people [Note: Two manuscripts: “and exceedingly needy people.” One of the Floriacensian manuscripts reads: “For he also ordered very many sacred vessels to be broken and melted down.” Salinas, from Vatican Codex 1191, has the same reading], and that the proceeds be distributed to the needy.

I would not have mentioned this had I not seen that it was contrary to the fleshly understanding of certain people. The venerable Ambrose also unquestionably said and wrote that this should be done in such necessities (*On the Duties*, book 2, chapter 18).

He also sometimes spoke in church about the treasury and storeroom neglected by the faithful, from which the necessities of the altar are brought in. He had once told us that the most blessed Ambrose had likewise discussed this matter in church in his presence.

## CHAPTER XXV — Domestic discipline. The punishment of one who swears.

The clerics always lived with him, in the same house and at the same table, and were supported and clothed from common resources. To prevent anyone, through easy swearing, from falling into perjury, he both preached in church before the people and instructed his own household that no one should swear [Note: Salinas, from Codex Regius 541: “And he instructed his own people by his words that no one should swear”]—not even at table [Note: The printed editions read “even in a small matter”; all the manuscripts read “even at table.” Salinas, from Vatican Codex 1190, has “in a small matter”] [Col. 0055].

If anyone slipped into doing so [Note: The manuscripts read: “If anyone had done so”], he forfeited one of the prescribed drinks; for a fixed number of cups had been established for those who lived and dined with him.

He rebuked the lack of discipline and transgressions of his people against the proper rule and good conduct [Note: Salinas, from two manuscripts: “and good practice.” One manuscript lacks “good conduct”], and tolerated them as much as was fitting and necessary. In such matters above all he taught that no one’s heart should turn toward evil words in order to make excuses for sins (Psalm 140:4).

When anyone brought his gift to the altar and there remembered that his brother had something against him, the gift was to be left before the altar, and he was to go and be reconciled to his brother [Note: The printed editions: “and that the same brother should be reconciled.” The manuscripts correct this reading]; then he was to return and offer his gift at the altar (Matthew 5:23–24).

If he himself had something against his brother, he was to rebuke him privately; and if the brother listened, he would have gained his brother. If not, one or two others were to be brought in. If he disregarded them as well, the Church was to be involved. If he did not obey even the Church, he was to be treated as a gentile and a tax collector.

He added that when a sinning brother asked forgiveness, the offense was to be forgiven not seven times, but seventy-seven times (ibid. 18:15–17, 21–22), just as each person daily asks the Lord to forgive him.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Concerning the association of women.

No woman ever lived within his household or remained there—not even his own sister, who, as a widow serving God, lived for a long time until the day of her death as the superior of the women servants of God. Nor did his uncle’s daughters or his brother’s daughters, who likewise served God, live there [Note: Our manuscripts do not have: “his uncle’s daughters and his brother’s daughters.” The same words are absent from Salinas’s manuscripts]. The councils of holy bishops placed such persons among the exceptions.

He said that, although no evil suspicion could arise concerning his sister and nieces living with him, those women could not remain there without other necessary persons and women living with them; and since other women would also enter from outside on their account, some occasion of offense or scandal could arise from them for the weaker. Those who happened to live with a bishop or any cleric could, through all these women living with them or visiting them, either perish through human temptations or at least be most disgracefully defamed by the evil suspicions of men [Note: The most ancient Fossatensian manuscript reads: “or be most disgracefully defamed by women visiting,” omitting “or perish through temptations,” and so forth].

For this reason, he said that women should never live in the same house with servants of God, even the most chaste, lest, as has been said, such an example place some scandal or occasion of offense before the weaker. If some women happened to ask to see him or greet him, they never entered to him without clerical witnesses [Note: The Louvain edition: “he entered to them,” contrary to the manuscripts and Ulimmerius. Salinas, from Codex Regius 541: “she entered to her”]; nor did he ever speak alone with women alone, unless some confidential matter was involved [Note: Salinas: “Nor did he ever speak alone with women alone, unless some confidential matter was involved,” adding this note: “Codex Regius 541: ‘unless some confidential matter was involved.’ Vatican Codex 1190: ‘unless some confidential matter were involved’; but earlier it reads: ‘nor, if some secret matter were involved.’”].

## CHAPTER XXVII — His care for the destitute and the sick. Ambrose’s notable saying at the end of life. Another eminent judgment of a bishop near death against the desire for a longer life here.

[Col. 0056]

In visitations he observed the rule laid down by the Apostle, visiting only orphans and widows in their affliction [Note: Ulimmerius and the manuscripts read: “those placed in affliction,” masculine] (James 1:27). And if the sick requested this of him—that he should pray to the Lord for them in their presence and lay hands upon them—he went without delay [Note: Salinas, from Codex Regius 541: “he performed it without delay”]. He visited monasteries of women only when urgent necessity required it.

He also used to say that, in the life and conduct of a man of God, one should observe what he had learned from the practice [Note: The printed editions read: “practices.” Salinas, from one manuscript: “practice.”] of Ambrose of holy memory: never to seek a wife for anyone, never to recommend for military service one who wished to serve, and never, when invited, to go to a banquet in his own native town. He gave reasons for each of these: namely, lest, if those joined in marriage should happen to quarrel with one another, they should curse the man through whom they had been joined; though, when they had already agreed, a priest ought indeed to be present when requested for this purpose, so that their agreements and arrangements already made might be confirmed [Note: The older manuscripts read: “their arrangements already made might be confirmed”] or blessed. He did this also lest blame for a person recommended for military service who behaved badly should be attributed to the one who recommended him [Note: This is exactly the manuscript reading; the printed editions read: “lest one acting badly should attribute his own blame to the one who recommended him”]; and lest, through frequent attendance at banquets in his native town, the measure of temperance should be lost.

He also told us that he had heard a very wise and pious reply from the aforesaid man of blessed memory when he was at the end of his life, and he greatly praised and commended it. For when that venerable man lay in his final illness, and honorable believers stood by his bed, seeing that he was about to pass from this world to God and grieving that the Church might be deprived of the ministry of the word and sacrament of God by the loss of so great and such a bishop, they begged him with tears to ask the Lord for a prolongation of life for their sake. He told them: “I have not lived so as to be ashamed to live among you; but neither do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord” [Note: Paulinus the presbyter relates the same thing in his *Life of Ambrose.*]

Our aged Augustine admired and praised these words as polished and well weighed. He held that Ambrose had said, “Nor do I fear to die, because we have a good Lord,” lest he should be thought, in confidence in his own most purified conduct, to have presumed when he said, “I have not lived so as to be ashamed to live among you” [Note: Three manuscripts read: “to have put forward”]. For he had said this with regard to what human beings could know about a human being. But, knowing the scrutiny [Note: Several manuscripts read: “for the scrutiny”] of divine justice, he said that he placed his confidence rather in the good Lord [Note: The printed editions add: “than in his own merits,” but this is absent from the manuscripts], to whom he also said in the daily Lord’s Prayer: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12).

Of another fellow-bishop, and a very close friend of his, he frequently related in the final days of his life the following saying. When he had gone to visit him, already near death, and the man indicated by a gesture of his hands that he was about to depart from this world, while he was answered that he might still live because he was necessary to the Church, the man replied—so that he would not seem to be held by a desire for this life:

“If never, all is well; if at some time, why not now?”

He marveled that such a judgment had been uttered by a man who indeed feared God, but who had been born and raised in a rural village and was not learned in extensive reading. He contrasted him, of course, with the thought of that sick bishop concerning whom the holy martyr Cyprian reported in his letter that he wrote *On Mortality*, saying:

“When one of our colleagues and fellow priests, worn down by illness and anxious about his approaching death, was praying that leave might be granted him, there stood beside the suppliant, already almost dying, a youth venerable in dignity and majesty, tall in stature and radiant in appearance—one whom human sight could scarcely behold with bodily eyes standing beside him, except that a person about to depart from this world could already see such a one. Then the youth growled, not without a certain indignation of spirit and voice, and said: ‘You are afraid to suffer; you do not wish to depart. What am I to do with you?’”

## CHAPTER XXVIII — What Augustine published shortly before his death. The books of the *Revisions*. The incursion of the barbarians. The siege of Hippo.

Before the day immediately preceding his death, he reviewed the books that he had dictated and published—whether those which, at the beginning of his conversion, he had dictated while still a layman, or those which he had dictated as a priest, or those which he had dictated as a bishop. Whatever he recognized in them as having been dictated and written by him otherwise than the ecclesiastical rule required, because he had still known ecclesiastical practice less well and had been less wise, he himself both criticized and corrected.

[Note: The manuscripts read *minusque sapuisset* (“and had been less wise”); the printed editions have *intelligeret* (“had understood less well”). Salinas likewise reads, from one manuscript, *minusque intelligeret*; from another, *minusque saperet* (“had been less wise”).]

For this reason he also composed two volumes whose title is *On the Revision of Books*.

[Note: *The Books of the Revisions*.]

He complained that certain books had been taken from him before more careful correction.

[Note: *On the Trinity*.]

Although he later corrected them, death overtook him while some of his books still remained unfinished. Wishing to be useful to everyone—to those who were able to read many books and to those who were not—he extracted from both Testaments of God, the Old and the New, after supplying a preface, the divine commands and prohibitions relating to the rule of life, and made one book from them, so that anyone who wished might read it and recognize in it whether he was obedient or disobedient to God. He wished this work to be called the *Mirror*.

Yet shortly afterward, by the will and power of God, it came about that a great host armed with various weapons and trained in war—composed of the savage enemies, the Vandals and Alans, together with the Gothic people and persons of various other nations—sailed from the regions overseas, from the direction of Spain, into Africa and invaded it. Raging with every kind of cruelty and brutality, it passed through all the regions of the Mauritanias and onward into our other provinces and territories, laying waste to everything it could through plunder, slaughter, various tortures, fires, and countless other unspeakable evils. It spared no sex, no age, not even the priests or ministers of God, nor the ornaments, vessels, or buildings of the churches.

That fiercest ravaging and devastation by the enemy, the man of God did not perceive and consider in the way other people did. He examined it more deeply and profoundly, foreseeing in it above all the dangers and deaths of souls. Consequently, more than usual—for, as it is written, “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1:18), and “an understanding heart is a moth to the bones”—his tears were his bread day and night (Psalm 41:4), and he led and endured the final, already almost terminal period of his old age more bitterly and mournfully than anything else.

He saw cities destroyed in ruin, and together with the buildings of the villages their inhabitants—some killed by the enemy, others driven away and scattered. He saw churches deprived of priests and ministers, and consecrated virgins and all those living in continence dispersed everywhere. Among them, some had succumbed under torture, others had been killed by the sword, and others, in captivity and having lost the integrity of mind and body and their faith, were serving their enemies through evil custom and harsh compulsion.

He saw the hymns and praises of God disappear from the churches; the buildings of the churches burned by fire in very many places; the solemn sacrifices owed to God cease in their proper places; and the divine sacraments either not sought at all, or, when sought, with no one easily found to administer them.

[Note: This is the reading of some manuscripts of good quality. The printed editions read: “The solemn sacrifices owed to God ceased in their proper places, and the sacrifices and divine sacraments were either not sought,” and so forth. Salinas reads: “The solemn sacrifices owed to God ceased in their proper places, and the sacrifices and divine sacraments were either not sought,” adding the note: “Thus the Louvain edition reads, and rightly, with the manuscripts.”]

He saw people fleeing into mountain forests, rocky caverns, and caves, or to whatever fortified places they could find. Some had been overcome and killed.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “and intercepted”; one of these continues: “Others, thus deprived of the necessities,” and so forth.]

Others had been so stripped and deprived of the supports necessary for life that they wasted away from hunger. Even the superiors and clergy of the churches who, by God’s favor, had either not encountered those disasters or had escaped them when they did encounter them—stripped and bereft of everything, reduced to the utmost poverty, and forced to beg—could not be assisted in all their needs.

Only three churches survived out of innumerable others: the Carthaginian, Hipponensian, and Cirtensian churches. By God’s favor they were not destroyed; their cities remained and were supported by both divine and human assistance. Nevertheless, after his death the city of Hippo, abandoned by its inhabitants, was burned by the enemy.

In the midst of these evils he consoled himself with the saying of a certain wise man:

“He will not be great who considers it a great matter that wood and stones fall and mortals die.”

[Note: The Louvain edition alone reads: “It will not be a great thing that wood and stones fall and mortals die.”]

Thus, being deeply wise, he wept daily and abundantly over all these things. His grief and lamentation increased when the same city of Hippo Regius, while it still stood in its former condition, was about to be besieged by those same enemies.

[Note: The printed editions read *Hipponensium-Regionum*, incorrectly. It is well known that this city was called Hippo Regius, as above, chapter 3, in order to distinguish it from Hippo Diarrhytus.]

At that time Count Boniface had been stationed there for its defense with an army of allied Goths.

[Note: All our manuscripts read this way; the printed editions instead have: “A certain Count Boniface with an army formerly allied with the Goths.” Salinas follows the printed reading because it better accords with historical truth.]

They besieged the city, almost completely shut in, for about fourteen months. They even cut it off from the sea by a blockade of the shore.

[Note: One of the Florentine manuscripts reads: “For they also took away its shore by a maritime blockade.” Salinas, from a Vatican manuscript, reads: “For they also took away that maritime shore by a blockade.” Royal Manuscript 541 reads: “For they took away its maritime shore by enclosing it.”]

We too had fled there from the neighboring area with certain other fellow-bishops, and we remained there throughout the entire siege. We therefore spoke with him very frequently, considering the terrifying judgments of God placed before our eyes, and saying:

“You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgment is upright” (Psalm 118:137).

At the same time, grieving, groaning, and weeping, we prayed to the Father of mercies and God of all consolation (2 Corinthians 1:3), asking that he deign to support us in that tribulation.

## CHAPTER XXIX — Augustine’s final illness

It happened that, while we were seated at table with him and conversing there, he said:

“Know that at this time of our calamity I ask God either to deign to free this city, surrounded as it is by the enemy, or, if he judges otherwise, to make his servants strong enough to endure his will; or at least to receive me from this world to himself.”

When he said this and instructed us, thereafter we—all of us, and those who were in that city—likewise asked the Most High God for the same things with him.

And behold, in the third month of the siege, he took to his bed, exhausted by fevers, and suffered that final illness. The Lord certainly did not deprive his servant of the fruit of his prayer. In due time he granted both to him personally and to that city what he had sought with tearful prayers.

I also know that he, both as a priest and as a bishop, was asked to pray for certain afflicted demoniacs, and that he prayed to God with tears, whereupon the demons departed from the people.

[Note: Salinas, from Vatican Manuscript 1191, reads *pro quibusque* (“for each of whom”).]

[Note: Salinas, from Vatican Manuscript 1191, reads: “For certain demoniacs who asked him to pray.”]

Likewise, someone came to him who was ill and confined to his bed, bringing his sick person with him, and asked him to lay his hand upon the man so that he might be healed. Augustine replied that if he had any power in such matters, he would certainly have first used it for himself. The man then said that he had been visited and had been told in a dream:

“Go to Bishop Augustine, so that he may lay his hand upon him, and he will be saved.”

When Augustine learned this, he did not delay in doing what was requested, and the Lord immediately caused the sick man to leave him healed.

## CHAPTER XXX — Whether bishops should withdraw from the churches when the enemy approaches

It must by no means be left unmentioned that, when the aforesaid enemies were threatening,

[Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, reads: “When the enemies of Mauritania were threatening.”]

our holy fellow-bishop Honoratus, bishop of the Church of Thiava,

[Note: The printed editions have *Thabennensis*; the manuscripts have *Thiabensis* or *Thiavensis*.]

consulted our holy man by letter about whether, when the enemy approached, bishops and clergy should withdraw from the churches or not. In his reply Augustine explained what was more greatly to be feared from those destroyers of the Roman world.

I have wished to insert that letter into this work, for it is highly useful and necessary for the conduct of priests and ministers of God. Augustine’s reply to him was as follows:

“To the holy brother and fellow-bishop Honoratus, Augustine sends greeting in the Lord.

“When I sent your Charity a copy of the letter—which is not extant—that I wrote to our fellow-bishop Quodvultdeus, I thought that I had been relieved of the burden you imposed upon me by asking what you should do amid the dangers that our times have encountered.

[Note: The Louvain edition reads: “Which have come upon our times.”]

“For although I wrote that letter briefly, I do not think I omitted anything that should have been enough both for one answering to say and for one asking to hear. For I said both that those who wished to migrate to fortified places, if they could, should not be prevented, and that we must not break the bonds of our ministry by which the love of Christ has bound us, nor abandon the churches that we are obliged to serve.

“These, then, are the words I included in that letter:

“‘It remains, therefore,’ I said, ‘that we, whose ministry is so necessary to the people of God who remain where we are—however small that people may be—that they ought not to remain without it, should say to the Lord: “Be to us a God of protection and a fortified place”’ (Psalm 30:3).

“But, as you write, this advice does not satisfy you, lest we attempt to act contrary to the Lord’s command or example, where he teaches that one should flee from city to city. For we recall the words of him who said: ‘When they persecute you in this city, flee into another’ (Matthew 10:23).

“Who, however, would believe that the Lord wished this to be done in such a way that the flocks he purchased with his own blood should be abandoned, together with the ministry necessary for them to live? Did he do this when, carried by his parents into Egypt, he fled as a child (Matthew 2:14)—he who had not yet gathered churches that we could say he had abandoned? Or when the Apostle Paul, lest the enemy seize him, was lowered in a basket through a window and escaped his hands (2 Corinthians 11:33)—was the Church that was there abandoned in its necessary ministry, or was what had to be done not fulfilled by other brothers established there?

“He did this at their wish, in order to preserve himself for the Church, since that persecutor was seeking him personally. Let Christ’s servants, therefore, the ministers of his word and sacrament, do what he has commanded or permitted. Let them certainly flee from city to city when one of them is specifically sought by persecutors, so that the Church may not be abandoned by others who are not being sought in the same way, but may provide sustenance to their fellow servants, whom they know cannot otherwise live.

“But when there is a common danger to all—that is, to bishops, clergy, and laity—those who need others must not be abandoned by those whom they need.

[Note: The printed editions omit “and laity,” which is restored from the manuscripts.]

“Either all should move to fortified places, or those who are under the necessity of remaining should not be abandoned by those through whom their ecclesiastical needs must be supplied, so that they may either live together or endure together whatever the Master of the household wills them to endure.

“If it should happen that some suffer less and others more, or that all suffer equally, it is clear which of them suffer for the sake of the others: namely, those who, although they could have escaped such evils by fleeing, preferred to remain rather than abandon the needs of others.

“This is above all proved by the love that the Apostle John commends when he says: ‘As Christ laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for the brothers’ (1 John 3:16). For those who flee—or who, bound by their own necessities, cannot flee—if they are captured and suffer, suffer for themselves, not for their brothers. But those who suffer because they did not wish to abandon their brothers, who needed them for Christian salvation, unquestionably lay down their lives for their brothers.

“Thus we have heard a certain bishop say: ‘If the Lord commanded us to flee in those persecutions in which the fruit of martyrdom can exist, how much more ought we to flee barren sufferings when there is a barbarian and hostile invasion?’ This is indeed true and acceptable,

[Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, reads: “It is useful.”]

“but only for those who are not held by the bonds of ecclesiastical office.

“For the one who does not flee hostile disasters, although able to escape, because he does not wish to abandon the ministry of Christ,

[Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 1025, reads: “Lest he abandon the ministry for Christ.”]

“without which people can neither become nor remain Christians, finds a greater fruit of love than the one who flees, not for the sake of his brothers but for his own sake, and, when captured, does not deny Christ but accepts martyrdom.

“What, then, is the meaning of what you wrote in your previous letter? You say:

“‘If we must remain in the churches, I do not see what benefit we can provide either to ourselves or to the people, except that men should fall before our eyes, women be violated, churches burned, and we ourselves perish under torture when they ask us for what we do not possess.’

“God is certainly powerful enough to hear the prayers of his household and avert these feared events. Nevertheless, because of things that are uncertain, the certain abandonment of our office must not be undertaken—an office without which certain destruction awaits the people, not in the affairs of this life, but in those of the other life, which must be cared for with incomparably greater diligence and concern.

“For if these evils were certain—the evils feared as possibly occurring in the places where we are—then all those for whose sake we must remain there would first flee and free us from the necessity of remaining. No one would say that ministers ought to remain where there were no longer any people whom they needed to serve.

“Thus certain holy bishops fled from Spain, after their peoples had partly escaped by flight, partly been killed, partly been consumed by siege, and partly been scattered into captivity. But many more remained there, because those for whose sake they were to remain were still there, remaining amid the density of the same dangers.

“If some abandoned their peoples, this is precisely what we say must not be done. For such men were not taught this by divine authority; rather, they were deceived by human error or overcome by fear.

“Why do they think they must obey without distinction the command in which they read that they should flee from city to city, while they do not shrink from being hirelings, who see the wolf coming and flee because they do not care for the sheep (John 10:12–13)?

“Why do they not strive to understand these two true sayings of the Lord—one in which flight is permitted or commanded, the other in which it is condemned and blamed—in such a way that they discover them not to be contrary to one another, just as they are not?

“How can this be discovered unless attention is paid to what I have already discussed above: that the ministers of Christ should flee from the places where they are under the pressure of persecution when either the people of Christ whom they should serve are not there, or when they are there but the necessary ministry can be fulfilled by others who do not have the same reason for fleeing?

“This is what happened when the Apostle fled, as I mentioned above, lowered in a basket, because he himself was specifically sought by the persecutor, while others who did not have the same necessity were there, and it would have been far from right for them to abandon the ministry of the Church.

“This is also what happened when the holy Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, fled because the emperor Constantius specifically wished to seize him, while the Catholic people who remained in Alexandria were by no means abandoned by the other ministers.

“But when the people remain, while the ministers flee and the ministry is withdrawn, what is it except that condemned flight of hirelings who do not care for the sheep?

“For the wolf will come—not a human being, but the devil—who has often persuaded the faithful to become apostates when the daily ministry of the Lord’s body was lacking. And the weak brother will perish, not through your knowledge

[Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, reads: “not through your conscience.”]

“but through your ignorance—the brother for whom Christ died (1 Corinthians 8:11).

“As for those who are not deceived by error in this matter but are overcome by fear, why do they not rather fight courageously against their fear, with the Lord’s mercy and help, lest evils incomparably worse, and much more to be dreaded, occur?

“This happens where the love of God burns, not where desire for the world smolders. For love says: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I am not inflamed?’ (2 Corinthians 11:29). But love is from God.

“Let us therefore pray that it may be given by him from whom it is commanded. Through it let us fear more that the sheep of Christ be slaughtered by the sword of spiritual wickedness in their hearts than by iron in their bodies, since at some time and by some kind of death they are all destined to die.

“Let us fear more that, with their inner understanding corrupted, the purity of faith may perish than that women should be violated in the flesh. For violence does not violate modesty if it is preserved in the mind; nor is it violated in the flesh when the will of the one suffering does not shamefully use her body, but without consent endures what another does.

“Let us fear more that the living stones may be extinguished when we abandon them than that the stones and timbers of earthly buildings may be burned while we are present.

“Let us fear more that the members of Christ’s body, deprived of spiritual nourishment, may die than that the members of our own bodies, overwhelmed by the enemy’s assault, may be tortured.

“Not because these things should not be avoided when they can be avoided, but because they must rather be endured when they cannot be avoided without impiety—unless someone should contend that the minister is not impious who withdraws the ministry necessary for godliness precisely when it is most necessary.

“Do we not consider, when matters reach the extreme point of these dangers and there is no power to flee, how great a gathering there is customarily in the Church from both sexes and every age? Some demand baptism, others reconciliation, others even the performance of penance,

“and all seek consolation and the preparation and distribution of the sacraments.

“If ministers are absent, how great a destruction follows for those who depart from this world either unregenerated or bound! How great also is the grief of the faithful who will not have them with them in the rest of eternal life! And finally, how great is the groaning of all, and how great the blasphemy of some, because of the absence of the ministries and ministers!

[Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 1025, reads: “Because of the absence of the mysteries and ministers.”]

“See what the fear of temporal evils does, and how great an increase of eternal evils it contains.

“But if the ministers are present, then, according to the strength that the Lord supplies them, everyone is assisted. Some are baptized, others reconciled, and none are deprived of communion in the Lord’s body.

[Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, reads: “Not many are deprived.”]

“All are consoled, strengthened, and exhorted to pray to God, who is powerful to avert everything that is feared. They are prepared for either outcome, so that, if this cup cannot pass from them, the will may be done of him who cannot will anything evil (Matthew 26:42).

“You now certainly see what you wrote that you did not see: how much good the Christian peoples receive if, amid present evils, the presence of Christ’s ministers is not lacking. You also see how greatly their absence harms them, since the ministers seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21), do not possess the love of which it is said, ‘It does not seek its own’ (1 Corinthians 13:5), and do not imitate the one who said, ‘I do not seek what is useful to me, but what is useful to many, so that they may be saved’ (1 Corinthians 10:33).

[Note: Salinas, from both Royal Manuscripts, reads: “Not what is useful to me.”]

“He would not have fled the plots of that persecuting ruler unless he had wished to preserve himself for those to whom he was necessary. For this reason he says: ‘I am constrained by both desires: I have the desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake’ (Philippians 1:23).

[Note: The remainder may be found in volume 2, Letter 228, sections 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14.]”

## CHAPTER XXXI — Augustine’s death and burial. The penitential psalms. The offering of sacrifice for the dead. The library. The monasteries. The epitaph of a certain poet.

That holy man lived seventy-six years in all, during a long life divinely granted for the usefulness and welfare of the holy Catholic Church; he spent nearly forty years in the clergy and episcopate.

[Note: The manuscript codices read: “For he lived seventy-six years … he was accustomed to say to us,” omitting *autem* (“however”).]

In familiar conversation he was accustomed to say that, after receiving baptism, even Christians of acknowledged merit and priests ought not to depart from the body without worthy and appropriate penance.

[Note: Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, reads: “Even Christians of praiseworthy conduct.”]

He himself did this during the final illness by which he died. For he had ordered the penitential Psalms of David—which are very few—to be written out, and while lying in bed during the days of his illness he gazed upon and read those quires, placed against the wall, and wept continually and abundantly.

So that no one might interrupt his concentration, about ten days before he departed from the body he asked us, in our presence,

[Col. 0064]

that no one should enter to see him except at those hours when the physicians came in to examine him

[Note: Salinas: Three manuscripts read *intrabant* (“when they entered”); one continues: “or when food was brought to him.”]

or when food was brought to him. This was observed and done, and throughout that entire time he devoted himself to prayer.

Until the very last illness he preached the word of God in the church without interruption, eagerly and courageously, with a sound mind and sound judgment. With all the members of his body intact, his sight and hearing unimpaired, and—as it is written—with us standing beside him, seeing him, and praying together with him,

[Note: All our manuscripts omit “praying together with him.”]

he fell asleep with his fathers,

[Note: The Louvain edition adds “in peace.”]

nourished in a good old age. In our presence, a sacrifice was offered to God for the commendation of the deposition of his body, and he was buried.

[Note: The German manuscript omits *enutritus* (“nourished”); and below, instead of “with us present for the commendation of his body,” it reads “by us for his …” Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, reads: “With us present.”]

He made no will, because, being God’s poor man, he had nothing from which to make one.

He always ordered the Church’s library and all its books to be carefully preserved for posterity. Whatever the Church possessed, whether in funds or ornaments, he left in the trust of the faithful priest

[Note: This is how the manuscripts read; the printed editions have “to the faithful priest.”]

who, under him, managed the affairs of the Church’s household.

Nor in life or death did he treat his blood relatives, whether they remained in the religious calling or lived outside it, according to the custom of the world. While he was still alive, he distributed to them, if they needed it, what he distributed to others as well—not so that they might have riches, but so that they might suffer no want, or less want.

He left the Church a fully sufficient clergy and monasteries of men and women, filled with those living in continence

[Note: The printed editions have “filled with those practicing continence.” Salinas likewise.] 

together with their superiors. He also left libraries containing books and treatises, his own and those of other saints, in which it can be recognized what sort of man and how great a man he was in the Church by God’s gift, and in which the faithful find that he continues always to live.

In a similar way, one of the secular poets, ordering that a tomb be placed for him after his death on a public mound, composed an inscription, saying:

> Traveler, do you wish to know that the poet lives after death?  
> Behold, I speak what you read: your voice is, in fact, mine.

[Note: The printed editions have “he composed an epitaph”; all the manuscripts have “he composed an inscription,” and most of them read “he fixed it, saying.” Salinas, from Royal Manuscript 541, reads: “He composed an epitaph, saying.”]

In his writings, that priest beloved and accepted by God is shown—so far as the truth, when it shines upon us, permits us to see—to have lived rightly and soundly according to the Catholic Church’s faith, hope, and love. Those who read him writing about divine matters recognize this and make progress.

But I think that those who were able to hear and see him speaking in person in the church, and especially those who knew his manner of life among human beings, could have benefited still more from him.

[Note: The German manuscripts read: “Those who were able to hear and see him present in the church.”]

For he was not only a learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven, bringing forth from his treasure things new and old, and one of those merchants who, having found one precious pearl, sold what he had and bought it (Matthew 13:52, 45–46); he was also one of those concerning whom it is written:

“Speak in this way, and act in this way” (James 2:12);

and of whom the Savior says:

“Whoever does and teaches these things to people will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:19).

I earnestly ask your Charity, you who read these writings, to give thanks with me to almighty God and bless the Lord, who granted me understanding so that I might both wish and be able to bring these matters to the knowledge of people of the present and absent, of the present time and of the future.

Pray with me and for me, so that, in this world, I may be an imitator and follower of that man with whom, by God’s gift, I lived in intimacy and sweetness for nearly forty years without any bitter disagreement, and that in the future I may enjoy with him the promises of almighty God.

Amen.

[Note: Salinas records that in Royal Manuscript 541 there is added here, together with certain other words concerning the transfer of the holy Doctor’s body: “Who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and is glorified and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.” This ending is an interpolation and does not belong to Possidius’s text. It is well known to students of ecclesiastical antiquity that at the end of both sermons and lives published by the ancients various additions and insertions are made, just as passages are often cut away—whether according to the preference of the speaker or writer, according to the requirements of a solemn occasion, or according to the needs of the times. When this is not carefully noticed, it drives one into serious and shameful errors.]

[Col. 0065]

# LIFE OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, COMPOSED CHIEFLY FROM HIS OWN WRITINGS

## BOOK ONE — On Augustine’s first twenty-nine years, from his birth to his departure for Italy

## CHAPTER ONE — 1. Augustine’s homeland. 2. His birthday. 3. His name. 4. His parents and relatives.

### 1

Aurelius Augustine, a man given to the Church by divine favor, ennobled by his birth the obscure African town of Thagaste, situated in the inland part of Numidia, not far from Madaura and Hippo Regius.

(Cf. Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1; Augustine, Letter 7, section 6; *Confessions*, book 2, chapter 3, section 5.)

That city had once adhered entirely to the wicked schism of the Donatists. But around the year 349, compelled by fear of the imperial laws to return to Catholic communion, it afterward united with such zeal of spirit that in the sixtieth year thereafter its inhabitants seemed never to have been involved in those errors.

(Augustine, Letter 93, section 17.)

### 2

Augustine was born on the Ides of November, in the year of Christ which, as we understand from Prosper and Possidius, was 354.

(Prosper, *Chronicle*; Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 30.)

For he departed this life on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the year of salvation 430, when he had nearly completed his seventy-sixth year. This matter will have to be discussed more fully in the place where we address the time of his conversion.

### 3

When his name began to be celebrated throughout the world, he already had the first name Aurelius. Whether he received it as an infant from his very cradle, or whether the holy Doctor acquired it later through the merit of his life and teaching, he retained it always.

For Paul Orosius honored him by this very first name in the title of his *History*: “To Aurelius Augustine.”

[Col. 0066]

His nearly contemporary Claudianus Mamertus likewise adorned him with that name (*On the Status of the Soul*, book 2, chapter 10). The venerable Bede did so as well (*Life of Saint Cuthbert*). And that name adorns and enhances the finest and oldest volumes of his works that have come into our hands.

Born, Possidius tells us, of respectable parents, he belonged to the *curiales*, that is, to those who administered the office of the curia in the municipalities and discharged civic duties (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 1). His father was Patricius, a very poor municipal citizen of Thagaste, a man endowed more in spirit than in wealth, as Augustine himself records with profound humility (*Confessions*, book 2, ch. 3, §5). With the same modesty, Augustine once admitted in a public gathering that expensive clothing might perhaps suit a bishop, but certainly not Augustine, a poor man born of poor parents (*Sermon* 356, §13).

Patricius was generous and well disposed toward everyone, but also very irascible and fierce. For a long time he was estranged from the Christian faith; near the end of his life, however, he was converted and, together with the faith, assumed a chaste and Christian manner of life (*Confessions*, book 9, ch. 9, §§19, 22).

Patricius’s wife, named Monnica—for this is how the copyists wrote her name everywhere in the ancient manuscripts—gave birth to Augustine in spirit no less than in flesh. She bore Patricius many children. Augustine testifies that, when his mother was dying at Ostia on the Tiber in the year 388, one of his brothers was present (*ibid.*, ch. 11, §27). This brother seems to have been Navigius, who, while living with his brother Augustine—who had not yet been regenerated—in the villa of Verecundus, took part in his philosophical discussions while suffering from a diseased spleen (*On the Blessed Life*, §§7, 14). By this father, without doubt, were begotten those nieces of Augustine, daughters of his brother, who likewise served God (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, ch. 26), together, it seems, with the full sister of the same holy bishop, who, after being widowed, presided for many years, until the day of her death, over a monastery of the handmaids of God while serving Christ (*Augustine, Letter* 211, §4).

Augustine also mentions Patricius, his nephew and a subdeacon of the Church of Hippo (*Sermon* 356, §3), who had several sisters and whose mother held the usufruct of the properties belonging to him. During his retreat at Verecundus’s, Augustine also had two of his cousins with him, Lastidianus and Rusticus. That Severinus, whom Augustine tried through a letter full of duty and charity to bring over from the Donatist faction to the unity of the Catholic Church, was likewise bound to Augustine by kinship (*Letter* 52). Finally, Licentius, the son of that prominent citizen of Thagaste, Romanianus, distinguished by both birth and wealth, seems to imply that he sprang from the same stock as Augustine (*Letter* 26, §3).

Paulinus, however, writes in one and the same place that Alypius was Licentius’s brother by blood, whereas Augustine was his teacher in the sciences and the cultivator of his intellect. For this reason, Licentius, as a young man seeking more eagerly to flatter his teacher, may be understood to have spoken with poetic license, according to which the citizens of a single city are sometimes said to be born of one blood. This is what we have learned concerning Augustine’s family. As for his mother Monnica, a woman certainly worthy of every praise, a longer account must be devoted to her than can be included here.

## CHAPTER II

1. Augustine is enrolled among the catechumens.  
2. Seized by illness in childhood, he asks for Baptism.  
3. As a little boy, he calls upon God not to be beaten at school.  
4. Sent to school to learn letters, he loves Latin.  
5. He hates Greek.  
6. The faults of his childhood.

### 1

As soon as that most holy and excellent woman had given birth to her child, she had nothing more at heart than to have him enrolled among the catechumens, marked with the sign of the cross of Christ, and seasoned with mystical salt (*Confessions*, book 1, ch. 11, §17). This rite of initiating a catechumen, retained among the solemn ceremonies of Baptism, is still observed with the greatest reverence.

From this it is clear that Augustine professes that the Christian religion had been implanted in him as a little boy by his parents, and that he had been a Christian Catholic before he fell into the errors of the Manichaeans (*On the Usefulness of Believing*, §2). As a child he had already heard of the eternal life promised to us through the mystery of the Incarnation of our Lord and God, who came to heal our pride by his humility (*Confessions*, book 1, ch. 11, §17).

Thus even then he believed in Christ, as did his mother and the entire household, with the sole exception of his father. Yet his father’s wicked counsels and exhortations were never able to overcome in his heart the authority of his mother’s piety. Moreover, the most sweet name of Jesus Christ, which he had imbibed together with his mother’s milk, became so deeply fixed in his tender heart that no enticements of eloquence, however fluent and polished, could wholly carry him away unless they were seasoned with the sweetness of that name (*ibid.*, book 3, ch. 4, §8).

### 2

Thus imbued with this faith from his earliest years, the little boy gave a noble proof of it when, seized by a sudden and extremely violent attack of stomach trouble, so severe that he seemed almost at the point of death, he demanded Baptism from his most devout mother with all the fervor of faith and mind of which he was capable. She hastened to ensure that he might be washed as soon as possible in the sacred font.

But when the force of the illness meanwhile subsided, his prudent mother thought that Baptism ought to be postponed to another time, fearing that, through the instability of the years that lay ahead, he might defile himself with new sins and incur a much greater guilt by violating the sanctity of the saving bath. Augustine, however, does not approve this postponement sufficiently:

> How much better it would have been if I had been healed quickly, and if, through the diligence of my family and of myself, it had been arranged that the salvation of my soul, once received, would be kept safe under your protection, you who would have granted it!

(*Confessions*, book 1, ch. 11, §§17–18.)

### 3

In addition to the excellent instruction he received from his mother, he also learned from certain devout people whom he encountered as a child that God—as far as he could understand about him at his age—was some great being who, even though he was not visible to our senses, could hear us and come to our aid.

Accordingly, he addresses God as follows:

> As a boy I began to ask you for help and refuge, and at your invocation I broke the knots of my tongue. As a little boy I asked you, not with little feeling, not to be beaten at school. Yet we were sinning, because we wrote, read, or thought about our lessons less than was required of us. For memory and intelligence were not lacking, Lord—those which you wished us to possess in sufficient measure for that age—but we delighted in play; and punishment was inflicted upon us by those who themselves were doing such things. The trifles of adults are called business; but when boys do such things, though they are the same, adults punish them. I was sinning by acting against the commands of my parents and teachers. For I could later have made good use of the letters they wanted me to learn, whatever their intentions may have been. I was not disobedient because I chose something better, but because I loved to play.

(*ibid.*, ch. 9, §§14–15; ch. 10, §16.)

### 4

Both parents ardently desired that he should become skilled in letters and polished in the liberal arts. His father desired this because, being almost forgetful of God, he formed empty hopes for himself concerning his son; his mother, because she believed that the study of learning and the best arts would bring him great assistance in attaining God (*ibid.*, book 2, ch. 3, §8).

Therefore, since he had quickly shown evidence of his talent, he was entrusted to a schoolmaster to be instructed in the first elements of letters, through which one learns to read, write, and count (*ibid.*, book 1, ch. 9, §14). When his age permitted, he was sent to the neighboring city of Madaura to acquire literary learning and the art of public speaking (*ibid.*, book 2, ch. 3, §5).

Yet the difficulties inherent in the first rudiments of letters discouraged the boy’s mind, although he excelled in talent and memory. He especially disliked those lessons in which the rules of writing, reading, and counting were taught, even though they bring far more practical benefit than what are considered the more honorable and extensive branches of learning (*ibid.*, book 1, ch. 13, §§20–21).

Later, however, when he had emerged from these difficulties, he applied himself with somewhat greater enthusiasm to Latin literature. This was either because, from his earliest childhood, he had acquired some familiarity with it amid the caresses of his smiling nurse, or because he was especially delighted by the inventions of poets and by the stories with which all the noblest authors of the Roman language filled their books.

He repeatedly read of Dido’s death, not without tears, and would have been extremely displeased if this reading had been forbidden him. Yet although his delight in such things made him wretched, it was for that very reason that he was called a boy of good promise (*ibid.*, ch. 16, §26):

> What, he says, is more wretched than a wretch who does not pity himself, mourning the death of Dido, which happened because she loved Aeneas, but not mourning his own death, which happened because he did not love you, O God, light of my heart? And yet at school he was loudly applauded above many of his contemporaries and fellow pupils. I did not love you, and I fornicated away from you, while the sound of applause rose all around me: “Well done! Well done!” For friendship with this world is fornication away from you, and “Well done! Well done!” is said so that a man may be ashamed if he is not such.

(*ibid.*, ch. 13, §21; ch. 17, §27.)

### 5

Although the Greeks are exceptionally skilled at weaving tales, he was nevertheless very far removed from the language itself because of its foreignness, and he rejected Homer altogether, despite the poet’s amusing ravings that entertain the mind.

The boy was driven by harsh terrors and punishments to learn Greek letters. But since little progress is made in a subject one undertakes unwillingly, Augustine admits that he acquired only a slight knowledge of these letters. He also does not conceal that, because of his lack of this language, he and his fellow Africans were unequal to reading books written in Greek on the divine Trinity (*On the Trinity*, book 3, §1).

Yet he made such successful use of whatever small knowledge of Greek he had acquired that, unless he had himself professed, out of his native modesty, to be unlearned in it, he might have appeared thoroughly educated in Greek literature. For he read Epiphanius’s *Commentary on Heresies*, or at least its abridgment, which had not yet been translated into Latin. He then read through the books of other Greek Fathers, from which he drew quite a number of testimonies against heretics. Finally, the frequent interpretation of Greek words found throughout his shorter works, together with the restoration of many passages of Scripture through comparison of Greek manuscripts with Latin ones, can serve as evidence that Augustine knew Greek by no means poorly.

### 6

He acknowledges that his life at that age was not free from just reproach: he was carried away into vanities and went out from his God; he was more afraid of committing a grammatical barbarism than he was careful not to envy those who committed none. Nevertheless, he was praised in such studies by those whose approval at that time constituted, for him, honorable living.

The holy man does not pass over in silence the other errors of his childhood. Yet there is nothing in them especially remarkable or contrary to the ordinary behavior of boys that should detain us.

## CHAPTER III

1. He returns home from Madaura and spends a year away from study.  
2. From leisure he falls into debauchery.  
3. He binds himself to theft.

### 1

These are roughly the matters Augustine reports about himself up to the completion of his fifteenth year, that is, apparently, up to the school holidays of the year 369.

Then, returning from Madaura to Thagaste, he spent his sixteenth year—the year 370 after the restoration of salvation—in his father’s house, his studies being interrupted for the time while funds were gathered for a more distant journey. For Patricius, eager for his son’s glory and endowed more in spirit than in wealth, intended to send him to the academy at Carthage.

Everyone at that time praised Patricius enthusiastically because he generously provided his son with the expenses necessary to continue his studies in that distant city, beyond what his domestic means allowed. None of his fellow citizens, although they were much wealthier, devoted as much care and effort to advancing the studies of their children.

Yet he was not equally concerned that his son should progress, as his age advanced, in the fear of God and in the practice of chastity. His sole aim was that the boy should become eloquent and polished, accomplished and persuasive (*Confessions*, book 2, ch. 3, §5). Indeed, although he ought to have restrained him with measured severity according to the dictates of prudence and gentleness, he allowed him free rein in games and amusements, and, by granting him liberty and license beyond all measure, let him rush headlong in obedience to various unbridled desires (*ibid.*, §8).

### 2

During this period, while he was free from every school and wasting away in idleness, he began to experience the goads of shameful lust and, like almost all idle adolescents, to suffer the tyrannical servitude of pleasure. These thorns suddenly grew so high that they rose above his head, and there was no healing hand to pull them out.

Indeed, his father once happened to see him in the baths, already reaching puberty, and, as though he hoped shortly to have grandchildren from his son’s marriage, happily reported this to Monnica. Patricius had not long before been a catechumen; but his wife, more advanced in piety, sprang up in agitation, trembling with fear and holy alarm lest the young man should plunge into depravity.

She therefore took him aside and warned him with profound concern to shun obscene loves, and especially the violation of another man’s marriage bed. But he regarded these admonitions—which had certainly been given to him by God through a woman—as womanish advice, and thought it disgraceful to obey them.

He was rushing headlong with such blindness that, among his contemporaries who openly boasted of their debaucheries and gloried in them all the more brazenly the more shameful they were, he was ashamed to be judged guilty of lesser disgrace. Whenever he lacked something by which he might equal the most depraved, he pretended that he had committed that very thing as well, lest, being more chaste and innocent, he should be considered more abject and contemptible (*ibid.*, §§7–8).

He himself deplores at length the filth of the conduct in which he meanwhile lay. It was then, as he says, that he burned to be sated with the depths of hell (*ibid.*, ch. 1, §1).

Nor does he complain only of the excessive license granted to him. He also complains that, after his mother had heard her husband’s report mentioned above, she thought it sufficient merely to give him warnings concerning the observance of chastity, and did not take care to restrain the pestilential and more dangerous lust of the future by imposing the bridle of lawful marriage, if it could not be cut out to the quick.

Yet his parents’ only concern was that he should learn the art of speaking and persuading well. They feared that, if their son were then bound by the ties of marriage, all the hopes they had conceived for him would vanish.

At the very beginning of his adolescence, as he himself writes, he asked God for chastity, but with a foolish and ambiguous prayer:

> I had said, “Give me chastity and continence, but not yet.” For I feared that you might hear me too quickly and heal me too quickly from the disease of lust, which I preferred to be satisfied rather than extinguished.

(*Confessions*, book 8, ch. 7, §17.)

### 3

During the same period, while he was spending his idle leisure at home, he had joined the company of several depraved and equally idle young men. He remembers being led by them into an association in theft, which he confesses that he committed solely out of contempt for justice and as though from an accumulation of aggravated iniquity. In this theft he sought nothing but theft itself and preferred to enjoy the shamefulness of the vice rather than any profit.

> There was a pear tree, he says, near our vineyard, heavily laden with fruit that was attractive neither in appearance nor in taste. To shake it and carry it off, we most wicked young men went out in the dead of night, after we had prolonged our games in the playing fields in the customary manner of pestilence. We carried away enormous loads, not for our own feasts, but to throw to the pigs; and even if we ate some of it, our purpose was simply that we might do what was forbidden because it was forbidden.

(*ibid.*, book 2, ch. 4, §9.)

Considering before God what the inclination of his mind had been in so wicked a theft, he says:

> There was laughter, as though my heart were being tickled by the thought that we were deceiving those who did not think we would do such things, and who vehemently opposed them. I would not have done it alone—not at all alone. I would not have enjoyed doing it alone, nor would I have done it. O friendship excessively hostile, unfathomable seduction of the mind; eagerness to harm arising from play and jest, and appetite for another’s loss; no desire for my own profit, no desire for revenge, but simply when someone says, “Come, let us do it,” and one is ashamed not to be shameless!

(*ibid.*, ch. 9, §17.)

## CHAPTER IV

1. While studying rhetoric at Carthage, he recoils from the corrupt behavior of the students.  
2. There he is seized by impure love.  
3. He exercises some restraint in it.  
4. He has Adeodatus by a concubine.  
5. Adeodatus’s remarkable talent and premature death.

### 1

Having obtained the necessary travel funds, he went to Carthage to complete his literary studies. There he was supported not only by the money his father had prepared for this purpose, but also by the resources of Romanianus, a leading citizen of Thagaste, who received the poor young man going abroad for study with lodging, financial support, and—what was more—with goodwill (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §3).

In this school of eloquence he immediately took first place, and he triumphed with no little pride and elation of mind. Nevertheless, he behaved more moderately than the other students and recoiled from their insane license. They brazenly displayed the name “Overturners,” which had rightly been imposed upon them as a mark of infamy, as though it were a badge of urbanity (*Confessions*, book 3, ch. 3, §6).

Their foul and intemperate license advanced so far that they boldly thrust their brazen faces into the classrooms of other teachers and, once inside, disrupted with a kind of furious impudence the order established by the masters for the progress of the students. In their extraordinary stupidity and disgraceful frenzy they committed many such insults, acts that certainly deserved punishment under the laws, had custom not approved them as their patron (*ibid.*, book 5, ch. 8, §14).

> Among them, Augustine says, I lived with an impudent sense of shame, because I was not like them. I was with them, and I sometimes enjoyed their friendship, although I always recoiled from their conduct—that is, from the disturbances with which they insolently attacked the modesty of strangers, gratuitously mocking it and thus feeding their malicious pleasures.

(*ibid.*, book 3, ch. 3, §6.)

Among these companions, therefore, while still weak in age, he studied books of eloquence. He desired to excel in it, inflamed by that perverse and unhappy ambition which labors solely for glory and places its more substantial joys in the windy breath of human vanity (*ibid.*, ch. 4, §7).

These studies led him directly to the forum, which he already regarded as his goal, so that, once famous there, he might acquire greater glory for himself by becoming better able to defend falsehood even when truth had been suppressed. “Such,” he says on this subject, “is the blindness of men who even glory in their blindness!” (*Confessions*, book 3, ch. 3, §6.)

### 2

But why should we pass over in silence what he previously committed to memory in that same book of his *Confessions* as disgraceful matters concerning himself? A singular humility of spirit impelled the holy man to confess publicly, before everyone, even those things that can scarcely be read without shame.

> I came to Carthage, he says—which seems to have occurred toward the end of the year 370—and everywhere around me roared the frying-pan of shameful loves. I did not yet love, but I loved to love, and from a deeper need I hated myself for being less needy. I also fell into the love in which I desired to be caught.

This does not seem to refer to the love of anyone other than the woman whom he took as the sole companion of his bed, for he immediately continues:

> My God, my mercy, with how much bitterness you made that sweetness for me, and how good you were to sprinkle it with bitterness! For I was both loved and came secretly to the bond of enjoyment, and I was happily bound in painful chains, so that I might be scourged by the burning iron rods of jealousy, suspicion, fear, anger, and quarrels.

(*ibid.*, ch. 1, §1.)

Thus the faithful mercy of God hovered from afar over the sinner and scourged him in all his evil deeds.

> I dared, he says, even amid the solemn celebration of your festivals, within the walls of your Church, to desire and undertake the business of procuring the fruits of death. For this you scourged me with grievous punishments—but they were nothing compared with my guilt.

(*ibid.*, ch. 3, §5.)

Theatrical spectacles, to which he was devoted beyond measure and in which he saw the images of his lusts represented, increasingly weakened his character (*ibid.*, ch. 2, §2).

Many years later, in a public sermon that he delivered at Carthage, he confessed that he had led an especially wicked life in that city and that he had once been among those whom the Apostle calls foolish and unbelieving, rejected for every good work (*Exposition on Psalm* 36, sermon 3, §19).

### 3

Nevertheless, although stained by those impurities of desire, he wished to appear an elegant and cultivated young man. Such was the natural beauty of virtue that even those who scarcely practice it most eagerly desire to display its appearance.

> Though foul and dishonorable, he says, I was eager to be elegant and cultivated, with an abundance of vanity.

(*Confessions*, book 3, ch. 1, §1.)

He was certainly naturally disposed to every kind of urbanity, and therefore, even while studying eloquence at Carthage and though captivated by a shameful love, he was nevertheless regarded as a cultivator of decency.

There is an illustrious testimony to this in the words of Vincentius, bishop of the Rogatists in that same city, in a letter that he wrote to Augustine when Augustine was already a bishop. He praises him in these words:

> Since I know very well that, although you were still far removed from the Christian faith and were formerly devoted to literary studies, you were a cultivator of tranquility and decency.

(*Among Augustine’s Letters*, letter 93, §51.)

The young man had not, in fact, cast off all shame so thoroughly that he took pleasure in being polluted everywhere by indiscriminate and promiscuous love. Rather, even in immoderate lust he maintained a certain restraint, content with what at that time did not seem unbecoming in a man who had not yet professed the Christian religion.

He remained attached to one concubine, preserving toward her a fidelity of the bed not unlike that of marriage. He had taken her during the first year of his stay at Carthage and did not allow himself to be separated from her until Milan, when he began to consider taking a wife. She, however, after returning to Africa, bound herself by a vow of perpetual continence (*Confessions*, book 6, ch. 15, §25).

Nevertheless, through his own unhappiness Augustine experienced the difference between the sacred covenant of marriage, which is entered into for the begetting of children, and the pact of lustful love, in which offspring is born even against the wishes of the parents, although, once born, it may compel love from those who did not want it.

### 4

Perhaps in the second year of his stay in that city, he had a son by her, whose name was Adeodatus. That he was born in the year 372, when Augustine was eighteen years old, is established by the fact that in the year 387, when Augustine was initiated into the Christian sacraments during the Easter season, Adeodatus was approximately fifteen years old (*ibid.*, book 9, ch. 6, §14).

### 5

Augustine acknowledges that he had contributed nothing to him except sin. Yet God had heaped upon him splendid gifts and endowed him with talent so precocious that, at fourteen or fifteen years of age, he already surpassed many serious and learned men.

As early as the year 386, the boy appeared to his father to offer the greatest promise. Augustine already admitted him to those learned conversations that he was accustomed to hold with his friends. Once, when the question was raised as to who possessed God within himself and each person had expressed an opinion on the matter, Adeodatus declared that it was the person who did not have an unclean spirit.

Monnica preferred this answer to all the others. When Augustine asked him the following day to explain the statement—perhaps the boy had spoken with a somewhat calmer and purer spirit—he replied:

> It seems to me that the person who does not have an unclean spirit is the one who lives chastely.

When his father pressed him and asked whom he called chaste—whether someone who committed no sin, or someone who merely abstained from unlawful intercourse—he answered:

> How can someone be chaste who merely abstains from unlawful intercourse while continuing to defile himself with other sins? The truly chaste person is the one who attends to God and holds fast to him alone.

This pleased Augustine so much that he judged the boy’s very words should be written down (*On the Blessed Life*, §§12, 18).

He likewise testifies that all the statements attributed to Adeodatus in the book *On the Teacher* were his own thoughts, although he was then only sixteen years old. He adds that he experienced in this boy many things even more worthy of admiration, and that his intelligence filled him with awe (*Confessions*, book 9, ch. 6, §14).

Adeodatus was initiated into the sacrament of regeneration together with his father Augustine. Augustine then took his son, now of the same age as himself in the grace of Christ, into the community of the holier life he had undertaken, so that he might increasingly imbue him with the precepts of Christian discipline.

Adeodatus was present when Monnica was dying at Ostia on the Tiber. When she had breathed her last, he suddenly burst into a cry of mourning; but, immediately restrained by the words of those standing by, he fell silent (*ibid.*, ch. 12, §29).

When his father returned to Africa, the son crossed over with him. He plays his part in the book *On the Teacher*, which Augustine published in Africa.

God took him from the earth prematurely, though he was already mature for heaven in his youth. Hence his father says:

> I remember him with greater security, fearing nothing for his childhood, his adolescence, or indeed for that human being at all.

(*ibid.*, ch. 6, §14.)

Augustine meant that he could recall that Adeodatus had never violated the sanctity of the Baptism he had received.

## CHAPTER V

1. Deprived of his father, Augustine is supported at Carthage by his mother’s resources and Romanianus’s assistance.  
2. After reading Cicero’s *Hortensius*, he is inflamed with the pursuit of wisdom.  
3. He disdains the sacred Scriptures because of their humbler style.  
4. By his own talent he grasps Aristotle’s Categories and all the liberal arts.

### 1

From the age of seventeen, which corresponded to the year 371 from the restoration of salvation, Augustine was already deprived of his father. This was a great loss for the young man, and he seemed to have been brought into the open ruin of both his studies and, indeed, his fortunes.

Nevertheless, such was Monnica’s greatness of spirit that, devotedly concerned for her son’s progress, she continued to support him at Carthage by whatever means she could. Augustine therefore says that his eloquence had been purchased with his mother’s wages (*Confessions*, book 3, ch. 7, §7).

At that time Romanianus also supplied part of the expenses. He did not cease to support and console the sorrowful orphanhood of the outstanding young man through goodwill, advice, and resources.

> When you had been deprived of your father, Augustine says, you consoled me through friendship, encouraged me through exhortation, and assisted me with your resources.

(*Against the Academics*, book 2, §3.)

### 2

He had reached his nineteenth year in the year 373, when, following the customary course of study, he came upon Cicero’s book entitled *Hortensius*, which contained an exhortation to wisdom (*Confessions*, book 3, ch. 4, §7; book 6, ch. 11, §18; *Soliloquies*, book 1, §17).

Although that book united the highest eloquence with admirable learning, Augustine did not read it in order to hunt for verbal ornament. Setting aside concern for style, he directed his mind solely toward its subject matter and ideas.

Through reading that book he began to burn with such a desire for wisdom that, compared with that passion, he cast away and despised every mortal hope. He had already begun to rise in order to return to God.

> How I burned, my God, how I burned to fly back from earthly things to you! Yet this one thing cooled the ardor of that flame: the name of Christ was absent from Cicero’s exhortation. For this name, Lord, this name of my Savior, your Son, my tender heart had drunk in, by your mercy, together with its mother’s milk, and it held it deeply. Whatever lacked this name, however learned, polished, and truthful it might be, did not wholly carry me away.

(*Confessions*, book 3, ch. 4, §8.)

### 3

For this reason he resolved to turn his attention to the sacred Scriptures, to discover what they were like. But here he was offended by that simplicity which was impenetrable to great and lofty minds and, in his judgment, unworthy of comparison with the dignity of Cicero.

At that time he was not yet capable of descending to the humility by which access to those Scriptures is opened. He disdained to be little, and, swollen with pride, seemed great to himself (*ibid.*, ch. 5, §9).

### 4

The more readily and acutely he grasped all the sciences without any assistance from a teacher, the more violently he was carried toward arrogance.

At approximately twenty years of age he encountered Aristotle’s *Categories*. He had heard them commended with such extravagant displays of language by his Carthaginian teacher of rhetoric and by others who were regarded as learned that he eagerly wished to read them as something great and divine.

Yet when he read them alone, he understood them so thoroughly that, after conversing with those who had scarcely learned the same works from highly skilled teachers, through oral explanation and diagrams drawn in the dust, he received from them nothing beyond what he had discovered by his own talent.

Nevertheless, he suffered no small harm from this reading because of the false conception of God that he absorbed into his mind.

As time went on, he likewise read all the books of the liberal arts that came into his hands. Whatever he was able to read concerning the power of speaking and disputing, whatever concerned geometry, and whatever concerned music and numbers, he understood by himself, with ease, without anyone teaching him.
