Consequently, he did not realize how difficult those arts were for even the most studious and talented people to grasp—except when he tried to explain them to others. Among them, the most outstanding was whoever followed him as he explained no more slowly.

> You know, my Lord God, that both the quickness of understanding and the sharpness of discernment are your gift; but I did not sacrifice to you because of them. Therefore they benefited me not for use, but rather for destruction.

(*ibid.*, book 4, ch. 16, §§28–30.)

## CHAPTER VI

1. He falls into the heresy of the Manichaeans.  
2. He entices several of his close associates into it.  
3. Among the Manichaeans he remains in the rank of the hearers.  
4. He listens to them for nine full years.  
5. Monnica mourns the fall of her son and is divinely commanded to hope for his salvation.

[Column 0076]

1. When Augustine, already ardently desirous of wisdom but not knowing where to turn in order to attain it, was intercepted by the Manichaeans—a kind of men arrogantly delirious, carnal and talkative, but otherwise displaying an appearance of piety (Confessions, book 3, chapter 6, no. 10)—it is not relevant here to recount the monstrous, or rather incredible, ravings of these heretics, which are sufficiently known from the holy Doctor’s writings against them. But, as regards the matter undertaken here, it will be useful to learn from Augustine himself by what arts they enticed and entangled in their heresy and society a young man endowed with outstanding intelligence.

Above all, they captivated minds by promising that they would teach the truth, accusing the Catholic Church chiefly on the ground that it commanded faith rather than teaching. Augustine testifies that he was deceived by this hope alone, because he was eager to discover the truth and because, in the innate swelling of his mind, he regarded as old wives’ tales whatever had not been established by reasoning:

> What else, then, compelled me for nearly nine years, after spurning the religion implanted in me as a boy by my parents, to follow and diligently listen to those men, except that they said we were terrified by superstition and commanded to believe before reasoning, whereas they pressed no one to faith unless the truth had first been examined and disentangled? Who would not have been ensnared by such promises, especially a young mind eager for truth, proud and talkative because of the disputations of certain learned teachers at school? Such was the person they found me then: one who despised those things as childish tales and desired to grasp and drink in the open and sincere truth they promised (On the Usefulness of Believing, no. 2).

No less alluring to him was the appearance of piety and the conspicuous dignity of continence that the Manichaeans falsely displayed. In their mouths were the devil’s snares, and mistletoe fashioned from the mingling of the syllables of your name, Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit, our Paraclete and Consoler. These names did not depart from their mouths, but only as sound and the clatter of the tongue; otherwise their heart was empty of truth. They said, “Truth, truth,” and they said it often to Augustine, but nowhere was it in them (Confessions, book 3, chapter 6, no. 10).

Indeed, the opinion is almost implanted in our minds that virtue and truth are bound together by a close relationship, and that truth cannot be absent where the virtue of chastity shines forth. Hence Augustine writes that there are two principal lures of the Manichaeans by which the unwary are deceived into wishing to have them as teachers: the first, when they display the image of a chaste and remarkable continence of life; the second, when they criticize the Scriptures, either because they themselves misunderstand them or because they wish them to be misunderstood (On the Morals of the Catholic Church, book 1, no. 2).

What the heretics uttered against the genealogy of Christ the Lord as described by Matthew and Luke also deeply disturbed him. Since, still inexperienced and unskilled in the sacred Scriptures, he could not extricate himself from their objections, he readily fell into their opinion. Concerning this there survives the following sincere confession, delivered by him in a sermon to the people:

> I speak to you as one who was once deceived, when, as a boy, I first wished to bring to the divine Scriptures the acuteness of disputation rather than the piety of inquiry. I myself, by my perverse ways, was closing the door of my Lord against myself, when I ought to have knocked so that it might be opened; I added [my own efforts] so that it might be closed. For in my pride I dared to seek what no one can find unless he is humble. These things disturbed me, and now, secure in the name of the Lord, I set them before you (On the Harmony of Matthew and Luke in the Construction of Christ’s Genealogy) and explain them (Sermon 51, no. 6).

The Manichaeans also commonly disparaged the Scriptures of the Old Testament, and especially by that disparagement mocked and deceived the weak and the simple, who could not find how to answer them (On Genesis against the Manichaeans, book 1, no. 2).

Furthermore, the difficulty that he experienced in discovering the origin of evil, especially the evil with which we are here concerned, led him into this heresy (Confessions, book 3, chapter 7, no. 12). For his mind, wearied by this inquiry, when no light shone upon it, was easily induced to assign to evil a true and eternal principle, contrary to God as the principle of good alone, together with those insane deceivers. Lacking the support of knowledge, he could not withstand their sophistical arguments when they asked him where evil came from.

2. After Augustine had enrolled himself among the Manichaeans, nothing was more important to him than to saturate his mind fully with the teachings and institutions of the heresy he had adopted. He therefore listened to them assiduously, investigated all their fictions with curiosity, and rashly placed his faith in them. Indeed, he also urgently persuaded others to accept whatever he could and defended it stubbornly and passionately against others.

Nor was success lacking for his counsels and rash efforts. He later mournfully acknowledged that he had devastated the Catholic faith with the most wretched and frenzied loquacity (On the Gift of Perseverance, no. 53). He tormented many ignorant people with the frivolous subtleties of questions (Confessions, book 3, chapter 12, no. 21), and deceived many of his friends. Among them he entangled especially Alypius, whom we shall often mention below, and Romanianus, his Maecenas, in the same errors. He finally reconciled and attached to the Manichaeans Honoratus as well—a man not yet a Christian, but ardently devoted to the discovery of truth, and one who strongly detested the Manichaeans (On the Usefulness of Believing, no. 2).

3. Nevertheless, from the association and intimacy that Augustine had formed with those heretics, he discovered that they were more eloquent in demolishing the opinions of others than firm in establishing their own (ibid.). This prevented him from adhering to them completely, so that he followed them cautiously and timidly and remained among the Auditors, which was their lowest rank and nearly the equivalent of the catechumens in the Church (Against the Letters of Petilianus, book 3, no. 20).

For he was not a presbyter of the Manichaeans, as someone later reproached him for being (ibid.), nor an Elect—that is, one initiated into their mysteries (Against Fortunatus, no. 3). Consequently, the crimes of which the Manichaeans were accused remained hidden from him, for these concerned the Elect. He had attended only their prayer, in which he had noticed nothing disgraceful except that they always turned toward the sun.

He had also heard that they received the Eucharist; but what they received and when they received it he did not know. Nevertheless, certain opponents attributed all the crimes of this sect to him, falsely supposing that the Manichaean catechumens or Auditors received their baptism.

Augustine had learned from the Catholic Church a distinctive observance of the solemnity of Easter. The Manichaeans celebrated that feast with almost no festivity, no vigils, no prolonged fast, and no more joyful ceremonial display (Against the Epistle of the Manichaean, no. 9). He often asked them the reason for this. But since, at roughly the same time, the Manichaeans celebrated the death of their own Manichaeus with great pomp, Augustine transferred to that observance the religious devotion and reverence with which he had been accustomed to honor holy Easter.

4. Since he found little support or firmness among the Manichaeans, he did not abandon the hopes and affairs of the world. He did not cease to be held by love of the world for as long as he followed them (On the Usefulness of Believing, no. 2).

He repeatedly testifies that he was devoted to the Manichaean sect for nine full years. Below we shall see that he departed from them at Milan only in the year 385. It must therefore be said that he fell into this heresy in the year 376.

Augustine himself testifies that during these nine years, while he listened to the Manichaeans, he was waiting for the arrival of Faustus (Confessions, book 5, chapter 6, no. 10). Faustus had already arrived when Augustine was in his twenty-ninth year (ibid., chapter 3, no. 3), in the year 383 of Christ. We must therefore count these nine years from the twentieth year of his life, the year 374 of Christ, and understand of these same years what he himself writes: that for nine years—namely, from his nineteenth year until his twenty-ninth year, when it was completed—he was deceived and deceived others (ibid., book 4, chapter 1, no. 1).

Thus it can be seen that when he first read Cicero’s *Hortensius*, in the nineteenth or twentieth year of his life, he fell into the Manichaean heresy. Nor did he immediately separate himself from them in his twenty-eighth or twenty-ninth year. Rather, he had grown thoroughly weary of them, and he followed them only so long as nothing better presented itself to him (ibid., book 5, chapter 7, nos. 12–13).

5. Monnica was struck by Augustine’s fall into so wicked a heresy with the deepest grief. The mother mourned her son’s departure from the faith no less than if she had carried him to the grave at a final funeral—indeed, all the more bitterly because she understood that immortal life surpasses mortal life, and that he seemed to have destroyed in himself its hope by the deadly wound of heresy:

> When my mother, your faithful servant, wept for me before you, she wept more than mothers weep over the bodily deaths of their children (ibid., book 3, chapter 11, no. 19).

With many tears she begged God for his conversion. She asked as many suitable people as she could find to speak with her son, refute his errors, and, instructing him in the doctrine of truth, recall him from falsehood.

But his arrogance, swollen by the novelty of this heresy, still made him excessively unteachable. Hence, when a certain holy bishop was asked by her to speak with her son, he refused, asserting that once Augustine had read the Manichaeans’ complete books, he would finally recognize their errors. When she persisted more and more, he said:

> Go away from me; as you live, it cannot be that the son of these tears should perish.

She received this answer as though it were a divine oracle (ibid., chapter 12, no. 21).

God also consoled her concerning her son’s salvation in several other ways, but especially through a dream. When she was exhausted with grief, she saw a radiant young man with a cheerful, smiling face approaching her. After asking the cause of her sorrow, he ordered her to be at peace and at the same time instructed her to look and observe that her son was standing with her in the same place.

When she had related this to her son, and he tried to apply the dream to himself, saying that the vision signified that his mother would one day be drawn into his opinion, she immediately replied without hesitation:

> No; for it was not said to me, “Where he is, there you are,” but, “Where you are, there he is” (ibid., chapter 11, no. 20).

He was more deeply moved by this spontaneous reply of his mother—who had not been disturbed by his attractive interpretation—than by the vision itself.

This occurred approximately nine years before Augustine emerged from the mire of the depths and the darkness of falsehood in which he lay. He often tried to rise, but was always plunged more deeply. We do not know whether these nine years, as some of the preceding ones, ended with the arrival of Faustus, before whom we do not read of any attempt on his part to emerge; or whether they ended at the time when he departed from the Manichaeans, in the year 385; or finally at the time when he was perfectly converted to God, namely, in the year 386.

## CHAPTER VII

1. At Thagaste Augustine teaches grammar, where he has Alypius as a pupil. 2. After the death of a friend he falls into the deepest grief and leaves Thagaste under the pressure of sorrow. 3. He returns to Carthage and teaches rhetoric there.

### 1

Augustine had perhaps returned to Thagaste when his mother had the dream mentioned above. He writes that, after this vision, she was so revived that she allowed him to live under the same roof and sit at the same table with her; shortly before, Monnica had begun to refuse this, so greatly did she abhor that heresy (Confessions, book 3, chapter 11, no. 9).

To this period, therefore, what he reports seems to belong: that, after returning to his homeland, he was received as a guest by Romanianus and was so honored by his friendship and familiar association that he seemed in the city of Thagaste to be his partner and sharer in honor and dignity (Against the Academics, book 2, no. 3).

He had undoubtedly reached the goal of his studies when he departed from Carthage, and those studies looked toward the contentious forum. We do not, however, read that he practiced as an advocate or applied his art to anything other than educating pupils. He therefore began to teach in his native city (Confessions, book 4, chapter 4, no. 7). Possidius writes that he taught grammar there (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1).

But since Augustine himself recalls that during those years he taught rhetoric (Confessions, book 4, chapter 2, no. 2), if this statement is interpreted according to the sequence of the narrative, he seems to have taught it at Thagaste. Nevertheless, there are weighty reasons that persuade us that this should be understood of Carthage, as we shall show below.

He certainly indicates the period in which he was teaching grammar when he writes that, like the prodigal son, he was excluded from the husks of the pigs which he had been feeding (ibid., book 3, chapter 6, no. 11). Immediately afterward he speaks of the fables of grammarians and poets, which Jerome also calls food for pigs or demons (Epistle to Damasus on the Prodigal Son).

The following passage, unless we are mistaken, belongs to the same context:

> We were both deceived and deceiving, false and deceiving in various desires; publicly through the teachings called liberal, but secretly under the false name of religion. Here we were proud, there superstitious, everywhere vain. In the former pursuit we followed the emptiness of popular glory, even to theatrical applause, contentious songs, contests for crowns of hay, the trivialities of spectacles, and the intemperance of lusts. In the latter we sought to be cleansed from these impurities with those who were called Elect and Saints. We brought them foods from which, in the workshop of their stomach, they fashioned angels and gods for us, through whom we might be liberated. I pursued and practiced these things with my friends, deceived by me and with me (Confessions, book 4, chapter 1, no. 1).

While he was teaching at Thagaste, Alypius was among his pupils—a young man of outstanding character and the greatest promise, descended from one of the leading municipal families of Thagaste. Augustine himself embraced him with exceptional affection because of the signs of virtue that already shone forth in him; and he says that he, in turn, was greatly loved by Alypius because Augustine seemed to him good and learned.

### 2

During this period, when a very dear friend—whose name he does not disclose—died, grief overwhelmed Augustine and compelled him to leave Thagaste for Carthage. He writes:

> During those years, when I had first begun to teach in the municipality where I was born, I had acquired a friend, exceedingly dear to me through our shared studies, my contemporary and blossoming with me in the flower of youth. He had grown up with me from childhood, and we had gone together to school and played together. But he was not yet my friend in the true sense, although even then he was dear to me as true friendship is dear; for friendship is not true unless you bind it together, Lord, among those who cleave to you through the love poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.
>
> Nevertheless, he was exceedingly sweet to me because our similar studies had kindled the bond between us. For I had turned him away from the true faith, which he did not yet hold as a youth in a genuine and profound manner, toward superstitious and pernicious fables, for which my mother mourned me. That man was already wandering with me in mind, and my soul could not exist without him.
>
> And behold, you were hanging over the backs of your fugitives, God of vengeance and fountain of mercies, who in marvelous ways turn us toward yourself. Behold, you took that man from this life when he had scarcely completed a year in my friendship, a friendship sweeter to me than all the sweetnesses of that life. Who can recount your praises, each person recounting what he has experienced in himself alone? What did you do then, my God, and how unfathomable is the abyss of your judgments?
>
> While he was suffering from fevers, he lay for a long time without consciousness in a deadly sweat. When his life was despaired of, he was baptized without knowing it. I did not care, for I presumed that what he had received from me would retain his soul rather than what was taking place in the body of one who did not know. But it was altogether otherwise: he was restored and saved.
>
> As soon as I was able to speak with him—for I was able as soon as he was able, since I did not leave him and we depended excessively upon one another—I tried to mock with him the Baptism he had received while his mind and senses were entirely absent, although he had since learned that he had received it. But he recoiled from me as from an enemy and, with marvelous and sudden freedom, warned me that if I wished to be his friend I should cease saying such things to him.
>
> I, astonished and confused, postponed all my emotions until he had recovered and was strong enough in health for me to deal with him as I wished. But he was taken away from my madness so that he might be preserved with you for my consolation. After a few days, while I was absent, the fever returned and he died.
>
> My heart was darkened by this grief, and whatever I looked upon was death. My homeland was a torment to me, and my father’s house an extraordinary unhappiness; and everything that I had shared with him, without him, had become a monstrous torture. Weeping alone was sweet to me and had succeeded my friend in the delights of my soul (Confessions, book 4, nos. 7–9).

He continues at greater length to describe the exceedingly bitter grief by which he was then struck. He was not unaware that his friend could be healed by God; but he had neither the will nor the ability to implore help, because when he thought of God, God was not for his mind something solid and firm, but an empty phantom (ibid., book 4, chapter 7, no. 12).

At last, excessive sorrow compelled him to change his place and return to Carthage:

> I fled from my homeland. My eyes sought him less where they were not accustomed to see him, and from the town of Thagaste I came to Carthage (ibid.).

There, time and the companionship of friends gradually softened his grief (ibid., chapter 8, no. 13).

### 3

It was not grief over his friend’s death alone that compelled him to leave Thagaste. Elsewhere he writes that he returned to Carthage for the sake of a more distinguished profession (Against the Academics, book 2, no. 3): either because he was moved by the desire to teach oratory there, whereas previously he had taught grammar at Thagaste; or because the profession of the same art in Carthage, a principal city, was more honorable than in Thagaste, an obscure municipality.

He made only Romanianus, his Maecenas, aware of and a participant in the plan he had undertaken and the hope he had conceived. Romanianus, moved by love for the homeland in which Augustine was then teaching, first tried to dissuade him from this decision. But when he could not overcome the young man’s desire, which was directed toward what seemed better, he changed from a dissuader into an assistant with remarkable benevolent moderation. He supplied him with the necessary means of travel; and the man who had fostered the cradle and, as it were, the nest of his studies there now supported the first efforts of one daring to fly (ibid.).

Thus Augustine came to Carthage to teach rhetoric there (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1), and he sold the art that conquers minds, himself conquered by the desire for profit and honor (Confessions, book 4, chapter 2, no. 2).

Yet he was not so led by gain and profit that he did not prefer, above these, to have good pupils, as they are commonly called “good,” since he could not endure the customary license of the students of Carthage (ibid., book 5, chapter 8, no. 14).

He taught the tricks of rhetorical art without trickery—not tricks by which they might bring an innocent person into danger of execution, but those by which they might sometimes free a guilty person from the snares of the courts (ibid., book 4, chapter 2, no. 2).

Thus, while Augustine himself was wavering on slippery ground, the faith that he displayed in that teaching shone like a spark in the densest smoke.

At Carthage he acquired distinguished pupils, especially the sons of his Maecenas, Romanianus: Licentius, namely, and, it seems, his younger brother. For Augustine calls the latter a boy when, together with Licentius, who was somewhat older, he is engaged in discussion (Against the Academics, book 2, nos. 16, 19).

We also find that Eulogius, a distinguished rhetorician of Carthage, used Augustine as his teacher in learning this art, which he was practicing in that city around the year 386 (On Care for the Dead, no. 13; the title is printed *De Curâ pro motuis gerendâ*).

Finally, Alypius, who had attended Augustine’s teaching at Thagaste, continued to listen to him at Carthage. Although, out of respect for his father, who happened to have some disagreement with Augustine, he had for a time refrained from attending his lectures, nevertheless he came into his lecture room, listened to him for a while, and then departed (Confessions, book 6, chapter 7, nos. 11–12).

It happened on one occasion that, while explaining a lesson, Augustine used an analogy drawn from the circus games and, taking the opportunity, unwittingly mocked with a biting jest those devoted to that madness. Alypius, infected by that plague, took the remark personally and believed that what Augustine had not said intentionally had been said about him alone.

Yet the honorable young man accepted this not as a reason to be angry with him but as a reason to love him more ardently. From then on he abstained from the circus and finally obtained from his reluctant father permission to use Augustine as his teacher. His only misfortune was that, deceived by the appearance of continence displayed by the Manichaeans, he became entangled in their superstition during this period.

## CHAPTER VIII

1. How greatly Augustine abhors magic. 2. He records something astonishing about Albicerius the diviner. 3. By attributing more than was proper to judicial astrology, he cannot be drawn away from it by Vindicianus and Nebridius. 4. Firminus unknowingly releases him from this error. 5. Books *On the Beautiful and the Fitting*, written to Hierius.

### 1

It was customary among the learned men of ancient times to announce a public prize and compete in verse before the people and in the theater. This exercise had been devised to foster the liberal arts, nourish studies, and sharpen and stimulate every outstanding talent through honorable rivalry.

Since this solemn contest was held at Carthage, Augustine decided to enter it, whether because of the office he had undertaken, or to display his talent, or to advertise his art. While he was considering this, a certain diviner sent word asking what payment Augustine wished to give him so that, through the diviner’s assistance, he might win.

But Augustine detested and abhorred those foul rites and replied that, even if the crown were golden and immortal, he would never permit a fly to be killed for the sake of his victory (Confessions, book 4, chapter 2, no. 3). He said this because, in those execrable sacrifices, the diviner was going to kill animals in order to invite demons to support Augustine with these impious honors.

Nevertheless, having rejected this superstition, Augustine won the agonistic crown by the strength of his talent. He writes that it was placed upon his head by the physician Vindicianus, then proconsul, although Augustine’s head was not sound.

From the order of narration that Augustine follows, we might refer this event to the period when he was teaching at Thagaste, were it not that Possidius clearly indicates that at Thagaste he taught only grammar (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1), and were it not established that Numidia, in which Thagaste was situated, was administered by a consular governor, not by a proconsul as Carthage was.

It should also be added that contests of this sort were more appropriate to principal cities. Augustine therefore seems, in these early chapters of the fourth book of the *Confessions*, to narrate without preserving the order of events and times, indiscriminately and in various places, things that happened to him from the nineteenth year of his life up to his twenty-eighth year, as he suggests at the beginning of the first chapter. Most of these events undoubtedly occurred after his return to Carthage, although no mention of that return appears before the seventh chapter of the same book.

### 2

During those years at Carthage he saw a man named Albicerius, celebrated for such skill in divination that, for this reason, he was consulted not only by the ignorant multitude but also by learned men.

Among other things Augustine records about this diviner something that, by its extraordinary character and magnitude, seems to surpass belief. One of Augustine’s students challenged him and petulantly asked Albicerius to declare what the questioner himself was silently turning over in his mind. Albicerius replied that he was thinking of a line of Virgil.

When the young man could not deny this, he went on to ask what the verse was. Although Albicerius had scarcely ever passed through a grammar school, he immediately recited the verse confidently and cheerfully.

Flaccianus, also a highly distinguished man who had served as proconsul in Africa, was considering the purchase of an estate and asked Albicerius whether he could reveal the plan he had formed concerning the matter. Albicerius immediately pronounced both the nature of the business and the name of the estate, although the matter was so absurd that Flaccianus himself scarcely remembered it.

Nevertheless, Flaccianus, a man of profound intelligence, ridiculed this kind of divination, attributing it to some most contemptible spirit. When that spirit inspired Albicerius, he was accustomed to give such answers, since demons possess sufficient acumen and subtlety even to perceive what has entered our memory.

For this reason Flaccianus exhorted those who spoke of this prophetic power to set their minds above that divination and strengthen them so that they might transcend the nature of those invisible spirits of the air.

It could be believed all the more readily that the whole thing was a demon’s sport because Albicerius was not only utterly ignorant of every branch of learning, but also infamous for crimes and every kind of disgrace. Even when he answered in agreement with the truth, he often hallucinated or went astray (Against the Academics, book 1, nos. 17–18).

### 3

Augustine did not abhor astrology, which is called judicial, as he abhorred magic. Since it employed no prayers for divination and sacrificed no victims, and seemed to him to be free from every commerce with demons and finally from every superstitious rite, he did not cease consulting those astrologers whom people once called mathematici. Christian and true piety, however, rejects and condemns this practice.

The familiar speech of such men was doubtless agreeable to the young man, for by it they greatly indulged wicked desires:

> From heaven comes the unavoidable cause of your sinning; Venus did this, or Saturn, or Mars. Thus man is without blame—flesh and blood and proud corruption—while the creator and arranger of heaven and the stars is to be blamed (Confessions, book 4, chapter 3, no. 4).

And since his talent was ready and agile in every discipline to which he applied himself, he seemed to have progressed so far in that frivolous art of divination that curious inquirers into future events sometimes consulted him as though he were highly skilled in it.

At that time Vindicianus was at Carthage. He was proconsul and, in that capacity, had placed the aforementioned crown upon Augustine (ibid., no. 5). He was an astute man, highly skilled and renowned in the medical art. Augustine describes him in these words:

> Consulted by someone, he ordered that something be applied to his pain which seemed appropriate at the time; after it was applied, health followed. Then, several years later, when the same bodily condition returned, he thought that this same remedy should be applied. After it was applied, the condition became worse. Astonished, the man returned to the physician and reported what had happened. But the physician, being an extremely shrewd man, replied: “You have received it badly because I did not order it.” Everyone who heard this and did not know the man well would have thought that he did not trust in medical skill but in some illicit power of an unknown kind. Later, when certain people who were astonished by this questioned him, he disclosed what they had not understood: namely, that by that age he would no longer have ordered that remedy (Letter 138, no. 3).

Such is Augustine’s account of Vindicianus. When Augustine had entered more deeply into this man’s friendship and, in conversation, disclosed his devotion to the books of the astrologers, Vindicianus left nothing undone to draw the young man away from that deceptive art. Kindly and paternally—for he was already well advanced in age—he urged him not to waste upon that vanity the care and effort necessary for useful things.

Vindicianus said that he himself had been so devoted to this empty study from his earliest youth that he had even considered making a living from it. But after exposing the fraud of the art, he had turned his attention to medicine, judging it unworthy to earn his livelihood by deceiving and misleading people.

Even so, he thought himself not unequal to learning that discipline, since he had read and understood without great difficulty the books of Hippocrates, which were extremely difficult to grasp. For that reason he thought Augustine should all the more abandon pursuits to which no necessity of maintaining his household compelled him, since rhetoric was available to him—a profession by which he could not only support his life but also increase his dignity.

Although Vindicianus’s speech was without verbal ornament, it was lively, pleasant, and weighty in its ideas. Augustine hung constantly and attentively upon his words, receiving with the impartial ears appropriate to the occasion everything that the venerable old man said—not merely as an adviser, but, more importantly, as an experienced teacher.

Yet one argument in particular prevented Augustine from abandoning his former opinion:

> What, then, would cause many true things to be foretold through it?

Vindicianus dissolved this objection as best he could by referring whatever element of divination there might be to a certain mysterious power of chance implanted in the nature of things.

If, when someone happened to consult the pages of a poet who was singing and intending something quite different, a verse often emerged that wonderfully agreed with the matter at hand, Vindicianus said that it was not astonishing if, through some higher impulse, the human soul—without knowing what was happening within it—should utter something not by art but by chance, something that harmonized with the affairs and actions of the person who was asking (Confessions, book 4, chapter 3, no. 5).

4. These things were undoubtedly impressed upon his mind by God’s will. Yet neither Vindicianus, that keen old man, nor Nebridius—especially dear to him and, as he himself describes him, “a wonderful young man in soul, very good and very cautious”—who ridiculed the entire art of divination, could then persuade him to abandon and reject his study of that art (Ibid., bk. 7, ch. 6, no. 8). Evidently, the authority of those who had practiced the art itself moved him far more than the opinion of those who condemned it without support from any certain arguments by which it might clearly appear to him that future events were sometimes foretold through the mere rashness of chance rather than through any definite reasoning based on the position and aspect of the stars (Ibid., bk. 4, ch. 3, no. 6).

Nevertheless, Vindicianus’s words remained fixed in his mind, obstinate and still resolute though it was; through them he was, as it were, initiated into a fuller inquiry by which he might one day free himself from error. He had already begun to incline toward Nebridius’s view. Nebridius did not indeed assert it emphatically, but repeatedly and again and again he said that there was no art of foreseeing the future, whereas human conjectures often possessed the force of chance: by saying many things, people predicted many future events, without knowing that they were doing so, but encountering them because they did not cease speaking.

At last, with God’s help, he rejoiced that he had been freed from all error more by chance than by deliberate purpose. This happened on the following occasion.

Firminus, a liberally educated man and by no means untrained in eloquence, though little versed in astrology, was nevertheless an extremely curious consulter of mathematicians. He came to Augustine as to a very dear friend, wishing to consult him about certain matters which were leading him to entertain great hopes of advancing fortune, and to ask what Augustine thought the outcome would be according to his configurations of the stars. Augustine did not refuse to disclose to Firminus what his conjecture suggested; yet he added that he was now almost persuaded that the whole business of prediction was mere emptiness and ridiculous folly.

Firminus then told Augustine that his father had in fact been passionately devoted to such books, and that he had a friend no less interested in them. They were so ardently devoted to these absurdities that they even observed the birth of animals born in their households [Col. 0086] and examined the position of the heavens at that moment, in order to collect the results of their art. Firminus said that he had heard from his father that, when his mother was pregnant with him, a maidservant of his father’s friend was also carrying a child. This could not escape the notice of her master, who observed even the births of his dogs with such precision. Thus it happened that when the one carefully investigated the day, hour, and moment of his wife’s delivery, and the other those of his maidservant’s, both women gave birth at precisely the same point in time. They were therefore compelled to record the same configurations of the stars, down to the same minute details, for the two newborn children: the one for his son, the other for a little slave.

For when the women began to give birth, both men informed each other of what was taking place in their respective homes and prepared messengers to send to one another as soon as the women had delivered. Firminus added that the messengers sent by each man met one another at such equal distances between the two houses that they could not record any different position of the stars or any different subdivisions of time at the births of the two infants.

And yet Firminus, born of noble family, was a man of great reputation among all; he grew daily richer in wealth and was advanced in honors. The other, however, remained under the yoke of his condition and served his masters without any relaxation of his slavery.

When Augustine had accepted these facts without hesitation, reported by a trustworthy witness, whatever doubt still remained in him vanished, and all his resistance dissolved and collapsed. First, he tried to draw Firminus away from that curiosity which the story he had told showed to be futile and ridiculous. Then, when the narration of this history had caused a great light to shine upon his mind for the complete exposure of the frauds of this art, he directed his attention especially to those who are born as twins.

Most twins, like Jacob and Esau, emerge from the womb one immediately after the other, so quickly that an astrologer cannot observe the interval of time or mark down different configurations of the stars for them. Yet their future lots are utterly unlike. But God, the most just and wisest governor of the universe, acts by a hidden impulse—while both those who consult and those consulted remain ignorant—so that, when each person consults, he hears what he ought to hear according to the hidden merits of souls, issuing from the abyss of God’s just judgment (Ibid., bk. 7, ch. 6, nos. 8–10).

Whether this conversation between Firminus and Augustine took place at Carthage or after Augustine had crossed into Italy is uncertain. It is beyond dispute that it occurred before his conversion; for he had not yet freed himself from all error, since he was still investigating the origin of evil (Conf. bk. 7, ch. 7, no. 11).

5. In the twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh year of his life he devoted himself to composing two or three books on the Beautiful and the Fitting (Ibid., bk. 4, ch. 15, no. 27). In these works he defined the Beautiful as that which is beautiful in itself, and the Fitting as that which, being adapted to something else, gives it grace (Ibid., no. 24). Since we love nothing except what is beautiful or becoming—for unless the things we love possessed beauty and form, they could in no way move us—he demonstrated that, in bodies themselves, one thing is like a whole and is therefore Beautiful, while another [Col. 0087] is fitting because it is suitably adapted to something else, as a bodily part is adapted to the whole body (Ibid., ch. 13, no. 20).

From there he turned also to the nature of the soul. But the false opinion about spiritual things that had been handed down to him by the Manichaeans prevented him from seeing the truth (Ibid., ch. 15, no. 24). These books had already been lost when he wrote his Confessions, and he himself no longer remembered how many he had written (Ibid., ch. 13, no. 20).

He had written them for Hierius, an orator of the city of Rome. Hierius had cultivated Greek literature with exceptional distinction, had become a remarkable teacher of Latin eloquence, and was at the same time the most renowned philosopher of his age. Augustine did not know him by sight, but loved him on account of his reputation for learning and the brilliance of his name. He had also heard certain words of his which had pleased him. Since, therefore, Augustine held Hierius in the highest esteem, he thought himself especially fortunate that his own writings might reach the notice of so great a man (Ibid., ch. 14, no. 21).

# CHAPTER IX

1. Augustine discovers the depraved morals of the Manichaeans.  
2. Constantius, one of their Auditors, attempts in vain to reform them and takes refuge in the bosom of the Catholic Church.  
3. Augustine also discovers their errors.  
4. Who and how great was that Faustus whom the Manichaeans praised so highly.  
5. Augustine detects his ignorance.  
6. After hearing Faustus, Augustine understands the weakness of the Manichaeans.

1. Although Augustine appeared to have joined the sect of the Manichaeans with great enthusiasm and to have labored no less zealously to defend and propagate it, he had not surrendered himself to it so completely that he did not sometimes distrust the doctrine handed down within it. That this suspicion soon arose in his alert mind is apparent even from the fact that, as we observed above (above, ch. 6, no. 3), he refused to pass beyond the rank of the Auditors. He later understood that his suspicion had been greatly strengthened and confirmed when he realized that the Manichaeans were more eloquent in refuting the doctrines of others than in asserting their own.

For he could not fail to see how easy it was for anyone of only moderate education to attack the errors of others with a great tumult of words. In this alone lay the whole strength of those heretics. By making it impossible to adhere to any opinion, they necessarily compelled people to pass over to their own position. “Thus,” Augustine says, “they treated us as treacherous bird-catchers do, who plant branches smeared with birdlime near water in order to deceive thirsty birds. They cover over and conceal, by whatever means they can, the other waters nearby, or even frighten the birds away from them by terrifying contrivances, so that the birds fall into their traps not by choice but through want” (On the Usefulness of Believing, no. 2).

Moreover, many serious causes combined to inspire him with disgust for the heresy he had embraced. None, however, moved him more powerfully than the fact that he had discovered the obscene conduct of the Manichaeans, conduct that deviated as far as possible both from the laws of Christ and from their own regulations.

“For nine whole years,” he says, “I listened to you with great care and diligence. I could not become acquainted with a single one of the Elect [Col. 0088] who, according to these precepts, had not either been caught in sin or at least subjected to suspicion. Many were found drinking wine and eating meat; many were found bathing in the public baths. But these things we merely heard. Some were proved to have seduced other women, so that in this matter I can have no doubt at all. Yet perhaps even this was more rumor than truth.

“I myself saw—not alone, but together with men some of whom had already been freed from that superstition and others whom I still desire to see freed—we saw, then, at a crossroads in Carthage, in a very crowded street, not one but more than three of the Elect together. As certain women passed by, they brayed after them with such wanton gestures that they surpassed the indecency and shamelessness of every street-corner libertine.

“That this arose from a widespread custom, and that they lived among themselves in this manner, was sufficiently evident: none of them feared the presence of his companions, and all, or nearly all, showed that they were infected with the same plague. They were not from a single household; rather, living in entirely different places, they had happened by chance to come down together from the place where their whole assembly had taken place.

“We were deeply shocked and made equally serious complaints. Who, then, judged that this ought to be punished—not, I do not say, by separation from the Church, but at least by a severe rebuke proportionate to the enormity of the crime? Their whole excuse for allowing such conduct to go unpunished was that, since their meetings were prohibited by public law at that time, they feared that the injured parties might expose them.

“The same answer was given to us when we brought before the leading men a woman’s complaint that, in a room where she was staying with other women, secure in the reputation of their holiness, several of the Elect had entered. One of them extinguished a lamp—it was uncertain which one—and in the darkness she had been assaulted and forced into a disgraceful act, unless she had escaped by raising an alarm. This crime, which was also well known to us, must surely have arisen from how widespread a custom? And this deed was committed on the very night on which your festive vigils are celebrated” (On the Morals of the Manichaeans, nos. 68–70).

As for the prohibition under which the Manichaeans were forbidden to hold assemblies, a law on the subject was issued by the emperor Valentinian in the year 372, although this ruler was by disposition so inclined that he readily left everyone free to choose and practice his religion.

“As for suspicions,” Augustine continues, “how many doors were opened when we found them envious, greedy, extremely eager for elaborate banquets, frequently engaged in quarrels, and highly excitable over trivial matters? Surely we did not think that they could restrain themselves from the things from which they professed to abstain whenever they found places of concealment and darkness.

“There were two men of fairly good reputation, of ready intellect, and among the leaders of their own disputations. They were more closely and familiarly connected with us than the others. One of them, who was attached to us more closely because of his liberal studies and is now said to be a presbyter there, bitterly envied the other. The second accused the first—not by an open charge, but in conversation with anyone who would listen and in whispers—of having violently assaulted the wife of a certain Auditor.

“The accused, while clearing himself, meanwhile charged before us another Elect with the same crime. That man lived with the same Auditor as though he were his most trusted friend. Since the Auditor had unexpectedly entered and found him with a woman, he said [Col. 0089] that the woman and her adulterer had been advised by that enemy and envious man to fabricate this false accusation against him, so that, if he exposed anything, he would not be believed.

“We were distressed and deeply troubled. Even if it was uncertain whether the woman had actually been assaulted, the bitter jealousy displayed between those two men—among whom we found no better in that community—was nevertheless unmistakable and compelled us to infer other things.

“Finally, we very often found Elect in the theaters, men serious both in age and, as they appeared, in character, together with an old presbyter. I say nothing of the young men whom we were accustomed to find quarreling over theatrical performers and charioteers. This is no small indication of how they can restrain themselves from secret sins when they cannot overcome the desire that displays and exposes them, blushing and fleeing, before the eyes of their own Auditors.

“Would that great crime have been exposed even in the case of that holy man to whose disputations we used to go in the street of the fig-trees, if he had been able to make a consecrated virgin merely a woman, and not also pregnant? But the hidden and incredible evil could not conceal the swelling womb. When the mother disclosed the matter to her young brother, he was deeply distressed, but was restrained from a public accusation out of respect for religion. He nevertheless succeeded in having the man expelled from that church—for who could have endured such a thing? And, so that the matter might not go entirely unpunished, he resolved, with the support of some friends, to beat the man to pieces with fists and kicks” (Ibid., nos. 71–72).

2. On this subject he further reports a particularly notable story, which had become so widely known that rumor carried it even to people who were absent and far away. It happened at Rome while Augustine was absent from that city. He learned the entire story from a trusted friend, a man of good faith who had witnessed it with his own eyes. Afterward, when Augustine came to Rome, several others related the same story to him in the same sequence, and he testifies that he found it wholly verified and established.

He himself relates it as follows:

“One of your Auditors”—he is addressing the Manichaeans—“who in that celebrated abstinence yielded nothing to the Elect, and who was both liberally educated and willing and accustomed to defend your sect at length, was extremely distressed because the utterly depraved conduct of the Elect, who lived scattered about in the worst manner and without discipline, was repeatedly thrown in his face whenever he argued with them.

“He therefore desired, if possible, to gather into his own house all those who were prepared to live according to those precepts and to support them at his own expense. For he was both no ordinary despiser of money and no ordinary possessor of it. He complained that his great efforts were obstructed by the dissolution of the bishops, whose assistance he needed in order to carry them out.

“In the meantime there was a certain bishop of yours, a man plainly—as I discovered for myself—rustic and unpolished, but somehow, precisely because of that hardness, seemingly stricter in guarding good morals. This Auditor seized upon him, long desired and finally present, and explained his wishes to him. The bishop praised and approved them; it was agreed that he himself should first begin living in the Auditor’s house.

“When this had been done, all the Elect who could be found in Rome gathered there. A rule of life was proposed from a letter of Mani. Many found it intolerable and departed; nevertheless, quite a few remained out of shame. Life began to be conducted as had been agreed and as so great an authority prescribed. Meanwhile, that Auditor compelled everyone vigorously to do everything, but no one to do anything he himself had not first undertaken.

“Before long, quarrels arose very frequently among [Col. 0090] the Elect. They accused one another of crimes, all of which the Auditor heard with groans, taking care that they did not expose themselves recklessly in their disputes. They exposed abominations and monstrous deeds. It became clear what sort of men they were—men who nevertheless thought that, among the rest, they ought to submit to the force of those precepts.

“What, then, was to be suspected—or rather judged—about the others? What more need be said? At last, compelled by circumstances, they began to murmur that those commands could not be endured, and then they rose in rebellion.

“The Auditor stated his case in the briefest terms: either all those commands had to be observed, or the man who had prescribed such things under conditions that no one could fulfill must be judged a complete fool. Nevertheless, the unrestrained tumult of the majority prevailed over the opinion of one man—for it could not have turned out otherwise.

“Afterward the bishop himself also withdrew and fled in great disgrace. It was reported that he had secretly taken food contrary to the rule, and had often been found doing so, since a considerable supply of money was available to him from his own purse, which he carefully kept hidden.

“If you say that these things are false, you are resisting matters that are too open and too widely known. But would that you said so! For since these things are manifest and easily known to those who wish to know them, it becomes clear how truthful those men customarily are who deny that these things are true” (On the Morals of the Manichaeans, nos. 74–75).

There can be no doubt that this Manichaean Auditor was Constantius. Augustine elsewhere writes that Constantius gathered very many Manichaeans into his house in order to compel them to fulfill the precepts of Mani. When those precepts seemed too severe, some dispersed in different directions; those who persevered in observing them separated from the other Manichaeans and formed a schism. Because they slept on mats, they were called the Mattarians (Against Faustus, bk. 5, ch. 5).

At last this Constantius embraced the Catholic faith. He was still alive when Augustine wrote against Faustus, around the year 404.

3. It was not only the scandalous conduct of the Manichaeans that offended Augustine; their doctrine itself also began to arouse suspicion in him, especially after he had heard Helpidius disputing against them openly and publicly at Carthage and producing several arguments from Scripture with which the Manichaeans had difficulty dealing.

They nevertheless answered as best they could, so that they would not appear to have abandoned their cause. But their very answer increased rather than removed the suspicion. They alleged that the Scriptures of the New Testament had been falsified by certain unknown corrupters of manuscripts who had thought fit to insert the laws of the Jews into Christian institutions. Yet, apart from the fact that they whispered this answer more secretly into the ears of their Auditors than they proclaimed it publicly, they produced no uncorrupted copy in which the passages charged with falsification did not actually appear (Conf. bk. 5, ch. 11, no. 21).

For this reason the answer appeared weak and futile not only to Augustine or Honoratus, but also to everyone who exercised somewhat greater care in judging than the multitude of believers (On the Usefulness of Believing, no. 7).

Above all, Augustine could not understand, given the Manichaean doctrine, why God had thrust souls into the bodies of mortals, which were subject to countless calamities. Since the sect’s adherents could not extricate themselves from this difficulty, [Col. 0091] Augustine writes that he was divinely admonished by it to renounce his error and turn to the faith of the Church (Against Fortunatus, disputation 2, no. 37).

This was Nebridius’s constant and most powerful argument, which by itself would have been sufficient to repel the error had Augustine paid sufficient attention. The keen young man asked the Manichaeans what that race of darkness—which they regularly set over against God as the principle of evil—would have done to God if God had not wished to fight against it.

If they answered that it would have inflicted some harm, God would be vulnerable and corruptible. But if they said that it could have done Him no harm, they supplied no reason for fighting, and especially not for fighting in such a way that a portion, member, or offspring of God’s very substance—namely, the soul—would be mingled with hostile powers and with natures not created by God, and would be so corrupted and changed for the worse by them that it would be transformed from blessedness into misery and require assistance by which it could be rescued and purified (Conf. bk. 7, ch. 2, no. 3).

He was also troubled by the fact that he had heard from someone that no substance was evil. Nor did that Manichaean leader remove this scruple from his mind—the leader who thought he had brilliantly solved the question by the following childish quibble:

“I should like,” he said, “to place a scorpion in a man’s hand and see whether he would not withdraw his hand. If he did so, he would be convicted not by words but by the fact itself that some substance is evil, since he would not deny that the animal is a substance.”

“Thus,” Augustine says, “he answered children in a childish manner. For who, being even moderately instructed and educated, would not see that these things cause harm through an incompatible bodily constitution, and again cause no harm through compatibility, often even conferring considerable benefits? For if that poison were evil in itself, it would first and more readily destroy the scorpion itself” (On the Morals of the Manichaeans, no. 11).

He had now reached the point at which he not only compared the teachings of the philosophers, by which he had diligently cultivated his mind, with the Manichaeans’ lengthy fables, but even preferred the former (Conf. bk. 5, ch. 3, no. 3).

As a perceptive man, he saw that the causes of the movements of the heavens, the equinoxes, the solstices, and finally the eclipses of the sun and moon were explained much better by the philosophers than by Mani, although Mani had raved at great length on the subject (Ibid., no. 6).

Although knowledge of these natural matters does not belong to the instruction of true piety, the fact that Mani was deceived or deceived others in this respect deprived him of all faith and authority in the remaining matters as well. A strong suspicion naturally arose that he was even more mistaken in dealing with matters remote from the senses, and that he was not equipped with true and sincere wisdom, since he rashly taught what he had not understood.

How much less could he be believed to be inspired by the divine Spirit—or, as he most of all wished to be regarded, to have the Holy Spirit personally residing in him with full authority (Ibid., ch. 5, no. 8)—when he blundered so disgracefully in matters accessible to anyone of moderate education that he seemed rather blinded than merely dim-sighted?

Meanwhile Augustine was commanded to believe him, even though the Manichaean fables in no way cohered with the explanations that Augustine had tested by his own reasoning [Col. 0092] and observation, but were in fact wholly at variance with them. Yet he had not sufficiently discovered whether, even according to Mani’s words, the alternations of longer and shorter days and nights, of night and day themselves, the eclipses of the heavenly lights, and whatever similar matters he had read in other books could be explained (Ibid., no. 9).

He therefore awaited with burning eagerness the arrival of Faustus, who was considered highly skilled in every honorable discipline and exceptionally learned in the liberal arts (Ibid., ch. 6, no. 10). The other Manichaeans were unequal to solving his questions, but they continually promised him Faustus, saying that upon his arrival and after a conversation with him, not only all the knots of astronomical matters but also any questions that might occur to his mind, even ones far more intricate than these, could be completely unraveled.

4. This Faustus was an African by race and a native of Milevis (Against Faustus, bk. 1, ch. 1), born of an obscure and impoverished father (Ibid., bk. 5, ch. 5). Having embraced the Manichaean sect, he obtained among them the title of bishop (Conf. bk. 5, ch. 3, no. 3).

He boasted that he had abandoned his father, mother, wife, children, and everything else that the evangelical law commands one to leave; that he had rejected gold and silver and carried no copper in his belts; that he was content with daily food, did not concern himself with the morrow, and was not anxious about where he would fill his stomach or cover his body. In short, he preached that he was poor, meek, peaceful, pure in heart, mourning, hungry, thirsty, and enduring persecutions and hatred for the sake of righteousness.

Yet Faustus’s softness was better known—especially to those who had associated with him intimately at Rome—than to require any lengthy refutation. His shamelessness was exposed by the delicate feathers on which he slept, the goatskins with which he covered himself, and all the abundance of luxuries by which he seemed to disdain not only the stricter discipline of the Mattarians but even the household of his own father, the poor man of Milevis.

As for that part of his empty self-praise in which he boasted that, because he had defended the truth, he had endured persecutions and hatred, it cannot be denied that certain pious men brought a charge of heresy against him. He was summoned to court and either convicted or confessed. Then, with Catholics themselves interceding on his behalf, he was sentenced to the mildest punishment merited by his conduct: he was deported, together with some of his associates, to an island by sentence of the African proconsul. Not long afterward, owing to the customary clemency of the emperors toward condemned persons in that period, he was recalled (Against Faustus, bk. 5, chs. 1, 5, 7, 8).

These events appear to have taken place around the year 386, when a great multitude of Manichaeans was ordered to plead its case before the proconsul Messianus and, as may be inferred, was condemned by him.

5. Just as Faustus did not stand out above the other Manichaeans for his morals, so he was not superior to them in doctrine and learning. He was ignorant of and unacquainted with all the liberal disciplines except grammar. Even in that field, in which he appeared to excel, he possessed nothing drawn from some hidden or esoteric branch of learning, but merely what he had taken [Col. 0093] from common sources.

Yet because he had read and reread several speeches of Cicero, only a very few books of Seneca, some works of the poets, and anything elegantly and ornamentally written by authors of his own sect, he had acquired through constant use and practice a considerable facility of speech. This made him all the more suited to deceiving the unwary, since his eloquence was accompanied by great moderation of spirit and a certain natural charm (Conf. bk. 5, ch. 6, no. 11).

Although he had taken up the art of speaking rather late, he was nevertheless keen and shrewd by nature (Against Faustus, bk. 21, ch. 10), with a face composed to modesty and a sweet, flattering eloquence (Conf. bk. 5, ch. 6, no. 10). He chattered about ordinary and familiar matters much more pleasantly and agreeably than others.

Because of this sweetness of speech, he became for not a few Catholics a great snare of the devil (Ibid., ch. 3, no. 3). To his own people he was regarded as a very great teacher, appearing wise and prudent in proportion to the eloquence and fluency with which he seemed endowed.

Armed with all these resources of eloquence, he dared to write a book in which, with a sacrilegious tongue, he impiously attacked the Law and the Prophets, their God, and the Incarnation of Christ. And lest he be refuted by the Scriptures of the New Testament, he confidently asserted that they too had been falsified in those passages by which he felt he might be impeded.

When the book came into Augustine’s hands, he immediately refuted it word for word. As a result, we still possess that same book.

Such, then, was the character and stature of that famous Faustus whom Augustine had eagerly awaited for almost nine years, hoping that the man whom the Manichaeans celebrated as though he had descended from heaven would remove from his mind every scruple by which he had long been troubled.

This happened far more successfully than Faustus himself could have imagined. “That very Faustus,” Augustine says, “who became a snare of death to many, had already begun, though neither willing nor knowing it, to loosen the snare in which I was caught” (Ibid., ch. 7, no. 13).

6. Faustus had already come to Carthage when Augustine was in his twenty-ninth year, which he had begun on the Ides of November in the year 382. Although Faustus could not entirely sustain and fulfill the expectation that he had aroused concerning himself, his eloquence nevertheless equaled his reputation. Augustine does not deny that he was greatly delighted by Faustus at their first hearing.

“I was delighted,” he says, “and, together with many others, or even above many others, I praised and exalted him” (Ibid., ch. 6, no. 11).

Yet, as a fair judge of matters, Augustine distinguished by acute judgment the abundant facility of speech that he rightly praised from the truth of the matters being discussed.

Meanwhile he was distressed that he had no opportunity to interrupt Faustus while he was speaking in a public assembly or to engage him in a familiar exchange, so that they might examine together the difficulties arising in his mind. As soon as the opportunity presented itself, he visited Faustus frequently with his friends and shared with him the scruples that troubled him.

“I brought forward,” Augustine says, “certain matters that disturbed me. I discovered that he was ignorant of the [Col. 0094] liberal disciplines except grammar, and even that only in the ordinary manner” (Conf. bk. 5, ch. 6, no. 11).

From that point a great despair arose that Faustus would ever calm the agitation of mind from which Augustine suffered or unravel the knots of the questions by which he was impeded. Augustine greatly desired to compare the mathematical explanations he had read in the commentaries of the philosophers with those contained in the books of the Manichaeans, and to have it explained whether the movements of the heavens and the revolutions of the stars could be accounted for with equal certainty according to the opinion of that sect and according to the discipline of the astrologers.

When the discussion reached these matters, Faustus, conscious of his limitations and, as Augustine says, “not entirely unlearned,” modestly excused himself on account of his ignorance and did not dare to enter the hazards of disputation.

That modest confession was more pleasing and acceptable to Augustine than the shameless rashness of other members of the sect, who attempted to teach what they had never known. Faustus displayed and consistently maintained the same moderation of mind in other subtle and difficult questions as well. He thereby gained much more favor with Augustine than he would have if, through chattering loquacity, he had clothed the falsehoods of the Manichaeans in the appearance of truth, or even if he had fully satisfied Augustine’s inquiry.

To a man who judged correctly, that restraint of mind seemed more beautiful than an open knowledge of the very matters about which he was being questioned (Ibid., ch. 7, no. 12).

Nevertheless, Augustine courteously and humanely accommodated himself to Faustus. He either began to converse familiarly with him about the art of rhetoric, read together with him whatever Faustus especially wished to hear, or selected passages that seemed more suited to Faustus’s intellectual ability.

Afterward the great enthusiasm with which Augustine had burned for the doctrine of Mani cooled, and all hope collapsed of finding within that sect men capable of disentangling the questions which its celebrated Faustus had been unable to solve.

Accordingly, once this was understood, Augustine abandoned all concern for making progress in that heresy. He wavered in mind, hesitating and remaining stuck in the same mud, and his hesitation increased day by day after Faustus had given him the opportunity to speak with him but had not lived up to his expectations (On the Usefulness of Believing, no. 20).

This may be regarded as the limit of those nine years during which he writes that he adhered to the Manichaeans, as we observed above (above, ch. 6, nos. 4–5). Yet at that age he did not entirely separate himself from their company:

“But as though I could find nothing better,” he says, “I resolved for the time being to remain content with that into which I had already rushed in whatever manner, unless perhaps something more worthy of choice should appear” (Conf. bk. 5, ch. 7, no. 13).

In this state of mind he left Africa and crossed into Italy on his way to Rome. Since he mentions this journey immediately after recounting his conversation with Faustus (Ibid., ch. 8, no. 14), he seems to indicate that he undertook it as he was approaching his twenty-ninth year, perhaps during the academic recess of the year 383. Nevertheless, there is no reason why it should not be thought that he undertook it at the beginning of that same year of Christ.

# BOOK TWO

On Augustine’s departure for Italy and on the events that took place there until his return to Africa.

[Col. 0095]

# CHAPTER ONE

1. Augustine sets out for Rome.  
2. He leaves secretly and against his mother’s wishes.  
3. There he falls ill with a dangerous illness.  
4. He associates with the Manichaeans and considers what still held him within their sect.  
5. He teaches rhetoric in the City.

1. When Augustine resolved to cross into Italy, he certainly did not promise himself the fruit that, with God’s help, he was destined to gain from that voyage. He was making for Rome in order to teach rhetoric there, not because he hoped for greater profit or higher honor, although those incentives, which his friends put before him, did move him to some extent. Rather, he was driven chiefly and almost solely by the fact that he had heard that young men studied more quietly at Rome than at Carthage and were brought to order by stricter discipline.

Yet, if we trace the matter back to its deeper cause, he was being directed by God’s particular will. By a hidden plan God both applied the goads that would tear him away from Carthage and added the enticements that would draw him toward Rome, so that through various winding paths He might ultimately lead him, wandering, to the harbor of salvation.

Recognizing this, Augustine says: “In these events, too, your highest hidden purposes and your most immediate mercy toward us must be considered and proclaimed” (Confes. bk. 5, ch. 8, no. 14).

His adversaries later alleged that he had fled Africa after being struck by the sentence pronounced by the proconsul Messianus against the Manichaeans (Against the Letter of Petilianus, bk. 3, no. 30). Nothing could be more absurd than this claim. The sentence of Messianus was pronounced in the year 386, whereas Augustine was unquestionably already at Milan before the year 385. He himself had ready evidence of this and was fully equipped, should necessity require, to establish it by the testimony of many distinguished men.

2. He undertook this journey secretly; he sailed without the knowledge of Romanianus himself, with whom he was accustomed to share his plans, and whose children he was also leaving behind at Carthage. Yet it does not seem that he would have concealed this from one to whom he was bound by so many and such great benefits, had Romanianus not been absent at the time. For this reason Romanianus neither took even slight offense at him nor relaxed anything of his former goodwill toward him (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §3): he understood Augustine’s character too well to suspect that he could be ungrateful or forgetful toward him.

Monnica was not unaware that Augustine was turning over in his mind the plan of departure. Since, as mothers do—and indeed much more than most—she delighted in her son’s company and could not calmly endure being separated from him (whether he was leaving from Thagaste or Carthage is uncertain), she resolved to follow him, either to bring him home with her or, if he remained firmly set upon continuing his journey, to attach herself to him as his travelling companion. Augustine then pretended that he wished only to remain with a friend who was about to sail until the latter had put out from the harbor. But the pious anxiety of his mother was not deceived by this stratagem, nor could he persuade her to return home alone. Indeed, when she obstinately refused to go back, he could scarcely convince her to spend that night in a place near the ship and consecrated by the memorial of the martyr Cyprian. While she remained there intent upon prayer, earnestly beseeching God to prevent her son from sailing, he secretly withdrew and, with favorable winds, sailed to Rome. When she discovered this in the morning, she poured herself out wholly in miserable tears and filled the entire shore with mournful cries, now lamenting her own bereavement, now turning over in her mind her son’s deception and cruelty. Nevertheless, when the pain of her spirit had been somewhat softened, she became calmer, abandoned the empty complaints with which she had been exhausting herself, and returned home, once again commending her son’s salvation to God in prayer (*Confessions*, book 5, chapter 8, §15).

3. Augustine had scarcely arrived in Rome when, behold, he fell into a most serious illness; and as the danger grew worse day by day, he was close to death. Yet he gave no thought to those saving waters by which the stains of the soul are washed away, for he had gone so far in madness that he mocked this divine remedy. Although his pious mother did not know what danger to his life had overtaken her son, she nevertheless continued to pray to God for him. He records, with grateful remembrance, that through the intervention of her prayer he recovered and was preserved for the life-giving bath. “I cannot express sufficiently,” he says on this subject, “what disposition she had toward me, and how much greater anxiety she suffered in giving me birth in spirit than she had suffered when she gave birth to me in the flesh” (*ibid.*, chapter 9, §16).

4. At that time Augustine was staying with one of the Auditors of the Manichaean sect, and he associated more familiarly not only with that man and with other Auditors but also with the Elect, than with the rest of humanity who did not adhere to that heresy. Although he no longer defended the ravings of the Manichaeans with quite the same vehemence as before, his close association with the large number of them whom Rome concealed nevertheless considerably delayed his search for truth. He had not yet abandoned the error by which, according to their doctrine, he seemed to himself not to be the one who sinned, but rather some other nature within him. This sacrilegious fiction, flattering his pride, readily persuaded him that he was beyond all guilt.

“For it still seemed to me,” he says, “that it was not we who sinned, but I know not what other nature in us that sinned; and I delighted that my pride should be outside guilt. When I had done something evil, I loved not to confess that I had done it, so that you might heal my soul, because it was sinning against you; rather, I loved to excuse it and accuse I know not what other thing that was with me and was not myself” (*ibid.*, chapter 10, §18).

This, however, was by far the greatest and almost the sole obstacle preventing him from emerging from the depths: he could not conceive of God as separate from every corporeal mass, and he thought that absolutely nothing existed that was not body. From this principle, many errors sprang like foul streams from a corrupt spring. Accordingly, he concluded his books *Against Faustus* with this salutary admonition: “Think, or believe, that the nature and substance of God is wholly immutable and wholly incorruptible, and you will immediately cease to be a Manichaean, so that at some time you may also become a Catholic” (*Against Faustus*, book 33, chapter 9).

He was further held back by despair of finding truth in the Catholic Church. The Manichaeans had made that Church so suspect to him through lies fabricated to arouse hatred that he suggests they had persuaded him that Catholics believed God to consist of a corporeal form resembling ours, to be joined together by human limbs, and to be bounded and adorned by the contours of flesh. This seemed to him shameful to believe and even to contemplate (*Confessions*, book 5, chapter 10, §20; book 6, chapter 2, §4). The friendship that united him to the Manichaeans also made him sluggish in investigating anything more certain, since he had decided to remain content with their teaching until something better and more thoroughly established should present itself (*ibid.*, book 5, chapter 10, §19). Moreover, he did not think that what the Manichaeans criticized in the divine Scriptures could be defended by Catholics, although he ardently desired to discuss, point by point, the matters in dispute with someone highly skilled in those books, so that he might discern that person’s judgment on the subject (*ibid.*, chapter 11, §21).

And since he had long since abandoned all hope of making progress within that sect, he was already retaining with increasing laxity and negligence the very positions by which he had resolved to stand if he found nothing better and clearer. Thus he did not hesitate to restrain his own host, who attributed excessive weight and confidence to the tales that the Manichaean had scattered through his books (*ibid.*, chapter 10, §19).

Yet scarcely had the cloud that the errors of the Manichaeans had spread around his mind been cleared away when a more violent storm descended again: his studies turned toward the hesitation and philosophical sect of the Academics, whom he regarded as far the wisest of all, either because they withheld assent from everything or because they had determined that no truth could be grasped by human beings (*On the Happy Life*, §4). “For,” he says, “they seemed to me to have thought just so, as they are commonly understood, since I did not yet understand their real intention” (*Confessions*, book 5, chapter 10, §19).

5. In any event, since the profession of rhetoric had been one, or perhaps the principal, reason for his going to Rome, once he had recovered from his illness he began diligently to devote himself to that pursuit. He first gathered at home the students by and through whom he had already become known. He soon learned that the license of the young Carthaginians did not prevail in Rome, but that another abuse, no less serious, was rampant there. He became aware of the fraud practiced by students who, in order to avoid paying their fees, generally deserted their teacher and, after forming a conspiracy, transferred themselves to another. The disgraceful character of this fraud—which was otherwise ruinous to him—undoubtedly moved him to consider accepting the position that was being offered to him elsewhere (*ibid.*, chapter 12, §22).

## CHAPTER II

1. He is sent by the prefect of the City to Milan to teach rhetoric. 2. Ambrose receives him kindly; after hearing his sermons, Augustine decides to withdraw from the Manichaeans and remain a catechumen in the Catholic Church until something certain should become clear to him.

[Col. 0098]

1. Since the city of Milan was without a professor of eloquence, a request was sent from Milan to Rome, to Symmachus, prefect of the City, asking him to provide a professor for that city; public transportation was also granted. Augustine sought this position through the very Manichaeans, he says, “from whom I was going away” (*Confessions*, book 5, chapter 13, §23). Nor was his effort fruitless. After he had tested his abilities and commended himself to Symmachus by delivering a public speech, he obtained what he desired and was sent to Milan, where the younger Valentinian then maintained his court (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1).

He arrived there before the consulship of Bauton—that is, before the year of Christ 385. If he had not reached Rome until late in 383, he could not have moved to Milan before 384, the year in which we find that Symmachus held the prefecture of the City.
