Alypius, who had gone to Rome before Augustine (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 8, §13), and who had there renewed and strengthened his former friendship with him by a closer bond, likewise resolved to follow him to Milan. “He did not abandon me,” Augustine says, “and he practiced there the law that he had learned, more in accordance with his parents’ wishes than his own” (*ibid.*, chapter 10, §16).

2. The bishop Ambrose administered the Church of Milan with a reputation for both great wisdom and great integrity (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1). When Augustine himself came to him to perform the duty of a respectful greeting, Ambrose received him with a father’s affection and embraced him with episcopal charity.

“But to him,” Augustine says, “I was being led by you, though I did not know it, so that through him I might knowingly be led to you. That man of God received me as a father, and as a bishop he welcomed my pilgrimage with sufficient affection. I began to love him, at first not as a teacher of truth—for I had utterly despaired of finding that in your Church—but as a man who was kind toward me.”

From that time onward he frequently and assiduously listened to him addressing the people—not with the disposition he ought to have had, but in order to test whether his eloquence fell below or rose above its reputation. He was unconcerned with the substance of what was said and merely pursued the allurements of language, whose sweetness delighted him wonderfully. Although Faustus’ speech seemed to him somewhat more polished and sweeter in its power to charm the ears, in his own judgment there was no comparison between the two in seriousness or learning (*Confessions*, book 5, chapter 13, §23).

Thus, little by little and without his knowing it, the truth was entering his mind. That very heresy whose teachings had formed him made him more attentive; for that reason he listened with greater suspense than others, lest anything should be said either for it or against it. The mercy of God the Liberator anticipated him, moving the heart of his priest Ambrose so that he might resolve, against that error, the questions arising from the Law (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1).

Augustine himself relates this at length and elegantly in the following manner:

“For since I was not concerned to learn what he was saying, but only to hear how he was saying it—for to me, a human being who had already despaired that a way to you lay open, only this vain concern remained—I found entering my mind together with the words that I loved also the matters that I neglected. For I could not separate them. And while I opened my heart to receive how eloquently he spoke, there entered at the same time, gradually, how truly he spoke.

“At first, even those things themselves began to seem capable of being defended; and the Catholic faith, which I had thought unable to answer the attacks of the Manichaeans, no longer seemed to me indefensible. This was especially so after I had heard one or another passage from the ancient Scriptures explained, and after an obscure passage had often been resolved. When I took such passages literally, they killed me. Thus, when many passages of those books were expounded spiritually, I began to reproach my despair—namely, the despair in which I had believed that no resistance at all could be offered to those who detested and mocked the Law and the Prophets.

“Yet I did not at that point feel that I ought to hold to the Catholic way because it too could have learned defenders who might refute the objections fully and without absurdity; nor did I therefore think that what I held ought now to be condemned because the two sides were evenly matched in defense. The Catholic position did not seem defeated to me, but neither did it yet appear victorious.

“Then I resolutely applied my mind to discovering, if somehow I could, certain proofs by which I might convict the Manichaeans of falsehood. If I had been able to conceive of a spiritual substance, all those contrivances would immediately have been broken apart and cast out of my mind; but I could not. Nevertheless, as I considered and compared these matters more and more, I judged that most philosophers had held views far more plausible concerning the body of this world and every nature accessible to the senses of the flesh.

“Thus, in the manner in which the Academics are thought to proceed, doubting everything and wavering among all things, I resolved that the Manichaeans ought to be abandoned. I did not think that, at that time of my doubt, I should remain in that sect, to which I was already preferring certain philosophers. Yet because those philosophers lacked the saving name of Christ, I utterly refused to entrust to them the healing of my soul’s sickness.

“I therefore resolved to remain a catechumen in the Catholic Church, the Church commended to me by my parents, until something certain should shine forth by which I could direct my course” (*Confessions*, book 5, chapter 14, §§24–25).

He writes the same thing again to Honoratus in these words:

“I took counsel with myself and engaged in lengthy deliberation, once I was already established in Italy—not whether I should remain in that sect into which I regretted having fallen, but how truth might be found. No one knows better than you how deeply I sighed for its love. Often it seemed to me that it could not be found, and the great waves of my thoughts were carried into the camp of the Academics. Often again, contemplating as far as I could the human mind, so lively, so keen, so perceptive, I did not think that truth could be hidden from it, except that the method of seeking it might be hidden; and that this very method had to be received from some divine authority.

“It remained to seek what that authority might be, since amid such great disagreements each party promised that it would offer that authority. There appeared before me an impenetrable forest, into which I was very reluctant to insert my axe; and amid these things, without any rest, my mind was agitated by the desire to find the truth.

“Nevertheless, I was detaching myself more and more from those whom I had already resolved to abandon. Nothing else remained amid such dangers except to implore divine providence, with tearful and pitiable cries, to bring me help. I did this diligently.

“By now certain discussions of the bishop of Milan had almost moved me to desire, not without some hope, to investigate many things in the Old Testament itself, which, as you know, had been badly commended to us and which we used to curse. I had resolved to remain a catechumen in the Church to which I had been entrusted by my parents until I either found what I wanted or became convinced that it ought not to be sought. At that time, therefore, I would have been found most ready and highly teachable, if there had been anyone able to teach” (*On the Usefulness of Believing*, §20).

## CHAPTER III

1. Monnica comes to Milan. 2. Augustine is given no opportunity to ask Bishop Ambrose what he wishes. 3. He continues to hear Ambrose’s sermons to the people and, through them, understands more fully day by day the true teaching of the Catholic Church. 4. He recognizes the necessity of faith and the salutary authority of the Scriptures. 5. He still struggles with the question of the origin of evil. 6. Through reading the Platonists he advances in the knowledge of God, but not in the knowledge of the incarnate Word. 7. He is moved by compassion for those entangled in the error of the Manichaeans.

1. The despair of finding the truth in which Augustine was involved was full of danger, because from it arose a sluggishness and negligence in his search. Yet this condition of mind—or rather this instability and uncertain wavering to which hearing Ambrose had brought him—was like a critical relapse, through which, with a more acute danger intervening, he was to pass from sickness to health (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 1, §1).

He was in this condition when Monnica, having followed her son by land and sea, arrived at Milan. Once he had informed her more fully of the whole situation, she experienced some pleasure because she saw that he had been rescued from falsehood. Yet she did not, as though she had heard something unexpected, give herself over to turbulent joy. With a calm mind full of confidence, she said that she trusted in Christ that, before she departed this life, she would see him a faithful Catholic (*ibid.*).

2. Meanwhile, although Augustine ought to have been assiduous in groaning and beseeching God to come to his aid, his mind was intent upon inquiry and restless for discussion. He had no opportunity to communicate his doubts and anxieties to Ambrose, since crowds of busy people, whose infirmities Ambrose served, shut Augustine off from the bishop’s ear and speech.

No one was ever forbidden to approach Ambrose, nor was it customary for him to be told when someone came to him. This man, born and devoted to the public good, freely made himself accessible to everyone. But when Augustine frequently visited him and occasionally found him at leisure from the disturbance of other people’s lawsuits, he nevertheless considered it improper to draw him away from his reading (*ibid.*, chapter 3, §3).

Accordingly, Augustine was given no opportunity to ask whatever he wished, except perhaps about matters that could be explained briefly. Thus, concerning the relaxation of the fast on the Sabbath—a matter about which Monnica was uncertain—he writes that, while still a catechumen and little concerned with such things, he asked Ambrose about it [Col. 0101]. But the scruples that tormented him day and night had taken deeper root in his mind than could easily or quickly be pulled out. The various waves of thought by which he was agitated required a teacher who was at leisure and free from every other concern, into whom he could pour them; but he never found Ambrose in such a condition.

The holy bishop often broke into praise of Monnica. “He congratulated me,” Augustine says, “that I had such a mother, not knowing what kind of son she had in me—one who doubted all those things and thought that the way of life could scarcely be found” (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 2, §2).

Augustine himself lacked the money to purchase books by whose assistance he might educate himself; he had no opportunity to borrow them from friends; and even if they had been available, he had no time to read them. His mornings were occupied by his students, while the remainder of the day was consumed either in preparing his lectures, caring for his frail body, restoring his mind after the strain of his occupations, or finally paying the dutiful calls owed to friends and powerful men, whose favor he needed for the advancement of his affairs (*ibid.*, chapter 11, §18).

Although he writes that he saw Philastrius of Brescia, then famous for his learning, at Milan (*Letters*, 222.2), it nevertheless does not appear that any close relationship existed between him and that bishop, or that he ever discussed religion with him.

3. The one remedy that remained for his wound was this: he continued diligently to hear Ambrose, each Sunday, discussing matters publicly before the people. Augustine testifies that, through the sermons of so great a man, he became increasingly convinced that all the knots of cunning slanders which the Manichaeans tied against the divine Books could be untied by Catholics without great difficulty.

When he discovered that Catholics did not understand the human being made in the image of God in such a way that God was thought to be bounded by the limbs of a human body, as the Manichaeans maliciously alleged (*On Heresies*, heresy 46), the matter was still not sufficiently clear to him, since he had not yet grasped the nature of spiritual substance. Nevertheless, he felt a joy mingled with shame, because at last he saw that he had rashly barked more against the fabrications of his own thoughts than against the faith of the Catholic Church, when he ought humbly and reverently to have investigated how the matter actually stood (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 3, §4).

For this reason he burned with a still more ardent desire to discern the truth, in proportion as he was ashamed to realize that he had been shamefully deceived by the empty promises of the Manichaeans. He had not yet clearly discovered whether the teachings handed down by the Church of God were true; but he held without any doubt that the Church did not teach there the things that he himself had once so bitterly accused on the basis of a false conception.

“Thus I was confounded and converted,” he says, “and I rejoiced, my God, that the one Church, the body of your Only-begotten, in which the name of Christ had been given to me when I was an infant, did not savor of childish fables; and that its sound doctrine did not contain the idea that you, the creator of all things, were enclosed within a spatial extent, however vast and broad, yet bounded on every side, and confined within the shape of human limbs.

“I rejoiced also that the ancient writings of the Law and the Prophets were now set before me to be read with a different eye from that with which they had previously appeared absurd, when I accused your holy servants as though they thought in that way. But they did not think so. And I was glad to hear Ambrose frequently say in his public sermons, as though commending it most carefully as a rule, ‘The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life’ (2 Corinthians 3:6), when he opened spiritually, after removing the mystical veil, those passages which, taken literally, seemed to teach perversity. He said nothing that offended me, although he said things whose truth I still did not know.

“For I kept my heart from every assent, fearing a precipice; and by suspending judgment I was being killed even more. I wanted to become as certain about things I could not see as I was certain that seven and three make ten. I was not so insane as to think that even this could not be grasped; but, just as I desired certainty about this, so I desired it about everything else—whether corporeal things that were not present to my bodily senses, or spiritual things, which I did not know how to think of except corporeally.

“Yet I could be healed by believing, so that the purified vision of my mind might somehow be directed toward your truth, which remains forever and fails from nothing. But just as it often happens that someone who has had experience of a bad physician is afraid to entrust himself even to a good one, so was the condition of my soul. It could not be healed except by believing, yet, in order not to believe falsehood, it refused to be healed. It resisted your hands, which prepared the medicines of faith and scattered them over the diseases of the world” (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 4, §§5–6).

4. He then began to understand that the Church acted more sincerely and modestly when it required faith in things that could neither be perceived by the senses nor demonstrated by certain reasoning than did the Manichaeans. They mocked such belief and made grand promises that they would hand down nothing except what was open and evident; but when they later proved unable to fulfill this promise, they finally sank to the point of wanting their own invented fables to stand and be accepted by their own faith (*ibid.*, chapter 5, §7).

After the most gentle hand of God had gradually touched and softened his heart, he considered how countless things he believed without hesitation on the testimony of others—things which, unless faith were granted to them, would have to be removed from human society altogether. From this he understood that those who placed faith in the sacred Books could not be reproached, since God himself had established their authority so powerfully in almost every part of the world.

Because human nature is too weak to investigate truth with complete clarity, and because we need divine authority for this purpose, God would not have conferred such authority upon that Scripture which the Church reveres unless he had wished both to be believed through it and to be sought through it. He used the humblest manner of speaking in order to attract all peoples.

If he did not yet grasp certain passages of Scripture in his mind, he readily understood that the obscurity of those statements ought to be referred to the depth of the mysteries. On this occasion he addresses God in the following words:

“I thought about these things, and you were present to me; I sighed, and you heard me; I wavered, and you guided me; I walked along the broad way of the world, and you did not abandon me” (*ibid.*, §8).

He judged that the sacred Scriptures ought to be granted primacy of authority all the more readily because the various and mutually conflicting opinions of the philosophers, with which he had imbued his mind, had never expelled his innate conviction that God exists and that the administration of human affairs belongs to him.

“I believed this,” he says, “sometimes more firmly, sometimes more faintly; yet I always believed both that you exist and that you care for us, even though I did not know either what should be thought concerning your substance or what way led or led back to you” (*ibid.*).

There also remained fixed in his mind a fear of death, dread of the future divine judgment, hope of immortality, and the future reckoning and recompense of the merits of his past life. No diversity of opinions displaced these convictions from his heart. He writes that they restrained him like reins and drew him back from the deeper whirlpool of obscene pleasures (*ibid.*, chapter 16, §26).

5. Although he could conceive of God in thought only as some most noble body, spread and extended in every direction through an immense mass, he nevertheless held firmly that God’s nature—whatever it might be—was undefiled, incorruptible, and incapable of change in any respect (*ibid.*, book 7, chapter 1, §2). For this reason he considered the Manichaeans all the more insane in their ravings: they thought it preferable to regard the divine substance as subject to suffering from evil than to regard themselves as guilty because they perpetrated evil (*ibid.*, chapter 3, §4).

Nevertheless, he could not yet clearly discern the origin of evil. It repeatedly occurred to him, as he heard it stated, that free choice of the will was the cause of the evil we did, while the just judgment of God was the cause of the evil we suffered. Yet he could not understand clearly why things stood that way. For although, when he felt that he possessed free choice of the will, some light arose by which he could readily recognize that it was the source of those sins he had committed freely and willingly, the question nevertheless remained inextricable: whence came the inclination toward evil implanted in free will by the supremely good God? Whence came the will to do evil and the unwillingness to do good? (*ibid.*, §5).

Agitated by these and similar waves of thought, he was consumed and tormented by cares, all the more because he was less able to explain them to his friends and share them through explanation. Yet those silent torments of his heart were like the clearest voices striking at the throne of divine mercy. His own arrogance, however, kept him away from it; and the swelling that had inflated his face closed his eyes so that he could not admit the light of truth (*ibid.*, chapter 7, §11).

“You were stirring me,” he says, “with inward goads, so that I would be impatient until you became certain to me through my inner vision. My swelling subsided under the hidden hand of your medicine, and the vision of my mind, confused and darkened, was healed day by day by the sharp eye-salve of salutary sorrows” (*ibid.*, chapter 8, §12).

6. Much assistance in this matter came to him from reading certain books of Plato and of his followers. They had been translated into Latin by Victorinus, the most distinguished rhetorician of the city, and had come into Augustine’s hands through a certain man who was excessively arrogant and conceited (*ibid.*, chapter 9, §13).

For while the other philosophers, clinging only to corporeal things and rising no higher, are full of deceit and deception, the Platonists attempt through all their reasoning to raise the mind toward knowledge of God and of his eternal Word. In their books he found, though not in the same words, everything that John himself teaches at the beginning of his Gospel concerning the glory of the Word, and that Paul teaches concerning the Word’s equality with the Father. There too he found that the Son is coeternal with his Father and remains immutable before all things and above every time; that souls receive from his fullness so that they may be blessed, and are renewed through participation in the Wisdom that remains in itself, so that they may be wise.

“Warned by this,” he says, “to return to myself, I entered into my inmost self, with you as my guide; and I was able to do so because you had become my helper. I entered, and with whatever eye of my soul I possessed, I saw above that eye of my soul, above my mind, an immutable light—not this common light, visible to all flesh, nor something of the same kind. It was greater, as though it shone much, much more brightly and occupied the whole of space by its magnitude. It was not this light, but something else, something very different from all these things.

“It was not above my mind in the way that oil is above water or heaven above earth; it was superior because it made me, while I was inferior because I was made by it. Whoever knows truth knows it, and whoever knows it knows eternity. Love knows it” (*ibid.*, chapter 10, §16).

Afterward he describes at length and magnificently how he was divinely enlightened to know eternal truth, the condition and order of created things, and also the true origin of evil. He adds the following:

“I marveled that I already loved you, not a phantom in place of you. Yet I was not standing firm in the enjoyment of my God; I was being swept toward you by your beauty, and soon torn away from you by my own weight, and I fell back into these things with a groan. That weight was carnal habit. Yet the memory of you remained with me, and I had no doubt that there was one to whom I should cling; but I was not yet one who could cling” (*ibid.*, chapter 17, §23).

He therefore sought a way by which he could acquire sufficient strength to enjoy God, but he found none except in the knowledge and love of the Mediator between God and human beings, Jesus Christ, God and man. Yet he did not hold Jesus Christ as humble, because he did not understand him to be humble; nor did he know what his weakness was meant to teach.

Moreover, he held no other opinion concerning the Lord Christ than that he was a human being like the rest, consisting of body, soul, and rational mind, distinguished only by an excellence of wisdom that no one could equal. He believed that God, in a singular providence toward us, had willed him to be miraculously born of a Virgin and to possess the highest authority and mastery over all, so that by his example we might learn to despise temporal things and attain immortality.

He could not even faintly suspect what mystery was hidden beneath the words, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). Only somewhat later did he learn how Catholic truth differed from the error of Photinus concerning this mystery. In the books of the Platonists he had indeed found the majesty and divinity of the Word, but he had read nothing of his abasement, nothing of his incarnation, nothing of his death and cross.

7. The more effort and labor Augustine had spent in investigating the truth, the more tenderly he afterward felt compassion toward those to whom God had not yet granted this benefit. Thus he addresses the Manichaeans:

“Let those rage against you who do not know with what labor truth is found and how difficult it is to avoid errors. Let those rage against you who do not know how rare and arduous it is, with the serenity of a pious mind, to rise above corporeal phantoms. Let those rage against you who do not know with what difficulty the eye of the inner person is healed so that it may gaze upon its sun. Let those rage against you who do not know through what sighs and groans it comes about that God can be understood, even in some small measure.

“Finally, let those rage against you who have never been deceived by an error such as that in which they see you deceived. But I, who after being tossed about for a long time and at length was able to behold what that sincerity is which is perceived without the telling of an empty fable; I, who, miserable as I was, scarcely succeeded, with the Lord’s help, in refuting the vain imaginings of my mind, gathered from various opinions and errors; I, who so late submitted myself to the most merciful physician calling and coaxing me in order to wipe away the darkness of my mind; I, who for a long time wept that the immutable and undefiled substance might deign, through the agreement of the divine Books, to persuade me inwardly of its existence; I, finally, who both diligently sought all those fabrications that hold you entangled and bound by long habit, listened to them attentively, believed them rashly, urgently persuaded others of them as far as I could, and defended them against others stubbornly and passionately—I cannot rage against you at all.

“I must now bear with you as I bore with myself at that time, and deal with you with as much patience as my neighbors dealt with me when, raging and blind, I wandered in your doctrine” (*Against the Letter of the Manichaean*, §§2–3).

## CHAPTER IV

1. Augustine pursues the truth while nevertheless still yearning for earthly things. 2. From a beggar who jokes and rejoices he understands the misery of ambitious people. 3. He wavers in choosing a way of life. 4. He dismisses his concubine in order to marry, and takes another. 5. He unsuccessfully consults with his friends about entering a common way of life. 6. The Platonists increase his love for wisdom. 7. He makes very great progress through reading the Apostle.

1. It was not ignorance of the truth alone that prevented Augustine from flying swiftly into the bosom of philosophy: he was still held back by the allurements of marriage and public distinction. He greatly desired first to obtain both, and only then to hasten with every sail and oar toward that secure harbor and rest there. At times he would burst out in these words, addressing his friends:

> Why do we delay, abandoning the hope of this world, and devote ourselves wholly to seeking God and the blessed life? But wait: these things too are pleasant; they possess no small sweetness of their own. One cannot easily cut oneself off from them, because it is shameful to return to them later. Look how little it would take to obtain some public office! And what more is there to desire in these matters? We have plenty of influential friends; if nothing else, and if we hasten greatly, a governorship can be obtained; and one can marry a wife with some money, so that she will not burden our expenses—and that will be the limit of our desire. Many eminent men, worthy of imitation, devoted themselves to the pursuit of wisdom while married.  
> (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 11, §19)

For he thought that he would be exceedingly miserable if he led a celibate life. Hence he regarded Bishop Ambrose—who was held in high honor even by the rulers of the Roman world—as fortunate according to worldly standards. Ambrose’s celibacy alone seemed to Augustine laborious and burdensome; he could not even imagine what hope Ambrose possessed, what struggle he maintained against the temptations assailing his excellence, or what consolation he found in adversity, nor how savory his joys were (*ibid.*, chapter 3, §3). Thus he longed for public honors, wealth, and marriage (*ibid.*, chapter 6, §9). But God, frustrating his wishes, tormented him amid the very heat of his desires with the bitterest difficulties. He was all the more gracious to Augustine insofar as he allowed nothing outside himself to become sweet to him, so that, setting everything else aside, he might turn to God.

2. Augustine himself records the occasion on which he clearly understood his misery, when he was preparing to deliver a panegyric to the younger Valentinian Augustus. Elsewhere he speaks of a panegyric that he had delivered on the Kalends of January before a very large gathering, in fulfillment of his profession as a teacher of rhetoric (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 3, §30). That speech, however, was a panegyric addressed to Bauto, consul in the year 385. Of this panegyric to the Emperor he speaks as follows:

> As I was preparing to recite praises to the Emperor—praises containing many lies, and for which those who knew the truth would nevertheless applaud the liar—and as my heart was panting under these cares and fevered with the fevers of thoughts that consumed me, I passed through a certain street in Milan and noticed a poor beggar, already, I believe, satisfied, joking and rejoicing. I groaned and spoke with the friends who were with me about the many sorrows of our madness. For in all our efforts of this kind, such as those with which I was then laboring, dragging under the goad of desire the burden of my unhappiness and increasing it by dragging it, we wanted nothing else but to attain secure happiness—a happiness to which that beggar had already preceded us, though we might perhaps never arrive there. What he had already acquired with a few small coins begged from others, I was pursuing through such sorrowful windings and circuits: namely, the happiness of temporal prosperity. He did not possess true joy; yet I was seeking it through those ambitions in a far more false manner.  
> (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 6, §9)

This was the constant subject of the groans into which he would burst with his friends. He discussed it increasingly often and openly with Alypius and Nebridius. Nebridius had left his mother, his homeland, and his estates, and had come from Carthage to Milan for no other reason than to live with Augustine and devote himself with him, with every effort, to the investigation of truth and wisdom. He was an ardent seeker of the blessed life and an exceptionally keen investigator of the most difficult questions.

“There were,” Augustine says, “the faces of three needy men, panting their poverty to one another and waiting for you to give them food at the proper time. And amid all the bitterness that followed our worldly activities because of your mercy, when we considered the end for which we endured these things, darkness confronted us. We turned away groaning and said: ‘How long will this last?’ We said this repeatedly, yet in saying it we did not abandon those activities, because no certain alternative shone forth which we could seize after leaving them” (*ibid.*, chapter 10, §17).

3. “I too,” Augustine continues, “was especially astonished, striving to understand and recalling how long it had been since my nineteenth year, when I had begun to burn with enthusiasm for wisdom and had resolved, once I had found it, to abandon all the empty hopes and deceitful insanities of vain desires. And now I was already thirty, still stuck in the same mire, greedy to enjoy present things, while they fled from me and scattered me, as I said: ‘Tomorrow I shall find it; look, it will become clear, and I shall grasp it’” (*ibid.*, chapter 11, §18).

He then proceeds to describe with remarkable vividness the doubts by which he was distracted concerning the kind of life he should choose as most suitable for the search for truth. At that time the light of truth had scarcely begun to shine upon him, since he had not yet read the books of the Platonists. Amid this manifold turmoil of impulses and thoughts, by which he was simultaneously tossed and driven here and there like a ship carried away by opposing winds, time slipped away, and, still uncertain in mind, he postponed his conversion day after day. Loving the blessed life, he feared it in the very place where it dwells—namely, in contempt for all things in order to cleave to the one God—so that, while seeking it, he fled from it (*ibid.*, §20).

Conscious of his weakness and not yet having experienced the power of grace, he could not bring himself to embrace a celibate life. Alypius, a young man of extraordinary chastity, made every effort to turn him away from marriage, arguing that, if Augustine married, it would be entirely impossible for them to live together in tranquility and in the love of wisdom, as they had long desired. But Augustine says:

> Bound by the disease of the flesh, I dragged my chain with deadly sweetness, afraid to be released and, as though a wound had been shaken, repelling the words of one who advised me well, as though they were the hand of one releasing me.

Alypius, who held a high opinion of Augustine’s intellect, was then himself stimulated by curiosity to desire marriage; astonished by another’s bondage, he freely inclined toward the same bondage (*ibid.*, chapter 12, §§21–22).

4. Since Augustine was thus disposed in mind, it is not surprising that Monnica took care to have him married before Baptism, toward which she rejoiced to see him preparing himself day by day (*ibid.*, chapter 13, §23), lest after the sacred regeneration he should still remain exposed to the danger of incontinence. She frequently prayed to God, even when urged by her son, to indicate to her in a vision something concerning this marriage; but she never obtained her request.

Nevertheless, a girl was sought and the arrangement was concluded. Since, however, she would not be marriageable until two years later, it was decided to wait for the appropriate time, and that condition did not seem negligible. [Col. 0108] Meanwhile, because Augustine’s concubine stood in the way of the marriage, she was taken away from his side. She returned to Africa, vowing to God that she would know no other man. Augustine, however, was unable even to imitate that little woman with manly resolve: since he could not wait two years, he took another woman in place of the one who had departed (*ibid.*, chapter 15, §25), as though he had determined either always to prolong or to aggravate the sickness of his soul.

Nor does he deny that he was restrained from a deeper abyss of lust solely by fear of death and divine judgment:

> That fear, he says, amid various opinions, nevertheless never departed from my breast.

When he sometimes disputed with Alypius and Nebridius about the ends of good and evil, he said that he would have awarded the palm to Epicurus if he had not believed what Epicurus refused to believe: that after death life remained for the soul, together with the consequences of its merits. By this thought he showed clearly enough his own misery and that he could not perceive the pure light of that heavenly beauty which ought to be loved for its own sake.

5. “Many friends,” he says, “had discussed in our minds and in conversation, and, detesting the turbulent troubles of human life, had almost firmly resolved to live in leisure, withdrawn from the crowds. We planned that leisure in such a way that, if we possessed anything, we would place it all in common and form one household from everything, so that through the sincerity of friendship there would not be one thing belonging to this man and another to that, but what came from all would become one, and the whole would belong to each, and everything would belong to everyone […]. It had pleased us that two of us each year, as though magistrates, should manage all necessities while the others remained at rest.

“But when we began to consider whether the women whom some of us already had, and whom we wished to have, would permit this, the entire plan that we had been shaping so well fell apart in our hands, was shattered, and was cast aside. From there came sighs and groans, and steps toward following the broad and well-trodden ways of the world, since many thoughts were in our hearts, but your counsel remains forever. By that counsel you mocked our plans and prepared yours, to give us food at the proper time, to open your hand, and to fill our souls with blessing” (*ibid.*, chapter 14, §24).

There seemed to be about ten men whom this common life pleased. Among them were several extremely wealthy men, especially Romanianus, who had been Augustine’s intimate friend from childhood. No one desired this community of life more eagerly or possessed greater authority for recommending it, since his resources were more ample than those of the others. At that time he was living in Milan in order to pursue lawsuits brought against him by a powerful adversary. Through these lawsuits divine providence was awakening him from a certain sleep and torpor of this life.

Augustine perhaps refers to this plan for a common life when he addresses him in these words:

> Whatever joy I now derive from my leisure—because I have escaped the bonds of superfluous desires; because, having laid down the burdens of deadening cares, I breathe again, recover my senses, return to myself; because I seek the truth with the greatest concentration, am beginning to enter upon its discovery, and trust that I shall reach the highest goal—you inspired, urged, and accomplished. Whose servant you were, I have conceived more by faith than grasped by reason.

> For when I had disclosed to you, face to face, the inner movements of my soul, and had repeatedly and vehemently asserted that no favorable fortune seemed favorable to me unless it afforded leisure for philosophizing, and that no life seemed blessed unless it was lived in philosophy, but that I was restrained by the great burden of my dependents, whose lives depended upon my official duties, and by many necessities—whether of my vain shame or the foolish misery of my own people—you were lifted up by so great a joy and inflamed with so holy a passion for this life that you said that, if you could somehow be freed from the bonds of those troublesome lawsuits, you would break all my bonds as well, even by sharing your patrimony with me.

> Thus, after you had departed, having applied fuel to our zeal, we never ceased to yearn for philosophy and to think of nothing else but that life which had pleased and suited us. We pursued this steadily, though less ardently; nevertheless, we thought that we were doing enough. Since the flame that was to seize us completely had not yet arisen, we supposed that the flame with which we were slowly burning was the greatest possible.  
> (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §§4–5)

6. After this he read the books of the Platonists, as he testifies in these words:

> And then, look, certain books—books which, as Celsinus says, breathed out good Arabian fragrances upon us—instilled into us a very few drops of the precious ointment. Incredible, Romanianus, incredible, and beyond what you perhaps believe of me! What more shall I say? They stirred up in me an incredible fire, incredible even to myself concerning myself. What honor, what public admiration, what desire for empty fame, what support or attachment of this mortal life could then move me?  
> (*ibid.*, §5)

Yet, however incredible that fire was, it would never have affected Augustine so as to turn him from the depravity of his life to the cultivation of wisdom unless other causes had also moved him. The words of the philosophers, without the assistance of Christ the mediator, possess no power to raise the human heart to God.

Elsewhere, where he says that reading the Platonists had greatly helped him to break the bonds by which he was tied to the world, he simultaneously testifies that he received this benefit when he compared their authority with that of those who transmitted the divine mysteries—namely, the Prophets and Apostles (*The Happy Life*, §4). Moreover, although he had discovered certain sublime teachings in the books of the philosophers, from them he had learned only to chatter about such things as though he had become an expert. Nevertheless, unless he sought the way of God in Christ our Savior, he would be, as he says, not learned but lost (*Confessions*, book 7, chapter 20, §26).

From that time he had begun, although weighed down by the punishment and burden of his sins, to court a reputation for learning and to exalt himself, puffed up by the esteem attached to his doctrine, while giving no thought to the cleansing away of his sins. Thus at that time he belonged to those who, “although they knew God, did not glorify him as God” (Romans 1:21).

This condition seems to have been expressed by him in *The Happy Life*, which he composed immediately after his conversion. There, after presenting all mortals as tossed upon a stormy sea from which they must make their way into the harbor of philosophy, he admirably warns that those who are carried by any route toward the region of the blessed life must greatly fear and carefully avoid one enormous mountain standing before the harbor and producing severe difficulties for those who enter it. By this mountain he wishes nothing else to be understood as feared by those approaching or entering philosophy than, in Augustine’s words, “the proud pursuit of utterly empty glory.” It possesses nothing inward that is full or solid; therefore, as those inflated men walk over it, the fragile ground resounds beneath them, plunges them down, and swallows them, and, once they have been hurled back into darkness, deprives them of the radiant house which they had almost seen (*The Happy Life*, §3).

7. Augustine saw himself being carried up this mountain by the books of the Platonists. Yet those books could never have taught him that charity which establishes and strengthens the structure of our salvation upon the foundation of humility, which is Christ Jesus.

When, therefore, he began to consider returning to himself as soon as possible, he turned the eyes of his mind toward the Catholic religion, which had been implanted in him since childhood and, as he says, entwined with him to the very marrow, and which was recalling him to itself even while he was unaware (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §5).

Augustine says:

> I believe that you wanted me to encounter these books before I considered your Scriptures, so that it might be impressed upon my memory how I had been affected by them. Then, when I had afterward been gentled by your books and my wounds were handled by the fingers of your care, I would discern and distinguish the difference between presumption and confession; between those who see where they must go but do not see the way, and the way that leads to the blessed homeland—not merely to be seen, but to be inhabited.

> For if I had first been formed by your holy writings, and had grown accustomed to their sweetness through familiarity with them, and afterward had fallen upon those volumes, perhaps they would have swept me away from the firm foundation of piety. Or, if I had remained in the disposition that I had healthfully absorbed, I might have thought that it could also be conceived from those books, if someone had learned them alone.  
> (*Confessions*, book 7, chapter 20, §26)

Accordingly, he seized the sacred books with the greatest eagerness and revered those divine oracles of the Holy Spirit. Yet nothing affected him more deeply than reading the Epistles of the Apostle Paul. The difficulties that had previously led him to suppose that Paul spoke contradictorily in certain passages, and that his words did not agree with the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets, immediately vanished.

He recognized that those chaste and entirely unvarnished utterances were animated by one Spirit and embraced the same mysteries. In contemplating them, he learned to rejoice with trembling. At first glance he also recognized that whatever truth he had read in profane books was found in these writings. But these writings communicated truth in such a way that they commended the power of grace and instructed us in various mysteries—something those pages did not do, nor did they generate knowledge of that devout humility found only in the Christian religion.

Indeed, it is one thing to see the homeland of peace from the summit of a lofty, wild, uncultivated mountain, without finding the road to it, and to strive in vain through pathless places while renegade angels hem one in; it is another to keep to the road leading to that blessed homeland, fortified by the protection of the good angels. These truths descended deeply into Augustine’s mind through wondrous and mysterious means as he read the Apostle, and, considering the marvelous works of God, he was struck with astonishment (*ibid.*, chapter 21, §27).

Elsewhere, addressing Romanianus, he says:

> “Stumbling, hurrying, hesitating, I seized the Apostle Paul. I read him through with the utmost concentration and care. Then, when even the slightest light had already been shed upon me, so magnificent a vision of philosophy was revealed to me that, I will not say to you, who have always burned with desire for knowledge of it, but if I could have displayed it even to your adversary—whom I do not know whether you are more exercised by than hindered by—he would surely have cast aside and abandoned Baiae, pleasant gardens, delicate and splendid banquets, household performers, and finally every pleasure that sharply excites him. As a gentle and holy lover, astonished, panting, and burning, he would have flown toward this beauty.”  
> (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §§5–6)

This remarkable change in conduct, which reading the sacred books produced in Augustine’s soul, does not seem to have occurred before the Easter festival of the year of his conversion, which we assign to 386, and indeed not before the end of June. When Justina was persecuting Ambrose around the feast of Easter, God had not yet dissolved the ice of his heart by the life-giving warmth of his Spirit, although Augustine himself was powerfully stirred by the tumult of the troubled city (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 7, §15). Nor was he yet running after God when Ambrose discovered the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius (*ibid.*, §16), apparently on June 18.

## CHAPTER V

1. He wishes to renounce everything for God’s sake, but cannot.  
2. He consults Simplicianus.  
3. Through Pontitianus’s account of Antony’s life, he learns also of the conversion of two imperial officials.  
4. The conflict in Augustine’s mind and will after hearing Pontitianus.  
5. At the prompting of an extraordinary voice, he opens the book of Paul and is suddenly converted upon reading the passage.

1. Since the sacred words of God, as we have said, had sunk deeply into Augustine’s mind, he now desired not merely to become more certain concerning them, but to become more firmly established in them. Yet his mind remained undecided, and he did not know what resolution to make regarding the pattern of his life. His heart had to be cleansed of the old leaven with which it had been infected.

Although he rejoiced that the Savior himself was the way leading us to salvation, he nevertheless still shrank from walking through the narrowness of that way. He found it painful and burdensome that he was still entangled in the affairs of the turbulent world. For, unlike before, the hope of acquiring wealth and honor no longer lifted his spirits so that he could endure this most burdensome servitude. Those things no longer delighted him, because of the sweetness he was thirstily drinking from the divine fountain.

What delayed him was his concern and desire to avoid offending certain people—perhaps those whose children he was instructing in the liberal arts. In addition, he was held very strongly by the desire for marriage. Because of this one thing he was languid in all else and wasted away under cares gnawing at his mind, since married life, toward which he was carried with such inclination, brought with it various difficulties that he did not wish to endure (*Confessions*, book 8, chapter 1, §§1–2).

[Col. 0112] 2. While he was in this condition, God put it into his mind to visit Simplicianus, then Ambrose’s spiritual father and later his successor. The grace of God shone in him; from his youth he had devoted himself to its service. He had always lived in the highest devotion and was now worn out by age. This led Augustine to believe—and the reality was as he thought—that, after so many years spent practicing virtue, Simplicianus had acquired knowledge of the spiritual life through long experience.

Augustine therefore resolved to disclose to him all the turmoil and agitation of his soul, so that, once his state of mind was understood, Simplicianus might show him the course he considered most suitable for following the way of God. He visited him and laid open to him the winding paths of his errors.

When Simplicianus learned that Augustine had read the books of the Platonists translated into Latin by Victorinus, he rejoiced. Taking this opportunity, he told him of the conversion of that same Victorinus, whom he had known most intimately at Rome. He related this to encourage Augustine to pursue the humility of Jesus Christ, which is hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones, and to kindle in him a desire to imitate so great a man, so distinguished in the same profession that Augustine himself practiced. In fact, Augustine was inflamed to imitate him.

Simplicianus added that Julian’s edict had forbidden Christians to teach literature and rhetoric, and that Victorinus, obeying this law, had dismissed his school. Augustine says:

> He seemed to me not braver than happier, because he had found an opportunity to devote himself to you.

He soon burst out in these words:

> I was sighing for that devotion while bound—not by another’s iron, but by my own iron will. The enemy held my will and had made a chain from it, binding me with it. For from a perverse will came desire; and when desire is served, habit is formed; and when habit is not resisted, necessity is formed. By these links, as though interwoven with one another—which is why I called it a chain—an oppressive bondage held me fast.

> The new will that had begun to arise in me—a will to serve you freely and to desire to enjoy you, O God, the only certain joy—was not yet strong enough to overcome the former will, strengthened by long age. Thus my two wills, one old and one new, one carnal and the other spiritual, were in conflict with one another and, by their discord, tore my soul apart.

> By my own experience I understood what I had read: how the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh […] (Galatians 5:17). The excuse was no longer available by which I had been accustomed to think that I had not yet begun to serve you after despising the world because my apprehension of the truth was uncertain. The truth itself was now certain, but I was still bound to earth and refused to enlist in your service. I feared being freed from all impediments in the same way that one ought to fear being impeded.  
> (*Confessions*, book 8, chapter 5, §§10–11)

He continues to describe vividly the power of the tyranny that his ingrained habit of sin exercised over him.

3. But at last God shattered all his bonds through a miracle both visible and invisible. His customary cares and anxieties grew more intense day by day. He continually sighed for God and attended church as often as the affairs beneath whose weight he groaned permitted.

“One day,” he says, “a fellow citizen of ours, Pontitianus, came to me and Alypius. As an African, he held an excellent position in the imperial service. I do not know what he wanted from us. We sat down to converse, and by chance he noticed a book lying on the gaming table before us. He picked it up, opened it, and unexpectedly found the Apostle Paul. For he had supposed it to be one of the books whose study exhausted me.

“Then, smiling and looking at me, he congratulated me and expressed his astonishment that he had suddenly found those writings, and those alone, before my eyes. He was a Christian and faithful, and often prostrated himself in church before you, our God, with frequent and prolonged prayers.

“When I told him that I devoted the greatest attention to those Scriptures, he began to speak—on his own initiative—of Antony the Egyptian monk, whose name was held in high renown among your servants but had remained unknown to us until that hour. When he discovered this, he lingered over the subject, making such a great man known to us who were ignorant of him and marveling at our ignorance.

“We were astonished as we listened to accounts of miracles so recent in memory and so fully attested in our own times within the true faith and Catholic Church. We all marveled: we, because the things were so great; he, because they were unknown to us.

“From there his conversation turned to the communities of monasteries, to the fragrant conduct of your servants, and to the desert breasts of the wilderness, of which we knew nothing. There was a monastery in Milan filled with good brothers, outside the city walls, under the care of Ambrose their fosterer; we did not know of it.

“He continued speaking, and we listened in silence. Then he happened to say that, when he and three of his companions were at Trier, while the Emperor was occupied with the afternoon spectacle in the Circus, they had gone out for a walk in gardens adjoining the walls. There, as they happened to walk in pairs, one of them went off separately, while the other two likewise departed together.

“But those two wanderers came upon a hut where certain servants of yours lived—poor in spirit, such as possess the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:3). There they found a book containing the life of Antony. One of them began to read it, marveling and becoming inflamed; and while reading, he began to consider embracing such a life and, abandoning secular military service, serving you. They were among those called *agentes in rebus*—official agents.

“Then, suddenly filled with holy love and wholesome shame, he became angry with himself, fixed his eyes upon his friend, and said: ‘Tell me, I beg you, what do we hope to reach through all these labors of ours? What are we seeking? For what purpose do we serve? Can our hope in the imperial court be greater than becoming the Emperor’s friends? And even there, what is not fragile and full of dangers? Through how many dangers does one reach a greater danger? And when will that be? But if I wish, I can become God’s friend now.’

“He said this, and, troubled by the labor of giving birth to a new life, returned his eyes to the pages. He read, and he was inwardly changed, where you saw him, and his mind was stripped of the world, as soon became evident. For while he read and turned over the movements of his heart, he sometimes groaned deeply, distinguished and decided upon better things, and was already yours.

“He said to his friend: ‘I have now torn myself away from that hope of ours and resolved to serve God; from this hour, in this place, I begin. If you are unwilling to imitate me, do not oppose me.’

“His friend replied that he would remain with him as a companion in so great a reward and so great a service. And both, now yours, were building the tower of abandoning all their possessions at an adequate cost and following you (Luke 14:26–35).

“Then Pontitianus and those who had been walking with him in another part of the garden, searching for them, came to the same place. When they found them, they urged them to return, since the day was declining. But after explaining their decision and purpose, and how such a will had arisen and become firm in them, the two asked that they not be troubled if they refused to return with them.

“The others, however, unchanged from their former state, nevertheless, as he said, wept, piously congratulated them, and commended themselves to their prayers. Dragging their hearts along the earth, they returned to the palace; the two, fastening their hearts to heaven, remained in the hut. Both had fiancées; when these women heard what had happened, they too dedicated their virginity to you.”  
> (*Confessions*, book 8, chapter 6, §§14–15)

4. After Pontitianus had told this story, Augustine continues:

> But you, Lord, were turning me back toward myself through his words, taking me away from the place behind my own back where I had put myself because I did not wish to look at myself. You set me before my own face, so that I might see how ugly I was, how distorted and filthy, stained and covered with sores. I saw and shuddered, and there was nowhere for me to flee from myself. If I tried to turn my gaze away from myself, he continued telling his story, and you again placed me before myself and thrust me into my own eyes, so that I might find my iniquity and hate it.

> I knew it, but I pretended not to; I closed my eyes and forgot it. But then, the more ardently I loved those men of whom I heard such healing dispositions, because they had given themselves wholly to you to be healed, the more hateful I found myself in comparison with them.

> For many of my years had passed away with me—perhaps twelve years—since, in my nineteenth year, after reading Cicero’s *Hortensius*, I had been awakened to the pursuit of wisdom. Yet I kept postponing the abandonment of earthly happiness in order to devote myself to seeking it […]. Thus I was gnawed inwardly and overwhelmed by terrible shame when Pontitianus was speaking in this way.

> When his conversation and the business that had brought him were finished, he departed. And I turned to myself: what did I not say against myself? With what blows of words did I not lash my soul so that it would follow me as I tried to go after you? But it resisted; it refused, and it offered no excuse. All arguments had been exhausted and refuted; only a silent trembling remained. It was as though my soul feared death—that is, being restrained from the flow of the habit by which it was wasting away toward death.

> Then, amid that great struggle within my inner house, which I had stirred up against my soul in the chamber of my heart, disturbed in both face and mind, I seized Alypius and cried out: “What are we suffering? What is this? What have you heard? The uneducated rise up and seize heaven, while we, with all our learning and without a heart, look where we are rolling about in flesh and blood! Is it because they have gone before us that we are ashamed to follow, while we are not ashamed even not to follow?”

> I said something of this kind, and my agitation carried me away from him while he remained silent, staring at me in astonishment. For it was not merely my familiar words that I was uttering; my forehead, cheeks, eyes, complexion, and tone of voice spoke more of my mind than the words I was producing.

> There was a small garden at our lodging, which we used, as we used the whole house. The owner of the house did not live there. The turmoil in my breast had carried me there, where no one would interrupt the fierce struggle that I had begun with myself, until it reached the outcome known to you, though unknown to me. I was only raving in a way that brought healing, and dying in a way that brought life, aware of what evil I was and unaware of what good I would shortly become.

> I went into the garden, and Alypius followed step by step. For my secret was not secret from him when he was present; and when had he ever abandoned me in such a state? We sat as far as possible from the house. I was raging in spirit, burning with the most turbulent indignation, because I was not entering into the agreement and covenant with you, my God, into which all my bones cried out that I must enter and lifted me toward heaven with their praises […]

> If I tore my hair, struck my forehead, or clasped my knee with interlocked fingers, I did so because I willed it. I could have willed it and not done it if the mobility of my limbs had not obeyed. I performed many actions, therefore, in which willing was not the same as being able; yet I did not do what pleased me with incomparably greater feeling and what I could do as soon as I willed it—for as soon as I willed it, I would certainly will it. There the ability was the will, and the willing itself was already the doing.  
> (*ibid.*, chapter 7, §18; chapter 8, §§19–20)

He then teaches at length that the struggle of the human will desiring to return to God arises because the will is divided against itself and is not complete in what it commands. It does not arise because there are two minds, or two natures mutually opposed, as the Manichaeans falsely asserted.

He subsequently relates how, on one side, pleasures shamefully flattering him delayed his hesitation, while on the other a chaste dignity, honorably and gently alluring him, drew him onward. Meanwhile Alypius, clinging to his side, silently awaited the outcome of so extraordinary a movement.

5. But at last he describes the miracle of his conversion in these words:

“But when deep reflection, drawn from the hidden depths, drew together and brought before the sight of my heart all my misery, a mighty storm arose, carrying with it a mighty rain of tears. And in order to pour it all forth together with its accompanying words, I rose from Alypius. Solitude presented itself to me as more suitable for the task of weeping, and I withdrew far enough that even his presence could not burden me. Such was my condition then, and he perceived it: for I think I had said something in which the sound of my voice, already heavy with weeping, could be heard, and so I had risen. He therefore remained where we had been sitting, exceedingly astonished.

“I threw myself down somehow beneath a certain fig tree, and gave free rein to my tears; and streams poured from my eyes, an acceptable sacrifice to you. And although not in these words, yet in this sense, I said many things to you: ‘And you, O Lord, how long? How long, Lord, will you be angry to the end? Do not remember our former iniquities.’ For I felt myself held fast by them, and I uttered pitiable cries: ‘How long, how long shall it be “tomorrow and tomorrow”? Why not now? Why not at this very hour put an end to my uncleanness?’ I said these things and wept with the bitterest contrition of my heart.

“And behold, I hear a voice from a neighboring house, with the sound of singing, saying and repeatedly saying, as though it were a boy or girl—I do not know: ‘Take up and read; take up and read.’ Immediately my countenance changed, and I began most intently to consider whether children were accustomed to sing something like this in any kind of game; nor did I recall ever having heard anything of the sort anywhere. Checking the force of my tears, I rose, interpreting it as nothing other than a divine command to me to open the book and read the first chapter I should find.

“For I had heard of Antony that, from the Gospel reading [Col. 0116] upon which he had happened, he had been admonished as though what was being read were addressed to him: ‘Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’ (Matthew 19:21); and that by such an oracle he had immediately been converted to you.

“Thus I hurried back to the place where Alypius was sitting—for there I had placed the Apostle’s book when I rose. I seized it, opened it, and in silence read the passage upon which my eyes first fell: ‘Not in reveling and drunkenness, not in bedrooms and indecencies, not in strife and rivalry; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires’ (Romans 13:13–14). I had no wish to read further, nor was there any need. For immediately, as the sentence ended, it was as though the light of security had been poured into my heart, and all the darkness of doubt fled away.

“Then, I know not how, I marked the place with either a finger or some other sign, closed the book, and with a now tranquil countenance told Alypius. But he, in turn, indicated what was happening within him—something of which I was unaware. He asked to see what I had read. I showed him, and he read beyond the point where I had stopped, though I did not know what followed. What followed was: ‘But receive the weak in faith’ (Romans 14:1). He applied this to himself and disclosed it to me.

“Strengthened by such an admonition, and by a resolve and purpose entirely suited to his character—by which he had long stood far and greatly apart from me in the better direction—he joined me without any agitated hesitation. From there we went in to my mother and told her. She rejoiced. We recounted how it had happened, and she exulted and triumphed; and she blessed you, who are able to do more than we ask or understand, because she saw that you had granted her far more concerning me than she had been accustomed to ask in her miserable and tearful groans. For you converted me to yourself, so that I would seek neither a wife nor any hope in this world . . .” (*Confessions*, Book 8, chapter 12, §§28–30).

“How sweet it suddenly became for me to be without the sweetnesses of trifles! And what I had feared losing was now a joy to relinquish. For you were casting them out from me, you who are the true and supreme sweetness; you were casting them out and entering in their place, sweeter than every pleasure” (ibid., Book 9, chapter 1, §1).

## CHAPTER VI

1. Why he did not lay down the burden of his teaching before the approaching vintage vacation.  
2. He withdraws with his friends to Verecundus’s estate.

### 1

Augustine, eager to live henceforth for God alone, thought that he ought to do as soon as possible what was required of him: lay down the burden of his public profession. But it seemed best to wait for the vintage vacation, which was conveniently approaching; only about twenty days remained until it, and when they had passed he could, according to customary practice, withdraw and quietly send back his notice resigning the teaching of rhetoric.

“Moreover,” he himself says, “because during that summer my lungs had begun to give way under excessive literary labor, and I had difficulty drawing breath, while pains in my chest testified that they were injured and refused to produce a louder or more sustained voice, I was initially troubled, because this almost compelled me by necessity to lay down the burden of that teaching—or, if I could be treated and recover, at least to interrupt it. But when a full desire arose and was strengthened [Col. 0117] in me to have leisure and to see that you are the Lord, you know, my God, that I also began to rejoice that this too supplied a genuine excuse, which would soften the offense felt by those who, for the sake of their children, were never willing for me to be free” (Confessions, Book 9, chapter 2, §§2–4).

In the earlier books which he had then written, he attributes the reason for his withdrawal to this illness of the chest, silently passing over what had happened to him in the garden (*Against the Academics*, Book 1, §3; *On the Happy Life*, §4; *On Order*, Book 1, §5). He did so, without doubt, out of the same modesty of spirit by which he resolved to communicate his purpose only to his closest friends and to keep it concealed from everyone else (*Confessions*, Book 9, chapter 2, §2).

His heart had been pierced deeply enough by the arrows of divine love and sufficiently fortified with burning coals that he had no fear of the deceitful tongues of those who might have tried by malicious talk to deter him from his purpose. Besides, the examples of holy men, by which he had been stirred to serve God, were applying such ardent torches beneath him that the contrary breath of detraction could only have caused the fire kindled in his spirit to burn more fiercely, not to be extinguished.

Yet, just as there would be good men who would praise his decision, so it seemed to him almost like boastfulness to resign his rhetorical profession before the approaching academic vacation, thereby turning everyone’s attention toward himself, since those who might have attributed this premature abdication from teaching openly to ostentation would have had grounds for doing so. To give rise to so many rash judgments and false reports, and to provide an occasion or cause for criticizing so holy a work and asking with what motive he was undertaking it, seemed contrary to prudence (ibid., §3).

He therefore endured that interval of time until it ran its course. Although it was short, he endured it with difficulty. For that desire for glory, which had habitually come to share the burden with him, had already withdrawn; and, forced to bear the burden alone, he would have collapsed beneath its weight had patience not come to his aid in place of his former ambition. However prudently he had conducted himself in this matter, he nevertheless did not dare to declare himself free from all fault, since, after embracing a firm purpose of serving God, he had still allowed himself to sit for a short time in the chair of falsehood (ibid., §4).

### 2

Verecundus was tormented by anxiety concerning Augustine’s good purpose (ibid., chapter 3, §5). He was Augustine’s friend, a citizen and grammarian of Milan (ibid., Book 8, chapter 6, §13), and his goodwill toward everyone—and especially toward Augustine—was extraordinary (*On Order*, Book 1, §5). He was therefore deeply distressed that, entangled in so many snares of the world, he saw himself about to be deprived of such delightful companionship.

He was not yet a Christian. Although he had married a faithful wife, he was held back from the path on which his friends were embarking by that very tight bond. For he was unwilling to undertake that course except by the lofty rule which he was least able to follow: namely, to separate himself from his wife so that, having abandoned all earthly things, he might devote himself entirely to God. Accordingly, Augustine and Alypius consoled him and urged him to serve God within the married life in which he was bound.

Nothing in his sorrow diminished Verecundus’s goodwill toward them. He kindly offered them his estate at Cassiciacum, so that they might live there for as long as they stayed. They gratefully accepted the [Col. 0118] dwelling he offered them. Hence Augustine, residing on that estate, jokingly said that he was using carelessly the words of grammarians who had given their own property for his use (*On the Happy Life*, §31).

“May you repay him, Lord,” Augustine says, “in the resurrection of the righteous, because you have already repaid him with the very lot he received. For although we were absent—already being at Rome—when he was seized by bodily illness and, having become a Christian and a faithful man in that illness, departed from this life, you had mercy not only on him but also on us, lest, as we considered the exceptional human kindness of our friend toward us while not counting him among your flock, we should be tortured by intolerable grief.

“We give you thanks, our God; we are yours. Your exhortations and consolations show it. Faithful promiser, you will repay Verecundus, in place of that estate of his at Cassiciacum, where we rested from the heat of the world in you, with the beauty of your ever-green paradise; for you forgave him his sins upon the earth, on the cheese-covered mountain, your mountain, the fertile mountain” (*Confessions*, Book 9, chapter 3, §5).

This estate of Verecundus, therefore, seems to have been situated among mountains. At last those days which remained until the academic vacation passed away—the days which, because of his love for the leisure of seeking the face of God, had seemed long and numerous to Augustine. Thus dawned the day on which he actually abandoned the teaching of rhetoric, and on which God drew his tongue away from that profession, from which he had first drawn away his heart (ibid., chapter 4, §7).

So, rejoicing and giving thanks to God, he immediately went with all his companions—that is, his mother Monnica, his brother Navigius, his students Trygetius and Licentius, his cousins Lastidianus and Rusticus, his son Adeodatus, and Alypius—to Verecundus’s estate (*On the Happy Life*, §6).

## CHAPTER VII

1. The source of the controversy concerning the year in which Augustine’s conversion occurred.  
2. Two opinions assign it to the year 387, each twisting Possidius’s and Augustine’s statements on this subject in a different direction.  
3. Nothing prevents us, when those statements are accepted in their proper sense, from asserting that he was converted in 386 and baptized in 387.  
4. Support for this view is gained from a passage of Augustine compared with the time when Ambrose was being harassed by Justina.  
5. The contrary argument drawn from the time when he delivered imperial praises is dissolved.  
6. An opinion placing Augustine’s conversion in 385 is altogether improbable.

### 1

He had spent only a few days at the estate when he began his books *Against the Academics* (*Against the Academics*, Book 1, §4). He interrupted them, however, in order to write the book *On the Happy Life* (*Revisions*, Book 1, chapter 2), a work completed in three days and begun on the birthday of the person in whose honor it was written (*On the Happy Life*, §6), which fell on the Ides of November.

Therefore his withdrawal to the estate at Cassiciacum must have occurred in October, and his conversion in September—or at least toward the end of August. For, after completing his lectures, he could still have remained for several days at Milan. At that time he was in the thirty-third year of his life, as he himself testifies near the end of the books he wrote *Against the Academics* (*Against the Academics*, Book 3, §43), which he completed after the Ides of November. He asserts the same in the books of the *Soliloquies* (*Soliloquies*, Book 1, §17), which he published at about the same time. And when [Col. 0119] his mother Monnica departed this life shortly after his Baptism, he had not yet completed the thirty-third year of his life (*Confessions*, Book 9, chapter 11, §28).

These facts establish that he was converted at the end of his thirty-second year and baptized in his thirty-third year, eight or nine months after his conversion, since he received Baptism at the Easter solemnity.

Possidius, however, reports that he died at the age of seventy-six (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 31), and no one disputes that his death occurred on the fifth day before the Kalends of September in the year 430, as recorded in Prosper’s chronicle. He must therefore have been born on the Ides of November in the year 354; converted in August of 386; and baptized at Easter in 387, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May. For Ambrose had taught that Easter was to be celebrated that year on the seventh day before the Kalends of May (Ambrose, *Letter to Aemilius*).

This chronology would admit no controversy if Augustine had not said that his mother departed this life while he, returning to Africa, was preparing at Ostia on the Tiber to resume his voyage (*Confessions*, Book 9, chapter 8, §17; chapter 10, §23). For it is established, on the one hand, that she died—as we have said—while Augustine was in his thirty-third year, that is, according to our calculation, before the Ides of November 387. On the other hand, we know with certainty that Augustine did not return to Africa until after the death of the usurper Maximus (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, §30), who was killed at the end of July or in August of 388.

### 2

The difficulty of reconciling these two facts divides even the most learned authorities into differing opinions. Some maintain that Possidius, when he writes that Augustine lived seventy-six years, counted his years by consulates. They take the first year to mean the period extending from the Ides of November to the Kalends of January, and the final year to mean the period from the Kalends of January to the fifth day before the Kalends of August. Thus they maintain that Augustine was born on the Ides of November 355, converted in 387, and baptized in 388; and that he actually lived not seventy-six years, but seventy-four, with more than nine or ten additional months.

Others hold that in the third book *Against the Academics* or the first book of the *Soliloquies* he counted only his completed years, not those already begun. Thus, they say, he was born in 354, converted only in 387, and baptized only in 388, after completing his thirty-third year—that is, at the beginning of his thirty-fourth.

Both opinions unquestionably do violence to the words of Augustine or Possidius, forcing us to say that Possidius, who passed forty years together with Augustine and received Augustine’s age from Augustine himself, nevertheless calculated it differently from Augustine. For if Augustine [Col. 0120] had marked his years by consulates, he would not have assigned his books *Against the Academics*, written in November, to the thirty-third year of his life; nor would he have assigned Monnica’s death to that same year, since it occurred so much later. And if only completed years were counted, he should have been credited with seventy-five years of life, and no more.

It may also be observed against the first opinion that, although it was not entirely unusual to count the years of bishops of the city and of emperors by consulates—though this occurred infrequently—their accession and death were recorded in public documents in which the consuls were named, and no one was ignorant of the year. The same cannot reasonably be supposed concerning the birth of a very humble municipal citizen of Thagaste.

As for the second opinion, although it must be admitted that when someone is said to be thirty-three years old the expression can refer either to years begun or to years completed—as when we say that kings become independent in the fourteenth year and others in the twenty-fifth, although the former enter their own authority upon beginning their fourteenth year and the latter upon completing their twenty-fifth—nevertheless it seems wholly contrary to fact to extend this ambiguity of expression to every passage in which Augustine mentions his age, and especially to the passage which ought to serve us as the rule for determining the date of his Baptism:

“On the ninth day of her illness, in the fifty-sixth year of her age and the thirty-third year of mine, that religious and devout soul was released from the body” (*Confessions*, Book 9, chapter 11, §28).

There is no verbal ambiguity here. No one has ever referred an event to the thirty-third year of his life in order to indicate that it occurred as the thirty-fourth year was advancing and more than half of it had already passed. Who, moreover, could suppose that when Augustine said that he was about to recount the history of his twenty-ninth year—“I will speak in the presence of my God of that twenty-ninth year of my life” (ibid., Book 5, chapter 3, §3)—he thought his readers should understand him to mean the history of his thirtieth year?

When he writes that, in the sixteenth year of his life, as he was entering adolescence, he began to obey lust and luxury (ibid., Book 2, chapter 2, §2), we do not know whether it is difficult to believe that an African youth, with the fiery vigor of his spirit, had by then reached sufficient maturity for this.
