Nevertheless, he seems not to have fallen completely into vice until Carthage (ibid., Book 3, chapter 1), that is, in the seventeenth year of his life.

### 3

Since, therefore, both opinions encounter such serious difficulties that those who follow one consider the other forced and wholly improbable, nothing seems to prevent us from standing by Augustine’s words and acknowledging, on his own testimony, that Monnica died when he, returning to Africa, was preparing to resume his voyage, without inferring that immediately after his mother’s death he completed the journey and boarded ship, since he says nothing of the kind.

Nor are formulas of speech such as these foreign to historical narratives: “We were setting out when he arrived”; “We were preparing ourselves for the journey.” Indeed, it seems to belong to the historian’s diligence and duty that, after recounting an event which caused a delay once a plan had been made, he should also [Col. 0121] explain whether the plan was merely postponed or entirely abandoned.

But it is clear that Augustine did not intend to carry the history of his life so far in the first part of his *Confessions*. His sole purpose may have been to bring into view, for the praise and glory of God’s grace, his own character from infancy to his conversion and Baptism. Hence, after narrating his mother’s death, he says not a word about his return to Rome, although it is certain that he stayed there for some time and wrote several books there (*Revisions*, Book 1, chapters 7–9). Moreover, he himself warns us that, being in great haste, he passed over many things in silence (*Confessions*, Book 9, chapter 8, §17).

We therefore in no way contradict his words when we say that, after his mother’s death, he postponed his plan of returning to Africa and completed it only in the following year. The reasons for which he postponed it—of which there may have been many—are unknown to us. It is enough for us that he could have delayed it, although substantial reasoning suggests that the delay and interruption were imposed upon him.

For he writes that, when his mother fell ill, he was at Ostia, where he was recovering his strength after the exertion of a long journey before boarding the ship: “We were preparing ourselves for the voyage” (ibid., chapter 10, §23). Thus, resting at Ostia on the Tiber, he was taking a break from the labor of the journey which he had endured on his return from Milan.

He had therefore certainly remained at Rome for as much time as could have been sufficient for writing the three or four short works which he published there after his Baptism (*Revisions*, Book 1, chapters 7–9). Consequently, his stay in the city must be placed not before but after his mother’s death, and it must be admitted that something prevented him from returning to Africa so quickly.

It could quite plausibly be said that Monnica died at the beginning of November; that, through her death, the opportunity Augustine had intended for his departure slipped away; that no suitable opportunity presented itself during the rest of the year; or that he did not wish to sail in already unfavorable weather and upon a dangerous sea; and finally that, for certain reasons, he was still detained at Rome until August of the following year.

We read, moreover, that navigation was closed from the third day before the Ides of November. Gratian himself decreed in 380 that ships bringing grain to Rome were thereafter not to leave the harbor beyond the Ides of October (*Theodosian Code*, edition of Gothofredus, volume 5, pages 107–108).

The history of the period itself also provides a sufficiently plausible conjecture by which we may infer what could have detained Augustine at Rome until the death of Maximus. In that very year, 387, the usurper invaded Italy around August and, after driving Valentinian from it, likewise occupied Africa, as Pacatus testifies. It could therefore easily have happened that Augustine, informed of these events while he was detained at Ostia on account of his mother’s death, changed his plan and decided to await the outcome of the upheaval at Rome, where he could live more safely from the disasters of civil war than at Thagaste.

From this, we think, it is sufficiently clear that there is no reason requiring us to twist the words of Augustine and Possidius away from their proper sense. [Col. 0122] Indeed, there are several considerations that draw us back from that perverse interpretation.

For if we place Augustine’s conversion in the year 387, we shall be forced to say that he was living in retirement in the countryside near Milan at precisely the time when Maximus, as the history of that period establishes, was invading all Italy and expelling Valentinian from it—that is, in the midst of the storm of war, which was raging nowhere more fiercely than in the region of Milan, since Milan customarily provided the emperor with his residence and seat. Hence Baronius thinks it can be inferred from Ambrose’s words that the citizens of Milan were then considering flight (Baronius, on the year 387, §62).

### 4

When Augustine received Baptism, a year or more had passed since the singing of psalms had begun in the church at Milan, namely when Justina, the mother of the boy-king Valentinian, having been led astray by the Arians, was persecuting Ambrose (*Confessions*, Book 9, chapter 7, §15). Hence Baronius concludes that Augustine was baptized in the year immediately following the end of this persecution (Baronius, on the year 388, §74).

This is correct if we place Augustine’s Baptism in 387, provided that Ambrose’s *Sermon on the Basilicas Not Being Surrendered* was delivered on Palm Sunday, which in 386 fell on the final day of March. For around the time when this sermon was delivered, or a few days before it, the people of Milan began singing psalms in unison. Thus, by the time Augustine was baptized on the eighth day before the Kalends of May in 387, approximately a year and a month had passed.

The chronology of this persecution against Ambrose can be confirmed by the law which Justina arranged to be issued against the orthodox in favor of the Council of Rimini, dated the twelfth day before the Kalends of February in 386. For in Ambrose’s fourteenth letter to his sister Marcellina, which seems to concern the first year of the persecution—for it raged for two years—not a word of that law appears. By contrast, it is frequently mentioned in the *Sermon on the Basilicas Not Being Surrendered*, which unquestionably belongs to the second year.

It is therefore probable that this law was enacted when the persecution was already well advanced. If so, the persecution must necessarily have begun in 385 and ended in 386. Accordingly, Augustine’s Baptism must be placed in 387.

It is likewise worthwhile to observe that Justina’s persecution was still continuing when the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius were discovered, that is, toward the end of June. Since Augustine establishes that the solemnity of this translation was celebrated in Africa (*Sermon* 286, §4), and since this same day is recorded in the old calendar of the Church of Carthage (Mabillon, *Annals*, volume 3, page 398), while there is no other evidence that those holy martyrs were known at that time, it is entirely probable that the nineteenth day of June, which is sacred to them, [Col. 0123] was the day of their translation.

It follows, therefore, that Justina’s persecution did not cease until the end of the June preceding the year of Augustine’s Baptism. All these facts fit together perfectly if we place his Baptism in 387 and his conversion in 386; but we encounter a difficult knot if we assign his conversion to 387.

For it is certain that in that year Maximus invaded Italy, and I think no one will doubt that Ambrose had shortly before carried out the second embassy entrusted to him by Valentinian to Maximus. From Ambrose’s own account it is clear that Maximus, then residing at Trier, was preparing for war; and according to Zosimus, Domninus was sent by Valentinian to Maximus after Ambrose (Zosimus, Book 4). It is not easy or straightforward to place all these events after June.

Furthermore, according to this calculation, Justina must not have ceased harassing Ambrose until she sent him to Maximus to negotiate peace. Yet it is scarcely credible that Justina immediately placed so much hope and confidence in a man against whom she had just employed so many devices to drive him out and who did not appear especially suited to undertaking this mission; for Ambrose’s own account shows that Maximus complained that he had been deceived by Ambrose on the first embassy.

### 5

Those who maintain that Augustine was born only in 355, or that he counted only his completed years, cite another passage in which, as they think, he testifies that he was in his thirtieth year when he delivered an imperial panegyric (*Confessions*, Book 6, chapter 6, §9, and chapter 11, §18).

They take it as certain that this panegyric was the one which he delivered to Bauton when Bauton entered the consulship (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, Book 3, §30), on the Kalends of January in 385. From this they conclude that, since he counted his thirtieth year in 385, he was either born in 355 or did not count the beginning of his thirty-first year.

We observed above that some methods of counting are doubtful and ambiguous, while others are fixed in a single sense. We believe that the expression “I am in my thirtieth year of life” belongs to the latter category and means nothing other than “I have not yet completed my thirtieth year of life.” If you say, “I am thirty years old,” we admit that this can equally mean that you have reached thirty years, whether those years have begun or have been completed.

Accordingly, we shall not deny that the panegyric Augustine mentions, if he delivered it at the age of thirty-one, belongs to the year 385. And in fact, since the various emotional agitations by which he was then tossed appear to have been stirred up by Ambrose’s sermons (*Confessions*, Book 6, chapter 4, §6), it may be conjectured that he had already come to Milan some time before, though not before the Ides of November in 384—if indeed he came to that city only in order to reopen the public schools after the vintage [Col. 0124] vacation of that year.

This, however, is not entirely established or certain; he may have come to Milan at the beginning of 384. Indeed, Rivius places his arrival in 383, and we have nothing to bring forward against that view. Faustus could have come to Carthage before Augustine’s twenty-ninth year, and this seems to be indicated by the words:

“I will speak in the presence of my God of that twenty-ninth year of my life. A certain Manichaean bishop named Faustus had already come to Carthage” (ibid., Book 5, chapter 3, §3).

Augustine could therefore have seen Faustus and become alienated from him as early as the end of 382; he could have come to Rome at the end of that year or the beginning of 383, and could have been sent to Milan before the vintage vacation of 383 had ended.

For if arguments are lacking to prove that Symmachus held the prefecture of the City in 383, arguments are equally lacking on the opposite side. According to this calculation, the panegyric which he appears to imply was delivered in his thirtieth year could have been given either at the beginning of 384 or at another time during that year.

No arguments can establish that it was the same panegyric which he delivered to the consul Bauton; and it is much more probable that it was another panegyric, since he calls it praise of the emperor (ibid., Book 6, chapter 6, §9).

As for why Augustine—something which also caused some people to err—when showing that he had been absent from Africa in 386, when the Manichaeans were condemned, silently passed over that earlier imperial panegyric (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, Book 3, §30), and merely testified that he had come to Milan before Bauton’s consulship (ibid.), at whose entry into office he had delivered a panegyric, the answer is easy and straightforward.

Since frequent opportunities for praising the emperor could have arisen, he needed to demonstrate by new arguments that the panegyric in question had been delivered to the emperor in 384, not in 387. He was therefore content to provide an adequate and entirely certain proof, all the clearer because the condemnation of the Manichaeans appears to have been dated in these words: “In the year after the consulship of Bauton,” and so forth.

For the same reason, doubtless, he says nothing of having stayed at Rome before setting out for Milan. Nevertheless, we have preferred to record Augustine’s arrival at Milan only in 384, because that opinion is more widely accepted and is entirely consistent with Augustine’s words, while it does not require us to suppose that Symmachus had already held the prefecture of the City from 384 onward, for which there is no visible evidence.

If Augustine arrived at the beginning of 384, it may be held that he delivered the imperial panegyric before completing his thirtieth year.

### 6

Another difficulty may arise from a different passage: [Col. 0125] namely, when he was converted to Christ, many years had already passed—as he relates in the *Confessions*—perhaps twelve, since he had read Cicero’s *Hortensius* in the nineteenth year of his life (*Confessions*, Book 8, chapter 7, §17).

There is no better way of removing this difficulty than the one suggested by Augustine himself. By adding the word “perhaps,” he sufficiently indicates that he is not speaking there with exactness and precision, just as in nearly the same passage he expresses that period as “ten years and more” (*Confessions*, Book 8, chapter 7, §18).

In his *Soliloquies*, however, which, as we have said, he wrote shortly after his conversion, he testifies that approximately fourteen years had passed (*Soliloquies*, Book 1, §17).

Nevertheless, relying on this one passage of the *Confessions*, Baronius placed Augustine’s conversion in the thirty-first year of his life, in the year 385. He was thereby forced to insert two years and several additional months between Augustine’s conversion and Baptism.

But it is clear from what has been said that this cannot in any way be defended, nor can the claim that Monnica died only on the fourth day before the Nones of May in 389, that is, after a year and more had elapsed since Augustine’s conversion, and that Augustine did not return to Africa until that same year, 389. According to that calculation, no more than two years would have elapsed between his return and his presbyterate, whereas Possidius places three years between them.

## CHAPTER VIII

1. What exercises occupied Augustine in the countryside.  
2. How he educated two young men there.  
3. He first composes the book *Against the Academics*.  
4. From there he turns his hand to certain other short works.  
5. He returns to the Academics and completes the second and third books on them.  
6. On Romanianus, to whom he dedicated these books *Against the Academics*.  
7. The book *On the Happy Life*, written for Theodorus.  
8. The two books *On Order*.  
9. He restrains movements of rivalry and empty boasting in his students.  
10. Why the work *On Order* was dedicated to Zenobius.

1. To resume the sequence of Augustine’s history: “I resigned,” he says, “when the vintage season was over, so that the people of Milan might provide another seller of words for their schoolboys; for I had chosen to serve you, and I was not equal to that profession because of difficulty in breathing and chest pain. And through a letter I disclosed to your bishop, the holy man Ambrose, my former errors and my present desire, asking him to advise me what I should read above all from your Books, so that I might become readier and better prepared to receive so great a grace. But he ordered the prophet Isaiah. I believe this was because, more clearly than the others, he announces beforehand the calling of the nations and the Gospel. Yet, not understanding the first reading of this book, and judging the whole work to be of the same character, I deferred returning to it until I had become more practiced in the Lord’s eloquence” (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 5, §13).

While they were staying at the country estate of Cassiciacum, Monnica had undertaken, as one may properly suppose, the household responsibilities and prepared their food (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §13; *Confessions*, book 9, chapter 4, §8, and chapter 9, §22). Augustine distributed the agricultural labor among the peasants and directed their work (*Against the Academics*, book 1, §15, and book 2, §10). He spent a large part of his time—sometimes unwillingly—in these domestic duties and in writing letters (*ibid.*, book 2, §25, and book 3, §2). He took only as much food as was sufficient to restrain hunger (*ibid.*, book 2, §14), and his lunch had the same beginning and end (*ibid.*, book 3, §7).

He did not rise from his bed before daylight. Yet, since at that time he performed this activity in darkness—a practice which, he testifies, was almost necessary even for the wealthy in Italy—he had long been accustomed, out of a desire to seek the truth, to spend the first, or the last, and certainly nearly half, of the night awake in meditation. He also instructed the young men to do something inwardly after his example and to accustom their minds to dwell with themselves (*On Order*, book 1, §6). Rising from his bed, he paid his daily vows to God (*ibid.*, §25) and presented humble complaints about his ignorance and wounds (*ibid.*, §13). Then, conversing with his companions about something useful, whatever came before his eyes sometimes provided him with material for discussing the highest matters (*Against the Academics*, book 3, §§33–34).

2. Among others, he had brought with him Trygetius and Licentius, both from Thagaste (*The Happy Life*, §6). Licentius, the son of Romanianus, had already been Augustine’s student when Augustine taught at Carthage (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §3). He embraced these young men with singular affection and devoted all his thought and care to forming their character (*On Order*, book 1, §29). He also worked to imbue them with liberal and humane letters, since this was why he kept them with him. “For,” he says, “the education provided by the liberal disciplines, if modest and concise, makes lovers of truth more alert, more persevering, and more refined, so that they desire it more ardently, pursue it more steadfastly, and finally cling more sweetly to what is called, Licentius, the happy life” (*ibid.*, §24).

Later, however, he realized that in this praise of the liberal disciplines he had exceeded proper limits. Even then he encouraged Licentius toward them only timidly and hesitantly; although Licentius was still a young man, Augustine was more intent on kindling in him a love of truth and wisdom—both of which are truly Christ (*Against the Academics*, book 3, §7; Paulinus, among Augustine’s letters, 32.5).

With Licentius and his companion Trygetius, Augustine himself often discussed very grave and serious matters, both to test their learning and to strengthen and advance them toward higher things by rousing them through planned disputation. “For,” he used to say, “when great matters are sought from the small, they commonly make them great” (*Against the Academics*, book 1, §6). Accordingly, whereas those who are driven to dispute not by a desire to find the truth but by childish intellectual vanity scarcely allow themselves to return to what their opponent has rashly conceded, he prescribed the opposite rule for them: matters that had perhaps been stated too cautiously were to be examined afresh from the beginning. Thus they were led to regard it as no small progress in philosophy when, in comparison with the discovery of what is right and true, the disputant’s victory was despised (*ibid.*, §8). He delivered a remarkable speech on this subject in their presence, which we reproduce below (see §9).

This method of training, which Augustine adopted, benefited Trygetius and Licentius so greatly that those who had previously known them could scarcely believe that they had become so ardent in investigating great matters and, at that age, had declared war on pleasures (*On Order*, book 2, §29). Licentius therefore quite reasonably wished afterward to recall those happiest days which he had spent with the holy Teacher in the heart of Italy amid the most delightful leisure (*Poem to Augustine, his teacher*, lines 52 ff., in volume 2, Letter 26). Whatever was said in these conversations was immediately taken down in writing by a shorthand writer (*On Order*, book 1, §5). Augustine always made use of this practice, both so that he would not allow anything good to be lost and because he saw that it was beneficial to his health. He suffered from some difficulty in speaking, and at that time he was in such poor health that he could not write with his own hand (*Soliloquies*, book 1, §16).

3. From these conversations came various short works by Augustine, published in dialogue form, in which those familiar and learned gatherings are presented in entirely natural and pleasant speech. He reports the very words that he and Alypius had used in those conversations; for the others, however, he reproduced only their opinions (*Against the Academics*, book 1, §4).

Of all the works that he composed during that period, when, after renouncing everything, he withdrew into the leisure of Christian life, while he was still unbaptized, the first was the work written *Against the Academics*, or *On the Academics* (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 1). As we have said, he had fallen into the errors of those philosophers who forbade the wise person to assent to anything as certain and evident, and wanted everything to appear obscure and doubtful to us; by this means they instilled despair of finding the truth in many people.

The opinion which their false arguments had impressed upon his mind had not yet been completely erased. Yet when, at one point in this work, he says that he still has no certain opinion except that it seemed probable to the Academics that the truth could not be found, while to him it seemed probable that it could be found (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §23), who would not understand that he said this figuratively, in the customary manner of dialogues? For, as he expressly says elsewhere, he already possessed a certain apprehension of the truth (*Confessions*, book 8, chapter 5, §11).

Since the matter was of the greatest importance for salvation, he resolved to attack, with every argument at his disposal, those philosophers who closed the door of truth by removing all hope of finding it. Accordingly, a few days after his withdrawal to the country estate, he ordered Trygetius and Licentius to debate this matter with each other: the latter was to support the Academic position, while the former was to attack it in the presence of Augustine and Alypius.

Navigius was present but contributed little. Alypius also departed shortly afterward (*Against the Academics*, book 1, §8), since he had to travel to Milan (*ibid.*, §5). The others, however, continued the conversation for three successive days (*ibid.*, §§11, 15), apparently on November 10, 11, and 12, or on November 4, 12, and 13, during the morning hours. This three-day disputation formed the first of the three books written *Against the Academics*. Augustine completed it, saying that the controversy could have been concluded in a few words if he had not wished to exercise the young men and especially to test their strength and zeal.

4. After that conversation they rested from disputation for about seven days (*ibid.*, book 2, §10). During this interval, before he had completed the books *On the Academics*, he composed the book *The Happy Life* (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 2), from conversations held over three days—November 13, 14, and 15—in the afternoon. He also composed two books *On Order* (*ibid.*, chapter 3), the first of which contains the conversations of two days, apparently November 16 and 17 (*On Order*, book 1, §27).

Thus, in the book *The Happy Life*, Augustine writes that, from their statements, the entire undertaking which they had begun against the Academics had been completed, and that Licentius everywhere supported the Academic side (*The Happy Life*, §13). In the first book *On Order*, however, Trygetius exclaims: “We have now, what is more, a Licentius who is not an Academic” (*On Order*, book 1, §10), for Licentius had been accustomed to defend them with the greatest zeal.

5. After only a few days—three or four at most—had passed since the two-day conversation from which the first book *On Order* arose, Alypius returned from Milan (*ibid.*, book 2, §1). Augustine then resumed the discussion of the Academics, which had been interrupted for eight days (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §10).

For some time Licentius supported the Academic position against Trygetius and Augustine himself; afterward he yielded his place to Alypius. With Alypius, Augustine no longer engaged in preliminary play for the amusement of the mind, as he had earlier with Licentius, but treated the matter seriously, as though it were of the greatest importance. On that day, however, and also on the following day, they merely touched upon the question. On the third day, when Alypius himself abandoned the Academic cause which he had been defending, Augustine concluded the entire disputation in a rather lengthy speech. From that speech, any prudent person can readily understand the danger faced by those who order their lives according to probability (*ibid.*, book 3, §§35–36).

Augustine also attempted to clear the Academics and to show that they had not held the opinion that the truth could not be found (*ibid.*, §§37–38). This conjecture was useful, even if it was not certain (*Letter 1*). He further observes that the various philosophical schools then appeared to have been reduced to one.

In any case, this debate, through the arguments of the Academics—which perhaps still troubled him—freed his mind, with God’s mercy and assistance (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 1, §1), and completely severed the restraint by which, before his conversion, his mind had been held back from the breast of philosophy by despair of finding the truth (*Letter 1, §3).

Therefore, as he brings the work to an end, he declares that he no longer despairs of attaining wisdom; that he has resolved to labor toward its attainment, setting aside all the other things that mortals esteem; and that, since we are driven to learn by the twofold weight of authority and reason, he will never depart from the authority of Christ, as the strongest of all. He also declares his confidence that he will find among the Platonists whatever does not conflict with the sacred Scriptures and can be grasped through understanding (*Against the Academics*, book 3, §43).

In his books *Retractions*, however, he condemns and rejects the praise by which he had exalted Plato and his followers so highly (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 1, §4).

Alypius declared that he had nothing to set against Augustine’s arguments. At the same time, in a very beautiful compliment, he added that he was leaving happily, defeated, and that he and his fellow disputants had Augustine as their leader—a leader who, by the gift of divine light, would lead them into the very secrets of truth (*Against the Academics*, book 3, §44).

When Hermogenianus, a friend of Augustine, had read these books, he congratulated him by letter on his victory over the Academics. His approval was especially pleasing to Augustine because he knew that Hermogenianus’s judgment was free from error and his friendship free from pretense. Accordingly, in the letter he writes to him, Augustine asks him to consider more carefully what he has said in these books about the true position of the Academics and to inform him by letter of his own view on the matter (*Letter 1, §3).

6. Augustine dedicated these books *On the Academics* to Romanianus, both to delight him with the literary progress of his son Licentius and to lead him toward the love of truth. Augustine earnestly desired that Romanianus should devote his mind to the love of wisdom, hoping that he would drink it in more eagerly the longer he had seemed to thirst for it.

He also considered him better prepared to investigate and love the truth because he had often been angered by the Academics, who called everything into doubt. Yet he was still entangled in the superstition of the Manichaeans, into which Augustine himself had recklessly thrown him (*Against the Academics*, book 1, §3).

But when Romanianus apparently visited Augustine at Cassiciacum, he departed almost shaken from his former opinion and now prepared to seek the truth, which the holy man hoped to demonstrate to him either in some conversation or in a discussion of religion sent to him. Since Augustine had conceived the hope that he would lead him to true wisdom, he tried by daily prayers—which he offered to Divine Wisdom for Romanianus’s sake—to obtain this gift for him, “if,” he says, “I am worthy to obtain it.”

Did Augustine, then, say this of Romanianus in vain: “He to whom I have wholly given myself, whom I have now begun somewhat to recognize, will not permit it” (*ibid.*, book 2, §2)?

In order to instill in him some taste for the philosophy to which he was urging him, Augustine inscribed to him his books *On the Academics*. He believed that this stimulus would be more effective because it would also be more pleasant, since Romanianus’s son Licentius could claim a share in them. Augustine admits that he envies only one thing in Romanianus’s fortune: that he alone enjoys his “Lucilianus” (*ibid.*, §9).

This person was undoubtedly very close to Romanianus, and perhaps his brother; for at one point they are joined as two almost equal persons. Augustine promises Romanianus a poem on philosophy composed by Licentius (*ibid.*, §7).

7. Among the conversations that constitute the three books *On the Academics*, the book *The Happy Life* was composed (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 2). It should not seem surprising, therefore, if Alypius was not present at it (*The Happy Life*, §6), for he had left for Milan after the discussion against the Academics had begun and did not return until ten days later.

While he was absent, Augustine’s birthday arrived—the day falling on the Ides of November. Augustine invited all his companions to a modest meal: his mother Monnica, his brother Navigius, his students Licentius and Trygetius, his cousins Lastidianus and Rusticus, and his son Adeodatus. Afterward he invited them to sit together in the baths.

He asked them many questions about happiness, intending to lead them into this harbor. In that conversation, it is certain that Monnica and Adeodatus excelled among them all in the prudence of their understanding and the gravity of their words. He continued the same discussion during the afternoon of the second and third days, and concluded it with a beautiful and sublime discourse on the Most Holy Trinity.

The purpose of these conversations was to teach that the happy life consists in perfect knowledge of God (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 2). Yet he later regretted having maintained in that discussion that happiness could also be attained by the wise person in this life and that it resided solely in the mind.

Augustine notes in his *Retractions* that he does not possess the work in its entirety (*ibid.*), since all copies, both his own and those of others, are found mutilated and considerably abridged. Nevertheless, we do not see which part of the book now lacks anything.

He dedicated the work to Mallius Theodorus, whose conversations, he writes, taught him that when one thinks about God or the soul, one must think of nothing bodily. Theodorus stood out greatly in the world. He was undoubtedly the same man who held the highest offices and served as consul in the year 399.

The poet Claudian celebrates him with the highest praise, especially for his singular moderation and integrity of spirit (*Claudius Claudianus, Panegyric on the Consulship of Flavius Mallius Theodorus*). Yet the praises Augustine bestows on him are more certain and far greater. At one point Augustine testifies that he was both Christian and learned (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 2); elsewhere he commends him as a man outstanding in talent, glory, the very insignia of fortune, and—what is most important—in mind (*On Order*, book 1, §31).

When dedicating the work in question to him, Augustine calls him both most cultivated and a great man. He was certainly very close to him, since Augustine appeals to the bond and communion of their souls, asking him to love him and to believe that he, in turn, is loved by him.

Augustine declares that he is not at all intimidated by Theodorus’s eloquence. Since eloquence was the ability he loved, he could not fear it, although he had not yet attained it. Still less did he fear the height and splendor of Theodorus’s fortune. “For although it is great among you,” he says, “it is secondary: for it makes those over whom it rules themselves secondary.”

He adds that Theodorus is the one person whom he looks up to and admires, and from whom he confidently expects help. He earnestly begs him, therefore, to extend his helping hand in accordance with his goodwill toward him. “If I obtain this,” he says, “I shall approach the happy life, to which I presume you already cling, with little effort and the greatest ease” (*The Happy Life*, §5).

This is undoubtedly the passage which Augustine, now more advanced in age and piety, testifies displeased him because he had attributed too much to a human being (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 2).

Theodorus was a very devoted student of Platonic philosophy. Through his favor toward learned men, he worked to ensure that no one, either in his own age or among posterity, could complain that his times had produced fewer learned men than other ages.

8. After the book *The Happy Life*, Augustine places the discussions *On Order*, arranged in two books (*ibid.*, chapter 3). He composed the first before Alypius had returned from Milan (*On Order*, book 1, §7, and book 2, §1), and therefore before the second book *Against the Academics*.

Navigius, who was still staying at the country estate of Cassiciacum on November 15, or at least November 14, had gone to Milan when the first book *On Order* was begun (*The Happy Life*, §20). He had left Cassiciacum early in the morning (*On Order*, book 1, §7), apparently on November 16.

The second book *On Order* cites the book *The Happy Life* more than once, as does the third book *Against the Academics*, which must consequently have been written between the two books *On Order*.

These two books contain conversations held with Licentius and Trygetius, in which Monnica sometimes took part. Alypius was also present at the discussions of the second book.

In these books the serious question is discussed whether the order of divine providence contains all good and evil things (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 3, §1). But since the most difficult matters arose, and Augustine understood that his listeners could be led to grasp them only with great effort, in the final part of the second book he preferred to speak about the order of study—how one must rise from bodily things to knowledge of spiritual realities.

9. Nothing more pleasant or agreeable can be imagined as the occasion and origin of this conversation, which is reported in the opening chapters of the first book, than the fight between gamecocks which Augustine describes there vividly (*On Order*, book 1, §25).

Yet what is read near the end of that book is too important to be passed over. There, this excellent teacher—not merely of language but also of the mind and of virtue—shows, by a grave and serious rebuke of his students, how the impulses of rivalry and empty boasting must be restrained in young men devoted to study.

Trygetius had said something for which Augustine had been forced to rebuke him. When Trygetius realized that he had spoken wrongly, he asked that his words be erased. Licentius insisted that they remain, “as boys do—or rather, disgracefully, as nearly all human beings do—as though we were doing this among ourselves for the sake of boasting.”

“When I rebuked this movement of his mind with rather severe words, he blushed. From his agitation I noticed that Trygetius was laughing and rejoicing. And I said to both of them:

‘Is this how you behave? Are you not moved by the great burdens of vice and the darkness of ignorance under which we are weighed down and buried? Is this the attentiveness and rising toward God and truth which you displayed a little earlier, and over which I foolishly rejoiced?

‘If only you could see—even with eyes as bleary as mine—in what dangers we lie, and what madness of disease that laughter reveals! If only you could see! How quickly, how immediately, and how much more fully you would turn it into tears!

‘Wretches, do you not know where we are? It is common to all foolish and ignorant people that their minds are submerged; but Wisdom does not extend help and a hand to all who are submerged in one and the same way. Believe me, there are some who are called upward, and others who are allowed to sink into the depths.

‘Do not, I beg you, double my miseries. Let my wounds be enough—the wounds for which I ask God almost daily with tears to be healed, though I often prove to myself that I am less worthy to be healed as quickly as I wish.

‘Do not, I beg you. If you owe me any love or affection, if you understand how much I love you, how highly I value you, and how greatly concern for your character agitates me; if I am worthy of not being neglected by you; if, finally, with God as my witness I am not lying when I say that I desire nothing more for myself than for you—repay me this favor.

‘And if you willingly call me teacher, pay me my reward: be good.’

At this point, so that I might say no more, tears imposed silence upon me. Licentius was extremely distressed that everything was being written down.

‘What have we done, I ask you?’ he said.

‘Even now,’ I replied, ‘you do not at least confess your sin? Do you not know that in that school I used to become deeply angry because the boys were driven not by the usefulness and dignity of their studies but by the most empty love of praise, so much so that some were not ashamed to recite the words of others and to receive applause—an evil to be lamented—from the very people whose words they were reciting?

‘Although you have never, as I think, done anything of that kind, you nevertheless attempt to introduce and propagate into philosophy, and into the life which I rejoice to have finally embraced, the final—and more harmful than all the others—plague of wasting rivalry and empty boasting.

‘Perhaps, because I am deterring you from this vanity and disease, you will become more sluggish in your studies; and, driven back from the ardor of windy fame, you will freeze into the torpor of inactivity.

‘Wretched me, if I must still endure people of such a kind—people from whom vices cannot depart without other vices taking their place!’

‘You will see,’ said Licentius, ‘how much more purified we shall become. We ask you by everything you love to forgive us and to order all those words erased.’

‘Let our punishment remain,’ said Trygetius, ‘so that the very fame which tempts us may, by its own scourge, deter us from loving it. We shall take no small pains to ensure that these writings become known only to our friends and intimates.’

Augustine agreed” (*ibid.*, book 1, §§29–30).

Augustine ordered Licentius to write a poem against lustful loves and in praise of pure love, by which the soul is joined through philosophy to the intellect (*ibid.*, §24). We do not know whether this is the poem on philosophy which the holy Teacher promised to Romanianus.

10. Augustine dedicated his books *On Order* to Zenobius, who was concerned about Licentius because he was very close to Licentius’s father.

Zenobius had often discussed the order of things with Augustine. Yet when he asked him about sublime matters, Augustine had never been able to satisfy him fully, whether because of the loftiness of the subjects or because of lack of time; he had always deferred the answer to another occasion. Wearied by this delay, Zenobius challenged Augustine in an elegant poem to give a fuller and more precise response.

But when Zenobius was unexpectedly forced to leave Milan because of a sudden disturbance, whose cause is not reported, he forgot to leave the poem with Augustine so that Augustine might answer it (*ibid.*, §20).

We do not know whether this was the very matter about which Augustine, writing to Zenobius, said that the discussion begun with him was to be completed with him (*Letter 2*). Zenobius was absent at that time. Augustine tells him that, although he had not yet attained the state in which he loved nothing whose absence could distress him, he was held by longing for his absent friend and wished likewise to be missed by his friends.

When this letter was sent cannot be determined, nor whether it was sent during Augustine’s retreat. In the later book *On Order*, Augustine promises that, if he has leisure, he will speak afterward about the soul (*On Order*, book 2, §17). Yet we do not see that he fulfilled this promise in the course of his discussion. Perhaps he was already meditating in his mind upon the book *On the Quantity of the Soul*, which he composed at Rome about a year later.

## CHAPTER IX

1. Augustine strives to advance more and more in the knowledge of truth.  
2. The fiery ardor of his devotion.  
3. With God’s help he frees himself from his ingrained habit of swearing.  
4. He is divinely healed of toothache.  
5. The *Soliloquies*, in which the state of his soul is examined.  
6. Why they were called *Soliloquies*, and the subject of those books.

1. From the books which Augustine wrote during conversations with his friends in his retreat, one can see how he lived there, what fruit he drew from his leisure, and in what studies he finally invested the learning and education granted to him by God. Although he had devoted all of this to divine worship, he nevertheless still seemed to retain something of the school of pride, as happens to those who gasp after a long race even when they pause to catch their breath (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 4, §7).

Moreover, in this respect his devotion was somewhat opposed by Alypius, who at first forbade him to insert the name of our Savior Jesus Christ into his books, preferring Augustine’s style to breathe the fragrance of the lofty cedars of philosophy and eloquence rather than the humble grasses of the Gospel and the Church—grasses wholesome to souls and hostile to serpents.

During that retreat Augustine rejoiced as though freed from the snares of the world’s superfluous desires; he breathed as though released from the burden of earthly cares; he repented of his error; he returned to himself; and he sought the truth with the greatest concentration (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §4).

At that time he felt how heavily he was burdened by vices and how densely he was overwhelmed by the darkness of ignorance. He asked God almost daily, with tears, for healing of his wounds; nevertheless, he persuaded himself that he was less worthy to be healed as quickly as he wished (*On Order*, book 1, §29).

He was still wavering over the question of the soul (*The Happy Life*, §5), and did not know that the Spirit of Truth, the Paraclete, had been sent by Christ the Lord (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 4, §9). He was therefore fully convinced that his ignorance was greater than he understood (*On Order*, book 2, §9), and he confessed that he was a child in philosophy, far from considering himself wise (*ibid.*, book 1, §13).

Yet he burned with an extremely ardent desire to learn, and for that one reason he stayed awake night and day (*ibid.*, §12). He devoted himself solely to cleansing his mind of the false and harmful opinions that disturbed it (*Against the Academics*, book 2, §9).

Since he already knew that the truth cannot be grasped without divine assistance, he expected it from God alone in order to refute falsehood, and from him he sought help in his studies with every form of devotion and piety. Although he questioned God himself every day with humble complaints and tears, he was nevertheless ready to receive an answer in whatever manner God might deem appropriate.

2. In Augustine’s earliest short works one can see more fully how much, though recently converted and having scarcely emerged from the darkness of his ignorance and error, he already possessed in learning and wisdom. It was certainly far greater than is usually found even among more advanced believers.

Yet one may affirm that his charity—that is, his love of truth—was much greater than that learning, of which charity was the source and origin. It is therefore not at all surprising that he later said that some catechumens are occasionally found who surpass many of the faithful both in learning and in conduct (*Exposition on Psalm 90*, sermon 2, §6).

Later it was sweet for him to recall how God was then driving his heart like a goad and subduing it: while God pressed down the mountains of empty and proud thoughts, leveled the valleys, straightened the crookedness of his character and disposition, and smoothed what was rough (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 4, §7).

“What words I gave you, my God,” he says in his *Confessions*, “when I read the Psalms of David, faithful songs and sounds of devotion that exclude the swelling spirit—still untrained in your genuine love, a catechumen resting in the country estate with the catechumen Alypius, while my mother clung to us, in womanly dress, manly faith, an old woman’s serenity, a mother’s love, and Christian devotion?

“What words I gave you in those psalms, and how I was inflamed toward you by them, and kindled to recite them, if I could, throughout the whole world against the pride of the human race! And yet they are sung throughout the whole world, and no one hides from your warmth.

“How vehemently and bitterly I was indignant against the Manichaeans, and yet again pitied them, because they did not know those sacraments, those remedies, and were mad against the antidote by which they could have been made whole!

“I wished that they might be somewhere nearby; then, without my knowing that they were there, they could look upon my face and hear my voice when I read the fourth psalm and learn what that psalm had done with me in that time of leisure.

“I shuddered in fear, and there I grew fervent in hope and rejoicing in your mercy, Father. All these emotions issued through my eyes and my voice when, turned toward us, your good Spirit said to us:

‘Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?’

“I heard this and trembled, because such words were addressed to people such as I remembered myself to have been. And I uttered many words, grave and forceful, in the pain of my recollection. Would that those who still love vanity and seek falsehood had heard them! Perhaps they would have been disturbed and vomited it forth.

“I read: ‘Be angry, and do not sin.’ And how was I moved, my God, I who had already learned to be angry with myself because of my past sins, so that I might sin no more in the future? …

“No longer were my goods outside me, nor were they sought by bodily eyes in this sun. If only they could see the inner and eternal reality which I had tasted and for which I gnawed with longing, because I could not show it to them!

“For there, where I was angry with myself inwardly in my chamber, where I was pierced with remorse, where I had sacrificed my old self by slaying it, and where, with the meditation of my renewal begun, I hoped in you—there you had begun to grow sweet to me, and you had given gladness to my heart.

“And I cried out while reading these words outwardly and recognizing them inwardly. I no longer wished to multiply earthly goods, devouring time and devoured by time, since I possessed another grain, wine, and oil in eternal simplicity.

“And in the following verse I cried out with a loud cry from my heart: ‘O in peace! O into the same state!’ What did he say? ‘I shall lie down and sleep.’ For who will resist us when the word is fulfilled which is written: ‘Death is swallowed up in victory’” (1 Corinthians 15:54)?

“And you are that same One, very truly, who do not change; and in you there is rest, forgetful of all labors, for there is no other beside you, nor are there many other things to attain that are not what you are; but ‘you, Lord, have established me uniquely in hope.’

“I read, and I burned; yet I could find nothing to do with those deaf dead among whom I had been a pest, a bitter and blind barker against the writings sweeter than honey from heaven and radiant with your light. And I wasted away over the enemies of this Scripture when I recalled all the days of that leisure” (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 4, §§8–12).

3. At about this time, apparently, he corrected the habitual practice of swearing which he had acquired.

“We too swore indiscriminately,” he says to his people; “we had this most dreadful and deadly habit. I tell your Charity: from the time we began to serve God, and saw how great an evil perjury is, we became exceedingly afraid, and by fear we restrained this most deeply rooted habit” (*Sermon* 180, §10).

“I struggled against my habit; in that struggle I called upon the Lord as my helper. The Lord granted me help not to swear. Nothing is easier for me than not to swear” (*Sermon* 307, §5).

“This habit, once restrained, is tightened; once tightened, it grows weak; once weakened, it dies; and a good habit takes the place of the evil one” (*Sermon* 180, §10).

From that time onward he still occasionally swore, but only when compelled by great necessity. For when he saw that he was not believed unless he swore, and that it was not beneficial for the person who did not believe him to remain unbelieving, after weighing and carefully considering the matter he would say, with great fear, in the solemn words of Paul: “Before God” (Galatians 1:20); or, “God is my witness” (Romans 1:9); or, “Christ knows that this is so in my heart” (2 Corinthians 11:31). Examples of such oaths may perhaps be found here and there in his writings. Apart from this necessity, no one ever heard him swear.

### 4

While the holy Man was living in retirement, God permitted him to be afflicted by such an acute toothache that he had never experienced anything comparable. He could not direct his mind toward learning anything new, and could scarcely turn over in his thoughts even what he had perhaps already learned. Nevertheless, it seemed to him that, if the splendor of truth shone upon his mind, he would either not feel that pain or would at least endure it more easily (*Soliloquies*, book 1, no. 21).

But God, who had chastised him so severely, raised him up with no less wondrous speed. “When the pain,” he says, “grew so severe that I was unable to speak, it came into my heart to urge all my companions who were present to pray to you for me, God of complete salvation. And I wrote this on a wax tablet and gave it to them to read. As soon as we bent our knees in supplication, that pain fled. But what pain was it, and how did it flee? I was astonished, I confess, my Lord and my God; for I had experienced nothing like it since childhood. And your signs were impressed upon me in the depths; rejoicing in faith, I praised your name. Yet that faith did not permit me to feel secure about my former sins, which had not yet been forgiven me through your Baptism” (*Confessions*, book 9, no. 12).

### 5

During this period that devout Catechumen published his books of the *Soliloquies*, in which he wonderfully expresses the inward condition of his soul. First of all, he declares that he is held by an extraordinary desire to know God, and that he does not know anything in the way in which he longs to know God (*Soliloquies*, book 1, no. 7). For it is not enough for him to know God in the way in which he knows his friend Alypius (*ibid.*, no. 8), nor even to know the more certain principles of mathematics, which had almost slipped from his memory because of his love of God (*ibid.*, nos. 10–11).

When he asks himself whether he loves anything besides the knowledge of God and of himself, he says:

> “I could answer that I love nothing more, according to the understanding I now possess; but I answer more safely that I do not know. For it often happens to me that, although I thought I was moved by nothing else, something nevertheless comes into my mind and pricks me quite differently from what I had supposed. Likewise, although some matter has entered my thoughts without penetrating me, yet when it actually comes it disturbs me more than I had thought. But at present I seem able to be moved by only three things: fear of losing those whom I love, fear of pain, and fear of death” (*ibid.*, no. 16).

The desire for riches and honors had departed from his soul. The pleasantness of foods did not entice him in those things from which he had determined to abstain. He did make use of other foods, not without some pleasure, but in such a way that he could easily restrain himself from them; nor did the appetite for food ever draw him away from those matters upon which he wished to meditate. In short, from food, drink, baths, and the other things of that kind belonging to the body, he took only what concern for his health required.

As for love of a wife:

> “However much you may wish to portray her and heap upon her every good quality, I have resolved that nothing is to be fled from more than sexual intercourse. I perceive that nothing casts a manly soul down from its citadel more than the caresses of women and that bodily contact without which a wife cannot be possessed. Therefore, if it belongs to the duty of a wise man—a matter I have not yet discovered—to provide children, anyone who has intercourse solely for this purpose may seem to me worthy of admiration, but in no way of imitation. For to attempt this is more dangerous than it is possible to accomplish successfully. Accordingly, I believe that I have imposed upon myself, with sufficient justice and usefulness, for the freedom of my soul, that I should neither desire, seek, nor marry a wife. I seek nothing of this kind at all; I desire nothing, even when I recall such matters with horror and disgust. What more do you want? This good also increases in me day by day: for the more my hope of seeing that beauty for which I burn grows, the more all my love and pleasure are turned toward it” (*ibid.*, book 1, no. 17).

Nevertheless, at times, by God’s permission, he was pierced by the sharp goads of lust, which had exercised such tyranny over him, so that he might recognize both the illness from which he had escaped through the care of the heavenly Physician and what still remained in him to be cured. When this occurred, he was flooded with shame and poured out a torrent of tears, even at the cost of his health. He dared promise himself nothing and presume nothing about himself; his sole consolation was to flee into God’s embrace and entrust himself to God’s providence.

> “May he whom I burn to see know when I am well; let him do what pleases him, and show himself when it pleases him. I now entrust my whole self to his mercy and care. I have once believed concerning him that he never ceases to lift up those who are so disposed toward him. I shall pronounce nothing about my own health until I have seen that beauty” (*ibid.*, no. 26).

> “I love wisdom alone for its own sake,” he says; “but I wish the other things—life, tranquility, and friends—to be present for its sake, and I fear their absence for its sake. What measure, however, can there be in love of that beauty in which I not only do not envy others but even seek many who may desire it with me, strive after it with me, possess it with me, and enjoy it with me? They will be all the dearer to me, the more widely the beloved object is shared among us” (*ibid.*, no. 22).

Accordingly, in his familiar conversations he urged his companions toward tireless love and pursuit of wisdom.

### 6

Augustine’s retirement also produced these *Soliloquies*, at almost the same time as the preceding books; for he appended them to those works and indicates that he wrote them shortly after abandoning his desire for honors and offices (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 4). In his other books he held conversations with his friends, but in these he speaks with himself. Hence he wished them to be entitled *Soliloquies*—a new and somewhat harsh name, but appropriate for designating the subject.

“For since,” he says, “truth cannot be sought more effectively than by asking and answering, and scarcely anyone is found who is not ashamed to be refuted in argument, so that it almost always happens that a matter properly introduced for discussion is shattered by an unruly outcry of obstinacy, even with the wounding of minds—usually concealed, but sometimes open—it seemed most peaceful and convenient, with God’s help, to seek the truth by questioning myself and answering myself” (*Soliloquies*, book 2, no. 14).

At the very beginning of the work he says that he does not know with whom he is conversing, whether with someone within or someone outside him. He says that he is beginning this conversation in order to know that interlocutor, after having spent many days diligently reflecting upon self-knowledge and upon the knowledge of seeking the good and avoiding evil (*ibid.*, book 1, no. 1). In his *Retractions* he testifies that he carried on a conversation with himself (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 4, no. 1).

This work is divided into two books. In the first he investigates what sort of person one must be who wishes to pursue wisdom, which is perceived not by the bodily senses but by the mind; and in the latter part of the book he demonstrates by various arguments that the things which truly exist are immortal. In the second he discusses the immortality of the soul, but does not bring the question to completion. “For the finishing hand was not applied to this work” (*ibid.*, chapter 5, no. 1), as he himself indicates, intending to discuss the matter with learned and right-minded men (*Soliloquies*, book 2, no. 28).

He mentions two writers who at that time were treating the immortality of the soul: one in Milan in prose, the other in Gaul in verse (*ibid.*, no. 26). The first, to whom he says he is unable, according to his own wish, to disclose his devotion to him and to wisdom (*ibid.*, and *Confessions*, book 6, no. 18), seems to have been Ambrose. But who the other familiar friend was—conscious of all his anxieties, living quietly in Gaul, and so far away that letters could scarcely be sent to him—we cannot conjecture unless we say that he was Zenobius, to whom Augustine had dedicated the two books *On Order* while Zenobius had long been absent from Milan.

In a letter sent to Nebridius immediately after the *Soliloquies*, which Nebridius evidently had not yet seen, Augustine places this work above all his earlier studies (*Letters*, 3, no. 1). He likewise asserts that in this work he had come to understand that the intellect is truth and that nothing in which there is anything immortal can die; since the intellect is in the soul and truth is immortal, it follows that the soul is immortal (*ibid.*, no. 4).

## CHAPTER X

1. On Nebridius, Augustine’s friend.  
2. On Augustine’s letter to Nebridius.

### 1

Augustine himself identifies these books of the *Soliloquies* in his *Confessions*, where he speaks of the books he composed from conversations held with himself alone in the presence of God (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 4, no. 7). He adds that his letters testify to what he dealt with in writing to the absent Nebridius.

The letters written to Nebridius must therefore be assigned partly to this period. Augustine was connected with him by a relationship scarcely less close than that which united him with Alypius. Nebridius, a young man of singular goodness, supreme prudence, and remarkable intelligence, came from a homeland near Carthage. Since he was very frequently in that city, he had formed a close friendship and association with Augustine, who was then teaching rhetoric there (*Confessions*, book 4, chapter 3, no. 6; book 6, chapter 10, no. 17; book 7, chapter 6, no. 8).

Nevertheless, following Augustine’s example, he did not allow himself to be deceived by the fictions of the astrologers. Indeed, he rejected and ridiculed them and tried to draw Augustine away from his extraordinary devotion to this kind of divination. It is also probable that Nebridius was not entangled in the errors of the Manichaeans, since he not only attacked them with an argument from which they could not extricate themselves but also overthrew them by it; thus he shook both Augustine himself and those who were listening (*ibid.*, book 7, chapter 2, no. 3).

For some time, however, he remained in the error of those heretics who believed that Christ’s flesh was an apparition; from this error he finally emerged even before he had embraced the Christian faith (*ibid.*, book 9, chapter 3, no. 6).

When Augustine had come to Milan, Nebridius too left his homeland, Carthage itself, his estate, and his house, and came to Milan without any other plan than to live together with Augustine and to assist him in the ardent pursuit of truth and wisdom that consumed him (*ibid.*, book 6, chapter 10, no. 17).

He sighed as Augustine sighed and wavered as Augustine wavered. He sought the happy life with the utmost intensity and examined the most difficult questions with wonderful intellectual acuity. “Since,” Augustine says, “he was a most diligent and keen investigator of obscure matters especially relevant to the teaching of piety, he greatly disliked a brief answer to a great question. Whoever demanded such an answer he endured with the greatest difficulty; and, if the person’s status permitted it, he restrained him with an indignant expression and voice, judging him unworthy to ask such questions because he did not know how much could and should be said about so important a matter” (*Letter* 98, no. 8).

With him and Alypius, especially and most intimately, Augustine shared his anxieties before his conversion (*Confessions*, book 6, chapter 7, no. 11); and the same anxiety afflicted all three friends (*ibid.*, no. 17).

When Augustine turned to Christ, Nebridius was absent. “For,” Augustine says, “he had yielded to our friendship in order to assist Verecundus, our most intimate friend, a Milanese citizen and grammarian, who was ardently desirous of and earnestly demanding, by right of friendship, faithful assistance from our group, which he greatly needed. Thus Nebridius was not drawn there by the desire for material advantage; he could have gained more from literary work if he had wished. But that sweetest and gentlest friend did not wish to disregard our request as an act of kindness. He carried out this duty with great prudence, taking care not to become known to persons who were prominent according to this age, avoiding any disturbance in those people whose minds he wished to remain free and to have as many hours as possible at leisure for seeking, reading, or hearing something concerning wisdom” (*ibid.*, book 8, chapter 6, no. 13).

### 2

Since Nebridius was detained by this occupation and could not follow Augustine into the country, they nourished their friendship through letters exchanged between them (*ibid.*, book 9, chapter 4, no. 7).

Among these letters, the third must undoubtedly be counted. From it we learn that the books Augustine had composed in November, before the *Soliloquies*, pleased Nebridius so greatly as he read them that, carried away as though by the excitement of his rejoicing spirit, he could not restrain himself from calling Augustine blessed.

Augustine therefore explains to him his thoughts on this matter and speaks of his *Soliloquies*. After concluding that truth is in the soul—namely, in the mind and intellect—he adds:

> “What opposes this? The senses? Then we must resist the senses with all the powers of the soul. It is clear. But what if sensible things delight us too much? Let it come about that they do not delight us. How does that happen? By becoming accustomed to going without them and desiring better things” (*Letter* 3, no. 4).

He adds that during his retirement he had clearly recognized that the blessedness of the soul, even if the soul were not immortal, could not consist in the delight and enjoyment of sensible things.

At the end of the letter he proposes to Nebridius several little questions concerning the conjugation of verbs (*ibid.*, no. 5)—something that may seem surprising in Augustine, who had professed both grammar and rhetoric.

The fourth letter also seems to belong to this period, when Augustine still needed to raise the eyes of his mind, disturbed by cares and weakened by the wounds inflicted by sensible things, so that he might become convinced that the things we understand are more real than those we perceive subject to our eyes.

He was led to this conclusion by Nebridius’s reasoning: namely, that the mind and intellect are better than the bodily eyes and ordinary sight, and that this would not be so unless the things we understand were more real than the things we see. Although Augustine asks Nebridius to consider whether anything strongly opposed to this reasoning exists, it pleased him so much that he later employed it in his books against the Manichaeans (*On Two Souls*, no. 3).

> “In the meantime,” he writes to Nebridius, “refreshed by this, when I have entreated God for help and begin to rise toward him and toward the things that are most truly true, I am sometimes filled with such confidence regarding enduring realities that I am astonished that I need reasoning in order to believe that these things exist with as much presence as each person has to himself” (*Letter* 4, no. 2).

In this letter he answers Nebridius, who had asked him to explain in writing how much progress he had made during his leisure in distinguishing sensible from intelligible things. Augustine replies that he is progressing in the former as we gradually progress with age; in the latter, however, he is still a child, though perhaps endowed with good hope.

At that time Nebridius had not yet been instructed in any of the sacred rites of the Church and was not yet a Christian, but he was nevertheless seeking the truth with the most ardent zeal (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 3, no. 6). Although, when Augustine turned to Christ, he had begun planning to leave Milan—and Nebridius would consequently be deprived of his friend’s companionship—Augustine nevertheless congratulated him on the good grace of his conversion. Nebridius himself was not far from it, since he was already on the point of following Augustine’s example; for not long afterward he too was cleansed in the sacred font.

## CHAPTER XI

1. Augustine returns to Milan to enroll among the Competentes.  
2. During this period he writes one book *On the Immortality of the Soul* and several others on the liberal disciplines.  
3. He receives Baptism, administered by the priest Ambrose.  
4. The Church’s congratulation and joy on this account.  
5. On this occasion the custom of singing hymns and psalms in the church was introduced at Milan.  
6. Having renounced everything, Augustine embraces the purpose of serving God, joins several companions to himself who share the same purpose, and returns with them to Africa.

### 1

When the time arrived in which catechumens were required to give their names for sacred regeneration and enroll among the *Competentes*—something customarily done at least at the beginning of Lent—Augustine left the countryside and returned to Milan together with Alypius, who desired to be reborn in Christ with him. He also brought with him his son Adeodatus, who was to share in the same grace and subsequently to be instructed in Christian morals and practices in their company.

Alypius was already clothed in the humility appropriate to the Christian Sacraments and was a most powerful conqueror of the body, even daring, in an extraordinary act, to trample the icy Italian ground with bare feet (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 6, no. 14).

We understand how suitably prepared Augustine himself was from what he wrote many years later both about himself and about others:

> “Are we so utterly estranged from our own feelings that we do not even remember how attentive and anxious we were about what those who instructed us in the catechumenate commanded us, when we were seeking the Sacraments of that font and for that reason were also called *Competentes*?” (*On Faith and Works*, no. 9).

Then, as he says, almost exhausted and dried up after a very long thirst, he returned with complete eagerness to the breasts of the Church. Weeping and groaning more deeply, he shook and pressed them, so that what flowed from them might be sufficient to refresh him in his condition and restore him to hope of life and salvation (*On the Advantage of Believing*, no. 2).

### 2

During those days he wrote his book *On the Immortality of the Soul*, as a memorandum for completing the *Soliloquies*, which had remained unfinished (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 5, no. 1). It should therefore not seem surprising that he described the arguments of this book as so compressed and briefly expressed that he himself could scarcely understand them. In the book there is a passage whose meaning he confesses that he does not grasp (*ibid.*, no. 3).

Nevertheless, this unwanted offspring came into the light and was numbered among his works. At that time he also began writing several books on the liberal disciplines, questioning his companions about these subjects when they did not shrink from such studies. His intention was either to reach spiritual realities through bodily things by certain definite steps, or to lead others to them in this way (*ibid.*, chapter 6).

He began these studies at Milan and completed there only the book on Grammar. The work on Music, however, which had also been begun at that time (*ibid.*, chapter 11, no. 1), was not completed until after his Baptism and after his return to Africa, when he finished it in six books (*ibid.*, chapter 6).

Of the other five disciplines begun in Milan—Dialectic, Rhetoric, Geometry, Arithmetic, and Philosophy—only the beginnings remained, that is, perhaps merely the opening sections of the respective books. Yet by the time he published his *Retractions*, he had already lost both these beginnings and the book on Grammar, although he thought that some people still possessed them (*ibid.*). In fact, all these little works are recorded in Possidius’s *Catalogue*.

### 3

At last, by the gracious assistance of God, it came about that through the bishop Ambrose Augustine received both the saving teaching of the Catholic Church and the divine Sacraments, as Possidius records. Immediately before these words we read:

> “The ardor of love for advancing in religion was innate in him, so that, as the holy days of Easter approached, he might receive the water of salvation” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1).

These words seem to indicate that, when Augustine turned to Christ, he resolved to receive Baptism at the approaching Easter solemnity. Baronius, however, inferred from this that he was regenerated at Easter, evidently with the intention of assigning his Baptism to the fifth of May, the day on which the Church now celebrates his conversion (*Baronius*, under the year 388, no. 71).

Yet if Possidius’s words are interpreted according to the custom then observed by the Church, they indicate that Augustine was baptized on the vigil of Easter. That day was devoted especially to the Baptism of adults, so that to wash many people at once with the saving waters outside that day, as happened at Augustine’s regeneration, would have been unusual and extremely rare.

This therefore occurred on the night preceding the twenty-fifth of April, the day on which Ambrose had demonstrated in a public letter that Easter was to be celebrated in the year 387.

### 4

It is beyond the weakness of our powers to speak worthily of the joy of God’s Angels in heaven over Augustine’s repentance and Baptism. Certainly the Church of Christ on earth still bears joyful witness to it every year. Recognizing that so eminent a Doctor had been granted such an extraordinary gift of divine grace, it established the fifth of May as sacred to his conversion. The Church celebrates by an appointed feast no other conversion except those of Paul and Augustine.

Augustine’s conversion or Baptism, however, could not have occurred on the fifth of May. Nevertheless, that day is not very far removed from the day that was festive for the Church of Milan when Augustine came to Baptism. No one, surely, will hesitate to suspect that the holy man was especially moved by the memory of that fortunate day when he took care to preserve in memory the joy of the Roman Church over Victorinus’s conversion, expressing and proclaiming it in such eloquent and devout words.

Accordingly, from what Augustine says about Victorinus (*Confessions*, book 8, chapter 2, no. 5), we may equally say of Augustine himself, changing only the name, that when he ascended to recite the creed in the church, everyone began to call out his name to one another, each according to the familiarity with which he knew him, amid the noise of rejoicing.

And who there did not know him? His name sounded softly through the mouths of all who rejoiced together:

> “Augustine! Augustine!”

They quickly cried out in exultation because they saw him, and quickly became silent in attentiveness in order to hear him. He professed the true faith with splendid confidence, and they all wanted to carry him inward into their hearts; and they carried him there by loving and rejoicing. These were the hands of those who seized him.

Many indeed return to God from a deeper hell of blindness than Augustine did. But if they are less well known among the people, even those who know them rejoice less over them. Those who are known to many, however, are an authority for salvation to many and go before many who will follow them.

The enemy is defeated more completely in one whom he holds more tightly and through whom he holds more people. He holds the proud more tightly through the name of nobility, and through the name of authority he holds more people.

How much more gratefully, then, was Augustine’s heart to be considered—a heart which the devil had possessed as an impregnable fortress—and Augustine’s tongue, a great and sharp weapon with which he had slain many. Therefore your children ought to have rejoiced all the more abundantly, because our King had bound the strong man, and they saw his vessels rescued, cleansed, fitted for your honor, and made useful to the Lord for every good work (*ibid.*, chapter 4, no. 9).

### 5

“We were baptized,” Augustine says, “and the anxiety of our former life fled from us. In those days I could not be satisfied with the wonderful sweetness of contemplating the depth of your plan for the salvation of the human race. How greatly I wept during your hymns and songs, intensely moved by the sweetly resonant voices of your Church! Those voices flowed into my ears, and the truth melted into my heart; from it the feeling of devotion overflowed, tears ran down, and I was happy in all this” (*ibid.*, book 9, chapter 6, no. 14).

It was a year, or scarcely more—approximately thirteen months since this custom had begun at Milan—when Justina Augusta, the mother of the boy-emperor Valentinian, persecuted your man Ambrose because of the heresy by which she had been deceived by the Arians. Augustine continues his account in these words:

> “The devout people kept watch in the church, prepared to die with their bishop, your servant. There my mother, your handmaid, holding the first place in anxiety and vigilance, lived in prayer. We were still cold, not warmed by your Spirit, yet we were stirred by the astonished and troubled city.
>
> “Then it was instituted that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions, so that the people might not waste away from the weariness of sorrow. From that time to the present the practice has been retained by many, indeed almost all, of your congregations, and it has been imitated throughout the other regions of the world” (*ibid.*, chapter 7, no. 15).

Whenever the holy Man remembered the beneficial effect received from the Church’s sacred singing, and the tears which the divine songs had drawn from his eyes at the beginning of his recovery of the faith, this always led him to approve that institution of the Church (*ibid.*, book 10, chapter 33, no. 50).

### 6

After receiving the grace of Baptism, Augustine immediately renounced from the depths of his heart whatever hope he might have been able to place in the world. He no longer pursued a wife, children, riches, or offices, but resolved to serve God alone with his companions, so that he might be enrolled among that little flock to which the Lord promises his kingdom and which he exhorts to sell its possessions and distribute them to the poor.

Accordingly, he resolved to build upon the foundation of faith nothing but gold, silver, and precious stones, and to be content with only the food necessary to preserve bodily health, although previously he had been entangled in various desires and anxieties (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 2).

There can be no doubt that Alypius, among others, was bound to him by fellowship in the same purpose. Evodius of Tagaste, through the work of God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house, joined himself to them as a companion. He had turned to God and been baptized before Augustine (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 8, no. 17).

All united together in God, they lived together, and Monnica cared for all of them as though she had been the parent of each (*ibid.*, chapter 9, no. 22). Each had likewise resolved to lead the perfect life; they were concerned only to find a place suitable for their plans and vows.

“We were together,” Augustine says, “and had resolved to live together in a holy purpose. We were seeking what place might best contain us in your service” (*ibid.*, chapter 8, no. 17).

Their holy purpose had no other end than that, having rejected the world, they should serve God together. They were now not merely Catholic Christians by the faith they had received and by sacred regeneration, but also, having despised earthly happiness, servants of God (*ibid.*, book 9, chapter 10, no. 26)—truly monks from that time onward, striving toward the perfection of Christ’s commandments.

For Augustine himself does not hesitate to call Albina, Pinianus, and Melania by these very names when, traveling in Africa, they distributed their possessions to the poor according to a very similar holy purpose.
