They are the very people whom he argues could not be released from the obligation of fulfilling an oath, even though that oath had been extorted from Pinianus, because the oath had been given through the ministry of preeminent holy servants of God—monks striving toward the perfection of Christ’s commandments even by distributing their possessions (*Letter* 126, no. 11).

Augustine therefore decided to return to Africa with his fellow citizens and friends who had likewise devoted themselves to God’s service (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 3).

His brother Navigius was with him (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 11, no. 27). When Augustine reached Ostia on the Tiber, he was deprived of his mother in the thirty-third year of his age (*ibid.*, no. 28), and therefore before the Ides of November of this year, 387. Yet it seems that this occurred somewhat earlier, for Augustine admits that he omits many things for the sake of brevity (*ibid.*). We therefore cannot determine how long he remained at Milan after his Baptism.

## CHAPTER XII

1. The blessed Monnica was born to Christian parents and was brought up among them chastely and soberly.  
2. How praiseworthy her conduct was in marriage.  
3. Deprived of her husband in the fortieth year of her age, she spent the remainder of her life entirely in pious works.  
4. With how much greater anxiety she gave birth to Augustine in spirit than she had borne him in the flesh.  
5. She took part in Augustine’s philosophical conversations, in which she distinguished herself among the others by her penetrating and serious remarks.

### 1

When the Man of God came, in his narrative, to his mother’s death, he testified that, although he was in great haste and had many things to pass over, he nevertheless could not refrain from bringing forth something of what came to mind concerning that most holy woman—not in order to praise her own merits, but to praise Christ’s gifts in her.

“For she,” he says, “gave birth to him both in the flesh, for this temporal light, and in the heart, for eternal light” (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 8, no. 17).

Augustine was truly the son of her tears (*ibid.*, book 3, chapters 11–12). Since he possessed a mind as sincere as it was mindful of benefits, he freely acknowledged that he owed her whatever life he possessed (*On the Happy Life*, no. 6).

Monnica was born in the year of Christ 332, in a faithful household, a good member of the Church; there, under Christ’s guidance, she had absorbed the fear of God.

When she spoke with Augustine about the manner in which she had been raised, she repeatedly declared that she owed less to her mother’s care than to the diligence of a certain aged maidservant. Because of her old age and excellent character, this woman was held in honor by the masters of that truly Christian household and had been placed in charge of educating their daughters.

She carefully fulfilled the care entrusted to her. In restraining the girls, when necessary, she was vigorous with holy severity; in teaching them, she was measured and temperate with prudent moderation.

Besides the hours during which they were fed very moderately at their parents’ table, she did not allow them to drink even water when they were burning with thirst. She guarded against the formation of a bad habit and added this sound advice:

> “For now you drink water, because you do not have wine at your disposal. But when you come to your husbands and become mistresses of storerooms and cellars, water will seem beneath you, but the habit of drinking will prevail” (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 8, no. 17).

By these most wise admonitions, and by the authority she had acquired among the tender minds of the girls, she restrained the thoughtless desires natural to an early age. She instructed them how to moderate their thirst according to the law of temperance, so that they would no longer even desire what was unbecoming.

Monnica nevertheless told Augustine that, despite the vigilance of that prudent old woman, a tendency toward drinking wine had crept into her mind. Whenever she was customarily sent by her parents to draw wine, as a girl whose sobriety had been tested, she would take from the cup that she filled from the wine jar a tiny sip with the tips of her lips, since her palate could bear no more.

She was not driven to this by an inborn desire for wine, but by certain free and playful impulses that boil up from the ardor of early childhood and must be restrained in children’s minds by the authority of their elders.

But since contempt for lesser faults gradually leads to more serious vices, it happened that, drinking a little more wine each day under the pressure of bad habit, she eventually drained nearly full cups of unmixed wine with eagerness and pleasure.

“Where then,” her devout son exclaims, “was that shrewd old woman and her vigorous prohibition? Could it have availed anything against the hidden illness, unless your medicine, Lord, had watched over us?

“Father, mother, and nurses were absent; yet you were present, you who created us, who call us, and who even through misguided human beings accomplish some good for the salvation of souls. What did you do then, my God? From where did you heal her? From where did you cure her?

“Did you not bring forth a harsh and sharp rebuke from another soul, like a medicinal blade from your hidden provisions, and by a single stroke cut away that corruption?

“For the maidservant who usually accompanied her to the wine jar quarreled with her younger mistress—as happens, one woman alone with another—and reproached her for this fault, calling her, with the bitterest insult, a ‘little winebibber.’ Struck by that goad, she looked upon her own disgrace, immediately condemned it, and cast it off” (*ibid.*, no. 18).

Monnica received the Baptism of Christ not when she lay at the point of death, but many years before her death. From that time onward she ordered her life in such a way that, by the purity of her faith and conduct, she might encourage anyone to praise the name of God (*ibid.*, chapter 13, no. 34).

## 2

Thus, having been raised chastely and temperately, and, in obedience to God, subject to her parents more by God’s grace than by her parents’ care, when she was of marriageable age she obeyed the husband to whom she was given as though he were her master. In order to win him for God, she directed all her thoughts toward this end, using the most effective means of persuasion: integrity of conduct. Adorned with this divinely bestowed quality, she shone in her husband’s eyes with such beauty that she secured his love and veneration, not without a certain admiration on his part (ibid., chapter 9, no. 19).

Her husband, whose name was Patricius, a citizen of Thagaste, was still enslaved to the worship of idols (ibid., book 2, chapter 3, nos. 5–6). In all matters that did not concern religion, Monnica, although the better of the two, served him; for in this she was obeying God himself, by whom the law of obedience had been imposed upon her (ibid., book 1, chapter 11, no. 17). She bore the injuries of the marriage-bed with such patience that she never reproached her husband on that account, plainly awaiting the gift of chastity for him from faith and God’s mercy.

She knew never to resist an angry man, either by deed or by word. But when his passion had cooled, finding an opportune moment, she explained to him her manner of acting, if he happened to have flared up somewhat rashly. When other women, whose husbands were more gentle, bore upon their [Col. 0146] faces the marks of blows, and in friendly conversation laid the blame upon their husbands’ intemperance, she taught them that the blame ought rather to be assigned to their own tongues. Gravely, yet with a certain pleasant humor, she warned them that, when they had first heard the marriage contract read aloud, they ought to have regarded it as the document by which they had become their husbands’ servants; and therefore, remembering their condition, they ought not to behave arrogantly toward their masters.

Accordingly, those who knew what a fierce-tempered husband she endured could never sufficiently marvel that no one had ever heard, or detected any trace, of Patricius violently laying hands upon his wife, or that they had disagreed with each other in a domestic quarrel even for a single day. When they asked her familiarly how she had achieved this, she explained to them the principle of conduct mentioned above. Those who imitated her learned its usefulness by their own experience and thanked her for it (ibid., book 9, chapter 9, no. 19).

She also won over her mother-in-law, who at first had been alienated from her by the whispers of certain wicked maidservants, through such patient and gentle attentiveness that the older woman herself exposed their malice to her son Patricius and begged him to punish them. When he had inflicted upon those same servants, with his mother’s approval, the penalties they deserved—both to gratify his mother and to preserve domestic discipline and peace—she declared that no other reward should be expected by anyone who, in the desire to please her, spoke evil of her daughter-in-law. Since no one thereafter dared to do so, they lived together in an extraordinary sweetness of mutual goodwill (ibid., no. 20).

God had also granted that holy woman a great gift: among any souls who were at odds and in conflict, wherever she could, she presented herself as a peacemaker. Even when she heard from both sides many bitter things about each other—such as swollen and undigested discord commonly belches forth, when the sourness of hatred exhales through harsh conversation about an absent enemy to a friend who is present—she revealed nothing to either about the other except what could serve to reconcile them (ibid., no. 21).

Such was Monnica’s conduct, taught by the inner Teacher in the school of her heart. Finally, the seed of grace that the heavenly Farmer had scattered in his handmaid’s mind bore abundant fruit in patience. Her conduct toward her husband was so effective that at the end of his life she won him wholly for God; and, once he had become a believer, she no longer had to mourn in him the evils she had endured while he was not yet a believer (ibid., book 9, chapter 13, no. 37).

When Augustine was sixteen years old—that is, approximately in the year 370—Patricius was counted among the catechumens (ibid., book 2, chapter 3, no. 6); he died in the following year, when Monnica was forty.

## 3

After losing her husband, before whom and after whom she married no one else (ibid., book 9, chapter 13, no. 37), she spent the remainder of her life as a chaste and temperate widow, frequent in almsgiving (ibid., book 5, chapter 9, no. 17), acting mercifully toward those who sinned against her and forgiving her debtors their debts (ibid., book 9, chapter 13, no. 36). She offered [Col. 0147] service and attendance to the saints, truly a handmaid of the servants of God. Whoever knew her praised, honored, and loved God greatly in her, since he perceived and recognized God’s presence in her heart through the fruits of her holy conduct, as through reliable witnesses (ibid., chapter 9, no. 22).

Ambrose himself also loved her greatly because of her deeply religious conduct, by which she frequented the church, fervent in spirit and devoted to good works (ibid., book 6, chapter 2, no. 2). Twice each day, morning and evening, she came to the church of God without fail—not for empty tales and old women’s chatter, but with the intention both of hearing God speak to her in the divine word and of being heard by him in her prayers (ibid., book 5, chapter 9, no. 17).

She never let a day pass without bringing an offering to the altar of God (ibid.). Or, as Augustine later recalled the matter in slightly different words, she served the altar every day without omission—“the altar from which she knew that the holy Victim was dispensed, by which the bond written against us was erased, by which the enemy who counted our sins and sought something to accuse us of was vanquished, finding nothing in the one through whom we conquer; against whom no one can repay innocent blood, to whom no one can restore the price by which he bought us in order to take us away from him. To the sacrament of this price of ours the handmaid of God had bound her soul with the bond of faith” (ibid., book 9, chapter 13, no. 36).

When it was customary in Africa to bring porridge, bread, and wine to the graves of the martyrs, Monnica would bring a basket filled with food, of which she would offer a portion in honor of the saints and afterward distribute the remainder to the poor. She did not bring a cup, but only a little vessel of wine, and that wine diluted with water, from which she might herself take a modest portion. If there happened to be many graves that seemed to deserve honoring in this manner, she carried that same single little vessel around and placed it everywhere. Thus the wine was not only extremely diluted but also very tepid, and she distributed it among the companions of this religious observance in tiny sips, because she was seeking devotion there, not pleasure.

Ambrose, however, had ordered that this not be done, not even by those who acted temperately: first, so that drunkards might not be given an opportunity to gorge themselves; and also because these offerings resembled the ancestral rites of the Gentiles almost to the point of superstition. When Monnica therefore brought her little gifts according to her custom and was stopped by the doorkeeper, as soon as she learned that Ambrose—whom she loved as an angel of God—had forbidden the practice, she accepted this so devoutly and obediently that Augustine himself wondered whether she had been brought to condemn the custom she had followed rather than to inquire why it was forbidden.

Thus she willingly abandoned her former practice and learned to bring to the memorials of the martyrs, instead of a basket full of earthly fruits, a heart full of purer vows: both to give to the needy whatever she could and to celebrate there the communion of the Lord’s body, in imitation of whose passion the martyrs had been sacrificed and crowned (ibid., book 6, chapter 2, no. 2).

When that religious widow was troubled by uncertainty about whether at Milan she ought to fast on Saturday, according to the custom of the [Col. 0148] Church of Thagaste, or dine according to the Milanese practice, Augustine—still not converted, although not greatly concerned about the matter—consulted Ambrose in order to free her from her hesitation. Ambrose replied that he could teach them nothing about this except what he himself practiced, since, if he knew a better practice, he would observe it instead. He added: “When I am here, I do not fast on Saturday; and wherever you come, follow the custom of that church, if you do not wish either to give or to suffer scandal” (Epistle 36, no. 32, and Epistle 54, no. 3).

He reported this answer to his mother, and it was sufficient for her; she had no doubt that obedience was required. During the same period, while he was living at Milan and Ambrose was enduring persecution from Justina for almost two full years, the devout people kept vigil in the church, Augustine says, “prepared to die with their bishop, your servant. There my mother, your handmaid, holding the foremost place in anxiety and watchfulness, lived by her prayers” (Confessions, book 9, chapter 7, no. 15).

At last she fulfilled everything that the Apostle requires in true Christian widows (1 Tim. 5:9). She had been the wife of one man, had repaid her parents, had piously governed her household, had testimony in good works, and had raised children, giving birth to them as often as she perceived them turning away from God (Confessions, book 9, chapter 9, no. 22)—something that was certainly evident in Augustine.

## 4

We have seen with what zeal that most holy woman worked to implant the Christian religion in the child Augustine and continually inspire him with piety (ibid., book 1, chapter 11, no. 17). At her breast he drank in the name of Christ our Savior, so that his tender heart retained it very deeply (ibid., book 3, chapter 4, no. 8).

With what ardor did she strive to have the same child initiated through the saving sacraments while he was still in danger of death—“giving birth to him more dearly in a chaste heart through faith than she had borne him in the flesh” (ibid., book 1, chapter 11, no. 17). Later, when he was an adolescent, with what concern did she admonish him, in order to deter him from shameful loves? (ibid., book 2, chapter 3, no. 7).

How greatly did she weep before God over his falling into the Manichaean heresy? Certainly she wept more than mothers weep over the bodily deaths of their children. “For she saw,” Augustine says, “my death from the faith and spirit which she had from you; and you heard her, Lord. You heard her and did not despise her tears, when they flowed and watered the earth beneath her eyes in every place of her prayer. You heard her.

“For whence was that dream by which you consoled her, so that she consented to my living and sharing the same table with her in the house, which she had begun to refuse, rejecting and abhorring the blasphemies of my error? For she saw herself standing on a certain wooden rule, and a radiant young man, cheerful and smiling at her, coming toward her while she was mourning and crushed by grief. When he asked her the reasons for her sadness and her daily tears—not to learn, but, as is customary, to teach—and she replied that she was lamenting my perdition, he ordered her to be secure and admonished her to pay attention and see that where she was, there I also was.

“When she paid attention, she saw me standing beside her on the same rule. Whence came this, unless your ears were turned toward her heart? Whence also came the fact that, when she told me of this vision and I tried to draw from it the conclusion [Col. 0149] that she rather ought not to despair of becoming what I was, she immediately replied, without hesitation: ‘No. For it was not said to me, “Where he is, there you are also,” but, “Where you are, there he is also”’” (ibid., book 3, chapter 11, nos. 19–20).

This occurred nearly nine years before his amendment, which took place around August of the year 386, and therefore approximately toward the end of 376. Throughout that entire period, the chaste, devout, and temperate widow never ceased groaning before God for her son. Indeed, with the lively faith of the promises made to her, she spurred herself on so intensely that she became not at all more sluggish; rather, she allowed no rest to her sighs, no pause to her tears, and no limit to her vows and prayers.

“From the blood of her heart she sacrificed to God for him through tears, by day and by night” (ibid., book 5, chapter 7, no. 13). Divine mercy preserved him until he reached the water of grace; when he had been washed in it, the streams of his mother’s eyes were dried—the eyes with which she watered the earth before God’s face each day for her son (ibid., chapter 8, no. 15).

Moreover, God was not content to give her this first pledge of Augustine’s future conversion. He added another through a bishop raised in the Catholic Church and trained in the divine books. When that woman asked him, Augustine says, to be willing to speak with me, refute my errors, disabuse me of evil, and teach me what was good—for he did this whenever he found someone capable—he wisely refused, as I later understood.

“For he replied that I was still unteachable, because I was puffed up with the novelty of that heresy and had already harassed many inexperienced people with certain little questions, as she had told him. ‘But leave him there,’ he said, ‘and only ask the Lord for him. By reading he will discover for himself what that error is and how great its impiety.’

“He also told her that he too, when still a little boy, had been handed over to the Manichaeans by his deluded mother, and that he had not merely read almost all their books but had actually written them; yet it had become clear to him, without anyone disputing with him and convincing him, that the sect ought to be avoided, and so he had fled from it.

“When he had said this, and she was unwilling to accept it but persisted in begging and weeping abundantly that he see me and converse with me, he, already somewhat irritated by her persistence, said: ‘Go away from me; as surely as you live, it cannot be that the son of these tears should perish.’ She often recalled in her conversations with me that she had received these words as though a voice had sounded from heaven” (ibid., book 3, chapter 12, no. 21).

Other testimonies of her son’s future amendment were also divinely given to her. She kept them in her faithful heart and continually presented them to God in prayer as though they were written guarantees (ibid., book 5, chapter 9, no. 17).

When Augustine sailed for Italy, while she was vainly attempting to hold him back and had been left on the shore, she remained behind praying and weeping. “And what was she asking of you, my God,” he says, “with such tears, except that you would not allow me to sail? But you, consulting her more deeply and hearing the central desire of her heart, disregarded what she then asked, in order to accomplish in me what she had always asked” (ibid., chapter 8, no. 15).

After reaching Rome, Augustine fell gravely ill. He professes that he was delivered from the illness through his mother’s prayers, although she did not know of his danger. If he had happened to die in the heresy that he was then [Col. 0150] following, that event would have inflicted so deep a wound upon his mother’s heart that she would have admitted no consolation for the rest of her life. For it cannot be expressed with what love she embraced her son, or with how much greater anxiety she was giving birth to him in spirit than she had borne him in the flesh.

“I do not see, therefore,” Augustine says, “how she could have been healed if such a death of mine had pierced through the inward parts of her love” (ibid., chapter 9, nos. 16–17).

She could not endure being separated from her son for long. Strong through piety and considering nothing too difficult, she followed him by land and sea and finally caught up with him at Milan, the city to which he had gone in the year 384 for the purpose of teaching (ibid., chapter 13, no. 23).

Trusting in divine assistance, she feared no danger, to such a degree that during the perils of the sea she herself comforted the sailors—although sailors usually comfort those who are unaccustomed to travel by sea and are shaken by a rising storm—promising them a safe arrival, because God had promised this to her in a vision (ibid., book 6, chapter 1, no. 1).

She found her son in considerable danger because of his despair of finding the truth. Yet when he told her that he was no longer a Manichaean but was not yet a Catholic Christian, “When I had indicated this to her,” Augustine says, “she did not leap for joy as though she had heard something unexpected. For she had already become secure concerning that part of my misery over which she had wept to you as over one dead, though destined to be resurrected, and had carried me forth upon the bier of her thoughts, so that you might say to the widow’s son: ‘Young man, I say to you, arise’ (Luke 7:14–15); and he would revive, begin to speak, and you would give him to his mother.

“Her heart therefore did not tremble with any turbulent exultation when she heard that what she daily wept before you should come to pass had already occurred to a considerable extent: I had not yet attained the truth, but had already been rescued from falsehood. Indeed, because she was certain that what remained would also be given by you, who had promised the whole, she replied to me with the calmest confidence and a heart full of trust that she believed in Christ that, before she departed this life, she would see me a faithful Catholic.

“And to you, fountain of mercies, she offered more abundant prayers and tears, asking you to hasten your help and illumine my darkness. She ran more eagerly to the church and hung upon the lips of Ambrose, the fountain of water springing up into eternal life. She loved that man as an angel of God, because through him she had learned that I had meanwhile been brought to that precarious fluctuation through which I would pass from sickness to health, though an even more dangerous crisis intervened—like the attack physicians call critical—and she confidently anticipated my recovery” (Confessions, book 6, chapter 1, no. 1).

At last, around August of the year 386, the blessed widow obtained what she had prayed for, when Augustine broke the chains by which he had been bound both to the world and to himself through the grace of Christ the liberator. He immediately went to his mother, who rejoiced when she heard the news. When he explained the whole course of events, she exulted, triumphed, and blessed God, who is able to do far more than we ask or understand. She saw that much more had been granted her for her son than she had been accustomed to ask with groans and tears.

For he had recovered so completely that he entirely abandoned the thought of taking a wife and trampled underfoot every hope of this world, now standing immovable in that [Col. 0151] rule of faith in which, through divine revelation, his mother had learned many years before that he would one day be with her. Thus she found that her tears had been changed into a joy far richer than she had promised herself, and that he had become much dearer and purer to her than if she had seen him beget in lawful marriage the children she had desired (ibid., book 8, chapter 12, no. 30).

## 5

After his conversion, Augustine withdrew with his companions to the villa at Cassiciacum. Monnica also joined them in that retreat as a companion, distinguished in womanly dress by manly faith, in the security of old age, in maternal love, and in Christian piety (ibid., book 9, chapter 4, no. 8).

There she took part even in their philosophical discussions, however elevated they might be. When they were discussing the blessed life on the Ides of November, she asserted that the soul is nourished by nothing other than the understanding and knowledge of things, and that no one can be blessed unless he both wills and possesses what is good:

“If he wills and possesses good things,” she said, “he is blessed; but if he wills evil things, he is wretched, even if he possesses them.”

Augustine declared that in this she had reached the highest summit of philosophy, and that not even Cicero himself, had he possessed equal eloquence, could have surpassed her. He then recited a beautiful passage from that orator’s *Hortensius*:

“In these words,” he said, “she cried out in such a way that, having completely forgotten her sex, we thought that some great man was sitting among us. Meanwhile, as far as I could, I understood from what divine source those words flowed and from whom” (*The Blessed Life*, discussion 1, nos. 8, 10).

She later added that even a person who possessed all the happiness of the world in such a way that he was sure he would never lose it would nevertheless be wretched if he could not be satisfied with it, since by that very fact he would always be in need. A person, therefore, is not blessed by such things but by the moderation of his own spirit. On hearing this, Augustine replied that she could have said nothing either truer or more worthy of herself (ibid., no. 11).

When it had been explained to her who the Academics were, Monnica said: “These people are *caducarii*”—a popular term for those whom the comitial disease, or epilepsy, overthrew (ibid., no. 16).

She also uttered words worthy of remembrance in the conversation held the following day. On the third day, when the question arose whether all those who possessed earthly happiness while deprived of the highest good were wretched, and therefore ought also to be called needy, Monnica said:

“I do not know, and I do not yet fully understand how wretchedness can be separated from need, or need from wretchedness. For this man, who was rich and wealthy and, as you say, desired nothing more, was nevertheless in need because he feared that he might lose what he had: he lacked wisdom. Would we call him needy if he lacked silver and money, but not call him needy when he lacked wisdom?”

Everyone present cried out and admired the saying. Augustine himself was greatly delighted that his mother had discovered the solution which he had obtained from the books of the philosophers and reserved for the end as something especially beautiful:

“Do you see,” he said, “that many and various teachings are one thing, and a mind wholly attentive to God another? For whence do these things that we admire proceed, unless from there?” (ibid., discussion 3, no. 27).

Toward the end of this discussion, when Augustine had introduced the subject [Col. 0152] of the Trinity, Monnica recalled words that were deeply fixed in her memory and, as though awakening into her faith, joyfully poured forth that verse from the hymn of the priest Ambrose: “Foster those who pray, O Trinity.” She then added:

“This is, without anyone’s doubt, the blessed life, which is the perfect life. We must presume that by solid faith, lively hope, and burning charity we can be brought to it as we hasten toward it” (ibid., no. 35).

Although Augustine had already perceived his mother’s remarkable intelligence through their long association, in this discussion he recognized her mind as so lofty and upright that he judged no one could be found better suited to true philosophy (*On Order*, book 2, no. 1). For this reason he made sure that, whenever leisure permitted, she was always present at such philosophical discussions.

In the second conversation on *Order*, she expressed this noble thought:

“I do not think that anything could have happened apart from God’s order, because the evil that arose was in no way brought forth by God’s order. But that justice did not allow it to remain disordered; rather, it restored and compelled it to return to an order merited by itself” (ibid., no. 23).

By these words she seems to have wished to signify what one encounters so frequently in Augustine: namely, that God is not the author of sin but its ordainer.

Toward the close of that conversation, Augustine praises and addresses her in these words:

“Let us pray, therefore, not that riches, honors, or such fleeting and unstable things, which pass away whenever anything resists them, should come to us, but that those things may come which make us good and blessed. That these prayers may be fulfilled with the greatest devotion, Mother, we especially entrust this task to you. I unshakably believe and affirm that through your prayers God has given me this frame of mind: that I place absolutely nothing before the discovery of truth, that I will, think about, and love nothing else. Nor do I cease to believe that we shall obtain, through your asking, this great good which, through your merit, we have desired” (ibid., no. 52).

After Augustine had been baptized, together with certain friends and relatives who were already united with one another in God, Monnica continued for some time to live in their company. She cared for all of them as much as if she had been the mother of them all, and showed them as much respect as if she had been the daughter of them all (Confessions, book 9, chapter 9, no. 22).

When they were all returning together to Africa and had reached Ostia on the Tiber, making preparations to sail, Monnica was seized by her final illness and paid the debt owed to nature (ibid., chapter 8, no. 17).

# CHAPTER XIII

1. Monnica’s conversation with Augustine concerning the blessedness of eternal life.  
2. The most excellent saying of the most holy woman concerning the abandonment of concern for her tomb; her blessed death.  
3. Monnica’s funeral; Augustine’s most bitter grief at her death and his restrained weeping.

## 1

About five or perhaps six days before the blessed Monnica fell ill, she and her son were resting at a window at Ostia on the Tiber, from which there was a view into the garden of the house where they were staying. Withdrawn from the crowds after the labor of their long journey, they were preparing themselves for the voyage and conversing about eternal life with the greatest delight [Col. 0153] of mind, forgetting what lay behind and stretching forward toward what lay ahead.

“We were gaping,” Augustine says, “with the mouth of our heart toward the supernal streams of your fountain, the fountain of life which is with you, so that, sprinkled from it according to our capacity, we might in some manner contemplate so great a reality.

“And when our conversation had reached the point where the pleasure of the bodily senses, however great and in whatever bodily light, seemed in comparison with the joy of that life not merely unworthy of comparison but not even worthy of remembrance, we raised ourselves with a more ardent affection toward that same life. While we were speaking and yearning for it, we touched it slightly with the whole thrust of our heart; then we sighed, left the first fruits of our spirit bound there, and returned to the sound of our own mouths, where a word both begins and ends.”

The fruit of that conversation and ecstasy was that all the pleasures of the world seemed worthless to them in comparison with the sweetness of that foretaste of blessedness. Then she said to Augustine:

“My son, as far as I am concerned, nothing now gives me pleasure in this life. What am I still doing here, and why I am here I do not know, since my hope in this world has been exhausted. There was one reason why I wished to remain for a while in this life: that I might see you a Christian Catholic before I died. My God has granted me this more abundantly, so that I also see you, having despised earthly happiness, as his servant. What am I doing here?” (Confessions, book 9, chapter 9, nos. 23–26).

## 2

On another day at Ostia on the Tiber, Monnica was conversing most familiarly with several of Augustine’s friends—for he himself was absent—about contempt for this life and the goodness of death. Astonished at the woman’s virtue, they asked her whether she feared leaving her body so far from her own city.

“Nothing is far from God,” she replied, “and there is no reason to fear that at the end of the age he will not know where to raise me.”

Previously she had been extraordinarily concerned about a tomb. For this reason she had arranged and prepared one for herself beside her husband’s body: after spending the years of their marriage in the deepest harmony, she wished this happiness to be added to theirs—that people might remember that, after her overseas pilgrimage, she had been granted that the earth covering both spouses should be joined together. But by then God had healed this weakness and filled the emptiness of her heart with the fullness of grace (ibid., chapter 10, no. 28).

She had clearly indicated this to Augustine when, in the conversation mentioned above at the window, she burst out with the words: “What am I doing here?” Yet he did not fully understand her mind until she revealed it more plainly at the end of her life.

For approximately the fifth day after that conversation she fell into a fever. While it lasted for nine days, she was comforted by the attentions Augustine gave her; she called him the pious one and, with the tenderest affection of heart, recalled that no little word had ever fallen from his mouth that could have wounded her even slightly (ibid., chapter 12, no. 30).

On one day of her illness she suffered a loss of consciousness and was briefly withdrawn from those present. “We rushed to her,” Augustine says, “but she was quickly restored to consciousness. She looked at my brother and me standing nearby and said to us, as though asking a question: ‘Where was I?’

“Then, seeing us stunned with sorrow, she said: ‘You will bury your mother here.’ I was silent and [Col. 0154] restrained my tears. But my brother said something by which he expressed the wish that she might die not abroad but in her homeland, as though that were more fortunate.

“When she heard this, she fixed him with an anxious look, rebuking him with her eyes for thinking such things. Then, looking at me, she said: ‘See what he is saying.’ And immediately she said to both of us: ‘Bury this body wherever you will; do not let concern for it trouble you. I ask you only to remember me at the altar of the Lord, wherever you may be’” (ibid., book 9, chapter 11, no. 27).

“Thus,” Augustine continues shortly afterward, “as the day of her dissolution approached, she did not think about having her body covered expensively, or embalmed with spices; she did not desire a chosen monument or care about a family tomb. She did not give us these instructions. She desired only that she be remembered at your altar, to which she had served without omitting a single day, and from which she knew that the holy Victim was dispensed, by which the bond written against us was erased” (ibid., chapter 13, no. 36).

After she had expressed her mind as far as her illness allowed, she was overcome by the worsening disease. In that torment the blessed soul left the body, destined to fly upward, on the ninth day of her illness, in her fifty-sixth year and in Augustine’s thirty-third year, perhaps a few days before the Ides of November in the year 387. Nevertheless, the Church celebrates her feast on the fourth day before the Nones of May. Why this is so is unknown to us.

## 3

Augustine closed his mother’s eyes, and immediately the most bitter grief pierced his inmost heart. When it sought an outlet through tears, he compelled his eyes and forced the tears back within. Nor was the anguish slight that he suffered in this most grievous struggle of himself against himself.

He considered it unseemly to accompany his mother’s death with tears, since he could not doubt that she lived in the better part of herself. He held this firmly both from the evidence of her conduct and from her sincere faith and certain reasoning (ibid., chapter 12, no. 29).

Nevertheless, he bitterly grieved that her most beloved companionship had been taken from him by death. “Life was torn apart,” he says, “which had been made one from my life and hers” (ibid., no. 30).

Then, when she breathed out her final spirit, the boy Adeodatus cried out in lamentation. Restrained by everyone present, he fell silent. Once Adeodatus had been checked from weeping, Evodius immediately seized the Psalter and began to sing, while Augustine and the others joined in:

“I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (ibid., no. 31).

When news of the holy widow’s death spread through the city, many Christians and devout women gathered at the house. While those whose duty it was took care of the funeral, Augustine withdrew to a place where he could suitably remain among those who judged that he ought not to be abandoned in this anguish of spirit.

“I discussed,” he says, “what suited the occasion, and by this nourishment of truth I mitigated the anguish known to you but unknown to them. They listened attentively and thought that I was without any feeling of grief. But in your ears, where none of them could hear, I reproached the softness of my feelings and restrained the flood of sorrow. It yielded to me a little, then again was carried along by its own force—not to the point of bursting into tears, nor to the point of altering my expression; but I [Col. 0155] knew what I was suppressing in my heart.

“And because I was deeply displeased that these human things, which must necessarily occur according to the proper order and the condition of our lot, should have such power over me, I grieved my grief with another grief and was worn down by a double sorrow” (Confessions, book 9, chapter 12, no. 31).

When the body had been carried out and placed near the tomb, as was customary there, the sacrifice of our redemption was offered for her. Meanwhile Augustine restrained his tears.

“Behold,” he says, “the body was carried out; we went and returned without tears. For even in the prayers that we poured out to you when the sacrifice of our price was offered for her, with the corpse already placed beside the tomb before it was laid in the grave, as is customary there, I did not weep. But throughout the day I was grievously sorrowful in secret and, with my mind troubled, prayed to you as best I could that you might heal my grief. You did not do so, I believe, in order to impress even this one lesson upon my memory: that every habit is a bond even against a mind that is no longer nourished by deceptive words.”

He decided to take a bath, having heard that bathing could drive anxiety from the mind, but his grief was not washed away by those waters. Yet when he had fallen asleep, he awoke and felt that his grief had been considerably eased by sleep (ibid., book 9, chapter 12, no. 32).

Nevertheless, when he gradually recalled the memory of his loss and bereavement, he wished to weep before God for his mother and on behalf of his mother, for himself and on behalf of himself. Thus he broke open the tears that he had kept restrained, as though a barrier had been shattered, and freely allowed them to flow in order to discharge the sorrow of his heart.

At last he found rest, because he had poured them out before God, not before the eyes of men who might perhaps have interpreted them wrongly through pride.

His weeping, however, did not exceed a small part of an hour.

“Let whoever wishes read this and interpret it as he wishes,” he says. “If he finds it a sin that I wept for my mother for a small part of an hour—my mother who was for the moment dead to my eyes, though she had wept for me for many years so that I might live in your eyes—let him not mock me, but, if he possesses great charity, let him himself weep before you, Father of all the brothers of your Christ, for my sins” (ibid., no. 33).

# CHAPTER XIV

1. Augustine postpones his return to his homeland and writes several books at Rome, including *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*.  
2. *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*.  
3. *On the Quantity of the Soul*.  
4. He begins the work *On Free Will* and learns certain customs of the Roman Church.

We have seen that Augustine reached Ostia on the Tiber in order to recover his strength there for the voyage and prepare his return to Africa. Yet he did not cross over until after the death of Maximus—that is, in August or September of the year 388. We have discussed this matter at sufficient length above (Book 2, chapter 7). He himself testifies that, after his baptism and before returning to Africa, he remained for some time at Rome (Retractions, Book 1, chapters 7–9). During these days he composed two books, one on the Morals of the Catholic Church, the other on the Morals of the Manichaeans. He also wrote the dialogue On the Magnitude of the Soul and three books On Free Choice of the Will.

The book On the Morals of the Church was published against the Manichaeans. For since Augustine recognized himself to be profoundly indebted to the grace of Christ, through whose [Col. 0156] aid he had at last emerged from the whirlpool of that heresy, he earnestly desired that others also might be rescued from the danger into which he himself had fallen. And in fact he received this consolation: that God, through his ministry and through the books composed by him under divine inspiration, had liberated very many from that wicked error.

The Manichaeans had two principal attractions with which to deceive the unsuspecting and inexperienced: first, their criticism of the books of the Old Testament, which they did not understand; second, their pretended profession of a chaste life and exceptional continence (On the Morals of the Catholic Church, §2). Augustine therefore resolved to explain the teaching and discipline of the Catholic Church, in order to turn the faithful away from this latter snare. He hoped that from this book it might become clear how easily virtue can be pretended and how difficult it is to maintain.

At the very beginning he declares that in other books he had sufficiently shown how the error and impiety with which the Manichaeans attacked the Old Testament could be refuted. Yet we do not find that he dealt with this subject in the earlier short works. Accordingly, we think that the books he there mentions were none other than the two in which, after his return to Africa, he expounded the beginning of Genesis against the calumnies of the Manichaeans.

If this is so, the books On the Morals of the Catholic Church and On the Morals of the Manichaeans were indeed written at Rome, as the author himself testifies; yet they were neither published there nor brought fully to completion until Augustine was already established in Africa. For in several passages he speaks as though he were then absent from Rome, as may be seen in chapter 33 of the first book and chapter 20 of the second. Moreover, in chapter 12 of the same second book he mentions a certain new reply on behalf of the Manichaean heresy, which he says he had recently heard near Carthage. Thus something may have been added in Africa to these books, first written at Rome, before they were circulated.

Augustine therefore could no longer silently endure the Manichaeans’ boastful claims concerning a false continence and deceptive abstinence—claims by which they led the uneducated into error while insolently placing themselves above true Christians, with whom they were not worthy to be compared. He broke his silence and took up his pen. Yet he wished to maintain such moderation that, when attacking their depraved practices, which he knew very well, he would not inveigh against them as harshly as those heretics inveighed against things they did not understand. He desired rather to heal them than to attack and defeat them.

Nor does he there disclose the mysteries that he himself discerned in the Scriptures, since, with God’s favor, he had undertaken not to teach them what was true but to unteach them what was false. Near the end of the first book, moving from moral instruction to examples of virtue that shone forth in the Church, he discusses those perfect inhabitants of the desert who had completely withdrawn from human society; the remarkable multitude of coenobites who, living in deserted places under the governance of a single father, supported themselves by the work of their hands; the consecrated women who, separated from the sight of men, lived according to the same discipline; the many most holy bishops and clergy, whose virtue was all the more wondrous because it is more difficult to preserve it among the wicked; and finally the various Christians of both sexes who, in the midst of cities, pursued the same manner of life that others pursued in solitude. He had seen a similar refuge of the saints at Milan [Col. 0157], and at Rome too he had learned of several such communities.

2. In that book he promises another volume in which he will show how empty, indeed how harmful and sacrilegious, was the virtue of which the Manichaeans boasted, and that scarcely one, or perhaps not even one, of the rules they imposed upon themselves through irrational superstition was observed (On the Morals of the Catholic Church, §75). He accomplishes this in the book On the Morals of the Manichaeans. After refuting their theological principles, he demonstrates what their moral teaching ultimately consisted in. Finally, he points out how carefully they observed it, on the basis of what he had either seen himself or learned from eyewitnesses. We have noted above various examples that he recalls concerning this matter (above, Book 1, chapter 9).

3. At Rome, not long after he had departed from Milan, Augustine composed the book On the Magnitude of the Soul. It is a dialogue that appears sufficiently natural and true to life that it should not be regarded as entirely fictitious. Augustine himself states that it was held with Evodius, in a letter addressed to him (Letter 162, §2).

In this book he investigates and considers many questions about the soul: namely, from where it derives its origin, what it is, how great it is, why, when infused into the body, it becomes what it becomes united with the body, and what it becomes when it has been separated from the body’s structures [Col. 0158]. But because he discusses more fully and carefully how great the soul is, in order to demonstrate both that it is free from quantity and from bodily nature and yet is something great, the work came to be called On the Magnitude of the Soul.

4. Finally, while still residing in the City, he began three books On Free Choice of the Will. He completed the two later books only after an interval of several years, when he had already been ordained a presbyter.

While he was living at Rome, he undoubtedly learned certain customs proper to the Roman Church, which he himself mentions in his writings. One was the frequent practice of fasting on three days of the week—Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday—and especially on Saturday, contrary to the custom of almost all Christians of the East and West, who did not fast on Saturday. Yet even at Rome the Saturday fast was not observed during the Paschal season, and there it was not thought necessary to fast on Thursday (Letter 36, §§8–9).

At Rome also he learned by report of the detestable crimes that the Manichaeans had perpetrated in their sacrifices, as was established by their confession made publicly in court in Gaul (On the Nature of the Good, against the Manichaeans, chapter 4).

# BOOK THREE

On Augustine’s Return to Africa and on the Events That Occurred There until His Episcopate

[Col. 0157]

## CHAPTER ONE

1. He returns to Africa, where he learns from Eulogius that, while Augustine was living at Milan, he had appeared to him in a dream.  
2. He takes part in the miraculous healing of Innocentius.

[Col. 0157]

1. Maximus, who had seized imperial power through tyranny in the year 383 and had expelled the younger Valentinian from Italy in 387, was killed the following year, on the fifth day before the Kalends of August or the sixth day before the Kalends of September. After his death Augustine crossed over to Africa (Against the Letter of Petilianus, Book 3, §30). Yet how greatly he had changed from the Augustine who had departed from Africa in 383!

“They know,” he says, “that we once sailed; they know that we also traveled abroad; they know that we went away as one person and returned as another” (Expositions of the Psalms, Psalm 36, Sermon 3, §19).

He is believed to have landed at Carthage and to have remained there for some time before proceeding to Thagaste. There he heard something marvelous to relate, which had happened while he himself was living at Milan.

“Eulogius,” he says, “the rhetorician of Carthage, who had been my student in that same art, told me this after we had returned to Africa. While he was assigning Cicero’s rhetorical books to his students, he was reviewing a passage that he intended to teach the following day. He encountered an obscure passage which, because he did not understand it, left him so troubled that he could scarcely sleep. That night, as he was dreaming, I explained to him what he did not understand—indeed, not I, but an image of me, without my knowledge, while I was so far away across the sea, occupied with something else or perhaps dreaming, and entirely unconcerned with his anxieties” (On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead, §13).

2. But he recalls another event from this same period, much more pleasing: namely, the healing of the distinguished man Innocentius, formerly an advocate of the vicariate prefecture. Augustine himself, if he was not the author of the account, was certainly an eyewitness.

He describes it carefully in these words:

“When we came from overseas, he—Innocentius—being, together with his entire household, a man of deep religious devotion—had received me and my brother Alypius, who were not yet clergy but were already serving God; and at that time we were staying with him.

“He was being treated by physicians. They had already cut open the fistulas, numerous and complicated, that he had in the back and lower part of his body, and were treating the remaining wounds with the other remedies of their art. In that operation he had suffered prolonged and severe pain. But one among the many channels had deceived the physicians and remained so hidden that they did not touch it, although they ought to have opened it with the knife. Thus, when all the wounds that had been opened and treated were healed, this one alone remained, and their labor was being expended on it in vain.

“Suspecting these delays and greatly fearing that he would be cut again—as another household physician had predicted, a man whom they had not permitted to be present even to observe how they performed the operation when he was first cut, and whom Innocentius had angrily expelled from the house and only reluctantly received again—he burst out and said: ‘Are you going to cut me again? Am I to submit to the words of the man whom you refused to have present?’

“They mocked the inexperienced physician and sought to calm the man’s fear with kind words and promises. Many more days passed, and everything that was done achieved nothing [Col. 0159]. Yet the physicians persisted in their assurances that they would close the channel not with the knife but with medicines.

“They also called in another physician, already very old and highly esteemed in that art—Ammonius, who was still alive. After examining the site, he promised the same thing as the others, relying on their care and expertise. Made confident by his authority, Innocentius mocked his household physician, who had predicted that another operation would be necessary, with playful cheerfulness, as though he were already saved.

“What more is there to say? After so many days had passed uselessly that the physicians, weary and confused, confessed that he could not possibly be cured except by the knife, he was terrified and grew pale, overwhelmed by excessive fear. When he had regained his composure and could speak, he ordered them to leave and not to come near him again.

“Nothing else occurred to the man, exhausted by tears and compelled by that necessity, except to call in a certain Alexandrian, who was then considered a remarkable surgeon, so that he might do himself what he had angrily refused to let the others do. But when the man arrived and, as an expert, saw the work of the other physicians in the scars, he fulfilled the duty of a good man. He persuaded Innocentius to allow those who had labored over him so greatly—so greatly that the surgeon himself marveled as he inspected their work—to enjoy the completion of his cure. He added that he truly could not be saved unless he were cut, but that it was entirely contrary to his own character to deprive of the prize of so great a labor men whose most skillful work, industry, and care he admired as he observed them in the scars, merely because a small part remained.

“The man recovered his courage, and it was agreed that, with the Alexandrian assisting, the physicians themselves should open with the knife that channel which, by the unanimous judgment of all, was now thought incurable by any other means.

“The operation was postponed until the following day. But when the physicians had left, such grief arose in that household from the master’s excessive sorrow that it could scarcely be restrained, like the mourning at a funeral, by any of us.

“Holy men visited him daily: Saturninus, then bishop of Uzalis, of blessed memory; the presbyter Gelosus; and deacons of the Church of Carthage. Among them was Aurelius, who alone of them is now still living and must be named with the honor due to him, since he is now a bishop. We have often spoken with him about God’s marvelous works in this matter, and we found that he remembered very well what we are relating.

“When they visited him in the evening, as they usually did, he begged them with pitiful tears to be willing to be present in the morning at his funeral rather than at his suffering. For such fear of the earlier tortures had seized him that he did not doubt he would die in the physicians’ hands.

“They consoled him and urged him to trust in God and bear his will bravely. Then we entered for prayer. When we had knelt as usual and prostrated ourselves upon the ground, he threw himself down as though someone had violently struck him to the earth, and began to pray.

“Who could express in words the manner, the feeling, the movement of his soul, the flood of tears, the groans and sobs that shook all his limbs and almost cut off his breath? I did not know whether the others were praying or whether their attention had been turned away from this. I myself could not pray at all. I said only this briefly in my heart: ‘Lord, whose prayers of your servants do you hear, if you do not hear these?’

“For it seemed to me that nothing more could be added except that he should breathe his last while praying.

“We rose, received the bishop’s blessing [Col. 0160], and departed; he asked them to be present in the morning, and they urged him to be of good courage.

“The dreaded day dawned. The servants of God were present, as they had promised. The physicians entered. Everything required at that hour was prepared. The dreadful instruments were brought out, while everyone stood stunned and anxious.

“Those of greater authority raised his failing spirit by consoling him. The limbs of the man who was to be cut were arranged on the bed; the knots of the bindings were loosened; the site was uncovered. The physician inspected it and, armed and intent upon cutting the channel, began his examination. He scrutinized it with his eyes, touched it with his fingers, and finally tested it in every way. He found a firm scar.

“Then the joy, praise, and thanksgiving to the merciful and almighty God that poured from everyone’s lips, amid tears of joy, should not be entrusted to my words. It should rather be imagined than spoken” (The City of God, Book 22, chapter 8, §3).

## CHAPTER TWO

1. Augustine distributes his property to the poor.  
2. He follows a communal way of life with companions serving God, whose care he undertakes.  
3. He converses by letter with Nebridius and considers his questions.

1. At last Augustine attained the full measure of his desires and successfully completed, upon returning to Thagaste, what he had purposed in his heart from the time of his baptism (Confessions, Book 9, chapter 8, §17; Possidius, chapter 3), indeed from the time of his conversion, when long before his baptism he had chosen to serve God (ibid., Book 9, chapter 5, §13).

First, he sold the fields left to him by his father, which had come to him by hereditary right, and immediately distributed their price among the poor, reserving absolutely nothing for himself, so that he might enjoy God’s free service with greater freedom from impediment (Letter 126, §7).

For he desired to belong to that “little flock” and to be one of its members, to which the Lord speaks, saying: “Do not be afraid, little flock, because your Father has been pleased to give you the kingdom. Sell what you possess and give alms” (Luke 12:32–33).

He also desired to build upon the foundation of faith not with wood, hay, and straw, but with gold, silver, and precious stones (Possidius, chapter 2). Thus, when he later faced the necessity of restraining the arrogance of the Pelagians, who wished to exclude the rich who did not give up their possessions from the kingdom of God (Letter 156), and wished to demonstrate that he was not moved by private considerations or advantages in refuting them, he said:

“I, who write these things, greatly loved the perfection of which the Lord spoke when he said to the rich young man, ‘Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me’ (Matthew 19:21), and I acted in this way, not through my own strength but with the help of his grace. It will not be counted to my account any less because I was not rich. For the Apostles themselves, who did this first, were not rich. But whoever gives up both what he has and what he desires to have gives up the whole world.

“How far I have advanced along this path of perfection, I know better than any other human being; but God knows better than I. And toward this goal I exhort others with all the strength I can.”

He adds: “And in the name of the Lord I have companions who, through my ministry, have been persuaded to embrace this way of life” (Letter 157, §39).

Among these companions, who were moved by his exhortation to embrace this purpose, were those fellow citizens and friends of his who, serving God together with him, returned to Africa and to their own home and fields (Possidius, chapter 3).

2. These fields were not in the countryside or far from the city but adjoining Thagaste. Writing to Nebridius from there, Augustine says that he could live there according to his wishes more readily than at Carthage or even in the countryside (Letter 10, §1).

In these fields—already alienated by him, for this is how the ancient manuscripts of Possidius read—that is, in fields no longer his own but now subject to another’s legal ownership, he spent nearly three years together with those fellow citizens and friends who clung to him as to a father. Freed from the cares of the world, he lived for God, devoting himself to fasting, prayers, and good works, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord, and, as far as he could, imitating the life of the Egyptian monks and of the others whom he had praised so warmly in the book On the Morals of the Catholic Church (Possidius, chapter 3).

He had not merely abandoned every hope in the world; rather, since he had refused to be what he might have been in the world, he was not thinking at all about pursuing the dignity to which he was later raised in the Church. He had chosen “to be despised in the house of God rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Psalm 83:11). He had separated himself from those who love the world, but he did not place himself on a level with those who rule over peoples (Sermon 355, §2).

He followed the manner and rule of life established under the Apostles, especially the principle that no one in his community should call anything his own, but that everything should be held in common and distributed to each according to his need. “Augustine himself had already done this earlier,” says Possidius, “when he returned from overseas to his own country” (Possidius, chapter 5).

That school of the Lord’s service, established under Augustine’s direction—if we may use the words of blessed Benedict when he speaks of the monastic institution—had Augustine himself as its teacher. To his companions, namely those who had professed the holy service together with him (Rule of Benedict, chapter 5), he was like a father to sons begotten by him in Christ Jesus. He continually cultivated their minds and instructed them in sacred writings and teachings; he nourished them in piety and strengthened them so that one day they might stand by their own strength, without his assistance, in their place of retreat.

When Nebridius urged him to come and live with him, Augustine replied in these words:

“Here are those who cannot come with me and whom I would consider it wrong to abandon. You can live pleasantly in your own mind; but care is being taken that they too may be able to do the same” (Letter 10, §1).

Elsewhere he adds that, from the earliest time of his conversion, after he came to Africa, whenever the brothers questioned him while they saw him at leisure, he dictated those answers from which, when he was already a bishop, he formed the book of Eighty-Three Questions (Retractions, Book 1, chapter 26).

He also attended to their affairs and interests, although such care and concern deprived him of the leisure he desired. Perhaps this was why Nebridius, having once learned that his friend was prevented by the business of his fellow citizens from enjoying the quiet he desired, sent him this brief letter:

“Is this really so, my Augustine? Are you devoting strength and endurance to the business of your fellow citizens, and has that longed-for leisure still not been restored to you? I ask you: what sort of people keep interrupting you? I suppose they are people who do not know what you love and what you desire. Do you have no friend who can tell them of your loves—not Romanianus, not Lucinianus? Let them listen to me: I will cry out, I will testify that you love God and desire to serve and cling to him.

“I would like to invite you to my estate and let you rest there. I will not be afraid of being called your seducer by your fellow citizens, whom you love too much and by whom you are loved too much” (Letter 5).

For the man devoted to God did not manage the affairs of just any fellow citizens, but only of those who had entrusted themselves to his discipline, whose needs he was bound to attend to and serve. Nevertheless, it may be believed that even in his retreat, since he was excessively loved by his fellow citizens and loved them in equal measure, he sometimes undertook responsibility for more serious matters that they brought to him.

In any event, among his companions from the beginning he had Alypius and Evodius, and, apparently, Severus, later bishop of Milevis. He remembers having meditated on the word of God with him for a long time when writing to Novatus (Letter 84, §1).

3. Nebridius, already returned from Milan, as we learn from the preceding letter, was at that time in Africa. He lived either at Carthage or on an estate near the city, together with his mother and his entire household (Letter 10, §1), which God had brought to the faith through his ministry (Confessions, Book 9, chapter 3, §6).

After his baptism he himself served God among his family in perfect chastity and continence. Since he was therefore far away from his friend and they could not often visit one another, they conversed with each other through an exchange of letters.

Nebridius proposed great and difficult questions to Augustine, while Augustine dissolved his knots through letters. “I greatly desire,” says Nebridius, “to preserve them as I do my eyes. They are great, not in quantity but in subject matter, and they contain great proofs of great things. They will sound to me of Christ, of Plato, and of Plotinus. Thus they will be sweet to hear because of their eloquence, easy to read because of their brevity, and wholesome to understand because of their wisdom” (Letter 6, §1).

In one letter to him, one observes that Augustine calls Plato’s recollection a most noble discovery and seems to assert, as though it were his own view, that the soul once saw the truth and later separated itself from it after being united to the body (Letter 7, §2). Something similar can be found in the dialogue On the Magnitude of the Soul (§34), although Augustine interprets it more soundly in his books of Retractions.

It should not, however, seem surprising if Augustine did not immediately reject the opinions he had absorbed from the sources of philosophy. He himself asserts that anyone who reads his works in the order in which they were written will easily notice how he progressed through writing (Retractions, prologue, §3). One will also discover without difficulty many things in his earlier works that he corrected in later ones.

In this connection it may be noted that he was at one time of the opinion of the Millenarians [Col. 0163], though in such a form that the view could in some measure be tolerated—namely, if it were believed that only spiritual delights would come to the saints in that thousand-year kingdom (Sermon 259, §2; The City of God, Book 20, chapter 7).

As for Nebridius’s questions, since they did not all concern divine matters, Augustine writes to him that the questions asked about this world did not seem to him sufficiently relevant to attaining the blessed life. Even if they bring pleasure when investigated, one must nevertheless fear that they may occupy time that ought to be devoted to better things.

Accordingly, among the remaining questions that had to be resolved, he selected the one proposed concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, attempting to explain how, although the actions of the three divine persons are undivided, our mysteries and the religion in which we have been instructed nevertheless attribute the assumption of human nature to the one Son (Letter 11).

From this question it seems possible to conclude with certainty that Nebridius had already been baptized.

That he died somewhat before Augustine’s presbyterate—not in Augustine’s monastery but in his own home—is clearly indicated by Augustine himself in this splendid eulogy for his deceased friend:

“Not long after our conversion and our regeneration through baptism, you released him from the flesh. He was already a faithful Catholic, serving you in Africa among his own people in perfect chastity and continence, while his entire household had become Christian through him. And now he lives in Abraham’s bosom.

“Whatever that bosom signifies, there my Nebridius lives, my sweet friend, but your adopted son, Lord, from a freedman’s household. For where else would such a soul have its place? There he lives, from where he used to ask me, an inexperienced little man, many questions. Now he no longer places his ear to my mouth, but his spiritual mouth to your fountain, and he drinks as much wisdom as he can, according to his thirst, blessed without end.

“Yet I do not think that he becomes so drunk with it that he forgets me, since you, Lord, whom he drinks, remember us” (Confessions, Book 9, chapter 3, §6).

## CHAPTER THREE

1. He composes the books on Genesis against the Manichaeans.  
2. He completes six books on Music.  
3. He publishes the dialogue On the Teacher.  
4. Then the book On True Religion.  
5. He writes to Maximus of Madaura.  
6. To Caelestinus.  
7. To Gaius.  
8. And to Antoninus.

1. Augustine had not withdrawn from worldly cares and occupations in order thereafter to enjoy an empty and sterile leisure in retreat. Therefore he endeavored to benefit not only those who were present—namely, his companions—but also those who were absent and those who were strangers, communicating, as Possidius testifies, through books and conversations what had been revealed by God to him as he meditated and prayed (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 3).

Some traces of those same conversations that he held with his companions still survive in the volume mentioned above, the Eighty-Three Questions.

As for the books he composed at that time, he lists in his Retractions two books on Genesis against the Manichaeans, six books on Music, the book entitled On the Teacher, and the book On True Religion.

In the books he wrote on Genesis, he began to defend the Old Testament against the insane calumnies of the Manichaeans. In the first book he expounds the beginning of Genesis up to the passage where God is said to have rested on the seventh day. In the second he continues the same exposition up to the passage where Adam and his wife are described as having been expelled from paradise. At the end of the book he clearly and concisely opposes the errors of the Manichaeans to the faith of Catholic truth.

In this exposition he followed only the allegorical sense:

“I did not dare,” he says, “to expound literally such great secrets of natural things—that is, to explain how what is said there could be understood according to its historical literal meaning” (Retractions, Book 1, chapter 18).

Later, speaking about these books, Augustine says:

“I composed two books shortly after my conversion, wishing quickly to refute the ravings of the Manichaeans or to raise their attention toward seeking Christian and evangelical faith in the writings they hate. Since at that time I did not yet see how everything could properly be understood, and since many things seemed either incapable of being understood, or scarcely or with difficulty capable of it, I did not wish to be delayed. I explained, with as much brevity and clarity as I could, what those things signified figuratively which I was unable to discover in their literal meaning, so that they would not be deterred by the length of the reading or the obscurity of the argument and thus refuse to take the books in hand.

“Yet I remembered what I had especially desired but had not been able to accomplish: that everything should first be understood not figuratively but properly. Nor did I entirely despair that this could also be done. Thus, in the first part of the second book, I wrote:

“‘Certainly, whoever wishes to accept everything that has been said according to the literal sense—that is, not to understand it otherwise than the letter sounds—can avoid blasphemies and proclaim everything consistent with the Catholic faith. Such a person is not merely undeserving of envy but must be regarded as an outstanding and highly praiseworthy interpreter’” (On Genesis Literally, Book 8, §5).

Later, relying upon God, he published his twelve books On Genesis Literally, which he had not initially dared to undertake, after he had examined the sacred words more carefully.

Yet from the very threshold of that work, On Genesis against the Manichaeans, he offers us in his own person a remarkable example of humility. For he writes that certain men who were educated in the liberal arts but were truly Christian, and who had read his first labors against those same heretics, observed that they could scarcely or only with difficulty be understood by the less educated.

“And they,” he says, “most benevolently warned me not to abandon the ordinary manner of speaking if I intended to drive those very dangerous errors from the minds even of the uneducated. For educated people also understand this customary and simple style, whereas the uneducated do not understand that other style” (On Genesis against the Manichaeans, Book 1, §1).

The holy man accepted this advice with an even temper and put it into practice beginning with this work. In it he professes that he would convict the vanity of the Manichaeans not with an ornate and polished style but with manifest facts.

2. During the brief period in which he remained at Milan in order to receive baptism, Augustine devoted himself, as we have seen, to writing books on the disciplines. Among his other labors he had begun something on Music. After returning to Africa, however, he composed the six surviving books on this subject after the work on Genesis (Retractions, Book 1, chapters 6 and 11).

He wrote those books as a kind of preliminary exercise during the leisure he was then beginning to enjoy (Letter 101, §3), and for the benefit of those who, although divinely endowed with good minds and devoted to more refined literature, become entangled in the errors and illusions of the world and wear out their excellent intellects on trifles, even though they do not understand what delights them in such things.

If they recognized what pleases them in the harmony of created things, they would see both how to escape the allurements by which they are ensnared and where they could find the harbor of blessed security and freedom (On Music, Book 6, §1).

In this work he intended to show how one advances, as though by certain steps, from mutable numbers—whether bodily or spiritual—to immutable numbers existing in the one immutable truth, and thus how “the invisible things of God” may be perceived through understanding by means of the things that have been made.

But he accomplishes this only in the sixth book, in which the entire fruit of the others is found, and which was especially celebrated because it contains matters most worthy of knowledge (Letter 101, §4).

In the first five books he dwells on numbers concerned with the durations of time, which he calls rhythms. These books are extremely difficult to understand. Augustine himself admits that many will regard them as childish trifles, but he hopes that others will judge this arduous labor fairly:

“We thought it should be undertaken,” he says in the preface to the sixth book, “for no other reason than that adolescents, or people of any age whom God has endowed with good intellects, might be drawn away—not precipitously but by certain steps—from the senses of the flesh and from fleshly literature, to which it is difficult for them not to cling. Guided by reason, they might cleave through love to the one God and Lord of all things, who presides over human minds without any intervening nature, and to immutable truth.

“Whoever reads those books will find that we have moved among grammatical and poetic minds, not by a choice of dwelling but by the necessity of traveling. But when he comes to this book, if—as I hope and humbly beseech—our God and Lord has guided my purpose and will and brought them to the goal toward which they are directed, he will understand that the way by which we now choose to walk with the weaker, since we ourselves are not particularly strong, is not a worthless path to a worthless possession. We preferred to proceed along it rather than hurl those with weaker wings through freer airs.

“Thus, I think, he will judge that we have either not sinned at all or not sinned greatly” (On Music, Book 6, §1).

He asserts that those who are not sufficiently educated to follow the path disclosed in this work can nevertheless, if they live by faith in Jesus Christ, complete the journey easily, as it were in flight, supported not by their feet but by the wings of charity. After the course of this life, they will reach the place to which that path leads more surely and happily than the others. Those who can understand these things, however, if they lack faith in the Mediator, will perish most miserably with all their knowledge.

Bishop Memorius requested these books on Music from Augustine. Augustine replied to him through Possidius that he had not yet had leisure to correct them, and sent only the sixth book, which he had found revised and corrected and which alone he considered worthy to be sent.

He adds that he had intended, besides those six books on Rhythm, to compose six others on Melody when he found leisure. But after he had advanced to the priesthood and assumed the burden of ecclesiastical cares, all those delights had slipped from his hands (Letter 101).

### 3.

We have already mentioned the books *On the Teacher*, in which Augustine converses with his son Adeodatus and testifies that all the thoughts inserted there in the son’s person are actually Adeodatus’s, although he was then only sixteen years old (*Confessions*, book 9, chapter 6, §14). From this it may be inferred that the book was written around the middle of the year 389, since Adeodatus was about fifteen when he received Baptism in the year of Christ 387, on the eighth day before the Kalends of May (*ibid.*). In that book, after the matter had been carefully discussed and investigated, he discovered that our true teacher is not one who imparts knowledge to human beings, but God (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 12).

### 4.
