At that time he also composed the book *On True Religion*, in which he demonstrates at length, by many arguments, that the one true God—that is, the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is to be worshiped through true religion. He likewise shows that, through the infinite mercy of God, true—that is, Christian—religion was granted to human beings through the temporal dispensation and incarnation of Jesus Christ. He also explains how a person ought to conform his life to the holiness of this religion. Above all, this book attacks the Manichaeans’ doctrine of two natures, or their error concerning the origin and nature of evil (*ibid.*, chapter 13, §1).

Hardly any of Augustine’s works is more effective in demonstrating the greatness of his extraordinary intellect. Nothing is more worthy of admiration or wonder than that a man newly instructed in the mysteries of the Christian religion, and not yet honored in the Church by any title other than that of “Faithful,” should have been able to discuss that divine religion with such distinction and to portray so excellent an image of its dignity and excellence. In this book he addresses all human beings at certain points, but especially Romanianus, to whom several years earlier—in the year 386, specifically—he had promised to send a discussion of this subject (*On True Religion*, §12). Many years later he refers Evodius back to this book, so that he might form a sound judgment concerning the rational demonstration of God’s existence (*Letter* 162, §2). This book is also to be numbered among the five that Alypius sent to Paulinus in the year 394 (*Letter* 25, §1).

Augustine also informed Romanianus by letter that he had published this book. He wrote to him while traveling, when he was soon to return to Tagaste, from which city he indicated that he was then absent. Romanianus had made Augustine a participant in the favorable outcome of his affairs. Although Augustine rejoiced at this news, he nevertheless warned him not to trust in fleeting prosperity, still less to cling to it, but to devote the leisure granted him by God increasingly to the pursuit of eternal goods (*Letter* 15).

### 5.

There is no doubt that he was still living at Tagaste when he wrote to Maximus of Madaura (*Letter* 17). For the association that appears to have existed between him and this pagan seems to have arisen from no other circumstance than their proximity. Madaura was adjacent to Tagaste (*Confessions*, book 2, chapter 3, §5).

Moreover, since no trace of either an episcopate or a presbyterate of his appears there, and since the worship of idols—which was forbidden by imperial law at the beginning of the year 391—was still public, as is repeatedly indicated there, it may be inferred that the letter was written in the year 390. Maximus, who was called a grammarian, openly professed pagan superstition. The people of Madaura were still, indeed for many years afterward, deeply devoted to it, although a Catholic church had already been established in that town.

Occupied by the pagan error, Maximus acknowledged in his letter to Augustine one supreme God without beginning, whose various powers—and, as it were, whose members—the other gods were. Then, with tasteless and frigid jokes, he mocked the names of certain martyrs of Madaura, although he unwillingly admitted that his thunder-wielding Jupiter and the throng of other immortal gods were placed below them.

As though he were about to assert the truth of his own gods, he added that they were openly worshiped and that sacrifices were offered to them before everyone’s eyes, whereas Christians claimed that their God was present and visible to them in hidden places. He therefore urged Augustine, after laying aside for a little while the eloquence celebrated by the reputation of all mortals, and also setting aside the sharp and compressed arguments of Chrysippus with which Augustine was accustomed to fight, finally to remove dialectic—which makes everything equally probable—and actually demonstrate to him who the Christians’ God was (*Letter* 16).

Augustine replied by telling him to regard the whole of his letter as playful, as though Maximus himself had wished to mock pagan superstition. Nevertheless, Augustine showed that at least a very broad opportunity had been opened to him for demonstrating how much there was in pagan religion that deserved ridicule. He warned him, however, not to burst into blasphemous speech by speaking jestingly about God. For the rest, the matter was worthy of serious discussion; and when Maximus treated it seriously, Augustine would not fail to answer him. At present, he said, he was not permitted to jest at leisure, since friends could rightly demand something else from his purpose (*Letter* 17, §5). By these words the monastic profession customary in those times was being indicated.

### 6.

He had already sent his friend Caelestinus his works against the Manichaeans to read. In a very brief letter—perhaps written before his ordination to the presbyterate, since it contains no indication of that office—Augustine asked him not to delay returning them and to write what he thought of them, and what he found lacking in them for the complete overthrow of those heretics.

He said that he wished continually to place something before Caelestinus’s ears, so that Caelestinus might strip himself of superfluous concerns and clothe himself in what was useful and necessary. There he included in a single expression all the duties of a Christian: not to love the lowest good, not to become arrogant in the intermediate good, or in what is properly one’s own, and thus to make oneself fit to cling to the highest good (*Letter* 18).

### 7.

His letter to Gaius does not appear to belong to any other period. Gaius was perhaps a Manichaean or a Donatist; certainly he was separated from the Catholic flock of Christ. Nevertheless, Augustine hoped that the merciful providence of God would come to his aid.

In a brief conversation that he had had with Gaius, Augustine had noticed his great eagerness in seeking the truth, as well as his considerable strength and wisdom in never abandoning the truth once he had recognized it.

“We recall,” he says, “that, although the ardor of your inquiry was remarkable, your modesty in discussion was not disturbed. For I have scarcely found anyone who questioned more passionately or listened more calmly.”

At that time Augustine could not converse with him frequently. To make up for this, he sent him the letter under discussion, and at the same time gave the brother who carried the letter instructions to place before Gaius for reading everything that Augustine had written against the heresy that Gaius followed.

He writes as follows:

> He will not force anything of mine upon you against your will; for I know what benevolence you harbor toward us. Yet if, after reading these things, you approve them and perceive their truth, do not think them ours except in the sense that they have been given, and so turn to the source from which it was granted to you also to approve them. For no one sees that what he reads is true in the book itself or in the person who wrote it, but rather in himself—if a light of truth, not ordinary but utterly removed from the dregs of the body, has been impressed upon his mind. But if you discover anything false and unworthy of approval, know that it has been sprinkled with human obscurity, and consider such things truly to be ours (*Letter* 19).

### 8.

At about the same time, and perhaps before he had been ordained presbyter, Augustine received a letter from Antoninus full of expressions of duty and friendship. He replied to thank him for regarding him as a faithful servant of God and for loving him greatly on that account. In this connection he says many very beautiful things.

Antoninus’s wife adhered to the Donatist schism. Augustine therefore urged her husband either to implant the fear of God in her mind or to nourish it through the reading of the divine word and serious conversation. For no one who is concerned about the condition of his soul and therefore sincerely and without obstinacy is devoted to seeking the divine will can fail to recognize—provided he makes use of a good guide—what he ought either to flee or to pursue (*Letter* 20).

## CHAPTER IV

1. Augustine is ordained presbyter at Hippo in the year of Christ 391.  
2. On Hippo-Regius.  
3. On Valerius, bishop of that city.  
4. Augustine asks him for a period of time in which to prepare himself in seclusion, through prayer and the study of the sacred Scriptures, for the duties of the presbyterate.  
5. Valerius appears to have granted this request.  
6. At Valerius’s command, the presbyter Augustine expounds the word of God to the people, even in the bishop’s presence.

### 1.

Nearly three years had now passed since Augustine had been living with his companions at the retreat of Tagaste according to the custom and discipline of monks, when some necessity was imposed upon him of going to Hippo in order to secure the salvation of a friend (*Sermon* 355, §2).

He feared promotion to the episcopate so greatly that, when his reputation had already begun to spread and become celebrated among the servants of God, he took care not to approach places that lacked a bishop. He did what he could to be saved in a humble station and to avoid the dangers of an exalted rank.

He saw that in this life, and especially at that time, nothing was easier, pleasanter, or more acceptable to people than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon if it was performed superficially and flatteringly; but nothing was more wretched, sadder, or more condemnable before God. Likewise, he considered that in this life, and especially at that time, nothing was more difficult, laborious, or dangerous than the office of bishop, presbyter, or deacon; but before God nothing was happier, if one served in the manner commanded by our Emperor. What that manner was, however, he was only beginning to learn (*Letter* 21, §1).

Such was his frame of mind when he was divinely called to the ministry that he feared so greatly. He did not ascend to it except because a servant ought not to contradict the Lord.

“I came,” he says, “to that city in order to see a friend whom I thought I might win for God, so that he might be with us in the monastery—almost secure because the place had a bishop. I was seized and made presbyter, and through this step I reached the episcopate” (*Sermon* 355, §2).

Possidius relates the matter somewhat more fully:

> It happened, perhaps at that same time, that a certain man of those called *Agentes in rebus*, who was stationed at Hippo-Regius, a good Christian and one who feared God, having learned of his good reputation and doctrine, desired and longed to see him. He promised that he could despise all the desires and enticements of this world if only he might at some time deserve to hear the word of God from his mouth.
>
> When this had been faithfully reported to him, Augustine, desiring to free the man’s soul from the dangers of this life and from eternal death, went of his own accord and without delay to the aforesaid city. After seeing the man, he spoke with him repeatedly and exhorted him, as far as God granted, to fulfill what he had vowed to God.
>
> The man promised that he would do so from day to day, yet he did not fulfill it in Augustine’s presence at that time. Nevertheless, what divine providence was accomplishing through such a pure vessel, honorable and useful to the Lord and prepared for every good work, could not be idle or fruitless in any place (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 3).

We do not know whether Possidius wished by these words to indicate that this *Agens in rebus* later obeyed Augustine’s counsel, or whether he intended to point out the benefit that the Church afterward derived from Augustine’s journey when he had been promoted to the presbyterate.

Augustine therefore came to Hippo secure in the knowledge that the city had a bishop, namely the holy old man Valerius. But perhaps the Church of Hippo then needed a presbyter, a fact unknown to Augustine. When the people had assembled, he came into the church suspecting nothing of the sort and mingled with the congregation, which had come to know his virtue and doctrine and greatly loved him because, after abandoning his patrimony, he had devoted himself entirely to God (*Letter* 126, §7).

When Valerius was addressing the people and explaining the necessity of ordaining a presbyter, the people suddenly seized Augustine (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 4). They could rightly do so, since the Church of Tagaste had not enrolled Augustine in the clerical service (*Letter* 126, §7).

They therefore presented him, while still a layman, to the bishop for ordination. Everyone, with one accord and desire, demanded that this be done and accomplished, pressing for it with great zeal and loud cries. But Augustine, judging this holy ministry to be extremely dangerous and already foreseeing in his mind the waves and storms to which he would soon be exposed in governing the Church, poured forth a flood of tears (*Letter* 21, §2).

His tears were noticed, and some who did not know their cause attempted to apply a remedy wholly unsuitable to his wound. For they suspected that his tears flowed from a desire for empty glory—namely, because he was not immediately advanced to the episcopate—and they suggested that the presbyterate was indeed beneath his merit, but nevertheless came immediately before the episcopate.

### 2.

Although Augustine resisted in vain, the people’s wish was fulfilled (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 4). Having been made presbyter of the Church of Hippo, he enriched it—not with gold and silver, for he brought it nothing except the clothing he wore (*Sermon* 355, §2)—but with such illustrious doctrine and piety that Hippo-Regius, otherwise little celebrated, was counted among the most distinguished cities of the Christian world because of Augustine’s fame.

According to the geographers, that city was situated on the maritime coast of Numidia. It was strongly defended by nature and by its location, since it endured the siege of the Vandals for fourteen months (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 28). It was approximately eighty-four leagues from Carthage and thirty-eight from Cirta, the metropolis of Numidia.

Geographers observe that this city, now called Bona, under Constantine in the kingdom of Algiers, is still of considerable renown. It was a colony and appears to have been the metropolis of the region that took its name from it, since several bishops are numbered in the territory of Hippo.

Silius Italicus celebrates that city in these words:

> Hippo, beloved of ancient kings  
> (*Punic War*, book 3, verse 259).

It is commonly called Hippo-Regius by the Latins, to distinguish it from the other Hippo, called Zarritus or Diarrhitus, on the same coast in the province of Proconsular Africa.

In the Council of Carthage held under the bishop Cyprian, mention is made of a certain Theogenes of Hippo, who is said to have been crowned with martyrdom. Augustine speaks of the memorial of Saint Theogenes as a place where sacrifice was customarily offered (*Sermon* 273, §7). He also writes of the very famous memorial of twenty martyrs at Hippo (*City of God*, book 22, chapter 8, §9).

Although the episcopal sees in Africa were very numerous, that of Hippo nevertheless extended widely, since even the territory of Fussala, sixteen leagues distant, belonged to the Church of Hippo (*Letter* 209, §2).

### 3.

Valerius, a Greek by birth, then presided over this Church. He was pious and God-fearing, but since he was not fluent in the use of the Latin language and consequently understood that he was less useful to the Church, he repeatedly begged God to provide him with a suitable man for the people entrusted to him, someone who could instruct them through word and doctrine (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 5).

When he was granted the opportunity to ordain Augustine, he believed that his prayers had been divinely heard. Having obtained what he had prayed for, he rejoiced triumphantly and gave abundant thanks to God (*Letter* 29, §7).

He embraced Augustine with the tenderest affection of heart. Although he was not at all unaware of how great a glory the holy presbyter would acquire for himself, no stain of envious jealousy ever polluted the pure mind of the blessed old man. Rather, he rejoiced intensely that his people were being instructed through Augustine’s ministry.

Indeed, he ardently desired Augustine as his successor. And God, to complete his wishes, granted Augustine to him as a colleague while he was still alive, as will be explained below (*Letter* 32, §2).

Augustine, for his part, honored and respected Valerius to such a degree that he dared to do nothing for a time that might displease him—not even something that he knew would redound to the salvation and advancement of his own soul (*Letter* 21, §6).

Writing to Aurelius of Carthage about abolishing the drinking parties customarily held at the tombs of martyrs, he says the following about Valerius:

> We have a bishop from those regions of which I have spoken, where this intemperance does not prevail, and for this we give great thanks to God. His modesty and gentleness, and finally his prudence and concern in the Lord, are such that, even if he were an African, he would quickly be persuaded from the Scriptures that one must take care of the wound inflicted by a licentious and wrongly “free” custom (*Letter* 22, §4).

At that time the Church of Hippo was being torn apart by the Donatist schism. Augustine, who was working to restore it to its former harmony, promised Proculeianus, the Donatist bishop, that Valerius, who was then absent, would gladly approve whatever they might do together.

“I confidently give you my word,” he says, “concerning the mind of the most blessed and venerable father Valerius, who is now absent: he will learn of this with great joy. For I know how much he loves peace and does not boast with any empty vanity of foolish pride” (*Letter* 33, §4).

Augustine relates that once Valerius encountered two countrymen speaking Punic to each other and repeatedly using the word *Salus* as a name. Valerius asked a man who knew both Latin and Punic what that name meant. The countryman replied that it signified three. Valerius then learned with joy that it was not by chance that the name had this signification, but by the most hidden dispensation of divine providence: the true Trinity, our salvation, was signified in Punic by the same word by which salvation is signified in Latin (*Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, begun, §13).

Augustine considered this observation worthy of including in his works to delight the minds of readers.

### 4.

It may be thought that Valerius conferred the rank of presbyter upon Augustine with the intention of entrusting the entire government of his Church to him. This explains why Augustine speaks with such gravity in his letter to Maximinus, a Donatist bishop, in a manner more suited to a bishop than to a presbyter (*Letter* 23).

He also undertook responsibility for conferring Baptism. Hence Licentius calls him “appointed over the fonts of infants” (*On Letter* 26, §3, verse 27).

In ordaining Augustine, however, Valerius appears to have had above all the intention of entrusting him with the task of preaching the word. Augustine therefore writes that, when he began to perform this duty, he experienced far more fully than before how many and how great were the difficulties and dangers surrounding the presbyterate.

He had a sufficiently clear understanding of what pertained to salvation, but he had not yet learned how this same knowledge ought to be ministered for the salvation of others. When he considered so many difficulties, he formed so humble an opinion of himself that he believed force had been used to make him presbyter, with God permitting this as punishment for his sins and correction of his former rashness, since he had criticized the faults of presbyters and bishops too freely.

“I did not know my own strength at all,” he says, “and thought it to be of some importance. But the Lord mocked me and wished to show me by the facts themselves what I was to myself.”

Nevertheless, trusting in God’s mercy, he believed that God was not condemning him but correcting him. Having therefore recognized his sickness, he resolved to seek medicines in the sacred Scriptures and to prepare for himself, through prayer and reading, the health of soul suitable for so dangerous a ministry.

He had no doubt that in the sacred books he would find both counsels and commands by which, once they were known and grasped, a person of God might minister more orderly to ecclesiastical affairs, or at least, amid the hands of the wicked, might either live with a sounder conscience or die in such a way that he would not lose the life for which alone humble and gentle Christian hearts sigh.

“But how can this be done,” he asks, “unless one asks, seeks, and knocks—that is, prays, reads, and mourns?”

To devote himself to these exercises, he earnestly desired at least a postponement until the following Easter. He begged Valerius for this opportunity through the prayers of his brothers and friends.

But Valerius, who was certain that Augustine had been equipped with every resource for all the offices and duties of a presbyter, answered his request in no other way than by declaring his sincere love for him, calling God himself and Jesus Christ as witnesses to it.

Augustine was therefore compelled to present him with a supplicatory written petition, in the form of a letter, requesting permission to withdraw for a time in order to study the sacred Scriptures. This remarkable letter still exists (*Letter* 21). While it reveals Augustine’s singular humility, it also warns those who are considering the ministry of evangelical preaching—an observation made by a man illustrious not only in rank but also in learning and piety, Antonius Godeau, bishop of Grasse, in his *Life of Saint Augustine*, book 1, chapter 28—to prepare themselves for this ministry through prayer, retreat, and meditation on the divine word.

As the same letter makes clear how fully Augustine understood the holiness and difficulty of that ministry, into which so many in our own age rashly involve themselves without reverence or divine vocation, so the zeal and fervor with which he humbly begs for a short delay as an immense benefit most severely condemn the precipitous haste of others.

In any case, that devout fear of so exalted and dangerous a ministry belongs to those who are called by God. By contrast, nearly all those who assume the honor not through the impulse of the Holy Spirit but through their own impulse may be seen imitating those of whom the Lord says: “I did not send the prophets, yet they ran” (Jeremiah 23:21).

### 5.

It is credible that Valerius yielded to Augustine’s earnest and justified prayers and granted him permission to defer the duties of the presbyterate for a time, perhaps until the tradition of the Creed, which occurred near the Paschal feast. At that time Augustine delivered the sermon on the Creed whose beginning is:

> In proportion to our age and our rudimentary beginnings, in proportion to the novitiate of the ministry undertaken and to the affection of our love for you, we who are already ministering at the altar before which you are soon to stand must not deprive you of the ministry of the word (*Sermon* 214, §1).

A few days later, while instructing the Competentes after the exorcism, he addressed them as follows:

> The beginnings of our ministry and your conception  
> (*Sermon* 216, §1).

Since, after undertaking the presbyterate, he had already tested his strength to some extent in that office, and especially in preaching the divine word, and since, having found himself unequal to so great a task, he had asked permission to withdraw for a short time, at least until Easter, in order to devote himself to the sacred Scriptures, it is easily understood that he was ordained not merely at the beginning of Lent, as Rivius maintains, but somewhat earlier.

Accordingly, the beginnings of his ministry can appropriately be referred only to the period when, having emerged from the retreat granted to him, he devoted himself entirely to this office. In this way, it is understood that he was setting aside the duties he had performed before that retreat.

It is unknown where he withdrew. Certainly it was not far from Hippo, for at this first period, or immediately afterward, the people of Hippo greatly and excessively feared Augustine’s prolonged absence and were entirely unwilling to believe him in this matter (*Letter* 22, §9).

From what we have said, it is necessary to place Augustine’s ordination at least at the very beginning of the year. It is commonly assigned to the year 391, in accordance with what Possidius writes: namely, that after returning from Italy to Africa he lived at Tagaste for three years, and that in the clerical state—that is, the presbyterate—or in the episcopate, he lived for nearly forty years until the fifth day before the Kalends of September in the year 430 (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapters 3 and 31).

In the year 391, Easter fell on the sixth of April. At that time Augustine was entering his fortieth year.

### 6.

At that time it was the established custom and practice of the African Church that presbyters either never preached the word of God—as seems possible to infer from certain statements of Optatus, who speaks of preaching as an episcopal duty (*Optatus*, book 3)—or at least did not expound it in church in the presence of bishops.

Jerome mentions this custom, which prevailed in certain Churches, that presbyters should remain silent and not speak in the presence of bishops. He calls it an extremely bad practice, since it gave occasion to suspect that bishops either envied the glory of their presbyters or disdained their sermons (*Jerome, Letter 2 to Nepotianus*).

Valerius, free from these perverse sentiments, knew that in the Eastern Churches presbyters customarily taught the people in the presence of bishops, and he did not hesitate to relax the African custom. Since he saw that he did not possess sufficient fluency in the Latin language to instruct the people, he entrusted his functions to Augustine and ordered him to expound the Gospel very frequently in church in his presence (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 5).

Some bishops criticized this. But that venerable and prudent old man judged that less account should be taken of the tongues of detractors than of the usefulness and fruit that he was securing for his Church through the ministry of a presbyter who instructed it, especially since Valerius himself was less able to do so.

Thus Augustine, like a burning and shining lamp placed upon the Church’s lampstand, illuminated all who were in the house of God with the rays of his teaching.

When the reputation of the sacred sermons that he delivered to the people of Hippo spread far and wide, several Churches followed this good example, so that in them presbyters, after receiving permission from their own bishops, began to expound the word of salvation in the bishops’ presence.

There still exists a letter of Augustine and Alypius, already bishops, to Aurelius of Carthage. In it they congratulate him especially for permitting presbyters, for the first time, to deliver a sermon to the people in his presence (*Letter* 41, §1). This letter appears to have been written during the early years of Augustine’s episcopate.

At the end of one of his sermons, Augustine himself urged the people not to be reluctant to listen to the presbyters who would minister the word of God after him (*Sermon* 20, §5).

## CHAPTER V

1. He establishes a monastery at Hippo.  
2. On his disciples.  
3. Several of them are raised to the episcopate.  
4. Augustine’s monastic life is propagated throughout Africa through his efforts.  
5. How deeply he grieved over the fall of certain monks from his own number.  
6. He demonstrates that it is impossible for the monastic profession to contain no wicked persons mixed among the good.  
7. He orders people of the lowest condition to be admitted to it, and says that those who wish to be admitted while rich are not to be thanked more highly, since they have given their possessions to the poor wherever they may be rather than to the monastery.  
8. On the community of life professed by the nuns of Hippo in the monastery established by him.

### 1.

Although that fortunate day of his ordination might seem to have brought him a different life and the rank of presbyter to have demanded different habits—as Martianus perhaps suggested to his friend on that occasion, namely, after he had perhaps returned to Tagaste following his ordination and was about to depart from there for Hippo (*Letter* 258, §5)—the holy man nevertheless began thinking at once about establishing a monastery, where he might continue steadfastly with the servants of God to maintain a humble and lowly manner of life.

When Bishop Valerius learned of this, he accommodated Augustine’s wishes and granted him a garden for this purpose. He related this to his people in a public sermon, in a very familiar manner of speaking and with the sequence of events somewhat neglected. This gave some people occasion to assert that, after cultivating that way of life at Tagaste, Augustine had come to Hippo in order to establish a monastery because no monastery had yet been organized by him there (Baronius, on the year 391, §24).

This does not appear probable. It is unlikely that, after spending approximately three years in retreat occupied with the exercises of monastic life together with the servants of God, he had been without a monastery, or that the monastery at Tagaste—whose inhabitants Paulinus greeted in the year 394 (*Augustine, Letter* 24, §6)—had been founded by anyone other than Augustine.

Augustine should therefore be read in the following way. When he says:

> I whom, by God’s favor, you see as your bishop came to this city while still young, as many of you know. I was seeking where I might establish a monastery and live with my brothers;

after the words “I was seeking,” one should mentally supply: “since, having become presbyter of Hippo, I had to remain in this city.” Then, separating the words that immediately follow as a parenthesis, one should connect the following sentence back to the earlier words:

> And because I was planning this—to be in a monastery with my brothers—when the old man of blessed memory learned of my purpose and intention, he gave me that garden in which the monastery now stands. I began to gather brothers of good purpose, companions of my own, possessing nothing, as I possessed nothing, and imitating me. Just as I had sold my modest little poverty and distributed it to the poor, so those who wished to be with me would do likewise, so that we might live from a common fund. Our common and great and exceedingly rich estate would be God himself (*Sermon* 355, §2).

Thus, together with the servants of God whom he had gathered, Augustine followed the same way of life that the first Christians had adopted at Jerusalem in the time of the Apostles—a way of life displayed for us in the Acts of the Apostles and one that Augustine himself had already begun to practice while still a layman.

Possidius records the establishment of that monastery at Hippo in these words:

> Having therefore been made presbyter, he immediately established a monastery within the church and began to live with the servants of God according to the manner and rule established under the holy Apostles: above all, so that no one in that fellowship should possess anything as his own, but that everything should be common to them and distributed to each according to his need. He himself had already done this when he returned from overseas to his own country (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 5).

Possidius writes that this community was within the church, perhaps because the garden granted to Augustine by Valerius belonged to the Church of Hippo and was situated near it. The monastery that he established in the episcopal residence was a different one from the former, and he did not begin to build it until he had already become bishop.

Baronius writes that Possidius confused these two monasteries (Baronius, on the year 391, §25). This does not, however, appear credible, nor is there anything that compels us to assert it.

Augustine, while still a presbyter, thanks Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, because through his care and generosity some estate had been given to the brothers (*Letter* 22, §9). By “the brothers” we must understand either the community at Tagaste or that at Hippo. Since both had been gathered by Augustine, each in some manner belonged to his care.

He says that this community of brothers was deeply indebted to Aurelius’s benefaction, since Aurelius showed by his care for them how closely he was united in spirit with the one from whom he was separated by such great distances.

## 2

No one doubts that Alypius, Severus, and Evodius, who while Augustine was still a layman were bound to him by the closest ties, gave their names to this holy community. Aurelius of Carthage himself congratulated Augustine by letter that Alypius had remained in his fellowship and community, so that he might serve as an example to those wishing to avoid the cares of the world (ibid., n. 1). In the two later books of *On Free Choice of the Will*, which he composed shortly before his episcopate, Augustine introduces Evodius as speaking with him, just as in the earlier book, which he had composed at Rome. It is in fact certain that Evodius lived in the monastery (Epist. 158, n. 11), and that he did not reside far from Hippo: on one occasion, apparently by chance, he came into the same house as Proculeianus, the Donatist bishop of Hippo, conversed with him, and subsequently reported his opinion and thinking to Augustine (Epist. 33, n. 2).

Possidius, the distinguished bishop of Calama, who committed Augustine’s deeds to memory, undoubtedly withdrew first of all into his monastery. For he records that he remained attached to Augustine’s charity for very many years and lived in his society and friendship pleasantly and familiarly, without any bitter disagreement, for nearly forty years (Possid., *Life of Augustine*, Preface and ch. 31). Augustine himself writes that Possidius had been nourished by his ministry—not, indeed, by those liberal studies which the slaves of their lusts call liberal, but by the Lord’s bread and heavenly food, as much as, he says, could be dispensed to him through our straitened circumstances (Epist. 101, n. 1).

The same man of God testifies that he had assisted his brother Profuturus in his endeavors (Epist. 28, n. 1), who was raised to the bishopric of Cirta at least by the year 395. Evodius, moreover, writes to Augustine concerning Profuturus, Privatus, and Servilius, who had gone before that holy man from the monastery and whom he asserts had spoken to him after their death (Epist. 158, n. 9). Augustine mentions a certain monk Privatus, who at his death had not transferred several solidi by way of gift to anyone (Epist. 83, n. 4).

Urbanus, later bishop of Sicca, had been a presbyter of Hippo (*Sermon Fragments*, no. 1 of the first fragment). It is also probable that Bishop Peregrinus was the very man who had formerly been Augustine’s deacon (Epist. 171, and Epist. 139, n. 4). Augustine everywhere testifies that he had such a close relationship with Boniface, bishop of Cataqua (Epist. 96, n. 2, and Epist. 97, n. 3), that it can certainly be inferred that Boniface was one of the holy man’s disciples. The same seems to be asserted of Fortunatus, bishop of Cirta (Epist. 115 and Epist. 116).

## 3

But no one should ask us to enumerate the many distinguished men who emerged from Augustine’s school. Possidius, who knew them well, seems to have taken care that the names of those whose outstanding services to the Church he was making public should remain hidden. As he says:

> As divine teaching advanced under the holy Augustine and with the holy Augustine, clerics began to be ordained for the Church of Hippo from among those serving God in the monastery. Then, as the truth of the Catholic Church’s preaching and the purpose, continence, and profound poverty of God’s holy servants became known and increasingly clear from day to day, peace and unity began, and afterward continued, to seek and receive bishops and clerics from the monastery which through that memorable man had begun both to exist and to grow, with great eagerness. For the blessed Augustine, when asked, supplied nearly ten holy and venerable men whom I myself knew—men continent and most learned—to different Churches, including some of the more eminent ones. Likewise, those who came from that holy way of life, as the Churches of the Lord were extended, established monasteries; and, as zeal for the edification of God’s word increased, they supplied to other Churches brothers promoted to receive the priesthood. Thus, as the salutary doctrine of faith, hope, and charity became known through many people and in many places—not only throughout all the regions of Africa but also overseas, and through books published and translated into the Greek language—many things from that one man and through that man were, by God’s favor, made known to many others.

(Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 11)

Of these ten bishops who, summoned from Augustine’s monastery to the episcopate, won for themselves a reputation for holiness by their own merits, eight have already come to our notice and have been praised above: Alypius of Thagaste, Evodius of Uzalis, Profuturus of Cirta, metropolitan of Numidia, Fortunatus, his successor, Severus of Milevis, Possidius of Calama, Urbanus of Sicca, and Peregrinus.

Augustine could not send his beloved disciples, whom he loved as pupils joined to him by the strictest and sweetest intimacy, to the needs of Churches situated far away without suffering because of their departure and being, as it were, pierced by the goads of grief. Nevertheless, he placed the public needs of the Churches before his private interests, hoping that he would one day live eternally with Christ in heaven with those whom, for Christ’s sake, he allowed himself to be separated from on earth (Epist. 84, n. 1).

After he himself had been made bishop, he customarily admitted to his clergy only those from among the members of the monastery who remained steadfast in their holy way of life and were better and more fully tested. Yet he sometimes found that a good monk could scarcely become a good cleric if he possessed sufficient continence but lacked the necessary instruction, or lacked the integrity proper to his person and calling (Epist. 60, n. 1).

## 4

Not only did the bishops summoned from Augustine’s monastery establish other coenobia, each in his own diocese; it is also reasonable to think that Aurelius and many others had done the same even before Augustine’s episcopate. For when Augustine attained the episcopate, more than a year had already passed since Paulinus had not only commended himself through Alypius to the prayers of the holy men—“who,” he says, “are companions in the clergy of Your Holiness and rivals in faith and virtue in your monasteries”—but had also, at the end of his letter, sent greetings to the brothers of the Churches and monasteries of Carthage, Thagaste, Hippo-Regius, and other places in Africa (Epist. 24, n. 2).

Augustine too sent him greetings in the name of the brothers: “not only those who live with us,” he says, “but also those who live anywhere and likewise serve God” (Epist. 27, n. 6). Even the cedars of Lebanon—that is, the noble and wealthy of this world—thought themselves especially fortunate if sparrows and the poor, who had abandoned everything for Christ’s sake and the profession of a common life, gathered beneath the shade of their branches and built their nests. They granted them fields and gardens and constructed churches and monasteries for them (*Exposition on Psalm* 103, sermon 3, nos. 16–17).

Hence it sometimes happened that several coenobia were found in one and the same city. Besides the one that Augustine founded near Hippo immediately after his ordination, a second seems to have been established in the same city by the presbyter Leporius, and a third there by Eleusinus (*Sermon* 356, nos. 10, 15).

For this reason Possidius writes that, when Augustine departed this life, he left his Church enriched with many monasteries of men and women devoted to continence and filled with them (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 31). These must have been established in the city; otherwise, since the Vandals besieged it for many months, they would have been destroyed. These are the abundant fruits that sprang from Augustine’s piety as from a root. Therefore he was not undeservedly regarded as the founder of monks and monasteries, since in reality we see that he was the founder of the monastic order in Africa.

Yet the adversaries of the Church, who did not hesitate to charge Augustine with this as a serious crime, showed that they were ignorant of that way of life—or rather, pretended not to know what was famous throughout the whole world (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 3, no. 48). What is more, they cast off all shame to such an extent that they dared to compare this most holy institution with their Circumcellions. Concerning this Augustine says to the Catholics:

> If they are to be compared, you must decide; if your words are needed, you are already in difficulty. Nothing is necessary except that you admonish each person to pay attention—only to pay attention and compare. What need is there for your words? Let drunkards be compared with sober men, the reckless with the thoughtful, the raging with the simple, the wandering with the gathered. Nevertheless, dearest brothers, there are also false monks, and we know such men; but the pious brotherhood has not perished because of those who profess to be what they are not.

(*Exposition on Psalm* 132, nos. 3–4)

## 5

Among his own people he endured such men with grief—men who were not unknown and were bound not merely by lesser crimes. For, as he repeatedly reminded his people, there is no state of life so perfect that it contains no weak persons, indeed even traitors; nor is there any society so holy that scandal is not sometimes found within it.

When the Lord included all people under three categories—those in the field, those at the mill, and those in bed—“by those in bed,” Augustine says, “he wished to indicate those who loved quiet; for by the bed he wished quiet to be understood: those who do not mix with the crowds or the turmoil of the human race, but serve God in leisure. Yet from there also one will be taken and one will be left. There are upright people there, and there are rejected people there” (ibid., no. 4).

Thus he says somewhere:

> However vigilant the discipline of my household may be, I am a human being, and I live among human beings. Nor do I dare arrogate to myself that my household is better than Noah’s ark, where, among eight human beings, one was nevertheless found to be rejected, and so forth; or better than the household of the Lord Christ himself, in which eleven good men tolerated the treacherous thief Judas; or finally better than heaven, from which angels fell.  
>   
> I frankly confess to your Charity, before the Lord our God, who is witness over my soul, that from the time I began to serve God, just as I have scarcely found anyone better than those who have made progress in monasteries, so I have not found anyone worse than those who have fallen in monasteries. Thus I think it is written in the Apocalypse: “Let the just person become more just, and let the filthy person become still filthier” (Rev. 22:11).  
>   
> Therefore, although we grieve over certain impurities, we are nevertheless consoled by the many more adornments. Do not, then, detest the winepress because of the dregs that offend your eyes, when it is from that winepress that the Lord’s storehouses are filled with the fruit of brighter oil.

(Epist. 78, nos. 8–9)

As bishop, he wrote this to the people of Hippo on the occasion of a certain scandal that had arisen in his own household between the presbyter Boniface and another man named Spes. He used these experiences to cultivate a low opinion of himself and at the same time to urge others to place their confidence not in him, nor in the discipline of his household, however good it might be, but in God alone.

“There was,” he says, “a certain man in our monastery who, when the brothers reproved him for doing certain things that ought not to be done and failing to do things that ought to be done, replied: ‘Whatever I am now, I shall be such as God foresaw that I would be.’ He was indeed speaking the truth, but that truth did not advance him toward the good. Rather, he advanced so far toward evil that, abandoning the fellowship of the monastery, he became a dog returning to its vomit. Yet what he will be in the future remains uncertain” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 38).

Donatus had left Augustine’s monastery with his brother so that, driven by ambition, both might hurry elsewhere to undertake the clerical life (Epist. 60). Augustine had begotten in Christ Jesus through the Gospel Paul, the bishop whom Boniface succeeded in the see of Cataqua. Yet he could not prevent Paul, by his wholesome counsels, kindness, or severity, from wounding the entire Church of Hippo through his perverse conduct. Consequently Augustine was forced to withdraw from communion with him (Epist. 85).

Antonius, whom Augustine had with him in his monastery and had brought up there from childhood, he advanced to the episcopate of Fussala. Yet Antonius discharged that office so perversely that Augustine himself, tormented by grief because he had supported his episcopate, considered renouncing his episcopal dignity in order to give himself over to laments appropriate to his error (Epist. 209, nos. 3, 10).

He gives a remarkably strange account of a monk who likewise had been brought up with him from childhood; yet after recounting the story, he says that the man did not persevere in his resolve to holiness (*On Genesis Literally*, book 12, nos. 37–38).

## 6

The more dearly he loved the monastic order, the more painfully he bore the falls and disgrace of monks, since these plainly opposed his zeal and desire that the holy institution should be propagated and flourish throughout Africa, as it already did in other parts of the Christian world.

He tempered his grief, however, when he reflected that, by God’s ordering, the condition of this life is such that nowhere are there grains without chaff, nowhere wheat except among weeds; and that everywhere souls—even those nearest to God in purity—live amid daughters like lilies among thorns. That is, they must necessarily live with those who, although daughters because of the Lord’s sacraments, are nevertheless thorns because of their conduct (*Exposition on Psalm* 99, no. 8).

Therefore, just as he did not want any condition of life praised in such a way that the evils mixed into it were concealed, so he did not approve of those who praised the monastic profession excessively, as though it alone, by some special prerogative, could be thought free of wicked people.

“You who praise it,” he says, “mention the wicked mixed in with it; you who condemn it, look also for the good there.” So too in that common life of the brothers which exists in a monastery:

> Great and holy men live there daily in hymns, prayers, and praises of God. They occupy themselves with reading; they labor with their hands and thereby support themselves. They do not ask greedily for anything; whatever is brought to them by pious brothers, they use with sufficiency and charity. No one appropriates for himself anything that another does not have; they all love one another, and they all support one another.  
>   
> You have praised it—you have praised it. Anyone who does not know what takes place within, who does not know how, when that wind enters, ships collide even in harbor, enters as though expecting security and thinking that he will have no one to tolerate. He finds wicked brothers there, who could not be found wicked unless they had been admitted. And they must first be tolerated, lest perhaps they be corrected; nor can they easily be excluded unless they have first been tolerated.  
>   
> Then he himself becomes unbearably impatient. “What was I seeking here? I thought there was charity here.” Irritated by the annoyance of a few people, and failing to persevere in fulfilling what he vowed, he becomes a deserter from so holy a way of life and guilty of a vow not fulfilled. Once he has left, he becomes a critic and reviler as well. He reports only what he claims he himself could not endure—and sometimes what he says is true.  
>   
> But the evils that are true must be tolerated for the sake of fellowship with the good. Scripture says to him: “Woe to those who have lost endurance!” (Ecclus. 2:16). Moreover, he belches forth the foul odor of indignation, by which he discourages those about to enter, because he himself, after entering, could not endure to remain. “What are they like? Envious, quarrelsome, tolerating no one, greedy. That man did this there, and the other did that there.”  
>   
> Why, wicked man, are you silent about the good? You denounce those whom you could not tolerate; you are silent about those who tolerated you, a wicked man.  
>   
> He compared this profession, therefore, with a harbor, in which ships indeed lie more safely than on the open sea, but not in complete security. “For,” he said, “a harbor also has an entrance from somewhere. If a harbor had no entrance on any side, no ship would enter it; therefore it must be open on one side. Sometimes, however, through the opening by which it lies open, the wind rushes in; and where there are no rocks, ships collide with one another and are wrecked. Where, then, is security, if not even in a harbor? And yet it must be confessed, it must be granted, it is true: they are in any event safer in harbor than on the open sea.  
>   
> “Let ships love one another in harbor; let them lie properly alongside one another and not collide. Let equality and uniformity be preserved there, together with steadfast charity. And when perhaps the wind rushes in through the side that is open, let prudent steering be exercised there.  
>   
> “For what will whoever happens to preside over such places—or rather, whoever serves the brothers in what are called monasteries—say to me? What will he say? ‘I shall be cautious; I shall admit no wicked man, no wicked brother who enters; with a few good men things will go well for me.’ How will you admit no wicked man? How will you recognize the person whom you perhaps wish to exclude? To discover whether he is wicked, he must be tested within. How, then, do you exclude one who is about to enter but must afterward be tested, and cannot be tested unless he enters?  
>   
> “Will you repel all wicked men? You say that you know how to inspect them. Do all come to you with their hearts laid bare? Those who are about to enter do not know themselves; how much less do you know them? Many have promised themselves that they would fulfill that holy common life in which all things are held in common, where no one says that anything is his own, and where there is one soul and one heart directed toward God. They were sent into the furnace, and they burst apart. How, then, do you recognize one who is still unknown even to himself?  
>   
> “Do you exclude wicked brothers from the assembly of the good? Whoever you are who say such things, exclude all wicked thoughts from your own heart, if you can. Where, then, is security? Here, nowhere; in this life, nowhere except in the sole hope of God’s promises.”

(*Exposition on Psalm* 99, nos. 10–11)

## 7

He did not wish to exclude people of the humblest station, although it was less clear whether they came with a genuine intention of serving God or rather out of love for a more comfortable and respectable life.

“Now,” he says, “people generally come to this profession of service to God from a servile condition, or as freedmen, or because they have been or are to be freed by their masters, and from rural life, from the practice of crafts, and from plebeian labor—people who have in any case been raised all the more happily because they have been trained more vigorously. If such people are not admitted, it is a grave fault. For many from this number have proved to be truly great and worthy of imitation.

“For this reason, ‘God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and the base things of the world, and things that are not, as though they were, to bring to nothing the things that are, so that no flesh might glory before God’” (1 Cor. 1:27–29).

This pious and holy consideration therefore leads such people to be admitted even when they bring no evidence of a life changed for the better. For it is not apparent whether they have come with a resolve to serve God, or whether, fleeing a poor and laborious life, they have wished to be fed and clothed without contributing anything, and, in addition, to be honored by those who had been accustomed to despise and oppress them (*On the Work of Monks*, no. 25).

Nor did he want the poor in his society ever to be distinguished from those who had brought something with them (*Sermon* 356, no. 9). With this attitude, he certainly did not depart from the rule concerning the reception of believers into Christ’s household, which he expressed in these words:

> Far be it that in your tabernacle the persons of the rich should be preferred to the poor, or the noble to the lowly, when you rather chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and chose the base and contemptible things of this world, and things that are not as though they were, to bring to nothing the things that are.

(*Confessions*, book 8, ch. 4, no. 9)

As for the rich, who leave their possessions and distribute them among the poor, thereby offering substantial evidence of their interior disposition:

> It should not be considered in which monasteries or in what place someone has spent what he possessed on needy brothers. For all Christians share one commonwealth. Therefore, whoever, wherever, distributes what Christians need, wherever he himself receives what he needs, receives it from Christ’s possessions. For wherever he gave to such people, who but Christ received?

(*On the Work of Monks*, no. 33)

Moreover, the holy man had become convinced that the good work of such people contributed in some degree to the monastery into which they withdrew, indeed that it belonged to that monastery, provided that the brothers regarded it with gratitude. Thus, after recounting that Leporius, although distinguished by worldly birth and born into a highly honorable family, was already serving God and had been received as a poor man after abandoning everything he possessed, because he had already distributed his property among the poor, Augustine says:

> He did not do it here, but we know where he did it. The unity of Christ and of the Church is one. Wherever he has done a good work, it also belongs to us, if we rejoice with him.

(*Sermon* 356, no. 10)

Besides the monastic coenobium that provided the setting for this account, and which Augustine appears to have wished to establish on the model of the many communities he had seen at Milan and Rome, once he was bishop he founded another for clerics, as we shall see in its proper place.

## 8

With the same zeal and purpose with which he had handed on the institution of the common life to men serving God, the holy Bishop—whose whole mind was directed toward the salvation of all—was also moved to provide such assistance to virgins dedicated to Christ.

Although the Church had always had virgins, whom she regarded as the most noble part of the Christian flock, they had not always lived together in monasteries, where they could kindle one another’s zeal for piety and protect one another from the attacks of human beings and demons. Nor are we informed whether any traces of such monasteries can be found in Africa before Augustine. It is certain that several existed in his time, although not all who professed virginity confined themselves within them (*Sermon* 355, no. 6).

There were very many at Hippo-Regius (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 31), and one in particular which Augustine had planted, as he himself says, like a garden of the Lord (Epist. 211, n. 3). His sister had presided over this monastery for many years, serving God in holy widowhood until her death. His nieces on his brother’s side also lived there (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 26).

He wrote a letter to the holy women of this coenobium (Epist. 211), which can appropriately be assigned to the final years of Augustine’s life. His sister, who had long served as superior of that coenobium, had already died, and another superior had succeeded her. Under the latter, as under their own mother, the holy women had by then grown old over many years (Epist. 211, n. 4).

Augustine drew great consolation from this monastery, of which he speaks as follows:

> I am accustomed to rejoice over you and, amid the many scandals with which this world everywhere abounds, sometimes to be consoled when I think of your abundant congregation, chaste love, and holy way of life, and of the greater grace of God that has been given to you, so that you have not only despised carnal marriages but have also chosen to live together unanimously in one household, so that you may have one soul and one heart directed toward God.  
>   
> When I consider these good things in you, these gifts of God, my heart, shaken by many storms arising from other evils, is accustomed somehow to find rest.

(Ibid., nos. 2–3)

Although he diligently cultivated and carefully watered this garden of the Lord, which he himself had planted through his own labor, he very rarely went to visit the holy women. For he visited women’s monasteries only when compelled by the greatest necessity, as Possidius considered worth noting (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 26).

Some think that the superior was Felicitas herself, to whom Augustine entrusted a letter with this inscription: “To the most beloved and most holy mother Felicitas, and to the brother Rusticus, and to the sisters who are with you” (Epist. 210). We do not know whether Rusticus was a presbyter of that monastery. There was a man of this name among the presbyters of Hippo in the year 426 (Epist. 213, n. 1).

In the coenobium mentioned earlier, however, the holy women were in great turmoil and urgently desired that their superior be replaced; for this reason they strongly wished to see Augustine. The holy Bishop thought it sufficient to send them a letter of reproof, in which he rebuked their fault forcefully but lovingly. He exhorted them to persevere in their good resolve; if they did so, they would no longer speak of changing their superior.

“May God quiet and compose your minds,” he says. “May the work of the devil not prevail in you, but may the peace of Christ conquer in your hearts. Do not, because you are grieved that what you want is not done, or because you are ashamed to have wanted what you ought not to have wanted, run shamefully toward death. Rather, by repenting, recover your strength. Do not have the repentance of Judas the betrayer; have instead the tears of Peter the shepherd” (Epist. 211, n. 4).

Immediately after these words begins the Rule prescribed by Augustine for the holy women, wholly worthy of its author.

# CHAPTER VI

1. Aurelius is made bishop of Carthage, from which immense benefits flow to the African Churches.  
2. Augustine writes to him so that he may remove banquets and other abuses from the churches.  
3. He grieves that contentiousness and the desire for empty praise are found even among the clergy themselves.

## 1

When Augustine returned from Italy toward the end of the year 388, Aurelius was at that time a deacon of Carthage (*City of God*, book 22, ch. 8, no. 3). While still occupying that rank, he lamented intolerably—and indeed detested—certain vicious customs that reigned with impunity throughout Africa. Therefore, when he was advanced to the Carthaginian see, no one seemed more worthy of healing those abuses through the authority of his office.

Those who sincerely loved the Church, such as Augustine, had previously seemed to despair that the shameful vices disfiguring most of its members and eliciting groans from a few others could ever be driven out. But once they saw that Aurelius had been divinely granted authority, they began to lose their despair. Indeed, since they believed that he excelled inwardly in virtue more than he stood out outwardly in dignity, they were led to the firmest hope that those shameful customs would be abolished both by the prudence of this bishop and by the authority of the councils he was to convene.

Nor did their hope deceive them. For as long as Aurelius governed the Church of Carthage, he always showed himself a successor worthy of Cyprian. The African Church never flourished more than under this bishop. No part of the Catholic Church displayed greater grace and piety. Without any charge of rashness, it seems possible to assert that, after the apostolic age, nowhere did the dignity of the Christian religion, the learning of ecclesiastical doctrine, and the form of episcopal government shine forth with such distinction as they did in the African Church during those fortunate times when Aurelius was its head and Augustine its soul.

These two outstanding bishops were always so closely joined for the support of their brothers that neither the distinction of Aurelius’s see nor the illustrious and widespread fame of Augustine appears ever to have diminished their friendship through any movement of rivalry or envy.

## 2

The first evidence of their mutual friendship that comes before us is a letter written by Aurelius, already bishop of Carthage, to Augustine. Augustine replied to it in his twenty-second letter, which he seems to have composed shortly after his own ordination, when he was beginning to establish his monastery at Hippo and at the very beginning of Aurelius’s episcopate—for in it he mentions the hope that all good people had conceived concerning him.

Accordingly, it may be affirmed that Aurelius was not made bishop before the year 390. In fact, we see his predecessor Genethlius presiding at the Second Council of Carthage on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June in the year 390. Aurelius, however, held the Carthaginian see in the year 393, since the Council of Hippo, recorded as having been held on 8 October of that year, belongs among those held under his authority.

The letter that Aurelius wrote to Augustine is not extant. We can gather only that he commended himself to Augustine’s prayers, congratulated him that Alypius was living with him, and mentioned in that letter the land that had been given to Augustine’s monastery.

Augustine had already honored and loved this holy bishop. When he read in Aurelius’s letter the marks of sincere affection, he was so moved that he remained for a long time uncertain in what words he should reply. At last he entrusted himself to God, so that God might suggest a response appropriate to the zeal and devotion that both men displayed for the good of the Church.

Aurelius’s letter gave Augustine confidence to converse with him as though he were speaking with himself. After informing Aurelius of the prayers that he himself and the brothers poured out before God, so that the outcome might answer the hope conceived concerning his episcopate, Augustine exhorted him to abolish the banquets at which Africans, even under an outward appearance of piety, indulged in the churches.

He also promised that, provided Aurelius first put his hand to the work, Valerius of Hippo would not fail to support him. Augustine says many excellent things on this subject, and includes a passage of the greatest importance concerning the observance of offerings for the dead (Epist. 22, nos. 1–6).

Aurelius undoubtedly fulfilled his duty to the Church in this matter. Augustine testifies in a sermon delivered to the people that, when he wished to drive drunkenness from the basilica in which he was preaching—drunkenness that was in fact removed despite the futile opposition of a disturbance raised by worldly people—he incurred great danger. This seems to have happened at Carthage, since in that sermon he speaks at length about spectacles and treats an argument that had been proposed to him by others (*Sermon* 252, no. 4).

## 3

To return to the remainder of Augustine’s letter to Aurelius: in it he also says splendid things about empty glory and the desire for praise. He adds that he is saying these things not so much to instruct Aurelius as to rouse himself to fight bravely against the enemy, whose strength is felt only by the person who has declared war upon him.

“While I fight the adversary fiercely,” he says, “I often receive wounds from him, because I cannot take away from myself the pleasure of praise when it is offered. I have written these things so that, if they are no longer necessary for Your Holiness—either because you yourself consider more numerous and more useful matters of this kind, or because Your Holiness has no need of this medicine—my illnesses may nevertheless be known to you, and you may know what you should deign to ask God for on account of my weakness. I beg you to do this with the utmost earnestness, by the humanity of him who gave the command that we should bear one another’s burdens” (Ep. 22, nos. 8–9).

He adds that much remained in his life and conduct over which he would have to grieve if he were permitted to discuss these matters with Aurelius face to face rather than by letter. The people of Hippo, moreover, would not consent; fearing that he would abandon them, they could not endure his long absence.

Nevertheless, he asks Aurelius to join him in urgently entreating Saturninus, whom both men sincerely loved, not to be reluctant to come to him. Augustine was deeply respectful toward that old man, and had himself witnessed his exceptional devotion to Aurelius; consequently, he says, he would scarcely recognize any difference between a conversation he might have with Saturninus and one he might have with Aurelius himself.

We do not know whether this Saturninus—whom we cannot doubt was an ancient and celebrated bishop—was the blessed-memory bishop Saturninus of Uzalis, whom Augustine saw at Carthage together with Aurelius (*City of God*, book 22, ch. 8), in the year 388.

# CHAPTER VII

1. He writes the book *On the Usefulness of Believing* to Honoratus, who was devoted to the Manichaeans.  
2. Then he writes the book *On the Two Souls* against the same Manichaeans.  
3. He refutes Fortunatus, a Manichaean presbyter, in a public debate.  
4. He refutes Adimantus, a disciple of the Manichaeans.

1. Although Augustine, at Valerius’s command, instructed the people of Hippo by preaching and diligently carried out the other duties of his presbyterate, these responsibilities nevertheless did not prevent him from educating the universal Church through his published writings. He first devoted himself to attacking the Manichaeans, who were numerous at Hippo Regius because of a certain Manichaean presbyter—his name was Fortunatus—who had infected many citizens and foreigners there with the poison of his perverse teaching (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 14). He dedicated his first work to his friend Honoratus, who was entangled in the snares of the Manichaeans, into which Augustine himself had once cast him (*On the Usefulness of Believing*, no. 2).

Honoratus had a keen judgment and sufficiently recognized how weak some of the Manichaeans’ answers were; he was also tossed about by almost the same waves of anxiety and concern by which Augustine’s mind had formerly been shaken, before his conversion. Yet he had been deceived by those attractive promises of the Manichaeans in which they assured people that they would affirm nothing except what was clear, evident, and manifest. Likewise, he ridiculed the discipline of the Catholic faith because faith was imposed upon human beings, while the truth was not demonstrated to them by reason.

Since, therefore, Honoratus had been deceived by a false appearance of truth and clung to the error not because he had been drawn by any temporal advantage, but was more a man misled by the heretics than himself a heretic, Augustine believed that he could lead him to knowledge of the truth by the same path by which he himself had arrived there. For this purpose he wrote him a distinguished book, entitled *On the Usefulness of Believing*, in order to show that the Manichaeans rashly and sacrilegiously attack those who, following the authority of the Catholic faith, prepare themselves for understanding the mysteries while believing what they are not yet able to grasp intellectually and cleansing their minds to receive the rays of the divine light. This single subject is treated in the work. He reserved for other works a refutation of the fables invented by the Manichaeans and a fuller discussion of Catholic teaching, if he judged that these would contribute to Honoratus’s salvation; indeed, he had already dealt with these matters in other volumes that had been published.

He says that he is treating Honoratus as a familiar friend, in a simple style—that is, as he was then able to do—setting aside the depth of learning that he had admired in other highly educated men (*ibid.*, no. 10). He adds that he was not yet sufficiently practiced in the sacred Scriptures. He had asked God that this work might be useful to Honoratus and to others into whose hands it might come.

“And I hope that this will be so,” he says, “if I am rightly conscious of myself: that I approached this style with a pious and dutiful spirit, not from a desire for an empty reputation or a trivial display. God knows—for he knows the hidden things of my conscience—that I am doing nothing maliciously in this discussion, but, as I think it ought to be received, for the purpose of testing the truth. To this one task we have long since determined to devote our lives, and with extraordinary anxiety: lest it should be very easy for me to go astray with you, while keeping the right path with you should be, to put it no more harshly, exceedingly difficult.

“Yet I venture to believe that even in this hope—in which I hope that you will attain the way of wisdom together with me—he to whom I am consecrated will not abandon me. Day and night I strive to gaze upon him; and because, on account of my sins and because I bear the soul’s eye wounded by the blows of long-standing habits of opinion, I recognize that I am weak, I often beg him with tears. Just as, after a long blindness and darkness, people whose eyes have scarcely been opened still tremble before and turn away from the light, although they desire it—especially if someone attempts to expose them to this sun—so it now happens to me. I do not deny that there is something ineffable and unique that can be seen by the mind as the soul’s good; yet with weeping and groaning I confess that I am not yet fit to contemplate it.

“He therefore will not abandon me, if I am inventing nothing, if duty guides me, if I love the truth, if I cherish friendship, and if I greatly fear that you may be deceived” (*ibid.*, nos. 1, 4).

The outcome desired by Augustine’s efforts on behalf of Honoratus was achieved, if indeed Honoratus was the man who, as is thought, sent various questions from Carthage to Augustine around the year 412 for him to resolve (*Letter* 140, no. 83).

2. After the book *On the Usefulness of Believing*, Augustine wrote *On Two Souls* (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 15). The Manichaeans say that two souls exist in the human being: one good, and the other belonging to the flesh and deriving from the race of darkness, which they oppose to God. They attribute all the good in a human being to the good soul, and all the evil to the evil soul.

Augustine proves this opinion false. The arguments he employs carry all the greater weight and force for persuading and moving his readers because he does not set them out as a disputant, but only with sorrow, regretting that he had not used them when he allowed himself to be deceived by the Manichaeans, although he shows that he could have used them. They are drawn from the nature of the matter itself and from the common judgment of humanity [Col. 0187] (*On Two Souls*, no. 22).

He asserts that he had been turned away from consideration of matters so evident by his habit of sinning, and that he now perceives, in the loss suffered by his closest friends, what he had not at all perceived at that time in the danger threatening himself. He therefore concludes the work by praying and pleading with God to recall them from error through the help of the same grace that he himself had experienced. By praying in this way, he acknowledges not only that those who have turned to God are helped by his grace so that they may make progress, but also that their conversion itself belongs to the grace of God (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 15, no. 8).

In this work he gives hope that in other writings he will show how the Catholic Scriptures can be defended against the accusations and slanders of the Manichaeans; this he accomplished especially when writing against Faustus. There are various passages in this same work that the Pelagians and other opponents of grace could twist in support of their errors. Julian, writing against Augustine, specifically congratulates him after producing one such passage, exclaiming: “O shining gold in dung! What truer or fuller statement could anyone, even an orthodox person, have made?” Yet Augustine himself shows in no way that these passages support them (*Unfinished Work*, book 1, chapters 44–45).

The books *On the Usefulness of Believing* and *On Two Souls* should be assigned to the year 391 or 392, since Augustine places them before the disputation that he held with Fortunatus on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the year 392.

3. We have already said that this Fortunatus was a Manichaean presbyter who, after having lived for a long time at Hippo Regius, had seduced so many people there that he loved living in that city because of them (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 16). Eventually, however, all the Catholics of that city, together with the foreigners then residing there, and even the Donatists themselves, approached Augustine and asked him to discuss the Law with Fortunatus, who was regarded by them as learned.

Augustine, always ready to give an account of his faith and of the hope and trust that he had placed in God, and fully capable of exhorting people in sound doctrine and refuting those who contradicted it, did not refuse the conversation. He did, however, inquire whether Fortunatus himself wished to undertake it. They immediately conveyed this request to Fortunatus, asking, urging, and entreating him not to refuse the encounter.

Fortunatus had known this formidable adversary at Carthage while Augustine was following the Manichaean cause, and for a long time he wavered, helpless and uncertain what to do. Yet he could not resist the earnest requests of the people—especially of the Manichaeans—lest by declining the contest of disputation he should silently betray the weakness of his cause. He therefore promised that he would enter the arena and defend his side (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 6).

A day and place were appointed, and it was agreed that the question should be examined by reasoning: whether there could be two natures, eternal and opposed to one another, as the Manichaeans maintained. Since those heretics rejected various parts of Scripture at will, it was difficult to overcome them by authority. Accordingly, they met at Hippo in the Baths of Sossius on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the year 392 [Col. 0188], with very many learned men gathering there, along with others drawn either by a desire to learn or by curiosity (*Against Fortunatus*, first disputation, no. 1).

At the end of the *Acts*, one might suppose that only baptized believers were present at the second disputation (*ibid.*, second disputation, no. 37). Nevertheless, it is clear from Possidius that many Manichaeans were also present when Fortunatus fell silent during it (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 6); indeed, it is scarcely, if at all, credible that the matter took place otherwise. On both sides, notaries recorded what was said as though in public proceedings.

Augustine pressed Fortunatus with an argument that he had received from Nebridius: if God could suffer nothing from the race of darkness that the Manichaeans imagine, because he is inviolable, then he ought not to have sent souls there—that is, according to their opinion, a part of his own substance—so that they might suffer afflictions. But if he could suffer something from the race of darkness, he is not inviolable. From this Augustine wished to infer that evil proceeds from the free choice of the will, while Fortunatus was attempting to persuade them that the nature of evil and of darkness was coeternal with God himself.

The disputation continued until Fortunatus burst into this blasphemous statement: “The Word of God is bound in the race of darkness.” When those present recoiled from this, the meeting ended. The conversation on the same subject was resumed on the following day. In that discussion Augustine forced Fortunatus into such straits that Fortunatus asked Augustine himself what he should say, confessing that he could find nothing to say.

Augustine then voluntarily promised him that he would explain the Catholic faith, provided that the audience permitted and wished it. Fortunatus replied that he would report Augustine’s argument to the most learned members of his sect; and if they did not adequately answer his question, then, since he wished to take care of his soul, he would come to the investigation of the Catholic faith that Augustine was offering.

Since this was the outcome of the disputation, those who had held Fortunatus’s learning and doctrine in very high regard judged that he had been unable to defend his error. Although he ought then to have embraced the Catholic faith, he could not endure the public disgrace. Some time afterward he left the city, covered with shame, and never returned to it.

Augustine took care to commit this disputation to a book for the sake of remembrance. With God favoring his pious labors, all who had attended the conversation or had read its *Acts*, having renounced their error, embraced the sincere and orthodox faith of the Catholic Church (*ibid.*).

The Manichaeans subsequently sent another presbyter of their sect to Hippo, whose name is not recorded. There is nevertheless no lack of conjecture that he was that Felix about whom we shall speak in the year 404.
