Augustine wrote to him and proposed the same argument by which Fortunatus had been unable to extricate himself, while warning him either to solve the question or to depart (*Letter* 79).

4. So that we may not separate the writings that Augustine composed against the Manichaeans while he was still a presbyter, we must discuss here his book against Adimantus (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 22), although it follows certain other short works about which we have not yet spoken [Col. 0189].

This Adimantus, also called Addas, was one of the first and most prominent disciples of Mani. He had collected many passages from both Testaments and, craftily setting them against one another as though they were contradictory, argued that they could not come from one and the same God.

When the disputations of this Adimantus came into Augustine’s hands, Augustine thought that he should refute them. He therefore wrote a book against them and demonstrated the agreement and harmony of both laws in the passages where Adimantus wished to show that they contradicted one another.

In this book he answers certain questions once and again, because the answers he had given at first had been lost, although they were later found after the second response. He also clarified some matters in his sermons to the people (*Sermon* 12, nos. 1–2). Finally, he omitted a few questions—very few indeed—partly because he had forgotten them and partly because pressing business had distracted him.

## CHAPTER VIII

1. A general council of all Africa is held at Hippo, at which Augustine explains the Creed.  
2. He writes to Jerome.  
3. He publishes an unfinished book on the literal interpretation of Genesis.  
4. Later, books on the Sermon on the Mount.  
5. He writes on the Epistle to the Romans.  
6. Likewise on the Epistle to the Galatians.  
7. A short work on Lying.

1. In the year 393, on the eighth day before the Ides of October, the Council of Hippo was held in the Church of Peace, a church that Augustine mentions more than once (*Letter* 213, no. 1). This was, as one may reasonably conjecture, the church that they called the Greater Basilica.

It was a general council of all Africa, and Aurelius undoubtedly presided, since he then occupied the see of Carthage. Augustine had already won great esteem for himself. For although, only two years earlier, it had been entirely unheard of for a presbyter to speak in the presence of a bishop, the bishops themselves ordered him at this famous assembly to discuss the Faith and the Creed. Since his friends pressed him very earnestly, he was compelled to reduce this discussion to the book that still exists (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 17).

In this work he explains each article of the Creed. Nevertheless, he does not report them in the same words in which they were handed down for memorization to the *Competentes*—those preparing for baptism—perhaps because it was permitted or customary for the Creed to be written only in the heart and memory (*Sermon* 212, no. 2; *Sermon* 214, no. 1). In the same book he repeatedly attacks the Manichaeans in express terms, though without naming them.

Although this glory of Augustine brought Valerius greater pleasure than anything else, it also caused him no small anxiety. For the more tenderly he loved Augustine, the more he feared that Augustine might be placed over another church and thereby taken away from Hippo. This almost happened, except that, once he understood what was taking place, Valerius secretly concealed him so effectively that those looking for him could not find him at all.

This experience led the holy old man to arrange that Augustine should be made his successor in the episcopate while Valerius was still alive. We shall explain below how this came about.

The Council of Hippo, which we have just discussed, undoubtedly enacted several decrees, most of which were inserted into the first thirty-three canons of the African Collection [Col. 0190]. It appears to have been the first council that Aurelius assembled from all Africa in order to restore ecclesiastical discipline, which had collapsed throughout this very extensive province. There can be no doubt that Augustine contributed his efforts more than the others to the decrees enacted by the council.

Baronius calls this council the Archetype (*Baronius*, under the year 393, chapter 33), from which many of the other councils later held in Africa borrowed several provisions, adding those that experience had taught them would be more beneficial.

2. Baronius assigns to this year, 393, the journey to Palestine of Alypius, not yet a bishop but already worthy of the episcopate (*Letter* 28, no. 1). In fact, when we see him writing to Paulinus in the year 394, he had already been made a bishop (*Letter* 24, no. 1, and its title).

Nothing is known about this journey except that Alypius saw Jerome (*Letter* 28, no. 1), who had been living at Bethlehem since 386 and had there acquired great renown through various scholarly works in which he chiefly expounded the sacred books.

Through this most peaceful leisure and genuinely liberal intellectual activity, Jerome first became known to Augustine. Since Augustine knew him through the fruits of his intellect, it remained only for him to know him by sight. This was the lesser part of Jerome; nevertheless, Augustine possessed such a disposition that he eagerly longed even to see his friends (*ibid.*). What he could not accomplish personally, he achieved through Alypius, with whom he was one in spirit. Through the eyes of that closest companion, and through Alypius’s account after his return, Augustine saw Jerome.

Jerome, in turn, first came to know and love Augustine through what he learned about him from Alypius in the year 394. Thus, when a certain Profuturus was about to travel to Palestine, Augustine—whose disciple he appears to have been—considered himself bound to Jerome by a sufficiently close relationship to commend Profuturus to him and to disclose to Jerome his own views, both concerning various passages in the works of this holy teacher and especially concerning the dispute between Peter and Paul.

Augustine also wished Jerome, in reading his writings—some of which he was sending him through Profuturus—to enjoy the same liberty and freedom (*ibid.*, no. 6). He wrote this letter while still a presbyter (*Letter* 71, no. 2), and therefore in 394 or 395.

It was not delivered to Jerome until a long time afterward, since Profuturus, to whom Augustine had entrusted it, did not make the journey. When he was preparing to set out, he was made a bishop and died not long afterward (*Letter* 72, no. 1). He seems to have been the Profuturus who was bishop of Cirta and who died a few years before Augustine wrote *On Baptism, against Petilianus* (*On the Uniqueness of Baptism*, no. 29).

3. Since we shall assign Augustine’s episcopate to the end of the following year—that is, to 395—we shall review in the present year the works that he composed after the Council of Hippo while he was still a presbyter [Col. 0191].

He places first the unfinished book *On Genesis according to the Letter*. It was also the first work of this kind that he composed on sacred Scripture. The two books that he had written on Genesis against the Manichaeans contained only an allegorical exposition.

He composed this work to investigate whether he was sufficiently capable of perceiving the secrets of natural things and explaining them literally—that is, according to their historical character—which he calls a very laborious and extremely difficult undertaking. He adds that he discovered at that time that his strength was so unequal to the task that, overcome by so great an undertaking, he left the little work unfinished and did not publish it.

Moreover, when reviewing his books, he had decided to destroy it, chiefly because he had completed a fuller and more finished work on the same subject. Nevertheless, he judged that this short work might serve as a useful indication of his first efforts in elucidating and examining the divine utterances, and he decided to preserve it. He also added approximately half a page at the end of the book, but still did not complete it. For this reason he entitled it *On Genesis according to the Letter, Unfinished*.

4. At about the same time he produced two books *On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount according to Matthew* (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 19). In them he observes the custom of receiving Communion daily, a practice that he followed together with the other faithful of Africa, although that custom did not prevail in the Eastern Church (*On the Sermon of the Lord on the Mount*, book 2, no. 26).

In the same place he reports that he asked a certain Jew what the word *Racha* meant, and he preferred the interpretation he received from him to the others (*ibid.*, book 1, no. 23). Many years later a certain Pollentius, examining this work, encountered several difficulties concerning divorced wives and presented them to the holy Doctor; Augustine resolved them in the first book *On Adulterous Marriages*.

5. While still a presbyter, Augustine traveled to Carthage. There, when the Epistle of Paul to the Romans was being read among the brethren, various questions concerning the most difficult passages of the Epistle were put to him on the occasion that arose. The brethren with whom he was staying persuaded him to allow his answers to be recorded in writing.

Thus another book was added to his earlier short works, entitled *An Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle of Paul to the Romans*. In his books of the *Retractations*, he admits that at that time he had not yet investigated carefully enough what the election of grace was. Hence he speaks there as though the beginning of faith came not from grace but from us (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 23, no. 2).

For this reason the Semi-Pelagians approved this book as though it supported them and cited it in defense of their position. They were not entirely without justification, as Augustine himself admits; he adds, however, that by reading the book they ought to have advanced together with him and abandoned their error by following his example (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, nos. 6–7).

6. At this time he also expounded the Epistle of the same apostle to the Galatians—not in excerpts, as he had treated the Epistle to the Romans, but continuously and in its entirety. Nevertheless, he contained this exposition in a single volume [Col. 0192] (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 14).

He may already have seen Jerome’s Commentary on this Epistle. Certainly he had read it while he was not yet a bishop (*Letter* 28, no. 3). He had also undertaken to comment on the Epistle to the Romans in the same continuous manner; that work would have filled many books. But discouraged by the size and labor of the undertaking, he turned to easier matters (*Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 25).

Thus he completed only a single book, dealing solely with an exposition of the Epistle’s greeting, as though it were its title, since he had been compelled to linger for a long time over a question that had arisen in his discourse concerning sin against the Holy Spirit.

7. The last book that Augustine notes as having been composed by him while a presbyter is entitled *On Lying* (*ibid.*, chapter 27). He wrote it to show that lying is unlawful. A large part of it, however, is occupied with the back-and-forth examination of the question itself and with the investigation of the truth.

He himself admits that the book seems obscure, entangled in winding passages, and altogether burdensome. For this reason he had not published it; indeed, especially since he later wrote *Against Lying*, he had decided to remove it from the number of his works.

Nevertheless, when he was about to review his short works, he found that this book had survived intact and allowed it also to remain after revision. He judged that it contained certain necessary matters absent from the later work, and that although it was laborious to understand, it would still provide a useful exercise for both intellect and mind and would be all the more suitable for instilling a love of truth.

He does not wish eloquence to be sought in it, since he had labored over the examination of the subject alone, neglecting concern for wording so that this work, indispensable for regulating life, might be completed quickly.

At the conclusion of the work he sharply attacks those who maintained that the Apostle had committed a courteous lie in the Epistle to the Galatians. This undoubtedly refers to Jerome’s Commentary on that Epistle. Perhaps Augustine composed this work at the very time when he wrote his twenty-eighth letter to Jerome on the same subject.

In a certain work composed around the year 419, he seems to indicate that he had not yet examined the scriptural testimonies concerning lying, since he did not number this book—which he had ordered to be suppressed—among his works.

He may also, while still a presbyter, have delivered *Sermon* 100 on the words of the Lord in Luke, chapter 9. In it he says that God chose the Apostles both according to his grace and according to their righteousness, since he saw them placing their confidence not in themselves but solely in his grace (*Sermon* 100, no. 3).

## CHAPTER IX

1. An outline history of the Donatists.  
2. How powerful they were in Africa in numbers when Augustine became a presbyter, and how he immediately attacked them.  
3. The Donatists do not dare to meet him.  
4. He composes an abecedarian psalm against them.  
5. He refutes Donatus’s letter.  
6. He writes to Maximinus, the Donatist bishop of Siniti, concerning a deacon whom, as was reported, Maximinus had rebaptized.

[Col. 0193]

1. Until now we have seen Augustine fighting in the arena only against the Manichaeans; but he had to struggle far more fiercely with the Donatists.

These heretics had separated themselves from communion with Caecilian, bishop of Carthage, around the year 311, on the pretext that Felix of Aptunga, by whom Caecilian had been ordained, had handed over the sacred books during the persecution. They themselves had requested judges from the emperor Constantine Augustus. Although they were first condemned by these judges and afterward also by Constantine himself, they stubbornly remained attached to their schism.

To seek support for their obstinacy, they relied upon what they presented as their foundation: all who communicated with the accused were held guilty of the same crime. Since the entire Christian world communicated with Caecilian, they separated themselves from all the other Catholics and created a complete schism.

Adding crime to crime, they rebaptized all who had not received baptism within their sect, maintaining that baptism conferred outside the legitimate Church—which they claimed as their own—was entirely invalid.

They also joined violence and cruelty to their error. Those among them who were called Circumcellions roamed about with impunity, contrary to every rule of law, beating, robbing, setting fires, and committing murders. Since they raged no less violently against themselves than against others, they voluntarily threw themselves into water and fire; above all, they were accustomed, with more than bestial savagery, to hurl themselves in groups from the highest mountain peaks.

From that one schism many others gradually sprang up. The most notorious among them was the schism of the Maximianists. In 393 they condemned Primian, the Donatist bishop of Carthage, and installed Maximian in his place.

The other Donatists, however, assembled at the city of Bagai in the province of Numidia in the very year under discussion, 394. They restored Primian to his see and pronounced judgment against those by whom he had been condemned: against twelve of them without setting any day, but against the others on condition that they return to their communion before Christmas.

Although they had pronounced this sentence of condemnation, they afterward admitted some of them once the prescribed period had elapsed. Indeed, they even received several of those to whom they had granted no delay, receiving them as bishops, while not rebaptizing any of those whom these same men had baptized during the schism. In this way, of course, they undermined the foundations of their own heresy.

2. Although this sect had no sound foundation, it nevertheless possessed such power in Africa when Augustine began to rise to prominence in the Church that 310 bishops assembled at the Council of Bagai, in addition to 100 others who adhered to Maximian. Possidius teaches that it included within its embrace a greater multitude of Africans (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 3).

At Hippo Regius the number of Catholics was so small and the Donatists held such authority that Faustinus, their bishop in that city, shortly before Augustine’s arrival, forbade bread to be baked for Catholics. As a result, a Catholic baker who was a tenant of a certain Hipponian deacon threw away the uncooked bread belonging to the deacon’s household [Col. 0194] (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 2, no. 184).

When Augustine arrived at Hippo, he summoned every resource of his eloquence in order to uproot the detestable practice of people who, while boasting of the Christian name, did not hesitate to rebaptize Christians (*Letter* 23).

As soon as he proclaimed the word of salvation, with God favoring his labors, the Catholic Church—which had lain afflicted and oppressed—began, in Possidius’s words, to lift up its head, and every day its numbers increased through the great multitude of those who renounced the schism.

This fruit was produced by Augustine’s unremitting labor as he taught the people privately and publicly, within domestic walls and in the church, by voice and in writing. He preached the word of God boldly and freely, and he attacked most vigorously every heresy that deviated from the path of truth.

The Catholics of Hippo, marveling with extraordinary joy, celebrated their triumph and acted so that this fact might be spread everywhere. Therefore even the heretics themselves, flocking together with the Catholics, eagerly hung upon those remarkable discourses of his, whose teaching he derived from the fountain of divine grace and strengthened always by the force of the strongest arguments and by the authority of the sacred Scriptures. Anyone who could employ notaries gladly had the words being spoken recorded.

Thus that singular teaching and the sweetest fragrance of Christ were spread throughout all Africa. Nor did the Church of God overseas remain long unaware of it; she rejoiced that so great a good had been divinely bestowed upon her brothers, with whom she formed one body (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 7).

Those who possessed written copies of his sermons or treatises—even the Donatists of Hippo and the surrounding region—carried them to Donatist bishops. When the bishops heard them and perhaps said something in response, they were either refuted by their own people or their replies were brought back to Saint Augustine. Once he had learned of them, he patiently and gently, as it is written, worked for the salvation of all “with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:12). He showed how they had been unwilling and unable to refute anything, and how true and manifest was what the faith of the Church of God holds and teaches (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 9).

Augustine himself, describing how greatly the Church was harassed by them, says: “We see and endure it, and as far as we can we try to restrain them by disputing, convincing, confronting, and frightening them” (this was after the year 405), “yet loving them in everything” (*Exposition on Psalm* 39, no. 1).

### 3

“And these things,” says Possidius, “were continually carried on by him day and night. For he also sent private letters to various bishops of the same error and, of course, to distinguished laymen, admonishing and exhorting them, with reasons given, either to correct themselves from that perversity or at least to come to a disputation. But they, distrusting their cause, were never willing even to reply; rather, in their anger they spoke madly and proclaimed both privately and publicly that Augustine was a seducer and deceiver of souls. They said and maintained that, in defense of their flock, he ought to be killed like a wolf; and they held that one could confidently believe that all sins would certainly be forgiven by God to those who could do and accomplish this—fearing neither God nor being ashamed before human beings. He also worked to make their distrust of their cause known to everyone; and when summoned before the public Acts, they did not dare to enter into conference” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 9).

“Sometimes,” says Augustine, “we came to them saying, ‘Let us seek the truth; let us find the truth.’ And they: ‘You keep what you hold; you have your sheep, I have mine. Do not trouble my sheep, because I too do not trouble yours.’ Thanks be to God: ‘Mine are sheep, his are sheep; what did Christ purchase?’” (*Enarration on Psalm* 21, tractate 2, no. 31).

They seem at times to have used Augustine’s mastery of learning and eloquence—which was exceptionally great—as a pretext for their refusal to engage with him (*Letter* 34, no. 6), although everything in which he surpassed them consisted rather in the force of the words of Scripture and in the weight of his arguments and proofs than in the elegance and vigor of his speech. They attributed the power with which truth prevailed in his mouth to his eloquence. Petilian and Cresconius at one point made this a reproach under the appearance of praise, comparing the holy man with Tertullus, Paul’s accuser. They also accused him of being a dialectician; and, as though that art were wholly incompatible with Christian truth, they judged that he ought rather to be avoided than refuted (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 3, no. 19; *Against Cresconius*, book 1, nos. 2, 16).

Their distrust, by which they rejected discussion with Catholics, although they boasted that they had been sent to them as prophets, was so great that they even feared that their own writings might fall into their hands. For when Augustine once wished to obtain the latter part of a letter written by one of their chief bishops, namely Petilian, no one from whom it was requested was willing to give it to him after they learned that he intended to reply to the former part (*Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 1, no. 21). Nor did the holy Doctor think that, if the author of that letter himself were pressed to acknowledge it as his own by subscribing it in his own hand, he would ever dare to do so.

Nor was it enough for them always to turn away from the light of the truth when it was offered, unless they also fiercely persecuted its proclaimers. But neither their stubbornness nor their fury could extinguish or delay Augustine’s burning zeal. Thus he addresses his own people:

“Here, somehow, we are moving among the hands of robbers and the teeth of raging wolves, and because of these dangers of ours we ask you to pray. And the sheep are obstinate: the straying are sought, but they say that, through their error and their destruction, they are strangers to us. ‘What do you want with us? Why do you seek us?’ As though this were not itself the reason why we want them and why we seek them: because they are straying and perishing. ‘If I am in error,’ he says, ‘if I am in destruction, what do you want with me? Why do you seek me?’ Because you are in error, I want to call you back; because you have perished, I want to find you. ‘So I want to stray; so I want to perish.’ So you want to stray; so you want to perish! How much better that I do not want it! I dare to say plainly: I am troublesome. For I hear the Apostle saying, ‘Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season’ (2 Tim. 4:2). ‘For whom in season? For whom out of season?’ ‘In season’ certainly for those who are willing, ‘out of season’ for those who are unwilling. I dare to say plainly: I am troublesome. You want to stray; you want to perish: I do not want it. Finally, he who terrifies me does not want it. If I should desire it, see what he says, see what he rebukes: ‘You did not bring back the straying, and you did not seek what had perished’ (Ezek. 34:4). Shall I fear you more than him? ‘We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ’ (2 Cor. 5:10). I do not fear you; for you cannot overturn Christ’s judgment seat and set up the judgment seat of Donatus. I will call back the straying; I will seek the lost: whether you wish it or not, I will do this. And if, while I am searching for you, the thorns of the forests tear me, I will force myself through every narrow place; I will search every hedge. As much strength as the terrifying Lord grants me, I will traverse everything; I will call back the straying; I will seek the perishing. If you do not want to endure me, do not stray; do not perish” (*Sermon* 46, no. 14).

He then notes that this was also necessary lest Catholics, regarding schism as something indifferent, slip into it more readily.

“If I neglect the straying and the perishing,” he says, “the one who is strong will also delight in straying and perishing. I desire external gains, but I fear internal losses more. If I treat your error as indifferent, the one who is strong takes notice and thinks that it is nothing to go into heresy. When some advantage from the world appears, by which he may be changed, that strong man who is about to perish immediately says to me, when I do not seek you who are lost: ‘God is here and there; what difference does it make? Human beings, quarreling among themselves, have made this distinction; God is to be worshiped everywhere.’ If some Donatist should perhaps say to him, ‘I will not give you my daughter unless you belong to my party,’ he must take notice and say: ‘If it were not evil to belong to their party, our pastors would not say so much against them, nor labor on account of their error.’ If, therefore, we cease and remain silent, he will say the opposite” (*ibid.*, no. 15).

“Much I fear,” he says elsewhere, while not yet a bishop, “that, if I remain silent and pretend not to notice, others too may be rebaptized by you. Therefore I have resolved, insofar as the Lord deigns to provide strength and opportunity, to conduct this matter in such a way that, through our peaceful conferences, all who share communion with us may know how far the Catholic Church differs from heresies or schisms, and how greatly the destruction must be avoided, whether of the tares or of the branches cut off from the Lord’s vine. If you willingly undertake such a conference with me, so that the letters of both of us may be read to the people in agreement, I shall rejoice with unspeakable joy. But if you do not accept this with an even mind, what shall I do, brother, except read our letters to the Catholic people even against your will, so that they may be better instructed? And if you do not deign to reply, I have nevertheless resolved to read my letters alone, so that, at least once your distrust is known, they may be ashamed to be rebaptized” (*Letter* 23, no. 6).

### 4

The first work that we learn Augustine wrote against the Donatists is the Psalm which he calls the *Abecedarian* (*Retractions*, book 1, chap. 20), because it was divided into various sections, each of which begins with a Latin letter according to the order of the alphabet. It is a kind of rhythm and song, to whose individual sections a *hypopsalma*—a refrain or undersong—is sung. In this Psalm he embraces the entire history of the schism, which he seems to have drawn from Optatus, together with a refutation of the schismatics’ error, with as much clarity of expression and simplicity of style as he could achieve. He composed the work to instruct an unlearned and uncultivated multitude; therefore, so that it could be sung and more easily fixed in memory, he enclosed it in rhythms. He did not, however, bind it to poetic meters, lest metrical necessity compel him to use words less familiar to the common people. He also testifies that a prologue intended to be sung had been prefixed to this Psalm, though outside the alphabetical order. We do not find this prologue, appended to the *hypopsalma*, in the Psalm that we have before us.

We have already observed that this work, and the others of which we are now speaking, were placed by him after the book *On Faith and the Creed*, composed in October of the year 393. In this Psalm he makes no mention of the history of the Maximianists; for it was not properly completed until the year 397.

### 5

During the time of his presbyterate Augustine also wrote another work against the Donatists: namely, a refutation of the great Donatus of Carthage, the founder and architect of the entire schism, who is also believed to have given it his name (*ibid.*, chap. 21). He had long since died; but among the works he left behind at his death there was found a letter in which he argued that Baptism could not be conferred outside his sect. Augustine refuted this letter, but the work itself has been lost.

In his books of *Retractions* the holy Doctor notes several passages in that work where he himself had gone wrong. Above all, with the greatest humility, he confesses that he had unjustly attacked Donatus as though he were a thief or violator of divine eloquence, and had falsely accused him of cutting out from the middle of a sentence certain words from the book of Ecclesiasticus that were necessary to the matter; for he later found the same error in many manuscripts that were older than the Donatist schism itself.

### 6

While Augustine was not yet a bishop, he wrote a letter to Maximinus, the Donatist bishop of Sinitum. This might lead us to believe that Maximinus’s see was at Hippo, were it not that Augustine testifies that Proculeianus had been bishop of the Donatists in that very city for many years, while Augustine himself had only recently assumed the episcopate there (*Letter* 34, no. 6). For this reason we readily accept the opinion of Holstenius, who considers this Maximinus to be that bishop of Sinitum whom Augustine records as having eventually returned to Catholic unity, around the year 407 (*Letter* 105, no. 4).

Sinitum was a fortified town near the colony of Hippo, over which its own bishop presided (*City of God*, book 22, chap. 8, no. 11). Nevertheless, this town seems, since it had no Catholic bishop, to have belonged to the diocese of Hippo, or at least the care of the Catholics living there to have belonged to the bishop of Hippo. For, when Augustine reports what had happened in the year 406 before Maximinus’s conversion, he says:

“For what other purpose had we sent a presbyter to Sinitum, except that, troubling no one, he might visit our people and, placed in a house under his jurisdiction, preach Catholic peace to those who desired it? You expelled him from there with grave insult” (*Letter* 105, no. 4).

The reason that led Augustine to write to Maximinus was supplied by a deacon of the Church of Mutugenna, which he mentions as though subject to the Church of Hippo [Col. 0198] (*Letter* 23, no. 2), and which elsewhere he calls a village (*Letter* 173, no. 7). At the Carthaginian Conference, however, there was a certain Antonius, a Catholic, together with Splendonius, a Donatist and bishop of Mutugenna—either because bishops were later established in that village, or because there was both a city and a village bearing the same name.

As soon, therefore, as Augustine arrived at Hippo, he began vigorously to attack the impious custom of the Donatists who rebaptized. Some people did indeed assert that the Maximinus of whom we are speaking did not practice this detestable custom. But when Augustine later learned by report that the Catholic deacon of Mutugenna had been rebaptized by Maximinus, he grieved intensely both over the deacon’s fall and over Maximinus’s crime.

Nevertheless, wishing to investigate the matter more thoroughly, he himself went to Mutugenna. He could not see that most shameful deserter from the faith, but he learned from his parents that he had already been made a deacon by the Donatists. Valerius was absent at that time. But Augustine, who was pierced by the sharpest pain at the deacon’s fall and feared a similar fate for others, did not think that he ought to wait for the return or command of his own bishop. For he had not undertaken the presbyterate in order to spend the briefest span of this mortal life in ecclesiastical honors; rather, he reflected that he would have to render an account to the supreme Prince of shepherds for the sheep entrusted to him.

Since, therefore, he judged that he could not remain silent without endangering his own salvation, he wrote the letter that still survives to Maximinus (*Letter* 23). He begins by giving an account of the respectful title with which he honors him in the letter’s address; then, after setting forth his complaint, he asks him to deign to write back and explain what he had done. Augustine thought so well of him that he could not persuade himself that he had rebaptized the deacon.

He also encourages him not to be frightened by the counsels of his fellow bishops, provided that he disagreed with them about the repetition of Baptism. Likewise, he urges him not to refuse to examine with him, by letter, the truth of the Catholic Church, so that that impious schism might be removed. He asks him to allow the letters they exchanged to be read to both peoples; if he did not accept this calmly, Augustine declared that he would do it nevertheless.

And if Maximinus did not deign to reply, Augustine would still read his own letters publicly, so that the Catholics, once they knew of the Donatists’ distrust, might not allow themselves to be rebaptized. He nevertheless promised that he would read nothing to the people so long as a soldier was present at Hippo, lest any Donatist think that he had wished to act tumultuously or to compel Donatists against their will to join his communion—something he declares to be entirely contrary to his purpose.

As we have said, this letter was unquestionably written during Augustine’s presbyterate. Its date is uncertain, as is the result it produced. If the Maximinus to whom it is addressed was the bishop of Sinitum, as may rightly be thought, we have already observed that he emerged from his error and returned to Catholic communion after returning from overseas, apparently in the year 405, shortly before Augustine composed his 105th letter to the Donatists.

Before his conversion, and while he was absent, the Catholics—and probably Augustine himself—had sent a presbyter to the fortified town of Sinitum, as we have just said. After he had returned to communion with the Church, the Donatists sent a herald to proclaim at Sinitum: “Whoever communicates with Maximinus, his house shall be burned” (*Letter* 105, no. 4).

Possidius records a sermon against the Donatists and against idols preached by Augustine at Sinitum (Possidius, *Catalogue*, chap. 3). In the year 409 or 410 Augustine advises Donatus, proconsul of Africa, to urge those whom he had in the territory of Sinitum to join the communion of the Catholic Church (*Letter* 112, no. 3).

The same holy Doctor, recounting a miracle that had occurred in his own diocese, writes that Maximinus, his colleague and bishop of the Church of Sinitum, was with him (*City of God*, book 22, chap. 8, no. 6). Shortly afterward he mentions Lucillus, who was bishop of the fortified town of Sinitum, near Hippo-Regius (*ibid.*, no. 11), from which the relics of Stephen the protomartyr had been brought to Africa in the year 416. Lucillus was perhaps Maximinus’s successor.

At the Carthaginian Conference no Catholic bishop of Sinitum is found. Cresconius was present on the Donatist side; he had doubtless been substituted for Maximinus after Maximinus’s conversion. Nevertheless, this Cresconius did not say that no Catholic bishop stood opposite him (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, chap. 202).

## CHAPTER X

1. Augustine becomes known to Paulinus through his own writings and Alypius’s report. 2. Paulinus sends separate letters to Alypius and Augustine. 3. Licentius sends a poem to Augustine. 4. Augustine replies to Paulinus’s letter. 5. Not having received Augustine’s reply, Paulinus writes him a second letter.

### 1

At the time when God was displaying in Augustine to Africa a miracle of grace, he was also presenting to the whole Church, in Paulinus, another example of his mercy. In that same year, 394, Paulinus had withdrawn to Nola in Campania, having despised the splendor of the noblest birth and renounced his vast wealth, so that there, together with his wife Therasia—or rather his sister and companion in piety—he might lead the humble and poor life of a monk.

Alypius, who while at Milan, when he was baptized there, had already heard about Paulinus (*Letter* 24, no. 4), hastened, as soon as he learned of the manner of Paulinus’s life at Nola, to address him and to behold him with the eyes of love and with that spirit of true affection which is everywhere both penetrating and diffused (*Letter* 25, no. 1).

Thus, although he did not yet know him personally and was separated from him by a great interval of land and sea, he nevertheless wrote to him through Julian, one of Paulinus’s household, who was returning from Nola to Carthage, in order to establish a friendship (*Letter* 24, no. 1). In this letter he had adorned Augustine with praise; and so that Paulinus might learn from Augustine’s works what sort and how great a man he was, and might regard him with no ordinary goodwill, Alypius sent the five books of Augustine against the Manichaeans as a first gift to this new friend—like a pledge of his concern for him, a bond of perfect charity, and a most certain token of his affection. Among these, however, was the book *On True Religion*, which does not directly attack the Manichaeans.

He also asked Paulinus to send him Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, translated into Latin by Jerome around the year 380, and to forward it to Comes and Evodius, who were to copy it. He advised him that this manuscript could be found at Rome in the possession of the holy Domnio, a close friend of Jerome.

Alypius likewise indicated to Paulinus his own location—that is, where Paulinus could send a reply to him—and seems to have designated Carthage or Hippo-Regius for this purpose. Tagaste was too distant and not sufficiently prominent for such correspondence. It is nevertheless clear from Paulinus’s earlier letter to Augustine that Alypius was already bishop of that city when those letters were written.

Alypius added that he had commended Paulinus to the prayers of several holy persons. He also mentioned a hymn that he had read, composed by Paulinus.

Paulinus professes that he owes much to the holy bishops Aurelius and Alypius, since through their kindness he had come to know Augustine from his writings against the Manichaeans. Accordingly, it seems that Aurelius of Carthage wrote to Paulinus at the same time as Alypius. To this letter may probably be referred what Paulinus wrote to Sulpicius Severus around the year 396: that several friends had been divinely granted to him in regions previously unknown, whose goodwill he valued in place of his homeland, his relatives, and his patrimony (in Paulinus, *Letter* formerly 5, now 11, no. 4).

### 2

When Paulinus received Alypius’s letter, he rejoiced exceedingly and gave the greatest thanks to God, who bound together by so close a bond of friendship people who did not know one another by sight and who were separated by so great a distance. But he was especially delighted by the first books of Augustine that Alypius had sent him as a gift.

In replying to Alypius, he testifies to this and declares at the same time that he marvels so greatly at the words of this holy and perfect man that he believes they were dictated by divine inspiration (in Augustine, *Letter* 24, no. 2).

He delayed replying to Alypius because he did not have with him the *Chronicle* of Eusebius that Alypius had requested. He was therefore forced to borrow it at Rome from the holy Domnio, who lent the manuscript all the more willingly because he knew that it was to be delivered to Alypius.

He accordingly sent it to Aurelius of Carthage together with a letter addressed to Alypius, asking Aurelius to forward the manuscript and letter to Alypius at Hippo-Regius, if he happened to be living there. At the same time he asked Comes and Evodius to transcribe the *Chronicle* for Alypius, so that Domnio would not be deprived of his own manuscript for too long.

In return for this history of the ages, however, Paulinus asks Alypius to write him the entire history and sequence of his own life, so that he might first learn with certainty whether Alypius had received Baptism or the priesthood from the hands of Ambrose, and might love him more ardently because of the closest relationship that connected him with that holy bishop, who was still alive.

He likewise asks Alypius, by his recommendation and favor, to make acceptable the letters that Paulinus had dared to write to the holy Augustine. Paulinus himself, struck with wonder at the miracles of divine wisdom that he found in the works of that holy Doctor, was wholly inflamed with love for him; and he did not doubt that Alypius, through the charity by which he had given him knowledge of Augustine, had also already secured Augustine’s friendship for him.

Thus he embraced Augustine in love from that time onward, so that he seemed not to be entering upon a new friendship with him but renewing an old one. The Spirit who united them and made them members of the same body led Paulinus to write him a letter (*ibid.*, *Letter* 25), in which he praises with marvelous commendation the works of Augustine that he had read.

He asks Augustine to send him any other books he had written. In turn, he sends him bread as a gift, as was his custom, a symbol of friendship and of their common communion. At the same time he sent a letter to Aurelius of Carthage. He sent all these letters through one of his household, whom he had dispatched to convey his greetings to Augustine and to other friends of God.

When that messenger was delayed on his return journey, Paulinus wrote to Augustine again (*ibid.*, *Letter* 30), to whom he testifies that he had sent his earlier letter before winter. These later letters, therefore, which were written in the same year in which Augustine was made bishop, seem to have been composed around springtime, while the earlier ones were written in autumn. We therefore assign all these events to the year 394.

### 3

Around the same time Licentius, the son of Romanianus, wrote to Augustine from the city of Rome and also sent him a poem (*Letter* 26, no. 3). Augustine replied to him by a letter sent a considerable time later, although he himself testifies that he had scarcely found an opportunity to write to him.

In this letter he mentions Paulinus as someone already very well known to him through the reputation of his virtue (*ibid.*, no. 5). He therefore seems to have written it after receiving Paulinus’s letters and seeing the person whom Paulinus had sent to convey his greetings to Augustine.

It must be acknowledged that the letter to Licentius was written before the one sent to Paulinus through Romanianus in the year 395. Augustine himself sufficiently indicates this when he tells Paulinus that, from Licentius’s poem and the letter that Augustine sent him, Paulinus would clearly understand what Augustine regretted in Licentius, what he feared, and what he desired for him (*Letter* 27, nos. 4, 6).

### 4

Although Paulinus had a thoroughly established knowledge of Augustine’s virtue and held it in high esteem, he did not yet know the holy man fully and deeply, since he thought Alypius’s recommendation necessary in order that Augustine might receive his letters favorably, and in order to excuse himself, as he says, for his lack of skill.

Augustine’s disposition toward his friends—and even less toward Paulinus—was neither doubtful nor hesitant. Indeed, nothing more ardent or tender can be imagined than the letter he wrote in reply; nothing can inspire greater admiration than that vehement and inflamed eagerness with which he declares himself to be burning to see Paulinus.

He returns him even greater praise than he had received from him. Yet it cannot be said that these praises proceeded either from flattery or falsehood, but from a love no less fiery than clear-sighted.

“The brothers,” he says, “have read and rejoice tirelessly and unspeakably in your goods, so abundant and so excellent, the gifts of God. All who have read them are carried away, because they are carried away as they read. How sweet the fragrance of Christ is, and how it breathes forth from them, cannot be said” (*ibid.*, no. 2).

Every word of the letter is worthy of admiration. In this letter he sends greetings to Therasia, whom Paulinus, according to custom, had joined with himself in the address of the letter.

Augustine wrote to Paulinus through Romanianus, his most intimate friend, who nevertheless had not yet reached the disposition of mind that Augustine so earnestly desired for him. Therefore Augustine begs and implores Paulinus with every prayer to assist both Romanianus and his son Licentius, and to promote, insofar as he could, the salvation of both.

He nevertheless asks Paulinus not to believe what this friend might perhaps have said about Augustine in praise of him, out of a tendency to love. Since Romanianus was carrying all of Augustine’s works with him, Augustine promises to make them available to Paulinus. But he asks Paulinus to read them carefully, so that he may inform him of any errors he notices. On this subject Augustine has a passage of exceptional beauty.

He also promises that he will write for Paulinus the history of the blessed bishop Alypius, which Paulinus had requested from Alypius himself. Alypius’s goodwill toward Paulinus compelled him to undertake this task, but his modesty of spirit held him back.

When Augustine therefore saw Alypius wavering between modesty and friendship, he transferred the burden from Alypius onto his own shoulders—partly as a duty, since Alypius had requested this of him by letter, but chiefly so that he might set forth more fully and abundantly the gifts divinely bestowed upon Alypius than Alypius himself could do. Alypius had doubtless remained silent about many things out of modesty and might have feared to provide a stumbling block to others who would later read the work without understanding with what intention he spoke about himself.

When Augustine wrote to Paulinus, he was preparing to send him this work. But because Romanianus unexpectedly departed, Augustine could do no more than promise that he would send it to Paulinus as soon as possible. Nevertheless, neither in Augustine nor in Possidius do we read that he fulfilled this promise in any other way than through what he records about Alypius in his books of the *Confessions*. Perhaps he carried it out in some later letter that has been lost.

At the end of the letter Augustine asks Paulinus, if he had leisure from ecclesiastical duties, to cross over to Africa, where he himself would see how greatly he was loved and honored by all the brothers who were serving God there.

### 5

This letter, which seems to have been written at the end of the winter of 395, was delivered to Paulinus later than Augustine would have wished; but this very delay proved beneficial to him.

For when Paulinus saw that the man whom he had sent to Africa before winter was delayed on the journey and was uncertain whether his letters had been delivered, he could not suspend his duty any longer. He wrote to Augustine again to testify to his goodwill toward him and to his desire to see him.

“Not only would great joy be added to our desires,” he says, “but light would also increase in our minds, and our poverty would be enriched from your abundance” (in Augustine, *Letter* 30, no. 3).

He wrote through Romanus and Agilis, whom he was sending to Africa for some work of charity. In the letter he commends them to Augustine and asks him, when they returned—for he had ordered them to return as quickly as possible—to deign to send them some reply [Col. 0203].

Augustine rejoiced greatly that the delay of the letters to which he had replied in his earlier letter had brought him the gain of this later letter, which he read with no less delight.

He received Romanus and Agilis, the bearers of this letter, with a joy all the greater because he longed more ardently to see its author, whom he also beheld as present in his spiritual sons. He calls them another letter from Paulinus, all the more pleasant because this letter did not merely speak to him like an ordinary written message, but allowed him to hear and answer actual voices.

He learned far more about Paulinus from their mouths than Paulinus could have reported in writing. Hence Augustine adds the following in his reply:

“There was also present something that cannot be present in any sheet of paper: so great a joy in those who were telling us that, through the very faces and eyes of the speakers, we read with unspeakable delight that you were written in their hearts. This too was an additional advantage: whatever page may contain, however much good writing, it accomplishes nothing by itself, even though it is unfolded for the benefit of others. But we read this letter of yours—that is, your brotherly soul—in their conversation, so that it appeared to us all the more blessed the more abundantly it had been written out of you. Therefore, in imitation of that same blessedness, by diligently questioning them about everything concerning you, we transcribed it into our hearts” (*Letter* 31, no. 2).

## CHAPTER XI

1. He preaches to the people of Hippo against the very bad custom of holding banquets in the church. 2. On the following day he attacks the same custom more vigorously. 3. On the next day he abolishes it completely. 4. He puts the finishing hand to his work *On Free Choice of the Will*. 5. Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians claimed that certain passages in that work supported them.

### 1

While Paulinus and Augustine were pleasantly conversing with one another through letters filled with piety, Augustine meanwhile received the greatest addition to his joy when an especially happy event, divinely granted in response to his prayers, occurred.

It has already been related above (chap. 6, no. 2) how indignantly the holy Presbyter had borne the dishonoring of sacred places when he saw drunken banquets being frequently held in the cemeteries and memorials of the martyrs. The ignorant people thought that by these banquets they were paying not only honor to the holy martyrs but also offering consolation to their own dead.

As soon as he heard that Aurelius had been installed in the see of Carthage, Augustine did not delay writing to him about this matter (*Letter* 22). He urged him to remove this disgrace from Africa by the authority of councils and by the example that the Church of Carthage would set for the others.

Later, in the year 393, the general Council of Hippo, by an established canon, forbade any bishops or clerics to hold banquets in the church. It likewise ordered that the people be kept away from such banquets as far as possible (*African Code of Canons*, canon 42).

We do not know whether Aurelius was able to correct this abuse so quickly at Carthage. Certainly, in the year of which we are speaking, 395, Augustine successfully abolished it at Hippo. We learned this from a letter recently discovered by us, which the holy man, still a presbyter, wrote to Alypius, already a bishop (*Letter* 29, no. 2).

There was a solemn celebration at Hippo on the sacred memorial day of some saint, which the citizens called *Laetitia*—“Joy”—thereby concealing the disgrace of drunkenness under this scarcely less indecorous name. The Donatists of Hippo held no less splendid a celebration on that day than the Catholics, nor was their intemperance more restrained.

Before the solemn day arrived, when Augustine was informed that the people were in turmoil and saying that they could not endure the prohibition of that celebration, it happened opportunely that, on the Wednesday before the beginning of Lent, the next Gospel passage to be treated in sequence presented itself: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7:6).

Applying this passage to the matter at hand, Augustine made them see how wicked it was to do within the walls of the church what, if they continued doing it in their own houses, would require them to be barred from what was holy and from the ecclesiastical pearls.

Although these words were well received, the matter was not yet settled, because few had gathered for the sermon. Moreover, when the sermon was discussed outside by those who had heard it, according to each person’s ability and zeal, it encountered many opponents.

2. Accordingly, after the day of Lent had dawned, when a larger crowd gathered for the hour of instruction, that passage in the Gospel was read in which the Lord drove the sellers of animals from the temple and overturned the tables of the money-changers (the same, XXI, 12). Augustine himself also recited this passage, having first raised the question of drunkenness, and added an exposition in which he showed how much more forcefully and vehemently our Lord would drive drunken banquets—which are disgraceful everywhere—from the temple, since he had driven out from it even permitted commercial transactions. Then, drawing on the readings he had prepared, he added that the still carnal Jewish people, in that temple where the body and blood of the Lord were not yet offered, had never celebrated banquets there—not merely drunken ones, but even sober ones—and that history records them as publicly intoxicated in the name of religion only when they were celebrating the festival of the manufacture of an idol (Exodus XXII, 6).

[Note: [Col. 0204] This is how the various editions we consulted read, though not clearly. More correctly one should read, “our Lord.” M.]

Then, having taken the book, he recited the entire passage. He added, with as much sorrow as he could express: If Moses had shattered the two stone tablets because of those drunkards, how could we not break the hearts of those who, as people of the New Testament, wished solemnly to display on the days of the saints what the people of the Old Testament had celebrated only once, and then in honor of an idol? Then, returning the book and intensifying his denunciation of drunkenness, he took up the Apostle and showed among which sins it had been placed, reading this passage: “If anyone is named a brother and is either a fornicator, or a servant of idols, or greedy, or abusive, or drunk, or rapacious, with such a person not even to take food” (1 Corinthians V, 11). With a groan he warned them of the great danger in which they were dining with those who became drunk even in their own homes.

He also read the passage that follows not long afterward: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor servants of idols, etc.” Having read this, he urged them to consider how they could hear the words, “But you were washed” [Col. 0205] (ibid., VI, 9–11), while they still allowed such filthy desires—desires against which the kingdom of heaven is closed—to remain in their hearts, the inner temple of God.

From there he came to the passage, “When you come together, therefore, into one place, etc.” (the same, XI, 20). After reciting it, he emphasized more carefully that not even respectable and sober banquets were permitted to be celebrated in the church. He also recalled the Gospel passage that he had expounded the day before, where it is said of false prophets, “You will know them by their fruits” (Matthew VII, 16). He then brought to mind that in that passage “fruits” means nothing other than deeds; and after reciting the passage in the Epistle to the Galatians, “Now the works of the flesh are manifest, etc.” (Galatians V, 19), he asked how Christians could be recognized by the fruit of drunkenness, which is named among the works of the flesh.

He urged them to observe how shameful and mournful it was that they wished not only to live privately by those fruits of the flesh but also to confer upon them the honor of the Church; whereas, concerning the spiritual fruits to which both the authority of Scripture and his own groans invited them, they were unwilling to offer gifts to God or, above all, to celebrate the feasts of the saints with those fruits.

When this was finished, he returned the book and, after ordering prayer, set before their eyes the common danger—not only that of those entrusted to his care, but also his own, since he would have to render an account of them to the Prince of pastors. By the humility of Christ, by his extraordinary insults, blows, spitting in his face, beatings, crown of thorns, cross, and blood, he implored them that, if they had offended him, they should at least show pity toward him; and that they should consider the ineffable love of the venerable old man Valerius toward him, who had imposed upon him, for their sake, the perilous burden of expounding the words of truth, and who had often told them that his prayers concerning Augustine’s arrival had been heard. Valerius had rejoiced that Augustine had come to him not, of course, for their common death or to witness their death, but for their common striving toward eternal life.

Finally, he also said that he was certain and trusted in God that, if they despised these great things that had been read and spoken to them, God would visit them with the rod and the scourge, and would not permit them to be condemned along with this world. “I did not move their tears,” Augustine said, “by my own tears; but when such things were being said, I confess that, overtaken by their weeping, I could not restrain my own. And when we had already wept together, with the fullest hope of their correction, my sermon came to an end” (Epistle 29, no. 7).

3. The next day, when dawn broke—the day on which their throats and bellies were accustomed to prepare themselves—it was reported to the holy Presbyter that some people, including some who had attended the sermon, had not yet ceased their murmuring. The force of the worst habit prevailed so strongly in them that they relied only on this objection and said: “Why only now? Surely those who previously did not forbid these things were not Christians?”

When he heard this, he had no idea what greater strategies he might prepare to move them. Nevertheless, he was planning, if they thought they must persist, to read that passage from Ezekiel, “The watchman is acquitted if he has announced the danger, even if those to whom it is announced are unwilling to take precautions” (Ezekiel XXXIII, 9), and then to shake out his garments and depart.

But God favored his wishes and efforts. Those who had complained about the attack on their old custom—perhaps now fearing that they might force the holy man either to leave Hippo or at least to withdraw from that present assembly—entered to see him before the hour at which he would ascend the platform. He received them graciously and, with a few words, brought them over to sound judgment. When the time for the discourse arrived, he omitted the reading he had prepared, since it was no longer necessary, and said a few words about the question itself. He could offer nothing against those who said, “Why only now?” that was either shorter or truer than to say himself, “Even now.”

Then, lest those who had previously permitted such banquets at the feasts of the saints, or who had not dared to prohibit them, seem to be subjected to some insult by him, he explained to the people the circumstances in which he believed these practices had arisen in the Church. After the persecutions had ended and peace had been restored, crowds of pagans wishing to join the Christian name were hindered by the fact that they were accustomed to spend their festal days with their idols in abundant feasting and drunkenness, and could not easily abstain from these most pernicious and deeply rooted pleasures. It had seemed to our forebears that this aspect of their weakness should for the time being be spared, and that, after the festivals they were abandoning, they should celebrate other festivals in honor of the holy martyrs—not with a similar sacrilege, although with similar luxury. In this way, salutary teachings of sobriety could be delivered to those already gathered under the name of Christ and subjected to the yoke of such authority, so that they would no longer be able to resist on account of the honor and fear inspired by the one who commanded.

Therefore, the time had now come for those who did not dare deny that they were Christians to begin living according to Christ’s will, and for those things that had been permitted in order that they might become Christians to be rejected once they were Christians.

Next he urged them to imitate the churches overseas, where such practices had either never been accepted or had already been corrected. Since examples of daily drunkenness were being cited from the basilica of the blessed Apostle Peter, he first said that he had often heard that this had been forbidden, but that, because the place was far from the bishop’s residence, and because in so large a city there was a great multitude of carnal people—especially foreigners, who continually arrived as newcomers and retained that custom with all the greater force because of their ignorance—it had not yet been possible to restrain and quiet so monstrous a plague.

Nevertheless, if they honored the Apostle Peter, they ought to listen to his precepts, and to consider much more devoutly the letter in which his will is apparent than the basilica. Immediately, taking up the book, he recited: “Since Christ therefore suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same understanding. For the time that has passed is sufficient for having fulfilled the will of the pagans, walking in licentiousness, desires, drunkenness, revelries, and abominable service of idols” (1 Peter IV, 1, 3).

When he had done these things, and saw that all were proceeding with one mind toward a good disposition, having rejected the evil custom, he urged them to attend divine readings and psalms at midday. In this way they would celebrate that day much more purely and sincerely; and it would certainly be easy to see, from the number of those gathering, who were following their mind and who their belly. Thus, after all the readings had been completed, the sermon ended.

In the afternoon a larger crowd was present than in the morning. At the hour when the presbyter Augustine was to leave with the bishop, readings were given and psalms sung alternately for them; and after they had gone out, two psalms were read. Then Valerius compelled the reluctant Augustine, who was already eager for such a perilous day to be over, to say something to the people. He delivered a brief sermon in which he gave thanks to God.

Since he had heard that in the basilica of the heretics they were accustomed to celebrate their usual banquets, while at that very time, when the Catholics were holding these observances, the others continued drinking, he said that the beauty of the day was enhanced by comparison with the night, and that a bright color was made more pleasing by its proximity to black. In the same way, he said, their spiritual gathering might perhaps have been less pleasing had not carnal drunkenness been set over against it. He urged them to desire such banquets eagerly, if they had tasted how sweet the Lord is.

After words appropriate to the occasion had been spoken in this vein, with the Lord supplying what was to be said, the evening rites were performed as they were every day. As Augustine departed together with the bishop, the brothers—perhaps monks—sang a hymn in the same place, while a considerable multitude of both sexes remained and sang psalms as daylight faded.

Augustine promptly and eagerly reported the entire course of events by letter to Alypius, so that the man who only a few days earlier had joined him at Hippo in offering prayers to obtain this benefit might also join him in giving thanks to God for the benefit received.

4. A few months later he attained the episcopate of Hippo, to which the holy Presbyter was showing himself daily more worthy. But before we set out the history of his ordination, we must discuss the books on Free Will that he wrote or completed at this time.

For when Romanianus departed for Italy at the beginning of the year 395, Augustine testifies that he did not yet possess that work—or at least the three books of which it entirely consists (Epistle 31, no. 7), although he believed that he had handed over to him all his writings (Epistle 27, no. 4). It is therefore very likely that this work had not yet been completed at that time—that is, as we think, at the beginning of the year 395.

Nevertheless, he brought it to completion while still a presbyter, after adding the two later books (Retractions, book 1, chapter 9, no. 1). For he had already written the first book at Rome in the year 388. In this way it could have happened that Romanianus carried the work away with him.

He composed these books in the form of dialogues, in which he engages in conversation with Evodius. The subject of their mutual conversation is an inquiry into the origin from which evil proceeds.

“When we were still staying at Rome,” Augustine says, “we wished by discussion to seek the origin of evil. And we discussed it in such a way that, if we could, reason, considered and examined with God’s assistance as far as we were able to achieve by discussion, would lead even to our understanding that which, in submission to divine authority, we believed concerning this matter.”

And since, after careful rational examination, it was agreed between them that evil arose from nothing other than free choice of the will, the three books produced by that discussion were called On Free Will. “I completed the second and third of them in Africa, after I had already been ordained presbyter at Hippo-Regius, as I was then able. In these books so much was discussed that certain questions arising in the course of the argument—which I either could not untangle or which required a lengthy discussion at the time—were deferred in such a way that, from either side or from all sides of those questions, where it was not apparent what best accorded with the truth, our reasoning nevertheless reached this conclusion: that, whichever of the alternatives were true, God should be believed, or even shown, to be worthy of praise.

“For that discussion was undertaken on account of those who deny that the origin of evil derives from free choice of the will, and who maintain that, if this is so, God must be blamed as the creator of all natures. In this way they wish, in accordance with the error of their impiety—for they are Manichaeans—to introduce a certain immutable nature of evil coeternal with God.

“Nothing was argued in these books concerning the grace of God by which he predestined his elect in such a way that, in those of them who already make use of free will, he himself also prepares their wills, because that question was not then proposed. Whenever a place arose for mentioning this grace, it was mentioned in passing, not as though the matter were being treated, and not defended by elaborate reasoning.

“For it is one thing to ask from where evil comes, and another to ask from where one returns to one’s former good or reaches a greater good. Therefore, let the new heretics, the Pelagians, who assert free choice of the will in such a way as to leave no place for the grace of God—since they claim that grace is given according to our merits—not exalt themselves as though I had acted on their behalf. For I said many things in these books in favor of free will, as the purpose of that discussion required” (ibid., nos. 1, 2).

5. Pelagius actually cites these books. But Augustine demonstrates that, in the very passage he cites, he overturned the distorted meaning that Pelagius was trying to attach to his words. And although the work had been written against the Manichaeans, not against the Pelagians, who had not yet arisen, he nevertheless had thoroughly weakened the latter’s heresy—so thoroughly that, if Pelagius himself were willing to acknowledge what is contained in the passage he cites, no further controversy on this matter would remain between them (On Nature and Grace, nos. 7, 8).

These same books also gave the Semi-Pelagians an opportunity for error. From them they argued that they could overturn everything Augustine had later said concerning predestination (Epistle 226, no. 8). But the holy Doctor shows that they could derive no support for their cause from his words. Nor, he says, did he in any way intend to call into question that ignorance and difficulty were punishments of original sin. Moreover, although at that time he had understood the truth less correctly, he was no less bound to undertake the defense of what he later came to know (On the Gift of Perseverance, nos. 26, 27).

As soon as he had been made bishop, Augustine sent this work to Paulinus, and testified that he wished the great question that constituted the subject of the entire work to be disentangled in these books with as much certainty and clarity as the abundance of expression with which it was treated (Epistle 31, no. 7).

A little later he wrote to the Roman Manichaean Secundinus that, if he wished to read his three books On Free Will, he would find them at Nola in Campania, in the possession of the holy Paulinus (Against Secundinus, chapter 11).

Writing later to Jerome, he notes how he had discussed in these books the incarnation of the soul, or the soul’s origin in the body. At that time he was thinking nothing of the Priscillianists, of whom he had still heard nothing, although while Augustine was at Milan they had already caused great disturbances. He likewise observes that he wrote very little about the Baptism of infants, and nothing at all about the condemnation of those who died without Baptism, since these matters were foreign to his purpose (Epistle 166, nos. 7, 18).

# BOOK FOUR

In which it is shown how Augustine lived as a bishop and what he published from his ordination through the fifth year thereafter.

[Col. 0209]

## CHAPTER ONE

1. Augustine is requested by Valerius to become his colleague.  
2. Megalius, primate of Numidia, opposes his ordination on the charge of a false accusation, of which he soon repents.  
3. Augustine finally consents to his ordination and sits as co-bishop with Valerius.  
4. His ordination took place at the end of the year 395.  
5. In a letter to Paulinus he informs him of his ordination.  
6. Paulinus writes to Romanianus about the same matter, adding a poem to Licentius.

[Col. 0209]

1. After Augustine had worthily discharged the office of presbyter for nearly five years, he was advanced to the episcopate when he had just entered upon his forty-fifth year. That holy man did not take this honor for himself. “Rather,” Paulinus says, “the African Church deserved this care from God, that it should receive heavenly words through Augustine’s mouth” (Epistle 32, no. 2).

This benefit was divinely bestowed upon the peace and purity of heart of the blessed bishop Valerius. He was not stung by any impulse of envy toward Augustine; rather, he rejoiced and gave thanks above all others for the glory won by his presbyter (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 8).

Valerius himself could not bear to have Augustine remain beneath him as presbyter. He compelled him to become his colleague and to undertake the burden of the co-episcopate (Epistle 31, no. 4).

At first, Valerius was concerned only with this and earnestly asked God that Augustine might become his successor in the priesthood (Epistle 32, no. 2). But when he saw that Augustine had almost been taken away from him to be placed over another church, and when, already weakened by poor health and advanced age, he realized that he needed another’s assistance to bear the episcopal burden, he secretly wrote to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, requesting that Augustine be ordained bishop—not so much to succeed him in the see of Hippo as to join him as colleague and co-bishop.

His wish was fulfilled, and he obtained by written reply what he had requested from Aurelius (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 8).

2. Shortly afterward Megalius, bishop of Calama and at that time primate, or dean, of the bishops of Numidia, came to Hippo-Regius to visit the church. His presence was required for the ordination of a bishop.

Accordingly, Valerius seized the opportunity to disclose to Megalius and the other bishops who happened to be present, to the entire clergy of Hippo, and to all the people, his plan—until then unknown to everyone—for advancing Augustine to the episcopate (ibid.). The proposal was received with the greatest eagerness and joy by the people and all those present, and they demanded with immense acclamation that it be carried out (Epistle 31, no. 4).

Only Augustine and Megalius opposed it. Why Megalius was hostile to Augustine is not clear. This alone is certain: he angrily intervened against Augustine’s ordination (Against Cresconius, book 3, no. 92), and he also wrote letters in which he accused him of some offense (ibid., book 4, no. 79).

What that offense was cannot be identified by name or with precision. For although, immediately before mentioning Megalius’s letters, Augustine observes that the Donatist Petilianus wished to persuade people that Augustine had supplied love magic to a certain woman, he nevertheless clearly indicates that this slander had been invented by Petilianus alone and was not taken from Megalius’s letters (Against the Letters of Petilianus, book 3, no. 19).

Whatever the case, Augustine testifies that he would have paid no attention to Megalius’s letters, even if Megalius had persisted in the accusation. But when Megalius was pressed in a council of bishops to prove what he had alleged against Augustine, he acknowledged the falsity of the accusation, explicitly condemned in writing the slander he had advanced, and asked the holy council for forgiveness for the offense he had committed against Augustine (Against Cresconius, book 3, no. 92).

He did not consider himself exempt from correcting his fault on account of the title and dignity of primate. Rather, he wisely remembered the divine oracle: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you will find grace before God” (Ecclesiasticus III, 20). Therefore, when he humbly asked that he be forgiven, the council mercifully forgave him.

As for that council, if the bishops who had first assembled at Hippo were not numerous enough to form a council, the matter was sufficiently important to warrant its being convened for that reason alone—unless perhaps another provincial synod in Numidia happened to be held at that time on another matter and examined this one as well.

Not long afterward, writing to his intimate friend Profuturus about Megalius’s death, Augustine immediately added: “There are scandals, but there is also refuge; there are sorrows, but there are also consolations” (Epistle 38, no. 2). Shortly afterward he showed at length that anger must be avoided lest it eventually assume the nature of hatred. He concluded by asserting that he was writing these things deliberately, because of what Profuturus had recently said to him.

We do not know whether those words referred to Megalius’s case, in which Profuturus, perhaps already a bishop, may at that time have taken the side of Augustine, once his teacher.

When Megalius’s letter fell into the hands of the Donatists, they attempted to use it to cast infamy upon Augustine. But Augustine found it easy to convict them by producing the accuser’s recantation.

At the Carthaginian Conference, the Donatists—who were always on the lookout for some opportunity to cause disturbance—asked Augustine who had ordained him, intending thereby to seize an occasion for dispute. For this reason Augustine for some time delayed answering them about a matter irrelevant to the question under discussion.

But when he noticed that they were gaining an advantage from his silence, he answered them confidently that he had been ordained by Megalius, primate of the Catholic Church’s bishops in Numidia, at the time when Megalius had the authority to ordain. They could say anything they wished about the matter and connect their slanders with the truth.

Then, since they did not dare to answer or even utter a word, they turned to other matters (Carthaginian Conference 3, chapter 247).

3. Just as Megalius refused to inaugurate Augustine, so Augustine in turn refused to be inaugurated by him (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 8). His modesty and religious scruple were no less than those of the many distinguished men who, in that age, as he writes, were compelled against their will to accept the episcopate, led away, confined, guarded, and subjected to so many things they did not want, until they became willing to undertake the good work (Epistle 173, no. 2).

For, besides fearing the burden of episcopal dignity, Augustine remembered that it was contrary to the custom of the Church for another man to be placed over a church while its bishop was still alive. He was nevertheless informed that this was neither new nor unusual, and many examples were brought before him—not only African but also overseas examples—so that every excuse was closed to him (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 8; Augustine, Epistle 31, no. 4).

Since he greatly feared resisting divine providence, if he continued to refuse what was being offered to him through such great affection from his bishop and such great enthusiasm from the people, he believed that God’s will was being announced to him through their public wishes and desires. Accordingly, he yielded and reluctantly accepted the care and insignia of episcopal dignity.

Paulinus writes that this unusual ordination added a new splendor and distinction to his episcopate, and that no one could have believed it before it occurred (in Augustine, Epistle 32, no. 2). This certainly confirmed the esteem already formed for Augustine’s learning and piety.

Nevertheless, that ordination was criticized, and Augustine himself, both orally and in writing, acknowledged that it had been prohibited by the eighth canon of the Council of Nicaea (Epistle 213, no. 4). In that canon the holy synod clearly declares that its primary intention was for one bishop alone to preside over each church, although it sometimes permits the contrary.

At that time, however, neither Augustine nor Valerius knew that decree of the council. Once Augustine learned of it, he carefully observed the council’s sanction. He did indeed advise that Donatist bishops who returned to communion with the Church should be permitted to sit with the Catholic bishop, just as the Council of Nicaea had permitted in the case of the Novatians.
