But apart from such very rare cases, in which the wound inflicted upon ecclesiastical discipline would be abundantly compensated by the greater benefit of reconciliation, he did not allow others to do what he himself regretted.

Therefore, although he thought that he ought to arrange for the election of the presbyter Heraclius to succeed him, he nevertheless left him a presbyter and did not promote his ordination (ibid., nos. 4, 5).

For this reason he also took care that the following rule be enacted in councils: before men were ordained, the ordinands were to have all the decrees of the Fathers read to them by the ordaining bishop (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 8).

That decree survives in the Third Council of Carthage. Its third canon, inserted as the eighteenth canon in the Code of African Canons, reads: “It was decided that, before bishops or clerics are ordained, the decisions of the councils should be impressed upon their ears by those who ordain them, lest they later regret having done anything contrary to the statutes of the council” (Labbe, *The Most Extensive Collection of Councils*, volume 2, page 1057); or, as it is read in the Third Council of Carthage, chapter 3: “It was decided that those to be ordained . . . should assert that they had carried out the decrees of the councils” (ibid., page 1167).

4. This, then, was Augustine’s advancement, the memory of which he renewed every year. The bishops of Rome, too, were accustomed in those times to do something similar, summoning many bishops to this celebration. We also read that Donatist bishops were accustomed to gather in large numbers for the birthday festival of their Optatus Gildonianus (Epistle 108, no. 5; Against the Letters of Petilianus, book 2, no. 53).

This anniversary of Augustine’s consecration was a most joyful day for all Africa. Its public rejoicing seems to have been expressed by Paulinus in the congratulatory letter that he immediately composed to Augustine upon receiving news of the ordination. In it, rejoicing, he breaks forth in these words:

“Let us exult and rejoice in him who alone works wonders, and who makes people dwell together in unity in a house, because he himself has looked upon our humility and has visited his people for good; he who raised up the horn in the house of David his servant, and has now exalted the horn of his Church in his chosen ones, so that he may break the horns of sinners, as he promises through the prophet—that is, the horns of the Donatists and the Manichaeans” (in Augustine, Epistle 32, no. 2).

For Augustine, however, this festival was rather a day of grief and sadness, since it renewed in his mind the memory of the burden placed upon his shoulders and of the account he had to render to God. And the older he grew, the more sharply that thought pierced his mind.

An especially excellent sermon on this subject survives (Sermon 339, no. 1), delivered to the people on the very day of his episcopal ordination, in which he says that the Lord’s nativity is approaching (ibid., no. 3).

This observation makes it impossible to place his consecration later than the year 396, although it has seemed appropriate to assign it to the end of the year 395. For in the year 397 Augustine subscribed among the bishops to the enactments of the Third Council of Carthage, held on September 1 or August 28. Through his influence, as we have said, that synod also established that the decrees of the councils should be read aloud to bishops or clerics being ordained.

Yet another observation seemed to prevent placing that ordination before the same year 396: namely, that of the books Augustine composed as bishop, the first were the two books addressed to Simplicianus of Milan. Both in the dedicatory letter and at the beginning of the work, Augustine calls him “father.” It might be thought that he honored him with this title because Simplicianus had already succeeded Ambrose; yet Ambrose did not depart from this life until the year 397, on the day before the Nones of April.

Thus, if Augustine’s ordination is said to have preceded the year 396, it seems necessary to admit that he spent nearly two years inactive, publishing no work. This can scarcely be believed of that holy teacher, who said that he placed his chief duty in the care he was bound to devote to his brothers, serving them especially by his tongue and his pen, the two chariots driven within him by charity (On the Trinity, book 3, no. 1).

Nevertheless, Prosper writes concerning the year 395: “Augustine, a disciple of the blessed Ambrose, a man outstanding in eloquence and learning, was ordained bishop at Hippo-Regius in Africa” (Prosper, *Chronicle*, under the year 395). All who have written about Augustine’s deeds have treated this clear authority as a fixed, certain, and unquestionable chronological marker.

Accordingly, so as not to depart from it, we shall later ask when the books addressed to Simplicianus were written, and how Simplicianus, although still a presbyter, could have been considered worthy of the title “father” by Augustine, who was already a bishop.

5. Once the date of Augustine’s ordination is established, it is clear that Romanus and Agilis, through whom Paulinus had sent his later letters to Augustine, could have been present at the consecration. They certainly did not return during the winter, but rather at the beginning of the spring of the year 396—yet earlier than Augustine would have wished. Augustine dismissed them only reluctantly, although they were hurrying to return for the sake of visiting Paulinus once more.

“They had to be dismissed all the more quickly,” Augustine says, “the more earnestly they wished to obey you. But the more earnestly they wished this, the more present they made you to us; for they thereby showed how dear your hearts were to us; Therefore, we wished to dismiss them less the more justly they pressed to be dismissed.”

He entrusted them with a letter addressed to Paulinus and Therasia, in which he replied to the later letters he had received from Paulinus. In this letter he showed no less tender affection for Paulinus, and no less ardent desire to see him, than in the letter carried by Romanianus.

He informed Paulinus of his promotion to the episcopate, both to tell him that he could not contemplate traveling to Italy in order to visit him and to invite him—once freed from ecclesiastical responsibilities, since Paulinus was not yet a bishop—to cross over to Africa. Paulinus’s arrival would bring consolation both to Augustine and to the others who wondered at the gifts divinely bestowed upon him, and would also instruct those who could neither believe in those gifts nor wished to do so unless they first saw Paulinus and his bride in person.

Augustine goes so far as to say: “I do not know whether you are doing anything more merciful than this: refusing only to conceal how much you are what you are, insofar as you wished to be what you are” (Epistle 31, nos. 3, 6).

He commends to Paulinus a boy named Vetustinus, who seems to have been guilty and wretched. He likewise wishes Romanianus and his son to be aided by Paulinus’s recommendation.

He sends Paulinus his three books On Free Will. In return, he asks him to send the commentary he was said to be writing against the pagans, together with some books of Ambrose. In those works the holy teacher had refuted at great length certain ignorant and proud men—perhaps philosophers—who maintained that Christ had learned from Plato’s books.

None of these books by Ambrose now survives for us. Nevertheless, since Augustine often praises them as though he knew them, there is no doubt that Paulinus sent them to him.

Augustine also asked Paulinus to accept kindly the bread he was sending. In the name of all the brothers serving God, he sent him greetings, including greetings in the words of the blessed Valerius, whom he still calls his father and who burned with the same desire as Augustine to see Paulinus.

He also extended to Paulinus the courteous service of Severus, bishop of the Church of Milevis. Therefore, we do not know whether this Severus is the same man who also gave Paulinus a letter, since the same brothers who carried Augustine’s letter and the news of his ordination to Paulinus likewise delivered letters from the holy bishops Aurelius, Alypius, Profuturus, and Severus (Epistle 32, no. 1).

It could easily have happened, however, that the same Severus, who at first wished merely to offer Paulinus the services of his courtesy through Augustine, was afterward compelled by some necessity to write to him personally.

6. Paulinus was already awaiting these brothers, Agilis and Romanus, while Romanianus was still present; but they did not arrive until after Romanianus’s departure. The day after their arrival, Paulinus wrote to Romanianus to inform him that he had received the most desired news, especially the news of Augustine’s advancement to the episcopate. In this matter, as was fitting for a holy man, he offered his congratulations.

Then he strongly exhorted Licentius. He first addressed him through his father, and afterward appealed to him in both a free and a more formal style, in order to satisfy Augustine’s most ardent concern, which, as he says, Augustine had renewed in his later letters.

He wished that this trumpet of the Lord, through which the Lord thundered by means of Augustine, might strike the hearing of Licentius’s heart. He also hoped, through his confidence in God, that the young man’s carnal desires would yield to faith and to Augustine’s wishes. For Augustine desired nothing more earnestly than that the one whom Romanianus, his father, had brought forth as a worthy son in letters might also be born worthily as a son in Christ to Augustine himself (in Augustine, Epistle 32).

There is no doubt that Paulinus replied to Augustine’s letter, and that he carefully and diligently nourished that noble bond which the piety of both men had created through their mutual friendship and correspondence. If only a few traces of it survive for us, this must be attributed to the fate of the times. These letters, like countless others, have perished.

In any event, Possidius records no more than eight letters from Augustine to Paulinus (in the *Catalogue*, chapter 7), and that is the number we now possess in the printed editions.

## CHAPTER II

1. What the disposition of Augustine’s soul and his conduct were once he was bishop. 2. He is forbidden by God to flee into solitude; his delights are the Scriptures of God and leisure for God. 3. What kind of bodily dress he accepted in clothing and footwear. 4. His table. 5. He would have liked to work with his hands every day, if health and responsibilities had permitted. 6. His poor health and responsibilities. 7. He established a monastery for clergy in the bishop’s house. A letter to Laetus, perhaps a member of that monastery. 8. In that monastery he lived with his clergy according to a strict rule and in poverty. 9. How he conducted himself toward women: he did not permit even one of his female relatives to live in his house.

[Col. 0215]

### 1

Augustine did not permit the episcopal burden to be imposed upon him until he had firmly resolved that he would spend his entire life in duties pertaining to it. Hence, throughout the rest of his life, he will be found to have undertaken and attempted nothing else except what his charity toward his brethren required—brethren whom he reverenced as his lords (Confessions, book 10, chapter 4, no. 6).

Before we examine, in the order of the years, the labors, writings, and journeys by which brotherly love involved him, we shall here gather some details concerning his activities on behalf of the Church, which cannot be assigned to a definite chronological order.

To begin our account with matters relating to his character: what the disposition of his soul was at the beginning of his episcopate, he himself set forth openly before everyone in his Confessions, written in the fourth or fifth year after his ordination. For although he wished to lie hidden and to count for nothing among human beings, the holy man found it exceedingly burdensome that he was, on the contrary, in everyone’s mouth and even regarded as supremely worthy of honor under the name of holy conduct.

Therefore, Possidius says, lest anyone believe him to be more than he knew himself to be, he portrayed not only what he had been before receiving grace, but also how he lived after receiving it (Possidius, Life of Augustine, Preface). Moreover, he saw that he would give pleasure, and not without great benefit, to many good Christians who likewise wished to know what he was like at the very time when he wrote his Confessions. They would give thanks to God for the gifts bestowed upon him and, having seen his faults, would pray for him (Confessions, book 10, chapter 3, no. 4).

Thus the very man who seemed to be most holy and most deserving before God, and in whom anyone might readily place his hope, professes that his entire hope rests only in the very great mercy of God. He asks God to grant what He commands, and in this way to command what He wills. He knows that no one can be continent unless God grants it, since by the commandment of continence we are instructed to gather ourselves together and be brought back into unity, from which we have flowed out into many things. For the person who loves something together with God, but does not love it for God’s sake, loves God less. Augustine confesses that he is not sufficient by himself to fulfill this command, but needs to be kindled by God Himself:

> O love, which always burns and is never extinguished! O Charity, my God, kindle me. You command continence; grant what You command, and command what You will.  
> (Ibid., chapter 29, no. 40)

Although, by divine gift, he had already been brought to such spiritual health that he could confidently say to God, “With no doubtful but certain conscience, Lord, I love You” (Ibid., chapter 6, no. 8), nevertheless he acknowledges that his illnesses were many and great, and that the medicinal grace of Christ the Mediator was necessary for their healing (Ibid., chapter 43, no. 68).

He testifies that images of shameful things still lived in his memory and confronted him: while he was awake, they lacked the power to affect him; in dreams, however, they proceeded not only to pleasure but even to something closely resembling consent and the deed itself. Yet he often resisted even in dreams and, mindful of his resolution and remaining most chastely faithful to it, gave no assent to such enticements even while asleep (Ibid., chapter 30, no. 41).

When he discovered that he was still in this condition of evil, he rejoiced with trembling over what God had granted him, while mourning what remained incomplete in him.

He proceeds to another kind of temptation, arising from the necessity of eating and drinking. God had indeed taught him to approach food as he would medicines, taking it as something necessary for health (Ibid., chapter 31, no. 44). But as he passed from the discomfort of need to the relief of satiety, a snare of desire lay in wait for him in that very transition. For since it is often uncertain whether the body is still seeking help because its care is necessary, or whether the deceitfulness of pleasure is supplying a service, the unhappy soul grows cheerful amid this uncertainty and prepares a defense for itself, glad that what is sufficient for the moderation of health does not appear clearly, so that, under the pretext of preserving health, the business of pleasure may be concealed.

He strove daily to resist these temptations and called upon God’s right hand for his salvation. He referred his agitations to God, because he could not settle the matter for himself.

Drunkenness was far from him; gluttony, however, sometimes crept upon him—gluttony of the sort by which not the heart itself but the emotions and the weakened stomach are occasionally burdened even in fully formed Christians. He was never a drunkard, something he attributes wholly to God’s favor.

Placed amid these temptations, he fought daily against the desire to eat and drink. Since this was not something he could cut off once and for all and decide never again to touch, the reins of the throat had to be held by moderate loosening and tightening. Yet he was not yet a man who was never carried somewhat beyond the limits of necessity. Nevertheless, he magnified the name of God, who conquered the world and interceded for his sins, counting Augustine among the weak members of His body.

As for the attraction of smells, he did not concern himself with it excessively. When pleasant odors were absent, he did not seek them; when they were present, he did not reject them, always prepared to do without them. Yet although this was how he seemed to himself, he feared that he was mistaken in this matter, since his own capacity was hidden from him and his mind did not readily consider itself trustworthy concerning its own strength. What is within us is generally hidden unless experience reveals it.

The pleasures of the ears had entangled and subdued him more tenaciously, but God had loosened and freed him. Thus, in sounds enlivened by the divine words when they were sung with a sweet and skillful voice, he rested for a little while—not so as to become fixed upon them, but so that he could rise whenever he wished.

Nevertheless, at times he seemed to himself to grant those sounds more honor than was fitting, because he felt his mind moved more religiously and ardently into the flame of piety by the sacred words when they were sung in this way than when they were not (Ibid., chapter 33, no. 49). For bodily pleasure often deceived him, attempting to run ahead of and lead even the reason for which he had deserved to be admitted. Thus he sinned in these matters without noticing it, and noticed it only afterward.

Sometimes, while guarding against this very deception, he erred through excessive severity. He would at times strongly wish to remove from his ears—and from the ears of the Church—the entire melody of the beautiful songs with which the Davidic psalter is commonly sung. It seemed safer to him to follow what he remembered having often been told about Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria: he made the reader sing the psalm with so slight a modulation of the voice that he was closer to speaking than to singing.

Yet when he remembered the tears he had shed at the singing of the Church in the early days of his recovered faith, and how he was afterward moved—not by the singing, but by the things that were sung when they were sung with a clear voice and most appropriate modulation, he again recognized the great usefulness of this practice.

But when it happened that the singing itself moved him more than the subject sung, he recognized that he was sinning in a manner deserving punishment, and then he would have preferred not to hear the singer:

> Behold where I am, he says; weep with me and weep for me, you who inwardly do something good with me from which actions proceed. For those who do not do so are not moved by these things.  
> (Ibid., no. 50)

He also resisted the seductions of the eyes and raised invisible eyes toward God. He knew that beautiful things, passing through souls into the hands of craftsmen, came from that Beauty which is above souls, to which his soul sighed day and night.

Even to these beautiful things he attached his step, from which God mercifully drew him away. He was miserably seized, and God mercifully pulled him away: sometimes without his noticing, because he had fallen more deeply; sometimes with pain, because he had already become attached (Ibid., chapter 34, nos. 52–53).

As for the sickness of curiosity, Augustine had cut away and driven many things from his heart, but he did not dare say that nothing ever held his attention for viewing or seized him through empty concern. The theaters no longer carried him away; he did not care to know the courses of the stars; his soul had never sought answers from shades; he detested all sacrilegious rites.

The enemy, however, employed every device of suggestion he could, trying to induce him to ask God for some sign. But the holy man was far from consenting to this (Ibid., chapter 35, no. 56).

Nevertheless, curiosity was tested daily in many very small matters, and he often slipped. At first he would tolerate people relating trivialities, as though merely to avoid offending the weak; then little by little he would listen willingly.

He no longer watched a dog chasing a hare when such a thing occurred in the circus. But in the countryside, if he happened to pass by while it was occurring, the hunt might turn him away from some important thought and draw him back to itself—not by forcing the body of the animal on which he happened to be riding to deviate, but by inclining his heart.

A lizard catching flies while he sat at home, or a spider entangling the flies rushing into its webs, would also hold his attention. He would indeed proceed to praise God, the wonderful Creator and arranger of all things, but his attention would first be captured by the spectacle.

His life was full of such things, and his one hope was the very great mercy of God (Ibid., no. 57).

At the beginning, God healed him of the desire for vengeance, so that He might also become favorable toward all his other iniquities. He had restrained his pride through fear of Him and tamed his neck beneath His yoke, so that the yoke had already become gentle to him as he bore it (Ibid., chapter 36, no. 58).

But he was tested daily, without interruption, by the temptation of human praise. “You know,” he says to God, “the groaning of my heart and the rivers of my eyes concerning this matter. For I do not easily gather how much cleaner I am from this plague, and I greatly fear my hidden things, which Your eyes know, but mine do not.

“Sometimes I am saddened by my praises, when either those things are praised in me with which I myself am displeased, or lesser and trivial goods are valued more highly than they ought to be. But again, how do I know whether I am affected in this way because I do not wish my praiser to disagree with me about myself, rather than because I am moved by his benefit? Is it not because the same goods that please me in myself are more pleasing to me when they also please another?

“I see that I ought to be moved by my praises not for my own sake but for the benefit of my neighbor. Whether this is so, I do not know.

“Speech proceeding from the mouth and deeds that become known to human beings possess a most dangerous temptation from the love of praise, which draws begged-for approval toward a private kind of excellence. It also tempts me when I criticize it in myself, precisely through the act of criticism; and often a person takes still more empty pride in despising empty glory” (Ibid., chapter 37, nos. 60–63).

Elsewhere he explains what he fears in human praise, why he does not reject it entirely, and how it affects him:

> My danger is this: if I attend to how you praise me and disregard how you live. But He knows, beneath whose eyes I speak—rather, beneath whose eyes I think—that I am not so much delighted by popular praise as stimulated and distressed by the question of how those who praise me live.  
>   
> I do not wish to be praised by those who live badly; I shrink from it and detest it. It is a source of pain to me, not pleasure. But if I say that I do not wish to be praised by those who live well, I lie; if I say that I do wish it, I fear that I am more desirous of emptiness than of substance. What, then, shall I say? I neither wholly wish it nor wholly do not wish it. I do not wholly wish it, lest I be endangered by human praise; I do not wholly reject it, lest those to whom I preach prove ungrateful.  
> (Sermon 339, no. 1)

Finally, concerning that other evil of temptation by which those who please themselves become empty—whether they regard God’s gifts as their own, or as arising from their merits, or behave as though envying others—Augustine himself was affected with trembling of heart. He felt that his wounds were continually being healed by God rather than that they were simply not being inflicted upon him (Confessions, book 10, chapter 39, no. 65).

### 2

When the holy Bishop acknowledged and confessed that he was subject to sins of every kind, whatever others might think of his uprightness and merit, he considered these sins far from contemptible. Rather, he testifies that he was shaken by such great fear that he contemplated fleeing into solitude.

> Terrified by my sins and by the burden of my misery, I had stirred the matter in my heart and reflected upon flight into solitude; but You forbade me and strengthened me, saying: “Christ died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for Him who died for them” (2 Cor. 5:14).  
> (Confessions, book 10, chapter 43, no. 70)

He therefore recognized that nothing remained for him except to cast his care upon God, so that he might live.

> You wished Your children to be my masters, and commanded me to serve them if I wished to live with You and from You. And this word of Yours would have been insufficient for me if it commanded merely by speaking, unless it also went before me by acting. And I do this in deeds and words; I do it beneath Your wings, with very great danger, except that beneath Your wings my soul is subject to You and my weakness is known to You.  
> (Ibid., chapter 4, no. 6)

Finally, as he says, he would scarcely ever have been sufficient to express with a pen all the exhortations, terrors, consolations, and directions by which God led him to undertake the burden of pastoral office (Ibid., book 11, chapter 2, no. 2).

Once established in this position, when he had formerly burned with eagerness to meditate upon divine law, he did not wish the hours he found free from the necessities either of restoring his body or of serving the people entrusted to his care to flow away into anything else. This was especially because he wished such study to benefit not himself alone but brotherly love as well.

His chaste delights were the Scriptures of God. Their voice was his joy; their voice was more to him than an abundance of pleasures (Ibid., no. 3).

Moreover, as he sought God in the consideration even of created things, consulting Him about all things—whether they are, what they are, and how each ought to be valued—he heard Him speaking and commanding:

> And I often do this, he says; this delights me, and, so far as I can be released from the activities necessity requires, I flee to this pleasure. In all these things through which I range, consulting You, I find no safe place for my soul except in You, where my scattered parts may be gathered together and nothing of me may depart from You. And sometimes You admit me inwardly to an altogether unusual affection, to I know not what sweetness; if this should be perfected in me, I do not know what it will be—something this life will not be. But I fall back under burdensome weights into these miseries, am swallowed up again by my accustomed ways, and am held fast; I weep greatly, yet am held fast greatly: so heavy is the burden of habit! I can remain here, yet I do not wish to; I wish to be there, yet I cannot: wretched in both places.  
> (Ibid., book 10, chapter 40, no. 65)

Thus the requirements of his office called him away to other labors and other cares, making his way narrower and rougher than it would have been had he exercised himself through bodily labor. Yet hope continually flooded him with joy, and the example of Christ the Lord made His yoke gentle and light for him.

Once he had learned of God, he did not hold Him uselessly in his memory. There he found Him and delighted in Him:

> These are my holy delights, which You have given me, looking with mercy upon my poverty.  
> (Ibid., chapter 24, no. 35)

### 3

As for bodily dress, his clothing, footwear, and bedding were of a moderate and suitable kind: neither excessively elegant nor excessively shabby. For people generally use such things either to display themselves insolently or to abase themselves; in both cases they seek not the things of Jesus Christ but their own. Augustine, however, as I have said, kept to the middle way, turning neither to the right nor to the left (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 22).

Augustine writes that it was customary for his undergarments to be linen and his outer garments woolen; he includes himself with others in these words concerning “our clothing” (Sermon 37, no. 6).

He also wore another kind of garment called a *byrrhus*, which laymen likewise wore. One of his sermons contains a particularly fine passage about his clothing:

> Let no one give a *byrrhus*, or a linen tunic, or anything else except for common use. I accept from the common fund, and I want whatever I possess to be held in common.  
>   
> I do not want Your Holiness to offer things that I alone might use more suitably. For example, offer me an expensive *byrrhus*. Perhaps it suits a bishop, although it does not suit Augustine—that is, a poor man born of poor parents.  
>   
> People would then say that I have acquired expensive clothing such as I could not have possessed either in my father’s house or in my former secular profession. It is not fitting. I ought to have the kind of garment that I could give to my brother if he lacked one. I want to receive what a presbyter can have, what a deacon and subdeacon can decently have, because I receive it for common use.  
>   
> If someone gives me something better, I sell it; and this is what I usually do, so that when the garment itself cannot be common, its price may be common. I sell it and distribute the proceeds to the poor.  
>   
> If it pleases him that I should have it, let him give me something I will not be ashamed to wear. For I confess to you that I am ashamed of expensive clothing: it does not suit this profession, this admonition; it does not suit these limbs; it does not suit these gray hairs.  
> (Sermon 356, no. 13)

When a certain holy virgin named Sapida was grieving intensely over the death of her brother Timothy, a Carthaginian deacon, she asked Augustine to accept for her consolation a tunic that she herself had woven with her own hands for her brother’s use. The holy Bishop did not refuse, lest he grieve her, and he used the tunic. Nevertheless, he urged her by letter to seek better consolations from her faith and to hope that she would one day live with her brother, whose eternal happiness he speaks of without hesitation (Letter 263, no. 1).

As for footwear, Augustine did not think himself bound to observe literally the prohibition that Christ the Lord had made concerning it, since he knew from the Gospel that Christ Himself had worn sandals. He proposed this to himself as a consolation in poor health, which imposed upon him the need for such relief.

At the same time, he loved the fortitude of those who went barefoot (Confessions, book 9, chapter 6, no. 14). Yet he did not think that they fulfilled the evangelical law in this matter more carefully than he did, or that they could on this account grow insolent through proud harshness.

In matters of this kind—good but by no means necessary—he wished both those who observed such practices and those who did not to be joined in charity, so that although their external practices differed, their hearts might burn with the same love (Sermon 101, chapter 6, no. 7).

### 4

He used a frugal and spare table, with nothing superfluous and nothing immoderate. It consisted of vegetables and legumes, with meat sometimes included for guests or for the weaker, and always wine (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 22).

For he feared not impurity in food but impurity of desire, knowing that every creature of God is good and is sanctified by the word of God and prayer (Confessions, book 10, chapter 31, no. 46).

A fixed number of cups was prescribed for his guests. If any of his clergy swore an oath, he forfeited one of the prescribed drinks (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 25).

He used silver spoons, but the other vessels in which food was brought to the table were earthenware, wooden, or marble—not from necessity or poverty, but from a deliberate devotion to voluntary poverty and modesty (Ibid., chapter 22).

Since he had always practiced hospitality, he received very many travelers at his table (Ibid.). In fact, he could not excuse himself from performing this duty toward all who came and went without diminishing the charity required of a bishop (Sermon 355, no. 2).

He showed the same kindness in receiving unknown guests, following this maxim: “It is far better to receive a bad person than to exclude a good one, provided that we take care not to receive a bad one” (Letter 38, no. 3).

This did not, however, disturb the order he had established. At table he preferred reading or discussion to eating and drinking. As a protection against the plague of human custom, he had the following inscription placed there:

> Whoever delights in gnawing at the lives of the absent  
> Must know that this table is unworthy of him.

For this reason he admonished every guest to abstain from unnecessary and harmful talk and from slander.

Once, when some of his most intimate fellow bishops had forgotten this inscription and were speaking against it, he rebuked them so sharply in his agitation that he said either the lines were to be erased from the table or he would rise from the middle of the meal and go to his room.

“This,” says Possidius, “I and the others who attended that table experienced” (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 27).

### 5

He did not provide his sustenance by the labor of his hands, since he could not carry this out because of poor health or because of the constant responsibilities with which the care of his Church involved him without interruption (Letter 126, no. 10).

If he could have done so without violating the requirements of his office, he would have preferred to work with his hands every day for certain hours, as was prescribed in well-ordered monasteries, and to keep the remaining hours free for reading, prayer, or devotion to the divine Scriptures (On the Work of Monks, no. 37):

> No one would surpass me in that most peaceful leisure. Nothing is better, nothing sweeter, than to search out the divine treasure without disturbance: it is sweet, it is good.  
>   
> To preach, rebuke, correct, build up, and labor for each person is a great burden, a great weight, a great labor. Who would not shrink from such work? But the Gospel terrifies me.  
> (Sermon 339, no. 4)

Thus the requirements of his office called him away to other labors and other cares, making his path narrower and harsher than it would have been had he exercised himself through bodily work. Nevertheless, hope continually flooded him with joy, and the example of Christ the Lord made His yoke gentle and light for him.

### 6

By nature he could not endure cold (Letter 124, no. 1), and he had a delicate and weak constitution (Letter 122, no. 1), as was evident to everyone who knew him more intimately (Letter 151, no. 13).

For this reason he testifies that he had grown old through bodily weakness long before he had grown old through age (Sermon 255, no. 7).

He speaks only very rarely of his illnesses, which sometimes forced him to go into the countryside to recover his strength (Letter 118, no. 34). We can nevertheless infer how patiently he endured his customary ailments from a letter he wrote during a most troublesome bodily illness (Letter 38, no. 1).

His constant responsibilities allowed him so little leisure that only a few drops of time—this is his own expression—remained from ecclesiastical cares. These scarcely sufficed to refresh him, whether he was thinking through something, dictating what pressed more urgently and would benefit more people, or restoring the bodily strength necessary for his service (Letter 261, no. 1).

Indeed, he seemed to himself to be acting against his duty if he devoted even those very few drops of time to other matters (Letter 110, no. 5).

In the year 404 he wrote to Jerome that if he possessed any ability in knowledge of the divine Scriptures, he devoted all of it to instructing the people of God. He could devote himself to study only insofar as necessity required him to prepare what the instruction of the people demanded (Letter 73, no. 5).

He also confessed that he had read little. Consequently, he avoided unusually great cares and responsibilities (Letter 82, no. 23). When Severus requested a lengthy letter from him, Augustine asked him to excuse him and added that Severus and his other closest friends would do him a very great favor if they demanded no extended writing from him and dissuaded others from making the same requests, lest, if he could not satisfy their wishes, they should take offense (Letter 110, no. 6).

Nor should we pass over the fact that, when writing longer letters to his close friends, whether laymen or bishops, he committed them to paper in a particular manner and format—perhaps less elegant, but well suited to being written quickly and to allowing the paper itself to be held more conveniently while it was read.

He wished the physician Maximus to know this, lest, being unfamiliar with Augustine’s practice, he should think that an insult had been committed against him (Letter 171).

When sending a letter to Victorinus, he warned him that it had been sealed with a ring bearing the image of a man looking to the side (Letter 59, no. 2). Since, according to Possidius, he never had a ring on his hand (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 24), he had perhaps borrowed for use the ring with which he sealed the letter in question.

### 7

We saw above that, as soon as Augustine was ordained a presbyter, he established a monastery for men in the city of Hippo. From it, as from a most abundant spring, the monastic life spread throughout all Africa. He lived there throughout the whole period of his presbyterate (Ibid., chapter 5).

But when he was made bishop, he understood that his office obliged him to show constant hospitality to guests, and he judged that this would interfere with the tranquility of monastic life. Therefore he wished to have with him in the bishop’s house a monastery of clergy—that is, of the presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons serving his Church (Sermon 255, no. 2).

It appears that Spes, who lived with Augustine, was the only layman in that monastery, although he was in some manner destined for the clerical state (Letters 77, no. 2, and 78, no. 2).

The same may be thought of Laetus, a young man who had begun his training in the perfect life under Augustine and had remained with him for some time—perhaps in his house, if Augustine admitted laymen whom he intended for the clergy.

Laetus had brought the brethren the greatest joy through the fervor of his spirit. Augustine nevertheless noticed that domestic responsibilities were holding him back from divine study, and that he was being carried and led by his cross and by the weakness of his flesh rather than carrying and bearing them himself.

In reality, Laetus was forced to leave Augustine and return to his own home so that he could arrange his domestic affairs, intending that, once he had shaken off the yoke of worldly servitude, he would freely submit himself to the bonds of wisdom.

At home, however, he was beset by many temptations. He found there a runaway slave, the deaths of female servants, the poor health of his brothers, and above all the tears of his mother, which drew him back from the course he had undertaken.

Accordingly, wishing to obtain some consolation for his anxieties from his brethren—whether laymen or clergy of the monastery at Hippo—he sent them a letter in which he indicated that he desired a letter from Augustine.

The grief Augustine had conceived over Laetus’s unhappy condition pressed him sufficiently that he did not refuse the young man’s request, since he saw that charity required it of him. He therefore wrote him a most ardent letter (Letter 243), exhorting him to despise earthly things and to subordinate love of his mother to the charity of Christ, the Church, and his own salvation.

He advised him to leave his possessions to his mother and household, if they should perhaps need them, and then to bid them farewell, lest through his sluggishness he cause his brethren greater sorrow than his former eagerness had given them joy.

He urged him to devote himself to the study of truth and to prepare himself for the office of preaching the Gospel. The Church needed help so that she might be defended against the attacks of her enemies and so that her little children might be warmed by the fervor of other children—children of whom Laetus was one—in opposition to the laziness and sluggishness of some of their fellow children.

From this we may infer that Augustine had destined him for the ministry of the Church.

### 8

Since Augustine therefore kept his clergy with him in the bishop’s house, he followed with them, as far as he could, the pattern of life of the first Christians living in Jerusalem, among whom everything was held in common and nothing was privately owned (Sermon 355, chapter 1, no. 2; Sermon 356, no. 1).

In his community no one was permitted to call anything his own; everything belonged to everyone. All who were admitted into it knew that this rule had been imposed upon them (Sermon 355, chapter 2, no. 2; Sermon 356, no. 2).

Nor did he ordain anyone as a cleric unless that person was willing to remain with him under this condition: if anyone departed from his purpose, Augustine would remove his clerical office and cast him down from his rank as a deserter from the sacred society he had entered and the holy profession he had undertaken (Sermon 356, nos. 6, 14).

Thus all the clergy were poor with him, jointly awaiting the mercy of God from the revenues of the Church’s properties or from the offerings of the faithful, which were distributed to each according to his need (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 23).

Those who possessed some private property were required either to distribute it to the poor, place it in common, or relinquish it in whatever manner they could (Sermon 355, no. 2). Those who had contributed nothing were not distinguished from those who had brought something (Sermon 356, no. 8).

If necessity forced any sick person or anyone recovering from illness to eat before the hour of the midday meal, Augustine did not forbid that person to be sent food offered by the piety of others; but he did not permit him to take lunch or dinner separately from the rest (Ibid., no. 13).

Augustine was always nourished and clothed with them in one house, at one table, and from common resources. He did not wish to possess anything except in common or to accept anything except for common use. If someone offered him something that could not be made common, he sold it so that its price might be common.

Possidius says that Augustine reproved and tolerated the undisciplined conduct and transgressions of his people against the proper rule and moral order as far as was suitable and necessary. In such matters he taught especially that no one’s heart should turn toward malicious words in order to devise excuses for sins.

He also taught that when someone brought his gift to the altar and there remembered that his brother had something against him, he should leave his gift before the altar and go to be reconciled with his brother; then he should return and offer his gift at the altar.

If, however, he himself had something against his brother, he was to rebuke him privately. If the brother listened, he had gained his brother. If not, one or two others were to be brought in. If the brother disregarded them too, the Church was to be involved. If he refused to obey even the Church, he was to be treated as a pagan and a tax collector.

Augustine added that when a sinning brother asked forgiveness, the offense was to be forgiven not seven times but seventy times seven, just as each person daily asks the Lord to forgive him (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 25).

Possidius surely included this among Augustine’s deeds for no other reason than to commend the holy Bishop’s particular concern and diligence: namely, that he labored especially to ensure that, without any exception, what our Lord had commanded in this matter should be carried out.

### 9

No woman ever lived or remained within his house—not even his full sister, who, as a widow serving God, lived for a long time until the day of her death as superior of the handmaids of God. Nor did his paternal uncle’s daughters or his brother’s daughters live there, although they likewise served God. Councils of holy bishops placed such persons among the exceptions.

Augustine used to say that although no evil suspicion could arise concerning his sister and nieces living with him, nevertheless such persons could not live with him without other female relatives and attendants. Other women would also come in from outside on their account, and from these circumstances offense or scandal could arise among the weak.

Those who happened to live with a bishop or any cleric could, through all these female persons living with or visiting them, either perish through human temptations or at least be grievously defamed by the evil suspicions of men.

For this reason, he said, women should never live in the same house with servants of God, even the most chaste, lest, as has been said, such an example place some scandal or stumbling block before the weak.

If he happened to be asked by some women to see or greet them, they never entered to him without clergy as witnesses. He was never alone with a woman alone, nor did he ever speak privately with one, even if some confidential matter was involved (Ibid., chapter 26).

## CHAPTER III

1. Augustine was always inwardly free in administering the goods of his Church. 2. In increasing those same goods when the opportunity was given, how completely free he was from all greed. 3. He approved and accepted pious offerings. 4. The sharply differing opinions of Augustine and Alypius concerning the inheritance of the presbyter Honoratus. 5. He arranged for basilicas and a hospice to be built.

1. He entrusted and committed the care of the Church’s household and all its property to clerics who were, in rotation, more capable of handling it (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 24). Each, apparently, discharged this office—called the superintendentship—for the period of a year; they were also permitted to borrow money (Serm. 356, no. 15). He himself never held a key, never a ring in his hand; rather, everything received and expended was recorded by those same household superintendents. When the year was complete, the accounts were read to him, so that it might be known how much had been received, how much disbursed, and what remained to be disbursed; and in many matters he relied more on the superintendent’s good faith than on knowledge confirmed and demonstrated.

He never wished to buy a house, a field, or an estate. Nor was he absorbed or entangled by love of, or involvement in, those possessions that the Church held and owned. Rather, suspended from and attached to greater and spiritual matters, he scarcely ever relaxed or withdrew himself from contemplation of eternal things in order to attend to these temporal concerns. Once he had arranged and ordered them, he would turn his mind back from these biting and troublesome matters toward the interior and higher regions of the mind, either to reflect on divine matters yet to be discovered, to dictate something concerning those already discovered, or at least to correct something already dictated and transcribed. He did this by laboring during the day and keeping vigil at night. He was like that most religious Mary, bearing the figure of the heavenly Church, of whom it is written that she sat at the Lord’s feet and listened attentively to his word (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 24).

Below we shall see that he entirely rejected the administration of his Church’s properties and wished wholly to relinquish it (ibid., ch. 23). That very contempt for wealth, by which from the time of his conversion onward he distributed his possessions to the poor, had won him the goodwill of the entire people of Hippo (Epist. 126, no. 7); nor was this virtue diminished in him after he had been made bishop. For although he seemed to possess Church property much greater than the private fortune he had abandoned, he was nevertheless only its distributor and steward. Thus, when he was once falsely suspected of avarice, he called God himself as witness to his mind:

> God is my witness, he says, that I endure all this administration of ecclesiastical property—of which we are believed to love the ownership—for the sake of the service I owe to the love of the brethren and to the fear of God; I do not love it. Indeed, if I could do so without failing in my duty, I would wish to be without it (ibid., no. 9).

What he writes on this subject to refute the calumnies of the Donatists may still be seen, on the occasion of the laws that assigned their ecclesiastical possessions to the bishops of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0226]

2. Yet from his actions it shone forth more clearly than from his words how free he was from the desire for money. When someone had bequeathed something to the Church by will, he preferred that it be offered to him voluntarily rather than demanded by him. “We know,” says Possidius, “that he refused certain inheritances—not because they could have been useless to the poor, but because he saw that it was just and right that they should rather be possessed by the children, parents, or relatives of the deceased, to whom the deceased had been unwilling to leave them when they were dying” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 24).

He also related the deed of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, which had provided everyone with an example of virtue:

> How praiseworthy, he said, was the deed of the holy and venerable bishop Aurelius of Carthage! How it filled with praises of God the mouths of all who know it! A certain man, having no children and no hope of having any, donated all his property to the Church while retaining the usufruct for himself. Children were born to him, and the Bishop returned to him, though he did not expect it, what he had donated. The Bishop had the legal power not to return it—but only the power of the earthly court, not of heaven (Serm. 355, no. 5).

He also considered this rule worth retaining: that he should not accept the inheritance of a father who, in anger, had disinherited his son, but should return it to the son. Accordingly, when he was to explain the reasoning behind his decision to his people, he addressed them as follows:

> If the father were alive, would I not appease him? Would I not have to reconcile him with his son? How, then, can I wish him to be at peace with his son while I seek his inheritance? Certainly, when I gave the son what his angry father took away at his death, I did well. Let those who wish praise it; let those who do not wish to praise it refrain.

At times he was also afraid to accept inheritances, lest they entangle the Church in anxieties and losses. For this reason he did not wish either to be praised or blamed in this matter:

> I did not wish to accept Boniface’s inheritance—not from compassion, but from fear. I did not wish the Church of Christ to become a shipping company. There are indeed many who acquire wealth even from ships. Yet it would be a temptation: the ship might set out and be wrecked. Would we have to hand men over to torture, so that the judge might investigate the shipwreck according to custom and torture those who had been saved from the waves? We would not hand them over; for the Church could in no way rightly do this. Would it then pay the fiscal charge? But from where would it pay it? We are not permitted to keep an *entheca*.

Here the passage is understood from what is found in Roman law: namely, that those who were required to transport public grain to Rome or Constantinople were called *navicularii*, and that their heirs succeeded to the same obligation. If a shipwreck occurred, they were compelled to compensate the fisc unless they proved that the loss had resulted solely from the violence of the storm and not from their own fault. To establish this, at least two or three sailors had to be subjected to examination, especially the shipmaster whose vessel had been wrecked.

The word *entheca* in this passage means nothing other than a repository for treasure, since Augustine immediately adds: “For it is not the bishop’s task to keep gold and turn away the hand of a beggar” [Col. 0227] (ibid., nos. 4, 5). Augustine did nevertheless have a treasury for receiving the offerings of the faithful, but it was quickly exhausted for the use of the poor (ibid., no. 13).

3. Some disapproved of his reluctance to accept inheritances. There were those who murmured and complained that, for this reason, nothing was being donated to the Church of Hippo. Augustine was not moved by this murmuring, which was so alien to reason; yet his wisdom compelled him in certain matters to do what he would by no means have done in others. For although he rejected offerings that were disgraceful or burdensome and troublesome to the Church, he nevertheless professed that he accepted holy offerings, and in fact accepted many of this kind (ibid., no. 4).

Therefore, if anyone donated or bequeathed to the Church a house, field, or estate, he did not reject it but ordered that it be accepted (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 29). He also frequently reminded the faithful to count Christ among their children and call him to share in their inheritance; when they had done so, he willingly accepted this portion (Serm. 355, no. 4). Likewise, he urged them carefully to inquire whether the servants of God and ministers of the Church lacked anything, and to anticipate their prayers as soon as possible by their generosity (Enarr. on Ps. 103, sermon 3, nos. 10, 12). He said this all the more willingly because everyone knew that in this matter he took no care to have such benevolence and concern directed toward himself (Enarr. on Ps. 147, no. 17; and Enarr. on Ps. 103, sermon 3, no. 12).

Possidius also records that Augustine sometimes spoke in church about the treasury and sacristy neglected by the faithful, from which the necessities of the altar are supplied. He had once reported to us that the most blessed Ambrose had treated the same subject in church in his presence (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 24).

He judged it more secure and safer for the Church to accept legacies by will alone than entire inheritances; nevertheless, he sometimes accepted inheritances, as in the case of Julian’s inheritance, because Julian had died without leaving any children (Serm. 355, no. 4).

“Moreover,” says Possidius, “a certain distinguished man of Hippo, living at Carthage, wished to donate a property to the Church of Hippo. He voluntarily sent the completed deed to the blessed Augustine, while retaining the usufruct for himself. Augustine gladly accepted his offering, rejoicing with him that he had remembered his eternal salvation. But after some years, when we happened to be present with him face to face, behold, that donor sent a letter through his son asking that the deed of donation be returned to his son; he directed that one hundred solidi be distributed to the poor. When the holy man learned of this, he groaned, thinking that the man had either pretended to make the donation or had repented of his good work. With as much grief as God inspired in his heart, he spoke against and corrected the man’s reversal: he immediately returned the deed that the man had voluntarily sent, though it had neither been requested nor demanded; he rejected the money and, in his written reply, rebuked and reproved him as was fitting. He admonished him to make satisfaction to God with the humility of repentance for his pretense or wrongdoing, lest he depart from this world with so serious a crime” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 24).

[Col. 0228]

4. A certain Honoratus, who had not disposed of his property, embraced the monastic life in the monastery at Thagaste and was later ordained a priest in the Church of Thavi. After his death, the people of Thavi claimed his property, either on the sole ground that he had been ordained a priest among them or under some title of donation.

Alypius, on the other hand, tried to assert that this property belonged to his own monastery, since Honoratus had been trained there in the monastic life; and because a monk ought to possess nothing of his own, he argued that whatever Honoratus had possessed belonged to his monastery. If it were decided that monks could possess anything, he argued that they should be given a period in which to postpone, as long as possible, the sale of their property.

For this reason Augustine went with Alypius to Thavi. But since the pressure of time did not allow them to deliberate long over the matter, he opposed the legal claim that the people of Thavi were asserting. He seemed to approve Alypius’s judgment: Alypius wished one half of Honoratus’s property to be assigned to the people of Thavi and the other half to the poor—that is, to the monks of his monastery at Thagaste—provided that Augustine would supply the people of Thavi elsewhere with the half of which they would be deprived by this division.

The people of Thavi did not approve this partition. Indeed, they seem to have accused Alypius of paying less attention to equity in the matter than to his own interests and advantages. The controversy was nevertheless left at that point.

After Augustine’s return, however, when he had long weighed the matter carefully on its merits, he saw that the proposed division of the disputed property was not free from the suspicion of avarice. It plainly suggested men concerned with pecuniary advantage rather than with justice. He saw that they were falling into the appearance of evil from which the Apostle commands us to abstain (1 Thess. 5:22); that they were casting a stain upon bishops who were highly renowned among the people; and that they were bringing death upon the minds of the weak, whose salvation depended greatly upon their being convinced that bishops were not led by sordid greed for money in such matters.

This was all the more necessary to avoid at that time because these communities had recently joined the Catholic peace, after many labors had been undertaken for that purpose. Augustine had especially shared in those labors, and he declares that he could in no way abandon them. Possidius himself records two letters of Augustine to the people of Thavi against the Donatists (*Index*, ch. 3).

As for the difficulty that Alypius saw in assigning this property to the Church of Thavi—namely, that the monks would be obliged to renounce their possessions—Augustine sufficiently recognized that the same difficulty existed in the proposed division. He therefore judged that there would be less danger if nothing at all were granted to the people of Thavi.

He thought Alypius’s reasoning invalid on another point and held that, in these civil possessions, one ought to follow the authority of the civil laws. According to those laws, monks at that time retained their property until they had sold it or made a donation of it; so much so that if monks died before making a donation, their private heirs, not the monastery, succeeded to the property under the provisions of the law. Several examples of this had already occurred.

[Col. 0229]

Augustine therefore strongly approved requiring monks, before they were received, to sell or donate their possessions. But if they died without having sold their property or transferred it to anyone by donation, he held that their goods ought to follow the provisions of civil law. In this way bishops would remain entirely free and pure even from the appearance of avarice and would preserve intact the reputation for integrity so necessary to their administration.

According to this rule, Honoratus’s property belonged to the people of Thavi. But even if the rule were false, since its falsity could not be demonstrated to the people of Thavi, Augustine judged it better both to accommodate their weakness and, in order to avoid giving offense, to yield possession of the property to them.

He was moved by the example of the Lord Christ, who paid a tax from which he had declared himself free, for this very reason; and also by the example recorded in the Acts of the Apostle, who, in order to protect his reputation, spared the weak even where he had a right belonging to the Church, and at times did not demand the support due to him.

Although Augustine was convinced by these arguments, lest he should err by being too inclined toward his own opinion, he nevertheless explained the matter to Samsucius, bishop of Thurris. He reported to him only what he had originally decided with Alypius. Samsucius was not highly trained in polished letters, but he was instructed in true faith; at this he was horrified and expressed amazement that so disgraceful a matter, unworthy of anyone’s life and character, had entered the minds of Augustine and Alypius.

Accordingly, Augustine wrote to the people of Thavi, so that he might yield Honoratus’s inheritance to them entirely, and sent the letter to Alypius, asking him to forward it to them as soon as possible. At the same time, he explained to Alypius at length the reasons that had led him to change his judgment.

He also wished this rule to be maintained: that whatever belonged by civil law to a cleric should belong to that cleric’s Church. Yet he does not state either that this occurred by virtue of a previously established donation or that Honoratus had made any disposition concerning his property.

The canons of Antioch (Council of Antioch, canon 24; Labbe, vol. 2, pp. 571, 580, etc.) and those of Hippo (Code of the African Canons, canon 32) nevertheless permit clerics to leave their property to whomever they wish; they assign to their Churches only what they acquired in their own names during the period of their clerical office. It appears, moreover, that this freedom was later restricted by certain limitations. We read that the third Council of Carthage, held on the Ides of September in the year 401, even struck with anathema those bishops who had preferred to the Church strangers, or even their own relatives who were pagans or heretics (ibid., canon 81). Perhaps this decree was expanded in later councils and strengthened by the authority of some imperial edict.

As for Alypius’s expectation that Augustine would pay to the monastery at Thagaste the half that he wished to grant to the people of Thavi, Augustine testifies that, provided Alypius clearly perceived this to be just, he did not refuse; but he said he would repay it when he had the means—in other words, when so large an alms had come to him that, after that sum had been deducted, no less than an equal portion according to the number of brothers would reach the monastery at Hippo.

When this entire controversy took place (Epist. 83), we do not know. It is clear only that Samsucius held his episcopal see at the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate and that nothing further is known about him after the year 407.

5. Although Augustine himself, keeping his mind entirely free from avarice and especially from the burdensome turmoil of business, never wished to buy a house, field, or estate (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 24), he nevertheless testifies that he had advised one of his clerics to acquire some property for the benefit of the Church. His intention was that, if the man should perhaps not persevere in his rank, the property would be returned to him, so that every occasion for complaint would be removed both from him and from his relatives (Serm. 356, no. 7).

“Possidius says that he never had a passion for new buildings, avoiding the entanglement of his mind in them, since he always wished to keep it free from every temporal burden. Yet he did not prevent those who wished to build from doing so, except when their building was excessive” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 34).

He ordered the priest Leporius to build a hospice with Church funds that had been collected for this purpose. At the same holy bishop’s command, Leporius also built a basilica to the Eight Martyrs with the money that remained (Serm. 356, no. 10). Heraclius, who was at most a deacon, apparently erected a shrine to the holy martyr Stephen at his own expense (ibid., no. 7).

It is likely that the shrine of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius was built during Augustine’s time. There he preached a sermon on the anniversary of their discovery at Milan (Serm. 286, no. 4), though not on their feast day, as the old books had indicated. There was also another shrine of the same martyrs at the estate of Victoriana in the diocese of Hippo; but it was ten or twelve leagues from the city (*City of God*, book 22, ch. 8, no. 7).

## CHAPTER IV

1. He devotes himself to relieving the poor.  
2. He writes to the people of Hippo on behalf of Fascius, burdened by debt.  
3. He conducts himself modestly when providing recommendations and interceding for others before the authorities.  
4. He writes to Romulus on behalf of the peasants.

1. No testimonies are needed to show for what purposes Augustine spent the revenues of his Church. Nevertheless, we shall observe that he writes that he had distributed what he received from Pinianus’s alms as he had deemed appropriate: he had given part to the monastic clerics and to a very few needy persons outside the monastery; the remainder was still in his possession, to be distributed in the same way (Epist. 126, no. 8). These alone did he make participants in the Church’s offerings.

We stated above that he kept no money set aside for himself. “For it is not the bishop’s task,” he says, “to keep gold and turn away the hand of a beggar. Every day so many ask, so many groan, so many needy people appeal to us, that we leave more people sorrowful because we do not have what we could give to everyone” (Serm. 355, no. 5).

He was always mindful of the poor and distributed to them from the same sources from which he and all who lived with him were supplied: that is, either from the revenues of the Church’s properties or from the offerings of the faithful. [Col. 0231] When the Church’s money ran out, he announced this very fact to the Christian people, saying that he had nothing to distribute to those in need (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 24). He seems to have done the same in the sermon he delivered on the anniversary of his episcopal ordination (Serm. 339, no. 3).

Elsewhere he congratulates his people because they took care that he himself lacked nothing and showed fraternal mercy toward their brothers (Epist. 268, no. 1). Nevertheless, those who administered the Church’s revenues were sometimes compelled to borrow money and incur debt (Serm. 356, no. 15).

It would be superfluous to append a list of the passages in which he exhorts the people to distribute alms to the poor. He established among his people an annual custom of clothing the needy (Epist. 122, no. 2). He speaks of this custom in a sermon, and the people received his exhortation with a public expression of joy (Serm. 2, no. 8). In his absence, however, this custom was interrupted once. Later, in letters that he wrote to his clergy and to the people of Hippo, he reproved this forgetfulness.

And because those were calamitous times, when, apparently, an invasion of Africa by Alaric was feared, he urged the faithful all the more strongly to bind themselves to relieve the poverty of the poor (Epist. 122).

2. A certain Catholic Christian, named Fascius, was being pressed by his creditors over a debt of seventeen solidi, and, unable to pay, fled to the Church for help so that he would not be dragged into prison.

In the year 397, the emperor Theodosius had decreed that debtors of the fisc who had taken refuge in a church were to be removed from it, or that the bishops who concealed them were to discharge the debts by which they were bound. Arcadius had extended this law to private debts in the year 398.

Therefore, whether relying on the authority of those laws or on the equity of Fascius’s case, his creditors—who were required to depart and therefore could not grant him a postponement—began to complain vehemently to Augustine about the matter, demanding either that he hand Fascius over to them or provide the means by which Fascius’s debt could be paid.

Augustine offered Fascius the opportunity to speak publicly about his situation, but Fascius, deterred by shame, begged the holy bishop not to do so. Since no other means of assisting him was available, Augustine borrowed seventeen solidi from Macedonius and gave them to Fascius’s creditors. Fascius in turn promised that he would repay Augustine this sum by a fixed date; if he failed to do so, he agreed that Augustine should address the people about the matter.

Fascius did not come on the appointed day. Augustine had not been informed of this, so that he might speak about it on Pentecost, when a larger crowd was present; and he soon afterward set out on a journey. Therefore, from the place where he then was, he wrote to the people of Hippo, asking them to contribute this sum as alms—not so much to release Fascius as to release the pledge by which Augustine himself had bound himself to Macedonius.

At the same time he wrote to his clergy that, if the money collected from the people was insufficient, the remainder should be supplied from the Church’s property. Yet he preferred that the sum be drawn from the pious generosity of his people, so that it might be, as it were, a fruit produced by the heavenly rains with which God continually watered it through Augustine’s ministry (Epist. 268).

Possidius notes that his compassion toward the miserable advanced so far that, in order to aid numerous captives and poor people, he ordered consecrated Church vessels to be broken up and melted down. In this, even if he offended the worldly sensibilities of some, he was certainly following the teaching and example of Ambrose with willing spirit (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 24).

3. Those whom God had entrusted to his care and love he also assisted by his recommendations and letters before the powers of this world. Yet he regarded this occupation, which drew him away from better things, as a kind of forced labor. He always found sweetness in speaking or conversing about the things of God with the familiarity of a brother and member of the household (ibid., ch. 19).

He considered it part of his priestly office to intercede for accused persons before judges. When someone’s life was in danger at trial, people would gather in the church and ask the bishop, even if he was occupied with the most serious matters, to plead for the accused. Augustine did this with modesty and restraint.

“We know,” says Possidius, “that when his dearest friends asked him for letters of intercession before the powers of this world, he did not grant them. He said that one ought to preserve the saying of a certain wise man, of whom it was written that, out of great regard for his reputation, he had not rendered services to his friends. He added this of his own: ‘For the power that often grants a request also oppresses.’”

When he saw that intercession ought nevertheless to be made, he acted so honorably and temperately that he appeared not merely free from burdening or troubling anyone, but even admirable (ibid., ch. 20).

Possidius then reports the testimony that Macedonius, the African vicar, gave him on this subject. Yet Augustine’s modest humility and innate gentleness did not prevent him from sometimes interceding in a more forceful and almost threatening manner. For “truth is both sweet and bitter: when it is sweet, it spares; when it is bitter, it heals” (Epist. 247, no. 1).

4. A certain Romulus, whom Augustine had begotten in Christ through the Gospel, had placed his agent Ponticanus in charge of his estate and of the tenant farmers subject to that estate. After Ponticanus had collected from them the taxes owed to Romulus—which Romulus could not deny—he diverted the money to himself.

Romulus, who possessed some fear of God from another source, insisted that these peasants, who had scarcely been able to pay even once, should be required to pay the taxes again. This unjust procedure deeply disturbed Augustine, though less on account of the needy tenants who were being oppressed than on account of Romulus himself, who by this tyranny was provoking divine vengeance against himself.

“For I am not so wretched,” he says, “nor so estranged from the compassion of Christ, that my heart is not struck by a grievous wound when those whom I have begotten through his Gospel act in this way.”

Augustine therefore confronted Romulus, who maintained that the tenants ought not to have paid Ponticanus. Yet Augustine had not instructed them to do the opposite in writing; and without such a written instruction, it was impossible for the peasants, who saw Ponticanus placed over them by Romulus, to refuse to pay money owed to their master.

When Augustine accomplished nothing with Romulus on this occasion, he sent to him on Saturday, while Romulus was still dining, asking him not to leave Hippo-Regius before visiting Augustine. Romulus announced that he would do so. Nevertheless, the next day he came into the church, prayed, and departed without greeting the holy bishop.

This was to treat Augustine with the greatest contempt. Yet the most devout bishop, in order to avenge himself in a holy manner, begged God in his prayers to forgive Romulus. But since Romulus could not obtain forgiveness without correcting himself, the holy bishop was compelled to write him a very stern letter. In it he entreated and implored him to consider the injury by which he was harming himself more than his tenant farmers, toward whom—as he could not deny—he was acting most unjustly.

> At present, he says, you must not be asked but rebuked; for it is also written: “I reprove and discipline those whom I love” (Rev. 3:19). If you were to be asked on my behalf, I might perhaps not ask you. But because you must be asked on your own behalf, I ask you, though angry: spare yourself, make peace with yourself, so that the one whom you entreat may be at peace with you. May he open your understanding, so that you may see what you are doing, recoil from it, and correct it. For the things that are such great evils seem to you small and almost nothing; but when your subdued desire permits you to consider them, you will water the earth with tears so that God may have mercy on you.

Augustine was afraid that Romulus, further exasperated by this letter, might rage more fiercely against his tenants. He therefore added that, if this should happen, it would be counted to their credit as a good work that they endured his anger for the sake of his salvation, which was the reason Augustine was writing to him.

He threatened Romulus with the judgment of God alone, since before human beings—who are bound to follow the forms established by law in order to prevent other unjust acts—Romulus could prevail in his case. Hence it follows that, although we must not deny others what we are bound by the provisions of human law to return to them, we are not always permitted to demand from others what those same laws say they owe us (Epist. 247, no. 1).

## CHAPTER V

1. Augustine’s rule and prudence in visits and in the performance of other duties.  
2. He writes to Pancarius on behalf of the parish of Germaniciana.  
3. He labors, according to his share and ability, for the universal Church.  
4. He complains that he is occupied with settling disputes.

1. To continue explaining the care and conduct of the holy bishop in administering the Church: “In his visits,” says Possidius, “he observed the rule established by the Apostle, visiting only orphans and widows who were in distress. If the sick happened to ask him for this reason to pray to the Lord for them in person and lay hands on them, he went without delay. He visited women’s monasteries only when urgent necessity required it.

“He also reported that the following practice, which he had learned from the conduct and character of Ambrose of blessed memory, ought to be observed in the life and behavior of a man of God: he should never seek a wife for anyone, never recommend anyone who wished to enter military service, and never go to a banquet in his native city when invited.

“He gave the reasons for each matter. He should not seek a wife for anyone, lest, when the married couple happened to quarrel with each other, they should curse the person through whom they had been joined; but the priest should clearly attend only when both parties had already agreed to the union, so that he might either confirm their agreements and decisions or bless them. He should not recommend anyone for military service, lest, if the man behaved badly, the fault should be attributed to his sponsor. And he should not attend banquets in his native city too frequently, lest he lose the proper measure of temperance” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 27).

Below we shall see the most vigilant bishop performing for his entire diocese the duties that he performed at Hippo-Regius.

2. In his diocese there was a parish called Germaniciana, whose priest Secundinus had always pleased the people. When, however, a certain Pancarius arrived there, he wrote to Augustine (Epist. 251) that the inhabitants were preparing to accuse Secundinus of crimes.

Pancarius apparently had a dispute with someone else over possession of this village, and the inhabitants suffered greatly on that account. Since he did not find Secundinus supporting his wishes in the matter, he had summoned Donatists to that village—where previously there had been none—to bring charges against the priest.

Augustine replied to Pancarius that he was surprised that the people of Germaniciana were complaining about Secundinus. Nevertheless, if those making the accusations were Catholics, he could not disregard what was being alleged; but he neither could nor should admit the accusations of heretics. Pancarius should therefore first ensure that there were no heretics where none had existed before his arrival; then Augustine would hear the priest’s case as it ought to be heard.

At the same time, he urged Pancarius not to allow Secundinus’s house to be plundered and destroyed or Secundinus to be removed from his church. He also advised him to settle the case as quickly as possible, lest the local inhabitants be afflicted longer on that account.

3. He considered the care of the Church of Hippo alone—of which he said that he had been divinely appointed servant—to belong especially to him (Epist. 124, no. 2). Therefore he was never absent from it except unwillingly (Epist. 34, no. 5). In turn, the people always felt his absence keenly (Epist. 122, no. 1); and since they were weak in almost every respect, they sometimes suffered from it to the point of the most dangerous offense and scandal. For this reason he was more constantly present in the city (Epist. 124, no. 2).
