Even when physically absent, he was always present with them in spirit and in the affection of his heart. As he says, he never left the city through arbitrary freedom, but through necessary service, in order to perform the duties owed to other members of the Church (Epist. 122, no. 1). For this reason he traveled almost every year to Carthage, frequently to other places, and sometimes even to Mauretania (Epist. 193, no. 1).

He would also gladly have exposed himself to the labors and dangers of sea travel to visit overseas regions on behalf of the Church and even the imperial court, as his colleagues regularly did, had not his weak health prevented him (Epist. 122, no. 1).

In other churches he did only as much as the diocesan bishops either permitted or imposed upon him (Epist. 34, no. 5). Whenever he could, he did not fail to attend councils held throughout the various provinces. He was inflamed by a desire to serve not his own interests but the honor of Christ, and to do his part so that the faith of the holy Catholic Church might remain inviolate and its discipline unimpaired (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 21).

When synods were held by bishops appointed for that purpose, or when ecclesiastical judges were selected to settle certain disputes, he was almost always chosen in the name of the bishops of Numidia. He likewise attended the ordinations of bishops and sometimes the dedications of basilicas, as may be seen in his letter to Bishop Nobilius (Epist. 269), who had invited him to the dedication of his building.

Augustine excuses himself from making such a long journey by citing the winter season and his own old age; nevertheless, he writes that he would gladly undertake it if he were not prevented by bodily weakness.

4. When the Apostle determined that the faithful ought not to be judged in the tribunals of secular magistrates, but by wise and holy men of the Church itself, who were established in those places, he imposed upon bishops the necessity of hearing cases belonging to others (*De Opere monachorum*, no. 37). Christian emperors, too, had confirmed this power of judging granted to bishops by more than one law. Thus Augustine, whether summoned by Christians or by people of any sect to hear cases, devoted himself diligently to them; and he conscientiously discharged this duty, which he regarded as part of his pastoral service.

At the same time, he kept before his eyes the saying of a certain man: “He would rather hear cases among strangers than among friends, because among strangers he might acquire as a friend the one in whose favor, according to the rule of law, judgment was pronounced; whereas among friends he might perhaps lose the one against whom judgment was delivered” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 19; Augustine, *Epistle* 33, no. 5).

In carrying out this duty he sometimes remained occupied until the hour of eating, and at other times fasted throughout the entire day. This was an exceedingly laborious and burdensome occupation for a man devoted to the contemplation of truth alone (*Exposition of Psalm* 118, sermon 24, no. 3). Hence he frequently complained about it and would have preferred to spend fixed hours each day at manual labor rather than become entangled in these labyrinths and vexations of business (*On the Work of Monks*, no. 37). Yet he could not deny this service to his brothers, especially to the weaker among them. Accordingly, he endured this labor not without consolation, hoping that one day he would receive from his patience the fruit of eternal life.

“Our prayers,” he says, “are often wounded and weakened by the darkness and tumult of secular affairs. Even when they are not our own affairs, those of people who compel us to go one mile and order us to go with them another two are imposed upon us in such number that we can scarcely breathe. Yet we believe that he in whose sight the groaning of the prisoners enters will, as we persevere in the ministry in which he has deigned to place us, free us from every distress, with the promised reward and with the help of your prayers” (*Epistle* 48, no. 1).

When he spoke to the people, he urged those against whom unjust lawsuits were brought to try to buy themselves free and secure their release with money; and he himself did the same, whenever he could, in the cases brought before him. “Someone,” he says in one sermon, “wants to distract you from your God by lawsuits. You will have no quiet heart, no tranquil mind; your thoughts will be overturned, and you will be provoked against your adversary himself. Behold, you have lost time. How much better, then, to lose a coin and buy back your time?

“My brothers, in your cases and affairs, when they come to us for judgment, if I say to a Christian that, in order to buy back time, he should lose something of his own, with how much greater care and [Col. 0236] confidence ought I to say that he should return what belongs to another? For I hear both parties as Christians.

“Now that slanderer who wants to bring a case against another and take something from him, even by way of settlement, rejoices at these words. The Apostle said: ‘Redeeming the time, because the days are evil’ (Ephesians 5:15). So I bring a charge against that Christian; whether he wishes it or not, he gives me something in order to buy back his time, because he has heard a bishop. Tell me: if I am going to say to him, ‘Lose something so that you may be at leisure,’ am I not going to say to you, ‘Slanderer, wastrel, son of the devil, why are you trying to take away another’s property? You have no case, and you are full of slander’?

“He then adds: ‘But perhaps you laugh at this because you are seizing money. Laugh, laugh, and despise it: I will spend it, and the one who exacts payment will come’” (*Sermon* 167, chap. 3, no. 4).

He undoubtedly urged litigants, in order to avoid provocation, to settle matters amicably, even when he had no doubt that one party’s case was unjust and the other’s right. In connection, probably, with such business, he eventually obtained from his people that for five days of each week no one should interrupt him. But when this arrangement had been observed only for a short time, it was violently broken in upon, and he was forced to be occupied with people’s business both before and after midday (*Epistle* 213, no. 5).

Finally, in the year 426, he transferred this burden to the presbyter Heraclius, whom he designated as his successor. By the extraordinary patience with which he endured the annoyance of these occupations, he strove to turn them not only toward his own salvation but also toward that of those who pleaded their cases before him. For when he heard the litigants, he simultaneously considered the inward state of their souls and the various dispositions of their hearts. From the manner in which each pursued his business and his rights, he observed how far each was progressing in faith and good works, or falling away from them.

Whenever a suitable opportunity presented itself, he taught the parties the truth of divine law. Impressing it upon them with all his heart and every effort, he exhorted them in his sermons to attain eternal life. In settling other people’s disputes, he sought precisely this gain: that they might fulfill what, according to the rule of Christian devotion, we owe to God and to human beings.

He did this as a watchman appointed by the Lord over the house of Israel, preaching the word and insisting upon it in season and out of season, reproving, exhorting, and rebuking with all patience and instruction; and he took particular care to teach those who were capable of teaching others (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 19). Thus, using every opportunity that arose, he never failed to labor at instructing others, whether privately or publicly.

## CHAPTER VI

1. The holy Bishop devotes himself diligently to preaching the divine word.  
2. Firmus the Manichaean is converted to the faith of Christ after hearing him preach.  
3. Some noteworthy features of his sermons.  
4. He preached in Latin at Hippo.  
5. He preferred the practice of hearing the word of God while seated to that of the African churches, namely, hearing it while standing.

### 1

Augustine’s episcopate brought the African churches the greatest benefit, chiefly, in the judgment of Paulinus, because they were permitted to receive heavenly words from his mouth (*Epistle* 32, no. 2). For although, while still a presbyter, he proclaimed the Gospel [Col. 0237] as far as his ability allowed, it came about that as a bishop he preached the word of eternal salvation much more insistently and fervently, with greater authority—not merely in one region, but wherever he was asked to go—as the Lord’s Church flourished and increased (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 19).

These are Possidius’s words. He likewise records the following about Augustine’s unceasing labor in preaching:

“He preached the word of God without interruption in the Church, even to his final illness, eagerly and courageously, with sound mind and sound judgment” (ibid., chap. 31).

Such esteem was shown him, even when he was young, that wherever he was present, if something had to be said to the people, that duty was always assigned to him; and he was rarely permitted to remain silent and listen to others (*Retractions*, prologue, no. 2).

Indeed, conducting himself modestly and content with the care of the single church of Hippo, in other cities he attended to ecclesiastical business only insofar as the bishops of those cities permitted—or rather imposed—it upon him (*Epistle* 34, no. 5). We have already seen that he was accustomed to spend almost whatever free time he had preparing what he was going to say to the people (*Epistle* 73, no. 5).

Sermon 351 appears to have been written out word for word and committed to memory. At times he preached extemporaneously. When we discuss his *Tractates on John*, we shall see that he preached for five consecutive days. On the same day he delivered two sermons on Psalm 88, one in the morning and the other in the afternoon.

Nor did he refrain from the ministry of the word even when his weakness almost prevented him from speaking; and by speaking he recovered his strength (*Sermon* 42, chaps. 1, 3). He was evidently so inflamed by his people’s eagerness for progress that he seemed insensible to fatigue and pain.

### 2

Sometimes he judged from accidental circumstances what God was commanding him to say to the people. For example, if the reader—who was often a boy—had chosen the psalm himself, or had made a mistake (*Sermon* 352, chap. 1, no. 1), he could scarcely bring himself to speak to the people on certain questions. Yet he did not omit to do so when, from an inward movement of his heart, he perceived that God willed it (*Sermon* 52, chap. 8, no. 20). At times God suggested to him something other than what he had been planning (*Sermon* 71, chap. 5, no. 8).

Possidius gives a remarkable example of this in the following words:

“I know likewise that not I alone but also other brothers and fellow servants who at that time lived with us in the Church of Hippo together with that holy man heard him say, as we sat together at table: ‘Did you notice my sermon in church today, and how its beginning and its end proceeded contrary to my custom? For I did not finish explaining the matter I had proposed, but left it hanging?’

“We replied: ‘We know that at the time we were greatly surprised, and we recognize it now.’

“But he said: ‘I believe that perhaps the Lord wished, through our forgetfulness and error, to instruct and heal someone in the congregation who was in error; for we and our sermons are in his hand. While I was examining the hidden aspects of the question proposed, I went off in another direction in the course of my sermon. Thus, without concluding or explaining the question, I ended the discussion, [Col. 0238] speaking more against the error of the Manichaeans—although I had resolved to say nothing about it—than about the matters I had proposed to assert.’

“After this, if I am not mistaken, on the following day, or two days later, a certain man named Firmus, a merchant, came. While holy Augustine was seated inside the monastery and we were present, he threw himself on his knees at Augustine’s feet, shedding tears and asking that the priest, together with the saints, pray to the Lord for his sins. He confessed that he had followed the sect of the Manichaeans and had lived in it for many years, and that for this reason he had foolishly spent a great deal of money on the Manichaeans, or on those whom they call the Elect. He further confessed that, through God’s mercy, he had recently been corrected by Augustine’s discourses in the Church and had become a Catholic.

“Both the venerable Augustine himself and we who were present carefully questioned him about what, above all, had satisfied him in that discourse. When he had reported it, and we all reviewed the sequence of the sermon, we admired and marveled at the profound plan of God for the salvation of souls, glorified his holy name, and blessed him—he who, whenever he wills, through whatever means he wills, and in whatever manner he wills, works the salvation of souls through those who know and those who do not know.

“From that time forward, this man adhered to the way of life of God’s servants, abandoned the occupation of a merchant, and, advancing among the members of the Church, in another region—being sought and compelled by God’s will—undertook even the office of the presbyterate, preserving and guarding the sanctity of his way of life. Perhaps he is still alive in human affairs, established across the sea” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 15).

### 3

In old age he preached with greater gravity but with less prolixity (*Sermon* 350, no. 3). At times, his strength broken by excessive fatigue, he was forced to interrupt a sermon, as happened on Easter Day itself because of the labor he had endured while fasting during the vigil of the feast (*Sermon* 320).

He more frequently brought his sermons to an end so as not to burden his listeners with too many instructions. At times he abstained from preaching in order to give the people time to recall attentively what he had said earlier (*Sermon* 352, chap. 1, no. 1).

Yet when the people received his sermons eagerly and profitably, their hunger provoked him rather than being satisfied by him. Thus he was compelled to yield to their pious and beneficial requests. The people displayed their eagerness and attention in listening to him: sometimes indicating that they understood the most difficult matters he was explaining; sometimes anticipating what he was about to say; and often interrupting him with the greatest applause.

This gave Augustine joy, because from it he recognized their zeal for and love of the truth; but it also struck terror into his modesty and humility. When the matters were of greater importance, he was not satisfied with their applause but continued speaking until he saw tears flowing from their eyes (*On Christian Doctrine*, book 4, no. 53).

“Almost always,” he says, “my sermon displeases me. For I am eager for something better, which I often enjoy inwardly before I begin to express it in sounding words. When I have rendered it less effectively than it is familiar to me, I am saddened that my tongue has not been sufficient for my heart.

“For I want the one who hears me to understand everything that I understand, and I feel that I do not speak in such a way as to accomplish this—especially [Col. 0239] because that understanding floods the mind like a swift flash of light, whereas speech is slow and extended, and altogether unlike it. While speech is unfolding, that understanding has already withdrawn into its own hidden places. Yet because it has impressed certain traces upon the memory in a wondrous way, those traces endure along with the small pauses of the syllables; and from those same traces we produce the sounding signs.

“Yet we, often burning intensely for the benefit of our listeners, want to speak as we understand at that moment, although we cannot do so through the very act of speaking. Because we do not succeed, we are distressed and, as though spending our labor in vain, waste away in weariness. From that weariness the same sermon becomes weaker and duller than the understanding from which it led us into weariness.

“But the eagerness of those who desire to hear me often shows me that my speech is not as lifeless as it seems to me; and I recognize from their enjoyment that they derive some benefit from it. I therefore make every effort with myself not to fail in discharging this ministry, in which I see that they gladly receive what is offered” (*On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, nos. 3, 4).

Among his sermons to the people, many were undoubtedly composed for the benefit of those who, although the requirements of their office and duty demanded that they preach in church, had no ability to devise what they should say. Two sermons of this kind were sent to a Carthaginian deacon in the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, and perhaps sermon 214 in the collection of his sermons was another. For he maintained that it was useful for many preachers of the truth to be produced in this way as well (*On Christian Doctrine*, book 4, chap. 29, no. 62).

In his diction he did not hesitate to violate the rules of grammar so that he might be understood more easily by the uneducated and inexperienced. Although in his discourses to the common people he was accustomed to use a somewhat simpler style, he did not so abandon care for his speech that his language became coarse. Rather, he considered it a significant part of the art of oratory to adapt oneself to the capacity of one’s listeners; and he preferred to be criticized by grammarians than not to be understood by the people (*Exposition of Psalm* 38, no. 20).

Above all, he approved the saying of the orator who taught that in speaking there should be a certain diligent negligence, provided that this removes ornament in such a way that it does not acquire coarseness.

“It is,” he says, “a mark of excellent minds to love the truth in words, not the words themselves. For what good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can? For we seek nothing except that what is closed may be opened” (*On Christian Doctrine*, book 4, chap. 10, no. 26).

Finally, as he himself observes, the simple diction that solves the most difficult questions, especially when it possesses a certain beauty that is not sought after but in a certain way natural, often arouses such acclamations that it can scarcely be recognized as simple (*ibid.*, no. 56). This happened very frequently when he was speaking to the people.

### 4

There can be no doubt that he delivered in Latin the sermons to the common people that have survived. In fact, since Hippo Regius was a celebrated city, a Roman city—or one enjoying the rights of a colony—and a maritime port to which very frequent arrivals came (*Epistle* 35, no. 3; *City of God*, book 22, chap. 8; *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 2, chap. 83, no. 184), it is credible that the people generally knew [Col. 0240] Latin.

In one sermon he renders a Punic proverb into Latin: “I shall speak to you in Latin,” he says, “because not all of you know Punic” (*Sermon* 167, chap. 3, no. 4).

He sought clerics who were skilled in the Latin language. What may seem surprising is that he complains of being without such men and, for that reason, of the progress of evangelical preaching being hindered. For this reason he did not wish to dismiss from him the deacon Lucillus, whom he appears to have educated.

This Lucillus was the brother of Novatus, apparently the bishop of Sitifis, who asked Augustine to return him so that he might benefit his diocese. But since the Church of Sitifis had no real need of ministers who knew Latin, Augustine asked Novatus, while attending to the needs of his own church, to allow him to retain Lucillus and not demand him back again.

Novatus consented in a most gracious manner. He acknowledged that it was harsh for a brother to deny a brother; that he was doing great violence to his own affection; but that he was nevertheless persuaded to grant the request by concern for his own episcopal office and by the salvation of the faithful. Novatus seems to have asked for his brother back as soon as he became bishop (*Epistle* 84, nos. 1, 2). This, therefore, must have occurred before the year 411, when Novatus took part in the Carthaginian conference.

### 5

The holy Doctor prescribed in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine* the rules to be observed in public instruction; but the rules to be followed in private instruction, especially with those being initiated, he recorded in the book entitled *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*.

In it we read that in the African Church the preacher alone sat while the listeners stood; whereas in certain overseas churches the people themselves listened while seated. Augustine approves the latter practice more, because the labor and difficulty of standing distract the mind from listening attentively to the word of God (*On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, no. 19).

There is a sermon of Caesarius, once attributed to Augustine, in which the preacher indicates that a few days earlier he had asked the weak and infirm to sit while the Acts of the Martyrs and longer readings from Scripture were being recited. Subsequently, however, almost all the women—even those whose health was not inconveniently poor—had adopted the custom not of sitting modestly in order to listen more attentively to what was read, but of reclining as though on their own beds and chattering (*attributed to Augustine, Appendix, Sermon* 300, no. 1).

In this sermon the preacher rebukes them on this matter and teaches them with what religious devotion and reverence they ought to receive the word of God.

When only a few people were being instructed privately, Augustine writes that it was intolerable arrogance not to offer them seats, especially when one noticed the weariness of the listeners, which could sometimes impel them to leave under some other pretext. Having experienced this himself while instructing a countryman in the mysteries, he learned how necessary it was to guard against it (*On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, no. 19).

He is said to have been accustomed to conclude his sermons with these words:

“Turning to the Lord God, the almighty Father, let us give him, with a pure heart and as far as our smallness permits, the greatest and most abundant thanks. Let us pray with all our heart for his singular gentleness, that he may deign to hear our prayers according to his good pleasure; that by his power he may drive the enemy [Col. 0241] from our actions and thoughts; that he may increase our faith, govern our mind, grant us spiritual thoughts, and lead us to his blessedness, through Jesus Christ his Son. Amen” (*Sermon* 67, no. 10; *Sermon* 106, no. 4; *Sermon* 183, no. 15; and after the *Exposition of Psalm* 150, etc.).

## CHAPTER VII

1. He attacks vices.  
2. His prudence and charity in correcting sinners.  
3. He avoids the company of shamefully living Christians more than that of pagans.  
4. He does not approve of excommunicating an entire household on account of one person’s sin.  
5. He admits a certain astrologer among the penitents.  
6. He instructs Lampadius, who is entangled in the question of the fate imposed by the stars.

### 1

They observe that the Africans were inclined toward luxury, drunkenness, and swearing. Therefore Augustine, according to Possidius, labored above all to eradicate completely from his people the ingrained habit of swearing (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 25).

Several sermons delivered by him against these vices have in fact survived. He had always postponed speaking about this matter, fearing that by admonishing his listeners he might make them worse. But at last he feared that he himself would fail to obey a command which, when he read it together with the Epistle of James, he believed had been imposed upon him by divine inspiration (*Sermon* 180, chap. 12, no. 14).

He also attacks drunkenness repeatedly. Once, when he was about to rebuke drunkards, he said: “If you do not listen to me, and yet I do not remain silent, I shall free my soul. But I do not want to be saved without you” (*Sermon* 17, chap. 2, no. 2).

With regard to luxury, he seeks above all to show that husbands are bound by the same fidelity toward their wives that they themselves demand from them (*Sermon* 9, chap. 9, nos. 11, 12; *Sermon* 392, chap. 5, no. 5). In this respect Roman laws differed greatly from the Gospel laws. Consequently, almost all men fell into this corruption of morals, which was nevertheless concealed and encouraged in silence.

Augustine preferred to speak the truth and expose himself to the hatred of all who refused to follow it rather than incur the guilt of concealing the truth, whose authority commanded him to speak. This is the principal argument of the sermon entitled *On the Ten Strings*, because in it he compares the ten commandments of God, which he explains, with the ten-stringed psaltery mentioned in Scripture.

### 2

He carefully observed the rules that the Apostle prescribed to Timothy for preaching the word of God; and, in order to inspire fear in others, he did not hesitate to rebuke publicly those who sinned publicly (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 19). Hence everyone praised him, although he himself privately rebuked himself first.

There were, however, vices so customary that, although they were public, he scarcely dared to attack and prohibit them except slowly and with a smile, lest he provoke sinners to anger and himself be regarded as an innovator (*Sermon* 17, chap. 3, no. 3; *Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*, no. 35).

Charity did not permit him to rebuke publicly hidden sins, especially when they carried grave consequences, such as homicide and adultery. Yet he did not neglect them. When those bound by such crimes were alone with him, he admonished them, set the day of divine judgment before their eyes, and persuaded them to repent by instilling fear in them. Finally, [Col. 0242] as far as he was able, he sought their cure without the severity of legal proceedings.

Consequently, it sometimes happened that people who knew about those crimes complained that he did not rebuke them, since they failed to notice that he was restrained either by the law of prudence or by the fact that he did not always know everything (*Sermon* 82, chaps. 7 and 8, nos. 10, 11).

### 3

At times he abstained from the company of Christians who lived disgracefully, both to cover them with shame and by this means to recall them to better conduct. He preferred to associate with pagans and impious people rather than with wicked Catholics; in this practice he followed the Apostle (*Exposition of Psalm* 100, no. 8).

He employed excommunication in crimes that required it, insofar as the peace of the Church allowed and insofar as he himself judged it useful for sinners. For example, the more common and widespread the vice of drunkenness was, the less he dared to strike drunkards with anathema and cast them out of the Church, even when they deserved it. Since they did not sufficiently recognize the gravity of their crime, he feared that those struck by the scourge might become worse because of it. Therefore he more often corrected them with words alone (*Sermon* 17, chap. 3, no. 3).

Addressing husbands who were not faithful to their wives, he said in one sermon: “Let those who know that I know their sins refrain from communion, lest they be cast out from the railings” (*Sermon* 392, chap. 5, no. 5).

Although this sentence may have been inserted into the sermon—which we have judged should be numbered among the doubtful works—when compared with what Augustine declares in sermon 351: “We cannot prohibit anyone from communion—although this prohibition is not yet mortal but medicinal—unless that person has either confessed voluntarily or has been named and convicted in some secular or ecclesiastical judgment” (*Sermon* 351, chap. 4, no. 10).

Although he was sometimes deeply moved by crimes committed monstrously against the Church, he never dared to strike the perpetrators with anathema together with their entire household, since he could find no way in which this could rightly be done, even if others perhaps adopted such a practice (*Epistle* 250, no. 2).

### 4

When certain men who had sworn falsely by the Gospel had taken refuge in a church, seeking refuge for their violated faith in the very house of faith, a faithful Christian magistrate named Classicianus came to the church with the retinue appropriate to his rank. He intended to deal with Auxilius, the diocesan bishop, so that Auxilius would not favor these perjurers against his lawful authority. His demand was certainly just.

Nevertheless, Auxilius—who, while still a catechumen, had been connected with Classicianus by friendship—gave such free rein to his anger that, after the written record of the proceedings had been drawn up, he struck Classicianus and his entire household with anathema. He had no doubt that Classicianus had violated the church’s sacred asylum and that the guilty men had consequently been forcibly taken away.

But when Classicianus complained of this injury to Augustine by letter, he stated that the offenders, burdened by the consciousness of their crime, had left the church voluntarily and without force.

Auxilius was still young and had not yet completed a year in the episcopal office; Augustine, however, had grown old after so many years as a bishop. Nevertheless, he wrote to Auxilius that if he could show [Col. 0243] in any way that the entire household could rightly be excommunicated on account of one person’s sin, Augustine was prepared to learn from him. But if he could not, the fault lay with the man who had undertaken an action for which he could not give an account.

He also asked Auxilius that, if Classicianus was free of guilt, he should correct his error, into which he had fallen through human frailty, and rescind the ecclesiastical proceedings brought against him.

“Do not suppose,” he says, “that unjust agitation cannot steal upon us because we are bishops. Rather, let us consider that we live most dangerously amid the snares of temptation, because we are human beings” (ibid., no. 3).

Auxilius, bishop of Nurco, was present at the Carthaginian conference. If this is the same man, the letter cannot have been written later than the year 412. Yet it would be difficult to suppose that it was written much earlier, since in 412 Augustine was only in the seventeenth year of his episcopate and the fifty-seventh year of his life. At that time he scarcely seems sufficiently advanced in age to speak to Auxilius as an old man to a young man, and as a bishop of many years to a colleague not yet a year in office.

To Classicianus himself, from whom he had received a letter about the matter, Augustine disclosed his counsel and his mind in a reply:

“I wish, with the Lord’s help, to bring before our council, and, if necessary, to write to the Apostolic See, the case of those who, on account of one person’s sin, bind his entire household—that is, a great many souls—with anathema, especially lest anyone there depart from the body without Baptism; and also the question whether those who flee to the Church in order to break faith with their guarantors should not be expelled from the Church. Thus, in these cases, what we ought to follow may be established and confirmed by the concordant authority of all.

“I can certainly say without rashness that if any of the faithful should be unjustly anathematized, it will harm the one who imposes this penalty rather than the one who suffers the injury. For the Holy Spirit dwelling in the saints, through whom each person is bound or loosed, imposes no undeserved punishment upon anyone. Through him charity is poured into our hearts, and charity does not act wrongly” (*From the Epistle to Classicianus*, following *Epistle* 250, vol. 2, p. 1334).

### 5

In his sermons Augustine attacks the empty superstitions of judicial astrology. He complains that many Christians were so devoted to them that some confidently said in his presence—as though there were nothing wrong in the matter—that they would not set out on certain days.

This vice was so widespread that scarcely anyone dared to condemn it. Hence he was forced to exclaim: “Woe to the sins of human beings, which we shudder at only when they are unfamiliar!” (*Enchiridion*, no. 21).

Nevertheless, when adherents of this empty and impious art—then called “mathematicians”—came forward for conversion, he assigned them to public penance and admitted them to it only after repeated petitions and delays. We have a notable example of this at the end of his sermon on Psalm 61.

“The thirst of that Church,” he says, indicating to the people one of these mathematicians among the penitents, “wants this man whom you see to drink as well. At the same time, so that you may know how many people bless with their mouths and [Col. 0244] curse in their hearts amid the company of Christians, this man returns as a Christian and faithful penitent. Terrified by the power of the Lord, he turns to the mercy of the Lord.

“When he was faithful, he was deceived by the enemy and was a mathematician for a long time: deceiving and being deceived, he enticed and misled people, speaking many lies against God, who gave human beings the power to do what is good and not to do what is evil.

“He used to say that adultery was not committed by one’s own will but by Venus; that homicide was not committed by one’s own will but by Mars; and that a just man was made not by God but by Jupiter—and many other sacrilegious things, no small matters.

“How many Christians do you think he robbed of their money? How many bought a lie from him? Now, as we must believe of him, he has shuddered at the lie, and he has perceived that although he once enticed many people, he himself was at some time enticed by the devil; he turns to God as a penitent.

“We think, brothers, that this happened through great fear of heart. For what shall we say? If a mathematician were converted from paganism, there would indeed be great joy; yet it might be thought that if he were converted, he would be seeking the clerical office in the Church. He is a penitent; he seeks nothing except mercy alone. He must therefore be commended to your eyes and your hearts.

“Love in your hearts the man whom you see; guard him with your eyes. Look at him, recognize him, and wherever he passes, point him out to the other brothers who are not present now. This attentiveness is mercy, lest that deceiver draw back his heart and attack him.

“Guard yourselves; do not let his conduct and his way escape your notice, so that by your testimony it may be confirmed to us that he has truly been converted to the Lord. For no report of his life will be silent, when he is presented to you in such a way that you must both see him and have pity on him.

“You know that it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that many who had been ruined—that is, people engaged in such arts and followers of wicked doctrines—brought all their books to the Apostles; and so many books were burned that it was worthwhile for the writer to estimate their value and record the total price (Acts 19:19).

“This was done, certainly, for the glory of God, so that those who had been ruined would not despair of the one who knows how to seek what was lost. This man, then, had been lost; now he has been sought, found, and brought back. He carries with him books to be burned, through which he himself had been burned, so that when they are cast into the fire, he may pass into refreshment.

“Know, brothers, that he had been knocking at the Church before Easter. Before Easter he began to seek medicine from the Church of Christ. But because the art in which he had been trained was one suspected of falsehood and deceit, he was delayed lest he should be put to the test; yet eventually he was admitted, lest he be tested more dangerously.

“Pray for him through Christ; pour out today’s prayer for him to the Lord our God. For we know and are certain that your prayer wipes away all his impieties. The Lord be with you” (*Exposition of Psalm* 61, no. 23).

### 6

A certain man named Lampadius placed some confidence in this art. When Augustine first understood this from conversation, and then learned it more certainly from a letter received from Lampadius himself, he sent him a brief reply (*Epistle* 246).

He wrote that the divine and human laws, and all the institutions of public and domestic discipline, were utterly weakened and overturned by the perverse opinions concerning fate and the power of the stars over human actions. Even the mathematicians themselves were not so [Col. 0245] insane, he added, as to regulate the management of their own household exactly according to the rule and standard of the science that they sold to others for a large sum of money.

He also asked Lampadius to inform him by letter what he thought of this epistle. If it did not satisfy his eagerness, Augustine promised him a complete book on the matter—provided that Lampadius would wait until Augustine could carry it out in his free time and would not object to reminding him repeatedly of his promise.

## CHAPTER VIII. AUGUSTINE’S ADMONITIONS AND EXHORTATIONS TO PRIVATE PERSONS

1. He enkindles Christinus to piety.  
2. He strengthens Sebastian against scandals.  
3. And Restitutus.  
4. He recalls Chrisimus from despair.  
5. He reproves the ill-considered course of action of Ecdicia, a devout woman.  
6. He presses the hardened heart of Cornelius.  
7. He does not refuse to instruct Florentina by letter.  
8. He warns Fabiola that the presence of the saints in bodily form is not greatly to be desired.  
9. He takes care of a female ward.

### CHAPTER VIII. AUGUSTINE’S ADMONITIONS AND EXHORTATIONS TO PRIVATE PERSONS

**1.** Of the many works written by Augustine for instructing or exhorting private persons, in this book we mention only those for which no more suitable place for discussion seems available. A certain man named Christinus, Christian by profession but only a catechumen—or at least entangled in the snares of the world—had written him a courteous letter and requested a letter in reply. Augustine thanked him for his polite courtesy and exhorted him to piety in this brief saying:

> When, on God’s path, easier and fruitful things are avoided through cowardly fear, while on the worldly path harder and barren things are endured through laborious toil.

(*Letter* 256.)

**2.** The monk and abbot Sebastian—or superior of a holy household—had for some time enjoyed an intimate association with Augustine and had left behind a very high reputation for his piety. Later he wrote to Augustine and, apparently, to Alypius also. Augustine received the letters gratefully; and when Sebastian declared in them that he was wearied by the sins and scandals of wicked people, the most holy Bishop warmly praised his zeal, while nevertheless exhorting him to perseverance and to seek his consolation in the goodness of good brothers and in God’s promises to the faithful.

Alypius, although he could have written him a separate letter, preferred to append a few courteous words to Augustine’s letter and subscribe it, so that their unanimity might be attested on a single page as well (*Letter* 248).

**3.** When Deogratias—perhaps that same man to whom Augustine writes elsewhere—reported to him the troubled state of mind of a certain Catholic deacon named Restitutus, who, like Sebastian, seems to have borne the faults of Catholics with excessive resentment, Augustine wrote back to Restitutus and advised him to read the Donatist Tychonius’s book *On the Church*. From its reading he would learn that the good and the wicked would live intermixed until the end of the age.

He nevertheless warned him that Tychonius had produced only a few scriptural testimonies on this subject, and that the arguments he advanced in defense of the schism to which he adhered had to be avoided (*Letter* 249).

**4.** A certain faithful man named Chrisimus, initiated through Baptism, had always listened attentively to the word of God and was regarded as intelligent. After suffering the loss of his property, he fell into such a disturbance of mind that he appeared ready to lay violent hands upon himself.

When the report reached Augustine, he was moved by the deepest compassion. In a letter filled not only with goodwill but also with esteem, he exhorted Chrisimus not to lose heart amid the adversities that God had sent for his salvation. The letter is brief, but completely full of piety and ingenious charity. At the same time he sent him the letter that he had written on Chrisimus’s behalf to the Count (*Letter* 244).

**5.** The letter to Ecdicia deals with a more serious matter. She was a Christian woman, married to a Christian man, by whom she had borne a son. Nevertheless, without awaiting her husband’s consent, she made a vow of continence. She did not realize that, although she did not practice this virtue, she would not be deprived of its reward if she yielded not to her own weakness but to that of her husband.

A fortunate outcome repaired this fault: her husband followed his wife’s example and bound himself by the same vow of continence. Thus, for many years, the couple remained together—the holier and chaster, and therefore the more truly and harmoniously united.

In this shared undertaking the woman appeared stronger, both in renouncing worldly ways and in distributing alms to the poor. Yet because she did not make a sufficient effort to accommodate herself to her husband’s judgment and wishes, she did not deal with his mind with the prudence that was required, nor did she moderate feminine zeal with knowledge and charity.

Although she was bound by a vow of continence, she ought nevertheless to have obeyed her husband in other matters. Yet, despite being perhaps ordered by her husband to wear the dress of married women, when she ought to have adopted a modest one—which would certainly have had her husband’s agreement—she put on a black garment like that of a widow or nun.

She compounded this fault with another. Her husband was slow to give alms, either because of a defect in his character or because of the necessary care he was obliged to devote to their still-young son. He ought indeed to have encouraged the boy toward what was better, but he could not compel him to adopt the monastic way of life. Ecdicia, on the contrary, desired to pour all their resources out among the needy.

Thus, while her husband was absent, when two traveling monks stopped at her house, she gave them everything—or nearly everything—that she possessed. When her husband learned of this, he became excessively angry with his wife and with those two impostors who, as he supposed, had approached his house under the false appearance of monks in order to exhaust it.

Augustine himself admits that there was reason to doubt whether men who had received so much from an unknown married woman were servants of God. But a much graver misfortune followed: the husband turned his anger upon himself, violated the vow of continence that he had made, and plunged himself into the deep whirlpool of adultery.

In this extremely calamitous situation Ecdicia consulted Augustine by letter, wishing to know what she ought to do. In his reply Augustine devoted most of the letter to pointing out the things she had done wrongly in the conduct of her former life. As for the future, he wrote that, since her husband had approved the vow of continence that she had made, she was bound to keep it until the end and, insofar as it depended on her, to redeem her husband’s fault.

> “Therefore,” he says, “put on humility of mind; and, so that God may preserve you in perseverance, do not despise your husband as he perishes. Pour forth pious and continual prayers for him; offer tears like the blood of a wounded heart; and write to him with an acknowledgment of fault, asking pardon because you sinned against him by doing with your property what you thought ought to be done without his advice and will—not so that you should repent of giving to the poor, but because you did not wish to have him share in and direct your good work. Promise that henceforth, with the Lord’s help, if he too repents of his disgrace and returns to the continence that he abandoned, you will serve him in everything as is fitting.”

Finally, Augustine ordered her to devote herself all the more earnestly to winning her husband’s heart because, without harmony between their minds, their son could not be brought up in the fear of God and in wisdom, as she desired. The boy was under his father’s authority and necessarily had to be granted to him when he demanded him by right (*Letter* 262).

What Augustine writes here—that married women may preserve a humble heart while wearing splendid attire, if they adorn themselves solely in order to obey their husbands—is consistent with what he writes to Possidius: adornments are not absolutely to be forbidden to married women, except cosmetics and things that bear the scent of magical superstition (*Letter* 245).

**6.** If Augustine attacks Ecdicia with vigorous language, he rebukes Cornelius in far more severe terms. Cornelius had once been entangled with Augustine himself in the most destructive error of the Manichaeans.

He was then a young man, although older than Augustine. After withdrawing from his love for a woman through the greatest strength of self-restraint, he immediately immersed himself more deeply in it. At the extreme danger of his life he received Baptism, when Augustine had already grown old as a bishop and Cornelius himself was likewise advancing in age.

Yet, after recovering from his illness, he did not withdraw from his shameful habit of sinning; instead he went about surrounded by an ever-growing herd of mistresses. Augustine, who always held him most dear, repeatedly and unsuccessfully warned him to correct his ways.

Cornelius had married Cypriana, a most chaste woman. Unlike her husband, she loved him even though he was entangled in obscene affairs and was consumed by the desire for his conversion. She departed this life and was received into the company of chaste and faithful souls.

After her death Cornelius wrote to Augustine, asking him to send a lengthy letter of consolation because he had been deeply shaken by the death of his excellent wife, just as he remembered that the holy Paulinus had done for Macarius.

Augustine replied that Cornelius’s wife had no need of human praises. Such praises were customarily bestowed upon the living, not the dead. Cornelius ought to earn an encomium for his wife by changing his life. Augustine promised to do so on the condition that his wife, even after death, would have desired it, just as she would have sought it while alive. To wipe away sorrow in any other way, he said, would be flattery rather than consolation.

At the same time he plainly exposed to Cornelius’s eyes the shameful condition in which he was living, and with great force of speech, both vehemently and affectionately, urged him to emerge from it (*Letter* 259).

**7.** Outside the boundaries of the diocese of Hippo there lived a girl named Florentina who, although still an adolescent, was devoted to an ardent pursuit of piety and true wisdom. Her excellent parents, rejoicing in their daughter’s piety, asked Augustine, who was staying in those parts, to offer his assistance in instructing her wherever necessary.

Augustine could not refuse. In fact, he undertook responsibility for her not only in prayers before God; when he wrote to her mother, he also gave her a great deal of instruction. But Florentina’s mother replied to Augustine that she first wanted her daughter to receive a letter from him; only then would she write more confidently and consult him about necessary matters.

Augustine therefore wrote to the girl to open the door of confidence to her, and at the same time urged her to bring forward herself whatever she thought she ought to ask him:

> “Either I know what you will have asked, and I shall not refuse you; or I do not know it in such a way that my ignorance causes no injury to faith or salvation—and I shall, if I can, make you yourself secure about this by giving an explanation. Or, if I both do not know and yet the matter ought to be known, either I shall obtain from the Lord that I not fail you—for often the duty of giving is the merit of receiving—or I shall answer you in such a way that you will know, concerning this very matter which we equally do not know, whom we ought to approach.

> “I have said this beforehand so that you may not confidently expect to hear from me whatever you ask, and, when this does not happen, judge that I acted boldly rather than prudently in giving you the opportunity to ask whatever you wish.

> “For I have done this not as a perfect teacher, but as one who must himself be perfected together with those who are to be taught, distinguished lady, deservedly worthy of honor in Christ and a daughter to be received.

> “Indeed, even in matters that I know to some extent, I desire more that you should be knowledgeable than that you should need our knowledge. For we ought not to wish others to be ignorant merely so that we may teach what we know. Much better, surely, are we all teachable by God.”

He then went on to demonstrate the danger he had discovered in instructing others. His particular consolation was that souls might advance in piety so far that they would reach the point where they no longer needed the ministry of a human teacher (*Letter* 266).

**8.** Another girl named Fabiola wrote back to Augustine and told him of the sorrow in her mind because she was still delayed in this earthly pilgrimage and could not always enjoy the company of the saints. This apparently referred to Augustine himself.

He considered it his duty to reply, commending the love by which she was carried toward heavenly things, while also teaching her that the presence of bodies must be placed after the presence of souls (*Letter* 267).

This Fabiola seems to be the same woman whom Jerome calls his holy daughter when, writing to Marcellinus, who was living in Africa, in the year 411 or 412, he says that Marcellinus could borrow from her the first two books on Ezekiel, which he had sent to her (Jerome, *Letter* 82).

**9.** At Hippo-Regius there was a certain girl who apparently had been deprived of her father; her mother also did not appear. She had been entrusted to the protection of the Church, so that it might defend her against the violence of wicked people, by a distinguished man whose name Augustine withholds.

He does not seem to have been the same person as Bishop Benenatus, who would not have been designated by the title “distinguished man” and who, if the matter had been within his authority, ought himself to have undertaken her care. Nevertheless, we do not deny that this Benenatus may have been related to the girl. He certainly wrote to Augustine proposing a match for her.

Augustine, diligently devoting himself to her protection because of the special care owed to orphans, replied that he was not displeased with the proposed arrangement. But the girl was still of too tender an age for her to be promised to anyone while she was growing up. Her mother, whose authority in giving away her daughter ought to take precedence over all others, might perhaps appear. A better arrangement might perhaps arise—one that, for the sake of God, he himself would be obliged to secure for her. Finally, it was uncertain whether she wished to marry. She was accustomed to say that she wanted to become a religious woman. Although, because of her age, such statements should not be relied upon, Augustine nevertheless ought to wait until she was able to choose a way of life of her own accord.

He added that Felix, who had married the girl’s maternal aunt and with whom Augustine had necessarily discussed the matter, had approved the proposed arrangement, but had rightly complained as a friend that he had received no letter about it (*Letter* 250, §4).

A certain pagan named Rusticus sought this girl in marriage for his son, who was likewise a pagan and did not promise that he would embrace the Christian faith. Augustine, however, strongly objected to handing her over to him, as he informed Rusticus by letter (*Letter* 255), apart from the considerations that he says he had indicated in his letter to Bishop Benenatus, which prevented him at that time from promising anything concerning the girl’s marriage.

We are scarcely persuaded that this was the same arrangement that Augustine, as we have said, explicitly declared in his letter to Benenatus to be acceptable to him. For even if Benenatus had proposed the girl to Augustine only on the condition that Rusticus’s son accept the Christian faith, Augustine would certainly not have been silent about so serious a circumstance.

Apparently concerning the same girl, Felix’s niece, Felix himself had written to Augustine and had sent him the letter of the distinguished man by whom she had been entrusted to the Church. Augustine replied that, since he did not dare entrust this orphan indiscriminately to anyone, he would await the arrival of the man whose letter had been sent to him. He would deliberate with him in person about what ought to be done and would do what the Lord inspired him to do (*Letter* 252).

We do not know whether Augustine is still writing about the same girl when he tells Benenatus that he has heard that Benenatus was considering settling the matter. Augustine declares that he cannot be brought to believe it. Nevertheless, if it is true, Benenatus knows how he ought to consult the Church and how he ought to make an arrangement only with a Catholic household that could benefit, rather than harm, the Church (*Letter* 253).

### CHAPTER IX

1. He strives to bring the people of Madaura to the Christian religion.  
2. He deals by letter with Longinianus, a pagan priest, in order to lead him to embrace it.  
3. He consoles and strengthens Maxima, who has been deeply disturbed by errors arising in her province.  
4. He enters into conflict with various heretics and writes to Seleuciana against a certain Novatian.  
5. In his presence the heresy of the Tertullianists is destroyed.  
6. The Abelonians, or Abelites, are likewise removed from the region of Hippo through his ministry and labor.

**1.** Augustine became illustrious and renowned chiefly through his own struggles with the enemies of the Church. He vigorously attacked the pagans in various works, and especially in his work *The City of God*.

When a certain Florentinus, who seems to have been one of the leading men of Madaura, had some business at Hippo, all the civic orders wrote to Augustine through him, asking that he graciously assist him in the matter. The letter bore this heading: “To Father Augustine, eternal salvation in the Lord”; its subscription read: “We wish you, lord, in God and in his Christ, to rejoice for many years always in your clergy.”

Augustine had long been grieved that idols were enclosed no more in the temples of the people of Madaura than in their hearts. He was therefore astonished by the title of the letter:

> “I was suddenly raised up by such great hope that I believed you had already been converted to the Lord himself and to eternal salvation itself, or that you desired to be converted through our ministry. But when I read the rest, my spirit cooled. Nevertheless, I asked the bearer of the letter whether you were already Christians or wished to become Christians. When his reply showed me that you had not changed at all, I was more deeply grieved that you had thought the name of Christ—whom you see to have already subjected the whole world—not merely something to be rejected by you, but also something to be mocked in us, when you imposed upon me the task of managing your affairs.”

Nevertheless, Augustine assisted Florentinus with every effort; but the matter was one that could easily be completed. He therefore believed that God had inspired the people of Madaura to write to him in order to offer him an opportunity to announce the truth to them.

He seized the opportunity. After showing that they had been mockers when they pretended, under the name of Christ, to offer him honor and respect while they still remained enemies of Christ, he defended the Christian religion with several arguments and exhorted them to embrace it. Yet he professed that he did this for them with trembling of heart:

> “For I know how much graver and more destructive a case you will have before God if I have told you these things in vain. My feeling toward you, expressed as far as I could on this page, will bear witness; it will bear witness for you at the judgment of him who will strengthen those who believe in him and confound those who do not believe.”

He called them his brothers and relatives, perhaps because he had learned his childhood letters at Madaura. In the same letter he recalled that the emperors themselves knelt with their diadems laid aside and prayed at the tomb of the fisherman Peter. In the same passage he also indicates, not obscurely, that he was writing after the laws against idols had been enacted in the year 399 (*Letter* 232).

**2.** Augustine once engaged in discussion with Longinianus, a pagan man and, apparently, a priest of idols. In this conversation, as in a mirror, he perceived that Longinianus acknowledged that God ought to be worshiped, thought well of Christ, and sincerely aspired to virtue. This was certainly an excellent disposition of mind for attaining virtue in reality.

Augustine therefore began to love him, just as Longinianus loved Augustine in return. Believing that friends could discuss nothing more fruitfully than the means by which we become good and blessed, Augustine willingly entered into an exchange of letters with Longinianus on this subject.

He accordingly asked him by letter to write back and explain how he believed God should be worshiped; what he thought about Christ the Lord; whether he believed that blessed life could be attained by any way other than the one Christ had shown us; and, if he believed this to be the only way, for what pious reason he delayed entering upon it (*Letter* 233).

Longinianus replied with a remarkable and truthful encomium. He points to Augustine as a truly excellent Roman, a good man—if ever there was one:

> “If, after the memory of mankind, you allow the pattern of a story composed from the fictions of Xenophon, I have still heard, read, or seen no one—or certainly, after one [perhaps Cyrus], no one else whom, with God as my witness, I can confidently and safely call good—except you, who always strive to acknowledge God, and who can very easily pursue him with purity of soul and with the burden of the body cast aside, and hold him with the undoubting faith of perfect conscience.”

In answer to Augustine’s questions, Longinianus says that one must approach the one true God, the incomprehensible Maker of all things, through integrity of life, fellowship with the gods—or, as Christians call them, angels—and the expiations of the ancient rites.

Concerning Christ and the gift of the Spirit, however, he says that he neither dares nor is able to express his opinion, since he has no knowledge of them. He therefore asks Augustine to write back and tell him what he thinks of these matters (*Letter* 234, §1).

From such a promising beginning Augustine derived extraordinary pleasure and prayed that the end might correspond to the beginning. To ensure that he himself did not fail, he wrote back to Longinianus that he did not disapprove of his judgment that nothing concerning Christ should rashly be denied or affirmed. He asked only that Longinianus reply whether the expiations of the ancient rites of which he had spoken necessarily belonged to a complete life, or whether they were its cause, its effect, or something like a part of it. This question, he said, had to be resolved before proceeding to other matters (*Letter* 235).

What the further course and outcome of this conversation were is unknown to us. We would gladly assign it to the period when Augustine was still a layman, unless Longinianus frequently called him “father,” a title that seems appropriate only to a bishop or to a man already advanced in age.

**3.** No one can grasp in thought—much less express in speech—the labors that the holy Doctor undertook throughout the rest of his life in defense of the Catholic faith against heretics.

A certain servant of God named Maxima perhaps wrote to him from Spain that the province in which she lived was gravely endangered by destructive errors spreading widely throughout it. She also set forth her faith concerning the mystery of the Incarnation, submitting it to his judgment, and seems to have requested from him the works he had written against heretics.

Augustine replied that, whenever she wished, she could send someone to copy his smaller works—for she appears to have been wealthy. He approved her faith concerning the incarnate Son of God and asked her, if she could, to send him some books of these heretics, so that he might learn their teaching more thoroughly and refute it more effectively.

He displays the bitterest grief at the growth of heresies. Nevertheless, he consoles himself with the thought that God would not permit these things unless he intended to draw from them a greater good for his elect:

> “He permits them to exist only to the extent that he knows it to be useful and sufficient for admonishing and exercising his holy household. Therefore he consoles our sadness concerning them, because the very sadness that we feel on their account relieves us, while it weighs upon them if they persist in their perversity. But the joy that we experience when some of them are corrected and changed for the better and joined to the company of the saints cannot be compared with any joy in this life.

> “For this reason I greatly approve and praise both your sorrow concerning such people and the vigilance and caution against them that you have expressed in your letter. And so that you may continue steadfastly on this path, I exhort and admonish you, as far as my strength permits and as you require: show them mercy as one who is simple like a dove; but beware of them as one who is shrewd like a serpent. Do everything you can so that those who adhere to you may remain with you in the true faith, or, if some have been corrupted in some respect, may be corrected and brought back to the right faith” (*Letter* 264).

**4.** Augustine wrote two books directly against the Marcionists and other heretics of that kind, under the title *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*. We shall see below that he wrote against the Spanish Priscillianists to Orosius, Consentius, and Ceretius. In the same book addressed to Orosius he attacks various errors attributed to Origen.

At that time the heresy of the Novatians was widespread and common in the West. When the noblewoman Seleuciana had held discussions with someone who claimed to belong to this sect and desired to win him for Christ, she asked Augustine to provide her with certain instructions. At the same time she wrote to him that this Novatian acknowledged no repentance except that which occurred before Baptism, and even maintained that Peter had not been baptized.

He also seemed to believe that the Apostles had sometimes imposed repentance upon neophytes in place of Baptism. This, however, was not the Novatian position.

Augustine therefore wrote back to Seleuciana. After briefly proving the threefold repentance recognized by the Church, he demonstrated at greater length that there was no room for doubt that Peter had been baptized. He did not wish, however, to use the example of that Apostle to prove canonical repentance after Baptism had been received (*Letter* 265).

**5.** The heresy of which the celebrated Tertullian had been the founder, and which was in fact called that of the Tertullianists, still flourished at Carthage in Augustine’s time. But after gradually losing strength, it was finally extinguished completely several years before the death of that holy Bishop.

When Augustine was at Carthage, the very few Tertullianists who remained were undoubtedly brought back, through his exhortations, to the unity of the Catholic Church. They handed over to the Church and to Bishop Aurelius the basilica that they had previously held (*On Heresies*, heresy 87).

**6.** God also extinguished another heresy in the region of Hippo during Augustine’s lifetime and, undoubtedly, through his ministry as well, although the holy Bishop modestly passes over this in silence. He reports the following about it in his book *On Heresies*:

> “There is a certain rustic heresy in our countryside—that is, in the territory of Hippo—or rather, there was one. For, gradually diminished, it had remained in one small village, in which there were indeed very few, but all of them belonged to it. Now all of them have been corrected and made Catholics, and no one remains in that error.

> “They were called Abelonians, by the Punic derivation of the name. Some say that they were named after Adam’s son who was called Abel; hence we may call them Abelites or Abelonians.

> “They did not unite with wives; yet their sect’s doctrine did not permit them to live without wives. Thus a man and a woman lived together under a profession of continence and adopted a boy and a girl, who were to become their successors under the terms of that union. Whenever death overtook one of them, others were substituted, provided that two persons of different sex succeeded the two in the society of that household.

> “For when either parent died, the children served the one who remained until that person also died. After that person’s death, they too adopted a boy and a girl in the same way. They were never without someone to adopt, because the neighbors around them had children and willingly gave their needy children the hope of another’s inheritance” (*ibid.*).

The remaining course of this history will explain what Augustine wrote against the Manichaeans, Donatists, and Pelagians. What he composed against the Arians at various times we shall gather together toward the end of his life.

### CHAPTER X

1. He attempts to confer with Proculeianus, the Donatist bishop of Hippo.  
2. He writes to Eusebius about this matter.  
3. He complains to the same man that a young man who had struck his mother was received by Proculeianus and rebaptized among his party.  
4. He protests against Primus, a subdeacon of Spain and a scandalous man, who was rebaptized by the Donatists.  
5. The death of Bishop Valerius.  
6. Augustine writes back to the presbyter Casulanus concerning fasting.

**1.** We have already noted that the Church of Hippo was divided by the schism of the Donatists. Their bishop at Hippo was Proculeianus. Augustine held him in considerable esteem, both because of the bond of human society that united them and because certain signs of a peaceful disposition shone forth in him, while many people praised his humanity.

For a long time, however, from the time he was made bishop, Augustine remained silent before him, believing that Proculeianus was avoiding an encounter and conversation with him. Later it happened by chance that Evodius and Proculeianus met in the same house, and a discussion arose between them concerning the hope of the faithful—that is, concerning the inheritance and Church of Christ.

Evodius, who wished to be regarded not as a flatterer but as a defender of the truth, for which he was most zealous, perhaps pursued the matter more vigorously than Proculeianus desired. Proculeianus complained that Evodius had answered him insultingly.

Nevertheless, Proculeianus indicated that he wished to converse with Augustine in the presence of serious and honorable men. Evodius joyfully reported this opinion and wish to Augustine. Augustine received it no less willingly and seized the opportunity offered by Proculeianus to examine the cause and origin of that sorrowful schism which was disturbing both families and people bound most closely together through a most wretched division.

He therefore wrote Proculeianus a letter full of courtesy and goodwill. After excusing Evodius’s vehemence and asserting that he took care not to injure anyone by his words, Augustine promised to come for a discussion before those whom Proculeianus himself should choose, provided that the words of both parties were recorded in writing; or, if Proculeianus preferred, they could first meet privately, or even correspond by letter.

The only condition was that either the proceedings of the discussion or the mutual letters should be read aloud to the common people, so that at last there might be not many peoples but one people and one Church. He promised that this would be pleasing to Valerius, who was then absent.

In the remainder of the letter he begged and earnestly entreated Proculeianus to place the pursuit of peace above fleeting honors and advantages. This may perhaps have been said because the African Church had not yet decreed that Donatist bishops should be admitted to their rank.

It is unclear whether Augustine was a presbyter or a bishop when he wrote this letter. Nevertheless, we consider it more likely that he was already a bishop, chiefly because of what he writes there about the honors with which people surrounded him:

> “People wishing to settle their secular affairs with us, when they have need of us, salute us daily with bowed heads.”

It is scarcely possible to establish that men who were only presbyters possessed the right to settle business and disputes.

Certainly, since this occurred before he wrote his first letter to Eusebius, in which he confesses that he was still a novice bishop (*Letter* 34, §6), and while Valerius was still alive, it cannot be placed very far after the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate.

What followed from this letter to Proculeianus is unknown to us. It is nevertheless certain that the Donatists generally avoided conversation with Augustine.

2. As for letters, he also wrote to the principal bishops of the Donatists (Epistle 43)—not letters of communion, since by dissenting from the Catholic Church they had made themselves unworthy of such letters, but private letters of the sort that one might also write to pagans: courteous, nevertheless, and suitable for bringing about peace. He invited them to a common conference in which the cause of the schism and other matters of that kind could be discussed. Yet he himself testifies that his letters were sometimes read by them and rejected, and that they never replied, whether through contempt or, rather, through ignorance and distrust (Against the Letters of Petilianus, book 1, no. 1). Of Proculeianus himself he writes that he had discovered his letters to be refused by him (Epistle 35, no. 1). For he sent him at least four letters, although only the one of which we have just spoken survives today.

If the following should be referred to this matter—that Proculeianus replied through one of his presbyters, Victor by name, who addressed the officials sent on public business to receive Proculeianus’s response—then this response, which those same officials entered in the public records, agreed sufficiently with what Proculeianus had said to Evodius and, as it seems, committed him to a common conference. Perhaps, however, this relates to another protest [Col. 0255], to which he had ordered that the following response be given: “If you are a Christian, preserve this judgment of God” (Epistle 35, no. 4).

At any rate, it began to be widely reported throughout the city of Hippo that Proculeianus had not given the order reported by the public Office (Epistle 34, no. 5). It was also reported that he had said that, if Augustine were so eager to debate, he ought to go to Constantina, where they had frequently assembled, or else go to Milevis, where they would shortly be holding a council.

At that time there was living near Hippo-Regius a prominent man named Eusebius, a follower of the Donatist sect and a friend of Proculeianus, but endowed with exceptional wisdom, seriousness, and moderation. Since Augustine did not wish to write to Proculeianus because Proculeianus rejected his letters, he approached this Eusebius, asking him through good and honorable men to inquire of Proculeianus whether he had given Victor the order which Victor had reported to the public Office in his own words, or whether the officials placed in charge of that public duty had fabricated false records from Victor’s statement.

Afterward he wrote to Eusebius about the same matter, asking him to inquire generally what Proculeianus’s mind was regarding the discussion of the entire question of the schism. Augustine declares that he would willingly come down to discuss it calmly with him if Proculeianus agreed—something he hoped would happen on the basis of reports that had reached him. For he had heard that Proculeianus had said that, with ten serious and honorable men from each side brought together, and without popular tumult, the two of them should investigate the truth from the authority of Scripture.

The holy Doctor adds that, if Proculeianus would be reluctant to come to a conference with him because, as was reported, he was less polished in the more humane disciplines, the learning of the liberal arts had no bearing on this question, which was to be discussed either from the Holy Scriptures or from ecclesiastical and public documents. Proculeianus could nevertheless choose as his colleague whomever he wished from among his own people; or Augustine would entrust his place at the conference to Samsucius, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Turris, who was then staying at Hippo (Epistle 35, no. 6).

This Samsucius wrote to Severus together with Alypius and Augustine (Epistle 62), being named third in the inscription itself. Augustine sometimes consulted him in his uncertainties, and discovered that he judged rightly concerning a matter on which Augustine himself had remained doubtful and hesitant (Epistle 83, no. 4). Although he was unpolished in speech, he was nevertheless thoroughly instructed in the true faith (Epistle 34, no. 6). Augustine therefore did not hesitate to pit him against Proculeianus, confident that, while contending for the truth, he would receive divine assistance.

As for the proposal that he should go to the city of Milevis, Augustine replies that the whole reason for this question concerned him especially with Proculeianus, and that he was not permitted to do anything in other cities, since the particular care of a single Church, that of Hippo, belonged to him.

3. Another matter at the same time compelled Augustine to write to Eusebius. A certain young Catholic from Hippo was accustomed to beat his mother, a widow, poor, elderly, and deprived of every support. His madness had advanced so far that not even on those days when the severity of the laws spares the most wicked—such as Sundays and the eight days of Easter [Col. 0256]—did he restrain his impious hands from her.

Augustine reproved him for his crime. But when the young man saw that his wickedness was being prohibited by the Church, he was seized with fury and threatened his mother in these words: “I will transfer myself to the party of Donatus, and I will drink your blood.” These appear to have been his very words.

He did not delay carrying out the first part of his threats. The Donatists received him; in his frenzy they rebaptized him; and, thirsting for his mother’s blood, they clothed him in white garments. He was placed within the railings, in a prominent position, for all to look upon, as though he had been perfectly renewed by the gift of the Holy Spirit, although he was thinking of nothing other than matricide.

The only thing remaining was for those who had baptized him in this condition to press him toward the rest of what he knew had to be fulfilled within their octave. At this spectacle, it seems, no one—not even among the Donatists—failed to groan. Augustine was profoundly shaken by so abominable a crime. Hence, however great the fury of the Donatists might be, he judged that he was at least compelled to speak.

He therefore wished so sacrilegious an outrage to be entered in the public records, so that, whenever he thought it appropriate to denounce so great a crime, whether within the city of Hippo or outside it, he could do so without suspicion of falsehood. At that very moment, before the octave of this unhappy neophyte had been completed, he wrote to Eusebius, hoping that Eusebius would condemn the deed. At the same time he solemnly called God to witness and declared to him that, as much as he loved Christian peace, so much was he moved by those sacrilegious acts which the schismatics perpetrated in their dissent.

Nevertheless, he added that this movement of his heart was peaceful, and that he was not acting so that anyone should be forced unwillingly into Catholic communion, but so that the truth might be openly declared to all who were in error and might thus persuade them sufficiently that it ought to be embraced (Epistle 34).

4. Eusebius replied to Augustine, confessing that he did not approve of the son who had struck his mother being received; and that, if Proculeianus had known of it, he would have prevented so wicked a young man from belonging to his communion. He expressed his astonishment, however, that Augustine himself had appointed him judge and arbiter between bishops.

Augustine replied by sending him another letter. He said that he had merely asked for Eusebius’s kindness, and was still asking him to inquire of Proculeianus whether he himself had given Victor the order which Victor had reported to the public Office as having been given to him; and at the same time to ask what Proculeianus thought about a conference.

As for the young man, if Proculeianus was prepared to exclude him from his communion once the crime had become known to him, he could not in any way claim either not to know what had happened or that there had been a delay in prohibiting him.

Augustine likewise warned Eusebius about another man whom Proculeianus was still obliged to exclude from his communion. His name was Primus, formerly, as appears, a subdeacon of the Spanish Church in the diocese of Hippo. Since he had been forbidden undisciplined access to consecrated women and had despised orderly and sound instructions, he had been removed from the clergy.

Taking this indignantly, he crossed over to the party of the Donatists. They rebaptized him together with two consecrated women from the same village who had followed him. From that time onward he devoted his life to every kind of intemperance, amid the degraded crowds of little women [Col. 0257] and the accursed banquets of the Circumcellions.

Augustine adds that Proculeianus ought likewise to observe the rule which he himself maintained: those who defect from the Church in order to escape discipline should not be received without the humiliation of repentance.
