He therefore asks Eusebius to inform Proculeianus of all these matters; otherwise he threatens to denounce them to Proculeianus through public records. He says that he cannot remain silent when God commands him to speak; and that, if they attempted to proceed against him by force, the Lord would not abandon His Church.

He also explains to him another reason for lodging a complaint. A certain tenant of a Church had a daughter who was a catechumen. She had been seduced by the Donatists and had received from them both baptism and the status of a consecrated woman. Her father wished to restore her to Catholic communion by paternal authority and by beatings inflicted upon her. Augustine, however, forbade him to use force, unwilling to receive her unless she returned willingly and of her own accord.

Although he had maintained a course of action so entirely opposed to every form of violence, Augustine nevertheless, while at some point passing through the village of Spanishus, encountered there a presbyter of Proculeianus on the estate of a most devout Catholic woman. The presbyter bitterly attacked Augustine and the woman, calling them traitors and persecutors.

Augustine not only restrained himself from engaging in the dispute, but also restrained the crowd accompanying him. Nevertheless, moved by this and other matters, he asks Eusebius to admonish Proculeianus to restrain the license of his clergy. He should no longer allow good pastors to remain silent while his people attempt, like wolves, to prey upon their sheep with lurking bites (Epistle 35).

Augustine wrote these two letters to Eusebius while he was still a recently consecrated bishop; for this reason we have assigned them to this period.

5. Bishop Valerius, who was still alive when Augustine invited Proculeianus to a mutual conference by letter (Epistle 33, no. 4), appears to have departed this life shortly afterward; at least, we have learned nothing further about him.

Hieronymus Vignierius included in his Supplement a sermon which, he thinks, Augustine delivered when he first spoke to the people after Valerius’s death, after three days of assemblies had passed in silence because of the force of his own tears and those of the entire people. This sermon contains a great many events and, if it could be accepted as genuine, would provide us with a very rich harvest of material for discussion.

Because it deals with a certain subdeacon who had been rebaptized by the Donatists and ordained a deacon, we have relegated it to the end of the ninth volume, which contains the writings against the Donatists. Without stopping to examine whether its style possesses sufficient gravity for it to be attributed to Augustine, this sermon is for the most part concerned with Rusticianus, a deacon—or subdeacon—of Mutugenna. After defecting from the Church to the Donatists, he had been rebaptized by Macrobius and ordained a deacon.

This Rusticianus appears, from numerous indications and conjectures, to be the same as that Mutugennian deacon about whom Augustine wrote to Maximinus, as we noted above (Book 3, chapter 9, no. 6).

6. Among the friends of the holy Bishop was a presbyter of another [Col. 0258] Church named Casulanus. Augustine took great pleasure in his studies and style and, because of the ability he displayed in his letters, encouraged him to advance in the word of God and to abound more and more in service to the Church.

He appears to have lived in an African Church in which some people observed the Saturday fast and others did not. At that time there was not one uniform ecclesiastical custom everywhere concerning this fast. The Roman Church and some Churches of the West, although they were few, observed it outside the fifty days of the Easter season. But throughout the Eastern peoples, and among many Christians in the West as well, no one fasted on that day except on Holy Saturday.

In this disagreement of customs, Casulanus appears to have written to a certain friend in Rome to learn what should be observed. His friend then replied and sent him a fairly lengthy dissertation, in which he argued that the custom of the Roman Church should be followed and that one ought to fast on Saturday. He attacked in insulting language those who acted otherwise—that is, almost the entire Christian world.

But since it would have been difficult to support that invented command to fast with strong arguments, he ranged freely in praise of fasting and, with mocking abuse, attacked feasts and drunken banquets. This was irrelevant to the question under discussion; alternatively, he was condemning everyone who did not fast every day, including the Roman Church itself as well as the others.

Casulanus sent this dissertation to Augustine so that he might refute it and reply to him whether it was permissible to fast on Saturday. He wished Augustine not to know the name of the person whose discussion he was sending him, calling him merely a certain Urbicus.

Augustine forgot to reply to Casulanus until he received another letter in which Casulanus, by the right of the charity that united them, urgently demanded an answer at last. Augustine therefore interrupted his most pressing occupations in order to discharge this obligation and to explain to him that, in matters of this kind not prescribed by divine law, the more certain rule—which he had received from blessed Ambrose—was the custom of the place where one lived; or, if that custom was not uniform, that one should follow the example of the bishop.

He thoroughly dissolved the false arguments of the dissertation sent to him, but did not linger over refuting each point individually, so that he could devote his leisure to other and more urgent works (Epistle 36).

When he praises Ambrose in these words—“I shall tell you what the venerable Ambrose, from whom I was baptized, the bishop of Milan, answered me when I asked him about this” (ibid., no. 32)—he gives grounds for suspecting that he wrote before Ambrose’s death, which occurred on the day before Easter in the year 397. Nothing stands in the way of this opinion.

## CHAPTER XI

1. On the books written to Simplicianus, in whose composition the truth of predestination was revealed to him by God.  
2. When these books were published.  
3. Augustine refutes the Manichaean letter called *The Foundation*.  
4. He publishes a book *On Christian Combat*.

1. In this year, on the day before the Nones of April, Ambrose departed this life [Col. 0259], and Simplicianus succeeded him. Augustine had known Simplicianus at Milan and had made use of his advice when he had already begun to think seriously about his conversion. Even then he had experienced the fatherly affection with which that most kindly heart burned toward him (Epistle 37, no. 1).

After Augustine had labored over various compositions, some of them fell into Simplicianus’s hands, and he read them with singular pleasure. Indeed, in a letter he informed Augustine that, as his devoted and grateful admirer, he rejoiced over the gifts divinely bestowed upon him. At the same time he proposed several questions to him, asking that they be explained in a single short work (*On Various Questions to Simplicianus*, book 2, question 6).

Augustine, who was not unaware of the illustrious merits of so holy a man, received with gladness the signs of his affection and the support by which he approved Augustine’s literary labors. He judged that God had wished to bring this consolation to his cares, since previously he had always been compelled to remain fearful and anxious lest, through ignorance or negligence, he should make some mistake in expounding the Scriptures.

As for the questions which he says Simplicianus had proposed to him as a most devout father—not so that Simplicianus might learn anything from him, but so that he might test one who was making progress and correct one who was in error—Augustine testifies that he would have been not merely disobedient but also ungrateful if he had failed to answer them (*ibid.*, Preface).

Since the questions concerned partly the Epistle to the Romans and partly the Books of Kings, he composed two books: the first on the questions concerning Paul, of which there were two altogether; the second on the remaining questions, whose prophetic meaning Simplicianus was seeking.

The questions which Simplicianus proposed for solution concerning the Apostle had already been discussed and committed to writing by Augustine. But he judged that Simplicianus would not have proposed them if their meaning had been easy and straightforward. Therefore, lest he had overlooked anything through carelessness in his earlier discussion, he examined them again with greater caution and attention.

In fact, when he reconsidered the second question, concerning the Apostle’s words, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7), he changed the opinion he had previously held. He had formerly thought that faith came from man (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 4, no. 8), and that, after the proclamation of the truth, a person determined by the choice of his own will whether to believe or not to believe (*ibid.*, no. 7).

He had indicated this opinion—which later became that of the Semi-Pelagians—in several short works he had written while still a presbyter. But as he advanced through the practice and exercise of writing and reading, he learned by divine revelation, more clearly in this work than ever before, that the beginning of faith, just as the entire sequence of the good works that follow it, is a gift of God (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 20, no. 52).

Thus, after he had labored on behalf of free choice, at last the grace of God prevailed (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 1, no. 1). In the latter part of the first book he establishes as a matter requiring no doubt that God’s grace is not given according to our merits. He also proves that the beginning of faith is a gift of God. And he lays down principles from which it is easy to infer—although he does not say so in explicit words—that we cannot possess perseverance to the end unless it is bestowed upon us by the One who predestined us to His kingdom and glory [Col. 0260] (On the Gift of Perseverance, chapter 21, no. 55).

For this reason he asks Prosper and Hilary to ensure that this work is read by the people of Marseilles who were attacking this doctrine, if they had perhaps not yet read it (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 4, no. 8).

Thus he received the fruit of his faith. It was under its impulse that he had written to Simplicianus, saying that, although he understood less well the questions proposed to him because he was entangled by his own slowness, he nevertheless trusted in Simplicianus’s merits and would open them up (Epistle 37, no. 3).

As he proceeded to the second question, he testifies that, aided by Simplicianus’s prayers, he was undertaking a matter so intricate and obscure, since he was certain that, because of Simplicianus’s good will toward him, he would never have ordered him to disclose these mysteries unless he had at the same time prayed to God that Augustine might be able to do so (*On Various Questions to Simplicianus*, book 2, question 1, Preface).

Augustine likewise asks Simplicianus, in this work and in others that might come into his hands, to devote not only the care of a reader but also the judgment of one who corrects (Epistle 37, no. 3). At the conclusion of the book, after asking him to pray for Augustine’s errors, he says:

“But I earnestly request your judgment concerning this work—very brief, but of the greatest weight; and, provided that it is entirely truthful, I do not refuse the severest judgment” (*On Various Questions to Simplicianus*, book 2, question 6).

Among the questions proposed to him by Simplicianus was one concerning the pythoness who presented Samuel’s soul to Saul (*ibid.*, question 3). Later, when Dulcitius consulted him about the same matter, Augustine merely repeated what he had already written to Simplicianus. At the end of the work, however, he added that, in view of what he subsequently discovered in Ecclesiasticus, it seemed to him that it was not a counterfeit image of Samuel presented through the wicked ministry of the pythoness, but Samuel himself who had appeared in visible form (*On Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, question 6, no. 5).

2. Although Augustine testifies that the first two of the books he composed as a bishop were those addressed to Simplicianus (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 1, no. 1), and that he wrote them at the beginning of his episcopate (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, no. 8; *On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 55), this does not prevent John Rivius from assigning them to the year 397, being quite certain that Simplicianus was already bishop at that time (Rivius, pp. 125, 636). In this he appears to have followed Baronius’s opinion (Baronius, under the year 397, no. 55).

We have not dared to depart from the judgment of either of them, since in these books Augustine calls Simplicianus his father (Epistle 37, title and no. 1; *On Various Questions to Simplicianus*, book 1, Preface), and repeatedly asserts that he wrote the work now to Simplicianus, bishop of the Church of Milan, now to Simplicianus, bishop of the Milanese Church (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 1; *On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 21, no. 55), the successor of blessed Ambrose (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, no. 8), or elsewhere says that Simplicianus, bishop of Milan, had asked him about the matter (*On Eight Questions of Dulcitius*, question 6, no. 2). He never, however, suggests that Simplicianus later became bishop.

Nevertheless, one may reasonably suppose that Simplicianus, while still a presbyter, was called “father” by Augustine out of his exceptional reverence for so great a man. Augustine himself calls him Ambrose’s father in Ambrose’s reception of Christ’s grace [Col. 0261] and relates that Ambrose was truly loved by him as by a father (*Confessions*, book 8, chapter 2, no. 3).

Ambrose himself expressly indicates that he honored Simplicianus as a father. He asks him to continue loving him with parental affection (in Ambrose, Epistle 65, no. 10); and elsewhere he says: “I recognize the affection of an old friendship and, what is more, the love of fatherly grace; for antiquity has something that can unite it with many people, but fatherly love does not” (ibid., Epistle 37, no. 1).

Since Ambrose held Simplicianus in such high honor, there is sufficient reason to think that Augustine, who was inferior to Ambrose both in age and rank, may have wished to call him “father” even though he was not yet a bishop.

Indeed, we do not read that Augustine bestowed this title either upon the Roman bishops or upon the bishop of Carthage, whom he generally calls “brothers.” From this it may be understood that he granted the title of “father” to Simplicianus himself, not to the see of Milan.

It may also be added that, if Simplicianus had already been bishop of Milan, Augustine would probably have bestowed upon him the title “pope,” just as he did upon Aurelius of Carthage (Epistle 41, no. 60) and also upon Ambrose himself (Epistle 31, no. 8).

Those sees were regarded as almost equal in dignity within the Church, and the very distance between the places—quite apart from the venerable gray hair of Simplicianus—would have required still greater expressions of duty and honor toward the see of Milan.

Moreover, Gennadius, who appears to have read Simplicianus’s letter, testifies that Simplicianus wrote to Augustine while Augustine was still a presbyter.

Simplicianus therefore must have sent these letters to Augustine at the beginning of the year 396. Hence we are led to believe that Augustine wrote to him in that year, but that, when he later mentioned these books addressed to Simplicianus, he called him bishop of Milan in order to honor and identify the man.

3. After the books addressed to Simplicianus, Augustine places a short work which he composed against the Manichaean letter called *The Foundation* (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 2), since in reality it embraced almost everything that the Manichaeans believed (*Against the Fundamental Epistle of Manichaeus*, chapter 5, no. 6).

He refutes only its basic principles, that is, the earlier portions of the letter. For the remainder of the letter he merely dictated notes, which nevertheless contained everything necessary to overturn it, so that these might serve as signs and indications to remind him, should he ever have leisure to write against the whole letter (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 2). Those notes have been lost.

At the beginning of this work against the Manichaeans he beseeches God to give him a peaceful and tranquil mind, one that would think more about their correction than their overthrow. He is moved toward them by mercy, not hatred, since he sees them entangled in the same errors from which he himself had escaped only with great difficulty.

4. To this book he appends the work which he entitled *On Christian Combat* (*ibid.*, chapter 3), because in it he instructs Christians for the battle they must wage against the devil and against themselves.

In it he sets forth the rule of faith and the precepts of right living in a few words, though many passages of exceptional beauty occur within them. He also briefly includes the principal heresies, among them the sects of the Donatists and the Luciferians [Col. 0262].

He likewise observes that the Donatists had been divided into various schisms (*On Christian Combat*, nos. 31–32). Yet he does not turn to the advantage of his own cause the fact that they had received Praetextatus and Felicianus into their communion after previously expelling them with dreadful curses, although this had occurred around the beginning of the year 397.

This fact lends considerable support to what we have said: perhaps Augustine had written to Simplicianus as early as the year 396.

He notes that he composed this book, *On Christian Combat*, in a humble style suited to brothers who had only a slight acquaintance with the Latin language (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 3).

## CHAPTER XII

1. Four books of *On Christian Doctrine* composed by Augustine.  
2. Then the book *Against the Party of Donatus* and the thirteen books of the *Confessions*.  
3. The work against Faustus published around the same time.  
4. What seemed necessary to observe in assigning certain short works to their proper places.  
5. Augustine writes a book on chants at the altar.  
6. The *Questions on the Gospels*.  
7. Notes on Job.  
8. The book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*.  
9. And fifteen books *On the Trinity*.

1. The order which Augustine follows in listing his works leads us to assign his composition *On Christian Doctrine* to this period (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 4).

In its first three books he lays down rules for understanding Scripture; in the fourth book he teaches how what has been understood and grasped should be conveyed to others.

When he undertook to publish this work, he already had many thoughts about the subject and hoped that, once he began to devote them to others, God, who had given him these things, would not deny him whatever else was still necessary (*On Christian Doctrine*, book 1, no. 1).

This work, however, perhaps begun in the year 397, was not completed at that time. He brought it only as far as the middle of chapter 25 of the third book (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 4), and immediately allowed it to circulate unfinished, since he cites it in the books which he wrote shortly afterward against Faustus (*Against Faustus*, book 22, chapter 91).

But when, while reviewing his works, he discovered that the book was incomplete, he judged that he ought to finish it before proceeding to revise anything else. He therefore completed the third book and added the entire fourth book (*On Christian Doctrine*, book 4, chapter 24, no. 53), eight or nine years after the journey he had undertaken to Caesarea in Mauretania in September of the year 418—that is, in the year 406 or 407.

In the second book, where he praises the work of Ambrose which he had requested from Paulinus, he calls that holy prelate “our Ambrose” (ibid., book 2, chapter 28, no. 43). From this, however, as we think, it cannot be inferred whether Ambrose was still alive at that time or had already departed this life.

Augustine reports that not long before he had learned from very serious and entirely trustworthy men of a Christian barbarian slave who did not know letters but, through three days of prayer, had divinely obtained complete knowledge of them, so that, to the astonishment of those present, he rapidly read through a book that was offered to him [Col. 0263] (ibid., book 1, Prologue, no. 4).

2. After mentioning the books *On Christian Doctrine*, Augustine speaks of two books which he had entitled *Against the Party of Donatus* (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 5); but they have not survived to our time.

He then places the books of his *Confessions*. In them, by commending God’s justice and goodness through the recollection of his sins and the remembrance of the benefits divinely received, he raises the human intellect toward that supreme good and the infinite majesty of God.

He testifies that this was what he accomplished in himself when they were written and what he continues to accomplish in those who read them, and that they pleased and continue to please many of the brothers (ibid., no. 6).

Elsewhere he writes that none of his works was read either more frequently or with greater pleasure (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 53). Yet he was not unaware that some people might perhaps disapprove of it (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 6).

Indeed, when these words of his were once being recalled at Rome by a certain bishop—“Give what You command, and command what You will”—Pelagius, who was present and had not yet disclosed the poison of his heresy, could not endure them. At one point he contradicted them rather heatedly and almost quarreled with the man who had recalled them (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 53).

There are, however, many more passages in this work which should offend Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians, since it repeatedly attacks their errors before those errors had yet arisen.

It appears that Petilianus took certain words from the third book of the *Confessions* in a distorted sense, so that he might seize upon them as an opportunity for accusation, although they were clear in themselves and evident from many statements made both before and afterward (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 3, no. 60).

When Count Darius had requested the books of the *Confessions* from Augustine, Augustine sent them to him and addressed him in these words:

“Look at me there, so that you do not praise me beyond what I am; there do not believe about me what others say, but what I say; there attend to me and see what I was in myself and through myself. And if anything in me pleases you, praise there with me Him whom I wished to be praised on account of me—and not me. For ‘He Himself made us, and not we ourselves.’ We had destroyed ourselves, but He who made us remade us [Col. 0264]. When you have found me there, pray for me, that I may not fail” (Epistle 231, no. 6).

Possidius says:

“In this work he showed what he had been before receiving grace and how he lived after receiving it. For he wished to do what the Apostle says, so that no one should believe or suppose concerning any human being more than he knew that person to be, or had heard him to be (2 Corinthians 12:6). He used the manner of holy humility and deceived no one; rather, he sought not his own praise but that of his Lord, for his own deliverance and gift, on the basis of what he had already received. He asked for the prayers of his brothers concerning what he desired to receive” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, Preface).

Since Paulinus had asked Alypius, though unsuccessfully, to write out for him the whole history of his life (in Augustine, Epistle 24, no. 4), Baronius, relying on this example, supposes that Augustine wrote his books of the *Confessions* at the request and urging of that same Paulinus (Baronius, under the year 395).

Yet it was not Paulinus alone, but many good Christians who knew Augustine—or rather, who did not know him in the way that mattered for the formation of the soul and therefore wished to know what his life was like. Augustine complied with their request. He hoped that they would both rejoice with him over the good things God had granted him and pray to God concerning certain remnants of his former vices, which still delayed his progress along the way of God (*Confessions*, book 10, chapter 3, nos. 4–5).

3. In the sequence of the *Retractations*, the work against Faustus follows the books of the *Confessions* (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 7).

We have spoken above about Faustus and about the book which he had written on behalf of the Manichaeans against the Church (Book 1, chapter 9, no. 4). When this book came into Augustine’s hands and had been read by the brothers, they earnestly demanded that the holy Bishop, by the right of the charity through which he served them, reply to it.

He therefore replied and placed his responses beneath the words of Faustus as they were proposed. Thus the work became very long, divided into thirty-three disputations, which Augustine prefers to call “books,” although some of them are very brief. Several, however, are extremely lengthy, especially the twenty-second, in which he defends the lives of the Patriarchs against Faustus’s calumnies.

He quotes a passage from this twenty-second book in the *Questions to Dulcitius* (Question 7). This book appears to be the work entitled *On the Life of the Patriarchs against Faustus*.

Around the year 405 Augustine sent his work against Faustus, together with a letter, to Jerome (Epistle 82, no. 17).

4. It is our responsibility to observe carefully the time of each work, whenever it can be discovered. The books mentioned above, however, offer either very slight indications of their date or none at all.

As for the books against Faustus, Augustine merely reports that he wrote them long before receiving from Jerome Letter 82, which could not have been delivered to him before the year 405.

We were therefore unable to do anything other than follow the sequence established by Augustine himself in the *Retractations*, where he testifies that he preserved the chronological order as far as he could (*Retractations*, Prologue, no. 3).

Nevertheless, he was not entirely accurate in this. Immediately after the books against Faustus he places the disputation against Felix the Manichaean, which he certainly held in December of the year 404 (*Acts with Felix*, book 1, chapter 1).

And when he had listed several other treatises, he places the books against Petilianus after them, although Augustine wrote those books under Pope Anastasius—that is, at least in the year 402 (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 2, chapter 15, no. 118).

Perhaps Augustine intended to attach continuously to the work against Faustus the other works which he later wrote against the Manichaeans. In fact, after the books which he mentioned in that place, we find no further work by him against this heresy.

We shall follow this order and shall likewise place here the other works which he subjoins to the books concerning the Manichaeans, until we encounter works whose date we can identify more precisely.

### 5

The first work that meets us in this series is the book that he wrote against a certain Hilarus, a tribune and a Catholic layman (Retractations, book 2, chapter 11). Inflamed with anger—for the reason is unknown to us—against the ministers of the Church, he maliciously attacked, as Augustine says was customary, the practice that had then begun to be introduced at Carthage, namely, that hymns from the [Col. 0265] Book of Psalms should be sung at the altar, either before the offering or while what had been offered was being distributed among the people. Since Hilarus was assailing this custom everywhere as erroneous, Augustine was compelled by the prayers of his brethren to refute him. Possidius calls this work *A Book against Hilarus, on the Songs Sung at the Altar* (Possidius, *Index*, chapter 6). It does not exist today.

### 6

After this book Augustine places explanations of certain passages from the Gospel according to Matthew and Luke, contained in two books, which he entitled *Questions on the Gospels* (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 12). He composed this work for the use of a certain person who, while reading the Gospel together with him, consulted him whenever something seemed obscure, and sometimes led him to reconsider matters that he himself had initially passed over. Hence these questions do not always follow the sequence of the Gospel text. To remedy this inconvenience Augustine drew up a table of contents. Moreover, these books do not resolve all the difficulties, nor even some of the more serious ones that might be proposed, because the person consulting Augustine already knew most of them.

### 7

The *Annotations on Job* consist only of certain scholia, which the holy Doctor had written in the margin of the text, but which others copied rather inaccurately and assembled into a single work. Hence Augustine doubts whether he ought to acknowledge this product as his own and legitimate. He admits that these *Annotations* would be understood and be suited to comprehension by very few; and that even those few would encounter much in them that they would fail to understand, both because of the brevity of the statements and because of the errors that had crept into them so frequently that he had been unable to correct them. Whatever the quality of the work may have been, it was requested by the brethren; and since Augustine could not refuse their earnest entreaty, he acknowledged it as his own in his books of *Retractations* (ibid., chapter 13).

### 8

These *Annotations* are followed by the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed* (ibid., chapter 14), addressed to Deogratias, a Carthaginian deacon to whom those being instructed in the first elements of faith were frequently brought. He was exceptionally learned in the Christian religion and possessed a pleasing eloquence and an outstanding ability to catechize.

Nevertheless, in this exercise he did not feel that he himself was adequate. He almost always found himself in difficulty, uncertain and perplexed about how he should explain those things whose faith makes us Christians; where the instruction ought to begin and where it ought to end; and whether some exhortation ought to be added to the instruction, or whether only those precepts should be explained whose observance the catechumen ought to know to be necessary for living in a Christian manner. He also complained that, often exhausted by a lengthy discourse, he would become languid through weariness, and that, being in such a state of mind, he neither inspired the catechumen nor kindled the attention of his hearers.

Deogratias therefore believed that Augustine would give him advice on this matter. Since he was familiar with Augustine, he asked him by letter not to begrudge him, amid his other occupations, some model of catechizing. Augustine considered that the duty and charity by which he was bound not merely to one friend but generally to the [Col. 0266] whole Church required him willingly to grant the other’s request. “For the more I desire,” he says, “that the Lord’s money be distributed more widely, the more it is incumbent upon me, if I learn that my fellow-servants, the stewards, experience difficulty in distributing it, to do whatever lies in my power so that they may easily and readily accomplish what they eagerly and diligently wish to do” (*On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, chapter 1, §2).

Accordingly, he wrote to him the book with which we are concerned on this subject. At the outset he consoles him for the weariness that usually crept over him while he was speaking. Augustine admits that almost the same thing happened to him whenever, in explaining the mysteries of faith, his tongue could not keep pace with his mind. As a result his spirit was discouraged, and he supposed himself burdensome to others; yet, judging from the zeal and eagerness displayed by his hearers, he inferred that his eloquence, however cold it might seem to him, inflamed them.

Among the other instructions that he gives, he advises that those being privately instructed should be offered a seat: partly because of the appearance of arrogance involved when people standing are made to listen to someone sitting, and partly because it may happen that, wearied by standing, they withdraw under some other pretext. He testifies that this happened to him while he was instructing a certain rustic in the first rudiments of faith (ibid., chapter 13, §19).

Deogratias, to whom this treatise is addressed, was later advanced to the priesthood—if indeed he is the same person to whom Augustine replied around the year 406 in Letter 102 concerning questions sent to him at Carthage. Augustine addresses this priest not merely as his familiar friend, to whom he could refuse nothing, but also as an experienced man who might be consulted in cases of doubt, and whose style was approved both by Augustine and by others.

### 9

To the book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed* Augustine appends fifteen books *On the Trinity* (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 15). He worked over them for several years, since, as he himself writes, he began them as a young man and published them as an old man (Letter 174). He interrupted them whenever he became involved in another work that he thought would benefit more people (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 16), considering this work more laborious and less useful than most others because it contained matters less necessary and intelligible to fewer people (Letter 169, chapter 1, §1).

He undertook the work chiefly for the sake of those who rejected the authority of faith and wanted the truth of the mysteries demonstrated to them by reason (*On the Trinity*, book 1, chapter 1, §1). Yet while he meditated on the law of the Lord as far as he was able, charity did not permit him to deny to others what he had received through God’s gift and revelation. He promised himself that, by ministering these things to others, he too would make progress; and that, while wishing to answer those who asked what he himself was seeking, he would discover what he was looking for (ibid., chapter 3, §5).

“Therefore,” he says, “I undertook these things at the command and with the help of the Lord our God, not so much to discuss known matters with authority as to come to know them by discussing them with piety” (ibid., chapter 5, §8).

The mind of the holy Doctor is evident in very many passages of this work, especially in its prefaces. He declares that he would gladly have suppressed his pen if either Latin authors had already provided sufficient explanations of matters of this kind, or Greek writers had been translated into Latin, or finally if someone else had been willing to undertake the task of answering the questions put to him.

At the beginning of the fifteenth book he [Col. 0267] summarizes, in a concise discourse, what he had explained in the preceding books (ibid., book 15, §3). He did not wish to publish these books individually, as he later published the books *On the City of God*, but all together, because the final books are connected with the first by something like a chain of reasoning.

But certain people who had heard something about these books and ardently desired to possess them, unwilling to endure such delay and postponement, took a copy away from him while the twelfth book was not yet finished, and while the others were less corrected and revised than he would have wished them to be when publishing them. When he discovered this, he decided not to publish them at all, interrupting his labor, but instead to complain in another little work about the theft of these books. Yet he was unable to resist the most ardent prayers of the brethren, and especially the commands of Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage.

Accordingly, he completed what remained to be done, bringing the work to its conclusion, and corrected the earlier books—not, however, as though he thought such an effort necessary for explaining and illuminating matters so difficult, but doing what he could so that they would not differ greatly from those that had appeared against his will (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 15, §1).

He subsequently sent them through a certain deacon to Aurelius of Carthage, together with a letter (Letter 174), which he asked to have prefixed to the books as a kind of preface, because in that letter he noted the matters we have just reported.

In a letter to Evodius he writes that he had not yet published this work (Letter 162, §2); and in another letter to the same man, written only toward the end of the year 415, he testifies that he had not yet completed it (Letter 169, chapter 1, §1), although he had already worked out the first five books *On the City of God*.

From another letter sent to Marcellinus near the end of the year 412, one can understand that his friends had urged him to publish these books, so that Marcellinus himself might undertake their defense if anything in them were attacked either by malicious enemies or even by friends who understood them imperfectly. Augustine, however, had held them back longer than his friends wished or could bear, because of the danger that he might be mistaken in the subject he was treating:

> “So that, if they could not avoid containing some things that deserved criticism, at least there might be fewer of them than there could be if they were published in precipitate and ill-considered haste” (Letter 143, §4).

Writing also to Consentius, he mentions the work *On the Trinity* that he had in hand but could not yet complete because of the importance and difficulty of its subject (Letter 120, chapter 3, §13).

In all these passages—perhaps with the exception of the last—he speaks of his work as though it had not yet been published. Accordingly, one may conjecture that the first edition, which appeared before the work was complete, was not published before the year 412.

It is clear, however, that the second edition was published only after a long interval, since in the thirteenth book he says that he had already explained something in the twelfth book *On the City of God*, which was not composed before the year 416.

When Augustine mentions the books *On the Trinity*, he also mentions those *On the Agreement of the Evangelists*, which, apparently, he composed after the destruction of the temples in the year 399. Therefore [Col. 0268] we are not dealing with the latter here.

We have already noted that we do not claim that all the works just mentioned were composed in this year, but only that they occurred approximately in the order we have assigned to them—and indeed before the books *On the Agreement of the Evangelists* and the other works that will be listed later.

## CHAPTER XIII

1. Possidius’s appointment as bishop of Calama.  
2. Jerome, writing to Augustine, honors him with the title of pope.  
3. The letter sent to Jerome through Paul is delivered to him only after delay.  
4. Two letters in which Augustine asks Paulinus to reply.

### 1

To resume the sequence of events that can be assigned to the year 397: the death of Megalius, the dean or primate of Numidia, must be placed in this year. At the Council of Carthage held in that year, on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, Aurelius testifies that he had recently received a letter from Crescentianus, the bishop of the principal see of Numidia—as Crescentianus himself indicated (African Code of Canons, canon 33). It is therefore clear that Aurelius did not then know that Crescentianus was the dean, although he ought above all to have known this.

About twenty-four days after Megalius’s death, Augustine wrote to Profuturus, bishop of Cirta, asking whether he had found a successor to Megalius in the primacy; for Augustine had promised that he would inquire about this (Letter 38, §2).

He writes to the same man that, because of the pain and swelling of his *rhagades* or *exochades*—terms for a painful lesion, though the precise condition is uncertain—he could neither sit, stand, nor walk, but was confined to bed. Nevertheless, since this was pleasing to the Lord, all was going very well with him (ibid., §1).

In the same letter he has very beautiful remarks on restraining anger, lest it degenerate into hatred (ibid., §2). He speaks deliberately on this subject because Profuturus had recently said something to him while they were traveling, although what exactly it was cannot be inferred.

Augustine wrote to Profuturus through Victor, who had told him in advance that he intended to go to Constantina. Consequently, there can be no doubt that this Profuturus was the same man who is elsewhere read to have been bishop of Cirta, or Constantina.

Augustine asks him to have Victor return through the city of Calama—as Victor had promised—because of a matter of which Profuturus himself would have knowledge, and about which Nectarius the elder was pressing Augustine very urgently. What the matter was is unclear.

A few years later, as we shall see, Augustine wrote to Nectarius (Letter 91), one of the leading men of Calama, very advanced in age but still a pagan, although his father had professed the Christian faith.

Megalius, as we have said, was bishop of Calama. Possidius, Augustine’s disciple, therefore must have succeeded him; for we shall later see Possidius illuminating this see by the glory of his labors and courage.

Nevertheless, the see of Calama must either have remained vacant for some time after Megalius or have had, for a short period, another bishop before Possidius. For Fortunatus, the successor of Profuturus, the bishop of Cirta to whom Augustine’s letter was sent after Megalius’s death, is placed before Possidius in all the African councils.

### 2

In this same year, apparently, Jerome—who had sent Augustine a letter through Asterius in the preceding year—[Col. 0269] wrote to him again (apud Augustine, Letter 39) to commend to him his close friend Praesidius, who had crossed over to the West for specific reasons.

Praesidius was devoted to cultivating the friendship of good men, and regarded it as the greatest benefit if someone secured such friendships for him. Jerome therefore asks Augustine to do this for Praesidius, since he needed nothing else.

In the same letter Jerome sends greetings to Alypius. He also testifies that he is enduring the troubles attached to our present pilgrimage and is being tossed about and buffeted in the monastery by various waves from every direction.

We are therefore compelled to assign this letter to the year 397, before the reconciliation that took place between Jerome and John of Jerusalem in that same year. For we do not read that, from that reconciliation with John until the persecutions stirred up against Jerome by the Pelagians in the year 416, he had any occasion to complain in this manner.

He honors Augustine once and again with the title of pope (ibid., heading and §2); hence the letter cannot be assigned earlier than the year 396.

Since Jerome does not congratulate Augustine in this letter on his advancement to the episcopate, it is probable that he had already done so when he wrote to him through Asterius in the preceding year.

The Praesidius whom Jerome commends to Augustine in this letter seems certainly to be the man whose services Augustine used to reconcile Jerome to himself after Jerome’s anger had been provoked, by offering an apology (Letter 74).

Praesidius had already been ordained bishop after serving as a deacon. In the year 410 he obtained from the Council of Carthage, as its envoy to the Emperor against the Donatists, the famous Carthaginian conference held in the following year. He also subscribed the letter of the Council of Numidia against the Pelagians to Pope Innocent in the year 416 (apud Augustine, Letter 176).

### 3

At about this time Augustine perhaps wrote a letter to Jerome, to be delivered through Paul (Letter 40, chapter 1, §1).

At first Augustine had courteously greeted Jerome by subscribing to another person’s letter, and Jerome, in return for his courtesy, had sent him a letter of his own. This was, unless we are mistaken, the letter that Jerome sent to him through the deacon Asterius in perhaps the year 396, returning Augustine’s greeting.

Since Augustine was therefore obliged to write back, he took the opportunity to ask Jerome what he thought about the dispute between Peter and Paul.

He also mentions a book written by Jerome on ecclesiastical writers, which Augustine himself had recently read. At the same time, he makes the friendly observation that, if Jerome had wished not to omit heretics from that book, he would, in Augustine’s opinion, have done better, after naming them, to add the points on which they should be avoided.

He likewise asks why Jerome had omitted some of them from the same work; or, if this had been done to avoid making the volume too large, why, after mentioning only the heretics, he had not added the matters on which Catholic authority condemned them.

Since, in replying about Origen, Jerome had implied that Origen was to be approved and praised in some respects but disapproved and censured in others, Augustine informs him that he already knows that [Col. 0270] not only in ecclesiastical literature but in all writings one ought to approve and praise whatever is right and true, while disapproving and censuring whatever is false and corrupt.

What Augustine had wanted, and still wanted, was for Jerome to point out the errors by which that great man was shown to have departed from the faith of truth.

Thus Augustine wrote to him through Paul, whose distinguished reputation he commends. But Paul changed his plans for the voyage, and the result was that the letter circulated through Italy before it reached Jerome (Letter 72, §1). This could have sown discord between the two men, had not Augustine’s humility and moderation, together with the charity of both, stifled the seeds of offense.

### 4

Just as, in the preceding letter, Augustine earnestly asks Jerome to maintain a literary correspondence with him—because this is especially effective in preserving friendship and prevents bodily absence, as he puts it, from separating friends too far—so in the letter that he sent at this same time to Paulinus, a holy man whose friendship he valued very highly, he presses him vehemently to send the replies that Augustine had long and eagerly desired.

“O you who daily give away your possessions,” he says, “repay what you owe.”

A year and more had already passed since Paulinus’s last letters, delivered to Augustine in the year 395. This is clearly indicated by Augustine’s complaint:

> “Why are we compelled to thirst through two summers, and those in Africa?” (Letter 42, §1).

In that letter he sends greetings to Romanus and Agilis, whom he also mentions honorably in a letter sent to Paulinus the following year. In that later letter he again insists that Paulinus finally write back after two years of silence:

> “It is not that your inexplicable delay in writing—by which, behold, for the entire two years since our sweetest brothers Romanus and Agilis returned to you from us, we have received no letters from you—has made us slow to write. For in other matters, the more someone is loved, the more worthy of imitation he seems; in this matter it is the opposite. The more ardently we love you, the less we can bear your not writing to us; nor do we wish to imitate you in this” (Letter 45, §1).

In both letters Augustine asks Paulinus to send him the work against the pagans that he had heard Paulinus was preparing.

## CHAPTER XIV

1. Augustine, traveling to Cirta with Alypius to ordain Fortunatus as bishop, meets Fortunius, the Donatist bishop of Tubursicum, for a discussion.  
2. The time at which this discussion took place.  
3. A letter written after the discussion to Glorius and certain other Donatists.  
4. Another discussion held with the same men before the meeting with Fortunius.  
5. Augustine begins a written dispute with Fortunatus, the Donatist bishop.  
6. On the Caelicolists.

### 1

We saw above that, nearly a month after Megalius’s death, Augustine wrote to Profuturus, bishop of Cirta. Profuturus seems to have died shortly afterward, for he did not hold the episcopate long (Letter 71, chapter 1, §2), and he died several years before Augustine wrote the book *On the One Baptism* (*On the One Baptism*, §29).

He was succeeded by Fortunatus, [Col. 0271] one of the seven men chosen by all the Catholic bishops of Africa in the year 411 to defend the cause of the Church against the Donatists at the celebrated Carthaginian conference.

Augustine praises Fortunatus for his devotion to poverty, and was present with Alypius at his ordination (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, chapter 99, §228). For we read that these two prelates hastened together to Cirta for the ordination of a bishop (Letter 44, chapter 1, §1, and chapter 3, §6).

It is clear that this occurred before the Carthaginian conference in which Fortunatus took part.

As they were traveling to Cirta, they passed through Tubursicum. The bishop of that city on the Donatist side was Fortunius, a man advanced in age whose kindness certain Donatists—Glorius, Eleusius, and Felix—had praised to Augustine. They, in turn, had spoken honorably of Augustine to Fortunius.

It appears from the word *soletis* (“you are accustomed”), with which Augustine addresses them (ibid., §1), that he had a habitual association and familiarity with them, although they were not natives of Hippo Regius but of another city, apparently Geliza, which was itself near Hippo (Letter 43, chapter 2, §5).

They had often kindly promised Augustine that Fortunius would not refuse to discuss with him the reconciliation of the division between the Churches (Letter 44, chapter 1, §1).

Accordingly, when Augustine arrived at Tubursicum, he told Fortunius that what he had heard about him had induced him both to see him and to address him. Fortunius agreed.

Augustine soon met with him, accompanied by a considerable number of people whom chance had brought along with him. He thought this should be attributed to Fortunius’s age.

When Augustine sat down with him, a large crowd of citizens, summoned by the rumor of the discussion that had spread through the city, gathered there. Yet amid so great a crowd, very few had been moved by a desire to learn the truth; most had come merely out of curiosity about the debate, as though to a spectacle.

This gathering of the people caused disorder. Neither prayers nor threats from Augustine or Fortunius could secure the silence necessary for the discussion.

Nevertheless, the proceedings began somehow, and for several hours the two men exchanged arguments. From almost the beginning Augustine asked that the words spoken by both sides be recorded by notaries, so that the discussion might be more peaceful and moderate. Fortunius reluctantly agreed.

But when the notaries who were present refused to undertake the recording, others took up the task and were forced to abandon it because of the disorderly interruptions and uproar of the crowd.

Fortunius first maintained that his communion was spread throughout the entire world, but he did not dare to affirm that he could send letters of communion wherever he wished. If he had made that claim, Augustine would have compelled him to write with him also to the Churches named in the apostolic Scriptures.

Fortunius then turned to the persecutions that, as he said, his fellow believers had endured. Augustine replied that persecutions numbered among the blessed only those who suffered for the sake of justice. Therefore, if Macarius—about whom they complained so bitterly—had harassed them only because of the schism that had arisen in the year 348, they could derive no advantage for their cause from this.

Fortunius answered [Col. 0272] that the Churches of the overseas regions had remained innocent until they consented to the shedding of the blood of those whom the persecution of Macarius had destroyed.

But when Augustine pressed him as to whether his fellow believers had at least until that time remained in unity with the Eastern Churches and with the other regions of the world, Fortunius produced a letter that the Council of Sardica had written in the year 347 to Donatus, whom he insisted was his Carthaginian Donatus.

It is evident that Augustine had hitherto known nothing of this letter or of the Council of Sardica. But when he saw that the letter condemned Athanasius of Alexandria and Julius, bishop of Rome, he easily recognized that it had come from an Arian workshop.

He therefore asked to be allowed to take it with him for a more careful investigation of the chronology. Fortunius refused, and would not even allow Augustine to write anything down in his own hand. Augustine had wanted to do this so that, if the circumstances later required him to request the letter, another might not be substituted for it.

Fortunius continued to insist that the justice of his party should be understood from the fact that it had suffered persecution. Augustine demonstrated that persecution was not sufficient evidence for establishing the justice of a cause. He confirmed this by the examples of Maximian, persecuted by the Donatists themselves, and Ambrose, whom they were forced to admit had been a Christian and a just man, yet who had been harassed by Justina.

Again, Fortunius brought forward the death of a certain intermediary whom he said had been killed by Augustine’s side, and began insistently to ask Augustine whom he considered just: the one who had killed, or the one who had been killed.

Augustine immediately opposed this single alleged and unproved death with many other examples, and above all with the manifest frenzy and frequent killings of the Circumcellions.

But Fortunius concealed these matters and persisted with his questions. When Augustine cited the deeds of Elijah, in which this man of God is said to have killed numerous false prophets with his own hand, Fortunius finally began to see that at least in the times of the Old Testament a just man had been permitted to kill.

He nevertheless continued to ask whether this could also be proved from the New Testament.

Augustine replied that he could not recall any just man in the New Testament who had killed someone, but that it was clearly demonstrated there that the wicked must be tolerated by the innocent within the Church, since Christ himself tolerated Judas and first offered him the sacrament of his body and blood.

When almost everyone was moved by this example, Fortunius attempted to evade it by asserting that communion with the wicked had not harmed the Apostles because at that time they had received no baptism other than John’s.

But here too Fortunius was unable to withstand Augustine, who proved that they had already been cleansed by Christ’s Baptism and was preparing to bring forward further evidence for this.

Augustine then turned the discussion to a subject from which it may be understood that the Donatists were afraid that some persecution was then threatening them. Fortunius asked Augustine what he himself would do if such an event occurred.

Augustine declared that he would not agree with Fortunius, and indeed would resist it with all the strength he could muster (ibid., §11). At that time he truly held this view, but experience later drove him from it (Letter 185, chapter 7, §25).

When they had risen and were about to leave their seats, [Col. 0273] Fortunius praised the leniency of Genethlius, Aurelius’s predecessor in the see of Carthage. Augustine added:

> “Yet if that Genethlius had fallen into your hands, he would have been judged worthy of rebaptism.”

Fortunius admitted that his people had established the rule that anyone who came to them from the ranks of the faithful was to be rebaptized. Yet it was clear that he said this unwillingly and with distress, disapproving in his heart of the practice of his sect.

Indeed, the testimony of the entire city made it evident how far he was from the violent acts of his party, about which he often complained among his own people, and for which he expressed sorrow in this discussion even together with the Catholics.

Accordingly, they agreed that the violent crimes with which the Donatists and Catholics reproached one another should not be brought forward in these discussions.

The question of the schism raised by the Donatists against Caecilianus remained to be addressed. Augustine therefore earnestly entreated Fortunius to work with him in a calm spirit toward resolving so serious a controversy.

When Fortunius replied that the Catholics did not wish the matter to be discussed, Augustine promised that he would produce his colleagues—certainly at least ten—who would subscribe to his position. Fortunius made the same promise on behalf of the Donatists.

At this point they separated.

### 2

On the following day Fortunius met with Augustine, and they again discussed the same matter, but only briefly, because Augustine had summoned the chief of the Caelicolists in order to speak with him, and was due to depart as soon as possible to ordain a bishop. Fortunius himself was also pressed by the need to undertake a journey.

Since Augustine was traveling to Cirta, there can be no doubt that the bishop of that city was to be ordained—namely, Fortunatus, the successor of Profuturus. For, as we have shown, Profuturus preceded Augustine in the episcopate, and his successor Fortunatus was among the leading participants in the Carthaginian conference of 411.

It is furthermore established that Augustine’s meeting and discussion with Fortunius occurred before the year 411. This may be inferred from Augustine’s own mind, which was still opposed to persecuting heretics.

It is also clear that the Donatists were then living in peace, and the entire letter indicates that they enjoyed complete freedom—something that never occurred after the year 411.

It is equally clear that, when Fortunius showed Augustine the letter of the pseudo-synod of Sardica, Augustine did not yet know what it was. Nevertheless, he mentions it in the books against Cresconius, written before the year 411, and dismisses it as an Arian work that he had already had in hand for a long time (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, chapter 34, §38).

Furthermore, this Fortunius, an older bishop than Augustine, had died before the year 411, since Januarius, as bishop of Tubursicum in Numidia on the Donatist side, took part in the Carthaginian conference.

But that Fortunius was undoubtedly the same man who is counted tenth among the 310 bishops of the Council of Bagai in the year 394 (ibid., book 4, chapter 10, §12).

When Ambrose was mentioned in the discussion, Augustine’s words may suggest [Col. 0274] that the holy bishop was still alive. And when the persecution of the Donatists against the Maximianists was discussed, no mention appears to have been made of Praetextatus and Felicianus, whom the Donatists had received at the beginning of the year 397.

These considerations seem to require us to acknowledge that the discussion took place no later than the beginning of the year 397.

But since it is certain that Augustine held it while departing to ordain the successor of Profuturus, it would follow that Megalius—who survived Profuturus, who had by then died—must have died before the year 397 itself, and that nearly a year had elapsed before his successor in the primacy was announced.

For Crescentianus, who is believed to have succeeded him, was not primate until approximately the beginning of August in this year, 397.

Although another primate might be inserted between Megalius and Crescentianus, there is nevertheless no reason to assert that this actually happened.

We therefore prefer to place this discussion either toward the end of the year 397 or, more probably, at the beginning of the year 398, when the death of Gildo could have caused the Donatists to fear persecution on account of their own Optatus, a supporter of Gildo.

### 3

Afterward Augustine informed Eleusius and the others who had spoken to him about Fortunius of the discussion that he had held with him. He testified that it would be very difficult to find among the Donatist bishops a mind and disposition as useful as those he had observed in this old man.

By the blood of the Lord he entreats these Donatists to remind Fortunius of his promise to continue the discussion, so that the matter, once begun and already pursued to a considerable extent, might at last be completed.

For resolving it, he advises that some place far from tumult and the disorderly crowding of people should be selected, such as the estate of Titiana, or any other place in the diocese of Tubursicum or Tagaste where there was no church, but where Catholics and Donatists lived together, so that each party could lodge with a host of its own communion.

The canonical books should be brought there, as well as any documentary evidence relevant to the case that ought to be produced by either side. Time should then be devoted to examining each point of dispute for as long as the matter required.

Finally, Augustine asks Eleusius and the others to write back with their opinion—or Fortunius’s opinion—on this matter (Letter 44, chapter 6, §12).

We do not know the outcome of these proceedings, which charity inspired Augustine to undertake in the cause of securing peace.

### 4.

There is still extant another letter of Augustine, addressed to the same Glorius, Eleusius, and Felix, to whom he adds Grammaticus and all the others to whom this might be agreeable (Epistle 43). In this letter, too, the schism is discussed, and nearly the same account is given of Maximian as in the preceding one; nor does anything seem to prevent us from judging that it was written at about the same time, or even somewhat earlier. Augustine mentions there, with the greatest freedom of speech, the tyranny of Optatus of Thamugadi, yet in words that imply it had not yet come to an end. He also demonstrates how justly the Donatists could be punished by civil penalties; but this can most appropriately be referred to the period of Macarius [Col. 0275].

This letter also records another conference that Augustine had held with the same Donatists in their own city. When he was discussing with them participation in Christian unity, they produced certain records in which Caecilianus and Felix were said to have been condemned by the Council of Carthage. Augustine showed them how defective that council was, and by what process its decree had been annulled: by the Roman council, which consisted of bishops sent by Constantine at the request of the Donatists themselves; by the Council of Arles; by Constantine himself, to whom they had appealed; and finally by the proconsul, who had acquitted Felix by his own judgment.

Augustine did not have all these documents of the case at hand, but he immediately arranged for them to be summoned. In the meantime, he made a journey to the Church of Gelizum. What that church was, or what he did there, we do not know. After returning, when he had received the documents he had requested after an interval of not quite two days, he ordered each of them to be read aloud to the Donatists in a single day.

He began with the records of the Council of Cirta. Since some of the Donatists tried to reject them, alleging that it was not credible that Caecilianus could have been condemned for the same crime by those who had obtained pardon for the offense of handing over sacred objects at the Council of Cirta, Augustine set forth at greater length the entire policy of Secundus in that affair. He then ordered the official records concerning the case of Felix of Aptunga to be read.

When one of them mocked Felix, as though he had suffered something unworthy of a bishop because he had been acquitted by a proconsular judgment, and because someone in his case had been subjected to torture, the man’s quibble, being absurd, displeased the others. These documents were read before noon. In the afternoon, the Donatists’ petitions to Constantine, the records of the Roman council, and Constantine’s letters concerning the judgment that he had rendered at Milan in favor of Caecilianus were read aloud.

Augustine had likewise arranged for the records in which Nundinarius had shown that, in the year 320, before Zenophilus, bishops had been corrupted by Lucilla’s money so that they would condemn Caecilianus. But, because of the shortage of time, these could not be read. He granted them complete freedom to examine and transcribe these records.

After this conference, therefore, he wrote to the same Donatists, urging them to inspect these records; and he dwells at length on the need to impress their importance upon them. At the very beginning of his letter he indicates plainly enough that some might disapprove of his writing to people separated from Catholic communion about the matter of their salvation, although they would approve if he did the same thing concerning worldly affairs: “So dear,” he says, “is this world to human beings, and so cheap have they become in their own eyes!”

He wrote to these Donatists all the more willingly because he saw that they were more inclined to seek the truth sincerely from the heart, so that, after abandoning the error they had received from their parents, they might follow it honestly. Indeed, his letter concerning the conference that he held with Fortunius sufficiently indicates that they were not hostile to concord and peace. He concludes the letter with these words:

> “This discourse of ours, which God himself knows with what love both for peace and for you we have drawn forth from the gift he has granted, will be correction for you if you are willing, but a witness even if you are unwilling.”

### 5.

The Donatists were not yet opposing the truth with such hostility of mind [Col. 0276]. Accordingly, Augustine was still in the earlier years of his episcopate when Honoratus, a bishop of that party and a neighbor of Hippo, informed him through Erotes that he would gladly discuss the schism with him by letter, so that they might debate a matter of such importance with the gentleness and tranquility of mind that it required.

Augustine, who had long desired a conference with him, wrote back that his proposal pleased him greatly. To induce him to undertake the discussion, he showed him that, since Scripture promises us that the Church of God would be spread throughout the world, this prophecy is fulfilled in the Catholic Church. He therefore asks him not to hesitate to reply: if this is how matters stand, how can the party of Donatus be that Church divinely foretold, and how could Christ have lost the inheritance promised to him throughout the whole world, so that it remained only in one part of Africa? (Epistle 49, no. 1.)

### 6.

We noted above that, when Fortunius came to Augustine, that holy bishop summoned Major of the Caelicolists to speak with him about something (Epistle 44, chapter 6, no. 13). The name “Caelicolists” still appears in certain laws of the Emperor Honorius (Theodosian Code, *On Heretics*, law 43; and *On the Judges of the Caelicolists and Samaritans*, law 19), but it is not sufficiently clear who they were.

It nevertheless appears that they were not a sect of heretics, nor, as we suppose, people who combined Jewish observance with Christianity, like the Nazoraeans, and consequently appropriated for themselves the name of Christians. For Augustine, who knew them well, does not mention them in his book *On Heresies*. In laws issued in the years 408 and 409, Honorius accuses the Caelicolists of a new doctrine, a new superstition, and a name previously unheard of.

It is possible that they had spread through the West only a few years earlier, or that they had replaced their original name there with the name “Caelicolists.” We also learn from Augustine that their leader, or “Major,” as he calls him—the man whom Augustine summoned while passing through Tubursicum—had instituted among them a new kind of baptism. By this sacrilege he had already led very many people astray (Epistle 44, chapter 6, no. 13).

Therefore, this sect, which, so long as it had nothing joined or shared with the Church, had scarcely possessed any significance, subsequently became all the more deadly the more closely it approached the Church and attempted to usurp its sacraments.

## CHAPTER XV

1. Augustine writes to Eudoxius the abbot.  
2. He preaches against Christians who join the pagans in their festivals.  
3. The statue of Hercules at Carthage treated disgracefully.  
4. Publicola’s questions are resolved.

### 1.

Gildo, having ruled Africa for ten or twelve years under the title of *Comes* and *Master of the Soldiers*, defected from Honorius toward the end of the year 397, on the pretext that he wished to transfer Africa to the dominion of Arcadius. But at the beginning of the following spring, his brother Mascezel, sent from Italy with troops, won a notable victory over him through divine assistance.

After his defeat, Optatus, the Donatist bishop of Thamugadi and one of his chief supporters, was thrown into prison and died there [Col. 0277]. Petilianus, a bishop of the Donatist party, later accused Augustine of having contributed by his counsels to Optatus’s condemnation (*Against the Letter of Petilianus*, book 3, chapter 40, no. 48).

When Mascezel then set out for Africa, he brought with him several monks from the island of Capraria, situated between Etruria and Corsica (Orosius, *History*, book 7, chapter 36). Perhaps these are the very monks of whom Augustine speaks in a letter written to Eudoxius the abbot and his brothers (Epistle 48, no. 4).

He testifies that he first learned of their piety by reputation, and later through the report of Eustasius and Andreas. These men, having come from their monastery, had brought the good fragrance of it to Africa and had spread the report of their holy manner of life. He informed them of Eustasius’s death: Eustasius would no longer long for Capraria, since he no longer sought to be clothed in a haircloth.

From this it may be inferred that the monastery of Eudoxius, from which Eustasius had come, was situated on that island. It also follows that it was customary for the monks, or at least for Eustasius, to wear a haircloth woven from goat’s hair.

Augustine therefore opens to Eudoxius and his monks how deeply in mind and affection he thinks of their holy repose. He earnestly requests their prayers, and strives to merit them through pious exhortations by which he urges them toward progress and perseverance. Above all, he warns them to seek the glory of God alone in all their good works; to be so devoted to solitude that neither eager ambition draws them away from it toward the governance of churches, nor flattering idleness holds them back when they are called to the duties of the Church (Epistle 48, nos. 2–3).

### 2.

In this very year, apparently 398, and certainly before the following year, that distinguished sermon was delivered in which Augustine reproved Christians who, so as not to offend the powerful or suffer injury at their hands, did not dare to refuse their commands when those men ordered them to be led to idols. These Christians not only accompanied the pagans when they went to the shrines, but also reclined with them in the idol-temple.

This encouraged the impious error of the pagans, who saw their idols honored even by Christians themselves. Thus all the labor that bishops expended in converting the remnants of paganism was often rendered fruitless. For the pagans, strengthened by the example of these Christians, said to themselves: “Why should we abandon the gods whom the Christians themselves worship along with us?”

Moreover, at these banquets Christians learned both to utter blasphemous words against Christ and to call his divinity into question. Deeply disturbed by this scandal, Augustine complained of it with all the gentleness available to him, yet in a sharp and serious discourse (Sermon 62), apparently at Carthage. For he mentions another sermon that he had delivered a few days earlier at the Mappalia, where the martyr Cyprian rested.

He also observes that these Christians were accustomed to say that they were not reclining beside false gods, but beside the genius of Carthage—a mere stone, though worshiped as a god by the pagans—and that an altar had been placed before its statue.

Augustine teaches in the same place that the way to conquer the pagans and bring them into the Christian faith would be almost a shortcut if Christians abandoned their festivals and did not involve themselves in their follies: “So that, if they do not agree with our truth,” he says, “they may at least be ashamed of their smallness.”

In this sermon he mentions someone who, after converting to the faith, had given a piece of land to the Church on which there were idols that he wanted destroyed. The Christians quickly complied with his wish, while the pagans raged and complained that bishops were seeking opportunities everywhere to smash idols.

Augustine denies this, asserting that there were many places in which they knew that statues existed, yet left them untouched because God had not entrusted them with authority over them; that they undertook nothing about which the owners of those places could complain; that they first acted to break the idols in the hearts of the people; and that they prayed to God for the conversion of human beings.

When owners of places had converted to the faith, they were asked to destroy the idols found on their property; if they failed to do so, they would be guilty. Idols were often smashed by the converts themselves. It was the mark of depraved people and frenzied Circumcellions to want to destroy things not under their authority and recklessly expose themselves to danger of death.

It is clear from this that, although certain laws had already been enacted against the pagans, the rescript by which the Emperor decreed that statues were to be removed had not yet been promulgated. We shall discuss it in the following year. After that rescript, the pagans were permitted to preserve those statues only secretly.

Toward the end of the same sermon, Augustine also seems to speak of certain new laws against the Donatists, enacted rather against the crimes of individuals than against the entire sect. For he writes that heretics in some places had paid the penalties for their impiety and madness according to the provisions of the laws, and consequently complained that the Catholics were stirring up a public persecution against them to their destruction.

In addition, in the same sermon he mentions the Jews. When they had been rebuked in certain places for their misconduct, they seized the opportunity to accuse, invent, or suspect that the bishops were always intent on seeking an opportunity to harm them.

Thus Jews, pagans, and heretics, although they had the whole Church hostile to them, joined together with united minds in an alliance of complaints against it, forming unity against unity.

### 3.

A sermon on the verse of Psalm 82, “O God, who is like you?” (Sermon 24), also seems to belong to this period, since sacrifices were still being offered to idols and their worship was flourishing at Carthage.

Among the other statues there was one made of stone, bearing in its inscription the name of the god Hercules. A new magistrate, seduced by the pagans, had permitted the statue’s beard—upon which all the strength of Hercules was thought to reside—to be covered with gold.

Yet, to the disgrace of its worshipers, the false deity glittered with gold. A Christian was consequently moved, not to worship but to take vengeance, and involved himself in that superstition by shaving its beard.

It is uncertain whether one man alone dared to do this, since Augustine immediately adds that the beard of Hercules was shaved by God through his faithful people, through his Christians, through the authorities whom he had appointed.

On this occasion Augustine delivered the sermon in question. The people interrupted him, shouting and crying out: “As Rome, so Carthage!” They evidently meant that they desired and demanded that every pagan superstition be destroyed, and that Hercules and the other Roman gods—who had already disappeared even in the city of Rome—should no longer be permitted at Carthage, so that in this respect Carthage might be entirely like Rome.

Augustine praises the piety and zeal of the people so highly that he nevertheless seems to fear that they might undertake some action tumultuously and without sufficiently lawful authority. If our conjecture is not mistaken, the bishop of Carthage had already restrained the impetuous zeal of his people that very morning.

For what other reason would Augustine congratulate them on having obeyed their bishop in what he had said to them that morning, and then urge them to follow him and not depart from that path? At the same time, he never ceases exhorting them to be content with having made their wish for the abolition of superstition known and confirmed, and to await from the bishops the plan and method by which it should be fulfilled. They should not fear that the bishops would fail in their duty in this matter.

He also gives them hope that their prayers will have a favorable outcome, since God had foretold that the superstitions of the pagans would be destroyed, and had already fulfilled his oracle in many regions of the world, including Rome.

From this sermon, which everyone acknowledges was delivered at Carthage, it is readily understood that the bishops then residing in that city had already decided to send a delegation to the Emperor Honorius to obtain the extinction of the superstition. It also appears that the famous laws enacted on this matter in 398 and carried into execution in Africa the following year were enacted through the persuasion and influence of those who had been sent to arrange this.

### 4.

At the time when Publicola submitted his questions to Augustine (Epistle 46), sacrifices to idols were certainly still flourishing. For what is read in Augustine’s reply concerning the destruction of temples, idols, and sacred groves (Epistle 47, no. 3) clearly refers not to authority granted by a public or general law to destroy them, but to authority given by some special order in particular cases.

Who this Publicola was is uncertain. He possessed estates in the Arzuges, a nation bordering on barbarous pagans. Consequently, the local inhabitants made use of the services of these barbarians, after first binding them by an oath of loyalty.

Various difficulties concerning this oath troubled Publicola, as did the use of many things that seemed to be polluted by the worship of idols. He proposed these and similar questions to Augustine as to a father, an elder, and a pontiff from whose mouth the law ought to be sought.
