Augustine replied to his requests and, among other matters, answered that he did not approve the opinion of those who held that a person could kill another to prevent being killed by him—unless perhaps the person acted with lawful authority for the protection of others. He therefore approves only the repelling of an attacker or ambusher by terror (ibid., no. 5).

He likewise judges that, if a person were pressed by hunger and could find nothing anywhere except food that he knew with certainty had been offered to idols, it would be better for him, even without anyone else knowing, to reject it through Christian virtue (ibid., no. 6).

## CHAPTER XVI

1. Pagan superstition is overthrown everywhere at the time when it was expected to be restored according to the oracles of demons.  
2. In the East it is prohibited and destroyed by the authority of Arcadius.  
3. In the West likewise, by the authority of Honorius.  
4. Jovius and Gaudentius arrange for this emperor’s law on the matter to be carried out.  
5. The temple of the goddess Caelestis at Carthage is dedicated to Christ by Aurelius.  
6. Certain remnants of idolatry are left in some places.  
7. The martyrs of Suffectum. Augustine writes to the leading men of the colony of Suffectum.  
8. A rescript granted by Julian in response to the Donatists’ flattering petitions is ordered to be affixed in public places.

[Col. 0280]

### 1.

When the pagans saw that Christianity could not be destroyed even by the many and great persecutions it had endured for nearly three hundred years, but had rather gained astonishing growth through them, they devised certain Greek verses—allegedly poured forth by a divine oracle consulted by someone—in which they declare Christ innocent of what they present as a kind of sacrilege, but add that Peter had brought it about by magical arts that the name of Christ should be worshiped for 365 years, after which, once that number of years had been completed, it should immediately come to an end (*City of God*, book 18, chapter 53, no. 2).

These 365 years began, at least, on the day when the Holy Spirit was sent—that is, in Augustine’s view, on the Ides of May, during the consulship of the two Gemini, Rubellius and Rufus, which was the twenty-ninth year of the common era. Thus the 365 years were to be completed on the Ides of May in the year 394.

Augustine, however, holds that they ended during the consulship of Honorius and Eutychianus, which fell in the year 398 of Christ. In reality, they would have been completed then if we suppose that Christ suffered in the thirty-third year of the common era.

According to that oracle of the demons, therefore, pagan superstition ought then to have risen again and the Christian religion to have fallen. But God, in order to demonstrate the falsehood of this oracle, willed the Christian religion to flourish with fresh growth day by day.

This became plainly evident from the following year, when Mallius Theodorus held the consulship—that is, in the year 399, the year in which we are now situated.

“In the following year,” Augustine writes, “during the consulship of Mallius Theodorus, when, according to that oracle of the demons, or fiction of human beings, there ought no longer to have been any Christian religion, there was no need to investigate what might perhaps have happened in other parts of the world. Meanwhile, what we know is that in the famous and eminent city of Carthage in Africa, Gaudentius and Jovius, counts of the Emperor Honorius, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, destroyed the temples of false gods and broke their statues” (*City of God*, book 18, chapter 54, no. 1).

Augustine therefore records only what was known to him and what had happened at Carthage; he did not investigate what had taken place in other regions of the world. In the *Fasti* of Idacius, however, we read that the temples of false deities were demolished in this year. Prosper of Tyre also notes, under the year following the disaster of Gildo—that is, under the present year—that the temples of the ancient superstition were destroyed throughout the Roman world.

### 2.

The Emperor Theodosius had undertaken this great work. After he died, having greatly extended the Church far and wide, his sons Arcadius and Honorius proved heirs no less of their father’s piety toward the Christian religion than of his empire [Col. 0281].

Their devotion to religion grew still stronger in their minds because of the favorable circumstances and the victories granted them by God over those who attacked their authority either openly in war or by secret plots. Since they attributed their success to their father’s piety, they defended with greater zeal the privileges granted to the Church by their predecessors and added to them through new edicts.

Their piety set a torch before their subjects. The pagans were brought to the faith of Christ without difficulty; and the heretics, exhausted by the divisions through which God permitted them to be torn apart, voluntarily returned to the unity of the Catholic Church.

But, to discuss here only matters concerning the pagans, and to begin with the East, we find a rescript of Arcadius to Rufinus, prefect of the praetorian guard in the East, issued on the seventh day before the Ides of August in the year 395. In it he prohibits the pagans, under threat of the gravest penalties, from entering shrines and temples or sacrificing to idols anywhere; and for this reason he renews all the laws enacted by his father against heretics and pagans (Theodosian Code, *On Pagan Sacrifices and Temples*, law 13).

In the following year, on the sixth day before the Ides of December, he deprived the priests and ministers of idols of the privileges that had previously been granted to them, as to people whose profession had been condemned by the laws (ibid., law 14).

It is necessary that very many temples throughout the East were demolished at that time, since in a rescript sent to Asterius, Count of the East, on the Kalends of November in the year 397, Arcadius decreed that the ruins of destroyed temples were to be used for restoring bridges, public roads, aqueducts, and the walls of cities (*On Public Works*, law 36).

In the year 399, on the third day before the Ides of July, Arcadius enacted a law for the removal of every source of superstition, ordering all rural shrines to be destroyed, but requiring that this be done without disturbance or tumult (*On Pagan Sacrifices and Temples*, law 16).

This law was issued at Damascus—or, as some hold, posted and promulgated there. They believe it to be the very law by which, according to Theodoretus, Chrysostom, who had been made bishop of the Church of Constantinople on the third day before the Kalends of March in the year 398, armed the zeal of the monks whom he sent to Phoenicia to demolish these shrines. Damascus is counted among the chief cities of that province (Theodoretus, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 29).

### 3.

As for the Emperor Honorius, no law concerning this matter issued by him is extant from before the year 399. We have nevertheless seen that the idols at Rome were destroyed while they still remained standing in Africa, although at that time, apparently, no law generally directed against the worship of idols had been established in the West.

It is nevertheless inferred from the law issued on the fourth day before the Kalends of February in the year 399 that Honorius had already promulgated, in the preceding year, a rescript ordering the complete destruction of all remnants of idolatry (Theodosian Code, *On Pagans*, etc., law 15).

Unless we are mistaken, this is also noted by the author of the book *On Predictions*, who uses the name of Prosper, when he testifies that Honorius, entirely obedient to his Christian piety, then transferred all the temples of the gods, with the areas adjoining them, to the churches and granted Christians permission to break all the statues (*On Predictions*, book 3, chapter 33).

In a work that we believe he wrote in the following year, Augustine states that the statues of the pagans had been ordered to be overturned and broken by recent laws, and that sacrifices had also been prohibited under penalty of death. He testifies there that throughout almost the whole world temples were in fact being demolished, idols broken, sacrifices abolished, and worshipers of demons, when discovered, subjected to punishment (*Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, book 1, chapter 9, no. 15).

Elsewhere he relates that Catholics and Donatists alike had labored, wherever they could, to destroy the temples of the pagans, and had broken the demon’s musicians’ pipes and benches (*Against Gaudentius*, book 1, no. 51).

Since the law made no exception concerning idols, it seems to have been extended generally to everything connected with the worship of idols, and the destruction of the very statues that served as ornaments to public buildings also seems to have been intended.

To prevent this, Honorius issued a rescript on the fourth day before the Kalends of February in the year 399 to Macrobius and Proclianus, the deputies of the prefects (Theodosian Code, *On Pagans*, etc., law 15): one of them governed in Spain, the other in the five provinces of Gaul, which, as is generally thought, were First and Second Aquitania and Second, Third, and Fourth Lugdunensis.

### 4.

The responsibility for carrying out Honorius’s law concerning the destruction of pagan temples seems to have been entrusted to the counts Jovius, or Jovianus, and Gaudentius, since we read in the *Fasti* of Idacius that temples were demolished by the counts in this year, and Prosper asserts that all the temples were stripped by the counts Jovius and Gaudentius (*On Predictions*, book 3, chapter 38).

He himself refers this event to the time of the great Theodosius. Either the same responsibility was entrusted to those men twice—first under Theodosius and then under Honorius, which seems less probable—or the author, still relatively young in these matters, did not preserve a sufficiently accurate memory of events.

The commission given to those two counts is recorded in the year 399 not only in the *Fasti* of Idacius but also by Augustine. He testifies that in this year, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April, the temples at Carthage were demolished and the statues broken by the counts Gaudentius and Jovius (*City of God*, book 18, chapter 54).

We do not know whether this Jovius was the same man who was prefect of the praetorian guard in 409. It seems likely to us, however, that Gaudentius was the man who became Count of Africa at the beginning of the year 401, as the subscription to the law in which he is mentioned indicates (Theodosian Code, *On the Levy of Horses*, law 3).

Since that law bears the twelfth indiction, however, it perhaps leaves room for the view that it was issued in the year 399 rather than in 401, for which year Marcellinus’s *Chronicle* records the fourteenth indiction. It is also established that Bathanarius was Count of Africa from the thirteenth day of July in the year 401.

Thus it is highly probable that Gaudentius, his predecessor, succeeded Gildo in that office. Among other things recorded about this Gaudentius is that he was the father of Aetius, that celebrated general in the time of the Emperor Valentinian.

Although Augustine, Idacius, and Prosper record that the temples of the pagans were demolished during this period, and although there can be no doubt that very many actually were destroyed, we cannot say that all of them were demolished. For even in the year 401 the Council of Carthage decreed that permission to demolish certain temples had to be requested from the Emperor (African Code of Canons, canon 84).

And according to the author of *On Predictions*, the commission given to Jovius and Gaudentius concerned the removal rather than the breaking of idols (*On Predictions*, book 3, chapter 38).

Since the temples were presumably handed over to the Church, it should not seem surprising if the bishops demolished many of them. Nevertheless, either because the Emperor’s rescript did not expressly order this, or because the complaints of the pagans moved his mind, on the third day before the Kalends of September in the year 399 he issued another rescript to Apollodorus, the proconsul of Africa.

In it he decreed that temples, stripped of all illicit objects—namely, altars and idols—were to be left standing with their buildings entirely intact (Theodosian Code, *On Pagans*, etc., law 18).

### 5.

Baronius refers to this period, as though it followed from the responsibility assigned to Jovius and Gaudentius (Baronius, under the year 399, no. 63), an event that the author of *On Predictions* says occurred concerning the temple of Caelestis during the reign of Honorius and before the rule of Constantius, who was taken by Honorius as his colleague in the empire in the year 420 or 421.

Baronius discusses this Caelestis at greater length, believing her to be the same as Astarte, the goddess of the Sidonians. It is generally acknowledged that she was the supreme deity of Carthage. A temple of astonishing size had been built for her there, surrounded by smaller temples of all the gods and extending over a circuit of nearly two miles. Its square was decorated with a paved pavement, precious columns, and walls (*On Predictions*, book 3, chapter 38).

This temple had already been closed for some time, perhaps since the year 391, when we find two laws prohibiting access to temples (Theodosian Code, *On Pagans*, etc., laws 10 and 11). These are the first laws enacted on the matter since the time of Julian the Apostate.

Since the temple had therefore long remained inaccessible, thorny bushes had grown up around it and buried it. When Christians wished to enter and consecrate it for the use of the true religion, after Honorius had transferred all temples to the churches, the pagans spread the rumor that dragons and vipers were hiding among those thorns and bushes to guard the temple and prevent entrance.

The Christians were thereby inflamed with still greater zeal, and removed everything without harm so that they might consecrate the temple to the true heavenly King and Lord.

For when the holy solemnity of Easter was being celebrated, a crowd gathered there from every direction, including many visitors drawn by curiosity. Aurelius, a father among the priests and a bishop worthy of remembrance, already a citizen of the heavenly homeland, had both his chair placed there in the place of Caelestis and sat upon it.

“I myself,” says the author, “was present then with companions and friends. And, as the restless age of youth turned us in every direction, while we carefully examined each thing according to its size, something marvelous and incredible presented itself to our sight: an inscription in larger bronze letters written on the front of the temple:

> AURELIUS THE BISHOP DEDICATED THIS.

When the people read it, they marveled that events had been accomplished by a prophetic spirit, events that God’s foreknowing order had brought to this definite conclusion” (*On Predictions*, book 3, chapter 38).

This temple was later leveled to the ground in the year 421. Thus Augustine was speaking not of the temple of Caelestis but of the idol when, shortly after the capture of Rome, he said: “Carthage remains in the name of Christ, and Caelestis was once overthrown; for she was not heavenly, but earthly” (Sermon 105, chapter 9, no. 12).

### 6.

The author of *On Predictions* writes that in a certain city of Mauretania many ancient statues were dug out of caves, where they had been hidden. On account of this discovery, the whole city, including the clergy themselves, was held guilty or convicted of perjury (*On Predictions*, book 3, chapter 38).

Perhaps cities were required to swear an oath by which they confirmed that no idols were hidden anywhere. The clergy of this city, however, knowing that statues had been concealed, had not dared to report the fact.

Fear of offending the powerful sometimes caused Christians themselves to connive at the crimes of idolatry. Augustine indeed makes a serious complaint on this matter in the sermon already mentioned to the people, where he condemns some who frequented temples and reclined with pagans in an idol-temple (Sermon 62, chapter 4, nos. 7–8).

This may still have been occurring after Honorius had enacted laws against idolatry. The Emperor himself supported this practice by a law issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of September in the year 399. In it he declared to Apollodorus, the proconsul of Africa, that, although he had prohibited the profane rites of pagan superstition, he did not wish public festivals to be abolished. The celebrations of the games were to continue, provided that no sacrifices or any other idolatrous superstition were mixed into them (Theodosian Code, *On Pagans*, etc., law 17).

Accordingly, the Council of Carthage, assembled on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July in the year 401, considered it its duty to petition Honorius to abolish completely those banquets at which Christians were compelled to participate with pagans. Such banquets cast the appearance of a kind of persecution, since pagans frequently committed many insolent acts against the dignity of religion (African Code of Canons, canon 60).

Augustine writes that, when temples, idols, and sacred groves were being destroyed insofar as the emperors’ permission allowed, private individuals ought to derive no advantage from their ruins, lest they seem to be led by greed rather than piety to destroy the monuments of pagan superstition. This, however, did not prevent those monuments from being converted to common and public uses or consecrated to the honor of the true God, just as human beings themselves, through their conversion to God, are transformed into his temples (Epistle 47, no. 3).

### 7.

Theodosius had spared no effort to purge Rome of the superstitions of idolatry, which had taken deeper root there than in any other city under his rule. There can be no doubt that Honorius had ordered the idols there to be cast down everywhere, just as elsewhere; for even before the defeat of Radagaisus—that is, before the year 406—and indeed while they were still standing in Africa, they had already been thrown down and destroyed there (Serm. 105, ch. 10, no. 13; Serm. 24, no. 6). But since, during this destruction of the idols, those images of the gods which served as ornaments in public places and buildings remained untouched, eleven years later God completely abolished those remaining traces of pagan superstition, partly by the hands of the Goths and partly by thunderbolts hurled from heaven.

This destruction of the images, which took place in the year 399, provided the occasion for the conversion of many pagans. They had clung stubbornly to their error until then and had been led to hope that, once 365 years had been completed, their ancestral worship would, according to the oracle of the demons, be restored as though by a return from exile to its former splendor. Only from the outcome did they finally learn that the oracle had been false and empty (The City of God, book 18, ch. 54).

Augustine testifies that from this time until that at which he completed the eighteenth book of *The City of God*—approximately thirty years later—the Christian religion had continued to make still greater advances, although the pagans persistently maintained that it would eventually perish (Exposition on Psalm 70, sermon 2, no. 4), and assigned a definite and fixed time for that event on the basis of oracles (Exposition on Psalm 4, no. 1). Meanwhile, those who intended to sacrifice were forced to seek hiding places and even to conceal their gods, lest, if discovered by Christians, they should be shattered in accordance with the laws of the emperors, just as the divine oracles had long before foretold through the Jewish prophets (On the Harmony of the Gospels, book 1, ch. 27).

A pagan poet of that period complains that the verses of the Sibyls were consigned to the fire at the command of Stilicho (Baronius, under the year 369, no. 82). Baronius attributes to an edict of Honorius [Col. 0286] what Augustine reports to have happened at the colony of Suffetana (the same, under the year 399, no. 77). There, when the statue of Hercules had been thrown down and broken, its impious worshipers attacked the Christians and slaughtered sixty of them. They are recorded in the Roman Martyrology among the martyrs of Christ on 30 August.

On this matter Augustine wrote that brief but vehement letter (Epistle 50) to the leading men and elders of that colony. He reproaches them for trampling underfoot the Roman laws, the sanctity of judicial proceedings, and above all the reverence and fear owed to the emperors—for they had elevated to the highest honors and dignities of their city men who had plainly displayed greater cruelty and savagery than the rest in that massacre. He promises them—and does so in language full of mockery and irony—that he will see to the restoration of their god, but only on the condition that they too restore the lives of those whom they had killed.

A city called Suffetensis is placed in Byzacena, while another, named Suffetula, also existed. It is in the latter that the Martyrology places the sixty men then killed by the pagans.

### 8.

The African Canons assign to this year, 399, a council held at Carthage on 27 April. From it we learn only that the bishops Epigonius and Vincentius were sent to the emperor to request, in the name of the council, a law providing that no person bound by any crime whatsoever should be forcibly removed from the church into which he had taken refuge (African Code of Canons, canon 56).

At the request of these envoys, as is sufficiently probable, Honorius issued that law on 25 February 400. He ordered that a rescript be posted in the more frequented and prominent places—the rescript which the Donatists had obtained from Julian the Apostate in the year 362. In it were contained their disgraceful petitions to that same emperor (Theodosian Code, On Heretics, law 37).

## BOOK FIVE. On Augustine’s activities from the year 400 to the year 405 after Christ.

[Col. 0285]

### CHAPTER ONE

1. He demonstrates the harmony of the Four Evangelists against unbelievers.  
2. He responds to Januarius’s inquiries about the sacraments and various customs of the Church.  
3. He writes *On the Work of Monks* for the benefit of those who supported themselves by their own hands.

[Col. 0285]

#### 1.

Meanwhile, while the profane worship of false gods was being exterminated throughout the Roman Empire, it was also necessary to refute the objections which unbelievers raised against the worship of the name of Christ. Although matters had reached the point at which they scarcely dared even to mutter their accusations among themselves, constrained by the faith of the nations and the devotion of all peoples, nevertheless they still held some back from the faith by their slanderous arguments, preventing them from believing; and they disturbed those who already believed, harassing them as much as they could. For this reason Augustine, under God’s inspiration, resolved to refute their clever accusations against the four Gospels in particular by demonstrating the harmony among them.

“For this,” he says, “they are accustomed to bring forward as though it were the chief palm of their vanity: that the Evangelists themselves disagree among themselves” (On the Harmony of the Gospels, book 1, ch. 7, no. 10).

Accordingly, he set aside for a time the work on the Trinity which he had in hand and undertook and completed, through continuous labor, another work of the greatest necessity, by which he might show the complete harmony of the Evangelists (Retractations, book 2, ch. 16). He does not silently pass over the fact that the images worshiped by the blindness of the nations were at that time being destroyed at the emperors’ command (On the Harmony of the Gospels, books 1, chapters 20 and 27). This proves that he did not begin the work [Col. 0287] before the end of 399.

For we have no law on this matter expressed in clearer terms than those laws which were promulgated and enforced in Africa in the year just mentioned. Before those laws had been enacted, Augustine admitted that he was not permitted to break images unless permission was given by those to whom they belonged (Sermon 62, ch. 11, no. 17).

Since the purpose of this work is to show how passages in the Gospels which appear to disagree with one another can be reconciled, he entitled it *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*. The first book of the work, however, is entirely occupied in refuting those who, while not denying that Christ should be honored as a human being far superior to others in wisdom, nevertheless refused to believe the Gospel because it had not been written by Christ himself but by his disciples. They alleged that Christ’s disciples had imposed their master upon others as God and had preached the abandonment of the worship of the gods, a doctrine which Christ himself had not handed down to them (On the Harmony of the Gospels, book 2, preface, no. 1).

In the other three books he demonstrates that the four Evangelists are invariably in agreement with one another. He does not deny that he expended much effort and labor on this portion of the work (Tractates on the Gospel of John, 112 and 117). Indeed, he lacked the aids available to all those who later treated the same subject. Yet even they, following in his footsteps, scarcely discovered anything of importance which he had not already taught.

#### 2.

Through such learned works Augustine had already acquired a great reputation when a certain Christian distinguished for piety, and well known to that holy Teacher, arranged for various inquiries about the sacraments and the rites of the Church to be referred to him as an outstanding teacher to whom nothing was unknown. His name was Januarius.

Since these many questions had been gathered together in a certain memorandum, as it is called, Augustine first answered one of them—the first in order, if one considers their arrangement. Januarius had asked what ought to be done on Thursday of the last week of Lent: whether the offering should be made in the morning and again after supper; whether one should fast and make the offering only after supper; or whether one should fast and, after the offering, dine, as we are accustomed to do (Epistle 54, ch. 5, no. 6).

The remaining questions were postponed to another time. But when, after a long interval, Januarius asked him by letter not to be unwilling to answer those as well, the holy Bishop interrupted the many occupations which then engrossed him, so that he might respond to his wishes in a second letter, or rather book, addressed to him (Epistle 55, no. 1).

Among other things Januarius asked why the feast of Easter was not always celebrated on the same day, as was the Nativity of the Lord, and why the Sabbath and the moon were observed in determining it (ibid., no. 2).

These two books discuss many customs which prevailed either in all Churches or only in some. After explaining them, Augustine concludes the work in these words:

“If you should not think that this is sufficient for the matters about which you have inquired, you are profoundly ignorant both of my abilities and of my occupations. For I am so far from being what you supposed—someone to whom nothing is unknown—that I have read nothing in your letter with greater sadness, because that supposition is both most plainly false, and I am amazed that you are unaware of this: not only are many things unknown to me in innumerable other matters, but even in the holy Scriptures I know far more things that I do not know than things that I know. Yet for this reason I maintain an unfailing hope in the name of Christ: not only have I believed my God that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon those two commandments, but I have also experienced, and experience daily, that whenever no sacrament or any particularly obscure saying from the sacred Scriptures is opened to me, I find those same commandments there. For the end of the commandment is charity” (ibid., ch. 20, no. 38).

To the books written for Januarius around the year 400 Augustine immediately adds the book *On the Work of Monks* (Retractations, book 2, ch. 21).

#### 3.

We saw above that the institution of monastic life, from the time when Augustine introduced it into Africa and began to observe it there, was quickly spread through many places. Soon a great number of monasteries were established at Carthage, though not one uniform manner of life was maintained in all of them.

Some followed the Apostle’s command and obtained their livelihood through their own labor. Others, on the contrary, preferred to be supported by the gifts of devout people and abstained from all work by which they might provide themselves with necessities. They did not do this because they were occupied with any ecclesiastical ministry, as though, serving at the altar, they might justly claim a stipend from it; nor because they had been delicately and softly brought up and were unequal to the labor of their hands. They had joined a holy fellowship in which they enjoyed abundant leisure, and most of them had come there from lives exercised in the most demanding labors.

They considered it much better to devote themselves to prayer, psalms, and reading, and also to study and meditation on the word of God, which might at times have to be distributed and explained to brothers coming to them from another kind of life. Finally, they had decided to fulfill without working the command in the Gospel concerning the birds and the lilies of the field, which neither sow nor reap; although, regarding what is added—“nor gather into storehouses” (Matthew 6:26)—they were less concerned, since they had by no means abandoned the care of storing provisions; indeed, they wished to have idle hands and full storerooms.

But whenever those who abstained in this way from manual labor ought to have acknowledged either their own bodily weakness or their own laziness, they instead placed themselves above those who sought their livelihood through daily and strenuous work.

The holy bishops therefore feared that true monks, who directed their lives according to the rule of the sounder way of life, might finally be enticed into idleness by the deceptive appearance of a higher piety. Their embarrassment was especially acute when they saw themselves regarded by the uneducated as violators of the Gospel.

Moreover, that manner of life gave authority to wandering monks who could not be induced to work quietly and silently. They deceived the people, captivated by reverence for the monastic habit, and used various frauds and deceptions to scrape together money, bringing the monastic institution into the greatest disgrace. It was also exceedingly troublesome that many laypeople, who in an admirable impulse of charity provided these men with their necessities, undertook to defend their very idleness, while others condemned this way of life.

Hence serious controversies arose among them, by which the Church was disturbed. Some of these idle men also habitually grew their hair contrary to Paul’s command; and some did so for no other purpose than to acquire greater veneration for themselves and to make a more abundant profit by this pretense of humility.

Monks otherwise very holy, and held in high honor by bishops of outstanding prudence, were falling into this fault. Through it they disturbed the Church by provoking the most dangerous disagreements. Some orthodox Christians, unwilling to condemn men so renowned for holiness, were forced to twist Paul’s explicit words to another meaning; others preferred to defend the proper sense of Scripture rather than accommodate themselves to any human being.

Since the disturbances in the Church of Carthage looked above all to Aurelius, as its bishop, he asked Augustine to write something on the matter. That holy man greatly desired the monastic institution to spread throughout Africa, just as it had throughout the other regions of the Christian world, and therefore could hardly refuse the task assigned to him by Aurelius, especially since he did not doubt that Christ himself was commanding it through Aurelius’s mouth.

He accordingly composed the work for rebuking the idle, entitled *On the Work of Monks*. At its conclusion he asks Aurelius, if he should find anything in it that ought to be removed or altered, not to hesitate to inform him.

In this book he speaks honorably of recluses, as they are called, including those who devoted themselves to no labor whatsoever. He also indicates the controversy which had arisen at that time between himself and Jerome concerning Peter and Paul.

## CHAPTER TWO

1. He urges Crispinus, the Donatist bishop of Calama, to discuss in writing the question of the cause of the schism.  
2. Alypius and Augustine discuss the same question with Clarentius in letters sent through Naucelius.  
3. Augustine endeavors to rescue his kinsman Severinus from the schism.  
4. He writes to Generosus so that he will not allow himself to be deceived by a certain Donatist presbyter.

#### 1.

At the same time Augustine was laboring indefatigably to reconcile the friends of catholic unity to the Church. Several substantial works published around this very year, 400, as well as various letters, have this aim.

Among them are two letters to Crispinus, bishop of the Donatist party at Calama. Since the first of these was written after the death of Optatus but before the death of Praetextatus, it cannot be placed more suitably at any other time. Augustine always mentions Praetextatus and Felicianus in the same manner, and of both—an especially decisive point—he says:

“All whom they baptized they now have with themselves and with you” [Col. 0290] (Epistle 51, no. 4).

But Praetextatus had already died when Augustine, around this same year, put the finishing touches to his books against Parmenianus (Against the Letter of Parmenianus, book 3, ch. 6). Therefore, when he reports that the Donatists complained of being harassed by the assistance of earthly rulers, this must not be referred to the laws enacted in 405, but to earlier ones. Some had been enacted in 377, and some at a later time.

Indeed, in 402 Augustine admitted that imperial edicts had provided that the Donatists were not permitted to reside in cities (Against the Letter of Petilianus, book 2, no. 184). At times he also applied to them laws generally enacted against heretics (Against the Letter of Parmenianus, book 1, ch. 12).

Augustine had repeatedly invited Crispinus, who happened to be at Carthage, to discuss the separation made from the Church (Epistle 51, no. 1). After a somewhat prolonged and sufficiently sharp dispute, Crispinus had excused himself on some pretext for the time being, though he promised to resume the interrupted conversation when a more convenient opportunity presented itself.

After both men had returned to Numidia and their respective Churches, a rumor arose that the difficulty had not been examined only because Crispinus was unwilling. Augustine therefore wrote to him and pressed him to proceed, since at that time nothing stood in the way, and because the proximity of the two Churches allowed them, by exchanging written arguments back and forth, to remove all obscurity from the question.

He had determined to deal with this matter in writing and in no other way, lest anything discussed only orally should slip from memory, and also so that those who wished to know the question might learn it from the letters if they had been unable to attend the debate. He even adds that this very letter, joined to the reply which he earnestly requests from Crispinus, might perhaps by itself suffice to untie all the knots of the difficulties.

Accordingly, he first demonstrates that a more serious crime is involved in schism and separation than in the transmission of the sacred books. Yet this was the only charge which they brought against Caecilianus—or rather against the man by whom he had been ordained—without relying on any trustworthy testimony or authority. They therefore had no right whatever to separate from the Church, however guilty Caecilianus might have been.

They themselves acknowledged this when they received Felicianus and Praetextatus—whom they had previously condemned on account of the schism—while allowing them to retain their episcopates. If those men had been free of the alleged crime, it could equally have been the case that Caecilianus too was free of the charge laid against him.

Moreover, by their own conduct toward the Maximianists they had openly shown that not all persons are justly condemned by those who persecute others, and even that it is not always necessary to baptize again all those who had received baptism outside the true Church.

After establishing these points, on which the whole controversy between the Church and the Donatists turned, and collecting them in summary form at the end of the letter, Augustine adjures Crispinus to reply and, if he can, to show even the slightest shadow of a difficulty which could perplex the most ignorant among them.

The letter has no title prefixed to it; indeed, Augustine had inscribed it either not at all or with a very simple heading. He excuses this to Crispinus by explaining that he had done so because, whenever Catholics dealt with the Donatists in a more courteous manner, the Donatists criticized their modesty. He adds that he would not be displeased if Crispinus followed the same manner of dealing with him.

We do not know whether Crispinus replied to this letter. It is certain, however, that he persevered in the schism and fell from the self-control and moderation which he had displayed at the beginning into a state of violent temper wholly at odds with them. For it is just that those who abuse gifts bestowed by God should be stripped of the very qualities with which they appeared to be adorned.

#### 2.

Augustine and Alypius, as we infer, entered into a similar discussion with Clarentius, whom they call “father,” perhaps because of his more advanced age. A certain Clarentius is recorded as a Donatist bishop of Tabraca (Carthaginian Conference 1, ch. 187).

In the discussion itself they used Naucelius as intermediary. The only information we possess is that Naucelius reported to these holy men that Clarentius had confessed that, after Felicianus of Musti had been condemned by the Donatists, he had later been received by them again with his honor restored. Clarentius claimed, however, that the condemnation had been unjust because it had been imposed on an absent man.

Augustine and Alypius take up this point and turn it to the advantage of their own case in a letter addressed to Naucelius himself (Epistle 70). Since this letter makes no mention of Praetextatus, it was unquestionably written after the year 400.

#### 3.

Augustine had a Donatist relative named Severinus. Like many others, Severinus remained in the schism for no other reason than habit. Augustine had long seen him miserably entangled in it, not without sorrow and groaning, and greatly desired to speak with him in person in order to free him from his error.

He had already sent Severinus several letters on this subject. For when he received a letter from him, Augustine reproached him for his excessive delay in writing. Yet although the contents of Severinus’s letter by no means answered Augustine’s wishes, he was glad that it had been delivered, especially when he learned that the courier had been sent by Severinus for no other reason than to carry it to Hippo.

From this Augustine judged that Severinus would never have undertaken such a service unless his mind had been prepared to receive the truth. In his reply, therefore, he set out several arguments which he customarily used to undermine the foundations of the schism. Among other points, he maintained that innumerable wicked men had been tolerated by the Donatists for so many years lest the party of Donatus be divided.

By these words he very often indicates the decade during which Optatus exercised his tyranny. If this consideration did not move us, we would readily believe that this letter (Epistle 52), in which the Maximianists are not mentioned at all, had been written by Augustine before he became bishop.

#### 4.

The letter sent to Generosus (Epistle 53) may also be assigned to approximately this period. It was certainly written during the pontificate of Anastasius, while Praetextatus of Assuritanum apparently was still alive, and therefore before the three books against Parmenianus had been published.

The Generosus in question was from Cirta and belonged to the catholic communion. We also learn that he later became governor of Numidia (Epistles 115 and 116), but only after a certain law had been enacted on 21 January 409 (as noted in the preface to volume 2, on Epistles 115 and 116). Therefore, if he held some office at Cirta in the year 400, as is sufficiently probable, it must have been something other than that of governor.

At that time there was at Cirta a certain presbyter belonging to the Donatist party. It occurred to him to write to Generosus that an angel had appeared to him and commanded him to reveal to Generosus the true succession of Christianity in the city of Cirta. He was also to urge him to embrace the party of Donatus, as was explained in a letter by Petilianus, bishop of that same city.

The presbyter also displayed to him a succession of bishops of that see and spoke especially honorably of Silvanus. It was clear that an angel of darkness had transformed himself into an angel of light in order to deceive him—unless, perhaps, this was the invention of that Donatist presbyter, who, acting as Satan’s minister, intended by this falsehood to lead others into fraud.

Generosus, therefore, being a genuine Catholic, mocked his letter and sent it to Fortunatus, the Catholic bishop of Cirta, and also to Alypius and Augustine, who happened at that time to be together at Cirta. The three bishops replied to Generosus, though the letter was written in Augustine’s hand, hoping and laboring to recall the presbyter to the faith (Epistle 53, ch. 1, no. 1). They therefore asked Generosus to share their letter with him.

They demonstrate in it that, if reliance must be placed on episcopal succession, it ought rather to be traced back to the Roman See. For this reason they compile a list of the Roman bishops down to Anastasius, who was then seated in that office.

After this they produce the documents most relevant to understanding the history of the Donatists, especially those which make it clear that Silvanus of Cirta had been a traditor. They also recount the deeds of the Maximianists and do not omit the fact that Felicianus and Praetextatus had been received by them; they apparently still confidently regarded both men as alive at that time.

They do not send Generosus the work written against Petilianus’s letter. From this it may be judged that Augustine had not yet published anything on that subject, since there can scarcely be any doubt that Petilianus’s letter praised by the presbyter was that well-known letter which Augustine refuted.

## CHAPTER THREE

1. Who Petilianus, a bishop of the party of Donatus, was.  
2. On his letter against the Catholic Church.  
3. Augustine refutes its first part.  
4. When he undertook this task.  
5. He refutes Parmenianus’s letter written against Tichonius in favor of the schism.  
6. He publishes books against the Donatists on baptism.  
7. On the book *Against What Centurius Brought Forward from the Donatists*.  
8. On the letter to Celer.

#### 1.

The author of the letter just mentioned, Petilianus, then the most widely known of all the Donatist bishops, had at one time practiced as an advocate in civil courts. For this reason, at the Carthaginian Conference, a certain Catholic bishop not unjustly ordered him to return to the laws of his own forum.

He had been accustomed to boast of his former power in forensic advocacy and foolishly proclaimed that, because of it, he had acquired a name associated with the Holy Spirit, since he had obtained the title “Paraclete” (Against the Letter of Petilianus, book 3, ch. 16, no. 19).

When he was first a catechumen in the Catholic Church, the Donatists seized him by force and bound him to their party by the deadly bond of honor—that is, by the episcopal dignity. Augustine spoke of this violence inflicted on Petilianus in a sermon to the people of Caesarea:

“When the party of Donatus prevailed at Constantina, it took Petilianus, our layman and catechumen, born of Catholic parents; it used force against him unwilling, searched for him as he fled, found him in hiding, dragged him out trembling, baptized him shaking with fear, and ordained him unwilling” (Sermon to the People of the Church of Caesarea, no. 8).

Thus, willingly or unwillingly, he was made bishop by them at Constantina, or Cirta—for the same city bears both names and was recognized by civic Numidia as its metropolitan center. He held that dignity while Optatus was still alive.

Although reputation was accustomed to praise Petilianus as the man who most excelled among his own people in learning and eloquence (Against the Letter of Petilianus, book 1, ch. 1), Augustine sometimes censures his speech as inflated, tumultuous, and suited to stirring up the crowd, and as occasionally composed of foolish and deranged expressions (ibid., book 2, ch. 73).

At the Conference he was the chief support of the schism. There he employed every conceivable form of cleverness and fraud, every evasion and obstinacy, in defense of falsehood. He produced documents and ensured that nothing was settled in the meantime; eventually, when his rambling had been curtailed, he was forced into silence.

#### 2.

Many years before the Carthaginian Conference, Petilianus had dared to write a pastoral letter against the Catholic Church to the presbyters and deacons subject to him. In it he recklessly attacked the Catholic Church with disgraceful accusations, without producing any evidence, and maintained that true and legitimate baptism was found only among his own sect (ibid., book 1, ch. 1, no. 2).

A person would possess this letter in full if he were to join together appropriately the beginnings of the individual chapters excerpted by Augustine in the second book against Petilianus.

In it Petilianus denounces the orthodox as traditors, or as descended from traditors, without relying on any testimony. He complains of injuries inflicted on him by them, although his party was not then experiencing any persecution; the magistrates were content merely to deprive them of their sacred buildings, perhaps under force of the law enacted by Gratian in 377.

Catholics retained many buildings which the Donatists had seized from them by force, as well as others which the Donatists themselves had constructed during the period of the schism, although a considerable number—including some that had belonged to the Catholic communion—still served the schismatic party.

Petilianus attempted to deprive the Catholic Church of the title “Catholic.” When that hope failed, he turned instead to praise of the few who walk along the narrow road. He reproached the Catholics for appealing to the emperors concerning the Church buildings occupied by the Donatist sect.

Laws already existed which prohibited Donatists from residing in cities, and there is no doubt that many edicts of Honorius against them were then in circulation. Petilianus had serious complaints about this as well, namely, that the Catholics appealed to imperial authority.

In the midst of these arguments he exhorted his people to defend the innocence which he attributed to them even at the cost of losing all earthly goods. He counted himself and his followers among those whom Christ calls poor in spirit, who fear riches rather than desire them. Yet such praises applied very poorly to some Donatist bishops, and Augustine was entirely unaware that Petilianus had suffered any loss of his own goods, or had given any of them up.

Petilianus had reached such a degree of madness and arrogance that he seemed to believe that the bishops of the true Church were subject to no sins and therefore had no need of the prayers of the people. He thus considered himself also more righteous than Paul, John the Evangelist, Daniel, and others.

#### 3.

This letter was in the hands of many people, who even memorized various sentences from it word for word, as though it were a work of great strength against the Catholic Church (On the Unity of the Church, no. 1).

Augustine first read some portions of it at Cirta (Against the Letters of Petilianus, book 1, no. 1), perhaps, as we have said, at the time when he received from Generosus the letter of the Donatist presbyter in which it was praised (Epistle 53).

While Augustine was in the church together with Fortunatus, the Catholic bishop of that place, some orthodox Christians brought the letter to him, with Absentius present. Perhaps “Alypius” should be read here, since Alypius, together with Augustine and Fortunatus, replied to Generosus.

This was only the beginning and a very small portion of the letter, since the Catholics had not yet been permitted to copy more of it. Augustine observes at the outset that the letter completely overturns the party of Donatus from its very beginning, since it teaches that the justification of those who are baptized depends upon the undefiled conscience of the baptizer.

For that reason he found it difficult to persuade himself that the letter was really Petilianus’s, even though it bore his name. But those who knew the writing style of this Donatist assured Augustine that it was indeed his style (Against the Letters of Petilianus, book 1, no. 1).

He therefore resolved to refute it in writing, and did so with the greatest diligence, clarity, and sincerity of which he was capable, so that the less educated might not suppose that it contained anything substantial against the Catholic faith. Nor does his modesty prevent him from asserting that the truth is established so firmly and illuminated with such light in his response that Petilianus has nothing by which he could overcome it (ibid., book 3, no. 1).

He dedicates this response to the faithful people of his diocese and does not call it a book, but a letter (Retractations, book 2, ch. 25).

Here he makes use of the history of Optatus, though much more of that of the Maximianists, and urges his people to impress this final point deeply upon their minds, since it is especially suited to refuting all the petitions of the Donatists without any support from argument.

He adds:

“Retain these things, brothers, so that they may be done and proclaimed with tireless gentleness: love the people, kill the errors; presume upon the truth without pride, contend for the truth without cruelty. Pray for those whom you rebuke and convict” (Against the Letters of Petilianus, book 1, no. 31).

Augustine took care to obtain the remaining parts of Petilianus’s letter. But when the Donatists learned that he had refuted its beginning, none of those from whom he requested the other portions was willing to provide them. They were so afraid that something from their writings might fall into Catholic hands.

Indeed, Augustine thinks that Petilianus would never be induced even to acknowledge that very letter as his own or to seal it with his own hand. Augustine did not behave in that way. He asks the Catholics not to refuse the letter to anyone who requests it, but rather to thrust it upon those who do not request it.

He allows the Donatists to send a reply, so that if they do not wish to send it to Augustine himself, they may at least send it to supporters of their sect, provided that they do not order the response to be concealed from him.

He also discourages them from pressing Petilianus’s letter so zealously, lest the portion which he had not happened to see should contain something which, as he wittily says, could not be refuted (ibid., no. 27).

### 4. The First Book Against Petilian’s Letter

He composed this first book after the deaths of Gildo and Optatus—that is, not before the end of the year 398 (ibid., nos. 10, 27). Indeed, if the letter to Generosus, written during the pontificate of Anastasius, preceded this work, it would not be possible to assign it to a date before the year 399, since Anastasius was appointed to that dignity only toward the end of 398. Indeed, from the sequence of the *Retractations*, in which this first book is joined to the second, published around the year 402, it might seem that it should be placed not long before that year, were it not that Augustine repeatedly remembers Praetextatus of Assuri and Felicianus of Musti as still living (ibid., nos. 10, 26). Praetextatus, however, had died before Augustine completed his work against Parmenianus (*Against Parmenian’s Letter*, book 3, chapter 6), which we do not think can be assigned to a date later than the year 400.

Accordingly, one might reasonably say that Augustine joined the two books together because of the similarity of their subject, and that, in assigning a place to both simultaneously, he took account of the second rather than the first. He himself regarded the first merely as occupying the place of a letter, and did not list it among the number of his books except on account of the second and third. Nevertheless, so that this first book against Petilian’s letter would not be separated by too long an interval from the other two, he chose to assign it a place immediately before the three books against Parmenianus.

### 5. The Work Against Parmenianus

Parmenianus, who is under discussion here, was the very man whom the Donatists had appointed bishop of Carthage in succession to the deceased Donatus (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 17). He had by then already died (*Against Parmenian’s Letter*, book 1, chapter 1). But when Augustine’s hands received the letter that Parmenianus had written against Tichonius, the defender of the Catholic Church could not refuse the brothers who requested and, as he himself says, demanded that he refute it—especially because Parmenianus was abusing various passages of the sacred Scriptures to defend his party’s separation.

Augustine therefore undertook to clear the Church, spread throughout the whole world, of the accusations and calumnies by which the Donatists attempted to defend their separation from it as legitimate. For this reason he examines and resolves that celebrated question: whether the wicked contaminate the good with whom they are joined by fellowship in the same Church and participation in the same Sacraments. He demonstrates that the good are in no way contaminated by them.

He makes particular use of what had occurred through the schism of the Maximianists, and employs with great advantage the very weapons that the Donatists had supplied him when they admitted Felicianus of Musti and Praetextatus of Assuri, together with all those baptized in the Maximianist schism, back into communion. Praetextatus had died not long before, whereas Felicianus was still living. Augustine also speaks at length there about Gildonian Optatus and the violent acts committed by him, and he clearly determines how long his tyranny continued (*ibid.*, book 2, no. 4). That tyranny was finally overthrown only in the year 398.

He testifies that, at the time when he was writing, almost everywhere throughout the world the temples of the false gods were being leveled to the ground, their images being destroyed by force of recently enacted laws, and their rites and ceremonies being suppressed (*ibid.*, book 1, no. 15); this began to take place in the year 399. Accordingly, that work cannot be placed before this year, although Augustine himself places it immediately after the book *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*.

### 6. The Seven Books on Baptism

In that work against Parmenianus, the holy Doctor promises that elsewhere he will treat the question of Baptism at greater length. In fact, he later composed seven books on Baptism, which in the *Retractations* he places immediately after this very work (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 18).

He undertook this further labor mindful of his promise, yet he would not refuse it to the brothers who earnestly requested it, even though he had made no promise concerning it in the book against Parmenianus. In these seven books he proposes to refute what the Donatists were bringing forward against the Church’s teaching concerning Baptism, but especially to answer the authority of Cyprian, whom they opposed as though he were the strongest shield of truth. He aims to show that, for those who judge matters fairly and are not corrupted by prejudice, nothing could more powerfully compel them to silence or undermine the foundations of their separation from the Church than the judgment and conduct of this most blessed martyr in that very controversy over Baptism.

He also fights them with the authority of the Donatists themselves, who, by receiving Felicianus, had shattered the supports of their own cause. There was now no serious reason to contend with the principal and larger part of Donatus, but only with certain small fragments which, as though torn away from their own body, accused that larger part because it had approved the Baptism of the Maximianists. Each of these tiny groups arrogated true Baptism to itself alone, insisting that it existed nowhere else—not in the Catholic Church, not in the larger body of Donatus, and not in any other group except itself.

In the final part of the work Augustine examines all the opinions of the council celebrated at Carthage under Cyprian’s authority concerning the rejection of heretics’ Baptism, and responds to each of them word for word.

### 7. The Book Against What Centurius Brought from the Donatists

At the time when Augustine was frequently preaching against the Donatists, one of them, a layman named Centurius, brought into the Church certain writings directed against the Catholics. They contained nothing whatever except several passages from the sacred Scriptures gathered together, which the schismatics claimed supported their position.

Augustine answered them briefly in a published writing entitled *Against What Centurius Brought from the Donatists*. Possidius records it under the same title in his catalogue (*Possidius, in the Catalogue*, chapter 3), and he seems to have intended to indicate the same work in the *Life of Augustine* (*ibid.*, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 9). It is no longer extant in our time.

### 8. The Letter to Celer

Perhaps Augustine sent Celer one of the books against the Donatists mentioned above, so that he might teach him that the Donatists had no just cause for separating themselves from the Catholic Church, which was spread throughout the entire world (*Letter* 57).

He always speaks of Celer as a man distinguished by the nobility of his birth and conspicuous on account of the offices he had held. He followed the faith of Christ with steadfast spirit and had adopted a life worthy of imitation in his own station. Nevertheless, he was overly intimate with the Donatists and did not seem entirely free from their errors.

Since he happened to possess estates in the region of Hippo, and through this circumstance had formed a connection with Augustine, the holy bishop, at Celer’s request, had promised to provide him with certain materials relating to an understanding of the schism. He fulfilled this promise later than he had wished, because he had been compelled to set out on a journey in order to visit his diocese. He nevertheless commissioned a certain presbyter named Optatus to read to Celer whatever was relevant to the matter.

For this reason he wrote Celer a special letter (*Letter* 56). He later wrote him another (*Letter* 57), informing him that he had arranged for the book which Celer had requested through his son Caecilianus to be delivered to him. Once Celer had read the book, it would become clear to him that the Donatists had wrongly separated themselves from the Catholic Church. Augustine promises him that, if any doubt should still remain in his mind, he would satisfy him on the matter as soon as Celer wished.

Celer must already at that time have been alienated from Donatus’s party, since Augustine asks him to commend Catholic unity to his dependents in the Hipponian countryside. He also asks Celer to assist him in this matter, since Augustine himself wished to reach agreement with a certain friend who was said at that time to be living on Celer’s estate.

Those letters contain a profound silence concerning the Conference of Carthage; they therefore seem to have been written by Augustine when he was still a recently appointed bishop. In the year 412, Spondeus, Celer’s property manager, was a formidable opponent of the Donatists (*Letter* 139, no. 2). In 423, when Augustine wrote his letter to Pope Caelestine, Celer held no office (*Letter* 209, no. 5). In 429, however, as can be understood from the titles of certain laws sent to him (*Theodosian Code*, *On the Grain Supply*, law 34, and *On Appeals*, law 68), he administered Africa as proconsul.

## CHAPTER IV

1. The book *On the Good of Marriage*, published on the occasion of the Jovinianist heresy.  
2. Also the book *On Holy Virginity*.  
3. The commentaries *On Genesis Literally*.

### 1. The Book *On the Good of Marriage*

When the heresy of Jovinian first appeared—he began preaching around the year 390 that virginity was not more meritorious than conjugal chastity (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 22)—it was first vigorously attacked and condemned at Rome and then at Milan. Jerome also opposed it in two highly celebrated books written in the year 392, with the result that no one thereafter dared openly to defend it.

Nevertheless, some remnants of the error could still be found at this time, occasionally disseminated in secret conversations. The circumstances therefore demanded that this poison be confronted—not less dangerous because it spread covertly.

For this reason Augustine wrote the book *On the Good of Marriage*. He deliberately chose to treat this subject because some people maintained that Jovinian could not be refuted in any other way than by condemning marriage, as they claimed Jerome had done.

Augustine, however, demonstrates both that the sanctity of marriage can be defended against the Manichaeans and that virginity, although marriage is not to be condemned, is nevertheless to be preferred to it. We nowhere find Jovinian named in this work, except where Augustine designates him somewhere as “an impudent questioner” (*On the Good of Marriage*, no. 27).

In one passage Augustine states that, according to the Roman custom then in force, it was not lawful for a man to take another wife so as to have more than one living wife. He also implies that it was forbidden for a sterile wife to be dismissed in order to marry another. In the same place he touches upon the question why those who had taken one wife and then another, either before or after receiving the grace of Baptism, were removed from episcopal office (*ibid.*, chapter 7, no. 7; chapter 18, no. 21).

He mentions the same work in the ninth book of *On Genesis Literally*, saying that he had recently made it public (*On Genesis Literally*, book 9, no. 12).

### 2. The Book *On Holy Virginity*

After praising the good of marriage at great length and admonishing Christian virgins in the preceding book not to place themselves above the ancient married women of God’s people (*On Holy Virginity*, no. 1), there was no longer any danger that, if he asserted the excellence of virginity against the remnants of Jovinian’s error, he would appear to condemn marriage.

Accordingly, free from that suspicion, he later published another book, *On Holy Virginity* (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 23). In it he endeavors, in accordance with the grace divinely granted to him, to urge people toward this virtue. He also seeks to plant in their minds modest thoughts concerning themselves, so that they will not become arrogant because of the dignity of their profession.

On the one hand, he sets before their eyes how great a gift God has bestowed upon them; on the other, how carefully that gift must be preserved through the pious humbling of the spirit.

### 3. The Commentaries *On Genesis Literally*

At this same time he undertook the twelve books *On Genesis Literally*. He gave them this title because, setting aside allegorical interpretations, he explains Scripture in them according to the truth of the events narrated (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 24).

As we observed above, while he was still carrying out the duties of a presbyter he had attempted the same task and had already written a book on this subject. Experience, however, had shown him that he did not yet possess sufficient strength to complete the work he had undertaken.

Thus, returning to it only after a long interval, he composed eleven books extending from the beginning of Genesis to the expulsion of Adam from paradise, and added a twelfth book on paradise itself. In that book he discusses at length how we perceive bodily things with the eyes of the mind.

He frankly admits that, although this work is in many respects preferable to what he had written while still a presbyter, in many passages he is investigating the truth rather than finding it. Even when he has found it, he does not usually present it as certain; rather, he generally postpones a definitive judgment about matters until a more exact examination can be made.

“We are not so much prescribing to each person what he should think about obscure matters,” he says, “as showing what we ourselves should be taught in matters where we have been uncertain, and removing from the reader the rashness of affirming where we have not been able to provide firmness of judgment” (*On Genesis Literally*, book 12, chapter 1, no. 1).

He does not propose to explain the mysteries enclosed in the context of the words. He is content to demonstrate that it contains nothing which cannot be true literally, as they say, and according to the actual meaning of the history, or which conflicts with what can be known by the natural light of reason. Finally, if anything appears superfluous, he maintains that it is necessary for the sake of the mystery (*ibid.*, book 9, chapter 12, nos. 20–22).

He believes that this method of interpretation will bring considerable economy and benefit to the Church, as well as to those whom he was especially eager to instruct for the sake of their salvation. Nevertheless, he does not concern himself with solving the problems of natural philosophy, since he neither has the time for this nor, indeed, ought to have it—neither for himself nor for those whom, as he says, he desires to form for their salvation and for the necessary benefit of the holy Church (*ibid.*, book 1, chapters 40–41; book 2, chapter 10, no. 23).

He did not complete this work in uninterrupted labor (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 24, no. 1). Although his friends pressed him to publish it, he kept it back for a long time, just as he had done with his reflections on the Trinity before putting the final hand to them (*Letter* 43, no. 4). He did so both because of the great difficulty of the questions treated in it and because he hoped that, as long as it remained unpublished, he would continue to correct certain errors in it.

In the eleventh book he promises, in a certain manner, the work *The City of God*, which was written on the occasion of the capture of Rome in the year 410 (*On Genesis Literally*, book 11, chapter 15, no. 20).

In fact, he had not yet released these writings on Genesis to the public when he wrote to Marcellinus toward the end of the year 412 (*Letter* 43, no. 4), nor when he wrote other letters to Evodius, probably in the years 414 or 415 (*Letters* 159, no. 2; 162, no. 2). Nevertheless, he completed them before finishing the work on the Trinity (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 24, no. 1).

He cited the twelfth book in another letter to Evodius, written around the year 414, and was hastening, as far as he was able, to revise the entire work so that he might make it public as soon as possible and not, by delaying longer, keep many people’s expectation and desire in suspense.

Augustine, however, in revising his works, assigned the volumes mentioned above a place before the books against Petilianus, which were completed no later than the beginning of the year 402. We therefore think that the works discussed above were composed partly in the year 400 and partly in 401.

## CHAPTER V

1. The council held at Carthage on 16 June decrees that bishops should be sent to the churches overseas, so that Donatists returning to unity might be admitted to the clergy; and that certain requests should be made to the emperor through the same envoys.  
2. A second council of Carthage, held on 13 September of the same year, discusses the restoration of the same schismatics to the Church and decrees that their clergy should be received in their existing honors.  
3. The manner and conditions for admitting Donatists into the Church.  
4. Certain provisions of the constitution of the Council of Carthage are noted.

### 1. The Council of 16 June

In the African collection, two councils are assigned to the same year, 401: one on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, or 16 June, and the other on the Ides of September, or 13 September. Both were held at Carthage in the secretariat of the Basilica of Restituta.

Aurelius, who alone speaks in the first synod, testifies that only some of those who ought to have assembled there were present. He first sets forth that Africa was suffering from such a shortage of ministers that in many churches not even a single, uneducated deacon was available. From this it may be inferred that the higher ranks, since they require more qualifications than the diaconate, were even more seriously deprived of suitable ministers.

“We can no longer endure,” he says, “the daily lamentations of almost lifeless congregations in various places. Unless some assistance is eventually provided for them, a grave and inexcusable responsibility for countless souls who are perishing will remain with us before God” (Labbe, *Councils*, volume 2, p. 1642).

He was convinced that no one could doubt that a remedy would be supplied for this evil if those who returned from Donatus’s party to the Church were not denied access to ecclesiastical dignities. Yet this had apparently been forbidden by the Roman and Milanese sees, perhaps in the Synod of Capua held in 392.

Aurelius therefore requests that a bishop be sent from their own number to Anastasius, the bishop of Rome, and at the same time to Venerius, the bishop of Milan, to explain to them the need of the African Church and ask them to agree that those baptized as infants by heretics might be enrolled among the clergy, provided that a piety worthy of so great a rank was evident in them, as the African Church had determined in the preceding council (*African Code of Canons*, canon 57).

It is clear that the question of receiving Donatists who had converted to the Church in their former honor and rank had already been discussed either at the Council of Hippo in 393 or at the Council of Carthage in 397. The condition was that they had not rebaptized anyone while in the schism or that they brought their own congregations back with them. Nevertheless, the councils had refused to decide anything on this matter without first consulting the churches overseas.

Aurelius then proposes other matters of considerable necessity which ought to be requested from the emperor. Among them was a request that the profane banquets held in many places be prohibited (*ibid.*, canon 60). This was sought not only because the pagans engaged there in dancing and other practices full of indecency and shamelessness, to the dishonor of the Christian religion, but also because they compelled Christians to attend. In this respect a new persecution was being stirred up under emperors devoted to Christ.

Aurelius plainly testifies that these banquets arose from pagan errors and were contrary to divine commands. By these words he seems to refer to the banquets customarily celebrated in temples, which Augustine likewise attacked in his sixty-second sermon, a sermon having considerable connection with this subject.

Furthermore, Constantine had granted, by three laws, that anyone wishing to manumit his slaves might do so in a church before bishops, without observing any other legal formalities. This practice perhaps had not yet become customary in Africa, where there was uncertainty about the proper method and lawful ritual.

Aurelius therefore requests that the envoy sent to Italy be charged with investigating how the bishops of Italy conducted themselves in this matter, so that the Africans might claim the same authority for themselves (*ibid.*, canon 82). At the council held on the Ides of September it was decided that the emperor should be asked to grant the power of manumitting slaves in a church (*ibid.*). Augustine shows that this permission was in fact granted (*Sermons* 21, no. 6; 356, no. 6).

### 2. The Council of 13 September

At the second Council of Carthage held that same year, 401, on the Ides of September, since it was a general council of all Africa, the bishops assembled in very large numbers. So many attended that, for a private matter, no fewer than twenty delegates were appointed, among them Alypius, Augustine, and Evodius.

Augustine’s genius is especially evident in the decrees of this council. First, a letter written by Pope Anastasius to the African bishops was read. In it he urged them not to overlook in any way the wickedness, injuries, and losses inflicted by the heretical Donatists, which were harassing the African Church with such terrible force.

They then gave thanks to God because he had kindled the heart of this holy bishop with such great charity toward them. Afterward, with great care, they discussed what course of action toward the Donatists would prove most useful (Labbe, *Councils*, volume 2, p. 1651).

By God’s inspiration they adopted the plan that they should act with great kindness and peace, and that, as far as possible, all the Donatists should be shown before their eyes how miserable a state they had fallen into (*African Code of Canons*, canon 66). It was hoped that, through the assistance of such friendly corrections, God would remove the darkness from their minds, soften their hearts, and loosen the bonds of the snares by which the devil held them entangled.

For this reason it was decided that the council should send letters to the African magistrates, asking them to order that authentic documents concerning what had taken place between the Donatists and the Maximianists be handed over to the bishops (*ibid.*, canon 67).

It was also decided that bishops should be selected to invite bishops and congregations separated from the Church by the schism to peace and unity, and to convince them that there was no reason for them to criticize the Catholic Church—especially since their own indulgence toward the Maximianists excluded every possible justification for their separation (*ibid.*, canon 69).

It was likewise agreed that bishops sent to the Donatists throughout all the provinces of Africa should be given authority in the form of instructions, from whose prescriptions they would not be free to depart (*ibid.*, canon 85).

Nothing was better suited to restoring harmony than receiving Donatist clergy who returned to the Church in their existing honors (*ibid.*, canon 68). This practice had been observed both at the very beginning of the schism and when unity was restored through Macarius around the year 347, as almost all the African churches could testify.

Later, however, various synods had forbidden it, especially the Council of Hippo and the overseas council, perhaps the Council of Capua held in 392. The African bishops greatly desired to restore that ancient practice, especially toward those who brought their congregations back with them. Nevertheless, they had not dared to decide anything on the matter before obtaining the agreement of the bishops of Italy.

Accordingly, at the council convened on 16 June of that year, they had remained disposed toward the matter in this way and had decided to leave the whole question to the judgment of the Roman and Milanese bishops.

At the present council, however, it was decreed that letters should be sent to the Italian bishops, and especially to Pope Anastasius, informing them that peace and the welfare of the African Church required that the local bishops have the authority to receive Donatists into their former honors whenever this appeared useful for recalling others to unity.

The overseas decision, however, would remain valid against those alone whose return would not bring the Church as much benefit as would be sufficient to compensate for the wound inflicted upon discipline by this concession.

Nevertheless, the heading of this article—“That the clergy of the Donatists be received into the clergy of the Catholic Church”—seems to indicate that it was regarded as a definite constitutional provision enacted by the African Church, rather than as something dependent upon the agreement of the churches overseas.

### 3. The Reception of Donatists

Writing against Cresconius around the year 406, Augustine declares that the provision of the preceding article was customarily observed at that time. Bishops and other clergy of lower rank who returned to the Church either continued to exercise their former ministries or refrained from doing so, according as it was judged expedient for the peace of the Church and the salvation of the peoples, for whose sake these dignities and ministries had been established (*Against Cresconius*, book 2, chapter 11, no. 13).

Augustine himself defended this discipline against the Donatists, who criticized it (*ibid.*, chapter 10, no. 12). Later, when writing to Count Boniface, he said that the matter was like cutting the bark of a tree in order to graft a shoot onto it (*Letter* 185, chapter 10, no. 44).

Certainly, Donatist bishops in places lacking a Catholic bishop were allowed, when they brought their congregations back to the Church, to continue governing those congregations (*African Code of Canons*, canon 99), at least until the year 407.

For this reason, at the Conference of Carthage there are found quite a number of Catholic bishops who had previously followed Donatus’s party. Indeed, some who had rebaptized others were permitted to retain their dignity (*Against Cresconius*, book 2, chapter 16, no. 19).

A certain Theodorus asked Augustine how he would receive Donatist clergy who wished to renounce the schism, since the council had left this matter to the judgment of each bishop. Augustine replied orally that he would deprive none of them of his dignity. He later wrote the same thing to Theodorus in his own hand, asking him to inform them of it and offering, if they wished, to leave his own letter with them as a pledge of good faith (*Letter* 61, no. 1).
