This Theodorus, whom Augustine calls “brother,” was, as is credible, a man of considerable authority at Hippo, whom Augustine used in negotiations with the followers of Donatus. For it was through the service of Theodorus and Maximus, whom he calls “most dear and honorable sons” (*Letters* 107 and 108, no. 1), that he first arranged for a letter to be delivered to Macrobius, the Donatist bishop of Hippo (*Letter* 106).

There is no reason for anyone to be troubled by Augustine’s calling Macrobius “brother,” since Augustine sometimes used this title to honor laymen as well.

As he had promised, Augustine admitted two deacons of Proculeianus (*Letter* 78, no. 8). Later, when they fell into some fault, they gave the people occasion to insult the administration of Proculeianus and, in their delight at Augustine’s virtue, to declare repeatedly that no one formed among the clergy under his discipline would fall into such sins.

Augustine did not approve this. He did not want people to boast of him, nor did he want anything besides their heresy to be reproached to heretics.

While explaining Psalm 36, he commends to the prayers of the people a Donatist subdeacon whose return to communion with the Church he declares himself glad to see (*Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 36, sermon 2, no. 11).

The Church, however, did not show itself equally ready to receive those who had defected from unity to Donatus’s party and had then wished to be baptized again, as it did toward those who had been entangled in the schism from childhood (*Against Cresconius*, book 2, chapter 16, no. 19).

The Church loved both groups and served their healing with truly maternal charity. Yet, although it received neither group without repentance, it was somewhat more lenient toward those whom it had not yet counted among its children. It imposed much heavier penalties upon those who had defected from its unity (*Letter* 93, no. 53).

It excluded the latter from ecclesiastical honors, treating them as those who, after once renouncing the schism, had returned again to their vomit and defected from the Church—whether they had been merely lay members among the Donatists or had held a place in their clergy. If any bishop either failed to remove such persons from ecclesiastical dignities or even wished to promote them to those dignities, the more diligent bishops reproved him as violating fraternal law (*On the Singular Baptism Against the Donatists*, chapter 12, no. 20).

On the other hand, Augustine was deeply displeased, and his inmost being was wrung with grief, when he heard that a certain person returning from the Donatists, who confessed the sin of rebaptization, had been barred from access to the Church and from penance on the pretext that he had requested admission perhaps only out of fear of the laws.

“Suppose,” he says, “that he was compelled to be a Catholic. Will he therefore be penitent? Who compels him to seek a place of reconciliation, except his own will? Let us therefore admit his weakness for the moment, so that afterward we may test his will” (*Sermon* 296, chapter 11, no. 12).

Although there were Donatist clergy who were forbidden to exercise their offices, hands were not laid upon those who were permitted to perform them before the people, lest this be turned into an insult to the sacred ordination which could never be erased from them.

If such a public imposition was ever carried out through ignorance, the deed was not obstinately defended but corrected in a pious manner once it became known, and forgiveness was readily obtained (*Against Parmenian’s Letter*, book 2, chapter 13, no. 28). The same rule applied to all presbyters and deacons whom their committed crimes had made worthy of being removed from their rank.

The blessed Optatus testifies that the holy chrism with which those who had been anointed among the Donatists had been anointed was preserved by the Catholic Church untouched and undefiled (*Optatus*, book 7).

Indeed, men who had held only the honor of the presbyterate within that faction were sometimes promoted to the episcopate. Several such cases can be observed in the Conference. The most distinguished among them is Sabinus. While he was serving as a presbyter in the diocese of Milevis at Tucca, his congregation was brought into the Church and requested that he himself be given to them as bishop; he was appointed to that dignity (*Carthaginian Conference*, session 1, chapter 130).

As for laymen who had been baptized by the Donatists while still children, it was sometimes granted that they might be initiated into the sacred orders (*African Code of Canons*, canon 57). Since this had been established only because of the extreme shortage of clergy, Augustine was once consulted by Possidius about whether he should ordain a certain man baptized among Donatus’s followers. Augustine indicated that he neither recommended this nor, if necessity compelled it, condemned it (*Letter* 245, no. 2).

Concerning those who had been removed by the schismatics from their rank and order because of an offense, Augustine stated from the beginning of his episcopate that he observed the following rule: if they wished to pass over to the Catholic Church, they were received in that humility of repentance to which the Donatists themselves might perhaps have subjected them for the sake of discipline, had they retained them in their fellowship.

He considered that it must never be tolerated for anyone to migrate with impunity from one Church to another in order to evade the severity of discipline (*Letter* 35, no. 3).

It is by no means unlikely that this was the situation of the man of whom Augustine speaks in connection with Psalm 36, using words especially suited to stir feelings of compassion:

“A certain man,” he says, “had come to us from the party of Donatus, accused and excommunicated by his own people, seeking here what he had lost there. But because he could not be received except in the condition proper to him—for he had not left that party while remaining upright among them, so that it might be clear that he acted not from necessity but by choice—because, therefore, he could not have there what he was seeking, and because he was seeking empty exaltation and false honor” (by which words something more than simple communion is meant), “and because he did not find here what he had lost there, he himself perished.

“He groaned, wounded, and was not comforted; for there were terrible, silent goads in his conscience. We tried to comfort him with the word of God, but he was not one of those wise ants that gathered for themselves in summer what they would live on in winter.

“When things are peaceful, a person ought to gather the word of God for himself and store it in the innermost recesses of his heart, just as an ant hides the labors of summer in secret chambers. For during summer one is free to do this; but winter comes—that is, tribulation overtakes him—and unless he finds within himself something to eat, he must perish from hunger.

“This man had not gathered the word of God for himself. Winter came, and he did not find here what he was seeking. He could not be comforted except by that source, but not at all by the word of God. Within himself he had nothing; outside himself he could not find what he was seeking. He burned with the flames of indignation and sorrow. His mind was violently agitated, and remained so in secret until it finally burst into certain groans, so that the sound reached the brothers while he himself did not know that he was being heard.

“We saw him and grieved deeply. God knows the great suffering of his soul—the many crosses, hells, and torments he endured. What more need be said? Impatient with the lowly place which, if he had been wise, could have been a place of healing for him, he appeared in such a condition that he was eventually expelled” (*Expositions of the Psalms*, Psalm 36, sermon 2, no. 11).

Augustine nevertheless seems to acknowledge that a certain man named Quodvultdeus, whom the Donatists had expelled as convicted of a double adultery, was received either into communion or into the clerical dignity. This, however, did not happen until he had lawfully proved his innocence (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 3, chapter 32, no. 37).

### 4

To return to the Council of Carthage: after the enactments concerning the Donatists had been made, certain other measures were decreed there for the sake of discipline. Among these was a provision concerning temporary bishops, since it had perhaps become customary among the Africans that, whenever some church was vacant, it should be entrusted to a particular bishop. They called such men *Interventores* or *Intercessores*. Augustine preserves an accusation made by the Donatists, who calumniated the orthodox by alleging that they had killed an *Interventor* whom they had sent to Carthage at a time when Majorinus had not yet been ordained against Caecilianus (Letter 44, ch. 4, §8). Before they began ordaining bishops of their own for their followers, they likewise sent to Rome such adventitious *Interventores*, as Augustine calls them (*On the Singular Baptism*, ch. 16, §28).

The council therefore forbids anyone to become bishop of a church which he had previously governed under the title of *Interventor*. If he could not bring about the completion of the episcopal election within a year, it ordered that, once the year had elapsed, another *Interventor* should be substituted in his place (*Code of the African Canons*, canon 74).

The same council decreed that clerics separated from the Church on account of some crime should be granted a year in which to prove their innocence; after that period had elapsed, every opportunity for clearing themselves was to be taken away from them (ibid., canon 79). Augustine mentions this decree in the letter of which we shall presently have to speak (Letter 65, §2).

He also appears to cite the following canon, which he says was established at the last synod: those who had withdrawn from a monastery or had been expelled from it were not permitted to be promoted either to the clerical order in another church or to the administration of any monastery (*Code of the African Canons*, canon 80). He likewise alludes to it in a letter to Aurelius and urges that it be observed.

The synod included within its general prohibition monks of a monastery situated in another diocese, and separated from communion with all—except his own people—the bishop by whom they had been promoted. The case of Cresconius of Villa-Regis was heard at this council (ibid., canon 77), as was that of Equitius, bishop of Hippo Diarrhytus (ibid., canon 78). What the latter had perpetrated is unknown. This alone is certain: he had long before been condemned by the judgment of the bishops on account of his crimes; yet not only did he fail, as was proper, to submit to their decision, but, through the fault of a restless disposition and shamelessness, he also disturbed the Church.

For this reason the council, convened on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July in the year 401, instructed the envoys whom it was sending to the Emperor that, if they happened to find that Equitius in Italy, they should proceed against him by every legal means (ibid., canon 65).

There were people in his city who were excessively devoted to his cause and awaited his return from flight; others, however, who disagreed with them, withdrew from communion with them. These latter occupied the sacred buildings and had not yet received any bishop. Since the council did not think that this church ought to be left deserted any longer, it selected twenty bishops, among them Alypius, Augustine, and Evodius. They were to go there and establish a bishop with the common consent of the entire people, provided that Equitius’ supporters could be induced to join fellowship with the others; if not, they were to ensure that those supporters caused no delay in the episcopal election.

Writing immediately after that synod had concluded, Augustine states that the bishop of Vigesilita—or at least the bishop to whose diocese the church of Vigesilita belonged—had been deposed from his rank in the plenary council of Africa. He says that, for this reason, the people of that place would act properly if they refused to receive him, and that no one either could or ought to compel them to do so. If the bishop in question attempted to force them into this action by the fear of secular power—which he appears to have threatened—he would show what sort of man he was now and what sort of man he had previously been, when he wanted no evil to be believed about him.

“For no one,” Augustine says, “is exposed in such a way as to reveal the sort of cause he has as the man who, through secular authorities or any kind of violence, tries, amid disturbance and complaint, to recover the honor he has lost. He does not wish to serve Christ willingly, but to dominate Christians against their will” (Letter 64, §4).

Finally, the council concluded by granting the bishop of Carthage authority to dictate and seal, in the name of all the bishops, the letters which the councils had decided should be sent—just as though their written instructions concerning whatever was absolutely to be observed with regard to the Donatists had been delivered to him (*Code of the African Canons*, canon 85).

## CHAPTER VI

1. Victorinus and Xantippus contend over the primacy.  
2. Pammachius recalls to the Church his tenant farmers who adhered to the Donatist party.  
3. Donatus leaves Augustine’s monastery with his brother.  
4. Augustine writes back concerning the case of the presbyter Quintianus before Aurelius.  
5. The complaint of the same man concerning Privatio’s admission into Augustine’s monastery.  
6. Augustine removes Abundantius, a presbyter of his diocese, from office.  
7. At the end of the year 401, Crispinus rebaptizes the peasants of the Mappalian estate.

### 1

The primate of Numidia, to whom the Council of Carthage had decided that a letter should be written concerning Cresconius of Villa-Regis (*African Code*, canon 77), unquestionably died not very long afterward. For, at the beginning of the year 402 at the latest, Xantippus, bishop of Tagosa, had already obtained the primacy of that same province (Letter 65, §2), and he still held it in the year 407 (*Code of the African Canons*, canon 100).

When he was entering upon the primacy, a controversy arose. On the fifth day before the Ides of November, as the day was already declining toward night, Augustine received Victorinus’ encyclical letter. Acting as primate, Victorinus invited him to the council of Numidia (Letter 59). The same letter—or, as it was called, the *tractoria*—also stated that the matter had been addressed to the Mauritanias, although those provinces had their own primates.

Even if a council was to be summoned from them for Numidia, the names of certain Moors who were senior there ought to have been placed in the *tractoria*. Since Augustine did not find them in it, he was greatly astonished. He was also displeased that, although several bishops were senior to him, he was listed in third place.

He was no less troubled by the fact that Xantippus himself—who said that the primacy belonged to him, with many people readily agreeing, and who sent letters of the sort appropriate to a primate—was not even mentioned in the same document, although he above all ought to have come to the council and been named first.

Because of these errors, Augustine feared that the *tractoria* might be spurious. This single doubt could by itself have prevented him from attending, lest his presence lend support to the summons. In addition, the shortness of the time, and the various serious cares with which he was then occupied—perhaps together with ill health—made it difficult for him to prepare himself for the synod.

He therefore contented himself with writing to Victorinus: first, to excuse himself; then, to remind him that Victorinus and Xantippus ought above all to settle between themselves which of them possessed the primacy and the right to summon the council; or rather, that the council should be convoked jointly by both of them, without prejudice to anyone, and that the matter should be examined with the senior bishops to determine which surpassed the other in antiquity.

Disputes of this kind concerning the seniority or primacy of the African provinces were referred by councils for judgment to the bishop of Carthage. This controversy may also have been the reason why the council of the following year established various regulations intended to remove every uncertainty concerning the date of bishops’ ordinations (*Code of the African Canons*, canon 86).

### 2

It was perhaps during this same year, 401, that Augustine sent Pammachius a letter written through the envoys of the Council of Carthage (Letter 58, §3). He tells him that he is not at all informing him of the plots which the Donatists, with hostile intent toward the Catholics, were contriving against him; rather, Pammachius would hear of them more appropriately from the brothers whom Augustine commends to him.

Pammachius possessed estates in central Numidia, whose inhabitants adhered to the party of Donatus. Moved therefore by charity and piety, he wrote to them concerning the acceptance of the unity of the Church. His letters displayed such fervor of spirit that, contrary to expectation, they immediately chose, with the greatest zeal, to follow what they persuaded themselves that they ought to follow only under the guidance of truth—and of so great and good a man.

This was so pleasing to Augustine that he considered it necessary to communicate his joy to Pammachius in the letters now under discussion. Yet he does not want Pammachius to suppose, from the words of his joy, that he derives pleasure from his own happiness or that he is inflamed with love for him. “Go on,” he says, “by thought into my heart, and see what is taking place there concerning you. The eye of charity will reveal the chamber of charity, which we close against the tumultuous frivolities of the world when we worship God there; and you will see there the delights of my joy over your good work, which I can express neither with my tongue nor with my pen—warm and burning in the sacrifice of his praise, by whose inspiration you desired this and by whose help you were able to accomplish it.”

He adds that he ardently desires that other Christian senators might be persuaded to undertake the same action, but that he does not have sufficient confidence to dare exhort them to it.

“For they,” the holy Bishop adds, “may perhaps not do so; and, as though the enemies of the Church had overcome us in their minds, they may lie in wait to deceive the weak.” He therefore asks him for only one thing: that he read aloud before them the letter Augustine had received from him. This might be done, since it could be shown that they were neglecting the conversion of their own tenant farmers for no other reason than that they despaired of bringing it about.

It is sufficiently clear that this occurred at a time when examples of Donatists returning in large numbers together to the unity of the Church were still rare, and therefore before the year 405; indeed, before the Circumcellions had committed the acts of violence with which they raged against the Catholics when they saw the history of the Maximianists being urgently published everywhere by the Catholics, in accordance with what the Council of Carthage had decreed that year.

Augustine mentions only the dangers which were feared from them, nor does he deny that his fear might be regarded by some as groundless. He therefore asks Pammachius not to despise those who fear even what may prove unnecessary.

### 3

Augustine found no small consolation in his monastery; nevertheless, he sometimes experienced there certain vexations. However carefully he looked after the discipline of those who lived with him, he still recognized both that he was a human being and that he lived in the company of human beings. He could in no way hope that, in the fellowship of life, he would have no companions except saints, since this was not to be found even in the household of those who had excelled in holiness of life, nor in the company of Christ the Lord, nor even in heaven itself (Letter 78, §§8–9).

At this time he experienced the misery of human affairs. There were two brothers in his monastery, born at Carthage or in its vicinity; one of them was named Donatus. Moved by a certain desire for vain glory, they planned to leave the monastery, apparently claiming as their reason a desire to serve their native city in the clerical ministry.

Anxious for their salvation, Augustine placed before them every obstacle he could devise to prevent them from carrying out their misguided intentions. But when they could not be dissuaded from their purpose, they went to Carthage. There Aurelius, perhaps supposing that they had come with Augustine’s approval, admitted Donatus to the clergy.

Augustine testifies that Donatus’ brother had given him the reason for leaving. This, however, occurred before the council at which the desertion of monasteries and the ordination of those who deserted them was discussed—namely, before the Ides of September in the year 401.

We do not find that Augustine spoke with Aurelius about this matter at that synod, although, by saying “we decided in the same place,” he clearly suggests that he was present. But in the letter which Augustine received from Aurelius soon after they had parted, Donatus and his brother were discussed.

The holy Bishop long hesitated over what reply he should give. At last, moved by concern for the salvation of those whom he was obliged to advise, he wrote back that monks were being exposed to a dangerous temptation, and that clerics—including the bishops themselves—were being subjected to no slight insult if deserters from monastic life were admitted into their order. Previously, this honor had ordinarily been granted only to monks of proven excellence, and even they were not rarely found unsuitable for ecclesiastical offices.

He adds that Aurelius could, according to his own judgment, make use of Donatus if Donatus had laid aside his pride, since Aurelius had ordained him before the council had established anything on the matter.

“As for his brother,” Augustine says, “once you understand what I think, I do not know what answer to give.” He plainly indicates by this that the brother could not be ordained without violating the council’s decree.

Nevertheless, he adds that he does not wish to interfere with Aurelius’ prudence and charity; indeed, Aurelius could follow in this matter whatever he judged more useful for the Church.

The title *Papa*, by which Augustine addresses Aurelius in the inscription of the letter, leaves no doubt that Aurelius was bishop of Carthage (Letter 60).

### 4

We do not know whether this is also the Aurelius whom Augustine twice calls “the old man Aurelius” in his letter to Quintianus (Letter 64, §§2–3). For the term was customarily applied in Africa to deans or primates; whether it was likewise regularly extended to the bishop of Carthage because of the dignity of his see is not sufficiently clear.

This, however, is beyond doubt: if the aforementioned letter was written after the Nativity of the Lord in that same year—as there is no real reason to question—it cannot have been Aurelius who was primate of Numidia, since Victorinus, or at any rate Xantippus, held that dignity.

Yet we do not dare determine whether the primacy might be attributed to that Aurelius in some other province of Africa, such as Byzacena, to which the church of Vigesilita—mentioned in the same letter—belonged (ibid., §4).

Whoever this Aurelius was, the presbyter Quintianus governed the church of Badezilita, or one near it, in either his diocese or at least his province. Quintianus had ordered that certain books be read in his church which were not included in the canon of Scripture established by synodal authority. They belonged to the number of the apocrypha, which heretics commonly misused to lead people into error, especially the Manichaeans, who were actually said to lie concealed willingly in that place (ibid., §3).

There was surely no other reason why Aurelius removed Quintianus from communion with him, although, being occupied with other matters, he had not yet delivered a final judgment concerning his case. He had, however, decided to go to the church of Badezilita around the feast of the Nativity of the Lord (ibid., §2).

### 5

At the same time it also happened that a young man named Privatio, who had read something of this sort from the apocryphal books only once in that church, came to Augustine and asked to be received into his monastery (ibid., §3).

The holy Bishop did not think that Privatio should be regarded as a reader, and therefore did not think that he was subject to the canon which prohibited the admission of a cleric from another diocese. Nevertheless, he informed Aurelius of the matter by letter, declaring that he would follow Aurelius’ judgment in it.

Quintianus therefore wrote to Augustine both concerning Privatio, whom he maintained could not be admitted without violating the canons, and concerning his own dispute with Aurelius, complaining that Aurelius had not judged his case.

Augustine received Quintianus’ letter on the day before the Nativity of the Lord, or at most two days earlier. He wished it to be delivered to Aurelius so that Aurelius might understand the matters about which Quintianus was protesting and the arguments which he had resolved to employ in his defense.

Augustine then replied to Quintianus with every sign of courtesy. At the same time, he urged him to bear with equanimity the decision being made concerning him, as though he considered him innocent; yet it is sufficiently clear that Augustine did not wish to claim for himself the right to decide the matter.

Indeed, he reproved Quintianus quite explicitly for having ordered that apocryphal books be read. He also observes that, with regard to Privatio, Quintianus had been more agitated than was reasonable.

Augustine excuses himself from undertaking Quintianus’ case, since there were other bishops who, because of their greater authority and closer proximity, could more easily do so. Nevertheless, he says that he had forwarded Quintianus’ letter to Aurelius.

He could not write to the people entrusted to Quintianus’ care, from whom he had received no letters: first, because he himself had received Quintianus’ letter late; and second, because he neither dared nor, in his own judgment, could rightly write of his own accord to a people who had not been committed to his administration. His own reply to Quintianus, however, would readily satisfy everyone.

Augustine indicates that Quintianus could come to him whenever he wished and that his arrival would not be burdensome. Yet Augustine could not admit into his communion a man who was not in communion with Aurelius.

In this letter Augustine also notes what the council had recently decreed concerning monks who deserted their monasteries. This leads us to believe that the letter was written during the course of that year, after Quintianus’ letter had been received around the Nativity of the Lord, since Augustine cites nothing else from the council apart from what had been established at Carthage on the Ides of September.

### 6

At approximately this time Augustine delivered his judgment in the case of Abundantius, as he himself states, one hundred days before the Lord’s Easter, which was to fall on the eighth day before the Ides of April (Letter 65, §2).

Xantippus was then primate of Numidia (ibid., heading). Easter is found to have fallen on the eighth day before the Ides of April only in the year 402. Augustine therefore judged this case on the sixth day before the Kalends of January in the year 401.

Abundantius was a presbyter of the place called Straboniana, in the diocese of Hippo. While governing the church there, he began to acquire a bad reputation. Although the holy Bishop was alarmed by this, he believed nothing rashly. Yet, becoming more concerned, he took pains to discover whether he could obtain any certain indications of Abundantius’ corrupt life.

First he learned that Abundantius could give no plausible account of money entrusted to him by a peasant. Indeed, he had converted it to his own use.

He was then convicted of the following offense. On a day of the fast established for the Nativity of the Lord, he had left the presbyter Gippitanus at about the fifth hour—that is, in our manner of speaking, the eleventh hour—supposedly to return home. Instead, he had turned aside, without any cleric accompanying him, to the house of a woman of ill repute in the same place. Although the fast was observed in the church of Gippita just as in the other churches, he had nevertheless eaten lunch and dinner at that woman’s house and, what was more blameworthy, had spent the night there.

At that time a cleric of Hippo was also staying in the same lodging—so that one might readily suppose it to have been a public inn. Consequently, when Augustine questioned him about Abundantius’ conduct, he could not deny this principal charge.

The holy Bishop therefore left to God the matters which Abundantius denied, and judged that this confession alone was sufficient to remove him from the administration of the Church, which was surrounded on every side by heretics; or even, because of his unfavorable reputation, to depose him from the rank of presbyter.

This took place, therefore, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, one hundred days before Easter.

Abundantius decided to withdraw to the presbyter Armemanus in the Bullensian field, from which he had come. Bulla, or Bulla-Regia, is situated in the Proconsular Province. Abundantius therefore asked Augustine to write to that presbyter and inform him of the whole matter, lest he suspect something more serious.

Augustine granted this request out of a certain compassion, so that, removed from the presbyteral office, Abundantius might live there with greater care for his reputation—or, as the holy Bishop says, in a more corrected state.

In his catalogue of Augustine’s letters, Possidius lists one addressed to Victor, presbyter of the Bullensian field (*In the Catalogue*, ch. 7).

Augustine also warned Abundantius that, if he wished to appeal the sentence pronounced against him, he was free to do so within a year under the final council (Code of the African Canons, canon 79); once that period had elapsed, he would no longer be admitted to bring the matter forward.

Augustine likewise wrote to Xantippus as the primate of the province, in order to give an account of what he had done. Abundantius was permitted to request that six bishops pronounce a final judgment on his case. Augustine declares that, if Abundantius were not found worthy of deposition in that examination, anyone whom Xantippus wished could entrust him with a church under his jurisdiction. Augustine himself, however, could not do so in any way, lest the resulting harm should perhaps fall back upon him.

This letter must have been written at the latest at the beginning of the year 402, and unquestionably before Easter.

### 7

That sad event should probably be assigned to the end of the year 401, since Augustine was still mourning it at the beginning of the following year.

Crispinus, a bishop of Calama belonging to the party of Donatus, was held not by the fear of wealth which Petilianus claimed existed among the members of his sect, but rather by love of wealth (Against the Letters of Petilianus, book 2, ch. 99, §228). Having assembled a considerable sum of money, he purchased an estate in the Mappalian district, not far from Hippo (Letter 66, §1). He oppressed and disturbed its wretched inhabitants so violently that, in a single assault of terror, he did not hesitate to plunge nearly eighty souls, muttering in pitiable lamentation, into rebaptism (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 2, ch. 83, §184).

Overcome by grief at this mournful event, Augustine informed Crispinus by letter that he could arrange for payment of the ten pounds of gold with which Theodosius had fined heretical clerics. He preferred, however, to warn Crispinus to consider what answer he would give to God himself.

If Crispinus claimed that the Mappalian tenants had voluntarily entered into his communion, Augustine asked that, in their presence, a disputation be held between Crispinus and Augustine concerning the case of the Church. Everything said on both sides was to be written down, sealed, and explained to those same peasants in the Punic language. When this had been done, they were to be given by Crispinus the freedom to choose whichever communion they wished.

Furthermore, if Crispinus thought that any other peoples had been compelled by fear of their masters to abandon the Donatists, Augustine declared that he would by no means refuse to have the same procedure carried out there: they should hear both men and, after hearing them, choose what they preferred.

He adjures Crispinus through the Lord Christ to reply to these proposals (Letter 66, §§1–2).

Although Crispinus could not evade the challenge without at the same time showing that he did not rely upon truth, it is nevertheless likely that he did not dare accept the condition, lest it bring upon him an obvious defeat more shameful than flight.

## CHAPTER VII

1. A controversy arises between Augustine and Severus of Milevis concerning Timotheus.  
2. Augustine sends Timotheus to Severus, who persistently demands him.  
3. A highly elaborate eulogy is delivered to Augustine by Severus.  
4. Augustine’s reply to the eulogy delivered to him by his friend.  
5. The extent of Augustine’s intimacy with Severus, together with certain episodes from his history.

### 1

Two letters to Severus were written at approximately this time (Letters 62 and 63), before the council of Milevis had been held, as we shall see later.

That Severus is unquestionably the same man who, after spending several years in Augustine’s monastery, was made bishop of Milevis (see above, book 3, ch. 5, §3). He had already acquired considerable distinction in that see when Augustine, himself still newly elevated to the episcopate, greeted Paulinus in friendly terms in Severus’ name (Letter 31, §9).

Severus also appears to have sent a letter to Paulinus at that time, since Paulinus testifies to his joy at having received letters from him, as well as from several other holy and venerable bishops (Letter 32, §1).

Somewhat later, Augustine asked Profuturus of Cirta to greet Severus on his behalf, since for the time being Profuturus was not permitted to write to him (Letter 38, §3).

Severus owed his birth to the same city as Augustine, and both of them had long and abundantly nourished themselves on the divine word (Letter 84, §1). Thus, however strong the bond of kinship by shared brotherhood may be, it could not surpass the bond of friendship by which they clung to one another.

This, however, did not prevent some disagreement from arising between them. The matter is considerably complicated, but we think it can be disentangled in the following way.

A certain Timotheus had begun to read the Scriptures publicly at Subsanum, in the diocese of Hippo, and also in certain other churches perhaps belonging to the same diocese. Consequently, once he had obtained the office of reader there, he was not permitted to transfer to another church.

Nevertheless, we understand that he had considered going to Milevis. Severus forbade him to come unless he had the permission of Carcedonius, although it is not sufficiently clear whether Carcedonius was the presbyter of Subsanum.

Timotheus nevertheless went to Severus, paying no attention to this command and without having requested Carcedonius’ consent. This was the origin of the entire dispute (Letter 63, §§1–2).

For when Severus, as was proper, advised him to return to Subsanum and serve God there, Timotheus affirmed under oath that he would never withdraw from Severus for any reason (Letter 62, §2).

It happened, however, that he returned to Subsanum. Meanwhile Severus conferred with Augustine, perhaps at Hippo, and in all probability for no other reason than to obtain Timotheus from him.

While Augustine was considering what should be decided concerning Timotheus, he thought that Severus might have been persuaded by their conversation to allow Timotheus to remain with him. The presbyter of that church and another man named Verinus therefore arranged, without Augustine’s advice or consent, for Timotheus to be ordained subdeacon at Subsanum (Letter 63, §1).

Not long afterward Augustine went to Subsanum with Alypius and the bishop Samsucius (Letter 62, §1). There, after an inquiry into what had been done in their absence and against their wishes, they discovered that some of the reports they had received were false and others true, but that all were troubling.

They nevertheless attempted to remedy the situation as far as they could—partly by rebuking, partly by warning, and partly by prayer. They rebuked those who had failed throughout the entire affair; then they warned these men and others what they would have to do in the future in order to correct what had been done wrongly.

“In praying,” to use Augustine’s words, “we corrected ourselves, so that we might commend both the administration and the outcomes of our plans to God’s mercy; and, if any indignation had bitten us, we might be healed by taking refuge beneath his healing right hand” (Letter 63, §2).

When they tried to persuade Timotheus not to leave the church of Subsanum, he openly declared that he had promised under oath never to withdraw from Severus’ company. If he were not bound by that obligation, he said, he would not refuse to comply with them.

The holy bishops demonstrated to him that, if Severus himself, being bound by no oath, wished to release him and consented that Timotheus should remain at Subsanum in order to avoid scandal, Timotheus could do so without any charge of perjury.

After hearing this, he did what a servant of God and son of the Church ought to do: he promised that he would observe whatever they had arranged with Severus.

At once the three bishops wrote to Severus. They informed him of what they had done together and adjured him, by the charity of Christ, to recall what they had said to one another and to revive them by his reply.

Timotheus himself did not write to Severus, since his own brother—whose name is not mentioned here—kept Severus informed of everything (Letter 62, §2).

### 2

Severus considered himself injured because, at the very time when he was asking that Timotheus be granted to his church, Timotheus had been made subdeacon of the church of Subsanum.

In his reply, therefore, Severus indicated that he was astonished that they were willing to tolerate an ordination which they professed to dislike, although the error could finally be corrected by returning Timotheus.

Having perceived this attitude of Severus, whether from his reply or before receiving it, Augustine judged that their charity could be preserved in no other way than by sending Timotheus back to him.

He therefore wrote him a letter beginning as follows:

“If I say what the case itself compels me to say, where will be the concern of charity? But if I do not say it, where will be the freedom of friendship? Nevertheless, while I wavered, I chose for the moment to clear myself rather than to accuse you” (Letter 63, §1).

He then explains the course he had followed in this matter. Although he does not regret having sent Timotheus back to Severus, he nevertheless hopes that Severus will consider before God that no one can retain a cleric of another church on the pretext that the man has sworn never to withdraw from him. Such a practice would open a great avenue for undermining the discipline of the Church.

By contrast, Augustine says, Severus would fail neither against the laws of concord nor into anyone’s reproach if, disregarding an oath by which Timotheus could not be bound, he returned him to the church of Subsanum.

Augustine submits his case to Severus’ judgment, asking only that he consult Christ, whom Augustine says he is fully persuaded dwells in Severus’ heart and presides over his mind, which is subject to him.

Augustine maintains that Timotheus was a cleric of Severus’ church not because of his subdiaconate—for he had been raised to that rank only after he had bound himself to adhere to Severus, and after Severus himself had asked Augustine for him—but solely because of the office of reader.

The holy Bishop asks Severus whether a man who had begun to perform that office in his diocese and had read in many places, including at Subsanum in the presence of the presbyter of the church of Subsanum, would not rightly be regarded as a reader.

He does not, however, assert that Timotheus must be counted among the clergy by a canonical definition. This leads us to assign the letter to a time before the Council of Milevis, held on the sixth day before the Kalends of September in the year 402. That council decreed that anyone who had read even once in any place could no longer be enrolled among the clergy of another church.

If this controversy was, as is quite probable, the reason for establishing that canon, Severus certainly could not refuse to return Timotheus to Augustine. Indeed, it is not inconsistent with the evidence that Timotheus had already been sent back by him beforehand.

### 3

Moreover, that intimate friendship which existed between Severus and Augustine was in no way diminished by this dispute. Nothing in the letters written back and forth several years later (Letters 109 and 110) could be more tender or fuller of sincere affection. Severus wrote his letters in the countryside, where he had spent some time with Augustine—that is, in reading his works. We shall here set down part of them, from which one may understand both what the mind of that bishop was like and, so to speak, the character of his intellect, but above all the esteem in which he held the books of the holy Doctor.

Severus accordingly breaks out in these words:

> Thanks be to God, brother Augustine, whose gift is whatever good and joyful things there are in us. I confess that I am well with you; I read you much. I shall say something wonderful, but entirely true: just as presence is usually absent from me, so your absence has become present to me. No turbulent activities of temporal affairs come between us. I do as much as I can, although I cannot do as much as I wish. Why should I say how much I wish? You know very well how greedy I am for you; nevertheless I do not complain that I do not do as much as I wish, since, in turn, I do no less than I can.
>
> Thanks, then, to God, dearest brother. I am well with you; I rejoice that I am more closely joined to you and, so to speak, as completely as possible clinging to you. Receiving the abundance of your breasts, I gather strength, if I can become capable of shaking and pressing them, so that whatever they guard more secretly and inwardly enclosed—once the skins have been removed which they insert to be sucked by those still at the breast—your very inward parts may, if possible, deign to pour out for me.
>
> I desire, I say, that your inward parts be poured back into me: your inward parts, your rich inward parts, fattened with heavenly nourishment and seasoned with every spiritual sweetness; [Col. 0316] your inward parts, pure inward parts, simple inward parts—except that they are bound with a double bond, the twin bond of charity; your inward parts, suffused with the light of truth and radiating truth. I submit myself to their outpouring or reflection, so that my night may fade in your light and we may walk together in the brightness of day.
>
> O truly skillful bee of God, constructing honeycombs full of divine nectar, dripping mercy and truth! As my soul moves through them, it delights in them and strives by this living nourishment to repair and support whatever it finds deficient or feels weak in itself.
>
> The Lord is blessed through the proclamation of your mouth and your faithful ministry, since you make him who sings to you, the Lord, sing and respond in such harmony that whatever flows down to us from his fullness becomes more pleasing and more welcome through your elegant service, your concise purity, and your faithful, chaste, and simple ministry. You make it shine so brightly through your ingenuity and vigilance that it dazzles the eyes and draws them to itself—unless you also indicate that the Lord is the source, so that, referring to him whatever delightful thing shines in you, we may recognize it as belonging to him, from whose goodness you are good and from whose purity, simplicity, and beauty you are pure, simple, and beautiful.

*(Letter 109, §§1–2.)*

At the end of the letter Augustine asks Severus to answer him with a long letter, although he declares that it will nevertheless seem short to him (ibid., §3). Some matter appeared to require Severus to go to the holy man; nevertheless he asks that, if it can be done, he be excused from this journey and not be drawn away from his course. We do not know whether by these words he means his retreat or a visitation of his diocese.

### 4

Quodvultdeus and Gaudentius brought those letters to Augustine, who shortly before had written to Severus through the deacon Timothy about some other matter. That deacon had not yet departed; but since he was already making ready and seemed likely to leave at any hour, Augustine could not use him to answer those most courteous letters. “But even if I had answered through him,” he says, “I should still have been in your debt. When shall I ever be adequate to your sweetness and to such eagerness of mind?” (Letter 110, §1).

The difficulty of replying arose because Augustine thought that, since Severus had praised him so magnificently, he ought on the one hand to return the favor and on the other to spare him out of modesty; but if he spared him, he would return less and consequently remain in debt. He says that he would have paid no attention to those excessive praises of himself if they had come from a flatterer, since then he would in no way have been obliged to repay such things. But since he knew for certain that they had arisen from sincere love and from a heart that displayed outwardly nothing other than what it felt within, he judged that either course was inconvenient, whether he matched like with like or did not.

Nevertheless, with no small sense of humility and affection, and displaying no less his zeal for consulting and cultivating justice, he replied as follows. Although he could not deny that Severus knew him no less thoroughly than he knew his own soul—for, he says, his other soul was contained in Severus, or rather the souls of both had grown together into one—Severus could nevertheless be mistaken in his opinion of him, since no one knows himself sufficiently. [Col. 0317] He found this especially difficult to bear, not only because he did not want his friend to be led into error, but also lest Severus should thereby pray less for him to God, as though he were already what Severus believed him to be.

Augustine says that it would also be easy for him to adopt a similar course toward Severus and to explain without disguise how many good qualities and gifts he knew divine generosity had bestowed upon him. But he preferred to spare Severus’s modesty—not because he feared that he himself might be mistaken in his judgment, but lest Severus, commended by another Severus, should appear to be the commendation of himself, and lest he should give Severus cause to complain of the very thing about which Augustine himself had complained in Severus.

As for the lengthy letter Severus had urgently requested, Augustine denies that his occupations allowed it. The order of justice required that what he owed to one Severus should give way to those duties which he was equally bound to perform for him and for others—that is, for the whole Church. He therefore asks Severus and the others to whom he was joined by a particularly close bond of friendship not to impose any new burden upon him, but rather, by all the authority and holy kindness they possessed, to prevent others from doing so. He indicates that he is expecting Severus to visit him (Letter 110, §4).

### 5

In one letter, after earnestly asking Bishop Novatus to send him a brother necessary for the welfare of the Church, he addresses him in these words:

> To leave your thought far aside: however strong the kinship of your blood may be, it does not overcome the bond of friendship by which I and brother Severus cling to one another; and yet you know how rarely I am able to see him. This has happened certainly not through the will either of myself or of him, but because we place the needs of our mother Church, for the future age in which we shall live together inseparably, before the needs of our present time.
>
> How much more reasonably, then, ought you to endure the absence, for the benefit of that same mother Church, of the brother with whom you do not chew the Lord’s food for as long as I do with my sweetest fellow citizen, Severus, who now speaks with me only with difficulty, and sometimes through very short letters—letters indeed more filled with other cares and business than with anything that carries to us the meadows of Christ’s sweetness.

*(Letter 84, §1.)*

That association between Augustine and Severus was known and widely celebrated among everyone. An unknown writer, in a letter to Augustine that had intruded into Jerome’s works, addresses the blessed bishop in these words:

> When I had come to the city of Leges some time ago, I was deeply saddened that I could not find you there in your entirety. For I found you divided, and, so to speak, your soul’s other half, your dearest Severus; and on one side I rejoiced. I would have rejoiced completely if I had found you whole. Thus, for the part in which I had found you, I gave thanks, while because of the part of you that I could not see I was saddened in every way.
>
> Therefore I said to my soul: “Why are you sad, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God” (Psalm 41:6); and he will make present the friend whom you love. Hence I trust in the Lord and hope that he will make me rejoice in seeing you.

*(In Augustine, Letter 270.)*

And, so that we may gather here whatever else can be found concerning Severus, Augustine records a remarkable experiment involving a magnet, which [Col. 0318] Severus had witnessed when he was dining one day with Bathanarius, the count of Africa. Augustine testifies that he gives the account no less credence on Severus’s testimony than if he himself had been present (The City of God, book 21, chapter 4, §4).

In settling the disturbances that, as we shall see below, were stirred up against the Church in Africa in the year 408, Severus labored as much as his charity required. Indeed, he also came to confer with Augustine, so that by their united counsels they might seek a suitable remedy for such great evils. Later, when a certain presbyter from the diocese of Milevis was going to the imperial court, Severus instructed him to travel through Hippo. Augustine took advantage of this opportunity to write to Olympius about the same matter and sent him many greetings in Severus’s words (Letter 97, §3).

Severus’s name is not found among those who attended the conference at Carthage. In the year 416, however, he sent a letter with the other bishops of Numidia assembled at Milevis to Pope Innocent (Letter 176). Finally, he died in the year 426, after designating a successor in the presence of his clergy; that successor in fact obtained his position through Augustine’s efforts (Letter 213, §1). In the same city there were servants of God—that is, monks—whom Severus had established there (ibid.), just as Possidius relates that all those who were taken from Augustine’s monastery to the episcopate had done (Life of Augustine, chapter 11, and above, book 3, chapter 5, §§2–3).

## CHAPTER VIII

1. The second book against Petilian was composed in the year of Christ 402.  
2. In this book Augustine refutes Petilian’s entire letter.  
3. He writes a letter to the Catholics, which is now called the book On the Unity of the Church, though that title was not assigned from the beginning.  
4. In reply Petilian heaps insults and curses upon Augustine.  
5. A remarkable response to Petilian’s abuse and insults.  
6. While expounding Psalm 36 to the people of Carthage, Augustine argues against the Donatists.

### 1

On the fifth day before the Kalends of May of the present year, 402, Pope Anastasius departed this life. His death had not yet been announced in Africa at the time when Augustine was composing the second book against Petilian’s letters; for in that work he remembers Anastasius as though he were still occupying the chair of Peter (Against the Letters of Petilian, book 2, chapter 51, §118). Certainly, however, Augustine placed this book among his other works in such an order that it cannot be said to have been composed before the present year.

Indeed, while Petilian was replying to Augustine’s first book before this second book had been completed, he complained that Quodvultdeus, a Donatist cleric, had been admitted in his own rank (ibid., book 3, chapter 32, §37). Therefore the work could not have been written before the council held at Carthage on the Ides of September in the year 401, where a decree was issued concerning the reception of Donatist clerics in their own dignity.

Moreover, in one passage of this second book Augustine testifies that the tyranny of Optatus Gildonianus had been endured in recent times (ibid., book 2, chapter 23, §53). [Col. 0319] These words indicate that a considerable period of time—not merely one or two months—had elapsed since that tyranny, which ended toward the close of the year 398. This observation completely overturns Baronius’s opinion, which assigns that book of Augustine to the same year, 398. We pass over in silence the laws of Honorius concerning the destruction of idols, mentioned in the same book (ibid., chapter 92, §202), which belong to the year 399.

Finally, Augustine mentions Felicianus repeatedly while omitting Praetextatus. This proves with complete certainty that Praetextatus had already died, although we have seen that he was still alive when Augustine wrote to Generosus during the pontificate of Anastasius (Letter 53, §6).

### 2

As for the occasion of the second book against Petilian, it was possible to understand from what we said above that the letter written by Petilian, the Donatist bishop of Cirta, against the Church had been refuted in the holy Doctor’s first book, but not in its entirety. Augustine had been able to read only part of it, since the Donatists had carefully kept the remainder from him. Their efforts were ultimately unsuccessful, however, and the entire letter came into Augustine’s hands. Certain Catholics of Cirta found it, copied it, and sent it to him (Against the Letters of Petilian, book 2, chapter 1, §1; On the Unity of the Church, §1; Against Cresconius, book 1, chapter 1, §1). As soon as he had received it, Augustine interrupted his books on the Trinity and on Genesis in order to answer it fully (Retractions, book 2, chapter 25).

Augustine says:

> It is not because he says anything new, to which an answer has not already been given in many ways and often; but for the sake of the slower brothers, who cannot apply to every matter what they have read in one place as though it were equal to everything else, I shall accommodate those who compel me to answer point by point, so that, as it were, we may discuss the matter in one another’s turns.
>
> I shall place the words from his letter under his name and give the response under my own name, as though, while we were speaking, they had been taken down by notaries. Thus no one will be able to complain that I have omitted something or that, because of the indistinctness of the speakers, he could not understand.
>
> At the same time, the Donatists themselves, who do not wish to debate with us face to face, will not escape, through the letters they published for their own people, the truth answering them point by point, as though they were conversing with us in person.

*(Against Petilian, book 2, chapter 1, §1.)*

He had used the same method in refuting the books of Faustus. Below he declares that he is sorry to have to spend time dissolving trifles, lest they perhaps trouble the weak and give them an occasion for falling (ibid., chapter 92, §209). Yet that diligence caused him much less annoyance than it did the Donatists.

Petilian, having nowhere else to turn, resorted to slander. He maintained that Augustine had falsely arranged his response in the form of a dialogue, since they had never held a conversation with one another.

“What are we to do,” Augustine asks, “with men who have such a heart, or who suppose that those to whom they wish their writings to become known have such a heart?” (On the Unity of the Church, §1).

This, then, was the reason why Augustine wrote a second book against Petilian, and a sufficiently lengthy one at that. In it he also again [Col. 0320] refutes the beginning of Petilian’s letter, which he had already refuted in his first book. He judged that everything he brought forward was so firmly supported by the authority of Scripture that it could be denied only by one who openly declared himself an enemy of the divine word. Nor did he hesitate to assert that those who had previously held Petilian’s letter in high esteem would, after reading Augustine’s refutation, finally recognize on which side the truth lay. Nevertheless, he did not deny Petilian the opportunity to be heard, if he wished to defend his letter.

### 3

At approximately the same time as he published the second book against Petilian, and before he set his hand to the third, Augustine wrote a fairly long letter to the faithful entrusted to his pastoral care. It is now entitled the book On the Unity of the Church. There he confirms the truth of the Catholic Church by the authority of Scripture and demonstrates at the same time that the Donatists can produce nothing from Scripture that supports their position. Clear testimonies all stand opposed to them; but ambiguous or obscure statements, as well as allegorical expressions, cannot establish the matter under dispute.

A certain Donatist bishop, however, had used such passages while preaching at Hippo and had won remarkable applause from those who, unable to distinguish appearance from substance, rejoiced that something new had been brought forward in favor of their sect.

The Donatists also, it is clear, were accustomed to produce miracles performed by their own people, benefits granted to those who prayed at the memorials of their dead, and visions finally sent down from heaven to some of their followers.

Augustine says:

> Let these things be removed, whether they are the inventions of lying men or the wonders of deceitful spirits. For either what is said is not true, or, if some remarkable things have occurred among heretics, we must be still more on our guard. When the Lord had said that certain deceivers would arise who, by performing some signs, would mislead even the elect, if that were possible, he added, strongly emphasizing the point: “Behold, I have told you beforehand” (Matthew 24:25).
>
> Moreover, if someone praying at the memorials of heretics is heard, he receives either good or evil not on account of the merit of the place but on account of the merit of his desire. Many are heard by God when he is angry, and to many, when he is favorable, God does not grant what they want, in order that he may grant what is useful.
>
> Do we not read that some were heard by the Lord God himself on the high places of the mountains of Judea? Yet those high places displeased God so greatly that kings who did not destroy them were condemned, while those who destroyed them were praised. From this it is understood that the petitioner’s disposition has greater force than the place of petition.
>
> As for deceptive visions, let them read what has been written: that Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light (2 Corinthians 11:14), and that many have been led astray by their dreams (Ecclesiasticus 34:7). Let them also hear what the pagans recount concerning things wonderfully done or seen in their temples and concerning their gods.
>
> Many, then, are heard, and in many ways—not only Catholic Christians, but also pagans, Jews, and heretics, devoted to various errors and superstitions. They are heard either by seductive spirits, which nevertheless do nothing unless they are permitted, God in his lofty and ineffable judgment deciding what should be granted to each person; or by God himself, either as punishment for wickedness, as consolation in misery, or as an admonition to seek eternal salvation.
>
> [Col. 0321] But no one reaches salvation itself and eternal life unless he has Christ as his head. No one can have Christ as his head unless he is in his body, which is the Church. We must recognize the Church, like Christ its head, in the canonical holy Scriptures; we must not seek it in the various rumors and opinions, deeds, words, and visions of human beings.

*(On the Unity of the Church, chapter 18, §46.)*

In this letter Augustine indicates that Praetextatus of Assuri had already died while belonging to the Donatist communion, whereas Felicianus of Musti was still living within it (ibid., §46). In the passage where he discusses persecutions (ibid., §55), several statements are found which, although they may be referred to the laws of Honorius of the year 405, seem to us to concern earlier laws, promulgated either specifically against the Donatists or generally against all heretics.

The holy Doctor had certainly not yet seen Petilian’s reply, which is refuted in Augustine’s third book against him, when he composed this work. For at its beginning he asks Petilian to answer either this work itself or the first two books that he had published against Petilian’s letters. Since Petilian had done so before Augustine completed his second book against him (Retractions, book 2, chapter 25), he could have replied only to the first book (Against the Letters of Petilian, book 3, §1).

Petilian therefore attacked several passages of this book, although in no way answering them; he left many others entirely untouched (ibid., §§22–23, 60–62). In particular, when he came to the question of why the Donatists had accepted the baptism of the Maximianists whom they had condemned, every attempt at a simulated struggle failed him, and he could extricate himself only by referring the matter to the second book that he promised to write (ibid., §42).

### 4

Finally, when Petilian realized how weak his position was concerning the central point of the case, he preferred to abandon it. At the same time he chose a subject on which his eloquence would be more pleasing to the followers of his party. These men were so implacably hostile to the holy Bishop that they regarded anyone who spoke in his favor as his enemy for that very reason.

Accordingly, Petilian substituted Augustine himself for the Church, against which he could find nothing to say; and thus, as Augustine puts it, he became “abundant in words because of the utmost poverty” of his case (ibid., §24). He turned all his anger against Augustine (Retractions, book 2, chapter 25) and lacerated him with innumerable insults (Against the Letters of Petilian, book 3, §17).

Yet although he poured out many things against him, he said nothing that was not either completely false, undeserving of any reproach, or at least in no way applicable to Augustine after he had received the grace of baptism. In this matter Petilian disregarded the judgment of sensible people, who would recognize that he had changed a public issue into a private quarrel for no other reason than the consciousness of his own weakness.

He declaimed at length about the life Augustine had led before his conversion, even attaching crimes to him that Augustine had never committed and sometimes passing over those into which he had actually fallen (ibid., §11). He twisted certain words from Augustine’s Confessions into a different meaning (ibid., §20). He asserted that Augustine had served as a presbyter among the Manichaeans, to whom [Col. 0322] he attributed every kind of disgrace (ibid., §§20, 19).

He also expanded upon this claim: namely, that Augustine had been forced to go into exile from Africa as a Manichaean in the year 386, although Augustine had already spent more than a year in Milan before that year (ibid., §30). Indeed, Petilian maintained with intolerable rashness that Augustine was still held by the same error (ibid., §11).

Because of the rhetoric Augustine had taught, Petilian gave him the name Tertullus, the orator by whom Paul was accused (Acts 24:1). At the same time, in order to bring into disrepute the force of Augustine’s arguments against the Donatists, he paraded him as a dialectician. He directed all the swelling and noise of his eloquence toward persuading people that dialectic was useful only for confirming a lie (Against the Letters of Petilian, book 3, §19).

He used sentences pronounced against certain men, some of whom were unknown to the holy Bishop, and wanted Augustine himself to be regarded as convicted of wrongdoing merely because, when questioned in court, one of his former friends had named him in order to defend himself. He reported that the titles of Augustine’s letters had been written by Augustine or his associates according to their own pleasure, simply to find some pretext for criticizing him.

When Augustine had informed a certain friend and the friend’s wife that he was sending them bread as a blessing, Petilian claimed that abominable crimes were concealed beneath these blessings. Despite the contrary judgment of everyone, he was not ashamed to say that love-magic had been given to the woman under the name of that sacred gift, of which her husband was not merely aware but also a companion and participant.

In the cited passage of the book against Petilian, after the words “with the husband not only aware,” we think that the readings “but also a companion” or “participant” should be preferred to “but also consenting,” which rests on Erasmus’s conjecture. It is very likely that Petilian was there pointing out and twisting into such a foul slander what Augustine, writing simply to Paulinus and his wife Therasia, says:

> The bread which we have sent will become a more abundant blessing through the love with which your Kindness receives it.

*(Letter 31, §9.)*

Moreover, Petilian maintained that account had to be taken of what Megalius had angrily written against Augustine when Augustine was still beginning the episcopal office. He wished to regard as worthless the fact that Megalius had soon asked the holy council for pardon for this offense. Indeed, he even treated as a crime the fact that Megalius had graciously forgiven Augustine when Augustine humbly asked him to do so (Against the Letters of Petilian, book 3, §19).

He charged Augustine with theft because, when quoting Petilian’s text, Augustine had omitted two words that were absent from the copy sent to him and that had no bearing whatsoever on the question at hand (ibid., §§18, 21, 19, 20). Finally, he made it a charge against Augustine that he had been the founder of monastic life in Africa (ibid., §48).

### 5

Petilian was completely mistaken if he hoped that by this method he would draw Augustine away from defending the Church and toward defending himself. Augustine was dealing with a man who labored not to attract people to himself but to convert them with himself to God; who was ready [Col. 0323] to abandon his own cause sooner than the cause of the Catholic Church; and who finally desired to humble and cast himself down while proclaiming and exalting the Church as the house of God.

> I shall exalt the house of my God, whose beauty I have loved, by the proclamation of my voice; but I shall humble and cast myself down.

*(ibid., §2.)*

The false reproaches of his opponents, which he had brought upon himself by preaching the words of truth and refuting the empty talk of error, brought him not sadness but the greatest consolation. He considered not how bitter was what he heard, but how false it was, and how truthful was the one for whose name he heard it—the one who promises a great reward to those who endure reproaches for his sake (ibid., §7).

In Petilian’s insults he perceived the devil’s stratagem, by which the devil sought to drive him into hatred of the man who treated him so disgracefully. Therefore the holy man applied himself with great vigilance and courage to afflicting one hidden enemy, loving the one who was openly visible, and winning divine mercy for the latter through his prayers (ibid., §14).

Thus, when he was about to publish the response that necessity required, he in no way violated the rule that he habitually observed in speeches and writings directed against himself: namely, that he served not his own just pain but the advantage of his hearers or readers, striving to overcome his adversary’s errors with invincible arguments rather than to overcome insults with insults.

In the third book against Petilian, therefore, he did only this: he made it clear that Petilian had in no way answered the first of the books that Augustine had written and that Petilian had undertaken to refute. Augustine promises that he will demonstrate this so clearly that even the Donatists themselves—however devoted to their party and hostile to Augustine—could certainly recognize it, provided they were not too reluctant to read through both authors’ writings (ibid., §15).

For this purpose nothing was really required beyond placing Augustine’s first book alongside Petilian’s response. Yet Augustine’s charity toward people of slower understanding led him, by adding a third book, to cast still more light upon the question (Retractions, book 2, chapter 25).

At the beginning of this work he repels Petilian’s insults with remarkable simplicity of spirit and gentleness. He declares that he detests all his former life after receiving baptism and does not wish to remember it except in order to proclaim the glory of the one who, as he says, “by his grace also delivered me from myself.”

> Therefore, when I hear that my former life is being reproached, whatever the intention of the one who does it, I am not so ungrateful as to grieve. For to the extent that he accuses my illness, I praise my physician.

*(Against the Letters of Petilian, book 3, §11.)*

As for the part of Augustine’s life that he led after baptism, his outward actions required no defense among the sons of the Church, who knew his manner of life. Those who did not yet know it sufficiently could be expected not to be so unjust as to give greater authority to the testimony of a declared enemy such as Petilian than to that of Augustine’s acquaintances.

If Petilian wished to examine even the innermost recesses of Augustine’s mind, the only witness to what was happening there was Augustine’s conscience, and its testimony had to be accepted entirely on Augustine’s own word. [Col. 0324] He testifies that, although he could not claim the Apostle’s words, “I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Corinthians 4:4), he could nevertheless affirm truly and before God that his conscience recognized none of the things with which Petilian attempted to stain the life he had led after baptism (Against the Letters of Petilian, book 3, §9).

Yet far from wishing to induce the Church to undertake his defense, Augustine instead undertakes to establish against the heretics that human confidence must be rejected, so that all our glory and hope may be transferred to God alone; and consequently that the house of God must not be abandoned because of the wicked who are presently tolerated within it.

He therefore tells the Catholics who loved the truth in Augustine himself and listened with pleasure to the truth from his mouth that they should be secure—not because of the honorable reputation he enjoyed among them, but because of the hope they had placed in God himself (ibid., §3).

The Donatists, however, ought not to consider what Augustine himself was or what Petilian said he was. They should consider with what force and effectiveness Augustine demonstrated that the Catholic Church, whose cause he defended whatever his own character might be, had gained victory over their errors (ibid., §§11–12, 17).

He then urges Petilian to abandon useless insults and answer the actual points (ibid., §18).

Nor does Augustine spend much effort clearing other persons whom Petilian attacked in his writing. Augustine had maintained that no one might withdraw from communion with the Church on the pretext of separating himself from evil people who could not be convicted. Petilian distorted this into another meaning and asserted that every crime among the Catholics remained unpunished (ibid., §§43–44).

To support his claim, he said that a certain bishop, deposed from his dignity on account of the crime of the Sodomites, had later been restored to his former rank even though another had already been appointed in his place. Augustine replies only that Petilian does not know what he is saying.

Petilian also mentioned another man who had been ordered to do public penance among the Donatists; Augustine seems to imply that this was said as a slander. Similarly, he alleged that a certain Quodvultdeus, whom the Donatists had cut off from communion as though convicted of two adulteries, had nevertheless been admitted by the Catholics to ecclesiastical honors—for it is clear that this was Petilian’s meaning (ibid., §37).

But this had not been done until Quodvultdeus had either demonstrated, or at least persuaded everyone, that he was free from guilt. The holy Bishop maintains that Petilian was falsely attributing to the Church a neglect of discipline.

> There are countless examples among those who were bishops or clerics of some other such rank and who have now been degraded, or who have gone away to other lands out of shame, or who have passed over to you or to other heresies, or who are known in their own regions.

*(ibid., §43.)*

He names specifically a certain Honorius of Milevis, who may have been Severus’s predecessor in the episcopate (ibid., §44).

He adds Splendonius, who had been stripped of the diaconate in Gaul. When Splendonius came to Cirta, Petilian baptized him again and raised him to the rank of presbyter. [Col. 0325] For this reason Fortunatus, the Catholic bishop of Cirta, ordered the documents of his deposition that had been sent to him to be read publicly.

Petilian himself had suffered an abominable betrayal at the hands of this same Splendonius and was subsequently forced to cast him out.

But since it had to be proved to Petilian that corrupt ministers could also lurk for a time among the Donatists, Augustine found it necessary to point out to him Cyprian, the bishop of Thubursicuburum. Cyprian had been caught with a prostitute in a brothel and brought before Primianus, his bishop at Carthage. Primianus condemned and deposed him for this reason; nevertheless, none of those whom Cyprian had baptized was compelled to repeat baptism (Against the Letters of Petilian, book 3, §40).

Augustine closes his book by addressing the Donatists in these words:

> But in the meantime, you whom I have placed as judges between myself and that man, do you have enough understanding to distinguish between truth and falsehood, between what is inflated and what is solid, between what is turbid and what is tranquil, between what is swollen and what is healthy, between divine predictions and human presumptions, between proofs and accusations, between evidence and fabrications, between conducting a case and turning away from a case?
>
> If you have such understanding, well and rightly. But if you do not, we shall not regret having cared for you; for even if your heart is not converted to peace, our peace will nevertheless return to us.

*(ibid., §71.)*

As for Petilian’s second book, in which he promises to treat the case of the Maximianists, Augustine speaks of it as though he had never seen it. Even if he testifies that he knows this for certain, namely, that nothing consistent with reason can be found in it.

6. The matters that he reports at the end of his exposition of Psalm 36 have so much affinity with the third book against Petilian that one could readily believe that it was composed by him at approximately the same time. In it he testifies that, because the Donatists are unable to defend their succession, they turn their tongues against him and indiscriminately pour forth things known and unknown. “What they know,” says the holy man, “belongs to our past: for at one time we too were, as the Apostle says, foolish, unbelieving, and rejected for every good work (Tit. 3:3). We were deceivers and madmen in perverse error: we do not deny it; and the more we do not deny our past, the more we praise God, who forgave us. Why, then, heretic, do you abandon the case and turn to the person? You reproach my past evils—what great thing are you doing? I am more severe toward my own evils than you are: what you reproached, I condemned. Would that you wished to imitate me, so that your error too might someday belong to the past.”

“But what they now criticize,” Augustine adds, “they do not know. There are things in me that they might still criticize; yet it is too much for them even to know these things. For I do much in my thoughts, fighting against my evil suggestions and enduring a long, almost continual struggle with the temptations of the enemy who wishes to overthrow me. I groan to God in my weakness; and he knows what my heart is bringing forth, he who knows my birth” (*Enarrationes in Psalmos* 36, sermon 3, §19). “But what we are, he knows to whom we groan” (ibid., §20).

Yet he does not linger long in his own defense; rather, he grants them complete freedom to judge him as they please (ibid., §19). He begs the Catholic Carthaginians to whom he was speaking—and whose goodwill toward him he declared himself to have recognized from the love with which he himself embraced them—to abandon his cause and not to enter into any dispute with the Donatists on that matter; instead, let them press the question of the Church, which he denied in any way depended upon his own case (ibid., §20).

“For what am I—what am I?” he exclaimed. “Am I perhaps the Catholic Church? Am I perhaps Christ’s inheritance spread among the nations? It is enough for me to be in it” (ibid., §19). Again, he explains in the following manner how the Donatists should be brought back to the essential issue:

“By all means: if you call me evil, I too call myself innumerably other things. Quickly remove me from the discussion; end my case; deal with the matter itself; attend to the Church’s cause; see where you are. Let truth speak to you from whatever source; receive it while you hunger, lest bread never reach you while, always fastidious and slanderous, you search for something to criticize in the vessel” (ibid., §20).
