We have said that he delivered this speech at Carthage, since it is plainly understood that he pronounced it both outside his own Church and in that same city where the errors of his youth had been most widely publicized (ibid., §19). Accordingly, there is no reason to wonder that he mentions Cyprian there as well (ibid., §13).

First, before beginning the Psalm, he interpreted the Gospel concerning the judgment—namely, “Two in the field” (Matt. 24:40), and so forth (*Enarrationes in Psalmos* 36, sermon 1, §2). After that first sermon, continual rain detained him as he was considering his return; and meanwhile, so that this delay would not be fruitless, the Catholics asked him to continue the exposition of the same Psalm (ibid., sermon 2, §1). When he had granted their request, the course of his speech led him to mention the Donatists, and he recited a large part of the synodal letter of the Maximianists against Primianus (ibid., §20). He lingered so long over this subject that even then he was unable to finish the Psalm. He therefore returned to it a third time, compelled, willingly or unwillingly, by God himself—that is, delayed contrary to his own plan—in order to discharge his obligation completely (ibid., sermon 3, §1).

He seems also to have arranged for a number of other documents concerning the Donatists, besides the synod of the Maximianists, to be read publicly in the church. For he excuses the fact that many papers, and many things not contained in the canon of Scripture, had been read; but he says that the Donatists had furnished the reason for doing so. “Even if they criticize this,” he says, “because we have read such things to you, let us be criticized, provided that you are instructed” (ibid., §18).

He indicates that Felicianus of Musti was still alive at that time (ibid., sermon 2, §§20, 22); afterward he scarcely ever mentions him except by himself—something that very clearly proves that Praetextatus had already ceased to live. There the holy Bishop also touches upon certain acts of the Donatists, in which they called Catholics “the offspring of traditors” and asserted that the Catholics were sharpening their swords, although the latter neither demanded the return of what had been taken from them nor defended themselves by any weapons other than the Gospel (ibid., §18).

Indeed, there is no doubt that this was the document that Primianus prepared before the magistrate of Carthage, brimming with highly abusive language against the Catholics, in which these words were also read: “They take away what belongs to others; we leave alone what has been taken” (*Contra Cresconium*, book 4, §57). He sent this document to all the bishops of his communion (*Enarrationes in Psalmos* 36, sermon 2, §18); and, so far as one may judge, it contained nothing other than the response that he published toward the end of September 403, when he was questioned about entering into a conference with the Catholics. It is certain that he then replied in these terms: “It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditors should meet together” (*Codex Canonum Africorum*, canons 91, 92, etc.).

In this state of affairs Augustine, who had attended the Council of Carthage on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, expounded Psalm 36 before returning to Hippo, after he had recently completed the third book against Petilian. Augustine also quotes from the little book that Primianus had submitted to the magistrate of Carthage these words: “Your ancestors harassed our parents with various exiles” (*Ad Donatistas post Collationem*, §20); and also these: “They carry,” he said, “the sacred decrees of many emperors; we offer only the Gospels” (ibid., §53).

After the books against Petilian, Augustine next lists those written against Cresconius (*Retractationes*, book 2, chapter 26), although he did not compose the latter books before 405. We think that this sequence was adopted because of the kinship of their subject matter, since Petilian’s letter provided the occasion for both works. Nor should anyone easily persuade us that no other work appeared between the two. Nevertheless, we shall insert none unless exceptionally clear evidence should arise, so that, as far as lies within our power, we may carefully adhere to Augustine’s chronological order.

# CHAPTER IX

1. Certain enactments of the first Council of Milevis.  
2. Maximianus of Bagai voluntarily resigns the episcopate for the peace and welfare of the Church; Castorius is urged to succeed his brother.  
3. Toward the end of this year Augustine and Jerome voluntarily exchange letters.  
4. Other matters in the following year.

## 1.

This year a general African council was held at Milevis in Numidia on the sixth day before the Kalends of September. We have seen above (chapter 6) that in the preceding year there had been some dispute between Xanthippus and Victorinus concerning primacy; and that Xanthippus had already obtained this dignity before Easter of the present year, since Augustine bestowed that title upon him in letters written at this very time.

It appears, however, that the same controversy furnished the occasion for several canons of the Council of Milevis, which have some affinity with it. For Bishop Valentinus requested that it be established by decree that what had always prevailed among bishops should be confirmed—namely, that their order should be determined by the antiquity of their consecration (*Codex Canonum Africanorum*, canon 86). This petition was approved by Aurelius and afterward, at Xanthippus’s request, confirmed by the votes of the entire council, while preserving the right of the primates of Numidia and Mauretania, who perhaps took precedence even over others more senior.

At least, we frequently find the primate of Numidia signing second after the Bishop of Carthage. Likewise, at Cirta, or Constantine, which was the civil metropolis of Numidia, one may reasonably believe that its bishop claimed some exceptional place for himself; for in the heading of a certain letter (*Epistle* 53), the names of Alypius and Augustine are read only after that of Fortunatus. Yet no one, we think, will doubt that this Fortunatus was the Bishop of Cirta, whom we know to have been junior to Augustine.

In the same council the Fathers also decreed that if someone had once read in a particular church, that was sufficient for him to be regarded as its lector, and that thereafter he was not free to transfer to another church (*Codex Canonum Africanorum*, canon 90). The dispute that arose between Augustine and Severus concerning Timothy may perhaps have occasioned this decree (Epistle 63); we discussed it above (chapter 7).

## 2.

The same council resolved to write to Maximianus, Bishop of Bagai, and to his people: to Maximianus, that he should resign the episcopate; to the people, that they should consider choosing another bishop for themselves (*Codex Canonum Africanorum*, canon 88).

There survives a letter of Augustine (*Epistle* 69) that agrees most plainly with this canon, as others have already observed. In it we read that Maximianus, Bishop of the Church of Vaga, and his brother Castorius, having renounced Donatus’s schism, had returned to the bosom of the Church; but that the joy brought by their return had been disturbed by a scandal diabolically stirred up against Maximianus.

Nevertheless, God so calmed that offense that the Church derived more pleasure from it than it had previously suffered distress from the scandal. For when Maximianus understood that he could not retain episcopal honor without the Church being agitated by a shameful dissension that might perhaps bring great destruction even upon Christ’s members, he laid down his dignity and declared that he sought not what was his own but what belonged to Jesus Christ; that he had defected from the party of the schismatics out of a sincere zeal for charity and peace; that true humility was present in him; and finally, that the building Christ had raised in his heart was so firm that it could withstand the storm of so troublesome a temptation without being shaken.

After his resignation, Castorius, his own brother, was elected to succeed him. The people of Vaga were ordered to restrain him, lest he flee in order to avoid this dignity. Alypius and Augustine also exhorted him by letter to accept the episcopate of his brother Maximianus, whom they call their son and whom they praise at length because of his voluntary resignation from his office.

Augustine had this example especially before his eyes when, several years later, he addressed the Donatists in these words: “Certain men endowed with holy humility, because of certain offenses in themselves that moved them piously and religiously, laid down the office of bishop not only without blame but even with praise” (*Contra Cresconium*, book 2, §13).

We shall see under the year 404 the astonishing cruelties of the Donatists against Maximianus of Bagai, or Vaga. At first Baronius thought that this was the same Maximianus who is being discussed here; afterward, however, he asserted that they were different men and bishops of different sees (Baronius, under the year 402, §62).

The latter opinion may also be supported by the fact that Augustine reports a special reason for the hatred with which the Donatists burned against Maximianus the confessor; yet he does not say that Maximianus had ever followed their party—something that would certainly have been more than sufficient to inflame them against him (Epistle 185, §§27–28).

## 3.

In this very year, 402, unless our conjecture deceives us, Augustine sent Jerome a letter (*Epistle* 67), asking him to provide a response to another letter (*Epistle* 40), which he had arranged to have delivered to Jerome as early as 397.

Those letters had circulated for a long time through Rome and Italy, against Augustine’s wishes, before reaching Jerome. Since Augustine had amicably challenged several of Jerome’s opinions in them, especially his account of the dispute between Peter and Paul, the result was that it was commonly said that Augustine had composed a book against Jerome and sent it to Rome (*Epistle* 67, §2).

The holy Bishop, who had not yet learned where that rumor had originated, repeatedly assured Jerome that he had in no way done what was being alleged. He not only did not wish to offend Jerome in any matter; he would also experience no small pleasure if he were permitted to live together with him, or at least to consult him frequently by letter.

The subdeacon Asterius was preparing to travel from Palestine to Africa when Jerome received that later letter from Augustine. Jerome therefore immediately sent Augustine a reply through the same subdeacon (*Epistle* 68), with exceptional expressions of his love for Augustine, though not without some indication of irritation concerning the letters of 397; nevertheless, Jerome still denied that he was entirely convinced that they were Augustine’s (ibid.; *Epistle* 72, §2).

He therefore asked Augustine to inform him as soon as possible of the truth of the matter. At the same time he arranged for his second apology against Rufinus to be delivered to the holy Bishop.

## 4.

What Jerome had entrusted to Asterius for delivery to Augustine reached Africa only much later. Meanwhile Augustine sent Jerome two letters (*Epistle* 72, §1). The first has been lost through the injury of time; the second, which begins, “From the time when I began to write to you” (*Epistle* 71), occupies a place among his letters under the year 403.

He sent it through the deacon Cyprian, together with copies of his earlier letters, since he did not know whether Jerome had received them. In this letter he openly admits that he was not at all pleased that Jerome was translating the sacred Scriptures into Latin from the Hebrew.

On this subject he warned him about a disturbance that had arisen in an African church because of the word “ivy,” which Jerome had used in a passage of Jonah in place of “gourd,” the term used by the Septuagint translators.

Jerome replied to Augustine’s missing letter with a letter beginning, “You send me frequent letters” (*Epistle* 72). In it he is somewhat more irritated than in his earlier letter sent through Asterius, though never without expressing his love and respect for Augustine. As for Augustine’s books, Jerome indicates that he has none in his hands except the *Soliloquies* and some commentaries on the Psalms.

It is enough for the moment to have touched briefly upon this dispute between them; we shall pursue it toward the end of the year 404.

# CHAPTER X

1. Provoked by the preaching of the truth, the Donatists undertake many acts of violence.  
2. Augustine is rescued from danger after losing his way.  
3. Because of the violence they endured, certain men acquire the name of confessors.  
4. The Catholic bishops publicly summon the Donatist bishops to hold a conference.  
5. They arrogantly refuse; Augustine writes to their laity.

## 1.

We have seen elsewhere what the history of the Maximianists was and how greatly it served the interests of the Church (above, book 3, chapter 9, §1). We have also seen what the Council of Carthage decreed in 401 concerning the search for original documents relating to that history (*Codex Canonum Africanorum*, canon 67).

It specifically wished bishops to be sent to exhort the Donatists to peace, and it wished those who were sent to employ, above all, this history—attested by the reliability of public records—to convince their minds (ibid., canon 69).

Those chosen for this task admirably obeyed the council’s decisions. Wherever they could, they spread this same history with fervent persistence. The matter was so recent and so clearly established that the Donatists could find absolutely nothing to bring forward in opposition.

Accordingly, many, overcome by salutary shame and afraid to deny a matter so thoroughly established, renounced their error; and returns to the Church became much more frequent than before, especially in those places where the savagery of the Circumcellions raged with less license (ibid.; *Epistle* 185, §17).

But the same light of truth that illuminated some increased the blindness of others. For those who delighted in the darkness of falsehood, distressed that every means of defense had been taken from them, began, says Augustine, “with customary frequency and greater audacity, to try to deter us by the violence and frenzied disturbances of the Circumcellions from preaching the Catholic truth and refuting their deceit” (*Contra Cresconium*, book 3, §49).

The Catholic bishops desired nothing except to be permitted to preach the truth, so that those who wished might freely and without any coercion embrace it. But the heretics deprived the bishops of this opportunity and terrified everyone by their violence (*Epistle* 105, §3).

They became so inflamed, to use Augustine’s words, and were driven by such powerful goads of hatred that, in the face of their ambushes, violence, and outright brigandage, scarcely any Church of our communion could be secure; scarcely was there any safe road for those who traveled to preach Catholic peace against their fury and to refute their madness by the evident truth.

Thus an extremely harsh condition was imposed in a certain sense not only upon the laity and ordinary clergy but also upon the Catholic bishops themselves. Either the truth had to be silenced, or their savagery had to be endured.

If the truth were silenced, not only would no one be freed by that silence, but many would also be lost through their seduction. If, on the other hand, the preaching of the truth provoked their fury to violence, then, although some might be freed and our own people strengthened, fear would again prevent the weak from following the truth (*Epistle* 185, §18).

This was the reason why, as we shall see in the following year, the bishops sought the Emperor’s protection. In the preceding year the holy Bishop had complained of the furious attempts of the same faction in these words:

“Would we not be driven from the countryside on every side by the violent attacks of your Circumcellions, who serve under your leadership in frenzied bands, unless we kept you as hostages in the cities—you who are unwilling in any way to endure the very face of public authority and the reproof of respectable persons, if not through fear, then at least through shame?” (*Contra Litteras Petiliani*, book 2, §184).

## 2.

At approximately this same time, after the care of preaching concord to the schismatics had been entrusted to various bishops—and certainly above all to Augustine (*Codex Canonum Africanorum*, canon 69)—the same holy Bishop encountered a danger that must not be passed over in silence.

He was often invited to visit Catholic communities in order to instruct and strengthen them by exhortation. When the Circumcellions learned of this, they sometimes lay in ambush for him while armed and blocking the roads.

On one occasion they had prepared to await him along a route where neither he nor any of his traveling companions could possibly have avoided falling into their hands. But by God’s extraordinary providence, they were misled at a fork in the road by the error of a false guide and turned away from the correct route.

Thus, wandering by the road they had intended to take, they reached their destination by a detour and escaped the ambush of the enraged men. Later, when they learned of the Donatists’ plan, they rejoiced at this providential mistake and gave thanks to God for having turned the danger away from them (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 12; *Enchiridion*, §5).

The Circumcellions, however, directed all their anger with their customary cruelty against Catholic clergy and laity. As a result, an investigation was conducted and an official document was drawn up against them (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 12).

## 3.

The clergy of Hippo, recalling what the Circumcellions had perpetrated before the edicts of Honorius, and perhaps even before the council of this year, say:

“They laid ambushes for our bishops on their journeys; they battered our fellow clergy with atrocious blows; they inflicted extremely serious wounds upon the laity as well, and set fire to their buildings” (*Epistle* 88, §6).

They add the well-known story of the presbyter Restitutus, as Augustine relates it. Restitutus had been a presbyter of the Donatist sect at Victoriana, a place situated in the diocese of Hippo. Moved by the force of truth, by a wholly voluntary choice and without anyone’s coercion, he had embraced Catholic unity. At that time Honorius had not yet issued the laws by which the Donatists were ordered to renounce the schism (*Contra Cresconium*, book 3; *Epistle* 88, §6; *Epistle* 105).

When these same heretics could not bear Restitutus’s change, their clergy and Circumcellions dragged him from his house in broad daylight to a neighboring fortress. A crowd watched, but no one dared to resist. They beat him with clubs until their fury was satisfied, rolled him in a muddy pool, and dressed him in a garment made of rushes, which they called a *buda*.

After exposing him for some time in this attire to the mockery of some and the grief of others, they led him away to a place whose entrance was forbidden to all Catholics, and released him only after twelve days (*Contra Cresconium*, book 3, §53).

Perhaps they would not have allowed him to leave at all if Proculeianus, their bishop at Hippo, had not feared that he would be brought to trial on that account (*Epistle* 105, §3).

Augustine did not wish to complain to Caesar about this violence and the many other acts by which the Donatists were tormenting the Catholics of his diocese (*Epistle* 88, §7). He complained only to Proculeianus. So that Proculeianus could not pretend ignorance, Augustine informed him through an official proceeding by which he called upon him to repair so great an injury (*Contra Cresconium*, book 3, §53).

Proculeianus’s response was committed to writing, but we nowhere read what it was. This alone is certain: he had no intention whatsoever of avenging the violence; indeed, he completely pretended not to investigate it.

When this prompted Augustine to repeat the same official complaint immediately, Proculeianus declared in the proceedings that he would say nothing further. Later, the guilty parties were to be seen among the presbyteral order, threatening Catholics daily and harassing them in every way they could (*Epistle* 88, §§6–7).

On this occasion Restitutus first earned the title of confessor, and later also that of martyr (*Epistle* 133, §1). This, however, did not occur until several years afterward, as we shall relate in its proper place.

For the rest, we do not know whether certain acts of violence committed by the Donatists—acts that Augustine mentions together with those against Restitutus—should be assigned to this period.

A certain presbyter of Casphalianum, named Marcus, had returned voluntarily and without compulsion to Catholic unity. The Donatists persecuted him so fiercely that he was on the point of being slaughtered by their hands, had God not restrained their violence through the arrival of some people (*Epistle* 105, §3).

They also forced Marcianus of Urga—whether presbyter or bishop—to save himself by flight after he had returned to Catholic communion. Then their clergy seized his subdeacon and, after beating him almost to death, buried him beneath stones. Their buildings were razed to the ground as punishment for the crime they had committed (ibid.).

## 4.

Among those ensnared by the errors of the Donatists, many were neither equal in wickedness to the Circumcellions nor sufficiently capable by themselves of judgment to embrace the truth immediately. Nevertheless, they did not show themselves wholly alienated from it. Whenever Catholics pressed them, they repeatedly declared that the matter had to be discussed with their bishops; they said that they desired a conference between the two parties, so that, after the arguments on both sides had been weighed, it might be determined which party possessed the truth (*Contra Cresconium*, book 3, §49).

When the orthodox understood that their minds were disposed in this way, they set themselves to arranging that debate. At the general council held at Carthage in the Basilica of the Second Region on the eighth day before the Kalends of September in the present year, 403, they discussed the means by which it could most conveniently be accomplished.

Alypius, Augustine, and Possidius were among those present. Of what was done at this council after the legates had been examined, nothing now survives that does not concern the Donatists.

The day before, a speech had been delivered about them, and it had been unanimously decided that each bishop, either alone or accompanied by a neighboring bishop, should summon the Donatist bishop through the magistrates or elders of the locality. The purpose was that, after a meeting had been held with their colleagues, the Donatists themselves should choose several from among their number to discuss peacefully with the Catholic legates, at a fixed place and time, the controversy arising from the schism, and to bring at last to the desired conclusion that most troublesome dissension by which all the communities were being divided (*Codex Canonum Africanorum*, canon 91; *Contra Cresconium*, book 3, §49).

The Catholics eagerly wished to offer this testimony to their inclination toward peace. They hoped that, if the Donatists accepted the conference, they would easily be convicted of error; but if they refused it, their refusal would show how little they trusted the justice of their own cause. This could usefully be employed to draw their followers away from error.

Moreover, so that it would be easier for all the bishops to follow the same procedure, Aurelius supplied a formula for the summons they were to use. It was read and approved by all alike, and today is found incorporated into the Council’s acts.

At its beginning there is a petition to be submitted to the magistrate of each city. The Catholic bishop who speaks in it declares that he has obtained this summons by the authority and command of that most important see, and that it was to be entered into the official record (*Codex Canonum Africanorum*, canon 92).

Indeed, the council had decided to send those letters to the judges or governors for no other reason than to obtain such commands; and it wished them to be sealed in the name of the council by the Bishop of Carthage.

There still exists a petition presented in the name of the Council of Carthage to Septiminus, proconsul of Africa, on the Ides of September in the year 403. In it the bishops declare that, although they could suppress the violence perpetrated by the Donatists by force of the laws enacted for that purpose by the emperors—just as the Donatists themselves had used those same laws to coerce the Maximianists—they nevertheless preferred to admonish them gently, so that they might either renounce their schism or defend it, if they trusted that they could do so, not through the savagery of the Circumcellions but by peaceful means in a legitimate debate.

For this reason they requested permission to summon them through the local magistrates whenever necessary (*Collatio Carthaginensis*, session 3, chapter 174). Septiminus immediately granted this request.

## 5.

The Catholics therefore did not fail to summon the Donatists for this purpose. But the Donatists, with their minds always firmly determined, obstinately declined and refused the conference. Augustine says that it would now take too long to demonstrate in what words they did so, and with what deceit, curses, and bitterness (*Contra Cresconium*, book 3, §49).

They alleged, as an unmistakable sign of intolerable arrogance, that it was unlawful for them to enter into a conference with sinners (*Epistle* 105, §13).

A witness to this is the response of Primianus of Carthage, full of arrogance. When he was summoned to hold the conference, he said: “It is unworthy that the sons of martyrs and the offspring of traditors should meet together” (*Ad Donatistas post Collationem*, §1).

He gave this response in writing to the magistrate of Carthage and ordered it to be communicated through his deacon to the scribes—or, as Augustine says, to be entered into the official record.

Above (chapter 8, §6) we saw certain words excerpted from a document that Primianus sent to the other Donatist bishops. We think that these words were contained in the response just mentioned.

We also said that it is entirely plausible that, not long afterward, shortly before returning to Hippo, Augustine delivered his exposition of Psalm 36 before the people of Carthage. After returning to his see, he arranged, in accordance with the council’s instructions, for Proculeianus to be summoned.

Proculeianus replied that a council of his own party would be compelled to meet, and that it would be decided collectively what answer should be given (*Epistle* 83, §7).

There is no doubt that this assembly of theirs took place, but it was held for no other purpose than to decide that the conference should be refused. When Proculeianus was again summoned to disclose his position, as he had promised, he cut off all hope of holding the conference.

It is sufficiently clear that this response was given as the decision of their assembly. Augustine plainly indicates this when he says: “If the wolves have held a council so that they may not answer the shepherds” (*Epistle* 76, §4). These words are taken from a letter that Augustine perhaps wrote at this very time concerning the conference refused by the Donatists.

He addresses that letter to all the followers of the schism. After demonstrating to them the truth of the Catholic Church, first by passages collected from divine Scripture, then by the three judgments issued in favor of Caecilianus, then by the crimes of Optatus, their martyr, whom they had not excluded from their communion (ibid., §3), and finally by the history of the Maximianists and the indulgence with which they had received Felicianus of Musti—Augustine does not mention Praetextatus—together with those whom Felicianus had baptized outside their Church, he urges the Donatist laity to press their bishops to resolve these difficulties, since the bishops were unwilling to enter into conference with the Catholics.

They should recognize that this very refusal contained unmistakable evidence of weakness. This letter makes no mention at all of the laws of Honorius.

# CHAPTER XI

1. When summoned to a conference, Crispinus responds with bitter and abusive words.  
2. The Donatists attack Possidius.  
3. The defender of the Church arranges for Crispinus to be condemned to a monetary penalty imposed upon heretics; Possidius subsequently proves him to be a heretic.  
4. Nevertheless, the Catholics later obtain remission of this penalty.  
5. A delegation from the Council of Carthage seeks moderate laws against the schismatics from the Emperor.  
6. This delegation is entrusted to Theasius and Evasius.  
7. The Donatists’ savagery against Maximianus.  
8. They also attack Bishop Servus.

## 1.

To return to the summons by which the Donatists were to be challenged by the Catholics: when Possidius, Bishop of Calama, arranged for it to be communicated to Crispinus, the Donatist bishop of that city—who was both senior in age and highly esteemed among his own people—Crispinus replied to the summons that he would consult with his colleagues to determine what answer should be given.

Much later, in the year 404, when summoned again, he gave the following response in the official record:

“Do not fear the words of a sinful man” (1 Macc. 2:62).

And again:

“Take care to say nothing to the ears of the imprudent, lest, when he hears, he mock your sensible words” (Prov. 23:9).

Finally, he concluded this response of his own “in patriarchal language”:

“Let the ungodly depart from me; I do not wish to know their ways” (*Contra Cresconium*, book 3, §50).

Crispinus’s response provoked laughter among the educated and uneducated alike, since he boasted that he did not fear the words of a sinful man, yet did not dare to answer him.

Its meaning was sufficiently obvious. There were also people who pointed out how useless the response was and how harmful it was to the very man who gave it because of the harshness of its language. At the same time, it demonstrated that all the celebrated learning of Bishop Crispinus—as he was regarded among the Donatists—could accomplish nothing against the truth when confronted by a young and inexperienced man such as Possidius.

## 2

When this attempt failed, another course had to be taken; and this seemed by far the most effective. A few days later Possidius set out from Calama to visit the Figulinian estate in his diocese, intending to strengthen the Catholics who were few in number there, to encourage others, if they wished, to embrace unity, and finally to impart to everyone the doctrine of peace which he had learned in Augustine’s monastery and clergy, from which he had been chosen for the episcopate (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 12; *Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 50; Letter 105, no. 4).

The Donatists, however, under the leadership of another Crispinus, presbyter of Crispinus, bishop of Calama, and, as was said, his relative, occupied the roads with armed men in the manner of bandits and laid ambushes. Possidius had almost fallen into one of them when, informed of what was happening, he turned aside and withdrew to a place called Livetum—where, clearly, Crispinus either would not dare to act, or would not be strong enough, or, if he did anything, could not deny it.

They then surrounded with armed men the house in which Possidius had shut himself in with his companions; pelted it with stones; encircled it with flames; and attempted to force an entrance from every side. The crowd of inhabitants who were present, mindful of the danger to themselves if so great a crime were carried out in that place, partly begged him to spare Possidius, whom they did not dare to offend by resisting him, and partly extinguished the fires that had been set. They suppressed the flames three times; had they not done so, Possidius, together with the house and the others enclosed within it, would have been burned alive.

But when Crispinus, no less fervent in his undertaking and unmoved by pity, continued to press on, the door eventually yielded to the blows. They entered, wounded and slaughtered the animals they found in the lower part of the house, and dragged the bishop down from the upper floors, subjecting him to blows and insults. To prevent them from raging still more violently, Crispinus himself intervened, as though moved by the pleas of others—although in his anger he seemed less concerned to heed their entreaties than to fear their serving as witnesses to his crime (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 50).

Possidius himself, reporting the same event as though it had happened to someone else, is content to say that when the Donatists attacked him on the road, they plundered his animals and possessions and inflicted upon him insults and extremely severe violence (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 12).

## 3

After these events had become known in the town of Calama, Augustine continues, people awaited your bishop Crispinus—he is addressing the Donatists—to see how he would avenge the matter upon his presbyter. There was also a formal protest, recorded in the municipal acts, by fear or shame of which he would be compelled to exercise ecclesiastical vengeance. When he utterly disregarded this, and the uproar of your people grew so great that they seemed likely to close the roads against the preaching of the truth, to which they could not reply—or rather, were already visibly doing so (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 51)—then, lest such violence obstruct the course of ecclesiastical peace, the Church’s defender, following the established legal procedure, brought complaints concerning the matter before the magistrate (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 12). It was obtained—perhaps from the proconsul of Numidia—that Bishop Crispinus should pay the fine established by law against heretics, namely ten pounds of gold (Letter 105, no. 4; *Against Cresconius*, no. 51).

Theodosius had promulgated this law against all heretics as early as 15 June of the year 392: anyone who among them conferred or received clerical rank was to be fined ten pounds of gold, and all places in which they assembled with the owner’s consent were to be confiscated to the treasury; but if this occurred without the owner’s knowledge, or in places already assigned to the treasury, the tenant of the estate was likewise to be fined ten pounds of gold (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 21). Augustine frequently mentions this same law (*Against the Letter of Parmenianus*, book 1, no. 19), in addition to quite a few others that permitted the Church to deal with heretics.

Although those laws were entirely consistent with justice, the Catholics possessed such great gentleness that they neglected them and, if one may put it so, allowed them to lie dormant, making no demand that their provisions be enforced (Letter 88, no. 7; *Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 51). Indeed, nothing else stirred the Catholics to recall those laws except the necessity of warding off the violence inflicted upon them by the Circumcellions. The Catholics first used these laws to restrain, if they could, the tyranny of Optatus Gildonianus (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 3, no. 184).

They later employed them against Bishop Crispinus as well, but much less in order to exact punishment for the crimes committed than to provide evidence of their own clemency and to make it clear that the Church, far from tyrannically usurping any power for itself—as the Circumcellions did, was unwilling even to use the authority which it had received from legitimate authority, serving it according to prophetic truth (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 51).

Crispinus refused to obey the judgment pronounced against him. He appeared before the proconsul and maintained that the charge of heresy did not in any way attach to him (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 12; *Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 51). It was not the responsibility of the Church’s defender—we believe this man was a layman—to prove that charge. When he withdrew, Possidius was therefore forced to resist Crispinus and to demonstrate that he really was entangled in heresy; otherwise the weak would be given a stumbling block, and there would be a danger that the ignorant themselves would consider Possidius a heretic.

Augustine was not far away. With all the strength at his disposal, he urged that the two bishops of Calama should debate one another. Thus, coming together three times for disputation, they argued about the very separation of communion by which the Donatists had been torn away from the true Church, while a large multitude of people both at Carthage and throughout the rest of Africa awaited the outcome with eager attention.

At last Crispinus was convicted of heresy without much difficulty, and was declared such by a written judgment issued in a formal document by the proconsul (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 12).

## 4

Nevertheless, Possidius showed such gentleness that he interposed his influence with the proconsul to prevent Crispinus from being fined ten pounds of gold, and in fact obtained this exemption for him (Letter 105, no. 4; *Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 52; Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 12).

Yet, although this judgment was exceedingly mild, Crispinus refused to comply with it (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 51). Showing himself most ungrateful, he appealed to the Emperor (Letter 88, no. 7, and Letter 105, no. 4).

This was said to have displeased the other Donatist bishops (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 51), and not without reason, since they could expect nothing from it except an unfavorable outcome. The appeal was nevertheless admitted, and the Emperor replied that Donatists, wherever they lived, were subject to the fine of ten pounds of gold, just as they were subject to all the other laws promulgated against heretics; those laws were therefore to be enforced against them.

Moreover, the ten pounds of gold were not to be exacted only from Crispinus, but also from the judge who had granted him remission of the fine, and from the *officium*, that is, from the other court officials who had assisted in that judgment (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 39; and Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 12).

Thus Crispinus preferred to turn the danger that threatened him alone, and which he could easily have averted himself, against the entire Donatist faction rather than punish his own presbyter, guilty of so atrocious a crime, at least by degrading him (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 52).

Nevertheless, the Catholic bishops, and Augustine above all, obtained from the Emperor’s clemency an exemption from the aforesaid fine for the Donatists, so that, through their intervention, even Crispinus was not compelled to pay it (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 12).

This indulgence of the bishops brought great additions to the Church. But Augustine always carried off the palm in such matters: in everything undertaken to bring about peace, he yielded first place to no one, and thus day by day increased ever more the crown of righteousness which God reserved for him in heaven.

## 5

After the history of Crispinus, Augustine adds a mention of the embassy which the council held at Carthage on 26 June of this year, 404, in the basilica of the Second Region, sent to the Emperor (Letter 88, no. 7).

At that time the Church was being savagely afflicted. The Donatists, indignant that, although so often challenged to a conference, they could find nothing to say in reply, attempted to avenge their defeat by new and utterly unheard-of acts of brutality (Letter 185, no. 18).

Yet quite a few among their communion detested such a course of action; because they abhorred it, they considered themselves free from all guilt (ibid., no. 16). On this point the Catholics objected that, if they judged themselves capable of being free from crimes committed within their communion, they could not consistently claim that the whole world had been polluted by the crimes of Caecilianus—whether those crimes were false or at least unknown.

This argument moved some so deeply that they resolved among themselves to abandon the schism and endure all the injuries they might fear from the fury of the Circumcellions. But the great majority of those who desired to return to Catholic unity did not dare provoke the anger of those depraved men against themselves, deterred by the example of people who had suffered atrocities because they rejected the schism.

In these circumstances the Catholic bishops would have incurred not the reputation of praiseworthy patience but the stigma of blameworthy negligence if they had preferred to endure this oppression rather than take refuge in the protection which divine providence offered them through imperial authority, and if they had not implored the defense of the Christian rulers for the Church itself—whose sons those rulers also were—so that, under their rule, the wicked would not be permitted to terrify the weaker and compel them by fear to do what they despaired of persuading them to do by reason (ibid., no. 18).

Very many bishops, especially those advanced in age, thought that laws should be requested ordering all Donatists without exception to embrace Catholic communion (ibid., no. 25). They cited the examples of many cities and places which, out of fear of the laws of Constantine and the emperors who followed him, had accepted Catholic communion even unwillingly and thereafter retained it with the greatest sincerity and steadfastness (Letter 185, no. 25; Letter 93, no. 16).

They specifically mentioned Tagaste. Although once entirely attached to Donatus, it had later abandoned him through fear of the imperial laws; and, having sincerely embraced unity, had conceived such hatred for the Donatist sect that one would have thought it had never belonged to it. In this way Augustine’s own city was held up above all others, so that the others might more easily be brought to the desired position (Letter 93, no. 17).

For at first Augustine’s position had been that no one should be compelled to the unity of Christ: one should proceed by speech, fight by disputation, and conquer by reason, lest the Church contain false Catholics who had previously been openly known as heretics. In the end, however, he yielded, overcome both by the arguments and by the examples of his colleagues; yet he judged it preferable still to pursue a milder course (ibid., no. 19).

“Some of our brothers,” he says, “among whom I was one, thought that, although the fury of the Donatists raged everywhere, we ought not to ask the Emperors to order that the heresy itself should altogether cease, imposing a penalty upon those who wished to remain in it. Rather, we thought they should decree that those who either preached the Catholic truth by speaking or read it aloud by public enactment should not suffer their mad violence.

“We thought that this could be achieved to some extent if the law of Theodosius of most blessed memory, which he promulgated generally against all heretics—‘Whoever among them, whether bishop or cleric, is found anywhere shall be fined ten pounds of gold’—were confirmed more explicitly against the Donatists, who denied that they were heretics. The provision would be that not all of them should be struck by the fine, but only those in whose regions the Catholic Church suffered any violence from their clerics, their Circumcellions, or their people. Thus, after the Catholics who had suffered such things had lodged a protest, the bishops or other ministers would then, through the agency of the municipal councils, be held responsible for paying the fine.

“We thought that, once they had been frightened and dared to do nothing of the kind, the Catholic truth could be freely taught and held: no one would be compelled to embrace it, but whoever wished could follow it without fear, so that we would not have false and hypocritical Catholics” (Letter 185, ch. 7, no. 25).

This proposal yielded to the opinion of the other bishops, and a decree was made at the synod in question. Envoys were chosen who, upon approaching the imperial court, would humbly ask the Emperor for the law which the Church was believed to require.

There was another law which deprived heretics of the ability either to make wills, to transfer anything by donations, or to receive anything from donations or wills. On account of this law—which is now absent from the Code—the Emperor, before the year 400, had rescinded the will of a certain Donatist woman by an edict that also touched upon the madness of the Circumcellions.

The council of Carthage therefore resolved to ask the Emperor to confirm this law, but with the qualification that it should apply only to those who obstinately persisted in the schismatic faction. Those who returned to reconciliation with the Church were to have the right and lawful authority to recover whatever had come to them before their reconciliation, provided that they had not transferred to Catholic unity only after litigation had begun over property which they claimed. For then they would be judged to have been moved more by the desire for earthly advantage than by fear of God.

The council also thought it should request that the municipal councils and those whose estates lay nearby be required to provide protection for the churches against the fury of the Circumcellions—a fury sufficiently well known to the Emperors and frequently condemned by law—and, in the meantime, while the envoys were returning, that the same protection should be requested from the prefects of the provinces (*African Code of Canons*, canon 93).

## 6

This embassy was entrusted to the bishops Theasius and Evodius (ibid.). The *Collation* mentions a certain Theasius, bishop of Memblosis in the Proconsular Province (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, ch. 133). Evodius may be the same as the bishop of Uzalis who, in a letter to Augustine, mentions Bishop Theasius, calls him an old man, and seems to imply that he lived in a monastery (Letter 158, no. 10).

Petilianus rages against both men in these words:

“Those, that is, whom they always have as their forerunners and navigators, the envoys of their madness, who seek blood, seek proscriptions, inflict fears, bring dangers, and kill men throughout the various provinces” (*Carthaginian Conference* 3, ch. 141).

Because of the persecutions they endured for the sake of the faith in the year 408, both obtained the title of confessor (*African Code of Canons*, in the Council of Carthage of 408, after canon 106).

The mandates given to them by the council concerning the embassy still survive. They prescribe what, according to the decision of the Fathers, was to be requested from the Emperor, while leaving them complete freedom to request whatever they judged conducive to the Church’s welfare (ibid., canon 93).

It was also decided that they should be commended by letter to the bishop of Rome and to the bishops of the places where the Emperor might happen to be. Other letters to the Emperor and to his principal ministers were also entrusted to the same envoys. They bore witness to the instructions given by the synod, and Aurelius alone sealed them in the name of all the Fathers.

Beyond doubt these letters were written by Augustine, since Possidius, when listing Augustine’s letters, places four of them in immediate succession: “To Innocent, the bishop”; “To the Emperors”; “To Stilicho”; “To the Prefects of Italy.” None of these letters, however, remains to us.

## 7

At least, in the foregoing account we have seen what counsel Augustine’s gentleness inspired in the African Church. “But God’s greater mercy,” says the same saint, “who knew how necessary the terror of these laws and a certain medicinal severity would be for the perverse or cold minds of many, and for that hardness which cannot be corrected by words but can be corrected by some degree of disciplinary severity, brought it about that our envoys could not obtain what they had undertaken” (Letter 185, no. 26).

For by then some extremely serious complaints from other places had preceded us. They came from bishops who had suffered many evils at the hands of the Donatists and had been driven from their sees. Above all, the dreadful and incredible slaughter of Maximianus, the Catholic bishop of the Church of Bagai, caused our embassy to have nothing further to do (ibid.).

After a judicial sentence had been pronounced between the parties by the ordinary judge, Maximianus had secured the basilica of the Calvian estate, which the Donatists had at one time unlawfully occupied even though it belonged to the Catholics. While he was retaining it by an unmistakable legal right, they attacked him as he stood at the altar itself, rushing upon him with terrifying force and savage fury. They broke apart the altar under which he had taken refuge, and beat him cruelly with its timbers and other clubs, even with iron, until the entire place was filled with his blood.

He had also received a great wound in the groin from a dagger. Blood flowed so copiously from it that he would have died immediately, had not their greater cruelty, through God’s hidden mercy, proved beneficial. For while his limbs were stripped bare on that side and he was dragged along half alive and face downward, dust secretly blocked the veins that were pouring out blood.

After the Catholics attempted to carry him away, having been abandoned by his attackers and singing psalms, the Donatists, inflamed by even fiercer anger, snatched him from the hands of those carrying him. They severely beat and drove away the Catholics, whom they greatly outnumbered and easily terrified by their violence.

Thus, after violently tearing him from them and beating him still more severely, they carried him to a high tower. Thinking that he had already died, although he was still alive, they threw him down. He fell softly upon a layer of dung-ash and lay there, having lost consciousness and barely drawing his final breath.

There a poor man found him when he happened to withdraw to that place to relieve himself. He recognized him after fearfully sending for his wife, whom he had kept at a distance out of modesty, carrying a lamp. The two of them then carried him home, either out of compassion or with some hope of gain, so that, whether alive or dead, he might nevertheless be recovered and shown to our people.

What more need be said? With great care and miraculous treatment, after many days he was restored from the brink of death and healed. News had reached the lands across the sea that he had been killed, and the enormity and grave outrage of the deed had stirred everything with terrible grief wherever it was heard.

When he himself later followed there, and his wholly unexpected survival became known, his scars—so enormous, so numerous, and so fresh—showed that the report of his death had not announced it without reason. Those who saw him then could scarcely believe that he was alive; and it seemed that the report of his death had not been rashly asserted.

He therefore sought help from the Christian Emperor, not so much to avenge himself as to protect the Church entrusted to him. Had he omitted to do so, his conduct would not have deserved praise for patience but would rightly have been blamed as negligence (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 52; Letter 185, nos. 26–28).

Augustine’s words seem to allow the conclusion that Maximianus went to Rome to see the Emperor (Letter 88, no. 7). Nevertheless, laws issued in February 405 on his behalf were promulgated at Ravenna (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 58).

In the following year, or the year after that—that is, when the holy Doctor was writing against Cresconius—Maximianus was still alive, and the scars on his body outnumbered his limbs (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 47).

His name does not appear in the Carthaginian Conference; but in the Roman Martyrology he is added to the holy confessors on 3 October.

## 8

When he arrived at the imperial court, he found there quite a few people who had fled to it and who had been treated by the Donatists in the same way as he had been, or at least scarcely more humanely (ibid.).

Among them was the bishop of Thubursica, which they called Bura and, in a single name, Thubursicabura; it seems to have been situated in the Proconsular Province. This bishop was named Servus, or Servus-Dei. He took part in the Carthaginian Conference of 411 (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, ch. 121).

He was reclaiming a place occupied by the Donatists (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 47). At that time a certain Donatus was their bishop—perhaps after Cyprianus had been condemned for his crimes (*Against the Letters of Petilianus*, book 3, no. 38; *Carthaginian Conference* 1, ch. 121).

While these two bishops were disputing over that place and the representatives of the parties were awaiting the proconsular inquiry, armed Donatists suddenly attacked Servus in the aforementioned town of Thubursicabura, so that he barely escaped alive.

His father, however, a presbyter grave in age and character, died a few days later from the wounds which the same men had inflicted upon him with great violence (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, ch. 43).

What laws the Donatists gave reason to be enacted against themselves on account of all these crimes, we shall explain in the following year.

# CHAPTER XII

1. A scandal arises at Hippo because of the presbyter Boniface and Spes.  
2. Augustine’s letter on this matter to strengthen the people of Hippo.  
3. He convicts Felix the Manichaean and recalls him from error.  
4. He writes the book *On the Nature of the Good* against the Manichaean heresy.  
5. He completely overthrows it, especially in the book published against Secundinus.  
6. By his humility he calms Jerome’s embittered spirit.  
7. Their letters sent back and forth.

## 1

Perhaps around the time of the Carthaginian council of which we were speaking, Augustine sent a letter to his people at Hippo concerning the affair of Boniface and Spes (Letter 78). It was certainly written after the decree concerning the restoration of Donatist clerics to their own rank, issued at the Carthaginian council in 401; but Proculeianus was still alive.

There was in Augustine’s household a presbyter named Boniface, together with a certain layman called Spes (Letter 77, no. 2). Boniface reported to Augustine that he had felt an impure and unchaste impulse, to which he himself was unwilling either to consent or to remain silent.

Spes, on the contrary, maintained that Boniface had solicited him to commit an immoral act and had decided to transfer his own crime to Spes, whom he had been unable to entice into the offense.

Augustine was exceedingly distressed that, of two members of his household and companions at table, one necessarily had to be regarded as leading a depraved life, while the other, though innocent of crime, was considered criminal in the minds of some and at least suspect in the minds of others.

He regarded Boniface as free from the charge, while he suspected nothing good of Spes; and certainly the conduct of both men confirmed this preconceived judgment. Since, however, there was no evidence by which either could be convicted, after weighing the matter carefully and at length, Augustine decided to entrust it to divine judgment, while awaiting some just and evident reason for expelling from his household the man whom he regarded as suspect.

Meanwhile, he was in no frame of mind to think that a man burdened in his presence by suspicion of so great a crime should be chosen for the clergy. Yet Spes—whether he wished to test Augustine’s attitude toward him or was driven by some innate ambition—brought every means to bear so that either he might be admitted to Augustine’s clergy through the holy bishop, or, having received letters of recommendation from him, might be permitted to receive ordination elsewhere.

Augustine could in no way be induced either to lay hands upon him or, through his recommendation, to introduce him into the clergy of any of his fellow bishops.

Because of this rejection, Spes began to act more turbulently and to declare that, if access to the clergy were closed to him, Boniface ought likewise to be removed from his rank. Nothing could have been more unjust than this proposal.

Nevertheless, Boniface declared himself ready to agree with him, because he preferred to be deprived of the honor of the presbyterate before men rather than provide Spes with any opportunity to disturb the Church.

Augustine thought that he should take a middle course in the matter: namely, that both men should promise in a written agreement to go to some place renowned for miracles, where either fear or divine vengeance would compel the guilty party to confess his crime.

Accordingly, he ordered them to go to Nola, to the tomb of Saint Felix, because there, more certainly than anywhere else, Paulinus would learn what had happened to each of them.

Boniface showed such modesty that he requested no letters testifying to his dignity in the Church. He was unwilling to refuse to be treated at Nola on equal terms with the other man, since in that place both were entirely unknown.

## 2

The matter had remained concealed, and Augustine tried to apply every remedy in such a way that the profound anguish of his heart would not become known to the people. He had good reason to fear that the steadfast would thereby be tormented fruitlessly, the weak dangerously disturbed, and the schismatics given an opportunity to mock the Catholic people.

Nevertheless, against his will, the affair became public and produced precisely the offense which he had foreseen—indeed, an even more bitter one because it had previously been asserted that Augustine’s clerics were not accustomed to fall into crimes, as did those upon whom Proculeianus had laid hands.

Some even demanded that Boniface’s name be removed from the list of presbyters whose names were customarily recited at the altar, so that the Donatists would be left no opportunity to proclaim that crimes remained unpunished among Catholics.

Augustine had not wanted this, lest in that way the judgment of God, before whose tribunal Boniface’s case had been transferred, be anticipated, and lest the statute of the council be violated, according to which a cleric who had not yet been convicted could not be suspended from communion unless he refused to appear for judgment (Council of Carthage 3, year 397, canons 7–8).

Nevertheless, he permitted the clergy and people to decide this as well, if they thought it expedient, so that those who were unwilling to approach the Church but were seeking at least something to use as a pretext would not thereby be provided with a plausible excuse. In that event, he said, the action would belong not to them but to those on whose account it had been taken; nor would any harm come from it to the man whom an innocent conscience had not erased from the book of the living.

While these things were taking place, Augustine was absent from Hippo. He therefore sent a letter to his clergy, the elders, and the entire people of the Church of Hippo. In it he tried to console those who were distressed by the unfortunate affair, although they felt much less pain over it than he did.

He taught that such scandals had long before been foretold by Christ. They themselves had to take the greatest care not to fall into the snares of the devil by judging their brother on the basis of false suspicions—something he says in Boniface’s favor.

He implored them not to add new wounds to his own wounds, not to increase his torments, and not finally to heap sorrow upon sorrow by failing through either false suspicions or the sins of others—speaking of those who had some hope in God and for whom he himself exposed his head to continual dangers.

As for the schismatics, who with utterly diabolical wickedness derived joy from such grievous events and searched out certain vices in the members of the Church in order to mock her entire body, Augustine thought it more expedient to despise them and regard them as the dogs that licked Lazarus’s wounds.

He warned the people of Hippo that perhaps God had not wished to conceal this scandal from them so that they might devote themselves more earnestly with him to prayer and that the truth of the affair might be discovered by divine revelation.

At the same time, he reproved them severely yet humbly because, in opposing Proculeianus, they had gloried in themselves rather than in God. He also urged them not to condemn monasteries on the ground that some wicked people might be found in them.

When a certain Felix and Hilarinus had written to him about the affair, he replied to their letter that it was not surprising if such offenses arose or if sinister rumors were spread among the people against the servants of God.

He had discovered nothing criminal in Boniface and had not believed anything of the kind. For that reason he had not ordered Boniface’s name to be removed from the number of presbyters, because he did not dare anticipate the divine judgment to which the presbyter’s case had been referred.

At the time when those letters were written by the blessed man, Boniface and Spes had already undertaken their journey to Nola, or at least were preparing to do so. We do not know what outcome their case had.

Later we shall also speak of a certain Boniface, a man of the highest character and a very close friend of the holy bishop, who was consecrated bishop of Cataqua around the year 408.

Although, from the presbyter’s humility, one might reasonably infer that God both clearly demonstrated his innocence and raised him to episcopal dignity after testing his faith and patience, there is nevertheless no evidence proving that the two men were one and the same.

### 3

Before the end of this year, Augustine’s disputation with Felix took place. Felix was one of the Manichaean Elect (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 16) and one of their teachers (*Retractations*, book 2, ch. 8). He was indeed unversed in the liberal disciplines; nevertheless, he was far more crafty than Fortunatus, whom Augustine, while still a presbyter, had defeated in a public debate in the year 393. Felix had come to Hippo to disseminate his errors.

We do not know with certainty whether this was the same Felix to whom Augustine’s letter survives (*Epistle* 79), which is addressed simply “to Felix, a Manichaean presbyter.” From it we understand that this man had attempted to conceal what sort of person he was; but after he had spoken with certain Catholics, they immediately detected him and reported him to the holy Bishop. He professed that he despised death and repeatedly declared that he was held in high regard by Augustine, since Augustine was so concerned to suppress his efforts.

Augustine therefore sent him a short but forceful letter. In it he mocks Felix’s boasting and places before him the very argument that his predecessor Fortunatus had been unable to dissolve, demanding that Felix either resolve it or leave the place. If this Manichaean presbyter was indeed the same person as Felix, we know that the following events happened to him.

His writings were brought forward—that is, perhaps five volumes of Manichaean doctrine that he had with him, kept under the public seal (*Acts with Felix*, book 1, ch. 1). On 6 December he went to the Curator, or Mayor, of the city and presented him with a written petition, publicly proclaiming that he was prepared to be burned together with his books if anything evil were found in them [Col. 0345] (*ibid.*, ch. 12).

Perhaps on that very day Augustine spoke with him for some time, since Possidius says that they debated two or three times (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 16), although the Acts written concerning the matter contain only two disputations. The first of these was conducted on 7 December, which was a Wednesday, in the year 404, in the church of Hippo (*Acts with Felix*, book 1, ch. 1). The people stood at the barrier (*ibid.*, ch. 20), listening in complete silence and decorum, while notaries were present to record the words of both men (*ibid.*, ch. 12).

The outcome of the debate was this. Augustine had put to Felix the same argument that he had previously put to Fortunatus: if God was by nature incorruptible, how could the race of darkness harm him? But if it could inflict no injury upon him, why had he fought against it in such a way as to permit a part of his own nature, sent here for this purpose, to be mixed with that race of darkness and polluted through it? (*ibid.*, ch. 19). Felix requested that the time for his reply be extended until the following Monday, 13 December—specifically, for five additional days (*ibid.*, book 2, ch. 1).

These precise notices concerning the time of the conversation remove every suspicion of error on that point. Felix promised that during the interval he would remain with a certain Christian whom he chose from among those present. But if he fled—and indeed he was not being detained—he agreed that he would be regarded, not as having anathematized Manichaeus, but as defeated by his own judgment, a transgressor of his law, and guilty before the city of Hippo (*ibid.*, book 1, ch. 20).

In fact, on the appointed day he came to the Church of Peace, where, in the presence of the people, the disputation began again (*ibid.*, book 2, ch. 1). Augustine resumed his argument. When Felix attempted to evade the necessity of replying by alleging that his books had not been returned, and that he would recover them and return to the discussion two days later, the holy Teacher declared that, if Felix thought those books necessary to him, he ought to have asked for them when he requested the postponement.

The disputation was therefore renewed and dealt chiefly with free will, by which good or evil is done. Grace, however, by which we are asserted in freedom, was not discussed at all, since that question had no bearing on the Manichaean heresy (*Retractations*, book 2, ch. 8; *Acts with Felix*, book 2, chs. 2–4).

At first Felix conceded that anyone who said that God was subject to corruption ought to be struck with anathema (*Acts with Felix*, book 2, ch. 14). But when Augustine had made it clear that this blasphemy was taught by Manichaeus, he compelled Felix, though not without difficulty, to profess that he would do whatever was commanded of him (*ibid.*, ch. 22).

The holy Bishop added that Manichaeus himself had to be anathematized—and sincerely so, since no one was compelling him to do this. Felix called God as witness that he was fully prepared in mind to carry this out; but he asked that Augustine, in order to strengthen him, go before Felix and first anathematize Manichaeus, as well as the spirit that had spoken through him.

The holy Bishop immediately received a sheet of paper and wrote the anathema. Felix did the same [Col. 0346], but used words that showed both that he clearly perceived the abomination of such blasphemies and that they were genuinely horrifying to him.

Afterward both men sealed the record of the conference. These acts have rightly been inserted among Augustine’s works, since they testify to the victory that he won over the heresy—not merely by striking down and confounding its error with his arguments, but also by bringing over to the true faith those by whom it was defended (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 16).

### 4

After that conversation with Felix, Augustine places his book *On the Nature of the Good* (*Retractations*, book 2, ch. 9). In it he demonstrates against the Manichaeans that God is an immutable nature and the supreme Good, and that he is the author of all other natures, both bodily and spiritual, which are all good in themselves.

At the same time, he demonstrates what evil is, from where it arises, how many goods are contained in the nature that they call evil, and, conversely, how many evils are involved in the nature of the good as they imagine it. He also recalls the dreadful immoralities that had been discovered among certain members of this sect, both in Paphlagonia and in Gaul (*On the Nature of the Good*, ch. 47).

He is silent about similarly detestable acts committed in Africa, because those events did not occur there until approximately the year 421. Nevertheless, he shows that those abominations rested upon the actual principles of the Manichaeans (*ibid.*, ch. 46).

He concludes the work with a prayer in which he appeals to divine goodness: just as God had already begun, through Augustine’s ministry, to release not a few people from the snares of this error, so may he continue to free others who are entangled in them (*ibid.*, ch. 48).

### 5

Secundinus was among the Manichaean Auditors (*Retractations*, book 2, ch. 10). He was a Roman, which is why he mentions the marble of the Anician house (*Letter of Secundinus*, no. 3); Augustine refers him to Paulinus (*Against Secundinus*, ch. 11).

After reading some of the holy Teacher’s books against the Manichaeans, Secundinus observed in them, as he admits, an orator perfect in every respect, almost a god of the whole art of eloquence. Yet, since he regarded the errors of his sect as thoroughly convincing, he was never able to discover the truth in Augustine’s writings (*Letter of Secundinus*, no. 3).

He therefore decided to write to Augustine—who was not even known to him by sight—as though to a friend. Yet, while maintaining a tone of urbanity and courteous language, he repeatedly inserted rather sharp criticisms, reproaching Augustine for attacking the Manichaean doctrines in his writings. He urged him to desist from this and even to return to the same sect (*Retractations*, book 2, ch. 10).

For this reason he attempted both to lend credibility to those doctrines and, as far as he could, to diminish the authority of Catholic teaching. Augustine wrote a much longer reply to Secundinus’s letter. It is counted among Augustine’s books because he had not prefixed to it the customary epistolary address; instead, he had placed before it only Secundinus’s letter, which is still found there.

In this reply Augustine dismissed, in a few words and with the greatest expression of modesty, the accusations that Secundinus had directed personally against him (*Against Secundinus*, chs. 1–2). But in defending the Church he was more lengthy and forceful, and he so overturned and shattered the principles of the Manichaean heresy [Col. 0347] that he professes to value this little work more highly than any other work he had published against that plague (*Retractations*, book 2, ch. 10).

### 6

Asterius the subdeacon, to whom Jerome had entrusted a letter for Augustine (*Epistle* 68), together with the second of his *Apologies against Rufinus*, arrived in Africa, apparently toward the end of the year 403. Not long afterward he was elevated to the episcopate (*Epistle* 82, no. 1).

Only then, after reading Jerome’s letters, did Augustine understand that Jerome’s attitude toward him had been alienated because of Augustine’s letter whose opening is “I Give Thanks” (*Epistle* 40). Therefore, at the first opportunity, he wrote to Jerome through certain friends who were perhaps travelling to Palestine in the year 404. His letter was full of humility and goodwill and intended to soothe Jerome’s feelings (*Epistle* 73).

In it he speaks with extraordinary delicacy about the hostility between Jerome and Rufinus. He does not presume to pronounce judgment in favor of either one. Instead, sighing at the thought of being in the presence of both, he declares what he might perhaps do or say, if such an opportunity were granted him, so that he might restore them to harmony.

He had read what Jerome had sent him on this subject. But with regard to Rufinus’s writings against Jerome, although they had been brought to Africa, Augustine makes it sufficiently clear that he had never read them—in fact, that he did not even know them.

He asked Bishop Praesidius—whom Jerome had once commended to him as a man joined to him by an exceptional bond of intimacy (Jerome, in Augustine, *Epistle* 39, no. 1)—to arrange for his letter (*Epistle* 74) to be delivered to Jerome, and, by adding another letter of his own, to urge Jerome to accept Augustine’s apologies.

Later he sent Jerome’s letter to Praesidius together with a copy of his own, so that Praesidius might more easily know how he ought to write to that holy presbyter [Col. 0348]. At the same time Augustine begged him that, if he found anything less than satisfactory in Augustine’s letter to Jerome (*Epistle* 73), he should point it out, so that Augustine could correct it.

### 7

Jerome had not yet received Augustine’s letter whose opening is “Although I Think” (*ibid.*), when he wrote to Augustine, after Chrysostom had been driven from his see and therefore toward the end of the year 404, the letter beginning “Three Letters at Once” (in Augustine, *Epistle* 75).

In it Jerome attempts to answer Augustine’s various questions and, above all, to respond satisfactorily to Augustine’s objections concerning a well-intentioned lie and the dispute between Peter and Paul.

Afterward the aforementioned letter of Augustine (*Epistle* 73) was delivered to Jerome. It undoubtedly calmed his agitated mind, although on that occasion he did not think it necessary to write back. Instead, when Firmus, a close associate of the holy Bishop, came to Palestine from Africa without any letter from Augustine—who had not known that his friend was making the journey—Jerome gave Firmus, on his return, a letter for Augustine (in Augustine, *Epistle* 81) bearing the sweetest testimony to his love and goodwill.

In it Jerome excused his last letter to Augustine (*Epistle* 75) and declared that in the future he wished to abstain from such questions. He also sent greetings to Alypius.

This did not prevent Augustine from afterward writing Jerome, through some of his own friends, a lengthy letter (*Epistle* 82), in which he discusses at length the same dispute between Peter and Paul. He took great care, while preserving the truth for which he was contending, not to irritate Jerome’s mind. At the same time he sent Jerome his work on Faustus.

This was the end of that celebrated dispute between Augustine and Jerome. Jerome himself eventually came over to Augustine’s position when the struggle against the Pelagians had to be undertaken in the year 415.

## BOOK SIX

In this book are related the deeds of Augustine from the new laws enacted against the Donatists in the year 405 until the Conference with those same schismatics at Carthage.

[Col. 0347]

## CHAPTER ONE

1. A severe law issued by Honorius against the Donatists.  
2. Other laws against the same group.  
3. Augustine’s letter to Paulinus.  
4. The Church derives the greatest benefit from the laws of Honorius.  
5. A council is held at Carthage after unity has begun to be restored there.

### 1

Having digressed briefly from the Donatist controversy, we are now brought back to it in the actual order of the narrative.

When the bishops who had been appointed as legates by the Council of Carthage arrived at the imperial court, they discovered that there was nothing for them to accomplish there (*Epistle* 185, no. 26). A law against the party of Donatus had in fact already been issued and promulgated before their arrival.

The Emperor had been moved by the complaints of all those who, having been badly punished, did not dare return home, and especially by the dreadful and very recent scars of the bishop of Bagai. Moreover, as Augustine says, the notorious madness of the Circumcellions, which supplied the clerics with a dreadful bodyguard, had become hated everywhere. Great hatred had consequently arisen against the Donatists, and this led both to the revival of all the earlier laws against them and to the enactment of new ones (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 47).

For the religious and pious Emperor, once such matters had been brought to his attention, preferred to correct the error of impiety completely by the most devout laws and to bring those who carried the standards of Christ against Christ back to Catholic unity by frightening and restraining them, rather than merely removing their license to rage while leaving them free to err and perish.

Accordingly, a law was promulgated so that the Donatist heresy, whose being spared seemed a greater cruelty than its own violence, would not be allowed to continue with impunity—not, however, by capital punishment, because Christian gentleness was to be preserved even toward the undeserving, but by imposing financial penalties and assigning exile to bishops and their ministers.

We therefore possess an edict issued by Honorius on 12 February 405. In it the Emperor declares that he no longer wishes to tolerate the errors of those who repeated Baptism or to hear the name “Donatists” any longer. He orders everyone to follow Catholic unity.

If any continue to commit unlawful acts, they are to suffer the penalties prescribed by the earlier laws, as well as by the law recently enacted—perhaps against Crispinus. Those who dare to assemble seditious gatherings are to be restrained more harshly and severely.

These are precisely the provisions that can now be found from that edict, divided into at least two parts and preserved in two places in the Code. One part appears under the title “That Holy Baptism Be Not Repeated,” law 3; the other under the title “Concerning Heretics,” law 38.

Some scholars (*In the Theodosian Code*, vol. 6, p. 196) believe that the following splendid words, which Augustine cites around the year 409 from a certain law, should be referred to this same edict:

“For if, among those who have been initiated once, the sacrament of Baptism is judged invalid for the reason that those by whom it is administered are thought to be sinners, the sacrament that has been handed down will have to be renewed as often as an unworthy administrator of the Baptism conferred is found. And our faith will depend not upon the judgment of our will, nor upon the grace of the divine gift, but upon the merits and character of priests and clerics.””

After the Emperor’s pronouncement, the holy Bishop said:

“Let your bishops hold a thousand councils and let them respond to this one judgment; and we agree with you in whatever you wish” (*Epistle* 105, no. 12).

Some call this edict the Edict of Union, or the Henoticon. The Council of Carthage in 407 likewise calls it the Law of Unity. Honorius himself also testifies that he had sent an edict concerning unity to Africa, so that everyone might understand that the one true Catholic faith was to be retained (Theodosian Code, *On Religion*, law 2).

### 2
