On the same day, namely 12 February, Honorius sent a law to the praetorian prefect Hadrian, in which he declared that he had decided to eradicate the Donatist heresy completely, chiefly because of the sacrilege of repeating Baptism, to which they forcibly compelled slaves and others subject to them (*ibid.*, “That Holy Baptism Be Not Repeated,” laws 4 and 5).

This provision is generally judged to have been aimed especially at the crime of Crispinus. The Emperor therefore decreed that those discovered to have administered Baptism a second time after the promulgation of this law should be stripped of all their property. Their property was nevertheless to be restored to their children if the children returned to the Church.

The estates on which such gatherings had taken place were to be confiscated by the treasury if the owners had been aware of the matter. If they had not, those who had held such meetings were to be scourged with leaded whips and sent into perpetual exile.

Their clients or slaves, whom they wished to baptize again, were permitted to take refuge in Catholic churches and thereafter obtain the rights of freedom. Those who had initiated or knowingly assisted in the repetition of Baptism were to be deprived not only of the right to make a will but also of the ability to acquire anything under the appearance of a gift or to enter into contracts until they renounced the heresy.

Anyone who had helped them was to be subjected to the same penalty. Provincial prefects who had given them consent or assistance were to pay twenty pounds of gold; their staffs—that is, their judicial officials—the same amount. Finally, the magistrates and defenders of the cities were to be condemned to the same fine if they either neglected to carry out those commands or allowed the churches to be harassed in their presence.

This last provision certainly relates to the request of the Council of Carthage that the cities be obliged to undertake the protection of the churches.

That law imposes no penalty upon the entire Donatist sect, nor does it send all their clerics into exile, as Augustine teaches that Honorius had decreed. We do not know whether the Emperor had prescribed these matters in another edict or whether the surviving constitution has not come down to our time intact.

In addition to the laws issued on 12 February 405, which Honorius clearly indicated when, two years later, he declared that he had recently shown what he thought of the party of Donatus (*ibid.*, “Concerning Heretics,” law 40), he also sent another law on 3 March of the same year to Diotimus, proconsul of Africa. In it he ordered him to arrange for the Edict of Unity that he had sent to Africa, so that it might become known to everyone, to be posted in various places (*ibid.*, “Concerning Religion,” law 2).

The same Emperor informed Diotimus on 8 December of the following year that the fine prescribed by law was to be exacted without any postponement from all who were found in the Donatist heresy (*ibid.*, “Concerning Heretics,” law 39).

### 3

The return to Africa of Theasius and Evodius, whom the Council of Carthage had sent to Honorius the previous year against the Donatist party, was thought to be imminent when Augustine sent Paulinus a letter through Celsus (*Epistle* 80).

Paulinus had recently sent the holy Bishop another letter concerning a certain question, which Paulinus had indeed resolved too hurriedly and briefly, but with an entirely Christian mind and piety, affirming that he had decided to remain at Nola, where he lived, in such a way that, if God should ask anything else of him, he would be prepared to place God’s will before his own.

Paulinus appears to have entrusted this very brief reply to someone named Celsus. Before Augustine had received it, he wrote again to Paulinus through Fortunatianus, a presbyter of Hippo who was travelling to Rome at that time. Those three letters—one from Paulinus and two from Augustine—have been lost.

Celsus came to Hippo intending to spend several days in Augustine’s company. But, having found an opportunity to sail, he notified the holy Bishop very late that he would be leaving the next day and asked him to give him a reply for Paulinus.

Augustine therefore dictated a letter in haste. In it he asked Paulinus to explain how we can recognize the divine will in choosing, from among several good actions, the one that God requires of us, and therefore the one that we ought to prefer to all others if we intend to obey God’s will. Augustine admits that it is difficult not to be mistaken in this matter and not to fall into sins of which we are unaware.

He promised to write to Paulinus at greater length [Col. 0351] as soon as Theasius and Evodius, whose arrival was expected each day, had returned and Augustine himself had seen God’s will in the minds and words of those bishops.

They returned, as may reasonably be believed, in March or at least in April, by which time the laws against the Donatists had already been granted and sealed on 12 February.

### 4

Augustine relates that when the laws themselves reached Africa, those who had been looking for an opportunity, or feared the violence of the furious, or were ashamed to offend their own people, immediately crossed over to the Church.

Many others had previously been held only by the custom handed down to them by their parents. They had never considered what basis the heresy itself possessed and had never wished to inquire or reflect upon it. But as soon as they began to pay attention and found nothing in it worthy of the great losses they would have to endure, they became Catholics without difficulty. Concern taught those whom security had made negligent.

Many others followed the authority and persuasion of all these people, although they were less capable of understanding for themselves the difference between the Donatist error and Catholic truth.

Thus, while the true mother received great crowds of people joyfully into her bosom, hard-hearted groups remained, persisting in that wretched plague with obstinate zeal. Many of these also pretended to conform, while others concealed themselves because of their small numbers.

Those who pretended, however, gradually became accustomed to the change and listened to the preaching of the truth. Especially after the conference and disputation held between us and their bishops at Carthage, most of them were corrected.

In certain places, however, where a more obstinate and unruly multitude prevailed—one that the smaller number, whose judgment concerning communion was better, could not resist—or where the crowds obeyed the authority of a few powerful men in an evil cause, the work continued for somewhat longer (*Epistle* 185, nos. 29–30).

In a letter to Vincent, apparently written before the Conference, the holy Bishop explains still more fully how much benefit the severity of those laws had brought to the Church. It will be enough to quote a few words. He says:

“We rejoice at the correction of many who now hold and defend Catholic unity with such sincerity, and rejoice that they have been freed from their former error, that we look upon them with great congratulation.”

A little farther on:

“If only I could show you how many notorious Catholics we now have from the Circumcellions themselves, condemning their former life and their miserable error, by which they thought that they were acting on behalf of God’s Church in whatever they did with restless recklessness!” (*Epistle* 93, nos. 1–2), and so forth.

“Many of them, whose devout fervor of faith and marvelous charity in the unity of Christ we now admire, give thanks to God with great joy because they have been freed from that error, in which they considered evils good. They would not now willingly give those thanks unless they had first been compelled, even against their will, to withdraw from that wicked association.

“What shall we say about those who confess to us every day that they long ago wished to be Catholics, but lived among people among whom, because of the weakness produced by fear, they could not be what they wished to be? For if they had spoken even a single word on behalf of the Catholic cause, they and their households would have been utterly destroyed” (*Epistle* 185, no. 13).

Writing also against Cresconius, he says that the Catholic Church is spreading and expanding in every direction, while the party of Donatus is diminishing day by day throughout Africa (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 71).

“For if you could see,” he says, “how far and wide that error had spread through Africa, and how little of it remains that has not yet been corrected and passed over into Catholic peace, you would by no means regard the insistence of those who defend Christian peace and unity as fruitless and empty” (*ibid.*, book 1, no. 7).

Toward the end of the year 408 he speaks as follows:

“We rejoice greatly over the firm and steadfast faith of certain people—and they are not few—who, taking the laws themselves as an occasion, have been converted to the Christian religion or to Catholic peace. For their eternal salvation we are glad to place ourselves in danger even during this present life. For this reason above all we now endure the heavier attacks of hostility from excessively harsh and perverse men, attacks which some of them bear with us most patiently” (*Epistle* 97, no. 4).

Very many confessed that it had been a great favor to them to be compelled to return to the bosom of the Church, and thus, by their return, to give the Circumcellions no occasion to harass them (*Epistle* 105, no. 5).

Indeed, some of those who seemed to renounce the party of Donatus not sincerely but out of sheer fear displayed greater steadfastness in the difficulties of the following period than those who had never departed from Catholic truth (*Epistle* 89, no. 7).

“Thus,” Augustine says, “many were corrected by those laws and are corrected every day. They give thanks that they have been corrected and freed from that mad destruction. Those who hated now love; and to the extent that in their madness they detested the laws that had been burdensome to them, to that same extent, once restored to health, they rejoice in them. They are also stirred by a similar love toward those who remain, with whom they would have perished, and together with us they strive to prevent those people from perishing” (*Epistle* 185, no. 7).

The laws also benefited many—a fact that we have established and continue to establish by experience—because they were first compelled by fear or pain, so that afterward they could be taught, or could practice by their actions what they had already learned in words (*ibid.*, no. 21).

Such were the fruits produced by that paternal severity joined to the instruction with which the Church, especially through Augustine’s speech and writing, nourished those who returned.

“For if they were frightened,” the same holy Bishop says, “but not taught, it would appear to be an improper form of domination. Again, if they were taught but not frightened, they would move more sluggishly toward taking up the path of salvation, hardened by the oldness of their custom” (*Epistle* 93, no. 3).

### 5

The chronicle of Idacius therefore does not without reason record that unity between the Catholics and the Donatists was achieved in this year.

It first began at Carthage before 23 August (African Code of Canons, canon 94), not indeed through the conversion of all the Donatists—for Primianus continued always to claim for himself the title of Bishop of Carthage—but certainly through the conversion of a considerable number of them.

Their sacred buildings were also taken from them, either to be handed over to the Catholics or at least to be closed. We have already found that this had been done in the diocese of Hippo (*Epistle* 139, no. 2).

After unity had been achieved or had begun, a council of Carthage was held on 23 August in the Basilica of the Second Region [Col. 0353]. That it was a council of all Africa is sufficiently and abundantly demonstrated by the date alone; this is also confirmed by the mention of legations sent to the synod from all the provinces.

It was decided to write to the provincial prefects and ask them to work toward establishing throughout Africa the harmony that at that time had been restored only at Carthage. It was likewise decided to write to the imperial court—that is, to the Emperor and his ministers—so that thanks might be offered to him in the name of all Africa for the expulsion of the Donatists (African Code of Canons, canon 94).

Two men were chosen to carry those letters—not bishops, but only clerics. The reason was that the letter of Pope Innocent, which they had undoubtedly quoted as having been brought by the legates of the preceding council, warned the African bishops not easily to allow bishops to travel to Italy.

In this matter the bishops or legates of the council held exactly the same view as Innocent. From this it may be inferred that the overseas journey of the bishops, although they had fled to the Emperor because of the Donatists’ attacks, had nevertheless not escaped criticism.

There is no room for doubt that Augustine attended this general council, just as he had attended the earlier ones.

## CHAPTER TWO

1. The brutality of the Donatists of Hippo.  
2. Augustine appeals for the assistance of Caecilianus.  
3. The fury of the schismatics throughout the rest of Africa.  
4. The Church flourishes despite their bloodshed.  
5. The Donatists send legates to the Emperor.  
6. The clergy of Hippo complain to Januarius about their injuries.

### 1

If the followers of Donatus had placed any confidence in their cause, when they saw themselves so severely pressured by the imperial laws they ought to have followed the example of the Catholics and challenged them to a conference for the clarification of the truth (*Epistle* 88, no. 7).

Instead, they neglected this course of action, took the entirely opposite path, and resolved to rage through still more crimes than before and to trample upon the laws with the same fury that had given occasion for their enactment (*Epistle* 108, no. 18).

“Every day,” Augustine says, “we suffer unbelievable deeds from your clerics and Circumcellions, much worse than those of any robbers or bandits. Armed with frightful weapons of every kind and roaming about terribly, they disturb not merely ecclesiastical peace, but human quiet and peace itself.

“By nocturnal attacks they invade the houses of Catholic clerics and leave them stripped and empty. They even carry off the clerics themselves, beat them with clubs, cut them with iron, and throw them away half alive.

“Moreover, in a new and previously unheard-of form of crime, they pour and force lime mixed with vinegar into their eyes. Although they could have blinded them quickly by tearing out their eyes, they choose to torture them further rather than blind them at once.

“At first they used only lime for this crime; but after learning that those to whom they had done this quickly recovered their sight, they added vinegar” (*Against Cresconius*, book 3, no. 46).

They practiced this savagery especially in the diocese of Hippo, a savagery unknown even among barbarians (*Epistle* 111, no. 1). For this reason, in the following year the clergy of Hippo protested about the matter before the Donatist Primate.

“They live like robbers,” they said; “they die like Circumcellions; they are honored like martyrs. Yet we have never even heard that robbers blinded those whom they had plundered. They take the slain away from the light; they do not take the light away from the living” (*Epistle* 88, no. 8).

At the Conference their cruelty was reproached as exceeding, in a certain sense, the cruelty of the devil himself against Job (*Brief Account of the Conference* 3, no. 22; *Carthaginian Conference* 3, ch. 298).

They also wounded the other limbs with terrible blows and injuries. They plundered some houses and set them on fire; they carried off dry fruits and poured out the moist ones (*Epistle* 111, no. 1).

They forged huge and terrifying weapons, with which they ran about in various places, threatening and panting for slaughter, robbery, arson, and blinding (*Epistle* 88, no. 8).

By instilling such terror into people’s minds, they terrified many so greatly that they allowed themselves to be defiled by a second Baptism (*Epistle* 111, no. 8).

Thus, amid the very severe laws that had been promulgated against them and about which they complained as though about the harshest persecution, they not only sat securely on their own and others’ possessions, but also afflicted the orthodox beyond all belief.

Moreover, the clergy of Hippo relate:

“If they voluntarily inflict deaths upon themselves, they want those deaths to be hateful to us and glorious for you. What they do to us they do not attribute to themselves; and what they do to themselves they attribute to us” (*Epistle* 88, no. 8).

The fear of the laws was not so much the cause of such great and unheard-of savagery—which even caused them to become objects of hatred among their own followers—as was their grief at the progress of the Catholic Church, which Augustine’s especially constant preaching was wonderfully enlarging.

“For while,” Possidius writes, “the word of God was diligently preached and the cause of peace was maintained even with those who hated peace, they attacked the speaker without cause. And as the truth against their doctrine became known to those who wished and were able to escape from it, they either freed themselves or withdrew from it and clung, together with as many of their own people as they could bring, to the peace and unity of the Church.

“Therefore, seeing that the gatherings of their error were diminishing and envying the Church’s growth, they were inflamed and burned with the fiercest anger and, united in a compact body, inflicted intolerable persecutions upon the unity of the Church” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 10).

## 2. At that time, when the fierce audacity of the heretics was raging with the greatest violence through the countryside around Hippo, that letter was sent to Caecilian (Epistle 86). In it Augustine asks him to employ the authority which he possessed in Africa—not, indeed, to avenge injuries with just severity, but to apply intimidation toward healing those who inflicted them. This Caecilian was praetorian prefect in the year 409. Toward the end of 413 Augustine wrote to the same man as one held by him in great honor and bound to him by an exceptionally close friendship (Epistle 151). He professed the Christian religion as a catechumen and was administering the office entrusted to him in Africa with a considerable reputation for diligence and piety. He had already issued a very severe edict against the Donatists, by which he admirably promoted the reconciliation of the schismatics with the Church in various parts of Africa.

[Col. 0355] But the fruits of this edict had not yet reached Hippo or the other regions of Numidia adjoining Hippo. Therefore, not wishing to be accused of negligence in a matter of such importance, the holy Bishop asked Caecilian by letter to assist that region as well; and he sent a presbyter, so that Caecilian might learn more certainly how urgent the necessity was. He addresses him as though Caecilian had not yet come to know him.

No one can doubt that Caecilian was in Africa at that time and administering that province. From this one may conclude that the letter should be assigned neither to the year 409, when Caecilian himself was praetorian prefect in Italy, nor to 413, when we have no reliable evidence that he held any office there. Indeed, it will scarcely seem probable to anyone that, after attaining the dignity of praetorian prefect, he presided over any province. Yet it is observed that in 404 he held the honor of vicarius (Gothofredus, *Codex Theodosianus*, title 6, p. 354). Hence it may reasonably be thought that in 405 he exercised the same office in Africa. For the letter cannot be placed in 404, before the laws of Honorius.

## 3. The unrestrained fury of the Donatists was not confined to the boundaries of the region of Hippo; its criminal traces were also evident throughout other parts of Africa. At Bagai, at whose city—so it seems to us—Maximianus, the man so grievously punished by them, was bishop, they perpetrated deeds horrifying to relate (*Breviculus Collationis* 3, no. 23). There they burned a basilica and threw into the fire the sacred books which they boasted of having preserved for themselves during the persecution of Diocletian. The judge himself, while attempting to restrain their violence and attacks, was placed in danger of his life; and when he was compelled to repel the force inflicted upon him by force and arms, some of them were killed.

When they exaggerated this matter at the Conference (*Collatio Carthaginensis* 3, ch. 258), repeatedly asserting that the Catholics had furnished the occasion for the blood of many Christians to be shed (*Breviculus Collationis* 3, no. 13), the Catholics replied that such punishments were insignificant in comparison with the injuries which the Donatists themselves had first inflicted. They said that the Donatists had suffered these things while resistance was being offered to their violence, which they had also attempted to inflict upon the judge himself (*ibid.*, no. 23).

Augustine’s words may refer to this devastation at Bagai:

> You too know how many evils the most deranged clerics and Circumcellions of the party of Donatus have inflicted upon our people. Churches have been burned; holy books have been thrown into the flames; private houses too have been burned; people have been dragged from their homes, and after everything they possessed had been taken away or destroyed, they themselves were beaten, torn apart, and blinded. Nor could they refrain from murder—although it is milder to kill one who must die than to take this light from one who lives. Men were attacked, not so that they might be detained and led away somewhere, but merely so that they might suffer these things. Yet we do not justify our people merely because they endured these things, but because they endured them for Christian truth, for the peace of Christ, and for the unity of the Church.

(*To the Donatists, after the Conference*, no. 22.)

Gorgonius, bishop of the people of Liberalia, complained at the Conference that his church had been leveled to the ground by the heretics (*Collatio Carthaginensis* 1, ch. 133). Fortunatus of Cirta likewise complained that all the altars in the city had been smashed by the same men (*ibid.*, ch. 139). Aurelius of Macomades lamented that the bishop of Rotaria had been killed and that his church had been forcibly occupied by them (*ibid.*, ch. 187).

When a portion of the people of Caesarea had defected from the heretics, Cresconius, the Donatist bishop there, subjected the Catholic presbyter who governed the faithful to various punishments; he plundered whatever the presbyter or his church possessed, carried off the Church’s money and grain as well, and drove away wagons loaded with this booty (*ibid.*, ch. 188).

At Pudentiana they demolished the sacred buildings of the Catholics and carried away all their furnishings. Cresconius, their bishop in that place, demolished four basilicas in one and the same location. When the Catholics, compelled by their fury and violence, appealed for the assistance of the magistrates in breaking their attacks, certain unpleasant and odious consequences necessarily followed; for these the Donatists bitterly complained at the Conference (*ibid.*, ch. 201).

These things certainly occurred against the will and intention of the good and distinguished Catholics, since they had requested laws by which they themselves might be protected, not laws by which they might persecute their adversaries. Meanwhile, the people of Hippo say:

> If at any time we have any of your people in our keeping, we preserve them unharmed with great affection. We speak with them and read to them all those things by which the error itself is refuted—an error that separates brothers from brothers. Thus, when some of them consider the clarity of truth and the beauty of peace, we join them not to the Baptism which they had already received, like deserters, as a royal mark, but to the faith which they lacked, to the love of the Holy Spirit, and to the body of Christ.
>
> But if, whether because of excessive stubbornness or shame—they cannot bear the insults of those with whom they had spread so many falsehoods against us and devised so many evils—or rather because of fear that they might now suffer from us the same things that they had previously inflicted upon us, they refuse to consent to the unity of Christ, then, just as they were kept unharmed, so they are dismissed by us unharmed.
>
> We also admonish our laypeople, as far as we can, to keep them unharmed and bring them to us to be corrected and instructed. Some listen to us and do so, if they are able. Others treat them as they would robbers, because they truly regard them as such. Some repel by striking the blows directed at their own bodies, so that they may not first be struck by them. Some hand over those whom they have seized to the judges and, despite our intercession, do not spare them, because they fear suffering monstrous evils at their hands.
>
> In all these matters the Donatists do not lay aside the deeds of robbers, yet they demand for themselves the honor of martyrs.

(*Epistle* 88, no. 9.)

## 4. Yet even at that time God, through the harms which the fury of the Donatists inflicted upon the Catholics, confirmed the statement pronounced many years earlier—namely, that the blood of martyrs is the seed of Christians. Augustine also attests this in the following words:

> The fruit that followed consoled us, afflicted as we were by such evils. For wherever these things were committed by the lost, there Christian unity advanced more fervently and more perfectly; and the Lord is praised more abundantly, since he deigned to grant that his servants, through their sufferings, might win their brothers, and that they might gather into the peace of eternal salvation, by their own blood, his sheep scattered through a deadly error.

(*Epistle* 185, no. 31.)

This happened especially through the labors of Augustine, who among all the members constituting the mystical body of the Lord was of particular importance. With tireless care he watched over the advancement of the Church’s affairs, and by divine kindness he obtained the joy of still living to see the fruits of his exertions. He saw peace and harmony first established at Hippo, whose city and diocese had been entrusted especially to his care; and then throughout Africa, where he brought great growth to the Church both personally and through the bishops whom he had given her by his formation and discipline (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 18).

Nevertheless, he did not complete this work in his own diocese until many years later. For the present, all that can be established is that the basilica which had belonged to the Donatists there was taken from them either at that time or shortly afterward (*Retractations* 2.27). The Church of Cirta, so dreadfully harassed by the heretics, likewise showed how greatly the sufferings of God’s servants had availed with him. Without doubt, in consideration of and in response to those sufferings, he finally brought the Donatists of that place back to Catholic unity (*Epistle* 144). This does not seem to have occurred before 412.

From the Conference we also learn that all the schismatics at Libertina, without exception, returned to the Church (*Collatio Carthaginensis* 1, ch. 116). The same had happened among the people of Bazarita, with the result that Calipotius, their bishop, seeing that everyone had deserted him, was compelled to move elsewhere (*ibid.*, ch. 129).

## 5. There was certainly no other reason why some of the Donatist bishops crossed the sea and presented themselves before the praetorian prefect than to ask that the severity of the laws enacted against them be mitigated (*Epistle* 88, no. 10). We think that Maximinus of Siniti was one of their number.

Before he had returned from his overseas journey, Augustine sent a presbyter to Siniti to care for the Catholics there and, residing in a house under his own jurisdiction, to proclaim Catholic peace without injuring anyone to those who wished to hear it. But the heretics treated the presbyter cruelly and eventually expelled him from the place (*Epistle* 105, no. 4).

The Donatist bishops who had come to the imperial court went to the tribunal of the prefect and earnestly demanded that they be heard—indeed, in a discussion with Valentinus, the Catholic bishop who happened at that time to be present there. They repeatedly affirmed that they had come for no other reason (*Collatio Carthaginensis* 3, ch. 124). The official records of this affair were drawn up at Ravenna on the third day before the Kalends of February in the year 406 (*ibid.*, ch. 141).

The Catholics had a copy of these proceedings transcribed from the archives and requested that it be read at the Conference of Carthage, in order to show that the request for a conference had been made by both sides. Consequently, Augustine’s words at the Conference must be assigned to this period:

> When some of them recently came to the imperial court, they said even in the prefectural records that they wished to be heard and wished to have the matter examined.

(*ibid.*, ch. 110.)

At that time, therefore, they were pressing Valentinus, the Catholic bishop who was then at the Emperor’s court, to debate the matter with them (*Epistle* 88, no. 10). But that bishop had not come there for the purpose of holding a discussion with them, nor had he received any instruction concerning the matter from his fellow bishops. The prefect himself, before whom these proceedings were taking place, had no authority to grant such a conference; he was obliged to pronounce judgment according to the laws enacted against the Donatists.

Meanwhile, the assent which the Donatists themselves had thus given to the holding of a conference turned to the advantage of the Catholics. Under this pretext they opportunely secured from the Emperor the authorization for the conference, although only four years later (*Collatio Carthaginensis* 3, ch. 110; *Breviculus Collationis*, chs. 4–5).

For Marcellinus also testifies in the edict which he promulgated at the beginning of 411 for the purpose of convening the Conference that, only a very short time earlier, the Donatists had requested one before the tribunal of the prefects. Augustine relates that they had damaged their own cause in the prefectural records by certain ill-considered and rash replies, and that for this reason they had taken the greatest care to prevent those replies from being read at the Conference (*Breviculus Collationis* 3, no. 5). In those same records they had applied to themselves the name “Donatists,” which they afterward repudiated (*Collatio Carthaginensis* 3, ch. 31).

## 6. Moreover, after this journey Maximinus of Siniti embraced Catholic unity, as we observed above (Book 3, ch. 9, no. 6). After that embassy of the Donatists, the clerics of Hippo also complained to the Donatists themselves about the abuses of the Circumcellions. A letter on this matter was sent to Januarius, their primate in Numidia (*Epistle* 88); its author is shown by its style to have been Augustine.

First, the letter demonstrates from a condensed account of the history of Caecilian that the Donatists had brought that controversy before the emperors before the Catholics did; and therefore that there was no reason to blame the Catholics for appealing to the aid of Honorius. Second, it shows that the atrocities of the Circumcellions had furnished the occasion for laws to be issued against them. Third, it shows that those same laws did not prevent the Catholics from treating the Donatists with the greatest kindness, even though the Donatists inflicted every kind of harm upon them, returning evil for good.

Mention is also made there of the lime, vinegar, and other cruelties. To these matters they add that it is their desire that the Donatists confer peaceably with the Catholic bishops, so that the schism—not the people—may be removed; that is, so that the people may not be punished but corrected. The Donatists had indeed declared before the prefects that they wished to hold a conference, but the judge could not grant it to them because of the laws already enacted. Yet they would not attempt it in vain before the Emperor, who was not bound by those same laws and had the power to enact others.

They add that they press so earnestly for this conference not so that a case settled long ago might be settled again, but so that what has already been settled might be demonstrated to those who do not know it. If they disapprove of this method of debate, they ask at least that they listen to the clerics of Hippo disputing before them with the Donatists of that same place, and that, if the clerics seem to depart from the truth in anything, they instruct them. Finally, they ask that the Donatists themselves, either personally or through others, investigate the wicked deeds perpetrated by the army of their Circumcellions; and if they think they must refrain from condemning those men, at least forbid them from murder, robbery, and blinding.

They close the letter with these words:

> But if you disregard our complaints, we shall not at all regret that we wished to act in an orderly and peaceful manner. The Lord will be with his Church, so that you, rather, may regret having disregarded our humility.

(*ibid.*, no. 12.)

# CHAPTER III

1. Augustine writes against Cresconius.  
2. He vainly attempts to bring Paul of Cataqua back to a manner of life worthy of a bishop.  
3. He writes to Emeritus, grieving that he is entangled in schism.  
4. Three short works against the Donatists perhaps published at that time.  
5. The book *On the Divination of Demons*.  
6. Six questions explained against the pagans, addressed to the presbyter Deogratias.  
7. An exposition of the Epistle of James to the twelve tribes.  
8. The book *On the One Baptism*, addressed to Constantinus.

## 1. Augustine also testifies in his books against Cresconius that the Catholics had asked the Donatists to come with them to a conference (*Against Cresconius* 4.83), at which they would demonstrate that the case had already been settled (*ibid.* 1.6).

The laws against those heretics had indeed already been enacted by Honorius (*Retractations* 2.26), but they were still recent when he composed this work (*Against Cresconius* 3.51). The Donatists were already harassing the Catholics because of those laws no less with lime and vinegar than with sword and fire (*ibid.*, no. 46).

Cresconius belonged to the Donatist sect and was of the lay order (*Against Cresconius* 1.1); by profession he was a grammarian (*Retractations* 2.26). After he had first read Augustine’s book against the letter of Petilianus, he undertook to defend his own party against Augustine, relying on the writing ability with which he was moderately equipped (*Against Cresconius* 1.2), and also undertook to defend Petilianus’s letter (*ibid.* 4.1).

Although Cresconius had dedicated his short work to Augustine, it did not reach him until long after it had been published (*ibid.* 1.1). Augustine then thought that courtesy required him to reply to its author, and that his office and duty required him not to evade the defense of the truth.

Accordingly, he refuted Cresconius in four books. In the first he teaches that the Donatists’ feigned modesty was entirely unworthy of approval—the modesty by which they refused to debate the cause of the schism with the Catholics—and that the defenders of truth need fear neither the eloquence nor the dialectic of any adversary. He further shows that, although the Catholics concede that the Donatists’ Baptism is true, it cannot from this be inferred that the same schismatics receive it rightly.

In the second book he demonstrates that Cresconius has said nothing by which Augustine’s book against Petilianus is refuted, although Cresconius may perhaps have taught him that the Donatists should not properly be called *Donatists* after Donatus, but *Donatians*, along with certain other grammatical trivialities on which Cresconius dwelt (*ibid.* 2.2).

After answering those statements of Cresconius which seemed to be of greater importance—lest the less educated should think that something had been left unanswered—Augustine added a third book dealing with the remaining chapters of the work Cresconius had written. Finally, in the fourth book he dismantled the whole work from beginning to end, using only the history of the Maximianists.

[Col. 0360]

## 2. You may also infer that the letter to Paul, the bishop, was not written before this period from the fact that its addressee is praised for having brought many people back to the Catholic Church (*Epistle* 85, no. 1). Since Augustine had begotten Paul for Christ, he therefore thought that Paul’s conduct was especially his own responsibility and that of the Church of Hippo.

If Paul is the same man as the Paul mentioned in the letter to Olympius (*Epistle* 96, no. 2), as Holstenius believes and the facts themselves seem to suggest, he held episcopal rank at Cataqua in Numidia (*Epistle* 97, no. 3). After attaining this office, however, he brought Augustine far more grief than consolation. For although he gathered not a few Donatists into the bosom of the Church, he drove away many more through his corruption of morals.

He lived so entangled in worldly business that one would have thought he regarded the episcopate as a profitable trade (*Epistle* 85, nos. 1–2). Yet God, in order to show Paul—if only he had possessed any understanding—that apart from the riches of the soul, for whose sake he had been chosen for the episcopate, he ought to seek no others, ensured that he would obtain no benefit from his odious profits. He was so unable to pay the sums he owed to the treasury that he was compelled to surrender all his possessions (*Epistle* 96, no. 2).

Nevertheless, he resumed the commercial enterprise he had previously undertaken, contrary to the very order of human laws, relying doubtless on the protection of some extremely powerful man of that period, perhaps Bathanarius. Thus he immersed himself more and more deeply in business and adopted a manner of life which the poverty of his Church could in no way sustain.

Augustine judged that he owed to the man whom he had brought forth in Christ through the Gospel, more than to anyone else, the salutary sharpness of charity expressed through truthful correction (*Epistle* 85, no. 1). Accordingly, he tried to heal him with every admonition which he thought might serve that purpose. But it was in vain.

Therefore, although Paul had been condemned by no ecclesiastical judge, the holy man separated himself from his communion, without depriving him of the title of brother, colleague, or bishop. Paul requested Augustine’s communion by letter and at the same time complained that Augustine—even calling him inexorable—placed excessive trust in those who had always maintained open hostility toward Paul.

For this very reason Augustine wrote to him the letter in question, full of both severity and charity. He declares that he does not wish to communicate with Paul because he cannot be induced to flatter him. If Paul wished to heal the wounds he had inflicted upon the Church of Hippo, he had to be freed by the Lord from worldly cares and burdens and restored to a life and livelihood appropriate to the episcopal order.

Without doubt, this letter produced little result, since Augustine speaks of this bishop, even after his death, with little honor. He relates that, at the time when Paul was compelled to surrender his property, he received some money that was owed to him and purchased, as though for his Church and under the name of a very powerful household, several small estates offered for sale by public proclamation, so that even from those properties—since he paid nothing to the treasury in his customary manner—he might suffer no harassment from the tax collectors [Col. 0361] (*Epistle* 96, no. 2).

Paul afterward left these estates to his successor Boniface. Boniface could perhaps have retained them without any dispute; but, being a man of more sincere faith, he feared that before God he might be considered a participant in fraud and injustice. Therefore he preferred frankly and openly to acknowledge that the estates left to him by his predecessor had been purchased with money owed to the treasury.

Boniface had already been appointed to the episcopate in August of 408, as we shall say in its proper place.

## 3. There is no doubt that Honorius had already issued those more severe laws against the Donatists in the year 405 when Augustine wrote his letter to Emeritus, the Donatist bishop of Caesarea (*Epistle* 87, no. 8). It is equally certain that the letter was written before the Conference took place, at which Emeritus defended the cause of his party as vigorously as anyone else. Augustine testifies in the aforementioned letter that he knew Emeritus only by reputation (*ibid.*, no. 1).

Emeritus had been initiated through Baptism among the schismatics and had never stood within the bosom of the Catholic Church (*Sermon to the People of the Church of Caesarea*, no. 2). Such was his authority among his own people that he was even believed to have composed, in 394, the celebrated judgment of the Council of Bagai against the Maximianists (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 10).

He was regarded as endowed with a happy disposition, cultivated in honorable disciplines, and liberally educated (*Epistle* 85, nos. 1, 10). He was hostile to the violent attempts of his own people and, finally, possessed as much integrity as could exist in a schismatic.

Augustine was not unwilling to believe the favorable reports circulated about him; indeed, he wished them to correspond to the truth. For he was especially inclined toward men of the sort in which Emeritus was portrayed. When he saw such men bound by some gross error, the more he wondered at it, the more he desired to enter into their knowledge and conversation, so that he might free them from that fault.

This was the reason he wrote to Emeritus once and again, although they were separated by a great distance, after receiving from trustworthy men the assurance that Emeritus would reply to him (*ibid.*, no. 6). Possidius also records two letters to this bishop (Possidius, *Index*, ch. 3), the first of which has been lost.

When Augustine received no reply to these letters and was uncertain whether his own letter or Emeritus’s response had perished, he added the second letter, which still survives. In it he demonstrates how powerless were the arguments that could be advanced in favor of separation. Then, after making clear by the example of Optatus Gildonianus that even the most manifest crimes committed within some communion, when tolerated for legitimate reasons, stain no one but their own perpetrators, he begs Emeritus to reply to him.

We nowhere read whether Emeritus satisfied the holy Bishop in this matter. But afterward he displayed, above all other Donatists, remarkable obstinacy and a mind hardened in error.

## 4. After the books against Cresconius, Augustine adds several other works against the Donatists [Col. 0362] which are missing in our time.

First, he addressed a short book to the Donatists in which he promised to hand over to them whatever could assist in deciding the cause of the schism—namely, all the records, both ecclesiastical and civil, as well as all the relevant passages of the sacred books—in order to induce them to demand these materials.

One of those into whose hands this promise fell published a counter-writing in which he called himself only a Donatist (*Retractations* 2.27). Consequently, Augustine entitled his own book, in which he replied to him, *Against Some Donatist or Other* (*ibid.* 2.28).

After publishing the materials he had promised, together with the short book in which those promises had first been made, Augustine gave the whole work the title *Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists* (*ibid.* 2.27). To make it more widely known among the people, he affixed it to the walls of the basilica recently taken from the Donatists.

When he realized that most people did not even read somewhat more extended works, he published, in accordance with his innate charity, a very brief one, so that the ease with which it could be copied would carry it through many hands and make it easy to commit to memory. This short work was entitled *Admonition to the Donatists concerning the Maximianists*. From the history of the Maximianists alone it demonstrated that the faction of Donatus rested on neither foundation nor truth (*ibid.* 2.29).

## 5. At the same time he wrote his book *On the Divination, or Prophecy, of Demons* (*ibid.* 2.30). It was occasioned by a conversation which he held one morning with certain Christian laymen who were present with him in large numbers during the holy days of the octave, before the divine mysteries were celebrated (*On the Divination of Demons*, nos. 1, 6).

The subject arose from a report that the destruction of the temple of Serapis—which was demolished at Alexandria around the year 389, during the reign of Theodosius—had been foretold by a certain magician. In this conversation Augustine attempted to explain the basis of the alleged divination and of other similar events which demons are able to announce in advance.

As soon as leisure permitted, he committed to writing what had been said at that time. At the end of the same book he promises that, if pagans should wish to oppose anything to the arguments he had set forth there, he would answer to the best of his ability.

He first observes that the worship of idols was declining day by day and that there was no year in which a smaller number of unbelievers was not found than in the preceding year (*ibid.*, no. 14).

## 6. Next in the sequence of his books Augustine places the *Six Questions Explained against the Pagans* (*Retractations* 2.31). Nevertheless, in printed manuscripts this short work is included among his letters (*Epistle* 102).

A certain pagan provided the occasion for writing it. Augustine held him in exceptional affection and greatly desired that he should become a Christian (*Retractations* 2.31). Augustine had also sent him several letters, but had received no reply from him, as though the man were ashamed to be regarded as Augustine’s follower [Col. 0363] (*Epistle* 102, no. 1).

At last the man proposed to the presbyter Deogratias six questions concerning religion, boasting that he had received some of them from the philosopher Porphyry. Augustine thinks that this Porphyry was different from the celebrated Porphyry, a Sicilian by nationality, who lived toward the end of the third century (*Retractations* 2.31).

The presbyter immediately sent the proposed questions from Carthage to Augustine, preferring to receive their solution from Augustine’s mouth rather than to convey it himself. The holy Doctor accommodated him in this matter, although he was exceedingly busy at the time. Yet in the letter prefixed to his short work he asks him not to hesitate to answer that pagan himself on every point, and to show him the work he was sending only to those persons whom he judged it appropriate to see it.

In the final section, since he anticipated that the man who had proposed the questions was already considering embracing the faith of Christ but wished first to have obscure matters in Scripture explained to him, Augustine judged that he ought to be carefully admonished to become a Christian at once and not remain any longer occupied with questions of the sort he had proposed:

> For fear, he says, that while he waits to finish his questions about the sacred books before becoming a Christian, he may finish this present life before passing from death to life. There are innumerable matters which must not be finished before faith, lest life be finished without faith. But once faith has been firmly retained, such matters should be diligently sought in order to exercise the devout delight of the minds of the faithful; whatever becomes clear in them should be shared without arrogant self-confidence, while whatever remains hidden should be endured without danger to salvation.

(*Epistle* 102, no. 38.)

The Pelagians cited this writing, thinking that they could turn to their own advantage what is read there: that Christ wished to appear to human beings and have his teaching preached among them at the time and in the place where he knew there would be people who would believe in him.

Augustine explains, however, that he intended to say only this about Christ’s foreknowledge because it seemed sufficient to refute the unbelief of the pagans who had raised that question. He did not wish to undertake elsewhere a full exposition of everything that might bear upon the matter. In addition, he shows that the statement in question has no bearing at all upon the cause of the Pelagians. He also explains several expressions in the same passage, although the Pelagians had not used them against him (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, nos. 17–20).

## 7. In his *Retractations* Augustine next places after the preceding work the *Exposition of the Epistle of James to the Twelve Tribes* (*Retractations* 2.32). This was nothing more than a collection, arranged through the diligence of his brothers, of notes which he had written in the margins of the text. Nevertheless, it provided some assistance toward understanding the words of this Epistle.

That work, however, does not survive in our time. Augustine next places after it the three books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, in which he first undertook to defend the grace of Christ against the Pelagian heresy (*ibid.* 2.33). Yet he did not write these books until after the condemnation of Caelestius—that is, as will be demonstrated below, in the year 412.

Since this is so, it is clear that in this matter he paid little attention to chronological order, for he places these same books far earlier in the brief summary of the Conference, a work which was published toward the end of 411 or not long afterward [Col. 0364].

8. As for the work *On the One Baptism*, which he discusses next (*ibid.*, chap. 34), that it preceded the *Conference* would already be evident from the fact that it contains no mention whatsoever of that *Conference*. The same point is further shown by the fact that here he says the Donatists had not attempted to substantiate the insults they directed against Marcellinus and certain other Roman bishops with any evidence, although in the *Conference* they produced some evidence, fabricated though it was (*On the One Baptism*, no. 27). In the same work he also persists in an error of fact (*ibid.*, no. 28), for which he himself reproaches himself in the revision of nearly all his books against the Donatists (*Retractions*, book 2, chap. 34): namely, that he places the judgment of Felix of Aptunga after the judgment that Constantine issued in favor of Caecilian. At the time of the *Conference* he had not yet been informed about this matter; but by the time he abridged that same *Conference*, he had already recognized his error (*Brief Account of the Conference*, 3, no. 42). Indeed, before 14 June of the year 412 he composed the *Book on the One Baptism*, or *On the Unity of Baptism*, with the intention of replying to another work bearing the same title (*Retractions*, book 2, chap. 34). Its author, whom they claimed to be Petilian of Cirta, maintained that Baptism could be validly administered only within the Donatist sect.

Apart from inflated language and incredible slanders, that book contained nothing deserving serious consideration (*On the One Baptism*, no. 1). Its author brought forward arguments and testimonies that favored the Catholics more than his own side (*ibid.*, no. 10). He accused several Roman bishops of idolatry, but without offering any proof (*ibid.*, no. 27). By asserting that the well-known Catholic bishops of the Church of Cirta followed the Manichaean heresy (*ibid.*, no. 29), he thereby demonstrated most clearly how much credence should be given to his accusations against others, whom he did not know: for he attacked with such savagery Profuturus of Cirta, who had died only a few years earlier, and his successor Fortunatus, who was still alive—men of such tested and conspicuous innocence.

A certain Donatist presbyter gave this book to one of Augustine’s friends, named Constantinus. Augustine received it from him while he was staying in the country, and Constantinus at the same time earnestly begged him to write a refutation of it. Although he had already treated the subject several times, Augustine did not think he should refuse his friend, judging that the abundance of good books could be increased with benefit, both so that they might more easily reach everyone’s hands and especially so that they might satisfy those who regard an old argument, when presented in a new form, as something new. He dedicated this work to Constantinus himself (*ibid.*, no. 1).

We have already mentioned a certain little book that Augustine had published in order to make it clear that the history of the Maximianists alone was sufficient to overthrow completely the impious and arrogant error of the Donatists against the Catholic Church. After some years he added to it a second book on the same subject, [Col. 0365] much longer and more exact than the first (*Retractions*, book 2, chap. 35). Both books, likewise, have perished. We have no information by which the proper date of either work can be established; but from the order in which they are arranged in the *Retractions*, we may at least conjecture that they were composed between the year 406 and the beginning of 411.

In that very year 406, in our opinion, the war of Radagaisus, king of the Goths, broke out. While Augustine was then at Carthage, he heard with the deepest sorrow of the opportunity which the unbelievers at Rome were taking from that event to disparage the Christian religion. But the swift defeat of Radagaisus soon covered the authors of this impious taunt with disgrace.

# CHAPTER IV

1. The decision of the Carthaginian council of 407 concerning the appointment of a bishop over communities converted from the Donatist schism.  
2. The laws granted to the council’s delegation to the emperor.  
3. The schism of the Rogatists, confined to the town of Carthena and neighboring places.  
4. Augustine refutes the letter of Vincentius, the principal Rogatist bishop.

## 1

The African council held at Carthage in the year 407 has transmitted to us certain matters relating to the history of Augustine and of the Donatists. Earlier synods had prohibited the establishment of new bishoprics when the bishop of the diocese from which the new see was to be detached objected. The council of the present year further decreed that the consent both of the primate and of the provincial synod was required (*African Code of Canons*, canon 98).

It nevertheless exempted from this rule those Churches that, while they had previously possessed their own bishop on the Donatist side, should request that the same bishop be retained after their return to unity. Such a request, it ordered, was to be granted without difficulty and without awaiting the synod (*ibid.*, canon 99). If, however, after the death of their bishop, the people preferred to be joined to a neighboring diocese rather than ask for a successor of their own, the council decreed that this too was not to be denied them.

It further established that whatever communities each bishop had restored to communion with the Church before Honorius’s law of 405, he was to govern by episcopal right as subject to his jurisdiction. The Churches of those who, after the law enacted concerning unity, had either returned to the Catholic Church or remained in heresy, together with all their instruments and rights, were to be under the authority of the Catholic bishop in whose diocese they were situated. It is therefore clear that, by the right established through the edict of Unity, the Donatist Churches belonged to the Catholics.

At that time the people of Germania Nova were in dispute with the bishop Maurentius (*ibid.*, canon 100). The council decided that bishops were to be chosen from both sides who, after traveling to Thubursica, would deliver a considered judgment on the matter. Maurentius immediately chose Xantippus, Augustine, Florentius, Theasius, Samsucius, Secundus, and Possidius. The council approved them and assigned the province to Xantippus, so that he might arrange for the people of Germania to nominate the other men needed to complete the number [Col. 0366].

Maurentius’s choice sufficiently indicated that he had no lack of confidence in his legal position. A certain Maurentius of Thubursica is found in the *Conference* (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, chap. 143); Holstenius considers him to be the same person as the bishop of Germania. It is certainly possible that Germania Nova was once included in his diocese, although in later times a separate diocese was formed from Germania alone.

## 2

The same council sent the bishops Vincentius and Fortunatianus as envoys to the emperor (*African Code of Canons*, canon 97)—the former perhaps from Sicca, the latter from Culusi—men to whom, together with the other envoys, the defense of the Church’s cause at the *Conference* had been entrusted (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, chaps. 138–139).

Those envoys were instructed to ask the emperors, in the name of the entire province, for permission to appoint advocates as defenders of the Church. Whenever they judged in the Church’s interest, these advocates were never to be denied access to the tribunals of the prefects—which the council calls the judges’ secretariats—whether to present petitions or to intervene. This was a right that had formerly belonged to the provincial priests of the pagans.

They were also granted free authority to act against the Donatists, the pagans, and superstitions connected with idolatry. It is commonly believed that, in response to the council’s petitions, the two laws issued on 16 August and subsequently combined into one were granted (*Theodosian Code*, “On Bishops and Churches,” law 38).

Both laws were issued at Rome in the year 407 and sent to Porphyrius, proconsul of Africa. The first confirms all privileges previously granted either to the Church or to the clergy and adds a new authorization: namely, to select defenders of Churches and ecclesiastical privileges from among the advocates, as the council had requested. The second orders that the laws enacted against the Donatists and Manichaeans be upheld and put into effect (*ibid.*, “On Heretics,” law 41).

Moreover, on 24 November of the same year 407, Honorius wrote a law to Curtius, the prefect of the praetorium, closely corresponding to the instructions that Vincentius and Fortunatianus had received from the Carthaginian synod. It concerned both pagans and heretics, especially the Donatists, Manichaeans, Priscillianists, and Caelicolists. This law was publicly posted at Carthage on 5 June 408 under the official notice of the proconsul Porphyrius (*Sirmond, Appendix to the Theodosian Code*, chap. 12).

A substantial portion of it was inserted in two places in the *Theodosian Code* (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” laws 43 and 44, and “On Pagans,” law 19); everywhere it is dated to the year 408 and to 15 November. Yet it is certain that in November 408 Honorius was not at Rome, from which the aforesaid law is said to have been issued, but at Ravenna. Nor could it have been posted at Carthage in 409 under the proconsul Porphyrius, since Donatus had already succeeded him toward the end of 408. At the end of that same year Theodorus was prefect of the praetorium; Curtius, however, held that office in 407 and at the beginning of 408 [Col. 0367].

## 3

At about this time Vincentius the Rogatist lodged a complaint by letter with Augustine against the Catholics—certainly not much later, for Augustine’s reply, although lengthy and concerned exclusively with the Donatist secession, contains not even the slightest trace of the Carthaginian Conference. Moreover, it says nothing about the freedom to choose one’s religion that was granted to everyone toward the end of 409, although the entire letter is devoted to defending the severity of the laws that had been enacted. Add to this that it says nothing about the killing of Stilicho, nor about the events that occurred as the year 408 unfolded.

This Vincentius, a bishop of the Donatist party, was the man from whom the Rogatist schism took its name (*Against Cresconius*, book 4, no. 73). He was “a very short fragment cut from a larger fragment” (*Letter* 93, no. 24). He had previously been a presbyter (*ibid.*, no. 47), but at that time was Rogatus’s successor (*ibid.*, no. 1). His see was at Cartenna, a town of Caesarean Mauretania (*ibid.*, no. 20).

Within Africa itself so many parties had arisen from the party of Donatus that even the Donatists themselves, if questioned, would not have been able to enumerate them (*ibid.*, no. 25). The Rogatists, moreover, had not yet separated from the Donatists when Julian assumed imperial power, which occurred toward the end of the year 361 (*ibid.*, no. 12). After their defection, the Donatists inflicted harsh and bitter treatment upon them. They did not merely exploit the imperial commands issued against heretics; they also used the tyranny of the general Firmus, who rebelled in 372, for the destruction of the same Rogatists (*Against the Letter of Petilian*, book 2, no. 184). For this reason they called the Rogatists “Firmians” (*Letter* 87, no. 10).

The Rogatists wished to appear more moderate and to recoil from the savagery of the other Donatists. Augustine, however, thought that this was attributable not so much to any devotion to Christian gentleness as to their recognized weakness. “You say,” he writes, “that you do not wish to rage; I think rather that you are unable to do so. For you are so few in number that you do not dare to stir yourselves against the multitudes opposed to you, even if you wish to” (*Letter* 93, no. 11).

Nevertheless, Augustine maintained that they interpreted the evangelical saying, “If anyone wishes to take your tunic and bring you to court, let him have your cloak as well” (Matthew 5:40), to mean that those who persecuted them should be resisted neither by force nor by any legal right. He argued that Rogatus, their founder, had either not understood the saying in this way or had failed to carry out what he understood, since he had engaged in fierce and persistent disputes—even in the courts—over certain matters that they claimed as their own.

Vincentius cared for the little flock left by Rogatus (*Letter* 93, no. 49) at Carthena and in the surrounding districts, together with nine or ten colleagues and associates (*ibid.*, nos. 20–22).

## 4

Vincentius had known Augustine as a young man when Augustine was still studying at Carthage and Rogatus was still alive (*ibid.*, nos. 1, 51). Even then he had noticed Augustine’s love of peace and uprightness. When he learned that Augustine, having embraced the religion of Christ, was devoting himself to the sacred Scriptures, he assumed that Augustine was now much more desirous of and eager for [Col. 0368] tranquility than before, and entirely averse to every form of violent action.

Accordingly, he wrote to Augustine concerning the severity exercised against the Donatists through the laws enacted at the request of the Catholic bishops. He argued that no one ought to be compelled to embrace justice and unity (*ibid.*, nos. 5, 14); that it was unlawful to bring complaints before the emperor against the enemies of their communion (*ibid.*, no. 13); that neither in the Gospels nor among the Apostles was anything found to show that earthly rulers had been asked to act against the adversaries of the Church (*ibid.*, no. 1); that no Apostle had ever invaded another person’s property under the pretext of faith (*ibid.*, no. 11); and that, in any case, those acts of violence were being applied uselessly to a very large portion of the population (*ibid.*, no. 3). He feared that, as a result, the name of God might instead be blasphemed by Jews and pagans (*ibid.*, no. 26).

He denied that the Church had been given the promise that it would always grow and spread throughout the world. On the contrary, he asserted that it could be extinguished throughout the rest of the world and preserved in a single region (*ibid.*, no. 21). In support of this he cited Hilary, who wrote that ten provinces of Asia for the most part truly did not know God (*ibid.*, nos. 31–32).

He maintained that the region in which Christian faith and religion flourished appeared small when compared with the whole world (*ibid.*, no. 22). Consequently, he interpreted the name “Catholic” not from communion with the entire world but from the observance of all divine commandments and all the sacraments. In this way he arrogated the title “Catholic” to his own Rogatist fragment (*ibid.*, nos. 23, 49).

He argued that Baptism administered outside the Church was invalid, citing both the martyr Cyprian and Cyprian’s predecessor Agrippinus as witnesses, and asserting that people were to be baptized after heretics (*ibid.*, nos. 35–36): “For even after John,” he said, “the Apostle Paul baptized” (*ibid.*, no. 47).

He asked why, if the followers of Donatus were wicked and heretical, the Catholics nevertheless sought them out with such eagerness and received them without difficulty (*ibid.*, no. 46).

This letter was delivered to Augustine by a Catholic whom Vincentius knew well. Since there was therefore no room for doubt that Vincentius the Rogatist had written it, Augustine sent him a reply (*ibid.*, no. 1). The reply was quite substantial—not so much with Vincentius’s state of mind in view as the benefit of those who might perhaps read it with fear of God—and Augustine hoped that, even if Vincentius himself gained nothing from it, at least others might derive some benefit (*ibid.*, no. 53).

# CHAPTER V

1. Melania the Elder comes to Africa.  
2. Augustine writes to Paulinus and in turn receives a letter from him.  
3. The insolence and ferocity of the pagan idolaters of Calama.  
4. Nectarius pleads with Augustine on behalf of his fellow citizens of Calama who were accused.  
5. Because of their crime, Possidius goes to the imperial court.  
6. Augustine replies to Paulinus.  
7. He also writes to Bishop Memor, to whom he sends the sixth of his books on Music.

## 1

Melania the Elder, or grandmother, a matron celebrated above all others in the writings of ecclesiastical authors, had returned to Rome a few years earlier after spending a very long period in the East, when she undertook a journey to Africa. [Col. 0369] Augustine bore witness to the moderation with which she endured the death of her only son (*Paulinus in Augustine*, *Letter* 94, no. 2).

We do not see how this can be assigned to the very period in which Albina, her daughter-in-law, crossed over there with her entire household—namely, toward the end of 410. For if Publicola, Melania’s son, had still been alive at that time, Albina, his wife, would have accompanied him rather than the younger Melania, her daughter, or Pinianus, her son-in-law.

Moreover, the upheaval at Calama followed Publicola’s death, and we find no basis for placing it after the year 408. This consideration prevents us from assigning Publicola’s death to the end of 410. There is also a stronger reason: that revolt at Calama took place on 1 June and on 8 June, in the presence of Possidius. It therefore cannot have occurred in 411, since Possidius was at the Carthaginian Conference on precisely those days.

Nor can the disturbance be placed in 410, since at that time no recent law against the pagans had been promulgated, whereas Augustine says that the crime had been committed against the most recent laws (*Letter* 91, no. 8). Immediately after those disturbances Augustine spent the winter at Carthage (*Letter* 121, chap. 3, no. 14), whereas he spent the winter that began in 410 at Hippo (*Letter* 124, nos. 1–2).

We shall explain later why we assign the revolt to 408 rather than 409. Baronius states that it occurred in 399. Apart from the arguments that undermine that opinion, however, we cannot confidently assert that Melania came to Africa in 398. The sequence of the history will shed greater light on these matters.

## 2

Perhaps when Melania came to Africa she brought with her the earlier letters of Paulinus, in which he had already praised Publicola’s developing virtue at length, before writing to him at the beginning of 408 the letter that begins, “Your word is always a lamp for my feet” (*Letter* 94).

It is not at all established that Publicola died in Africa; it is certain only that his death occurred while his mother was staying there. Augustine saw how many tears she shed over this death, and how pious and restrained they were. He could not refrain from writing to Paulinus about it and telling him that Melania seemed to be mourning not so much the death of her only son as the fact that he had not yet completely renounced the pomp and vanity of the world (*ibid.*, nos. 2–3).

At the same time, he asked Paulinus what he thought the activity of the blessed would be in heaven after they had resumed their bodies (*ibid.*, no. 4). He also discussed with him that happy leisure necessary for acquiring or expounding Christian wisdom, which Augustine thought Paulinus was then enjoying, although he later learned of Paulinus’s extraordinary occupations (*Letter* 95, no. 9).

He entrusted this letter to the deacon Quintus for delivery at the beginning of 408 (*Letter* 94, no. 8). Quintus had already been in Rome for some time [Col. 0370] when Paulinus arrived with him, as he did every year after the Paschal feast, to visit the monuments of the Apostles and martyrs (*ibid.*, no. 1). Easter in 408 fell on 29 March.

Paulinus therefore received the letter there. He did not read it, however, until he was at Formiae, where, on his journey home, he had decided to stop for a full day. The noise unavoidable at Rome would not have allowed him to read it there continuously and at leisure, so as to satisfy his desire. This indicates that the letter, which is now lost, was quite extensive and was rightly given by Paulinus the title of a little book (*ibid.*).

Paulinus commended it with no ordinary praises in his reply, which he wrote rather hastily on 15 May, since Quintus had informed him of his departure on the day before he actually left (*ibid.*, no. 8). As a result, he forgot to answer some sections of Augustine’s letter (*Letter* 95, no. 9).

With profound humility and piety he discussed the activity of the blessed in the future age after the resurrection, and at that point he honored the holy bishop, who had asked him for his opinion on the matter, with great praises (*Letter* 94, no. 6).

## 3

As we have said, the law issued at Carthage on 24 November 407 was not promulgated before 5 June 408 (*Sirmond, Appendix to the Theodosian Code*, chap. 12). It appears, however, to have been promulgated earlier in Numidia, if the event that occurred at Calama on 1 June (*Letter* 91, no. 8) is assigned to this year rather than the following one.

The following observation leads us to this conclusion: the matter arising from that revolt had still not been settled at the end of March of the following year (*Letter* 104, no. 1). Thus, if it is assigned to 409, Possidius would still have been at the imperial court in April 410; and he would scarcely have returned to Africa—something no one will readily believe—when he was sent as an envoy to the emperor by the Carthaginian council on 14 June of that same year 410.

Whether the event occurred in 408 or in 409, this is what happened at Calama:

“Against the most recent laws,” Augustine says, “on the first of June, during a pagan festival, a sacrilegious celebration was conducted, with no one preventing it, and with such insolent boldness that a most shameless crowd of dancers passed along that same street directly before the doors of the church—something that had not occurred even in the time of Julian.

When the clergy attempted to prevent this unlawful and utterly disgraceful act, the church was stoned. Then, about eight days later, after the bishop had repeated the well-known laws to the council and they were preparing to carry out what had been ordered, the church was stoned again.

On the following day, when our people were trying to impose fear on the criminals, public legal recourse was denied to our people, who, it seemed, wished to make a statement for the record. On that very day, as though they were to be terrified by divine intervention, hail answered the stonings. When it had passed, they immediately carried out a third stoning and finally set fire to the ecclesiastical buildings and to the people.

They killed one servant of God—that is, one of the monks—who happened [Col. 0371] to come within their reach. The others hid wherever they could or fled by whatever route they could find. Meanwhile the bishop, pressed and hemmed in, concealed himself in a certain place, where he heard the voices of those searching for him in order to kill him and reproaching one another because, since they had not found him, they had committed so great a crime for nothing.

These events lasted from about the tenth hour until a substantial part of the night. No one among those whose authority might have been decisive attempted to restrain them or come to their aid, except for one foreigner. Through him many servants of God—that is, monks—were rescued from the hands of those attempting to kill them, and much was taken away from the plunderers.

Through this it became clear how easily these things would either not have happened at all or would have been abandoned once begun, if the citizens, and especially the leading men, had forbidden them to be done and completed” (*Letter* 91, no. 8).

Augustine says elsewhere that things stored for feeding the most devout poor—namely, in the monastery established under Possidius’s care—were exposed to the unfortunate populace for plunder. He also says that their blood was shed, one of them having been killed (*Letter* 104, no. 5).

He likewise indicates that the disturbance arose from certain silver images which the pagans were extremely eager either to melt down themselves or to preserve, worship, or publicly honor with sacrilegious rites and distinctions. The entire city was therefore at fault, except that those who, fearing to provoke against themselves the enemies of the Church—whom they knew to possess great influence in that town—were content to commend the bishop and the monks to God in their prayers, were less culpable than the rest (*Letter* 91, no. 9; *Letter* 104, no. 17).

There is consequently a considerable presumption that these cowardly and timid people were nevertheless counted among the Christians. Augustine expressly records that not a few of them fell into the public sin, either because they had not brought help to the burning church or because they had taken something from the sacrilegious pagan plunder. Later, however, they cleansed their guilt by confession, prayers, and the mourning of repentance (*Letter* 104, no. 9).

Baronius assigns this history to the year 399, after the laws enacted by Honorius against the idolaters (*Baronius*, under the year 399, no. 78). Nevertheless, the pagan festivals were not prohibited by the laws of 399; indeed, they were confirmed by the law issued on 20 August of that year (*Theodosian Code*, “On Pagans,” law 17). On the basis of this observation, some assign their prohibition to the law addressed to Curtius (*ibid.*, law 19), as though it were the first of all the laws on this matter.

## 4

Not long after this impious crime Augustine went to Calama. “So that our people,” he says, “might either be consoled in their great grief or calmed in their inflamed state, we dealt with the Christians as far as we could and as we thought the circumstances required.

Then we also admitted the pagans themselves—the source and cause of so great an evil—when they asked to see us, so that on this occasion we might admonish them what they ought to do, if they had any sense, not merely for removing their present anxiety—for they had good reason to fear that they would suffer the most severe punishments for so great a crime—but also for seeking eternal salvation.

They heard many things from us, and they themselves [Col. 0372] made many requests. But far be it from us to be servants of the sort who take pleasure in being asked by those who do not ask our Lord” (*Letter* 91, no. 10).

Nectarius, whom we mentioned above, must be counted among the principal citizens of that city. He himself was a pagan (*Letter* 90), though at least his father had been a Christian before his death (*Letter* 91, no. 2). When he saw his country exposed to such danger because of the revolt—although it is credible that he himself had not participated in it—he wrote to Augustine, addressing him as “brother.” He admitted that Calama was liable under the laws to the severest punishment and begged Augustine to display the love of gentleness so appropriate to a bishop.

He offered complete and undiminished restitution for what had been lost and requested that the innocent not be involved with the guilty and that punishments not be imposed (*Letter* 90).

Taking the opportunity offered by the zeal he displayed for his homeland, Augustine urged him in his reply to love his true homeland as well and to embrace the Christian religion, so holy and so beneficial.

Regarding the revolt at Calama, Augustine replied that the bishops had decided to pursue a punishment that would deter the other cities from imitating so hideous an example, while nevertheless not exceeding the limits of Christian and episcopal gentleness. Its purpose was not to avenge injuries but to correct sinners and promote their salvation (*Letter* 91, no. 6).

Finally, Augustine said that the accused were to be left their lives and the necessities required to preserve life, even if they refused to repent; only those things were to be taken away that they had used for wrongdoing. As for the investigation, whatever could be extracted only by force and torture—for example, who had first initiated the revolt—was to be omitted.

But since this matter lay in the hands and at the discretion of the emperor and the civil judges, Augustine added that, if it pleased God that the crime should either be punished more severely or remain unpunished for the present under the weight of His more severe anger, the bishops would have nothing left but to submit their minds to the divine plan. They could nevertheless console themselves with the fact that they had attempted to accomplish what they judged best and most beneficial (*ibid.*, no. 9).
