He wrote this letter about eight months before 27 March—that is, around the beginning of August (*Letter* 104, no. 1). Nectarius did not reply throughout that entire period. This fits quite well with the year 408, when, as we shall see, people were generally arguing and spreading the report that the laws issued during Stilicho’s ascendancy had been annulled by his death, which occurred in August of that year. Perhaps Nectarius therefore thought that, both for this reason and because of the disturbances that had arisen at that very time, the revolt at Calama would be forgotten, and so he refrained from pressing Augustine.

## 5

Possidius was still in Africa when Augustine wrote to Nectarius (*ibid.*). Later, however, after crossing the sea, Possidius went to the imperial court to conduct his case against the pagan idolaters of Calama. He loved them more truly and more holily than those who would have wished their crime to go unpunished.

We have not discovered when he undertook that journey [Col. 0373]. Nevertheless, since on 27 March Augustine still did not know whether Possidius had obtained anything, it may reasonably be believed that he did not depart until late in that year or even at the beginning of the following year.

In fact, the letter sent by Possidius himself—or certainly not long after his departure—to Paulinus (*Letter* 95, no. 1) was written during the winter that Augustine spent at Carthage (*Letter* 121, no. 14). That letter replies to the one which the deacon Quintus had brought to Augustine from Paulinus, written on 15 May, as can be understood from Paulinus’s own words quoted in it.

In the same letter Augustine indicates, with evident sorrow, the necessity that was taking Possidius to Italy. Yet he expresses it only by saying that Possidius was compelled all the more imperiously to serve the illnesses of the sick, the more dangerously ill they were. He nevertheless confesses that he finds consolation in the joy Possidius derives from seeing Paulinus.

From this passage we may understand the spirit in which those holy African bishops so frequently traveled to the imperial court. Augustine testifies there that he would easily have been drawn to sail to Italy solely by his longing to see Paulinus, if the duties of his office had not detained him.

Speaking of the circumstances that were driving Possidius to make the journey to Italy, he says: “Whether we are being exercised by these things or rather punished by them, I do not know—except that he who mingles such great consolations with our sorrows and acts with marvelous medicine does not deal with us according to our sins or repay us according to our iniquities, lest we love the world and lest we fail in the world” (*Letter* 95, no. 1).

## 6

Augustine then replied to Paulinus’s letters (*ibid.*, no. 2 and following). Paulinus had said that it was more worthwhile to inquire how one ought to live here than what our future state in heaven would be. Augustine seized this opportunity to propose a question which seemed to him to be of no small importance: namely, how one ought to live among and for the sake of people who had not yet been released and freed from their desires.

He then confessed the anxiety, distress, and fear of his own mind amid the many duties of life, and asked Paulinus to discuss the matter with some truly devout or, as Augustine puts it, gentle physician of the heart whom he might find either at Nola, where he lived, or at Rome, where he went each year. Whatever the Lord revealed to Paulinus, he asked him to write back.

He then turned to the state of the resurrection, especially in matters concerning the body. He also raised the question whether angels possess bodies adapted to their functions, since Paulinus had apparently treated it as certain that they were simply spiritual creatures.

He therefore asked that the blessed man satisfy him both on this point and on another question proposed in his earlier letter concerning Christian leisure for the pursuit of wisdom, since Paulinus’s early departure with Quintus had prevented him from answering everything.

It is thought that this was the very letter on the form of the resurrection (*Letter* 121, no. 14) that Augustine had written in response to Paulinus’s second inquiry, in which he had discussed the use of the bodily members. Paulinus asked Augustine to send it to him again [Col. 0374], although he indicates that it was brief (*Letter* 95, no. 7; *Letter* 149, no. 2).

It is clear that Paulinus calls it brief only in comparison with writings that constitute entire books. It could also undoubtedly be called brief in view of the doctrines of faith with which it was filled.

### 7

Among the bishops most closely connected with Augustine through correspondence was Memor, or Memorius, the father of that Julian who later miserably fell into the Pelagian heresy (*Against Julian*, book 1, §12). Yet the unfortunate fate of his son in no way prevented Augustine from always regarding Julian’s parents as honorable Catholic Christians, and from considering them fortunate in this respect: that they had died before seeing their son become a heretic (*Unfinished Work*, book 1, chapter 68).

Memor had therefore written Augustine a letter full of affection and respect, asking him for the books he had composed on music (*Letter* 101). The holy Doctor had undertaken to correct them and send them to him. But since he was extremely pressed by business, he not only had no time to devote himself to this revision, but could scarcely even locate those books—at least the first five of them. His occupations left him so little leisure for such relaxation.

Nevertheless, since Possidius was unwilling to depart for that region without being introduced to Memor, Augustine entrusted him with the sixth book to deliver to Memor on his arrival. He also added a letter in which he discusses certain disciplines that are commonly, but falsely, called “liberal,” since true piety is absent from them; and he asks Memor to send his son Julian, then a deacon, to stay with him for a while.

Memor had asked him in what meters the verses of David consisted. Augustine frankly admits that he did not know, since he was inexperienced in the Hebrew language; nevertheless, he says that learned men in that language had assured him that the verses were composed according to entirely definite meters.

## CHAPTER VI

1. Olympius succeeds to Stilicho’s authority.  
2. Augustine writes to him concerning the case of Boniface, bishop of Cataqua.  
3. Augustine explains the questions of Bishop Boniface.  
4. After Stilicho’s death, the Church is disturbed by the upheavals of Pagans and heretics.  
5. New laws are obtained against them from the Emperor.  
6. Augustine asks Donatus, remembering Christian gentleness, to restrain the Donatists when power is given him, but not to kill them.  
7. He writes to Italica concerning the vision of God and the siege of Rome.

### 1

When Honorius had left Rome at the end of May, after first marrying Thermantia, Stilicho’s second daughter—just as in 398 he had married her elder sister Maria—he reached Ticinum. There a very serious mutiny broke out, and the soldiers killed the Empire’s principal officials. The outcome of this disturbance was that Stilicho himself was thrown into chains and was slaughtered at Ravenna on 22 August 408.

The common agreement of historians is that Olympius brought about Stilicho’s downfall; for this reason some praise him and others condemn him. Augustine reports that he was a Christian and commends his piety, which he appears to have regarded as genuine and substantial (*Letters* 96.1; 97.1). Augustine maintained a correspondence with him. He may have become acquainted with him through some African bishops who had seen him at court and had found him favorably disposed toward advancing their holy councils.

Zosimus, although necessarily hostile to Olympius if he considered him truly a Christian, admits that Olympius devoted himself assiduously to the duties of Christian piety. Zosimus nevertheless contends that this outward appearance served him as a mask by which he concealed his wickedness and won the Emperor’s favor. He likewise reports that Olympius regularly visited sick soldiers as though performing a religious duty. He adds that, amid the Empire’s divisions, Honorius placed his confidence in Olympius’s prayers (*Zosimus, History*, book 5).

Even while Stilicho was alive, Olympius had already attained the highest honors. After Stilicho’s death he obtained the office of master of the offices, whom some call the *magister palatii*; finally, he was appointed chief minister and arbiter of affairs at court.

Augustine considered him worthy of this honor. Since he knew that Olympius had learned from God not to be high-minded but to associate with the lowly (*Letter* 96.1), he did not doubt that Olympius would wisely use his temporal prosperity to acquire eternal merits. And because he was a true son of the Church, Augustine believed that Olympius would devote himself to the Church’s interests with all the greater diligence in proportion to the authority he possessed in the Empire.

Thus, as soon as Olympius’s advancement was reported in Africa—even before the truth of the matter had been fully ascertained, that is, apparently at the beginning of September or thereabouts—Augustine commended Boniface’s case to him.

### 2

This Boniface, bishop of Cataqua, perhaps a place in Numidia, had succeeded Paul, whose conduct we have seen Augustine criticizing above (chapter 3, §2). Paul had not only purchased, under another person’s name, certain fields with money that he himself owed to the imperial treasury, but also, while collecting the produce of those fields in the name of the Church, had failed to pay the taxes that he owed the treasury on their account.

Boniface, his successor, appears to have been summoned to pay these taxes. He could have asked the Emperor for exemption from the amount and then retained without dispute the property that his predecessor had acquired and had already begun to possess in the Church’s name. Yet he could not endure to conceal the fraud committed against the treasury, nor could he bear the burden on his conscience of retaining property acquired by dishonest means.

He therefore explained how the matter had been handled and asked the Emperor for the use of those lands, judging it preferable that they should be credited to the manifest generosity of the ruler rather than to the concealed wrongdoing of his predecessor. Indeed, even if he were refused in this matter, he judged that it was better for God’s servants to endure the hardship of poverty than to obtain what they needed with a guilty conscience.

He had already obtained from the Emperor certain written orders concerning this matter, apparently through Augustine’s influence, since Augustine had commended him to Olympius. Yet the affair had not proceeded entirely according to his wishes (*ibid.*, §3). Accordingly, when these written orders proved wholly insufficient, Boniface refused to use them as a means of obtaining others.

Augustine therefore wrote to Olympius on Boniface’s behalf and asked him to assist the bishop in obtaining this favor—or else to request the lands himself, so that he might later donate them to the Church of Cataqua.

Boniface of Cataqua is mentioned in the Conference (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, chapter 142). From the integrity of conscience that he displayed throughout this affair, we may reasonably infer that he was the same Boniface who strongly detested lying and whose questions Augustine answered (*Letter* 98.7); the Boniface whom Augustine calls his holy brother in various places (*Letter* 97.3); and the one with whom Augustine says that he was staying around 414 (*Letter* 149.2).

### 3

Boniface’s questions were twofold.

The first was whether parents harmed their infant children when, for the purpose of curing them, they employed either superstitious remedies or sacrifices to imaginary gods. Boniface said that he could not understand how the faith of parents benefited infants brought to the life-giving waters of Baptism, if the parents’ unbelief did them no harm (*Letter* 98.1).

Augustine maintains that parents can in no way deprive their infants of spiritual life. He then responds by appealing to certain passages of more obscure meaning drawn from Cyprian. He further observes that infants are brought to Baptism by those whose hands carry them, provided that these people are truly faithful; but above all they are brought by the whole community of saints and believers.

Boniface seemed to think that infants were not cleansed from original sin unless they were brought to the saving waters by both parents. Augustine demonstrates to him, on the basis of the Church’s constant practice, that they may also be brought by any persons whatsoever.

Boniface’s second question concerned how parents are permitted, when they present infants at the sacred font, to say that they believe on the infants’ behalf and to answer the other customary questions (*ibid.*, §7). This question seemed difficult to him because he strongly abhorred lying.

At the end of his letter he asked Augustine to answer his doubts, relying not merely on the authority of custom but also on arguments drawn from reason itself. Augustine therefore gives him a full answer by explaining, insofar as was necessary, the rationale of ecclesiastical practice.

### 4

The disturbances that followed Stilicho’s fall at court immediately produced further disturbances in the African Church. Pagans and Donatists openly asserted that the laws enacted while Stilicho was alive had died together with him (*Letters* 97.2; 100.2), since they had supposedly been promulgated solely on the authority of that minister, without the Emperor’s knowledge or even against his will. Consequently, they claimed, the measures enacted either to repress heretics or to destroy idols were no longer valid. The Donatists even circulated a false report that Honorius had granted them a special indulgence (*Letter* 105.6).

These empty rumors, spread and propagated by the Church’s enemies, suddenly swept through the whole of Africa. They began everywhere to produce immense disturbances and to inflame the people against the bishops to such an extent that the bishops could in no way feel secure about their lives.

At about this time, in September, Severus and Macarius were killed by Pagans or heretics, while the bishops Evodius, Theasius, and Victor were subjected to blows and wounds (*African Code of Canons*, canon 106).

If the fourteenth constitution of the appendix to the Theodosian Code applies in its entirety to the events that took place in Africa at that time, it is clear from it that some bishops were forcibly dragged from their houses, and even from their churches, and subjected to various punishments. Others were treated less cruelly but more insultingly: part of their hair was torn out, and various injuries were inflicted upon them as an insult and disgrace to the Christian faith.

Although these crimes, committed in the very centers of the cities, could not have escaped the notice of the magistrates, they were nevertheless restrained by no punishments on the magistrates’ part; indeed, they were not even brought to the Emperor’s attention.

### 5

Moved by these events, the bishops at the Council of Carthage sent two of their number, Florentius and Restitutus, to the court on 13 October, against the idolaters and heretics (*ibid.*).

Augustine seems to have been referring to this mission when he says that the bishops sent to the Emperor could indicate some means of confronting these evils, insofar as they had been more carefully considered by the common counsel of their colleagues, within the narrow limits imposed by time (*Letter* 97.3). He himself, however, says that he had been unable to share his advice with them (*ibid.*, §2).

These words show that Augustine did not attend that Council of Carthage, which was very probably only a provincial council. He also states that many bishops, amid that immense disturbance and alarm in the Church, were compelled to hasten to the court and almost to flee there (*ibid.*). These were doubtless the men who had suffered the most severely and who had joined the council’s delegates.

They had decided to pass through Rome.

Augustine’s letter to Olympius concerning Boniface had made no mention of these troubles, since he had not yet heard that they had occurred. But later, after receiving a letter from Olympius, who had voluntarily contacted him and asked to be informed of matters necessary for the welfare of the Church so that he could devote his efforts to arranging them (*ibid.*, §1), Augustine finally found a suitable opportunity through the agency of Bishop Severus (*ibid.*, §3).

He used as his courier a presbyter of Milevis who, driven by urgent necessity to travel to that region on behalf of the safety of one of his fellow citizens, was compelled to undertake the journey even in midwinter. Through him Augustine sent Olympius a second letter, explaining how necessary the protection was that Olympius himself had spontaneously offered to the African Church.

The confidence Augustine placed in Olympius is shown by his willingness to entrust him with a memorandum explaining what he thought should be done, so that Olympius might hand it to the bishops after they reached the court (*ibid.*, §4). Augustine thought that the presbyter, although he had set out before the bishops, would arrive ahead of them.

Nevertheless, he presents his suggestions in such a way as to leave it to the bishops themselves to explain by what means the Church could most effectively be assisted.

But he asks, entreats, and demands that Olympius immediately declare in official documents that the laws enacted against the Pagans and heretics had proceeded from the Emperor’s will and knowledge, and therefore could not have been repealed by Stilicho’s death. It was important that this be done without any delay, without even waiting for the bishops to arrive at court (*ibid.*, §3), because that storm was placing many weak believers in danger of salvation—people who, since their faith was not yet strong enough, could not rise above merely human considerations.

Augustine explains how he himself was disposed in these extremely difficult circumstances:

> “We certainly rejoice on account of the firm and steadfast faith of some—and they are not few—who have been converted to the Christian religion or to Catholic peace by the opportunity provided by these very laws. For their eternal salvation we are glad even to suffer danger in this temporal life. It is especially for this reason that we now endure more violent assaults of hostility from men who are excessively harsh and wicked” (*ibid.*, §4).

Although Augustine says that he wrote this letter in midwinter (*ibid.*, §2), some nevertheless believe that it was through the efforts made on its behalf—certainly with all possible diligence—that Olympius arranged for a law dated 24 November of that same year and addressed to Donatus, then acting as proconsul in Africa, to be enacted (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 44).

That law appears to have decreed that if anyone attempted anything against religion or profaned the sacraments—with the Donatists expressly named—the full force of the law should be brought against him.

On 14 November Honorius had already forbidden anyone not bound to him by the bond of faith and religion—that is, anyone belonging to the opponents of Catholic truth—from accepting any office at the imperial court (*ibid.*, law 42). Zosimus testifies that at that time Pagans were excluded from such honors (*Zosimus, History*, book 5).

In addition, on 27 November Honorius issued to Theodorus, prefect of the praetorium, an edict ordering that the defenders and all other magistrates prohibit from holding any assembly, whether in the cities or in the countryside, all those alien to communion with the Catholic bishops. They were to confiscate all places in which such unlawful gatherings had been held, and to proscribe and compel to go into exile those who taught a doctrine condemned by the teaching we have received from God (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 45).

On that same day, if we accept the date given by the Sirmondian Appendix (*Appendix to the Theodosian Code*, chapter 9)—or on 1 December, if we follow the edition of the Code (*Theodosian Code*, “On Bishops,” law 39)—Honorius entrusted another constitution to the same Theodorus. In it he established and confirmed ecclesiastical discipline, decreeing that those who had been deprived of the clerical order by bishops, or who had abandoned it voluntarily, should also lose its privileges and be burdened with public duties and obligations like laymen. Access to military offices, however, was to be entirely denied them.

Those who had broken faith with God could in no way prove themselves faithful to human beings.

### 6

These constitutions made it sufficiently clear that the court’s intentions and policies toward the Catholic Church had not changed in the least. It is therefore not unreasonable to believe that, upon first hearing of these laws, Augustine wrote to Donatus the letter in which he tried to persuade him to signify as soon as possible by an edict that the laws which the Donatists declared obsolete still retained their force (*Letter* 100.7).

He says nothing about the idolaters, since the laws enacted that year did not expressly prescribe measures concerning them to the same extent as the law promulgated immediately afterward.

He earnestly and vehemently begs Donatus not to condemn anyone to death for violence inflicted upon the Church (*ibid.*, §§1–2). This had not been necessary with respect to past crimes after the law of 15 January 409, since that law removed the death penalty for such offenses, while imposing it upon those who might attempt anything of the kind in the future.

Donatus had apparently only recently become proconsul when he received Augustine’s letter. The two men were connected by an old and distinctive relationship (*Letter* 112.1), so that even if Augustine lacked episcopal rank while Donatus held a position far higher than the proconsulate, Donatus nevertheless allowed Augustine great freedom in dealing with him (*Letter* 100.2).

Augustine calls him a most sincere son of the Catholic Church. He believed that, while Donatus wielded proconsular authority, God had given the African Church someone who could comfort it amid its greatest troubles and break the audacity of its enemies.

Augustine feared only one thing from Donatus’s zeal for justice: that he might punish crimes committed against the Church with the full severity they deserved—that is, with the ultimate penalty. To prevent this, Augustine solemnly appeals to him in the name of Jesus Christ. Otherwise, the clergy would no longer dare to bring such matters before him; when the others neglected this duty, those crimes would remain unpunished; and the Church’s enemies would gain new boldness to commit them.

> “We desire that they be corrected, not killed. We do not want discipline to be neglected in their case, nor do we want them to be subjected to punishments they deserve. Therefore restrain their sins in such a way that there remain people who regret having sinned” (*ibid.*, §1).

With no less earnestness he urges Donatus not to suppress the Donatists’ utterly vain and impious sect through imperial laws in such a way that they might appear, either to themselves or to their fellows, to be enduring any kind of hardship for the sake of truth or justice. If any of them were detained on Donatus’s orders, Donatus should allow the Catholics, whenever they requested it, to convict and instruct them before the official records by the clearest evidence of established facts.

> “Diligence is more burdensome than useful,” Augustine says, “when people are merely forced and not taught, even though the aim is to abandon a great evil and hold fast to a great good” (*ibid.*, §2).

Since Augustine had observed Donatus’s gifts and excellences and considered his heart a fitting vessel for Christ to pour himself into most abundantly, he was seized by the strongest possible desire to see him. Yet, while Donatus held office, he never found an opportunity to satisfy that desire, although Donatus had come to Tibilis, which, as we may reasonably suppose, was not far from Hippo Regius (*Letter* 112.1).

When Augustine later saw him released and free from earthly cares, he tried to establish some association with him by exchanging letters. In these letters he urges him toward the pursuit of virtue—not from a desire for human esteem or praise, but from love of virtue and justice themselves.

> “As you have begun,” he writes, “behold our Lord Jesus Christ with the most courageous vision of your heart. Rising above all empty arrogance, ascend toward him, who does not puff up those who turn to him with empty boasting, but establishes those who rely upon and ascend by the sure steps of faith in the everlasting summit of heavenly and angelic dignity” (*ibid.*, §3).

He congratulates Donatus on the father whom Donatus’s efforts had brought into the embrace of the Church. He also begs Donatus to visit him, so that they might work together with equal purpose for the salvation of certain people who cultivated Donatus’s estates in the territory of Siniti and Hippo. In the meantime, Augustine says, he would like Donatus to write to them and kindly and humanely encourage them to embrace communion with the Catholic Church.

It is not clear when Donatus left the proconsular office. It is certain, however, that this had occurred before 25 June 410, on which date we find a law addressed to Macrobius, proconsul of Africa (*Theodosian Code*, “On Indulgences,” law 6).

### 7

When Augustine sent Olympius his second letter (*Letter* 97), informing him that the delegates of the council would shortly arrive in Rome, he had not yet heard of that city’s siege, since he makes no mention of it. The event occurred not long afterward.

We read that African bishops were then present at Rome, when reports arrived that the city and its surrounding territory were being afflicted by the gravest calamities and losses (*Letter* 99.1). If we are to accept Zosimus’s testimony, that siege must be assigned to the end of 408 (*Zosimus, History*, book 5).

Rome was besieged and reduced to the utmost extremity of food supplies and money, while the plague also overtook the city. Augustine was informed of the miserable condition of Rome, as he indicates, by letters from fellow bishops (*Letter* 99.1). From these he learned matters that were grievous and harsh, though public rumor added still more bitter reports.

He subsequently received a letter from Italica, a noble Roman woman, which told him nothing at all about this matter. Augustine, whose charity would not allow him to remain unmoved by the sufferings of his fellow Christians, was astonished at this. He was no less surprised that the holy bishops—certainly the African bishops who were then in that region—had not written back through Italica’s household.

It is clear that communication with the city had not then been entirely cut off. From this one may infer that the letter was sent either before Alaric had closed the approaches to the Tiber—that is, at the beginning of the siege—or only after the siege had already ended.

Baronius thinks that the matter relates to the capture of Rome in 410. Yet the law against the heretics addressed to Heraclianus—which, not without reason, is thought to have been granted in response to the prayers of the delegates of the African Church—bears the date 25 August, precisely the period when Rome was captured (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 51).

How, then, are the delegates to be said to have been there when the city was captured? As for 409, the year in which Alaric likewise surrounded Rome with his forces, there was no African bishop in Italy, so far as we have learned from our reading.

We reasonably suppose that the Italica whom Augustine calls a most religious and deservedly praiseworthy servant of God (*Letter* 99) was the same woman whom Chrysostom, harassed by the wickedness of his enemies, encouraged by letter to lend her assistance in settling the divisions of the Eastern Church (*Chrysostom, Letter* 70). He expressly indicates that she was then at Rome, but adds nothing further.

She had children who were not yet grown, and Augustine greets them in the reply he now sends her, without mentioning her husband (*Letter* 99.3). From this it is clear that she had already lost her husband. She must also be the same woman whom Augustine comforts, in the opening of another letter to Italica, concerning her husband’s death (*Letter* 92.1), where he also orders that his greetings be conveyed to her children (*ibid.*, §6).

In this letter Augustine is almost entirely occupied with refuting those who claimed that God could be seen with the eyes of the body. He deliberately does not identify who they were, for one of them was an African bishop whose name he considered it necessary to spare (*Letter* 148.1, 4).

Some of them had previously said only that Christ had been granted the privilege of seeing the divine substance through bodily vision. They had finally gone so far as to assert that all the saints would see God in the same way after the resurrection, and even to grant the possibility of seeing God to the impious (*Letter* 92.4).

Augustine rebukes them in very harsh and severe terms, fearing that the result would eventually be belief in a corporeal God divisible through local spaces (*ibid.*, §3; *Letter* 148.1). He asks Italica, if they should happen to discuss their ravings with her, to read them this letter and write back to him what they had replied (*Letter* 92.6).

In another later letter to the same woman, he shows how deeply he is affected by Rome’s troubles (*Letter* 99.1). He also observes that Italica’s children, in view of what was happening, could already at so tender an age understand how dangerous and harmful love of this world is.

> “Would that, when great and harsh things are shaken, the small and pliable might be corrected” (*ibid.*, §3).

## CHAPTER VII

1. Honorius confirms the laws enacted against Pagans and heretics; Nectarius again asks Augustine on behalf of the people of Calama.  
2. Honorius grants freedom to heretics and Pagans.  
3. Augustine writes to the Donatists.  
4. He also writes to Festus.  
5. He earnestly urges Macrobius not to rebaptize Rusticianus, a subdeacon who had apostatized.  
6. He writes letters to various people on Faventius’s behalf.  
7. He strengthens Victorianus, whose spirit has been broken by the world’s intolerable calamities.

### 1

The Theodosian Code supplies us with a law issued by Honorius on 16 January 409 (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 46). We think that it was obtained through the prayers of the bishops who, by decree of the Council of Carthage on 13 October of the preceding year, had been sent as delegates to him to request protection and assistance against the Pagans and heretics who were claiming that, after Stilicho’s death, the laws enacted against them had ceased to be in force.

To prevent the Donatists or other heretics, Pagans, or Jews from flattering themselves that these laws had been repealed, the Emperor ordered all judges to observe them and to ensure their execution with the greatest possible diligence. Those who neglected to carry out his orders were threatened with monetary fines, loss of honors, confiscation of property, and exile.

Since this made it perfectly clear how well disposed the Emperor was toward the Church, the idolaters of Calama had good reason to fear that they would suffer the penalties deserved for their wicked attempts of the previous year.

For this reason Nectarius resolved once more to seek Augustine’s help and to reply to the letter he had received from him seven or eight months earlier (*Letter* 104.1). He tries to obtain pardon for everyone who had been in any way connected with that crime, taking advantage of the false opinion that all sins are equal (*Letter* 103.3).

Augustine received Nectarius’s letter on 27 March. In his reply he first asks him to inform him if, as rumor had prematurely reported, Possidius had obtained some edict harsher than justice permitted. Augustine wishes to know this so that he can determine either what should be done to prevent anything harsher from occurring or what answer should be given to those who had rashly believed the false report.

As for the monetary fines, the severity of whose consequences Nectarius had greatly exaggerated, Augustine demonstrates to him, even from the teachings of the philosophers, how needlessly he was troubling himself so much about them. In any case, it was not the Christian disposition to reduce the guilty to a condition in which they lacked the necessities of life. The Christians’ purpose was not to take revenge on their opponents but to provide for their salvation.

Augustine then refutes Nectarius’s claim concerning the equality of sins and earnestly urges him to embrace the Christian faith. Finally, referring to Nectarius’s son, whose name was Paradoxus, he skillfully demonstrates once again how dangerous was the Stoic doctrine about sins just mentioned (*Letter* 104).

### 2

In addition to these measures, on 26 June of this year, 409, Honorius decreed, for the sake of the Church, that judges should decide without delay matters relating to it; and that any edicts they might obtain from him contrary to the laws repeatedly enacted against heretics should be entirely deprived of force and authority and should in no way be put into execution (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 47).

Perhaps he foresaw that, in the Empire’s extreme weakness and amid his own severely troubled circumstances, there would be no shortage among his principal ministers of men whose wicked counsels might lead him to do something unworthy of himself and of his religion.

His fears were not mistaken. For from the Council held at Carthage on 14 June 410 it is clear that a law was then in force providing that no one should embrace the Christian religion except by free choice (*African Code of Canons*, canon 107).

This amounted to leaving everyone free to follow whatever religion he wished and, at the same time, annulling everything that had previously been enacted against heretics or Pagans.

In the edict issued on 25 August 410, Honorius acknowledges that the heretics had fraudulently extracted from him a rescript permitting them to hold their own assemblies (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 51). Likewise, in another edict issued on 14 October, the Emperor declares that if he had made any provision that the followers of Donatus considered favorable to their interests, he had done so only with the intention of gently moving their minds toward abandoning their superstitions and correcting their errors (*ibid.*, “On Religion,” under law 3).

Baronius holds that this law of liberty was enacted at the urging of Heraclianus, count of Africa, and Macrobius, who was serving there as proconsul in 410. Their aim, he thinks, was to prevent the Donatist faction and the Pagan sect from being alienated from Honorius by the excessive severity of the earlier laws and from being transferred to the side of Attalus.

Heraclianus, as Jerome portrays him (*Jerome, Letter* 8), had a character such that he could readily have offered such advice. Macrobius, however, if he was the same man whom some identify as the author of the *Saturnalia*, is found to have been openly devoted to the worship of idols.

Zosimus also seems to have had this same law in view when he stated that Honorius opened access to both civil and military offices to everyone, provided that each retained his own religion; and that for this reason the law enacted on 14 November 408 was repealed (*Zosimus, History*, book 5).

He says that this repeal was occasioned by a certain Generidus, a Pagan by religion. When the Emperor wished to place Generidus in command of the Dalmatian legions, the Emperor offered him an exemption from the law that excluded him from the office. Generidus refused the dignity unless the law were entirely repealed.

Zosimus says that this occurred shortly before Attalus was made Emperor by Alaric; it could therefore reasonably be assigned to the middle of 409.

It is generally thought that Honorius’s indulgence toward the heretics lasted through the final months of 409 and the first months of the following year, 410. At that time Olympius had fallen from the Emperor’s favor and, deprived of his position, had been compelled to withdraw to Dalmatia. For this reason he was no longer able to turn Honorius away from the wicked counsels being suggested to him (*ibid.*).

The Emperor nevertheless did not follow them for long. In the following year we shall see how, amid the most turbulent circumstances, he repealed the law that he had allowed himself to be forced into issuing by misguided counsels.

### 3

We believe that Augustine wrote at the beginning of this year the letter addressed generally to all the Donatists (*Letter* 105). It mentions the false indulgence, or repeal of the laws enacted against them, whose rumor they had spread during the previous year, 408. Augustine there undertakes to demonstrate to them, provided that they do not refuse to come to a conference with him, certain matters relating to the case of Caecilian, which had been the principal subject of the Conference of Carthage. He does not indicate that anything had yet been decided concerning that Conference.

At the end of the letter he gathers together many passages from Scripture demonstrating that the Catholic Church is spread among all nations. Yet he devotes most of the letter to defending the severity of Honorius’s laws against their accusations. From this one may understand that the letter was written before Honorius granted freedom to practice any religion, at the end of this year, 409.

The occasion for writing the letter was provided by certain presbyters of the Donatist party, who ordered Augustine to be given these very words:

> “Withdraw from our congregations, if you do not want us to kill you” (*ibid.*, §1).

4. Those insane threats of the Donatists that are mentioned at the beginning of the letter to Festus (Epistle 89, §1) are perhaps the very threats that we have just quoted from Augustine’s letter to the same men. The trials by which he says that those who had returned to the bosom of the Church were tested (ibid., §7) can equally well be referred to the events that, as we have said, followed either Stilicho’s death or Honorius’s orders against the Donatists from the year 405 onward. For at the time when this letter was delivered, imperial edicts were certainly being vigorously enforced against them (ibid., §§1, 2, 3, 6). There is no mention of the Conference in the letter itself.

Festus, moreover, was a layman who was involved in the administration of public offices. In the district of Hippo he had Donatists subject to him (ibid., §8), and he had urged them by letter to be reconciled with the Church. Yet something perhaps prevented this from succeeding as he wished. Augustine was concerned for their salvation, not only on their account but also on account of those who, after returning to the Catholic faith, suffered some harm from the proximity of the others. He therefore wrote to Festus, asking him to send some trustworthy person from among his household or friends who, without going there directly, would turn aside to Augustine without the knowledge of the others. After they had exchanged counsel, they could decide by what means in particular the men might be drawn back to the Church.

And lest anyone should dissuade Festus from the undertaking by which he had begun to labor for the recovery of his subjects to the faith, Augustine explains to him the cause of the schism and the manner in which the Church receives those who return to her. Possidius records Augustine’s admonition to Festus against the Donatists (*In the Index*, chap. 3).

5. Just as Augustine devoted all his mind and energy to uprooting the Donatist heresy completely from his diocese of Hippo, so the Donatists, for their part, strove with all their strength to establish it there and even to increase its influence. The vigilance and labor of that most watchful shepherd could not, in fact, prevent some man expelled from his flock, ruined by crime and poverty, from fleeing to their sheepfolds.

At this very time, a certain Rusticianus, a Catholic subdeacon of the diocese of Hippo, had been excommunicated by his presbyter because of his immoral conduct and had also become indebted to many people in that region. While seeking to provide himself with some means of support both against his creditors and against the discipline of the Church, he judged it best to approach Macrobius, the bishop of the schismatics at Hippo, and receive a second Baptism from him. In this way, he would presumably become dear to the Circumcellions as though he were perfectly pure, and would be defended by them (Epistle 108, §19).

As soon as Augustine learned of Rusticianus’s plan, he wrote to Macrobius. The letter was brief, but no less forceful: he adjured him, by the salvation of his soul, not to confer repeated Baptism on this subdeacon—or at least to answer the question concerning the Baptism that Felicianus had administered during the Maximianist schism. If Macrobius would do the latter, the holy Doctor declared himself ready to receive Baptism again. But if he doubted what Felicianus had done, Augustine accepted the challenge of proving it, on the condition that, if he failed, he would lose his episcopate (Epistle 106).

He entrusted this letter to Macrobius to Maximus and Theodore. At first Macrobius refused to admit them to an interview, lest they read Augustine’s letter to him; but at length, yielding to their persistence, he allowed it to be read. His answer was as follows:

> “I can do nothing except receive those who come to me and give them the faith they have requested. That is repeated Baptism.”

As for Primianus, by whom both Felicianus and those whom Felicianus had baptized had been received, Maximus and Theodore asked what answer he had to make to this. He replied:

> “Since I was only recently ordained, I cannot sit in judgment on my father; I must remain in what I received from my predecessors” (Epistle 107).

When they reported Macrobius’s answer to Augustine, he was moved at once by fear and grief and judged that he should write to Macrobius again at greater length. In this letter he continued to press him, arguing from Felicianus’s action itself and from the case of Primianus and Maximianus. He showed with still greater care that whatever Macrobius might bring forward or devise against the Church was wholly overturned by this single history. For that reason he calls it a mirror of correction placed before their eyes by divine mercy, so that every difficulty had been entirely removed.

He therefore urges Macrobius to examine the objection just mentioned and, if possible, to dispel it; but if he cannot do so, he must not prefer the cause of Donatus, which he had undertaken, to the fear of God and his own salvation. For this reason Augustine sets before him both the evils of schism and the blessings of unity (Epistle 108).

The style of the letter, everywhere tempered by great gentleness, fits well with the period of the freedom granted by Honorius. We do not know whether anything prevents referring to this period the words: “Before that law by which you rejoice that liberty has been restored to you.” Augustine no longer threatens Macrobius with the severity of the laws in order to deter him from repeating Baptism, as he had threatened Crispinus before the later laws were issued. Perhaps he conducted himself toward Macrobius in this way so as not to exasperate him, hoping that he could more easily overcome him by gentleness. Besides, Augustine regarded Macrobius as a young man of good character, and he also credits him with talent and eloquence.

When Augustine wrote to him, Macrobius had recently been ordained and had been solemnly escorted to Hippo, where he was to exercise the episcopal office (Carthaginian Conference 1, chapters 138, 201). In that city he had his own congregation (Epistle 108, §§17, 20). As he entered the city, the leaders of the Circumcellions escorted him, surrounded by their bands, shouting “Praise be to God!” amid songs (ibid., §14). With such cries, like the trumpet of their battles, they were accustomed to encourage one another to slaughter.

Macrobius, however, was more offended by their insolence than pleased by their attentions. On the following day, through an interpreter of the Punic language, he addressed harsh words to them, expressing his indignation with the freedom befitting an upright and honorable man. They bore this so impatiently that, before the assembly had been dismissed, they withdrew, displaying unmistakable signs of indignation and fury.

Some Catholics witnessed the event. After these Catholics had likewise departed, Macrobius’s clerics washed with salt water the pavement where they had stood. Optatus testifies that this was a practice familiar to them (Optatus, book 6). The place occupied by the Circumcellions, however, was not purified in the same manner.

6. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of February in the present year, Honorius issued a law which, among other provisions, ordered that those who were being detained, and who were afterward to be transferred elsewhere for presentation at trial, should first be asked before the magistrates whether they wished to remain for thirty days under moderate guard in the city where they had been arrested. This was so that they might attend to their household affairs and provide themselves with the expenses they required. If they indicated that they wished to use this period, the law promulgated by Theodosius on the third day before the Kalends of January in the year 380 provided that it should not be denied them (*Theodosian Code*, “On Persons to Be Presented or Transferred for Trial,” law 6). Otherwise, they were to be taken immediately, together with their accusers, to the place appointed for the trial (ibid., law 3).

Augustine mentions this law in several letters written for one and the same reason (Epistles 113–115). A certain Faventius, therefore, who had leased an estate and feared something from its owner, fled to the church at Hippo and remained there for a time while the holy Bishop settled the matter. As the affair dragged on, he gradually became somewhat more confident and had almost abandoned concern for preserving himself and remaining within the boundaries of the church.

Thus it happened that, while returning from a meal with a friend, he was intercepted by a certain Florentinus, an apparitor of the Count of Africa, with a military force, and dragged away to an unknown destination. Augustine asserts that the laws were not observed in this matter (Epistle 115).

As soon as he learned of the abduction, Augustine immediately informed Cresconius by a written note. Cresconius was the tribune entrusted with the defense of the maritime coast (Epistle 113). Cresconius sent several of his men, but they found nothing (Epistle 115).

When daylight came on the following day, Augustine learned that Faventius had spent the night in a certain house and had been transferred at first light by Florentinus to a designated place. He immediately sent one of his presbyters, named Caelestinus, furnished with the Emperor’s law, to compel Florentinus to observe it. Caelestinus read the law to him, but could not even obtain permission to see the prisoner (Epistle 114).

On the following day Augustine sent Florentinus another letter, together with the very law itself. He begged him, both out of concern for his own reputation and out of the obedience owed to the Emperor, whose servant he was, not to deny the prisoner what the law granted him, especially in view of the intervention of a bishop who was making a kind and earnest request.

At the same time, unless he had already done so the previous day, Augustine sent another letter to be delivered to Cresconius, the tribune to whom the custody of the coast had been entrusted; Augustine had already written to him earlier about the same matter. He explains that, since Faventius had fled to the protection of his Church, it was not permissible for him to abandon him or fail to defend him to the best of his ability, lest he incur guilt before God—and even before the very man by whom Faventius was being harassed. For Augustine could reasonably imagine that he too would have been abandoned by the Church if he had happened to flee to it in a similar situation.

He therefore asks Cresconius to join him in requesting Florentinus, the apparitor, not to prevent the prisoner from using the benefit of the law. Augustine hoped that the matter could be settled amicably within the thirty-day period (Epistle 113).

All his diligence, however, was fruitless. For, taking no account of the law, Florentinus transferred Faventius to a more distant place, where, as was believed, he was to be brought before the tribunal of consular Numidia. The judge was named Generosus, and he was reputed to be a man of the highest fairness and integrity. But since Faventius was dealing with an exceedingly wealthy man, the holy Bishop feared that Faventius might suffer something contrary to justice and equity at the hands of Generosus’s officers.

He therefore wrote to Generosus about the matter (Epistle 116), but did not explain what the affair was. Instead, he asked him not to refuse to be informed of the whole case by Fortunatus, bishop of Cirta, from whose hands Generosus would receive the letter and to whom Augustine had sent another letter to be read to him (Epistle 115). The letter addressed to Fortunatus sets out the entire sequence of events and indicates Augustine’s desire that the judge grant Faventius some delay and extension, since he had been carried away in violation of the laws and deprived of the benefit of postponement.

7. In this year the Empire of the West was everywhere afflicted by many great calamities. Alaric, to whom Rome had surrendered her wealth in the preceding year in order to ransom herself from plunder, continued to hold the very heart of Italy with his forces. Since he found no proposed arrangement with Honorius acceptable, he came once more to besiege the City and compelled it to accept Attalus as emperor.

The new Caesar sent certain forces to seize Africa; but they perished through the strategy and prudence of the Count Heraclianus. By placing garrisons in all the province’s harbors, Heraclianus soon reduced Rome to the extremity of famine and freed Honorius from the necessity of laying aside the insignia of his rank and fleeing to the East.

For more than two years Gaul had been exposed to the incursions of countless barbarians, and it was also burning in the flames of the civil war that Constantine had stirred up there. In Spain, at the end of September or somewhat later, the barbarians found the passes of the Pyrenees undefended and poured through them with such force that afterward the Romans were never able to expel them. It is scarcely possible to describe the disasters that those provinces suffered at their hands.

Africa, too, was not untouched in those mournful times. There can be no doubt that Victorianus, a presbyter, wrote to Augustine about some calamity of this kind, and that Augustine replied to him shortly afterward. Certainly the district of Hippo, which the barbarians had spared, was savagely tormented by the fury of the Donatists and Circumcellions, lest it should be treated more gently than the other regions. We have already spoken of this above.

At this very time, when the first reports were arriving of the barbarians’ descent upon Spain—perhaps toward the end of October—forty-eight people in one place were compelled by those heretics to receive Baptism again. The holy Bishop learned of that most grievous event on the day before he replied to the presbyter Victorianus concerning the barbarian devastation. Victorianus had reported that certain servants of God—that is, monks—had been slaughtered, while sacred virgins had been led into captivity and exposed to the lust of men stripped of every religious scruple and sense of shame.

Victorianus asked Augustine to give him a somewhat fuller reply on this matter, especially because the Pagans were seizing upon it as an opportunity to attack God with blasphemous words and to attribute those evils to the Christian religion. The holy man gave him, considering his other occupations, a substantial answer sufficient for the matter.

In it he demonstrates that nothing more suitable or advantageous can be offered either to Pagans or to Christians than the assertion that those who despise the will of the Lord—which they cannot be unaware of—deserve heavier punishments than those who have never had the opportunity to hear anything about it. The pious, however, no matter how brightly they shine in holiness of life, cannot claim precedence in integrity and innocence of conduct over Daniel and his companions, those most holy young men, or even over the Maccabees. Yet all of them, though afflicted by terrible sufferings, declared that they were being punished deservedly and justly for their own sins.

Augustine therefore urges Victorianus to use every effort to prevent God from being provoked by unworthy complaints over these disasters and losses. He also urges him not to cease groaning before God on behalf of the captive virgins, but to investigate with the greatest diligence what had become of them and in what way they might be helped. Finally, he tells him to hope that God will bring them assistance, either by preventing dishonor from being inflicted upon their bodies or by strengthening their minds through grace so that they may preserve the virginity that they had vowed to God.

He adds that perhaps God will turn the captivity of these maidservants both to his own glory and to their benefit, yielding a rich return. As evidence of this he relates an event that had occurred a few years earlier in the case of a consecrated virgin from the region of Sitifis, the niece of Bishop Severus.

“For the household of the barbarians,” he says, “where she had entered as a captive, suddenly began to be afflicted by the illness of its masters, so that all those barbarians—three brothers, if I am not mistaken, or more—were suffering from a most dangerous disease. Their mother noticed that the girl was devoted to God and believed that her sons could be delivered from the danger of death, which was already threatening them, through her prayers. She asked her to pray for them, promising that, if they recovered, they would return her to her parents.

“She fasted and prayed, and her prayer was immediately heard. For this, as the outcome showed, was the purpose of the event. Thus, having received health through so sudden a benefit from God, they marveled at and honored her, and fulfilled what their mother had promised. By the wonderful mercy of God, she was therefore restored to her parents with great honor.”

Finally, Augustine adds that purity of chastity has such power in the mind that, if it remains inviolate, modesty cannot be violated even in the body (Epistle 111).

# CHAPTER VIII

In the year 410, after the conquest of the City, he delivers various discourses on that subject to the people. 2. He excuses his absence to the people of Hippo and urges them to consider clothing the poor according to their customary practice. 3. Recovering from illness in the countryside, he replies to Dioscorus concerning the questions sent by him. 4. He instructs Consentius, who was in error through simplicity of mind and without arrogance, and imbues him with sounder doctrine. 5. Honorius abolishes the freedom that had been granted to each person to practice his own religion. 6. He also orders the Catholics to enter into conference with the Donatists. 7. Marcellinus is appointed to arrange the procedure and order of the forthcoming Conference.

1. In the preceding year Augustine had tried to strengthen Victorianus, whose spirit had been broken by the intolerable evils that the barbarian invasions had inflicted upon the Empire. But the holy Bishop needed remedies of that kind—which his compassion for all supplied so readily—even more amid the hardships brought by the year 410. In that year Alaric, king of the Goths, surrounded the City with a siege and finally captured it on the ninth day before the Kalends of September.

He permitted his barbarian soldiers to plunder it, but imposed this condition: they were to spare Christian blood and dare not touch anything that had been taken into the basilicas, especially those of the Apostles Peter and Paul.

The sad reports of the disasters that had ravaged that most illustrious city drew frequent groans from the heart and a great stream of tears from the eyes of the pious Bishop. He admits that he could scarcely find consolation in them (*On the Destruction of the City*, §3).

What especially troubled him was that the Pagans—including even those whose safety would certainly not have been secured had they not pretended to be Christians or taken refuge in Christian churches—nevertheless showed themselves so blind and forgetful of the benefit they had received that they blamed the losses of the Empire on the Christian religion. They declared that the City had been conquered for no other reason than that its idols had been overthrown.

He frequently refuted these blasphemies in his sermons to the people. A number of those sermons still survive, especially one in which he says that the Gentiles reproached him for mentioning the Roman disaster too often, as though he intended to mock and insult the misfortunes of others—something utterly contrary to his character (Sermon 105, §§12, 13).

And indeed, in that sermon, where he teaches the faithful how they should receive hardships and adversity and what they should answer, in hope, to the Pagan insulters and blasphemers of the Christian name, he also deeply laments the Pagans’ condition and prays that, once converted to the faith, they may attain eternal salvation.

On another occasion, when he was treating in a speech the devastation of Rome, which was already imminent—or rather had recently occurred—he appealed to his hearers at the end of the sermon: the more they saw the number of foreigners, poor people, and afflicted persons increasing on that occasion, the more they should intensify their own charity and mercy. For in this way, when Christians fulfilled Christ’s commandment, the Pagans’ impious words against God would turn only to their own destruction.

> “Let Christians do what Christ commands,” he says, “and the Pagans blaspheme only to their own harm” (Sermon 81, §9).

Another sermon also survives, delivered on the recent sack of that same city, whose title is itself: *On the Destruction of the City*. In it the holy man demonstrates that such disasters must be attributed to our sins. By many arguments and examples he shows that no one among mortals is entirely just and free from the contagion of sin. He seems to have done this in order to counter the emerging doctrines of the Pelagians.

There too he mentions that fiery cloud which appeared hanging over Constantinople in the year 396. We shall say no more here. The proper place will be given below to explaining how, stirred by the impious complaints of the Gentiles over the conquest of the City, he turned his mind to undertaking the great work *On the City of God*.

2. During those most mournful times the holy Bishop happened to be absent from Hippo for some while; he did not return until winter had begun. We do not know why he had then left his Church, at a time when, amid the Empire’s troubles, it needed his presence more than ever. Certainly he was never absent from his diocese through any freer exercise of personal choice, but only because necessity compelled him to help others (Epistle 122, §1). There is no doubt that some unusually urgent reason drove him to undertake the journey at this particular time.

“For the people of Hippo,” he says, “to whom the Lord has made me a servant, are weak to a great degree and in almost every respect, so that even the pressure of a lighter tribulation could make them seriously ill. Now they are being struck by so great a tribulation that, even if they were not so weak, they would scarcely endure it with any spiritual well-being.

“When I returned,” the same holy man continues, “I found them dangerously scandalized by my absence, especially since there are many here who, by speaking against us, are trying to disturb against us the minds of the others, by whom we seem to be loved, so that they may make room for the devil in them. When they are angry with us, though we are concerned for their salvation, their great plan of revenge is the desire to die—not in the body, but in the heart” (Epistle 124, §2).

By these words he seems quietly to indicate that they wished to pass over to the Donatist side. This was the reason why, throughout the entire winter, he did not set foot outside Hippo.

During this same period of absence he appears to have written a letter to the clergy and people of Hippo (Epistle 122). In it he mentions the calamities raging through nearly the entire world, by which the people of Hippo needed to be stirred to take precautions lest they likewise be overwhelmed.

For after Alaric had plundered Rome and devastated Italy, he intended to cross into Sicily (Orosius, *History*, book 7, chap. 43), and, if we believe Jordanes, from there to invade Africa (Jordanes, *On the Affairs of the Goths*).

Fear of these disasters cooled the piety of the citizens of Hippo to some degree. For many years they had been accustomed to clothe the poor, and they had not failed to perform this duty even when Augustine was occasionally absent. Before setting out, the holy Bishop had carefully urged them to continue that pious work according to their custom. Nevertheless, he learned that they had neglected it.

He therefore tried with great affection to persuade them by letter that, as each person had the means, none should refuse to perform the same duty of Christian charity that he had formerly been accustomed to perform, now that the ruin and collapse of the world were already impending.

Rather, let them imitate those who, when their houses threaten to collapse, transfer their possessions to a safer place, remembering the apostolic declaration: “The Lord is near; do not be anxious about anything” (Philippians 4:5–6).

At the beginning of the letter he justifies his absence, asserting that he had been compelled to it by the necessity of coming to the aid of other members of Christ. Had illness not prevented him, this same necessity would have induced him to cross the sea, as some of his fellow bishops had often done.

Nor does he conceal that the people of Hippo had taken his absence very badly. This too fits well with the year 410, as we said above. We may also add that clothing had to be distributed to the poor at the beginning of winter.

3. Perhaps in this same year of Christ 410 Augustine undertook to satisfy the questions of Dioscorus. For he says that he was already advanced in years and white-haired, something that could apply to a man fifty-six years old (Epistle 118, §9). On this occasion, when speaking of the heretics who were causing disturbances in Africa at that time and of opinions that it was worthwhile to know, he names the Donatists, Maximianists, and Manichaeans (ibid., §12). He makes no mention of the Pelagians or of the other enemies of Christ’s grace, against whom a council had to be convened in the following year.

Dioscorus was a young man from Greece. After acquiring the first rudiments of the Greek language, he had come to Rome and then to Carthage, where he was living at the time, to be educated in Latin literature (ibid., §§9, 10). He preferred Christian teaching to all other doctrines and professed that it alone could offer hope of eternal life (ibid., §11).

As he was preparing to revisit his family and set out again for Greece (ibid., §§1, 2), he sent a certain Cerdon to Augustine, laden with extremely difficult questions—questions concerning Cicero’s dialogues, so that he might understand the various opinions of the philosophers, and also concerning Cicero’s *Orator* and his books *On the Orator* (Epistle 117).

Augustine found it astonishing that, when he was almost overwhelmed by so many cares, questions so difficult should be put to him—questions so far removed from the studies and occupations of a bishop, and concerning subjects that either age had erased from his memory or investigation into more useful knowledge had itself obscured. He would therefore have had to recall them from books that he could not even have found at Hippo.

Since all the questions concerned the gratification of intellectual curiosity, they were utterly contrary to the bishop’s duties. One of the bishop’s chief responsibilities, after all, is to restrain those who indulge curiosity excessively.

In his letter Dioscorus called God himself as witness that he had been compelled by absolute necessity to question Augustine about these matters. The holy man therefore read with the greatest attention what followed that appeal, in order to discover what this supposedly urgent necessity was.

He easily discovered that it was nothing other than the young man’s fear that, if he returned to his homeland and happened not to be able to answer these questions, he would be regarded as slow-witted and foolish.

“Here,” Augustine says, “I was inflamed to write back to you; for through this sickness of your spirit you pierced my heart and burst into my concerns, so that I could not conceal how greatly God was helping me to heal you—not by thinking about disentangling and explaining your questions, but by breaking your happiness free from its dependence on and instability before the tongues of men, tearing it away from so unhappy a tether, and fastening it to a seat altogether unshaken and firm” (Epistle 118, §3).

He therefore demonstrates that Dioscorus’s desire was mere vanity, to which bishops could in no way accommodate themselves. It would also be useless, since at that time no one could be found who would devote his labor to investigating and examining the opinions of philosophers of that sort from ancient times, whose names themselves had for the most part been buried in oblivion.

If a Christian ought to concern himself with such matters at all, he might gain some reputation and distinction by reading the Greek philosophers who were still famous. But as for Cicero’s books, which were then treated with considerable neglect among the Latins, Dioscorus could be certain that no one would be found in Greece to mention them.

“For you will hear crows more readily in Africa,” the holy man says, “than in those regions you will hear a word of this kind” (ibid., §9).

He therefore tries to persuade Dioscorus to devote himself to some more necessary branch of knowledge, for example, the study of heresies—especially those that at that time were troubling the East, toward which Dioscorus intended to travel.

But Augustine repeatedly urges him to apply himself to piety, and above all to humility, a virtue strongly opposed by the study of that vain philosophy. Nevertheless, he explains certain philosophical opinions to him and, as it were, in passing untangles some of his questions. What he says about the Platonists is especially worthy of attention.

He also adds several brief observations concerning the other philosophical problems that he had not addressed in his reply. He wrote these on the same sheets on which Dioscorus had sent his questions.

As for the matters relating to rhetoric, had Augustine undertaken to explain them, he would have seemed to himself to be wasting time on mere trifles and absurdities. He tells Dioscorus that he was unable to do more; indeed, he would not have done even what he did if illness, after abating somewhat, had not compelled him to leave Hippo in order to restore his health.

He asks Dioscorus to inform him how he had received the letter. When the messenger delivered Dioscorus’s letter to Augustine, Augustine was still confined by poor health. Later, even in the place where he was staying in the countryside for the sake of purer air, he was afflicted by a recurrence of fever for several days.

### 4

It may also be conjectured that the letter written to Consentius in the countryside, where the holy Man had been compelled to withdraw for a time (Letter 119, no. 1), was composed while he was still preparing his books *On the Trinity* (Letter 120, no. 13), and that it was sent when he had leisure for restoring his health. Whatever the precise date, we find that the reason for writing it was as follows.

That Consentius was living with many others on certain islands—where it is indeed probable that he led a solitary life—is clear from Letter 119, no. 6. He had resolved to publish books in which he represented God as resembling an immense light, though nevertheless corporeal. Using this fiction as his starting point, he attempted, according to his capacity, to explain both the mystery of the three Persons in God and that of the Incarnation (ibid., no. 3).

Yet since, beneath his simplicity, there was so much integrity and humility that he deserved admission to the knowledge of truth, he sent his books to Augustine. In the letter that served as a preface, he declared that he intended to establish his wavering faith by Augustine’s judgment, and that he had sent the books not merely to be read, but to be subjected to the judgment of so great a Doctor and corrected (Letter 120, no. 1).

Whether the holy Man later saw him in person or addressed him only by letter is not known, although the former possibility is more probable. In either case, however, Augustine clearly and openly declared to him that his understanding was falling into the blindness of idolatry (Letter 119, no. 6), and that God must not be conceived in the mind as resembling a body, but rather in the manner of justice and piety, neither of which has a corporeal image (ibid., no. 5).

Since he also perceived that Consentius possessed not only no ordinary virtue but also an intellect by no means contemptible, and that he was capable of expressing in writing even those things which he had correctly conceived, Augustine resolved to take particular care of him. Accordingly, he lovingly invited him more than once to come to him, so that he might read in more accurate copies certain passages from his shorter works which Augustine judged would be more useful to him. Consentius had complained that he had fallen in with extremely corrupt copies. Whenever he found anything somewhat obscure, he would hear Augustine’s explanation of it from his own lips; thus, instructed by oral teaching as far as divine goodness allowed, he might himself correct his own errors in his books.

Augustine even ordered him, until he had leisure to come to Hippo, to place marks before those passages which he understood less well, so that later, when present together, he might bring them before Augustine. The benefit he offered Consentius was certainly not to be considered ordinary. For however great the advantage derived from Augustine’s writings, those who heard him addressing the people or speaking in familiar conversation perceived it much more vividly (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 31).

Consentius undoubtedly valued the favor shown him as highly as was proper. Yet he desired to be taught by Augustine both orally and in writing, because many of those who lived with him on the islands were held by the same error (Letter 119, no. 6). He was not satisfied merely to be brought back into the way by the holy Man’s admonitions; he wished that those who needed the same assistance should not be deprived of it. He desired that Augustine should also become the Augustine of his brothers, whose authority they would obey, whose teaching they would follow, and whose supreme intellect they would submit to.

The familiar discussion which the holy Bishop, in his fatherly kindness, offered him would have better safeguarded his modesty than a public refutation. But since Consentius sought with the greatest ardor the benefit of his soul, not the applause of the world, he thought that nothing bitter could be present in a remedy which would be useful to him and which would bring heavenly life and solid, genuine praise both to himself and to others. He did not think that people would be so unjust in their judgment as to condemn him for having been in error for a while rather than commend him for having emerged from it into the light of truth.

He opened his mind to Bishop Alypius, whom we may reasonably believe had then returned from his journey to Mauritania, and asked him to obtain this favor for him from Augustine (ibid., no. 1). He later came in search of Augustine, but could not enjoy even the sight of him, much less his conversation. For the holy Bishop, compelled by some necessity, had withdrawn to the countryside, where he happened to be obliged to remain for some time.

Therefore, impatient of a longer delay, Consentius asked him by letter not to disdain correcting his opinions and books in writing. He added these words:

> Why then, O man, summit of this doctrine which is in Christ, do you hesitate openly to rebuke and henceforth correct your son, when the anchor of your judgment, unless it presses its bite more deeply, cannot establish us with greater certainty? (ibid., no. 6)

The remaining portions of this letter likewise reveal Consentius’s humility and repeatedly declare, in magnificent and distinguished language, the place he assigned to Augustine’s authority and intellect. He frankly confessed that he had not yet grasped in thought how justice is substantial and living, and therefore had hitherto been unable to conceive God—that is, a living nature—as resembling justice.

For this reason he especially entreated Augustine to hold out a torch before him for understanding both the unity of God and the distinction of the Persons (Letter 120, no. 2). He had already determined in his mind that the divine mysteries must be known by the light of faith, not of reason.

The holy Doctor satisfied his wishes by writing him a fairly long letter. Aided by reading it and by further instruction requested elsewhere, Consentius would more easily correct his own work (ibid., no. 20). At the outset Augustine showed that Consentius was wrong to assure himself in his own mind that he could understand the divine mysteries. Faith itself, he explained, rests upon reason, and reason is useful for grasping the secrets of religion to the extent that each person’s intelligence permits, provided that we use it prudently and never abandon the foundation of faith.

For this reason he advised him to ask God, with fervent prayers grounded in faith, for the ability to understand rightly:

> Pray strongly and faithfully that the Lord may grant you illumination, so that the things externally supplied through the diligence of a teacher or instructor may be fruitful (Letter 120, no. 14).

And, in order to provide Consentius with assistance on his own part, Augustine explained to him what must be held with unshaken faith concerning the Trinity, and at the same time in what manner God may be conceived in the mind. He again urged him to come to him and spend several days with him, asking about each matter that troubled him. He even humanely reproached him for not having done so earlier:

> You would rightly feel ashamed and be reluctant to do it if you had tried even once and had found me difficult to approach (ibid., no. 1).

From these words one may recognize the holy Man’s humanity and affability.

He also promised that he would arrange for Consentius to read everything he had already written, or was still writing, on the Trinity and on seeing God, although he had not yet been able to reach the end of the work because of the breadth and difficulty of the subject (ibid., no. 13). It is perfectly clear that by this he meant no other books than those *On the Trinity*.

### 5

We have already seen that Honorius, led by the evil counsels of certain men, in effect annulled all the holy and salutary laws which he had previously enacted against pagans and heretics, by granting everyone freedom to choose his religion.

While this license among religions continued, the African bishops assembled at Carthage on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July in the year 410, in the basilica of the Second Region. From the acts of this council we find only that a delegation was entrusted by the council to the Emperor, consisting of the bishops Florentius, Possidius, Praesidius, and Benenatus (*African Code of Canons*, canon 107).

The purpose of this delegation may be inferred from a constitution of Honorius addressed to Count Heraclianus of Africa and issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. By it, the permission granted to heretics to perform their own religious rites was completely and plainly revoked; the penalty of proscription, or even death, was established; and they were forbidden to hold any public assembly (*Theodosian Code*, *On Heretics*, law 51). This law is reasonably attributed to the efforts and diligence of the legates of this council.

The same law is praised in the mandate written to Marcellinus concerning the organization of the conference, issued on the day before the Ides of October of that year. In this mandate Honorius expressly ordered that whatever he himself or earlier emperors had decreed for the sake of the Catholic religion should be observed with the greatest exactness (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, ch. 4).

Accordingly, in his edict issued at the beginning of March in the year 411, Marcellinus states that certain men had been appointed throughout each province to pursue or summon the followers of Donatus (ibid., ch. 5).

### 6

The bishop-legates who had obtained the revocation of the liberty granted to the heterodox also had instructions to secure another matter of no small importance. There is no reason to doubt that the mandate for holding the conference at Carthage, issued by Honorius on the day before the Ides of October, was owed to their petitions (ibid., ch. 4).

We have already seen with what zeal the Catholic bishops urged the Donatists to meet with them for a conference in the years 403 and 404; with what arrogance the Donatists refused; and yet how, only in the year 406, they were brought to the point of pretending that they wished and desired it. The Catholics judged that they ought to take advantage of this apparently favorable disposition on the part of their opponents (*Carthaginian Conference* 3, ch. 110; *Brief Account of the Conference* 3, no. 4).

They saw that many of the common people belonging to the Donatist sect, and almost all of them, were accustomed to say:

> Oh, if only they would meet in one place! Oh, if only they would confer at last, and truth would appear while they disputed!

(*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 58).
