Moreover, Augustine says:

> Their fury had occupied all Africa, and they would not allow the truth to be preached by Catholics against their error. By violent assaults, brigandage, blockades of roads, plunder, fires, and killings, they laid waste many things and terrified everyone. With such men, before bishops whom we did not share as colleagues, we could accomplish nothing; and what our forefathers had done with them nearly a hundred years earlier was no longer retained in the memory of the peoples. This necessity therefore compelled us, at least by means of the official acts completed in our Conference, to crush their shamelessness and restrain their audacity.

(*Against Julian*, book 3, no. 5).

These were chiefly the reasons that induced the African bishops to seek this conference, not because they thought that such a remedy was always expedient against heretics (*Unfinished Work*, book 1, ch. 10).

Augustine was both the originator and the consummator of this arduous undertaking, whose completion was of the greatest importance to the Church, although the other bishops also gave their consent and supported his efforts by their own diligence (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 13).

Legates were therefore sent to the Emperor to ask that he order the bishops of both parties to assemble at Carthage, where a number of men selected from each side would dispute (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, ch. 4), so that truth might appear once falsehood had been plainly exposed (ibid. 3, ch. 110).

The legates produced before Honorius the document in which the Donatists themselves had requested a conference in the year 406 (*Brief Account of the Conference* 3, no. 4).

The dreadful confusion of the Empire did not prevent Honorius from readily and generously consenting to the assembly they had requested. In this matter he proved by a most striking argument that his assertion was not empty: namely, that the welfare and honor of the Catholic Church were either his sole concern or at least his first concern; that he sought nothing, in peace or in war, except that God should reign in his dominions; and that he was grieved to see the province of Africa, which had assisted him in his undertakings—especially against Attalus—torn apart by the division of the Donatists (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, ch. 4).

Honorius showed an even readier willingness to authorize the conference because both parties had requested it (ibid., ch. 5). His rescript still survives. In it, after again abolishing the freedom he had granted to the heretics, he permits the conference requested by the Catholics (ibid., ch. 4).

He appointed it for the fourth month after the promulgation of the edict. If the Donatists refused to assemble by that time, he ordered that they be summoned a second and a third time, thereby extending the matter for another two months. If even then they failed to appear at the appointed time, he finally ordered all the peoples to be bound to obey the Catholic bishops, with all the churches restored to their authority (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, ch. 30).

This document was issued at Ravenna on the day before the Ides of October, although the year is not stated. It was undoubtedly the year 410, since the Conference was held in 411. Add to this the fact that part of the same rescript was inserted into the Theodosian Code and dated to the consulship of Varro, which fell in the year 410, although the day there is given not as the day before the Ides but as the fourth day before the Ides of the same month (*Theodosian Code*, *On Religion*, law 3).

### 7

The imperial order concerning the holding of the conference was sent to all the judges of the African provinces (*Carthaginian Conference* 3, ch. 140). It was also addressed to Flavius Marcellinus, with instructions that he preside over the tribunal (ibid. 1, ch. 4).

Marcellinus is everywhere called a tribune and notary. This rank differed little from the office which we call the king’s secretary. He belonged to the Catholic communion (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 2). Orosius describes him as a man of outstanding prudence and industry, and exceptionally eager for every good pursuit (Orosius, *History* 7, ch. 42).

His first two qualities shone forth remarkably at the Conference, where he displayed outstanding examples not only of fairness and moderation but also of judgment and wisdom. Augustine testifies to his intense devotion to sacred Scripture (Letter 190, no. 20). In due course below we shall relate his unimpeachable character and his noble death.

In his rescript Honorius ordered Marcellinus to inform him by letter of any magistrates who showed themselves negligent in providing the assistance necessary for the assembly, so that they might be punished, and to report at the earliest opportunity the sentence he had pronounced in the matter (*Carthaginian Conference* 1, ch. 4).

The proconsul and the vicar of Africa were also ordered to place at his disposal all the officials whom he needed for carrying out the task entrusted to him.

Thus Marcellinus came from the imperial court to Africa on account of the Conference (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 13). Augustine states that he had been sent for the benefit of the Church and that ecclesiastical matters had been especially entrusted to him, so that he could judge the undertakings and schemes of the heretics, investigate them under the severity of the laws, and, when circumstances required, punish them even with the ultimate penalty (Letter 133, nos. 1–3).

The Catholics received great joy when they were first informed of the reconciliation which the Emperor intended to bring about through the benefit of the conference. The Donatists, however, could not restrain themselves from displaying the resentment and grief they felt over the matter (Sermon 357, no. 3).

## CHAPTER IX

1. Pinianus and Melania, together with her mother Albina, arrive at Tagaste.  
2. Augustine is unable to visit them there.  
3. Pinianus comes to Hippo.  
4. The people of Hippo demand him as a presbyter.  
5. Pinianus suppresses the ensuing tumult by promising under oath that he will remain at Hippo.  
6. Albina and Alypius complain about what happened to them or to Pinianus.  
7. Augustine clears himself before them.  
8. The people of Hippo undoubtedly later granted Pinianus permission to depart wherever he wished.  
9. Augustine urges Armentarius and Paulina to despise the world and to fulfill their vow of continence.

### 1

What results were produced, during the course of this year 411, by the zeal and care of the Emperor Honorius or of the tribune Marcellinus in advancing the Conference so long desired by the Catholics will be explained in what follows. We must now disclose what happened at the beginning of that same year.

Not long before the capture of Rome, the elder Melania had led away her household from the city: namely, her daughter-in-law Albina, her granddaughter the younger Melania, and Pinianus, the husband of this younger Melania. All of them, illustrious among the Romans by birth and wealth, abandoned equally the pleasures of that most noble city and their dwelling there, and migrated with no other purpose than to devote themselves and their possessions to Christ and to live a truly monastic life (Letter 126, no. 11).

When Alaric captured Rome not long afterward and burned the city of Rhegium, Pinianus was still staying in Sicily with his companions (Valois, on Eusebius, p. 129; Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, p. 25). The *Life of the Younger Melania* relates that she crossed from Sicily first to Carthage and from there to Tagaste, where she spent the winter with Pinianus and Albina (Letter 124, no. 1) (Surius, December 31 or January 2).

The people of Tagaste were greatly favored by divine providence in possessing such illustrious guests, who could offer them consolation during those bitter times. They had already heard what the splendor of their birth and the grace of Christ had bestowed upon them, and, moved by charity, they had believed what they heard. But to those who did not possess the same charity, the story could scarcely be told without seeming to surpass all credibility.

Alypius, the bishop of Tagaste, was skilled in speech and by the power of a certain holy eloquence implanted in human hearts the love of salvation. He received the greater share of this joy and, together with his guests, devoted himself to meditation on the divine word (Surius, December 31 or January 2).

The guests, on the other hand, as we read in the *Life of Melania*, enriched his church with various ornaments, decorated with gold and many kinds of gems, and with substantial estates. They also built two monasteries at Tagaste: one for men, in which eighty monks lived, and another for women, in which one hundred and thirty virgins lived, assigning sufficient revenues for their support.

Augustine likewise left it on record that they had bestowed various kinds of gifts upon the church of Tagaste, and that, for this reason, the people displayed unusual joy—yet joy wholly free from the taint of private desire (Letter 126, no. 7). For the entire benefit of such generosity returned not to private citizens but to ecclesiastics, monks, nuns, and the poor (Letter 125, no. 2).

### 2

The only reason those most illustrious lights of the Christian religion had undertaken so long a journey to Tagaste was that they might enjoy Augustine’s presence and conversation (Letter 124, no. 1).

Yet although the holy Man was exceptionally devoted to honoring his friends and would gladly have crossed the seas to visit them, he was not at liberty to travel even to Tagaste, both to greet them and to congratulate his fellow citizens on the happiness that had befallen them.

The severe and dreadful winter seemed to oppose the journey, since his health was such that his constitution could not endure the cold. Nevertheless, this circumstance did not deter him from setting out for Tagaste. But when he learned that, as the year 410 was drawing to a close, the people of Hippo had been offended by his absence, he judged that he would be failing in his duty and office if he undertook another journey so soon.

Accordingly, he decided that the service he owed to his own church must be preferred to the pleasure he would enjoy at Tagaste. He therefore wrote to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania to excuse himself. He declared that the very fault he incurred by not visiting them was itself the greatest punishment that could be imposed upon him. Yet he added that, if he should be so unfortunate as not to be able to see them at Hippo, he hoped that an opportunity would not be lacking by which, somehow freed from this constraint, he might meet them wherever in Africa they might be.

### 3

Apparently only a few days after this letter was sent, Pinianus came to Hippo with the younger Melania.

Because of his humility, he feared that he might suffer the same violence which Augustine had endured from the people of Hippo and Paulinus from the people of Barcelona. He therefore wished Augustine to give him an assurance that Augustine would never ordain him presbyter against his will (Letter 126, no. 1). The holy Bishop also promised him that, if he accepted that dignity, Augustine would neither urge nor persuade him to do so (ibid., no. 2).

Apart from one witness—undoubtedly Alypius, who at that time happened to be staying at Hippo with Pinianus—there was no witness to at least the latter part of this promise.

Pinianus gave Augustine many and various gifts. Augustine, using them as he judged most beneficial, distributed some among clergy and monks and some among certain needy laypeople (ibid., no. 8).

Because of the wealth which Pinianus entrusted to Augustine and Alypius, both feared that they might fall under suspicion of unjust administration. Their own consciences did not suffice in this matter. It was also necessary to make clear and evident to the people whom they were bound by the Lord’s command to instruct and before whom they were required to lead the way by their example, how completely they abhorred the pursuit of private advantage (Letter 125, no. 2).

They therefore discussed the matter among themselves and carefully considered, in one another’s presence, how they might make it evident to the children of the Church—and even to their opponents—that, in administering ecclesiastical goods, their minds were not stained by any mark of desire or greed (ibid., no. 1; Letter 126, no. 9).

How necessary this precaution was for them became clear from a temptation which, by God’s permission, occurred not long afterward.

### 4

It happened that, while Pinianus and Melania were one day attending an ecclesiastical gathering together with Alypius, the entire congregation, without yet dismissing the catechumens, demanded with loud cries that Pinianus be ordained their presbyter (Letter 126, nos. 1–3, 5).

Augustine approached them. After allowing their shouting to continue for a short time, he declared that he was not at liberty to do what they demanded, because he had promised that he would not ordain Pinianus against his will. He added that, if they had Pinianus as their presbyter contrary to the promise he had given, they would no longer have Augustine himself as their bishop.

After saying this, he withdrew to his seat, which in that place he calls the benches and shortly afterward the apse—a kind of platform raised much higher by many steps (ibid., no. 1).

Pinianus and Melania were also present, though somewhat removed from Augustine. As the tumult increased—and the Bishop’s answer had not calmed it—they approached him (Letter 125, no. 2).

The holy Bishop says:

> At first they hesitated and were disturbed by my unexpected answer, like a flame briefly pressed down by the wind; then they began to blaze much more fiercely, thinking that either I might be compelled to break my promise or, while I kept faith with my promise, Pinianus might be ordained by another bishop.

> I told those whom I could, the more honorable and influential men who had come up to us in the apse, that I could not be moved from keeping my promise, and that Pinianus could not be ordained by another bishop in the church entrusted to me unless I had been consulted and had given permission. If I gave permission, I would nevertheless depart from my promise.

> I also added that they would gain nothing by his being ordained against his will except that, once ordained, he would depart. They did not believe that this could happen.

> The crowd standing on the steps persisted in the same intention with a dreadful and unceasing roar of shouting, leaving us uncertain in mind and deliberation.

(Letter 126, no. 1).

The people then hurled many insults at Alypius, as though he desired to keep Pinianus with them for no other reason than to divert his generosity and liberality to his own uses.

Augustine was deeply moved by this, although he had discovered that none of the clergy or monks present was guilty of the insult (Letter 125, no. 5). It was merely the ignorant crowd, which he had been unable to restrain (ibid., no. 2), and which he earnestly desired to be absolved from so great a fault through Alypius’s prayers (Letter 126, no. 1).

Amid these disturbances, Augustine, Alypius, and Pinianus all had good reason to fear the worst. For, Augustine says, there was reason to fear that some wicked men, who are often mingled with the multitude even when the majority are good, might seize the opportunity provided by the riot and what appeared to be a just indignation, and break out into criminal violence from desire for plunder (Letter 125, no. 3; Letter 126, no. 1).

### 5

The danger immediately before him could not induce Augustine even briefly to advise Pinianus to comply with the people’s will, although he had promised, in the presence of only one witness, that he would not do so.

Augustine says:

> I was thinking of leaving, but there was reason to fear that, if I were absent, the people—less restrained by reverence and more inflamed by grief—might do something still more atrocious.

> Moreover, if I left with my brother Alypius through the tightly packed crowd, it was necessary to fear that someone might dare to lay hands upon him. If I left without him, what would become of my reputation if something happened to him? Would it not appear that I had abandoned him for that very reason, in order to deliver him to the raging crowd?

> Amid these agitations of mind, this profound sorrow, and my inability to find any relief in counsel, behold, suddenly and unexpectedly our holy son Pinianus sent to me a servant of God named Barnabas. He told me that Pinianus wished to swear to the people that, if he were ordained against his will, he would leave Africa altogether. I suppose he thought that, since he could not swear falsely, they would no longer continue their fruitless shouting to drive away a man whom at least we ought to have as a neighbor.

> I kept silent within myself, because I thought that after this oath a still more violent grief on their part might be feared. But since he had also asked me to come to him, I did not delay.

> After he had told me this, he immediately added something else to the oath. While I was going to him, he had sent me word through another servant of God, Timasius: namely, that he would remain at Hippo, if no clerical burden were imposed upon him against his will.

> Here, in such great distress, I was refreshed as though by a breath of air. I could not be so foolish as to prefer that the Church which I serve should be overturned by such a tumult or offense rather than accept what was being offered to us by such a man.

> I answered him nothing, but went at a quicker pace to my brother Alypius and told him what Pinianus had said. But Alypius, as I suppose, fearing that something might occur on his authority which he thought would offend you, Albina, said: “Let no one consult me about this.”

> On hearing this I went to the shouting people. When silence had been made, I disclosed what had been promised, together with the oath.

> Those who were thinking only of and desiring his presbyterate did not receive what had been offered in the manner I had expected. After murmuring among themselves for a little while, they asked that this be added to the promise and oath: that, if Pinianus should ever consent to undertake the clerical office, he should consent only in the church of Hippo itself. Their hope was that, through his remaining present, he might eventually consent to undertake the clerical office when those who desired it urged him.

> I reported this to him, and he agreed without hesitation. I announced it to them, and they rejoiced. Soon afterward they demanded the promised oath.

> I returned to our son and found him hesitating over the words by which that promise, together with the oath, might be framed, because unforeseen necessities might arise and compel him to leave.

> At the same time he explained that he feared some hostile incursion might occur, which would make departure necessary. He wished holy Melania and the danger of unhealthy air to be mentioned, but her answer led him to reject this.

> I said that he had put forward a serious and by no means contemptible cause of necessity—one that might compel even citizens to emigrate. But if these things were told to the people, we had to fear that we would appear to be uttering an evil omen; whereas, if an excuse were made under the name of necessity, it would be regarded as nothing but a feigned necessity.

> Nevertheless, it seemed best to test the people’s attitude on this matter, and we found nothing other than what we had expected. When the deacon recited his words and everything was approved, as soon as the mention of the alleged necessity was heard, there was an immediate outcry. The promise displeased them, the tumult flared up again, and the people thought that we were dealing with them by fraud.

> When our holy son saw this, he ordered the word “necessity” to be removed. The people returned to joy.

> When I excused myself on the ground of weariness, he refused to approach the people without me. We approached them together.

> He told them that he had dictated what they had heard from the deacon, that he had sworn it, and that he would carry it out. He then repeated everything in the form in which he had dictated it.

> The answer was, “Thanks be to God,” and they asked that the entire document be signed.

> We dismissed the catechumens, and immediately he signed the document.

> Afterward we bishops were asked to sign as well—not by the voices of the people themselves, but by respectable believers acting on behalf of the people. When I began to sign, holy Melania objected.

> I was surprised that she had objected so late, as though the promise and oath could be rendered void if we did not sign them. Nevertheless, I obeyed; thus my signature remained incomplete, and no one afterward thought it necessary to press us to sign.

(Letter 126).

During these disturbances, Albina’s holy children—Pinianus and Melania, who were in the apse—openly complained that the people of Hippo were seeking not a presbyter but a wealthy man, out of greed for his money (Letter 125, no. 2).

Apart from certain omitted details which had no bearing on the matter, Augustine testifies that this account is the exact truth of what happened. Pinianus had not sworn because Augustine, as was reported, ordered him to do so, nor because the people compelled him; he had offered it himself, freely and spontaneously. Augustine cites Barnabas and Timasius as witnesses, sending each of them separately to him (Letter 126, no. 6).

He calls both of them servants of God—that is, monks.

Whether Barnabas, whom he honors with the title “holy,” should be identified with that presbyter of Hippo (Letter 213, no. 1) whom Augustine had placed over his household and whose reputation he publicly defended in a sermon (Sermon 356, no. 15), we do not determine.

At that time Timasius was a monk who, on Pelagius’s advice and urging, had renounced the world (Letter 177, no. 6). We shall encounter him again below.

### 6

After Pinianus had sworn that he would live at Hippo, a certain necessity arose which compelled him to leave the following day.

When the people of Hippo learned of this, they were thrown into considerable tumult, and many things were said in the heat of their feelings, which they also took care to commit to writing. But when it became clear that he had acted because of a private necessity and with the intention of returning, no one failed to judge the matter favorably (Letter 126, nos. 6, 13).

For their intention had not been to retain him there like an exile. They thought they had been fully satisfied provided that, like other citizens, he established his seat and residence there and never departed except with the intention of returning (Letter 125, no. 4).

Baronius reports that Pinianus secretly slipped away from Hippo and returned with his companions to Tagaste, since he knew perfectly well that the sanctity of a promise into which he had been led by force and fear could not bind him (Baronius, under the year 409). But it is for Baronius himself both to prove this principle and to establish the event which he asserts contrary to Augustine’s clear authority.

Pinianus’s mother-in-law Albina, however, took the matter badly. She wrote Augustine a letter full of grief (Letter 126), in which, using an offensive term, she called the presence which Pinianus had promised the people of Hippo “exile,” “deportation,” or “banishment.” She also asked whether Augustine thought that an extorted oath ought to be enforced, especially since Pinianus had made an exception for necessity in his oath not to depart.

She reproached Augustine for not having prevented this promise. She accused the people of Hippo of having wanted to have a presbyter, or to retain among them a wealthy man who despised riches sufficiently to distribute them to others, after being moved by the most shameful desire for money.

Alypius, who had perhaps withdrawn to Tagaste, also recalled in a letter to Augustine the insulting words that had then been directed against him. He advised that they should discuss by common counsel what ought to be determined concerning oaths extorted by force, although in what he had written in his advisory letter he indicated that Pinianus ought to live at Hippo like the other citizens, and indeed like Augustine himself (Letter 125).

7. In his reply to Alypius (ibid.), Augustine testified that he deeply grieved over the injuries inflicted upon him. As for Pinianus’s oath, however, after citing certain celebrated Roman examples concerning this very matter, he declares that it would be disgraceful if they themselves were to introduce even the question whether the oath ought to be observed or not. For otherwise no one would trust the promise, or even the oath, of bishops, if they allowed what had been given by so great a man to be broken or evaded by some empty pretext. Indeed, the oath is fulfilled not according to the words of the person swearing, but according to the expectation of the one to whom the oath is sworn—an expectation known to the person who swears. He nevertheless hoped that, through both divine goodness and the virtue of Pinianus, who guarded with such religious devotion the pledge he had made to God and the Church, that harvest of scandal and offense would not arise. Together with this reply, he sent Alypius a copy of Pinianus’s promise, transferred and corrected from the document Pinianus himself had signed.

In his response to Albina’s letter (Epistle 126), Augustine first declares that he is writing to her not to aggravate her grief but to relieve it; nor to disturb with harsher words the soul he revered as consecrated to God, but to heal her suspicions. He then explains the circumstances, so that she herself may perceive that the people of Hippo had asked Pinianus to become a presbyter solely for the spiritual advantage of the Church and because of the virtues with which Pinianus was adorned. In this matter, not even the slightest appearance of avarice or covetousness was evident. Consequently, no one except herself was touched by that accusation, although Albina had taken pains to suggest that the vice with which she judged Augustine to be afflicted should be attributed to him—not directly, lest she appear to act somewhat too freely or shamelessly toward a bishop, but indirectly and as though under another person’s name. Augustine says that he counted this kindness of hers among her benefits and did not take it in a bad sense. Yet, since he knew himself to be free from that very vice and could produce no testimony concerning a matter hidden within his conscience, he calls God as witness that the administration of the Church’s goods, which he necessarily undertook out of love for the brethren and fear of God, was something he endured, not loved, so that, if he could do so without failing in his duty, he desired to be rid of it. He further asserts that he is convinced Alypius held the same view in this matter.

Then, following the example of Paul, who in a similar case had appealed to God as witness, he approves his own oath. Finally, he turns to the oath Pinianus had taken, about which he speaks in the same way as in the letter sent to Alypius, to which he refers Albina. From this one may infer that Albina remained at Tagaste until that time, since there is no evidence that she had previously departed from there. Moreover, Augustine arranged for Albina to receive a memorandum in which the complaints of the people of Hippo against Pinianus, who was absent from Hippo, had been fully written out.

8. What happened afterward is nowhere recorded, except that the Life of the blessed Melania, Pinianus’s wife, reports that after spending seven years in Africa with astonishing holiness of life, she crossed over to Egypt and from there to Palestine (Surius, December 31, or January 2). For it is hardly likely that she was in that province in the year 415, the year in which Jerome wrote his letter to Ctesiphon, in which he speaks rather uncharitably of Melania’s grandmother. But when, in the year 418, Zosimus condemned Pelagius, who was at that time living in Palestine (Retractions, book 2, chapter 50), Albina, Pinianus, and Melania consulted Augustine by letter about the conference they had held with that heresiarch. In reply, he dedicated to them his two books On the Grace of Christ and On Original Sin. In them he declares that he rejoiced beyond anything that can be said both that they were physically well and, even more, that they were sound in soul. In the following year, Jerome, who was then living in the monastery at Bethlehem, sent greetings to the holy Bishop on their behalf (Augustine, Epistle 202, no. 2).

These mutual signs of love and respect are sufficient to make us believe that Pinianus departed neither contrary to his pledged word nor contrary to Augustine’s intention. Perhaps the holy Bishop had also prevailed, by his authority and prayers, upon the people of Hippo to release Pinianus from his oath.

9. Augustine wrote a letter to Armentarius and Paulina (Epistle 127), probably in this year, 411, since he reports that the City had recently been plundered by barbarians and that the world was being afflicted by such great calamities that it retained scarcely any of those vain and false attractions by which it had been accustomed to lead people into error and lure fools into loving it. Armentarius, together with his wife Paulina, had bound himself by a vow to consecrate the remainder of his life to God and, it seems, to undertake the monastic way of life. Paulina had no obstacle preventing her from dedicating perpetual continence to God. Armentarius, however, does not appear to have been equally prepared to renounce conjugal relations, but to have postponed the matter somewhat. Accordingly, after Augustine had been informed by their kinsman Ruferius of their state of mind (ibid., no. 1), he addressed to both of them a remarkably beautiful letter, although throughout he speaks to the husband. With very forceful arguments he urges him to fulfill, without any further delay, the vow he had made—a vow that could not be broken without grave sacrilege.

## CHAPTER X

1. The conference held at Carthage between the Catholic and Donatist bishops: Marcellinus summons it. 2. At Carthage Augustine preaches as the conference approaches. 3. The Donatists’ insolent entry into that city, and their numbers. 4. Marcellinus prescribes the entire procedure of the conference by edict. 5. The Donatists wish all their members who have come to attend the conference and refuse to give their signatures to the records. 6. The Catholics offer them this condition: if the Church prevails, they may either retain their episcopal sees when they return to unity, or divest themselves of them together with the Catholics. 7. Another of Augustine’s sermons before the conference, on peace. 8. The Catholics designate the bishops who are to dispute with the schismatics and strengthen them with an excellent mandate.

1. Marcellinus was the tribune to whom the Emperor had entrusted the task of compelling the Catholics and Donatists to meet for a conference. As soon as he came to Africa, he doubtless omitted nothing that could advance so important a matter with every care and diligence. Yet nothing is recorded as having been done by him before the edict that he ordered to be promulgated four months before the Kalends of June—or, more accurately, before the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, that is, about the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February in the year 411.

By this edict, which he sent throughout Africa together with Honorius’s command (Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 2), he established that all bishops, both Catholic and Donatist, were to be summoned in legal fashion by the magistrates of their localities, so that each party might elect its more experienced men to come to Carthage for the conference within the four months specified in the imperial command (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 5). He swears by all that is most sacred that he would judge nothing except what had been shown to be true by the documents produced by both sides. Nevertheless, since he might be suspected by the Donatists of being a Christian of the Catholic communion (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 4), he attempts to demonstrate his fairness to them by granting concessions that seemed to go beyond the limits of the law and that, as he himself admitted, would have been made without the Emperor’s authorization (Marcellinus, sentence after the Conference; Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 2).

He therefore promises that all Donatist bishops who, when summoned to the conference, replied that they would attend would be restored, before the conference itself, to possession of their churches and all their rights, which the Catholics might perhaps have been enjoying by force of the imperial decrees (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 5). As though by way of intercession, he also decrees that all lawsuits and legal proceedings brought or to be brought against them should already be suspended. Moreover, under oath he promises that, whatever the outcome of the conference, the Donatists who came there would be entirely free to return to their own places.

What is especially astonishing is that, if they regarded him with suspicion, he declares himself ready to admit to the proceedings as his colleague in judgment anyone from their communion of equal or even higher rank. Marcellinus fixes the Kalends of June as the date, within the four months, on which the conference was to be held (ibid.). Augustine had read this in the later edict of Marcellinus, in which he states that the same day had been fixed as in the earlier edict (Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 3).

At the conference, however, the secretary declared that the deadline fixed by the edict closed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 27). Augustine also agrees with this and acknowledges that the edict sent to the province—that is, the first edict—had contained this provision (Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 8). Marcellinus, on the other hand, states that the day of the Kalends of June had been assigned to the conference by the second edict (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 23).

Accordingly, in the first edict one ought to read not “within the day of the Kalends of June” but “within the day of the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June” (ibid., chapter 5), unless one prefers to suppose that the secretary made an error there, as Augustine observes that he made elsewhere as well (ibid., chapter 27). The second edict assigns the Kalends of June to the assembly in such a way that it gives no indication that another date had previously been fixed. Indeed, in both the second and the third conference the Catholics insisted that the four months prescribed by the edict—namely, the first edict, whose wording they use in that passage—ended on the day of the Kalends of June (Conference of Carthage 2, chapter 50; ibid. 3, chapter 404; Short Account of the Conference 2, chapter 3).

They proved this by pointing out that when Primianus was summoned to attend the conference, he had promised that he would be present on that day, and that the Donatists themselves, after selecting the bishops who were to represent their side at the conference, had not sent them their mandate before the eighth day before the Kalends of June. They had neither requested any earlier postponement relating to the date of the conference nor sought a judicial ruling (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 28).

2. In that year Easter was celebrated on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, and therefore Pentecost fell on the day before the Ides of May. According to the Church’s customary discipline, this feast was followed by a fast (Sermon 357, no. 5), whether that was the fast observed throughout the year on Wednesdays and Fridays outside the Easter season, or some more solemn fast. The latter interpretation seems closer to Augustine’s words. Possidius indeed included two of Augustine’s sermons on the fast of Pentecost in his Index (Index, chapter 9).

At any rate, during this period the holy Doctor delivered a sermon on peace beginning, “It is time to exhort” (Sermon 357). In it he complains that the Donatists displayed an extremely hostile disposition toward peace and reconciliation. He urges the Catholics to pursue peace, so that they might draw the Donatists toward it, and asks them to avoid with the greatest care every occasion for quarrel and strife with the heretics, lest the latter become even more angry and irreconcilable as a result.

“Now,” he says, “we must attend to the sick; the eyes of the wounded are inflamed; they must be treated cautiously and handled gently” (ibid., no. 4).

He advises them to endure patiently whatever the Donatists might utter against the Church or against the Church’s bishops. They should address God alone with prayers poured out for the Donatists’ salvation, and offer him the fasts of that season, both for the return of the schismatics to Catholic communion and for the bishops who were to defend the Church’s cause. Their prayers, moreover, should be supported by a more generous liberality toward the needy. He also urges his hearers to take advantage of the arrival of the servants of God and practice hospitality. No one can doubt that this refers to the bishops coming to Carthage for the conference, or at least to the monks accompanying them. From this it may be understood that Augustine delivered this sermon in that city; and in the immediately following sermon, which is certainly known to have been preached at Carthage, he in fact mentions it (Sermon 358, no. 6).

3. The Catholics came to the place of the conference without the elaborate display and pomp arranged for ostentation, but individually and far removed from the Donatists’ showiness (Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 11). The Donatists, by contrast, entered Carthage on Thursday, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, with such magnificence and such a multitude of companions that they held the eyes of all the citizens of that great city fixed upon them (Conference of Carthage 1, chapters 14, 29).

They themselves even boasted that all Carthage, indeed all Africa, was witness to their arrival, so that no one could plead ignorance of it. They added that they had been driven there by the edict that Marcellinus had issued, ordering them to hasten to Carthage; that old men, even those of advanced and decrepit age, had not pleaded weakness as an excuse; and that no one had been left in the provinces except those whom ill health unwillingly detained.

And this was indeed how matters stood. Their primates had ordered all their bishops to hasten there, abandoning every other concern, declaring that those who refused to come with the others would deprive their cause of its principal defense (To the Donatists after the Conference, no. 41). Accordingly, when they were summoned to the conference by the public records, they promised readily that they would attend; nor did they reject Marcellinus as judge in a matter of faith, although they knew that he professed the Catholic religion (Possidius, Life of Augustine, chapter 4).

What their primates so strongly commended to them as especially advantageous to their cause, however, was—as Augustine testifies—nothing other than the effort to make them appear as numerous as possible (To the Donatists after the Conference, no. 41). They even tried, through various frauds and lies, to increase the number of their followers. Yet they achieved only this much: they were counted as 279, somewhat fewer than the Catholics (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 213), who numbered 286 (Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 14; Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 214).

Besides these, as the records of the conference report, another 220 members of the Catholic communion (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 215)—or, more accurately, no more than 120 (Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 14)—had remained in the provinces, detained by illness, old age, or some other necessity. Augustine and the manuscript copy of the Conference give the latter number. In addition, sixty churches had been left without their bishops.

Therefore, if one wishes to calculate the total in this way, it is necessary to say that there were 466 sees of Catholic bishops in Africa. Yet at the conference the schismatics boasted that they had more absent bishops and vacant churches than the Catholics. Later they even proclaimed themselves to have more than 400 bishops throughout Africa (To the Donatists after the Conference, no. 41). None of them, however, was named individually. How futile and foolishly boastful this claim was became abundantly clear both from the frauds they had employed in exaggerating the number of their own people and from the fact that, with the sole exception of the sick, they had most explicitly declared in their own Notice that no one was absent.

4. When the bishops of both communions had arrived at Carthage, Marcellinus established by a second edict the place, time, and procedure of the conference (Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 3). At the same time, by introducing safeguards, he carefully provided that no one would afterward be permitted to deny what he had said at the conference.

He therefore decreed that seven bishops from each party, who were to dispute with one another, should be chosen by all the rest. An additional seven were to be appointed, whom the principal disputants would be free to consult whenever circumstances seemed to require it. Four others were also to be appointed to supervise the writing of the records. The assembly was to meet on the Kalends of June at the Gargilian Baths, a place chosen as especially suitable for everyone (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 18).

The baths stood in the middle of the city. They were very spacious, bright, and cool, and altogether worthy of so celebrated an assembly. It is observed that an epigram survives concerning their restoration through the care and expense of Thrasamund, king of the Vandals (Rivius, Life of Augustine, p. 359). They could easily have accommodated all the bishops, both Catholic and Donatist, since they all entered there together.

But because so great a number would undoubtedly have caused confusion, Marcellinus ruled that no bishop should be admitted except the twenty-eight or thirty-six already mentioned. He asked the bishops to warn their peoples in advance not to assemble there on the day of the conference.

He further declared that he wished the bishops of both communions, before the day of the meeting, to promise that they would regard as valid whatever action was taken by the seven selected for the conference, and that the record drawn up concerning this matter should be handed to him, in his presence, sealed by all. Whatever was said was to be immediately taken down by the public stenographers present and written at the same time by four ecclesiastical notaries from each side. The bishops appointed in groups of four to supervise the writing of the records were to guard them with vigilant and careful attention, so that no one could cast doubt upon their fidelity.

Moreover, so that these records might never be accused of even the slightest alteration or corruption, each bishop was to subscribe to what he had said. Marcellinus promised that he himself would be the first to do the same with his own statements. Finally, the tablets written and arranged in this manner, together with the signatures of the fourteen bishops whom they had chosen for the debate, were immediately to be posted publicly, so that everyone might read them and the entire people of Carthage might judge them.

“For since,” Marcellinus says, “the August Dignity has appointed me judge for those whom, out of reverence for so great a name, I recognize as superior to me, I have provided for the security of my concern for the faith by this consideration: I wished to be judged by my judgment. Thus the entire order of the dispute, not only before the eyes of this city but also of the whole province, will be displayed, so that both the arguments of the disputing bishops and the sequence of my judgments may be explained in publicly arranged volumes. For this is the security of faith in a judge: that he does not fear being judged concerning himself” (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 10).

The individual sheets were also to remain sealed until the controversy had been completely decided, bearing the seals of Marcellinus and of the eight bishops appointed as custodians.

All these safeguards proceeded from God’s singular kindness toward the Donatists. They therefore could not disregard them without incurring the gravest charge of ingratitude (Epistle 141, no. 2). Marcellinus even declares that if anyone evaded observing them, he would make public how little confidence that person had in his own cause and how little good faith he intended to show.

He likewise ordered that letters signed by the primates of both parties, in which they declared their agreement with the conditions proposed in the edict, should be presented to him. He expressly excluded the Maximianists from the conference (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 10). They had sought admission by submitting a humble petition, apparently wishing to obtain some honor for their insignificance and lowly status; but the Catholics treated this vanity with contempt (Against Julian, book 3, no. 5).

5. On the eighth day before the Kalends of June in the year 411, the Donatists arranged for Marcellinus to be notified of an act that they called the Notice. In it Januarius and Primianus—the only two who signed it—and the other bishops “of sincere Christianity and Catholic truth,” as their own words put it, declared that they could not agree with the second edict, especially as regards the signatures. They earnestly requested that all of them be permitted to attend the conference (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 14).

They seemed unwilling to sign because they wished to retain the ability, should it serve their interests, to accuse the judge of having corrupted the records (To the Donatists after the Conference, no. 15). Although that Notice asked that none of their people be absent from the conference, on that very day, the eighth day before the Kalends of June, they appointed seven of their own number to defend the cause of the Church of God—as they themselves expressed it—against their betrayers and persecutors. They promised that whatever those seven did would be regarded by them as valid (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 148).

All of them subscribed to this act (ibid., chapter 149), though not in Marcellinus’s presence (ibid., chapter 154). Although the document had been drawn up in the form of a letter, they testify that they had given it to the chosen representatives in the presence of the electors, or that those present had given it to those present (ibid., chapter 148). They were eventually compelled to provide the signatures necessary to authenticate the records, which they had initially refused to give (To the Donatists after the Conference, no. 15).

Those designated by them to dispute were Primianus of Carthage, Petilianus of Cirta, Emeritus of Caesarea, Protasius of Thubursicum, Montanus of Zama, Gaudentius of Thamugadi, and Adeodatus of Milevis.

6. Since the Donatists repeatedly claimed that they were offended by many provisions of Marcellinus’s second edict, the Catholics, by contrast, promised that they agreed with him in everything and would religiously observe whatever he prescribed. On this matter they presented Marcellinus with a letter—by this name he himself distinguishes it from the Donatists’ Notice (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 17). Aurelius of Carthage and Silvanus of Summa, dean and primate of Numidia, signed it on behalf of the other bishops (ibid., chapters 16, 18).

In it they cite the example of the Maximianists, whom the Donatists had received together with all those baptized by them, preserving even for bishops whom they had previously condemned the honor proper to their office. They declare that this was their sole purpose in seeking a conference: to demonstrate that the Church spread throughout the whole world could not perish through the sins of any human beings mixed within it. The case of Caecilianus, they say, had been brought to an end once his innocence had been exposed and those who accused him had been regarded as slanderers. As for the others whom the Donatists accused, they were either innocent or their sins did not harm the Church at all.

What chiefly gave this letter its renown, however, was the Catholics’ declaration that, if the Donatists proved that the Church remained solely in their communion, the Catholics would come under the Donatist rules in such a way that they would not at all consider retaining their episcopal dignity. Conversely, if the Catholics demonstrated that all the guilt rested with the Donatists, they nevertheless wished to keep them with themselves in unity without depriving them of episcopal honor.

Wherever two bishops were found, one Catholic and one Donatist, they would occupy the episcopal see in turn, while the other sat beside him for the time being, though in a somewhat lower position—the place customarily assigned to a visiting bishop. Or at least each would be assigned his own church until one had died, after which the other would alone possess the dignity, according to accepted practice.

If the peoples of a place were too impatient to tolerate two bishops in one location, then both would be stripped of the episcopate equally, and another would be appointed in their place by those bishops who had had no competitors.

“For what should we hesitate,” the Catholic Fathers say, “to offer our Redeemer the sacrifice of this humility? Did he descend from heaven into human members so that we might be his members, while we fear to descend from our seats lest his members be torn apart by cruel division? For our sake nothing is more sufficient than that we are faithful and obedient Christians; therefore let us always be just that. We are ordained bishops for the sake of Christian peoples. Whatever therefore benefits Christian peoples for Christian peace, let us do with respect to our episcopate.

“If we are useful servants, why do we begrudge the eternal gains of the Lord for the sake of our temporal exaltation? Episcopal dignity will be more fruitful for us if, by being laid down, it gathers Christ’s flock, rather than dispersing it by being retained. For with what face shall we hope in the age to come for the honor promised by Christ if our honor in this age hinders Christian unity?” (ibid., chapter 16).

After reading part of this letter aloud during a sermon at Augustine’s command, Augustine expounded the passage as follows:

“I shall tell Your Charity, and recall a very sweet and pleasant event that, with the Lord’s help, we experienced. Before the conference itself, when some brethren among us were discussing this matter—for bishops ought either to exist for Christ’s peace or ought not to exist—you must know that, as we looked around at all our brethren and fellow bishops, we could not easily find anyone who would be willing to undertake this and sacrifice to the Lord this humility.

“We said, as is customary, ‘That man can do it; this one cannot. That man consents to it; this one cannot tolerate it,’ speaking more from our suspicions, since we could not see their hearts at all. But when the time came for this to be made public, in the very large council of nearly three hundred bishops, all were of one mind and all were so inflamed that they were ready to lay down the episcopate for Christ’s unity—not to lose it, but to entrust it more securely to God.

“Only two were scarcely found who disliked the proposal. One was an aged old man who dared to say this rather freely; the other expressed his will by a silent look. But after the old man, who had spoken so freely, was overwhelmed by the fraternal correction of all, and changed his opinion, the other also changed his expression” (On the Proceedings with Emeritus, no. 6).

This thoroughly Christian proposal was not only confirmed by the signatures of the bishops but also consecrated by the prayer of the entire council to God (Sermon to the People of the Church at Caesarea, no. 1).

Although the Donatists resisted the truth, the Catholics nevertheless did not cease to offer them the same condition, and they fulfilled it in good faith toward those whom they received into the Church. At least this is established by the council held at Carthage in the year 419, where Donatists were customarily received into episcopal dignity (African Code of Canons, canons 118, 119).

7. Augustine also mentions in other places that remarkable promise by which the foremost of the African bishops undertook to renounce their own honor (Sermon 359, no. 5). He prays to God that, since it proceeded from the fountain of charity, God might regard it as pleasing and acceptable (Sermon 358, no. 4).

If one desires a fuller account of this matter, one may consult the sermon on Peace and Charity. We infer from what it says about the condition offered by the bishops that it was delivered after the letter just mentioned, but nevertheless before the day of the conference. In it the second edict of Marcellinus is cited, and even the third, by which, as we shall soon explain, he published the Catholics’ letter.

There the holy Bishop appeals to the people not to violate Marcellinus’s edict by rushing to the place of the conference. Indeed, he asks them not even to pass through that place until the matter had been completely settled, so that no opportunity for disorder might be offered to those who wanted nothing at all except disorder (ibid., no. 6).

In this sermon the devout Bishop displays a very ardent desire to recall the schismatics to unity, which would be their true victory. “For,” he says, “only truth conquers; the victory of truth is charity” (ibid., no. 1).

He shows how Caecilianus’s case ought to be defended and with what care each person must avoid becoming attached to any individual human being (ibid., no. 3). “What shall we assign to you?” he asks the people. “Perhaps abundant works of piety. We shall dispute on your behalf; you pray on our behalf. Support your prayers also with fasts and almsgiving. Add wings to them, by which they may fly to God. In acting thus, you may perhaps be more useful to us than we are to you. For none of us relies upon himself in this dispute; all hope is in God” (ibid., no. 6).

8. In their letter the Catholics asked Marcellinus to display it as soon as possible before everyone’s eyes. Perhaps, even before the conference, the weak or hardened hearts of the schismatics might thereby be healed or subdued by the testimony of pious charity presented in it (Conference of Carthage 1, chapter 16).

Marcellinus was more than sufficiently compelled to do this by his own promise, by which he had undertaken to submit his procedure to everyone’s judgment (ibid., chapter 17). Accordingly, he ordered by a new edict that both the Catholics’ letter and the Donatists’ Notice be posted publicly.

When this had been done and the Notice became known to the Catholics, they presented Marcellinus with another letter, likewise signed by Aurelius and Silvanus. In it they stated that they feared that some sedition might arise from the Donatists, who were demanding, plainly without any justification, that all their members be admitted to the conference.

Nevertheless, they agreed to the Donatists’ request on the condition that only the eighteen Catholic bishops designated according to Marcellinus’s second edict should attend, lest, if any disturbance were stirred up, it could be attributed to anyone other than the Donatists. They added that they would consider the matter to have turned out very well for them if that fear proved unfounded and if the Donatists had wished all their members to participate in the council for no other reason than that, after the matter had been concluded by a solemn reconciliation, they might enter the same church together with the Catholics and give thanks to God for the restoration of their communion (ibid., chapter 18).

In this letter the entire case is set forth so clearly, forcefully, and briefly that, after reading it, the Donatists complained—though not without absurdity—that the Catholics had acted before discussion had begun concerning the conditions preliminary to the conference (ibid., chapters 18, 20; Short Account of the Conference 1, chapters 7, 8).

On the third day before the Kalends of June in the year 411, all the bishops of the Catholic communion designated the bishops for the conference and wrote in the church at Carthage, in Marcellinus’s presence, the mandate with which they wished those bishops to be equipped. The assembly itself consisted of 266 bishops, presided over by Aurelius of Carthage and Silvanus, primate of Numidia.

Those appointed to dispute at the conference were Aurelius of Carthage, Alypius of Tagaste, Augustine of Hippo, Vincentius of Culusita, Fortunatus of Constantinopolis, Fortunatianus of Sicca, and Possidius of Calama.

The seven advisers were Novatus of Sitifis, Florentius of Hippo Diarrhytus, Maurentius of Thubursicum, Priscus of Cudia, Serenianus of Mididi, Boniface of Cataquae, and Squillacius of Scillium.

Those appointed to guard the writing of the records were Deuterius of Caesarea, Leo of Mopta, Asterius of Vicus, and Restitutus of Tagaste (Conference of Carthage 1, chapters 55, 57).

It is likely that these 266 bishops signed in the order of their consecration. The names of the eighteen chosen bishops, however, with the exception of Aurelius, who signed first of all, are subscribed at the end (ibid., chapters 136, 142).

All the bishops observed the following form when subscribing:

“[Name], bishop of [place], established at Carthage, in the presence of Vir Clarissimus Marcellinus, Tribune and Notary, have agreed to and subscribed the mandate made by us”; or, “I have commissioned and subscribed” (ibid., chapter 57).

Those to whom the task of disputing had been entrusted replaced the words “I have agreed to the mandate made by us” with “I have undertaken this mandate.”

The Catholics’ mandate and their response to the schismatics’ Notice contained everything of greater importance that needed to be said—and this was deliberate. For it had become widely known that the Donatists intended to argue about certain procedural objections and formulas that would merely delay the decision of the case. If these were denied them, there was a fear that they would dissolve the conference (Short Account of the Conference 1, chapter 10).

The Catholics therefore wished those writings to testify how invincible were the weapons of truth on whose side they stood, so that if the conference should be dissolved by the Donatists, everyone would nevertheless know fully that they had refused to confer for no other reason than that they despaired of victory, having no answers at all.

## CHAPTER XI

1. The opening of the conference held on the Kalends of June. 2. The Donatists demand that all the Catholics be summoned, so that they may satisfy themselves concerning the subscriptions to their mandate. 3. The Donatists refuse the opportunity offered them to sit, but announce those chosen to argue on their behalf. 4. They are convicted of having erred several times in the subscriptions to the mandate given to their disputants. 5. Likewise, they are shown to have lied concerning Bishop Quodvultdeus. 6. On the appointed day for the second conference, only the seven disputant bishops come from the Donatists, whereas the eighteen Catholic delegates are present. 7. A postponement is granted to the Donatists.

1. On the day appointed for the conference—namely, the Kalends of June in the year 411, which fell on a Thursday—Marcellinus entered the secretariat of the Gargilian Baths with men of various ranks, twenty officials of the courts, and ecclesiastical notaries, two Catholic and an equal number of Donatist. He also ordered the bishops who were standing at the door to be brought in: eighteen chosen Catholics and all the Donatists (Carthaginian Conference 1, ch. 1). Thus the Donatists abandoned that arrogance with which, some years earlier, they had loudly declared it unworthy for the sons of martyrs to meet with the offspring of the Traditores (On the Donatists after the Conference, nos. 1, 39).

At the outset Marcellinus ordered the Emperor’s rescript, his own edicts, and various letters addressed to him by bishops of both communions to be read aloud. Since, in his earlier edict, Marcellinus had promised the schismatic faction that he would accept as his colleague in this judgment anyone else whom they wished, Petilian replied that it was not fitting for those to whom a first judge had been assigned without their requesting one to choose a second judge for themselves (Carthaginian Conference 1, chs. 6–7). But their own conscience and their own fear found, in the very official whom Honorius had appointed, another examiner and judge for themselves, far more perceptive and severe (On the Donatists after the Conference, no. 46). Before the case was argued, this judge had already judged it.

After these documents had been read, Emeritus maintained that the time for disputing had already passed and that the four months prescribed by the Emperor had elapsed from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June [May 19] (Carthaginian Conference 1, ch. 20). Marcellinus, however, showed that the period extended through the Kalends themselves [June 1], and indeed that, after the four months had expired, two more could still be added (ibid., ch. 30). Nevertheless, this did not prevent the Donatists from later trying to burden the Catholics with the charge that they had not appeared on the legally appointed day; they made the same allegation at the second hearing as well, where they were refuted even more decisively by the Catholics (Carthaginian Conference 2, chs. 48, 50).

The result was that, by this maneuver, the Donatists achieved nothing except that it became clear and certain to everyone how greatly they feared that, once the case had been thoroughly examined, both the weakness of their faction and the strength of the Catholics would be exposed. Marcellinus had complained that the Donatists were employing petty legal quibbles unworthy of the gravity of the case. Therefore they asked him, once forensic formulas had been removed from consideration, to order that only the authority of Scripture should prevail in this judgment (ibid. 1, chs. 30–31).

Marcellinus thought that the proceedings should begin with the selection of persons, something which, in his presence, the Donatists had not yet carried out. They, however, insisted that this too was a forensic formality and should consequently be omitted along with the others. Nevertheless, when, at the Donatists’ insistence, Marcellinus asked the Catholics whether they preferred to proceed according to the custom of the courts or by the authority of divine Scripture alone, and the answer was given that the mandate contained the will of everyone, whose limits they were not permitted to exceed, while they were not in any way entangled in forensic technicalities, Marcellinus finally succeeded in having the mandate read, although the Donatists objected and loudly declared that the formality was entirely unnecessary. “For in one person,” Emeritus said, “the whole person of the Church is represented” (ibid., ch. 47).

When the mandate had been read, they honestly acknowledged that it excluded the formulas of court and law, and therefore that they ought to answer the Catholics from the testimonies of divine law (ibid., ch. 70). In a short time, however, they forgot this promise.

2. After the mandate had been read, they requested that those who had signed it be brought in, lest perhaps subordinate clerics had secretly inserted signatures in place of bishops. The Catholics suspected that, since the Donatists had so far dared to provoke no disturbance and feared that all the odium would fall upon themselves, who were almost alone, they were insisting on calling in the Catholics for the purpose of breaking off the discussion by gradually stirring up a disturbance amid the confusion of a crowd (ibid., chs. 81, 83, 84).

Accordingly, the Catholics resisted for some time, until the Donatists themselves proposed that their own people should be seated on one side and the Catholics on the other, so that, if any disturbance arose, the blame for it could not nevertheless be transferred to the innocent. Later, however, it became clear that the Donatists had been moved to demand the presence of the Catholics for no other reason than that they could not persuade themselves that there were as many of them as the signatures appeared to indicate, since they had not seen those Catholics enter the city with display and pomp.

The Catholics therefore agreed that their fellow bishops, who had perhaps arranged to meet among themselves in some church, should be summoned [Col. 0415] (ibid., ch. 89). Since, however, quite a few might have been scattered in different places, Alypius undertook to bring them on the following day. Yet after those found at the doors had been brought in—men whom we cannot doubt had been summoned by prior arrangement—no one was found to be absent from among those who had signed the mandate, except those who were ill at Carthage.

In this examination of the signatures, the schismatics reproached the Catholics because, where there was only one of their bishops in a given district, the Catholics sometimes had two or even more (ibid., chs. 65, 117). The Catholics demonstrated that the same thing was also found among the Donatists (ibid., ch. 125, or 126). They accused one another of establishing bishops in villages, estates, and rural properties, or in sees without a people (ibid., chs. 181–182). Finally, they did not cease to throw back at one another the wrongs each had suffered from the other. Marcellinus, however, cut short such disputes insofar as he could, since they merely diverted attention from the central issue.

When Felicianus of Musti, formerly of the Maximianist faction, was mentioned, Alypius insisted that the Donatists openly acknowledge him as belonging to their communion (ibid., ch. 122; Brief Account of the Conference 1, ch. 12). They refused to do so. In one case, a certain bishop signed in place of Paulinus, a Catholic bishop who was present but did not know how to write (Carthaginian Conference 1, ch. 133).

3. After all the names of the Catholics had been read, Marcellinus asked the bishops to sit, since, naturally, he found it uncomfortable to sit while they were standing. The Donatists declined the honor offered to them, while lavishing the most magnificent verbal flattery both on themselves and on Marcellinus (ibid., chs. 144–145). Although they praised him so extravagantly that, as Augustine reports, they called him “honorable, just, respectful, and kind,” they nevertheless did not want the case for which so many had assembled to be argued before him (Brief Account of the Conference 1, ch. 13).

At last they were compelled to appoint men to argue on their behalf—or rather, to name those to whom they had already delegated this responsibility from the eighth day before the Kalends of June [May 25] (Carthaginian Conference 1, ch. 143). The mandate concerning this matter was therefore read. It contained only seven men who were to argue; but Augustine records that another seven, who were to serve as advisers to the first group, and four others, who were to preserve the records, had also been selected (Letter 141, no. 2). The same arrangement may be read explicitly at the end of the First Conference (Carthaginian Conference 1, ch. 218).

4. The reading of the mandate was followed by the signatures, which they again confirmed—at the urging of the Catholics, certainly, but with the Donatists themselves pressing even more insistently (ibid., chs. 152, 154, 165, 175). They demanded this earnestly from Marcellinus, openly professing that they placed their chief confidence in the number of their adherents. Marcellinus pointed out that the case was not at all concerned with this and declared that he would be satisfied if the first ten testified concerning the signatures of the others; the Catholics did not object to this either. Nevertheless, it was necessary to accommodate the Donatists.

Felix, who signed third among them, declared himself to be the bishop of the city of Rome [Col. 0416] (ibid., ch. 157). The Catholics did not dwell on this either, except to say that Innocent’s right must be preserved (ibid., chs. 161, 163).

The names of certain men were read who had not come to Carthage at all; but, in place of these absent men, others had signed, even though they were forwarding their mandate while present to those who were present (Brief Account of the Conference 1, ch. 14). Thus Manilius, a presbyter of Bazia, signed in place of his bishop, who had been prevented by blindness from coming, without even stating the bishop’s name (Carthaginian Conference 1, chs. 182–183). Likewise, Rufinus the presbyter was found to have signed in place of his absent bishop Julian (ibid., chs. 193, 195). Other bishops also acknowledged that they had been asked to lend their hands for four of their colleagues, who, as they claimed, had been detained on the journey by ill health (ibid., chs. 208–209).

Felix Zummensis [of Zummi] was found neither in person nor through anyone who had signed in his name. Consequently, after conferring among themselves, the Donatists were forced to take refuge in the claim that the names of that man and of a certain Felix of Lambesis, who was then ill, had perhaps been confused (ibid., chs. 200–201). Previously, however, they had asserted that this Felix of Zama was confined by illness (ibid., ch. 114).

Novatus, the Catholic bishop of Sitifis, seeing Donatus presenting himself as bishop of a place subject to his jurisdiction, declared that there was no bishop there and no Donatist of any kind (ibid., chs. 203–204). Asellicus, bishop of Tusurita, also solemnly affirmed that on the third day before the Kalends of May [April 29], when he had departed from Arzuges, a region situated south of Africa, Victorianus—who arrogated to himself the title of Donatist bishop of Aquae—had been only a presbyter. He further maintained that Victorianus had been ordained on the journey, although he was accused of adultery, a charge whose examination was still pending (ibid., ch. 207, or 208).

5. What happened in the case of Quodvultdeus, bishop of Cessita, seems especially worthy of notice (ibid., chs. 206–207). In that matter they were convicted of the most manifest falsehood (Letter 141, no. 1).

The signature of this bishop was included among the others as though he had written it at Carthage, yet when his name was read aloud he did not answer. When it was asked where he was, they were suddenly blinded by confusion and themselves admitted that he had died on the journey. When the Catholics asked how he could have signed at Carthage if he had died on the journey, they remained for a long time in confused uncertainty, not knowing what to answer.

At first they said that the reference was not to him but to someone else. When the Catholics understood them to mean another person—namely, a cleric who could have signed in place of the dead man—they asked whether the cleric had signed in his own name or in the dead man’s name. After great distress, confusion, and the inconsistency and variability of their replies, they answered that he himself had signed while present when the mandate was drawn up on the eighth day before the Kalends of June [May 25], but that, since he had signed while ill, he had died on the journey as he returned home.

When the Catholics heard this, they requested that their earlier statements be read aloud, so that the very inconsistency might become clear. When this had been done, and it became evident how little consistency there was in their answers, the Judge asked whether they would at least affirm under oath before God that he had been at Carthage when they, being present, sent the mandate to those who were present, instructing them to sign. At this they were even more confused. Not daring to bind themselves by perjury, they replied: “What if someone else also signed in his place?”

Leaving their detected falsehood to the judgment of God, the Judge ordered the remaining names to be read (Brief Account of the Conference 1, ch. 14). Thus the Donatists, who had wanted the Catholics’ signatures examined because they believed that some false ones might be discovered among them (Against the Donatists after the Conference, no. 56), became entangled in their own nets.

During this dispute, Petilian said somewhat coldly, “Is it not human to die?” Alypius immediately replied, “It is human to die, but it is inhuman to deceive” (Carthaginian Conference 1, ch. 207).

After the Donatist signatures had been read, Alypius produced sixteen more Catholic bishops who were prepared to sign the mandate, in addition to four others who were detained by illness in the city (ibid., chs. 212, 215). As a result, when all the bishops were counted, the Catholics outnumbered the Donatists.

Then all the bishops were dismissed except the thirty-six who had been selected for the Conference (ibid., ch. 216). But since the eleventh hour of the day had already passed—that is, it was six o’clock in the afternoon—Marcellinus, with the agreement of both parties, postponed the Conference until the day after the next, namely Saturday, the third day before the Nones of June [June 3], so that what had been said and merely captured in notes could be transcribed during the intervening day and arranged in a clearer form (ibid., ch. 219).

6. On the following day, the fourth day before the Nones of June [June 2] in the eleventh year above four hundred [411], which was a Friday, the Donatist advocates—who arrogated to themselves the title of defenders of the truth of the Church—submitted to Marcellinus a Notoria. After explaining that the records of the preceding Conference were too lengthy to be transcribed in a short time, they requested that a copy of the Catholics’ mandate be supplied to them in the meantime, so that they might be prepared to defend the case they had undertaken (ibid. 2, ch. 12).

Marcellinus ordered a copy of the mandate to be given to them. This, as they themselves admitted, threw their minds into no small confusion (ibid., chs. 33, 36), since in truth they could think of nothing to answer him. Consequently, although they had bound themselves by strict promises to continue the Conference on the following day—that is, the third day before the Nones of June [June 3]—they changed their plan, hoping that a delay would allow them to recover their composure.

Nevertheless, on this third day of June they went to the place of the Conference. Of their number, only the seven disputants appeared; of the Catholics, however, not one of the eighteen delegates was absent (ibid., ch. 2).

Marcellinus again asked them to sit. The Catholics immediately complied. The Donatists, however, not only rejected this honor but also loudly declared that divine laws forbade them to sit together with the Catholics. The Catholic Fathers ignored this, lest they waste time refuting matters irrelevant to the case. Nevertheless, all of them immediately rose. Indeed, when the chair was ordered removed, Marcellinus himself stood up, declaring that, out of the reverence with which he regarded the bishops, he could not sit while they refused to do the same (ibid., chs. 3–4).

By this conduct the Donatists sufficiently displayed their own arrogance. In the Third Conference, on the occasion of certain letters they had written and to which the Catholics were replying, the Catholics touched upon that ridiculous vanity: the Donatists, they said, were misinterpreting Scripture. If, because of the words of the psalm, “I have not sat in the council of the ungodly,” they were forbidden to sit with those whom they wished to mark as ungodly, then they ought not even to have entered the same place, because of the words immediately following in the same psalm, “And with those who act wickedly I will not enter” (Psalm 25:4). But since they had not hesitated to enter the same place with the Catholics, they ought not to refuse to sit with them as well (Brief Account of the Conference 3, no. 18).

7. Accordingly, while Marcellinus and all the others were standing, the Notoria which the Donatists had submitted the previous day was read aloud (Carthaginian Conference 2, ch. 12). The Tribune then asked whether the bishops were prepared to sign their own statements individually (ibid., ch. 13).

At first the Donatists denied that this was customary. Then they said that they would answer only when a copy of the records of the preceding Conference had been given to them, since those records had not yet been entirely transcribed. They wished first to read them again before the proceedings advanced any further and to examine them with more careful judgment, something they could do less readily in a copy written in notes, since they did not know the notes; whereas, otherwise, no one knew another person’s notes (ibid., chs. 16, 20, 33, 38, 43).

This amounted to nothing other than dragging out the time and seeking to use postponements to prevent the case from reaching judgment (ibid., ch. 36). The Catholics therefore replied that, at the First Conference, the Donatists ought to have arranged for a copy of the records if they needed one, and ought not to have promised that they would return to the Conference only when they were prepared to do so. Now, after giving their word, it was by no means honorable for them to procrastinate further. The previous day they had requested the Catholics’ mandate and had mentioned no other matter (ibid., ch. 49).

Moreover, the preceding Conference had consisted chiefly in reviewing the bishops’ signatures and similar matters, rather than in dealing with anything of importance to the case (ibid., ch. 40). Still dissatisfied, they irritatingly insisted, as they had done the previous day, that the day appointed for the Conference had already elapsed from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June [May 19] (ibid., chs. 48, 50).

Finally, when they obstinately persisted in requesting a postponement, Augustine succeeded in obtaining this concession from the judge (ibid., ch. 56). Their request itself was not unreasonable; but since the previous day they had bound themselves by a promise to conduct the case on this day, there was no longer any reason to give such requests consideration (ibid., ch. 66).

Marcellinus therefore granted them a postponement, although they accepted it reluctantly (ibid., ch. 61). When the notaries promised that they would complete the corrected sheets that same day (ibid., ch. 63), the Donatists likewise promised that they would sign them (ibid., ch. 64).
