In this way they eventually admitted the very point to which they had initially objected (Against the Donatists after the Conference, no. 15).

They were not unaware that, if they refused to confirm their own statements by their signatures, it would become plainly evident that they feared being convicted by their own words. They therefore judged it preferable later to seek disguise and obscurity for their words than to condemn them from the beginning.

Accordingly, once the Donatists had undertaken to sign the records, the notaries also gave their word that, if the records were signed that same day or the next, the scribes, who were laboring day and night, could complete them in such a way that they would be published to the public on Wednesday, the seventh day before the Ides of June [June 7] (Carthaginian Conference 2, ch. 65).

Then both Catholics and Donatists promised that they would assemble in council on Thursday, the sixth day before the Ides of June [June 8], so that the substance of the case might finally be debated (ibid., chs. 66–67).

At the Donatists’ request, Marcellinus also agreed that, early in the morning of the seventh day already mentioned [June 7], copies of both Conferences should be delivered to both parties, and they were required to attest in writing that this had been done (ibid., chs. 67–68).

Thus the Second Conference ended. The Tribune promised to publish an edict declaring that the extension had been granted at the request of the Donatists themselves (ibid., chs. 72–73). Alypius had requested this, fearing that the Donatists might seize the opportunity to disturb the people with false rumors, as they had done the previous day.

When, during this discussion, Augustine once addressed the Donatists as “brothers,” Petilian took the expression offensively and complained of it as nothing other than an insult (ibid., chs. 49–50).

The scribes displayed even greater diligence than their promises required (ibid. 3, ch. 3). On the eighth day before the Ides of June [June 6], at the third hour of the day—that is, according to our method of reckoning in Gaul, about nine in the morning—they brought the records of the two Conferences to the Donatists in a church they called Theoprepia. Montanus of Zama gave written testimony to this (ibid., ch. 5).

Two hours later they brought the records to the Catholics in the Basilica Restituta and delivered them to them; Fortunatianus of Sicca also attested this in writing (ibid., ch. 4). In their written statement, however, the schismatics recorded that they had sustained these two Conferences against their Traditores and persecutors.

Both parties promised that they would return on the appointed day for the Third Conference. There is no doubt that, in order to fulfill his word, Marcellinus ordered the records of both Conferences to be publicly posted as soon as they had been transcribed. Perhaps this is to be understood as the edict mentioned at the beginning of the Second Conference, where he declares that he would display before everyone’s eyes, as he had promised, what had already taken place among the bishops and the opening stage of the contest.

## CHAPTER XII

1. The Third Conference is held on the sixth day before the Ides of June. The Donatists insist that it be determined who should be regarded as the plaintiffs and that the Catholics’ mandates concerning the request for the Conference be examined.

2. The same men acknowledge that the Catholic Church is the Church spread throughout the whole world.

3. In order to determine which party is the plaintiff, various records are read aloud; thus, despite the Donatists’ opposition, the discussion reaches the central issue.

4. The Donatists produce a document concerning the purity of the Church, as they call it.

5. Augustine refutes it and resolves the dispute concerning that most serious point.

6. The discussion turns to Caecilianus and the schism.

7. Disturbed and overwhelmed by the history of the Maximianists, the Donatists admit that neither the cause should prejudice the cause nor the person the person.

8. They raise a controversy concerning the truth of the Council of Cirta.

9. They wish to examine a passage of Optatus by which they are refuted.

10. The same men, when documents were produced establishing the innocence of Caecilianus and Felix, cut through all the knots of the difficulties.

11. At last the Judge adjudicates the case to the Catholics.

[Col. 0420]

1. On the sixth day before the Ides of June [June 8], they began the Conference early in the morning, as they had agreed. Marcellinus ordered eighteen Catholics, as usual, but only eleven Donatists found there, to be brought in. He then decreed that, after the evasions of unnecessary delays had been set aside, they should finally debate the central point of the entire case.

The Catholics immediately said that, since the Donatists had attacked them in their mandate as their persecutors and Traditores, the Donatists ought to support the crimes they alleged with legitimate arguments and should also state in general the causes of their separation from the Church (Carthaginian Conference 3, ch. 14).

The schismatics replied that the first matter to be examined was which party was assuming the role either of plaintiffs or of defendants, and that it should therefore be investigated by which party the Conference had been requested (ibid., ch. 16).

They pressed this point obstinately so that, once the Catholics had accepted the role of plaintiffs, they could quibble in forensic fashion. From this, endless delays and complications would have arisen.

Marcellinus nevertheless did not appear unwilling to conduct that inquiry. But the Catholics had clearly understood what their opponents were aiming at. Although they had already shown sufficiently in their mandate that the Donatists were truly the accusers, they did not want the matter investigated any further. They urged that the central issue itself should be addressed first (ibid., chs. 18, 98).

Above all, they asked the Donatists to show for what reasons they had separated from the Church promised in the divine Scriptures and spread throughout the whole world (ibid., ch. 82). They then asked them to prove the claim they had accepted—namely, that the Catholic Church was on their side (ibid., ch. 75).

On this occasion Augustine said:

> God, he said, wanted us to be disputants and conference-partners rather than litigants. Let nothing be introduced that is not necessary to the case. The Church we assert is known to all through the testimonies of the divine Scriptures; it is established on a very high mountain, as it is written, and all nations come to it. If anything is to be said against this Church, let it now be said, and let there be no further delays. How long will this great expectation of the people remain suspended? Everyone is thinking about his own soul, while we introduce procedural postponements in order never to reach the end of discovering the truth! (ibid., ch. 21)

They did not deny that the Emperor had granted the Conference at their own request, as he himself testified in the rescript that was read again. But the heretics were not satisfied with that admission. They further insisted that the petition submitted to Honorius should be produced, that the names of the envoys should be disclosed, and that the mandates which the Catholics had received concerning this matter should be published. Unless this were done, they argued, the rescript they had obtained would be entirely without force.

The Catholics maintained that this was wholly irrelevant to the case. Although Marcellinus supported them in this, the Donatists’ obstinacy could never be overcome.

“The expectation,” Augustine exclaimed, “not merely of this city but of almost the whole human race, is suspended. It wishes to hear something about the Church, while we are still examining forensic formulas and carrying on the most wretched litigation!” (ibid., ch. 41). “How much is being done so that nothing may be done!” (ibid., ch. 40).

Another Catholic bishop likewise said:

> What else is it to abandon the case and seek out persons than to want to escape? Why have you come? (ibid., ch. 56)

This controversy concerning the Catholic embassy to Honorius continued up to the ninety-seventh section of the Conference, where the Catholics were again pressed by the heretics to acknowledge that they were the plaintiffs.

2. Some discussion also arose concerning the name “Catholics” (ibid. 3, chs. 22, 30, 75, and elsewhere). Marcellinus declared that what judgment should be made concerning this name would be explained after the substance of the entire case had been decided (ibid., chs. 36, 94). In the meantime, he said, he was not permitted to deny this title to those whom the Emperor had honored with it in his rescript (ibid., chs. 92, 94, 147).

When the Tribune wished to determine which party should truly be called the plaintiffs, the Catholics refused to accept that role, lest they give the Donatists an opening for their quibbles. Augustine replied that the Catholics’ plan was to dissolve the accusations with which the Donatists attacked the Church in their mandate, and that they had requested the Conference for no other reason than that the same Donatists, by whom it had also been requested, might either approve the justice of their separation or recognize and correct its injustice (ibid., chs. 110, 116). It was now Marcellinus’ task to pronounce which party deserved the name of plaintiffs (ibid., ch. 108).

For the time being the schismatics disputed the meaning of “Catholic.” They nevertheless admitted that the name could not be denied to their opponents, provided that the Catholics could demonstrate that the whole world was joined to them by the bond of communion (ibid., ch. 102).

A great advantage for the cause of truth arose from the following fact. When the Catholics said that the Church spread throughout the whole world had been attacked by the Donatists with false accusations, the schismatics openly declared that they did not wish to bring a lawsuit against all the Churches of the entire world. Those Churches, they said, were wholly removed from the African Christian controversy; rather, they were awaiting the outcome of the contest so that they might join in communion with whichever party won at this Conference and might wish to rejoice with them in the name “Catholic” (ibid., ch. 99).

In this way they acknowledged that they had nothing to bring against the Church spread throughout the whole world. From this admission it also followed that Caecilianus had not been cut off from that same Church, either because he himself was innocent or because it was impossible for those who retained his communion to be polluted by his guilt.

The force of this argument likewise applied to all the African Catholics, since, joined to that same Church, they had always retained the name “Catholic” in its unity. This was plainly a victory for them, and one granted not without divine favor.

The heretics denied that the Catholics were in this universal communion. Yet the Catholics recognized with great satisfaction that the difficulty of the case had been reduced to this point. Alypius therefore immediately asked permission to demonstrate by arguments the matter under investigation (ibid., ch. 102).

The schismatics, however, tried to turn the discussion elsewhere and again demanded that the mandates of the envoys be shown to them, abandoning the case of the Church which they had already begun to address (Brief Account of the Conference 3, no. 3).

When Augustine declared that he intended to take his stand upon the Church spread throughout the whole world, saying, “We have chosen to retain this Church,” Emeritus replied, “You have always been accustomed to choose in this way—and then to change” (Carthaginian Conference 3, chs. 100–101).

Without doubt he was silently reproaching him with the heresy of the Manichaeans, in which Augustine had been entangled as a young man. But the holy man did not utter even a single word in response to that personal insult; he simply continued his discourse.

### 3

At last the Examiner pronounced that those who brought accusations against others were to be regarded as plaintiffs, provided it could be established that the Conference had been requested by both parties (ibid., chap. 120). To make this clear, the Catholics offered for reading the record of what the Donatists had declared before the Prefects on 30 January 406 (ibid., chap. 124). But they were absolutely not permitted to continue reading beyond the day whose date was prefixed. For since the Donatists had entangled and compromised themselves in that document, so that they might not be held convicted by their own words—as Possidius aptly charged them—they left nothing undone to prevent its being read (ibid., chap. 141).

For this reason they again thrust forward the already worn-out point, so often rejected by the Examiner: they wished to examine the instructions of the envoys through whom the Conference had been obtained. Although they demanded this with such passionate insistence that they seemed almost ready to dissolve the council for its sake, Marcellinus nevertheless persisted in refusing what was unjust, since he had promised that he would order nothing read except what either party wished to bring forward (ibid., chap. 140).

Accordingly, after they realized that they were making no progress by this route, they produced certain Catholic records drawn up before the sixth year counted from 400. These records accused the Donatists of various crimes and declared that, as schismatics, they were obliged to come together for a conference. The Donatists therefore demanded that these records, as older than those produced by the Catholics, be read first, and that the Catholics be declared plaintiffs on account of the crimes alleged in them (ibid., chap. 141).

Meanwhile the Catholics produced Anulinus’s report to Constantine, so that, if it was thought proper to follow the order of dates, the proceedings might begin with it as by far the earlier document (ibid., chaps. 144, 148). Marcellinus in fact ordered that this sequence be observed (ibid., chap. 150). Thus it came about that the question of which party were the plaintiffs—a question introduced by the Donatists solely to divert attention from the principal issue—gradually led, not without divine providence, to that very issue (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 7; *To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 43).

The Donatists noticed this and could not in any way restrain themselves from expressing their displeasure and declaring openly: “We are gradually being brought into the case” (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 151). By these words they made it sufficiently clear that throughout all their maneuvers they had only one aim: to ensure that nothing was accomplished. They therefore could not conceal that they knew the truth was against them. They repeated the same complaints a little later (ibid., chap. 193).

“O violence of truth,” Augustine exclaims, “stronger than any rack, stronger than any claws for forcing out a confession! Who could wring this most explicit utterance of fear from their closed hearts—not, I say, if we enriched them with the most lavish gifts, but even if we tortured them with the most savage punishments? The distinguished men who seemed to have been chosen to act cry out and testify that they were rather chosen not to act, and they maliciously complain to the judge that they are gradually being led into the heart of the case” (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 43). “O great, though not astonishing, confusion! For when has a demon ever feared an exorcist?” (ibid., no. 44).

Therefore, to evade that deeper investigation, they alleged that the Catholics were violating their pledge to stand solely by the Scriptures while making use of public documents ( *Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 149). Augustine answered this petition by saying that the Catholics claimed the Church to be catholic and were always entirely ready to establish her authority by divine utterances; but that, as for laws, official records, or anything else from the archives being offered for reading, the Donatists themselves were forcing them to do this, since they had been the first to proceed by such means. “They accuse us,” he said, “of the crime of handing over [the Scriptures], and either they do not prove it from the archives—in which case they say nothing—or they do prove it, and they compel us in turn to proceed by the archives” (ibid., chap. 155).

When Marcellinus supported this answer (ibid., chap. 156), the Donatists did not blush to resort once more to their long-rejected complaint about producing the envoys’ instructions, but with no greater success than before (ibid., chaps. 157, 164). Marcellinus therefore ordered the record brought forward by the Donatists, drawn up in 403, to be read (ibid., chap. 174), asking the Catholics meanwhile to allow their own documents, although older, to be postponed (ibid., chap. 170).

When this reading had been completed, Marcellinus said that it did indeed appear that the Catholics were the plaintiffs, since they charged the Donatists with schism and heresy; nevertheless, so that judgment on this matter might be made more fairly, other records likewise had to be read (ibid., chaps. 177, 180). Nothing was less agreeable to the evasive Donatists. Accordingly, here too they returned to their customary devices, introducing quibbles about the prescribed day, which they claimed had elapsed, about the instructions, and about the procedure. With the same refrain they incessantly deafened the ears of their hearers, so that either the principal issue might be omitted altogether, or at least no one might be found willing to read through records so lengthy and so tedious (ibid., chaps. 181, 183, 188, 215).

At last, however, the Examiner overcame their prolonged obstinacy and ordered Anulinus’s report, by which the Donatists’ complaints against Caecilian had been conveyed to Constantine, to be read (ibid., chaps. 216, 220). In this way the case began to be examined.

After Anulinus’s letter concerning Caecilian had been read, the Donatists—doubtless to forestall what was to follow from it—asked Augustine on what grounds he defended Caecilian, and whether Caecilian was his son or not (ibid., chaps. 221, 227). Augustine replied that Catholics acknowledged no true and proper father or head in matters pertaining to faith and salvation except Christ alone. Accordingly, when Paul called himself the father of the Corinthians, this must not be understood in that sense, but only because he was the steward of the ministry of the gospel (ibid., chaps. 222, 242).

Caecilian, therefore, held among the Catholics neither the place of father nor of mother—as they had foolishly asked—but only that of a brother, whether good or bad; for this made no difference to the Church (ibid., chap. 231). Augustine said that he was defending Caecilian’s case because they regarded him as innocent; but if the contrary should prove true, Caecilian alone would suffer from his guilt. If the opponents wished to withdraw their accusation against him, the Catholics would not defend him either, and the case would consequently be much shorter (ibid., chaps. 230, 232, 233).

This dispute continued for some time. Meanwhile, when Marcellinus occasionally replied to the Donatists with Augustine’s words, Petilian accused him—swearing an oath—that he favored the Catholics more than was proper (ibid., chaps. 233, 234).

### 4

When Augustine had finished his speech concerning the proper meaning of the name “father,” the Donatists asked by whom he had been consecrated bishop (ibid., chap. 243). Possidius, who had perceived the mind of that great man, his teacher, replied that the Catholics had not undertaken to defend Augustine’s case, whatever it might ultimately prove to be (ibid., chap. 245).

Nevertheless, they persisted and seemed to be searching for some ground of accusation in the ordination of the holy Bishop. But when Augustine himself openly stated that Megalius had laid hands upon him, and at the same time asked whether they had anything to say against this, they turned the discussion in another direction (ibid., chap. 247).

They therefore produced, in the name of their entire council, a written statement in which they attempted to prove from divine authorities that evil shepherds were stains and blemishes upon the Church, and that no wicked person ought to be among her children—at least none who had been detected and exposed. They were compelled by the force of truth itself to admit that some hidden wicked persons lurked within her (ibid., chap. 249).

Marcellinus declared that this document ought to have been drawn up not in the name of the entire party but only in the name of the seven disputants (ibid., chaps. 252, 253). The Catholics were therefore free to reject it and to object to its being read. Yet they did not wish to cause even the slightest delay or hesitation, lest they appear to fear the force of the arguments used by their opponents (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 49).

The Donatists therefore arranged for their document to be read by one of their bishops. The Catholics listened to him without interruption, with fair and kindly attention (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 257–259, 264).

They had composed that document in order to answer the mandate of the Catholics that had been read at the First Conference. Augustine demonstrated, however, that they had brought forward nothing that satisfied that mandate; this was clear from the mere reading of the two documents (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 10).

It was therefore especially advantageous to the Catholics that they had issued their own mandate to the opponents when the latter requested it through a formal notice (*Notoria*), and had likewise granted them the requested delay of seven days, so that they might produce some carefully prepared answer, meditated over for all those days. For it could clearly be seen from this that the points to which they gave no answer—points which were certainly very serious—had not been omitted through a failure of memory, but because they were beyond all possible answer (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 49).

### 5

After this document had been read, the schismatics themselves called upon the Catholics to answer it (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 260). Nothing could have been more welcome to the Catholics, and Augustine undertook the task, although the opponents continually interrupted him (ibid., chaps. 264, 267).

When he pressed the opponents concerning the necessity of tolerating the chaff of the Lord’s threshing floor until the winnowing, Emeritus denied that the threshing floor was mentioned in the Gospel (ibid., chap. 262). But the holy Bishop defeated him by quoting words from John; indeed, the Donatists themselves secretly warned Emeritus of his error. He corrected it in such a way, however, that he did not thereby assert a heretical or schismatic perversity. He immediately added that by the name “chaff” hidden wicked persons were signified (*Against Gaudentius* 2, no. 4). This answer is nevertheless attributed to Petilian in the records (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 263).

At last, only through the authority of the tribunes, Augustine scarcely obtained permission to speak in an uninterrupted sequence and without anyone intervening (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 16). He himself reduced to a summary the speech which he generally attributes to the Catholics. There he undertook with all his energy to establish the point that openly manifest as well as hidden wicked persons are tolerated in the Church, and that the good are not defiled by the sins of those who associate with them.

The beginning of this speech still survives in the records of the Conference (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 281); the remainder, together with the sequence of the proceedings—of which nothing survives except the titles of the sections—is lost.

The Donatists attempted to refute Augustine’s statement that the wicked had been sown in the Church by the devil (ibid., chaps. 282, 283). The Catholics confirmed this from other sources and especially by the authority of Bishop Cyprian, whom the schismatics professed to hold in the highest veneration. Whenever Cyprian’s words were brought against them, they neither dared nor were able to answer them, yet they refused to yield to his authority (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 20; *To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 10).

They also accused the Catholics of teaching that there were two Churches, one of which was mortal. This charge rested upon the distinction Augustine had made between the Church’s present condition, in which she is mortal—that is, composed of human beings subject to death—and her future condition, in which the saints will reign, freed from the laws of mortality (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 283, 287; Brevic. Collat. 3, nos. 16, 19).

It was not difficult to dispel this calumny. For when Augustine requested that his own words be reread, the Donatists were reduced to accusing not what he had said but what they claimed he had intended (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 284, 285).

In this way the case of the Church seemed to have been concluded. The Catholics had set out to demonstrate that she was stained by no one’s guilt—not Caecilian’s, nor anyone else’s. The Donatists themselves finally acknowledged this principle when, driven into difficulty by the history of the Maximianists (Epist. 141, no. 6; Brevic. Collat. 3, nos. 21–23, 27), they allowed truth to force from them the words Augustine so often applied to them: “Neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person” (*Nec causa causae, nec persona personae praejudicat*) (Epist. 141, no. 6; Epist. 142, no. 3; *To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 24, and elsewhere).

Marcellinus therefore pronounced that this point required no fuller discussion, and that after all the other matters had been examined he would also give judgment on it. The cause and origin of the schism must now be investigated (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 289).

Both parties insisted that judgment should be pronounced on each matter as soon as its examination had been completed (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 21). But Marcellinus replied that the law did not permit this: it was the duty of a judge to give judgment on the entire case at once and to keep his opinion restrained until the case had been completely concluded (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 292, 314).

### 6

When Marcellinus wished to investigate the original source and cause of the separation, the Donatists began to resist the inquiry with greater determination (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 21). They claimed that Christ alone was judge of a matter touching bishops and sought to bring the Catholics into disrepute because they had brought it before a human tribunal (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 245, 297).

They also inserted their customary complaints about the persecutions they claimed to be suffering. But the Catholics demonstrated that they themselves had first committed the very acts they denounced so spitefully. Nor did it help them to insist that the crimes of the Circumcellions had nothing to do with the bishops, since it was established that those frenzied men, under the leadership of their clergy, had committed so many and such dreadful atrocities.

This dispute about acts of harassment and injury was prolonged. But when Marcellinus ordered the documents produced by the Catholics to be read, it was finally brought to an end.

“Therefore, with the Church’s cause safe—confirmed, immutably fixed, and established as upon a rock’s foundation which the gates of hell cannot overcome—with the Church’s cause safe,” Augustine says, “we have also come to Caecilian’s case, now secure whatever he may be found to have committed. And we said: With the Church’s cause safe, since Caecilian’s sin prejudices it in nothing, let us examine his own case and see what it is. If we find him innocent, where will you then be, you who have failed even in your human accusation? But if he is found guilty, if he is found culpable, even then we are not defeated, because we possess the unity of the Church, which is unconquered. Let him be found altogether guilty; I anathematize the man, but I do not abandon Christ’s Church. This is what we did and said: henceforth we shall not name him at the altar among the bishops whom we believe to be faithful and innocent. This alone we did. Are you therefore going to rebaptize the whole world on account of Caecilian? With this security established and confirmed, Caecilian’s case began to be examined” (*Serm.* 359, no. 6).

Accordingly, Anulinus the proconsul’s letter to the emperor Constantine concerning the Donatists’ accusations against Caecilian was read; likewise another letter by the same Anulinus informing Constantine that he had sent Caecilian and his opponents to the Roman synod. This letter has not survived (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 316, 318).

To this reading were added Constantine’s letters to Miltiades and the other bishops appointed to the Roman council, as well as the first session of the Roman council held in 313 (ibid., chaps. 319, 321).

Here the Donatists interrupted, and they did not cease their uproar until the Tribune granted that the documents bearing upon Caecilian’s condemnation should be read (ibid., chaps. 322, 333).

They then argued that the schism had arisen because, during the persecution, Caecilian’s predecessor Mensurius had handed over the sacred books. To prove this accusation they read both Mensurius’s letter to Secundus of Tigisis and Secundus’s reply to Mensurius (ibid., chaps. 334–342).

These letters were private, and it could not in any way be established whether they were genuine or not. Yet they by no means made it clear that Mensurius had handed over the sacred books; nevertheless, they hinted at this none too obscurely concerning Secundus (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 27).

Next, with the Catholics’ agreement, the sentence issued against Caecilian by the council of Carthage was read (ibid., no. 26; *Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 346, 347).

The Catholics wished it to be noted that Mensurius had not been condemned by any public judgment, and that the Carthaginian council whose proceedings against Caecilian they had read had neither the name of a consul nor a date. They themselves willingly attributed this more to simple negligence than to fraud. Finally, Caecilian had been condemned in absentia by bishops who had themselves pardoned in another council the same offense for which they condemned him (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 351).

To make this last point clear, they requested that the council of Cirta, held in 305, be read. When its testimony was read with the consul and date, the schismatics attempted to weaken it on the ground that a date had been added to it contrary to the customary practice they wished to impose upon ecclesiastical records (ibid., chap. 353).

The Catholics, on the contrary, maintained that it had always been their custom to append the consul and date to councils (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 27). Nevertheless, the Donatists did not end the dispute until the Examiner openly declared that the authority of a decree was not destroyed by the addition of the consul’s name (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 393, 396).

The discussion therefore returned from the council of Cirta to the council of Carthage. The Donatists insisted that the Catholics acknowledge the authority of that council and confess Caecilian to be guilty, since he had been condemned by it. The Catholics replied that the Donatists themselves had clearly indicated that such a condemnation was entirely insufficient when they brought the matter before Constantine (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 30).

### 7

How weak the argument drawn from that Carthaginian council was, however, was demonstrated still more clearly by the history of Primianus, condemned in exactly the same manner by the Maximianists. The schismatics were thus caught in the nets of truth and driven into dreadful straits; in the confusion into which the mention of the Maximianists had thrown them, they could find nothing to say except what served as the Catholics’ foundation: neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, chap. 30; *Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 372).

Here Augustine bursts out with the words: “O brief, clear, true answer! No shorter, surer, or clearer judgment could have been delivered on our behalf” (*Serm.* 164, no. 13).

The Catholics wanted to extract nothing else from them. “If we offered mountains of gold,” he says, “when could we purchase that?” (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 52).

The same saint adds that they burdened the records with many unnecessary words; and since they could not prevent the case from being heard, they accomplished this by speaking at such length: they made what had been done difficult to read. “But even these few words of theirs ought to be sufficient for you, so that because of the crimes of I know not which people you may not hate the unity of the Catholic Church; for, as they themselves said, reread, and subscribed: ‘Neither does one case prejudice another case, nor one person another person’” (Epist. 141, no. 7).

Augustine goes on at greater length to show what uses the Church can draw from the truth confessed by the Donatist whose tongue had uttered it, although he was the most distinguished defender of his cause (Brevic. Collat. 3, nos. 2–4). “For he did not know what he said,” Augustine declares; “but, like Caiaphas, although he was high priest, he prophesied” (*Serm.* 164, no. 13).

After the Conference they attempted to turn their words into a meaning different from their own; but in vain. Hence Augustine exclaims: “O remarkable defense! The place where their feet have become stuck is so dense and tight that, as they try to pull themselves out, they plant both hands and head in vain, and, struggling in the same mud, become entangled even more tightly” (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 25).

This explains why even the most obstinate Donatists did not conceal that this one statement left them no room for any reply (Epist. 173, no. 7).

### 8

To continue the history of the Conference: the Tribune asked whether the Donatists had fled to Constantine before the council of Carthage or only after it had been held (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 377). What they answered him is not recorded.

The Catholics insisted that, whether this had occurred before or after the council in question, Constantine’s judgment had to be considered and the reading of the records continued (ibid., chaps. 379, 382). Thus, after various quibbles by the schismatics concerning the council of Cirta, the reading of the Roman synod—which had freed Caecilian from the charge—was continued and completed (ibid., chap. 403).

After this had been done, when the Donatists were required to answer concerning the Roman synod, as Marcellinus had asked them (ibid., chap. 405), they returned to the council of Cirta and asserted that it was spurious, on the ground that during the persecution it had not been possible to hold any council freely (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 32; *Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 407, 408).

Marcellinus wished the matter to be investigated (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 413). The Catholics therefore demonstrated, especially from the acts of the martyrs, that Christian congregations were accustomed to assemble even during an active persecution. The martyrs testified in their sufferings that they had gathered together and celebrated the Lord’s service.

Accordingly, they requested permission to send some of their own people, who could bring records containing such testimonies (ibid., chap. 419). When this was denied and the Catholics protested, the Donatists themselves produced certain acts of the martyrs for reading (ibid., chap. 432).

The Catholics also brought forward other acts of martyrs on their own behalf. From these it was clear that certain private individuals had offered their homes for assemblies of the faithful—which the Donatists claimed could in no way have happened—and that some people had even received baptism in prison itself, in a congregation gathered there (ibid., chaps. 433, 449, 451, 453).

After these documents had been read, the Tribune declared more than once that a council of twelve bishops, such as the council of Cirta had been, could easily have assembled even during a persecution (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 33; *Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 444).

The Donatists produced their own records—evidently those of the holy Saturninus, Dativus, and others—to show that the council of Cirta had been held during a persecution, since those records were dated 12 February 304. The Catholics, however, before the chronological indications had yet been examined, maintained that it had not been held until eleven months later. Indeed, thirteen months had elapsed since the martyrs’ suffering, since the council had been held on 5 March 305.

But the Office was ordered to calculate the interval between the date of that council and the date of those records by considering the consuls and the days; it reported that precisely one month had intervened. The Catholics were somewhat disturbed by this, since only after the Conference had ended did they discover that the acts of the martyrs were dated to the consulship of Diocletian and Maximian, whereas the acts of the council of Cirta were recorded after that consulship. The Office had therefore made a mistake because, in both sets of records, it had read the phrase not as “after the consulship” but simply as “in the consulship” (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 433, 435; Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 32).

The dispute over the acts of the council of Cirta was prolonged, and the Donatists did not cease pressing the Catholics to admit that they were spurious and falsified, although they themselves provided no evidence whatever that fraud had been committed here (Epist. 141, no. 11).

When Marcellinus at last compelled them to answer concerning the Roman synod, they declared Miltiades, under whose presidency it had been held, guilty of handing over the Scriptures. They embellished this accusation with various worthless and frivolous testimonies (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chap. 471).

### 9

When the question concerning the Roman and Cirtense councils appeared to have been sufficiently discussed, Constantine’s letters to Eumal­ius were read. In them Constantine himself had pronounced Caecilian innocent after hearing both parties (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 515, 530).

The Donatists found nothing to object to except to quibble that the letters did not bear the names of the consuls. But the Examiner declared that the rescript was in no way weakened by this omission (ibid., chaps. 523, 525, 528). Immediately afterward, however, a copy of the same letters was found in which the consuls were named (ibid., chap. 534).

They then resorted to another answer, considerably more substantial—if only it had rested upon the truth. They said that after that rescript Caecilian had been condemned by the same emperor, and that Optatus was a witness to the fact (ibid., chap. 532).

They had previously requested that the passage from Optatus be read, and Marcellinus had promised to arrange for this. Therefore, when they requested it a second time, the Catholics also agreed, while openly declaring beforehand that, if the same author happened to have fallen into error, this could in no way harm them, since his writings were not to be regarded as free from the possibility of error; that privilege belonged to canonical Scripture alone (ibid., chaps. 480, 482, 533).

One thing alone was discovered: Optatus wrote that Caecilian had been detained for some time at Brescia for the sake of peace (ibid., chap. 536). The Donatists then insisted that Optatus had wished to diminish Caecilian’s condemnation by using milder words.

The reply was that they must therefore find some other testimony by which they could prove this more clearly; their diligence in that search was fruitless. Marcellinus ordered the entire page of the codex to be read, so that Optatus’s meaning might be understood. From its reading it became clear that Optatus had recorded that the Roman council, by its judgment, had removed every suspicion of guilt from Caecilian.

For the Office read from it: “Caecilian was pronounced innocent by the judgment of all those mentioned above.” When this was read, the Donatists said that they had not requested this to be read and at the same time complained angrily against those who had been unable to restrain their laughter when they heard how openly the page produced by the Donatists themselves had contradicted them.

But since laughter could not be entered into the notaries’ records, the Donatists themselves testified in the Acts that they had been laughed at, saying: “Let those who laughed hear this.” The words were written down by the recorders and subscribed by the Donatists (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 38; *To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 54).

### 10

“Here they began to help us most openly,” Augustine says, “as though they had been instructed by us, or as though they had been chosen together with us to defend and establish Caecilian’s innocence” (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 54).

Indeed, in this respect they surpassed the diligence even of the Catholics themselves. For the Catholics produced two documents on Caecilian’s behalf, whereas the Donatists produced four (Epist. 14, no. 12): namely, Optatus’s testimony together with three other readings, two of which the Catholics, since they had not been equipped with them, would have been willing to purchase at a very high price (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 54).

The Donatists had to prove that Caecilian, whom the Catholics had shown to have been acquitted by Constantine in an earlier judgment, had been condemned by the same emperor in a subsequent hearing. To accomplish this, they produced a petition that they themselves had presented to the emperor (Brevic. Collat. 3, nos. 39, 40). By it, however, it was established both that they themselves had been condemned by him and that Caecilian’s innocence had been declared.

Next they brought forward the emperor’s letter to Verinus. In it Constantine expressed severe abhorrence of them and left their wickedness to the judgment of the Lord, who had already begun to avenge it upon them.

Nothing could have been clearer against them, and perhaps this was not hidden from them. Yet they hoped to obtain from the Tribune the same freedom that, as these letters made clear, Constantine had granted them. But the Tribune replied that Honorius had given him a different command (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 155, 552).

Thus, by producing all these documents, they achieved nothing except to make it clear that they themselves had been condemned. At the same time they were convicted of how unjustly they had stirred up hatred and hostility against the Catholics on the ground that the Catholics had brought the Church’s case before the emperor. For the Donatists themselves admitted that Caecilian had been accused before Constantine by their predecessors and, as a result of their prosecution, condemned by him—although they falsely kept proclaiming this (Epist. 141, no. 8).

They now seemed unable to produce anything that could assist the Church more fully. Yet they did produce something, and, like Balaam, who against his will blessed God’s people, they too, against their will and with God compelling them, rendered remarkable service to the Catholic party.

For it was in the Church’s interest to demonstrate the innocence also of Felix of Aptunga, by whom Caecilian had been ordained. The Catholics had documents concerning this matter at hand, which they could produce when the circumstances of the case required it. Yet they might not have used them, since Caecilian’s innocence was sufficiently clear from other evidence.

The Donatists, however, forestalled them. They placed before the court Constantine’s letters—something no one would have expected them to do—in which the emperor acknowledged that, after the case had been examined, Felix had been acquitted of the charge of handing over the Scriptures. He also decreed that Ingentius, who had confessed that he had given false testimony against Felix, should be sent to the imperial court, where Caecilian’s accusers, excessively troublesome and persistent, were to be refuted.

The Donatists produced those letters, which were strongly against them, because they wanted them to be regarded as later than Constantine’s judgment against themselves. Their aim was evidently to persuade the court that the case had by no means been settled by that judgment, and that it was therefore necessary to examine what had followed from Ingentius’s being sent there (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 55).

The Catholics replied that there could no longer be any doubt that Caecilian had been acquitted by Constantine, and that it was now incumbent upon the Donatists to prove by legitimate arguments that the other trial had actually been instituted (Brevic. Collat. 3, no. 42).

Later, when the chronological indications were compared, it was understood that Ingentius’s case had occurred before Caecilian’s acquittal. Meanwhile, the Catholics gained this advantage: the testimonies used by their opponents wonderfully strengthened Felix’s innocence.

The Catholics themselves also further confirmed it by producing the report of Aelianus the proconsul, who had investigated Felix’s case, to Constantine, and even the records of that investigation. The Donatists found nothing of any weight to oppose these documents.

### 11

At last, when the Catholics saw that the matters they had been obliged to defend had been sufficiently examined, they requested that the Examiner bring the lawsuit to an end by his judgment (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 571, 576).

The Donatists, on the contrary, continued endlessly to introduce the same objections and complained that the documents they themselves had produced on their own behalf had been falsified at the opponents’ initiative (ibid., chap. 583).

When it had become clear that no new document remained to be read, Marcellinus ordered both parties to withdraw so that he might have room to write his judgment. At last night came on (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 16)—for in that age it often happened that judges were compelled by the necessity of hearing cases to sit until late at night and could settle lawsuits only during the night.

When the bishops had again been ordered to enter, Marcellinus read his judgment. In it he summarized the entire case and declared that the Donatists had been refuted by the manifest force of all the arguments brought forward by the Catholics.

After this judgment had been published, extraordinary joy arose among everyone, because God had at last revealed on whose side the truth stood and on whose side falsehood and error (*Collat. Carthag.* 3, chaps. 584, 585).

## CHAPTER XIII

1. How greatly Augustine distinguished himself in the Conference.  
2. The many evasions and subterfuges of the Donatists.  
3. How prudently Marcellinus conducted himself.  
4. The Donatists appeal to the Emperor.  
5. Marcellinus publishes the records of the Conference in a written edict against the schismatics.  
6. Augustine reduces them to a summary.  
7. After the Conference, many Donatists return to the Church.  
8. Among them, Gabinus and the virgin Felicia are mentioned by name.

1. Such was the outcome of that celebrated assembly, which the African Church had now been seeking for a full eight years, and which we rightly count among the chief fruits of Augustine’s episcopate. Certainly there can be no dispute that, on the Catholic side, he was virtually its guiding mind; nor, in our judgment, is anything else better suited to show how powerful that doctor and defender of the Church was in intellectual ability. For although he everywhere extols Alypius’s outstanding gifts, and although those entrusted with the task of disputation were beyond doubt the most distinguished and learned of all the African bishops of their age, nevertheless in all Augustine’s words there shines such force of intellect, such fluency and grace, and finally such a combination of charm and vigor, that the brilliance of the others fades and is extinguished before him. He leaves the juridical formulas, and the task of watching whether the Donatists should make any mistake, to Alypius and Possidius; but whenever some difficult and important question is debated, or the faith of the Church must be upheld, then everyone entrusts to him the duty and role of disputing. This is why one finds him scarcely speaking at all in the first two Collations, whereas in what has survived for us from the third, we hear him almost everywhere. If some have observed that he treated the same matters much more clearly and forcefully in his books than in the Collation, they also acknowledge that the Donatists’ frequent interruptions did not allow him to exercise there the same intellectual freedom (Baldus, *Historia Collationis*, p. 125 C–D). Perhaps one may likewise attribute to that kind of disturbance, or to the heat of the debate, the fact that some have observed—although they regarded it as the result of carelessness—that the Catholics did not sufficiently distinguish between the lawful rites of the kingdom of Judah and those of the kingdom of Israel, where worship was celebrated contrary to the law; rather, they affirmed in general that communion in Jewish rites had never been rejected by the Prophets.

2. From the entire course of the proceedings it is certainly possible to perceive how many devices and quibbles the Donatists employed. Petilianus, who had practiced as an advocate in the courts and played the leading role in this case, revealed himself to be much more skilled in forensic technique than in ecclesiastical doctrine. Emeritus, who himself held second place, although he seems to have possessed some ability in speaking, expressed his meaning with such a tangle of words that we usually grasped it only with the greatest difficulty (Baldus, *Historia Collationis*, p. 123). All their delaying quibbles and evasions aimed at prolonging the decision of the case. As a result, far more time and speech were spent on trifling matters unrelated to the issue than on the very heart of the case. Indeed, one should rather say that they pursued only this: by doing much, to ensure that absolutely nothing would be done.

Hence Saint Augustine addresses the Donatists in these words:

> Behold the bishops of your party, whom all had chosen to speak for everyone. They tried, as far as they could, to prevent the very case from being heard, the case for which so great a number of bishops of both parties from all Africa and from such distant places had come to Carthage. And while every soul, suspended in expectation, awaited what would be done in so great an assembly, they pressed vehemently that nothing should be done. Why was this, unless they knew that their case was bad and could not doubt that, if it were heard, they would very easily be defeated? Their very state of mind, by which they feared that the case would be heard, showed that they were already defeated. For if they had extorted what they wanted—namely, that the Collation itself should not take place and that the truth should not appear through our disputations—what answer would they have had to give you on returning from Carthage? What would they have demonstrated? I believe they would have produced the proceedings and said to you: “We pressed that the case should not be heard; they pressed that it should be heard. You are waiting to see what we accomplished. Here, read where we defeated them: by doing nothing.” Perhaps you would have replied, if you had any heart: “If you were going to do nothing, why did you come against these men? Or rather, since you did nothing, why did you return?”

(*Epist.* 141, no. 3).

He writes elsewhere:

> So many bishops are gathered from all Africa; they enter Carthage with such a splendid display of procession that the eyes and attention of so great a city are turned toward them. Those who are to speak for everyone are chosen by everyone. A place worthy of so important a matter is also secured in the center of the city. Both parties assemble; the judge is present; the records lie open; everyone’s hearts, held in suspense, await the outcome of so great a Collation. Then, by men of the highest distinction and eloquence, with as much power as possible, something ought to have been done; yet they act with such force that nothing is done.

(*Ad Donatistas post Collationem*, ch. 25, no. 43).

Nothing could have demonstrated more certainly how suspicious they themselves were of their case than their extreme fear that the matter should be unraveled and explained. Thus, above all, the schismatics—conscious of their weakness and poverty—desired that the controversy should not be discussed at all. When they could not achieve this, at least they prolonged the proceedings with such lengthy and superfluous speeches that scarcely anyone could endure reading them.

“As to whether they did this,” Augustine says, “more from lack of truth or from the skill of their cunning, I do not know. Yet by this means they could only somehow assist so extremely bad a case, which they ought rather to have abandoned. Finally, if the others who took part in the proceedings accuse them and claim that they had been corrupted by us, so that by so many arguments, or by the readings they themselves produced, they should aid our case and destroy their own, I do not know how they could defend themselves or clear themselves of this suspicion, unless perhaps they say: ‘If we had been corrupted, we would have brought to an early conclusion a case so bad, and convicted both by us and by them. But now believe this very fact: we were present sincerely and wished to be of some help; by speaking at such length, we ensured that what was done would not easily be read and that it would quickly become known that we had been defeated.’ If they did not say this, perhaps no one would believe—even if they swore it, either they or we—that they had freely provided us with all the many things they said and read against themselves in our favor. Yet we give thanks for this not to them, but rather to God. For when they brought forward and disclosed all those things, whether by speaking or by reading, in support of our case, truth tormented them; charity did not move them” (*Ibid.*, no. 57).

They tried to weaken the strength of truth and, as far as they could, to cloud its clarity with the mists of empty arguments. “The Lord was present; his clarity overcame their clouds” (*Serm.* 164, no. 12). Thus almost nothing did they bring forward that worked against the Catholics rather than against themselves.

3. Marcellinus, who presided over this tribunal, brought to a case of such importance an altogether exceptional diligence, combined with expertise in both civil and ecclesiastical law. This was not in order to determine on which side the truth stood—for even if he had been bribed by the Donatists, he could not have failed to condemn them when they had been convicted by their own proofs—but in order to disentangle the tricks and evasions of such litigants and, removing their tergiversations, bring them to address the matter at issue. He also displayed extraordinary gentleness and patience, so much so that he might have been suspected of a greater partiality toward the Donatists, had his reputation for integrity and uprightness been less established. In fact, he deliberately conducted himself in this manner. For when he saw them oppressed by the truth, and did not wish them to think that he was hostile to them, he tolerated with extreme patience men wandering through empty matters, saying so many superfluous things, and returning again and again to points that had already been refuted (*Ad Donatistas post Collationem*, no. 57).

4. Although the Donatists themselves had anticipated his judgment—whether by producing documents against themselves, or by the distrust and despair concerning their case that they could not conceal—they nevertheless appealed to the Emperor. Those who had witnessed the proceedings and examined their own words, written down and subscribed there, by which they themselves had destroyed their case, were astonished at this (Possidius, *Vita Augustini*, no. 15; Augustine, *Ad Donatistas post Collationem*, no. 16). Yet while appealing from the judge, they nevertheless boasted that they had departed from the contest as victors (*Serm.* 359, no. 6).

It is not sufficiently clear whether their appeal was the same as that written statement which, according to reports, they issued immediately after the Collation and which Augustine refuted in his book *To the Donatists after the Collation* (*Ad Donatistas post Collat.*, no. 32). Nevertheless, they did not hesitate to produce again the very passages of Scripture that had already been discussed in the Collation: namely, this one taken from the Apostle, “Do not be yoked with unbelievers” (2 Cor. 6:14), and others of the same kind; but above all they displayed the passage from Haggai, “Whoever approaches it shall be defiled” (Hag. 2:14). There they attempted to explain what they had said in the Collation: “The case does not prejudice the case, nor the person the person” (*Ad Donatistas post Collat.*, no. 25).

They complained that the sentence had been pronounced at night (*Ibid.*, nos. 16, 20, 58); that they themselves had been shut up in the place of the Collation as though in a prison; that they had been deprived of the opportunity freely to bring forward whatever they wished; and that, because the judge professed the Catholic faith, he had also been more favorably disposed toward the Catholics (*De Gestis cum Emerito*, no. 2). Emeritus, their principal defender at the Collation (Possidius, *Vita Augustini*, ch. 14), later said that whether he had been overcome by authority or crushed by force was apparent to anyone from the proceedings themselves (*De Gestis cum Emerito*, no. 3). Then he himself joined the others in spreading publicly that the judge had been bribed with gold by the Catholics (*Ibid.*, no. 2; *Ad Donatistas post Collat.*, nos. 1, 39, 57, etc.).

Although they had appealed to the Emperor, they nevertheless subscribed the proceedings of the third Collation just as they had those of the preceding two, though almost everywhere adding that they subscribed “without prejudice to the appeal.” Marcellinus’s subscription, although he had initially promised that he would subscribe, is entirely absent from the records of the three days. It could certainly have happened that, with both parties consenting to this, he was relieved of the obligation.

5. No one, we think, should doubt that the proceedings of the Collation were publicly posted as soon as they had been more neatly transcribed. The Cognitor’s edict appended to the end of the Collation must undoubtedly be understood in this connection. It is not equally clear, however, whether this should be regarded as a sentence pronounced in favor of the Catholics, in which, according to Augustine, Marcellinus summarized everything he could remember from the lengthy proceedings of the three days (*Brevic. Collat.* 3, no. 43).

In the edict he declares the following points to have been established with the utmost clarity (Labbe, vol. 2, p. 1505): that one person absolutely cannot be made guilty by another person’s crime; consequently, the Church could not have been defiled by the charges brought against Caecilianus; nor had Caecilianus in any way been convicted of any offense, since the Council by which he had been condemned unheard and in his absence could no more harm him than the synod of the Maximianists could harm Primianus, who likewise was absent. He had, moreover, been acquitted of the charge in many subsequent judgments; Donatus had been declared the author of the schism; and Felix of Aptunga had likewise been cleared of a false accusation in a solemn judgment.

There he touches upon the Donatists’ obstinacy, since they seemed to prefer perishing in their error to returning freely to the way of salvation. To test whether severity might perhaps extract from them what the force of truth had been unable to obtain—or at least to prevent them from bringing upon others the same destruction they had brought upon themselves—he decrees, by imposing a very heavy fine, that men of every rank should do everything in their power to prevent their assemblies from meeting either in the cities or anywhere at all. He further orders them to ensure that the churches which, by his own earlier command, had been restored to the Donatists before the Collation should as soon as possible be handed over to the Catholics.

He solemnly declares that those who now defect to the Donatist faction can no longer avoid the penalty established by the laws promulgated on this matter, although those laws had not yet been fully enforced. He also orders all who harbor Circumcellions on their estates to restrain their seditious efforts; if they do not obey, those places are immediately to be seized by the imperial treasury, since this concerns not only the Catholic faith but also the public peace.

Nevertheless, confirming the security of passage that he had granted the Donatists in his earlier edict, he forbids anyone to obstruct their return, until, restored to their respective homes, they declare whether they have decided to return to the Church and finally accept the conditions that the Catholics had offered them before the Collation and were still offering them at that time.

Augustine also testifies that, after the Collation had been completed, those who returned to Catholic communion were not deprived of their episcopal dignity, although those who stubbornly persisted in error took this as an opportunity for arrogance (*Ad Donatistas post Collat.*, no. 58).

Marcellinus does not explicitly mention the Donatists’ appeal in his edict. He simply orders the observance of the earlier laws, renewed by the Emperor’s command that the Collation be held. After Marcellinus had died, Honorius confirmed the proceedings of the Collation by a law issued on the third day before the Kalends of September in the year 414, and ordered that they be regarded as valid and lawful (*Codex Theodosianus*, *De Haereticis*, law 55).

6. The most vigilant of the bishops—especially those of Carthage, Hippo, Tagaste, and Constantine—had these proceedings read aloud from beginning to end during the Lenten fast, when the people had greater leisure to hear this reading. Augustine himself, when he was at Caesarea in the year 418, presented himself as an example and exhorter to Deuterius, bishop of that city, so that he might imitate the same practice (*De Gestis cum Emerito*, no. 4).

Idacius undoubtedly records these proceedings in his *Chronicle*, where, under the year 412, he says: “Augustine is held distinguished; among his magnificent labors, the authenticated proceedings demonstrate that, by God’s help, the Donatists were overcome.”

Nor were these events unknown to the Greeks, since the Fifth Council, from the 187th article of the third Collation, quotes certain words of Augustine by which it demonstrates that it is permissible to pronounce an anathema against the dead.

The proceedings of the first two Collations, together with part of the third, have survived to our own age, but have been disfigured by numerous errors. Since they are extremely long, entangled in highly complicated digressions, and burdensome to read, a certain Marcellus—whom Marcellinus had wished to possess some authority in this tribunal—was asked by Severianus and Julianus, evidently Catholics, to reduce them to an abridgment. A letter still survives in which Marcellus informs them that he had fulfilled what they requested and had also added numerical markings throughout the articles, so that whatever one wished might be found more conveniently (Labbe, vol. 2, p. 1337).

We do not determine whether this little work of Marcellus should be identified with the titles of the articles of the Collation, which one sees appended to that letter and prefixed to each Collation. Certainly, they provide some sort of summary of the proceedings. But since this summary is itself obscure and incomplete, it did not prevent Augustine from preparing another, which still exists, divided according to the number of sessions of the Collation.

He believed that this labor would be useful because it made it possible to learn what had taken place in the Collation and, by the same means, to consult the proceedings themselves whenever one wished, thanks to the numbers that had been written in the margin of the work—though they are now absent—and that indicated the articles of the Collation.

The holy Doctor testifies that this work, which he calls the *Brief Summary of the Collation* (*Breviculum Collationis*) (*Retractationes*, book 2, ch. 39), was a work of great toil. Nevertheless, he did not consider himself free to decline it, because no one would read through proceedings so lengthy (*Epist.* 139, no. 3). He refers Count Boniface to this same abridgment (*Epist.* 185, no. 6). He did not undertake it, however, until after completing his books on the baptism of infants, namely in the year 412, as we shall later demonstrate, God willing.

7. The sermon on the Apostle to the Galatians seems, however, to belong to the year 411. Augustine may perhaps have delivered it at Carthage when the proceedings of the Collation were just about to be posted publicly (*Serm.* 164, no. 13). In it he indicates, among other reasons, why the Donatist leaders hardened their minds in schism: namely, that they feared offending those to whom they had sold falsehood for so long.

At the same time he explains what disposition the love of truth—had they possessed it in their hearts—ought to have suggested to them in addressing the peoples whom they had deceived. “Let them say to their people,” he says: “We have gone astray together; let us withdraw from error together. We were your leaders to the pit, and you followed us when we led you to the pit; now follow us when we lead you to the Church. It would indeed have been better if we had never gone astray; but let us at least do what comes second, so that we may eventually correct our error” (*Ibid.*, no. 14).

Then he adds:

> They could say such things; they could say them to those who were indignant, to those who were angry. At some point they too might lay aside their indignation and love unity, even if late.

Finally, turning his address to the Catholics, he speaks to them as follows:

> Nevertheless, brothers, let us be patient toward them; they are in a state of heat and swelling—the eyes that we are treating. I do not say that we should cease treating them, but that we should not provoke them by taunts to still greater bitterness. Let us give our explanation gently; let us not exult arrogantly over the victory.

(*Ibid.*, no. 15).

That prudent method of action adopted by Augustine was not entirely without the success he hoped for, since after the Collation many returned to the faith of the Church, including even Circumcellions. Speaking of them, Augustine says:

> Charity must be exercised; they too must be loved. Many, when corrected, wept—many who were corrected. We know that they came to us from the number of those madmen. Every day they weep over their former conduct, and they are not satisfied with their tears, when they consider the madness of those who, their intoxication with vanity not yet dispelled, still rage.

(*Serm.* 359, no. 8).

Elsewhere he says of the same people:

> Who does not know how many of this kind formerly went through various deaths and perished, and how few now, in comparison with them, burn in their own fires? But if you think that we ought to be moved because so many thousands die in this way, how great do you think our consolation must be that many more thousands, far more and beyond comparison, are freed from the great madness of the party of Donatus, where not only the error of an unholy division but also this madness itself had become law? For those who perish do not even equal the number of those who, from that very group, are now held under the order of discipline, cultivate their fields, and, having abandoned both the work and the name of the Circumcellions, devote themselves to labor, preserve chastity, and maintain unity. How much less do these lost people equal the number of both sexes—not only boys and girls, young men and maidens, but also married people and the elderly—of whom countless numbers are passing from the wicked dissension of the Donatists into the true and Catholic peace of Christ? Those who set themselves on fire are not even as numerous as the places filled with peoples that are being rescued, through this persistent effort to achieve unity, from the deadly plague of that error and madness.

(*Contra Gaudentium*, book 1, no. 33).

8. Among those who withdrew from the faction of Donatus, a certain Gabinus is mentioned first, as a man distinguished above others by his rank (*Ibid.*, nos. 12, 13, 43). In the year 418 there was scarcely any Donatist at Caesarea who had not returned to the bosom of the Catholic Church, although the truth was still not fully known and understood by very many of them (*De Gestis cum Emerito*, no. 2).

Nor could it have happened otherwise than that, amid the ranks of so many great peoples, some were still disturbed by the novelty of the matter; yet these too were gradually healed of their weakness. And even if some continued in pretense, the truthful were not therefore to be left unassembled on their account (*Contra Gaudentium*, book 1, no. 27).

Among Augustine’s sermons there also survives a brief address to the people, beginning: “Thanks be to God, brothers; rejoice with your brother” (*Serm.* 360). From its inscription and style, one might reasonably infer that Augustine composed it, but in the name of that Donatist who gives public thanks to God because he had been freed from error.

This same sermon is prefaced as having been delivered at the vigil of Maximianus or Maximinus—that is, if we are not mistaken, during the nocturnal Office of an African martyr bearing that name, whose identity has not come down to our memory. Augustine likewise expounded Psalm 72 at the vigil of Saint Cyprian; he does not specify whether this took place at Carthage. The only point beyond doubt is that it occurred not long after the present year had elapsed, since in a letter written approximately in the middle of the year 412 he refers Honoratus to the same exposition (*Epist.* 140, no. 13).

There he indicates with what eagerness the people lent him their ears, and he denies that he could now equal their ardor; finally, he pleasantly complains that their enthusiasm compels him (*Enarr. in Ps.* 72, no. 34).

Among those whom God willed to be compelled by his servants to enter the wedding hall, a certain virgin named Felicia is recorded. Christ did not permit her, steadfast in the fruit of the virginity she had dedicated to him, to remain abandoned in schism. In later years Augustine evidently regarded her, while she lived in his diocese, as a daughter especially dear and honorable to him, and as a living member of Christ’s body through the presence of the Holy Spirit.

A letter addressed to her has survived, in which he comforts her after she had been disturbed by some scandal and urges her to rely upon the one God, not upon human beings; at the same time he encourages her to continue loving the Church, into whose bosom she had withdrawn, no less on that account. He asks her to inform him by reply with what disposition she had received the letter, assuring her that concern and solicitude for her salvation had moved him to write to her (*Epist.* 208).

After returning to Hippo from the Collation, Augustine arranged for its proceedings to be read aloud to the people. He perhaps indicates this when, in Sermon 99, delivered during the summer heat not long after the Collation had ended, he refers to certain events that had occurred in it and adds: “You can also read this in the proceedings themselves” (*Serm.* 99, no. 8). In that sermon he inveighs vigorously against the Donatists.

# BOOK SEVEN

It comprises the eight years from 411, the year in which Augustine began to have dealings with the enemies of God’s grace.

[Col. 0439]

## CHAPTER ONE

1. Pelagius begins to put forward his heresy. 2. His disciple Caelestius is condemned by the Council of Carthage. 3. Augustine attacks the Pelagians and writes for Marcellinus two books *On the Baptism of Infants*. 4. He appends an Epistle to the same man, or a third book added to the preceding books against the Pelagians. 5. The book dedicated to the same Marcellinus, *On the Spirit and the Letter*. 6. At Carthage he delivers a sermon to the people against the error of the Pelagians. 7. He replies to Pelagius. 8. In his letter to Anastasius he proves the necessity of grace for fulfilling the law. 9. Replying to Honoratus, he discusses the grace of the New Testament.

1. The Donatist war, after approximately one hundred and five years during which the African Church had been most violently harassed by them, was at last happily ended; but another war against the Pelagians immediately had to be undertaken, one that would be far more dangerous to the whole Church in magnitude and more troublesome in duration. Yet just as Augustine bore off the palm in all the battles waged with the Donatists for the peace of the Church—for through him the whole benefit of restored unity was both begun and completed (Possidius, *Vita Augustini*, ch. 13)—so, in every contest with the enemies of God’s grace, from the very time when battle against them began, the Catholic battle-line fights and conquers under the leadership of this same holy man (Prosper, *Contra Collatorem*, no. 2).

No one is unaware that these hostile forces against God’s grace, which strive to overthrow the very foundations of the entire Christian faith, are called Pelagians after Pelagius, their author and leader (*Epist.* 176, nos. 3–4). He was born in Britain, whence his surname “the Briton,” of humble rank. Having adopted the monastic way of life, he enjoyed for some time a reputation for holiness that was by no means ordinary. He gathered the seeds of his error from the ancient philosophers and also from Origen (*Epist.* 178, no. 2; *Epist.* 157, no. 21; *Epist.* 175, no. 6). At Rome, where he lived for a very long time, he disseminated them both in writings and in private conversations and debates, though in the latter he proceeded cautiously and avoided commotion as far as possible (*De Peccato originali*, no. 24).

Augustine first learned the name of the absent Pelagius, then living at Rome, together with great praise of him; later reports began to reach him that Pelagius argued against God’s grace (*De Gestis Pelagii*, no. 46). When the words of the holy Doctor, “Give what you command, and command what you will,” were mentioned at Rome, in Pelagius’s presence, by a certain bishop, Pelagius could not bear them and, objecting with some agitation, almost quarreled with the man who had mentioned them (*De Dono perseverantiae*, no. 53).

Afterwards, when he came to Africa, he was received on the shore of Hippo while Augustine was away, apparently in the year 410; but nothing whatever was heard from him there that savored of his heresy, because he left sooner than had been expected. Subsequently Augustine saw him once and again at Carthage, namely in 411, when he was occupied with the very weighty business of the conference which Catholics were to hold with the Donatists. Pelagius, however, then departed from Carthage and hurried overseas (*De Gestis Pelagii*, no. 46).

2. Meanwhile, through the mouths of those said to be Pelagius’s disciples, the doctrines of the new heresy were rife in Africa (*Ibid.*). There were certain persons there who scattered these new seeds of their error wherever they could. One of them, Caelestius by name, easily the foremost of Pelagius’s disciples, had already begun to insinuate himself into the Church of the city of Carthage with a view to attaining the honor of the presbyterate. Because of these very arguments against Christ’s grace, he was brought before episcopal judgment by Catholic men animated by love of the Christian faith (*Epist.* 157, no. 22).

Aurelius held a council on the matter at Carthage with his colleagues, perhaps at the very beginning of 412, certainly nearly five years before the other Carthaginian synod held in 416 in the same case of Pelagius and Caelestius (*Epist.* 175, no. 1). Two written accusations, containing the charges brought against Caelestius, were presented to the council, and the deacon Paulinus appeared against him. Augustine adduces a fragment from the proceedings of this council, showing that at this episcopal trial Caelestius refused to condemn those who say: “Adam’s sin harmed himself alone and not the human race”; and: “The infants who are born are in the state in which Adam was before his transgression” (*De Peccato originali*, nos. 2–3).

Nevertheless, Caelestius, unable to withstand Christian countenances (*Contra Julianum*, book 3, no. 9), was compelled in his very brief written statement to confess, because infants are baptized, that redemption is necessary even for them (*De Peccatorum meritis*, book 1, no. 62; *Epist.* 157, no. 22; *De Peccato originali*, no. 21), although he would not confess that sin had passed to them from Adam (*De Peccatorum meritis*, book 2, no. 58; *De Peccato originali*, no. 21). But although he would not speak more expressly about original sin, nevertheless, the holy Doctor says, he gave himself no small disadvantage by the very word “redemption.” For from what were they to be redeemed, if not from the devil’s power, in which they could not be unless bound by original sin? Or at what price are they redeemed, if not by Christ’s blood, of which it is written most plainly that it was shed for the remission of sins (*Epist.* 157, no. 22)?

At the Synod of Diospolis it was reported, in addition to the two heads just mentioned, that Caelestius had also been accused before the Council of Carthage of teaching that Adam had been made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin; that the Law sends to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel; that there had been persons without sin before Christ’s coming; and that neither does the entire human race die through Adam’s death or transgression, nor does the entire human race rise through Christ’s resurrection (*De Peccato originali*, no. 12). Augustine records these things in two places, in one of which he testifies that some of these heads were not, as he remembered, contained in the ecclesiastical proceedings of this Carthaginian council. He himself had not been present at it, but when he came to Carthage, he reviewed the same proceedings (*De Gestis Pelagii*, no. 23).

It was not difficult, however, to convict Caelestius in that council; to correct him was altogether impossible.
