Therefore, after he had been heard, convicted, and had even confessed his own opinions, the doctrines of which he had been accused were condemned (*Epist.* 157, no. 22); he himself received a sentence worthy of his perversity (*De Gestis Pelagii*, no. 46), being punished by excommunication (*Retractationes*, book 2, ch. 33). After that judgment he departed in disgrace and fled from Africa (Orosius, *Apology*).

### 3

Although those who had allowed themselves to be imbued with the Pelagian error were undoubtedly fewer in Africa, and, deterred by Caelestius’s condemnation, no longer dared openly to mutter against the Church’s thoroughly established faith, but only in secret (Epist. 157, no. 22), nevertheless the holy Bishop resolved to oppose vigorously this new heresy, which in his judgment was no less deadly than impious. Previously he had dealt with it only in sermons and conversations, whenever it seemed appropriate and useful (Retractations, book 2, chapter 33). But a necessity that soon arose [Col. 0442] led him to refute it in writing as well.

Marcellinus—the same man who had been the judge at the Carthaginian conference—was unable to answer the followers of this heresy, whom he had to endure every day as most troublesome disputants. He therefore sent their questions by letter from Carthage to Augustine, asking him not to hesitate to write out their solution for him (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 25). Above all, he sought an explanation of the question concerning the baptism of infants. They maintained that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned, and that nothing had passed from his sin to his descendants by propagation (On the Merits and Remission of Sins, book 3, no. 1). For although, as Marcellinus reported in his letter, they now admitted that sins were forgiven even in infants through Baptism, “they nevertheless said that this was not original sin; rather, after they were born, they began to have sin in their own life” (ibid., book 1, no. 62).

Marcellinus further reported that they were twisting into another new opinion that apostolic testimony: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death” (Romans 5:12). Nor did he omit the question by which they attempted to persuade people that in this life there are, have been, and will be children of human beings who have absolutely no sin (On the Merits and Remission of Sins, book 3, no. 1).

At that time the holy Doctor was greatly hindered by troubles and anxieties arising from the affairs that sinful men—and perhaps Donatists—were causing him; in his characteristic humility, he attributes this to the merits of his own sins (ibid., book 1, no. 1). Nevertheless, he could not fail to accommodate the praiseworthy desire of a man to whom he was joined by a great and holy bond. Moreover, the charitable concern that he ought to have had for Christ’s Church by no means allowed him, when he saw the minds of many weak people disturbed by the fiercely contentious assertions of these opinions, which were already raging everywhere, to impose silence upon himself in the meantime (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 25). This was especially so because those new heretics were spreading the poison of their doctrine publicly and privately, not only by word of mouth but also in books, and these books were all the more harmful because they had been written with greater cunning and skill (Possidius, Life of Augustine, no. 21).

Among the works that he composed to refute the Pelagians and to answer Marcellinus’s questions, the two books *On the Merits and Remission of Sins* take the leading place. This is how Augustine calls them in the *Retractations* (book 2, chapter 33). Elsewhere, however, he calls them *On the Baptism of Infants*, the title by which Jerome also refers to them (Against the Pelagians, dialogue 3, chapter 6).

In the first book he demonstrates that human death comes from the guilt of Adam’s sin, that Adam’s entire stock is held bound by that sin, and that infants are therefore baptized so that they may receive remission of their original sin. In the second he teaches that a human being can be without sin in this life through God’s grace and his own free will, but that no one in this life is entirely without any sin. No one wills as much as the situation requires, either because what is just remains hidden or because doing it is not pleasing. Finally, with the one Mediator [Col. 0443], Christ, excepted, there is no human being who is, has been, or will be immune from every sin.

In this second book he obscurely indicates the booklet submitted by Caelestius to the Council of Carthage, in which Caelestius admitted that infants needed redemption (On the Merits and Remission of Sins, book 2, no. 58). In the *Retractations*, however, he openly states that he wrote these books only after that council, whose sentence had excommunicated Caelestius himself (book 2, chapter 33)—that is, in the year 412.

Even so, he still thought it necessary to keep his opponents’ names silent, because he hoped that by this method they could more easily be corrected. In this work Augustine mentions a certain man belonging to that class of fools who provide amusement for others, commonly called buffoons. “One of these,” he says, “was so much a Christian that, although with remarkable foolishness he was the most patient of all the injuries done to him, nevertheless he could not endure an injury to the name of Christ, or to the religion with which he had been imbued, in such a way that he would not continue attacking with stones those who blasphemed—men whom he heard saying such things in order to provoke him—and he did not spare even their masters.

“I therefore think that such people are predestined and created so that those who are able may understand the grace of God, and the Spirit who breathes where he wills, and may understand that for this reason he does not pass over every kind of character among the children of mercy, nor does he pass over every kind of character among the children of Gehenna, so that ‘whoever boasts may boast in the Lord’” (On the Merits and Remission of Sins, book 1, no. 32).

A little later he adds that this fool was to be preferred, in Christ’s grace, to many extremely clever people.

### 4

Now that these books had been completed and sent to Marcellinus, it is probable that the blessed Bishop went to Carthage. For he addresses that same Marcellinus as follows:

“I have forgotten why I received again from you the books *On the Baptism of Infants*, since I had already sent the very codex to Your Excellency—unless perhaps, when I examined them, I found them faulty and wished to correct them; but, being extraordinarily hindered, I have still not done so” (Epist. 139, no. 3).

A few days later, when Pelagius’s commentaries on Paul’s Epistles had come into his hands, Augustine found in them an argument against original sin that he had not refuted at all. It had simply never entered his mind that anyone could think or say such things (On the Merits and Remission of Sins, book 3, no. 1). Since he judged that nothing could be added to the earlier books, which he had brought fully to completion, he wrote a separate letter on this subject to Marcellinus and appended it to his work as a third book (Retractations, book 2, chapter 33). At that time Marcellinus was in Carthage (On the Merits and Remission of Sins, book 3, no. 10).

Pelagius, however, did not attack the Church’s faith in his own person, but reported it as though it were an objection made by others. Nevertheless, once he had raised the standard of his heresy, he defended it with the most obstinate determination (Retractations, book 2, chapter 33). Indeed, in Rome, where many already knew well what sentiments he held in his mind, people did not hesitate to say that under this disguise he was insinuating his own doctrine (On Original Sin, no. 24).

Nevertheless, Augustine, still thinking that Pelagius ought to be treated with moderation, followed in refuting him precisely the method and procedure that Pelagius himself had abused. Indeed, since [Col. 0444] many praised Pelagius for the holiness of his conduct, Augustine did not hesitate to address him in especially respectful terms.

This is surely the letter to Marcellinus that Augustine had begun in Carthage, intending to join it to the first two books, but had not yet entirely completed when he wrote Marcellinus another letter concerning the publication of the proceedings composed against the Donatists (Epist. 139, no. 3).

### 5

In the second book Augustine had taught that it is possible for a person to be without sin, if he wills it, with God’s assistance, although no one in this life, Christ excepted, possesses such perfect righteousness. Marcellinus wrote in reply that he had been troubled because Augustine had said that something could exist of which there was no example.

Augustine answered this new question with a new book, entitled *On the Spirit and the Letter*. In explaining the question, he took the opportunity to argue against the Pelagians concerning the assistance of God’s grace. He showed that God does not help us to perform righteousness merely by giving a law full of good and holy commandments, but by assisting our will itself through the Spirit of grace bestowed upon us. Without this assistance, the teaching of the law is a letter that kills, because it holds people guilty of transgression rather than justifying the ungodly (Retractations, book 2, chapter 37; *On the Spirit and the Letter*, no. 1).

He testifies that in this work, insofar as God helped him, he argued vigorously against the enemies of God’s grace, by which the ungodly are justified (Retractations, book 2, chapter 37). Yet even against them he still maintained such moderation that he did not name any of his opponents individually.

### 6

Indeed, in his excessive zeal to recall people from error, the holy man showed them such indulgence that he ordered Catholics to bear patiently even when these people did not hesitate, during debate, to treat defenders of the ancient faith as heretics and innovators.

“For it is not enough,” he says, “that these men discuss and argue about I know not what impious novelties; they also try to accuse us of saying something new” (*Sermon* 294, no. 19).

Thus he spoke to the people of Carthage in a sermon delivered at the urging of Bishop Aurelius (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 25), some time after the earlier books sent to Marcellinus had been published, but, as it seemed to us, not before the year 413 (see Preface to volume 10, § 6). He preached it in the Basilica of the Majores on the feast of the martyr Guddentis, on the fifth day before the Kalends of July.

After treating the question of Baptism at greater length—first producing divine authorities, then also holding in his hands the letter of the most glorious martyr Cyprian to Fidus, reciting and examining Cyprian’s words on this matter so that the wicked error might be removed from the hearts of certain people—the pious Bishop concluded the discussion in these words:

“Let us therefore obtain from our brothers, if we can, that they not call us heretics as well. We could perhaps call them so, if we wished, when they argue such things; yet we do not call them so. Let the mother endure them with pious compassion, to be healed; let her carry them, to be taught, lest she mourn the dead.

“They are going too far; it is much, scarcely bearable, that such conduct should still be endured with great patience. Let them not abuse the Church’s patience; let them be corrected. That is good. We exhort them as friends; we do not quarrel with them as enemies.

[Col. 0445] “They insult us, and we endure it; let them not insult the canon, let them not insult the truth. Let them not contradict the holy Church, which labors daily for the remission of the original sin of infants. This matter is established.

“An erring disputant may be endured in other questions that have not been carefully worked out and have not yet been confirmed by the full authority of the Church; in those matters error may be endured. But he must not go so far as to attempt to shake the very foundation of the Church. That is not expedient.

“Perhaps our patience should not yet be criticized; but we must fear that it may also be blamed as negligence. Let your Charity be satisfied. With those whom you know to be such, deal with them in a friendly, brotherly, peaceful, loving, and sorrowful manner. Let piety do whatever it can, because afterward impiety will not deserve to be loved” (*Sermon* 294, no. 20).

### 7

About this same time Augustine also replied to a letter that Pelagius had sent him. Although he refrained from praising Pelagius, he nevertheless treated him with such honor that Pelagius brought Augustine’s letter forward for reading at the Council of Diospolis, so that by the testimony of so great a man he might drive away from himself the charge of heresy that had not yet been brought against him.

The letter was as follows:

> To my most beloved and most longed-for brother Pelagius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.
>
> I give you very great thanks because you have deigned to gladden me with your letter and to inform me of your well-being. May the Lord repay you with good things, so that you may always be good and live with him forever and ever, my most beloved and most longed-for lord and brother.
>
> Although I do not recognize in myself the praises of me contained in your letter, written with such kindness, I cannot nevertheless be ungrateful for your goodwill toward my insignificance. At the same time I urge you instead to pray for me, so that by the Lord’s making I may become such as you already think me to be.
>
> And in another hand:
>
> > Remembering us, may you remain safe and please the Lord, my most beloved and most longed-for lord and brother.  
> > (Epist. 146)

There Augustine said that Pelagius was most longed for by him because he greatly desired to converse with him when he was present. For he had already heard that, whenever the subject arose, Pelagius openly attempted to contend against the grace by which we are justified.

Examining the individual words of this letter, Augustine showed that Pelagius had no reason to claim that it could serve him in repelling the charge not yet brought against him. In it Augustine admonished him to hold a right understanding of God’s grace, insofar as this could be done without offending him or discussing any particular question.

Later, however, the holy man regretted that, because he had then feared causing pain, he had increased the swelling of the wound, as he now understood (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, nos. 50–52).

### 8

The letter to Anastasius was also written to refute the Pelagians (Epist. 145). After teaching in it that righteousness is fulfilled not through the law but through grace, and not through servile fear but through free charity, Augustine explains that he had treated this question with Anastasius in writing not on Anastasius’s account, but on account of certain people who attribute too much to human will and think that, once the law has been given, the will is sufficient by itself to fulfill it.

This letter, in which he still spares his opponents’ name, was certainly written before the year 416, by which time he no longer hesitated to name Pelagius.

That Anastasius was at this time in the midst of the disturbances and calamities that were then oppressing the world [Col. 0446]—perhaps in Spain—is evident. Augustine therefore asks him what condition his affairs were in and whether God had wished to grant him some measure of peace. At the same time he urges him to overcome the world’s adversities through charity and to implore this virtue from God, who alone can bestow it.

The holy Bishop had received a letter from Anastasius. He admits that he does not know at all whether he had replied to it, so completely was he being distracted by cares at that time.

### 9

While Augustine was writing the letter to Marcellinus mentioned above (Epist. 139, no. 3), which he appended to the books *On Baptism*, he also had in hand the letter to Honoratus, whose inquiries he above all wished to satisfy (Epist. 140; Retractations, book 2, chapter 36).

“For charity,” he says, “which, like a nurse, cherishes her children, places the weaker before the stronger—not according to the order of loving, but according to the order of providing assistance. She wishes the weaker to become such as those already are whom she passes over for the time being, not by despising them, but by relying upon them” (Epist. 139, no. 3).

Since Honoratus was among the catechumens and had not yet been initiated through Baptism (Epist. 140, no. 48), he wrote from Carthage to Augustine, with whom he was acquainted, and proposed five questions for him to explain.

At that time Augustine was intensely occupied in opposing the Donatists. Nevertheless, he thought it preferable to seize the opportunity that Honoratus had offered him to attack the Pelagians. Thus, after Honoratus had proposed his five questions, Augustine added a sixth of his own: what should be understood as the grace of the New Testament? He examined this question with such particular care and diligence that he referred all the others back to it. He also attached to them an explanation of Psalm 21, at whose beginning one of Honoratus’s questions had been included (Retractations, book 2, chapter 36).

This composition, which he counts among his works (ibid.; Epist. 139, no. 3) and honors with the designation “book,” although it is in fact quite long (Epist. 140, no. 85), has long held a place among his letters. After it Augustine appends the short work entitled *On the Spirit and the Letter* (Retractations, book 2, chapter 37). There can certainly be no doubt that the latter was written afterward.

## CHAPTER II

1. Augustine writes to the lay Donatists after the Conference.  
2. The Donatists are condemned by an imperial rescript.  
3. Their fury.  
4. Restitutus is beaten by them.  
5. How vigorously Augustine acts to prevent those guilty of the killings from being punished capitally.  
6. He works to restrain the violence of the schismatics in the diocese of Hippo and in the rest of Numidia.  
7. He writes various short works.

### 1

In the same letter to Marcellinus in which Augustine indicates that he is devoting himself to preparing a reply to Honoratus, he reports that he had abridged the Carthaginian Conference and had also recently completed a letter to the Donatist people concerning that same Conference (Epist. 139, no. 3).

We have already spoken above about this abridgment of the Conference. As for the letter written at that time to the Donatist laity, it should perhaps be identified with the book entitled *To the Donatists after the Conference* (Retractations [Col. 0447], book 2, chapter 40), in which the holy man in fact does not address their bishops at all.

In this work, which is both of considerable size and carefully and accurately composed, he dispels the calumnies and empty fabrications that they put forward in order to avoid submitting to Marcellinus’s judgment. He treats the same matter, though much more briefly, in another letter, which he later published together with the Council of Zerta—or, as he himself says, published again (ibid.). The letter of the Fathers of Zerta is dated the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July in the year 412.

If the earlier work is the one *To the Donatists after the Conference*, as the word “again” seems to indicate, then it must necessarily have preceded it, together with all the other writings of that same period, in July of the year 412. Since all these works followed Caelestius’s condemnation, we have therefore judged that the condemnation should be assigned to the year 411, and that the writings produced afterward should be placed from the beginning of 412 to approximately June.

In the same book Augustine openly indicates that the Catholics had resolved to persecute the Donatists and to restrain their insolence and injuries by the authority of the laws when they would not allow themselves to be called back from this course of action by words and teaching. Nevertheless, they did not wish anyone to be punished with bloody execution, but with some very mild penalty (*To the Donatists after the Conference*, no. 21). From this intention of the Catholics one may infer that Augustine wrote after the law issued on the third day before the Kalends of February in 412 (*Theodosian Code*, On Heretics, law 52).

### 2

Marcellinus had undoubtedly informed the Emperor of the outcome of the Conference, as he had been instructed to do. Moreover, the Donatists had appealed elsewhere to the Emperor against Marcellinus’s judgment. It was therefore necessary for Honorius to speak.

Possidius testifies that the Emperor himself answered their appeal and condemned them, as was proper, as heretics (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 13). Nor does it seem doubtful that the law under discussion was issued by him for this very reason (*Theodosian Code*, On Heretics, law 51). Yet, insofar as one can reach a conclusion by conjecture, it is nothing more than a fragment of the complete law.

First, it revokes whatever had been granted to the Donatists in the year 409; conversely, it renews whatever had been decreed against them. Next, it establishes that any Donatists who refused to return to Catholic fellowship—bishops and clergy as well as laymen and Circumcellions—should, according to each person’s rank, be subjected to a monetary fine. Women were to be condemned separately to pay it just as their husbands were.

Those who did not repent after the fine had been imposed were to be stripped of all their property. Whoever received them or provided them refuge against the official appointed to enforce this measure was to be subjected to the same fine.

Slaves and tenant farmers were to be compelled by bodily punishment to renounce the schism. Their masters, even if Catholic, were to be fined in the same way as Donatist bishops and other clergy who persisted in the division. The latter were to be exiled, each to a different place [Col. 0448], from the whole of Africa. Finally, their churches and all other meeting places, together with the estates belonging to them, were to be assigned to Catholic bishops, in accordance with the decree made on this matter in 405, or at least with the proposal set forth in the law issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of December in 407.

This was the provision about which the Donatists complained most bitterly and indignantly. They thought that it would easily persuade people that the Catholics harassed and persecuted them for no other reason than to enrich themselves with their property (Epist. 185, no. 35).

Augustine repeatedly reports that, even before the Conference, the Donatists had been accustomed to use this unjust complaint against Catholic bishops in order, in a certain way, to mitigate their own grief when they saw their sect increasingly diminished.

“Look,” they would say, “where Gaius Seius has donated an estate to the Church over which Faustinus presided” (*Tractates on the Gospel of John* 6, no. 25)—that is, Faustinus, the Donatist bishop at Hippo.

But the holy Bishop demonstrates everywhere both how unjust such complaints were and, conversely, how entirely just the Emperor’s edict was. To force them completely into silence, he declares in the name of the whole Church:

> “Whoever, taking advantage of this law—which the kings of the earth, serving Christ, promulgated to correct your impiety—greedily desires your possessions displeases us. Whoever, finally, possesses through avarice rather than justice the very property of the poor, or the basilicas of congregations that you held under the name of the Church—possessions that belong entirely only to that Church which is the true Church of Christ—displeases us.
>
> “But you do not easily demonstrate these things; and if you do demonstrate them, we tolerate some whom we cannot correct or punish. Nor do we abandon the Lord’s threshing floor on account of the chaff” (Epist. 93, no. 50).

On the same matter he adds:

> “If we are fellow-poor with the poor, these things are both ours and theirs when they become Catholics. But if we possess privately what is sufficient for us, those things are not ours but the poor’s. We exercise a kind of stewardship over them; we do not claim ownership of them for ourselves by a damnable usurpation” (Epist. 185, no. 35).

Elsewhere, clearing himself before the people entrusted to his care, he says:

> “You know, my brothers, that these estates do not belong to Augustine. And if you do not know this, and think that I rejoice in possessing estates, God knows—he himself knows—what I think about those estates, or what I suffer there. He knows my groans, if he has deigned to grant me something from the dove” (*Tractates on the Gospel of John* 6, no. 25).

Moreover, from the zeal that orthodox Christians displayed in recalling the schismatics, the holy Doctor teaches that they were accustomed to be guided by charity, not by greed. For as soon as one of their bishops returned to the Church, all his possessions—money, clothing, produce, vessels, fields, and buildings—were immediately restored to him (*Against Gaudentius*, book 1, nos. 50–51).

### 3

Thus, enlightened by Catholic truth through the benefit of the Conference and confirmed by the Emperor’s edict, more Donatist bishops than before were returning courageously into the bosom of the Church together with their clergy and people. They endured with unbroken spirit being harassed, and even being punished in their bodies [Col. 0449] and lives, by those who had stubbornly hardened their minds in error (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 13).

For God had not granted repentance to everyone. Indeed, the obstinacy of certain people was so great that, even after Catholic truth and the perversity of the Donatists had been demonstrated to them, they denied that they would ever be drawn away from the schism (Epist. 139, no. 1).

Some of their bishops fled (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 17); others hid themselves, as Emeritus of Caesarea did. When he came out to meet the Catholics in the year 418, they let him go (ibid., no. 41). Besides him, they had left many others, though not men of such renown, free to withdraw without punishment, although the Donatists declared that no one who fell into the hands of the Catholics had escaped safely. They complained that they were being harassed by a persecution more savage than any that had ever existed, and that no hiding place remained for them anywhere (ibid., no. 47).

Nevertheless, they continued to hold assemblies and to appoint bishops in place of those who had burned themselves. Before the year 420, as it seems, more than thirty bishops met with Petilianus. At that synod they decreed that bishops and priests who had unwillingly embraced Catholic communion could obtain forgiveness for that fault and be restored to their offices, provided that they had neither performed the sacred rites nor spoken publicly to the people (ibid., no. 48).

By this decree they themselves were undermining the foundation of their sect. Yet however diligently the Catholics labored to recall the schismatics to harmony, there were still many who not only refused to enter the banquet of eternal salvation and the holy unity of the Church, but also raged against the Catholics with dreadful violence (Epist. 173, no. 10), especially against bishops (Epist. 185, no. 30) and clergy (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 7).

The sacred buildings that they possessed near Carthage were handed over to the Catholics; not long afterward they were burned, and there was no doubt that the Donatists themselves had set them on fire out of spite.

When a band of Circumcellions attacked Rogatus—whom they had formerly established as bishop of Assuras, but who afterward escaped from the storms of the schism—they cut out his tongue and severed one of his hands. He was still living in this mutilated state in the year 418 (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 9).

“The frenzied,” says Augustine in a sermon on charity and concord delivered shortly after the Conference, “are troublesome: they have lost their minds, and, mad and raging, they wander armed here and there, seeking people to kill and people to blind. For new things have been reported to us: they cut out the tongue of one of our priests. These men are frenzied. Charity must be exercised; they too must be loved” (*Sermon* 359, no. 8).

### 4

At that same time nothing was more widely discussed than the savagery that the Donatists inflicted upon Restitutus and Innocentius, priests of the Church of Hippo Regius (Epist. 133, no. 1).

We have already mentioned the harassment that Restitutus, a priest of the Victoriana district in the territory of Hippo Regius, had suffered from them because, intending to follow the truth [Col. 0450] divinely shown to him, he had defected from their faction (above, book 5, chapter 10, no. 3). It is probable that he was the same man who at this time crowned his life with the honor of martyrdom.

When the Circumcellions and Donatist priests ambushed and captured him, they not only refused to listen to his words, by which he urged them to repent, but also drove swords into his throat and took his life by a bloody murder (Epist. 134, nos. 2, 4).

The priest Innocentius was likewise guilty of the same zeal, and they therefore wished to make him share the same crown. Either the same Circumcellions or others dragged him violently from his house, gouged out one of his eyes, and, as Augustine says, horribly mutilated him by cutting off one finger with blows from a stone (ibid., no. 2).

Among these marauders and assassins the leading place was held by a certain Donatus, formerly a tenant of the Church. After allowing himself to be polluted by a second Baptism and even to be adopted by the Donatists as a deacon, he was rightly regarded as one of the boldest and most depraved of them all (Epist. 139, no. 2).

### 5

That most cruel crime could undoubtedly have turned to the advantage of the Church. Apart from the fact that the suffering of God’s servants provided an especially suitable example for strengthening the weaker in patience and redounded to the praise and honor of the whole Church, nothing else could have been found by which those who claimed that they refused to return to the Catholic Church lest they be polluted by contact with the crimes of others—or who boasted that they defended the truth because they endured persecution—could have been forced more effectively into silence (Epist. 133, 134, 139).

Augustine therefore strongly desired that the official records of this crime should come into his hands, so that they might be read both in the Church of Hippo and before the large congregations of the other churches of the same diocese.

Nevertheless, neither Augustine himself nor any other member of his clergy accused them of homicide. Rather, the civil magistrates, who were responsible for public order and discipline, referred the matter to Marcellinus. They also sent him, under guard, the Circumcellions and Donatist clergy responsible for both killings, so that he might investigate them.

The examination of ecclesiastical cases had been entrusted especially to Marcellinus, apparently by the law issued on the third day before the Kalends of February. That law mentions an *Exsecutor* against the Donatists; Dulcitius the tribune was later given the same title, as well as that of notary (*Theodosian Code*, On Heretics, law 52).

Although the crime under investigation was atrocious, Marcellinus extracted a confession from the accused and their accomplices without stretching them on the rack, without tearing them with claws, and without burning them with flames, but only by blows of rods. “This form of coercion,” Augustine says, “is customarily employed by teachers of the liberal arts, by parents themselves, and often by bishops in legal proceedings” (Epist. 133, no. 2).

The holy man therefore praises Marcellinus because, in investigating the crime, he had used great leniency, and indeed rather the concern of a father than the severity of a judge (ibid.; Epist. 134, no. 2).

It now seemed that only one thing remained: that, in proportion to the atrocity of the deed, the accused should be punished—that is, with capital [Col. 0451] execution.

The Church could certainly have left the entire matter to the judges without any intervention, since these men had been brought to trial not by the clergy but by officials responsible for civil discipline. Indeed, there were members even of the clergy who, inflamed by that first heat which such great and serious crimes ordinarily kindle, thought that allowing the criminals to receive lighter penalties would involve some damage to and neglect of discipline.

Augustine, however, rightly judged that the Church would suffer very substantial harm if the Donatists were put to death, while it would gain by far the greatest advantage if, taking this opportunity, it openly displayed how great its clemency and charity were toward its most hostile enemies.

He hoped that others would soon return to this opinion once the first emotions had subsided—the emotions that the horror of recent events had aroused in their minds. It would indeed have been troubling if the proceedings of this trial, which the Church’s welfare required to be read before the people, could not be recited to the end, lest the bloody conclusion offend the minds of the hearers.

Moreover, the sufferings of God’s servants could not be avenged by the blood of their enemies without the splendor of those sufferings being in some way obscured.

The holy Bishop therefore feared that the strictest application of the law might be used in this case. He earnestly begged Marcellinus by letter not only to moderate his own severity, but also to ensure that others did the same. For he suspected that this trial might be referred to Apringius, the proconsul—a Christian and a son of the Church, certainly, and by nature averse to such bloody punishments, but nevertheless a man who appeared to have decided that the guilty should be deprived of their heads.

He therefore also sent Marcellinus a letter to be delivered to Apringius.

In these two letters (Epist. 133 and 139) he directs all the power of argument and eloquence at his disposal toward ensuring that the accused be condemned not to death, but to some other lighter penalty—one that would both deprive them of the freedom to commit wrongdoing and yet leave them time to repent and the opportunity to occupy themselves in some useful labor.

This was what lay closest to his heart, both because of his conscience and because he wished Catholic communion to be commended.

### 6

At about this same time Marcellinus wrote to Augustine, promising that he would send him the *Acts* containing the confession of the accused. At the same time he asked whether these ought to be posted in the Theoprepia, which during the time of the Conference had been the Donatist church at Carthage (*Collation of Carthage* 3, ch. 5); and he also reminded him to discharge his obligation concerning a certain written promise (*Epistle* 139, §§1, 3, 4).

Augustine replied that he earnestly desired the promised *Acts* to be sent to him, so that he might arrange for them to be read as soon as possible not only in the church at Hippo, but also, if it could be done, in all the other churches of the same diocese. As for posting them at Carthage, he said that the most frequented place should be selected, whether in the Theoprepia or elsewhere.

He also implored him to spare the lives of the accused; but if this could not be granted, he asked him to insert in the sentence the two letters which he had written separately on this matter, one to Marcellinus and one to the Proconsul; or at least to keep the guilty men in custody for a while, [Col. 0452] until he could seek pardon for them from the clemency of the Emperors. For he knew that, some years earlier, the Emperor had readily granted the request that the Gentiles who had killed the martyrs of Anaunia should not be punished with death.

He also complained of the injuries and acts of violence by which the schismatics in his diocese, led by Bishop Macrobius, continued to rage and run riot. The landowners, out of fear of the laws, had closed the Donatist basilicas; but Macrobius, rushing about in every direction with a band of abandoned men and women, ordered them to be opened for him by force. The audacity of the heretics had been curbed to some degree by Spondeus, the steward of the estates which the most distinguished Celer possessed in the territory of Hippo. But when Spondeus had gone to Carthage, Macrobius immediately reopened the churches and held his assemblies on the very properties of Celer or Spondeus.

Moreover, it was not only the Church of Hippo Regius but also other churches throughout Numidia that were enduring more serious harassment from the Donatists. To obtain some assistance against the danger threatening them, these churches sent Bishop Delphinus to Carthage. There was there a certain presbyter of Augustine, to whom Augustine arranged for a memorandum to be delivered through the deacon Peregrinus, who had accompanied Bishop Boniface to that place. He also sent the same presbyter another memorandum together with this letter to Marcellinus.

Whether this presbyter was the same man as Urbanus, from whom Augustine had received the letter brought to Marcellinus, is uncertain. Augustine states elsewhere that the deacon Peregrinus had departed from Hippo Regius with Urbanus, whom he was summoning for the purpose of undertaking the episcopate (*Epistle* 149, §34). Accordingly, he implores Marcellinus to read the memoranda which he had sent from Hippo to Carthage and, together with Delphinus and Boniface, to consider by what means the best assistance might be provided to that province, which he commends to Marcellinus’s care and fidelity.

The holy Bishop also asks him not to allow Rufinus of Cirta, the *Principalis*, to be deprived of his protection (*Epistle* 139, §§2, 4).

### 7

As we have already said, Marcellinus pressed Augustine to send him a certain written account. Augustine excuses himself on the ground that, although he desired this most earnestly, he was entirely unable to do it, partly because of the crowds of people who were continually coming to him concerning their own affairs, and partly because of various tasks which at that time did not allow themselves to be set aside.

Perhaps it will be better to explain the matter in Augustine’s own words:

> If I could give you an account of all the days and night-watchings spent on other necessities, you would be deeply saddened and astonished at how many things occupy me—things that cannot be postponed at all and that do not allow me to undertake what, by requesting and reminding me, you urge me to do, although I am willing, and although I grieve beyond words because I cannot do it. For whenever I obtain even a little freedom from the necessities of those who press upon me in such a way that they cannot be avoided and ought not to be disregarded, there are always matters which I must place before everything else, fixed as they are at particular moments and unable to tolerate delay.

After some intervening material he continues in this manner:

> And I truly do not know what I should do. You have heard from what source you should pray with me to the Lord; but although you remind me so urgently and so frequently, I do not want you to cease, while accomplishing something of no small value (*Epistle* 139, §§3, 4).

He lists various treatises which he had been preparing during the same period. We have already discussed all of them except the letters mentioned there to Marcellinus and to Volusianus.

## CHAPTER III

1. Augustine and Marcellinus endeavor to bring Volusianus from the worship of idols to the Christian faith.  
2. Augustine’s celebrated letter to Volusianus.  
3. The Council of Zerta.  
4. Certain Donatist presbyters and clerics, and also citizens of Cirta, return to the Catholic Church.  
5. The esteem in which Augustine holds his writings, and in which he wishes his friends to hold them.

### 1

Augustine’s profound respect for Volusianus, which he consistently displayed toward him, compels us to acknowledge that Volusianus was a man born into the highest rank. Baronius certainly thinks that he was the maternal uncle of Melania the Younger (*Baronius*, under the year 412), that is, the full brother of her mother Albina; for Melania the Younger’s father was the only son of Melania the Elder.

If the *Metaphrast* calls him his paternal uncle, this error must be attributed to the translator. The same thing is presented in Photius’s version, although the Greek text has θεῖος (*theios*), a word that signifies equally a brother of one’s father or of one’s mother (*Photius, Bibliotheca*, codex 53).

Augustine and Marcellinus commend his intelligence and eloquence exceptionally. Yet from the questions which he raises against the Christian faith, one can understand either that he had not yet professed it or, at least, that he had in no way been firmly established in it. Consequently, for the sake of his soul, he needed to be given a fuller exposition of the Church’s teaching.

Augustine calls Volusianus’s mother holy and worthy of the highest honor in Christ (*Epistle* 137, §20). She ardently desired the salvation of her son (*Epistle* 132) and sought it from God with devout prayers (*Epistle* 137, §20). She had even persuaded Marcellinus to visit Volusianus from time to time and, as far as he could, to establish and strengthen him in his good purpose through conversation (*Epistle* 136, §1).

It is not equally certain whether Augustine undertook to secure her son’s salvation at her request; but it is beyond doubt that he was as concerned for the same matter as she was. Accordingly, he had written to Volusianus (*Epistle* 132), exhorting him to read the divine Scriptures, especially Paul’s letters, and promising that, if he encountered any difficulty there, Augustine would answer everything in writing.

Volusianus replied with a very courteous letter, which still survives (*Epistle* 135). He indicated that Augustine’s promise was pleasing to him and, so that he might immediately derive some benefit from it, described a conversation which had taken place in his presence. In it, someone had raised certain questions about the Incarnation, arguing that it contained many things unworthy of God.

Volusianus therefore asked Augustine to explain these difficulties, using words which are worth quoting here:

> It is in your interest, he says, that we should know the answers to these questions. Among other priests, ignorance may be tolerated without detriment to divine worship; but when one comes to Bishop Augustine, anything that happens to be unknown is lacking to the reader [Col. 0454] (*ibid.*, §2).

Here he proposes only the question concerning the Incarnation, lest he appear to have forgotten the brevity appropriate to a letter. But to Marcellinus and many others he admitted that many additional matters remained which he wished to have clarified.

Among these were the alteration and abolition of the sacraments of the Old Testament, as well as the teaching of the Gospel concerning certain major precepts which, as he himself thought, conflicted with civil life and the public welfare of kingdoms.

Marcellinus informed Augustine of all this and implored him to answer not only the questions Volusianus had put forward but also the other questions. For Augustine’s reply would come into the hands of many who were held entangled and impeded by those same difficulties.

Above all, Marcellinus asked him carefully to refute the claim made by the pagans that Christ had never accomplished anything exceeding human powers, and that Apollonius of Tyana, Apuleius, and many others among the magicians had performed miracles greater than those of Christ (*Epistle* 136, §§2, 3).

### 2

Augustine decided that all the other writings on which he was laboring should be interrupted so that he might answer Volusianus without any delay and also provide for the instruction of many others. Accordingly, with the utmost modesty he minimized the praises Volusianus had bestowed upon him, while setting before him the loftiness of the sacred books. He then took up the question requiring discussion and argued with great clarity about the mystery of the Incarnation.

Afterward he began to speak of the Church, establishing and defending it in a remarkably beautiful manner—one that is almost a summary of his great work *The City of God*. He also endeavors to persuade Volusianus to communicate all his doubts to him, without fearing that he might exceed the customary limits of letters. Finally, he sends him greetings in the words of Possidius, from which one may reasonably infer that Possidius was then at Hippo Regius (*Epistle* 137).

Augustine considered it sufficient to answer Volusianus concerning the matters about which Volusianus had questioned him. As for the other questions, which he had learned from Marcellinus’s letter were troubling both Volusianus and many others, he preferred to write his opinion on them to Marcellinus himself. If Marcellinus judged this useful, he could show the letter to those who continually harassed him by raising such objections; or he could first inform Augustine what addition seemed necessary to him in order to make the answer sufficient (*Epistle* 138, §1).

We shall see under the year 421 that the reply ordering Volusianus, prefect of the City, to send Coelestius and Pelagius into exile was issued by Constantius (*Photius, Bibliotheca*, codex 53). Volusianus added his own edict, calling Coelestius a disturber of the divine faith and of the public peace (*Baronius*, under the year 420, §3).

But this does not at all prove that Volusianus had thereby given his allegiance to Christ, if he was indeed the same man who, as one reads in Photius, was the uncle of the holy Melania. For, according to that account, after being earnestly entreated by his niece to cleanse his soul through Baptism, he was finally, as death approached, brought to Christ and baptized after renouncing the error of the Gentiles [Col. 0455] (*Photius, Bibliotheca*, codex 53).

This is how the matter is related in the *Life* of that blessed woman. It says that he died at the time when Proclus was occupying the see of Constantinople (*Surius*, December 31 or January). This led Baronius to place his death in the year 434.

### 3

After Augustine had written his book to the Donatists following the Conference, the Council of Zerta was held in the year 412. Nothing remains of it except the letter written to the same Donatists on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July (*Epistle* 141).

Their bishops were claiming that the judge had been bribed by the Catholics to pronounce against their opponents. This foul and ridiculous slander found credence among the minds of the uneducated multitude and prevented many from submitting to the truth.

Nothing could have refuted it more powerfully than the reading of the *Acts* themselves. In those records it had been set down that the Donatists themselves had brought forward so much that was contrary to their own cause that, even if Marcellinus had allowed his religious convictions to be corrupted by them, he would never have dared to pronounce judgment against them.

Yet not everyone was able to read those *Acts*, and many who could do so were deterred by their very length. The Catholic bishops therefore thought it useful—both to advance the salvation of the people and to leave the obstinate no pretext for excuse—to place before their eyes in a more concise form everything of somewhat greater importance that had taken place at the Conference.

They accomplished this through the letter which, moved by divine charity, they sent to the Donatists. Augustine wrote it by the common agreement and in the name of the entire council (*Retractions* 2, ch. 42). At its head he names Silvanus of Summa, dean of Numidia; Valentinus of Vaga; Aurelius of Macomades; Augustine himself; and, besides those whom he omits, several others.

This assembly was, in all likelihood, provincial, since Augustine calls it the Council of Numidia.

### 4

Augustine was away from Hippo, perhaps because of this Council of Zerta, when he sent another letter to the presbyters Saturninus and Euphrates and to certain clerics who had been converted with them to unity (*Epistle* 142). In it, certain statements concerning the Donatist bishops convicted at the Conference of Carthage are expressed in the same words which we read in the letter of this council, as we have noted elsewhere (*Preface to volume 2*).

Their reconciliation undoubtedly took place during Augustine’s absence. He therefore joyfully congratulates them on their return to the Church and asks them to regard his own absence as excused. He then produces various testimonies of divine authority by which he establishes the universality of the Church. Finally, he urges them each diligently and eagerly to fulfill his own part and duty.

The conversion of all Cirta to Catholic unity may be assigned to the period immediately following this. For in that city, the chief city of Numidia, everyone returned to the Church except a very few whom either love or fear of a man [Col. 0456]—perhaps Petilianus—kept in the schism. They were not permitted to assemble with him except secretly.

This occurred after Augustine had undertaken a journey there, though after he had already returned from it. He therefore took the opportunity to attribute this most fortunate event not to his own labors but to God alone. Most of the people of Cirta, however, believing that God had used Augustine’s work in this matter, sent him a letter informing him of what had happened among them and at the same time asking him to visit them.

The holy Bishop replied that he very much desired to make the journey and was praying to God to grant an end to this desire. He would undertake it with all the greater willingness because he would be going to see not his own work but God’s work (*Epistle* 144, §§1–3).

### 5

We observed above that Bishop Boniface and a presbyter of Hippo—perhaps the man named Urbanus—were at Carthage when Augustine wrote the letter beginning, “The *Acts* which Your Eminence promised” (*Epistle* 139). Each of them, however, brought from Marcellinus a separate letter to the holy Bishop.

Augustine replied to the two letters with a single response beginning, “Your letter” (*Epistle* 143). In it he professes not to know what place he had inadvertently assigned to the letter brought to him by Boniface. He nevertheless remembers well that the question and request made of him there concerned the source from which Pharaoh could have obtained more water to turn into blood, since all the water of Egypt had already been turned into blood.

In the letter which Urbanus had delivered to him, Marcellinus was asking for the explanation of a difficulty arising from Augustine’s books *On Free Choice of the Will*. At the same time he indicated that a certain friend of his—perhaps Volusianus—had not been entirely satisfied with what Augustine had written in his letter to Volusianus concerning the virginity of Saint Mary.

In replying to the passage in the third book of *On Free Choice of the Will*, Augustine first declares that he does not wish it to be read, or defended by his friends, as though he were himself immune from every error, as were the sacred writers—that is, those men of God who spoke under the influence of the Holy Spirit. Indeed, he already indicates there that he was considering a review of all his works, intending to publish a written statement openly demonstrating which parts of them he considered less satisfactory and how little he spared himself.

Nevertheless, he asserts that in the passage under discussion he had said nothing that anyone could rightly criticize. It is certainly clear that no one except followers of the Pelagian doctrine had dared to attack the words in question.

## CHAPTER IV

1. Augustine publishes his book *On Faith and Works*.  
2. He writes to Paulina about seeing God, and also to Fortunatianus, whose assistance he seeks in restoring friendship with a certain bishop who had taken offense at statements Augustine had made against an erroneous opinion.  
3. Paulinus and Augustine send various letters to one another.  
4. Augustine turns his attention to writing *The City of God*.

### 1

Augustine had published his work *On the Spirit and the Letter* not long before he turned his attention to writing *On Faith and Works* (*On Faith and Works*, §21). He did so in order to answer certain writings which some laymen, though brothers devoted to the divine Scriptures, had sent him (*Retractions* 2, ch. 38).

The authors of these writings distinguished faith in Christ from good works in such a way that they thought we could attain eternal life without good works, though not without faith. They therefore taught that everyone should be admitted to the sacrament of Baptism and to the Lord’s table, and that it should not matter at all whether they considered correcting their life. Indeed, even if it were clear that they had resolved to remain in their crimes and vices, they should be admonished about correcting them only after receiving Baptism (*On Faith and Works*, §§1, 10). For it was new, indeed perverse and backward, first to teach how a Christian ought to live and only afterward to baptize him (*ibid.*, §§33, 1).

They had been driven headlong into this exceedingly dangerous opinion by their affection for certain people who had perhaps been denied Baptism because, after rejecting an earlier wife, they had married another (*ibid.*, §2).

This compelled Augustine not only to teach how those regenerated by Christ’s grace ought to order their lives, but also what sort of people should be admitted to the laver of regeneration. What he had argued throughout the book he gathers and summarizes as though into a bundle in its final chapter (*Retractions* 2, ch. 38).

### 2

At approximately the same time Augustine composed the little work which he had written to Paulina about seeing God (*ibid.*, ch. 41). In that work the holy Doctor does not intend to investigate what the bodies of the blessed will be like after the general resurrection, or whether the eyes can see a spiritual nature such as God is (*ibid.* and *Epistle* 147, §49). He promises that, if God helps him, he will discuss the matter expressly in a treatise of some kind (*Epistle* 147, §54). He deals with it in the twenty-second book of *The City of God*.

He also treated this subject in a letter which he calls a memorandum to Fortunatianus, Bishop of Sicca (*Retractions* 2, ch. 41; and *Epistle* 148), and in another letter written somewhat earlier to Italica (*Epistle* 92).

In the latter he had said that the eyes of this body neither see nor will see God. He was led to make this assertion because he feared that God might consequently be thought corporeal and visible within a spatial interval and distance (*Epistle* 148, §1, and *Epistle* 92, §3).

By this argument he was refuting somewhat forcefully a certain bishop among his friends, neighboring the diocese of Sicca in the Proconsular Province. He had been carried away by the ardor of his criticism to such an extent that he did not sufficiently adjust his words to the respect owed to episcopal dignity. He thought himself less bound by this obligation because in his letter he had not named anyone.

Nevertheless, that bishop interpreted the matter in the worst sense and took it as an insult to himself. Augustine wished to meet him, hoping that he might reconcile the bishop’s mind to him by humbly asking pardon. When he attempted this, he says that the bishop wrote to him—“a venerable man, and one preferred in honor to us all,” clearly, as we understand it, Aurelius of Carthage [Col. 0458]—but that the bishop refused to come, perhaps suspecting that Augustine intended to deceive him, mock him, or insult him over his error. Nothing could have been further from Augustine’s character.

Nevertheless, Augustine did not think he should go to the bishop’s house, lest, if the bishop refused to accept his apology, the visit produce offense and scandal (*Epistle* 148, §4).

When he happened to see Bishop Fortunatianus, Augustine explained to him how deeply and sincerely he was pained by the alienation of his friend. He also asked Fortunatianus to visit the bishop and make him aware of Augustine’s sincere disposition. Augustine did not despise him; rather, he venerated and feared God himself in him, and implored him to forgive this offense (*ibid.*, §1).

He afterward wrote to Fortunatianus the letter just mentioned. In it, repeating the same requests, he begged as humbly and affectionately as possible that Fortunatianus would gladden him with news that he had obtained the bishop’s pardon.

Yet however great his desire to appease this man, it did not prevent Augustine from steadfastly defending the truth he had already maintained. He declares that he does not regret what he had written in order to restore the bishop’s friendship. He confirms, on the authority of Athanasius, Ambrose, Gregory, and especially Jerome, that God cannot be seen in the way we see things perceived by the senses—not even by glorified bodies.

If, however, the bishop thought that bodies would come so near to the nature of spirits that they could apprehend incorporeal things with their eyes, Augustine was entirely prepared to hear the arguments by which he established his opinion (*ibid.*, §4). Meanwhile, until the question had been discussed accurately and peacefully, the heart—which, without doubt, is the means by which we shall see God—had to be prepared and purified.

Augustine seems to imply that those whose testimony he employs had already departed this life. If that were so, the letter would have to be assigned to a date after the year 420, in which Saint Jerome died. But we do not think those words should be interpreted so strictly. Fortunatianus of Sicca took part in the Conference of Carthage in 411, and we shall see that Urbanus succeeded him in the episcopate, presiding over the Church of Sicca in 416 and again in 419. It is also quite plausible that Urbanus had become bishop of that see as early as 413. Consequently, the letter mentioned here cannot have been written later than that year.

### 3

We have no doubt that the presbyter Urbanus mentioned by Augustine in his letter to Marcellinus, written near the end of 412 (*Epistle* 143, §2), is the same man of whom Augustine says in a sermon to the people:

> “Our holy brother and fellow bishop, our Urbanus, who was a presbyter here and is now Bishop of Sicca” (*Sermon Fragments*, §1, first fragment).

Nor does Augustine refer to anyone else when he states that the Hipponensian deacon Peregrinus accompanied Urbanus when Urbanus departed, probably in 413, to undertake the episcopal office [Col. 0459] (*Epistle* 149, §34).

Urbanus had returned from Rome, where he had undertaken his journey, to Africa by 416 (*Sermon Fragments*, §1, first fragment). Peregrinus, however, who had gone with him to Sicca, had not yet returned to Hippo when Augustine wrote to Paulinus the letter beginning, “As to your arrival being so prosperous” (*Epistle* 149). It was therefore written neither before 413 nor after 415.

This letter contains a response to several letters from Paulinus. Augustine had sent him a letter from Carthage during the winter of 408 or 409 (*Epistle* 95). Paulinus, whose copy had perhaps been lost, asked that a transcript be sent to him, or that Augustine explain in full the subject of the resurrection discussed in that same letter.

At the same time Paulinus proposed nine questions to Augustine concerning the Old and New Scriptures. He himself examined them with the utmost care and implored Augustine to write back his opinion on them, especially on the ninth, which concerned Simeon’s words to Mary (*Paulinus, in Augustine, Epistle* 121, §14).

After receiving this letter, which Paulinus had written about the year 410, Augustine immediately replied. He resolved some of Paulinus’s questions but omitted others because the messenger was hurrying. He also arranged for the copy of the letter which Paulinus had requested to be enclosed with the reply.

The reply which we desire was probably sent only a few days before Paulinus added another letter—likewise lost—in which he again consulted Augustine concerning the sixteenth psalm and Simeon’s words to Mary.

When this letter was brought to Hippo, Augustine was staying at Cataqua with Boniface, the bishop of that city. Accordingly, he received the letter which had been forwarded to him from Hippo and answered it at Cataqua; but he did not find there a Greek psalter from which he could draw an exposition of the sixteenth psalm.

This reply too has been lost, and it was not returned to Paulinus, just as the earlier letter in which Augustine had answered his nine questions was not returned. Paulinus therefore had to write to him again when, in 412 or 413, he announced the arrival of the presbyter Quintus and several others, of whose journey we know nothing further.

In that letter he informed Augustine of a certain plan of mercy, as he called it, which he had conceived (*Epistle* 149, §1). He sent greetings to Augustine’s companions, who were devoted to divine service, collectively, and specifically to the deacon Peregrinus, as we infer (*ibid.*, §34).

On the first opportunity after receiving Paulinus’s final letter, Augustine replied through the deacon Rufinus, who was sailing from the harbor of Hippo. This was probably around 414. Augustine answered Paulinus’s questions, although he touched only briefly on the question concerning Simeon’s words, because he had already discussed that subject in another letter to the same man. He sent Paulinus a copy of that letter, as well as of the one beginning, “When our brothers” [Col. 0460] (*Epistle* 95; *Epistle* 149, §33).

In the same letter he discusses predestination, not indeed expressly as his principal subject, but with great clarity and force (*Epistle* 95).

### 4

Augustine began in this year to compose his work *The City of God against the Pagans*, who were assailing the Christian religion with insults and slanders because Rome had been conquered. The work was developed over a period of many years.

Augustine wrote it to the tribune Marcellinus, who was killed and ceased to live on the Ides of September in that very year, 413. Yet he had not begun the work long before Marcellinus’s murder, since when that event occurred he had scarcely completed two books.

This undoubtedly explains why, although he began by addressing Marcellinus in the opening of the first and second books, he never addresses him again in the remainder.

Marcellinus himself had asked Augustine to compose books on this subject (*Epistle* 136, §3). Augustine had replied to him in 412 that he was then dealing with such questions, not in the manner required for a full book, but in the manner sufficient for an exchange of letters (*Epistle* 138, §1). This easily leads us to suppose that he had not yet begun the work at that time.

But when Augustine also asked Marcellinus to inform him if he thought anything further necessary for refuting unbelievers, so that, “if God helps us, we may undertake to answer everything either in letters or in books” (*ibid.*, §20), it is clear how the holy Doctor was gradually led to compose the books of *The City of God*.

Accordingly, inflamed—as he says—by zeal for the house of God against the blasphemies of the pagans, he resolved in his heart to undertake its defense (*Retractions* 2, ch. 43, §1). Yet from this particular subject he transferred his pen to a general treatment of the two cities, namely, the city of the world and the City of God. At the same time he undertook both to overthrow everything that could be brought forward with greater splendor in defense of pagan worship and to establish the Christian religion by irresistible arguments.

The principal subjects treated in that great work, extending over twenty-two books, are summarized by Augustine in the *Retractions*. He was able to bring so many books to completion only over several years and at interrupted intervals, repeatedly having to remove his pen from the work in order to turn it to matters that appeared more urgent (*ibid.*).

As we have already stated, he composed the first two or three books in this year and the next two in 415, beginning them shortly before Lent (*Epistle* 169, §1).

He first published the first three books, and they soon reached the hands of very many people. Some idolaters were not lacking who considered refuting them. Indeed, they were said to be waiting for nothing except some opportunity that would allow them to publish their response without fear of the imperial laws.

Augustine warns them:

> “Do not desire what is not good for you. It is easy for anyone who does not wish to remain silent to appear to have answered. For what is more talkative than vanity? It cannot do what truth can do, because, if it wishes, it can shout even more loudly than truth.  
>   
> “But let them consider everything carefully. If, judging without partisan zeal, they should find that these are matters which can more readily be harassed than overthrown by the most shameless babbling and by a kind of satirical or theatrical frivolity, let them restrain their nonsense and choose rather to be corrected by the prudent than praised by the foolish.  
>   
> “For if they are waiting not for an opportunity to speak the truth freely but for permission to slander, may what Cicero said about a certain man whom he called fortunate because he was permitted to sin not happen to them: ‘O wretched man, who was permitted to sin!’  
>   
> “Therefore, whoever thinks himself fortunate because he is permitted to slander will be much more fortunate if he is not permitted to do so at all. He can still, after laying aside the emptiness of boastfulness, contradict whatever he wishes in a spirit of seeking advice; and, as far as they are able, those whom he consults can tell him in friendly discussion, honestly, seriously, and freely what he ought to hear” (*The City of God* 5, ch. 26, §2).

When Augustine encouraged Orosius to write his history—probably in 416 or 417—he himself was composing the eleventh book of this great work, having already published the first ten. The rays issuing from those books, as we may reproduce Orosius’s own words here, “as soon as they rose from the watchtower of ecclesiastical brilliance, shone throughout the whole world” (*Orosius, History*, Preface).

Augustine mentions the fourteenth book when writing against the *Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, probably around 420. At the end of the eighteenth book he also states that nearly thirty years had passed since the consulship of Theodorus, which fell in the year 399. Thus he indicates that he was writing under the year 426 of Christ.

## CHAPTER V

1. Marinus, conqueror of Heraclianus, loses the reputation he had gained through the murder of Marcellinus.  
2. This is the same man whose death is related in the letter to Caecilianus.  
3. Marcellinus is held in custody with his brother by order of Marinus.  
4. Marinus persuades the Church to send men to the Emperor to seek pardon for them.  
5. Marcellinus is condemned with his brother and struck with the sword.  
6. Marinus falls from the Emperor’s favor; Marcellinus becomes renowned for his integrity, innocence, and martyr’s crown.  
7. Augustine secretly leaves Carthage, deeply grieving Marcellinus’s death.

### 1

In this year we must place the rebellion of Heraclianus, the Count of Africa, who came to attack Rome with a fleet equipped with more than three thousand ships. He was defeated and put to flight in Italy by Count Marinus. Later, at Carthage, where he had withdrawn after his flight, he was subjected to the ultimate punishment before the third day before the Nones of August, as conjecture seems to suggest.

Marinus then crossed over to Africa. There, without doubt, his principal concern was to carry into effect the rescript of Honorius against Heraclianus and all those associated with his rebellion, promulgated on the third day before the Nones of July (*Theodosian Code*, “On Punishments,” law 21; *Orosius, History* 7, ch. 42).

But Marinus marked his name with the stain of everlasting infamy by removing the tribune Marcellinus, whose services to the Church had been so numerous and so great [Col. 0462].

It must indeed be admitted that Jerome reports that Marcellinus was killed by heretics (*Jerome, Against the Pelagians*, dialogue 3). But when Jerome adds that Marcellinus’s death was connected with the tyranny of Heraclianus, although Marcellinus himself was free from guilt, he clearly indicates that the Donatists did not inflict death upon him except through the agency of those who administered the laws and the courts.

Orosius certainly asserts that Marcellinus was punished by a capital sentence imposed by Count Marinus, whether driven by private resentment or, as is quite easy to believe, corrupted by the money of the Donatists (*Orosius, History* 7, ch. 42).

## 2.

Much that concerns his death may be found in Augustine’s letter to Caecilian (Epistle 151); yet there you will find no one explicitly named. Rather, it was written about two brothers, whose innocence he always regarded as completely established, struck down by the sword at Carthage. The holy Doctor celebrates one of them with remarkably singular praises, portraying the man as adorned with every kind of virtue and as renowned for the Christian disposition of his heart and life. He asserts that this man had come to Africa for the sake of the Church, and that persecution had thereby been directed especially against the Church herself.

He writes that Marinus had inflicted atrocious grief upon the Church through gratuitous cruelty and without any necessity—although there may perhaps have been other causes which one could suspect but which there was no need to commit to writing—and that he had attempted to please the impious by this punishment, or had rejoiced that he had pleased them. The author of so wicked a slaughter was trying to shift the responsibility onto necessity and the Emperor’s command, although the imperial court had so thoroughly established the innocence of both brothers that it did not even seem appropriate to grant them a pardon, lest any suspicion should thereby cling to their reputation. Indeed, we shall see that Marcellinus’s death was disapproved by the court.

Those were times remarkably exposed to calumny, so that even when only a single witness was produced, anyone could be punished with impunity by the ultimate penalty—especially someone whom it was easy plausibly to accuse of a crime that was inherently hateful. This would fit no other charge more suitably than that of rebellion, particularly after so great a revolt as Heraclian’s. Moreover, the considerable power then possessed by the man who condemned him had, within a not very long period, been substantially diminished. In fact, immediately after Marcellinus’s death, Marinus was recalled from Africa and lost both his position and his favor.

All these considerations lead us to believe that Marcellinus himself is designated in that letter. Certainly we see nothing that conflicts with this opinion, and we may rightly affirm that no one can be found to whom the matters reported in those letters would better apply.

There is, to be sure, no doubt that the letters were written during the time of Pope Innocent, who lived on until the year 417. They are addressed to Caecilian, a man already advanced in age and held in great esteem for his integrity, though still a catechumen. He was involved in the administration of the state and burdened with many public cares and affairs (ibid.). [Col. 0463] Therefore, for our part, we see no reason not to be persuaded that he was the same man who became prefect of the praetorium at the beginning of the year 409, and also the very man to whom Augustine sent a letter around the year 405 concerning the restraint of the Donatists in the territory of Hippo (Epistle 86). For the holy man calls him an old friend (Epistle 151, no. 1).

## 3.

After Heraclian’s defeat, it happened that Caecilian was in Africa together with Count Marinus, to whom, as was reported, he was joined by a long-standing friendship. When Caecilian had once come to him, the Count summoned Marcellinus and his brother. After they had been dismissed, Caecilian remained, as was reported, and held a private conversation with him. At the same time, men were sent to lay hands on the brothers and thrust both of them into a foul and dark prison.

Nevertheless, Marcellinus was there flooded with joy and possessed a greater happiness than Marinus himself, since Marinus could not attain such dignity or power as to avoid being miserably tormented by the goads of his own madness.

One day, when the brothers were being held together in custody, Marcellinus’s brother said to him: “If I am suffering these things for the merits of my sins, then you, whose life we know to be so carefully and fervently Christian—by what evil merits have you been brought to this?”

He replied: “Do you think that a small benefit is being bestowed upon me by God, if your testimony about my life is true: that what I am suffering—even if I suffer it to the shedding of blood—may there punish my sins and not reserve them for the judgment to come?”

At this point, Augustine adds, someone might perhaps suppose that he was conscious of some secret sins of sexual impurity. “I shall therefore say,” he continues, “what the Lord God willed me to hear from his mouth, to my great consolation, and to know with certainty. Since, as human affairs go, I was concerned about this matter and was alone with him, who was already confined in the same custody, lest there should be anything for which he ought to appease God by a greater and more conspicuous repentance, he—being a man of exceptional modesty, who blushed at my suspicion, although it was false, yet received my admonition most gratefully—smiled modestly and gravely, grasped my right hand with both his hands, and said: ‘I call to witness the sacraments administered through this hand: I have known no sexual intercourse except with my wife, neither before nor afterward’” (ibid., no. 9).

## 4.

These events were taking place at Carthage, where the blessed Augustine was undoubtedly already present; for it is not likely that he would have had an opportunity afterward to travel there deliberately. He left nothing unattempted to prevent Marinus from striking the heart of the Church with grief through Marcellinus’s death, and from destroying his own soul by so great a crime.

Indeed, Caecilian himself—although certain considerations burdened him with suspicion that he had arranged this imprisonment—joined his prayers to those of the Church. After repeatedly warning Marinus and repeatedly entreating him, he showed no slight hope of a more favorable outcome. From time to time he assured the bishops that he was devoting every effort and resource to the matter; and they convinced him that this was absolutely necessary to remove the odium directed against him. [Col. 0464]

Marinus made many splendid promises, but only in order to deceive the bishops and prevent them from releasing the captives from their bonds. For it was believed that this could be accomplished by them either through the Church’s intercession and intervention with the Emperor, or even by employing some force. This seems to be what the holy Bishop’s words signify: “the ecclesiastical hand could rescue them” (ibid., no. 5).

For that reason, when it was proposed that one of the bishops should be sent to the Emperor to plead the brothers’ case, Marinus not only consented but even requested it, promising in the meantime that, until he learned what the bishop sent had obtained, he would postpone his decision. In fact, a certain bishop was sent to the court together with a deacon. He did not obtain pardon for the brothers, lest their reputation should be injured even by the slightest suspicion; but he did obtain an imperial order to Count Marinus that he release them as soon as possible and inflict upon them neither punishment nor injury. The Count, however, anticipated the Emperor’s reply.

## 5.

On the third day before the feast of the martyr Cyprian—that is, on the day before the Ides of September—Caecilian visited Augustine and gave him better hope than ever before. He said that he would soon depart for Rome, and hoped that before leaving the Count would grant him this favor.

He solemnly affirmed to the blessed Bishop that, when he had gone to Marinus, he had openly declared that the familiarity with which Marinus honored him through such frequent conversations would, if he were going to condemn these brothers, prove not an honor but a very great disadvantage to him. For since no one was unaware of the reasons for the estrangement between Caecilian and the brothers, everyone would easily believe that he had been seized neither without his knowledge nor against his wishes, and that he had participated in the plan to remove them both.

Finally, stretching out his hand toward the altar, he swore that he had truly said all these things to Marinus. Marinus, he claimed, had been so moved by them that Caecilian had no doubt that he would grant pardon to both men as his viaticum—that is, in place of the gifts with which departing friends were customarily presented.

When Augustine heard this, he admits that he was so firmly persuaded that Caecilian was earnestly and sincerely laboring for their release that he did not abandon this opinion even when he saw the outcome prove entirely contrary. For when, on the following day, he learned that both men had been brought out of prison and taken before the Count for sentence to be pronounced, he was certainly struck with considerable shock. Nevertheless, strengthened by what he had heard from Caecilian and almost certain of their release, he thought that the Count had chosen the eve of the martyr Cyprian’s feast in order to discharge his obligation to Caecilian, and that he would therefore ascend to the place of the holy Martyr to gladden the faithful by this unexpected event, raised higher by the mercy of sparing than by the power of killing.

But Marinus had a very different intention. Augustine had not yet been able to inquire what was being done in the matter when, behold, the sad news of the brothers’ execution was brought to him. Since the Count feared nothing so much as that the Church’s intervention might snatch them from his cruelty, he condemned both men when this was least expected and ordered them to be beheaded immediately. [Col. 0465]

Moreover, to hasten the affair still further, he assigned them a place that had previously been intended not for the punishment of men but for the adornment of the city.
