It had never before been polluted with the blood of the condemned, except that a few days earlier he had ordered several criminals to suffer the capital penalty there. It was firmly believed that he had done this deliberately, so that, if Marcellinus were struck down in the same place, the disgrace and horror of the deed might be increased by the novelty of the location.

For it could not be unclear to him how grievous that condemnation would be to the Church. By not shrinking from inflicting torment upon that holy mother, he bound himself to an even heavier crime, since he himself had been counted among her children and had received from her the benefit of baptism.

The brother whose advice he followed in so great a crime had once been placed in danger of his life and had been forced to seek the Church’s aid. Indeed, Marinus himself, when he had once incurred the displeasure of a patron—for through unexpected success that man had risen to such great power—had begged the Church’s protection as a favor, and it had by no means been denied him.

## 6.

He did indeed attempt to invoke the necessity of obedience to an imperial order, which he claimed had been communicated to him by letter. But the fact that the bishop sent as envoy had obtained from the Emperor an entirely contrary command made the Count’s lie perfectly clear. And certainly he was immediately recalled from Africa, stripped of every office and dignity, and left to his own conscience, so that it might serve as a witness to his repentance or punishment (Orosius, *Histories*, book 7, chapter 42).

As for Marcellinus, he departed this life not merely to receive the reward and fruit of his virtues and of the labors he had undertaken for the Church, but also the deserved martyr’s crown through the shedding of his blood. The Church honors him by this title in the Roman Martyrology. Yet there they offer no reason or authority for celebrating his memory on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

In fact, we have seen that he was struck down on the Ides of September—that is, on the day before the feast of Cyprian’s passion. Once this is established, there can be no doubt that his execution occurred in the present year, since it followed Heraclian’s revolt and preceded the law issued by Honorius after his death, on the third day before the Kalends of September in the year 414. In that law the Emperor wished to give perpetual validity to the acts of the Conference over which Marcellinus had presided (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 55).

There the Emperor, while showing that he wished to preserve the reputation of a man who had been slain under the appearance of rebellion, calls him “a man of illustrious memory.” Augustine, however, honors him not only with the title “of religious memory” (Epistle 166, no. 7; Epistle 169, no. 13), but also “of holy memory” (*On Nature and Grace*, no. 25). Lamenting the death of one whose friends were especially dear to him (Epistle 190, no. 20) and especially beloved in the love of Christ (Epistle 166, no. 6), he says:

“What integrity he possessed in character, what fidelity in friendship, what zeal in learning, what sincerity in religion, what chastity in marriage, what self-restraint in judgment; patience toward enemies, kindness toward friends, humility toward the saints, love toward all; readiness in granting favors, modesty in requesting them, love of good deeds, grief over sins! What dignity of uprightness, what splendor of grace, what care for piety! What mercy in helping, what goodwill in forgiving, what confidence in prayer! How modestly he spoke of what he knew to be beneficial! With what diligence he investigated what he knew not to be useless! How great was his contempt for present things! How great his hope and desire for eternal goods!

“Although he had abandoned all secular pursuits in order to take up the military service of Christ, the bond of marriage held him back; already bound by it, he had begun to desire better things, when it was no longer possible to break away from those things, although they were inferior. What evil, then, happened to this man in death—or rather, what very great good—since, possessing these gifts, which are possessed in vain without Christ, he departed from this life to Christ?” (Epistle 151, nos. 8, 10.)

## 7.

After the impious and cruel treachery of Count Marinus, Augustine could not bring himself to remain longer at Carthage. Accordingly, on the following day he set out; and when Caecilian wished to speak with him, he learned that Augustine had hastened his departure.

He secretly slipped out of the city so as not to be detained by the groans, tears, and cries of many distinguished citizens who had taken refuge in the church to escape the Count’s fury and sword. For although their lives were not actually in danger, they would undoubtedly have begged him to intercede for them with the Count; and propriety certainly did not permit this. For if the holy man had used against the Count such terrifying language as seemed necessary for securing the salvation of his soul, Marinus would never have taken it well.

Therefore, unable to endure such an outrage, Augustine departed. “I was deeply grieved,” says the great Bishop, “at the plight of my venerable fellow bishop, the ruler of so great a Church, whose duty, it was said, required him, after such a wicked deception by that man, still to present himself humbly so that others might be spared—namely, those who had taken refuge in the church, unless perhaps some others were also being held in custody. I confess that, since I could not endure so great an evil with any strength of heart, I departed” (ibid., no. 3).

Elsewhere he gives other reasons for his departure besides Marcellinus’s death. One, he says, was this: “Because I can no longer endure the labor which it is necessary to undergo in that city and which, if I wished to explain it, would require as much speaking again; for, in addition to my own weakness, which is known to all who know me more intimately, old age has also come upon me, the common weakness of the human race. The second reason is that I have resolved, if the Lord wills, to devote all the time granted me by those occupations which the needs of the Church, whom I serve by my office, demand, to the labor of studies concerning ecclesiastical learning. In this work I think that, if it pleases God’s mercy, I may also benefit those who come after me” (ibid., no. 13).

Then he gravely admonishes Caecilian, formerly a catechumen and one who sought to learn the truth from the holy Doctor, not to delay any longer joining himself to the faithful through baptism on the empty pretext that the faithful cannot administer the state properly [Col. 0467] (Epistle 151, no. 14).

He also did not fail to teach him how he ought to conduct himself toward Marinus: “If you love him, detest him; if you do not want him to be punished eternally, shudder at him. Thus must you care for your own reputation and for his life” (ibid., no. 11).

This letter may reasonably be said to have been written toward the end of that year.

# CHAPTER VI

1. Demetrias, after the Goths capture Rome, is sent to Africa together with her mother and grandmother.  
2. Augustine instructs Proba, Demetrias’s grandmother, by letter and gives her directions concerning prayer to God.  
3. At his urging Demetrias embraces virginity.  
4. Augustine rejoices with the whole Church at Demetrias’s veiling.  
5. He writes his mother Juliana a book *On the Good of Widowhood*.  
6. Under the pretext of instructing the virgin Demetrias, Pelagius publishes a letter steeped in the poison of his heresy.

## 1.

Although the wound inflicted upon Augustine’s heart by the utterly disgraceful murder of Marcellinus was exceedingly grave, his grief was greatly diminished when he witnessed a remarkable work of divine grace. He himself had served as an instrument in that same journey to Carthage, during which his friend’s blood had been shed almost before his eyes. This miracle of grace may properly be assigned to the present year, if one wishes to place here that memorable event: Demetrias, the foremost virgin in the Roman world in nobility and wealth, in whom the blood of the Probi, the Olbrii, and the Anicii had converged, bid farewell to all things when she was thought to be on the point of marriage, so that she might have Jesus Christ as her bridegroom; and thus she increased that family—among whose members the consulship and every highest dignity of the Empire were familiar—with the honor and renown of virginity as well.

Her father was Anicius Hermogenianus Olibrius, born to Sextus Petronius Probus and Proba Anicia Faltonia; her mother was Juliana. Demetrias was living at Rome with her grandmother Proba and her mother Juliana when the city was captured by the Goths in the year 410. They left Rome together while it was still, so to speak, smoking from the fire (Jerome, Epistle 8).

Proba, fearing that Alaric, who had departed after laying waste Italy, might return to Rome, entrusted her own life and safety, and those of all her companions—including Juliana and her daughter Demetrias—to a small boat. She reached Africa with good fortune; but there she encountered Count Heraclian, who, while pretending to manage the Emperor’s affairs, was cruelly harassing the entire province. Since the chastity of the women accompanying her, of whom she had a considerable number, had to be preserved, she was forced to ransom it, as it were, from the tyrant by surrendering part of her wealth. This nevertheless did not prevent her from remaining extremely rich.

## 2.

Since there was no one in all Africa more illustrious than Augustine, Proba and Juliana did not fail to introduce themselves to his acquaintance by letter (Epistle 188, no. 1). Perhaps that correspondence gave rise to the letter from which we learn that Proba, wishing to receive news of Augustine’s health, had written to him that, “since the soul is placed in a corruptible body, it is constrained by a certain earthly contagion; and, weighed down and bent by this burden, it more easily desires and thinks about many things below than about one thing above” (Epistle 131).

Augustine replied that she rightly recognized how powerless human nature is and how entirely it inclines toward earthly things, but that Christ had descended to us in order to raise it up. He also told her that she was doing rightly to regard present calamities as bearable through hope of future goods. At the same time, he taught her that those very calamities and misfortunes bring no small benefit. He prayed to God for the rewards of the future life and the consolations of the present, and finally commended himself to the love and prayers “of all of you,” he says, “in whose hearts Christ dwells through faith.”

Proba was already of an age at which she seemed to have less reason to fear for herself; therefore it was especially her duty to struggle in prayer for her own people (*On the Good of Widowhood*, no. 29). She rightly asked the holy Bishop to write something to her about praying to God, so that she might be taught both what should be requested from God and in what manner it should be sought (Epistle 130, nos. 1, 9).

Augustine promised that he would satisfy the request of so worthy a Christian widow. As soon as he found leisure, he endeavored to fulfill his promise and sent her a longer letter on this subject, which he himself mentions in his book *On Widowhood* (*On the Good of Widowhood*, no. 29).

In that letter he exhorted Proba, with no less seriousness than modesty, to embrace the greater perfection commanded by the Gospel—and not without effect. For although she already possessed by nature an extraordinary inclination toward works of kindness, Augustine’s exhortation seized her with a renewed ardor of charity. This occurred, as Jerome writes:

“She is said to sell the possessions inherited from her ancestors and to make friends for herself from the mammon of iniquity, who may receive her into eternal dwellings, so that every rank of ecclesiastical ministry and the empty titles of monks may blush to purchase estates while a woman of such nobility is selling them” (Jerome, Epistle 8).

In this letter to Proba, Augustine mentions Juliana, her daughter-in-law (Epistle 130, no. 30), but he entirely forgets Demetrias. This is evidence that the letter was written before that noble virgin had devoted herself to Christ. Indeed, Augustine later mentions this same letter to Proba in his book *On Widowhood*, which, as the words “she has just begun” make clear, was published not long after Demetrias’s consecration (*On the Good of Widowhood*, no. 24).

## 3.

Baronius seems to place Demetrias’s consecration as early as the year 411 (Baronius, under the year 413, no. 13). This would indeed be necessary if, when Augustine first saw her, God had implanted this purpose in her; but the holy Bishop by no means relates that the matter happened in this way.

If Jerome wrote to Demetrias only in the year 413—or rather, as Baronius himself reports, in 414—why should he be said to have waited two or three years before writing about a matter that had immediately spread throughout the entire world? We find no reason for such a claim.

As we have already said, Augustine first became acquainted with Proba and Juliana through their letters (Epistle 188, no. 1). He later saw them in person, beginning in the year 411, and whenever he subsequently came to Carthage he did not cease to scatter in their hearts the seeds of saving instructions that he had learned from God [Col. 0469]. They received these instructions not as the words of some human being, but—as they truly were—as the words of God himself.

Through Augustine’s exhortations, with the help of God’s grace, the greatest fruits were produced in that household. For not long after he had departed from Carthage, Demetrias, rightly and successfully following the instructions he had given her, professed virginal sanctity. She preferred the chaste embraces of her heavenly Bridegroom to the earthly husband to whom she was on the point of being given.

Augustine testifies that he and Alypius labored together in this matter. His praise or reward is not diminished because he shared the work with such a unanimous and intimate friend. Demetrias was already prepared for marriage when she pronounced her vow of virginity.

Jerome gives many remarkable and beautiful details about the deed of that most noble virgin (Jerome, Epistle 8). He had received them from certain holy and noble women who, having been forced to leave Gaul because of hostile devastation and traveling through Africa on their way to Jerusalem, happened to see Demetrias there.

After the name of God had been invoked, the bishop—Aurelius, bishop of Carthage—publicly placed the *flammeum*—as the holy Presbyter calls it, the insignia of virginity—upon Demetrias’s head, and consecrated that chaste virgin to Christ the Lord (ibid.).

## 4.

Proba and Juliana did not fail to inform Augustine by letter of Demetrias’s decision (Epistle 150), and they sent him some gift as a testimony of the solemnity at which she had been veiled, declaring that this great benefit of God was the fruit of his exhortations (Epistle 143, no. 1).

Their letter outran the speed of rumor and brought the holy Augustine so joyful a message that he experienced the pleasure of certainty before he could have doubted its truth. That would surely have happened had he learned of the matter only through widespread rumors.

Anyone wishing to know how greatly the holy Bishop was filled with joy by this great miracle of grace need only read the letter he wrote about it to Proba and Juliana around the beginning of the year 414 (Epistle 150). Wherever Proba’s name had reached—that is, throughout all regions—the fame of the virginity professed by Demetrias had also spread (ibid.).

“All the Churches throughout Africa,” in Jerome’s words, “celebrated with a kind of rejoicing: the famous report penetrated not only to cities, towns, and villages, but even to the isolated farmsteads. All the islands between Africa and Italy were filled with this rumor, and the rejoicing ran farther still without hindrance.”

Immediately before this he says: “As though from a fertile root, many virgins sprang up at once, and the crowd of clients and servants followed the example of their patron and mistress” (whose vows Augustine had supported) (ibid.).

Therefore Augustine rightly calls Juliana’s household no small church of Christ (Epistle 188, no. 3), and elsewhere calls her family a domestic church (*On the Good of Widowhood*, no. 29).

## 5.

A few days after Demetrias had professed her decision to adopt the more holy way of life, Augustine wrote to Juliana, her mother, a book—or letter—*On the Good of Widowhood*. Juliana had asked him for it personally; and when he could neither resist nor refuse the holy woman, she repeatedly reminded him by letter of his promise.

He therefore had to steal several hours from the occupations that pressed upon him in order to satisfy her wishes. In this work he proposed both to teach Christian widows their duties and to exhort them to undertake courageously and eagerly the good which they knew they ought to do.

Although he was writing to Juliana alone, he was not writing for Juliana alone, nor merely for Proba Faltonia, her mother-in-law who lived in her household, but also for all the widows who would read this work of his (ibid., no. 1). Among other things, he especially advised Juliana to avoid conversations harmful to the grace of Christ with opponents (ibid., no. 21).

## 6.

At that time, while the more distinguished men of the Church, at the request of Demetrias’s grandmother and mother, were striving to instruct her and strengthen her in her holy purpose, Pelagius also did not wish to be absent. He seized this opportunity both to acquire fame and to convey his error.

He therefore wrote a letter for the instruction of that noble virgin. It appears in the appendix to Augustine’s letters and begins, “If with the highest genius” (*Appendix*, Epistle 17).

Among the instructions with which Pelagius teaches Demetrias, he advises her to establish solitude for herself in the City—a term that properly means Rome (ibid., chapter 23). Certainly nothing prevents Proba from having returned there by that time.

At least we see Jerome advising Demetrias to follow the faith of Innocent, without mentioning either Aurelius or Augustine (Jerome, Epistle 8). It further appears that the fame of Pelagius’s letter did not reach Augustine before the year 416 or 417. If Demetrias had remained in Africa throughout, this could scarcely have happened.

At least this much is beyond doubt: Augustine did not see the letter until after the Palestinian synod, which was held only toward the end of the year 415, since he is uncertain whether it was written before or after that synod (*On the Grace of Christ*, no. 23).

Augustine may already have seen this letter when he and Alypius warned Demetrias’s mother not to lend her ears to men who corrupted the faith by their speeches (Epistle 188, no. 2). Juliana replied that she owed them very much for this warning and assured them that such men were hateful to her no less than to her household. Finally, she informed them that her entire family had always been so steadfast in the Catholic faith that no one in it had ever adhered to any heresy, not even the slightest.

It happened conveniently that Alypius was at Hippo when Juliana’s reply was delivered to Augustine. Accordingly, they sent her a joint reply in both their names (ibid., no. 1).

First they affirm that, since they had contributed their efforts to promote the veiling of her daughter Demetrias, no one could think it improper if they presumed to admonish them about their salvation and about the enemies of grace [Col. 0471].

Then they ask her to inform them about a certain book addressed to Demetrias and filled with extremely dangerous errors: whether she herself had read it, who was considered its author, and with what assurance Demetrias had accepted a work teaching her that she owed her virginal holiness and all her spiritual riches to herself alone, and thus—before she became fully blessed—should learn to be, God forbid, ungrateful to God.

They themselves do not conceal that they assigned this letter to Pelagius, but they were seeking fuller confirmation of the matter (Epistle 188, no. 4). Their opinion did not deceive them. For in his book *On the Grace of Christ*, published in the year 418, Augustine repeatedly cites the same composition without hesitation as Pelagius’s.

From this one may understand that Augustine and Alypius’s reply to Juliana is indeed earlier than that work, but only by a very few days, since in it they mention Pelagius’s letters to Innocent, delivered to Zosimus around September of the year 417 (ibid., no. 14).

# CHAPTER VII

1. Honorius issues a more severe law against obstinate Donatists.  
2. Donatus of Mutugenna and another presbyter of the Donatist party are placed in custody with him.  
3. Augustine writes to Macedonius about bishops’ intercessions for criminals.  
4. Macedonius testifies how prudently and modestly Augustine conducted himself in such intercessions; Augustine instructs him concerning the duties of a Christian magistrate and true virtues.  
5. He replies to Hilary concerning questions sent from Sicily against the Pelagians.

## 1.

The Donatists easily persuaded themselves that, through Marcellinus’s murder, they had inflicted upon the Church no less injury than anguish. But not long afterward God taught them that, even after Marcellinus’s death, the power by which he had protected the Church before Marcellinus was born had not been taken from him.

For on the tenth day before the Kalends of July in this very year, 414, Honorius issued a law against them. It followed almost chapter by chapter the law promulgated on the third day before the Kalends of February in the year 412, but added greatly to its severity (*Theodosian Code*, “On Heretics,” law 44).

Indeed, whereas the law of 412 imposed a fine of only fifty pounds of gold even upon the highest-ranking offender, this law fined the same persons two hundred pounds of silver. It added that the imposed sum was to be exacted from each individual every time he returned to the communion of the schismatics. If anyone relapsed more than five times, his name was to be reported to the Emperor so that an even harsher punishment might be sought for him.

It further added that masters who left unpunished their agents, by whom the Donatists had not been prevented from holding assemblies on their estates, were to be fined all the produce gathered from those estates during one year; that clerics were to be stripped of all their property before being subjected to the prohibition of water and fire; and that Donatists generally were to be declared infamous, excluded from every gathering and association, legally incapable of making wills, and finally deprived of every right to enter into contracts.

Furthermore, on the third day before the Kalends of September in that same year, 414, he confirmed by his authority, as has already been stated, the acts of the Conference (*ibid.*, law 55).

## 2.

Although Augustine was exerting himself before the judges with great zeal, so that they might temper the severity of the imperial laws against the Donatists with Christian gentleness, nevertheless he thought it his duty to ensure that, by the authority of those laws, they should gradually be brought over to the Catholic Church—especially those whose welfare, as residents within his own diocese of Hippo, he was obliged to safeguard (Epistle 133 and Epistle 134).

Among these were undoubtedly those two presbyters of Donatus’s party who, whether through the holy Bishop’s efforts or at least at his desire, were arrested and brought to Hippo, so that they might perhaps be presented to the judges, whose duty it was to enforce the commands of the laws, and so that they might be kept in custody lest they do violence to themselves. One of them, named Donatus, not only refused a horse that was offered to him but also threw himself against the ground and severely injured himself. Later, after he had been brought to Hippo, he threw himself headlong into a well, from which the Catholics pulled him out against his will and resistance.

So great was this man’s obstinacy that he continually shouted that he wished to persist in error and wished to perish in it; that no one ought to be compelled to what was good, whatever that might be, since God had willed us to be our own masters and to possess freedom of choice; that Christ, when his disciples wished to depart from him, had not detained them, but had allowed his Apostles the choice and complete freedom either to leave or to remain; and, finally, that he ought not to be blamed for having resolved to do himself violence, since the Apostle had counted among actions deserving goodness and praise the act of anyone who handed over his body to be consumed by flames.

When the provisions established at the Conference were brought up against him, he boasted that he could defend the cause of his party even against Augustine, provided that what the Donatists had conceded—that one person should not prejudice another—were recalled. Augustine was deeply distressed by the pitiable condition of this wretched presbyter, and the care of his salvation caused him the greatest anxiety. Moved, therefore, by this concern, he sent him a letter (Epistle 173), full alike of love and forcefulness, in which he overturned the empty arguments and sophistries by which the man deceived himself in his obstinacy and blindness.

There he explains what induces the Church to employ some degree of force. As for the Donatists’ admission that one person should not prejudice another, he demonstrates that, if what they had conceded so solemnly could not harm this man, a private presbyter, still less could it injure the universal Church on account of what Caecilianus had committed or might have been able to commit. Finally, he challenges him to answer, if he can more effectively, the argument that the Catholics had drawn from the history of the Maximianists.

## 3.

As we have seen, Augustine began his work *On the City of God* in the preceding year, and completed its fourth and fifth books in the following year. Since this was so, it will certainly not seem out of place to assign to this year [Col. 0473] Augustine’s letters to Macedonius, then the vicar of Africa, some of which he wrote after sending him the first three books of this work (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 20).

We possess two letters from Macedonius to Augustine, written with considerable skill and elegance (in Augustine, Epistles 152 and 154), and an equal number of excellent replies from Augustine to him (Epistles 153 and 155). Augustine held Macedonius in high esteem both because of his outstanding abilities and because of his prudence and integrity in conducting public affairs, but especially because, as he says, he recognized that Macedonius’s spirit, “thirsting for the divine and heavenly commonwealth, whose ruler is Christ, with a love of eternity and truth and with the affection of that very love,” was “drawing near to it” and “burning to possess it” (Epistle 155, §1).

Therefore, when so great and eminent a man eagerly desired to enter into friendship with the holy Bishop, to converse with him by letter, and to see some of his writings (ibid., §11), Augustine received this with gratitude and pleasure. He promised to send him some of his shorter works (Epistle 152, §3), and sent him, by Bishop Boniface—perhaps the bishop of Cataquum—a letter in which he asked Macedonius to intercede on behalf of a certain defendant (ibid., §1).

Macedonius certainly was not the kind of man who would allow the Bishop whom he regarded as uniquely worthy of veneration and true reverence to suffer any refusal (Epistles 152 and 154, titles). Indeed, he himself was so inclined toward clemency that, although he did not dare of his own accord to acquit defendants, lest he appear to be defending crimes, he considered those from whom he had been asked to remit punishments to have rendered him an excellent service (Epistle 152, §3).

Yet, wishing—as he said—to repay Augustine for the favor granted him, he asked him in a letter full of the utmost courtesy to disclose the reasoning behind his advice, and whether it was consistent with the duties of the Christian religion for bishops to intercede on behalf of defendants. At the same time, he requested that the writings Augustine had promised him be sent, so that, since he could not meanwhile enjoy Augustine’s presence, he might at least be nourished by his teaching (ibid., §1).

Accordingly, Augustine arranged for the first three books of *The City of God* to be delivered to him. To the question Macedonius had put to him he replied briefly that bishops sought life and salvation for defendants with the aim that they might be permitted to correct their deeds and cleanse them through repentance:

> “So that they may not end this life by punishment in such a way that, once it has ended, they cannot end their punishment” (Epistle 153, §3).

On this subject, however, he argues at somewhat greater length for the benefit of those who might read this letter without possessing the same discernment that Macedonius possessed. He also explains on what grounds it is permissible to intercede for defendants, and gives many instructions concerning the laws to be observed in restoring another person’s property.

He likewise notes that Macedonius, moved by a certain innate humanity, had pleaded on behalf of a cleric who had committed some offense. Aurelius, apparently softened by his prayers, had moderated the punishment owed by that cleric; Augustine speaks of this action in such a way as to indicate that he himself was present (ibid., §§16, 10).

## 4.

[Col. 0474] Augustine had approved bishops’ intercessions in that same letter, and had placed himself under an obligation to Macedonius through the confidence by which he had, in a sense, undertaken not to refuse such requests. Therefore, making diligent use of his right, he did not allow defendants who fled to him to be deprived of his protection (Epistle 152, §3; Epistle 154, §1). Yet in this matter he displayed such wisdom and modesty that Macedonius not only could not reject his requests, but could not restrain himself from heaping praise upon Augustine’s modesty.

Possidius copied the following words into the *Life of the Holy Man*:

> “In a marvelous way I am moved by your wisdom, both in what you have published and in what, when interceding for criminals, you do not hesitate to send. For the former possess such keenness, knowledge, and holiness that nothing could surpass them; and the latter such modesty that, unless I do what you command, I judge that the fault remains with me, not in the matter itself—lord deservedly venerable and father truly worthy of reverence. For you do not press me—as most people in this position do—to extort whatever you anxiously desire; rather, with accommodating modesty, you remind me of what you have judged may be requested from a judge burdened by so many cares. This modesty is the most effective instrument among good men for difficult undertakings” (ibid.; Possidius, *Index*, §25).

At the same time, Macedonius extols in magnificent praise what he had read from Augustine’s works (Epistle 154, §2). That these works were the first books of *The City of God* is indicated clearly enough both by his own words (ibid.) and by Augustine’s (Epistle 155, §2).

Macedonius appears to have been on the point of returning to Italy, and promised that he would write to Augustine from there, if this could be done, “so that,” as he says, “a work of such great learning may be repaid by services that, although not sufficient, are at least appropriate” (Epistle 154, §3).

Before his departure Augustine wished to present him with a gift worthy of him. He therefore replied in a most distinguished letter (Epistle 155), in which he placed before him the principal duties of a Christian man, and especially of one who holds authority. Above all, he warned him to attribute all his virtues to the goodness of God and to set this goal before himself in all the duties of his magistracy: to lead his subjects to God and to eternal life.

Possidius calls this work *On True Virtues*, and the other letter to Macedonius *On the Intercessions of Bishops* (Possidius, *Index*, chapter 1).

## 5.

Perhaps in this year, 414, Augustine wrote the book, or letter, to Hilary concerning the questions sent from Sicily (Epistle 157). Jerome and Orosius mention it in the year 415 and testify that it had recently been written.

No one throughout the Christian world was unaware of how far the Bishop of Hippo surpassed the teachers of the Church in learning and knowledge. Even Volusianus himself, though not yet a believer, had heard that Augustine was ignorant of nothing pertaining to sacred doctrine. “When one comes to Augustine,” he said, “whatever may have happened to be unknown is absent from the reading” (Epistle 135, §2). He even maintained that Augustine’s reputation was at stake unless his own questions were explained through him.

When Hilary therefore noticed [Col. 0475] that certain people in Syracuse were teaching the following new doctrines—that a human being could be without sin and, if he wished, could easily keep God’s commandments; that an unbaptized infant prevented by death from receiving baptism could not justly perish, since it was born without sin; that a rich man remaining in his wealth could not enter the kingdom of God unless he sold everything he possessed; and that it would not benefit him if, from those riches, he happened to keep the commandments, and so forth—he consulted Augustine about them. He was persuaded by Augustine’s grace, that is, by the divinely granted ability to teach that was known to everyone.

He seems to indicate Augustine’s supreme authority in these words:

> “Concerning all these matters, I beg your Holiness with all the prayers of which I am capable to order that we be instructed more clearly, so that we may know to what extent we ought to hold these opinions” (Epistle 156).

Accordingly, after Augustine had explained at length what he thought about those Pelagian questions, he said:

> “You have received what seems right to me. Let better men explain these matters more fully—not those whose opinion I now know must be rejected, but others who can do so truthfully. For I am more ready to learn than to teach; and you will confer a great benefit on me if you do not allow me to remain ignorant of what the holy brothers there are saying against the empty talk of these men” (Epistle 157, §41).

# CHAPTER VIII

1. Several psalms explained both in the year of Christ 415 and earlier.  
2. The presbyter Orosius comes from the farthest part of Spain to Augustine.  
3. To satisfy his inquiry, Augustine writes a book against the Priscillianists and Origenists.  
4. He sends Orosius with some of his writings to Jerome, from whom he wishes especially to learn about the origin of the soul.  
5. He recalls Timasius and James from Pelagius’s error and publishes a short work against him, *On Nature and Grace*.  
6. He replies in several letters to certain questions of Evodius, especially to the principal ones.  
7. He composes a book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*.

## 1.

In the letter given to Evodius during this year, 415, various works are mentioned which Augustine, as he himself reports, had begun before Easter, when Lent was already approaching, and had at that time brought to completion (Epistle 169, §1).

Among these he mentions two books, namely the fourth and fifth books of *The City of God*. To them he adds extensive expositions of Psalms 61, 71, and 77, dictated by him. He had already explained many other psalms, either in writing or by preaching. For we have seen that he had explained Psalm 36 at Carthage in the course of preaching as early as the year 403 (above, book 5, chapter 8, §6). In the letter just mentioned he says that the remaining psalms, for which he had not yet produced an exposition either in writing or in a sermon delivered to the people, were eagerly awaited and demanded from him (Epistle 169, §1).

He also suggests that at that time, namely toward the end of the year 415, he intended to devote himself entirely to completing this work and, at the same time, the work *On the City of God*. For that reason he was postponing the books *On the Trinity*, since they were more difficult and, at least in the opinion of most [Col. 0476] people, less useful.

In fact, he put the finishing hand to this great work and explained all the psalms, partly by dictating and partly by preaching; indeed, he explained some of them in both ways.

## 2.

After the expositions of the three psalms just mentioned, Augustine adds the books that he sent to Jerome through Orosius, as well as another work addressed to Orosius, entitled *Against the Priscillianists and Origenists* (ibid., §13).

Orosius was a Spanish presbyter who is also called Paul in the works that survive from him. He had been born in the farthest part of Spain, on the shore of the Ocean (ibid.; Epistle 166, §2). Since he was not merely Catholic in communion but also inflamed with piety and zeal for the Christian faith, he grieved less over his homeland being plundered and devastated by the barbarians than over the faith being attacked throughout Spain by various errors.

When he heard of Augustine’s reputation, he concluded that, with Augustine as his teacher, he could learn whatever he wished about the questions that troubled him, and that Augustine would fully and abundantly satisfy his love of the sacred Scriptures. Augustine, a witness beyond all objection, testifies that this single purpose moved him to cross from the farthest part of Spain into Africa (Epistle 169, §13).

Nevertheless, he seems to have been forced by the cruelty of the barbarians to carry out his plan sooner than he had intended. He himself says that, during a certain disturbance, struck with fear of misfortune, he fled (Orosius, *History*, book 5, chapter 2); that he barely escaped the barbarians’ ambushes; and that, even after he had boarded ship, he was attacked with stones and weapons, finally escaping through the sudden appearance of a mist when he seemed on the point of being captured. He adds that these dangers were so great that no one could hear of them without tears unless he were hard-hearted (ibid., book 3, chapter 20).

He further says that, having been driven from his homeland by some hidden force and having departed without will, necessity, or consent, he crossed into Africa, and did not discover that his voyage was tending there until he reached the shore of that province. Only then, after considering by what route he had been carried there, did he understand the end and purpose of his course; and, recovering and recollecting his mind, he recognized that divine providence was directing him to Augustine, so that he might find in him a remedy for the evils of Spain (in Augustine, *Orosius’s Inquiry*, §1).

Thus it is not implausible that, as he hurried in precipitous haste toward a ship, he boarded a vessel that was sailing elsewhere, yet, with God guiding its course, landed on the African shore.

## 3.

Orosius ardently desired a conversation with Augustine and was awaiting an opportunity to set down in a short book the questions about which he wished to be instructed and present them to him. It happened that, moved by the same desire to promote the salvation of all, the bishops Paul and Eutropius brought to the holy Teacher a memorandum concerning certain heresies.

Since they had exposed not all heresies but only certain ones, Orosius therefore judged it necessary to gather together all the trees of heretical doctrines, with their roots and branches. For this purpose he presented the blessed Bishop with an inquiry, or memorandum, in the form of a letter, [Col. 0477] in which he explained what poisons of Priscillian and Origen were then infecting Spain (ibid.).

The desire for learning with which Orosius burned could not fail to be most welcome to Augustine. Therefore, to satisfy his wishes, Augustine wrote a book entitled *Against the Priscillianists and Origenists* and dedicated it to Orosius.

In it he used as much brevity and clarity as he could. He said almost nothing against the errors of the Priscillianists because the principles by which the Priscillianists too could be overthrown had already been established in his arguments against the Manichaeans, which Orosius had either already read or could conveniently read (Against the Priscillianists and Origenists, §1).

At the end, while speaking about the distinction among heavenly spirits, Augustine argues beautifully about obscure questions of this kind, especially questions that are not necessary; and he candidly admits to Orosius that he is entirely unable to answer that particular question:

> “So that you may despise me, whom you think a great teacher: I do not know what these things are, or how they differ from one another” (ibid., §14).

Elsewhere, too, he says that Orosius would gain this benefit from his journey: that thereafter he would not place so much confidence in what rumor might proclaim about him (Epistle 166, §2).

Augustine assigns this treatise among the works he composed in the year 415. Since it must have been published not long after Orosius’s arrival in Africa, we do not see why Orosius should not be said to have come to that province earlier in the same year 415.

## 4.

Although Orosius received in abundance the benefit he had expected from his voyage when he saw and heard Augustine, Augustine wished to enrich him with full interest. Not content with giving him what he himself knew, he pointed out to him the richest source from which he might easily draw whatever Augustine did not think himself able to teach him, and urged him to visit Jerome.

Orosius accepted this advice—or command—from Augustine very willingly and gladly resolved to comply with it. The holy Bishop asked him to turn aside to Augustine first on his return, before going back to his homeland; Orosius undertook to do so.

Augustine was especially pleased to have found an opportunity for presenting his questions to Jerome. Because of his supreme zeal for truth, he greatly desired to converse with Jerome by letter, since he held his intelligence and learning in the highest regard.

For this task, however, a man was needed who was trustworthy in action, prompt in obedience, and practiced in enduring the hardships of travel. The holy Bishop had long been seeking such a person, but he did not easily find one. When he discovered all these and other qualities in the still-young Orosius, he believed that divine providence had sent him for this very purpose.

He therefore seized the opportunity and arranged for two rather lengthy writings to be delivered to Jerome. Augustine himself calls them “books” (Epistle 169, §13; Epistle 190, §20), and lists them under that title in his *Retractions*, although in our time they are numbered among his letters (Epistles 166 and 167).

In the first he consults Jerome about the origin of the human soul; in the second, about the statement of James:

> “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one [Col. 0478] point has become guilty of all” (James 2:10).

Jerome mentions these books with expressions of respect, but refused to reply to them because he did not have the leisure necessary for the task and because it would not benefit the interests of the Church for Augustine and Jerome to appear divided in opinion, even on minor matters.

This was perhaps, besides Augustine’s hope that Jerome would eventually answer him on these subjects, the principal reason why Augustine did not wish to make those books public during Jerome’s lifetime (in Augustine, Epistle 172, §1; *Retractions*, book 2, chapter 45).

From then on, he could not be persuaded to give a copy of them to anyone; nor did he entrust them to his friends to take home. He granted only that they might come to him and read them there. Before he received Jerome’s letter (in Augustine, Epistle 172), he seems to have acted more freely in this respect, for he counts these works among several other books that he offered to have Evodius copy (Epistle 169, §13).

He also seems to have asked Jerome, through Orosius, for his translation of the Septuagint, made by Jerome and distinguished by asterisks and obeli (Epistle 172, §2). Jerome is likewise said to have written several letters to the virgin Eustochium and to her mother, Paula the Younger, exhorting them to continue advancing and progressing in virtue.

## 5.

Augustine had perhaps already begun writing the book *On Nature and Grace* when Orosius departed from Africa. Not long afterward, when Orosius had reached Palestine and Pelagius himself was present, Orosius affirmed that he had responded fully, at the request of Pelagius’s disciples, to the book of that heretic which they had given him (*Orosius, Apology*).

At about the same time Jerome speaks of a certain work by Augustine that had not yet reached his hands and that was said to attack Pelagius directly (Against Pelagius, dialogue 3, chapter 6). Augustine likewise places this book last among the works that he mentions in a letter given during the course of the year 415.

Timasius and James had sent Pelagius’s book to Augustine (*On Nature and Grace*, §1). They were young men of highly respectable birth and educated in the liberal disciplines (Epistle 179, §2), who, at Pelagius’s own encouragement, had rejected every worldly hope and devoted themselves to the service of God (Epistle 177, §6; Epistle 179, §2).

Yet scarcely had they freed themselves from worldly bonds through Pelagius’s teaching when they became entangled in much more disastrous snares, namely the heresy introduced by him. God nevertheless rescued them from these snares through Augustine’s assistance and admonitions.

For Augustine immediately set aside what he had in hand and read the book with considerable attention (*On Nature and Grace*, §1). He found that Pelagius was defending human nature against the grace of God with every argument at his disposal (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 42).

The book was composed in the form of a dialogue, as is clear from the passages Augustine quotes. In it Pelagius posed to himself the question whether he was not excluding grace when he maintained that a human being could live without sin. In explicit terms he professed that the help of grace and divine mercy was necessary for this.

[Col. 0479] Augustine, who detested with horror those who spoke of human justification while excluding grace, was suddenly filled with joy at this open confession of grace. But as he continued reading the rest, it eventually became clear that an equivocation lay hidden beneath this expression (*On Nature and Grace*, §§11–12). Pelagius not only failed there to acknowledge the true grace of Christ, but also said many things contrary to it (Epistle 169, §3), and was altogether attempting to persuade people of doctrines that would erase from the hearts of believers their faith in that grace (Epistle 186, §1).

Augustine therefore replied to this book, as he saw that he ought to do, in a published disputation. He entitled his work *On Nature and Grace* because in it he defends grace, not against nature, but grace by which nature is liberated and governed (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 42).

Orosius states that Augustine condemned Pelagius’s claim that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes (*Apology*). Augustine examines and refutes every statement in Pelagius’s book, showing both how strongly the error of other statements must be avoided and detested, and how much suspicion nevertheless adheres even to those very statements that do not appear to be bad, because Pelagius deliberately keeps silent about true grace and its assistance (in Augustine, Epistle 168).

When Timasius and James received Augustine’s work, they wrote to thank him and testified that they had derived extraordinary pleasure from reading it. They declared that, although they had already renounced their error, they nevertheless owed him a great deal because he had supplied them with weapons by which they could attack it in others.

In this letter, which by Augustine’s favor we still possess in full, Timasius and James say that they regretted not having received this great gift of God’s grace earlier—for that is what they call the book. It had happened that some people whose blindness required illumination by so clear a revelation of the truth were absent at that time; nevertheless, they hoped that those people would receive the same gift of grace, even if later.

Augustine suspected that by these words they meant Pelagius above all (On the Proceedings of Pelagius, §49).

## 6.

The disputation *On Nature and Grace* had already been completed. Yet the year had not run its course when Augustine wrote his reply to Evodius’s questions concerning the Trinity and the dove (Epistle 169).

That holy Bishop of Uzalis had been bound to Augustine by a close relationship from the time of his baptism. He was accustomed to propose various questions concerning especially difficult matters, as the portions of both surviving letters make clear.

The holy Teacher had indicated to him that he was then occupied with matters and studies of such importance that he did not wish to be drawn away from them. Nevertheless, he satisfied him concerning the principal questions, partly in the present year and partly in the preceding one, while postponing others whose explanation would probably yield less benefit. For he was firmly resolved not to allow himself to be diverted from labors that were more necessary and useful to more people in order to clarify difficulties that concerned scholars alone.

When he deals with the question of certain miraculous visions reported by Evodius, Augustine declares that he wished he had some means [Col. 0480] readily available by which he could distinguish the visions of pious and holy people from imaginations closely resembling them, which error or impiety very often introduces as a deception. He adds that he would sooner run out of time while recounting examples of deceptive visions than run out of examples of such illusions (Epistle 159, §5).

From this one may understand that at that time there were both true and false visions, and that Augustine exercised the greatest caution lest he rashly reject or accept them all (above, book 5, chapter 8, §3).

## 7.

We were not permitted to place the book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness* before this period, since Possidius, in his *Index* (chapter 4), not without reason places it after *On Nature and Grace*. Augustine does not mention it in the letter to Evodius just cited (Epistle 169).

Nevertheless, it seems sufficiently reasonable to assign it a place immediately after that letter, for this single reason among others: it was written to the bishops Paul and Eutropius, the very men who had shortly before presented Augustine with a short work against certain heresies, before Orosius arrived in Africa and wrote to him about those same matters.

At that time a small document perhaps came into the hands of those bishops. It had been brought from Sicily by some brothers or Catholics, and bore the following heading at the front:

> “Definitions, as they are called, of Caelestius.”

They immediately gave it to that distinguished defender and vindicator of the faith and asked him to answer it.

Augustine judged that the heading did not belong to Caelestius, but, after examining another work whose authorship by Caelestius was established, he discovered that these brief definitions—or rather arguments—were not inconsistent with Caelestius’s character.

Attached to the definitions were testimonies from Scripture. The whole purpose of the document was to assert human powers and to persuade people that a human being could be without sin in this life (*On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, §1).

Augustine refutes the document in such a way that he does not yet dare to condemn those who said that some human beings had been or were righteous in this life without sin (ibid., §44). Nevertheless, he later attacks this opinion, condemned by the authority of the Council of Carthage in the year 418, as a pernicious error and orders people to beware of it (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 4, §28).

Meanwhile, in this book he teaches and insists upon the following: throughout our pilgrimage, in which we walk by faith, our righteousness is to be understood as consisting in this—that we now advance toward that perfection and fullness of righteousness in which love will already exist in complete and perfect form, advancing by the rightness and perfection of our course (*On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, §18).

# CHAPTER IX

1. Pelagius’s heresy is attacked in Palestine by Jerome, and the same heresy is examined at the Jerusalem assembly.  
2. Pelagius, accused by Heros and Lazarus, is brought before an episcopal tribunal held at Diospolis, where Pelagius’s heresy is condemned after Pelagius himself is acquitted.  
3. Violent acts are committed against Jerome and the virgin Eustochium by the Pelagians after the judgment of that synod.  
4. After the same Synod of Diospolis, Pelagius publishes various writings.

## 1.

When Orosius came to Palestine, Jerome [Col. 0481] received him according to his merit and according to the recommendation he had from Augustine (in Augustine, Epistle 172, §1).

Pelagius had arrived there perhaps two or three years earlier and had initially formed some relationship with Jerome, although Jerome was not yet acquainted with him. The holy Presbyter indicates this in the words:

> “So that we may not seem to injure an old relationship” (*Commentary on Jeremiah*, book 4, preface).

After Jerome learned that Pelagius was secretly disseminating and gradually fostering what he calls a most pernicious heresy, he resolved to work toward removing it from the churches (in Augustine, Epistle 172, §1).

His first writing against that heresy was the letter to Ctesiphon, in which he promised a fuller discussion of the subject. He then composed three books against the Pelagians in the form of dialogues, beginning work on them at the end of July of the present year.

The presbyters of Jerusalem, likewise struck with horror at the Pelagian error, came against the enemy of the ancient faith at the same time as Jerome. With them, and perhaps at their prompting, Bishop John held an assembly at Jerusalem in this same year, 415, on the fourth or third day before the Kalends of August.

Orosius was summoned to it. He declared that Caelestius had already been condemned by the Council of Carthage; that Augustine had refuted the book of Pelagius, which had been brought forward by Pelagius’s disciples; and that, at this very assembly, he read Augustine’s letter concerning several Pelagian questions, recently sent to Sicily.

Pelagius was then brought in and questioned by everyone as to whether he had taught the things that Augustine had refuted. When he replied, “And who is Augustine to me?”, those present were offended by this answer, which was insulting to the Bishop through whose mouth the Lord had granted the whole of Africa the health of unity by extinguishing the Donatist schism. They all cried out that Pelagius ought to be expelled not only from the assembly but also from the Church.

John then, in order to forgive Pelagius more freely for the insult offered to Augustine, professed to take the insult upon himself:

> “I am Augustine,” he said.

Orosius—or perhaps someone else—immediately replied:

> “If you assume the person of Augustine, follow Augustine’s judgment.”

Orosius continued to press Pelagius. After a long dispute, during which John himself seems to have supported Pelagius with zeal and effort, many objected that the same person could not be both advocate and judge. John then declared that brothers should be sent with letters to Pope Innocent, and that everyone would follow whatever he decided. Meanwhile, silence was imposed upon both parties (Orosius, *Apology*).

At that assembly John understood Pelagius’s position so poorly—whether through error or through the deception of an interpreter—that a few days later he accused Orosius himself of blasphemy. Orosius was compelled to repel this charge by publishing an apology soon afterward.

### 2.

Before five months had yet elapsed since the Jerusalem gathering—which may properly be called a presbyteral assembly—Pelagius was summoned to another episcopal trial in Palestine (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 53). His accusers were two Gauls, Heros, bishop of Arles, and Lazarus, bishop of Aix. Offended by the perversity of his disputations, [Col. 0482] they presented to Eulogius, bishop of Caesarea, a document filled with errors that they had copied from the books of Pelagius and Coelestius, together with the chapters that had been brought against Coelestius and condemned at the Council of Carthage, and with those matters that had been sent from Sicily to Augustine.

For this reason the council was held at Diospolis, a city called Lydda in Scripture (Acts 9:32, 35, 38), in this same year, 415, around 20 December. Fourteen bishops attended; among them Eulogius presided in the first place. Heros and Lazarus, however, were unable to be present because one of them was seriously ill (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 1).

When their document had been read aloud, Pelagius acknowledged some of the chapters brought against him; but at the same time he denied that he had said them in the sense intended by his opponents, claiming that he had meant something entirely different, and something that in no way conflicted with the true faith. Others he flatly denied, dismissing them as mere absurdities; indeed, he pronounced an anathema against those who defended them (Photius, *Bibliotheca*, cod. 54).

As for the teaching of Coelestius, which they asserted had been condemned by the Council of Carthage and by Augustine, Pelagius maintained that it in no way concerned him (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 57–58); nevertheless, he pronounced an anathema against those who held or had held it (*ibid.*, no. 47).

The matters brought against him, as Pope Innocent says, he partly suppressed by avoiding them; partly he confused them in complete obscurity by throwing many words back at his accusers; and some he cleared himself of, as it might seem for the moment, by false arguments rather than true reasoning—denying some, and twisting others through a false interpretation (Augustine, *Letter* 183, no. 3).

Yet, besides those charges that he dared to defend in some fashion, however he could, certain others were brought forward which, unless he had anathematized them without any evasion whatsoever, he would have left the council himself anathematized (*Letter* 186, no. 32). This may be read at greater length in Augustine, since he reports the words both of the bishops and of Pelagius faithfully from the original documents that had been sent to him, adding his own observations and refutations wherever the matter seemed to require them (*ibid.*; *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 23–24, 65; *On Original Sin*, no. 12).

Since no one at the council was present to defend the accusations made against Pelagius or to expose his evasions and falsehoods, and since the Greek prelates were unable themselves to examine his books, which had been published in Latin, only one course remained: to judge Pelagius’s opinions from his own words and testimony. Thus, deceived—as men are—without an opponent pressing him from the other side, they pronounced him Catholic, treating him as a Catholic (*Against Julian*, book 1, no. 19).

Thus, as far as human observation was concerned, Pelagius emerged from the judgment at Diospolis as though acquitted; yet his doctrine had plainly been condemned by himself (*ibid.*, book 2, no. 34).

### 3.

After this judgment, Augustine relates that, at the hands of some band of wicked men who were said strongly to support Pelagius, such great evils were perpetrated with incredible audacity that the servants and handmaids of God attached to the care of the presbyter Jerome were subjected to a most criminal slaughter; a deacon was killed; the buildings [Col. 0483] of the monasteries were burned; and scarcely did a fortified tower, through God’s mercy, protect Jerome himself from the attack and assault of the impious. As news of these crimes flew everywhere, people’s hearts were grievously wounded (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 66).

When Pope Innocent was informed of these events, he wrote two letters concerning them: one to John, bishop of Jerusalem, and the other to the presbyter Jerome.

### 4.

After the same synod of Diospolis, publication of its proceedings was deliberately delayed (*ibid.*, no. 55). Meanwhile, a letter of carnal boasting and arrogance, said to have been written by Pelagius to one of his presbyter friends (*ibid.*, no. 54), rushed ahead and quickly found its way into people’s hands. In it the affair was presented in such a way that, with divine grace passed over in silence, only miserable and self-deceiving human pride appeared, as though victorious.

Moreover, Pelagius made a brief summary of the Palestinian proceedings on a small sheet of paper, so that it might easily and quickly circulate everywhere and serve him in place of an apology (*ibid.*, no. 57). Perhaps for this reason Augustine, to whom Pelagius sent it without a letter specifically addressed to him (*ibid.*, no. 1), calls it “his document of defense” (*ibid.*, no. 57), and refers to it as the defense that Pelagius had written, in which he claimed to have answered the accusations of the Gauls (*Letter* 169, no. 7). Yet in that document, under cover of abbreviation, he altered or obscured the proceedings at certain points (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, nos. 57–58).

Finally, around the same time he wrote a short work in four books in defense of free will, in which he gloried in the proceedings of the Palestinian synod (*On Original Sin*, no. 15). We find him mentioning this work in a letter sent to Rome and written around the beginning of the year 417 to Pope Innocent (*On Grace and Free Will*, no. 32). In these four books, whatever he seemed to say in favor of grace—the grace by which we are helped to turn away from evil and do good—he expressed in such a manner and with such verbal ambiguity that he did not altogether depart from his own doctrine (*ibid.*, no. 45).

## CHAPTER X

1. Jerome’s letter, together with others from Heros and Lazarus, is brought to Africa by Orosius.  
2. The Council of Carthage, and, following its example, the Council of Milevis, write to Pope Innocent against Pelagius.  
3. Five African bishops jointly do the same.  
4. Augustine makes the African decrees against the Pelagian errors known to Hilary of Narbonne.  
5. He writes to John of Jerusalem about the same errors detected in Pelagius.  
6. A letter is sent by him to Oceanus.  
7. Two councils assign Augustine the task of investigating more deeply the Church’s teaching in Scripture.

### 1.

When Orosius, whom Augustine had sent the previous year to Jerome in order to learn from him what ought to be believed concerning the soul, returned to the West in the year 416, Jerome took advantage of the opportunity and entrusted him with a letter. In it he excused to Augustine the difficulty of the times for not having replied to his two books, namely, *On the Soul* and *On the Opinion of James*—a delay that was clearly understood to have fallen during the period [Col. 0484] of Pelagius’s acquittal. He declared that he had resolved to love, esteem, honor, and admire Augustine, and to defend his statements as though they were his own; he also said that, in the dialogue against the Pelagians that had already been published, he had remembered Augustine as he deserved (Augustine, *Letter* 172, no. 1).

The holy presbyter had expressed this in the following words:

> Some time ago the holy and eloquent bishop Augustine wrote two books to Marcellinus—who was later innocently killed by the heretics under the accusation of the tyranny of Heraclian—*On the Baptism of Infants*, against your heresy, and so forth. Therefore I judge that this labor should be set aside, lest Horace’s words be applied to me: “Do not carry wood into the forest” (*Satires* 1.10.34). Either we would say the same things unnecessarily, or, if we wished to say something new, the better material has already been taken up by a most distinguished intellect (*Against the Pelagians*, dialogue 3).

Moreover, Orosius brought to Africa letters from Heros and Lazarus, in which Pelagius and Coelestius were accused as the authors of a criminal and accursed error (*Letter* 175, no. 1). One of them—that is, Coelestius—was said even to have attained the presbyterate in Asia; the other, namely Pelagius, was said to be active at Jerusalem and to be deceiving certain people there, although far more of those who had investigated his opinions more carefully, and especially Jerome, were fighting against him on behalf of the grace of Christ (*Letter* 176, no. 4).

### 2.

Orosius delivered these letters to the bishops of the Proconsular Province, who at that time were celebrating their customary annual council at Carthage. After the letters had been read in the synod, the bishops recognized that the Catholic faith faced the gravest danger from the teachers of this detestable error.

Accordingly, they ordered the proceedings of the episcopal judgment by which Coelestius had been condemned at Carthage five years earlier to be read aloud. Although that judgment had seemed at the time to excise from the Church only that particular wound, they nevertheless decided by common deliberation that the authors of such an error ought themselves to be anathematized unless they most explicitly anathematized it, so that, even if their own health could not be restored, at least the well-being of those who had been deceived or might be deceived by them could be secured, once the sentence pronounced against them had become known.

They took care to inform Pope Innocent of what they had done, so that apostolic authority might also be added to their own decrees. For many who are said to be or to have been their disciples do not cease, by every means in their power, to assert these evils by which they attempt to overthrow the foundations of the Christian faith (*Letter* 175, nos. 1–2).

At that time Innocent held the Apostolic See, not without God’s singular providence. He devoted himself so diligently to the affairs of the Church that, if the African bishops failed to bring any matters requiring recommendation before him, this would arise from negligence rather than from any fear that he himself would either disregard them or receive them with annoyance and resentment (*Letter* 176, no. 1).

For this reason the synod of the province of Numidia, assembled in the city of Milevis, asked him by letter, following the example of the Council of Carthage, to deign to apply pastoral care to the grievous dangers threatening the weak members of Christ. It urgently and promptly requested that he take measures so that they would not be entangled in the snares of a new and exceedingly destructive heresy, which removed from adults the necessity of prayer, and from infants likewise the necessity of Baptism [Col. 0485].

### 3.

The Christian faith appeared to those holy bishops to have been brought into a danger so open and so near that, from among those who had sent letters in their own names from the two councils of the provinces of Carthage and Numidia to Pope Innocent against the enemies of Christ’s grace (*Letter* 177), five—namely Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius—jointly wrote to him in their own names, in a private letter that treated the matter with somewhat greater diligence (*Letter* 186, no. 2).

From this letter we learn that Augustine had written to Pelagius in response to the document of his defense, or purification, at the synod of Diospolis. They sent this letter to Innocent, asking him to forward it to Pelagius, whom they thought would read it more willingly if induced to do so by Innocent’s authority (*Letter* 177, no. 15).

Innocent replied to the African bishops in the manner that was right and proper for a bishop of the Apostolic See (*Letter* 186, no. 2).

### 4.

After the letters sent by the two councils mentioned above to Innocent—and perhaps before the five bishops had written to him—it happened that a certain Palladius, who was about to cross the sea, asked Augustine for a letter of recommendation to Hilary, perhaps the bishop of Narbonne (*Letter* 178, no. 1). Augustine gladly took advantage of this occasion to inform that bishop of what had recently been decreed in Africa against the Pelagian heresy.

He briefly disclosed its principal points to him, asking him in his pastoral care to beware of people who contradicted our prayers with that pestilential impiety (*ibid.*, no. 3). They asserted that a person could reach such great righteousness by his own powers that it would not be necessary for him to say, “Forgive us our debts,” or to understand, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matthew 6:12–13), in the ordinary sense. Rather, they interpreted the latter prayer as asking God not to allow some human accident to fall upon us bodily, not as asking him to help us overcome the temptations of sins, since they held that overcoming them lay so entirely within our power, by the possibility belonging to nature, that they considered it pointless to seek this from God through prayer (*Fragments of Sermons*, first fragment, no. 3).

### 5.

Augustine had sent a letter to John, bishop of Jerusalem, who in the previous year had held a gathering with several presbyters concerning Pelagius’s case, but he had received no reply from him. The holy bishop did not take this amiss; nevertheless, he wrote to him again.

Because he had heard that Pelagius was greatly loved by John, Augustine warned him that he ought to show Pelagius such love that he would not appear to be deceived by him. He therefore exposed Pelagius’s heresy, contained in a book that Pelagius had composed to exalt the powers of nature. He sent John that work together with his own treatise *On Nature and Grace*, written against it, and asked him in return to send the ecclesiastical proceedings of the Palestinian synod, by which Pelagius was said to have been cleared (*Letter* 179).

### 6.

Also in this year, not long after Orosius’s return, Augustine wrote a response to two or three letters from Oceanus. We have no doubt that Oceanus was that celebrated [Col. 0486] friend of Jerome (Augustine, *Letter* 165, no. 3), since he not only devoted himself to reading Jerome’s writings but also received his teaching directly from his spoken words (*Letter* 180, no. 2).

In his letters Oceanus first treated the origin of the soul, proposing, on the basis of Jerome’s opinion, the question of how God could justly bestow souls even upon adulterous conceptions. Augustine replied that this was not the troubling question; rather, the troubling question was this: If individual new souls are created from nothing for each person who is born, how are they justly condemned when they depart from their bodies without Baptism?

The holy Doctor did not approve Oceanus’s use, in solving another question concerning a well-intentioned and useful lie, of the Lord’s statement that not even the Son knew the day and hour when the age would end. Augustine judged that a figurative expression of this kind could in no way properly be called a lie.

Finally, he asked Oceanus not to delay in sending him a new book by Jerome on the resurrection of the flesh.

### 7.

Baronius and several writers who followed him attribute to the councils held at Carthage and Milevis in the present year what Augustine reported in 426 (*Letter* 213, no. 5): namely, that a duty of meditating upon or expounding Scripture had been imposed upon him by his brothers and fathers, his fellow bishops at two councils, one in Numidia and the other at Carthage, a few years earlier (Baronius, under the year 416).

Yet, from the end of the year 413, Augustine had already testified that he had resolved to devote whatever time he would have free from the necessary duties of his own Church entirely to the study of ecclesiastical teaching, so that he might transmit something useful even to posterity (*Letter* 151, no. 13).

After the synods had assigned him this task, the holy bishop, in order to fulfill it, obtained from his people five free days—one, as it were, in each week (*Letter* 213, no. 5). After a formal agreement had been drawn up concerning this matter, the people acclaimed it and kept faith for a little while. But soon the obstinacy of those who wanted to consult the bishop about their own affairs broke the agreement and forcibly dragged him away from his leisure.

He was not allowed to rest either before or after midday. He was compelled to attend to other people’s business and to abandon and cast aside the very work for which he had wished to be free.

Among the fruits of this leisure, the expositions on John seem to deserve a prominent place. Although Augustine may have begun them somewhat earlier, he did not complete them until after the revelation of the body of the martyr Stephen, which occurred near the end of the year 415 and had already become known and widely publicized almost everywhere among the nations. This is what he refers to in the 120th treatise:

> “This,” he says, “has certainly just now been made known to almost all nations through the revelation of the body of the blessed Stephen” (*Tractates on the Gospel of John* 120, no. 4).

## CHAPTER XI

1. At Augustine’s urging, Orosius writes his history.  
2. In replying to the Africans, Pope Innocent condemns Pelagius and Coelestius, imposing an anathema upon both and condemning their doctrine.  
3. Augustine publishes for general circulation a book on the proceedings of the Palestinian synod.  
4. The outstanding qualities of the count Boniface and his inclination to surrender himself wholly to God after renouncing all worldly affairs.  
5. Augustine writes a book to him on the correction of the Donatists.  
6. His book to Dardanus on the presence of God.  
7. Augustine writes a letter to Paulinus in his own name and that of Alypius against the Pelagians.

[Col. 0486]

[Col. 0487]

### 1.

In the year after 400—according to Marcellinus’s chronicle, the sixteenth year, or, according to several others, the seventeenth—Orosius composed his *History*. It is possible that he began it in the earlier year but did not complete it until this later one.

It is certain that he did not write it until after he had gone to Bethlehem and obtained an audience with Jerome (Orosius, *Histories* 7.43). He seems to indicate that he wrote it in Africa (*ibid.* 5.2), a claim that is not very difficult to believe, since at the beginning and end of the work he addresses Augustine, who had prompted him to undertake it.

The pagans, neither considering the future nor recalling the past, were seizing upon the capture of the City and upon other disasters of the Roman Empire as opportunities for blasphemy. They attempted to attribute these calamities to the Christian religion, loudly asserting that they had resulted from the extinction of the worship of idols.

Augustine, Orosius says, instructed him to select from all writers the most disastrous events preserved in human memory: wars, pestilences, famines, earthquakes, floods of rivers, eruptions of subterranean fires, extraordinary violence of hail, the most remarkable crimes, and finally every tragic subject that could be read in the records of history. From all these materials he was to weave a historical sequence and a kind of unified whole, so that it might be understood whether such calamities had occurred more frequently since the coming of the Christians (*ibid.* 1, preface).

Augustine could not carry this out himself, since he was occupied with many other duties, especially the composition of his books *On the City of God*, the eleventh of which he was then working on (*ibid.*). He therefore assigned this task to Orosius, whom he also encouraged to undertake it through Julian of Carthage, a servant of God, since Orosius was perhaps then staying at Carthage.

Orosius obeyed readily and willingly, out of a desire to comply with the wishes of one whom he revered as a father and without anxiety about the success of the work. Indeed, he entirely entrusted his book to the holy Doctor, so that, if Augustine judged it unworthy of publication, he might condemn it to darkness (*ibid.* 7.43).

Accordingly, Orosius undertook a general history of all nations, tracing it from the creation of the world itself to the year 417 after Christ. He explained, as briefly and simply as he could, the passions and punishments of sinful people, the conflicts of the world, and the judgments of God.

He further declares that, after careful investigation, he discovered that the days of the past [Col. 0488] had been not merely as grievous as the present, but miserable to a far greater degree, because they were farther removed from the remedy of the true religion (*ibid.* 1, preface).

### 2.

At the beginning of this year Pope Innocent replied separately to the letters of the Council of Carthage, the Council of Milevis, and the five bishops, which had been sent to him the previous year. In each response he approved their action and teaching against the Pelagians and confirmed their judgment and sentence.

The principal part of the apostolic decree against Pelagius and Coelestius was as follows:

> We decree, by the authority of apostolic vigor, that Pelagius and Coelestius—that is, the inventors of novel expressions—are to be deprived of ecclesiastical communion until they repent. Therefore, dearest brothers, let this sentence remain fixed against the men mentioned above. Let them be absent from the Lord’s courts and deprived of pastoral oversight, lest the dreadful contagion of two sheep perhaps spread among the unwary flock (Augustine, *Letter* 182, no. 6).

In this same year Augustine preached a sermon at Carthage on Sunday, 23 September. In it he openly declared that he scarcely ever addressed the people without proclaiming the necessity of divine grace, because of certain ungrateful people who recognized it too little, while attributing far too much to the powers of nature (*Sermon* 131, no. 6).

He urged the faithful to have compassion on such people, but not, if they discovered anyone of this kind, to allow him to remain hidden out of a false kind of mercy. He ordered that they be corrected and, if they stubbornly hardened their minds in error, brought before him.

“For already,” he said, “two councils have sent their decisions concerning this matter to the Apostolic See; replies have also come from there. The case is finished; would that the error might sometime be finished as well!” (*ibid.*, no. 10).

### 3.
