Augustine thought that the first step toward ending the error was to examine the judgment of the Palestinian synod, where Pelagius boasted that he had been cleared. He had become convinced that Pelagius had renounced his heresy before Catholic bishops in order to be acquitted by them, and that he had professed the Christian faith to them in its entirety.

When at last he received the proceedings of the synod, he discovered with the greatest satisfaction that the matter was indeed so. To expose the heretic’s fraud, he immediately began writing a book against the abbreviated proceedings that Pelagius had circulated in his document of defense (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 2), lest anyone, regarding him as acquitted, should also suppose that the judges had approved his doctrines.

Accordingly, in this book, entitled *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, Augustine examines with the greatest care each of the errors brought against Pelagius before the synod, together with Pelagius’s replies to them.

Although Pelagius had been pronounced Catholic by the synod because he condemned the doctrines hostile to Christ’s grace that had been read against him from the document of Heros and Lazarus, Augustine nevertheless shows that the suspicion of heresy still clung to him. Finally, he shows that Pelagius was acquitted by the sentence of the synod only in such a way that the heresy for which he had been brought before the episcopal tribunal was nevertheless condemned without hesitation (*Retractions* 2.47).

### 4.

Augustine states that, at the time when he wrote *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, he also composed a book *On the Correction of the Donatists* (*ibid.* 2.48).

Boniface, to whom the book is addressed, was counted among the greatest men of the Roman Empire. Procopius left it written that he and Aetius, both because of their courage [Col. 0489] and military expertise and because of their greatness of spirit and other virtues, could rightly be called the last of the Romans (Procopius, *Vandalic History* 1.195).

He was held in such honor by everyone on account of his human greatness that the holiest bishops of his age revered him no less for his outstanding piety. Yet he did not retain that glory to the end. When he turned his mind and thoughts away from God, he was plunged into calamities so numerous and so terrible that, in order to support his temporary and fleeting fortune, he was compelled to inflict an immense wound upon the Church and the Empire—a wound that neither he himself nor all the Roman forces were able to heal for a hundred full years.

Augustine marveled that, amid the cares of war and arms, Boniface sought knowledge of divine matters with such passionate zeal (*Letter* 185, no. 1). He could add nothing to his commendation beyond what he appended to the advice he had given Boniface, at his request, for properly ordering his life: Augustine’s letter, he said, was more a mirror in which Boniface might see what he was like than a place where he might learn what he ought to be (*Letter* 189, no. 8).

Above all, Augustine urged him to attend to conjugal chastity (*ibid.*, no. 7). Boniface, however, wished to go beyond this advice. Although he was married and had raised at least one daughter, whom he gave in marriage to Count Sebastian (Victor of Vita, *History of the Vandal Persecution* 1.6), he nevertheless shrank from worldly vanity and desired nothing more than, after renouncing worldly affairs, to live as a monk and devote himself wholly to God (*Letter* 220, no. 3).

After his wife had died, he soon afterward encountered Augustine and Alypius alone at Tubunae in Numidia and disclosed his plan to both of them. He intended to renounce all public and military affairs and spend the rest of his life in blessed quiet, so that he might thereafter fight only against demons, in the silence of solitude, together with a few soldiers of Christ (*ibid.*, no. 12).

The holy men dissuaded him from this plan, reminding him that his service at his present rank would be exceedingly useful to the Church. He should direct his weapons only toward securing peace for the Church by restraining the incursions of the barbarians. Among men he should seek nothing beyond what was necessary for himself and his people (*ibid.*, nos. 3, 12). He should neither reject earthly wealth when it was offered nor pursue it when it was withheld—not even when it had been taken away, lest he be reduced to such necessity that, as Augustine says, “when possessions are loved, evil deeds are committed” (*ibid.*, no. 5).

Finally, so that he might be more securely and more strongly armed with spiritual weapons amid bodily arms, he was to preserve continence with the utmost severity. Boniface therefore resolved to remain among men while nevertheless cultivating a celibate life (*ibid.*, no. 4).

When this was done is unknown. Augustine and Alypius offered this advice to Boniface with no other intention than that they judged it beneficial to his salvation. Yet, apart from God, no one can know who is not deceived. By a judgment inscrutable to human thoughts, God allowed two of the holiest men to be blind in so important a matter; and thus, while innocently bringing ruin and destruction upon Boniface, they provided the Vandals with an opportunity to invade Africa [Col. 0490].

### 5.

To return to the book, whose occasion required an explanation of who Boniface was: the work deals entirely with the Donatists, who perhaps quite frequently made themselves troublesome to Boniface.

Since that noble man wished to learn about the Donatist sect, he wrote to Augustine asking what difference there was between the Donatists and the Arians (*Letter* 185, no. 1). Augustine disclosed to him the whole character of this schism, undermined its foundations, rejected the paralogisms by which they tried to strengthen it, and above all explained the justice, usefulness, and necessity of the laws that Honorius had enacted against them (*Retractions* 2.48).

At the end of the letter he addressed him in these words:

> The mother Church commends these people to you, as to a faithful son, to be corrected and healed with the Lord’s help wherever and however you can—whether by speaking and answering yourself, or by bringing them to the teachers of the Church (*Letter* 185, no. 51).

He also asked Boniface to read the acts of the Conference, which Augustine had reduced to a summary; these might perhaps be found in the possession of Bishop Optatus (*ibid.*, no. 6).

It would not be unreasonable to suppose that this bishop was Optatus of Vesceris in the province of Sitifis (*Conference of Carthage* 1.120), since Augustine says that, if the book was not with Optatus, it could easily be obtained from the Church of Sitifis. From this it is sufficiently clear that Boniface was then in that region.

Although Augustine lists this work among his books, it is now preserved among his letters.

### 6.

The book *On the Presence of God*, which is also counted as a letter, was composed during the summer of this year (*Letter* 187, no. 1). For this reason Augustine reviewed it immediately after his books *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* and *On the Correction of the Donatists* (*Retractions* 2.49).

This distinguished work is to be credited to Dardanus, a man of exceptionally high rank in this age (*Letter* 187, no. 1). Moved by a certain religious love, he asked that two questions be explained to him with intense attention and eagerness to learn.

The first was how Christ could now be in heaven when he had said to the thief on the cross that he would be with him that day in paradise: whether perhaps this was because Christ exists everywhere, or because paradise is located in heaven.

The second was whether infants, even while still in the womb, know God, since John leaped in the womb at the presence of the mother of the Lord (*ibid.*, no. 3).

In answering the first question accurately and carefully, Augustine discusses how it should be said that the divine nature is present in all things, and especially in its temple, that is, in the faithful person. For this reason he entitles the treatise *On the Presence of God* (*Retractions* 2.49).

When he reaches the second question, he directs his attention chiefly to the Pelagian heresy, though he does not explicitly name it, and provides an extensive and very necessary discussion of the regeneration of infants. He shows how absurd it is to attribute the use of reason and will to infants [Col. 0491]. He immediately explains how the Holy Spirit dwells in those who have been baptized, even though they do not know it, and how this is rightly to be understood (*Letter* 187, no. 25).

### 7.

Writing to Paulinus, bishop of Nola, after the death of Pope Innocent, in his own name and that of Alypius (*Letter* 186), Augustine attacks this heresy more openly and with much greater force. He announces that its author is Pelagius, who was called the Briton, perhaps to distinguish him from Pelagius of Tarentum, and whom Paulinus had loved as a servant of God just as Augustine and Alypius had.

He sends Paulinus the letters written on this matter to Pope Innocent by the two African councils and by the five bishops, together with Innocent’s replies to them. He undoubtedly also attached the proceedings of the Palestinian judgment, from which, he says, Pelagius would have emerged condemned unless he himself had condemned the statements brought against him concerning God’s grace—statements that he could not obscure (*ibid.*, no. 31).

Nevertheless, Augustine maintains that it is perfectly clear from the books Pelagius published after that judgment that Pelagius did not hold a correct view of the help of divine grace. At one point Pelagius weighs the power of the will in an even balance, defining it as having some power even not to sin. At another point he confesses that we are fortified by the daily help of God’s grace, although we may possess a strong and firm free will not to sin. Thus he seems to regard the help of grace as something granted in addition, so that what human beings are commanded to do through free will they may more easily accomplish through grace.

Moreover, Augustine had heard that certain people in the city of Nola were so obstinately committed to the error that unbaptized infants possess eternal life that they would sooner withdraw from Pelagius himself than abandon that opinion.

He also mentions others who were held by a different error concerning the Baptism of infants. They made infants who die without Baptism guilty of sins of their own, committed through the exercise of free will. Thus, although infants cannot think of good or evil, they were thought capable through free will either of deserving punishment or of deserving grace.

Augustine does not pass over this refuge, however absurd, in silence:

> For whatever great and acute intellects have been able to devise, either poverty of mind avoids by keeping silent, or arrogance passes over by contempt (*ibid.*, no. 13).

Nearly twelve years later, some people who had resolved to foster the remnants of the Pelagian heresy rather than profess the Catholic doctrine concerning predestination and the gift of perseverance began to object to certain statements in this letter (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 55).

Before the end of the same letter, Augustine sets out twelve errors that Pelagius, whether willingly or unwillingly, condemned at the Palestinian synod, and adds an equal number of opposing statements that the Catholic Church had always held.

A document formed from this portion of the letter is found in the *Code of the Canons of the Roman Church* (*Roman Code of Canons*, canon 18). It is not far from the truth, as a learned scholar judged (Quesnel, on Leo, volume 2, dissertation 13, chapter 21), to suppose that this document—which sets out more distinctly what Coelestius or Pelagius and his disciples were required to profess—was sent to Pope Zosimus by the bishops of the Council of Carthage held in this year [Col. 0492]. They evidently thought it insufficient for them merely to profess in general terms that they agreed with the teaching of the Apostolic See (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians* 2.5).

## CHAPTER XII

1. Coelestius comes to Rome. Zosimus treats him with the greatest gentleness and writes to the African bishops on his behalf.  
2. Pelagius’s letter to Innocent is delivered to Zosimus, who is also deceived by its ambiguous language and writes to Africa in Pelagius’s favor.  
3. The Council of Carthage, consisting of 214 bishops, replies to Zosimus and defends the sentence pronounced by Innocent against the heretics mentioned above.  
4. Zosimus replies to the Africans that he has changed nothing since receiving their letters. A plenary council of Africa issues eight or nine canons against the Pelagians.  
5. The same council enacts certain measures concerning matters relating to the Donatists.  
6. The Pelagians are condemned both by Pope Zosimus and by the emperor Honorius.  
7. All the bishops confirm their condemnation by their subscriptions, except eighteen, who appeal to a plenary synod.  
8. The Pelagians are defeated by the Church, not without much labor on Augustine’s part.  
9. He writes two books against Pelagius to Pinianus.

1. Pelagius and Coelestius were not long unaware of the sentence pronounced against them both by the African Church and by the Apostolic See; nor did they fail to try immediately to clear themselves. Coelestius, indeed, going to Rome, approached Zosimus, the successor of Innocent, complained about the judgment passed against him in Africa, and maintained that he had falsely come under suspicion before the Apostolic See. He presented a statement of his faith, skillfully composed so that Zosimus could by no means reject it—especially since he professed that he wished to be instructed and expressly said there: “If, as can happen to human beings, some error arising from ignorance has perhaps crept in, let it be corrected by your judgment” (*On Original Sin*, no. 26).

Zosimus was not satisfied with this, however. He probed the man’s mind by various questions and, as he attempted to clear himself, repeatedly constrained him to agree with Innocent’s letters (*Against Two Letters of Pelagius*, book 2, no. 5). Thus Coelestius answered that he condemned everything about which he had been questioned, according to the judgment of that pope of blessed memory (*ibid.*, no. 6), and promised that he would condemn everything condemned by the Apostolic See (*On Original Sin*, no. 8). Induced by these answers of Coelestius, Zosimus did not indeed immediately release him from the bonds of excommunication, but treated him with the greatest possible leniency. After allowing a period of two months, until a reply should come from Africa, he granted him an opportunity to repent, under a certain medicinal mildness of judgment.

Indeed, concerning what had taken place with him, he sent Aurelius and the other African bishops a letter full of benevolence toward Coelestius. In it he seems to censure their judgment concerning his case as excessively hasty; the man’s accusers, moreover, he treats more harshly and punishes with excommunication. The letter assigns the year of Christ 417, but gives no day (*Appendix to volume 10*, part 2, Zosimus’s letter to the African bishops concerning the case of Coelestius).

2. Pelagius, who at that time was living in Palestine, likewise attempted to clear himself by letters written to Innocent, unaware that he had died (*On the Grace of Christ*, no. 32). The letters were delivered to his successor, Zosimus, together with the statement of faith that Pelagius had sent at the same time. It ended with these words:

> “This is the faith, most blessed pope, which we learned in the Catholic Church and have always held and do hold. If anything has perhaps been set down in it with insufficient skill or caution, we wish it to be corrected by you, who hold both the faith and the see of Peter” (*Appendix to volume 10*, part 2, *Pelagius’s Statement of Faith*, etc., no. 14), and so forth.

Deceived by this man also, Zosimus, as he had acted on behalf of Coelestius, sent another letter on behalf of Pelagius to the African bishops in that same year, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. In it he attacked Heros and Lazarus with much harsher language than in his earlier letter. He promised that the African bishops too would consequently be persuaded along with him and would regard Pelagius and Coelestius as Catholics, since both men condemned what ought to be condemned and followed what ought to be followed. They had not, he said, come back to life after death and destruction and been found again—namely, by returning to the faith—but had not been dead at all and had not perished; false reports, evidently, had been spread about them (*Part 1 of the Hypomnesticon against Pelagius*, book 5, chapters 9–10).

3. That Pelagius imposed upon Zosimus is certainly not surprising. He had composed his words so craftily and cast such an artful fog of ambiguity over the truth that, when Zosimus sent his writings to Africa, even Augustine himself scarcely managed to refrain from judging them Catholic and rejoicing over Pelagius’s return to the right faith (*On Original Sin*, no. 20). But the poison that Augustine had noticed in Pelagius’s longer books caused these writings also to seem suspect to him; and when he inspected them more carefully, he finally detected their ambiguity and defect.

As for Coelestius, Augustine says that the African bishops replied that it was not enough for him to profess general agreement with the letters of Bishop Innocent; he had to anathematize openly the wrong things that he had set down in his statement (*Against Two Letters of Pelagius*, chapter 3). From their letter to Zosimus, written at the council of 214 bishops, Prosper reports this decree:

> “We have determined that the sentence pronounced against Pelagius and Coelestius through the venerable Bishop Innocent from the See of the most blessed Apostle Peter shall remain in force until they confess with the utmost clarity that by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord we are assisted, not only in knowing righteousness but also in doing it, in each and every act, so that without that grace we are able to possess, think, say, or do nothing belonging to true and holy piety” (Prosper, *Against the Collator*, no. 15).

4. In the following year Zosimus replied to the African bishops in a letter dated the twelfth day before the Kalends of April (*Appendix to volume 10*, part 2, Zosimus’s letter to the African bishops concerning the case of Coelestius). He informed them that, after receiving their letter, he had changed nothing, but had left everything in the same condition, just as they had requested. It was not because of him that Coelestius’s case was not investigated more carefully, according to their wishes and counsel.

But when Coelestius was summoned to appear, so that either the man’s cunning or his correction might become clear through definite and lucid answers, leaving no ambiguity for anyone, he withdrew and refused the examination (*Against Two Letters of Pelagius*, book 2, no. 5). Pelagius likewise, although for a time he seemed to say something consistent with the Catholic faith, was unable to deceive the Roman See to the end (*On Original Sin*, no. 24).

After the African council’s reply, not only those pernicious doctrines of his that had reached Africa but also other doctrines of his, brought forth by faithful brethren in Rome—where he had lived for a very long time and had previously engaged in these discussions and disputes—were exposed. Pope Zosimus finally judged them worthy of execration by all Catholics.

Those later letters of Zosimus reached Africa on the third day before the Kalends of May. At that time the bishops were gathering at Carthage for a council, which is recorded as having been held in that city on the Kalends of May and which Augustine calls a plenary council of all Africa (*Letter* 215, no. 2). From it came the eight or nine canons against the Pelagian heresy that had falsely been attributed to the Council of Milevis (*see the Preface to volume 10*).

5. The Pelagians were not the only reason for this very frequent council. Several canons were also enacted there concerning matters relating to the Donatists. A general council convened at Carthage on the Ides of June in the year 407 had decreed that the churches and peoples who had abandoned the Donatist secession before the law of Honorius issued in 405 should belong to the bishop by whom they had been converted; others, however, were to follow the bishop of the city to whom they had been subject while they adhered to the schismatic party (*Code of the African Canons*, canons 98, 99).

Disputes consequently arose among the bishops concerning the boundaries of their dioceses, and these moved the council of the present year to alter something in that decree (*ibid.*, canons 117, 118). Furthermore, however much the African bishops had shown zeal for extinguishing the Donatist schism, some among them nevertheless displayed very little concern for converting those whom they knew to be mingled with their own people. The council took action against such men and ordered that certain who were negligent in this duty should be punished by excommunication (*ibid.*, canon 113).

There remained, as one may infer, many matters that required a rather long delay before they could be settled. Therefore, so that so many bishops would not be detained at Carthage any longer, three were selected from each province to settle with Aurelius whatever remained. Augustine was chosen from Numidia together with Alypius and Restitutus.

Accordingly, until he set out for Mauretania, where he was engaged on the fourteenth and twelfth days before the Kalends of October, he remained at Carthage. Various affairs kept him extremely busy in that city (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 1).

6. Augustine had not yet left Carthage when, through news brought to Africa, he learned that the Pelagians had been condemned both by an imperial law and by the authority of the Apostolic See. Honorius issued the law for this purpose on the day before the Kalends of May in the year 418. It ordered that Pelagius and Coelestius, authors of impious speculation and detestable doctrine, should be expelled from the City if they happened to be there; and that, if adherents of this sacrilege should thereafter be found anywhere, they should, once duly convicted, be sent into exile (*Appendix to volume 10*, part 2, *Imperial Rescript against Pelagius and Coelestius*).

The emperors expressly stated in letters separately addressed to Aurelius and Augustine, in the year 419 on the fifth day before the Ides of June, that in establishing this law they had followed the judgment of both men (*apud Augustine*, *Letter* 201, no. 1). They were speaking, of course, of the judgment of the African council held against the Pelagians in the preceding year. As Prosper sings, Aurelius was its leader and Augustine its intellect, just as they were for the council of the present year (*Poem against the Ungrateful*, part 1, chapter 3).

The reputation and authority of these bishops undoubtedly had no small influence in inducing Zosimus finally to pronounce a sentence of condemnation against the same heretics. He condemned throughout the entire Christian world the authors—or at least the most vehement and notorious advocates—of this new heresy, Pelagius and Coelestius, unless they had corrected themselves and also repented (*apud Augustine*, *Letter* 190, no. 22; *On Original Sin*, no. 25).

For this reason he sent some letters specifically to the Africans and others generally to all bishops. In these letters, which Pope Zosimus composed to be carried throughout the Catholic world, he appended the doctrines of Pelagius and Coelestius as worthy of execration (*On Original Sin*, no. 24).

The Roman clergy themselves were witnesses that they had embraced their bishop’s judgment with all their hearts—indeed, the Pelagians themselves testify to this when they accuse them of not being ashamed to commit the crime of treachery (*Against Two Letters of Pelagius*, book 2, no. 5). Certainly the same report did not omit to say that Sixtus, a presbyter of the Roman Church—the very man whom rumor had previously proclaimed favorable to the enemies of Christian grace (*Letter* 194, no. 1) and a principal patron of those men—had first, that is, either before everyone else or before the sentence of condemnation was promulgated, pronounced an anathema against them before a very large assembly (*Letter* 191, no. 1).

Augustine, who, as we have said, had remained at Carthage after the council of the Kalends of May, was delighted by this news, which was exceedingly welcome to him, before he departed from there. The holy man learned it not merely from common report but also from Sixtus’s own letter to Aurelius, brought by the acolyte Leo.

In that letter Sixtus explained, briefly, what he thought about the most pernicious Pelagian doctrine—or, rather, about the grace of God. The bishops who were present hurried to copy his letter, so great was their joy, and eagerly wished to display it to everyone.

7. All the Catholic bishops confirmed the condemnation of the Pelagian heresy with their signatures. The Pelagians, complaining about this, repeatedly claimed:

> “A signature was extorted from simple bishops, sitting in their own places, without a gathering of a synod” (*Against Two Letters of Pelagius*, book 4, no. 34).

The bishops who refused to sign numbered eighteen (*ibid.*, book 1, no. 3). Their leader was undoubtedly Julian, Bishop of Eclanum, who was condemned by Zosimus for this reason (*Against Julian*, book 1, no. 13).

Julian, together with his followers, separated himself from the Catholic Church (*Sermon* 181, no. 3). He testified that he and his associates had resolved not to communicate with the Manichaeans (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, nos. 4, 42). They requested a hearing (*ibid.*, no. 42), and in a statement presented to Zosimus the Pelagian bishops appealed to a plenary synod (*Appendix to volume 10*, part 2, *Statement of Faith of the Pelagian Bishops*). They even petitioned the emperor to order that judges be assigned to their case (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 42).

But, Augustine says, “far be it from Christian rulers of the earthly commonwealth that they should doubt the ancient Catholic faith and therefore grant its attackers a place and time for examination.” Their pride, plainly, is understood to seek even this glory: that a synod of East and West should be convened on their account. Since they cannot corrupt the Catholic world because the Lord resists them, they at least try to disturb it. Rather, after a proper and sufficient judgment has been made concerning them, they must be crushed everywhere these wolves appear, whether so that they may be healed and changed or so that others may avoid them for the sake of their own salvation and integrity (*ibid.*, book 4, no. 34).

How troublesome they became, under the pretext of requesting a general council, to the Churches of the East, in order to draw them over to their side, is shown by a letter sent by eighteen Pelagian bishops—including Julian—to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica (*ibid.*, book 1, no. 3). In it they earnestly sought the fellowship of Rufus and other Eastern bishops against the impious heresy of the Manichaeans (*ibid.*, book 2, no. 1).

Their entire strength and ingenuity lay in this: they wished to fasten a detestable heresy upon orthodox Christians, so that they might conceal their own errors and, by commending nature, the law, and free choice, condemn grace (*ibid.*, book 4, no. 26). Augustine refuted this letter in three later books addressed to Boniface; Julian himself mentions and acknowledges it (*Unfinished Work*, book 2, chapter 178).

8. Prosper, not unjustly, proclaims that the glory of the victory won over the Pelagians belongs chiefly to Augustine, whose industry was greater and whose labor was more substantial than that of all the others who contributed their efforts to expelling them from the Church (*Poem against the Ungrateful*, part 1, chapter 3).

Nevertheless, this victory cost the holy Doctor not only the greatest labors but also the gravest troubles, as Jerome clearly shows in a letter sent to him around this time. There Jerome indicates the difficulties that the truth had suffered even at Rome when he says:

> “Against the winds that blow upon you, you have stood firm through the ardor of faith.”

He also signifies the evil that threatened the champion of invincible grace from the supporters of Pelagius and Coelestius, and which Augustine himself had bravely scorned, when he adds:

> “You preferred, insofar as it lay within you, to be saved alone from Sodom rather than to remain among those who were perishing. Your prudence knows what I mean.”

Finally, he adds those magnificent and splendid words:

> “Courage! You are celebrated throughout the world. Catholics venerate and honor you as the restorer once again of the ancient faith; and, what is a sign of greater glory, all heretics detest you. They persecute me with the same hatred, so that those whom they cannot kill with swords they may kill by their wish” (*apud Augustine*, *Letter* 195).

In another letter written afterward, Jerome congratulates Augustine on the heresy of Coelestius, which Augustine had slaughtered (*ibid.*, *Letter* 202, no. 1).

9. After the Pelagian heresy and its authors had been condemned by Pope Zosimus and by the emperor Honorius, Augustine wrote two books against the authors of that heresy, addressed to Pinianus, his mother-in-law Albina, and his wife Melania (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 50; *On Original Sin*, no. 18).

These people had advised Pelagius—who was at that time living with them in Palestine—to condemn in writing whatever was said against him. He replied to them with such craft that anyone who had not clearly perceived his mind could easily be persuaded that he held nothing except what was sound and Catholic (*see the Preface to volume 10*, chapter 20).

Indeed, he declared anathema against anyone who denied that the grace of God, through which Christ came into this world to save sinners, was necessary at every moment and for every act (*On the Grace of Christ*, no. 2). He acknowledged that there was one and the same Baptism, and that it was to be administered to infants in the same words used for adults (*ibid.*, no. 35). When he was questioned further, he admitted that infants received Baptism for the remission of sins, reciting to them his teaching on the Baptism of little children from the statement that he had sent to Rome (*On Original Sin*, no. 1).

He therefore said that he, whose innocence had also been proved at the Palestinian judgment, ought not to be held in the same opinion as Coelestius (*ibid.*, no. 9). What Pelagius had professed brought them considerable joy; nevertheless, they still thought that Augustine should be consulted about his words (*ibid.*, no. 5).

Accordingly, they sent a letter in their common name asking what he thought of this statement. The bearer of the letter found the holy bishop at Carthage and brought back a reply from him, even though he was hindered there by exceptionally pressing affairs—and the reply was not a brief one (*On the Grace of Christ*, no. 1).

For Augustine had learned that those holy people read, with an ever-unfulfilled desire, whatever is written for the edification and confirmation of the faith (*On Original Sin*, no. 48). He therefore did not hesitate to send them two complete volumes: one *On the Grace of Christ*, the other *On Original Sin*. In these books he demonstrates Pelagius’s true mind on both subjects from Pelagius’s own works—the very works from which Pelagius had quoted passages in his letter to Innocent in order to clear himself.

# CHAPTER XIII

1. Augustine travels to Caesarea on Church business.  
2. Emeritus comes to that city to dispute with him; in his presence and while he remains silent, Augustine preaches.  
3. On the following day, with Emeritus stationed inside the church and persisting in his silence, the holy Bishop turns the situation advantageously to the benefit of his case.  
4. In a sermon to the people, he abolishes a wicked custom of the citizens of Caesarea.  
5. He replies to Optatus concerning the question of the origin of the soul.  
6. He also replies to Mercator.  
7. Likewise to Coelestinus and Sixtus.  
8. He writes to Asellicus against Aptus concerning avoidance of Judaism.

1. The holy Bishop did not abandon the important affairs with which he had been occupied at Carthage in order to recover from his labor. Rather, he left the city to undertake new labors and thereby demonstrate his devotion to the Church.

Accordingly, departing from that city, he set out for Caesarea of Mauretania. He was staying in that city on the fourteenth and twelfth days before the Kalends of October of this same year (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 1).

This city, as some think, is called Algiers today and is situated approximately 120 leagues from Hippo Regius. Since Augustine traveled there by this route, we do not doubt that he passed through it; nevertheless, it may be inferred from his letter to Mercator that he did not remain there long (*Letter* 193, no. 1).

He was induced to undertake this journey with several other bishops by a letter from Pope Zosimus (*Letter* 190, no. 1), evidently to settle certain serious affairs of the Church. What those affairs were, we do not know, except that it is certain they had nothing to do with the Donatists (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, no. 16).

The following words seem to indicate that Augustine traversed the whole region:

> “As we passed through all those lands, the various things presented to our senses carried our attention here and there” (*Letter* 193, no. 1).

What happened at Caesarea, however, is unknown. Among others, Deuterius, the bishop of that see—and, unusually in Africa, called a metropolitan—assembled there, as did Alypius of Thagaste, Possidius of Calama, Rusticus of Cartenna, and Palladius of Tigava. The names of the others are not recorded (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 1). Bishops of the same province were also present (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 51).

2. Emeritus, whom we have already mentioned several times, presided over the Donatists of Caesarea. He was especially renowned for what he had done on behalf of his faction at the Conference of Carthage. When that gathering had ended, he returned to Caesarea, where, stubborn in his schism, he had invented and loudly proclaimed many things intended to diminish the victory won by the Church (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 3).

Augustine had sent him a certain writing, which has since been lost through the ravages of time. It was particularly useful, since the holy Doctor had compressed into it, in a brief and straightforward manner, everything that could serve to extinguish the schism. He composed this work around the year 416, since he places it between the works that he sent to Jerome in 415 and the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 46).

But when this work of peace failed to find in Emeritus a son of peace, it returned to its author. Nevertheless, the Caesarean Donatists did not imitate their bishop. Almost all of them returned to Catholic communion, although not all with the same sincerity. For many still remained who doubted the truth; indeed, some of both sexes continued in mind and will to cling to the schism (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, nos. 1–2).

But so that the former might be freed from their blindness and the latter strengthened, God permitted what we are about to relate.

When Augustine arrived there, Emeritus was absent. It is clear that at that time he had gone into hiding so as not to be captured. But when he learned that the bishop of Hippo was present, he came of his own accord on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October to see him.

Augustine was unexpectedly informed that Emeritus was there, and the holy Bishop immediately hurried out to meet him. Finding him standing in the street, Augustine, after the first expressions of honor and courtesy, pointed out that the place was neither convenient nor suitable for either of them. He therefore asked Emeritus not to object to coming with him into the church.

Emeritus agreed without reluctance. Augustine consequently began to hope that he would soon embrace Catholic communion with a good and willing spirit. Indeed, rumor spread that he had already done so (*Against Gaudentius*, book 1, no. 15).

In that event Deuterius might have been compelled to yield his episcopate to Emeritus, who was beloved by his fellow citizens, just as the Catholics had promised before the Conference that they would yield to the Donatists. Reconciliation, however, would not have been delayed on that account, since Deuterius was entirely ready for it. Augustine affirms that he had long known the mind of this bishop, who would never have allowed private honor to be preferred to the good of the Church (*Sermon to the People of the Caesarean Church*, no. 1).

But Emeritus did not permit him to display this example of virtue. Emeritus entered the church together with Augustine, and a very large crowd from both communions gathered there (*Against Gaudentius*, book 1, no. 15; *Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 14).

He had scarcely entered when he was addressed in the first sermon. He replied in these ambiguous words:

> “I cannot be unwilling for what you want, but I can will what I want” (*Sermon to the People of the Caesarean Church*, no. 1).

He was unable, however, to add anything in defense either of himself or of his faction; he persisted instead in refusing communion. He had undoubtedly come for no other reason than to act as the champion of his schism. But before he could express what he had planned, he understood that Augustine had already overturned it so completely by what he had said beforehand that he could find nothing to answer (*Against Gaudentius*, book 1, no. 15).

When Augustine saw that the matter was being prolonged and that Emeritus was stubbornly persisting in schism and heresy within the very walls of the Catholic church, he began to address the assembled people. He said:

> “I have spoken much about peace, much about charity, much about the unity of the holy Catholic Church, which God promised and bestowed. In that speech I was addressing you and exhorting him; and, insofar as the compassion of charity could accomplish anything in me, in that speech I was giving birth to all who were placed in danger of their souls, and I desired to give birth to them for the Lord” (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 1).

Throughout the entire speech the devout Bishop continually showed that he hoped divine mercy would recall Emeritus from his error. But however much effort and zeal his charity employed, after hearing the sermon Emeritus hardened his mind in obstinacy. Even then Augustine did not despair of him. Emeritus was also granted a period during which he could remain safely in the city (*Against Gaudentius*, book 1, no. 15).

3. Two days later, that is, on Friday, the twelfth day before the Kalends of October in the year 418, bishops, presbyters, deacons, the entire clergy, and a very large crowd of people assembled in the larger basilica of Caesarea.

Deuterius is named first of all and as if president of the assembly. Emeritus was also present. Notaries were appointed to write everything down and enter it into the records.

Augustine prudently judged that he should use this opportunity, if not to secure Emeritus’s salvation, at least for the benefit of those who needed a clearer explanation of the schism (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 1).

Since Emeritus himself and others of his faction complained that, through the authority of Marcellinus, they had been overpowered at the Conference of Carthage and had not been allowed to bring forward everything they had to say on behalf of their cause (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 14), Augustine recounted to that very large assembly what had taken place on Wednesday and asked Emeritus to bring forward whatever he judged most important to do in response.

Augustine said that he was ready to answer; that the disputation would prejudice neither side; that it would nevertheless depart from the presence of the assembled people not without benefit; that Emeritus had nothing to fear; and that the matter would bring him great glory, whether he should prevail before his fellow citizens or yield to the victorious truth.

Emeritus replied that whether he had departed victorious or defeated, whether he had yielded to truth or power, could easily be understood from the records of the Conference of Carthage. When Augustine then asked him why he had come if he had decided to say nothing, Emeritus replied that he had come with the intention of saying precisely what Augustine was asking him to say.

The holy man continued to press him about the reason that had brought him there, while the notary waited for an answer. Emeritus said:

> “Do it—that is, write it down” (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, nos. 2–3; *Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 14).

After this word, as though he had become mute, he neither wished nor was able to answer anything further.

Augustine allowed him additional time to speak; then, finally understanding that he was obstinately maintaining silence, he continued the course of the sermon he had begun to deliver to the people. He discussed the Conference of Carthage and begged Deuterius to arrange for its records to be read every year during Lent.

He wished Alypius to read the letter in which the Catholic bishops, out of regard for peace and unity, had offered the Donatists a voluntary renunciation of their own dignities. Augustine himself inserted into the reading exceptionally distinguished observations and examples of Christian charity and humility (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus*, no. 4).

Finally, he overturned the entire foundation of the schismatic party by recounting the history of the Maximianists. He lingered over it at some length and drew no response from Emeritus, addressing him as though he were dumb (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 51).

Emeritus’s relatives and fellow citizens earnestly begged him to enter into conversation with the holy Bishop. They promised that, if he defeated the Catholics, they would delay no longer in restoring themselves to his communion, even at the risk of their property or their lives. But greater distrust had settled in Emeritus’s mind than would permit him to utter or even murmur anything (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 14).

Augustine says that this had the effect of bringing about Emeritus’s ruin and punishment, but also of confirming and saving the others:

> “For if they had seen Emeritus communicating with us, they would have suspected that he was afraid. But when they saw him remaining in the party of Donatus and nevertheless keeping silent against the Catholics, it appeared to them more clearly that by his silence he was crying out against his own people. Or, when he stood there with a sound and free voice and mouth, was that Emeritus—not just any Emeritus, but that Emeritus, both an enemy and mute—not a suitable witness on your behalf against us?” (*Against Gaudentius*, book 1, no. 15).

At last Emeritus was dismissed without suffering any injury, so that the Church’s gentleness, worthy of the truth, might crown its victory. He then went into hiding thereafter (*ibid.*, no. 41).

Augustine cites the tablets, or records, of what had been disputed on this matter on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 51). To make it plain to everyone that Emeritus had been silenced by lack of arguments, he challenged Gaudentius, Bishop of Thamugadi and a man of the highest authority among the Donatists, to answer (*Against Gaudentius*, book 1, no. 15).

4. We cannot refrain from reporting here the very great benefit that Augustine’s journey produced among the people of Caesarea. We shall recount the matter in the holy man’s own words:

> “Finally, when at Caesarea in Mauretania I was dissuading the people from a civil—or rather more than civil—battle, which they called the Caterva—for not only citizens, but also relatives, brothers, and finally parents and children, divided into two parties, used to fight one another with stones for several consecutive days at a fixed season of the year, and each person killed anyone he could—I exerted myself vigorously, as far as I was able, to tear out and drive away by my speaking that cruel and deeply rooted evil from their hearts and habits. Yet I did not think that I had accomplished anything when I heard them shouting, but only when I saw them weeping.

> “For by their acclamations they indicated that they were being instructed and delighted, but by their tears that they were being moved. When I saw those tears, I believed that the monstrous custom handed down to them by their fathers and grandfathers and by ancestors even more remote—a custom that had occupied, or rather possessed, their hearts in a hostile manner—had been defeated, before they showed it in fact. And immediately, when my speech was finished, I turned their hearts and mouths toward giving thanks to God.

> “And behold, it has now been almost eight years or more, through Christ’s mercy, since anything of that kind has been attempted there” (*On Christian Doctrine*, book 4, no. 53).

### 5.

During that same Caesarean journey, or not long after he had departed from there, he wrote a letter on the origin of the soul to Bishop Optatus (Epist. 190). Optatus was troubled about the soul’s origin and wished to know whether it descended by propagation from a soul created by God and implanted in Adam, or whether God created a new soul individually for each human being. Nevertheless, it appears that he had inclined toward this latter opinion; he had published a short work on the same subject and had sent letters to certain very close friends of his. When these writings reached Caesarea, they were delivered to Augustine, who was still staying there, by a servant of God named Renatus. Renatus urged the holy teacher so strongly to reply that, although he was occupied with other matters at the time, he could not refuse.

Optatus himself also seems to have expressed in his letter a wish to become more certain of the holy Doctor’s judgment on the matter. A certain Muressis [Col. 0502], a close associate of Optatus, likewise induced Augustine to undertake this task. When Muressis came to Caesarea at that time, he said that he too had received a letter from Optatus on the same subject, and he asked Augustine to explain to him, orally or in writing, what he thought about it, so that he might communicate it to Optatus. Accordingly, the holy Doctor gave a letter to Optatus himself from Caesarea, as is sufficiently clear from the words, “when we were staying in the same town,” when he was now departing.

In his reply concerning the proposed difficulty, Augustine wrote that he had no firm conclusion to establish, because arguments could be advanced on both sides. The only point that had to be guarded against was that no one, abusing this question, should begin to doubt original sin, which was an established and catholic doctrine, and thus unwittingly admit the new heresy of Pelagius and Coelestius, which councils and the Roman bishops Innocent and Zosimus had recently condemned. He enclosed their letters—or at least those of the latter, lest they had not yet reached Optatus.

Optatus was evidently not satisfied with this reply, for Augustine sent him two further letters on the same subject, which have been lost through the ravages of time. Fulgentius praises the learning and intellectual power with which the holy Doctor examined this question both in these three letters and in certain other works of his; but above all he praises his modesty, which deterred him from deciding anything concerning a matter equally grave and obscure. “Seeing,” he says, “that the depth of this question was inscrutable to him, he did not wish to put forward any definite judgment on it, considering it entirely inappropriate to wish to affirm without hesitation something that another person could overthrow by a contrary answer” (Fulgentius, *On Predestination and Grace*, book 5, chapter 18).

After therefore treating more fully the opposing opinions—both that which Jerome chose, abhorring every error of Origen, Manichaeus, Priscillian, and Tertullian, namely, that God creates individual souls for each person at birth (apud Augustine, *Epist.* 165, no. 1, and *Against Rufinus*, book 2), and the other according to which souls are propagated and are not created by God each day, while nevertheless avoiding the errors of every heretical view concerning the nature of the soul—Augustine never dared either to reject or to affirm one side of the question (Epist. 66, nos. 8, 28, and Epist. 190, no. 21).

Accordingly, nothing is more consistent with the mind of the holy Doctor, nor does anything detract from his teaching, than what we read at the end of Celestine’s letter: “As for the deeper and more difficult aspects of the questions that arise, which those who resisted the heretics have treated at greater length, just as we do not dare to disregard them, so we are not obliged to establish them” (*Appendix to volume 10, part 2*, Letter of Pope Celestine, for Prosper and Hilary, etc., no. 15).

Following the footsteps of this most prudent pope, the synod of the exiled African bishops, when it likewise transmitted rules of catholic faith concerning grace, added a similar warning: “As for the question of souls, we ought either to leave it unspoken or to treat it without contention” (ibid., Letter of the synod of the exiled African bishops, no. 16).

Augustine conducted himself in precisely this way whenever, in disputing with the Pelagians, he encountered questions not clearly explained by the aid of divine revelation [Col. 0503]. For the same reason he more than once treated without contention the question of whether those found alive at the Lord’s coming at the end of the world will pass from mortality to immortality without an intervening death (Epist. 193, no. 9 ff., and *City of God*, book 20, chapter 20).

### 6.

After Augustine returned to Hippo, he took up his pen to reply to Mercator. Before departing for Caesarea, he had received at Carthage a letter from Mercator, but, being occupied with more serious affairs and sometimes lacking an opportunity to send a message by a courier, he had not yet been able to answer it. Therefore Mercator, whose writings indicate a vehement and fiery temperament, sent him a second letter. Since he had received no reply, he complained as though Augustine had neglected and despised him; at the same time he sent him another short work against the new heretics, namely the Pelagians, for Augustine to examine and approve.

After reading these writings, the holy Doctor not only did not take amiss the agitation which Mercator displayed, but found it especially pleasing. He considered Mercator’s complaints signs of sincerity and affection, not of anger or hostility. Thus, having found an opportunity to reply through Albinus, an acolyte of the Roman Church, he excused the delayed response to him in a manner worthy of his own kindness and humility, and answered certain doubts that Mercator had proposed concerning the Pelagian denial that death was the effect and punishment of sin.

They objected that neither Enoch nor Elijah had died, and that Paul asserted that those who would remain alive at Christ’s coming would not die but would be caught up alive to meet him in the air. From this they concluded that, since not all human beings undergo death, either those people were born without sin—which Catholics maintained could be affirmed only of Christ—or death was not the punishment of sin.

Augustine rejected this objection. Even if it were entirely certain that some would be exempt from the necessity of dying, it could nevertheless readily be understood that this had been granted as a particular privilege of God, who can exempt some from this punishment if he wills, just as he does not exempt many others.

He ended his letter with that profession of humility so characteristic of him: he preferred to learn the solution of obscure questions from others rather than hand it on to them as though it came from himself. “I love learning,” he says, “more than teaching. Therefore, in order that we may learn, the sweetness of truth ought to invite us; but in order that we may teach, the necessity of charity ought to compel us” (Epist. 193, no. 13).

### 7.

That same Albinus, the acolyte who carried the preceding letter, also carried two others. One (Epist. 192, no. 1) was addressed to Celestine, then a deacon of the Roman Church and afterward its bishop. Augustine replied to his letter, which had been brought to Hippo while he himself was far away, in order to testify to their mutual goodwill. The other (Epist. 191) was addressed to a presbyter of the same Church, Sixtus, who later succeeded Celestine in the episcopate. As we have already noted, Augustine congratulated him warmly because he had undertaken the defense of grace against the Pelagians, whom rumor said he favored.

In this letter Augustine promised to send him another, more extensive one [Col. 0504]. In fact, shortly afterward he entrusted it for delivery to him to the presbyter Firmus (Epist. 194, no. 1). The holy Doctor later placed this letter before the eyes of the enemies of grace, saying: “Let them inspect the letter I sent to Sixtus, presbyter of the Roman Church, when we were engaged in the fiercest struggle against the Pelagians” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 55).

In that letter he closes the Pelagians’ customary avenues of escape, dissolves their objections against grace, and finally asks Sixtus to inform him if he knew of any other arguments they had devised against the catholic faith, as well as of anything he himself had argued in defense of the faith against them (Epist. 194, no. 47).

### 8.

Whenever any matter at that time offered an opportunity to expose the destructive character of the Pelagian heresy, Augustine made use of it skillfully and gladly. A certain Aptus—perhaps the same Donatist bishop of Tusurrita who, at the Conference, acknowledged Asselicus as his opponent (Conference of Carthage, chapter 120)—wanted to be called a Jew and an Israelite. He also taught Christians to Judaize, that is, to abstain from foods forbidden by the Law and to observe the other Jewish rites (Epist. 196, no. 16).

Accordingly, that Asselicus—or Assellicus—who, unless we are mistaken, was the Catholic bishop of Tusurrita and had taken part in the Conference with Aptus, the Donatist bishop of Tusurrita, sent a letter concerning the controversy over the avoidance of Judaism to Donatianus, primate of the province of Byzacena, in the year 418. Donatianus arranged for it to be delivered to Augustine so that he might answer it, earnestly begging him to do so (ibid., no. 1).

Augustine complied. He demonstrated that Christians are truly Jews and Israelites, and likewise children of Abraham and Sarah, not according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Nevertheless, he taught that these terms should be used only very rarely and should not be employed in ordinary speech, lest the established usage of language be disturbed and Christians be confused with the Jews who descend from Abraham by carnal generation (ibid., nos. 9–16). Those works of the Law which belong to the ancient sacraments, however, are by no means to be observed by them now that the New Testament has been revealed.

But those things commanded in the Law in such a way that they serve to form the conduct of the faithful must be understood and observed so that whatever progress anyone makes through them is attributed not to himself but to grace (ibid., nos. 1–8). For those who profess to be Christians but oppose the grace of Christ so fiercely that they believe they fulfill the divine commandments by human strength “Judaize,” says the holy Doctor, “not in name, but in error.”

“This class of people,” he says, “had found for itself Pelagius and Coelestius as leaders, the fiercest defenders of this impiety. By God’s recent judgment, through his diligent and faithful servants, they have been deprived even of catholic communion, and because of their unrepentant heart they still remain in their condemnation” (ibid., no. 15).

## CHAPTER XIV

1. In the year 419 Honorius sent a mandate to Aurelius and Augustine requiring every bishop to give his signature against the Pelagian heresy.  
2. Augustine recounts in a sermon at Carthage prodigies recently seen in Jerusalem and elsewhere.  
3. Jerome, inflamed with love for Augustine, especially because through Augustine’s help the Coelestian heresy had been crushed.  
4. Augustine writes to Hesychius of Salona concerning the end of the world.  
5. He first publishes the book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.  
6. *Questions and Expressions in the Heptateuch*.  
7. Vincentius Victor is refuted by Augustine in books *On the Origin of the Soul*, and compelled to retract statements wrongly made by him.  
8. Two books *On Adulterous Marriages* are written to Pollentius.  
9. The adversary of the Law and the Prophets is refuted.

[Col. 0504]

[Col. 0505]

### 1.

The case of Apiarius began to be agitated in the preceding year. He was the presbyter of Sicca who had been excommunicated by his bishop Urbanus and deposed from his rank. He appealed to the Apostolic See, although the customs or laws of the African Church by no means permitted him to do so (Code of the African Canons, canon 125). This matter gave rise to a long and very troublesome dispute between the Roman bishop and the African bishops, which could not be brought to an end before Zosimus died at the close of the preceding year.

Boniface, the successor of Zosimus, did not take the conduct of the Africans, nor the letters they sent him—however serious and forceful they were—in the worse sense. This did not at all prevent him from maintaining an exceptional friendship with the bishop of Hippo, who had played a major part in the councils held in Africa concerning the case of Apiarius.

Prosper praises this pope of holy memory because he acted against the enemies of God’s grace not only by his own apostolic authority but also through decrees of the emperors, whose piety supported his efforts (Prosper, *Against the Collator*, no. 57).

Perhaps the edict inscribed to Aurelius, dated the fifth day before the Ides of June in the year 419, should be attributed to his care (apud Augustine, Epist. 201). In it Honorius indicates that he has renewed by a recent sanction the edict of the preceding year against Pelagius and Coelestius. He also decrees that anyone who knowingly failed to denounce or expel them, wherever within his jurisdiction they might be found, would himself be driven into exile.

He orders Aurelius to admonish those bishops who did not resist these heretics or who silently agreed with them concerning their duty. He wishes all bishops without exception to be compelled to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius, so that those who refused would be stripped of their rank, expelled forever from their cities, and deprived of communion.

An edict very similar to this was sent by the emperor to Augustine, who by his own merits had acquired such authority and esteem that he was considered worthy of the honor proper to the principal see of Africa.

### 2.

Augustine had attended the Council of Carthage held in the present year. Perhaps before leaving that city he delivered a sermon in the Basilica of Restituta, in which he mentioned, as though they had occurred very recently, the prodigies that, according to the chronologists, had been seen in Jerusalem in the year 419. In the same place he also related that the city of Sitifis had been shaken by an extremely violent earthquake (Serm. 19, no. 6).

The title indicates that the sermon was delivered “on the Day of the Games.” From this Sirmond understands that a gladiatorial contest was exhibited on that day. But it is less contrary to the truth to suppose that the title merely identifies the customary day on which such an event had once been held, or some other kind of public spectacle that had begun to be exhibited in place of gladiatorial contests [Col. 0506] from the year 403 or 404, when Honorius abolished gladiators (Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book 2, and Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 25).

### 3.

Innocent the presbyter had been sent from the Carthaginian council mentioned above to Alexandria, so that he might receive from Cyril the genuine and authentic canons of the Council of Nicaea. As far as conjecture allows us to determine, this same Innocent carried there a letter written by Augustine against the Pelagians.

In it, as Julian reports, the holy Doctor declared that Pelagius had been crushed by Jerome beneath the weight of arguments from Scripture (Julian, *Unfinished Work*, book 4, chapter 88). This letter, however, has been lost, as has another letter which Augustine and Alypius at that time gave to the same Innocent for delivery to Jerome. In it they asked whether he had replied to books published against him by a certain Pelagian who called himself Anianus, a deacon of Celeda.

Jerome replied to them through the same Innocent that, because of the grief caused by the death of the blessed Eustochium, he was not yet in a condition to undertake the task. Nevertheless, he hoped that he would soon accomplish it without great difficulty; and he added that they would still do him a favor if they were willing to take this labor upon themselves. He sends greetings in the names of Albina, Pinianus, Melania, and the younger Paula (apud Augustine, Epist. 202, no. 2).

Jerome departed this life in the following year. Thus, as Baronius thought, in this letter the holy presbyter wished his final declaration of love for those holy bishops to contain his last words to them:

“For every opportunity is most welcome to me by which I write to Your Reverence. I call God as witness that, if it could be done, taking wings like a dove, I would entwine myself in your embrace—always because of the merit of your virtues, but now especially because, with you as fellow-workers and authors, the Coelestian heresy has been strangled” (ibid., no. 1).

### 4.

Around this year Augustine wrote to Hesychius, bishop of Salona, the metropolis of Dalmatia. At the time when he wrote to him, approximately 420 years were reckoned from the birth of Christ and somewhat more or less than 390 from his resurrection or ascension (Epist. 199, no. 20). It is also clear that Jerome was still alive (Epist. 197, nos. 1, 5, and Epist. 198, nos. 1, 7).

Certain prodigies had occurred at that time (Epist. 198, no. 5; Philaster, 12.8; Idacius, under the year 418; Marcellinus and Prosper). This appears to have given Hesychius an occasion to write to Augustine through one of his presbyters, named Cornutus, asking whether he thought the time of the Lord’s final coming might not be near, and wishing to learn this from him.

It is sufficiently clear that Hesychius himself wished to derive that time from Daniel’s seventy weeks, which he applied to Christ’s second coming. He therefore asked Augustine for his opinion. Through the same presbyter, the most wise bishop replied that it seemed unreasonable to inquire into a matter which Christ himself had wished to remain hidden. Nothing more certain could be affirmed about it than that the evangelical law had not yet been proclaimed throughout the whole world [Col. 0507].

As for the seventy weeks, he had no doubt that they had to be interpreted as referring to the first coming. When Hesychius asked him to explain them, Augustine sent him Jerome’s commentary on Daniel concerning that very passage and asked him to write back with his opinion of it.

The letter ends with this very beautiful conclusion:

“I would certainly prefer to possess knowledge of what you have asked me rather than ignorance; but since I have not yet been able to do so, I choose rather to confess a cautious ignorance than to profess a false knowledge” (Epist. 197, no. 5).

Hesychius’s reply survives (apud Augustine, Epist. 198). It is devoted chiefly to acknowledging that we cannot know either the day or the year of the judgment, while maintaining that its time can in some way fall within the scope of our knowledge and that we are even obliged to investigate it.

He then adds that, from the prodigies that had appeared and from the other calamities and wars that continually raged in those times, it could not without good reason be concluded that the event was now not very far off. Peoples who had not yet embraced the faith, he thought, could be brought to it within a not very long period.

Regarding the seventy weeks, he says that Jerome defines nothing, since he is doubtful and wavering on this point. Finally, he places before those who applied the weeks to the first coming one difficulty which they must resolve.

Augustine answers this letter with another (Epist. 199). First of all, he distinguishes the desire for the Lord’s coming from the investigation of the time when it will occur. He teaches that the former belongs to the duty of Christians, whereas the latter is contrary to the Gospel, since no one ought to claim knowledge which Christ wished to be denied to his apostles.

He then admits that, since Christ was born, the final hour—that is, the last age—is underway; but how long it is to last remains unknown. Those who believe Christ will come soon can be mistaken, just as those who believe he will come late can be mistaken. The safest course, and the one closest to the Gospel, is for people to refrain from making pronouncements on this matter.

To affirm that Christ will soon be present, if he is in fact not to come until after a long interval, is dangerous. The calamities and wars of the present differ in no way from those seen under Gallienus and at other times. Likewise, the signs that were being reported contained nothing beyond the ordinary pattern of events. Nor did it seem contrary to reason to transfer to a spiritual interpretation the things read in the Gospel concerning this matter.

Finally, Augustine maintains that what David declared—“Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm XVIII, 5)—had not been fulfilled in his own age, much less in apostolic times. Taking this passage as his occasion, he explains that Africa was inhabited by innumerable barbarian nations who had hitherto been unfamiliar with the Gospel. This could be discovered every day from those who were brought from there to Rome into slavery (Epist. 199, no. 46).

### 5.

In his *Retractions*, Augustine lists the books *On Marriage* dedicated to the comes Valerius second, after the *Acts with Emeritus*, which belong to the year 418 (Retractations, book 2, chapter [Col. 0508] 53).

The blessed Doctor had written to Valerius repeatedly, perhaps as early as the year 417, without receiving any reply. This caused him some anxiety. At last, however, he was greatly cheered by three letters from Valerius, received at nearly the same time: the first was returned to Augustine through Bishop Vindemialis, and the second and third followed not long afterward through the presbyter Firmus, from whom Augustine had received the letters of Sixtus about the middle of the year 418 and whom he calls a man of God (Epist. 200, no. 1).

At that time, perhaps also from the same presbyter, Augustine learned that a Pelagian treatise addressed to Valerius himself had fallen into Valerius’s hands. In it the Pelagians asserted that Augustine condemned marriage by defending original sin. Although Valerius had laughed at this slander with the strongest confidence, Augustine nevertheless thought that he had to defend the Church’s teaching against such an accusation.

For this reason he first composed the first of two books entitled *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. In them he demonstrates the goods of marriage, distinguishing them from concupiscence. He teaches that concupiscence is an evil, not belonging to the nature of marriage but deriving from human sin into marriage; nevertheless, marital chastity makes good use of this evil for the procreation of children.

He worked on this book after Pelagius and Coelestius had been condemned, and dedicated it to the comes Valerius for several reasons: because Valerius had received a writing directed to him by the Pelagians; because he had steadfastly and effectively resisted those heretics; and finally because he practiced conjugal chastity with the greatest strictness, which was relevant to the subject of this dispute (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 5).

Apart from such weighty considerations, Augustine was not the sort of person who would thrust his books upon a man of such rank, occupied with affairs, and not asking for them; he considered that closer to impudence than to courtesy.

The book was accompanied by a letter filled with praise of the same comes. There is no reason to fear that Augustine exceeded the bounds of truth in it. For, besides the fact that nothing was more sincere than his affection for Valerius, he also had to take care, as he himself testifies, not to incur the suspicion of flattery (Epist. 200, no. 1).

Indeed, the Pelagians seized this as an opportunity to boast that Augustine had written to a military official for no other reason than to incite his power against them (*Unfinished Work*, book 2, chapter 14).

### 6.

Between this first book to Valerius and the second one addressed to him, Augustine inserts in his *Retractions* a considerable number of books. The first of these are seven books of *Expressions* on the first seven books of divine Scripture, to which he added seven books of *Questions* on those same divine books (Retractations, book 2, chapters 54–55).

He was engaged on both works at the same time. He composed the books of *Questions*, which are cited more than once in the *Expressions*, by reading the sacred Scriptures (Questions on the Heptateuch, book 2, question 62; book 6, question 29; book 7, questions 49, 51) and by comparing various copies of the Septuagint, sometimes also adding material from the versions of Aquila and Symmachus and from a translation made from the Hebrew (ibid., book 1, Preface) [Col. 0509].

We do not doubt that this was Jerome’s version, since no other work under this title existed among the Latins and since the passages Augustine quotes from it agree with our Vulgate edition (Questions on the Heptateuch, book 5, question 20; book 6, questions 7, 15, 19, 24, 25; book 7, questions 21, 55).

Thus, while devoting himself to reading Scripture in this way, Augustine resolved to commit to writing whatever difficulty he encountered. For the time being, he was content to note some matters, examine others cursorily, and resolve only those that did not require a longer delay.

For this reason he wished this commentary to be entitled *Questions*, although most of the questions are treated in such a way that they may seem fully illustrated and explained. Yet even those which he thought it sufficient merely to record in writing are not entirely without usefulness, since the beginning of discovery is to recognize what must be investigated.

He had begun to inquire into the books of Kings in the same manner; but after making some progress in that work, certain more necessary matters recalled him from it (Retractations, book 2, chapter 55, no. 1).

As for the books of *Expressions*, they are a collection of phrases proper to Scripture that arose from the character and usage of the Greek or Hebrew idiom rather than from anything else. Since these expressions are less familiar in Latin usage, they give careless readers an opportunity to seek out certain mystical meanings. “Sometimes,” says the holy Doctor, “they carve out something that indeed does not conflict with the truth; yet it is not found that the author who wrote this passage intended that meaning” (ibid., chapter 54).

He therefore thought that, in order to understand many passages that seemed to contain some obscurity, nothing more was required than to observe in what sense the same expressions were used elsewhere, where their meaning was clear, and then apply that sense to the less clear expressions as well.

He devoted himself to extracting such forms of speech, or idioms, from the five books of Moses, Joshua, and Judges. These extracts make up the seven books entitled *Expressions*. Sometimes he merely copies the expressions; at other times he explains them.

### 7.

After the books of *Questions* and *Expressions*, he places the four books published on the occasion of Vincentius Victor, entitled *On the Soul and Its Origin* (ibid., chapter 56).

Vincentius Victor was a young man born in Caesarea of Mauretania who had converted to the Church from the faction of the Rogatists, which was a subdivision and schism of the Donatists. While staying with a certain Peter, a Spanish presbyter, he came across a treatise by Augustine in which the holy man confessed—with his characteristic modesty—that he did not know whether all souls were propagated from Adam’s one soul or whether God created an individual soul for each person at birth. He did not, however, doubt that the soul was spirit and not body.

Victor was equally displeased that Augustine did not teach without hesitation what should be held concerning the origin of the soul, but considered the propagation of souls probable, and that he declared without hesitation that the nature of the soul was incorporeal.

Therefore he composed two books on this subject for the same Peter the presbyter. They were filled with several Pelagian propositions and other errors [Col. 0510] (*On the Soul and Its Origin*, book 3, no. 2).

At that time the monk Renatus was staying in Caesarea (Retractations, book 2, chapter 56). He was perhaps the same man who, in that city, had delivered to Saint Augustine the letter of Optatus, who had inquired about the origin of the soul in the year 418.

Although Renatus belonged to the lay order, he was nevertheless entirely orthodox in faith. When he encountered these books, whose teaching he did not approve and in which he saw Augustine treated with indignity, he carefully had them copied and arranged for them to be delivered to Augustine (*On the Soul and Its Origin*, book 2, no. 1; book 1, no. 35).

Augustine received the books, sent from Caesarea to Hippo during the summer, only at the end of autumn, since he had been absent throughout that period on some journey unknown to us.

Here the holy Doctor displayed his customary wisdom and humility. He took in good part what Victor had undertaken against him and was most grateful that, although Victor disagreed with his position, he had expressed his mind in published writings. Augustine thought that Victor may perhaps have acted out of goodwill, wishing to free him from what he judged to be an error.

For the holy man had established this rule for himself: whenever he was uncertain about someone’s disposition, he would approve that person’s judgment as good rather than condemn it as evil. “When a person’s attitude toward me is unknown and uncertain,” he says, “I think it better to assume that he has good intentions than to condemn what I have not investigated” (*On the Soul and Its Origin*, book 1, no. 2).

The fact that Victor had opened his mind to someone else rather than, as was proper, to Augustine, he attributed to Victor’s modesty. Moreover, he did not think that a person who believed his own opinion entirely certain could have been obliged to consult Augustine.

If, while disputing, the young layman had let some word fall insulting Augustine, the holy bishop believed that he had done so not out of a desire to abuse him but from the necessity of holding a different opinion.

Nevertheless, just as the holy bishop was moved by the modesty and humility of his spirit to correct whatever evil might perhaps have clung to him, so the love of truth did not permit him to leave undefended what was sound (*On the Soul and Its Origin*, book 4, no. 1). The things Victor attacked belonged to this category.

Accordingly, Augustine produced four books in reply: one to the monk Renatus, another to the presbyter Peter, and two to Victor himself. Although the work addressed to Peter was a letter, it received the title of a book because it was not to be separated from the others (Retractations, book 2, chapter 56).

In all these books, which discuss many matters necessary to know, Augustine defends his hesitation concerning the origin of the souls given to individual human beings and exposes many of Victor’s errors and corruptions arising from his presumption. Nevertheless, he did not think the young man should be condemned prematurely. Since he had heard that Victor had only recently become a Catholic, he treated him with the greatest possible gentleness (ibid.; *On the Soul and Its Origin*, book 1, no. 2).

This method and labor of the holy Doctor had such a fortunate outcome that he received from Victor a written reply correcting his errors (Retractations, book 2, chapter 56).

### 8.

After the books *On the Origin of the Soul*, the two books *On Adulterous Marriages* addressed to Pollentius occupy the next place in the *Retractions* [Col. 0511].

Who that Pollentius was cannot be discovered anywhere. This alone may safely be said: he was a man distinguished for piety, whom Augustine calls his religious brother (*On Adulterous Marriages*, book 2, no. 1).

As Pollentius was reading the works in which Augustine had explained, many years earlier, the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, he was surprised that the holy bishop maintained that women lawfully separated from adulterous husbands were not permitted to marry another man while those husbands were alive, but had to preserve continence themselves.

Therefore Pollentius asked Augustine by letter to remove this doubt for him. He thought rather that only women who separated from their husbands for a reason other than fornication were forbidden a second marriage during the husbands’ lifetime.

When Pollentius learned that Augustine was preparing a reply for him, he sent him some additional new questions on the same subject (ibid.).

After receiving these questions, once he had already completed his work, Augustine had intended to answer them by adding a supplement. But when his book was published by friends sooner than he had wished, he was forced to compose a new work.

In these two books he examines the question of marriage on the authority of Scripture. In his judgment it was a very difficult question (Retractations, book 2, chapter 57), exceedingly obscure and deeply entangled (*On Adulterous Marriage*, book 1, no. 32).

When it was objected, among other things, that men separated from their wives could not preserve continence, Augustine overturned the objection, especially by adducing the example of clerics.
