The necessity of continence was imposed upon them, and often they were suddenly compelled to accept clerical office; nevertheless, with the assistance of divine grace, they bore with the greatest religious devotion this burden, whose assumption they had never previously considered (*On Adulterous Marriage*, book 2, no. 22).

Pollentius also asked Augustine whether he believed that Baptism should be conferred upon catechumens who had been struck by illness and were unable to request it (*On Adulterous Marriage*, book 1, no. 33).

The holy Doctor wishes each person to have the freedom to follow in this matter whatever seems best to him. For his own part, however, he thinks it right to confer the same sacrament upon such people even if, before their illness, they had given no other indication of a desire to receive it than what was known from their faith.

A much more effective support for this opinion is provided by an event that he recalls having happened to one of his friends in his *Confessions* [Col. 0512] (*Confessions*, book 4, no. 8).

Indeed, he extends that grace even to those who, while maintaining adulterous relationships, would not have been admitted to Baptism had they been in bodily health.

He also says that what he establishes concerning the baptism of catechumens must likewise be observed in reconciling penitents. “For Mother Church,” he says, “ought not to wish them to depart from this life without the pledge of her peace” (*On Adulterous Marriages*, book 1, no. 35).

9. Around the same time, an anonymous book by some Marcionite, or by someone belonging to one of those sects which, together with the Manichaeans, condemned the Law and the Prophets and moreover attributed the creation of the world to a demon rather than to God—a doctrine foreign to the Manichaeans—was offered for sale at Carthage (Retractations, book 2, chapter 58; Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, book 1, no. 1). The author related that his teaching had been handed down to him by a certain Fabricius, whom he had encountered at Rome and whose disciple he proudly claimed to be. He had undertaken to undermine the authority of the Old Testament, employing various testimonies both from it and from the New Testament (Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, book 2, nos. 3, 40). He used the authority of apocryphal writings (ibid., no. 14), and at the end of his work commended his heresy on the ground that it had only a few adherents (ibid., no. 41).

Since this volume, filled with errors, was openly available, many people, led by curiosity and by a most dangerous pleasure, either read it or lent their ears to those who read it. When some faithful Christians learned of this, acting with a truly Christian spirit, they sent the book to Augustine and asked him to refute it in writing as soon as possible. He therefore complied with their wish and entitled his response *Against the Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*. Concerned for the benefit of his readers, he divided it into two books. In the first he defended those passages of the Old Testament which that scoundrel mocked, showing that they contained nothing either evil or ridiculous; in the second he answered the testimonies from the New Covenant which the same heretic employed against the Old. In the first book he cites the fourteenth book of *The City of God* (ibid., book 1, no. 18).

Moreover, if Augustine composed the four books *On the Origin of the Soul* toward the end of the autumn of the year 419, there is no reason to deny that he wrote these two books around the beginning of 420.

# BOOK EIGHT

Concerning the remaining acts of Augustine, from the year of Christ 420 to the year 430.

[Col. 0511]

## CHAPTER ONE

1. The Donatists, driven by their own madness, kill and burn themselves.  
2. Dulcitius, tribune and notary, endeavors to dissuade Gaudentius, a bishop of the Donatist party, from the plan of burning himself, and receives two letters from him.  
3. At Dulcitius’s request, Augustine answers Gaudentius.  
4. He writes a book to Consent(i)us against lying, arguing that Catholics may not use it to investigate the Priscillianists.  
5. He explains the same Consentius’s questions, especially whether the Lord’s body now has bones and blood and the remaining features of the flesh.  
6. He writes to Ceretius against the Priscillianists, who abused apocryphal Scriptures and perjury.

[Col. 0512]

### 1.

We have already seen what advances the Catholic Church made against the Donatist schism through both the Conference at Carthage and the laws enacted by Honorius to enforce its decrees [Col. 0513]. We have also seen what violent crimes were produced by the grief of those who refused to endure the defeat of their obstinacy. Yet this was by no means the end of their madness. For, as Augustine says, just as the Church’s charity labors to free them from that destruction so that none of them may die, so their madness labors either to kill us, that they may feed the appetite of their cruelty, or even to kill themselves, lest they appear to have lost the power of killing others (Letter 185, no. 11).

Those horrible and lamentable deaths which they had once practiced, and by which the name of the Circumcellions had become so famous throughout the world—and indeed hateful even to the somewhat more moderate members of their own sect—were therefore revived. The emperor punished them only with exile (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 21); the Catholics, for their part, did not unwillingly allow them to remain in hiding (ibid., no. 41), since they sought their exile only so that they would not obstruct the salvation of others (ibid., no. 12).

Nevertheless, although extreme punishments were deservedly due to their crimes, they themselves both decreed and carried them out against themselves, becoming at once the judges and executioners of their own deeds. Whereas holy martyrs meet death for the truth, these men perished in order to prevent the truth from being proclaimed, the truth from being held, unity from being loved, charity from being embraced, and eternity from being attained (Sermon 325, no. 2).

If Gaudentius is to be believed, an innumerable multitude was taken away by this kind of death (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 32). Augustine, however, insists that there were not as many men who laid violent hands upon themselves as there were entire villages, towns, cities, and peoples who, out of fear of the imperial laws, defected from the schism. When they threatened to turn the sword against their own lives and to surrender themselves either to a precipice or to fire, they hoped by this device to delay the persecution directed against them by the Catholics and to diminish their zeal. But it seemed better to the Catholics that a few lost and desperate people should perish than that innumerable persons should be left in the deadly schism—persons whom, through the benefit of laws supplied to them not without divine providence, they might be able to rescue from it (Letter 204, nos. 1–2).

Heavenly favor so supported this policy that, without anyone taking his own life, a great number both in Numidia and in the other provinces of Africa returned to peace with the Church. If such an evil occurred somewhere, the Church, like David mourning the slain Absalom while finding consolation in the peace restored to his kingdom, softened the grief of her maternal heart and healed it through the restoration of unity and the liberation of so many peoples.

“If you were to see,” he says to Boniface, “the joys, gatherings, and enthusiasm of these people in the peace of Christ; their numerous and joyful assemblies both to hear and sing hymns and to receive the word of God; the great sorrow with which many among them recall their former error; the joy with which they contemplate the truth they have come to know; and the indignation and detestation with which they regard the lies of their teachers, now that they understand how falsely those teachers boasted about our sacraments; and also the confessions of many among them that they had long wished to be Catholics but had not dared to do so among men of such great madness—if you were to see, gathered together under one view, the assemblies of these peoples liberated from that destruction throughout the many regions of Africa [Col. 0514], then you would say that it had been excessive cruelty if, while people feared that desperate men, incomparable in number with this innumerable multitude, might burn themselves in their own voluntary fires, these others had been left to be lost forever and tortured by everlasting fires” (Letter 185, no. 32).

### 2.

Among those whose madness was especially conspicuous, Gaudentius, bishop of Thamugadi, distinguished himself. He was the successor of that celebrated Optatus Gildonianus and one of the seven whom the Donatists chose as patrons of their party at the Conference of Carthage (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 52; Retractations, book 2, chapter 59).

After first fleeing, he later returned (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 17), swearing that, if he were compelled to communicate with the Catholics, he would burn himself together with his church and several other madmen who still adhered to him (ibid., no. 1; Retractations, book 2, chapter 59).

The emperor Honorius had entrusted Dulcitius with enforcing the laws enacted for unity. Dulcitius was a layman and a military man of the Catholic communion and, like Marcellinus a few years earlier, had been honored with the rank of tribune and notary (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 12). The nature of his office permitted him to inflict on them not the penalty of death but only exile (Letter 204, no. 3).

He possessed great gentleness, and through his efforts God had brought not a few from the schism to Catholic unity. Since the people of Thamugadi were more obstinate than the others, Dulcitius, intending to deal with them with the mildness that was appropriate, admonished them by an official edict. Among other things, knowing that they intended to burn themselves, he declared that they would endure the death they deserved. By this statement he plainly meant the death which they would inflict upon themselves with their own hands. They, however, interpreted it as though he had threatened them with capital punishment.

In another edict he explained his meaning more clearly. He also sent Gaudentius a letter exhorting him to Catholic unity and dissuading him from the burning by which he threatened to consume himself and his followers together with the church in which he was staying (Retractations, book 2, chapter 59). Dulcitius said that there were innocent people there whom Gaudentius was holding against their will for destruction—that is, people who, unless restrained by regard and reverence for his authority, would freely return to the Catholic Church (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 6).

He added that Gaudentius should take care lest it be said that he himself had burned so large a basilica, where he had so often invoked the name of God. Dulcitius said that he had been glad, on arriving in the province or perhaps even in the city of Thamugadi, to find Gaudentius absent; but that he was distressed to see him return. He did not wish to be given an occasion to persecute him, nor did he wish Gaudentius’s presence to become an obstacle to the salvation of others. If Gaudentius believed himself innocent, he should flee, in accordance with the Lord’s command, rather than burn himself (ibid., no. 12).

Dulcitius testified that he had learned from the report of certain persons that Gaudentius was a man endowed with prudence. He always treated him more honorably than a Catholic ought to treat a heretic, hoping by this method to make him more teachable (ibid., no. 3).

After receiving this letter, Gaudentius promptly replied in the briefest possible form, lest, as he said, he cause delay for the messengers [Col. 0515] (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 12). He declared that he had firmly determined and resolved, if he saw any violence threatening, to bring his life to an end within the Lord’s camp—that is, to burn himself together with his church. As for the others, however, he said that he was so far from intending to compel them that he would instead urge all who wished to leave the church to declare their desire openly and freely (ibid., no. 7).

On the following day he sent another response, more verbose than the first, in which he attempted to defend his madness by scriptural testimonies, including the example of Razis, whose death is narrated in the Second Book of Maccabees (ibid., no. 12). He also recalled what had happened to Emeritus when Augustine had gone to Caesarea in the year 418, but he concealed the truth of the matter (ibid., no. 15).

### 3.

Dulcitius arranged for both letters to be delivered to Augustine and asked him to refute them (Retractations, book 2, chapter 59) and to instruct him how he should answer the heretics (Letter 204, no. 1)—that is, unless we are misled by our conjecture, how he ought to deal with the threats by which they boasted that they would use sword and fire against themselves.

The holy bishop replied that such threats should be disregarded and that fear of the destruction of a few wretched people ought not to deter Dulcitius from caring, insofar as possible, for the salvation of others. As for refuting Gaudentius’s letters, Augustine said that his occupations scarcely allowed him to do so and that he had already answered elsewhere the arguments contained in them (ibid., no. 4). Nevertheless, he promised to refute them carefully, both for Dulcitius’s sake and for that of Eleusinus, who had made the same request, and out of his own charity toward the people of Thamugadi (ibid., no. 9).

He also briefly dismantled those letters, especially the example of Razis, in the very letter to Dulcitius. This Eleusinus, whom Augustine calls his honorable and most beloved son and whom he testifies to have served as tribune among the people of Thamugadi, may reasonably be thought to be the same Eleusinus, a man of tribunitian rank, who possessed an estate in the territory of Hippo, where there was also a small shrine or memorial of blessed Stephen.

When Eleusinus’s infant son had been taken away by illness, he placed the child upon the memorial—or perhaps upon the small shrine containing the sacred relics of the Martyr. After he had prayed to God with abundant tears, he carried the child back alive and unharmed (The City of God, book 22, chapter 8, no. 19).

The holy bishop further relates that his beloved and honorable son Eleusinus donated a villa to the monastery at Hippo (Sermon 356, no. 15). You may infer that it produced no modest income from the fact that people said Eleusinus had sold it, since no one would readily believe that such a valuable gift had proceeded from him gratuitously. Augustine, however, declared that this rumor was false and professed himself a witness to the donation.

As soon as he was able, Augustine discharged his promise to refute Gaudentius’s two letters and composed one book for this purpose. In it, the opponent’s text was presented first, followed by Augustine’s own response, so that even the less educated might clearly see that he had omitted nothing without answering it (Against Gaudentius, book 1, no. 1).

After reading this book, Gaudentius sent a reply directly to Augustine—not in order to refute him, but merely so that he would not be thought to acknowledge his defeat by remaining silent (ibid., book 2, no. 1; Retractations, book 2, chapter 59). Yet while he intended to conceal his weakness, he made it far more evident. Anyone could see that he had wished to respond but had opposed nothing sound or substantial.

Thus no one could doubt that his case was desperate. Even men of moderate intelligence could recognize, by comparing the writings of the two authors, how ineptly Gaudentius had answered Augustine. To demonstrate this point in detail, however, required a more extended discussion. Augustine was fully prepared for such labor if it seemed necessary. But so that Gaudentius would not meanwhile be left without an answer, he supplied a very brief one, which is the second book against him.

That this satisfied public expectation may be inferred from the fact that the holy man is not afterward found to have added anything to it. He refers to these two books as though they were addressed directly to Gaudentius himself. Possidius, however, records them separately in his *Catalogue*: “One book of Responses against the two letters of Gaudentius, bishop of the Donatists,” and “One letter to Gaudentius, bishop of the Donatists” (Possidius, *Catalogue*, chapter 3).

We nowhere find what happened to Gaudentius and the other Donatists thereafter, up to Augustine’s death.

### 4.

While Augustine was answering Gaudentius, he was also working on the book *Against Lying*, which he sent to Consentius, who was living perhaps not far from Spain, where the Priscillianist heresy was flourishing (Retractations, book 2, chapter 60).

Consentius had sent Augustine many things to read, reporting individually on the doctrines of the Priscillianists after careful investigation and after learning a great deal from a certain Fronto (Against Lying, nos. 1, 4).

Since these heretics believed that their heresy had to be concealed not only by lying but also by perjury, Consentius thought that Catholics should use deception in investigating them, pretending to be Priscillianists so that they might penetrate their hiding places. Augustine entirely rejected this idea and wrote a book on the subject entitled *Against Lying* (Retractations, book 1, chapter 27). In it he attacks the vice openly and resolves the scriptural passages by which some people—and perhaps Consentius himself—attempted to support it.

Above all, Augustine demonstrates that even if it were sometimes perfectly true that lying was permitted, it could nevertheless never be used in matters pertaining to religion without great guilt and danger. He urges Consentius to engage the Priscillianists with his pen once God had equipped him with the strength necessary for this task. It would be pointless, he says, to investigate and expose their doctrines if they were left without refutation (Against Lying, no. 25).

Above all else, however, he commands him to attack their teaching that lying may be used in a religious cause and, for this purpose, to refute the book of the Priscillianist bishop Dictinius entitled *The Scales* (*Libra*) (ibid., no. 5).

This work against lying appears to have been composed around the spring of the present year. There is no doubt that Augustine referred to this very work when he said: “Here arises a most difficult and obscure question, concerning which, when the necessity of answering pressed us, we completed a substantial book” (*Enchiridion*, no. 6).

As for the book *On Lying*, we do not see that it was composed in response to anyone. It should also be added that it did not appear until Augustine had begun revising his works (Retractations, book 1, chapter 27).

### 5.

We may readily believe that the letter beginning “As far as the bodily eyes are concerned” (Letter 205) was written both to the same Consentius and in the same year. The letter from Consentius which Augustine mentions there may well be the very one that provided the occasion for writing the book just discussed.

In addition to this letter, Consentius had asked Augustine, on a separate sheet, to solve several questions: whether the Lord’s body now has bones and blood, or the remaining features of the flesh; whether the features of the bodies that are now being formed are fashioned individually by God the Creator; whether all baptized persons will eventually obtain forgiveness, even if they die entangled in various crimes without repentance; and whether the breath of God in Adam is Adam’s soul itself.

Augustine replied to him concerning these matters, but discussed especially the state of the Lord’s body and of the blessed in heaven. The author of these questions may also have been that same Consentius who, approximately ten years earlier, had asked certain questions about the Trinity. Augustine had then written to him: “In your books I have been greatly delighted by your talent. For you possess the ability to explain what you have understood” (Letter 120, no. 1).

Likewise, now writing to him about lying, Augustine says: “I have been greatly delighted by your eloquence, by your recollection of the holy Scriptures, and by your intellectual skill” (Against Lying, no. 1).

In the year 410 Consentius lived on certain islands (Letter 119, no. 6), and he had sailed to Africa in order to see Augustine (ibid., no. 1). But Augustine had been unable to see him because he had gone into the countryside for some necessity.

At that time, however, Augustine said that he had heard something from him. Unless Augustine said this in such a way that it was understood that he had learned it from Consentius not in person but by some other means, the statement does not suit the Consentius whose questions Augustine is now considering. For Augustine places him among those whom he had never seen but nevertheless loved and whose presence he eagerly desired in order to fulfill the affection he bore them (Letter 120, no. 1).

### 6.

Augustine attacks the same Priscillianist heresy in his letter to the bishop Ceretius (Letter 237), whose date we do not know.

Ceretius had informed him about a certain Argirius and had sent him two volumes, apparently apocryphal, together with a hymn said to be by the Lord Christ. He especially wished to learn from Augustine’s letter what opinion he should hold concerning it.

The many and continuous affairs by which the holy man was almost overwhelmed [Col. 0518] scarcely left him enough leisure to read through one of these volumes. As for the other, it was misplaced during some interruption, and afterward it could not be found.

After a not particularly short interval, therefore, Augustine replied to Ceretius. He informed him that he thought Argirius had either adopted the name of the Priscillianist sect or, at least, was imprudently following its errors. Augustine said that he had no doubt that the writings which had been brought to him at Argirius’s request were the same as those apocryphal works which the Priscillianists abused as though they were divine.

He quotes a great many words from the hymn which the heretics themselves claimed was the very hymn spoken by Christ after the Last Supper and which supposedly contained mysteries beyond the capacity of ordinary people to understand.

Augustine shows that, if the manner in which the hymn was publicly interpreted were considered, it contained nothing that books of canonical authority did not contain. Nevertheless, he says it was extremely likely that the heretics were concealing there the doctrines of their sect, which they revealed only to their own members, because those doctrines were truly impious and detestable.

They also gave their followers the following command, instructing them to lie—even with false oaths—in order to conceal their doctrines:

“Swear, forswear yourself; do not reveal the secret.”

Augustine testifies that he had learned this and other crimes of the sect in abundance from men who had formerly been involved in it but had afterward been rescued from it by divine favor.

## CHAPTER TWO

1. Julian writes four books against Augustine and several letters on behalf of the Pelagians.  
2. Augustine refutes excerpts from the first of Julian’s books by publishing a second book addressed to Valerius; he also writes four books to Boniface against two letters of the Pelagians.  
3. Alypius carries all these books of Augustine to Italy.  
4. Augustine publishes six further books against Julian.  
5. A rescript of the emperor Constantius is promulgated against the Pelagians, and the temple of the goddess Caelestis is razed to the ground.

### 1.

We saw in the preceding year how Augustine sent to the count Valerius the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. This book had scarcely appeared when Julian, bishop of Eclanum and a member of the Pelagian faction, published four books against it in a single work.

In reality, however, he touched upon not even a fourth part of Augustine’s book, content to attack what he considered weaker points, as though no one would ever examine the whole of either work (Against Julian, book 1, no. 2).

Having abandoned the truth, he turned to insults (ibid., no. 3). He abusively called Catholics Manichaeans and, above all, Augustine, whom he also contemptuously called the “Punic disputant” (ibid., book 3, no. 32).

He also disparaged certain people who, after renouncing the Pelagian heresy, had returned to the orthodox faith. Augustine appears to say that some of them were known to him and lived extremely chaste lives; as for the others, he says he did not know who they were (ibid., book 6, no. 35). He treated Count Valerius more respectfully (Unfinished Work, book 1, chapter 10).

He labored in vain (ibid., chapter 67) to twist to his own meaning those famous words of the Apostle: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Romans 7:24).

He brought forward certain sayings of Basil and Chrysostom which he claimed favored his heresy [Col. 0519] (Against Julian, book 6, no. 69). Finally, he promised that he would answer all the arguments brought forward by Catholics to prove original guilt (Unfinished Work, book 1, no. 1).

He dedicated these four books to Turbantius, a bishop of his own faction, whom he praises in other books addressed to Florus as a man distinguished by the great splendor of his virtues.

But immediately after these later books had been published, and after Julian had offered these praises to him, God—entreated by the prayers of the Church on Turbantius’s behalf—freed Turbantius from the Pelagian error and converted him to the Catholic faith through his own action and mercy. Perhaps God used for this purpose the very work by which Julian had attempted to strengthen him in heresy (ibid., book 2, chapter 11; book 5, no. 4).

“Perhaps holy Turbantius,” Augustine says, “after reading the very work which you say you wrote to him, breathed again into the Catholic faith for this reason also: because he recognized that you had failed in such a cause” (ibid., book 4, no. 30).

After completing this work, Julian immediately sent a letter to Rome, through which, as the holy Doctor says, he either found or made as many of his supporters as he could (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book 1, no. 3). In it he also mentions the hearing—that is, the synod—which the Pelagian faction was demanding (ibid., no. 12).

Augustine refutes this letter in his first book addressed to Boniface. Julian seems, however, to have wished to disown it for some rather foolish reason; Augustine did not prevent him from doing so: “If you do not acknowledge it,” he says, “then let it not be yours” (Unfinished Work, book 1, no. 18).

In the same letter one could read the very statement contained in the letter sent in the name of eighteen Pelagian bishops to the bishop of Thessalonica: namely, that Augustine’s words had been taken up by their own enemies in hatred of the truth (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book 1, no. 9; book 4, no. 20). From this one may infer that both letters were written around the same time. At least this much is entirely certain: they were published no later than that.

### 2.

When both letters had come into the hands of Pope Boniface, certainly only through the most vigilant diligence of the Roman Catholics (ibid., book 1, no. 3), he arranged for them to be delivered to Augustine through Saint Alypius. We do not know what prompted Alypius to undertake an overseas journey at this time.

While Valerius was at Ravenna, he then sent Augustine a letter in which he thanked the holy Doctor for the book sent to him and at the same time warned him, through the aforementioned Alypius, to learn what the heretics were saying against certain passages of the book (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, no. 1).

Afterward, when Alypius had gone from Ravenna to Rome, Valerius sent him a note to carry to Augustine. It contained extracts from Julian’s first book, selected by someone at will and with some alterations, and sent to the same count so that he might have a shorter and more convenient response to Augustine’s book (Unfinished Work, Preface).

Valerius therefore arranged for these extracts to be carried to Augustine, asking him to refute them with the greatest possible speed.

Alypius was received most kindly at Rome by Pope Boniface. Though he lived with him for only a short time, he became bound to him by great affection and also formed for Augustine a most intimate bond of friendship with him (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book 1, no. 1).

For this reason Boniface entrusted Alypius with the two letters, as we have already observed: one which Julian had written to Rome and the other which the eighteen bishops had written to Rufus of Thessalonica. His principal reason was that he saw the holy Doctor treated calumniously in both (ibid., book 2, no. 3).

Alypius therefore returned to Africa carrying these two books and the aforementioned sheet of extracts.

Augustine inferred that these extracts had been taken from Julian’s books and judged that it would be better to devote himself to refuting the entire work. Nevertheless, he thought he had to hurry in order to satisfy Count Valerius (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 2, no. 3).

Accordingly, he quickly published a second book addressed to Valerius under the same title, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, after approximately a year had passed since the publication of the first book. There he refuted Julian’s calumnies and showed that the Catholic doctrine concerning original evil was very far removed from the heresy of the Manichaeans.

He also composed four books to refute the two aforementioned letters. In the first book he answered the letter allegedly written by Julian; in the next three he refuted the other letter, which belonged to the eighteen bishops.

Since he saw that the enemies of grace did not cease trying, through various arguments, to disturb the minds of the weaker, he judged it his duty to confront them in the same manner—both so that no Catholic might be deceived by them and so that they themselves might not strengthen either themselves or their followers in that wicked error.

He decided above all to send the work to Boniface, so that Boniface might read it not so much for the purpose of learning as of examining and correcting it whenever he came upon a passage that seemed less satisfactory to him.

While recalling there the insulting manner in which the Pelagians treated him, Augustine says:

“I hope in the Lord our God that they who tear me with a malicious tooth, because I oppose them on behalf of the little ones, so that they may not be abandoned to the deceptive praiser Pelagius but offered for liberation to the truthful Savior Christ, do not do so without receiving a reward in heaven” (Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, book 1, nos. 2–3).

### 3.

Toward the end of the same year 420, or at the beginning of the following year, Alypius crossed once more to Italy and carried the new works which Augustine had composed against the Pelagians: namely, the four books addressed to Boniface (Unfinished Work, book 1, no. 85) and the second book addressed to Valerius (ibid., no. 7).

At that time it was necessary to confront the most troublesome enemies of God’s grace, because in those regions they were making every effort to rescue their heresy from destruction.

Those people, supposing that this was either the sole or the principal reason for Alypius’s repeated voyage, seized upon it as an opportunity to disparage the orthodox, making particularly insolent use of Julian’s style for this purpose.

Julian accused Alypius of bringing with him on this journey more than eighty horses, fattened throughout Africa, for the tribunes (ibid., no. 42). He then flattered himself in these words:

“The dignity of our cause is exceedingly great, as both the consideration and weighing of the matters we defend show—and so also does your fear: you who fight against our blood by the pouring out of money, the lavish distribution of inheritances, the sending of horses, the sedition of peoples, and the corruption of authorities, while you are ashamed to profess the faith which we attack” (Unfinished Work, book 1, no. 74).

After returning at length to the same purpose of calumny, he says:

“Why, then, have you stirred up all Italy with such great factions? Why have you provoked riots at Rome by hiring crowds? Why have you fattened throughout nearly all Africa herds of horses from the resources of the poor, horses which, through Alypius, you sent to tribunes and centurions? Why have you corrupted the secular authorities with the inheritances offered by matrons, so that the straw of public fury might burn against us? Why have you disturbed the peace of the churches? Why have you stained the reign of a religious prince with the impiety of persecutions?” (ibid., book 3, no. 35).

Augustine, however, repelled the man’s impotence and remarkable impudence with this response:

“Either you are making a calumny, or you do not know what you are saying; and therefore you speak these things either as a liar or as a reckless man. But what is worse than you if you invented these things yourself? What is more foolish if you believed those who invented them?

“And now, as for what you also dared to write, without fearing that your books might reach those places which welcomed my colleague Alypius as he crossed by sea or travelled by land—places where your utterly false statements cannot be read without mockery of you, or rather detestation of you—to what can this be compared, not in impudence but in madness?” (ibid., book 1, chapter 42).

Finally, once again correcting Julian’s shameless mockery, Augustine says:

“Just as the crimes you bring against us are false, so the doctrines you invent for yourselves are false” (ibid., book 3, no. 35).

### 4

Augustine had not yet seen Julian’s four books when he refuted extracts from them; but it is understood from this that they came into his hands not much later, since he places their refutation immediately after the books addressed to Boniface (*Retractations* II.62). A certain bishop—his name was Claudius [*Epistle* 207]—sent them to him before Augustine requested them. The holy Doctor therefore examined the books carefully after receiving them and found, on reading, that they were just as he had supposed they would be before possessing them: namely, filled with deceptions and lies. Indeed, they could assail the truth they opposed only with weapons of that kind (*Unfinished Work* I.17).

During that same reading he detected that the extracts Valerius had sent him differed in certain respects from Julian’s work. Hence he feared that Julian, or someone else, seeing a published response to those extracts, might accuse him of fraud (*Retractations* II.62). Julian certainly did not fail to charge him with that offense in the most insulting manner, although his accusations collapsed under their own weight; indeed, he plainly identified the holy Doctor as the author of the extracts to which he had replied (*Unfinished Work* I.19).

Thus, besides other considerations, fear of this accusation moved him to refute Julian’s work; and he accomplished this clearly in six books. Since Julian applied the impious doctrine of the Manichaeans to all who said that original sin was transmitted from Adam, Augustine showed that this calumny fell upon the most illustrious Fathers of the Church, adducing testimonies both Greek and Latin in support of his case. He further demonstrated that the Manichaeans were rather assisted by certain rash opinions of Julian himself [*Col. 0522]. The second book, moreover, consists of statements by the Fathers, which are there opposed to Julian’s subtleties and sophisms.

Augustine feared, however, that Julian would yield to the authority of so many holy and learned Fathers—or rather, he had no doubt that Julian would even say that those Fathers had erred in this matter. Therefore, so that nothing in Julian’s entire work might remain unrefuted and overthrown, he refuted each of Julian’s four books with one of his own, confirming by carefully reasoned arguments both that Catholic doctrine is true and that the Pelagian teachings establish the heresy of the Manichaeans (*Against Julian* III.1).

At the beginning of the entire work he openly declares that he does not wholly disregard Julian’s insults. Yet—and this is something that Catholic disputants, who are abused by the enemies of God’s grace, should note—he declares that he is moved by them for no other reason than that they provide him with material both for joy and exultation, because of the greater reward he would receive in heaven, and for grief and sorrow, because of Julian’s danger. Out of his greater love for Julian, and for those who were deceived by him, he grieved over Julian’s plight (*ibid.* I.1).

As for the single combat Julian offered him, Augustine by no means thinks it should be accepted. “Far be it from me,” he says, “to claim among Catholics what you are not ashamed to claim for yourself among the Pelagians. I am one among many who, as we are able, refute your profane novelties, according as God has apportioned to each of us the measure of faith” (*ibid.* VI.22).

“Far be it from me to challenge you to single combat, for wherever you appear, everywhere the army of Christ, spread throughout the world, defeats you. It defeated Caelestius at Carthage, when I myself was not there; and again at Constantinople, so far from the African regions. It defeated Pelagius in Palestine, where, fearing his own condemnation, he condemned your cause” (*ibid.* III.4).

In the first book he mentions Jerome as though he had already died (*ibid.* I.34). Yet that holy presbyter died only in the year 420, on the day before the Kalends of October. Consequently, we do not hesitate to date these books to the year 421.

### 5

The chronographers agree that the emperor Constantius, Honorius’s brother-in-law, died this year, 421, after having ruled for exactly six months, entering upon his seventh according to Olympiodorus. Among the other memorials he left of his zeal for the Church is a rescript to Volusianus, prefect of the City, ordering that Caelestius be expelled from Rome. Volusianus obeyed the rescript and ordered Caelestius—whom he called a disturber of the divine faith and of the public peace—to be driven from Rome and the entire surrounding region, threatening the penalty of proscription against those who concealed him.

Under the same emperor, a tribune named Ursus demolished to the foundations all the buildings of the celebrated temple of the goddess Caelestis belonging to the Carthaginians and assigned the site for the burial of the dead (*Prosper, On Predestination* III.38). This temple had already been handed over to the Christians and consecrated as a church by Aurelius. Nevertheless, on the authority of a certain vain prophecy, the unbelievers hoped that they would one day see their ancient superstitions revived in this magnificent building. It was therefore necessary that God utterly remove this confidence from them.

## CHAPTER III

1. Some Manichaeans discovered at Carthage.  
2. Augustine expels Victorinus the Manichaean.  
3. He composes the *Enchiridion* for Laurentius.  
4. He writes to Paulinus, who consulted him, the book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*.  
5. He responds to Dulcitius’s eight questions.

### 1

From the passage of Prosper recently cited, where we learn that the tribune Ursus was at that time living in Africa, we are additionally reminded that we should report here what was done there concerning the Manichaeans through the efforts of that same Ursus.

This man—whom they call not only a tribune but also an administrator of the imperial household—professed the Catholic faith. He apprehended several persons from the number of those whom the Manichaeans called the Elect and the Elect Women, among whom was a girl named Margarita, not yet twelve years old, and a certain Eusebia, apparently a religious woman. He brought them into a church at Carthage, where they were questioned by the bishops, especially by Augustine.

Since Augustine knew this detestable sect better than the others and demonstrated their blasphemies from their own books, he compelled them to confess them. He drew from the mouths of the Elect Women a confession of the disgraceful lusts they practiced among themselves, the least serious of which was the violation of virgins.

Margarita was the first to confess those abominations. Afterwards Eusebia, who had proclaimed herself a virgin, was compelled by her to confess her own disgrace and shame, and she disclosed other detestable crimes of her sect as well. Throughout the entire inquiry everything was committed to the ecclesiastical records. This is perhaps why Possidius says that the Manichaeans were heard “from the records.”

He adds that, through the care and diligence the bishops devoted to this matter, the Church of the Lord was enriched by a new accession and equipped with new weapons by which it could defend itself against thieves and robbers. Later the bishops also exposed what was not their sacrament but, to use Augustine’s expression, their “execrament,” through the confession of another Manichaean named Viator. The Carthaginian deacon Quodvultdeus sent the records of this affair to Saint Augustine (*Possidius, Life of Augustine* 16; Augustine, *On Heresies* 46).

Augustine probably refers to this same affair when, around the year 427, he asks that deacon to inform him about Theodosius, who had exposed several Manichaeans—whether both he and those whom he had exposed, and who he said had corrected their errors, were persevering in the Catholic faith (*Epistle* 222.2).

A fragment of records of this kind is extant, concerning the investigation and examination of Manichaeans (*Admonition to the Book on the Proceedings with Felix*, vol. 8). Felix, who had renounced that sect, binds himself by oath to denounce all whom he knew to be devoted to the same superstition. For this purpose he names two men and several women [*Col. 0524], some of whom lived in the district of Caesarea and others at Hippo Regius.

Felix’s denunciation is followed by a *Memorandum* bearing Augustine’s name and worthy of its author, in which instructions are given concerning what should be observed with regard to Manichaeans returning to the Church (*Appendix*, vol. 8).

There he orders them, above all, to submit a written statement containing their former errors. They are to ask pardon for these errors and to renounce the Manichaean sect, together with its disgraceful ravings, in the wording prescribed in the *Memorandum*. If the bishop approves their statement, he is to give those who had been merely Auditors among the Manichaeans letters dated and countersigned with the current day and consulate. In these letters he is to testify that they have taken refuge in the mercy of the Church, so that they could not be summoned either before ecclesiastical tribunals or before secular magistrates, despite having adhered until that time to a heresy punished with the utmost severity by the civil laws enacted even under Diocletian.

If they returned to their vomit, the *Memorandum* orders that the severity of the law appropriate to them be applied—that is, that the faithful abstain from their company, friendship, and every kind of Christian association.

As for the others, after they had received letters of recommendation from the bishop, it was established that they should be entrusted to certain devout men, whether clergy or laity, who lived with them or nearby. These men were to encourage them to hear the word of God more frequently and to provide testimony concerning their manner of life. Thus it could be determined when they ought to be admitted to Baptism, if they had not yet received it—for the Manichaeans appeared to regard this sacrament as superfluous—or to reconciliation, if they had been placed among the penitents. In general, neither should easily be granted to them unless the danger of death required otherwise.

With regard to the Elect, the *Memorandum* warns that the bishop should grant them testimony of repentance only with difficulty, so that they might not readily abandon the places where they had been assigned for a period of probation—namely, monasteries or hospices—where they had to remain until it was clear that Baptism or reconciliation should no longer be denied them.

### 2

There was a certain Victorinus from the sect of the Manichaeans who, under the pretense of Catholic faith, had been appointed subdeacon of the Church of Malliana in Caesarean Mauretania (*Epistle* 236.1).

He had come to Hippo, where he taught his errors to quite a few people. He opened his mind to them because he supposed that they were coming to him for the sake of learning. Once the matter became known, Augustine therefore had no difficulty convicting him. When he questioned the man about his doctrine, Victorinus—who had revealed his opinions to too many people to hope that denial would benefit him—confessed of his own accord that he was a Manichaean. He maintained, however, that he had been enrolled not among the Elect but only among the Auditors.

He even begged the holy Bishop to lead him back to the way of truth and Catholic doctrine. But Augustine was horrified by the heresy concealed in the old man under the sacred dignity of the clergy. He ordered him to be restrained and expelled from the city.

To prevent him from infecting the province of Mauretania, Augustine informed Deuterius, the metropolitan bishop of Caesarea, so that, forewarned, he might meet the danger. He instructed him to ensure that Victorinus was not granted penance until he had first exposed all the Manichaeans of Malliana—and indeed of the entire province—whom he knew. Finally, he ordered that Victorinus be avoided and deprived of his dignity, or that it be announced at Hippo that he had been deprived of it (*On the Proceedings with Emeritus* 1). At the same time, Augustine explained to Deuterius what blasphemies the Manichaean Auditors believed and what discipline they observed.

### 3

Augustine did not compose his *Enchiridion*, or *Manual*, before this year, 421, since in it Jerome is praised with the designation “of holy memory” (*Enchiridion* 23).

This work is addressed to Laurentius, the brother of Dulcitius (*On Dulcitius’s Eight Questions* 1.10). Laurentius had asked Augustine by letter to write him a book in the form of a handbook, which he could always keep in his hands. In it he wished to learn what we ought especially to embrace; what, because of the various heresies, we ought above all to avoid; in what matters reason follows and confirms faith, and in what matters it contradicts faith and ought to abandon it alone, since it is unequal to tracing its footsteps; within what limits our hope is contained; what constitutes the sum of Christian doctrine; and what is the certain and proper foundation of the Catholic faith. He greatly desired that all these matters, so numerous and difficult, should be defined for him in a few words (*Enchiridion* 1).

Saint Augustine, who took great pleasure in Laurentius’s learning and desired even more earnestly that he be joined to the truly wise, did not refuse him the instruction he requested. Since all Laurentius’s questions concerned learning what should be believed, what should be hoped for, and finally what should be loved, the holy Bishop discussed these matters in his treatise *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*. He also gave the work this title in various places, although he allowed Laurentius’s judgment to call it the *Enchiridion* if he preferred (*Retractations* II.63; *Epistle* 231; *On Dulcitius’s Eight Questions* 1).

Augustine testifies that he had carefully discussed the manner of worshiping God, which is the true wisdom of man. Regarding the question of those practices that the Church commonly performs for the dead—namely, whether they were contrary to the apostolic teaching, which Paulinus was asking him about at that time—the holy Doctor affirms that such practices benefit those for whom they are beneficial because, while alive, they had merited that they might benefit them after death, either toward a complete remission or at least toward making their damnation itself more tolerable.

### 4

After the *Enchiridion*, Augustine places the book entitled *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead* (*Retractations* II.64). Its subject was suggested by Paulinus, who had certainly always cultivated Augustine’s friendship, although for many years previously we have found no evidence of this.

It happened that a certain matron named Flora, a widow living in Africa, asked Paulinus for a place in the shrine of some saint where she might bury her son. It is quite credible that the young man had died not far from Nola. Paulinus consoled her by sending a letter, while also informing her that the matter concerning the body of the faithful young man Cynegius, whom she desired with maternal and pious affection, had been settled, so that it might be placed in the basilica of the most blessed confessor Felix.

In this basilica of Saint Felix, which Paulinus had built, there were sacred chambers or chapels intended for prayer and the burial of the dead.

When Paulinus wrote back to Flora, he took advantage of the occasion to send a letter to Augustine. In it he asked whether Augustine believed that it benefited someone after death if his body were buried near the memorial of a saint. Paulinus said that it seemed to him that the religious and faithful emotions of those who cared for these things on behalf of their dead were not empty movements. He added that what the entire Church customarily did in praying for the dead could not be without effect. From this, he thought, one might infer that it benefited a person after death if, through the faith of his relatives, a place were provided for the burial of his body in which the aid of the saints appeared to have been sought in this manner as well (*On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead* 1).

On the other hand, he said that something else raised a doubt in his mind: he did not sufficiently see how that opinion could be reconciled with the Apostle’s statement, “Each person will receive according to what he has done in the body” (II Cor. 5:10).

That modest inquiry by so eminent a bishop and so learned in the sacred Scriptures differs remarkably from the confidence of those who, because of the same difficulty, prohibited the prayers customarily offered for the spirits of those who sleep. Paulinus saw the force of the difficulty no less than they did; but the holy man thought more humbly of himself than they did. He did not dare condemn either Paul or the Church. With a tranquil mind, he waited until God should reveal the matter to him as he sought it in faith; and at last, through Augustine’s assistance, he reached the fulfillment of his desire.

Augustine long delayed answering Paulinus. Perhaps he would even have entirely forgotten this duty, so heavily was he burdened by the weight of other affairs, had the presbyter Candidianus not compelled him to undertake it without allowing any delay (*On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead* 1, 23). In that work he resolves, on the basis of Paul’s teaching, the doubt proposed to him concerning prayers for the dead (*ibid.* 2).

As for burial near the memorials of martyrs, Augustine holds that it benefits the deceased for no other reason than that the affection expressed in prayer for him may be increased by commending him also to the patronage of the martyrs (*ibid.* 22).

“When,” he says, “a faithful mother desired that the body of her faithful deceased son should be placed in the basilica of a martyr, because she believed that his soul was aided by the merits of the martyr, the very fact that she believed this was a kind of prayer; and this was beneficial, if anything was beneficial. And when she returns in spirit to that same tomb and commends her son more and more earnestly in her prayers, it is not the place of the dead body but the living affection of the mother, revived by the memory of the place, that assists the spirit of the deceased” (*ibid.* 7).

Augustine recounts visions of many of the dead and saints appearing to the living; and finally, in a remarkable manner, he sets forth what his own state of mind was in these difficulties, whose solution he had not yet received (*ibid.* 21).

### 5

As we saw above, Dulcitius was in Africa around the year 420, having been appointed to carry out the emperor’s laws against the Donatists. He was still staying there when he consulted Augustine by letters sent from Carthage concerning various questions; Augustine received them during the Easter festivities (*On Dulcitius’s Eight Questions*, Preface).

At that time the holy Doctor was entirely unable to write a response to them [*Col. 0527], because immediately after those sacred days he went to Carthage, from which he was not permitted to return to his own people until three months had elapsed. No one can doubt that he was occupied there with very serious business, although nothing is known about it except what he himself disclosed in a letter: he was so constrained by the multitude of the occupations that were never lacking for him in that city that he had absolutely no leisure to dictate anything.

After returning from there, he had to devote his mind for fifteen days to more pressing affairs, namely those of his own diocese. When these had been completed and he had obtained a little leisure, he immediately set himself to satisfying Dulcitius.

Dulcitius had asked him about eight questions concerning Scripture or ecclesiastical doctrine. With the exception of the fifth, Augustine had explained all of them in various places in his works. Therefore, in the case of the other seven, he was content to extract what he had already discussed. In this way he both satisfied Dulcitius’s most praiseworthy desire and spared himself the labor of recasting the same material from the beginning—a task that would have been burdensome to Augustine and useless to Dulcitius.

In this written work he relates a remarkably unusual story, which we shall reproduce in his own words:

“I shall tell what happened in Sitifian Mauretania. For the God of the holy Fathers is also our God. A young catechumen named Celticchius abducted a widow who was resolved upon continence, intending to have her as his wife. Before they had intercourse, overcome by sleep and terrified by a dream, he restored her untouched to the bishop of Sitifis, who had earnestly demanded her. Those of whom I speak are still alive. After he was baptized, and converted to the Lord by the miracle that had occurred in his own case, he attained the episcopate through venerable integrity; and she persevered in holy widowhood” (*On Dulcitius’s Eight Questions* 7.3).

In the letter of the Council of Carthage to Caelestine, Celticchius is named eleventh among the bishops.

The structure of this book shows that the Lord’s day of Easter fell this year on the third day before the Kalends of April. During Augustine’s episcopate, this occurred only in the years 419 and 430. No one should understand the latter year here, since the second book of the *Retractations*, in which this same treatise is reviewed, does not extend that far. We must therefore assign it to the year 419, when the holy Bishop was at Carthage at the turn of May.

But although this opinion is supported by such a plausible argument, the *Enchiridion*, cited in this same treatise, prevents us from accepting it (*ibid.* 1.10; 2.4). The *Enchiridion* could not have been written before the year 421, when Jerome is called “of holy memory” in it. Prosper reports that Jerome died only in the year 420, on the day before the Kalends of October. Augustine, moreover, still placed him among the living in September of the year 418, and we have also shown that he sent a letter to Augustine in the year 419.

Nevertheless, we must admit that an error has entered Augustine’s text and that, instead of the third day before the Kalends of April, we should read either the seventh day before the Kalends of April, on which Easter fell in the year 422, or the tenth day before the Kalends of April, on which, Bucherius asserts, certain Latins celebrated Easter in the year 425. It is likely that the Church of Hippo should be associated with those Latins [*Col. 0528].

## CHAPTER IV

1. Augustine arranges for Antonius to be ordained bishop of Fussala.  
2. He is compelled to remove the administration of that Church from him.  
3. Antonius deceives the primate of Numidia and Pope Boniface in order to be restored completely.  
4. Augustine beseeches Caelestine to allow the sentence passed against him to remain in force and to cooperate with him for the peace of the Church of Fussala.  
5. Otherwise, since he had imprudently supported Antonius’s ordination, the holy man considers resigning his own dignity.

### 1

Baronius places the death of Pope Boniface in the year 423, on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, and the election of Caelestine, his successor, on the third day before the Nones of November. But it is not easy to ascertain the truth of this matter. It seems at least equally probable that Boniface ceased to live toward the end of the year 422, while Caelestine was appointed in his place in the year 423.

This is why we place the beginning of the history of Antonius of Fussala in the year 422—a history for which it would not be easy to find another more worthy of remembrance in Augustine’s life.

Fussala was a fortified town or settlement situated on the boundary of the territory of Hippo (*Epistle* 209.2), sixteen Gallic leagues—that is, forty miles—from Hippo itself. Nevertheless, it was included within the boundaries of the diocese of Hippo, since until Augustine’s time it had never had its own bishop.

Augustine recorded several miracles that occurred in this place while he governed it and after the conversion of Maximinus of Siniti—that is, after the year 405 (*City of God* XXII.8.6).

There was a numerous population at Fussala and in the neighboring places, but through a most miserable misfortune all of it had rushed headlong into schism (*Epistle* 209.2). Only a few Catholics remained in its territory; in the town itself, not even one. The first presbyters whom Augustine appointed there were stripped of their possessions, beaten, maimed, blinded, and even murdered. Yet their sufferings were not useless or fruitless. After countless labors and dangers, finally, through the inspiration of divine mercy, no place in that region failed to return to peace with the Church, and the few Donatists who remained were now thinking not of harassing others but of concealing themselves.

The holy Bishop of Hippo, who had brought forth others through his own fears and sorrows, desired to win these people also for Christ the Lord (*ibid.* 4).

When he therefore understood that, because of the remoteness of the place, he could not devote as much care to this matter as was necessary, he resolved to arrange for a bishop to be established there, without considering any diminution of his own dignity, which would be reduced by cutting away that portion of his jurisdiction (*ibid.* 2).

He therefore sought someone suitable for the office, for whose discharge knowledge of the Punic language was necessary or at least useful [*Col. 0529] (*ibid.* 3). For this purpose he designated from his own clergy a presbyter who seemed ready for the task.

He then wrote to the primate of the province of Numidia—who at that time, unless we are mistaken, was Silvanus of Summa—whose see was far distant from Hippo Regius, asking him to undertake this ordination.

When the primate arrived, all the arrangements having already been made, the presbyter whom the holy man had designated for this episcopate absolutely refused to accept him. Subsequent events showed that it would have been better to postpone a matter of such importance to another time than to rush it. But Augustine then thought that, having summoned so venerable and holy an old man from so great a distance, he could not send him away with nothing accomplished.

Therefore, he offered the people of Fussala—who had not requested one—a young man named Antonius, whom he then had with him. This may have taken place at Fussala. Augustine had raised Antonius from childhood, but his age was not yet sufficiently mature and his character had not been sufficiently tested (*ibid.* 9), since Augustine had examined him in no clerical office except that of lector (*ibid.* 3).

Nevertheless, the people of Fussala welcomed him with open arms when their Bishop proposed him, being as ignorant as he was of what would later happen. In this way Antonius was ordained and placed in the episcopal see.

We do not know when this ordination took place, although it does not seem unreasonable to place it after the Council of Carthage, in which Antonius’s name is not found. It is thought that he was named among the last bishops at the Council of Milevis, held in the year 416; if so, Silvanus of Summa must necessarily have laid hands upon him.

### 2

This caused Augustine’s heart an even sharper grief because, while he had wished to provide for those whom he regarded as his children, he had instead unwillingly inflicted the greatest injuries upon them.

He denies that he wishes to expose the life of Antonius, whom he had raised; yet he admits that Antonius’s conduct had produced such serious offenses that an inquiry into it necessarily had to be instituted (*ibid.* 4).

He was accused by men outside his own diocese of capital crimes and adulteries. The people of Fussala, however, accused him of intolerable domination, plundering, and many acts committed by force. They declared that they could not be induced to endure his authority any longer; and no one doubted that they were stung by just indignation (*ibid.* 5).

Nevertheless, since the more serious crimes of which he was accused could not be proved, this circumstance obtained for him only so much mercy that the other offenses, which had been detected and clearly established, aroused less indignation and did not appear all together to deserve his abdication.

He was therefore condemned only to restore everything he had taken from the people of Fussala, and he was deprived of communion until he had satisfied them (*ibid.* 4). Since Antonius consented to this sentence, the honor of the episcopate was left intact for him (*ibid.* 6), in the hope, namely, that since he had not yet passed beyond youth, he might be able to improve (*ibid.* 5).

It should also be observed that the question of permitting him to administer his own Church was considered in the trial, and this matter was presented to the representatives of Fussala. They, however, protested vehemently, declaring that they would sooner descend to every extreme than allow this to happen—namely, either return to their former schism or perhaps even kill Antonius himself.

Celer, a distinguished man whom Antonius claimed was hostile to him and had incited others against him by his power, held no office at that time. It was therefore clear that the alienation of the people of Fussala from Antonius did not originate in Celer’s instigation.

It was consequently necessary to remove from Antonius the administration of his diocese, while granting him permission to live there, lest, if he were sent elsewhere, he be said to have been unlawfully transferred to another’s see contrary to the statutes of the councils (*ibid.* 7).

Whatever was decreed in that trial was entered simultaneously into the records. No one doubts that this was customary throughout Africa at that time.

Augustine admits that the judgment might appear less rigorously framed than exact severity would require, and he testifies that the matter was handled there with excessive leniency. He does not say, however, whether another bishop was meanwhile appointed at Fussala or whether Antonius returned to his administration.

The latter possibility is less inconsistent with the evidence, if it is not regarded as entirely certain. Since the episcopal honor was preserved for Antonius in his own see, if they had introduced another bishop there, the Church would have become two-headed.

Add to this that, toward the end of his life, Augustine commended a certain presbyter of Fussala in these words: “For we cannot abandon the needs of people of this kind, who are not our colonists but, what is more, our brothers, and who in the charity of Christ belong to our care” (*Epistle* 224.1, 3).

This in no way prevents another bishop from having been appointed there after Antonius’s death. For from the *Notitia of Africa* we learn that a bishop named Melior held the see of Fussala.

### 3

When the trial had ended, the amount Antonius ought to repay to the people of Fussala was assessed, and he deposited that money in order to obtain communion.

As for the other part of the penalty imposed upon him, the very indulgence that had been shown toward him supplied him with a pretext for arranging that it be rescinded by the Apostolic See. He claimed, namely, that if he had been found guilty, he ought to have been compelled to resign the episcopate; since this had not happened, it was an argument that he could not justly have been deprived of his see (*Epistle* 209.7).

He therefore approached the primate, perhaps Valentinus of Baia, who had succeeded Silvanus of Summa in that dignity. Although this holy and venerable old man possessed authority, Antonius nevertheless imposed upon him by his own cunning, and perhaps also by false and altered records. Thus the primate believed everything Antonius said and commended him to Pope Boniface as entirely free from blame (*ibid.* 6).

Boniface judged in Antonius’s favor and wrote to Africa that he should be restored to his rights, provided that he had sincerely disclosed the state of affairs in his written petition (*ibid.* 9).

The people of Fussala were now threatened with nothing less than the power of imperial judges and magistrates; indeed, a military force was to be employed to compel those wretched people to obey the judgment of the Apostolic See. Thus the unfortunate population, while within the Catholic Church, feared from a Catholic bishop cruelties worse than those they had feared in schism from the authority of the laws of a Catholic emperor.

### 4

In the meantime, after Boniface had been removed from human affairs, the people of Fussala implored the assistance of Caelestine, who had succeeded him. They besought him by the mercy of Christ to rescue them from the evils Antonius was inflicting upon them or threatening to inflict upon them (*Epistle* 209).

They also complained about Augustine, from whom they had received such a bishop. The holy Bishop humbly and modestly acknowledged that they had done so with justice.

Accordingly, he was not angered by them; rather, he presented himself to Pope Caelestine as an advocate of their requests. He sent him the outstanding letter on this subject that we still possess (*ibid.*), which, according to the order we have adopted, should be placed in this year, 423.

It also appears that the primate himself understood the deception by which Antonius had misled him, since he arranged for all the records and documents relating to this case to be conveyed to Caelestine.

In his letter to that same pontiff, Augustine first congratulates him on having been raised to the summit of apostolic dignity without disturbances or any division. He then explains how deeply Antonius’s case afflicted him.

Next, after relating the entire history of the affair, he begs the Pope to read and weigh the documents sent to him by the primate. He asks him to sympathize with his distress, to free the Church of Fussala from the man by whom it was being miserably harassed, and thereby to earn a good name both with this people and with Antonius himself: he should prevent Antonius from inflicting enormous evils and prevent the people from suffering the same, while also forestalling the crimes that would follow Antonius’s restoration.

By the blood of Christ and by the memory of the Apostle Peter, who warned the rulers of Christian peoples not to lord it over their brothers by force (I Pet. 5:3), Augustine beseeches Caelestine not to allow the people of Fussala to be compelled by force to obey Antonius (*Epistle* 209.9).

For it appears that in those times clerics from Rome were sent by the Apostolic See—or at least requested by the prayers of those whose interests were involved—to Africa as executors of its judgments (*African Code of Canons*, canon 138). They were doubtless instructed to invoke the assistance of the civil authorities whenever circumstances required it.

Augustine never mentions Antonius except with the greatest moderation and as his son. Yet the more ardently he loved him, the more firmly he resisted Antonius’s desire to be restored.

### 5.

He openly admits everywhere what an imprudent fault he had committed by enrolling Antonius among the bishops; but how far could the humility and repentance of the holy man have gone beyond this? “For my own part,” he says, “as I must confess to Your Beatitude, amid the danger threatening us both, such fear and grief torment me that I am considering withdrawing from the duty of exercising the episcopate and giving myself over to laments befitting my error, if I should see the Church of God laid waste through the man whose episcopate I imprudently supported—and, may God Himself avert it—even perish together with the destruction of its destroyer. For, remembering what the Apostle says, ‘If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord’ (1 Cor. 11:31), I shall judge myself, so that He who will judge the living and the dead may spare me. But if you restore the members of Christ who are in that region from their deadly fear and grief, and if by this merciful justice you console my old age, He who through you comes to our aid in this tribulation, and who established you in that see, will repay you both in the present life and in the life to come, good for good” (Epistle 209, §10).

Without doubt, Celestine was deeply moved by that most forceful letter and was entirely unwilling to deprive the Church of a bishop whose teaching and reputation he had defended, as its most illustrious patron. Therefore, since Augustine presided over the Church of Hippo until his final breath and also governed Fussala in the year 427 or 428, it is inferred that Celestine consented to Antonius’s remaining deprived of the administration of that see. This is further confirmed by the same pontiff’s love and veneration for Augustine after the latter’s death.

Yet even if Augustine had received a refusal from the Pope in this most equitable petition, he would nevertheless have been entitled to vindicate himself against that injustice by relying on the declaration in which the African Fathers stated that they no longer wished to tolerate even African bishops appealing thereafter to the Roman See (Code of the African Canons, canon 138).

## CHAPTER V

1. The relics of the martyr Stephen are received at Hippo around the year of Christ 424.  
2. Januarius, a presbyter of Hippo, dies, leaving to the Church the money he had retained contrary to the rule of common life.  
3. Augustine preaches to the people on this matter; he rejects Januarius’s inheritance and leaves it to his children, and declares that he allows clerics who wish to possess something of their own to preserve the dignity of their order while living outside the episcopal residence.  
4. In a later sermon he testifies that all his clerics wish to remain committed to the rule of common life and reject private property, and that those who retained anything for themselves were to be removed from the list of clerics; he also clears before the same people those who were reputed rich and possessed of money.  
5. The horrible punishment of ten children against whom their mother had pronounced a curse.  
6. Of those ten, Paul is divinely healed at Hippo.  
7. Palladia is healed there on another day.  
8. Augustine commends Galla and Simpliciola to Quintilian.

### 1.

Not yet two years had passed since Augustine had obtained the relics of the martyr Stephen at Hippo when he was laboring over the final book of *The City of God*, which, as we stated above, was completed in the course of the year 426 (above, Book 7, chapter 4, §4) (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §20). Accordingly, he could not have acquired those sacred relics earlier than, at the very least, the end of the year 424.

It would not be far from the truth to suppose that the fourth sermon on Saint Stephen (*Sermon* 317) was delivered when the relics were received, and the fifth on the same martyr (*Sermon* 318) before they were placed beneath the altar. For the holy Bishop deposited this venerable pledge in a sacred chamber of one of his churches, what we call a chapel; and he ordered four verses to be carved in its vault, so that all the faithful might thereby be reminded that the extraordinary miracles performed at that time through the prayers and relics of Saint Stephen ought to be attributed to God Himself (*Sermon* 319, §7).

To publish these same miracles, Augustine was the first in Africa to introduce the practice that those for whose benefit they had been performed should present and attest them by having a written account read before all the people (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §20). Within two years, nearly seventy such accounts were produced at Hippo, and he ordered one of them to be read on the day when he delivered his sixth sermon on the martyr Stephen (*Sermon* 319).

Among all the miracles performed at Hippo during the first two years after the relics of the blessed Protomartyr had been brought there, Augustine names only three dead persons who were restored to life (*ibid.*, §§17–19), adding the healings of Paul and Palladia (*ibid.*, §22), which we shall mention in the following year.

Now, if we suppose that the relics in question were brought to Hippo in this very year, 424, nothing prevents us from interpreting as referring to the little shrine where they were kept what the holy Bishop says in his second sermon on the life and conduct of his clerics, delivered around the beginning of 425, not long after Epiphany (*Sermon* 355, §7): namely, that a memorial of Saint Stephen had been constructed through the labor and money of the deacon Heraclius (*Sermon* 356, §7).

But if the relics of Saint Stephen reached Hippo only in 425, it would be more difficult to call the little shrine erected by Heraclius a shrine dedicated to Stephen. For in that case the sermon in which those relics are mentioned could not have been delivered before the beginning of the year after 426. Yet Heraclius, who at that time was distinguished only by the office of deacon, was afterward raised to the rank of presbyter (*Epistle* 213), and then, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October in the year 426, was designated by Augustine as his successor, while in the meantime he was to administer and manage the affairs of the Church of Hippo.

### 2.

Whatever the precise circumstances, it is entirely clear that the holy Bishop was advanced in years and completely gray-haired when he delivered those two celebrated sermons on the life of his clerics to the people of Hippo (*Sermon* 355, §7; *Sermon* 356, §§7, 13). The occasion was as follows.

We have seen that at the beginning of Augustine’s episcopate that most holy man gathered all his clerics into the episcopal residence, where, after renouncing ownership of every kind of property, he lived with them in perfect common possession of all goods (*Sermon* 355, §§1–2). He did not lay hands on anyone for the clerical office unless on the condition that the man would follow this common life with him (*ibid.*, §6); and it appears that he explicitly declared this before the entire people.

He was satisfied that all his clerics knew this to be the manner of life they were obliged to embrace in his household (*ibid.*, §2). As for actual practice, however, he preferred to leave the matter to their consciences rather than investigate too scrupulously whether they possessed absolutely nothing, because such an inquiry would carry an unpleasant appearance of suspicion.

Nevertheless, a certain presbyter named Januarius imposed upon him. Januarius came to him, promised to live the common life, lived with him, and was supported from the resources of the Church. He had two children, a son and a daughter, whom Augustine placed in the monasteries at Hippo to be raised—the boy among the men and the girl among the women. He was thought to have renounced every possession and to have arranged his property in the manner appropriate to a man of his profession. Yet it was not unknown that he had reserved a certain sum of money; he declared that it belonged to his daughter.

Since the girl had not yet passed beyond childhood, and nothing certain could be decided concerning her inclination toward the celibate life—although she apparently was already bound to it by some commitment—no one was permitted to interpret the matter unfavorably if her father kept what he repeatedly said was hers, until, once she was grown, she might use it in a manner befitting a virgin of Christ, when she was fully able to do so.

Meanwhile Januarius fell ill. In his will he made provision concerning this money as though it were his own; he disinherited his son with reproach and his daughter with praise, and died, leaving the inheritance of his property to the Church of Hippo (*ibid.*, §3).

When Augustine discovered this fraud committed by a presbyter of his community, he felt deep grief. He detested the act because, besides harming Januarius’s salvation, it also caused offense and scandal to the Church and entirely extinguished the good reputation that the clerics themselves spread among the people (*Sermon* 356, §2).

Accordingly, Augustine, who was accustomed to reject inheritances that parents wished to leave to the Church after disinheriting their children, could not be induced to accept this one (*Sermon* 355, §4). “Let what he left belong to his children,” he said; “let them do with it whatever they wish. For it seems to me that if I accept it, I shall become a participant in this action, which displeases me and causes me grief” (*ibid.*, §3).

### 3.

Having thus satisfied his conscience, Augustine considered it his duty to clear his own reputation before the people among whom he lived and whose eyes were upon him, and to explain his conduct publicly, lest anyone seize upon it as an occasion for error.

He therefore asked the people to assemble in greater numbers on the following day. When they had all gathered, he addressed them in a thoroughly simple and familiar sermon, but one especially suited to moving their hearts.
