He set before them the rule of life that he had always resolved to maintain with his clergy; he also set forth Januarius’s fault and his own decision to prevent the Church from accepting the inheritance in question. Then he added the reasons that had persuaded him to resolve to reject other inheritances as well, although some people might disapprove of and criticize this prudent and generous decision (*Sermon* 355, §1).

Afterward he declared that he had ordered all his clerics who still appeared to possess something of their own—for example, those who had not yet divided their father’s property with their brothers, or who had not yet reached the age at which they were permitted to dispose of it—to sell and distribute all their possessions, or to give and transfer them to the common fund, if they wished to remain in his household. He had ordered this to be done before Epiphany, a feast that perhaps would not be celebrated for several months (*ibid.*, §6).

Previously he had established this rule: anyone who wished to depart from the common life was to resign his clerical office, because he would be abandoning the promise and fellowship of the holy community that he had begun. But now he declared that he had resolved to alter that rule. Accordingly, if any cleric preferred to possess something of his own rather than be content with God and the Church, he could retain his rank while living wherever he wished outside the episcopal residence.

Augustine acknowledged that this was an evil, a falling away from the rule, an abandonment of the holy profession, and a violation of one’s vow—just as if a virgin were to leave the monastery she had entered while continuing to practice virginity. But hypocrisy seemed to him far worse. He therefore did not wish to force such men into a necessity by which they would be utterly ruined through continual pretense, nor to give them cause to continue disturbing the Church with complaints over the loss of their clerical office—complaints that some bishops might perhaps not consider unjust. “I would rather have the lame than mourn the dead” (*Sermon* 356, §14).

It was enough, then, that he had set before them how great a danger and evil it was to fall away from the rule; afterward he left them to the divine judgment. He promised them preservation in their clerical office; it was for them to consider whether they could hope for eternal blessedness.

He ended his address by promising the people that after Epiphany he would report to them what he had decided concerning his clerics, from whose service he expected everything, and what he had decided concerning the children of Januarius, to whom their unhappy father had left, besides other troubles, a lawsuit.

The sister claimed that whatever had been left by their father belonged to her, as he himself had so often affirmed; but the brother relied upon their father’s will, which had instructed what was to be done with the money as his own, not as a deposit belonging to his daughter.

The holy Bishop, acting as their common father, resolved to settle the dispute and to take with him a reputable layman so that they might judge it together according to the rule of equity (*Sermon* 355, §3). The children, however, spared him this labor: they settled the matter amicably and followed the blessed man’s advice that they divide the money between them (*Sermon* 356, §11).

Nor did Augustine’s own clerics cause him any greater trouble. He found all his presbyters, deacons, subdeacons, and, among these, his nephew Patricius, as he wished them to be—that is, every one of them poor in spirit and intention (*ibid.*, §3).

For if anyone was permitted to retain anything, he retained it from a religious and charitable necessity, for the sake of others, not for his own, and without any inclination toward greed. Accordingly, they all embraced the common life anew and gladly received the holy man’s decision to remove from the list of clerics anyone thereafter discovered to possess property of his own (*ibid.*, §14).

### 4.

After the feast of Epiphany had passed, Augustine reported these welcome tidings to the people, as he had promised. He understood that, since his conduct was exposed both to the praise of some and to the accusations of others, those who loved him should not be covered with shame by those who did not love him.

First, then, he ordered the deacon Lazarus to read from the Acts of the Apostles the passage describing the life of the first Christians, a life according to which he intended to shape the conduct of his clergy; he himself also recited the passage.

Then he gave an account, one by one, of all his clerics: both those who for legitimate reasons had not yet been able entirely to renounce their possessions and those who were falsely said to possess property of their own.

Having done this, he revoked the permission he had granted them to live outside the episcopal residence while retaining private property. He declared that, since they had all agreed to the common life, anyone found possessing property of his own would be deprived by him of his clerical rank.

“Let him appeal against me,” said the holy man, “to a thousand councils; let him sail against me wherever he wishes; let him certainly be wherever he can. God will help me, so that where I am bishop, he cannot be a cleric. You have heard; they have heard. But I hope in our God and in His mercy that, just as they received this decision of mine gladly, so they will preserve it purely and faithfully” (*ibid.*).

He also mentioned the agreement reached between Januarius’s children. Afterward he added that he hoped those who loved him would boldly testify to their joy, while the others would suppress their grief in silence. But if there were any who wished to mutter or quibble against him, he would refute them publicly if the circumstances seemed to require it (*ibid.*, §11).

“I wish our life,” he said, “to be before your eyes. I know that those who seek permission to do evil seek examples of people living badly, and defame many so that they may appear to have found companions. Therefore we have done what is ours to do; we have no more that we can do. We are before your eyes. We desire nothing from anyone except your good works” (*ibid.*, §12).

From this sermon one can learn what condition most of his clerics were in, for he speaks only of those in whom something seemed worthy of reproach.

As for his presbyters, therefore, he asserts only that, whatever the people might commonly boast concerning their possessions, they were poor and had brought nothing with them into his community except charity itself, which is more precious than anything.

The subdeacons likewise were poor. “By God’s favor,” he says, “they await the mercy of God. They have nothing from which to make a living; possessing no resources, they have ended their desires for the world. They live with us in the common fellowship, and no one distinguishes them from those who brought something with them. The unity of charity must be placed before the earthly advantage of inheritance” (*Sermon* 356, §8).

If any of the deacons had perhaps come under suspicion of abandoning the rule in order to possess private property, Augustine removed that accusation by clearing each of them by name.

Finally, he ended his address with these words:

“Let no one tear apart the servants of God, for it is not profitable to those who tear them apart. The reward of God’s servants increases through false accusations, but the punishment of their accusers increases as well. We do not wish to have a great reward at your expense. Let us have less of it there, and yet reign there with you” (*ibid.*, §15).

### 5.

The healings of Paul and Palladia were divinely granted in this same year. This miracle was not greater than the others that occurred at Hippo at that time through the relics of the martyr Stephen (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §20, in the note beginning “Hence”), but it was so clear and renowned that no one in that city could be found who had not seen or learned of it, and no one could in any way forget it (*ibid.*, §22).

At Caesarea in Cappadocia there was a family of no low standing, consisting of ten children—seven boys and three girls. Among them, Paul claimed the sixth place and Palladia the seventh.

After their father’s death, only a few days later, while all the brothers were still at home, the eldest son inflicted grave and intolerable injuries upon his widowed mother, to the point that he did not hesitate even to strike her. Meanwhile none of the other children took care either to oppose that impiety or even to restrain their brother’s madness with a word.

The unhappy woman endured this atrocious injury with the greatest bitterness. Inflamed by those movements of anger so familiar to that sex, she resolved to avenge her grief upon her firstborn by pronouncing dreadful curses against him.

“When she was hurrying to the font of holy Baptism,” Paul says in the written account of his healing, “after the cockcrow, intending to invoke God’s wrath against her aforesaid son, then some demon, apparently in the likeness of our uncle, met her and first asked her where she was going. She replied that she was going to curse her son because of the intolerable insult. Then that enemy, since he could easily find a place in the woman’s maddened heart, persuaded her to curse them all. Inflamed by those viperous counsels, she threw herself before the sacred font, and with her hair loosened and her breasts uncovered, asked God above all that, banished from our homeland and wandering through foreign lands, we might terrify the whole human race by our example” (*Sermon* 322).

God heard the prayer suggested by her grief, and, although it was wicked, He allowed Himself to be entreated by it. For since He is just in every respect, His judgment could regard as just nothing other than punishing children guilty of impiety toward their mother.

The eldest son was immediately seized by a horrible trembling, so that even in sleep his limbs were shaken. Then, in the order in which they had been born, all the other brothers and sisters were afflicted by the same punishment within one year (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §22).

The wretched and accursed mother was punished all the more severely because she saw herself answered so promptly and completely. Unable to endure either the consciousness of her impiety or human disgrace any longer, she tightened a noose around her throat and brought her sorrowful life to a more terrible end (*Sermon* 322).

Thus one family taught children the honor and obedience they owed their parents, and warned parents not to forget their own dignity or allow themselves to be carried away against their children by a burst of anger.

Unable to endure the sight of their fellow citizens while in that mournful condition, the children left their homeland and departed in different directions, wherever each wished. In this way they wandered through almost the entire Roman world, displaying their misery before everyone’s eyes (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §22), and deterring the proud by the example of their punishment (*Sermon* 323, §1).

The second of the brothers recovered his health at Ravenna through the help of the relics of Saint Lawrence, which had recently been placed there.

Paul and Palladia set out to visit every place where miracles were said to occur, with a great desire to regain their health. As a result, they became famous in various regions because of their misery.

Among other cities, they visited Ancona in Italy and Uzalis in Africa, both renowned because of the miracles of blessed Stephen. Nevertheless, in neither place could they be restored to their former condition—or rather, God, who could easily have granted this, did not wish to do so, reserving the healing of both for Hippo-Regius to witness.

He therefore made this known to them through a clear vision on the very day of the Kalends of January, a vision that occurred three months before the event. “A certain man,” Paul testifies while addressing Augustine, “bright in appearance and venerable with white hair, said to me that within three months the health I desired would come to me.

“Your Holiness appeared to my sister in the form in which we now see you in person. By this it was signified to us that we ought to come to this place. Indeed, afterward, as we traveled through other cities on the road by which we were coming, I often saw Your Beatitude exactly as I see you now.

“Thus, warned by evident divine authority, we came to this city about fifteen days ago” (*Sermon* 322)—that is, approximately on the eighth day before the Ides of March.

Here they attended the church and the memorial of Saint Stephen every day, praying to God with poured-out tears that He might forgive their sin and restore the health they desired. Both there and wherever they went, they drew the eyes of the city upon themselves. Some who had seen them elsewhere and knew the cause of their trembling explained it to others as best they could (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §22).

### 6.

Easter arrived. On the morning of that Sunday, when a large crowd was already present and the same young man was praying while holding the railings of the holy place where the martyr’s shrine was located, he suddenly fell forward and lay there looking like someone asleep; yet he was not trembling, as he often did even in sleep.

Those present were astonished; some were frightened and others grieved. When certain people wished to lift him up, others prevented them, saying that they should rather wait for the outcome (*ibid.*).

He himself, deprived of consciousness, did not know where he had been. But when he rose a little later, he realized that he had been freed from that agitation and was completely healed (*Sermon* 322).

“He stood unharmed,” Augustine says, “looking at those who were looking at him. Who, then, could restrain himself from praising God? The church was filled everywhere with the voices of those crying out and rejoicing: ‘Thanks be to God! Praise be to God!’ No one was silent; cries came from every side.

“They ran from there to me, where I was already sitting, preparing to go out. One after another rushed in, each later arrival announcing as though it were something new what the earlier one had reported. While I rejoiced and gave thanks to God within myself, he himself also entered with several others, bowed at my knees, and rose to kiss me.

“We went out to the people. The church was full and resounded with joyful cries: ‘Thanks be to God! Praise be to God!’ No one was silent; they were shouting on every side. I greeted the people, and again they shouted in the same words, but with a more fervent voice.

“At last silence was made, and the appointed readings from the divine Scriptures were read. When the time came for my sermon, I said a few words, suited to the occasion and to their joyful happiness. For I allowed them to contemplate, rather than hear, a certain eloquence of God in His work” (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §22).

We still possess the brief address that he delivered on this event (*Sermon* 320), or at least an abridgment of that address; for it is difficult to believe that he restrained himself from saying more.

Nevertheless, he excuses the brevity of his sermon and gives as its reason his own exhaustion and the magnitude of the labor of the preceding day. He says that he would not have been equal to enduring it, weakened as he was by fasting, had the assistance of the prayers of Saint Stephen not supported him. Indeed, Paulinus observed (*Life of Saint Ambrose*, §38) that, on the Saturday when Saint Ambrose passed to heaven, scarcely five bishops sufficed for the baptismal ceremonies, which Ambrose himself had customarily performed alone.

Paul’s presence close beside Augustine can also be understood from this sermon. Augustine displayed him to the people and said that his presence took the place of the written accounts that others supplied to publicize benefits obtained through the prayers of blessed Stephen.

Indeed, it appears that Augustine, satisfied with this, would never have requested a written account from Paul (*Sermon* 321). But after bringing him home to dinner and ordering him to relate carefully the whole history of his own, his mother’s, and his brother’s calamity, Augustine considered that it ought to be presented to the people, so that they might perceive divine providence more clearly and proclaim it as marvelous in the memorials of His saints.

Accordingly, on the following day, after speaking in his usual manner, he delivered the brief address that still survives. In it he promised that he would arrange for this narrative to be written down and read on the next day (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §22).

### 7.

On the Tuesday after Easter, Augustine mounted the platform from which he addressed his people. He ordered Paul and his sister Palladia, who had not yet recovered her health, to climb the steps of the same platform, after first obtaining the people’s consent in a certain manner, so that they might be exposed to everyone’s gaze.

“The entire people,” says the holy man, “men and women alike, looked upon one standing without any disfiguring movement and the other trembling in all her limbs. Those who had not seen him could see in his sister what divine mercy had done in him. They saw in him what was cause for rejoicing and in her what called for prayer” (*ibid.*).

Paul’s written account was then read. He concluded it by asking them to implore divine kindness on behalf of his sister and to offer and return thanksgiving on his own behalf.

After the reading, the holy Bishop dismissed both of them from the steps. Palladia went to pray at the memorial of the martyr in question. Augustine, however, began to teach the people what was appropriate to the things they had just read and heard. He first testified that he hoped the remaining brothers would be restored to the health that Paul already enjoyed (*Sermon* 323, §1).

Paul had stated in his account that the blessed Bishop had frequently appeared to him. Augustine seriously forbade this from being turned to his own honor:

“What are we,” he said, “that I should have appeared to them without knowing it? They saw me, and I did not know it; and they were instructed to come to this city. Who am I? I am one human being among many, not one of the great ones” (*ibid.*, §2).

He had begun to speak about the miracles performed at Ancona and Uzalis through the relics of the same holy martyr, when suddenly a shout arose from the memorial, repeated again and again: “Thanks be to God! Praise be to Christ!” (*ibid.*, §4).

Those acclamations had been provoked by Palladia’s healing. She had scarcely approached the railings enclosing the memorial when, like her brother, she collapsed onto the ground as though asleep, and soon rose fully restored to health (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §22).

Those who had witnessed the miracle immediately began with loud applause to cry out their thanks to God. The people who had been listening to Augustine rushed there. While the holy man was asking what had happened, the girl was brought into the basilica and to the platform from which he had been speaking (*Sermon* 323, §4).

“Then,” he says, “such a cry of astonishment arose from both sexes that the continuous voice, mingled with tears, seemed unable to end. She was led to the place where a short while before she had stood trembling. They rejoiced to see her like her brother, whereas they had grieved that she remained unlike him; and although they had not yet poured out their prayers for her, they saw that their prior wish had been answered so quickly.

“They rejoiced in praise of God with a sound without words, with such a volume that our ears could scarcely endure it. What was in the hearts of those rejoicing except faith in Christ, for which Stephen’s blood was shed?” (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §22).

When the uproar had subsided, the holy Doctor added nothing more than a few words commending the mercy of God, who had heard even the mere desire of their hearts to pray.

On the following day he continued, as he had done the day before, to inquire why God had wished this miracle to occur at Hippo rather than at Ancona or Uzalis (*Sermon* 324). Yet what survives from that same sermon contains only an account of the famous miracle performed at Uzalis upon an infant who died before receiving Baptism. From this one may infer that the sermon has not come down to us complete.

### 8.

Perhaps in this same year, after Augustine had nourished Galla, who had professed widowhood, and her daughter Simpliciola, who had vowed her virginity to Christ, for some time with the food of divine eloquence, he dismissed them to their homeland and commended them by letter to Quintilian, who exercised the episcopal office there.

“They carried with them relics of the aforementioned martyr. ‘Your Holiness,’ he writes to Quintilian, ‘knows, just as we do, how appropriately you ought to honor them’” (*Epistle* 212).

Not long after this time, he also went to Uzalis, where he induced the illustrious woman Petronia to explain in writing the miracle that the same Stephen had performed on her behalf; and he encouraged Evodius to require the same from those who had been healed in the same manner (*The City of God*, Book 22, chapter 8, §21).

## CHAPTER VI

1. The death of Severus, bishop of Milevis.  
2. Concerning the presbyter Heraclius.  
3. Augustine transfers the administration of affairs to the man designated as his successor.  
4. Disputes among the monks of Hadrumetum concerning grace and free will.  
5. Defenders of free will against grace approach Augustine; he instructs them and gives them, together with two letters, the book *On Grace and Free Will*, addressed to Valentinus and the monks with him.  
6. The holy Doctor sends them another book, *On Rebuke and Grace*.

### 1.

Severus, bishop of Milevis, a friend and close associate of Augustine, departed this life at the beginning of the year 426 (*Epistle* 213, §1).

Before his death he had designated the man whom he wished to succeed him. But, since he had not additionally presented the matter to the people, as was proper, he considered it sufficient to have appointed him before his own clerics.

This omission caused them, after his death, to fear that disturbances might arise among the people. Accordingly, the brothers—by which we may reasonably understand the clerics and, above all, the servants of God, that is, the monks—asked Augustine to go there to secure the peace.

Divine mercy favored him. Although some displayed a certain resentment because Severus had not shared this plan with them, that cloud of sadness soon gave way to the clear sky of joy. As soon as they learned who had been designated as their future bishop, they accepted him willingly and gladly. In this way he was consecrated peacefully and with everyone’s consent.

This event led Augustine to reflect again upon the disturbances that he had often observed, not without grief, arising in other Churches after the deaths of bishops—disturbances provoked in some cases by the bishops’ ambition and in others by their successors’ natural inclination toward contention.

Therefore, judging that, having been born more than seventy-two years earlier, he could not prolong his life much further, he resolved to provide for the security of his own Church and, for that reason, to designate his successor.

The Church had sometimes prohibited this. Yet in matters of this kind, which in themselves are reckoned neither among good things nor among evil things, the same Church can sometimes permit and sometimes prohibit the practice, according to what it judges more advantageous.

At that time, however, the prohibition against appointing one’s own successor certainly did not prevail in Africa. Saint Augustine himself designated his successor, and he approved the same action in the case of Severus. There is no doubt that he was led to do this neither by ambition nor by concern for his own advantage, but that he had before his eyes solely the welfare of the Church.

Accordingly, when he returned to Milevis on Saturday, the seventh day before the Kalends of October in the year 426, he asked the people to assemble the following day in as great a number as possible, since they were to hear something of the greatest importance.

## 2

Accordingly, on Sunday, the sixth day before the Kalends of the same month, a numerous congregation gathered in the Basilica of Peace of Hippo Regius. Augustine also came, accompanied by the two bishops Religianus and Martinianus, seven presbyters, and the rest of the clergy (ibid.). As was his custom, he delivered no sermon, being certain that, because of their impatience to learn what he had promised to report, the people could not turn their attention to anything else.

Therefore, after briefly explaining how necessary it was for him to safeguard the peace of his congregation, he declared that, in order to avoid the difficulty that had arisen at Milevis and to leave no one any occasion for complaint, he wished to make known his decision. He believed it also consonant with the divine will: namely, that the presbyter Heraclius should succeed him in the episcopate. Immediately everyone expressed agreement with applause and acclamation.

Eraclius—or Heraclius, as he is sometimes called—is named last among the seven presbyters who were present with the holy Bishop at that assembly; from this one may infer that he was not among the older men. Certainly he was still young and at that time held only the office of deacon (ibid., no. 5), when Augustine delivered his Sermons on the Life and Conduct of His Clergy (Sermon 356, no. 7). Yet even then his life shone forth so conspicuously that it gave joy to the holy Prelate. Augustine had no need to say anything in his commendation to a people who knew him well and would have preferred him to everyone else; nor did he wish, by praising his wisdom, to injure his modesty (Epistle 213, no. 2).

Even while he was still a deacon, Heraclius’s works shone before the eyes of the entire people. It appears that he had received a very substantial paternal inheritance. Part of it he had spent, as we have seen above, on establishing a memorial to the Martyr—that is, Saint Stephen—and he had wished to entrust the remainder to Augustine for distribution as Augustine judged best.

Indeed, if the holy Prelate had been led by any desire for money and had considered nothing except the needs of the poor entrusted to his care, he would not have rejected such a gift. But since he was extremely concerned for his reputation—not for his own sake, but for the sake of the people committed to him, for his own conscience was sufficient for him—he advised Heraclius to purchase an estate with the money. Heraclius followed this advice and donated the property to the Church.

Yet the Saint had another matter in view as well:

> “For I confess to you,” he said to the people, “that I was still suspicious of his age; and I feared that perhaps, as people are, his mother might be displeased by this and say that I had induced the young man to squander his paternal goods and leave him destitute. Therefore I wished his money to be preserved in that property, so that, if something happened otherwise than we wished—God forbid—the estate could be returned, and the bishop’s reputation would not be blamed. For I know how necessary my reputation is to you; my conscience is sufficient for me.

> “He also purchased a plot of land,” Augustine continued, “from this Church afterward—you know of it—and built a house with his own money; you know this too. A few days ago, before I spoke with you about this matter, he donated it to the Church. He was waiting to complete it and then donate it when finished.

> “He had no need to build a house except that he thought his mother would come here. If she had come, she would have lived in her son’s property; if she comes now, she will live in her son’s work. I bear witness for him: he remained poor, but he remained in possession of charity.

> “Some little servants had been left to him. They are now living in the monastery, but today he will set them free through the ecclesiastical records. Let no one therefore say, ‘He is rich’; let no one suppose it; let no one speak ill; let no one tear himself or his own soul to pieces with his own teeth. He has no money kept in reserve—if only he may restore what he owes!” (Sermon 356, no. 7).

## 3

Augustine gave this testimony before the people of Hippo concerning Heraclius’s preserved holy purpose while Heraclius was still among the deacons. Without doubt, his virtue had made considerable progress since that time, for the Bishop of Hippo judged him worthy not merely of the presbyteral office but also adopted him as his successor.

As we have said, Augustine declared this to the people and designated Heraclius in Christ’s name for that office (Epistle 213, no. 5). Moreover, so that the matter might remain firm and legally established as far as human affairs were concerned, and so that authoritative validity might be given to the proceedings, he ordered the ecclesiastical notaries to record in writing both his own words and the acclamations of the people responding to him.

As for the will and decrees of God, he exhorted the people to seek from God, through united prayers, confirmation of what God himself had brought about among them:

> “This, then, is what I desire,” he said, “this is what even now, in the chill of old age, I ask from the Lord our God with fervent prayers. I exhort, admonish, and beseech you to pray with me, so that God may confirm, through the minds of all brought together and united in the peace of Christ, what he has worked in us. May he who sent him preserve him; preserve him safe and sound; preserve him without blame; so that he who brings joy to the living may fill the place of the dying” (ibid., no. 2).

Nothing more ardent or more full of affection could be found.

Having been content to designate Heraclius as his successor, Augustine refused to have him consecrated bishop, believing that there was sin in doing so because he himself had been consecrated while Valerius was still alive (ibid., nos. 4–5). He therefore wished Heraclius to remain in the presbyteral order, while nevertheless transferring the entire burden of affairs to him. He entreated the people, and bound them by Christ, to go to Heraclius in matters that arose, so that Heraclius might provide for them according to his wisdom, or that they might seek counsel and assistance from him himself, as from a father, whenever necessary.

Augustine was not thinking of withdrawing from his people or of failing them in any necessary matter. He was seeking only some measure of quiet, not in order to idle or waste time through indolence, but so that, for as long as God granted him to remain in this life, he might devote himself wholly to the study of the Scriptures.

We have already observed that, a few years earlier, the two councils of Numidia and Carthage had entrusted this responsibility to him. The people had granted him five days each week for that purpose. But this arrangement did not last long: the holy Man was compelled to hear cases no less in the morning than after the midday meal.

This, indeed, was why he begged the people to permit and consent to the transfer of this burden to Heraclius. The people, without hesitation, indicated that they gladly accepted his request (ibid., no. 5).

Finally, Augustine asked that those who were able should seal the record of the events then taking place, and that the people should ratify everything with their final vote. This was immediately done by various acclamations, which were probably the same as those customarily used in the election of bishops (ibid., no. 6).

After this the holy Man proceeded to offer the sacrifice, having first earnestly admonished the people that, during the hour of this sacred supplication, each person should withdraw from other concerns and pray diligently for the Church of Hippo, for himself, and for Heraclius (ibid., no. 7).

These, then, are the proceedings of that assembly, which have been inserted among Augustine’s letters.

Two sermons of the presbyter Heraclius are extant. One was delivered in Augustine’s presence, in which Heraclius declares that he had recently been compelled by necessity to undertake the ministry of preaching the word of God, and that he had already begun to preach it. The other is on the words of the Lord in Matthew chapter fourteen, where the Lord walked upon the waters and Peter faltered.

Maximinus, a bishop of the Arian sect, came to Hippo at about this time. At first he disputed with the presbyter Heraclius, or Eraclius; afterward Augustine himself was summoned by Heraclius to enter into discussion with the heretic (Conference with Maximinus, no. 1).

## 4

The books addressed to the monks of Hadrumetum were written neither after this period nor before it. They are included in the Retractations, published around the year 427, yet there they occupy the final place.

At Hadrumetum, a distinguished city in the province of Byzacena, there was a community of monks whose abbot at that time was Valentinus. One of his pupils, a certain Florus, came to the city of Uzalis, which was his native place, together with Felix, likewise a monk of the Hadrumetine community. There Florus found a letter of Augustine to Sixtus (Epistle 194) and copied it at Felix’s dictation (In Augustine, Epistle 216, no. 2).

When the letter was brought to Hadrumetum, some—perhaps five monks, or not many more—twisted it into a foreign meaning. They argued against their companions, who plainly understood the letter more correctly, maintaining that grace was defended in such a way that free will was taken away, and that it consequently followed that the Lord would not repay each person according to his works at the final judgment (ibid., no. 3).

As the division grew more serious day by day, and those ignorant men stirred up hostility against innocent monks and threw everything into confusion, Florus thought it his duty at last to inform Valentinus, the abbot, of the matter.

Valentinus, having no doubt that the letter was genuinely Augustine’s and that it taught no doctrine other than the orthodox one, resolved to work toward removing the impious questions that had arisen from the ignorance of some of his pupils (In Augustine, Epistle 216, no. 1). For this reason he sent to Evodius, bishop of Uzalis, asking him to send a written response concerning these questions (ibid., no. 3).

When Evodius learned that the monks of Hadrumetum were engaged in such vehement disputes concerning grace, free will, and the justice of God, he replied that he approved their devotion to investigating the truth, but that this pursuit ought to be free from every harshness and contentiousness. Turmoil arises from contention, whereas piety is required by love of the truth.

He then explained to them, according to Augustine’s doctrine, that free will certainly exists in human beings, but that it is wounded and weakened by Adam’s transgression, and that Christ the Savior was sent to heal it.

After adding other evidence relevant to the matter, he admonished them that, whenever they encountered in the writings of distinguished men something they found difficult to understand, they ought not rashly to rush into condemning those authors. Rather, they should strive through prayer to attain the meaning of what they had read (volume 10, Letter of Valentinus to Augustine, in the note to *Rescripsit*).

## 5

The complaints of the ignorant men were satisfied neither by the response of Bishop Evodius nor by the explanation given by a certain holy presbyter, Sabinus, concerning the letter under discussion (Epistle 216, no. 3).

Accordingly, two of them—Cresconius alone and Felix, this Felix being different from the companion of Florus at Uzalis—came to Augustine. After these two had departed, the other brothers remained in peace.

They complained before the holy Doctor that some of their brothers preached grace in such a way that they denied free will and asserted that we would not be judged according to our works. They testified, however, that many others acknowledged free will together with grace (Epistle 214, no. 1). They also attributed the disturbance that had arisen among them to Florus (ibid., no. 6).

Augustine therefore explained his letter to Sixtus to them in person (Epistle 215, no. 1). In addition, he wrote a letter to Valentinus and the monks of his community concerning that difficult question of will and grace (ibid., no. 2).

In it he asked that Florus be sent to him. He rightly conjectured that some were causing an uproar against Florus for no other reason than that they did not sufficiently understand him when he attempted to solve and disentangle a most difficult question intelligible to only a few (Epistle 214, no. 6).

He gave this letter to the monks as they were preparing to return to their monastery, where they were to celebrate Easter, which in that year, 427, fell on the third day before the Nones of April.

But either something intervened to prevent their departure, or Augustine kept them with him somewhat longer for the sole purpose of sending them back to their brothers better instructed against the new heresy of the Pelagians (Epistle 215, no. 1).

After Easter he gave them another letter for Valentinus and his monks, again urging that Florus be sent to him, in these words:

> “If I deserve anything from you, let brother Florus come to me” (ibid., no. 8).

Through the same men he also sent them the letters of the two councils of the province of Carthage and of Numidia, as well as the letters of five bishops to Innocent and three replies from that same pope. He sent also the letters of the African council to Zosimus and of Zosimus to all the bishops throughout the world; finally, he sent the decrees of the plenary council of all Africa against the Pelagian errors.

He believed that all these documents ought to be sent to them so that they might learn how the Catholic Church, through the mercy of God, had driven away the poisons of the Pelagian heresy (ibid., no. 2).

To these he added a new book written by him for their benefit on the very question with which they were struggling. He entitled it *On Grace and Free Will, to Valentinus and the Monks with Him*. There he demonstrates at length that human beings possess free will, but demonstrates at still greater length that free will, deprived of the assistance of grace, can do nothing.

Exhorting them to read it, he says:

> “Read this book over and over again; and if you understand it, give thanks to God. But where you do not understand, pray that you may understand; for the Lord will give you understanding” (*On Grace and Free Will*, no. 46).

Before their departure, he had read this book and the other documents mentioned above, which concerned the condemnation of the Pelagians, in the presence of the monks who were to carry them. He also read to them Cyprian’s book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, in which that holy martyr commends grace with great clarity.

## 6

Valentinus received Augustine’s letter and the book dedicated to himself and his brothers with the reverence that was fitting. He did not fail to send brother Florus to Augustine, and he added a letter (In Augustine, Epistle 216) in which he related everything that had taken place in his monastery to the holy Prelate. He also affirmed and professed that his own faith was the same as that of brother Florus.

After reading Valentinus’s letter, which brother Florus and others who came with him had brought to him, Augustine gave thanks to God because from it he had learned of their peace in the Lord, their agreement in the truth, and their fervor in charity.

With regard specifically to brother Florus, he rejoiced that he had found in him a Catholic faith concerning grace and free will:

> “Those, then, must rather be corrected,” he said, “whom, by God’s favor, I already consider corrected, namely, those who did not understand him” (*On Rebuke and Grace*, nos. 1–2).

Nevertheless, the holy Doctor learned—perhaps from Florus himself—that there was someone in the monastery at Hadrumetum who said:

> “If God works in us both to will and to act, those in authority command in vain when they prescribe what ought to be done or avoided. Or, at least, after they have commanded what is good and right, they should merely pray to God that the disciples may do it; but they ought not rebuke them if they do not do it, since God has not given them that faithful love of God and neighbor by which his commandments are fulfilled” (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 67; *On Rebuke and Grace*, nos. 3–6).

To drive away from the received doctrine of grace this weapon—which seemed impossible for those who are earthly-minded to hurl with greater force—Augustine wrote for Valentinus and the monks with him another book entitled *On Rebuke and Grace*. He did not contend against those men themselves, whose hearts were rightly disposed toward God, but, as he says, against human thoughts themselves, in defense of the love of heavenly and divine grace.

The monk in whose mind such a thought had arisen may have disclosed his view of the matter to Augustine with a heart rightly disposed toward God for no other reason than that this most diligent and clear-sighted Doctor of grace might explain this knot as well.

He explained it with great care, aided by divine revelation. Thus, not without reason, he concludes his book with these words:

> “Since these things are so, neither does grace prevent rebuke, nor does rebuke deny grace. Therefore righteousness must be prescribed in such a way that the grace by which what is prescribed may be done is sought from God by faithful prayer. Both things must be done in such a way that just rebuke is not neglected” (*On Rebuke and Grace*, no. 49).

This book is small in size but immense in doctrine. It is wholly filled with mysteries and places before our eyes the entire economy of divine grace; rightly, therefore, the most learned have called it golden.

> “I customarily call this book,” says the eminent man, “the key by which access is opened to the whole of Augustine’s teaching concerning divine grace and free will” (Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book 1, chapter 23).

The holy Prosper rightly called this book full of divine authority in his letter to Augustine (In Augustine, Epistle 225, no. 2).

# CHAPTER VII

1. Augustine combats the remnants of the Pelagian error detected in Vitalis and presents twelve propositions concerning grace.  
2. He admonishes Palatinus to seek from God the assistance of grace for perseverance in the good.  
3. Leporius’s errors against the faith of the Incarnation and of grace are condemned in Gaul.  
4. Through Augustine’s efforts Leporius is recalled to sound faith.  
5. Augustine applies himself to reviewing his works.  
6. He composes a *Mirror* from passages of the whole of Scripture suitable for forming or correcting conduct.

## 1

A certain Vitalis was struggling with the question of the grace of God and free will, just as the monks of Hadrumetum had done. He was an educated man in the Church of Carthage (Epistle 217, no. 2), and perhaps by his way of life and profession was a monk. For that reason Augustine honors him with no other title than “brother.” Augustine also adopts the manner of addressing himself as a servant of Christ and, through Christ, a servant of his servants, in keeping with the address “to the servant of God” to whom he wishes salvation.

Augustine did not believe him to be a Pelagian heretic; rather, he wanted him to be so orthodox that none of this error should pass over to him or remain in him (ibid., no. 25).

“For the Pelagians,” says the holy Doctor, “attribute everything pertaining to the faithful and devout life of human beings to the free choice of the will in such a way that they think these things are to be obtained from ourselves, not requested from the Lord. But you, if what I hear about you is true, do not wish the beginning of faith—which is also the beginning of a good, that is, a devout, will—to be God’s gift. You insist that we possess from ourselves the beginning by which we begin to believe. As for the other goods of the religious life, you agree that God grants them by his grace to those who already ask, seek, and knock in faith” (ibid., no. 29).

Vitalis therefore twisted divine authorities opposed to his error into another meaning, so that they would not establish that God’s grace is also necessary for the beginning of faith and of a devout will.

When confronted with the Apostle’s statement, “It is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish” (Philippians 2:13), he replied that God works through his law and his Scriptures to make us willing, since we either read or hear them. But whether we consent or refuse to consent to them, he said, remains so entirely our own that, if we wish, God’s work becomes effective in us, whereas, if we do not wish, we make God’s work powerless within us (Epistle 217, no. 1).

He interpreted the Psalmist in the same way. He thought that the statement “The steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he wills his way” (Psalm 36:23) meant that a person follows God’s teaching, preceded by persuasion and followed by consent; and that he does so by natural freedom—if he wills, he does it, and if he does not will, he does not do it—receiving reward or punishment according to what he has done.

In the same manner, he was said to explain through the law of God and the teaching of the Scriptures what is written: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8:15), rather than through the hidden inspiration of God’s grace.

Against this error of Vitalis, Augustine, in a letter written to him around this time, advances an argument drawn from the prayers of the Church, from his own judgment, and from the matter itself—an argument of the greatest force and highly suited to persuading him of the truth.

The Church prays for unbelievers that they may be converted, and gives thanks for those same people once converted to the faith. In the same way, it prays to God for the faithful themselves, that they may persevere by his gift in what they have begun to be.

“Yet,” Augustine says, “you do not deny that these things ought to be requested from the Lord. What remains, brother Vitalis, except that you acknowledge that they are given by the one from whom you agree they must be requested?” (Epistle 217, nos. 5 ff.).

He presses the same point by the authority of Saint Cyprian’s book *On the Lord’s Prayer* and his book *On Mortality*.

Then, warning Vitalis that, if we truly wish to defend free will, we must not attack the source from which it becomes free, Augustine teaches that the will of those who become believers is liberated through Christ from the power of the devil, so that, with the devil no longer obstructing them, they may believe in Christ by a free will.

Since the question to be treated against Vitalis was ultimately whether grace precedes or follows the human will—that is, whether it is given to us because we will, or whether God himself produces through it even this, that we will—Augustine sets before him twelve propositions concerning grace that settle the whole question.

From all of them together, and even from each one individually, it follows that we must confess that God’s grace precedes human wills, and that through grace those wills are prepared, rather than grace being given on account of their merit.

He reduces these propositions to the number twelve so that they may more easily be committed to memory and retained more distinctly.

He asserts that, since by Christ’s favor he is a Catholic Christian, he knows without hesitation that these twelve doctrines are Catholic teachings, placed beyond all controversy. One may not depart from them, and even Vitalis could not deny that they pertain to the faith.

If, however, there were any one of them about which Vitalis thought he ought to doubt, Augustine asked him to indicate it, so that he himself might answer him according to the ability the Lord granted.

Meanwhile, the arguments that brother Vitalis could bring forward—and those that were later brought forward in part by people commonly called Semi-Pelagians—the distinguished defender of grace dissolves and overturns.

Finally, at the end of the letter he adds that, if Vitalis were to contend on behalf of those who are unwilling to believe that one ought not pray for them so that they may will to believe, and that one ought not give thanks to God when those who were unwilling to believe come to will precisely that, then Vitalis would have to be refuted by another method. If he persisted in his error, care would have to be taken that he could not draw others into it—namely, that he should be cut off from the body of the Church.

## 2

At about the same time Augustine gave Palatinus this admonition:

> “Pray that you may not enter into temptation. Prayer itself admonishes you that you need the assistance of your Lord, so that you may not place the hope of living well in yourself. Since you have already begun to do good, you have reason to give thanks. But knowing from whom you have received it, ask him to bring it to completion—the one by whom it was granted that you should begin.

> “Work out your salvation, therefore, with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure, since the will is prepared by the Lord, and the steps of a man are directed by him, and he will his way.

> “This holy thought will preserve you, so that your wisdom may be piety—that is, so that you may be good from God and not ungrateful for the grace of Christ” (Epistle 218, no. 3).

This Palatinus was apparently a native of Hippo. Whatever he had hoped for in the world, he had despised through the working of Christ’s grace, so that, freed from the burden, he might take up the Lord’s yoke and his burden. He was serving God in a place where he had abundant access to the exhortations he needed, perhaps in a monastery at Carthage.

Palatinus had written to Augustine and sent him garments of haircloth. Augustine encouraged him by letter to persevere in his good purpose and declared that he had received the haircloth garments most gratefully, as tokens of humility to be preserved and of prayer to be practiced frequently.

## 3

In the aforementioned book *On Rebuke and Grace*, when Augustine was teaching that we are helped by the more powerful grace of the Savior, he took the opportunity to discuss the incarnate Son of God and said that no one could be so blind or so ignorant in the faith as to dare say that, although he was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary as a son of man, he nevertheless merited becoming the Son of God by living well through free will and performing good works without sin (*On Rebuke and Grace*, no. 30).

Accordingly, since Leporius openly confesses in his book of correction that he had fallen into this error, Leporius’s correction—which is attributed chiefly to Augustine’s labor and diligence (Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 59)—must have followed the book mentioned above.

Yet it was also preceded by the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, in which the holy Doctor attacked this very error as it emerged from the Pelagian heresy.

Leporius, therefore, a monk by profession, arrogated to free will and his own powers the innocence of life in which he flourished in Gaul, following Pelagian doctrine rather than relying on divine assistance.

Indeed, he has been counted among the first and most prominent leaders of those who at that time renewed, from the principles of the Pelagian heresy, the ancient impiety of the Ebionites (Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book 1, chapter 4), and laid the foundations of the Nestorian heresy (Facundus of Hermiane, book 4).

He hesitated to say that God had been born from a virgin or had become man, and brought himself only to concede that Jesus Christ had been produced as a perfect man together with God (Leporius, in the *Book of Correction*).

In this way he so separated the divine properties from the human that he made two Christs and even added a fourth person to the Trinity.

He also loudly proclaimed that Christ had acquired glory for himself through labor, religious devotion, faith, and good works, attributing to him things that properly belong only to mere human beings and reducing him, almost, though unintentionally, to the condition of holy men.

He further published his errors in a written letter that gave offense to all orthodox believers.

Learned men of Gaul attempted to oppose him and persuade Leporius to correct his perverse opinions, but in vain. Consequently, after his impious doctrines had been condemned by the authority of the Gallic bishops Proculus and Cillinus, he was forced to leave the country.

## 4

Expelled from Gaul, Leporius went to Africa with several companions in error. There Aurelius of Carthage, Augustine, and several others joined their efforts to recall him from his error, but Augustine above all.

At last Leporius acknowledged his error and detested it. He publicly confessed its poison with vivid sorrow and a certain holy boldness. Those who had crossed over with him also changed their judgment with him.

Just as his error had first been made public in Gaul, so he wished his repentance to become publicly known there, so that those who had been witnesses of his sin might also be witnesses of his penitence.

For this reason he sent there a little book full of tears and groans expressing his sorrow. In it he magnificently condemned his badly conceived belief, so that his correction is scarcely less admirable than the unshaken faith of many others (Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book 1, chapter 4).

Leporius therefore sent his book of correction to Proculus and Cillinus and entreated them to forgive him.

He sealed it in the Basilica of Carthage—whence it may be inferred that these events took place there—in the presence of bishops, at least Aurelius, Augustine, Florentius, and Secundinus. Dominus and Bonus, perhaps companions of Leporius, also signed it, declaring by their signatures that they too shared this faith.

The same four bishops strengthened the aforementioned letter with their own signatures, both to testify that it was Leporius’s letter and to approve his doctrine.

They also sent a letter to Proculus and Cillinus concerning the conversion of Leporius and his companions (In Augustine, Epistle 219), wishing all its glory to be attributed to divine mercy.

They do not condemn the severity that these Gallic bishops had employed against Leporius. On the contrary, they praise it, admitting that, had it not come first, the gentleness they themselves afterward employed would have been useless.

They ask the Gallic bishops to approve by their support what had been done by them; to receive Leporius through the letter—or little book—he had sent to them, which gave proof of his correction, just as they themselves had received him through his repentance, of which they were eyewitnesses; and to make his correction known to all whom his fault had offended, communicating to them through their reply the joy they had received from this fraternal correction.

They do not indicate that they are awaiting the Gallic bishops’ agreement so that they may restore to Leporius the communion of which he had been deprived by them. On the contrary, they state unreservedly that they themselves had already received him. They undoubtedly believed that, once he had renounced the perverse opinions for which he had incurred the sentence of condemnation, they could rescind that sentence and that he ought not to be sent back to his first judges.

From the style of this letter, Jacques Sirmond judges that it was dictated by Augustine.

### 5.

As we have already observed, the series of all the books which Augustine revised is closed by the book *On Correction and Grace*. From this one may reasonably conclude that this book and the work of the *Retractations* were completed at almost the same time, namely toward the end of the year 427. For although that book had been seen in Gaul before the holy Doctor published the *Retractations*, no one will think that this labor was completed much later than the end of the preceding year, since it does not include the books against Maximinus, which were composed in 428. Nor could it have been completed much earlier, since in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, which he wrote when he had scarcely begun the second book of the *Retractations*, Augustine states that nearly eight years or more had elapsed since he had gone to Caesarea in September of the year 418.

Augustine had long since proposed to review all his books, letters, and sermons with the severity of a judge, and, like a strict censor, to collect in a work undertaken for this very purpose whatever he thought ought to be censured in them (*Retractations*, Preface 1). There was certainly no shortage of things which he would have preferred not to have said or written. As early as 412 he testified to Marcellinus that he desired to be allowed to devote himself to this labor (*Letter* 143.2–3), thereby making clear how little he was disposed to favor himself.

Accordingly, he composed a catalogue of his books and arranged them according to the date of each, so that anyone who wished to read through them in that order might observe how he himself had progressed in writing (*Retractations*, Preface 3):

> Therefore I am now making these books in which I have undertaken to revise my little works, so that I may demonstrate that I did not follow myself in everything; rather, I consider that, by God’s mercy, I wrote as one making progress, though I did not begin from perfection. Indeed, I speak more arrogantly than truly if even now I say that at this age I have arrived at perfection in writing without any error. But it matters how much one errs and in what matters, and how readily each person corrects his error, or with how much obstinacy he tries to defend it. A person is surely one of good hope if the last day of this life finds him progressing in such a way that what was lacking to him as he progressed is added to him, and he is judged rather as one to be perfected than as one to be punished (*On the Gift of Perseverance* 55).

He also wished to include in the same catalogue the treatises which he had published after his conversion while he was still a catechumen, because they had been made public and were read with benefit, provided that certain errors in them were excused, or at least that they were not thought worthy of being embraced (*Retractations*, Preface 3).

In each work he carefully notes whatever might offend either himself or others, clarifying obscure passages and those liable to erroneous interpretations (*Letter* 224.2), and correcting whatever he judged to be foreign to ecclesiastical rule—namely, matters into which, as Possidius says, he had allowed himself to enter when he had not yet sufficiently mastered the practice or teaching of the Church (*Life of Augustine* 28).

When the blemishes which had crept in could not be removed from so many examples of his labors, he thought it necessary to warn everyone about them and thus to judge himself under the one Master whose judgment concerning offenses he desired to escape (*Retractations*, Preface 2–3). Led by this purpose, he paid no attention to whatever thoughtless people might say. For concerning the prudent he knew this with certainty: they would never count it as a fault against him that he corrected his errors with humble modesty, since it had not been permitted him to attain, by human strength, to a perfection in which he would never stumble (*Letter* 143.2–3).

The holy Doctor composed the first book from works written before his episcopate, and the second from those which he had published after becoming a bishop. By this means he discovered—for until then he had not known it (*Letter* 224.2)—that he had issued ninety-three works in two hundred and thirty-two books (*Retractations* 2.67).

The brothers compelled him to make these two books public before he had reviewed his letters and sermons. Possidius testifies that their title was *On the Review of Books* (*Life of Augustine* 28). Nevertheless, whenever Augustine refers to them, he generally uses the verb *retractare*. Hence these books are now entitled *Retractations*, just as they are found titled in Augustine himself and, following him, in Prosper and Cassiodorus.

One must not suppose, however, that this word means the same as what is commonly called “singing a palinode.” In Augustine it generally means to review and to apply a second treatment. And in reality, however rigorously he exercises this criticism, he is chiefly occupied in disclosing his thought, taking care that certain somewhat obscure words not be understood in a worse sense, or correcting a few other matters. Meanwhile, he retracts no error into which he had fallen except the Semi-Pelagian one, lest someone perhaps be deterred by his observance and authority from departing, in this matter, from his opinion.

He himself also cites various passages from these two books in which he renounced the error into which he had fallen before his episcopate. It was reported in Gaul that the holy Doctor was laboring over the review of his works even before he had published anything on the subject; and Hilary begged him to send it to him as soon as this review appeared (*Letter* 226.10). Accordingly, in his reply to Hilary, Augustine takes it as certain that Hilary had not yet read it (*On the Gift of Perseverance* 27).

He then undertook the review of his letters, many of which he had already reread, when it became necessary for him to respond to Julian’s eight books (*Letter* 224.2). Even then he did not interrupt the labor which he judged extremely necessary: when no other business of greater importance intervened, he devoted the day to one work and the night to the other.

Yet although he was held by the greatest desire to complete the work mentioned, he was compelled first by the Vandal war and afterward by his own death to leave it unfinished. For Possidius recognizes only two books of the *Retractations*. In a certain way Possidius supplied what was lacking through the catalogue which he compiled from the holy man’s books, letters, and sermons. He states that these writings altogether amounted to 1,030 compositions, adding that there were others which could not be counted because he had not specified their number (*Possidius, Catalogue*, 10).

Victor of Vita declares that Augustine’s letters and sermons were innumerable (*On the Vandal Persecution* 1.3). Nor should anyone find this difficult to believe of that bishop who for thirty years was, as it were, an oracle for the entire Latin Church; who was compelled, whenever occasion arose, to speak at the request of others (*Retractations*, Preface 2); and who preached the word of God unceasingly until his final illness (*Possidius, Life of Augustine* 31).

### 6.

Possidius seems to suggest that Augustine composed the work entitled *The Mirror* at approximately the same time as his *Retractations*, and shortly before the Vandals either descended upon Africa or reached Hippo Regius (*ibid.*, 28).

This treatise consists of excerpts from both Testaments containing things which God commands or forbids us. It was not composed so that we might learn only those things which we ought to believe, nor so that passages in which we might be exercised by a certain sacred obscurity would be set before us. Rather, it was composed so that our conduct might be instructed by simple precepts, free from the covering of figures, which all the faithful must observe.

He arranged this collection for the benefit of those who, already believing, wish to obey God, and especially for those who are unable to devote themselves to extensive reading. By contemplating themselves in this collection—seeing where they obey or disobey God—they might discover how far they had advanced in good works and what still remained for them to attain perfection. Thus they might give thanks for the good things they observed in themselves, devote all their cares and prayers, with faithful devotion, to preserving them, and direct their strength toward acquiring those things of which they saw themselves deprived.

This was the reason why he gave these excerpts the title *The Mirror*. To them alone he added a preface in which he explains the rationale of his undertaking. He cites the passages in the order of the books of Scripture. Since some of them appear to be mutually contradictory, the holy bishop promises, after completing *The Mirror*, to explain and reconcile them by proposing questions.

This work is nowhere to be found. Indeed, one may judge that it was never published at all by Augustine from the fact that Possidius makes no mention of it, although he did not pass over even the preface placed before *The Mirror* by its author [Col. 0554].

## CHAPTER VIII

1. Boniface takes a second wife and afterward suffers great calamities.  
2. War is declared against him as an enemy of the Empire, and Mavortius and other commanders are sent against him.  
3. Augustine urges Boniface by letter to return to his duty.  
4. Segisvultus assumes command of the war begun against Boniface.  
5. By God’s will the Vandals pour into Africa, so that some may be punished and others crowned.  
6. Africa’s savage and dreadful devastation by the Vandals.  
7. Whether bishops may seek safety by flight in such calamities.

### 1.

Before we close this year, the history of Count Boniface must be taken up again. He is now astonishingly changed from the man whom we mentioned several years ago. We said that in 417, while occupied in conducting war against the barbarians in Africa, he had considered renouncing everything; but Augustine and Alypius persuaded him to remain in the office of count and to devote himself—as indeed he was doing—to the interests of God and the Church, while preserving his resolve to practice perfect continence and taking no concern for increasing the advantages of fortune or empty honors (*Letter* 220.3).

He followed Castinus into Spain in 422 and fought there with him against the Vandals (*Prosper, Chronicle*). There is no doubt that his military skill would have averted the disastrous outcome of that war, had he not, out of respect for Castinus’s arrogant character, withdrawn into the harbor of the City and from there into Africa. Prosper certainly states that this departure was the beginning, for the Empire, of many subsequent calamities and evils.

This was not immediately apparent, however. On the contrary, when Placidia was compelled at the beginning of 423 to flee to Constantinople, historians commend Boniface because he alone remained loyal to her and sent her the money she needed from Africa. Likewise, after Honorius died—which occurred on 15 July of this year—he helped her recover the Western Empire, which John had seized (*ibid.*).

After John had been defeated and killed in 425, and Valentinian had been proclaimed Augustus at Rome on 23 September of the same year under his mother’s guardianship, Placidia summoned Boniface from Africa to Rome and increased his honors with new dignities (*Letter* 220.4). Almost everyone attributed his downfall to this great accumulation of honors, since it had aroused against him the jealousy of Aetius, who had already begun to wield great influence at court.

Yet according to the judgment of holy men, the chief cause of his fall was that, yielding to desire, he abandoned the continence which he had undertaken to practice (*ibid.*, 5), and again brought home as his wife a certain extremely wealthy woman named Pelagia (*Marcellinus, Chronicle*).

She professed the Arian heresy, but he refused to marry her unless she first became Catholic. This was some consolation to Augustine, who was overwhelmed with profound grief at the wholly unexpected news of this marriage [Col. 0555] (*Letter* 220.4).

Moreover, this marriage was attended by the further disgrace that, although his wife was said to have embraced the Catholic faith, the Arians had arrogated such authority to themselves in his household that they baptized his daughter, perhaps born of this marriage. As was observed above, he had one daughter by his former wife, whom he had given in marriage to Count Sebastian. But since that count was devoted to the Catholic faith, it does not seem credible that he had married an Arian woman.

It was also reported that the same heretics had rebaptized women dedicated to God who belonged to Boniface’s household. Rumor further spread that, not content with his lawful wife, he kept concubines at home as well.

But if this marriage proved to be a source of crimes, it was followed by an innumerable multitude of notable calamities. Boniface himself is said to have partly provided the cause of these calamities (*ibid.*, 5).

### 2.

Prosper has handed down that war was declared against him in the name of the state because, when ordered to return to Italy, he had refused to obey (*Prosper, Chronicle*). Procopius relates the matter at somewhat greater length.

From Augustine, however, it is understood that Boniface was accustomed to lay the cause of the war upon those who, although he had served the state exceptionally well, had repaid him with ingratitude and hostility (*Letter* 220.8). He also blamed the fact that he grieved over the worldly goods—which he either hoped for or possessed—being denied to him or assigned to others (*ibid.*, 5).

Boniface came to Hippo at that time, but found the holy bishop scarcely able to speak because of bodily weakness, and therefore could not hear from him what was necessary for his salvation (*ibid.*, 2).

The war which he sustained against the Empire was a new fault and the source and origin of almost innumerable others:

> Who does not see that many people attach themselves to you to protect your power or safety, and that, even if they are all loyal to you and no ambushes are feared from any of them, they nevertheless desire through you to attain those goods which they too love—not according to God but according to the world? Thus, although you ought to have restrained and curbed your own desires, you are compelled to satisfy those of others. For this to happen, many things displeasing to God must be done. Yet even then such desires are not satisfied; for they are more easily cut away in those who love God than they are ever satisfied in those who love the world. You see so many things crushed that scarcely anything worth seizing remains (*Letter* 220.6).

Moreover, although Boniface had remained under arms solely to protect the province from the African barbarians, and it was generally expected that they would be completely subdued as soon as he obtained supreme command of the forces, the opposite occurred. Although he now possessed that authority and led a considerable army, those same barbarians were penetrating deep into the province, laying everything waste, plundering and devastating it. They turned many places which had been crowded with inhabitants into deserts, with no one resisting and with Boniface making no provision to restrain them, since concern for his own safety occupied him intensely (*ibid.*, 7).

When he had likewise been declared an enemy of the Empire, Felix arranged for an army to be sent against him under the commanders Mavortius, Galbio, and Sinocis [Col. 0556]. While they were besieging Boniface—though the place is not specified—Mavortius and Galbio were killed during the siege through Sinocis’s treachery. Boniface afterward discovered Sinocis’s betrayal and killed him as well (*Prosper, Chronicle*).

### 3.

While Boniface was in danger, Augustine did not write to him, fearing that either the bearer of the letter might be endangered or the letter itself, in which the Count’s plans were disapproved, might fall into the hands of his adversaries (*Letter* 220.2).

Later, however, when he found a trustworthy man who was also dear to Boniface himself—namely, the deacon Paul—the blessed Bishop’s love for Boniface led him to say something to him concerning his eternal salvation in Christ (*ibid.*, 1).

In considering the losses which Africa was suffering from the war, Augustine paid attention rather to the higher causes, since he knew that people ought to attribute whatever evil they endure to their own sins. Yet because he loved the Count deeply, he wished Boniface not to be among those through whom God temporarily avenged the crimes of peoples and whom he afterward punished with eternal penalties (*ibid.*, 8).

First he recalls to him his former piety, his desire to abandon everything, and his resolve to preserve continence. Then, with the greatest affection of charity, he places before his eyes the deplorable condition to which he had been reduced, both by his second marriage and by the war which he had undertaken—crimes which he either committed himself or caused others to commit on his account.

As for the reasons by which Boniface thought himself justified, Augustine testifies that it was not his place to pronounce judgment on them, since he had not heard both sides. It belonged to Boniface to defend his innocence, if not before human beings, then certainly before Christ himself, whose faithful servant he professed to be, and before his own conscience, in which he would perceive that he had reached this state through his love of secular vanity. Finally, even if it were entirely true that the Empire had not repaid his labors with an equivalent service, it was not Christian—as Boniface was—to return evil either for good or for evil (*ibid.*, and 5).

He adds that, if Boniface consulted him about what seemed necessary in so great a crisis, he had no advice to offer concerning the preservation of his dignities and wealth. But if he wished to care for his soul, which ought to be more precious to him than everything else, he would hear from Augustine the words of John: “Do not love the world or the things that are in the world” (1 John 2:15).

> “Here is the counsel,” the holy man continues: “Seize it and act. Let it now be shown whether you are a brave man. Conquer the desires by which this world is loved; do penance for past evils, when you were overcome by those desires and dragged along by improper longings” (*Letter* 220.9).

Earlier he had addressed him in these words (*ibid.*, 5):

> You are a Christian; you have a heart; you fear God. Consider for yourself those things which I do not wish to say, and you will discover how many evils you ought to do penance for. For this reason I believe that the Lord spares you and will deliver you from every danger, so that you may do penance as it ought to be done. But hear what is written: “Do not delay turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day” (Sirach 5:8).

Given Boniface’s circumstances at that time, it was not easy for him to follow this advice. Therefore Augustine urges him to pray and implore God again and again to release him from the bonds of the necessities in which he was entangled. “For,” Augustine says, “these necessities come to an end when those desires are overcome” (*Letter* 220.10).

He wishes almsgiving to be joined to the prayers, and, insofar as Boniface’s health allowed, fasting as well (*ibid.*, 11).

If Boniface had no wife, Augustine says that he would advise him not only to preserve continence but also to withdraw into a life among the servants of God, spending it in pious works—a course which he had previously forbidden him to take. But because of his wife, who had married him without knowing of the continence he had vowed and who therefore prevented him from keeping his vow, Augustine did not have the freedom to urge him toward this way of life.

Boniface would be happy if she allowed herself to be led to practice the same virtue, so that in this way he might discharge what he knew he owed to God. If that was impossible, he should at least remain within the bounds of marriage and meanwhile ask God that what was not then permitted him might someday become possible.

“Nevertheless,” Augustine says, “in order that you may love God, do not love the world; in order that, if you still need to be involved in wars, you may keep faith and seek peace; in order that you may use the goods of the world to do good works and not do evil works for the sake of the goods of the world—your wife either does not hinder this or ought not to hinder it” (*ibid.*, 12).

### 4.

This letter perhaps moved Boniface to return to his duty somewhat later. At that time, however, he could not comply with it except by an altogether extraordinary miracle of grace. He had to abandon either his own fortune and that of his family entirely, or be driven to the extremity to which we shall see him reduced.

Indeed, those who desired his downfall brought it about that command of the war begun against him was transferred to Count Segisvultus (*Prosper, Chronicle*). He was a Goth and, apparently, an Arian, for he made use of the services of Maximinus, the Arian bishop who had come to Africa with the Goths.

Since Segisvultus was placed in command of this war only after Mavortius and the other commanders sent against Boniface had been killed, he could scarcely have crossed into Africa before the year 428. We know that Maximinus came from Carthage to Hippo at his command (*Conference with Maximinus* 1). If this is so, those two great cities must have been subject to him. Beyond this, however, nothing concerning his military exploits is found anywhere.

Indeed, if we are to rely on Procopius, Boniface was at Carthage after the Vandals’ landing.

### 5.

The present year witnessed the Vandals’ invasion of Africa, an event more remarkable and more grievous than any which Augustine saw during his entire life.

Boniface, having entered into an alliance with the Vandals in order to defend himself against the Empire, summoned them from Spain to Africa in May of the year 428—according to the opinion which comes closest to probability—and handed over to their lust this vast and flourishing province. Except for three cities, they occupied it entirely within two years.

They crossed over at the summons of God rather than of Boniface, namely so that they might exact punishment from the peoples for the crimes they had committed. They themselves even acknowledged that in this expedition they were moved not so much by their own initiative as by divine impulse.

Salvianus demonstrates how just that impulse was from the customary and familiar crimes of the Africans, especially from their shamelessness and blasphemies—that is, from those matters which concern the honor of God and of religion. He shows divine justice shining forth all the more clearly in this Vandal invasion because the Vandals removed from that province its filthy and disgraceful lusts (*Salvianus, On the Government of God* 7).

He is very expansive on this subject and paints so dreadful a picture of Africa that he seems scarcely to have been able to keep within the limits of the matter.
