Yet since there were many most holy bishops there, who could doubt that through their care and labors God had assisted a great many among the people?

At the same time, it is entirely true that the more richly this province had been equipped with means of salvation, the more monstrous was the crime of those who had abused them—whether by remaining in the unbelief of the pagans, in the schism of the Donatists, in the impious doctrines of the Manichaeans and other popular heretics, or, finally, in obstinate vices and crimes.

The holy African bishops themselves acknowledge with grief that this scourge had been completed both by the sins of the wicked and by the timidity of the good, who, in order not to lose their temporal possessions, were afraid to resist the evils over which they groaned (*Sermon on the Time of the Barbarians* 1).

Since God is equally merciful and just, we may rightly say that these punishments of Africa were tempered by mercy no less than by justice. For those temporal calamities undoubtedly purified many good Christians who endured them with patience.

Moreover, since God had prepared very many people for martyrdom through the work of the holy bishops whom he had placed over them, and especially through Augustine, it belonged to his glory to display before everyone the virtue with which he had adorned them. The outcome certainly taught this lesson. For the tyranny of the Vandals, by which they held Africa for a hundred years, became less renowned for its dreadful devastation than for the immense number of confessors and martyrs whom their cruelty crowned there (*Victor of Vita, On the Vandal Persecution* 1.1ff.) [Col. 0558].

### 6.

Genseric crossed over with a vast army composed not only of Vandals but also of Alans, Goths, and peoples of every kind. He found Africa prosperous, enjoying leisure and abundance in every respect. Salvianus speaks of it in such a way as to indicate that no province in the entire Roman Empire had been richer (*Salvianus, On the Government of God* 7).

But the barbarians soon changed its appearance. Possidius writes:

> By the will and power of God it came to pass that a vast force, armed with various weapons and trained in war, composed of the savage enemies, the Vandals and Alans, together with the Gothic people and persons of many other nations, flowed across from the regions of Spain and burst into Africa in ships. It then passed through every region of the Mauretanias and into our other provinces and territories, raging with every cruelty and savagery, and devastated everything it could through plunder, killings, various tortures, fires, and innumerable other unspeakable evils. It spared no sex, no age, not even God’s priests or ministers, nor the furnishings, instruments, or buildings of the churches.

> This most savage attack and devastation by the enemy was perceived and considered by that man of God—not as other human beings perceived it—but with deeper and more profound reflection. He foresaw in these events especially the dangers and deaths of souls, and therefore his tears were more abundant than usual. For, as it is written, “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1:18), and “A discerning heart is a moth to the bones” [the cited text is corrupt or uncertain]. Thus “tears were his bread day and night” (Psalm 42:3), and he led and endured the final, almost terminal portion of his old age with greater bitterness and mourning than others.

> That man of God saw cities destroyed by ruin, and together with the buildings of the country estates their inhabitants—some killed by the enemy, others driven away and scattered. He saw churches deprived of priests and ministers, and sacred virgins and all who practiced continence dispersed everywhere. Among them, some had perished under torture, some had been killed by the sword, and some, having lost the integrity of soul and body and of faith in captivity, were forced by evil custom and harshness to serve their enemies.

> He saw the hymns and praises of God disappear from the churches, the buildings of the churches burned by fire in very many places, and the solemn sacrifices owed to God cease in their proper locations. The divine sacraments were either no longer sought, or it was not easy to find anyone to administer them to those who sought them.

> Some who fled into the forests of the mountains, the caverns in the rocks, and the caves, or to various fortified places, were conquered and killed; others were so stripped and deprived of the necessities of life that they wasted away from hunger.

> He saw the heads of the churches and the clergy who, by God’s favor, had either not encountered the enemy or had escaped after encountering them, stripped and deprived of everything, reduced to the greatest poverty and forced to beg, while it was impossible to provide all of them with all the support they required.

> He saw scarcely three churches surviving from among innumerable others—namely, the Carthaginian, Hipponensian, and Cirtense churches—which, by God’s favor, had not been destroyed, and whose cities continued to exist, supported by divine and human protection. Yet after his death the city of Hippo, deprived of its inhabitants, was burned by the enemy.

> Amid these evils he consoled himself with the saying of a certain wise man: “He is not great who thinks it a great thing that wood and stones fall and mortals die.”

> Thus, being profoundly wise, he wept abundantly over all these things every day (*Possidius, Life of Augustine* 28) [Col. 0559].

### 7.

The man of God did not allow either his faith or his episcopal courage to be broken or weakened by the grief with which he was afflicted amid such great calamities. He clearly demonstrated this in a letter addressed to Bishop Quodvultdeus.

Quodvultdeus had asked what the duty of bishops was in such circumstances: whether they were permitted to allow their people to flee and to withdraw themselves in order to avoid danger. Augustine replied briefly, but sufficiently for the necessity of the matter: those who wished, if able, to migrate to fortified places were not to be prohibited; but bishops could not break the sacred bonds of their ministry by which Christ’s love had bound them, so that they would not abandon their churches. Therefore, as long as their presence would remain necessary for their people, nothing at all was left to them except to commit themselves wholly to the divine will and place their hope in heavenly assistance (*Letter* 228.1).

Honoratus, bishop of Thibaris and also called a holy man by Possidius (*Possidius, Life of Augustine* 30), later asked Augustine the same question concerning bishops and clergy.

Honoratus indicated to the holy bishop that he could not see what benefit bishops could provide either to themselves or to their people by remaining in their places, except that men would fall before their eyes, women would be violated, churches would be burned, and they themselves would perish under torture while people were asking about them, though they had no resources.

Augustine thought it sufficient to send him his letter to Quodvultdeus. But Honoratus again indicated that this had not satisfied him, since Christ had commanded flight and had confirmed his command by his own example. This, therefore, was why the holy Doctor wrote him a new letter on the matter (*Letter* 228.2). Possidius says that Augustine regarded it as especially useful and necessary for instructing bishops and other ministers of the Church, and for that reason thought it appropriate to insert it, though somewhat lengthy, into the *Life* of the holy Bishop (*Possidius, Life of Augustine* 30).

In that letter Augustine teaches that flight is permitted to bishops only when either they themselves are being specifically sought and the necessary ministry can be fulfilled by others who are not being sought in the same way, or when the entire people have departed.

To support the latter condition, he adduces the example of certain Spanish bishops; for the former, that of Athanasius. He could also have added Cyprian. Apart from these two conditions, he maintains that only ignorance or cowardice could induce a cleric, and especially a bishop, to allow the people to be abandoned by his ministry at the very time when they most need it.

Another bishop had objected that if Christ commanded people to flee in persecutions where there could be the fruit of martyrdom, then sterile sufferings ought much more to be avoided when there was a barbarian and hostile invasion.

Augustine replies that this is indeed true of those who are not held by the bonds of ecclesiastical office, but not of those who remain because they owe their service to the faithful. Through this benefit of charity, they acquire for themselves the merit of a more glorious martyrdom than if they suffered merely for the sake of preserving their faith.

Yet when charity itself seemed to suggest that some portion of the clergy should withdraw, so that those escaping the barbarian fury would not lack assistance, Augustine advises that those who voluntarily embraced this course could, lest they be marked by cowardice or seem, in their own judgment, more necessary to the Church than others, entrust the matter to lots. He says that no one except the ignorant would blame this procedure, although he admits that it was less customary.

Augustine asserts that this greatness of soul, by which a bishop remains amid dangers with the people divinely entrusted to him, is generated not by the smoke of worldly desire but by the flame of heavenly love. He further says that this love comes from God and must be earnestly sought from him in prayer:

> Let us therefore pray that it may be given by him by whom it is commanded (*Letter* 228.7) [Col. 0561].

Finally, as a conclusion, he adds that in these calamities no counsel more useful remains than to take refuge in the protection of prayer and earnestly implore the divine mercy.

From this letter one may judge that the city of Calama and many other places had been entirely deserted and left desolate by their inhabitants, since Possidius—who would never have brought himself to depart from Augustine’s opinion, which he praises with such great and abundant commendation—testifies that he and other neighboring bishops had fled for refuge to Hippo (*Possidius, Life of Augustine* 28).

## CHAPTER IX

1. The holy Doctor undertakes his final work against Julian.  
2. He enters into a disputation with Maximinus, an Arian bishop, and refutes him in published books.  
3. He urges Maximus, converted from the Arian heresy, to strive to lead his own people and others entangled in the same error to the Catholic faith.  
4. He refutes the *Sermon of the Arians*.  
5. He publishes in writing his disputation with Pascentius, who adhered to the same Arian heresy.  
6. He replies to Elpidius, who was in error concerning the faith of the Trinity.

1. In that devastation of all Africa, while nearly everyone was concerned only either to assist their suffering homeland or at least to save themselves from destruction, the holy Bishop nevertheless steadfastly maintained his established practice of aiding the Church through his continual labors and of defending the truth and faith against its enemies. We have already observed that, when Julian had written four books against Augustine’s first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, the holy Doctor refuted certain excerpts from the first of them in his own second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*; and that, after obtaining all four books, he subsequently published a longer work against them all together, whose title is recorded in the *Retractations* simply as *Six Books against Julian*. Alypius had taken the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* with him to Italy as early as the year 421, so far as we can infer. Julian, however, undertook this response once it had been prepared, at a time when he did not yet know the six books in which Augustine had refuted his four, since he doubts whether Augustine had even read them (*Unfinished Work*, book 4, no. 38).

Julian’s response consisted of eight books, in which he was not copious through wandering verbosity but, to those who cling to the substance of things and disdain superfluous words, wearisome (*Ibid.*, book 3, no. 20). Augustine wittily jokes about this, saying that, if Julian had decided to continue along the same path, he could easily complete more than a thousand volumes in answering the six books with which Augustine had refuted Julian’s four (*Ibid.*, book 1, no. 34; book 4, no. 5). Nevertheless, Julian continually boasted of his devotion to brevity, as though he had left unsaid much that he could have added. Hence Augustine’s reply to him: “You wrote eight books against one of mine because, through your dialectical abridgements, you were unwilling to debate at length” (*Ibid.*, book 1, no. 34).

Yet Julian does not even attack Augustine’s entire book in his eight books (*Ibid.*, book 2, no. 127); indeed, refuting no part of it, he scarcely touches a third (*Ibid.*, book 4, no. 5). Six of Julian’s books are included in Augustine’s refutation. In them Julian scarcely ever calls Catholics anything other than “Traducians” and “Manichaeans”; and he repeatedly calls the holy Bishop himself the “Punic Debater,” while calling Alypius “the home-born slave (*vernula*) of Augustine’s sins” (*Ibid.*, book 1, no. 7). Augustine, however, considers those insults worthless—or rather, believes they should be valued highly: “When I hear insults from heretics in defense of the Catholic faith,” he says, “I regard them as praises” (*Ibid.*, book 3, chapter 18).

Julian dedicates this work to Florus, a prominent bishop among the Pelagian faction. At Florus’s request, or rather at the prompting of his paternal authority, Julian declares that he was induced to undertake this great work after abandoning his plan for a shorter one (*Ibid.*, book 1, nos. 2, 7). Elsewhere he boasts that this burden was imposed upon him by holy men and confessors of his time—that is, by those who had been ordered to leave their homeland solely because of the Pelagian doctrine (*Ibid.*, book 1, no. 51).

Augustine had already completed two books of the *Retractations* when he happened to see this work. At that time Alypius had gone to Rome for the third time. After receiving the work there, he had not yet copied it in full when he seized the opportunity to arrange for five books of it to be sent to Augustine, promising to send the other three shortly and urgently pressing him not to delay his reply (*Epistle* 224, no. 2).

The holy Doctor was then occupied with reviewing his letters and sermons. He had already read many of his letters, although he had not yet dictated anything from them, when Julian’s books also began to demand his attention. But since he regarded the revision of his works as a necessity too serious to be abandoned, he divided his leisure between the two labors, as we have already noted, devoting himself to one by day and to the other by night. Other concerns, however, of such a kind and importance that he could not neglect them, drew him away from the task he had in hand.

He answered Julian in such a way as first to present the heretic’s text and then to append what seemed appropriate for refuting it (*Ibid.*, no. 1). This method repeatedly compelled him to give the same answers, because Julian persisted in reiterating the same errors. But the holy man preferred that his excessive diligence be pardoned by quicker minds rather than that slower ones complain to him about having neglected their slowness (*Unfinished Work*, book 6, no. 17).

There he also relates the following history, which is by no means unworthy of notice:

> “There was among us a certain Acatius, born of an honorable family among his people. He said that he had been born with his eyes closed; but because, while the interior of the eyes was sound, the lids adhered and the eyes could not open, a physician wished to open them with an iron instrument. His devout mother did not allow this, but accomplished it by applying a poultice made from the Eucharist, when the boy was already about five years old or somewhat older. He said that he remembered this quite well” (*Ibid.*, book 3, no. 162).

The holy Doctor continued working on this book against Julian until the end of his life. He was still engaged upon it in the city of Hippo, already besieged by the Vandals, but death overtook him and forced him to leave the work unfinished [Col. 0563] (*Prosper, Chronicle*). Possidius also clearly reports this when he mentions it in these words: “Against the second response of Julian, the *Unfinished Work*” (*Possidius, Index*, chapter 4).

2. We said above that Maximinus had come to Hippo at the command of Segisvultus (above, chapter 8, no. 4). He had come, as he himself claimed, “for the sake of peace” (*Debate with Maximinus*, no. 1), although he does not explain this more clearly. Later he likewise states that he had been brought forward to reply by fear of God and by his desire to gather together his brothers, or disciples, whom Augustine had attempted to take from him and reconcile to the Church, not only through private exhortations but also through a public discourse in which he had discussed the invisibility of God (*Ibid.*, Maximinus’s debate, no. 26).

Perhaps he was referring to certain Goths belonging to Segisvultus, who were unable to ensure that the Catholic party did not prevail at Hippo. For Maximinus feared the imperial laws (*Debate with Maximinus*, no. 4), whereas Augustine spoke as one protected by the authority of the rulers (*Ibid.*, Maximinus’s debate, no. 1).

Maximinus first held a conversation with the presbyter Heraclius, claiming that he had been challenged by him (*Ibid.*, no. 1). Heraclius subsequently summoned Augustine. At the urging of many people, Augustine agreed to enter into the discussion; Maximinus did not dare refuse, lest he be deserted by his own followers (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 17).

They therefore met before a large gathering of distinguished persons and others, both clergy and laity, as well as notaries who would record the statements of both sides. At the beginning Maximinus, adopting a certain appearance of modesty, openly acknowledged that Augustine had done him an injury, if only by deeming him worthy to meet with him in discussion. He then professed that he held the faith of Ariminum and proceeded to explain its various doctrines, which the holy Doctor refuted as far as the time permitted him (*Debate with Maximinus*, no. 1).

From this controversy one may learn what the doctrine of this heresy was, by what deceptions heretics attempted to conceal its weakness and impose upon simpler minds, and, finally, what faith concerning the divine Trinity the Catholic Church followed.

Maximinus expressed his thoughts not merely with great fluency but also pleasantly and elegantly, although he claimed that he had never studied either rhetoric or humane letters. He certainly possessed a remarkably good memory and had at his fingertips a great many testimonies from Scripture, which he delivered with great verbal facility. He said many things, and many of them were very beautiful, but they were entirely irrelevant to the matter at hand. Thus, although he had declaimed at length, he was found to have accomplished nothing and to have answered none of the questions put to him.

He showed clearly that he was doing this deliberately in his final debate, which he prolonged until the end of the day. For there was no time to read it over again so that Augustine could refute it. Nor was it possible to persuade Maximinus to continue the discussion on the following day, since he alleged that pressing necessity was calling him back to Carthage.

Augustine was therefore obliged to answer him briefly [Col. 0564]. Yet this holy man undertook to commit the debate to writing and to demonstrate to Maximinus what false doctrines he was defending. He confirmed this promise with his signature. Maximinus likewise wrote in his own hand that he would be at fault if, after receiving Augustine’s book, he did not answer each of its chapters.

Augustine fulfilled his pledge, and it was all the more necessary for him to do so because, after returning to Carthage, Maximinus boasted that he had departed from the debate victorious—because, evidently, he had shown himself the more talkative there (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 17).

Although this alleged victory was fictitious, it was not easy for slower minds and those less instructed in the faith to judge the matter. The holy man therefore wrote two very lengthy books. In the first he made it clear that Maximinus had not answered the points he himself had raised; in the second he refuted in full the longer discourse of the same heretic, to which the shortage of time had prevented him from replying during the debate.

The holy Bishop does not mention these books in the *Retractations*, because he had already put the finishing touches to them. Possidius, however, mentions them both in the *Life* and in the *Index* (*Ibid.*, and *Index*, chapter 5).

The holy Bishop refuted certain statements of Maximinus in a sermon to the people, whose title reads: *Against a Certain Statement of Maximinus, Bishop of the Arians, Who, Stationed in Africa with Count Segisvultus, Was Blaspheming* (*Sermon* 140). It is unknown, however, whether that sermon preceded the discussion mentioned above or followed it.

3. This debate between the holy Bishop and Maximinus reminds us to gather here, as it were into a single bundle, the other short works against the Arian heresy, especially those whose date we have been unable to determine.

There was a certain Maximus, called in ancient manuscripts “the physician of Thenita,” an Eunomian, who had long been ensnared in Arian doctrines and, through his own persuasion, had infected others of his household with the same plague (*Epistle* 170, no. 10). Nevertheless, when already advanced in age, he emerged from it by divine favor and joined himself to the Catholic Church, in the presence of Augustine and Alypius; and we cannot doubt that they contributed their assistance to this end.

It nevertheless appears that he showed too little zeal in bringing back those whom he had turned away from the truth, as well as others of his family whom he had hoped would follow his return. This moved the holy Bishops to write to Maximus. They exhort him to urge those people, pray for them, and finally bring them to the Church. They devoted the remainder of the letter to explaining the mystery of the divine Trinity, in order to strengthen Maximus more and more in the faith.

They also asked Bishop Peregrinus, perhaps the bishop of Thenita, in a letter sent to him at the same time (*Epistle* 171), to inform them at the first opportunity whether Maximus had received their letter gratefully and had obeyed their admonitions. They further implore Peregrinus to tell him in their own words that they customarily wrote lengthy letters to their closest friends, including bishops, in the form in which that letter had been written, so that they might be composed quickly and the paper might be held more conveniently [Col. 0565] when read. “Otherwise,” they say, “not knowing our custom, he might think that an insult had been offered him.”

4. Although no adherents of the Arian sect otherwise lived at Hippo, the frequent arrival of travelers had brought some of them there (*Tractates on the Gospel of John* 40, no. 7). At some point, therefore—apparently in the year 418, as may be understood from the sequence of the *Retractations*—a *Sermon of the Arians*, whether of the people of Hippo or of others, had been published (*Retractations*, book 2, chapter 52) and sent to the holy Doctor by Catholic believers. Augustine refuted it with as much diligence and brevity as he could. Moreover, so that he would not be forced to insert throughout his own short work the text he was examining, he placed the entire sermon at its beginning and added numbered divisions by which each passage of his refutation could be identified (*Against the Sermon of the Arians*, chapter 39).

5. A certain Pascentius, a count of the imperial household and an adherent of the Arian heresy, as Possidius relates, “through the authority of his position, a most violent collector of the treasury, savagely and continually attacked the Catholic faith and harassed and troubled very many priests of God who lived by a simpler faith, through his mockery and power” (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 17). He challenged Augustine to discuss the matter with him at Carthage, with distinguished and noble men present (*Epistle* 228, no. 9).

But the same heretic, Possidius continues, “absolutely refused to allow tablets and stylus—that is, notaries to record what our teacher [Augustine] most insistently wanted recorded both before and during the encounter—to be present. And when he obstinately refused this, saying that he did not wish to risk the danger of the public laws through written records, and when Bishop Augustine saw that this pleased those who were present, including his fellow priests, that they should debate privately without any writing, he undertook the discussion. He predicted, as later happened, that after the gathering had been dissolved anyone might perhaps freely say, without any written evidence, that he had said what he had not said or had not said what he had said.

“He entered into discussion with him and stated what he believed, and heard from him what he held—that is, what he said against the Catholic faith—for otherwise he could not obtain from Pascentius a clear statement of his faith. He proved and taught the foundations of our faith by sound reasoning and the authority of Scripture; but he showed that Pascentius’s assertions were supported by no truth and by no authority of the sacred Scriptures, and he exposed their futility.

“When the parties departed from one another, Pascentius, increasingly angry and enraged, made many false boasts about his faith, proclaiming that he himself had defeated Augustine, whose name was praised by the mouths of many. Since these things were by no means concealed, Augustine was compelled to write to Pascentius. Omitting the names of those who had taken part in the discussion, out of fear of Pascentius, he faithfully reported in those letters everything that had been said or done between the parties. If these matters were denied, he had an ample supply of witnesses to prove them—namely, the most distinguished and honorable men who had been present at the time.

“Pascentius scarcely returned a reply to the two letters addressed to him; in it he was more capable of offering insult than of explaining the reasoning of his own sect. This is confirmed by those willing and able to read it” (*Possidius, Life of Augustine*, chapter 17).

6. Possidius also lists a letter to Elpidius among the works undertaken against the Arians (*Ibid.*, *Index*, chapter 5). This Elpidius was indeed in error concerning the Trinity and considered it foolish to say that the Son was equal to the Father (*Epistle* 242, no. 2). He had never seen Augustine; nevertheless, he conceived the idea of attempting, as he claimed, out of goodwill to bring him back from error (*Ibid.*, no. 1).

For this reason he sent Augustine a short work by a bishop of his own sect and encouraged him to cross the sea so that he might hear Bonosus and Jason, very learned men from whose conversation he would derive abundant benefit. Although Elpidius’s proposal was absurd, the holy Doctor replied to him kindly. Since Elpidius had thereby testified to his goodwill and wished Augustine to be freed from error, Augustine said that he ought to give him thanks and acknowledge the favor. But, he added, whether one of them was in error concerning the faith or concerning knowledge of the Trinity was another question; and he wished that God might make Elpidius know what Elpidius thought he knew.

As for the short work published by Elpidius’s bishop, Augustine promises that he will demonstrate the author’s vanity and weakness if he is allowed, when time permits, to examine it point by point (*Ibid.*, no. 5). Without doubt, however, the various affairs with which he repeatedly complains of being burdened prevented him from undertaking that work.

## CHAPTER X

1. The Massilians and certain others in Gaul, not wholly opposed to the Pelagians, rise against the doctrine of predestination and grace explained by Augustine in his earlier books.  
2. At the urging of Prosper and Hilary, Augustine defends the Catholic faith against them in his books *On the Predestination of the Saints*.  
3. Quodvultdeus asks the holy Doctor to write on heresies.  
4. At Quodvultdeus’s insistence, Augustine undertakes the work *On Heresies*, which he is forced to leave unfinished.  
5. In a letter to the elder Alypius, he recounts the miraculous conversion of Dioscorus.

1. However great the multitude of cares pressing upon him, the holy Doctor did not therefore remove from his memory the conviction that God had assigned him the task of defending grace. Thus, besides never ceasing to contend in writing with Julian until the end of his life, he immediately confronted new enemies of grace who arose not long before his death.

Many servants of Christ—that is, monks—who lived in the city of Massilia (*Epistle* 225, no. 2), and certain others in various places in Gaul (*Epistle* 226, no. 2), were reading Augustine’s writings. Whatever the holy Doctor argued in them concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose, they repeatedly declared to be contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding.

They claimed that this purpose of God’s calling, by which the distinction between those to be chosen and those to be rejected is said to have been made either before the beginning of the world or at the very creation of the human race, both removes from the fallen the concern to rise again and gives the saints an occasion for lethargy (*torporis*). They further said that, under the name of predestination, a certain fatal necessity was being introduced. In short, whatever Augustine sets against them in the book *On Rebuke and Grace* or in his books against Julian, they opposed with the greatest determination and struggle.

They also said that this doctrine was contrary to the edification of those who heard it and therefore, even if true, ought not to be publicly taught. Defending their obstinacy in the name of antiquity, they maintained that Paul, on whose authority Augustine relied, had never until then been understood in this way.

With respect to infants, in whom divine predestination is manifest, they said that such children were lost or saved according to what divine foreknowledge had foreseen they would become in adulthood, if they reached that age (*Epistle* 225, no. 5). In a similar way they explained the question concerning adults: why is the Gospel not preached to everyone? They asserted that this belonged to divine foreknowledge, so that the Gospel was not preached to certain peoples because they would not receive it (*Ibid.*, and *Epistle* 226, no. 3).

Moreover, they were troubled by the distinction Augustine established between the grace given to Adam and the grace given to us (*Epistle* 226, no. 6). They did not wish anyone to be given a perseverance from which he could not fall through transgression, but only one from which he could defect by his own will, and which could either be obtained through humble petition or lost through obstinacy (*Ibid.*, no. 4).

Some of the same Gauls, moving still closer to the Pelagian heresy, distinguished saving grace from initial grace. They held that initial grace was nothing other than reason and free will, granted by the Creator’s favor to a human being who had previously merited nothing, since he did not yet exist; and that, with its aid, a person, while making good use of the good of nature, could attain saving grace (*Epistle* 225, no. 4).

Thus, since in adults who exercise free will there are two things that bring about human salvation—namely, God’s grace and human obedience—they wanted obedience to precede grace, so that the beginning of salvation should be believed to depend upon the one who is saved, not upon the one who saves; and so that the human will should procure for itself the help of divine grace, rather than grace subject the human will to itself (*Ibid.*, no. 6).

Finally, they taught that each person possessed as much capacity for good as for evil, and that the soul could move itself with equal force either toward vices or toward virtues: when it desired good, God’s grace would support it; when it pursued evil, just condemnation would overtake it (*Ibid.*, no. 4).

These and other arguments against the faith concerning predestination and grace were advanced by men who surpassed others in the merit of their lives or in the dignity of their position within the Church to such an extent that scarcely anyone, except a few fearless lovers of perfect grace, dared resist their arguments (*Ibid.*, no. 7). Prosper and Hilary therefore considered it necessary—both men being laymen—to notify Augustine by letter and ask him to oppose his own authority to them, and not to shrink from opening up through the clearest explanations those matters in these questions that were more obscure and difficult to understand.

They hoped, in fact, not only to be strengthened by the protection of his arguments but also that the adversaries themselves would receive the purest light of grace (*Ibid.*, no. 9). “Whatever,” Hilary says, “you may wish or be able to do for that grace which, in you, we little ones admire together with the great, we shall receive with the greatest gratitude, as though it had been decreed by an authority most dear and revered by us” [Col. 0568] (*Epistle* 226, no. 10).

Hilary informs Augustine that he had obtained from Prosper a letter, which he sends together with his own, in which Prosper had, as far as he could, addressed all the adversaries’ doctrines and principles. At the beginning of that letter Prosper declares to the holy Doctor that he is no longer writing to him merely as a matter of courtesy, as he had done in an earlier letter, but out of love for the faith by which the Church lives.

“For while your most vigilant diligence keeps watch over all the members of Christ’s body,” he says, “and while you fight against the snares of heretical doctrines with the power of truth, I in no way thought that I should fear being burdensome or troublesome to you in a matter that concerns the salvation of many and therefore your own piety. Rather, I believed that I would be guilty if I did not refer matters that I understand to be highly destructive to the faith’s special protector” (*Epistle* 225, no. 1).

2. Augustine was distressed that the divine utterances in which God’s grace is proclaimed—grace that is altogether nothing if it is given according to our merits—were not accepted despite their number and clarity. Yet, moved by the efforts of Prosper and Hilary and by a pious concern for those in error, he was induced to undertake still more on their behalf, after so many books and letters of his own on the subject, although he believed that he had already done enough (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, book 1, nos. 1, 2).

He therefore wrote two books to Prosper and Hilary, both entitled *On the Predestination of the Saints*—although one of them is now commonly called *On the Gift of Perseverance*—and not without reason were they given this title (*Note on book 2 of On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *Preface to volume 10*, chapter 29). In both books the holy Doctor’s aim is to defend the Catholic Church’s doctrine of predestination, by which God chose us not because we were going to be holy, but, as the Apostle teaches, so that we might be holy (Eph. 1:4) (*On the Predestination of the Saints*, nos. 35–39, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*, nos. 34, 48, etc.).

In each book he also attacks individually the errors of the Gauls who, as could be learned from the letters of Prosper and Hilary, placed both the beginning of faith and perseverance to the end so entirely within our power that they did not regard these as gifts of God. Nor did they believe that, in order for us to possess and retain them, God worked upon our thoughts and wills, although they conceded that God gives all other things when they are obtained from him through the faith of believers (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 42).

In the first book Augustine teaches that not only the growth but also the beginning of faith is God’s gift; that grace removes hardness of heart; and that all who are taught by the Father to come to Christ do come to him. Those whom he teaches, he teaches through mercy; those whom he does not teach, he does not teach through judgment.

He shows the difference between grace and predestination. Through predestination, moreover, God foreknew what he himself was going to do. He wonders that the opponents of predestination, who are said to be unwilling to be led into uncertainty concerning God’s will, prefer to entrust themselves to their own weakness rather than to the firmness of God’s promise.

He teaches that the truth of grace and predestination shines forth in the infants who are saved, who are distinguished from the others who perish by none of their own merits. They are not distinguished on the basis of foreknown merits that they would have possessed had they lived longer. The Savior himself, however, is the most illustrious example of predestination and grace.

Finally, he commends that the predestined were chosen before the foundation of the world, not because they were foreknown as going to believe and become holy, but so that they might become such through the election of grace.

In the second book he proves that the perseverance by which one perseveres in Christ to the end is a gift of God. This gift may indeed be obtained through humble petition, but once it has been given, it cannot be lost through obstinacy. It is not given according to the merits of those who receive it: to some it is given through God’s mercy, while to others it is not given through his just judgment.

Why one adult rather than another is called, just as why one of two infants is taken up and the other left behind, is inscrutable; more inscrutable still is why, among two devout persons, perseverance is granted to one and not to the other. Yet this is completely certain: the former belongs to the predestined, while the latter does not.

Augustine then refutes what the adversaries claim: that defining predestination is contrary to the usefulness of exhortation and correction. He asserts that predestination is beneficially preached so that a person may glory not in himself but in the Lord. Whatever they object against predestination may likewise be objected either against God’s foreknowledge or against that grace which they agree is necessary except for the beginning of faith and the perfection of perseverance, even though they concede that God gives these other things when they are obtained from him through the faith of believers.

For the predestination of the saints is nothing other than the preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. Nevertheless, he commands that predestination be preached in a suitable manner, and not in such a way that, among an uninstructed multitude, it might seem to be refuted by the very act of preaching it.

Finally, he again commends to us the Lord Jesus, the most illustrious example of predestination, set before our eyes.

Pope Hormisdas wished it to be understood especially from these books what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church professes concerning free will and the grace of God. On the authority of these books, the African bishops exiled in Sardinia most strongly commend them for the sake of the faith in their synodical letter:

> “Above all, take pains to have the books of Saint Augustine, which he wrote to Prosper and Hilary, read by the brethren mentioned. The glorious bishop of the Apostolic See, Hormisdas of blessed memory, inserted a reference to them, with great praise of Catholic doctrine, in the letter by which he replied to the holy brother and fellow priest Possessor when consulted by him. His words are these: ‘Concerning free will, however, and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church follows and preserves may indeed be recognized sufficiently in the various books of blessed Augustine, and especially in those addressed to Prosper and Hilary; nevertheless, explicit chapters are also contained in the ecclesiastical archives’” (*Appendix to volume 10*, *Letter of the African Bishops*, no. 17).

Augustine does not mention those remnants of the Pelagian error in his book *On Heresies*, because he had perhaps already brought this part of the work addressed to Quodvultdeus, which was still supposed to consist of a second book, nearly to completion when he received the letters of Prosper and Hilary.

3. Quodvultdeus, a deacon of Carthage, reflected upon the great grace God had granted the Bishop of Hippo for instructing others. He therefore decided to approach him, although the holy Doctor was burdened by old age and bodily weakness, and to ask him to compose an account of all the heresies that had arisen from the foundation of the Church: what doctrines they held, in what opinions they dissented from the truth, what Scripture and reason suggested for refuting them, in what manner the Church received those who renounced them, and, finally, which of them accepted or rejected Baptism.

Since it would have been an immense labor for Augustine to refute all heresies, Quodvultdeus immediately confined himself within narrower limits. He declared himself satisfied if Augustine would briefly record the character of their teachings and the doctrine that the Catholic Church defended against them, directing those who desired fuller knowledge to the disputations that either the holy man himself or others had composed on the same subject.

This work could undoubtedly have brought considerable benefit both to the uneducated and to the learned. Therefore Quodvultdeus adjures the holy Doctor, in the name of Christ who had granted him the gift of being learned without envy, not to refuse it. He does not deny that he is imposing a very serious burden upon a holy old man who was contemplating and arranging greater things and suffering the complaints of his body.

“But your Beatitude’s goodwill, universally acknowledged, encouraged me,” he says. “When I considered it, I feared more that the Lord might judge me proud for not asking, sluggish for not seeking, and lazy for not knocking” (*Epistle* 221, no. 1).

Augustine had long before considered undertaking this labor, and he would certainly have done so had he not weighed the difficulty of the matter and judged that the burden far exceeded his strength (*On Heresies*, preface). He therefore took advantage of the opportunity provided by a leading citizen of Hippo named Philocalus (*Epistle* 222, no. 1) and immediately sent Quodvultdeus a letter, now lost through the passage of time, in which he pointed out that the requested task and undertaking were excessively burdensome.

A few days later he added another letter, sending it through one of his subdeacons, whom some matter had compelled to travel to Carthage. In these letters he states that catalogues of heresies had already been compiled by Philastrius and Epiphanius. If Epiphanius, who was much more learned than Philastrius, assigned them a smaller number, this was because it was extremely difficult to determine what ought to be regarded as a heresy (*Ibid.*, no. 2).

Augustine says that he is prepared to send Quodvultdeus Epiphanius’s book. It was written in Greek, but a person who could render it into Latin could easily be found at Carthage. Augustine asks Quodvultdeus to write to him about Theodosius, about the Manichaeans whom Theodosius had exposed, and about the departure of the holy bishops.

We discussed this Theodosius above (book 8, chapter 3, no. 1). As for the bishops’ journey, it may refer to the fact that we observed Alypius to have been staying in Rome in the year 428 (*Ibid.*, chapter 9, no. 1), since nothing prevents Augustine’s letter from having been sent before that time.

### 4.

Quodvultdeus had received only this second letter to Augustine, when he complained of his misfortune to the blessed Doctor in another letter [Col. 0571], namely, that he had been prevented by his own sins from obtaining something that would have been of such great benefit to the whole Church. Nevertheless, he said that, relying on Christ’s mercy and on those compassionate affections by which the holy man was always ready to benefit others, he hoped that Augustine would not refuse the nourishment which he requested for himself and for others. His letter does not answer at all the other matters which Augustine had mentioned in his own letter; but the reason seems to be that the editors decided to cut away what belonged elsewhere, so that only what related to the book *On Heresies* would be printed. For not even the little salutation which it was customary for him to add in his own hand at the end has been preserved. There he openly declares that he would nevertheless continue to trouble Augustine until he granted what was requested: so that, although he could not obtain the privilege on the ground of merit, at least unwearied persistence might deserve it (*Epist.* 223, §3).

Augustine states that, driven by Quodvultdeus’s increasingly frequent requests and pressed by his urgent insistence, he undertook this work, and that no one else had ever persisted so much in asking him for anything. He therefore finally thought that he ought to yield; and he says that he was moved in this also by divine will, which the deacon’s very name signified (*On Heresies*, Preface). Accordingly, when by chance a presbyter of Fussala was about to travel to Carthage, the holy man reread Quodvultdeus’s first letter, intending at least to begin this little work, so that, by sending him something like a specimen, he might show him how difficult a burden he had wanted imposed upon him. Yet he was entirely unable to write anything because of pressing occupations, which were also the reason that he interrupted his response to Julian. He therefore did nothing more than commend to Quodvultdeus the presbyter of Fussala and his cause; nevertheless, he added that he hoped that, as soon as he had dealt with the matters that were occupying him and had answered Julian’s five books, he would undertake the work which Quodvultdeus desired, and at the same time revise his other little works, devoting a night to one and a day to another—provided that Julian’s three books had not first been brought to him (*Epist.* 224, §1).

At last, in order to discharge his pledge, he applied himself to the work toward the end of the year 428 or at the beginning of the following year. He planned to divide it into two parts: the first, concerning the heresies that had arisen after Christ’s coming and ascension against his teaching; the second, concerning the highly useful question of what makes a heretic, so that one might readily avoid every kind of heresy, whether known or unknown, and pronounce judgment on all those that might arise in the future (*On Heresies*, Preface). This plan would certainly have been of great value if it could have been brought to completion; but the matter was full of difficulty, since no general rule can show how a heretic is to be defined, because not every error ought to be regarded as heresy. From the time of Christ’s passion down to his own day, he enumerates eighty-eight heresies in the first book. Nor does he persuade himself that he has reviewed all that ever existed, or all the doctrines of those about which he speaks [Col. 0572]; he considers that task beyond human ability (*ibid.*, conclusion).

He derives what he says chiefly from Epiphanius, although he does not follow him in every respect. To Epiphanius he also adds Philaster and Eusebius in Rufinus’s translation, whom he seems deliberately to have read for this very purpose; he further employs the knowledge which he had acquired for himself. Finally, he mentions the Pelagians, while he did not yet have sufficient knowledge of the new heresy of the Nestorians. As soon as he had put the finishing hand to his book, he arranged for it to be carried to Quodvultdeus, so that both Quodvultdeus and the others who would read it might be stirred more ardently to implore from God the grace and light which Augustine needed in order to complete the second part, which was destined to be so useful. But God’s providence did not permit him either to compose or to finish that part; and for this reason Possidius calls the book *On Heresies* an unfinished work.

### 5.

The letter entitled *To Alypius the Elder* belongs approximately to this period, unless this Alypius was someone other than the bishop of Thagaste—although it is not unreasonable to think that the latter had only at this time attained the rank or primacy of the province of Numidia. In any event, whatever year the letter was written, Augustine there relates to Alypius a memorable event in these words:

> “The chief physician Dioscorus is also a faithful Christian, having received grace at the same time. Hear also how this happened; for surely neither that neck nor that tongue would have been subdued except by some miracle. His daughter, his only child and his sole comfort, fell ill and, as the father himself reported, reached the point of complete despair regarding her temporal recovery.  
>   
> “It is said—and it is established, since the admirable and thoroughly Christian man Peregrinus, who had been baptized at the same time as they, reported it to me before the return of brother Paul—that the old man at last turned to imploring Christ’s mercy and bound himself by a vow that he would become a Christian if he saw her restored to health. This happened. But he concealed his intention of fulfilling what he had vowed. Yet the hand was still outstretched. For he was suddenly covered with blindness, and it immediately came to mind why this had happened. He cried out in confession and vowed again that, once his sight had been restored, he would fulfill what he had promised. He recovered his sight and fulfilled his vow; yet the hand was still outstretched.  
>   
> “He had not learned the Creed, or perhaps he had refused to learn it, and had excused himself by saying that he had been unable to do so. God had seen this. Then, after all the rites connected with his reception had been completed, he was struck with paralysis in many, almost all, of his limbs, and even in his tongue. At that point, warned in a dream, he confessed in writing that this had happened to him because he had not recited the Creed. After that confession, the functions of all his limbs were restored except that of his tongue. Nevertheless, he admitted in writing that he had learned the Creed and therefore now knew it by heart, though he remained under the same affliction. Thus all his frivolity was removed from him—frivolity which, as you know, greatly disfigured a certain natural kindness in him and made him a most sacrilegious scoffer at Christians” (*Epist.* 227).

## CHAPTER XI

1. Boniface is reconciled with Placidia, apparently through the intervention, among others, of Count Darius; Augustine seeks Darius’s friendship.  
2. Defeated by the Vandals [Col. 0573], Boniface withdraws to Hippo Regius; the Vandals advance against him to besiege the city; meanwhile Augustine is seized by illness.  
3. Miraculous healings are performed at Augustine’s prayers; he devotes himself entirely to tears and repentance in preparation for his departure; he dies, and after a sacrifice has been offered for the commendation of his burial, he is buried.  
4. The year of Augustine’s death; in that very year he was summoned by Theodosius to the Council of Ephesus.  
5. Some time later Hippo Regius is devastated by fire, but Augustine’s writings are nevertheless preserved there; Possidius appended a catalogue of them to the Life of Augustine which he committed to writing. (See the final volume of this edition.)

### 1.

In the preceding year we saw that Count Boniface, in order to preserve his temporal fortunes, had entered into an alliance with the Vandals. Nevertheless, God was content to exact from Africa the punishments he had decreed through the unjust will of this count. He showed mercy toward Boniface, however, and gave him the opportunity of repairing, in some measure, what he had done, reconciling him with Placidia.

Procopius attributes Boniface’s restoration to favor to the services of the friends whom he had in Rome. Placidia may perhaps have made use of Count Darius’s assistance in this affair. For Darius came to Africa after the publication, in the year 421, of the *Enchiridion on Faith, Hope, and Charity*, and during the final period of Augustine’s life (*Epist.* 231, §7; 229, §1). He had been sent to negotiate peace, to settle the war by discussion, and to prevent anyone’s blood from being sought. In this respect Augustine asserts that Darius surpassed in glory the bravest and most faithful soldiers who, with God assisting them by their own arms, had broken an untamed enemy and secured peace for the state and the provinces (*Epist.* 229, §2).

That Boniface was certainly reconciled with the Empire is clear not only from Procopius but also from Possidius, who says that Boniface was besieged by the Vandals within the walls of Hippo Regius in the year 430 (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 28). Nor is there any doubt that the war was either ended by Darius, or at least postponed, and that the evils which had then reached the height of calamity were temporarily quieted (*Epist.* 230, §3). But from the year 421 no occasion presents itself to which this can suitably apply, unless we say that, while dealing with Boniface, the count was also negotiating with the Vandals and concluded a truce with them. For nothing else seems to be meant by this postponement of the war.

Darius received as a hostage of the peace a certain Verimodus, who, so far as conjecture permits us to determine, was a Roman by birth or at least related by marriage to Boniface. Augustine sends him greetings, and Verimodus returns them; he declares that he rejoices exceedingly that Augustine had remembered him (*ibid.* and *Epist.* 229, §2; 231, §7). Darius professed the Christian religion handed down to him by his ancestors, but he had not sufficiently rejected the vain superstition of the pagans. After reading Augustine, however, he despised pagan rites more fully and more decisively than ever before (*Epist.* 230, §4).

Indeed, he reached such a degree of devotion that the holy Bishop is found speaking of him as a great man, and rejoicing that Darius praised him because Darius loved Christ’s servants for Christ’s sake and was a good man—Christian not merely outwardly, but in Christian charity (*Epist.* 231, §§2, 6). Therefore the holy man considered it important to win his friendship. He wrote to congratulate him on the peace or truce he had made (*Epist.* 229), perhaps displaying the greatest pleasure because what had happened to his friend Boniface was especially welcome. As for his books, Augustine says that they may perhaps not have displeased Darius, provided that Darius had approached their reading with more charity than severity. Finally, he asks Darius to honor him with one of his letters.

Darius complied with his wishes and testified in a very lengthy letter to his goodwill and singular reverence toward the holy man (*Epist.* 230). There he informs Augustine of what he had done to bring about peace, adding that he hoped that, with the support of Augustine’s vows and prayers, the war which he himself had merely postponed might be completely abolished. He mentions the history of Abgar and entreats the holy Bishop to write to him and to send him the books of the *Confessions* as well.

Through the presbyter Lazapus, Darius sent him certain medicines which a physician had said might relieve his illness. He also seems to have added money for the purchase of books for Augustine’s library, although he passed over this matter in silence. The holy man received the count’s gifts and praises with gratitude, because they showed the good intention of the giver and praiser. Accordingly, he answered him with such lively and tender affection that he departed from his usual practice in this respect.

He sent him not only the *Confessions*; wishing to exceed Darius’s request, he added four treatises, which he calls books: *On Faith in Things Not Seen*, *On Patience*, *On Continence*, and *On Providence*, as well as the substantial work *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, commonly called the *Enchiridion* (*Epist.* 231, §7). He asks Darius to write back with his judgment concerning these works, if he should be able to read them before leaving Africa; if not, he should leave that judgment at Carthage, from where his master and brother, Lord Aurelius, might order it to be brought to Augustine.

### 2.

After Placidia had restored Boniface to favor, he left nothing undone to induce the Vandals—with whom he later regretted having entered so close an alliance—to leave Africa, using now prayers and now promises. But he accomplished nothing, and the barbarians complained that he was deceiving them (Procopius). He was therefore forced to take up arms and attack them in order to expel them by force and the sword.

When he engaged them in battle, perhaps toward the end of the year 429, he was defeated and compelled to flee to Hippo, a city that at that time was strongly fortified. In this way God restored him to Augustine, who was soon to depart from the living. Hence one may suppose that God granted Augustine this favor because he had determined to reconcile Boniface not only with the Empire but also with Augustine himself. At the very least, there is no reason to doubt that the holy Bishop exerted every effort in this matter and wisely used so opportune an occasion.

Possidius and several other neighboring bishops also took refuge in Hippo [Col. 0574]. Boniface’s admission into the city was the reason why the Vandals came to besiege it under their king Gaiseric (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 28) in the year 430, toward the end of May or at the beginning of June. At that time blessed Augustine, who departed to heaven on the fifth day before the Kalends of September of that same year, fell into his final illness in the third month of the siege. It is likely that it lasted, as such illnesses commonly do, two or three weeks, since it is observed to have been neither prolonged nor exceptionally brief, and it is otherwise certain that it lasted more than ten days (*ibid.*, ch. 31).

The sorrow which the holy Bishop had felt at the ruin of the other cities of Africa was increased by the siege of his own city in a measure that anyone can easily imagine. “Then,” says Victor of Vita, “that river of eloquence which flowed abundantly through all the fields of the Church was dried up by fear; and the sweetness of a charm poured forth with greater sweetness was turned into the bitterness of wormwood” (Victor of Vita, *On the Vandal Persecution*, book 1, §3).

Augustine was immediately refreshed by the consolation that he then had several bishops with him, among them Possidius, the most distinguished of his disciples. Possidius says:

> “We very frequently conversed with him about these misfortunes and considered the terrible judgments of God set before our eyes, saying: ‘You are just, O Lord, and your judgment is right’ (Psalm 118:137). Likewise grieving, groaning, and weeping, we prayed to the Father of mercies and God of all consolation that he might deign to support us in the same tribulation.  
>   
> “It happened, perhaps, that while we were seated at table with him and conversing there, he said to us: ‘Know that at this time of our calamity I am asking God either to deign to free this city, surrounded by enemies, or, if this is his will, to make his servants strong enough to endure it; or certainly to receive me from this world to himself.’  
>   
> “When he had said this and instructed us, we and all our people, as well as those who were in that same city, thereafter likewise asked the supreme God for these things. And behold, in the third month of the siege he lay down, exhausted by fevers, and suffered that final illness. The Lord certainly did not defraud his servant of the fruit of his prayer. For in due time he obtained both for himself and for that city what he had sought with tearful prayers” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chs. 28–29).

By these words Possidius seems to indicate what Procopius relates: that the barbarians, wearied by the length of the siege, finally withdrew. This gave the citizens the opportunity to abandon the city—a step which Possidius says they took—and to preserve their lives.

### 3.

There is no doubt that Possidius intended to refer this final illness to what he adds shortly afterward in these words:

> “Likewise, I know that a certain sick man came with his illness to one who was himself ill and confined to bed, and asked him to lay his hand upon him so that he might become well. The latter replied that, if he had any power in such matters, he would first have exercised it for himself. The sick man then said that he had been visited and that in a dream he had been told: ‘Go to Bishop Augustine, so that he may lay his hand upon you, and you will be saved.’ When he learned this, he did not delay doing what was requested; and the Lord immediately caused that sick man to leave him healed” (*ibid.*, ch. 29).

It seemed fitting to divine mercy, by this miracle performed through Augustine at the end of his life, as though to seal his holiness in action and his learning and piety in writing.

“I also know,” says the same author, “that the same man, both as presbyter and as bishop, was asked to pray for certain persons suffering from demonic possession. As he prayed, shedding tears, he entreated God, and the demons departed from the people” (*ibid.*). These are all the external miracles of this saint that you will find recorded.

Possidius continues:

> “He used to say to us in familiar conversation that after receiving Baptism even Christians and priests of good reputation ought not to depart from the body without worthy and suitable repentance. He himself did this in the final illness by which he died. For he had ordered that the very few Psalms of David concerning repentance be written out, and while he lay in bed he kept looking at and reading those gatherings of pages, which had been placed against the wall opposite him during the days of his illness; he wept continually and abundantly.  
>   
> “And so that no one might interrupt his concentration, about ten days before he departed from the body he asked us, in the presence of others, not to allow anyone to enter to him except at the hours when the physicians came in to examine him or when food was brought to him. This was observed and done, and throughout that time he devoted himself to prayer.  
>   
> “Until his very last illness he preached the word of God in the Church without interruption, eagerly and courageously, with sound mind and sound judgment. With all the members of his body healthy, his sight and hearing unimpaired, and—as Scripture says—with us standing by and seeing him and praying together with him, he fell asleep with his fathers, nourished in a good old age. In our presence a sacrifice was offered to God for the commendation of his bodily burial, and he was buried” (*ibid.*, ch. 31).

Prosper records his death under the year 430, that is, when Theodosius was consul for the thirteenth time and Valentinian for the third, in these words:

> “Augustine, bishop, outstanding in every respect, dies on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, responding to Julian’s books amid the attacks of the besieging Vandals at the very end of his days, and persevering gloriously in defense of Christian grace” (Prosper, *Chronicle*, under the year 430).

He departed this life at the age of seventy-six, nearly forty of those years having been spent in the duties first of the presbyterate and then of the episcopate. God had granted him such a prolonged life so that he might serve the usefulness and welfare of the Church.

Possidius continues:

> “He made no will, because, as a poor man of God, he had nothing from which to make one. He always ordered that the Church’s library and all its books be carefully preserved for posterity. Whatever the church possessed in money or ornaments he left to the faithful presbyter who, under him, administered the household of the Church. He did not treat his relatives, whether they were in the religious life or outside it, in the ordinary manner of the world, either during his life or at his death. While he was still alive, whenever there was need, he gave them what he gave to others—not so that they might have riches, but so that they might have little or no want.  
>   
> “He left the Church a sufficiently numerous clergy and monasteries of men and women, full of those who practiced continence together with their superiors, along with libraries containing his own books and treatises and those of other holy men” (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 31).

### 4.

Marcellinus assigned Augustine’s death to the year 429 (Marcellinus, *Chronicle*). But Prosper’s testimony, according to which it occurred in 430, supports that date; no more splendid testimony could be desired for the consecration of the memory of the holy Bishop.

For when the heresy of the Nestorians moved Theodosius the Younger to summon an ecumenical council at Ephesus, and for this reason to send letters to all the metropolitans, he also sent to Africa through a certain *magistrianus* named Ebagnio (Liberatus, *Brief Account*, ch. 5) a sacred imperial rescript addressed especially to Augustine—that is, rather to Augustine than to Capreolus, then bishop of Carthage (Capreolus, *Letter to the Council of Ephesus*, part 2, act 1). In this rescript the Emperor made a special request that Augustine deign to attend the council.

Another letter, sent in July of the following year to those same metropolitans whom the Emperor had invited to the council, also shows the place which Augustine held in his estimation (Noris, *History of the Pelagian Heresy*, book 2, ch. 9). For in that letter the most illustrious Bishop is placed immediately after the Bishop of Thessalonica and before all the other metropolitans.

The Emperor’s sacred letter to the metropolitans is dated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December in the year 430 (Council of Ephesus, part 1, canon 32). Therefore no one can rightly say that Augustine died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September in the year 429.

### 5.

After Augustine’s death, Hippo Regius continued to withstand the attacks of the Vandals. Although they had blockaded the port itself (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 28), they were never able to take the city, either by force or by surrender. Thus, after a long period during which they had expended their efforts uselessly before its walls, they lifted the siege, which had lasted almost fourteen full months (Procopius).

Not long after the siege of Hippo had been lifted, Boniface, having received substantial aid from Rome and Constantinople, again fought the Vandals in battle, but with equally unfortunate results. The Romans were completely routed; each fled in a different direction; Boniface, however, set sail for Italy in the year 432. The inhabitants of Hippo, finally deprived, as is most probable, of every hope of defense, abandoned their city.

The enemy destroyed it by fire, except for the library which the holy man had left to the Church. This library was preserved amid the flames and the Arian barbarians, since Possidius directs to the library at Hippo those who might wish to read or copy more accurate copies of Augustine’s works (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 18). This could certainly have happened only through God’s extraordinary protection (Baronius, under the year 430; Rivius, *Life of St Augustine*, book 4, ch. 11, §8).

The envious devil, since he had been wholly unable to destroy the works of so great a Doctor through the Vandals, employed various devices and slanders in order at least to weaken their authority and teaching, spreading them in many places among different people. But we do not think it belongs to our purpose to discuss that matter here, or to explain how God continually raised up against him outstanding defenders in Prosper, Hilary, and Pope Celestine. Nor is it our purpose to heap together here all the praises with which men distinguished in the Church honored Augustine both living and dead.

Possidius, bishop of Calama, who had lived in his company for nearly forty years (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, ch. 31), committed Augustine’s deeds to memory on the basis both of what he had himself observed and of what he had heard from Augustine in familiar conversation. He judged that he ought to employ for this purpose the abilities of intellect and speech which he had received by divine gift, so that he might contribute something to the edification of the Catholic Church.

Moreover, in order to satisfy in every way those who were inflamed by a holy thirst for truth, he appended to the Life of the holy Doctor a catalogue of his works. Thus those who preferred divine truth to earthly riches could, amid that astonishing multitude of writings, select the works they judged most useful to themselves and share them without envy with those in need (*ibid.*, ch. 18).

He composed this work after Hippo Regius had already fallen into ashes and, as seems likely, after Boniface had died (*ibid.*, ch. 28)—that is, after the year 432. It is nevertheless evident that it was written before the year 439, when Carthage was conquered by the Vandals, since Possidius indicates that Carthage and Cirta had not yet been destroyed but were still standing, supported by divine and human protection.

As for the quality and greatness of the man whom he commits to memory and writing, Possidius wishes us to see them in the books and treatises Augustine published for the Church; in these, he asserts, Augustine is always found living among the faithful.

“And indeed,” the same Possidius continues, “in his writings that priest, acceptable and dear to God, is shown—so far as the truth shining upon us permits us to see—to have lived in the Catholic Church in right and sound faith, hope, and charity. Those who, by reading him as he writes about divine things, make progress acknowledge this. But I think that those who were able to hear and see him speaking in the Church while present, and especially those who knew his conduct among men, could have profited still more from him.

“For he was not only a learned scribe in the kingdom of heaven, bringing forth new and old things from his treasure, and one of those merchants who, having found a precious pearl, sold all that he had and bought it (Matthew 13:45–46); he was also one of those of whom it is written, ‘So speak and so act’ (James 2:12), and of whom the Savior says, ‘Whoever does and teaches these things to men shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5:19).”

## [THE FIRST VOLUME OF ST AUGUSTINE.]

[Col. 0579]

## PREFACE TO THE FIRST VOLUME

[Note: [Col. 0579] Here begins the first volume of the Benedictine edition, preceded only by the dedicatory letter. M.]

Learned Reader, there is no need for us to write a lengthy preface concerning the edition of this volume. This part contains precisely the same little works of Augustine that were included in the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars. The only difference is that we have relegated to the Appendix certain works which learned men had regarded as genuine compositions of Augustine; and that we have moved some of the holy Doctor’s works from their previous positions in order, as far as possible, to preserve the sequence and chronological order in which each work was produced by its author.

The works which Augustine wrote when he was young and not yet a presbyter have indeed been arranged appropriately in this volume. Nevertheless, first place has been given to the books of the *Retractations*, which he published in old age, as a preliminary introduction to the other books. The books of the *Retractations* are followed, not without reason, by the books of the *Confessions*, which he published as bishop. For just as, if anything obscure, doubtful, or insufficiently consonant with truth had slipped into his writings, he explained, unraveled, and corrected it by revising them, so in the books of the *Confessions*, if anything in his conduct and life had strayed from the path of the true piety which he teaches, he expiated it by penitential confession.

Thus, in the books of the *Retractations*, he inspires a sincere and entirely unfeigned love of truth together with singular modesty; in the *Confessions*, true piety and discipline. Anyone who approaches his teaching wholeheartedly ought to be equipped with these qualities.

After these works had been read through with abundant profit and great pleasure, the editions of Erasmus and the Louvain scholars placed certain little works next: namely, *On Grammar*, the *Categories*, the *Principles of Dialectic*, and the *Principles of Rhetoric*. Thoughtful readers, who desired in them Augustine’s learning, intelligence, and skill, turned back from reading the works of the first volume almost at its threshold, as though works of the same kind were to follow.

But when we examined these trifles more closely and discovered by certain arguments that they did not belong to Augustine, we sent them off into the class of spurious writings. In this way, after reading the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, students would encounter no obstacle to reading the books which Augustine composed soon after his conversion.

Nor should the first monuments of his noble intellect therefore be passed over hastily, as commonly happens to many, or merely greeted as though from the threshold, on the assumption that they contain no deeply stored learning. They were composed by a catechumen and neophyte in polished style and in the form of dialogues. Certainly, he himself vigorously discusses and most sagaciously resolves there questions of the greatest difficulty—questions over which once the greatest intellects labored and failed.

Who would not admire the seriousness and force with which, in the course of discussion, he treats the apprehension of truth against the Academics, the blessed life, the order of things, the magnitude and immortality of the soul, and other matters of great importance that arise along the way? Then, in the five final works of the same volume, which he composed against the Manichaeans, with how many varied and manifold arguments does he weaken and overthrow their heresy—arguments powerful and unconquerable!

Saint Paulinus used to say that he admired and revered these works so greatly that he believed the words dictated in them had been given by God (*Epist.* 24, §2). Finally, while fulfilling the duties of his novitiate and thoroughly subjecting to the Catholic faith a mind recently converted from heresy, Augustine omitted nothing that could free others from those pernicious errors into which he had unfortunately fallen.

Whether he attacks the philosophers or the Manichaeans, he fortifies the reader’s mind against their errors and fixes more deeply in it the foundations of true faith and Christian religion. Moreover, from the beginning of his life the holy man was so disposed toward a better purpose that he did not treat the liberal arts in the barren manner of ordinary authors, but with an entirely Christian mind, so far as to lead the minds of his readers toward love of the Creator. He explains his mind on this subject in book 1 of the *Retractations*, chapter 6. For this reason, after completing five books on music, he added a sixth, which directs and raises the entire subject toward God.

Now anyone who wishes to accustom his mind to Augustinian teaching and to imbue it thoroughly with Augustine’s precepts and institutions must necessarily advance through the same stages and gradually rise to its complete perfection. One should not be reluctant to follow the path taken by so great a man as Augustine. Either the dignity of the subject or the method of treating it invites us onward, for everything is worthy of so great and truly Christian a man; everywhere one finds something to learn, or a lesson in how to learn it.

Indeed, in the books under discussion, profound judgments frequently occur, extremely useful for educating students; any one of them could serve anyone as a summary of an entire book. Moreover, in the works we are discussing, which he wrote in youth, the style moves more richly and is fuller of the sap of eloquence; it possesses more of the vitality of a lively intellect than the works we meditate upon in already sluggish age.

Experience establishes this especially in these first books, which Augustine, perfectly trained in the precepts of rhetoric, polished shortly before and shortly after his baptism. These works therefore possess very great importance, whether one considers his intellect and eloquence or his learning and piety.

What we say about all of them was experienced in particular with regard to the work Augustine entitled *On Free Will* by Odo, later bishop of Cambrai. By chance, after purchasing this book from a certain cleric, Odo threw it into a corner of his chest, since, still devoted to worldly wisdom, he took more pleasure in reading Plato than Augustine.

But when, after nearly two months, while lecturing to his students on Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*, he reached the fourth book, in which free will is discussed, he remembered the book he had bought and ordered his servant to bring it to him. After reading two or three pages, he summoned his students and said: “Truly, until now I did not know that Augustine possessed such great and such delightful eloquence.”

As he read through the third book, he was changed into another man; he gradually abandoned his schools, attended the church, and finally renounced the world. We learn this from Herimann, the monk of Tournai [Note: [Col. 0581] Herimann, *Narrative of the Restoration of the Abbey of St Martin of Tournai*, §4, *Spicilegium*, vol. 12.]

Paulinus, whom we have already praised, had experienced the same thing (*Epist.* 25, §1). He used to read most eagerly Augustine’s earliest writings against the Manichaean heresy, writings overflowing with scholastic learning and sweet as heavenly honeycombs, as medicines and nourishment for his soul.

“These books,” he says, “I keep for reading; in them I delight; from them I take food—not food that perishes, but that which produces the substance of eternal life.” Then he exclaims in Augustine’s praise: “O truly the salt of the earth, by which our inmost hearts are seasoned, lest they be made to perish through the error of the world,” and so forth.
