Moreover, it is unnecessary to explain in detail how much labor we devoted to correcting this volume. We prefixed admonitions to the individual works and supplied the subject of each book at the beginning. We have frequently altered the headings of the chapters, which were often inelegant, but have retained their numerical markings in the margins so that confusion would not arise in the citations already in use; nevertheless, we have sometimes altered and multiplied the sections and have thought it useful to divide them into numbered paragraphs as well, so that Augustine might be read more easily. We have added notes in the lower margin wherever we have explained the basis of the more important corrections. We have also compiled an Index of Subjects and of Scripture for the works in this volume, which, as we hope, will be of some use to students. [Note: [Col. 0581] We have thought fit not to follow the arrangement of the Maurist Fathers entirely. For a separate analytical index appended to each volume is useless, since the whole work is to be concluded with a general index; at least it will be much more useful to have placed an index of subjects, as they occur in each volume, at the end of each individual volume. This is lacking in the Benedictine edition, a lack which many people, and not without reason, regret. M.] Finally, we have done other things that are fully explained above in the general preface.

[Col. 0581]

# THE TWO BOOKS OF THE RETRACTATIONS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO

[Note: [Col. 0583] Written in the year 426 or 427.]

## MANUSCRIPTS USED TO CORRECT THE BOOKS OF THE RETRACTATIONS

The Corbie manuscript, of excellent quality and nearly nine hundred years old; the Theodoric manuscript, formerly belonging to Hincmar of Rheims; and the Joly manuscript, eight hundred years old, were used. Also the very ancient manuscripts of Fleury, Albi, and Saint-Bénigne; and, somewhat later in date, those of Pratelles, Saint-Michel, Bec, three Victorine manuscripts, three Sorbonne manuscripts, the Royal manuscript, the Royal Aachen manuscript, and the German manuscript; besides several others which, through the efforts of learned men, were collated for our purposes.

These are the manuscripts of Arnulf, Cîteaux, Saint-Vaast, and the Vatican; six English manuscripts, namely, three from the Bodleian Library, two from Merton College, and one from the Laudian archive. The readings of these six manuscripts, transmitted to us after this edition had already been completed by the distinguished scholar E. Bernard, Professor of Astronomy at Oxford, confirm in many places the corrections made here. We were also assisted by readings collected by the Louvain scholars from four Belgian manuscripts. Consult the *Notice of the Manuscripts* in the volume entitled *Augustiniana*.

Finally, the following earlier and more carefully corrected editions were used: Am., that is, the edition printed by Johann Amerbach in 1505; Er., the edition printed under the care of Desiderius Erasmus by the Froben press in 1529; and Lov., the edition issued from the Plantin press in 1577 according to the revision of the Louvain theologians.

## EDITIONS ALSO COLLATIONED

1. Er. Guill., that is, the second edition of Erasmus, published at Paris in the house of Charlotte Guillard in 1541, and much enlarged over the Basel edition.

2. Lugd., that is, the Lyon edition of 1561.

3. Venet., that is, the Venetian edition of 1584.

4. Lov. Par., that is, the Louvain edition published at Paris in 1651.

5. Lov., that is, the second Louvain edition, published at Antwerp in 1662.

6. Benedict., that is, the Benedictine edition reprinted at Antwerp in 1700–1702. M.

In these books of the *Retractations*, we represent the chapter headings, as well as the beginnings of the works cited at the end of each chapter, as they appear in the manuscripts, though occasionally somewhat differently from the form in which they were presented in the printed editions.

## (C)

# NOTICE CONCERNING THE TWO BOOKS OF THE RETRACTATIONS

[Col. 0581]

What impelled Saint Augustine to review and correct his writings is disclosed by his preface to the following books. He undertook this task toward the end of his life, certainly not long before the year of Christ 427. For in the fourth book of *On Christian Doctrine*, which in the *Retractations* he testifies that he wrote while engaged in this task, he counts approximately eight years or more from his journey among the Caesareans; from this it is clear that he returned from there in the latter part of the year 418.

Since he had resolved to subject all his writings to examination—books, letters, and sermons, whether he had dictated them or delivered them—he began with his books. He had already reviewed all those published up to that time when he wrote his second letter to Quodvultdeus (*Letter* 224), perhaps in the year 428. At that time Prosper and Hilary in Gaul had not yet learned that any part of this work had been published, as is evident from Hilary’s letter (*Letter* 226). Nevertheless, Augustine writes in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3, that the two books had been completed before he received their letter.

Thus, what Possidius says in chapter 28—“Shortly before the day of his death, he reviewed the books he had dictated and published”—should not be interpreted strictly from the literal details of the wording, especially since, in that same passage, he reports that two volumes on this subject had been completed before the Vandals’ invasion of Africa.

Augustine was also devoting attention to revising his letters. He had already reread a good many of them diligently, although he had not yet committed any observations on them to writing, when suddenly he heard that Julian the Pelagian’s later eight books had appeared. At Alypius’s urging, he undertook to refute them; meanwhile he pursued the work he had begun with less intensity, and finally, overtaken by death, was unable to complete it.

Moreover, the holy Doctor arranged his books, generally reviewed in chronological order, into two classes. One volume was to contain the corrections of those he had written from the day of his conversion until he became bishop; the other, those of all the rest. Here he follows the titles, dates, subjects, and occasions of all of them, and finally carefully records the beginnings of each.

Possidius gives this work the title *On the Review of the Books*. Nevertheless, all the published and manuscript copies call it the books of the *Retractations*, with perhaps one exception: the very ancient Corbie manuscript, which, changing the word, has at the end of the first book: “Here ends the first book of the *Recognitions*.” In Augustine himself—both in his letter to Quodvultdeus and in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapters 3 and 4, and also in the brief epilogue appended to these books—the title *Retractation*, or *Retractations*, is applied to this work.

This title is especially appropriate, because it makes clear that the work involves not only the censure of errors but also the defense of what was correctly said, and the strengthening, through renewed treatment, of passages that uninformed readers had disturbed. “I was revising my little works,” he says in the aforementioned letter to Quodvultdeus, “and if anything in them offended me or could offend others, I dealt with it partly by criticizing and partly by defending what ought and could be read.”

Finally, the ancients celebrated this work under that name: Prosper, in his letter to the Genoese; Cassiodorus the senator, *On the Institution of Divine Scripture*, chapter 16; Bede, preface to the book of the *Retractations on the Acts*, and elsewhere.

## Prologue

[Col. 0583]

### 1

It is a long time since I began and resolved to do what, with the Lord’s assistance, I am now undertaking, because I do not think it should be postponed: namely, to review my little works—whether in books, letters, or treatises—with a certain judicial severity, and to mark with a censor’s pen whatever displeases me. [Note: [Col. 0583] The Louvain editors read, “It is a long time since that.” But the manuscripts designated above prefer the reading, “It is a long time since,” which is certainly familiar to Augustine. Thus in Letter 71 to Jerome, no. 2, one reads: “which it is a long time since I have been expecting.” Er. Guill. reads “It is a long time since that,” like the Louvain editors. M.]

No one, unless he is foolish, will dare to criticize me because I criticize my own errors. But if someone says that I should not have said things which later displeased even me, he speaks the truth and agrees with me. For he is criticizing things of which I too am a critic. I ought not to criticize them if I ought to have said them.

[Note: [Col. 0583] The Louvain edition adds: “But whoever could not occupy the first place in wisdom should at least occupy the second place in modesty, so that whoever was unable to say everything that should not be repented of may at least repent of what he recognizes should not have been said.” This is not found in the editions of Johann Amerbach or Desiderius Erasmus, nor in the fourteen manuscripts that we examined. It seems to have been borrowed from Augustine’s *Letter* 143 to Marcellinus. Er. Guill. agrees with the Louvain edition. M.]

### 2

But let everyone understand what I am doing as he wishes. Nevertheless, in this matter too I ought to have kept before me that apostolic saying: “If we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:31).

The statement also written in Scripture, “You will not escape sin through much speaking” (Proverbs 10:19), greatly frightens me—not because I have written much, or because many things that were not dictated were nevertheless written down from what I said—for heaven forbid that I should count as “much speaking” what is necessary, however numerous and lengthy the words in which it is said—but because I fear this saying of Holy Scripture on account of the many discussions I have held. From them, without doubt, many things can be gathered which, if not false, at least may appear, or even be proved, unnecessary.

And whom among Christ’s faithful did he not frighten when he said: “Every idle word that anyone speaks, he will give an account of it on the day of judgment” (Matthew 12:36)? Hence also his apostle James says: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19). And elsewhere: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, knowing that you will receive the greater judgment. For we all offend in many ways. If anyone does not offend in word, he is a perfect man” (James 3:1–2).

I do not claim this perfection even now, when I am already old; how much less when I began to write or speak publicly as a young man. So much was granted to me that whenever it was necessary to speak to the people in my presence, I was very rarely allowed to keep silent and listen to others, and to be quick to hear but slow to speak.

It remains, therefore, that I should judge myself under the one Teacher, whose judgment concerning my offenses I desire to escape. I consider that there are many teachers when they hold opinions that are different and opposed to one another. But when they all say the same thing—and say what is true—they do not depart from the instruction of the one true Teacher. They offend not when they say many things belonging to him, but when they add things of their own. Thus, through much speaking, they fall even into false speaking.

### 3

I have decided to write this so that I may place it in the hands of people from whom I cannot recall for correction what I have already published. Nor do I pass over those things which I wrote when I was already a catechumen, although I had abandoned the hope that I had entertained as earthly, yet was still inflated by the habit of secular literature.

Those writings too have entered the knowledge of those who copy and read them, and they are read profitably if some things are forgiven; or, even if they are not forgiven, one should not remain attached to the errors. Therefore, whoever will read these works should not imitate me in error but in progress toward what is better.

For anyone who reads my little works in the order in which they were written will perhaps discover how I progressed through writing. In this work, therefore, I shall take care, as far as I can, that the reader may know that order.

# BOOK ONE

## IN WHICH THE BOOKS HE WROTE BEFORE BECOMING BISHOP ARE REVIEWED

[Col. 0585]

# CHAPTER ONE

## Against the Academics: Three Books

### 1

After I had abandoned both the things I had acquired through the desires of this world and those I wished to acquire, and had devoted myself to the leisure of the Christian life, I wrote my first work, while still unbaptized, against the Academics, or concerning the Academics. I did this so that, with whatever arguments I could, I might drive from my mind—since their arguments had also disturbed me—their claims that induce many people to despair of finding the truth, that prevent anyone from assenting to anything, and that prevent the wise person from approving anything at all as manifest and certain, since everything appears obscure and uncertain to them. This was accomplished through the Lord’s mercy and assistance.

### 2

Nevertheless, in those same three books of mine, I do not approve of having referred so many times to Fortune (*Lib.* 1, ch. 1, nos. 1 and 7). I did not intend by this name to suggest some goddess, but the fortuitous outcome of events, whether involving our body or external goods and evils.

That is why there are also those words which no religion forbids one to utter: *forte*, “perhaps”; *forsan*, “perhaps”; *forsitan*, “possibly”; *fortasse*, “perhaps”; *fortuito*, “by chance.” Yet all of this must be referred to divine providence. I did not conceal this there either, when I said: “For perhaps what is commonly called Fortune is governed by some hidden order; and in things we call nothing else ‘chance’ except that whose reason and cause are hidden.”

I did say this, but nevertheless I regret having used the word Fortune in that passage, since I see that people have acquired a very bad habit: where they ought to say, “This is what God willed,” they say, “This is what Fortune willed.”

Again, where I said: “It is so arranged, whether on account of our merits or of the necessity of nature, that the divine mind joined to mortals does not in any way attain the harbor of philosophy” (*ibid.*), either neither of those two qualifications should have been stated, since even without them the meaning could remain complete, or it would have been enough to say, “on account of our merits,” as is true of the misery inherited from Adam. I should not have added, “or of the necessity of nature,” since the harsh necessity of our nature arose as a result of preceding iniquity.

Likewise, where I said there that “nothing at all should be worshiped, and everything should be rejected that mortal eyes behold or that any sense perceives” (*ibid.*, no. 3), the words should have been added so that it would say, “whatever any sense of the mortal body perceives.” For there is also a sense belonging to the mind.

At that time, however, I was speaking in the manner of those who say that sense belongs only to the body and that sensible things are only corporeal. Thus, wherever I have spoken in this way, the ambiguity has not been sufficiently avoided except among those accustomed to this manner of speaking.

I also said: “What else do you think it is to live happily than to live according to what is best in a human being?” Then, explaining shortly afterward what I meant by “what is best in a human being,” I said: “Who would doubt that the best thing in a human being is nothing other than that part of the soul to which, when it rules, everything else in a human being ought to obey?” And, so that you would not ask for another definition: “This may be called mind or reason” (*ibid.*, ch. 2, no. 5).

This is true, for as far as human nature is concerned, nothing in a person is better than mind and reason. But the person who wishes to live happily ought not to live according to mind and reason alone; otherwise he lives according to the human being, when he ought to live according to God in order to attain happiness. To attain that happiness, the mind must not be content with itself but must be subjected to God.

Again, in replying to the person with whom the discussion was being held, I said: “Here you are certainly not mistaken; and, that this may be a favorable omen for what follows, I should gladly wish it for you” (*ibid.*, ch. 4, no. 11). Although this was said not seriously but jokingly, I nevertheless wish I had not used that word. I do not remember ever having read the word *omen*, either in our sacred Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0586] We nevertheless read *omen* in 3 Kings 20:33. But Augustine either had not read it in the version he used, or, because the passage concerns pagan men, did not think that its use there justified approving a profane term.], or in the speech of any ecclesiastical writer. The word *abomination*, however, is derived from it and occurs frequently in the divine books.

### 3

In the second book, the quasi-fable about Philocalia and Philosophy—that they are sisters born of the same parent—is entirely foolish and tasteless (*Lib.* 2, ch. 3, no. 7).

For either the thing called *philocalia* is concerned only with trifles and therefore has no rational kinship with philosophy, or, if this name deserves honor because, translated into Latin, it signifies love of beauty, and the beauty of true and supreme wisdom is involved, then the very same *philocalia* that is philosophy exists in incorporeal and supreme realities; they are not in any way like two sisters.

Elsewhere, when I was discussing the soul, I said: “I shall return to heaven more secure” (*Lib.* 2, ch. 9, no. 22). I ought rather to have said “I shall go,” than “I shall return,” since I would then have spoken more securely in view of those who think that human souls, because of the merits of their sins, fell or were cast down from heaven and thrust into these bodies [Note: [Col. 0587] The Platonists, as can be seen in *The City of God*, book 12, chapter 26.].

I nevertheless did not hesitate to say this because I said “to heaven” as though I had said “to God,” who is its author and creator. The blessed Cyprian likewise did not hesitate to say: “Since we possess a body from the earth and a spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven” (Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*). And it is written in Ecclesiastes: “The spirit will return to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7).

This must certainly be understood in such a way that we do not contradict the Apostle when he says that those not yet born had done neither good nor evil (Romans 9:11). Without question, then, there is a certain original region of the soul’s blessedness, and that is God himself. He did not generate the soul from himself, but created it from nothing else, just as he created the body from the earth.

As for the soul’s origin, by which it comes to be in the body, whether each soul derives from that one soul who was first created when the human being was made a living soul, or whether individual souls are similarly made individually, I neither knew then nor know now.

### 4

In the third book I said: “You ask what I think; I believe that the highest good of the human being is in the mind” (*Lib.* 3, ch. 12, no. 27). I should more truly have said, “in God,” for the mind enjoys God in order to be blessed, as its highest good.

Nor do I approve of what I said: “It is clearly permissible to swear by every divine thing” (*ibid.*, ch. 16, no. 35). [Note: [Col. 0587] Erasmus and the Louvain edition read, “It is pleasing to swear”; but, more correctly, Amerbach and eighteen manuscripts read, “It is clear to swear,” a phrase taken from Terence, *Eunuchus*, act 2, scene 3.]

Again, what I said about the Academics—that they knew the truth, which they called something like the probable, and that I called this very probable thing false, which they approved—was incorrectly stated for two reasons. Either it was false to say that something which in some way resembles a truth is false, since in its own kind it too is true; or it was false to say that they approved these things which they called probable, since they approved nothing and maintained that the wise person approves nothing. But because they also called this very thing “probable” *approvable*, I came to speak of them in this way.

The praise with which I exalted Plato, or the Platonic or Academic philosophers, so highly (*ibid.*, ch. 17, no. 37) that it was not fitting to exalt impious men so greatly, also displeased me, and not without reason—especially since Christian doctrine must be defended against their great errors.

Again, when comparing Cicero’s arguments, which he used in his Academic books, I said that my arguments were “trifles” (*ibid.*, ch. 20, no. 45), although I refuted those arguments with the greatest certainty. Even though I said this jokingly, and it appears more a case of irony, it nevertheless should not have been said.

This work begins as follows: “Would that, Romanianus, a man suited to himself—”

# CHAPTER TWO

## On the Blessed Life: One Book

It happened that I wrote the book *On the Blessed Life* not after the books *Against the Academics*, but in the midst of them. It arose from the occasion of my birthday and was completed through a three-day discussion, as the book itself sufficiently indicates.

In that book it was agreed among us, who were jointly seeking the answer, that the blessed life is nothing other than the perfect knowledge of God.

But I do not approve of the fact that there I attributed more than I should have to Manlius Theodorus, to whom I dedicated the book, although he was a learned and Christian man (in the preface, no. 7 and following). Nor do I approve of having referred to Fortune so often there.

Nor do I approve of having said that, during this present life, the blessed life dwells solely in the mind of the wise person, regardless of the condition of his body (Disputation 3). The Apostle hopes for perfect knowledge of God in the life to come—that is, knowledge greater than which none can be possessed by a human being—and this alone should be called the blessed life. In that life the incorruptible and immortal body will also be subjected to its spirit without any distress or resistance.

I found this book interrupted in our manuscript, with a considerable portion missing; it had been copied in this form by certain brothers, and when I wrote these *Retractations* I had not yet found an intact copy from which to correct it.

This book begins as follows: “If I were approaching the harbor of philosophy—”

# CHAPTER THREE

## On Order: Two Books

### 1

At the same time, amid the books written about the Academics, I also wrote two books *On Order*. In them a major question is discussed: whether divine providence’s order encompasses all good and evil.

But when I saw that the matter was difficult to understand, and that it could be brought to the comprehension of those with whom I was discussing it only with considerable difficulty, I preferred to speak about the order of study, by which one can advance from corporeal things to incorporeal things.

### 2

Nevertheless, in these books too I am displeased by the frequent insertion of the word Fortune (*Lib.* 2, ch. 9, no. 27). I am also displeased that I did not add the word “body” when I spoke of bodily sense (*ibid.*, book 1, chapters 1, 2, and elsewhere).

And I am displeased that I attributed so much to the liberal disciplines (*ibid.*, ch. 8; and book 2, ch. 14), which many saints know very little about; indeed, some who know them are not saints.

I also regret that I mentioned the Muses as though they were certain goddesses, although I did so jokingly (*ibid.*, ch. 3, no. 6). I regret that I called wonder a vice (*ibid.*, no. 8). I regret that I said philosophers who were not endowed with true piety shone with the light of virtue.

I also regret that I commended two worlds—one sensible, the other intelligible (*ibid.*, ch. 11, nos. 31–32)—not in the person of Plato or the Platonists but in my own voice, as though the Lord too had wished to signify this by saying not, “My kingdom is not of the world,” but, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36).

Yet this could be found expressed in another way. If another world is signified by the Lord Christ, it could more appropriately be understood as the world in which there will be a new heaven and a new earth, when what we pray for will be fulfilled as we say: “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10).

Nor was Plato mistaken in saying that there is an intelligible world, if we attend not to the term—which is not customary in ecclesiastical usage in this matter—but to the reality itself.

He called the intelligible world the very eternal and unchangeable reason by which God made the world. Anyone who denies that this exists must consequently say either that God made what he made irrationally, or that, when he was making it—or before he made it—he did not know what he was making, if he had no reason for making it. But if he did have such a reason, as he certainly did, Plato seems to have called that reason the intelligible world.

Nevertheless, we would not use this name if we were already sufficiently instructed in ecclesiastical literature.

### 3

Nor do I approve of the fact that, after saying, “The greatest effort must be devoted to the best morals,” I immediately added: “For our God will not be able to hear us in any other way, but he will hear those who live well very readily” (*Lib.* 2, ch. 20, no. 52).

This was said as though God does not hear sinners. Someone said this in the Gospel, but he was a man who had not yet known Christ, by whom he had already been enlightened in body (John 9:30–31).

Nor do I approve of having given the philosopher Pythagoras so much praise (*ibid.*, ch. 20, no. 53) that anyone who hears or reads this might think that I believed there were no errors in Pythagorean doctrine, although there are many, and serious ones.

This work begins as follows: “When I consider the order of things, Zenobius—”

# CHAPTER FOUR

## The Two Books of the Soliloquies

### 1

During this period I also wrote two volumes, in accordance with my study and love of investigating the truth [Note: [Col. 0589] The Louvain edition reads, “of reason.” But most manuscripts, as well as Amerbach and Erasmus, read, “by reason.” The Paris Louvain edition reads, “by reason.” M.], questioning myself about the matters I most desired to know and answering myself as though we were two persons—reason and I—although I was alone.

For this reason I called the work *Soliloquies*. It nevertheless remained unfinished. Even so, the first book asked, and to some extent made clear, what kind of person someone who wishes to attain wisdom ought to be. Wisdom is perceived not by bodily sense but by the mind. At the end of the book it is gathered by a certain line of reasoning that the things which truly exist are immortal.

In the second book, the question of the soul’s immortality is discussed at length but is not completed.

### 2

In these books I certainly do not approve of what I said in my prayer: “God, who did not wish anyone except the pure to know the truth” (*Lib.* 1, ch. 1, no. 2). [Note: [Col. 0589] “God, who wished only the pure to know the truth.” This is the reading of the Vatican manuscript and of book 1 of the *Sentences*, distinction 2; it is indeed clearer, but the other reading, which we have retained, is more familiar to Augustine. Thus in book 3 *Against the Academics*, chapter 17: “which would be unknown except to a few wise men.”]

It can be answered that many who are not pure nevertheless know many truths. Nor is it stated here what “the truth” is, which only the pure can know, or what it means to know.

Nor do I approve of the statement there: “God, whose kingdom is the whole world that sense does not perceive” (*ibid.*, ch. 1, no. 3). If God is to be understood, the words should have been added so that it would say, “which the sense of the mortal body does not perceive.”

If “world” is intended—“the world which sense does not perceive”—then it is rightly understood as the world that will exist with a new heaven and a new earth. But even here the words “of the mortal body” should have been added to clarify that the sense is the sense of the mortal body.

At that time I was still speaking in the manner in which sense is properly called bodily sense. There is no need constantly to repeat what I have already said above about this (*Retractations* 1, chapters 1 and 3), but this should be remembered wherever this expression occurs in my writings.

### 3

When I said concerning the Father and the Son, “He who generates and he who is generated are one” (*Lib.* 1, ch. 1, no. 4), I should have said, “They are one,” as the Truth himself plainly says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Nor do I approve of having said that, once God is understood in this present life, the soul is already blessed, unless perhaps this is understood as a matter of hope.

Again, what I said—“There is not just one path by which one reaches union with wisdom” (*Lib.* 1, ch. 13, no. 23)—is badly expressed, as though there were another path besides Christ, who said: “I am the way” (John 14:6).

This offense against religious ears should therefore have been avoided, although there is one universal way, while there are other paths of which we sing in the Psalm: “Make your ways known to me, O Lord, and teach me your paths” (Psalm 24:4).

And when I said there that “these sensible things must be utterly fled” (*Lib.* 1, ch. 14, no. 24), I should have taken care not to appear to hold the opinion of that false philosopher Porphyry, who said: “Every body must be fled.”

I did not say “all sensible things” but “these,” that is, corruptible things. Yet I should rather have said: “Such sensible things will not exist in the heaven and the new earth of the future age.”

### 4

In another passage I said that those educated in the liberal disciplines, “without doubt, bring out by learning those disciplines buried in themselves through forgetfulness, and in a certain way dig them up again” (*Lib.* 2, ch. 20, no. 35).

I reject this as well. It is more credible that uneducated people can give true answers concerning certain disciplines when they are questioned properly because the light of eternal reason is present in them to the extent that they are capable of grasping it, and in that light they perceive these unchangeable truths—not because they once knew them and have forgotten them, as Plato or others of that kind thought.

Against this opinion, I discussed at length, in the twelfth book *On the Trinity*, the opportunity provided by the work I had undertaken (*On the Trinity* 12.15).

This work begins as follows: “As I turn over many varied matters within myself—”

# CHAPTER FIVE

## On the Immortality of the Soul: One Book

### 1

After the books of the *Soliloquies*, when I had returned from the countryside to Milan, I wrote the book *On the Immortality of the Soul*. I had intended it to serve as a kind of memorandum for completing the *Soliloquies*, which had remained unfinished.

But somehow, against my will, it fell into people’s hands and came to be counted among my little works. At the beginning, because of the compression and brevity of its reasoning, it is so obscure that, when it is read, it tires even my own attention, and it is scarcely intelligible to me myself.

### 2

Then, while considering that only human souls were involved, I said in one argument in that book: “There can be no discipline in that which learns nothing.”

Elsewhere I said: “No thing comprehends through knowledge except what belongs to some discipline” (ch. 1, no. 1). It did not occur to me that God does not learn disciplines and yet possesses knowledge of all things, including foreknowledge of future events.

The same is true of what is said there: “There is no life with reason for anything except the soul” (ch. 4, no. 5). For God too has life with reason, since in him are supreme life and supreme reason.

There is also what I said earlier: “Whatever is understood is always of such a kind” (ch. 1, no. 1), when the mind too is understood, although the mind is certainly not always of such a kind.

But when I said that the mind cannot be separated from eternal reason because it is not joined to it locally (ch. 6, no. 11), I certainly would not have said this if I had then been so instructed in the sacred Scriptures that I remembered what is written: “Your sins separate between you and your God” (Isaiah 59:2).

From this it is clear that separation can also be spoken of concerning things joined not spatially but incorporeally.

### 3

I was also unable to remember what I meant when I said: “If the soul lacks a body, it is not in this world” (ch. 13, no. 22). [Note: [Col. 0591] Erasmus and two manuscripts read: “I was unable to remember the dead.”] For do the souls of the dead either not lack a body, or are they not in this world? As though the underworld were not in this world.

But because I placed the absence of a body among good things, perhaps by the word “body” I meant bodily afflictions. If so, I used the word excessively and presumptuously.

The following was also said rashly: “From the supreme essence a form is given to the body through the soul, by which it exists, insofar as it exists. Through the soul, therefore, the body subsists, and by that very fact it exists by which it is animated, whether universally, as the world, or particularly, as each individual animal within the world” (ch. 15, no. 24).

All of this was said entirely rashly.

This book begins as follows: “If discipline exists anywhere—”

# CHAPTER SIX

## The Books on the Disciplines

During the period when I was at Milan, preparing to receive baptism, I also attempted to write books on the disciplines. I questioned those who were with me and who did not shrink from studies of this kind, wishing by means of corporeal things to reach or lead others toward incorporeal things by certain apparently measured steps.

But I was able to complete only a book on Grammar, which I later lost from our library, and six volumes on Music, insofar as they concern the part called Rhythm.

I wrote those six books after I had been baptized and had returned from Italy to Africa; while at Milan I had merely begun this discipline.

Of the other five disciplines begun there in the same way—Dialectic, Rhetoric, Geometry, Arithmetic, and Philosophy—only the beginnings remained, and even these we have lost. I nevertheless think that some people possess them.

[Note: [Col. 0591] The printed editions add: “This work begins: ‘All the thirteen names—.’” This is the beginning of the book on Grammar, and therefore this clause fits badly with what immediately precedes it; it is also absent from the manuscripts. Of the books on the disciplines listed here, which Augustine says he wrote in dialogue form and with the intention of leading “through corporeal things to incorporeal things,” only the six books on Music have been found.]

# CHAPTER SEVEN

## On the Morals of the Catholic Church and on the Morals of the Manichaeans: Two Books

### 1

After I had been baptized, while I was in Rome, I could not silently endure the Manichaeans’ boast concerning their false and deceptive continence or abstinence. In order to deceive the uninstructed, they even set themselves above true Christians, although they cannot be compared with them.

I therefore wrote two books: one *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, the other *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*.

### 2

In the book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, I cited a testimony in which we read: “For your sake we are afflicted all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm 43:22; Romans 8:36).

The corruption of our manuscript misled me, since I was not yet sufficiently familiar with the Scriptures. For other manuscripts of the same translation do not read, “For your sake we are afflicted,” but, “For your sake we are afflicted unto death”; others expressed it in one word: “we are put to death.”

The Greek books indicate that this is the more accurate reading. From Greek, the translation of the ancient divine Scriptures into Latin was made according to the Septuagint translators.

Nevertheless, on the basis of these words—namely, “For your sake we are afflicted”—I made many arguments (*Lib.* 1, ch. 9, nos. 14–15), and I do not reject them as false in their substance. Yet I certainly did not demonstrate from these words alone the agreement between the Old and New Scriptures that I wished to demonstrate.

I therefore explained where the error had crept in: “From other testimonies, however, I have shown that same agreement sufficiently” (*ibid.*, ch. 16, nos. 26–29).

### 3.

Likewise, shortly afterward I quoted a passage from the Book of Wisdom, according to our manuscript, in which it was written: “For wisdom teaches sobriety, and justice and courage” (Wis. 8:7). On the basis of these words I discussed matters that were indeed true, but which had been suggested by the occasion of a textual error (Book 1, chap. 16, §27). For what could be truer than that wisdom teaches the truth of contemplation, which I thought was signified by the name “sobriety,” and the uprightness of action, which I wished to understand through the other two terms, “justice” and “courage,” when the more reliable manuscripts of the same translation read: “For it teaches sobriety and wisdom, and justice and courage”?

By these names the Latin translator designated the four virtues that are most commonly on the lips of philosophers: calling temperance “sobriety,” assigning prudence the name “wisdom,” expressing fortitude by the term “courage,” and translating only justice by its own name. Much later we found these four virtues called by their proper names in the same Book of Wisdom, as they are called by the Greeks, in Greek manuscripts.

Likewise, concerning what I quoted from the Book of Solomon—“Vanity of the vain” [*vanitas vanitantium*], said Ecclesiastes (Eccl. 1:2)—I did indeed read it in many manuscripts, but the Greek does not have this. It has instead, “Vanity of vanities” [*vanitas vanitatum*], as I later discovered; and I found those Latin manuscripts to be more reliable which read *vanitatum*, not *vanitantium*. Nevertheless, whatever I discussed on the occasion of this textual error is shown by the matters themselves to be true (Book 1, chap. 21, §39).

[Note: We have restored *vanitantium* from the sounder manuscripts, in place of *vanitatum*, which the printed editions have. A little later Am. and Er. continue as follows: “But it has ‘Vanity of the vain,’ which I saw later; and I found those Latin manuscripts to be more reliable which read ‘of the vain,’ not ‘of vanities.’” The text is exceedingly corrupt, and here too the manuscripts vary no more successfully. The marginal reading of Er. Guill. supports the Benedictine reading. M.]

### 4.

As for what I said, “Let us first love with complete charity the very one whom we wish to know—that is, God” (Book 1, chap. 25, §47), it would have been better to say “with sincere,” rather than “with complete,” charity, lest it be thought that the love of God will not be greater when we see him face to face.

It should therefore be understood as though I had said “complete,” meaning a love that cannot be greater so long as we walk by faith; for it will be fuller—indeed, completely full—but by sight.

[Note: In nearly all the manuscripts the reading is *nisi forte putatur* (“unless perhaps it is thought”). In the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus: *nisi forte putaretur* (“unless perhaps it were thought”).]

Likewise, concerning those who assist the needy, whom I called merciful even if they were so wise that they were no longer disturbed by any grief of spirit (ibid., chap. 27, §53), this should not be understood as though I had defined such wise people as existing in this life. For I did not say, “since they are”; I said, “even if they are.”

### 5.

Elsewhere, where I said:

“Now, when this human love has nourished and strengthened the soul clinging to your breasts, and has made it fit to follow God, when his majesty begins to reveal itself to it in such measure as is sufficient for a human being while he is an inhabitant of this earth, such an ardor of charity is kindled, and so great a fire of divine love arises, that, when all vices have been burned away and the human being has been sanctified and purified, it becomes sufficiently clear how divinely it was said: ‘I am a consuming fire’” (Deut. 4:24; Heb. 12:29),

the Pelagians may think that I said this perfection can occur in this mortal life.

But they should not think so. The ardor of charity, once made fit to follow God, can be born and grow in this life, and it can become so great as to consume every vice. But it cannot here accomplish the purpose for which it is born—namely, that no vice may remain in a human being. Nevertheless, this great reality is perfected by that same ardor of charity where and when it can be perfected. Just as the bath of regeneration cleanses from the guilt of all sins that human birth has brought with it and iniquity has contracted, so that perfection cleanses from every stain of vices, without which human weakness cannot exist in this age.

The same understanding should be applied to what the Apostle says: “Christ loved the Church and gave himself for her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind” (Eph. 5:25–27). For this is the washing of water in the word by which the Church is cleansed. But since, throughout her entire present existence, she says, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), she is certainly not here without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind. Nevertheless, from what she receives here she is brought to that glory and perfection which are not here.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts agree almost unanimously. The editions read *hoc est*, “that is,” but the sequence of the sentence proves this to be an error.]

### 6.

In another book, entitled *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, I said that “the goodness of God so orders all deficient things that they are where they can most suitably be, until, through ordered movements, they return to the place from which they fell away” (Book 2, chap. 7, §9). This should not be understood as though everything returns to the place from which it fell away, as Origen thought, but rather all those things which do return.

For those who will be punished in everlasting fire do not return to God, from whom they fell away. Yet all deficient things are so ordered that they are where they can most suitably be, since those who do not return are also most suitably in punishment.

Elsewhere I said: “Almost no one doubts that beetles arise from dung, which they roll into a round ball and bury” (ibid., chap. 17, §63), although many doubt whether this is true, and many have never even heard it.

This work begins as follows: “In the other books I think we have dealt sufficiently.”

## CHAPTER VIII  
### *On the Quantity of the Soul*, one book

[Vol. 1]

### 1.

While living in the same city, I wrote a dialogue in which many questions concerning the soul are raised and discussed: where it comes from, what sort of thing it is, how great it is, why it was given to the body, what it becomes when it comes to the body, and what it is when it departs.

But since its magnitude was discussed with the greatest care and subtlety, in order that we might show, if possible, that it is not corporeal in quantity and yet is something great, the entire book received its title from this one inquiry and was called *On the Quantity of the Soul*.

### 2.

In this book I said that it seemed to me that the soul had brought all the arts with it, and that what is called learning is nothing other than recollecting and remembering (chap. 20, §34). This should not be understood as though it were thereby approved that the soul had once lived either here in another body or elsewhere, whether in a body or outside a body, and had learned in another life beforehand those things which it answers when questioned, although it did not learn them here.

[Note: See *On the Trinity*, Book 12, chap. 15, §24.]

For it is possible, as we already said above in this work, that it can do this because it is intelligible in nature (above, chap. 4, §4), and is connected not only with intelligible realities but also with immutable realities. It was made in such an order that, when it turns toward those realities with which it is connected, or toward itself insofar as it sees them, it gives true answers about them to the extent that it sees them.

Nor did it bring all the arts with it in that manner, nor does it possess them all with it. For concerning the arts that pertain to the bodily senses—such as much of medicine and all of astrology—it cannot speak unless it has learned them here. But those matters which the intellect alone grasps, because of what I have said, it answers after remembering them, whenever it has been properly questioned by itself or by another.

[Note: In the editions the words are printed with almost no connection as follows: “But also with immutable realities. It was made in such an order that, when …” We have altered the punctuation and removed *est* (“is”), which is absent from the best manuscripts.]

### 3.

Elsewhere I said:

“I would like, I say, to say more about this and to place myself under constraint, while, as though I were giving you an instruction, I command myself to do nothing other than be restored to myself, to whom I owe myself above all.”

Here I seem rather to have needed to say, “May I be restored to God, to whom I owe myself above all.” But since a human being must first be restored to himself, so that, having made that as it were a step, he may rise and ascend from there to God—just as the younger son first returned to himself and then said, “I will arise and go to my father” (Luke 15:18)—I therefore spoke in this way.

Indeed, immediately afterward I added: “And thus the slave becomes a friend of the Lord” (chap. 28, §55).

Therefore, when I said “to whom I owe myself above all,” I was referring to human beings: I owe myself more to myself than to other human beings, although I owe myself more to God than to myself.

This book begins as follows: “Since I see that you have abundant leisure.”

## CHAPTER IX  
### *On Free Choice*, three books

[Vol. 1]

### 1.

While we were still staying in Rome, we wished, by discussion, to inquire where evil comes from. We conducted the discussion in such a way that, if possible, reason, considered and worked out with God’s assistance insofar as we could achieve this through argument, might bring even to our understanding what we believed concerning this matter while submitting to divine authority.

And since, after the matter had been carefully examined by reason, we agreed that evil arises only from the free choice of the will, the three books produced by that discussion were called *On Free Choice*. I completed the second and third books in Africa, after I had already been ordained a presbyter at Hippo-Regius, insofar as I was then able.

### 2.

Many matters were discussed in these books. Certain questions arose which I either could not untangle or which required a lengthy discussion at the time; these were therefore deferred in such a way that, whether from both sides or from all the aspects of those questions in which it was not apparent what best accorded with the truth, our reasoning was nevertheless brought to this conclusion: whichever of the alternatives was true, God should be believed—or even shown—to be worthy of praise.

That discussion was undertaken on behalf of those who deny that the origin of evil is derived from the free choice of the will and maintain that, if this is so, God must be blamed as the creator of all natures. In this way, following the error of their impiety—for they are Manichaeans—they wish to introduce a certain nature of evil that is immutable and coeternal with God.

Nothing was discussed in these books concerning the grace of God by which he predestined his elect in such a way that he himself also prepares the wills of those among them who now exercise free choice, because this question had been proposed for another purpose.

[Note: Several manuscripts, together with Amerbach and Erasmus, read *propter hanc propositam quaestionem*, “because this question had been proposed.”]

Whenever an occasion arose for mentioning this grace, it was mentioned in passing, not defended through elaborate reasoning as though the discussion concerned it. For it is one thing to ask where evil comes from, and another to ask from where one may return to one’s former good, or attain to a greater good.

### 3.

Therefore, let the recent heretics, the Pelagians, who assert free choice of the will in such a way as to leave no place for the grace of God—since they maintain that it is given according to our merits—not exalt themselves as though I had argued their case. I said many things in these books in favor of free choice because the purpose of that discussion required them.

In the first book I said that evil deeds are punished by the justice of God, and I added: “For they would not be punished justly unless they were done voluntarily” (Book 1, chap. 1, §1).

Likewise, when I showed that the good will itself is so great a good that it is rightly preferred to all bodily and external goods, I said:

“You see, then, as I think, that it has been established in our will whether we enjoy or lack so great and so true a good. For what is situated in the will as much as the will itself?” (ibid., chap. 12, §26).

And elsewhere:

“What reason, then,” I said, “is there for us to think it doubtful that, even if we have never previously been wise, we nevertheless merit and live a praiseworthy and blessed life by our will, and by our will a disgraceful and wretched one?” (ibid., chap. 13, §28).

Again, elsewhere:

“From this it follows,” I said, “that whoever rightly and honorably wishes to live, if he wishes this rather than fleeting things, may attain so great a reality with such ease that having what he wished requires nothing else of him than the very act of wishing” (ibid., §29).

And elsewhere I said:

“For that eternal law, to whose consideration it is now time to return, established with unchangeable stability that merit lies in the will, while reward and punishment lie in blessedness and misery” (ibid., chap. 14, §30).

And elsewhere:

“It has been established,” I said, “that what each person chooses to pursue and embrace lies in the will” (ibid., chap. 16, §34).

And in the second book:

“For the human being himself,” I said, “insofar as he is human, is some good, because when he wishes to live rightly, he can do so” (Book 2, chap. 1, §2).

And elsewhere I said:

“Right action is impossible except through that same free choice of the will” (ibid., chap. 18, §47).

And in the third book:

“What need is there,” I said, “to ask where this movement comes from, by which the will is turned away from the immutable good toward a changeable good, when we acknowledge that it is nothing other than a movement of the soul, voluntary, and therefore blameworthy? Every useful teaching concerning this matter serves the purpose that, once this movement has been rejected and restrained, we may turn our will away from the fall into temporal things and toward the enjoyment of the eternal good” (Book 3, chap. 1, §2).

And elsewhere:

“Truth itself cries out most clearly concerning you,” I said: “‘You could not regard anything as being within our power except what we do when we wish.’ Therefore nothing is so much within our power as the will itself. For it is immediately present, without any interval, as soon as we wish” (ibid., chap. 3, §7).

Likewise, elsewhere:

“For if you are praised,” I said, “when you see what you ought to do, although you do not see it except in him who is immutable truth, how much more should he be praised who both commanded you to will, gave you the ability, and did not permit you to be unwilling without penalty?”

Then I continued:

“For if each person owes what he has received, and a human being has been made in such a way that he must necessarily sin, then he owes it that he should sin. When, therefore, he sins, he does what he owes. But if it is a crime to say this, no one is compelled by his nature to sin” (ibid., chap. 16, §46).

And again:

“What, then,” I said, “could be the cause of the will before the will? For either it is itself a will, and we do not depart from this root of the will; or it is not a will, and there is no sin. Therefore either the will is the first cause of sinning, or no one is the first cause of sinning; and sin can rightly be imputed to no one except the sinner. It can therefore rightly be imputed to no one except the willing person” (ibid., chap. 17, §49).

[Note: Lovaniensis and the Corbie manuscript read *nisi voluntati*, “except to the will.” But Amerbach and Erasmus, together with most of the other manuscripts, more correctly read *nisi volenti*, “except to the willing person”; thus also Lovaniensis in Book 3 of *On Free Choice*. Erasmus and Guill. have *volenti* in the margin. M.]

And shortly afterward:

“Who sins in something that cannot in any way be avoided?” I said. “But sin occurs; therefore it can be avoided” (ibid., chap. 18, §50).

Pelagius used this statement of mine in one of his books. When I answered that book, I wished my own book to be entitled *On Nature and Grace*.

### 4.

Because grace is not mentioned in these and similar statements of mine—for it was not then the subject of discussion—the Pelagians think, or may think, that we held their position. But they think this in vain.

For it is the will by which one sins and by which one lives rightly; this is what we were discussing in those statements. Therefore, unless the will itself is liberated by God’s grace from the slavery by which it has been made a slave of sin, and unless it is assisted in overcoming its vices, mortals cannot live rightly and devoutly.

And unless this divine benefit by which the will is liberated preceded it, it would already be given on account of its merits and would not be grace, which is given freely.

We dealt sufficiently with this matter in other works, refuting these recent heretics, enemies of grace. Yet even in these books, *On Free Choice*, which were not written against them at all—for they did not yet exist—but against the Manichaeans, we did not remain wholly silent concerning this grace of God, which they attempt to remove with unspeakable impiety.

In the second book we said that not only great goods but also the least goods cannot exist except from him from whom all goods come, that is, God. Shortly afterward I said:

“The virtues by which one lives rightly are great goods. The forms of any bodily things, without which one can live rightly, are the least goods. The powers of the soul, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods. No one makes evil use of the virtues; but the other goods—that is, the intermediate and least goods—can be used well or badly.

“And therefore no one makes evil use of virtue, because the good use of these things, which we can also use badly, is the work of virtue; but no one uses something badly by using it well. Thus the abundance and greatness of God’s goodness has provided not only great goods but also intermediate and least goods. His goodness is more worthy of praise in great goods than in intermediate ones, and more in intermediate than in least goods; but it is more worthy of praise in all of them than it would be if he had not bestowed them all” (Book 2, chap. 19, §50).

And elsewhere:

“Hold fast,” I said, “to an unwavering devotion, so that no good may occur to you—whether through sensation, understanding, or thought of any kind—that is not from God.”

[Note: Four manuscripts read: “Hold fast with unwavering devotion.”]

Likewise, elsewhere I said:

“But since a human being cannot rise voluntarily in the same way that he fell voluntarily, let us hold firmly in faith the hand of God extended to us from above—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ” (ibid., chap. 20, §54).

### 5.

And in the third book, after I had said the statement that I mentioned Pelagius had also used from my writings—“Who sins in something that cannot in any way be avoided? Sin occurs; therefore it can be avoided”—I immediately continued:

“Nevertheless, certain acts committed through ignorance are also disapproved and judged to require correction, as we read in the divine authorities. For the Apostle says, ‘I obtained mercy because I acted ignorantly’ (1 Tim. 1:13); and the prophet says, ‘Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance’ (Ps. 24:7).

“There are also acts done under compulsion that must be disapproved, when a person wishes to act rightly but cannot. For what else are the words: ‘For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I hate, that I do’? And: ‘To will lies at hand for me, but to accomplish the good does not’ (Rom. 7:15, 18). And: ‘The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish’?” (Gal. 5:17).

But all these conditions belong to human beings who come from that condemnation of death. For if this is not a punishment of the human being but his nature, then none of these things are sins. If he does not depart from the condition in which he was naturally made, so that he cannot be better, then, when he does these things, he does what he ought.

But if the human being were good, he would be otherwise. Now, however, because he is in this condition, he is not good, nor does he have it within his power to be good—whether because he does not see what he ought to be, or because he sees it but is unable to be what he sees he ought to be.

Who could doubt that this is a punishment? Every punishment, however, if it is just, is a punishment for sin and is called a penalty. But if the punishment is unjust—since no one doubts that it is a punishment—it has been imposed upon the human being by some unjust ruler.

But since it is madness to doubt the omnipotence and justice of God, this punishment is just and is paid on account of some sin. No unjust ruler could either seize a human being as though God were unaware, or extort this punishment from him against God’s will as though God were weaker, whether by frightening or by fighting, so as to torment the human being with an unjust punishment.

It therefore remains that this just punishment arises from the condemnation of the human being” (Book 3, chap. 18, §§50–51).

And elsewhere:

“To approve false things as true and so to fall into error unwillingly, and, while the pain of the bodily bond resists and torments him, to be unable to abstain from lustful deeds—this is not the nature in which the human being was created, but the punishment of one who has been condemned.

“When we speak of the free will by which one does what is right, we are speaking of that will in which the human being was created” (ibid., §52).

[Note: Several manuscripts, including the more authoritative ones, read *conturbando*, “by disturbing.”]

[Note: Two manuscripts, as well as the margins of Amerbach and Erasmus, read *calore*, “heat.” Erasmus and Guill. have *dolore*, “pain,” in the margin. M.]

[Note: Lovaniensis, with several manuscripts, reads *de illa voluntate*, “of that will.” But *illa* is absent from the Corbie manuscript; Amerbach and Erasmus therefore have *libera*, “free.” Thus also Book 3 of *On Free Choice*, from which we have restored the reading here. Lovaniensis and Paris read *de libera voluntate*, “of free will,” without *illa*. M.]

### 6.

Behold, long before the Pelagian heresy existed, we discussed matters as though we were already arguing against them.

Since all goods were said to come from God—that is, great, intermediate, and least goods—free choice of the will is found among intermediate goods, because we can use it badly; yet it is such that we cannot live rightly without it. Its good use is already virtue, which is found among the great goods, and no one can use those goods badly.

And since all goods, as has been said—great, intermediate, and least—come from God, it follows that the good use of free choice, which is virtue and is counted among the great goods, also comes from God.

It was further said from what misery, justly inflicted upon sinners, God’s grace delivers us: a human being could fall voluntarily, that is, by free choice, but could not rise in the same way. To this misery of just condemnation belong the ignorance and difficulty suffered by every human being from the beginning of his birth; and no one is freed from this evil except by God’s grace (Book 2, chap. 20; Book 3, chap. 18).

The Pelagians do not wish this misery to descend from a just condemnation, since they deny original sin. Yet even if ignorance and difficulty were the natural beginnings of the human being, God would not thereby be blamed but praised, as we argued in the same third book (Book 3, chaps. 20–21).

That discussion should be understood as directed against the Manichaeans, who do not accept the sacred Scriptures of the Old Testament, in which original sin is related; and whatever is read concerning it in the apostolic writings, they contend with detestable impudence was inserted by corruptors of the Scriptures, as though it had not been spoken by the Apostles.

Against the Pelagians, however, we must defend what both Scriptures commend, since they profess to accept them.

This work begins as follows: “Tell me, I beg you, whether God is not the author of evil.”

## CHAPTER X  
### *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, two books

### 1.

After I had settled in Africa, I wrote two books *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*. Although in the preceding books everything I discussed was directed toward showing that God is the supremely good and immutable creator of all mutable natures, and that no nature or substance is evil insofar as it is nature and substance, my intention was directed against the Manichaeans; nevertheless, these two books were published most explicitly against them, in defense of the Old Law, which they attack with the vehement zeal of their deranged error.

The first book extends from the words, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1), through the completion of the seven days, where it is read that God rested on the seventh day.

The second extends from the words, “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth” (ibid. 2:4), until Adam and his wife were expelled from paradise and a guard was placed over the tree of life.

Then, at the end of the book, I set the faith of Catholic truth against the error of the Manichaeans, briefly and clearly summarizing what they say and what we say.

### 2.

But concerning what I said—“That food does not nourish the eyes of irrational birds, but the pure hearts of those who believe in God and turn from the love of visible and temporal things toward fulfilling his commands; which all human beings can do if they wish” (Book 1, chap. 3, §6)—the recent heretics, the Pelagians, should not think that this was said in accordance with their position.

It is entirely true that all human beings can do this if they wish; but the will is prepared by the Lord, and is so greatly increased by the gift of charity that they are able to do it. This was not stated here because it was not necessary for the question then under consideration.

But where it is read that the blessing of God expressed in the words “Be fruitful and multiply” (Gen. 1:28) should be understood as having been turned toward carnal fecundity after the sin, if this cannot be understood in any other way except that those human beings would not have had human children unless they had sinned, I entirely reject it.

Nor does it follow that what is said in Genesis—that green plants and fruit-bearing trees were given as food to every kind of beast, and to all birds and serpents—must therefore be understood only allegorically, because there are quadrupeds and flying creatures that appear to live solely on flesh (ibid., chap. 20, §31).

For it could be that they were also fed by human beings with the fruits of the earth, if, because of the obedience by which the human beings themselves served God without any iniquity, all beasts and birds deserved to have them serving them in every way.

Likewise, it may cause difficulty that I said concerning the people of Israel: “Still through bodily circumcision and sacrifices, as though in the sea of the nations, that people served the law” (ibid., chap. 23, §40). For they could not sacrifice among the nations, just as we now see that they remain without sacrifices—unless perhaps the sheep they sacrifice at Passover is counted as a sacrifice.

[Note: Deuteronomy 16:6 prescribes that the Passover could not be slaughtered just anywhere. Hence, it is said that the Jews dispersed throughout the world celebrate the Passover each year while nevertheless religiously abstaining from the slaughter of sheep. See Jerome, Letter 2, to Nepotian.]

### 3.

In the second book also, concerning what I said—that life could be signified by the term “food” (Book 2, chap. 3, §4)—since the more accurate manuscripts do not read *pabulum*, “food,” but *fenum*, “hay,” the statement seems insufficiently appropriate. For the term “hay” does not correspond to the meaning of life as “food” does.

Likewise, I seem not to have correctly called the prophetic words “Why is earth and ashes proud?” (Sir. 10:9) prophetic, since they are not found in a book whose author we can be certain should be called a prophet (ibid., chap. 5, §6).

Nor did I understand correctly the Apostle’s statement when, citing Genesis, he says, “The first human being, Adam, was made a living soul” (1 Cor. 15:45), as he intended, when I explained the words, “God breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7). For the Apostle used that testimony to prove that the body is animal; I, however, thought it should be used to show that the human being was first made animal, and not merely the human body (Book 2, chap. 8, §10).

As for what I said—that sins harm no nature except its own (ibid., chap. 29, §43)—I said this because sin does not truly harm the righteous person who is harmed, since it even increases his reward in heaven; but by sinning he truly harms himself, because on account of the very will to harm he will receive what he has inflicted.

The Pelagians can indeed draw this statement toward their doctrine and therefore say that the sins of others have not harmed infants, because I said that sins harm no nature except its own. They fail to observe that infants, who certainly belong to human nature, contract original sin because human nature sinned in the first human beings; consequently, no sins harmed human nature except its own.

“For through one human being, in whom all sinned, sin entered the world” (Rom. 5:12). I did not say that sins harm no human being except through his own sins, but that they harm no nature except its own.

Likewise, concerning what I said shortly afterward—that there is no natural evil (Book 2, chap. 29, §43)—they can seek a similar hiding place unless this statement is referred to a nature such as it was originally created, without defect. For that is truly and properly called human nature.

By a transferred use of the word, however, we also call nature that condition in which a human being is born. In accordance with this usage the Apostle said: “For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

This work begins as follows: “If the Manichaeans would choose those whom they deceived.”

## CHAPTER XI  
### *On Music*, six books

### 1.

Then, as I mentioned above (Book 1 of the *Retractations*, chap. 6), I wrote six books *On Music*. The sixth book became especially well known, because it deals with a matter worthy of knowledge: how one proceeds from bodily and spiritual but mutable numbers to immutable numbers, which already exist in immutable truth itself, and thus how the invisible things of God may be perceived through understanding by means of the things that have been made.

Those who cannot do this but nevertheless live by faith in Christ will come after this life to perceive those realities more certainly and more happily. But those who can do it, if they lack the faith of Christ, who alone is the mediator between God and human beings, perish with all their wisdom.

### 2.

In this book I said:

“For bodies are better in proportion as they are more numerous according to such numbers; but the soul becomes better by renouncing the things it receives through the body, when it turns away from bodily senses and is reformed according to the divine numbers of wisdom” (Book 6, chap. 4, §7).

This should not be understood as though there will be no bodily numbers in incorruptible and spiritual bodies, since they will be much more beautiful and comely; nor as though the soul will not perceive them when it is at its best, just as here it becomes better by renouncing them.

Here the soul must turn away from bodily senses in order to grasp intelligible realities because it is weak and less capable of directing its attention to both at once. At present, moreover, it must avoid the allure found in bodily things, so long as the soul can be enticed by them into shameful pleasure.

Then, however, it will be so strong and perfect that it will not be turned away from the contemplation of wisdom by bodily numbers. It will perceive them without being enticed by them, and it will not become better by renouncing them; rather, it will be so good and rightly ordered that they can neither remain hidden from it nor occupy it.

### 3.

Likewise, concerning what I said—that “this health will then be most firm and certain, when, at its appointed time and in its proper order, this body has been restored to its former stability” (ibid., chap. 5, §13)—this should not be understood as though bodies after the resurrection will not be better than the bodies of the first human beings in paradise, since those future bodies will no longer need the bodily nourishment by which these were nourished.

“Former stability” should instead be understood only to the extent that those bodies will suffer no sickness, just as these bodies could have suffered none before sin.

### 4.

Elsewhere I said:

“More laborious is the love of this world. For what the soul seeks in it—namely, constancy and eternity—it does not find, because frail beauty is completed by the passing of things, and what in it imitates constancy is conveyed from the supreme God through the soul. For a form changeable only in time is prior to one changeable both in time and place” (ibid., chap. 14, §43).

If these words can be understood in such a way that “the lowest beauty” is understood to exist only in the bodies of human beings and of all animals that live with bodily sensation, the evident reasoning supports that interpretation.

For what imitates constancy in this beauty is that the same bodies remain in their structure, insofar as they remain. This, however, is conveyed into them from the supreme God through the soul. For the soul holds their structure together so that it does not dissolve and disperse; we see this occur in the bodies of animals when the soul departs.

But if “the lowest beauty” is understood to exist in all bodies, this statement also compels one to believe that the world itself is an animal, so that what imitates constancy in it is likewise conveyed into it from the supreme God through the soul.

[Note: Lovaniensis reads *idipsum*, “that very thing.” Other editions read *in ipsum*, “into it.”]

[Note: See *The City of God*, Book 7, chap. 23.]

But although Plato and many other philosophers thought that the world is an animal, I have neither been able to establish this by certain reasoning nor discovered that it can be persuaded by the authority of the divine Scriptures.

Therefore, I noted as rashly said anything of this kind that I had stated in such a way that it could be understood in that sense, even in the book *On the Immortality of the Soul* (Book 1 of the *Retractations*, chap. 5, §3). I did not do so because I affirm that this is false, but because I do not comprehend that it is true that the world is an animal.

I am nevertheless firmly convinced that we must hold without wavering that this world is not God for us, whether it has a soul or not. For if it has one, the one who made that soul is our God; but if it has none, this world cannot be the god of anything—how much less our God?

It is nevertheless entirely right to believe that there exists a spiritual and living power, even if the world is not an animal, which serves God in the holy angels in adorning and administering the world, though it is not understood by those who believe this.

By the name “holy angels” I would now designate every holy spiritual creature established in God’s secret and hidden service. But sacred Scripture does not ordinarily signify angelic spirits by the name “souls.”

Accordingly, toward the end of this book I said:

“Rational and intellectual numbers of blessed and holy souls, receiving without the interposition of any nature whatsoever the very law of God—without which not even a leaf falls from a tree, and according to which even the hairs of our head are numbered—transmit it down to earthly and infernal laws” (Book 6, chap. 17, §58).

I do not see how it can be shown that the word “souls” here has been used in accordance with the sacred Scriptures, since I wished here to understand only the holy angels. I do not recall ever having read in the canonical divine utterances that they possess souls.

[Note: Lovaniensis reads *canonicisque recolo*, “and I recall in the canonical writings.” Other manuscripts lack *-que*.]

This book begins: “It has been long enough, almost…”

[Note: The editions read: “This first book begins: ‘What is the measure of the foot?’ But the sixth begins: ‘It has been long enough, almost.’” This reading is not very coherent. We have adopted our text from the most complete manuscripts.]

## CHAPTER XII. *On the Teacher*, one book

At about the same time I wrote a book entitled *On the Teacher*. In it the question is discussed and investigated, and it is found that no one is a teacher who teaches a human being knowledge except God, in accordance also with what is written in the Gospel: “One is your Teacher, Christ” (Matthew 23:10). This book begins as follows: “What do you think we are trying to accomplish when we speak?”

## CHAPTER XIII. *On True Religion*, one book

### 1

At that time also I wrote a book *On True Religion*. In it, in many different ways and at great length, it is argued that the one true God—that is, the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—is to be worshiped through true religion; that the Christian religion, which is the true religion, has been granted to human beings through his temporal dispensation with what great mercy; and how a human being is to be fitted, through a certain way of life, to that same worship of God. [Note: [Column 0602] Some manuscripts of no lesser authority read: “through a certain sweetness is to be fitted.”]

The book speaks chiefly, however, against the Manichaean doctrine of two natures. [Column 0603]

### 2

In this book I said at one point: “Let this be clear and understood by you: no error could have existed in religion if the soul had not worshiped as its god either a soul, or a body, or its own phantasms.” Here I used “soul” for the whole incorporeal creation, without speaking in the manner of Scripture. When Scripture uses the word “soul” without a figurative meaning, I do not know whether it intends anything other than that by which mortal animals live, among whom human beings are included so long as they are mortal.

A little later, however, I expressed the same meaning better and more briefly, where I said: “Therefore let us not serve the creature rather than the Creator, nor let us vanish in our thoughts; and this is perfect religion.” For by the single word “creature” I signified both kinds, spiritual and bodily. What remains is what I said there, “or its own phantasms,” which is why I said here, “nor let us vanish in our thoughts.”

### 3

Likewise, when I said, “This is the Christian religion in our times, whose knowledge and observance are the surest and most certain salvation,” this statement was made with reference to the name, not to the reality designated by that name.

For the reality itself that is now called the Christian religion existed among the ancients and was not absent from the beginning of the human race, until Christ himself came in the flesh; from that time the true religion that already existed began to be called Christian. When, after his resurrection and ascension into heaven, the Apostles began to preach him and very many believed, the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch, as it is written (Acts 11:26). Therefore I said, “This is the Christian religion in our times”—not because it did not exist in earlier times, but because it received this name in later times.

### 4

Elsewhere I said: “Therefore attend carefully and reverently, as far as you can, to what follows; for God helps such people” (chapter 10, §§18–20). This should not be understood as though he helps only such people, since he also helps those who are not yet such, so that they may become such—that is, so that they may seek carefully and reverently. He helps those who are such so that they may find.

Again, elsewhere I said: “Then, I say, it will follow that after the bodily death which we owe to the first sin, at its proper time and in its proper order, this body will be restored to its original stability” (chapter 12, §25). This should be understood in the following way: the body’s original stability, which we lost by sinning, possessed such great blessedness that it did not tend toward the decline of old age. This body, then, will be restored to that original stability in the resurrection of the dead. But it will possess something more: it will not be sustained by bodily nourishment, but will be given life in sufficiency by the spirit alone, when it has risen as a spiritual body; for this reason it will also be spiritual. The body that existed at first, although it would not have died unless the human being had sinned, was nevertheless an animal body, made into a living soul.

### 5

Elsewhere I said: “So evil is voluntary sin that in no way is there sin if it is not voluntary” (chapter 14, §27). This definition may appear false, but if it is carefully examined, it will be found to be entirely true. What must be understood as “sin” is that which is merely sin, not that which is also the punishment of sin, as I showed above when I recalled certain points from the third book *On Free Will* (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 9, §5).
