Although even those acts that are rightly called involuntary sins, because they are committed either by the ignorant or by those under compulsion, cannot in every respect be committed without the will: for the person who sins in ignorance does indeed act willingly [Note: [Column 0604] Am. and Er. read: “he sins willingly.” Six manuscripts read: “he sins by the will”], doing what he thinks ought to be done although it ought not to be done.

Likewise, when the flesh desires against the spirit, the person does not do what he wills: he desires unwillingly, and in that respect does not do what he wills. But if he is overcome, he willingly consents to the desire, and in that respect does nothing except what he wills—free, of course, with respect to righteousness, but a slave of sin.

Even what is called original sin in infants, although they do not yet exercise the freedom of the will, is not absurdly called voluntary as well, because it was contracted from the first evil will of the human being and thereby became, in a certain sense, hereditary.

Therefore what I said is not false: “So evil is voluntary sin that in no way is there sin if it is not voluntary.” For this reason, through the grace of God, not only is the guilt of all past sins released in all who are baptized in Christ, which occurs through the Spirit of regeneration; in adults, the will itself is also healed and prepared by the Lord, which occurs through the spirit of faith and charity.

### 6

Elsewhere, concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, I said: “He did nothing by force, but everything by persuasion and admonition” (chapter 16, §31). It had not occurred to me that he drove the sellers and buyers from the temple by scourging. But what of that, and how significant is it? He also drove out demons unwillingly from human beings—not by persuasive speech, but by the force of his power.

Again, elsewhere I said: “First, those people are to be followed who say that there is one supreme God, the only true God, and that he alone is to be worshiped; if the truth does not shine forth among them, only then must one depart.” This may appear to have been said as though I doubted the truth of this religion. But I spoke as was appropriate for the person to whom I was writing. For I said, “If the truth does not shine forth among them,” without doubting that it would shine forth among them—just as the Apostle says, “If Christ has not been raised” (1 Corinthians 15:14), without doubting that he has been raised.

### 7

Likewise, when I said, “Nor have those miracles been permitted to continue into our times, lest the soul should always seek visible things and the human race grow cold through familiarity with those things whose novelty had inflamed it” (chapter 25, §§46–47), this is indeed true. For even now, when hands are laid upon the baptized, they do not receive the Holy Spirit in such a way that they speak in the languages of all nations; nor are the sick even now healed by the shadow of passing preachers of Christ. And if similar things were then done, it is clear that they subsequently ceased.

But what I said should not be understood to mean that no miracles are now believed to occur in the name of Christ. For when I myself wrote this very book, I already knew that a blind man had been healed in the same city at the bodies of the Milanese martyrs [Note: [Column 0604] Protasius and Gervasius; *Confessions*, book 9, chapter 7, §16], as well as several other events of the kind that occur even in these times in such abundance that we can neither learn of them all nor enumerate those of which we do learn.

### 8

Elsewhere I said: “As the Apostle says, ‘Every order is from God.’” The Apostle did not say this in those same words, although the meaning appears to be the same. For he says: “Those things that exist have been ordered by God” [Note: [Column 0605] Lov. reads: “have been ordered by God.” We have restored *ordinatae* from the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek *tetagménai eisin* (“they have been ordered”)]. (Romans 13:1).

Again, elsewhere I said: “Let absolutely no one deceive us: whatever is rightly criticized is rejected in comparison with something better” (chapter 41, §§77–78). This was said about substances and natures, for that was the subject under discussion, not good actions and sins.

Likewise, elsewhere I said: “But even so, a human being is not to be loved by a human being in the way in which fleshly brothers, children, spouses, or other relatives are loved—whether relations by marriage or fellow citizens—for this love too is temporal. We would not have any such relationships, which arise through birth and death, if our nature, remaining in God’s commandments and image, had not been banished into this corruption” (chapter 46, §88).

I entirely reject this meaning, as I already rejected it above in the first book *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* (*Retractions*, book 1, chapter 10, §2). For it leads to the belief that the first married couple would not have produced human offspring unless they had sinned—as though it were necessary for human beings destined to die to be born if they were born through the intercourse of male and female.

At that time I had not yet seen that it could have happened that those who would not die were born from those who would not die, if human nature had not been changed for the worse by that great sin. Consequently, if fecundity and blessedness had remained both in the parents and in their children, human beings would have been born until the number of the saints predetermined by God had been reached—not to succeed their parents when they died, but to reign with them while they lived. Thus these relationships of kinship and affinity would also have existed if no one had sinned and no one had died.

### 9

Again, elsewhere I said: “As we move toward the one God and bind our souls to that one God—for religion is believed to have received its name from this binding—let us be free from all superstition” (chapter 55, §111).

In these words of mine, I preferred the explanation given there of the origin of the word *religion*. For I was not unaware that the authors of the Latin language had explained another origin for this name: that *religio* was so called because it is *relegitur*, “chosen again,” a compound verb formed from *legere*, that is, “choosing,” so that *religo* in Latin would appear analogous to *eligo*, “I choose.”

This book begins as follows: “Since every path of a good and blessed life…”

## CHAPTER XIV. *On the Benefit of Believing*, one book, addressed to Honoratus

### 1

While I was still a presbyter at Hippo Regius, I wrote a book *On the Benefit of Believing*, addressed to my friend whom I knew had been deceived by the Manichaeans and was still being held in that error. He mocked the discipline of the Catholic faith because people were ordered to believe, but were not taught by the most certain reasoning what the truth was.

In this book I said (chapter 3, §9): “Yet in those precepts and commandments of the Law which it is not now lawful for a Christian to use—such as the Sabbath, circumcision, sacrifices, and anything of that kind—such great mysteries are contained that every devout person understands that nothing is more destructive than to take whatever is found there literally, that is, according to the word; and nothing is more beneficial than for it to be revealed spiritually. Hence: ‘The letter kills, but the spirit gives life’” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

But I explained these words of the Apostle Paul differently, and, as it seems to me—or rather, as the realities themselves make evident—much more appropriately in the book entitled *On the Spirit and the Letter*, although this interpretation too should not be rejected.

### 2

I also said: “There are two kinds of persons worthy of praise in religion. One consists of those who have already found what they seek; they must also be judged most blessed. The other consists of those who seek with the greatest zeal and in the right way. The first are already in possession; the others are on the way, although it is a way by which they will arrive with absolute certainty.”

In these words of mine, if those who have already found what they seek—whom we have said are already in possession—are understood to be most blessed not in this life but in the life that we hope for and toward which we advance by the way of faith, the meaning contains no error. For those who are already there, where we desire to arrive by seeking and believing—that is, by holding to the way of faith—must be judged to have found what ought to be sought.

But if they are thought to be or to have been in this life, that does not seem true to me. This is not because nothing true at all can be found in this life and perceived by the mind rather than believed by faith, but because whatever it is that can be found is not enough to make us most blessed [Note: [Column 0606] Er., Lugd., and Ven. read: “But because whatever it is is not enough to make us most blessed.” M.].

For when the Apostle says, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma,” and, “Now I know in part” [Note: [Column 0606] We have restored “and now I know in part” from the manuscripts; the earlier printed editions read corruptly, “and now it is seen”], this is not something that the mind does not perceive. It is plainly perceived, but it does not yet make us most blessed.

That is what makes us most blessed which he says: “But then face to face,” and, “Then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13:12). Those who have found this must be said to stand in possession of blessedness, to which the way of faith that we hold leads, and to which we desire to arrive by believing.

But who those most blessed persons are who already possess what this way leads to is a major question. That the holy angels are there is not in question. But concerning holy human beings who have already died, it is rightly asked whether they too should be said to stand already in that possession.

They have indeed been stripped of their corruptible bodies, by which the soul is weighed down; but they too still await the redemption of their bodies, and their flesh rests in hope, not yet shining in the incorruption that is to come. Whether, however, they are thereby in any way less able to contemplate the truth with the eyes of the heart, “face to face,” as it is written, is not the place to investigate here.

Likewise, when I said, “To know great, honorable, or even divine things is supremely blessed,” we must refer this to that same blessedness. For in this life, however much one may know, one is not yet supremely blessed, since what remains unknown is incomparably greater.

### 3

When I said that it makes a great difference whether something is held by the mind through certain reasoning—which we call knowledge—or whether it is profitably commended to posterity for belief through report or written testimony, and shortly afterward, “What we know, therefore, we owe to reason; what we believe, to authority” (chapter 11, §25), this should not be understood as though, in more ordinary speech, we should hesitate to say that we know what we believe on the testimony of reliable witnesses.

Strictly speaking, we call “knowledge” only what we grasp through the mind’s firm reasoning. But when we speak in language more suited to common usage, as even divine Scripture speaks, let us not hesitate to say that we know both what we perceive through the senses of our bodies and what we believe through trustworthy witnesses—provided that we understand the difference between these things and the former kind of knowledge.

### 4

Likewise, when I said, “No one doubts that all human beings are either foolish or wise” (chapter 12, §27), this may appear contrary to what is read in the third book *On Free Will*: “As though human nature admitted no intermediate condition between folly and wisdom” (chapter 24, §71).

But that statement there was made when the question concerned the first human being: whether he was made wise, foolish, or neither. We could in no way call him foolish, since he was made without fault and folly is a great fault; yet it was not sufficiently clear how we could call him wise, since he could be seduced. Therefore, for the sake of brevity, I wished to say, “As though human nature admitted no intermediate condition between folly and wisdom.”

I was also considering infants [Note: [Column 0607] The Louvain editors allowed the conjunction *etiam* (“also”), which here has the force of “in addition,” to be omitted. We have restored it, since it is found in all the editions], who, although we confess that they bear original sin, cannot properly be called either wise or foolish, since they do not yet use free will, whether well or badly.

But here I said that all human beings are either wise or foolish, intending those who already use reason, by which human beings are distinguished from beasts, just as we say that all human beings wish to be blessed. Surely, in this statement, which is so true and evident, we need not fear that infants will also be understood, since they are not yet capable of having this wish.

### 5

Elsewhere, after recalling what the Lord Jesus did when he was present in the flesh, I added: “Why, you ask, do such things not happen now?” And I replied: “Because they would not move people unless they were extraordinary; if they were customary, they would not be extraordinary” (chapter 16, §34).

I said this because such things are not now as numerous, nor do all of them occur now—not because none occur even now.

### 6

At the end of the book I said: “But since this speech of ours, I say, has gone on much farther than I thought, let us bring this book to an end. I want you to remember that I have not yet begun to refute the Manichaeans, nor yet attacked those absurdities, nor disclosed anything substantial about Catholic teaching itself. I have merely wished, if I could, to extract from you the false opinion maliciously or incompetently insinuated to us concerning true Christians [Note: [Column 0607] Lov. and Er. read “insinuated to you.” The manuscripts and Am. read “insinuated to us.” Augustine indicates that he and Honoratus, to whom he is speaking, had once been deceived by the Manichaeans], and to raise you up to the study of certain great and divine matters. Therefore let this volume stand as it is; when your mind has become more peaceful, perhaps I shall be more ready to address the rest” (chapter 18, §36).

I did not say this as though I had not yet written anything against the Manichaeans, or had committed nothing concerning Catholic doctrine to writing, since the many books published above on both subjects testify that I had not been silent about either. Rather, in this book written to him, I had not yet begun to refute the Manichaeans, had not yet attacked those absurdities, and had not disclosed anything substantial about Catholic teaching itself, because I hoped that, after making this beginning, I would write to him the things that I had not yet written here.

This book begins as follows: “If, Honoratus, it seemed to me that one and the same thing…”

## CHAPTER XV. *Against the Manichaeans, On Two Souls*, one book

### 1

After this book, while I was still a presbyter, I wrote *On Two Souls* against the Manichaeans. They say that one soul is a part of God, while the other belongs to the nation of darkness, which God did not create and which is coeternal with God. They deliriously claim that both souls—one good and the other evil—exist in one human being.

They say, naturally, that the evil soul belongs properly to the flesh, and they also say that this flesh belongs to the nation of darkness. The good soul, on the other hand, comes from an adventitious part of God, which fought against the nation of darkness and mingled both together. They attribute everything good in a human being to the good soul, and everything evil to the evil soul.

In this book I said: “There is no life whatsoever that, precisely insofar as it is life, and insofar as it is life at all, does not belong to the supreme source and principle of life” (chapter 1, §1). I said this so that it might be understood generally of a creature’s relation to the Creator, not so that it would be thought to come from him as a part of him.

### 2

Likewise, when I said that sin exists nowhere except in the will, the Pelagians may think that this was said on their behalf because of infants. They deny that infants have any sin to be remitted to them in baptism because they do not yet use the freedom of the will.

As though the sin that we say they draw originally from Adam—that is, by which they are implicated in his guilt and consequently held liable to punishment—could exist anywhere except in the will by which the transgression of the divine command was committed [Note: [Column 0608] Am., Er., and the Pratel manuscript read: “could nowhere have existed.” The Sorbonne and Regiomontanus manuscripts read: “is nowhere found to exist.” Shortly afterward, Corb. and other manuscripts of no inferior quality read: “except from the will.”].

This statement may also be thought false: “Sin exists nowhere except in the will,” because the Apostle says: “If I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.” For this sin is so far from being in the will that he says: “What I do not will, that I do.” How, then, does sin exist nowhere except in the will?

But the sin of which the Apostle speaks in this way is called sin because it was brought about by sin, and is the punishment of sin. For he is speaking of the desire of the flesh, as he makes clear in what follows: “I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh; for the willing is present with me, but the accomplishing of the good is not” (Romans 7:16–18).

The perfection of the good is that the desire of sin itself should not be in a human being. When one lives well, the will does not consent to it; nevertheless, one does not accomplish the good because the desire remains within, and the will struggles against it. The guilt of this desire is released in baptism, but its weakness remains. Until it is healed, every believer who makes good progress struggles against it with the greatest zeal.

But the sin that exists nowhere except in the will must be understood especially as that which was followed by just condemnation. “Through one human being this entered into the world.” Yet even the sin by which one consents to the desire of sin is committed only by the will [Note: [Column 0609] Four manuscripts read: “by which one consents to sinful desire.”]. For this reason I also said elsewhere: “Therefore one sins only by the will” (chapter 9, §12).

### 3

Likewise, elsewhere I defined the will by saying: “The will is a movement of the mind, compelled by no one, toward either retaining or acquiring something” (chapter 9, §14).

This was said so that, by this definition, a willing person might be distinguished from an unwilling one, and so that attention might be directed to those who were the first origin of evil for the human race in paradise [Note: Six copies read: “who made the origin of evil for the human race.”]. No one compelled them to sin—that is, they sinned by free will—for they knowingly acted against the commandment, and the tempter persuaded them to do this but did not compel them.

Even someone who sinned in ignorance may appropriately be said to have sinned unwillingly, although what he did in ignorance he nevertheless did willingly; thus his sin too could not have existed without the will. The will, as it was defined, was a movement of the mind, compelled by no one, toward either retaining or acquiring something. If he had not wanted to do what he did, he would not have done it; he was not compelled to do it.

Therefore, because he wanted to, he did it, even if he did not sin because he wanted to sin, being unaware that what he did was sin. Thus even such a sin could not exist without the will—but it was the will of the act, not the will of sin, although the act itself was sin, since what ought not to have been done was done.

But whoever knowingly sins, if he can resist the one compelling him to sin without sinning and nevertheless does not resist, sins willingly, since one who can resist is not compelled to yield.

Whoever, however, cannot resist with a good will the desire that compels him [Note: [Column 0609] Am. and Er. read: “the willing desire.”], and therefore acts against the precepts of righteousness, is already guilty of sin in such a way that the sin is also the punishment of sin. Therefore it is entirely true that sin cannot exist without the will.

### 4

Likewise, the definition of sin in which I said, “Sin is the will to retain or obtain what justice forbids, and from which one is free to abstain” (chapter 11, §15), is true because what is defined is merely sin, not what is also the punishment of sin.

For when the condition is such that it is both sin and the punishment of sin, what power does the will possess under the domination of desire, except perhaps the power, if it is devout, to pray for help? It is free to the extent that it has been liberated [Note: The editions read: “because it has been liberated to that extent.” But the more elegant manuscripts, omitting *quia* (“because”), read: “to the extent that it has been liberated.”], and to that extent it is called a will.

Otherwise, the whole matter should more properly be called desire than will [Note: Lov. reads: “otherwise desire is more safely [or: more readily] called…” We have preferred the reading of Am. and Er., which is supported by the manuscripts except for one German manuscript, which incorrectly reads “so much desire,” and another, Pratel., which, with three English manuscripts, reads “more readily the whole of desire.” That reading is sound, but the comparative is better removed, as Saint Augustine likes to leave such things unspoken. Compare *Retractions* 2.6: “What seems to me like a light declamation seems a grave confession.”]—and this is not, as the Manichaeans foolishly imagine, an addition belonging to another nature, but a defect of our own nature, from which it is healed only by the grace of the Savior.

If someone says that desire itself is nothing other than will, though a defective will enslaved to sin, there is no need to resist him or to quarrel over words when the reality is clear. Even in this way it is shown that no sin exists without the will, whether in an act or in its origin.

### 5

Again, when I said: “I had begun to ask whether that evil kind of souls, before it was mingled with the good, had possessed any will. For if it did not possess one, it was without sin and innocent, and therefore in no way evil” (chapter 16, §17), they ask: “Why, then, do you call infants’ condition sin, when you do not hold their will guilty?”

The answer is that they are held guilty not through the property of their own will, but through their origin. For what is every earthly human being by origin other than Adam? Adam, moreover, certainly possessed a will; and when he sinned by that will, sin entered the world through him.

### 6

Likewise, regarding my statement that souls cannot in any way be evil by nature, if the question is how we should understand the Apostle’s words, “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3), I answer that by “nature” in my statement I wished to be understood as referring to that which is properly called nature, in which we were created without defect.

This nature is called “nature” because of its origin; but that origin certainly has a defect, which is contrary to nature.

Again, when it was said, “It is the height of injustice and madness to hold anyone guilty of sin because he did not do what he could not do,” they ask: “Why, then, are infants held guilty?”

The answer is that they are held guilty through the origin of the one who did not do what he could have done—namely, preserve the divine commandment.

When I said, “Whatever those souls do, if they do it by nature rather than by will—that is, if they lack a free movement of the mind both to do and not to do it; if, finally, they are granted no power to abstain from their action, we cannot hold them guilty of sin” (chapter 12, §17) [Note: Am., Er., and the Beccensis manuscript read: “to be held guilty of their sin.” Lov. likewise has this reading in *On Two Souls*], the question concerning infants is not troubling for this reason: they are held guilty through the origin of the one who sinned by his will, when he did not lack a free movement of the mind both to do and not to do, and when he had complete power to abstain from the evil act.

The Manichaeans do not say this of the nation of darkness, which they introduce in a most fabulous manner and insist was always evil by nature and never good.

### 7

It may be asked how I could have said: “Even if there are souls—although for the time being this is uncertain—that are devoted to bodily functions not through sin but by nature, and that touch us, although they are inferior, through some inward proximity, they ought not on that account to be considered evil, because when we follow them and love bodily things, we are evil.”

I said this concerning those about whom I had begun to speak above, saying: “Even if it is granted that we are enticed to shameful things by another, inferior kind of souls, it does not follow either that those souls are evil by nature or that these are the supreme good” (chapter 13, §20).

I carried the discussion of these matters up to the point where I said: “Even if there are souls—although for the time being this is uncertain—that are devoted to bodily functions not through sin but by nature,” and so forth.

It may therefore be asked why I said “although for the time being this is uncertain,” since I ought not to have doubted at all that there are no such souls.

I said this because I had encountered people who claimed that the devil and his angels are good in their own kind and in the nature in which God created them, possessing their own proper order and being what they are; but that they are evil for us if we are enticed and deceived by them, whereas if we avoid and conquer them, this is noble and glorious.

Those who say this seem to themselves to bring suitable testimonies from Scripture to prove it—either what is written in the book of Job, when the devil is described: “This is the beginning of the Lord’s creation, which he made to be mocked by his angels” (Job 40:14); or: “This dragon whom you formed to mock him” (Psalm 103:26).

At that time I did not wish to examine and resolve this question—which would have had to be taken up not against the Manichaeans, who do not hold this view, but against others who do—lest I make the book much longer than I wished. I saw that even if this were granted, the Manichaeans nevertheless ought to be and already could be refuted for introducing, in their utterly insane error, a nature of evil coeternal with the eternal good.

Therefore I said “although for the time being this is uncertain,” not because I myself doubted it, but because, between me and those whom I had found holding this view, the question had not yet been resolved. I later resolved it in other books of mine, written much later, *On Genesis Literally*, with as much clarity as I could, in accordance with the holy Scriptures.

### 8

Elsewhere I said: “Therefore we sin by loving bodily things, because we are commanded to love spiritual things, are able by nature to love them, and then are best and most blessed in our own kind” (chapter 13, §20).

Here it may be asked why I said “we are able by nature,” rather than “we are able by grace” [Note: Am. and several manuscripts read: “why I said rather by grace.”].

But the question under discussion against the Manichaeans concerned nature. Grace, certainly, acts so that a healed nature may be able, through him who came to seek and save what was lost, to do what a corrupted nature cannot.

Nevertheless, even then, remembering this grace, I prayed for my closest companions, who were still held in that deadly error, and said: “Great God, almighty God, God of supreme goodness, whom it is right to believe and understand to be inviolable and incorruptible [Note: Four manuscripts add: “and unchangeable.” Am. and Er. read: “and immutable”], Triune Unity, whom the Catholic Church worships, I humbly beseech you, having experienced your mercy in me, not to permit the men with whom I had shared the closest harmony in every association since childhood to disagree with me in your worship” (chapter 15, §24).

In praying in this way, I already held by faith that not only are those who have turned to God helped by his grace so that they may progress and be perfected—in which case it might still be said that this grace is given in accordance with the merit of their conversion—but that it also belongs to God’s grace that they should turn to God. For I prayed for people who were excessively alienated from him, and I prayed that they might turn to that grace.

This book begins as follows: “With the help of God’s mercy…”

## CHAPTER XVI. *Proceedings against Fortunatus the Manichaean*, one book

### 1

At the same time, during my presbyterate, I disputed against a certain Fortunatus, a presbyter among the Manichaeans, who had lived for a long time at Hippo and had led so many astray that, for their sake, he was pleased to remain there.

The disputation was recorded by notaries as though official proceedings were being drawn up; it even gives the day and the consul. We took care to commit it to a book for remembrance.

The question discussed there was the origin of evil: I maintained that human evil had arisen from the free choice of the will, while he attempted to persuade us that the nature of evil was coeternal with God.

On the following day, however, he finally confessed that he could find nothing to say against us. He did not, in fact, become a Catholic, but nevertheless he departed from Hippo.

### 2

In this book I said: “I say that the soul was made by God, just as all other things made by God were made; and among the things that almighty God made, the soul was given the principal place” (Disputation 1, §13). I said this intending it to be understood generally of the whole rational creation, although it may either not be found at all in the holy Scriptures, or may not easily be found there, that the angels are called “souls,” as we have already said above.

Elsewhere I said: “I say that there is no sin if one does not sin by one’s own will” (Disputation 2, §21). By “sin” I wished to be understood that which is not also the punishment of sin; for elsewhere in the same disputation I spoke of such punishment, as had to be said (Disputation 1, §15).

I also said: “So that afterward this same flesh, which tormented us while we remained in sins, may be subjected to us in the resurrection, and may not shake us by any adversity so as to prevent us from keeping the divine law and commandments” (Disputation 2, §22).

This should not be understood as though, in that kingdom of God where we shall have an incorruptible and immortal body, the law and commandments must be taken from the divine Scriptures. Rather, the eternal law will there be observed with perfect completeness, and those two commandments concerning love of God and of neighbor will be held not in reading but in perfect and everlasting love.

This work begins as follows: “On the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of the emperors Arcadius, for the second time, and Rufinus, most illustrious men.”

## CHAPTER XVII. *On Faith and the Creed*, one boo[k]

During the same period, at the command of the bishops who were holding at Hippo Regius the plenary council of all Africa, I, a presbyter, disputed before them on Faith and the Creed. At the earnest insistence of some of those who loved us with particular affection, I committed that disputation to a book. In it the subjects themselves are discussed, though without that connected sequence of words which is taught to catechumens for memorization.

In this book, when the resurrection of the flesh was being discussed, I wrote: “The body will rise, I say, according to the Christian faith, which cannot deceive” [Col. 0613] [Note: Some manuscripts have *falli* (“be deceived”) instead of *fallere* (“deceive”).]. Whoever considers this incredible attends to what the flesh is now, but does not consider what it will be in the future: “for at the time of that angelic transformation it will no longer be flesh and blood, but only a body” (Chapter 10, §23). I also discussed there the transformation of earthly bodies into heavenly bodies, since the Apostle, speaking of this, said: “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God.”

But whoever understands this in such a way as to suppose that the earthly body which we now have is changed by resurrection into a heavenly body, so that neither these limbs nor the substance of flesh will exist in the future, must unquestionably be corrected by being reminded of the Lord’s body. After the resurrection it appeared with the same limbs, not only to be seen by the eyes but also to be handled by the hands; and He affirmed even in words that He had flesh, saying: “Touch me and see, because a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me have” (Luke 24:39).

It is therefore clear that the Apostle did not deny that the substance of flesh would exist in the kingdom of God; rather, he either called human beings who live according to the flesh “flesh and blood,” or he referred to the corruption of the flesh itself, which certainly will then no longer exist. For when he had said, “Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,” it is rightly understood as though, explaining what he had said, he immediately added: “Nor will corruption possess incorruption” (1 Corinthians 15:50).

Whoever reads the final book of *The City of God* will discover how carefully, as far as I was able, I discussed this difficult matter in order to persuade unbelievers [Note: See *The City of God*, Book 22, chapters 5 and 21.]. This book begins as follows: “Since it is written…”

## CHAPTER XVIII. *On Genesis Literally*, an unfinished book

After I had composed two books against the Manichaeans on Genesis, I had treated the words of Scripture according to their allegorical meaning and had not dared to expound literally such profound secrets of natural things—that is, to explain how what is said there might be understood according to its historical sense. I wished to test in this extremely laborious and difficult work what I was capable of doing. But in expounding Scripture my apprenticeship collapsed under the great weight of the task. Before completing even one book, I rested from a labor that I was unable to sustain.

While revising my smaller works in this work, this very book, unfinished as it was, came into my hands. I had neither published it nor had resolved to destroy it, since I later wrote twelve books entitled *On Genesis Literally*. Although in those books many things seem rather to have been sought than discovered, this work is nevertheless in no way comparable to them. Yet after revising this book also, I wished it to remain as, in my judgment, a not-useless indication of my beginnings in analyzing and investigating the divine utterances; and I wanted its title to be *On Genesis Literally, Unfinished*.

I found that it had been dictated up to these words: “The Father is only Father, and the Son is nothing other than Son; for even when He is called the likeness [Col. 0614] of the Father, although this shows that no dissimilarity intervenes, the Father is not alone if He has a likeness” (Chapter 16, §60) [Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, and the Benignian manuscript, read: “but he has a likeness.”].

After this I returned to the words of Scripture in order to consider and discuss them again: “And God said, ‘Let us make man in our image and likeness’” (Genesis 1:26). I had left the dictated book unfinished up to this point. When I revised it, I thought that what follows should be added; yet even then I did not complete it, but left it unfinished after this addition as well.

For if I had completed it, I would at least have discussed all the works and words of God belonging to the sixth day. In this book I considered it superfluous to note what displeases me or to defend what might rightly displease others because they have not understood it well. I simply give the brief admonition that the twelve books should be read—the books I wrote much later, after I had become a bishop—and that this work should be judged from them.

This book therefore begins as follows: “Concerning the obscure matters of natural things which we perceive to have been made by God the almighty craftsman, one must proceed not by affirming but by investigating.”

## CHAPTER XIX. *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, two books

### 1.

During the same period I wrote two volumes on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount according to Matthew. In the first, because it is written, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9), I said: “Wisdom belongs appropriately to peacemakers, in whom all things have already been ordered, and no rebellious movement is directed against reason; rather, everything obeys the human spirit, while the spirit itself obeys God” (Book 1, chapter 4, §11).

This rightly raises the question of how I could have spoken in that way. No one in this life can reach the point at which the law opposing the law of the mind is altogether absent from his members. Even if the human spirit resisted it so completely that it never yielded assent to it, that law would nevertheless still be opposed to it. Therefore, what was said about there being “no rebellious movement against reason” can rightly be understood of the peacemakers’ present activity: they are subduing the desires of the flesh so that they may eventually arrive at that fullest peace.

### 2.

Accordingly, elsewhere, when repeating the same evangelical saying, I said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9), and added: “These things can indeed be fulfilled in this life, just as we believe they were fulfilled in the Apostles” (Book 1, chapter 4, §12). This must be understood not as though we should suppose that, while the Apostles were living here, no movement of the flesh opposed the spirit, but rather that these things can be fulfilled here to the extent that we believe they were fulfilled in the Apostles—that is, according to the measure of human perfection possible in this life.

For it was not said, “These things can be fulfilled in this life, for we believe they were fulfilled in the Apostles,” but, “just as we believe they were fulfilled in the Apostles,” so that they may be fulfilled as they were fulfilled in them: with a certain perfection of which this life is capable, not in the manner in which they will be fulfilled in the complete peace for which we hope, when it will be said: “Where is your contention, O death?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

### 3.

Elsewhere (Book 1, chapter 6, §17), I inserted the testimony: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34). At that time I had not yet understood that this is more properly and more truly taken as referring to Christ. If the Spirit were given to other human beings without measure, Elisha would not have asked for twice as much as there had been in Elijah.

Again, when explaining what is written—“Not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things have taken place” (Matthew 5:18)—I said that nothing else could be understood except a forceful expression of perfection (Book 1, chapter 8, §20). Here it is rightly asked whether this perfection can be understood in such a way that it nevertheless remains true that no one living here with the use of free will is without sin.

For by whom can the Law be perfected down to a single stroke, except by one through whom all the divine commandments are fulfilled? Yet among those commandments is also the one by which we are commanded to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12); and the whole Church says this prayer until the end of the age. Thus all the commandments are reckoned as fulfilled when whatever is not done is forgiven.

### 4.

As for what the Lord says—“Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches others to do so,” and so forth, up to the passage where He says, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:18–20)—I explained this much better and more appropriately in other sermons I wrote later; it would be lengthy to reproduce that explanation here.

In this work, however, the interpretation is brought to the point (Book 1, chapter 9, §21) that those have a righteousness greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees who “say and do” [Note: Earlier printed editions read, “who say and do not do.” We have removed the negating particle, which is absent from the manuscripts, so that the relative pronoun “who” refers to those whose righteousness is greater.]. For elsewhere the Lord Himself says of the scribes and Pharisees: “They say, and do not do” (Matthew 23:3).

We also later understood better what is written: “Whoever is angry with his brother” (Matthew 5:22). The Greek manuscripts do not have *without cause* [Note: Nowadays it is difficult to find a Greek manuscript that does not have *eikē*, “without cause,” which Chrysostom also read in his copy. Jerome says that it should be erased, whereas Augustine here restores it to its proper meaning.], although the sense is nevertheless the same. We said that one must consider what it means to be angry with one’s brother, since a person is not angry with his brother when he is angry with his brother’s sin. Therefore, whoever is angry with his brother rather than with his sin is angry without cause.

### 5.

Again, what I said—“This is also to be understood of father, mother, and the other bonds of blood, so that in them we hate what the human race has acquired by being born and dying” (Book 1, chapter 15, §41)—sounds as though these relationships would not have existed if, without any preceding sin of human nature, no one had died. I already rejected that interpretation above.

Kinships and affinities would certainly have existed even if, with no original sin, the human race had grown and multiplied without death. Accordingly, the question must be resolved in another way: why the Lord commanded us to love our enemies (Matthew 5:44), while elsewhere He commands us to hate parents and children (Luke 14:26). It should not be resolved as it was here, but as we often resolved it later: we are to love enemies in order to win them for the kingdom of God, and to hate our relatives if they hinder us from the kingdom of God.

### 6.

Regarding the commandment forbidding a wife to be dismissed except on account of fornication, I argued here with the greatest care (Book 1, chapter 19). But what kind of fornication the Lord wishes to be understood as permitting the dismissal of a wife must be considered and investigated again and again: whether it is the fornication condemned in adulterous acts, or that of which it is said, “You have destroyed everyone who fornicates away from you” (Psalm 72:27)—in which the former is also included. For one who takes Christ’s members and makes them members of a prostitute certainly fornicates away from the Lord.

I do not want the reader to think that, in a matter so important and so difficult to distinguish, our discussion here ought to suffice. Let the reader also consult other writings, whether our own written later or those of others that have been considered and treated more carefully; or, if able, let the reader examine with a more watchful and intelligent mind the matters that can rightly cause difficulty here.

This is not because every sin is fornication. God does not destroy everyone who sins, since He daily hears His saints saying, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12), whereas He destroys everyone who fornicates away from Him. But how this fornication is to be understood and limited, and whether a wife may also be dismissed on account of it, is a most obscure question. That it is permitted on account of the fornication committed in adulterous acts, however, is beyond question.

And when I said that this was permitted, not commanded, I failed to take account of another Scripture, which says: “He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and ungodly” (Proverbs 18:22). Nor would I say that the woman was to be counted an adulteress after she had heard the Lord say, “Neither will I condemn you; go, and from now on do not sin” (John 8:11), provided that she heard this obediently.

### 7.

Elsewhere, I defined the “sin unto death” of a brother, concerning which the Apostle John says, “I do not say that anyone should pray for it” (1 John 5:16), as follows: “I think that a brother’s sin unto death occurs when, after coming to know God through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, someone attacks the brotherhood and is inflamed by the fires of envy against the very grace by which he has been reconciled to God” (Book 1, chapter 22, §73).

I did not affirm this, since I said only that I thought it so. Nevertheless, I should have added that this applies if he ended this life in such a wicked perversity of mind. For one who is still living in this life, however wicked he may be, must never be despaired of; nor is it rash to pray for someone of whom one has not despaired.

### 8.

In the second book I also said: “No one will be permitted to be ignorant of the kingdom of God, since His Only-begotten Son will come from heaven—not only intelligibly but also visibly, in the Lord’s man (*homo dominicus*)—to judge the living and the dead” (Book 2, chapter 6, §20).

But I do not see whether it is correct to call the man who is the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, “the Lord’s man” (*homo dominicus*), since He is certainly Lord. A “lordly man” (*homo dominicus*) can be said to be anyone in His holy household. I found this expression in certain Catholic interpreters of the divine utterances [Note: Perhaps in Athanasius, *Exposition of the Faith*, and in Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*.]. But wherever I used it, I would prefer not to have done so. Later I saw that it ought not to be said, although it can be defended on a certain interpretation.

Again, when I said, “For scarcely anyone’s conscience can hate God” (Book 2, chapter 14, §48), I do not see that this ought to have been said. There are many of whom it is written: “The pride of those who hate you” (Psalm 73:23).

### 9.

Elsewhere, when I said that the Lord’s saying, “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matthew 6:34), was spoken because necessity itself would compel us to take food, and that I think it is called “evil” because it is punitive for us and belongs to the weakness we merited by sinning (Book 2, chapter 17, §56), I failed to take account of the fact that bodily nourishment had also been given to the first human beings in paradise before they merited this punishment of death through sin.

They were therefore immortal in body—not yet spiritual, but animal—while nevertheless using bodily nourishment in that kind of immortality.

Again, when I said (Book 2, chapter 19, §66) that God chose for Himself “a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27), I did not mean that it is already such in every respect. Yet there is no doubt that it was chosen in order to become such when Christ, who is its life, appears. Then it too will appear with Him in glory; and it is on account of that glory that the Church is called glorious.

Again, although I took pains to explain how the three commands differ from one another—“Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7)—it is much better to refer all three to persistent asking. This is shown where He gathered everything together in the same expression, saying: “How much more will your heavenly Father give good things to those who ask Him?” (Matthew 7:11). He did not say, “to those who ask, seek, and knock.”

This work begins as follows: “The sermon which the Lord spoke…”

## CHAPTER XX. *A Psalm against the Donatist Party*

Because I wanted the cause of the Donatists to reach the knowledge of the humblest common people, and of those altogether uneducated and illiterate, and because I wanted it, as far as possible, to remain fixed in their memory through us, I composed a Psalm for them to sing, using Latin letters—but only up to the letter V. Such compositions are called alphabetic poems.

I omitted the final three letters, but in their place I added a final passage, almost an epilogue, as though the Church, their mother, were addressing them. The *hypopsalma*, the response that was to be sung, and the preface to the controversy, which was likewise to be sung, do not follow the order of the letters; the order of the letters begins after the preface.

I wanted this to be done without any particular poetic form, so that the demands of meter would not compel me to use words less familiar to ordinary people.

This Psalm begins as follows: “All you who rejoice in peace, now judge truly”—which is its *hypopsalma*.

## CHAPTER XXI. *Against the Letter of the Heretic Donatus*, one book

*[This work is not extant.]*

### 1.

During the same period of my presbyterate I also wrote a book against the Letter of Donatus, who was the second bishop of the Donatist party at Carthage after Majorinus. In that letter he argued that Christ’s baptism should be believed to exist only in communion with him. In this book we contradict him [Note: “Whom we contradict in this book”: “in which I said.” This should be read thus, in accordance with the English manuscripts and some of our own.].

In one passage I said of the Apostle Peter that the Church was founded in him as upon a rock. This interpretation is also sung by many mouths in the verses of the most blessed Ambrose, where, speaking of the cockcrow, he says: “At its crowing, the very rock of the Church washes away guilt.”

But I know that afterward I very frequently explained what the Lord said—“You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church”—as meaning that the Church was built upon the one whom Peter confessed by saying, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:18, 16). Thus Peter was named from this rock and represented the person of the Church, which is built upon this rock and received the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

For it was not said to him, “You are the rock,” but, “You are Peter.” The rock was Christ. Simon, having confessed Him, as the whole Church confesses Him, was called Peter. Let the reader choose which of these two interpretations is the more probable.

### 2.

Elsewhere I said, “God seeks no one’s death.” This should be understood in the sense that the human being acquired death for himself by abandoning God, and acquires it by failing to return to God, according to what is written: “God did not make death” (Wisdom 1:13).

But this too is no less true: “Life and death are from the Lord God” (Sirach 11:14)—life from the One who gives it, death from the One who exacts punishment.

### 3.

Again, I said that Donatus, whose letter I was refuting, had asked the Emperor to appoint overseas bishops as judges between himself and Caecilian. It is more probable that this was done not by him but by another Donatus, although he too belonged to the same schism.

The latter was not the Carthaginian bishop of the Donatists, but Donatus of Casis-Nigris; nevertheless, it was he who first committed that wicked schism at Carthage [Note: “This man, coming from Numidia,” Augustine says, “and dividing the Christian people against Caecilian, joined by bishops of the same faction, ordained Majorinus bishop at Carthage. Another Donatus succeeded Majorinus, and by his eloquence strengthened this heresy.” From the book *On Heresies, to Quodvultdeus*, chapter 69.].

Nor did Donatus of Carthage institute the rebaptism of Christians; I had believed that he instituted it when I replied to his letter.

Nor did he remove from the middle of a sentence in the book of Ecclesiasticus [Note: The manuscripts, together with the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, read “from the book of Wisdom.”] the words necessary to the meaning, where it is written: “He who is baptized by a dead person and again touches him, what does his washing profit?” (Sirach 34:30). He presented it as though it were written: “He who is baptized by a dead person, what does his washing profit?”

But we later learned that, even before the Donatist party existed, many copies—African copies, to be sure—had the text in this form, without the words “and again touches him.” If I had known this then, I would not have said so much against him as against a thief of the divine utterance or its violator.

This book begins as follows: “I had heard this from you yourself, while you were present…”

## CHAPTER XXII. *Against Adimantus, a Disciple of Manichaeus*, one book

### 1.

At the same time, certain disputations of Adimantus came into my hands. He had been a disciple of Manichaeus and had written against the Law and the Prophets, attempting to demonstrate that the evangelical and apostolic writings were contrary to them.

I replied to him by setting out his words and giving my response to them. I completed the work in a single volume. In it I answered certain questions not once but twice, because the answer I had first given had been lost and was discovered only after I had answered again.

I also resolved some of the same questions in popular ecclesiastical sermons. Even now I have not answered certain others; some remain because they were set aside in favor of more pressing matters, with forgetfulness adding to the accumulation.

### 2.

In this work I said: “Before the Lord’s coming, that people which received the Old Testament was held under certain shadows and figures of realities, according to the wondrous and perfectly ordered distribution of the ages. Nevertheless, there is so much proclamation and prefiguration of the New Testament in it that no difficult and divine commandments or promises are found in evangelical and apostolic teaching that are absent even from those ancient books” (Chapter 3, §4).

But I should have added *almost*, and said: “so that almost no difficult and divine commandments or promises are found in evangelical and apostolic teaching that are absent even from those ancient books.”

For what is the meaning of the Lord’s saying in the evangelical Sermon on the Mount: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients; but I say to you” (Matthew 5:21), if He Himself commanded nothing more than what had been commanded in those ancient books?

Moreover, we do not read that the kingdom of heaven was promised to that people among the promises made in the Law given through Moses on Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:3–6), which is properly called the Old Testament. The Apostle says that this was prefigured by Sarah’s slave woman and her son; but the New Testament was also prefigured there by Sarah herself and her son (Galatians 4:22–31).

Accordingly, if the figures are examined, everything is found to have been prophesied there that has been presented, or is expected to be presented, through Christ. Nevertheless, because certain commandments that are not figurative but proper to the New Testament are found not in the Old Testament but in the New, it would be said more cautiously and moderately: “Almost none,” rather than “none,” are found here that are not also found there.

Even so, the two commandments concerning love of God and neighbor are found there, and all the commandments—legal, prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic—are most properly referred to them.

### 3.

Again, what I said—“The name ‘sons’ is used in three ways in the holy Scriptures” (Chapter 5, §1)—was said with insufficient consideration. We had undoubtedly omitted several other ways, such as “son of Gehenna” (Matthew 23:15) and “adoptive son” (Romans 8:14–15). These are not spoken according to nature, doctrine, or imitation.

We gave examples as though these three were the only forms: according to nature, as the Jews are sons of Abraham (John 8:37); according to doctrine, as the Apostle calls those whom he taught the Gospel his sons (1 Corinthians 4:14); and according to imitation, as we are sons of Abraham because we imitate his faith (Galatians [Col. 0620] 4:28).

When I said (Chapter 12, §5), “When it has put on incorruption and immortality, it will no longer be flesh and blood” (1 Corinthians 15:54), I was speaking of the corruption belonging to the flesh: I meant that flesh would no longer be subject to corruption, not that it would cease to exist in substance. According to its substance, the Lord’s body was called flesh even after the resurrection (Luke 24:39).

### 4.

Elsewhere (Chapter 26) I said: “Unless each person changes his will, he cannot do good. Scripture teaches that this lies within our power where it says: ‘Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad’” (Matthew 12:33).

This is not contrary to the grace of God that we proclaim. It is within a human being’s power to change his will for the better; but that power exists only if it is given by God, of whom it is said: “He gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12).

For that lies within our power which we do when we will; and nothing is so much within our power as the will itself. Yet the will is prepared by the Lord. In this way, therefore, He gives power.

The same must be understood of what I said later: that it lies within our power whether we deserve to be grafted into God’s goodness or cut off by His severity. For nothing lies within our power except what follows our will; and when the will is prepared by the Lord as strong and powerful, an act of piety is easily accomplished, even when it had been difficult or impossible.

This book begins as follows: “Concerning what is written: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth.’”

## CHAPTER XXIII. *An Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Apostle’s Letter to the Romans*

### 1.

While I was still a presbyter, it happened that the Apostle’s Letter to the Romans was being read among us who were together at Carthage, and the brothers asked me certain questions. When I answered them as I was able, they preferred that what I said should be written down rather than poured forth without being committed to writing. By complying with them, I added one book to my earlier small works.

In this book I said: “When he says, ‘We know that the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal,’ he sufficiently shows that the Law cannot be fulfilled except by spiritual people, whom the grace of God makes so.”

I did not at that time wish this to be understood as spoken in the person of the Apostle, who was already spiritual, but of a person placed under the Law and not yet under grace. This was how I formerly understood these words. Later, after reading certain interpreters of the divine utterances whose authority moved me, I considered them more carefully and saw that what he says—“We know that the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal”—could also be understood of the Apostle himself. In the books I recently wrote against the Pelagians, I demonstrated this as carefully as I could.

In this book, therefore, I said that the words “But I am carnal,” and everything that follows up to the passage where he says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:14–25), describe a person still under the Law and not yet established under grace: one who wants to do good but, overcome by the desire of the flesh, does evil (Propositions 41–46).

No one is freed from the dominion of this desire except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Through that Spirit, love poured into our hearts conquers the desires of the flesh, so that we do not consent to them in order to do evil, but rather do good.

This overturns the Pelagian heresy, which wishes the love by which we live well and piously to come not from God but from ourselves.

Yet in the books we published against them, we showed that these words can also be better understood of the spiritual person, already established under grace, on account of the body of the flesh, which is not yet spiritual but will be spiritual in the resurrection of the dead. They can also be understood on account of the very desire of the flesh, against which the saints struggle, not consenting to it for evil, yet not being free in this life from its movements, which they resist as they oppose them.

They will not have these movements in the life to come, where death will be swallowed up in victory. On account of this desire, therefore, and of the movements themselves—which are resisted in such a way that they nevertheless remain within us—a holy person already under grace can say all these things, which here I said were the words of a person not yet under grace but under the Law.

It would take too long to demonstrate this here; it is stated at the place where I demonstrated it (Chapter 6).

### 2.

Again, when discussing what God chose in the case of the one not yet born to whom He said that the elder would serve, and what He similarly rejected in that same elder, likewise not yet born—matters recalled on account of the prophetic testimony uttered much later, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Romans 9:13)—I carried my reasoning to the point of saying:

“Therefore God did not choose anyone’s works in foreknowledge, works which He Himself would give; rather, He chose faith in foreknowledge, so that the one whom He foreknew would believe in Him He would choose to receive the Holy Spirit, in order that, by doing good, he might also attain eternal life” (Proposition 60).

At that time I had not yet investigated carefully enough, nor had I yet discovered, what the election of grace is. Concerning it the same Apostle says: “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5). This is certainly not grace if any merits precede it, since what is then given is no longer given according to grace but according to debt, being repaid on the basis of merits rather than bestowed as a gift.

Accordingly, when I immediately went on to say, “For the same Apostle says, ‘The same God works all things in all people’ (1 Corinthians 12:6); but nowhere is it said, ‘God believes all things in all people,’” and then added, “Therefore what we believe is ours, but what good we do belongs to Him who gives the Holy Spirit to those who believe” (Proposition 61), I certainly would not have said this if I had already known that faith itself is also found among God’s gifts, which are given in the same Spirit.

Both, therefore, are ours on account of the freedom of the will, and yet both have been given through the Spirit of faith and love. For it is not love alone, but, as it is written, “Love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 6:23).

### 3.

A little later I also said: “It is ours to believe and to will, but it belongs to Him to give those who believe and will the ability to do good through the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts” (Proposition 61).

This is true, but according to the same rule both things also belong to Him, because He prepares the will; and both are ours, because nothing is done unless we will it.

Accordingly, what I also said later is true: “For we cannot even will unless we are called; and when, after the call, we have willed, our will and our course are not sufficient unless God both supplies strength to those who run and brings them to the place to which He calls them.” Then I added: “It is therefore clear that it belongs not to the one who wills or to the one who runs, but to God who has mercy, that we do good” (Romans 9:16).

This is entirely true. But I said too little about the call itself, which occurs according to God’s purpose. For the call is not of this kind for everyone who is called, but only for the elect.

Accordingly, what I said a little later is entirely true: “Just as among those whom God chooses, faith—not works—begins the merit by which they do good through God’s gift, so among those whom He condemns, unbelief and ungodliness begin the merit of punishment, so that through that punishment they also do evil.”

But I did not think it necessary to ask, nor did I say, that the merit of faith itself is also a gift of God.

### 4.

Elsewhere I said: “For the one of whom He has mercy, He makes him do good; and the one whom He hardens” (Romans 9:18), “He leaves to do evil. But that mercy is attributed to a preceding merit of faith, and that hardening to preceding ungodliness” (Proposition 62).

This is true, but it still needed to be asked whether the merit of faith itself comes from God’s mercy [Note: Amerbach reads: “May the merit of faith precede God’s mercy.” Erasmus and some manuscripts read: “May God’s mercy precede the merit of faith.”]—that is, whether this mercy is shown to a person only because he is faithful, or whether it is also shown so that he might become faithful.

For we read the Apostle saying, “I received mercy in order to be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25); he does not say, “because I was faithful.” Mercy is therefore given to one who is faithful, but it was also given so that he might become faithful.

Accordingly, I rightly said elsewhere in the same book: “Since we are called to believe not on the basis of works but by God’s mercy, and since those who believe are enabled to do good, this mercy is not to be begrudged to the Gentiles” (Proposition 64). Yet there I treated less carefully the call that occurs according to God’s purpose.

This book begins as follows: “These are the meanings found in Paul’s Letter to the Romans.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. *An Exposition of the Letter to the Galatians*, one book

### 1.

After this book I expounded the Letter of the same Apostle to the Galatians—not piecemeal, omitting some portions, but continuously and in its entirety. I contained this exposition in a single volume.

In it, where I said, “The earlier apostles were true apostles, sent not by human beings but by God through a human being—namely, through Jesus Christ while He was still mortal. The last apostle was also true, sent through Jesus Christ, who after His resurrection was already wholly God,” the expression “already wholly God” was spoken on account of the immortality which He began to possess after the resurrection, not on account of the divinity that had always been immortal and from which He never departed, in which He was wholly God even while He was still going to die.

The following words make this meaning clear. I added: “The other Apostles are earlier, through Jesus Christ who was still partly human, that is, mortal; the Apostle Paul is later, through Jesus Christ who was already wholly God, that is, immortal in every respect” (Proposition 2).

I said this while explaining the Apostle’s words: “Not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father,” as though Jesus Christ were no longer human. For it follows: “Who raised Him from the dead” (Galatians 1:1), so that this would show why he said, “nor through a human being.”

Therefore, on account of immortality, Christ is now no longer a human being but God; yet on account of the substance of human nature in which He ascended into heaven, He is still “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5), since He will come in the same way as those who saw Him going into heaven saw Him go (Acts 1:11).

## 2. Likewise, concerning what I said: “The grace of God is that by which sins are forgiven us, so that we may be reconciled to God; peace, however, is that by which we are reconciled to God” (No. 3), it must be understood in such a way that we nevertheless recognize that both belong to the general grace of God—just as, among the people of God, one thing is specifically Israel and another Judah, yet both are generally Israel.

Likewise, when I was expounding the words, “What then? Was the Law added because of transgressions?” [Note: [Col. 0623] Thus most manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek *prosetéthē*; likewise the Louvain editions in the passage under revision, although here they follow the Vulgate, “was given.”] (Gal. 3:19), I thought it should be punctuated so that the question would be, “What then?” and the answer would follow: “The Law was added because of transgressions” [Note: [Col. 0623] Thus most manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek *prosetéthē*; likewise the Louvain editions in the passage under revision, although here they follow the Vulgate, “was given.”] (No. 24). This indeed is not contrary to the truth; but this punctuation seems better to me: let the question be, “What then is the Law?” and let the answer follow: “It was added because of transgressions.”

But when I said, “Therefore he added most orderly: ‘But if you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the Law,’” so that we might understand those to be under the Law whose spirit so lusts against the flesh that they do not do the things they will—that is, they do not remain invincible in the love of righteousness, but are overcome by the flesh lusting against them (No. 47)—this reflected the understanding I then had: that the words, “The flesh lusts against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you will” (Gal. 5:17–18), referred to those who are under the Law and not yet under grace.

For I had not yet understood that these words also apply to those who are under grace and not under the Law, because they too have desires of the flesh against which they lust spiritually; although they do not consent to them, they would nevertheless wish to have none of them if they could. And therefore they do not do whatever they wish, because they wish to be free of these desires but cannot. They will not have them then, when they will no longer have corruptible flesh.

This book begins as follows: “The reason for which the Apostle writes.”

## CHAPTER XXV. An Unfinished Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, one book

I had also undertaken an exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, just as of the Epistle to the Galatians. But if this work had been completed, several books would have been required. I completed one of them in the discussion of the salutation itself alone, from the beginning up to the words, “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

It happened that, when we wished to resolve a very difficult question that arose in our discussion concerning the sin against the Holy Spirit—which is not forgiven either in this age or in the age to come—we lingered over it. But afterward I ceased adding further volumes in order to expound the whole Epistle, deterred by the magnitude and labor of the work, and turned to easier subjects.

Thus it came about that I left alone the first book I had composed, and wished its title to be *An Unfinished Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*. Wherever I said that grace consists in the forgiveness of sins and peace in reconciliation with God, this must not be understood as though peace and reconciliation themselves did not belong to the general grace of God; rather, by the specific name “grace” I signified the forgiveness of sins. So too we speak of the Law both specifically, as when it is said, “The Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40), and generally, so that the Prophets are included within it.

This book begins as follows: “In the Epistle that the Apostle Paul wrote to the Romans.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. On Eighty-Three Different Questions, one book

Among the works we wrote there is also an extensive work which is nevertheless counted as a single book, entitled *On Eighty-Three Different Questions*. Since these questions had been scattered over many sheets—dictated from the very beginning of my conversion, after we came to Africa, as the brethren asked me questions whenever they saw me at leisure, without my preserving any arrangement—I ordered, once I had become bishop, that they should be gathered together and made into one book, with numbers added so that anyone wishing to read a particular question might easily find it.

The first of these questions is whether the soul exists from itself. The second concerns free choice. The third asks whether man is made worse by God as author. The fourth asks what causes man to be worse. The fifth asks whether an irrational animal can be blessed. The sixth concerns evil. The seventh asks what is properly called “soul” in a living creature. The eighth asks whether the soul moves by itself. The ninth asks whether truth can be perceived through bodily senses.

In this ninth question, where I said, “Everything touched by bodily sense, which is also called sensible, is changed without any interruption of time,” this is certainly not true of the incorruptible bodies of the resurrection. But none of our bodily senses now touches such bodies, unless perhaps something of this kind should be revealed by divine power.

The tenth asks whether the body is from God. The eleventh asks why Christ was born of a woman. The twelfth has the title *The Judgment of a Certain Wise Man*. It is not mine; but because it became known through me to certain brethren who were then carefully collecting these materials from me, they were pleased to write it among my works. It belongs to a certain Fonteius of Carthage [Note: [Col. 0624] The Louvain edition adds: “Who wrote something about the life of the Brahmans”; this is entirely absent from the Ambrosian, Erasmian, and manuscript witnesses.], and concerns the cleansing of the mind in order to see God. He wrote it as a pagan, but died baptized as a Christian.

The thirteenth asks by what evidence it is established that human beings surpass beasts. The fourteenth asks whether the body of our Lord Jesus Christ was not a phantom. [Col. 0625] The fifteenth concerns understanding. The sixteenth concerns the Son of God. The seventeenth concerns the knowledge of God. The eighteenth concerns the Trinity [Note: [Col. 0625] The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and manuscripts of no lesser quality read, “On the Triune Unity.”]. The nineteenth concerns God and creation. The twentieth concerns the place of God.

The twenty-first asks whether God is not the author of evil. Here it must be considered lest what I said—“He is not the author of evil”—be misunderstood, since he is the author of all things that exist, and insofar as they exist, they are good; nor should it be thought from this that the punishment of the wicked, which is certainly evil for those who are punished, is not from him. But I said this in the sense in which it is written, “God did not make death” (Wis. 1:13), although elsewhere it is written, “Death and life are from the Lord God” (Ecclus. 11:14).

The punishment of the wicked, therefore, which comes from God, is indeed evil for the wicked; but it belongs among God’s good works, since it is just that the wicked should be punished, and everything just is certainly good.

The twenty-second asks whether God is subject to necessity. The twenty-third concerns the Father and the Son. There I said that he himself generated the wisdom by which he is called wise; but we treated this question better later in the book *On the Trinity*. The twenty-fourth asks whether both sin and right action lie within free choice of the will. This is altogether most certainly so; but in order that the will may be free for right action, it is freed by the grace of God.

The twenty-fifth concerns the cross of Christ. The twenty-sixth concerns the difference among sins. The twenty-seventh concerns providence. The twenty-eighth asks why God wished to make the world. The twenty-ninth asks whether anything is above or below in the universe. The thirtieth asks whether all things were created for the benefit of man.

The thirty-first [Note: [Col. 0625] Here the Louvain editors insert the title of the first sentence from book 21 of the *Sentences*: “XXXI. That the person who lives as he wishes is blessed.” It is not mine either. We detected the interpolation with the help of the Ambrosian, Erasmian, and more reliable manuscripts.] is not mine either, but Cicero’s—Tullius, *On Duties*, book 1. But because this too became known through me to the brethren, they wrote it among the materials they were collecting, wishing to know how he had divided and defined the virtues of the soul.

The thirty-second asks whether one person understands a given matter more than another, and whether understanding of the same matter therefore proceeds to infinity. The thirty-third concerns fear. The thirty-fourth asks whether anything should be loved except freedom from fear. The thirty-fifth asks what should be loved.

In this question I said that what should be loved is that to possess which is nothing other than to know it; I do not sufficiently approve this statement. For those to whom it was said, “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Cor. 3:16), did possess God, yet did not know him, or did not know him as he ought to be known.

Likewise, when I said, “Therefore no one knows the blessed life, and is miserable,” by “knows” I meant “knows how it ought to be known.” For who among those who already use reason is entirely ignorant of it, since they know that they wish to be blessed?

The thirty-sixth concerns the nurturing of love. There I said: “Therefore God and the mind by which he is loved are properly called the most pure and perfected love, if nothing else is loved.” But if this is true, how then does the Apostle say, “No one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:29)? From this he urges that wives should be loved.

But it was said that love is “properly” so called because flesh is indeed loved, though not properly, but for the sake of the soul to which it is subject for use. For even if it seems to be loved for its own sake, when we do not want it to be deformed, its beauty must be referred to something else—namely, to that from which all things are beautiful.

The thirty-seventh concerns the One who is eternally begotten. The thirty-eighth concerns the formation of the soul. The thirty-ninth concerns nourishment. The fortieth asks: if the nature of souls is one, whence come the different wills of human beings? The forty-first asks: since God made all things, why did he not make them equal? The forty-second asks how the Wisdom of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, was both in his mother’s womb and in heaven.

The forty-third asks why the Son of God appeared in a human being and the Holy Spirit in a dove (Matt. 3:16). The forty-fourth asks why the Lord Jesus Christ came so long afterward.
