When I was recalling the ages of the human race as though of one human being, I said: “Nor was it fitting for the teacher sent from heaven, by whose imitation it would be formed toward excellent conduct, to come except at the time of youth.” I added that this was related to what the Apostle says, namely, that those under the Law were guarded as children under a pedagogue (Gal. 3:23).

But it may cause difficulty that elsewhere we said that Christ came in the sixth age of the human race, as in its old age (*On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book 1, ch. 23, no. 40). What was said there about youth refers to the strength and fervor of faith, which works through love; what was said about old age refers to the number of the ages.

Both may be understood in the whole human race, though not in the ages of individual human beings. Just as youth and old age cannot coexist in the body, they can coexist in the soul: the former on account of liveliness, the latter on account of seriousness.

The forty-fifth is against the astrologers. The forty-sixth concerns ideas. The forty-seventh asks whether we can ever see our thoughts.

There I said that the angelic bodies which we hope to possess should be believed to be most luminous and ethereal. If this is understood as meaning that they will exist without the members we now have and without substance, although incorruptible, of flesh, the statement is erroneous. The question of seeing our thoughts was treated much better in the work *The City of God* (book 22, ch. 29).

The forty-eighth concerns things to be believed. The forty-ninth asks why the children of Israel visibly sacrificed victims from livestock. The fiftieth concerns the equality of the Son. The fifty-first concerns man made in the image and likeness of God.

There I said: “A man without life is not rightly called a man,” although a human corpse is also called a man. Therefore I should at least have said, “He is not properly so called,” where I said, “He is not rightly called.”

I also said: “Nor is it ineptly distinguished that one thing is the image and likeness of God, and another is ‘according to the image and likeness of God,’ as we understand man to have been made.” This must not be understood as though man were not called the image of God, since the Apostle says, “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God” (1 Cor. 11:7). But he is also said to be “according to the image of God”; the Only-Begotten is not so called, since he is simply the image, not “according to the image.”

The fifty-second concerns the statement, “It repented me that I had made man” (Gen. 6:6–7). The fifty-third concerns the gold and silver which the Israelites received from the Egyptians [Col. 0627] (Exod. 3:22; 12:35). The fifty-fourth concerns the statement, “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28).

There I said, “What is better than every soul, we call God.” It should rather have been said, “What is better than every created spirit.”

The fifty-fifth concerns the statement, “There are sixty queens, eighty concubines, and maidens without number” (Song 6:7). The fifty-sixth concerns the forty-six years during which the Temple was built. The fifty-seventh concerns the one hundred and fifty-three fish. The fifty-eighth concerns John the Baptist. The fifty-ninth concerns the ten virgins.

The sixtieth concerns the statement, “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son of Man, but the Father alone” (Matt. 24:36). The sixty-first concerns the Gospel passage in which the Lord fed the crowds on the mountain with five loaves (ibid. 14:15–21).

There I said that the two fish signified those two persons, namely the royal and priestly persons, to whom that most sacred anointing also pertained. I should rather have said, “It pertained especially,” since we sometimes read that the Prophets too were anointed.

I also said that Luke, who indicated Christ as a priest ascending after the abolition of sins, ascended through Nathan to David (Luke 3:31), because Nathan the prophet had been sent, and through his rebuke David obtained the abolition of that sin by repentance. This must not be understood as though he himself were the prophet Nathan, who was David’s son. For it is not stated here that he himself was the prophet who had been sent; rather, it is stated that the prophet Nathan had been sent, so that the mystery might be understood not in the same person but in the same name.

The sixty-second concerns the Gospel statement that Jesus baptized more people than John, although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples did (John 4:1–2).

There I said that the thief to whom it was said, “Truly I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43), had not even received baptism. We find that this view was also held in their writings by other leaders of the holy Church before us [Note: [Col. 0627] Among them was Cyprian, *Epistle* 73, to Jubaianus.]. But by what evidence it can be sufficiently established that that thief had not been baptized, I do not know.

This matter was discussed more carefully in some of my later short works, especially in the work I wrote to Vincentius Victor *On the Origin of the Soul* (book 3, ch. 9, no. 43).

The sixty-third concerns the Word. The sixty-fourth concerns the Samaritan woman. The sixty-fifth concerns the resurrection of Lazarus. The sixty-sixth concerns the statement, “Do you not know, brothers—for I am speaking to those who know the Law—that the Law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives?” through the passage, “He will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 7–8:11).

When I wished to explain the Apostle’s words, “We know that the Law is spiritual; but I am carnal,” I said: “That is, I consent to the flesh, not yet freed by spiritual grace.” This must not be understood as though a spiritual person already established under grace could not also say this about himself, and the rest [Note: [Col. 0628] The printed editions have: “Could say these things: ‘I was sold under sin; for I do not understand what I do. For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I hate,’” and the following words up to the passage in question. We, retaining all the words of the better manuscripts, have moved the remainder to the place required by the sense.] up to the passage, “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” (ibid. 7:14–24). This I later learned, as I have already confessed.

Again, when explaining the Apostle’s statement, “The body indeed is dead because of sin” (ibid. 8:10), I said: “He calls the body dead so long as it is such that the need for temporal things afflicts the soul.” But afterward it seemed much better to me that the body is called dead because it already has the necessity of dying, which it did not have before sin.

The sixty-seventh concerns the statement, “For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that will be revealed in us,” through the words, “For in hope we were saved” (ibid. 8:18–24).

When I was explaining the statement, “And creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption,” I said: “And creation itself—that is, man himself—when, after losing the seal of the image on account of sin, he remained merely creation.”

This must not be understood as though man had lost everything he possessed of the image of God. For if he had lost it altogether, there would be no reason for the saying, “Be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Rom. 12:2), and, “We are transformed into the same image” (2 Cor. 3:18). But, again, if he had lost it all, nothing would remain as the basis for saying, “Although man walks in the image, he is nevertheless troubled in vain” (Ps. 38:7).

I also said that the highest angels live spiritually, but the lowest live in an animal manner. This was said more boldly concerning the lowest angels than can be demonstrated either from the holy Scriptures or from the facts themselves—for even if it can be demonstrated, it can be demonstrated only with great difficulty.

The sixty-eighth concerns the statement, “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20).

There I said: “Even if someone, whether through lighter sins or certainly through graver and many sins, has nevertheless become worthy of God’s mercy through great groaning and the pain of repentance, this is not his own doing—for if abandoned to himself he would perish—but the doing of the merciful God, who comes to the aid of his prayers and sorrows. For it is not enough to will unless God has mercy; but God does not have mercy on one whom he calls to peace unless the will toward peace has gone before.”

This was said after repentance. For God’s mercy also precedes the will itself; if it did not, the will would not be prepared by the Lord. The calling itself, which even precedes faith, belongs to this mercy.

When I dealt with this shortly afterward, I said: “This calling, which operates either in individual human beings, or in peoples, or in the whole human race, at suitable times, belongs to a lofty and profound ordering.” To this also belongs the statement, “In the womb I sanctified you” (Jer. 1:5); and, “When you were in the loins of your father, I saw you”; and, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Rom. 9:13; Mal. 1:2–3), and the rest.

However, I do not know from where the testimony, “When you were in the loins of your father, I saw you,” which presented itself to me as though it were written, came.

The sixty-ninth concerns the statement [Col. 0629], “Then the Son himself will also be subject to the one who subjected all things to him” (1 Cor. 15:28).

The seventieth concerns what the Apostle says: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the Law” (ibid. 15:54–55).

The seventy-first concerns the statement, “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2). The seventy-second concerns eternal times. The seventy-third concerns the statement, “And being found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7).

The seventy-fourth concerns the statement in Paul’s Epistle to the Colossians: “In whom we have redemption and the forgiveness of sins, who is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1:14–15). The seventy-fifth concerns the inheritance of God. The seventy-sixth concerns what the Apostle James says: “But do you wish to know, O empty man, that faith without works is idle?” (James 2:20).

The seventy-seventh concerns fear and whether it is a sin. The seventy-eighth concerns the beauty of images. The seventy-ninth asks why Pharaoh’s magicians performed certain miracles just as Moses, the servant of God, did (Exod. 7:22). The eightieth is against the Apollinarians. The eighty-first concerns Lent and Pentecost. The eighty-second concerns the statement, “For whom the Lord loves he chastises, and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

The eighty-third concerns marriage, with reference to the Lord’s statement, “If anyone divorces his wife, except for the cause of fornication” (Matt. 19:9).

This work begins as follows: “Whether the soul exists from itself.”

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Lying, one book

I also wrote a book *On Lying*. Although it is understood with some difficulty, it nevertheless provides a useful exercise for the intellect and mind, and contributes more to the cultivation of a love for truth in one’s conduct. I had decided to remove it from my works because it seemed obscure, involved, and altogether burdensome to me; for this reason I had not published it.

Then, after I had written another work entitled *Against Lying*, I decided and ordered even more firmly that this one should not remain. But this was not carried out. Therefore, when during this revision of my works I found it still intact, I ordered that it too should remain revised—especially because it contains certain things that are necessary and are not found in the other work.

For this reason the title of the other is *Against Lying*, whereas this one is *On Lying*: the former consists throughout in an open attack on lying, while a large part of the latter is devoted to an investigative discussion. Nevertheless, both are directed toward the same end.

This book begins as follows: “Lying is a great question.”

# BOOK TWO. IN WHICH THE BOOKS WRITTEN BY THE BISHOP ARE REVISED

[Col. 0629]

## CHAPTER I. To Simplicianus, two books

[Col. 0629]

### 1

The first two books I composed as bishop are addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of the Church of Milan, who succeeded the most blessed Ambrose. They concern various questions, two of which, drawn from the Epistle of the Apostle Paul to the Romans, I gathered into the first book.

The first of these concerns the passage, “What then shall we say? Is the Law sin? By no means,” through the words, “Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:7–25).

In this passage I explained the Apostle’s words, “The Law is spiritual, but I am carnal,” and so forth, in such a way that a person still under the Law, not yet established under grace, seemed to be described as one whose flesh struggles against the spirit. Much later I came to recognize that these words can also—and more plausibly—belong to a spiritual person.

The second question in this book begins at the passage, “And not only this, but Rebecca also, having conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father,” and continues through the words, “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah” (ibid. 9:10–29).

In resolving this question, an effort was indeed made on behalf of the free choice of the human will; but the grace of God prevailed. It was possible to arrive only at the point where the Apostle is understood to have spoken with perfectly clear truth: “For who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

The martyr Cyprian, wishing also to demonstrate this, expressed the whole matter in the title itself, saying: “There is nothing in which one should boast, since nothing is ours” (Cyprian, book 3, *Testimonies*, 4).

### 2

The remaining questions are treated in the second book and are resolved according to our limited ability. All of them concern the Scripture called *The Books of Kingdoms*.

The first concerns the statement, “And the Spirit of the Lord rushed upon Saul” (1 Sam. 10:10), whereas elsewhere it is said, “And an evil spirit from the Lord was upon Saul” (ibid. 16:14). In explaining this I said: “Although it is in each person’s power what he wills, it is not in anyone’s power what he can do” (*Various Questions*, book 2, question 1).

This was said because we call only that within our power which occurs when we will it; and here the first and most important thing is the willing itself. For the will is immediately present, without any interval of time, when we will something. Yet even this power for living well we receive from above, when the will is prepared by the Lord.

The second question asks how the statement, “It repents me that I made Saul king” (1 Sam. 15:11), is to be understood. The third asks whether the unclean spirit that was in the medium could have caused Samuel to appear to Saul and speak with him (ibid. 28:7–20). The fourth concerns the statement, “King David entered and sat before the Lord” (2 Sam. 7:18). The fifth concerns what Elijah said: “O Lord, witness of this widow with whom I dwell, you have done evil by killing her son” (1 Kings 17:20).

This work begins as follows: “Most welcome indeed.”

## CHAPTER II. Against the Epistle They Call *The Foundation*, one book

The book *Against the Epistle of the Manichaeans Which They Call The Foundation* refutes only its fundamental principles; but in the other parts of that epistle [Note: [Col. 0631] In seven manuscripts it is read approximately as follows: “But in the final parts of that work, all the winding passages, wherever it seemed appropriate, were refuted; and also in the other parts [there were] annotations.” In the Parcensis manuscript the Louvain editors read: “But in its final parts, since all the winding passages, wherever it seemed appropriate, had been refuted, [there were] annotations.”] annotations have been attached wherever it seemed appropriate. By these the whole work is overthrown, and they would have reminded me to write against the entire epistle if I had ever had the opportunity.

This book begins as follows: “The one true God.”

## CHAPTER III. On the Christian Struggle, one book

The book *On the Christian Struggle* was written in humble language for brethren uneducated in Latin eloquence. It contains the rule of faith and instructions for living.

In it I wrote: “Nor should we listen to those who deny that there will be a resurrection of the flesh and cite what the Apostle Paul says: ‘Flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God,’” without understanding what the Apostle himself says: “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:50, 53).

When this has happened, there will no longer be flesh and blood, but a heavenly body (ch. 32, no. 34). This must not be understood as though there will not be a substance of flesh; rather, by the name “flesh and blood” the Apostle must be understood to have referred to the corruption of flesh and blood, which certainly will not exist in that kingdom, where the flesh will be incorruptible.

It can also be understood in another way: the Apostle may be taken to have called the works of flesh and blood “flesh and blood,” and to have said that those will not possess the kingdom of God who persistently love such things.

This book begins as follows: “The crown of victory.”

## CHAPTER IV. On Christian Teaching, four books

### 1

When I discovered that the books *On Christian Teaching* were incomplete, I preferred to complete them rather than leave them unfinished and pass on to revising other works.

I therefore completed the third book, which had been written up to the passage (ch. 25, no. 36) where the Gospel testimony was recalled concerning the woman who hid leaven in three measures of flour until the whole was leavened (Luke 13:21). I also added the final book and completed the work in four books. The first three assist in understanding Scripture, while the fourth concerns how what we understand should be expressed.

### 2

In the second book, concerning the author of the book which many call *The Wisdom of Solomon*, I said that it too had been written by Jesus Sirach [Note: [Col. 0631] The Ambrosian, Louvain, and Venetian editions read: “Jesus son of Sirach.” M.], just as *Ecclesiasticus* was. I later learned that this was not as certain as I had said (ch. 8, no. 13), and found it altogether more probable that he was not the author of that book.

Where I said, “The authority of the Old Testament concludes with these forty-four books,” I used the expression “Old Testament” according to the custom by which the Church already speaks. But the Apostle does not seem to call anything the Old Testament except what was given on Mount Sinai (Gal. 4:24).

And where I said that Saint Ambrose had resolved the question concerning the history of the ages (ch. 28, no. 43), as though Plato and Jeremiah had been contemporaries, my memory deceived me. What that bishop actually said about this matter can be read in the book he wrote *On the Sacraments*, or *On Philosophy*.

This work begins as follows: “There are certain precepts.”

## CHAPTER V. Against the Party of Donatus, two books—[They no longer exist]

There are two books of mine entitled *Against the Party of Donatus*. In the first I said that I did not approve of schismatics being forcibly compelled to communion by the power of any secular authority.

At that time I truly did not approve of this, because I had not yet experienced either how much harm their impunity could cause or how much the careful application of discipline could contribute to changing them for the better.

This work begins as follows: “Since the Donatists for us…”

## CHAPTER VI. The Thirteen Books of the *Confessions*

### 1

The thirteen books of my *Confessions* praise God, just and good, for my evils and my goods, and they arouse the human intellect and affection toward him. As far as I am concerned, this is what they did in me when they were written, and what they do when they are read.

What others think of them, let them see for themselves; nevertheless, I know that they have greatly pleased and continue to please many of the brethren.

From the first book through the tenth they concern me. In the remaining three they concern the holy Scriptures, beginning with the statement, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and continuing to the rest of the Sabbath (Gen. 1:1; 2:2).

### 2

In the fourth book, when I confessed the misery of my soul over the death of a friend, saying that our soul had somehow become one soul out of two, and therefore, I said, perhaps I feared death lest the whole of him should die whom I had loved greatly (ch. 6), this seems to me more like a light rhetorical exercise than a serious confession, although the foolishness is somewhat moderated by the addition of the word “perhaps.”

And in the thirteenth book, where I said that a firmament was made between the spiritual waters above and the bodily waters below (ch. 32), I did not speak with sufficient care; the matter is exceedingly obscure.

This work begins as follows: “Great are you, Lord.”

## CHAPTER VII. Against Faustus the Manichaean, thirty-three books

### 1

I wrote a large work against Faustus the Manichaean, who blasphemed the Law and the Prophets and their God, and the incarnation of Christ, and who said that the Scriptures of the New Testament had been falsified, even though they refute him. I set forth his words and replied to them.

There are thirty-three discussions. Why should I not call them books? Although some of them are very brief, they are nevertheless books. One of them, in which we defend the lives of the Patriarchs against his accusations, is so extensive that scarcely any of my books is equally long.

### 2

In the third book, when I was resolving the question of how Joseph could have had two fathers, I did say that he was born from one and adopted by another (ch. 3); but I should also have stated the kind of adoption. For what I said sounds as though another father adopted him while he was still alive.

But the Law adopted sons even for the dead [Note: [Col. 0633] The printed editions read, “adopted the dead.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “for the dead.”], commanding that the brother should marry the wife of a brother who died without children and raise up offspring for his deceased brother from her (Deut. 25:5–6). This provides the more straightforward explanation here of the two fathers of one man.

The men involved were uterine brothers. This occurred when one, named Heli, died, and the other, Jacob, married his wife. Matthew says that Joseph was begotten by Jacob; but Jacob begot him for his uterine brother, whose son Luke says Joseph was—not begotten by him, certainly, but adopted according to the Law.

This account is found in the writings of those who, with recent memory, wrote about the matter after the Lord’s ascension. Africanus did not omit even the name of the same woman who bore Jacob, Joseph’s father: by her first husband, Mathan, who was Jacob’s father and Joseph’s grandfather according to Matthew; and by her later husband, Melchi, she bore Heli, whose adopted son Joseph was.

When I replied to Faustus, I had not yet read this account; nevertheless, I could not doubt that it was possible for one man to have two fathers through adoption.

### 3

In the twelfth and thirteenth books, the discussion proceeded as though the second son of Noah, who was called Ham, had been cursed by his father in his own person, rather than in his son Canaan, as Scripture demonstrates (book 12, ch. 23; book 13, ch. 10).

In the fourteenth book, things were said about the sun and moon as though they were capable of perception and therefore tolerated their foolish worshipers (ch. 12). Nevertheless, the words there can be understood as transferred from an animate thing to an inanimate one, according to the figure of speech called in Greek *metaphora* (“metaphor”). Thus it is written of the sea that it roars in its mother’s womb, wishing to advance (Job 38:8, according to the Septuagint), although it certainly has no will.

In the twenty-ninth book I said: “Far be it that there should be any shamefulness, even in the genital members of the saints. They are indeed called dishonorable because they do not possess that appearance of beauty which the members placed in view possess” (ch. 4).

But in other writings of ours a more probable explanation was later given for why the Apostle also called them dishonorable (1 Cor. 12:23): namely, because of the law in the members that opposes the law of the mind (Rom. 7:23), which arose from sin and not from the original constitution of our nature.

This work begins as follows: “There was a certain Faustus.”

## CHAPTER VIII. Against Felix the Manichaean, two books
Against a Certain Manichaean Named Felix, I Debated for Two Days in the Presence of the People in the Church

He had come to Hippo to sow the same error; for he was one of their teachers, although uneducated in the liberal arts, yet more cunning than Fortunatus. The proceedings were ecclesiastical, but they are counted among my books. There are therefore two books; in the second, free choice of the will is discussed, whether for doing evil [Col. 0634] or for doing good. But since the man with whom we were dealing was such that we were not compelled by any necessity to discuss more carefully the grace by which people truly become free—of whom it is written, “If the Son shall make you free, then you shall be truly free” (John 8:36)—we did not do so.

This work begins as follows: “In the consulship of Honorius Augustus for the sixth time, on the seventh day before the Ides of December.”

## CHAPTER IX. On the Nature of the Good, One Book

The book On the Nature of the Good is directed against the Manichaeans. It demonstrates that the immutable nature is God and the supreme good; that all other natures, whether spiritual or bodily, come from him; and that all things, insofar as they are natures, are good. It also discusses what evil is and from where it comes, and how many evils the Manichaeans posit in the nature of the good, and how many goods in the nature of evil—natures fabricated by their error.

This book begins as follows: “The supreme good, than which nothing is higher, is God.”

## CHAPTER X. Against the Manichaean Secundinus, One Book

A certain Secundinus, not one of those whom the Manichaeans call the Elect, but one of those whom they call Hearers, whom I had not even seen face to face, wrote to me as a friend, respectfully reproving me for attacking that heresy in writing, warning me not to do so, and rather exhorting me to follow it, while defending it and criticizing the Catholic faith.

I replied to him. But because at the beginning of the same little work I did not state who was writing to whom, it is counted not among my letters but among my books. His letter too is transcribed there from the beginning. The title of this volume of mine is Against the Manichaean Secundinus. In my judgment, I readily place it before everything else that I was able to write against that plague.

This book begins as follows: “Your goodwill toward me.”

## CHAPTER XI. Against Hilarus, One Book.—[Not Extant]

Meanwhile a certain Hilarus [Note: [Col. 0634] The editions print *Hilarius* and *Hilarium*. In the manuscripts, however, the forms are *Hilarus* and *Hilarum*, as we have had them printed.]—a man of tribunician rank, a Catholic layman—had become irritated, I do not know for what reason, against the ministers of God, as often happens. Wherever he could, he attacked with malicious criticism the practice that had then begun at Carthage, namely, that hymns should be sung at the altar from the Book of Psalms, either before the offering or while what had been offered was being distributed to the people. He maintained that this ought not to be done.

At the request of the brethren I replied to him, and the book itself is called Against Hilarus. This book begins as follows: “Those who say that mention of the Old Testament…”

## CHAPTER XII. Questions on the Gospels, Two Books

These are explanations of certain passages from the Gospel according to Matthew, and other explanations similarly taken from Luke. The former were arranged into one book, and the latter into another. The title of the work is Questions on the Gospels.

My prologue, with the questions themselves appended and numbered so that anyone may find whatever he wishes to read by following the numbers, sufficiently explains why, among the passages from the Gospels mentioned above, only those contained in these books of mine were expounded, and what those passages are.

In the first book (Question 27), where it is stated that the Lord privately related his passion to two disciples (Matthew 20:17), a scribal error misled us: the text says “twelve,” not “two.”

In the second book, when I wished to explain how Joseph could have had two fathers, although his wife was called the virgin Mary, I said that the statement that a man took his deceased brother’s wife in order to raise up offspring for him according to the Law (Deuteronomy 25:5) was weak, because the Law commanded that the one who was born should take the name of the deceased (Question 5). This is not true. For the Law prescribed that the deceased’s name should serve the purpose of having the child called his son, not that he should be called by the name by which the deceased himself was called [Note: [Col. 0635] “For when Boaz took Ruth in order to raise up offspring for his kinsman, the one born from her was reckoned, in respect of the deceased’s name, as his son; and thus it came about that the deceased’s name was not erased from Israel. Yet he was not called by the deceased’s name.” Saint Augustine discusses this matter at greater length in Book 5 of his Questions on Deuteronomy, Question 46.].

This work begins as follows: “This work was not written in this manner…”

## CHAPTER XIII. Notes on Job, One Book

Whether the book entitled Notes on Job should be considered mine, or rather the work of those who, as they were able or wished, copied the notes from the margins of the codex and collected them into one body, I cannot easily say.

They are pleasing to very few readers who understand them, though even these readers must be offended by much that they do not understand. For in many places the very words being explained have not been copied in such a way that it is clear what is being expounded. Moreover, such obscurity follows upon the brevity of the statements that the reader can scarcely endure it and must pass over much without understanding it.

Finally, I found the work itself so corrupt in our manuscripts that I could not emend it, nor would I wish it to be called an edition of mine, except that I know the brethren possess it, and their diligence could not be denied.

This book begins as follows: “And great works were being done for him upon the earth.”

## CHAPTER XIV. On Catechizing the Uninstructed, One Book

There is also our book On Catechizing the Uninstructed, bearing this very title. In that book, where I said, “Nor did the angel who, together with his other attendant spirits, proudly abandoned obedience to God and became the devil harm God in any way, but himself; for God knows how to order the souls that abandon him” (Chapter 18, §30), it would be more appropriate to say, “the spirit,” since the discussion concerned angels.

This book begins as follows: “You asked me, brother Deogratias…”

## CHAPTER XV. On the Trinity, Fifteen Books

1. I wrote fifteen books on the Trinity, which is God, over a period of several years. But before I had completed the twelfth, and while I kept them longer than those who ardently desired to possess them could bear, they were taken from me less carefully corrected than they ought to have been and could have been when I wished to publish them.

When I discovered this, because other copies of them had remained in our possession, I had decided not to publish them myself, but to keep them in such a way that in some other little work of mine I could explain what had happened to me concerning them. Nevertheless, when the brethren pressed me—those whom I was unable to resist—I corrected them as far as I thought they needed correction, completed them, and published them. I added at the beginning a letter that I wrote to the venerable Aurelius, bishop of the Church of Carthage. In it, as in a prologue, I explained what had happened, what I had intended to do in my own judgment, and what I had done under the compulsion of the brethren’s affection.

2. In the eleventh book, while discussing the visible body, I said: “Consequently, to love it is to be alienated” (Chapter 5, §9). This was said with reference to that kind of love by which something is loved in such a way that the one who loves it considers himself blessed by enjoying it. For it is not alienation to love bodily beauty in praise of the Creator, so that each person may truly be blessed by enjoying the Creator himself.

Again, in the same book, where I said, “I do not remember a four-footed bird, because I have not seen one; but I can very easily contemplate such an image by adding to some winged form of the sort I have seen two other feet, likewise of the sort I have seen” (Chapter 10, §17), in saying this I failed to recall the four-footed winged creatures mentioned by the Law (Leviticus 11:20). For the Law does not count as feet the two hind legs with which locusts leap—locusts that it calls clean—and thus distinguishes them from similar unclean winged creatures that do not leap with those legs, such as beetles. All such winged creatures are called four-footed in the Law.

3. In the twelfth book (Chapter 10, §15), where, as though explaining the Apostle’s words, I said, “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body,” I am not satisfied with what I wrote. Nor do I think the statement, “But whoever commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Corinthians 6:18), should be understood as though the person who does this were someone who, in order to obtain the things perceived through the body, acts so as to place the end of his happiness in them. For this interpretation includes far more sins than the fornication committed through unlawful intercourse, which the Apostle evidently had in mind when he said this.

This work, apart from the letter later added at its beginning, begins as follows: “The reader of these things that we discuss concerning the Trinity…”

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Harmony of the Evangelists, Four Books

During the same years in which I was gradually dictating the books on the Trinity, I also wrote other works with continuous effort, inserting them among the periods in which those books were being composed. Among them are the four books On the Harmony of the Evangelists, written against those who accuse the Evangelists as though they were in disagreement.

The first book was written against those who either honor, or pretend to honor, Christ as supremely wise and therefore refuse to believe the Gospel, because they think it was not written by Christ himself but by his disciples, who, through error, attributed to him the divinity by which he was believed to be God.

In that book I said, “The nation of the Hebrews began with Abraham” (Chapter 14, §21). This too is plausible, so that the Hebrews may appear to have been called, as it were, Abrahamites. But more correctly they are understood to have been named after the man called Heber, as though “Heberites” [Note: [Col. 0637] Nevertheless, authors of no little authority, especially Greek authors, favor a third opinion: namely, that the Hebrews—meaning “Those Who Crossed Over”—were so called because the patriarch Abraham had crossed the Euphrates from the region of the Chaldaeans into Palestine. For this reason, they say, the surname “Hebrew” was added to Abraham in Genesis 14:13; that is, according to the Septuagint interpreters, who render the word in their customary manner, *Peratē*, “the one who crossed over,” or “the one from beyond the river,” as was generally found in Saint Augustine’s manuscript. Augustine himself, in Question 29 on Genesis, thinks that Abraham was called “the one from beyond the river” from the region from which he had come.], concerning which I discussed the matter sufficiently in Book 16 of The City of God (Chapter 11).

In the second book, when discussing Joseph’s two fathers, I said that he was begotten by one and adopted by the other (Chapter 3, §5). I should have said, “adopted by the other.” For, after the death of the man, as is more credible, he had been adopted according to the Law, since the man who begot him had married the wife of his deceased brother.

Again, where I said, “But Luke ascends to David himself through Nathan, the prophet through whom God expiated his sin” (Chapter 4, §12), I should have said, “through the prophet of that name,” so that it would not be thought that the two were the same man, since they were different, although this one too was called Nathan.

This work begins as follows: “Among all the divine authorities…”

## CHAPTER XVII. Against the Letter of Parmenianus, Three Books

In the three books Against the Letter of Parmenianus, the Donatist bishop of Carthage and successor of Donatus, a major question is raised and resolved: whether, within unity and the common participation in the sacraments, the wicked contaminate the good; and how they do not contaminate them is discussed. The issue concerns the Church spread throughout the whole world, against which they formed a schism by their accusations.

In the third book, when it was being discussed how the Apostle’s statement should be understood, “Remove the evil person from among yourselves” (1 Corinthians 5:13), I said, “So that each person may remove the evil from himself” (Chapter 1, §2). This should not be understood in that way, but rather as meaning that the evil person is removed from among good people, which is accomplished through ecclesiastical discipline. The Greek wording sufficiently indicates this: there, without ambiguity, it is written that the meaning is “this evil person” [Note: [Col. 0637] Greek: *ton ponēron*], not “this evil,” although I also replied to Parmenianus according to the former interpretation.

This work begins as follows: “Although I have often written many things against the Donatists…”

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Baptism, Seven Books

Against the Donatists, who sought to defend themselves by the authority of the most blessed bishop and martyr Cyprian, I wrote seven books On Baptism. In them I taught that nothing is so effective for refuting the Donatists and completely closing their mouths, so that they may not defend their schism against the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0637] The editions read, “so that they may not defend their schism against the Catholic Church.” The word “Church” is absent from the manuscripts. Augustine frequently made “Catholic,” an adjective, into a substantive noun, and he loved by this usage to commend the Church spread throughout the whole world.], as the letters and conduct of Cyprian.

Whenever in these books I mentioned the Church “without spot or wrinkle” (Ephesians 5:27) (Book 1, Chapter 17; Book 3, Chapter 18; and Book 4, Chapters 3 and 4), this should not be understood as though she already possesses that condition, but as referring to the Church being prepared to possess it when she will appear glorious. For now, because of certain ignorances and weaknesses of her members [Col. 0638], she has reason each day, as a whole, to say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12).

In the fourth book, when I said that martyrdom could take the place of baptism (Chapter 22, §29), I offered an insufficiently suitable example in the case of the thief, since it is uncertain whether he had not been baptized.

In the seventh book, concerning the golden and silver vessels placed in a great house (Chapter 51, §99), I followed Cyprian’s interpretation, according to which these are understood as the good, while the wooden and earthen vessels are understood as the wicked (Cyprian, Letter 51, to Maximus, etc.). I referred to the former the statement, “Some for honor,” and to the latter, “Others for dishonor” (2 Timothy 2:20). But I approve more strongly what I later found or noticed in Tychonius: that in both categories some are to be understood as being for honor—not only the golden and silver vessels—and again in both categories some as being for dishonor—not only the wooden and earthen vessels.

This work begins as follows: “In those books that I wrote against the Letter of Parmenianus…”

## CHAPTER XIX. Against What Centurius Brought from the Donatists, One Book.—[Not Extant]

While we were conducting many frequent debates against the party of Donatus, a certain layman who at that time belonged to them brought to the Church several dictations or writings against us, presented as a few testimonies that they thought supported their cause. I replied to them very briefly.

The title of this little book is Against What Centurius Brought from the Donatists. It begins as follows: “You say that it is written by Solomon: ‘Abstain from foreign water.’”

## CHAPTER XX. Replies to the Questions of Januarius, Two Books

The two books entitled Replies to the Questions of Januarius contain discussions of many matters concerning the sacraments, whether those observed universally by the Church or those observed only in particular places—that is, not equally everywhere. It was not possible to mention everything, but a sufficient response was given to the questions asked.

The first of these books is a letter; for at its beginning it states who is writing and to whom. Nevertheless, this work is counted among the books because the second book, which does not contain our names, is much longer and treats many more subjects.

In the first book, therefore, where I said of the manna, “Because it tasted in each person’s mouth according to his own preference” (Chapter 3, §4), I did not recall where this could be proved except from the Book of Wisdom (Wisdom 16:20), which the Jews do not accept as canonical authority. Nevertheless, this could have happened to the faithful, not to those who murmured against God; they certainly would not have desired other foods if the manna had tasted to them as they wished.

This work begins as follows: “Regarding the matters about which you questioned me…”

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Work of Monks, One Book

The necessity that compelled me to write a book On the Work of Monks arose when monasteries began to exist at Carthage. Some monks supported themselves by the work of their own hands, obeying the Apostle; others, however, wished to live from the offerings of religious people, so that, doing no work by which they might obtain or supplement what was necessary, they instead considered and proclaimed that they were fulfilling the evangelical command in which the Lord says, “Consider the birds of the air and the lilies of the field” (Matthew 6:26).

As a result, among laymen of a lower calling, though fervent in their zeal, tumultuous disputes also began to arise, disturbing the Church, with some defending one position and others another. Added to this was the fact that some of those who said that work was unnecessary wore their hair long. Thus disputes increased between those who criticized them and those who, as it were, defended them [Note: [Col. 0639] The editions read “those who fight.” But several manuscripts more correctly have “those who purge,” that is, those who remove from the monks the basis for criticism.], in accordance with the interests of the opposing parties.

For these reasons the venerable old man Aurelius, bishop of that city’s Church, ordered me to write something on the matter, and I did so.

This book begins as follows: “Your command, holy brother Aurelius…”

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Good of Marriage, One Book

1. The heresy of Jovinian, by equating the merit of holy virgins with marital chastity, gained such influence in the city of Rome that it was said to have driven some religious women into marriage, although no suspicion had previously touched their chastity. His principal argument in pressing them was this: “Are you therefore better than Sarah, better than Susanna, or Anna?” By recalling these and other women highly commended by the testimony of Holy Scripture—women whom they could not imagine themselves better than, or even equal to—he weakened the holy celibacy of men as well by recalling and comparing married patriarchs.

The holy Church there resisted this monstrosity with complete fidelity and courage. Yet these arguments of his remained in the little speeches and whispers of certain people, and no one dared openly to recommend them. But it was necessary to counter them even as their poisons secretly crept about, by the ability that the Lord granted—especially since it was being asserted that Jovinian could not be answered with praise [Note: [Col. 0639] The manuscripts have “cannot be [answered]”; the editions have “could not be [answered] with praise.”], but only by condemning marriage.

For this reason I published a book whose title is On the Good of Marriage. In it, the question of the propagation of children before human beings merited death by sinning was deferred for extensive discussion, because intercourse appears to pertain to mortal bodies. But in other writings of mine composed later, I believe the matter is explained sufficiently.

2. I also said in one place: “For what food is for the health of a person, that intercourse is for the health of the human race; and neither is without carnal pleasure, which, when moderated and restrained by self-control and reduced to natural use, cannot be lust” (Chapter 16, §18).

This was said because lust is not the good and proper use of lust [Note: [Col. 0639] With the word “of lust” removed here, the object of the revised passage was not sufficiently clear in the editions. The point is that one must never suppose that all lust is absent from carnal union, even when it is moderated and reduced to natural use. Saint Augustine repeatedly insists that it is the cause of original sin: “That very lawful and honorable intercourse cannot occur without the ardor of lust, so that what belongs to reason, not lust, may be carried out,” from Book 1 of On Marriage and Concupiscence, Chapter 24. On the basis of the older manuscripts, we have therefore restored the word “of lust”; seven manuscripts add “natural.” This is not inappropriate, for lust is present from the origin and condition of birth.]. For just as it is evil to use good things badly, so it is good to use bad things well. I have discussed this matter elsewhere, especially against the new Pelagian heretics, at greater length.

Concerning Abraham, what I said—“From this obedience that father Abraham, who was not without a wife, was prepared to be without his only son and to have him killed by himself” (Chapter 23, §31)—I do not approve sufficiently. For he should rather be understood to have believed that, if his son were killed, he would soon be restored to him by resurrection, as we read in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebrews 11:19).

This book begins as follows: “Since each human being is a part of the human race…”

## CHAPTER XXIII. On Holy Virginity, One Book

After I wrote On the Good of Marriage, it was expected that I would write On Holy Virginity, and I did not delay. In a single volume I demonstrated, as I was able, that this gift of God is very great and must be guarded with what great humility.

This book begins as follows: “We recently published a book On the Good of Marriage…”

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Literal Meaning of Genesis, Twelve Books

1. During the same period I wrote twelve books on Genesis, beginning at the beginning and continuing until Adam was expelled from paradise and the flaming sword was placed to guard the way to the tree of life.

When eleven books had been completed up to this point, I added a twelfth, in which paradise was discussed more carefully. The title of these books is On Genesis Literally—that is, not according to allegorical meanings, but according to the actual character of the events narrated.

In this work more questions were raised than answered, and of the matters answered, fewer were established with certainty; the rest were set forth as though they still required investigation. I actually began these books later but completed them before the books on the Trinity. For that reason I have now recalled them in the order in which I began them.

2. In the fifth book (Chapter 19, §38), and wherever in these books I wrote, “Concerning the seed that was promised, which was ordained through angels in the hand of the mediator” (Galatians 3:19), the Apostle does not say this, as I later discovered by consulting more accurate manuscripts, especially Greek ones. For the statement concerns the Law, whereas many Latin manuscripts, through the translator’s error, read it as though it concerned the seed.

In the sixth book, where I said that Adam lost through sin the image of God according to which he had been made (Chapter 27, §28), this should not be understood as though no image of God remained in him, but rather that it had become so disfigured that it required restoration.

In the twelfth book, concerning the underworld (Chapter 33, §62), I should rather have taught that the underworld is beneath the earth than have given a reason why it is believed—or said—to be beneath the earth, as though that were not in fact the case.

This work begins as follows: “All divine Scripture is divided into two parts.”

## CHAPTER XXV. Against the Letters of Petilianus, Three Books

Before I had finished the books On the Trinity and the books On Genesis Literally, the need to reply to the Letters of Petilianus the Donatist, which he had written against the Catholic Church, suddenly arose; I could not postpone the matter.

I wrote three volumes on it. In the first, I replied to the first part of his Letter, which he had written to his own people. Since the whole letter had not come into our hands, but only its short opening portion, I responded to that portion with as much speed and accuracy as I could.

This too is a letter to our people, but it is counted among the books because the other two works are books on the same subject. Later we found the entire letter, and I replied to it with as much care as I had shown toward Faustus the Manichaean: first setting down his words piece by piece under his own name, and then placing my response to each under mine.

But what I had written before we found the whole letter reached Petilianus first. He attempted to reply in anger, saying about me whatever he pleased [Note: [Col. 0641] The editions have “whatever pleased him.” The manuscripts have “whatever pleased him” with the pronoun in the accusative form used here; we have not regarded this expression, which is accepted by Augustine, as objectionable. Because the wording was less well understood, Augustine’s sermon On the Beheading of Saint John was later corruptly printed in breviaries as “Yet he did not have it in this way,” instead of “It did not please him to rage in this way.”], but he failed entirely in the case itself.

Although this could easily be recognized by comparing the writings of both of us, I nevertheless took care, by replying myself, to demonstrate it for slower readers. Thus the third book was added to our work.

In the first book this work begins as follows: “You know that we have often wished…”

In the second it begins: “The opening portions of Petilianus’s Letter…”

In the third it begins: “I have read your letter, Petilianus…”

## CHAPTER XXVI. To Cresconius the Grammarian of the Party of Donatus, Four Books

A certain Donatist grammarian, Cresconius, having found my letter in which I had refuted the opening portions of Petilianus’s Letter that had at that time come into our hands, thought that he ought to reply to me, and wrote this very thing to me.

I answered his work in four books, completing in three of them what the whole response required. But when I saw that the matter of the Maximianists alone—those whom they had condemned as their schismatics [Note: [Col. 0641] The editions read, “those whom they condemned.” We have restored “those” from the manuscripts; it refers to the Maximianists mentioned earlier.] and some of whom they had again restored to their offices, without repeating the baptism administered by them outside their communion—could answer everything he had written, I added a fourth book. In it I showed this very point as carefully and clearly as I could.

When I wrote these four books, the emperor Honorius had already issued laws against the Donatists.

This work begins as follows: “Not knowing when my writings could reach you, Cresconius…”

## CHAPTER XXVII. Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists, One Book.—[Not Extant]

After this, I took care to send the Donatists the documents necessary against their error and in support of Catholic truth, whether from ecclesiastical records, public proceedings, or the canonical Scriptures.

First I directed to them a promise concerning these materials, so that, if possible, they themselves might request them. When the documents reached the hands of some of them, someone appeared who wrote against them without disclosing his name, confessing himself to be a Donatist as though “Donatist” were his proper name. I replied to him and wrote another book.

The documents I had promised I joined to the same little work in which I had made the promise, wishing the two to constitute a single work. I published it in such a way that it was first posted for reading on the walls of the basilica that had belonged to the Donatists. Its title is Proofs and Testimonies against the Donatists.

In this book we did not place the acquittal of Felix of Aptunga, the ordainer of Caecilianus [Note: [Col. 0642] In several and better manuscripts, here and below in Chapter 34, the form is *Aptugnensis*. The Ambrosian manuscript agrees, as does Erasmus below. Other manuscripts have *Aptugenensis*.], in the correct chronological order that later became clear to us after careful examination of the consuls. Instead, we placed it as though Felix had been acquitted after Caecilianus, although it had occurred before him.

Also, after quoting the testimony of the apostle Jude, where he says, “These are the ones who separate themselves, worldly, not having the Spirit” (Jude 19), I added: “Concerning them the Apostle Paul also says, ‘The worldly person does not receive the things that belong to the Spirit of God’” (1 Corinthians 2:14). These people should not be equated with those whom schism has entirely cut off from the Church.

For the Apostle Paul calls these people infants in Christ, whom he nevertheless nourishes with milk because they are not yet able to receive solid food (1 Corinthians 3:1–2). The others, however, must be counted not among infant sons but among the dead and lost, so that, if one of them is corrected and joined to the Church, it may rightly be said of him, “He was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found” (Luke 15:32).

This book begins as follows: “You who fear consenting to the Catholic Church…”

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Against Some Donatist Whom I Do Not Know, One Book.—[Not Extant]

I wished the other book mentioned above to bear the title Against Some Donatist Whom I Do Not Know. In it too the true chronological order concerning the acquittal of Caecilianus’s ordainer is not preserved.

Also, where I said, “To the multitude of weeds, by which all heresies are understood,” one necessary conjunction is lacking. I should have said either, “by which all heresies also are understood,” or, “by which even all heresies are understood.”

As it now stands, the statement seems to imply that weeds exist only outside the Church and not also within the Church, although the Church herself is the kingdom of Christ from which his angels will gather all stumbling blocks at the time of the harvest (Matthew 13:36–42).

For the martyr Cyprian says: “Although weeds appear to be in the Church, neither our faith nor our love ought therefore to be hindered, so that, because we see that weeds are in the Church, we ourselves withdraw from the Church” (Cyprian, Letter 51, to Maximus, etc.).

We too defended this interpretation elsewhere, especially in the conference against these same Donatists who were then present.

This book begins as follows: “We promised to collect in a little booklet the proofs of the necessary facts…”

## CHAPTER XXIX. Admonition to the Donatists concerning the Maximianists, One Book.—[Not Extant]

Since I saw that many people were prevented by the labor of reading from learning how little reason and truth the party of Donatus possessed, I composed a very short little book in which I thought they should be admonished concerning the Maximianists alone. Thus, through the ease with which it could be copied, it could reach the hands of many, and through its very brevity it could more easily be committed to memory.

I gave it the title Admonition to the Donatists concerning the Maximianists.

This book begins as follows: “All of you who are moved by the slanders and accusations of men…”

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Divination of Demons, One Book

[Col. 0643]

Around this same time, a discussion created the necessity for me to write a little book On the Divination of Demons, which is also its title.

In one passage of it, where I said, “Demons can sometimes learn with complete ease not only the dispositions of human beings expressed in spoken words, but also those conceived in thought, when certain signs are expressed from the mind in the body” (Chapter 5, §9), I spoke of an extremely obscure matter with a more audacious assertion than I ought to have made.

For it has been established by certain experiments that these things do come to the knowledge of demons. But whether certain signs proceed from the bodies of those who are thinking and are perceptible to the demons but hidden from us, or whether they know these things by some other power, specifically a spiritual one, is something human beings can discover only with the greatest difficulty, or perhaps cannot discover at all.

This book begins as follows: “One day during the holy days of the Octave…”

## CHAPTER XXXI. Six Questions Explained against the Pagans

During this period six questions were sent to me from Carthage. A certain friend had proposed them, and I desired him to become a Christian; they were to be answered against the pagans, especially because he said that some of them had been proposed by the philosopher Porphyry.

I do not think, however, that this was that famous Porphyry the Sicilian. I collected discussions of these questions into one book, not a long one, whose title is Six Questions Explained against the Pagans.

The first question concerns the resurrection; the second, the time of the Christian religion; the third, the distinction among sacrifices; the fourth, the statement, “In whatever measure you measure, it shall be measured to you” (Matthew 7:2); the fifth, the Son of God according to Solomon; and the sixth, the prophet Jonah.

In the second question I said: “The salvation of this religion, through which alone true salvation is truly promised, has never been lacking to anyone who was worthy; and to the one to whom it was lacking, it was because he was not worthy.”

I did not say this as though anyone had been made worthy by his own merits. Rather, it is to be understood as the Apostle says: that it was said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” not from works but from him who calls (Romans 9:12–13). He asserts that this calling belongs to God’s purpose.

Hence he says, “Not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace” (2 Timothy 1:9). Again he says, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called saints according to his purpose” [Note: [Col. 0643] The word “saints” is absent from the ancient manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.] (Romans 8:28).

Concerning this calling he says, “That he may deem you worthy of his holy calling” (2 Thessalonians 1:11).

This book, after the letter later added at its beginning (Letter 102, to Deogratias), begins as follows: “Certain people are troubled and ask…”

## CHAPTER XXXII. Exposition of the Epistle of James to the Twelve Tribes.—[Not Extant]

Among my little works I found an exposition of the Epistle of James. On reviewing it, I noticed that it was rather a collection of notes on certain passages of that epistle, compiled into a book through the diligence of the brethren [Col. 0644], who did not wish these notes to remain in the margins of the codex.

They are therefore of some assistance, except that the Epistle itself, which we were reading when I dictated these notes, had not been carefully translated for us from the Greek.

This book begins as follows: “To the twelve tribes that are in the Dispersion, greetings…”

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, and on the Baptism of Infants, Three Books to Marcellinus
There also came a necessity that compelled me to write against the new Pelagian heresy. Previously, when the need arose, we had dealt with it not in writing but through speeches and conversations, each of us as he was able or ought to do. Accordingly, when questions from Carthage were sent to me for resolution in a written reply [Note: [Col. 0644] The editions read *dissolveram*, “I had resolved.” The manuscripts read *dissolverem*, “I might resolve,” more correctly.], I first wrote three books, whose title is *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*. In them the chief discussion concerns the baptism of infants on account of original sin, and the grace of God by which we are justified—that is, made righteous—although in this life no one keeps the commandments of righteousness so perfectly that it is not necessary for him to say in prayer concerning his sins, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). Those who held contrary views on all these matters established a new heresy.

In these books I still thought that their names should be withheld, hoping that they might thereby be corrected more easily. Indeed, in the third book, which is a letter but is counted among the books because I thought it should be joined to the other two, I mentioned Pelagius himself with some praise (chapter 3, section 5), because many people were commending his life. I refuted statements that he had not put forward in his own person in his writings, but had merely explained as things said by others; nevertheless, he later defended them, once he had become a heretic, with the utmost obstinacy. His disciple Caelestius, however, had already earned excommunication at Carthage for such assertions in an episcopal judgment at which I was not present.

In the second book I wrote at one point: “To some, I say, he will finally grant this, that they may not experience death in a sudden transformation” (chapter 31, section 50), reserving the matter for a more careful investigation. For either they will not die, or, passing from this life into death and from death into eternal life by the swiftest transformation, as in the blink of an eye, they will not experience death. This work begins as follows: “Although amid the central and great storms of cares…”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the One Baptism, against Petilian, to Constantine, one book

At that time a certain friend of mine received from some unknown Donatist presbyter a book *On the One Baptism*, with the information that Petilian, their bishop of Constantina, had written it. He brought it to me and earnestly asked me to answer it; and I did so. I also wanted my own book, in which I replied to him, to bear the same title, namely, *On the One Baptism*.

In that book I said that the emperor Constantine, when the Donatists accused Felix of Aptunga, the ordainer of Caecilian, had not denied them the opportunity to bring an accusation, although he had discovered them to be slanderers in their fabricated charges against Caecilian (chapter 16, section 28). Later, however, when the order of events was considered, the matter was found to have occurred differently. For the emperor mentioned above first had Felix’s case heard by the proconsul, where Felix is recorded as having been acquitted; afterward he himself had Caecilian heard together with his accusers and discovered Caecilian to be innocent, having found them to be slanderers in their charges against him. This sequence of events, established by the names of the consuls, refutes and completely overturns the Donatists’ slanders in that case far more forcefully; we have shown this elsewhere.

This book begins as follows: “To answer those who hold contrary opinions…”

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Maximianists, against the Donatists, one book—[Not extant]

I also wrote, among other works, a book against the Donatists—not as brief as the one I had written earlier, but a substantial work, treated with much greater care. In it one can see how the case of the Maximianists alone completely overturns their impious and arrogant error against the Catholic Church: the schism had arisen from Donatus’s own party.

This book begins as follows: “We have already said many things; we have already written many things…”

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Grace of the New Testament, to Honoratus, one book

At the very time when we were vigorously engaged against the Donatists and had already begun to be engaged against the Pelagians, a certain friend sent me five questions from Carthage and asked me to explain them to him in writing. They were these: What does the Lord’s cry mean, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Psalm 21:1; Matthew 27:46)? What does the Apostle mean when he says, “Rooted and grounded in love, may you have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Ephesians 3:17–18)? Who are the five foolish virgins, and who are the wise (Matthew 25:1–12)? What is “the outer darkness” (Matthew 22:13)? And how should we understand, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14)?

But, observing that the heresy mentioned above was a new enemy of God’s grace, I proposed a sixth question to myself, concerning *The Grace of the New Testament*. In discussing it, I inserted an exposition of the twenty-first Psalm, at whose beginning is written the cry that the Lord uttered on the cross—the matter that this friend had first asked me to explain—and I resolved all five questions (Letter 140, to Honoratus), though not in the order in which they had been proposed, but in the order in which they could fittingly occur to me while I was discussing the grace of the New Testament.

This book begins as follows: “You proposed five questions for me to treat…”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Spirit and the Letter, to Marcellinus, one book

The man to whom I had written three books entitled *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, in which the baptism of infants is also discussed at length, wrote back that he had been troubled because I had said that it could be possible for a person to be without sin if his will did not fail, with divine assistance [Col. 0646]—although no one in this life ever has been, is, or will be of such perfect righteousness.

For he asked how I could say that something was possible when there was no example of it. Because of this inquiry of his I wrote a book entitled *On the Spirit and the Letter*, treating the apostolic statement: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6). In this book, insofar as God helped me, I argued vigorously against the enemies of God’s grace, by which the ungodly person is justified.

When I was discussing the observances of the Jews, who abstain from certain foods according to the old law, I said, “the ceremonies of certain foods” (chapter 21, section 36). This word is not found in the usage of the sacred Scriptures [Note: [Col. 0646] We have certainly searched carefully for this word and nowhere encounter it in the version of the Seventy; but in the passages where the Vulgate has *caeremonias*, that version has *dikaiōmata*, “justifications”; or *prostagmata*, “commands”; or *phylakas*, “observances”; or *latreian*, “service”; *nomon*, “law”; and so forth.]. Nevertheless, it seemed suitable to me because I remembered that *ceremonies* (*cerimoniae*) was derived from *carere*, “to lack” or “to be without,” as though they were *carimoniae*, since those who observe them are without the things from which they abstain. If this word has another origin that is incompatible with true religion, I did not use it in that sense, but in the sense I have just mentioned.

This book begins as follows: “Having read the little works that I recently prepared for you, dearest son Marcellinus…”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On Faith and Works, one book

Meanwhile, certain lay brothers—though laymen, they were devoted students of the divine Scriptures—sent me some writings that distinguished Christian faith from good works in such a way as to argue that one could not attain eternal life without faith, but could attain it without works. In reply to them I wrote a book entitled *On Faith and Works*.

In it I discussed not only how those regenerated by Christ’s grace ought to live [Note: [Col. 0646] So the manuscripts read here and below in chapter 47; the editions have *the grace of God* in these passages.], but also what sort of people should be admitted to the washing of regeneration.

This book begins as follows: “It seems to some…”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. A Brief Account of the Conference with the Donatists, three books

After our conference with the Donatists had taken place, I briefly recalled what had been done and committed it to writing according to the three days on which we conferred with them. I considered this work useful so that anyone who was informed by it might either learn without difficulty what had been done or, by consulting the numbered references that I marked beside each matter, read in the official Acts themselves whatever passage he wished, since their excessive length tires the reader.

The title of this work is *A Brief Account of the Conference*. It begins as follows: “When the Catholic bishops and those of Donatus’s party…”

## CHAPTER XL. After the Conference, against the Donatists, one book

I also wrote a substantial book, sufficiently careful in my judgment, addressed to the Donatists themselves after the conference we had held with their bishops, so that they might no longer be led astray by them. In it I also answered certain of their empty claims that had reached us, which, although defeated, they proclaimed wherever and however they could. This was apart from what I had said concerning the official Acts of the conference, from which one could learn briefly what had been done.

I treated the same subject much more briefly in another letter to them. But because, at the council of Numidia, it seemed good to all of us who were present that this should be done, it is not among my letters [Note: [Col. 0647] It is now found among the Letters, numbered 141.]. It begins in this manner: “The old man Silvanus, Valentinus, Innocentius, Maximinus, Optatus, Augustine, Donatus, and the other bishops of the council of Zertum” [Note: [Col. 0647] Lov. reads *Cirtensis*. Some manuscripts read *Zersensis* or *Teriensis*. The Bodleian manuscript and two Merton College manuscripts read *Zirtensis*. Another Bodleian manuscript reads *Hetensis*. But the Am. and Er. editions, together with thirteen manuscripts, read *Zertensis*. This reading is confirmed by the manuscripts containing the book in full.] “to the Donatists.”

This book begins as follows: “Why are you still being led astray, Donatists?”

## CHAPTER XLI. On Seeing God, one book

I wrote a book *On Seeing God* (Letter 147, to Paulina), in which I postponed a more careful investigation of the spiritual body that will exist in the resurrection of the saints: whether, or in what manner, God, who is spirit, can also be seen through such a body. Later, in the final book—that is, the twenty-second book—of *The City of God* (chapter 29 and following, section 1 and following), I explained this exceedingly difficult question sufficiently, as I think.

I also found in one of our manuscripts, which contains this book as well, a memorandum that I had written on this subject to Fortunatianus, bishop of Sicca. In the catalogue of my little works it was not listed either among the books or among the letters [Note: [Col. 0647] It is now found among the Letters, numbered 148, volume 2, page 739.].

This book begins as follows: “Mindful of my obligation.” It also contains the words: “As I asked you in person…”

## CHAPTER XLII. On Nature and Grace, one book

At that time a certain book of Pelagius came into my hands. In it he defended human nature, with as much argumentation as he could muster, against the grace of God by which the ungodly are justified and by which we are Christians. I therefore named the book in which I replied to him, defending grace—not against nature, but as that by which nature is liberated and governed—*On Nature and Grace*.

In that book I defended certain statements that Pelagius attributed to Xystus, bishop and martyr of Rome, as though they truly belonged to Xystus; for that is what I had thought. Later, however, I read that they belonged to the philosopher Sextus, not to the Christian Xystus [Note: [Col. 0647] Augustine apparently learned that those sayings belonged to the philosopher Sextus from Jerome, who, in his Letter to Ctesiphon and in his commentaries on Jeremiah chapter 22 and Ezekiel chapter 18, attributes the source of the error to Rufinus. Jerome accuses Rufinus of having translated Sextus’s sayings from Greek into Latin and published them under the name of Saint Xystus, martyr and bishop of the city of Rome. Consequently they came to be read everywhere by devout men and carried in the hand like a ring, since Rufinus had given that title to his collection, and they came to be held so familiarly that Saint Benedict quoted one of the sayings in chapter 7 of his Rule: “As it is written, ‘The wise man is known by few words.’”].

This book begins as follows: “The book that you sent…”

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the City of God, twenty-two books

1. Meanwhile Rome was overthrown by the invasion of the Goths, who were acting under King Alaric, and by the violence of a great disaster [Col. 0648]. Its overthrow was attributed to the Christian religion by the worshipers of many false gods—whom we commonly call pagans—and, in their attempt to lay the blame upon Christianity, they began to blaspheme the true God with their customary bitterness and hostility, but more fiercely and bitterly than before.

Therefore, inflamed with zeal for the house of God, I began to write books *On the City of God* against their blasphemies and errors. This work occupied me for several years, because many other matters intervened that could not be postponed and first occupied me in resolving them.

At last this great work *On the City of God* was completed in twenty-two books. The first five refute those who want human affairs to prosper in such a way that they believe the worship of the many gods whom the pagans customarily worship is necessary for that prosperity; and because this worship is prohibited, they argue that these evils arise and abound. The next five books address those who admit that such evils have never been absent and will never be absent from mortal beings, and that they vary according to places, times, and persons, being sometimes great and sometimes small; but who argue that the worship of the many gods, to whom sacrifices are offered, is useful for the life that will follow death. Thus these ten books refute the two empty opinions opposed to the Christian religion.

2. But so that no one might criticize us for merely refuting the views of others without asserting our own, the second part of the work is devoted to this purpose, and it consists of twelve books. Nevertheless, whenever necessary, we assert our own positions in the first ten books and refute opposing positions in the twelve later ones.

The first four of the twelve following books contain the origin of the two cities, one of which is the city of God and the other the city of this world. The second four contain their course or progress. The final four contain their appointed ends. Thus, although all twenty-two books were written concerning both cities, they received their title from the better one and were therefore called *On the City of God*.

In the tenth book it should not have been stated as a miracle that, during Abraham’s sacrifice, a flame from heaven passed between the divided victims (chapter 8), since this was shown to him in a vision.

In the seventeenth book, concerning Samuel, I wrote, “He was not one of the sons of Aaron” (chapter 5, section 2). It would have been better to say, “He was not the son of a priest.” For it was more in accordance with legitimate custom for the sons of priests to succeed their deceased fathers in the priesthood. Samuel’s father is indeed found among the sons of Aaron [Note: [Col. 0648] On the contrary, Samuel is found among the sons of Korah, Aaron’s rival, in 1 Chronicles 6. Thus Saint Augustine either encountered a corrupt manuscript or was deceived by someone else.]. But Samuel was not a priest, nor is he called a son among the sons of Aaron in the sense that Aaron himself had fathered him; rather, he is called a son as all members of that people are called sons of Israel.

This work begins as follows: “The most glorious city of God…”

## CHAPTER XLIV. To Orosius, against the Priscillianists and Origenists, one book

In the midst of these matters I replied, as briefly and clearly as I could, to the questions of a certain Spanish presbyter named Orosius concerning the Priscillianists and certain opinions of Origen that the Catholic faith rejects. The title of this little work is *To Orosius, against the Priscillianists and Origenists* [Col. 0649]. The consultation itself was also attached at the beginning to my reply.

This book begins as follows: “In replying to your inquiry, dearest son Orosius…”

## CHAPTER XLV. To Jerome the presbyter, two books: one on the Origin of the Soul, and the other on the Saying of James

I also wrote two books (Letters 166 and 167) to Jerome the presbyter, who was residing at Bethlehem: one *On the Origin of the Human Soul*, and the other *On the Saying of the Apostle James*, where he says, “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James 2:10). In both books I consulted him.

In the first, I did not resolve the question that I myself had proposed.
