In the second, I did not conceal what seemed to me to be the solution to the question, but I consulted him as to whether he also approved it. He replied by praising my consultation, but said that he did not have the leisure to answer it.

I did not wish to publish these books while he was still alive, lest he perhaps answer at some later time and his response be published together with them instead. After his death, however, I published the first so that anyone who reads it may be warned either not to ask at all how souls are given to those who are born, or at least to accept, concerning this most obscure matter, that solution to the question which is not contrary to the clearest truths known through the Catholic faith concerning original sin—truths according to which infants are undoubtedly condemned unless they are regenerated in Christ. I published the second so that the solution to the question treated there, insofar as it appeared to us, might also become known.

This work begins as follows: “Our God, who called us…”

## CHAPTER XLVI. To Emeritus, bishop of the Donatists, after the conference, one book—[Not extant]

Some time after our conference with the Donatists, I wrote to Emeritus, the Donatist bishop who had appeared to be their principal spokesman in the conference we held with them. The book is quite useful, since it sets out with convenient brevity the matters by which they are defeated or shown to have been defeated.

This book begins as follows: “If even now, brother Emeritus…”

## CHAPTER XLVII. The Proceedings concerning Pelagius, one book

At about the same time, in the East—that is, in Syria Palestina—Pelagius was brought before episcopal proceedings by certain Catholic brothers. Those who had submitted a written accusation against him were absent because they had been unable to arrive by the day of the synod. Pelagius was therefore heard by fourteen bishops, who declared him a Catholic after he condemned the doctrines hostile to Christ’s grace that had been read against him from the written accusation.

But when those proceedings came into our hands, I wrote a book about them, lest the judges should be thought, by absolving him, also to have approved those doctrines—doctrines from which he could not possibly have emerged without being condemned unless he had condemned them himself.

This book begins as follows: “After the proceedings had come into our hands…”

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On the Correction of the Donatists, one book

At the same time I also wrote a book *On the Correction of the Donatists* (Letter 185, to Boniface) for the sake of those who did not want them to be corrected by the imperial laws.

This book begins as follows: “I praise, rejoice, and marvel…”

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the Presence of God, to Dardanus, one book

I wrote a book *On the Presence of God*. In it my principal concern is directed against the Pelagian heresy, although it is not expressly named. The book also discusses, with careful and subtle argument, the presence of the nature that we call the supreme and true God, and his temple.

This book begins as follows: “I confess, dearest brother Dardanus…”

## CHAPTER L. Against Pelagius and Caelestius, on the Grace of Christ and on Original Sin, to Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, two books

After the Pelagian heresy, together with its authors, had been convicted and condemned by the bishops of the Roman Church—first Innocent and then Zosimus—with the assistance of letters from the African councils, I wrote two books against them: one *On the Grace of Christ*, and the other *On Original Sin*.

This work begins as follows: “How greatly we rejoice in your bodily, and especially your spiritual, salvation…”

## CHAPTER LI. The Proceedings with Emeritus the Donatist, one book

Some time after the conference we had held with the Donatist heretics, it became necessary for us to travel to Caesarean Mauretania. There, at Caesarea itself, we saw Emeritus, the Donatist bishop—one of the seven whom they had chosen to defend their cause and who had labored most energetically in that cause.

The ecclesiastical proceedings, which are preserved among my little works, testify to what we did with him in the presence of the bishops of that province and of the people of the church of Caesarea, in which city he had been both a citizen and the bishop of the aforementioned heretics. Since he found nothing to answer, he listened like a mute to my entire speech, which I delivered concerning the Maximianists alone in the hearing of him and everyone who was present.

This book, or these proceedings, begin as follows: “In the consulship of the most glorious emperors Honorius for the twelfth time and Theodosius for the eighth time” [Note: [Col. 0650] The Bodleian manuscript reads: “In the consulship of the most glorious Honorius Augustus twelve times, and Constantius for the second time, distinguished men, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, at Caesarea, in the church of Major.” Several of the principal manuscripts read: “In the consulship of the most glorious Honorius Augustus and Constantius for the second time, distinguished men, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, at Caesarea, in the church of Major.” Most of the others agree, although some insert “twelve” or “twelve times” after “Honorius Augustus.” Yet this year does not coincide with the second consulship of Constantius, which all the editions that we have been able to examine nevertheless assign. A few of them also read “in the greater church,” as in the editions. We have not changed the text here.].

## CHAPTER LII. Against the Sermon of the Arians, one book

Meanwhile, a certain sermon of the Arians came into my hands, without the name of its author. At the request and insistence of the person who had sent it to me, I replied as briefly and quickly as I could [Col. 0651]. I attached the same sermon at the beginning of my reply and added numbers to each section, so that, by consulting them, one could easily see what I had answered at each point.

This book, after their sermon, which is attached at the beginning, begins as follows: “I answer their preceding argument with this argument…”

## CHAPTER LIII. On Marriage and Concupiscence, to Count Valerius, two books

I wrote two books to the distinguished Count Valerius after hearing that the Pelagians had written something or other to him about us—namely, that we condemned marriage by asserting original sin. The title of these books is *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

We defend the goodness of marriage, lest anyone suppose that the concupiscence of the flesh, and the law in the members that resists the law of the mind, is a defect of marriage—a defect of lust that marital chastity nevertheless uses well for the procreation of children.

The reason there are two books is that the first came into the hands of Julian the Pelagian, who wrote four books against it. A certain person extracted some passages from those books and sent them to Count Valerius, and Valerius sent them on to us. After receiving them, I replied to those same matters in another book.

The first book of this work begins as follows: “New heretics, dearest son Valerius…”

The second begins: “Amid the duties of your military service…”

## CHAPTER LIV. Seven books of Expressions

I composed seven books on seven books of divine Scripture: the five books of Moses, one book of Joshua son of Nun, and one book of Judges. In them I marked expressions in each book that are less customary in our language. Readers who pay too little attention seek the meaning of such expressions in the divine utterances, although the expression is merely a particular form of speech. Sometimes they extract a meaning that does not indeed conflict with the truth, but it is nevertheless clear that the author who wrote the passage did not intend that meaning; rather, he more probably used this form of expression.

Many obscure passages in the sacred Scriptures become clear once the forms of speech are recognized. For this reason these forms should be learned where the meaning is evident, so that when the meaning is hidden, this knowledge may come to its aid and open the passages to the reader’s understanding.

The title of this work is *Expressions from Genesis*, and similarly from each of the individual books.

In the first book I stated (number 18) that it is written, “And Noah did all the words that the Lord commanded him; so he did” (Genesis 6:22), and I said that this expression was similar to the wording used in the creation of the creatures: after it says, “And so it was done,” it adds, “And God made…” (Genesis 1). This no longer seems to me to be similar in every respect. Indeed, in the first passage the meaning is also hidden; here there is only a form of expression.

This work begins as follows: “Expressions of the Scriptures…”

## CHAPTER LV. Seven books of Questions

1. At the same time I also wrote seven books of *Questions on the Same Divine Books*. I wanted to call them this because in them I proposed matters for investigation more often than I resolved questions already asked. Nevertheless, many more matters seem to me to have been treated in such a way that they can reasonably be judged to have been resolved and explained.

We had also begun to examine the books of Kings in the same manner, but, having made little progress, we directed our attention to other matters that pressed more urgently.

In the first book, where the matter concerns the variegated rods that Jacob placed in the water so that the sheep, seeing them while they drank, would conceive and give birth to various offspring (Question 93), we did not explain correctly why he did not put them there again when they conceived—that is, when they conceived other offspring—but only during the earlier conception. The explanation of another question (Question 95), in which the question is why Jacob said to his father-in-law, “You defrauded me of my wages by ten ewe-lambs” (Genesis 31:41), is sufficiently and truthfully unfolded and demonstrates that the former question was not resolved as it ought to have been.

2. In the third book, too, where the discussion concerns the high priest and how he could father children when he was required to enter the Holy of Holies twice a day, where the altar of incense stood, in order to offer incense morning and evening (Exodus 30:7–8)—for the Law says that no unclean person could enter, and the same Law says that a man becomes unclean through marital intercourse, commanding him to wash with water but declaring him unclean even after washing until evening (Leviticus 15:16)—I said, “It followed that he was either continent or that the incense was omitted on certain days” (Question 82). I did not see that this did not follow.

For the statement “He shall be unclean until evening” can be understood to mean that by evening itself he was no longer unclean, but only until that point, so that, once evening had come, he could offer the incense in a clean state, even though, for the purpose of fathering children, he had intercourse with his wife after the morning incense [Note: [Col. 0652] Some manuscripts and Am. read, “after evening itself.” This is not coherent unless “when it had begun” is understood.].

Likewise, when the question was asked how the high priest could be forbidden to enter upon the death of his father (Leviticus 21:11), since, when there was only one high priest, he could not properly become a priest until after the death of his priestly father, I said that for this reason it was necessary for the son to be appointed immediately after his father’s death, before the father had been buried, so that he could succeed him; and that this was also necessary because the incense had to be offered continually, twice each day (Question 83), even though the priest was forbidden to enter upon the death of his father before his burial.

But I paid too little attention to the possibility that this command was given rather for those who were destined to become high priests, not because they were succeeding high-priestly fathers, but because they were descendants—sons—of Aaron, in case the high priest had no sons or had sons so unworthy that none of them ought to succeed their father. Thus Samuel succeeded Eli the high priest (1 Samuel 1), although Samuel himself was not the son of a priest, but was nevertheless descended from Aaron, that is, from Aaron’s descendants [Note: [Col. 0652] Although there are substantial reasons why more recent interpreters of the sacred Scriptures think that Samuel should be counted only among the Levites, as one not descended from Aaron but from the elder branch of Levi, nevertheless most of the ancients, together with Saint Augustine, ascribe priestly dignity to him: Cyprian, Letter 65; Ambrose, on Psalm 118, sermon 18; and others.].

3. Concerning the robber to whom it was said, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), I stated as though it were certain that he had not been visibly baptized (Question 84), although this is uncertain, and it is more reasonable to believe that he had been baptized, as I later argued elsewhere.

Likewise, in the fifth book I said that, where the mothers are mentioned in the Gospel genealogies, they are never listed without the fathers (Question 46, section 2). This is true, but it is irrelevant to the matter under discussion. The question concerned those who took the wives of their brothers or relatives who had died childless, because of the two fathers of Joseph, one of whom Matthew mentions and the other Luke.

I discussed this question carefully in this work when we revised our book against Faustus the Manichaean.

This work begins as follows: “When I read the sacred Scriptures that are called canonical…”

## CHAPTER LVI. On the Soul and Its Origin, four books

At the same time, a certain Vincentius Victor, in Caesarean Mauretania, found among a certain Spanish presbyter named Peter one of my little works. In it I had confessed, in a certain passage concerning the origin of the individual human souls, that I did not know whether they are propagated from the one soul of the first human being and subsequently from parents, or whether, as happened with that first soul, each individual soul is given to each individual person without any propagation. Nevertheless, I did say that the soul is not a body but a spirit.

Against these statements of mine, that man wrote two books to Peter himself. The monk Renatus sent them to me from Caesarea. After reading them, I responded with four books: one to Renatus the monk, another to the presbyter Peter, and two to Vincentius Victor himself. Although the book addressed to Peter is as long as a book, it is nevertheless a letter, which I did not wish to separate from the other three.

In all these works, in which many necessary matters are discussed, I defended my hesitation concerning the origin of the souls given to individual human beings and exposed the many errors and perverse presumptions of Victor’s position. Nevertheless, I treated the young man with as much gentleness as I could, since he should not be rashly condemned but still instructed; and I received from him a written reply indicating his correction.

The book of this work addressed to Renatus begins as follows: “Your sincerity toward us…”

The one addressed to Peter begins: “To my most beloved brother and fellow presbyter Peter…”

Of the final two books, addressed to Vincentius Victor, the first begins as follows: “What I thought I ought to write to you…”

## CHAPTER LVII. To Pollentius, on Adulterous Marriages, two books

I wrote two books *On Adulterous Marriages*, seeking, insofar as I could, to resolve a most difficult question according to the Scriptures. Whether I did so with complete clarity, I do not know. Indeed, I recognize that I did not reach perfection in this matter, although I opened many of its recesses; anyone who reads intelligently will be able to judge this.

The first book of this work begins as follows: “The first question, dearest brother Pollentius, is…”

The second begins: “Concerning what you had written to me…”

## CHAPTER LVIII. Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets, two books

Meanwhile, a book by a certain heretic—whether a Marcionist or one of those whose error holds that God did not make this world and that the God of the Law given through Moses, and of the Prophets belonging to that same Law, is not the true God but an utterly evil demon—was being read at Carthage, in the seaside marketplace, while many people gathered and listened with the greatest attention.

Some highly zealous Christian brothers came upon it and sent it to me to refute without any delay, earnestly asking me not to postpone my reply. I refuted it in two books, which I entitled *Against an Adversary of the Law and the Prophets*, because the book itself that had been sent to me bore no author’s name.

This work begins as follows: “The book that you sent, dearest brothers…”

## CHAPTER LIX. Against Gaudentius, bishop of the Donatists, two books

At about the same time Dulcitius, a tribune and notary, was in Africa executing the imperial orders issued against the Donatists. He had sent a letter to Gaudentius, the Donatist bishop of Thamugadi, one of the seven whom they had chosen in our conference as the authors of their defense. He exhorted him to Catholic unity and dissuaded him from the fire with which he threatened to consume himself and his followers, together with the church in which he was situated. He also added that, if they considered themselves righteous, they should flee according to the command of the Lord Christ rather than burn themselves in impious flames.

Gaudentius sent back two letters: one brief, because, as he claimed, the messenger was in a hurry; the other lengthy, as though he were replying more fully and carefully. The tribune mentioned above thought that these should be sent to me so that I might refute them myself. I answered both in a single book.

When this reached the hands of Gaudentius himself, he sent me a reply containing what seemed appropriate to him. He did not answer rationally, but rather declared that he could neither reply nor remain silent. Although this could readily be understood by intelligent readers when our words and his were compared, I nevertheless did not wish to leave the matter—whatever it was—without a written reply. Thus these two books of ours addressed to him came into being.

This work begins as follows: “Gaudentius, Donatist bishop of Thamugadi…”

## CHAPTER LX. Against Lying, one book

At that time I also wrote a book *Against Lying*. The occasion for this work was that certain Catholics thought they ought to pretend to be Priscillianists in order to penetrate the hiding places of the Priscillianist heretics, who believed that their heresy could be concealed not only by denying and lying but also by perjury.

I prohibited this course of action and composed this book.

This book begins as follows: “You have sent me many things to read…”

## CHAPTER LXI. Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, four books

There follow four books that I wrote against two letters of the Pelagians, addressed to Boniface, bishop of the Roman Church [Col. 0655]. When these letters had come into his hands, he sent them to me because he found that my name had been inserted in them slanderously.

This work begins as follows: “I certainly knew you, as your widespread fame proclaimed…”

## CHAPTER LXII. Against Julian, six books
Julian the Pelagian’s four books, which I mentioned above, meanwhile also came into our hands. In them I discovered that the passages extracted from them by the person who had sent them to Count Valerius were not all written to that same count in the form in which Julian had stated them, but that some had been altered to a certain extent. Accordingly, I wrote six books against those four. The first two of my books refute Julian’s shamelessness by the testimonies of the saints who defended the Catholic faith after the Apostles. Julian had thought that the dogma of the Manichaeans should be brought against us because we say that original sin is derived from Adam and is removed through the washing of regeneration—not only in adults but also in infants. In the latter part of my first book I showed how Julian himself, by certain of his statements, assists the Manichaeans. Each of the other four of our books is directed against one of those books individually.

In the fifth volume of this extensive and painstaking work, however, where I mentioned that a deformed husband was accustomed to place before his wife, during intercourse, a beautiful picture so that she would not bear deformed children (Book 5, chapter 14, §51), I gave the name of the man who used to do this as though it were certain, although it is uncertain, because my memory deceived me. Soranus, the author of a medical work, wrote that the king of Cyprus used to do this, but he did not give his proper name.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions that differ from them here have “a master of the medical art.” But in Book 5 Against Julian, chapter 14, the text returns to agreement with the manuscripts.]

This work begins: “Your insults and abusive words, Julian.”

## CHAPTER LXIII. To Laurence, On Faith, Hope, and Charity, one book

I also wrote a book on Faith, Hope, and Charity, when the person to whom it was written had asked me to provide him with a little work of mine that would not leave his hands. The Greeks call this kind of work an *Enchiridion* (“Handbook”). In it I seem to have explained with sufficient care how God should be worshiped and what wisdom Scripture defines as truly human wisdom.

This book begins: “It cannot be said, my most beloved son Laurence, how greatly I rejoice in your learning.”

## CHAPTER LXIV. To Bishop Paulinus, On Care for the Dead, one book

I wrote a book On Care for the Dead when I had been asked by letter whether it benefits anyone after death that his body is buried near the memorial of some saint.

This book begins: “For a long time, my venerable fellow bishop Paulinus, I have…”

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius, one book

The book entitled On the Eight Questions of Dulcitius would not need to be mentioned in this work among my books, since it was compiled from things that I had previously written in other works, unless some discussion by us were also found to have been inserted into it, and unless I had given one of the answers not from some other short work of mine but as the answer that occurred to me at that time.

This book begins: “As it seems to me, my most beloved son Dulcitius…”

## CHAPTER LXVI. To Valentinus and the Monks with Him, On Grace and Free Choice, one book

Because there are people who, when God’s grace is defended, think that free choice is being denied, and who defend free choice in such a way as to deny God’s grace, asserting that grace is given according to our merits, I wrote a book entitled On Grace and Free Choice. I wrote it to the monks of Hadrumetum, in whose monastery a dispute on this subject had begun, so that some of them were compelled to consult me.

This book begins: “Because of those who [defend] the free choice of the human being…”

## CHAPTER LXVII. To the Same Persons, On Rebuke and Grace, one book

I wrote another book to the same persons, entitled On Rebuke and Grace, when I had been informed that someone there had said that no one should be rebuked if he does not perform God’s commandments, but that one should merely pray for him so that he may do so.

This book begins: “After reading your letter, my most beloved brother Valentinus…”

I recalled that I had dictated these ninety-three works in two hundred and thirty-two books when I revised them, not knowing whether I would still dictate any others. I published the revision itself in two books, at the urging of the brethren, before I began to revise the letters and sermons addressed to the people—some dictated by others and some dictated by me.

[Note: In several old manuscripts, after the final chapter, we found the following written by the first hand:

“Books written and published by the blessed Bishop Augustine after the correction of these works:

“These two books of the *Retractions*.

“The book called the *Speculum*, consisting of testimonies from Scripture.

“To Prosper and Hilary, two books On the Predestination of the Saints.

“To the deacon Quodvultdeus, two books On Heresies.

“Against the Proceedings Held with Maximinus, Bishop of the Arians—for the day on which they met was consumed by his lengthy disputation—two books.

“Against Julian the Pelagian, six books. He left a seventh unfinished, and did not even begin an eighth. The heretic himself has eight books to which he replied, setting out his words and adding his own responses to them.”

This is how it is read in the Pratellian manuscript and in that of Saint Arnulf of Metz, and others.]

---

# ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: THIRTEEN BOOKS OF THE CONFESSIONS

[Note: Written about the year 400.]

## NOTICE BY THE BENEDICTINE FATHERS

The books of the *Confessions* are here issued newly corrected against the best-quality old manuscripts: the Fossatensis, Thuaneus, Corbeiensis, Germanensis, and Benignianus manuscripts, which appear to have been written seven or eight hundred years ago.

In addition, we consulted other manuscripts of a later period, or manuscripts unknown to us because we did not examine all of them with our own eyes: namely, the Theodericensis, Albinensis, Lyranus, Valinensis, Regius, Vedastinus, and Vaticanus manuscripts; one from the library of the Reverend Fathers of the Dominicans in Paris on the Rue Saint-Jacques; two from the Sorbonne; three from the Victorine library; and four from the library of the Reverend Fathers of the Augustinians of the Great Convent in Paris.

Finally, we consulted the various readings of the Louvain scholars, collected from five manuscripts, as well as four English manuscripts: one from the Bodleian Library, two from Merton College, and one from the Laudian Archive.

The following older and more carefully corrected printed editions were used in correcting the books of the *Confessions*:

**Am.** That is, the book printed at Basel by Johann Amerbach in the year of the Lord 1489.

**Bad.** The edition that Jodocus Badius had printed in Paris by Jean Petit in 1502.

**Er.** Corrected under the supervision of Desiderius Erasmus and printed at Basel by the Froben press in 1529.

**Lov.** The book that appeared at Antwerp in 1777 from the Plantin press, according to the revision of the Louvain theologians.

**Arn.** The edition that appeared at Paris in 1649, revised through the efforts of Dr. Antoine Arnauld of the Sorbonne against twelve manuscripts.

## WE ALSO COMPARED THE FOLLOWING EDITIONS

1. **Lugd.** That is, the Lyon edition of 1561.

2. **Er. Guill.** That is, another edition of Erasmus, published in Paris in the house of Carole Guillard in 1541.

3. **Ven.** That is, the Venetian edition of 1584.

4. **Somm.** That is, the edition of H. Sommalius of the Society of Jesus, published at Cologne in 1629. Two more recent editions also exist, **P. Desb.** and **GG.**: one published by Parent-Desbarres and the other by the booksellers Gaume brothers in Paris. We compared both. M.

5. **Lov. Par.** That is, the Louvain edition published at Paris in 1651.

6. **Lov.** That is, another Louvain edition, reprinted at Antwerp in 1662.

7. **Dub.** That is, the edition of D. Dubois, published at Paris in 1687.

8. **Benedict.** That is, the Benedictine edition, which was again published at Antwerp in 1700–1702.

9. **Mart.** That is, the edition revised by Dom J. Martin Maurin against the old edition of Ulimmerius and twelve manuscripts, published at Paris in 1741.

10. **Flor.** That is, the edition revised by Fr. Archangel of the Presentation, a priest, a professed Discalced Carmelite, and lecturer in theology and sacred Scripture, against several editions and thirteen Tuscan manuscripts, published at Florence in 1757.

11. **Rond.** That is, the edition collated through the efforts of L. St. Rondet with sixteen manuscripts and with the preceding editions, published at Paris in 1776. M.

(C)

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOKS OF THE CONFESSIONS

[Note: See also Book 2, chapter 6, of the *Retractions*, page 632, §§1–2, from the words “Of my *Confessions*” to the words “Great are you, Lord.” M.]

The same reason that caused the life of each author customarily to be placed at the beginning of the books he published undoubtedly also moved the first editors of Saint Augustine’s works to place his *Confessions* immediately after the books of the *Retractions*, which properly ought to precede them, in the first volume. For it is of the greatest importance that anyone who undertakes to read an author’s writings with pleasure and benefit should have a clear understanding of his character, interests, habits, integrity, faith, and other qualities.

Now Augustine expressed himself completely and with exceptional accuracy in his *Confessions*. In them he set out individually not only those deeds that could have been exposed to human eyes, but also those things—both good and evil—that he had pondered in his inmost self, with God alone as witness. In them he commemorates at length both the slightest errors of his former life and the benefits he received from God, intending to leave to posterity an enduring memorial either of a penitent or of a grateful heart, and also an outstanding example of both the justice and the goodness that God constantly displays toward us. Above all, he was concerned to praise God as just and good for both his evils and his goods and to awaken the human intellect and affection toward him—to express the matter in his own words.

He carries this out as follows.

In the first book, after invoking God, he recalls the beginnings of his life up to his fifteenth year. He acknowledges the sins of infancy and childhood, and confesses that at this age he was more inclined toward play and every sort of childish amusement and vice than toward the study of literature.

In the second book he advances to another period, recalling the first year of his adolescence—that is, his sixteenth year—which he had spent in his father’s house, having abandoned his studies and indulging his temperament and lusts. He recalls it with profound grief, judging with particular severity the theft that he and his companions committed at that time.

The third book concerns the years of his seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth years, spent at Carthage. While completing his literary studies there, he remembers having become entangled in the snare of lustful love and having fallen into the heresy of the Manichaeans. He argues lucidly against their errors and absurdities. He recounts his mother’s tears and the divinely given response concerning her son’s conversion.

In the fourth book he is ashamed that he had been attached to that sect for nine years and had drawn others with him into the same error. He then recalls that, in the meantime, his dearest friend had been taken from him by death and that he had mourned him with a grief more bitter than was fitting. On this occasion he says a good deal about vain and genuine friendship. Finally, he mentions the books *On the Beautiful and the Fitting*, which he composed in his twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh year, as well as how easily, when he was about twenty, he had understood for himself the books of the liberal arts and Aristotle’s *Categories*.

In the fifth book he presents himself at the age of twenty-nine. At that time, having discovered the ignorance of Faustus the Manichaean, he abandoned his intention of advancing within that sect. At the same time he was sent from Rome, where he was then teaching rhetoric, to Milan to teach the same art. After hearing Ambrose, he began to recover his senses and resolved to renounce Manichaeism and return to the status of a catechumen.

In the sixth book, when his mother Monica had already arrived at Milan and he himself was thirty years old, he increasingly understood the truth of Catholic doctrine, which the Manichaeans falsely calumniated. He relates the character of his friend Alypius. He was being pulled in different directions while deliberating how to order his life more rightly; and, struck also by fear of death and judgment, he was daily becoming more fervent in turning his life around.

In the seventh book he brings before the eyes of his mind the beginning of his youth, that is, his thirty-first year. He relates that at that age he was still wrapped in denser darknesses of ignorance and wandering concerning the nature of God and the origin of evil. In searching into this matter he was tormented in a remarkable way, but at last he arrived at a true knowledge of God, although he did not yet think rightly about the Lord Christ.

The eighth book touches on the most celebrated period of his life, namely his thirty-second year. After consulting Simplicianus and learning from him about Victorinus’s conversion, and after learning from Ponticianus about the life of Antony, the Egyptian monk, he underwent a fierce struggle between flesh and spirit. Then, admonished by a heavenly oracle, he opened the Apostle’s book; immediately afterward, through reading it, he was transformed with his whole soul toward a better way of life and was completely converted to God.

In the ninth book he speaks of the decision he had made to abandon the profession of rhetoric, although not before the period of the approaching autumn vacation had arrived. He then speaks of his retreat to the country estate of his friend Verecundus, of his baptism, and of the virtues and death of his mother Monica, which occurred in that same year after he had been baptized—namely, Augustine’s thirty-third year.

In the tenth book he subsequently examines himself and openly declares not what he had formerly been but what he was then. He strives to make known the God whom he loves, and, as he leads the reader through each class of things, he explains the astonishing power of memory in many ways, rejoicing that God has a place in his memory. He investigates all his actions, perceptions, and emotions under the threefold temptation of pleasure, curiosity, and pride. He confesses Christ the Lord as the one mediator between God and human beings and trusts that through Christ all the weaknesses of his soul must be healed.

In the eleventh book and those that follow he treats of the sacred Scriptures. He explains the whole of the first chapter of Genesis, in which the creation of the world is described, illuminating it with discussions, resolving the difficulties that arise, and defending it against the objections of opponents. In the eleventh book he discusses time at somewhat greater length. In the twelfth he discusses formless matter and the manifold meaning of Scripture. In the thirteenth he commends God’s goodness from the production of created things; he proclaims God as Trinity and a certain proper conception of the Holy Spirit. Finally, he interprets the history of the created world allegorically.

We judge that these books were written around the year of Christ 400 because Augustine lists them immediately before those works that the bishop composed against Faustus the Manichaean not long before or after that year, as will be said in its proper place. Certainly, when works bear no indisputable and distinct chronological indication and the date cannot be established by other arguments, it seems that the sequence of the *Retractions* should be decisive, since Augustine took care, as far as he could, that we should learn from that very work the order in which his writings were composed.

[Note: *Retractions*, Prologue, §3.]

Nevertheless, we will not deny that at times he paid less attention to chronology and more to the sequence of the subject matter treated.

## ST. AUGUSTINE, LETTER 231, TO COUNT DARIUS, §6

“Take the books of my *Confessions* that you desired. There you may look upon me; do not praise me beyond what I am. There, believe not what others say about me, but me. There attend to me and see what I was in myself and through myself. If you find anything in me that pleases you, praise with me there the one whom I wished to be praised because of me—for it is not I. He made us, and we did not make ourselves; we had destroyed ourselves, but he who made us remade us. When you find me there, pray for me, that I may not fail but be perfected.”

## FROM THE BOOK ON THE GIFT OF PERSEVERANCE, CHAPTER XX

“What of my shorter works could have become known more frequently and more pleasingly than the books of my *Confessions*? I published them before the Pelagian heresy arose, and in them I certainly said to our God—and said it often: ‘Give what you command, and command what you will.’ When these words of mine were mentioned at Rome in the presence of Pelagius by a certain brother and fellow bishop, he could not endure them; and, objecting with rather greater agitation, he nearly quarreled with the man who had recalled them.”

# BOOK ONE

After invoking God, Augustine recalls the beginnings of his life up to his fifteenth year. He acknowledges the sins of infancy and childhood, and confesses that at this age he was more inclined toward play and every sort of childish amusement and vice than toward the study of literature.

## CHAPTER ONE. He Wishes to Praise God, Moved by God Himself

### 1

“Great are you, Lord, and greatly to be praised” (Psalm 144:3); “great is your power, and your wisdom has no measure” (Psalm 146:5). Yet human beings, a small part of your creation, wish to praise you—human beings who carry their mortality and carry the testimony of their sin and the testimony that you resist the proud (1 Peter 5:5). [Note: Sommal., Lov., and Mart., from five manuscripts, and Rond., from three manuscripts: “God, you resist the proud.” M.] And yet human beings, a small part of your creation, wish to praise you.

You stir them so that they delight to praise you, because you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Grant me, Lord, to know and understand whether I should first invoke you or praise you; and whether I should first know you or invoke you. But who invokes you without knowing you? For someone who does not know you might invoke one thing in place of another. Or rather, are you invoked so that you may be known? But how will they invoke one in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe without someone preaching? (Romans 10:14.) And they will praise the Lord who seek him (Psalm 21:27). For those who seek him will find him, and those who find him will praise him.

I will seek you, Lord, by invoking you; and I will invoke you by believing in you, for you have been preached to us. My faith, which you have given me and inspired in me through the humanity of your Son and through the ministry of your preacher, invokes you, Lord.”

## CHAPTER TWO. The God Whom He Invokes Is in Him, and He Himself Is in God

### 2

“And how shall I invoke my God, my God and my Lord? For surely I shall call him into myself when I invoke him. And what place is there in me to which my God may come, the God who made heaven and earth? Is it really so, Lord my God, that there is anything in me that can contain you? Or do the heaven and earth that you made, and in which you made me, contain you? Or, since nothing that exists would exist without you, does it follow that whatever exists contains you?

Since, then, I also exist, why do I ask you to come into me, when I would not exist unless you were in me? For I am not yet in hell, and yet you are there too. [Note: The Theoderic manuscript has, “I am hell,” a reading that is not inadmissible. Most others have, “I now [am] hell,” apparently through a scribal error. One manuscript used by Rondet has, “For I am not in hell.” M.] For if I descend into hell, you are present (Psalm 138:8). I would not exist, my God, I would not exist at all, unless you were in me. Or rather, I would not exist unless I were in you, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, in whom are all things (Romans 11:36). Even so, Lord, even so.

Where do I invoke you when I am in you? Or from where can you come into me? Where could I withdraw beyond heaven and earth, so that from there my God might come into me, who said: ‘I fill heaven and earth’?” (Jeremiah 23:24.)

## CHAPTER THREE. God Is Entirely Everywhere, Yet Nothing Contains Him Entirely

### 3

“Do heaven and earth, then, contain you because you fill them? Or do you fill them and yet something remains, because they do not contain you? And where do you pour out whatever of you remains after heaven and earth have been filled? Or do you have no need to be contained anywhere, you who contain all things, since you fill what you contain by containing it?

The vessels that are full of you do not make you stable; for even if they are broken, you are not spilled. And when you pour yourself over us, you do not fall, but you raise us up; nor are you scattered, but you gather us. [Note: The older editions—namely those of Jodocus Badius Ascensius, Johann Amerbach, and Desiderius Erasmus—together with three manuscripts, read “you are dispersed.”]

But do you, who fill all things, fill all things with your whole being? [Note: B. reads *quae* (“which”); Somm., Dub., Mart., and Rond. read *qui* (“who”). M.] Or, because nothing can contain you wholly, does everything contain a part of you, and do all things together contain that same part? Or do individual things contain individual parts, larger things larger parts and smaller things smaller parts? Then there is some part of you that is greater and some that is smaller. Or are you wholly everywhere, and does nothing contain you wholly?”

## CHAPTER FOUR. God’s Majesty and Inexpressible Perfections

### 4

“What are you, then, my God? What, I ask, except the Lord God? For who is Lord besides the Lord, or who is God besides our God? (Psalm 17:32.)

Supreme, best, most powerful, almighty, most merciful and most just; most hidden and most present; most beautiful and most strong; stable and incomprehensible; unchanging, changing all things; never new, never old; renewing all things and bringing the proud into old age, and they do not know it; always active, always at rest; gathering and yet needing nothing; carrying, filling, and protecting; creating, nourishing, and perfecting; seeking, although nothing is lacking to you.

You love, yet you do not burn with passion; you are jealous, yet secure; you repent, yet do not grieve; you become angry, yet remain tranquil; you change your works, yet do not change your plan; you receive what you find, yet you never lost anything [Note: Somm., Flor., and Rond. read “you lose.” M.]; never in want, you rejoice in gains; never greedy, you demand interest. More is paid to you than is owed, so that you become a debtor; and who possesses anything that is not yours? You repay debts while owing nothing; you forgive debts and lose nothing.

And what have we said [Note: Somm. and Rond., from one manuscript, read “do we say.” M.], my God, my life, my holy sweetness? Or what can anyone say when speaking of you? And woe to those who are silent about you, since even those who speak much are mute.”

## CHAPTER FIVE. He Asks for the Love of God and Forgiveness of Sins

### 5

“Who will grant me rest in you? Who will grant that you come into my heart and intoxicate it, so that I may forget my evils and embrace you, my one good?

What are you to me? Have mercy, so that I may speak. What am I to you, that you command me to love you and become angry with me if I do not, threatening me with immense misery? Is it, indeed, a small misery if I do not love you? [Note: The word “misery” is added in the old editions of Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus, and in one manuscript.]

Alas for me! Tell me, through your mercies, Lord my God, what you are to me. Say to my soul: ‘I am your salvation’ (Psalm 34:3). Speak so that I may hear. Behold, the ears of my heart are before you, Lord; open them and say to my soul: ‘I am your salvation.’ I will run after that voice and seize you. Do not hide your face from me: let me die, lest I die, so that I may see it.

### 6

“The house of my soul is too narrow for you to enter; let it be enlarged by you. It is in ruins; restore it. It contains things that offend your eyes; I confess and know this. But who will cleanse it? Or to whom besides you shall I cry: ‘Cleanse me from my hidden faults, Lord, and spare your servant from those belonging to others’? (Psalm 18:13–14.)

‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’ (Psalm 115:10). Lord, you know. Have I not confessed my sins against myself to you, my God, and have you not forgiven the wickedness of my heart? (Psalm 31:5.) I do not contend with you in judgment, for you are truth (Job 9:2–3); and I do not wish to deceive myself, lest my iniquity lie to itself (Psalm 26:12). I do not contend with you in judgment, therefore, because if you should observe iniquities, Lord—Lord, who could endure it?” (Psalm 129:3.)

## CHAPTER SIX. He Describes His Infancy and Praises God’s Providence and Eternity

### 7

“But allow me to speak before your mercy—I who am earth and ashes. [Note: Sommal.; Rond., from nine manuscripts; and Mart., from two manuscripts, read “Allow me.” M.] Allow me to speak, for behold, it is your mercy, not a mocking human being, to whom I speak. And perhaps you mock me, but you will turn and have mercy on me.

What is it that I wish to say, Lord my God, except that I do not know from where I came here, into this mortal life—or whether I should call it a living death? I do not know. [Note: This is the reading of almost all manuscripts and of the edition prepared by Antoine Arnauld, Doctor of the Sorbonne; there *I do not know* refers to the preceding clause, “from where I came here,” by which Augustine indicates uncertainty about the origin of the soul. Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus read: “into this, I say, mortal life: whether I should call it mortal life or a living death, I do not know.” The Louvain editors altered this, on the authority of three manuscripts, to: “into this I should call mortal life, or a living death, I do not know.”] And the consolations of your mercies received me, as I heard from the parents of my flesh, from whom and in whom you formed me in time, for I do not remember it. [Note: Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read “from whom and in whom” with both relatives feminine. The manuscripts and Arnauld’s edition more correctly read the masculine and feminine forms, to designate both parents.] The consolations of human milk received me.

My mother and my nurses did not fill their own breasts for themselves; rather, through them you gave me the nourishment of infancy according to your ordinance and according to the riches you have stored even in the depths of creation. You also gave me the desire not to want more than you gave me, and you gave those who nourished me the desire to give me what you gave them. For they wanted to give me, through an ordered affection, what they abundantly received from you.

Their good was my good, which came through them but not from them [Note: B. reverses the word order: “which from them not.” Somm., Dub., Mart., and Rond., with four manuscripts, read “which not from them.” M.]: for all good things come from you, God, and from my God comes all my salvation. I understood this later, when you called to me through the very things you grant, inwardly and outwardly. At that time I knew only how to suck and to rest in pleasures, and to weep at bodily discomforts—nothing more.

### 8

“Afterward I also began to laugh, first while asleep and then while awake. This was reported to me about myself, and I believed it, because we see others do the same; for I do not remember it of myself. And behold, little by little I began to sense where I was, and I wanted to make my wishes known to those through whom they could be fulfilled, but I could not, because my wishes were within me while they were outside me, and they could not enter my soul by any sense of their own.

Thus I moved my limbs and uttered sounds—signs resembling my wishes—as best I could and in such forms as I could manage; for they did not truly resemble them. When I was not obeyed, either because I was not understood or because my request might have been harmful, I became angry with adults who did not submit to me, though they were free and were not my servants, and I took revenge on them by weeping.

I learned that infants are like this from those whom I was able to observe, and they themselves, without knowing it, showed me more clearly that I had been like this than did my knowing nurses.”

### 9

“And behold, my infancy died long ago, while I live. But you, Lord, who always live, and in whom nothing dies—for before the beginnings of the ages and before anything that can be said to be ‘before,’ you are, and you are God and Lord of all that you have created; and with you the causes of all unstable things remain stable, the origins of all changeable things remain unchanging, and the eternal principles of all irrational and temporal things live—

Tell me, God, your suppliant, and in your mercy tell me, miserable as I am: did my infancy, which has now died, succeed some other age of mine? Or was it the age that I lived within my mother’s womb? For I have also been told something about that, and I myself have seen pregnant women.

What came before even this, my sweetness, my God? Was I somewhere, or was I someone? I have no one to tell me these things—not my father, nor my mother, nor the experience of others, nor my own memory. Or do you mock me for asking such questions and command me to praise you and confess to you for what I do know? [Note: Sommal., Lov., and Rond., from several manuscripts, read: “asking you, who command yourself to be praised by me and confessed to for what I know.” M.]”

### 10

“I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth, praising you for the beginnings and infancy of my life, which I do not remember. You have granted human beings to infer these things about themselves from others and also to believe much about themselves on the authority of little women.

For even then I existed and lived; and, near the end of infancy, I was already seeking signs by which I could make my perceptions known to others. From where could such a living creature come except from you, Lord? Or can anyone be the craftsman of his own making? Or can any vein be drawn from elsewhere through which being and life might flow into us, apart from your making us, Lord, for whom being and living are not two different things, because supreme being and supreme living are the same?

You are supreme and do not change. Nor does the present day pass away in you, although in you it does pass, because all these things are in you. They would have no paths by which to pass away unless you contained them. And because your years do not fail [Note: Lov. reads “or your years”; this *or* is absent from our manuscripts and from most other editions. Sommal. and Rond., with six manuscripts, read “will fail.” M.], your years are one day. How many days of ours and of our fathers have passed through your one day, receiving from it their forms, existing in some fashion, and passing onward to receive them again and exist in some fashion!

But you remain the same; today you will make all tomorrows and all that follows them, and all yesterdays and all that came before them; today you made them. What does it matter to me if someone does not understand this? Let him rejoice nevertheless, saying, ‘What is this?’ Let him rejoice even in this, and let him love finding you by not finding, rather than by finding failing to find you.”

## CHAPTER SEVEN. Infancy, Too, Is Subject to Sin

### 11

“Hear me, God. Woe to the sins of human beings! And yet a human being says this, and you have mercy on him, because you made him, and you did not make sin in him.

Who reminds me of the sin of my infancy? [Note: Lov. and Arnauld read, “Who reminds me”; Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus, “Who recalls with me.” The genuine reading is that restored with the aid of the manuscripts, in accordance with Augustine’s usage in *On the Teacher*, chapter 1: “I now establish two purposes of speaking: either that we may teach, or that we may remind either others or ourselves.”] For no one is clean before you, not even an infant whose life on earth is but a single day (Job 25:4). Who reminds me? Perhaps some tiny child now, in whom I see what I do not remember about myself.

What, then, was I sinning in that period? Was it that I longed for the breast, crying? For if I now did this—not for the breast, certainly, but longing in this way for food appropriate to my years—I would rightly be mocked and rebuked. Then, therefore, I was doing things worthy of rebuke; but because I could not understand the one who rebuked me, neither custom nor reason allowed me to be rebuked. As we grow, we uproot and cast such things out. Nor have I seen anyone who knowingly cleanses something [Note: The English manuscripts read “was cleansing.” Rond. has this reading with eight manuscripts. M.] throw away what is good.

Or were such things good for that time: to ask by weeping even for something harmful; to become violently angry with people who were not subject to me, whether free people or adults; and with those from whom I had been born; and with many others wiser than I who did not obey the nod of my will; to strive to harm them by striking as much as possible, because they did not obey commands that it would have been harmful to obey?

Thus the weakness of infant limbs is innocent, but not the mind of infants. I myself have seen and observed a jealous little child. He could not yet speak, but he gazed with a pale and bitter look at his fellow nursling. Who is unaware of this? Mothers and nurses claim that they expiate such things by some remedies or other.

Unless this too is innocence: when, in a spring of milk flowing abundantly and overflowing, one who is desperately in need and still living on that one nourishment cannot endure having a companion share it. Such things are gently tolerated, not because they are no evils or only slight evils, but because they will pass away with advancing age. You may prove this from the fact that the same things cannot be tolerated with equanimity when they are found in someone older. [Note: This is the correct manuscript reading. Augustine means that the evils gently tolerated in infants can be shown to be evils precisely because they cannot be borne with equanimity in persons of more advanced age. The printed editions therefore read erroneously: “Although you may prove this, they are nevertheless tolerated.”]

### 12

“Therefore, Lord my God, you gave life to an infant and fashioned the body that we see with its senses, joined it together with its limbs, adorned it with its form, and implanted in it all the impulses of a living creature for its wholeness and preservation. You command me to praise you in these things, confess you, and sing praises to your name, O Most High (Psalm 91:2), because you are God, almighty and good, even if you had made only these things, which no one else can make except you, from whom comes all order; most beautiful, who shapes all things and orders all things by your law.

This age, then, which I do not remember having lived through [Note: Erasmus, Lugd., Ven., Lov., Sommal., and Rond., with ten manuscripts, and Mart., with three manuscripts, read: “which I do not remember that I lived”; and shortly afterward, “which I live … which I lived.” M.], about which I believed what others told me, and which I inferred from other infants that I had passed through—although this is a very reliable inference—I hesitate to count as part of this life of mine that I live in this world. For, insofar as the darkness of my forgetfulness is concerned, it is equal to the life I lived in my mother’s womb.

But if I was conceived in iniquity and my mother nourished me in sins in her womb (Psalm 50:7) [Note: *if also* is omitted in the Louvain edition.], where, I ask you, my God, where, Lord, was I, your servant, or when was I innocent? But behold, I set aside that period. What have I now to do with a time of which I recall no trace?”

## CHAPTER EIGHT. How He Learned to Speak as a Child
13. Did I not, from infancy onward, proceed hither into childhood—or rather, did childhood itself come into me and succeed infancy? It did not depart: where could it have gone? And yet it was no longer there. For I was not an infant incapable of speech, but already a speaking child. I remember this, and only afterward understood how I learned to speak. Older people did not teach me by presenting words in some definite order of instruction, as they did shortly afterward with letters. Rather, I myself, with the mind you gave me, my God, wished to express the feelings of my heart by groans, cries, and various movements of my limbs, so that my will might be obeyed. I was unable to express everything I wanted, or to everyone I wanted; therefore I kept trying to grasp it by memory [Note: [Col. 0666] Lov.: “I grasped it by memory.” Bad., Am., Er., and Arnald., with several manuscripts: “I considered it by memory.” The reading of the manuscripts Corb., Fossat., and others of the best quality, which have “I kept trying to grasp it,” seemed preferable.]. When they named some object, and in accordance with that word moved their bodies toward something, I observed this and retained it: that object was called by the word they uttered when they wished to point it out. Their intention was revealed by the movement of their bodies, as if by the natural language of all peoples, expressed through the face, the nodding of the eyes, and the actions of the other limbs, as well as by the sound of the voice indicating the mind’s feeling when seeking, possessing, rejecting, or avoiding things. Thus, by gradually gathering words placed in various sentences in their proper contexts and frequently heard, and recognizing what things they signified, I tamed my mouth to these signs and began to express my own wishes through them. In this way I shared with those among whom I lived the signs by which wishes are expressed, and entered more deeply into the stormy fellowship of human life, dependent on the authority of my parents and the nod of my elders.

## CHAPTER IX. His hatred of letters, his love of play, and his fear of punishment in children

14. My God, my God, what miseries and mockeries I experienced there! For it was presented to me as proper for a child to live rightly by obeying those who admonished me, so that in this world I might prosper and excel in the arts of eloquence, which serve human honor and false riches. For this reason I was sent to school, to learn my letters. Miserable that I was, I did not know what benefit they had; yet if I was slow in learning, I was beaten. This was praised by my elders, and many before us, living this kind of life, had constructed the painful roads through which we were compelled to pass, multiplying labor and sorrow for the children of Adam.

Yet, Lord, we found people praying to you, and from them we learned—sensing, insofar as we could, that you were some great being who, though unseen by our senses, could hear us and help us. As a child I began to pray to you, my help and refuge; and in calling upon you I broke the knots of my tongue. I prayed to you, a little child but with no little feeling, that I might not be beaten at school. And when you did not hear me—for this was not to my foolishness (Ps. XXI, 3)—my punishments were laughed at by my elders, even by my parents, who wanted no harm to come to me. Those blows were then my great and grievous evil.

15. Is there, Lord, any spirit so great, bound to you with such overwhelming devotion? Is there, I ask, any such person? For a certain kind of foolishness can also produce this. Is there, then, one who is so profoundly attached to you in piety that he would regard the rack, the claws, and various tortures of this kind—against which people pray to you with great fear throughout the world for deliverance—as so insignificant that he would mock those who dread them most bitterly, just as our parents mocked the punishments with which we children were afflicted by our teachers? [Note: [Col. 0667] Some manuscripts: “loving them.” A little later, however, Bad., Am., and Er.: “they inflict most cruelly.”] We did not fear them less, nor did we pray to you less earnestly to escape them; yet we sinned less by failing to write, read, or think about our letters than was required of us. For we were not lacking, Lord, in memory or intelligence, which you wished us to possess in sufficient measure for our age; [Col. 0668] but we delighted in playing, and those who themselves engaged in such things punished us for it.

The trifles of adults are called business; but when children engage in similar things, they are punished by adults. No one pities either children or adults—or both. Unless, perhaps, some good judge of things would approve of my being beaten because, as a boy, I played ball, and that game hindered me from learning my letters quickly, so that as an adult I might play more disgracefully; or because [Note: [Col. 0668] In Bad., Am., Er., and Lov.: “not.”] the same person who beat me did something else. If he had been defeated by his fellow teacher in some little dispute, he would have been tortured more by anger and envy than I was when I was beaten in a game of ball by my playmate.

## CHAPTER X. He is diverted from the study of letters by his love of play and spectacles

16. And yet I sinned, Lord God, arranger and creator of all natural things, but arranger only of sins [Note: [Col. 0668] In the editions of Am., Er., and Lov. the reading was: “arranger, but not arranger, only.” This was an error, corrected by the editions of Bad. and Arn. and by many more authoritative manuscripts, which lack the negation. For it is commonly known that Augustine repeatedly affirms that God, most just, is the arranger of sins. Thus, in *The City of God*, book 11, chapter 17: “God,” he says, “just as he is the best creator of good natures, so is he the most just arranger of evil wills.” Likewise, in Psalm 7: “He made and arranged one thing; he did not make another, but nevertheless arranged even this.” This doctrine is illustrated somewhat by another passage in the book *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 16, where we read: “It is in the power of evil people to sin. But that, by sinning, their evil should do this or that is not in their power, but in God’s, who divides the darkness and arranges it.”].

I sinned, my Lord God, by acting against the commands of my parents and teachers. I could later have made good use of the letters they wanted me to learn, whatever their own intention may have been. I was not disobedient because I chose better things, but because I loved playing, loved proud victories in contests, and loved having my ears scratched by false stories so that they would itch more intensely, while the same curiosity shone forth more and more through my eyes into spectacles [Note: [Col. 0668] Lov.: “with dangerous curiosity shining through the eyes into spectacles”; other manuscripts: “shining through the eyes.” Er., Lugd., Ven., and Somm. read as Lov.]. and the games of adults. Yet those who produced such entertainments possessed such dignity that nearly everyone wished the same for their little children; and nevertheless they willingly allowed the children to be beaten if such spectacles distracted them from the study by which they hoped the children would eventually become producers of such entertainments.

Look upon these things mercifully, Lord, and free us who now call upon you; free also those who do not yet call upon you, so that they may call upon you and you may free them.

## CHAPTER XI. When afflicted by illness, he asks insistently for baptism, which his mother postpones for a sound reason

17. While I was still a child, I had heard of the eternal life promised to us through the humility of our Lord God, who descended to our pride. I had already been marked with the sign of his cross and seasoned with his salt [Note: [Col. 0668] He indicates that from his earliest years he had already been initiated into the sacrament of catechumens. He makes this clearer again in this work, book 6, chapter 16: “I shall fix my feet,” he says, “on that step on which I was placed by my parents as a boy, until the clear truth is discovered.” Concerning the sacrament of salt, which was given to catechumens during the days of Easter, there is the fifth canon of the first Council of Carthage; and St. Augustine mentions this rite more than once, most explicitly in *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, chapter 26, where a significant error entered the editions in the words “what is seasoned in it,” instead of “what seasons in it.”], from the womb of my mother, who had placed great hope in you. You saw, Lord, when I was still a child and one day suddenly burned with stomach pressure, almost at the point of death [Note: [Col. 0669] Thus it is found in the better manuscripts. In Arn. and some manuscripts: “pressed by the stomach.” Bad., Am., Er., and Lov.: “pressed by the pain of the stomach.”]. You saw, my God, for you were already my guardian, with what movement of soul and with what faith I demanded from the piety of my mother the baptism of your Christ, my God and Lord, and of your Church, the mother of us all.

My mother of the flesh was disturbed, for in her pure heart, through faith in you, she was giving birth to my eternal salvation with even greater tenderness. She was already hastening to ensure that I should be initiated into the saving sacraments and cleansed, confessing you, Lord Jesus, for the forgiveness of sins, had I not immediately recovered. My cleansing was therefore postponed, as though it were necessary that I should become dirty again if I lived; for, clearly, after that washing the guilt of sins would be greater and more dangerous if I became soiled again.

Thus I already believed, as did she and the whole household, except my father, who nevertheless did not prevail over my mother’s claim of devotion so as to prevent me from believing in Christ, as he himself did not yet believe. For she was concerned that you, my God, should be my father rather than he; and in this you helped her to overcome her husband, whom she served because he was better served by her. In this too she was serving you, who had commanded it.

18. I ask you, my God—I should like to know, if you also willed it, for what reason my baptism was postponed then: were the reins of sinning loosened for my benefit, as it were, or were they not loosened [Note: [Col. 0669] “Were,” according to Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., Somm., Flor., Rond., with six manuscripts, and Mart. with six other manuscripts. M.]? Why, then, does the saying still resound from every side in our ears concerning others and others: “Let him be; let him do what he wants” [Note: [Col. 0669] “Let him do what he wants” is absent from the best manuscripts.], “for he has not yet been baptized”? And yet, when bodily health is concerned, we do not say, “Let him be wounded further, for he has not yet been healed.”

How much better and more quickly would I have been healed [Note: [Col. 0669] “So that I might be healed quickly,” according to Somm., Dub., Mart. with six manuscripts, and Rond. with four manuscripts.], and how much better would it have been if my family and I had taken care that, once the health of my soul had been restored, it should remain secure under your protection, since you had given it? Better indeed. But my mother already knew how many and how great the waves of temptation seemed to threaten after childhood; and she did not wish to entrust to them the earth from which I was later to be formed [Note: [Col. 0669] Aroald. reads this way, and most manuscripts likewise; but the passage was variously corrupted in the editions. Am., Er., and Lov. have: “And to you so much through them.” Bad. has: “And terrified through them.” Others, inserting a particle, have: “And the earth more through them.” Augustine sometimes leaves this particle elegantly understood.], rather than entrust to them the image already formed.

## CHAPTER XII. He was compelled to study letters, which God nevertheless used for good

19. Yet in that very childhood, which was less feared for me than adolescence, I did not love letters, and I hated being forced into them. Nevertheless I was forced, and it benefited me, although I did not act well. I would not have learned unless compelled. But no one does well what he does unwillingly, even if what he does is good. Nor did those who forced me act well; but it benefited me [Col. 0670] through you, my God. They did not consider where I would direct [Note: [Col. 0670] In the manuscript of Lyre: “would be directed.”] what they compelled me to learn, except toward the satisfaction of the insatiable desires of abundant poverty and disgraceful glory.

But you, before whom the hairs of our head are numbered (Matt. X, 30), used for my benefit the error of all who pressed me to learn. You used my own error—my unwillingness to learn—for my punishment, and I, so small a child and so great a sinner, was not undeserving of being chastised by it. Thus, from those who did not act well, you did good for me; and from my own sin you justly repaid me. For you commanded, and so it is, that every disordered spirit should itself be its own punishment.

## CHAPTER XIII. The studies in which he was chiefly delighted

20. Why I hated Greek letters, with which I was being instructed as a little boy, is not even now sufficiently clear to me. For I had come to love Latin—not the Latin taught by the first teachers, but that taught by those called grammarians. Yet I found the first lessons, in which one learns to read, write, and count, no less burdensome and punitive than all the Greek lessons.

And what is the source of this, unless sin and the vanity of life, because I was flesh [Note: [Col. 0670] Many manuscripts: “because I was flesh.”], a passing spirit that does not return? (Ps. LXXVII, 39.) Those first lessons were certainly better, because they were more reliable: through them I acquired—and have acquired—the ability to read whatever writing I find and to write whatever I wish. This was better than being compelled to retain the errors of some Aeneas or other, while forgetting my own errors; and to weep for the dead Dido because she killed herself for love, while all the while I was miserably dying in these things away from you, God, my life, and bore it with dry eyes.

21. For what is more miserable than a miserable person who does not pity himself, weeping over Dido’s death, which occurred because she loved Aeneas, but not weeping over his own death, which occurred because he did not love you, God, light of my heart, bread within the mouth of my soul, and power joining my mind to the bosom of my thought?

I did not love you, and I fornicated away from you; and everywhere it was said to the fornicator, “Well done, well done!” For friendship with this world is fornication away from you, and “Well done, well done!” is said so that a person may be ashamed not to be such. I did not weep over these things, but I wept for Dido, extinguished and pursuing her end with the sword (Aeneid VI, 456), while I myself pursued the ends established by your creation, abandoning you and going from earth to earth [Note: [Col. 0670] Am., Er., and Lov.: “out of the earth.”]. If I had been prevented from reading these things, I would have grieved because I could not read what made me grieve.

Such madness is considered more honorable and more fruitful learning than that by which I learned to read and write.

22. But now, in my soul, let my God cry out, and let your truth say to me: “It is not so; it is not so. That earlier instruction is altogether better.” For behold, I am more ready to forget the errors of Aeneas and everything of that kind than to forget how to write and read.

But the curtains hang at the entrances of the schools of grammar. They signify the honor of secrecy no more than they signify a covering for error. Let not those whom I no longer fear cry out against me while I confess to you what my soul desires, my God, and acquiesce in the reproach of my evil ways, so that I may love your good ways.

Let not the sellers or buyers of grammar cry out against me. If I asked them whether it were true that the poet says Aeneas once came to Carthage, the less learned would answer that they did not know, while the more learned would even deny that it was true. But if I asked them in what letters the name *Aeneas* is written, all who have learned these things would give me the correct answer, according to the agreement and convention by which human beings established these signs among themselves.

Likewise, if I asked which of these things a person would forget with greater detriment to this life—reading and writing, or those poetic fictions—who would not see what answer would be given by anyone who had not entirely forgotten himself?

I was therefore sinning as a boy when, out of love, I preferred those empty things to these more useful ones—or rather, when I hated these and loved those. “One and one are two, two and two are four” was a hateful song to me; but the wooden horse filled with armed men, the burning of Troy, and the shadow of Creusa herself (Aeneid II) were the sweetest spectacle of vanity.

## CHAPTER XIV. He hated Greek

23. Why, then, did I also hate Greek grammar, which sang such things? Homer too was skilled at weaving such tales, and is most sweetly vain; yet he was bitter to me as a boy. I believe Virgil is likewise bitter to Greek boys when they are forced to learn him as I was forced to learn Homer.

Clearly, the difficulty [Note: [Col. 0671] Thus the more distinguished manuscripts; but Lov. and Arn. have “with difficulty, difficulty.” “With difficulty, difficulty,” according to Somm. and Mart. with five manuscripts, and Rond. with three editions. M.] of learning a foreign language thoroughly sprinkled all the sweetness of those Greek stories with gall. I knew none of those words, and I was pressed vehemently to learn them amid savage threats and punishments.

For I too, as an infant, knew no Latin words; yet I learned it without fear or torment, amid even the coaxing of nurses, the jokes of those who smiled at me, and the joyful play of those who amused themselves with me. I learned it without the painful burden of people forcing me, when my heart itself pressed me to give birth to what it had conceived—something I could not have done unless I had learned certain words, not from teachers but from speakers, in whose ears I too gave birth to whatever I felt.

From this it is sufficiently clear that free curiosity has greater power for learning these things than fearful compulsion. But your laws, God, restrain its flow—your laws extending from the teachers’ rods to the trials of martyrs, your laws able to mingle healing bitterness and recall us to you from the destructive pleasure by which we departed from you [Note: [Col. 0671] Rond., with seven manuscripts: “by which we had departed from you.” M.].

## CHAPTER XV. A prayer to God

24. Hear my prayer, Lord, so that my soul may not fail under your discipline; and may I not fail in confessing your mercies, by which you rescued me from all my most evil ways, so that you may become sweet to me above all the seductions I pursued. May I love you with all my strength, embrace your hand with all my inmost heart, and may you rescue me from every temptation to the end.

For behold, you, Lord, my King and my God: let everything useful that I learned as a child serve you. Let what I speak, write, read, and count serve you, because while I was learning vain things, you were giving me discipline; and in those vain things you forgave me the sins of my pleasures. For through them I learned many useful words, as well as things that can be learned in matters that are not vain; and that is a safe path on which children may walk.

## CHAPTER XVI. He condemns the method by which the young are educated

25. But woe to you, flood of human custom! Who can resist you? How long will you not dry up? How long will you roll the sons of Eve into the great and fearful sea, which those who have climbed aboard the wood scarcely cross?

Did I not read in you of thundering and adulterous Jupiter? Certainly he could not be both; yet it was arranged that he should possess authority for imitating real adultery, with a false thunderbolt acting as his procurer. But what teacher wearing the cloak listens with sober ear when a man from that same dust cries out and says: “Homer invented these things and transferred human traits to the gods; I would rather he had transferred divine traits to us”? (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* 1.) More truthfully it is said that he did indeed invent these things; but by attributing divine things to immoral human beings, he ensured that they would not regard immoralities as immoralities [Note: [Col. 0672] Lov.: “that immoralities might not be regarded.” Incomplete.], and that anyone who did such things would appear to imitate not ruined men but heavenly gods.

26. And yet, O infernal flood, the sons of men are hurled into you, paying fees to learn these things. A great matter is being transacted when this is done publicly in the forum, in the presence of laws that decree salaries above the fees. You strike your rocks and resound, saying: “Here words are learned; here eloquence is acquired, which is especially necessary for persuading people of things and expounding opinions.”

Yet we would not know these words—“a shower of gold,” “lap,” “seduction,” “temples of heaven,” and the other words written in that passage—unless Terence introduced a wicked young man setting Jupiter before himself as an example of sexual misconduct, while looking at a painted picture on a wall. The picture showed this:

“They say that Jupiter once sent a shower of gold into Danaë’s lap, playing a deception upon the woman.”

And see how he excites himself to lust, as though instructed by a heavenly teacher:

“But which god?” he says. “The one who shakes the highest temples of heaven with a great crash of thunder.

Would I, a mere little man, not do that? Indeed I did it—and gladly.” (*The Eunuch*, act 3, scene 5.)

Those words are not learned more effectively through this depravity; rather, through those words this depravity is committed more confidently. I do not accuse the words, as chosen and precious vessels; I accuse the wine of error poured into them for us by drunken teachers. If we did not drink it, we were beaten, and we were not permitted to appeal to any sober judge.

And yet I, my God, in whose presence my memory is now secure, gladly learned these things, and miserable as I was, took pleasure in them; and for this I was called a boy of good promise.

## CHAPTER XVII. He continues his attack on the method of literary education

27. Permit me, my God, to say something about my talent, your gift, by which my talent was worn down in those ravings.
