A sufficiently unsettling task for my soul was set before me, rewarded by praise and enforced by the fear of disgrace or blows: I had to recite the words of Juno, angry and grieving that she could not turn the king of the Teucrians away from Italy (Aeneid I, 36–75). I had never heard Juno say these words; nevertheless we were compelled to follow the wandering traces of poetic fictions and to say in prose something like what the poet had said in verse. The student was praised more highly when, in a manner appropriate to the dignity of the character represented, he appeared more like that character in anger and grief, with words suitably clothing the thoughts.

What was the point of that, O my true life, my God, when I was applauded above many of my peers and fellow students as I recited? Behold, were not all those things smoke and wind? Was there nowhere else for my talent and tongue to be exercised? May the praises of you, Lord—your praises through your Scriptures—have suspended the vine-shoot of my heart, so that it would not be carried away through empty trifles as shameful prey for flying things. For the transgressor angels are not sacrificed in only one way.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How people take care to preserve the laws of grammar but neglect the divine commandments

28. What wonder, then, that I was carried so far into vanities and went outward from you, my God, when people were set before me for imitation who, if they uttered some morally harmless deed with a barbarism or solecism, were rebuked and ashamed; but if they narrated their lusts in correct, properly constructed, copious, and ornate language, they were praised and boasted?

You see these things, Lord, and remain silent—patient, exceedingly merciful, and truthful. Will you always remain silent? And now you rescue [Note: [Col. 0673] Am., Er., and Lov.: “And you do not rescue.” But Bad., Arn., and the chief manuscripts much more suitably have: “And now you rescue.”] from this monstrous abyss the soul that seeks you, thirsts for your delights, and whose heart says to you: “I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. XXVI, 8).

For one is far from your face when in a dark affection [Note: [Col. 0673] Lov. adds: “I had withdrawn.” Am. and Er.: “I had departed.” In the manuscripts Alb. is found: “I was in a dark affection.” Bad., Arn., and nearly all the other manuscripts express the more general sense without the addition, so that we understand those who are in a dark affection to be far from God.]. One does not go away from you or return to you by feet or distances of place.

Or did that younger son of yours seek horses, chariots, or ships, or fly away on a visible wing, or travel by moving his legs, so that, living in a distant region, he might waste prodigally what you had given him when he departed? Sweet father, because you had given it; and sweeter to the needy son when he returned (Luke XV, 12, 32). He was therefore in a lustful affection—for that is a dark affection—and that is being far from your face.

29. See, Lord God, and patiently observe as you observe, how carefully the sons of men preserve the agreements of letters and syllables received from earlier speakers, while neglecting the eternal agreements of everlasting salvation received from you. Thus, if someone who retains or teaches the old conventions of sounds should say *ominem* instead of *hominem*, without the aspiration at the beginning of the syllable, he displeases people more than if, contrary to your commandments, he hates a human being, though he himself is human.

As though he could feel any human enemy to be more destructive than the hatred itself by which he is provoked against that enemy, or as though anyone could devastate another more severely by persecution than he devastates his own heart by enmity. Certainly the inner knowledge of letters is not more profound than the written conscience: that one should not do to another [Note: [Col. 0674] “Not to another,” according to Rond. with four manuscripts. M.] what one does not wish to suffer.

How hidden you are, dwelling on high in silence, God alone who is great, scattering with tireless law punitive blindness over unlawful desires! When a man seeks a reputation for eloquence, standing before a human judge and surrounded by a crowd of human beings, he attacks his enemy with monstrous hatred and most carefully guards against saying, through a mistake of the tongue, *inter hominibus* [“among human beings”] [Note: [Col. 0674] Lov.: *inter homines*. It is clear that, according to the manuscripts, *inter hominibus* should be read; or, without aspiration, *inter omines*. Augustine gives this as an example of an incongruous expression that must be avoided.]. Yet through the madness of his mind he does not guard against removing a human being from among human beings.

## CHAPTER XIX. The faults of childhood that continue into later ages

30. As a child I lay miserably at the threshold of these customs, and that arena was my training ground. There I feared making a barbarism more than I guarded against envying those who did not make one. I say these things and confess them to you, my God, in which I was praised by those whose approval then seemed to me the mark of living honorably. I did not see the abyss of disgrace into which I had been cast away from your eyes.

For what was uglier in me than those things by which I even displeased such people—deceiving my tutor, my teachers, and my parents with innumerable lies, out of love of playing, eagerness to watch frivolous spectacles, and restless desire to imitate games?

I also committed thefts from my parents’ storeroom and table, whether driven by gluttony or in order to have something to give to boys who sold me their games, in which they were equally delighted. In those games, overcome by a vain desire [Note: [Col. 0674] “Vain,” according to Rond. with eight manuscripts, supported by two manuscripts cited by Mart. M.] for superiority, I often hunted after fraudulent victories.

What did I so hate to suffer, and so fiercely rebuked when I detected it, as what I did to others? Yet if I were detected and rebuked, I preferred to rage rather than yield. Is this the innocence of childhood? It is not, Lord; it is not, I beg you, my God.

For these same things pass from tutors and teachers, from nuts, balls, and sparrows, to prefects and kings—these very things that pass into succeeding ages, just as greater punishments succeed the teachers’ rods. You approved the sign of humility in the stature of childhood, our King, when you said: “The kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these” (Matt. XIX, 14).

## CHAPTER XX. He gives thanks to God for the good things granted to him in childhood

[Col. 0675]

31. Yet, Lord, to you, most excellent and best creator and ruler of the universe, our God, be thanks—even if you had wished me to be nothing more than a child. For even then I existed, I lived [Note: [Col. 0675] Thus the manuscripts and most editions, whereas Lov. has: “And even then I dared.” “And even then I lived,” according to Sommal. and Rond. with four manuscripts. M.], and I felt; and I cared for my own preservation, the trace of that most secret unity from which I came. By my inner sense I guarded the integrity of my senses, and in the very thoughts of small things I delighted in truth.

I did not wish to be deceived; my memory was vigorous; I was instructed in speech; friendship soothed me; I avoided pain, humiliation, and ignorance. What in such a living creature is not marvelous and praiseworthy?

Yet all these things are gifts of my God. I did not give them to myself. They are good, and I am all these things. Good, therefore, is he who made me; he himself is my good; and in him I rejoice for all the good things that belonged even to me as a child.

For this was my sin: that I sought pleasures, exalted things, and truths not in him but in myself and in other creatures [Note: [Col. 0676] Bad., Am., Er., and Lov.: “other things.” This has been corrected from Arn. and the manuscripts to “in other creatures.” In this passage Augustine confesses that he sinned by seeking pleasures, exalted things, and truths not in God but in himself and other creatures.], and thus rushed into pains, confusions, and errors.

Thanks be to you, my sweetness, my honor, and my confidence, my God. Thanks be to you for your gifts; but preserve them for me. For in this way you will preserve me; what you have given me will grow and be perfected; and I shall be with you, because you also gave me existence.

# BOOK TWO

He proceeds to another period of life. He recalls with great sorrow the first year of his adolescence—that is, the sixteenth year of his life—which he spent in his father’s house, his studies having been interrupted, while he indulged his inclination and his lusts. He is especially severe in judging the theft he committed at that time with his companions.

[Col. 0675]

## CHAPTER I. He recalls the period and faults of adolescence

1. I wish to remember my past foulness and the carnal corruptions of my soul—not because I love them, but so that I may love you, my God. I do this for love of your love, recalling my most wicked ways in the bitterness of my recollection, so that you may become sweet to me, sweetness that does not deceive, sweetness that is happy and secure, gathering me from the dispersion in which I was torn apart piecemeal while, turning away from you, the One, I vanished into many things.

For at one time, in adolescence, I burned to be sated with hell [Note: [Col. 0675] Lov., with the older editions: “to be satisfied in things below.” We have removed *in* in accordance with the manuscripts and Arn.], and dared to grow wild amid various and shadowy loves. My appearance withered, and I rotted before your eyes while pleasing myself and wishing to please human eyes.

## CHAPTER II. He spends the sixteenth year of his life in the heat of lust

2. And what was it that delighted me except to love and be loved? But the proper limit was not maintained by the soul from one soul to another, insofar as it is a luminous boundary [Note: [Col. 0675] In the editions published by Henricus Sommalus of the Society of Jesus and by Thomas Blasius, we read: “a muddy boundary.” In the codex Corb., “a muddy boundary.” Both are corrupt. For here Augustine laments that he did not keep himself within the limits of honorable friendship; therefore the reading should be, with the manuscripts and other editions, “a luminous boundary.”] of friendship. Rather, mists rose from the muddy lust of the flesh and the bubbling spring of puberty, clouding and darkening my heart, so that the serenity of affection could not be distinguished from the darkness of lust.

Both seethed together in confusion, carrying my weak age over the precipices of desire and plunging it into a whirlpool of wickedness. Your anger had grown strong against me, and I did not know it. I had become deaf to the screeching of the chain of my mortality, the punishment of my proud soul [Col. 0676]; and I was going farther from you, while you allowed it. I was tossed about, poured out, dissipated, and boiling over through my fornications, while you remained silent.

O my tardy joy! You were silent then, and I went farther and farther from you into many barren seeds of sorrow, in proud degradation and restless weariness.

3. Who could have moderated [Note: [Col. 0676] The first-rate manuscripts and nearly all others have “modulated,” a reading we came very close to preferring.] my misery and turned the fleeting beauties of the lowest things to proper use, setting limits to their pleasures, so that the waves of my age might surge as far as the shore of marriage? If tranquility could not be found in them, they might at least be content with the procreation of children, as your law prescribes, Lord, you who also form the offspring of our mortality [Note: [Col. 0676] The best manuscripts have “of our death.”], being powerful enough to place a gentle hand for the tempering of the thorns excluded from your paradise.

For your omnipotence is not far from us even when we are far from you. Or at least I might have listened more attentively to the sound of your clouds: “Those who are such will have trouble in the flesh. But I am sparing you”; and, “It is good for a man not to touch a woman”; and, “The unmarried man thinks about the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but the married man thinks about the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Cor. VII, 28, 1, 32–34).

I would have heard these words more attentively, and, made a eunuch for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XIX, 12), I would have waited more happily for your embraces.

4. But miserable that I was, I boiled over, following the impulse of my own flux and abandoning you. I transgressed all your lawful bounds, yet I did not escape your scourges. For who among mortals could do so?

You were always present, mercifully raging, sprinkling my unlawful pleasures with exceedingly bitter vexations, so that I might seek to enjoy myself without vexation. Yet wherever I could have found this, I found nothing except you, Lord—except you, who fashion pain according to your commandment (Ps. XCIII, 20), strike in order to heal, and kill us so that we may not die away from you (Deut. XXXII, 39).

Where was I, and how far was I exiled from the delights of your house, in that sixteenth year of my bodily life, when lust took the scepter within me and I handed myself over entirely to it—lust made licentious by human disgrace but unlawful according to your laws [Note: [Col. 0677] Lov., Somm., and Blas.: “luxury took the scepter within me, and I handed myself entirely over to the madness of lust.” Most of the other manuscripts have *vesania* [“madness”] correctly, and the word *luxuria* [“luxury”] is absent.].

My family did not take care to restrain my fall through marriage; their only concern was that I should learn to speak as effectively as possible and persuade through eloquence.

## CHAPTER III. His journey for the sake of study and his parents’ plans
5. In that year, my studies had indeed been interrupted, while, after I had been brought back from Madaura—where, in that neighboring city, I had already begun traveling abroad in order to receive instruction in literature and rhetoric—the expenses of a more distant journey to Carthage were being prepared for me, more through my father’s determination than through his means, since he was a very poor municipal citizen of Thagaste. To whom am I telling these things? Not to you, my God, but in your presence I recount them to my race, the human race, however small a portion of it may fall into these writings of mine. And why this? Clearly so that I and whoever reads this may consider from how profound an abyss one must cry out to you. And what is nearer to your ears than a confessing heart and a life founded on faith?

For who then did not praise my father, saying how generously he was spending, beyond the resources of his household, whatever his son needed even for studies far away? Many citizens much wealthier than he had made no such provision for their children. Meanwhile, the same father took no care what sort of person I was becoming before you, or how chaste I was, provided only that I became eloquent—or rather, deserted by your worship, O God, who are the one true and good Lord of the field of my heart.

6. But when, in that sixteenth year, having taken a year off because of domestic necessity and being idle from every school, I began living with my parents, the thorny growth of lust rose above my head, and there was no hand to uproot it. Indeed, when that father of mine saw me in the baths, already reaching puberty and clothed in the restless excitement of adolescence, as though he were already eagerly looking forward to grandchildren, he joyfully reported it to my mother—joyful with the drunkenness in which this world, having forgotten you, its creator, has loved your creature instead of you: with the invisible wine of a will perverted and inclined downward.  
[Note: The Lyrensis manuscript reads: “perverted and inclined.”]

Yet you had already begun to build your temple in my mother’s breast, and the foundation of your holy dwelling had been laid, for he was still a catechumen, and this was recent. Thus she leapt up in devout alarm and trembling; and although I was not yet a believer, she nevertheless feared the crooked paths in which those walk who turn their back toward you rather than their face.

7. Woe is me! And do I dare to say that you were silent, my God, while I was going farther from you? Were you really silent to me then? Whose words were those, if not yours, which you sang into my ears through my mother, your faithful servant? Yet nothing descended from them into my heart so that I might act on them. For she wanted this, and I secretly remember that she warned me with great anxiety not to fornicate, and especially not to commit adultery with anyone’s wife.

Those warnings seemed to me womanish admonitions, which I would have been ashamed to obey. Yet they were yours, and I did not know it. I thought that you were silent and that she was speaking—the very woman through whom you were not silent to me—and in her you were despised by me, her son, the son of your handmaid, your servant. But I did not know this, and I rushed headlong with such blindness that, among my contemporaries, I was ashamed of a lesser disgrace: I heard them boasting of their crimes and glorying all the more the more shameful they were. I took pleasure not only in the lust of the deed itself but also in the praise it brought.

What deserves blame if not vice? So that I would not be blamed, I became more vicious. And whenever I lacked some deed by which I could equal the depraved, I pretended that I had done what I had not done, lest I appear more contemptible because I was more innocent, and be considered more worthless because I was more chaste.

8. Behold the companions with whom I traveled the streets of Babylon and wallowed in its mire as though in cinnamon and precious perfumes. At its center, where I might cling to it more tenaciously, an invisible enemy trampled me and seduced me, because I was easily seduced.

For that mother of my flesh, who had already fled from the midst of Babylon but was proceeding more slowly among the rest of it, did not take care to restrain what she had heard from her husband about me and already sensed would be pestilential and dangerous in the future, by confining it within the bounds of conjugal affection—if it could not be cut out at the living root—just as she warned me about chastity. She did not do so because she feared that my hope might be impeded by the fetter of marriage: not the hope my mother had in you for the age to come, but the hope of literary studies, which both parents greatly wanted us to know. He wanted this because he thought almost nothing about you, but empty things about me; she, however, because she judged that those customary studies of learning would lead to you not only without harm but even with some benefit.

This, at least, is how I infer it as I recall, insofar as I can, the character of my parents. The reins were also loosened for me in play beyond the proper moderation of severity, into the dissolution of various affections. And in everything there was a darkness blocking me from the serenity of your truth, my God; my iniquity emerged as though from abundance of fatness (Ps. LXXII, 7).

## CHAPTER IV. The Theft Committed with His Companions

9. Theft is certainly punished by your law, Lord, and by the law written in human hearts, which not even iniquity itself erases. For what thief tolerates a thief with an even temper? Not even the wealthy man tolerates one driven by poverty.

And I wanted to steal, and I did steal, compelled by no need or poverty, but by contempt for justice  
[Note: More numerous manuscripts read: “not by poverty, but by contempt for justice.”]  
and by an abundance of iniquity. For I stole something of which I had an ample supply, and something much better besides. I did not want to enjoy the thing I desired through theft, but the theft itself and the sin.

There was a pear tree near our vineyard, loaded with fruit that was attractive neither in appearance nor in taste. To shake it and carry away its fruit, we extremely wicked young men went out at dead of night, after we had prolonged our game in the courtyards in the customary manner of pestilence. We carried away enormous loads, not for our own feasts, but either to throw them to the pigs—even if we ate something from them—provided only that we did what pleased us precisely because it was forbidden.

Behold my heart, O God; behold my heart, which you pitied in the deepest abyss. Let it now tell you what it was seeking there: that I should be gratuitously evil, and that the cause of my evil should be nothing but evil. It was foul, and I loved it; I loved my ruin; I loved my defect. I loved not that toward which I was defective, but the defect itself. My soul was ugly and leaping away from your firmament into destruction, seeking not some disgrace  
[Note: “Not seeking some honor, but disgrace,” according to Somm. and Rond. Mart. from three manuscripts.]  
but disgrace itself.

## CHAPTER V. No One Sins Without a Cause

10. There is indeed beauty in beautiful bodies, in gold and silver, and in all things; and in the contact of the flesh, harmony has great power, while in the other senses each has its own suitable arrangement of bodies. Temporal honor also has its attraction, as does the power to command and conquer, from which even the desire for revenge arises.

Yet in pursuing all these things one must not depart from you, Lord, or deviate from your law. The life we live here has its own allure because of a certain beauty and harmony with all these lower beautiful things. Human friendship also is sweet because of the beloved bond by which many souls are united.

Because of all these and similar things, sin is committed, when, through immoderate attachment to them, although they are among the lowest goods, the better and highest goods are abandoned: you, Lord our God, your truth, and your law. These lower things too have their pleasures, but not like my God, who made all things; for the just person delights in him, and he himself is the delight of those upright in heart.

11. Therefore, when the cause of a crime is sought, it is usually not believed unless it appears that there could have been a desire to obtain one of those goods we have called lower, or fear of losing one. For they are beautiful and attractive, although, in comparison with the higher and blessed goods, they are degraded and prostrate  
[Note: “And riches,” according to Somm. and Rond. Mart.].

He committed murder. Why did he do it? He loved the man’s wife or estate; or he wanted to plunder what would provide him a living; or he feared losing something of his to that man; or, having been injured, he burned to avenge himself. Would anyone commit murder without a cause, taking pleasure in murder itself? Who would believe it?

For even concerning that foolish and exceedingly cruel man who was said to be evil and cruel for no reason, a cause was nevertheless given: “So that,” he says, “his hand or spirit might not grow sluggish through inactivity” (Sallust, *The War of Catiline*, chapter IX). Why that as well? Why so? Clearly so that, through that exercise in crime, once the city had been captured, he might obtain honors, commands, and riches, and be free from fear of the laws and from the difficulty of circumstances caused by poverty of resources and consciousness of his crimes.

Therefore Catiline himself did not love his crimes, but something else for whose sake he committed them.

## CHAPTER VI. All Things That Invite Us to Vices Under the Appearance of Good Are True and Perfect in God Alone

12. What did I, wretched man, love in you, O my theft, O that nocturnal crime of mine in my sixteenth year? For you were not beautiful, since you were a theft; or, to address you directly, were you even anything at all?

Those pears were beautiful because they were your creation  
[Note: “They were,” according to Erasmus, Lyons, Louvain, Somm., Dub., Mart., and Rond.],  
most beautiful creator of all things, good God, God the supreme good, my true good. Those pears were beautiful, but it was not them that my miserable soul desired. For I had an abundance of better things; I picked them only in order to steal. Having picked them, I threw them away, having feasted only on the iniquity in which I took delight  
[Note: Louvain reads “in iniquity alone”; the other manuscripts have the better reading, “on iniquity alone.”]  
and from which I enjoyed myself  
[Note: Two English manuscripts read “raging”; the others read “enjoying myself.”].

For if any of those pears entered my mouth, the seasoning there was the crime itself  
[Note: Four manuscripts and Arnobius read “for me.”].

And now, Lord my God, I ask what delighted me in that theft, and behold, it has no beauty. I do not mean beauty like that found in justice and prudence; it had none even like that found in the human mind, memory, senses, and living activity. It was not beautiful like the stars, beautiful in their places, or like the earth and sea, full of living things that succeed one another as they are born and die. It was not even like that defective and shadowy beauty found in deceptive vices.

13. Pride imitates elevation, although you alone, God, are exalted above all. And ambition—what does it seek but honor and glory, although you alone are to be honored above all and are glorious forever? The cruelty of the powerful wants to be feared; but who is to be feared except the one God? From whose power can anything be snatched or withdrawn  
[Note: “Can” should be omitted, according to Somm., Louvain, Florence, and Rond. Mart.]  
—and when, or where, or by what means, or by whom could this be done?

The flatteries of the lustful want to be loved; but nothing is more flattering than your love, nor is anything loved more healthfully than your truth, beautiful and radiant above all. Curiosity appears to seek a zeal for knowledge, although you know all things supremely. Ignorance and stupidity themselves are concealed under the name of simplicity and innocence, because nothing is simpler than you. And what is more innocent than you, since your works are hostile to the wicked?  
[Note: This is how the manuscripts and older editions read. Louvain and Arnobius instead have: “Your works are hostile to the wicked.” The former reading is retained because Augustine seems to intend to prove that the punishment inflicted on the wicked detracts nothing from God’s innocence: if they suffer any harm, it must be wholly charged to their own works.]

Sloth seems to seek rest; but what rest is certain apart from the Lord? Luxury wants to be called satiety and abundance; but you are the fullness and unfailing abundance of incorruptible sweetness. Lavishness of generosity displays a shadow; but you are the most abundant giver of every good. Avarice wants to possess many things; but you possess all things. Envy quarrels over superiority; what is superior to you? Anger seeks revenge; who avenges more justly than you?

Fear shudders at what is unusual and sudden, at things opposed to what is loved, while it takes precautions for security. But what is unusual or sudden to you? Or who can separate from you what you love? Or where is there firm security except with you?

Sorrow withers over lost things in which desire took delight, because it would not want them to be taken away from it as nothing can be taken away from you.

14. Thus the soul fornicates when it turns away from you and seeks outside you what it cannot find pure and undiluted except when it returns to you. All who distance themselves from you imitate you perversely and raise themselves against you. Yet even by imitating you in this way they show that you are the creator of every nature, and therefore that there is no place where one can wholly depart from you.

What, then, did I love in that theft? In what respect did I imitate my Lord, even viciously and perversely? Did I at least take pleasure in acting against the law through deception, because I could not do so through power, so that, as a captive, I might imitate imperfect freedom by doing with impunity what was forbidden—a dark likeness of omnipotence?

Behold that servant fleeing from his Lord and pursuing a shadow. O corruption, O monstrous life, O depth of death! Could I freely do what was forbidden for no other reason than that it was forbidden?

## CHAPTER VII. He Gives Thanks to God for the Remission of His Sins and for Having Been Preserved from Many

15. What shall I repay the Lord, since my memory recalls these things and my soul is not afraid of them? I shall love you, Lord, and give thanks to you, and confess to your name, because you have forgiven me so many evils and wicked deeds. I attribute to your grace and mercy the fact that you melted my sins like ice.

I attribute to your grace also whatever evils I did not commit. For what could I not have done, I who even loved a gratuitous crime? I confess that everything has been forgiven me: both the evils I committed willingly and those I did not commit under your guidance.

Who is there among human beings who, reflecting on his own weakness, dares to attribute his chastity and innocence to his own strength, so that he loves you less, as though your mercy—by which you forgive the sins of those who turn to you—had been less necessary for him?

Let whoever, called by you, followed your voice and avoided the things that I remember and confess about myself not mock me for being healed by that physician by whom he was granted not to fall ill, or rather, to fall less ill. Let him therefore love you just as much—or indeed more—for through the one by whom he sees me freed from such great illnesses of sin, he sees himself preserved from becoming entangled in such great illnesses of sin.

## CHAPTER VIII. In the Theft He Loved the Fellowship of Fellow Sinners

16. What fruit did I once gain, wretched man, from those things of which I am now ashamed as I recall them (Rom. VI, 21), especially from that theft in which I loved the theft itself? None; since the theft itself was nothing, and by that very fact I was more wretched.

Yet I would not have committed it alone. I remember my mind at that time: I certainly would not have done it alone. Did I therefore also love the companionship of criminals with whom I committed it? Then I did not love only the theft. Indeed, I loved nothing else, because that too is nothing.

What is it really? Who can teach me except the one who illumines my heart and distinguishes its shadows? What is this that comes to mind for me to seek, examine, and consider? If at that time I had loved the pears I stole and desired to enjoy them, I could have done so alone, if committing that iniquity was sufficient to bring me to my pleasure. I would not have inflamed the itch of my desire through the rubbing together of guilty minds. But since I found no pleasure in those pears, the pleasure was in the crime itself, and that pleasure was produced by the companionship of those who sinned together.

## CHAPTER IX. Evil Companions Are a Contagious Thing

17. What was that feeling of the soul? Certainly it was plainly exceedingly shameful, and woe to me for possessing it. Yet what was it? “Who understands his offenses?” (Ps. XVIII, 13.)

It was laughter, as though the heart had been tickled, because we were deceiving those who did not think we would do such things and vehemently disapproved of them. Why, then, did I take pleasure in not doing it alone? Is it because no one easily laughs alone? No one does so easily; yet even solitary and individual people are sometimes overcome by laughter when something excessively ridiculous presents itself to their senses or mind.

But I would not have done that alone; I would not have done it alone at all. Behold, before you, my God, is the living memory of my soul. I would not have committed that theft alone, in which what I stole did not please me, but the fact that I stole it—a thing I would not have wanted to do and would not have done alone.

O excessively hostile friendship, inscrutable seduction of the mind, eagerness to harm arising from play and joking, and desire for another’s injury—not for any gain of my own, nor from any desire for revenge, but simply when someone says, “Come, let us do it,” and one is ashamed not to be shameless!

## CHAPTER X. Every Good Is in God

18. Who can unravel that most crooked and intricate knot? It is foul; I do not want to concentrate on it, I do not want to see it. I want you, justice and innocence, beautiful and attractive to the pure in vision, and possessing an insatiable fullness.

With you there is profound rest and undisturbed life. Whoever enters into you enters into the joy of his Lord (Matt. XXV, 21); he will not fear, and he will fare exceedingly well in the one who is supremely good.

I departed from you and went astray, my God, wandering too far from your stability during adolescence, and I became for myself a region of poverty.

# BOOK THREE

On the years of his life—the seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth—spent at Carthage, where, while completing the course of his literary studies, he remembers that he became entangled in the snare of lustful love and also fell into the heresy of the Manichaeans. He argues brilliantly against their errors and absurdities. He recounts the tears his mother shed for him and the response divinely given concerning his recovery of his senses.

[Col. 0683]

## CHAPTER I. He Is Captured by the Love He Was Hunting

1. I came to Carthage, and all around me a cauldron of disgraceful loves seethed. I did not yet love, but I wanted to love  
[Note: Louvain reads: “And I wanted to be loved”; shortly afterward it has: “Loving in order to be loved.” Bad., Ambrose, Erasmus, and Arnobius, together with the manuscripts, have *amare* (“to love”) rather than *amari* (“to be loved”) in both places, and this is better.]  
and, from a more secret need, I hated myself for being less needy. I sought what I might love, loving to love, and I hated safety and a path without snares.

For I was hungry inwardly for the inner food that is yourself, my God, and in that hunger I was not hungry; I was without desire for incorruptible nourishment—not because I was full of it, but the emptier I was, the more disgusted I became. And therefore my soul was not well; wounded, it threw itself miserably outward, eager to be scratched by contact with sensible things.

But if they had no soul, they would certainly not be loved. It was sweet to me to love and to be loved, especially when I could also enjoy the body of the one who loved me. Thus I polluted the vein of friendship with the filth of lust and clouded its brightness with the pitch of desire  
[Note: Ambrose, Erasmus, and Louvain read: “with the pitch-like lust”; Bad., Arnobius, and the manuscripts: “with the pitch of desire.”]  
and, although foul and dishonorable, I eagerly wanted to be elegant and urbane through abundant vanity.

I also fell into the love by which I wanted to be captured. My God, my mercy, how much gall you mixed into that sweetness for me—and yet how good you were in doing so! For I was loved, and I secretly reached the bond of enjoyment, and I was bound, rejoicing, in grievous chains, so that I might be scourged by the iron rods of jealousy, suspicion, fear, anger, and quarrels.

## CHAPTER II. He Loved Tragic Spectacles

2. Theatrical spectacles seized me, full of images of my own miseries and fuel for my fire. Why does a person want to suffer when watching sorrowful and tragic events that he himself would not want to endure? Yet the spectator wants to suffer through them, and the suffering itself is his pleasure. What is this but miserable madness  
[Note: Seven manuscripts read: “wondrous madness.”]?

For a person is moved more by such things the less healthy he is in relation to such emotions. Nevertheless, when he himself suffers, it is usually called misery; when he sympathizes with others, compassion. But what sort of compassion is there in fictitious and theatrical events? The audience is not summoned to offer help, but only invited to grieve; and the actor who presents these beloved images receives greater favor the more the audience grieves  
[Note: Ambrose, Erasmus, and Louvain read “the author.”].

If those human calamities, whether ancient or fictitious, are acted in such a way that the spectator does not grieve, he leaves bored and critical. But if he grieves, he remains attentive, weeping and rejoicing.

[Col. 0684]

3. Are pains therefore loved as well?  
[Note: The theologians of Louvain read: “Therefore tears and pains are loved.” The word “tears” is absent from most manuscripts and editions.]

Certainly every human being wants to rejoice. Or, although no one wishes anyone to be miserable, does one nevertheless wish to be compassionate—and, because this cannot occur without pain, are pains loved for that one reason? This too comes from that vein of friendship.

But where does it go? Where does it flow? Why does it run into a torrent of boiling pitch, into the fever of dark lusts, into which compassion itself is changed and transformed by its own impulse, twisted and cast down from heavenly serenity?

Let compassion therefore be rejected? Certainly not. Then let pains sometimes be loved. But beware impurity, my soul, under the guardianship of my God, the God of our fathers, who is praised and exalted above all forever (Dan. III, 32); beware impurity.

For it is not that I do not now feel compassion. But then, in the theaters, I rejoiced together with lovers when they enjoyed one another through crimes, although these things were enacted imaginatively in the play of the spectacle  
[Note: “Were enacted,” according to Erasmus, Lyons, Louvain, Somm., Mart., and Rond.].

When they lost one another, I grieved as though compassionate; yet both responses pleased me. Now, however, I feel more compassion for one who rejoices in wrongdoing than for one who, as though suffering some harsh injury, has lost a harmful pleasure and the wretched happiness it brought.

This is certainly the truer compassion; but in it pain does not give pleasure  
[Note: Bad., Ambrose, Erasmus, and Louvain read: “The heart takes pleasure”; the manuscripts and Arnobius prefer our reading.].

For although the person who grieves over someone miserable is approved for the duty of charity, the one who is truly compassionate would certainly prefer that there were no cause for grief. If there were such a thing as malevolent goodwill—which cannot be—then the one who truly and sincerely feels compassion could desire that people be miserable so that he might pity them.

Therefore some pain is to be approved, but none is to be loved. You, Lord God, who love souls, feel compassion for these things far more purely and widely than we do, and more incorruptibly, because you are wounded by no pain. And who is sufficient for this?

4. But at that time I, wretched man, loved to grieve and sought something over which I could grieve. In another’s misery—fictitious and theatrical—the actor’s performance pleased me all the more and attracted me more forcefully when it drew tears from me.

What wonder, when I, an unhappy sheep wandering from your flock and impatient of your protection, was defiled by a shameful disease? From this came my love of grief—not the kind that penetrated me more deeply, for I did not love enduring such things as I loved watching them, but the kind by which, through hearing and imagining them, I was scratched as though on the surface.

Yet that burning swelling, corruption, and dreadful discharge followed them, like the feverish tumor of fingernails scratching. Such was my life. Was it truly life, my God?

## CHAPTER III. In the Rhetorician’s School He Shrank from the Deeds of the “Subverters”

[Col. 0685]

5. And your faithful mercy hovered over me from afar. Into how many iniquities did I wander, and what sacrilegious curiosity did I pursue, so that, while I was abandoning you, it led me down to treacherous depths and the deceptive services of demons, to whom I sacrificed my evil deeds—and in everything you scourged me!

I even dared, amid the public celebrations of your solemnities, within the walls of your church, to desire and conduct business aimed at procuring the fruits of death. For this you struck me with severe punishments—but they were nothing compared with my guilt, O my exceedingly great mercy, my God, my refuge from the terrible harms among which I wandered with an arrogant neck, seeking to depart far from you, loving my own ways and not yours, loving fugitive freedom.

6. Even those studies that were called honorable had their own course, directed toward contentious lawcourts, so that I might excel in them and be praised all the more the more fraudulent I was. So great is the blindness of human beings that they even glory in their blindness.

I was already older in the rhetorician’s school. I rejoiced proudly and swelled with arrogance, although, as you know, Lord, I was far more restrained and wholly removed from the overturnings practiced by the *Eversores*—for this was their sinister name  
[Note: According to the ancient manuscripts, this should be written *scaevum*, meaning “left” or “sinister,” not *saevum*, “savage,” as it is written by Erasmus and Louvain.]  
and, as it were, their diabolical badge of urbanity.

I lived among them with shameless shame, because I was not like them. I was with them, and at times I enjoyed their friendship, although I had always recoiled from their deeds—namely, their overturnings, by which they insolently persecuted the modesty of strangers, disturbing it through gratuitous mockery and feeding their malicious joys on the result.

Nothing resembles the deeds of demons more closely than that behavior. What, then, could be more fitting than that they should be called *Eversores*, “subverters”? They themselves had first been utterly overthrown and perverted, mocked and seduced by deceitful spirits secretly, precisely in that by which they loved to mock and deceive others.

## CHAPTER IV. Cicero’s *Hortensius* Stirred Him to Love Philosophy

7. Among them, at that weak age, I was learning the books of eloquence, in which I desired to excel for a damnable and windy end, amid the pleasures of human vanity. Following the customary order of study, I had reached a certain book by Cicero, whose language almost everyone admires, though not so much his heart. That book contains an exhortation to philosophy and is called *Hortensius*.

That book changed my affections; it changed my prayers to you, Lord, and made my vows and desires different. Every vain hope suddenly became worthless to me, and I began to desire the immortality of wisdom with an incredible ardor of heart. I began to rise up in order to return to you.

I was not turning to that book in order to sharpen my tongue—as I seemed to be purchasing with my mother’s earnings when I was nineteen years old, my father having already died two years earlier. No, I was not turning to that book to sharpen my tongue; it was what the book said, not its manner of expression, that persuaded me.

[Col. 0686]

8. How I burned, my God, how I burned to fly back from earthly things to you—and I did not know what you were doing with me! For wisdom is with you. The love of wisdom has a Greek name, *philosophia* (φιλοσοφία), and those writings kindled me with it.

There are people who deceive through philosophy, disguising and coloring their errors with a great, attractive, and honorable name. Almost all who were such in those times and earlier are marked out and exposed in that book. There too that saving admonition of your Spirit is revealed through your good and devout servant: “See that no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to human tradition, according to the elements of this world, and not according to Christ; because in him the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II, 8–9).

And at that time, you know, light of my heart, those apostolic words were not yet known to me. Yet in that exhortation I was pleased by this alone: that I was urged and inflamed by its words to love, seek, attain, hold, and firmly embrace wisdom itself, whatever it might be. This alone restrained me amid so great a fervor: that the name of Christ was not there.

For, by your mercy, Lord, this name—the name of my Savior, your Son—I had drunk in with my tender heart already at my mother’s milk  
[Note: “Had drunk in,” according to Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, Louvain, Florence, and Mart. with six manuscripts.]  
and had deeply retained. Whatever lacked this name, however learned, polished, and truthful it might be, did not wholly seize me.

## CHAPTER V. He Was Disgusted with Sacred Scripture Because of the Simplicity of Its Style

9. Therefore I resolved to direct my mind to the Holy Scriptures, to see what sort of books they were. And behold, I see a work not discovered by the proud and not laid bare to children, but humble in its manner of walking, exalted in its progress, and veiled in mysteries. I was not such as could enter it or bend my neck to its footsteps.

For when I turned my attention to that Scripture, I did not feel as I speak now. It seemed to me unworthy to compare with the dignity of Cicero. My swelling pride recoiled from its measure, and my vision could not penetrate its interior. Yet it was the kind of work that grows with the little ones. But I disdained to be little, and, swollen with pride, I seemed great to myself.

## CHAPTER VI. How He Was Captured by the Manichaeans

10. Thus I fell among people who were arrogantly delirious, excessively carnal and talkative, in whose mouths were the snares of the devil and birdlime compounded by mixing syllables of the name of you, of the Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Paraclete, our Comforter, the Holy Spirit.

These names did not leave their mouths  
[Note: Louvain reads: “For all these things did not.”],  
but remained only as sound  
[Note: Four manuscripts read “in a thin sound”; others read “only as sound.”]  
and the clatter of the tongue; otherwise, their hearts were empty of truth.

They said, “Truth,” and “truth.” They spoke it to me at great length, but nowhere was it in them. They spoke falsely not only about you, who truly are Truth, but also about these elements of the world, your creation. Even the philosophers who spoke truly about them, I ought to have gone beyond for love of you, my Father, supremely good, beauty of all beautiful things.

O Truth, Truth, how deeply even then the marrow of my soul sighed for you, while they spoke your name to me frequently and in many ways, with their voices alone and through many large books! Those were the dishes in which, while I hungered for you, the sun and moon—your beautiful works—were served to me in your place. Yet they were your works, not you, and not even your first works, for your spiritual works are prior to these bodily works, however radiant and heavenly they may be.

But I hungered and thirsted not even for those prior works, but for you yourself, Truth, in whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning (Jas. I, 17). Yet on those dishes they continued to place splendid fantasies. It would have been better to love this sun, at least the true sun perceived by these eyes, than those false things imagined by a mind deceived through the eyes.

And yet, because I thought they were you, I ate them—not eagerly, for you did not taste in my mouth as you truly are; nor were you those empty fabrications. I was not nourished by them but rather drained by them. Food in dreams resembles the food of waking people, yet sleepers are not nourished by it, for they are asleep.

Those things, however, were in no way like you, as you have now spoken to me. They were bodily fantasies, false bodies, while these true bodies that we see with bodily sight, whether heavenly or earthly, are more certain than they. We see these with animals and birds; and they are more certain than when we imagine them.

Again, we imagine these bodies more certainly than we imagine other grand and infinite things inferred from them—things that do not exist at all. With such empty things I was then being fed, and I was not being fed.

But you, my love, into whom I fail so that I may become strong, are not these bodies that we see, even if they are in heaven; nor are you those things that we do not see there, because you created them and do not possess them among your highest creations  
[Note: Erasmus reads *abes*, “you are absent.”].

How far, then, you are from those fantasies of mine—the fantasies of bodies that do not exist at all! The fantasies of bodies that exist are more certain than those; and the bodies themselves are more certain than those fantasies, although you are not those bodies. Nor are you the soul, which is the life of bodies. Therefore the life of bodies is better and more certain than bodies. But you are the life of souls, the life of lives, living through yourself and unchanging, the life of my soul.

11. Where, then, were you for me at that time, and how far away? I was wandering far from you, excluded even from the pods of pigs whom I was feeding with pods (Luke XV, 16). For how much better were the little tales of grammarians and poets than that snare? Verse, song, and the flying Medea were certainly more useful than the five elements painted in various colors on account of the five caves of darkness—things that do not exist at all and destroy the one who believes them.

I can even transfer verse and song to true nourishment. As for the flying Medea, although I sang of her, I did not assert that she existed; although I heard her sung, I did not believe in her. But I believed those things.

Woe, woe! By what stages was I led down into the depths of hell? I was struggling and burning with want of truth, while I sought you, my God—this I confess to you, who had mercy on me even before I confessed—but sought you not according to the understanding of the mind, by which you intended me to excel the beasts, but according to the sensation of the flesh.

Yet you were more inward than my inmost self and higher than my highest self. I encountered that bold woman, lacking prudence, Solomon’s riddle, sitting on a seat at the doors and saying: “Eat willingly the hidden bread, and drink the stolen sweet water” (Prov. IX, 17).

She seduced me because she found me dwelling outside, in the eye of my flesh, and ruminating within myself on such things as I had devoured through it  
[Note: “Through her,” according to Erasmus and Venice.]

## CHAPTER VII. The Absurd Doctrine of the Manichaeans, Which He Supported
12. For I knew nothing else that truly exists; and, as though I were somewhat clever, I was moved to support foolish deceivers when they asked me where evil came from; whether God was bounded by bodily form and had hair and fingernails; and whether those should be considered righteous who had several wives at once, killed human beings, and sacrificed animals. Ignorant of such matters, I was thrown into confusion; and, turning away from the truth, I seemed to myself to be moving toward it, because I did not know that evil is nothing but the privation of good, extending even to that which altogether does not exist. But how could I see this, when my capacity for seeing reached only as far as the body through my eyes, and through my mind only as far as phantasms? Nor did I know that God is spirit—not one possessing limbs extended in length and breadth, nor one whose being consists in mass: for a mass is smaller in a part than in its whole; and if it is infinite, it is smaller in any part defined by a fixed extent than it is through infinity; and it is not wholly present everywhere, as spirit is, as God is. And what there was in us by which we were like God and were rightly said in Scripture [Note: [Col. 0688] Thus the English manuscripts: “And if we were rightly said in the Scriptures.” Am.: Two Florentine manuscripts and the Florentine edition read: “And rightly in Scripture.” M.] to be made in the image of God (Gen. 1:27), I was utterly ignorant.

13. Nor did I know true inner justice, which judges not according to custom but according to the perfectly right law [Note: Four manuscripts read “most choice” (*lectissima*)] of almighty God. By that law the practices of regions and days are shaped according to regions and days, while justice itself is everywhere and always the same—not one thing in one place and another elsewhere, nor one way at one time and another at another. According to this justice Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, and all those praised by the mouth of God were righteous. Yet the unlearned judge them unjustly, judging according to their own human day and measuring all the customs of the human race by the portion of custom familiar to themselves—as if someone ignorant of military equipment wanted a greave to cover the head and a helmet to be put on the foot, then complained that the arrangement was unsuitable; or as if, on a single day when a public suspension of business had been proclaimed from the afternoon onward, someone became angry because he was not allowed to offer something for sale, since it had been permitted in the morning; or as if, in one house, he saw some task being performed by the hands of a servant which the servant who served the cups was not permitted to do; or saw something being done behind the stalls which was forbidden before the table, and became indignant that, although there was one dwelling and one household, the same thing was not granted everywhere and to everyone.

So are those who become indignant when they hear that in another age the righteous were permitted something that is not permitted to the righteous in this age; and because God commanded one thing to those people and another to these for temporal reasons, although both served the same justice. They see that, in one person, on one day, and in one house, one thing suits one member and another suits another; that something was permitted long ago but is not permitted after an hour has passed; that something is allowed or commanded in one corner which is justly forbidden and punished in another. Is justice therefore varied and changeable? No; but the times over which it presides do not proceed in the same way, for they are times. Human beings, however, whose life on earth is brief, are unable—because their understanding is insufficient—to connect the causes of earlier ages and of other peoples, which they have not experienced, with those they have experienced. In one body, or one day, or one house, they can easily see what suits which member, at which moments, in which circumstances, and to which persons; in the former matters they take offense, while in the latter they obey.

14. At that time I did not know or consider these things. They struck my eyes from every side, yet I did not see them. I sang poems, but I was not permitted to place just any foot anywhere; rather, in one meter one way and in another meter another way, and even within a single verse the same foot could not occupy every position. The art by which I sang, moreover, had nothing different in one place and another, but possessed everything together. And I did not contemplate the justice served by good and holy people: a justice that, far more excellently and sublimely, possesses together all that it commands [Note: [Col. 0689] In Lov. “God” is added; but the word is absent from the manuscripts and most editions, because the Justice praised here is none other than God himself, who commanded.], varies in no respect, and yet at different times distributes and commands not everything together, but what is proper to each time. Blind, I criticized the pious fathers—not only because they used present things as God commanded and inspired them to do, but also because, as God revealed the future, they foretold it.

## CHAPTER VIII. Against the Manichaeans: Which acts of shame are always to be detested, and which crimes.

15. Is it ever or anywhere unjust to love God with all one’s heart, with all one’s soul, and with all one’s mind, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself? Therefore acts of shame that are contrary to nature must everywhere and always be detested and punished, such as those of the Sodomites. If all peoples committed them, they would be held under the same guilt by divine law, for God did not make human beings to use themselves in that way. The very fellowship that ought to exist between us and God is violated when the same nature, of which he is the author, is polluted by perverse lust.

Acts of shame that are contrary to human customs, however, must be avoided according to the diversity of customs, so that no citizen’s or foreigner’s lust may violate the compact established among them by the custom or law of a city or nation. For every part that does not accord with its whole is disgraceful.

But when God commands something contrary to the custom or agreement of any people, even if it has never been done there, it must be done; if it has been omitted, it must be restored; and if it had not been instituted, it must be instituted. For if a king may command in the state over which he rules something that neither anyone before him nor he himself had ever commanded, and obedience to him is not contrary to the fellowship of the state—in fact, disobedience is contrary to that fellowship—for it is a general compact of human society to obey its kings, how much more must God, the ruler of all his creation, be served without hesitation in whatever he commands? For just as, within the authorities of human society, the greater authority is placed over the lesser for the purpose of obedience, so God is placed over all.

16. Likewise, in crimes where there is a desire to do harm—whether by insult or injury—whether for the purpose of revenge, as an enemy against an enemy; or to obtain some advantage, as a robber against a traveler; or to avoid an evil, as someone against one whom he fears; or out of envy, as a wretched person against someone more fortunate; or when someone who has prospered fears that another may become his equal, or grieves that another is already his equal; or from the mere pleasure of another’s misfortune, as with spectators at gladiatorial shows, mockers, or deriders of anyone—these are the chief sources of iniquity. They spring from the desire to rule, to look on, and to experience, whether from one, two, or all three together. Thus one lives wickedly against the three and the seven, the ten-stringed psalter, your Decalogue, O most high and most gentle God.

But what acts of shame can there be against you, who are not corrupted? Or what crimes can there be against you, who cannot be harmed? Yet you punish what human beings perpetrate against themselves, because even when they sin against you, they act impiously against their own souls. Iniquity deceives itself, whether by corrupting and perverting its own nature, which you made and ordered; by using permitted things without restraint; by burning with desire for things not permitted, for a use contrary to nature; or when, as one held guilty, it rages against you in mind and words and kicks against the goad. It also deceives itself when, after breaking the boundaries of human society, it rejoices boldly in private alliances or separations, according as each thing pleases or displeases.

These things happen when you are abandoned, you who are the fountain of life, the one true creator and ruler of the universe, and private pride loves one false thing as though it were the whole. Therefore, by humble devotion we return to you; you cleanse us from evil habit, show mercy to the sins of those who confess, hear the groans of those bound, and release us from the chains we have made for ourselves—provided that we no longer lift against you the horns of a false liberty: the greed of possessing more, and the fear of losing everything, by loving our own possessions more than you, the good of all.

## CHAPTER IX. The distinction among sins, and between God’s judgment and that of human beings.

17. Among acts of shame, crimes, and so many iniquities, there are the sins of those who are making progress. These are condemned by those who judge well according to the rule of perfection, but praised in hope of their fruit, like the grass of a crop. There are also certain actions resembling either an act of shame or a crime which are not sins, because they offend neither you, Lord our God, nor the fellowship of society: for example, when things suitable for the use of life are arranged according to the time, while it remains uncertain whether this was done from a desire to possess; or when punishments are imposed by an authorized power for the purpose of correction, while it remains uncertain whether they arose from a desire to harm.

Many actions, therefore, which would seem blameworthy to human beings have been approved by your testimony; and many praised by human beings are condemned when you bear witness. Often the appearance of an action is one thing, the intention of the person performing it another, and the hidden circumstance of the moment still another.

But when you suddenly command something unusual and unforeseen—even if you once forbade it, even if you conceal the reason for your command according to the time, and even if it is contrary to the agreement of some human society—who would doubt that it must be done, when that human society is just which serves you? Yet blessed are those who know that you have commanded it. For everything is done by those who serve you either to provide what is needed for the present work or to foretell the future.

## CHAPTER X. The Manichaeans’ foolish notions about the fruits of the earth.

18. Not knowing these things, I mocked those holy servants and prophets of yours. And what was I doing when I mocked them, except arranging to be mocked by you, gradually and little by little being led to such foolish notions that I believed that a fig wept when it was plucked, and that its mother, the tree, shed milky tears? Yet if some holy person ate that fig—plucked, to be sure, by another’s crime, not his own—he would mingle it with his entrails and breathe angels out of it, or rather particles of God, groaning in prayer and belching them forth. Those particles of the highest and true God, they said, would have been bound in that fruit unless the tooth and belly of a holy elect person released them.

And in my misery I believed that greater mercy ought to be shown to the fruits of the earth than to human beings, for whose sake those fruits were born. If someone who was hungry asked for food and was not a Manichaean, the morsel seemed almost condemned to capital punishment if it were given to him.

## CHAPTER XI. The mother’s lament and dream concerning her son.

19. And you stretched out your hand from on high and drew my soul from this deep darkness (Ps. 143:7), while my faithful mother, your servant, wept before you for me more than mothers weep over bodily deaths. For she saw my death through the faith and spirit that she had from you; and you heard her, Lord. You heard her and did not despise her tears, which flowed and moistened the ground beneath her eyes wherever she prayed; you heard her.

For where did that dream come from, by which you consoled her, so that she allowed me to live [Note: The editions of Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read “so that she believed me to be with her”; but the better manuscripts should be followed: “so that she allowed me,” or, with Arn., “so that she allowed me to be with her.” The Florentine edition reads “believed me to be with her,” a reading supported by the authority of Bad., Am., Er., Lov., Somm., and eleven Etruscan manuscripts.] and to share with her the same table in the house—the very thing she had begun to refuse, turning away from and detesting the blasphemies of my error?

For she saw herself standing on a certain wooden rule, and a radiant young man, cheerful and smiling at her, coming toward her while she was mourning and overcome with grief. When he asked her the cause of her sorrow and daily tears—not to learn, but, as is customary, to teach—and she replied that she was lamenting my destruction, he ordered her to be at ease and instructed her to pay attention and see that where she was, there I also was. When she paid attention, she saw me standing beside her on the same rule. Where did this come from, except that your ears were close to her heart? O you, good and almighty God, who care for each one of us as though you cared for that one alone, and for all as though they were individuals!

20. There was also this: when she told me of that vision and I tried to turn it toward the interpretation that she should instead not despair of becoming what I was, she immediately, without hesitation, said: “No. It was not said to me, ‘Where he is, there you also are,’ but, ‘Where you are, there he also is.’”

I confess to you, Lord, so far as I recall—a memory I have often not kept silent—that even then I was more moved by this reply you gave through my watchful mother, who was not disturbed by so plausible a false interpretation and so quickly saw what had to be seen, which I certainly had not seen before she said it, than by the dream itself, by which the joy of that pious woman, so long afterward to come, was foretold so long beforehand as a consolation for her present anxiety.

For nearly nine years followed during which I rolled about in that mire and darkness of falsehood. Often I tried to rise, only to be dashed down more heavily. Yet that chaste, devout, and temperate widow—such as you love—already more cheerful in hope, but no less assiduous in weeping and groaning, never ceased at every hour of her prayers to lament me before you. Her prayers entered into your presence, while you still allowed me to be rolled and entangled in that darkness.

## CHAPTER XII. What answer Augustine’s mother received from a certain bishop concerning his conversion.

21. In the meantime you gave another answer, which I remember. I pass over many things, for I am hastening toward those matters that press me more urgently to confess to you, and I remember many things no longer.

You therefore gave another answer through one of your priests, a certain bishop brought up in the Church and trained in your Scriptures. When that woman asked him to be willing to speak with me, refute my errors, unteach me evil, and teach me good—for he did this whenever he found people suitable for it—he refused, wisely indeed, as I later understood.

For he replied that I was still unteachable, because I was puffed up by the novelty of that heresy and had already troubled many unlearned people with various little questions, as she had told him. “But leave him there,” he said, “and only pray to the Lord for him. By reading, he will discover what that error is and how great its impiety.”

He also related that he himself had been given to the Manichaeans as a small child by his seduced mother, and had not merely read nearly all their books, but had even written books of theirs. Yet, without anyone arguing against him and convicting him, it had become apparent to him how that sect ought to be avoided, and so he had fled from it.

When he had said this and she refused to accept it, but persisted in pleading and weeping abundantly that he see me and converse with me, he, already somewhat irritated by her persistence, said: “Go away from me; so may you live: it cannot happen that the son of these tears should perish.” [Note: Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., Flor., and Rond. read *fieri enim* (“for it can happen”). It seemed appropriate here to record a passage from Augustine, *Against the Letter of Petilianus the Donatist*, Book 3, chapter 17: “Let someone assert, either falsely or deceitfully and with astonishing audacity, that I was also a Manichaean presbyter. Let him set forth and argue, according to whatever interpretation seems to him, the words of the third book of my *Confessions*, which are perfectly clear to readers in themselves and in relation to the many things said before and afterward, and so on.” We do not know what those words were which Petilianus, torn from their context, interpreted insolently; perhaps the words from chapter 6: “For I transfer verse and song even to true foods.” For, as can be seen in chapter 16 of the same book *Against Petilianus’s Letter*, Augustine was reproached with having given love-magic to a woman.]

She remembered this reply in her frequent conversations with me as though it had sounded from heaven.

# BOOK FOUR

Augustine is ashamed that he had been devoted to the Manichaean sect for nine years and had drawn others with him into the same error; that he had also consulted astrologers; and that, in the meantime, a friend had been taken from him by death, whom he mourned with grief more bitter than was fitting. On this occasion he says much about vain and substantial friendship. He mentions books on *The Beautiful and the Fitting*, written by him in his twenty-sixth or twenty-seventh year; and also how easily, at about the age of twenty, he understood by himself the books of the liberal arts and Aristotle’s *Categories*.

[Col. 0693]

## CHAPTER I. How long and in what manner he led others astray.

1. During those same nine years, from my nineteenth year until my twenty-eighth, we were led astray and led others astray, deceived and deceiving, amid various desires: openly through the disciplines called liberal, but secretly under the false name of religion. In the former, we were proud; in the latter, superstitious; everywhere, vain.

In one pursuit we followed the emptiness of popular glory, even to theatrical applause, competitive poems [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read “contests” (*certamina*).], contests for crowns of hay, the nonsense of spectacles, and the intemperance of lust. In the other, we sought to be cleansed from these defilements by bringing food to those called the elect and holy, who, in the workshop of their stomach, would manufacture angels and gods for us, through whom we might be liberated. I pursued and practiced these things with my friends, deceived through me and along with me.

Let the arrogant mock me, those not yet healthfully cast down and crushed by you, my God; yet I will confess my disgraces to you in praise of you. Allow me, I beg, and grant me to pass in my present memory around the past circuits of my error and to sacrifice to you a sacrifice of jubilation. For what am I to myself without you, except a guide toward the abyss? Or what am I when things go well for me, except one sucking your milk or enjoying you as food that does not perish? And what is any human being, since he is a human being? Let the strong and powerful mock us; we, weak and needy, will confess to you.

## CHAPTER II. He teaches rhetoric, keeps a concubine, and rejects a diviner who promised him victory.

2. During those years I taught the art of rhetoric, and sold victorious loquacity out of a desire for profit. Yet, Lord, you know that I preferred to have good students, as they are called “good,” and I taught them deceit without deceit on my part—not so that they might act against the life of an innocent person, but sometimes on behalf of a guilty one.

And you, God, saw from afar my faith slipping on a slippery path and sparkling amid much smoke—the faith I displayed in that teaching to those who loved vanity and sought falsehood, as their companion.

During those years I had one woman, not joined to me in what is called a lawful marriage, but one whom wandering desire, lacking prudence, had sought out. Yet she was the only one, and I kept faith with her in the bed. In her I learned by my own example the difference between the restraint of a marital agreement, established for the sake of procreation, and a pact of lustful love, in which offspring is born even against one’s will, although once born it compels itself to be loved.

3. I also remember that when I had decided to enter a contest in theatrical poetry, some diviner sent word asking what fee I would give him to make me victorious. I detested and abhorred those foul rites, however, and replied that even if the crown were immortally golden, I would not permit a fly to be killed for my victory. For he was going to kill living creatures in his sacrifices, and by those honors he seemed to be inviting demons to support me.

But even in rejecting this evil I did not act from your chastity [Note: Bad., Am., and Er. substitute “charity.”], God of my heart. For I did not know how to love you, since I knew how to imagine nothing but bodily splendors. As the soul sighs after such inventions, does it not commit fornication away from you, trust in false things, and feed on the winds? Yet evidently I did not want sacrifices to be made for me to the demons to whom, through that superstition, I myself was sacrificing. For what else is “feeding on the winds” (Hos. 12:1) than feeding them—that is, becoming a source of pleasure and mockery to them through wandering in error?

## CHAPTER III. He is recalled from astrology, to which he was devoted, by an old man skilled in medicine and other matters.

4. For that reason I did not cease consulting those frauds [Note: Some editions read “astrologers” (*planetarios*). This occurs in the Louvain edition itself through the typographical carelessness of the printers, since in their corrections they say that *planos*, meaning impostors, seems to them the more correct reading. It is clear that mathematicians were once called by this name. Augustine uses the term elsewhere as well, as in *Against the Academics*, Book 3, chapter 15.] whom they call mathematicians, because, as I thought, they offered no sacrifice and directed no prayers to any spirit for purposes of divination. Yet true Christian devotion rightly rejects and condemns this as well.

For it is good to confess to you, Lord, and to say, “Have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5), and not abuse your indulgence as permission to sin, but remember the Lord’s words: “Behold, you have been made well; sin no more, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14).

They try to destroy all this healing when they say: “The unavoidable cause of your sin comes from the heavens; Venus did this, or Saturn, or Mars.” Thus, apparently, the human being is without blame—flesh and blood and proud corruption—while the creator and arranger of heaven and the stars is to be blamed. And who is this, if not our God, the sweetness and source of justice, who repays each person according to his works (Matt. 16:27) and does not despise a contrite and humbled heart? (Ps. 51:19.)

5. At that time there was a shrewd man, highly skilled and eminent in the medical art, who, as proconsul [Note: [Col. 0695] “As proconsul,” according to Er., Lugd., Ven., and Benedict. “Proconsul, with his own hand,” according to Lov.], had placed that agonistic crown on my unsound head with his own hand—not as a physician. For you are the healer of that disease, you who resist the proud but give grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5:5).

Yet did you fail me through that old man, or cease to heal my soul? I had become more intimate with him, and I clung constantly and attentively to his conversation—for his remarks, though without verbal ornament, were pleasant and weighty in the liveliness of their thoughts. When he learned from our conversation that I was devoted to books of genethliacal astrology, he kindly and fatherly advised me to cast them aside and not waste on that vanity the care and effort required for useful matters.

He said that he had studied it so thoroughly that, in the first years of his life, he had wanted to make it his profession and earn his living from it; and that if he had understood Hippocrates, he could certainly have understood those writings as well. Yet he had afterward taken up medicine and abandoned them for no other reason than that he had discovered them to be utterly false and, as a serious man, did not wish to seek a livelihood by deceiving people.

“But you,” he said, “support yourself among human beings by practicing rhetoric; you pursue this deception through free choice, not because of financial necessity. Therefore you ought all the more to believe me about it, since I worked so hard to learn it perfectly that I wanted to live from it alone.”

When I asked him what, then, caused many true statements to be made through it, he replied as best he could that this resulted from the power of chance, diffused everywhere throughout nature. If someone happened to consult a poet’s pages, in which the poet was singing and intending something altogether different, and a verse often emerged that wonderfully harmonized with the matter at hand, he said it was not surprising that something might sound forth from the human soul—under the impulse of something higher, though it did not know what was happening within it—not by art but by chance—which agreed with the affairs and actions of the person asking.

6. Through him, or by means of him, you arranged this for me. And what I was afterward to seek by myself, you outlined in my memory. At that time, however, neither he nor my dearest Nebridius, a very good and very cautious young man [Note: “Chaste,” according to Mart. with three manuscripts.], who mocked the whole art of divination, could persuade me to abandon these practices. The authority of the authors themselves moved me more strongly, and I had not yet found any certain proof of the kind I sought by which it might appear to me without ambiguity that the truths reported by those consulted were spoken by chance or lot, not through the art of observing the stars.

## CHAPTER IV. He recounts the illness and baptism of his friend, whom he had also entangled in his errors; after his friend’s death, he grieves most bitterly. The marvelous efficacy of the sacrament of baptism.

7. During those years, when I had first begun to teach in the town where I was born, I acquired a friend through our shared studies, extremely dear to me, my contemporary and flourishing with the bloom of youth. We had grown up together as boys, gone to school together, and played together.

Yet he was not then such a friend, although even then our friendship was not what true friendship is; for it is not true unless you bind it together among those who cling to you, through the love poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). Still, it was exceedingly sweet, formed by the ardor of shared studies.

For I had led him away from the true faith—which, as a young man, he did not hold genuinely and deeply—and into superstitious fables and destructive practices, on account of which my mother wept for me. That man was now wandering in spirit with me, and my soul could not exist without him.

And behold, you were already threatening the backs of your fugitives, God who is both the God of vengeance and the fountain of mercies, who turn us to yourself in wondrous ways. Behold, you took that man from this life when he had scarcely completed a year in my friendship, a friendship sweeter to me than all the sweetnesses of that life.
