8. Who can recount your praises, one person recounting what he himself has experienced? What did you do then, my God, and how unsearchable is the abyss of your judgments?

When he was suffering from fevers, he lay for a long time without consciousness, covered in the sweat of death. When he was despaired of, he was baptized without knowing it, while I did not care and presumed that what he had received from me would retain his soul rather than what was taking place in the body of one who did not know it.

But it was altogether otherwise: he revived and was saved. As soon as I was first able to speak with him—which was as soon as he was able, since I did not leave him and we depended excessively upon one another—I tried to mock the baptism he had received, as though he too would mock it with me, having been utterly absent from it in mind and senses; yet he had already learned that he had received it.

But he recoiled from me as from an enemy and, with marvelous and sudden freedom, warned me that if I wished to be his friend I should stop saying such things to him. I, astonished and disturbed, postponed all my reactions until he had recovered and his health had restored his strength, so that I could deal with him as I wished.

But he was snatched away from my madness, so that he might be preserved by you for my consolation. A few days later, while I was absent, the fevers returned, and he died.

9. My heart was darkened by this grief, and whatever I looked upon was death. My homeland was a punishment to me, my father’s house a strange misery; and whatever I had shared with him had become, without him, an immense torture.

My eyes sought him everywhere, but he was not given to me. I hated everything because it did not contain him and could no longer say to me, “He will come,” as it did when he was alive and absent. I had become a great question to myself, and I asked my soul why it was sad and why it disturbed me so greatly, but it knew nothing to answer me.

If I said, “Hope in God” (Ps. 42:6), it rightly did not obey, because the real human being whom I had most dearly lost was more true and better than the phantasm in which I was commanded to hope. Weeping alone was sweet to me and had succeeded my friend as the delight of my soul.

## CHAPTER V. Why weeping is sweet to the wretched.

10. And now, Lord, those things have passed away, and time has softened my wound. Can I hear from you, who are truth, and bring the ear of my heart near your mouth, so that you may tell me why weeping is sweet to the wretched?

Or have you, although you are everywhere present, cast our misery far from you? You remain in yourself, while we are tossed about in our experiences. Yet unless we wept before your ears, nothing of our hope would remain.

From where, then, is a sweet fruit plucked from the bitterness of life—groaning, weeping, sighing, and complaining? Is this sweet there [Note: [Col. 0697] Am., Er., and Lov. read: “Is this sweet to you?”] because we hope that you will hear us? That is rightly so in prayers, because they contain the desire to reach you.

But was it so in the grief over the loss of that thing and the mourning with which I was then covered? For I did not hope that he would return to life, nor did I ask this with my tears; I merely grieved and wept. I was wretched, and I had lost my joy.

Or is weeping itself a bitter thing, which nevertheless delights us because we are disgusted by the things we previously enjoyed and, while we recoil from them, take pleasure in weeping?

## CHAPTER VI. The magnitude of his grief at his friend’s death.

11. Why am I saying these things? For now is not the time to complain, but to confess to you. I was wretched, and every soul bound by friendship to mortal things is wretched; it is torn apart when it loses them, and then feels the misery in which it was already wretched even before it lost them.

That is how I was then. I wept most bitterly and rested in bitterness. I was so wretched that I held that wretched life itself dearer than my friend. Although I wanted to change it, I did not want to lose it any more than I wanted to lose him.

And I do not know whether, in his place, I would have been willing to die for him, as the story is told—if it is not fiction—of Orestes and Pylades, who wished either to die for one another or to die together, because for them it was worse to live apart than to die together.

But in me there arose some feeling altogether opposed to this: an extreme weariness of living, and a fear of dying. I believe that the more I loved him, the more I hated and feared death, which had taken him from me, as my most savage enemy; and I thought it would suddenly consume all human beings, because it had been able to consume him.

That is exactly how I was; I remember it. Behold my heart, my God; behold it within and see that I remember, my hope, you who cleanse me from the impurity of such affections, directing my eyes toward you and drawing my feet out of the snare (Ps. 25:15).

I wondered that other mortals lived, because the one whom I had loved as though he would never die was dead; and I wondered even more that I, who had been another self to him, continued to live after his death.

Someone rightly said of his friend, “Half of my soul” (Horace, *Odes*, Book 1, Ode 3). For I felt that my soul and his soul had been one soul in two bodies; and therefore life was a horror to me, because I did not want to live half a life, and perhaps for that reason I feared death, lest the whole of him whom I had loved so greatly should die (see *Retractations*, Book 2, chapter 6).

## CHAPTER VII. Impatience with grief causes him to change his location.

12. O madness that does not know how to love human beings humanly! O foolish human being suffering human things without measure—such as I was then!

I burned, sighed, wept, and was troubled; there was neither rest nor counsel. I carried my lacerated and bleeding soul, impatient of being carried by me, and I could not find where to place it.

It did not find rest in pleasant groves, games and songs, sweet-smelling places, prepared banquets, or the pleasure of the bedroom and bed. Finally, it did not rest in books and poems either. Everything, even the light itself, bristled with horror; and whatever was not what he had been was wicked and hateful, except for groaning and tears. For in those alone there was a little rest.

But whenever my soul was taken away from them, the great burden of misery weighed upon me. I knew that it had to be lifted and healed by you, Lord [Note: This is found with broad agreement among the manuscripts; the editions, however, read “the misery that comes from you.”], but I neither wished nor was able to do so, especially because, when I thought of you, you were not something solid and firm to me.

For it was not you, but a vain phantasm; and my error was my god. If I tried to place my soul there so that it might rest, it slipped through the void and again fell upon me, while I myself remained for myself an unhappy place in which I could neither be nor depart from.

For where could my heart flee from my heart? Where could I flee from myself? Where could I go without myself following me?

And yet I fled from my homeland. For my eyes sought him less where they were not accustomed to see him; and I went from the town of Thagaste to Carthage.

## CHAPTER VIII. Time and the conversations of friends heal grief.

13. Time does not stand idle, nor does it roll pointlessly through our senses; it accomplishes wondrous works in the soul. Behold, day by day they came and passed away, and by coming and passing away they implanted in me one set of impressions after another and one memory after another, and little by little they restored me to my former kinds of pleasure, to which that grief of mine yielded; yet there followed not indeed other griefs, but the causes of other griefs. For from where had that grief penetrated me most easily and into my inmost being, unless because I had poured out my soul upon the sand, loving one who was going to die as though he were not going to die? Most of all, however, the consolations of other friends renewed and refreshed me, friends with whom I loved what I loved in your place. Yet this was a huge fiction and a prolonged lie, whose adulterous rubbing corrupted our minds, itching for things to hear. But that fiction did not die for me if one of my friends died. Other things were those that more fully captivated the mind in them: talking and laughing together; mutually rendering kind services; reading together books sweet in their speech; joking together and honoring one another; occasionally disagreeing without hatred, as a person might with himself, and seasoning with that very rare disagreement our many agreements; teaching one another something, or learning from one another; longing with sorrow for those who were absent and welcoming those who arrived with joy. Through such signs and others like them, proceeding from the hearts of those who loved and were loved in return, through the mouth, the tongue, the eyes, and a thousand most pleasing movements, they seemed to kindle our spirits as though with fuel, and to make one out of many.

## CHAPTER IX. Human friendship. Blessed is the one who loves in God.

14. This is what is loved in friends, and it is loved in such a way that the human conscience considers itself guilty if it has not loved one who loves it in return, or if it has not returned the love of one who loves it, seeking nothing from the other’s body except signs of goodwill. Hence comes grief when someone dies; hence the darkness of sorrows, the heart drenched in bitterness after sweetness has been turned into gall, and the death of the living arising from the life lost by the dying. Blessed is the one who loves you, and a friend in you, and an enemy for your sake. For only the one loses no beloved who has all beloved in the One who is not lost. And who is this but our God—the God who made heaven and earth and fills them, because by filling them he made them? No one loses you except the one who abandons you; and the one who abandons you, where does he go, or where does he flee, except from you, who are at peace, to you, who are angry? For where does he not find your law in his punishment? And your law is truth, and you are the truth.

## CHAPTER X. Creatures are transitory, and the soul cannot find rest in them.

15. God of hosts, restore us, and show us your face, and we shall be saved (Psalm 79:4). For wherever the human soul turns, it fastens itself to sorrows elsewhere than in you, even though it fastens itself upon beautiful things outside you and outside itself. Yet these things would not exist at all unless they existed from you. They arise and pass away; by arising they begin, as it were, to exist; they grow so as to reach completion; and once complete, they grow old and perish—and not all things grow old, and all things perish. Therefore, when they arise and tend toward being, the more rapidly they grow so as to be, the more swiftly they hasten toward not being. Such is their condition. You have allotted them only so much, because they are parts of things that do not all exist simultaneously; yet, by departing and succeeding one another, all the parts together accomplish the whole of which they are parts.

Behold, our speech is likewise completed through sounding signs. The speech would not be whole if one word did not depart when it had sounded out its parts, so that another might succeed it. Let my soul praise you through these things, God, creator of all; but let it not be fastened to them by the glue of love through the bodily senses. For they go where they were going, toward not being, and they tear the soul apart with diseased desires, because it itself wants to exist and loves to rest in the things it loves. But in them there is no place for it: they do not remain; they flee. And who can follow them with the sense of the flesh? Or who can grasp them, even when they are present? The sense of the flesh is slow, because it is the sense of the flesh, and this too is its limitation. It is sufficient for the purpose for which it was made; but it is not sufficient to hold what is passing from its appointed beginning to its appointed end. For in your Word, through which they are created, they hear: “From here—and thus far.”

[Note: [Col. 0699] We follow the manuscripts; in the editions, with the negation removed, one reads instead: “For indeed all things grow old.”]

[Note: [Col. 0700] Three manuscripts read: “For they go where?—that they may not be.”]

## CHAPTER XI. All created things are unstable. God alone is stable.

16. Do not be vain, my soul, and become deaf in the ear of your heart amid the tumult of your vanity. You too, listen: the Word himself cries out that you should return; and there is the place of undisturbed rest, where love is not abandoned if it itself does not abandon. Behold, those things depart so that others may succeed them, and the lowest universe is made complete through all its parts. “Do I depart anywhere?” says the Word of God. “Establish your dwelling there; entrust there whatever you possess from there, my soul, at least you who are weary of deceptions. Entrust to the Truth whatever you have from the truth, and you will lose nothing. Your decayed things will bloom again; all your sicknesses will be healed; your fleeting things will be restored, renewed, and gathered together around you. They will not lay you down where they descend; rather, they will stand with you and remain forever with the God who always stands and remains.”

17. Why do you perversely follow your flesh? Let it follow you, once converted. Whatever you perceive through it is a part, and you do not know the whole of which these are parts; yet they delight you. But if the sense of your flesh were capable of grasping the whole, and had not itself received, as a punishment for you, its proper measure within a part of the universe, you would want whatever exists in the present to pass away, so that all things might please you more. For you also hear what we are saying through this same sense of the flesh; and surely you do not want the syllables to remain, but to fly past so that others may come and you may hear the whole. Thus, all things of which one thing consists, and whose constituent parts do not all exist simultaneously, delight more as a whole than individually, if all can be perceived. But far better than these is the One who made all things, and he is our God; and he does not depart, because no one succeeds him.

## CHAPTER XII. Love is not condemned, provided that in the things which please us we love God.

18. If bodies please you, praise God because of them and turn your love back toward their maker, lest in the things that please you, you yourself become displeasing. If souls please you, let them be loved in God, because they too are changeable and are established in him, who is stable; otherwise they would go away and perish. Let them therefore be loved in him; and carry with you to him as many as you can, and say to them: “Let us love this One, let us love this One. He made these things, and he is not far away.” For he did not make them and then depart; rather, they are from him and in him. Behold, there he is, where truth gives delight.

[Note: [Col. 0701] In the Sorbonne manuscript: “Behold, there he is, where truth gives delight.”]

He is most inwardly present to the heart, but the heart has wandered away from him. Return, transgressors, to the heart, and cling to the One who made you. Stand with him, and you will stand; rest in him, and you will be at rest. Where are you going into rough places? Where are you going? The good that you love is from him; but insofar as it is directed toward him, it is good and sweet. Yet it will rightly become bitter, because whatever is from him is loved unjustly when he is abandoned. Why do you continue to walk along difficult and laborious roads? There is no rest where you seek it. Seek what you seek—but it is not there where you seek it. You seek the blessed life in the land of death; it is not there. For how can there be a blessed life where there is not even life?

19. And Life itself descended here, and took our death, and killed it from the abundance of its own life. It thundered, crying out that we should return from here to him, into that hidden place from which he came forth to us: into that first virginal womb itself, where the human creature, mortal flesh, was joined to him in marriage, so that it might not remain forever mortal. From there, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, he rejoiced like a giant to run his course (Psalm 18:6). He did not delay but ran, crying out through words, deeds, death, life, descent, and ascent; crying out that we should return to him.

And he withdrew from our eyes so that we might return to our heart and find him. For he departed—and behold, he is here. He did not wish to remain long with us, yet he did not abandon us. For he departed to the place from which he never withdrew, because the world was made through him; and he was in this world (John 1:10), and he came into this world to save sinners (1 Timothy 1:15). To him my soul confesses, and he heals it, because it sinned against him (Psalm 40:5). “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:3.) [Note: [Col. 0701] The Benignian manuscript, of excellent quality, reads discessum, “departure.”] Even after Life’s descent, do you not wish to ascend and live? But where will you ascend, when you are on high and have set your mouth against heaven? (Psalm 73:9.) Descend, so that you may ascend—ascend to God. For you fell by ascending against him. Say these things to them, so that they may weep in the valley of weeping, and thus carry them with you to God; for you speak these things to them from his Spirit, if you speak while burning with the fire of love.

[Note: [Col. 0701] Lov., Arn., and Mart., together with five manuscripts, as well as Rond. with four manuscripts, read: “so that he may heal it.” M.]

## CHAPTER XIII. From where love arises.

20. At that time I did not know these things, and I loved lower beauties, and was descending into the depths, and said to my friends: “Do we love anything except what is beautiful? What, then, is the beautiful? And what is beauty? What is it that attracts us and reconciles us to the things we love? For unless there were in them grace and appearance, they would in no way move us toward themselves.”

I observed and saw in bodies themselves that one thing was, as it were, the whole and therefore beautiful; while another was pleasing because it was suitably fitted to something else, as a part of the body is fitted to its whole, or a shoe to the foot, and similar things. This reflection sprang up in my mind from its innermost heart, and I wrote books On the Beautiful and the Fitting; I think, two or three. You know, God, for it has slipped from my memory. We do not possess them, for somehow they have gone astray from us.

## CHAPTER XIV. The books On the Fitting and the Beautiful, dedicated to Hierius. Why he had loved him.

[Col. 0702]

21. What was it, then, Lord my God, that moved me to write those books to Hierius, the orator of the city of Rome? I did not know him by sight, but I had come to love the man because of the reputation for learning that surrounded him, and because I had heard some of his words, which pleased me. Yet I loved him more because he pleased others, and they exalted him with praises, amazed that a man from Syria, first learned in Greek eloquence and later also an extraordinary speaker in Latin, should have become so learned in matters pertaining to the pursuit of wisdom. This pleased me.

A man is praised and loved while absent. Does that love enter the heart of the listener from the mouth of the one praising him? Far from it. One lover kindles another. For the praised man is loved when he is believed to be proclaimed by the praiser with a heart free from deceit—that is, when someone who loves him praises him.

[Note: [Col. 0702] Hierius is the spelling in the Lov. edition and in most manuscripts; Bad., Am., Er., Arn., and four manuscripts have Icherius.]

[Note: [Col. 0702] The editions read doctor, “teacher.” Two Lov. manuscripts read dictator, evidently corrupt for dictor, “speaker.” It seemed appropriate to restore the latter word on the authority of our manuscripts.]

22. For at that time I loved people according to human judgment, not according to yours, my God, in whom no one is deceived. Yet why did I not love someone as I loved a famous charioteer or a hunter celebrated by popular enthusiasm, but in a very different and serious way, and in the manner in which I too wished to be praised? I would not have wished to be praised and loved as actors are, although I myself praised and loved them; but I preferred to remain hidden rather than to be known in that way, and I would rather have been hated than loved in that manner.

Where are these weights of various and diverse loves distributed within one soul? What is it that I love in another which, if I did not hate it, I would not myself reject and drive away, since both of us are human beings? It is not like loving a good horse when one would not wish to be a horse oneself, even if one could; and the same must be said of an actor, who shares our human nature. Do I therefore love in a human being what I hate to be, although I am a human being? Great is this depth—the human being, whose very hairs you, Lord, have counted, and they do not diminish in your sight. Yet his hairs are more easily counted than his feelings and the movements of his heart.

23. But that orator belonged to the kind whom I loved in such a way that I wished to be like him. I was wandering in pride, carried about by every wind, and governed by you in a manner hidden even from me. How do I know, and how can I confess to you with certainty, that I loved him more in the love of those who praised him than in the things for which he was praised? If those same people had criticized him instead of praising him, and while criticizing and despising him had recounted those very same accomplishments, I would not have been inflamed or stirred toward him. Certainly the accomplishments would not have been different, nor would the man himself; only the effect produced by those who narrated them would have been different.

Behold where the weak soul lies, not yet clinging to the solidity of truth. As the breezes of tongues blow from the breasts of those who form opinions, so the soul is carried and turned, twisted and turned back, and the light is clouded for it, so that truth is not seen. Yet behold, it is before us. It seemed a great thing to me if my speech and studies became known to that man. If he approved them, I would burn with greater eagerness; but if he disapproved, my vain and empty heart, lacking your solidity, would be wounded. Nevertheless, I gladly revolved in my mind that beautiful and fitting thing which I had written to him, before the gaze of my contemplation, and, with no one to join in praising it, admired it.

[Note: [Col. 0703] Arn., together with Moretus’s 1650 edition, reads: “I revolved it in my mind for the display of my contemplation.” Six manuscripts read: “the modes of my contemplation.”]

## CHAPTER XV. Obscured by bodily images, he could not grasp spiritual things.

24. But I did not yet see the central principle of so great a matter in your art, Almighty One, who alone do wondrous things (Psalm 71:18). My mind moved among bodily forms, and I defined and distinguished the beautiful as that which is beautiful through itself, while the fitting was that which, by being adapted to something, was appropriately pleasing; and I supported these definitions with bodily examples.

Then I turned toward the nature of the soul, but the false opinion that I held concerning spiritual things prevented me from seeing the truth. The very force of truth rushed into my eyes, yet I turned my trembling mind away from the incorporeal reality toward outlines, colors, and swollen dimensions. Because I could not see these things in the soul, I thought that I could not see my own soul.

And while I loved peace in virtue and hated discord in vice, I observed unity in the former and a kind of division in the latter. In that unity, the rational mind and the nature of truth and the highest good seemed to me to exist; but in that division of irrational life I imagined some substance and nature of the highest evil, which would not merely be a substance but would altogether be a life, and yet would not exist from you, my God, from whom all things exist. Miserably, I held this opinion.

I called the former a monad, as though it were a mind without any sex; the latter a dyad—anger in crimes, lust in shameful acts—without knowing what I was saying. For I did not know or understand either that evil was not a substance or that our mind itself was the highest and unchangeable good.

[Note: [Col. 0703] The English manuscripts, together with ours, read: “in the division of irrational life,” or “of non-rational life.” Lov. has rationalis, “rational,” evidently incorrectly.]

[Note: [Col. 0703] In five manuscripts of no inferior quality one finds: “a mind without any sensation,” instead of “without any sex.”]

25. For just as there are crimes when the movement of the soul is vicious—the movement in which there is an impulse that throws itself about insolently and turbulently—and shameful acts when the soul’s affection is immoderate, by which carnal pleasures are imbibed, so errors and false opinions contaminate life when the rational mind itself is vicious, as mine then was, unaware that another light had to illumine it so that it might share in truth, because it is not itself the nature of truth.

For “you will illumine my lamp, Lord; my God, you will illumine my darkness” (Psalm 18:28); and “from your fullness we have all received.” You are the true light that illumines every human being coming into this world (John 1:16, 9), because in you there is no change or shadow caused by turning (James 1:17).

26. But I was striving toward you and was driven back from you, so that I might taste death, because you resist the proud. And what is prouder than to assert, in astonishing madness, that I was naturally what you are? For although I was changeable—and this was evident to me because I wished to become wise precisely so that I might become better from a worse state—I nevertheless preferred to imagine even you changeable rather than admit that I was not what you are.

And so I was driven back, while you resisted my wind-swollen neck. I imagined bodily forms, and I accused flesh with flesh; and, as a spirit walking on, I had not yet returned to you (Psalm 78:39). As I walked, I continued to walk among things that do not exist—not in you, not in me, not in the body. They were not created for me by your truth; they were fashioned from the body by my own vanity. And I said to your little faithful ones, my fellow citizens, from whom I was unknowingly an exile: “Why, then, does the soul that God made go astray?”

But I did not wish anyone to say to me: “Why, then, does God go astray?” I contended instead that your unchangeable substance was compelled to err rather than that my changeable substance had voluntarily gone astray, and I acknowledged that I erred through punishment.

[Note: [Col. 0704] The editions read pene errare confitebar, “I confessed that I erred almost”; this is manifestly an error.]

27. I was perhaps twenty-six or twenty-seven years old when I wrote those volumes, turning over within myself bodily fantasies that clamored in the ears of my heart. I directed those ears toward your inner melody, sweet Truth, as I contemplated the beautiful and the fitting, wishing to stand still, to hear you, and to rejoice with joy because of the Bridegroom’s voice (John 3:29); but I could not. The voices of my error carried me outward, and the weight of my pride cast me down into the depths. For you did not grant my hearing joy and gladness, nor did my bones rejoice, since they had not been humbled (Psalm 51:10).

## CHAPTER XVI. He understood Aristotle’s Categories and the books of the liberal arts by himself.

28. And what did it profit me that, when I was nearly twenty years old, certain Aristotelian works came into my hands, which are called the Ten Categories? My teacher, a rhetorician at Carthage, would pronounce their name with cheeks loudly puffed up by pride, as did others who were considered learned; and I, hanging as though suspended before something great and divine, gaped in wonder. Yet I read them by myself and understood them.

When I compared my understanding with those who said that they had scarcely understood them, under the instruction of highly learned teachers who not only spoke but drew many diagrams in the dust, they could tell me nothing beyond what I had discovered by reading them alone. They seemed to me to speak quite clearly about substances, such as a human being; and about what exists in them, such as the human form; what kind of stature it has, how many feet tall it is; its relation—whose brother it is; where it is situated; when it was born; whether it stands or sits; whether it is shod or armed; whether it does something or undergoes something; and whatever is found in the other nine categories, of which I have offered some examples, or in the category of substance itself, where innumerable things are found.

29. What did this profit me, when it also harmed me? I tried to understand you, my God, wondrously simple and unchangeable, as though you were wholly comprehended by those ten categories, imagining that you too were subject to your own magnitude or beauty, so that these qualities existed in you as in a subject, as they do in a body. Yet your magnitude and your beauty are yourself; whereas a body is not large and beautiful simply insofar as it is a body, since even if it were smaller and less beautiful, it would nonetheless be a body.

The conception I had of you was false, not true; it was a product of my misery, not a foundation for your blessedness. For you had commanded, and so it happened to me, that the earth should bring forth thorns and thistles for me, and that with labor I should reach my bread (Genesis 3:18–19).

30. And what did it profit me that I myself read and understood all the books of the arts they call liberal, whatever I was able to read, while I was then the most wicked slave of evil desires? I rejoiced in them, and did not know where came whatever was true and certain in them. I had my back toward the light and my face toward the things illuminated by it; therefore my face itself, by which I saw the illuminated things, was not illumined.

Whatever I understood without great difficulty about the art of speaking and reasoning, about the dimensions of figures, about music and numbers, without anyone teaching me, you know, Lord my God. For both the rapidity of understanding and the sharpness of discernment are your gifts.

[Note: [Col. 0705] Earlier editions read discendi, “of learning”; Lov. and Arn. read disputandi, “of debating.” But several manuscripts have dispiciendi acumen, “the sharpness of discernment,” which appears to be the genuine reading.]

Yet I did not sacrifice to you with these gifts. Therefore they served me not for useful purposes but rather for my destruction, because I strove to possess such a good part of my substance under my own control. I did not keep my strength for you (Psalm 59:9); instead, I departed from you into a distant land, to squander it upon prostituted desires (Luke 15:12–13, 30).

[Note: [Col. 0705] Lov., together with earlier editions, reads meretricias cupiditates, “prostituted desires.” [Col. 0706] But the manuscripts, together with Arn., have meretrices, “prostitutes,” a word Augustine employed from the Gospel passage to which he alludes.]

For what did a good thing profit me when I did not use it well? I did not realize that even by students and gifted people those arts are understood only with the greatest difficulty, unless they attempt to explain the same things to others; and that the one most excellent in them is the person who, when I explain them, follows me without delay.

31. But what did this profit me, when I thought that you, Lord God of truth, were a luminous and immense body, and that I was a fragment of that body? Excessive perversity! Yet that was how I was. I am not ashamed, my God, to confess to you your mercies toward me and to call upon you, who did not blush at that time to profess my blasphemies before human beings and to bark against you.

What, then, did an intellect made agile by those disciplines profit me, and what did all those intricate books, unraveled without the aid of a human teacher, profit me, when I was wandering deformously and with sacrilegious shame in the doctrine of piety? Or what did the much slower intellects of your little ones harm them, when they did not depart far from you, so that they might grow safely feathered in the nest of your Church and nourish the wings of love with the food of sound faith?

O Lord, our God, let us hope in the shelter of your wings (Psalm 63:8); protect us and carry us. You will carry the little ones, and even to old age you will carry them (Isaiah 46:4). For when you are our strength, then there is strength; but when it is our own, there is weakness. Our good lives with you forever. Because we have turned away from it, we have become perverse. Let us now return, Lord, so that we may not be overturned; for our good, which is you yourself, lives with you without any failing. We need not fear that there is nowhere for us to return, because we fell away from there; [Note: [Col. 0706] “We shall fear,” according to Somm., Lov., Arn., and Mart. with seven manuscripts, and Rond. with thirteen manuscripts. M.] while we are absent, your house, your eternity, does not fall.

# BOOK FIVE

He presents the twenty-ninth year of his life, in which, having discovered the ignorance of Faustus the Manichaean, he abandoned his intention of advancing in that sect. In the same year he was sent from Rome, where he was then teaching rhetoric, to Milan to teach the same art; after hearing Ambrose, he began to recover his senses and to decide both to renounce Manichaeism and to resume the catechumenate.

[Col. 0705]

## CHAPTER I. He stirs his mind to praise God.

1. Receive the sacrifice of my confessions from the hand of my tongue, which you formed and awakened so that it might confess your name; and heal all my bones, and let them say: “Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 35:10.)

For the one who confesses to you does not teach you what is happening within him. A closed heart does not shut out your eye, nor does human hardness repel your hand; but you loosen it when you will, whether in mercy or in judgment, and no one can hide from your heat.

But let my soul praise you, so that it may love you, and confess your mercies to you, so that it may praise you. All your creation does not cease or fall silent in your praises: nor does every spirit of a human being through a mouth turned toward you; nor do animals or bodily things, through the mouths of those who contemplate them. Thus our soul may rise up in you from weariness, relying upon the things you have made and passing over to you, who made these things wondrously; and there is refreshment and true strength.

## CHAPTER II. The wicked cannot escape God’s presence; therefore they must turn to him.

2. Let the restless and wicked go away and flee from you; yet you see them and distinguish their shadows. And behold, all things are beautiful with them, while they themselves are ugly. What harm have they done to you? Or in what have they dishonored your rule, which is just and whole from the heavens to the furthest depths?

For where did they flee when they fled from your face? Or where do you not find them? They fled so that they would not see you seeing them, and, blinded in you, they might stumble; for you do not abandon anything that you have made. The unjust stumble against you and are justly tormented, withdrawing themselves from your gentleness, stumbling against your uprightness, and falling upon their own harshness.

[Note: [Col. 0706] Most manuscripts have this reading, which seems more elegant than the version in which the connection of the sentence is broken and a new sentence begins: “The unjust stumbled against you so that they might be justly tormented,” as some manuscripts, together with Arn., read.]

[Note: [Col. 0707] We have substituted suam, “their own,” from manuscripts of better quality, for tuam, “your,” which is found in the commonly transmitted codices and in some manuscripts.]

Clearly they do not know that you are everywhere, that no place confines you, and that you alone are present even to those who make themselves far from you. Let them therefore turn and seek you, because just as they have abandoned their Creator, so you have not abandoned your creature.

Let them turn and seek you; and behold, there you are in their heart—in the heart of those who confess to you, throw themselves upon you, and weep in your bosom after their difficult ways. And you, who are gentle, wipe away their tears; and they weep and rejoice even more in their tears, because you, Lord—not some human being of flesh and blood, but you, Lord, who made them—refresh and console them.

And where was I when I sought you? You were before me, but I had departed even from myself and could not find myself; how much less could I find you?

## CHAPTER III. Faustus the Manichaean, and the blindness of the philosophers who did not know the Creator through his creatures.

3. In the presence of my God I shall speak of that year, the twenty-ninth of my life. A certain Manichaean bishop named Faustus had already come to Carthage, a great snare of the devil, and many were being entangled by the charm of his smooth eloquence. Although I praised that eloquence, I nevertheless distinguished it from the truth of the matters I was eager to learn. I did not look at the kind of vessel in which his speech was served, but at what knowledge the famous Faustus among them would set before me to consume.

For reputation had already spoken in advance about him, saying that he was highly skilled in every honorable discipline and especially learned in the liberal arts. Since I had read many philosophers and retained what I had committed to memory, I compared certain of their teachings with the Manichaeans’ long fables. The teachings of those who had been capable enough to assess the universe seemed more probable to me, although they had not in the least found its Lord.

For you are great, Lord, and you look upon the lowly, but the exalted you know from afar (Psalm 138:6). You do not draw near except to those crushed in heart; and you are not found by the proud, even if they count the stars and the sand with inquisitive skill, measure the regions of the heavens, and track the paths of the stars.

4. They investigate these things with their minds and with the intelligence you gave them. They have discovered much and foretold, many years in advance, the eclipses of the sun and moon—on what day, at what hour, and to what extent they would occur. Their calculations did not deceive them, and things happened as they predicted. They wrote down the rules they had discovered, and these are read today; from them it is predicted in what year and month of the year, on what day of the month, at what hour of the day, and by what portion of its light the moon or sun will be eclipsed. And it will happen as predicted.

People who do not understand these things marvel and are astonished; those who do understand them exult and raise themselves up. In impious pride they withdraw and fall away from your light. They foresee the future eclipse of the sun long beforehand, but do not see their own eclipse in the present. They do not religiously seek to know from whom they have the intelligence with which they investigate these things.

When they discover that you made them, they do not give themselves to you so that you may preserve what you made. They do not put to death for you the selves they have made, nor slaughter their exaltations like birds, their curiosities like the fish of the sea, by which they range through the secret paths of the abyss, and their lusts like the beasts of the field, so that you, God, a consuming fire, may consume their dead cares and restore them to immortality.

[Note: [Col. 0708] Arn. and two manuscripts read occidant se tibi, “let them kill themselves for you,” followed shortly by trucident, “let them slaughter.” Most other codices support the alternative reading, which is somewhat obscure because of the distance separating the negative particle, which must also be understood with occidunt and trucidant.]

5. Yet they did not know the way—your Word—through which you made the things they count, and those who count them, and the sense by which they perceive what they count, and the mind from which they count; and there is no number to your wisdom (Psalm 147:5). The Only-Begotten himself became for us wisdom, righteousness, and sanctification (1 Corinthians 1:30), and he was numbered among us and paid tribute to Caesar (Matthew 22:21).

They did not know this way, by which they might descend from themselves to him and through him ascend to him. They did not know this way, and they think themselves exalted and luminous with the stars; yet behold, they fell to the earth, and their foolish heart was darkened.

They say many true things about creation, but they do not piously seek the Truth, the maker of creation, and therefore they do not find him. Or, if they do find him, while knowing God they do not glorify him as God or give thanks; instead, they become futile in their thoughts and say that they are wise, attributing to themselves what belongs to you. Consequently, in the perversity of their blindness they also strive to attribute to you what belongs to them—namely, falsehoods—inflicting lies upon you, who are truth.

They exchange the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and snakes; and they exchange your truth for a lie, worshiping and serving the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:21–25).

6. Nevertheless, I retained from them many true statements drawn from creation itself. Reason presented itself to me through numbers, the order of times, and the visible testimony of the stars; and I compared these with the statements of Manichaeus, who had written very extensively and deliriously about these matters. I could find no reason in his teaching for the solstices and equinoxes, the eclipses of the heavenly bodies, or anything of the sort that I had learned in books of secular wisdom. There I was ordered to believe, and nothing corresponding to the calculations verified by my numbers and my eyes presented itself to me; it was altogether different.

## CHAPTER IV. The knowledge of God alone makes blessed.

7. Is it the case, Lord God of truth, that whoever knows these things already pleases you? Wretched is the person who knows all those things but does not know you; blessed, however, is the one who knows you, even if he does not know those things. And the one who knows both you and them is not more blessed because of them, but is blessed because of you alone, if, knowing you, he glorifies you as God and gives thanks, and does not become futile in his thoughts.

For just as the person who knows how to possess a tree and gives you thanks for its use is better—even if he does not know how many cubits high it is or how widely it spreads—than the one who measures it, counts all its branches, and neither possesses it nor knows or loves its Creator, so the faithful person, whose entire world is a world of riches, and who, as having nothing, possesses all things by clinging to you, whom all things serve—even if he does not know the circuits of the northern constellations—is certainly better than the measurer of the heavens, the counter of the stars, and the weigher of the elements, who neglects you, although you have ordered all things in measure, number, and weight (Wisdom 11:21). There is no doubt of this.

## CHAPTER V. Manichaeus’ ignorance concerning the stars made him unworthy of belief in other matters.

8. Yet who was looking to some Manichaeus to write even about these matters, without knowledge of which piety could still be learned? For you said to humanity: “Behold, piety and wisdom” (Job 28:28, according to the Septuagint). He could have been ignorant of piety even if he had known these things perfectly. But because he did not know them, while audaciously and shamelessly undertaking to teach them, he could certainly not know piety.

It is vanity to profess knowledge even of these worldly matters; piety, however, is to confess you. Therefore that misguided man spoke at great length about these subjects so that, once refuted by those who had truly learned them, the nature of his understanding in the other, more hidden matters might become clearly apparent.

For he did not wish to be thought insignificant. Rather, he attempted to persuade your faithful that the Holy Spirit, their consoler and enrich­er, was personally present in him with full authority. Thus, when he was discovered to have spoken falsely about the heavens and the stars and the movements of the sun and moon—although such matters do not belong to the doctrine of religion—it became sufficiently clear that his audacity was sacrilegious. He asserted these things not merely in ignorance but with such a senseless vanity of pride that he tried to attribute them to himself as though he were a divine person.

[Note: [Col. 0709] This reading is supported by Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., and Flor.]

[Note: [Col. 0709] Thus four English manuscripts. Mart. and Rond., together with some manuscripts, read fulsa, tam, “falsified, so,” a reading that is evidently corrupt.]

9. For when I hear a Christian brother—this one or that one—who is ignorant of these matters and holds one opinion in place of another, I patiently observe the man forming an opinion; nor do I see that it harms him if, concerning you, Lord, the Creator of all things, he believes nothing unworthy, even if he happens to be ignorant of the arrangement and disposition of bodily creation. It does harm, however, if he supposes this to belong to the very form of the doctrine of piety and dares stubbornly to assert what he does not know. Yet even such weakness in the cradle of faith is sustained by charity, its mother, until the new man rises to mature manhood and can no longer be carried about by every wind of doctrine (Ephesians 4:13–14).

But in the case of one who was teacher, author, guide, and leader to those to whom he offered these doctrines, and who dared to act in such a way that his followers believed they were following not merely any human being but your Holy Spirit—who, if he were convicted of having spoken falsely anywhere, would not judge such madness worthy of abhorrence and complete rejection? Nevertheless, I had not yet clearly discovered whether, according to his words, the alternations of longer and shorter days and nights, and of night and day themselves, the eclipses of the heavenly bodies, [Col. 0710] and whatever of this kind I had read in other books could be explained. Thus, if perhaps they could be explained, I would indeed be uncertain whether matters stood that way or otherwise; but, because of the sanctity attributed to him, I would have placed his authority above my faith.

## CHAPTER VI. Faustus eloquent, but without training in the liberal disciplines

10. During nearly those same nine years, while I listened to them with a wandering mind, I awaited the coming of this Faustus with an excessively eager longing. For the others among them whom I happened to encounter, when they failed before the questions I put to them about such matters, promised him to me: with his arrival and a conversation with him, they said, these questions—and any greater ones I might perhaps raise—would most easily and most lucidly be untangled.

Therefore, when he came, I found him a pleasant and agreeable man in speech, chattering much more sweetly about the very things they were accustomed to say. But what was the use to my thirst of a most accomplished server of more precious cups? My ears were already sated with such matters; nor did they seem better to me because they were expressed better, nor true because they were eloquent, nor the soul wise because the face was well matched to the speech and the language graceful.

Those who had promised him to me were not good judges of things; and therefore he seemed prudent and wise to them because they were delighted when he spoke. I also perceived another kind of people who were suspicious even of the truth and unwilling to accept it if it were offered in polished and abundant language.

But you had already taught me, my God, by wondrous and hidden means; and for that reason I believe that you taught me, because what you taught is true, and no one besides you is the teacher of truth, wherever and from whatever source it may shine forth. I had therefore already learned from you that something should not be considered true merely because it is spoken eloquently, nor false because the sounds of the lips come forth without order; and, conversely, that it is not true merely because it is expressed inelegantly, nor false because the speech is splendid. Wisdom and folly are like useful and useless foods: both kinds of food can be served in ornamented or unornamented vessels, just as in elegant or rustic dishes.

11. Accordingly, my eagerness—the eagerness with which I had awaited this man for so long—was delighted by the movement and passion of his disputation, by words that fitted together and readily presented themselves for clothing his thoughts. I was delighted, and, together with many others—or even above many others—I praised and extolled him. But I was troubled that, in the gathering of listeners, I was not allowed to thrust myself upon him and share with him the concerns of my questions, by conversing familiarly, giving and receiving speech.

When I was able to do so, and began to occupy his ears together with my friends, at a time when it would not be improper to converse in turn, I brought forward some matters that troubled me.  
[Note: [Col. 0710] “*Eo quoque*” (“at that same time also”), according to Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. M.] I discovered first that the man was untrained in the liberal disciplines, except for grammar—and even in that only in its ordinary form. Because he had read some of Cicero’s speeches, a very few books of Seneca, and some poetry, as well as whatever volumes of his own sect had been written in Latin and with some elegance; and because he possessed the daily practice of conversation, he had at his disposal an eloquence that became more acceptable and more seductive through the guidance of his intelligence and a certain natural charm.

Is this really how it was, as I recall it, Lord my God, judge of my conscience? Before you are my heart and my memory—you who were then guiding me through the hidden secret of your providence and were already turning my shameful errors before my face, so that I might see and hate them.

## CHAPTER VII. He is alienated from the sect of the Manichaeans

12. After it became sufficiently clear that he was ignorant of those disciplines in which I had thought him excellent, I began to despair that he would be able to explain and resolve for me the matters that troubled me—matters of which, though ignorant, he might still possess the truth of piety, if only he were not a Manichaean.

Their books are full of very long fables about the heavens and the stars, the sun and the moon. I had come to doubt that he could explain these matters with the subtlety I desired, by comparing the numerical calculations I had read elsewhere, and determining whether they were as the books of the Manichaeans claimed, or whether at least an equally plausible account could be given on that basis.

When I brought these matters forward for consideration and examination, he modestly declined to undertake the burden itself. For he knew that he did not know these things, and he was not ashamed to confess it. He was not like the many talkers I had endured, who tried to teach me such matters while saying nothing. This man, however, had a heart, though not rightly directed toward you; and yet he was not excessively incautious with respect to himself. He was not altogether ignorant of his own ignorance, and he did not wish, by arguing rashly, to confine himself within a position from which he could find neither escape nor an easy return. This, too, made me like him more.

The self-restraint of a confessing mind is more beautiful than the knowledge I desired; and I found him like this in all the more difficult and subtle questions.

13. My enthusiasm for the writings of Mani having therefore been broken, and my despair of the other teachers of the sect having grown—since this celebrated man had appeared so inadequate in many matters that troubled me—I began to conduct my life with him according to the enthusiasm with which he himself was devoted to those writings that I was then teaching as a rhetorician to the young men of Carthage.  
[Note: [Col. 0711] “*Quo*” (“by which”), according to Rond. M.] I read with him whatever he desired to hear or whatever I myself thought suited to such an intelligence.

But my entire endeavor, by which I had resolved to advance in that sect, came wholly to an end once I had come to know this man—not so that I separated from them altogether, but because, finding nothing better, I decided for the time being to remain content with the place into which I had already rushed by one means or another, unless something more deserving of choice should perhaps appear.

Thus this Faustus, who had proved a snare of death to many, had already begun to loosen the snare by which I was caught, unwillingly and unknowingly. For your hands, my God, in the hidden depths of your providence, did not abandon my soul. From the blood of my mother’s heart, through her tears offered for me day and night, sacrifice was made to you; and you dealt with me in wondrous ways.  
[Note: “In wondrous and hidden ways,” according to Somm. and Arn., with seven manuscripts, and Rond., with eleven manuscripts.]

You brought this about, my God. For “the steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he wills his way” (Psalm 36:23). And what provision is there for salvation apart from your hand, which restores what you have made?

## CHAPTER VIII. He sets out for Rome against his mother’s will

14. You therefore brought it about that I was persuaded to go to Rome and teach there what I was teaching at Carthage. How I was persuaded of this I will not pass over without confessing it to you, since in these events too your highest purposes and your most present mercy toward us must be considered and proclaimed.  
[Note: [Col. 0712] “*Sit*” (“may be”), according to Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., Dub., Mart., Flor., and Rond. M.]

I did not wish to go to Rome because greater earnings and greater distinction were promised me by friends who urged this course, although these considerations also influenced my mind at that time. The greatest and almost sole reason was that I heard that young men there studied more quietly and were restrained by a more orderly discipline, so that they could not burst into their teacher’s school indiscriminately and insolently; nor were they admitted at all unless he permitted it.

At Carthage, by contrast, there is a disgraceful and uncontrolled license among students. They burst in shamelessly and, with an almost deranged boldness, disturb the order that each teacher has established for the advancement of his pupils. They commit many insults with astonishing stupidity—acts punishable by law, unless custom acts as their patron. This shows them to be all the more wretched, since, as though it were permitted, they do what your eternal law will never permit. They think they act with impunity, although by the very blindness with which they act they are punished, and suffer incomparably worse things than those they inflict.

Thus the customs that, while I was a student, I did not want to be mine, I was compelled to endure as a teacher in others; and therefore I was pleased to go where, everyone who knew the situation told me, such things did not occur.

But you, my true hope and my portion in the land of the living (Psalm 141:6), were secretly using both their perversity and mine to correct my steps. To change the place of my earthly life for the salvation of my soul, you applied goads at Carthage to tear me away from it, and set before me at Rome attractions to draw me there, through people who loved a dead life: here doing insane things, there making empty promises.  
[Note: [Col. 0712] “*Diligebant*” (“loved”), according to Somm., Dub., Arn., Mart., and Rond. M.]

Those who disturbed my leisure were blind with foul madness; those who invited me elsewhere were earthly-minded. But I, who detested genuine misery here, was seeking false happiness there.

15. But why I should leave here and go there, you knew, God; you did not reveal it either to me or to my mother, who bitterly lamented my departure and followed me as far as the sea. I deceived her when she was forcibly holding me back, either to make me return or to travel with me. I pretended that I did not wish to abandon a friend until the wind arose and he sailed. I lied to my mother—and to that mother—and escaped.

You mercifully forgave me this too, preserving me from the waters of the sea, filled as I was with detestable impurities, until I reached the water of your grace, by which, after I had been washed, the streams of my mother’s eyes would be dried—the eyes with which, on my behalf, she daily watered the earth before your face.

Yet when she refused to return without me, I scarcely persuaded her to spend that night at a place near our ship, where there was a memorial of the blessed Cyprian. But that night I secretly departed, while she remained—[Note: The manuscripts, in great agreement, read “she did not remain.” That may perhaps be the more authentic reading, by which the mother is shown to have accompanied her son with her weeping and prayers.]—praying and weeping.

And what were you asking of God, my God, with such abundant tears, except that you would not allow me to sail? But you, taking counsel from above and hearing the central desire of her heart, did not attend to what she was then asking, in order to do for me what she was always asking.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] The manuscripts read “in order to make me” (*ut me faceres*).] The wind blew, filled our sails, and removed the shore from our sight. On that shore she raved in grief, filling your ears—which disregard none of these things—with complaints and groans.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] “*Contemnentes ista*” (“disregarding these things”), according to Lugd., Ven., Lov., Somm., Mart., Flor., and Rond. M.]

At the same time, you were carrying me away through my desires in order to bring those very desires to an end, while her carnal longing was being chastised by the just scourge of sorrow. She loved my presence with her in the manner of mothers, but far more intensely than most; and she did not know what joys you were going to make for her from my absence. She did not know; therefore she wept and wailed, and through those torments the remnant of Eve within her was exposed, as she sought with groaning the one whom she had borne with groaning.  
[Note: We restore this reading from the very ancient Corbie manuscript, since the passage is corrupt in most other manuscripts, which read “the remnants of Eve were exposed in her.” Bad., Am., and Er. follow those manuscripts. Others, wishing to emend the corrupt passage, substitute *rea* (“guilty”) for *in ea* (“in her”), although the manuscripts oppose this. There is no doubt that the passage was first corrupted by scribes to whom the unusual and unfamiliar word *reliquiarium* was unknown. The scribes made the same mistake in Book 1 of the *Questions on Genesis*, question 148, where the more accurate manuscripts prefer “to nourish your *reliquiarium*, according to the Greek of the Septuagint, *cataleipsin*,” rather than “remnants” or “of the remnants,” as others have it. The Corbie manuscript is strengthened by the authority of two Florentine manuscripts.]

Yet, after accusing me of deceit and cruelty, she once more turned to entreat you on my behalf, went back to her customary prayers, and I went to Rome.

## CHAPTER IX. Seized by fever, he suffers dangerously

16. And behold, there I was met by the scourge of bodily illness, and I was descending to the underworld, carrying all the evils I had committed against you, against myself, and against others—many and grievous evils—together with the bond of original sin by which we all die in Adam.

For you had forgiven me none of these things in Christ; nor had he released, upon his cross, the enmity I had contracted against you through my sins.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] This is to be read with the manuscripts, Bad., and Arn., not “in the flesh,” as Am., Er., and Lov. have it, although the apostolic passage to which Augustine alludes has that wording. Here he preferred “nor had he released [them] on his cross,” because he recalled his earlier error with the Manichaeans, in which he denied not Christ’s cross but his flesh.] For how could he release it on the cross of a phantom, which was what I had believed him to be? Thus, as false as the death of his flesh seemed to me, so real was the death of my soul; and as real as the death of his flesh was, so false was the life of my soul, which did not believe it.

As the fever grew worse, I was already departing and perishing. Where would I have gone, if I had then departed from this life, except into the fire and torments deserved by my deeds according to the truth of your order?

She did not know this, yet she prayed for me in my absence. But you, present everywhere, heard her where she was and had mercy on me where I was, so that I might recover my bodily health, though I was still insane in my sacrilegious heart.

For I did not desire your baptism in that great danger; and I was better as a boy, when I urgently requested it out of filial devotion, as I have already recalled and confessed. But I had grown to my disgrace, and, in my madness, mocked the counsels of your medicine—you who did not allow me to die such a death twice. If that wound had pierced my mother’s heart, it would never have been healed. I cannot adequately express what she felt toward me, or with how much greater spiritual anxiety she gave birth to me than that with which she had borne me in the flesh.

17. I therefore do not see how she could have been healed if my death in such a state had pierced the inward parts of her love. And where would there have been such prayers, so frequent and uninterrupted? Nowhere but with you.

Would you, God of mercies, despise the contrite and humbled heart of a chaste and sober widow—one who frequently gave alms, obeyed and served your saints, never omitted an offering at your altar, and came twice each day, morning and evening, without interruption, to your church—not for empty tales and old wives’ chatter, but to hear you in your sermons and to have you hear her in her prayers?

Would you despise her tears, with which she asked you not for gold or silver, nor for any changeable or fleeting good, but for the salvation of her son’s soul? Would you, whose gift had made her such a woman, reject those tears and drive her away from your help? Certainly not, Lord. Rather, you were present, heard her, and acted according to the order you had predestined.

Far be it from you to have deceived her in those visions and responses of yours that I have already mentioned, and in those I have not mentioned, which she kept in a faithful heart and, always praying, presented to you as though they were your written promises. For you deign—because your mercy endures forever—to become a debtor even through your promises to those whose every debt you forgive.

## CHAPTER X. Errors before receiving the teaching of the Gospel

18. You therefore restored me from that illness and saved the son of your handmaid—at that time in body, so that there might remain one to whom you could give a better and more certain salvation.

Even then at Rome I was attached to those false and deceitful “saints”—not only to their hearers, among whom was also the man in whose house I had fallen ill and recovered, but also to those whom they call the Elect.

For it still seemed to me that it was not we who sinned, but some other nature—I knew not what—which sinned within us. My pride delighted in being outside guilt; and when I had done something evil, instead of confessing that I had done it, so that you might heal my soul because it had sinned against you, I loved to excuse it and accuse something else that was with me but was not myself.  
[Note: [Col. 0714] The oldest manuscripts read thus, where the Louvain edition has: “I sinned against you; but I loved to excuse myself.” Somm., Mart., and Rond. M. read “I was sinning” (*peccabam*).] In truth, however, I was wholly myself, and my impiety had divided me against myself. This was the more incurable sin: that I thought myself not to be a sinner. It was an execrable iniquity to prefer that you, almighty God, should be overcome in me—to my destruction—by the nature of evil, as I conceived it, rather than that my evil should be overcome by you for my salvation.  
[Note: Lov. and the older editions read “you from me.” The manuscripts and Arn. more rightly read “you in me,” in accordance with the Manichaean error, according to which they believed a portion of God in man to struggle against the nature of evil.]

You had not yet set a guard over my mouth and a door of restraint around my lips, so that my heart would not turn toward evil words, to make excuses for sins with people who work iniquity; and therefore I was still joining myself to their Elect (Psalm 140:3–4).  
[Note: This alludes to verse 4 of Psalm 140 and follows here and elsewhere a reading of the Septuagint, which has *SUNDUASO* (“I will join myself,” literally “I will pair myself”). We therefore write *combinabam* (“I was joining myself”), following the older manuscripts; other manuscripts have *convivebam*, *combibebam*, *convivabar*, or *communicabam*.]

19. Nevertheless, I was already despairing of making progress in that false doctrine, and I was retaining even those teachings—with which I had decided to remain content if I found nothing better—in a more relaxed and negligent manner.

For the thought had also arisen in me that those philosophers whom they call Academics were wiser than the rest, because they had judged that everything should be doubted and had decided that no truth could be apprehended by human beings. So, as they are commonly understood—and because I did not yet understand their purpose—they seemed to me to have clearly held this view.

Nor did I conceal from my host that I was trying to restrain him from the excessive confidence I perceived him to have in the fabulous matters with which the Manichaean books are filled. Nevertheless, I cultivated their friendship more familiarly than that of the other people who had not belonged to that heresy. I no longer defended it with my former zeal; yet their companionship—for there are many of them hidden in Rome—made me slower to seek something else.

This was especially so because I despaired of finding truth in your Church, Lord of heaven and earth, Creator of all things visible and invisible. They had turned me away from it, and it seemed to me very shameful to believe that you had the form of human flesh and were bounded by the bodily outlines of our limbs.

Since, whenever I wished to think of my God, I knew no way to think except in terms of masses of bodies—for nothing seemed to me to exist that was not such—I was thereby led into an unavoidable error, and this was its chief and almost its sole cause.

20. From this arose my belief that evil too was some kind of substance, possessing a dark and misshapen mass of its own—either coarse, as they said the earth was, or fine and subtle, like the body of air—which they imagine the malignant mind crawling through that earth.

And because whatever piety I possessed compelled me to believe that the good God had created no evil nature, I set up opposite one another two masses, both infinite, but the evil one more restricted and the good one larger.

From this pestilential beginning, all my other sacrileges followed. For whenever my mind tried to return to the Catholic faith, I was driven back, because what I believed to be the Catholic faith was not Catholic at all.

I seemed more pious if I believed you, my God—to whom your mercies confess through me—to be infinite in every respect except that in one direction the mass of evil was opposed to you, and thus I was forced to acknowledge you finite, than if I imagined you bounded on every side in the form of a human body.

It seemed better to me to believe that you had created no evil—which, in my ignorance, appeared to me not only to be some substance but also bodily—because I did not know how to think of a mind except as a subtle body, one that nevertheless extended through the spaces of place, than to believe that the nature of evil was such as I imagined it to be apart from you.  
[Note: Bad., Am., and Er. read “extended from you.” The words *abs te* were removed by the Louvain editors, and we have found them nowhere except in the Regiomontanus manuscript.]

I also imagined our only-begotten Savior, your Son, as though he had been stretched out for our salvation from the mass of your most luminous substance; I believed of him only what I could imagine in my vanity. I therefore thought that such a nature could not be born from the Virgin Mary unless it became entangled with flesh. But I could not see how it could become entangled without being polluted, since I imagined it in such a form. Thus I was afraid to believe that he had been born in the flesh, lest I be compelled to believe that he had been polluted by the flesh.

Now your spiritual people will gently and lovingly laugh at me if they read these confessions of mine; but such was I.

## CHAPTER XI. How Augustine conferred with Catholics

21. I did not think that the objections they had raised against your Scriptures could be defended.  
[Note: “They had raised objections,” according to Mart. and Rond.]

Yet I sometimes earnestly desired to confer with one of the most learned in those books, point by point, and discover what he thought about them.

For even at Carthage the speeches of a certain Helpidius, who spoke and argued publicly against those same Manichaeans, had begun to move me. He brought forward passages from Scripture that could not easily be resisted, and their reply seemed to me weak.

They did not readily produce this reply in public, but told it to us more privately, saying that the Scriptures of the New Testament had been falsified by certain people who wished to insert the law of the Jews into the Christian faith; yet they themselves produced no uncorrupted copies.

But those bodily masses weighed me down most of all and, in a sense, strangled me. I was thinking in bodily terms, and beneath them I could not breathe freely in the clear and simple air of your truth.

## CHAPTER XII. The fraud of the students at Rome against their teachers

22. I therefore began diligently to carry out the task for which I had come: to teach rhetoric at Rome. First I gathered some students in my house, through whom and among whom I had begun to become known.

And behold, I learned that other things occurred at Rome that I had not endured in Africa. For it was made clear to me that those overturnings by ruined young men did not occur there.

“But suddenly,” they said, “so that they may not pay the teacher’s fee, many young men conspire and transfer themselves to another teacher—deserters from their pledged faith, for whom justice is cheap in comparison with love of money.”

My heart hated such people too, though not with perfect hatred. What I was going to suffer from them I perhaps hated more than what they did unlawfully to anyone else.

Yet such people are certainly disgraceful: they fornicate against you by loving the fleeting deceits of time and the muddy profit which, when grasped, stains the hand; by embracing a world that is passing away and despising you, who remain, call them back, and forgive those who return to you—the human soul that has become a prostitute.

Even now I hate such perverse and distorted people, although I love them so that they may be corrected and may prefer the teaching itself, which they are learning, to money; and may prefer you, God, the truth, the abundance of a certain good, and the most chaste peace.

But at that time I was more unwilling to suffer their wickedness on my account than desirous that they should become good for your sake.

## CHAPTER XIII. He is sent to Milan to teach rhetoric and is received by Ambrose

23. After a request had been sent from Milan to the urban prefect that a teacher of rhetoric be provided for that city, and public transportation had also been granted, I myself canvassed those same people intoxicated with Manichaean vanities—the very vanities from which I was going away. Neither of us knew this, so that the prefect Symmachus might send me, after testing me in a public address.

I came to Milan, to Ambrose the bishop, known throughout the world as one of the best, your devoted servant. At that time his discourses diligently supplied your people with the fatness of grain, the joy of oil, and the sober intoxication of wine.

I was led to him by you without knowing it, so that through him I might be led knowingly to you. That man of God received me like a father and, in a manner worthy of a bishop, welcomed my journey.

I began to love him—not at first as a teacher of truth, which I had entirely despaired of finding in your Church, but as a man kindly disposed toward me.

I listened attentively to him when he spoke to the people—not with the attention I ought to have given him, but as though I were examining his eloquence, to see whether it matched his reputation, or whether his speech flowed more or less impressively than had been reported.

I hung upon his words, intent on their sound but unconcerned with their substance; and I stood there delighted by the sweetness of his speech, which was more learned, though less cheerful and soothing in its delivery than Faustus’s.

But there was no comparison between the matters themselves: the former wandered through Manichaean deceptions, whereas the latter taught salvation most healthfully. Yet “salvation is far from sinners,” such as I then was; and nevertheless, gradually and unknowingly, I was drawing near.  
[Note: Thus the English manuscripts agree with ours. Am., Er., and Lov. read “and I did not know”; Somm. and Blas. read “and I was not knowing.”]

## CHAPTER XIV. Having heard Ambrose, he gradually recovers from his errors

24. Since I was not concerned to learn what he said, but only to hear how he said it—for, having already despaired of a way by which a human being might reach you, that empty concern was all that remained to me—the matters I neglected entered my mind together with the words I loved. I could not separate them.

And while I opened my heart to receive how eloquently he spoke, there entered at the same time, though gradually, how truly he spoke.  
[Note: Lov. reads “to be deceived.”]

At first, even the matters themselves began to seem capable of defense; and I began to think that the Catholic faith, about which I had believed nothing could be said against the attacks of the Manichaeans, could be asserted without shame—especially after hearing one or another passage from the ancient Scriptures explained repeatedly through the solution of an enigma. When I took those passages literally, I was killed.  
[Note: Somm. and Rond. read “I was spiritually killed. Therefore.”]

When most of those books’ passages had thus been explained spiritually, I began to condemn my despair—specifically the despair by which I had believed that no resistance at all could be made to those who detested and mocked the Law and the Prophets.

Yet I did not therefore feel that I should now hold to the Catholic way, simply because it too could have learned defenders who might refute the objections fully and without absurdity; nor did I therefore already condemn what I held, because the two sides seemed equally matched in defense. The Catholic faith did not appear defeated to me, but neither did it yet appear victorious.

25. I then applied my mind vigorously to discovering whether I could somehow convict the Manichaeans of falsehood by certain proofs. If I could think of a spiritual substance, all those contrivances would immediately be undone and cast out of my mind—but I could not.

Nevertheless, as I considered and compared matters more and more, I judged that most philosophers had held many views about the body of this world and every nature accessible to the senses of the flesh that were more probable.

Accordingly, following the manner in which the Academics are thought to proceed—doubting everything and wavering among all possibilities—I decided that the Manichaeans should be abandoned. I did not think that, at that very time of my doubt, I should remain in that sect, since I was already placing certain philosophers above it.

Yet I refused entirely to entrust the healing of my soul’s illness to those philosophers, because they lacked the saving name of Christ. I therefore resolved to remain a catechumen in the Catholic Church, commended to me by my parents, until some certainty should appear by which I could direct my course.

# BOOK SIX

By this time Monnica, his mother, had arrived at Milan, and he himself was entering his thirtieth year. Warned by Ambrose’s sermons, he was increasingly coming to understand the truth of Catholic doctrine, which the Manichaeans falsely accused. He continues with the account of the character of his friend Alypius. He was drawn in different directions while deliberating how to order his life better; and, struck also by fear of death and judgment, he was daily inflamed toward a change of life.

[Col. 0717]

## CHAPTER I. Augustine neither a Manichaean nor a Catholic

1. My hope from my youth, where were you for me, and where had you withdrawn? Had you not made me and set me apart from the four-footed animals and the birds of heaven? You had made me wiser, and I was walking through darkness and slippery places. I was seeking you outside myself and did not find the God of my heart. I had come into the depths of the sea, and I distrusted and despaired of finding the truth.

My mother had already come to me, strong in piety, following me by land and sea, secure in you amid every danger. For even during the perils of the sea she comforted the sailors themselves, whom inexperienced travelers of the abyss customarily comfort when they are distressed, promising them a safe arrival because you had promised this to her in a vision.
