She found me in grave danger, indeed, through my despair of discovering the truth. But when I told her that I was no longer a Manichaean, though I was not yet a Catholic Christian either, she did not leap for joy as though she had heard something unexpected. She had already become confident regarding that part of my misery over which she had wept to you as though I were dead but destined to be raised again; in the bier of her thought she carried me forth so that you might say to the son of the widow, “Young man, I say to you, arise,” and he might revive, begin to speak, and you might give him to his mother (Luke 7:14–15).

Her heart therefore did not tremble with any turbulent exultation when she heard that so much of what she daily wept to you should come to pass had already occurred: I had not yet attained the truth, but I had been rescued from falsehood.

Indeed, because she was certain that you, who had promised everything, would give what remained, she replied to me with the greatest calm and a heart full of confidence that she believed in Christ: before she departed this life, she would see me a faithful Catholic.

To you, however, fountain of mercies, she poured forth more abundant prayers and tears, so that you might hasten your help and enlighten my darkness; and I began to run more eagerly to the Church and to hang upon Ambrose’s lips, at the fountain of water springing up into eternal life (John 4:14).  
[Note: The manuscript of Alb. adds “to pour forth.”]

She loved that man as an angel of God, because through him she had learned that I had by then been brought to that state of uncertain wavering by which, she confidently presumed, I would pass from sickness to health through an intervening and more severe danger, as through the crisis that physicians call a critical turn.  
[Note: “A sharper danger,” according to Er., Lugd., and Lov.]

## CHAPTER II. Feasts and the gathering at the martyrs’ tombs
## 2. Therefore, when she had brought to the memorial shrines of the saints, as was customary in Africa, gruel, bread, and unmixed wine, and was prevented by the doorkeeper, as soon as she learned that the bishop had forbidden this, she embraced the prohibition so devoutly and obediently that I myself wondered [Note: [Col. 0719] Thus the manuscripts and Am., Er., Arn.; but Bad. and Lov. read *miraretur*.] how easily she became an accuser of her own custom [Note: [Col. 0719] Although the custom in question had long been accepted throughout Africa, because it had degenerated into feasting and drunkenness, Augustine likewise undertook to abolish it. He writes about this in Letter 22, to Aurelius of Carthage. Indeed, while not yet a bishop, he himself completely withdrew the Church of Hippo from this practice, as Letter 29, to Alypius, makes clear.], rather than a disputant against that prohibition.

For wine-drinking did not besiege her spirit, nor did love of wine spur her to hate the truth, as happens to many men and women who, at the song of sobriety, nauseate as though at watered drink when they are drunk. But when she had brought a basket with the customary foods, to be tasted beforehand and distributed, she did not set down more than a single little cup—tempered sufficiently for her very sober palate—from which she might herself partake. And if there were many memorials of the dead that seemed to require such honor, she carried around the same single measure, which she would distribute in tiny sips among those present with her, now not only very heavily watered but also very tepid [Note: [Col. 0720] Somm., Arn., Dub., Flor., and Rond. read: “which was not only very heavily watered ...”; other copies read: “which was now not only very heavily watered.”]. For she sought piety there, not pleasure.

Therefore, when she learned from that outstanding preacher and bishop of piety that this practice had been forbidden—not even by those who observed it soberly, lest it provide drunkards with any opportunity to gorge themselves, and because it was almost identical with the pagan custom of honoring the dead—she abstained from it most willingly. In place of a basket full of earthly fruits, she learned to bring to the memorial shrines a heart full of more purified vows, so that she might give to the needy whatever she could give, and so that the communion of the Lord’s body might be celebrated there: in imitation of whose passion the martyrs had been sacrificed and crowned.

Yet it seems to me, my Lord God—and thus my heart stands in your sight concerning this matter—that my mother would perhaps not easily have given up this custom if she had been forbidden by someone whom she did not love as she loved Ambrose, whom she loved chiefly because of my salvation. He, in turn, loved her because of her most devout way of life, by which, fervent in spirit in good works, she frequently attended church. Thus, when he saw me, he would often burst into praise of her [Note: [Col. 0720] Lov., Somm., and Blas. read: “in her praise.”], congratulating me that I had such a mother—without knowing what kind of son she had in me, who doubted all those things and thought that the way of life could scarcely be found.

## CHAPTER III. Ambrose’s occupations and studies

### 3.

I no longer groaned in prayer that you might come to my aid; but my mind was intent on seeking and restless in discussion. I regarded Ambrose as a happy man according to the standards of this world, one whom such great powers honored; only his celibacy seemed burdensome to me. What hope he possessed, however; what struggles he endured against the temptations of his own excellence; what consolation he had in adversity; what his hidden mouth was—that is, his heart—and what savory joys he chewed over from your bread: I neither knew how to conjecture nor had experienced. Nor did he know my anxieties or the pit of my danger.

For I could not ask him what I wished, in the way I wished, because crowds of busy people, whose weaknesses he served, kept me from his hearing and his speech. When he was not with them—and that was for only a very brief time—he was either restoring his body with the necessities of nourishment or his mind with reading. When he read, however, his eyes traveled across the pages and his heart searched out the meaning, while his voice and tongue were silent.

Often when we were present—for no one was forbidden to enter, nor was it customary for anyone to announce to him the arrival of visitors—we saw him reading silently, and never otherwise. Sitting in prolonged silence—for who would dare to burden someone so intent?—we would leave. We supposed that, in that brief time which he obtained for restoring his mind, he wished to be free from the noise of other people’s affairs and did not want to be called away to something else. Perhaps he was also taking care lest, if the reader had put something less clearly, he should be required to explain it to a listener who was suspended in attention; or lest he should have to debate some more difficult questions and, by spending time on that task, turn fewer volumes than he wished. There could also have been a more just reason for his reading silently: preserving his voice, which was very easily strained.

Whatever his purpose in doing so, that good man was certainly acting well.

### 4.

But I was given no opportunity to ask what I wished about so holy an oracle of your truth within his heart, except when something could be heard briefly. My anxieties, however, needed someone with abundant leisure to whom they could be poured out, and they never found such a person.

Every Sunday I heard him rightly handling the word of truth before the people, and I became increasingly convinced that all the knots of the crafty accusations which those deceivers of ours tied against the divine Books could be untied. When I also learned that the human being whom you made in your image was not understood by your spiritual children, whom you regenerated by grace from the womb of the Catholic Church, as though they believed and thought that you were bounded by the form of a human body—although I had not even the faintest suspicion, not even in an enigma, of what the nature of spiritual substance might be—I rejoiced and was ashamed that for so many years I had barked not against the Catholic faith, but against the fabrications of bodily imaginings.

For I had been rash and impious in saying, by accusing, what I ought to have learned by inquiry [Note: [Col. 0721] The manuscripts read *dicere* (“to say”) rather than *discere* (“to learn”).]. You, most high and most near, most secret and most present, who have no members larger or smaller but are wholly everywhere and nowhere confined by place—you are certainly not this bodily form. Yet you made the human being in your image; and behold, that human being is located in a place from head to foot.

## CHAPTER IV. He understands the Church’s doctrine while Ambrose preaches

### 5.

Since, then, I did not know how this image of yours could exist, I raised the question, asking how one ought to believe, not insolently objecting as though this were how it was believed [Note: [Col. 0721] This is how it should be read according to the manuscripts, Somm., and Arn.; Lov. and the other printed editions read *pulsansque* (“and knocking”).]. The more deeply I was ashamed of having been deceived and deluded for so long by the promise of certainty, and of having, through childish error and obstinacy, chattered about so many uncertain things as though they were certain, the more sharply an anxiety gnawed my inmost being concerning what certainty I should retain.

Later it became clear to me that those teachings were false. Yet it was certain that they were uncertain and that I had once taken them for certainties, when in my blind disputes I accused your Catholic Church—even though I had not yet discovered that it taught the truth, I nevertheless knew that it did not teach the things of which I so gravely accused it.

Therefore I was confounded and converted. And I rejoiced, my God, that your one Church, the body of your Only-Begotten One, in which the name of Christ had been impressed upon me when I was an infant, did not savor childish nonsense [Col. 0722] [Note: [Col. 0722] After the word “Church,” the printed editions add “your,” a word absent from the manuscripts.], nor did it possess in its sound doctrine the notion that you, the creator of all things, were compressed into the space of a place—however immense and vast—yet bounded on every side by the form of human limbs.

### 6.

I also rejoiced that the ancient writings of the Law and the Prophets were now being presented to me for reading with eyes different from those with which they had previously seemed absurd, when I accused your saints as though they held such views. They did not hold them. And I was glad to hear Ambrose often saying in his public sermons, commending it as a rule with the greatest care: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). When he opened spiritually, after removing the mystical veil, those passages which seemed, if taken literally, to teach perversity, he said nothing that offended me, although he said things whose truth I did not yet know.

I kept my heart from every assent, fearing a precipice; yet I was being killed all the more by suspense. I wanted to become as certain about what I could not see as I was certain that seven and three make ten. I was not so insane as to think that even this could not be grasped. But just as I desired certainty about this, so I desired it about everything else—whether bodily things that were not present before my senses, or spiritual things, which I did not know how to conceive except bodily.

I could have been healed by believing, so that the purified vision of my mind might somehow be directed toward your truth, which always remains and never fails from itself. But just as it commonly happens that someone who has experienced a bad doctor is afraid to entrust himself even to a good one, so was the condition of my soul. It could not be healed except by believing, yet it refused treatment lest it believe falsehood. It resisted your hands, though you had prepared the medicines of faith, scattered them over the illnesses of the world, and granted them such great authority.

## CHAPTER V. The authority of the sacred Books and their necessary use

### 7.

Nevertheless, because I was now giving preference to Catholic teaching, I thought that it was more modest and entirely free from deceit to be commanded there to believe what was not demonstrated—whether it was something that existed but perhaps not for that person, or whether it did not exist at all—than to have credulity mocked there by a rash promise of knowledge, followed by orders to believe so many fabulous and absurd things because they could not be demonstrated.

Then, little by little, you, Lord, with the gentlest and most merciful hand, touched and arranged my heart. I considered how innumerable were the things I believed without seeing them [Note: [Col. 0722] *Videram* (“I had seen”), according to Mart. M.], things at which I had not been present when they occurred: so many events in the histories of peoples; so many facts about places and cities I had not seen; so many things told by friends, by physicians, and by all sorts of other people. Unless these things were believed, we would do absolutely nothing in this life.

Finally, I considered how firmly I held by faith the identity of my parents, something I could not know unless I had believed what I heard. You persuaded me that the people who believed your Books—which you had established with such authority among almost all peoples—were not to be blamed, and that those who refused to believe should not be heeded if they happened to say to me: “How do you know that those Books were given to the human race by the Spirit of the one true and most truthful God?”

That was precisely what had to be believed most firmly, because no contentiousness arising from slanderous questions, amid the many conflicting philosophers I had read, could ever force me not to believe that you were whatever you were—something I did not know—or that the administration of human affairs belonged to you.

### 8.

Yet I believed this sometimes more strongly and sometimes more weakly; nevertheless, I always believed both that you exist and that you care for us, even though I did not know either what should be thought about your substance or what path leads or leads back to you.

And so, since we were weak in discovering the truth by clear reasoning, and therefore needed the authority of the sacred Scriptures, I had already begun to believe that you would never have granted such outstanding authority to that Scripture throughout all lands unless you had wished that you should be believed through it and that you should be sought through it.

For when I heard many passages from those Books expounded plausibly, I referred the absurdity that had previously offended me in them to the depth of their mysteries. Their authority appeared to me more venerable and more worthy of sacred faith precisely because it was readily available to everyone for reading while preserving the dignity of its secret in a deeper understanding. It presented itself to all in words of the greatest clarity and in the humblest style of speech, exercising the attention of those who are not lighthearted, so that it might receive everyone into its popular embrace and convey a few through narrow openings to you—yet many more than it would have conveyed if it had neither stood out with such a pinnacle of authority nor gathered the crowds into the lap of holy humility.

I reflected on these things, and you were with me. I sighed, and you heard me. I fluctuated, and you guided me. I traveled along the broad road of the world, and you did not abandon me.

## CHAPTER VI. The misery of ambitious people, illustrated by the example of a joyful beggar

### 9.

I longed for honors, profits, and marriage, while you mocked me. I suffered the bitterest difficulties in those desires, though you were gracious toward me—more gracious the less you allowed what was not you to become sweet to me.

See my heart, Lord, who wished me to remember and confess this to you. Now let my soul cling to you, whom you have stripped from the glue of death so tenaciously adhering to it. How wretched it was! You pricked the awareness of its wound so that, abandoning everything, it might turn to you who are above all things and without whom nothing would exist; that it might turn and be healed.

How wretched I was, then, and how you acted so that I should feel my misery, on the day when I was preparing to recite praises before the Emperor [Note: [Col. 0723] Perhaps before Valentinian the Younger, since, according to Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 1, his “court was then established at Milan,” when Augustine was teaching rhetoric there. Moreover, in *Against the Letters of Petilian*, book 3, chapter 25, Augustine writes that in the same city he “recited praise for the consul Bauton on the Kalends of January, in fulfillment of his profession of rhetoric at that time.”]—praises containing many lies, for which those who knew the truth would nevertheless favor the liar—while my heart panted after these concerns and burned with the fevers of thoughts that consumed me.

As I passed through a certain street of Milan, I noticed a poor beggar, already, I think, satisfied, joking and rejoicing. I groaned and spoke with the friends who were with me about the many pains of our madness. Under the goads of desire, I was then dragging along the burden of my unhappiness through all such efforts as those with which I was laboring, increasing it by dragging it along. We wished nothing else than to reach secure joy, a place to which that beggar had already preceded us, though we might perhaps never reach it.

What he had already obtained with a few coins begged from others, I was seeking through such sorrowful twists and turns: namely, temporal happiness. He did not possess true joy, but I was seeking it through those ambitions much more falsely. Certainly he was joyful while I was anxious; he was secure while I trembled.

If someone had asked me whether I preferred to rejoice or to fear, I would have answered, “To rejoice.” If he had asked again whether I preferred to be as that man was or as I then was, I would have chosen myself, worn out by cares and fears—but perversely, not truthfully. For I ought not to have preferred myself to him because I was more educated, since I did not rejoice in that education but sought to please people through it—not to teach them, but merely to please them. Therefore, with the staff of your discipline, you were also breaking my bones.

### 10.

Let those who say to my soul, “It matters what a person rejoices in,” depart from it. That beggar rejoiced in drunkenness; you wished to rejoice in glory. What glory, Lord? Glory that is not in you. For just as his joy was not true, so neither was that glory true; and it turned my mind even more.

That man was going to sleep off his drunkenness that very night. I had slept with my anxiety, had risen with it, and was going to sleep and rise with it again—consider for how many days.

It certainly matters what a person rejoices in, I know; and the joy of faithful hope is incomparably different from that vanity. But even then there was a difference between us. Clearly he was happier—not only because he was drenched in merriment while I was being disemboweled by cares, but also because he had obtained his wine by wishing for it, whereas I was seeking an inflated reputation by lying.

I said many things along these lines to my dear friends, and I often observed in them what my own condition was. I discovered that I was in a bad way; I grieved, and by grieving I doubled the very evil. If anything favorable smiled upon me, I was reluctant to seize it, because almost before it could be held, it flew away.

## CHAPTER VII. He turns Alypius away from the madness of the Circus

### 11.

We groaned together over these things, we who lived together in friendship, and I discussed them especially and most familiarly with Alypius and Nebridius. Alypius had come from the same municipal town as I, from parents who were leading citizens of the town, and he was younger than I.

He had studied under me when I began teaching in our own town, and later at Carthage. He loved me greatly because I seemed to him good and learned, and I loved him because of the great promise of virtue that stood out in him even at a relatively young age [Col. 0725].

Yet the whirlpool of Carthaginian customs, where frivolous spectacles burn fiercely, had swallowed him into the madness of the Circus. While he was being miserably swept about in it, I was teaching rhetoric there and using a public lecture hall. He did not yet listen to me as a teacher because a certain dispute had arisen between me and his father. I had learned that he loved the Circus disastrously, and I was deeply distressed, since he seemed destined either to lose—or already to have lost—such great promise.

But I had no opportunity to admonish him or recall him by some restraint, whether because of the goodwill of our friendship or because of my authority as his teacher. I thought that he shared his father’s feelings toward me, but that was not so. Therefore, setting aside his father’s wishes in this matter, he began to greet me, coming into my lecture hall, listening to something, and then departing.

### 12.

But I had forgotten to deal with him so that his excellent talent might not be destroyed by the blind and headlong passion for empty games. Yet you, Lord, who preside over the helm of all that you have created, had not forgotten that he would one day become a bishop among your children, administering your sacrament. And so that his correction might clearly be attributed to you, you accomplished it through me, although I did not know it.

One day, when I was sitting in my customary place with my students before me, he came, greeted me, sat down, and paid attention to what was taking place. As it happened, a reading was at hand. While I was explaining it, and a comparison with the Circus seemed appropriately useful to make what I was conveying more pleasant and clearer, I mocked with biting irony those whom that madness had captivated.

You know, our God, that at that moment I was not thinking of healing Alypius from that plague. But he took the words personally and believed that I had said them only on his account. What another person might have taken as an occasion for anger against me, that honorable young man took as an occasion for anger against himself and for loving me more ardently.

For you had said long ago and woven it into your Scriptures: “Reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Prov. 9:8). I had not, in fact, reproved him; but, using everything—those who knew and those who did not know—in the order known to you, and in the order that is just, you made burning coals from my heart and tongue, with which you scorched and healed a mind wasting away, yet possessing good hope.

Let him be silent in praising you who does not consider your mercies, which confess you from the depths of my being. For after those words he tore himself out of the pit so deep into which he willingly descended and in whose miserable pleasure he was blinded [Note: [Col. 0725] Three English manuscripts read: “with wondrous pleasure.”]. He shook his mind free through strong self-control, and all the filth of the Circus sprang away from him. He never went there again.

Then he overcame his resisting father so that he might use me as his teacher. His father yielded and consented. Beginning to listen to me again, Alypius became entangled with me in that superstition, loving the ostentatious continence of the Manichaeans, which I thought true and genuine. It was in fact foolish and deceptive, ensnaring precious souls who did not yet know how to touch the heights of virtue and were easily deceived by appearances, though it was nevertheless a shadow and imitation of virtue.

## CHAPTER VIII. Alypius is seized by the madness of gladiatorial games, although he had previously detested them

[Col. 0726]

### 13.

Without abandoning the earthly path that had been charmed for him by his parents, he had gone ahead to Rome to study law. There he was seized with incredible force, and incredibly carried away, by the gaping attraction of the gladiatorial spectacle.

Although he detested and abhorred such things, some of his friends and fellow students, returning from a meal, happened to encounter him on the way [Note: [Col. 0726] “They encountered him,” according to Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., and Mart.; “They encountered him on the road,” according to Somm. and Rond.]. He refused vehemently and resisted, saying: “If you drag my body into that place and set it there, can you also turn my mind and eyes toward those spectacles? I shall be present while absent, and in this way I shall overcome both you and them.”

When they heard this, they nevertheless brought him along with them, perhaps wishing to test whether he could actually do what he had said. When they arrived and took whatever seats they could, everything was seething with the most savage pleasures.

He shut the doors of his eyes and forbade his mind to advance into such evils. If only he had also stopped his ears! For, when a great roar from the entire crowd struck him forcefully in the course of some chance in the combat, overcome by curiosity and as though prepared to despise and overcome whatever it might be even by seeing it, he opened his eyes.

He was struck in his soul by a wound more severe than that in the body of the man whom he desired to see. Alypius fell more miserably than the man whose fall produced the shout that entered through his ears and opened his eyes, so that his still daring rather than courageous mind might have something by which it could be struck down; and it was all the weaker because it had presumed upon itself rather than upon you.

When he saw that blood, he immediately drank in savagery. He did not turn away but fixed his gaze. He absorbed the madness without knowing it, delighted in the wickedness of the combat, and became intoxicated with the pleasure of bloodshed.

He was no longer the man who had come, but one of the crowd into which he had come, a true companion of those by whom he had been brought there. What more need I say? He watched, shouted, became inflamed, and carried away with him the madness that would urge him to return—not only with those who had first dragged him away, but even ahead of them, dragging others along.

Yet from that place you eventually snatched him out with your powerful and most merciful hand, and taught him to place his confidence not in himself but in you—though only much later.

## CHAPTER IX. Alypius is arrested as a thief

### 14.

Nevertheless, this event was already being stored in his memory for the sake of his future healing. So too was what happened when he was still studying under me at Carthage. At midday, while he was thinking in the forum about what he was going to recite, as students commonly practice, you allowed him to be seized by the officials of the forum as though he were a thief.

I do not believe, our God, that you permitted this for any other reason than that this man, who was destined to become so great, might already begin to learn how difficult it is for one human being to condemn another through rash credulity when the facts of a case have not been distinguished.

He was walking alone before the tribunal, carrying writing tablets and a stylus, when suddenly a certain young man from among the students—a genuine thief—secretly brought an axe. Without Alypius noticing, he entered the enclosure beneath the lead grilles that project above the silversmiths’ street and began cutting through the lead.

When the sound of the axe was heard, the silversmiths below murmured among themselves and sent men to seize whoever they might find. Hearing their voices, the thief abandoned his tool and departed, fearing that he might be caught with it.

Alypius, who had not seen the man enter, noticed him leaving and quickly saw him going away. Curious to know the reason, he entered the place and found the axe. He stood examining it in amazement.

At that moment, the men who had been sent found him alone carrying the iron whose sound had aroused them. They seized and dragged him away. After the inhabitants of the forum had gathered, they boasted that they had caught a manifest thief, and he was being led away to be presented to the judge.

### 15.

But this was as far as he needed to be instructed. Immediately, Lord, you came to the aid of the innocence of which you alone were witness.

As he was being led either to imprisonment or to punishment, a certain architect met them, a man responsible for the public buildings and deeply concerned with them. They rejoiced that this particular man had encountered them, for they were accustomed to be suspected by him of having stolen objects that had disappeared from the forum. They thought that at last he would discover who was responsible for such deeds.

But this man had often seen Alypius in the house of a certain senator whom he regularly visited to pay his respects. He immediately recognized him, took him by the hand, and pulled him away from the crowd. Seeking the cause of such a grave misfortune, he heard what had happened and ordered all who were present—those shouting tumultuously and growling threats—to come with him.

They came to the house of the young man who had committed the crime. The boy was in front of the door and was so young that, fearing nothing from his master, he could easily reveal everything. For the boy had been that young man’s attendant in the forum.

When Alypius remembered the servant, he informed the architect. The architect showed the boy the axe and asked whose it was. He immediately replied, “Ours,” and, when questioned further, disclosed the rest.

Thus the matter was transferred to that household, and the crowd that had already begun to triumph over Alypius was confounded. The man destined to become an administrator of your word and an examiner of many cases in your Church departed from the affair more experienced and better instructed.

## CHAPTER X. Alypius’ integrity and Nebridius’ arrival

### 16.

I had found Alypius in Rome, and he became attached to me by an exceptionally strong bond. He went with me to Milan, both so that he would not leave me and so that he might practice something in the law he had learned, more in accordance with his parents’ wishes than his own.

He had already served three times as an assessor [Note: [Col. 0727] Bad., Am., Er., and Blas. read “and there.” Lov. and Somm. read “and during this time.” But the more numerous and better manuscripts, together with Arn., read: “And he had already served three times as an assessor.” We have preferred this reading, since Alypius is also said later to have served a third term as assessor, in book 8, chapter 6: “Alypius was with me, free from the work of the lawyers after his third term as assessor, waiting to see to whom he might once again sell his advice.”] with remarkable self-restraint, while he wondered all the more at those who preferred gold to innocence.

His character was also tested not only by the lure of greed but by the goad of fear. At Rome he was serving as assessor to the count of the Italian largesses [Note: [Col. 0728] Lov. reads *Italicarum* (“of the Italian [largesses]”); but the ancient manuscripts read *Italicianarum*, as it is also written in the *Notitia Dignitatum* of the Empire and by those who discuss the official responsible for distributions to be made in Italy.].

At that time there was a certain extremely powerful senator, whose favors bound many people to him and whose authority made many his subjects. He wished to be permitted to do something, according to the custom of his power, that was unlawful under the laws. Alypius resisted. A reward was promised; he dismissed it with contempt. Threats were held out; he trampled them underfoot.

Everyone marveled at a spirit so unusual: a man who neither desired as a friend nor feared as an enemy someone who was merely human, though celebrated by immense fame and by innumerable means of conferring benefits or doing harm.

The judge whose counselor Alypius was did not wish to comply either, but he did not openly refuse. Instead, he shifted the matter onto Alypius, claiming that he was prevented by him, since in fact, if the judge acted, Alypius would withdraw.

Alypius had almost been enticed by his literary interests alone, to the point of arranging for books to be copied at praetorian prices. But after consulting justice, he changed his deliberation for the better, judging the equity that prohibited him more useful than the power that permitted him.

This is a small matter; but “whoever is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much.” Nor will what proceeded from the mouth of your Truth be empty: “If you have not been faithful in unrighteous mammon, who will entrust the true riches to you? And if you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is yours?” (Luke 16:10–12.)

Such was Alypius then, clinging to me and wavering with me in our deliberation over what way of life should be pursued.

### 17.

Nebridius also had left his nearby homeland, Carthage itself—where he was constantly present—and his excellent paternal estate, as well as his house and his mother, who would not follow him. He had come to Milan for no other reason than to live with me in the most ardent pursuit of truth and wisdom.

He sighed along with me and fluctuated along with me: an ardent seeker of the blessed life and a most acute investigator of the most difficult questions. We were the mouths of three needy men, panting toward one another in our poverty and waiting for you to give us food at the proper time.

In all the bitterness that followed our worldly activities because of your mercy, whenever we looked toward the end and asked why we were suffering these things, darkness confronted us. Groaning, we turned away [Note: [Col. 0728] B. reads *adversabamur* (“we opposed”). Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., Somm., Arn., Dub., Mart., Flor., and Rond. also read *adversabamur*.] and said, “How long will this last?” We said this frequently, yet in saying it we did not abandon those activities, because no certain alternative shone forth which we could grasp after abandoning them.

## CHAPTER XI. Augustine anxiously deliberates about establishing a way of life

### 18.

I was especially astonished, as I labored and recalled how much time had passed since my nineteenth year, when I had begun to burn with the pursuit of wisdom and had planned, once I found it, to abandon all the empty hopes and deceptive madnesses of vain desires.

And now I was already thirty, still stuck in the same mire, greedy to enjoy present things that were fleeing and dissipating me, while I said: “Tomorrow I shall find it. Behold, it will become clear, and I shall grasp it. Behold, Faustus will come and explain everything.”

O great men of the Academy! Nothing certain can be grasped for the conduct of life. Rather, let us investigate more diligently and not despair. Behold, the things in the ecclesiastical Books that seemed absurd are no longer absurd and can be understood in another and honorable way.

I shall plant my feet on the step where my parents placed me when I was a child, until the transparent truth is found. But where will it be sought? When will it be sought? Ambrose has no leisure; he has no leisure to read. Where shall we look for the Books themselves? From where, or when, shall we obtain them? From whom shall we borrow them? Let times be assigned; let hours be distributed for the salvation of the soul.

A great hope has arisen: the Catholic faith does not teach what we thought, and what we foolishly accused it of teaching. Its learned adherents regard it as impious to believe that God is bounded by the figure of a human body. And do we hesitate to knock, so that the rest may be opened to us?

The students occupy the morning hours [Note: [Col. 0729] “Hours,” according to Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., Somm., Flor., and Rond.]. What shall we do with the remaining time? Why do we not pursue this? But when shall we pay our respects to influential friends whose support we need? When shall we prepare what the students will purchase? When shall we restore ourselves by relaxing our minds from the strain of our cares?

### 19.

Let everything perish, and let us abandon these vain and empty things. Let us devote ourselves solely to the search for truth. This life is miserable; death is uncertain. If it suddenly overtakes us, how shall we leave this life? And where shall we learn what we have neglected here? Or should we not rather suffer the punishments for this negligence?

What if death itself will remove and end all care together with consciousness? This too, then, must be investigated. But far be it from us that this should be so. It is not without significance that so eminent a summit of authority belonging to the Christian faith is spread throughout the whole world. Such great and remarkable things would never be divinely accomplished for us if bodily death also consumed the life of the soul.

Why, then, do we hesitate—abandoning the hope of the world—to devote ourselves entirely to seeking God and the blessed life? But wait: these things too are pleasant. They have their own considerable sweetness. One must not easily cut oneself off from them, because it is shameful to return to them afterward.

Behold, how little remains before some honor is obtained! And what more is there to desire in these matters? There is an abundance of influential friends. If nothing else, and if we hurry greatly, a governorship can be obtained. A wife can also be taken, with some money, so that she will not burden our expenses; and that will be the limit of our desire. Many great men, highly worthy of imitation, devoted themselves to the pursuit of wisdom while married.

### 20.

While I was saying these things, and these winds alternated and drove my heart here and there, time passed. I delayed turning to the Lord, and I postponed from day to day living in you, while I did not postpone dying in myself each day.

Loving the blessed life, I feared it in its proper dwelling; and while fleeing from it, I sought it. For I thought I would be excessively wretched if I were deprived of women’s embraces. I did not consider the medicine of your mercy for healing that very weakness, because I had not experienced it. I believed continence to be a matter of my own strength, though I was not conscious of possessing such strength—so foolish was I that I did not know, as it is written, that no one can be continent unless you grant it (Wis. 8:21).

Certainly you would grant it if, with an inward groaning, I knocked at your ears and cast my care upon you with firm faith.

## CHAPTER XII. The dispute between Alypius and Augustine concerning marriage and celibacy
21. Alypius was indeed trying to dissuade me from taking a wife, arguing that in no way could we live together in the secure leisure of the love of wisdom, as we had long desired, if I did so. [Note: [Col. 0730] *Cantans* (“singing”), according to Arn. Flor. and Mart., on the basis of six manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0730] *Desideraveramus* (“we had desired”), according to Somm. Rond. and Mart., on the basis of three manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0730] Lov. and Blas., with several manuscripts, read *delicatus* (“pampered”); Somm. and Arn., *delectatus* (“delighted”). Manuscripts of better authority support our reading.] For even then he himself was exceptionally chaste in this matter, so much so that it was remarkable: he had perhaps experienced intercourse at the beginning of his adolescence, but he had not become attached to it; rather, he had been distressed by it and rejected it, and thereafter lived in the utmost continence.

I, however, resisted him, citing the examples of those who, though married, had cultivated wisdom, won God’s favor, and faithfully possessed and loved their friends. Yet I was far removed from their greatness of spirit. Bound by the disease of the flesh and its deadly sweetness, I was dragging my chain, afraid to be released and, as though from a shaken wound, repelling the words of one who was giving good advice, as though he were a hand trying to loosen me. Moreover, through me the serpent itself was also speaking to Alypius, weaving and scattering through my tongue sweet snares in his path, in which his honorable and unencumbered feet might become entangled.

22. For when he marveled at me—although he did not despise me—for clinging so tenaciously to the glue of that pleasure that, whenever we discussed the matter between ourselves, I insisted that a celibate life could in no way be lived; and when, seeing his astonishment, I defended myself by saying that there was a great difference between that which he himself had experienced hastily and secretly, which he could scarcely even remember and therefore could easily disregard without any distress, and the pleasures of my habitual practice—which, if accompanied by the honorable name of marriage, he ought not to find astonishing, so that he should not wonder why I could not despise that life—he himself had begun to desire marriage, not at all overcome by lust for such pleasure, but out of curiosity.

For he said that he wanted to know what that thing was without which my life, which pleased him so greatly, seemed to me not life but punishment. His spirit, free from that bondage, was astonished at my slavery; and, in its astonishment, it moved toward a desire to experience it, destined to arrive at the experience itself and perhaps thereby to fall into the slavery at which it marveled. For he wanted to make a wager with death; and “whoever loves danger will fall into it.” Neither of us, however, was guided except faintly by whatever marital honor there may be in the duty of governing a household and begetting children. For the greater part, and with great force, habit in satisfying insatiable desire held me captive and tormented me; while astonishment drew him toward captivity.

So we remained until you, Most High, without abandoning our earthly condition, took pity on us in our misery and came to our aid by wondrous and hidden means.

### CHAPTER XIII. A Wife Is Sought for Augustine

23. And the effort to make me take a wife was pursued energetically. I was already asking for one, and one was already being promised, chiefly through my mother’s efforts, so that once I was married, saving Baptism might wash me clean—the Baptism toward which she rejoiced to see me being fitted day by day—and so that she might see her own vows and your promises fulfilled in my faith.

Indeed, at my request and in accordance with her own desire, she daily begged you with a strong cry of the heart to show her something in a vision concerning my future marriage; but you never willed it. She did see certain empty and phantasmal things, produced by the force that drives the human spirit when it is consumed with anxious concern over such a matter, and she told me about them—not with the confidence she usually had when you revealed something to her, but with contempt for them. For she said that, by some taste which she could not explain in words, she could distinguish the difference between you revealing something and her soul dreaming.

Nevertheless, the effort continued, and a girl was sought whose age was approximately two years short of marriageable age; and because she was pleasing, she was awaited.

### CHAPTER XIV. He Deliberates About Living in Common with His Friends

24. Many of us had also turned the matter over in our minds, and, speaking together and detesting the turbulent troubles of human life, had almost firmly resolved to live in leisure, withdrawn from the crowds. We planned that leisure in this way: if we possessed anything, we would contribute it to a common fund and form one household from all our resources, so that, through the sincerity of friendship, there would not be one thing belonging to this man and another to that, but that all would become one from the contributions of everyone, and the whole would belong to each individual, and everything to all.

We thought that we might be about ten men in the same association. Among us were men of considerable wealth, especially Romanianus, our fellow townsman, whom the serious pressures of his affairs had then drawn to the imperial court and who had been my closest friend from early youth. He was particularly insistent on this plan and had great authority in persuading others, since his substantial resources far exceeded those of the rest. We had agreed that two men each year, as though magistrates, would take care of all necessities while the others remained at leisure.

But when it began to be considered whether the little women would permit this—some of us already having wives or wanting to have them—the whole plan that we had been forming so well [Note: [Col. 0731] *Firmabamus* (“we were making firm”), according to the oldest editions and several manuscripts; *pene firmaveramus* (“we had almost firmly resolved”), according to Flor. M.] fell apart in our hands, was shattered, and cast aside. From there we turned to sighs and groans [Note: [Col. 0731] The Codex, Alb., and the older editions read: “From there we turned to sighs and groans, and to our steps.”], and our steps to following the broad and well-trodden roads of the world, because there were many thoughts in our hearts, but your purpose remains forever (Ps. 32:2). By that purpose you mocked our plans and prepared your own, intending to give us food at the proper time and to open your hand and fill our souls with blessing (Ps. 144:15–16).

### CHAPTER XV. Another Concubine Takes the Place of the One Who Departed

25. Meanwhile my sins were multiplying. When she with whom I had been accustomed to lie was torn from my side as an impediment to marriage, the heart to which it had clung was cut and wounded in me, and it streamed with blood. She had returned to Africa, having vowed to you that she would know no other man, leaving with me the natural son she had borne me.

But I, wretched man, unable even to imitate that woman and impatient of delay—as though, after two years, I would receive the one I was seeking, because I was not a lover of marriage but a slave of lust—procured another woman, certainly not a wife. Through her, my disease of the soul might be sustained and carried forward, whether unchanged or increased, by the escort of my continuing habit into the realm of marriage.

Nor was the wound caused by the cutting away of the former woman healed. Rather, after its intense heat and sharp pain, it festered; and, as though becoming colder, it caused a more desperate pain.

### CHAPTER XVI. He Never Laid Aside His Fear of Death and Judgment

26. To you be praise, to you glory, fountain of mercies. I was becoming more wretched, and you were drawing nearer. Your right hand was already close—indeed, at that very moment—to snatch me from the mire and wash me, and I did not know it.

Nothing recalled me from the deeper whirlpool of carnal pleasures except fear of death and of your future judgment. Through various opinions, that fear nevertheless never withdrew from my heart. With my friends Alypius and Nebridius I discussed the ends of good and evil. Epicurus would have carried the victory in my mind had I not believed that after death there remained a life for the soul and a reckoning of merits—something Epicurus refused to believe.

I asked: if we were immortal and lived in perpetual bodily pleasure without any fear of its loss, why would we not be happy, or what else would we seek? I did not know that it belonged to great misery that, so sunk and blinded, I could not conceive the light of moral goodness and the beauty that must be embraced freely—a beauty that the eye of the flesh does not see, but that is seen from within.

In my misery I did not consider from what source it came that I could discuss these very ugly matters sweetly with my friends; nor could I be happy without friends, even according to the understanding I then possessed, amid however great an abundance of carnal pleasures. I loved these friends freely, and in turn felt that I was freely loved by them.

O tortuous ways! Woe to the daring soul that hoped that, if it withdrew from you, it would possess something better! Turned and turned again, onto its back, its sides, and its belly—everything is hard; and you alone are rest. And behold, you are present, and you free us from our miserable errors, and establish us on your way, and console us, and say: “Run! I will carry you, and I will lead you through, and there I will carry you.” [Note: [Col. 0732] The Lyrensis Codex reads: “and there I will set you free.”]

## BOOK VII. He recalls before his mind’s eyes the beginning of his youth, that is, his thirty-first year. He relates that at that age, still enveloped in the denser darkness of ignorance and wandering over the nature of God and the origin of evil—a question which distressed him extraordinarily—he finally came to a true knowledge of God, although he did not yet hold a worthy view of the Lord Christ.

[Col. 0733]

### CHAPTER I. He conceives God as something bodily, spread through infinite spaces

1. My evil and wicked adolescence was now dead, and I was passing into youth; the older I grew in years, the more disgraceful I became in vanity. I could conceive no substance except one like those which are ordinarily seen through these eyes. I did not conceive you, God, under the figure of a human body—ever since I began to hear something about wisdom, I had always avoided this—and I rejoiced to have found this in the faith of our spiritual mother, your Catholic Church. [Note: [Col. 0733] Bad., Am., and Er.: “Yet I did not conceive you.”] But no other way of conceiving you occurred to me. And I, a human being, strove to conceive you as a human being—yet as such a human being: the supreme, sole, and true God. With all my inmost being I believed you to be incorruptible, inviolable, and unchangeable; for although I did not know whence or how, I nevertheless clearly saw and was certain that what can be corrupted is worse than what cannot be corrupted; that I unhesitatingly preferred what cannot be violated to what can be violated; and that what suffers no change is better than what can be changed.

My heart cried out violently against all my phantasms, and with this one blow I tried to drive from the gaze of my mind the flying swarm of uncleanness. Scarcely had it been dispersed in a moment, when, behold, it was gathered together again and present, rushing upon my sight and clouding it, so that, although not under the form of a human body, I was nevertheless forced to conceive something bodily, whether infused through the world or diffused beyond the world through infinity—something itself incorruptible, inviolable, and unchangeable, which I preferred to the corruptible, violable, and changeable. For whatever I deprived of such spaces seemed to me to be nothing at all—not even emptiness, but absolute nothingness; as if a body were removed from a place and the place remained empty of every body, terrestrial, watery, aerial, and celestial, yet were still an empty place, like a spacious nothing.

2. Thus, with my heart grown gross, unable even to see myself, I thought that whatever was not extended, diffused, gathered together, swollen, or capable of receiving or being able to receive something of that sort, was utterly nothing. For as my eyes ordinarily moved through forms, so my heart moved through images; and I did not see that the very act of attention by which I formed those images was not something of that kind, though it could not form them unless it were something great. Thus I conceived you also, Life of my life, as great, penetrating the whole mass of the world on every side through infinite spaces, and beyond it everywhere through immeasurable spaces without end [Col. 0734], so that earth might contain you, heaven might contain you, and all things might contain you, and these might end in you, while you yourself ended nowhere.

As the body of this air above the earth does not obstruct the sunlight from passing through and penetrating it—not by breaking or cutting it apart, but by filling it wholly—so I thought that not only the bodies of heaven, air, and sea, but also that of earth, were pervious to you and penetrable in all their greatest and least parts so as to receive your presence, secretly governing inwardly and outwardly everything you created. Thus I supposed, because I could conceive nothing else; but it was false. For in that manner a larger part of the earth would contain a larger part of you, and a smaller part a smaller one; and all things would thus be full of you in such a way that the body of an elephant would contain more of you than that of a sparrow, because it is larger and occupies more space. In this way you would make your parts present piecemeal to the parts of the world, great parts to great things and small parts to small things. But you are not so. Yet you had not then illumined my darkness.

### CHAPTER II. The argument by which Nebridius refuted the Manichaeans

3. It was enough for me, Lord, against those deceived deceivers and talkative mutes [Note: [Col. 0734] Am. and Er.: “talkative mutes, and therefore mutes, because …”], since your word did not sound from them. Enough, therefore, was the point which Nebridius had long been accustomed to raise, from Carthage onward, and by which all who heard it were shaken. What could that unnamed race of darkness, which they customarily set against you as an opposing mass, have done to you if you had been unwilling to fight it? [Note: [Col. 0734] Bad., Er., Somm., and Blas. read *voluisses*, “had wished.”] If the answer were that it could have harmed you in some respect, you would be violable and corruptible. But if it were said that it could have harmed you in nothing, there would be no reason for fighting—and for fighting in such a way that a certain portion of you, a member of you, or an offspring from your very substance, should be mingled with hostile powers and natures not created by you, and be corrupted and changed by them for the worse to such an extent that it should be turned from blessedness into misery and need help in order to be rescued and purified. This, they say, is the soul, to which your Word—free when it comes to the aid of one enslaved, pure when it helps one defiled, whole when it helps one corrupted—would bring assistance; though the Word itself would then be corruptible, since it is of one and the same substance. Therefore, if they called you—whatever you are, that is, the substance by which you are—incorruptible, all those things were false and abominable; but if corruptible, that very assertion was already false and to be abhorred at the first word. This, therefore, was enough against men to be cast out of the oppression of my breast altogether, since they had no way out without a horrible sacrilege of heart and tongue, in thinking and speaking such things of you.

### CHAPTER III. Free choice is the cause of sin

[Col. 0735]

4. Yet although I already called, and firmly believed and felt, our Lord God to be true—incorruptible, unalterable, and in no respect mutable, the maker not only of our souls but also of our bodies, and not only of our souls and bodies but of all things and everything—I had not grasped the explicit and disentangled cause of evil. Whatever it might be, I saw that I must seek it in such a way as not to be compelled by it to believe the immutable God mutable, lest I myself become what I was seeking. I therefore sought it securely, certain that what those men said was not true; with my whole soul I fled from them, for I saw that in asking whence evil comes they were full of the evil by which they supposed that your substance suffered evil rather than that their own did evil.

5. I strained to discern what I heard: that the free choice of the will is the cause of our doing evil, and your righteous judgment the cause of our suffering it. But I could not discern this clearly. [Note: [Col. 0735] This is the reading of the English manuscripts and nearly all ours. A little below, they read, “no one other than myself.” Arn., Mart., Flor., and Rond., with some manuscripts: “No one other than myself.”] Thus, whenever I tried to draw the gaze of my mind up from the depths, I was plunged down again; and often trying, I was plunged down again and again. Yet what raised me toward your light was that I knew myself to have a will just as certainly as I knew myself to live. Therefore, whenever I willed or did not will something, I was most certain that none other than I myself willed or did not will it; and I was beginning to observe that there lay the cause of my sin. But whatever I did unwillingly, I saw myself as suffering rather than doing; and I quickly acknowledged that this was not a fault but a punishment, by which, thinking you just, I confessed that I was not punished unjustly.

But again I said: Who made me? Was it not my God, not merely good but goodness itself? Whence, then, comes my willing evil and unwillingness to will good, so that there should be cause for me justly to pay penalties? Who put this in me and planted in me the nursery of bitterness, when I was made wholly by my most sweet God? If the devil is its author, whence came the devil himself? And if he too, by a perverse will, was made a devil out of a good angel, whence came in him the evil will by which he became a devil, when as a whole angel he had been made good by the best Creator? [Note: [Col. 0735] *Bonus* is omitted in the Benignus and Theodericanus manuscripts and several others.] By these thoughts I was again crushed and suffocated; but I was not drawn down to that hell of error where no one confesses to you, because people suppose that you suffer evil rather than that a human being does evil.

### CHAPTER IV. God must be incorruptible

6. For I was striving to discover the rest as I had already discovered that the incorruptible is better than the corruptible, and therefore I confessed that you, whatever you might be, are incorruptible. No soul has ever been, or can be, able to conceive anything better than you, who are the supreme and best good. Since the incorruptible is most truly and certainly preferred to the corruptible, as I already preferred it, I could in thought attain something better than my God unless you were incorruptible. Therefore, where I saw that the incorruptible was to be preferred to the corruptible, there I ought to seek you and from there observe whence evil comes—that is, whence corruption itself comes, by which your substance cannot in any way be violated. [Note: [Col. 0736] In B., “where”; most editions, “whence.”]

For corruption in no way at all violates our God: not by any will, necessity, or unforeseen chance. For he is God, and what he wills for himself is good, and he himself is that good. But to be corrupted is not good. Nor are you compelled unwillingly to anything, because your will is not greater than your power. It would be greater if you yourself were greater than yourself; for God’s will and power are God himself. And what can be unforeseen by you, who know all things? No nature exists unless you know it. And why say much about why the substance which is God is not corruptible, when, if it were so, it would not be God?

### CHAPTER V. He again asks whence evil comes and what its root is

7. I asked whence evil comes, and I asked badly; and in the very inquiry I did not see evil. Before the sight of my spirit I set the whole creation, whatever we can see in it—earth, sea, air, stars, trees, and mortal animals—and whatever we do not see in it, such as the firmament of heaven, and besides it all angels and all its spiritual beings. My imagination, however, arranged even these in places and places as though they were bodies. And I made your creation one great mass, distinguished by kinds of bodies [Note: [Col. 0736] Four manuscripts read “your creatures.”], whether they were true bodies or bodies I had myself imagined for spirits. I made it large, not as large as it was, for that I could not know, but as large as I pleased, yet finite in every direction.

But I conceived you, Lord, as surrounding and penetrating it on every side, yet everywhere infinite: as though the sea were everywhere, an infinite sea alone extending in every direction through immeasurable spaces, and contained within itself a sponge of whatever great size, yet finite. That sponge would surely be full, in every part of itself, from the immeasurable sea. Thus I thought your finite creation full of you who are infinite, and said: Behold God, and behold what God has made; and God is good and vastly and incomparably superior to these things. Yet, being good, he made good things; and behold how he surrounds and fills them. Where, then, is evil? Whence and by what way has it crept in here? What is its root and what its seed? Or does it not exist at all? Why, then, do we fear and avoid what does not exist? Or, if we fear vainly, surely the fear itself is evil, by which the heart is needlessly goaded and tormented; and the graver evil because there is nothing to fear and yet we fear. Therefore either the evil we fear exists, or this is evil: that we fear.

Whence, then, is it, since God made all these things, good things as a good maker? The greater and supreme good made lesser goods, yet both the Creator and the things created are all good. Whence is evil? Was the matter from which he made them evil, and did he form and order it while leaving something in it which he did not convert into good? [Note: [Col. 0736] The manuscripts, with Bad. and Arn., read thus; Am., Er., and Lov., with altered punctuation, read: “Or was some matter evil from which he made them?”] Why this too? Was he unable to turn and change it all so that no evil remained, though he is almighty? Finally, why did he will to make anything out of it, rather than by the same omnipotence bring it about that it did not exist at all? Or could it exist against his will? Or if it was eternal, why did he allow it to be so for so long through the infinite backward spaces of time, and only much later choose to make something from it? Or if he suddenly willed to act, ought not the Almighty rather to have acted so that it did not exist and he alone was the whole, true, supreme, and infinite good? Or if it was not good that he should not also make and create something good, since he was good, then, after removing and reducing to nothing that evil matter, he should himself have established good matter from which to create all things. For he would not be almighty if he could not create something good unless aided by matter which he had not created.

I turned such things over in my miserable breast, pregnant with the sharpest anxieties from fear of death and failure to find the truth. Yet the faith of your Christ, our Lord and Savior, remained fixed in my heart, in the Catholic Church—still for the most part unformed and wavering outside the rule of doctrine [Note: [Col. 0737] Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read “fluctuating.”], but my mind did not abandon it; rather, day by day it drank it in more and more.

### CHAPTER VI. He rejects the divinations of astrologers

8. I had also rejected the deceptive predictions and impious ravings of the astrologers. Let your mercies, my God, be confessed to you in this also from the deepest recesses of my soul. For it was you, wholly you; for who else recalls us from the death of every error but the Life that cannot die, and the Wisdom that illumines needy minds while itself needing no light, by which the world is governed even to the flying leaves of trees? You provided for my obstinacy, by which I resisted Vindicianus, a keen old man, and Nebridius, a young man of remarkable soul—the former strongly affirming, the latter saying with some hesitation yet frequently, that there is no art of foreseeing the future [Note: [Col. 0737] The manuscripts read: “that that art does not exist.”], but that human conjectures often have the force of chance, and that, by saying many things, people say many things that will happen, though they do not know it, because by not keeping silent they happen upon them.

You therefore supplied a friend, not indeed an idle consulter of astrologers, nor a person well versed in those writings, but, as I said, a curious consulter, who nevertheless knew something which he said he had heard from his father, though he did not know how much force it had for overthrowing the reputation of that art. [Note: [Col. 0737] From the English manuscripts: “he said [that he had heard from his father] how much force it had.”] This man, named Firminus, liberally educated and polished in eloquence, consulted me as a very dear friend about certain affairs of his in which his worldly hope had swelled, asking what I thought, according to his so-called constellations. I had already begun to incline to Nebridius’s opinion on this subject. I did not refuse to conjecture and say what occurred to a wavering mind [Col. 0738], but added that I was now almost persuaded that those things were ridiculous and empty.

Then he told me that his father had been an eager student of books of this kind and had a friend who pursued the same studies with him. By equal zeal and interchange they fanned the fire of their hearts upon these trifles [Note: [Col. 0738] Most editions read: “and by interchange burned over these trifles with the fire of their hearts.” Arn. corrected this to *flabant ignem*; from the manuscripts the editors restore *flatabant*: because the word was less familiar, copyists stumbled and corrupted the passage. Arnobius also uses it, *Against the Nations*, book 2, near the middle: “Why [speak of] mimes, actors, singers, blowing with trumpet, pipe, and reed?”], so that they even observed the moments of birth of dumb animals born at home and noted the positions of the sky at those moments, gathering from them experimental evidence for that alleged art.

Accordingly, he said that he had heard from his father that, when Firminus’s mother was pregnant with him, a slave woman of his father’s friend was likewise far along in pregnancy. This could not escape the master, who took the greatest care to know even the births of his dogs. Thus it happened that, while the one carefully counted the days and hours and the smaller divisions of hours of his wife, and the other those of the slave woman, both women gave birth at the same time. They were therefore compelled to draw up the same constellations, to the same smallest intervals, for each newborn: the one for his son, the other for his little slave. For when the women began to be in labor, the two men informed one another what was happening in each of their homes and arranged to send messengers to one another as soon as the birth had been announced to each. They could easily ensure its immediate announcement, as though in their own kingdoms.

Thus, he said, the messengers sent by each met one another at precisely equal distances from the two houses, so that neither man was able to note a different position of the stars or different portions of time. Yet Firminus, born to high rank among his own people, ran along the brighter roads of the world, grew in wealth, and rose in honors; while that slave, with the yoke of his condition in no way loosened, served masters, as Firminus himself, who knew him, reported.

9. When I heard and believed this—for such a man had told it—my whole resistance collapsed and dissolved. First I tried to recall Firminus himself from that curiosity. I said that, on inspecting his constellations, in order to make true predictions [Note: [Col. 0738] Mart. and Arn. read “foretell.”], I should surely have had to see there parents eminent among their fellows, a noble family in his native city, free birth, honorable upbringing, and liberal studies. But if that slave had consulted me from the same constellations, since they were also his, in order to give him true answers too, I should again have had to see there a most abject family, servile status, and everything else wholly unlike and far removed from the former case. How, then, could it happen that, looking at the same thing, I should say different things if I spoke truly? But if I said the same things, I should speak falsely. From this I most certainly concluded [Note: [Col. 0738] The English manuscripts support: “If I spoke? From this I most certainly concluded that the things which were true …”] that whatever true things were said after considering constellations were said not by art but by chance; and whatever false things were said were false not because of the art’s lack of skill, but because of chance’s deceit.

10. Having gained this opening [Note: [Col. 0739] Bad., Am., Er., and five manuscripts read “hearing.”], I reflected with myself that no one of those madmen who pursued such a profit—men whom I was now eager to attack and refute with ridicule—could resist me by saying that either Firminus or his father had related a falsehood. I directed my consideration to those who are born twins. Most of them are brought from the womb one immediately after the other, so that the small interval of time, however great an influence they maintain it has in the nature of things, cannot be gathered by human observation or at all recorded in writing, though the astrologer must inspect those written records in order to make true predictions. His predictions will not be true, for, looking at the same records, he ought to have said the same things about Esau and Jacob; yet the same things did not happen to both. Therefore he would speak falsely; or, if he spoke truly, he would not say the same things even if he inspected the same things. [Note: [Col. 0739] Er., Lugd., and Ven.: “if he said the same”; Somm., Arn., and Mart.: “but the same.”] Therefore he would speak true things not by art but by chance.

For you, Lord, most just governor of the universe, act by a hidden prompting upon those who consult and those consulted, though they do not know it, so that when a person consults, he hears what he ought to hear according to the hidden merits of souls, from the abyss of your just judgment. Let no one say to you, “What is this? Why is this?” Let him not say it, let him not say it; for he is a human being.

### CHAPTER VII. He is miserably tormented while inquiring whence evil comes

11. By now, therefore, my Helper, you had released me from those bonds, and I asked whence evil comes, but there was no way out. Yet you did not allow any waves of thought to carry me away from the faith by which I believed that you exist, that your substance is unchangeable, that you care for and judge human beings, and that in Christ, your Son, our Lord, and in the holy Scriptures commended by the authority of your Catholic Church, you had established the way of human salvation toward the life which is to come after this death. With these things preserved and unwaveringly strengthened in my mind, I asked in anguish whence evil comes. What torments of my laboring heart there were! What groans, my God! Yet there were your ears, though I did not know it. When I searched vigorously in silence, great cries toward your mercy were the silent contritions of my mind. You knew what I suffered, and no human being did. For how little of it was digested through my tongue into the ears of my closest friends! Did the whole tumult of my soul, for which neither time nor my mouth sufficed, sound to them? Yet all that I roared from the groaning of my heart entered your hearing, and before you was my desire, while the light of my eyes was not with me (Ps. 37:9–11).

For that light was within, while I was outside; and it was not in a place. Yet I attended to things contained in places and found no place there in which to rest. Nor did those things receive me so that I might say, “It is enough, and it is well”; nor did they allow me to return where it would be enough and well for me. For I was superior to those things, but inferior to you; and you are the true joy to me when I am subject to you, and you had subjected to me the things you created beneath me. This was the right order and the middle region of my salvation: that I should remain in your image and, serving you, rule my body. But when I rose proudly against you and ran against the Lord with the thick neck of my shield (Job 15:26), even these lowest things were set above me; they pressed upon me, and nowhere was there relief or breathing-space. They met my sight everywhere in heaps and masses; and when I tried to think, bodily images opposed me as I returned, as though saying, “Where are you going, unworthy and filthy man?” These things had grown out of my wound, because you had humbled the proud man as one wounded (Ps. 88:11); and by my swelling I was separated from you, while my grossly inflated face closed my eyes.

### CHAPTER VIII. How divine mercy aided Augustine

12. But you, Lord, remain forever and are not angry with us forever. For you have pitied earth and ashes, and it pleased you in your sight to reform my deformities. By inward goads you stirred me, so that I was impatient until you should become certain to me by inward sight. The swelling in me subsided by the hidden hand of your healing, and the troubled and darkened gaze of my mind was healed day by day by the sharp salve of salutary pains.

### CHAPTER IX. In the books of the Platonists he finds the divinity of the eternal Word, not the humility of the incarnate Word

13. First, wishing to show me how you resist the proud but give grace to the humble (1 Pet. 5:5), and how great was the mercy shown to human beings in the way of humility, because your Word was made flesh and dwelt among human beings, you provided for me, through a man swollen with monstrous pride, certain books of the Platonists translated from Greek into Latin. In them I read—not indeed in these words, but with this very thing urged in many and varied arguments—that in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; that this Word was in the beginning with God; that all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made that was made; that in him was life, and the life was the light of human beings, and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

And I read that although the human soul bears witness to the light, it is not itself the light; but the Word of God, God, is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world. And I read that he was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. But that he came unto his own, and his own did not receive him, while to as many as received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name: this I did not read there.

14. Likewise there I read that God the Word was born not of flesh, nor of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God. But that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:1–14)—I did not read there. For I found in those writings, expressed in various ways and by many arguments, that the Son is in the form of the Father, that he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, because he is naturally the very same. But that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being; that he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross; and that therefore God exalted him from the dead and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 2:6–11)—those books do not contain.

That your only-begotten Son remains unchangeably before all times and above all times, coeternal with you; that souls receive from his fullness so as to be blessed (John 1:16); and that through participation in the wisdom abiding in him they are renewed so as to become wise—that is there. But that he died in time for the ungodly (Romans 5:6), and that you did not spare your only Son but delivered him up for us all (Romans 8:32)—that is not there. For you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to little ones, so that those who labor and are burdened might come to him and he might refresh them; because he is gentle and humble in heart, directs the gentle in judgment, and teaches the meek his ways, seeing our humility and our labor and forgiving all our sins (Psalm 24:9, 18).

But those who, as though raised upon the cothurnus of a loftier doctrine, do not hear him saying, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:25, 28–29)—even if they know God, they do not glorify him as God or give thanks; instead, they become futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart is darkened. Claiming to be wise, they become fools.

15. And therefore I also read there of the exchange of the unaltered glory of your incorruptibility for idols and various images, made in the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, and of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents (Romans 1:21, 23)—namely, the Egyptian food by which Esau lost his birthright (Genesis 25:33–34):

[Note: It is helpful to illuminate this passage from another work. In fact, in his Expositions on Psalm 46, no. 6, Augustine argues as follows: “We find that the lentil was food of the Egyptians, for it is abundant there in Egypt; hence Alexandrian lentils are highly prized and reach even our lands, as though lentils did not grow here. Thus Esau, by desiring Egyptian food, lost his primacy. So also the Jewish people, of whom it is said, ‘Their heart turned back to Egypt,’ desired, as it were, lentils and lost their primacy.”]

For the firstborn people, having turned their heart toward Egypt, honored the head of a quadruped in your place and bowed your image—its own soul—before the image of a calf eating grass (Exodus 32:1–6; and Psalm 105:19–20). I found these things there, but I did not eat them.

For it pleased you, Lord, to remove from Jacob the reproach of diminution, so that the greater might serve the lesser (Romans 9:13); and you called the Gentiles into your inheritance. And I had come to you from among the Gentiles, and I fixed my attention upon the gold that you desired your people to carry away from Egypt (Exodus 3:22; 11:2), because it was yours wherever it was. And through your Apostle you said to the Athenians that in you we live and move and are, just as some of their own people had said (Acts 17:28); and indeed those books came from there. Yet I did not attend to the idols of the Egyptians, for which those who changed the truth of God into falsehood, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, supplied material from your gold (Romans 1:25).

### CHAPTER X. Divine things now become clearer to Augustine
