16. And thus admonished to return to myself, I entered into my inmost self, with you as my guide; and I was able to do so because you had become my helper. I entered, and with whatever eye of my soul I could use, above that same eye of my soul, above my mind, I saw an unchangeable light—not this ordinary light visible to all flesh, nor something larger of the same kind, as though it had merely become much, much brighter and occupied everything by its vastness. It was not that; it was something else, altogether different from all these things.

Nor was it above my mind in the way that oil is above water, or heaven above earth; it was above because it made me, and I was below because I was made by it. Whoever knows truth knows it, and whoever knows it knows eternity. Love knows it.

O eternal truth, true love, and beloved eternity! You are my God; to you I sigh day and night. And when I first came to know you, you took me up so that I might see that what I saw existed, while I myself did not yet exist as one who saw. And you struck back the weakness of my sight, shining upon me with overwhelming brightness; I trembled with love and dread. And I found myself far from you in the region of dissimilarity, as though I heard your voice from on high: “I am the food of the mature; grow, and you will eat me.” Nor will you change me into yourself, as food of your flesh; rather, you will be changed into me.

And I learned that you discipline a person because of iniquity and make my soul waste away like a spider (Psalm 39:12). And I said: “Is truth therefore nothing, since it is not spread out through finite or infinite spaces?” And you cried out from far away: “No indeed, I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14). And I heard this as one hears within the heart, and there was absolutely no reason for me to doubt. I would more easily have doubted that I was alive than that truth exists, which is perceived through the things that have been made (Romans 1:20).

[Note: The manuscripts, by a strong consensus, read “are perceived.”]

[Note: In the editions, “Lord” is added here; the manuscripts lack the word.]

### CHAPTER XI. How creatures both are and are not

17. And I looked upon the other things beneath you, and I saw that they neither wholly exist nor wholly do not exist. They do exist, because they come from you; yet they do not exist, because they are not what you are. For that truly exists which remains unchangeably.

But for me to cling to God is good (Psalm 72:28), because if I do not remain in him, neither will I be able to remain in myself. Yet he, remaining in himself, renews all things (Wisdom 7:27). And you are the Lord my God, because you have no need of my goods (Psalm 16:2).

### CHAPTER XII. Everything that exists is good

[Col. 0743]

18. It was revealed to me that the things that are corrupted are good. They could not be corrupted either if they were the highest goods or unless they were goods: if they were the highest goods, they would be incorruptible; but if they were no goods at all, there would be nothing in them to be corrupted. For corruption causes harm, and it would not cause harm unless it diminished something good.

Therefore either corruption causes no harm—which is impossible—or, as is most certain, everything that is corrupted is deprived of good. But if it is deprived of all good, it will altogether cease to be. For if it continues to exist and can no longer be corrupted, it will be better, because it will remain incorruptibly. And what is more monstrous than to say that things become better after losing all good?

Therefore, if they are deprived of all good, they will not exist at all; therefore, for as long as they exist, they are good; therefore, whatever exists is good.

And that evil whose origin I was seeking is not a substance, because if it were a substance, it would be good. For either it would be an incorruptible substance, and therefore a great good, or it would be a corruptible substance, which could not be corrupted unless it were good.

Thus I saw, and it was made clear to me, that you made all things good, and that there are absolutely no substances that you did not make. And because you did not make all things equal, therefore all things exist: each is good individually, and all things together are very good, because our God made all things very good (Genesis 1; and Sirach 39:21).

### CHAPTER XIII. All created things praise God

19. There is absolutely no evil for you—not only no evil for you, but none for your whole creation—because outside it there is nothing that can break in and corrupt the order you established for it.

[Note: In Louvain and the older editions this was read, “because outside you there is nothing.” Arnaldus removed “you,” since the word is absent from the manuscripts and ought to be absent, as the meaning is that there is nothing outside the whole creation that can break in to disturb the order established by God.]

But within its parts, some things are thought evil because they do not suit certain others; yet the very same things suit others and are good, and are good in themselves. And all these things that do not suit one another suit the lower part of the world, which we call earth, having its own cloudy and windy sky appropriate to it.

And far be it from me now to say, “These things should not exist.”

[Note: The manuscripts read this way, as does Arnaldus; Somner has, “so that I should say, ‘There should be nothing but these things.’” The other editions have, “so that I should say, ‘These things should not exist.’”]

For even if I saw only these things, I would indeed desire better things, but I should already praise you on account of these alone; for they show that you are worthy of praise. From the earth, dragons and all abysses praise you; fire, hail, snow, ice, and storm-wind, which perform your word; mountains and all hills; fruitful trees and all cedars; beasts and all cattle; creeping things and winged birds; kings of the earth and all peoples; princes and all judges of the earth; young men and maidens; elders together with the young—all praise your name.

And when they also praise you from the heavens, let all your angels praise you, our God, in the heights; all your powers; sun and moon; all stars and light; heavens of heavens; and waters that are above the heavens—let them praise your name (Psalm 148:1–12).

I no longer desired better things, because I considered everything: I judged that the higher things were indeed better than the lower, but that all things together were better than the higher things alone, according to a sounder judgment.

### CHAPTER XIV. A sound-minded person is displeased by nothing among God’s creatures

20. Those who are displeased by any of your creatures are not in sound health, just as I was not when many things you had made displeased me. And because my soul did not dare to be displeased with my God, it did not want whatever displeased it to be yours. From this it had fallen into the opinion of two substances; it found no rest and spoke alien things.

Returning from there, it had made for itself a god extending through the infinite spaces of all places, and had thought that this was you. It had installed him in its heart, and had again become a temple of its own idol, abominable to you.

But after you had cherished the head of one who did not know, and closed my eyes so that they would not see vanity, I withdrew for a little while from myself, and my madness fell asleep. I awoke in you and saw you as infinite in another way; and this vision was not drawn from the flesh.

### CHAPTER XV. How truth and falsehood exist in creatures

21. And I looked upon other things and saw that they owe it to you that they exist, and that in you all things are bounded—not as though you were contained in a place, but because you are the one who holds all things in your hand through truth. And all things are true insofar as they exist; there is no falsehood except when something is thought to be what it is not.

And I saw that things suit their own places, but also their own times. And because you alone are eternal, you did not begin to act after innumerable stretches of time; for all stretches of time, both those that have passed and those that will pass, would neither depart nor arrive unless you were acting and remaining.

### CHAPTER XVI. All things are good, even if unsuitable for some

22. I perceived and experienced that it is no wonder that bread, which is pleasant to a healthy palate, is painful to an unhealthy one; and that light, which is beloved by pure eyes, is hateful to diseased eyes.

Your justice is displeasing to the unjust—how much more the viper and the worm, which you created as good and which are suitable to the lower parts of your creation! The unjust themselves are suitable to those parts insofar as they are unlike you, but they are suitable to the higher things insofar as they become like you.

And I sought what iniquity was, but I did not find it to be a substance. Rather, it was a perversion of the will, twisted away from the highest substance—from you, God—toward the lowest things, casting away its inner possessions (Sirach 10:12) and swelling outward.

[Note: This is the reading of Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus, and likewise of the English manuscripts and many of ours. Arnaldus and some manuscripts have “twisted toward the lowest substance.” Supply “substance.” Louvain has “twisted toward the lowest [thing],” with the intended sense, “twisted toward the lowest perversion of the will.”]

### CHAPTER XVII. What delays the knowledge of divine things

23. And I marveled that I already loved you, not a phantom in your place. Yet I did not stand firm in the enjoyment of my God; I was swept toward you by your beauty, and soon torn away from you by my own weight, falling into these things with a groan. This weight was carnal habit.

[Note: Amerbach and Erasmus, together with four manuscripts, read, “and I did not persist.”]

But the memory of you remained with me. I had no doubt at all that there was one to whom I should cling, but I was not yet one who could cling; for the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things (Wisdom 9:15).

And I was absolutely certain that your invisible attributes, understood through the things that have been made, are seen from the foundation of the world—your eternal power and divinity (Romans 1:20). For I was seeking the basis on which I might judge the beauty of bodies, whether heavenly or earthly, and what enabled me to judge mutable things correctly and say, “This ought to be so; that ought not to be so.”

In seeking the basis of such judgments, I had found the unchangeable and true eternity of truth, above my changeable mind. And so I proceeded gradually from bodies to the soul that perceives through the body; from there to its inner power, to which the bodily senses report external things; and as far as animals can go; and from there again to the reasoning power, to which what is received through the bodily senses is referred for judgment.

When this power discovered that it too was mutable in me, it raised itself toward its own understanding. It withdrew its thought from habit, separating itself from the conflicting crowds of phantasms, so that it might find the light by which it was illumined when, without any doubt, it cried out that the unchangeable must be preferred to the changeable. How could it know the unchangeable itself unless it knew it in some way? Without such knowledge, it could in no way confidently prefer it to the mutable.

And it reached what is, in a flash of trembling vision.

[Note: This excellent passage is restored by the manuscript copies. In the printed editions it was corruptly read, “and it might reach.”]

Then indeed I saw your invisible attributes, understood through the things that have been made. But I could not fix my gaze upon them; and when my weakness rebounded, I returned to my customary ways, carrying with me only a loving memory, and, as it were, longing by scent for what I was not yet able to eat.

[Note: “I was able” is found in Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, Louvain, Martin, Florence, and manuscript M.]

### CHAPTER XVIII. Christ alone is the way to salvation

24. And I was seeking a way to acquire strength sufficient to enjoy you, but I did not find it until I embraced the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), who is God blessed above all forever (Romans 9:5), calling and saying, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), and mixing with flesh the food that I was too weak to receive—for your Wisdom, through which you created all things, became flesh so that it might provide milk for our infancy.

For I, though humble, did not yet grasp my humble Lord Jesus, nor did I understand of what his weakness was the teacher. For your Word, eternal truth, surpassing the higher parts of your creation, raises those subject to him toward himself. In the lower parts, however, he built for himself a humble house from our clay, through which he would bring those who were to be subjected to him down from themselves and lead them across to himself, healing their pride and nourishing love.

Thus they would not advance farther through self-confidence, but would instead be weakened when they saw before their feet the weakened divinity resulting from participation in our garment of skin; and, weary, they would fall upon it, while it, rising, would lift them up.

### CHAPTER XIX. What he thought about Christ’s incarnation

25. I, however, thought otherwise, and held of my Lord Christ only what one might hold of a man of outstanding wisdom, whom no one could equal—especially since, having been wondrously born of a virgin, he seemed, as an example of despising temporal things in order to attain immortality, to have merited through divine providence such great authority as a teacher for our sake.

But what mystery was contained in the Word becoming flesh (John 1:14), I could not even begin to suspect. From what had been written and handed down about him, I knew only that he ate and drank, slept, walked, rejoiced, was saddened, and spoke; that his flesh was not joined to your Word except together with a human soul and mind.

Everyone who knows the unchangeability of your Word knows this—an unchangeability that I already knew as far as I was able—and I had no doubt about it at all. For to move or not to move the bodily limbs according to the will; to be affected or not to be affected by some emotion; to express wise judgments through signs or remain silent—these are proper to the mutability of soul and mind.

If these things had been falsely written about him, everything would also be endangered by falsehood, and no salvation of faith would remain for the human race in those Scriptures. Therefore, because these things were truly written, I recognized in Christ the whole human being—not merely a human body, nor a soul with a body but without a mind,

[Note: “Animam” (“soul”) is read in Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, Rondinelli, and manuscript M.]

but the human being himself. I thought that he was set above the rest not as the person of Truth, but by a certain great excellence of human nature and a more perfect participation in wisdom.

Alypius, however, thought that Catholics believed God to be clothed in flesh in such a way that, apart from God and flesh, there was no soul in Christ; he did not believe that a human mind was affirmed to exist in him. And because he firmly held the reasonable conviction that the things committed to memory about him could not occur without a living and rational creature, he was moved more slowly toward the Christian faith.

But afterward, recognizing this as the error of the heretical Apollinarians, he rejoiced in and was reconciled to the Catholic faith. I, however, confess that somewhat later I learned how, in the statement that the Word became flesh, Catholic truth is distinguished from the falsehood of Photinus.

For the refutation of heretics causes what your Church believes and what sound doctrine possesses to stand out clearly. For heresies had to exist, so that those who were approved might become manifest among the weak (1 Corinthians 11:19).

### CHAPTER XX. He became more learned from the Platonic books, but more puffed up

26. But at that time, after reading those books of the Platonists, when I had been prompted by them to seek incorporeal truth, I saw your invisible attributes, understood through the things that have been made. Repelled, I perceived what, because of the darkness of my soul, I was not permitted to contemplate. I was certain that you exist and that you are infinite, yet that you are not spread out through finite or infinite spaces; and that you truly are the one who is always the same, in no part and through no movement otherwise or otherwise.

All other things, however, exist from you. The firmest evidence for this was simply that they exist. I was certain of these things, yet still too weak to enjoy you.

I chattered as though I were learned; and unless I had sought your way in Christ our Savior, I would have been not learned but lost. For I had already begun to want to appear wise, filled with my own punishment; I did not weep, and moreover I was puffed up with knowledge.

Where was that love which builds, with its foundation in humility, which is Christ Jesus? Or when would those books teach me this? I believe that you wanted me to encounter them before I considered your Scriptures precisely so that the manner in which I had been affected by them would be impressed upon my memory. Then, when I had afterward been gentled by your books and my wounds were handled by your fingers as they tended them, I would discern and distinguish the difference between presumption and confession; between those who see where they must go but do not see the way, and the way leading to the blessed homeland—not merely to be seen but to be inhabited.

For if I had first been formed by your holy Scriptures, and you had sweetened them for me through familiarity, and only afterward I had fallen upon those books, perhaps they would have snatched me away from the foundation of piety. Or, if I had remained in the disposition that I had healthfully absorbed, I might have thought that it too could be conceived from those books, if someone studied those books alone.

### CHAPTER XXI. What he found in the sacred books that was not found in the Platonic books

27. Therefore I eagerly seized the venerable writing of your Spirit, and above all the Apostle Paul. And those questions in which he had once seemed to me to contradict himself, and in which the wording of his discourse did not agree with the testimonies of the Law and the Prophets, disappeared.

One face of pure eloquence appeared to me, and I learned to rejoice with trembling. And I began—

[Note: “I began” is read by Dubois, Martin, Rondinelli, and manuscript M.]

—and I found that whatever truth I had read there was expressed here with the commendation of your grace: so that whoever sees may not boast as though he had not received not only what he sees but also the ability to see—for what does anyone have that he has not received? (1 Corinthians 4:7).

And so one who sees is admonished not only to see you, who are always the same, but is also healed so as to hold fast to you. And whoever cannot see from far away may nevertheless walk along the way by which he can come, see, and hold fast.

For even if a person delights in the law of God according to the inner human being, what will he do about the other law in his members, warring against the law of his mind and taking him captive in the law of sin that is in his members? For you are just, Lord; but we have sinned, we have acted wickedly, we have behaved impiously, and your hand has grown heavy upon us. In justice we were handed over to the ancient sinner, the ruler of death, because he persuaded our will to adopt the likeness of his will, by which he did not stand in your truth (John 8:44).

What will wretched humanity do? Who will free it from this body of death except your grace through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 7:23–25), whom you begot coeternal with yourself and created at the beginning of your ways (Proverbs 8:22), in whom the ruler of this world found nothing deserving death (John 14:30), and yet killed him—and the record that stood against us was canceled (Colossians 2:14)?

Those writings do not contain this. Those pages do not contain the face of this piety, the tears of confession, your sacrifice, a spirit troubled, a heart contrite and humbled (Psalm 51:19), the salvation of the people, the city as bride (Revelation 21:2), the pledge of the Holy Spirit (2 Corinthians 5:5), or the cup of our ransom.

No one there sings: “Will not my soul be subject to God? For from him comes my salvation. Indeed, he is my God and my salvation, my protector; I shall not be moved any further” (Psalm 62:2–3).

No one there hears him calling: “Come to me, you who labor.” They disdain learning from him that he is gentle and humble in heart. “For you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11:28–29, 25).

It is one thing to see the homeland of peace from a wooded summit and not find the way to it, and to attempt in vain to cross impassable places while fugitive deserters, with their leader the lion and dragon, surround and lie in wait. It is another thing to hold the way leading there, fortified by the court of the heavenly Emperor, where those who have deserted the heavenly army do not commit robbery; for they avoid it as punishment.

These things were entering into my very being in wondrous ways as I read the least of your Apostles, considered your works, and was filled with awe.

# BOOK EIGHT

This book touches upon the most celebrated part of his life, his thirty-second year: after consulting Simplicianus and learning from him about the conversion of Victorinus, and after learning from Pontitianus about the life of Antony, the Egyptian monk, following a vehement struggle between flesh and spirit, he opened the Apostle’s book after receiving a heavenly oracle; and immediately, through reading it, he was wholly changed in spirit toward a better way of life and fully converted to God.

[Col. 0747]

### CHAPTER I. He decides to visit Simplicianus in his desire to organize his life better

[Col. 0747]

1. My God, let me remember you in thanksgiving and confess your mercies toward me. Let my bones be drenched with your love—

[Note: Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus, together with the Codex of Alba, read “your delight.”]

—and let them say: “Lord, who is like you?” (Psalm 35:10). You have broken my bonds; I will sacrifice to you a sacrifice of praise (Psalm 116:17). How you broke them I shall tell, and all who worship you will say this when they hear it: “Blessed is the Lord in heaven and on earth; great and wondrous is his name.”

Your words had clung to my innermost being, and from every side I was enclosed by you. I was certain of your eternal life, although I had seen it in a riddle and as through a mirror (1 Corinthians 13:12). Every doubt concerning an incorruptible substance—that every substance came from it—had been removed from me. I did not wish to be more certain about you, but to be more firmly established in you.

But concerning my temporal life, everything was unsteady. My heart had to be cleansed of the old leaven, and the way itself pleased me—the Savior—but I was still reluctant to proceed through its narrow passages.

And you put into my mind, and it seemed good in my sight, to go to Simplicianus, who appeared to me to be your good servant and in whom your grace shone. I had also heard that from his youth he had lived in the most devoted service to you. He was already old, and through his long life in so good a pursuit of following your way, he seemed to me to have experienced and learned much; and so indeed it was.

Therefore I wanted him to bring forth, as I discussed my struggles with him, what manner of proceeding would be suitable for one disposed as I was, so that I might walk in your way.

2. For I saw the Church full of people, and one walked in one way, another in another. But I was displeased with what I was doing in the world, and it was a very great burden to me—not because desires for honor and money were inflaming me as they once had, so that I might endure that grievous servitude.

For they no longer delighted me in comparison with the sweetness of you and the beauty of your house, which I loved (Psalm 26:8). Yet I was still tenaciously bound by a woman. The Apostle did not prohibit me from marrying, although he urged what was better, wishing especially that all people might be as he was (1 Corinthians 7).

But I, being weaker, chose the softer place; and because of this one thing I languished and wasted away in the other matters, exhausted by sluggish anxieties. For in other matters that I did not wish to endure, I was compelled to conform to married life, to which I was devoted and bound.

[Note: “To which” is read by Martin, together with three manuscripts.]

I had heard from the mouth of Truth that there are eunuchs who have mutilated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. But he says, “Let the one who is able to receive this receive it” (Matthew 19:12).

“Vain are all people in whom there is not the knowledge of God; and from the things that are seen they were unable to discover him who is” (Wisdom 13:1). But I was no longer in that vanity. I had gone beyond it, and with all your creation bearing witness, I had found you, our Creator, and your Word, God with you, and, together with the Holy Spirit, one God, through whom you created all things.

[Note: The words “together with the Holy Spirit” could have been omitted, since they are absent from many and better manuscripts.]

There is also another kind of impious people, who, although they know God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks. I too had fallen into this; but your right hand received me (Psalm 18:35) and took me away from there, placing me where I might recover, because you said to humanity: “Behold, piety is wisdom” (Job 28:28); and, “Do not wish to appear wise” (Proverbs 3:7), because “claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1:21–22).

And I had already found the good pearl; it had to be purchased by selling everything I possessed, and I was hesitating (Matthew 13:46).

### CHAPTER II. The rhetorician Victorinus converted to the faith

3. So I went to Simplicianus, the father in receiving your grace of Bishop Ambrose at that time, whom Ambrose truly loved as a father. I told him about the circuits of my error.

[Col. 0750]

When I mentioned that I had read certain books of the Platonists which Victorinus, once a rhetorician of the city of Rome, whom I had heard had died a Christian, had translated into Latin, he congratulated me that I had not come upon the writings of other philosophers, full of deceptions and delusions according to the elements of this world (Colossians 2:8). In these books, however, God and his Word were insinuated in every possible way.

Then, to exhort me to the humility of Christ, hidden from the wise and revealed to little ones (Matthew 11:25), he recalled Victorinus himself, whom he had known most intimately while in Rome, and told me about him. I will not keep silent about it, for it contains a great praise of your grace, to be confessed to you.

That highly learned old man, thoroughly skilled in every liberal discipline—for he had read, assessed, and clarified so many works of the philosophers—

[Note: The manuscripts do not add “and clarified.”]

—the teacher of so many distinguished senators, who, because of the distinction of his renowned teaching, which the citizens of this world regard as extraordinary, had earned and received a statue in the Roman forum—had remained a worshiper of idols into old age and a participant in sacrilegious rites. Almost the whole Roman nobility at that time, puffed up, breathed into the people the monstrous forms of gods of every kind and barking Anubis—forms which had once borne arms against Neptune and Venus and against Minerva (Aeneid 8.678–700), and to which Rome, now conquered by them, offered supplication. This old man Victorinus had defended them for so many years with a thunderous voice.

[Note: The manuscripts vary extraordinarily here. The oldest and more carefully corrected copies—Fossatianus, Benignianus, Corbeiensis, and others—read, instead of “breathed upon the people even,” “breathed upon the people, already . . .” Five others, together with Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, Somner, and Blasius, read “breathed upon the people’s . . .”; Victorinus, the German manuscript, and others read “breathed upon the people, and already . . .”; some read “breathed upon the people even.” Louvain reads “breathed upon the people also.” We follow this reading, although we are by no means certain that it is genuine. We have also added the conjunction “and” before “monstrous,” because it occurs in all the manuscripts.—The Benedictine Fathers add in a supplementary correction: “Three English manuscripts read, ‘puffed up, breathed upon the people even monstrous gods,’ etc. This reading is superior to the others and should be adopted.” We have therefore adopted it and placed it in the text, following the Benedictines’ advice. M.]

Yet he was not ashamed to become a child of your Christ and an infant at your font, submitting his neck to the yoke of humility and bowing his forehead to the reproach of the cross.

4. O Lord, Lord, who bent the heavens and descended; who touched the mountains, and they smoked (Psalm 144:5)—by what means did you insinuate yourself into that heart? As Simplicianus said, Victorinus read the holy Scripture and investigated and diligently searched through all Christian writings. He said to Simplicianus, not openly but more privately and familiarly: “Know that I am already a Christian.”

But Simplicianus replied: “I will not believe it, nor count you among Christians, unless I see you in the church of Christ.” Victorinus mocked him, saying: “So, do walls make Christians?” He often said that he was already a Christian, and Simplicianus often gave the same reply; and the mockery of the walls was often repeated by him.

For he was afraid of offending his friends, proud devil-worshipers, from whose height of Babylonian dignity, as from the cedars of Lebanon that the Lord had not yet crushed (Psalm 29:3), he thought hostile attacks would fall heavily upon him.

But after reading and thirstily drinking in strength, he feared that Christ would deny him before the holy angels if he feared to confess him before human beings (Matthew 10:33). He appeared guilty to himself of a great crime: he was ashamed of the sacraments of the humility of your Word, yet was not ashamed of the sacrilegious rites of proud demons, which he, a proud imitator, had accepted.

He blushed at his vanity and was ashamed of the truth. Suddenly and unexpectedly he said to Simplicianus, as Simplicianus himself related: “Let us go to the church; I wish to become a Christian.”

Unable to contain his joy, Simplicianus went with him. Once Victorinus had been instructed in the first sacraments of Christian teaching, he soon afterward also gave his name so that he might be regenerated through Baptism, to the amazement of Rome and the joy of the Church.

The proud saw and were enraged; they gnashed their teeth and wasted away (Psalm 92:10). But the Lord God was the hope of your servant,

[Note: “His servant” is read by Rondinelli together with several manuscripts.]

and he did not look upon vanities and lying madnesses (Psalm 40:5).

5. Finally, when the hour came for making the profession of faith—which those who are about to receive your grace in Rome customarily recite before the faithful people from a raised place, in fixed and prescribed words committed to memory—Victorinus said that the presbyters had offered him the opportunity to recite it privately, as was customary to offer this to some who seemed likely to tremble from embarrassment.

But he preferred to profess his salvation in the presence of the holy multitude. The salvation he taught in rhetoric was not such a thing, yet he had publicly professed it. How much less, then, ought he to have feared your gentle flock when proclaiming your Word, since he had not feared the crowds of madmen when speaking his own words?

Therefore, when he ascended to recite the profession, everyone who knew him began to cry out his name to one another with the sound of rejoicing. And who there did not know him? A restrained but joyful sound passed through the mouths of all who rejoiced together: “Victorinus! Victorinus!”

They quickly cried out in exultation because they saw him, and quickly became silent in attentive expectation so that they might hear him. He proclaimed the true faith with splendid confidence, and they all wanted to snatch him into their hearts; and they did snatch him there by loving and rejoicing. Those were the hands of those who snatched him.

## CHAPTER III. That God and the Angels Rejoice More in the Conversion of Sinners

**6.** Good God, what happens in a human being, that he rejoices more over the salvation of a soul rescued from despair and greater danger than if hope had always been present for it, or its danger had been less? For you also, merciful Father, rejoice more over one repentant person than over ninety-nine righteous persons who have no need of repentance. And we too listen with great delight when we hear how, amid exulting angels [Note: [Col. 0751] In several editions: “of the exultant shepherd.” In the manuscripts: “of the shepherd exulting”; except the Valinensis, which has: “of the shepherd, with the angels exulting”; and this is better.], the sheep that had wandered is carried back on the shepherd’s shoulders; and how the drachma is restored to your treasuries, while the neighbors rejoice with the woman who found it; and how the joy of your household’s celebration brings tears from our eyes when it is read in your house concerning your younger son, that he was dead and came to life again, that he was lost and was found (Luke 15). For you rejoice in us, and your holy angels rejoice with a holy love for those whom you make holy. Yet you are always the same [Col. 0752], and you always know in the same way all things that are not always present or in the same condition.

**7.** What, then, happens in the soul, when it takes greater pleasure in things found or restored—things it loves—than it would have taken if it had always possessed them? Other things also bear witness, and everything is full of testimonies crying out: “It is so.” A victorious commander triumphs, yet he would not have conquered had he not fought; and the greater the danger in battle, the greater the joy in triumph. The storm tosses sailors about and threatens shipwreck; all grow pale at the prospect of death. Then the sky and sea become calm, and they rejoice exceedingly because they feared exceedingly. A beloved person is sick, and his pulse announces danger; all who desire his recovery are sick in spirit along with him. He improves, and still does not walk with his former strength; yet a joy arises such as there was not when he had previously walked safe and strong.

Human beings acquire even the pleasures of this life not only through unexpected troubles that break in against their will, but also through troubles deliberately undertaken and willingly accepted. The pleasure of eating and drinking does not exist unless the discomfort of hunger and thirst precedes it. Drunkards even eat certain salty morsels so that an unpleasant burning may arise; when drinking extinguishes it, pleasure follows. And it is customary not to give a betrothed bride immediately to her husband, lest the husband should regard as cheap the woman he was given without having longed for her while she was delayed.

**8.** This is true of shameful and detestable joy; it is true of joy that is permitted and lawful; it is true even of the most sincere honesty of friendship. It is true of the one who was dead and came to life again, who was lost and was found. Everywhere, greater joy is preceded by greater distress.

What is this, Lord my God, when you yourself are eternally your own joy, and certain things around you always rejoice in you? What is it that this part of creation alternates between decline and progress, estrangement and reconciliation? Is this their condition, and did you assign to them such a condition when, from the heights of heaven to the depths of earth, from the beginning to the end of the ages, from the angel to the worm, from the first movement to the last, you established every kind of good and placed all your righteous works, each in its proper place, carrying them out at their proper times?

Alas for me, how exalted you are in the heights, and how deep in the depths! Yet nowhere do you withdraw, and we scarcely return to you.

## CHAPTER IV. Why There Should Be Greater Rejoicing in the Conversion of the Noble

**9.** Come, Lord, act; stir us up and call us back; kindle us and seize us; burn us and make us sweet: let us love, let us run. Do not many return to you from a deeper hell of blindness than Victorinus did, and draw near and are enlightened, receiving the light which, when people receive it, gives them power to become your children? (John 1:9, 12.) But if they are less well known among the people, even those who know them rejoice less over them. For when many rejoice together, the joy in each individual is richer, because they kindle and inflame one another.

Moreover, those who are known to many possess authority with many for salvation and lead many who will follow. Therefore those who went before them also rejoice greatly over them, because their joy is not confined to them alone.

Far be it from your tabernacle that the persons of the rich should be preferred to the poor, or the noble to the obscure. Rather, you chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; and you chose the obscure things of this world, and the despised, and things that are not, as though they were, to bring to nothing the things that are (1 Corinthians 1:27–28).

And yet that very least of your apostles (ibid., 15:9), through whose tongue you uttered these words—when the proconsul Paulus, his pride defeated through the apostle’s service, had been placed under the gentle yoke of your Christ and made a provincial ruler of the great king (Acts 13:7, 12)—also loved to be called Paul instead of his former name, Saul, as a mark of so great a victory.

The enemy is more thoroughly conquered in the one whom he holds more completely and through whom he holds more people. He holds the proud more strongly through the name of nobility, and through the name of authority he holds more people.

Accordingly, the more joyfully Victorinus’ heart was thought of [Note: [Col. 0753] Eight manuscripts read “was compelled” (cogebatur), not inappropriately, to signify the violence done to the devil. We follow the received reading, found in many manuscripts as well; indeed, it can bear the same sense.]—the heart that the devil had occupied as though it were an impregnable fortress—and Victorinus’ tongue, the great and sharp weapon with which he had slain so many, the more abundantly your children ought to exult, because our King had bound the strong man, and they saw his vessels (Matthew 12:29) cleansed and prepared for your honor, and made useful to the Lord for every good work (2 Timothy 2:21).

## CHAPTER V. What Delayed His Conversion

**10.** But when your servant Simplicianus told me these things about Victorinus, I burned to imitate him; for that was why he had told the story. When he added that, during the reign of the emperor Julian, Christians had been forbidden by law to teach literature and rhetoric, and that Victorinus, embracing this law, had preferred to abandon his loquacious school rather than abandon your word, by which you make the tongues of infants eloquent (Wisdom 10:21), he seemed to me not so much stronger as more fortunate, because he had found an opportunity to devote himself to you.

For this I was sighing, though bound—not by another’s chains, but by my own iron will. The enemy held my will, and from it he had made a chain for me and had bound me. For from a perverse will came lust; and when lust was served, habit was formed; and when habit was not resisted, necessity was formed. These links, joined one to another—as I have called them a chain—held me fast in harsh slavery.

But the new will that had begun to arise in me, by which I might serve you freely and desire to enjoy you, O God, the sole certain happiness, was not yet strong enough to overcome the earlier will, hardened by age. Thus my two wills—one old, the other new; the one carnal, the other spiritual—were in conflict with each other and, by their discord, tore my soul apart.

**11.** Thus, through my own experience [Note: [Col. 0753] In B.: “In myself.” Lugd., Ven., and Lov.: “by my own self.” Er., Somm., Ann., Mart., and Flor., with several manuscripts: “through my own experience.” M.], I understood what I had read: how the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh (Galatians 5:17). I was present in both, but I was more truly myself in what I approved within me than in what I disapproved. In the latter I was already less myself, because to a great extent I suffered it unwillingly rather than did it willingly [Note: [Col. 0753] “Great,” according to Lov. M.] [Col. 0754] [Note: [Col. 0754] Lov.: “which I did willingly.” But “rather than” (quam) is to be read, as the other codices have it; and “more” is to be supplied, a particle Augustine likes to leave unexpressed.]

Yet habit had become more combative against me because it had arisen from me: willingly I had reached the point where I no longer wished to be. And who could rightly object when a just punishment followed sin?

Nor was there any longer that excuse [Note: [Col. 0754] Bad., Am., Er., Lov.: “no excuse.”] by which I used to persuade myself that I had not yet abandoned the world and served you because my apprehension of the truth was uncertain. For now the truth itself was certain. Yet I, still bound to the earth, refused to serve you; and I feared to be freed from all impediments just as one ought to fear being impeded.

**12.** Thus the burden of the world pressed sweetly upon me, as sleep usually does; and the thoughts by which I meditated on you were like the efforts of those who wish to wake but, overcome by the depth of sleep, sink back again. No one wishes to sleep forever, and everyone of sound judgment prefers to remain awake; yet a person often delays throwing off sleep when a heavy stupor weighs upon his limbs, and, although the time for rising has already arrived, he continues more willingly in the sleep that has begun to displease him.

In the same way I knew that it was better to surrender myself to your love than to yield to my desire; but the former pleased me and prevailed, while the latter delighted me and bound me [Note: [Col. 0754] Four manuscripts have: “and did not prevail.” But the reading of the other manuscripts, without the negation, is more correct. The thing that prevailed was what was preferred by the sounder judgment of the mind, although it was not chosen by the inclination of the still weaker will. Hence he says shortly afterward: “I had absolutely nothing to answer, convicted by the truth.”].

For I had nothing to answer you when you said to me, “Awake, sleeper, and rise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14). And when you showed me on every side that you were speaking the truth, I had absolutely nothing to answer, convicted by the truth, except slow and sleepy words: “Now, behold, now; wait a little.”

But “Now” and “now” had no end, and “Wait a little” went on for a long time. In vain I delighted in your law according to the inward person, while another law in my members resisted the law of my mind and led me captive into the law of sin that was in my members. For the law of sin is the force of habit, by which the mind is dragged and held even against its will, according to the penalty deserved by willingly slipping into it.

Wretched that I was, who would free me from this body of death, except your grace through Jesus Christ our Lord? (Romans 7:22–25.)

## CHAPTER VI. Pontitianus Tells of the Life of Antony

**13.** I shall tell how you freed me from the bond of my desire for sexual intercourse, by which I was held with the tightest constraint, and from slavery to secular affairs; and I shall confess to your name, Lord, my helper and my redeemer.

I continued my customary activities, while my anxiety increased, and every day I sighed for you. I attended your church as far as I was free from those affairs beneath whose burden I groaned [Note: [Col. 0754] Lov.: “in which I lived.”]. Alypius was with me, having withdrawn from the work of the lawyers after the third sitting and waiting for those to whom he might once again sell advice, just as I sold the ability to speak, insofar as it can be supplied by teaching.

Nebridius, however, had yielded to our friendship so that he might assist as a subordinate teacher to Verecundus, the most intimate friend of us all, a citizen and grammarian of Milan. Verecundus greatly desired this and, by the right of friendship, urgently requested faithful assistance from our group, which he very much needed.

Nebridius was not drawn there by a desire for profit. He could have earned more from literary work if he had wished; but our sweetest and gentlest friend did not wish to disregard the request of kindness. He acted with great prudence, taking care not to become known to persons who, according to worldly standards, were of higher rank, and avoiding in them every disturbance of mind. He wanted his mind to remain free and, for as many hours as possible, unoccupied, so that he might seek, read, or hear something concerning wisdom.

**14.** One day—I do not remember the reason for Nebridius’ absence—Pontitianus, a fellow citizen of ours insofar as he was an African, and a distinguished military officer at the imperial court, came to our house to see Alypius and me [Note: [Col. 0755] Thus in the manuscripts. But the printed books write “Potitianus.”]. He wanted something from us. We sat down to converse, and by chance he noticed a codex lying on the gaming table before us. He took it, opened it, and unexpectedly found the apostle Paul. He had supposed it to be one of the books connected with the profession that was wearing me down.

Then, smiling and looking at me, he expressed his astonishment and congratulated me that he had suddenly found those writings—and those alone—before my eyes. For he was a Christian and a believer, and he often prostrated himself in church before you, our God, in frequent and prolonged prayer.

When I told him that I devoted the greatest care to those Scriptures, he began to speak—he himself telling the story—of Antony the Egyptian monk, whose name shone brilliantly among your servants, though it had remained unknown to us until that hour. When he learned this, he lingered over the subject, introducing this great man to us who knew nothing of him, and expressing amazement at our ignorance.

We were astonished to hear of things so recently remembered and so fully attested, almost in our own time: your marvelous works in the true faith and catholic Church. We were all amazed—both we, because these things were so great, and he, because they were unknown to us.

**15.** From there his conversation turned to the communities of monasteries, to the ways fragrant with your sweetness, and to the fertile solitudes of the desert, of which we knew nothing. There was a monastery at Milan, full of good brothers, outside the city walls, under the care of Ambrose; and we did not know of it.

He continued speaking, and we listened attentively in silence. This led him to say that once, at Trier, he and three of his companions had gone out for a walk in gardens adjoining the walls while the emperor was occupied at the afternoon Circus games. As they happened to walk in pairs, one of them went off separately with one companion, and the other two likewise went off together.

Those two wanderers entered a cottage where some of your servants lived—poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5:3)—and there they found a codex containing the life of Antony. One of them began to read it, marvel, become inflamed, and, while reading, consider embracing such a life: abandoning secular military service [Col. 0756] and serving you. They belonged to those called agents of affairs [Note: [Col. 0756] Am., Er., and Lov. read the singular: “he was” (erat).].

Then, suddenly filled with holy and sober love, and angry with himself, he cast his eyes upon his friend and said to him: “Tell me, I beg you, where do we hope to arrive through all these labors of ours? What are we seeking? For what purpose do we serve in the army? Can our hope at court be greater than that we should become friends of the emperor? And there, what is not fragile and full of dangers? And through how many dangers does one arrive at a greater danger? And when will that be?” [Note: [Col. 0756] Most editions read: “and how long?” But the better manuscripts and Arn. read: “and when?” We prefer this so that the antithesis is retained, since the following clause says, “Behold, I become [one] now.” Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., Mart., Flor., and Rond. read “this” (istud), not “there” (istuc). M.]

“But if I wish,” he said, “I can become a friend of God—behold, even now.” He said this, and, troubled by the birth pangs of a new life, returned his eyes to the pages. He read, and he was inwardly changed where you saw him; his mind was stripped of the world, as soon became evident.

For as he read and wrestled with the waves of his heart, he sometimes groaned; then he discerned and resolved upon better things. Already yours, he said to his friend: “I have now broken away from that hope of ours, and I have decided to serve God; and from this hour, in this place, I am beginning. If you are unwilling to imitate me, do not oppose me.”

The other replied that he would remain his companion in so great a reward and so great a service [Note: [Col. 0756] Thus in the manuscripts. Lov.: “a companion of so great a reward.”]. And now both belonged to you, building a tower at the proper cost of abandoning all their possessions and following you (Luke 14:26–35).

Then Pontitianus and those who were walking with him through other parts of the garden, searching for them, came to the same place. When they found them, they urged them to return, since the day was declining. But after the two had described their decision and purpose, and how such a will had arisen and been strengthened in them, they asked the others not to trouble them if they refused to join them.

Those men, however, unchanged from their former ways, nevertheless wept, as he said [Note: [Col. 0756] “It was fitting,” according to Somm. and two German manuscripts. M.], piously congratulated them, commended themselves to their prayers, and, dragging their hearts along the earth, departed for the palace. The others, fastening their hearts to heaven, remained in the cottage.

Both had fiancées. When these women heard what had happened, they too dedicated their virginity to you.

## CHAPTER VII. Augustine Is Inwardly Consumed When He Hears Pontitianus

**16.** Pontitianus was telling these things; but you, Lord, were turning me back upon myself through his words, taking me away from my own back—where I had placed myself because I did not wish to look at myself—and setting me before my own face, so that I might see how ugly I was, how misshapen and filthy, stained and ulcerous.

I saw, and I shuddered; but there was nowhere for me to flee from myself. If I tried to turn my gaze away from myself, he continued telling what he was telling, and you again set me opposite myself and thrust me into my own eyes, so that I might find my iniquity and hate it.

I knew it, but I pretended not to; I closed my eyes [Note: [Col. 0756] Lov. in four of its manuscripts read “I lived with it”; in ours we found “I restrained myself.” He had his iniquity with him, living alongside it, yet he forgot it. “I restrained myself,” according to the Florentine edition. M.] and forgot.

**17.** The more ardently I loved those whose salutary emotions I was hearing about—those who had surrendered themselves wholly to you to be healed—the more detestably I hated myself in comparison with them.

For many years of mine had passed with me—perhaps twelve years since, at the age of nineteen, I had read Cicero’s *Hortensius* and been roused to pursue wisdom. I had postponed setting aside earthly happiness and devoting myself to seeking that wisdom, whose discovery—or even the mere search for it—ought already to have been preferred to found treasures, kingdoms of nations, and bodily pleasures flowing around me at my command.

Yet I, a wretched young man—very wretched—at the beginning of my youth had even asked you for chastity and said: “Give me chastity and continence, but not yet.” For I feared that you would hear me too quickly and heal me too quickly from the disease of lust, which I preferred to have satisfied rather than extinguished.

I had traveled along crooked paths through sacrilegious superstition—not certain even in that, but as though I were placing it above all else [Note: [Col. 0757] Er. with one manuscript: “above certain other things.”]—things that I did not seek in a godly manner, but attacked as an enemy.

**18.** I had thought that I delayed from day to day abandoning the hope of the world and following you alone because nothing certain appeared to me by which I could direct my course. Then came the day when I was laid bare before myself, and my conscience reproached me: “Where is your tongue?” [Note: [Col. 0757] “You are,” according to Er., Lugd., Lov., Mart. M.]

You were saying that, because the truth was uncertain, I did not wish to throw off the burden of vanity. Behold, now the truth is certain, and it still weighs upon you; while those whose shoulders are freer are receiving wings, those who have not been worn down by such searching, nor spent ten years and more meditating on these matters.

Thus I was inwardly consumed and overwhelmed by a terrible shame while Pontitianus was speaking in this way. When his conversation and the business for which he had come were finished, he departed.

And I turned to myself: What did I not say against myself? With what scourges of words did I not beat my soul so that it would follow me as I struggled to go after you? And it resisted [Note: [Col. 0757] The English manuscripts: “was held back”; others: “resisted.”]; it refused, and it did not excuse itself.

All arguments had been exhausted and refuted. A silent trembling remained; and my soul, as though fearing death, recoiled from being restrained from the flow of the habit by which it was wasting away toward death.

## CHAPTER VIII. He Withdraws into the Garden and What He Did There

**19.** During that great internal struggle in my own house—which I had vigorously stirred up in the chamber of my heart, with both face and mind in turmoil—I seized Alypius and cried out: “What are we suffering? What is this? What have you heard? The uneducated are rising up and taking heaven by force, while we, with all our learning and without a heart, behold where we roll about in flesh and blood!

“Is it because they have gone before us that we are ashamed to follow, while we are not ashamed even not to follow?”

I said things of this kind—I do not know exactly what—and my agitation carried me away from him, while he remained silent, staring at me in astonishment. For the usual sound did not come from my lips; my forehead, cheeks, eyes, complexion, tone of voice, and manner spoke more of my mind than the words I was uttering.

There was a small garden belonging to our lodging, which we used like the whole house; the owner of the house did not live there. The tumult of my heart had taken me there, where no one could interrupt the fierce struggle I had begun with myself, until it ended in the way you knew, but I did not [Note: [Col. 0758] “I did not know,” according to Er., Lugd., Ven. M.]. I was only raging in a health-giving way [Note: [Col. 0758] B.: “I was raging.” Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., Somm., Flor., and Rond.: “I was raging.” M.], and dying in a life-giving way, knowing what evil I was and not knowing what good I would shortly become.

I withdrew into the garden, and Alypius followed step by step [Note: [Col. 0758] This is the reading according to the manuscripts. The editions instead have: “step after step.”]. For my solitude was not truly solitary while he was there; and when had he ever abandoned me in such a state?

We sat down as far as possible from the house. I was raging in spirit, indignant with the most turbulent indignation that I was not entering into the agreement and covenant with you, my God, into which all my bones cried out that I must enter and lifted me toward heaven in praise. Yet it was not necessary to travel there by ships, chariots, or feet—at least not as far as I had traveled from the house to the place where we were sitting.

For to go there—and even to arrive there—was nothing other than to wish to go, but to wish strongly and wholeheartedly, not to toss and turn a half-wounded will this way and that, struggling as one part rose while another fell [Note: [Col. 0758] The old Corbie manuscript: “with one part rising, while another part lay elsewhere and fell, struggling.” Two English manuscripts: “with one part rising while another.” “The rising part,” according to Er. and Lugd. Ven. The Florentine edition reads as the Corbie manuscript; two Florentine manuscripts as the two English manuscripts. M.].

**20.** Finally, during the very fever of my hesitation, I performed many bodily actions that people sometimes wish to perform but cannot if they do not possess the necessary limbs, or if those limbs are bound by chains, weakened by illness, or impeded in some other way.

If I tore my hair, struck my forehead, or clasped my knee with interlocked fingers, I did so because I willed it. I could have willed it and not done it if the mobility of my limbs had not obeyed. Thus I did many things in which willing was not the same as being able; yet I was not doing what pleased me far more intensely and what, as soon as I willed it, I could do—because as soon as I willed it, I would certainly will it.

There, ability was identical with will, and the willing itself was already the doing; yet it was not done. The body obeyed the slightest will of the mind more easily, so that the limbs moved at the mind’s command, than the mind obeyed itself in carrying out its great will by will alone [Note: [Col. 0758] Lov., Somm., Blas.: “for its pleasure”—incorrectly, for Augustine is speaking of accomplishing the will. In the manuscripts, almost without exception, and in the earlier editions and Arn., the reading is “for its own will.”].

## CHAPTER IX. How It Happens That the Mind Commands Itself and Is Resisted

**21.** What is this monstrosity? And why is it so? Let your mercy shine, and let me ask whether perhaps the hidden places of human punishments and the darkest anguishes of the children of Adam can answer me.

What is this monstrosity? And why is it so? The mind commands the body, and it is obeyed immediately; the mind commands itself, and it is resisted. The mind commands that the hand move, and the ease is so great that the command can scarcely be distinguished from service—yet the mind is mind, while the hand is body.

The mind commands that the mind will, yet there is not another mind, and nevertheless it does not do so. What is this monstrosity? And why is it so?

The mind commands, I say, that it will, and it would not command unless it willed; yet what it commands is not done. But it does not will completely; therefore it does not command completely. For it commands to the extent that it wills, and what it commands is not done to the extent that it does not will.

The will commands that there be a will, and not another will, but itself. It does not command completely, and therefore what it commands does not exist. For if it were complete, it would not need to command itself to exist, since it would already exist.

It is therefore not a monstrosity partly to will and partly not to will, but a sickness of the mind, because it does not wholly rise, lifted by truth and weighed down by habit. Thus there are two wills, because neither of them is complete, and what one possesses is lacking to the other.

## CHAPTER X. Against the Manichaeans, Who Assert Two Contrary Natures on the Basis of Two Contrary Wills

**22.** Let them perish from your presence, O God, as vain talkers and deceivers of the mind perish—those who, when they notice two wills in deliberation, assert that they are two natures belonging to two minds, one good and the other evil.

They themselves are truly evil when they think such evil things; and they will themselves be good if they think and assent to what is true, so that your apostle may say to them: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

For while they wish to be light—not in the Lord but in themselves—and suppose that the nature of the soul is what God is, they have thus become denser darkness, because in their horrible arrogance they have withdrawn farther from you, the light that enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9).

Pay attention to what you say, be ashamed, draw near to him, and be enlightened; and your faces shall not be ashamed (Psalm 33:6).

When I was deliberating about serving my Lord God, as I had long resolved to do, I was the one who willed and the one who did not will; I—I was the one. I neither willed completely nor did I not will completely. Therefore I struggled with myself and was torn apart by myself.

This division indeed took place against my will, yet it did not reveal the nature of another mind; it revealed the punishment of my own. Therefore it was no longer I who carried it out, but the sin dwelling in me (Romans 7:14), arising from the punishment of sin committed in greater freedom, because I was a son of Adam.

**23.** For if there are as many contrary natures as there are wills resisting one another, there will no longer be two, but many. If someone deliberates whether to go to their gathering or to the theater, they cry out: “Behold two natures! One, the good one, leads him here; the other, the evil one, leads him back there.”

Where, they ask, does this hesitation of mutually opposed wills come from? But I say that both are evil: both the will that leads to their gathering and the will that leads back to the theater. Yet they believe that the will by which one goes to them is good.

What, then, if one of us deliberated and, with two wills arguing within him, wavered between going to the theater and going to our church? Would they not waver over what answer to give?

For either they will admit what they do not want to admit—that it is by a good will that people go to our church, as those go who have been instructed and held by its sacraments—or they will suppose that two evil natures and two evil minds are struggling in one person. Then what they are accustomed to say, that one is good and the other evil, will not be true. Or they will turn to the truth and not deny that, whenever someone deliberates, one soul is agitated by different wills.

**24.** Let them no longer say, then, whenever they perceive two wills opposing each other in one person, that two contrary minds, arising from two contrary substances and two contrary principles, are contending—one good and the other evil.

For you, truthful God, disapprove of them, refute them, and convict them, as is clear from the fact that the same person, when deliberating whether to kill someone with poison or with a sword; whether to invade this or that person’s estate, when he cannot invade both; whether to purchase pleasure through extravagance or save money through greed; whether to go to the circus or the theater, if both are offered on the same day; and I add a third possibility, whether to go steal from another’s house if the opportunity presents itself; and a fourth, whether to commit adultery if that opportunity also simultaneously opens—if all these things converge upon one moment in time and everything that cannot be done at once is desired equally—the soul is torn apart by four wills opposed to one another, or even by more, amid such an abundance of things desired.

Yet they do not usually say that there are so many different substances. The same is true of good wills.

I ask them whether it is good to delight in reading the apostle, whether it is good to delight in a sober psalm, and whether it is good to expound the Gospel. They will answer each time: “It is good.”

What, then, if all these things delight someone equally and at the same time? Do not different wills stretch the human heart when one deliberates which to seize first? All are good, and they contend with one another until one is chosen, toward which the whole will is directed—the one will that had been divided among many.

So too, when eternity delights us above, while temporal pleasure holds us back below, it is the same soul, not willing either the one or the other with its whole will. Therefore it is torn apart by grievous distress, while it places the former above the latter through truth, yet does not set aside the latter because of familiarity [Note: [Col. 0760] The Corbie manuscript and several others: “does not punish.”].

## CHAPTER XI. The Struggle of Spirit and Flesh in Augustine

**25.** Thus I was sick and tormented, accusing myself with an unusually bitter severity, turning and twisting myself within my chain, until the whole of that chain was broken—the small remnant by which I was already held, yet still held.

And you pressed upon my hidden places, Lord, with severe mercy, redoubling the lashes of fear and shame, lest I should again cease and the small, slender remnant that remained should not be broken, but grow strong again and bind me more firmly.

For inwardly I said to myself: “Let it happen now; let it happen now.” And with the word I was already moving toward the decision. I was almost doing it, yet I was not doing it. Nevertheless I was not falling back into my former state; I stood close by and drew breath.

Again I tried, and I was almost there—almost touching and holding it now—but I was not there, nor did I touch or hold it. I hesitated between dying to death and living to life. What had become deeply rooted in me through habit had greater force than what was unfamiliar and better. And the very moment in which I was to become someone else inspired greater horror the nearer it approached; yet it did not drive me backward or turn me away—it suspended me.

**26.** Trifles of trifles and vanities of vanities [Note: [Col. 0761] B.: “vanities of those who vanish.” Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., Somm., Dub., Mart., Flor., and Rond.: “vanities of vanities.” M.], my former companions, still held me back. They tugged at the garment of my flesh and murmured: “Are you abandoning us? From this moment shall we no longer be with you forever? From this moment shall you no longer be permitted to do this or that forever?”

And what were they suggesting by “this or that,” my God? What were they suggesting? May your mercy turn such filth away from the soul of your servant! What disgraceful things they were suggesting!

I heard them now much less than half clearly—not as though they were openly contradicting me and going out to meet me, but as though they were muttering behind my back and, as I was departing almost secretly, plucking at me so that I would look back.

Yet they delayed me, hesitating as I tried to tear myself away from them, shake them off, and leap over to where I was being called, while violent habit said to me: “Do you think you will be able to live without these things?”

**27.** But it was now saying this only very faintly. For from the side toward which I had turned my face, and across which I trembled to pass, there appeared the chaste dignity of continence—serene and joyfully cheerful without dissipation, honestly and gently inviting me to come and not hesitate, and stretching out pious hands to receive and embrace me, hands full of flocks of good examples.

There were so many boys and girls there; there was a great multitude of young people and people of every age; there were serious widows and aged virgins. And in all of them continence itself was not barren, but a fruitful mother of children of joy, born from you as her husband, Lord.

She mocked me with an encouraging mockery, as though she were saying: “Can you not do what these men and women do?” [Note: [Col. 0761] “What these men and women do,” according to Er., Lugd., Somm., Lov., and Rond.]

“Or can these men and women do it in themselves, and not in the Lord their God?” The Lord their God gave them to me. Why do you stand on yourself, and yet do not stand? Cast yourself upon him; do not be afraid—he will not withdraw so that you fall. Cast yourself confidently; he will receive and heal you.

I was exceedingly ashamed, because I still heard the murmuring of those trifles and hung there hesitating. Again continence seemed to say: “Be deaf to the unclean members that belong to you upon the earth, so that they may be put to death. They tell you of pleasures, but not as does the law of the Lord your God” (Psalm 118:85).

This dispute in my heart was nothing other than a dispute of myself against myself. Meanwhile Alypius, attached to my side, silently awaited the outcome of my extraordinary agitation.

## CHAPTER XII. How He Was Wholly Converted at the Admonition of a Voice

**28.** But when profound reflection drew my entire misery from its hidden depths and gathered it before the sight of my heart, a great storm arose, bringing a great downpour of tears.

And so that I might pour everything out with all its cries, I rose from beside Alypius. Solitude seemed more suitable for the task of weeping, and I withdrew farther away, far enough that even his presence could not burden me.

That was my state then, and he perceived it. I do not know what I had said—perhaps something in which the sound of my voice revealed that it was already heavy with tears [Note: [Col. 0761] Lov.: “And he perceived something.” For he certainly perceived something. So also Er., Lugd., Ven., Somm., and Rond. M.]—and in that state I had risen.

He therefore remained where we had been sitting, utterly astonished. I threw myself down somehow beneath a fig tree and gave free rein to my tears; and floods poured from my eyes, an acceptable sacrifice to you.

Not in these exact words, but with this meaning, I said much to you: “And you, Lord, how long?” (Psalm 6:4.) “How long, Lord, will you be angry forever? Do not remember our former iniquities” (Psalm 78:5, 8).

For I felt myself held by them, and I uttered miserable cries: “How long? How long—tomorrow and tomorrow? Why not now? Why not at this hour put an end to my uncleanness?”

29. I was saying these things and weeping with the bitterest contrition of my heart. And suddenly I hear a voice from a neighboring house, singing and repeatedly saying, as though it were a boy or a girl—I do not know which: “Take it, read it; take it, read it.” Immediately my expression changed, and I began most intently to consider whether children were accustomed to sing something like this in any kind of game; yet I could not recall ever having heard anything of the sort. Suppressing the rush of my tears, I rose, interpreting it as nothing other than a divine command to open the book and read the first chapter upon which my eyes should fall. For I had heard of Antony that, when he happened to come upon a reading from the Gospel, he had been admonished as though what was being read were addressed to him: “Go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21); and that, by this oracle, he had immediately been converted to you.

So I hurried back to the place where Alypius was sitting, for there I had left the Apostle’s book when I rose. I seized it, opened it, and read in silence the passage upon which my eyes first fell: “Not in revelry and drunkenness, not in sleeping chambers and debaucheries, not in strife and jealousy; but put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13:13–14). I did not wish to read further, nor was there any need. For as soon as the sentence ended, it was as though the light of security had been poured into my heart, and all the darkness of doubt fled away.

30. Then, inserting either a finger or I do not know what other mark, I closed the book and, with a calm expression, told Alypius. He, in turn, indicated what was happening within him—something of which I was unaware. He asked to see what I had read. I showed him, and he continued reading even beyond the point I had read, without my knowing what followed. It continued: “Receive the weak in faith” [Note: [Col. 0762] Lovaniensis: “assume”; other manuscripts: “receive.”] (the same work, 14:1). He applied this to himself and disclosed it to me. But by this admonition he was strengthened, and, with a settled and excellent resolution entirely suited to his character—by which he had long stood far above me—he joined me without any troubled hesitation.

From there we entered to my mother and told her. She rejoiced. We related how it had happened; she exulted and triumphed, and blessed you, who are able to do far more than we ask or understand (Ephesians 3:20), because she saw that you had granted her much more concerning me than she was accustomed to ask in her pitiable and tearful prayers. For you had converted me to yourself, so that I would neither seek a wife nor cherish any hope in this world, standing in that rule of faith which many years earlier you had revealed to her concerning me. And you had turned her mourning into joy (Psalm 29:12), far more abundantly than she had desired, and far more dearly and chastely than she had asked for grandchildren of my flesh.

# BOOK NINE

He speaks of the decision he had made to abandon the profession of rhetoric, though not before the time of the vintage vacation, which was then approaching. He then speaks of his retreat to the country estate of his friend Verecundus, of his Baptism, and of the virtues and death of his mother Monica, which occurred in that same year, namely, when Augustine was thirty-three years old.

[Col. 0763]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### He praises God’s goodness, acknowledging his own misery

1. O Lord, I am your servant; I am your servant and the son of your handmaid. You have broken my bonds; to you I will offer a sacrifice of praise (Psalm 115:16–17). Let my heart and my tongue praise you, and let all my bones say: “Lord, who is like you?” Let them say it, and answer me; and say to my soul, “I am your salvation” (Psalm 34:10, 3). Who am I, and what kind of person am I? What evil did I not do—or, if not in my deeds, in my words—or, if not in my words, in my will? [Note: [Col. 0763] Thus the manuscripts and Arnobius; Louvain reads: “What evil was I not? Or, in my deeds?” Other editions also have “I,” but change “or” into “or else.”] But you, Lord, are good and merciful, and your right hand regarded the depth of my death and drew out from the bottom of my heart the abyss of corruption. And this was the whole of it: to refuse what I wanted and to will what you willed.

[Note: Most editions read: “And this was the whole of it: to refuse what you willed and to will what you willed.” We prefer, with Arnobius, the reading of the manuscripts.]

But where, for so many years, and from what deep and hidden recess, was my free will summoned in an instant, so that I might bow my neck to your gentle yoke and my shoulders to your light burden (Matthew 11:30), Christ Jesus, my helper and my redeemer? How sweet it suddenly became for me to be without the sweetnesses of trifles! The things I had feared to lose were now a joy to relinquish. For you were driving them out from me, you who are true and supreme sweetness; you were driving them out, and entering in their place, sweeter than every pleasure—but not to flesh and blood; brighter than every light—but more inward than every secret; loftier than every honor—but not lofty in the eyes of those who exalt themselves.

Now my mind was free from the gnawing cares of ambition and acquisition, and from wallowing in and scratching the itch of lust. I was chattering to you, my glory, my wealth, and my salvation, Lord my God.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### He postpones abandoning the profession of rhetoric until the vintage vacation

2. In your sight it pleased me not to seize my ministry of speech tumultuously, but gently to withdraw it from the marketplace of verbal bustle,

[Note: In the Benignian manuscript: “from the marketplaces of verbal bustle.”]

so that children, who were studying not your law and not your peace but deceptive insanities and forensic battles, would no longer purchase weapons for their fury from my mouth. And now, appropriately, only a very few days remained before the vintage vacation. I decided to endure them so that I might leave in due and customary fashion, and, having been redeemed by you, no longer return to be sold.

Our plan, therefore, was known to you; to human beings, except our own people, it was not known. We had agreed that it should not be disclosed indiscriminately to anyone. Yet, as we ascended from the valley of weeping (Psalm 83:6–7) and sang the Song of Ascents, you had given us sharp arrows and destructive coals against the deceitful tongue (Psalm 119:3–5), as though it were contradicting us under the guise of advice and, as food is accustomed to do, consuming us through love.

3. You had shot our heart through with your love, and we carried your words transfixed in our inward parts. The examples of your servants—those whom you had made radiant from darkness and alive from the dead—piled up in the breast of our thoughts, burning away and consuming our heavy torpor, lest we sink to the depths.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “lest we be plunged into the depths.”]

They raised us powerfully, so that every breath of contradiction from the deceitful tongue might inflame us more intensely, not extinguish us.

Nevertheless, since, on account of your name, which you have sanctified throughout the earth, our resolve would certainly have its praisers, it seemed like an act of vanity not to wait for the approaching vacation, but to withdraw beforehand from the public profession, set before the eyes of everyone. [Note: [Col. 0764] “If I were to withdraw in this way,” according to six manuscripts; two German manuscripts have this reading, and one of them also has the words “if in this way.”] Then, when the faces of all those unaccustomed to it had turned toward what I had done, they would say many things about my wish to anticipate the approaching day of the vintage vacation,

[Note: “Many would say,” according to Martianay from four manuscripts.]
