as though I had wished to appear important. And what advantage would this have been to me—that my mind should be guessed at and discussed, and our good should be blasphemed?

4. Moreover, that very summer my lungs had begun to give way under the excessive labor of teaching, and I was breathing with difficulty; the pains in my chest testified that they were injured, and I could no longer sustain a louder or longer voice. At first this disturbed me, because it almost compelled me, by necessity, to lay down the burden of that teaching—or, if I could be treated and recover, at least to interrupt it.

But when a full desire arose and became firm within me to be free for leisure and to see that you are the Lord, you know, my God, that I even began to rejoice that this too provided a genuine excuse which might soften the offense of those who, for the sake of their children, never wished me to be free. Filled with such joy, I endured that interval of time until it ran its course. I do not know whether it lasted even twenty days, but they were endured bravely, because the desire that used to bring with it a grave burden had withdrawn, and I would have remained crushed unless patience had come to my aid.

Let any of your servants, my brothers, say that I sinned in this: that, though my heart was already wholly enlisted in your service, I allowed myself to sit even for one hour in the chair of falsehood. I do not argue. But you, most merciful Lord, did you not also forgive and remit this sin, together with my other dreadful and deadly sins, in the holy water?

## CHAPTER THREE  
### Verecundus grants him his country estate

5. Verecundus was distressed by this good of ours, because he saw that, on account of the bonds by which he was held most tightly, he was being abandoned by our companionship. He was not yet a Christian, and his faithful wife—though she was bound by an even stricter chain than the others—kept him back from the journey we had undertaken. He said that he wished to become a Christian in no other way than the way in which he could not.

Yet he kindly offered that, for as long as we remained there, we should stay at his country estate.

[Note: Almost all manuscripts read: “that we should be at his property.”]

You will repay him, Lord, in the resurrection of the just,

[Note: “Repay him,” according to Martianay from four manuscripts.]

for you have already repaid him that very portion. Although, while we were absent and already in Rome, he was seized by bodily illness and, having become a Christian and faithful, departed this life, you showed mercy not only to him but also to us, lest, while thinking of our friend’s outstanding kindness toward us and not counting him among your flock, we should be tortured by unbearable grief.

Thanks be to you, our God; we are yours. Your exhortations and consolations show it. Faithful promiser, you will repay Verecundus, for his estate at Cassiciacum, where we rested in you from the heat of the world, with the beauty of your eternally verdant paradise, because you forgave him his sins on earth, on the rich, cheese-bearing mountain, your mountain, the fertile mountain (Psalm 67:16).

6. At that time, then, Verecundus himself was distressed, while Nebridius rejoiced. For although Nebridius too, still not a Christian, had fallen into that pit of most destructive error, believing the flesh of the Son of your Truth to be a phantom, nevertheless, as he emerged from it, he was already such a man—still untouched by any sacrament of your Church, but a most ardent seeker of truth.

Not long after our conversion and regeneration through your Baptism, you released him from the flesh in Africa among his own people, as he served you as a faithful Catholic in perfect chastity and continence, after his entire household had become Christian through him. And now he lives in Abraham’s bosom. Whatever that bosom signifies,

[Note: Augustine later explained what he believed Abraham’s bosom to signify in Book 4 of *On the Soul and Its Origin*, chapter 16, section 24: “Understand Abraham’s bosom as a distant and secluded dwelling of rest, where Abraham is. It is called Abraham’s not because it belongs only to him, but because he is the father of many nations and is set before them as the leader of faith for imitation.”]

there my Nebridius lives, my sweet friend, but your adopted son, Lord, from a freedman’s condition; there he lives. For what other place could there be for such a soul? There he lives, from where he used to ask many questions of me, an inexperienced little man. He no longer places his ear at my mouth, but his spiritual mouth at your fountain, and drinks, as much as he can, wisdom according to his desire, blessed without end. Nor do I think that he becomes so intoxicated by it that he forgets me, since you, Lord, whom he drinks, remember us.

[Note: Two manuscripts read: “from whom he is given to drink.”]

Thus we were consoling the sorrowful Verecundus, without damage to our friendship, concerning this conversion of ours,

[Note: The Louvain edition, together with the older editions, reads: “concerning this association of ours.”]

and exhorting him to the faith appropriate to his station, even though it was a married life. We were also awaiting Nebridius, who could follow us very soon and was already on the point of doing so. Then, suddenly, those days finally passed. They had seemed long and numerous because of our love for the leisure of freedom, during which we sang from the depths of our being: “My heart said to you, ‘I have sought your face’; your face, Lord, I will seek” (Psalm 26:8).

## CHAPTER FOUR  
### Books written at Cassiciacum; letters to Nebridius; the sudden removal of severe toothache while he devoutly read the psalms

7. The day came on which I was also released in action from the profession of rhetoric, from which I had already been released in thought. It happened, and you freed my tongue, just as you had already freed my heart. I joyfully set out for the country with all my companions, and blessed you.

What I did there in writing—works that already served you, but still breathed, as though pausing after exertion, toward the school of pride—

[Note: Sommalius reads: “but still breathing toward the school of pride as though pausing.” Arnobius and our manuscripts prefer our reading. Augustine is alluding to what happens to fugitives: when they first stop, they continue panting for some time. The books he says were written at the villa are those listed in Book 1 of the *Retractions*, chapters 1–4.]

—is attested by the books discussed with those who were present and with me alone before you; what I wrote with Nebridius absent is attested by the letters.

And when would I have enough time to recount all your great benefits toward us at that time, especially when I am hastening toward greater matters? My memory calls me back, and it is sweet to me, Lord, to confess to you by what inward goads you subdued me, how you leveled me by humbling the mountains and hills of my thoughts, straightened my crooked ways, and smoothed my rough places; and how you subjected even Alypius, my brother in the heart, to the name of your only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ—a name he had initially disdained to have inserted in our writings.

For he preferred that our writings should breathe the fragrance of the cedars of the schools, which the Lord has now shattered, rather than the healing herbs of the Church that oppose serpents.

8. What words did I offer you, my God, when I read the Psalms of David, those faithful songs and sounds of devotion that exclude the swollen spirit? I was still inexperienced in your true love, a catechumen spending a holiday at the country estate with Alypius, himself a catechumen, while my mother clung to us in womanly dress, manly faith, the security of old age, maternal love, and Christian devotion.

What words I offered you in those psalms! How I was inflamed toward you by them, and set on reciting them, if I could, throughout the whole world, against the arrogance of the human race! Yet they are sung throughout the whole world, and no one can hide from your heat.

With what vehement and bitter indignation I resented the Manichaeans, and yet again pitied them, because they did not know those sacraments, those remedies, and were insane against the antidote by which they could have been made well! I wished that they were somewhere nearby then,

[Note: “That they were there then, while I did not know whether they were listening, and while I did not know that they were there,” according to Erasmus, the Louvain edition, Lovaniensis, Sommalius, and Rondellus.]

and, without my knowing that they were there, might look upon my face and hear my words when I read the fourth psalm—what that psalm had done to me during that time of leisure:

“When I called, the God of my righteousness heard me; in tribulation you enlarged me. Have mercy on me, Lord, and hear my prayer.”

Let them hear, while I did not know whether they were hearing, so that they would not think that I was saying the words because of them—those things I said among these words. For in truth I would neither have said them nor said them in that way if I had sensed that they were hearing and seeing me. And even if I had said them, they would not have received them as I did, and as I spoke them to myself and to you, before you, out of the familiar affection of my soul.

9. I shuddered with fear, and in that same place I burned with hope and exulted in your mercy, Father. All these feelings came forth through my eyes and my voice, when your good Spirit, turned toward us, said: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?”

For I had loved vanity and sought falsehood. And you, Lord, had already glorified your Holy One, raising him from the dead and placing him at your right hand (Mark 16:19), from where he would send from on high his promise, the Spirit of Truth, the Paraclete (John 14:16–17). And he had already sent him (Acts 2:1–4), but I did not know it. He had sent him because he had already been glorified, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven. “But the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

And prophecy cried out:

[Note: “The prophet,” according to the Florentine edition. “And the prophet cries,” according to Erasmus, the Louvain edition, Venice, Lovaniensis, Sommalius, Dubravius, Martianay, and Rondellus.]

“How long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? And know that the Lord has glorified his Holy One.”

It cries out, “How long?” It cries out, “Know!” And I, for so long, ignorant, loved vanity and sought falsehood. Therefore I heard and trembled, because these words were spoken to people like the person I remembered myself to have been. For in the phantoms that I had held in place of truth there was vanity and falsehood.

[Note: Badenius, with two manuscripts, reads “imaginations.” This is erroneous: Augustine, in Book 3, chapter 6 of this work, calls the images of things that exist *phantasiai*, but the images of bodies that do not exist at all *phantasmata*. While formerly attached to the Manichaeans, he had embraced these as truth. The Benignian manuscript has “of phantoms.” Erasmus, the Louvain edition, Venice, Lovaniensis, Sommalius, Dubravius, Martianay, Florence, and Rondellus read “in phantoms.”]

And I uttered many things with gravity and force in the pain of my recollection. Would that those who still love vanity and seek falsehood had heard them! Perhaps they would have been shaken and vomited it out; and you would have heard them when they cried out to you, because he who intercedes for us with you died for us by the true death of the flesh.

10. I read: “Be angry, and do not sin.” And how I was moved, my God! I had already learned to be angry with myself over my past sins, so that I would not sin thereafter. And rightly angry, because it was not some other nature belonging to the race of darkness that sinned through me, as those say who are not angry with themselves but store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and the revelation of your just judgment (Romans 2:5).

My good things were no longer outside me, nor were they sought with bodily eyes in this sun. For those who wish to rejoice in external things quickly fade away; they pour themselves into things that are seen and temporal, and with hungry thought they lick their images.

Oh, if they would grow weary from hunger and say: “Who will show us good things?” Then let us say, and let them hear: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, Lord.” For we are not the light that illuminates every human being (John 1:9); rather, we are illuminated by you, so that although we were once darkness, we may be light in you (Ephesians 5:8).

Oh, if they could see the eternal reality within!

[Note: The editions read: “Oh, if they could see the inward eternal light!” The Corbie manuscript reads: “Oh, if they could see in you the inward eternal light!” We have followed other manuscripts of the highest quality, including all the English manuscripts, which, omitting the other words, prefer: “Oh, if they could see the inward eternal!” Six Florentine manuscripts support this reading.]

Because I had tasted it, I was gnashing my teeth, since I could not show it to them if they brought before me, externally and apart from you, a heart in their eyes and said: “Who will show us good things?” For there, where I was angry with myself inwardly in my chamber, where I had been pierced, where I had sacrificed my old self by slaughtering it, and, having begun to reflect on my renewal, was hoping in you—there you had begun to grow sweet to me, and had given joy to my heart.

And I cried out while reading these words outwardly and recognizing them inwardly. I no longer wished to multiply earthly goods, devouring time and being devoured by time,

[Note: The manuscripts read this way; the editions have “by temporal things.” The Florentine edition and six manuscripts likewise support the reading.]

since in eternal simplicity I possessed other grain, wine, and oil.

11. In the following verse I cried out with a loud cry from the depths of my heart: “O in peace! O in the selfsame! O, what did he say: ‘I will lie down and sleep’!” For who will resist us when the word is fulfilled that is written: “Death is swallowed up in victory”? (1 Corinthians 15:54.)

And you are supremely the selfsame, you who do not change. In you there is rest, forgetting all labors, because there is no other one with you, nor are there many other things to attain that are not what you are. Rather, you alone, Lord, have established me in hope.

I read and burned; yet I could not discover what to do with those deaf and dead people, of whom I had once been a plague—a bitter and blind barker against the Scriptures, sweet with the honey of heaven and radiant with your light. And I wasted away over the enemies of this Scripture.

[Note: “Formerly,” according to three Martianay manuscripts; “in preference to these,” according to Rondellus and Martianay with one manuscript.]

[Note: Ambrose, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read: “And I wasted away over the hostile writings of this Scripture.” The manuscripts of Badenius and Arnobius lack the word “writings.”]

12. When will I recall all the events of those days of leisure?

[Note: The Benignian manuscript reads “When I recalled,” and thus begins chapter 12: “But I have not forgotten.”]

Yet I have neither forgotten nor will I remain silent about the severity of your scourge and the wondrous swiftness of your mercy. At that time you tortured me with toothache. When it became so severe that I could no longer speak, it entered my heart to inform all those who were present that they should pray for me to you, the God of every salvation. I wrote this on a wax tablet and gave it to them to read.

As soon as we bent our knees in supplication, that pain fled. But what pain? Or how did it flee? I was astonished, I confess, my Lord, my God; for from my earliest youth I had experienced nothing like it. Your signs were impressed upon me in the depths, and rejoicing in faith I praised your name. Yet that faith did not allow me to feel secure concerning my past sins, which had not yet been remitted and forgiven me through your Baptism.

## CHAPTER FIVE  
### He consults Ambrose about what he should read

13. When the vintage vacation had ended, I resigned my office, so that the people of Milan might provide their schoolchildren with another vendor of words, since I had chosen to serve you, and, because of my difficulty in breathing and the pain in my chest, was no longer adequate to that profession.

I also informed your bishop, the holy man Ambrose, by letter, of my former errors and my present resolve, asking him to advise me what I should read above all from your books, so that I might become more ready and better prepared to receive such a great grace. He ordered me to read the prophet Isaiah, I believe because, more clearly than the others, he announces the Gospel and the calling of the Gentiles. However, when I did not understand the beginning of this book and judged the whole work to be of the same character, I postponed reading it until I had become more practiced in the Lord’s eloquence.

## CHAPTER SIX  
### He is baptized at Milan with Alypius and Adeodatus

14. When the time came for me to give my name, we left the country and returned to Milan. Alypius also wished to be reborn in you with me. He had already put on the humility appropriate to your Sacraments and was so formidable a conqueror of the body that, with an extraordinary boldness, he trampled the frozen soil of Italy barefoot.

We also took with us the boy Adeodatus, born carnally from my sin. You had made him good. He was nearly fifteen years old, and in intelligence surpassed many serious and learned men.

I confess your gifts to you, Lord my God, creator of all things, and exceedingly powerful in reshaping our deformities. For in that boy I had nothing but sin.

[Note: Many and better manuscripts read: “Exceedingly powerful in forming”; and shortly afterward: “Apart from sin, I had nothing.”]

Whatever was being nourished by us in your discipline, you had inspired in us; no one else had done so. I confess your gifts to you.

There is a book of ours entitled *The Teacher*; he himself speaks with me there. You know that all the thoughts inserted there in the person of my interlocutor belong to him, although he was sixteen years old. I experienced many other things in him that were even more remarkable. That intelligence filled me with awe. And who besides you could be the creator of such wonders?

You quickly removed his life from the earth, and I remember him with greater security, fearing nothing for that boyhood, or adolescence, or indeed for that human being. We joined him, our contemporary, to ourselves in your grace, to be educated in your discipline. We were baptized, and the anxiety of our former life fled from us.

During those days I could not be satisfied with the astonishing sweetness of contemplating the depth of your plan for the salvation of the human race. How much I wept over your hymns and songs, moved intensely by the sweetly resonant voices of your Church! Those voices flowed into my ears, and the truth melted into my heart; from it the feeling of devotion boiled over, and tears ran down,

[Col. 0770]

and I was happy through them.

## CHAPTER SEVEN  
### The institution of ecclesiastical singing at Milan; the discovery of the bodies of Saints Protasius and Gervasius

15. The Church of Milan had only recently begun to celebrate this form of consolation and exhortation, with great zeal, the brothers singing together with voices and hearts. It was about a year, or not much more, since Justina, the mother of the boy-emperor Valentinian, persecuted your servant Ambrose on account of heresy, by which she had been led astray by the Arians. [Note: “Which,” according to six Martianay manuscripts and Rondellus with two manuscripts.]

The devout people kept watch in the church, prepared to die with their bishop, your servant. There my mother, your handmaid, held the foremost place in concern and vigils, living in prayer. We were still cold, far from the warmth of your Spirit, but we were nevertheless stirred by the astonished and troubled city.

Then it was established that hymns and psalms should be sung according to the custom of the Eastern regions, lest the people waste away from the weariness of grief. From that time this practice has been retained to the present day by many, indeed almost all, of your flocks, and imitated throughout the other parts of the world.

[Note: Sommalius and Martianay read: “Imitated throughout the other regions.” Rondellus reads: “Throughout the other parts of the world.”]

16. Then you revealed in a vision to the bishop mentioned above where the bodies of the martyrs Protasius and Gervasius lay hidden—bodies that, for so many years, you had preserved incorrupt in the treasury of your secret will, from which you brought them forth at the appropriate time to restrain a woman’s—though royal—rage.

When they had been brought to light and exhumed and transferred with due honor to the Ambrosian basilica, not only were those tormented by unclean spirits healed when the demons themselves confessed it, but also a certain citizen who had been blind for many years and was well known throughout the city. When he asked the reason for the joy of the tumultuous crowd and heard it, he leaped up and asked his guide to lead him there.

When he had been led there, he obtained permission to touch with his handkerchief the bier of your saints, whose death is precious in your sight (Psalm 115:15). As soon as he did so and brought it to his eyes, they were immediately opened.

From there the report spread; from there your praises burned brightly;

[Note: “Burning brightly,” according to Sommalius and Rondellus.]

from there the mind of that hostile woman, although it was not enlarged toward the health of belief,

[Note: This is the proper reading according to three English manuscripts, so that the contrast with the following “was restrained” is preserved. “Was brought to bear” is found in Erasmus, the Louvain edition, Venice, Lovaniensis, Sommalius, and Martianay.]

was nevertheless restrained from its fury of persecution.

Thanks be to you, my God. From where and to where have you led my memory, so that I should also confess to you these things, which I had forgotten and passed over despite their greatness? And yet, when the fragrance of your ointments was wafted in this way, we did not run after you (Song of Songs 1:3). Therefore I wept all the more amid the singing of your hymns, having long sighed for you and at last breathed freely,

[Note: Three manuscripts read: “but only breathed freely.”]

as much air as can enter a house of hay.

## CHAPTER EIGHT  
### The conversion of Evodius; the death of his mother and her upbringing from childhood

17. You make those who dwell together in unity inhabit one house (Psalm 67:7), and you joined to us Evodius, a young man from our own municipality. While he was serving in the imperial service, he was the first of us to turn to you and be baptized. He abandoned secular military service and was girded for yours.

We were together and intended to live together according to a holy resolve.

[Note: The manuscripts and Arnobius have this reading; Badenius, Ambrose, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read: “We lived together.” The following words, “according to a resolve,” are found in Sommalius and Rondellus.]

We were seeking what place would best accommodate us in serving you. Together we were returning to Africa. When we were at Ostia on the Tiber, my mother died.

I am passing over many things because I am hurrying. Receive my confessions and thanksgivings, my God, concerning countless matters, even those spoken in silence. But I will not pass over whatever my soul brings forth concerning that handmaid of yours who gave birth to me—bodily, so that I might be born into this temporal light, and in her heart, so that I might be born into eternal light.

[Note: This should be read with the manuscripts. Rondellus, from eight manuscripts, has: “so that I might be born.”]

I will speak not of her gifts but of yours in her. For she did not make herself, nor educate herself. You created her; neither father nor mother knew what sort of person would come from them. And she was trained in your fear by the rod of Christ, the rule of your only Son, in a faithful household, a good member of your Church.

Nor did she praise her mother’s diligence concerning her discipline as much as that of a certain aged maidservant who had carried her father when he was an infant, just as little children are commonly carried on the backs of somewhat older girls. Because of this, and because of her old age and excellent character, she was greatly honored by her masters in the Christian household.

She therefore diligently exercised the care entrusted to her over the daughters of the household. When necessary, she was forceful in restraining them with holy severity, and soberly prudent in teaching them. Apart from the hours during which they were fed very moderately at their parents’ table, she did not allow them to drink water, even if they burned with thirst, taking precautions against a bad habit and adding this sound saying:

“Now you drink water because you are not permitted to have wine. But when you have come to your husbands and become mistresses of storerooms and cellars, water will seem contemptible, but the habit of drinking will prevail.”

By this method of instruction and authority in commanding, she curbed the appetite of their tender age and trained the girls’ thirst toward an honorable moderation, so that they would no longer desire what was unbecoming.

18. Yet drunkenness had crept upon her, as my mother, your handmaid, related to me, her son. When, as was customary, she was ordered by her parents, like a sober girl, to draw wine from the cup, she would lower the vessel through the opening at the top. Before pouring the pure wine into the flask, she would sip a little with the edges of her lips, because she could take no more, her senses refusing it.

She did not do this out of any desire to become drunk, but because of certain excesses of youth that overflow in playful behavior and are usually suppressed in childish minds by the weight of their elders. Thus, by adding a small amount each day to that small amount—for “whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Sirach 19:1)—she had slipped into the habit of eagerly draining cups that were almost full of wine.

Where then was that shrewd old woman and her forceful prohibition? Could it have achieved anything against a hidden illness unless your medicine, Lord, were watching over us?

[Col. 0772]

In the absence of father and mother and nurses, you were present—you who created her, who call, and who also accomplish something for the salvation of souls through those placed over human beings.

[Note: Antoninus and Arnaldus suspect that the reading should be “through perverse people” or “through untoward people.”]

What did you do then, my God? From where did you cure her? From where did you heal her? Did you not bring forth a hard and sharp rebuke from another soul, like a medicinal blade from your hidden provisions, and by a single stroke cut away that rottenness?

For the maidservant with whom she was accustomed to approach the cup quarreled with her younger mistress—as happens, one alone with another—and threw this crime in her face, calling her, in a most bitter insult, a “winebibber.” Struck by that goad, she looked upon her own disgrace and immediately condemned and abandoned it.

As flattering friends corrupt, so quarrelsome enemies often correct. You do not repay them for what you accomplish through them, but for what they themselves intended. For that angry woman wished to provoke the younger mistress, not to cure her, and therefore she disclosed it secretly—either because the place and time of the quarrel had brought them together alone, or because she feared that she herself might be endangered for having revealed it so late.

But you, Lord, ruler of the heavenly and earthly realms, turning the depths of the torrent toward your purposes and ordering the turbulent flow of the ages,

[Note: The better manuscripts read: “ordering it.”]

even from the madness of one soul healed another, so that when anyone observes this, no one may attribute to his own power the correction by his word of someone whom he wishes to be corrected.

## CHAPTER NINE  
### He continues to praise his mother’s conduct
19. Thus she was brought up chastely and soberly, more subject to her parents than her parents were subject to her; and, when she had reached marriageable age, she was given to a husband and served him as though he were her master. She took pains to win him for you, speaking of you to him through her conduct—by which you made her beautiful, reverently lovable, and admirable to her husband. She endured the injuries of the marriage bed so patiently that she never had any quarrel with her husband on this account. For she awaited your mercy toward him, so that, believing in you, he might be made chaste.

He was, moreover, as outstanding in kindness as he was passionate in anger. Yet she knew not to resist an angry husband, not merely by deed but not even by word. Once he had calmed down and become composed, when she saw that the time was suitable, she would explain the reason for her conduct, if perhaps he had been provoked more thoughtlessly than was appropriate.

Finally, when many married women whose husbands were gentler nevertheless bore the marks of blows, even with disfigured faces, they would, in friendly conversation, complain of their husbands’ conduct. She, on the other hand, would blame their speech, seriously admonishing them, as though in jest, that from the time they had heard those documents called marriage contracts read aloud, they ought to have regarded them as instruments by which they had become slave-women, and therefore, remembering their condition, ought not to grow proud against their masters.

When these women, knowing how fierce a husband she endured, marvelled that they had never heard, or discovered by any indication, that Patricius had beaten his wife, or that the two had disagreed with one another in a domestic quarrel even for a single day, and when they asked her privately for the reason, she taught them the practice I have mentioned above. [Col. 0773] Those who observed it, having experienced its benefit, rejoiced; those who did not observe it were subjected to vexation.

20. Her mother-in-law, too, who at first had been provoked against her by the whispers of wicked servant girls, she overcame by such attentiveness, persevering patience, and gentleness that the older woman herself voluntarily disclosed to her son the double-tongued speech of the servants by which domestic peace between herself and her daughter-in-law was being disturbed, and requested punishment.

Accordingly, after he—both obeying his mother, maintaining household discipline, and caring for the harmony of his family—had restrained the exposed women with beatings, at the discretion of the one who had exposed them, she promised that they ought to expect such rewards from her for anything they might say maliciously about their daughter-in-law to please her. After this, when no one dared to do so any longer, they lived together with a memorable sweetness of mutual affection.

21. This great gift, too, you had bestowed upon that good servant of yours, in whose womb you created me, my God, my mercy: among any souls who were divided and at odds, wherever she could, she showed herself so peaceable that, when she heard from each side many bitter things about the other—such as swelling and undigested discord usually spews forth, when, in the presence of a friend, the undigested mass of hatred is exhaled in acrid conversations about an absent enemy—she nevertheless disclosed nothing to one about the other except what could serve to reconcile them. [Note: [Col. 0773] Bad., Am., Er., and several manuscripts read *crudelitas*, “cruelty,” rather than *cruditas*, “rawness.”]

This would seem a small virtue to me, unless I had experienced countless disturbances caused by some dreadful plague of sins spreading everywhere—not only the disclosure to angry enemies of what angry enemies had said, but also the addition of things that had not been said. Yet, on the contrary, it ought not to be enough for a human being merely neither to stir up nor to increase human enmities by speaking ill, unless that person has also endeavoured to extinguish them by speaking well. Such was she, taught by you, her inner teacher, in the school of her heart.

22. Finally, she won you her husband as well, when his temporal life was already approaching its end, and she did not mourn in him, now faithful, what she had endured when he was not yet faithful. She was also a servant of your servants. Whoever among them knew her praised, honoured, and loved you greatly in her, because they sensed your presence in her heart, attested by the fruits of her holy conduct.

For she had been the wife of one man, had repaid her parents with reciprocal devotion, had piously managed her household, and had testimony in good works. She had nourished children, giving birth to them as often as she saw them straying from you. Finally, for all of us, Lord—since by your gift you allow your servants to speak—who before her falling asleep were already joined together in you through the grace of your Baptism, she cared as though she had given birth to us all, and served as though she had been born from us all.

## CHAPTER X  
### A conversation with his mother about the kingdom of heaven

23. As the day on which she was to depart this life approached—a day known to you but unknown to us—it came about, I believe through your hidden arrangements, that she and I alone stood leaning against a certain [Col. 0774] window from which the garden within the house that sheltered us could be seen. This was at Ostia on the Tiber, where, withdrawn from the crowds after the exertion of a long journey, we were preparing ourselves for the voyage.

We were conversing there alone very sweetly. Forgetting the past and stretching forward toward what lay ahead (Philippians 3:13), we sought together, in the presence of the Truth—which you are—to understand what the eternal life of the saints would be, that life which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and which has not entered the human heart (1 Corinthians 2:9).

Yet we opened our mouths of the heart toward the heavenly streams of your fountain, the fountain of life that is with you (Psalm 35:10), so that, sprinkled from it according to our capacity, we might in some manner contemplate so great a reality.

24. When our conversation had reached the point at which the delight of bodily sensations, however great, and in whatever bodily light, seemed, in comparison with the joy of that life, unworthy not merely of comparison but even of mention, we raised ourselves with a more ardent affection toward that same reality. Gradually we passed through all bodily things, and the very heaven, from which the sun, moon, and stars shine upon the earth.

Still we ascended inwardly by thinking, speaking [Note: [Col. 0774] Lov. reads *loquendo te*, “speaking you.” The word *te* is absent from the manuscripts.], and marvelling at your works. We came to our own minds and transcended them, so that we might reach the region of inexhaustible abundance, where you feed Israel forever with the nourishment of truth, and where life is Wisdom, through which all these things came to be—both those that were and those that will be.

Wisdom itself does not come to be, but is as it was and will always be. Indeed, “having been” and “being about to be” do not belong to it; only “being” does, because it is eternal. For “having been” and “being about to be” are not eternal.

And while we were speaking and longing for it, we touched it slightly with the whole impulse of our heart. We sighed [Note: [Col. 0774] The manuscripts of Corbie read *susum spiravimus*, “we breathed upward.”] and left there, bound to it, the first-fruits of our spirit; then we returned to the sound of our mouths, where a word both begins and ends. And what is like your Word, our Lord, who remains in himself without growing old and makes all things new? (Wisdom 7:27.)

25. So we said: If the tumult of the flesh were silent for anyone, if the images of earth, water, and air were silent, if the heavens too were silent, and the soul itself were silent to itself, passing beyond itself by no longer thinking of itself; if dreams and imaginary revelations were silent, and every tongue and every sign, and whatever comes to be by passing away—if all these things were wholly silent, since, if anyone listened, all of them would say: “We did not make ourselves, but he made us who remains forever” (Psalm 99:3, 5)—if, after saying this, they too were silent, because they had raised their ear toward the one who made them, and he alone spoke, not through them but through himself, so that we might hear his word, not through the tongue of flesh, nor through the voice of an angel, nor through the sound of a cloud, nor through the riddle of a likeness; but might hear without these things the very one whom we love in them, just as even now we stretched ourselves out and touched, with swift thought, the eternal Wisdom that remains above all things [Note: [Col. 0774] Somm., Lov., and four manuscripts cited by Mart. read *attingimus*, “we touch.” M.];

if this were prolonged, and other visions of a far unequal kind were withdrawn, and this one vision seized, absorbed, and concealed its beholder within inward joys, so that eternal life were like this moment of understanding [Col. 0775] for which we sighed—would this not be, “Enter into the joy of your Lord”? (Matthew 25:21.) And when will this be? Will it be when we all rise, though we shall not all be changed? (1 Corinthians 15:51.)

26. I was saying such things [Note: [Col. 0775] Mart., with four manuscripts, reads *dicebamus talia*, “we were saying such things.” M.], though not in this manner or with these words. Yet you know, Lord, that on that day, while we were speaking in this way and this world was becoming worthless to us, together with all its pleasures, she said:

“My son, as far as I am concerned, nothing in this life now delights me. What am I still doing here, and why am I here, I do not know, now that my hope in this world has been exhausted. There was one reason why I wanted to remain in this life for a little while: to see you a Christian Catholic before I died. My God has granted me this more abundantly, so that I see you also, having rejected earthly happiness, as his servant. What am I doing here?”

## CHAPTER XI  
### The ecstasy and death of his mother

27. I do not adequately remember what I replied to this. Meanwhile, within scarcely five days, or not much more, she was laid up with fevers. During her illness, one day she suffered a failing of consciousness and was briefly withdrawn from present things. We rushed to her, but she soon returned to her senses and looked at my brother and me standing beside her. Then, as though asking a question, she said to us:

“Where was I?”

Then, seeing us stunned with grief, she said:

“Will you bury your mother here?”

I remained silent and restrained my tears. But my brother said something expressing his wish that she might die not abroad but in her homeland, as though that would be happier.

When she heard this, she rebuked him with an anxious expression, looking at him as though startled that he could think such things. Then, turning her eyes toward me, she said:

“See what he is saying.”

And immediately she said to both of us:

“Lay this body wherever you please. Do not let concern for it disturb you. I ask only this: wherever you are, remember me at the altar of the Lord.”

When she had explained this thought in whatever words she could, she fell silent, and as the illness grew worse she was afflicted by it.

28. I, however, reflecting on your gifts, invisible God, which you send into the hearts of your faithful and from which wonderful fruits arise, rejoiced and gave you thanks. I recalled what I knew: how anxiously she had always concerned herself with the tomb she had provided and prepared for herself beside her husband’s body.

Since they had lived together in great harmony, she also wished—as the human spirit, less capable of divine things, tends to do—to have herself joined to that happiness and to be remembered by people as having been granted, after her journey across the sea, that, joined in the same earth, the earth might cover both spouses.

When this vanity had begun to disappear from her heart through the fullness of your goodness, I did not know, and I rejoiced in wonder that she had revealed it to me in this way [Note: [Col. 0775] Thus Arn. and several of the principal manuscripts; Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read *apparuisset*, “had appeared.” Rond. likewise reads this, supported by its manuscripts and by Flor., with the same number of manuscripts. M.].

Yet even in our conversation by the window, when she said, “What am I doing here now?” she did not seem to desire to die in her homeland.

I also heard afterward that, when we were already at Ostia, she was speaking one day with some of my friends, with the confidence of a mother, about contempt for this life and the goodness of death. I was not present. They marvelled at the virtue you had given her and asked whether she did not fear leaving her body so far from her city.

“Nothing,” she said, “is far from God; nor is there any reason to fear that he will not know at the end of the world where to raise me.”

Thus, on the ninth day of her illness, in the fifty-sixth year of her life and the thirty-third of mine [Note: [Col. 0776] All manuscripts, both printed and written, assign this number without exception. It follows that the passage is hardly corrupt, as Caesar Baronius suspected, *ad an.* 388, no. 71, and in the note to Mart., 3 May.], that religious and devout soul was released from the body.

## CHAPTER XII  
### How he mourned his mother’s death; sacrifice for the dead

29. I closed her eyes, and immense sorrow flowed together into my heart and poured itself out in tears. At the same time my eyes, under the violent command of my spirit, drew their fountain back into themselves until it was dry, and I felt very wretched in this struggle.

Then, when she breathed out her last breath [Note: [Col. 0776] Most manuscripts omit the word *spiritum*, “breath/spirit.”], the boy Adeodatus burst into loud weeping, but all of us restrained him, and he fell silent. In the same way, something childish in me, which was slipping into tears in the youthful voice of my heart, was restrained and became silent.

For we did not think it appropriate to celebrate that funeral with lamentations, tearful groans, and wailing, because such things usually express grief for some misery of the dying or an extinction as though complete. But she was neither dying miserably nor dying altogether. We held this to be true both from the evidence of her conduct and from her sincere faith and certain reasons.

30. What, then, was it that caused me such deep inward pain, except the fresh wound caused by the sudden rupture of our sweetest and dearest habit of living together? I did indeed rejoice in her testimony, when, during that final illness, while flattering me with her attentions, she called me dutiful and recalled, with great affection, that she had never heard from my mouth a harsh or insulting sound directed at her [Note: [Col. 0776] Lov. and other editions read *sermonem*, “speech.”].

Yet what comparable honour, my God, who made us, was there between the honour I had shown her and the service she had shown me? Since I was therefore deprived of so great a comfort, my soul was wounded, and my life, which had become one from hers and mine, was somehow torn apart.

31. After that childish weeping had been restrained, Evodius took up the Psalter and began to sing a psalm. The whole household responded:

“I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 100:1).

When word was heard of what was happening, many brothers and religious women gathered. While those whose duty it was cared for the funeral according to custom, I withdrew to a place where I could decently do so and, with those who thought I ought not to be left alone, discussed what was appropriate to the moment. By this nourishment of truth I was soothing the anguish known to you, while they did not know it and listened intently, believing that I was without any sense of pain [Col. 0777].

But in your ears, where none of them heard, I reproached the softness of my feelings and restrained the flow of sorrow. It yielded to me for a little while, then was carried along again by its own force—not to the point of breaking into tears or altering my expression, but I knew what I was suppressing in my heart.

And because I was deeply displeased that these human feelings, which necessarily arise according to the proper order and condition of our nature, should have so much power over me, I grieved over my grief with another grief and was tormented by a double sorrow.

32. And behold, the body was carried out [Note: [Col. 0777] Rond. completes the preceding sentence in this way: “And behold, the body was carried out.” M.]. We went and returned without tears.

For even during the prayers we poured out to you, when the sacrifice of our redemption was offered for her, with the corpse already placed beside the tomb before it was laid in it—as is customary there—I did not weep. Yet throughout the day I was deeply sorrowful in secret, and with my mind disturbed I prayed to you as best I could, asking you to heal my pain, but you did not do so. I believe that you were commending to my memory, by this one lesson at least, how difficult it is for every habit to be avoided, even by a mind that is no longer nourished by deceptive words [Note: [Col. 0777] Three English manuscripts read *pascitur, difficile posse vitare. Visum etiam.*].

It also seemed to me that I should go and bathe. I had heard that the name for baths had been derived from the Greek word *βαλανεῖον* (*balaneion*), because it drives anxiety from the mind. Behold, I confess this also to your mercy, Father of orphans: I bathed, and I was just as I had been before bathing. The bitterness of sorrow had not sweated out of my heart.

Then I slept and awoke, and found that my grief had been eased to no small degree. While I was alone in my bed, I recalled the truthful verses of your Ambrose—for you are:

> God, creator of all,  
> and ruler of heaven’s sphere,  
> clothing the day with lovely light,  
> and the night with sleep-giving grace:

> so that rest may restore  
> relaxed limbs to the use of labour,  
> lighten weary minds,  
> and release anxious grief.

[Note: [Col. 0777] Earlier printed editions read *soporis*, “of sleep”; many manuscripts read *sopora*, from the verb *soporo*, “to lull to sleep,” which is better, since in the hymn for night a peaceful sleep is requested for the renewal of body and mind. According to Flor. and Mart., with seven manuscripts, and Rond., with six manuscripts, one should read *soporis*. M.]

33. Thereupon I gradually returned to my former awareness of your servant, of her devout conduct toward you, and of her holy [Note: [Col. 0777] Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read *sanctam*, “holy,” agreeing with *conversationem* rather than *sancte*.] gentleness and obedience toward us, of which I had suddenly been deprived. And I wanted to weep in your presence for her and on her behalf, for myself and on my own behalf.

I let the tears I had been restraining flow as much as they wished, spreading them beneath my heart; and I found rest in them [Note: [Col. 0777] Mart., with three manuscripts, and Arn. read *requievi in eis*, “I found rest in them.” M.], because your ears were there, not those of any human being who might arrogantly interpret my weeping.

And now, Lord, I confess this to you in writing. Let whoever wishes read it and interpret it as he wishes. If he finds it sinful that I wept for a small part of an hour over my mother—my mother, who for the moment had died before my eyes, though she had wept over me for many years so that I might live before your eyes—let him not mock me. Rather, if he possesses great charity, let him weep to you for my sins, Father of all the brothers of your Christ [Col. 0778].

## CHAPTER XIII  
### He prays for his deceased mother

34. Now that my heart has been healed of that wound in which a carnal affection could be reproved, I pour out to you, our God, on behalf of that servant of yours, a very different kind of tears. They flow from a spirit shaken by consideration of the dangers of every soul that dies in Adam.

Although she had been made alive in Christ (1 Corinthians 15:22), and, while not yet released from the flesh, had lived in such a way that your name was praised in her faith and conduct, I nevertheless do not dare to say that, from the time you regenerated her through Baptism, no word ever came from her mouth against your command.

Your Son, the Truth, said:

“If anyone says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ he will be liable to the fire of Gehenna” (Matthew 5:22).

And woe even to the praiseworthy life of human beings if, setting mercy aside, you examine it. Yet because you do not investigate sins with excessive severity, we confidently hope that she may find some place with you for pardon [Note: [Col. 0778] These words, “may find some place for pardon,” are absent from almost all manuscripts. They are present, however, in the Florentine edition. M.].

Whoever enumerates his true merits to you, what does he enumerate to you but your gifts? O that human beings would recognize themselves as human beings, and that whoever boasts would boast in the Lord! (2 Corinthians 10:17.) [Note: [Col. 0778] Thus the manuscripts with Arn.; Lov., following older editions, reads: “O that all human beings would recognize themselves, and that those who boast would boast in the Lord.” The final part of the sentence is also preserved in Ven. in this form: “And let those who boast boast in the Lord.” M.]

35. Therefore, my praise and my life, God of my heart, setting aside for a little while her good deeds, for which I joyfully give you thanks, I now appeal to you for my mother’s sins. Hear me through the Medicine of our wounds, who hung upon the tree and, seated at your right hand, intercedes for us (Romans 8:34).

I know that she acted mercifully and from the heart forgave the debts of those who owed her. Forgive her debts also, if she contracted any during so many years after the water of salvation (Matthew 6:12). Forgive, Lord, forgive, I beseech you; do not enter into judgment with her (Psalm 143:2). Let mercy triumph over judgment (James 2:13), for your words are true, and you have promised mercy to the merciful (Matthew 5:7). You granted them the ability to be merciful, since you will have mercy on whomever you have mercy, and you will show mercy to whomever you are merciful (Exodus 33:19; Romans 9:15).

36. And I believe that you have already done what I ask of you, but accept, Lord, the voluntary offering of my lips (Psalm 119:108).

For, when the day of her release was impending, she did not think of having her body covered expensively or embalmed with spices, nor did she desire an honoured monument or concern herself with a family tomb. She did not give us these instructions, but only wished that she be remembered at your altar, which she had served without missing a single day. From that altar she knew that the holy Victim was dispensed, by which the record that stood against us was erased (Colossians 2:14), by which the enemy who counted our sins and sought something to accuse us of was defeated, finding nothing in the one through whom we conquer.

Who will restore to him innocent blood? Who will return to him the price by which he bought us, so that he might take us away from him [Note: [Col. 0779] Arn., with several manuscripts, reads *offerat*, “might offer us”; but Bad., Arn., Er., and Lov., with more manuscripts, read *auferat ei*, “might take us away from him,” namely, from Christ the buyer, as it seems to us.]?

To the sacrament of this price of our redemption your servant bound her soul by the bond of faith. Let no one tear her away from your protection. Let neither the lion nor the dragon intervene against her by force or deceit. For she will not answer that she owes nothing, lest she be convicted and seized by the cunning accuser; rather, she will answer that her debts have been forgiven by the one to whom no one can repay what he, though owing nothing, paid on our behalf.

37. Let her therefore rest in peace with her husband, before whom and after whom she was married to no one else, and whom she served, bearing fruit for you with perseverance (Luke 8:15), so that she might win him also for you.

And inspire, my Lord, my God [Note: [Col. 0779] Ven. reads “Lord, my God.” M.], inspire your servants, my brothers, your sons, my masters, whom I serve by voice, heart, and writing, so that all who read this may remember at your altar Monnica, your servant [Note: [Col. 0780] I have followed the ancient manuscripts, which use the double *n* in *Monnica*. The name is likewise written in the prayer composed by Abbot William out of devotion to Augustine’s wishes, in these words: “Remember, O Lord, the soul of your servant Patricius and of your servant Monnica; and if I, a wretched sinner, may lawfully desire anything for the soul of their son, my lord Augustine, your most beloved confessor, even with the innermost affection of my heart,” and so forth. The complete prayer is found in the first volume of the *Veterum Analecta*.], together with Patricius, once her husband, through whose flesh you brought me into this life, though I do not know how.

Let them remember my parents with pious affection in this transitory light, my brothers under you as Father in the Catholic Mother, and my fellow citizens in the eternal Jerusalem, toward which the pilgrimage of your people sighs from its departure to its return. Thus may what she asked of me at the end be granted to her more abundantly through the prayers of many who confess you [Note: [Col. 0780] Several editions read “both through their confessions”; the word “both” is absent from the manuscripts that we consider preferable.], than through my prayers.

# BOOK TEN

He now searches into himself and openly declares not what he had been before, but what he now is. He strives to make known the God whom he loves; and, proceeding through the several classes of created things, he expounds at length the entirely astonishing power of memory and rejoices that God has a place in his memory. He examines his actions, senses, and affections in relation to the threefold temptation of pleasure, curiosity, and pride. He confesses Christ the Lord as the one mediator between God and human beings, and trusts that through him all the weaknesses of his soul must be healed.

[Col. 0779]

## CHAPTER I  
### Hope and joy in God alone

[Col. 0779]

1. May I know you, my knower; may I know you as I have also been known (1 Corinthians 13:12). Power of my soul, enter into it and make it suited to yourself, so that you may possess and hold it without spot or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:27).

This is my hope; therefore I speak, and in this hope I rejoice whenever I rejoice soundly [Note: [Col. 0779] Somm. and six manuscripts cited by Mart. read *sane*, “soundly.” M.]. The other things of this life are less to be mourned in proportion as they are mourned more, and more to be mourned in proportion as they are mourned less.

For behold, you have loved truth (Psalm 51:8), since whoever does it comes to the light (John 3:21). I wish to do it in my heart before you through confession, and in my writing before many witnesses.

## CHAPTER II  
### Since God knows hidden things, what does it mean to confess to him?

2. What could be hidden in me from you, Lord, whose eyes see the naked depths of human consciousness, even if I did not wish to confess it to you? I would conceal you from myself, not myself from you.

But now, because my groaning is witness that I am displeasing to myself, you shine forth and please me, and you are loved and desired, so that I may be ashamed of myself, reject myself, and choose you, and please neither you nor myself except because of you.

To you, therefore, Lord, I am manifest, whoever I may be, and I have said with what benefit I confess to you. For I do this not with words of the flesh and bodily voices, but with words of the soul and the cry of thought, which your ear knows.

When I am wicked, confessing to you means nothing other than that I displease myself. When I am devout, confessing to you means nothing other than that I do not attribute this to myself, for you bless the righteous (Psalm 5:12), but first justify the ungodly (Romans 4:5).

Thus my confession, my God, is made silently and not silently in your presence. It is silent in sound, but cries out in affection. For I do not say anything right to human beings that you have not first heard from me, nor do you hear from me anything of that kind that you have not first told me.

## CHAPTER III  
### For what benefit he will henceforth confess what he is, not what he was

3. What, then, have I to do with human beings, that they should hear my confessions, as though they were going to heal all my illnesses? They are curious to know another’s life, but slow to correct their own.

What do they want to hear from me about who I am, when they do not want to hear from you about who they are? And how do they know, when they hear from me about myself, whether I am telling the truth? For no one knows what is happening in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him (1 Corinthians 2:11).

But if they hear from you about themselves, they will not be able to say, “The Lord is lying.” For what does it mean to hear from you about oneself except to know oneself? And who knows himself and says, “It is false,” unless he himself is lying?

But because charity believes all things (1 Corinthians 13:7), at least among those whom it joins together and makes one, I too, Lord, confess to you in such a way that human beings may hear me—human beings to whom I cannot demonstrate whether I am confessing the truth. Yet those whose ears charity opens to me believe me.

4. Nevertheless, my innermost physician, make clear to me for what benefit I do this. When the confessions of my past evils—which you have forgiven and covered, so that you might make me blessed in yourself (Psalm 32:1), changing my soul through faith and your sacrament—are read and heard, they rouse the heart so that it does not sleep in despair and say, “I cannot,” but awakens to the love of your mercy and the sweetness of your grace, through which every weak person is made strong, once that person becomes conscious through it of his weakness.

Good people delight in hearing about the past evils of those who are now free from them. They do not delight because those things are evil, but because they existed and no longer exist.

For what benefit, then, my Lord, to whom my conscience confesses daily, more secure in the hope of your mercy than in its own innocence—for what benefit, I ask, do I also confess before you to human beings through these writings what I now am, not what I was?

I have seen and described that benefit. But who I still am—behold, many wish to know this at the very time of my confessions: many who know me and do not know me, who have heard something from me or about me. Yet their ear is not at my heart, where I am whoever I am.

They therefore wish to hear me confess what I am inwardly, where they cannot direct eye, ear, or mind. Yet they want to believe—do they also want to know? For the charity by which they are good tells them that I am not lying when I confess about myself, and that same charity in them believes me.

## CHAPTER IV  
### The great benefits of this kind of confession

5. But for what benefit do they want this? Do they perhaps wish to rejoice with me when they hear how far I have advanced toward you through your gift, and to pray for me when they hear how much I am held back by my own burden?

I will reveal myself to such people. For it is no small benefit, Lord my God, that many give thanks to you for us and that many ask you on our behalf.

Let brotherly affection love in me what you teach it to love, and let it grieve in me what you teach it to grieve over. Let that affection be brotherly, not foreign, not that of the sons of strangers, whose mouth has spoken vanity and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity (Psalm 144:8); but let it be brotherly affection which, when it approves me, rejoices over me, and when it reproves me, grieves for me—for whether it approves or reproves me, it loves me.

I will reveal myself to such people. Let them breathe freely over my good deeds and sigh over my evil ones. My good deeds are your institutions and gifts; my evil deeds are my sins and your judgments. Let them breathe freely over the former and sigh over the latter, and let hymn and weeping rise into your presence from fraternal hearts as from your censers (Revelation 8:3).

But you, Lord, pleased by the fragrance of your holy temple, have mercy on me according to your great mercy (Psalm 51:1), for the sake of your name; and, never abandoning what you have begun, bring my unfinished works to completion.

6. This is the benefit of my confessions: not what I was, but what I am, so that I may confess this [Note: [Col. 0781] B. does not contain the words: “not what I was, but what I am, so that I may confess this.” They are also absent from several editions and manuscripts, but are preserved by the finest witnesses. M.] not only before you with a secret exultation mingled with trembling and a secret sorrow mingled with hope (Philippians 2:12), but also in the ears of believing human beings, companions in my joy and partners in my mortality, my fellow citizens and fellow pilgrims, those who go before, those who follow, and those who travel with me along the way.

These are your servants, my brothers, whom you wished to be your sons, my masters, whom you commanded me to serve if I wish to live with you and from you.

And your Word would have been insufficient for me if, by speaking, it had commanded without going before me by acting. I too do this in deeds and words; I do it beneath your wings, with exceedingly great danger, except that beneath your wings my soul is subject to you and my weakness is known to you.

I am little, but my Father lives forever, and my guardian is capable of protecting me. For he himself is the one who begot me and guards me. And you yourself are all my good, you almighty one who are with me and who were before I was with you.

Therefore I will reveal to those whom you command me to serve not what I was, but what I now am and what I still am. Yet I do not judge myself (1 Corinthians 4:3). Thus let me be heard.

## CHAPTER V  
### A human being does not know himself entirely

7. For you judge me, Lord. Although no one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him (1 Corinthians 2:11), nevertheless there is something in a human being that even the human spirit within him does not know. But you, Lord, know everything about the one whom you made.

Although, in your presence, I despise myself and consider myself earth and ashes, I nevertheless know something about you that I do not know about myself. And certainly now we see through a mirror in an enigma, not yet face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). Therefore, as long as I am a pilgrim away from you, I am more present to myself than to you, yet I know that you cannot in any way be violated. But I do not know against which temptations I am able to resist and against which I am not.

There is hope, because you are faithful: you do not allow us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, but with the temptation you also provide a way out, so that we may be able to endure it.

Let me therefore confess what I know about myself, and confess also what I do not know about myself. For what I know about myself, I know because you shine upon me; and what I do not know about myself, I shall remain ignorant of until my darkness becomes like midday in your presence (Isaiah 58:10).

## CHAPTER VI  
### What he loves when he loves God; and how God is known through creatures

8. With a consciousness that is not doubtful but certain, Lord, I love you. You struck my heart with your word, and I loved you.

But heaven and earth and all that is in them—behold, from every side they say to me that I should love you, and they do not cease saying this to everyone, so that they are without excuse (Romans 1:20). Yet you will have mercy on whom you will have mercy and will show mercy to whom you will be merciful; otherwise heaven and earth speak your praises to the deaf.

What, then, do I love when I love you? Not bodily appearance, nor temporal beauty, nor the brightness of light—so welcome to these eyes [Note: [Col. 0782] Ven. also reads *etiam*, “also/even.” M.]—not sweet melodies of every kind of song, not the fragrance of flowers, ointments, and spices, not manna and honey, not limbs pleasing to the embraces of the flesh.

I do not love these things when I love my God. And yet I love a certain light, a certain voice, a certain fragrance, a certain food, and a certain embrace when I love my God—the light, voice, fragrance, food, and embrace of my inner self; where there shines for my soul what no place can contain, where sounds what no time can seize, where smells what no breeze scatters, where tastes what no appetite diminishes, and where clings what no satisfaction tears away.

This is what I love when I love my God.

9. And what is this? I questioned the earth, and it said, “I am not”; and whatever things are in it confessed the same. I questioned the sea and the abysses, and the creeping things of living souls, and they answered: “We are not your God; seek above us.” I questioned the breezes that blow, and the whole air with its inhabitants said: “Anaximenes is mistaken; I am not God.” I questioned the sky, the sun, the moon, and the stars; and they said: “Neither are we the God whom you seek.” And I said to all those things that surround the doors of my flesh: “You have told me about my God that you are not he; tell me something about him.” And they cried out in a loud voice: “He made us” (Ps. 99:3). My questioning was my attention; their answer, their appearance. And I turned toward myself and said to myself, “Who are you?” And I answered, “A human being.” And behold, body and soul are present within me, one outward and the other inward. From which of these should I have sought my God, whom I had already sought through the body, from earth to heaven, as far as I was able to send messengers—the rays of my eyes? But the inward is better. For all the bodily messengers reported to the one presiding and judging over their individual responses—the sky and earth and all that is in them saying: “We are not God, but he himself made us.” The inward human being knew these things through the ministry of the outward; I, the inward, knew them—I, the mind—through the senses of my body. I questioned the mass of the world about my God, and it answered me: “I am not he, but he made me.”

10. Does not this appearance become evident to everyone whose senses are sound? Why does it not speak the same way to everyone? Small and large animals see it, but they cannot question it; for rational judgment has not been set over the senses that announce things in them. Human beings, however, can question it, so that “the invisible things of God may be understood and seen through the things that have been made” [Note: [Col. 0783] “May see,” according to five manuscripts, M.]; but they become subject to these things through love, and once subjected they cannot judge. Nor do these things answer those who question them except those who judge; nor do they change their voice—that is, their appearance—if one merely sees while another sees and questions, so that they appear one way to the former and another way to the latter. Rather, appearing in the same way to both, they are mute to the one and speak to the other; indeed, they speak to everyone, but those understand who inwardly compare their voice, received outwardly, with the truth. For the Truth says to me: “Your God is not the sky and earth, nor any body.” Their nature says this to the one who sees: “It is a mass; a mass is smaller in a part than in the whole.” You are already better, then; to you I speak, soul, because you give life to the mass of your body, supplying it with life, something no body supplies to another body. But your God is also the life of your life [Note: [Col. 0783] Thus Arn. and the manuscripts; but Am., Er., and Lov. read, “also life for you.” The same reading is found in Ven. and Lugd. M.].

## CHAPTER VII. God Is Not Found through Bodily or Sensory Power

[Col. 0784]

11. What, then, do I love when I love my God? Who is this one above the summit of my soul? Through my soul itself I shall ascend to him. I shall pass beyond the power by which I am joined to the body and vitally fill its structure. I do not find my God through that power; for a horse and a mule would find him through it as well, “which have no understanding” (Ps. 32:9), since it is the same power by which their bodies also live. There is another power, by which I not only give life to my flesh but also make it capable of sensation—the flesh that the Lord fashioned for me—commanding the eye not to hear and the ear not to see, but giving the eye the power by which I see and the ear the power by which I hear; and assigning their proper places and functions to the other senses individually. Through these different senses I, one mind, perform different actions [Note: [Col. 0784] “I, one mind, perform,” according to the Venetian manuscript.]. I shall pass beyond this power as well; for a horse and a mule possess it too, since they also perceive through the body.

## CHAPTER VIII. The Power of Memory

[Col. 0784]

12. I shall therefore pass beyond this power of my nature as well, ascending by degrees to him who made me; and I come to the fields and broad halls of memory, where are the treasuries of countless images brought into it from all manner of objects perceived by the senses [Note: [Col. 0784] “Of this kind,” according to Er., Ven., and Lugd. M.]. There is stored whatever we think about, whether by enlarging, diminishing, or in any way varying what the senses have touched; and whatever else has been entrusted to and stored there that oblivion has not yet swallowed and buried. When I am there, I bring forth whatever I want. Some things come out immediately; others are sought for a longer time and dragged, as it were, from more hidden receptacles; some pour forth in a crowd [Note: [Col. 0784] “They bring themselves forth,” according to the Venetian manuscript.]; and while one thing is being requested and sought, others leap into the midst as though saying, “Perhaps we are what you want?” And I drive them away with the hand of my heart from the face of my memory, until what I want is cleared of obscurity [Note: [Col. 0784] “That which,” according to Er., Ven., and Lugd. M.] and comes forth from its hiding place into view. Other things are suggested easily and in an undisturbed sequence, as they are requested; those that precede yield to those that follow, and by yielding are stored away, to come forth again when I wish. All this occurs when I recount something from memory.

13. There everything is preserved distinctly and by kinds, each entering through its own avenue: light, all colors, and the forms of bodies through the eyes; all kinds of sounds through the ears; all odors through the avenue of the nostrils; all flavors through the avenue of the mouth; and, through the sense of the whole body, what is hard or soft, hot or cold, smooth or rough, heavy or light, whether external or internal to the body. The vast recesses of memory and I know not what secret and ineffable folds of it receive all these things, to be recalled and brought forth when needed; each enters through its own gate and is stored there. Yet the things themselves do not enter; rather, their images of perceived things are present there for the mind that remembers them. Who can say how they were formed, though it is clear through which senses they were snatched up and stored within? For even in darkness and silence, when I am dwelling there, I can, if I wish, bring colors forth into my memory [Note: [Col. 0785] “Into my memory,” according to the Bertinian manuscript.]; I can distinguish white from black, and from whatever other colors I wish. Nor do sounds intrude and disturb what I am considering, having been taken in through the eyes, although the sounds too are present and lie hidden, as though stored separately. For if I wish, I can summon them, and they are immediately present. With my tongue at rest and my throat silent, I sing as much as I wish; and those images of colors, which are nevertheless present there, do not intervene or interrupt me when another treasury is recalled, one that entered through the ears. Thus I recall, as I please, the rest of what has entered and been accumulated through the other senses. I distinguish the scent of lilies from that of violets without smelling anything; and I prefer honey to grape syrup, the smooth to the rough, without then tasting or touching anything, but by remembering.

14. Within, I perform these things in the immense hall of my memory. There, sky and earth and sea are present to me, together with everything I have been able to perceive in them, except what I have forgotten. There too I encounter myself and recall what I did, when and where I did it, and how I felt while doing it. There are all the things that I remember either having experienced or having believed. From the same abundance I also weave together various likenesses of things I have experienced, or of things believed on the basis of what I have experienced; and from these I construct future actions, events, and hopes, and again meditate on all these as though they were present. “I shall do this or that,” I say to myself, in that immense inner fold of my soul, full of images of so many and such great things; “and this or that will follow.” “Would that this or that were so! May God avert this or that.” I say these things to myself; and when I say them, the images of everything I say are present from the same treasury of memory. I could not say any of it at all if those images were absent.

15. Great is this power of memory, exceedingly great, my God: a vast and boundless inner chamber. Who can reach its depths? And it is a power of my mind, belonging to my nature; yet I myself cannot grasp the whole of what I am. Thus the mind is too narrow to contain itself. And where is that which it does not contain of itself [Note: [Col. 0785] Lov. reads: “So that it does not grasp where it is or what it is.” Er., Ven., and Lugd. read: “So that it does not grasp where that which belongs to it is.” Mart. reads: “Is it too narrow for that which belongs to it to be there?” It continues: “Or is it outside itself? Is it not within itself?” The word “is” is omitted in Somm. and Rond. M.]? Is it outside itself and not within itself? How, then, does it not contain itself? Great wonder arises in me concerning this; astonishment seizes me. And people go off to admire the heights of mountains, the immense waves of the sea, the broad courses of rivers, the circuit of the ocean, and the revolutions of the stars, while they abandon themselves—and do not wonder that, when I spoke of all these things, I was not seeing them with my eyes, and yet I could not have spoken of them unless I were seeing inwardly, in my memory, the mountains and waves and rivers and stars that I had seen, and the ocean that I had believed in, with spaces as vast as though I were seeing them outwardly. Yet I did not absorb these things by seeing them when I looked at them with my eyes; nor are the things themselves present to me, but their images [Col. 0786]. And I know which of my bodily senses impressed each thing upon me.

## CHAPTER IX. The Memory of Disciplines

16. But this immense capacity of my memory does not contain only these things. Here too are all those things concerning the liberal disciplines that have not yet fallen from memory, as though stored in an inner place—not in a place [Note: [Col. 0786] Lov. reads “places”; Ven. and Lugd. M. support this reading.]; and I carry not their images but the things themselves. For whatever literature is, whatever skill in disputation is, whatever the kinds of questions are, and whatever else of this sort I know, is in my memory in such a way that I have not left the thing outside while retaining an image of it, nor has it sounded and passed away, like a voice impressed through the ears, leaving a trace by which it could be recalled [Note: [Col. 0786] “Is recalled,” according to six manuscripts cited by Mart. M.]; nor is it like a scent that passes and vanishes into the winds, affecting the sense of smell and then transferring into memory an image of itself for us to retrieve by remembering; nor is it like food, which certainly no longer has flavor in the stomach, yet somehow still tastes in memory; nor is it like something perceived by touching the body, which memory imagines even when it has been separated from us. These things are not brought into memory; only their images are seized with astonishing speed and stored in wondrous compartments, as it were, and brought forth through the act of remembering in a marvelous way.

## CHAPTER X. The Disciplines Are Not Introduced into Memory through the Senses but Drawn from Its More Hidden Recess

17. But when I hear that there are three kinds of questions—whether something is, what it is, and what kind it is—I retain images of the sounds from which these words are composed; and I know that they have passed through the air with a noise and now no longer exist [Note: [Col. 0786] Thus Arn. and the manuscripts; but Am., Bad., Er., and Lov. read “through the ears.” The same reading is found in Ven. and Lugd. M.]. But the things themselves signified by those sounds I have touched through no bodily sense, nor seen anywhere except within my own mind; and I stored in memory not images of them but the things themselves. Let those who can tell me say from where they entered me [Note: [Col. 0786] “Let me say, if I can,” according to Er., Ven., and Lugd. M.]. For I pass through all the doors of my flesh, yet I do not find through which of them they entered.
