The eyes say: “If they are colored, we reported them.” The ears say: “If they sounded, we indicated them.” The nostrils say: “If they smelled, they passed through us.” The sense of taste also says: “If there is no flavor, ask me nothing.” The sense of touch says: “If it has no bodily substance, I did not touch it; if I did not touch it, I did not report it.” From where, then, and by what route did these things enter my memory? I do not know how. For when I learned them, I did not believe another person’s heart; rather, I recognized them in my own, approved that they were true, and entrusted them to memory, as though storing them away so that I might bring them forth whenever I wished. Therefore they were there even before I learned them, but they were not in my memory. Where, then, were they, or why, when they were spoken, did I recognize them and say, “That is so; it is true,” unless they were already in my memory, but so remote and deeply hidden—as though in more secret recesses—that, unless someone had reminded me, I might perhaps not have been able to think of them?

## CHAPTER XI. What It Means to Learn

[Col. 0787]

18. Accordingly, we find that learning these things—of which we do not draw images through the senses, but perceive inwardly, without images, just as they are in themselves—is nothing other than collecting by thought what memory held scattered and disordered, and attending to it so that, placed as it were within reach in memory, where it previously lay scattered and neglected in hiding, it may now readily present itself to familiar attention. And how many such things my memory contains—things already discovered and, as I have said, placed as though within reach—which we are said to have learned and to know! If I cease recalling them at modest intervals of time, they sink again so deeply and slip away into more remote inner chambers that they must once more be thought out as though new, from that same place [Note: [Col. 0787] Thus the better manuscripts; and this should be the reading, as the following passage proves: “For there is no other region of them” from which, naturally, they could be gathered. Hence the printed editions should be emended where they read “and into the same place” or “and in the same place.”], “for there is no other region of them,” and gathered again so that they may be known—that is, collected, as it were, from a kind of dispersion. This is the origin of the word “think” (*cogitare*). For *cogo* and *cogito* relate as *ago* and *agito*, *facio* and *factito*. Nevertheless, the mind has claimed this word for itself in a special sense, so that what is gathered—that is, collected—not elsewhere but in the mind is now properly called “thought.”

## CHAPTER XII. The Memory of Mathematical Things

19. Memory also contains innumerable principles and laws of numbers and dimensions, none of which bodily sensation has impressed upon it, since they have neither color nor sound nor smell, and have not been tasted or touched. I heard the sounds of the words by which they are signified when they are discussed; but the sounds are one thing and these realities another. The sounds are different in Greek and Latin, whereas these realities are neither Greek nor Latin, nor do they belong to any other kind of language. I saw the lines drawn by craftsmen, even extremely fine ones, like a spider’s thread; but those lines are something else. They are not images of the lines reported to me by the eye of the flesh. Anyone who has recognized them inwardly without any kind of bodily thought knows this. I have also perceived, through all the bodily senses, the numbers that we count; but they are different from the numbers by which we count, are not images of those numbers, and for that reason truly exist. Let the person who does not see them laugh at me for saying this, and let me grieve over the one who laughs at me.

## CHAPTER XIII. We Remember That We Remember

20. I retain all these things in memory, and I retain in memory how I learned them. I have also heard and retain in memory many arguments that dispute against these things with the greatest falsity. Although those arguments are false, it is not false that I remember them; and I remember that I distinguished between those true things and these false arguments that contradict them. I now see that I distinguish them in one way, but I remember that I often distinguished them in another way when I repeatedly thought about them. Therefore I also remember that I understood these things many times; and what I now distinguish and understand I store in memory, so that later I may remember that I understood it now. Therefore I also remember that I remember [Col. 0788]; just as, if later I recall that I was able now to remember these things, I shall certainly recall it through the power of memory.

## CHAPTER XIV. How Memory Contains the Affections of the Mind. How We Remember Joy Without Being Joyful

21. My memory also contains the affections of my mind—not in the way the mind itself has them when it experiences them, but in another way, altogether different, corresponding to the power of memory. For I remember having been joyful without being joyful; I recall my past sadness without being sad; I remember that I was once afraid without being afraid; and I remember my former desire without desire. At other times, on the contrary, I recall my past sadness joyfully, and my joy sadly. This is not surprising in the case of the body, for the mind is one thing and the body another. Thus, if I remember a past bodily pain with joy, that is not so surprising. But here, since memory itself is also mind—for when we entrust something to be retained in memory, we say, “See that you keep it in mind”; and when we forget, we say, “It was not in my mind,” or, “It slipped from my mind,” calling memory itself the mind—since this is so, what is happening when I remember my past sadness joyfully? The mind possesses joy, while memory possesses sadness; and the mind is joyful because joy is present in it, while memory is not sad because sadness is present in it? Or perhaps memory does not belong to the mind? Who would say that? Clearly, then, memory is like the stomach of the mind, while joy and sadness are like sweet and bitter food. When these are entrusted to memory, as though passed into the stomach, they can be stored there but cannot be tasted. It is absurd to think that these things are altogether alike, yet they are not altogether unlike.

22. But behold, when I say that there are four disturbances of the mind—desire, joy, fear, and sadness—and whatever I am able to discuss about them, dividing each into the species belonging to its own genus and defining them, I find in memory what I am to say and bring it forth from there. Yet I am not disturbed by any of these disturbances when, by remembering, I speak of them. Before they were recalled and reconsidered by me, they were there; and for that reason they could be drawn forth from there through recollection. Perhaps, then, just as food is brought forth from the stomach by chewing, so these things are brought forth from memory by remembering. Why, then, does the sweetness of joy or the bitterness of sadness not become perceptible in the mouth of thought—that is, to the person who discusses and remembers? Or is the comparison unlike because it is not alike in every respect? For who would willingly speak of such things if, whenever we named sadness or fear, we were compelled each time to grieve or be afraid? And yet we would not speak of them unless in our memory we found not only the sounds of their names, according to the images impressed upon the bodily senses [Note: [Col. 0788] The earlier editions read “impressed upon the bodily senses,” but the manuscripts read “by the senses.” The Florentine edition has the same reading as the manuscripts. M.], but also the notions of the things themselves—things that no door of the flesh received, but that the mind itself, sensing them through its experience of suffering, entrusted to memory, or that memory itself retained even without their being entrusted to it [Col. 0789].

## CHAPTER XV. We Remember Even What Is Absent

23. But who could easily say whether this occurs through images or not? I name a stone; I name the sun, when the things themselves are not present to my senses. Their images, certainly, are present in my memory. I name bodily pain, which is not present to me while nothing hurts; yet unless its image were present in my memory, I would not know what I was saying, nor distinguish it from pleasure in discussion. I name bodily health when I am physically healthy: the reality itself is indeed present to me; nevertheless, unless its image were also present in my memory, I could in no way remember what sound this name signified. Nor would sick people recognize what was meant when health was named, unless that same image were retained by the power of memory, even though the reality itself were absent from the body. I name the numbers by which we count, and they are present in my memory—not their images, but the numbers themselves. I name the image of the sun, and that image is present in my memory; for I do not recall an image of its image, but the image itself. It is the image itself that is present to me when I remember. I name memory, and I recognize what I name. And where do I recognize it except in memory itself? Is memory itself present to itself through its own image, and not through itself?

## CHAPTER XVI. There Is Also a Memory of Forgetfulness

24. What happens when I name forgetfulness and likewise recognize what I name? From where would I recognize it unless I remembered it? I am not speaking of the same sound of the name, but of the thing it signifies. If I had forgotten that, I certainly could not recognize what that sound meant. Therefore, when I remember memory, memory itself is present to itself through itself; but when I remember forgetfulness, both memory and forgetfulness are present—memory by which I remember, and forgetfulness which I remember. But what is forgetfulness except the deprivation of memory? How, then, is it present so that I can remember it, when, while it is present, I cannot remember? Yet if we retain in memory whatever we remember, and if we could not recognize the thing signified by the name “forgetfulness” upon hearing it unless we remembered it, then forgetfulness is retained in memory. It is present, therefore, so that we may not forget, and yet when it is present we forget. Or is this understood to mean that forgetfulness is not present in memory through itself when we remember it, but through its image? For if forgetfulness were present through itself, it would cause us not to remember but to forget. And who, in the end, will investigate this? Who will understand how it is?

25. Certainly, Lord, I labor here, and I labor within myself. I have become for myself a land of difficulty and of excessive toil. For we are not now examining the regions of the sky, measuring the distances of the stars, or seeking the balance of the earth: I am the one who remembers; I am the mind. It is not so surprising if whatever I am not is far from me. What, then, is closer to me than I am to myself? And behold, the power of my memory cannot be comprehended by me, though I cannot speak of myself apart from it. What am I to say when I am certain that I remember forgetfulness [Col. 0790]? Am I to say that what I remember is not in my memory? Or am I to say that forgetfulness is in my memory for the purpose of preventing me from forgetting? Both statements are utterly absurd. What is the third possibility? How am I to say that the image of forgetfulness is held in my memory, and not forgetfulness itself, when I remember forgetfulness? How can I say even this, since, whenever the image of some thing is impressed upon memory, the thing itself must first be present, so that its image can be impressed? Thus I remember Carthage; thus I remember all the places where I have been; thus I remember the faces of people I have seen and the reports of my other senses; thus I remember the health or pain of my own body. When these things were present, memory received their images, which I could contemplate as present and reconsider in my mind when I remembered them even in their absence. If, then, forgetfulness is held in memory through its image and not through itself, it was certainly present so that its image could be captured. But when it was present, how did it inscribe its image in memory, when forgetfulness, by its presence, erases even what it finds already written down? Yet in whatever way this may happen—even if the manner is incomprehensible and inexplicable—I am certain that I remember forgetfulness itself, by which what we remember is overwhelmed.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Great Power of Memory, but We Must Go Beyond It to Reach God

26. Great is the power of memory, something I do not know how to describe—something terrible, my God—deep and boundlessly manifold. And this is the mind, and this am I myself. What, then, am I, my God? What kind of nature am I? A varied, multifaceted life, immense beyond measure. Behold, in the fields and caves and innumerable caverns of my memory, filled beyond numbering with innumerable kinds of things, there are things either through images, as with all bodies; or through their presence, as with the disciplines; or through I know not what notions or marks, as with the affections of the mind—which memory retains even when the mind is not experiencing them, since whatever is in memory is in the mind. Through all these I run and fly; I penetrate here and there as far as I can, and nowhere is there an end. So great is the power of memory, so great is the power of life in a human being who lives mortally!

What, then, shall I do, my God, my true life? I shall pass beyond this power of mine called memory; I shall pass beyond it in order to reach you, sweet light. What are you saying to me? Behold, I am ascending through my mind to you who remain above me. I shall pass beyond this power of mine called memory, wishing to touch you where you can be touched and to cling to you where one can cling to you. For animals and birds also have memory; otherwise they would not return to their dens and nests, nor to the many things to which they become accustomed. Indeed, they could not become accustomed to anything without memory. I shall therefore pass beyond memory, so that I may reach him who separated me from the four-footed animals and made me wiser than the birds of the sky. I shall pass beyond memory; and where shall I find you, truly good and secure sweetness? Where shall I find you? If I find you apart from my memory, I am forgetful of you. And how shall I find you now if I do not remember you?

## CHAPTER XVIII. A Thing That Has Been Lost Would Not Be Found Unless It Were Retained in Memory

27. A woman had lost a drachma and sought it with a lamp (Luke 15:8); and unless she remembered it, she would not have found it. For once it had been found, how would she know whether it was the same one if she did not remember it? I remember having sought and found many things that I had lost. From this I know the matter: when I was seeking one of them and someone said to me, “Perhaps this is it; perhaps that is it,” I kept saying, “It is not,” until what I was seeking was offered to me. If I did not remember whatever it was, then even if it were offered to me, I would not find it, because I would not recognize it. And this always happens when we seek and find something that has been lost.

Yet if something disappears from the eyes but not from memory—for example, any visible body—its image is held inwardly, and it is sought until it is restored to sight. When it has been found, it is recognized from the image within. We do not say that we have found what was lost if we do not recognize it; nor can we recognize it if we do not remember it. It had been lost to the eyes, but was held in memory.

## CHAPTER XIX. What It Means to Remember

28. What happens when memory itself loses something, as occurs when we forget, and we seek in order to remember? Where, finally, do we seek except in memory itself? And if something else is perhaps offered there in place of what we seek, we reject it until what we are seeking comes before us; and when it appears, we say, “This is it.” We would not say this unless we recognized it, nor recognize it unless we remembered it. Certainly, then, we had forgotten it. Or had it not wholly fallen away, but while one part remained, another part was being sought? For memory sensed that it was not simultaneously bringing forth what it had been accustomed to bring forth together, and, limping as though its habit had been cut short, demanded that what was missing be restored [Note: [Col. 0791] Mart. reads “we had forgotten it,” rather than “and not . . . demanded.” Elsewhere, “for.” M.]. It is like a person known to us: whether seen with the eyes or thought of, if we have forgotten the person’s name and seek it, whatever else comes to mind does not connect with that person because it was not accustomed to be thought of together with that person, and so it is rejected until the name appears, at which point the recognition that had been accustomed to be joined with it settles into place without inequality.

And from where does the name appear except from memory itself? For even when another person reminds us, it appears from there. We do not believe it as though it were new; rather, by remembering, we approve that this is what was said. But if it were utterly erased from the mind, we would not remember it even when reminded. For we have not altogether forgotten what we remember that we have forgotten [Note: [Col. 0791] In B. one reads *cam*, corruptly. M.]. Therefore we cannot seek what has been lost if we have forgotten it altogether.

## CHAPTER XX. In Order for Everyone to Desire Blessedness, They Must Know It

29. How, then, do I seek you, Lord? For when I seek you, my God, I seek the blessed life. I shall seek you so that my soul may live. For my body lives from my soul, and my soul lives from you. How, then, do I seek the blessed life? Since it is not mine until I say, “That is enough,” in the place where I ought to say it, how do I seek it? Is it through recollection, as though I had forgotten it but still retained the memory that I had forgotten it? Or is it through the desire to learn something unknown—something I have never known, or something I have forgotten so completely that I do not even remember having forgotten it?

Is not this the blessed life that everyone wants, and is there anyone at all who does not want it? Where did they come to know it, that they want it so? Where did they see it, that they love it? Surely, somehow, we possess it. And there is another manner in which someone is blessed: when he possesses it, he is blessed; and there are those who are blessed in hope. The latter possess it in an inferior manner to those who are already blessed in reality, but they are nevertheless better off than those who are blessed neither in reality nor in hope. Yet even the latter, unless they possessed it in some manner, would not so desire to be blessed—which they certainly do desire.

I do not know how they know it, and therefore possess it in some kind of knowledge; and I am concerned to know whether this knowledge is in memory. For if it is there, then we were blessed at some time—whether individually, all of us, or in that one human being who first sinned, in whom we all died and from whom we were all born in misery, I do not ask now. I ask whether the blessed life is in memory. For we would not love it unless we knew it.

We hear this name, and we all admit that we desire the reality itself; we are not delighted merely by the sound. For when a Greek hears this in Latin, he is not delighted, because he does not know what has been said; but we are delighted, just as he would be if he heard it in Greek. For the reality itself is neither Greek nor Latin, yet Greeks and Latins—and people of every other language—long to attain it. It is therefore known to everyone. If everyone could be asked in a single voice whether they wished to be blessed, they would answer without any hesitation that they did. This would not happen unless the reality designated by this name were held in their memory.

## CHAPTER XXI. How Memory Contains the Blessed Life

30. Is it in the way that someone who has seen Carthage remembers Carthage? No. The blessed life is not seen with the eyes, because it is not a body. Is it like the way we remember numbers? No. Whoever possesses numbers in knowledge does not still seek to attain them; but we possess the blessed life in knowledge, and for that reason love it, yet still wish to attain it in order to be blessed.

Is it like the way we remember eloquence? No. For although, upon hearing this name, those who are not yet eloquent remember the reality itself, and many desire to be eloquent—whereby it is evident that the reality is present in their knowledge—they have nevertheless noticed eloquent people through the bodily senses, have taken delight in them, and desire to be like them. (Yet they would not take delight in eloquence, nor wish to be eloquent, unless they had some inward knowledge of it [Note: [Col. 0792] Thus Am., Arn., and the manuscripts; Er. and Lov. read “in an outward knowledge.”].) But we do not experience the blessed life in others through any bodily sense.

Is it like the way we remember joy? Perhaps it is. For I remember my joy even when I am sad, just as I remember the blessed life when I am miserable. I have never seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or touched my joy through a bodily sense; but I experienced it in my mind when I rejoiced, and knowledge of it adhered to my memory, so that I can recall it sometimes with aversion and sometimes with desire, according to the different things over which I remember having rejoiced. For I was once suffused with a kind of joy over shameful things, which I now detest and execrate when I remember it; at other times, I rejoiced over good and honorable things, which I recall with desire, although perhaps they are not present, and for that reason, in sadness, I recall my former joy [Col. 0793].

31. Where and when did I experience my blessed life, that I remember it and love it and desire it? And this is not true of me alone, or of only a few: we all want to be blessed. Unless we knew this with a certain knowledge, we would not want it with such certainty of will.

But what is this? If two people are asked whether they wish to serve as soldiers, it could happen that one would answer that he wished to and the other that he did not. But if they are asked whether they wish to be blessed, it could happen that both would immediately say, without any hesitation, that this was what they desired [Note: [Col. 0793] Somm., Mart., Flor., and Rond. read “it may be possible.” M.]. And does one wish to serve as a soldier, and the other not, for any reason other than that they may be blessed? For perhaps one rejoices in one thing and the other in another [Note: [Col. 0793] Er., Lugd., Dub., Mart., and Rond., together with eleven manuscripts, omit “it could happen that.” M.]. Thus they all agree that they wish to be blessed, just as they would agree if they were asked whether they wished to rejoice; and they call joy itself the blessed life. Although one attains it by one route and another by another, there is nevertheless one goal toward which all strive: to rejoice. Since no one can say that he has never experienced this reality, the name of the blessed life, when heard, is therefore recognized as something found in memory.

## CHAPTER XXII. What the Blessed Life Is and Where It Is

32. Far be it, Lord—far be it from the heart of your servant, who confesses to you—that I should think myself blessed whatever joy I may enjoy. For there is a joy “that is not given to the wicked” (Isa. 48:22), but to those who worship you freely, whose joy you yourself are. And this is the blessed life: to rejoice in you, from you, and because of you. This is the blessed life, and there is no other. Those who think there is another pursue another joy, and not the true one. Yet their will is not turned away from some image of joy.

## CHAPTER XXIII. He Continues His Account of What the Blessed Life Is and Where It Is
33. It is not therefore certain that all desire to be blessed, since those who do not wish to rejoice in you—which is the only blessed life—do not in fact desire the blessed life. Do all desire this? But because the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that they do not do what they wish (Gal. V, 17), they fall into what they are able to attain and are content with it, because what they are unable to attain they do not desire with sufficient strength to make them able to attain it. For I ask everyone whether they would rather rejoice in truth than in falsehood: they are no less certain to say that they would rather rejoice in truth than they are certain to say that they wish to be blessed. For the blessed life is joy in the truth. This is joy in you, who are the truth (John XIV, 6), my God, the light of my face and my salvation (Ps. XXVI, 1), my God. Everyone desires this blessed life, everyone desires this life which alone is blessed, everyone desires joy in the truth. I have encountered many who wished to deceive, but no one who wished to be deceived. Where, then, did they come to know this blessed life, if not where they also came to know the truth? For they love the truth itself, since they do not wish to be deceived. And when they love the blessed life—which is nothing other than joy in the truth—they surely love the truth as well; nor would they love it unless some knowledge of it existed in their memory. Why, then, do they not rejoice in it? Why are they not blessed? Because they are more powerfully occupied with other things that make them miserable rather than with that which they remember only faintly and which would make them blessed. For there is still but a little light in human beings; let them walk, let them walk, lest the darkness overtake them (John XII, 35).

34. Why, then, does truth produce hatred, and why has your servant, who proclaims the truth, become their enemy, when the blessed life is loved, and is nothing other than joy in the truth? Is it not because truth is loved in such a way that all who love something else wish what they love to be the truth; and because they do not wish to be deceived, they do not wish to be convicted of being in error? Thus they hate the truth for the very reason that they love what they love as truth. They love it when it shines, but hate it when it reproves them. For because they do not wish to be deceived and wish to deceive, they love it when it reveals itself, but hate it when it reveals them themselves [Note: [Col. 0794] Lov., “judges.”]. Therefore it will repay them by both revealing those who do not wish to be revealed by it and by remaining itself unrevealed to them. Thus, yes, thus the human mind—even when miserable, blind, and weak, shameful and indecent—wishes to remain hidden; yet it does not wish anything to remain hidden from it. In return, it is made unable to hide from the truth, while the truth remains hidden from it. Yet even so, while miserable, it prefers to rejoice in what is true rather than in what is false. It will therefore be blessed if, without any troubling interruption, it rejoices in the truth alone, through which all things are true.

### CHAPTER XXIV. He rejoices that God has a place in his memory

35. Behold, I have ranged far and wide through my memory, seeking you, Lord, and I have not found you outside it. For I have found nothing concerning you that I had not remembered from the time I learned to know you. From the time I learned to know you, I have not forgotten you. For where I found the truth, there I found my God, the truth itself, which, from the time I learned to know it, I have not forgotten. Thus, from the time I learned to know you, you remain in my memory, and there I find you whenever I remember you and delight in you. These are my holy delights, which your mercy granted me as you looked upon my poverty.

### CHAPTER XXV. At what level of the memory God is found

36. But where do you remain in my memory, Lord—where do you remain there? What sort of chamber have you built for yourself there? What sort of sanctuary [Note: [Col. 0794] In some manuscripts, “sacrarium.”] have you built for yourself? You granted my memory the honor of your remaining in it; but I am considering in which part of it you remain. For when I remembered you, I passed beyond those parts of it which animals also possess, because I was not finding you there among the images of bodily things; and I came to those parts where I had entrusted the affections of my mind, but I did not find you there either. And I entered into the very seat of my mind, which it has in my memory, since the mind also remembers itself—but you were not there. For just as you are not a bodily image, nor the affection of a living being, such as occurs when we rejoice, grieve, desire, fear, remember, forget, and whatever else is of this kind, so neither are you the mind itself, since you are the Lord God of the mind. All these things change, but you remain unchangeable above all things; and from the time I learned to know you, you have deigned to dwell in my memory. Why, then, do I search for the place in it where you dwell, as though places existed there? Certainly you dwell in it, since I have remembered you from the time I learned to know you, and I find you in it whenever I remember you.

### CHAPTER XXVI. Where God is found

37. Where, then, did I find you, so that I might learn to know you? For you were not yet in my memory before I learned to know you. Where, then, did I find you, so that I might learn to know you, if not in you, above me? Yet nowhere is there a place; we withdraw and draw near, and nowhere is there a place. Everywhere, O Truth, you preside over all who consult you, and at the same time you answer all who consult you about different things. You answer clearly, but not all hear clearly. Everyone consults you about what he wishes, but does not always hear what he wishes. Your best servant is the one who does not look chiefly to hear from you what he himself wants, but rather wants what he has heard from you.

### CHAPTER XXVII. How the beauty of God seizes a person

38. Late have I loved you, beauty so ancient and so new! Late have I loved you! And behold, you were within, while I was outside, and there I sought you; and in the beautiful things you made I rushed about, deformed. You were with me, but I was not with you. Those things held me far from you which, if they did not exist in you, would not exist. You called, cried out, and broke through my deafness. You flashed, shone, and dispelled my blindness. You gave forth fragrance [Note: [Col. 0795] “You burned brightly,” according to Er., Lugd., Flor., and M.], and I drew breath and gasped for you. I tasted you, and I hunger and thirst. You touched me, and I was inflamed with desire for your peace.

### CHAPTER XXVIII. The miseries of this life

39. When I cling to you with my whole being, nowhere will there be pain or labor for me, and my life will be alive, wholly full of you. But now, since you raise up the one whom you fill, and since I am not full of you, I am a burden to myself. My joys, which ought to be mourned, contend with my sorrows, which ought to be rejoiced in, and I do not know on which side victory stands. Woe is me! Lord, have mercy on me. My evil sorrows contend with my good joys, and I do not know on which side victory stands. Woe is me! Lord, have mercy on me. Woe is me! Behold, I do not hide my wounds: you are the physician, I am the sick person; you are merciful, I am miserable. Is not human life upon earth a trial (Job VII, 1)? Who would want troubles and difficulties? You command that they be endured, not [Col. 0796] loved. No one loves what he endures, even if he loves to endure it. For although he rejoices that he is enduring it, he nevertheless prefers that there be nothing for him to endure. In adversity I desire prosperity; in prosperity I fear adversity. Where is the middle ground between these, where human life is not a trial? Woe, again and again, to the prosperity of the world, because of fear of adversity and corruption through joy! Woe, again and again and a third time, to the adversity of the world, because of desire for prosperity! And since adversity itself is hard, and endurance founders [Note: [Col. 0796] Bad. and many of the older manuscripts read, “and lest endurance break”; this reading is preferred by the Somm. and Rond. editions, with four manuscripts.], is not human life upon earth a trial without any interval?

### CHAPTER XXIX. All hope is in God

40. And all my hope is nowhere but in your exceedingly great mercy. Give what you command, and command what you will. You command us to be continent. “And when I knew,” someone said, “that no one can be continent unless God grants it, and this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was” (Wis. VIII, 21). For through continence we are gathered and brought back into unity, from which we had dispersed into multiplicity. For the one who loves something with you that he does not love for your sake loves you less. O love, always burning and never extinguished! Love, my God, set me ablaze. You command continence; give what you command, and command what you will.

### CHAPTER XXX. He confesses his condition with regard to temptations of carnal desire

41. Certainly you command me to abstain from the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition (John II, 16). You commanded abstinence from sexual intercourse, and concerning marriage itself you gave a better admonition than the permission you granted. And because you granted it, it was accomplished even before I became a steward of your sacrament. Yet there still live in my memory—which I have discussed at length—the images of such things, fixed there by habit; and they confront me while I am awake, though without power, but in dreams not only up to the point of pleasure, but even up to consent and an act almost identical with the reality. So powerful is the illusion of the image in my soul and in my flesh that false appearances persuade the sleeper of what they cannot persuade the waking person of as true. Am I not then present, Lord my God? And yet how great is the difference between myself and myself in the moment when I pass from wakefulness into sleep, or pass back again from sleep to wakefulness! Where then is reason, which, while awake, resists such suggestions? And if the things themselves are brought before me, I remain unmoved [Note: [Col. 0796] Seven manuscripts read, “it remains unmoved,” correctly referring the phrase to reason. The Florentine edition, supported by Somm. and Rond. and claiming the authority of better manuscripts, reads: “Where then is reason by which the waking mind remains unmoved by such things . . .?” Yet, perhaps through a typographical error, it omits the first part of that reading.]. Is it closed when the eyes are closed? Does it fall asleep with the bodily senses? And why is it that even in dreams we often resist, remembering our purpose and remaining most chaste in it, and offer no assent to such enticements? Yet the difference is so great that, when something else happens, we wake and return to the rest of conscience; and in that very difference we discover that we did not do what nevertheless we grieve was somehow done in us.

42. Is your hand not powerful, almighty God, to heal all the sicknesses of my soul and, by your more abundant grace, to extinguish even the wanton movements of my sleep? You will increase your gifts in me more and more, Lord, so that my soul may follow me to you, freed from the birdlime of desire, so that it may not be rebellious against itself, and so that even in dreams it may not only refrain from perpetrating these shameful acts of corruption through animal images, even to the emission of the flesh, but may not consent to them at all. For that I should feel no pleasure in anything of this kind, not even the slightest [Note: [Col. 0797] “So slight,” according to Rond. with eleven manuscripts.], however small a movement might be restrained by a nod, even in the chaste disposition of one asleep—not only in this life but even at this age—is no great thing for the Almighty, who is able to do beyond all that we ask or understand (Eph. III, 20). Yet for now I have told my good Lord what I still am in this form of my evil, rejoicing with trembling (Ps. II, 11) in what you have granted me, and mourning because I am not yet perfected, hoping [Note: [Col. 0797] “And hoping,” according to Rond. from six manuscripts.] that you will complete your mercies in me unto full peace, which my inward and outward parts will possess with you when death has been swallowed up in victory (I Cor. XV, 54).

### CHAPTER XXXI. His condition with regard to temptations of gluttony

43. There is another evil of the day; would that it were enough for the day. For we repair the daily ruin of the body by eating and drinking, before you destroy food and belly, when you kill my need with marvelous satiety and clothe this corruptible body with everlasting incorruption (ibid., 53). But for now necessity is pleasant to me, and I fight against this pleasantness lest I be captured by it; and I wage a daily battle through fasts, more often bringing my body into subjection (I Cor. IX, 27); and my pains are driven away by pleasure. For hunger and thirst are certain pains: they burn and, like a fever, kill unless the medicine of nourishment comes to the aid. Since that medicine is at hand, through the consolation of your gifts, in which earth and water and heaven serve our weakness, calamity is called pleasure [Note: [Col. 0797] Am., Er., and Lov. read, “calamities are called pleasures,” but most manuscripts and Arn. read, “calamity.” The former reading is supported by Somm. and Rond. with four manuscripts.].

44. You taught me to approach food as I would medicines, in the manner of one about to take them. But as I pass from the distress of need to the repose of satiety, the snare of desire lies in ambush for me in the very passage. For the passage itself is pleasure, and there is no other [Note: [Col. 0797] “Other,” according to Somm. and Rond. with two manuscripts.] way by which one may pass to that place to which necessity compels us to go [Note: [Col. 0797] In all editions before Arn. it read, “than by which one may pass.” “Than” has been deleted, as required by the authority of the manuscripts and by the sense.]. And although health is the reason for eating and drinking, dangerous pleasure attaches itself like a treacherous attendant and usually tries to go first, so that what I either say or wish to do for the sake of health may instead be done for its sake. The measure of the two is not the same: what is enough for health is too little for pleasure. [Col. 0798] And often it becomes uncertain whether the body’s necessary care is still seeking assistance, or whether the deceptive service of pleasurable desire is supplying it. In this uncertainty the unhappy soul smiles, and prepares there a defense for its excuse, rejoicing that what is sufficient for the moderation of health does not appear, so that under the pretext of health it may cast a shadow over the business of pleasure. Every day I try to resist these temptations, and I call upon your right hand for my salvation, and I refer my agitations to you, because I have not yet reached a settled judgment concerning this matter.

45. I hear the voice of my commanding God: “Do not let your hearts be weighed down with gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke XXI, 34). Drunkenness is far from me; you will have mercy, so that it may not approach me. But gluttony sometimes steals upon your servant; you will have mercy, so that it may be far from me. For no one can be continent unless you grant it. You grant us many things when we pray; and whatever good we received before we prayed, we received from you; and that we might later recognize this, we received it from you. I have never been a drunkard, but I have known drunkards whom you made sober. Therefore it was by you that those who had never been drunkards were made not to be so; by you that those who had been drunkards were made no longer to be so; and by you also that both learned from whom this had come about. I heard another word of yours: “Do not go after your desires, and turn away from your will” (Ecclus. XVIII, 30). I also heard, through your gift, a saying I have loved greatly: “Neither if we eat shall we abound, nor if we do not eat shall we lack” (I Cor. VIII, 8). That is to say: “Neither will the one thing make me rich, nor the other make me wretched.” I heard another saying: “I have learned to be content in whatever circumstances I am; I know how to abound, and I know how to suffer need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Phil. IV, 11–13). Behold the soldier of the heavenly camp—not dust, as we are. But remember, Lord, that we are dust, and that from dust you made human beings (Ps. CII, 14; Gen. III, 19), and that one had perished and was found (Luke XV, 24, 32). Nor was he able to do this of himself, since he too was dust—the one who, speaking such words through the breath of your inspiration, I loved: “I can do all things,” he said, “through him who strengthens me.” Strengthen me, so that I may be able. Give what you command, and command what you will. This man confesses that he received, and whatever he boasts of, he boasts in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0798] “So that whatever he boasts of, he may boast in the Lord,” according to five manuscripts cited by Mart.]. (I Cor. I, 30, 31.) I heard another man asking to receive: “Take away from me,” he said, “the desires of the belly” (Ecclus. XXIII, 6). From this it is clear, my holy God, that you grant what occurs when what you command is done.

46. You taught me, good Father: “All things are clean to the clean,” but that it is evil for a person to eat through giving offense (Rom. XIV, 20); that every creature of yours is good, and that nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving (I Tim. IV, 4); and that food does not commend us to God (I Cor. VIII, 8); and that no one should judge us concerning food or drink (Col. II, 16); and that the one who eats should not despise the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat should not judge the one who eats (Rom. XIV, 3). I have learned these things; thanks to you, praise to you, my God, my teacher, the one who knocks at my ears and illumines my heart: deliver me from every temptation. It is not the uncleanness of food that I fear, but the uncleanness of desire. I know that Noah was permitted to eat every kind of flesh useful as food (Gen. IX, 2, 3); that Elijah was nourished with flesh as food (III Kings XVII, 6); that John, endowed with extraordinary abstinence, was not defiled by animals—namely, locusts—being used as food (Matt. III, 4). And I know that Esau was deceived by his desire for lentils (Gen. XXV, 34); that David was reproved by himself because of his desire for water (II Kings XXIII, 15–17); and that our King was tempted not with flesh but with bread (Matt. IV, 3). Therefore the people in the wilderness deserved condemnation not because they desired flesh, but because, from desire for food, they murmured against the Lord (Num. XI).

47. Placed amid these temptations, I wage a daily battle, certainly, against the desire to eat and drink. For it is not a matter which I can decide to cut off once and never touch again, as I was able to do with sexual intercourse. Therefore the reins of the throat must be held by measured relaxation and tightening. And who, Lord, is not carried a little beyond the boundaries of necessity? Whoever is, is great; let him magnify your name. But I am not such a one, for I am a sinful human being. Yet I too magnify your name; and he intercedes with you for my sins (Rom. VIII, 34) who conquered the world (John XVI, 33), counting me among the weak members of his body, because your eyes saw its imperfection, and in your book all will be written [Note: [Col. 0799] Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read, “my imperfection”; but the manuscripts, with Arn., have “its imperfection,” namely, Christ’s, from whose person Augustine interprets this verse in his Expositions on Psalm 138, no. 23.].

### CHAPTER XXXII. His condition with regard to the enticements of odors

48. I am not excessively concerned about the enticement of odors. When they are absent, I do not seek them; when they are present, I do not reject them, and I am always prepared to do without them. So it seems to me; perhaps I am mistaken. For these too are darknesses to be mourned, in which my capacity, which lies within me, is hidden from me. Thus, when my mind questions itself about its own powers, it does not easily consider itself trustworthy, because what exists within it is often hidden unless experience reveals it. And no one ought to feel secure in this life, which is wholly called a trial (Job VII, 1), as to whether one who could become better from a worse state might not also become worse from a better one. Your mercy is my one hope, my one confidence, my one firm promise.

### CHAPTER XXXIII. His condition with regard to the pleasures of the ears

49. The pleasures of the ears had entangled and subdued me more tenaciously, but you loosened and freed me. Now, in the sounds animated by your words, when they are sung with a sweet and skillful voice, I confess that I rest a little; not indeed so as to cling to them, but so that I may rise whenever I wish. Yet, together with the meanings by which they live, when they seek admission to me, they ask for a place of some dignity in my heart, and I scarcely grant them one that is appropriate. For sometimes I seem to give them more honor than is fitting, when I feel that our minds are moved more religiously and ardently into the flame of piety by those holy words when they are sung in this way than when they are not sung in this way; and that all the affections of our spirit, according to their diversity, have their own proper modes in voice and song, by some hidden affinity with which they are stirred [Note: [Col. 0800] “Of the sounds,” according to one manuscript cited by Mart.; “sweet,” according to another; “of its own,” according to one manuscript cited by Rond.]. But the pleasure of my flesh, to which the mind ought not to be surrendered so as to be weakened, often deceives me, when feeling does not follow reason in such a way that it remains patiently in second place; rather, because it earned admission on account of reason, it also tries to run ahead and lead. Thus I sin in these matters without realizing it; afterward I realize it.

50. Sometimes, however, by guarding against this very deception too immoderately, I err through excessive severity. At times I almost wish that all the melodies of the sweet songs with which the Davidic Psalter is regularly sung would be removed from my ears, and from the ears of the Church itself. I consider it safer to recall what I have often been told about Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria: he made the reader chant the psalm with so slight a modulation of the voice that it was closer to recitation than to singing. Nevertheless, when I remember my tears, which I shed at the singing of your Church during the early days of my recovered faith, and now, when I am moved—not by the singing but by the things that are sung, when they are sung with a clear voice and entirely suitable modulation—I again acknowledge the great usefulness of this practice [Note: [Col. 0800] Moret’s edition, in Rond., reads, “and now I myself am moved.”]. Thus I fluctuate between the danger of pleasure and the experience of its beneficial effect; and I am inclined—though I do not pronounce an irrevocable judgment—to approve the custom of singing in the Church, so that through the delight of the ears the weaker mind may rise into an affect of piety. Yet whenever it happens that the singing moves me more than the thing that is sung, I confess that I am sinning in a punishable way, and then I would rather not hear the singer. Behold where I am: weep with me, and weep for me, you who inwardly undertake some good work from which actions proceed. For those who do not undertake such work are not moved by these things. But you, Lord my God, hear me; look upon me and see [Note: [Col. 0800] Somm. and Rond. read, “look upon me and hear; see.”], have mercy, and heal me, in whose eyes I have become a question to myself, and this is my sickness.

### CHAPTER XXXIV. His condition with regard to the enticements of the eyes

51. There remains the pleasure of these eyes of my flesh, concerning which I shall speak [Note: [Col. 0800] “I speak,” according to Somm. and Mart. with six manuscripts.] confessions for the ears of your temple, the ears of a brotherhood both fraternal and devout, so that we may conclude the temptations of the desire of the flesh, which still assail me as I groan and desire to be clothed over with my dwelling that is from heaven (II Cor. V, 2). The eyes love beautiful and varied forms, bright and pleasing colors. Let these things not hold my soul; let God, who made them, hold it—things that are indeed very good, but he himself is my good, not they. They touch me while I am awake throughout the day, and I am given no rest from them, as I am sometimes given from melodious voices—from all voices—in silence. For this light itself, queen of colors, which pours over everything we see, wherever I am during the day, caresses me with manifold approaches while I am engaged in something else and do not notice it. It insinuates itself so forcefully that, if it is suddenly taken away, it is sought with longing; and if it is absent for a long time, it saddens the mind [Note: [Col. 0801] “May it sadden,” according to Somm. and Rond. with two manuscripts.].

52. O light that Tobias saw when, with these eyes closed, he taught his son the way of life and went before him with the foot of charity, never straying (Tob. IV)! Or the light that Isaac saw when, his bodily eyes weighed down and covered by old age, he was granted to bless his sons without recognizing them—and to recognize them by blessing them (Gen. XXVII). Or the light that Jacob saw when, himself blinded in his eyes by great age, he radiated with a luminous heart in his sons the kinds of the future people marked out in advance; and when he laid his mystically crossed hands upon the sons of Joseph—not as their father corrected him outwardly, but as he himself discerned inwardly (Gen. XLVIII, XLIX). That is the light; it is one [Note: [Col. 0801] “It is one, and there is no other,” according to Er., Lugd., Somm., and Rond. with six manuscripts.], and all who see and love it are one. But this bodily light of which I was speaking seasons the life of the world with an alluring and dangerous sweetness for its blind lovers. Those who know how to praise you even for it, God, creator of all things, take it up into your hymn; they are not consumed by it in their sleep. Such I wish to be. I resist the seductions of the eyes, lest they entangle the feet with which I walk in your way; and I raise to you invisible eyes, so that you may draw my feet out of the snare (Ps. XXIV, 15). You continually draw them out, for they are ensnared. You never cease to draw them out, but I repeatedly become caught in the traps scattered everywhere, because you neither sleep nor slumber, you who guard Israel (Ps. CXX, 4).

53. How innumerable are the things human beings have added, by various arts and crafts, in clothing, footwear, vessels, and all kinds of workmanship [Note: [Col. 0801] Lov. reads, “all kinds of manufactured objects”; but the manuscripts have “all kinds,” a term Augustine frequently uses for “whatever kind,” and which we have already restored in chapter 8, no. 12 of this book.], as well as in paintings and diverse images—things that far exceed necessary and moderate use and devout symbolism—in order to entice the eyes! They follow outwardly what they make, abandoning inwardly the one by whom they were made, and destroying what they were made to be. But I too, my God and my glory, offer you a hymn even concerning these things, and sacrifice praise to my sacrificer [Note: [Col. 0801] The manuscripts and many editions read, “to my sanctifier.” A few read, “to my sacrificer.”], because beautiful things conveyed through souls into artistic hands come from that beauty which is above souls, for which my soul sighs day and night. But the makers and lovers of outward beauties draw from there the standard by which they are approved; they do not, however, draw from there the standard by which they should use them. He is there, and they do not see him, so that they may not go farther and may preserve their strength for you (Ps. LVIII, 10), rather than scatter it in pleasurable weariness. But I, even as I speak of and distinguish these things, entangle my steps in these beauties; but you draw me out, Lord, you draw me out, for your mercy is before my eyes (Ps. XXV, 3). For I too am pitifully captured, and you mercifully draw me out—sometimes without my realizing it, because I had fallen in too deeply; sometimes with pain, because I had already become attached.

### CHAPTER XXXV. His condition with regard to the second kind of temptation, which is curiosity

[Col. 0802]

54. To this is added another form of temptation, more manifold and dangerous. Besides that desire of the flesh which is present in the pleasure of all the senses and pleasures, and by serving which those who distance themselves far from you waste away, there is also in the soul, through those same bodily senses, a certain desire—not to take pleasure in the flesh, but to make trial through the flesh of vain and curious things, concealed under the name of knowledge and learning. Since this desire lies in the appetite for knowing, while the eyes hold first place among the senses for knowing, it is called by divine speech “the desire of the eyes” (I John II, 16). Seeing properly belongs to the eyes. Yet we use this word also with respect to the other senses when we direct them toward knowing. For we do not say, “Hear how it sparkles,” or, “Smell how it shines,” or, “Taste how it gleams,” or, “Touch how it glows.” All these things are said to be seen. We say not only, “See what shines,” which only the eyes can perceive, but also, “See what sounds; see what smells; see what tastes; see how hard it is.” Therefore the general experience of the senses is called, as has been said, the desire of the eyes, because the other senses appropriate to themselves by analogy the function of seeing—in which the eyes hold primacy—when they investigate something for the sake of knowledge.

55. From this it is more clearly distinguished what is pleasure and what is curiosity exercised through the senses: pleasure pursues what is beautiful, musical, sweet-smelling, tasty, and smooth; curiosity, however, pursues even things contrary to these for the sake of testing them—not in order to undergo discomfort, but from the appetite for experience and knowledge. What pleasure is there in seeing a mangled corpse at which you shudder? And yet, wherever one lies, people flock to it, so that they may be distressed and turn pale. They are even afraid that they might see such a thing in their dreams, as though anyone had forced them to see it while awake, or any report of its beauty had persuaded them. So it is also with the other senses, though it would take too long to pursue them. From this disease of desire, all sorts of spectacles are displayed as marvels. From this impulse one proceeds to investigate the hidden things of nature—which lies outside us [Note: [Col. 0802] Thus the manuscripts, with Arn.; Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read, “one proceeds to investigate the secrets of nature, which has acted outside us.”]—things whose knowledge is of no benefit, and which people desire for no other reason than to know them. From this impulse also, if something is sought through magical arts for the same perverted purpose of knowledge. From this impulse, too, God himself is tempted within religion when signs and portents are demanded, desired not for some salvation but solely for the sake of experience.

56. In this immense forest, full of snares and dangers, behold how much I have cut away and driven from my heart, as you granted me to do, God of my salvation. Yet when do I dare to say, since so many things of this kind clamour around our daily life on every side, when do I dare to say that no such thing captures my attention for viewing and seizes me with vain concern? Certainly the theaters no longer carry me away; I do not care to know the courses of the stars; my soul has never sought answers from the shades; I detest all sacrilegious rites. From you, Lord my God, to whom I owe humble and simple service, how many machinations of suggestion does the enemy set in motion within me, trying to make me ask for some sign? But I beseech you by our King and by the simple, chaste Jerusalem that, just as such consent is far from me, so it may always be farther and farther away. When I pray to you for someone’s salvation, however, the purpose of my intention is quite different; and as you do what you will, you grant me—and will grant me—the willingness to follow.

57. Nevertheless, who can count how often our curiosity is tested every day in the smallest and most contemptible things [Note: [Col. 0803] “May it be tested,” according to Mart. with six manuscripts and Rond. with four manuscripts.], and how often we slip? How often, when others tell empty stories, do we initially tolerate them, as though merely to avoid offending the weak, and then gradually begin to listen willingly? I no longer watch a dog running after a hare when this happens in the circus. But in the countryside, if I happen to pass by, that hunt perhaps turns me aside even from some great thought and turns me toward itself—not forcing the body of my mount to deviate, but by the inclination of my heart. And unless, now that my weakness has been shown to me, you quickly warn me either to rise through some reflection from the sight to you, or to despise the whole thing and pass on, I become foolishly dull. What happens when, sitting at home, a lizard catching flies, or a spider entangling in its webs those that rush into them, often makes me attentive? Is the same thing not happening merely because the animals are small? From there I proceed to praise you, the marvelous creator and ordering principle of all things; but I do not thereby cease to be absorbed in it. It is one thing to rise quickly; it is another not to fall. And my life is full of such things, while my one great hope is your exceedingly great mercy. For when our heart becomes a receptacle [Note: [Col. 0803] According to Rond., “a repository.”] of things of this kind and carries crowds of abundant vanity [Note: [Col. 0803] According to Rond., from five manuscripts cited by Mart.: “When our heart is such a receptacle, and carries …”], our prayers are often interrupted and disturbed by this; and while we direct the voice of our heart before your sight toward your ears, some great matter is cut short by trivial thoughts rushing in from I know not where.

### CHAPTER XXXVI. His condition with regard to the third kind of temptation, which is pride

58. Shall we count even this among the things to be despised, or can anything bring us back to hope except your entire mercy [Note: [Col. 0803] Some manuscripts, with Arn., read, “except your known mercy”; others, “except your entire mercy.”], since you have begun to change us? And you know how much you have changed me, you who first heal me from the desire to avenge myself, so that you may be gracious also toward all my other iniquities, heal all my sicknesses, redeem my life from corruption, crown me with compassion and mercy, and satisfy my desire with good things (Ps. CII, 3–5); you who have restrained my pride through fear of you and have gentled my neck beneath your yoke. And now I bear it, and it is easy for me, because you promised and accomplished this (Matt. [Col. 0804] XI, 30); and truly it was so, though I did not know it when I feared undertaking it. But has this third kind of temptation, Lord, ceased from me—or can it cease throughout this whole life? You alone rule without arrogance, because you alone are the true Lord who have no lord.

59. To wish to be feared and loved by human beings, not for any other reason than that one may derive joy from it—a joy that is no joy [Note: [Col. 0804] Somm. and Rond., supported by nine manuscripts, begin the sentence thus: “But surely”; and complete it: “which is no joy?” M.], is a wretched life and shameful boasting. Hence, above all, it comes about that we do not love you, nor fear you chastely. Therefore you resist the proud but give grace to the humble (I Peter V, 5); you thunder against the ambitions of the world, and the foundations of the mountains tremble.

Thus, since certain duties of human society make it necessary for us to be loved and feared by human beings, the adversary of our true blessedness presses upon us, everywhere scattering into snares the cry, “Well done, well done!”—so that, while we greedily gather it up, we are caught unwarily, and set down our joy from your truth and place it in human deceit. We may then desire to be loved and feared, not for your sake but in your place; and, having thereby been made like him, he may keep us with himself—not for the harmony of love, but for fellowship in punishment—he who determined to set his throne in the north, so that, dark and cold, they might serve him who imitates you along a perverse and distorted path (Isaiah XIV, 13–15) [Note: [Col. 0804] We read this as it stands in the Fossatensis manuscripts; in most others it is *imitandi* or *imitati*, which we judge less suitable.].

But we, Lord, behold, are your little flock (Luke XII, 32); possess us. Spread out your wings, and let us flee beneath them. You be our glory; for your sake may we be loved, and may your word be feared in us. Whoever wishes to be praised by human beings while you condemn him will not be defended by human beings when you judge him, nor rescued when you condemn him.

But when a sinner is not praised in the desires of his soul, nor is one who does what is unjust blessed (Psalm X, 3), but a person is praised on account of some gift that you have given him, and he rejoices more that he himself is praised than that he possesses the gift for which he is praised, then even this person is praised while you condemn him; and the one who praised him is already better than the one who was praised. For the former was pleased by God’s gift in the person; the latter was more pleased by the human gift than by God.

### CHAPTER XXXVII. How he is moved by human praise

60. We are tested by these temptations every day, Lord; without ceasing we are tested. Our daily furnace is the human tongue. In this also you command us to practice self-restraint: give what you command, and command what you will. You know the groaning of my heart concerning this matter, and the streams of my tears before you. For I do not easily determine how much cleaner I am from this plague, and I greatly fear my hidden faults (Psalm XVIII, 13), which your eyes know, but mine do not.

In other kinds of temptation I have some means of examining myself; in this one, almost none. For I can see how much I have managed to restrain my mind from the pleasures of the flesh and from the unnecessary curiosity of knowing, when I am deprived of those things either by choice or when they are absent [Col. 0805] [Note: [Col. 0805] Somm. reads: “either by choice when they are present, or by necessity when they are absent.” Rond. does likewise, substituting *absunt* for *desunt*. M.]. For then I ask myself how much more or less distressing it is for me not to have them.

As for riches, which are sought for the purpose of serving one or two or all three of these desires, if the mind cannot discern whether, possessing them, it despises them, they can also be relinquished so that it may prove itself. But as for doing without praise, and testing what we can do in that regard, must we live wickedly, and so ruinously and monstrously that no one who knows us fails to detest us? What greater madness can be spoken or imagined?

Yet if praise both accompanies and ought to accompany a good life and good works, we must not abandon either its companionship or the good life itself. I do not, however, perceive whether I can be without it either calmly or with distress, except when it is absent.

61. What, then, do I confess to you, Lord, concerning this kind of temptation? What but that I take pleasure in praise, though more in the truth itself than in praise? For if I were offered the choice between being praised by everyone while raging mad or mistaken in everything, and being blamed by everyone while steadfast and completely certain in the truth, I see what I would choose.

Nevertheless, I would not want the approval of another’s mouth to increase my joy in any good of mine. Yet it does increase it, I confess; and not only that, but blame also diminishes it. When I am troubled by this misery of mine, an excuse enters my mind—what kind of excuse it is, you know, God—for it makes me uncertain.

Since you have commanded us not only self-restraint—that is, from which things we should withhold our love—but also justice—that is, to what we should direct it—and since you wished us to love not only you but also our neighbor, I often seem to take pleasure in my neighbor’s progress or hope when I take pleasure in the praise of one who understands well; and again to grieve at his misfortune when I hear him blame what he does not understand, or what is good.

For I am sometimes saddened by my own praises, either when things are praised in me in which I myself am displeased with myself, or when lesser and trivial goods are valued more highly than they ought to be. But again, how do I know whether I am affected in this way because I do not want my praiser’s judgment of me to differ from my own—not because I am moved by his benefit, but because the same goods that please me in myself are more pleasing to me when they also please another?

In a certain sense I am not praised when my own judgment is not praised; for either those things are praised which displease me, or those which please me less are praised more highly. Am I, then, uncertain about myself in this matter?

62. Behold, in you, Truth, I see that I ought to be moved by my praises not for my own sake but for the benefit of my neighbor. Whether that is really so, I do not know. I know myself less in this matter than I know you [Note: [Col. 0805] Lov. reads “than I know myself to you,” but the older editions and manuscripts read “than you.” Here he plainly confesses what he said above in chapter 5: “I am more present to myself than to you, and yet I know that you cannot in any way be harmed; but I do not know which temptations I can resist and which I cannot.”—Somm. and Rond., with seven manuscripts, read “than to you,” as Lov. M.].

I beseech you, my God, and reveal myself to me, so that I may confess to my brothers praying for me what I discover to be wounded in me. Let me question myself again more carefully. If I am moved by the benefit of my neighbor when I am praised, why am I less moved when someone else is unjustly blamed than when I am? Why does an insult hurled against me before my eyes wound me more than the same injustice hurled against another? Do I not know this as well? Does it remain for me to deceive myself and fail to speak the truth before you in my heart and on my tongue?

Keep this madness far from me, Lord, lest my mouth become the oil of the sinner, used to fatten my head (Psalm CXL, 5).

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. Even virtue is endangered by vainglory

63. I am needy and poor, and I am better when, in hidden groaning, I displease myself and seek your mercy, until my weakness is restored and brought to that peace which the eye of the arrogant does not know.

But speech issuing from the mouth, and deeds that become known to human beings, have an exceedingly dangerous temptation arising from the love of praise, which draws together solicited approval for a certain private eminence. It makes its attempt even when I condemn it in myself, by the very fact that I condemn it; and often a person boasts even more vainly of his contempt for vainglory. Therefore he no longer boasts of that very contempt [Note: [Col. 0806] Am., Er., and Lov. read “of that very contempt for vainglory.” The word *vainglory* is absent from the manuscripts, some of which also punctuate the following words thus: “For he does not despise it when he boasts.” “Within, indeed, within, there is something else.” Moreover, in the following sentence several manuscripts omit the word *homo* (“person”).]—for inwardly, while boasting, he does not despise it.

### CHAPTER XXXIX. The power and nature of self-love

64. There is also, inwardly, another evil of the same kind of temptation, by which those who are pleased with themselves become empty, even though they do not please others, or displease them, and do not seek to please others [Note: [Col. 0806] This is the reading of the better manuscripts. Lov., without the negation, reads “or please them.”].

Yet those who please themselves greatly displease you—not only when they regard things that are not good as good, but also when they regard your goods as their own; or when they regard them as yours, but as arising from their own merits; or even when they regard them as arising from your grace, yet do not rejoice in them communally, but envy others who possess them [Note: [Col. 0806] Most editions interpolate the passage as follows: “Or even as arising from your grace, but not from their own merits, and yet …” We have removed the words “but not from their own merits,” because they are absent from the manuscripts.].

Amid all these and similar dangers and troubles, you see the trembling of my heart; and I feel that my wounds are continually being healed by you, rather than that they are not being inflicted upon me.

### CHAPTER XL. How he investigated God in himself and in other things

65. Where did you not walk with me, Truth, teaching me what to avoid and what to pursue, when I referred to you the inferior perceptions I was able to form and consulted you?

I surveyed the world outside with the bodily sense I could use, and attended to the life of my body as it came to me, and to the senses themselves. From there I entered the recesses of my memory, its manifold and vast chambers filled in wondrous ways with innumerable stores. I considered them, and was terrified, and could discern nothing among them without you; yet I found that none of them was you.

Nor was I myself the discoverer who traversed all these things and attempted to distinguish them and assess each according to its proper worth—receiving some through the senses as messengers, questioning others that I sensed mingled with myself, recognizing and counting the messengers themselves, and then, amid the broad resources of memory, handling some things, storing others away, and bringing others out [Note: [Col. 0807] Lov. reads “among the riches raised up in memory.”].

Nor, while I was doing these things—that is, was the power by which I did them—were you yourself; for you are the enduring light whom I consulted about all things: whether they existed, what they were, and how highly they should be valued. And I heard you teaching and commanding.

I often do this; it delights me, and whenever I can withdraw from the duties of necessity, I retreat to this pleasure. Yet amid all these things that I pass through while consulting you, I find no safe place for my soul except in you, where my scattered parts may be gathered together, and nothing of me may depart from you.

Sometimes you admit me into an exceedingly unusual inward affection, toward a sweetness I cannot describe; if it were perfected in me, I do not know what life would then be, but it would not be this life. Yet I fall back into these things under the weight of troubles, am swallowed up again by my customary ways, held fast, and weep greatly—though I am held fast even more strongly. So great is the burden of habit! [Note: [Col. 0807] In nearly all the manuscripts, without exception: “So great is the burden of habit worthy of this.” The same reading is found in Bad.].

Here I can remain, but do not wish to; there I wish to be, but cannot. Wretched in both places.

### CHAPTER XLI. The threefold desire

66. Therefore I considered the illnesses of my sins in the threefold desire, and called upon your right hand for my salvation. For I saw your splendor with a wounded heart, and, driven back, I said: “Who can reach it?” I was cast away from the sight of your eyes (Psalm XXX, 23).

You are the Truth presiding over all things; but through my greed I did not want to lose you—I wanted to possess falsehood together with you, just as no one wishes to tell a falsehood in such a way that he himself does not know what is true. Thus I lost you, because you do not deem it worthy to be possessed together with falsehood.

### CHAPTER XLII. Some unhappily turned to demons as mediators for returning to God

67. Whom could I find to reconcile me to you? Should I have approached the angels? With what prayer? By what rites?

Many who tried to return to you, and, as I hear, were unable to do so by themselves, attempted these things and fell into a desire for curious visions and were deemed worthy of deceptions. For, lifted up by the pride of their learning, they thrust out their breasts rather than beat them, and they brought upon themselves, by the likeness of their own hearts, the powers of the air that conspired with them and shared their pride (Ephesians II, 2). Through magical powers they were deceived by these beings, seeking a mediator by whom they might be purified—and there was none.

For the devil was disguising himself as an angel of light (II Corinthians XI, 14). And he greatly enticed proud flesh by the fact that he himself was not clothed in a fleshly body. For they were mortal and sinful; but you, Lord, with whom they proudly sought reconciliation, are immortal and without sin.

Now a mediator between God and human beings (I Timothy II, 5) had to possess something like God and something like human beings: otherwise, if he were like human beings in both respects, he would be far from God; or if he were like God in both respects, he would be far from human beings, and so would not be a mediator.

That deceptive mediator, then, through whom, by your hidden judgments, pride deserved to be mocked, has one thing in common with human beings—sin; he wishes to appear to have another thing in common with God, so that, because he is not covered by the mortality of flesh, he may display himself as immortal. But since the wages of sin are death, he shares this with human beings, and by it he is condemned together with them to death.

### CHAPTER XLIII. Christ the true mediator

68. But the true mediator, whom your hidden mercy revealed to the humble and sent so that by his example they might also learn humility itself—that mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus—appeared between mortal sinners and the immortal righteous: mortal with human beings, righteous with God.

Since the wages of righteousness are life and peace, by the righteousness united to God he might abolish the death of justified ungodly persons [Note: [Col. 0808] The Benignian manuscript reads “of the ungodly who were to be justified.” The Corbeiensis manuscript reads “of the righteous who were justified.”], a death he chose to share with them.

He was shown in this way to the ancient saints, so that they might be saved through faith in his future passion, just as we are saved through faith in his past passion. Insofar as he was human, he was a mediator; insofar as he was the Word, he was not intermediate, because he was equal to God, God with God, and, together with the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0808] Most manuscripts do not contain the words “together with the Holy Spirit.”], one God.

69. How you loved us, good Father, you who did not spare your only Son but delivered him up for us ungodly people! (Romans VIII, 32.) How you loved us, for whose sake he, who did not consider equality with you something to be grasped, became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians II, 6).

He alone among the dead was free (Psalm LXXXVII, 6–8), having authority to lay down his life and authority to take it up again (John X, 18); for us, before you, victor and victim—and therefore victor because victim; for us, before you, priest and sacrifice—and therefore priest because sacrifice; making us from servants into sons, by being born from you and serving us.

Rightly my hope in him is strong: that you will heal all my illnesses through him who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us (Romans VIII, 34); otherwise I would despair. For many and great are my illnesses—many and great; but your medicine is greater. We might have thought that your Word was removed from union with humanity and despaired of ourselves, unless he had become flesh and dwelt among us.

70. Terrified by my sins and by the burden of my misery, I had pondered and turned over in my heart the idea of fleeing into solitude; but you prohibited me and strengthened me, saying: “Christ died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who died for them” (II Corinthians V, 15).

Behold, Lord, I cast my care upon you so that I may live, and I will consider the wonders of your law (Psalm CXVIII, 18). You know my ignorance and my weakness: teach me and heal me. Your only Son, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians II, 3), redeemed me with his blood.

Let not the proud slander me, for I contemplate my price, and eat, and drink, and distribute it; and, poor as I am, I long to be satisfied from it among those who eat and are filled and praise the Lord who seek him (Psalm XXI, 27).

# BOOK ELEVEN

Augustine now intends to praise God by professing his own knowledge or ignorance of the Holy Scriptures, and also the zeal with which, by divine gift, he burned for them. He begins by explaining the Book of Genesis, and here first expounds the words: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” He answers those who objected, asking what God was doing before he founded heaven and earth, and what finally prompted him to make them, since he had not made them before. While laboring to refute them, he composes an extensive discussion of Time.

[Col. 0809]

### CHAPTER I. Why we confess to God, who already knows

1. Since your eternity is yours, Lord, do you not know what I say to you, or do you see in time what occurs in time? Why, then, do I set before you so many accounts of events? Certainly not so that you may know them through me, but to arouse my affection toward you and that of those who read these things, so that we may all say: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise” (Psalm XCV, 4).
