I have already said, and I shall say again: I do this for love of your love. For we pray, and yet Truth says: “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew VI, 8).

We therefore disclose our affection to you by confessing to you our miseries and your mercies toward us, so that you may wholly deliver us, since you have begun to do so, and so that we may cease to be miserable in ourselves and be blessed in you. For you have called us to be poor in spirit, meek, mourning, hungering and thirsting for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, and peacemakers (Matthew V, 3–9).

Behold, I have told you many things that I could and wished to tell, because you first willed that I should confess to you, Lord my God, that you are good and that your mercy endures forever (Psalm CXVII, 1).

### CHAPTER II. He asks God for understanding of the Holy Scriptures

2. When would the tongue of my pen be sufficient to declare all your encouragements, all your terrors, consolations, and guidance by which you led me to preach the word and administer your sacrament to your people? And even if I were sufficient to declare these things in order, the drops of time would be precious to me.

Long ago I burned to meditate on your law, and in it to confess to you my knowledge and ignorance, the beginnings of your illumination and the remnants of my darkness, until weakness is swallowed up by strength. I do not want the hours I find free from the necessities of restoring the body, directing the mind, and serving human beings—services we owe them, and services we do not owe them yet nevertheless render—to dissipate into other things.

3. Lord my God, attend to my prayer, and in your mercy hear my desire, for it does not burn for me alone but wishes to serve fraternal love; and you see in my heart that this is so. Let me offer you the service of my thought and my tongue, and grant me something to offer you.

For I am needy and poor; you are rich toward all who call upon you (Romans X, 12), and you securely care for us. Circumcise from all rashness and every lie the inward and outward lips of my mouth. May the Scriptures be my chaste delights; may I neither be deceived in them nor deceive through them.

Attend, Lord, and have mercy, Lord my God, light of the blind and strength of the weak, and at once light of those who see and strength of the strong: attend to my soul and hear it crying from the depths. For if your ears are not present even in the depths, where shall we go? Where shall we cry?

The day is yours, and the night is yours (Psalm LXXIII, 16); at your command the moments fly past. Grant our meditations room within the hidden places of your law, and do not close it against those who knock. For you did not wish the shadowy secrets of so many pages to be written without purpose; surely those forests have their deer, which withdraw into them, recover their strength, walk and feed, lie down [Note: [Col. 0810] This is the reading of Arn. and twelve manuscripts. Lov. reads “lie back.”] and ruminate.

O Lord, perfect me and reveal them to me. Behold, your voice is my joy, your voice surpasses an abundance of pleasures [Note: [Col. 0810] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads “above an abundance.” Bad. and Am., with four manuscripts, read “above the overflowing of pleasures.”]. Grant what I love—for I do love it, and you gave me this love. Do not abandon your gifts, nor despise your thirsty plant.

Let me confess to you whatever I find in your books, and hear the voice of praise (Psalm XXV, 7), and drink you in, and consider the wonders of your law, from the beginning at which you made heaven and earth, to the everlasting kingdom with you of your holy city.

4. Lord, have mercy on me and hear my desire. For I think it is not for things of earth—not for gold, silver, or stones, nor for beautiful garments, honors, or powers, nor for the pleasures of the flesh, nor for the necessities of the body and this life of our pilgrimage—all of which are added to us when we seek your kingdom and righteousness.

See, Lord my God, where my desire comes from. The wicked have told me of delights, but not such as your law, Lord (Psalm CXVIII, 85). Behold where my desire comes from.

See, Father; look, and see, and approve. May it please your mercy that I find grace before you, so that the inner meanings of your words may be opened to me when I knock. I beseech you through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, the man at your right hand (Psalm LXXIX, 18), the Son of Man whom you established for yourself as mediator, your mediator and ours, through whom you sought us when we were not seeking you—and sought us so that we might seek you; your Word through whom you made all things, among which you made me; your only Son through whom you called the believing people to adoption, among whom you called me also.

Through him I beseech you, who sits at your right hand and intercedes for us, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians II, 3). Him I seek in your books [Note: [Col. 0811] The earlier editions read “I seek them.” The older and better manuscripts read “I seek him.”]. Moses wrote about him (John V, 46); he himself says this, and Truth says this.

### CHAPTER III. What Moses wrote about the creation of heaven and earth cannot be understood unless God grants understanding

5. Let me hear and understand how, in the beginning, you made heaven and earth (Genesis I, 4). Moses wrote this, wrote it, and departed, passing from here—from you to you [Note: [Col. 0811] The words “from you to you” are absent from the editions but found in nearly all the manuscripts.]; nor is he now before me.

For if he were, I would hold him, ask him, and beseech him through you to disclose these things to me; I would offer the ears of my body to the sounds issuing from his mouth. If he spoke in Hebrew, he would knock in vain upon my senses, and nothing from it would touch my mind; but if he spoke in Latin, I would know what he said.

Yet how would I know whether he spoke the truth? And if I knew even that, would I know it from him? Surely the truth would speak inwardly to me, within the dwelling place of thought—not in Hebrew, Greek, Latin, or any barbarian tongue, without the organs of mouth or tongue and without the noise of syllables: “He speaks the truth.” And I, immediately certain, would say confidently to that servant of yours: “You speak the truth.”

Since, then, I cannot question him, I ask you, Truth, with whom he was filled when he spoke the truth. I ask you, my God; spare my sins. You who gave that servant of yours the ability to say these things, give me also the ability to understand them.

### CHAPTER IV. Creation cries out that God is its creator

6. Behold, heaven and earth exist: they cry out that they were made, for they change and vary. Whatever has not been made, yet exists, contains nothing in itself that previously was not there—nothing that can change or vary.

They also cry out that they did not make themselves: “We exist because we were made; therefore we did not exist before we existed, so that we could make ourselves.” Their voice is the very evidence of the matter.

You therefore, Lord, made them—you who are beautiful, for they are beautiful; you who are good, for they are good; you who are, for they are. Yet they are not so beautiful, so good, or so existent as you, their creator; compared with you, they are neither beautiful, good, nor existent.

We know this; thanks be to you. And our knowledge, compared with your knowledge, is ignorance.

### CHAPTER V. The world was created from nothing

7. But how did you make heaven and earth [Note: [Col. 0811] In Am., Er., and Lov., chapter 5 begins as follows: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth. How …” The same words occur here in Bad., but they are absent from the manuscripts and from the Arnaldine edition.]? What instrument did you use for so great an operation?

Not as a human craftsman forms one body from another, according to the decision of a soul able somehow to impose upon the material a form that it sees within itself with its inner eye. And whence would he have this ability, unless you had made him? He imposes a form upon something that already exists and possesses being—earth, stone, wood, gold, or any similar thing.

And whence would these things exist unless you had established them? You made the craftsman’s body, the soul that commands his limbs, the material from which he makes something, the skill by which he grasps an art and sees within what he is to do without, the bodily sense through which, as interpreter, he transfers from the soul to the material what he is making and reports to the soul what has been made, so that the soul may consult the Truth presiding within it as to whether it has been made well.

All these things praise you as their creator. But how do you make them? How did you make heaven and earth, O God? Certainly not in heaven or on earth did you make heaven and earth; nor in the air or in the waters, since these too belong to heaven and earth. Nor did you make the whole world in the whole world, because there was no place where it could be made before it was made so as to exist.

Nor did you hold in your hand anything from which to make heaven and earth; for whence would you have had what you had not made, from which you could make something? What is there, then, except that you are?

Therefore you spoke, and they were made; and in your Word you made them (Psalm XXXII, 9, 6).

### CHAPTER VI. How God spoke so that the world might be made

8. But how did you speak? Was it in the manner in which the voice came from the cloud, saying: “This is my beloved Son”? (Matthew III, 17; XVII, 5.)

That voice was produced and passed away; it began and ended. The syllables sounded and passed away—one after another, the second after the first, the third after the second, and so on in order, until the last followed the others, and silence followed the last.

This makes clear and prominent the fact that the movement of a creature expressed it, the temporal movement itself serving your eternal will. These words, made for a time, were announced by the outer ear to the discerning mind, whose inner ear is placed toward your eternal Word.

The mind compared these words sounding in time with your eternal Word in silence and said: “One thing is this, and something altogether different is that. These things are far beneath me; indeed, they do not exist, because they flee and pass away. But the Word of my Lord remains above me forever.”

If, then, you spoke through sounding and passing words so that heaven and earth might be made, and so made heaven and earth, there was already a bodily creation whose temporal movements could cause that voice to pass through time. But there was no body before heaven and earth; or, if there was, you had certainly made it without a transitory voice, so that from it you might make the transitory voice by which you would say that heaven and earth should be made.

Whatever that thing was from which such a voice could arise, unless it had been made by you, it simply would not exist. Therefore, when the body from which these words were to arise was made, by what word did you speak it?

### CHAPTER VII. The Word of God is coeternal with God

9. You therefore call us to understand the Word, God with you, God, which is spoken eternally, and through which all things are spoken eternally. For what was being said does not come to an end, with something else being said so that all things may be said; rather, all things are said together and eternally [Col. 0813]. Otherwise there would already be time and change, not true eternity or true immortality.

I know this, my God, and I give you thanks. I know it, I confess it to you, Lord; and whoever is not ungrateful to certain truth knows and blesses you together with me.

We know, Lord, we know: insofar as anything is not what it was and is what it was not, insofar does it die and arise. Therefore nothing of your Word gives way or succeeds to anything else, because it is truly immortal and eternal.

And therefore, with your Word coeternal with you, you speak all that you speak both together and eternally [Note: [Col. 0813] Some manuscripts read “you speak together and eternally.” A little later, many of the better manuscripts, with Arn., read “and all things are made both together and eternally.” “And together and eternally,” according to Er., Ven., and Lugd.; “together and eternally,” omitting the earlier “and,” according to Somm. and Flor. M.]. Whatever you say to be made comes to be; nor do you make anything in any other way than by speaking. Yet not all the things you make by speaking are made both together and eternally.

### CHAPTER VIII. The Word of God itself is the Beginning by which we are taught all truth

10. Why is this so, I ask, Lord my God? I see it somehow, but I do not know how to express it, except that everything that begins and ceases to exist begins to exist and ceases to exist when it is known in the eternal reason that it ought to begin or cease—there where nothing begins or ends.

This is your Word, which is also the Beginning, because it speaks to us [Note: [Col. 0813] The editions read “which also speaks.” The manuscripts read “because it also speaks,” corresponding to the Greek *hoti kai lalō hymin*. Augustine appears to have read it in this way elsewhere, for example in chapter 28 of the following book and in Treatise 38 on John.].

Thus he spoke in the Gospel through flesh, and this sounded outwardly in human ears so that it might be believed, sought inwardly, and found in eternal truth, where the good and only Teacher teaches all disciples.

There I hear your voice, Lord, saying to me that he speaks to us who teaches us. But whoever does not teach us, even if he speaks, does not speak to us. And who teaches us except stable Truth?

For even when we are admonished through mutable creation, we are led to stable Truth, where we truly learn when we stand and hear him, and rejoice with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice (John III, 29), returning ourselves to him from whom we are.

Therefore he is the Beginning, because unless he remained, when we went astray there would be nowhere for us to return. When we return from error, we return by knowing; and so that we may know, he teaches us, because he is the Beginning and speaks to us.

### CHAPTER IX. How the Word of God speaks to the heart

11. In this Beginning, God, you made heaven and earth—in your Word, in your Son, in your Power, in your Wisdom, in your Truth—speaking in a wondrous way and making in a wondrous way. Who can comprehend it? Who can recount it?

What is this that shines through to me and strikes my heart without injury, so that I shudder and burn? I shudder insofar as I am unlike it; I burn insofar as I am like it.

It is Wisdom itself that shines through to me, tearing apart my cloud, which again covers me when I fall away from it, with the darkness and mass of my punishments. For my strength has been so weakened by poverty (Psalm XXX, 11) that I cannot bear my good until you, Lord, who have become gracious toward all my iniquities, also heal all my illnesses; for you will redeem my life from corruption, crown me with mercy and compassion, and satisfy my desire with good things, so that my youth will be renewed like the eagle’s (Psalm CII, 3–5).

For we were saved in hope, and through patience we await your promises (Romans VIII, 24–25). May whoever can hear you hear you speaking inwardly. I shall confidently cry out from your oracle: “How magnificent are your works, O Lord! You have made them all in Wisdom” (Psalm CIII, 24)—and she is the Beginning, and in that Beginning you made heaven and earth.

### CHAPTER X. He answers those who object, asking what God was doing before he founded heaven and earth

12. Are they not, behold, full of their old nature, those who say to us: “What was God doing before he made heaven and earth?”

“For if he was idle,” they say, “and was not doing anything, why did he not remain idle forever afterward, just as he had always previously ceased from work? For if a new movement arose in God, and a new will arose by which he founded a creation that he had never before founded, how can that be a true eternity, in which a will arises that previously did not exist?

“God’s will is not a creature, but precedes creation; for nothing would be created unless the will of the Creator preceded it. Therefore his will belongs to the very substance of God. But if something arose in God’s substance that previously did not exist, that substance cannot truly be called eternal. If, however, God’s will was eternal that creation should exist, why was creation not eternal also?”

### CHAPTER XI. He responds to the objection that God’s eternity knows no times
13. Those who say these things do not yet understand you, O Wisdom of God, light of minds; they do not yet understand how the things that are made through you and in you come to be. They try to comprehend eternal things, but their hearts still flit about amid the past and future movements of created things, and so remain vain. Who will grasp and fix the heart, so that it may stand for a little while, seize for a little while the radiance of the eternity that always stands, and compare it with times that never stand still, and see that it is incomparable? Who will make it see that a long period of time is not long except through many passing movements, which cannot all be extended simultaneously; that nothing passes away in the eternal, but everything is present; whereas no time is wholly present? Who will make it see that every past is driven on by the future, and every future follows from the past; and that both past and future are created and proceed from that which is always present?

Who will grasp the human heart so that it may stand still and see how, while standing, it may declare future and past times—though eternity is neither future nor past? Can my hand accomplish this, or the hand of my mouth bring about so great a thing by words?

## CHAPTER XII. What God did before the creation of the world

[Col. 0815]

14. Behold, I answer the one who says, “What was God doing before he made heaven and earth?” I do not answer what someone is said to have replied jokingly, evading the force of the question: “He was preparing hell for those who pry into lofty matters.” It is one thing to see and another to laugh; I do not give that answer. I would rather reply, “I do not know what I do not know,” than give the answer that ridicules the one who asked about lofty matters and praises the one who gave a false answer.

But I say to you, our God, creator of every creature: if by the name “heaven and earth” every creature is understood, I boldly say, “Before God made heaven and earth, he was not making anything.” For if he was making something, what was he making except a creature? And would that I might know whatever I profitably desire to know in the same way that I know that no creature was being made before any creature was made [Note: [Col. 0815] The Benignianus manuscript reads, “that he was making no creature.”].

## CHAPTER XIII. That before the times created by God there was no time

15. But if someone’s flighty mind wanders through images of times long past and marvels that you, almighty, creator of all things, sustainer of all things, and maker of heaven and earth, ceased from so great a work for innumerable ages before you made it, let him awaken and attend, because what he marvels at is false. For how could innumerable ages have passed which you yourself had not made, since you are the author and founder of all ages? Or what times could there have been that were not established by you? Or how could they have passed if they had never existed?

Since, then, you are the maker of all times, if there was any time before you made heaven and earth, why is it said that you were then inactive? You had made that very time, and no times could have passed before you made times. But if there was no time before heaven and earth, why ask what you were doing then? There was no “then” where there was no time.

16. Nor do you precede times in time; otherwise you would not precede all times. You precede all past things by the height of your ever-present eternity, and you transcend all future things because they are future and, when they arrive, will be past. But you are always the same, and your years do not fail (Ps. 101:28). Your years neither go nor come; but our years both go and come, so that all may come.

All your years stand simultaneously, because they stand; and, since they do not pass away, those that go are not excluded by those that come. But all our years will exist when all of them no longer exist. Your years are one day, and your day is not day after day but today, because your today does not yield to tomorrow, nor does it follow yesterday. Your today is eternity; therefore you begot one coeternal with you, to whom you said, “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2:7; Heb. 5:5). You made all times, and you are before all times; nor was there ever a time when there was no time.

## CHAPTER XIV. The three distinctions of time

17. Therefore there was no time when you had not made something, because you had made time itself. And no times are coeternal with you [Col. 0816], because you remain; but if they remained, they would not be times. What, then, is time? Who could easily and briefly explain it? Who could grasp it even in thought, so as to put its meaning into words? Yet what do we mention more familiarly and knowingly in speech than time? We certainly understand it when we speak of it, and we also understand it when we hear another speaking of it.

What, then, is time? If no one asks me, I know; if I wish to explain it to someone who asks, I do not know. Yet I confidently say that I know this: if nothing passed away, there would be no past time; if nothing arrived, there would be no future time; and if nothing existed, there would be no present time.

How, then, are those two times—the past and the future—when the past no longer is and the future does not yet exist? As for the present, if it were always present and did not pass into the past, it would no longer be time but eternity. If, then, the present becomes time because it passes into the past, how can we say that it exists, when its reason for existing is that it will not exist? Thus we cannot truly say that time exists except insofar as it tends toward nonexistence [Note: [Col. 0816] Lovaniensis reads, “tends toward nonexistence.” The particle “toward” is absent from the manuscripts, and Augustine elsewhere likewise does not use it after the verb “tends,” as in Book 4 of this work, chapter 10: “Therefore, when they arise and tend toward existence.”].

## CHAPTER XV. The measure of time

18. Yet we speak of a long time and a short time, and we say this only of the past or the future. We call a past time long—for example, one hundred years ago—and likewise a future time long, one hundred years from now. We call a past time short, say, ten days ago, and a future time short, ten days from now.

But how can what does not exist be long or short? The past no longer exists, and the future does not yet exist. So let us not say, “It is long,” but of the past let us say, “It was long,” and of the future, “It will be long.”

My Lord, my light, will not your truth here also mock the human being? When the past time was long, was it long when it was already past, or when it was still present? It could be long then, when there was something that could be long; but the past no longer existed, and therefore what did not exist at all could not be long. Let us not say, then, “The past time was long”; for we shall not find what was long when, from the moment it became past, it no longer exists. Rather, let us say, “That present time was long,” because, while it was present, it was long. It had not yet passed away so as no longer to exist, and therefore there was something that could be long. But afterward, when it passed away, it simultaneously ceased to be long, because it ceased to exist.

19. Let us see, then, O human soul, whether present time can be long; for you have been given the ability to perceive durations and measure them. What will you answer me? Is one hundred present years a long time? First see whether one hundred years can be present. If the first of them is passing, that year alone is present; the other ninety-nine are future, and therefore do not yet exist. If the second year is passing, one year is already past, one is present, and the rest are future.

And so, whichever year of this hundred-year number we take as present, the years before it will be past and those after it future. Consequently, one hundred years cannot be present. See at least whether the one year that is passing is itself wholly present. If its first month is passing, the remaining months are future; if its second month is passing, the first has already passed and the rest do not yet exist. Therefore even the year that is passing is not wholly present; and if it is not wholly present, it is not a present year.

A year consists of twelve months. Whichever one month is passing is present; the others are past or future. Yet even the month that is passing is not present as a whole, but only one day. If it is the first day, the others are future; if it is the last, the others are past; if it is any middle day, some are past and some future.

20. Behold, the present time—the only time we found that could be called long—has scarcely been reduced to the span of a single day. But let us examine even that, because not even one day is wholly present. It is completed by all twenty-four hours, night and day; the first has all the others as future, the last has all the others as past, and any intervening hour has those before it as past and those after it as future.

That single hour itself passes in fleeting particles: whatever of it has flown away is past; whatever remains is future. If any period of time can be conceived that cannot be divided into any further, or even the tiniest, portions of moments, that alone is what may be called present. Yet it flies so swiftly from future into past that it has no duration at all. For if it had duration, it would be divided into past and future; but the present has no extent.

Where, then, is the time that we can call long? Is it future? We do not say, “It is long,” because what could be long does not yet exist; we say, “It will be long.” When, then, will it be long? If, while it is still future, it will not be long—because what is to be long does not yet exist—but if it will be long when it has begun to exist as what was future and has become present, so that there is something that can be long, then the present time itself cries out through what we have already said that it cannot be long.

## CHAPTER XVI. What kind of time can and cannot be measured

21. Yet, Lord, we perceive intervals of time, compare them with one another, and say that some are longer and others shorter. We also measure how much shorter or longer one time is than another, and say that one is double or triple, the other single, or that one is equal to another.

But we measure passing times as we perceive them; who can measure past times, which no longer exist, or future times, which do not yet exist—unless someone dares to say that what does not exist can be measured? Therefore, when time is passing, it can be perceived and measured; but when it has passed, because it no longer exists, it cannot.

## CHAPTER XVII. Where past and future time are

22. I ask, Father; I do not assert. My God, preside over me and rule me. Who will tell me that there are not three times, as we learned as children and taught children—the past, the present, and the future—but only the present, because the other two do not exist?

Or do they also exist, but emerge from some hidden place when the future becomes present, and withdraw into some hidden place when the present becomes past? For where did those who foretold the future see it, if it does not yet exist? What does not exist cannot be seen. And those who recount the past would certainly not recount the truth if they did not see it in their minds; but if it did not exist at all, it could not be seen. Therefore both future and past exist.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How past and future times are present

23. Allow me, Lord, to inquire further; my hope, do not let my attention be disturbed. If future and past exist, I want to know where they are. Even if I cannot yet know this, I do know that wherever they are and whatever they are, they are not there as future or past, but as present. If they are future there, they are not yet there; if they are past there, they are no longer there. Wherever they are and whatever they are, they exist only as present.

Yet when past events are truthfully narrated, they are brought forth from memory—not the events themselves, which have passed away, but words formed from images of them, which they fixed in the mind as traces while passing through the senses.

My childhood, which no longer exists, belongs to past time, which no longer exists. But when I recall and narrate its image, I behold it in the present, because it is still in my memory. Whether the same explanation applies to the prediction of future events—so that already existing images of things that do not yet exist are made present [Note: [Col. 0818] Most editions read, “so that the images are presented,” and shortly afterward, “and the future things are present.” We follow the reading of the manuscripts, which is supported at the later passage by Arnaldus]—I confess, my God, that I do not know.

This much I do know: we often deliberate beforehand about our future actions, and this deliberation is present, while the action about which we deliberate does not yet exist because it is future. But when we have begun to undertake it and to do what we had deliberated, then the action will exist, because then it is not future but present [Note: [Col. 0818] “Will exist,” according to Erasmus, Venetiensis, Lugdunensis, and M.].

24. Whatever the mysterious foreknowledge of future things may be, nothing that does not exist can be seen. Whatever already exists is not future but present. Therefore, when future things are said to be seen, perhaps it is not the things themselves that do not yet exist—that is, the things that are future—that are seen, but their causes or signs, which already exist. For this reason they are present to those who see them, and from them the future things are foretold as conceived in the mind. These conceptions, in turn, already exist, and those who foretell such things behold them as present within themselves.

Let the vast multitude of things provide me with an example. I behold the dawn and announce the rising of the sun. What I behold is present; what I announce is future—not the sun, which already exists, but its rising, which does not yet exist. Yet I could not foretell that rising unless I imagined it in my mind, just as I do now while speaking of it.

But neither is the dawn that I see in the sky the rising of the sun, although it precedes it, nor is the image in my mind. Both of these are seen as present, so that the future rising may be foretold beforehand. Future things, therefore, do not yet exist; and if they do not yet exist, they do not exist. If they do not exist, they cannot be seen at all; but they can be foretold from present things, which already exist and are seen.

## CHAPTER XIX. The manner in which God teaches future things cannot be grasped

25. You, then, ruler of your creation, what is the manner in which you teach souls the things that are future? For you taught your prophets. What is that manner in which you teach future things, when nothing is future for you—or rather, in which you teach present things concerning the future? For what does not exist cannot be taught. This manner is far beyond my vision; it has become too great for me, and I cannot reach it (Ps. 138:6). But I shall be able to reach it through you, when you give me the sweet light of my hidden eyes.

## CHAPTER XX. How the distinctions of time should be named

26. What is now clear and evident is that neither future nor past things exist. Strictly speaking, therefore, it is not correct to say, “There are three times: past, present, and future.” Perhaps it would be correct to say, “There are three times: a present of things past, a present of things present, and a present of things future.”

For these three do somehow exist in the soul, and I do not see them anywhere else: the present of past things is memory; the present of present things is direct perception; the present of future things is expectation. If we are permitted to speak in this way, I see three times and acknowledge that there are three.

It may also be said, according to customary usage, “There are three times: past, present, and future.” Let it be said; I do not object or resist or criticize, provided that what is said is understood, and that it is not taken to mean that what is future already exists or that what is past still exists. We speak few things strictly and many things loosely, but what we mean is recognized.

## CHAPTER XXI. How time may be measured

27. A little earlier I said that we measure passing times, so that we can say that one period is twice as long as another, or that one is equal to another, and make whatever other statements about parts of time we can make by measuring. Therefore, as I said, we measure passing times.

If someone asks me, “How do you know?” I can answer, “I know because we measure; and we cannot measure what does not exist, while past and future things do not exist.” But how do we measure present time, when it has no extent? It is measured while it passes; when it has passed, it is not measured [Note: [Col. 0819] Several editions and manuscripts read, “We measure, then, while it passes ... we do not measure; for what would be measured?” This is awkward. M.].

For what could be measured will no longer exist. But from where, through what, and toward what does it pass when it is measured? From where, except from the future? Through what, except the present? Toward what, except the past? Thus it passes from what does not yet exist, through what has no extent, into what no longer exists.

But what do we measure except time in some extent? We do not speak of single, double, triple, equal, or any other such relationships in time except in relation to periods of time. In what extent, then, do we measure passing time? Is it in the future, from which it passes? But what does not yet exist cannot be measured. Or in the present, through which it passes? But we do not measure what has no extent. Or in the past, into which it passes? But what no longer exists cannot be measured.

## CHAPTER XXII. He asks God to solve this riddle

28. My mind burns to know this most intricate riddle. Do not, O good Lord my God and Father, I beg you through Christ, shut these familiar yet hidden matters against my desire, so that it cannot penetrate them and they cannot grow bright through the illumination of your mercy, O Lord.

Whom shall I question about these things? And to whom can I confess my ignorance more fruitfully than to you, whose patience is not troubled by my eager studies, burning intensely over your Scriptures? Give me what I love; for I love it, and you gave me that love. Give, Father, you who truly know how to give good gifts to your children (Matt. 7:11). Give, because I have undertaken to know, and the labor lies before me (Ps. 72:16), until you open the way [Note: [Col. 0820] Badianus, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read, “to know you.” “You” should be removed, in accordance with the manuscripts and Arnaldus, because Augustine is speaking of knowing time, not of knowing God.].

Through Christ I beg you, in the name of that Holy One who is holy among the holy, let no one obstruct me. I believed, and therefore I spoke (Ps. 115:1). This is my hope; for this I live [Note: [Col. 0820] Lovaniensis reads, “for this I long”; the reading given here is preferable, unless the other editions and manuscripts, which agree in large numbers, are to be rejected].—that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.

Behold, you have set my days as days of old (Ps. 38:6), and they pass away; how they pass away, I do not know. We say, “Time and time,” “times and times”; “How long did that person say this?” “How long did that person do that?” “For how long did I not see that?” And, “This syllable has twice as much time as that short syllable.”

We say these things, hear these things, and are understood and understand. They are most evident and familiar; yet again they are deeply hidden, and discovering them is something new.

## CHAPTER XXIII. What time is

29. I heard from a learned man that the movements of the sun, moon, and stars are themselves times, and I did not assent [Note: [Col. 0820] This seems to be the correct reading, supported by two Vedastine manuscripts and one Corbie manuscript: “and I did not assent”; or, with Arnaldus, “and I did not assent.” The German codex has, “and I did not decline”; Lovaniensis, with several manuscripts, “and not years”; Erasmus, “and years”; finally, Badianus and Ambrosianus, “and not minds.” According to Venetiensis: “times and years; not ‘I did not assent.’”].

Why should the movements of all bodies not rather be times? If the lights of heaven ceased and a potter’s wheel moved, would there not be a time in which we could measure its revolutions and say that they were made in equal intervals? Or, if it moved sometimes more slowly and sometimes more quickly, could we not say that some revolutions lasted longer and others less long?

When we said this, would we not also be speaking in time? Or would there be different long and short syllables in our words unless the former sounded for a longer time and the latter for a shorter time?

God, grant human beings the ability to see, in small matters, the common knowledge of small and great things. There are signs in the stars and in the lights of heaven, and they are for times, years, and days (Gen. 1:14). They are indeed so; but I would not say that the revolution of that little wooden wheel [Note: [Col. 0820] All the English manuscripts read, “the revolution of that [wheel],” or explicitly, “the double revolution of the wooden wheel.” “Of the little fiery [wheel]” is found in Erasmus, Venetiensis, and Lugdunensis. M.] is a day, nor would that mean that it is not time.

30. I want to know the power and nature of time by which we measure the movements of bodies and say that one movement lasts, for example, twice as long as another. For I ask: since “day” means not only the time during which the sun is above the earth—just as day is one thing and night another—but also its entire circuit from sunrise to sunrise, as when we say, “So many days have passed,” and those days are counted with their nights, the spans of the nights not being excluded—since, then, a day is completed by the sun’s movement and circuit from sunrise to sunrise, I ask whether the movement itself is the day, or the duration through which it is completed, or both.

If the first is the case, then there would be a day even if the sun completed that course in as much time as one hour. If the second is the case, then there would be no day if the interval from one sunrise to the next were as short as one hour; rather, the sun would have to circle twenty-four times to complete a day. If both are the case, neither would it be called a day if the sun completed its entire circuit in one hour, nor would it be called a day [Note: [Col. 0821] “That one,” according to Erasmus, Venetiensis, Lugdunensis, and M.] if, while the sun remained still, as much time passed as the sun normally takes to complete its entire circuit from morning to morning.

I am not asking now what that thing called a day is, but what the time is by which we measure the sun’s circuit and would say that it had been completed in half the usual time if it had been completed in as much time as twelve hours last. Comparing the two times, we would say that one was single and the other double, even if the sun sometimes completed its circuit from sunrise to sunrise in the single period and sometimes in the double period.

Therefore let no one tell me that the movements of the heavenly bodies are times. For when, at someone’s request, the sun stood still (Josh. 10:13) so that the victorious battle might be completed [Note: [Col. 0821] Badianus, Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis, with a smaller number of manuscripts, read, “so that Joshua the victor ...”], the sun stood still, but time moved on. The battle was fought and completed within the period of time sufficient for it.

I see, then, that time is a kind of extension. But do I see this, or do I merely seem to see it? You will show me, O Light, O Truth.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Time is that by which we measure the movement of a body

31. Do you command me to approve the statement that time is the movement of a body? You do not command me. For I hear you say that no body moves except in time. But I do not hear you say that the movement of the body itself is time.

When a body moves, I measure in time how long it moves—from when it begins to move until it stops. If I did not see when it began and it continued moving so that I did not see when it stopped, I could not measure it, except perhaps from when I began to see it until I ceased to see it.

If I watch it for a long time, I can report only that the time is long, not how long it is, because when we say “how long,” we say it by comparison: “This is as long as that,” or “This is twice as long as that,” or whatever else we say in this manner.

But if we can mark the distances of the places from which and to which the moving body—or its parts, if it moves as on a wheel—travels, we can say how much time has passed from the moment when the movement of the body or one of its parts was completed from one place to another [Col. 0822].

Since, then, the movement of a body is one thing, and the measure by which we determine how long it lasts is another, who does not see which of these should rather be called time? For although a body sometimes moves and sometimes stands still, we measure not only its movement but also its rest by time. We say, “It stood still for as long as it moved,” or, “It stood still twice or three times as long as it moved,” and whatever else our measurement either grasps or estimates, as the saying goes, more or less.

Time, therefore, is not the movement of a body.

## CHAPTER XXV. He again appeals to God

32. And I confess to you, Lord, that I still do not know what time is. Yet again I confess to you, Lord, that I know I am saying these things in time, that I have been speaking about time for a long time, and that the very “long time” is nothing other than a duration of time.

How, then, do I know this, when I do not know what time is? Or perhaps I do not know how to say what I know? Woe is me, for I do not even know what I do not know!

Behold, my God, before you I do not lie; as I speak, so is my heart. You will light my lamp, Lord my God; you will illumine my darkness (Ps. 17:25).

## CHAPTER XXVI. How we measure time

33. Does my soul not confess to you, in a truthful confession, that I measure times? Is it so, my God, that I measure, yet do not know what I measure? Do I measure the movement of a body by time, and not measure time itself? Could I measure how long a body moves and how long it takes to get from here to there unless I measured the time in which it moves?

By what, then, do I measure time itself? Do we measure a longer period by a shorter one, as we measure the length of a beam by the space of a cubit? Thus we seem to measure the space occupied by a long syllable by the space occupied by a short syllable, and call it twice as long.

In the same way we measure the lengths of songs by the lengths of verses, the lengths of verses by the lengths of metrical feet, the lengths of feet by the lengths of syllables, and the lengths of long syllables by short ones—not on pages, for in that way we measure places, not times—but as sounds pass by in utterance, and we say, “The song is long, for it is composed of so many verses; the verses are long, for they consist of so many feet; the feet are long, for they extend through so many syllables; the syllable is long, for it is twice as long as a short one.”

But even in this way no exact measure of time is grasped, since it may happen that a shorter verse, if pronounced more slowly, sounds for a longer period of time than a longer verse pronounced more quickly. The same applies to a song, a foot, and a syllable.

Therefore it seemed to me that time is nothing other than an extension—but of what, I do not know. And it would be astonishing if it were not an extension of the mind itself.

What, then, do I measure, I beg you, my God, when I say either indefinitely, “This time is longer than that,” or definitely, “This is twice as long as that”? I measure time, I know that; but I do not measure the future, because it does not yet exist; I do not measure the present, because it has no extent; and I do not measure the past, because it no longer exists.

What, then, do I measure? Is it passing times, not past times? For that is what I had said.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How we measure time as it remains in the mind

34. Persist, my soul, and attend courageously: God is our helper; he made us, and not we ourselves (Ps. 99:3). Attend to where the truth begins to grow bright.

Suppose that a bodily voice begins to sound, sounds, continues sounding, and then ceases. Now there is silence, and that voice is past; it is no longer a voice. Before it sounded, it was future and could not be measured, because it did not yet exist; now it cannot be measured, because it no longer exists. It could therefore be measured while it sounded, because then there was something that could be measured. But even then it did not stand still; it was moving and passing away.

Or was it more measurable for that very reason? As it passed, it was extended through some period of time in which it could be measured, since the present itself has no extent.

Suppose, then, that another voice begins to sound and continues sounding in an unbroken flow without any distinction. Let us measure it while it sounds; for when it ceases, it will already be past, and there will be nothing that can be measured. Let us measure it, then, and say how long it is. But it is still sounding, and it can be measured only from its beginning, when it began to sound, to its end, when it ceases.

For we measure the interval from some beginning to some end. Consequently, a voice that has not yet ended cannot be measured so as to be called long or short, nor can it be called equal to another, or single or double in relation to another, or anything of that sort. But once it has ended, it will no longer exist. How, then, can it be measured?

Yet we do measure times—neither those that do not yet exist, nor those that no longer exist, nor those that have no duration, nor those that have no boundaries. Therefore we measure neither future, past, present, nor passing times; and yet we do measure times.

35. “God, creator of all things”: this verse has eight syllables, alternating short and long syllables. Thus the four short syllables—the first, third, fifth, and seventh—are single in relation to the four long ones—the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth. Each of the latter has twice the time of its corresponding short syllable. I pronounce them and report this, and it is so, insofar as it is perceived by clear sense.

Insofar as clear perception reveals it, I measure the long syllable by the short one and perceive that it has twice the duration. But when one sounds after the other—if the first is short and the second long—how will I retain the short syllable, and how will I apply it as a measure to the long one, so as to discover that the latter has twice its duration, since the long syllable does not begin to sound until the short one has ceased?

Nor do I measure the long syllable while it is present, since I measure it only when it is complete. But its completion is its passing away. What, then, do I measure? Where is the short syllable by which I measure [Note: [Col. 0823] Lovaniensis and the older editions read, “by which I measure it”; but Arnaldus, with the manuscripts, more correctly has “by which,” since Augustine has just said that he measures the long syllable by the short one]? Where is the long syllable that I measure? Both have sounded, flown away, and passed; they no longer exist. Yet I measure, and confidently answer, insofar as trained perception can be trusted, that one is single and the other double, specifically in the extent of time.

I could not do this unless they had passed and ended. Therefore I do not measure the syllables themselves, which no longer exist, but something in my memory that remains fixed there.

36. In you, my soul, I measure times; do not obstruct me. What I mean is: do not obstruct yourself with the tumult of your emotions. In you, I say, I measure times. I measure the affection that passing things produce in you and that remains after they have passed away; I measure that affection, which is present, not the things that passed away to produce it. I measure it when I measure times.

Therefore either this affection is time, or I do not measure time. What happens when we measure silences and say that a particular silence lasted as long as a particular voice? Do we not extend our thought toward the measure of the voice as though it were sounding, so that we can report something about the intervals of silence within the span of time?

Even when voice and mouth are silent, we mentally recite songs, verses, and every kind of speech, as well as any measurements of movement; and we report how one span of time compares with another as if we were expressing these things aloud.

If someone wishes to produce a somewhat long sound and has decided beforehand how long it will be, he has already enacted a span of time in silence and, committing it to memory, begins to produce the sound, which continues until it reaches the appointed limit. Indeed, part of it has sounded and part will sound: what has already been completed has sounded; what remains will sound. Thus it proceeds while present attention transfers what was future into the past, the future diminishing and the past increasing, until, when the future has been exhausted, the whole is past.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. We measure times through the mind

37. But how is the future diminished or exhausted when it does not yet exist? Or how does the past increase when it no longer exists, unless because there are three things in the mind that performs this action? For the mind both expects, attends, and remembers, so that what it expects passes, through what it attends to, into what it remembers.

Who, then, denies that future things do not yet exist? Yet there is already in the mind an expectation of future things. Who denies that past things no longer exist? Yet there is still in the mind a memory of past things. Who denies that the present time has no extent, because it passes in an instant? Yet attention endures, and through it what will be present proceeds toward passing away [Note: [Col. 0824] Earlier editions omit “what will be present” and read, “through which it may accomplish what is absent.” The manuscripts more correctly read, “through which it proceeds toward what will be absent”—that is, through which attention proceeds to pass into the past what is future. Martianus and Rondellus read, “proceeds toward what will be present, which will be absent.” M.].

Therefore it is not a long future time—for that does not exist—but a long expectation of the future that is long. Nor is it a long past time—for that does not exist—but a long memory of the past that is long.

38. I am going to recite a song that I know. Before I begin, my expectation is extended over the whole song. But once I have begun, whatever I have plucked from that expectation into the past is extended in my memory [Note: [Col. 0824] “From that,” according to Erasmus, Venetiensis, Lugdunensis, Somm., Dub., Florentinus, and Rondellus, with seven manuscripts.]. The life of this action of mine is extended into memory, because of what I have recited, and into expectation, because of what I am going to recite; yet my attention is present, through which what was future passes over to become past.

The more this proceeds and proceeds, the more expectation is shortened and memory lengthened, until the whole expectation is exhausted, when the entire action has ended and passed into memory. What happens in the whole song also happens in each of its parts and in each of its syllables. It happens in the longer action of which that song may perhaps be a part; it happens in the whole life of a human being, whose parts are all the actions of a human being; and it happens in the whole age of the children of humanity, whose parts are all human lives.

## CHAPTER XXIX. He desires to be gathered into God from his extension among temporal things
39. But because your mercy is better than lives (Ps. 62:4), behold, my life is a distension, and your right hand has received me in my Lord, the mediator, the Son of Man, between you, the One, and us, the many, amid many things and through many things, so that through him I may grasp that in which I have also been grasped, and, forgetting what lies behind, may be gathered together from former days as I follow the One—not being distended toward those things that are future and passing away, but stretched out toward the things that lie ahead—not according to distension but according to intention, as I pursue the prize

[Note: [Col. 0825] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read *intentus*, “intent.”] of the heavenly calling (Phil. 3:13–14); there I shall hear the voice of your praise and contemplate your delight, neither coming nor passing away. But now my years are in groans. And you, Lord, my comfort, are my eternal Father; yet I have been scattered into times whose order I do not know,

[Note: [Col. 0825] The Benignus, Corbie, and other not inferior manuscripts read *dissolui*, “I have been dissolved.”]

and my thoughts—the inmost organs of my soul—are torn apart by tumultuous variations, until I flow together into you, purified and made clear by the fire of your love.

[Note: [Col. 0825] Thus the manuscripts; but the editions have *intentus*, “intent.”]

## CHAPTER XXX. He again rebukes those who ask what God was doing before the creation of the world

40. And I shall stand and be made firm in you, in my own form, which is your truth; nor shall I endure the questions of people who, afflicted by a punitive disease, thirst for more than they can grasp and say, “What was God doing before he made heaven and earth? Or what came into his mind so that he should make something, when previously he had never made anything?” Grant them, Lord, to think well about what they say, and to discover that one does not say “never” where there is no time.

[Note: [Col. 0825] *Qui*, according to Erasmus, Venice, Lyons, Martianay, and Rondon, with eight manuscripts.]

Therefore, when it is said that he “never made” anything, what else is being said but that he made it at no time? [Col. 0826] Let them see, then, that no time can exist without a creature, and let them cease speaking this vanity. Let them also stretch themselves toward the things that lie ahead, and understand that you are, before all times, the eternal Creator of all times; that no times are co-eternal with you, nor is any creature co-eternal with you, even if there is some creature above times.

## CHAPTER XXXI. How God knows, and how the creature knows

41. My Lord God, what is that recess of your deep secret, and how far have the consequences of my sins cast me from it? Heal my eyes, and let me rejoice with your light. Certainly, if there is a mind endowed with such great knowledge and foreknowledge that all past and future things are known to it just as one particular song is perfectly known to me, that mind is exceedingly wondrous and terrifyingly astonishing: for nothing that has been accomplished, nor anything that remains throughout the ages, is hidden from it, just as, when I sing that song, I am not unaware of what and how much of it has gone by from the beginning, or what and how much remains until the end.

But far be it from you, Creator of the universe, Creator of souls and bodies, that you should know all future and past things in this way. Far, far more wondrous are you, and far more secret. For just as the feeling and perception of a singer or of one listening to a known song are varied and distended by expectation of the future sounds and memory of those already past, so nothing of this sort happens to you, who are unchangeably eternal—that is, truly the eternal Creator of minds. Therefore, just as you knew heaven and earth in the beginning without any alteration in your knowledge, so you made heaven and earth in the beginning without any distension in your action.

[Note: [Col. 0826] In the common editions and in some manuscripts, “without distinction”; but in more numerous and better manuscripts, “without distension,” which corresponds more closely to what precedes: “for just as the feeling and perception of a singer ... are varied and distended.”]

Let whoever understands confess to you; and let whoever does not understand confess to you. O how exalted you are, and how humble in heart are the house of your dwelling! For you raise up those who are bowed down (Ps. 145:8), and those whose exaltation you are do not fall.

# BOOK TWELVE

He continues his interpretation of the verse, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” By the name “heaven” he understands the spiritual or intellectual creature that always contemplates the face of God; by the term “earth,” the formless matter from which the forms of bodily things were afterward fashioned. He acknowledges, however, that other methods of interpretation are by no means to be rejected, and indeed confesses that from the depth of divine Scripture a multiplicity of meanings can be drawn.

[Col. 0825]

## CHAPTER I. The difficult search for truth

[Col. 0825]

1. My heart, Lord, struck by the words of your holy Scripture amid the poverty of my life, is busily occupied with many things; and therefore human understanding is often poor in speech, because inquiry speaks more than discovery, asking is longer than receiving, and the hand that knocks works harder than the hand that takes. We hold fast to the promise; who will corrupt it? If God is for us, who can be against us? (Rom. 8:31.) “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, [Col. 0826] and to the one who knocks it will be opened (Matt. 7:7–8). These are your promises; and who should fear deception when Truth itself makes the promise?

## CHAPTER II. On the twofold heaven and earth

2. The humility of my tongue confesses to your exaltedness, because you made heaven and earth: this heaven that I see, and the earth that I tread upon. From where is this earth that I carry? You made it. But where is the heaven of heaven, Lord, of which we have heard in the voice of the Psalm: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men” (Ps. 113:16)? Where is the heaven that we behold, for which all that we behold is earth? For this whole bodily creation, although not everywhere in its entirety did it receive such a beautiful form [Col. 0827] in its final state, whose foundation is our earth, is nevertheless itself earth in relation to that heaven of heaven; and in relation to that heaven which belongs to the Lord, even our earth’s heaven is earth. And this entire twofold great body is not absurdly called earth in relation to that heaven—whatever sort of heaven it may be—which belongs to the Lord and not to the children of men.

[Note: [Col. 0827] *Cui*, “for which,” according to Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain.]

## CHAPTER III. What “darkness over the face of the abyss” means

3. Surely this earth was invisible and unformed, and there was some deep abyss over which there was no light, because it had no form; hence you commanded that it be written that “darkness was over the abyss” (Gen. 1:2). What else does this mean but the absence of light? For where would light be, if it existed, except above, by rising over and illuminating? Therefore, where light did not yet exist, what did it mean for darkness to be present except that light was absent? Darkness was therefore above, because light was absent above—just as where sound is absent there is silence. And what does it mean for silence to be there except that sound is not there?

Have you not, Lord, taught this soul that confesses to you? Have you not, Lord, taught me that before you formed and ordered this formless matter, there was nothing—not color, not shape, not body, not spirit? Yet it was not altogether nothing: it was a certain formlessness without any appearance.

## CHAPTER IV. What is meant by the invisible and unformed earth

4. What, then, could it be called, so that it might in some way be suggested even to those whose senses are slow, except by some familiar term? And what can be found throughout all the parts of the world more nearly resembling complete formlessness than earth and the abyss? For, in keeping with their lowest rank, they are less beautiful than all the other higher things, which are transparent and radiant. Why, then, should I not understand the formlessness of matter—which you had made without appearance, from which you would make the beautiful world—as being suitably brought to human notice by calling it “the invisible and unformed earth”?

## CHAPTER V. Why formless matter seems to have been so called

5. When thought seeks in it what the mind can grasp, and says to itself, “It is not an intelligible form, like life or justice, because it is the matter of bodies; nor is it sensible, since what can be seen and what can be perceived is not present in the invisible and unformed,” let human thought, while saying these things to itself, attempt either to know it by not knowing, or to fail to know it by knowing.

[Note: [Col. 0827] Thus in the manuscripts, and more coherently than the reading in the common editions, “And when in it.” Somm. has neither *et* nor *ut*, admitting simply: “when in it.”]

## CHAPTER VI. What he formerly thought about formless matter with the Manichaeans, and what he thinks now

6. But I, Lord, if I confess to you with my mouth and my pen everything

[Note: [Col. 0827] All manuscripts read “if I confess everything”; the sense of this construction is completed by the words, “who among my readers could endure to grasp it?”]

that you have taught me about this matter—when formerly, hearing its name but not understanding it, I imagined it, according to the accounts of those who did not understand it, together with innumerable and varied forms, and therefore was not imagining it—my mind rolled about foul and horrible forms in confused arrangements, but they were nevertheless forms. I called it formless, not because it lacked form, but because it possessed such a form that, if it appeared, my senses would reject it as strange and incongruous, and human weakness would be disturbed. But

[Note: [Col. 0828] Martianay, from two manuscripts, reads *verumtamen*, “nevertheless”; one manuscript reported by Rondon has the same reading.]

what I was thinking was formless not through deprivation of every form, but by comparison with more beautiful forms.

True reason persuaded me that I should remove altogether every remnant of every sort of form if I wished to think of something completely formless; but I could not. For I more readily judged that what was deprived of every form did not exist than I could think of something between the formed and nothing—neither formed nor nothing, almost nothing.

[Note: [Col. 0828] We follow the manuscripts of Benignus, Theodoricus, and others. Many, however, with Louvain and Arnold, read “something between form and nothing, neither ...” But Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus, with two manuscripts, have: “than I could think of something formless and nothing formed, neither nothing formless, almost nothing.”]

And my mind ceased questioning my spirit, which was full of images of formed bodies and changed and varied them at will. I turned my attention to the bodies themselves and examined more deeply their mutability, by which they cease to be what they were and begin to be what they were not. I suspected that this same transition from form to form occurred through some formlessness, not through absolute nothing; but I wanted to know, not merely to suspect.

And if my voice and pen were to confess to you everything that you have untangled for me concerning this question, who among my readers could endure to grasp it? Yet my heart will not therefore cease to give you honor and a song of praise for those things which it is not sufficient to express. For the mutability of mutable things is itself capable of all the forms into which mutable things change. And what is this? Is it mind? Is it body? Is it a form of mind or of body? If it could be said, “Something nothing,” and “It is, it is not,” I would call it that. Yet it already existed in some manner, so that it could receive these visible and ordered forms.

[Note: [Col. 0828] Thus in all but a few manuscripts. Louvain, along with the older editions, has: “nothing is something, and is not”; “I would call it this.”]

## CHAPTER VII. God made heaven—that is, the angels—and earth—that is, formless matter—from nothing

7. And from where did it exist in some manner, unless it were from you, from whom all things are insofar as they are? Yet it was farther from you in proportion as it was unlike you—not spatially, of course. Therefore you, Lord, who are not at one time one thing and at another another, nor at one time in one way and at another in another,

[Note: [Col. 0828] The printed editions read *alibi aliud*, “elsewhere another.”]

but are the same, the same, the same—“Holy, holy, holy, Lord God almighty” (Isa. 6:3)—in the Beginning, which is from you, in your Wisdom, which was born from your substance, made something from nothing.

For you made heaven and earth, but not from yourself. For then it would be equal to your Only-Begotten, and therefore also equal to you; and it would in no way be right that what was not from you should be equal to you. And there was nothing else besides you from which you could make these things, O God, one Trinity and triune Unity. Therefore from nothing you made heaven and earth, something great and something small, because you are almighty and good for making all good things: the great heaven and the small earth. You existed, and there was nothing else from which you made heaven and earth, two things of a sort: one near you, the other near nothing; one above which you would be, the other beneath which nothing could be.

## CHAPTER VIII. Formless matter from nothing; from it all visible things

8. But that heaven of heaven belongs to you, Lord; whereas the earth that you gave to the children of men to see and touch (Ps. 113:15) was not such as we now see and touch. For it was invisible and unformed, and there was an abyss over which there was no light; or, “There was darkness over the abyss” (Gen. 1:2), that is, darkness was rather above the abyss than in it.

[Note: [Col. 0829] Thus in the better manuscripts and in Badius. Other editions have, “But there was darkness.”]

For this abyss of already visible waters, even in its depths, has some perceptible light of its own kind for the fish and the creatures that crawl along its bottom. But that whole substance was almost nothing, because it was still altogether formless; yet it already existed in such a way that it could be formed. For you, Lord, made the world from formless matter, which you made from nothing—almost nothing—from which you would make the great things that we, the children of men, marvel at.

For this bodily heaven is exceedingly wondrous, which, on the second day after the establishment of light, you commanded to be made between water and water, saying, “Let there be a firmament”; and so it was made (Gen. 1:6–7). You called that firmament heaven; but it is the heaven of this earth and sea, which you made on the third day, giving visible form to the formless matter that you had made before every day.

For you had already made heaven before every day, but the heaven of this heaven—the heaven of heaven—because “in the beginning you made heaven and earth.” The earth itself that you had made was formless matter, because it was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss.

[Note: [Col. 0829] In the earlier common editions, “and there was darkness over the abyss.” But *erant*, “there was,” is absent from the manuscripts.]

From this invisible and unformed earth, from this formlessness, from this almost nothing, you would make all these things of which this changeable world consists and does not consist, in which changeability itself appears, through which times can be perceived and counted. For times arise through the changes of things, as their forms vary and turn; and the matter of these forms has been called the invisible earth.

## CHAPTER IX. Why it is written without mention of days that God made heaven and earth in the beginning

9. Therefore the Spirit, the teacher of your servant, when he recalls that you made heaven and earth in the beginning, is silent about times and says nothing of days. For surely the heaven of heaven that you made in the beginning is some intellectual creature. Although by no means co-eternal with you, the Trinity, it nevertheless participates in your eternity; and, through the sweetness of its most blessed contemplation of you, it restrains its great mutability. By cleaving to you from the moment it was made, without any lapse, it surpasses every revolving change of times.

But that formlessness—the invisible and unformed earth—was not itself numbered among the days.

[Note: [Col. 0829] Louvain and other editions have, “the formlessness of the invisible earth.”]

For where there is no form, there is no order; and nothing comes or passes away. And where this does not happen, there are certainly no days and no succession of temporal intervals.

## CHAPTER X. He desires to be taught by God

[Col. 0830]

10. O Truth, light of my heart, let not my darkness speak to me. I fell away into these things and was darkened; but even from here, even from here, I came to love you. I wandered, and I remembered you. I heard your voice behind me, calling me to return, and I scarcely heard it because of the tumult of the unquiet.

[Note: [Col. 0830] Louvain and Arnold have “because of the tumult of sinners.” But Badius, Amerbach, and Erasmus have the better reading, “of the unquiet,” as do almost all the manuscripts. By this name the Manichaeans seem to be designated, as enemies of the sacred Scriptures.]

And now, behold, I return, burning and panting toward your fountain. Let no one prevent me; I shall drink from it and live from it. Let me not be my own life; I lived badly from myself, and I became death to myself; in you I come alive again.

[Note: [Col. 0830] Thus in the earlier editions: “I shall drink from it, and then live; for I am not my own life. If I lived badly, I was death to myself from myself, and in you I come alive again.”]

Speak to me yourself; speak with me yourself. I have believed your Books, and their words are exceedingly mysterious.

## CHAPTER XI. What he learned from God

11. You have already said to me, Lord, in a strong voice in my inner ear, that you are eternal, alone possessing immortality (1 Tim. 6:16), because you are changed by no form or movement, and your will is not varied by times; for a will that is one thing and then another is not immortal. This is clear to me in your sight; and may it become increasingly clear, I pray, and may I remain sober beneath your wings in that revelation.

Again you said to me, Lord, in a strong voice in my inner ear, that you made all natures and substances that are not what you are, yet nevertheless exist; and that the only thing not from you is what is not, and the movement of the will from you, who are, toward what is less. For such movement is fault and sin; and no one’s sin either harms you or disturbs the order of your rule, whether at the highest or at the lowest level. This is clear to me in your sight; and may it become increasingly clear, I pray, and may I remain sober beneath your wings in that revelation.

12. Again you said to me in a strong voice in my inner ear that even that creature is not co-eternal with you whose will is you alone,

[Note: [Col. 0830] Six manuscripts, including the German and Fossatensis, read *voluptas*, “delight.”]

and which, drawing you in through the most persistent chastity, never and nowhere displays its mutability. Since you are always present to it, and it clings to you with its whole affection, it has nothing future to await, nor does it transfer anything into the past to remember; it is changed in no succession and is not distended into any times.

O blessed creature, if there is one such, by clinging to your blessedness! Blessed by having you as its everlasting inhabitant and illuminator! And I do not find what I would more gladly call “the heaven of heaven belonging to the Lord” than your house, contemplating your delight without any failure that would make it depart into something else: a pure mind, most harmoniously one in the stability of the peace of the holy spirits, the citizens of your heavenly city above these heavens.

13. From this, let the soul whose pilgrimage has been made far away understand

[Note: [Col. 0830] Louvain and Arnold read: “Whence may the soul understand how much by pilgrimage.” The reading adopted here is supported by more manuscripts and is especially apt: “whence may the soul understand” refers to how far God is eternal above all times.]

—if it already thirsts for you, if its tears have already become its bread while it is told each day, “Where is your God?” (Ps. 42:3–4, 11); if it already asks one thing of you and seeks this alone, that it may dwell in your house all the days of its life (Ps. 27:4). For what is its life except you, and what are your days except your eternity, like your years that do not fail because you are the same? From this, then, let the soul that is capable of it understand how far you are eternal above all times, when your house, though it has not been on pilgrimage and is not co-eternal with you, nevertheless, by clinging to you without interruption or failure, undergoes no succession of times.

This is clear to me in your sight; and may it become increasingly clear, I pray, and may I remain sober beneath your wings in this revelation.

14. Behold, I do not know what formlessness exists in these changes of the most extreme and weakest things. And who will tell me—unless it is someone who wanders and rolls about through the emptiness of his heart with his phantasms—who but such a person will tell me that, when every form has been diminished and consumed, if formlessness alone remains, through which a thing was changed and turned from form to form, it could exhibit the succession of times?

For it absolutely cannot, because without variation of movements there are no times; and there is no variation where there is no form.

## CHAPTER XII. The twofold creature that lacks time

15. Having considered these things insofar as you grant them, my God—how much you stir me to knock, and how much you open to the one who knocks—I discover two things that you made which lack times, although neither is co-eternal with you.

One is so formed that, without any failure in contemplation and without any interval of change, although mutable it is not changed, and it enjoys your eternity and immutability. The other was so formless that it had no form from which or into which it could be changed, whether by movement or by rest, and therefore had no time to which it could be subjected.

But you did not leave it formless, because you made it before every day: in the beginning, heaven and earth, these two things of which I was speaking. The earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss. These words indicate formlessness, so that those who cannot conceive of a complete privation of form, yet not a passage into nothing, may gradually be led to understand from what the other heaven and the visible and ordered earth, the beautiful water, and everything else that is subsequently recalled as having been made in the establishment of this world—not without days—would arise. Such things are of a kind in which the successions of times take place, because movements and forms undergo ordered changes.

## CHAPTER XIII. Why Scripture says, without mentioning days, that God made heaven and earth in the beginning

16. For the moment, my God, this is what I understand when I hear your Scripture say, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth; but the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss” (Gen. 1:1–2), without mentioning on which day you made these things.

For the moment, this is what I understand: it is because of that heaven of heaven, the intellectual heaven, where understanding means knowing simultaneously—not in part, not in an enigma, not through a mirror, but wholly, in manifestation,

[Note: [Col. 0832] “With unveiled face,” according to the Louvain manuscript.]

face to face (1 Cor. 13:12). It does not know now this and now that, but, as it has been said, it knows simultaneously, without any succession of times.

And it is also because of the invisible and unformed earth, which exists without any succession of times, whereas succession ordinarily involves having now this and now that; for where there is no form, there is nowhere this and that.

Because of these two things—the one first formed and the other utterly formless: the former heaven, but the heaven of heaven; the latter earth, but the invisible and unformed earth—I understand, for the moment, why your Scripture says, without mentioning days, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” For it immediately added which earth it meant. And the fact that the firmament is recalled as having been made on the second day and called heaven indicates which heaven was being discussed earlier without days.

## CHAPTER XIV. The depth of Scripture

17. Wondrous is the depth of your utterances! Behold, their surface, caressing the little ones, lies before us; but wondrous is the depth, my God, wondrous the depth! It is terrifying to enter into it: the terror of honor and the trembling of love. I vehemently hate its enemies. O that you would slay them with a double-edged sword, and that they might cease to be its enemies!

[Note: [Col. 0832] Somm. and Rond. have “slay them with the sword.”]

For I love them to be slain to themselves, so that they may live to you. But behold, there are others who are not critics but praisers of the book of Genesis. “The Spirit of God,” they say, “who wrote these things through his servant Moses, did not intend this to be understood in these words.
