He did not intend what you say, but something else that we say.” To these, with you as judge, O God, I reply as follows.

## CHAPTER XV. What Augustine thinks about God, the angels, and formless matter, which his opponents cannot deny

18. Will you say that the things which Truth tells me in a strong voice in my inner ear about the true eternity of the Creator are false—that his substance is in no way varied through times, and that his will is not outside his substance? Therefore he does not at one time will this and at another that, but wills all that he wills once, simultaneously, and always; not again and again, nor now this and now that, nor later willing what he did not will, or no longer willing what he previously willed. For such a will is mutable, and everything mutable is not eternal; but our God is eternal.

Again, Truth tells me in my inner ear that the expectation of future things becomes perception when they arrive, and that this same perception becomes memory when they have passed. Every intention that is thus varied is mutable; and everything mutable is not eternal; but our God is eternal. I gather and join these things together, and I find that my God, the eternal God, did not create the creature by some new will, nor does his knowledge undergo anything transitory.

[Note: [Col. 0832] According to the English manuscripts, this should be read *dicitur*, “is said.”]

19. What, then, will you say, you who contradict? Are these things false? “No,” they say. What about this? Is it false that every formed nature and every matter capable of being formed exists only from him who is supremely good, because he supremely is? “We do not deny this,” they say. What, then? Do you deny that there is a certain sublime creature so joined to the true and truly eternal God by chaste love that, although it is not co-eternal with him, it nevertheless neither dissolves nor flows away from him into any variation or succession of times, but rests in the contemplation of him alone, most truly?

For you, God, reveal yourself to the one who loves you as much as you command, and you are sufficient for that one; therefore it does not turn away from you or toward itself. This is the house of God—not earthly, nor composed of any heavenly bodily mass, but spiritual and sharing in your eternity, because it stands forever without stain.

[Note: [Col. 0833] Arnold, with four manuscripts, has “stands forever without stain.”]

For you established it forever and unto the age of ages; you gave a command, and it shall not pass away (Ps. 148:6). Yet it is not co-eternal with you, God, because it did not exist without a beginning; for it was made.

20. For even if we do not find time before it—since Wisdom was created before all things (Ecclus. 1:4)—this is not, of course, that Wisdom which is plainly co-eternal and equal with you, its Father, our God, through whom all things were created and in whom you made heaven and earth in the Beginning. Rather, it is the wisdom that was created, namely, an intellectual nature that is light through contemplation of the Light. It too is called wisdom, although created.

But as great as the difference between the light that illuminates and the light that is illuminated, so great is the difference between the Wisdom that creates and this wisdom that was created; just as between the justice that justifies and the justice produced by justification. For we too are called your justice. One of your servants says that we are “the justice of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:21).

Therefore, because a certain created wisdom was created before all things—a rational and intellectual mind of your chaste city, our mother who is above and is free (Gal. 4:26), eternal in the heavens—what heavens, except those that praise you, the heavens of heavens (Ps. 148:4), since this too is “the heaven of heaven belonging to the Lord”?—even if we do not find time before it, because it precedes the creature of time, having been created before all things, yet before it is the eternity of the Creator himself, from whom it received the beginning of its existence. This beginning was not in time, since time did not yet exist, but it was nevertheless the beginning of its creation.

21. Therefore it is from you, our God, in such a way that it is plainly something other than you and not the same as you. For although we find no time not only before it but even within it, because it is capable of always seeing your face and is never turned away from it, so that it is not varied by any change, nevertheless mutability itself is present in it, by which it could become dark and grow cold, unless, cleaving to you with great love, it shone and burned like perpetual midday from you.

O luminous and beautiful house, I have loved your beauty and the place where the glory of my Lord, your Maker and Possessor, dwells (Ps. 26:8)! To you my pilgrimage sighs; and I say to the one who made you, “May he possess me also in you,” because he made me as well. I wandered like a lost sheep (Ps. 119:176); but on the shoulders of my shepherd, your builder, I hope to be carried back to you (Luke 15:5).

[Col. 0834]

22. What do you say to me, you whom I was addressing, you who contradict, yet also believe that the pious Moses, the servant of God, and his books are oracles of the Holy Spirit? Is this the house of God—not indeed co-eternal with God, but nevertheless eternal in the heavens according to its own measure—where you vainly seek the successions of times, because you will not find them? For it surpasses every distension and every revolving span of age; and it is always good for it to cling to God (Ps. 73:28).

“It is,” they say. What, then, among the things that my heart cried out to my God when it heard inwardly the voice of his praise, do you finally contend is false? Is it because there was formless matter, where, because there was no form, there was no order? But where there was no order, there could be no succession of times. Nevertheless, this almost nothing—insofar as it was not altogether nothing—was certainly from him from whom is everything that exists, everything that is in any way something.

“We do not deny this either,” they say.

## CHAPTER XVI. He does not wish to engage with those who contradict divine truth

23. With these people I wish to converse before you, my God, who grant that all these things are true—those things that your truth, which does not remain silent within my mind, tells me. As for those who deny these things, let them bark and make as much noise against themselves as they wish. I shall try to persuade them to be quiet and to make way for your word to reach them. But if they are unwilling and repel me, I beg you, my God, do not be silent toward me (Ps. 28:1).

Speak truthfully in my heart, for you alone speak in this way; and I shall leave them outside, blowing dust and stirring up earth into their own eyes. I shall enter my chamber and sing songs of love to you, groaning with inexpressible groans during my pilgrimage and remembering Jerusalem, with my heart stretched upward toward her: Jerusalem, my homeland; Jerusalem, my mother; and you, her ruler, illuminator, father, protector, and husband; her chaste and strong delights, her solid joy, and all her ineffable goods, all together, because you are the one supreme and true good.

I shall not turn away until you gather into the peace of that most beloved mother, where the first fruits of my spirit are found and from which these certainties come to me, all that I am from this dispersion and deformity; until you conform and establish me forever, my God, my mercy.

But with those who do not say that all those things that are true are false—who honor that holy Scripture of yours, issued through holy Moses, and place it with us at the summit of the authority to be followed, yet nevertheless contradict us on certain matters—I speak in this way: Be yourself, our God, the judge between my confessions and their contradictions.

## CHAPTER XVII. How different things may be understood by the names “heaven” and “earth”

24. For they say: “Although these things are true, Moses was not contemplating those two things when, under the revelation of the Spirit, he said, ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth’ (Gen. 1:1). By the name ‘heaven’ he did not signify that spiritual or intellectual creature which always contemplates the face of God; nor by the name ‘earth’ did he signify formless matter.”

“What, then?”

“What we say,” they reply, “is what that man understood; that is what he expressed in these words.”

“What is that?”

“By the names ‘heaven’ and ‘earth,’ he wished first to signify this entire visible world universally and briefly, so that afterward he could set out, in the enumeration of the days, as if point by point, all the things that pleased the Holy Spirit to express in this manner. For those to whom he spoke were a crude and carnal people, such that he judged that the works of God should be commended to them only as visible things. They agree, however, that the invisible and unformed earth and the dark abyss, from which it is subsequently shown that all these visible things known to everyone were made and arranged through those days, should appropriately be understood as this formless matter.”

25. What if someone else should say that the same formlessness and confusion of matter were first indicated by the name “heaven and earth,” because this visible world, together with all the natures that most clearly appear within it and which is often called by the name “heaven and earth,” was created and perfected from it?

What if another should say that it was not improperly called “heaven and earth,” referring to an invisible and visible nature; and that, accordingly, the whole creature that God made in Wisdom—that is, in the Beginning—was comprehended under these two terms? Yet, because all things were made not from God’s own substance but from nothing, because they are not the same as God, and because some mutability is present in all things—whether they remain, like the eternal house of God, or change, like the human soul and body—what if he should say that the common matter of all invisible and visible things, still formless but certainly capable of being formed, from which heaven and earth would be made—that is, the invisible and visible creature, both already formed—was expressed by these names: “the invisible and unformed earth” and “darkness over the abyss”?

The distinction would be this: “the invisible and unformed earth” is understood as bodily matter before the quality of form; whereas “darkness over the abyss” is spiritual matter before the restraint, as it were, of its flowing immoderation and before the illumination of Wisdom.

26. There is still another possibility, if someone wishes to propose it: when we read, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” the names “heaven” and “earth” may not signify already perfected and formed invisible and visible natures. Rather, they may name the still formless beginning of things, matter capable of being formed and created, because in it there already existed, confused together and not yet distinguished by qualities and forms, the things that are now ordered and called “heaven” and “earth”: the former, spiritual creation; the latter, bodily creation.

## CHAPTER XVIII. What harmless error may occur concerning the Scriptures
27. Having heard and considered all these things, I do not wish to contend over words; for this is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear (2 Tim. 2:14). But the law is good for edification, if one uses it lawfully, because its end is “love from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Tim. 1:8, 5). And our Teacher knows upon which two commandments he suspended the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:40). When I ardently confess these things to you, my God, the light of my eyes in secret, what harm does it do me if different meanings can be understood in these words, meanings that are nevertheless true? What harm, I ask, does it do me if I think something other than what another man thought that he meant who wrote them? Certainly, all of us who read strive to investigate and grasp what the man we read intended. And because we believe him truthful, we dare not suppose that he said anything which we either know or think to be false. Therefore, while each person tries to understand in the Holy Scriptures what the writer understood in them, what harm is there if he understands what you, the light of all truthful minds, show to be true, even if the writer whom he reads did not understand this—since he too understood something true, though not this particular thing?

## CHAPTER XIX. Things that are plainly true

28. For it is true, Lord, that you made heaven and earth; and it is true that your Wisdom is the Beginning in which you made all things (Ps. 103:24). It is likewise true that this visible world has as its great parts heaven and earth, a brief comprehending of all the natures that have been created and established. And it is true that everything mutable reveals to our understanding a certain formlessness by which it receives form, or by which it is changed and turned. It is true that no times affect what is so joined to unchangeable form that, although it is mutable, it does not change. It is true that formlessness, which is almost nothing, cannot undergo the alternations of time.

[Note: [Col. 0836] Lov. reads *proprie* (“properly”) for *prope* (“almost”).] It is true that what something is made from may, in a certain manner of speech, already bear the name of the thing made from it; hence any formlessness from which heaven and earth were made could be called “heaven and earth.” It is true that of all formed things nothing is closer to the formless than earth and the abyss. It is true that you made not only what has been created and formed, but also whatever can be created and formed, from which all things exist. It is true that everything formed from the formless is first formless and afterward formed.

## CHAPTER XX. “In the beginning he created,” etc., understood in various ways

29. From all these truths—which those do not doubt whom you have granted the gift of seeing such things with their inward eye, and who firmly believe that Moses, your servant, spoke in the Spirit of truth—each person takes a different conclusion.

One says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the intelligible and sensible, or spiritual and bodily, creation.

Another says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the whole mass of this bodily world, together with all the manifest and known natures that it contains.

Another says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the formless matter of spiritual and bodily creation.

Another says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, in his Word, coeternal with himself, God made the formless matter of bodily creation, in which heaven and earth were still confused—those things which we now perceive as distinct and formed within the mass of this world.

Another says: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, at the very outset of making and working, God made formless matter, containing heaven and earth in a confused state, from which they now stand forth and appear in formed condition, together with all that is in them.

## CHAPTER XXI. “The earth was invisible,” etc., understood in various ways

30. Likewise, with regard to the meaning of the words that follow, each person takes a different conclusion from all these truths.

One says: “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss,” that is, the bodily thing which God made was still the formless matter of bodily things, without order and without light.

[Note: [Col. 0837] Thus read several and better manuscripts, together with Arn.; but Bad., Am., Er., Somm., and Blas., with five manuscripts, have *id est, incorporale* (“that is, incorporeal”); Lov., *id est, corporabile* (“that is, capable of becoming bodily”).]

Another says: “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss,” that is, the whole that was called heaven and earth was still formless and dark matter, from which bodily heaven and bodily earth would be made, together with all that is known to the bodily senses in them.

Another says: “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss,” that is, the whole that was called heaven and earth was still formless and dark matter, from which the intelligible heaven would be made, which elsewhere is called “the heaven of heaven” (Ps. 113:16), and the earth—that is, the whole bodily nature, under which name this bodily heaven too is understood; in other words, from which every invisible and visible creature would be made.

Another says: “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss.” Scripture did not call that formlessness by the name of heaven and earth; rather, it says that the formlessness itself already existed, and called it the invisible and unformed earth and the dark abyss. From it, Scripture had said, God made heaven and earth—that is, the spiritual and bodily creation.

Another says: “But the earth was invisible and unformed, and darkness was over the abyss,” that is, there was already a certain formless matter from which Scripture had declared that God made heaven and earth: namely, the whole bodily mass of the world, divided into two greatest parts, upper and lower, together with all the customary and familiar creatures that are in them.

## CHAPTER XXII. There is no contradiction in supposing that something was created by God of which Genesis is silent

31. Suppose someone attempts to resist these two last opinions in this way: “If you do not want this formlessness to be understood as having been called by the name of heaven and earth, then there was something which God had not made, from which he made heaven and earth. For Scripture did not relate that God made this matter, unless we understand that it was signified by the name of heaven and earth, or of earth alone, when it said, ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth.’ Thus, even if it pleased someone to call the formless matter that follows—‘But the earth was invisible and unformed’—by this name, we must nevertheless understand it to be only that matter which God made in the statement, ‘God made heaven and earth.’”

[Note: [Col. 0837] Somm.: “Someone should attempt this in this way: if he does not want this to be understood.” Mart.: “If he does not want this to be understood.” M.]

When the advocates of the two opinions that we have placed last hear this, they will answer and say: “We do not deny that this formless matter was made by God, by whom all very good things exist. For just as we say that what has been created and formed is more good, so we acknowledge that what has been made capable of being created and formed is less good, but nevertheless good. Scripture did not mention that God made this formlessness, just as it did not mention many other things, such as the Cherubim and Seraphim (Isa. 6:2; 37:16), and those which the Apostle expressly distinguishes as Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Powers (Col. 1:16), although it is clear that God made all these things.

“Or, if everything is included in what was said—‘He made heaven and earth’—what are we to say about the waters over which the Spirit of God was borne? For if, when earth is named, they too are understood at the same time, how is formless matter understood under the name of earth, when we see such beautiful waters? Or, if it is understood in this way, why is it written that the firmament was made from the same formlessness and called heaven, while it is not written that the waters were made? For those waters are not still formless and unseen, since we see them flowing in so fair a form.

“Or, if they received this form when God said, ‘Let the water under the firmament be gathered together’ (Gen. 1:9), so that the gathering itself was their formation, what will be said about the waters above the firmament? They would not have been worthy to receive so honorable a place if they were formless, nor is it written by what word they were formed.

“Therefore, if Genesis was silent about God’s making something which neither sound faith nor certain understanding doubts that God made, and if for that reason no sober teaching will dare to call these waters coeternal with God merely because we have heard them mentioned in the book of Genesis, but do not find where they were made, why should we not understand, taught by the truth, that that formless matter also—which Scripture calls the invisible and unformed earth and the dark abyss—was made by God from nothing, and therefore is not coeternal with him, although this narrative omitted to state where it was made?”

[Note: [Col. 0838] Nearly all books read *nisi ut intelligamus* (“unless we understand”), through a scribal error; the copyists may perhaps have changed *ut* into *aut*. We have removed this particle in accordance with Arn. and the Benignian manuscripts.]

[Note: [Col. 0838] *Audimus* (“we hear”), according to Rond. and seven manuscripts. M.]

## CHAPTER XXIII. Two kinds of disagreement in interpreting Scripture

32. Having heard and examined these things, insofar as my weakness permits—which I confess to you, my God who know all things—I see that two kinds of disagreement can arise when something is announced by truthful messengers through signs: one, when there is disagreement about the truth of things; the other, when there is disagreement about the intention of the person who announces them.

For we inquire in one way what is true about the creation of the universe, and in another way what Moses, that outstanding household-servant of your faith, wanted the reader and hearer to understand in these words.

In the first kind of disagreement, let all those depart from me who think they know things that are false. In the second kind also, let all those depart from me who think that Moses said things that are false. But let me be joined to those, Lord, in you, and rejoice with them in you, who are nourished by your truth in the breadth of love. Let us approach together the words of your Book and seek your will through the will of your servant, by whose pen you dispensed them.

## CHAPTER XXIV. From many truths one ought not confidently assert that Moses understood this or that

33. But which of us has discovered his intention among so many truths—which arise for those who seek them when these words are understood in different ways—so that he can say as confidently that Moses understood this and wanted this to be understood in that narrative, as he can say confidently that this is true, whether Moses understood this or something else?

[Note: [Col. 0839] Lov., Somm., and Rond., with nine manuscripts: *inveniet* (“will find”). M.]

[Note: [Col. 0839] Lov., Somm., and M.: *verba* (“words”).]

For behold, my God, I am your servant, and in these writings I have vowed to you the sacrifice of confession; I ask that by your mercy I may fulfill my vows to you. Behold, I say with confidence in your unchangeable Word that you made all things, invisible and visible. But do I say with equal confidence that Moses, when he wrote, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” had no other meaning in view than this? I do not see in his mind that he thought this when he wrote these words as clearly as I see it to be certain in your truth.

For he could have thought of the very beginning of making when he said, “In the beginning.” And by “heaven and earth” in this passage he could have wanted no already formed and perfected nature, whether spiritual or bodily, to be understood, but both in their beginning and still formless. I see that whatever of these meanings was said could truly have been said; but which of them he had in mind in these words, I do not see in the same way. Nevertheless, whether he saw in his mind one of these things, or something else that I have not mentioned, when he uttered these words, I do not doubt that so great a man saw the truth and expressed it fittingly.

## CHAPTER XXV. Against those who rashly reject the interpretations of others

34. Let no one now trouble me by saying, “Moses did not understand what you say, but what I say.” If he said to me, “How do you know that Moses understood what you express concerning his words?” I ought to bear it patiently and perhaps answer what I answered above, or somewhat more fully if he were obstinate. But when he says, “He did not understand what you say, but what I say,” while nevertheless not denying that what both of us say is true, then, O God, the life of the poor, in whose bosom there is no contradiction, pour gentleness into my heart, so that I may patiently endure such people. They do not say this because they are divine and have seen in the heart of your servant what they say, but because they are proud. They do not know Moses’ meaning, but love their own—not because it is true, but because it is theirs.

Otherwise, they would love another true interpretation equally, just as I love what they say when they say what is true—not because it is theirs, but because it is true. And for that reason it is no longer theirs, because it is true. If they love it because it is true, then it is both theirs and mine, since it belongs in common to all who love the truth.

But what they insist upon—that Moses did not understand what I say, but what they say—I do not want and do not love. Even if it is so, such rashness is not knowledge but boldness; it was not vision but conceit that produced it. Therefore, Lord, your judgments are fearful: for your truth is neither mine nor his nor that other man’s, but belongs to all of us whom you publicly call to share in it, solemnly warning us not to want it to be private, lest we be deprived of it.

For whoever claims for himself what you set before all to enjoy, and wants what belongs to all to be his own, is driven from the common possession to his private possession—that is, from truth to falsehood. For “whoever speaks a lie speaks from his own” (John 8:44).

35. Attend, best Judge, God who are truth itself; attend to what I say to this contradictor—attend. For I speak before you and before my brothers who use the law lawfully, unto the end of love (1 Tim. 1:8). Attend and see what I say to him, if it pleases you.

I give him this fraternal and peaceful answer: If we both see that what you say is true, and we both see that what I say is true, where, I ask, do we see it? Certainly not I in you, nor you in me, but both of us in the unchangeable Truth itself, which is above our minds.

Since, then, we do not contend about the light of the Lord our God himself, why do we contend about the thought of our neighbor, which we cannot see as we see the unchangeable Truth? Even if Moses himself had appeared to us and said, “This is what I thought,” we would still not see it; we would believe it.

Therefore, “let no one be puffed up for one against another beyond what is written” (1 Cor. 4:6). Let us love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves (Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37). Unless we believe that Moses understood these two commandments of love—whatever he understood in those Books—we shall make the Lord a liar when we form an opinion about the mind of our fellow servant different from what he taught.

Now see how foolish it is, amid such an abundance of entirely true interpretations that can be drawn from those words, rashly to assert which of them Moses chiefly understood, and through harmful disputes to offend the very love for whose sake he said everything and whose words we are trying to explain.

## CHAPTER XXVI. What kind of discourse is suitable for Scripture

36. And yet, my God, height of my humility and rest from my labor, who hear my confessions and forgive my sins—for you command me to love my neighbor as myself—I cannot believe less of Moses, your most faithful servant, than I would wish and desire you to grant me as a gift, if I had been born in that age and had placed me in the position that, through the service of my heart and tongue, those writings were to be dispensed which would later benefit all nations and throughout the whole world surpass, by the summit of their authority, the words of all false and proud teachings.

For if I were Moses at that time (for we all come from the same mass, and what is a human being except that you remember him? [Ps. 8:5]), if, then, I were what he was, and the writing of the book of Genesis were entrusted to me by you, I would wish to be given such a capacity for expression and such a method of composing the discourse that:

- those who are not yet able to understand how God creates would not reject the words as exceeding their powers;
- those who are already able to understand would find, in the few words of your servant, no true interpretation that they might reach by reflection omitted;
- and if another person saw another meaning in the light of truth, that meaning too would not be absent from the understanding of those same words.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Scripture is suited by a humble and simple kind of language

37. For just as a spring in a small place is more abundant and supplies its flow through many channels into wider spaces than any one of those channels that is led from the same spring through many places, so the narrative of your steward, destined to benefit many who would speak about it, pours forth streams of liquid truth in a small measure of language. From it each person draws, through longer winding courses of speech, whatever truth he can about these matters—this person one thing, that person another.

For some, when they read or hear these words, imagine God as a human being, or as some immense mass endowed with immense power, who by a new and sudden decision made heaven and earth outside himself, as though in distant places: two great bodies, above and below, containing everything. And when they hear, “God said, ‘Let that be,’ and that came to be,” they imagine words beginning and ending, sounding through time and passing away, after whose passage what had been commanded to exist immediately came into existence.

[Note: [Col. 0841] B. has *existere* (“to exist”); Somm., Lov., Arn., Dub., Mart., with four manuscripts, and Rondet., with six manuscripts, have *existeret* (“would exist”). M.]

They may perhaps hold some other opinion of this kind through familiarity with bodily things. Among such little creatures, while their weakness is carried as though in a mother’s lap by this most humble kind of language, faith is healthfully built up: they become certain and hold firmly that God made all the natures which their senses behold surrounding them in wondrous variety.

But if one of them, scorning the supposed lowliness of the words, stretches himself beyond the nourishing cradles in proud weakness—alas, the wretched one will fall. And, Lord God, have mercy, lest those who pass along the road trample the unfledged chick; send your angel to replace him in the nest, so that he may live until he can fly.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. How Scripture is understood in various ways by the learned

38. Others, for whom these words are no longer a nest but shadowy thickets, see hidden fruits in them. They fly about joyfully, chirp as they investigate, and pluck the fruits.

For when they read or hear these words, they see that all past and future times are surpassed by your eternal and stable permanence, O God; yet they also see that there is nothing in temporal creation which you did not make. Your will, because it is what you are, did not change, nor did some previously nonexistent will arise by which you made all things.

You did not fashion from yourself a likeness of yourself, the form of all things; rather, from nothing you made a formless unlikeness, which would be formed according to your likeness, returning to you, the One, in an ordered manner, insofar as was granted to each thing according to its kind. Thus all things would become very good, whether they remained near you or, through times and places, made or underwent beautiful variations at progressively greater distances.

[Note: [Col. 0842] Thus Lov.; but other printed and manuscript books have *narrationes* (“narratives”), except the Benignian manuscript, which substitutes *rationes* (“reasons”).]

They see these things and rejoice in the light of your truth, however little they are able to do so here.

39. One of them fixes his attention on what is said, “In the beginning God made,” and looks to Wisdom as the Beginning, since Wisdom herself speaks to us. Another likewise fixes his attention on the same words and understands “beginning” as the beginning of created things; he takes “In the beginning he made” as though it said, “First he made.”

Among those who understand “In the beginning”—that in Wisdom you made heaven and earth—one believes that heaven and earth itself means the matter capable of becoming heaven and earth, and so called; another understands already formed and distinguished natures; another understands one formed nature, spiritual, under the name of heaven, and another formless nature, bodily matter, under the name of earth.

Those who understand the names “heaven” and “earth” as referring to still formless matter from which heaven and earth would be formed do not understand this in one way either. One understands matter from which the intelligible and sensible creation would be completed; another understands only the sensible bodily mass, holding within its vast embrace the evident and readily accessible natures.

Nor do those who believe that already ordered and arranged creatures are called “heaven and earth” in this passage understand it in one way. One understands the invisible and visible creation; another only the visible creation, in which we behold the luminous heaven and the dark earth, together with what is in them.

## CHAPTER XXIX. In how many ways something is said to be prior

40. But the person who understands “In the beginning he made” only as though it said, “First he made,” cannot understand “heaven and earth” truthfully unless he understands the matter of heaven and earth—namely, of the whole intelligible and bodily creation.

For if he wants the whole to be understood as already formed, it can rightly be asked of him, “If God made this first, what did he make afterward?” He will find nothing after the whole, and consequently will hear unwillingly: “How was it first, if there was nothing afterward?”

But when he says that it was first formless and afterward formed, he is not speaking absurdly—provided he is able to distinguish what precedes in eternity, what precedes in time, what precedes by choice, and what precedes by origin.

By eternity, as God precedes all things; by time, as the flower precedes the fruit; by choice, as the fruit precedes the flower; by origin, as sound precedes song.

Of these four, the first and the last are understood with the greatest difficulty; the two intermediate ones most easily. For it is rare and exceedingly difficult to behold, Lord, your eternity unchangeably making changeable things, and thus being prior.

[Col. 0843]

Who can then perceive with such an acute mind as to distinguish without great labor how sound is prior to song, simply because song is formed sound, and something can exist unformed, whereas what does not exist cannot be formed?

[Note: [Col. 0843] Somm. and Rond., with four manuscripts, and Mart., with five manuscripts: *sic acuto cernat animo* (“perceive with so acute a mind”). M.]

So matter is prior to what is made from it—not because it itself produces the thing, since it is rather produced, and not because it is prior by an interval of time. For we do not first utter unformed sounds without song and then, at a later time, fit or shape them into the form of a song, as we do timber from which a chest is made, or silver from which a vessel is fashioned.

Such materials do precede in time the forms of the things made from them; but in a song it is not so. When a song is sung, its sound is heard. It does not first sound formlessly and then become formed into a song. Whatever sounds first in any way passes away; you will find nothing in it that can be taken up again and composed by art. Therefore, the song is transformed in its sound, and its sound is its matter.

The very thing that is formed becomes a song; and thus, as I was saying, the matter of sounding is prior to the form of singing—not by the power of making.

[Note: [Col. 0843] The editions read *perficiendi potentia prior* (“prior by the power of bringing about”); the manuscripts oppose this reading, which is therefore rejected.] For sound is not the craftsman of song; rather, it is subject to the singing soul through the body, from which the soul makes the song.

Nor is sound prior in time, for it is produced together with the song. Nor is it prior by choice, for sound is not better than song, since song is not merely sound but beautiful sound. It is prior by origin, because song is not formed so that it may be sound; rather, sound is formed so that it may be song.

Let whoever can understand by this example that the matter of things was made first and called “heaven and earth,” because heaven and earth were made from it. It was not made first in time, because the forms of things unfold time, whereas that matter was formless; and it is already perceived together with time. Nevertheless, nothing can be related about it except as though it were prior in time, since it is understood to be more remote at the extreme point: formed things are plainly better than formless things, and the matter is preceded by the eternity of the Creator, so that there might be from nothing something from which something else would be made.

[Note: [Col. 0843] It seems that *variari* (“to be varied”) should be read. Augustine means that, just as sound precedes song by origin, since song is formed from it, so matter ought to precede, as it were, in time—that is, by origin—so that something might be varied from it.]

[Note: [Col. 0843] Thus the manuscripts and Arn.; Bad. has *praecedantur* (“are preceded”); other printed editions have *praecedunt* (“precede”).]

## CHAPTER XXX. Those who interpret Scripture differently should agree with one another in love and devotion to truth

41. In this diversity of true interpretations, may Truth itself bring forth harmony; and may our God have mercy on us, so that we may use the Law lawfully, with pure love as the end of the commandment.

Therefore, if someone asks me what that Moses, your servant, understood, these are not the words of my confessions. If I do not confess this to you, I do not know it. Yet I know that these interpretations are true, except for the carnal interpretations, about which I have spoken as far as I thought appropriate. Nevertheless, these words of your Book do not frighten the little ones of good hope: they speak lofty things humbly and abundant things briefly.

[Col. 0844]

But let us love one another—all those whom I acknowledge to perceive and express truths in these words—and let us together love you, our God, the source of truth, if it is not vanity but truth itself that we thirst for. Let us likewise honor your servant, the steward of this Scripture, filled with your Spirit, in such a way that we believe that, when he wrote these things, he attended to what you revealed to him: that which excels most greatly in them both by the light of truth and by the fruit of usefulness.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Moses should be thought to have understood whatever truth can be found in his words

42. Thus, when one person says, “He understood what I say,” and another, “No, he understood what I say,” I consider it more religious to ask, “Why not rather both, if both are true?” And if someone sees in these words a third, a fourth, or any other true meaning at all, why should we not believe that Moses saw all of them, through whom the one God adapted the sacred writings for the many minds that would see different truths in them?

For my part, I boldly declare from my heart that, if I were writing something intended to possess the summit of authority, I would prefer to write in such a way that my words would echo whatever truth anyone could grasp concerning these matters, rather than set down one true interpretation more plainly in such a way as to exclude the others, whose falsity could not offend me.

Therefore, my God, I do not wish to be so rash as not to believe that this man received such a gift from you. He certainly understood and thought, when he wrote these words, whatever truth we have been able to find here—and whatever we have not been able to find, or cannot yet find, but nevertheless can be found in them.

## CHAPTER XXXII. The true meanings of Scripture are revealed by the Holy Spirit

43. Finally, Lord, who are God and not flesh and blood: if a human being sees something less clearly, could anything have been hidden from your good Spirit, who will lead me into a right land (Ps. 142:10), whatever you yourself were going to reveal in those words to later readers—even if the man through whom they were spoken perhaps had one of many true meanings in mind?

If this is so, then let that meaning which he had in mind be higher than the others.

[Note: [Col. 0844] *Excellentior* (“higher” or “more excellent”), according to several printed editions. M.]

But to us, Lord, reveal either that meaning itself or whichever other true meaning you approve, so that whether you disclose to us what you disclosed to that man of yours or something else prompted by the same words, you may nevertheless nourish us, and error may not deceive us.

Behold, Lord my God, how many things we have written from a few words—how many things, I ask you! What strength do we possess, and what amount of time, to suffice for all your Books in this manner?

[Note: [Col. 0844] *Sufficiant* (“may suffice”), according to Somm., Arn., and Mart., with four manuscripts. M.]

Therefore, allow me to confess to you more briefly concerning them, and to choose one thing that you inspire as true, certain, and good, even if many things present themselves where many things can present themselves. Let this be the faith of my confession: if I say what your minister understood, I shall have said it rightly and excellently—for this is what I ought to strive for. But if I do not attain that, I shall nevertheless say what your Truth wishes to say to me through his words, the Truth that also told him what it wished.

# BOOK THIRTEEN

The goodness of God shines forth in the production and perfection of things; moreover, the Trinity of God, and the particular nature of the Holy Spirit, are intimated in the first words of Genesis. Later, the entire history of the created world is transferred, through allegorical interpretation, to the works by which God brings about human holiness and glory in the Church.

[Col. 0845]

## CHAPTER I. He invokes God, whose prevenient goodness he acknowledges

[Col. 0845]

1. I call upon you, my God, my mercy, who made me and did not forget the one who had forgotten you. I call upon you in my soul, which you prepare to receive you through the desire that you inspire in it. Do not abandon me now that I call upon you—you who, before I called upon you, came before me and pressed upon me, repeating your call in many ways, so that I might hear from afar, turn back, and call upon you as you called me.

For you, Lord, wiped away all my evil merits, so that you would not repay me according to the deeds by which I had departed from you; and you went before all my good merits, so that you might reward me through the hands by which you made me. For before I existed, you were; nor was there anyone to whom you could grant existence. And yet, behold, I exist through your goodness, which preceded this whole fact: that you made me, and that from which you made me.

For you did not need me, nor am I such a good as could help you, my Lord and my God—not so that I might serve you as though you would grow weary in acting, or as though your power would be less if it lacked my service; nor so that I might worship you as one tills the earth, as though you would remain uncultivated if I did not worship you. Rather, I serve and worship you so that it may be well with me through you, from whom comes my existence as one for whom it may be well.

## CHAPTER II. Creatures subsist and are perfected through God’s goodness

2. For from the fullness of your goodness your creation subsists, so that a good thing which would contribute nothing to you, and would not be equal to you from you, might nevertheless not be lacking, since it could be made from you.

What did heaven and earth, which you made in the beginning, deserve from you? Let the spiritual and bodily natures say what they deserved from you—those natures which you made in your Wisdom, so that even their beginnings and formless states, each in its own spiritual or bodily kind, might depend on it while tending toward immoderation and distant unlikeness to you.

The formless spiritual nature was better than a formed body would have been; the formless bodily nature was better than if it had been nothing at all. Thus the formless things would depend upon your Word, unless through that same Word they were recalled to your unity, formed, and made into all very good things by you, the one supreme Good.

What had they deserved from you so that they should exist at least in a formless state, when they would not even be this except from you?

[Note: [Col. 0845] *Spirituales corporalesque naturae* (“spiritual and bodily natures”), according to Somm. and five manuscripts in Mart. M.]

3. What did bodily matter deserve from you, so that it should exist at least as invisible and unformed (Gen. 1:1)? For it would not even be this unless you had made it; and since it did not exist, it could not deserve from you that it should exist.

Or what did the beginning of spiritual creation deserve, so that it should at least flow darkly, like an abyss, unlike you, unless through that same Word it were turned toward the One from whom it was made, and, illuminated by him, became light—not equally, but conformed to the form equal to you?

For just as for a body being is not the same as being beautiful—for otherwise it could not be deformed—so also for a created spirit living is not the same as living wisely; otherwise it would possess wisdom unchangeably.

It is good for it always to cling to you, lest it lose through turning away the light which it gained by turning toward you, and fall back into a life resembling a dark abyss.

And we too, who according to the soul are a spiritual creation, once lived as darkness when we had turned away from you, our light (Eph. 5:8); and we labor amid the remnants of our darkness until we become your righteousness in your Only-Begotten, like the mountains of God. For we were your judgments, like a great abyss (Ps. 35:7).

## CHAPTER III. Everything is from God’s grace

4. As for what you said in the first acts of creation, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Gen. 1:3), I understand this not inappropriately as referring to spiritual creation, because there already existed some kind of life which you could illuminate.

But just as it had not deserved from you that it should exist as such a life as could be illuminated, so, once it existed, it did not deserve from you that it should be illuminated. For its formlessness would not please you if it did not become light—not by existing in itself, but by contemplating the light that illuminates it and clinging to it.

Thus both its existence in any degree and its blessed existence would be owed only to your grace, when it was turned through a better change toward that which cannot be changed for better or worse—which you alone are, because you alone simply are. For with you, living is not one thing and living blessedly another, because your blessedness is yourself.

## CHAPTER IV. God does not need created things
5. What, then, would be lacking for the good that you are to yourself, even if these things either did not exist at all or remained formless—things you did not make out of need, but from the abundance of your goodness, restraining and turning them toward form—not so that your joy might somehow be completed by them? For their imperfection is displeasing to you in your perfection, so that they may be perfected from you and please you; but not to you as though you were imperfect and needed to be perfected by their perfection. For your good Spirit was borne over the waters (ibid., 2); he was not borne by them, as though he rested in them. For those in whom your good Spirit is said to rest (Isa. XI, 2), he causes to rest in himself. But your incorruptible and immutable will was borne over them, itself sufficient to itself, above the life that you had made—a life for which to live is not the same as to live blessedly, since it also lives while drifting in its own darkness; and it remains for it to turn toward him by whom it was made, to live more and more fully beside the fountain of life, and in his light to see light (Ps. XXXV, 10), and to be perfected, illumined, and blessed.

## CHAPTER V. From the first words of Genesis the Trinity, who is God, is understood.

6. Behold, in an enigma the Trinity appears to me, the Trinity who is my God: for you, Father, in the Beginning of our wisdom—which is your Wisdom born from you, equal and coeternal with you, that is, in your Son—you made heaven and earth. We have said much about the heaven of heaven, and about the invisible and unformed earth, and about the dark abyss, according to the wandering lapses of spiritual formlessness, unless it were turned toward him from whom came whatever life it possessed, and by illumination became a beautiful life, and became his heaven of heaven, which was afterward made between water and water. I already understood the Father in the name of God, who made these things, and the Son in the name of Beginning, in which he made these things; and, believing the Trinity to be my God, as I did believe, I sought for it in his holy utterances—and behold, your Spirit was borne over the waters. Behold the Trinity, my God: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, creator of the whole creation.

[Note: This notable passage is restored by the manuscripts. In the printed editions it had been mutilated, with the words “of our wisdom” omitted.]

## CHAPTER VI. Why the Spirit is said to have been borne over the waters.

7. But what reason was there for this, O true light? I bring my heart near to you; scatter its darkness, lest it teach me vanity, and tell me, I beseech you by that motherly charity: tell me what reason there was that, after heaven and the invisible and unformed earth and darkness over the abyss had been named, your Scripture should then finally name your Spirit. Was it because he had to be introduced in such a way that he would be said to be borne over something, and this could not be said unless what your Spirit could be understood to be borne over had first been mentioned? For he was not borne over the Father or the Son; nor would it rightly be said that he was borne over anything if he were borne over nothing. Something, therefore, had first to be named over which he could be borne, and then the one who could not fittingly be mentioned in any other way than by saying that he was borne over it. Why, then, could he not be introduced in any other way than by saying that he was borne over something?

## CHAPTER VII. The effects of the Holy Spirit.

8. Let whoever can follow your Apostle in understanding when he says that your charity has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5); and when, teaching about spiritual things, he demonstrates the surpassing way of charity, and bends his knees before you on our behalf, that we may know the surpassing knowledge of the charity of Christ (Eph. III, 14–19). Therefore, from the beginning, he who surpasses all was borne over the waters. To whom shall I speak? How shall I speak of the weight of cupidity plunging into the sheer abyss, and of the uplifting of charity through your Spirit, who was borne over the waters? To whom shall I speak? How shall I say: “We are submerged and emerge”?

[Note: The manuscripts do not have “we are submerged and emerge” here. The same words are absent from Somm. and Flor. M.]

For these are not places into which we are submerged and from which we emerge. What is more similar, and what more dissimilar? They are affections; they are loves. The uncleanness of our spirit, flowing downward through love of cares, and the holiness of yours, lifting us upward through love of security, so that we may have our heart above, toward you, where your Spirit is borne over the waters—and may come to the surpassing rest when our soul has passed through the waters that have no substance (Ps. CXXIII, 5).

## CHAPTER VIII. For an intellectual creature, whatever is less than God is insufficient for blessed rest.

9. The angel fell, the human soul fell, and they revealed the abyss of the whole spiritual creation in the depth of darkness, unless you had said from the beginning, “Let there be light,” and light had come to be, and every obedient intelligence of your heavenly city had adhered to you and rested in your Spirit, who is immutably borne over everything mutable. Otherwise even the heaven of heaven would be a dark abyss in itself; but now it is light in the Lord. For even in the miserable restlessness of spirits that flow downward and reveal their darkness, stripped of the garment of your light, you sufficiently show how great a rational creature you have made, one for whom whatever is less than you is in no way sufficient for blessed rest, and consequently neither is it sufficient for itself. For you, our God, will illumine our darkness (Ps. XVII, 29); from you our garments arise, and our darkness will be like midday (Ps. CXXXVIII, 12). Give me yourself, my God; restore yourself to me: for I love you; and if it is too little, let me love you more strongly. I cannot measure, so as to know how much love I lack for what is sufficient, so that my life may run into your embraces and not turn away until it is hidden in the secret place of your face (Ps. XXX, 21).

[Note: The manuscripts read “restore yourself to me: for I love you.” The same reading is found in Am., Er., and the Florentine edition of M.]

[Note: Lov. reads “until I am hidden.” But the other editions, with the manuscripts, more correctly read “until it is hidden.” Understand “my life.”]

This alone I know: outside you it is evil for me—not only outside myself, but even within myself; and all abundance that is not my God is poverty.

## CHAPTER IX. Why only the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters.

10. Was either the Father or the Son not borne over the waters? If this is understood spatially, as with a body, then neither was the Holy Spirit; but if it is understood as the eminence of immutable divinity above everything mutable, then the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit were all borne over the waters. Why, then, is this said only of your Spirit? Why is it said only of him? As though there were a place there—which is no place—and of that one alone it was said that he is your gift. In your gift we rest; there we enjoy you. Our rest is our place. Love lifts us there, and your good Spirit raises our lowliness from the gates of death (Ps. IX, 15). In good will we have peace (Luke II, 14).

A body strives toward its place by its own weight. Weight is not directed only downward, but toward its own place. Fire tends upward; a stone falls downward. Things are moved by their own weights; they seek their places. Oil poured beneath water rises above the water; water poured over oil sinks beneath the oil. They are moved by their own weights; they seek their places. Things that are less ordered are restless; they are ordered and come to rest. My weight is my love; wherever I am carried, it is that which carries me. By your gift we are kindled and borne upward. We burn and move onward. We ascend the ascents in the heart (Ps. LXXXIII, 6), and sing the song of degrees. By your fire, your good fire, we burn and move onward, for we move upward toward the peace of Jerusalem, because I rejoiced with those who said to me:

[Note: Earlier printed editions read “the things that they said to me.” Augustine alludes to Ps. 121:1, where he usually reads “who said”; the manuscripts have that reading here as well.]

> “We will go into the house of the Lord” (Ps. CXXI, 1).

There good will has placed us, so that we desire nothing other than to remain there forever.

## CHAPTER X. Everything comes from God’s gift.

11. Blessed is the creature that, though itself something else, knows nothing else [than you], unless by your gift, which is borne over everything mutable, it was raised, as soon as it was made and without any interval of time, by that calling in which you said, “Let there be light,” and light came to be (Gen. I, 3).

[Note: This is the reading of the manuscripts and Arn. Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. have “light was made”; shortly afterward they also read “in which we were darkness.”]

For in us there is a temporal distinction: we were darkness, and we become light (Eph. V, 8). But in that creature it was said what it would be if it were not illumined; and it was said as though it had first been fluid and dark, so that the reason would be evident why it came to be otherwise—namely, so that, turned toward unfailing light, it might be light. Let whoever can understand; and whoever cannot, let him ask you.

[Note: The manuscripts omit the words “and whoever cannot,” reading: “Let whoever can understand; let him ask you.”]

Why, then, should he trouble me, as though I illumined anyone coming into this world? (John I, 9.)

## CHAPTER XI. Symbols of the Trinity in the human being.

12. Who understands the omnipotent Trinity? And who does not speak of it, if indeed he speaks of it? Rare is the soul that, when it speaks of it, knows what it is speaking about.

[Note: “Let him know what he is speaking about,” according to Somm., Lov., Dub., Mart., and Rond. M.]

They argue and fight, yet no one sees this vision without peace. I wish that people would consider these three things in themselves. These three are vastly different from that Trinity; but I point out where they may exercise and test themselves, and perceive how far they are from it.

I mean these three: being, knowing, and willing. For I am, I know, and I will; I am knowing and willing; and I know that I am and that I will; and I will to be and to know. In these three, let whoever can see how inseparable a life they are, and one life; how inseparable a mind, and one mind; how inseparable an essence, and one essence; and finally, how there is an inseparable distinction, yet nevertheless a distinction. It is certainly before itself: let it attend to itself, see, and tell me.

But when it has found something in these things and has spoken of it, let it not suppose that it has already found that which is above them: that which is immutable, which exists immutably, knows immutably, and wills immutably. Whether because of these three things there is also a Trinity there; or whether these three things are in each, so that each has its own threefold set; or both, in wondrous ways, simply and multiply, in the infinite which is its own limit in itself, by which it exists, is known to itself, and immutably suffices to itself—the selfsame reality in the abundant greatness of unity. Who could easily conceive this? Who could express it in any way? Who would rashly pronounce upon it in any fashion?

[Note: Lov. reads “or threefold.” But the other editions, with the manuscripts, more clearly read “so that each member has them in a threefold manner.” What follows immediately—“or both”—shows that two alternatives have already been proposed: first, whether the Trinity there exists because of these three things; and second, whether these three things exist in each member, so that each member has them threefold. In Am. and Er. the passage after this reads: “Or whether both, in wondrous ways, simply and multiply, in the infinite, imperceptible, without which he is.” Bad. has the same, except that it reads “at the end” rather than “without.”]

## CHAPTER XII. The creation of the world prefigures the formation of the Church.

13. Advance in confession, my faith; say to your Lord God:

> “Holy, holy, holy, Lord my God, in your name we have been baptized, Father and Son and Holy Spirit; in your name we baptize, Father and Son and Holy Spirit.”

For in his Christ God also made among us heaven and earth: the spiritual and carnal members of his Church.

[Note: “In his Christ, his Son,” according to Somm. and Rond. M.]

And our earth, before it received the form of teaching, was invisible and unformed, and we were covered by the darkness of ignorance, because you disciplined humanity for its iniquity (Ps. XXXVIII, 12), and your judgments were like the great abyss (Ps. XXXV, 7). But because your Spirit was borne over the water (Gen. I, 2), your mercy did not abandon our misery, and you said, “Let there be light.”

> “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III, 12).

“Repent: let there be light.” And because our soul had been troubled in relation to itself, we remembered you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan and from the mountain equal to you, though made small for our sake (Ps. XLI, 7). Our darkness displeased us, and we turned toward you, and light came to be. And behold, once we were darkness, but now we are light in the Lord (Eph. V, 8).

## CHAPTER XIII. The renewal of the human being during this life is not yet complete.

14. Yet this is still through faith, not through sight (II Cor. V, 7). For we have been saved in hope. But hope that is seen is not hope (Rom. VIII, 24). Still the abyss calls to the abyss, but in the voice of your cataracts (Ps. XLI, 8).

[Note: “But now in the voice,” according to Som., Mart., and Rond. “But now not in the voice,” according to Er. and Lugd. M.]

Even the one who says, “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (I Cor. III, 1), still does not consider that he has comprehended; forgetting what lies behind and stretching toward what lies ahead (Phil. III, 13), he groans under his burden, and his soul thirsts for the living God as a deer for springs of water, and says, “When shall I come?” (Ps. XLI, 2, 3), desiring to put on over it his dwelling from heaven (II Cor. V, 2). He calls upon the lower abyss, saying:

> “Do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Rom. XII, 2);

and:

> “Do not become children in your minds; be infants in evil, so that you may be mature in your minds” (I Cor. XIV, 20).

[Note: Some of the older manuscripts read “become children in your perceptions.” According to Somm. and Rond., the text then reads: “be mature in your perceptions.” M.]

And:

> “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” (Gal. III, 1.)

But now it is no longer in his own voice; it is in yours, for you sent your Spirit from on high (Acts II, 2), through him who ascended on high (Ps. LXVII, 19) and opened the cataracts of his gifts, so that the rushing stream might gladden your city (Ps. XLV, 5).

For the friend of the bridegroom sighs for him, already possessing with him the first fruits of the Spirit, yet still groaning within himself and awaiting adoption, the redemption of his body (Rom. VIII, 23). He sighs for him, for he is a member of the bride; and he is jealous for him, for he is the friend of the bridegroom. He is jealous not for himself (John III, 19), because, in the voice of your cataracts and not in his own voice, he calls upon another abyss (Ps. XLI, 8), for which, in his jealousy, he fears lest, just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so their minds might be corrupted from the chastity that is in our bridegroom, your only Son (II Cor. II, 3).

What is that light of sight? When we shall see him as he is (I John III, 2), and the tears that have become my bread day and night shall have passed away, while it is said to me every day, “Where is your God?” (Ps. XLI, 4.)

## CHAPTER XIV. We are strengthened by faith and hope.

15. And I say: “My God, where are you?” Behold where you are.

[Note: Lov. omits “behold where you are.”]

I breathe in you for a little while when I pour out my soul over myself in the voice of rejoicing and confession, celebrating a festive sound (Ps. XLI, 5). Yet it is still sad, because it falls back and becomes an abyss—or rather, because it still feels itself to be an abyss. My faith, which you kindled at night before my feet, says to it:

> “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in the Lord” (Ps. XLII, 5, 6);

his word is a lamp for your feet (Ps. CXVIII, 105).

Hope and persevere until the night, the mother of the wicked, has passed; until the Lord’s anger has passed, whose children we also once were—darkness, the remnants of which we drag about in a body dead because of sin (Rom. VIII, 10); until the day breathes forth and the shadows are removed (Song II, 17).

Hope in the Lord: “In the morning I shall stand,” and I shall contemplate; I shall always confess to him.

[Note: The printed editions, with some manuscripts, read “in the morning I shall stand before you.” But “before you” is absent from the more reliable codices.]

“In the morning I shall stand, and I shall see” (Ps. V, 5) the salvation of my face (Ps. XLII, 5), my God, who will give life to our mortal bodies because of the Spirit who dwells in us (Rom. VIII, 11), because he was mercifully borne over our inner darkness and fluidity.

From this, in this pilgrimage, we have received a pledge (II Cor. I, 22), so that we may already be light (Eph. V, 8), while we have still been saved in hope (Rom. VIII, 24), and may be children of light and children of the day, not children of night or darkness (I Thess. V, 5)—though such we once were.

Between them and us, in this still uncertain state of human knowledge, you alone make the division: you who test our hearts, and call the light day and the darkness night (Gen. I, 5). For who distinguishes us except you? And what do we have that we have not received from you? (I Cor. IV, 7.) We are vessels for honor from the same mass from which others have also been made for dishonor (Rom. IX, 21).

## CHAPTER XV. “Let there be a firmament,” etc., Genesis 1:6. What the firmament is, and what the upper waters are.

16. Or who but you, our God, made for us a firmament of authority above us in your divine Scripture? For heaven will be folded up like a scroll (Isa. XXIV, 4), and now it is stretched out over us like a skin (Ps. CIII, 2). Your divine Scripture possesses the higher authority, now that those mortals through whom you administered it to us have undergone this death.

And you know, Lord, you know how you clothed human beings with skins when they became mortal through sin (Gen. III, 21). Thus, like a skin, you stretched out the firmament of your Book: your concordant utterances, which through the ministry of mortals you placed above us. For through their very death, the solid foundation of authority in the words issued through them is majestically stretched above all things beneath it—something that, while they lived here, had not been stretched out with such majesty. You had not yet stretched heaven out like a skin; you had not yet spread the fame of their death everywhere.

17. Let us see, Lord, the heavens, the work of your fingers; clear away from our eyes the cloud with which you have veiled them. There is your testimony, giving wisdom to the little ones (Ps. XVIII, 8). Perfect your praise, my God, from the mouths of infants and nursing children.

For we know no other books that so destroy pride, so destroy the enemy and the defender (Ps. VIII, 4, 3), who resists your reconciliation by defending his sins. I know of no other utterances, Lord, so chaste, which would persuade me so powerfully to confession, bend my neck beneath your yoke so gently, and invite me to worship you without seeking a reward.

Let me understand them, good Father; grant this to me in my lowliness, for you have made them firm for those who are beneath them.

18. There are other waters above this firmament, I believe: immortal waters, separated from earthly corruption. Let them praise your name; let the supercelestial peoples of your angels praise you. They have no need to look up to this firmament and come to know your word by reading.

[Note: Lov., together with the older editions, reads “receive”; and shortly afterward, “they would receive and know your mercy.” But the manuscript reading given in the text is clearly better.]

For they always see your face (Matt. XVIII, 10), and there they read, without the syllables of time, what your eternal will desires. They read, choose, and love; they always read, and what they read never passes away. For by choosing and loving they read the very immutability of your counsel.

Their book is not closed, nor is their scroll folded, because you yourself are this for them, and you are so forever. For you have ordered them above this firmament, which you established over the weakness of the peoples below, where they might look upward and know your mercy, which declares you in time, though you made time.

For in heaven, Lord, is your mercy, and your truth reaches to the clouds (Ps. XXXV, 6). The clouds pass away, but heaven remains. The preachers of your word pass from this life into another life, but your Scripture is extended over the peoples until the end of the age. Yet heaven and earth will pass away; your words will not pass away (Matt. XXIV, 35). For the skin will be folded up, and the grass over which it was stretched will pass away with its splendor; but your word remains forever (Isa. XL, 6).

Now it appears to us in the enigma of clouds and through the mirror of heaven (I Cor. XIII, 12), not as it truly is. For although we are loved by your Son, what we shall be has not yet appeared.

He looked through the nets of flesh, wooed us, kindled us, and we ran after his fragrance. But when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is (I John III, 2). As he is, Lord, is what our seeing shall be; but it is not yet ours.

[Note: The common editions read, “which is not yet—give it to us.” But the manuscripts do not have “give,” unless perhaps one of the more recent ones does.]

## CHAPTER XVI. God alone knows himself completely as he is.

19. For as you truly are, you alone know, who exist immutably, know immutably, and will immutably. Your essence knows and wills immutably; your knowledge exists and wills immutably; your will exists and knows immutably.

Nor does it seem just in your sight that, just as immutable light knows itself, so it should be known by a mutable creature that has been illumined. Therefore my soul is like land without water to you (Ps. CXLII, 6): for just as it cannot illumine itself from itself, so it cannot satisfy itself from itself. For with you is the fountain of life; in your light we shall see light (Ps. XXXV, 10).

## CHAPTER XVII. “Let the waters be gathered,” etc., Genesis 1:9. What the sea is, and what the dry land is. Genesis 1:11, “Let the earth bring forth,” is explained.

20. Who gathered together those who cause bitterness into one society? For they have the same end: temporal and earthly happiness, for the sake of which they do everything, although they are tossed about by an innumerable variety of cares.

Who, Lord, but you, who said that the waters should be gathered into one gathering and that the dry land should appear, thirsting for you? For the sea is yours, and you made it, and your hands formed the dry land (Ps. XCIV, 5). It is not the bitterness of wills that is called the sea, but the gathering of waters.

For you restrain even the evil desires of souls, fix limits to how far they may be permitted to advance, and cause their waves to break against themselves (Job XXXVIII, 10, 11). Thus, by the order of your command, you make the sea subject to everything.

[Note: This is the reading of Bad., Am., and Er., with eleven manuscripts. Lov. and Arn. read “how far the waters may be permitted to advance, so that they may break against themselves.”]

21. But you water souls thirsting for you and appearing before you, distinguished by another end from the society of the sea, with a hidden and sweet spring, so that the earth may also give its fruit. And it gives its fruit; and, at your command, Lord God, our soul brings forth works of mercy according to their kind: loving its neighbor by supplying bodily necessities, bearing within itself seed according to likeness.

For from our own weakness we are moved with compassion to help those in need, assisting them as we would wish to be assisted if we were in the same need—not only in easy matters, as in seed-bearing grass, but also in the protection of assistance, with strong vigor, like a fruit-bearing tree: that is, being beneficial in rescuing the one who suffers injury from the hand of the powerful and in providing the shelter of protection through the strong vigor of just judgment.

[Note: This should be read as “being beneficial,” according to four manuscripts of Ang. Mart. also has this reading, with one manuscript. The Florentine edition and three manuscripts cited by Rond. P. Benedictines in the first edition of the first volume printed “a benefit”; in the later edition, while retaining the preceding reading, they said it should be changed to “being beneficial.”]

## CHAPTER XVIII. “Let there be lights,” etc., Genesis 1:14. What the lights are that divide between day and night.

[Col. 0854]

22. Thus, Lord, thus, I beseech you: let truth arise from the earth, as you make it arise, as you grant joy and ability, and let righteousness look down from heaven (Ps. LXXXIV, 12), and let lights come to be in the firmament.

Let us break our bread for the hungry, bring the homeless poor into our house, clothe the naked, and not despise those of our own seed. When these fruits have been born on earth, see that it is good; let our temporal light burst forth (Isa. LVIII, 7, 8). And from this lower harvest of action, let us obtain the higher word of life amid the delights of contemplation, and appear like lights in the world, adhering to the firmament of your Scripture.

For there you dispute with us, so that we may divide between intelligible and sensible things, as between day and night—or between souls devoted, respectively, to intelligible and sensible things—so that now it is not you alone, in the hiddenness of your judgment, as before the firmament was made, who divide between light and darkness, but also your spiritual people, placed and distinguished in that same firmament, may shine over the earth with your grace made manifest throughout the world, divide between day and night, and signify the seasons.

For old things have passed away; behold, new things have come to be. Our salvation is nearer than when we believed (Rom. XIII, 11). The night has passed, and the day has drawn near. You bless the crown of your year (Ps. LXIV, 2), sending laborers into your harvest (Matt. IX, 38), in which others have labored by sowing, and sending them also into another sowing, whose harvest is at the end (John IV, 38; Matt. XIII, 39).

Thus you grant the desires of the one who desires, and bless the years of the righteous. Yet you are the same, and in your years, which do not fail (Ps. CI, 28), you prepare a storehouse for passing years. For by your eternal counsel you give heavenly goods to the earth at their proper times.

[Note: Four English manuscripts read “laborers of benevolence.”]

[Note: Lov. reads “you grant life to the one who desires”; shortly afterward it reads “you prepare the rising.” The other codices, which we follow in both places, have the readings represented in the text.]

23. For to one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, like the greater light, for those who delight in the clear light of truth, as in the beginning of day; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit, like the lesser light; to another, faith; to another, the gift of healing; to another, works of power; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues—and all these are like stars.

For one and the same Spirit works all these things, distributing gifts severally to each as he wills, and making the stars appear in manifestation for the common good (I Cor. XII, 7, 11). But the word of knowledge, which contains all the sacraments that vary with the seasons like the moon, and the other forms of knowledge of the gifts mentioned afterward like stars, differ from that brilliance of wisdom in which the day mentioned above rejoices as much as they belong to the beginning of night.

[Note: The better manuscripts read “at the beginnings,” that is, “among the lights of the night.” This reading might seem preferable, were it not that “at the beginning of day” occurs shortly above. Perhaps the phrase should read “at the beginning of the night,” as in Book 1 of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 14.]

For these things are necessary to those to whom your most prudent servant could not speak as spiritual people, but as carnal (I Cor. III, 1), although he speaks wisdom among the mature (ibid. II, 6). But the natural person, like a little one in Christ and a drinker of milk, until strengthened for solid food and able to fix his gaze upon the sun, should not have his night abandoned, but should be content with the light of the moon and the stars.

These things you discuss with us, our most wise God, in your Book, your firmament, so that we may discern all things with wondrous contemplation, although still through signs, seasons, days, and years.

## CHAPTER XIX. The same verse, “Let there be lights,” etc., is discussed.

24. But first, “wash yourselves; be clean. Remove wickedness from your souls and from before my eyes,” so that the dry land may appear. “Learn to do good; judge for the orphan and vindicate the widow,” so that the earth may bring forth the grass of pasture and the fruit-bearing tree. “Come, and let us reason together,” says the Lord, so that lights may come to be in the firmament of heaven and shine upon the earth.

That rich man was asking the good teacher what he should do to obtain eternal life. Let the good teacher, whom he thought to be a human being and nothing more, answer him—for he is good because he is God. Let him tell him that, if he wishes to enter into life, he must keep the commandments: he must separate from himself the bitterness of malice and wickedness; he must not kill, commit adultery, steal, or bear false witness, so that the dry land may appear and bring forth honor toward father and mother and love of neighbor.

“I have done all these things,” he said.

Then where do such great thorns come from, if the earth is fruitful? Go, uproot the wooded thickets of greed; sell what you possess, and be filled with fruits by giving to the poor; you will have treasure in heaven.
