And follow the Lord, if you wish to be perfect, joined to those among whom the one who knows what he should apportion to day and night speaks wisdom, so that you too may know, and lights may come to be for you in the firmament of heaven.

But this will not happen unless your heart is there; and that in turn will not happen unless your treasure is there, as you heard from the good teacher (Matt. VI, 21). But the barren earth was saddened, and the thorns choked the word (ibid. XIX, 16–22).

25. But you, an elect race, the weak things of the world, who have abandoned everything to follow the Lord, go after him and put the mighty to shame. Go after him, beautiful-footed, and shine in the firmament (I Pet. II, 9), so that the heavens may declare his glory, dividing between the light of the perfect—not yet like that of the angels—and the darkness of the little ones, though they are not despised.

[Note: Am., Er., and nine manuscripts read “of the despairing.”]

Shine over the whole earth; let the day, bright with the sun, pour forth the word of wisdom to the day, and let the night, shining with the moon, announce the word of knowledge to the night (Ps. XVIII, 2). The moon and stars shine for the night, but the night does not darken them, because they illumine it according to its measure.

For behold, as though God were saying, “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven,” suddenly there came from heaven a sound like the rush of a mighty wind, and divided tongues appeared as if of fire, which also rested upon each of them (Acts II, 2, 3); and lights came to be in the firmament of heaven (Matt. V, 14), possessing the word of life.

Run everywhere, holy fires, beautiful fires. For you are the light of the world, and you are not under a bushel. The one to whom you adhered was exalted, and he exalted you. Run everywhere and make yourselves known to all nations.

## CHAPTER XX. “Let the waters bring forth,” etc., Genesis 1:20. What the creeping things and the flying things are.

26. Let the sea also conceive and give birth to your works, and let the waters bring forth creeping things with living souls. For by separating the precious from the vile, you became the mouth of God, through whom he would say: “Let the waters bring forth,” not the living soul that the earth produces, but creeping things with living souls and flying things that fly over the earth.

For your sacraments crept forth, God, through the works of your saints, amid the waves of the world’s temptations, to imbue the nations with your name in your baptism. Amid these there also came to be great wondrous works, like enormous whales, and the voices of your messengers flying over the earth, close to the firmament of your Book, with that Book set over them as their authority, beneath which they would fly wherever they went.

For there are no languages or speech whose voices are not heard, when their sound has gone out into all the earth and their words to the ends of the world (Ps. XVIII, 4, 5), because, by blessing them, you multiplied these things, Lord.

27. Am I lying, or do I confuse things by mixing them together, failing to distinguish the luminous perceptions of these matters in the firmament of heaven from bodily works in the rolling sea and beneath the firmament of heaven?

For the things whose knowledge is firm and determinate, without the increase of generations, like the lights of wisdom and knowledge, have bodily operations that are numerous and varied. One thing is multiplied by growing from another, in your blessing, God, who have consoled the weariness of mortal senses, so that one reality in the mind might be represented and expressed in many ways through bodily movements.

The waters brought forth these things—but in your word. The needs of peoples alienated from the eternity of your truth brought forth these things—but in your Gospel, because the waters themselves cast them forth; their bitter sickness was the cause that these things proceeded in your word.

28. And all things are beautiful because you make them; and behold, you are inexpressibly more beautiful, who made all things. If Adam had not fallen from you, the saltiness of the sea would not have poured forth from his womb: the human race, deeply curious, stormily swollen, and unstably fluid. Thus there would have been no need for your stewards to perform and declare mystical deeds and words bodily and sensibly amid many waters.

For this is how the creeping things and the flying things now came before me: people imbued and initiated through bodily sacraments and subjected to them would not progress further unless the soul lived spiritually at another level and, after the word of initiation, looked toward completion.

## CHAPTER XXI. “Let the earth bring forth a living soul,” etc., Genesis 1:24.

29. And therefore, in your word it was not the depth of the sea but the earth, separated from the bitterness of the waters, that brought forth—not creeping things of living souls and birds, but a living soul. [Note: “It brings forth” (ejicit), according to Somm., Mart., and Rond. M.] For it no longer needs the Baptism that the Gentiles need, as it needed it when it was covered by the waters; for since that time when you established that entry should be made in this way, there is no other way to enter the kingdom of heaven. Nor does it seek great miracles by which faith may be produced; for “unless he sees signs and wonders, he does not believe” (John 4:48), since the faithful earth has now been separated from the waters of the sea, bitter with unbelief; and “tongues are a sign,” not for believers but for unbelievers (1 Cor. 14:22). [Note: “As a sign,” according to Somm. and Rond., with five M manuscripts.] Therefore the earth that you founded upon the waters has no need of that kind of bird which the waters brought forth by your word.

Send your word into it through your messengers. For we recount their works, but you are the one who works in them, so that they may bring forth a living soul. The earth produces it because the earth is the cause that they perform these works in it, just as the sea was the cause that creeping things of living souls and birds under the firmament of heaven should perform their works—things which the earth no longer needs, although it eats the fish “raised from the deep” in the meal that you have prepared in the sight of believers (Ps. 22:5 [21:6]). For this reason it was raised from the deep: to nourish the dry land.

And birds, though offspring of the sea, nevertheless multiply upon the earth. For the unbelief of human beings became the cause of the first words of those who evangelized; yet the faithful too are exhorted by them and are blessed by them in manifold ways from day to day.

But the living soul took its beginning from the earth [Note: “Takes,” according to Arn. and Mart., with six M manuscripts.], because it is no longer beneficial except for the faithful to restrain themselves from love of this world, so that their soul may live for you—a soul that was dead while living in pleasures, in “pleasures,” Lord, that bring death (1 Tim. 5:6); for you are the life-giving pleasure of the pure in heart.

30. Let your ministers, then, now work upon the earth—not as in the waters of unbelief, proclaiming and speaking through miracles, sacraments, and mystical utterances, where ignorance, intent upon the hidden signs, gives birth to wonder in fear. For such is the entrance to faith for the sons of Adam who have forgotten you, while they hide themselves from your presence (Gen. 3:8) and become an abyss. But let them work also as upon the dry land, separated from the gulfs of the abyss; let them be examples to the faithful by living before them and rousing them to imitation. Thus they hear not only in order to listen, but also in order to act: “Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live” (Ps. 68:33 [69:32]), so that the earth may bring forth a living soul.

“Do not be conformed to this world” (Rom. 12:2); restrain yourselves from it. The soul lives by avoiding what kills it through desire. Restrain yourselves from the savage violence of pride, from the inert pleasure of lust, and from the deceptive name of knowledge, so that there may be tame beasts, domesticated cattle, and harmless serpents. These are the movements of the soul in allegory. But the arrogance of self-exaltation, the pleasure of lust, and the poison of curiosity are movements of a dead soul, because it does not die in such a way as to be deprived of every movement; rather, by departing from the fountain of life it dies, and thus is taken up by the passing world and conformed to it.

31. Your word, O God, is the fountain of eternal life, and it does not pass away. Therefore that departure is restrained in your word when we are told, “Do not be conformed to this world,” so that the earth may bring forth, from the fountain of life, a living soul; in your word, through your evangelists, a soul practicing self-restraint, imitating those who imitate your Christ.

For this is “according to its kind,” since the imitation of a man comes from a friend: “Be as I am,” he says, “because I too am as you are” (Gal. 4:12). Thus, in the living soul, there will be good beasts in the gentleness of conduct. For you commanded, saying: “Complete your works in gentleness, and you will be loved by everyone” (Sir. 3:19).

And there will be good cattle, neither excessive if they eat nor lacking if they do not eat; and good serpents, not harmful for doing harm but shrewd for avoiding it. They investigate temporal nature only as far as is sufficient for eternity to be perceived intellectually through the things that have been made (Rom. 1:20). These animals serve reason when, restrained from a deadly advance, they live and are good.

### CHAPTER XXII  
“Let us make man in our image,” etc. (Gen. 1:26). The renewal of the mind.

32. For behold, Lord our God, our creator: when the affections by which we were dying through wicked living have been restrained from love of the world, and the soul has begun to be alive through good living, and your word has been fulfilled—the word that you spoke through your apostle, “Do not be conformed to this world”—then what you immediately added follows: “But be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Rom. 12:2).

This is no longer “according to its kind,” as though imitating the preceding neighbor, nor living by the authority of a better human being. For you did not say, “Let man be made according to its kind,” but, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), so that we may prove what your will is.

For this purpose your minister, who begets children through the Gospel (1 Cor. 4:15), lest he should always have little ones whom he nourished with milk and cherished like a nurse (1 Thess. 2:7), says: “Be transformed in the renewal of your mind, so that you may prove what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect” (Rom. 12:2). [Note: The printed editions omit “you”; it has been restored from the manuscripts, since Augustine usually cites the passage thus.]

Therefore you do not say, “Let man be made,” but, “Let us make man.” Nor do you say, “According to its kind,” but, “In our image and likeness.” Renewed in mind, and contemplating your truth as it is understood, man does not need a human teacher to imitate his kind; but, with you as teacher, he himself proves what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect.

And you teach him [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and Arn. read, “you now make him capable.” Two manuscripts likewise have this reading.] now capable of seeing the Trinity in unity and the unity in Trinity. Therefore, although it is said in the plural, “Let us make man,” it is nevertheless continued in the singular: “And God made man”; and although it is said in the plural, “In our image,” it is continued in the singular: “in the image of God.”

Thus man is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of the one who created him (Gen. 1:27; Col. 3:10); and, having become spiritual, he judges all things that ought to be judged, while he himself is judged by no one.

### CHAPTER XXIII  
“And let him have dominion over the fish of the sea,” etc. (Gen. 1:26). What the Christian judges.

33. That he judges all things means that he has authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, all cattle and beasts, the whole earth, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth. For he does this through the understanding of the mind, by which he perceives the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14).

Otherwise, man, placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them (Ps. 48:13 [49:12]). Therefore, in your Church, our God, according to the grace that you have given it—for we are your workmanship, created for good works (Eph. 2:10)—not only those who rule spiritually, but also those who are spiritually subject to those who rule (for you made man male and female [Gen. 1:27]), in this way within your spiritual grace, where according to bodily sex there is neither male nor female, because “there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free” (Gal. 3:28): spiritual people, then, whether those who rule or those who obey, judge spiritually (1 Cor. 2:15).

They do not judge spiritual lights that shine in the firmament—for it is not right to judge such exalted authority. Nor do they judge your very Book, even if something in it does not shine clearly, since we submit our understanding to it and hold it certain that even what is hidden from our sight has been spoken rightly and truthfully.

For thus, although man is already spiritual and renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of the one who created him (Col. 3:10), yet as a doer of the law he must be, not its judge (Jas. 4:11). Nor does he judge that distinction between spiritual and carnal people who are known to your eyes, our God, but whose works have not yet appeared to us, so that we may know them by their fruits (Matt. 7:20). But you, Lord, already know them, have divided them, and have called them in secret before the firmament came to be.

Nor does the spiritual man judge the turbulent peoples of this world, although he is spiritual. [Note: Most manuscripts, with Arn., read “although” (quanquam); the other editions read “as though” (tanquam), while three manuscripts read “anyone” (quemquam).] For what business has he judging those who are outside (1 Cor. 5:12), when he does not know who among them will come into the sweetness of your grace and who will remain in the perpetual bitterness of impiety?

34. Therefore the man whom you made in your image did not receive authority over the lights of heaven, nor over heaven itself in its hiddenness, nor over the day and night that you called into being before the establishment of heaven, nor over the gathering of the waters, which is the sea. Rather, he received authority over the fish of the sea, the birds of the air, all cattle, the whole earth, and all creeping things that creep upon the earth.

For he judges: he approves what he finds right and rejects what he finds wrong—whether in the solemnity of the sacraments by which those whom your mercy searches out in many waters are initiated; or in that sacrament in which the fish is displayed, which the devout earth, raised from the deep, eats; or in the signs of words and utterances subject to the authority of your Book, flying as though beneath its firmament—interpreting, explaining, discussing, disputing, blessing, and invoking you, with signs bursting and sounding from the mouth, so that the people may respond, “Amen.”

The abyss of the world and the blindness of the flesh are the cause that all these utterances must be pronounced bodily; for thoughts cannot be seen, and therefore there must be noise in the ears. [Note: Lov. and the other editions, except Arn., read “badly” (male), as is clear from the manuscripts and the course of the sentence.] Thus, although the birds multiply over the earth, they nevertheless derive their origin from the waters.

The spiritual person also judges, approving what he finds right and rejecting what he finds wrong in the works and conduct of the faithful: in almsgiving, as in fruitful earth; and in the affections tamed from the living soul, in chastity, fasting, and pious thoughts concerning the things perceived through bodily sensation. For it is said that he now judges these things, in which he also has authority to correct.

### CHAPTER XXIV  
“And God blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply,’” etc. (Gen. 1:28).

35. But what is this, and what sort of mystery is it? Behold, you bless human beings, O Lord, so that they may increase and multiply and fill the earth. Do you give us no indication through this that we should understand something? Why did you not likewise bless the light that you called day, nor the firmament of heaven, nor the lights, nor the stars, nor the earth, nor the sea?

I would say, our God, who created us in your image, that you specifically intended to bestow this blessing upon man—if you had not in the same way blessed the fish and the great sea creatures so that they might increase and multiply, fill the waters of the sea, and so that the birds might multiply upon the earth.

Again, I would say that this blessing belonged to those kinds of things that propagate by generating from themselves, if I found it among shrubs, bushes, and the cattle of the earth. Yet it was not said to the grasses and trees, nor to the beasts and serpents, “Increase and multiply,” although these too, like fish, birds, and human beings, increase by generation and preserve their kind.

36. What, then, shall I say, my light, O Truth? That this is meaningless, that it was said in vain? By no means, Father of mercy; far be it from the servant of your Word to say this.

And if I do not understand what you signify by this utterance, let those who are better—that is, more understanding than I—use it more profitably, each according to the wisdom you have granted him, my God. Yet let my confession also please you in your sight: I confess to you that I believe, Lord, that you did not speak in vain, and I will not keep silent about what this reading suggests to me.

For it is true, and I see no obstacle to my understanding the figurative statements of your books in this way. I know that what is understood in the mind in one way may be signified bodily in many ways, and that what is signified bodily in one way may be understood mentally in many ways.

Behold the one simple love of God and neighbor, proclaimed bodily through how many sacraments, how many languages, and how many innumerable modes of expression in each language! Thus the offspring of the waters increase and multiply.

Consider again, whoever you are who read these words: behold what Scripture expresses in one way, and the voice utters, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). Is it not understood in many ways—not through the deceit of errors, but through the variety of true interpretations? Thus the offspring of human beings increase and multiply.

37. Therefore, if we consider the actual natures of things not allegorically but literally, the words “Increase and multiply” apply to everything generated from seeds. But if we treat these things as figurative—which I rather think Scripture intended, since it certainly did not gratuitously attribute this blessing only to the offspring of aquatic creatures and human beings—we do indeed find multitudes both in spiritual and bodily creatures, as in heaven and earth; in righteous and wicked souls, as in light and darkness; in the holy authors through whom the law was administered, as in the firmament established between water and water; in the society of embittered peoples, as in the sea; in the zeal of devout souls, as in the dry land; in works of mercy according to the present life, as in seed-bearing grasses and fruit-bearing trees; in spiritual gifts manifested for the benefit of others, as in the lights of heaven; and in affections formed toward self-restraint, as in the living soul.

In all these we find multitudes, abundance, and increase. But that something should increase and multiply so that one thing is expressed in many ways and one expression is understood in many ways—we find this only in bodily signs that are produced and in intelligible things conceived by the mind.

We understand bodily signs that have been produced as generations of the waters, because of the necessary causes of carnal depth; and intelligible things conceived by the mind as human generations, because of the fecundity of reason. Therefore we believe that you, Lord, said to both these kinds, “Increase and multiply.”

In this blessing I understand that you have granted us the power and capacity both to express in many ways what we have grasped as one meaning, and to understand in many ways what we have read expressed obscurely in one way.

Thus the waters of the sea are filled, though they are moved only by varied signs [Note: “Only by varied signs,” according to Dub., Mart., and Rond., with eleven manuscripts.]; thus the earth too is filled with human offspring, whose dryness appears in their zeal, and over whom reason rules.

### CHAPTER XXV  
“Behold, I have given you every herb … for food,” etc. (Gen. 1:29).

38. I also wish to say, Lord my God, what your Scripture, which follows, reminds me of; and I will say it without fear. I will speak the truth, you inspiring me with what you intended me to say through those words. For I do not believe that I speak truth under the inspiration of anyone other than you, since you are truth (John 14:6), while “every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11 [116:11]). Therefore “whoever speaks a lie speaks from his own” (John 8:44). So, in order to speak truth, I will speak from what is yours.

Behold, you have given us for food every seed-bearing grass that sows seed over all the earth, and every tree that has in itself the fruit of seed-bearing plants. You gave these not only to us, but also to all the birds of heaven, the beasts of the earth, and the serpents; but you did not give them to the fish and the great sea creatures.

For we said that these fruits of the earth signify, and are figured allegorically as, works of mercy that are offered from fruitful earth for the necessities of this life. Such an earth was the devout Onesiphorus, whose household you granted mercy, because he often refreshed your Paul and was not ashamed of his chain (2 Tim. 1:16).

The brothers did this too, and bore fruit of this kind—those who supplied what he lacked from Macedonia (2 Cor. 11:9). But how painful are certain trees that did not give him the fruit owed to him, where he says: “At my first defense no one stood by me, but all deserted me; may it not be counted against them” (2 Tim. 4:16)!

These things are owed to those who minister rational teaching through their understanding of divine mysteries, and they are owed to them as human beings. They are owed to them, however, as living souls, when they offer themselves for imitation in complete self-restraint. They are also owed to them as birds, because of their blessings, which multiply over the earth, since “their sound has gone out through all the earth” (Ps. 18:5 [19:4]).

### CHAPTER XXVI  
Pleasure and usefulness from a benefit bestowed upon one’s neighbor.

39. Those who rejoice in these foods are nourished by them; but those whose god is their belly do not rejoice in them. For even in those who provide these things, what they give is not the fruit, but the spirit in which they give it.

Therefore I clearly see where the one who served God rather than his own belly rejoices; I see it, and I rejoice greatly with him. He had received from the Philippians what they had sent through Epaphroditus; yet I see where he rejoices. He is nourished by that in which he rejoices, because, speaking in truth, he says: “I rejoiced greatly in the Lord, because now at last you have revived your concern for me, in which indeed you were concerned, but had lacked opportunity” (Phil. 4:10).

They had withered through prolonged weariness, and had, as it were, dried up with regard to this fruit of good works; and he rejoices that they have revived, not that they had relieved his need. Therefore he goes on to say: “Not that I speak because anything is lacking; for I have learned to be self-sufficient in whatever circumstances I am. I know how to be brought low, and I know how to abound. In everything and in all things I have been instructed, both to be filled and to hunger, both to abound and to suffer need. I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (ibid., 11–13).

40. “Therefore, in all things” [Note: The words “in all things” are omitted by Somm., Arn., and Mart. with seven manuscripts, and by Rond. with eleven manuscripts.] “you rejoice,” O great Paul? Where do you rejoice, from what are you nourished, you man renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created you, and living soul of such self-restraint, and flying tongue speaking mysteries? Such living creatures are owed this food.

What is it that nourishes you? Joy. Let us hear what follows. “Nevertheless,” he says, “you did well by sharing in my affliction.” Here he rejoices, here he is nourished: because they did him good, not because the distress of the one who says to you, “In tribulation you enlarged me” (Ps. 4:2 [4:1]), was relieved. For he knows both how to abound and how to suffer need in you who strengthen him.

“For you Philippians yourselves know,” he says, “that in the beginning of the Gospel, when I departed from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving except you alone; for even when I was in Thessalonica, you sent something for my needs once and again” (Phil. 4:14–16). He now rejoices that they have returned to these good works, and delights that they have revived like a field whose fertility has been restored.

41. Did he rejoice on account of his own needs, because he said, “You sent something for my needs”? Was that why he rejoiced? No. And how do we know this? Because he himself continues, saying: “Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the fruit” (ibid., 17). [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. add “abundant”; but this word is absent from the manuscripts and from Arn.]

From you, my God, I have learned to distinguish between the gift and the fruit. The gift is the thing itself that the giver gives when he supplies necessities—such as money, food, drink, clothing, shelter, or assistance. But the fruit is the giver’s good and upright intention.

For the good Teacher did not say merely, “Whoever receives a prophet,” but added, “in the name of a prophet.” Nor did he say merely, “Whoever receives a righteous person,” but added, “in the name of a righteous person.” Thus the one will receive a prophet’s reward, and the other a righteous person’s reward.

Nor did he say merely, “Whoever gives one of my little ones a cup of cold water to drink,” but added, “only in the name of a disciple.” And so he continued: “Truly I say to you, he shall not lose his reward” (Matt. 10:41–42).

The gift is receiving a prophet, receiving a righteous person, or offering a cup of cold water to a disciple. But the fruit is doing these things in the name of a prophet, in the name of a righteous person, and in the name of a disciple.

Elijah is nourished by the fruit of the widow who knew that she was nourishing a man of God, and nourished him for that reason; but by what was given through the raven he was nourished [Note: 1 Kings 17:6]. It was not the inner Elijah who was nourished, but the outer one, who could even be corrupted by a lack of such food.

### CHAPTER XXVII  
What is signified by the fish and the great sea creatures.

42. Therefore I will say what is true before you, Lord. When ignorant and unbelieving people—for whom the sacraments of initiation and the great miracles that we believe are signified by the names of fish and great sea creatures are necessary for their initiation and conversion—receive your children for bodily refreshment or to be helped in some need of the present life, while they do not know why this should be done or to what it pertains, neither do those people nourish these children nor are the children nourished by them.

For neither do the former perform these things with a holy and upright intention, nor do the latter rejoice in what the former give, since they do not yet see the fruit. The soul is nourished by that in which it rejoices. Therefore fish and great sea creatures do not feed on foods produced only by the earth after it has been separated and set apart from the bitterness of the waves of the sea.

### CHAPTER XXVIII  
“And God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good,” etc. (Gen. 1:31).

43. And you saw, O God, everything that you had made, and behold, it was very good; for we too saw them [Note: The manuscripts read “we see.” Mart., Flor., and Rond., with several manuscripts, agree with this reading.], and behold, everything was very good.

In each kind of your works, when you had commanded that it should come to be and it had come to be, you saw this and that [Note: Lov. reads, “you saw this and another.”] because it was good. I counted seven times that it is written that you saw that what you had made was good; and this is the eighth, because you saw everything that you had made. And behold, it was not merely good, but very good, as though all things were seen together.

For individually they were only good; together they were both good and very good. This is also said of beautiful bodies: the body composed of all beautiful members is much more beautiful than the individual members themselves, whose most orderly union completes the whole, although those members too are beautiful individually.

### CHAPTER XXIX  
How it should be understood that God saw eight times that his works were good.

44. I paid attention in order to discover whether you saw seven or eight times that your works were good when they pleased you. In your vision I found no times by which I could understand that you saw what you made so many times, and I said:

“O Lord, surely your Scripture is true, since you who are truthful and truth produced it? Why, then, do you tell me that there are no times in your vision, while your Scripture tells me that on each day you saw the things you had made and that they were good? And when I counted them, I found how many times.”

To this you reply to me—for you are my God—and you speak with a strong voice in the inner ear of your servant, breaking through my deafness and crying out:

“O man, surely what my Scripture says, I say. Yet it speaks temporally, whereas no time befalls my Word, because it abides in equal eternity with me. What you see through my Spirit, I see; what you say through my Spirit, I say. And so, when you see these things temporally, I do not see them temporally; just as, when you say them temporally, I do not say them temporally.”

### CHAPTER XXX  
The ravings of the Manichaeans.

45. And I heard, Lord my God, and I tasted a drop of sweetness from your truth. I understood that there are certain people who are displeased with your works, and who say that you made many things under compulsion, such as the structures of heaven and the arrangements of the stars.

They say that these things were not created from you, but had already been created elsewhere and from another source; that you drew them together, joined them, and wove them together when you were constructing the ramparts of the world out of conquered enemies, so that, bound by that construction, they could not rebel against you again. [Note: “Bound” (devincti) is to be read according to the English manuscripts; Mart. and Rond., with three M manuscripts, read “conquered” (devicti).]

Other things, they say, you neither made nor joined together at all, such as all flesh, the tiniest living creatures, and whatever holds fast to the earth by its roots. Rather, they say that a hostile mind and another nature—not created by you and opposed to you—begets and forms these things in the lower regions of the world.

They say these things in their madness because they do not see your works through your Spirit, nor do they know you in them.

### CHAPTER XXXI  
The godly approve what has pleased God.

46. But those who see them through your Spirit—you see in them. Therefore, when they see that they are good, you see that they are good; and whatever pleases them for your sake, you are pleased with in them [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read “you are pleased together with them.”]; and what pleases us through your Spirit pleases you in us.

“For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. But,” he says, “we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:11–12).

And I am reminded to say: Certainly no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. How, then, do we too know the things given to us by God? The answer is made to me: Even with regard to the things we know through his Spirit, no one knows them except the Spirit of God.

For just as it is rightly said, “It is not you who speak” (Matt. 10:20), to those who speak in the Spirit of God, so it is rightly said, “It is not you who know,” to those who know in the Spirit of God. Likewise, then, it is rightly said, “It is not you who see,” to those who see in the Spirit of God.

Whatever they see in the Spirit of God to be good, therefore, is not seen by them but by God as good. It is one thing for someone to think that what is good is evil, as were those mentioned above; another thing for a human being to see that what is good is good, as many people are pleased by your creation because it is good, though you yourself do not please them in it, so that they prefer to enjoy it rather than you.

But it is another thing when, as a human being sees something to be good, God sees in it that it is good: namely, that the one who made it is loved in what he made—one who would not be loved except through the Holy Spirit whom he has given. For “the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Through him we see that whatever in any way exists is good; for it comes from the one who does not merely exist in some way, but who is what he is [Note: “But he is what he is,” according to four manuscripts cited by Mart.].

### CHAPTER XXXII  
A summary account of the works of God.

47. Thanks be to you, Lord. We see heaven and earth, whether the upper and lower bodily regions, or spiritual and bodily creation. And in the adornment [Note: “For the adornment,” according to three manuscripts cited by Mart.] of these regions, from which the entire mass of the world—or creation as a whole—is composed, we see light made and divided from darkness.

We see the firmament of heaven: whether it is between the higher spiritual waters and the lower bodily waters, the primary body of the world (Book 2 of the Retractions, chapter 6, §2); or this expanse of air, which is also called heaven, through which the birds of heaven wander among the waters carried above them like vapor, which sprinkle them even on clear nights with dew, and among those waters that float heavily upon the earth.

We see the appearance of the gathered waters spread across the plains of the sea, and the dry land, either laid bare or formed so as to be visible and ordered, together with the substance of grasses and trees.

We see the lights shining above: the sun sufficient for the day, the moon and stars consoling the night, and all these marking and signifying times.

We see the moist nature everywhere, made fertile with fish, beasts, and birds; for the corporeal substance of the air, which bears the flight of birds, is condensed by the exhalation of the waters.

We see the face of the earth adorned with terrestrial animals, and man, made in your image and likeness, placed above all irrational living creatures by that very image and likeness of yours—that is, by the power of reason and understanding.

And just as in his soul one thing rules by deliberating while another is subjected in order to obey, so also woman was made bodily for man: she has in her mind a nature equal in rational understanding, yet in bodily sex she is subjected to the male sex in the same way that the appetite for action is subjected to reason, in order to conceive from the mind’s reason the skill of acting rightly.

We see these things, each good and all very good.

### CHAPTER XXXIII  
Everything made either from nothing or from created matter.

48. Let your works praise you, so that we may love you; and let us love you [Note: English manuscripts read, “and may we be loved by you,”] so that your works may praise you—works that have a beginning and an end in time, a rising and a setting, progress and decline, form and deprivation.

They therefore have a succession of morning and evening, partly hidden and partly evident. For they were made by you from nothing, not from you, nor from some substance that was not yours [Note: So read the manuscripts and Arn.; but Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. have, “not from you some substance that was not yours,” or similar wording.], or that had previously existed, but from matter created together with them—that is, created by you at the same time—for you formed its formlessness without any interval of time.

For the matter of heaven and earth is one thing, and the form of heaven and earth another. You made the matter wholly from nothing, and the form of the world from formless matter; yet you made both simultaneously, so that form followed matter without any interval of delay.

### CHAPTER XXXIV  
The allegorical exposition of the whole creation of the world.

49. We also considered on whose account you willed these things to be made in such an order or written in such an order, and we saw that each was good and all were very good—in your Word, in your Only-Begotten: heaven and earth, the head and body of the Church, in predestination before all times, without morning or evening.

But when you began to execute temporally what had been predestined, so that you might reveal hidden things and bring our disordered condition into order—for our sins were upon us, and we had gone away from you into a dark abyss, while your good Spirit hovered above us to help us at the proper time—you justified the ungodly and separated them from the unrighteous.

You established the authority of your Book between those above who were teachable by you and those below who were subject to them. You gathered the fellowship of the unbelievers into one conspiracy, so that the zeal of the faithful might become apparent and works of mercy might be performed for you, as they distributed earthly resources even to the poor in order to acquire heavenly ones.

From this you kindled certain lights in the firmament—your saints, possessing the word of life and shining with lofty authority, exalted by spiritual gifts. From this same source, for the instruction of unbelieving nations, you produced from bodily matter visible sacraments and miracles, together with verbal utterances according to the firmament of your Book, by which the faithful too would be blessed.

Then you formed the living soul of the faithful through ordered affections and the strength of self-restraint [Note: The Codex Benignianus reads, “you strengthened.”]. From this same soul you renewed the mind subjected to you alone, needing no human authority for imitation, according to your image and likeness. And you subjected rational action to superior understanding, as woman is subjected to man.

You willed all your ministries necessary for perfecting the faithful in this life to be furnished by those same faithful for temporal uses, as fruitful works for the future.

We see all these things, and they are very good, because you see them in us—you who gave us the Spirit by which we would see them and love you in them.

### CHAPTER XXXV  
He desires peace.

50. Lord God, grant us peace—for you have supplied everything for us: the peace of rest, the peace of the Sabbath, the Sabbath without evening [Note: It is clearly to be read this way with the Albinensis codex, not, as most printed and manuscript copies have it, “peace without evening.”].

For this whole most beautiful order of very good things, once its appointed courses have been completed, will pass away; and morning has indeed come to be in them, and evening.

### CHAPTER XXXVI  
Why evening does not follow the seventh day.

51. But the seventh day is without evening and has no setting, because you sanctified it for everlasting permanence, so that what you did after your very good works—although you made them while remaining at rest, you rested on the seventh day—might by this word of your Book announce beforehand to us that, after our works, which are very good precisely because you granted them to us, we too may rest in you on the Sabbath of eternal life.

### CHAPTER XXXVII  
When God will rest in us.

52. For even then you will rest in us in the manner in which you now work in us; and your rest through us will be such as your works through us are. Yet you, Lord, are always at work and always at rest. You do not see for a time, nor are you moved for a time, nor do you rest for a time; and yet you bring about temporal visions, time itself, and rest arising from time. [Note: [Col. 0868] Here the editions, except the Arnaldine, insert the words “nor do you work for a time”; these are absent from most manuscript codices.]

### CHAPTER XXXVIII. God sees created things differently from human beings

53. Accordingly, we see these things that you have made because they exist; but they exist because you see them. We see outwardly that they exist, and inwardly that they are good; but you saw them made there where you saw them to be made. We were moved at one time to do good, after our heart had conceived from your Spirit; but at an earlier time we were moved to do evil, abandoning you. You, however, good God, never ceased doing good.

There are some good works of ours, indeed gifts from you, but they are not eternal. After them we hope to rest in your great sanctification. But you, who are good and need no good, are always at rest, because your rest is yourself. And who among human beings will give this understanding to another human being? What angel to an angel? What angel to a human being? Let it be sought from you, sought in you, knocked for at you: thus, yes thus, it will be received; thus it will be found; thus it will be opened (Matthew 7:8). Amen.

[Col. 0867]

## The Two Books of the Soliloquies of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo

[Note: [Col. 0869] Written at the beginning of the year of Christ 387.]

[Note: [Col. 0869] Collated against the manuscripts of Thuaneus, Victorinus, Navarricus, two Sorbonic manuscripts, Regio-Montensis, Audoenensis, Medardensis, one from the monastery of Vendôme, the Vatican manuscript, Vedastinus, and five English manuscripts—namely, the Bodleian, two Merton manuscripts, and two Cambridge manuscripts—and against the readings of five Belgian manuscripts collected by the Louvain scholars; also against the editions of Bad., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0869] We also compared all those editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.]

(C)

## Notice concerning the following two books of the *Soliloquies*

[Note: [Col. 0867] In the Benedictine edition these follow the books *On Order*; but we have transferred them here because, in their vivid expressions of devotion, they are more closely related to the nature of the *Confessions*. M.]

[Note: [Col. 0867] See Book 1, chapter 4, of the *Retractations*, cols. 589–590, from the words “Among these I wrote,” no. 1, through the words of no. 4, “Various things with me.” M.]

When Augustine undertook this work, he was still staying in the countryside at Cassiciacum, as appears from *Confessions* 9.4; and he was in his thirty-third year, as he himself testifies here in Book 1, chapter 10. It therefore seems that it should be assigned to the beginning of the year of Christ 387, unless someone should wish, with the other works so far catalogued, to assign it to the end of the preceding year.

In the first book he portrays himself vividly, adopting a new but extremely familiar method in order to teach what the person ought to be like who desires to pursue knowledge of God and of the soul. He speaks first of the need to secure the health of the mind through the aid of faith, hope, and charity; and he shows that the mind’s eye, once purified from every desire for lower things, cannot safely be raised to that sun, much less fixed upon it. The second book is concerned entirely with demonstrating that truth can never perish; from this the immortality of the soul itself, which is the seat of truth, is inferred.

## BOOK ONE

Augustine himself trains himself to pursue knowledge of God and of the soul. First he implores divine assistance; then, having recognized the excellence of the knowledge he desires, he converses with himself about advancing the health of his soul, so that at last he may safely rise to contemplate God. At the end of the book he gathers together the conclusion that whatever truly exists is immortal.

[Col. 0869]

### CHAPTER I. Prayer to God

[Col. 0869]

1. As I had long been turning over many and various matters within myself, and for many days had been diligently seeking myself and my good, and what evil ought to be avoided, suddenly someone—whether I myself or someone else from outside, or from within, I do not know, for this very thing is what I am striving most earnestly to discover—said to me:

[Note: [Col. 0869] R. signifies Reason; A., Augustine.]

**Reason:** Look: suppose you have actually found something. To whom will you entrust it, so that you may proceed to other things?

**Augustine:** To memory, of course.

**Reason:** Is it so great that it will preserve everything you have thought out well?

**Augustine:** It is difficult—indeed, impossible.

**Reason:** Then it must be written down. But what will you do, since your health refuses the labor of writing? Nor should these matters be dictated, for they require complete solitude.

**Augustine:** You speak truly. And so I simply do not know what to do.

**Reason:** Pray for the health and assistance by which you may reach what you desire, and commit this very matter to writing, so that through your offspring you may become more courageous. Then briefly gather what you discover into a few concise conclusions. Do not concern yourself now with inviting a crowd of readers; these things will be enough for a few of your fellow citizens.

**Augustine:** I shall do so.

2. God, creator of the universe, grant me first that I may ask you rightly; next, that I may conduct myself as one worthy to be heard by you; and finally, that you may set me free.

God, through whom all things that would not exist of themselves tend toward existence.

God, who do not permit even that which destroys other things to be destroyed.

God, who created this world from nothing, this world that all eyes perceive as exceedingly beautiful.

God, who do not make evil, yet cause it to exist so that it may not become the worst thing.

God, who show to the few who flee for refuge to what truly exists that evil is nothing.

God, through whom the universe is perfect even with its left or inferior part.

God, from whom there is no discord to the very end, since inferior things harmonize with superior things.

God, whom everything that can love loves, whether knowingly or unknowingly.

God, in whom all things are, yet for whom the ugliness of the whole creation is not ugly, wickedness does no harm, and error does not err.

God, who have willed that none know the truth unless purified.

God, Father of truth, Father of wisdom, Father of true and supreme life, Father of blessedness, Father of good and beautiful things, Father of intelligible light, Father of our awakening and illumination, Father of the pledge by which we are admonished to return to you.

3. I call upon you, God Truth, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that are true are true.

God Wisdom, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that possess wisdom are wise.

God, true and supreme Life, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that truly and supremely live have life.

God Blessedness, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that are blessed are blessed.

God, Good and Beautiful, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that are good and beautiful are good and beautiful.

God, intelligible Light, in whom, from whom, and through whom all things that shine intelligibly shine.

God whose kingdom is the whole world, which the senses do not perceive.

God from whose kingdom the law is also prescribed for these earthly kingdoms.

God, from whom to turn away is to fall; toward whom to turn is to rise again; in whom to remain is to stand firm.

God, from whom to depart is to die; to whom to return is to come back to life; in whom to dwell is to live.

God, whom no one loses except by deception; whom no one seeks except when admonished; whom no one finds except when purified.

God, to abandon whom is the same as perishing; to attend to whom is the same as loving; to see whom is the same as possessing.

God, to whom faith rouses us, hope raises us, and charity joins us—God, through whom we overcome the enemy, I beseech you.

God, through whom we have received [Note: [Col. 0870] In seven of the better manuscripts: “God, whom we have received.”] that we should not perish altogether.

God, by whom we are admonished to keep watch.

God, through whom we distinguish good from evil.

God, through whom we flee evils and pursue goods.

God, through whom we do not yield to adversities.

God, through whom we serve well and rule well.

[Col. 0871]

God, through whom we learn that the things we once thought ours are alien, and that the things we once thought alien are ours.

God, through whom we do not cling to the foods and enticements of evil things.

God, through whom small things do not diminish us.

God, through whom our better part is not subjected to what is worse.

God, through whom death is swallowed up in victory (1 Corinthians 15:54).

God, who convert us.

God, who strip us of what is not and clothe us with what is.

God, who make us worthy to be heard.

God, who fortify us. [Note: [Col. 0871] Seven manuscripts read: “God, who make us one.”]

God, who lead us into all truth.

God, who speak all good things to us, neither making us insane nor permitting anyone to make us so.

God, who call us back to the way.

God, who lead us to the door.

God, who cause the door to be opened to those who knock (Matthew 7:8).

God, who give us the bread of life.

God, through whom we thirst for the drink which, once drunk, leaves us never thirsty again (John 6:35).

God, who convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment (John 16:8).

God, through whom those who do not believe at all do not move us.

God, through whom we condemn the error of those who think that the merits of souls count for nothing with you.

God, through whom we do not serve weak and beggarly elements (Galatians 4:9).

God, who purify us and prepare us for divine rewards, come to me in mercy.

4. Whatever I have said, you are the one God. Come, come to my aid: one eternal, true substance, in which there is no disagreement, no confusion, no change, no need, no death.

Where there is supreme harmony, supreme clarity, supreme constancy, supreme fullness, supreme life.

Where nothing is lacking, nothing excessive.

Where the one who begets and the one begotten are one. [Note: [Col. 0871] See *Retractations* 1.4.3.]

God, whom all things that serve serve, whom every good soul obeys.

By whose laws the heavens revolve, the stars complete their courses, the sun governs the day, and the moon regulates the night; and the whole world, through days by the alternation of light and darkness; through months by the waxing and waning of the moon; through years by the succession of spring, summer, autumn, and winter; through lustrums by the completion of the sun’s course; through great cycles by the return of the stars to their risings, preserves, so far as sensible matter permits, the great constancy of things through the ordered sequence and repetition of times.

God, by whose laws, established throughout eternity, the unstable motion of changeable things is not permitted to become disordered, and by whose reins the revolving ages are continually recalled to an image of stability; by whose laws the soul possesses free choice, while rewards for the good and punishments for the wicked are distributed by fixed necessities throughout all things.

God, from whom all goods flow to us, and by whom all evils are restrained by us.

God, above whom there is nothing, outside whom there is nothing, without whom there is nothing.

God, beneath whom everything is, in whom everything is, with whom everything is.

You who made the human being according to your image and likeness—something which the person who knows himself recognizes.

Hear me, hear me, hear me, my God, my Lord, my king, my father, my cause, my hope, my possession, my honor, my home, my homeland, my salvation, my light, my life. Hear me, hear me, hear me in that manner of yours known to few.

[Col. 0872]

5. Now I love you alone, follow you alone, seek you alone, and am ready to serve you alone, because you alone rule justly; I desire to belong to you. Command, I beg you, and order whatever you will, but heal and open my ears, that I may hear your voices. Heal and open my eyes, that I may see your signs. Drive madness from me, so that I may recognize you. Tell me where I should direct my attention, that I may look upon you, and I hope to do everything you command.

Receive, I beg you, your fugitive, Lord, most merciful Father. By now I have suffered punishments enough; I have served your enemies, whom you hold beneath your feet, long enough; I have been the plaything of deceits long enough. Receive me, your servant, fleeing from those things, for they too received me as an alien when I was fleeing from you.

I perceive that I must return to you. May your door be opened to me as I knock; teach me how one reaches you. I have nothing but willingness; I know nothing except that transient and perishable things must be despised, and that what is certain and eternal must be sought.

I do this, Father, because this alone I know; but I do not know how one reaches you. Suggest it to me, show it to me, provide me with provisions for the journey. If those who flee for refuge to you find you through faith, give me faith; if through virtue, give me virtue; if through knowledge, give me knowledge. Increase faith in me, increase hope, increase charity. O your wondrous and singular goodness!

6. I hasten toward you, and from you again I ask by what means one hastens toward you. For if you abandon a person, that person perishes; but you do not abandon, because you are the supreme good, which no one rightly sought and failed to find. Everyone, however, has sought rightly whom you have made to seek rightly.

Make me seek you, Father; rescue me from error. As I seek you, let nothing else present itself in place of you. If I desire nothing except you, may I find you now, I beg you, Father.

But if there is in me a desire for anything superfluous, cleanse me yourself and make me fit to see you. As for the health of this mortal body of mine, so long as I do not know what benefit may come from it either to me or to those whom I love, I entrust it to you, most wise and best Father; and concerning it I shall pray for whatever you may indicate for the time being.

I ask only this of your supremely excellent mercy: that you turn me wholly toward yourself, and make nothing resist me as I strive toward you. Command that, while I bear and inhabit this body, I may be pure, magnanimous, just, and prudent; a perfect lover and apprehender of your wisdom; worthy of inhabiting, and an inhabitant of, your most blessed kingdom. Amen, amen.

### CHAPTER II. What must be loved

7. **Augustine:** Look: I have prayed to God.

**Reason:** What, then, do you wish to know?

**Augustine:** All these very things for which I prayed.

**Reason:** Gather them briefly.

**Augustine:** I desire to know God and the soul.

**Reason:** Nothing more?

**Augustine:** Nothing at all.

**Reason:** Then begin to inquire. But first explain how, if God were demonstrated to you, you could say, “That is enough.”

**Augustine:** I do not know how he ought to be demonstrated to me for me to say, “That is enough.” For I do not believe that I know anything in the manner in which I desire to know God.

**Reason:** What, then, shall we do? Do you not think that you must first know how it is enough for you to know God, so that when you have reached that point you will seek no further?

**Augustine:** I do think so; but I do not see how it can be done. For what have I ever understood that resembles God, so that I could say, “In the manner in which I understand this, so I wish to understand God”?

**Reason:** You do not yet know God. How, then, do you know that you know nothing resembling God?

**Augustine:** Because if I knew something resembling God, I would undoubtedly love it. But now I love nothing except God and the soul, neither of which I know.

**Reason:** Then you do not love your friends?

**Augustine:** How could I, loving the soul, not love them?

**Reason:** In that case, do you also love fleas and bedbugs?

**Augustine:** I said that I love the soul, not animals.

**Reason:** Either human beings are not your friends, or you do not love them; for every human being is an animal, and you said that you do not love animals.

**Augustine:** They are human beings, and I love them—not insofar as they are animals, but insofar as they are human beings; that is, insofar as they possess rational souls, which I love even in robbers. I may love reason in anyone, while rightly hating the person who misuses what I love. Accordingly, I love my friends all the more as they make better use of their rational soul—or at least as much as they desire to use it well.

### CHAPTER III. Knowledge of God

8. **Reason:** I accept that. Yet if someone said to you, “I shall make you know God in the way in which you know Alypius,” would you not give thanks and say, “That is enough”?

**Augustine:** I would indeed give thanks, but I would not say that it was enough.

**Reason:** Why, please?

**Augustine:** Because I do not know God even in the way in which I know Alypius, and yet I do not know Alypius sufficiently.

**Reason:** See, then, whether you do not presumptuously wish to know God sufficiently, when you do not know Alypius sufficiently.

**Augustine:** That does not follow. For, compared with the stars, what is cheaper than my dinner? Yet I do not know what I shall dine on tomorrow; whereas I do not presumptuously claim to know under which constellation the moon will be tomorrow.

**Reason:** Then is it enough for you to know God in the way in which you know under which constellation the moon will travel tomorrow?

**Augustine:** It is not enough, for I establish that by the senses. But I do not know whether God, or some hidden cause of nature, might suddenly alter the moon’s order and course. If that happened, everything I had assumed would be false.

**Reason:** And do you believe that this could happen?

**Augustine:** I do not believe it. But I am asking what I know, not what I believe. Everything that we know may perhaps rightly be said also to be believed; but not everything that we believe is also known.

**Reason:** Then in this matter do you reject all testimony of the senses?

**Augustine:** I reject it entirely.

**Reason:** What, then? That familiar friend of yours whom you said you still do not know—do you wish to know him by sense or by intellect?

**Augustine:** By sense, certainly, whatever I know in him—if indeed anything is known by sense—is both trivial and sufficient. But that part by which he is my friend, namely the soul itself, I desire to grasp by the intellect.

**Reason:** Can it be known otherwise?

**Augustine:** In no way.

**Reason:** Then do you dare to say that your very close and familiar friend is unknown to you?

**Augustine:** Why should I not dare? I consider that law of friendship most just by which it is prescribed that each person should love a friend neither less nor more than himself. Therefore, since I do not know myself, how could I insult someone whom I have said is unknown to me—especially since, as I believe, he does not even know himself?

**Reason:** If, then, the things you wish to know belong to the class grasped by the intellect, when I said that you presumptuously wished to know God while not knowing Alypius, you should not have brought forward your dinner and the moon as similar examples, if, as you said, these pertain to the senses.

### CHAPTER IV. What certain knowledge is

9. But what does that matter to us? Now answer this: if what Plato and Plotinus said about God is true, is it enough for you to know God in the way in which they knew him?

**Augustine:** Not necessarily. Even if what they said is true, it does not follow that they knew what they said. Many people speak at length about what they do not know. I myself said that I wished to know everything for which I prayed—something I would not desire if I already knew it. Was I therefore any less able to say those things? I said not what I had comprehended intellectually, but what I had gathered from various sources and committed to memory, assigning to it as much faith as I could. But knowing is something else.

**Reason:** Tell me, please: do you at least know, in geometry, what a line is?

**Augustine:** I certainly know that.

**Reason:** And in making that claim you are not afraid of the Academics?

**Augustine:** Not entirely. They did not wish the wise person to err; but I am not wise. Therefore I am not yet afraid to claim knowledge of things I know. If, as I desire, I attain wisdom, I shall do what they advised.

**Reason:** I object to nothing. But, to continue the inquiry I had begun: just as you know a line, do you also know the body they call a sphere?

**Augustine:** I do.

**Reason:** Do you know both equally, or do you know one more or less than the other?

**Augustine:** Entirely equally. For in neither case am I deceived.

**Reason:** Did you apprehend these things through the senses or through the intellect?

**Augustine:** Rather, I have found the senses to be like a ship in this matter. For when they had carried me to the place toward which I was heading, I dismissed them; and once I had been placed, as it were, on solid ground, I began to turn these matters over in thought, yet for a long time my footsteps tottered. Therefore it seems to me that one can navigate on land sooner than geometry can be apprehended by the senses, although the senses may appear to help beginners somewhat at first.

**Reason:** Then, whatever knowledge of these disciplines you possess, do you have no hesitation in calling it knowledge?

**Augustine:** No—if the Stoics allow it, for they grant knowledge to no one except the wise person. I do not deny that I possess an apprehension of these things, which they concede even to folly; but I am not afraid of them either. I firmly possess the knowledge about which you have asked. Continue; let me see where you are going with this.

**Reason:** Do not hurry; we have leisure. Take this attentively, so that you do not rashly concede anything. I am trying to make you rejoice in matters whose uncertainty you need not fear at all—and, as though it were a small matter, you order me to plunge ahead?

**Augustine:** May God bring it about as you say. So ask at your discretion, and rebuke me more severely if I ever do anything of that kind again.

10. **Reason:** Then it is clear to you that a line cannot in any way be split lengthwise into two lines?

**Augustine:** Clear.

**Reason:** What about transversely?

**Augustine:** What else but that it can be divided infinitely?

**Reason:** Is it equally clear that a sphere cannot, from any part at a distance from its center, have even two equal circles?

**Augustine:** Entirely equally clear.

**Reason:** What about a line and a sphere? Do they seem to you to be one thing, or do they differ in some respect?

**Augustine:** Who does not see that they differ very greatly?

**Reason:** But if you know this and that equally, and yet, as you admit, they differ greatly from one another, is knowledge of different things therefore undifferentiated?

**Augustine:** Who has denied it?

**Reason:** You did a little earlier. When I asked how you wished to know God so that you could say, “That is enough,” you replied that you could not explain this because you had apprehended nothing resembling the way in which you wished to apprehend God—for you knew nothing resembling God. What, then, now? Are a line and a sphere similar?

**Augustine:** Who would say that?

**Reason:** But I had asked not what you knew that was similar, but what you knew in the manner in which you desire to know God. For you know a line in the same manner as you know a sphere, although a line is not constituted in the same way as a sphere. Therefore answer whether it is enough for you to know God in the way in which you know that geometrical sphere—that is, to have no more doubt about God than about it.

### CHAPTER V. Equal or identical knowledge of dissimilar things

11. **Augustine:** I beg you: although you press and convict me very forcefully, I still do not dare to say that I wish to know God in the way in which I know these things. Not only do the things themselves seem dissimilar to me; the knowledge itself also seems dissimilar.

First, a line and a sphere do not differ so greatly that their cognition is not contained within one discipline; but no geometer has ever professed to teach God. Further, if knowledge of God and knowledge of these things were equal, I would rejoice as much that I know these things as I anticipate rejoicing once I know God. But now I hold these things in very low esteem in comparison with him, so that sometimes it seems to me that, if I understand him and see him in the manner in which he can be seen, all these things will perish from my knowledge. Indeed, now, out of love for him, they scarcely come to mind.

**Reason:** Let us grant that you will rejoice much more—indeed, incomparably more—in knowing God than in knowing these things. Yet this results from a dissimilarity of the things, not of the understanding, unless perhaps you look upon the earth with one kind of sight and upon the clear sky with another, even though the sight of the latter delights you much more than that of the former.

If the eyes are not deceived, I believe that, when asked whether it is as certain to you that you see the earth as that you see the sky, you ought to answer that it is equally certain, although you do not rejoice as much in the beauty and brilliance of the earth as in those of the sky.

**Augustine:** I admit that this comparison moves me, and I am led to agree that, to the degree that the earth differs from the sky in its own class, so those true and certain objects of the disciplines differ from the intelligible majesty of God.

### CHAPTER VI. The senses of the soul by which it perceives God

12. **Reason:** You are rightly moved. For the reason speaking with you promises to demonstrate God to your mind in the way in which the sun is demonstrated to your eyes. The senses of the mind are, as it were, the eyes of the soul. [Note: [Col. 0875] Louvain reads: “For minds are, as it were, senses for souls.” The other editions likewise read essentially the same, except that Bad. has “of the mind,” while Am. and Er. have “of the soul.”]

The most certain objects of the disciplines, however, are like those things illuminated by the sun so that they can be seen, such as the earth and all earthly things. God himself, on the other hand, is the one who illuminates. I, reason, am to minds what sight is to eyes.

For having eyes is not the same as looking; nor is looking the same as seeing. Therefore the soul requires three things in order to possess eyes with which it can already make good use of them: that it look, and that it see.

The healthy eyes are the mind, pure from every bodily stain—that is, already withdrawn and cleansed from desires for mortal things. Nothing supplies this to it except faith, first of all. For what cannot yet be demonstrated to it because it is polluted and sick with vices—since it cannot see unless it is healthy—will not attend to its own healing if it does not believe that otherwise it cannot see.

But what if it does believe that things are as they are said to be, and that, if it becomes able to see, it will see in this way, yet despairs of being healed? Does it not then cast itself down and despise itself entirely, and refuse to obey the physician’s instructions?

**Augustine:** Entirely so, especially since the illness must experience those instructions as harsh.

**Reason:** Then hope must be added to faith.

**Augustine:** I believe so.

**Reason:** What if it both believes that everything is as described and hopes that it can be healed, but does not love or desire the light that is promised? What if it thinks that for the time being it ought to be content with its darkness, which has already become pleasant through habit? Does it not nevertheless reject that physician?

**Augustine:** Entirely so.

**Reason:** Then a third thing, charity, is necessary.

**Augustine:** Nothing is at all more necessary.

**Reason:** Without these three, then, the soul is not healed so that it may see its God—that is, understand him.

13. When it has healthy eyes, what remains?

**Augustine:** That it look.

**Reason:** The soul’s act of looking is reason. But since it does not follow that everyone who looks also sees, a right and perfect act of looking—that is, one followed by vision—is called virtue. For virtue is either right or perfect reason.

Yet the act of looking itself, although its eyes are already healthy, cannot turn them toward the light unless those three things remain: faith, by which it believes that the reality toward which the gaze must be turned is such that, once seen, it makes one blessed; hope, by which, after looking well, it anticipates that it will see; and charity, by which it desires to see and enjoy.

Vision itself then follows the act of looking: the vision of God, who is the goal of looking—not because he is not already present, but because there is nothing further toward which the gaze may be directed. This is truly perfect virtue: reason arriving at its end, followed by the blessed life.

Vision itself, moreover, is that understanding which exists in the soul and which is constituted from the one who understands and the thing understood; just as what is called seeing with the eyes is constituted from the sense itself and the sensible object, without either of which nothing can be seen.

### CHAPTER VII. How long faith, hope, and charity are necessary

14. When it happens, then, that the soul sees God—that is, understands God—let us see whether those three things are still necessary for it.

Why should faith be necessary when it already sees? Why should hope likewise be necessary, since it already possesses what it hoped for? But nothing will be taken away from charity; rather, much will be added. For when it sees that singular and true beauty, it will love it more; and unless it fixes its eye upon it with immense love and never turns away from contemplating it, it will not be able to remain in that most blessed vision.

But while the soul is in this body, even if it sees—or understands—God most fully, nevertheless, since the bodily senses also exercise their proper function, although they indeed have no power to deceive, they nevertheless are not altogether without force for preventing doubt. [Note: [Col. 0876] So the manuscripts. The editions read: “They exercise their proper function, which, although it has no power to deceive, nevertheless does not do nothing; it can.”]

Thus faith may still be said to be that by which the soul resists them and believes that the other reality is true.

Likewise, in this life, although the soul is already blessed when it understands God, nevertheless, because it endures many bodily troubles, it must hope that after death none of these inconveniences will remain. Therefore hope does not abandon the soul while it is in this life.

But when, after this life, it has gathered itself wholly into God, charity remains, by which it is held there. For it should not be said to have faith that those things are true when it is troubled by no interruption from falsehood; nor does anything remain for it to hope for, since it possesses everything securely.

Three things, then, pertain to the soul: that it be healthy, that it look, and that it see. The other three—faith, hope, and charity—are always necessary for the first and second of those three; but for the third, they are all necessary in this life, while after this life only charity remains.

### CHAPTER VIII. What is necessary for knowing God

15. Now accept, insofar as the present moment requires, something about God that I am teaching you from that comparison with sensible things. God is intelligible, and those objects of the disciplines are also intelligible; yet they differ greatly.

The earth and the light are both visible, but the earth cannot be seen unless it is illuminated by the light. Therefore, concerning those things taught in the disciplines, which anyone who understands admits without hesitation to be most true, we must believe that they cannot be understood unless they are illuminated by another light, as it were their own sun.

Thus, just as in this sun one may observe three things—that it exists, that it shines, and that it illuminates—so in that most hidden God whom you wish to understand there are three things: that he is, that he is understood, and that he makes other things understood.

I dare to teach you how to understand these two things, namely yourself and God. But answer: how have you received them—as probable or as true?

**Augustine:** Clearly as probable; and, it must be admitted, I have risen into greater hope. For apart from those two matters concerning the line and the sphere, you have said nothing that I dare claim to know.

**Reason:** That is not surprising. Nothing has yet been set forth in such a way that an apprehension of it can rightly be demanded from you.

### CHAPTER IX. Love of ourselves

16. But why do we delay? The journey must be undertaken. Yet let us see whether we are healthy, since that precedes everything.

**Augustine:** You can judge this, if you can look to some extent either into yourself or into me. If I feel anything, I shall answer you as you inquire.

**Reason:** Do you love anything besides knowledge of yourself and of God?

**Augustine:** I could answer that, according to the feeling I now have, I love nothing more. But I answer more safely that I do not know. For it often happens to me that, although I believe I am moved by nothing else, something nevertheless comes to mind that pricks me quite differently from what I had supposed.

Likewise, although something entering my thoughts may not have shaken me, when it actually comes it nevertheless disturbs me more than I had thought. But at present I seem to myself to be capable of being moved by only three things: fear of losing those whom I love, fear of pain, and fear of death.

**Reason:** Then you love the lives of those dearest to you, your own good health, and your own life in this body; for otherwise you would not fear losing them.

**Augustine:** I admit that this is so.

**Reason:** Then the fact that not all your friends are with you, and that your health is less than complete, causes some distress to your soul; for I see that this follows as well.

**Augustine:** You see correctly; I cannot deny it.

**Reason:** What if you suddenly felt and confirmed that your body was healthy, and saw all those whom you love enjoying harmonious and generous leisure with you? Would you not also have to rejoice and exult to some degree?

**Augustine:** Indeed, to some degree; or rather, if these things had come about suddenly, as you say, when would I have time to collect myself? When would I even be permitted to conceal such joy?

**Reason:** Then you are still driven by all the illnesses and disturbances of the soul. What shamelessness of such eyes, then, to wish to see that sun!

**Augustine:** You have drawn your conclusion as though I did not at all perceive how much my health has advanced, or how many diseases have withdrawn, and how much remains. Let me grant you this point.

### CHAPTER X. Love of bodily and external things
17. R. Do you not see that even healthy eyes of the body are often struck back and turned away by this sunlight, and flee to their accustomed darkness? Yet you consider what progress you have made, but do not consider what you wish to see; nevertheless I shall examine this very matter with you, and ask what progress you think we have made. Do you desire no wealth?

A. This is certainly not something I have only now renounced. For although I am thirty-three years old [Note: In the Codex Regio-Montensis, and in three of those examined by the Louvain scholars, the reading is, “although I am thirty-four years old.” This is erroneous, since it was about fourteen years earlier that Augustine had read Cicero’s *Hortensius*; and he testifies that he read this book in the nineteenth year of his life, in *Confessions* 3.4 and *Against the Academics* 3.20], it is nearly fourteen years since I ceased desiring such things, nor have I considered anything else in them, if they should happen to be offered, except necessary support and honorable use. One book of Cicero quite easily persuaded me that wealth should in no way be sought, but that, if it should come, it should be administered with the greatest wisdom and prudence.

R. What of honors?

A. I admit that I have only recently—and almost within these past few days—ceased desiring them.

R. What of a wife? Would you not sometimes be pleased by a beautiful, chaste, well-mannered, educated woman, or one who could easily be instructed by you, bringing also such a dowry—since you despise wealth—as would make her in every respect no burden upon your leisure, especially if you hoped and were certain that you would suffer no trouble from her?

A. However much you wish to portray her and heap upon her every good quality, I have resolved that nothing must be fled from more than intercourse. I perceive that nothing casts a manly mind down from its citadel more than feminine blandishments and that bodily contact without which a wife cannot be had. Therefore, if it belongs to the duty of a wise man—which I have not yet discovered—to devote himself to children, whoever has intercourse for this reason alone may seem worthy of admiration to me, but in no way of imitation. To attempt this is more dangerous than success is fortunate.
