Thus, I believe that I have imposed upon myself, justly and usefully, for the freedom of my soul, the command neither to desire, seek, nor marry a wife.

R. I am not now asking what you have resolved, but whether you are still struggling, or whether you have already conquered lust itself. For the health of your eyes is at issue.

A. I seek and desire nothing of this kind at all; even when I remember such things, I do so with horror and loathing. What more do you want? This good also grows in me day by day: the more my hope of seeing that beauty for which I burn intensely increases, the more all my love and pleasure are turned toward it.

R. What of the pleasure of food? How much concern do you have for it?

A. Those foods which I have decided not to eat do not move me at all. As for those which I have not cut off, I admit that I enjoy them when present, but only so that they may be removed, whether seen or tasted, without any disturbance of mind. When they are entirely absent, this appetite does not dare intrude so as to obstruct my thoughts. But as for food and drink, baths, and every other bodily pleasure, ask me nothing at all: I desire only to have as much of them [Note: The editions read, “I seek from her”; the English manuscripts more correctly have, “I desire to have.” [“I seek from her.”]] as can contribute to the preservation of health.

CHAPTER XI.—External advantages may be admitted more truly for the sake of other true goods than desired for their own sake.

18. R. You have made much progress; nevertheless, the things that remain greatly hinder you from seeing that light. But I am devising something which seems to me easy to demonstrate: either nothing remains for us to tame, or we have made no progress at all, and the corruption of all those things which we think have been cut away still remains. For I ask you this: if you were persuaded that you could not live in the study of wisdom with many of your dearest companions unless some considerable household wealth could support your needs, would you not desire and wish for wealth?

A. I agree.

R. What if it should also become clear that you would persuade many people to wisdom if your authority grew through honor, and that those very companions of yours could not restrain their desires and turn themselves wholly toward seeking God unless they too were honored—and that this could not be achieved except through your honors and dignity? Would not these things also have to be desired, and would you not have to strive greatly that they might come about?

A. It is as you say.

R. I shall say nothing now about a wife. Perhaps such a necessity cannot arise for marrying one. Yet if it were certain that, through her ample property, all those whom you wish to live leisurely with you in one place could be supported, and she herself willingly agreed to this—especially if she possessed such distinction of birth that through her you could easily obtain those honors which you have already granted to be necessary—I do not know whether it would belong to your duty to despise such a woman.

A. When would I dare hope for such a thing?

19. R. You say this as though I were now asking what you hope for. I am not asking what does not please you when denied, but what pleases you when offered. For one thing is a disease exhausted, another is a disease merely lulled to sleep. Here applies what certain learned men have said: that all fools are insane, so that they perceive every cesspool to smell foul—not always, but whenever they stir it. It makes a great difference whether desire is overwhelmed by despair of the mind or driven away by health.

A. Although I cannot answer you, you will never persuade me that, in the state of mind in which I now find myself, I have made no progress.

R. I believe this seems so to you because, although you might be able to wish for these things, they would nevertheless appear desirable not for their own sake, but for the sake of something else.

A. That is what I wanted to say. When I desired wealth, I desired it in order to be wealthy; and the honors themselves—which I have just said that I have subdued my desire for—I wanted because I was pleased by some sort of luster belonging to them. And whenever I considered a wife, I always attended to nothing except the pleasure she would provide me together with a good reputation. At that time there was a genuine desire for these things in me. Now I utterly despise them all. But if there is no passage to the things I desire except through these, I do not desire them as things to be embraced, but submit to them as things to be endured.

R. Entirely excellent. For I do not think that desire should be called desire for any things that are sought for the sake of something else.

CHAPTER XII.—Nothing is to be desired except insofar as it contributes to the supreme good; nothing is dreadful except insofar as it turns us away from it.

20. But I ask you why you wish those people whom you love either to live or to live with you.

A. So that together we may seek our souls and God in harmony. For when one of us happens to make the discovery first, he easily leads the others there without labor.

R. What if they do not wish to seek these things?

A. I shall persuade them to wish to do so.

R. What if you cannot—either because they think they have already discovered them, or because they think such things cannot be discovered, or because they are obstructed by the cares and desires of other things?

A. I shall have them, and they me, as best we can.

R. What if their presence even prevents you from seeking? Would you not grieve and wish—if they cannot be otherwise—that they should not be with you rather than remain as they are?

A. I admit that it is as you say.

R. Then you desire either their life or their presence not for its own sake, but for the sake of discovering wisdom?

A. I entirely agree.

R. What if you were certain that your own life hindered you from grasping wisdom? Would you wish it to remain?

A. I would flee from it altogether.

R. What if you were taught that, after leaving this body as well as while established in it, you could attain wisdom? Would you care whether you enjoyed what you love here or in another life?

A. If I understood that I would suffer nothing worse that would drive me back from the progress I had made, I would not care.

R. Therefore, you now fear death because you fear becoming involved in some worse evil by which divine knowledge would be taken from you.

A. I fear not only that it might be taken away, if I have perhaps grasped something of it, but also that access to those things which I long to grasp might be blocked for me, although I think that what I already possess will remain with me.

R. Therefore, you wish this life to remain not for its own sake, but for the sake of wisdom.

A. That is so.

21. R. The pain of the body remains; perhaps its force moves you.

A. I fear it intensely for no other reason than that it hinders me from seeking. Although during these past days I was tormented by a very sharp toothache [Note: See *Confessions* 9.4.12], I was not entirely prevented from turning over in my mind anything I had perhaps already learned; but I was completely prevented from learning, which required the whole concentration of my mind. Yet it seemed to me that, if the radiance of truth should reveal itself to my mind, either I would not feel that pain or would certainly endure it as nothing.

But because, although I have never suffered anything worse, I often consider how much more severe pains may occur, I am sometimes compelled to agree with Cornelius Celsus, who says that the supreme good is wisdom, while the supreme evil is bodily pain. Nor does his reasoning seem absurd to me. “Since,” he says, “we are composed of two parts—namely, soul and body—the former part, the soul, is better, while the body is inferior. The supreme good is therefore the best of the better part, while the supreme evil is the worst of the inferior part. In the soul the best thing is wisdom; in the body the worst thing is pain. Thus it is concluded, without any falsehood, as I think, that the supreme good of a human being is wisdom, and the supreme evil is pain.”

R. We shall examine these matters later. For the wisdom itself to which we strive to attain may perhaps persuade us otherwise. But if it proves this to be true, we shall hold without hesitation this opinion concerning the supreme good and supreme evil.

CHAPTER XIII.—How and by what stages wisdom is discerned. True love.

22. We are now asking what kind of lover of wisdom you are—wisdom which you desire to see and grasp with the most chaste gaze and embrace, with no veil interposed, as though it were naked, although it does not permit itself to be seen in this way except by a very few and select lovers. If you were burning with love for some beautiful woman, she would rightly refuse herself to you if she discovered that you loved anything besides herself. Will wisdom, in her most chaste beauty, reveal herself to you unless you burn for her alone?

A. Why, then, am I still suspended, unhappy, and delayed by miserable torment? Surely I have already shown that I love nothing else, since whatever is not loved for its own sake is not loved. I alone love wisdom for her own sake; everything else—life, rest, friends—I either wish to be present or fear to be absent for her sake. What limit can there be to love of that beauty in which I not only do not begrudge it to others, but even seek many who may desire it with me, long for it with me, grasp it with me, and enjoy it with me? They will be dearer to me in proportion as what we love is more widely shared among us.

23. R. Such people ought indeed to be lovers of wisdom. She seeks such lovers, since her union is truly chaste and free from all contamination. But there is not one single road by which she is reached [Note: *Retractions* 1.4.3]. Each person comprehends that singular and most true good according to his own health and strength.

There is an ineffable and incomprehensible light of minds. Let this ordinary light teach us, as far as it can, how that light is to be understood. For there are some eyes so healthy and vigorous that, as soon as they are opened, they turn toward the sun itself without any trembling. For these, the light itself is in a certain sense their health; they need no teacher, but perhaps only an admonition. For them, believing, hoping, and loving are enough.

Others, however, are struck by the very brilliance which they ardently desire to see, and, having failed to see it, often return with pleasure into the darkness. Although they may already be such that they can rightly be called healthy, it is dangerous for them to wish to expose themselves to what they are still unable to see.

Therefore, these people must first be exercised, and their love must usefully be delayed and nourished. First, certain things must be shown to them which do not shine by themselves but can be seen by means of the light, such as a garment, a wall, or something similar. Then something which does not shine by itself but nevertheless gleams more beautifully through that light, such as gold, silver, and similar things, though not so radiantly as to harm the eyes. Then perhaps this earthly fire should be shown to them moderately; afterward the stars, then the moon, then the radiance of dawn and the brightness of the whitening sky.

Among these things, whether sooner or later, whether by passing through the whole sequence or by omitting certain stages, each person, growing accustomed according to the condition of his health, will see the sun without trembling and with great pleasure.

The best teachers do something similar for those most devoted to wisdom who, although not keen-sighted, are nevertheless beginning to see. To reach wisdom by a certain order is the duty of sound discipline; to reach it without order is scarcely credible good fortune. But I think we have written enough for today; we must spare our health.

CHAPTER XIV.—Wisdom itself heals the eyes so that it may be seen.

24. A. And on another day I said: “Please, if you can, now give me that order. Lead me—come, by whatever route you wish, through whatever you wish, in whatever manner you wish. Command any hardships, any difficulties, provided they lie within my power, through which I may be certain that I shall reach what I desire.”

R. There is only one thing I can command you; I know nothing more. You must flee entirely from these sensible things [Note: The same place], and take the greatest care, while we inhabit this body, lest our wings become caught in the glue of any of them. We need those wings whole and perfect if we are to fly from these darknesses to that light. It does not even deign to reveal itself to those imprisoned in this cage unless they are such that, once these things have been shattered or dissolved, they can escape into their own atmosphere.

Therefore, when you become such that nothing earthly pleases you at all, believe me: at that very moment, at that very instant of time, you will see what you desire.

A. When will that be, I beg you? For I do not think that these things can become utterly contemptible to me unless I have seen that in comparison with which they become filthy.

25. R. In this way the eye of the body could also say: “I shall not love darkness when I have seen the sun.” For it seems that this too belongs to the order, although the truth is far otherwise. It loves darkness because it is not healthy; and it cannot see the sun unless it is healthy.

The mind is also often deceived in this way: it thinks itself healthy and boasts of it, and because it does not yet see, it complains as though with justification. But that beauty knows when to reveal itself. For it performs the office of a physician and understands better who are healthy than do the very people who are being healed.

As much as we have emerged, we seem to ourselves to see; but how deeply immersed we were, and how far we had progressed, we are neither permitted to consider nor to feel. In comparison with a more serious illness, we think ourselves healthy.

Do you not see how, as though secure, we declared yesterday that we were no longer held by any disease, and that we loved nothing except wisdom, while seeking or desiring everything else only for her sake? How dirty, how foul, how accursed, how horrible did the embrace of a woman seem to you when we were discussing your desire for a wife! Surely, while we were awake during the past night and were again discussing the same matters among ourselves, you sensed how those imagined blandishments and that bitter sweetness tickled you differently from what you had supposed—far, far less than usual, but also far differently from what you had expected. Thus that most secret physician showed you both how far you had escaped his care and what remains to be cured.

26. A. Be silent, I beg you, be silent! Why do you torment me? Why do you dig so deeply and descend so far? I can no longer endure weeping; I promise nothing, I presume nothing—only do not question me about these matters. Surely you say that the one whom I burn to see knows when I am healthy. Let him do what he wishes; let him reveal himself when he wishes. I now commit myself entirely to his mercy and care. I have believed once and for all concerning him that he never ceases to raise up those who are disposed toward him in this way.

I shall pronounce nothing about my health until I see that beauty.

R. Do nothing else at all. But now restrain your tears and strengthen your mind. You have wept a great deal, and this disease of your heart feels it very heavily.

A. Do you wish to impose a limit on my tears when I see no limit to my misery? Or do you order me to consider the health of my body when I myself am consumed by disease? But, I beg you, if you have any power over me, try to lead me by some shortcuts, so that, even by coming somewhat nearer to that light—which, if I have made any progress, I can now endure—I may be reluctant to turn my eyes back toward the darkness I have left behind; if indeed those things may be called abandoned which still dare to flatter my blindness.

CHAPTER XV.—How the soul is known. Confidence in God.

27. R. If you agree, let us conclude this first book, so that in the second we may undertake whatever useful path presents itself. For we must not cease moderate exercise in response to this condition of yours.

A. I will not allow this little book to be concluded at all unless you reveal to me some small measure of what may keep me intent concerning our nearness to the light.

R. That physician accommodates you. For I do not know what radiance invites and touches me, drawing me toward where I may lead you. Therefore, receive this attentively.

A. Lead me, I beg you, and snatch me wherever you wish.

R. You certainly say that you wish to know the soul and God?

A. That is my entire concern.

R. Nothing more?

A. Nothing at all.

R. What? Do you not wish to grasp the truth?

A. As though I could know these things except through it!

R. Then it must first itself be known, through which those things can be known.

A. I reject nothing.

R. Let us therefore first examine this: since there are two words, *truth* and *true*, whether you think that these words signify two things or one.

A. They seem to signify two things. For just as chastity is one thing and a chaste person another, and similarly in many cases, so I believe that truth is one thing and what is called true another.

R. Which of these two do you think is superior?

A. I think truth. For it is not chastity that becomes chaste through a chaste person, but a person becomes chaste by means of chastity; similarly, if anything is true, it is true by means of truth.

28. R. What? When a chaste person dies, do you think chastity also dies?

A. Not at all.

R. Therefore, when something true perishes, truth does not perish.

A. But how does anything true perish? I do not see this.

R. I am surprised that you ask. Do we not see thousands of things perish before our eyes? Unless perhaps you think that this tree is either a tree but not a true tree, or that it cannot perish. Even if you do not trust your senses and could answer that you are entirely ignorant whether it is a tree, nevertheless, I think you will not deny that it is a true tree if it is a tree. For this is judged not by the senses but by understanding. If it is a false tree, it is not a tree; but if it is a tree, it must be true.

A. I grant that.

R. What of the other point? Do you not grant that this kind of thing exists which is born and perishes?

A. I cannot deny it.

R. Then it follows that something true perishes.

A. I do not object.

R. What then? Does it not seem to you that, while true things perish, truth does not perish—just as chastity does not die when a chaste person dies?

A. I now grant this too, and I eagerly await what you are attempting.

R. Then pay attention.

A. I am here.

29. R. Does this proposition seem true to you: “Whatever exists is compelled to exist somewhere”?

A. Nothing leads me so strongly to assent.

R. But you admit that truth exists?

A. I admit it.

R. Then we must ask where it exists. For it is not in a place, unless perhaps you think that something other than a body can be in a place, or that truth is a body.

A. I think neither of these.

R. Where, then, do you believe truth exists? It cannot be nowhere, since we admit that it exists.

A. If I knew where it existed, perhaps I would seek nothing further.

R. Can you at least understand where it does not exist?

A. If you remind me, perhaps I can.

R. It certainly does not exist in mortal things. For whatever exists cannot remain in something unless that in which it exists also remains. Yet we have just granted that truth remains even when true things perish. Therefore truth does not exist in mortal things.

But truth exists, and it is not nowhere. Therefore immortal things exist. Nothing, however, is true in which truth does not exist. It follows, then, that only those things which are immortal are true.

A false tree is not a tree; a false piece of wood is not wood; false silver is not silver; and, in general, whatever is false does not exist. But everything that is not true is false. Therefore nothing is rightly said to exist except immortal things.

Consider this little argument carefully with yourself, lest anything seem to you not to be granted. For if it is sound, we have almost completed the entire undertaking; it will perhaps become clearer in another book.

30. A. I am grateful. I shall carefully and cautiously consider these matters with myself—and indeed with you—when we are silent, provided no darkness intrudes and, as I greatly fear, even makes itself pleasing to me [Note: This is the reading of most manuscripts. The editions have “I shall reconsider.”].

R. Trust God steadfastly, and commit yourself entirely to him as far as you can. Do not wish to be as though you belonged to yourself and were in your own power; rather, profess yourself the servant of that most merciful and most beneficial Lord. For he will not cease to raise you up toward himself, and he will permit nothing to happen to you except what benefits you, even if you do not know it.

A. I hear, I believe, and I obey as far as I can. I also earnestly beseech him to grant me the ability to do so, unless perhaps you desire something more from me.

R. For now, that is good. Later you will do whatever the one whom you have now seemed to see commands [Note: The English manuscripts read, “whatever experience itself may later command.”].

## BOOK TWO

In this book Augustine discusses extensively with himself the true and the false, and finally, after properly perceiving the perpetuity of truth, concludes that the human soul itself, which is the seat of truth, is immortal.

[Col. 0885]

### CHAPTER I.—On the immortality of the human being.

[Col. 0885]

1. A. Our work has been interrupted long enough, and love is impatient; tears find no limit unless love is given what it loves. Therefore, let us begin the second book.

R. Let us begin.

A. Let us believe that God will be present.

R. Certainly, let us believe, if even this lies within our power.

A. He himself is our power.

R. Therefore pray as briefly and perfectly as you can.

A. “God, ever the same, may I know myself; may I know you.”

The prayer has been said.

R. You who wish to know yourself—do you know that you exist?

A. I know.

R. How do you know?

A. I do not know.

R. Do you perceive yourself as simple or multiple?

A. I do not know.

R. Do you know that you are moved?

A. I do not know.

R. Do you know that you think?

A. I know.

R. Therefore it is true that you think.

A. True.

R. Do you know that you are immortal?

A. I do not know.

R. Of all these things which you have said you do not know, which would you prefer to know first?

A. Whether I am immortal.

R. Then you love to live?

A. I admit it.

R. What if, once you have learned that you are immortal, that were enough?

A. It would indeed be a great thing, but it would be too little for me.

R. Yet how much will you rejoice in this thing that is too little?

A. Very greatly.

R. Will you no longer weep?

A. Not at all.

R. What if life itself should prove to be such that you could learn in it nothing more than you already know? Would you refrain from tears?

A. On the contrary, I would weep so much that there would be no life.

R. Therefore you do not love living for the sake of living itself, but for the sake of knowing.

A. I yield to the conclusion.

R. What if that very knowledge of things made you miserable?

A. I do not believe that this could happen in any way. But if it is so, no one can be happy; for I am miserable now only because of ignorance of things. If knowledge of things also makes one miserable, then misery is eternal.

R. Now I see the whole of what you desire. Since you believe that no one is made miserable by knowledge—and since it is probable from this that understanding makes one happy; while no one is happy except one who is alive, and no one lives who does not exist—you wish to exist, live, and understand; but you wish to exist so that you may live, and live so that you may understand. Therefore you know that you exist, you know that you live, and you know that you understand.

But you wish to know whether these things will always continue, whether none of them will continue, whether something will remain forever while something else perishes, or whether these things can diminish and increase while all remain.

A. That is so.

R. If, then, we prove that we shall always live, it will follow that we shall always exist.

A. It will follow.

R. It remains to inquire about understanding.

### CHAPTER II.—Perpetual truth.

2. A. I see an extremely clear and very brief order.

R. Then remain here now, so that you may answer the one questioning you carefully and firmly.

A. I am here.

R. If this world will always remain, is it true that the world will always remain?

A. Who could doubt this?

R. What if it will not remain? Is it not then true that the world will not remain?

A. I offer no resistance.

R. What when it has perished, if it is destined to perish? Will it not then be true that the world has perished? For as long as it is not true that the world has perished, it has not perished. Therefore it is contradictory that the world should have perished and that it should not be true that the world has perished.

A. I grant this too.

R. What of this? Does it seem possible to you that something could be true while truth does not exist?

A. Not at all.

R. Truth will therefore exist even if the world perishes.

A. I cannot deny it.

R. What if truth itself perishes? Will it not then be true that truth has perished?

A. Who denies that?

R. But nothing can be true if truth does not exist.

A. I granted that a little earlier.

R. Therefore truth will in no way perish.

A. Continue as you have begun, for nothing is truer than this chain of reasoning.

### CHAPTER III.—If falsehood will always exist, and cannot exist without sensation, it follows that some soul will always exist.

3. R. Now please answer me this: does it seem to you that sensation belongs to the soul or to the body?

A. It seems to belong to the soul.

R. What of understanding? Does it seem to you to belong to the soul?

A. It certainly does.

R. To the soul alone, or to something else as well?

A. I see nothing else besides the soul, except God, in whom I believe understanding exists.

R. Let us now examine this. If someone told you that this wall was not a wall but a tree, what would you think?

A. Either that his sense or mine was deceived, or that he called the wall by this name.

R. What if the appearance of a tree were presented to him, while the appearance of a wall were presented to you? Could both perceptions be true?

A. In no way; for one and the same thing cannot be both a tree and a wall. Although each of us may see it as something different, one of us must necessarily be suffering from a false imagination.

R. What if it is neither a wall nor a tree, and both of you are deceived?

A. That is possible.

R. Then you had omitted one possibility just mentioned.

A. I admit it.

R. What if you both recognize that what appears to you is different from what it is? Are you then deceived?

A. No.

R. Therefore what appears can be false, and the person to whom it appears need not be deceived.

A. It can.

R. We must therefore admit that the person who sees false things is not deceived, but the person who assents to false things is.

A. We must plainly admit it.

R. What is falsehood itself? Why is it false?

A. Because it is otherwise than it appears.

R. If, therefore, there were no one to whom it appeared, there would be nothing false.

A. It follows.

R. Falsehood, then, is not in things but in sensation; and the person who does not assent to false things is not deceived. It follows that we are one thing and sensation another, since, when sensation itself is deceived, we can remain undeceived.

A. I have nothing to say against this.

R. But when the soul is deceived, do you dare to say that there is no falsehood?

A. How could I dare say that?

R. Yet no sensation exists without the soul, and no falsehood without sensation. Therefore the soul either produces falsehood or cooperates with it [Note: The English manuscripts read, “falsehood cooperates.”].

A. The preceding arguments compel assent.

4. R. Now answer this: does it seem possible to you that falsehood might at some time not exist?

A. How could this seem possible to me, when the difficulty of finding truth is so great that it would be more absurd to say that falsehood cannot exist than that truth cannot exist?

R. Do you think that one who does not live can have sensation?

A. That cannot happen.

R. It is therefore established that the soul always lives.

A. You are driving me too quickly into joy; proceed gradually, I beg you.

R. But if those concessions were correctly made, I see no reason to doubt this matter.

A. It is too quick, I say. I am therefore more easily led to think that I rashly conceded something than to become already secure about the soul’s immortality. Still, unfold this conclusion and show how it has been established.

R. You said that falsehood cannot exist without sensation, and that it cannot fail to exist. Therefore sensation always exists. But no sensation exists without the soul. Therefore the soul is eternal. Nor can anything have sensation unless it lives. Therefore the soul always lives.

### CHAPTER IV.—Can the immortality of the soul be inferred from the perpetuity of falsehood or truth?

5. A. What a leaden dagger! You could have concluded that the human being is immortal if I had granted you that this world could never exist without a human being, and that the world itself is eternal.

R. You are rightly watchful. Nevertheless, what we have established is not insignificant: the nature of things cannot exist without a soul—unless perhaps falsehood will at some point cease to exist.

A. I admit that this follows. But I think we must now deliberate further about whether the earlier concessions are unstable. For I see that no small step has been taken toward the soul’s immortality.

R. Have you considered carefully enough to ensure that you have granted nothing rashly?

A. Carefully enough; I see nothing by which I can accuse myself of rashness.

R. Then it is established that the nature of things cannot exist without a living soul.

A. Established so far only that some souls can be born while others die in succession.

R. What if falsehood is removed from the nature of things? Will it not follow that everything is true?

A. I see that it follows.

R. Answer me: why does this wall seem to you to be a true wall?

A. Because I am not deceived by its appearance.

R. Therefore because it is as it appears?

A. Yes.

R. If something is false because it appears otherwise than it is, and true because it appears as it is, then, when that to which it appears is removed, there is neither anything false nor anything true. But if there is no falsehood in the nature of things, everything is true. And nothing can appear except to a living soul. Therefore the soul remains in the nature of things whether falsehood can be removed or whether it cannot.

A. I see that what was already concluded has been made stronger [Col. 0888], but we have advanced nothing by this addition. For that which troubles me most remains: souls are born and perish, and that they are not absent from the world results not from their immortality but from their succession.

6. R. Do corporeal things—that is, sensible things—seem to you capable of being grasped by understanding?

A. They do not.

R. What of this? Does God seem to you to use the senses in order to know things?

A. I do not dare rashly affirm anything about this; but as far as one may conjecture, God in no way uses the senses.

R. Then we conclude that only the soul can have sensation.

A. Conclude for now as far as is probable.

R. What of this? Do you grant that, if this is not a true wall, it is not a wall?

A. I could grant nothing more easily.

R. And that, if it is not a true body, it is not a body?

A. This too is the same.

R. Therefore, if nothing is true unless it is as it appears; if nothing corporeal can appear except through the senses; if nothing can have sensation except the soul; and if a thing cannot be a body unless it is a true body, it remains that a body cannot exist unless there is a soul.

A. You are pressing too hard, and I have no means of resisting.

### CHAPTER V.—What the true is.

7. R. Pay closer attention to this.

A. Here I am; I am present.

R. Certainly this is a stone; and it is a true stone if it is not otherwise than it appears; and it is not a stone if it is not true; and it can be seen only by the senses.

A. Yes.

R. Therefore there are no stones in the most hidden recesses of the earth, nor anywhere at all where there are no beings capable of sensation. Nor would this stone be a stone unless we saw it; nor will it be a stone when we have departed and no one else present sees it.

Nor, if you close your little chests securely, will they contain anything, even if you have enclosed many things in them. Nor is the wood itself, within, really wood. For whatever exists deep inside a body that is not at all transparent escapes all the senses, and is compelled not to exist at all.

For if it did exist, it would be true; and nothing is true except what is as it appears. But that inner thing does not appear; therefore it is not true—unless you have some answer to make to this.

A. I see that this follows from the things I have granted; but it is so absurd that I would more readily deny whatever you wish of those things than grant this to be true.

R. I offer no resistance. See, then, what you wish to say: whether corporeal things can be seen except by the senses; whether anything can have sensation except the soul; whether something can be a stone or something else without being true; or whether the true itself must be defined differently.

A. Please, let us examine this last point itself.

8. R. Then define the true.

A. The true is what is as it appears to the one who knows it, if that person wishes and is able to know it.

R. Then what no one can know will not be true? Further, if what appears otherwise than it is is false, what if this stone appears to one person as a stone and to another as wood? Will the same thing be both false and true?

A. The first point troubles me more: how can something become not true because it cannot be known? As for one thing being simultaneously true and false, I am not greatly concerned. I see that one thing, compared with different things, can simultaneously be greater and smaller. For these are names of comparison [Col. 0889].

R. But if you say that nothing is true in itself, do you not fear that it will follow that nothing exists in itself? From the same source by which this is wood, it is also true wood. Nor can it happen that, in itself—that is, without a knower—it is wood, but is not true wood.

A. Then I say this and define it in this way; nor am I afraid that my definition will be rejected because it is too brief: the true, to me, seems to be that which is.

R. Then nothing will be false, because whatever exists is true.

A. You have thrown me into great difficulties, and I find absolutely nothing to answer. Although I do not wish to be taught in any other way than through these questions, I am now nevertheless afraid of being questioned.

### CHAPTER VI.—Whence falsehood arises, and where it is.

9. R. The God to whom we have entrusted ourselves undoubtedly gives aid and delivers us from these straits, provided only that we believe and earnestly beseech him.

A. Nothing could I do more willingly at this moment; for nowhere have I endured such darkness. God, our Father, who urges us to pray, and who grants even this very thing for which you are asked—for when we ask you, we live better and become better—hear me, trembling in these shadows, and extend your right hand to me. Stretch out your light toward me; call me back from my errors. Under your guidance may I return to myself and to you. Amen.

R. Remain here as much as you can, and attend with the utmost vigilance.

A. Speak, I beg you, if anything has been suggested to you, lest we perish.

R. Remain here.

A. Behold, you have me doing nothing else.

10. R. Let us first examine again and again what the false is.

A. I wonder whether it will be anything other than that which is not as it appears.

R. Attend rather, and let us first question the senses themselves. Certainly what the eyes see is not called false unless it possesses some likeness to the true. For example, a person whom we see in dreams is plainly not a real person, but a false one, precisely because he bears a likeness to the true. For who, seeing a dog, would rightly say that he had dreamed of a man? That dog too, therefore, is a false dog because it resembles a real one.

A. It is as you say.

R. What if, while awake, someone should think, upon seeing a horse, that he was seeing a man? Is he not deceived because some likeness of a man appears to him? For if nothing appeared to him except the form of a horse, he could not think that he was seeing a man.

A. I entirely concede the point.

R. Likewise, we call the tree we see painted a false tree, the face reflected from a mirror a false face, the movement of towers to sailors a false movement, and the apparent breaking of an oar a false breaking, for no other reason than that these things resemble the true.

A. I admit it.

R. Thus we are deceived in twins, in eggs, in individual seals impressed with the same ring, and in other such things.

A. I follow and concede the whole argument.

R. The likeness of things that pertains to the eyes, then, is the mother of falsity.

A. I cannot deny it.

11. R. But this entire forest, unless I am mistaken, can be divided into two classes. For in part it occurs among equal things, and in part among inferior things.

Things are equal when we say that this is as similar to that as that is to this, as was said of twins or of impressions made by a ring. They are inferior when we say that what is inferior is similar to what is better. For who, looking into a mirror, would rightly say that he himself is similar to the image, and not rather that the image is similar to him? [Col. 0890]

This latter class is partly found in what the soul undergoes, and partly in the things that appear to the sight. What the soul undergoes, however, it undergoes either in sensation, as with the movement of a tower that does not exist, or within itself, from what it has received through the senses, as with the visions of dreamers and perhaps also of the insane.

Again, among those things that appear in the very objects we see, some are produced by nature and the rest are expressed and fashioned by living beings. Nature produces inferior likenesses either by generation or by reflection. By generation, when offspring are born resembling their parents; by reflection, as with mirrors of various kinds. For although most mirrors are made by human beings, they themselves do not fashion the images that are reflected in them.

The works of living beings, on the other hand, include paintings and all such fabrications; and this category may also include, if such things are in fact made, those produced by demons. The shadows of bodies, because it is not altogether beside the point to call them similar to bodies and, as it were, false bodies [Note: Absent, according to Lov. M.], must not be denied a place among things pertaining to the judgment of the eyes. I think they should be placed in that class which is produced by nature through reflection. Every body placed before a light reflects it and casts a shadow in the opposite direction.

Do you think anything needs to be said against this?

A. Nothing at all. But I am eagerly waiting to see where all this is leading.

12. R. We must patiently endure until the remaining senses inform us that falsity dwells in a likeness to the true. In hearing itself, too, almost as many kinds of likenesses occur: for example, when, hearing the voice of someone whom we do not see, we think it is the voice of another person whose voice it resembles; among inferior things, the echo bears witness, as does the ringing in the ears themselves, the imitation of a blackbird or crow in clocks, and those sounds which dreamers or the insane seem to hear.

The false little sounds spoken of by musicians bear astonishing testimony to the truth, as will become clear later; nevertheless, for the present it is enough to say that they too are not unlike the sounds which they call true.

Do you follow this?

A. Most willingly. I have no difficulty understanding it.

R. Then, so that we do not delay: does it seem to you that a lily can easily be distinguished by smell from another lily, honey from thyme-honey in another hive by taste, or the softness of a swan’s feathers from that of a goose by touch?

A. It does not seem so.

R. What, when we dream that we smell, taste, or touch such things? Are we not deceived by the likeness of images, the more deceptively the more insubstantial they are?

A. You speak the truth.

R. It therefore appears that in all the senses, whether among equal or inferior things, we are either deceived by an alluring likeness, or—even when we are not deceived, but suspend our assent or recognize a difference—we nevertheless call false those things that we discover to be similar to the true.

A. I cannot doubt it.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the True and the Similar; Why the Work Is Called *Soliloquies*

13. R. Now attend while we return once more to the same matters, so that what we are attempting to demonstrate may become clearer.

A. Here I am; speak as you wish. I have decided to endure this circuitous route once, and I shall not grow weary on it, with so great a hope of reaching the place toward which I sense that we are proceeding.

R. You are doing well. But consider whether, when we see similar eggs, we can rightly call any one of them false.

A. It does not seem possible at all. For if they are all eggs, they are true eggs.

R. What, when we see an image reflected from a mirror? By what signs do we understand that it is false?

A. Evidently because it cannot be grasped, makes no sound, does not move by itself, does not live, and for countless other reasons which it would take too long to enumerate.

R. I see that you do not wish to linger, and your haste must be accommodated. Therefore, not to repeat each individual case: if those people whom we see in dreams could live, speak, and be touched by people who are awake, and if there were no difference between them and those whom we address and see after waking in sound health, would we call them false?

A. How could that rightly be said?

R. Then, if they were true insofar as they appeared most like the true, and no difference at all existed between them and real people, while they were false insofar as they were proved unlike them by those or other differences, must we not admit that likeness is the mother of truth and unlikeness the mother of falsity?

A. I have nothing to say, and I am ashamed of my earlier consent, which was so rash.

14. R. It is absurd for you to be ashamed, as though we had not chosen this kind of conversation for that very reason. Since we converse only with ourselves, I wish it to be called and entitled *Soliloquies*—a new and perhaps harsh name, but sufficiently suitable for demonstrating the matter.

For since truth cannot be sought more effectively than by questioning and answering, and since scarcely anyone can be found who is not ashamed to be proved wrong in argument—so that almost always an improperly controlled cry of obstinacy bursts apart a matter well introduced for discussion, often with a concealed and sometimes even open wounding of the mind—it has seemed to me both most peaceful and most convenient, with God’s help, to seek the truth by questioning myself and answering myself.

Therefore there is no reason for you to fear returning and undoing anything in which you have rashly entangled yourself; for there is no other way to escape from here.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Whence the True and the False Arise

15. A. You speak correctly; but I do not clearly see what I have conceded wrongly—unless perhaps it is right to call false that which possesses some likeness to the true, since nothing else worthy of the name “false” occurs to me; yet I am again forced to admit that those things are called false insofar as they differ from the true. It follows that this very unlikeness is the cause of falsity.

Thus I am confused; for I do not easily think of anything that is produced by contrary causes.

R. What if this is the one and only kind of thing in nature that is so? Do you not know that, although you may run through countless kinds of animals, the crocodile alone is found to move its upper jaw when chewing? Especially since scarcely anything can be found so similar to any given thing that it is not also unlike it in some respect?

A. I see that, certainly. But when I consider what we call false—something that possesses both a likeness to the true and an unlikeness— I cannot discern by which aspect it has earned the name “false.”

For if I say it is called false because of what is unlike, there will be nothing that could not be called false; for nothing is unlike some other thing that we admit to be true.

Likewise, if I say that it should be called false because of what is like, not only will those eggs object, which are true precisely insofar as they are most alike, but even then I shall not escape the person who would compel me to confess that everything is false, since I cannot deny that everything is similar to itself in some respect.

But suppose I am not afraid to answer that likeness and unlikeness together make it right to call something false. What means of escape will you give me? I shall nevertheless be pressed to declare that everything is false, since, as was said above, all things are found to be both similar and dissimilar to themselves in some respect.

It would remain for me to say that nothing is false except what is otherwise than it appears—were I not afraid of those many monstrosities from which I thought I had already sailed away. For I am again driven back by an unexpected vertigo to say that what is true is what is as it appears.

From this it follows that nothing can be true without a knower; and here I fear shipwreck on utterly hidden reefs, which are true even if they are not known.

Or, if I say that what is true is what exists, it will be concluded, despite every objection, that nowhere is there anything false. Thus those waves return, and I see that nothing has been accomplished through your delays, despite all my patience.

## CHAPTER IX.—What Is False, What Is Deceptive, and What Is Lying

16. R. Attend rather; for I will not allow myself to believe that we have invoked divine assistance in vain. Having tested everything as far as we could, I see that nothing remains which can rightly be called false except what either pretends to be what it is not, or strives to be and is not.

The former kind of falsehood is also deceptive or lying. For that is rightly called deceptive which possesses a certain desire to deceive; and this cannot be understood without a soul. It occurs partly through reason and partly through nature: through reason in rational animals, as in human beings; through nature in beasts, as in a little fox.

What I call lying, however, is produced by those who lie. They differ from the deceptive in this respect: every deceptive thing desires to deceive, but not everyone who lies wishes to deceive. For actors, comedies, and many poems are full of lies, with the intention of entertaining rather than deceiving, and nearly everyone who jokes lies.

But that person is rightly called deceptive or deceiving whose business it is that someone should be deceived. Those who do not act in order to deceive but nevertheless fabricate something are, without dispute, called merely liars—or, if not even that, still “lying,” unless you have something to say against these points.

17. A. Continue, I beg you. Perhaps you have now begun to teach us something about false things that is not false; but I am waiting to learn what that class is which, as you said, strives to be and is not.

R. Why would you not wait for it? They are the very things of which we mentioned many examples above. Does it not seem to you that your image reflected in a mirror somehow wishes to be you yourself, but is false for the reason that it is not you?

A. It certainly seems so.

R. What of every painting or statue, and all such products of craftsmen? Do they not claim to be that in whose likeness each thing has been made?

A. I am entirely persuaded.

R. You concede, I suppose, that the things by which sleepers or the insane are deceived belong to this class.

A. More than anything else. For nothing more strongly strives to be what those who are awake or sound see; yet such things are false precisely because they cannot be what they strive to be.

R. What more need I say about the movement of towers, the submerged oar, or the shadows of bodies? It is clear, I think, that they must be measured by this rule.

A. Perfectly clear.

R. I say nothing of the remaining senses; for anyone who considers the matter will discover that, among the very things we perceive, that is called false which strives to be something and is not.

## CHAPTER X.—Things That Are True Precisely insofar as They Are False

18. A. You speak correctly; but I wonder why you thought those poems, jokes, and other deceptions should be separated from this class.

R. Because it is one thing to wish to be false and another to be unable to be true. Thus the works of human beings themselves—comedies, tragedies, mimes, and other things of that kind—may be joined to the works of painters and sculptors.

A painted man cannot be a real man, however much he tends toward the appearance of a man, any more than the things written in the books of comic poets can be real. They do not wish to be false, nor are they false through any desire of their own; rather, they are false by a kind of necessity, insofar as they were able to follow the fabricator’s intention.

But on the stage Roscius was, by his will, the false Hecuba, while by nature he was a true man; and by that same will he was also a true tragedian, insofar as he fulfilled the appointed role. He was a false Priam because he represented Priam, but was not Priam himself.

From this arises something remarkable, which nevertheless no one doubts to be so.

A. What is it?

R. What do you think, except that all these things are true in some respects precisely because they are false in others, and that what serves them as their own truth is only that they are false in relation to something else?

Thus they cannot in any way attain what they either wish or ought to be if they avoid being false. For how could the man I mentioned be a true tragedian if he did not wish to be the false Hector, the false Andromache, the false Hercules, and countless other characters? Or how could a painting be true if there were no false horse? How could there be a true human image in a mirror if there were no false human being?

Therefore, if it benefits some things, in order that they may be something true, to be something false, why do we fear falsehoods so greatly and desire truth as a great good?

A. I do not know, and I am greatly astonished—unless it is because I see nothing worthy of imitation in these examples. We ought not to be like actors, or like whatever is reflected in mirrors, or like Myron’s little bronze heifers, so that we too may be true in some particular guise while being shaded and assimilated to another guise and therefore false.

Rather, we should seek that truth which is not, as it were, by a two-faced and self-contradictory reasoning, true in one respect and false in another.

[Note: *Est*, according to Erasmus, Lovanius, and the manuscripts.]

R. You seek something great and divine. Yet if we should find it, shall we not admit that truth itself is constituted and, as it were, fused from these things—the truth from which everything called true in any way derives its name?

A. I willingly agree.

## CHAPTER XI.—The Truth of the Disciplines; What a Fable Is; What Grammar Is

19. R. What, then, do you think? Is the discipline of argument true or false?

A. Who could doubt that it is true?

But grammar is true as well.

R. In the same way as that?

A. I do not see what could be truer than it.

R. Surely that which contains nothing false—the very point at which you were troubled earlier by those things which, in some strange way, could not be true unless they were false. Do you not know that all those fabulous and plainly false things belong to grammar?

A. I do know that; but, as I think, they are not false by means of grammar. Rather, grammar demonstrates what sort of things they are, whatever their character may be.

A fable is a fabricated falsehood composed for utility or pleasure. Grammar, however, is the discipline that guards and regulates articulated speech. By the necessity of its profession, it is compelled to gather all the fabrications of human language that have been entrusted to memory and writing—not making them false, but teaching and affirming a certain true account concerning them.

R. Quite right. I am not now concerned with whether you have defined and distinguished these matters well; I ask instead whether grammar itself demonstrates that this is so, or whether that discipline of argument does.

A. I do not deny that the power and skill of definition, by which I have now attempted to separate these things, belong to the art of argument.

20. R. What of grammar itself? If it is true, is it not true insofar as it is a discipline? For “discipline” derives its name from learning; and no one can be said not to know what he has learned and retains, while no one knows false things. Therefore every discipline is true.

A. I do not see what is rashly conceded in this little argument. Yet I am troubled lest by it someone should think those fables true as well, since we learn and retain them too.

R. Did our teacher not want us to believe and know what he taught?

A. On the contrary, he strongly insisted that we should know it.

R. Did he ever insist that we believe Daedalus had flown?

A. Certainly never. But plainly, unless we retained the fable, he would scarcely have made us able to retain anything at all.

R. Do you therefore deny that it is true that this is a fable, and that Daedalus was thus represented in popular report?

A. I do not deny that this is true.

R. Then you do not deny that you learned something true when you learned this. For if it is true that Daedalus flew, and boys accepted and recited this as a fabricated fable, they would retain falsehoods precisely because the things they recited were true.

This is the source of what we wondered at earlier: that the fable about Daedalus’s flight could not be true unless it were false that Daedalus had flown.

A. I understand that now; but I am waiting to see what advantage we gain from it.

R. What else but that the reasoning by which we concluded that a discipline cannot be a discipline unless it teaches what is true is not false?

A. And what does that have to do with the matter?

R. Because I want you to tell me the source of grammatical discipline; for it is true from the same source from which it is a discipline.

A. I do not know what to answer you.

R. Does it not seem to you that, if nothing in it were defined and nothing distributed and distinguished into classes and parts, it could in no way have been a discipline?

A. Now I understand what you mean. Nor does any form of any discipline occur to me in which definitions, divisions, and reasonings do not perform the whole task by which it is called a discipline: declaring what each thing is; assigning to each part its own place without confusion; omitting nothing proper to it and including nothing alien.

R. Then the whole of that by which it is called true as well.

A. I see that this follows.

21. R. Answer now: what discipline contains the methods of definition, division, and partition?

A. It was said above that these are contained in the rules of argument.

R. Grammar, then, was created by the same art both as a discipline and so that it might be true—the grammar which you earlier defended against falsity. And I may conclude this not merely about grammar but absolutely about all disciplines.

For you said—and said truly—that you could think of no discipline in which the right to define and distribute had not performed the very work by which it is a discipline.

But if disciplines are true insofar as they are disciplines, will anyone deny that truth itself is that through which all disciplines are true?

A. I am almost entirely ready to agree; but I am troubled by the fact that we also count the art of argument among those same disciplines. I therefore think that truth is rather that by which this very art is true.

R. Very good, and very vigilant. But you do not deny, I suppose, that it is true insofar as it is a discipline.

A. On the contrary, that is precisely what troubles me. I have noticed that it is also a discipline, and for that reason is called true.

R. What then? Do you think that this could have been a discipline in any other way than by having everything defined and distributed within it?

A. I have nothing else to say.

R. But if this function belongs to it, then the discipline is true through itself. Will anyone think it surprising, then, if that by which all things are true is itself, through itself and in itself, true truth?

[Note: Thus in the manuscripts. Lovanius has: “Will anyone think it surprising if those things which are true are all true through it, if it too is truth?” Erasmus and the Venice edition have the same reading.]

A. Nothing prevents me from proceeding rightly toward that conclusion.

## CHAPTER XII.—The Several Ways in Which Something Is in Something Else

22. R. Then attend to the few things that remain.

A. Bring forward whatever you have, provided it is something I can understand and willingly concede.

R. We are not unaware that “being in something” is said in two ways. In one way, a thing is so situated that it can also be separated and exist elsewhere, as this piece of wood in this place, or the sun in the east.

In the other way, something is in a subject in such a manner that it cannot be separated from it, as the form and appearance we see in this piece of wood, light in the sun, heat in fire, and discipline in the soul, along with other similar things.

Does this seem otherwise to you?

A. These matters are very old acquaintances of ours, and we learned and understood them with the greatest diligence from early youth. Therefore, when questioned about them, I cannot help conceding them without any deliberation.

R. What of this? Do you not concede that what is inseparably in a subject cannot remain if the subject itself does not remain?

A. I see that this too is necessary. For anyone who carefully considers the matter understands that, while the subject remains, what is in the subject can fail to remain. The color of this body, for example, can change through health or age while the body itself has not yet perished.

And this does not apply equally to everything, but to those things in which what is in the subjects coexists with them without constituting the subjects themselves.

For this wall is not a wall because of the color we see in it. Even if by some circumstance it should become black or white, or change to some other color, it nevertheless remains and is called a wall.

But if fire is without heat, it will not even be fire; nor can we call snow snow unless it is white.

23. But who would concede what you asked, or to whom could it seem possible, that what is in a subject should remain when the subject itself has perished? It is monstrous and utterly alien to truth that what would not exist unless it existed in the subject should be able to exist even when the subject itself no longer exists.

R. Then what we were seeking has been found.

A. What are you saying?

R. What you hear.

A. Is it therefore now clearly established that the soul is immortal?

R. Most clearly—if the things you conceded are true; unless perhaps you say that, even if the soul dies, it remains a soul.

A. I would never say that. Rather, I say that precisely by perishing it ceases to be a soul.

Nor does what great philosophers have said turn me from this view: that a thing which, wherever it enters, bestows life cannot admit death into itself. For although light, wherever it can enter, makes that place luminous and, because of that memorable force of opposites, cannot admit darkness into itself, nevertheless it is extinguished, and the place is darkened when the light has gone out.

Thus that which resisted darkness and in no way admitted darkness into itself nevertheless, by perishing, made room for darkness, just as it could have done by departing.

Therefore I fear that death may come to the body as darkness comes to a place: sometimes when the soul departs as light departs, and sometimes when it is extinguished in the same place. In that case, security would not exist with respect to every kind of bodily death; rather, one kind of death might be desirable, by which the soul could be led unharmed out of the body and conducted to a place—if there is any such place—where it could not be extinguished.

Or, if even this is impossible, and the soul is kindled in the body like a light and cannot endure elsewhere, and every death is a kind of extinguishing of the soul in the body, or of life, then one should choose, insofar as human beings are permitted, a kind of life by which what is lived may be lived with security and tranquility—although I do not know how this could happen if the soul dies.

O greatly blessed are those who have been persuaded, whether by themselves or by anyone else, that death need not be feared even if the soul perishes! But as for miserable me, no arguments and no books have yet been able to persuade me of this.

24. R. Do not lament; the human soul is immortal.

A. How do you prove this?

R. From the things which, as I think, you conceded earlier with great caution.

A. I remember giving you nothing while you questioned me that I did not grant with full vigilance. But now gather the whole conclusion, I beg you. Let us see where we have arrived through so many windings; and I do not want you to question me any longer.

For if you are going to enumerate briefly what I conceded, why is my answer needed again? Is it so that you may needlessly prolong my anticipation of joy, if we have perhaps accomplished something good?

R. I shall do what I see you wish, but attend with the greatest care.

A. Speak now; I am here. Why do you torture me?

R. Everything that is in a subject, if it always remains, necessarily requires that the subject itself also always remain. Every discipline is in the soul as in a subject. Therefore the soul must always remain if discipline always remains.

But discipline is truth, and truth always remains, as the reasoning at the beginning of this book persuaded us.

Therefore the soul always remains, and the soul is not said to be dead. Only he does not absurdly deny that the soul is immortal who proves that one of the preceding propositions was not rightly conceded.

## CHAPTER XIV.—The Earlier Syllogism Is Examined

25. A. I want now to throw myself into joy, but two considerations hold me back somewhat.

First, I am troubled because we have made use of so great a circuit, following I know not what chain of reasonings, when the whole matter under discussion could have been demonstrated as briefly as it has just now been demonstrated. It therefore concerns me that the argument wandered about for so long, as though lying in ambush.

Second, I do not see how discipline—especially the discipline of argument—can always be in the soul, since so few people know it, and whoever does know it was uneducated for so long a period from infancy.

We cannot say either that the souls of the ignorant are not souls, or that the discipline they do not know exists in their souls. If this is profoundly absurd, it remains either that truth is not always in the soul, or that discipline is not truth.

26. R. You see why our reasoning made so many circuits, and that they were not pointless. For we were asking what truth is; and even now, after wandering through nearly all the paths in this forest of things, I do not see that we have been able to investigate it.

But what shall we do? Shall we abandon what we have begun and wait to see whether some writings by others fall into our hands that may satisfy this question?

I think that many were written before our time which we have not read. And now, so that we may not suppose anything unknown to us, we plainly know that this subject has been written about both in verse and in prose, by men whose writings cannot remain hidden from us and whose talents we know to be such that we cannot despair of finding in their works what we seek.

Especially since that man is before our eyes in whom we have recognized the eloquence we lamented as dead to have revived in perfection.

[Note: Apparently Ambrose, who wrote the books *On Duties* and who had no time for Augustine to hear him; see *Confessions*, book 6, chapter 2, section 3, and chapter 11, section 18.]

Will he allow us, after teaching through his writings how to live, to remain ignorant of the nature of life?

A. I certainly do not think so, and I place great hope in him. But I grieve over one thing: that we cannot reveal to him, as we wish, either our devotion toward him or our devotion toward wisdom.

Surely he would pity our thirst and would overflow toward us much sooner than is now possible. For he is secure, having already persuaded himself completely concerning the immortality of the soul; and he does not know that there may be some who have sufficiently understood the misery of this ignorance, and for whom, especially when they ask for help, it would be cruel not to provide it.

The other man knows the ardor of our affection because of our familiarity, but he is now so far away, and we are in such circumstances, that we scarcely have the opportunity even to send him a letter.

[Note: Perhaps Zenobius, skilled in poetry; concerning his sudden departure, see *On Order*, book 1, chapter 7, section 20.]

I believe that, in his Transalpine leisure, he has now completed a poem by which the fear of death may be charmed away, and the stupor and chill of the soul, hardened by ancient ice, driven off.

But while these things—which are not in our power—are coming to pass, is it not most shameful for our leisure to perish, and for the whole soul itself to remain suspended and bound to an uncertain decision?

## CHAPTER XV.—The Nature of the True and the False

27. Where is the God whom we have both asked and continue to ask to open a path for us who seek not riches, not bodily pleasures, not popular acclaim and honors, but our soul and himself? Will he abandon us, or shall we abandon him?

R. It is utterly foreign to him to abandon those who desire such things. Therefore it ought also to be foreign to us to abandon so great a guide.

So, if you agree, let us briefly review how those two conclusions were established: either that truth always remains, or that truth is the discipline of argument.

You said that these conclusions were unstable, and that for this reason the summary of the whole matter could not make us secure. Or shall we instead ask how discipline can exist in an ignorant soul, which we cannot avoid calling a soul? This was what moved you, so that it became necessary to doubt again the things you had conceded.

A. Rather, let us examine those matters first; afterward we shall see what this other point amounts to. In this way, I think, no controversy will remain.

R. Let it be so; but be wholly present and extremely cautious. I know what happens to you when you attend: while you are too intent upon the conclusion and expect it to be drawn at any moment, you concede what is asked without carefully examining it.

A. You may perhaps be right. But I shall resist this kind of illness as far as I can. Only begin asking now, so that we do not linger over unnecessary matters.

28. R. As I remember, we concluded that truth cannot perish because, even if the whole world should perish, and even if truth itself should perish, it would still be true that both the world and truth had perished.

But nothing is true without truth; therefore truth cannot perish.

A. I recognize these points, and I should be greatly surprised if they were false.

R. Let us then examine the other conclusion.

A. Allow me to consider it for a little while, I beg you, so that I do not return here shamefully once again.

R. Then will it not be true that truth has perished? If it will not be true, then it does not perish. If it will be true, from where will it be true after the destruction of truth, when no truth remains?

A. I have nothing further to think through and consider; proceed to something else.

Certainly we shall do what we can to ensure that learned and prudent men read these words and correct whatever rashness may be ours, if there is any. For I do not think that either now or at any time I shall be able to discover an argument against this.

29. R. Is truth called anything other than that by which whatever is true is true?

A. No.

R. Is anything rightly called true except what is not false?

A. To doubt that would be madness.

R. Is not that false which has been fashioned in the likeness of something else and yet is not that of which it appears to be the likeness?

A. I see nothing else that I would more willingly call false. Yet what is far removed from a likeness to the true is also commonly called false.

R. Who denies that? Yet it nevertheless possesses some imitation of the true.

A. How so? For when it is said that Medea flew with winged serpents yoked together, the statement in no respect imitates the true. The thing does not exist at all; and a thing that does not exist altogether cannot imitate anything.

R. You speak correctly, but you do not notice that something which is altogether nonexistent cannot even be called false. If it is false, it exists; if it does not exist, it is not false.

[Note: Thus in our manuscripts, and likewise in the English manuscripts. Lovanius has: “For if it is false, it does not exist; if it exists, it is not false.”]

A. Shall we not then say that that monstrous thing—whatever it is—about Medea is false?

R. Certainly not; for if it is false, how is it a monster?

[Note: Thus in the manuscripts of better quality. The earlier printed editions have instead: “For if it happened, how is it false? If it did not happen, how is it a monster?”]

A. I see something astonishing. So, when I hear:

> “Huge winged serpents joined to the yoke.”  
> *(Poet cited by Cicero, *On Invention* I.19.)*

I am not to call it false?

R. You certainly are to call it false, for there is something that you can call false.

A. What, I ask?

R. The proposition, of course, which is expressed in the verse itself.

A. And what likeness to the true does that possess?

R. It would be expressed in the same way even if Medea had really done that. The false proposition therefore imitates true propositions in its very enunciation.

If it is not believed, it imitates true propositions merely by being stated in that way, and is false but not deceptive. If it secures belief, it also imitates propositions that have been believed to be true.

A. Now I understand that there is a great difference between what we say and the things about which we say something. Therefore I agree. What held me back was the thought that whatever we call false cannot rightly be called so unless it contains an imitation of some truth.

For who would not rightly laugh at someone who said that a stone was false silver? Yet if someone says that a stone is silver, we say that he speaks falsely—that is, that he utters a false proposition.

But tin or lead we can, I think, reasonably call false silver, because the thing itself somehow imitates it. Our proposition is not false for that reason; rather, it is the very thing of which the proposition is uttered that is false.

## CHAPTER XVI.—Whether Better Things Can Be Called by the Names of Inferior Things
30. R. You understand well. But consider whether we can also appropriately call silver “false lead.”

A. I do not think so.

R. Why not?

A. I do not know—except that I see it is being said very much against my wishes.

R. Perhaps because silver is the better substance, and this is said as an insult to it, whereas lead receives a kind of honor when it is called false silver?

A. You have explained exactly what I meant. And for that reason I believe that those who parade themselves in women’s clothing are rightly regarded as infamous and legally incapable of making wills. I do not know whether it would be better to call them false women or false men. Yet we can undoubtedly call them genuine actors and genuinely infamous; or, if they conceal themselves and nothing is infamous except what is named from a disgraceful reputation, we may, I think, call them genuine scoundrels—not without truth.

R. We shall have another occasion to discuss such matters. Many things are done which, by their outward appearance to the public, seem disgraceful, but which, when judged by some laudable end, are shown to be honorable. And it is a serious question whether someone who has put on a woman’s tunic in order to free his country ought to deceive the enemy, since, by being a false woman, he might perhaps prove a truer man; and whether a wise man who has somehow become certain that his life will be necessary to human affairs would prefer to die of cold rather than, if there were no alternative, clothe himself in women’s garments. But, as I have said, we shall consider this elsewhere. You certainly see how much investigation is required to determine how far such matters may proceed, lest one fall into certain inexcusable disgraces. For the present, however, what is sufficient for our question already seems clear: nothing is false unless it possesses some imitation of the true.

## CHAPTER XVII. Whether anything is entirely false or entirely true

31. A. Proceed to the remaining matters; for I am well persuaded of this.

R. Then I ask whether, apart from the disciplines by which we are educated—and among which even the study of wisdom should properly be counted—we can find anything so true that it is not, like the theatrical Achilles, false in some respect, so that it may be true in another.

A. I think many such things can be found. For that stone is not one of the disciplines, and yet, in being a true stone, it does not imitate anything according to which it could be called false. Once this example has been mentioned, you see that we must dispense with countless other examples that readily occur to anyone who reflects.

R. I see that perfectly. But do you not think that all these things are included under the single name “body”?

A. They would seem to be, if I either knew with certainty that the void is nothing, or thought that the mind itself should be numbered among bodies, or even believed that God was some kind of body. If all these things are so, I see that they are false and true without imitating anything.

R. You are leading us into a lengthy discussion, but I shall make use of brevity as far as I can. Surely the thing you call “the void” is one thing, and truth another.

A. Entirely different. For what could be emptier than I would be if I thought truth was something empty, or if I desired something empty so intensely? What else do I desire except to discover truth?

R. Then perhaps you also grant that nothing is true unless it is made true by truth.

A. That has long been clear.

R. Do you doubt that nothing is empty except the void itself—or certainly a body?

A. I do not doubt it at all.

R. I suppose, then, that you believe truth to be some kind of body.

A. Not at all.

R. What is it in a body?

A. I do not know; that is irrelevant. For I imagine that you know this much: if the void exists, it is more truly where there is no body.

R. That is certainly clear.

A. Why, then, do we delay?

R. Do you think either that truth made the void, or that anything can be true where truth is absent?

A. I do not think so.

R. Then the void is not true, since what is not the void cannot make something into a void; and it is clear that what lacks truth is not true. Indeed, the very thing called “the void” receives that name from the fact that it is nothing. How, then, can what does not exist be true? Or how can what is utterly nothing exist?

A. Come, then, let us abandon the void as void.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Whether body truly exists

32. R. What do you say about the remaining things?

A. What else [could I say] but what you see?  
[Note: Er., Ven., Lov.: “What else but what you see,” in an uninterrupted sentence continuing through the words “How do you know?” M.]

R. What you see strongly supports my position. For the mind and God remain; and if these two are true because truth is in them, no one doubts God’s immortality. The mind, however, is believed to be immortal if it is proved that truth—which cannot perish—is also in it.

Let us therefore examine the final point: whether body is not truly true—that is, whether truth is not in it, but rather some kind of image of truth. For if we find in body—which is sufficiently certain to be subject to destruction—a kind of truth such as exists in the disciplines, it will not immediately follow that the truth of disputation is the discipline through which all disciplines are true. For body is also true, although it is evident that it was not formed by the method of disputation. But if body too is true through some kind of imitation, and therefore not true in the fullest sense, perhaps nothing will prevent us from showing that the method of disputation itself is truth.

A. For the moment let us investigate body; for even when this has been established, I do not see that the controversy will have been brought to an end.

R. How do you know what God wills? Pay attention, then. I think that body is contained by some form and shape; if it did not possess these, it would not be body, while, if it possessed a true form, it would be mind. Is there any other way this should be understood?

A. I agree in part, but I am uncertain about the rest. I grant that, unless it is held within some figure, it is not body. But I do not sufficiently understand how, if it possessed a true figure, it would be mind.

R. Do you not remember anything from the beginning of the first book, and from that geometrical discussion of yours?

A. You have reminded me well. I remember it completely, and with great pleasure.

R. Are figures found in bodies of the same kind as those demonstrated by that discipline?

A. On the contrary, it is incredible how much inferior they are shown to be.

R. Which of these, then, do you consider true?

A. Please do not suppose that I must be questioned even on that point.
