Who is so blind in mind that he does not see that the figures taught in geometry reside in truth itself—or that truth is also in them? The figures of bodies, however, since they seem somehow to strive toward those figures, possess I know not what imitation of truth, and for that reason are false. I now understand everything you were trying to demonstrate.

## CHAPTER XIX. Immortal truth proves the immortality of the soul

33. R. What need is there, then, to inquire further about the discipline of disputation? Whether geometrical figures are in truth, or truth is in them, no one doubts that our soul—that is, our understanding—contains them; and consequently truth is also compelled to be in our mind.

But if every discipline exists in the mind as in a subject, inseparably, and truth cannot perish, why, I ask, do we doubt the soul’s perpetual life, as though it had some familiar connection with death? Do that line, that square, or that circle possess other things which they imitate in order to be true?

A. I cannot believe that at all, unless perhaps a line is something other than length without breadth, and a circle something other than a line drawn around a center, tending equally toward it on every side.

R. Why, then, do we hesitate? Is truth absent wherever these things are?

A. May God avert such madness.

R. Is the discipline not in the mind?

A. Who would say that?

R. But perhaps, when the subject perishes, what exists in the subject can remain?

A. When will that be persuaded to me?

R. It remains, then, that truth must perish.

A. How could that happen?

R. The soul is therefore immortal. Now, now, believe your own arguments; believe the truth. It cries out that it both exists and dwells in you, that it is immortal, and that no death of the body can wrest its dwelling from it. Turn away from your shadow; return to yourself. Your destruction is nothing except your forgetting that you cannot perish.

A. I hear; I recover my senses; I am beginning to remember. But please explain how what remains can be understood to be in the mind of an unlearned person—for we cannot call that mind mortal—namely, discipline and truth.

R. That question requires another volume if you want it treated carefully. At the same time, I see that the matters we have investigated as best we could must be reviewed for you, because, if none of the things granted is doubtful, I think we have accomplished much and may investigate the rest with no small degree of confidence.

## CHAPTER XX. Some truths we believe, some we remember; some are apprehended neither by sensation nor imagination, but by reason alone

34. A. It is as you say, and I gladly obey your instructions. But grant me at least this, before you set the limit of the volume: briefly explain the difference between the true figure contained in understanding and the figure that thought imagines for itself—which in Greek is called either *phantasia* or *phantasma*.

R. You are asking about something that no one can see unless he is very pure, and for seeing which you have had little practice. Even now, through these circuits of discussion, we are accomplishing nothing other than exercising you so that you may become capable of seeing it. Nevertheless, I may perhaps make clear briefly how the difference can be explained.

Suppose that you have forgotten something and want others to recall it to your memory. They say to you, “Is it this, or that?” and offer different things as though they were similar. You do not see the thing you wish to remember, and yet you see that it is not what they have named. When this happens to you, does it seem that you are wholly in a state of forgetfulness? For the very discrimination by which you reject what you are falsely reminded of is a certain part of recollection.

A. That seems so.

R. Such people, then, do not yet see the truth; nevertheless they cannot be deceived or misled, and they know well enough what they are seeking. But if someone tells you that you laughed a few days after you were born, you do not dare to say that it is false; and if he is an authority who deserves belief, you will believe it rather than remember it. For that entire period is buried in you under the strongest forgetfulness. Do you think otherwise?

A. I entirely agree.

R. This, then, differs greatly from that forgetfulness, but it lies midway between them. There is another state nearer and more closely related to the recovery of memory and the re-examination of truth. It is like what happens when we see something and recognize with certainty that we saw it at some time, affirming that we know it; but we struggle to recall where, when, how, or through whom it first came to our knowledge.

For example, if the matter concerns a person, we also ask where we came to know him. When he reminds us, suddenly the whole matter pours into memory like a light, and no further effort is needed for us to remember. Is this kind of experience unknown or obscure to you?

A. What could be clearer—or what happens to me more frequently?

35. R. Such are those who have been well educated in the liberal disciplines. They undoubtedly bring forth, by learning, those disciplines buried within themselves by forgetfulness and, in a certain sense, dig them up again.  
[Note: 1 *Retractations*, chapter 4, no. 4.]

Yet they are not satisfied with this, nor do they stop until they contemplate as broadly and fully as possible the entire face of truth, whose radiance already glimmers to some extent in those arts. But from these disciplines certain false colors and forms pour themselves, as it were, into the mirror of thought, often deceiving and misleading those who inquire, because they suppose that the whole of what they know or seek is contained in them.

These are the imaginative representations that must be avoided with great caution. They are recognized as deceptive when they vary along with the changing mirror of thought, whereas the face of truth remains one and unchanging. For thought then paints for itself a square of one size and another of another size, and presents it as though before its eyes. But the inner mind, which wishes to see the truth, should turn rather toward that according to which it judges that all those things are square, if it is able to do so.

A. What if someone says that it judges according to what it is accustomed to see with its eyes?

R. Why, then, if it has nevertheless been properly educated, does it judge that a true sphere, however large, is touched by a true plane at a single point? What has the eye ever seen of this, or what can it see, since even the imagination of thought cannot form anything of this kind?

Do we not demonstrate this when, in imagining, we describe even the smallest circle in the mind and draw lines from it to the center? For when we have drawn two lines, between which scarcely a point could be pricked with a needle, we can no longer, in the imagination of thought itself, draw other lines in the middle so that they reach the center without any mingling; yet reason declares that innumerable lines can be drawn, and that they can meet one another in those incredible narrow spaces only at the center, so that a circle could even be inscribed within every interval between them.

Since that imagination cannot accomplish this, and fails even more than the eyes themselves—if indeed it was impressed upon the mind through the eyes—it is clear that it differs greatly from truth, and that, while this is seen, truth is not seen.

36. These matters will be discussed more laboriously and subtly when we begin to treat understanding, the part assigned to us, after we have clarified and examined as far as we can whatever concerns the soul’s life. For I do not think you are insufficiently afraid that human death, even if it does not kill the soul, may nevertheless bring forgetfulness of all things, and of truth itself, if truth is ever discovered.

A. It is impossible to say sufficiently how greatly this evil must be feared. For what will that eternal life be, or what death would not be preferable to it, if the soul lives as we see it living in a child immediately after birth? I say nothing of the life that takes place in the womb; for I do not think it is nonexistent.

R. Be of good courage. God will be present, as we now feel, to us who are seeking; and he promises something supremely blessed and completely filled with truth, without any falsehood, after this body.

A. May it happen as we hope.

[Col. 0903]

# Three Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Against the Academics

[Note: Written toward the end of the year 386.]  
[Note: For correcting these books, the following manuscripts were used: the Germanensis, Michaelinus, Theodericensis, Albinensis, Casalensis, two Victorini, three Sorbonici, the Regius, the Vaticanus, four readings of the Belgian manuscripts apud Lov., as well as the editions of Bad., Am., Er., and Lov.]  
[Note: In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.]  
(C)

## Notice concerning the following three books against the Academics

[Note: See also book 1, chapter 1, of the *Retractations*, cols. 585–587, from the words “Therefore, when I had left,” no. 1, through the words of no. 4, “a man suited to himself.” M.]

The correct order requires that the books against the Academics—being the first of all to be reviewed by Augustine and having been composed by him before the others, except for the work *On the Beautiful and the Fitting*, which was produced when he was younger and immediately disappeared—be restored here to their proper place.

For the holy Doctor had long before absorbed the Academics’ arguments against apprehending truth. Even after he had attained truth through God’s grace, those arguments still caused him some difficulty. To dispel them, he resolved not only to devote himself privately to diligent meditation but also to hold a discussion with his friends. He divided this discussion, conducted over several days, into three books and sent it to his fellow citizen and patron Romanianus, encouraging him to pursue philosophy.

The first book presents Licentius and Trygetius engaging each other, the former arguing on behalf of the Academics and the latter against them: whether the happy life consists in knowledge of the truth, or instead in the investigation of truth alone. What error and wisdom are is explained at length.

In the second book Saint Augustine reviews the Academics’ doctrines; Alypius develops the differences between the Old and the New Academy. The view of these philosophers is rejected: they thought that truth could not be apprehended, yet professed to follow what was probable.

In the third book Alypius denies, in keeping with the position he has undertaken, that truth can be found; Augustine proves that it can be known by the wise person, since such a person at least knows wisdom. Augustine then examines Zeno’s definition and refutes those two Academical statements: “Nothing can be apprehended,” and “One ought to assent to nothing.” Finally, he says that the Academics seem not to have thought as they are commonly believed to have thought.

He wrote these books at the beginning of his conversion, in the country estate at Cassiciacum, after only a few days had passed since he began living there (book 1, chapter 1, no. 4), and therefore toward the end of the year 386. At that time he had renounced his profession of rhetoric and withdrawn there in order to devote himself entirely to purifying his mind and to prepare himself worthily for holy Baptism. See the annotation on book 3, chapter 20.

## Saint Augustine, Letter 1, to Hermogenianus

“I would never dare attack the Academics, even in jest—for how could the authority of such great men fail to move me, unless I thought that their position was quite different from what is commonly believed? Therefore I imitated them as far as I was able rather than defeated them, something I am altogether unable to do.

“For it seems to me that it suited the times well that, if anything sincere flowed from the Platonic source, it should be led for the nourishment of very few people through shady and thorny thickets, rather than flowing through open places and being unable to remain clear and pure because herds rushed upon it from every side . . . .

“But in this age, when we see no philosophers except perhaps men wearing a little cloak—men whom I would scarcely consider worthy of so venerable a name—I think that those people should be led back to hope of finding truth if the Academics’ doctrine, through its verbal ingenuity, deterred them from grasping things. Otherwise what was temporarily suitable for uprooting deeply rooted errors may now begin to obstruct the planting of knowledge . . . .

“Indeed, whatever the case may be with those writings, I am not so much delighted that, as you write, I have defeated the Academics—you write this perhaps more affectionately than accurately—as that I have broken the most hateful restraint by which, through despair of truth, the nourishment of the soul, I was held back from the breast of philosophy.”

## From Book XV on the Trinity, chapter XII

“Against the Academics . . . who maintain that nothing can be known by a human being . . . are our three books, written at the beginning of our conversion. Whoever can and wishes to read them, and understands what he has read, will certainly not be disturbed by any of the many arguments they have devised against apprehending truth.”

See the *Enchiridion*, chapter 20.

# BOOK ONE

Romanianus is encouraged to pursue philosophy in the preface to this book, in which his son Licentius engages Trygetius in three discussions. The former argues that the happy life consists in the very investigation of truth; the latter, on the contrary, that it consists only in the apprehension of truth. The definition of error also enters into the debate, as does the definition of wisdom, which is explained lucidly.

## CHAPTER I. He exhorts Romanianus to true philosophy

1. O Romanianus, if virtue could in turn seize a person suited to itself away from hostile fortune, just as it permits no one to be taken away from it, fortune would by now surely have laid hands upon you, proclaimed you its own possession, and led you into the possession of the most certain goods, refusing to let you serve even favorable circumstances.

But since it has been arranged—whether because of our merits or because of the necessity of nature (*Retractations*, book 1, chapter 1, no. 2)—that the divine soul dwelling in mortals does not readily reach the harbor of wisdom, where it is moved neither by the opposing nor by the favorable breath of fortune, unless fortune itself, whether favorable or seemingly adverse, brings it there, nothing remains for us on your behalf except prayers. Through them we may ask God, who cares for these matters, to restore you to yourself; for he will thus easily restore you to us as well. May he permit that mind of yours, which has long been struggling for breath, finally to emerge into the air of true freedom.

For perhaps what is commonly called fortune is governed by some hidden order. We call nothing else “chance” in events except that whose reason and cause are concealed (*ibid.*); and nothing advantageous or disadvantageous happens in any part that does not agree and correspond with the whole.

Philosophy promises that she will reveal this doctrine—issued from the oracles of the richest teachings and placed very far from the understanding of the profane—to her true lovers. To her I now invite you.

Therefore, since many things unworthy of your character happen to you, do not despise yourself. For if divine providence extends even to us, as cannot reasonably be doubted, believe me: you must be dealt with in precisely the way you are being dealt with.

When, possessing such a great natural ability as I have always admired, you entered human life from the beginning of adolescence with reason still weak and your steps faltering, a life completely filled with every kind of error, you were met by the abundance of riches. It began to swallow that age and mind—eagerly pursuing what seemed beautiful and honorable—in its seductive whirlpools, unless those blows of fortune that are thought adverse had snatched you away when you were almost drowning.

2. But suppose that, when you produced the gifts of bears and spectacles never before seen there for our fellow citizens, the theatrical applause had received you with complete enthusiasm; suppose that, carried to heaven by the mingled and harmonious voices of foolish people, whose multitude is immense, no one dared to be your enemy; suppose that the municipal records marked you in bronze as the patron not only of your fellow citizens but also of your neighbors; that statues were erected, honors poured upon you, and powers added that exceeded the status of a municipal office; that rich banquets were prepared daily; that whatever anyone needed, and whatever anyone’s pleasures thirsted for, he requested without hesitation and drank without hesitation, while much was poured out even for those who had asked for nothing; and that your household property, carefully and faithfully administered by your people, proved itself adequate and ready for such enormous expenses.

Suppose that meanwhile you lived amid the most exquisite masses of buildings, in the splendor of baths, in games that honest people do not reject, in hunting, in banquets, in the mouths of clients, in the mouths of citizens, and finally in the mouths of peoples, celebrated as most humane, most generous, most refined, and most fortunate—as you were.  
[Note: In several old manuscripts and in Bad., Am., and Er., “as you were” is absent. In seven other manuscripts it is replaced by “as you are accustomed to be”; that reading may perhaps be the more genuine because it is farther removed from common usage.]

Would anyone dare mention to you another happy life—the only life that is truly happy? Would anyone, I ask, be able to persuade you that you were not merely not happy, but most miserable precisely to the extent that you least seemed so to yourself?

But now, how briefly the many and great adversities you have endured have made it necessary to remind you of all this! You do not need to be persuaded by examples belonging to others of how fleeting, fragile, and full of calamities are all the things mortals consider good. You have had such experience of them in one respect that through you we can persuade others.

3. That quality of yours—by which you have always desired what is honorable and good; by which you preferred to be generous rather than rich; by which you never desired to be more powerful than just, and never yielded to adversities or wickedness—that very quality in you which, I do not know through what sleep and torpor of this life, has been lulled into slumber, hidden providence has resolved to awaken through those various and harsh upheavals.

Awake, awake, I beg you. Believe me, you will greatly rejoice that the gifts of this world, by which the unwary are held, have scarcely flattered you with any prosperity. They were trying daily to ensnare me as well while I sang these same praises, unless the pain in my chest had forced me to abandon my empty profession and take refuge in the embrace of philosophy.

She now nourishes and shelters me in the leisure we have ardently desired. She has wholly freed me from that superstition into which I had plunged you headlong along with myself.  
[Note: Romanianus was evidently among those whom Augustine laments having drawn with him into the Manichaean heresy, *Confessions*, book 4, chapter 1. He too, however, eventually returned to sound faith, since he always held Augustine in the highest esteem, valued highly the book *On True Religion* and other writings Augustine dedicated to him, and was finally treated with great honor in letters from Paulinus, bishop of Nola, who sent him loaves under the name of “blessed offerings,” addressing him as a thoroughly Christian and Catholic man.]

For philosophy teaches—and truly teaches—that absolutely nothing should be worshiped, and that everything must be despised which mortal eyes behold or any sense touches (*Retractations*, book 1, chapter 1, no. 2). She promises to reveal plainly the truest and most hidden God, and even now deigns to display him, as it were, through luminous clouds.

4. Our Licentius lives with me in this philosophy with the greatest zeal. He has turned wholly away from youthful allurements and pleasures, so that I do not rashly dare to propose him to his father as an example for imitation.

For philosophy is the one whose breasts no age can complain of being excluded from.  
[Note: *Queritur*, according to Lov. M.]

To encourage you to hold fast to and drink deeply from them more eagerly, although I know your thirst well, I wished nevertheless to send you a taste. I ask that I not have hoped for nothing: may it be for you most pleasant and, so to speak, an introduction.

I have sent you in writing the discussion that Trygetius and Licentius held with each other. Trygetius too, as though he had taken up military service for a time merely to relieve the weariness of his studies, has returned to us ardently and voraciously eager for the great and honorable arts.

After only a few days had passed since we began living in the country estate, I saw that, when I urged and encouraged them toward study, they were prepared and eager beyond what I had hoped. I therefore wished to test what they could do at their age, especially since Cicero’s book *Hortensius* seemed already to have reconciled them to philosophy to a considerable extent.

I therefore employed a secretary, so that the breeze would not scatter our work, and permitted nothing to be lost. In this book, you will read the matters and opinions of those two, but also the words of Alypius and myself.

## FIRST DISCUSSION

## CHAPTER II. Whether apprehension of truth is necessary for the happy life, or only its investigation

5. When, then, at my urging we had all assembled for this purpose in one place, wherever it seemed convenient, I said: “Surely you do not doubt that we ought to know the truth?”

“Not at all,” said Trygetius. The others also indicated by their very expressions that they agreed.

“What if,” I said, “we can be happy even without apprehending the truth? Do you think apprehension of truth is necessary?”

Here Alypius said: “I think it safer for me to be the judge of this question. Since I am scheduled to travel to the city, I ought to be relieved of the burden of taking one side. At the same time, I can more easily delegate the role of judge to someone than that of advocate. Therefore, from this point on, expect nothing from me in favor of either side.”

When everyone had granted this to him and I had repeated the question, Trygetius said: “Certainly we wish to be happy; and if we can reach this state without truth, then we do not need to seek truth.”

“What does that mean?” I asked. “Do you think we can be happy even without discovering the truth?”

Then Licentius said: “We can, if we seek the truth.”

When I asked the opinion of the others by a nod, Navigius said:  
[Note: Augustine’s brother.]

“What Licentius has said moves me. For perhaps this itself may be to live happily: to live in the search for truth.”

“Then define,” said Trygetius, “what the happy life is, so that I may infer from that what answer is appropriate.”

“What do you think,” I said, “living happily is other than living according to what is best in a human being?”

“I will not recklessly pour out words,” he said. “For I think you must define for me what that best thing itself is.”

“Who,” I said, “would doubt that the best thing in a human being is nothing other than that part of the soul whose rule it is fitting that everything else in a human being should obey?”

“That part,” so that you do not demand another definition, “can be called mind or reason.”  
(*Retractations*, book 1, chapter 1, no. 2.)

“If this does not seem right to you, ask how you yourself would define either the happy life or the best thing in a human being.”

“I agree,” he said.

6. “What, then?” I said, “to return to our subject: does it seem to you that one can live happily without discovering the truth, provided one merely seeks it?”

“I repeat my earlier opinion,” he said: “It does not seem so.”

“What do the rest of you think?” I asked.

Then Licentius said: “It seems entirely possible to me. For our ancestors, whom we have accepted as wise and happy, lived well and happily for the sole reason that they sought the truth.”

“I thank you,” I said, “for making me judge together with Alypius, whom I confess I had already begun to envy. Since, then, one of you thinks that the happy life can be attained through the investigation of truth alone, while the other thinks it can occur only through its discovery, and since Navigius a little earlier showed that he wished to cross over to your side, Licentius, I am very eager to see what kind of advocates you can be for your respective opinions.

“The matter is important and thoroughly worthy of careful examination.”

“If the matter is important,” said Licentius, “it requires great men.”

“Do not look for what is difficult to find anywhere in the world, especially in this country house,” I said. “Instead, explain why the statement you have made, as I think not recklessly, seems correct to you, and by what reasoning. For even the greatest matters, when sought from small beginnings, usually make those who seek them great.”

## CHAPTER III. The Academical position that happiness lies in the investigation of truth is defended

7. “Since I see,” he said, “that you are pressing us very strongly to argue against one another—which I trust you wish for our benefit—I ask why the person who seeks the truth cannot be happy, even if he does not discover it at all.”

“Because,” said Trygetius, “we want the happy person to be perfect in wisdom in every respect. But the person who is still seeking is not perfect. I therefore cannot see at all how you can defend him as happy.”

“Can the authority of our predecessors have any influence with you?”
[Note: Six manuscripts read “conquer” (*vincere*) instead of “have influence” (*vivere*); likewise Er. and Ven. M.] he asked.

“Not everyone’s,” said Trygetius.

“Whose, then?”

“Those, of course, who were wise.”

Then Licentius said: “Does Carneades not seem wise to you?”

“I am not Greek,” he replied. “I do not know who this Carneades was.”

“What, then,” said Licentius, “do you think of our Cicero?”

After he had remained silent for a long time, he said: “He was wise.”

“Then Cicero’s opinion on this matter carries some weight with you?”

“It does,” he said.

“Then hear what it was, for I think it has slipped your mind. Our Cicero held that the person who investigates the truth is happy, even if he is unable to arrive at its discovery.”

“Where,” he asked, “did Cicero say that?”

Licentius replied: “Who does not know that he emphatically asserted that nothing can be apprehended by a human being, and that nothing remains for the wise person except the most diligent investigation of truth? For if he assented to uncertain things, even if they happened to be true, he could not be freed from error, which is the greatest fault of a wise person.

“Therefore, if we must believe both that the wise person is necessarily happy and that the investigation of truth alone is the complete task of wisdom, why do we hesitate to think that the happy life can be attained through the investigation of truth in itself?”

8. Then Trygetius said: “May we return at last to the matters that were rashly conceded?”
[Note: In B: “And when he departed: What.” Par., Er., Ven., and Lov.: “And when he had departed: That.” M.]

Here I said: “Those who are driven to debate not by a desire to discover truth but by childish boasting of their cleverness do not usually grant this. Therefore, in my judgment, especially since you are still in need of nourishment and education, you should not only be permitted but also instructed to return to the points you have conceded too carelessly and examine them again.”

Licentius said: “I consider it no small progress in philosophy when a disputant despises victory in comparison with the discovery of what is right and true. Therefore I gladly comply with both your instructions and your judgment, and I permit Trygetius to return to the point he thinks he conceded rashly, since the matter is within my authority.”

Then Alypius said: “You yourselves recognize with me that I have not yet performed the duties of the office I undertook. But since the departure already arranged compels me to interrupt this, my fellow judge will not refuse to share with me a doubled authority until my return, as part of my own responsibility. For I see that your contest will continue at greater length.”

When he had departed, Licentius said: “Bring forward what you conceded rashly.”

And Trygetius replied: “I rashly granted that Cicero was wise.”

“So Cicero was not wise,” said Licentius, “the man through whom philosophy in the Latin language was both begun and perfected?”

“Even if I grant that he was wise,” Trygetius replied, “I do not approve everything he said.”

“Yet you must refute many other things he said, if you do not want to seem impudent in rejecting the particular point under discussion.”

“What if I am prepared to assert that he was wrong only in this one matter?”

“As I think, it makes no difference to you except how much weight the arguments I produce will have in support of what I wish to establish.”

“Proceed,” said Trygetius.

“For what,” he said, “could I dare say against one who declares himself Cicero’s opponent?”

9. Then Trygetius said: “I want you, our judge, to pay attention to how you defined the happy life above. For you said that the happy man is one who lives according to that part of the soul which is suited to rule the others. But now, Licentius, I want you either to grant me—or at least grant me now—for I have shaken off that yoke of authority in the liberty which philosophy promises will vindicate us most fully—that the man who is still seeking the truth is not perfect.”

After a long silence he replied: “I do not grant it.”

“And why, please?” said Trygetius. “Explain. I am here, eager to hear how a man can both be perfect and still seek the truth.”

He replied: “I admit that whoever has not reached the end is not perfect. But I believe that only God knows that truth—or perhaps the human soul, once it has left this body, that is, this dark prison. The end of man, however, is to seek the truth perfectly. For we seek the perfect, but we are nevertheless human.”

“And so,” said Trygetius, “a man cannot be happy. For how can he be happy when he cannot attain [Col. 0911] what he ardently desires?”

[Note: [Col. 0911] Par.: “or, then, he can find the truth; or let him withdraw into himself.” M.]

“But a man can live happily,” he replied, “if he lives according to that part of the soul which is permitted to rule in man.”

“Then he can find the truth.”

“Or else,” he said, “he should withdraw into himself and not desire the truth, lest, when he cannot attain it, he necessarily be miserable.”

“But this very thing,” he replied, “is the happy condition of man: to seek the truth perfectly. For this is to reach the end beyond which he cannot advance. Whoever, therefore, seeks the truth less earnestly than he ought has not reached the end of man. But whoever devotes himself to finding the truth as much as a human being can and ought, is happy even if he does not find it; for he does everything that he was born to do. If discovery is lacking, what is lacking is something that nature did not give. Finally, since a man must be either happy or miserable, is it not madness to call miserable the man who, day and night, presses forward as far as he can in investigating the truth? He will therefore be happy.

“Moreover, that definition supports me, as I think, even more abundantly. For if the happy man is, as he is, the one who lives according to that part of the soul which is suited to rule the others—and this part is called reason—I ask whether the man who seeks the truth perfectly does not live according to reason. If that is absurd, why do we hesitate to call a man happy through the very seeking of the truth alone?”

## CHAPTER IV.—What Error Is

10. “In my view,” he said, “whoever errs neither lives according to reason nor is happy at all. But everyone who always seeks and never finds errs. Therefore, one of two things must now be demonstrated to you: either that a man who errs can be happy, or that the man who never finds what he seeks does not err.”

He replied: “A happy man cannot err.”

And after he had remained silent for a long time, he added: “But he does not err when he seeks, because he seeks perfectly, and thus does not err.”

“And so,” said Trygetius, “he seeks in order not to err, certainly; but he errs when he does not find.”

“You thought this would help your case,” said Trygetius, “because he refuses to err—as though no one ever errs unwillingly, or as though anyone at all errs except unwillingly.”

Then, when he hesitated for a long time about what to answer, I said: “You must define what error is. For you can more easily see its boundaries, since you have already entered deeply into it.”

“I am not capable,” said Licentius, “of defining anything—although defining error is easier than bringing it to an end.”

“I shall define it,” he said. “That is very easy for me, not because of my talent, but because the case is excellent. For to err is certainly always to seek and never to find.”

“If I could easily refute even that definition,” said Licentius, “I would long ago have had no lack of arguments for my case. But since either the matter itself is difficult, or at least appears so to me, I ask you to defer the question until tomorrow’s light, if, after carefully turning it over within myself, I am unable to find anything to answer today.”

Since I thought this should be granted, and the others did not object, we rose to go for a walk. While we were conversing among ourselves on many different matters, he remained absorbed in thought. When he realized that this was fruitless, he preferred to relax his mind and join our conversation. Later, when evening was already approaching, they had returned to the same conflict; but I put an end to it and persuaded them to allow the matter to be postponed to another day. From there we went to the baths.

## SECOND DISPUTATION

11. The next day, when we had taken our seats, I said: “Bring forward what you began yesterday.”

Licentius replied: “Unless I am mistaken, we postponed the discussion at my request because the definition of error seemed exceedingly difficult to me.”

“Here at least you are not mistaken,” I said; “and I gladly hope that this may be an omen for what follows” (*Retractions* 1.1.2).

“Listen, then,” he said, “to what I would have produced yesterday had you not intervened. Error seems to me to be the approval of what is false as though it were true. No one who always holds that the truth must be sought can fall into it. For one who approves nothing cannot approve what is false; therefore he cannot err. Yet he can very easily be happy. For, not to go farther afield, if we were permitted to live every day as we were permitted yesterday, I would see no reason to hesitate to call ourselves happy. We lived with great tranquillity of mind, freeing the soul from every bodily stain and keeping far removed from the torches of desire, devoting ourselves, as far as is permitted to a human being, to reason—that is, living according to that divine part of the soul which, by yesterday’s definition among ourselves, we agreed to be the happy life. And, as I think, we found nothing, but merely sought the truth. A happy life, therefore, can come to a man through the mere seeking of the truth, even if he is quite unable to find it.

“Consider how easily your definition is excluded by common understanding. For you said that to err is always to seek and never to find. What if someone seeks nothing and, when asked, for example, whether it is day, rashly and immediately supposes and answers that it is night? Does he not seem to you to be in error? Your definition has therefore failed to include this kind of error, which is perhaps the most monstrous. But if it has also included people who do not err, can any definition be more defective?

“For if someone is seeking Alexandria and proceeds toward it along the correct road, I do not think you can call him mistaken. But what if, hindered by various circumstances, he takes a long time on that same road and is overtaken by death before reaching the city? Has he not both always sought and never found, and yet not erred?”

“No,” he replied, “he has not always sought.”

12. “You speak correctly,” said Licentius, “and you remind me well. For your definition is altogether irrelevant to the matter. I did not say that the man who always seeks the truth is happy. Indeed, this cannot even happen: first, because a man is not always a man; and then, because from the moment he begins to be a man, he is not yet able to seek the truth, since age prevents him.

“Or, if you think that ‘always’ must be said whenever he allows no period of time to be lost in which he is already able to seek, you must return once more to your example of Alexandria. Suppose that, from the time when he is permitted by age or circumstances to begin traveling, someone sets out along that road; and, as I said above, without ever going astray, nevertheless departs this life before arriving. You will be greatly mistaken if this man seems to you to have erred, even though throughout all the time available to him he neither ceased seeking nor was able to find the place toward which he was traveling.

“Therefore, if my description is true, and if, according to it, the man who seeks perfectly does not err, even though he does not find the truth, and is happy for the reason that he lives according to reason; while your definition has been frustrated—and even if it had not been, I should not need to concern myself with it, if the case has been sufficiently established by what I defined—why, please, has this question between us not yet been resolved?”

## CHAPTER V.—What Wisdom Is

13. Then Trygetius said: “Do you grant that wisdom is the right way of life?”

“I do,” he replied, “without any doubt. But nevertheless I want you to define wisdom for me, so that I may know whether what seems to me to be wisdom seems the same to you.”

“Does it seem to you,” he said, “to have been insufficiently defined by the very answer you have just given? You have granted what I wanted. For, unless I am mistaken, wisdom is not falsely called the right way of life.”

Licentius replied: “Nothing seems more ridiculous to me than that definition.”

“Perhaps so,” he said. “Nevertheless, proceed step by step, please, so that reason may precede your laughter. For nothing is uglier than laughter deserving of ridicule.”

“What?” he said. “Do you not admit that death is opposed to life?”

“I admit it.”

“Then,” he said, “no way of life seems to me more truly a way of life than the one by which each person proceeds so as not to fall into death.”

Trygetius agreed.

“Suppose, then, that some traveler, avoiding a side road which he has heard is occupied by robbers, continues straight ahead and thereby escapes destruction. Has he not followed both the way of life and the straight way? Yet no one calls that wisdom. How, then, is every straight way of life wisdom? I granted that it is one, but not that it is the only one. A definition, however, ought not to include anything alien to the matter. So define again, if you please, what you think wisdom is.”

14. He was silent for a long time. Then he said: “There, I define it again, if you have decided never to bring this to an end. Wisdom is the straight road that leads to the truth.”

“This too,” he replied, “is refuted in the same way. For when, in Virgil, Aeneas is told by his mother:

> Go on now, and direct your steps wherever the road leads you.  
> (*Aeneid* 1.400),

he follows this road and reaches the thing that had been spoken of—that is, the truth. If you please, argue that the path on which he set his foot can be called wisdom. Yet I am utterly foolish to try to break down your description, since nothing could help my case more. For you said that wisdom is not the truth itself, but the road that leads to it. Therefore, whoever uses this road certainly uses wisdom; and whoever uses wisdom must be wise. The man who has sought the truth perfectly will therefore be wise, even if he has not yet reached it. For no road that leads to the truth is, in my opinion, understood better than diligent inquiry into the truth. By using this road alone, then, this man will already be wise. But no wise man is miserable; and every human being is either miserable or happy. Therefore, it is not only discovery but the investigation of the truth in itself that will make a man happy.”

15. Then he smiled and said: “I deserve this, since I confidently agree with my opponent on a matter that is not necessary—as though I were some great definer, or thought anything more superfluous in debate. For what limit will there be if I should again want you to define something, and then again demand, pretending that I understand nothing, that the words of the same definition, and likewise all the consequences of it, be defined one by one? For what is so perfectly clear that I could not compel it to be defined as a matter of right, if the definition of wisdom is rightly demanded of me? For what term has nature intended to be more clearly understood in our minds than wisdom?

“But somehow, when that very notion has departed from our minds as though from a harbor, and has stretched out its sails, so to speak, toward words, a thousand shipwrecks of sophistry immediately appear.”

[Note: [Col. 0914] B reads “will appear”; Par., Er., Ven., and Lov. read “appear.” M.]

Therefore, either let no definition of wisdom be demanded, or let our judge deign to descend in its defense.

Then, since night prevented me from writing and I saw something substantial arising that would have to be discussed almost from the beginning, I postponed it to another day. We had begun the discussion when the sun was already declining toward sunset, and nearly the entire day had been spent both in arranging rural affairs and in reviewing the first book of Virgil.

## THIRD DISPUTATION

## CHAPTER VI.—A Definition of Wisdom Is Given and Attacked. The Divinations of Albicerius

16. Then, as soon as daylight appeared—for the arrangements of the previous day had left us abundant leisure—the task undertaken was immediately resumed.

“Yesterday,” I said, “Trygetius, you asked me to descend from the role of judge to the defense of wisdom. As though wisdom would tolerate an adversary in your conversation, or, if someone defended it, would be in such difficulty that it needed to implore greater aid. For nothing else has arisen between you than the question of what wisdom is; and neither of you attacks it, since both desire it.

“Nor, if you think that you have failed in defining wisdom, should you therefore abandon the remaining defense of your position. Thus you will receive from me nothing other than a definition of wisdom which is neither mine nor new, but belongs both to ancient thinkers and to a tradition which I am surprised you do not remember. For you are not hearing for the first time that wisdom is knowledge of human and divine things.”

17. At this point Licentius, whom I had thought would spend a long time searching for something to say after that definition, immediately added: “Why, then, please, do we not call that most disgraceful man wise—the man whom we ourselves know well to be accustomed to squander himself among innumerable prostitutes? [Col. 0915] I mean Albicerius, who for many years at Carthage gave astonishing and accurate answers to those who consulted him.

“I could recall innumerable examples, except that I am speaking among people who have experienced them, and that a few will now suffice for what I want. Did he not, when a spoon was not found in the house—for he was speaking to me—answer, when questioned at your command, with the greatest speed and truthfulness, not only what was being sought but also whose object it was and where it was hidden?

“I shall omit what happened in my presence, in which he was not at all mistaken about the matter being asked. A boy who was carrying the money had stolen a certain portion of it while we were going to Albicerius. He ordered that all the coins be counted and compelled the boy to return before our eyes what he had taken, before Albicerius himself had either seen the coins or heard from us how much had been brought to him.”

[Col. 0915]

18. “What of the fact that we have heard from you that the highly educated and distinguished man Flaccianus was accustomed to marvel? When he had spoken to Albicerius about purchasing an estate, he brought the matter before that divine man in such a way that he asked him, if he could, to say what he had done. Albicerius immediately pronounced not only the kind of transaction but also, to Flaccianus’s vehemently expressed astonishment, the very name of the estate, even though it was so strange that Flaccianus himself scarcely remembered it.

“Now I cannot relate without amazement of mind the following incident. Our friend, your pupil, wanted to provoke Albicerius and insolently demanded that he say what the man was silently turning over in his own mind. Albicerius replied that he was thinking of a line of Virgil. When the man was stupefied and could not deny it, Albicerius continued by asking which line it was. Although he had scarcely ever passed through a grammarian’s school, Albicerius did not hesitate to recite the verse himself, confidently and volubly.

“Were the matters about which people consulted him, then, not human matters? Or could he have given such definite and truthful answers to those who consulted him without knowledge of divine things? Both alternatives are absurd. For human matters are nothing other than the affairs of human beings—money, coins, an estate, and finally even thought itself. And who would not rightly judge divine matters to be those through which divination itself comes to a human being?

“Therefore Albicerius was wise, if we grant the definition that wisdom is knowledge of human and divine things.”

## CHAPTER VII.—The Definition of Wisdom That Was Given Is Defended

19. He replied: “First, I do not call something knowledge if the man who professes it is at times mistaken.

[Note: [Col. 0915] Victorinus’s manuscripts, with three other manuscripts, read: “Then I said: First, I do not call knowledge …” This is erroneous, as is sufficiently clear from the final chapter, where this reply is unmistakably attributed to Trygetius.] Knowledge consists not merely in things apprehended, but in things apprehended so securely that no one can ever err in them or waver when driven by opposition of any kind. Hence certain philosophers very truly say that knowledge can be found nowhere except in the wise person. He must not only have grasped what he supports and follows, but also hold it unshaken.

“We know that the man you mentioned often said many false things. I learned this not only from reports given me by others but also from something I myself once witnessed in his presence. Shall I therefore call him knowledgeable when he often spoke falsely—someone whom I would not call knowledgeable even if he had spoken the truth hesitantly?”

[Note: [Col. 0915] Earlier printed editions read “steadfastly.” Five manuscripts read “without hesitation.” Six manuscripts of the best quality read “hesitantly,” and this is preferable. For Trygetius here refuses to call Albicerius and people of that sort knowing, because none of them, when consulted, has never doubted his answers or, finally, never given a false reply.]

Understand me to have said this about the soothsayers, augurs, all those who consult the stars, and interpreters of dreams. Produce, if you can, someone from this class who, when consulted, has never doubted his answers and, finally, has never given a false one. I do not think I need concern myself with prophets, who speak with another’s mind.”

20. [Col. 0916] “Further, even if I grant that human matters means human affairs, do you think anything belongs to us which chance can either give or take away from us? Or, when knowledge of human affairs is mentioned, is it knowledge by which someone knows how many estates we have, or what kind they are; how much gold or silver we possess; or even what lines belonging to others we are thinking about?

“That is knowledge of human affairs which knows the light of prudence, the honor of temperance, the strength of courage, and the sanctity of justice. These are the things which, fearing no fortune, we dare truly to call our own. If that Albicerius had learned them, believe me, he would never have lived so luxuriously and disgracefully.

“As for his saying what line the man who consulted him was turning over in his mind, I do not think this should be counted among our possessions either—not because I deny that the most honorable disciplines belong, in a certain sense, to the possession of our soul, but because even the most ignorant people are permitted to sing and recite someone else’s verse.

“Therefore, when such things happen to us by entering our memory, it is not surprising if they can be perceived by certain very low creatures of this air, whom they call demons. I grant that they can surpass us in keenness and subtlety of perception, but I deny that they can surpass us in reason. And this occurs, I do not know how, through some most secret means removed from our senses.

“For when we marvel that a little bee, after honey has been placed somewhere, flies to it by some sagacity with which it surpasses a human being, we should not therefore place it above ourselves, or even compare it with us.”

21. “Thus I would have preferred Albicerius, when questioned by someone eager to learn from him, to have taught the actual meters; or, when compelled by one of those who consulted him, to have recited verses of his own in response to a matter immediately put before him.

“You often recall that the same Flaccianus used to say, when he mocked and despised that kind of divination with great elevation of mind, attributing it—as he put it—to some most wretched little soul, by whose spirit, so to speak, Albicerius was prompted or inflated when he gave such answers. That most learned man used to ask those who marveled at such things whether Albicerius could teach grammar, music, or geometry.

[Note: [Col. 0916] B reads “geometrical science”; Par., Er., Ven., and Lov. read “geometry.” M.] And who could have known him without admitting that he was the most ignorant of all these subjects?

“Therefore, in the end, he urged those who had learned such disciplines to prefer their minds, without hesitation, to that divination, and to apply themselves to furnishing and supporting their minds with those disciplines by which they might leap beyond and soar above the airy nature of those invisible creatures.”

## CHAPTER VIII.—Whether the Soothsayer Is Wise, and What a Wise Man Is. A Description of Wisdom Suited to the Academic Position

22. “Now, since everyone grants that divine things are much better and more august than human things, how could he attain them when he did not know what he himself was? Unless perhaps you think that the stars which we contemplate every day are something great in comparison with the most true and most hidden God, whom perhaps understanding rarely reaches, but whom no sense reaches at all, while the stars are present to our eyes.

“These, then, are not those divine things which wisdom professes to know alone. The other matters which these so-called diviners exploit either for vain display or for profit are certainly more worthless than the stars.

“Therefore Albicerius did not possess knowledge of human and divine things, and you have attempted in vain to apply our definition in this way.

“Finally, since we ought to regard everything besides human and divine things as utterly worthless and altogether contemptible, I ask: in what matters does your wise man seek the truth?”

“In divine matters,” he replied. “For virtue in a human being is also undoubtedly divine.”

“Then Albicerius already knew those things which your wise man will always seek?”

Licentius replied: “He too knew divine things, but not those which must be sought by a wise man. For who would not overturn all ordinary usage of language if, while granting him divination, he deprived him of divine things from which divination takes its name?

[Note: [Col. 0917] “And deprived him,” according to Par., Er., Ven., and Lov. M.] Therefore, unless I am mistaken, that definition of yours included something else which did not belong to wisdom.”

23. Then Trygetius said: “The man who produced that definition will defend it, if he wishes. For now I want you to answer me, so that at last we may come to the matter under discussion.”

“I am here,” he replied.

“Do you grant,” said Trygetius, “that Albicerius knew the truth?”

“I grant it.”

“Then he is better than your wise man.”

“Not at all,” he replied. “For the kind of truth that the wise man seeks is attained not by that deranged soothsayer, but not even by the wise man himself while he lives in this body. Nevertheless, it is of such great value that seeking it always is far more advantageous than finding the other only once.”

“It is necessary,” said Trygetius, “that the definition come to my aid in this difficulty. Since you thought it defective because it included someone whom we cannot call wise, I ask whether you approve it if we say that wisdom is knowledge of human and divine things that pertain to the happy life.”

“That too is wisdom,” he replied, “but not wisdom alone. Thus the earlier definition invaded what was alien, while this one abandoned what was proper to it. The former can therefore be accused of greed, and the latter of folly.

“For, to explain my view through a definition, wisdom seems to me to be not merely knowledge but also diligent inquiry into human and divine things that pertain to the happy life. If you wish to divide this description, the first part, which contains knowledge, belongs to God; the other, which consists in inquiry, belongs to man. God is therefore happy through the former, while man is happy through the latter.”

Then he said: “I wonder how you can maintain that your wise man wastes his effort in vain.”

[Note: [Col. 0917] “Maintain,” according to Par., Ven., and Lov. M.]

“How,” said Licentius, “does he waste his effort in vain when he gains so great a reward?

[Note: [Col. 0917] The printed editions omit here “wastes his effort,” and subsequently read “when he seeks so great a reward,” except Bad., which, with the manuscripts, prefers “with so great a reward.” So also Par. M.] For by the very fact that he seeks, he is wise; and insofar as he is wise, he is happy. He loosens his mind, as far as he can, from all the wrappings of the body and gathers it into itself. He does not allow it to be torn apart by desires, but remains always peacefully intent upon himself and upon God. Thus, here he enjoys reason—which we agreed above among ourselves is what makes him happy—and at the final day of his life he is found prepared to attain what he desired. He enjoys the divine happiness deservedly, since he has previously enjoyed the human.”

## CHAPTER IX.—Epilogue

[Col. 0918]

24. Then, while Trygetius was spending a long time searching for what he should answer, I said: “I do not think, Licentius, that arguments would fail him either, if we allowed him to search at leisure. For what point has ever failed him when he had to answer?

“First, he himself introduced the argument that, since the question of the happy life had arisen, the wise man alone must be happy, since folly is miserable even in the judgment of fools. He argued that the wise man must be perfect, but that the man who is still inquiring what truth is cannot be perfect, and hence cannot even be happy.

“When you opposed to him the weight of authority, you were somewhat troubled by the name of Cicero,

[Note: [Col. 0918] Printed editions read “moderately.” But ten manuscripts read “troubled,” and this is preferable: Augustine is evidently alluding to “the weight of authority.”] yet you immediately recovered and, with a certain noble defiance, leapt to the summit of freedom. You seized again what had been violently wrenched from your hands, and asked whether he thought that the man who was still seeking was perfect. If he admitted that he was not perfect, you would return to the main point and show, if you could, through that definition, that the man who governed his life according to the law of the mind was perfect—and therefore that no one could be happy unless perfect.

“When you escaped that snare more cautiously than I had expected and called the diligent investigator of truth a perfect man, and when you had fought with greater boldness and clarity through that definition by which we had said that the happy life was the life conducted according to reason, he plainly answered you. For he seized your position, from which you had been driven, and would have deprived you entirely of the whole case, had the truce not restored you.

“For where did the Academics place their stronghold, whose position you defend, if not in the definition of error? Unless it should perhaps return to your mind at night in a dream, you no longer had anything to answer, since you yourself had already mentioned this very point when explaining Cicero’s position.

“Then we came to the definition of wisdom. When you tried to undermine it with such cleverness that perhaps not even your ally Albicerius could have detected your thefts, with what vigilance and strength did he resist you! He almost overwhelmed and crushed you, unless at last you protected yourself with your new definition, saying that human wisdom is the inquiry into truth, through which, because of the tranquillity of the soul, the happy life comes to us.

“He will not answer this position, especially if, in postponing the matter until another day or until the remaining part of the day, he asks that the favor be returned to him.”

[Note: [Col. 0918] Par. reads, “will answer this position.” M.]

25. “But, so that we do not make this too long, let this conversation now be closed, if you please. I think it superfluous to linger over it. The matter has been treated sufficiently for the task undertaken; it could be concluded in a few words, if I did not wish to exercise you and test your strength and zeal, which are a matter of great concern to me.

“For when I had resolved to urge you vigorously to seek the truth, I began to ask how much importance you would attach to it. But all of you attached so much that I desire no more.

“Since we desire to be happy—whether this is possible only after the truth has been found, or only after it has been diligently sought—we must put everything else aside and pursue it, if we wish to be happy.

“Therefore, as I said, let us now end this discussion and commit it to writing. Licentius, send it especially to your father, whose attitude toward philosophy I now thoroughly understand. But I am still waiting to see what fortune will permit. He may be inflamed more ardently toward these studies when he learns that you yourself are already devoted to them and live in this way with me—not merely by hearing them but also by reading them.”

“But if, as I perceive, you are pleased with the Academics, prepare stronger forces for defending them. For I have resolved to summon them as defendants.”

[Note: Ancient editions read, “I have resolved to accuse them.” Several older manuscripts likewise read this; a little later they omit the words “and it was announced that lunch was ready.”]

When these things had been said, it was announced that lunch was ready, and we rose.

# BOOK TWO

He again urges his patron Romanianus to embrace philosophy, with an expression of gratitude. He describes three discussions for him: in the first, the teachings of the Academics are explained; in the second, the differences between the New and Old Academy are reported, and the position of those philosophers is rejected who, thinking that the truth could not be apprehended, nevertheless professed to follow what appeared likely to be true; in the third, he explains what they called the “likely” or “probable.”

[Col. 0919]

## CHAPTER I.—Against the Arguments of the Academics, the Help of God Is Necessary

[Col. 0919]

1. If it were as necessary that the wise man could not be without the discipline and knowledge of wisdom as it would be necessary for him to find it while seeking, then every slander, obstinacy, or perversity of the Academics—or, as I sometimes think, the position appropriate to that period—would have been buried together with that period itself and with the bodies of Carneades and Cicero.

“But because of the many and varied upheavals of this life, Romanianus, in which you prove yourself to be the same man; or because of a certain dullness of minds that are sluggish through torpor, carelessness, or slowness; or because of despair of finding; because the star of wisdom does not rise in minds as easily as this light rises before the eyes; or because of the error common to all peoples, namely, the false belief that they have found the truth—so that people do not seek diligently, if they seek at all, and are turned away from the desire to seek—it has come about that knowledge rarely and in few people arises.

“For this reason the weapons of the Academics, whenever one comes to grips with them—not against mediocre men but against sharp and well-educated ones—seem unconquerable and almost Vulcanian.

“Therefore, against those waves and storms of fortune, we must both resist with the oars of whatever virtues we possess and, above all, implore divine help with every devotion and piety, so that the steadfast pursuit of good studies may hold its course and no accident shake it from the path by which the safest and most delightful harbor of philosophy may receive it.

“This is your first danger. Here I fear for you; here I desire your liberation; here, if I am worthy to obtain it, I never cease to pray daily that favorable winds may be granted you. I pray to the Power and Wisdom of the supreme God. For what else do the mysteries reveal to us as the Son of God?”

2. “You will greatly help me as I plead for you if you do not despair that we can be heard, and if you strive with us—not only through prayers and will, but also through that natural elevation of mind of yours for which I seek you, in which I take singular delight, and which I have always admired.

“Alas, that elevation is enveloped in you like lightning within the clouds of domestic affairs, and it remains hidden from many, almost from everyone. Yet it cannot remain hidden from me, or from one or two of your closest friends, who have often not only listened attentively to your murmurs but have also witnessed certain flashes closer to lightning.

“For, to say nothing for the moment of everything else and mention only one example, who has ever thundered so suddenly and so powerfully, or flashed forth with so much light of mind, that in a single roar of reason and a certain lightning-flash of temperance, the lust which had raged most savagely the day before died completely in a single day?

“Will that virtue, then, never break forth and transform the laughter of many who despair into dread and astonishment? Having spoken on earth as a kind of sign of things to come, will it not return to heaven once the burden of the entire body has been cast aside?

“Did Augustine say these things about Romanianus in vain? He whom I have given myself wholly to will not allow it—the one whom I am now beginning, in some measure, to recognize.”

## CHAPTER II.—He Offers Romanianus the Service of Gratitude and Urges Him Toward Philosophy

3. “Come, then, and undertake philosophy with me. Here is whatever is accustomed to trouble and amaze you, anxious and uncertain as you often are.

“For I do not fear either dullness of character or slowness of intellect in you. Who, when you have been granted a little breathing space, has appeared more alert than you in our conversations? Who more acute?

“Shall I not repay your kindness? Or perhaps I owe you only a little? You received me, a poor young man traveling abroad for study, both into your home and at your expense—and, what is more, into your heart.

“When I had lost my father, you consoled me with your friendship, encouraged me with exhortation, and assisted me with material support. In our own municipality, through your favor, intimacy, and the sharing of your house, you almost made me illustrious and foremost together with yourself.

“When I returned to Carthage for the sake of a more distinguished teaching position, although I had disclosed my plan and hope only to you and none of my family, you hesitated for a while because of the love of country implanted in you, since I was already teaching there. Yet when you could not overcome the desire of a young man striving toward what seemed better, you changed from discourager into helper with extraordinary moderation of goodwill.

“You supplied everything necessary for my journey. There again, you who had cherished the cradle and, as it were, the nest of my studies supported the beginnings of one who was already daring to fly.

“Even when I had sailed away while you were absent and unaware, you did not grow angry that I had not made a practice of sharing everything with you, nor did you suspect any kind of defiance. You remained steadfast in friendship. Before your eyes there was not more concern for children abandoned by their teacher than there was for the purity and inner sanctuary of our mind.”

[Note: [Col. 0921] Am. and Er. read “growing somewhat angry”; several manuscripts of better quality support this reading.]

### 4

Finally, whatever it is that I now rejoice in concerning my leisure: that I have escaped from the bonds of superfluous desires; that, having laid down the burdens of deadening cares, I breathe again, recover my senses, and return to myself; that I seek the truth with utmost concentration; that I am already beginning to find it; that I trust I shall reach the highest “measure” itself [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “to the highest good itself.” But Bad., Amerbach, and most manuscripts have the better reading, “to the highest measure itself,” that is, to wisdom; compare what Augustine was discussing at about the same time, *The Happy Life*, near the end: “Wisdom is nothing other than the measure of the soul, that is, the manner in which the soul balances itself, so that it neither rushes beyond what is excessive nor contracts below what is complete.”—The Paris manuscript likewise reads so.]: you encouraged, you impelled, you accomplished.

But whose agent you were, I have grasped by faith more deeply than I have comprehended by reason. For when, in your presence, I had laid before you the inward movements of my soul [Note: He had made use of Romanianus’s presence at Milan about two years earlier, at the time when he was deliberating with his friends about entering upon a common life, *Confessions* 6.14: “Romanianus, our fellow townsman, whom at that time the severe pressures of his affairs had drawn to the imperial court, had been my intimate friend from early youth. He was especially insistent upon this undertaking and had great authority in urging it, since his considerable resources far surpassed those of the others.”], and had repeatedly and vehemently maintained that no good fortune seemed good to me unless it granted leisure for philosophizing, and no life blessed unless it was lived in philosophy—but that I was restrained by the great burden of my dependents, whose lives depended upon my official duties, and by many necessities, whether arising from my vain sense of shame or from the wretchedness of my foolish dependents—you were so uplifted by joy, so inflamed by the holy ardor of this life, that you declared that, if only you could somehow be freed from the bonds of those troublesome lawsuits, you would break all my bonds as well, even by sharing your own patrimony with me.

### 5

Accordingly, when you had departed after supplying us with fuel, we never ceased yearning for philosophy and thinking of nothing else but that life which we had approved and agreed upon among ourselves. We pursued this steadily, though less intensely; nevertheless, we thought we were doing enough. And since that flame had not yet arrived which was destined to seize us completely, we supposed that the slow heat in which we were already simmering was perhaps the greatest possible.

Then suddenly, as Celsinus says, certain books filled with good Arabian spices breathed upon us; when they had poured out their fragrance upon us and sprinkled a very few drops of the most precious ointment upon that little flame, an incredible thing happened, Romanianus—incredible beyond anything that you, perhaps, believe about me; what more can I say? They kindled in me an utterly unbelievable fire. What honor then, what public display, what desire for empty fame, what, finally, support or attachment of this mortal life could move me? I was returning swiftly and wholly into myself.

I looked back only, I confess, as though from the road toward that religion which had been implanted in us as children and entwined with us to the marrow. But in truth it was itself drawing me toward it without my knowing. Thus, wavering, hastening, and hesitating, I seized the Apostle Paul. “Surely,” I said, “these men could not have possessed such power, nor could they have lived as it is evident that they lived, if their writings and arguments were opposed to so great a good.” I read the whole of him with the utmost concentration and care [Note: Bad., Amerbach, Erasmus, and very many manuscripts read, “with the utmost concentration and purity.” Shortly afterward, the editions hitherto published and some manuscripts read *incognitae fama*, “of unknown reputation,” or *incognitae famae*, “of an unknown reputation.” But other manuscripts preserve the more exact reading, *fame*, “hunger.”].

### 6

Then, once even a little light had been shed upon me, so great a vision of philosophy disclosed itself to me that—never mind telling you, who have always burned with a hunger for what was unknown to you—if I could have displayed it to your very opponent, by whom, I do not know, you are exercised more than hindered, he would have thrown aside and abandoned Baiae, the pleasant orchards [Note: Everywhere we find *pomoeria* or *pomeria*, apparently corrupt readings; for here the subject is clearly orchards, *pomaria*, a word with an entirely different meaning. M.], the delicate and elegant banquets, his household performers, and, finally, whatever sharply excites him toward every kind of pleasure. As an affectionate and holy lover, he would fly to its beauty, wondering, panting, and burning.

For he too possesses—this must be acknowledged—a certain beauty of soul, or rather something like a seedbed of beauty [Note: *Seminarium*, according to the Paris, Erasmus, Venetian, Lovaniensis, and M. manuscripts], which, striving to burst forth into true beauty, puts forth crooked and misshapen growth amid the rough places of vice and the thickets of false opinions. Yet it does not cease to put forth leaves, and, to the extent permitted, it stands out for those few who gaze sharply and attentively into the dense growth. From this comes his hospitality; from this, the many seasonings of humanity at his banquets; from this, the very elegance, polish, and immaculate appearance of all things; and from every side, the urbane refinement that suffuses everything with the shadow of reflected charm.

## Chapter III — Philocalia and Philosophy. He again kindles Romanianus toward philosophy

### 7

This is commonly called *philocalia*. Do not despise the name because it is a popular one: *philocalia* and *philosophia* are almost similarly named, and they wish to appear to be, as it were, kindred to one another—and they are. For what is philosophy? Love of wisdom. What is philocalia? Love of beauty. Ask the Greeks. What, then, is wisdom? Is it not itself true beauty?

These, therefore, are genuine sisters, born of the same parent (*Retractions* 1.1.3). But philocalia, stripped of its wings by the birdlime of lust and shut up in a popular cage, nevertheless retained the likeness of its name, to remind the fowler not to despise it [Note: *Illam*, according to the Paris, Erasmus, Venetian, Lovaniensis, and M. manuscripts]. Its sister, philosophy, fluttering freely, often recognizes this wingless and impoverished creature, but rarely sets it free. For philocalia does not recognize the source of its lineage unless philosophy does so.

Licentius will reveal this whole story to you in a sweeter poem—for I have suddenly become Aesop; he is almost a perfect poet. So, if he could behold true beauty, of which he is the lover of a false image, after his eyes had been healed and uncovered a little, with what delight would he wrap himself in the embrace of philosophy! How would he embrace you there, once he had recognized you as his true brother!

You are amazed at this, and perhaps you laugh. What if I explained it as I wished? What if at least the voice of philosophy itself could be heard by you, even though its face cannot yet be seen? You would certainly be amazed; but you would not laugh or despair. Believe me, no one should be despaired of, and least of all people of this kind. There certainly are examples: this kind of bird easily escapes and easily flies away again [Note: So Amerbach, Erasmus, and nearly all the manuscripts. Bad. and Lovaniensis read *evolat*, “flies away.”]—though many remain shut in, and many onlookers marvel.

### 8

But let us return to ourselves—I mean us, Romanianus. Let us philosophize. I shall repay you your kindness: your son has already begun to philosophize. I restrain him so that, first strengthened and made firm by the necessary disciplines, he may rise with greater vigor. You need not fear being without those disciplines yourself, if I know you well; I ask only that you have free air [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read *aures*, “ears.” But, with Bad. and the manuscripts, one should read *auras*, “breezes,” which Augustine wishes Romanianus to have freely, so that he may rise up and fly away again.—*Auras*, according to the Paris and M. manuscripts.] around you.

For what shall I say of your natural disposition? Would that it were not as rare among human beings as it is assuredly present in you! Two faults remain, and two impediments to discovering the truth; I do not greatly fear them in your case, though I fear them nonetheless: that you may despise yourself and despair of discovering the truth, or certainly that you may think you have discovered it.

The first of these, if indeed it is present in you, this discussion may perhaps remove. You have often been angry with the Academics—more seriously because you were less learned, but more willingly because you were attracted by love of the truth. Therefore, with Alypius as your supporter, I shall now engage you in battle, and I shall easily persuade you of what I wish—though only probably. For you will not see the truth itself unless you enter wholly into philosophy.

As for the other fault, that you perhaps presume to have discovered something, although you departed from us already seeking and doubting, it will certainly be expelled—either when I send you some discussion among us concerning religion, or when, present with you, I discuss many things with you.

### 9

For at present I am doing nothing other than cleansing myself from empty and destructive opinions. Therefore I do not doubt that my condition is better than yours. There is only one point on which I envy your fortune: that you alone enjoy my Lucilianus [Note: This is written thus in the older and more numerous manuscripts. In the earlier editions it is *Lucinianus meus*, and in four manuscripts *Lucianus*.].

Do you also envy me because I said “my”? But what else did I say than “yours,” and “belonging to all of us, whoever are one”? Nevertheless, to help satisfy my longing, what should I ask of you? Ask yourself for me, as much as you know how, because you ought to.

But now I speak to both of you: take care not to think that you know anything unless you have learned it at least as certainly as you know that one, two, three, and four, when added together, make ten. Yet take equal care not to think that in philosophy you will either fail to recognize the truth or that it cannot in any way be recognized. Rather, believe me—or, better, believe the one who says, “Seek, and you will find” (Matthew 7:7)—that knowledge is not to be despaired of and that the truth will become clearer than those numbers are.

Now let us come to the matter at hand. For I have begun rather late to fear that this introduction may have exceeded the proper measure, and that is no small matter. For measure is doubtless divine; but if I have been deceived while it gently leads me, I shall be more cautious when I have become wise.

# First Discussion

## Chapter IV — The Matters Discussed in the First Book Are Repeated

### 10

After the previous conversation, which we included in the first book, we were free from discussion for nearly seven days, while we reviewed the three books of Virgil after the first and discussed them as the occasion seemed to require. In this undertaking Licentius became so inflamed with zeal for poetry [Note: *Poetriae*, according to the Paris manuscript; *poeticum studium*, according to Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and Lovaniensis.] that he seemed to me to require some restraint. He was now scarcely willing to be diverted from this pursuit toward anything else.

At last, however, when I praised the light of philosophy as much as I could, he approached without reluctance the question concerning the Academics that we had postponed. Perhaps the day had shone forth with such serenity that it seemed suited to nothing so much as the calming of our minds.

We therefore left our beds earlier than usual and spent a little time with the country people, since time was pressing. Then Alypius said:

“Before I hear you discussing the Academics, I want that conversation of yours—which you say was completed in my absence—to be read aloud to me. Otherwise I cannot help either going wrong or at least struggling as I listen to you, since the occasion for this discussion arose from that conversation.”

When this had been done and we saw that nearly the whole morning had been spent on it, we decided to return home from the fields, which had received us while we walked about.

Then Licentius said:

“I ask you not to object to briefly repeating, before lunch, the entire position of the Academics by way of explanation, so that I do not miss anything in it that might support my side.”

“I shall do so,” I replied, “and all the more willingly because, while thinking about this matter, you will eat little.”
