“Do not be so confident of that,” he said. “I have often noticed, especially in my father, that a person is more voracious in proportion as he is more burdened with cares. Besides, you have not found me, when thinking about these verses, so disposed that my concern ensures the safety of the table.”

I am accustomed to marvel at this in myself: what does it mean that we crave food more stubbornly when we direct our minds toward something else? Or what is it that makes the mind imperious when our hands and teeth are occupied? [Note: Most manuscripts read, “or who is it that, when our hands and teeth are occupied, becomes too imperious for us?” A few shortly afterward read, “and when our hands and teeth are occupied, the mind becomes less imperious”; three others likewise read, “and when our teeth are occupied, the mind becomes less imperious.”]

“Listen instead,” I said, “to what you asked about the Academics, so that, while you are turning over these verses, I do not have to endure you not only at a meal without meter but also in the midst of questions.”

“But if you conceal anything on my behalf,” Alypius said, “I shall expose it.”

“You require good faith,” Alypius continued, “for if there is reason to fear that you may conceal something, I think it difficult for me to detect it—especially since no one who knows me is unaware from whom I learned these matters, and especially since, in revealing the truth, you will be concerned no more for victory than for your own mind.”

## Chapter V — The Teachings of the Academics

### 11

“I shall act in good faith,” I replied, “since you invoke a legal right. The Academics held that human beings could not attain knowledge—at least not knowledge of matters belonging to philosophy; Carneades said that he did not concern himself with other matters. Yet they maintained that a human being could be wise, and that the whole task of the wise person consisted, as you yourself explained in that conversation, Licentius, in the search for truth.

From this it follows that the wise person assents to nothing, for if he assented to uncertain things, he would necessarily be mistaken, and error is forbidden to the wise. They did not merely say that everything was uncertain; they affirmed it with very extensive arguments [Note: Five manuscripts read, “with very destructive arguments.”].

They seemed to have derived the claim that truth could not be grasped from the Stoic Zeno’s definition. He said that that could be perceived as true which was so impressed upon the mind by the source from which it arose that it could not have arisen from a source other than that one. Put more briefly and clearly: truth can be grasped by signs that cannot belong to what is false.

They exerted themselves with the greatest force to prove that such a thing could not be found. Hence arose the disagreements among philosophers, the deceptions of the senses, dreams and madness, the *pseudomeni* and the *soritae* in defense of that cause. And since they had accepted from the same Zeno that nothing was more disgraceful than forming an opinion, they cleverly concluded that, if nothing could be perceived and opinion was the most disgraceful thing, the wise person would never approve anything.”

### 12

“From this they incurred great unpopularity: it seemed to follow that a person who approved nothing would do nothing. Thus the Academics appeared to portray their wise person as always asleep and abandoning every duty, since they held that he approved nothing.

Introducing a certain ‘probable’ judgment, which they also called ‘verisimilar,’ they nevertheless asserted that the wise person did not cease performing his duties, since he had something to follow, while the truth lay hidden, either buried or obscured because of certain darknesses of nature or because of the resemblance between things. They also said that restraint itself, and the suspension, as it were, of assent, was a very great action of the wise person.

I think I have briefly explained everything, as you wished, and have departed in no way from your stipulation, Alypius—that is, I have acted, as they say, in good faith. For if I have said something not quite as it is, or perhaps failed to say something, I did nothing intentionally. Good faith, then, consists in speaking according to one’s mind. One person should regard another who is being taught as honest, but should be on guard against one who is deceptive. The former requires a good teacher; the latter, a cautious student.”

### 13

Then Alypius said:

“I am grateful, since you have satisfied Licentius and relieved me of the burden you imposed. You had less reason to fear that you might say something less than the whole truth in order to test me—for how else could it have been done?—than I would have had if it had been necessary for me to expose you in any respect.

Therefore, please do not hesitate to explain what remains—not so much for the question as for the questioner himself—namely, the difference between the New and the Old Academy.”

“I freely admit,” I replied, “that I am reluctant. Therefore you will confer a favor upon me—for I cannot deny that the point you mention is highly relevant—if you will allow me, while I rest a little, to distinguish these names within myself and explain the origin of the New Academy.”

“I would have thought,” he said, “that I too was trying to draw you away from lunch, if I had not thought that you were already more frightened by Licentius, and if his request had not prescribed for us that whatever this tangle contained should be unraveled for him before lunch.”

And as he was about to say the rest, our mother—for we were already at home—began pushing us toward lunch so insistently that there was no opportunity for further speech.

# Second Discussion

## Chapter VI — The Schism between the New and Old Academy

### 14

Then, after we had taken as much food as was sufficient to restrain our hunger, and after we had returned to the meadow, Alypius said:

“I shall adhere to your position, and I would not dare refuse. For if I have missed nothing, I shall congratulate both your learning and my memory. But if I have perhaps gone wrong in any respect, you will correct me, so that henceforth I may not fear undertaking such a delegation.

“I think that the schism of the New Academy was stirred up not so much against the Old Academy’s conception as against the Stoics. Nor should it be regarded as a schism, since the new question introduced by Zeno had to be dissolved and examined.

“For the opinion that nothing could be perceived, although it had not been set in motion by any controversies, was nevertheless present in the minds of the Old Academics and could reasonably be attributed to them. This is readily confirmed by the authority of Socrates, Plato, and the other ancient philosophers, who believed that they could protect themselves from error so long as they did not rashly commit themselves to assent. Yet they did not introduce a specific discussion of this matter into their schools, nor did they ever investigate clearly whether truth could or could not be perceived.

“When Zeno introduced this rough and novel doctrine and maintained that nothing could be perceived unless it were true in such a way that it could be distinguished from the false by marks unlike those of the false, and that the wise person must not submit to opinion—and when Arcesilaus heard this—he denied that anything of this kind could be found by a human being and that the life of the wise person should be entrusted to the shipwreck of opinion. From this he also concluded that assent should be given to nothing.”

### 15

“But when matters stood in such a way that the Old Academy seemed rather strengthened than attacked, Antiochus, a student of Philo, appeared. As some thought, he was more desirous of glory than of truth, and he brought the positions of both Academies into conflict.

“For he claimed that the New Academics were attempting to introduce something unprecedented and utterly remote from the opinions of the ancients. To this end he invoked the authority of the ancient physicists and other great philosophers, while also attacking the Academics themselves, who claimed to follow what was verisimilar even though they confessed that they did not know the truth itself.

“He had collected many arguments, which I think should be passed over for the present. Yet he defended nothing more strongly than the claim that the wise person could perceive the truth.

“I believe this was the controversy between the New and Old Academics. If the matter is otherwise, I ask you to instruct Licentius most fully on behalf of both sides. But if it is as I have been able to state it, continue the discussion you have undertaken.”

## Chapter VII — Against the Academics

### 16

Then I said:

“How long, Licentius, will you remain at rest in this conversation of ours, which has lasted longer than I expected? Have you heard who your Academics are?”

He smiled shyly, somewhat more embarrassed by this address, and said:

“I regret having so strongly maintained against Trygetius that the blessed life consists in the search for truth. For this question disturbs me so greatly that I am scarcely not miserable; and surely, if you possess any humanity, I seem to you deserving of pity.

“But why do I torment myself so foolishly? Why should I shrink back, supported as I am by so good a cause? I shall yield absolutely only to the truth.”

“Do you approve of the New Academics?” I asked.

“Very much,” he replied.

“Then do they seem to you to speak the truth?”

He was already about to assent, but, made more cautious by Alypius’s smile, he hesitated for some time. Then he said:

“Repeat the little question.”

“Do the Academics seem to you to speak the truth?”

Again he was silent for a long time. Then he said:

“Whether it is true, I do not know; nevertheless, it is probable. For I see nothing more that I can follow.”

“Do you know,” I said, “that they themselves also call the probable the verisimilar?”

“So it seems,” he said.

“Then,” I said, “the Academics’ position is verisimilar.”

“So it is,” he replied.

“Now,” I said, “please pay closer attention. If someone asserted that your brother appeared to resemble your father, while not knowing your father himself, would he not seem to you insane or foolish?”

He was silent for a long time. Then he said:

“This does not seem absurd to me.”

### 17

When I began to answer him, he said:

“Wait, please, a little.”

Then, smiling, he said:

“Tell me, I beg you, are you already certain of your victory?”

“Suppose that I am certain,” I replied. “Even so, you must not abandon your cause, especially since this discussion has been undertaken among us for the sake of exercising you and challenging you to polish your mind.”

“Have I read the Academics,” he said, “or have I been trained in all the disciplines with which you come to me equipped?”

“The Academics,” I replied, “had not been read even by those who first defended that position. And if you lack learning and an abundance of disciplines, your natural intelligence should not nevertheless be so weak that, without making any effort, you succumb to my very few words and questions.

“For I have already begun to fear that Alypius will succeed you sooner than I wish. With him as my opponent, I shall not walk about so confidently.”

“Would that I were already defeated,” he said, “so that I might at last hear you discussing and, what is more, see you doing so! No spectacle could be presented to me more happily.

“Since you have chosen to pour these things forth rather than spill them—since you receive in writing what bursts from your mouths and do not allow it, as they say, to fall to the ground—I shall also be able to read you [Note: Several manuscripts read, “you will also be able to read.”]. But somehow, when those very same persons whose conversation is being cut short [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read *editur*, “is produced.” But nearly all the manuscripts have *caeditur*, “is cut short.” Terence also uses the phrase in *The Self-Tormentor* 2.3: “But meanwhile, while we cut short our conversations.”] are brought before the eyes, a good discussion floods the mind—not more usefully, perhaps, but certainly more joyfully.”

### 18

“We are grateful,” I said. “But this sudden joy of yours has rashly led you to escape from the position in which you said that no spectacle could be presented to you more happily.

“What if you see your father—surely no one will drink philosophy more ardently after so long a thirst—inquiring and discussing these matters with us? If I shall never regard myself as more fortunate, what, then, ought you to feel and say?”

At this he shed some tears. When he was able to speak, he stretched out his hand and looked up toward heaven:

“And when shall I see this, O God?” he said.

“But there is no reason to despair of you.”

At this, when nearly all of us had begun to turn from the concentration of discussion toward tears, I struggled with myself and scarcely managed to recover my composure.

“Come now,” I said, “and return to your strength. I warned you long ago to gather your resources from wherever you could, since you were going to be the champion of the Academy—not, I think, so that trembling might now seize your limbs before the trumpet [*Aeneid* 11.424], or so that, from longing to watch another’s battle, you might wish to become a captive so quickly.”

Then Trygetius, when he noticed that our faces had become sufficiently serene, said:

“Why should this holy man not wish for that, when God has granted it to him before he even asked? Believe me now, Licentius: since you cannot find what to answer and still wish to be defeated, you seem to me a man of little faith.”

We smiled. Then Licentius said:

“Speak happily—not by finding the truth, but certainly by not seeking it.”

### 19

We were made happier by this amusement among the young men. Then I said:

“Pay attention to the question, and return to the path stronger and more vigorous, if you can.”

“I am here,” he said, “as much as I can be. For what if the man who has seen my brother has learned by widespread report that he resembles my father? Can he be insane or foolish if he believes it?”

“Can he at least be called foolish?” I asked.

“Not immediately,” he replied, “unless he claims to know it. For if he follows as probable what repeated report has spread, he cannot be accused of rashness.”

Then I said:

“Let us consider the matter itself for a little while and set it, as it were, before our eyes. Suppose the unknown man whom we are describing is present. Your brother arrives from somewhere. The man says: ‘Whose son is this boy?’ The answer is: ‘He is the son of a certain Romanianus.’ Then the man says: ‘How much he resembles his father! This is precisely what report had not rashly conveyed to me.’

“Then you, or someone else, say: ‘Do you know Romanianus, good sir?’

“‘I do not,’ he replies; ‘nevertheless, the boy seems to me to resemble him.’

“Could anyone keep from laughing?”

“Not at all,” he replied.

“Then,” I said, “you see what follows.”

“I have seen it for a long time,” he said. “Nevertheless, I want to hear the conclusion from you. You must begin to nourish the one whom you have captured.”

“Why should I not conclude?” I said. “The matter itself cries out that your Academics deserve similar ridicule: they say that in life they follow what resembles the truth, although they do not know what the truth itself is.”

## Chapter VIII — The Academics’ Sophistry

### 20

Then Trygetius said:

“The Academics’ caution seems to me very different from the foolishness of the man you described. For they arrive by arguments at what they say is verisimilar, whereas this fool followed a report, whose authority is the basest thing there is.”

“Surely,” I replied, “he would have been even more foolish if he had said: ‘I certainly do not know his father, nor have I learned from report how much he resembles his father; nevertheless, he seems to me to resemble him.’”

“Certainly more foolish,” he said. “But where are you going with this?”

“Because such are those who say: ‘We do not know the truth, but what we see resembles what we do not know.’”

“They call that probable,” he said.

“How do you say that?” I replied. “Do you deny that they call it verisimilar?”

“I wished to say that in order to exclude that kind of resemblance. For it seemed to me that report had intruded improperly into your question, since the Academics do not trust even human eyes, much less a report with a thousand eyes—as poets imagine—even though those eyes are monstrous.

“For who, after all, am I to be a defender of the Academy? Or do you begrudge me security in this question? Here you have Alypius, whose arrival, I pray, may grant us a holiday. We think that you have not feared him without reason for some time.”

### 21

Then they fell silent and both turned their eyes toward Alypius. He said:

“I should certainly like, insofar as my strength permits, to assist your side to some degree, were your omen not a source of terror to me. But, unless hope deceives me, I shall easily escape this fear [Note: In the editions hitherto published, “I shall easily flee.”].

“At the same time, I am consoled by the fact that the present opponent of the Academics has taken upon himself the burden of Trygetius, who has been nearly defeated, and now, by your admission, is probably the victor.

“What I fear more is that I may be unable to avoid both the negligence of abandoning my duty and the shamelessness of usurping it. I do not think you have forgotten that the office of judge was assigned to me.”

Then Trygetius said:

“That is one matter, and this is another. Therefore we ask you to allow yourself, for once, to be deprived of it.”

“I shall not refuse,” he replied. “Indeed, while I wish to avoid shamelessness and negligence, I might fall into the snares of pride—a fault more monstrous than any other—if I retained longer than you permit the honor you have granted me.”

## Chapter IX — The Position of the Academics Must Now Be Discussed Seriously

### 22

“Therefore, good accuser of the Academics, I want you to explain your office to me—that is, in whose defense you are attacking these men. For I fear that, while refuting the Academics, you may wish to prove yourself an Academic.”

“As I think you know well,” I replied, “there are two kinds of accusers. For even if Cicero very modestly said that he was the accuser of Verres in such a way that he was the defender of the Sicilians (*Against Verres*, First Action), it does not follow that everyone who accuses someone must have another person whom he defends.”

“And do you have anything,” he said, “on which your own position has now been firmly established?”

“It is easy to answer that question,” I replied, “especially for me, since it is not unexpected. I have already gone through this entire matter with myself and turned it over in my mind for a long time.

“Therefore listen, Alypius, to what, as I think, you already know very well: I do not wish to undertake this discussion merely for the sake of disputing. It is enough that we have played preliminary games with these young men, where philosophy willingly amused itself with us, as it were. Let us therefore remove these childish tales from our hands.

“Our life, our conduct, our soul are at stake. The soul presumes that it will overcome the enmity of every deception and, having grasped the truth, will return as if to the region of its origin and triumph over its lusts; then, having accepted temperance as a wife, it will reign and return more securely to heaven (*Retractions* 1.1.3).

“You see what I am saying? Let us now remove all these things from our midst: ‘the weapons that must be made ready for the fierce man’ (*Aeneid* 8.304). I have always desired nothing less than that, among people who have lived and conversed with one another at length, something should arise from which a new kind of conflict might emerge.

“But because memory is an unreliable guardian of what has been thought, I wanted what we have often discussed among ourselves to be committed to writing, so that these young men might learn both to attend to such matters and to attempt to undertake and confront them.”

### 23

“Then you do not know that I still have nothing certain that I hold as my opinion [Note: Augustine is employing here a figure customary in the solemn manner of his dialogues. He did in fact possess something certain to hold as his opinion, since he had already ‘arrived at that which is,’ as we read in *Confessions* 7.17. More explicitly, in the same work, 8.5, he confesses, concerning his delay in conversion: ‘And that excuse was no longer available to me by which I had been accustomed to think that I had not yet begun to serve you after despising the world because my apprehension of the truth was uncertain; for by then it was certain.’], but that I am prevented from seeking it by the Academics’ arguments and discussions?

“For somehow they produced in my mind a certain probability—for I shall not yet depart from their word—that a human being cannot discover the truth. As a result I became sluggish and utterly inactive, and I did not dare to seek what the sharpest and most learned men had been unable to discover.

“Unless, therefore, I first persuade myself that the truth can be discovered as thoroughly as they persuaded themselves that it could not, I shall not dare to seek it, and I have nothing to defend. So, if you please, remove this question and let us instead examine among ourselves, as shrewdly as we can, whether truth can be discovered.

“For my part, I seem already to have many arguments with which I am trying to withstand the reasoning of the Academics. At present the only difference between them and me is this: it seemed probable to them that truth could not be discovered, whereas to me it seems probable that it can be discovered. For ignorance of the truth is either peculiar to me, if they were pretending, or certainly common to both sides.”

## Chapter X — The Controversy with the Academics Concerns Things, Not Words

### 24

Then Alypius said:

“Now I shall walk confidently, for I see that you will be not so much an accuser as an assistant. Therefore, so that we do not wander too far, let us first see whether, in this question in which I seem to have prevailed over those who yielded to you, we might fall into a verbal dispute. You yourself, appealing to that authority of Tullius, have often confessed that such a dispute is most disgraceful.

“For, unless I am mistaken, when Licentius said that he approved the Academics’ position concerning probability, you added the question whether he knew that they also called it verisimilitude. And I know well—since I learned it from you—that the Academics’ teachings are not unfamiliar to you.

“Since these teachings, as I have said, are fixed in your mind, I do not know what words you are pursuing.”

“Believe me,” I replied, “this is not a great controversy over words but over the things themselves. I do not think those men were such as to be unable to assign names to things. Rather, it seems to me that they chose these terms both to conceal their position from those who were slow-witted and to signify it to those who were vigilant.

“I shall explain why and how this seems so to me, after I have first examined those statements which people think were made by them as enemies of human knowledge.

“I am therefore very pleased that our conversation has progressed this far today, so that it has become sufficiently clear what we are investigating among ourselves. For they seem to me to have been altogether serious and prudent men.

“If there is anything that we shall now discuss against them, it will be against those who believed that the Academics were opposed to the discovery of truth [Note: The Paris manuscript reads, “since what we shall discuss, we shall discuss against those who …” M.].

“And lest you think that I am frightened, I shall willingly arm myself even against those men themselves, if they defended what we read in their books not in order to conceal their position—lest certain sacred truths be revealed by minds polluted and, as it were, profane—but from genuine conviction.

“I would do this today, except that the setting sun is already forcing us to return home. This was the extent of the discussion that day.”

# Third Discussion

## Chapter XI — What the Probable Is
25. On the following day, although the dawn had been no less bright and calm, we nevertheless scarcely managed to free ourselves from our household business. We had spent most of the day, especially, in writing letters. When scarcely two hours remained, we went out to the meadow. The extraordinary clearness of the sky invited us, and we decided not to let even the little time remaining go to waste.

When we had reached the customary tree and settled in our place, I said: “Young men, since we are not undertaking any great matter today, I should like you to remind me how Alypius answered yesterday’s little question that disturbed you.”

Licentius replied: “It is so short that there is no difficulty in remembering it; but how slight it is, you may judge for yourself. For, as I understand it, he forbade you, once the matter itself was clear, to raise a question about the words.”

“And have you,” I said, “sufficiently noticed what this means and what force it has?”

“I think I see what it means,” he replied, “but I ask you to explain it briefly. I have often heard you say that, when disputants have no remaining disagreement about the things themselves, it is shameful to linger over a question of words. But this matter is too subtle for me to be expected to explain it.”

## CHAPTER XII — Again on the Probable and the Verisimilar

26. “Listen, then,” I said, “to what it means. The Academics call *probabile* or *verisimile* that which can invite us to act without assent. By ‘without assent’ I mean that we do not think the thing we are doing is true, or judge that we know it; nevertheless, we act.

“For example, if someone asked us whether, after such a clear and pure night, the sun would rise today so bright, I believe we would deny that we knew it, but we would nevertheless say that it appeared likely.

“Thus,” said the Academic, “everything that I thought ought to be called probable or verisimilar seems to me to be of this kind. If you wish to call it by another name, I have no objection. It is enough for me that you have now understood what I mean—that is, to what things I apply these names. For it is not fitting that a wise man be a maker of words, but an investigator of things.

“Have you understood sufficiently how those playful weapons with which I was harassing you have been knocked from my hands?”

When both replied that they understood, and by their very expressions seemed to demand my answer, I said: “What do you think? Do you suppose that Cicero, whose words these are, was so poor in the Latin language that he gave less suitable names to the things he perceived?”

27. Then Trygetius said: “Now that the matter is understood, we are pleased to stir up no quibbles about words. So consider instead what you will answer this man who has freed us, against whom you are trying once again to charge, having been driven back.”

“Wait, please,” said Licentius. “For something is beginning to dawn on me, by which I see that you ought not so easily to have allowed so great an argument to be snatched from you.”

After he had remained silent for some time, absorbed in thought, he continued: “I ask you: what could be more absurd than to say that one follows the verisimilar who does not know what the truth is? Nor does your comparison disturb me. For if I am properly asked whether, given this condition of the weather, no rain will be produced tomorrow, I answer that this is likely, although I do not deny that I know something true. I know that this tree cannot suddenly become silver, and I confidently say that I know many such true things, which I see to be like those things I call verisimilar.

“But you, Carneades—or whatever other Greek pest you are, to spare our own people—for why should I hesitate to cross over to the one to whom I owe my captivity by right of victory? You, then, when you say that you know nothing true, how do you follow the verisimilar?”

“But I could not give it any other name.”

“What, then, are we to debate with someone who cannot even speak?”

28. “I shall not fear deserters,” said Alypius, “and still less that Carneades whom, moved I do not know whether by youthful or childish levity, you thought should be attacked with insults rather than with any weapon. For, to strengthen his position, which was always founded, at least to some extent, on a probable argument, this will easily suffice against you for the moment: we are so far removed from discovering the truth that you yourself can serve as a major argument for the claim, since you were so shaken from your position by a single little question that you utterly lost sight of where you ought to stand.

“But let us postpone these matters—and your knowledge, which a little earlier you admitted you had acquired concerning this tree—to another time. For although you have now chosen another side, you must still be carefully taught what I said a little earlier.

“As I understand it, we had not yet advanced to the question of whether truth can be discovered. I merely thought that, at the very entrance to my defense, I should set down this point, since I saw you exhausted and prostrate: namely, that we should not be asking whether that which the Academics say is enough for them should be called verisimilar, probable, or by some other name.

“For if you now seem to yourself to be the finest discoverer of truth, that is no concern of mine. Later, if you are not ungrateful for my advocacy, perhaps you will teach me the same things.”

### Note

[Col. 0932] *Par.* *Er.* *Ven.*: “frequently founded on probable reasoning” (*saepetenus probabili ratione*), rather than simply “founded on probable reasoning” (*tenus probabili*). M.

## CHAPTER XIII — Whether the Academics Concealed That They Knew the Truth

29. When Licentius, with some embarrassment, feared Alypius’s attack, I said: “You preferred to talk about everything, Alypius, rather than explain how we are to debate with those who cannot speak.”

He replied: “Since it has long been known both to me and to everyone, and since you have now sufficiently indicated by your own profession that you are skilled in speaking, I should like you first to explain the usefulness of his inquiry. As I see it, it is either superfluous, in which case it is even more superfluous for him to answer it; or, if it should appear useful and I am unable to explain it, I ask you to grant me the favor of not refusing the duty of a teacher.”

### Note

[Col. 0933] *Bad.* *Er.* and *Lov.* read “your inquiry” (*inquisitionis tuae*). But *Am.* and the manuscripts better read “his inquiry” (*suae*), referring to Licentius.

“I remember,” I said, “that yesterday I promised to deal with these words later. And now the sun warns me to put away in boxes the toys I brought before the children, especially since I am now displaying them for the sake of adorning them rather than selling them.

“Before darkness overtakes our writing—darkness that is usually the Academics’ patron—I want it to be completely clear among us today what question we must rise tomorrow to explain. So answer me, please: do you think that the Academics held a definite opinion about the truth and were unwilling to disclose it rashly to minds that were ignorant or unpurified? Or did they really think as their discussions indicate?”

[Col. 0934]

30. He replied: “I shall not rashly affirm what their intention was. As far as one may gather from their books, you know better what words they commonly use to express their position. But if you ask me about myself, I think that the truth has not yet been discovered. I add what you demanded concerning the Academics: I think that it cannot be discovered—not merely because of my deeply rooted opinion, which you have almost always observed, but also because of the authority of the great and eminent philosophers. Whether our weakness or their insight compels us to bow our necks to them, I do not know; but it seems that nothing more can now be discovered.”

“This,” I said, “is precisely what I wanted. I was afraid that, if you also held the same view as I do, our discussion would remain incomplete, since there would be no one to force the matter from the other side into our hands, so that it might be handled as carefully as we could.

“Therefore, if that had happened, I was prepared to ask you to take up the Academics’ position as though they seemed not merely to have argued, but also to have believed, that truth cannot be comprehended.

“So the question between us is whether their arguments make it probable that nothing can be apprehended and that assent ought to be given to nothing. If you establish this, I shall gladly yield. But if I can demonstrate that it is much more probable both that the wise man can arrive at the truth and that assent ought not always to be withheld, then, as I think, you will have no reason not to allow yourself to cross over to my position.”

This pleased him and the others who were present, and, by then shaded by evening, we returned home.

# BOOK THREE

This book presents two discussions. At their beginning it is established that fortune is neither a help nor a hindrance to the wise man. Soon afterward Augustine, with Alypius opposing him in accordance with the position he has undertaken, proves that the wise man knows something, since at least he knows wisdom. He then examines Zeno’s definition and refutes those two Academical doctrines: “Nothing can be apprehended,” and “One ought to assent to nothing.” Finally, he says that it seems to him that the Academics did not actually think as they are commonly believed to have thought.

[Col. 0933]

## FIRST DISCUSSION

## CHAPTER I — Truth Must Be Sought with the Utmost Dedication, Since the Blessed Life Depends upon It

1. After the conversation contained in the second book, we sat down in the baths on another day, for the weather was too gloomy to make us want to go down to the meadow. I began as follows:

“I think you have already noticed sufficiently what question has been established for discussion among us. But before I come to my own side of the argument, I ask you willingly to listen to a few remarks about our hope, our life, and our undertaking—remarks that are not irrelevant to its explanation.

“I consider our task neither trivial nor superfluous, but necessary and of the highest importance: we must seek the truth with the utmost dedication. Alypius and I agree on this. For the other philosophers thought that their wise man had found it, while the Academics declared that their wise man must seek it with the greatest effort and devote himself diligently to that task. But because the truth either lay hidden beneath some covering or was confused and did not stand out clearly, they said that, in conducting his life, he should follow whatever presented itself as probable and verisimilar.

“This too was settled in your earlier discussion. For one of you asserted that a man becomes happy when he has found the truth, while the other said that he becomes happy merely by having sought it diligently. None of us doubts, therefore, that nothing should be placed before this undertaking.

“Accordingly, what sort of day yesterday do you think we spent? You were at least permitted to live in accordance with your studies. You, Trygetius, amused yourself with the verses of Virgil, while Licentius devoted himself to composing verses. He was so captivated by his love of them that, chiefly for this reason, I thought I had to bring this conversation upon him—one by which philosophy, since the time has now come, might claim and vindicate a greater portion of his soul, not only than poetry but than every other discipline.”

## CHAPTER II — Whether Fortune Is Necessary to the Wise Man

2. “But tell me, were you not sorry for us when, the day before yesterday, we went to bed in such a way that we would rise for the postponed question and for nothing else?”

### Note

[Col. 0934] B reads *miserati*, a reading neither adopted by *Er.*, *Ven.*, and *Lov.* nor to be adopted, since it is very un-Latin with the following genitive case. M.

“ So many matters concerning the household necessarily had to be dealt with that, completely occupied by them, we could scarcely breathe freely for ourselves during the final two hours of the day.

“Thus my opinion has always been that the man who is already wise has need of nothing, but that fortune is extremely necessary for one who is becoming wise” (*Retractions* I.1.1)—unless Alypius thinks otherwise.”

He replied: “I do not yet know how much authority you grant to fortune. For if you think that fortune itself is necessary in order to despise fortune, I offer myself as your companion in that view. But if you grant fortune nothing more than those things that cannot be supplied for the needs of the body unless fortune itself wills it, I do not agree.

“For either it is possible, even when fortune resists and is unwilling, for a man who is not yet wise but desires wisdom to obtain those things that we acknowledge to be necessary for life; or else it must also be admitted that fortune rules over the whole life of the wise man, since even the wise man cannot fail to need those things that are necessary for the body.”

3. “So you say,” I replied, “that fortune is necessary for the student of wisdom, but deny that it is necessary for the wise man.”

“It is not irrelevant to repeat the same point,” he said. “So I now ask you whether you think fortune contributes anything toward despising fortune itself. If you think it does, I say that the person who desires wisdom greatly needs fortune.”

“I think so,” I replied, “since through fortune he will become the kind of person who can despise it.”

“That is not absurd,” he said. “For even as small children we need breasts, by means of which we become capable later of living and prospering without them.”

“If our views do not differ in their underlying conception,” he said, “it is clear to me that they agree—unless someone thinks that we must distinguish between the fact that fortune or breasts make us despise them, and the breasts or fortune themselves, and some other thing makes us despise them.”

“There is no great difficulty,” I said, “in using another similar example. Just as no one crosses the Aegean Sea without a ship or some other vehicle—or, to avoid even fearing Daedalus, without any instruments adapted to the task or some more hidden power—even though his sole intention is to arrive, and, once he has arrived, he is ready to cast away and despise all the means by which he was transported;

“so whoever wishes to reach the harbor of wisdom, and, as it were, the firmest and most tranquil land, since—leaving other considerations aside—if he is blind and deaf he cannot do so, must, it seems to me, have fortune available for the purpose he desires, since this lies in fortune’s power.

“Once he has attained it, even if he is thought to need certain things pertaining to the health of the body, it remains clear that he does not need them in order to be wise, but in order to live among human beings.”

“Indeed,” he replied, “if he were blind and deaf, in my opinion he would rightly despise both the attainment of wisdom and life itself, for whose sake wisdom is sought.”

### Note

[Col. 0935] *Par.* *Er.* *Ven.*: “he despises” (*contemnit*), rather than “he would despise” (*contemnet*).

4. “Nevertheless,” I said, “since our very life—the life in which we live here—is in the power of fortune, and since no one can become wise except while living, must we not admit that we need fortune’s favor in order to reach wisdom?”

“But since wisdom is necessary only to the living,” he replied, “and once life has been removed there is no need for wisdom, I do not fear fortune in preserving life. For it is because I live that I want wisdom; it is not because I desire wisdom that I want life. Therefore, if fortune takes life from me, it will take away the reason for seeking wisdom. I have no reason, then, to desire fortune’s favor or fear its hindrances in order to become wise—unless you produce some further argument.”

“Then,” I said, “you do not think that the student of wisdom can be prevented by fortune from reaching wisdom, even if fortune does not take his life?”

“I do not think so,” he replied.

## CHAPTER III — The Wise Man and the Student of Wisdom Differ. The Wise Man Knows Something, Since at Least He Knows Wisdom

5. “I want you,” I said, “to explain briefly what difference you think there is between the wise man and the philosopher.”

“I think,” he replied, “that the wise man differs from the student in no respect except that, in the wise man, there is a certain settled condition of those things whose pursuit in the student is only ardent desire.”

“What things are these?” I asked.

“To me,” I said, “there seems to be no difference except that one knows wisdom while the other desires to know it.”

“If you define knowledge within a modest limit,” he replied, “you have expressed the matter more clearly.”

“However I define it,” I said, “we have all agreed on this: knowledge cannot consist in false things.”

“That,” he replied, “seemed to me a qualification that had to be introduced, lest, through my careless agreement, your speech should ride easily into the main field of the question.”

“Clearly,” I said, “you have left me nowhere to ride. For, unless I am mistaken, we have reached the very conclusion I have long been working toward.

“For if, as you have said both subtly and truly, there is no difference between the student of wisdom and the wise man except that the one loves wisdom while the other possesses the discipline of wisdom—and you did not hesitate to express this also by the very name, that is, as a certain settled condition—then no one can possess a discipline in the soul who has learned nothing; no one has learned anything who knows nothing; and no one can know what is false.

“Therefore the wise man knows the truth, since you have already admitted that he possesses the discipline of wisdom in his soul—that is, a settled condition.”

“I do not know how shameless I would be,” he replied, “if I wished to deny that I had admitted that the wise man possesses a settled condition of inquiry into divine and human matters. But I do not see why you think the settled condition of discovered probabilities is not the same thing.”

“You grant me,” I said, “that no one knows what is false?”

“That is easy enough,” he replied.

“Now say, if you can,” I continued, “that the wise man does not know wisdom.”

“Why,” he said, “do you confine everything within this limit, so that the wise man cannot seem to himself to have comprehended wisdom?”

“Give me your right hand,” I said. “For if you remember, this is what I said yesterday I would accomplish. And now I am glad that it has not been concluded by me but offered to me voluntarily by you.

“For when I said that the difference between me and the Academics was that they thought it probable that truth could not be comprehended, whereas I thought that, although I had not yet discovered it, it could nevertheless be discovered by the wise man, you were now pressed by my question whether the wise man does not know wisdom, and you said: ‘It seems to him that he knows it.’

“What follows?” he asked.

“If it seems to him that he knows wisdom,” I replied, “then it does not seem to him that the wise man can know nothing. Or, if wisdom is nothing, I want you to say so.”

6. “I would truly have believed,” he replied, “that we had reached the end of our discussion; but suddenly, when you extended your right hand, I see that we are utterly separated and have traveled a long way apart.

“Yesterday the only question established among us seemed to be this: you asserted that the wise man could attain the comprehension of truth, while I denied it. But now I think I have conceded nothing to you except that it can seem to the wise man that he has attained wisdom in probable matters.

“Yet I believe that we all agree that I have placed this wisdom in the investigation of divine and human matters. I do not see how these two claims fit together when we speak of one or the other.”

“No,” I said, “you have not unraveled the matter by wrapping it up. It seems to me that you are now arguing merely to exercise yourself. And because you know very well that these young men are still scarcely able to distinguish what is argued sharply and subtly, you are abusing the ignorance of your judges, so that you may speak as much as you please without anyone objecting.

“For a little earlier, when I asked whether the wise man knew wisdom, you said that it seemed to him that he knew it. To someone to whom it seems that the wise man knows wisdom, it certainly does not seem that the wise man knows nothing. This cannot be maintained unless someone dares to say that wisdom is nothing.

“It follows that what seems so to you now seems so to me as well. It seems to me that the wise man knows something, and, I think, it seems so to you also, since you accept that it seems to the wise man that the wise man knows wisdom.”

Then he said: “I do not think I am trying to exercise my own intellect any more than you are, and I am surprised that you think I need any such exercise. For, perhaps because I am still blind, it seems to me that there is a difference between ‘it seems to him that he knows’ and ‘he knows,’ and between wisdom, which lies in investigation, and truth. When we use either of these expressions, I cannot see how they fit together.”

At that point we were being called to lunch. I said: “I do not dislike the fact that you resist so strongly. Either neither of us knows what we are saying, in which case we must take care not to be so disgraceful; or one of us does know, which is likewise no less disgraceful to abandon and neglect. But we shall return to one another in the afternoon. For when it seemed to me that we had reached the end, you even brought your fists into the fight.”

When they laughed at this, we parted.

# SECOND DISCUSSION

## CHAPTER IV — Again: He Is Not Wise Who Knows Nothing

7. When we returned, we found Licentius, whom Helicon had never assisted when he was thirsty, absorbed in devising verses. For almost in the middle of lunch—although the beginning of our lunch had been the same as its end—he had secretly risen and had drunk nothing.

I said to him: “I certainly hope that you will someday embrace the poetry for which you have conceived such a desire—not because this perfection gives me excessive pleasure, but because I see that you have become so inflamed that you will not be able to escape this love except through disgust, which easily follows upon perfection.

“Since you are also very musical, I would rather have you impress your verses upon our ears than have you sing, like the little birds we see shut up in cages, words that you do not understand in those Greek tragedies.

“I do advise you, however, to go and drink if you wish, and to return to our school, if Hortensius and philosophy still deserve anything from you. You have already tasted their sweetest first fruits in that conversation of yours, which had moved you more powerfully than this poetry toward knowledge of great and truly fruitful matters.

“But while I am trying to call you back to those disciplines by which souls are cultivated, I fear I may turn them into a labyrinth for you, and I almost regret having restrained you from that impetuous course.”

He blushed and went away to drink. He was very thirsty, and this also gave him an opportunity to avoid me, since I might perhaps say more things, and harsher ones.

### Note

[Col. 0938] The printed editions read *circulum* (“a circle”), but ten manuscripts more correctly read *circum* (“around”).

8. When he had returned, and everyone was attentive, I began as follows:

“Is it really the case, Alypius, that we disagree about a matter which, as it seems to me, is now perfectly clear?”

“It is not surprising,” he replied, “if what you assert is obvious to you is obscure to me. For many things that are obvious can be more obvious to some people, and certain obscure things can be more obscure to others.

“If this too is truly obvious to you, believe me when I say that there is someone for whom this obvious point of yours is even more obvious, and likewise someone for whom what is obscure to me is more obscure still.

“But do not think me stubborn for much longer. I beg you to explain this obvious point more clearly.”

“Pay close attention, please,” I said, “and for a little while set aside your concern with answering. For if I know you and myself well, what I am saying will easily become clear, and each of us will quickly persuade the other.

“Did you say—or had I perhaps become deaf—that it seems to the wise man that he knows wisdom?”

He nodded.

“Let us set aside that wise man for a moment,” I said. “Are you yourself wise or not?”

“Nothing less,” he replied.

“Nevertheless,” I said, “I want you to answer me: what do you think of the Academic wise man? Does it seem to you that he knows wisdom?”

“Do you mean,” he replied, “whether it seems to him that he knows it, or whether he actually knows it? Do you think those are one and the same or different? I am afraid that this confusion may provide either of us with a refuge.”

9. “This is that Tuscan quarrel,” I said, “as it is commonly called, in which an objection to another question seems to remedy, not solve, the question that was posed.

“Our poet too,” I added, “so that I may indulge Licentius’s ears for a moment, appropriately judged this to be rustic and completely pastoral in his *Eclogue*, when one man questions another in a place where the expanse of sky is no wider than three cubits, while the other replies:

> Tell me in what lands flowers are born  
> Bearing the names of kings inscribed upon them.  
> (Virgil, *Eclogue* 3.105–106)

“But please do not think, Alypius, that such a thing is permitted to us in the country. At least these little baths should recall to us some of the decorum of the gymnasia. So, if you please, answer what I ask:

“Does it seem to you that the wise man of the Academics knows wisdom?”

“Lest we go on at length by repeating words with words,” he replied, “it seems that it seems to him that he knows it.”

“Then,” I said, “does it seem to you that he does not know it? For I am not asking what seems to you to seem to the wise man; I am asking whether it seems to you that the wise man knows wisdom. As I understand it, you can answer either yes or no.”

“O,” he replied, “if only it were as easy for me as it is for you, or as difficult for you as it is for me! Then you would not be so troublesome, and you would not hope for anything in this matter.

“When you asked me what I thought of the Academic wise man, I answered that it seemed to me that he seemed to himself to know wisdom, lest I rashly affirm that I knew it or say, with equal rashness, that he knew it.”

“As a great favor,” I said, “I beg you first to grant me the request that you answer what I am asking, not what you are asking yourself. Then, for a little while, set aside the hope that I know is no less dear to you than your own.

“Certainly, if this question deceives me, I shall quickly cross over to your side and we shall end the dispute. Finally, drive away the anxiety by which I see that you are troubled, and pay closer attention, so that you may easily understand what I want you to answer.

“You said that you would neither affirm nor deny because one or the other must be done in response to my question, and because you did not want rashly to claim that you knew what you did not know. But surely I asked not what you know, but what seems to you to be the case.

“So I ask the same question again, more clearly—if it can be said more clearly: Does it seem to you that the wise man knows wisdom, or does it not seem so?”

“If the wise man whom reason discloses can be found,” he replied, “then it can seem to me that he knows wisdom.”

“Then,” I said, “reason discloses to you a wise man who does not fail to know wisdom. And rightly so; for it could not reasonably seem otherwise to you.”

10. “I ask now, then, whether the wise man can be found. For if he can, he can also know wisdom, and every question between us is resolved.

“But if you say that he cannot be found, then the question will no longer be whether the wise man knows anything, but whether anyone can be wise at all. Once this has been established, we shall have to withdraw from the Academics and examine this question carefully and cautiously with you, as far as we are able.

“For they held—or rather, it seemed to them—that a man could be wise and yet that knowledge could not arise in a human being. Therefore they affirmed that the wise man knew nothing.

“But you think that he knows wisdom, which certainly is not the same as knowing nothing. For we have agreed among ourselves, as did all the ancients and the Academics themselves, that no one can know what is false.

“It remains, then, either for you to maintain that wisdom is nothing, or for you to admit that the Academics describe a wise man whom reason does not recognize.”

## CHAPTER V — The Academics’ Empty Refuge Is Closed Off

11. “Setting these matters aside, agree that we should ask whether such wisdom as reason discloses can arise in a human being. For we neither ought nor can rightly call anything else wisdom.”

“Even if I grant,” he replied, “what I see you pressing so strongly—that wisdom is known by the wise man, and that we have discovered something which the wise man can apprehend—I still do not see that the Academics’ entire position has been undermined.

“For I foresee that a considerable place remains open to their defense, and that the suspension of assent has not been cut away. They cannot fail to have something with which to support their cause, even in the very point by which you think they have been defeated.

“For they will say that nothing can be apprehended and assent ought to be given to nothing, to such an extent that even this conclusion—that nothing can be apprehended—which throughout almost their whole lives they had probably persuaded themselves of, has now been wrested from them by your conclusion.

“Whether the force of this argument is invincible because of the slowness of my intellect, or truly because of its own strength, it cannot move them from their position, since they can still boldly affirm that assent ought even now to be given to nothing.

“For perhaps at some time something may be discovered, either by themselves or by someone else, that can be said against this position with acuteness and probability. We must notice their own image and, as it were, their mirror in that Proteus who, as the story goes, was accustomed to be captured by the very form in which he would least be captured, and whose investigators never held him except through the indication of some divine power.”

### Note

[Col. 0940] This passage is mentioned in *On Order* II.15.43.

“If that power should be present and deign to demonstrate to us the truth for which we care so greatly, I too, even against their will—which I scarcely think likely—shall admit that they have been defeated.”

12. “That is excellent,” I said. “I could wish for nothing more. For see, please, how many and how great advantages have come to me.

“First, the Academics are now said to have been so completely defeated that nothing remains for their defense except what cannot be the case. Who could understand or believe that someone who has been defeated should glory in being victorious by the very means by which he was defeated?

“Moreover, if there is now any remaining conflict with them, it does not concern what they say about nothing being knowable, but what they maintain about assenting to nothing.

“So we are now in agreement. For it seems to me, as it does to them, that the wise man knows wisdom. Nevertheless, they advise that he refrain from assent. They say only that it seems to him that he knows, but that he knows in no way—as though I were claiming that I know.

“I too say that it seems so to me, for I am a fool, just as they are, if they do not know wisdom. But I think that we ought to approve something—that is, the truth. I ask them whether they deny this; that is, whether they think that one ought not to assent to the truth.

“They will never say this, but they will assert that the truth cannot be found. Therefore, even here they are in some respect my companions, since neither of us dislikes—and indeed both necessarily approve—the proposition that we ought to assent to the truth.

“But who, they ask, will demonstrate it? On this point I shall not trouble myself to quarrel with them. It is enough for me that it is no longer probable that the wise man knows nothing, lest they be compelled to say something utterly absurd: either that wisdom is nothing, or that the wise man does not know wisdom.”

## CHAPTER VI — Truth Cannot Be Apprehended Except through Divine Assistance

13. “But who can show the truth? You said this, Alypius, and I must work very hard not to disagree with you. For you said, both briefly and devoutly, that only some divine power can show a human being what the truth is.

“Nothing in this conversation have I heard more gladly, nothing more seriously, nothing more probably—and, if that divine power is present, as I trust it is, nothing more truly.

“And that Proteus: with what depth of mind you recalled him, and with what force you turned him toward the highest kind of philosophy! For that Proteus is introduced as an image of truth, so that you young men may see that poets are not wholly to be despised by philosophy.

“Proteus, I say, assumes and sustains the role of truth in poetry—a role that no one can maintain if, deceived by false images, he loosens or lets go the knots of apprehension.

“For these images, through the habit formed by bodily things and by those senses that we use for the necessities of this life, strive to deceive and mock us even when truth is held and, as it were, possessed in our hands.

“This, then, is the third advantage that has come to me, and I cannot determine its value. For my closest friend agrees with me not only concerning the probability of human life but also concerning religion itself. This is the clearest indication of a true friend, since friendship has been most correctly and most sacredly defined as agreement in human and divine matters accompanied by goodwill and love.”

## CHAPTER VII — At Alypius’s Request, Augustine Now Delivers a Speech Against the Academics. A Witty Passage of Cicero Is Cited

14. “Nevertheless, lest the arguments of the Academics seem to spread certain clouds over the matter, or lest we appear arrogantly to resist the authority of learned men—among whom Cicero in particular cannot fail to move us—if you agree, I shall first say a few things against those arguments by which their discussions seem opposed to the truth.

“Then, as it seems to me, I shall show what reason the Academics had for concealing their position.

“So, Alypius, although I see you wholly on my side, take up their cause for a little while and answer me.”

“Since today,” he replied, “you have proceeded, as they say, under favorable auspices, I shall not obstruct your complete victory. I shall now attempt to undertake those positions more securely, in the manner in which you impose them upon me—provided that, since you indicate that you intend to proceed by questions, you prefer to turn them into a continuous speech, if that is convenient for you. Otherwise, like a stubborn opponent—which is very far from your courtesy—I shall be tortured by those little weapons while already captured by you.”

15. When I noticed that the others were expecting this as well, I began as though opening a different introduction:

“I shall accommodate you. Although, after the labor of the rhetorical school, I had assumed that I would rest somewhat in this light armor and conduct the matter by questioning rather than speaking, still, because we are very few and I do not need to strain my health by shouting, and because I have wished to make this pen, for the sake of that same health, the charioteer and guide of my speech, so that my mind may not carry me more rapidly than my body’s care permits, listen to what I think in a continuous speech, as you wish.

“But first let us see what sort of thing it is from which the admirers of the Academics are accustomed to boast excessively. For in Cicero’s books, which he wrote in defense of this cause, there is a certain passage composed, as it seems to me, with remarkable wit—and, in the opinion of some, strengthened also by considerable force.

“It is altogether difficult for anyone not to be moved by what is said there: that the Academic wise man is granted second place by all the members of the other schools who consider themselves wise, since each of them must claim first place for himself.

“From this it may probably be concluded that the man who is rightly first in his own judgment is the one who, in everyone else’s judgment, is second.”

16. Suppose, for example, that a Stoic sage were present—for against them above all the Academic intellect blazed forth. [Col. 0942] Thus, if Zeno or Chrysippus were asked who is wise, he would answer that the wise person is the one he himself has described. Epicurus, on the other hand, or any other of their opponents, would deny this and insist that his own most accomplished hunter of pleasures is wise. From there, a quarrel: Zeno shouts, and the whole of that colonnade erupts in tumult, declaring that the human being was born for nothing other than moral excellence; that excellence, by its own splendor, draws minds to itself, with no external advantage whatsoever placed alongside it as a kind of seductive reward; and that Epicurus’ pleasure is shared only with beasts, among whose company it would be impious to thrust either a human being or a sage.

In opposition, Epicurus summons from his little gardens what is virtually a free mob of drunken revelers, who nevertheless are looking for someone whom they may tear apart with untrimmed nails and rough mouths, and, exaggerating before the assembled people the name of pleasure, sweetness, and repose, presses his case fiercely, so that no one seems capable of being happy without them. If an Academic should happen upon their quarrel, he will hear both sides dragging him over to their respective parties; but if he yields to either one or the other, those whom he abandons will denounce him as mad, ignorant, and reckless. And so, after carefully lending an ear in both directions, when asked what he thinks, he will say that he is uncertain.

Now ask the Stoic who is better: Epicurus, who shouts that he is delirious, or the Academic, who declares that he must still deliberate about so important a matter. No one doubts that the Academic will be preferred. Turn again to the Stoic and ask whom he loves more: Zeno, by whom he is called a beast, or Arcesilas, from whom he hears, “You may perhaps be speaking the truth, but I shall investigate more carefully.” Is it not clear that the whole of that colonnade would appear insane to Epicurus, while the Academics would appear, in comparison with them, modest and cautious men?

Thus Cicero provides his readers with an almost perfectly balanced and most entertaining spectacle concerning virtually all the philosophical schools, as though displaying that none of them, after assigning the first place to himself—which each is necessarily bound to do—fails to assign second place to the person whom he sees not resisting but merely doubting. On this point I shall offer no opposition, nor shall I [Note: Am. and Er. read, “nor shall I take glory from that Sulla.”] deprive them of any glory. Let Cicero here appear to anyone to have intended not a joke, but to have pursued and gathered certain empty and inflated notions, which are alien to the lightness of those little Greeklings themselves [Note: In the earlier printed editions, “would be alien” (*abhorreret*). But eight manuscripts have *abhorret*, “is alien,” which is no less satisfactory. [*Abhorreret*.]].

## CHAPTER VIII — The passage cited from Cicero is refuted

17. For what prevents me, if I wish to resist this vanity, from easily showing how much less harmful it is to be unlearned than to be incapable of learning? Hence, when that boastful Academic has offered himself as a pupil to each of them in turn, and no one has been able to persuade him of what he thinks he knows, afterward they all laugh at him in full agreement. Each of them will then judge that every one of his opponents has learned nothing, whereas this man is capable of learning nothing. Thereafter he will be thrown out of all the schools—not with schoolmasters’ rods, which would be more disgraceful than troublesome, but with the clubs and cudgels of those cloaked philosophers. [Col. 0943] For it will not be difficult to demand, against this common plague, something like the Herculean aid of the Cynics.

But if I should wish to contend with them for this very cheap glory—a contest that may indeed be granted with indulgence to me as one who is philosophizing, though not yet wise—what will they have with which they can refute me? Let us suppose that I and the Academic have burst into those quarrels of the philosophers. Let them all be present and briefly set out their opinions as circumstances permit. Let Carneades be asked what he thinks. He will say that he is uncertain. Thus each of them will prefer him to all the others. Therefore all will prefer him to all: surely a great and lofty glory! Who would not wish to imitate him? And so, when questioned, I too shall give the same answer; the praise will be equal.

Does the sage, then, take pleasure in a glory in which the fool is his equal? What if the fool even surpasses him with ease? Does shame have no effect? For I shall now hold this Academic back as he departs from the judgment-seat. Indeed, folly is all the more eager for this kind of victory. So, keeping him there, I shall reveal to the judges what they do not know, and say:

“Excellent gentlemen, I have this in common with him: he doubts which of you follows the truth. But we also have our own distinct opinions, and I ask you to judge between them. I am indeed uncertain where the truth lies, although I have heard your doctrines; but this is because I do not know which of you is wise. He, however, denies that even the wise person knows anything—not even wisdom itself, from which he is called wise.”

Who cannot see to whom that palm belongs? For if my opponent says this, I shall win by glory; but if, blushing, he admits that the wise person knows wisdom, I shall win by the verdict.

## CHAPTER IX — Zeno’s definition is examined

18. But let us now withdraw from this contentious tribunal to some place where no crowd will trouble us; and would that we might enter Plato’s own school, which is said to have received its name because it is set apart from the people. Here let us discuss, as far as we can among ourselves, not glory—which is a trivial and childish matter—but life itself and some hope of a blessed soul.

The Academics deny that anything can be known. Whence did this opinion please you, men most eager for learning and most learned? “Zeno’s definition moved us,” they reply. Why, I ask? For if it is true, the person who knows even that definition knows something true; but if it is false, it ought not to have moved men so steadfast.

Let us see, then, what Zeno says. He says, of course, that such an appearance can be grasped and apprehended as could not have the same distinguishing marks as a false appearance. Did this move you, Platonist, to draw students away from the hope of learning with all your strength, so that, with a kind of torpor of mind groaning along with you, they might abandon the whole enterprise of philosophy?

19. But how could it not have moved him, if no such appearance can be found and, unless there is such an appearance, nothing can be apprehended? If this is so, it would have been better to say that wisdom cannot befall a human being than that the wise person does not know why he lives, does not know how he lives, and does not know whether he lives; finally—and nothing more perverse, delirious, or insane can be said—that he is both wise and ignorant of wisdom.

For which is harsher: that a human being cannot be wise, or that a wise person does not know wisdom? There is nothing to debate here, if the matter as stated [Col. 0944] is not sufficient for judgment. But perhaps if that were said openly, people would be driven entirely away from philosophizing. As things stand, they must be enticed by the sweetest and holiest name of wisdom, so that, after having learned nothing when their life is worn away, they may later pursue with the most dreadful curses the one whom, having abandoned at least bodily pleasures, they followed into the torments of the soul.

20. But let us see by whom they are more likely to be deterred from philosophy. By the person who says:

“Listen, my friend. Philosophy is called not wisdom itself but the pursuit of wisdom. If you devote yourself to it, you will not indeed be wise while you live here—for wisdom is with God and cannot arise in a human being—but once you have sufficiently exercised and cleansed yourself through such study, your soul will easily enjoy wisdom after this life, that is, when you have ceased to be a human being”?

Or by the person who says:

“Come, mortals, to philosophy! Great is its fruit: for what is dearer to a human being than wisdom? Come, then, so that you may be wise—and yet not know wisdom”?

“No,” he says, “I shall not speak in that way.”

That is deception, for you will find nothing else in him. Thus, if you say this, they will flee from you as from a madman; if you lead them to this by another route, you will make them mad. But let us grant that, because of either opinion, people are equally unwilling to philosophize. If Zeno’s definition compelled him to say something harmful to philosophy, then, man, what ought to have been said to a human being: something that would make him grieve, or something that would make him laugh at you?

21. Nevertheless, let us examine, as far as our folly permits, what Zeno defined. He says that an appearance can be grasped when it appears in such a way that it could not appear false. It is clear that nothing else enters into perception. “I too,” says Arcesilas, “see this; and by this very point I teach that nothing is perceived. For no such thing can be found.”

Perhaps it cannot be found by you or by other fools; but why can it not be found by a wise person? Indeed, I think that even the fool himself could not answer if he told you, with that memorable sharpness of yours, to refute this very definition of Zeno and show that it too could be false. If you cannot do so, you possess the very thing that you perceive; but if you refute it, you have no basis for preventing perception.

I do not see that it can be refuted, and I judge it altogether most true. Therefore, since I know it, although I am a fool, I know something. But suppose that it yields to your cleverness. I shall use an utterly secure dilemma. For it is either true or false: if true, I grasp it correctly; if false, something can be perceived even if it has distinguishing marks in common with what is false.

“Whence,” he asks, “can that be?”

Zeno therefore defined the matter most truly, and whoever agreed with him at least on this point did not err. Or shall we think it a small achievement, and lacking in sincerity, that definition which, in opposition to those who were going to say many things against perception, while designating what could be perceived, showed itself to be of that very kind? Thus the definition is both an example of and a statement about apprehensible things.

“I do not know,” he says, “whether the definition itself is true; but because it is probable, by following it I show that nothing such as it describes can be grasped.”

You are perhaps showing something apart from the definition itself, and, I think, you see what follows. Even if we are uncertain about that, knowledge does not thereby abandon us: for we know that it is either true or false. [Col. 0945] Therefore we do not know nothing.

Although I shall never allow myself to be ungrateful, I judge that definition altogether most true. For either false things can be perceived—which the Academics fear more intensely, and which is in fact absurd—or even things resembling false things cannot be perceived; hence the definition is true. But let us now examine the remaining points.

## CHAPTER X — Two Academic pronouncements

22. Although this may, if I am not mistaken, be sufficient for victory, it may perhaps not be sufficient for satisfaction with victory. There are two claims made by the Academics against which we shall undertake to proceed as best we can: “Nothing can be perceived,” and “One ought to assent to nothing.” We shall speak about assent on another occasion; for now, let us say a little about perception.

Do you really say that absolutely nothing can be apprehended? Here Carneades awoke—for none of them slept less deeply than he—and looked around at the obviousness of things. Thus, I imagine, speaking with himself as people do, he said:

“Are you really going to say, Carneades, that you do not know whether you are a human being or an ant? Or will Chrysippus triumph over you?”

Let us say that we do not know those things investigated among philosophers; let the rest not concern us. Thus, if I stumble in ordinary daylight, I may appeal to those darknesses of the unlearned where only certain divine eyes can see. Even if they have seen me groping and falling, they cannot betray me to the blind—especially to the arrogant, and to those who are ashamed to be taught anything.

Gracefully indeed, O Greek ingenuity, you advance, compact and prepared; but you do not consider that definition and discovery, both the work of a philosopher, have been fixed and established in the vestibule of philosophy. If you try to cut it down, the double-headed axe will rebound upon your legs. Once it has been shaken, not only can something be perceived, but even what is extremely similar to the false can be perceived, if you do not dare to overturn it.

This is your hiding place, from which you burst forth violently and leap out against those wishing to enter unsuspectingly. Some Hercules will strangle you in your own cave like the half-human Cacus [Note: Eleven manuscripts read “will strangle the half-human,” omitting the name Cacus.] and crush you beneath the same mass, showing that there is something in philosophy which cannot be made uncertain by you as though it were similar to the false.

Certainly I was hurrying toward other matters; but whoever presses this point inflicts a great insult on you, Carneades, since he thinks that you, as though dead, can be overcome by me anywhere and by any means. If he does not think so, he is merciless, compelling me to abandon my defenses everywhere and fight with you in the open field. When I began to descend into it, terrified by your very name, I drew back my foot and hurled something from a higher position; whether it reached you or accomplished anything, let those under whose judgment we fight decide.

But why am I afraid, foolish man? If I remember correctly, you are dead, and Alypius no longer rightly fights before your tomb. God will easily help me against your shade.

23. You say that nothing can be perceived in philosophy. And, to spread your argument far and wide, you seize upon the quarrels and disagreements of philosophers and suppose that they supply you with weapons against them. For how shall we decide the dispute between Democritus and the earlier physicists about whether there is one world or countless worlds, when harmony could not even remain between him and his heir, Epicurus?

That luxurious fellow, allowing his atoms—almost his maidservants, that is, the little bodies he happily embraces in the darkness—not to keep to their own course but spontaneously to deviate everywhere into the boundaries of others, dissipated the whole inheritance even through quarrels.

But this has nothing to do with me. If knowing some of these things belongs to wisdom, they cannot be hidden from the wise person. But if wisdom is something else, the wise person knows that and despises these matters. Nevertheless, I, who am still far even from the neighborhood of wisdom, know something about these physical questions.

For I am certain that there is either one world or not one; and, if there is not one, that there are either a finite or an infinite number. Let Carneades show that this opinion resembles the false. Likewise, I know that this world of ours has been arranged either by the nature of bodies or by some providence; and that it either always has existed and always will exist, or began to exist and will not cease; or did not arise in time but will have an end; or both began to exist and will not remain forever. And I know countless physical propositions in this fashion.

For these alternatives are true as disjunctions, and no one can confuse them with the false by any resemblance. But “assume something,” says the Academic.

“I do not wish to. For this is equivalent to saying, ‘Abandon what you know and speak of what you do not know.’”

“But the proposition remains suspended.”

“Certainly it hangs better than it falls: it is plainly level” [Note: Seven manuscripts read “it is plainly full.”]; plainly it can now be called either false or true. Therefore I say that I know this.

You, who deny that these matters even belong to philosophy and assert that nothing concerning them can be known, show me that I do not know them. Say that these disjunctions are either false or have something in common with the false by which they cannot be distinguished at all.

## CHAPTER XI — The weakness of the senses does not establish that nothing true is perceived; nor do sleep and madness

24. “How do you know,” he says, “that this is the world, if the senses deceive?”

Your arguments have never had enough force to refute the senses so completely that you could convince us that nothing appears to us. Nor have you ever dared to attempt this; rather, you have labored vigorously to persuade us that something may be other than it appears.

I therefore call “world” this whole thing—whatever its nature—that contains and nourishes us, this thing, I say, which appears to my eyes and is perceived by me as having earth and sky, or something like earth and something like sky. If you say that nothing appears to me, I shall never be in error. For the person who errs is the one who rashly approves what appears to him. You say that something false can appear to those who perceive; you do not say that nothing appears.

Indeed, the whole basis of your argument will be removed wherever you wish to reign, if we not only know nothing but nothing even appears to us. But if you deny that what appears to me is the world, you are disputing about a name, since I have said that I call it “world.”
