25. “Even if you are asleep,” you will say, “is this thing you see the world?”

It has already been said that whatever of this kind appears to me I call the world. But if you are willing to call “world” only what is seen by those who are awake or even sane, then, if you can, maintain that those who sleep and those who are mad are not sleeping and raging [Col. 0947] in the world.

Therefore I say that this entire mass and structure of bodies in which we are situated—whether we are asleep, mad, awake, or sane—is either one thing or not one thing. Explain how this proposition could be false.

For if I am asleep, it may be that I said nothing; or, if words escaped from the mouth of a sleeping person, as often happens, it may be that I did not say them here, while sitting in this way, before these listeners. But that this is false cannot be the case.

Nor do I claim to have perceived that I am awake. You can say that this too could have appeared to me while I was asleep and therefore could be extremely similar to the false. But if there are one and six worlds, then that there are seven worlds is evident, whatever my condition may be, and I do not affirm shamelessly that I know it.

Therefore show that either this connection or those disjunctions mentioned above can be false because of sleep, madness, or the vanity of the senses; and, if I remember these things after waking, I shall concede that I have been defeated.

For I think it is already sufficiently clear which things appear false through dreaming and insanity—namely, those belonging to the bodily senses. For “three times three is nine,” and the square of intelligible numbers, must be true even while the human race snores.

Indeed, I see that many things can also be said in defense of the senses, which we do not find criticized by the Academics. I think that the senses are not blamed either because mad people experience false images or because we see false things in dreams. For if they reported the truth to those who are awake and sane, it is no concern of theirs what the mind of a sleeping or insane person imagines for itself [Note: Paris manuscript: “what the mind imagines for itself.”].

26. It remains to ask whether, when the senses themselves report something, they report it truly. Suppose some Epicurean says:

“I have no complaint to make against the senses. It is unjust to demand more from them than they can do; and whatever the eyes are capable of seeing, they see truly.”

Then, is what they see concerning an oar in water true?

“Entirely true. For since there is a cause that makes it appear so, if an oar submerged in water appeared straight, I would more properly accuse my eyes of a false report. For they would not be seeing what ought to be seen when such causes were present.”

Why say more? The same can be said about the apparent movement of towers, the wings of birds, and countless other things.

“But I am deceived if I assent,” someone may say.

“Do not assent to more than that it appears to you in this way, and there is no deception. For I do not see how the Academic can refute someone who says: ‘I know that this appears white to me; I know that this delights my hearing; I know that this smells pleasant to me; I know that this tastes sweet to me; I know that this feels cold to me.’”

Rather, say whether the leaves of the wild olive are bitter in themselves, when the goat pursues them so stubbornly.

“What an offensive man! Is not the goat itself more modest?”

“I do not know what they are like for the animal, but they are bitter to me. What more do you ask?”

“But perhaps there is also some human being to whom they are not bitter.”

“Are you trying to be troublesome? Did I say that they are bitter for everyone? I said that they are bitter for me—and I do not even [Col. 0948] assert this always. For what if at one time one cause makes one taste present itself in the mouth, and at another time another cause makes it taste sweet or bitter?”

This is what I say: when a person tastes something, he can swear in good faith that he knows it to be pleasant to his palate, or, conversely, unpleasant; and no Greek sophistry can dislodge him from this knowledge.

For who would be so shameless as to say to me while I am licking something with pleasure, “Perhaps you are not tasting it; perhaps this is a dream”?

“Do I resist?”

“Yet this would also delight me in a dream.”

Therefore no resemblance to false things confuses what I said I know.

The Epicurean, or the Cyrenaics, and perhaps many others may say much in defense of the senses, against which I have not learned that the Academics have said anything. But what is that to me? If they wish and are able, let them overturn these arguments, even with my support. For whatever they argue against the senses does not prevail against all philosophers.

There are those who admit that all these things which the mind receives through bodily sensation can generate opinion, but deny that they generate knowledge. Yet they wish knowledge to be contained in the understanding and to live in the mind, removed from the senses. Perhaps that wise person whom we seek is one of their number. But we shall discuss this on another occasion. For now, let us proceed to the remaining matters, which, because of what has already been said, we shall explain briefly, if I am not mistaken.

## CHAPTER XII — The Academics are pressed because they wrongly appeal to the deceptions of the senses, sleep, and madness

27. For what assistance or hindrance do bodily senses provide to someone investigating morals? Unless, indeed, those very people who placed the highest human good in pleasure—whom neither the neck of a dove, nor an uncertain voice, nor a heavy weight for a human being that is light for camels, nor six hundred other things prevents from saying that they know themselves to delight in what delights them or to be offended by what offends them, which I do not see how it could be refuted—will move the person who embraces the end of the good with his mind.

Which do you choose? If you ask what seems right to me, I think that the highest human good lies in the mind (*Retractions*, Book I, chapter 1, section 4). But now we are asking about knowledge.

Therefore question the wise person, who cannot be ignorant of wisdom. Meanwhile, even I, that slow and foolish man, may know that the end of human good, in which the blessed life resides, either does not exist, or exists in the soul, or in the body, or in both. Convince me, if you can, that I do not know this; your famous arguments cannot do so in any way.

But if you cannot—and you will not find anything to which it is similar as false—shall I hesitate to conclude that it rightly appears to me that the wise person knows whatever is true in philosophy, since I have learned so many truths from it?

28. Perhaps he fears that the wise person may choose the highest good while asleep. There is no danger: when he wakes, he will reject it if it displeases him and retain it if it pleases him. For who will rightly blame him for seeing something false in a dream?

Or perhaps he will fear that, while asleep, the wise person may lose his wisdom if he approves false things as true? He does not dare even to dream this: that he should call someone wise while awake and deny that he is wise if he sleeps.

The same things can be said about madness; but the argument is hastening elsewhere. Nevertheless, I shall not leave these matters without the most secure conclusion. For either wisdom is lost through madness, in which case the person whom you declare ignorant of truth will no longer be wise; or his knowledge [Col. 0949] remains in the understanding, even if the rest of his soul imagines, as in a dream, what it has received from the senses.

## CHAPTER XIII — Many things are perceived in dialectic

29. Dialectic remains. Certainly the wise person knows it well, and no one can know what is false. But if he does not know it, knowledge of it does not belong to his wisdom, since he could have been wise without it; and we ask needlessly whether it is true or can be perceived.

Perhaps someone will say to me: “You foolishly keep revealing what you know. Could you know nothing about dialectic?”

On the contrary, I know more about it than about any other part of philosophy. First, it taught me that all the propositions I used above are true. Then through it I learned many other truths. But count how many they are, if you can.

If there are four elements in the world, there are not five. If there is one sun, there are not two. One soul cannot both die and be immortal. A person cannot simultaneously be happy and miserable. The sun cannot be shining here while it is night. We are either awake now or asleep. Either there is a body that I seem to see, or there is not.

These and many other things, which it would take too long to enumerate, I learned through dialectic to be true in themselves, whatever the condition of our senses may be. It taught me that, if the antecedent part of any of the propositions I just presented by connection is assumed, what is joined to it necessarily follows.

It also taught me that, when the matter about which words are spoken is clear, we ought not to quarrel about words; and that anyone who does so should, if he acts from ignorance, be instructed; if from malice, be abandoned; if he cannot be taught, he should be advised to do something else rather than spend his time and effort on superfluities; and, if he does not comply, he should be ignored.

As for deceptive and fallacious little arguments, the brief rule is this: if they are inferred through an improper concession, one must return to what was conceded. If the true and the false conflict in a single conclusion, one should accept what is understood and leave aside what cannot be explained. But if the method lies entirely hidden from human beings in certain matters, knowledge of it should not be sought.

These things, and many others that need not be enumerated, I have from dialectic. Nor ought I to prove ungrateful. But that wise person either disregards these matters, or, if dialectic itself is truly the science of truth, knows it in such a way that by despising it, and not pitying it, he starves to death [Note: Am., Er., and Lov. omit *fame*, “by hunger.” Four manuscripts read “and not by a reputation to be pitied.” But nine others, more correctly, read “and, by not pitying it, starves it to death”; Bad. agrees with them.] the most mendacious slander of all:

“If it is true, it is false; if it is false, it is true.”

I think that this is sufficient concerning perception, because when I begin to speak about assent, the whole argument will once again turn on this point.

## CHAPTER XIV — The wise person ought at least to assent to wisdom

30. Let us now come to that part in which Alypius still seems to be uncertain. First, let us [Col. 0950] examine precisely what it is that moves you so acutely and cautiously.

For if, as you said, the Academic opinion—that the wise person knows nothing—is supported by so many and such great arguments, and if your discovery undermines it, forcing us to confess that it is much more probable that the wise person knows wisdom, then assent ought to be restrained all the more. For this very point shows that nothing, however abundantly and subtly argued, can be persuaded in such a way that, if ingenuity is present on the opposing side, it cannot be resisted just as sharply, or perhaps even more sharply.

Thus it comes about that, although the Academic has been defeated, he has won.

Would that he might be defeated! No Pelasgian art will ever make it possible for him to leave me both defeated and victorious at once. Certainly, if nothing else can be found to say against these arguments, I openly declare that I have been defeated. For we are not dealing with securing glory but with discovering truth.

It is enough for me, by whatever means, to cross this great obstacle that confronts those entering philosophy and, growing dark in I know not what hiding places [Note: “Concealing darkness,” according to Par., Er., and Ven. M.], threatens that all philosophy is of this nature and allows no hope that any light will be found in it.

But if it is already probable that the wise person knows something, I have nothing further to desire. For the only reason it seemed probable that he ought to withhold assent was that it seemed probable that nothing could be grasped. Once that has been removed—for the wise person perceives even wisdom itself, as is now conceded—no reason will remain why the wise person should not assent even to wisdom itself. For it is unquestionably more monstrous for the wise person not to approve wisdom than for the wise person not to know wisdom.

31. Let us, then, if we can, place before our eyes for a little while a spectacle of this kind: a quarrel between wisdom and the wise person.

What else does wisdom say but that it is wisdom?

But the other replies, “I do not believe it.”

Who says to wisdom, “I do not believe that you are wisdom”? Who, unless it is one with whom wisdom has been able to speak and in whom it has deigned to dwell—that is, the wise person?

Go now and look for me, who am fighting against the Academics. You have here a new contest: the wise person and wisdom are fighting with each other. The wise person does not wish to assent to wisdom; I shall safely await the outcome with you.

For who would not believe that wisdom is unconquerable? Nevertheless, let us fortify ourselves with a dilemma. Either the Academic will defeat wisdom in this contest—and he will be defeated by me, because he will not be wise—or wisdom will overcome him, and we shall show that the wise person assents to wisdom.

Therefore either the Academic is not wise, or the wise person assents to something—unless perhaps the person who was ashamed to say that the wise person does not know wisdom will not be ashamed to say that the wise person does not assent to wisdom.

But if it is now probable that even the perception of wisdom itself can befall the wise person, and there is no reason why he should not assent to what can be perceived, I see the conclusion I wanted to establish as probable: namely, that the wise person will assent to wisdom.

If you ask where he finds wisdom itself, I shall answer, “In himself.” If you say that he does not know that he possesses it, you return to that absurdity: that the wise person does not know [Col. 0951] wisdom.

If you deny that the wise person himself can be found, then, whoever holds that opinion, we shall discuss the matter with you in another conversation, not with the Academics. For when they debate these matters, they are certainly debating the wise person.

Cicero loudly declares that he himself is a great man of opinion, but that he is asking about the wise person. If this is still unfamiliar to you, young men, you have certainly read it in the *Hortensius*:

“If, then, nothing is certain, and it is not the part of the wise person to hold opinions, the wise person will never approve anything.”

From this it is clear that, in those discussions of theirs against which we are striving, they are asking about the wise person.

32. Therefore I think that wisdom is certain for the wise person—that is, that the wise person has perceived wisdom—and for this reason he does not hold an opinion when he assents to wisdom. For he assents to a thing which, if he had not perceived it, he would not be wise.

Nor do they assert that no one ought to assent except to things that cannot be perceived. Wisdom, however, is not nothing. Since the wise person both knows wisdom and assents to wisdom, he neither knows nothing nor assents to nothing. What more do you want?

Or are we asking about the error that they say is completely avoided if assent inclines the mind toward no thing? “For,” they say, “anyone who approves not only a false thing but even a doubtful thing, although it may be true, is in error.”

But I find nothing that is not doubtful.

The wise person, however, finds wisdom itself, as we have said.

## CHAPTER XV — Whether one who follows what is probable in action without assent avoids error

33. But perhaps you now wish me to leave this subject. Matters of the utmost security should not easily be abandoned when we are dealing with exceedingly crafty men. Nevertheless, I shall accommodate you.

But what shall I say here? What? What indeed? Surely the old argument must be stated—the one in which they themselves have something to say.

For what shall I do, when you thrust me outside my camp? Shall I call on the aid of more learned men, with whom, if I cannot win, it may perhaps be less shameful to be defeated?

I shall therefore hurl, with whatever strength I possess, a weapon that is already smoky and rough, but, if I am not mistaken, extremely powerful:

“He who approves nothing does nothing.”

“What a rustic fellow!”

“And where is the probable? Where is the likely?”

“This is what you wanted. Do you hear how the Greek shields ring?”

The strongest point has been caught [Note: Paris edition: “which indeed is the strongest.” M.]; but with what hand have we hurled it? My own forces suggest nothing more powerful, nor, as I see, have we inflicted any wound.

I shall turn to what the villa and the countryside provide: they burden me with things greater than they prepare for me.

34. For when, while I had been thinking at leisure for a long time in this country setting about how this “probable” and “verisimilar” principle could protect our actions from error, it first seemed to me—as things usually seem when I was selling these arguments—that it was neatly covered and fortified. Then, when I examined the whole matter more cautiously, I seemed to have noticed one entrance through which error could rush upon the unsuspecting. For I think that not only the person who follows a false road errs, but also the person who does not follow the true one.

Let us imagine two travelers heading toward the same place, one of whom has resolved to trust no one, while the other is excessively credulous. They come to a fork in the road. [Col. 0952] The credulous man says to a shepherd who happens to be there, or to some peasant: “Good day, honest fellow; please tell me which way one should go to reach that place.” The reply is: “If you go this way, you will not go astray.” And he says to his companion: “He is telling the truth; let us go this way.”

The extremely cautious man laughs, mocks so facetiously so quick an act of assent, and meanwhile, while the other departs, remains standing at the fork. Soon it begins to seem shameful to linger, when suddenly, from another branch of the road, a certain well-dressed and urbane man appears, mounted on a horse; he comes closer, and the cautious traveler rejoices. He greets the newcomer, explains his purpose, and asks the way. He also tells him why he has stopped, so as to make the man more favorably disposed toward him, preferring him to the shepherd.

But by chance the newcomer was one of those whom the common people already call *Samardaci* [Note: The word is written this way in the edition of Basel and in several manuscripts. In the old editions of Chrysostom, too, *samardakous* is read in Homily 17 on the Epistle to the Ephesians, where it means “makers of laughter” (*gelotopoious*). It is not very different in the Ambrosian manuscript and in three others, which read *Samardocos*. Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *Sarmadacos*, as does the old commentator on Horace, in his note on Book 1, Satire 6, “The deceitful crowd around him,” where he calls them “Sarmadaci and mathematical fortune-tellers, who stood around the turning-post as spectators and deceived the inexperienced with their nonsense.”]. The thoroughly wicked man maintained his customary practice, even without payment. “Go on this way,” he says, “for I have just come from there.” He deceived him and went away.

But when would this traveler have been deceived? “I do not approve this direction as true,” he says, “but because it is verisimilar.” And here, to remain inactive is neither honorable nor useful; let us go this way.

Meanwhile, the man who erred by assenting—thinking so quickly that the shepherd’s words were true—was already refreshing himself at the place toward which they had been heading. The other, who did not err, if indeed he follows what is probable, wanders around through I know not what forests and no longer finds anyone who knows the place he had intended to reach.

I tell you truly: when I was thinking about this, I could not restrain my laughter. Somehow, through the Academics’ arguments, it comes about that the man who happens, even by chance, to take the true road is said to err, while the man who has been led plausibly through trackless mountains and has not found the region he sought is not thought to err. For although I rightly condemn rash assent, it is easier for both men to have gone astray than for this man not to have erred.

From that point, more alert to the force of these arguments, I began to consider the actual deeds and habits of human beings. Then so many matters, and matters of such deadly seriousness, came to mind against these men that I no longer laughed, but partly grew angry and partly grieved that men so learned and sharp-minded had descended into such crimes of opinion and outrages of conduct.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### To do what seems probable even without assent is wicked.

35. Certainly, perhaps not everyone who errs sins; nevertheless, everyone who sins is either admitted to err or does something worse. What, then, if one of the young men, after hearing these people say, “It is shameful to err, and therefore we ought to assent to nothing; yet when someone acts on what seems probable to him, he neither sins [Note: The Basel edition and eleven manuscripts read: “what seems probable to him, he neither ceases, nor errs.”] nor errs,” should merely remember that whatever occurs to the mind or senses must not be approved as true?

Hearing this, the young man will lie in wait for another man’s wife. I appeal to you, Marcus Tullius: we are discussing the character and life of young men, and all your writings have been vigilant for their education and formation. What else will you say except that it is not probable to you that a young man [Col. 0953] should do such a thing? But to him it is probable.

For if we live according to what is probable to someone else, you too ought not to have administered the republic, because Epicurus thought that this should not be done. The young man will therefore commit adultery with another man’s wife. If he is caught, where will he find you as his defender? Yet even if he does find you, what will you say? You will certainly deny it. But what if the matter is so clear that you deny it in vain? You will surely persuade the court—as though in the gymnasium at Cumae, or rather at Naples—that he has committed no sin, indeed that he has not even erred. For he did not convince himself that adultery ought to be committed as a truth; something probable presented itself, he followed it, and he acted—or perhaps he did not act, but merely seemed to himself to have acted.

Meanwhile the husband, a foolish man, throws everything into confusion with lawsuits, crying out for his wife’s chastity, while perhaps he is now sleeping with her and does not know it. If the judges understand this, they will either disregard the Academics and punish him as though it were a most genuine crime, or, obeying the same principles, will condemn the man in a way that is verisimilar and probable, so that this advocate will no longer know what to do.

For he will have no one to be angry with, since everyone will say that he has not erred, once those who do not assent have made whatever seemed so into something probable. He will therefore lay aside the role of advocate and assume that of a philosopher offering consolation. Thus he will easily persuade the young man—who has already made such progress in the Academy—that he should think himself condemned as though in a dream.

But you think I am joking. It is plain that I may swear by everything divine [Note: Lovaniensis reads “it pleases.” The reading “it is plain that I may swear” is restored from the Ambrosian manuscript, Erasmus, and the manuscripts; as we observed in *Retractations* I.1, it is a usage from Terence. Augustine liked to emulate Terence and other authors of more polished Latin in writings “already indeed serving God, but still, as it were, catching their breath during a pause from the school of pride,” as he says in *Confessions* IX.4.] [*Retractations* I.1.4] that I simply do not know how this man has sinned, if whoever does what seems probable does not sin. Unless, perhaps, they say that erring is one thing and sinning another, and that they acted according to those precepts so that we might not err, while they considered sinning to be no great matter.

36. I say nothing of murders, parricides, sacrileges, and every kind of outrage or crime that can be committed or imagined—deeds which are defended in a few words, and what is more serious, before the wisest judges: “I assented to nothing, and therefore I did not err.” But how could I not do what seemed probable? Those who do not think that such things can be plausibly defended should read Catiline’s speech, by which he persuaded men to commit parricide against their country, a crime that contains all other crimes within itself (*Sallust, The War with Catiline* 12).

And who would not laugh at this? They themselves say that in acting they follow nothing except what is probable, and yet they earnestly seek the truth, although it is probable to them that truth cannot be found. O astonishing monstrosity! But let us set this aside: it concerns us less, threatens our lives less, and endangers our fortunes less.

The truly deadly and terrifying matter, the matter that every decent person ought to fear, is this: if this probable theory is valid, then every crime, whenever it has seemed probable to someone that it should be committed, can be committed—not merely without blame for crime, but even without blame for error—provided only that he does not assent to it as true.

What, then? Did they not see these consequences? Indeed, [Col. 0954] they saw them with the greatest skill and prudence. Nor would I in any way presume so much as to claim for myself any share of Marcus Tullius’s diligence, vigilance, intelligence, or learning. Yet if, when he asserted that a human being could know nothing, someone merely said, “I know that this seems so to me,” he would have no means by which to refute him.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Why the Academics concealed their opinion.

37. What, then, did such great men intend by their continuous and obstinate disputes, so that knowledge of the truth would appear to be attainable by no one? Listen now somewhat more attentively—not to what I know, but to what I think. I had reserved this for the end, so that, if I could, I might explain what the whole plan of the Academics seems to me to have been.

Plato, the wisest and most learned man of his age, who spoke in such a way that whatever he said became great, and expressed himself so that, however he said it, nothing became insignificant [*Retractations* I.1.4], is said after the death of his teacher Socrates, whom he loved uniquely, to have learned many things also from the Pythagoreans.

Pythagoras, dissatisfied with Greek philosophy—which at that time was either almost nonexistent or certainly very obscure—after being moved by the discussions of a certain Pherecydes of Syria and believing that the soul was immortal, had also heard many wise men while traveling far and wide.

Plato therefore added to the Socratic charm and subtlety that he possessed in moral matters a knowledge of natural and divine things, which he had carefully received from those whom I have mentioned. He also added dialectic, as though the shaper and judge of those branches of knowledge—either itself wisdom, or something without which wisdom could not exist at all. He is said to have composed a complete system of philosophy, about which there is no time [Note: The Basel edition reads “of time”; all the other editions read “time.” The manuscripts support the latter reading.] to speak now.

For my present purpose it is enough that Plato held there to be two worlds: one intelligible, in which truth itself dwelt; and this sensible world, which it is evident that we perceive by sight and touch. Thus the former is true, while this world is verisimilar and made in the image of that one. Therefore, in the soul that knows it, truth can be polished and, as it were, brought into serenity from that intelligible world; but from this world, in the minds of fools, not knowledge but opinion can be generated.

Whatever was done in this world through those virtues which he called civic virtues—virtues resembling other true virtues, which were unknown except to a few wise men—could be called only verisimilar.

38. These and similar doctrines seem to me to have been preserved, as far as possible, among his successors and guarded as mysteries. For either such things are not easily grasped except by those who, cleansing themselves from every vice, have claimed for themselves a kind of association surpassing the human; or else anyone who knowingly wished to teach them to just anyone would not be committing a light sin.

Thus I suspect that Zeno, the leading Stoic, when he came to the school Plato had left and which Polemo then held, after hearing and believing certain teachings, was regarded with suspicion and was not thought the sort of person to whom those Platonic decrees, almost sacred, should readily be revealed and entrusted before he had unlearned [Note: Lovaniensis reads “before they had taught him otherwise.”] what he had brought into that school after receiving it from others.

Polemo died, and Arcesilaus succeeded him—Zeno’s fellow student, but a pupil under Polemo. Since Zeno was pleased with a certain opinion of his own about the world, and especially about the soul, for whose sake true philosophy keeps watch, saying that the soul was mortal and that nothing existed except this sensible world, and that nothing occurred in it except through body—for he thought that God himself was fire—it seems to me that Arcesilaus, with the utmost prudence and usefulness, concealed the Academy’s opinion completely, when that evil was spreading widely, and buried it, as it were, like gold to be found by later generations.

Since the crowd is more inclined to rush into false opinions, and since, through habit formed from bodies, it is very easy—but harmful—to believe that everything is corporeal, that exceptionally sharp and humane man resolved to unteach those whom he found badly taught rather than teach those whom he did not consider teachable.

From this arose all those doctrines attributed to the New Academy, because the earlier Academics had no need of them.

39. If Zeno had ever awakened and seen that nothing could be grasped except what he himself defined, and that nothing of this kind could be found among bodies, to which he attributed everything, then this kind of disputation—which had burned with such great necessity—would have been extinguished long ago.

But Zeno, deceived by an image of steadfastness, as the Academics thought—and as it also seems to me—was obstinate. That destructive belief in bodies somehow survived into Chrysippus, who, since he was especially capable of doing so, gave it great strength to spread more widely. Unless Carneades, from the opposing side, sharper and more vigilant than all the others, had resisted it so successfully that I am amazed the opinion retained any force afterward.

For Carneades first abandoned that shameless habit of slander which he saw had brought considerable disgrace upon Arcesilaus, lest he appear to wish to contradict everything merely for show. Instead, he set himself specifically to pull down and overthrow the Stoics themselves, and Chrysippus in particular.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### How the Academics introduced the probable.

40. Then, when he was pressed from every side with the objection that, if the wise man assented to nothing, he would do nothing—O remarkable man, and indeed not remarkable at all, since he drew this from Plato’s own fountains—he wisely considered what kinds of actions those men approved. Seeing them to be similar to certain true actions, he called what one should follow in acting in this world “verisimilar.”

He knew well what those actions resembled, and prudently concealed it; he also called this “probable.” For anyone approves a good likeness if he observes its model.

How can the wise man approve anything [Note: Eight manuscripts read: “How, then, does the wise man approve nothing?”], or how can he follow what resembles the truth, if he does not know what the truth itself is? Therefore they knew and approved false things in which they discerned a praiseworthy imitation of true realities [*Retractations* I.1.4].

But because it was neither lawful nor easy to display this to the uninitiated, they left to posterity, and to those whom they could reach at that time, a certain sign of their opinion. They prevented those who were good dialecticians from raising questions about words [Col. 0956], assailing and ridiculing them. For this reason Carneades is also said to have been the leader and founder of the Third Academy.

41. Then this conflict lasted into the time of our Cicero, by then plainly wounded and about to breathe his last into Latin literature. For nothing seems to me more inflated than to say so many things with such abundance and ornament while not actually holding the opinion expressed.

Nevertheless, those winds seem to me to have thoroughly scattered and dispersed that *feneus* Platonist, Antiochus [the adjective is materially uncertain]. For the flocks of Epicureans established sunny stalls in the minds of pleasure-loving peoples.

Antiochus was a pupil of Philo, a man, as I believe, extremely circumspect, who had already begun, as it were, to open the gates as the enemy retreated and to restore the Academy to Plato’s authority and laws. Metrodorus had previously attempted the same, and is said to have been the first to confess that it was not by decree [Note: Almost all manuscripts read “not by the right judgment.”] that the Academics had decided that nothing could be grasped, but that they had necessarily taken up such weapons against the Stoics.

Antiochus, then, as I had begun to say, after hearing the Academic Philo and the Stoic Mnesarchus, had slipped into the Old Academy—as though it were empty of defenders and secure because it had no enemy—like an ally and citizen, bringing I know not what evil from the ashes of the Stoics that violated Plato’s sanctuary.

But when Philo once again seized those weapons, he resisted Antiochus until his death, and our Cicero crushed all the remnants of Antiochus, unable while alive to tolerate the weakening or contamination of anything he had loved. Thus, after those times, when all obstinacy and stubbornness had died within a short interval, that mouth of Plato, the purest and most luminous thing in philosophy, shone forth once the clouds of error had been dispersed—especially in Plotinus, the Platonic philosopher who was judged so similar to Plato that they seem scarcely to have lived at different times; yet so great is the interval between them that Plotinus must be thought to have revived Plato [Note: *Interesse*, according to Erasmus and the Venice edition.]

## CHAPTER XIX  
### The various kinds of philosophy.

42. Thus nowadays we scarcely see philosophers except Cynics, Peripatetics, or Platonists. The Cynics are present because a certain freedom and license of life pleases them.

As for learning and doctrine, and the habits by which the soul is cared for: because there have been men of exceptional sharpness and skill who, in their discussions, taught that Aristotle and Plato agree so completely that they seem to disagree only to the inexperienced and inattentive, one discipline of the truest philosophy has, in my opinion, emerged after many centuries and many disputes.

For this is not the philosophy of this world, which our sacred teachings rightly detest, but of another, intelligible world. The most subtle reasoning could never recall souls blinded by manifold darknesses of error and stained by the deepest filth of the body, unless the supreme God, through a kind of popular clemency, bent and lowered the authority of divine understanding all the way to the human body itself. Souls, awakened not only by his teachings but also by his actions, could then return to themselves and look back toward their homeland [Col. 0957], even without engaging in disputations.

## CHAPTER XX  
### Conclusion of the work.

43. This is what I have meanwhile persuaded myself about the Academics, plausibly and as best I could. If it is false, that does not concern me, since it is enough for me now not to believe that truth cannot be found by a human being.

But whoever thinks that this was the Academics’ opinion should listen to Cicero himself. He says that they had the habit of concealing their opinion and were accustomed to reveal it to no one except someone who had lived with them into old age [Note: So according to three manuscripts: “who had lived with them”—plural.]. What that opinion was, God knows; nevertheless, I think it was Plato’s.

But so that you may understand my entire purpose briefly: whatever the nature of human wisdom may be, I see that I have not yet attained it. Yet although I am now entering my thirty-third year [Note: He was thirty-three when he placed the final touch on this work. He had begun writing it before completing his thirty-second year, since he himself says in *Retractations* I.2 that he wrote the work on the Blessed Life “not after the books Against the Academics, but among them,” on the occasion of his birthday, which fell on November 13, as he testifies in the preface to *The Blessed Life*.], I do not think that I ought to despair of attaining it someday.

Despising all the other things that mortals consider good, I have resolved to devote myself to investigating this. Since the Academics’ arguments had seriously frightened me away from this undertaking, I think I have now sufficiently fortified myself against them through this discussion.

No one doubts that we are driven to learn by a double force: authority and reason. For my part, I am certain never to depart from the authority of Christ, for I find none stronger. As for what must be pursued through the most subtle reasoning—for I am now so disposed that I impatiently desire to grasp what is true not only by believing but also by understanding—I trust that, for the time being, I shall find among the Platonists whatever does not conflict with our sacred teachings.

[Col. 0958] 44. When they saw that I had brought the conversation to an end, although it was already night and something had even been written by lamplight, the young men nevertheless waited most intently to see whether Alypius would promise to answer on another day.

Then he said: “I am prepared to affirm that nothing has ever turned out so much according to my wishes as the fact that I am leaving today’s discussion defeated. Nor do I think this joy ought to belong to me alone. I shall share it with you, then, my opponents—or our judges. Perhaps the Academics themselves wished, in this way, to be defeated by their descendants.

“For what could appear or be displayed to us more pleasing than the charm of this conversation, more weighty than the seriousness of its arguments, more ready than its benevolence, or more learned than its instruction? I simply cannot admire enough how harsh matters were handled with such wit, desperate matters with such courage, matters conclusively established with such moderation, and obscure matters with such clarity.

“So now, my companions, turn the expectation with which you were urging me to answer toward learning with me, and do so with surer hope. We have a guide who, with God now showing the way, can lead us into the very secrets of truth.”

45. When they displayed on their faces a kind of childish disappointment because Alypius did not seem likely to answer, I said, smiling: “Are you jealous of my praises? But since I am now confident of Alypius’s steadfastness and fear nothing from him, I shall equip you also to thank me, by arming you against the man who has frustrated so great an eagerness on your part to hear his answer.

“Read the Academics; and when you find Cicero there victorious—what could be easier?—over these trifles [*Retractations* I.1.4], compel this man to defend our present conversation against those unconquered arguments.

“This is the harsh payment I return to you, Alypius, for my false praise.”

When they had smiled at this, we brought so great a conflict to an end—whether it was truly concluded I do not know—more modestly, and sooner than I had expected.

[Col. 0957]

# ST. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO  
## ONE BOOK ON THE BLESSED LIFE

[Note: Notice of the Benedictine Fathers. The text has been corrected from manuscript codices: three Sorbonne manuscripts; the manuscripts of Saint-Victor, Sainte-Geneviève, Saint-Michel, Thuaneus, Casalinus, Arnuensis, Cisterciensis, Vedastinus, Regius, and Regiomontanus; two from the library of the College of Navarre; one from the library of the larger Augustinian convent in Paris; from the variant readings extracted by the Louvain editors from four Belgian manuscripts; and from the editions of Basel, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]  
[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.] (C)

## NOTICE OF THE FOLLOWING BOOK, ON THE BLESSED LIFE

[Note: See Book I, chapter 2, of the *Retractations*, column 588, from the words “The book On the Blessed Life” through the words “the harbor of philosophy.”]

Here we present the book *On the Blessed Life*. It was undertaken after the work *Against the Academics* had already been begun and then temporarily set aside, and it was completed at Cassiciacum through a discussion continued over three days.

Since Augustine says that he found the occasion for publishing it when his birthday returned on the Ides of November—on which day he was entering the thirty-third year of his life—it must be entirely certain that both works, this one *On the Blessed Life* and the other *Against the Academics*, were composed toward the end of the Christian year 386, a year distinguished by his conversion.

For these discussions on the blessed life, which he presented as something like a festive and solemn banquet, he wished all his table companions to be present, especially his mother Monnica, who carried those present away in admiration by the weight and wisdom of her opinions. Augustine even exclaimed: “You have truly grasped, mother, the citadel of philosophy.”

He dedicated this book to Theodore, whose companionship he had enjoyed at Milan, as can be understood sufficiently from the preface. The man whose first name, Manlius, he indicates in the *Retractation* does not seem to be different from the one he mentions in *The City of God* XVIII.54: namely, the man who held the consulship in the year 399 and honorably performed other distinguished offices under various emperors. For this reason Claudian greatly commends him in the poem published as a panegyric on his consulship.

## [DISCUSSIONS]

[Col. 0959] This book contains three days of discussions dedicated to Theodore. The matter ultimately reaches the conclusion that the blessed life consists in nothing other than perfect knowledge of God.

# CHAPTER I  
## Preface. He dedicates the book to Theodore and explains by what winds, as it were, he was driven toward the harbor of Christian philosophy. The occasion of the discussion.

[Col. 0959]

1. If a course guided by reason, and the will itself, were to lead one to the harbor from which one proceeds toward the region and land of the blessed life, most humane and distinguished Theodore, I do not know whether I would be rash to say that far fewer people would reach it than do now—even though, as we see, those who reach it are still exceedingly rare and few.

For when either God, or nature, or necessity, or our own will, or some combination of these, or all of them together—for the matter is very obscure, but you have already undertaken to illuminate it—has cast us, as it were, blindly and randomly into this world as into a stormy sea, who would know what he ought to strive toward or by what route he should return, unless at some point a storm, which seems adverse to fools, should drive even the unwilling and resisting into the most desired land, although they do not know or intend it?

2. Among the human beings whom philosophy can receive, I seem to discern three kinds, as it were, of sailors.

The first consists of those who, as soon as they reach the age of rational judgment, flee from the shore with a small stroke and push of the oars, and conceal themselves in that tranquility from which they raise for the rest of their fellow citizens, as far as they can, a brilliant sign of some work of their own, so that, warned by it, they may strive to come to them.

The second kind is the opposite. Deceived by the deceptive appearance of the sea, they have chosen to advance into the open waters and dare to travel far from their homeland, often forgetting it. If, in some unknown and excessively hidden way, a wind from the stern follows them—a wind they think favorable—they are carried aloft and rejoicing into the deepest misery, because the utterly deceptive calm of pleasures and honors flatters them on every side.

What else can be wished for such people except that some adversity arise in the very things by which they are tossed about and received? And if that is insufficient, may a raging storm and a contrary wind drive them, even weeping and groaning, toward certain and solid joys [Col. 0960] [Note: Five manuscripts read: “a wind that crushes them and leads them to solid joys.”]

Most of this kind, however, have not yet wandered too far and are brought back by certain troubles that are not especially severe. These are the people whom either the tearful tragedies of their fortunes or the anxious difficulties of empty occupations—as though they had nothing else to do—have thrust into the books of the wisest and most learned men. In a certain sense they awaken in the very harbor, from which none of the promises of that sea, smiling with excessive deceit, can exclude them.

There is also a third kind among these: those who, either at the very threshold of adolescence or after having long and greatly been tossed about, nevertheless look back toward certain signs and remember, even amid the waves, their exceedingly sweet homeland. Either they return to it by a direct course, deceived in nothing and delaying nowhere; or, more often, wandering amid the clouds, gazing at stars that are sinking, or captured by certain enticements and postponing the time of a good voyage, they wander longer and often endanger themselves.

These too are often driven by some disaster amid their shifting fortunes—as though by a storm adverse to their efforts—into their most desired and tranquil homeland [Note: So in several manuscripts. The Louvain edition and other codices read: “into the most desired blessed life.”]

3. But before all these people who are traveling by whatever route toward the region of the blessed life, immediately before the harbor, stands one enormous mountain. It generates great difficulties even for those who are entering and must be feared with the utmost intensity and avoided with the greatest care.

For it shines so brightly and is clothed in that deceptive light in such a way that it offers itself not only to those who have arrived but have not yet entered, as a place to inhabit, promising to satisfy their desires in place of the blessed land itself; it also frequently invites people from the harbor itself to come to it and sometimes holds them captive, delighted by its height, from which they may enjoy looking down upon the others.

Yet these people often warn those who are approaching not to be deceived by hidden reefs beneath the surface, nor to think it easy to climb up to them; and, because of the nearness of that land, they teach them with great kindness how to enter without danger. Thus, while they begrudge them their empty glory, they point out a place of safety.

For what other mountain should reason understand as feared by those approaching or entering philosophy than the proud pursuit [Col. 0961] of utterly empty glory? It has nothing inward that is full or solid, and therefore, while inflated men walk over it, its fragile ground crackles beneath them, sinking and swallowing them. Once rolled back into darkness, it snatches from them the luminous dwelling they had almost seen.

4. Since this is so, my Theodore—for in seeking what I desire, I look to you alone, and I have always admired you as especially suitable—receive, I say, both which of those three kinds of men has given me to you, the place in which I seem to stand, and the sort of help I confidently expect from you.

From my nineteenth year onward, after I had received at the school of a rhetorician that book of Cicero called the *Hortensius*, I was kindled by such a great love of philosophy that I immediately planned to devote myself to it.

But clouds were not lacking to confuse my course, and for a long time, I confess, I looked up at sinking stars by which I was being led into error. A certain childish superstition frightened me away from the inquiry itself. Then, when I had become more upright, I scattered that darkness and persuaded myself that one ought to believe teachers rather than commanders.

I fell in with people who thought that the light visible to the eyes should be counted among the highest and divine things to be worshiped [Note: The Manichaeans; *Confessions* III.6]. I did not assent to them, but I thought that they concealed beneath those coverings something great which they would eventually reveal.

But after I escaped from them and had crossed that sea, the Academics for a long time held my rudders amid the waves, resisting every wind. Then I came to these lands; here I learned the north by which I should steer.

For I noticed, both often in the words of our priest [Note: Ambrose; *Confessions* VI.3.4] and sometimes in your discussions, that whenever God was being considered, nothing corporeal should be imagined at all—and the same was true when the soul was considered, since it is the one thing among created realities nearest to God.

But, I confess, I was prevented from flying quickly into the lap of philosophy by the allurements of a wife and of honor. I thought that once I had obtained these, I could at last—an opportunity granted to only a few fortunate people—be carried with all sails and every oar into that harbor and rest there.

After reading a few books of Plato [Note: Five manuscripts read: “After reading a few books of Plotinus,”]—for I have learned that you are especially devoted to him—and comparing them, as far as I could, with the authority of those who have handed down the divine mysteries, I was so inflamed that I wanted to cut all those anchors, had not the opinion of certain people disturbed me (*Confessions* VII.9, 20).

What else, then, remained except that, while I lingered among superfluous things, the storm thought adverse should come to my aid? Thus so great a pain seized my heart that, unable to bear the burden of the profession by which I was perhaps sailing toward the Sirens, I cast everything aside and brought my battered and split vessel into the tranquility I desired.

5. Therefore you see the philosophy in which I am sailing as in a harbor. But even this harbor is broad, and although its great size makes it less dangerous, it does not wholly exclude error. For I simply do not know to which part of the land—which is certainly one and blessed [Col. 0962] [Note: So thirteen manuscripts, together with the Basel and Amerbach editions and Erasmus. The Louvain text instead prefers: “which is the blessed life.”]—I should bring myself close and make contact.

For what solid ground have I grasped, while the question of the soul still trembles and fluctuates for me? Therefore I beg you, by your virtue, your humanity, and the bond and exchange between souls, to extend your right hand.

This means that you should love me, and believe that you in turn are loved and cherished by me. If I obtain this, I shall very easily approach the blessed life itself, to which I presume you already cling, with little effort.

But what I am doing, and in what way I am gathering my friends into this harbor, so that you may know, and so that you may understand more fully the beginning of my discussions [Note: Erasmus and Louvain omit the particle “and,” which is found in Basel, Amerbach, and the manuscripts. Shortly afterward, all editions have “by which I may show myself to you, or so that you may understand more fully the sea of my discussions”; several manuscripts support this. Other codices, and not a few, read “so that you may understand,” and some of these have “the sequence of my discussions.” The Cistercian manuscript reads “the burden of my discussions.” Finally, the codex of Saint-Arnulf of Metz reads “the beginning of my discussions,” which seemed the best reading. In fact, this book was the first of all those produced through discussion at Cassiciacum to be completed, and because of its subject it is not improperly said to have “become more religious,” that is, to have emerged in a more religious form. The verb is used in this sense in *Against the Academics* II.7; and it was more worthy of Theodore’s name.]—and because I could find no other signs by which to display my soul to you—I have thought that I should write to you and dedicate it to you under your own name.

This is entirely appropriate, since we have discussed the blessed life among ourselves, and I see nothing else that should more properly be called a gift of God.

I am not frightened by your eloquence. Whatever I love, even if I do not attain it, I cannot fear. And I am much less frightened by the exalted position of your fortune. For with you, although it is great, it is truly secondary; indeed, it makes those over whom it rules secondary as well.

But now, please attend to what I am about to bring forward.

6. It was my birthday, on the Ides of November. After a luncheon so light that none of our intellectual powers would be impeded by it, I invited all those who dined together—not merely on that day, but every day—to go to the baths and sit down there, for the place happened to be private and suitable for the occasion. They were, although I do not hesitate meanwhile to identify them by name to your singular kindness, first of all my mother [Note: [Col. 0962] Monnica.], to whose merits I believe I owe my whole life; my brother Navigius; Trygetius and Licentius, my fellow citizens and pupils; and my cousins Lastidianus [Note: [Col. 0962] Nearly all manuscripts read *Bartidianum*.] and Rusticus. Although they had never endured even a grammar lesson, I did not wish them to be absent, and I thought their common sense itself necessary for the undertaking I was preparing. Also with us was the youngest of them all, but one whose talent, if my affection does not deceive me, promises something great: my son Adeodatus. When they had taken their seats, I began as follows.

## CHAPTER II.—Discussion of the First Day

*We consist of soul and body. Food is necessary for the body. The soul too has its own food. He is not happy who does not possess what he wants. Yet not everyone who possesses what he wants is happy. What a person must acquire in order to be happy. Who possesses God. An Academic cannot be happy, and therefore cannot be wise.*

[Col. 0963]

### 7

“Does it seem clear to you that we are composed of soul and body?”

When everyone agreed, Navigius replied that he did not know.

“Do you mean,” I said, “that you know absolutely nothing, or is this simply one of the things you do not know?”

“I do not think I know nothing at all,” he said.

“Can you tell us something that you do know?”

“I can.”

“If it is not troublesome,” I said, “tell us something.”

When he hesitated, I asked, “Do you at least know that you are alive?”

“I know that,” he said.

“Then you know that you possess life, since no one can live except by life.”

“I know that too,” he said.

“Do you also know that you have a body?”

He agreed.

“Then you already know that you consist of body and life.”

“For the moment I know that; but I am uncertain whether these are the only things.”

“Then you do not doubt,” I said, “that there are these two things, body and soul; but you are uncertain whether there is something else that contributes to completing and perfecting a human being.”

“That is so,” he said.

“What that might be,” I said, “we shall investigate another time, if possible. For now I ask all of you: since we all admit that a human being cannot exist without body or without soul, for the sake of which of these do we desire food?”

“For the body,” Licentius said.

The others, however, hesitated and discussed among themselves in various ways how food could seem necessary for the body when it was desired for the sake of life, while life belonged exclusively to the soul.

Then I said: “Does it seem to you that food belongs to that part which we see grow and become stronger through food?”

They all agreed except Trygetius.

“Why, then,” he said, “did I not grow in proportion to my appetite?”

“All bodies,” I replied, “have a limit fixed for them by nature, beyond which they cannot advance. Yet they would be smaller if they lacked nourishment; this is more readily observed in animals. No one doubts that, when food is withdrawn, the bodies of all living creatures waste away.”

“They waste away,” Licentius objected, “not grow smaller.”

“That is sufficient for my purpose,” I said. “The question is whether food belongs to the body. It does, since when it is withdrawn the body is reduced to emaciation.”

Everyone agreed that this was so.

### 8

“What, then, of the soul?” I asked. “Does it have no nourishment of its own? Or does knowledge seem to you to be its food?”

“Certainly,” my mother said. “I believe the soul is nourished by nothing other than the understanding and knowledge of things.”

When Trygetius showed uncertainty about this opinion, she said: “Did you not yourself teach today where or from what the soul is nourished? After part of the meal, you said that you had not noticed what sort of vessel we were using, because you had been thinking about something else; yet you had not withdrawn your hands or bites from that portion of the food. Where, then, was your mind at the time when, while you were eating, it was not attending to the vessel? Believe me, the mind is nourished by such banquets as these—that is, by its own theories and thoughts—if through them it is able to apprehend anything.”

When they murmured uncertainly about this, I said: “Do you not agree that the minds of highly educated people are, in their own kind, much fuller and greater than those of the unlearned?”

They said that this was obvious.

“Then we rightly say that the minds of those who have been instructed in no disciplines and have absorbed none of the liberal arts are empty and, as it were, hungry.”

“I think their minds too are full,” Trygetius said, “but full of vices and wickedness.”

“That very thing,” I said, “believe me, is a kind of barrenness and, as it were, hunger of the soul. Just as a body deprived of food is usually filled with diseases and scabs, which reveal the defects resulting from hunger, so the minds of such people are full of diseases by which they confess their own fasting. Indeed, the ancients wished wickedness itself—the mother of all vices—to have been named from *nequidquam*, ‘to no purpose,’ that is, from the fact that it is nothing. The virtue opposed to this vice is called frugality. Thus, just as *frugality* is named from *frux*, ‘fruit,’ on account of a certain fertility of the soul, so *nequitia* is named from barrenness, that is, from nothingness. For everything that flows, dissolves, melts, and is, as it were, always perishing, is nothing. That is why we also call such people ‘lost.’ But something exists if it remains, is stable, and is always of the same character—as virtue is. A large and most beautiful part of virtue is called temperance and frugality. But if this is too obscure for you to see already, surely you concede that, if the minds of the unlearned are themselves full, then, just as there are two kinds of nourishment for bodies, so there are two kinds of nourishment for souls: one healthy and beneficial, the other diseased and destructive.”

### 9

“Since this is so,” I said, “on my birthday, given that we agree that there are two things in a human being—body and soul—I ought to provide not merely a somewhat more sumptuous luncheon for our bodies, but also one for our souls. If you are hungry, I shall bring out what this meal is. For if I try to feed you against your will, while you are reluctant and have no appetite, I shall labor in vain. Rather, we should pray that you may desire such fare more than bodily food. That will happen if your souls are healthy; for sick people, as we see in bodily illnesses, refuse and spurn their food.”

By their very expressions and by their unanimous voices, they all declared that they wanted to consume and devour whatever I had prepared.

### 10

Then I began again: “We want to be happy, do we not?”

I had scarcely said this when they all agreed with one voice.

“Does it seem to you,” I asked, “that someone is happy who does not possess what he wants?”

They denied it.

“What, then? Is everyone who possesses what he wants happy?”

Then my mother said: “If he wants and possesses good things, he is happy; but if he wants evil things, he is miserable even if he possesses them.”

Smiling and showing my delight, I said: “You have captured the very citadel of philosophy, mother. Without doubt, you lacked the words to express yourself as Cicero has done, although you have unfolded the same thought. In the *Hortensius*, the book he composed in praise and defense of philosophy, he says:

> ‘But behold: all those who are not philosophers, yet are ready to argue, say that all who live as they wish are happy. That is false. For to wish for what ought not to be wished is itself the greatest misery. Nor is it as miserable not to obtain what you wish as to wish to obtain what you ought not to wish for. A perverse will brings more evil than fortune brings good to anyone.’

As she uttered these words, she exclaimed in such a way that, completely forgetting her sex, we imagined some great man sitting among us. Meanwhile, as far as I was able, I understood from what source and from how divine a fountain her words flowed.”

“But you must tell us,” Licentius said, “what a person ought to want in order to be happy, and what things he ought to desire.”

“Invite me on your birthday,” I replied, “whenever you please, and whatever you set before me I shall gladly consume. On that condition I ask you to feast at my table today, and not demand something that perhaps has not been prepared.”

When he became embarrassed by his modest and respectful reminder, I said: “Then do we agree on this: that no one can be happy who does not possess what he wants, but that not everyone who possesses what he wants is happy?”

They agreed.

### 11

“Do you also concede,” I asked, “that everyone who is not happy is miserable?”

They did not hesitate.

“Then everyone who does not possess what he wants is miserable.”

Everyone approved.

“What, then,” I asked, “must a person acquire in order to be happy? Perhaps this too will be supplied at our present banquet, so that Licentius’s appetite is not neglected. For, in my opinion, he must acquire what he possesses whenever he wants it.”

They said that this was obvious.

“Then,” I said, “it must be something that always remains, that does not hang upon fortune, and that is not subject to any accidents. For whatever is mortal and perishable cannot be possessed by us whenever we wish and for as long as we wish.”

Everyone agreed.

“But there are many fortunate people,” Trygetius said, “who possess in abundance and lavishly, for the purposes of this life, those very things that are fragile and subject to accidents, yet find them pleasant, and lack none of the things they want.”

“Whoever is afraid,” I replied, “does he seem happy to you?”

“He does not,” he said.

“Then if someone can lose what he loves, can he fail to be afraid?”

“He cannot.”

“But those things dependent on fortune can be lost. Therefore someone who loves and possesses them cannot in any way be happy.”

No one objected.

At this point my mother said: “Even if he is confident that he will not lose all those things, he still cannot be satisfied by them.”

“Then he is also miserable,” I said, “because he is always in need.”

“What if someone,” she replied, “abounding and overflowing with all these things, sets a limit to his desires and enjoys them contentedly, decently, and pleasantly? Does he not seem happy to you?”

“Then he is happy,” she said, “not because of those things, but because of the moderation of his soul.”

“Excellent,” I said. “No other answer was required by this question, nor could any other answer have come from you. Therefore we have no doubt that, if someone decides to be happy, he must acquire what always remains and cannot be snatched away by any violence of fortune.”

“We agreed to that long ago,” Trygetius said.

“Does God seem to you to be eternal and always abiding?”

“Certainly,” Licentius replied. “That is so certain that it requires no question.”

All the others joined in with pious devotion.

“Then the person who possesses God is happy.”

### 12

They accepted this with great pleasure and rejoicing.

“Then,” I said, “I believe that we now have nothing left to investigate except which human beings possess God, since that person will certainly be happy. What do you think about this?”

Licentius said: “The person who lives well possesses God.”

Trygetius said: [Col. 0966] “The person who does what God wants to be done possesses God.”

Lastidianus agreed with him.

But the youngest boy of all, Adeodatus, said: “The person who does not have an unclean spirit possesses God.”

My mother approved all these answers, but especially this one. Navigius remained silent. When I asked his opinion, he replied that he favored the last answer. I also thought that Rusticus should not be neglected, and asked what his opinion was on so great a matter. He seemed to me to be kept silent less by deliberation than by shyness; he agreed with Trygetius.

### 13

Then I said: “I have before me everyone’s opinions on a truly important matter, beyond which nothing need be asked or can be discovered—provided that we investigate it, as we have begun, with complete serenity and sincerity. Since today this would take too long, and since even souls have a kind of luxury in their banquets if they rush upon them excessively and greedily—for they digest them badly in that way, and their mental health must be feared no less than from that very hunger—it would be better, if you agree, for this question to receive us tomorrow, when we are hungry.

“For now I want you to nibble willingly at something that has suddenly occurred to me and has suggested itself to your server as something to be brought out. If I am not mistaken, it is the sort of thing usually served last, as though prepared and seasoned with a scholar’s honey.”

When they heard this, they all stretched themselves forward as though toward a raised platter and urged me to hurry and say what it was.

“What do you think,” I asked, “except that the whole undertaking we have begun has been completed against the Academics?”

When the name was mentioned, the three who knew what I meant straightened up more eagerly. As though extending their hands, as people do, they helped the serving attendant who was bringing the dish forward, showing by every means available that they could hear nothing more delightful.

### 14

I then presented the matter as follows:

“If it is clear,” I said, “from what reason demonstrated a little earlier, that someone who does not possess what he wants is not happy; and if no one seeks what he does not want to find, while those people—the Academics—are always seeking truth, then they want to find it. Therefore they want to possess the discovery of truth. But they do not find it [Note: [Col. 0966] Erasmus, Venetian edition, Lovaniensis: ‘and they do not find it.’ Manuscript M omits the second clause.]; it follows that they do not possess what they want, and from this it also follows that they are not happy. But no one is wise unless he is happy. Therefore an Academic is not wise.”

At this, as though seizing the whole argument, they suddenly cried out together.

But Licentius, paying closer and more cautious attention, feared assenting and added: “I did seize it along with you, since I exclaimed, moved by that conclusion. But I shall not admit anything from it into my stomach; I shall reserve my portion for Alypius. Either he will lick it up with me, or he will warn me why I ought not to touch it.”

“Navigius,” I said, “with his diseased spleen ought to fear sweet things more.”

He smiled and said: “Such things will certainly cure me. I do not know how this twisted and prickly thing you have set before us is, as the saying has it, like Hymettian honey: sharply sweet and not at all bloating to the stomach. Therefore, although it has somewhat irritated my palate, I shall pass the whole thing into my inmost marrow as gladly as I can. For I do not see how this conclusion can be refuted.”

“It cannot be refuted at all,” Trygetius said. “That is why I rejoice that I have long been at enmity with them. [Col. 0967] For, driven by I know not what nature—or, to speak more truly, by God—even though I did not know how they could be refuted, I nevertheless opposed them intensely.”

### 15

“I have not yet abandoned them,” Licentius said.

“Then you disagree with us?” Trygetius asked.

“Do you disagree with Alypius?” Licentius replied.

I said: “I have no doubt that, if Alypius were present, he would yield to this little argument. He could not think so absurdly as to suppose either that the man was happy who did not possess that great good of the soul which he most ardently wished to possess, or that the Academics did not want to find the truth, or that someone who is not happy could be wise. For these three things—like honey, grain, and nuts—make up what you are afraid to taste.”

“He would yield to this little childish treat,” Licentius said, “after abandoning the Academics’ great abundance, which, pouring over this little morsel, would either bury it or drag it away?”

“As though we were looking for something lengthy,” I replied, “especially against Alypius. His own bodily condition could have shown well enough that these little things are very strong and useful. But you, who have chosen to depend on the authority of someone absent, which of these points do you reject? That someone who does not possess what he wants is not happy? Or do you deny that the Academics want to possess the truth they seek so intensely? Or does it seem to you that someone can be wise without being happy?”

“Of course the person who does not possess what he wants is happy,” he said, smiling as though irritated.

When I ordered this to be written down, he exclaimed: “I did not say that.”

When I nodded again for it to be written, he said: “I did say it.”

I had already ordered that no word be uttered unless it was committed to writing. Thus I kept the young man caught between embarrassment and determination.

### 16

But while we joked with him in these words, as though inviting him to eat his portion, I noticed that the others, who did not understand the whole matter but wanted to know what was taking place so pleasantly among us alone, were watching us without laughing. They seemed to me exactly like those who, when dining among the greediest and most rapacious guests, either refrain from snatching food because of their dignity or are held back by modesty.

Since I had invited them, and since at that banquet I was playing the part of a great man—or, to explain myself fully, of a host inviting genuine human beings—I could not endure the inequality and imbalance of our table, and it disturbed me [Note: [Col. 0967] Eleven manuscripts read: “You taught me to endure being the host at that banquet; it disturbed me.” Two others come close to this reading, having: “I was enduring, taught; it disturbed me.” Perhaps Theodorus had taught him what sort of matters should be handled with less educated people in conversations of this kind. This may be inferred from *On Order*, Book 1, chapter 11.].

I smiled at my mother. She, ordering most freely that whatever they lacked should be brought out as though from her own storeroom, said: “Now tell us, and explain who these Academics are and what they want.”

I explained the matter briefly and clearly, so that none of them departed without understanding it.

“These people,” she said, “are epileptics”—the common term used among us for those whom the disease of epilepsy knocks down.

With that she rose to leave, and we all departed happy and laughing after bringing the discussion to an end.

## CHAPTER III.—Discussion of the Second Day

*Who possesses God in such a way as to be happy. “Unclean spirit” is customarily used in two senses.*

[Col. 0968]

### 17

The next day, when we had again sat down in the same place after luncheon, though somewhat later than the day before, I said: “You have come late to the banquet. I do not think this happened because of indigestion, but because you felt secure on account of the small number of dishes: you did not think it necessary to attack them very early, since you thought you would soon be surfeited. There could hardly be many leftovers, when on a day and occasion of such solemnity so little had been found. Perhaps you are right. But I too do not know what has been prepared for you. There is another who never ceases to provide food for all—and especially such banquets—for everyone [Note: [Col. 0968] Erasmus reads *qui omnibus*, ‘who provides for all,’ or ‘who provides common things for all’; Lovaniensis reads *cum omnes*, ‘when all.’]. We usually abstain from eating either through weakness, satiety, or business. Yesterday, unless I am mistaken, we agreed among ourselves with pious and firm conviction that this provider, remaining within human beings, makes them happy.

“For when reason had demonstrated that the person who possesses God is happy, and none of you had opposed that judgment, we asked who, in your opinion, possesses God. If I remember correctly, three opinions were given. Some thought that the person who does what God wills possesses God. Others said that the person who lives well possesses God. To the rest, God seemed to be in those who do not have the spirit called unclean.”

### 18

“But perhaps you all meant one and the same thing in different words. For if we consider the first two opinions, everyone who lives well does what God wills, and everyone who does what God wills lives well; indeed, living well is nothing other than doing what pleases God—unless any of you thinks otherwise.”

They agreed.

“But the third opinion must be considered somewhat more carefully, because, as I understand it, in the ritual of the most chaste sacred rites, ‘unclean spirit’ [Note: [Col. 0968] Earlier editions read: “Because, in the ritual of the most chaste sacred rites and spirits, the unclean spirit …” This is less satisfactory, as is sufficiently clear from the context that follows and from the manuscripts we follow. Here the phrase ‘most chaste sacred rites’ commends the sacraments of initiation.] is customarily used in two senses. It may mean the spirit that attacks the soul from outside, disturbs the senses, and inflicts a kind of madness upon human beings; those in charge of expelling it are said to lay hands upon or exorcise it—that is, to drive it out by adjuring it through divine things. But ‘unclean spirit’ may also mean every unclean soul, that is, a soul polluted by vices and errors.

“Therefore I ask you, boy—who perhaps expressed that opinion with a somewhat clearer and purer spirit—which person seems to you not to have an unclean spirit: the one who does not have the demon by which deranged people become mad, or the one who has cleansed his soul from all vices and sins?”

“It seems to me,” he said, “that the person who lives chastely does not have an unclean spirit.”

“But whom do you call chaste?” I asked. “Someone who commits no sin, or someone who merely abstains from unlawful intercourse?”

“How can someone be chaste,” he replied, [Col. 0969] “who abstains only from unlawful intercourse while he does not cease to defile himself with other sins? The truly chaste person is the one who keeps his attention on God and clings to him alone.”

When I decided that the boy’s words should be written down exactly as he had spoken them, I said: “Then he must live well; and whoever lives well is necessarily such a person—unless you think otherwise.”

He agreed with the others.

“Then,” I said, “one and the same opinion has been expressed here.”

### 19

“But I ask you this for a little while: Does God want a human being to seek God?”

They agreed.

“Again I ask: Can we say that someone who seeks God is living badly?”

“Absolutely not,” they said.

“Answer this third question as well: Can an unclean spirit seek God?”

They denied it, though Navigius hesitated somewhat; afterward he yielded to the voices of the others [Note: [Col. 0969] Four manuscripts read: “he yielded to their expressions.”].

“If, then,” I said, “the person who seeks God does what God wills, lives well, and does not have an unclean spirit; but the person who seeks God does not yet possess God, then we must not immediately believe that everyone who lives well, or does what God wills, or does not have an unclean spirit possesses God.”

At this the others laughed at having been deceived by their own concessions. My mother, who had remained stunned for a long time, asked me to explain and loosen the very point I had stated in such a tightly argued conclusion.

When I had done so, she said: “But no one can reach God unless he has sought God.”

“Excellent,” I said. “Yet whoever is still seeking has not reached God, even if he lives well. Therefore not everyone who lives well possesses God.”

“It seems to me,” she said, “that no one does not possess God; but the person who lives well has him favorably disposed, while the person who lives badly has him hostile.”

“Then,” I said, “yesterday we wrongly agreed that the person who possesses God is happy, since everyone possesses God, yet not everyone is happy.”

“Then add ‘favorably disposed,’” she said.

### 20

“At least we agree on this much,” I said: “that the person who has God favorably disposed toward him is happy?”
