“I should like to agree,” Navigius said, “but I am afraid of the person who is still seeking, especially lest you conclude that the Academic is happy—the man whom yesterday’s discussion called *caducarius*, a vulgar and grammatically poor word, but, as it seems to me, a highly suitable one.

“For I cannot say that God is hostile to someone who is seeking God. If that is an impious thing to say, then God will be favorably disposed toward him; and whoever has God favorably disposed toward him is happy. Therefore the person who is seeking will be happy. But everyone who is seeking does not yet possess what he wants. Thus a person will be happy who does not possess what he wants, which yesterday seemed absurd to all of us; and from this we believed that the darkness surrounding the Academics had been dispelled.

“Accordingly Licentius will now triumph over us, and will prudently remind me that those sweet things which I rashly accepted against my health exact this penalty from me, like a wise physician.”

### 21

At this even my mother smiled.

“I, Trygetius,” he said, “do not grant that God is immediately hostile to anyone toward whom he is not favorably disposed; I think there is something intermediate.”

I said: “Do you nevertheless grant that this intermediate person, toward whom God is neither favorably disposed nor hostile, possesses God in some way?”

He hesitated.

“It is one thing,” my mother said, “to possess God, and another not to be without God.”

“Which, then,” I asked, “is better: to possess God, or not to be without God?”

“As far as I can understand,” she said, “this is my view: the person who lives well possesses God, but has him favorably disposed; the person who lives badly possesses God, but has him hostile. The person who is still seeking and has not yet found him possesses neither a favorably disposed nor a hostile God, but is not without God.”

“Is this also your opinion?” I asked the others.

They said that it was.

“Tell me, please,” I said: “Does it not seem to you that God is favorably disposed toward someone whom he favors?”

They admitted that he was.

“Then,” I said, “does God not favor a person who is seeking him?”

“He does,” they replied.

“Therefore the person who seeks God possesses God favorably disposed toward him; and everyone who possesses God favorably disposed toward him is happy. Therefore the person who is seeking is also happy. But the person who is seeking does not yet possess what he wants. Therefore a person will be happy who does not possess what he wants.”

“Absolutely,” my mother said, “it does not seem to me that someone who does not possess what he wants is happy.”

“Then,” I said, “not everyone who possesses God favorably disposed toward him is happy.”

“If reason requires this,” she replied, “I cannot deny it.”

“Then,” I said, “the distinction will be this: everyone who has already found God possesses God favorably disposed toward him and is happy; everyone who seeks God possesses God favorably disposed toward him but is not yet happy; and whoever alienates himself from God through vices and sins is not only not happy, but does not even live with God favorably disposed toward him.”

### 22

When everyone approved this, I said: “Very well. But I am still afraid that you may be troubled by what we conceded earlier: that everyone who is not happy is miserable. It would follow that the person who possesses God favorably disposed toward him is miserable, since we have said that the person who is still seeking God is not yet happy.

“Or, as Cicero says, do we call the owners of many estates in this world rich, while we call the possessors of every virtue poor? But consider whether, just as it is true that everyone who is in need is miserable, it is also true that everyone who is miserable is in need. For then it will be true that misery is nothing other than need—something you noticed me praising when it was said.

“It would take too long to investigate this today. Therefore I ask you not to find it tedious to meet again at this table tomorrow.”

When they all said that they would do so with the greatest pleasure, we rose.

## CHAPTER IV.—Discussion of the Third Day

*The question proposed the day before must be discussed. Everyone who is in need is miserable. The wise person, moreover, is in need of nothing. Whether everyone who is miserable is in need. The soul’s need. The soul’s fullness. Who, finally, is happy.*

### 23

The third day of our discussion dispersed the morning clouds that had forced us into the baths and made the afternoon sky perfectly clear. We therefore decided to go down to a nearby little meadow. After we had all sat wherever it seemed convenient, the rest of the conversation proceeded as follows.

“I have and retain,” I said, “nearly everything I wanted you to concede when I questioned you. Therefore today, when we can finally separate this banquet of ours by an interval of days, there will be, I think, either nothing or very little that you need to answer me. My mother had said that misery was nothing other than need, and we agreed among ourselves that everyone who is in need is miserable. But whether everyone who is miserable is also in need remains a question, which we were unable to resolve yesterday.

“If reason demonstrates that this is so, then we shall have found perfectly who is happy: it will be the person who is not in need. For everyone who is not miserable is happy. Therefore the person who is free from need is happy, if it is established that the need of which we are speaking is the same thing as misery.”

### 24

“What prevents this conclusion already?” Trygetius asked. “Since it is clear that everyone who is in need is miserable, cannot we conclude that everyone who is not in need is happy? I remember that we conceded that there is nothing intermediate between misery and happiness.”

“Do you think there is something intermediate between being dead and being alive?” I asked. “Is every human being not either alive or dead?”

“I admit that there is nothing intermediate here either. But what has that to do with the matter?”

“Because,” I replied, “I believe you also admit that everyone who was buried a year ago is dead.”

He did not deny it.

“What, then? Is everyone who was not buried a year ago alive?”

“No,” he said; “that does not follow.”

“Then,” I said, “it does not follow that, if everyone who is in need is miserable, everyone who is not in need is happy, although no intermediate state can be found between misery and happiness, just as none can be found between life and death.”

### 25

When some of them understood this somewhat slowly, I explained and worked it out in whatever words I could adapt to their understanding.

“Then,” I said, “no one doubts that everyone who is in need is miserable. Nor are we troubled by certain things necessary for the bodies of wise people. The soul itself, in which the happy life resides, has no need of them. For the soul is perfect; but nothing perfect is in need of anything. It will take whatever appears necessary for the body if it is available; if it is not available, the lack of such things will not break it.

“For every wise person is brave; but no brave person fears anything. Therefore the wise person does not fear bodily death or the pains whose removal, avoidance, or postponement requires those things whose absence may occur. Yet he does not cease to use them well if they are not absent.

“For that saying is completely true:

> For what you can avoid,  
> it is foolish to admit.  
> *(Terence, Eunuchus, Act 4, Scene 6)*

“Therefore he will avoid death and pain as far as he can and as far as is proper. Otherwise, if he fails to avoid them when he could have done so, he will be miserable not because these things happen to him, but because, though he could have avoided them, he was unwilling to do so. That is an obvious sign of folly. Thus the person who does not avoid them will be miserable not because he suffers such things, but because of his folly.

“But if he is unable to avoid them, although he has diligently and properly tried to do so, their assault will not make him miserable. For this saying of the same comic poet is no less true:

> Since what you wish cannot happen,  
> wish for what can.  
> *(Terence, Andria, Act 2, Scene 1)*

“How can someone be miserable to whom nothing happens contrary to his will?”

“Because,” I replied, “he cannot wish for what he sees cannot happen to him. He possesses a will directed toward the most certain things [Col. 0972]—namely, that whatever he does, he should do only according to the prescription of virtue and the divine law of wisdom. These cannot in any way be taken away from him.”

### 26

“Now consider whether everyone who is miserable is also in need. The difficulty in conceding this opinion is created by the fact that many people are established in great abundance of things dependent on fortune, and everything is so readily available to them that whatever desire demands is present at their command.

“That, to be sure, is a difficult life. But let us suppose someone such as Cicero says Orata was. Who could easily say that Orata suffered from need—a man of the greatest wealth, most agreeable circumstances, and greatest luxury, who lacked nothing for pleasure, social favor, or good and sound health? He abounded as much as he pleased in highly profitable estates and most congenial friends, and used all these things most suitably for the health of his body. In short, his whole way of life and every desire were attended by continuous success.

“Perhaps one of you will object that he wanted to possess more than he had. We do not know that. But, for the purposes of the question, let us suppose that he desired nothing more than what he possessed. Does he seem to you to have been in need?”

“Even if I grant,” Licentius said, “that he desired nothing—for I do not know how to accept that in a person who was not wise—he was nevertheless afraid, since he was, as they say, a man of no poor intelligence, that all those possessions might be snatched from him by a single hostile turn of fortune. It was not difficult to understand that all such things, however great they might be, were subject to chance.”

Then, smiling, I said: “You see, Licentius, that this most fortunate man was prevented from enjoying the happy life by the very goodness of his intelligence. For the sharper he was, the more clearly he saw that he could lose all those things; and the fear by which he was weakened confirmed that familiar saying: ‘A distrustful man is prudent to his own harm.’”

### 27

When both he and the others had smiled, I said: “Let us nevertheless consider the matter more carefully. Although this man was afraid, he was not in need; hence the question. To be in need consists in not possessing something, not in fearing to lose what one possesses.

“This man was miserable because he was afraid, although he was not in need. Therefore not everyone who is miserable is in need.”

My mother herself approved this, along with the others, though she remained somewhat uncertain, since it was her opinion that I was defending.

“Yet I do not know,” she said, “and I do not fully understand how misery can be separated from need, or need from misery. This man was rich and wealthy, and, as you say, desired nothing more; nevertheless, because he feared losing what he had, he was in need of wisdom. If he had been in need of silver and money, would we call him needy, but if he was in need of wisdom, would we not?

“When everyone cried out in amazement at this, and I myself was exceptionally eager and delighted that she had said precisely what I had prepared to produce as a major point from the books of the philosophers, I said:

“Do you see that one thing is possessing many different kinds of learning, and another is having a soul wholly attentive to God? For from where do these remarkable insights proceed, if not from there?”

[Col. 0973]

Then Licentius, exclaiming joyfully, said: “Nothing truer, nothing more divine, could have been said. For there is no greater or more pitiable need than to be in need of wisdom; and whoever is not in need of wisdom can be in need of nothing at all.”

28. “Therefore,” I said, “the poverty of the soul is nothing other than folly. For this is contrary to wisdom, and so contrary that it is like death to life, like misery to blessedness—without any intermediate state. For just as every person who is not blessed is miserable, and every person who is not dead is alive, so it is clear that everyone who is not foolish is wise. From this we may now also see that Sergius Orata was miserable not merely because he feared losing those gifts of fortune, but because he was foolish. Indeed, he would have been more miserable if, while those things he considered good were so precarious and unstable, he had feared nothing at all. He would have been secure not through the vigilance of courage but through the drowsiness of his mind, and would have been miserable, sunk in a deeper folly.

“But if everyone who lacks wisdom suffers great poverty, while everyone who possesses wisdom lacks nothing, it follows that folly is poverty. And just as every foolish person is miserable, so every miserable person is foolish. Therefore, just as all poverty is misery, so all misery is proved to be poverty.”

29. When Trygetius said that he understood this conclusion only imperfectly, I said: “What, then, do we agree about rationally between us?”

“He is poor,” he replied, “who does not possess wisdom.”

“What, then, is it to be poor?”

“Not to possess wisdom.”

“What is it not to possess wisdom?”

When he fell silent, I said: “Is this not to possess folly?”

“Yes.”

“Therefore, to possess poverty is nothing other than to possess folly; and from this it is now necessary that poverty be called by another name, since folly is being named. Yet I do not know how we should say, ‘He possesses poverty’ or ‘He possesses folly.’ It is like saying that a place lacking light possesses darkness, which is nothing other than not possessing light. Darkness does not, as it were, come or go; rather, to lack light is itself to be dark, just as to lack clothing is to be naked. For nakedness does not flee because some movable thing, clothing, approaches. Thus we say that someone possesses poverty as though we said that he possesses nakedness. Poverty, then, is a word signifying not possessing. Therefore, to explain what I mean as best I can, one says, ‘He possesses poverty,’ as though one said, ‘He possesses not possessing.’

“Accordingly, if it has been shown that folly itself is true and certain poverty, see now whether the question we had undertaken has been resolved. We were uncertain whether, when we called something misery, we were naming anything other than poverty. We have given a reason why folly is rightly called poverty. Therefore, just as every foolish person is miserable and every miserable person is foolish, so we must acknowledge not only that everyone who is poor is miserable, but also that everyone who is miserable is poor.

“But if from the fact that every foolish person is miserable and every miserable person is foolish it follows that folly is misery, why should we not likewise conclude, from the fact that everyone who is poor is miserable and everyone who is miserable is poor, that misery is nothing other than poverty?”

[Col. 0974]

30. When everyone acknowledged that this was so, I said: “It now follows that we should see who does not suffer poverty; for he will be wise and blessed. Poverty, however, is folly, and the word ‘poverty’ usually signifies a certain barrenness and lack.

“Attend, I ask, more deeply to how carefully the men of old—whether they created all words or merely those whose origin is evident—formed words especially for things whose knowledge was most necessary. You now concede that every foolish person is poor and everyone who is poor is foolish. I think you will also concede that a foolish soul is vicious, and that all the vices of the soul are included under the single name ‘folly.’

“On the first day of our discussion, we said that *nequitia* (‘wickedness’) was so called from the fact that it is nothing, while the contrary, *frugalitas* (‘frugality’), was named from *frux* (‘fruit’). Thus, in these two contraries—frugality and wickedness—two things appear prominent: being and not being.

“What, then, do we think is contrary to the poverty under discussion?”

When they hesitated for a while, Trygetius said: “If I say ‘wealth,’ I see that poverty is its contrary.”

“It is indeed closely related,” I said. “For poverty and want are commonly understood as one and the same. Yet another word must be found, so that the better side may not lack a single designation, while the side represented by poverty and want has an abundance of names and only the word ‘wealth’ is opposed to it. Nothing could be more absurd than for there to be a poverty of vocabulary where the contrary of poverty is concerned.”

“Fulness,” said Licentius, “if it may be said so, seems to me rightly opposed to poverty.”

31. “Later, perhaps, we shall investigate the word more carefully. In the inquiry into truth this is not the point that must concern us. Although Sallust, a most discerning judge of words, opposed *opulentia* (‘abundance’) to poverty (Sallust, *The War against Catiline*), I accept this *plenitudo* (‘fulness’). We shall not here be troubled by fear of grammarians [Note: [Col. 0974] Thus the manuscripts. Earlier printed editions, however, have: ‘For here too we shall not be free from fear of grammarians.’], nor need we fear their correction because we use words carelessly, since they have given us their possessions for our use [Note: [Col. 0974] He subtly indicates the benefit conferred by the modest grammarians.].”

When they smiled, I continued: “Since I have resolved not to disregard your minds, when you are intent upon God, as though they were certain oracles, let us see what this word means; for I think no word is more suitable to the truth.

“Fulness and poverty, then, are contraries. Here too, as in wickedness and frugality, those two things appear: being and not being. And if poverty is folly, fulness will be wisdom.

“Many have rightly called frugality the mother of all the virtues. In agreement with them, Tully also says in a public speech: ‘Let each person understand it as he wishes; nevertheless, I judge frugality—that is, moderation and self-restraint—to be the greatest virtue’ (*Speech for Deiotarus*). He spoke with complete learning and propriety. For he considered *frux*, that is, what we call being, to which not-being is contrary. But because of the common usage of speech, in which frugality is usually understood almost as thrift, he clarified what he meant by the two words that follow, adding ‘moderation’ [Col. 0975] and ‘self-restraint.’ Let us attend more carefully to these two words.”

32. “*Modestia* (‘moderation’) is plainly derived from *modus* (‘measure’), and *temperantia* (‘self-restraint’) from *temperies* (‘due proportion’). Where there is measure and due proportion, there is neither more nor less. This, therefore, is the fulness that we had set contrary to poverty, and much better than if we had posited abundance. For in abundance there is understood an outpouring, as it were, of something overflowing excessively. When this exceeds what is sufficient, measure is still lacking; and a thing that is excessive itself needs measure. Thus poverty is not wholly foreign even to excess; but both more and less are foreign to measure.

“If you examine abundance itself, you will find that it contains nothing other than measure. For *opulentia* is derived only from *ops* (‘help’ or ‘resources’). But how can what is excessive provide help, when it is often more troublesome than too little? Whatever is either too little or too much, because it needs measure, is subject to poverty.

“Therefore measure in the soul is wisdom. Wisdom, which is contrary to folly, is not denied; folly is poverty; and fulness is contrary to poverty. Wisdom, therefore, is fulness. In fulness there is measure. Therefore the measure of the soul is in wisdom.

“Hence that celebrated saying is rightly and deservedly made famous as the first useful principle in life:

> Let nothing be in excess.  
> (Terence, *Andria*, act 1, scene 1.)

33. “At the beginning of today’s discussion we had said that, if we discovered misery to be nothing other than poverty, we would acknowledge as blessed the person who did not suffer poverty. We have discovered this. Therefore to be blessed is nothing other than not to suffer poverty—that is, to be wise.

“If you ask what wisdom is—for reason has itself, as far as it could at present, unfolded and drawn this out—it is nothing other than the measure of the soul; that is, the way in which the soul balances itself so that it neither rushes into excess nor is confined below what is full.

“It rushes into extravagance, domination, arrogance, and other things of this kind, by which the unrestrained and miserable imagine that joys and powers are acquired for themselves. It is confined by sordidness, fears, grief, desire, and whatever else causes even miserable people to confess that human beings are miserable.

“But when the soul contemplates the wisdom it has found, and, to use this boy’s expression, holds fast to it; when it does not turn, moved by any vanity, toward the deceitfulness of images, whose weight it embraces and by which it is accustomed to fall and sink away from its God; then it fears neither immoderation—and therefore neither poverty—nor, consequently, misery. Whoever is blessed, therefore, possesses his measure, that is, wisdom.”

34. “What wisdom should be named except the Wisdom of God? We have also received by divine authority that the Son of God is nothing other than the Wisdom of God (1 Cor. 1:24); and the Son of God is certainly God. Therefore whoever is blessed possesses God—a point on which we all agreed earlier, when we entered this banquet.

“But what do you think wisdom is, unless it is truth? For this too has been said: ‘I am the Truth’ (John 14:6). Truth comes to be through some supreme measure, from which it proceeds and toward which it turns in perfection. No other measure is imposed upon the supreme measure; for if the supreme measure is measure through the supreme measure, it is measure through itself.

“Yet the supreme measure must also be the true measure. Just as truth is generated by measure, so measure is known through truth. Therefore neither truth ever existed without measure, nor measure without truth.

“What is the Son of God? It has been said: Truth. Who is the one who has no father, except the supreme measure? Whoever, therefore, comes through truth to the supreme measure is blessed. This is to possess God in the soul, that is, to enjoy God. For although all other things are received from God, they do not possess God.”

35. “A certain admonition that acts within us—urging us to remember God, to seek him, and, once every weariness has been driven away, to thirst for him—flows from the very fountain of truth to us. That hidden sun pours its radiance into our inner eyes. From it comes everything true that we say, even when we still hesitate, with eyes either not yet sound or suddenly opened, boldly to turn and gaze upon the whole of it. And this too appears to be nothing other than God, perfect, with no degeneration hindering him. For there everything is wholly and completely perfect, and at the same time God is almighty.

“Yet, as long as we are seeking, let us acknowledge that we have not yet been satisfied by the fountain itself, or, to use that word, by fulness; we have not yet reached our own measure. Therefore, although God is already helping us, we are not yet wise and blessed.

“That is the complete satiety of souls; this is the blessed life: to know devoutly and perfectly from whom you are led into truth, what truth you enjoy, and through what means you are joined to the supreme measure [Note: [Col. 0976] Lov. has: ‘by what truth you enjoy, through what means you are joined to the supreme good.’ But the other editions and the manuscripts more aptly agree with us in reading: ‘by what truth ... to the supreme measure.’]. These three, for those who understand one God and one substance, excluding the vanities of varied superstition, reveal one God.”

Here his mother, recognizing words that were deeply fixed in her memory, and as though awakening into her faith, joyfully recited that verse of our bishop:

> Foster those who pray, O Trinity,  
> (Ambrose, hymn, “God, Creator of All”)

and added: “This is unquestionably the blessed life, which is perfect life. We should confidently expect that, hastening toward it, we can be brought there by solid faith [Note: [Col. 0976] This should unquestionably be read thus, in agreement with the manuscripts and all the older editions—Basel, Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Cologne edition of 1529. It should not be read ‘by faith alone,’ as in Lov., evidently through an error, since the words that follow are added continuously: ‘with joyful hope and burning love.’], with joyful hope and burning love.”

36. “Therefore,” I said, “since measure itself admonishes us to separate this banquet by an interval of several days, I give as many thanks as I can, according to my strength, to the supreme and true God the Father, Lord and liberator of souls; and then to you, who were invited in harmony and have further heaped many gifts upon me. For you contributed so much to our conversation that I cannot deny that I have been satisfied by my guests.”

At this everyone rejoiced and praised God.

“How I wish,” said Trygetius, “that you would feed us in this way every day.”

“Measure,” I replied, “must everywhere be observed and everywhere loved, if our return to God is dear to you.”

After these words, bringing the discussion to an end, we departed.

[Col. 0977]

SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: TWO BOOKS ON ORDER [Note: [Col. 0977] Written toward the end of the year 386.] [Note: [Col. 0979] The present books of *On Order* have been collated with manuscripts nearly a thousand years old, namely the Theoderican and Corbie manuscripts; with the Vatican, Vedastine, two Thuane manuscripts, the Regiomontanus, Albinensis, Michaelinus, Arnulfensis, one from the monastery of Vendôme, one from the College of Navarre, and one from the College of the Reverend Fathers of the Bernardines in Paris; with the readings of four Belgian manuscripts cited by Lov.; and with the editions of Basel, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 0979] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.] (C)

INTRODUCTORY NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING TWO BOOKS ON ORDER. [Note: [Col. 0977] See book 1, chapter 3, of the *Retractations*, cols. 588–589, from the words ‘At that time,’ no. 1, through the words of no. 3, ‘the order of things,’ Zenobi. M.]

Augustine undertook to publish a work *On Order* at the urging of Zenobius. He recalls this man’s friendship and his great goodwill toward himself and his household in book 1, chapter 7, where he says that previously he had been unable to satisfy Zenobius, who questioned him extensively and profoundly about this subject, since not only the difficulty of the matter but also the pressure of time prevented him. But when his friend pressed him strongly not to delay any longer and challenged him in verse to give a fuller response, Augustine had to comply.

He therefore began to devote himself to writing these books at Cassiciacum toward the end of the year 386. He completed the first book before Alypius had returned from Milan. Alypius had gone there on 13 November, while the work against the Academics had already begun, and returned in time to take part both in completing the two later books of that work and in composing another book, *On Order*. The latter occasionally cites the book *On the Blessed Life* and also praises a passage from book 3 of *Against the Academics*. From this we understand that the second book of *On Order* was completed after those works.

The subject of both books is presented in the *Retractation* appended here. In the first book, the most notable passage is that in which Augustine restrains those impulses of rivalry and empty boasting by which young men devoted to literature are commonly agitated. In the second book, various questions arise from the definition and nature of order. Since the difficulty of the subject exceeded the capacity of the interlocutors, Augustine thought it appropriate to teach the proper order of study. Accordingly, he first discusses the proper formation of character and then the acquisition of the liberal disciplines, relying upon whose assistance the soul may finally be raised to apprehend higher things.

BOOK ONE. It presents two discussions. The first teaches that absolutely all things, both good and evil, are contained within the order of divine providence. The second touches somewhat upon the excellence and meaning of order. On this occasion Augustine severely censures the disordered movements of the soul and the quarrels of his pupils undertaken for the sake of childish glory; and he declares that Monica should by no means be excluded from philosophical discussion on account of her sex.

[Col. 0977]

[Col. 0977] PREFACE.

CHAPTER ONE.—ALL THINGS ARE GOVERNED BY DIVINE PROVIDENCE.

1. “To perceive or explain the order of things, Zenobius—the order proper to each thing and especially that of the universe by which this world is restrained and governed—is exceedingly difficult and exceedingly rare among human beings. Moreover, even if someone is capable of this, he is not necessarily able to find an auditor worthy of such divine and obscure matters, whether by merit of life or by some form of education.

“Yet nothing is sought more eagerly by the finest minds, and no subject do those who look upon the reefs and storms of this life with their heads raised as far as possible desire more to hear and learn, than how it comes about both that God cares for human affairs and that such great perversity is spread everywhere throughout human affairs that it seems attributable neither to divine administration nor even to the management of any servant, had such power been granted him.

“For this reason, those concerned with such questions are almost compelled to accept one of two conclusions: either divine providence does not extend to these lowest and most insignificant things, or else all evils are committed by God’s will. Both are impious, but the latter more so. For although believing that anything has been abandoned by God is both extremely ignorant and extremely dangerous to the soul, nevertheless, among human beings no one has accused another of being unable to do something; whereas the charge of negligence is much more readily excused than that of wickedness and cruelty.

“Thus reason seems compelled, without forgetting piety, to hold either that these earthly things cannot be administered by divine things, or that they are neglected and despised rather than governed in such a way that every complaint against God is gentle and blameless.”

2. “But who is so blind in mind as to hesitate to attribute to the governance and moderation of divine power anything of rational order in the movements of bodies that lies beyond human arrangement and will [Note: [Col. 0979] Here ten manuscripts omit *rationis* (‘of reason’); but a little later they read, ‘to the reason, power, and moderation of God.’]? Unless perhaps we are prepared to say either that the limbs of even the tiniest animals are formed by chance with such fixed and subtle proportion; or that, when someone denies that a thing happened by chance, he can acknowledge it as done only by reason; or that, throughout the whole of nature, we dare to remove from the secret judgment of the divine majesty, by any trifling opinion, what we marvel to see ordered in each individual thing without the activity of human art.

“Yet this very point makes the question more pressing: the limbs of a flea are arranged and distinguished with astonishing order, while human life meanwhile turns and fluctuates amid the instability of innumerable disturbances.

“But suppose someone’s sight were so limited that, on a mosaic pavement, he could take in no more than the size of a single tile. He would criticize the artist as ignorant of order and composition because he thought the variety of the stones disordered, since he could not see all those pieces at once, joined together and illuminated into the form of a single beauty.

“Nothing else happens to the less educated among human beings. Unable with their feeble minds to grasp and contemplate the universal fitting-together and harmony of things, they are offended by something and, because it is large in relation to their own thought, suppose that some great ugliness inheres in reality.”

3. “The chief cause of this error is that the human being is unknown to himself. Yet, in order to know himself, he greatly needs the habit of withdrawing from the senses (1 *Retractations* 3.2) and gathering the soul into itself and keeping it within itself. Only those achieve this who either burn away the wounds of opinion inflicted by the course of daily life through solitude, or heal them through the liberal disciplines.”

CHAPTER TWO.—HE DEDICATES THIS WORK TO ZENOBIUS.

“For once the soul has been restored to itself, it understands the beauty of the universe, which certainly derives its name from the One. Therefore the soul that proceeds into multiplicity and eagerly pursues poverty cannot see that beauty, since it does not know that poverty can be avoided only by separating itself from multiplicity.

“By multiplicity I do not mean human beings, but everything touched by the senses. Nor should you wonder that the soul suffers poverty more in proportion as it desires to embrace more things. For just as, in a circle of any size, there is one center toward which all things converge—the point that geometers call the center [Note: [Col. 0980] Most manuscripts read: ‘which mathematicians call the center.’]—and although the whole circumference may be divided into innumerable parts, there is nevertheless nothing besides that one point by which all the others are equally measured and which, as though by a law of equality, dominates them all; but if you wish to move outward in any direction, everything is lost in proportion as you proceed into multiplicity: so the soul, poured out from itself, is shattered by a kind of immensity and worn down by genuine poverty, since its nature compels it to seek the One everywhere, while multiplicity does not allow it to find him.

4. “You will certainly grasp, my Zenobius, both what these things I have said are like, what cause gives rise to the error of souls, how all things coincide in one and are perfect, and yet why sins must be avoided. For I know your character: a soul that loves beauty in every form, without the immoderation and sordidness of desire.

“This sign in you of future wisdom divine law prescribes against destructive desires, so that you may not abandon your own cause, enticed by false pleasures. Nothing more disgraceful or dangerous than such a betrayal can be found.

“Believe me, you will grasp these things when you have devoted yourself to education, by which the soul is cleansed and cultivated, though before then it is in no way fit to receive the divine seeds.

“These books, I think, will sufficiently teach you what the whole matter is like, what order it demands, what reason promises to the studious and good, what sort of life we, your dearest friends, are living, and what fruit we gather from our liberal leisure. They are sweeter to us because they bear your name than because of our own labor, especially if you are willing to insert and fit yourself into the very order about which I am writing to you, choosing better things.”

5. “When a stomach illness forced me to leave the school—although, as you know, even without any such necessity I was already trying to take refuge in philosophy—I immediately withdrew to the estate of our closest friend Verecundus. What need I say, when he was pleased to have me there? You know very well the man’s extraordinary goodwill toward everyone, and especially toward us.

“There we discussed among ourselves whatever seemed useful, with a stylus naturally employed to record everything, since I saw that this benefited my health. For because I was occupied with some care in speaking, no excessive contention crept into our discussions. At the same time, if we wished to commit anything of ours to writing, there would be neither the necessity of speaking otherwise nor the labor of recollection.

“Alypius, my brother Navigius, and Licentius—who had suddenly become remarkably devoted to poetry—were engaged in these activities with me. Trygetius had also been restored to us by military service; like a veteran, he had become enamored of history. And we had already committed a considerable amount to books.”

[Col. 0981] FIRST DISCUSSION.

CHAPTER THREE.—THE OCCASION OF THE DISCUSSION.

6. “But one night, when I had awakened as usual and was silently turning over in my mind things that I do not know from where were coming to me—for my love of discovering truth had by then become habitual, so that whenever such concerns occupied me I would remain awake for the first part of the night, or certainly the last, and usually about half the night in all, thinking about whatever arose—I did not allow myself to be distracted from myself by the young men’s nocturnal studies. They were already occupied throughout the whole day to such an extent that it seemed too much for them to devote even part of the night to the labor of study. They had also been instructed by me to do something with themselves beyond their books and to become accustomed to making the soul dwell within itself.

“As I said, I was awake. Suddenly, the sound of the water flowing behind the bathhouse came to my ears and drew my attention more closely than usual. It seemed very strange to me that the same water now made a louder, now a softer, noise as it rushed over the stones. I began to ask myself what the cause might be. I confess that nothing occurred to me.

“Then Licentius, striking the wooden object beside his bed to frighten away troublesome mice, announced in this way that he was awake. I said to him: ‘Licentius, have you noticed—for I see that your Muse has lit a lamp for you to study by [1 *Retractations* 3.2]—how this channel produces an irregular sound?’

“‘This is not new to me,’ he replied. ‘Once, awakened by a desire for clear weather, I brought my ear close to it so that I might know whether rain was approaching, and this water was doing then what it is doing now.’

“Trygetius approved. He too had been lying awake in his bed in the same room, though we did not know it; for it was dark, something that in Italy is almost unavoidable even for people with money.

7. “When I saw, therefore, that our school—however large it was, since Alypius and Navigius had gone into the city—was not asleep even at those hours, and when the course of the water prompted me to say something about it, I asked: ‘What do you think is the reason that this sound alternates in this way? We do not suppose that at these hours anyone is repeatedly interrupting that channel either by passing through it or by washing something.’

“‘What do you think,’ said Licentius, ‘except that somewhere some sort of leaves—which fall abundantly and continuously throughout autumn—have been forced together in the narrowness of the channel and at some point are pushed aside and give way; then, when the water that had been pressing against them has passed through, they gather and pack together again? Or perhaps some other shifting arrangement of floating leaves is taking place, which similarly serves now to restrain, now to release, the flow?’

“Since I had no other explanation, this seemed plausible to me. I confessed that, though I had searched for a long time to discover why it was so, I had found nothing, and I praised his ingenuity.”

8. “After a brief silence I said: ‘No wonder you found nothing astonishing and were keeping yourself inwardly with Calliope.’

“‘No wonder,’ he replied; ‘but just now you have given me great cause for wonder.’

“‘What is that?’ I asked.

“‘That you were surprised at this.’

“‘What else,’ I said, ‘usually gives rise to wonder, or what is the mother of this failing [ibid.], except an unusual event that occurs beyond the evident order of causes?’

“‘I accept “beyond the evident order,”’ he replied, ‘but nothing seems to me to happen beyond order.’”

Here I became more hopeful and livelier than usual, since I was asking these young men to produce something significant that the mind of a youth had conceived so suddenly, almost yesterday turning toward these matters, with no question about them having previously been discussed among us.

“‘Good, good,’ I said, ‘but entirely and exceedingly good: you have understood much and dared much. Believe me, at a great distance you surpass Helicon, toward whose summit you strive to reach as though it were heaven. But I should very much like you to remain with this opinion, for I am going to try to undermine it.’

“‘Let me be myself for now, I beg you,’ he replied, ‘for I have focused my mind very intensely on something else.’

“Here I began to fear that, wholly overcome by his devotion to poetry, he might be carried far away from philosophy. I said: ‘I am provoked by you to attack those verses of yours, singing and howling them in every kind of meter; they are trying to raise between you and truth a wall more monstrous than the one between your lovers. Yet those lovers themselves were breathing through even the smallest crack. For at that time he had begun to sing of Pyramus.’”

9. “When I had said this in a harsher voice than he expected, he fell silent for a while. I had now abandoned what I had begun and returned to myself, lest I foolishly try to occupy someone already preoccupied.

“Then he said:

“‘By my own judgment I am miserable, like a mouse. Terence could not have put it more aptly than I can now speak of myself. Yet that final point may perhaps be turned to the contrary. For where he says:

> Today I am lost,  
> (*The Eunuch*, act 5, scene 6),

I may perhaps be found today.

“‘If you do not disdain what superstitious people are accustomed to divine from mice, then, if by my noise I have warned that mouse or little mouse which revealed to you that I was awake—if it has any sense—to return to its hole and rest there with itself, why should I not be warned by the noise of your voice to philosophize rather than sing? For that, as I have begun to believe from your daily insistence, is our true and unshakable dwelling place.

“‘Therefore, if it is not troublesome to you and you think it should be done, ask whatever you wish. I shall defend, as far as I can, the order of things, and shall assert that nothing can happen outside order. I have absorbed and drunk in such a great conviction of it that, even if someone defeats me in this discussion, I shall attribute that too not to anyone’s rashness but to the order of things. For it will not be the truth itself that is defeated, but Licentius.’”

CHAPTER FOUR.—NOTHING HAPPENS WITHOUT A CAUSE.

10. “I was once again delighted that he had returned to us. Then I said to Trygetius: ‘What do you think?’

“‘I am strongly in favor of order,’ he replied, ‘but I am nevertheless uncertain and want so great a matter examined with the utmost care.’

“‘Then let that part have your support,’ I said [Note: [Col. 0982] The printed editions have: ‘Let that wall, then, have your support.’ Incorrectly; for Trygetius is being assigned the task of undertaking the defense of order on his side.], ‘for your uncertainty, I think, is shared by Licentius and me.’

“‘Absolutely,’ said Licentius. ‘I am certain of this opinion. Why should I hesitate to tear down the wall you mentioned before it has fully raised itself? Poetry cannot turn me away from philosophy as much as distrust of discovering the truth can.’

“Then Trygetius, with words of delight, said: ‘We now have something even greater: Licentius is no Academic. He used to defend them most zealously.’

“‘Please leave that aside for now,’ he replied, ‘lest this clever and captious remark divert and tear me away from some divine reality that has begun to display itself to me, and toward which I hang in longing.’

“Seeing my joys overflow much more abundantly than I had ever dared hope, I enthusiastically recited this verse:

> Thus may that Father of the gods, thus high Apollo,  
> Grant that you begin:  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.874–875)

“For he himself will lead us through if we follow where he commands us to go, and where he gives us a place to set our seat, he who now gives the oracle and slips into our souls (ibid. 3.88–89).

“For high Apollo is not the one who, in caves, mountains, and groves, stirred by the odor of incense and the slaughter of animals, fills madmen; there is another, certainly another, that high and truthful one—and what need have I to evade the word?—Truth itself. Its prophets are all who are able to be wise.

“Therefore, Licentius, let us undertake this task, trusting in piety as worshipers, and let us extinguish beneath our footsteps the destructive fire of smoky desires.”

11. “Now question me, I beg you,” he said, “if I can explain this great something-or-other both in your words and in my own.”

“Answer me this first,” I said, “why it seems to you that this water flows in this way not randomly but according to order. The fact that it runs over those wooden channels and is led to serve our needs can pertain to order. For human beings, using reason, arranged it so that by the same route they could both drink and wash, and its arrangement naturally followed the suitability of the locations.

“But as for the leaves, which, as you say, fell in such a way that the phenomenon we wondered at occurred: by what order of things shall we think this happened, and not rather by chance?”

“As though,” he replied, “anyone who looks calmly at the fact that nothing can happen without a cause could think that they ought or could have fallen otherwise than they did! Shall I now trace the position of the trees and branches themselves, the weight that nature imposed upon the leaves, the mobility of the air by which they fly, its softness by which they descend, and their various falls according to the condition of the sky, their weight, their shapes, and countless other causes, still more obscure? These things are hidden from our senses—profoundly hidden. Yet the point sufficient for the question we have undertaken [Note: [Col. 0983] In the manuscript of St Arnulf at Metz, the reading is ‘for the rustic question’; perhaps more aptly.] somehow does not remain hidden from the mind: nothing happens without a cause.

“An irritating questioner may continue to ask what the cause was for trees to be planted there. I will answer that human beings followed the fertility of the soil. What if the trees are fruitless and grew up by chance? Here too I will answer that we see too little; for nature, which produced them, is by no means random.

“What more is there to say? Either show me that something happens without a cause, or believe that nothing happens except according to a definite order of causes.”

[Note: [Col. 0983] Most manuscripts read, ‘May God grant.’ Then some have, ‘Thus high Jesus.’]

CHAPTER FIVE.—GOD ADMINISTERS ALL THINGS IN ORDER.

[Col. 0984]

12. I said to him: “You may call me an irritating questioner—for I can scarcely avoid being one, since I prevented you from conversing with Pyramus and Thisbe—but I shall nevertheless continue to question you.

“This nature that you wish to appear ordered: for what purpose, to say nothing of innumerable other things, did it produce these very trees that bear no fruit?”

While he was considering what to say, Trygetius remarked: “Are the uses of shrubs for human beings found only in their fruits? How many other uses there are for their shade, their wood, and finally their very branches and leaves!”

“Please,” he replied, “do not answer these questions for him. Innumerable things can be brought forward that offer human beings no benefit, or whose benefit is so hidden or so slight that human beings—especially people like us—cannot draw it out or defend it. Let him teach us instead how anything can happen without a cause preceding it.”

“We shall examine those points later,” I said. “For I no longer need to be the teacher, since you, who have already declared yourself certain about so great a matter, have still taught me nothing, though I am exceedingly eager to learn and for this very reason remain awake day and night.”

13. “Where are you sending me?” he said. “Is it because I follow you more lightly than these leaves follow the winds, by which they are thrown into the flowing water, so that falling is not enough for them unless they are also dragged along? For what else will happen when he instructs Licentius and Augustine, and teaches the things that belong to the very midst of philosophy?”

“Please,” I replied, “do not either abase yourself so greatly or exalt me. I too am a child in philosophy, and when I ask questions I am not overly concerned about who answers me through him who receives me daily as a complainer—I believe, indeed, that you will someday become his prophet; and perhaps that ‘someday’ is not far off. Yet others too, even those greatly removed from studies of this kind, can teach something when they are constrained, as though by the bonds of questioning, to join the company of disputants. But to teach something is not to teach nothing. Do you not see—for I shall gladly use an example like your own—that those very leaves which are carried by the winds and float upon the waves resist the rushing river to some extent, and remind human beings of the order of things, if what you are defending is true?”

14. At this he leapt up from his couch, overcome with joy, and said: “Who could deny, great God, that you administer all things in order? How closely everything holds together! How firmly successive events press onward into their own knots! How many and how great things have happened so that we might speak these words! How many are happening so that we might find you! For from where else does this very fact flow and proceed, unless from the order of things: that we awoke, that you noticed that sound, that you asked yourself for its cause, and that you did not find the cause of such a trifling matter? A mouse too comes forth, so that I may be revealed to be awake.

“Finally, even your own speech—though you perhaps did not make it do this, for no one has power over what comes into his mind—is somehow turned about so as to teach me what I ought to answer you. For, I ask you, if these things said by us should travel somewhat farther into public knowledge in writing, as you have undertaken, would not the matter appear so great that, if someone had been consulted about it, some great prophet or Chaldean ought to have answered long before it happened? And if he had answered, he would have been called divine and extolled with such universal praise that no one would nevertheless have dared ask him why a leaf had fallen from a tree, or whether a wandering mouse had troubled a man lying down.

“Did any of those men ever say such future events either on his own account, or was he ever compelled by a consulter to say them? Yet if he were to announce that some future book of no little distinction would appear, and saw that it would necessarily come to pass—for otherwise he could not prophesy—then surely whatever the fluttering of leaves does in the field, whatever the most insignificant little creature does in the house, is as necessary within the order of things as those writings. For it is through these words that things come to be which, without those preceding trifling events, could neither have entered the mind nor proceeded from the mouth nor been entrusted to posterity.

“Therefore, I beg you, let no one now ask me why each thing happens. It is enough that nothing happens and nothing is generated without some cause having generated and moved it.”

## CHAPTER VI.—The Order Encompasses Everything

15. “Here,” I replied, “it is evident that you do not know, young man, how many things, and by what sort of men, have been said against divination. But answer me now—not whether anything happens without a cause, for I already see that you are unwilling to answer that—but whether this order you have undertaken seems to you to be something good or something evil.”

Muttering, he replied: “You did not ask in such a way that I can answer one of the two. I see here a kind of middle position. For order seems to me neither good nor evil.”

“What, then, do you think is contrary to order, at least?”

“Nothing,” he said. “For how can anything be contrary to that which has occupied everything and possessed everything? Whatever is contrary to order must necessarily be outside order. But I see that nothing is outside order. Therefore, we ought to think that nothing is contrary to order.”

“Then,” said Trygetius, “error is not contrary to order?”

“Not at all,” he replied. “For I see no one erring without a cause. The series of causes, however, is encompassed by order. Error itself is not only generated by a cause, but also generates something of which it is the cause. Therefore, since nothing is outside order, it cannot be contrary to order.”

16. When Trygetius had fallen silent, and I myself could scarcely contain my joy—for I saw that the young son of my dearest friend was becoming my own as well, and not merely that, but was already rising and growing into a friend to me, although I had despaired of his interest even in ordinary literature, and now, as though he had looked back upon his own possession [Note: [Col. 0985] Lov. reads *despecta possessione*, “with his possession despised”; all other printed and manuscript codices read *respecta*, “with his possession looked back upon.”], was rushing with all his force into the midst of philosophy—I silently marveled and was inflamed with congratulation. Suddenly, as though seized by some inspiration, he exclaimed:

“O if only I could say what I want to say! Please—where, where are you, words? Come to my aid. Both good and evil are within the order.”

## CHAPTER VII.—God Does Not Love Evil, Although Evil Belongs to the Order

17. “Believe me, if you wish; for I do not know how to explain it.”

I marveled and remained silent. But when Trygetius saw that the man had become approachable [Col. 0986] and had returned to conversation, as though his intoxication had somewhat subsided, he said:

“It seems absurd to me, Licentius, and entirely contrary to the truth, what you are saying. But please allow me a little time, and do not disturb me by shouting.”

“Say what you wish,” he replied. “For I fear that you will not carry me away from what I see and almost grasp.”

“Would that you were not straying from the order you defend, nor carried away by such great carelessness toward God—to put it mildly. For what could be called more impious than to say that even evils are contained within the order? Certainly God loves order.”

“He truly loves it,” Licentius replied. “It flows from him and is with him. And if anything more fitting can be said about so lofty a matter, consider it yourself, I beg you. For I am not capable of teaching you these things now.”

“What am I to consider?” Trygetius asked.

“I accept exactly what you are saying,” he replied, “and what I understand is enough for me. Certainly you said both that evils are contained within the order and that the order itself flows from the supreme God and is loved by him. From this it follows that evils too come from the supreme God, and that God loves evils.”

18. At this conclusion I became afraid for Licentius. But he, groaning under the difficulty of finding words and considering how to bring forth what ought to be answered, said:

“God does not love evils; and for no other reason than that it is not part of the order for God to love evils. He therefore loves the order greatly because through it he does not love evils.

“But how can the evils themselves not be within the order, when God does not love them? For this is precisely the order of evils: that they are not loved by God. Does it seem to you a small order of things that God loves good things and does not love evil things? Thus evils that God does not love are not outside the order, and yet he loves the order itself. For he loves this very arrangement: to love good things and not to love evil things. This is a great order and a divine disposition.

“Because this order and disposition preserves the harmony of the universe through its very distinction, it follows that evils too must necessarily exist. Thus, as though by means of antitheses—or, in a way, contraries—which is also pleasing to us in speech, the beauty of all things together is shaped.”

19. After this he paused for a little while. Then suddenly, raising himself up toward the couch where Trygetius lay, he said:

“For I ask you, please: Is God just?”

The other remained silent, struck and horrified—as he later reported—by the discourse of his fellow student and companion, inspired by a new breath. While he was silent, Licentius continued:

“For if you answer that God is not just, you must consider what you are doing, since just a little earlier you accused me of impiety. But if, as tradition teaches us, and as we perceive from the necessity of that very order, God is just, then he is certainly just by distributing to each person what is his due. But what distribution can be spoken of where there is no distinction? Or what distinction is there if everything is good? And what can be found outside the order if, through God’s justice, each person receives what is his according to the merits of good and evil? We all acknowledge that God is just. Everything, therefore, is enclosed within the order.”

Having said this, he sprang from his couch. Since no one offered him a word, he now spoke in a gentler voice:

“Do you not answer me at all—even you who compelled me to say these things?”

20. “A strange new religious scruple has now come upon you—come, tell me,” I replied (Terence, *Andria*, act 4, scene 3). “But [Col. 0987] I shall answer during the day, which already seems to me to be returning—unless it is the moon whose radiance is being brought in through the windows. At the same time, we must take care that oblivion does not swallow up your many excellent thoughts, Licentius. For when have our writings not demanded that such things be committed to them?

“I shall tell you plainly what I think; I shall argue against you as far as I can. For if you defeat me, no greater triumph could be granted to me. But if your weakness should yield either to the cleverness or to some subtle error of those whose side I shall attempt to undertake, and if your mind, insufficiently nourished by the disciplines of learning, should perhaps be unable to sustain so great a god, the matter itself will remind you how much strength you must acquire in order to return to him with greater firmness. At the same time, I want this discussion of ours to turn out more polished, for I ought not to present it to crude ears.

“Our Zenobius often discussed the order of things with me. Though he questioned deeply, I was never able to satisfy him, either because of the obscurity of the matters or because of the narrowness of the time available. He was so impatient with my repeated postponements that, to force me to answer more carefully and fully, he even challenged me in verse—and in good verse, so that you may love him all the more. But at that time I could not read it to you, since you were far removed from studies of this kind; nor can I do so now. His departure was so sudden and disturbed by that upheaval that none of this could come to mind for us; for he had decided to leave it to me to answer. Many reasons converge for sending him this speech.

“First, because it is owed to him; then because it is fitting that even in this way the kind of life we now lead should indicate his goodwill toward us; finally, because in joy over your hope he yields to no one. When he was present, too, because of his friendship with your father—or rather, with all of us—he was greatly concerned that the sparks of your talent, which he carefully noticed, should not be kindled by my care only to be extinguished by your negligence. And when he learned that you were also devoted to poetry, he will rejoice so greatly that I seem already to see him exulting with me.”

## CHAPTER VIII.—Licentius Is Enkindled with Love of Philosophy. Monnica Rebukes Him for Singing a Verse of a Psalm While Going Out to Attend to Nature’s Needs. The Usefulness of the Liberal Disciplines

21. “You will do nothing more pleasing to me,” he said. “But whether you will laugh at my fickleness and childish frivolity, or whether this is happening in us through some truly divine prompting and order, I would not hesitate to tell you that I have suddenly become less inclined toward those verses. Something else—something entirely different—has now shone upon me, though I do not know what it is. Philosophy is more beautiful, I confess, than Thisbe, than Pyramus, than that Venus and Cupid, and than loves of every such kind.” As he spoke, he was giving thanks to Christ with a sigh.

I received these words gladly—what else shall I say? Or what need I not say? Let everyone receive them as he wishes; I care nothing, except that perhaps I was rejoicing beyond measure.

22. Meanwhile, after a short time, day began to open. They rose, and I, weeping, prayed at length, when I heard Licentius cheerfully and volubly singing that prophetic verse:

“God of hosts, restore us;  
and show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Psalm 79:8).

The previous day, after dinner, when he had gone outside to attend to nature’s needs, [Col. 0988] he had sung it somewhat too loudly for our mother to bear, since such words were being repeatedly sung in such a place. He was saying nothing else, because he had recently learned the tune itself and, as often happens, loved the unfamiliar melody. Our deeply religious mother rebuked him for this very reason: the place was inappropriate for the song. Then he had joked:

“As if, if some enemy were imprisoning me here, God would not hear my voice!”

23. So, when he had returned alone in the morning—for both of them had gone out for the same reason—he came to my little couch.

“But tell me the truth,” he said; “may what you wish happen to us: what do you think of me?”

I took the young man’s right hand.

“What do I think?” I replied. “You sense it, believe it, and understand it. For I do not think that yesterday you sang for so long without purpose, so that the God of hosts might restore you and show you his face.”

Then, recalling it with astonishment, he said:

“You speak of something great and true. For I myself am not a little moved by the fact that just now I was being drawn away from those trifling verses with such difficulty, whereas now I am reluctant and ashamed to return to them, so wholly am I being carried toward certain great and wondrous things. Is this not truly to be converted to God?

“At the same time, I rejoice that the scruple of superstition was needlessly planted in me because I was singing such words in such a place.”

“For my part,” I replied, “I do not dislike even this, and I think it belongs to that order that we should say something about it here as well. For I see that both the song and the very place that offended her, and also the night, are fitting.

“From what things do you think we are being asked to turn back to God and see his face, except from a certain filth and uncleanness of the body, and likewise from the darkness in which error envelops us? Or what else is it to be converted than to be raised up from the immoderation of vices into oneself through virtue and self-control? And what else is the face of God than truth itself, which we long for, and to which, when we love it, we render ourselves pure and beautiful?”

“It could not be said better,” he exclaimed. Then, lowering his voice as though to my ear, he said: “See, please, how many things have come together, so that I may believe that something is already taking place for us according to a more favorable order.”

24. “If you care about order,” I replied, “you must return to those verses. For a moderate and concise education in the liberal disciplines makes lovers of truth more alert, more persevering, and more refined, so that they desire it more ardently, pursue it more steadfastly, and finally cling to it more sweetly (1 *Retractationes*, chapter 3, no. 2)—to truth which, Licentius, is called the blessed life.

“When it is named, everyone raises himself and, as it were, looks toward your hands to see whether you have anything to give to those in need and afflicted by various diseases. When wisdom begins to command them to endure a physician and to allow themselves to be treated with some patience, they retreat into their rags. Wasted and diseased by the warmth of those rags, they scratch the scab of their miserable pleasures more willingly than they endure and undergo the physician’s advice, somewhat harsh and burdensome to their illnesses, so that they may be restored to the health and light of the healthy.

“Thus, content as though with an alms of that name and understanding of the supreme God, the wretched live—yet they do live. But he seeks other men—or, to speak more truly, other souls—who, while they inhabit this body, are already worthy of his chamber: that [Col. 0989] best and most beautiful spouse. For them it is not enough to live; they require blessed life.

“Go, then, for the moment, to those Muses. Yet do you know what I want you to do?”

“Order me to do what you wish,” he replied.

“When Pyramus and his beloved have killed themselves—the latter over him as he lies half-dead—as you are going to sing, you will have the most suitable opportunity in the very grief by which your poem ought to be inflamed more powerfully. Seize upon the execration of that foul lust and those poisonous fires through which those pitiable things happen. Then raise yourself wholly into praise of pure and sincere love, by which souls endowed with learning and made beautiful by virtue are joined through philosophy to the intellect; and by which they not only escape death but also enjoy the most blessed life.”

He remained silent for a long time, nodding thoughtfully, then moved his head and departed.

25. Then I too rose, and after offering God our daily prayers, we began to go to the baths. When we could not be in the countryside because the sky was gloomy, that place was suitable and familiar to us for discussion.

Then, behold, before the doors we noticed roosters entering into an exceedingly fierce fight. We were pleased to watch. For what do eyes, beloved of beauty, not encompass and traverse, lest beauty—by which reason, modifying and governing all things known and unknown, draws its eager followers to seek it everywhere and wherever it commands—should offer no sign from any quarter? [Note: [Col. 0989] Am., Er., and Lov. read *ne quid inde innuat* (“lest anything give a hint thence”); shortly afterward, *atque ubicumque sectari iubet* (“and commands them to pursue it wherever”). But the manuscript reading given in the text is more elegant.] For where or from what place can it fail to give a sign?

Thus, in those very roosters, one could see their heads thrust forward intently, their feathers puffed up, their vigorous blows, and their extremely cautious evasions; and in every movement of creatures devoid of reason, nothing was without decorum, since another reason was directing everything from above. Finally, one could see the victor’s law: his proud crowing, and his limbs gathered together into a kind of circle, as though in the pomp of domination. The sign of the defeated bird was his little feathers raised from his neck, and the whole of him was deformed in voice and movement; yet even in that very deformity he was, somehow, harmonious and beautiful according to the laws of nature.

26. We asked many questions: Why were they all like this? Why did they fight for domination over the females subject to them? Why did the very appearance of the fight lead us to take some pleasure in the spectacle, even apart from that higher consideration? What was there in us that sought many things removed from the senses [Note: [Col. 0989] Thus the manuscripts; the editions read *remotum*, “removed”]? And what, again, was there that was captured by the invitation of the senses themselves?

We said to ourselves:

“Where is there no law? Where is there no dominion owed to what is better? Where is there no shadow of steadfastness? Where is there no imitation of that truest beauty? Where is there no measure?”

Then, warned that there should be a limit to our watching, we continued toward our appointed destination. There, as best we could and with considerable care—for the events were recent, and how could they escape the memory of three students so deeply marked by them?—we gathered all the little works of our nocturnal labor into this part of the book.

Nothing else was done by me that day, in order to spare my health, except that before dinner I was accustomed each day to hear with them half a volume of Virgil, with no other [Col. 0990] subject anywhere for us than the consideration of measure. No one can fail to approve of this; but to perceive it while each person is diligently engaged in something is extremely difficult and rare.

## SECOND DISCUSSION

## CHAPTER IX.—Order Is the Guide to God

27. The next day, early in the morning, we cheerfully assembled at our usual place and sat down there. Addressing the two of them attentively:

“Be fully present, Licentius,” I said, “as far as you can—and you too, Trygetius; for this is no small matter: we are investigating order.” Why should I now, as though established in that school from which I am glad to have escaped somehow, praise order to you at length and with ornamented speech? Accept this, if you wish—or rather, make yourselves wish it—for nothing shorter, and, as it seems to me, nothing truer, can be said in praise of it:

“Order is that which, if we maintain it in life, will lead us to God; and if we do not maintain it in life, we shall not reach God. But unless my mind deceives me about you, we already presume and hope that we shall reach him.

“This question, therefore, must be examined and resolved among us with the greatest care. I wish the others who are accustomed to take part with us in these matters were present. If it were possible, I would wish to have with me not only them, but at least all our friends, whose talent I have always admired, as attentive as you are now [Note: [Col. 0990] Lov. reads *non minus mecum habere* (“to have [them] with me no less”); the other books read *nunc mecum habere* (“to have [them] with me now”).]; or at least that one Zenobius himself, whom I have never received as idle when he was undertaking so great a task concerning this matter. But since that has not happened, they will read our writings, since we have now undertaken not to squander words about these matters, but to bind matters themselves—which readily escape memory—with the bond of writing, so that they may be brought back.

“And perhaps order itself was demanding this, having arranged their absence. For you too, surely, rise up with more vigorous spirits toward so great a matter, since we alone are charged to carry it through. And when those who are most dear to us have read it, if anything moves them to object, this discussion will give birth to other discussions for us, and the succession of speeches will itself insert itself into the order of instruction.

“But now, as I promised, I shall oppose Licentius as far as the matter permits. He has nearly completed the whole case, if he can securely and firmly surround it with the wall of a defense.”

## CHAPTER X.—What Is Order? On Restraining the Movements of Rivalry and Empty Boasting in Young Men Devoted to Letters

28. When I saw that they were sufficiently moved by the seriousness of the matter—by their silence, expression, eyes, suspense, and immobility of limb—and inflamed with the desire to listen, I said:

“Therefore, Licentius, if it seems good to you, gather into yourself whatever strength you can; polish whatever acumen you possess; and encompass in a definition what this order is.”

When he heard that he was being compelled to define it, he shuddered as though sprinkled with cold water. Looking at me with a troubled expression and, as often happens, smiling amid his very agitation, he said:

“What is this matter? What do I seem to you to be? Do you truly believe that I have been inflated by some strange and adventitious spirit?”

Then, immediately encouraging himself, he said:

“Or perhaps there is something with me.”

He was silent for a little while, so that whatever notion of order he possessed might be brought together [Col. 0991] into a definition. Then, more upright and confident, he said:

“Order is that by which all things that God has established are carried on.”

29. “What of God himself?” I asked. “Does it not seem to you that he too is carried on according to order?”

“It certainly seems so,” he replied.

“Then God is carried on,” said Trygetius.

“What else?” Licentius replied. “Do you deny that Christ is God, who came to us according to order and says that he was sent by God the Father? If, therefore, God sent Christ to us according to order, and we do not deny that Christ is God, then God not only carries out all things, but God himself is also carried on according to order.”

At this Trygetius, hesitating, said:

“I do not know how to understand that. When we name God, Christ himself does not come before our minds, as it were, but the Father. He comes before us when we name the Son of God.”

“You are doing a fine thing,” Licentius said. “Shall we then deny that the Son of God is God?”

The other, although he seemed to feel that it was dangerous to answer him, nevertheless forced himself and said:

“He too is God, certainly; yet properly speaking we call the Father God.”

“Restrain yourself,” I replied. “The Son is not improperly called God.”

But Trygetius, moved by religious scruple and unwilling even for his own words to be written down, was pressed by Licentius to let them remain—after the manner of boys, or rather of human beings, alas, almost all of them—as though the matter were being pursued among us for the sake of boasting.

When I rebuked Licentius’s impulse in stronger words, he blushed; from his agitation I noticed Trygetius laughing and rejoicing. I addressed them both:

“Is this how you behave? Are you not moved by the great burdens of vice and the darkness of ignorance under which we are weighed down and covered? Is this the attentiveness and elevation toward God and truth that you displayed a little while ago, at which I foolishly rejoiced?

“O if only you could see—even with eyes as bleary as mine—the dangers in which we lie, and what disease this laughter reveals! O if only you could see! How quickly, how immediately, and with what abundance you would turn it into tears.

“Miserable men, do you not know where we are? That all the minds of fools and the unlearned are submerged is a common condition; but wisdom does not extend help and a hand to all who are submerged in one and the same way. Believe me, there are different kinds: some are called upward, while others are allowed to sink into the depths.

“Please do not multiply my miseries. Let my own wounds be enough for me. I beg God to heal them with almost daily tears, yet I often convince myself that I am less worthy to be healed as quickly as I desire.

“Please, if you owe me any love, if you owe me any affection, if you understand how much I love you and how highly I value you, how much concern for your character torments me; if I am worthy of not being neglected by you; if, finally, with God as my witness, I am not lying when I say that I desire nothing more for myself than for you—repay me this service. And if you gladly call me teacher, give me my reward: be good.”

30. Here, when tears prevented me from saying more, Licentius was greatly distressed that everything was being written down.

“What have we done, I ask you?” he said.

“Even now,” I replied, “do you not at least confess your fault? Do you not know how accustomed I was to grow seriously angry in that school because boys were led not by the usefulness and beauty of the disciplines but by the love of the emptiest praise—so much so that some were not ashamed even to recite the words of others, [Col. 0992] and to receive applause (an evil to be lamented!) from those very people whose words they were reciting?

“Thus, although, as I believe, you have never done anything of that kind, you are nevertheless trying to introduce and propagate into philosophy, and into that life which I rejoice to have finally taken hold of, the ultimate—and more harmful than all the others—plague of destructive rivalry and empty boasting. Perhaps, because I am deterring you from this vanity and disease, you will become less eager for the studies of learning; and, thrown back from the ardor of windy fame, you will freeze into the torpor of inactivity.

“Wretched me, if I must still endure men of such a kind, from whom vices cannot depart without being succeeded by other vices.”

“You will see,” Licentius replied, “how much purer we shall become. We ask only this, by everything you love: be willing to pardon us and order all those things to be erased; and at the same time spare the writing tablets, which we no longer possess. For none of what we discussed at length has been transferred into books” [Note: [Col. 0992] They first wrote on tablets; from these they subsequently transferred the material into books.].

“On the contrary,” Trygetius said, “let our punishment remain, so that the very things that entice us—fame—may deter us from its love by its own scourge. For ensuring that these writings become known only to our friends and intimates will cost us no little labor.”

Licentius agreed.

## CHAPTER XI.—Monnica Is Not to Be Excluded from Philosophical Discussion on Account of Her Sex

31. Meanwhile our mother entered and asked what progress we had made, for she too knew about the question. When I ordered that both her entrance and her question be written down in our customary manner, she said:

“What are you doing? Have I ever heard women brought into this kind of discussion in the books you read?”

“Very little do I care,” I replied, “for the judgments of arrogant and ignorant people, who rush upon books to be read just as they rush upon people to be greeted. They do not consider what sort of people those before them are, but what clothing they wear and with what pomp their possessions and fortune shine.

“Such people in literature pay little attention either to where the question comes from, or to where the disputants are striving to arrive, or to what has been explained and accomplished by them.
