Yet because some among them are found whose minds are not to be despised—for they have been sprinkled with certain seasonings of humanity and are easily led through golden and painted doors into the innermost sanctuaries of philosophy—our predecessors have done enough for them. I see that you are familiar with their books as we read them to you.

“In our own times too, to omit the others, there is Theodorus, whom you know well, outstanding in talent and eloquence, in the very honors and gifts of fortune, and above all in mind. He is working to ensure that no class of people may justly complain, now or among posterity, about the literature of our time.

“If my books should happen to fall into someone’s hands, and, on reading my name, he should not say, ‘Who is this?’ and throw the volume aside, but, whether out of curiosity or excessive devotion to study, should disregard the lowliness of the threshold and continue inside, he will not take offense at my philosophizing with you. Nor will he perhaps despise any of those whose speech is mingled with mine in my writings.

“For they are not [Col. 0993] only free men—which is enough for any liberal discipline, and especially for philosophy—but were born in the highest rank among their own people. Yet the writings of the most learned men also contain shoemakers who philosophized, and people of much humbler fortunes; nevertheless, they shone with such light of talent and virtue that they would in no way have wished to exchange their own good qualities for any nobility of this kind, even if they could have done so under any terms.

“Believe me, there will also be a class of people who will like this very fact—that you philosophize with me—more than anything else, whether pleasant or serious, that they may find here. For women too philosophized among the ancients, and I am exceedingly pleased with your philosophy.”

32. “For, mother, so that you may not be ignorant of anything: this Greek word by which *philosophia* is named is called in Latin *amor sapientiae*, ‘love of wisdom.’ Hence even the divine Scriptures, which you embrace so fervently, do not command us to avoid and ridicule philosophers altogether, but rather the philosophers of this world (Colossians 2:8).

“That there is another world, most remote from these eyes, which the understanding of a few sound minds perceives, Christ himself sufficiently indicates (1 *Retractationes*, chapter 3, no. 2). For he does not say, ‘My kingdom is not from the world,’ but, ‘My kingdom is not from this world’ (John 18:36).

“For whoever thinks that all philosophy must be avoided wants us to do nothing other [Col. 0994] than not love wisdom. I would therefore despise you in these writings of mine if you did not love wisdom; but I would not despise you if you loved it moderately, and still less if you loved wisdom as much as I do.

“But now, since you love it much more than you love yourself—and I know how much you love me—and since you have made such progress in it that you are no longer terrified either by the horror of any chance misfortune or by that of death itself, which is exceedingly difficult for the most learned men and which all acknowledge to be the highest summit of philosophy, should I not gladly give myself to you even as a pupil?”

33. At this she gently and piously said that I had never lied so much. When I saw that we had poured out so many words that they ought not to remain unwritten, that the book had now reached its proper length, and that no tablets remained, it seemed best to postpone the question, while also sparing my stomach. For it had been disturbed more than I wished by the things that had seemed necessary for me to vomit forth against the young men.

But when we began to leave, Licentius said:

“Remember how many things, and how necessary, are supplied to us by you through that most hidden and divine order, even without your knowing it.”

“I see it,” I replied, “and I am not ungrateful to God. And I presume that you yourselves, because you notice these things, will for that very reason become better.”

This was all that occupied me that day.

## BOOK TWO

This book contains two discussions. While the interlocutors examine the definition of Order, they encounter various questions: how the wise person remains unmoved with God; whether even the things wrongly done by human beings are carried on according to God’s order; whether God was just before the origin of evil; and whether evil arose from God’s order. Finally, the discussion turns more fully to the proper order of study, which requires that, once character has been properly formed and human disciplines acquired, the mind advance toward the apprehension of higher and divine things.

[Col. 0993]

[Col. 0993] FIRST DISCUSSION

## CHAPTER I.—The Definition of Order Is Examined

1. After a few days had intervened, Alypius arrived. The brightness of the sun invited us, and the mild temperature—as mild as winter could be in those regions—invited us to descend into the meadow, which we used more frequently and familiarly.

Our mother was also with us. I had previously come to know her talent and her mind, inflamed toward divine matters, through long companionship and careful observation. But on a certain occasion, in a discussion of no small importance that I held with my companions on my birthday and committed to a little book, her intelligence had appeared to me so great that nothing seemed more suited to true philosophy. Therefore, whenever leisure abounded, I had resolved to arrange matters so that she would not be absent from our conversation. You learned this from me in the first book of this work as well.

2. When we had sat down in the place just mentioned as conveniently as we could, I said to the two young men:

“Although I have been angry with you for dealing with great matters in a childish way, nevertheless it seems to me that, with God’s favor, it has happened not without order that the time was consumed in the speech by which I was drawing you away from that frivolity, so that so great a matter appears to have been postponed until Alypius’s arrival.

“Therefore, since I have now made the question thoroughly familiar to him and shown how far we have advanced in it, are you prepared, Licentius, to defend the case you undertook on the basis of your definition? For I believe I remember that you said order is that by which God carries out all things.”

“I am prepared,” he replied, “as far as I am able.”

“How, then,” I asked, “does God carry out all things according to order? Does he also carry himself on according to order, or are all other things governed by him according to order apart from that order?”

“Where everything is good,” he replied, “there is no order. For there is supreme equality, which has no need of order.”

“Do you deny,” I asked, “that everything with God is good?”

“I do not deny it,” he replied.

“Then,” I said, “it follows that neither God nor the things that are with God are administered according to order.”

He conceded this.

“Do you mean, then,” I asked, “that all good things seem to you to be nothing?”

“On the contrary,” he said, “they truly are.”

“Where, then,” I asked, “is your earlier statement that everything that exists is administered according to order, and that absolutely nothing is separate from order?”

“But evils exist as well,” he replied, “and through them it has come about that order encompasses good things too; for good things alone are not governed according to order, but good and evil together. When we say, ‘Everything that exists,’ we certainly do not mean good things alone. It follows that everything together that God administers is administered according to order.”

3. I said to him: “Do the things that are administered and carried on seem to you to move, or do you think they are immobile?”

“Those things that take place in this world,” he replied, “I admit do move.”

“Do you deny that the rest move?”

“Those things that are with God do not move; I think that everything else does move.”

“Since, then,” I said, “you think that the things which are with God do not move, but concede that everything else moves, you show that everything which moves is not with God.”

“Repeat that more clearly,” he said [Col. 0995].

He seemed not to have asked this because it was difficult to understand, but to gain time for finding an answer.

“You said,” I replied, “that the things which are with God do not move, while everything else moves. If, then, these things which move would not move if they were with God—since you deny that anything which is with God moves—it follows that the things which move exist apart from God.”

He remained silent for some time. At last he said: “It seems to me that even in this world, whatever does not move is with God.”

“That has no bearing on my point,” I said. “For you admit, I suppose, that not everything in this world is immobile. It follows that not everything in this world is with God.”

“I admit,” he said, “that not everything is.”

“Then there is something without God.”

“No,” he replied.

“Then everything is with God.”

At this point he hesitated. “Please,” he said, “do not make me say that nothing exists without God; for absolutely everything that moves does not seem to me to be with God.”

“Then this heaven,” I said, “which no one doubts is in motion, is without God.”

“Heaven is not without God,” he replied.

“Then there is something with God that moves.”

“I cannot explain what I think as I would like,” he said. “Nevertheless, I ask you to understand as perceptively as you can what I am trying to say, without waiting for my words to express it adequately. For it seems to me both that nothing exists without God and, again, that whatever is with God remains undisturbed. Yet I cannot say that heaven is without God—not only because I think that nothing exists without God, but also because I think that heaven contains something that does not move, something that is truly either God or with God, although I do not doubt that heaven itself turns and moves.”

## CHAPTER II  
### What it means to be with God. How the wise person remains unmoved with God

4. “Then define,” I said, “if you please, what it means to be with God and what it means not to be without God. For if our disagreement concerns words, it will easily be set aside, provided that we can see the thing itself which you have conceived in your mind.”

“I dislike defining,” he replied.

“What, then, shall we do?” I asked.

“You define, please,” he said. “For it is easier for me to see what I reject in another person’s definition than to explain anything properly by defining it myself.”

“I shall oblige you,” I said. “Does that seem to you to be with God which is governed and administered by him?”

“No,” he replied. “That is not what I had in mind when I said that the things which do not move are with God.”

“Then consider,” I said, “whether at least this definition pleases you: whatever understands God is with God.”

“I agree,” he said.

“What, then?” I asked. “Does the wise person not seem to you to understand God?”

“He does,” he replied.

“Since wise people, then, move not only within one house or one city, but also by travelling and sailing through immense regions, how can it be true that whatever is with God does not move?”

“You have made me laugh,” he replied, “as though I had said that whatever the wise person does is with God. The wise person is with God, but that which he knows is with God.”

“Does the wise person not know,” I said, “his own book, cloak, tunic, furniture, if he has any, and other things of that kind—things which even fools know well?”

“I admit,” he replied, “that knowing a tunic and knowing a cloak are not being with God.”

5. “Then this is what you are saying,” I replied: “Not everything that the wise person knows is with God; but the wise person knows whatever of his is with God.”

“Exactly,” he said. “For whatever he knows through the bodily senses is not with God, but that which he perceives with his mind is.”

“I may perhaps dare to say something more,” he continued, “but I shall say it nevertheless. You are to judge me, and either confirm me or teach me. Whoever knows only what the bodily senses touch seems to me not only not to be with God, but not even to be with himself.”

At this point I noticed that Trygetius seemed to want to say something, but was held back by embarrassment, lest he appear to intrude into another person’s place. Since Licentius was now silent, I gave him permission to speak if he wished.

He said: “No one seems to me truly to know those things that pertain to the bodily senses. To sense is one thing; to know is another. Therefore, if we know anything, I think it is contained in the intellect alone and can be grasped by it alone. It follows that, if what the wise person knows through understanding is with God, then everything the wise person knows can be with God.”

Licentius approved this, and added another point which I could in no way disregard. He said: “The wise person is certainly with God, for the wise person also understands himself. This follows both from what I learned from you—that whatever understands God is with God—and from what we have said—that whatever is understood by the wise person is with God. But as for that part through which he uses these senses—for I do not think that it should be counted when we call someone wise—I admit that I do not know it, nor can I even conjecture what sort of thing it is.”

6. “Then you deny,” I said, “that the wise person consists not only of body and soul, but also of the whole soul, since it would be madness to deny that this part through which he uses the senses belongs to the soul. It is not the eyes or ears themselves that sense, but some other faculty through the eyes. If sensing itself is not assigned to the intellect, it is assigned to no part of the soul. It remains that it be attributed to the body, and for the moment nothing seems to me more absurd than saying that.”

“The soul of the wise person,” he replied, “purified by the virtues and now cleaving to God, is worthy even of the name ‘wise person’; nor is it fitting to call anything else in him wise. Nevertheless, certain things—so to speak, stains and cast-off coverings by which he has cleansed himself, as though he had withdrawn into himself—serve that soul. Or, if this whole entity is to be called a soul, they certainly serve and are subject to that part of the soul which alone ought to be called wise. I think that memory itself dwells in this subordinate part.

“The wise person therefore uses it as a servant, commanding it and, once it has been subdued and brought under control, imposing on it the limits of the law. Thus, while using these senses for things that are now necessary not to the wise person but to the servant itself, he does not dare to exalt himself or become arrogant toward his master, nor to use even the things that belong to him indiscriminately and without restraint. For those things that pass away can belong to that most contemptible part. And to whom is memory necessary except to things that pass away and, as it were, flee?

“The wise person, then, embraces God and enjoys him who always remains. He is not awaited as though he might come into being, nor feared as though he might be absent; rather, by the very fact that he truly exists, he is always present. Remaining unmoved and abiding in himself, the wise person cares for the quasi-property of his servant, so that he may use it as a thrifty and diligent attendant and guard it sparingly.”

[Col. 0997] 7. As I considered this opinion of his with admiration, I remembered that I had once said essentially the same thing briefly, while he was listening.

Then, smiling, I said: “Give thanks, Licentius, to this servant of yours. If he had not supplied you with something from his own property, perhaps you would now have had nothing to say. For if memory belongs to that part which submits itself to be governed like a servant by the good mind, believe me, you have now been helped by it to say this.

“Before I return to that order, then, does it not seem to you that, even on account of such things—that is, on account of honorable and necessary studies—the wise person needs memory?”

“What need has he of memory,” he replied, “when he has and retains all his possessions present before him? Even in sensation itself, we do not summon memory to our aid for something that is before our eyes. Since, then, everything is present to the wise person before those inner eyes of the intellect—that is, since he looks fixedly and immovably upon God himself, with whom are all the things that the intellect sees and possesses—what need, I ask, has he of memory?

“As for me, I need it to retain what I heard from you because I am not yet master of that servant. For now I serve it; now I struggle not to serve it; and I dare, as it were, to assert myself into freedom. If at some point I command it and it obeys me, often making me think that I have conquered, then in other matters it rises up again in such a way that I, wretched man, lie beneath its feet. Therefore, when we inquire about the wise person, do not count me among them.”

“Nor me,” I said.

“But nevertheless,” I continued, “can this wise person abandon those who are his own? Or, while he acts through this body in which he keeps that servant bound by its law, will he in any way leave off the duty of conferring benefits upon those whom he can benefit—especially the duty most urgently demanded of him, teaching wisdom itself?”

“When he does this, so that he may teach appropriately and be less inept, he often prepares something to speak and discuss from an orderly arrangement. If he does not entrust it to memory, it must perish. Therefore, either you will deny that the duties of benevolence belong to the wise person, or you will admit that certain things belonging to the wise person are guarded by memory.

“Or perhaps he entrusts to that servant something of his own possessions—not for his own sake, but nevertheless as something necessary for his own people—to be preserved by it, so that, like a sober servant instructed according to the best discipline of his master, it may guard not what it would guard for its own sake, but what he has ordered it to guard for the purpose of leading fools to wisdom?”

“I do not think,” he replied, “that the wise person entrusts anything at all to this servant. For he is always fixed upon God, whether silent or speaking with human beings. But that servant, already well trained, carefully preserves what it may occasionally offer its master while he is engaged in discussion, and thereby performs its duty agreeably to him as to the most just of masters, under whose authority it sees itself living. It does this not by reasoning, as it were, but because that highest law and highest order prescribe it.”

“I do not now resist your arguments,” I said, “so that the undertaking we have begun may rather be brought to completion. But as for this matter, we shall examine elsewhere, when God himself has granted the opportunity according to his order, exactly how it stands—for it is not a small matter, nor one that can be contained in so brief a discussion.”

## CHAPTER III  
### Whether folly is with God

8. It has now been defined what it means to be with God [Col. 0998]. When I said that being with God means understanding God, you added still more: that the things understood by the wise person are also there. In this connection I am greatly troubled by the way you have suddenly placed folly with God. For if whatever the wise person understands is with God, and he can escape folly only after understanding it, then—an impious thing to say—that plague too will be with God.

Moved by this conclusion, they remained silent for a little while. Then Trygetius said: “Let him answer, whose arrival for this discussion, at the most opportune moment, I do not think we rashly celebrated.”

Then Alypius said: “Heaven forbid! Was my long silence finally preparing this for me? But my quiet has already been broken. Nevertheless, I shall now try somehow to satisfy this request, after first looking ahead for myself and obtaining from you a promise that you will demand no more such answer from me.”

“By no means,” I said, “may you, Alypius, deny our conversation the voice we desire from your benevolence and humanity. Go on now and accomplish what you have undertaken; the rest, as that order now stands, will follow.”

“Equally,” he replied, “I must hope for better things from the order whose defense you have meanwhile required me to undertake. But, unless I am mistaken, you thought that by the conclusion you drew, folly had been joined with God because they said that everything the wise person understands is with God. But I shall for now set aside the question of how far that statement should be accepted; turn your attention for a little while to your reasoning.

“You said: ‘For if whatever the wise person understands is with God, and he can escape folly only after understanding it.’ As though it were unclear that, before someone avoids folly, he should not be counted among the wise. It was said that what is understood by the wise person is with God. Since, then, someone understands folly in order to avoid it, he is not yet wise. When he becomes wise, folly is not to be counted among the things he understands. Therefore, since the things that the wise person now understands are joined to God, folly is rightly separated from God.”

“You have answered sharply, as is your custom, Alypius,” I said, “but as though you had been thrust into difficulties not your own. Nevertheless, since, as I suppose, you still deign to be foolish with me, what shall we do if we encounter some wise person who is willing to free us from so great an evil by teaching and discussing with us?

“I shall ask nothing of him first, as I suppose, except that he show me what folly is, what sort of thing it is, and what its nature is altogether. I could not readily assert this of you; but it holds me so completely and for so long as it remains unintelligible to me.

“He will therefore say, on your authority: ‘You should have come to me when I was foolish, if you wanted me to teach you this. But now you yourselves can become your own teachers, for I no longer understand folly.’

“If I heard him say this, I would not hesitate to advise the man to become our companion while we sought another teacher. For although I do not fully understand folly, I can nevertheless see that nothing could be more foolish than this reply.

“Perhaps he will be ashamed either to leave us or to follow us. He will therefore discuss and expound the evils of folly at great length. We, taking good care of ourselves, will either listen attentively to a man who does not know what he is saying, or believe that he knows what he does not understand, or folly will still be joined to God on account of the reasoning you have undertaken.

“Yet I see no possible defense for any of the preceding alternatives. What remains is the final possibility, which you do not want.”

“I had never thought you envious,” he replied. “For if I had received, as is customary, any honorarium from those who entrusted this case to me, then, while you cling too stubbornly to this line of reasoning, I would now be forced to return it to them. Let them therefore be satisfied either that, while I struggled along with you, I gave them no little time for reflection; or, if the defeated advocates, listening willingly to the advice though the defeat was not their fault, should yield to you in this matter, let them be more cautious in the rest.”

10. “I shall not disregard,” I said, “something that Trygetius was also trying to say, making some noise in your defense; and I shall do so with your kind permission. Perhaps you are not well prepared, since you have only recently arrived at this business. I would therefore rather remove the advocacy and patiently hear the parties themselves conduct their case, as I had begun to do.”

Then Trygetius, with Licentius entirely absent, said: “Understand it as you wish, and laugh at my folly. It does not seem to me that the faculty by which folly itself is understood should be called understanding, since folly is either the sole or the chief cause of failure to understand.”

“I am not quick to reject this,” I said. “Although what Alypius feels greatly troubles me—how can anyone rightly teach what a thing is if he does not understand it, or what harm it brings to the mind if he does not see it with his mind?—I think that this consideration was precisely why he hesitated to say what you have said, even though the statement is also familiar to him from the books of teachers.

“Nevertheless, when I consider bodily sensation itself—for the soul also uses this, and it alone provides whatever comparison there can be with the intellect—I am led to say that no one can see darkness. Therefore, if understanding is to the mind what seeing is to sensation, and although one may have open, sound, and clear eyes, one still cannot see darkness, then it is not absurd to say that folly cannot be understood, since we call no other things the darkness of the mind.

“Nor will it now trouble me how folly can be avoided without being understood. Just as we avoid darkness with our eyes by the very fact that we do not want not to see, so whoever wishes to avoid folly should not try to understand it. Rather, he should grieve that, through it, he does not understand the things that can be understood, and should perceive that folly is present to him not because he understands it more, but because he understands other things less.”

## CHAPTER IV  
### Whether the things a human being does wrongly are done according to order. Evil things brought into order contribute to the beauty of the universe

11. But let us return to order, so that Licentius may at some point be restored to us. For now I ask you whether whatever a fool does seems to you to be done according to order. Consider what traps this question contains. If you say “according to order,” where will that definition be: “Order is that by which God does everything that exists,” if even what the fool does is done according to order? But if order is not present in what the fool does, there will be something not held by order; and yet you want neither alternative. Take care, please, lest you disturb the whole defense of order.

Here again Trygetius spoke, for the other man was still entirely absent: “It is easy enough to answer this complication of yours, but for the moment I lack an analogy by which I see that my opinion ought to be asserted and illuminated. Nevertheless, I shall say what I think; you will do what you did a little earlier. For that reference to darkness brought us no little illumination concerning what I had brought forth in obscure form.

“The whole life of fools, although it is in no way stable or ordered through the fools themselves, is nevertheless necessarily included, through divine providence, within the order of things. It is arranged, as it were, in certain places assigned by that ineffable and eternal law, and is in no way allowed to exist where it ought not to exist.

“Thus, when someone considers it alone with a narrow mind, he recoils from it as though struck by great ugliness. But if he raises and expands the eyes of his mind and surveys everything together, he will find nothing that is not ordered, and everything distinguished and arranged in its own proper places, as it were.”

12. “How great and wonderful,” I said, “is the response which some hidden order of things makes to me through you—and I myself am increasingly moved to believe it! You are saying things which I understand neither how they can be said without having been seen, nor how you see them; and so I suspect that they are both true and profound.

“You perhaps sought a single example corresponding to this opinion. But innumerable examples now occur to me, drawing me altogether toward agreement.

“What is more dreadful than an executioner? What is more savage and terrible than his character? Yet he occupies a necessary place among the laws and is inserted into the order of a well-governed state; he is harmful in his own character, but, by an order not his own, he is the punishment of harmful people.

“What can be said to be more filthy, more empty of dignity, and fuller of disgrace than prostitutes, pimps, and the other plagues of this kind? Take prostitutes away from human affairs, and you will throw everything into disorder through lust; place them in the position of respectable married women, and you will dishonor them with stain and disgrace. Thus this class of people is most impure in its way of life, yet, by the laws of order, lowest in status.

“Do we not find certain limbs of living creatures intolerable if we consider them by themselves? Yet the order of nature has neither wished them to be absent, since they are necessary, nor permitted them to stand out, since they are unbeautiful. Nevertheless, by occupying their proper places, these deformed parts have yielded a better place to better things.

“What was more pleasing to us, or more fitting for the spectacle of a farm and country house, than that fight and contest between gamecocks which we mentioned in the preceding book (Book 1, chapter 8, no. 25)? Yet what did we see more base than the deformity of the defeated bird? Even through that deformity, however, a more complete beauty arose from the same contest.”

13. “I believe that everything is like this; but it requires eyes to see it. Poets have loved what are called solecisms and barbarisms; they have preferred to escape obvious faults by changing the names and calling them figures of speech and metaplasms. Yet remove these from poems, and we shall miss their sweetest seasonings.

“Pile many things together in one place, and I shall find the whole harsh, foul, and rancid. Transfer it into unrestrained and public speech, and who will not order us to flee from it and withdraw into the theaters?”

[Note: In editions published up to the present, the reading is “and withdraw into caves.” But nearly all manuscripts have “into the theaters,” and some have “withdraw”: this is the correct reading.]

“Order, then, governing and regulating these things, will not allow them to be excessive in themselves or out of place anywhere. Speech is illuminated when certain subdued and almost unpolished elements are interposed among its high points and graceful passages. If such elements stand alone, you reject them as worthless; but if they are absent, the beautiful passages do not stand out, do not rule in their own regions and possessions, as it were, but obstruct their own particular light and throw everything into confusion.”

## CHAPTER V  
### How to remedy the error of believers who think that things take place without order

Great thanks are owed to order here as well. Who would not fear or hate deceptive conclusions that creep gradually into assent to falsehood, either by diminishing or by adding? Yet in discussions, when placed in their proper and appropriate positions, they often possess such power that, somehow, the deception itself becomes sweet through them. Will order itself not be praised here too?

14. In music, geometry, the movements of the stars, and the necessities of numbers, order rules so completely that if anyone wishes to see, as it were, its source and innermost sanctuary, he will either find them in these disciplines or be led through them to it without any error.

For such education, if used with moderation—for nothing there is more to be feared than excess—nurtures a philosophical soldier, or even a commander, of such a kind that he may fly and arrive wherever he wishes at that highest measure beyond which he neither can, ought, nor desires to seek anything further, and may lead many others there as well.

Thus, while still occupied with human affairs, he despises them and distinguishes everything in such a way that he is not moved at all by the fact that one person desires to have children but does not, while another is tormented by his wife’s excessive fertility; that one person lacks money although he is prepared to give much generously, while a lean and scabrous moneylender lies upon money buried in the ground; that luxury scatters and dissipates great estates, while a beggar, weeping all day long, scarcely obtains a single coin; that honor raises up someone unworthy, while shining moral character remains hidden in the crowd.

15. These and other conditions in human life often compel people impiously to believe that we are not governed by any order of divine providence.

But there are others—pious and good people, endowed with brilliant intelligence—who cannot bring themselves to believe that we have been abandoned by the supreme God, yet, disturbed by the great darkness and confusion of things, see no order. Wanting the most hidden causes to be laid bare, they often complain of their errors even in verse.

[Note: In manuscript B, the reading is “and wanting.” We have followed the reading of Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition.]

[Note: He seems to be alluding to the poem of Zenobius, mentioned above, Book 1, chapter 7, no. 20.]

If they ask only why the Italians always pray for serene winters, while our Getulia is always miserably thirsty, who will easily answer them? Or where among us will any hint of that order be discovered?

For my part, if I can offer advice to my own people, I judge—so far as I see and understand—that they ought to be instructed in every discipline (Retractations I, chapter 3, no. 2). For these matters cannot possibly be understood in any other way so that they become brighter than daylight.

But if they are either too sluggish, occupied with other business, or already hardened against learning, let them prepare for themselves the supports of faith, so that he may draw them to himself by that bond and free them from these dreadful and most entangled evils—he who permits no one who has believed rightly through the mysteries to perish.

16. For there are two paths that we follow when the obscurity of things troubles us: reason, or certainly authority. Philosophy promises reason and scarcely liberates a very few. Yet it compels even those few not only not to despise those mysteries, but to understand them as they ought to be understood.

True and genuine philosophy has no other task than to teach what the principle of all things is, without a principle, how great an intellect abides in it, and what has flowed from it for our salvation without any degeneration. The venerable mysteries teach that this is the one omnipotent God, the threefold-powerful God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who liberates peoples through sincere and steadfast faith; neither confusedly, as some proclaim, nor insultingly, as many preach.

[Note: In the very old manuscripts of Corbie and Theodoric the reading is “with whom, threefold-powerful.” In the manuscripts of the Abbey of Vendôme, it is “by whom, threefold-powerful.” In another manuscript of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris, it is “and by whom, threefold-powerful.” The scribal error here was easy to make; but we consider it our duty to leave all the readings to the judgment of the learned whenever ancient and better-quality manuscripts disagree on a matter of some importance.]

And however great it may seem that so great a God has deigned to assume and act through even the body of our race for our sake, the more lowly it appears, the fuller it is of mercy and the farther removed it is, in every direction, from a certain arrogance of clever minds.

17. As for where the soul derives its origin, what it does here, how far it is from God, what it possesses uniquely that alternates between the two natures, to what extent it dies, and how it is proved immortal—how important do you think the order is by which these things are learned?

It is altogether important and certain; if there is time, we shall speak about it later, briefly. For now I want you to accept this from me: if someone rashly and without the ordered sequence of disciplines dares to rush into knowledge of these matters, he will become curious instead of studious, credulous instead of learned, and unbelieving instead of cautious.

Therefore I both marvel at the source of your excellent and appropriate answer to my recent question and am compelled to acknowledge it. Nevertheless, let us see how far your hidden intention can advance.

Let us now have Licentius’s words returned to us. For so long he has been occupied by some concern and absent from this conversation that I believe he will read these words just as he would read those concerning our familiar friends who are not present.

But return to us, please, Licentius, and make yourself wholly present here; I am speaking to you. For you approved my definition by which it was said what it means to be with God, and you wished to teach me, so far as I am able to grasp it, that the mind of the wise person remains immovable with the God with whom it is.

## CHAPTER VI  
### The immovable mind of the wise person

18. But I am troubled by how, since this wise person is not denied to be in a body as long as he lives among human beings, his mind can remain immovable while his body wanders here and there.

In this way you could say that, when a ship moves, the people who are in it do not move, although we admit that the ship is possessed and steered by them. For even if they guided it by thought alone and made it go wherever they wished, when it moved, those who were situated within it could not fail to move.

“No,” said Licentius, “the mind is not in the body in such a way that the body rules the mind.”

“I am not saying that,” I replied. “But neither is a rider in a horse in such a way that the horse rules him; nevertheless, although he drives the horse wherever he wishes to go, when the horse moves he must move as well.”

“He can sit there immovably,” he replied.

“You are forcing us,” I said, “to define what it means to move. If you can do so, I want you to.”

“Please,” he replied, “let your kindness remain as it is; for my request also remains. And do not ask me again whether I am willing to define it. When I am able to do so, I shall announce it myself.”

When these words had been spoken, a boy from the household to which we had assigned this task ran up to us and announced that it was time for lunch.

Then I said: “This boy, to whom we had assigned that task, is forcing us to demonstrate with our own eyes what it means to move, rather than define it. Let us go, then, and move from this place to another; for, unless I am mistaken, that is nothing other than moving.”

At this they smiled, and we departed.

## SECOND DISCUSSION

19. After we had refreshed our bodies, since the sky had become overcast, we sat in the bathhouse in our usual place.

Then I said: “So, Licentius, you concede that motion is nothing other than passing from one place to another?”

“I concede it,” he replied.

“Then you concede that no one who is in a place in which he was not before has failed to move?”

“I do not understand,” he replied.

“If something was previously in one place and is now in another,” I said, “do you concede that it has moved?”

He agreed.

“Then,” I said, “could the living body of some wise person be here with us while his mind was absent from this place?”

“It could,” he replied.

“Even if he were conversing with us and teaching us something?”

“Even if he were teaching us wisdom itself,” he replied, “I would not say that he was with us, but with himself.”

“Then not in the body?” I asked.

“Not in the body,” he replied.

“Would you not admit,” I said, “that the body deprived of a mind was dead, when I proposed that it was alive?”

“I do not know how to explain it,” he replied. “For I see that a human body cannot be alive if the mind is not in it; and yet I cannot say that wherever the body of the wise person may be, his mind is not with God.”

“I shall make you explain this,” I said. “Perhaps, since God is everywhere, wherever the wise person goes he finds God, with whom he can be. Thus we can both avoid denying that he passes from place to place—which is movement—and nevertheless maintain that he is always with God.”

“I admit,” he replied, “that the body passes from place to place, but I deny that the mind itself—the mind from which the name ‘wise person’ is derived—does so.”

## CHAPTER VII  
### How there was order when evil did not exist

20. “For now,” I said, “I yield to you, lest a matter of the greatest obscurity, requiring longer and more careful treatment, obstruct our present purpose. But let us see, since we have defined what it means to be with God, whether we can also know what it means to be without God, although I think it is already clear.

“For I suppose that it seems to you that those who are not with God are without God.”

“If I had words available to me,” he replied, “I might perhaps say something that would not displease you [Col. 1004]. But I ask you to bear with my childishness and, as befits you, to anticipate the matters themselves with a swift mind. For those people seem to me neither to be with God nor yet to be without God, since they are held by God. Thus I cannot say that those whom God holds are without God.

“I likewise do not say that they are with God, because they do not possess God. For it was agreed long ago among us, in that delightful conversation we held on your birthday, that to possess God means nothing other than to enjoy God (On the Happy Life, no. 34). But I admit that I fear these contrary alternatives: how can someone be neither without God nor with God?”

“Do not let this trouble you,” I said. “Where the matter is agreed, who would quibble over words? Let us therefore return at last to that definition of order. You said that order is that by which God does everything. Yet, as I see, there is nothing upon which God does not act, since it was from this that it seemed to you that nothing could be found apart from order.”

“My opinion remains,” he replied. “But I already see what you are going to say: whether God does things that, as we admit, are not done well.”

“Excellent,” I said. “You have indeed put the point directly before my mind. But just as you saw what I was going to say, I ask you to see what must be answered.”

He shook his head and shoulders. “We are confused,” he said.

At this point his mother may also have come in to join us. After remaining silent for a little while, he asked me to put the same question to him again. He had not noticed at all that Trygetius had already answered this point above (Chapter 4, no. 11).

Then I said: “Why, or for what purpose, should I repeat it to you? As they say, ‘Do not do again what has been done.’ I therefore advise you instead to take care to read what was said above, if you were unable to hear it.

“I did not resent your absence of mind from our conversation; indeed, I tolerated it for a long time, so that I neither interrupted what you were doing on your own behalf while you were intent upon and withdrawn from us, nor failed to pursue those matters which your pen did not allow you to abandon.”

22. “Now I ask about something which we have not yet attempted to examine with careful reasoning. For when some order—I do not know what order—first gave birth to this question about order, I remember that you said that this was the justice of God, which distinguishes between the good and the wicked and assigns to each what is his own (above, Book 1, chapter 7, no. 19).

“For, so far as I understand, there is no more evident definition of justice. I therefore want you to answer whether it seems to you that God was ever not just.”

“Never,” he replied.

“If God was therefore always just,” I said, “then good and evil always existed.”

“I can see nothing else that follows,” said his mother. “For there was no judgment of God when evil did not exist; nor, if at some time he did not assign to the good and the wicked what was due to each, can he be regarded as having been just.”

Licentius said to her: “Then do you think that we should say that evil always existed?”

“I do not dare to say that,” she replied.

“What, then, shall we say?” I asked. “If God is just because he judges between the good and the wicked, then, when evil did not exist, he was not just.”

While they were silent, I noticed that Trygetius wanted to answer, and I allowed him to do so.

He said: “God was absolutely just. For he could distinguish good and evil, if they had existed, and by the very fact that he could, he was just.

“For when we say that Cicero prudently investigated Catiline’s conspiracy, that he acted temperately and was corrupted by no reward to spare the wicked, that he justly put them to death with the highest punishment by authority of the Senate, and that he courageously endured all the weapons of his enemies and the burden of unpopularity—as he himself put it—we do not mean that those virtues would not have been in him had Catiline not prepared such destruction for the state.

“Virtue must be considered in itself, not through some action of this kind, and this is true in a human being; how much more so in God?—provided, of course, that in the narrowness of our circumstances and words we are permitted somehow to frame the matter in this way.

“For, so that we may understand that God was always just: when evil came into existence, so that he could separate it from good, he did not delay in assigning to each what was his own. He did not then need to learn justice; rather, he then used the justice that he had always possessed.”

[Col. 1005] 23. When both Licentius and my mother had approved this in such a pressing situation, I said: “What do you say, Licentius? Where is what you maintained so emphatically—that nothing happens except according to order? For the fact that evil came into being certainly did not happen according to God’s order; but, once it had come into being, it was included within God’s order.”

And he, astonished and distressed that so good a case had so suddenly slipped from his hands, said: “I say that order began precisely from the time when evil began to exist.”

“Then,” I said, “if order began after evil arose, evil itself did not come into being according to order. But order was always with God. Either what is called evil never existed at all, or, if it is found to have begun at some point, since order itself is either good or derives from good, nothing ever existed without order, nor will anything ever exist without it.

“Although something else—I do not know what—has occurred to me more forcefully, it has escaped me through that customary forgetfulness. I believe that it happened according to order, in accordance with the merit, rank, or order of life.” [Note: [Col. 1005] Here there is a notable omission in nine manuscripts, and those not of inferior quality, which immediately add after the words “order began”: “I do not know how it escaped me.”]

“I do not know how it escaped me,” he said, “that opinion which I now reject. I should not have said that order began after evil was born. Rather, just as there was that justice in God of which Trygetius spoke, so too there was order with God; but it did not come into use until after evil began to exist.” [Note: [Col. 1005] Bad., Am., Er., and Lov. read: “did not come into its use.” But *its* is absent from most witnesses.]

“You are falling back into the same position,” I said. “For what you least want remains unshaken: whether order existed with God, or began from the time when evil also began, that evil nevertheless arose outside order. If you concede this, you admit that something can happen outside order; and that weakens and mutilates your case. But if you do not concede it, evil begins to appear as having been born according to God’s order, and you will admit that God is the author of evil. Nothing seems to me more detestable than that sacrilege.”

As I repeatedly raised and turned this point over, whether he failed to understand it or pretended not to understand it, he had nothing to say and gave himself over to silence.

Then my mother said: “I do not think that nothing could happen outside God’s order, because the evil that arose was in no way born according to God’s order. But that justice did not allow it to remain disordered; it reduced it and compelled it into an order corresponding to its own merit.”

[Col. 1006] 24. When I saw that all of them were seeking God with the greatest devotion, each according to his strength, but were not maintaining the very order under discussion—the order by which one reaches an understanding of that ineffable majesty—I said: “I beg you, since, as I see, you love order greatly, do not allow us to be backward and disordered.

“For although the most hidden reason promises that it will demonstrate that nothing happens outside the divine order, nevertheless, if we heard a schoolmaster attempting to teach syllables to a boy whom no one had previously taught letters, we would think him not merely laughable as a fool, but deserving to be bound as a madman. This would be, I suppose, for no other reason than that he was not observing the order of teaching.

“Yet no one doubts that many such things are done by the uneducated—things which the educated criticize and ridicule—and by deranged people—things which do not escape even the judgment of fools. Nevertheless, a certain profound discipline, far removed from even the suspicion of the multitude, promises that it will reveal to students, to minds devoted solely to God and to souls, that even all those things which we acknowledge to be perverse are not outside the divine order, so that this will become no less certain to us than the highest truths of mathematics.”

## CHAPTER VIII  
### The principles of life are first imparted to the young, and then the order of education.

25. This discipline itself is God’s law. It remains fixed and unshaken with him forever, and is, as it were, transcribed into wise souls, so that they understand that they live better and more sublimely in proportion as they contemplate it more perfectly through understanding and observe it more diligently in their lives.

This discipline, then, commands those who desire to know it to follow a twofold order simultaneously, one part of which concerns life and the other education.

Young men devoted to study must live in such a way that they abstain from sexual affairs; from the enticements of the belly and the throat; from immoderate care and adornment of the body; from the empty business of games; from the sluggishness of sleep and laziness; from rivalry, detraction, and envy; from ambition for offices and powers; and even from an excessive desire for praise itself. They should believe that love of money is the surest poison of all their hopes.

Let them do nothing weakly, nothing rashly. In the sins of their associates, let them either wholly drive away anger or restrain it so that it resembles anger that has been driven out. Let them hate no one. Let them wish to neglect no vice. When they punish, let them take great care that it is not excessive; when they forgive, that it is not insufficient. Let them punish nothing that does not contribute to improvement; let them indulge nothing that turns toward deterioration.

Let them regard as their own all over whom authority has been given to them. Let them serve in such a way that they would be ashamed to rule them; let them rule in such a way that they take pleasure in serving them. In the sins of others, let them not be troublesome against their will. Let them avoid enmities with the greatest caution, endure them with the greatest equanimity, and bring them to an end with the greatest speed.

In every transaction and association with human beings, it is enough to observe this common proverb: “Let them do to no one what they do not want to suffer themselves.”

Let them not wish to administer the state unless they are fully formed. Let them hasten to become fully formed either before reaching senatorial age or, at any rate, before youth is past. But whoever turns to these pursuits late should not think that no precept applies to him, for with a more mature age he will certainly observe these things more easily. [Col. 1007]

Throughout life, in every place and at every time, let them either have friends or strive to have them. Let them show obedience even to the worthy who do not expect it. Let them pay little attention to the proud, and be least of all proud themselves. [Note: [Col. 1007] Thus the manuscripts and editions, except Lov., which reads *minimi sint* (“let them be least”).]

Let them live suitably and consistently. Let them worship, contemplate, and seek God, supported by faith, hope, and charity. Let them desire tranquility and a steady course for their studies and those of all their companions, and, for themselves and each other as far as possible, a good mind and a peaceful life.

## CHAPTER IX  
### We are led to learning by authority and reason.

26. Next I must explain how those devoted to study should be educated, once they have undertaken to live as described.

We are likewise led to learning in two ways: by authority and by reason. In time, authority comes first; in the matter itself, reason comes first. For one thing is what is given precedence in action, another what is valued more highly in desire.

Thus, although the authority of good men may seem more beneficial to the uneducated multitude, while reason is more suitable for the educated, nevertheless no human being becomes educated except from a state of ignorance. No ignorant person knows what attitude he ought to present to teachers or what kind of life can make him teachable. Consequently, for all who desire to learn great and hidden things, authority opens the door—and authority alone.

Once a person has entered through that door, he follows without hesitation the precepts of the best life. When he has thereby become teachable, he will finally learn both how much reason those very things possess which he followed before reason, and what reason itself is—the reason that, after the cradle of authority, he now follows and grasps, firm and capable; and what understanding is, in which all things exist, or rather which itself is all things; and what lies beyond all things: the principle of all things. [Note: [Col. 1007] Earlier printed editions read: “or rather all things themselves”; the manuscripts read more aptly: “or rather itself.”]

In this life, only a few can reach this knowledge; beyond it, no one can advance further even after this life.

But those who are content with authority alone and steadily devote themselves to good morals and upright desires—whether because they despise the liberal arts or are unable to be educated in them—how to call them blessed while they live among human beings, I do not know. Nevertheless, I firmly believe that as soon as they leave this body, they will be liberated more easily or with greater difficulty in proportion as they have lived better or worse.

27. Authority, however, is partly divine and partly human. True, firm, and supreme authority is that which is called divine.

In connection with it, one must beware of the astonishing deceitfulness of aerial creatures. Through certain predictions concerning things belonging to these bodily senses, and through certain powers, they are accustomed very easily to deceive souls that are either curious about perishable fortunes, eager for fragile powers, or fearful of empty miracles.

That authority, therefore, should be called divine which not only surpasses every human capacity in sensible signs, but, acting upon the human being himself, shows him how far it has humbled itself for his sake. [Col. 1008] It commands him not to remain attached to the senses by which those marvels appear, but to fly toward understanding, while at the same time demonstrating what power exists here, why it does these things, and how little it values them.

It must teach its power through deeds, its mercy through humility, and its nature through instruction. All these things are imparted more secretly and more firmly in the sacred rites by which we are initiated; through them the life of the good is cleansed most easily—not through the winding paths of disputation, but through the authority of mysteries.

Human authority, on the other hand, is usually deceptive. Nevertheless, it rightly seems to excel among those who, insofar as the understanding of the uneducated permits, offer many indications of their learning and do not live otherwise than they teach one ought to live.

If gifts of fortune have also come to such people, gifts whose greatness is evident in their use and even greater in their contempt, it is altogether difficult for anyone to be rightly blamed for trusting them when they give instructions about how to live.

## CHAPTER X  
### Few attain the principles of life.

28. Alypius then said: “You have set before our eyes a very great image of life, both fully and briefly established. Although we eagerly attend to it through your daily instructions, today you have made us still more desirous and ardent.

“If it were possible, I would wish not only that we but all human beings might already reach it and cling to it, so that these principles would be as easy to imitate as they are wonderful to hear. For I do not know how it happens—although may this be far from us—that while the human mind, on hearing these things, proclaims that they are heavenly, divine, and entirely true, it behaves differently in its desires. Thus it seems to me most true either that those who live in this way are divine human beings, or that they do not live so without divine assistance.”

I replied: “Although these principles of living, which—as always—you greatly approve, Alypius, have for the present been expressed in my words here, you know very well that I did not invent them. The books of great, almost divine men are filled with them. I thought I should say this not on your account but for the sake of these young men, so that they may not rightly despise my authority as though it were the source of these teachings.

“I do not want them to believe me at all unless I am teaching and giving an account of my reasons. I think that you introduced this speech in order to stir them to enthusiasm in proportion to the greatness of the subject.

“For these things are not difficult for you to follow. You seized them with such eagerness and entered upon them with such an impulse of your admirable nature that I have become your teacher in words, while you have become mine in realities. There is now no reason, or at least no opportunity, for you to lie: I do not think that you would become more devoted to study through false praise of yourself, and those who know both of us are present. Moreover, this speech will be sent to one for whom none of our affairs is unknown.”

29. “If you think and have spoken as you say,” I continued, “I believe that you think there are fewer good men devoted to the best morals than seems probable to me. But many are entirely hidden from you.

“Likewise, among many who are not hidden, the very things that are admirable remain hidden. These things are in the soul, which cannot be perceived by the senses. Often, while wishing to accommodate itself to the conversation of vicious people, the soul says things that it appears either to approve or desire.

“It also does many things unwillingly, either to avoid the hatred of others or to escape foolishness. When we hear or see these things, [Col. 1009] it is difficult for us to think otherwise than as this sense reports to us. Thus it happens that we believe many people are not what they themselves and their close associates know them to be.

“I would like you to be persuaded of this by some of the great virtues of soul possessed by our friends, which we alone know. For this error rests in no small measure upon the fact that many people suddenly turn toward a good and admirable life; [Note: [Col. 1009] Ten manuscripts read *nutritur* (“is nourished”); others, *innititur* (“rests upon”).] until they become known through some more conspicuous deeds, they are believed to remain what they formerly were.

“To come no farther afield, who would readily believe that these young men, whom no one previously knew, are now seeking great things so earnestly and have suddenly, at this age, declared such enmity toward pleasures?

“Let us therefore drive this opinion from our minds. That divine assistance which, as was fitting, you placed religiously at the end of your speech carries out the duty of its mercy among all peoples more widely than some suppose.

“But let us, if you please, return to the order of our discussion. Since enough has been said about authority, let us see what reason requires.”

## CHAPTER XI  
### What reason is, and its traces in sensible things. How the rational and the rationally produced differ.

30. Reason is the movement of the mind capable of distinguishing and connecting the things that are learned. Under its guidance, only a very rare kind of human being can proceed to understand God, or the soul itself—whether the soul is in us or exists everywhere.

The reason is simply that, once someone has advanced into the affairs of these senses, it is difficult for each person to return into himself. Thus, although people attempt to conduct everything by reason even in matters that are themselves deceptive, almost everyone is ignorant of what reason itself is and what kind it is.

This seems astonishing, but that is how things stand. For the present, it is enough to have said this. If I now wished to display so great a matter to you as it ought to be understood, I would be as foolish as I would be presumptuous if I professed that I had already grasped it myself.

Nevertheless, insofar as reason has deigned to advance into things that seem known to us, let us investigate it, if we can for the moment, as the discussion we have undertaken requires.

31. First, then, let us see where this word *reason* is usually employed. For this ought especially to move us: the ancient sages defined the human being in this way: “The human being is a rational mortal animal.”

Once the genus—what is called “animal”—has been established, we see two differences added. I believe that through them the human being was meant to be warned both of where he must return and from where he must flee.

For just as the soul’s advance was a fall into mortal things, so its return ought to be a return into reason. By one word, “rational,” the human being is separated from beasts; by another, “mortal,” from divine beings. Therefore, unless he maintains the former, he will be a beast; unless he turns himself away from the latter, he will not be divine.

But since the most learned men are accustomed to distinguish sharply and subtly between the *rational* and the *rationally produced*, this must by no means be neglected for our present purpose. They have said that something is rational if it uses or can use reason; but rationally produced if it has been made or spoken by reason.

Thus we can call these baths rationally produced, as we can call our speech rationally produced; but we call the person who made these baths, or us who speak, rational. [Col. 1010] Reason therefore proceeds from the rational soul, specifically into things that are either made or spoken rationally.

32. I therefore see two areas in which the power and force of reason can be brought even before the senses themselves: the works of human beings that are seen, and the words that are heard.

In both cases the mind uses a twofold messenger for the needs of the body: one belonging to the eyes and the other to the ears.

Thus, when we see something formed with parts that correspond to one another, we do not speak absurdly when we say that it appears rationally constituted. Likewise, when we hear something harmonize well, we do not hesitate to say that it sounds rationally.

No one would fail to be ridiculed if he said, “It smells rationally,” or “It tastes rationally,” or “It is rationally soft”—unless perhaps he meant things arranged by human beings for a purpose, so that they might smell, taste, or feel in a certain way, or something similar.

For example, if someone called a place from which snakes are driven away by strong odors “rationally odorous,” considering the reason why it had been made; or if he called a cup prepared by a physician rationally bitter or sweet; or if he called a bath which a physician had ordered to be tempered for a sick person rationally hot or warm.

But no one, on entering a garden and bringing a rose to his nose, would dare to say: “How rationally it smells!”—not even if a physician had ordered him to smell it.

In that case the command or gift may be called rationally given, but the odor is not called rationally odorous, nor is this because the odor is natural.

For although we can say that a dish has been rationally seasoned by a cook, we cannot, according to ordinary usage, say that it tastes rationally when there is no external reason but only present pleasure to be satisfied.

If one asks about the person to whom a physician has given a cup why he ought to perceive it as sweet, another cause is offered for its being so: namely, the kind of illness, which is no longer in that sensation but exists in another condition within the body.

But if a glutton, aroused by the stimulus of appetite, is asked why something is so sweet and answers, “Because I like it,” or “Because I enjoy it,” no one will call it rationally sweet—unless perhaps his pleasure is necessary for some purpose and what he is eating has been prepared in that way for that reason.

33. So far as we have been able to investigate, we have grasped certain traces of reason in the senses. In what concerns sight and hearing, they are found even in pleasure itself.

The other senses usually require this designation not in their own pleasure but for the sake of something else. That “something else” is an act of a rational animal performed for some end. [Note: [Col. 1010] Lov. reads, “But the other senses in their pleasure.” The other manuscripts read, “not in their pleasure.”]

As for the eyes, where correspondence among parts is called rationally constituted, it is usually called beautiful. As for the ears, when we call a harmony rational and say that a measured song has been rationally composed, it is called by its proper name, sweetness.

Yet when color attracts us in beautiful things, or when a struck string sounds as though liquid and pure, we do not ordinarily call that rational. It remains, therefore, that in the pleasure of these senses we should acknowledge something pertaining to reason wherever there is a certain measurement and modulation.

34. Thus, carefully considering the individual parts of this very building, [Col. 1011] we cannot help being annoyed that we see one door on the side and another near the middle, though not placed in the middle. In things constructed by human beings, when no necessity compels it, unequal measurement of the parts seems to inflict a kind of injury upon the sight itself.

But inside, three windows—one in the middle and two at the sides—pour light upon the bath-seat at equal intervals. How much this delights us when we look at it attentively, and how strongly it draws the mind toward itself, is evident and does not need to be disclosed to you in many words. [Note: [Col. 1011] Er. and Lov. read *solis* (“upon the sun”); twelve manuscripts, together with Bad. and Am., read *solio lumen infundunt* (“pour light upon the bath-seat”), that is, the vessel of the baths on which those bathing sat; see above, no. 32.]

Hence architects themselves already call this arrangement *reason* by their own term, and say that parts placed discordantly “lack reason.” This is widely evident and extends through almost all the arts and works of human beings.

Now in poems, in which we likewise say that there is a reason belonging to the pleasure of the ears, who does not perceive that measurement is the maker of all this sweetness?

But when an actor is dancing, and all his gestures are signs of things to attentive spectators, although a certain measured movement of the limbs delights the eyes by that same proportion, the dance is nevertheless called rationally constituted because it signifies and displays something well—apart from the pleasure of the senses.

For if he portrays winged Venus and Cupid wearing a cloak, even though he depicts them through a remarkable movement and arrangement of the limbs, he does not seem to offend the eyes; rather, through the eyes he affects the mind, to which those signs of things are displayed. The eyes would be offended if he did not move beautifully. That belongs to the sense in which the soul, by the very fact that it is mingled with the body, perceives pleasure.

Thus one thing is the sense, another what is conveyed through the sense. A beautiful movement soothes the sense; but through the sense, the beautiful significance in the movement reaches the mind alone.

This is more easily observed in the ears. Whatever sounds pleasantly is pleasing and attracts the hearing itself. [Note: [Col. 1011] B reads: “Whatever sounds pleasantly pleases and attracts that very hearing.” We have followed the reading of Er., Er., Guill., Ven., Lov., and Par., as preferable. M.] But whatever is signified well through the same sound is related, through the messenger of the ears, to the mind alone.

Thus, when we hear those verses:

> Why do the suns hasten so greatly to bathe themselves in Ocean,
>
> In winter, or what delay obstructs the slow nights?  
> (Virgil, *Georgics* 2.480–481.)

we praise the meter in one way and the meaning in another. We do not say, with the same understanding, “It sounds rationally” and “It has been rationally spoken.”

## CHAPTER XII  
### Reason as the inventor of all the disciplines. The origin of words. The origin of letters. The origin of numbers. The origin of the distinction between letters, syllables, and words. The origin of history.

35. There are therefore now three kinds of things in which the rationally produced appears. One is found in actions related to some end, another in speaking, [Note: [Col. 1011] Most manuscripts read *discendo* (“in learning”).] and a third in giving pleasure. The first warns us to do nothing rashly; the second, to teach correctly; the last, to contemplate happily.

The first belongs to morals; the other two to the disciplines with which we are now concerned.

For the rational element within us—that is, what uses reason and either makes or follows rationally produced things—[Col. 1012] was bound by a natural bond to the fellowship of those with whom reason itself was shared. Since one human being could not be joined most firmly to another unless they conversed and thereby poured their minds and thoughts, as it were, into one another, reason saw that names had to be imposed upon things: certain significant sounds, so that, since minds could not be perceived directly, they might use sense as an interpreter to join them to one another.

But the words of absent people could not be heard. Therefore reason brought forth letters, marking and distinguishing all the sounds of the mouth and tongue.

Yet it could do none of this if the multitude of things seemed to extend infinitely, without some fixed limit. Thus the usefulness of counting was recognized under great necessity.

Once these two discoveries had been made, there arose the profession of copyists and *calculoni*, as it were a kind of infancy of grammar, which Varro calls *litteratio*. I do not presently recall what it is called in Greek. [Note: [Col. 1012] Bad. and some manuscripts read *calculorum professio* (“the profession of counters”). But other manuscripts more correctly read *calculonum*. By this name, which most lexicographers have omitted, schoolmasters were formerly called who first undertook to train boys in reading, writing, and counting. This is relevant to the statement of Julius Capitolinus in *Pertinax*: “A boy trained in elementary letters and calculation.” Likewise Augustine says in *Confessions* 1.13: “I had come to love Latin letters—not those taught by the first teachers, but those taught by men called grammarians. For I found those first lessons, in which one learns to read, write, and count, no less burdensome and punitive.” From this one can finally understand Tertullian’s statement at the end of *On the Pallium*: “The first teacher of letters, the first disentangler of speech, and the first sand-counter of numbers.”]

36. Reason then advanced and observed that among the same sounds of the mouth with which we spoke, and which it had already marked with letters, some flowed from the throat without any collision, through a measured and varied opening, as though loosened and simple; others, through a different compression of the mouth, nevertheless retained some sound; while the final kind could not burst forth unless joined to the initial sounds.

Accordingly, it named the letters, in the order in which they have been described, vowels, semivowels, and mutes.

Next it marked syllables. Then words were divided into eight kinds and forms, and all their movement, integrity, and conjunction were distinguished with skill and subtlety.

Thereafter, not forgetting numbers and measurement, it applied its attention to the varying durations of sounds and syllables. From this it discovered that some intervals of time were double and others single, by which long and short syllables were extended. It also marked these distinctions and arranged them according to fixed rules.

37. Grammar could now have been complete. But because by its very name it professes letters—for which reason it is also called *litteratura* in Latin—whatever was committed to letters as worthy of remembrance necessarily came under its scope.

Thus one name, but an infinite and multifarious subject, fuller of cares than of pleasure or truth, was added to this discipline: history. It was laborious not so much for historians as for grammarians.

For who could endure its not being thought that a man is uneducated if he has not heard that Daedalus flew; a liar if he invented it; a fool if he believed it; or impudent if he asked? [Note: [Col. 1012] Most manuscripts read *dixerit* (“has said it”).]

Or consider what I often deeply pity in our own acquaintances: if they do not answer what Euryalus’s mother was called, they are accused of ignorance, even though they themselves would not dare to call foolish and inept, or lacking in curiosity, those who ask such questions of them.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### The invention of dialectic and rhetoric.

38. Thus reason, grammar having been perfected and ordered, was prompted to seek and attend to the very power by which it had produced the art. [Note: [Col. 1013] Er. and Lov. read *ratione* (“reason”), rather than *ratio* (“reason” as the subject).] For by defining, dividing, and collecting, it had not merely arranged and ordered things; it had also defended them against every intrusion of falsehood.

When, then, could it proceed to construct other things unless it first distinguished, marked, arranged, and made known its own devices and instruments, as it were, and disclosed the discipline of disciplines which they call dialectic? [Note: Er. and Lov. read *ratione* (“by reason”).]

Dialectic teaches how to teach; it teaches how to learn. In it reason displays and reveals itself: what it is, what it desires, and what it can do. It knows how to know. It alone not only wishes to make people knowledgeable but is able to do so.

But because foolish people generally follow, in matters rightly, usefully, and honorably urged upon them, not the utterly pure truth which a rare mind perceives but their own senses and customary habits, it was necessary not merely to teach them as much as they could grasp, but also often, and especially, to move them deeply.

This part of itself, which performed that task and was fuller of necessity than of purity, it called rhetoric. It filled its lap with delights to scatter among the people, so that they might deign to be led toward their own advantage.

Up to this point, that part which is called rationally produced in signification has been advanced through liberal studies and disciplines.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Music and poetry. The three kinds of sound. The origin of verse. Rhythm.

39. From there reason wished to carry itself toward the most blessed contemplation of divine realities. [Note: [Col. 1013] Bad., Am., Er., and the better manuscripts read *rapere* (“carry itself”); Lov. and four manuscripts substitute *reparare* (“restore itself”).] But, lest it fall from a height, it sought steps and fashioned a path for itself through its possessions and order. It desired a beauty that could be contemplated without these eyes, by itself and in its simplicity; the senses stood in its way.

Accordingly, it turned its attention for a little while toward those very senses. They were loudly claiming to possess truth and were calling it back, with unwelcome clamor, from its haste to proceed to other things.

First it began with the ears, because they said that the words themselves belonged to them—the words through which it had already made grammar, dialectic, and rhetoric.

But this power, supremely capable of distinguishing, quickly saw the difference between a sound and that of which it was the sign. It understood that nothing belonged to the judgment of the ears except sound, and that sound was of three kinds: either in the voice of a living being, or in what breath produced in instruments, or in what was produced by striking.

The first belongs to tragedians, comedians, choruses of every kind, and all who sing with their own voice. The second is assigned to flutes and similar instruments. The third belongs to zithers, lyres, cymbals, and everything that produces a musical sound by being struck.

40. It saw that this material was extremely base unless sounds were shaped by a fixed measurement of time and by a regulated variation of high and low pitch.

It recognized here the seeds which, when it carefully examined syllables in grammar, it had called feet and accents.

Since it was easy in speech to observe the shortness and length of syllables, [Col. 1014] scattered in almost equal numbers, it attempted to arrange and join those feet in fixed orders. At first, following the sense itself, it impressed measured articulations, which it called sections and members.

And lest the course of the feet roll on farther than its judgment could sustain, it established a limit at which it would turn back, and called it a verse from that very fact.

But what was not regulated by a fixed ending, yet proceeded through rationally ordered feet, it marked by the name rhythm—which in Latin could mean nothing other than number.

Thus poets were born from it. When it saw in them the great significance not only of sounds but also of words and things, it honored them greatly and granted them power over whatever rationally constituted fictions they wished.

And because they traced their origin to that first discipline, it permitted grammarians to be their judges.

41. At this fourth level, whether in rhythms or in modulation itself, reason understood that numbers reigned and completed everything.
