It examined carefully what kind they were and discovered them to be divine and everlasting—especially since, with their assistance, it had woven together all the higher disciplines.

It was already suffering greatly that their brilliance and serenity were being discolored by the bodily material of voices.

Since what the mind sees is always present and is judged immortal, and since numbers appeared to be of this kind, while sound, being a sensible thing, flows away into past time and is impressed upon memory, reason—now favoring poets in their rationally constituted fiction (one must ask whether something similar belonged to their offspring)—fashioned the story that the Muses were daughters of Jupiter and Memory. From this discipline, partaking of sense and understanding, the name music arose.

## CHAPTER XV  
### Geometry and astronomy.

42. From there reason advanced into the resources of the eyes. As it surveyed earth and heaven, [Col. 1015] it perceived that nothing pleased it except beauty; in beauty, figures; in figures, dimensions; and in dimensions, numbers.

It asked itself whether a line, a circle, or any other form and figure there was of the kind contained in understanding. It found the visible form far inferior, and discovered that what the eyes saw could in no respect be compared with what the mind perceived.

It likewise distinguished and ordered these things, reduced them to a discipline, and called it geometry.

The movement of the heavens deeply moved it and invited it to examine itself carefully. There too, through the most constant cycles of time, through the fixed and determined courses of the stars, and through the measured intervals of space, it understood that nothing other than that same dimension and those same numbers held dominion.

By defining and distinguishing these things in the same way and linking them into an order, it gave birth to astrology: a great argument for the religious, and a torment for the curious.

43. In all these disciplines, therefore, reason encountered everything arranged according to number, although these arrangements appeared more clearly in the dimensions which it contemplated as most true by thinking and revolving them within itself. In the things perceived by the senses, it recalled rather their shadows and traces.

Here it raised itself greatly and presumed greatly; it dared to establish the soul’s immortality. [Note: [Col. 1015] Lov. reads *ita ausa est* (“thus it dared”); *ita* is absent from the manuscripts.]

It examined everything carefully and fully grasped that it possessed very great power—and that whatever it could do, it could do through numbers.

A certain wonder moved it, and it began to suspect that it itself might perhaps be that very number by which all things were counted; or, if it was not this, that the number was nevertheless there, where it strove to arrive.

It grasped this number with all its strength. It was already destined to become the index of universal truth—the one whom Alypius mentioned when we were discussing the Academics—as though Proteus were in its hands (*Against the Academics* 3.5.11).

For false images of the things we count, flowing from that most hidden principle by which we count, seize thought and carry it into themselves; and often, when that principle is already being grasped, they cause it to slip away.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### The liberal disciplines raise the intellect toward divine things.

44. If anyone does not yield to these considerations, and reduces to one simple and certain truth all the things dispersed widely and variously throughout so many disciplines, he is most deserving of the name “learned”; and now he seeks those divine realities not rashly, no longer merely to be believed, but also to be contemplated, understood, and retained. But whoever is either still a slave to desires and gaping after perishable things, or, though already fleeing these things and living chastely, nevertheless does not know what “nothing” is; what unformed matter is; what is formed but lifeless; what body is; what form in a body is; what place is; what time is; what is in place; what is in time; what motion according to place is; what motion not according to place is; what stationary motion is; what an age is; what it is to be neither in a place nor nowhere [Note: [Col. 1015] Thus the manuscripts and the printed editions except Lov., which in the text prefers *usquam*, “anywhere.”]; what it is to be beyond time and always; what it is both to be nowhere and not to be nowhere; and what it is never to be and never not to be—whoever, then, does not know these things and wishes to inquire and dispute, I do not say about that supreme God, who is better known by not knowing, but about his own soul, will err as greatly as it is possible to err. Yet he will more easily understand these matters who has grasped the simple and intelligible numbers. Moreover, he will grasp these who, being gifted in intelligence, free from occupation by reason of age or any other good fortune, and ardently inflamed with zeal, has pursued the aforementioned order of disciplines as far as is sufficient. For although all those liberal arts are learned partly for the practical purposes of life and partly for the knowledge and contemplation of things, it is exceedingly difficult to attain their practical use unless one has devoted oneself to them from childhood with exceptional intelligence, the greatest diligence, and unwavering perseverance.

## CHAPTER XVII — The Uninstructed in the Disciplines Should Not Approach Difficult Questions

45. As for what we need from those disciplines for the matter we are investigating, please do not let this, as though it were some immense forest of things, frighten you, mother. For a very few things will be selected from them all, though extremely powerful in their force [Note: [Col. 1015] Lov.: “very few in number, that is, extremely powerful.”], and difficult for many to understand; yet for you, whose intelligence seems to me daily something new, and whose mind I recognize as having risen far above all trivialities, whether by age or by admirable self-control, and as emerging from the great stain of the body, they will be as easy as they are difficult for those who live most sluggishly and miserably.

For if I were to say that you would easily reach a form of speech free from defects of diction and language, I would certainly be lying. Even I myself, who had great necessity to learn these matters thoroughly, am still mocked by Italians in many sounds of words; and in turn I criticize them with regard to the sound itself. For it is one thing to be secure by art, another to be secure by nationality. As for the solecisms, as we call them, perhaps any learned person who pays close attention will find some in my speech; for there was no lack of someone who most skillfully persuaded me that Cicero himself had committed certain such faults. The kind of barbarism in our own times has been found to be such that even the speech by which Rome was saved appears barbarous. But you, disregarding these childish matters or matters that do not concern you, understand the almost divine power and nature of grammar so well that you seem to have grasped its soul and left its body to the eloquent.

46. I would say the same about the other arts of this kind. If you perhaps utterly despise them, I admonish you, insofar as I dare as your son and insofar as you permit me, to guard firmly and carefully the faith you have received through venerable mysteries; and then to remain throughout this life steadfastly and watchfully in conduct and character.

But concerning the most obscure and yet divine questions—how God both does no evil and is omnipotent, while such great evils occur; for what purpose he made the world, since he had no need of it; and whether evil has always existed or began at some point; and, if it always existed, whether it existed under God’s control; and, if it did, whether this world too has always existed, in which that evil held dominion by the divine ordering [Note: [Col. 1016] In B., *domitaretur*. So also Er. and Guill.; but Lov. and Par. have *dominaretur*. M.]; but if this world at some time began to exist, how evil was held by God’s power before the world existed; and what need there was to construct a world in which the evil already restrained by God’s power might be enclosed for the punishment of souls; but if there was a time when evil did not exist under God’s dominion, what suddenly happened that had not happened throughout the eternal ages before—concerning these questions, and others like them, either inquiry must be made according to that order of learning, or not at all.

For it is impious, or rather utterly foolish, to say that a new plan arose in God. But if we call evil troublesome and, as it were, rebellious against God, as some suppose, no learned person will refrain from laughter, and no unlearned person will fail to become indignant. For how could that evil nature of some unknown kind have harmed God? If they say that it could not, it will not be the reason for constructing the world; if they say that it could, it is an unforgivable sacrilege to believe that God can be violated—and not even merely in such a way that he provided by his power that his own substance should not be violated. For they admit that the soul suffers punishment here, while they wish there to be absolutely no difference between its substance and God’s. But if we say that this world was not made, it is impious and ungrateful to believe so, lest the consequence be that God did not construct it. Therefore, concerning these and similar matters, inquiry must be made either according to that order of learning or not at all.

## CHAPTER XVIII — The Order by Which the Soul Advances to Knowledge of Itself and of Unity Itself. All Things Tend Toward Unity

[Col. 1017]

47. And lest anyone think that we have embraced some exceedingly broad subject, I shall put it more plainly and briefly. No one ought to aspire to knowledge of these matters without that almost twofold science of sound reasoning and the power of numbers. If anyone thinks even this too much, let him know either numbers alone very well or dialectic alone. If even this is infinite, let him at least know perfectly what “one” is in numbers and how much power it possesses—not yet in that supreme law and supreme order of all things, but in those things that we perceive and do every day and everywhere.

For philosophy itself takes over this learning, and in it finds nothing more than what “one” is, but at a far higher and more divine level. Its inquiry is twofold: one part concerns the soul, the other God. The first makes us know ourselves; the second, our origin. The former is sweeter to us, the latter dearer; the former makes us worthy of the blessed life, the latter makes us blessed. The first belongs to those who are learning, the second to those who are already learned. This is the order of studies in wisdom, by which each person becomes capable of understanding the order of things—that is, of discerning the two worlds and the very Father of the universe, of whom there is no knowledge in the soul except knowing how it does not know him.

48. Keeping to this order, the soul, now committed to philosophy, first looks into itself. And since that prior learning has persuaded it either that its own [faculty] is reason, or that it itself is reason, and that in reason there is either nothing better or more powerful than numbers, or that reason is nothing other than number, it will speak to itself in this way:

“I can, by a certain inner and hidden motion of my own, distinguish and connect the things that are to be learned, and this power of mine is called reason. But what is there to distinguish except what is thought to be one but is not, or at least is not as much one as it is thought to be? Again, why is anything to be connected except that it may become one insofar as possible? Therefore, both in distinguishing and in connecting, I desire unity and love unity. But when I distinguish, I desire what has been purified; when I connect, I desire what is whole. In the former activity foreign elements are avoided; in the latter, proper elements are joined together, so that something perfect may become one.

“A stone, in order to be a stone, has all its parts and its entire nature solidified into one. What of a tree? Would it not cease to be a tree if it were not one? What of the limbs and internal organs of any living creature, and of everything from which it is constituted? Certainly, if they suffer separation from unity, it will not be an animal. What else are friends trying to do except to be one? And the more they are one, the more they are friends. A people is one state, and dissension is dangerous to it. But what is dissension except not having one judgment? From many soldiers there arises one army. Is not any multitude overcome less easily the more closely it gathers into one? Hence that gathering into one has been called a *cuneus* [“wedge”], as though from *co-uneus* [“one together”]. What is all love? Does it not wish to become one with what it loves, and, if this happens, does it not become one with it? Pleasure itself delights more intensely for no other reason than that bodies loving one another are forced together into one. Why is pain harmful? Because it attempts to tear apart what was one” [Col. 1018] [Note: [Col. 1018] Lov., *discindere nititur*, “attempts to cut apart.” Er., *disjicere*, “to scatter.” Bad., *dishiscere*, “to gape apart.” But Am. and ten manuscripts prefer *dissicere*. The learned observe that this verb was accepted by ancient authors and restore it in various places with the help of the manuscripts.].

## CHAPTER XIX — How Man Is Superior to Brutes, and How He Can See God

Therefore it is troublesome and dangerous to become one with something that can be separated.

49. From many things lying about here and there, then gathered into one form, I make one house. I am better, since I make it, while it is made; better, because I make it. There is no doubt that I am therefore better than the house. But for that reason I am not better than a swallow or a little bee. For the one constructs nests skillfully, the other honeycombs. Yet I am better than these because I am a rational animal.

But if reason is present in dimensions, are the things that birds construct any less suitably and harmoniously measured? On the contrary, they are full of number. Therefore I am not better because I make things possessing number, but because I know numbers. What then? Could they, without knowing, make things possessing number? They certainly could. How is this shown? By the fact that we too fit our tongue to our teeth and palate according to definite dimensions, so that letters and words burst forth from the mouth, and yet when we speak we do not consider by what movement of the mouth we ought to do this.

Furthermore, what good singer, even if untrained in music, does not, by natural sensation itself, preserve in memory while singing both rhythm and melody as perceived? What could be produced with more numerical order than this? The unlearned person does not know this, but nevertheless does it through nature at work. When, then, is he better, and to be preferred to animals? When he knows what he is doing. Nothing else, then, places me above the animal except that I am a rational animal.

50. How, then, is reason immortal, while I am defined as something both rational and mortal? Is reason not immortal? Yet the ratio of one to two, or of two to four, is most truly a ratio. It was no more true yesterday than it is today; nor will it be more true tomorrow or a year from now; and even if this whole world should collapse, that ratio could not cease to exist. For it is always such as it is.

But this world did not have yesterday what it has today, nor will it have tomorrow what it has today; indeed, even on this very day, it has not had the sun in the same place for the space of a single hour. Thus, since nothing remains in it, it possesses nothing in the same way even for a short interval of time.

Therefore, if reason is immortal, and I, who either distinguish or connect all these things, am reason, then what makes me mortal is not mine. Or, if the soul is not reason and yet I use reason and am made better through reason, I must flee from the worse to the better, from the mortal to the immortal.

The well-instructed soul speaks and reflects upon these and many other matters with itself. I do not wish to pursue them, lest, while I am eager to teach you the order, I exceed the measure that is the parent of order. For step by step it leads itself to the best character and life, no longer by faith alone but by certain reason.

To one who carefully observes the force and power of numbers, it will seem exceedingly disgraceful and exceedingly lamentable that, through his knowledge, he should make a verse run smoothly and a lyre sound harmoniously, while his life—and he himself, who is the soul—follows a crooked path and, with desire ruling him, resounds discordantly with the most shameful clamor of vices [Col. 1019].

51. But when it has composed and ordered itself, and made itself harmonious and beautiful, it will now dare to see God, the very source from which all truth flows, the very Father of Truth. Great God, what eyes those will be! How sound, how beautiful, how strong, how steadfast, how serene, how blessed!

But what is it that they see? What, I ask? What should we think, what estimate should we make, what should we say? Everyday words come to mind, and all have been sullied by the basest matters. I shall say nothing more than that we are promised a vision of a beauty in whose imitation other things are beautiful and in comparison with which they are ugly.

Whoever sees this—for he will see it who lives well, prays well, and studies well—when will he be troubled by the fact that one person, wishing to have children, does not have them; another exposes children in abundance; another hates those who are to be born; another loves those already born? How is it not contradictory that nothing will occur which is not with God, from whom all things must necessarily proceed according to order, and yet that God is not prayed to in vain?

Finally, when will any burdens, dangers, annoyances, or flatteries of fortune trouble the just man? In this sensible world, one must carefully consider what time and place are, so that what gives pleasure in a part, whether of place or of time, may nevertheless be understood to be far inferior to the whole of which that part is a part. Conversely, what is offensive in a part should be clear to the learned person as offensive for no other reason than that the whole, to which that part wonderfully corresponds, is not seen.

But in that intelligible world, every part, as though it were the whole, is beautiful and perfect [Note: [Col. 1019] Er. and Ven., “every part entirely beautiful and perfect.” Lov., “every part, as though it were the whole, entirely beautiful and perfect.” M.].

These matters will be discussed at greater length if your studies undertake to follow, as I urge and hope, either the order we have mentioned or perhaps another order that is shorter and more convenient, provided that it is nevertheless correct, and if they maintain it altogether seriously and steadfastly.

## CHAPTER XX — Epilogue Encouraging a Good Life

52. To make this possible for us, we must devote the greatest effort to the best character. For our God cannot otherwise hear us; but he will most readily hear those who live well (1 *Retractationes*, ch. 3, no. 3).

Let us pray, therefore, not that riches, honors, or things of this kind—which are unstable and fleeting and pass away whenever anything resists them—may come to us, but that those things may come which make us good and blessed.

And that these prayers may be fulfilled with the greatest devotion, we especially entrust this task to you, mother. I firmly and confidently believe that through your prayers God gave me this disposition of mind: to place absolutely nothing before the discovery of truth, to desire nothing else, to think of nothing else, and to love nothing else [Col. 1020]. Nor do I cease to believe that we shall obtain this great good, which we desired through your merit, because you ask for it as well.

But what should I exhort you to do, Alypius? What should I advise you? You are not excessive for this reason: because, however much one may love such things, perhaps it can always be called too little, but never rightly too much.

53. Then he said: “You have truly brought it about that, both through daily reflection and through this present admiration we have for you, we not only have no doubt about the memory of the most learned and great men—which once seemed incredible in view of the greatness of their achievements—but could even swear to it if necessary.

“For what? Has not that venerable and almost divine discipline of Pythagoras, which was rightly both practiced and approved, been opened up by you today almost before our very eyes [Note: [Col. 1020] Er.: “For what has not been opened up to us concerning that venerable …?” M.] (1 *Retractationes*, ch. 3, no. 3)? You have indicated, briefly yet so fully, both the rules of life and not merely the paths of knowledge but the very fields and clear waters, and—something that was held in great reverence by that man himself—the very shrines of truth: where they were, what they were like, and what sort of people sought them. Although we suspect and believe that you still possess more secret things, we nevertheless would think ourselves shameless if we supposed that anything further ought to be demanded from you.”

54. “I gladly accept this,” I replied. “For I am delighted and encouraged not so much by your words, which are not true, as by the true spirit in your words. And it is fortunate that we have decided to send this letter to the man who is accustomed gladly to tell many lies about us. If perhaps others should read it, I do not fear that they will be angry with you either. For who would not forgive an error in judgment arising from affection with the greatest kindness?

“But as for your mention of Pythagoras, I believe that it came to your mind through some hidden and divine ordering. A very important matter had entirely escaped me: something that I regularly admire in that man—if anything committed to writing is worthy of belief, though who would not believe Varro?—and, as you know, regularly extol almost every day in my praises (ibid.): namely, that he handed over the discipline of governing the state as the final subject to his pupils, when they were already learned, already perfected, already wise, already blessed.

“For he saw so many waves there that he did not wish to entrust them to anyone except a man who, in governing, could avoid the reefs almost divinely and, if everything failed, could himself become for those waves something like a reef. For it can most truly be said of the wise man alone:

> He, like a rock unmoved in the sea, withstands;

and the other things that have been said in shining verses to this effect (*Aeneid* 7.585–589).”

This brought the discussion to an end, and, with everyone joyful and full of hope, we dismissed the gathering when the nocturnal light had already been brought in.

[Col. 1019]

[Note: [Col. 1019]

## On the Following Book, *On the Immortality of the Soul*

See Book 1, chapter 5, of the *Retractations*, cols. 590–591, from the words “After the books of the *Soliloquies*,” no. 1, through the words of no. 3, “In some places there is a discipline.” M.]

# St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On the Immortality of the Soul*

One book [Note: [Col. 1021] Written in the year of Christ 387.] [Note: [Col. 1021] Revised against the manuscripts: the very old Corneliensis, Corbeiensis, Michaelinus, Sergiensis, Ebrulphensis, Vindocinensis, Regiomontensis, two Victorini, two Sorbonici, Bigotianus, Vedastinus, and Vaticanus; against variant readings excerpted by the Louvain editors from three Belgian manuscripts; and finally against the editions of Bad., Am., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 1021] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.] (C)

## [Collection of Arguments for the Immortality of the Soul]

[Col. 1021] This book contains a collection of arguments for the immortality of the soul, as well as solutions to difficulties arising along the way.

## CHAPTER I — The First Argument: The Soul Is Immortal Because It Is the Subject of a Discipline That Always Exists

[Col. 1021]

1. If discipline exists anywhere, and can exist only in something that lives, and is always present, then nothing in which something is always present can fail to be always present. What lives always is that in which discipline exists.

If we are the ones who reason—that is, if our mind is the one that reasons—then it cannot reason correctly without discipline; nor can the mind exist without discipline, unless it can exist in that in which discipline is not present. Discipline is present in the human mind.

Discipline exists somewhere, for it exists, and whatever exists cannot exist nowhere. Again, discipline cannot exist except in something that lives. For nothing that does not live learns anything; nor can discipline exist in something that learns nothing [Note: [Col. 1021] 1 *Retractations*, chapter 5, no. 2.].

Again, discipline always exists. For what exists and is unchangeable must necessarily always exist. No one denies that discipline exists. And whoever admits that it is impossible for a line drawn through the center of a circle not to be the longest of all lines not drawn through the center, and that this belongs to some discipline, does not deny that discipline is unchangeable.

Again, nothing in which something is always present can fail to be always present. For nothing that always exists can at some point suffer the removal of that in which it always exists.

Now, when we reason, the mind is at work. For only what understands can perform this activity; the body does not understand, nor does the mind understand with the body’s assistance, because when it wishes to understand, it turns away from the body. That which is understood is always of this kind [Note: [Col. 1021] Am., Er., and Lov.: “that which understands.” But Bad. and the manuscripts, both here and in Book 1 of the *Retractations*, chapter 5, have *intelligitur*, “is understood.”] [Note: [Col. 1021] Ibid.]; and nothing bodily is always of this kind. Therefore the body cannot assist the mind striving toward understanding, since it is enough if it does not impede it.

Again, no one reasons correctly without discipline. Correct reasoning is thought proceeding from certainties toward the investigation of uncertainties [Note: [Col. 1021] Six manuscripts have *cognitio*, “knowledge.”]. Nothing is certain in the mind that it does not know. Everything the mind knows, however, it has within itself; and knowledge embraces no matter except one that belongs to some discipline [Note: [Col. 1021] Ibid.]. For discipline is knowledge of things of every kind. Therefore the human mind always lives.

## CHAPTER II — Another Argument: The Soul Is the Subject of Reason, Which Does Not Change

[Col. 1022]

2. Reason is certainly either the mind or something in the mind. Our reason, however, is better than our body; and our body is a substance, while it is better to be a substance than nothing. Therefore reason is not nothing.

Again, whatever harmony belongs to the body must necessarily be inseparably present in the subject, the body; and nothing else should be thought to exist in that harmony which is not equally and necessarily present in that body as its subject, in which the harmony itself is no less inseparably present.

But the human body is changeable, whereas reason is unchangeable. For everything that is not always in the same way is changeable. And “two and four are six” is always in the same way [Note: [Col. 1022] In B., “and six.” Par. has “six,” without the little word *et*. We have judged the latter reading preferable. M.].

Likewise, it is always in the same way that what is four is what two and two have; but two do not have this. Therefore two are not four. This reason is unchangeable; therefore it is reason.

But when the subject is changed, that which is inseparably in it cannot fail to change. Therefore the harmony of the body is not the mind. Nor can death happen to unchangeable things. Therefore the mind always lives, whether it is itself reason or reason is inseparably in it.

## CHAPTER III — A Living and Unchangeable Substance: Even If the Soul Is Changeable in Some Way, It Does Not Therefore Become Mortal

3. There is a certain power of constancy, and all constancy is unchangeable; every virtue can do something, and when it does nothing, it is not virtue [Note: [Col. 1022] Lov. has “and when it does not do something.” But *non* is absent from the manuscripts and ought to be absent.].

Moreover, every action either is moved or moves. Therefore either not everything that is moved is changeable, or at least not everything that moves is changeable.

But everything that is moved by another and does not itself move is mortal. Nor is anything mortal unchangeable. Therefore, with certainty and without any remaining alternative, we conclude that not everything that moves changes.

No motion exists without a substance; and every substance either lives or does not live. Everything that does not live is lifeless, and there is no lifeless action. Therefore that which moves in such a way that it does not change can be nothing other than a living substance.

Every such substance moves the body through whatever degrees there are. Therefore not everything that moves the body is changeable.

The body, however, is moved only according to time. For slower and faster motion belong to time. It follows that there is something which moves in time and yet does not change.

But everything that moves the body in time, even if it tends toward a single end, cannot do everything simultaneously and cannot fail to do more than one thing. For, however it may be accomplished, neither can what is divisible into parts be made perfectly one by any means, nor is there any body without parts, nor any time without an interval of delay, nor even the briefest syllable can be uttered whose end you do not hear only when you are no longer hearing its beginning.

Moreover, what is performed in this way requires expectation in order to be completed and memory in order to be grasped as far as possible. Expectation concerns future things, while memory concerns things past. Attention to action belongs to the present time, through which the future passes into the past; and the end of a bodily motion that has begun cannot be awaited without some memory.

For how can one await the ending of what one has forgotten either began or even moved at all? Again, the present attention to completing something cannot exist without expectation of the future end. Nor is there anything that either does not yet exist or no longer exists.

Therefore, in action there can be something that belongs to things not yet existing. Several things can exist simultaneously in the agent, although the several things being done cannot exist simultaneously. They can therefore also exist in the mover, although they cannot exist in that which is being moved.

But whatever things cannot exist simultaneously in time and yet are conveyed from the future into the past must necessarily be changeable.

4. From this we now infer that there can be something which, while it moves changeable things, does not change. For when the mover’s intention to bring the body it moves to whatever end it wishes does not change, while the body from which something is being made changes through successive moments under the same motion, and when that intention of completing the work clearly remains unchanged, while it moves both the limbs of the craftsman and the wood or stone subject to the craftsman, who could doubt that the stated conclusion follows?

Therefore, if some change of bodies takes place while the mind is moving them, even though it is directed toward that change, we should not on this account necessarily judge that the mind itself changes and therefore also dies.

For in this intention it can simultaneously possess memory of past things and expectation of future things, neither of which can exist without life.

Although no destruction occurs without change and no change without motion, nevertheless not every change produces destruction, nor does every motion produce change. We may indeed say that our own body is often moved by some action and certainly changed by age, and yet that it has not already perished—that is, that it is not without life.

Let us therefore also be permitted not immediately to think that the mind is deprived of life, even if some change perhaps occurs in it through motion.

## CHAPTER IV — The Art and Reason of Numbers Are Unchangeable and Inhere in the Mind Without Its Being Lifeless

5. For if something unchangeable remains in the mind that cannot exist without life, then everlasting life must also remain in the mind. The matter is precisely such that, if the first is true, the second must be true.

The first is true. For, to omit other considerations, who would dare to say either that the reason of numbers is changeable, or that any art does not consist in this reason; or that an art is not in the craftsman even when he is not practicing it; or that it exists anywhere except in the mind; or that it can exist where there is no life; or that what is unchangeable can at some time fail to exist; or that art and reason are different things?

Although one art may be called a kind of gathering of many reasons, nevertheless one art can most truly be called and understood as one reason. But whether this or that is the case, it is no less established that art is unchangeable. It is also clear that art exists not only in the mind of the craftsman but nowhere except in the mind, and that it exists there inseparably.

For if art is separated from the mind, it will either exist somewhere other than in the mind, or it will exist nowhere, or it will pass continuously from one mind into another. But just as art has no seat without life, so life together with reason belongs to nothing except the soul [Note: [Col. 1024] 1 *Retractations*, chapter 5, no. 2.].

Moreover, what exists nowhere cannot exist, nor can what is unchangeable at some time fail to exist. But if art passes from one mind into another, leaving one mind while remaining in it, no one teaches art except by losing it; or someone becomes skilled only through the teacher’s forgetting, or through death [Note: [Col. 1024] In earlier printed editions, “without death.” But the manuscripts have the better reading, “or through death.”].

Since these conclusions are utterly absurd and false, as indeed they are, the human mind is immortal.

6. But if art is at one time present in the mind and at another time not present, as is sufficiently clear from forgetting and lack of expertise, the connection of this argument contributes nothing to its immortality unless the antecedent is denied in the following way:

“Either there is something in the mind that is not present in its present thought; or there is no musical art in the learned mind when it is thinking only about geometry.” The latter is false; therefore the former is true.

But the mind does not sense itself to possess anything except what has entered into thought. Therefore something can exist in the mind that the mind itself does not sense to be in it. How long it remains there makes no difference. For if the mind has been occupied with other matters for too long to be able easily to turn its attention back to what it previously thought about, this is called forgetfulness or lack of expertise.

But when either we ourselves, reasoning with ourselves, or when properly questioned by another, discover matters belonging to the liberal arts, we discover them nowhere other than in our own mind. To discover, however, is not to make or generate; otherwise the mind would generate eternal things through a temporal act of discovery. For it often discovers eternal things. What is as eternal as the ratio of a circle, or anything else of this kind in the arts, which is understood never to have failed to exist and never to be going to fail to exist?

It is therefore also clear that the human mind is immortal, and that all true reasons are hidden within it, although through ignorance or forgetfulness it may appear either not to possess them or to have lost them.

## CHAPTER V — The Mind Does Not Change So as to Cease to Be Mind

7. Let us now see how the mind’s change is to be understood. For if the mind is the subject and art exists in the subject, and if the subject cannot change without that which is in the subject also changing, how can we establish that art and reason are unchangeable if the mind in which they exist is shown to be changeable? What change is greater than the one that is usually found in opposites? Who denies that the mind, leaving aside other matters, is at one time foolish and at another wise?

First, then, let us see in how many ways what is called a change of the soul is understood. There are, as I think, two more evident and clearer kinds in general, though more kinds are found in particular. For the soul is said to change either according to the body’s affections or according to its own.

According to the body: through the stages of life, illnesses, pains, labors, injuries, and pleasures. According to its own states: through desiring, rejoicing, fearing, grieving, applying itself, and learning.

8. If all these changes are not necessarily arguments that the soul dies, they are not in themselves to be feared individually. But we must see that they do not conflict with our reasoning, according to which, when the subject is changed, everything in the subject must necessarily change.

They do not conflict. For the subject is said to change according to that change by which it is compelled altogether to change its name. If wax takes on a black color from white through some cause, it is no less wax; and if it assumes a round shape from a square one, becomes hard from soft, or grows cold from hot, these properties are in the subject, and wax is the subject.

Wax remains no more or less wax when these properties change. Therefore some change can occur in the things that are in a subject while the subject itself, according to what it is and is called, does not change.

But if such a great change occurred in the things that are in the subject that what was said to be beneath them could no longer be called that at all—for example, when through the heat of fire the wax disperses into the air, undergoing such a change that the subject that was wax is rightly understood to have changed and is no longer wax—then no one would in any way suppose that anything of those things which were in that subject because it was wax remained.

9. Therefore, if the soul is the subject, as we said above, in which reason exists inseparably; if, by the same necessity by which it is shown to exist in the subject [Note: [Col. 1025] Four manuscripts have: “by the necessity by which each thing is shown to exist in the subject.”]; the soul can exist only as a living soul; if reason cannot exist in it without life; and if reason is immortal, then the soul is immortal.

For it is utterly impossible that unchangeable reason should remain when its subject does not exist. This would happen if such a great change occurred in the soul that it ceased to be a soul—that is, if it were compelled to die.

But none of those changes that occur either through the body or through the soul itself—although whether any occur through the soul itself, that is, whether the soul is their cause, is a considerable question—acts so as to make the soul cease to be a soul.

Therefore these changes are not to be feared, not only for their own sake, but not even according to our arguments.

## CHAPTER VI — Unchangeable Reason, Whether It Is in the Mind, with the Mind, or the Mind Is in It, Cannot Be Separated from That Same Mind

10. I see, therefore, that every power of reasoning must be applied so that we may know what reason is and in how many ways it can be defined [Col. 1026], in order that the immortality of the soul may be established according to all these interpretations.

Reason is the mind’s act of seeing, by which it beholds truth through itself and not through the body; or it is the contemplation of truth itself, not through the body; or it is truth itself, which is contemplated.

No one doubts that the first of these is in the mind. The second and third may be questioned; but the second cannot exist without the mind either.

The third raises a major question: whether that truth which the mind beholds without the instrument of the body exists through itself and is not in the mind, or whether it can exist without the mind.

However the matter may stand, the mind could not contemplate it through itself unless there were some conjunction between it and that truth. For everything that we contemplate, or grasp in thought, we grasp either through sense or through understanding.

But things grasped through the senses are also perceived to exist outside us and are contained in places; hence they are said not even to be capable of being perceived. Things that are understood, however, are understood not as though they were placed somewhere other than in the mind that understands them; for at the same time they are understood not to be contained in a place.

11. Therefore this union of the contemplating mind and the truth which it contemplates is either such that the mind is the subject and that truth is in the subject; or, conversely, the truth is the subject and the mind is in the subject; or both are substances. If the first is the case, then, according to the preceding discussion, the mind is as immortal as reason, since that which is in it cannot exist unless it is alive. The same necessity applies in the second case. For if that truth which is called reason has nothing changeable in it, as appears to be the case, nothing that is in it as in a subject can be changed.

The whole dispute therefore remains about the third possibility. For if the mind is a substance, and reason, with which it is joined, is also a substance [Note: [Col. 1026] Thus in the manuscripts, and more coherently than if the reading found in the editions to date is followed, “joined to reason.”], one might reasonably think that it could happen that, while reason remains, the mind ceases to be here. But it is evident that, as long as the mind is not separated from reason and cleaves to it, it must necessarily remain and live.

By what force, then, could it be separated? By a bodily force, perhaps—whose power is weaker, whose origin lower, and whose order more remote? By no means. Or by an animal force? But how could that happen? Could some other, more powerful mind contemplate reason only by separating another mind from it? Yet reason would not be lacking to anyone contemplating it, if everyone contemplated it; and since nothing is more powerful than reason itself, than which nothing is more unchangeable, the mind that is not yet joined to reason could in no way be more powerful than the mind that is joined to it.

It remains, then, either that reason itself separate from itself, or that the mind separate from reason by an act of will. But there is nothing in that nature that resembles envy, preventing it from offering itself to the mind for enjoyment. Moreover, the more it exists, the more it makes whatever is joined to it exist; whereas destruction is opposed to this.

One might say, not altogether unreasonably, that the mind is separated from reason by its will, if there could be any separation from one another of things that are not contained in a place [Note: [Col. 1026] *Retractations* I.5.2.]. This, however, can be asserted against all the preceding arguments, to which we opposed other contradictions.

What, then? Must we now conclude that the mind is immortal? Or, even if it cannot be separated, can it nevertheless be extinguished? But if that power of reason, by its very union with the mind, affects it—and it certainly cannot fail to affect it—it affects it in such a way as to grant it existence. For reason itself is supremely what it is, and in it supreme unchangeability is understood. Thus it compels the one whom it affects from itself [Note: [Col. 1027] So in the manuscripts. The editions read: “Thus it causes whatever it affects from itself,” except Bad., which has “Thus it causes whatever.” Par. follows Bad. M.] to exist in some manner.

The mind therefore cannot be extinguished unless it is separated from reason; but it cannot be separated, as we reasoned above. It therefore cannot perish.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Even if the mind tends toward diminution through its substance, it does not therefore perish

12. Yet the very turning away from reason, through which folly comes upon the mind, cannot occur without some diminution of it. For if the mind is more turned toward reason and clings more closely to it, because it clings to an unchangeable reality, which is truth—and which is both primary and supreme—then, when it turns away from truth, it possesses less of that very being; and this is what it means to be diminished.

Every diminution tends toward nothingness, and no destruction ought to be understood more properly than when that which was something becomes nothing. To tend toward nothingness, therefore, is to tend toward destruction. Why this does not befall the mind, into which diminution does befall, is scarcely easy to say.

The remaining points are granted here, but it is denied that it follows that whatever tends toward nothingness—that is, toward reaching nothingness—must perish. This can also be observed in a body. For since any body is a part of the perceptible universe, and since the larger it is and the more space it occupies, the nearer it approaches the whole, the more it exists insofar as it does so. For the whole exists more than the part. Consequently, it must also exist less when it is diminished.

It therefore undergoes diminution when it becomes smaller. Moreover, it becomes smaller when something is removed from it by division. From this it follows that, through such subtraction, it tends toward nothingness. Yet no division brings it to nothingness. Every part that remains is a body, and whatever is a body occupies some place, however small the space may be. Nor could it do so unless it had parts into which it could repeatedly be cut.

A body can therefore be diminished infinitely by infinite division, and thus undergo diminution and tend toward nothingness, although it can never reach nothingness. The same may be said and understood of space itself and of any interval. For even when these are bounded, if one removes half of them, for example, and then continually removes half of what remains, the interval is diminished and advances toward an end which it nevertheless never reaches in any way.

There is still less reason to fear this with regard to the mind. For it is certainly better and more vigorous than the body, to which it gives life.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### Just as what makes a body a body cannot be taken away from the body, so what makes the mind a mind cannot be taken away from the mind

13. But if what makes a body a body is not its mass, but that which makes it exist in a particular form—and this view is supported by the stronger argument, since a body exists more insofar as it is more beautiful and well formed, and less insofar as it is uglier and more deformed [Col. 1028]—then this diminution does not occur through the subtraction of mass, about which enough has already been said, but through the deprivation of form [Note: [Col. 1028] Thus the manuscripts with Bad. Am., Er., and Lov. read “by a process of cutting away.”].

This matter must therefore be carefully investigated and examined, lest anyone assert that the mind perishes through such diminution. For since, while it is foolish, it is deprived of some form of its own, one might suppose that this deprivation could increase to such an extent that it stripped the mind of every form, reduced it to nothingness by this corruption, and forced it to perish.

Accordingly, if we can establish that this cannot happen even to a body—that it cannot be deprived of the form by which it is a body—we may perhaps rightly maintain that what makes the mind a mind can much less be taken away from it. Indeed, no one has looked carefully at himself who does not admit that any mind, however insignificant, ought to be preferred to every body.

14. Let the beginning of our reasoning, then, be this: no thing makes or generates itself; otherwise it would exist before it existed. If this is false, the following is true: whatever has not been made or generated, yet exists, must necessarily be everlasting.

Whoever attributes such a nature and excellence to any body is gravely mistaken. But why do we argue? We are compelled to attribute it to the mind much more strongly. Thus, if any body is everlasting, no mind is not everlasting. For any mind must be preferred to any body, and all everlasting things to things that are not everlasting.

But if what is truly called a body has been made, it has been made by some maker, and that maker is not inferior to it. For whatever it is that makes, it would not be capable of giving existence to what it makes unless it possessed the power to do so. Nor is the maker merely equal to what is made. The maker must possess something better for making than the thing he makes.

For of a generator it is not improperly said that he is what the thing generated from him is. The whole bodily universe, therefore, was made by some power and nature more powerful and better than it, and certainly not bodily. For if body were made by body, the universe could not have been made. It is entirely true that which we placed at the beginning of this reasoning: no thing can make itself.

This incorporeal power and nature, which produced the whole body of the universe, sustains the universe by its present power. It did not make it and then depart, abandoning what it had made. For that substance which is not body, and which, so to speak, does not move locally, cannot be separated from the substance that occupies a place; and that productive power cannot be idle, but must preserve what has been made by it and not allow it to lack the form by which it exists insofar as it exists.

For what does not exist through itself, if it is abandoned by that through which it exists, certainly will not exist. Nor can we say that, when it was made, the body received the power to be self-sufficient, even if it were abandoned by its creator.

15. Yet if this is so, the mind possesses this even more, since it is manifestly superior to the body. Thus it is immediately proved to be immortal, if it can exist through itself. Whatever is such must necessarily be incorruptible, and therefore cannot perish, because nothing abandons itself.

The mutability of the body, however, is obvious; the motion of the whole bodily universe sufficiently demonstrates this. Hence, for those who carefully examine as much of such a nature as can be examined, it is found, through ordered mutability, to imitate that which is unchangeable [Note: [Col. 1029] Am., Er., and Lov. read: “that which is changeable is found to change.” We have preferred the manuscript reading, which is also found in Bad. Shortly afterward the editions read, “nor does it have any motion.” But the manuscripts read, “nor does it need any motion,” or, “nor does it need motion of any kind.”].

But what exists through itself has no need even of motion, since it exists wholly and abundantly through itself; for every motion is toward something else, and that which moves needs that other thing.

Form, therefore, is present to the whole body of the universe, supplied and maintained by the better nature that made it. Consequently, mutability does not take away from a body its being a body, but makes it pass from form to form through the most orderly motion. No part of it is allowed to be reduced to nothingness, since that productive power embraces the whole, without labor or slackening, granting existence to everything that exists through it, insofar as it exists.

Therefore no one ought to be so far removed from reason as either not to be certain that the mind is better than the body, or, having granted this, to suppose that what happens to the body—that it ceases to be a body—could happen to the mind, so that it ceases to be a mind. If this does not happen, and the mind cannot exist unless it lives, then the mind certainly never dies.

## CHAPTER IX  
### The mind is life and therefore cannot lack life

16. But if someone says that the destruction to be feared for the mind is not that by which something that was something becomes nothing, but rather that by which we call things dead when they lack life, let him consider that no thing is deprived of itself.

The mind is a kind of life. Hence everything that is animated is understood to live, while everything inanimate that can be animated is understood to be dead—that is, deprived of life. The mind, therefore, cannot die. For if it could lack life, it would not be a mind but something animated.

If this is absurd, then this kind of destruction is even less to be feared for the mind, since life certainly is not to be feared for. For if the mind dies when that life abandons it, then the life itself that abandons it is much more properly understood to be the mind, so that whatever is abandoned by life is no longer the mind, but the very life that abandons it.

Whatever is said to be dead because it has been abandoned by life is understood to have been abandoned by the soul. But this life, which abandons things that die, is itself the mind; and because it does not abandon itself, the mind does not die.

## CHAPTER X  
### The mind is not a harmony of the body

17. Unless perhaps we ought to believe that life is some harmony of the body, as certain people have thought. They would certainly never have held this view if, with their minds withdrawn from and purified of the habit of bodily things, they had been able to see those realities that truly exist and remain unchangeable.

For who, looking carefully into himself, has not experienced that he understands something more clearly in proportion as he has been able to remove and withdraw the attention of his mind from bodily sensations? But if the mind were a harmony of the body, this could not happen.

For a thing that had no nature of its own and was not a substance, but existed inseparably in a subject body like color and form, could not in any way turn away from that same body in order to perceive intelligible realities, and, insofar as it could do so, contemplate them and become better and more excellent through that vision.

For in no way can form or color, or even the harmony of the body itself—which is a definite mixture of the four natures by which that body subsists—turn away from the body in which it exists inseparably as in a subject.

Moreover, the things that the mind understands when it turns away from the body are certainly not bodily; and yet they exist, indeed they exist supremely, for they always remain in the same condition. Nothing more absurd could be said than that the things we see with our eyes exist, while those we perceive by understanding do not exist, since only a mad person could doubt that understanding is incomparably superior to the eyes.

When the mind contemplates these intelligible things, which remain in the same condition, this sufficiently shows that it is joined to them in some wondrous and likewise incorporeal manner—namely, not locally. For either they are in the mind, or the mind is in them. Whichever is the case, either one is in the other as in a subject, or both are substances.

But if the first is the case, the mind is not in a bodily subject as color and form are. For either the mind itself is a substance, or it exists in another substance that is not body, as in a subject.

If the second is true, the mind is not in a bodily subject like color, because it is a substance. But the harmony of the body is in a bodily subject like color. Therefore the mind is not the harmony of the body; rather, the mind is life. No thing abandons itself, and that which life abandons dies. Therefore the mind cannot die.

## CHAPTER XI  
### The mind does not perish through falsehood, which is contrary to truth, even though truth is the cause of the mind

18. Let us return, then. If anything is to be feared, it is that the mind may perish through diminution—that is, while it is deprived of the form of existence itself.

Although I think enough has been said about this matter and it has been demonstrated by a firm argument that it cannot happen, we must nevertheless observe that the only cause of this fear is the admission that the foolish mind is in a state of diminution, while the wise mind is in a more certain and fuller state of being.

But if, as no one doubts, the mind is wisest when it contemplates truth, which always remains the same, and cleaves immovably to it, joined to it by divine love; and if all things that exist in any manner whatsoever derive their being from that essence which exists supremely and most fully [Note: [Col. 1030] Er. and Lov. read: “and which is supremely and most fully all things that exist in any manner whatsoever.”]—then either the mind derives from it whatever being it possesses, or it exists through itself.

If it exists through itself, then, since it is itself the cause of its existence and never abandons itself, it never perishes, as we have also argued above.

But if it derives its being from that essence, we must carefully ask what reality could be contrary to it and take away from the mind the being that truth grants it.

What, then? Perhaps falsehood, because truth is its opposite? But it is manifest and readily evident how much harm falsehood can do to the mind. Can it do anything more than deceive? Yet no one is deceived unless he lives. Falsehood, therefore, cannot destroy the mind.

If falsehood, which is contrary to truth, cannot take away from the mind the being that truth gave it—for truth is thus utterly unconquerable—what else can be found that could take away from the mind that which makes it a mind? Nothing at all. For nothing contrary is stronger than the thing it opposes, so as to take away what is produced by its contrary.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Nothing is contrary to truth, from which the mind has whatever being it possesses, insofar as truth itself exists

19. But if we seek what is contrary to truth not insofar as it is truth, but insofar as it exists supremely and most fully—although it is precisely as much of this as it is truth, since we call that truth by which all things are true insofar as they exist, and they exist insofar as they are true—I shall nevertheless in no way avoid what supports my position more evidently.

For if no essence, insofar as it is essence, has anything contrary to it, then still less does that primary essence called truth have anything contrary to it insofar as it is essence. The first truth is being. For every essence is essence for no other reason than that it is. Being has no contrary except nonbeing; therefore nothing is contrary to essence.

In no way, then, can anything be contrary to that substance which exists supremely and primarily. If the mind has from it the very being that it possesses—for it cannot have this from elsewhere, since it does not possess it from itself, but only from that reality which is superior to the mind precisely by this being—then there is nothing by which it could lose it, since nothing is contrary to the reality from which it has it. For this reason it does not cease to be.

But it can lose wisdom, because it possesses wisdom by turning toward that from which it is. It can lose it by turning away. For turning away is contrary to turning toward. But what it has from that to which nothing is contrary has no source from which it could lose it. It therefore cannot perish.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### The mind is not changed into a body

20. At this point perhaps a question may arise: just as the mind does not perish, does it likewise not change into a lesser essence? It may seem, and not without reason, that this reasoning has established that the mind cannot reach nothingness, but that it might perhaps be changed into a body.

For if what was previously the mind should become a body, it would not be altogether nothing. But this cannot happen unless either the mind itself wishes it or is compelled by another. Yet even if the mind either desired this or were compelled, it would not immediately be able to become a body.

It follows that, if it becomes a body, it must either wish this or be compelled. But it does not follow that, if it wishes this or is compelled, it becomes a body. The mind will never wish this. For every desire it has with respect to the body is either to possess it, to give it life, to fashion it in some way, or to care for it by whatever means. None of these things can happen unless the mind is better than the body.

But if it becomes a body, it will certainly not be better than the body. Therefore it will not wish to become a body. No clearer proof of this can be found than when the mind questions itself on this matter. It easily discovers that it has no desire except to do something, to know something, to perceive something, or simply to live insofar as its own power permits.

21. But if it is compelled to become a body, by whom is it compelled? Certainly by something more powerful. It cannot therefore be compelled by the body itself. For in no way is any body more powerful than any mind.

A more powerful mind, however, compels no one into anything unless the one compelled is subject to its power. Nor is a mind subject to the power of another mind except through its own desires. Thus one mind compels another only to the extent permitted by the desires of the mind it compels.

But it has been shown that the mind cannot have the desire to become a body [Note: [Col. 1032] Thus in the manuscripts. The earlier editions read: “But it has been shown that the mind cannot be compelled to become a body,” which is not sufficiently consistent with the argument.]. It is also clear that it cannot reach the fulfillment of any desire while losing every desire; and it loses every desire when it becomes a body.

Therefore the mind cannot be compelled to become a body by one who has no right to compel it except through the desires of a subordinate. Moreover, whoever has one mind under his power must necessarily wish to have it under his power more than he wishes to have a body under his power, and must wish either to benefit it through goodness or to command it through wickedness. He will not, therefore, wish it to become a body.

22. Finally, the mind that compels is either an animal or without a body (*Retractations* I.5.3). If it is without a body, it is not in this world. And if that is so, it is supremely good and cannot wish such a shameful transformation for another.

But if it is an animal, then either the one whom it compels is also an animal or he is not. If he is not, he cannot be compelled by another to become anything. For he has no more powerful being over him, since he is at the highest level.

But if he is in a body, then he is compelled again by one who is in a body, through the body, into whatever he is compelled to become. Yet who could doubt that such a transformation of the mind cannot in any way be effected through the body? It could happen only if that body were more powerful than the mind.

Whatever it is, however, into which he is compelled through the body, he is compelled not actually through the body but through his own desires, about which enough has been said.

But what is better than a rational soul is, by universal agreement, God. He certainly cares for the soul, and therefore the soul cannot be compelled by him to change into a body.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Neither sleep nor any similar condition of the body diminishes the power of the soul

23. If, then, the mind suffers this neither by its own will nor through the compulsion of another, from where could it suffer it? Must we fear that, because sleep often overwhelms us against our will, the mind may be transformed into a body through some such diminution?

It is as though, because our limbs grow slack in sleep, the mind therefore becomes weaker in any respect. It merely does not perceive sensible things, because whatever produces sleep comes from the body and operates in the body. For that which puts the bodily senses to sleep and, as it were, closes them causes the soul to yield to such a bodily change with pleasure, since this change is according to nature and restores the body from its labors.

Yet this does not deprive the mind of either the power of perceiving or the power of understanding. It also has images of sensible things present to it, with such a vivid likeness that at that very time they cannot be distinguished from the things of which they are images.

And if it understands something, what is true remains equally true for one who is asleep and one who is awake. For example, if in a dream someone seems to be debating and, following true arguments in the course of the debate, learns something, then, after awakening, those same truths remain unchangeable [Col. 1033], although other elements are found to be false: for example, the place where the debate occurred, the person with whom it seemed to take place, the words themselves insofar as their sound was concerned, by which the debate seemed to be conducted, and other things of this kind.

These things are also sensed and experienced by those who are awake through their very senses, but they pass away and in no respect attain the everlasting presence of true reasons. From this it follows that through such a bodily change as sleep, the soul’s use of the same body may be diminished, but not its own life [Note: [Col. 1033] Er. reads “power.”].

## CHAPTER XV  
### Again, the soul cannot be changed into a body

24. Finally, although the soul is joined to a body that occupies a place, it is not joined to it locally. It is affected first by those highest and eternal reasons, which remain unchangeably and are certainly not contained in a place; and the soul is affected before the body, not merely earlier but also more strongly.

It is affected earlier in proportion as it is nearer, and for the same reason more strongly in proportion as it is better than the body. This nearness is not to be understood spatially, but according to the order of nature.

According to this order, the highest essence gives form to the body through the soul, by which the body exists insofar as it exists. The body therefore subsists through the soul and exists precisely insofar as it is animated, whether universally, as the world, or particularly, as each individual animal within the world.

It would therefore follow that the soul becomes body through the soul, and that this could happen in no other way. But because this does not happen—for the soul remains in that condition in which it is soul, and through it the body subsists, receiving form rather than being deprived of it—the soul cannot be changed into a body.

For if the soul does not transmit the form it receives from the highest good, the body does not become body through it. And if the body does not become body through it, then either it does not become body at all, or it receives form as nearly as the soul does. But it does become body; and if it received form as nearly as the soul does, it would be what the soul is. For this is the distinction: the soul is better insofar as it receives form more nearly.

But the body would receive form just as nearly if it did not receive it through the soul. For it would receive it with no intermediary at all. Yet nothing is found between the highest life—which is unchangeable wisdom and truth—and that which is vivified at the lowest level, namely the body, except the vivifying soul.

If the soul transmits form to the body so that the body exists insofar as it exists, it does not, by transmitting form, deprive itself of form. But it would deprive itself of form by changing into a body. Therefore the soul cannot become a body either through itself—for the body becomes body through it only while the soul remains a soul—or through another. For the body becomes body through the soul only by the transmission of form, whereas the soul would be changed into a body, if it were changed, by the loss of form.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### A rational soul is not changed even into an irrational soul. The whole soul is present in the whole body and in each of its parts

[Col. 1034]

25. The same may be said of an irrational soul or life: a rational soul is not changed into it. For unless it were subjected to a rational soul in an inferior order, it too would receive form in the same way and would be of the same kind.

Thus more powerful natures transmit the form received from supreme beauty to weaker natures according to the natural order. And when they transmit it, they do not deprive themselves of it. Hence weaker things exist insofar as the form by which they exist is transmitted to them by more powerful things [Note: [Col. 1034] Lov. reads: “because form is transmitted to them, as it were, by more powerful things.” The more reliable manuscripts read: “because form is transmitted to them, by which they exist.”]. Those more powerful things are also, of course, better.

This has been granted to natures whose power does not arise from a greater mass over smaller masses, but which, without any swelling of local magnitude, are more powerful by the same form by which they are better. The soul belongs to this class: it is better and more powerful than the body.

Accordingly, since the body subsists through the soul, as has been said, the soul cannot in any way be turned into the body. For no body comes to be except by receiving form through the soul. But the soul could become a body only by not receiving form, but by losing it. For this reason it cannot become a body—unless perhaps the soul is contained in a place and joined locally to the body.

For if that were the case, perhaps a greater mass, however more beautiful, could turn it into its own inferior form, as a greater quantity of air turns a smaller quantity of fire into itself. But this is not the case.

For every mass that occupies a place is not wholly present in each of its parts, but only in all of them collectively. Thus one part of it is in one place and another part elsewhere.

But the soul is not only wholly present to the entire mass of its body; it is also wholly present to each of its smallest parts simultaneously. It feels the affection of a bodily part as a whole, though not in the whole body.

When something hurts in the foot, the eye turns toward it, the tongue speaks, and the hand is brought to it. This could not happen unless that which is present in those parts of the soul also felt what occurred in the foot; nor could it feel what happened there if it were absent.

For it is not credible that this happens through some messenger that does not itself feel what it reports. The affection that occurs does not run through a continuous bodily mass in such a way that it prevents the other parts of the soul, which are elsewhere, from being unaware of it. Rather, the whole soul feels what occurs in the small part that is the foot, and feels it only where it occurs.

The whole soul is therefore present simultaneously in each individual part, and the whole soul simultaneously feels in each part. Yet it is not present in this manner so that the whole of it is in each part of the body like whiteness or some other quality of this kind.

For what the body suffers in one part through a change of whiteness need not pertain to the whiteness that is in another part. Consequently, according to the bodily parts that are distant from one another, whiteness itself is shown to be distant from itself.

But this is not so in the soul, as is proved by the sense described above.

[Col. 1033]

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO  
## One Book on the Quantity of the Soul

[Note: [Col. 1035] Written around the beginning of the year 388.] [Note: [Col. 1037] For the correction of this book, two Sorbonne manuscripts, three Victorine manuscripts, the Regius, Cistercian, Floriacensian, Michaeline, Remigian, Corbie, Vendôme, Ebrulphian, Sergian, Vatican, and Vedastine manuscripts were used, in addition to readings drawn from four Belgian manuscripts by the Louvain editors; also the editions of Bad., Er., and Lov.] [Note: [Col. 1037] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.] (C)

## NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING BOOK, ON THE QUANTITY OF THE SOUL

[Note: [Col. 1035] See Book I, chapter 8 of the *Retractations*, col. 594, from the words “In the same city,” no. 1, through the words of no. 3, “To have abundant leisure.” M.]

[Col. 1033]

Augustine held the dialogue on the Quantity of the Soul with Evodius, as he himself reports in Letter 162, when, writing again to Evodius and proposing certain further questions about the soul, he says:

“If you reread those things [Col. 1035] . . . which I wrote when you were discussing and conversing with me, whether on the Quantity of the Soul or on Free Will, you will find in them enough to resolve your doubts even without my assistance” (*Epistle* 162.2).

Moreover, after examining those passages in which the editions, together with several manuscripts that are not very old, give the names of Augustine and Adeodatus as the interlocutors, we found nothing in the ancient codices except certain uncertain marks inserted to indicate questions and answers. Therefore Adeodatus’s name had to be removed. Indeed, at the time when this dialogue was held, Adeodatus had scarcely reached adolescence; but the person who converses with Augustine says that he is a young man, in chapter 24, no. 46.

It seemed best, however, not to move the work from the place it has hitherto occupied in the editions, where it follows immediately after the book on the Immortality of the Soul, since the arrangement of the argument requires that position.

Augustine further testifies in Book I, chapter 7 of the *Retractations*, that, after he had already been baptized and while he was in Rome, he wrote the books on the Morals of the Catholic Church and on the Morals of the Manichaeans. Then, in the following chapter, he records that he held this dialogue, the one under consideration, in the same city. Afterward he lists the books on Free Will, begun there. For this reason we place this dialogue near the beginning of the year of Christ 388.

For Augustine had come to Rome in the preceding year and spent a large part of the following year there; during that interval he composed the works mentioned above.

## [DIALOGUE ON THE SOUL]

In this dialogue the interlocutor proposes six questions about the soul to Augustine. In treating the third question more deeply—namely, how great the soul is—Augustine first distinguishes two kinds of quantity: one derived from mass and spatial extension, the other from power and capacity. He teaches that the former belongs properly to body and is excluded from the soul, which is wholly incorporeal, while the latter is found in the soul. He then assigns seven degrees of this magnitude, to which he refers whatever the human soul is capable of, whether in the body, in itself, or finally in relation to God.

## CHAPTER I  
### Evodius proposes six questions about the soul. From where the soul comes. God is the soul’s homeland. The soul’s proper and simple substance

1. **E.** Since I see that you have abundant leisure, I ask you to answer me about the matters that trouble me—not, as I think, at an inconvenient or inappropriate time. For often, when I had asked you many questions, you thought to frighten me away by citing that Greek maxim which forbids us to inquire into what is above us. But now I do not think that we ourselves are above ourselves.

Therefore, when I ask about the soul, I am not so unworthy as to be told, “What is above us, what has it to do with us?” [Note: [Col. 1035] A saying of Socrates: “That which is above us—what has it to do with us?” Greek: *ta hyper hēmas, ti pros hēmas?*]. Perhaps I am worthy to be told what we are.

**A.** Briefly enumerate what you wish to hear about the soul.

**E.** I shall do so, for these questions have been prepared in me by long reflection. I therefore ask from where the soul comes, what it is like, how great it is, why it was given to the body, and, when it has come to the body, what it becomes, and what it becomes when it has departed.

2. **A.** When you ask from where the soul comes, I am compelled to understand two different things. For we speak in one way when we ask where a human being comes from, wishing to know his homeland; and in another way when we ask where he comes from in the sense of what he consists of—that is, from what elements and things he is composed.

Which of these do you wish to know when you ask where the soul comes from? Do you wish to know, as it were, its region and homeland, from which it has come here? Or are you asking what its substance is?

**E.** I would certainly like to know both, but I prefer to leave it to your judgment which ought to be known first.

**A.** I believe that God himself is the soul’s proper dwelling and homeland [Col. 1036], since he is the one by whom it was created.

But I cannot name its substance. For I do not think that it is made from those familiar and well-known natures that we touch with the bodily senses. I do not think that the soul consists of earth, or water, or air, or fire, or of all these together, or of some combination of them.

But just as, if you asked me what this tree consists of, I would name those four familiar elements from which everything of this kind must be believed to consist; and if you continued to ask from what earth, water, air, or fire themselves consist, I would have nothing further to say; so, when one asks from what a human being is composed, I can answer, “From soul and body.”

Again, if you ask about the body, I shall return to those four elements. But when you ask about the soul, since it seems to be something simple and to possess a substance of its own, I am no less at a loss than if, as I have said, you asked from what earth consists.

**E.** I do not understand how you want it to have a substance of its own, when you have said that it was made by God.

**A.** I cannot deny that God himself made the earth; and yet I cannot say from what other bodies, as it were, the earth consists. Earth is a simple body, precisely insofar as it is earth, and therefore it is called an element of all those bodies that are made from the four elements.
