There is therefore no contradiction in saying both that God made the soul and that it possesses a nature of its own. God himself made this particular nature, its own and proper to it, just as he made the nature of fire, air, water, and earth, from which other things were to be composed.

## CHAPTER II  
### What the soul is like

[Col. 1037]

3. E. For the moment I accept where the soul comes from—that is, from God—and I shall carefully reconsider this with myself; if anything troubles me, I shall ask about it later. But I ask you to explain what the soul is like.

A. It seems to me to be like God. For unless I am mistaken, you are asking about the human soul.

E. That is precisely what I wanted you to explain to me: in what way the soul is like God, since we believe that God was made by no one, whereas you said above that the soul was made by God himself.

A. What? Do you think it was difficult for God to make something like himself, when you see that even we have been granted this ability amid such a great variety of images?

E. But we seem to make mortal things, whereas God made the soul immortal—or so I think, unless you see the matter otherwise.

A. Then you would like human beings to make things such as God made [Note: [Col. 1037] *Facit*, “makes,” according to Ven. Bar. M.]?

E. I certainly did not say that. But just as he, being immortal, made something immortal in his own likeness, so we, made immortal by God, ought also to make something immortal in our likeness.

A. You would be right if you painted a picture of what you believe to be immortal in yourself. But as it is, you represent in it the likeness of the body, which is certainly mortal.

E. How, then, am I like God, since I cannot make anything immortal as he can?

A. Just as an image of your body cannot possess the power that your body possesses, so it is not surprising if the soul does not have as much power as he does, in whose likeness it was made.

## CHAPTER III.—How great the soul is

4. E. For the moment this is enough. Now tell me how great the soul is.

A. How do you ask how great it is? I do not understand whether you are asking about something like its spatial breadth, length, or strength, or all of these together, or whether you want to know how powerful it is. We customarily ask how great Hercules was—that is, to how many feet his stature extended—and likewise how great a man someone was, meaning how great his power and virtue were.

E. I want to know both about the soul.

A. The former, however, cannot be said, nor can it in any way be understood of the soul. The soul should not be thought of as long, broad, or, so to speak, strong in any way. These are bodily properties, as it seems to me; and it is from our customary way of thinking about bodies that we ask such questions about the soul. Hence it is rightly commanded even in the mysteries that whoever desires to be made such as he was made by God—that is, like God—should despise everything bodily and renounce this entire world, which, as we see, is bodily. For the soul has no other salvation, renewal, or reconciliation with its creator.

Therefore I cannot answer you how great the soul is according to this inquiry; but I can affirm that it is neither long, nor broad, nor strong, nor anything of the kind that is ordinarily sought in measurements of bodies. If you wish, I shall give you the reason why I think this.

[Col. 1038]

E. I certainly wish it, and I await it eagerly. For it seems to me that the soul is virtually nothing if it is none of these things.

A. First, then, if you please, I shall show you that there are many things which you cannot call nothing, and yet in them you will not find any of the kinds of space that you are seeking in the soul. Thus the soul should not seem to you to be nothing merely because you do not find length or anything similar in it; indeed, it should be considered more precious and more highly valued precisely because it has none of these things. Then we shall see whether it truly has none of them.

E. Proceed in whatever order and manner you wish. I am ready to listen and learn.

## CHAPTER IV.—That the soul is something, although it is neither long nor broad

5. A. You are right to do so. But I want you to answer me when I ask you; perhaps you already know what I am trying to teach you. I assume that you do not doubt that this tree is not altogether nothing.

E. Who would doubt that?

A. What of this? Do you doubt that justice is much better than this tree?

E. That is certainly ridiculous—as though there could be any comparison.

A. You are generous toward me. But now consider this: since it is established that this tree is so much worse than justice that it does not even seem to you worthy of comparison, and since you have confessed that this piece of wood is not nothing, are you willing for us to believe that justice itself is nothing?

E. What madman would believe that?

A. Quite rightly. But perhaps this tree seems to you to be something because, in its own measure, it is long, broad, and strong; and if you take these properties away, it will be nothing.

E. That seems so.

A. What, then? Justice—which you have confessed to be not nothing, indeed something far more divine and far more excellent than this tree—does it seem to you to be long?

E. Justice cannot occur to my thought as long, broad, or anything of that kind.

A. If, then, justice is none of these things and yet is not nothing, why does the soul seem to you to be nothing unless it has some length?

E. Very well. The soul no longer seems to me to be nothing because it is neither long, broad, nor strong. But you know that you have not yet shown whether it truly is so. Many things may be highly valued despite lacking these properties, but I do not think that it immediately follows that the soul belongs to this class.

6. A. I know that this remains for us to unravel, and I promised that I would explain it next. But because the matter is exceedingly subtle and requires eyes of the mind very different from those which human custom ordinarily employs in the affairs of daily life, I urge you to proceed willingly along the paths by which I think you must be led, and not to become weary or resentful because, through the necessary turns of our argument, you reach what you desire somewhat more slowly.

First, then, I ask you whether you think there is any body that does not, according to its own measure, have some length, breadth, and height.

E. I do not understand what you call height.

A. I mean that by which the interior of a body can be conceived—or even perceived, if it is transparent like glass. Indeed, if this is removed from bodies [Note: [Col. 1039] According to Lov., “if you remove this from bodies.” M.], they can neither be perceived, in my opinion, nor properly regarded as bodies. Tell me what you think about this.

E. I have no doubt at all that bodies cannot be without these properties.

A. What of this? Can you conceive that these three exist anywhere except in bodies?

E. I do not understand how they could exist elsewhere.

A. Then you do not think that the soul is anything other than a body?

E. If we also admit that wind is a body, I cannot deny that the soul seems to me to be a body; for I conceive it to be something of that sort.

A. I grant that wind is a body just as readily as if you asked me about a wave. For we perceive wind to be nothing other than this air moved and stirred; this can be demonstrated in a place of complete calm, entirely sheltered from winds, even with a small fan, by which we stir the air while driving away flies and feel a breath. When this occurs through some more hidden movement of heavenly or earthly bodies across the vast extent of the world, it is called wind, and it receives different names according to the different regions of the sky. Do you see it otherwise?

E. Not at all; I accept what you say as plausible. But I said that the soul is not the wind itself, only something of that kind.

A. First tell me whether you perceive that the wind itself, which you mentioned, has some length, breadth, and height. Then we shall see whether the soul is something of this kind, so that we may investigate how great it is in this way.

E. What could easily be found longer, broader, and higher than this air, which you have now convinced me is wind when it is moved?

## CHAPTER V.—The soul’s boundless power

7. A. You are right. But do you think that your soul exists anywhere except in your body?

E. That is what I think.

A. Only inside, so that it fills [the body] like a wineskin [Note: [Col. 1039] The editions read, “so that it fills the wineskin as water does.” The word *aqua* is absent from the manuscripts.]; or only outside, like plaster; or do you think that it exists both inside and outside?

E. I think what you asked last. For if it were not inside, there would be nothing vital in our organs; and if it were not outside, it could not feel even a slight prick upon the skin [Note: [Col. 1039] *Possis*, “you could,” according to Erasmus, Venetus, and Lov. M.].

A. Why, then, do you ask how great the soul is, when you see that it is as great as the spaces occupied by the body itself?

E. If reason teaches this, I ask for nothing more.

A. You are right to ask for nothing more than reason teaches. But does this reasoning seem to you absolutely firm?

E. Since I find no other, it does. In its proper place I shall ask what greatly troubles me—whether this shape remains the same when the soul has departed from the body; for I remember having put that question last among those to be examined. But since asking about the number of souls seems to me to belong to the question of quantity, I do not think it should be passed over here.

A. You are right to think so, but first, if you please, let us explain the question of its spatial extent, which still troubles me, so that I too may learn something, if you are already satisfied.

[Col. 1040]

E. Ask whatever you wish. For your feigned doubt genuinely makes me doubt the very matter which I had assumed was already settled.

8. A. Tell me, please: does what is called memory seem to you to be an empty name?

E. To whom could it seem so?

A. Do you think memory belongs to the soul or to the body?

E. It would be ridiculous to doubt that as well. What? Can an inanimate body be believed or understood to remember anything?

A. Do you remember the city of Milan?

E. I remember it very well.

A. Now that it has been mentioned, do you recall how large it is and what it is like?

E. I certainly recall it, and nothing could be more recent or more distinct.

A. Although you do not now see it with your eyes, you see it with your mind.

E. That is so.

A. You remember, I suppose, that it is now distant from us by four geographical intervals.

E. I remember that as well.

A. You therefore see even the distance between places with your mind.

E. I see it.

A. Since, then, your soul is here where your body is, and does not extend beyond the space of your body, as the preceding reasoning demonstrated, how does it see all those things?

E. I think this happens through memory—not because it is present in those places.

A. So images of those places are contained in the memory.

E. That is what I think. For I do not know what is happening there now; and certainly I would not be ignorant of that if my mind extended as far as those places and perceived them as present.

A. You seem to me to be speaking correctly. But surely these are images of bodies.

E. Necessarily so, for cities and lands are nothing other than bodies.

9. A. Have you never looked into small mirrors, or never seen your own face in the pupil of another person’s eye?

E. On the contrary, very often.

A. Why does it appear much smaller than it is?

E. What else would you expect, except that it should appear according to the size of the mirror?

A. Images of bodies must therefore appear small if the bodies in which they appear are small.

E. Certainly.

A. Why, then, when the soul occupies as small a space as its body does, can such enormous images be represented in it that it can imagine cities, the breadth of lands, and any other immense things within itself? I want you to consider more carefully how great and how many things our memory contains, which are certainly contained in the soul. What kind of foundation, what recess, what immensity could contain these things, when the preceding reasoning also seemed to have taught us that the soul is as large as the body?

E. I find nothing to answer, nor can I adequately explain how much this troubles me. I greatly mock myself for having so quickly agreed with the preceding reasoning that I determined the size of the soul from the measure of the body.

A. Then does the soul no longer seem to you to be something like wind?

E. Not at all. For even if this air—whose kind of wave we plausibly believe wind to be—could fill the entire universe, the soul can imagine innumerable worlds as great as this one, and I cannot even conjecture what space could contain such images.

A. Consider, then, whether it is better to believe that the soul is, as I said above, neither long, nor broad, nor high, just as you conceded to me in the case of justice.

E. I would readily agree, were I not even more disturbed by the question of how the soul can contain innumerable images of such vast spaces without having any length, breadth, or height of its own.

## CHAPTER VI.—Pure and simple length

10. A. Perhaps we shall discover this as far as possible if we first examine carefully these three things: length, breadth, and height. Therefore try to conceive length that has not yet taken on any breadth.

E. I cannot conceive such a thing. For if I imagine a spider’s thread in my mind—nothing thinner than which we ordinarily see—there nevertheless presents itself to me in it length by itself, breadth, and height as well. Whatever their dimensions may be, I cannot deny that they exist.

A. Your answer is not altogether absurd. But certainly, when you understand that these three things are present in a spider’s thread, you distinguish them and know how they differ from one another?

E. Why would I not know how they differ? How else could I see that none of them is lacking in this thread?

A. By the same understanding with which you distinguished them, you can also conceive length alone, separating those properties, provided you do not turn any body over in your mind; for whatever body you conceive will lack none of them. What I now want you to understand is incorporeal: length alone can be conceived by the mind, but cannot be found in a body.

E. I understand now.

A. If, then, you wish to cut this length, as it were, by thinking along its length, you see that this cannot be done. For if it can be cut, breadth is present as well.

E. That is clear.

A. Let us therefore call this pure and simple length a line, if you please; many learned people customarily call it by this name.

E. Call it whatever you wish. I need not trouble myself about names when the thing itself is clear.

11. A. You do well; and I not only approve, but also urge you always to take greater pleasure in caring about things than about words. But this line, which you now understand well, I suppose, if extended either from one end or from both, as far as it can be extended in length, you see has no limit. Is the acuity of your mind less capable of contemplating this?

E. I contemplate it fully; nothing is easier.

A. You see, then, that no figure can be made if nothing is done except to extend that line.

E. I do not yet understand what you mean by a figure.

## CHAPTER VII.—The shorter and safer way for the multitude to perceive the truth is through authority rather than reason

A. For the moment I call a figure that which is enclosed by some space bounded by a line or lines—as when you make a circle, or join four lines at their ends to one another so that no end remains free from the joining with another.

E. I think I now see what you mean by a figure. But if only I could see as clearly where this is leading, or what you intend to accomplish by it, so that I may know what I am asking about the soul.

12. A. I warned you of this at the beginning and asked you to endure our somewhat circuitous route patiently. I ask you to do so again. What we are seeking is no trivial matter, nor is it easy to understand; if possible, we want to know and firmly grasp it.

For it is one thing when we believe authority, and another when we rely on reason. To believe authority is a great shortcut and involves no labor. If this pleases you, you can read many things in which great and divine men, concerning matters they considered necessary, have beneficially spoken to the less instructed as though by a kind of sign, wishing those people to believe them whose minds, whether slower or more entangled, could have no other means of salvation.

For such people—and their number is certainly very great—if they wish to grasp the truth by reason, are easily deceived by likenesses of reasoning and slip into various harmful opinions, from which they can emerge and be freed either never or only with the greatest difficulty. For them, therefore, it is exceedingly useful to believe the highest authority and to order their lives accordingly. If you think this safer, I do not merely offer no resistance but strongly approve.

If, however, you cannot restrain this desire by which you have convinced yourself that you will reach the truth through reason, you must endure many long turns, so that reason may lead you only by what ought properly to be called reason—that is, true reason—and not merely true, but so certain and so remote from every likeness of falsity, if indeed this can in any way be discovered by human beings, that no false or merely plausible arguments can draw you away from it.

E. I shall desire nothing prematurely. Let reason act and lead wherever it wishes [Note: [Col. 1042] Lov. reads, “wherever it wishes to lead.” Other manuscripts read, “wherever it wishes.”], provided that it leads me to the destination.

## CHAPTER VIII.—Mathematical figures. How many lines make a figure. How a figure can be made with three lines

13. A. God will accomplish this, and it is for such matters—or at least especially for such matters—that he must be entreated. But let us return to the subject I had begun. Since you now know what a line and what a figure are, answer my question: do you think that any figure can be made if a line extends infinitely in both directions, or infinitely in one direction?

E. I affirm that this cannot happen in any way.

A. What, then, must we do to make a figure?

E. What else but ensure that that line is not infinite and extend it into a circle, so that it touches itself on the other side? I do not see how a space could otherwise be enclosed by a single line; and unless this happens, according to your definition it will not be a figure.

A. What if I wish to make a figure with straight lines? Can this be done with one line or not?

E. In no way.

A. What about two?

E. Not even with two.

A. What about three?

E. I see that it can be done.

A. You therefore know and firmly understand that when a figure is to be made with straight lines, fewer than three will not suffice. Or, if any reasoning opposes you, will it draw you away from this judgment?

E. Certainly. If someone showed me that this was false, I would have no confidence that I could know anything.

A. Now answer this: how do you make a figure with three lines?

E. When they join at their ends.

A. What? When they join, does an angle not seem to be formed?

E. Yes.

A. How many angles, then, does this figure consist of?

E. As many as it has lines.

A. What? Do you make the lines themselves equal or unequal?

E. Equal.

A. What? Are all the angles equally open, or is one more contracted or more open than another?

E. I see that the angles too are equal.

A. Can it happen that, in a figure made with three equal straight lines, the angles are unequal, or can it not?

E. It is wholly impossible.

A. What if a figure consists of three straight but unequal lines? Can the angles in that figure nevertheless be equal, or do you understand otherwise?

E. They cannot be equal at all.

A. You are right. But tell me, please: which figure seems better and more beautiful to you, the one consisting of equal lines or the one consisting of unequal lines?

E. Who would doubt that the better is the one in which equality prevails?

## CHAPTER IX.—Which figure is superior. What is opposite an angle in a triangle

14. A. Then you prefer equality to inequality?

E. I do not know whether anyone would not prefer it.

A. Now consider, in a figure completed by three equal angles, what is opposed to an angle in it—that is, what is placed opposite it on the other side: a line or an angle?

E. I see a line.

A. What, then? If an angle is opposed to an angle and a line to a line, do you not admit that equality is superior in the figure in which this occurs?

E. I admit it, but I do not at all see how this can happen with three lines.

A. What about four lines? Can it happen then?

E. Certainly.

A. The figure consisting of four equal straight lines is therefore better than the one consisting of three.

E. Certainly better, since equality has greater force in it.

A. What, then? Do you think that this figure made of four equal straight lines can also be so formed that not all its angles are equal, or do you think it cannot?

E. I see that it can.

A. How?

E. If two are more contracted and two more open.

A. Do you also see how the two more contracted angles and the two more open angles are opposed to one another?

E. I see it both most truly and most clearly.

A. You therefore see that equality has been preserved here too, as far as it could be preserved. For you certainly see that when a figure is completed with four equal lines, it cannot happen that either all the angles, or at least pairs of them, are not equal; and that the equal angles correspond to one another in opposition.

E. I see it and hold it most firmly.

15. A. Does nothing move you in these matters as well—such great and unshakable justice?

E. How so?

A. Because, as I think, we say that justice is nothing but equity; and equity seems to derive its name from a certain equality. But what is equity in this virtue except that each person receives what belongs to him? And what belongs to each cannot be assigned without some distinction. Or do you think otherwise?

E. It is clear, and I entirely agree.

A. What? Do you think there can be any distinction if everything is equal, so that nothing differs at all from anything else?

E. In no way.

A. Justice, then, cannot be preserved unless, in the things in which it is preserved, there is a certain, so to speak, inequality and dissimilarity.

E. I understand.

A. Since, then, we admit that these figures of which we are speaking are dissimilar to one another—the one consisting of three angles and the other of four, although both are made with equal lines—does it not seem to you that a certain justice has been retained? The first, unable to possess equality among opposites, preserves the equality of its angles unshaken; whereas in the second, because there is such harmony among opposites, that law of the angles permits some inequality.

When this greatly moved me, it seemed that I should ask you how you could take pleasure in this truth, equity, and equality.

E. I now see what you mean, and I am greatly astonished.

A. Since you rightly prefer equality to inequality, and since, as I think, no one endowed with human understanding fails to see this, let us, if you please, seek a figure in which the highest equality can be found. Whatever it is, it will without doubt be preferred to all the others.

E. I gladly agree, and I am eager to know what it is.

## CHAPTER X.—The highest equality in figures

16. A. First answer this: of the figures we have already discussed as much as seemed sufficient, does the one seem superior to you which consists of four equal lines and an equal number of equal angles? For, as you see, in this figure both the lines and the angles are equal; and what we did not find in the one enclosed by three equal lines is present here: equality among opposites, since a line is opposed to a line and an angle to an angle, as you see.

E. It is exactly as you say.

A. Does it possess the highest equality, or do you see otherwise? If it does, then, as we had planned, we are seeking another in vain; but if it does not, I want you to demonstrate that very point to me.

E. It seems to me that it does. For where both the angles and the lines are equal, I do not see where I could find inequality.

A. I think otherwise. A straight line possesses the highest equality until it reaches the angles; but when another line is joined to it from the opposite side and forms an angle, do you not think that this itself is unequal? Or does the part of the figure enclosed by a line seem to you to correspond in equality or likeness with the part enclosed by an angle?

E. In no way. I am ashamed of my rashness, for I was led astray by seeing that the angles and sides in it were equal to one another. But who does not see the great difference between those sides and the angles?

A. Take another unmistakable indication of inequality. Surely you see that either the triangular figure consisting of equal lines or the square figure has some center.

E. I clearly see it.

A. What, then? When we draw lines from the same center to all parts of the figure, do the lines seem equal or unequal to you?

E. Entirely unequal. For those drawn to the angles must be longer.

A. How many are there in the square, and how many in the triangle?

E. Four here, three there.

A. And which are the shortest of all, and how many are there in each figure?

E. The same number—namely, those drawn to the middle of the sides.

A. You seem to me to be speaking most correctly, and there is no need to linger here any longer. What we want is sufficiently established: for you see, I think, that a great equality is preserved here, and yet it is not perfect in every respect.

E. I see it completely, and I eagerly await learning what figure possesses the highest equality.

## CHAPTER XI.—The superiority of figures. What a sign is; what a point is

17. A. Which figure could it be except the one whose boundary is everywhere harmonious with itself, without any angle disturbing its equality, and from whose center equal lines can be drawn to every part of its boundary?

E. I think I understand now. You seem to be describing the figure bounded by a single line drawn into a circle.

A. You understand correctly. Now consider this: since the preceding reasoning taught that a line is understood solely in length and does not take on any breadth, and therefore cannot be divided along its length, do you think that any figure without breadth can be found?

E. In no way.

A. What? Can breadth lack length, although it is breadth alone, just as above we understood length without breadth? Or can it not?

E. I see that it cannot.

A. You also see, unless I am mistaken, that breadth can be divided from every direction, whereas a line cannot be divided along its length.

E. That is clear.

A. What, then, do you think should be valued more highly: what can be divided, or what cannot?

E. Certainly what cannot.

A. You therefore prefer the line to breadth. For if what cannot be divided is to be preferred, then what can be divided less must also be preferred. Breadth is divided from every direction, whereas length is divided only from the opposite side, since it does not admit division along its length; therefore it is superior to breadth. Or do you think otherwise?

E. Reason absolutely compels me to admit that it is as you say.

18. A. Let us now ask, if you please, whether there is anything in this reasoning that cannot be divided at all. For that will be even better than the line. You see that a line can be divided innumerably from the opposite side, and so I leave it to you to discover this for yourself.

E. I think that what cannot be divided is the center that we placed in the figure, from which lines are drawn to the extremities. For if it is divided, it cannot lack length, or even breadth. But if it has length alone, it is no longer the point from which the lines are drawn; it is the line itself. If it is also broad, it requires another center from which lines may be drawn to the extremities of its breadth. Reason rejects both alternatives. It will therefore be something that cannot be divided.

A. You speak correctly. But does not something similar seem to be present even in that from which the line is drawn, although there is not yet a figure whose center we can conceive? I mean the beginning of the line, from which length begins, which I want you to conceive without any length whatsoever. For if you conceive length, you certainly do not conceive the point from which length itself begins.

E. Something entirely of that kind.

A. What you now understand, then, is the most powerful of all the things that have been demonstrated. For it is that which admits no division; and when it occupies the center of a figure, it is called a point. If it is the beginning or end of a line or lines, or if it marks anything at all that must be understood as without parts but does not occupy the center of a figure, it is called a sign.

A sign, therefore, is a mark without parts. A point, however, is a mark occupying the center of a figure. Thus every point is also a sign, but not every sign appears to be a point. I want us to agree about these names so that we may be less circumlocutory in our discussion. Many, however, call something a point not because it occupies the center of every figure, but because it occupies the center only of a circle or sphere; nevertheless, we should trouble ourselves less over terminology.

E. I agree.

## CHAPTER XII.—The power of the point

19. A. You certainly see how much power it has. A line begins from it and ends at it; we see that no figure made with straight lines can be formed unless an angle is closed by it; moreover, wherever a line is cut, it is cut through it, although it itself admits absolutely no division within itself; no line is joined to another except through it.

Finally, since reason has demonstrated that among the other plane figures—for we have not yet said anything about height—the figure enclosed by a circle must be preferred because of its highest equality, what other principle governs that equality than the point placed at the center?

Many things could be said about its power, but I shall observe restraint and leave more for you yourself to consider.

E. Certainly, as it seems. I shall not be reluctant to ask if anything is obscure. I see, at least moderately well, how great the power of this sign is.

20. A. Now consider this: since you have understood both what a sign is, what length is, and what breadth is, which of these seems to you to belong to another, and which requires another without which it cannot exist?

E. I see that breadth requires length, without which it cannot be understood at all. Again, I see that length does not require breadth in order to exist, but cannot exist without that sign. It is clear that the sign exists through itself and requires none of these things.

A. It is as you say. But consider more carefully whether breadth can truly be divided in every direction, or whether there is some direction from which even it cannot admit division, although it admits more division than a line.

E. I have no idea where it could not be divided.

A. I believe you do not remember; for you could not possibly be ignorant of this. I shall therefore remind you in the following way. Surely you understand breadth in such a way that your thought takes nothing from height?

E. Exactly so.

A. Let height, then, be added to this breadth, and answer whether anything has also been added by which it can be divided more completely in every direction.

E. You have reminded me wonderfully. Now I see that division can be admitted not only from above or below but also from the sides, and that nothing at all remains from which division cannot penetrate. It is therefore clear that breadth cannot be divided from those directions along which height is to rise.

21. A. Since, then, unless I am mistaken, length, breadth, and height are known to you, I ask whether the two higher dimensions can be absent where height is present.

E. I see that height cannot exist without length, but it can exist without breadth.

A. Return, then, to the conception of breadth. If you imagine it as lying flat, let it be raised in any direction, as though you wished to draw it through the thinnest crack where closed doors meet. Do you not yet understand what I mean?

E. I understand what you are saying, but perhaps not yet what you intend.

A. I mean that you should answer whether breadth, when raised in this way, seems to you to have changed into height and to have lost the name and description of breadth, or whether it still remains breadth, although placed in this position.

E. It seems to me to have become height.

A. Do you remember, I ask, how we defined height?

E. I remember perfectly, and I am ashamed that I answered as I did. For even when breadth is raised in this way, it does not admit division downward along its length; and so no interior parts can be conceived in it, although its center and extremities can be conceived. But according to your earlier demonstration of height, which you made me remember, there is no height at all where nothing within can be conceived.

A. You speak correctly, and I wanted you to remember it precisely in this way. Therefore answer me now whether you prefer what is false to what is true.

E. It would be incredible madness to doubt this any longer.

A. Tell me, then, please: is a true line one that can be divided along its length? Or a true sign one that can be divided in any way? Or is true breadth something which, when raised as we described, admits division downward along its length?

E. Nothing could be less so.

## CHAPTER XIII.—The incorporeal mind perceives incorporeal things. What the mind is

22. A. Have you ever seen with these bodily eyes either such a point, such a line, or such breadth?

E. Never at all. For these things are not corporeal.

A. Yet if corporeal things are perceived by bodily eyes through some wondrous kinship among things, then the mind by which we see incorporeal things must not be corporeal or a body. Or do you think otherwise?

E. Very well; I now grant that the mind is not a body or anything corporeal. But what, then, is it? Tell me.

A. First consider whether it has been established that it lacks all the quantity about which we are now inquiring. For I am astonished that you have forgotten what the mind is, since we discussed it in our earlier inquiry. You remember that you first asked where it came from. I remember that we treated this in two ways: first, as though you were asking about its region; second, whether it came from earth, fire, or any other of these elements, or from all of them, or from some of them.

In that inquiry we agreed that this question need no more be asked than where the earth comes from, or where any other individual element comes from. For although God made the mind, it must be understood to possess a definite substance that is neither earthly, nor fiery, nor airy, nor moist. Unless perhaps one should suppose that God granted earth to be nothing other than earth, but did not grant the mind to be nothing other than mind.

If you wish me to define the mind, and therefore ask what the mind is, I can answer easily. For it seems to me to be a certain substance sharing in reason, adapted to ruling the body.

## CHAPTER XIV.—How powerful the incorporeal mind is
23. Therefore attend rather to the point now in dispute: whether the soul has any quantity and, so to speak, any local extension. For assuredly, since it is not a body—for otherwise it could not perceive any incorporeal thing, as the preceding argument demonstrated—it is undoubtedly without the space by which bodies are measured; and for this reason its quantity cannot rightly be believed, imagined, or understood as such.

But if it troubles you that the soul retains in memory such vast spaces of heaven, earth, and sea, although it itself has no quantity, this is a remarkable power; nevertheless, insofar as your intelligence possesses light, you can discern it from what we have discovered. For if there is no body without length, breadth, and height, as reason has now shown—and none of these can exist in a body except together with the other two—yet the soul is permitted to see even a line alone with a kind of inward eye, that is, with understanding. I think we must grant that the soul is not a body, in such a way that it is superior to a body. Once this is granted, I do not think we should doubt that it is also superior to a line: for it would be ridiculous, when those three properties are present in a body in order for it to be a body, to say that one who is superior to a body is not superior to all of them.

But the line itself, to which the soul is shown to be superior, surpasses the other two because it can be divided less than they can. Moreover, those two are divided more than the line in proportion as they extend themselves into space; whereas the line has no space except length, and when that is removed, no space at all remains. Therefore whatever is superior to a line must necessarily be without space and altogether incapable of division or being cut. In my opinion, then, we labor in vain to discover a quantity of the soul—which has none—when we grant that it is superior to a line.

And if, among all plane figures, the best is that formed by a circle, in which reason has taught that nothing is better or more powerful than the point, which unquestionably has no parts, what wonder is it if the soul is neither corporeal nor extended in length, spread out in breadth, or solidified in height, and yet has such power in the body that the governance of all the limbs rests with it, and that it is, as it were, a kind of hinge in action for all bodily movements?

[Note: [Col. 1048] The editors read *illa cernere* (“to perceive that”), while the manuscripts read *ulla* (“any”).]

24. Since the middle of the eye, called the pupil, is nothing other than a kind of point of the eye, yet possesses such power that from some elevated place half the sky—whose extent is ineffable—can be seen and surveyed through it, it is not contrary to truth to say that the soul is without all corporeal magnitude, which is constituted by those three dimensions, although it can imagine any bodily magnitudes whatever.

Few people, however, can see the soul by the soul itself—that is, so that the soul sees itself [Col. 1049]; and it sees through understanding. For only understanding can see that nothing in reality is more powerful and magnificent than those natures which, so to speak, are understood to exist without swelling. “Swelling” is not improperly called bodily magnitude; and if magnitude deserved high esteem, elephants would certainly seem wiser to us.

If one of their kind should say that elephants are wise—for I have noticed, though with amazement, that people often doubt this too—he will at least, I think, grant that a little bee knows more than a donkey. To compare their sizes is surely more than asinine. Or, to return to what we were saying about the eye, who does not know that an eagle’s eye is much smaller than ours? Yet the eagle, flying so high that it is difficult for us to see it in such bright light, has been observed to see a little hare hiding beneath a bush and a fish beneath the waves.

If, then, even among the senses—which are incapable of sensing anything except corporeal things—the magnitude of the body contributes nothing to the act of sensing, should we fear, I ask, that the human soul, whose more excellent and almost solitary form of vision is reason itself, by which it also seeks to discover itself, is nothing, if that same reason—that is, the soul itself—proves it to be without every magnitude by which space is occupied?

[Note: [Col. 1049] The manuscripts have *se ipse* (“itself”); Erasmus and Lovaniensis read *ipsam* (“it”).]

Believe me, great things—very great things—must be conceived of the soul, but without any bulk. This is more easily achieved by those who approach these matters well educated, not inflamed by a desire for empty glory but kindled by divine love of truth, or by those who are already engaged in investigating them, even if they come to the inquiry less learned, provided that they patiently make themselves receptive to good instruction and turn themselves away, insofar as this life permits, from every association with bodily things. By a certain divine providence, it cannot happen that religious souls who seek themselves and their God—that is, truth—with devotion, purity, and diligence should lack the ability to find them.

### CHAPTER XV  
### It Is Objected That the Soul Grows with Age

25. But unless something still troubles you about this question, let us now leave it, if you please, and move on to other matters. Whatever we may perhaps have discussed at greater length than you wished concerning those figures, you will see how useful it is for what follows, if you grant that this discussion has contributed something to the inquiry. For this kind of discipline exercises the soul so that it may perceive subtler things, lest, dazzled by their light and unable to bear it, it willingly retreat into the very darkness from which it wished to flee. It also supplies, unless I am mistaken, arguments so certain that whatever has been discovered and established leaves no room for shameless doubt, insofar as human beings are permitted to investigate such matters.

[Note: [Col. 1049] Parisian and Erasmus read *quantum homini tali investigari* (“insofar as such a matter may be investigated by a human being”); the Venetian reads *investigare* (“to investigate”).]

[Note: [Col. 1049] At this point Erasmus and Lovaniensis insert the following words: “Shameless doubt is recognized as arising in two ways: either when a human being who is capable of using reason becomes so dull and lazy in seeking truth that he would rather remain in the darkness of vanity than labor, by true reasoning, to find and investigate himself and his God, for whose discovery and investigation he was created by his Creator; or when he doubts that what others have diligently and devoutly sought, discovered, and established can be found and established. They do this for no other reason than that they did not discover it themselves; reason proves this kind of envy to be utterly shameless.” All these words are absent from the Bad., the manuscripts, and Parisian M.]

[Col. 1050] I have less doubt about these matters than about things we see with these eyes, which are perpetually at war with phlegm. For what could be less tolerable and less worthy of being heard than to admit that we surpass beasts by reason, while admitting that the thing we perceive by bodily light is something—although some beasts see it better than we do—and yet to contend that what we behold by reason is nothing? If it were said to be such as that which the eyes see, nothing more dishonorable could surely be said.

[Note: [Col. 1050] Lovaniensis reads *nobis ratione praestare bestias* (“that beasts surpass us by reason”); but, with the other printed editions and manuscripts, one should read *nos ratione praestare bestiis* (“that we surpass beasts by reason”). Augustine here considers it intolerable if someone maintains that the object of reason is nothing while admitting that the object of bodily sight is something. His reason is that we surpass beasts by reason, whereas they often surpass us in the clarity of their vision.]

26. E. I gladly accept and approve this. But I am troubled by the following. It is so clear to me that the soul is not a thing of corporeal quantity that I altogether do not know how to resist those arguments or what part of them I should refuse to grant. First, why does the soul, just as the body grows with age, either grow or appear to grow? For who would deny that young children are not even comparable with the cunning of some animals? And who would doubt that, as they grow, reason itself somehow grows within them?

Further, if the soul is extended through the space occupied by its body, how is it without quantity? But if it is not extended, how does it feel what pricks it everywhere?

A. You are asking precisely the questions that have often troubled me as well. Therefore I am not unprepared to answer you, as I usually answer myself; whether I shall answer well, the reason that moves you will judge. Whatever the answer may be, however, I certainly cannot do more, unless something better occurs to us by divine inspiration as we discuss. But let us proceed, if you please, in our usual way, so that, with reason as your guide, you may answer yourself.

First, let us ask whether the fact that the soul grows with the body is securely proved by this: as age advances, a person becomes more suited to human society and increasingly skilled in it.

E. Proceed as you wish. I especially approve this manner of teaching and learning. For somehow, when I myself answer what I was seeking because I did not know it, the discovery becomes sweeter not only because of the thing itself but also because of the wonder it produces.

[Note: [Col. 1050] Lovaniensis reads *animi ratione* (“by the soul’s reason”), apparently through a scribal error for *admiratione* (“wonder”), as found in the ancient manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER XVI  
### The Objection Is Answered, and It Is Shown That the Soul Progresses Without Bodily Increase

27. A. Tell me, then: do “greater” and “better” seem to you to be two things, or one and the same thing called by two names?

E. I know that “greater” is one thing and “better” another.

A. Which of these two do you think possesses quantity?

E. Obviously, that which we call greater.

A. When we admit that, of two figures, the round one is better than the square, is quantity responsible for this, or something else?

E. In no way quantity. Rather, the equality of which we spoke earlier is the cause of this excellence.

A. Now consider whether virtue seems to you to be a certain equality of a life wholly consonant with reason. For if one part of life [Col. 1051] differs from another, we are more offended by it, I think, than if some part of a circle were farther from the center than the other parts, whether by a greater or lesser interval. Or do you think otherwise?

E. No, I agree. I approve the account of virtue that you have given: reason must neither be called nor considered reason unless it is true; and the person whose life conforms in every respect to truth is certainly either the only person, or at least the chief person, who lives well and honorably. Whoever is so disposed must be judged to possess virtue and to live by it.

A. You speak well. But surely you also see, I think, that among plane figures the circle resembles virtue more than any other figure. This is why we habitually praise in the highest terms that line of Horace in which, speaking of the wise man, he says:

> Strong, and wholly self-contained, smooth and rounded in himself.  
> (*Satires* 2.7.60.)

And rightly so. For among the goods of the soul you will find nothing that agrees with itself in every respect more than virtue; nor among plane figures anything more than the circle. Therefore, if the circle surpasses the others not by the magnitude of the space it occupies but by a certain configuration, how much more should we think of virtue as surpassing the other dispositions of the soul, not by occupying a larger place but by a certain divine congruence and harmony of reasons?

28. When a boy makes laudable progress, in what does he more properly get said to progress than in virtue? Or does this not seem clear to you?

E. It is obvious.

A. You should not, then, think that the soul progresses with age by growing as the body does. For by progressing it reaches virtue, which we admit to be beautiful and perfect not through any magnitude of space but through great strength of steadfastness. And since, as you have already granted, one thing is greater and another better, whatever the soul gains with age, becoming capable of reason, does not seem to me to make it greater but better. If the magnitude of the limbs caused this, each person would be wiser in proportion as he was taller or stronger—which, I think, you will not deny is otherwise.

E. Who could deny it? Yet since you too grant that the soul progresses with age, I am surprised how it can be aided by time while being free of every quantity—even if not by the space of the limbs, at least by the passage of time.

### CHAPTER XVII  
### The Soul Is Said Metaphorically to Grow Through Time

29. Stop being surprised, for here too I answer you by a similar argument. The magnitude of the limbs supplies no evidence that it aids the soul, since many people with thinner and shorter limbs are found to be wiser than some who possess bodies of great bulk. Likewise, since we see some younger people more industrious and energetic than most older people, I do not see why we should think that intervals of time in the stages of life give growth to souls as they do to bodies.

Even bodies themselves, which are permitted to grow over time and occupy larger spaces, are often shorter when they are older—not merely in old age, when they contract and diminish through the length of time, but even among children, whom we observe to be shorter in body than those who are older in age.

If, then, extended [Col. 1052] periods of time do not even cause bodies to become larger, but all that effect belongs to the power of the seed and to certain numbers of nature—quite hidden and difficult to discern—how much less should we suppose that the soul becomes longer through a long period of time because we see it learn much through experience and continual practice?

30. If it troubles you that we usually translate what the Greeks call *μακροθυμία* (*makrothymia*) as “longanimity,” you may observe that many words are transferred from body to soul, just as many are transferred from soul to body. Virgil called a mountain “unrelenting” and the earth “most just” (*Aeneid* 12.687; *Georgics* 2.460); you see that these expressions have been transferred from the soul to bodies. What wonder, then, if by a reciprocal transfer we speak of “longanimity,” since only bodies can be long?

That virtue which is called greatness of soul (*magnitudo animi*) is rightly understood as referring not to any spatial extent but to a certain force—that is, to the soul’s authority and power. A virtue is to be valued more highly in proportion as it despises more things. We shall speak of this later, when we ask how great the soul is, just as people customarily ask how great Hercules was, meaning the excellence of his deeds, not the bulk of his limbs; for that is how we divided the subject above.

But you must now recall what we have already sufficiently discussed concerning the point. Reason taught that the point is most powerful and exercises the greatest authority among figures. But do power and authority not display a certain greatness? Yet in the point we found no space at all. Therefore, when we hear or say that a soul is great or enormous, we must think not of how much space it occupies but of how much it can do.

Accordingly, if your first argument—that the soul seemed to you to grow with the body through age—has now been sufficiently examined, let us move on to the next.

### CHAPTER XVIII  
### The Capacity for Speech, Which a Child Gradually Acquires, Is Not to Be Attributed to Growth of the Soul

31. E. I do not know whether we have pursued everything that has often, and not without reason, troubled me. It may be that some things have escaped my memory. Nevertheless, let us examine what has now occurred to me: an infant child does not speak, but acquires speech as he grows.

A. This is easy. I suppose you think that everyone speaks the language spoken by the people among whom he was born and raised.

E. No one is unaware of that.

A. Imagine, then, someone born and raised among people who did not speak but expressed and signaled their thoughts to one another by gestures and movements of their limbs. Do you not think that he would do the same, and would not speak, having heard no one speak?

E. Do not ask me about something impossible. How could I imagine anyone born among such people?

A. Have you not seen at Milan a young man of the most respectable appearance and the greatest urbanity, yet mute and so deaf that he understood others only through bodily movement and himself communicated what he wished in no other way? He is very well known.

[Note: [Col. 1052] B has *hinc* (“from here”); Parisian, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis have *hic* (“this man”), which is indeed better. M.]

[Col. 1053] For I knew a certain rustic who spoke, though his wife also spoke, yet fathered nearly four—or perhaps more; I do not now remember exactly—sons and daughters who were mute and deaf. They were called mute because they could not speak, and deaf because they gathered no signs except through their eyes.

E. I know that man well, and I believe you concerning these others of whom you speak. But what is the point?

A. Because you said that you could not imagine anyone born among such people.

E. I say nothing different now. For you grant, unless I am mistaken, that these men were born among people who spoke.

A. I do not deny it. But since it is now agreed between us that some such people can exist, imagine, I ask, that a man and woman of this kind were joined together and, having been carried by some chance into a solitude where they could nevertheless live, begot a son who was not deaf. How would this child speak with his parents?

E. How do you suppose, except that he would return signs by gestures, just as his parents gave them to him? Yet a very small child could not even do that; so my argument remains intact. For what difference does it make whether he acquires speech or gesture as he grows, when both belong to the soul, which we do not wish to admit grows?

32. A. It now seems to me that, when someone walks on a tightrope, you believe him to have a larger soul than those who cannot do so.

E. That is different. Who does not see that this is a skill?

A. Why, I ask, is it a skill? Is it because he learned it?

E. Certainly.

A. Why, then, if someone learns something else, does that not also seem to you to be a skill?

E. I do not deny that whatever is learned is a skill.

A. Did he not, then, learn from his parents to make gestures?

E. Certainly he learned it.

A. Therefore you must grant that this too results not from a larger soul produced by growth, but from a certain imitative skill.

E. I cannot grant that.

A. Then not everything learned is a skill, although you had just granted this.

E. It is entirely a skill.

A. Then he did not learn to make gestures, which you had likewise granted.

E. He learned it, but it is not a skill.

A. Yet just now you said that what is learned is a skill.

E. Very well, I now grant that both speaking and making gestures are skills because we learned them. Nevertheless, there are skills that we learn by directing our attention to others, and others that teachers implant in us.

A. Which of these do you think the soul acquires because it becomes larger? All of them?

E. I do not think all, but the former kind.

A. Does walking on a tightrope not seem to you to belong to this kind? For those who do it acquire it, I suppose, by watching it.

E. I believe so. Yet not everyone who watches and observes these things with great attention can acquire them, but only those who submit themselves to teachers of the skill.

A. You speak well. I could answer you in the same way concerning speech. Many Greeks hear us speaking more frequently than they watch a tightrope walker; and in order to learn our language, just as we wish to learn theirs, they are often placed under teachers. Since this is so, I am surprised that you wish to attribute people’s speaking to growth of the soul but not their walking on a tightrope.

E. I do not know how you confuse these matters. A person who is placed under a teacher in order to learn our language already knows [Col. 1054] another language of his own, which I think he learned because his soul had grown. But when he learns a foreign language, I attribute that to skill, not to a larger soul.

A. What if someone born and raised among the mute later, already a young man, encountered other people and learned to speak, while knowing no other language? Would you think that his soul had grown at the time when he learned to speak?

E. I would never dare say that. I now yield to reason, and I do not think that speaking is evidence of a larger soul, lest I be forced to admit that the soul acquired all other skills by growing. If I said that, the absurd consequence would follow that the soul diminishes whenever it forgets anything.

### CHAPTER XIX  
### How the Soul Is Said to Grow or Diminish

33. A. You understand correctly. And, to tell the truth, the soul is rightly said to grow through learning, as it is said to diminish through unlearning, but only by a transferred use of the word, as we showed earlier. Care must nevertheless be taken lest, when it is said to grow, it seem to occupy a greater spatial extent; rather, the more experienced soul has a greater power for action than the inexperienced one.

It makes a great difference, however, what the things are that it learns, by which it seems somehow to be enlarged. For just as there are three kinds of growth in the body, so there are corresponding distinctions in the soul.

The first is necessary growth, by which the natural proportion of the limbs is completed. The second is excessive growth, by which one part becomes different from the others while the body remains in sound health; thus people are sometimes born with six fingers, and many other things that, when they are excessive beyond custom, are called monstrous. The third is harmful growth, which, when it occurs, is called a swelling. For in this way too the limbs are said to grow, and they really do occupy more space, but at the cost of sound health.

Similarly, there are in the soul certain quasi-natural forms of growth, when it is said to be enlarged by disciplines that are honorable and suited to living well and happily. But when we learn things that are more marvelous than useful—although they are often advantageous for particular purposes—they are nevertheless superfluous and must be counted as belonging to the second kind.

For if, as Varro relates, some flute-player so delighted the people that he became king, we should not therefore think that our souls ought to be enlarged by that art. Nor would we wish to have teeth larger than human teeth if we heard that someone had killed an enemy by biting him because he possessed such teeth.

The harmful kind is that of skills by which the soul’s health is wounded. To distinguish food by smell and taste with extraordinary precision, to know in which lake a fish was caught, or to tell how many years old a wine is—[Note: [Col. 1054] Parisian M. reads *discere* (“to learn”).]—is a pitiable kind of expertise. When the soul seems to grow through such skills, having neglected the mind and flowed down into the senses, it must be judged to have done nothing except swell, or even waste away.

### CHAPTER XX  
### Whether the Soul Knows Anything from Itself

34. E. I accept and approve this, yet I am still troubled by the fact that the soul is ignorant and brutish with respect to all things, as far as we can observe in a newborn child. Why did it bring no skill with it, if it is [Col. 1055] eternal?

A. You raise an exceedingly great question—indeed, I do not know whether anything greater exists. In it our opinions oppose each other so sharply that you think the soul brought no skill with it, while I think that it brought all skills with it; and that what is called learning is nothing other than recollecting and remembering.

[Note: [Col. 1055] See *Retractions* 1.8.2.]

But do you see that it does not belong to the present inquiry to ask whether these matters are so? We are now concerned to establish, if possible, that the soul is not called small or great according to the spaces of place. If it is eternal, we shall investigate that appropriately when we begin to treat the fourth question you proposed: why it was given to the body, insofar as it is permitted to inquire into that.

For what bearing on the soul’s quantity does it have whether it has always existed or not, whether it will exist forever, or whether it is now ignorant and now learned? We have already proved that even a long period of time does not cause bodies to become larger; and it is well known that learning may be absent in those who are growing and may often be useful in those who are aging. Enough else has also been said, I think, to demonstrate that the soul does not become larger along with the bodily magnitude that age brings.

### CHAPTER XXI  
### Greater Strength at a More Advanced Age Is Not Evidence That the Soul Grows

35. Let us therefore examine, if you please, your other argument: that the soul feels touch throughout the entire extent of the body, although we wish to say that it has no extent.

E. I would allow us to pass to that point now, except that I think something must be said about strength. What is this, that bodies enlarged by age provide the soul with greater strength, if the soul does not become larger with them? Although the soul’s power and the body’s strength are usually distinguished, I would never separate strength from the soul, since I see that there is none in lifeless bodies.

It must indeed be admitted that the soul uses the body for strength, just as it uses it for sensation. Yet since these are functions of a living being, who would doubt that they belong to the soul rather?

Since, then, we see greater strength in somewhat older children than in infants, and then adolescents and young men surpass one another from day to day in strength until it again diminishes as the body grows old, this seems to me no slight indication that the soul first grows with the body and then grows old with it.

36. A. What you say is not entirely absurd. But I am accustomed to think that strength depends no more on the increase of bodily size and age than on a certain exercise and formation of the limbs. To prove this to you, I ask whether you think that one person’s walking more persistently and becoming less tired than another’s is a sign of greater strength.

E. I do.

A. Why, then, when I was a boy and exercised myself by walking in pursuit of birds, could I cover a much greater distance without fatigue than I could as a young man, when I had turned to other studies that required me to sit more, if greater strength must be attributed to advancing age and to the soul growing through it?

Further, in the very bodies of wrestlers, trainers in the wrestling school carefully inspect not [Col. 1056] bulk and size but certain knots of muscle, tightened sinews, and the entire proportionate form of the body; from these they gather their evidence of strength. Yet all these things are of little value unless the power of skill and exercise is added.

Often, too, men of enormous bodies have been seen to be defeated by small and short men, whether in moving or carrying weights or even in wrestling itself. Who does not know that an Olympic champion may become tired on a journey sooner than some traveling merchant who could be knocked down with one of the champion’s fingers?

[Note: [Col. 1056] Erasmus and the manuscripts read *circumforanum*; Lovaniensis has *circumforaneum*.]

Therefore, if we call the strengths themselves great not equally in every case but according to their fitness for different tasks; if the lines and form of bodies are more important than their size; and if exercise contributes so much that it is widely believed that a man who lifted a small calf every day thereby became able to lift and support even a bull without feeling the increase of the burden, which was added gradually—then strength in more advanced age by no means indicates that the soul has grown with the body.

### CHAPTER XXII  
### The Source of Greater Bodily Strength

37. If larger animals possess somewhat more strength precisely because their bodies are larger, the reason is that, by the law of nature, smaller weights yield to larger ones—not only when they are carried by their own impulse toward their proper place, as moist and earthy bodies move toward the center of the world, which is the lowest place, while airy and fiery bodies move upward, but also when, through some engine, throw, push, or repulsion, they are forced by an external power to move in a direction in which they would not move spontaneously.

For if you release two stones of unequal size from a height at the same time, the larger does indeed reach the ground sooner. But if the smaller is placed beneath it and is inevitably struck by it, it certainly yields and is brought down to the ground with it.

Likewise, if the larger is thrown downward from above while the smaller is thrown upward, when they meet, the smaller must be knocked back and recoil. And do not think that this happens because the smaller was being forced upward contrary to nature while the other was seeking its proper place with greater force. Have the larger hurled upward and meet the smaller as it is thrown down toward the earth: you will nevertheless see the smaller driven back toward the sky, though by the rebound itself it will fall to another side, so that it may be carried downward where its path is unobstructed.

Again, if both stones are thrown not by natural motion but by two combatants, as though on a field, against each other, and collide in the middle space, who would doubt that the smaller will yield to the larger and be driven toward the side from which it itself came and toward which the other was traveling?

[Note: [Col. 1056] Parisian, Erasmus, Venetian, and Lovaniensis read: “from where it itself is and toward where the other was traveling.”]

Since this is so—that smaller weights, as stated, yield to larger ones—the force with which they strike one another nevertheless makes a great difference. For if the smaller, launched by some violent engine with greater force, strikes the larger, whether the larger has been thrown more weakly or is already losing momentum, it will rebound from it but nevertheless slow it down, or even drive it backward, according to the force of the blows and the weights involved.

38. With these points stated and understood, insofar as the present [Col. 1057] matter requires, consider whether the strengths attributed to animals agree with this account. Who denies that all animal bodies possess weight? When that weight is moved by the soul’s impulse, it is greatly affected by its own magnitude, in whatever direction the impulse turns it.

But the soul’s impulse in moving the body’s weight uses the nerves as though they were engines. Dryness and moderate heat invigorate the nerves and make them more mobile; moist cold, on the contrary, relaxes and weakens them. Thus the limbs become sluggish in sleep, since physicians say and demonstrate that sleep is cold and moist; and the effort of those waking from sleep is much weaker. Nothing, therefore, is more broken and nerveless than the bodies of lethargic patients.

But certain victims of delirium, whose sleeplessness, the power of wine [Note: [Col. 1057] Parisian M. reads *vitii* (“of a vice” or “of a fault”).], and acute fevers—that is, so much excessive heat—stretch and stiffen the nerves beyond measure, visibly resist with greater strength than they would in sound health and perform many actions, although their bodies have been thinned and weakened by illness.

If, then, these things called strengths arise from the soul’s impulse, from a kind of mechanism of the nerves, and from the body’s weight, the will supplies the impulse. That impulse becomes more eager through hope or boldness, but is blunted by fear, and much more by despair—for when some hope is present within fear, stronger efforts usually appear. A certain bodily configuration fits together the mechanism; the body’s condition regulates it; diligent exercise strengthens it; and the mass of the limbs supplies the weight, which age and nourishment acquire, though only nourishment restores it.

[Note: [Col. 1057] The manuscripts have *valetudinis* (“of the body’s condition”); the editions have *valetudines* (“conditions”).]

Whoever prevails equally in all these respects is remarkable for strength; and one person is weaker than another in proportion as these factors fail him. It often happens that one person, through a persistent impulse and a better mechanism, overcomes another possessing a greater bodily mass, although he moves only a small weight. Conversely, sometimes the mass is so great that, even when moved by a weaker effort, it nevertheless overwhelms a small opponent who is exerting himself much more vigorously.

But when it is not the body’s weight or the regulation of the nerves but the impulse itself—that is, the soul—that gives way, so that someone altogether stronger is defeated by someone altogether weaker, or someone timid by someone bolder, I do not know whether this should be attributed to strength. Unless someone says that the soul possesses certain powers of its own, by which greater boldness or confidence is produced. When these are present in one person and absent in another, it becomes clear how much the soul surpasses its body even in what is performed through the body.

39. Since, in an infant, the impulse alone for pulling or pushing something is intact, while the nerves are unfit both because their formation is recent and incomplete and because the moisture abundant at that age makes them slack, and because the lack of exercise leaves them weak; and since the body’s weight is so slight that it would not press heavily even if struck by someone else, being more suited to receiving than to inflicting harm—who, when he observes all these deficiencies supplied by the passing years and recognizes the strength thereby provided, would rightly think that the soul has grown because it uses these things as they become greater from day to day?

[Col. 1058] For suppose such a person saw a young man, hidden from his view by an intervening curtain, shoot small, light reeds from a slack bow with all his strength, yet saw them travel only a short distance and soon fall back; then, shortly afterward, saw arrows already heavy with iron and made lively by their feathers, shot from a most tightly drawn bowstring, fly toward the remotest sky; and suppose he were assured that both had been done by the man with equal effort. Would he think that the man had grown in that brief time and had acquired greater strength? What could be more perverse than that?

40. Further, if the soul grows, consider how foolish it is to believe its growth from bodily strength but not from the abundance of learning, when the soul merely directs the former but possesses the latter by itself. Yet if we think that the soul grows when strength is added, we must think that it diminishes when strength is taken away.

Strength is taken away in old age; it is taken away through the labor of study. Yet it is precisely during these periods that learning is commonly accumulated and built up. Nor can anything increase and diminish simultaneously at the same time.

Therefore, greater strength at a more advanced age is no evidence that the soul grows. Many other things could be said, but if you are now satisfied, I shall impose a limit and move on to other matters.

E. I am indeed sufficiently convinced that greater strength does not result from the soul’s having grown. To omit the other points you have discussed so subtly, even a madman would not say that the soul grows through insanity and bodily illness while the body itself diminishes, although no one is unaware that the strength of the delirious is often much greater than that of the healthy.

Therefore it seems to me especially that everything remarkable in strength lies in the nerves. So now, I ask you, address the point to which I am wholly devoted: if the soul does not possess an extension as large as the body’s, why does it feel everywhere when the body is touched?

[Note: [Col. 1058] Parisian, Erasmus, and Venetian read *ubique illa* (“it feels it everywhere”); Lovaniensis has *ubique [.....]*.]

### CHAPTER XXIII  
### Although the Soul Feels Throughout the Whole Body, It Is Not Therefore Extended with the Body. What Sensation Is and How Vision Occurs
41. A. Come now, let us undertake what you wish, but I need you to be much more attentive than you perhaps suppose you ought to be. So make every effort to be fully present, and answer me: what do you think this sense is by which the soul makes use of the body? For it is already called “sense” by its proper name.

E. I usually hear that there are five senses: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching. I do not know what more to answer.

A. This division is very ancient and is commonly celebrated in public speeches. I should like you, however, to define for me what sense itself is, so that the same definition would include all those senses, while nothing else that was not sense would be understood in it. But if that cannot be done, I shall not press the matter. For what is sufficient—you can certainly either refute or establish my definition.

E. In this way, perhaps, I shall not fail you, as far as I am able; for even this is not always easy.

A. Attend, then. For I think sense is this: that what the body undergoes is not hidden from the soul.

E. I approve this definition.

A. Then take it as though it were your own, and defend it while I refute it for a little while.

E. I shall certainly defend it, if you help me; but if you do not, I already dislike it. For you did not think it needed refutation without reason.

A. Do not depend too much on authority, especially mine, which has none; and heed what Horace says: “Dare to be wise” (*Epistles* 1.2.39), lest reason fail to subdue you before fear does.

E. I am altogether unafraid, however matters may proceed; for you will not let me go wrong. But begin now, if you have anything to say, lest by delaying rather than opposing you wear me out.

42. A. Tell me, then: what does your body undergo when you see me?

E. It certainly undergoes something; for my eyes are parts of my body, unless I am mistaken. If they underwent nothing, how would I see you?

A. But it is not enough to persuade me that your eyes undergo something, unless you show what they undergo.

E. What else, then, except sight itself? For they see. If you asked me what a sick person undergoes, I would answer, sickness; what someone desiring something undergoes, desire; what someone fearing undergoes, fear; what someone rejoicing undergoes, joy. Why, then, when you ask what someone seeing undergoes, should I not properly answer “sight itself”?

A. But someone who is rejoicing feels joy. Do you deny it?

E. On the contrary, I agree.

A. I would say the same of the other disturbances.

E. That is my view.

A. But whatever the eyes feel, they see.

E. I will by no means grant that. For who sees pain, although the eyes often feel it?

A. It is clear that you are speaking about the eyes; you are paying close attention. Consider, then, whether, just as someone rejoicing feels joy by rejoicing, someone seeing likewise feels sight by seeing.

E. How could it be otherwise?

A. But whatever someone seeing feels by seeing, he must also see.

E. That is not necessary. For what if he feels love by seeing? Does he also see love?

A. You are extremely careful and perceptive; I am glad that you are not easily deceived. But attend now. Since we have established between us that not everything the eyes feel is seen, and that not everything felt by seeing is seen, do you think at least this is true: that everything which is seen is felt?

E. Certainly. Unless I grant this, how can what we see be called sense?

A. What, then? Do we not also undergo everything that we feel?

E. Yes.

A. Therefore, if we feel everything that we see, and undergo everything that we feel, we undergo everything that we see.

E. I offer no resistance.

A. Then you undergo me, and I in turn undergo you, when we see each other.

E. That is my view, and reason strongly compels me to this conclusion.

43. A. Consider the rest. For I suppose it would seem most absurd and foolish to you if someone asserted that you undergo a body in a place where the body you undergo is not itself present.

E. It seems absurd, and I think it is as you say.

A. What of this? Is it not clear that my body is in one place and yours in another?

E. It is clear.

A. Your eyes feel my body; and if they feel it, they certainly undergo something. They cannot undergo it where what they undergo is not present. Yet they are not where my body is. Therefore, they undergo it where they are not.

E. I granted all those points whose denial seemed absurd; but this final conclusion drawn from them is so much more absurd that I would sooner admit that I rashly granted some part of the earlier argument than agree that this is true. I would not dare say even in a dream that my eyes feel where they are not.

A. Consider, then, where you have fallen asleep. For what would have slipped from you more carelessly if you had remained as attentive as a moment ago?

E. Indeed, I am carefully examining and turning this over in my mind. Yet nothing sufficiently emerges that I regret having granted, except perhaps this: that our eyes feel when we see. For perhaps sight itself feels.

A. No, that is how it is. Sight stretches outward and flashes forth through the eyes as far as it can survey in every direction what we see. Thus it sees rather where the thing it sees is than where it bursts forth in order to see. So, when you see me, are you not seeing?

E. What madman would say that? I certainly see, but I see by sight extended through my eyes.

A. But if you see, you feel; if you feel, you undergo something; and you cannot undergo something where you are not. Yet you see me where I am; therefore, you undergo something where I am. But if you are not where I am, I do not at all understand how you dare say that I am seen by you.

E. I see you, I say, by sight extended to the place where you are; I see you where you are, but I admit that I am not there. Yet just as, if I touched you with a stick, I would certainly touch you and feel it, although I would not be where I touched you, so, when I say that I see by sight, although I am not there, I am not thereby forced to admit that I am not the one who sees.

44. A. Then you granted nothing rashly. For your eyes too can be defended in this way: their sight is, as you say, like a stick. Nor is the conclusion absurd that your eyes see where they are not. Do you see the matter differently?

E. It is certainly as you say. For I have now noticed this as well: if the eyes saw where they are, they would also see themselves.
