A. More correctly you would say not “they would also see themselves,” but “they would see only themselves.” For where they are—that is, the place they occupy—they occupy alone. The nose is not there where they are, nor anything else adjacent to them. Otherwise you too would be where I am, since we are beside one another. Since this is so, if the eyes saw only where they are, they would see nothing more than themselves. But since they do not see themselves, we are compelled not only to agree that they can see where they are not, but also that they cannot see except where they are not.

E. There is nothing that makes me doubt this.

A. Then you do not doubt that they undergo something where they are not. For where they see, there they feel; seeing itself is feeling, and feeling is undergoing. Therefore, where they feel, there they undergo something. But they see elsewhere than where they are; therefore, they undergo something where they are not.

E. It is astonishing how true I think all this is.

## CHAPTER XXIV — The Definition of Sense Is Examined

45. A. Perhaps you are right to think so. But answer me, please: do we see everything that we recognize through sight?

E. I believe so.

A. Do you also believe that everything we recognize by seeing, we recognize through sight?

E. I believe that as well.

A. Why, then, when we see only smoke, do we usually recognize that fire lies beneath it, although we do not see the fire?

E. You are right. I no longer think that we see everything we recognize through sight. For, as you have taught, by seeing one thing we can recognize another which sight has not reached.

A. What, then? Can we fail to see what we feel through sight?

E. In no way.

A. Therefore, feeling is one thing and recognizing another.

E. Entirely different. For we feel the smoke, which we see; and from it we recognize that fire, which we do not see, lies beneath.

A. You understand correctly. But you surely see that, when this happens, our body—that is, our eyes—undergoes nothing from the fire, but only from the smoke, which alone they see. For we have already agreed that seeing is feeling, and feeling is undergoing.

E. I understand and agree.

A. Therefore, when something is not hidden from the soul through an affection of the body, it is not immediately called one of the five senses mentioned earlier; rather, it is called sense when the affection itself is not hidden. For that unseen fire is neither heard, smelled, tasted, nor touched by us, yet it is not hidden from the soul because the smoke is seen. Since this not-being-hidden is not called sense, because the body underwent nothing from the fire, it is nevertheless called cognition through sense, because it was inferred and ascertained from an affection of the body, though from a different one—that is, from the sight of another thing.

E. I understand, and I see very clearly that this agrees with and supports your definition, which you gave me to defend as my own. For I remember that you defined sense as the condition in which what the body undergoes is not hidden from the soul. Thus, what is seen—the smoke—we call sense, for the eyes underwent it by seeing, and the eyes are both parts of the body and bodies themselves. But the fire, from which the body underwent nothing, we do not call sense, although it was recognized.

46. A. I approve your memory and your consistent understanding; yet that defense of the definition is weakening.

E. Why, please?

A. Because, as I suppose you do not deny, the body undergoes something when we grow or grow old. It is clear that we do not feel this through any sense, and yet it is not hidden from the soul. Therefore, something that the body undergoes is not hidden from the soul, but this cannot be called sense. For by seeing things larger than we once saw them when they were smaller, and by seeing people whom we know to have been young men and children now grown old, we infer that our bodies too are undergoing some such change even now while we speak. Nor, I think, are we mistaken in this. It is easier for me to say that I am mistaken about what I see than about my understanding that my hair is now growing or that my body is changing from moment to moment. If this change is an affection of the body—and no one denies that it is—and if it is not now felt by us, yet is not hidden from the soul because it is not hidden from us, then, as I said, the body undergoes something which is not hidden from the soul, but this is nevertheless not sense. Therefore, that definition, which ought to include nothing that was not sense, is certainly defective because it included this.

E. I see that nothing remains for me but to ask you either to define it differently or, if you can, to repair it. For I cannot deny that the definition I strongly approved for the reason you gave is defective.

A. It is easy to correct it, provided you dare to do what I want. You will do so, believe me, if you have understood where it goes wrong.

E. Is it anywhere except where it included something foreign?

A. How so?

E. Because the body that grows old, even in a young person, cannot be denied to undergo something; and when we know this, something the body undergoes is not hidden from the soul, yet it cannot be perceived through any sense. For I do not see myself growing old at this moment, nor do I feel it by hearing, smelling, tasting, or touching.

A. How, then, do you know it?

E. I infer it by reason.

A. On what evidence does your reason rely?

E. I see other people who are old, although they were young, as I am now.

A. Is not the sense by which you see them one of the five?

E. Who denies it? But from seeing them, although I do not see it, I infer that I too am growing old.

A. What words, then, do you think should be added to that definition to complete it, since sense is nothing other than that an affection of the body is not hidden from the soul, but not in such a way that the soul understands it through another affection or through anything else?

E. Tell me, please, somewhat more plainly.

## CHAPTER XXV — How a Definition Must Be Examined

47. A. I shall oblige you, and much more willingly because you are slowing me down than if you were hurrying me. But be wholly attentive; what I am about to say will be useful for many things.

A definition contains neither less nor more than what has been undertaken for explanation; otherwise it is altogether defective. Whether it is free from such defects is tested by conversion. The matter will become clearer to you through these examples.

If you asked me what a human being was, and I defined one in this way—“A human being is a mortal animal”—you should not immediately approve the definition merely because the statement was true. Instead, you should prefix the word “every,” convert it, and consider whether the converted statement was also true. That is, just as it is true to say, “Every human being is a mortal animal,” would it also be true to say, “Every mortal animal is a human being”? If you find otherwise, you should reject the definition because of the defect by which it includes something foreign. For a human being is not the only mortal animal; every beast is one as well.

The definition of a human being is therefore usually completed by adding “rational” to “mortal”: “A human being is a rational mortal animal.” Just as every human being is a rational mortal animal, so every rational mortal animal is a human being. The earlier definition was defective because it contained more than it should: it included a beast along with a human being. This definition is complete, for it contains every human being and nothing more than a human being.

But a definition is likewise defective if it contains less, as it would be if you added “grammatical.” Although every rational mortal grammatical animal is a human being, many human beings who are not grammarians are not included by this definition. For that reason it is false in its first proposition, although true when converted. It is false to say, “Every human being is a rational mortal grammatical animal,” but true to say, “Every rational mortal grammatical animal is a human being.”

When a definition is true neither in its first proposition nor in its conversion, it is still more defective in both respects. Such are these two: “A human being is a white animal,” or “A human being is a four-footed animal.” If you say either “Every human being is a white animal” or “Every human being is a four-footed animal,” you speak falsely; and the converted statements are false as well. They differ, however, in this respect: the first applies to some human beings, for many human beings are white; the second applies to no one, for no human being is four-footed.

For the present, you have learned enough to examine definitions by seeing how they are judged through proposition and conversion. There are many other matters of this kind that are taught—full of words and darkness—which, little by little, when the occasion seems suitable, I shall try to teach you.

48. Now turn your attention to our definition, and, having examined it more skillfully, correct it. We had found that, when it defined sense, it included something that was not sense, and therefore was not true when converted. For perhaps it is true to say, “Every sense is an affection of the body not hidden from the soul,” just as it is true to say, “Every human being is a mortal animal.” But just as it is false to say, “Every mortal animal is a human being,” because a beast is also a mortal animal, so it is false to say, “Every affection of the body not hidden from the soul is sense.” For our nails are now growing, and this is not hidden from the soul, since we know it; yet we do not feel it, but know it by inference.

Just as “rational” was added to the definition of a human being in order to complete it, thereby excluding the beasts that had been included along with human beings, so that the definition would contain both every human being and nothing besides a human being, do you not think that something must also be added to this definition, so that what it contains foreign to itself may be separated from it, and so that nothing but sense, and every sense, may be understood in it?

E. I certainly think so, but I do not know what could be added.

A. Every sense is certainly an affection of the body not hidden from the soul; but this statement cannot be converted because of that affection of the body by which it grows or diminishes while we know it—that is, because it is not hidden from the soul.

E. That is so.

A. What, then? Is this affection itself not hidden from the soul in itself, or through something else?

E. Clearly, through something else. For seeing larger nails is one thing, and knowing that they are growing is another.

A. Since growth itself is the affection, which we reach through no sense, while that size which we feel has been produced by the same affection but is not itself the affection, it is clear that we know such an affection not through itself but through something else. If it were not hidden from the soul through something else, would it not be felt rather than inferred?

E. I understand.

A. Why, then, do you hesitate over what must be added to the definition?

E. I now see that it should be defined in this way: sense is an affection of the body not hidden from the soul in itself. For every sense is this, and, as I think, everything that is this is sense.

49. A. If this is so, I admit that the definition is complete. But, if you agree, let us test whether it does not falter through that second defect, like the definition of a human being to which “grammatical” was added.

You must remember that it was said that a human being is a rational, mortal, grammatical animal, and that this definition is defective because it is true in conversion while false in its first proposition. For it is false to say, “Every human being is a rational, mortal, grammatical animal,” although it is true to say, “Every rational, mortal, grammatical animal is a human being.”

Therefore, this definition is defective because it contains nothing besides a human being but does not contain every human being. Perhaps our definition is of this kind, although we boast of it as though it were complete. For although every affection of the body not hidden from the soul in itself is sense, not every sense is this.

You may understand the matter as follows: beasts certainly feel, and almost all of them possess all five senses, to the extent allotted to each by nature. Will you deny this?

E. Nothing could be further from my intention.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Whether There Is Knowledge and Reason in Beasts

A. What, then? Do you not grant that knowledge exists only when something has been apprehended and known by firm reasoning?

E. I grant it.

A. But a beast does not use reason.

E. I grant that as well.

A. Therefore, knowledge does not belong to a beast. Yet whatever is not hidden is known. Therefore, beasts do not feel, if every sense is an affection of the body not hidden from the soul in itself. But they do feel, as was granted a little earlier. Why, then, do we hesitate to reject that definition, which could by no means encompass every sense, since the sense of beasts has been excluded?

50. E. I admit that I was deceived when I granted that knowledge exists when something is apprehended by firm reasoning. When you asked this, I was considering human beings alone. For I cannot say that beasts use reason, nor can I deny them knowledge. A dog, I think, knew its master, whom it is said to have recognized after twenty years ( *Odyssey* 17.291ff.), not to mention countless other examples.

A. Tell me, please: if two things are proposed to you, one which is the goal to be reached, and the other by which you can reach it, which do you value more, and which do you place first?

E. Who doubts that the goal to be reached is superior?

A. Then, since knowledge and reason are two things, do we reach reason through knowledge, or knowledge through reason?

E. Each is so connected with the other, I think, that either can be reached through the other. For we would not reach reason itself unless we knew that it was something to be reached. Knowledge therefore came first, so that through it we might reach reason.

A. What, then? Is the knowledge you say comes first reached without reason?

E. I would never say that; it would be the height of recklessness.

A. Through reason, then?

E. That is not the case.

A. Then through recklessness?

E. Who would say that?

A. Through what, then?

E. Through nothing, because knowledge is implanted in us.

51. A. You seem to have forgotten what we agreed earlier, when I asked whether you thought knowledge existed when something was apprehended by firm reasoning. You answered, I think, that this seemed to you to be human knowledge. Now, however, you say that a person can possess some knowledge without having apprehended the matter through any reasoning. Who does not see that nothing could be more contradictory than these two claims: that knowledge exists only when something is apprehended by firm reasoning, and that there is knowledge of something apprehended by no reasoning? I therefore want to know which of the two you choose, for they cannot both be true in any way.

E. I choose what I said a little earlier. I admit that I rashly granted the earlier claim. For since we are seeking the truth by reason, and this takes place through questioning and answering, how could we reach the final conclusion to which reasoning leads unless something were first granted? But how could something be rightly granted if it were not known? Thus, unless reason found something known in me on which it could rely in leading me toward the unknown, I would learn nothing through it, and I would not call it reason at all. Therefore, you object in vain when I say that some knowledge necessarily exists in us before reason, from which reason itself takes its beginning.

A. I shall oblige you, and, as I have undertaken, I shall allow you to correct yourself whenever you regret having granted something. But please do not abuse this permission by paying insufficient attention when I ask questions, lest your repeatedly mistaken concessions compel you to doubt even what has been properly granted.

E. Proceed instead to the rest. For although I shall add whatever I can to my vigilance—for I am ashamed of falling away from my position so often—I shall never be deterred from resisting this shame and correcting my error, especially with you extending your hand to me. For constancy is not to be rejected merely because steadfastness is desirable.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Reason and Reasoning

52. A. May that constancy of yours appear as quickly as possible. You have stated a position that pleases me. But now be fully present for what I want to ask. For I want to know what difference you think there is between reason and reasoning.

E. I am not sufficiently capable of distinguishing them.

A. Consider, then, whether you think reason is continuously present in a human being who is already an adolescent, an adult, or—in order to remove all circumlocution—a wise person, so long as his mind is sound, just as good health is present in the body so long as it is free from disease and wounds; or whether reason is present and absent in turn, like walking, sitting, and speaking.

E. I think reason is always present in a sound mind.

A. What of this? When, by means of things that have been granted and are evident, either by questioning another person or by connecting one thing with another, we lead ourselves to knowledge of something, do you think that we—or any wise person—are always doing this?

E. Not always. For, as I think, not every human being, or every wise person, is always seeking something by discussing it either with himself or with another. For one who seeks has not yet found; and if he were always seeking, he would never find. A wise person, however, has already found something—not to mention wisdom itself, which, while he was foolish, he perhaps sought by discussion or in some other way.

A. You speak correctly. I therefore want you to understand that this process—by which we are led through things that have been granted and are known to something unknown—is not reason, since, as we have now agreed, it is not always present in a sound mind; reason, however, is always present.

53. E. I understand; but where is this leading?

A. Because a little earlier you said that I ought to agree that we possess knowledge before reason on the ground that reason relies on something known while leading us toward the unknown. But we have now discovered that the process occurring here should not be called reason. For a sound mind does not always engage in it, although it always possesses reason. This process may more properly be called reasoning: reason is a certain gaze of the mind, while reasoning is the mind’s inquiry—that is, the movement of that gaze through the things that must be examined. Thus the latter is needed for seeking, the former for seeing.

Accordingly, when that gaze of the mind which we call reason is directed toward something and sees it, it is called knowledge. But when the mind does not see, although it directs its gaze, this is called ignorance or lack of knowledge. For even with these bodily eyes, not everyone who looks sees; we observe this most easily in darkness. It is therefore clear, I think, that looking is one thing and vision another. In the mind we call these two reason and knowledge.

Unless something in this troubles you, or you think I have not distinguished them clearly enough.

E. I am very pleased with this distinction [Note: [Col. 1066] All the editions we have read have this form; would it not be better to read: “This distinction greatly pleases me”? M.], and I readily agree.

A. Consider, then, whether you think we look in order to see, or see in order to look.

E. No one, not even a blind person, could doubt that looking exists for the sake of vision, not vision for the sake of looking.

A. We must therefore admit that vision is to be valued more highly than looking.

E. We must certainly admit it.

A. Then knowledge is also more valuable than reason.

E. I see that this follows.

A. Do you approve of beasts being better or happier than human beings?

E. May God avert such monstrous madness.

A. Quite properly you recoiled; but your position forces us toward this conclusion. For you said that beasts possess knowledge but do not possess reason. A human being possesses reason, by which he scarcely reaches knowledge. But even if I readily grant that knowledge is easily reached, how will reason help us to regard ourselves as superior to beasts, when they possess knowledge, and it has been established that knowledge is more highly valued than reason?

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Beasts Have the Power of Feeling, Not Knowledge

54. E. I am altogether forced either to deny knowledge to beasts or to refuse nothing to the claim that they are rightly placed above me. But please explain the case of Ulysses’ dog which I mentioned. Moved by my astonishment at it, I barked so pointlessly.

A. What do you think this is, then, except a certain power of feeling, not of knowing? Many beasts surpass us in sense; it is not the place here to inquire into the reason for this. But in mind, reason, and knowledge, God has placed us above them.

The sense of such souls can distinguish the things in which they delight when habit is added, for habit has great force. This happens all the more easily because the soul of animals is more firmly attached to the body. Their senses are directed toward nourishment and pleasure, which they obtain from that same body. The human soul, however, through reason and knowledge—the matters with which we are concerned, and which are far superior to the senses—withdraws itself from the body as far as it can and more willingly enjoys the pleasure that is within. The more it inclines toward the senses, the more it makes a human being resemble an animal.

This is why even crying infants, the farther they are from reason, more easily distinguish by sense the touch and closeness of their nurses, and cannot tolerate the smell of other women with whom they have had no habitual association.

55. Therefore, although one thing has arisen from another, I gladly linger in this discussion, by which the soul is warned not to pour itself into the senses beyond what necessity compels, but rather to gather itself back from them into itself and become a child again for God. This means becoming a new person after casting off the old—a process that must begin because of the neglected law of God. Nothing more true or more hidden is contained in the divine Scriptures.

I would like to say more about this, and to restrain myself while, as though instructing you, I command myself to do nothing other than give myself back to myself, to whom I owe myself above all ( *Retractions* 1.8.3); and thus to become for God what Horace calls “a friend, a slave to his master” ( *Satires* 2.1.2–3) [Col. 1067].

This cannot happen at all unless we are re-formed according to his image, which he gave us to guard as something most precious and most dear, when he made us such that nothing could be preferred to him himself. I see nothing more laborious than this activity, and nothing more like inactivity. Yet the mind can neither undertake nor complete it unless it is aided by the very one to whom it is restored. Thus a human being must be re-formed by the clemency of the one by whose goodness and power he was formed.

56. But we are compelled to return to our subject. Consider, then, whether you now accept that wild animals do not possess knowledge, and that the whole semblance of knowledge which we admire in them is the power of feeling.

E. I certainly accept it; and if anything further needs to be investigated on this matter, I shall look for another occasion. Now I want to know what conclusion you draw from it.

## CHAPTER XXIX — The Difference Between Knowledge and Sense

A. What else do you think, except that the definition of sense is now wavering from the opposite defect, just as earlier it included something more than sense, because it could not include every sense? Wild animals possess sense but do not possess knowledge. Whatever is not hidden is known; and everything known certainly belongs to knowledge. On all these points you now agree with me.

Either, then, it is not true that sense is an affection of the body not hidden from the soul, or beasts lack sense because they lack knowledge. But we grant that beasts possess sense. Therefore, that definition is defective.

E. I admit that I can find nothing with which to resist you.

57. A. Consider another point, which should make us even more ashamed of this definition. You remember, I think, that I showed you a third defect in a definition, one more disgraceful than any other: a definition that is true from neither side, such as the definition “A human being is a four-footed animal.” For whoever says and asserts either “Every human being is a four-footed animal” or “Every four-footed animal is a human being” is certainly insane, unless he is joking.

E. You are right.

A. What, then? If our definition too is found to have this defect, do you think anything could be more deserving of rejection and expulsion from the soul?

E. Who would refuse that? But, if possible, I would rather not be detained here so long and harried by little questions.

A. There is nothing for you to fear. The matter is already settled. Are you still not convinced that, when we were discussing the difference between beasts and human beings, feeling is one thing and knowing another?

E. On the contrary, I am entirely convinced.

A. Then sense is one thing and knowledge another.

E. That is so.

A. But we do not feel through reason; we feel either through sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch.

E. I agree.

A. And everything we know, we know through reason. Therefore, no sense is knowledge. Whatever is not hidden belongs to knowledge. Therefore, not-being-hidden belongs to no sense, just as no human being can rightly be called four-footed. Accordingly, this definition of ours, which you undertook to defend, has been shown not merely to have invaded foreign boundaries and retained nothing of its own, but to have possessed nothing proper at all and to have occupied the whole of what belonged to another.

E. What, then, shall we do? Will you allow it to leave the court in this condition? Although I offered it whatever defense I could, you yourself composed the very legal formula of the case that deceived us. I was present in good faith, even though I could not win the case, and that is enough for me. But if you are accused of collusion, what will you do, since you both produced it to argue boldly and attacked it so that it would withdraw in disgrace?

A. Is there anyone here as judge, from whom either it or I need fear anything? I wished to refute you privately, like a jurist called in for consultation, in order to instruct you, so that when we come to court you may stand prepared.

58. E. Then do you have something to offer in defense of this definition, which you rashly commended to me, so utterly weak, to defend and protect?

A. I certainly do.

## CHAPTER XXX — The Soul, Though It Feels Everywhere in the Body, Is Not for That Reason Diffused Throughout the Body

E. What is it, please?

A. Although sense is one thing and knowledge another, not-being-hidden is nevertheless common to both. It is like the fact that human beings and beasts, although they differ greatly, have in common that they are animals. Whatever appears to the soul is not hidden, whether through the body’s *temperatio* (“attunement” or “adjustment”) or through the purity of understanding; sense claimed the former for itself, and knowledge the latter [Note: [Col. 1068] Bad., Er., and Lov. read *per temperantiam corporis* (“through the body’s temperance”); but nearly all the manuscripts have *per temperationem* (“through the body’s tempering/attunement”).].

E. Then that definition remains secure and established?

A. It certainly remains so.

E. Where, then, was I deceived?

A. When I asked whether everything that is not hidden is known. You rashly agreed to this question.

E. What else would you have had me say?

A. That something is not immediately knowledge simply because it is not hidden, but only when it is not hidden through reason. When it is not hidden through the body, it is called sense, provided the affection of the body is not hidden in itself. Do you not know that certain philosophers, exceedingly acute men, have thought that even what is grasped by the mind should not be given the name “knowledge” unless the apprehension is so firm that the mind cannot be moved away from it by any reasoning?

59. E. I receive this with the greatest gratitude. But since, as I think, what sense is has now been explained with the utmost subtlety, let us return to the question for whose sake we undertook to explain it.

I had produced an argument by which I sought to prove that the soul is as large as the body it inhabits, on the ground that it feels the person touching it from head to the tip of the big toe, wherever the touch occurs. From there we were led, perhaps necessarily, into this extremely lengthy discussion of the definition of sense. So now, if you please, show me the fruit of so great an undertaking.

A. There is fruit indeed, and abundant fruit, for everything we were investigating has been accomplished. If sense is an affection of the body not hidden from the soul in itself—and we have spoken at greater length than you wished in order to establish this as firmly as possible—do you remember that we finally discovered that the eyes feel where they are not, or rather, that they undergo something there?

E. I remember.

A. You also granted, unless I am mistaken—and now you do not doubt that it had to be granted—that the soul is much better and more powerful than the entire body.

E. I consider it impious to doubt this.

A. Come, then. If the body can undergo something where it is not, because of a certain attunement with the soul, as was found to happen to the eyes in seeing, should we suppose the soul to be so gross and sluggish that, through it, the eyes themselves can do so much, yet the affection of the body remains hidden from it unless it lies in the very place where that affection occurs?

### 60

**E.** This conclusion greatly disturbs me—so greatly that I am utterly bewildered, and cannot find not only what I should answer, but even where I am. For what shall I say? That there is no sensation when a bodily affection does not, by itself, escape the soul? What else would sensation be, if it were not this? That the eyes undergo nothing when we see? That is utterly absurd. [Note: Col. 1069. In editions published thus far: “It is utterly absurd that they undergo it where they are, so that they do not see themselves”; except Bad., which comes close to the manuscript reading restored here.] Do they undergo it where they are? But they do not see themselves there, and where they are there is nothing besides themselves. To say that the soul is not more powerful than the eyes, when the eyes have the same power as the soul—what could be more senseless? Or should we say that it is more powerful to undergo something where the thing is than where it is not? But if that were true, sight would not be superior to the other senses.

**A.** What of this? When the eyes undergo a blow, or something striking them, or a disturbance caused by moisture, they undergo these things where they are; nor is this hidden from the soul. Yet this affection is not called sight but touch. An eye could undergo such things even in a lifeless body, although the soul, from which the affection would not be hidden, were absent. But that which the eye cannot undergo unless the soul is present—that is, what it undergoes in seeing—does it undergo only where it is not? From this, who would not conclude that the soul is contained in no place? For the eye, which is a body, undergoes outside its own place only that which it would never undergo without the soul.

### 61

**E.** What, then, shall I do, I beg you? Cannot these arguments establish that our souls are not in our bodies? And if that is so, do I not know where I am? For who can take from me the fact that I myself am a soul?

**A.** Do not be disturbed; rather, keep a good heart. This thought and consideration invites us toward our very selves and, as far as possible, tears us away from the body. As for what seemed to you absurd—that the soul is not in the body of a living creature—although it may appear absurd, there have nevertheless been, and I think still are, very learned men who approve it. But, as you yourself understand, the matter is extremely subtle, and to perceive it the mind’s vision must be sufficiently purified.

For now, attend instead to what else you can bring forward by which you might prove that the soul is long or broad, or something of that kind. For you perceive that your argument from the sense of touch does not reach the truth and is of no force for proving that the soul is diffused throughout the body like blood. Or, if you have nothing more to bring forward, let us examine what remains.

### CHAPTER XXXI  
**The parts of a cut-up worm move. Whether this is an argument that the soul extends throughout the whole body**

### 62

**E.** Perhaps I would have nothing, if I did not remember how greatly, as boys, we used to marvel at the severed tails of lizards, which continued to twitch after being cut off from the rest of the body. I cannot persuade myself that such movement occurs without a soul; nor do I understand how there could be no space belonging to the soul when it too can be cut away together with the body.

**A.** I might answer that air and fire—those two elements which are held in the earthly and moist body by the presence of the soul, so that all four elements form a balanced mixture—after [Col. 1070] the soul’s departure escape upward and free themselves, thereby moving those little particles all the more rapidly because they burst out suddenly through a fresh wound. Then the movement gradually weakens and finally ceases, as less and less of what is escaping remains, until everything has flown away.

But what I myself saw with these eyes—almost later than can be believed, though certainly not later than I ought to have seen it—draws me away from that explanation. Recently, when we were in the countryside of Liguria, some young men of ours who were then with me for the sake of their studies noticed, lying on the ground in a shady place, a crawling many-footed creature—a certain long little worm, I mean. It is commonly known, though I had never before tested what I am about to describe.

One of them happened to turn his stylus and struck the animal in the middle. Immediately the two parts of the body moved away from the wound in opposite directions, with such rapid movement of their feet and with no weaker effort than if they had been two creatures of this kind. Terrified by the marvel and eager to discover its cause, they brought the lively fragments briskly to us, where Alypius and I were sitting together.

Nor were we unmoved. We watched them run in every direction across a tablet as far as they could. When one of them was touched with the stylus, it twisted itself toward the place of pain, while the other, sensing nothing, carried on its movements elsewhere. What more need I say? We tested how far the phenomenon extended, and cut the little worm—or rather, by then, the little worms—into many pieces. They all moved in such a way that, had we not done the cutting and had the wounds not appeared fresh, we would have believed that as many creatures had been born separately and that each had lived independently.

### 63

But what I said to those young men when they were watching me intently, I now hesitate to say to you. We have already advanced so far that, unless I give you an answer which is probable and supports my position, our great effort, fortified by so long a discussion, may seem to have been pierced and defeated by a single worm.

I had instructed them to continue their studies along the course on which they had begun; thus, if circumstances required it, they would at some more suitable time be better prepared to investigate and learn these matters. But if I wished to set out what Alypius and I discussed after they had departed—while each of us, according to his ability, recalled, conjectured, and investigated—we would have far more to say than was said from the very beginning through all those long digressions and winding paths. Nevertheless, I shall not conceal from you what I think.

If I had not already known much about the body, about the form that is present in the body, about place, time, and motion—matters discussed with great subtlety and obscurity precisely because of this question—I would incline to grant the victory to those who say that the soul is a body. Therefore, as best I can, I repeatedly warn you not to rush recklessly into books or into the discussions of excessively talkative men who put too much trust in these bodily senses, until you correct and strengthen the steps that lead the soul even to God. Otherwise you may be turned away by studies and exertions, more easily than by inactivity and idleness, from that most secret and tranquil dwelling-place of the mind from which, while it inhabits this present life, it is an exile.

### 64

[Col. 1071]

Now accept the reply to that point which, as I perceive, has greatly disturbed you—not because it is stronger than the many arguments already given, but because it is shorter; and not because I could choose it as more probable than the others, but because it is better suited to you.

**E.** Speak, I beg you, as quickly as you can.

**A.** First I say this: even if the reason why such things occur when certain bodies are cut apart is completely hidden from us, we ought not immediately to be so disturbed by this one fact that we judge false the many things which earlier seemed to you brighter than daylight. It may be that the reason for this matter is hidden from us because it has been concealed from human nature; or it may be known to some person whom we cannot question; or perhaps our own understanding is such that, even if questioned, we could not be satisfied by the answer.

Should everything we learned with complete certainty from the opposing side, and acknowledged to be most true, slip away from us and be torn from us for that reason? If those things remain intact which, when questioned, you answered to be certain and indubitable, there is no reason for us to fear this little worm in a childish manner, even though we cannot explain the cause of its vitality and multiplicity.

Suppose you had firmly and immovably established in your mind that a certain man was good, and that you found him at a banquet of the robbers whom you were pursuing; then, by some chance, he died before he could be questioned by you. Would you prefer to suppose some cause of his association and banquet with the criminals—though it remained forever hidden from you—rather than suppose that he shared their crime? [Note: Col. 1071. Flor. MSS.: “than of crime and association.” Perhaps the reading here should be: “Than that it was an association in crime.”]

Why, then, when the many arguments set forth earlier and firmly confirmed by you have made it clear that the soul is not contained in a place, and therefore has none of the dimensions we observe in bodies, should you not suspect that there is some reason why a cut-up animal lives in all its parts? Why should you suppose that this reason is that the soul could be cut up together with the body? If we cannot discover the reason, ought we not rather to seek the true explanation than believe a false one?

### CHAPTER XXXII  
**The soul is not cut when the body is dissected. The pieces of a dissected body can live although the soul has not been cut. Next, the soul’s magnitude in respect of its power and force**

### 65

Next I ask you whether you think that in our words the sound itself is one thing and what is signified by the sound another.

**E.** I think they are both the same.

**A.** Tell me, then: from where does the sound itself proceed when you speak?

**E.** Who would doubt that it proceeds from me?

**A.** Then the sun proceeds from you when you name the sun?

**E.** You asked me about the sound, not about the thing itself.

**A.** So the sound is one thing, and the thing signified by the sound another; yet you had said that both were the same.

**E.** Very well; I now grant that the sound which signifies is one thing and the thing signified another.

**A.** Tell me, then: if you knew Latin, could you name the sun in speech if an understanding of the sun did not precede the sound?

**E.** In no way could I.

**A.** What then? Before the name itself comes from your mouth, if you keep silent for a while, intending to utter it, does not what another person will hear expressed aloud remain in your thought?

**E.** Clearly.

**A.** What then? Since the sun itself is so great, can the notion of it which you hold in thought before [Col. 1072] the sound be seen as long, or broad, or anything of that kind?

**E.** In no way.

### 66

**A.** Now tell me this: when the name itself bursts from your mouth, and I, hearing it, think of the sun—the sun which you thought of before the sound and together with the sound, and which perhaps we both now think of—does it not seem to you that the name itself has, as it were, received from you a signification which it carries to me through my ears?

**E.** It does.

**A.** Since, then, a name consists of sound and signification, and sound belongs to the ears while signification belongs to the mind, do you not think that in a name, as in some living creature, the sound is the body and the signification, as it were, the soul of the sound?

**E.** Nothing seems more similar.

**A.** Now consider whether the sound of a name can be divided through its letters, while its soul—that is, its signification—cannot. For you answered a little earlier that this signification seemed to you neither broad nor long in our thought.

**E.** I entirely agree.

**A.** What happens when that sound is divided through its individual letters? Do you think that signification remains?

**E.** How can individual letters signify what the name formed from them signifies?

**A.** But when the sound has been torn apart into letters, with its signification lost, do you think anything has happened other than that, when the body was mangled, the soul departed, and a kind of death overtook the name?

**E.** I not only agree; I agree so gladly that nothing in this discussion has given me greater pleasure.

### 67

**A.** If, then, you have understood sufficiently from this analogy how the soul can remain uncut when the body is dissected, now learn how the pieces of the body themselves can live although the soul has not been cut.

You have already granted—and, I think, rightly—that the signification which is, as it were, the soul of the sound while the name is uttered cannot in itself be divided in any way, although the sound, which is as it were its body, can be divided. But in the name *sun* the sound was divided in such a way that none of its parts retained any signification. Thus we considered those letters, after the body of the name had been torn apart, as lifeless limbs—that is, as deprived of signification.

If, therefore, we find a name which, when divided, can still signify something in each of its parts, you must grant that such a cutting has not brought about a complete kind of death, since the members, considered separately, will appear to you to signify something and to be, as it were, alive.

**E.** I shall certainly grant it; and I insist that you now utter such a word.

**A.** Here it is. As I was thinking of a neighboring subject—the sun, whose name we discussed earlier—*Lucifer* occurred to me. If it is cut between the second and third syllables, the first part still signifies something when we say *Luci*, and therefore it lives in more than half the body of the name. The final part also has a soul. For when you are ordered to carry something, you hear *fer*. How could you obey if someone said to you, “Carry the book” (*Fer codicem*), if *fer* signified nothing? When *fer* is added to *Luci*, the sound *Lucifer* is produced and signifies the star; but when it is removed, it still signifies something, and therefore, as it were, retains life.

### 68

Since place and time are the dimensions occupied—or rather, which occupy—all things that are sensed, what we sense with the eyes is divided by place, and what we sense with the ears by [Col. 1073] time. Just as that little worm occupied more place when whole than when it was a part, so it occupies a greater span of time when *Lucifer* is spoken than when only *Luci* is spoken.

Therefore, if it lives by its signification in that reduction of time which was produced when the sound was divided, while the signification itself was not divided—for it was not extended through time, but the sound was—then we should likewise think that, when the body of the worm was cut, although a part would live in a smaller place precisely because it was a part, the soul was not thereby cut at all, nor made smaller because of the smaller place, even though, when the living creature was whole, it simultaneously occupied a greater place with all its limbs extended through it.

The soul itself did not occupy the place; rather, it occupied the body which it moved. In the same way, that signification was not stretched out through time, yet it animated and filled all the letters of the name, each possessing its own duration and temporal extent.

For the present, I ask you to be satisfied with this analogy, since I perceive that you have enjoyed it. Do not expect at present the extremely subtle arguments that can be made about this matter—arguments that would satisfy us by the things themselves rather than by analogies, which are often misleading. This lengthy discussion must also be brought to a close, and your mind must first be prepared by many other matters that are still lacking before it can observe and examine these things. Then you will be able to understand with complete clarity whether what certain very learned men say is true: that the soul cannot in itself be divided in any way, but can nevertheless be divided through the body.

### 69

Now, if you wish, receive from me—or rather, recognize through me—how great the soul is, not in the dimensions of place and time, but in power and force. For, if you remember, this has long been our purpose and our assigned subject.

As for the number of souls, I do not know what answer to give you, since you have thought that this belongs to the present question. I would sooner say that the matter should not be investigated at all, or at least should be postponed for you at present, than either deny that number and multiplicity belong to quantity or pretend that I can now disentangle so involved a question for you.

For if I say that there is one soul, you will be troubled because in one person it is blessed and in another miserable; yet one thing cannot be blessed and miserable at the same time. If I say that there is one soul and also many, you will laugh, and I will not easily find anything with which to restrain your laughter. But if I say that there are only many souls, I myself will laugh at myself, and I shall endure my own displeasure less readily than yours.

Listen, then, to what I promise you can hear well from me. But do not undertake or impose upon yourself what may be burdensome to both of us—or perhaps overwhelming to one of us.

**E.** I entirely submit, and I await your explanation of how great the soul’s power is, insofar as you think it can properly be treated with me.

### CHAPTER XXXIII  
**The soul’s power in the body, in itself, and with God establishes seven degrees of its magnitude**

**The first degree of the soul**

### 70

**A.** Would that we could both question some person who was not only extremely learned and eloquent, but altogether wise and perfect! How would he explain in speech and discussion what the soul can do in the body, what it can do in itself, and what it can do with God, to whom it is nearest in purity and in whom it possesses its highest and entire good?

But since I lack such a person for this matter, I nevertheless [Col. 1074] dare to be sufficient for you. This is the compensation: while, as an unlearned man, I explain what the soul can do, I safely experience what I myself can do.

First, however, I must cut short a very broad and boundless expectation, lest you think I am going to speak about every soul. I shall speak only about the human soul, which alone we ought to care for if we care for ourselves.

The first thing about it—which anyone can easily observe—is that by its presence it gives life to this earthly and mortal body; gathers it into unity and holds it together, preventing it from dissolving and decaying; causes food to be distributed through the limbs, assigning to each its due; and preserves its proportion and order, not only in beauty but also in growth and generation.

But these functions may also seem common to human beings and plants. For we too say that plants live, and we see and acknowledge that each is preserved in its own kind, nourished, grows, and reproduces.

**The second degree of the soul**

### 71

Rise, then, to the second degree, and observe what the soul can do in the senses, where life is understood more clearly and manifestly. We must not listen to a certain rustic impiety—more wooden, indeed, than the trees themselves for which it provides a defense—which believes that the vine feels pain when its grapes are plucked, and that it not only feels such things when trees are cut down but also sees and hears. Another place is required for discussing that sacrilegious error.

For now, attend to what I began to discuss: the soul’s power in the senses and in the movement itself of a more manifestly living creature, with which we can have no communion with things fixed by roots.

The soul directs itself toward touch, and through it senses and distinguishes hot and cold, rough and smooth, hard and soft, light and heavy. Then, by tasting, smelling, hearing, and seeing, it judges innumerable differences of flavors, odors, sounds, and shapes.

In all these things it takes up and desires whatever accords with the nature of its body; it rejects and avoids what is contrary. It withdraws from these senses at certain intervals of time, and, restoring their movements as though through periods of rest, turns over within itself in groups and in many forms the images of things it has absorbed through them. This whole process is sleep and dreams.

Often, too, it takes pleasure in the ease of movement, whether leaping about or wandering, and without effort arranges the harmony of the limbs. In pursuit of sexual union it does what it can, and in the dual nature, fellowship, and love of the sexes it works toward unity. It joins in the generation of offspring—not merely in producing them but also in fostering, protecting, and nourishing them.

It entwines itself through habit with the things among which the body acts and by which the body is sustained, and is separated from them only with difficulty, as though they were its limbs. When the force of this habit is not severed even by the separation of the things themselves and by the passage of time, it is called memory.

Yet no one denies that the soul can do all these things also in animals.

**The third degree of the soul**

### 72

Rise, then, to the third degree, which now belongs particularly to human beings. Consider memory—not of things impressed by habit, but of innumerable things entrusted to and retained by attention and [Col. 1075] signs: the countless arts of craftsmen; the cultivation of fields; the construction of cities; the manifold marvels of various buildings and undertakings; the invention of so many signs in letters, words, gestures, sounds of every kind, paintings, and images; the languages of so many peoples; so many institutions; so many new creations and restorations; the immense number of books and monuments of every sort for preserving memory, and such concern for posterity; the orders of duties, powers, honors, and offices, whether in households, at home and in military and civil life, or in profane and sacred arrangements; the power of reasoning and devising; the streams of eloquence; the varieties of poetry; the thousand forms of pretense for play and amusement; skill in musical composition; subtlety in measurement; the discipline of counting; and the inference of past and future from present things.

These are great things and wholly human. Yet even here there is still a capacity shared partly by the learned and unlearned, and partly by good and evil souls.

**The fourth degree of the soul**

### 73

Look upward, then, and leap to the fourth degree, from which goodness begins and all true praise. Here the soul dares to place itself not only above its own body, insofar as it plays some part in the universe, but even above the whole body of the universe. It does not count the body’s goods as its own, and, comparing them with its own power and beauty, it distinguishes and despises them.

The more it delights in this, the more it withdraws itself from uncleanness, purifies its whole being, and renders itself most clean and most adorned. It strengthens itself against everything that attempts to divert it from its purpose and judgment. It values human fellowship highly, and does not wish anything for another that it would not wish to happen to itself. It follows the authority and instructions of the wise, and through these believes that God speaks to it.

Even in this exceedingly noble action of the soul there remains labor, together with a great and fierce struggle against the troubles and allurements of this world. In the very work of purification there is a fear of death—sometimes not great, sometimes extremely violent.

The fear is not great when one firmly believes—for only a thoroughly purified soul can see whether this is true—that everything is governed by God’s providence and justice in such a way that death cannot befall anyone unjustly, even if an unjust person happens to inflict it.

But at this degree death is feared intensely when that belief itself is considered weaker in proportion to the anxiety with which it is sought, and when the tranquility necessary for investigating the most obscure matters appears diminished in proportion to the fear. Then, the more the soul senses—and by the very fact that it advances—how great the difference is between what is pure and what is contaminated, the more it fears that, when it lays aside this body, God may be less able to endure it polluted than it is to endure itself.

Nothing is more difficult than both to fear death and, as the dangers themselves demand, to refrain from the allurements of this world. [Note: Col. 1075. Er. and one of our MSS.: “than both to fear death and not to fear death.”] Yet the soul is so great that, with the help of the justice of the supreme and true God, by which the universe is sustained and governed, it can even do this. By that same justice it has come about not only that all things exist, but that they exist in such a way that they could not possibly be better.

To this [Col. 1076] justice the soul devoutly and securely entrusts itself, so that it may be helped and perfected in the difficult work of its purification.

**The fifth degree of the soul**

### 74

When this has been accomplished—that is, when the soul has been freed from every corruption and washed clean of its stains—then at last it rests most joyfully in itself, fearing nothing at all for itself and feeling no anxiety on its own account.

This, then, is the fifth degree. It is one thing to achieve purity and another to retain it; one action restores the soul when it has been defiled, and an entirely different action prevents it from being defiled again.

At this degree the soul fully grasps how great it is. When it has grasped this, it proceeds toward God—that is, toward the contemplation of truth itself—with immense and incredible confidence. This is the highest and most secret reward for which so much labor has been undertaken.

**The sixth degree of the soul**

### 75

This action—the desire to understand what truly and supremely exists—is the soul’s highest vision; it has no more perfect, better, or more upright one.

The sixth degree, then, will be this action. For it is one thing to cleanse the eye of the soul itself, so that it does not look in vain or rashly and see wrongly; another to preserve and strengthen its health; and another to direct an already serene and upright vision toward what must be seen.

Those who wish to do this before they have been cleansed and healed are so struck by the light of truth that they think there is in it not only nothing good but an abundance of evil. They deny it the name of truth and flee back, with a kind of miserable lust and pleasure, into their own darkness—the darkness their sickness can endure—cursing the medicine.

Thus, by divine inspiration, the Prophet says in a completely orderly way:

> “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts” (Psalm L, 12).

For I think that the right spirit is what makes it impossible for the soul to deviate and go astray in its search for truth. This spirit is not renewed in it unless the heart has first been made clean—that is, unless thought itself has first restrained and filtered itself from every desire and impurity belonging to mortal things.

**The seventh degree of the soul**

### 76

Now, in the very vision and contemplation of truth—which is the seventh and final degree of the soul, or rather no longer a degree but a certain dwelling reached through those degrees—what shall I say of the joys, the enjoyment of the supreme and true good, and the breath of that serenity and eternity?

Certain great and incomparable souls, whom we believe both to have seen and to see these things, have said as much about them as they judged ought to be said.

This much I now dare to tell you plainly: [Note: Col. 1076. He frequently quotes it thus. See *1 Retractations*, ch. 7, no. 3.] if we hold with complete steadfastness to the course which God commands us and which we have undertaken to follow, we shall arrive, through God’s Power and Wisdom, at that supreme cause, or supreme author, or supreme principle of all things—or whatever other name may more suitably be given to so great a reality. Once we understand it, we shall truly see how all things under the sun are “vanity of vanities” (Ecclesiastes 1:2).

For vanity is deceit, while “the vain” are understood either as those who are false, those who deceive, or both. Yet it is possible to discern how great the difference is between these things and those that truly exist; and also how, nevertheless, all these things were created by God as their author, and, compared with those higher things, are nothing, while considered in themselves they are [Col. 1077] marvelous and beautiful.

Then we shall recognize how true are the things we were commanded to believe, how excellently and healthfully we were nourished in the mother Church, and what benefit there is in that milk which the Apostle Paul professed to have given the little ones as drink (1 Corinthians 3:2).

To receive this nourishment while one is being nursed by a mother is most beneficial; when one is already grown, it is shameful; to reject it when it is necessary is pitiable; at some point to criticize or hate it is criminal and impious; but to handle and dispense it properly is full of praise and love.

We shall also see such great changes and alternations in this bodily nature, while it obeys the divine laws, that we shall hold even the resurrection of the flesh—which some believe only with difficulty and others not at all—as certain as it is certain to us that the sun will rise after it has set.

As for those who mock the example of our salvation and its first fruits—the human being assumed by the most powerful, eternal, and unchanging Son of God, and that same human being born of a virgin, together with the other miracles of this history—we shall despise them as we despise children who, seeing a painter painting before displayed panels which he is looking at, think that a person cannot be painted unless the painter looks at another painting.

The pleasure in contemplating truth is as great as the extent to which each person can contemplate it; its purity, sincerity, and certainty concerning things are so great that no one, when he seemed to himself to know, will think that he had ever known anything else. And, so that the soul may be hindered as little as possible from cleaving wholly to the whole truth, death—which was formerly feared, namely, complete flight and escape from this body—will be desired as the highest gift.

### CHAPTER XXXIV  
**God alone is better than the soul, and therefore He alone is to be worshiped by it**

### 77

You have heard how great the soul’s force and power are. To summarize briefly: just as we must acknowledge that the human soul is not what God is, so we must suppose that among all things God has created nothing is closer to God.

Therefore, the Catholic Church divinely and uniquely teaches that no creature is to be worshiped by the soul. I prefer to use the words in which these matters were communicated to me: only the Creator of all things is to be worshiped—the one from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are; that is, the unchangeable principle, unchangeable wisdom, and unchangeable love; the one true and perfect God, [Note: Col. 1077. So most MSS., with Er. But Bad. and Lov. read: “that is, unchangeable truth, unchangeable eternity, unchangeable power, unchangeable love, the one true God.” Three MSS.: “that is, unchangeable eternity, unchangeable truth, unchangeable love, the one true God.”] who never was not, never will not be, who was never otherwise and will never be otherwise; than whom nothing is more hidden and nothing more present; who is difficult to find where He is, more difficult to find where He is not; with whom not everyone can [Col. 1078] be, and without whom no one can be; and whatever else human beings may be able to say about Him that is more incredible, yet more fitting and appropriate.

This God alone, then, is to be worshiped by the soul—neither separately nor confusedly. For whatever the soul worships as God, it must regard as better than itself.

But the nature of the soul must not believe that earth, seas, stars, moon, sun, or anything at all that can be touched or seen with these eyes—and finally not even heaven itself, which cannot be seen by us—is better than it. Indeed, sound reasoning proves that all these things are far inferior to any soul, provided that lovers of truth dare to follow the soul as it leads them through unfamiliar and therefore difficult paths, with complete steadfastness and care.

### 78

But if there is anything else in the nature of things besides what is known to the senses and what occupies some extent of space—things all of which we have said the human soul surpasses—then, among whatever else God has created, some thing is inferior and some equal. Inferior is the soul of an animal; equal are angels; but nothing is better.

And if any of these is ever better, this happens because of its sin, not through its nature. Yet it does not thereby become so much worse that the soul of an animal ought to be preferred or compared with it.

God alone, then, is to be worshiped by the soul, since He alone is its author. Any other human being, however wise and perfect, or indeed any rational and blessed soul, is to be loved and imitated only, and what is appropriate to it according to its merit and order is to be rendered to it.

“For you shall worship the Lord your God, and Him alone shall you serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13; Matthew 4:10).

Let us know that we must aid kindred souls who are wandering and laboring, as far as we are able and as we have been commanded, understanding that when this is done well, God Himself acts through us. Let us claim nothing as our own, deceived by the desire for empty glory—the one evil by which we are dragged down from the highest to the lowest. [Note: Col. 1078. Thus Par., Er., Ven., and Lov.; in B., “is dragged down.”]

Let us hate not those oppressed by vices, but the vices themselves; not those who sin, but the sins themselves. For we ought to wish to help everyone, even those who have harmed us, or wish to harm us, or wish to be harmed at all.

This is the true, perfect, and only religion: through it reconciliation with God belongs to the magnitude of the soul for which we are searching, by which the soul makes itself worthy of freedom. For He frees all people, and it is most beneficial for all to serve Him; and in His service, pleasing Him is perfect and the only freedom. [Note: Col. 1078. Thus to be read on the authority of the Ebrulph MSS.: “perfectly alone.”]

But I see that I have almost exceeded the boundaries of my purpose and, without your asking a question, have said many things to you at length. I do not regret it. For although these matters are scattered through many of the Church’s Scriptures, and although we seem to have collected them not ineptly, they cannot be fully understood unless each person, acting courageously at the fourth of those seven degrees and preserving devotion, acquires the health and strength needed to grasp them and investigates every point individually with the greatest diligence and intelligence.

Each of those degrees has its own distinct and particular beauty; we more properly call them acts.

### CHAPTER XXXV  
**The acts of the soul are variously named according to the seven degrees mentioned above**

[Col. 1079]

### 79

We are inquiring, in fact, into the soul’s power, and it may be that it performs all these acts simultaneously, but that it seems to itself to be performing only what it does with difficulty, or at least with fear. [Note: Col. 1079. In four MSS. of better standing: “with love.”] It performs this with much greater attention than the other acts.

As we ascend upward, then, let the first act, for purposes of instruction, be called animation; the second, sensation; the third, art; the fourth, virtue; the fifth, tranquility; the sixth, entry; and the seventh, contemplation.

They may also be named in this way: from the body; through the body; around the body; toward itself; in itself; toward God; with God.

They may also be named thus: beautifully concerning another; beautifully through another; beautifully around another; beautifully toward the beautiful; beautifully in the beautiful; beautifully toward beauty; beautifully with beauty.

You may ask about all these matters later, if anything seems to require explanation. For now, I wanted to mark them repeatedly by these names so that you will not be disturbed when others call the same things by other names or divide them differently, and so that you will not therefore reject either this arrangement or that one.

The same things can be named and divided in innumerable ways, each entirely correct and subtle. But amid such a wealth of methods, each person uses the one he thinks he can use appropriately.

### CHAPTER XXXVI  
**The remaining questions concerning the soul are touched upon. What true religion is**
80. Therefore the supreme and true God, by an inviolable and incorruptible law whereby He governs everything He has created, subjects the body to the soul, the soul to Himself, and thus all things to Himself; nor does He abandon the soul in any act, whether in punishment or in reward. For He judged it most beautiful that everything that exists should exist in the manner in which it does exist, and that nature should be ordered in degrees so that, when those who contemplate the universe consider it, no deformity should offend in any part; and that every punishment and every reward of the soul should always contribute something, in proportion, to the just beauty [Note: [Col. 1079] The editions read, “something to the proportion of just beauty.” But the manuscripts read “in proportion”; and three of them, “to just beauty.”] and arrangement of all things.

For free will was given to the soul. Those who try to undermine it with frivolous arguments are so blind that they do not even understand that they utter these very vain and sacrilegious arguments by their own free will. Yet free will was not given to the soul in such a way that, by attempting anything whatever with it, it could disturb any part of the divine order [Col. 1080] and law. For it was given by the wisest and unconquered Lord of the whole creation.

But to see these things as they ought to be seen is granted to few; and no one becomes fit for this except through true religion. True religion is that by which the soul binds itself again to the one God, from whom it had torn itself away, as it were, through sin, by being reconciled to Him. Thus religion entwines the soul in that third act, and begins to lead it; purifies it in the fourth; reforms it in the fifth; brings it in, in the sixth; and nourishes it in the seventh. This occurs more quickly in some and more slowly in others, according to the strength of their love and merits. Yet God does everything with the greatest justice, moderation, and beauty, however those for whom He does these things may have chosen to conduct themselves.

Moreover, how much the consecrations of infant children may accomplish is a very obscure question; nevertheless, we must believe that they accomplish something. Reason will discover this when it becomes necessary to inquire into it—although I have already brought forward many other matters for you to investigate someday rather than to know immediately. This will be done most fruitfully if they are sought under the guidance of piety.

81. Since these things are so, who could justly be indignant that the soul has been given to act upon and govern the body, when so great and so divine an order of things could not be more excellently joined together? Or who would think it necessary to ask what sort of soul is produced in this mortal and fragile body, when it has rightly been thrust into death because of sin and can nevertheless excel here also through virtue? Or what sort it will be after this body, when the punishment of death must necessarily remain so long as sin remains, while God Himself—that is, truth itself—is the reward of virtue and piety?

Therefore, if you are now willing, let us at last bring this very long discussion to an end, and devote ourselves with the utmost vigilance and religious seriousness to fulfilling God’s commandments; for there is no other escape from such great evils. If I have said anything more obscurely than you wished, make a point of committing it to memory and asking about it on another, more suitable occasion. For the Teacher of us all, who is above, will not be lacking to us when we seek Him.

E. I have indeed been so affected by this discourse that I would have thought it wrong to interrupt it. And if you are pleased with the manner of our discussion here, and if the three questions that remained seemed for the present to require only such brief treatment, I shall yield to your judgment; and henceforth, in investigating matters of such importance, I shall watch not only for a time more suitable to your occupations, but also for a time more suitable to myself.

[Col. 1079]

SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, SIX BOOKS ON MUSIC [Note: [Col. 1082] Begun in the year of Christ 387 and completed about the year 389.] [Note: [Col. 1081] The Books on Music have been purged of nearly innumerable errors by comparison with the manuscripts of excellent quality at Corbie, Arnulf, Albinus, Victorinus, Regius, and the Vatican; with readings collected from four Belgian manuscripts by the Louvain scholars; and with the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain. In addition, the first five books were compared with another manuscript of Victorinus and with the Navarre manuscript; the sixth book, finally, with another Navarre manuscript, another Victorinus manuscript, one manuscript of the larger Augustinian convent in Paris, and the manuscript at Saint-Bénigne.] [Note: [Col. 1081] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the Retractations and the Confessions, as well as two manuscripts of the Royal Library, designated by the numbers A, 7200, and B, 7231, and a certain epitome of Augustine’s work, composed chiefly from Augustine’s own words, which Angelo Mai found in a very ancient manuscript of the Vatican Library and published at Rome in 1828, in volume 3, part 3, pages 116–134, of the New Collection of Ancient Writers Transcribed from Vatican Manuscripts. M.] (C, S)

NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING SIX BOOKS ON MUSIC [Note: [Col. 1081] See also book 1, chapter 11, of the Retractations, cols. 600–602, from the words “Then, as above,” no. 1, to the words “For a sufficiently long time, almost,” no. 4. M.]

Of the books on the disciplines that Augustine sampled at Milan in the year of Christ 387, when he was about to receive baptism (see Retractations, book 1, chapter 6), although the others have perished—for we shall show in the appendix that the books on Grammar, the Principles of Dialectic, the Categories, and the Principles of Rhetoric, which have so far been published among his works, are spurious—these six books on Music, and these alone, have reached us in their entirety. They were evidently copied with particular care by scribes, since they appeared complete in all their parts around the year of Christ, apparently, 389. At that time, after publishing the books Against the Manichaeans on Genesis, Augustine indicates in book 1, chapter 11, of the Retractations, that he devoted himself to completing them in Africa.

Most manuscripts, including the more ancient ones, report that he held these dialogues with Licentius. It is uncertain whether this may be understood from the following verses of Licentius to Augustine in letter 26:

> They themselves will make you present to me, if you comply with my request  
> And hand over the books in which Music reclines languidly upon you;  
> For I burn wholly for them.

In the first book, the definition of Music is given, and the species of measured movements relevant to the consideration of this discipline are explained. In the second, the discussion concerns syllables and metrical feet. In the third, the intention is announced to treat separately of rhythm, meter, and verse; first, the nature and properties of rhythm are presented, and then the treatment of meter begins, which is continued in the fourth book. In the fifth, verse is discussed. What Augustine had treated thus far with great learning, he himself calls trifling, for which he apologizes to benevolent readers under the name of dutiful labor at the beginning of the sixth book; there he proceeds to raise the minds of students from consideration of numbers toward God.

SAINT AUGUSTINE, LETTER 101, TO MEMORIUS, BISHOP

“Since the power of numbers in all the movements of things is more easily considered in sounds, and since this consideration rests upon certain graded paths, as it were, leading toward the innermost heights of truth—in which paths Wisdom shows herself joyfully and, in every providence, meets those who love her—at the beginning of my leisure, when my mind was free from greater and more necessary concerns, I wished to make a preliminary effort in the writings you had requested of me. When I wrote six books on rhythm alone, I confess that I was also planning to write perhaps another six on melody, hoping that I should have leisure for this.

“But after the burden of ecclesiastical cares was laid upon me, all those delights escaped my hands, so that I can scarcely now find the very manuscript itself; nevertheless, I cannot disregard your will—not merely your request, but your command. If I can send you this little work, you will perhaps regret not that I have obeyed you, but that you pressed me so insistently to do so. For the first five books are exceedingly difficult to understand unless there is someone who can not only distinguish the speakers in the discussion, but also, by pronouncing them, make the small temporal divisions of the syllables sound in such a way that the kinds of numbers are expressed through them and strike the sense of the ears—especially since in some passages measured intervals of silence are also interwoven, which cannot be perceived at all unless the reciter instructs the listener.

“As for the sixth book, which I found corrected, and in which the entire fruit of the others is contained, I did not delay sending it to Your Charity. Perhaps it will not shrink very much from your gravity.”

BOOK ONE. The definition of Music is given, and the species and proportion of measured movements relevant to the consideration of this discipline are explained.

[Col. 1081]

CHAPTER ONE.—Observing definite measurements of sounds belongs not to grammar but to Music.

1. MASTER: Which foot is *modus*?

STUDENT [Note: [Col. 1081] At the beginning of the work, the Albinus manuscript has: “Here begins the first book of Augustine’s and Licentius’ dialogues on Music.” The Regius codex and the two manuscripts of Victorinus bear a very similar title. In the Corbie, Arnulf, and most other manuscripts, however, the speakers—[Col. 1082] Augustine and Licentius—are identified by name throughout the work wherever the printed editions attach the labels Master and Student.]: A pyrrhic.

M. How many time-units does it contain?

S. Two.

[Col. 1082] M. And *bonus*: which foot is it?

S. The same as *modus*.

M. Is *modus*, then, the same as *bonus*?

S. No.

M. Why, then, are they the same?

S. Because they are the same in sound, but different in meaning.

M. You therefore grant that the sound is the same when we say *modus* and *bonus*.

S. I see that they differ in the sound of their letters; in all other respects, however, they are equal.

M. What, then? When we pronounce *pone* as a verb and *pone* as an adverb, apart from the difference in meaning, do you not think that the sound differs?

S. It differs entirely.

M. In what way does it differ, when both consist of the same number of times and the same letters?

S. It differs because the accent falls in different places [Note: [Col. 1083] “They differ,” according to manuscript A and the editions of Erasmus and Lyons. M.].

M. To what art does the discernment of this belong?

S. I am accustomed to hear this from grammarians, and I learned it there; but whether it is proper to that same art or borrowed from elsewhere, I do not know.

M. We shall consider that later. For now I ask whether, if I were to strike a drum or a string with these sounds as rapidly and quickly as when we pronounce *modus* or *bonus*, you would recognize that they had the same temporal measure, or not.

S. I would recognize it.

M. You would therefore call it a pyrrhic foot.

S. I would.

M. From whom did you learn the name of this foot, if not from a grammarian?

S. I admit that I learned it from him.
