M. Will the grammarian, then, judge concerning all sounds of this kind? Or did you learn these beats through yourself, but hear the name you were to give them from the grammarian?

S. That is so.

M. And you dared to transfer a name taught to you by grammar to a thing that you admit does not belong to grammar?

S. I see that the foot was given its name only because of the measurement of times. Why should I not transfer that term wherever I recognize the same measurement? But even if other terms must be assigned when the sounds have the same measurement but do not belong to grammar, why should I trouble myself over names when the matter itself is clear?

M. Nor do I wish you to do so. Yet when you see innumerable kinds of sounds in which definite measurements can be observed, and when we admit that these kinds ought not to be assigned to the discipline of grammar, do you not think that there must be some other discipline embracing whatever is measured and artfully ordered in such sounds?

S. That seems probable to me.

M. What name do you think it has? For I suppose it is not unfamiliar to you that a certain all-encompassing power of singing is commonly granted to the Muses. This is, unless I am mistaken, what is called Music.

S. I too think that this is what it is.

CHAPTER TWO.—What Music is. What *modulari* is.

2. M. But we now agree not to trouble ourselves at all over the name. Let us simply inquire, as carefully as we can, into the whole power and nature of this discipline, whatever it may be.

S. Let us indeed inquire; for I greatly desire to know all that this whole matter contains.

M. Define Music, then.

S. I do not dare.

M. Can you at least approve my definition?

S. I shall try, if you state it.

M. Music is the science of good modulation. Does it not seem so to you?

S. It might seem so if it were clear to me what modulation itself is.

M. Have you never heard this word, *modulari*, or have you heard it anywhere except in connection with singing or dancing?

S. That is certainly so. But because I see that *modulari* is derived from *modus*, and because a measure must be observed in everything well done, while many things in singing and dancing, although pleasing, are nevertheless extremely base, I want to understand fully what modulation itself precisely is, since the definition of so great a discipline is contained in almost a single word. For what must be learned here is not something known by just any singers and actors.

M. Let the point you made earlier—that a measure must be observed in everything, even outside music, and yet in Music this is called modulation—not trouble you, unless perhaps you do not know that the speech of an orator is properly called a *dictio*.

S. I do know that. But what has that to do with the matter?

M. Because even your child, however unpolished and rustic, when he answers you with even a single word in response to a question, is he not, as you admit, saying something?

S. I admit it.

M. Is he therefore also an orator?

S. No.

M. When he has said something, then, he has not used *dictio*, although we admit that *dictio* is derived from *dicere*, “to say.”

S. I grant that. But I still ask what bearing this has.

M. It bears precisely on your understanding that *modulatio* can belong exclusively to Music, although *modus*, from which the word is formed, can also exist in other things—just as *dictio* is properly attributed to orators, although everyone who speaks says something, and although *dictio* is named from *dicere*.

S. I understand now.

3. M. Therefore, your later observation that there are many base things in singing and dancing, in which, if we accept the name of modulation, this almost divine discipline is degraded, was made with the greatest caution. Let us therefore first examine what *modulari* is, and then what it is to modulate well; for the word *bene* was not added to the definition without reason. Finally, the word *scientia*, “science,” which appears there, must not be disregarded either; for, unless I am mistaken, the definition is complete through these three elements.

S. Let it be so.

M. Since we admit that *modulatio* is named from *modus*, do you think there is any danger that a measure could either be exceeded or fail to be fulfilled except in things that occur through some movement? Or, if nothing moves, can we fear that anything will happen beyond measure?

S. Not at all.

M. Therefore, *modulatio* may reasonably be called a certain skill of moving, or at least that by which something is moved well. For we cannot say that something is moved well if it does not observe measure.

S. We certainly cannot. But it will again be necessary to understand this modulation in everything well done. For I see that nothing is done well except by moving well.

M. What if all these things are done through Music, although the name *modulatio* is more commonly used of instruments of various kinds [Note: [Col. 1084] Thus manuscript B; manuscript A has *hujuscemodi*. The editions have *ejuscemodi*. M.]—and not without reason? For I suppose you think that a turned object of wood, silver, or any material is one thing, and the movement of the craftsman while turning it another.

S. I agree that they differ greatly.

M. Is the movement itself, then, desired for its own sake, and not for the sake of what he wishes to have turned?

S. That is clear.

M. What if he moved his limbs for no other reason than that they should move beautifully and gracefully? Would we call what he did anything other than dancing?

S. It seems so.

M. When, then, do you think one thing is superior and, as it were, dominant: when it is desired for its own sake, or when it is desired for the sake of something else?

S. Who denies that it is when it is desired for its own sake?

M. Now repeat what we said earlier about modulation. We had posited it as a certain skill of moving, and see where this name ought more properly to reside: in the movement that is, as it were, free—that is, desired for its own sake and delightful through itself—or in the movement that is in some way servile. For everything that exists not for itself but in relation to something else is, as it were, servile.

S. Clearly, in the movement that is desired for its own sake.

M. It is therefore probable that the science of modulation is the science of moving well, in such a way that movement itself is desired for its own sake and therefore delights through itself.

S. Quite probable.

CHAPTER THREE.—What it is to modulate well, and why this is included in the definition of Music.

4. M. Why, then, was *bene*, “well,” added, when modulation itself cannot exist unless it moves well?

S. I do not know, and I do not know how that point escaped me; for the question had remained fixed in my mind.

M. There could have been no controversy at all over this word, so that we might define Music simply as the science of modulation, removing the word *bene* that was added.

S. Who would tolerate your wishing to unravel the whole matter in that way?

M. Music is the science of moving well.

But since whatever moves with measured arrangements of times [Note: [Col. 1085] Thus in the manuscripts; Louvain has “whatever moves with a measure of times.” Amerbach and Erasmus have “whatever moves with a measure which belongs to times.” The Benedictine reading is supported by the Vatican manuscript. M.] and intervals already can be called “moving well”—for it already gives pleasure, and for that reason is not improperly called modulation—it can nevertheless happen that this measured order and proportion gives pleasure when it is not appropriate; for example, if someone who sings most sweetly and dances beautifully wishes to indulge in that very activity when the occasion calls for seriousness. In that case he is not using measured modulation well; that is, he is using badly, or inappropriately, the movement that may already be called good because it is measured.

Thus to modulate is one thing, and to modulate well another. For modulation should be understood as belonging to any singer who does not err in the measurements of voices and sounds; but good modulation should be regarded as belonging to this liberal discipline, that is, to Music.

If you do not think that movement good because it is unsuitable, although you admit that it is artfully measured, let us hold to the principle that must be observed everywhere: we must not let a dispute over words torment us when the matter itself is perfectly clear. Let us not care whether Music is described as the science of modulating or of modulating well.

S. I do indeed like passing over and disregarding quarrels about words; nevertheless, I do not dislike this distinction.

CHAPTER FOUR.—Why “science” is included in the definition of Music.

5. M. It remains for us to ask why *scientia*, “science,” appears in the definition.

S. Let us do so; for I remember that the order of the argument requires this.

M. Answer me, then: does it seem to you that a nightingale modulates well during the springtime of the year? Its song is measured and most sweet, and, unless I am mistaken, appropriate to the season.

S. It certainly seems so.

M. Is it therefore skilled in this liberal discipline?

S. No.

M. You see, then, that the word *scientia* is indispensable to the definition.

S. I see that perfectly.

M. Tell me, then, I ask you: do not all those seem to you like that nightingale who, guided by a certain sense, sing well—that is, do so in a measured and pleasing way—although, when questioned about the measures themselves or about the intervals of high and low notes, they are unable to answer?

S. I consider them very much alike.

M. What of those who gladly listen to such performers without possessing this science? When we see elephants, bears, and certain other kinds of beasts moved by songs, and birds themselves delighted by their own voices—for they would not engage so earnestly in this activity without some pleasure—are they not comparable to cattle?

S. I think so. But this insult extends almost to the whole human race.

M. It does not extend as far as you think. Great men, even if they do not know Music, either wish to accommodate themselves to the common people, who differ little from cattle and are very numerous—and they do this with the greatest modesty and prudence, although this is not the place to discuss it—or they moderately take some pleasure in it to relax and restore their minds after great exertions. To enjoy it occasionally in this way is most modest; but to be captured by it, even occasionally, is shameful and unbecoming.

6. But what do you think? Can those who play the flute or the lyre, or instruments of this kind, be compared with nightingales?

S. No.

M. What, then, distinguishes them?

S. I see that there is some art in these performers, whereas in the nightingale there is only nature.

M. You speak plausibly. But do you think this should be called art even if they do it through a certain imitation?

S. Why not? For I see that imitation has such power in the arts that, if it were removed, almost all of them would perish. Teachers offer themselves for imitation, and this very thing is what they call teaching.

M. Does art seem to you to be a certain kind of reason, and do those who use art employ reason? Or do you think otherwise?

S. It seems so.

M. Whoever, then, cannot use reason does not use art.

S. I grant that as well.

M. Do you think dumb animals, which are also called irrational, can use reason?

S. Not at all.

M. Then you must either declare magpies, parrots, and crows to be rational animals, or you have rashly called imitation by the name of art. For we see these birds singing and producing many sounds in a manner acquired from human practice, and doing so only by imitation—unless you believe otherwise.

S. I do not yet clearly understand how you have established this, or how much force it has against my answer.

M. I had asked whether you would say that harpists, flute players, and other people of this kind possess art even if they achieved what they do in singing by imitation. You said that it was art, and asserted that imitation had such force that, once removed, almost all arts seemed to you to be endangered. From this it can now be inferred that everyone who achieves something by imitation uses art, even if it happens that not everyone who uses art acquired it by imitation.

But if every imitation is an art, and every art is reason, then every imitation is reason. An irrational animal, however, does not use reason; therefore it does not possess art. Yet it does possess imitation. Therefore imitation is not art.

S. I said that many arts consist in imitation; I did not call imitation itself an art.

M. Then do you not think that the arts which consist in imitation also consist in reason?

S. On the contrary, I think that they consist in both.

M. I offer no objection. But where do you place science—in reason or in imitation?

S. In both as well.

M. Then you will grant science to those birds from whom you do not remove imitation.

S. I will not grant it. I said that science exists in both in such a way that it cannot exist in imitation alone.

M. What, then? Does it seem to you that it can exist in reason alone?

S. It does.

M. You therefore think art one thing and science another. For science can exist in reason alone, whereas art joins imitation to reason.

S. That does not follow, in my view. I said that not all arts, but many, consist in reason and imitation together.

M. What, then? Will you call that science which consists in these two together, or will you attribute only the rational part to it?

S. What prevents me from calling it science when imitation is joined to reason?

7. M. Since we are now speaking of the harpist and flute player—that is, of musical matters—I want you to tell me whether, if these people do something by imitation, it should be attributed to the body, that is, to a certain obedience of the body.

S. I think it should be attributed both to the mind and to the body. Indeed, the word you used was quite properly chosen when you called it the body’s obedience; for nothing can obey except through the mind.

M. I see that you were very cautious in refusing to grant imitation to the body alone. But will you deny that science belongs to the mind alone?

S. Who could deny that?

M. You therefore cannot allow science in the sounds of strings [Note: [Col. 1087] “Of words,” according to manuscripts A and B. M.] and flutes to be attributed simultaneously to reason and imitation. For, as you admitted, that imitation does not exist without the body, whereas you said that science belongs to the mind alone.

S. From what I have granted you, I admit that this conclusion has been established. But what bearing does it have on the matter? The flute player will possess science in his mind. For when imitation is added to him—and I granted that it cannot exist without the body—it does not remove what he possesses in his mind.

M. It certainly does not remove it. Nor do I assert that all those who handle these instruments lack science; I say that not all of them possess it. We have pursued this question in order to understand, if possible, how rightly science has been placed in the definition of Music. If all flute players, lyre players, and any others of that sort possess it, I think nothing is more worthless or contemptible than this discipline.

8. But pay the closest attention, so that what we have long been working toward may become clear. You have certainly already granted me that science resides in the mind alone.

S. Why should I not grant that?

M. What of the sense of hearing? Do you attribute it to the mind, to the body, or to both?

S. To both.

M. What of memory?

S. I think it must be attributed to the mind. For if we perceive something through the senses and entrust it to memory, that does not mean that memory must therefore be located in the body.

M. This is perhaps a major question and not suited to our present discussion. But for what we have undertaken, I think you cannot deny that animals possess memory. Swallows return to their nests after a year, and the following has been said with complete truth about she-goats:

> And the she-goats themselves, remembering, return to their shelters.  
> (Georgics, book 3, verse 316.)

It is also reported that a dog recognized his master, the hero, although he had already been forgotten by his own people (Odyssey, book 17, verse 291 and following). And, if we wished, we could observe countless examples by which what I am saying would be evident.

S. I do not deny this either, and I am eagerly waiting to see how it helps you.

[Col. 1088] M. How could it help, except in this way? One who attributes science to the mind alone and removes it from all irrational animals has placed it neither in sensation nor in memory—for neither exists without the body, and both are also found in animals—but in the intellect alone.

S. I am waiting to see how this helps you as well.

M. It helps in no other way than this: all who follow sensation, commit to memory what delights them in sensation, and, moving their bodies accordingly, add a certain power of imitation—although they seem to do many things skillfully and expertly—do not possess science if they do not grasp, through the purity and truth of their intellect, the very thing they profess or exhibit.

But if reason demonstrates that these theatrical performers are such people, there will be no reason, in my opinion, for you to hesitate to deny them science and therefore to deny them Music, which is the science of modulation.

S. Explain this. Let us see what it amounts to.

9. M. I believe you attribute greater or lesser agility of the fingers not to science but to practice.

S. Why do you believe that?

M. Because earlier you attributed science to the mind alone, whereas you see that this activity, although commanded by the mind, nevertheless belongs to the body.

S. But when the knowing mind commands this of the body, I think it should be attributed more to the knowing mind than to the limbs that serve it.

M. Do you not think it possible for one person to surpass another in science, while the less skilled person moves his fingers much more easily and efficiently?

S. I do.

M. But if the quick and efficient movement of the fingers were attributable to science, each person would excel in it to the extent that he was more knowledgeable.

S. I grant that.

M. Consider this also. I suppose you have sometimes noticed craftsmen and workers of this kind striking the same spot repeatedly with an axe or hatchet, and directing the blow to exactly the place at which the mind intended it to land. When we try to do this and cannot manage it, they often laugh at us.

S. It is as you say.

M. When, therefore, we cannot do this, are we ignorant of what should be struck or of how much should be cut away?

S. Often we are ignorant; often we know.

M. Suppose, then, that someone knows everything that craftsmen ought to do and knows it perfectly, but is nevertheless less capable in the actual work, while he can dictate many things more skillfully to those very people who work most easily than they could judge for themselves [Note: [Col. 1088] B has *indicare*, “indicate”; so too Louvain. Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and manuscripts A and B have *judicare*, “judge.” M.]. Would you deny that this results from practice?

S. I do not deny it.

M. Therefore, not only the speed and ease of movement, but also the very manner of movement in the limbs, should be attributed to practice rather than to science. For if it were otherwise, each person would use his hands better in proportion to his greater skill. We may apply this to flutes and lyres, so that we do not suppose that what the fingers and joints do there—because it is difficult for us—comes from science rather than from practice, diligent imitation, and training.

S. I cannot resist this. I often hear physicians, highly learned men, surpassed by less skilled practitioners in cutting or otherwise compressing limbs, in whatever is done by hand and instrument. They call this kind of treatment surgery, a word that sufficiently indicates a certain practical habit of healing with the hands. Proceed, then, to the remaining points and now bring this question to an end.

CHAPTER FIVE.—Whether the sense of Music is implanted by nature.

[Col. 1089]

10. It remains, as I think, for us to discover, if we can, whether these very arts that please us through the hands [Note: [Col. 1089] Manuscript A has: “whether these very hands that greatly please us.” M.] follow sensation and memory, once they have become capable through practice, and not immediately science. Otherwise, you might say to me that science can indeed exist without practice, and is often greater than it is in those who excel through practice; yet even those performers could not have reached practice alone without any science at all.

S. Begin, then; for it is clear that this must be done.

M. Have you never listened especially attentively to performers of this kind?

S. Perhaps more than I wished.

M. How do you think it happens that the unskilled crowd often hisses at a flute player producing worthless sounds, but applauds one who plays well, and is moved more intensely and eagerly the more sweetly the music is played? Should we believe that the common people do this through the art of Music?

S. No.

M. What, then?

S. I think it happens by nature, which has given everyone the sense of hearing by which such things are judged.

M. You think correctly. But now consider also whether the flute player himself possesses this sense. If so, his judgment can move his fingers when he blows into the flute; he can mark and commit to memory whatever sounds sufficiently pleasingly according to his choice; and, by repeating it, train his fingers to go there without hesitation or error—whether he receives what he plays from someone else or discovers it himself, with the nature of which we spoke guiding and approving.

Thus, when memory follows sensation and the joints follow memory, having already been subdued and prepared by practice, he sings whenever he wishes, all the better and more pleasantly the more he excels in all those things that reason earlier taught us we share with animals: namely, the impulse to imitate, sensation, and memory.

Do you have anything to say against this?

S. I have nothing at all. I now wish to hear what sort of discipline this is, which I see has been most subtly vindicated from the knowledge of the lowest kinds of soul.

CHAPTER SIX.—That theatrical singers do not know Music.

11. What has been accomplished is not yet sufficient, and I will not allow us to pass to its explanation until it has been established that, just as actors can satisfy the pleasure of the popular ear without this science, so it is in no way possible for actors to be students and experts in Music.

S. It will be surprising if you accomplish that.

M. It is easy enough, but I need you to pay closer attention.

S. As far as I know, I have never been less attentive in listening since this discussion began. But now, I admit, you have made me much more alert.

M. I am grateful, although you are doing yourself an even greater favor. Answer me, then, if you please: does it seem to you that someone knows what a gold solidus is if, wishing to sell it at its proper value, he thinks it is worth ten coins?

S. Who could think that?

M. Now tell me: what should be considered more precious—the thing contained in our understanding, or what is assigned to us by the chance judgment of the ignorant?

S. No one doubts that the former is far superior to everything else, things that ought not even to be considered our own.

[Col. 1090] M. Do you therefore deny that all science is contained in understanding?

S. Who would deny it?

M. Music, then, is there as well.

S. From its definition, I see that this follows.

M. What of the applause of the crowd and all those theatrical rewards? Do they not seem to you to belong to the category of things placed in the power of fortune and the judgment of the ignorant?

S. I think nothing is more accidental, more exposed to chance, and more subject to the domination and nods of the common people than all those things.

M. Would actors, then, sell their singing at such a price if they knew Music?

S. I am considerably shaken by this conclusion, but I do have something to say in response. For the seller of the solidus does not seem comparable with this person. When he receives applause or any money given to him, he does not lose the science—if he happens to possess it—by which he pleased the crowd. Rather, laden with money and happier because of human praise, he returns home with the same discipline unharmed and intact. He would be foolish if he despised those advantages, without which he would be much less honored and poorer; once he has obtained them, however, he is no less learned.

12. M. See, then, whether we can achieve by this means what we want. For I think you agree that the thing for the sake of which we do something is much more excellent than the thing itself that we do. D. Clearly. M. Whoever, then, sings or learns to sing for no other reason than to be praised by the people, or by anyone at all—does he not judge that such praise is better than singing? D. I cannot deny it. M. What, then? Does a person who judges badly about something seem to you to know it? D. Not at all, unless perhaps he has been corrupted in some way. M. Therefore, whoever truly thinks something better which is in fact worse, unquestionably lacks knowledge of it. D. That is so. M. Whenever, then, you either persuade me or demonstrate to me that any stage performer has acquired whatever ability he possesses, or displays it, not in order to please the people for profit or fame, I shall grant that someone can both possess knowledge of music and be a stage performer. But if it is highly probable that there is no stage performer who does not establish and set before himself the goal of his profession in money or glory, you must admit either that stage performers do not know music, or that praise—or any other chance advantage—is more desirable to others than understanding is to ourselves.

[Note: [Col. 1090] Ms. A adds: “And because they seek praise and advantages from others, and do not seek understanding from ourselves, when they prefer what is cheaper to what is more valuable, it is clear that they do not possess its knowledge”; added improperly. M.]

D. I see that, since I have granted the preceding points, I must yield on these as well. For it does not seem at all possible to me that such a man could be found on the stage—one who loved his art for its own sake and not for external advantages—when such a man is scarcely found even in the gymnasium. Nevertheless, if anyone exists or has existed, stage performers might on that account appear not to be despised as musicians, but at times to be honored as stage performers. Therefore, now explain, if you please, this discipline, which no longer seems to me so base.

## CHAPTER VII—Long and Not Long in Motion

13. M. I shall explain it—or rather, you will. For I shall do nothing except ask and question you; you, by answering, will explain this entire matter, whatever it is, which you now seem to be seeking without knowing how to seek it.

[Col. 1091]

So I ask you now: can anyone run both for a long time and quickly? D. He can. M. What, then—slowly and quickly? D. Not at all. M. Therefore “for a long time” is one thing, and “slowly” another. D. Entirely different. M. Again I ask: what do you think is contrary to duration, just as speed is contrary to slowness? D. No customary word occurs to me. Therefore I see nothing to oppose “long-lasting” except “not long-lasting,” so that “not long” may be contrary to “long”; for even if I did not wish to say “quickly” and said “not slowly” instead, nothing else would be signified. M. You speak correctly. Nothing is lost from the truth when we speak in this way. For even if there is a word for this which, as you say, does not occur to you, either I do not know it or it does not come to mind at present. Let us therefore proceed by calling these two pairs of opposites “long” and “not long,” “slow” and “quick.” Let us first discuss the long and the not long, if you agree. D. Let it be so.

## CHAPTER VIII—The Proposition Concerning Long and Not-Long Motion

14. M. Is it clear to you that something is said to happen “for a long time” when it occurs over a long period, and “not for a long time” when it occurs over a short period? D. Clearly. M. A motion, then, that takes place over two hours has twice as much time as one that takes place over one hour, does it not? D. Who could doubt that? M. Therefore what we call “long” or “not long” admits dimensions and numbers of this kind: one motion may stand to another as two to one—that is, one may have twice as much as the other has once;

[Note: [Col. 1091] Manuscripts A and B and all the editions do not have, “one may have twice as much as the other has once.” The Vatican codex reads: “so that it has twice as much duration as the one which takes one hour.” M.]

another may stand to another as three to two—that is, one may have three portions of time as large as the other’s two. And one may proceed through all the other numbers, so that the intervals are not undefined and indeterminate, but two motions have some numerical relation to each other: either the same relation, such as one to one, two to two, three to three, four to four;

[Note: [Col. 1091] Thus the ancient manuscripts; but all the printed editions have: “Or the same, so that one occupies as much time as the other, or not the same, etc.” The same reading is found in Ms. A and the Vatican codex. M.]

or not the same, such as one to two, two to three, three to four; or one to three, two to six; and whatever relation one thing may have to another by way of dimension.

D. Please make this clearer. M. Return, then, to those hours, and consider throughout what I thought had been sufficiently stated when I spoke of one hour and two. Surely you do not deny that one motion can occur in the time of one hour and another in the time of two. D. That is true. M. What, then? Do you not admit that one can occur in two hours and another in three? D. I admit it. M. And that one can occur in three hours and another in four; again, one in one hour and another in three; or one in two and another in six—is this not clear? D. It is clear. M. Why, then, should the other point not also be clear? For this is what I meant when I said that two motions can have some numerical relation to each other—for example, one to two, two to three, three to four; one to three, two to six; and any others you may wish to enumerate. Once these are understood, it is possible to pursue the others as well, whether seven to ten, or five

[Col. 1092]

to eight, or whatever relation there may be at all between two motions whose parts are dimensioned in relation to each other so that they can be expressed as so many to so many—whether the numbers are equal, or one greater and the other smaller. D. I understand now, and I grant that it is possible.

## CHAPTER IX—Rational and Irrational Motions, Connumerated and Dinumerated

15. M. You also understand, I think, that every measure and proportion is rightly preferred to disproportion and infinity.

[Note: [Col. 1092] Most manuscripts rightly have “and formlessness” (*et informitati*) instead of “and infinity.” This is also what our manuscripts and the Vatican codex report. M.]

D. It is perfectly clear. M. Two motions which, as has been said, have some numerical dimension in relation to each other must therefore be preferred to those which do not. D. This too is clear and follows necessarily: a certain order and measure, which resides in numbers, joins the former to one another; those who lack it are not joined to one another by any rational principle. M. Let us therefore, if you agree, call those which are measured in relation to one another “rational,” and those which lack such measurement “irrational.” D. I agree.

M. Now consider whether it seems to you that there is greater concord in rational motions that are equal to one another than in those that are unequal. D. Who would not think so? M. Further, among unequal motions, are there not some in which we can say by what fraction the greater either equals the lesser or exceeds it—for example, two and four, or six and eight—and others in which the same cannot be said, as with three and ten, or four and eleven?

[Note: [Col. 1092] In B.: “Among unequal [motions], are there not some in which we can say by what fraction the greater either equals the lesser or exceeds it; and others in which the same cannot be said, as with these numbers, two and four, or six and eight?” We give the passage in the corrected form found in the Vatican codex. M.]

You certainly see that in the first two numbers the greater equals the lesser by one-half; while in the numbers I mentioned next, the greater exceeds the lesser by one-quarter of the greater. But in the other cases, such as three and ten or four and eleven, we do see some correspondence, because they have parts in relation to one another of which it can be said, “so many to so many”; but is it of the same kind as in the former cases? For it cannot in any way be said by what fraction the greater equals the lesser, or by what fraction the greater exceeds the lesser. No one, for instance, could say that three is some definite fraction of ten, or four some definite fraction of eleven. When I ask you to consider what fraction it is, I mean a clear fraction, without any additional subdivision, such as one-half, one-third, one-quarter, one-fifth, one-sixth, and so on—not that thirds, half-ounces, or any such minute divisions be added. D. I understand now.

16. M. Of these unequal rational motions, then, since I have set out two kinds with numerical examples, which do you think should be preferred: those in which such a fraction can be stated, or those in which it cannot? D. Reason seems to command me to prefer those in which, as has been demonstrated, it can be said by what fraction of itself the greater either equals the lesser or exceeds it, over those in which this does not occur. M. Correct. But would you also like us to give them names, so that when it becomes necessary to mention them later we may speak more efficiently? D. Certainly.

M. Let us therefore call those which we prefer “connumerated,” and those over which we prefer them “dinumerated.” For the former are not only counted individually; they also measure and count themselves by that fraction through which the greater equals or exceeds the lesser. The latter, however, are counted individually only in relation to one another; by the fraction through which the greater either equals or exceeds the lesser, they neither measure nor count themselves. For in their case it cannot be said either how many times the greater contains the lesser, or how many times both the greater and the lesser contain the amount by which the greater exceeds the lesser. D. I accept these terms too, and, insofar as I can, I shall make an effort to remember them.

## CHAPTER X—Complicated and Sesquate Motions

17. M. Come, let us now see what division connumerated motions may have; for I think it will be clear. One kind of connumerated motion is that in which the lesser number measures the greater—that is, the greater contains it a certain number of times,

[Note: [Col. 1093] “The greater contains the lesser a certain number of times,” according to the Vatican codex. M.]

as we said of the numbers two and four. For we see that four contains two twice; it would contain it three times if, instead of four, six were set against two; four times if eight were set against it; five times if ten were set against it.

Another kind is that in which the part by which the greater exceeds the lesser measures both: that is, both the greater and the lesser contain that part a certain number of times. We have already seen this in the numbers six and eight. For the part by which the lesser is exceeded is two; you see that two occurs four times in eight and three times in six.

Let us therefore mark and designate with names these motions under discussion, and the numbers through which what we wish to learn about motions is made clear. For their distinction has, if I am not mistaken, already become apparent. Accordingly, if you agree, let those in which the greater is formed by multiplying the lesser be called “complicated,” while the others may be called “sesquate,” by an already established name. For *sesque* is said to apply when two numbers are related to one another in such a way that the greater has as many parts in relation to the lesser as the fraction by which it exceeds it: for if the relation is three to two, the greater exceeds the lesser by one-third of itself; if four to three, by one-quarter; if five to four, by one-fifth; and so on. The same relation is found in six to four, eight to six, ten to eight; and from these examples it is possible to observe and investigate the same relation in subsequent and larger numbers.

I would not easily explain the origin of this name, unless perhaps *sesque* is formed as though from *se absque*, that is, “without itself,” because five is greater than four by a fifth of itself—

[Note: [Col. 1093] “If five is related to four,” according to Ms. A and the Vatican codex. M.]

that is, by what the lesser is without. What do you think about these matters? D. The account of dimensions and numbers seems to me entirely correct; and the terms you have introduced seem appropriate for designating the things we have understood. The origin of the name which you have now explained is not unreasonable either, even if it is perhaps not the one followed by the person who established the term.

## CHAPTER XI—How Motion and Number Proceeding to Infinity Are Restricted to a Definite Form

[Col. 1094]

18. M. I approve and accept your opinion. But do you see that all these rational motions—that is, those which have some numerical dimension in relation to one another—can proceed through numbers to infinity unless a definite principle again restrains them and brings them back to a certain measure and form? For, to speak first of equal motions themselves: if I pursue one to one, two to two, three to three, four to four, and so on, what end will there be, since number itself has no end? For this power belongs to number: everything stated is finite, but what is not stated is infinite. And you can observe that what occurs with equal numbers also occurs with unequal ones, whether complicated, sesquate, connumerated, or dinumerated.

For if you set one against two and wish to continue that multiplication by saying one to three, one to four, one to five, and so on, there will be no end. The same is true if you use only the double relation: one to two, two to four, four to eight, eight to sixteen, and onward—here too there is no end. Likewise, the triple relation alone, the quadruple relation alone, and whatever else of this kind you attempt, proceed to infinity.

The same is true of sesquate relations. When we say two to three, three to four, four to five, you see that nothing prevents us from pursuing the rest, with no end resisting us. Or if you wish to continue within the same kind in this manner—two to three, four to six, six to nine, eight to twelve, ten to fifteen, and so on—whether in this kind or in the others, no end presents itself. Why need I speak now of dinumerated relations, when anyone can understand from what has already been said that in those too, as they rise step by step, there is no end? Do you not agree? D. What could be said more truly than this? But I am now eagerly waiting to learn that principle which brings this infinity back to a definite measure and prescribes a form that must not be exceeded.

19. M. You will recognize this too, as with the other matters, as something you yourself know, when you answer correctly the questions I ask. First, then, I ask you: since we are dealing with numerical motions, ought we to consult numbers themselves, so that we judge that the definite and fixed laws they reveal to us should be observed and applied in those motions? D. Certainly; I do not think anything could be done in a more orderly way.

M. Let us therefore, if you agree, begin the consideration from the very beginning of numbers, and see, insofar as the power of our minds permits us to contemplate such things, what the principle is by which, although number proceeds to infinity, as has been said, human beings have established certain articulations in counting, from which they return again to one, which is the beginning of numbers.

In counting, we proceed from one up to ten, and from there return again to one. And if you wish to pursue the tenfold progression, advancing in this way—ten, twenty, thirty, forty—the progression continues up to one hundred. If you pursue the hundredfold progression—one hundred, two hundred, three hundred, four hundred—the articulation reaches one thousand, from which one returns.

What need is there to inquire further? You surely see which articulations I mean, whose first rule is prescribed by the number ten. For just as ten contains one ten times, one hundred contains those same tens ten times, and one thousand contains one hundred ten times; and so, for as long as one wishes to proceed, it will proceed in such articulations, according to what has been fixed in the number ten.

[Note: [Col. 1095] Lov. has: “they proceed in such quasi-articulations.” Am. and Er. have: “To proceed, it lives in such quasi-articulations,” etc.; but the better manuscripts have: “to proceed, it will go in such articulations,” etc.]

Do you fail to understand any of this? D. Everything is perfectly clear and entirely true.

## CHAPTER XII—Why Counting Proceeds from One to Ten and Then Returns from Ten to One

20. M. Let us therefore examine this as carefully as we can: what is the reason that counting proceeds from one to ten and then returns again to one? I ask you first whether what we call a beginning can exist at all without being the beginning of something. D. It cannot at all. M. Again, can what we call an end exist without being the end of something? D. That too is impossible. M. What, then? Do you think one can arrive from a beginning at an end except through some middle? D. I do not think so. M. Therefore, for something to be complete, it consists of a beginning, a middle, and an end. D. So it seems.

M. Tell me, then: in what number do you think beginning, middle, and end are contained? D. I suppose you want me to answer “the number three,” since there are three things about which you ask. M. You are right. Therefore you see that there is a certain perfection in the number three, because it is complete: it has a beginning, a middle, and an end. D. I see that clearly.

M. What, then? Have we not learned from early childhood that every number is either even or odd? D. You speak truly. M. Recall, then, and tell me which number we customarily call even and which odd. D. The number that can be divided into two equal parts is called even; the one that cannot is called odd.

21. M. You understand the matter. Since three is therefore the first complete odd number—for it consists of a beginning, a middle, and an end, as has been said—must not an even number also be complete and perfect, so that beginning, middle, and end may be found in it as well? D. Certainly it must.

M. But whatever number this may be, it cannot have an indivisible middle as an odd number does. For if it had one, it could not be divided into two equal parts, which we said is characteristic of an even number. An indivisible middle is one; a divisible one is two. The middle in numbers is that from which both sides are equal to each other. Have I said anything obscure, so that you understand it less well? D. On the contrary, this too is clear to me; and when I seek a complete even number, four is the first to occur to me. For how could those three things through which a number is complete—beginning, middle, and end—be found in two?

M. You have given precisely the answer I wanted, and which reason itself compels us to acknowledge. Return, then, to the number one itself and consider it. You will certainly see that one has no middle and end because it is only a beginning—or that it is a beginning because it lacks a middle and end. D. It is clear.

M. What, then, shall we say

[Col. 1096]

about two? Can we understand beginning and middle in it, when there can be no middle unless there is an end? Or beginning and end, when one cannot reach an end except through a middle? D. Reason compels me to admit the difficulty, and I am completely uncertain what answer to give about this number.

M. See whether

[Note: [Col. 1096] “See whether this,” according to Ms. A. M.]

this number too can be a beginning of numbers. For if it lacks a middle and an end—which, as you said, reason compels us to admit—what remains except that it too is a beginning? Or do you hesitate to posit two beginnings? D. I hesitate greatly.

M. You would be right to do so if they were established as two beginnings opposed to each other. But this second beginning derives from the first, so that the first is from no other, while the second is from the first. For one and one are two, and both are beginnings in such a way that all numbers indeed derive from one; but because they arise through a certain multiplication and addition, and the origin of multiplication and addition is rightly attributed to the number two, it follows that the first beginning is the source from which all numbers derive, while this second is the means through which all numbers come to exist. Unless you have something to argue against this. D. I have nothing, and I cannot consider these matters without amazement, although, questioned by you, I myself give the answers.

22. M. These matters are investigated more subtly and more obscurely in the discipline concerned with numbers; here, however, let us return as quickly as possible to the work we have undertaken. I ask, then: what does one joined to two make? D. Three. M. Therefore these two beginnings of numbers, joined together, make a complete and perfect number. D. That is so.

M. What number do we place in counting after one and two? D. The same three. M. The same number, then, which is formed from one and two, is placed in order after both of them, so that no other number can be inserted between them. D. I see that.

M. But you must also see that this cannot occur with any of the remaining numbers: when you have marked any two numbers joined together in the order of counting, the number formed from both does not follow them without another being inserted. D. I see that too. For two and three, which are joined numbers, make five in total; but five does not immediately follow them, since four comes first. Again, three and four make seven; but between four and seven, five and six are arranged. And the farther I wish to proceed, the more numbers are inserted.

M. There is therefore a great concord in the first three numbers. For we say one, two, and three, between which nothing can be inserted; and one and two themselves are three. D. A very great concord indeed.

M. What, then? Do you think it unworthy of consideration that the closer and more tightly joined this concord is, the more it tends toward a certain unity and makes one thing out of several? D. On the contrary, it is most worthy of consideration; and somehow I both marvel at and love this unity you commend. M. I approve greatly. But surely every joining and connection of things produces one thing most fully when the middle agrees with the extremes and the extremes with the middle. D. Certainly it must.

23. M. Pay attention, then, so that we may see this in the present connection.

[Col. 1097]

When we say one, two, three, is not one exceeded by two to the same extent that two is exceeded by three? D. That is entirely true. M. Now tell me: in this comparison, how many times have I named one? D. Once. M. Three? D. Once. M. What about two? D. Twice. M. One time, twice, and one time—how many do they make in total? D. Four. M. Therefore the number four rightly follows these three, since the comparison is assigned to it in this proportion.

You will gradually become accustomed to recognizing how much this means from the fact that the unity which you said you loved can be produced in ordered things by this one relation, whose Greek name is *ἀναλογία* (*analogia*), which some of our people have called *proportio*, “proportion.” Let us use that term if you agree; for I do not willingly use Greek words in Latin unless necessity requires it. D. I agree; but proceed toward the point at which you were aiming.

M. I shall. What proportion is, and how much force it has in things, we shall investigate more carefully in its proper place in this discipline; and the further you advance in learning, the better you will understand its force and nature.

But you surely see what is sufficient for the present: those three numbers whose concord you admired could not be compared with one another in the same connection except through the number four. Therefore it rightly obtained the privilege of being arranged after them, so that the concord may be joined to them even more closely. Thus the progression of numbers is now not merely one, two, three, but one, two, three, four, joined together in the most harmonious manner.

[Note: [Col. 1097] “It commanded,” according to Mss. A and B. M.]

D. I entirely agree.

24. M. Now examine the rest, lest you think that the number four has no distinctive property lacking in all the other numbers—a property relevant to the connection of which I speak, so that the progression from one to four may be definite and most beautiful. For we previously agreed that something is made most fully into one from several things when the middle agrees with the extremes and the extremes with the middle. D. That is so.

M. When, then, we arrange one, two, and three, tell me which are the extremes and which the middle. D. I see that one and three are the extremes, and two the middle. M. Now answer: what is made from one and three? D. Four. M. And the number two, which is one number in the middle, can it be compared except with itself? Therefore tell me also what two taken twice makes. D. Four.

M. Thus the middle agrees with the extremes, and the extremes with the middle. Therefore, just as three is distinguished by being placed after one and two, although it consists of one and two, so four is distinguished by being counted after one, two, and three, although it consists of one and three, or of two taken twice. This is the agreement of the extremes with the middle and of the middle with the extremes, in that proportion which in Greek is called *ἀναλογία* (*analogia*). Explain whether you have understood it. D. I understand it sufficiently.

25. M. Try, then, with the remaining numbers, whether what we said was distinctive of the number four is found in them. D. I shall. If we arrange two, three, and four, the extremes together make six; the middle also makes this when taken twice. Nevertheless, it is not six but five that follows them. Again, I arrange three, four, and five; the extremes make eight, and the middle likewise makes eight when doubled. But between five and eight I now see not one but two numbers inserted, namely six and seven. And the farther I proceed by this method, the larger these intervals become.

[Note: [Col. 1098] B has “these intervals become larger”; Ms. A has “are made.” M.]

M. I see that you have understood and entirely grasped what was said. But, so that we do not linger, you certainly observe that the progression from one to four is most justly constituted: either because of the odd and even numbers, since three is the first complete odd number and four the first complete even number, a matter discussed shortly before; or because one and two are the beginnings and, as it were, seeds of numbers, from which three is formed, so that there are now three numbers; and when they are compared with one another by proportion, four shines forth and is generated, and is therefore rightly joined to them, so that the measured progression we seek extends up to it. D. I understand.

26. M. Very well. But do you finally remember what we had undertaken to investigate? As I think you recall, the question was whether we could somehow discover, given that definite articulations had been established for those counting within the infinity of numbers, why the first articulation itself occurs at the number ten, which has the greatest power throughout all the others—that is, why those counting, after progressing from one to ten, return again to one. D. I clearly remember that we have gone around so much because of this question; but I do not see what we have accomplished that bears on solving it. For all our reasoning has reached the conclusion that the just and measured progression extends not to the number ten but only to the number four.

M. Do you not see, then, what sum is formed from one, two, three, and four? D. I see now—I see—and I marvel at everything, and admit that the question has been solved: one, two, three, and four together make ten. M. It is therefore fitting that these first four numbers, and their sequence and connection, should be held in greater honor than the others within the realm of numbers.

## CHAPTER XIII—The Beauty of Proportioned Motions, So Far as It Is Judged by the Senses

27. It is now time to return to the motions that properly belong to this discipline and to examine and discuss them—those for whose sake we considered matters concerning numbers, which belong to another discipline, insofar as seemed sufficient for our purpose.

I ask you, then: since, for the sake of understanding, we established motions in intervals of hours, and reason demonstrated that they have some numerical dimension in relation to one another, if one person runs for the duration of one hour and another afterward for two hours, could you, without looking at a clock, water-clock, or any similar indication of time, perceive that the two motions are related as one to two—that one is simple and the other double? Or, even if you could not state this, could you nevertheless take pleasure in that concord and be affected by some enjoyment? D. I could not at all.

M. What if someone were to clap rhythmically, so that one sound occupied one unit of time and another twice as much—the feet called iambs—and were to continue and connect them; while another person danced to the same sound, moving his limbs according to those same periods? Would you not either recognize or even state the very pattern of the times—that is, that intervals in the motions alternate as one to two, whether in the clapping that is heard or in the dancing that is seen—or at least take pleasure in the numerical structure that you perceive, even though you could not express the numbers of its dimension?

[Note: [Col. 1099] Ms. A adds “recognize.” M.]

D. It is exactly as you say. Those who know these numbers perceive them in the clapping and dancing and can easily state what they are; and those who do not know them and cannot state them nevertheless do not deny that they derive some pleasure from them.

28. Since, then, it cannot be denied that all well-measured motions belong to the very rational principle of this discipline—if indeed it is the science of measuring rhythmically—and especially those motions which are not referred to something else but preserve within themselves the end of beauty or pleasure, nevertheless these motions, as you have now rightly and truthfully said in answer to my question, if they take place over a long interval of time and occupy an hour or even more within that dimension which is beautiful, cannot harmonize with our senses.

[Note: [Col. 1100] The Vatican codex adds: “Although the same foot, while preserving the principle of comparison, may in singing be made with sounds that are sometimes longer and sometimes shorter.” M.]

Therefore, since music, proceeding in some way from its most secret inner chambers, has also left certain traces in our senses and in the things perceived by us, ought we not first to follow those same traces, so that, if we can, we may be led without error to those inner chambers I mentioned? D. Certainly we ought, and I urgently request that we do so at once.

M. Let us therefore set aside those temporal limits stretched beyond the capacity of our senses,

[Note: [Col. 1100] The Vatican codex has “outside” (*extra*). M.]

and discuss, insofar as reason leads us, the brief intervals of duration that delight us in singing and dancing. Unless you happen to think that the traces which this discipline is said to have placed in our senses and in the things we are capable of perceiving can be investigated in some other way. D. I certainly do not think so.

# BOOK TWO

In Which Syllables and Metrical Feet Are Discussed

[Col. 1099]

## CHAPTER I—The Grammarian Considers the Duration of Syllables in One Way, the Musician in Another

1. M. Pay close attention, then, and now receive what may be called the second beginning of our discussion. First answer whether you have properly learned the distinction between short and long syllables taught by grammarians, or whether, whether you know this or are ignorant of it, you would prefer us to investigate the matter as though we were entirely inexperienced in such things, so that reason may lead us to everything rather than established habit or prejudiced authority compelling us. D. I am driven to prefer that course not only by reason itself but also by my lack of knowledge of these syllables—for why should I hesitate to admit it?

M. Come, then, at least tell me whether you yourself have never observed, in our speech, that some syllables are pronounced rapidly and for a very short time, while others are uttered at greater length and for a longer time. D. I cannot deny that I have not been deaf even to these matters.

M. But I want you to know that the entire discipline which in Greek is called *grammatica* and in Latin *litteratura* professes to be the guardian of history—or only that, as more subtle reasoning teaches, or at least chiefly that, as even the less refined minds concede.

Thus, for example, when you say *cano*, or happen to place it in a verse, so that either you, in pronouncing it, lengthen the first syllable of this word, or you place it in a position in the verse where it ought to be long, the grammarian will correct you. He is, of course, the guardian of history, and asserts no other reason why this syllable ought to be shortened than that those who lived before us, whose books exist and are handled by grammarians, used it short

[Note: [Col. 1099] The Vatican codex has *pro correpta*, “in place of ‘shortened.’” M.]

rather than long. Thus, in this matter, whatever force there is belongs to authority.

But the rational principle of music, to which the measured arrangement and numerical structure of sounds belong, cares only that the syllable be shortened or lengthened according to the demands of its position within the system of its measures. For if you place this word where two long syllables ought to be placed, and by your pronunciation make the first syllable, which is short, long, music is not offended at all;

[Col. 1100]

for the durations of the sounds have reached the ears that were due to that numerical pattern.

[Note: [Col. 1100] “It is offended,” according to the Vatican codex. M.]

The grammarian, however, orders you to correct it and to substitute a word whose first syllable ought to be long, in accordance with the authority of our ancestors, whose writings, as has been said, he guards.

[Note: [Col. 1100] B has *custodiuntur*, “are guarded”; Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition have *custodiunt*, “they guard”; Ms. B likewise; but Ms. A has *custodit*, “he guards,” indicating that the grammarian, whom Augustine shortly before called the guardian of history, is meant. M.]

## CHAPTER II—The Grammarian Judges Verse by Authority, the Musician by Reason and Sense
2. Therefore, since we have undertaken to pursue the principles of music, even if you do not know which syllable should be shortened and which lengthened, we can nevertheless not be hindered by this ignorance of yours, and can be satisfied that you have observed—as you said—that some syllables are shorter and others longer. So I now ask whether the sound of verses has ever moved you through the ears with some pleasure.

D. Indeed, very often, so that I have scarcely ever heard a verse without delight.

M. If, then, in a verse whose sound delights you, someone should either lengthen or shorten syllables in a place where the structure of that verse does not require it, could you still be delighted in the same way?

D. On the contrary, I cannot hear that without offense.

M. There is therefore no doubt that, in the sound which you say delights you, you are delighted by a certain numerical measure; if it is disturbed, that delight cannot be conveyed to your ears [Col. 1101].

D. That is clear.

M. Tell me next, as far as the sound of the verse is concerned, what difference there is between saying, *Arma virumque cano, Trojae qui primus ab oris*—“I sing of arms and the man, who first from the shores of Troy”—and *qui primis ab oris*—“who from the first shores.”

D. To me, as far as that measure is concerned, both sound the same.

M. But [Note: [Col. 1101] B has *et*; manuscripts A and B have *at*. M.] that resulted from my pronunciation, with the fault that grammarians call a barbarism. For *primus* consists of a long and a short syllable, whereas in *primis* both syllables must be lengthened; but I shortened its final syllable. Thus your ears suffered no loss.

Therefore we must try again and again to see whether, when I pronounce the words, you can perceive what in syllables is long and what is not long [Note: [Col. 1101] Thus manuscripts A and B. B has *quod fit*, which is less idiomatic Latin. M.], so that our discussion may proceed—as we have arranged—with me asking and you answering. Accordingly, I shall repeat the same verse in which I committed a barbarism, and I shall lengthen the syllable that I shortened so that your ears would not be offended, as the grammarians prescribe. You must tell me whether, when the verse is measured in this way, it affects your sense with the same pleasure. I shall pronounce it thus: *Arma virumque cano, Trojae qui primis ab oris.*

D. Now I cannot deny that I have been offended by some disfigurement of the sound.

M. Not without reason. Although no barbarism has been committed, a fault has nevertheless occurred which both grammar and music condemn: grammar, because the word whose final syllable must be lengthened has been placed where a word with a shortened final syllable ought to have stood; music, however, only because some sound has been lengthened in a place where it ought to have been shortened, and the required time demanded by the rhythmic measure has not been supplied.

Therefore, if you now sufficiently distinguish what sense requires from what authority requires, it follows that we should see why that same sense is sometimes pleased by sounds that are lengthened or shortened and at other times offended by them. For this is what concerns the long and the not-long. I believe you remember that we undertook to explain this part.

D. I have distinguished the former, I remember the latter, and I await with the greatest attention what follows.

## CHAPTER III — The durations of syllables

3. M. What do you think remains except that we begin to compare syllables with one another and see what numerical relations they have to one another, just as we have already discussed motion among ourselves at such length? Everything that sounds is in motion, and syllables certainly sound. Can any of this be denied?

D. In no way.

M. When syllables are therefore compared with one another, certain motions are compared with one another, and in these certain numerical measures of duration can be investigated [Note: [Col. 1101] *Temporis, et* (“of time, and”), according to manuscript A. M.] [Col. 1101].

D. That is so.

M. Can one syllable, then, be compared with itself? For, unless you think otherwise, singularity eludes every comparison.

D. I think otherwise about nothing.

M. What, then? Do you deny that one can be compared with one, or one or two with two or three, and so on among larger numbers?

D. Who could deny that?

M. Consider this again: however short a syllable may be, and however briefly pronounced, ending as soon as it has burst forth, it nevertheless occupies some space in time [Col. 1102] and has a certain little duration of its own.

D. I see that what you say must be true.

M. Tell me now: from what do we begin counting?

D. From one, naturally.

M. It is therefore not unreasonable that the smallest extent of time, as it were, which a short syllable occupies, was called by the ancients one time; for we proceed from the short to the long.

D. True.

M. You must now observe this as well: just as in numbers the first progression is from one to two, so in syllables, by which [Note: [Col. 1102] *Quia* (“since”), according to manuscript A. M.] we proceed from the short to the long, the long syllable must have twice the duration. Thus, if the space occupied by a short syllable is rightly called one time, the space occupied by a long syllable is likewise rightly called two times.

D. Entirely correct; I agree that reason requires this.

## CHAPTER IV — Two-syllable feet

4. M. Come, let us now examine the comparisons themselves. I ask what relation one short syllable seems to you to have to another short syllable, or what these motions among themselves should be called. For, unless I am mistaken, you remember that in our earlier discussion we assigned names to all motions that agree with one another in some numerical relation.

D. I remember that they were called equal, since they contain the same amount of time in relation to one another.

M. But do you think this comparison of syllables, by which they now acquire certain numerical relations to one another, should be left without a name?

D. I do not think so.

M. Know, then, that the ancients called such a comparison of sounds a foot. But we must carefully observe how far reason permits a foot to extend. So tell me now: by what relation are a short and a long syllable compared?

D. I think this comparison proceeds from the class of numbers that we called compound. For I see in it one-to-two: one time belonging to the short syllable compared with two times belonging to the long syllable.

M. What if they are arranged so that the long syllable is pronounced first and the short syllable afterward? Does the relation of compound numbers cease merely because the order has changed? For just as in the former foot there is one-to-two, so in this one there is two-to-one.

D. That is so.

M. What of a foot consisting of two long syllables? Are not two times compared with two times?

D. Clearly.

M. From what relation, then, is this comparison derived?

D. From that of the numbers called equal.

5. M. Come, now tell me: since, beginning with two short syllables, we have reached two long syllables, how many foot-comparisons have we discussed?

D. Four: first, two short syllables; second, a short and a long; third, a long and a short; fourth, two long syllables.

M. Can there be more than four when two syllables are compared with one another?

D. In no way. For once syllables have been assigned this condition—that a short syllable has one time and a long syllable two—and since every syllable is either short or long, in what way can two syllables be compared and joined together to form a foot except as short and short, short and long, long and short, or long and long?

M. Tell me also how many times the smallest foot of two syllables contains, and how many the largest.

D. The former contains two, the latter four.

M. Do you see that progression, whether in feet or in times, could not proceed beyond the number four?

D. I see it clearly, and I recall the principle of progression in numbers; I feel with great pleasure that the same force is present here also.

M. Since feet consist of syllables—that is, of distinct and, as it were, articulated motions occurring in sounds—and syllables extend through times, do you not therefore think that the progression of the foot ought likewise to proceed up to four syllables, just as you see that the progression of feet and times has already reached the number four?

D. I feel exactly as you say, I recognize [Note: [Col. 1103] *Agnosco* (“I recognize”), according to manuscripts A and B. M.] that this is the mark of a perfect principle, and I demand what is due.

## CHAPTER V — Three-syllable feet

6. M. Come, then. First, as the order itself requires, let us see how many feet of three syllables there can be, just as we discovered that there are four of two syllables.

D. Let it be so.

M. You remember that we began this investigation with one short syllable, that is, with one time, and that you understood well why this was necessary.

D. I remember that we agreed not to depart from that law of counting by which we begin from one, the beginning of numbers.

M. Since, then, among feet of two syllables the first is the one consisting of two short syllables—for reason required one time to be joined first to one time before two could be joined—what do you think ought to be the first among feet of three syllables?

D. What else but the one consisting of three short syllables?

M. And how many times does it contain?

D. Three, naturally.

M. How, then, are its parts compared with one another? For every foot must have two parts, because of that comparison of numbers, and those parts must be compared with one another in some relation; I remember that we dealt with this above. But can we divide this foot of three short syllables into two equal parts?

D. In no way.

M. How, then, is it divided?

D. I see no alternative except that the first part contains one syllable and the second two, or the first two and the second one.

M. Tell me also [Note: [Col. 1103] B omits *hoc* (“this”), which is found in all printed editions and in manuscripts A and B. M.]: to what rule of numbers does this belong?

D. I recognize that it belongs to the class of compound numbers.

7. M. Come, now observe how many variations are possible in three syllables containing one long syllable and the others short—that is, how many feet they can form—and answer if you discover it.

D. I see one foot consisting of a long syllable and two short syllables; I understand no other.

M. Does it seem to you that only the foot having the long syllable in first place contains one long syllable among three?

D. I could not think that, since the two short syllables may come first and the long syllable last.

M. Consider whether there is a third possibility.

D. Certainly: the long syllable may also be placed in the middle of two short syllables.

M. See whether there is a fourth.

D. There cannot be one.

M. Can you now answer how many variations are possible in three syllables containing one long and two short syllables—that is, how many feet they can form?

D. I certainly can: they are varied in three ways and form three feet.

M. What, then? Do you now yourself understand how these three feet should be ordered, or must I lead you through this point in detail as well?

D. Do you disapprove of the order in which I discovered the variation? First I noticed one long and two short syllables; then two short and one long; finally a short, a long, and a short.

M. Do you really not disapprove of someone who orders them so that he goes from the first to the third and from the third to the second, rather than from the first to the second and then to the third?

D. I entirely disapprove. But what, I ask, have you noticed here?

M. Since you placed first in this threefold difference the foot that has the long syllable first because you perceived that the unity of the long syllable itself holds the leading position—for it is one there—you ought also to have seen that the foot in which it is second should be second, and that in which it is third should be third. Do you still think we should remain with that ordering?

D. On the contrary, I condemn it without hesitation. Who would not agree that this is the better order—or rather, that it is the order?

M. Now tell me by what numerical rule these feet too are divided, and their parts compared with one another.

D. I see that the first and last are divided according to the same rule, because both the first, which consists of a long and two short syllables, and the last, which consists of two short and a long syllable, can be divided so that each part contains two times and is therefore equal. But in the second, because it has the long syllable in the middle, whether that syllable is assigned to the earlier or the later part, the division is either into three and one or into one and three times. Thus the principle of compound numbers governs its division.

8. M. I now want you, if you can, to tell me on your own which feet you think should be ordered after those we have discussed. We first dealt with the four feet of two syllables, whose order was derived from the order of numbers, so that we began with short syllables. Then we undertook to discuss the somewhat longer feet of three syllables, and, following the earlier principle, we began with three short syllables. What followed except that we should see what forms one long syllable with two short syllables could produce? We have seen this, and the three feet after that first one have been ordered as they ought to be. Surely you should now see for yourself what comes next, so that we do not extract everything through the most minute questions.

D. You are right. Who would not see that the next are those in which one syllable is short and the others long? Since that short syllable, because it is one, receives precedence according to the earlier principle, the first will certainly be the one in which it is first, the second where it is second, and the third where it is third—which is also last.

M. You see, I think, by what principles these too are divided, so that their parts can be compared with one another.

D. I see it clearly. The foot consisting of one short and two long syllables can be divided only so that the first part has three times, containing the short and one long syllable, and the second has two times, belonging to the remaining long syllable. The third foot is like the first in that it permits one division, but unlike it in that the first is divided into three and two times, whereas the third is divided into two and three. For the long syllable occupying the first part has two times; what remains—the long and the short syllable—occupies three times. But the middle foot, which has the short syllable in the middle, can undergo a double division, because that same short syllable can be assigned either to the earlier or to the later part. It is therefore divided either into two and three or into three and two times. Accordingly, the relation of sesquialter numbers governs these three feet.

M. Have we now considered all the feet of three syllables, or does something remain?

D. I see one remaining: the foot consisting of three long syllables.

M. Then deal with its division as well.

D. Its division is one syllable and two, or two and one—two and four times, or four and two. Therefore its parts are compared with one another according to the principle of compound numbers.

## CHAPTER VI — Four-syllable feet

9. M. Let us now proceed in order to examine feet of four syllables, and you yourself say which of these ought to be first, adding the principle of its division.

D. Clearly, the foot of four short syllables, which is divided into two parts of two syllables according to the principle of equal numbers, containing two and two times.

M. You have it [Note: [Col. 1105] *Teneo* (“I have it”), according to the Erasmus, Louvain, and Venetian editions and manuscripts A and B. M.]. Now proceed on your own and pursue the rest. I do not think there is any need to question you about each one, since there is one principle: successively to remove short syllables and substitute long ones for them until all the syllables are long; and, as the short syllables are removed and long ones substituted, to consider what variations they make and how many feet they generate. The syllable that is one among the others, whether long or short, retains precedence in the order. You have already been trained in all this above. When there are two short and two long syllables—a case not found in the preceding groups—which do you think ought to have precedence?

D. This too is clear from what came before. The short syllable, which has one time, possesses unity more strongly than the long syllable, which has two. For that reason, at every beginning and in every first place we established as first the foot consisting of short syllables.

10. M. Nothing, then, prevents you from pursuing all these feet while I listen and judge rather than question.

D. I shall do so if I can. First, in the foot of four short syllables, one short syllable must be removed and a long syllable substituted for it in first place, because of the dignity of unity. This foot has two divisions: either into a long syllable and three short syllables, or into a long and a short syllable and two short syllables—that is, either into two and three, or into three and two times.

When the long syllable is placed second, it produces another foot, which is correctly divided in one way, namely into three and two times, so that the first part contains a short and a long syllable, and the second two short syllables.

When the long syllable is placed third, it produces a foot that is again correctly divided in one way, but so that the first part contains two times in two short syllables and the second three times in a long and a short syllable.

The long syllable in fourth place produces the fourth foot, which is divided in two ways, like the one in which the long syllable is first. For it may be divided either into two short syllables and a short and a long syllable, or into three short syllables and a long syllable—that is, into two and three, or three and two times. All these four feet, in which the long syllable is variously placed among three short syllables, have their parts compared with one another [Note: [Col. 1106] *Collocatas* (“placed together”), according to manuscript A and all printed editions. M.] according to the relation of sesquialter numbers.

11. Next, after removing two from the four short syllables, let us substitute two long syllables for them and see how many forms and feet can be produced when there are two short and two long syllables.

First, then, I see that two short and two long syllables must be placed, since it is more appropriate to begin with short syllables.
