This foot has a double division: it is divided either into two and four or into four and two times—either the two short syllables occupy the first part and the two long syllables the second, or the first part contains two short syllables and a long syllable, while the second contains the remaining long syllable.

Another foot is formed when the two short syllables that we had placed at the beginning are placed in the middle, as the order itself requires. Its division is into three and three times, for the first part is occupied by a long and a short syllable, and the second by a short and a long syllable.

When the short syllables are placed at the end—for this follows in the order—they form a foot with a double division: either the first part contains two times in one long syllable and the second four times in a long and two short syllables; or the first contains four times in two long syllables and the second two times in two short syllables.

The parts of these three feet are compared according to the principle of compound numbers in the case of the first and third; the middle foot has equal parts.

12. Next, the two short syllables that had been placed together must be placed separately. Their smallest separation is that in which they have one long syllable between them; this is also where we must begin. Their greatest separation is that in which they have two long syllables between them.

When there is one long syllable between them, two arrangements are possible, producing two feet. The first is: a short syllable at the beginning, then a long; afterward a short, and then the remaining long syllable. The second is for the short syllables to be in the second and fourth places, with long syllables in the first and third: thus the pattern is long and short, long and short.

The greatest separation occurs when the two long syllables are in the middle, with one short syllable first and the other last.

These three feet, in which the short syllables are separated, are divided into three and three times: the first into a short and a long, and a short and a long; the second into a long and a short, and a long and a short; the third into a short and a long, and a long and a short.

Thus six feet are formed by placing two short and two long syllables variously among one another, insofar as this is possible.

13. It remains to remove three short syllables from the four and substitute three long syllables for them. One short syllable will remain; and because a short syllable at the beginning followed by three long syllables forms one foot, placing it second makes a second foot, third a third, and fourth a fourth.

Of these four feet, the first two are divided into three and four times, while the latter two are divided into four and three. In all of them the parts are compared according to the relation of sesquialter numbers [Col. 1107].

For the first part of the first is a short and a long syllable, containing three times; its second part consists of two long syllables, containing four times.

The first part of the second is a long and a short syllable, therefore three times; its second part is two long syllables, four times.

The third has its first part in two long syllables, four times; its second part is occupied by a short and a long syllable, that is, three times.

The first part of the fourth is likewise formed by two long syllables, four times; its second part by a long and a short syllable, three times.

The remaining foot is the four-syllable foot in which all the syllables are long. It is divided into two and two long syllables according to equal numbers, that is, into four and four times.

You have what you wanted me to explain by myself. Now continue by questioning me about the rest.

## CHAPTER VII — A verse consists of a definite number of feet, just as a foot consists of a number of syllables

14. M. I shall do so. But have you sufficiently considered how much this progression up to the number four, which has been demonstrated in numbers themselves, applies also to these feet?

D. Certainly. I approve this principle of progression in them just as in numbers.

M. What of this? Just as feet are formed by joining syllables together, should we not likewise think that something can be formed by joining feet together—something that is no longer called either a syllable or a foot?

D. I certainly think so.

M. What, then, do you think it is?

D. I think it is a verse.

M. What if someone wished to join certain feet together continuously, imposing no limit or end upon them except the failure of his voice, some other interrupting circumstance, or the measure of time directing him to pass to something else? Would you still call it a verse if it had twenty, thirty, or even a hundred or more feet, according to the desire and ability of the person who joined them together in any length of continuity?

D. That is not so. I shall not call it a verse merely whenever I notice any feet mixed together in any fashion, or many feet joined through infinite length. Rather, I shall have to determine by some discipline both the kind and the number of feet—that is, which feet and how many make a verse—and from that judge whether a verse has struck my ears.

M. Whatever this discipline may be, it establishes a rule and limit for verses, not as one pleases, but according to some principle.

D. It could not be otherwise, if it is a discipline; nor ought it to be otherwise.

M. Let us therefore investigate and attain this principle, if you agree. For if we look only to authority, a verse will be whatever some Asclepiades or Archilochus—ancient poets, of course—or Sappho the poetess, or the others, wished to be called a verse. The kinds of verse that these first noticed and sang are even called by their names. Thus there is an Asclepiad verse, an Archilochian, a Sapphic, and six hundred other names of authors that the Greeks have given to verses of different kinds.

From this it might not unreasonably seem to someone that if a person arranges as he wishes as many feet as he wishes, and whichever feet he wishes, since no one before him established this order and measure for feet, he should rightly and legitimately be called the founder and propagator of a new kind of verse.

Or, if this liberty is denied to a person, one must ask with indignation what those earlier poets deserved: if they followed no principle, why did they make the combination of feet that they chose to join together be called and accepted as a verse?

Does it seem otherwise to you?

D. It is exactly as you say, and I entirely agree that a verse is generated by reason rather than authority. I ask that we now examine this without delay.

## CHAPTER VIII — Various names of feet

15. M. Let us therefore see which feet should be joined to one another, then what results from their being joined—for it is not verse alone—and finally we shall discuss the entire theory of verse.

But do you think we can conveniently pursue these matters unless we retain the names of the feet? They have indeed been arranged by us in such an order that they can be called by the names of their order itself: first, second, third, and so forth. But since ancient terms should not be despised, and one should not easily depart from customary usage unless it conflicts with reason, we must use the names of feet established by the Greeks and now employed by our writers in place of Latin names. We should use these names without investigating their origins. That subject has much verbosity and little usefulness. You do not speak less usefully when you call something bread, wood, or stone merely because you do not know why these things have those names.

D. I feel exactly as you say.

M. The first foot is called the Pyrrhichius, consisting of two short syllables and two times, as *fuga* (“flight”).

The second is the Iambus, consisting of a short and a long syllable, as *parens* (“parent”), and containing three times.

The third is the Trochaeus, or Chorius, consisting of a long and a short syllable, as *meta* (“goal”), and containing three times.

The fourth is the Spondeus, consisting of two long syllables, as *aestas* (“summer”), and containing four times.

The fifth is the Tribrachus, consisting of three short syllables, as *macula* (“spot”), and containing three times.

The sixth is the Dactylus, consisting of a long syllable and two short syllables, as *Maenalus* (“Maenalus”), and containing four times.

The seventh is the Amphibrachus, consisting of a short, a long, and a short syllable, as *carina* (“keel”), and containing four times.

The eighth is the Anapaestus, consisting of two short syllables and a long syllable, as *Erato* (“Erato”), and containing four times.

The ninth is the Bacchius, consisting of a short syllable and two long syllables, as *Achates* (“Achates”), and containing five times.

The tenth is the Creticus, or Amphimacrus, consisting of a long, a short, and a long syllable, as *insulae* (“islands”), and containing five times.

The eleventh is the Palimbacchius, consisting of two long syllables and a short syllable, as *natura* (“nature”), and containing five times.

The twelfth is the Molossus, consisting of three long syllables, as *Aeneas* (“Aeneas”), and containing six times.

The thirteenth is the Proceleumaticus, consisting of four short syllables, as *avicula* (“little bird”), and containing four times.

The fourteenth is the first Paeon, consisting of a first long syllable and three short syllables, as *legitimus* (“legitimate”), and containing five times.

The fifteenth is the second Paeon, consisting of a second long syllable and three short syllables, as *colonia* (“colony”), and containing five times.

The sixteenth is the third Paeon, consisting of a third long syllable and three short syllables, as *Menedemus* (“Menedemus”), and containing five times.

The seventeenth is the fourth Paeon, consisting of a fourth long syllable and three short syllables, as *celeritas* (“swiftness”), and containing five times [Col. 1109].

The eighteenth is the Ionicus a minore, consisting of two short and two long syllables, as *Diomedes* (“Diomedes”), and containing six times.

The nineteenth is the Choriambus, consisting of a long syllable, two short syllables, and a long syllable, as *armipotens* (“mighty in arms”), and containing six times.

The twentieth is the Ionicus a maiore, consisting of two long and two short syllables, as *Junonius* (“of Juno”), and containing six times.

The twenty-first is the Diiambus, consisting of a short and a long, and a short and a long syllable, as *propinquitas* (“nearness”), and containing six times.

The twenty-second is the Dichorius, or Ditrochaeus, consisting of a long and a short, and a long and a short syllable, as *cantilena* (“song”), and containing six times.

The twenty-third is the Antispastus, consisting of a short syllable, two long syllables, and a short syllable, as *Saloninus* (“Saloninus”), and containing six times.

The twenty-fourth is the first Epitritus, consisting of a first short syllable and three long syllables, as *sacerdotes* (“priests”), and containing seven times.

The twenty-fifth is the second Epitritus, consisting of a second short syllable and three long syllables, as *conditores* (“founders”), and containing seven times.

The twenty-sixth is the third Epitritus, consisting of a third short syllable and three long syllables, as *Demosthenes* (“Demosthenes”), and containing seven times.

The twenty-seventh is the fourth Epitritus, consisting of a fourth short syllable and three long syllables, as *Fescenninus* (“Fescennine”), and containing seven times.

The twenty-eighth is the Dispondeus, consisting of four long syllables, as *oratores* (“orators”), and containing eight times [Note: [Col. 1109] The old books, without explanation or any example, list the feet as follows: “The first foot is called the Pyrrhichius, the second the Iambus, the third,” and so on; and they consistently give *spondius*, *dispondius*, and *paean* instead of *spondeus*, *dispondeus*, and *paeon*. In some places they likewise have *tribrachys* and *amphibrachys* instead of *tribrachus* and *amphibrachus*.].

## CHAPTER IX — The structure of feet

16. D. I have these. Now explain which feet are joined to one another.

M. You will judge this easily if you consider equality and likeness superior to inequality and unlikeness.

D. I think no one would judge otherwise.

M. This equality must therefore be followed above all in joining feet together, and one must not depart from it at all except for some thoroughly justifiable reason.

D. I agree.

M. You will therefore have no doubt about joining Pyrrhichii to one another, or Iambi, or Trochae i—which are also called Chorii—or Spondees. In the same way, you will certainly join the remaining feet of the same kind to one another without hesitation. For there is complete equality when feet of the same kind and name follow one another. Does this not seem so to you?

D. It cannot seem otherwise to me.

M. What of this? Do you not approve of mixing different feet while preserving equality? For what could be more pleasing to the ears than when they are delighted both by variety and are not deprived of equality?

D. I approve it sufficiently.

M. Do you think feet should be regarded as equal except those of the same measure?

D. That is my view.

M. What, then? Should feet be considered of the same measure except those that occupy the same amount of time?

D. True.

M. Therefore, whenever you find feet containing the same number of times, you will join them together without offending the ears.

D. I see that this follows.

## CHAPTER X — The Amphibrachus forms no verse either by itself or mixed with others; on arsis and thesis

[Col. 1110]

17. M. Quite rightly. But the matter still contains a little difficulty. Since the Amphibrachus is a foot of four times, some deny that it can be mixed with Dactyls, Anapaests, Spondees, or Proceleumatics, for all these are feet of four times. They deny not only that it can be mixed with these, but also that a rhythmic sequence can proceed properly and, as it were, legitimately from the Amphibrachus alone, repeated and joined to itself.

We must consider their opinion, lest it contain some principle that we ought to follow and approve.

D. I greatly desire and eagerly await hearing what they have to offer. I am not slightly troubled that, although there are twenty-eight feet pursued by reason, this one alone should be excluded from a continuation of the numbers, even though it occupies in time as much space as the Dactyl and the other feet that you counted as equal, which no one forbids us to join together.

M. To discern this, however, you must consider the other feet and how their parts are compared with one another. Then you will see that something new and singular happens in this one foot, so that it was not without reason judged entirely unsuitable for rhythmic sequences.

18. As we consider this, we must commit two terms to memory: arsis and thesis, or lifting and placing. For in clapping, since the hand is lifted and placed, the arsis claims one part of the foot and the thesis another. By the parts of the feet I mean those about which enough was said above when we pursued them in order.

If you approve this, begin by briefly reviewing the measures of the parts in all the feet, so that you may know what distinctive feature has occurred in this one under discussion.

D. I see that the Pyrrhichius has as much in its arsis as in its thesis. The Spondeus, Dactylus, Anapaestus, Proceleumaticus, Choriambus, Diiambus, Dichorius, Antispastus, and Dispondeus are divided in the same way, for in them the clap places as much time as it lifts.

I see that the Iambus has the relation of one-to-two. I recognize this same relation in the Chorius, the Tribrachus, the Molossus, and both Ionici.

Now the arsis and thesis of this Amphibrachus—which has come before me in order, and for which I shall seek corresponding feet—consist in the relation of one-to-three. But I find no other foot afterward whose parts are related to one another by so great an interval.

When I consider those in which there is one short syllable and two long syllables—that is, the Bacchius, Creticus, and Palimbacchius—I see that their arsis and thesis are arranged according to the relation of sesquialter numbers. The same relation holds in the four feet in which there is one long syllable and three short syllables, which are called, in order, the four Paeones.

There remain the four Epitriti, likewise called in order, whose arsis and thesis are governed by the sesquitertian relation.

19. M. Does it therefore seem to you an insufficiently just reason why this foot [Note: [Col. 1110] Amphibrachus.] should not be admitted into the rhythmic sequence of sounds—that its parts alone are so far apart that one is onefold and the other threefold? The closer the parts are to equality, the more worthy of approval is their proximity [Col. 1111].

Thus, in that rule of numbers [Note: [Col. 1111] In B. the little word *in* is absent; we have restored it from Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions, and manuscripts A and B. It should be noted that, where the Benedictines have *illa*, the printed editions have *ista*. M.], when we progress from one up to four, nothing is closer to each number than the number immediately adjoining it.

Accordingly, the first thing to be approved in feet is that their parts have equal duration; next comes the joining of onefold and twofold, as in one and two; then the sesquialter joining appears in two and three; and finally the sesquitertian in three and four.

Although onefold and threefold are governed by the law of compound numbers, they are not adjacent to one another in that order. We do not count three immediately after one; rather, we reach three from one with two intervening.

This is the reason why the Amphibrachus is judged to be excluded from the joining about which we are inquiring [Note: [Col. 1111] B. has *quaesivimus* (“we inquired”); Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions, as well as manuscript A, have *quaerimus* (“we are inquiring”). M.]. If you approve this, let us examine the rest.

D. I certainly approve it, for it is exceedingly clear and certain.

## CHAPTER XI — The rational mixture of feet
20. M. Since it is agreed that, however their syllables may be arranged, feet can nevertheless be properly mixed without impairing equality if they occupy the same span of time—except only the amphibrach—one may reasonably ask whether those feet are properly mixed which, although equal in time, do not harmonize in their beat, by which the parts of a foot are joined to one another through raising and lowering. For the dactyl, anapaest, and spondee are not only equal in time but are also beaten equally: in each of them the raising claims as much as the lowering. Thus they are more properly mixed with one another than any ionic foot is with the other six-time feet. For each ionic is beaten in the relation of one to two, contributing two times to four times. The molossus agrees with them in this respect as well. The others—[Col. 1111] choriambus, diiambus, dichorius, and antispastus—are beaten in equal portions, for in them three times are assigned to the raising and three to the lowering. Therefore, although all are beaten according to legitimate principles—for the former three are beaten according to the relation of one to two, and the other four in equal parts—nevertheless, since this mixture produces an unequal beat, I do not know whether it ought rightly to be rejected, unless you have something to say in reply.

D. I am inclined toward that opinion. For I do not see how an unequal beat could fail to offend the ear; and if it offends, this can surely happen only through some defect in the mixture.

21. M. Yet you should know that the ancients judged these feet fit to be mixed and composed verses from their mixture. But so that I may not seem to press you with authority, take some of these verses and see whether they offend the ear. For if they not only do not offend but even give pleasure, there will be no reason for rejecting this mixture. The verses are these, and I want you to attend to them:

> But the consonants, unless you fit them to vowels,  
> will utter from themselves only half the work of the voice;  
> the mute part of the sound will restrain the mouths of those striving to speak;  
> for them the sound is more obscure and more obstructed,  
> yet both are uttered with the mouth half closed. (Terentianus.)  
> [Col. 1112]

I think this is enough to judge the matter I wish to have judged. So tell me, please, whether this rhythm has given your ears no pleasure.

D. On the contrary, nothing seems to run and sound more agreeably.

M. Consider the feet, then. You will certainly find that, although there are five verses, the first two proceed solely in ionic feet, while the remaining three have a dichorius mixed into them, even though all of them alike delight our sense through their common equality.

D. I have noticed that already, and more easily because you recited them.

M. Why, then, do we hesitate to agree with the ancients—not defeated by their authority, but now overcome by reason itself—who hold that feet of the same duration may rationally be mixed if they have a legitimate, though different, beat?

D. I yield completely now; that sound does not allow me to contradict anything.

## CHAPTER XII — Six-Time Feet

22. M. Attend likewise to these verses:

> I want you at last to spare yourself; the work is in the pages,  
> and to allow your open spirit to move through the breezes.  
> This is pleasing, for it is wise sometimes to relax  
> the attention suitably directed toward matters requiring action.

D. This too is sufficiently clear.

M. Especially since these verses are artless compositions, which I fashioned under the pressure of the moment. Nevertheless, in all four of them I ask for the judgment of your ear.

D. What else can I say here but that they sounded beautifully and harmoniously?

M. Do you also perceive that the two earlier verses are composed of the ionic called “minor,” while the two later ones have a diiambus mixed into them?

D. I perceived this too when you indicated it by your recitation.

M. What? Does it not strike you that in those verses of Terentianus the dichorius is mixed with the ionic called “major,” whereas in these verses of ours the diiambus is mixed with the other ionic, which is called “minor”? Or do you think there is no difference?

D. There is a difference, and I think I can see the reason itself. Since the major ionic begins with two long syllables, it demands that the foot joined to it should likewise begin with a long syllable—that is, the dichorius. The diiambus, however, because it begins with a short syllable, is more suitably mixed with the other ionic, which begins with two short syllables.

23. M. You understand correctly. Therefore this point too must be retained: apart from equality of duration, such congruence ought to have some force in the mixing of feet. It does not have the greatest force, but it has some. For you may judge, by questioning your sense, that every six-time foot can be substituted for every other six-time foot. Let these be our examples: the molossus, *virtutes*; the minor ionic, *moderatas*; the choriambus, *percipies*; the major ionic, *concedere*; the diiambus, *benignitas*; the dichorius, *civitasque*; the antispastus, *volet justa*.

D. I have them.

M. Now connect them all and recite them—or rather, listen while I recite them, so that your sense may remain freer for judgment. To impress upon you the equality of continuous rhythm without any offense to the ears, I shall recite this entire sequence three times, which I am sure will be enough:

> Virtutes moderatas percipies, concedere benignitas civitasque volet justa.  
> Virtutes moderatas percipies, concedere benignitas civitasque volet justa.  
> Virtutes moderatas percipies, concedere benignitas civitasque volet justa.

Has anything in this progression of feet deprived your ears of equality or sweetness?

D. In no way.

M. Has anything given you pleasure? Although in this kind of case it necessarily follows that everything which does not offend should give pleasure.

D. I cannot describe my response otherwise than as you have suggested.

M. You therefore approve that all these six-time feet can properly be joined and [Col. 1113] mixed with one another. [Editorial note: B reads “or”; more correctly, with Erfurt, Lyons, Venice, Louvain, and MSS. A, “and.” M.]

D. I approve.

## CHAPTER XIII — How the Order of the Feet Can Be Changed Harmoniously

[Col. 1113]

24. M. Do you fear that someone might think these feet could sound so equally when arranged in this order, but could not do so if their order were changed?

D. It does contribute something, but it is not difficult to test.

M. Do this, then, when you have the opportunity. You will find nothing other than that your sense is soothed by manifold variety and a single equality.

D. I shall do so, although anyone can foresee from this example that the result must necessarily be as you say.

M. You are right. But for the matter at hand, I shall go through these with a beat, so that you may judge whether anything or nothing limps in them. At the same time, you can test the change of order which, as I predicted, will introduce no limping. Change the order now itself, and, as you wish, allow me to sound and beat the same feet arranged differently from the way I arranged them.

D. Let the first be the minor ionic, the second the major ionic, the third the choriambus, the fourth the diiambus, the fifth the antispastus, the sixth the dichorius, and the seventh the molossus.

M. Attend, then, both your ear to the sound and your eyes to the beat. For the beating hand must not merely be heard but seen, and you must observe carefully how long the raising lasts and how long the lowering lasts.

D. I am attending with all my ability.

M. Then receive your arrangement with its beat:

> Moderatas, concedere, percipies, benignitas, volet justa, civitasque, virtutes.

D. I certainly feel that this beat does not limp at all, and that it raises for as long as it lowers. But I am greatly astonished at how those feet could be beaten in this way whose division is governed by the relation of one to two, as are both ionics and the molossus.

M. What else do you think is happening here, since three times are raised and the same number lowered?

D. I see nothing else happening here than that the long syllable which is second in the major ionic and in the molossus, but third in the minor ionic, is divided by the beat itself. Since it has two times, one is assigned to the earlier part and the other to the later part; thus the raising and lowering each receive three times.

25. M. Nothing else at all can be said or understood here. But why should the amphibrach, which we were completely excluding from this numerical arrangement, not also be mixed under this condition with the spondee, dactyl, and anapaest—or even, by being continued on its own, produce something rhythmical in music? [Editorial note: Thus the manuscripts; but Louvain and the other editions read “something rhythmical.”] For by a similar process the middle syllable of that foot, which is long, can also be divided by the beat. If one time is assigned to each side, the raising and lowering will no longer claim one and three times but two each, unless you have something to oppose this.

D. I have nothing to say except that this foot too must be admitted.

M. Let us therefore beat something arranged and connected in four-time feet, with this foot mixed into it, and test by the same method whether anything unequal gives offense. For ease of judgment, attend to this rhythm, repeated three times with its beat:

> Sumas optima, facias honesta.  
> Sumas optima, facias honesta.  
> Sumas optima, facias honesta.

D. Please, spare my ears now! Even without the beat being applied, the progression of these feet itself limps most violently at the amphibrach.

M. What, then, should we think is the reason that what was possible in the molossus and the ionics cannot happen here? Is it because in those feet the sides on either side of the middle are equal? For in an even number, where the middle is equal to its sides, the first example is the number six. Thus those six-time feet, since they contain two times in the middle and two on either side, allow the middle to fall, as it were, willingly onto the sides, with which it is joined by the most harmonious equality. But the same does not happen in the amphibrach, where the sides of the middle are unequal, since they contain one time each, while the middle contains two.

To this is added the fact that when, in the ionics and the molossus, the middle is released into the sides, three-time units result; and in these, in turn, equal sides are found on either side of an equal middle. [Editorial note: The earlier editions omit *pari* (“equal”); it is restored from the manuscripts. The manuscripts also support below “whereas these too give pleasure,” where the editions read “whereas this too gives pleasure.”] This too is lacking in the amphibrach.

D. The matter is as you say: and it is not without reason that the amphibrach offends the ear in that series, whereas these other feet give pleasure.

## CHAPTER XIV — Which Feet May Be Mixed with Which

[Col. 1114]

26. M. Come, now begin yourself with the pyrrhichius, and, according to the principles stated above, explain as briefly as you can which feet ought to be mixed with which.

D. No foot can be mixed with the pyrrhichius, since no other foot is found with the same number of times.

The chorius could be joined to the iambus; but this must be avoided because of the unequal beat, since one begins with the ratio of one to two and the other with that of two to one. The tribrach, therefore, can be fitted to both.

I see the spondee, dactyl, anapaest, and proceleumaticus as mutually compatible and joinable, since they agree with one another not only in duration but also in beat.

The excluded amphibrach, however, could not be brought back by any reasoning: equality of duration could not help it when its division and beat disagree.

The cretic can be joined with the bacchius and with the first, second, and fourth paeons. The same cretic, together with the first, third, and fourth paeons, plainly agrees with the palimbacchius both in duration and in beat. [Editorial note: B reads “in durations”; more correctly, with both manuscripts, “and.” M.] Therefore all the remaining five-time feet can be joined without any limping to the cretic and to the first and fourth paeons, since their division can begin either with two or with three times.

As for all the feet composed of six times, we have discussed sufficiently their remarkable harmony with one another. For they too do not differ in beating from those whose syllabic structure forces them to be divided differently: such power belongs to equality between the middle and the sides.

Furthermore, since there are four seven-time feet, called epitriti, I find that the first and second can be joined to one another. For the division of both begins with three times, and therefore they differ neither in duration nor in beat. Again, the third and fourth readily join one another, because the division of each begins with four times; thus they are measured and beaten equally.

[Col. 1116]

The remaining foot is the eight-time foot called the dispondeus, for which, as with the pyrrhichius, no equal partner exists. You have from me what you asked for and what I was able to do. Proceed to what remains.

M. I shall—but after so long a discussion, let us breathe a little and recall those verses which weariness itself suggested to me extemporaneously a little earlier:

> I want you at last to spare yourself; the work is in the pages,  
> and to allow your open spirit to move through the breezes.  
> This is pleasing, for it is wise sometimes to relax  
> the attention suitably directed toward matters requiring action.

D. It certainly pleases me, and I gladly comply.

# BOOK THREE

In this book the difference between rhythm, meter, and verse is explained; rhythm is then treated separately, and afterward the discussion of meter is begun.

[Col. 1115]

## CHAPTER I — What Rhythm and Meter Are

[Col. 1115]

1. M. Since enough has been said in this third discussion about a certain friendship and harmony among feet, we must now see what is produced from these feet when they are connected and continued. So I first ask you whether joined feet—feet which ought to be joined—can create a continuous numerical sequence in which no definite end appears. This is the case, for example, when musical performers strike footboards and cymbals with their feet, in definite numbers which are joined to one another with pleasure for the ears, yet with a continuous progression, so that if you did not hear the pipes, you could in no way determine how far the connection of the feet extends or where it returns again to its beginning.

It would be like your wishing to let one hundred or more pyrrhichii, or other feet that are mutually compatible, proceed in continuous connection for as long as you pleased.

D. I understand now, and I concede that a certain connection of feet can be made in which it is fixed how many feet one should advance before turning back.

M. Do you doubt that this is of that kind, since you do not deny that there is a definite discipline for making verses, and since you have confessed that you have always listened to verse with pleasure? [Editorial note: Louvain reads, “Do you doubt that it is certain?” The manuscripts read, “Do you doubt that it is of this kind?”; the Amsterdam and Erfurt editions add, “and do you grant that this differs from the former kind?” Manuscript A simply reads, “Do you doubt that it is?” M.]

D. It is clear both that this is so and that it differs from the earlier kind.

2. M. Therefore, since things which are distinct in reality must also be distinguished by their names, you should know that the earlier kind of connection is called *rhythm* by the Greeks, while the other is called *meter*. In Latin they might be called, respectively, *numerus* and *mensio* or *mensura*. But since these names have a broad range among us, and we must avoid speaking ambiguously, it is more convenient to use the Greek terms.

Yet I think you see how appropriately both names have been assigned to these things. Since the first proceeds through definite feet, and an error is made in it if discordant feet are mixed, it has rightly been called *rhythmus*, that is, “number.” But because this progression has no limit and no fixed point at which an end appears, it ought not to be called *meter*, since its continuation has no measure.

The other [Col. 1116] possesses both characteristics: it proceeds through definite feet [Editorial note: B reads “is proceeded through”; the Vatican manuscript and manuscript A read “proceeds.” M.] and ends in a definite manner. Thus it is not only meter, because of its conspicuous ending, but also rhythm, because of the rational connection of its feet. Therefore every meter is rhythm, but not every rhythm is also meter.

The name “rhythm” extends so broadly in music that the entire part of music concerned with duration and non-duration has been called rhythm. But learned and wise people have agreed that, when the matter is clear, one need not be anxious about the name.

Do you think anything I have said here should be contradicted or doubted?

D. On the contrary, I entirely agree.

## CHAPTER II — The Difference between Verse and Meter

3. M. Now consider with me whether, just as every verse is meter, every meter is also verse.

D. I am considering it, but I do not know what answer to give.

M. Why do you think this has happened to you? Is it because the question concerns words? For we cannot answer questions about names in the same way as questions about matters belonging to a discipline. Matters are commonly implanted in the minds of all, whereas names are assigned according to each person’s preference, and their force rests chiefly upon authority and custom. This is why languages can differ, while things established in truth itself obviously cannot.

So accept from me what you yourself could not possibly answer: the ancients called not verse alone but also meter by the name “verse.” As far as you are concerned, then, observe and answer this: the question is no longer about names, but whether there is some difference between two kinds of numerical sequence. In one, a definite number of feet is closed by a fixed ending, without its matter being affected by whether a certain articulation occurs before the end; in the other, it is not only closed by a definite ending, but also has before the end [Editorial note: These words, “before the end,” have here been restored from the manuscripts; they are absent from the editions hitherto printed. They are not absent in the Vatican edition. M.] a certain definite point at which a division appears, so that it is constructed, as it were, from two members.

D. I do not understand.

M. Then attend to these examples:

> Go now, Muses,  
> girls of the little spring,  
> who sing beneath the caves  
> honey-sweet sounds,  
> who wash your hair  
> [Col. 1117] in the purple Hippocrene spring,  
> where once the nourishing Pegasus  
> washed his foaming  
> mouth with watery mane,  
> as he flew through the shining  
> ether, about to fly through the shining sky.

You clearly see that the five verses at the beginning have a completed part of the sentence at the same point, namely in the choriambic foot, which is followed by a bacchius to complete the verse—for these eleven verses are composed of choriambic and bacchiac feet. The remaining verses, except one—namely, “mouth with watery mane”—do not have a completed part of the sentence at the same point.

D. I see that, but I do not see what it concerns.

M. It concerns your understanding that this meter does not have, as a regular feature, a point at which a part of the sentence ends before the end of the verse. For if that were the case, all of these verses would have this articulation at the same point, or at least it would occur only rarely that one lacked it. But now, since there are eleven, six have it in this way and five do not.

D. I understand that too, and I am still waiting to see where the reasoning leads.

M. Then attend also to this very well-known passage:

> Arms and the man I sing, who first from the shores of Troy …

And, not to make this lengthy, since the poem is so familiar, examine each verse from this one onward as far as you wish. You will find a completed part of the sentence in the fifth half-foot—that is, in two and a half feet. For these verses consist of four-time feet; therefore the ending of the part of the sentence in question is, as it were, regular at the tenth time.

D. That is clear.

4. M. You now understand, then, that there is some difference between the two kinds I proposed before these examples. One kind of meter, as we observed in those eleven little verses, has no definite and established articulation before it is closed; the other does, as the fifth half-foot in heroic meter sufficiently indicates.

D. What you say is now clear.

M. You should know, however, that the learned ancients, whose authority is great, did not call the first kind “verse.” Rather, the kind now defined and called “verse” is that which consists of two members, as it were, joined by a definite measure and rational structure.

But do not trouble yourself greatly over the name. Unless I, or someone else, had informed you of it, you could in no way have answered a question about it. Instead, direct your attention chiefly and above all to what reason teaches, as in the very matter we are now discussing. Reason teaches that there is some difference between these two kinds, whatever names they may be given. Thus, if properly questioned, you could answer this by relying on truth itself; but you could not answer the other unless you followed authority.

D. I now understand these matters most clearly, and I appreciate the importance of what you have so often urged upon me.

M. I would therefore like you to commit these three names to memory, which we shall necessarily use in our discussion: rhythm, meter, and verse. They are distinguished as follows: every meter is also rhythm, but not every rhythm is also meter. Likewise, every verse is also meter, but not every meter is also verse. Therefore every verse is both rhythm and meter; for I think you see that this follows.

D. I certainly see it, for it is clearer than daylight.

## CHAPTER III — Rhythms Made from Pyrrhichii

[Col. 1118]

5. M. Let us discuss first, if you agree, rhythm in which there is no meter; then meter in which there is no verse; and finally verse itself, as far as we can.

D. I agree.

M. Take pyrrhichii from the very beginning and construct a rhythm from them.

D. Even if I could do that, what would its extent be?

M. It is enough for you to extend it—for we are doing this by way of example—to ten feet. For a verse does not proceed beyond this number of feet, as will be carefully discussed in its proper place.

D. It is kind of you not to propose many feet for me to join. But you seem not to remember that you have already sufficiently distinguished the grammarian from the musician, when I told you that I do not possess the knowledge of long and short syllables taught by grammarians. Unless perhaps you permit me to exhibit this rhythm not in words but by some kind of beat. I do not deny that I can judge the temporal intervals and regulate their duration; but which syllable ought to be lengthened or shortened, since that depends upon authority, I do not know at all.

M. I admit that we distinguished the grammarian from the musician as you say, and that in this field you confessed your ignorance. So accept from me the following example:

> Ago celeriter agile quod ago tibi quod anima velit.

D. I have it.

6. M. By repeating this as often as you wish, you will produce a rhythm of whatever length you desire, although these ten feet are sufficient for an example. But I ask you this: if someone were to tell you that this rhythm consists not of pyrrhichii but of proceleumatic feet, what would you answer?

D. I simply do not know. Where there are ten pyrrhichii, I measure five proceleumatics; and my uncertainty is increased because we are being asked about rhythm, which flows continuously. For eleven pyrrhichii, or thirteen, or any odd number, cannot contain an integral number of proceleumatics. If there were a definite ending in the rhythm under discussion, we could at least say that it proceeds by pyrrhichii rather than by proceleumatics at the point where complete proceleumatics were not found. But now its very infinity confuses our judgment; and the same is true whenever counted feet are presented to us in an even number, as these ten are.

M. Yet even your conclusion about an odd number of pyrrhichii is not as certain as it seemed. For what if, when eleven pyrrhichii are proposed, someone says that the rhythm contains five proceleumatics and a half-foot? Can this be resisted, when we find many verses ending in a half-foot?

D. I have already said that I do not know what can be said about this matter.

M. Do you also not know that the pyrrhichius is prior to the proceleumaticus? A proceleumaticus is formed from two pyrrhichii. Just as one is prior to two, and two to four, so the pyrrhichius is prior to the proceleumaticus.

D. That is entirely true.

M. Since, then, we have fallen into an ambiguity in which both the pyrrhichius and the proceleumaticus can be measured in the rhythm, to which shall we give precedence: the earlier, from which the latter is composed, or the later, from which the former is not composed?

D. No one will doubt that precedence must be given to the earlier.

M. Why, then, when asked about this matter, do you hesitate to answer that this rhythm ought to be called pyrrhichiac rather than proceleumatic?

D. I do not hesitate at all now. I am ashamed that I did not quickly notice such an evident argument.

## CHAPTER IV — Continuous Rhythm

[Col. 1119]

7. M. Do you see that this reasoning also forces us to conclude that there are certain feet which cannot continue a rhythm? What has been discovered concerning the proceleumaticus—that the pyrrhichius deprives it of precedence—I think must also be discovered concerning the diiambus, dichorius, and dispondeus, unless you think otherwise.

D. How could I think otherwise, when, once that reasoning has been established, I cannot reject what follows from it?

M. Examine this too, compare it, and judge. When such an uncertainty arises, it seems that the foot in which the rhythm proceeds ought rather to be distinguished by the beat. [Editorial note: Manuscript A reads “determined.” M.] Thus, if you wish to proceed in pyrrhichii, one time must be raised and one lowered; if in proceleumatics, two and two. In this way the foot will appear, and no foot will be excluded from the continuation of the rhythm.

D. I favor more strongly the opinion which allows no foot to be excluded from this connection.

M. You are right. To make you approve this more fully, consider what answer we could give if someone nevertheless insisted that this rhythm proceeds not by pyrrhichii or proceleumatics but by tribrachs.

D. I see that the judgment must be referred to the beat: if one time is in the raising and two in the lowering—that is, one syllable and two—or conversely, two in the raising and one in the lowering, the rhythm should be called tribrachic.

8. M. You understand correctly. Now tell me whether the spondee can be joined to a pyrrhichiac rhythm.

D. In no way. The equal beat would not continue, since the pyrrhichius contains one time in the raising and one in the lowering, whereas the spondee contains two in each.

M. Then it can be joined to a proceleumaticus.

D. It can.

M. When it is joined to it, and we are asked whether the rhythm is proceleumatic or spondaic, what shall we answer?

D. What do you think, unless precedence must be given to the spondee? Since this dispute is not settled by the beat—for in both we raise and lower two times—what remains except that the foot which is earlier in the order of the feet should rule?

M. I approve that you have followed reason, and I think you see what follows.

D. What, finally?

M. What else could it be but that no other foot can be mixed with the proceleumatic rhythm? Since whichever foot is mixed with it must have the same number of times—for otherwise it cannot be mixed—the name of the rhythm must be transferred to that foot. For all the feet having the same number of times are prior to it. And since reason forces us to give precedence to those discovered earlier, as you have seen—that is, to name the rhythm after them—the rhythm will no longer be proceleumatic when another four-time foot is mixed into it, but spondaic, dactylic, or anapaestic. It is agreed that the amphibrach is rightly excluded from the joining of these numerical patterns. [Editorial note: B reads, “What do you think, unless both the proceleumatic and the pyrrhichian are excluded from rhythm?”—plainly corrupt. Since the pyrrhichius precedes all other feet, the rationale Augustine gives below would fit it badly, but fits the proceleumaticus most suitably. M.]

D. I admit that this is so.

9. M. Now consider in order the iambic rhythm, since we have sufficiently discussed the pyrrhichius and the proceleumaticus, which is generated by doubling the pyrrhichius. Tell me which foot you think should be mixed with this rhythm so that it retains the name “iambic.”

D. Which foot except the tribrach? It agrees with it both in duration and in beat; and because it is later, it cannot claim the sovereignty. The chorius is indeed later and has the same duration, but it is not beaten in the same way.

M. Come, now consider the trochaic rhythm and answer the same question about it.

D. I give the same answer, since the tribrach can harmonize with it not only in duration but also in beat. Who does not see that the iambus must be avoided? Even if it were beaten equally, once mixed in it would still take away the precedence.

M. What foot shall we join to the spondaic rhythm?

D. Here there is a very wide choice. I see that the dactyl, anapaest, and proceleumaticus can all be mixed with it, since nothing prevents them: there is no inequality of duration, no limping of the beat, and no deprivation of precedence.

10. M. I see that you can now easily follow the remaining cases in order. Therefore, without my questioning you further—or rather, as though you had been asked about all of them—answer briefly and clearly, as far as you can, how each of the remaining feet, when mixed legitimately with others, retains its own name in the rhythm.

D. I shall do so, since no difficulty remains after so much light has been shed by the reasoning.

Nothing can be mixed with the tribrach, since all the feet equal to it in duration are prior to it.

The anapaest can be mixed with the dactyl, since it is later and proceeds equally in duration and in beat. The proceleumaticus can likewise be joined to both, for the same reason.

The cretic can be mixed with the bacchius and with the first, second, and fourth paeons.

All the five-time feet that follow the cretic can rightly be mixed with it, though not all with the same division. Some are divided into two and three times, others into three and two. The cretic, however, can be divided in either way, because its middle short syllable can be assigned to either part.

The palimbacchius, since its division begins with two times and ends with three, has as compatible and joinable partners all the paeons except the second.

Among the trisyllabic feet, the molossus remains. From it begin the six-time feet, all of which can be joined to it, partly because of the relation of one to two, and partly because of that division which the beat showed us: the division of the long syllable, which grants one time to each side because, in the number six, the middle is equal to its sides.

For this reason the molossus and both ionics are beaten not only according to the relation of one to two but also in equal parts of three times each.

It follows that from this point onward all the later six-time feet can be joined to every six-time foot; only the antispastus remains, which wishes no foot to be mixed with it.

These are followed by the four epitriti. The first admits the second; the second admits none; the third admits the fourth; and the fourth admits none.

The dispondeus remains, and it alone can also produce a rhythm, since it has neither a later foot nor an equal one.

Thus there are eight feet which produce a rhythm when no other foot is mixed with them: the pyrrhichius, tribrachus, proceleumaticus, fourth paeon, antispastus, second epitritus, fourth epitritus, and dispondeus. The remaining feet allow those which are later than themselves to be joined to them, so that they retain the name of rhythm even if fewer feet are counted in that sequence.

I think I have explained and arranged sufficiently what you asked. It is now your task to see what remains.

## CHAPTER V — Whether There Are Feet of More Than Four Syllables

[Col. 1121]

11. M. On the contrary, the question is yours as well as mine, for we are both asking it. [Editorial note: Erfurt, Lyons, and Venice read, “On the contrary, mine too, and yours”; manuscript A, “On the contrary, mine and yours too”; manuscript B, “On the contrary, mine is more than yours.” M.] But what do you think remains concerning rhythm? Must we not consider whether some measurement of a foot, although it does not exceed the eight times possessed by the dispondeus, nevertheless exceeds the number of four syllables?

D. Why, please?

M. No—why do you ask me rather than yourself? Does it not seem to you that, without any fraud or offense to the ears, whether we consider the beat and division of the feet or their duration [Editorial note: Here and shortly below, the manuscripts read “that.” M.], two short syllables can be substituted for one long syllable?

D. Who could deny it?

M. This is why we substitute the tribrach for the iambus or chorius, and the dactyl, anapaest, or proceleumaticus for the spondee: either two short syllables are substituted for its second long syllable, or for its first, or four for both.

D. I agree.

M. Do the same, then, with any ionic or any other four-syllable six-time foot, and substitute two short syllables for any one of its long syllables. [Editorial note: Erfurt, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read, “and that you substitute”; manuscripts A and B, “so that you substitute.” M.] Does anything disappear from the measure, or does this resist the beat?

D. Nothing at all.

M. Consider, then, how many syllables result.

D. I see that there are five.

M. You see, surely, that the number of four syllables can be exceeded.

D. I certainly see it.

M. What if, for the two long syllables found there, you substitute four short syllables? Must not six syllables necessarily be measured in a single foot? [Col. 1122]

D. That is so.

M. What if you resolve all the long syllables of any epitritus into short syllables? Can there then be any doubt that seven syllables result?

D. None at all.

M. And the dispondeus itself—does it not produce eight syllables when we place two short syllables in the place of each of its long syllables?

D. That is entirely true.

### 12.

**M.** What, then, is the principle by which we are compelled both to measure feet of so many syllables and, in accordance with the arguments treated earlier, to refrain from exceeding four syllables in the foot used for rhythm? Do these things not seem to you to conflict with one another?

**D.** Indeed they do, most seriously; and I do not know how this can be reconciled.

**M.** This too is easy, if you ask yourself again whether we agreed a little earlier, reasonably enough, that the pyrrhic and the proceleusmatic should be distinguished and differentiated by their beat, so that no foot of legitimate division might fail to produce rhythm—that is, so that rhythm might be named from it.

**D.** I remember this, and I do not see why I should regret having approved it. But where are you going with this?

**M.** Clearly because all these four-syllable feet, with the exception of the amphibrach, produce rhythm—that is, they hold the chief place in rhythm and produce it both in practice and by their name. Those, however, which have more than four syllables can often be substituted for these [Note: [Col. 1122] The Vatican manuscript: “Those, however, which have more than four syllables can be substituted for others, but they themselves …” M.]; but they cannot by themselves produce rhythm or acquire the name of rhythm. For that reason, I would not even think that these should be called feet.

Thus the contradiction that was troubling us has now, I think, been resolved and laid to rest, since it is permissible both to substitute more than four syllables for a given foot and yet not to call the substitute a foot unless it is one by which rhythm is produced.

A certain measure of progression in syllables had to be assigned to the foot. The best measure that could be established was the one transferred from the very principle of numbers and fixed at four. Thus a foot could consist of four long syllables. When, however, we substitute eight short syllables for it, since they occupy the same amount of time, they can be substituted for another foot. But because they exceed the legitimate progression—that is, the number four—they are forbidden by the rule of the discipline to stand in their own place and generate rhythm, even though the ear does not forbid this. Unless you are preparing some objection.

### 13.

**D.** I certainly am, and I shall make it now. What prevented the foot from progressing as far as eight syllables, when we see that this same number may be admitted into rhythm? I am not moved by your saying that it is admitted in place of another; indeed, this makes me ask—or rather complain—all the more why one that can stand in place of another is not also admitted under its own name.

**M.** It is not surprising that you are mistaken here; but the truth is easily explained. Let us set aside all that was argued earlier concerning the number four and why the progression of syllables should extend only that far. Suppose that I have now yielded to you and agreed that the length of a foot should extend to eight syllables. Will you be able to deny that there can now be a foot of eight long syllables? For whatever number of syllables a foot reaches, it reaches not only in feet composed of short syllables but also in those composed of long syllables. Consequently, if we again apply that rule which cannot be abolished—the rule that two short syllables may be substituted for one long—we proceed to sixteen syllables. If you then wish to establish another increase of the foot, we advance to thirty-two short syllables. Here too your reasoning compels you to bring the foot, and again that rule places twice as many short syllables in the position of the long ones. Thus no limit will be established.

**D.** I now yield to the principle by which we advance the foot only as far as the number four in syllables. I do not object, however, that feet with more syllables should be substituted for these legitimate feet, provided that two short syllables occupy the place of one long.

## CHAPTER VI

### Feet longer than four syllables cannot produce rhythm under their own name

### 14.

**M.** It is therefore easy for you also to see and acknowledge that some feet stand in the place of those in which the chief power of rhythm resides, while others are placed alongside them. When individual long syllables are doubled into short ones, we place one foot in the place of the foot that possesses the rhythmic authority—for example, a tribrach in place of an iamb or trochee, or a dactyl, an anapest, or a proceleusmatic in place of a spondee.

When this does not happen, however, whatever foot is mixed in with the lesser feet is placed not in their place but alongside them: an anapest with a dactyl, for example, or, with an ionic, either a diiamb or a dichoree; and similarly the others, each in its proper relation with the rest. Does this seem insufficiently clear or false to you?

**D.** I understand now.

**M.** Answer, then: can those that are substituted for other feet also produce rhythm by themselves?

**D.** They can.

**M.** All of them?

**D.** All.

**M.** Then a five-syllable foot can also produce rhythm under its own name, since it can be substituted for a bacchius, a cretic, or any paeon.

**D.** It certainly cannot. But I no longer call that a foot, if I remember correctly that the progression extends only as far as the number four.

[Note: [Col. 1123] So in Manuscripts A and B; but in B it reads: “but I remember well that this is no longer called a foot if its progression passes beyond the number four.” Erasmus, Lyon, Venice: “if the progression …” M.]

When I answered “all,” I was certainly answering that all feet can do this.

**M.** I commend your care and vigilance in retaining the name. But know that some have thought that feet of six syllables should also be called feet; beyond that, so far as I know, no one has approved the practice. Those who approved this denied that feet so long ought to be used by themselves to produce rhythm or meter. They therefore did not even assign names to them.

Accordingly, the truest measure of progression is the one that reaches four syllables. All feet which, when divided, cannot become two feet were capable, when joined, of forming a foot. Thus those who extended their progression as far as the sixth syllable ventured to transfer the name of foot to those exceeding the fourth syllable; but they did not allow them in any way to aspire to the chief place that belongs to rhythms and meters.

When short syllables are doubled in place of long ones, the progression reaches, as reason has already shown, even to the seventh and eighth syllables. No one, however, extended the foot to that number.

But since I see that we agree that any foot of more than four syllables, when we put two short syllables in place of one long, can be placed not alongside these legitimate feet but in their place, and cannot produce rhythm by itself, I think that we have now said enough about rhythm. Let us pass to meters, if you agree.

**D.** I certainly agree.

## CHAPTER VII

### Of what and how many feet a meter is constituted at minimum

### 15.

**M.** Tell me, then: do you think that meter is made by feet, or feet by meter?

**D.** I do not understand.

**M.** Do joined feet create a meter, or are feet created by joined meters?

**D.** I know what you mean now, and I think that meter is made by joined feet.

**M.** Why do you think that?

**D.** Because you said that this is the difference between rhythm and meter: in rhythm, the joining of feet has no definite end, whereas in meter it does. Thus this joining of feet belongs both to rhythm and to meter; but in rhythm it is unlimited, while in meter it is bounded.

**M.** Then one foot is not a meter.

**D.** Certainly not.

**M.** What about one foot and a half?

**D.** Not even that.

**M.** Why? Is it because meter is constituted by feet, and feet cannot properly be said to exist where there are fewer than two?

**D.** That is so.

**M.** Let us therefore examine those meters that I mentioned a little earlier and see of what feet they consist. You ought not yet to be inexperienced in recognizing this kind of thing. They are:

> Go, then, Muses,  
>   
> Girls of the spring,  
>   
> You who sing beneath the grottoes  
>   
> Honey-flowing sounds.

I think these are sufficient for our present purpose. Now scan them and report what feet they contain.

**D.** I cannot possibly do so. I think that the feet must be those which can be joined together legitimately, and I cannot escape from this difficulty. If I make the first a chorius, an iamb follows, equal to it in time but not beaten in the same way. If I make it a dactyl, no other foot follows that is at least equal to it in time. If I make it a choriamb, the same difficulty arises: what remains agrees with it neither in time nor in beat. Therefore either this is not a meter, or what we have discussed among ourselves concerning the joining of feet is false; for I cannot find anything else to say.

### 16.

**M.** That it is indeed a meter is proved both by the fact that it is more than a foot and has a definite ending, and by the judgment of the ears themselves.

[Note: [Col. 1124] “We are brought together,” according to Erasmus and Manuscripts A and B. M.]

For it would not sound with such pleasant equality, nor would it be beaten with such harmonious movement, if it did not contain numerical structure—which certainly cannot exist except in this part of music.

I am surprised that you think the agreements we reached were false. Nothing is more certain than numbers, nor anything more orderly than our recollection and arrangement of the feet. From the very principle of numbers, which cannot in any way deceive, everything that we observed to be effective both in soothing the ears and in holding the chief place in rhythm has been expressed.

Instead, consider what happens when I often repeat:

> You who sing beneath the grottoes,

and soothe your sense with this numerical structure. What difference is there between this and my adding a short syllable at the end and repeating it in the same way:

> You who sing beneath the grottoes, or?

**D.** Both flow pleasantly into my ears. Yet I am compelled to admit that the latter, to which you added a short syllable, occupies more space and time, since it has become longer.

**M.** What if I repeat the earlier line,

> You who sing beneath the grottoes,

in such a way that I keep silent after the end? Does the same pleasure reach you?

**D.** On the contrary, something lame offends me, unless perhaps you have prolonged that final syllable more than the others.

**M.** Then, whether it is the additional prolongation or the silence that follows, do you think that it occupies some amount of space in time?

**D.** How could it be otherwise?

## CHAPTER VIII

### How much silence should be employed in meters; what is called a meter

### 17.

**M.** You are right. But tell me also how much space you think it is.

**D.** It is altogether difficult to measure.

**M.** You speak truly. But does it not seem to you that the short syllable measures it—that syllable which, when we added it, caused the sense to desire neither a prolongation of the final long syllable beyond the usual amount nor any silence in the repetition of the meter?

**D.** I entirely agree. For when you pronounced and repeated the earlier line, I too repeated the latter line silently to myself along with you. I thus felt that the same amount of time confronted both of us, since my final short syllable corresponded to your silence.

**M.** You must therefore hold that these spaces of silence are definite in meters. Accordingly, when you find something lacking from a legitimate foot, you must consider whether it is compensated by a measured and counted silence.

[Note: [Col. 1125] According to the Vatican manuscript: “whether it is compensated in the measured and counted silence.” M.]

**D.** I understand that now. Continue with the rest.

### 18.

**M.** I see that we must now inquire into the measure of the silence itself. In this meter, where we find a bacchius after a choriamb, one time is lacking for it to be a six-time foot like the choriamb. The ears very easily perceived this and compelled us, in repeating the line, to insert a silence as long as the space occupied by a short syllable.

But if a spondee is placed after the choriamb, we must perform two times in silence as we return to the beginning, as in:

> You who sing of the spring.

[Note: [Col. 1125] “Times in silence,” according to the Vatican manuscript, with the preposition *cum* omitted. M.]

For I think you already perceive that we must be silent so that, when we return to the beginning, the beat does not limp.

To test the measure of this silence, add one long syllable, so that the line becomes:

> You who sing of the spring, you;

and repeat this with the beat. You will see that the beat occupies as much time as it occupied above, when there were two long syllables after the choriamb, whereas here there are three. It is therefore clear that a silence of two times is inserted there.

But if an iamb is placed after the choriamb, as in:

> You who sing of places,

we are compelled to be silent for three times. To test this, add either another iamb, or a chorius, or a tribrach, so that the lines are:

> You who sing of good places;

or:

> You who sing of places in the hills;

or:

> You who sing of places in the grove.

When these additions are made, a pleasant and even repetition proceeds without silence. Since, with the beat applied, each of these three additions is found to occupy as much space as the interval in which we were silent, it is evident that the silence there consists of three times.

A single long syllable may be placed after the choriamb, so that four times are silent. For the choriamb can also be divided in such a way that the rising and falling correspond to one and two in proportion. An example of this meter is:

> You who sing of things.

If you add to it either two long syllables, or one long and two short, or one short, one long, and one short, or two short and one long, or four short syllables, you will fill out a six-time foot, so that the line can be repeated without any silence being required. Such examples are:

> You who sing of beautiful things;  
>   
> You who sing of things in the good;  
>   
> You who sing of things good—or;  
>   
> You who sing of tender things;  
>   
> You who sing of things just now well.

Once these matters have been recognized and granted, I think it is now sufficiently clear to you that it is possible to be silent for no less than one time and that one ought not to be silent for more than four times. This is the same measured progression about which so much has already been said; and in all feet neither the rising nor the falling occupies more than four times.

### 19.

Thus, whenever something is sung or pronounced that has a definite ending, is longer than one foot, and, by its natural movement before any consideration of numbers, soothes the sense with a certain evenness, it is already a meter.

[Note: [Col. 1126] “Equality,” according to the Vatican manuscript and Manuscript A. M.]

Although it may contain less than two feet, nevertheless, because it exceeds one foot and compels silence—not without measure, but for as much as is sufficient to fill the times belonging to the other foot—the hearing takes it as equivalent to two feet.

[Note: [Col. 1126] “And,” according to the Vatican manuscript. M.]

[Note: [Col. 1126] “Accepted,” according to the same manuscript. M.]

It takes up the times of two feet until we return to the beginning, while a definite and measured interval of silence is counted along with the sound.

But now, please tell me whether, having understood what has been said, you agree.

**D.** I understand it and agree.

**M.** Do you agree because you trust me, or because you yourself perceive that it is true?

**D.** I myself certainly perceive it, although I recognize, when you state them, that they are true.

## CHAPTER IX

### The greatest number of times and feet of which a meter can consist

### 20.

**M.** Come, then. Since we have discovered where a meter begins, let us also discover how far it extends. A meter begins with two feet, whether they are filled by sound itself or by silence counted to fill what is lacking. You must therefore now turn your attention to that fourfold progression and report to me how many feet a meter ought to extend.

**D.** This is easy. Reason sufficiently shows that there should be eight feet.

**M.** What? Do you remember our saying that learned men call that a verse which consists of two members measured and joined according to a definite rule?

**D.** I remember well.

**M.** Since, then, we did not say that a verse consists of two feet but of two members, and since it is evident that a verse does not contain one foot but several, does not the thing itself indicate that a member is longer than a foot?

**D.** It does indeed.

**M.** But if the members of a verse are equal, could not the order be reversed, so that the first part might become the last and the last the first without distinction?

**D.** I understand.

**M.** Therefore, to prevent this and to make it sufficiently clear and distinct that the member with which a verse begins is different from the member with which it ends, we cannot refuse to admit that the members must be unequal.

[Note: [Col. 1126] Erasmus: “lest it happen.” Venice, Louvain, and Manuscript A: “that this may not happen.” Likewise Lyon, though *hoc* is enclosed in brackets. M.]

**D.** Not at all.

**M.** Let us therefore first consider this in the pyrrhic, if you agree. I think you now see that a member cannot contain fewer than three times, since it must be more than a foot.

**D.** I agree.

**M.** How many times, then, will the shortest verse contain?

**D.** I would say six, unless that reversal of order held me back. It will therefore contain seven, because a member cannot contain fewer than three; but it has not yet been forbidden to contain more.

**M.** You understand correctly. But tell me how many pyrrhic feet seven times contain.

**D.** Three and a half.

**M.** Then a silence of one time is owed while we return to the beginning, so that the space of the foot may be filled.

**D.** It certainly is owed.

**M.** When this is counted, how many times will there be?

**D.** Eight.

**M.** Therefore, just as the shortest foot—which is also the first—cannot contain fewer than two, so the shortest verse—which is also the first—cannot contain fewer than eight times.

**D.** That is so.

**M.** What of the longest verse, beyond which it ought not to extend? How many times must it contain? Will you not see this at once if we turn our attention to that progression about which so much has so often been said?

**D.** I understand now that a verse cannot contain more than thirty-two times.

### 21.

**M.** What do you think about the length of a meter? Should it be longer than a verse, since the meter that is smallest is so much shorter than the smallest verse?

[Note: [Col. 1127] Manuscript B has “than the verse.” “Than a verse” is preferable with Manuscript A. M.]

**D.** I do not think so.

**M.** Since, then, a meter begins with two feet and a verse with four—or the former with the space of two feet, the latter with four, silence being counted—and since a meter does not exceed eight feet, must it not, since a verse is also a meter, likewise not exceed that number of feet?

**D.** That is so.

**M.** Again, since a verse is no longer than thirty-two times, and since a meter is also the length of a verse when it does not possess the particular joining of two members required in a verse but merely closes with a definite ending, and since it ought not to be longer than a verse, is it not clear that, just as a verse should not exceed eight feet, so a meter should not exceed thirty-two times?

[Note: [Col. 1128] “Nevertheless,” according to the Vatican manuscript. M.]

**D.** I agree.

**M.** There will therefore be the same amount of time and the same number of feet for both meter and verse, and a common limit beyond which neither should proceed.

[Note: [Col. 1128] The Vatican reads: “And the same number of feet; and a certain limit common to meter and verse, beyond which …” M.]

The difference is that the meter ends with fourfold feet, from which it begins, while the verse ends with fourfold times, from which it too begins. Thus, by preserving that fourfold measure of growth, the meter shares feet with the verse, while the verse shares times with the meter.

**D.** I understand and approve this; and I am pleased that this harmony and agreement are indeed so constituted.

# BOOK FOUR

## The discussion of meter continued

[Col. 1127]

## CHAPTER I

### Why the final syllable is indifferent in meter

### 1.

**M.** Let us return, then, to the consideration of meter. Because of its progression and length, I was compelled to discuss the verse with you, although a place has been assigned to us later for treating it.

But first I ask whether you do not reject the view that poets and grammarians who judge such matters have considered it irrelevant whether the final syllable that terminates a meter is long or short.

**D.** I reject it entirely. It does not seem reasonable to me.

**M.** Tell me what the shortest meter in the pyrrhic is.

**D.** Three short syllables.

**M.** How long, then, must we be silent while it is repeated?

**D.** One time, which is the space of one short syllable.

**M.** Come, now beat this meter—not with your voice but with your beat.

**D.** I have done so.

**M.** Beat an anapest in the same way.

**D.** I have done that too.

**M.** What difference did you perceive?

**D.** Absolutely none.

**M.** What? Can you state the reason why this is so?

**D.** It seems sufficiently clear to me. What in the one case is assigned to silence is assigned in the other to the prolongation of the final syllable. The final short syllable there is beaten in the same way as the long syllable here, and after exactly the same interval we return to the beginning. In the one case we rest until the space of the pyrrhic foot is filled; in the other, until the space of the long syllable is filled. Thus in both cases the delay is equal, and after inserting it we return.

**M.** They therefore did not absurdly decide that the final syllable of a meter, whether long or short, is irrelevant. Wherever the ending is, silence follows, so far as the meter that is ending is concerned.

Do you think that in this matter they ought to have considered any repetition or return to the beginning, rather than merely the fact that the meter ends, as though nothing were to be said afterward?

**D.** I now agree that the final syllable should be accepted indifferently.

**M.** Correctly. But if this happens because of the silence, since the ending is considered as though the one who has finished were not going to produce any further sound, and because of this generous interval it makes no difference which syllable is placed there, does it not follow that this very indifference of the final syllable—granted because of the ample space—has the effect that, whether the syllable there is short or long, the ears claim it for themselves as long?

[Note: [Col. 1128] “Will make sound,” according to the Vatican manuscript and Manuscript A. M.]

**D.** I clearly see that this follows.

## CHAPTER II

### Of how many syllables the shortest pyrrhic meter consists, and how long the silence should be

### 2.

**M.** Do you also see that, when we say that the shortest meter is a pyrrhic of three short syllables, with one short syllable’s space of silence while we return to the beginning, it makes no difference whether we repeat this meter or anapest feet?

**D.** I understood this a little earlier from the beating.

**M.** Do you not therefore think that whatever is confused here must be distinguished by some method?

**D.** I certainly do.

**M.** Tell me whether you see any other method of distinguishing these things except to say that the pyrrhic meter is not the shortest one you thought it was in three short syllables, but in five. For the equal duration of the anapest does not allow us to place the shortest meter in the pyrrhic after one foot and a half and to return to the beginning after the half-foot’s delay required to complete the foot, as has already been demonstrated. Therefore, if we wish to avoid confusion, that one time must be silent after two feet and a half.

**D.** Why should two pyrrhic feet not be the shortest meter in the pyrrhic—four short syllables, after which there is no need for silence—rather than five syllables, after which there is such a need?

**M.** You are alert indeed, but beware lest the proceleusmatic exclude you from this just as the anapest excludes you from the other.

**D.** You speak truly.

**M.** Do you therefore approve this arrangement of five short syllables and one time of silence?

**D.** I certainly approve it.

**M.** It seems that you have forgotten how we said that one could distinguish whether one was proceeding in a pyrrhic or a proceleusmatic rhythm.

**D.** You remind me correctly. We discovered that these numbers must be distinguished from one another by the beat. Thus I no longer fear the proceleusmatic here, since, by applying the beat, I shall be able to distinguish it from the pyrrhic.

**M.** Why, then, did you not see that the same beat should be applied so that the anapest could be distinguished from those three short syllables—that is, from the pyrrhic and its half-foot—after which one time would have to be silent?
