**D.** I understand now, and I return to the proper path. I affirm that the shortest pyrrhic meter consists of three short syllables, which, when the silence is counted, occupy the time of two pyrrhic feet.

**M.** Your ears therefore approve this kind of rhythm:

> If any things,  
>   
> You wish well,  
>   
> Speak well,  
>   
> Act well,  
>   
> The spirit,  
>   
> If anything,  
>   
> You wish evil,  
>   
> Speak evil,  
>   
> Act evil,  
>   
> The spirit,  
>   
> The middle way.

**D.** They approve it sufficiently, especially now that I remember how these lines ought to be beaten, so that the feet are not confused with anapests in a pyrrhic meter.

### 3.

**M.** Consider these also:

> If you are anything,  
>   
> Act well;  
>   
> He who acts badly  
>   
> Does nothing;  
>   
> And therefore  
>   
> He will be wretched.

**D.** These too insinuate themselves pleasantly, except in one place, where the ending of the third line is joined to the beginning of the fourth.

**M.** That is exactly what I wanted your ears to notice. The sense is not offended without reason when it expects the individual times of all the syllables without any intervening silence. That expectation is certainly disappointed by the meeting of the two consonants, *t* and *n*, which compel the preceding vowel to be long and extend it over two times. Grammarians call a syllable of this kind long by position.

But because of that indifference of the final syllable, no one condemns this meter, even though pure and strict ears condemn it without an accuser. For consider, I ask, how great the difference is if, instead of:

> He who acts badly, does nothing,

we say:

> He who acts badly, the man perishes.

**D.** This is certainly clear and sound.

**M.** Let us therefore observe, for the sake of musical purity, what poets do not observe for the sake of ease in singing: whenever, for example, we need to insert certain meters in which nothing is owed to the foot that must be compensated by silence, let us place as final syllables those which the rule of that rhythm itself requires. In this way, when we return from the end to the beginning, we avoid offending the ears and falsifying the measure.

We nevertheless allow poets to end such meters as though they were not going to say anything afterward, and therefore to place a final syllable that is either long or short with impunity. But in the continuation of meters they are most clearly convicted by the judgment of the ears: they ought not to place as the final syllable anything other than what must be placed there by the law and principle of the meter itself. This continuation occurs when nothing is owed to the foot that would compel us to be silent.

**D.** I understand, and I am glad that you promise examples of this sort, in which the sense suffers no injury.

## CHAPTER III

### The order and number of pyrrhic meters

### 4.

**M.** Come, now report these pyrrhic meters in order:

> What will a human be  
>   
> Who loves a human,  
>   
> If he loves in him  
>   
> What is fragile?  
>   
> Let him therefore love  
>   
> The human spirit,  
>   
> And he will be a human  
>   
> Loving something.

How do these seem to you?

**D.** What else could they be but extremely smooth and entirely sound?

**M.** What about these?

> Good will be love,  
>   
> If the soul is good;  
>   
> Love dwells within,  
>   
> And the soul is its house.  
>   
> Thus it dwells well  
>   
> Where the house is good;  
>   
> Where it is bad, badly.

**D.** I accept these too, when continued, as extremely smooth.

**M.** Now consider three and a half feet:

> The human spirit is  
>   
> Stirring good and evil.  
>   
> It desired good and has it;  
>   
> It desired evil and has it.

**D.** These too are pleasant when one time of silence is inserted.

**M.** Next come four full pyrrhic feet. Hear them and judge:

> The human spirit acts  
>   
> So that it may possess those goods  
>   
> In which a human may dwell;  
>   
> There nothing is feared.

**D.** Here too there is a definite and pleasant measure.

**M.** Now hear nine short syllables, and judge:

> An evil human loves and lacks;  
>   
> For the evil one loves those goods  
>   
> In which nothing satisfies him.

**D.** Produce five pyrrhic feet now.

**M.**

> Light, fragile goods,  
>   
> A human who loves has likewise.

**D.** That is enough, and I approve it. Now add a half-foot.

**M.** I shall:

> Wandering, light, fragile goods,  
>   
> A human who loves will be like them.

**D.** Very good indeed. I now expect six pyrrhic feet.

**M.** Hear these also:

> Wandering, little, fragile goods,  
>   
> A human who loves deeply will be like them.

**D.** That is enough; add a half-foot.

**M.**

> Fluid, little, fragile goods,  
>   
> The soul that loves them deeply will be like them.

[Col. 1131]

**D.** Enough, and it is good. Now give seven pyrrhic feet.

**M.**

> Little, fragile, slender, good things,  
>   
> The little soul that loves them deeply becomes like them.

**D.** Let a half-foot be added to these, for this is elegantly composed.

**M.**

> Wandering, fluid, little, fragile, good things,  
>   
> The little soul that loves them deeply becomes like them.

**D.** I see that eight feet remain, so that we may now escape these trifles. Although your ears approve what you utter by a certain natural measure, I would not want you to keep searching for so many short syllables. If I am not mistaken, it is more difficult to find them woven together in a combination of words than it would be if we were allowed to mix long syllables among them.

**M.** You are not mistaken. To prove to you my delight that we are at last permitted to pass beyond this point, I shall compose the remaining meter of this type with a more felicitous sentiment.

[Note: [Col. 1131] Manuscript B has “with an easier sentiment.” “With a more felicitous sentiment” is preferable according to Manuscripts A and B. M.]

> A good man loves solid goods, and whoever loves them has them.  
>   
> Thus love does not lack, and those goods are God.

**D.** I have pyrrhic meters completed most fully. Iambic meters follow; two examples of each will be sufficient for me, and it is a pleasure to hear them without interruption.

## CHAPTER IV

### On the iambic meter

### 5.

**M.** I shall oblige you. But how many are the meters we have now completed?

**D.** Fourteen.

**M.** How many iambic meters do you think there will also be?

**D.** Fourteen likewise.

**M.** What if I wished to substitute a tribrach for the iamb in them? Would there not be a more varied multiplicity?

**D.** It is obvious. But I wish to hear these examples in iambs alone, so that we do not make the discussion too long. The discipline that two short syllables may be substituted for any long syllable is easy enough.

**M.** I shall do what you wish, and I am glad that your receptive understanding lessens my labor. Give your ear to the iambic meter.

**D.** I am ready. Begin.

**M.**

> A good man: blessed.  
>   
> An evil man: wretched; he is an evil to himself.  
>   
> A good man is blessed; God is his good.  
>   
> A good man is blessed; God is his good.  
>

>

>

>

>

>   
> Blessed is the good man, for he enjoys God;  
>

>

>

>   
> Blessed is he who sees God; he desires no further good;  
>

>   
> Blessed is he who sees God; he wants no further good;  
>   
> The evil man seeks good outside; hence, needy, he wanders.  
>   
> Blessed is he who sees God; he will desire no further good;  
>   
> The evil man seeks good outside; hence he lacks the good, wretched.

## CHAPTER VII

### How many tribrachic meters there are

### 8.

**D.** I have nothing to ask further about the spondee. Let us come to the tribrach.

**M.** Indeed. But since each of the four preceding feet of which we have spoken has produced fourteen meters—fifty-six altogether—we should expect more from the tribrach. In those feet, when the space of a half-foot is assigned to silence, no more than one syllable is silent. In this one, however, when we are silent, do you think that only the space of one short syllable should be silent, or can the duration of two short syllables also be contained in the silence? No one will doubt that this foot has a twofold division: it either begins with one and ends with two, or, conversely, begins with two and ends with one.

Therefore it must produce twenty-one meters.

**D.** Most certainly. They begin with four short syllables, so that we are silent for two times. Then there are five, where we are silent for one time; third, six, where nothing is silent; fourth, seven, where again two times must be silent; then eight, where one time is silent; sixth, nine, where none is silent.

And so, as one syllable is added at a time until we reach twenty-four syllables—which are eight tribrachs—the total of twenty-one meters is completed.

**M.** You have followed the reasoning very efficiently. But do you think that examples must be produced by us in every case, or should we consider that the examples we supplied for those first four feet will provide sufficient illumination for the rest?

**D.** In my judgment, they are sufficient.

**M.** I too require nothing now except your judgment. Nevertheless, since you know very well that in pyrrhic meters tribrachs can be beaten by changing the beat, I ask whether the first pyrrhic meter can also be a tribrachic meter.

[Col. 1133]

**D.** It cannot, for a meter must be greater than a foot.

**M.** What about the second?

**D.** It can. For the four short syllables of two pyrrhic feet amount to one tribrach and a half, so that in the one case we are silent for no times, and in the other for two.

**M.** By changing the beat, then, you have examples of tribrachs even in the pyrrhic meters up to sixteen syllables—that is, up to five and a half tribrachs. You should be satisfied with these; you can compose the rest for yourself, either with your voice or with some kind of beat, if you still think that such numbers should be tested by the sensation of the ears.

**D.** I shall do what seems best. Let us see what remains.

## CHAPTER VIII

### On the dactyl
9. M. The dactyl follows; it can be divided once. Do you think otherwise?  
D. No, that is how it is.  
M. What portion of it, then, can be in silence?  
D. Half, naturally.  
M. What if, after a dactyl, someone places a trochee and wishes to be silent for one time-unit—the unit owed by the short syllable in the dactyl to complete it? What shall we answer? For we cannot say that one ought not to be silent for less than the duration of a half-foot. The reasoning treated above persuaded us that silence should be not less than, but more than, the time of a half-foot. For in a choriambus one is certainly silent for less than a half-foot, when a bacchius is placed after the choriambus itself, as in the example *Fonticolae puellae* (“girl of the little spring”). Here, as you recognize, we are silent for the duration of one short syllable, although six time-units must be completed.  
D. You speak truly.  
M. With a trochee therefore placed after the dactyl, will it also be permissible to be silent for one time-unit?  
D. I am compelled to admit it.  
M. Who, then, would compel you, if you remembered what came before? You have forgotten what was demonstrated concerning the indifference of the final syllable, and how the ears claim a final long syllable for themselves when there remains a space in which it may be extended, even if the syllable is short.  
D. I understand now. For if, when silence remains, the ears receive a final short syllable as long—as we learned above through reasoning and examples—it makes no difference whether a trochee or a spondee is placed after the dactyl. Therefore, when the repetition is to be marked off by silence, one must place a single long syllable after the dactyl, so that we may be silent for the duration of two time-units.  
M. What if a pyrrhic is placed after the dactyl? Do you think that is properly done?  
D. Not properly. For whether it is the same as an iambus makes no difference: it must be taken as an iambus because of its final syllable, which the ears require to be long since silence remains. Who does not understand that an iambus ought not to be placed after a dactyl because of the difference between arsis and thesis, neither of which ought to have three time-units in a dactyl?

## CHAPTER IX — The Bacchius

10. M. Entirely excellent and consistent. But what, finally, do you think about the anapaest? Is the same reasoning applicable?  
D. Precisely the same.  
M. Let us now consider the bacchius, if you please, and tell me what its first metre is.  
D. I think it consists of four syllables: one short and three long, of which two belong to the bacchius, while the final one belongs to the beginning of the foot [Col. 1134] that may be placed with the bacchius, so that what is owed to that foot may be supplied by silence. Yet I should like to test this with the ears in some example.  
M. It is easy enough to provide examples, although I do not think you will enjoy them as much as the preceding ones. For feet of five time-units, and likewise of seven, do not move as pleasantly as those divided either into equal parts or into one-and-two, or two-and-one. Such is the difference between sesquialterate movements and equal or compound ones, which we discussed sufficiently in that first conversation of ours. Thus these feet of five and seven time-units are taken up by prose more willingly, though by poets with somewhat greater reluctance. This can be seen more easily in the examples you requested, for they are:

> *Laborat magister docens tardos.*  
> “The teacher labors while instructing the slow.”

Repeat this with an intervening silence of three time-units. To make it easier for you to perceive this, I placed a long syllable after three feet, since that is the beginning of a cretic, which can be placed with a bacchius. I did not provide an example of the first metre—namely, the one of four syllables—lest a single foot be insufficient to remind your sense how much silence ought to follow it and one long syllable.

[Note: [Col. 1134] Er. and Lugd. have: “Nor did I give an example of the first metre”; and, in the margin, *adeo* for *ad*. Lov.: “nor indeed of the first metre.” Manuscript A: “not of the first metre”; but Manuscript B reads as the Benedictine editors. The Venetian edition follows the text of Er. and Lugd. M.] But I shall now present one and repeat it myself, so that you may perceive three time-units in my silence:

> *Labor nullus, Amor magnus.*  
> “No labor, great Love.”

D. It is sufficiently clear that these feet are more suitable to unconstrained prose, and there is no need to run through the remaining examples.  
M. You speak truly. But when silence is required, do you think that only one long syllable can be placed after the bacchius?  
D. Certainly not; a short and a long syllable may also be placed there, which is the first half-foot of that same bacchius. For if we were permitted to begin a cretic because it can be placed with that bacchius, how much more will it be permitted to do this with the bacchius itself, especially since we have not set down the whole cretic, whose duration is equal to the first part of the bacchius?

## CHAPTER X — What Is Added to a Complete Foot before the Silence

11. M. Now, if you please, with me listening and judging, run through the remaining cases yourself, and explain what is placed after a complete foot when the remainder is completed by silence in all the feet that remain.  
D. What you ask is now, I think, very brief and easy. For what was said about the bacchius can also be said about the second paeon. After a cretic one may place a single long syllable, an iambus, or a spondee, so that either three, two, or one time-unit is silent. What has been said about this also applies to the first and fourth paeons.

[Note: Manuscript A adds: “Because of the two divisions.” M.]

After a palimbacchius it is appropriate to place either one long syllable or a spondee; accordingly, in this metre either three or one time-unit will be silent. The same condition applies to the third paeon.

Certainly, wherever a spondee is permitted, an anapaest is also rightly permitted. After a molossus, as regards its division, we place either one long syllable, worth four time-units, or two [long syllables], so that we may be silent for two time-units. But since both reckoning and reason have established that all the feet of six time-units can be arranged [Col. 1135] with it, there will also be room after it for an iambus, and three time-units will remain to be silenced; there will also be room for a cretic, and one time-unit will be silent; under this condition there will also be room for a bacchius. But if we resolve the first syllable of the cretic and the second syllable of the bacchius into two shorts, there will also be room for the fourth paeon. What was said about the molossus may also be said about the other feet of six time-units.

I think the proceleusmatic is to be reckoned with the other feet consisting of four time-units, except when three short syllables are placed after it. This is equivalent to placing an anapaest, because of the final syllable, which, together with silence, is customarily received as long.

After the first epitrite an iambus is rightly joined, as well as a bacchius, a cretic, and the fourth paeon. Let this also be said of the second epitrite, so that either four or two time-units may be silent. The remaining two epitrites can rightly be followed by a spondee and a molossus, with permission to resolve the first syllable of the spondee, and the first or second syllable of the molossus, into two shorts. Thus in these metres either three or one time-unit will be silent.

The dispondeus remains. If we place a spondee after it, four time-units must be silenced; if a molossus, two, with the permission remaining to resolve a long syllable into two shorts, either in the spondee or in the molossus, except for the final syllable. You have what you asked me to run through, unless perhaps you will correct something.

## CHAPTER XI — An Iambus Is Improperly Placed after a Dichorius

12. M. No, not I, but you, when you apply your ear to judging. For I ask you whether, when I say and clap this metre,

> *Verus optimus*  
> “A true man, the best.”

and this,

> *Verus optimorum*  
> “A true man, one of the best.”

and this,

> *Veritatis inops*  
> “Lacking truth,”

your sense receives this third one as pleasantly as the preceding ones; by repeating them and clapping with the appropriate silences, it will easily judge.  
D. It is clear that it receives those pleasantly, but this one unpleasantly.

[Note: Manuscripts A and B have: “It is clear that those are received pleasantly, but this unpleasantly.” M.]

M. An iambus, then, is not properly placed after a dichorius.  
D. That is so.  
M. That it can properly be placed after the other feet is agreed by anyone who repeats these metres with a disciplined insertion of silences:

> *Fallacem cave.*  
> “Beware the deceitful.”

> *Male castum cave.*  
> “Beware the falsely chaste.”

> *Mutiloquum cave.*  
> “Beware the mutilated speaker.”

> *Fallaciam cave.*  
> “Beware deceit.”

> *Et invidum cave.*  
> “And beware the envious.”

> *Et infirmum cave.*  
> “And beware the weak.”

D. I understand what you are saying, and I approve it.  
M. See also whether anything displeases you when, with a silence of two time-units inserted, this metre is repeated as it proceeds unevenly.

[Note: *Inaequaliter*, according to Manuscript A and all printed editions. Manuscript B reads, as do the Benedictines, *inaequale*. M.]

Does it sound, then, like these?

> *Veraces regnant.*  
> “The truthful reign.”

> *Sapientes regnant.*  
> “The wise reign.”

> *Veriloqui regnant.*  
> “The truthful-speaking reign.”

> *Prudentia regnat.*  
> “Prudence reigns.”

> *Boni in bonis regnant.*  
> “The good reign among the good.”

> *Pura cuncta regnant.*  
> “All pure things reign.”

D. On the contrary, these proceed evenly and pleasantly, while that one is absurd.  
M. We shall therefore maintain that among metres of feet of six time-units, a dichorius closed by an iambus, and an antispastus closed by a spondee, are improperly formed.  
D. Certainly we shall.

13. M. What? Will you not approve the reason why this is so [Col. 1136] if you observe that a foot is divided by arsis and thesis into two parts, so that if it contains a medial syllable—whether one or two—it is assigned either to the first or to the second part, or divided between both?  
D. I know that, and it is true; but what does it have to do with the matter?  
M. Attend also to what I shall say, and then you will more easily see what you are asking about. For I think it is clear to you that some feet have no medial syllables, such as the pyrrhic and the other feet of two syllables; while in others the medial space belongs either to the first part, the final part, both, or neither.

It belongs to the first part in the anapaest, the palimbacchius, and the first paeon; to the final part in the dactyl, the bacchius, and the fourth paeon; to both in the tribrach, the molossus, the choriambus, and every ionic foot; and to neither in the cretic, the second and third paeons, the diiambus, the dichorius, and the antispastus. For in feet that can be divided into three equal parts, the middle part agrees with both the first and the final; those that cannot be so divided agree either with the first alone, the final alone, or neither.  
D. I know this equally well, and I await where you are heading.  
M. Where else, do you think, than toward your seeing that an iambus is therefore improperly placed after a dichorius with silence, because its middle does not equal either the first or the final part, and for that reason is discordant with arsis and thesis? The same is understood of the spondee, which likewise does not willingly stand after an antispastus with silence. Or do you have anything to say against this?  
D. Nothing, except that the offense the ears experience when these feet are placed in this way arises by comparison with the pleasantness that delights the hearing when these feet are placed with silence after the other feet of six time-units. For if, without comparing them with the others, you asked me how they sounded, and supplied examples in which an iambus stood after a dichorius or a spondee after an antispastus, both placed with silence, I might perhaps approve and praise them as I found them.  
M. I do not resist you. It is enough for me, however, that, as you say, this arrangement is offensive by comparison with such numbers that sound better. It must therefore be rejected because, since those feet too are of the same kind, and we admit that they glide more pleasantly when closed by these half-feet, they ought not to differ from them. But does it not seem to you, on this reasoning, that an iambus with silence ought not to be placed after the second epitrite either? For in this foot also the iambus occupies the middle position in such a way that it is equal in time to neither the preceding nor the following part.  
D. The preceding reasoning compels me to concede it.

## CHAPTER XII — The Total Number of All the Metres

14. M. Come now, if you please, give me the number of all the metres we have already treated: that is, those which begin with their own complete feet, but are closed either by their own complete feet, so that when the movement returns to the beginning we insert no silence, or by incomplete feet with silence, which reason has nevertheless shown to be compatible with them. Let the count begin with two incomplete feet and extend to eight complete feet, while not exceeding thirty-two time-units.  
D. What you impose is laborious, but it is worth the effort. Yet I remember that a little earlier we had already reached seventy-seven metres, from the pyrrhic to the tribrach, when each of the fourteen feet of two syllables produced seven metres, making fifty-six in all. The tribrach, however, produced twenty-one, because of its double division. [Col. 1137]

To these seventy-seven we add fourteen dactyls and an equal number of anapaests. When complete feet are placed without silence, with the metre beginning at two feet and extending to eight, they produce seven each; when half-feet with silence are added, with the metre beginning at one foot and a half and extending to seven and a half, they produce another seven each. Thus the total is now one hundred and five.

The bacchius cannot extend its own metre to eight feet, lest it exceed thirty-two time-units; nor can any foot of five time-units. But these can extend to six. The bacchius, therefore, and the foot equal to it not only in time but also in division—the second paeon—proceeding from two feet to six, produce five metres each when arranged complete and without silence. With silence, beginning from one half-foot and reaching five half-feet, they produce another five when one long syllable is placed after them, and likewise five with a short and a long syllable. Thus they produce fifteen each, which reduced to a total makes thirty. The total number of metres is now one hundred and thirty-five.

The cretic and the feet divided in the same way, the first and fourth paeons, reach seventy-five, since after them one may place a long syllable, an iambus, a spondee, or an anapaest. Since there are three feet, they produce five each without silence and twenty with silence; these together, as stated, make seventy-five. Added to the preceding total, they complete two hundred and ten.

The palimbacchius and the third paeon, which agrees with it in division, produce five complete metres without silence. With silence they produce five with a single long syllable, five with a spondee, and five with an anapaest. We add these to the greater total and have two hundred and fifty metres altogether.

15. The molossus and the other feet of six time-units, seven in all together with it, produce four complete metres each. With silence, since a single long syllable, an iambus, a spondee, an anapaest, a bacchius, a cretic, and a fourth paeon can be placed after each of them, they complete twenty-eight each. These together make one hundred and ninety-six; added to the four each, they complete two hundred and twenty-four. But eight must be subtracted, because an iambus is improperly arranged after a dichorius and a spondee after an antispastus. The remainder is two hundred and sixteen; added to the greater total, this makes four hundred and sixty-six metres altogether.

The proceleusmatic could not be counted with the feet compatible with it because of the half-feet that are placed after it in greater number. For a single long syllable can be placed after it with silence, as after the dactyl and its companions, producing two [time-units], and three short syllables can be placed after it, producing one time-unit of silence. This results in the final short syllable being received as long.

The epitrites produce three complete metres each, with the metre beginning with two feet and extending to four. For if a fifth is added, thirty-two time-units will be exceeded, which is impermissible. With silence, the first and second [Col. 1138] epitrites produce three each after an iambus, three each after a bacchius, three each after a cretic, and three each after a fourth paeon. Together with the three each that they produce without silence, these make thirty.

The third and fourth epitrites produce three before the silence, three with a spondee, three with an anapaest, three with a molossus, three with a lesser ionic, and three with a choriambus. Together with the three each that they produced without silence, these make thirty-six. Thus all the epitrites produce sixty-six metres; added to the twenty-one of the proceleusmatic, this makes five hundred and fifty-three when added to the preceding total.

The dispondeus remains. It too produces three complete metres; with silence, it produces three with a spondee, three with an anapaest, three with a molossus, three with a lesser ionic, and three with a choriambus. Added to the three produced in its complete form, these make eighteen. Thus the total number of metres will be five hundred and seventy-one.

## CHAPTER XIII — The Method of Measuring Metres and Inserting Silences

16. M. It would indeed be five hundred and seventy-one, were it not necessary to subtract three, because it was said that an iambus is improperly placed after the second epitrite. But that is satisfactory. Now tell me how this metre strikes your ear:

> *Triplici vides, ut ortu Triviae rotetur ignis.*  
> “You see how, at the rising of Trivia, the fire wheels threefold.”

D. Very pleasantly.  
M. Can you say of what feet it consists?  
D. I cannot. For I cannot discover how the feet I measure fit together. Whether I establish a pyrrhic at the beginning, or an anapaest, or a third paeon, the feet that follow do not agree with them. Here, indeed, I find a cretic after the third paeon, leaving a long syllable, which a cretic does not reject when placed after it. But this metre could not properly consist of these feet unless a silence of three time-units were inserted; yet now nothing is silenced, although its repetition delights the hearing.  
M. Consider, then, whether it ought to begin with a pyrrhic, after which we measure a dichorius, then a spondee, which completes the time-units of which two occur at the beginning. An anapaest can likewise occupy the beginning, followed by a diiambus, so that the final long syllable, placed together with the four time-units of the anapaest, completes six time-units, which agree with the diiambus. From this you may understand that portions of feet are placed not only at the end but also at the beginning of metres.  
D. I understand now.

17. M. What if I remove one final long syllable, so that the metre is:

> *Segetes meus labor.*  
> “My labor is the harvest.”

Do you not notice that it is repeated with a silence of two time-units? From this it is clear that a portion of a foot can be placed at the beginning of a metre, another at the end, and another in the silence.  
D. That too is clear.  
M. But this occurs if you measure a complete dichorius in this metre. For if you measure a diiambus and place an anapaest at the beginning, you see that a part of the foot is placed at the beginning and already contains four time-units; the two that are owed to it are silenced at the end. From this we learn that a metre can begin with a portion of a foot and end at a complete foot, but never without silence.  
D. That too is evident.

[Col. 1139] 18. M. What of this? Can you measure this metre and say of what feet it consists?

> *Jam satis terris nivis, atque dirae*  
> *Grandinis misit Pater, et rubente*  
> *Dextera sacras jaculatus arces.*  
> *(Horace, Book 1 of the Odes, Ode 2.)*
>
> “Already enough snow and dreadful hail has the Father sent upon the lands, and, with reddening right hand, hurled the sacred citadels.”

D. I can establish a cretic at the beginning and measure the two remaining feet of six time-units: one a greater ionic, the other a dichorius. I can then be silent for one time-unit, which is joined to the cretic so that six time-units are completed.  
M. Your consideration fell somewhat short. For when a dichorius is at the end and silence remains, its final syllable, which is short, is received as long. Will you deny this?  
D. On the contrary, I admit it.  
M. It is therefore not appropriate to establish a dichorius at the end unless no silence follows it in the repetition, lest it now be perceived not as a dichorius but as a second epitrite.  
D. That is clear.  
M. How, then, shall we measure this metre?  
D. I do not know.

## CHAPTER XIV — He Pursues the Method of Applying Silences in Measuring Metres

M. Consider, then, whether it sounds well when I pronounce it in such a way that I am silent for one time-unit after the first three syllables. In this way nothing will be owed at the end, and a dichorius can properly stand there.  
D. It sounds most pleasantly.

19. M. Let us therefore add this to our method: we must be silent not only at the end but also before the end whenever necessary. This is necessary when what is owed in order to complete the feet’ time-units is either improperly silenced at the end because of a final short syllable, as in the passage just mentioned, or when two incomplete feet are established, one at the beginning and the other at the end, as in this:

> *Gentiles nostros inter oberrat equos.*  
> “He wanders among our native horses.”

You perceived, I think, that after five long syllables I was silent for the duration of two time-units, and that the same amount must be silenced at the end while returning to the beginning. For if you measure this metre according to the rule of feet of six time-units, the first will be a spondee, the second a molossus, the third a choriambus, and the fourth an anapaest. Two time-units are therefore owed to the spondee in order to complete a foot of six time-units, and likewise to the anapaest. Thus two are silenced after the molossus before the end, and two after the anapaest at the end.

But if you measure it according to the rule of time-units of four, there will be one long syllable at the beginning; then we measure two spondees, then two dactyls, and one long syllable will conclude the metre.

[Note: Manuscript B has *collocata quatuor*, omitting the preposition *cum*, which is found in Manuscript A; *concludet* (“will conclude”) is supported by Manuscripts A and B. M.]

We therefore silence two time-units after the pair of spondees before the end, and two at the end, so that both feet may be completed, the halves of which we placed at the beginning and at the end.

20. Sometimes, however, what is owed to two incomplete feet placed at the beginning and the end is supplied only by final silence, if the amount does not exceed the space of a half-foot. Such are these two:

> *Silvae laborantes, geluque*  
> “The woods laboring, and with frost—”

> *Flumina constiterint acuto.*  
> “The rivers have stood still with sharp [frost].”

The first of these begins with a palimbacchius, proceeds from there into a molossus, and ends with a bacchius. Two time-units are therefore silenced; when you restore one to the bacchius and the other to the palimbacchius, six time-units will be completed everywhere.

[Col. 1140] The second begins with a dactyl, proceeds into a choriambus, and closes with a bacchius. It will therefore be necessary to silence three time-units. We shall restore one of these to the bacchius and two to the dactyl, so that there will be six time-units throughout.

21. What is owed to the final foot established at the end is restored before what is owed to the foot established at the beginning. The ears permit no other arrangement. Nor is this surprising, for when we repeat it, what is at the very end is joined to the beginning. Thus, in the metre just cited, *Flumina constiterint acuto*, since three time-units are owed in order to complete feet of six time-units, if you wish to render them not by silence but by voice, they can be rendered by an iambus, a chorius, or a tribrach, since all possess three time-units. Yet sense in no way permits them to be rendered by a chorius, in which the first syllable is long and the second short. What is owed to the final bacchius must sound first—that is, the short syllable—not the long syllable owed to the first dactyl. This can be tested by these examples:

> *Flumina constiterint acuto gelu.*  
> “The rivers have stood still with sharp frost.”

> *Flumina constiterint acute gelida.*  
> “The rivers have stood still, sharply frozen.”

> *Flumina constiterint in alta nocte.*  
> “The rivers have stood still in the deep night.”

Who could doubt that the first two can be repeated pleasantly, but the third in no way?

22. Likewise, when individual time-units are owed to individual incomplete feet, if you wish to render them by voice, sense does not allow them to be compressed into a single syllable—a remarkable justice indeed. For what must be restored separately ought also to be established separately. Accordingly, in the metre *Silvae laborantes, geluque*, if you add one long syllable in place of the final silence, as in *Silvae laborantes gelu duro* (“The woods laboring with hard frost”), the ears do not approve it, whereas they approve it when we say:

> *Silvae laborantes gelu et frigore.*  
> “The woods laboring with frost and cold.”

You perceive this most satisfactorily when you repeat each version.

23. Likewise, when two incomplete feet are placed, the larger ought not to be placed at the beginning rather than at the end. The hearing condemns this too, as if you were to say:

> *Optimum tempus adest tandem.*  
> “At last the best time is here.”

Here the first foot would be a cretic, the second a choriambus, and the third a spondee; we would silence three time-units, two of which are owed to the final spondee in order to complete six, and one to the first cretic.

But if it is said as follows:

> *Tandem tempus adest optimum.*  
> “At last the time is here, the best,”

with the same three-time-unit pause inserted in the silence, who would not feel that it is repeated most pleasantly? Therefore the incomplete foot at the end ought either to occupy as much space as the one at the beginning, as in *Silvae laborantes, geluque*, or the one at the beginning should be smaller and the one at the end larger, as in *Flumina constiterint acuto*. And rightly so: where there is equality, there is no discord; where the number is unequal, if we proceed from the smaller to the larger, as is customary in counting, the order itself again produces harmony.

24. From this it also follows that when the incomplete feet under discussion are placed, and silence is inserted in two locations—that is, before the end and at the end—we must be silent before the end for as much as is owed to the final foot, and at the end for as much as is owed to the first; for the middle tends toward the end, while from the end one must return to the beginning.

[Note: Am., Erasmus, and Lovaniensis have: “for as much as is owed to the beginning”; [Col. 1141] most manuscripts instead have: “for as much as is owed to the first [incomplete foot]”—understood. They subsequently lack the words “if you add one long syllable in place of the final silence,” which we have removed because the sense requires it. M.]

If the same amount is owed to both, there is no dispute that the same amount should be silenced before the end as at the end. Silence, however, ought to occur only where a portion of the utterance ends. In rhythms formed not by words but by some percussion, breath, or even the tongue itself, there is no difference in this matter after which sound or stroke the silence occurs, provided that the proper silence intervenes according to the principles stated above.

Accordingly, a metre can also begin with two incomplete feet, provided that their combined space is not less than what could constitute one and a half feet. For we said above that two incomplete feet are properly placed when what is owed to both does not exceed the space of half a foot. An example is:

> *Montes acuti.*  
> “Sharp mountains.”

Here we may either silence three time-units at the end, or one time-unit after the spondee and two at the end. For the metre cannot otherwise be measured appropriately.

## CHAPTER XV — Again on Inserting Silence in Metres

25. Let this also be part of the method: when we are silent before the end, a portion of the utterance must not end there with a short syllable, lest, according to the rule often mentioned, the sense receive it as long when silence follows. Thus, in this metre,

> *Montibus acutis.*  
> “With sharp mountains,”

we cannot be silent for one time-unit after the dactyl, as we were able to be after the spondee in the preceding example, lest it now be perceived not as a dactyl but as a cretic. In that way the metre would appear to consist not of two incomplete feet, as we are now demonstrating, but of a complete dichorius and a final spondee, with two time-units restored by silence at the end.

26. But it must be noted that what is owed to an incomplete foot placed at the beginning may be restored there by silence, as in:

> *Jam satis terris nivis atque dirae.*  
> “Now enough snow and dreadful [hail] for the lands.”

Or it may be restored at the end, as in:

> *Segetes meus labor.*  
> “My labor is the harvest.”

To an incomplete foot placed at the end, what is owed may either be restored there by silence, as in:

> *Ite igitur Camoenae.*  
> “Go, then, O Muses,”

or at some point in the middle, as in:

> *Ver blandum viget arvis, adest hospes hirundo.*  
> “Gentle spring flourishes in the fields; the swallow, a guest, is here.”

For the one time-unit owed to the final bacchius may either be silenced after the whole number, or after its first foot, the molossus, or after the second lesser ionic.

But what is owed to incomplete feet situated in the middle can be restored only there, as in:

> *Tuba terribilem sonitum dedit aere curvo.*  
> “The trumpet gave a terrifying sound with curved bronze.”

For if we measure this metre by making the first foot an anapaest, the second any ionic of five syllables—after resolving either its first or its final long syllable into two shorts—the third a choriambus, and the last a bacchius, there will be three time-units owed: one to be restored to the final bacchius and two to the first anapaest, so that six time-units may be completed. This entire space of three time-units can be silenced at the end.

But if you begin with a complete foot and measure the first five syllables as any ionic,

[Col. 1142] a choriambus follows; from that point you will no longer find a complete foot. It will therefore be necessary to be silent for the duration of one long syllable. Once this is counted, the second choriambus will be completed; the remaining bacchius will close the metre, and one time-unit owed to it will be silenced at the end.

27. Hence it should now be clear that when silence occurs in the middle, either the time-units owed at the end are restored, or those owed at the point where the silence occurs. Sometimes, however, it is not necessary to be silent in the middle, when the metre can be measured otherwise, as in the passage we placed shortly before.

Sometimes it is necessary, as in this:

> *Vernat temperies, aurae tepent, sunt deliciae.*  
> “The mild season blooms; the breezes are warm; there are delights.”

It is clear that this rhythm proceeds either in feet of four time-units or in feet of six.

If in feet of four, one time-unit must be silenced after the eighth syllable and two at the end. Measure first a spondee, second a dactyl, third a spondee, fourth a dactyl, counting the silence after the long syllable, since it ought not to follow a short; fifth a spondee; sixth a dactyl, whose final long syllable closes the rhythm, with the two time-units owed to it silenced at the end.

But if we measure the feet here as feet of six time-units, the first will be a molossus, the second a lesser ionic, the third a cretic—which becomes a dichorius when one time-unit of silence is added—the fourth a greater ionic followed by a final long syllable, after which four time-units will be silenced.

It could be done otherwise: one long syllable could be placed at the beginning, followed by a greater ionic, then a molossus, then a bacchius, which would become an antispastus when one time-unit of silence was added; the final choriambus would close the metre, with four time-units of silence at the end restoring the one long syllable established at the beginning.

But the ears reject this measurement, because a portion of a foot placed at the beginning, unless it is larger than a half-foot, is not properly restored by final silence after a complete foot where it is owed. We know how much is owed after the intervening feet, but the sense does not grasp that one should be silent for so much time—unless less is owed in silence than was placed in sound. For once the voice has completed the greater part of a foot, the smaller remainder is easily encountered wherever it occurs.

28. Accordingly, for the metre we placed under the example *Vernat temperies, aurae tepent, sunt deliciae*, although there is one necessary measurement, as we said—namely, one time-unit of silence after its tenth syllable and four at the end—there is another voluntary measurement if someone wishes to be silent for two time-units after the sixth syllable, one after the eleventh, and two at the end. In that case there will be a spondee at the beginning, followed by a choriambus; to the third spondee two time-units of silence will be added, so that it becomes either a molossus or a lesser ionic; the fourth bacchius, with one time-unit of silence likewise added, will become an antispastus; the fifth choriambus will complete the rhythm in sound, with two time-units restored by silence at the end to the spondee placed at the beginning.

There is also another measurement. If you wish, you may be silent for one time-unit after the sixth syllable, one after the tenth, the same amount after the eleventh, and two at the end. Then the first will be a spondee; the second, a choriambus; the third, a palimbacchius, will become an antispastus when one time-unit of silence is added; the fourth spondee will become a dichorius with one time-unit inserted and followed by one time-unit of silence; and the final choriambus will close the rhythm, with two time-units silenced at the end, owed to the first spondee.

There is also a third measurement: one time-unit may be silenced after the first spondee, while the remaining arrangements are preserved as in the immediately preceding case, except that one time-unit will be silenced at the end. For the spondee customarily placed at the beginning has become a palimbacchius through the following silence of one time-unit, so that nothing more than one time-unit is owed to it and must be silenced at the end.

From this you now see that silences are inserted into metres, some necessary and some voluntary. Necessary silences occur when something is owed in order to complete the feet; voluntary silences occur when the feet are complete and whole.

29. What was said above—that no more than four time-units should be silenced—was said of necessary silences, where the owed time-units are completed. In what we have called voluntary silences, however, it is permissible both to sound a foot and to silence a foot. If we do this at equal intervals, it will not be a metre but a rhythm, with no definite end apparent from which one returns to the beginning.

Therefore, if, for example, you wish to mark off the metre with silences, so that after the first foot you silence the time-units of another foot, this need not be maintained continuously. With any variation, it is permissible, once the silences have been counted, to extend the metre up to the proper number of time-units, as in this:

> *Nobis verum in promptu est, tu si verum dicis.*  
> “For us the truth is ready at hand, if you speak the truth.”

Here one may be silent for four time-units after the first spondee and for another four after the following two; after the three final feet nothing will be silenced, since thirty-two time-units have already been completed.

But it is much more suitable, and in a certain sense more orderly, to be silent either only at the end or in the middle and at the end. This can be done by subtracting one foot, so that it runs as follows:

> *Nobis verum in promptu est, tu dic verum.*  
> “For us the truth is ready at hand; speak the truth.”

This must also be observed in the metres of the other feet: with necessary silences, whether final or medial, what is owed must be restored so that the feet are completed. But one ought not to be silent for more than the portion of a foot occupied by arsis or thesis.

[Note: The manuscripts, together with Am., have *deberi* (“to be owed”). M.]

With voluntary silences, however, it is permitted to silence both portions of feet and complete feet, as we demonstrated in the examples given above.

[Note: Manuscript B has *supradictis* (“mentioned above”). Manuscripts A and B have *supra editis* (“given above”), which is more correct. M.]

But let this be enough concerning the method of inserting silences.

## CHAPTER XVI — The Mixture of Feet and the Joining of Metres
30. Now let us say a little about the combination of feet and the joining of the meters themselves, since much has already been said when we were asking which feet ought to be mixed with one another; and as for the joining of meters, some things will have to be said when we begin to discuss verses. For feet are joined and mixed with one another according to the rules that we explained in the second treatise.

Here, however, this must be understood: each kind of meter that has already been celebrated by poets had its own authors and inventors, by whom certain fixed laws were established; and we are forbidden to unsettle them. For when they have fixed these laws by reason, we ought not to change anything there, even though, in accordance with reason, we might be able to change something without offending the ears. [Col. 1144] [Note: Manuscripts A and B agree in this reading: “For when they have fixed these laws by reason, we ought not to change anything there, although we might be able to change something there according to reason without offending the ears.” Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and Lovaniensis read *finxerint* (“have fashioned”) instead of *fixerint* (“have fixed”).]

Knowledge of this matter is transmitted not by art but by history; hence it is believed rather than known. [Note: [Col. 1144] *Metrum* (“meter”), according to Erasmus, the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions and manuscript A.] For if some Phaliscus—I do not know who—composed meters in such a way that they sound as follows,

> *Quando flagella ligas, ita liga,*  
> “When you bind the vine-shoots, bind them thus,”
>
> *Vitis et ulmus uti simul eant;*  
> “So that vine and elm may go together,”

we cannot know this by reasoning; we can only believe it by hearing and reading. But it belongs to disciplined inquiry to determine whether this consists of three dactyls and a final pyrrhic, as most people untrained in music maintain—for they do not understand that a pyrrhic cannot be placed after a dactyl—or whether, as reason teaches, the first foot in this meter is a choriamb, the second an ionic foot with its long syllable resolved into two shorts, and the last an iamb, after which three time-units are silent. Half-educated people could perceive this if it were pronounced and marked by a trained person according to both principles. In that way they would judge by natural and common perception what the rule of the discipline prescribed.

31. Nevertheless, since that poet wanted these rhythms to remain fixed when we use this meter, that must be observed. For it does not deceive the ear, although the ear would likewise not be deceived if, instead of a choriamb, we placed a diiamb, or used the ionic without resolving it into shorts, or inserted anything else that fitted. In this meter, therefore, nothing will be changed—not for the reason by which we avoid inequality, but for the reason by which we respect authority.

Reason does indeed teach that some meters are instituted as fixed, that is, meters in which nothing ought to be changed, as is this very meter about which we have spoken at sufficient length; and that others are mobile, in which it is permissible to place one foot in place of another, as in:

> *Trojae qui primus ab oris, arma virumque cano.*  
> “The man who first came from the shores of Troy, I sing of arms and the man.”

For here an anapest may be placed anywhere in place of a spondee. Others are neither wholly fixed nor wholly mobile, as in:

> *Pendeat ex humeris dulcis chelys,*  
> “Let the sweet lyre hang from the shoulders,”
>
> *Et numeros edat varios, quibus*  
> “And let it produce varied rhythms, to which”
>
> *Assonet omne virens late nemus,*  
> “Every green grove far and wide may resound,”
>
> *Et tortis errans qui flexibus.*  
> “And that which wanders through twisting bends.”

(Terentianus, from Pomponius.)

For here you see that both spondees and dactyls may be placed everywhere except in the final foot, which the author of the meter wanted always to be a dactyl. In these three kinds, then, you see that authority has some force.

32. As for what in the combination of feet belongs solely to reason, judging matters that are perceived, this must be understood: those parts of feet that are pleasantly placed after certain feet, with a residual silence, such as an iamb after a dichory and after a second epitrite, and a spondee after an antispast, are badly placed after other feet with which those feet have been mixed. For it is clear that an iamb is well placed after a molossus, as this frequently repeated example shows, with three time-units silent at the end:

> *Ver blandum viret floribus*  
> “The gentle spring is green with flowers.”

But if, instead of a molossus, you establish a dichory first, as in:

> *Vere terra viret floribus*  
> “In spring the earth is green with flowers,”

the ear rejects and condemns it. [Col. 1145] The same can easily be tested in the other cases by the judgment of perception.

For the most certain rule is this: when feet that are mutually capable of being joined are connected with one another, those parts should be appended at the end that suit all the feet placed in that sequence, so that no sort of discord may arise among partners.

33. More remarkable still is the following: although a spondee pleasantly closes both a diiamb and a dichory, nevertheless, when these two feet—whether alone or mixed in any way with other feet capable of combination—occur in a single sequence, a spondee cannot be placed at the end with the approval of perception.

Who would doubt that the ears gladly receive these expressions when repeated separately:

> *Timenda res non est*  
> “There is nothing to fear,”

and likewise, separately:

> *Jam timere noli*  
> “Do not be afraid now”?

But if you join them in this way,

> *Timenda res, jam timere noli*  
> “There is nothing to fear; do not be afraid now,”

I would not want to hear it except in ordinary prose.

It is no less absurd if you connect another foot anywhere, for example a molossus, in this way:

> *Vir fortis, timenda res, jam timere noli*  
> “A brave man—there is nothing to fear; do not be afraid now.”

Or:

> *Timenda res, vir fortis, jam timere noli*  
> “There is nothing to fear, brave man; do not be afraid now.”

Or even:

> *Timenda res, jam timere vir fortis noli*  
> “There is nothing to fear; do not be afraid now, brave man.”

The reason for this absurdity is that a diiamb can be marked both as a twofold and as a single unit, just as a dichory can be marked as a single and a twofold unit. A spondee, however, is equal to the twofold part of each of them. But when the diiamb draws it toward the beginning and the dichory toward the end, a certain discord arises; and thus reason removes the cause for wonder.

34. The antispast produces no less a marvel. If no other foot, or at least only a diiamb, is mixed with it, it allows the meter to close with an iamb; but when placed with others, it does not allow this at all. With a dichory, indeed, this is because of the dichory itself; therefore I am not at all surprised by it.

But why, when joined with the other feet of six time-units, it rejects at the end the foot of three time-units just mentioned, I do not know; perhaps the cause is more hidden than can be extracted and displayed by us. I prove that this is so by the following examples. No one doubts that these two meters, when repeated separately with three time-units silent at the end, are pleasant:

> *Potestate placet*  
> “It pleases by authority,”
>
> *Potestate potentium placet*  
> “It pleases by the authority of the powerful.”

But the following are unpleasant with the same silence:

> *Potestate praeclara placet*  
> “It pleases by splendid authority.”
>
> *Potestate tibi multum placet*  
> “It greatly pleases you by authority.”
>
> *Potestate jam tibi sic placet*  
> “By authority it now pleases you thus.”
>
> *Potestate multum tibi placet*  
> “By authority it greatly pleases you.”
>
> *Potestatis magnitudo placet*  
> “The greatness of authority pleases.”

As far as perception is concerned, it has performed its function in this inquiry and has shown what it accepted and what it rejected. But we must consult reason about why this is so.

My own reason [Note: [Col. 1145] Manuscript A adds *ratio* (“reason”).], in such obscurity, sees nothing other than this: the antispast shares its first half with the diiamb, since both begin with a short and a long; but it shares its second half with the dichory, since both end with a long and a short. Therefore the antispast, either alone—as possessing its own first half—or together with the diiamb, with which it shares that half, allows an iamb to be at the end of the meter. It would also allow this with a dichory if such an ending suited that same dichory. But it does not allow it with the other feet, because it is not joined to them by such a partnership. [Note: [Col. 1145] Erasmus and Lovaniensis omit the negation here, but it is present in the manuscripts and in Ambrosianus.]

## CHAPTER XVII  
### On the joining of meters

35. As for the joining of meters, for the present it is enough to see that different meters [Col. 1146] can be joined to one another, provided that they agree in their marking, that is, in lifting and placing. They are different either in quantity, as when larger meters are joined to smaller ones, as in these lines:

> *Jam satis terris nivis atque dirae*  
> “Now the Father has sent enough snow and dreadful”
>
> *Grandinis misit Pater, et rubente*  
> “hail upon the earth, and with his glowing”
>
> *Dextera sacras jaculatus arces,*  
> “right hand hurling at the sacred citadels,”
>
> *Terruit urbem.*  
> “he terrified the city.”

(Horace, Book 1 of the *Odes*, Ode 2.)

You see how small the fourth line is when placed beneath the three preceding lines, which are equal to one another: it ends with one choriamb and one long syllable.

Or they differ in their feet, as in:

> *Grato Pyrrha sub antro,*  
> “Pyrrha, beneath a pleasant cave,”
>
> *Cui flavam religas comam.*  
> “for whom you bind up your golden hair.”

(Horace, Book 1 of the *Odes*, Ode 5.)

For you see that the first of these consists of a spondee, a choriamb, and a final long syllable, which would have been owed to the spondee in order to complete six time-units; while the second consists of a spondee, a choriamb, and two final short syllables, which likewise complete six time-units together with the first spondee. These lines are therefore equal in time-units, but differ somewhat in their feet.

36. There is another difference among these combinations: some are joined in such a way that they do not want any silences inserted between them, as do these two most recently quoted; others require some silence between them, as in:

> *Vides ut alta stet nive candidum*  
> “You see how it stands white with deep snow,”
>
> *Soracte, nec jam sustineant onus*  
> “Soracte, nor can the laboring woods now bear the burden,”
>
> *Silvae laborantes, geluque*  
> “and how, with the frost,”
>
> *Flumina constiterint acuto.*  
> “the rivers have come to a halt.”

(Horace, Book 1 of the *Odes*, Ode 9.)

If these are repeated separately, the first two require one time-unit to be silent at the end, the third two, and the fourth three. But when joined, in passing from the first to the second they require one time-unit to be silent; from the second to the third, two; from the third to the fourth, three. If you return from the fourth to the first, you will leave one time-unit silent.

The same principle that governs returning to the first governs passing to another such combination. We rightly call this kind of combination a circuit, which in Greek is called *περίοδος* (*periodos*).

A circuit therefore cannot be smaller than one consisting of two members, that is, two meters; nor did they want it to be larger than one extending to four members. Thus we may call the smallest two-membered, the middle one three-membered, and the last four-membered. The Greeks call these *δίκωλον* (*dicolon*), *τρίκωλον* (*tricolon*), and *τετράκωλον* (*tetracolon*).

Since, as I said, we shall discuss this entire subject more carefully in the treatise that will deal with verses, this will suffice for the present.

37. I think you now understand that there are innumerable kinds of meters—five hundred and sixty-eight that we had discovered—although examples had been given only of final silences, no mixing of feet had been made, and no resolution of long syllables into two shorts had been introduced that would extend a foot beyond four syllables. [Note: [Col. 1146] Earlier printed editions and several manuscripts have “forty-seven that we had discovered.” But, following the Albinian manuscript, one should read “sixty-eight.” Compare Book 4, sections 15 and 16, where this is reckoned as the total number of meters.]

But if you wished to collect the number of meters by employing every possible insertion of silences, every possible mixture of feet, and every possible resolution of long syllables, the number would be so great that perhaps it would not have a name.

Yet although these examples that we have presented, and any others that can be presented, are approved by the poet in composing them and by common nature in hearing them, they cannot be judged true unless the pronunciation of a learned and [Col. 1148] practiced person commends them to the ears, and the perception of the hearers is not slower than human refinement requires. [Col. 1147] [Note: [Col. 1147] Thus the manuscripts. Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read: “Although nature both seeks them in composition and approves them in hearing.”]

But let us rest for a little while and proceed next to discuss the verse.

D. Let it be so.

# BOOK FIVE  
## In which verse is discussed

[Col. 1147]

## CHAPTER I  
### How rhythm, meter, and verse differ

1. M. What verse is was investigated among learned men with no small amount of disputation, and the effort was not fruitless. For the thing was discovered, committed to writing for the knowledge of later generations, and secured not merely by weighty and certain authority but also by reason.

They therefore observed that there is some difference between rhythm and meter, so that every meter is rhythm, but not every rhythm is meter. For every legitimate connection of feet is rhythmical; and since meter possesses this rhythmical character, it cannot in any way be without number—that is, it cannot fail to be rhythm. [Note: [Col. 1147] Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis read “is number”; the manuscripts more correctly read “is rhythmical.”]

But since it is not the same thing for a sequence to proceed through legitimate feet without being driven toward any fixed ending, and for it likewise to proceed through legitimate feet but be confined by a fixed ending, these two kinds also had to be distinguished by names. The former was therefore called simply rhythm by its proper name; the latter was called rhythm and also meter.

Again, since among those rhythms that are closed by a fixed ending—that is, among meters—some do not take into account a certain division around the middle, while others do take deliberate account of it, this difference too had to be marked by terminology. Accordingly, the kind in which this principle is not observed was properly called meter, a kind of rhythm; but the kind in which it is observed they called verse.

As we proceed, reason itself may perhaps show us the origin of this name. Do not think, however, that the rule has been laid down so strictly that it is not permissible also to call those meters verses. It is one thing to misuse a name through a certain license of proximity; it is another to express a thing by its proper term.

But let the discussion of names end here. In these matters, as we have already learned, the permission of the interlocutors [Note: [Col. 1147] “Of those speaking among themselves,” according to the Vatican manuscript.] and the authority of antiquity have complete force. Let us investigate the rest, if you please, in our customary way: perception will report, and reason will point out. In this way you will understand that those ancient authors did not institute these things as though they had not existed whole and perfect in the nature of things, but discovered them by reasoning and marked them by naming them.

## CHAPTER II  
### Meters divisible into two parts are superior to the others

2. M. Let me first ask you this: does a foot delight the ear for any reason other than that its two parts—one of which is in the lifting and the other in the placing—correspond to one another in rhythmic harmony?

D. I have already been persuaded and convinced of that.

M. What then? Since it is clear that a meter is formed by the combination of feet, should we suppose that it belongs to the class of things that cannot be divided, when absolutely nothing indivisible can extend through time, and when it would be utterly absurd to consider indivisible something composed of divisible feet?

D. I would in no way deny that this kind of thing admits division.

M. But are not all things that admit division more beautiful when their parts agree in some equality than when they are discordant and dissonant?

D. No one doubts it.

M. And what number is the source of equal division? Is it the number two?

D. It is.

M. Since, then, we have discovered that a foot can be divided into two harmonious parts and that this very division delights the ear, if we also find a meter of this kind, will it not rightly be preferred to the others that are not so divided?

D. I agree.

## CHAPTER III  
### Why verse is so called

3. M. Quite rightly. Now answer this: since in everything that we measure by some portion of time, one thing precedes and another follows, one begins and another ends, does it not seem to you that there ought to be some difference between the preceding and beginning part and the part that follows and ends? [Note: [Col. 1148] The Vatican manuscript reads “follows and ends.”]

D. I think there should be.

M. Tell me, then, what difference there is between these two parts of the verse, one of which is:

> *Cornua velatarum*  
> “The horns of the veiled [sails],”

and the other:

> *vertimus antennarum*  
> “we turned the yards.”

(*Aeneid* 3.549.)

For the poet did not say *obvertimus* (“we turned toward”), but if the verse is pronounced in this way:

> *Cornua velatarum vertimus antennarum*  
> “We turned the horns of the sails,”

does it not become uncertain, when repeated several times, which part is first and which is second? For the same verse remains no less intact when uttered in this way:

> *Vertimus antennarum cornua velatarum*  
> “We turned the sails’ horns.”

D. I plainly see that it becomes uncertain.

M. Do you think this should be avoided?

D. I do.

M. See, then, whether it has been sufficiently avoided here. One part of the verse, and the preceding part, is:

> *Arma virumque cano*  
> “I sing of arms and the man”;

the following part is:

> *Trojae qui primus ab oris*  
> “who first came from the shores of Troy.”

These differ from one another so greatly that, if you reverse their order and pronounce:

> *Trojae qui primus ab oris, arma virumque cano*  
> “Who first came from the shores of Troy, I sing of arms and the man,”

it becomes necessary to measure different feet. [Note: [Col. 1148] “Of meter,” according to the Vatican manuscript.]

D. I understand.

M. Now see whether this principle has been preserved in other cases. You recognize that the beginning part,

> *Arma virumque cano*,

has the same measure as:

> *Italiam fato*  
> “Italy by fate,”
>
> *Littora multum ille et*  
> “The shores, that man, and,”
>
> *Vi superum saevae*  
> “By the power of the gods, savage,”
>
> *Multa quoque et bello*  
> “Many things also, and in war,”
>
> *Inferretque deos*  
> “And would bring in the gods,”
>
> *Albanique patres*  
> “And the Alban fathers.”

In short, pursue the remaining examples as far as you wish: you will find these preceding parts of the verses all have the same measure, that is, are articulated after the fifth half-foot. [Note: [Col. 1148] The Vatican manuscript adds “and ended after the seventh.”]

Very rarely, if ever, is this not so, so that the following parts are likewise equal among themselves:

> *Trojae qui primus ab oris*  
> “Who first came from the shores of Troy,”
>
> *Profugus Lavinaque venit*  
> “An exile, and came to Lavinian [shores],”
>
> *Terris jactatus et alto*  
> “Tossed over lands and the deep,”
>
> *Memorem Junonis ob iram*  
> “Because of the mindful Juno’s anger,”
>
> *Passus dum conderet urbem*  
> “Having suffered until he founded the city,”
>
> *Latio genus unde Latinum*  
> “From which came the Latin race in Latium,”
>
> *Atque altae moenia Romae*  
> “And the walls of lofty Rome.”

D. It is perfectly clear.

4. M. Thus five and seven half-feet divide the heroic verse into two members, which is well known to consist of six feet of four time-units each. [Note: [Col. 1149] The Vatican manuscript reads “is most equitable.”] Without the harmonious relation of two members—whether these or any others—there is no verse.

In all such cases reason has shown that the following must be preserved: the preceding part must not be able to occupy the place of the following, nor the following that of the preceding. If this happens otherwise, it will no longer be called a verse except by an abuse of the name. It will be rhythm and meter, such as it is not unbecoming to insert occasionally among long poems woven from verses, as is the very example I mentioned shortly before:

> *Cornua velatarum vertimus antennarum*  
> “We turned the horns of the sails.”

For this reason, I do not think that verse was called so, as some believe, because it returns from a fixed ending to the beginning of the same number, so that the name was derived from those who turn around while retracing their route. For this feature is apparently shared by those meters that are not verses as well.

Rather, the name may have been found from the opposite consideration: just as grammarians called a verb “deponent” when it does not lay aside the letter *r*, as in *lucror* (“I gain”) and *conqueror* (“I complain”), so that which consists of two members, neither of which can, without violating the law of its rhythms, be placed in the position of the other, is called a verse because it cannot be reversed.

But whether you approve either of these origins of the word, reject both, seek another, or dismiss this entire kind of question along with me, it has no bearing on the present matter. Since the thing signified by this name is sufficiently clear, there is no need to labor over the root of the word.

Unless you have something to say about this.

D. Nothing at all; go on to the rest.

## CHAPTER IV  
### The ending of verses is varied

5. M. We must next inquire about the ending of a verse. For they—or rather reason itself—wanted this also to be marked and distinguished by some difference.

Do you not think it better that the ending, by which the movement of the rhythm is restrained, should stand out without disturbing the equality of the time-units, [Note: [Col. 1149] The Vatican manuscript reads “then.”] than that it should be confused with the other parts that do not make an ending?

D. Who doubts that what is more evident is better?

M. Consider, then, whether some have rightly wanted the distinctive ending of the heroic verse to be a spondaic foot. In the other five places one may use either this foot or a dactyl; at the end, however, only a spondee. For what they think is a trochee results from the indifference of the final syllable, about which we have said enough in discussing meters.

But according to these people, the iambic senarius will either not be a verse or will be a verse without this distinction of ending. Both alternatives are absurd. For no one, whether among the most learned, the moderately learned, or even the slightly educated, has ever doubted that the following is a verse:

> *Phaselus ille quem videtis hospites*  
> “That boat which you see, visitors.”

(Catullus.)

Nor has anyone doubted that whatever is formed in words with such rhythm is verse. And the most authoritative writers, precisely because they were the most expert, have judged that no verse should be considered a verse without a distinctive ending.

[Col. 1150]

6. D. You speak truly. Therefore, I think another mark of the ending must be sought, and this one, which is placed in the spondee, must not be approved.

M. What do you mean? Do you doubt that, whatever this distinction may be, it lies either in the difference of the foot, or in that of the time-unit, or in both?

D. How could it?

M. Which of these three do you approve? Since the very act of ending the verse, so that it does not run on longer than it ought, pertains only to the measure of time, I do not think that this distinction should be taken from anywhere other than time. Do you think otherwise?

D. No; I agree.

M. Do you also see that, since time here cannot have a difference except in being either longer or shorter—for when the verse ends, the aim is to prevent it from proceeding farther—the mark of the ending must lie in the shorter time?

D. I see that; but what is the relevance of the added word “here”?

M. It is relevant because we do not everywhere understand a difference of time solely in terms of shortness and length. Do you either deny that there is a difference between summer and winter in time, or do you locate it in a shorter or longer span rather than in the force of cold and heat, or of moisture and dryness, and anything else of that kind? [Note: [Col. 1150] Manuscript B reads “or dryness”; manuscript A more correctly reads “and dryness.”]

D. I understand now, and I agree that the mark of the ending that we are seeking must be derived from the shortness of time.

7. M. Consider, then, this verse:

> *Roma, Roma, cerne quanta sit deum benignitas*  
> “Rome, Rome, see how great is the benevolence of the gods,”

which is called trochaic. Measure it and tell me what you discover about its members and the number of its feet.

D. I can easily answer about the feet: it is clear that there are seven and a half. But the members are not so evident, for I see the sentence ending in many places. Nevertheless, I think the division is at the eighth half-foot, so that the preceding member is:

> *Roma, Roma, cerne quanta*  
> “Rome, Rome, see how great,”

while the following is:

> *sit deum benignitas*  
> “is the benevolence of the gods.”

M. How many half-feet does it have?

D. Seven.

M. Reason itself has led you entirely to this answer. Since nothing is better than equality, and since we ought to seek it in division, if it cannot be attained, its proximity must be sought, lest we depart too far from it.

Since this verse has fifteen half-feet, therefore, it could not be divided more equally than into eight and seven; for seven and eight are equally close to one another.

But in this way the mark of the ending would not be preserved in the shorter time, as reason itself commands that it be preserved. For if the verse were:

> *Roma cerne quanta sit tibi deum benignitas*  
> “Rome, see how great the benevolence of the gods is to you,”

the member would begin with the seven half-feet:

> *Roma cerne quanta sit*  
> “Rome, see how great it is,”

and the other would end with the eight:

> *tibi deum benignitas*  
> “the benevolence of the gods to you.”

The half-foot could not close the verse, for eight half-feet make four complete feet. At the same time another deformity would result: we would not measure the same feet in the final member as in the first, and the preceding member would rather be ended by the mark of the shorter time—that is, by a half-foot—than the following member, to which this ending properly belongs.

For in the former there would be three and a half trochees:

> *Roma cerne quanta sit*  
> “Rome, see how great it is”;

in the latter, four iambs would be scanned:

> *tibi deum benignitas*  
> “the benevolence of the gods to you.”

But as it stands, we scan trochees in both members, and the verse is closed by a half-foot, so that the ending bears the mark of the shorter span. There are four trochees in the first:

> *Roma, Roma cerne quanta*  
> “Rome, Rome, see how great”;

but in the second there are three and a half:

> *sit deum benignitas*  
> “is the benevolence of the gods.”

Are you preparing to object?

D. Not at all; I gladly agree.

8. M. Let us therefore hold these laws unshaken, if you please:

- The verse must not lack a division of its two members that tends toward equality, as this one lacks it:

  > *Cornua velatarum obvertimus antennarum*  
  > “We turned toward the sails’ horns.”

- The equality of the members must not make the division reversible, as it does in:

  > *Cornua velatarum vertimus antennarum*  
  > “We turned the horns of the sails.”

- When this reversal is avoided, the members must not depart too far from one another, but must be brought as close as possible to equality in neighboring numbers. We should not say that this can be divided so that eight half-feet come first:

  > *Cornua velatarum vertimus*  
  > “We turned the sails’ horns,”

  followed by four, namely:

  > *antennarum*  
  > “of the sails.”

- Nor should the later member have an even number of half-feet, as in:

  > *tibi deum benignitas*  
  > “the benevolence of the gods to you,”

  lest a verse ending with a complete foot lack an ending marked by the shorter time.

D. I now understand these principles and will commit them to memory as far as I can.

## CHAPTER V  
### The ending of the heroic verse

9. M. Since we now hold that a verse ought not to end with a complete foot, how do you think the heroic verse should be measured, so that both that law of the members and this mark of the ending may be preserved?

D. I see that it has twelve half-feet. Since, in order to avoid reversal, the members cannot have six half-feet each, and since they ought not to be too far apart so as to be divided into three and nine or nine and three, nor should the later member be given an even number of half-feet, so that they would be eight and four or four and eight and the verse would end with a complete foot, the division must be into five and seven or seven and five.

For both these numbers are odd and adjacent, and the members approach one another more closely than they would in the numbers four and eight.

To hold this as firmly as possible, I see that the sentence always, or almost always, ends at the fifth half-foot, as in Virgil’s first verse:

> *Arma virumque cano*  
> “I sing of arms and the man”;

and in the second:

> *Italiam fato*  
> “Italy by fate”;

and in the third:

> *Littora multum ille et*  
> “The shores, that man, and”;

in the fourth likewise:

> *Vi superum saevae*  
> “By the power of the gods, savage”;
