and so through almost the entire poem.

M. You speak truly. But you must consider which feet you are measuring, so that you do not dare to violate any of the laws already firmly established.

D. Although reason is sufficiently clear to me, I am disturbed by the novelty. [Note: [Col. 1151] “Which,” according to the Vatican manuscript.] In this kind of verse we are accustomed to scan only a spondee and a dactyl, something almost no one is so uneducated that he has not heard, even if he is less able to do it.

If I now choose to follow this widespread custom, that law of the ending must be abolished: the preceding member would be closed by a half-foot, but the later one by a complete foot, whereas the reverse ought to be the case. [Note: [Col. 1151] Vatican: “That law of the ending must be abolished.”] But since it would be utterly unjust to abolish that law, and since I have already learned that in rhythm it is possible to begin from a non-complete foot, [Note: [Col. 1151] Vatican: “that we do not begin from a complete foot.”] it remains for us to judge that here an anapest, not a dactyl, is placed with the spondee.

Thus the verse begins with one long syllable; then two feet, either spondees or anapests or alternating feet, [Col. 1152] end the upper member; [Note: [Col. 1152] Vatican and manuscript A: “or anapests or alternating”; manuscript B: “or anapests, the other member.”] then three feet again—either anapests or, in any position, spondees, or all of them spondees—and finally one syllable, by which the verse is properly ended. [Note: [Col. 1152] Manuscript B reads “when”; Vatican, “while”; manuscript A, “then.”]

Do you approve this as well?

10. M. I too judge it entirely correct, but it will not easily be persuaded to the common people. For custom has such force that, when it has grown old from a false opinion, nothing is more hostile to truth.

You understand that for composing a verse it makes no difference whether an anapest or a dactyl is placed with a spondee in this kind of verse. But for measuring it rationally—which belongs not to the ears but to the mind—this is distinguished by true and certain reason, not by an irrational opinion. [Note: [Col. 1152] The older manuscripts have: “which belongs not to the ears but to the mind, and by how much this reason is distinguished from that opinion.” The Vatican manuscript reads: “This reason is very much distinguished from that opinion.”]

Nor has this now been discovered by us for the first time; it was noticed long before this established custom. [Note: [Col. 1152] Thus the Vatican manuscript: “But this was noticed by the ancients long before the established custom.”]

Therefore, if people read those who were most learned in this discipline, whether in Greek or Latin, they will not be excessively surprised if they happen to hear this. Yet it is shameful weakness when human authority is sought to strengthen reason, since nothing ought to be superior to the authority of reason and truth itself, which is certainly better than any human being.

For when we lengthen or shorten a syllable, we seek the authority of ancient speakers, using words as they used them, because in such a matter it is laziness not to follow any established practice, while instituting a new one is license. But in measuring a verse, it is not the long-established human preference that must be considered, but the eternal reason of things.

We first naturally perceive by the ear the measured length of the verse; then we approve it by rational consideration of its rhythms. Anyone who judges with certainty that it must be closed by a distinctive ending also judges that it must be ended more decisively than other meters, and it is clear that this ending must be marked in a shorter time, since this shorter time restrains and, as it were, reins in the length of the time-unit. [Note: [Col. 1152] Lovaniensis reads: “Anyone who judges with certainty that it must be ended more distinctly than other meters, which has an ending marked in a shorter span of time, as is clear.” Other editions likewise differ, except that Ambrosianus has “marked, as is clear”; Erasmus has “of the marked time, as is clear.” The manuscript reading restored here is preferable.]

## CHAPTER VI  
### Again concerning the ending of the verse

11. Since this is so, how can its later member end except with a non-complete foot? The beginning of the preceding member, however, must be either a complete foot, as in the trochaic verse:

> *Roma, Roma, cerne quanta sit deum benignitas*  
> “Rome, Rome, see how great is the benevolence of the gods,”

or a part of a foot, as in the heroic:

> *Arma virumque cano, Trojae qui primus ab oris*  
> “I sing of arms and the man who first came from the shores of Troy.”

Therefore, with every doubt removed, measure this verse as well, if you please, and tell me about its members and feet:

> *Phaselus ille quem videtis, hospites*  
> “That boat which you see, visitors.”

D. I see that its members are divided into five and seven half-feet, so that the first is:

> *Phaselus ille*  
> “That boat,”

and the second:

> *quem videtis, hospites*  
> “which you see, visitors.”

But I recognize the feet as iambs.

[Col. 1153]

M. Are you taking care not to end the verse with a complete foot?

D. You speak truly; I do not know where I was. Who would not see that, as in the heroic verse, one must begin with a half-foot? When this happens in this kind of verse, we measure it not with iambs but with trochees, so that a half-foot may properly close it.

12. M. It is as you say. But consider what you should answer about this verse, which they call Asclepiadic:

> *Maecenas atavis edite regibus*  
> “Maecenas, descended from ancestral kings.”

(Horace, Book 1 of the *Odes*, Ode 1.)

The sentence ends at the sixth syllable, not inconsistently but in almost all verses of this kind. Thus its first member is:

> *Maecenas atavis*  
> “Maecenas, from ancestral [kings]”;

the second:

> *edite regibus*  
> “descended from kings.”

By what method this division is made may be questioned. For if you measure the feet here as four time-units, there will be five in the first member but four half-feet in the second. Yet the law forbids the later member to consist of an even number of half-feet, lest the verse end with a complete foot.

It remains, then, to consider feet of six time-units. From this it follows that each member consists of three half-feet. For the preceding member is to end with a complete foot, so it must begin with two long syllables. Then the whole choriamb divides the verse, so that the later member also begins with another choriamb and the verse closes with a half-foot consisting of two short syllables. Together with the spondee placed at the beginning, these complete a foot of six time-units.

Unless you have something to say about this.

D. Nothing at all.

M. Then do you approve that each member consists of the same number of half-feet?

D. Why should I not? For here there is no need to fear that reversal: if the later member were placed in the position of the preceding one, so that what is first became second, the same law of the feet would not remain. Therefore there is no reason why the same number of half-feet should be denied to the members in this kind of verse, since this equality can be maintained without any defect of reversal, while the law of the more distinctive ending is also preserved, since the verse does not end with a complete foot. This must be observed with complete consistency. [Note: [Col. 1153] All editions and manuscript A read: “It is entirely pleasing that it must be observed.”]

## CHAPTER VII  
### How the inequality of half-feet in the members of verses is referred to equality  
### The members of four and three half-feet are reconciled  
### Members of five and three half-feet

13. M. You have seen the matter itself perfectly. Since reason has now established that there are two kinds of verses—one in which the members have the same number of half-feet, and another in which they have unequal numbers—let us carefully consider, if you please, how this inequality of half-feet is referred to a certain kind of equality by a somewhat obscure but certainly very subtle principle of numbers. [Note: [Col. 1153] The Vatican manuscript reads “nevertheless” instead of “but certainly.”]

For I ask you: when I say two and three, how many numbers am I saying?

D. Two, obviously.

M. Therefore two is one number and three is one number, and the same may be said of any other number.

D. That is so.

M. Does it not seem to you from this that one can not unreasonably be compared with any number? For we could not say that one is two, but we can in a certain sense say that two is one; and likewise it can correctly be said that three and four are one.

D. I agree.

M. Consider another point. Tell me: two multiplied by three—what is the total?

[Col. 1154]

D. Six.

M. Are six and three equal in number?

D. Not at all.

M. Now I want you to multiply three by four and give me the total.

D. Twelve.

M. You see that twelve is likewise greater than four.

D. And greatly so.

M. To avoid delay, a rule must now be established: [Note: [Col. 1154] Restored from manuscript A. Manuscript B reads: “And greatly. M. Indeed, that I may not delay.”] from two onward, whenever you take any two numbers, the greater multiplied by the lesser must exceed the lesser.

D. Who could doubt this? For what is so small among plural numbers as two? Yet if I multiply that number a thousand times, it will exceed one thousand so that it becomes twice as much.

M. You speak truly. But set down one and then any larger number, and multiply the lesser by the greater as we did in those cases. Will the greater be exceeded in the same way?

D. Not exactly; rather, the lesser will equal the greater. One multiplied by two is two; one multiplied by ten is ten; one multiplied by a thousand is a thousand; and whatever other number I multiply it by, one must always produce that same number.

M. One therefore possesses a certain right of equality with the other numbers—not merely because every number is one, [Note: [Col. 1154] “Of whatever number,” according to the Vatican manuscript.] but also because when multiplied by any number it produces exactly that amount.

D. It is perfectly clear.

14. M. Come now, turn your mind to the numbers of half-feet by which unequal members are formed in verse, and by the method we have discussed you will find a remarkable kind of equality. For, as I think, the shortest verse whose members contain an unequal number of half-feet consists of two members, having four and three half-feet, as in this example: “That stranger whom you see” (*Hospes ille quem vides*). Its first member, “That stranger” (*Hospes ille*), can be divided equally into two parts of two half-feet each; the second, “whom you see” (*quem vides*), is divided so that one part has two half-feet and the other one. This is as though there were two and two, by that law of equality which we have sufficiently discussed, whereby one has a relation of equality with all numbers. Thus, by this division, the earlier member is in a certain sense equal in value to the later one.

Accordingly, where there are four and five half-feet, as in “Rome, Rome, see how great it is” (*Roma, Roma, cerne quanta sit*), observe how much less satisfactory it is. It will therefore be a meter rather than a verse, because its members are so unequal that they cannot, by any division, be referred to any law of equality. You see, I think, that the four half-feet of the first member, “Rome, Rome,” can be divided into two pairs [Note: [Col. 1154] “Divided” (*discindere*), according to the Vatican manuscript. M.]; but the five half-feet of the second member, “see how great it is,” can be divided into two and three, where no equality appears by any law. For five half-feet cannot in any way, on account of the two and three, be worth as much as four, as we found above in the shorter verse that three half-feet, because of the one and two, were worth as much as four. Have you failed to grasp something, or are you dissatisfied?

D. On the contrary, everything is clear and satisfactory.

15. M. Come, let us now consider five and three half-feet, as in the little verse “That little ship whom you see” (*Phaselus ille quem vides*), and let us see how this inequality is held together by some law of equality. For everyone agrees that this form is not only a meter but also a verse. When, then, you divide the first member into two and three half-feet, and the second into two and one, join together the portions that you find equal in the two members [Note: [Col. 1155] So the Vatican manuscript: “joining the portions which you find on either side.” M.]. For in the first member we have two, and in the second two portions remain: one in the three half-feet of the first member, the other in the one half-foot of the second. We therefore join these together as well, in a mutually associating union, because one has fellowship with all numbers [Note: [Col. 1155] “A mutual fellowship” (*consocietatem*), according to the Vatican manuscript. M.]. In the total, one and three make four, which is equal to two and two. By this division, therefore, the five and three half-feet are also brought into harmony. But answer me: have you understood?

D. Indeed I have, and I approve it thoroughly.

## CHAPTER VIII — Members of Five and Seven Half-Feet

16. M. It remains for us to discuss five and seven half-feet, such as those two most celebrated verses, the heroic and the one commonly called iambic, which is itself also a senarius. Thus “I sing of arms and the man, who first from the shores of Troy” (*Arma virumque cano, Trojae qui primus ab oris*) is divided so that its first member is “I sing of arms and the man,” which contains five half-feet, and its second is “who first from the shores of Troy,” which contains seven half-feet. Likewise, “That little ship whom you see, guests” (*Phaselus ille quem videtis, hospites*) has “That little ship” (*Phaselus ille*) as its first member, in five half-feet, and “whom you see, guests” (*quem videtis, hospites*) as its second, in seven.

But this great distinction is troubled by the law of equality. When we divide the first five half-feet into two and three, and the later seven into three and four, the portions of three half-feet correspond to one another. But if the two remaining portions corresponded in such a way that one consisted of one half-foot and the other of five, they could be joined by that law according to which one can be joined with every number; together they would make six, which is also what three and three make. As it is, however, since two and four are found, they do indeed produce a total of six, but by no law of equality are two worth as much as four, so that they may be joined together in a relationship of this kind.

Unless perhaps someone should say that it is sufficient for some rule of equality that, just as three and three make six, so two and four also make six. I do not think that this reasoning should be rejected, for this too is some kind of equality. But I would not want five and three half-feet to be joined with greater agreement than five and seven. For the reputation of that verse is not as great as that of these; and you see that in the former not only is a total found, by combining one and three, equal to that found in two and two, but the parts are also much more harmonious when one and three are joined together, because of the affinity of one with all other numbers, than when two and four are joined, as happens in these.

Is anything unclear to you?

D. Nothing at all. But I do not know why it troubles me that these senarii, although more celebrated than the other forms and said to hold a certain primacy among verses, possess somewhat less in the harmony of their members than those verses of less familiar renown.

M. Take heart. I shall show you in them a harmony so great that they alone among all verses deserved to possess it, so that you may see that they were preferred with good reason. [Col. 1156] But since the treatment itself is somewhat longer, although altogether more agreeable, it should remain for the end, so that after we have discussed the others as much as seems sufficient, and are now freed from every other concern, we may come to examine their innermost structure.

D. I am pleased with that; but I already wish that what we undertook earlier had been explained, so that I might now hear about this more readily.

M. By comparison with what we discussed earlier, those matters that you expect will become sweeter.

## CHAPTER IX — Members of Six and Seven Half-Feet; Members of Eight and Seven Half-Feet; Members of Nine and Seven Half-Feet

17. Now, then, consider whether in two members, the first of which contains six half-feet and the other seven, that equality can be found which would properly make them a verse. You see that this must be examined after five and seven half-feet. An example of it is: “Rome, see how great is the kindness of the gods” (*Roma, cerne quanta sit deum benignitas*) [Note: [Col. 1156] In B: “Rome, Rome, see how great is the kindness of the gods” (*Roma, Roma, cerne quanta sit deum benignitas*), an erroneous repetition of the word “Rome,” since it grants eight half-feet to the first member and seven to the second, which conflicts with the explanation Augustine gives shortly afterward. M.].

D. I see that the first member can be divided into parts containing three half-feet each, and the second into three and four. Thus, when the equal parts are joined, there are six half-feet; but three and four make seven, and they are not equal to that number. But if we consider two and two in the part where there are four, and two and one in the part where there are three, the joining of the parts that contain two each produces a total of four. When, however, those parts are joined, of which one contains two and the other one, if we also treat these as though they were four, because of the harmony of one with all other numbers, eight are produced together, and they exceed the total of six even more than when there had been seven.

18. M. It is as you say. Therefore, setting this kind of combination apart from the law of verses, attend, as the order requires, to those members of which the first has eight half-feet and the second seven. This combination does contain what we are seeking. For, joining half of the preceding member with the larger part of the following member, which is closest to a half, since there are four half-feet in each, I make a total of eight. There remain, therefore, four half-feet from the first member and three from the second. Two from one side and two from the other, joined together, make four. Again, the two remaining on the one side and the one on the other, joined according to that law of correspondence by which one is equal, in a certain sense, to the rest, are taken for four. Thus the upper eight corresponds to the lower eight.

D. But why do I not hear an example of this?

M. Because it has often been mentioned. Nevertheless, so that you do not think it was omitted in its proper place, it is this: “Rome, Rome, see how great is the kindness of the gods”; or also this: “That excellent blessed man who is far from business” (*Optimus beatus ille qui procul negotio*).

19. Now examine the connection of nine and seven half-feet, an example of which is: “The excellent blessed man who is far from business” (*Vir optimus beatus ille qui procul negotio*).

D. This correspondence is easy to understand. The first member is divided into four and five half-feet, and the second into three and four. The smaller part of the first, joined with the larger part of the second, makes eight; and the larger part of the first with the smaller part of the second likewise makes eight. For the former combination is four and four half-feet, and the latter five and three.

To this is added the fact that, if you divide five into two and three half-feet, and three into two and one, another correspondence appears: that of two with two, and of one with three, because one is joined with all numbers according to the law mentioned earlier. But unless my reasoning deceives me, nothing further remains for us to seek concerning the combination of members. We have now reached eight feet, and, as we have sufficiently learned, a verse is not permitted to exceed that number. Come, then, disclose the secrets of those senarii, the heroic and the iambic or trochaic, with which you both aroused and delayed my eagerness.

## CHAPTER X — The Excellence of Senarian Verses: They Are Most Appropriate Only When Heroic or Iambic

20. M. I shall do so—or rather, reason itself will do so, the reason common to you and me. But do you remember, please, that when we were discussing meters we said, and approved by our own judgment, that those feet whose parts stand in sesquialteral proportion—whether in two and three, as in the cretic and the paeons, or in three and four, as in the epitrites—were excluded by poets because of their less pleasing sound, but were more suitably employed to adorn the severity of prose when clauses were joined with them?

D. I remember. But what does this concern?

M. I want us first to understand that, once feet of this kind have been excluded from the poets’ treatment, only those remain whose parts correspond to an equal total, as in the spondee; or to a double, as in the iamb; or to both, as in the choriamb. 

D. That is so.

M. But if this is the material of poets, and prose is hostile to verse, no verse should be made except from this class of feet.

D. I agree. I see that poems become grander in verses than in the other meters of lyric poets, but I do not yet understand where this reasoning is leading.

21. M. Do not hurry. We are now discussing the excellence of senarian verses, and first I wish, if I can, to demonstrate to you that the most appropriate senarii can belong only to these two forms, which are also the most celebrated of all. One is the heroic, as in “I sing of arms and the man, who first from the shores of Troy,” which ordinary usage measures by spondees and dactyls, while subtler reasoning measures it by spondees and anapaests. The other is what is called iambic, and by the same reasoning the trochaic form is found.

For I believe it is clear to you that long syllables, unless short ones are interposed, somehow dull the intervals of sound; and that short syllables, unless long ones are interposed, become too clipped and almost trembling. Neither arrangement is properly tempered, even though by equality of duration they fill the ears. [Note: [Col. 1157] “Fill” (*impleantur*), according to the Vatican manuscript.] Accordingly, neither verses containing six pyrrhichs or six proceleusmatics aspire to the dignity of the heroic, nor those containing six tribrachs to that of the trochaic.

Furthermore, in those forms that reason itself prefers to the others, if you reverse the members, everything will be changed in such a way that we must necessarily scan different feet as well. They are therefore, so to speak, less reversible than those composed entirely of short syllables or entirely of long ones. And so, whether the members in these more temperate forms are arranged as five and seven or as seven and five half-feet, it makes no difference: in neither arrangement can the verse be reversed without such a great change that it seems to proceed in different feet.

In the other forms, however, if a poem has begun with verses whose first members contain five half-feet, the poet should not mix in verses whose first members contain seven, lest it no longer be possible to reverse them all; for no change of feet prevents reversal. Nevertheless, heroic verses are allowed, though very rarely, to insert all spondees—a practice that our later age has by no means approved. In trochaic or iambic verses, although it is permitted to insert a tribrach in any position, it has nevertheless been judged most disgraceful in such poems to have a verse consisting entirely of short syllables.

22. After the epitrite feet have therefore been removed from the law of the senarian verse—not only because they are better suited to prose, but also because, if there are six of them, they exceed thirty-two durations, like the dispondees—and after the five-duration feet have likewise been removed, since prose has more willingly claimed them for clausulae; and after the molossi and other six-duration feet have also been excluded from the number of durations now under discussion, although they flourish most elegantly in poems—there remain verses of entirely short syllables, containing pyrrhichs, proceleusmatics, or tribrachs, and verses of entirely long syllables, containing spondees.

Although these are admitted to the senarian measure, they must nevertheless yield to the dignity and balance of those verses that vary long and short syllables, and which for that reason are much less capable of being reversed.

## CHAPTER XI — How Senarian Verses Are More Conveniently Scanned

23. But one may ask why those verses are judged better in which that subtler reasoning scans an anapaest, and those in which it scans a trochee, than if it scanned a dactyl in the former and an iamb in the latter. Without prejudice to the opinion—for we are now discussing numbers—if the verse were arranged as follows:

“Who first from the shores of Troy, I sing of arms and the man”  
(*Trojae qui primus ab oris arma virumque cano*)

or, from the other form:

“That blessed man who is far from evil”  
(*Qui procul malo pius beatus ille*),

each of these would be no less a senarius, no less governed by a balanced arrangement of short and long syllables, and no more capable of reversal. In each, moreover, the members are so arranged that a division of the words occurs at both the fifth and seventh half-foot. Why, then, should these be considered better if they are arranged instead as follows?

“I sing of arms and the man, who first from the shores of Troy”  
(*Arma virumque cano, Trojae qui primus ab oris*)

and:

“That blessed man who is far from evil”  
(*Beatus ille qui procul pius malo*)?

In answer to this question, I might more readily and plausibly say that it happened that these forms were noticed and used first [Note: [Col. 1158] In B: “or used more frequently.” The Vatican manuscript and manuscript A have “and used more frequently.” M.]; or, if this was not accidental, I believe it seemed preferable for the heroic verse to end with two long syllables rather than with two short syllables and a long one, because the ears more comfortably come to rest on long syllables. The other form, however, would preferably have a long rather than a short syllable in its final half-foot.

The situation is in fact such that whichever of these forms were chosen first would necessarily deprive the others of a place—those others that could be produced by reversing the same members. Therefore, if the form whose example is “I sing of arms and the man, who first from the shores of Troy” was judged better, it would be inept to produce by reversing it another form, such as “Who first from the shores of Troy, I sing of arms and the man.” The same must be understood of the trochaic form. For if “That blessed man who is far from business” is more honorable, the form produced by reversing it—“Who is far from business, that blessed man”—ought not to be made [Note: [Col. 1159] In B: “ought not to have been made.” The Vatican manuscript has “ought not to be made.” M.]. Nevertheless, if anyone dares to make such verses, it is clear that he will be producing other kinds of senarii, with respect to which these are superior.

24. These, then, the most beautiful of all senarii, could not both preserve their purity against human license. In the trochaic form, poets thought that not only in the senarius, but from the point where it begins with less than a full foot up to the greatest length, which has eight feet, all four-duration feet used in rhythmic composition should be intermingled. The Greeks, indeed, place these longer feet in alternating positions: first and third, and so on, if the verse begins with a half-foot; but if it begins with a complete trochee, in the second and fourth positions, and so on, preserving the intervals.

To make this corruption tolerable, they did not divide each individual foot by clapping into two parts, one of raising and the other of lowering; instead, they raised one foot and lowered another. Hence they referred the clapping of the senarius trimeter itself to the division of the epitrites. But if at least this practice had been maintained consistently, although epitrite feet are more suited to prose than to poetry, and although what would then be found would no longer be a senarian but a ternary verse, the equality of the rhythms would not have been entirely undermined.

As it is, however, provided they are placed in the positions mentioned, it is permitted to insert not merely all the four-duration feet, but whichever of them one wishes, wherever and as often as one wishes. Our own ancient poets were unable even to preserve the intervals between the positions when intermingling feet of this kind. Accordingly, in this form poets clearly achieved, through corruption and license, what they must be thought to have desired: that their poems in dramatic works should be as similar as possible to prose.

But since enough has been said about why these verses have acquired greater renown among senarii, let us now see why the senarii themselves are better verses than the others composed in any other number of feet—unless you have some objection to what I have argued.

D. I agree entirely. And I am eagerly awaiting the opportunity, if it is now permitted, to understand that equality of members to which you recently made me especially attentive.

## CHAPTER XII — Why Senarian Verses Are Superior to Others

25. M. Give me your full attention, then, and answer this: does it seem to you that any length can be divided into any number of parts?

D. I have been sufficiently persuaded of this, and I do not think it can be doubted that every length called a line has a half-part of itself [Note: [Col. 1159] “Has a measured part,” according to the Vatican manuscript. M.], and therefore can be divided crosswise into two lines. Since the two lines produced by this division are themselves undoubtedly lines, it is also clear that the same thing can be done in them. Thus any length, however small, can be divided into any number of parts.

M. Most readily and most truly. Now consider whether it is correctly asserted that every length extending toward a breadth arising from it is worth as much as the square occupied by that breadth. For if the extension into breadth is less or greater than the length of the line from which it proceeds, a square is not formed; but if it is equal, nothing other than a square is formed.

D. I understand and agree. What could be truer?

M. You now see, I think, what follows: if equal counters arranged lengthwise in a line are placed in place of the line, that length does not reach a square form unless the counters are multiplied by the same number. Thus, if you place two counters, you do not make a square unless two others are added breadthwise. If you place three, six must be added, distributed in two rows of three in the breadth [Note: [Col. 1160] “In the breadth,” according to the Vatican manuscript. M.]. For if they are added to the length, no figure is formed. Length without breadth is not a figure [Note: [Col. 1160] “Is not a formation,” according to the Vatican manuscript. M.].

In this way one may consider other numbers proportionally. Just as twice two and three times three form square figures in numbers, so four times four, five times five, six times six, and so on to infinity.

D. These points too are established and clear.

M. Now consider whether there is some length of time.

D. Who could doubt that no time exists without some length?

M. What then? Can a verse fail to possess some length of time?

D. On the contrary, it must possess one.

M. What shall we place in that length in place of counters more suitably: feet, which are necessarily divided into two parts, that is, raising and lowering [Note: [Col. 1160] “Are distributed,” according to manuscript A. M.]; or rather the half-feet themselves, which each possess a single raising or lowering?

D. I judge that half-feet are more suitably placed in the position of those counters.

26. M. Come, now recall how many half-feet the shorter member of the heroic verse contains.

D. Five.

M. Give an example.

D. “I sing of arms and the man” (*Arma virumque cano*).

M. Do you then desire anything other than that seven half-feet should correspond with these five according to some equality?

D. Nothing else at all.

M. What then? Can seven half-feet by themselves complete a verse?

D. Certainly they can. For the first and shortest verse has that many half-feet, if the silence at the end is counted.

M. You speak correctly. But how is it divided into two members so that it can be a verse?

D. Into four and three half-feet, of course.

M. Apply each of these parts to the law of the square, and see what four times four produces.

D. Sixteen.

M. And three times three?

D. Nine.

M. And the total together?

D. Twenty-five.

M. Since, therefore, seven half-feet can have two members, and each member, referred to the rule of squares, yields its square, they produce in total the number twenty-five; and this is one part of the heroic verse.

D. That is so.

M. The other part, then, which contains five half-feet, since it cannot be divided into two members [Col. 1161] and must correspond by some equality, must it not be taken as a whole into a square?

D. I think nothing else at all, and at last I recognize the astonishing equality. For five multiplied by five likewise completes twenty-five. It is therefore not without reason that senarian verses have become more celebrated and renowned than the others. It is scarcely possible to say how great is the difference between their equality in unequal members and that of all other verses.

## CHAPTER XIII — Epilogue

27. Your expectation, then—or rather reason itself, which both of us follow—has not deceived you. Therefore, to bring this discussion to a conclusion at last, you surely see that although meters are almost innumerable, a verse cannot exist unless it consists either of two members harmoniously corresponding to one another, or is bounded by an equal number of half-feet that are not reversible, as in “Maecenas, descended from ancient kings” (*Maecenas atavis edite regibus*); or with an unequal number of half-feet nevertheless joined by some equality, as in four and three, five and three, five and seven, six and seven, eight and seven, or seven and nine.

A trochaic verse can begin with a complete foot, as in “That excellent blessed man who is far from business” (*Optimus beatus ille qui procul negotio*), and it can also begin with an incomplete foot, as in “The excellent blessed man who is far from business” (*Vir optimus beatus ille qui procul negotio*); but a verse absolutely cannot end except with an incomplete foot.

These incomplete feet, whether they contain complete half-feet, as in the example just given; or less than half a foot, as in the two final short syllables of that choriambic verse, “Maecenas, descended from ancient kings”; or more than half a foot, as in the two first long syllables at its beginning, or in the final bacchius of another choriambic verse, whose example is “Your house, Evander, your lofty seat of Latinus” (*Te domus Evandri, te sedes celsa Latini*) [Note: [Col. 1161] “Your house of Evander” (*Te domus Evandrea*), according to Erasmus; “of Evandria” (*Evandria*), according to Lovaniensis. M.]. [Note: [Col. 1161] Terentianus places this verse among the phalecians.] All these incomplete feet are therefore called half-feet.

[Col. 1162] 28. Poems are not made only in such a way that a single form is maintained throughout, as in the works of epic poets or even comic poets. The larger periods, which the Greeks call *periodoi* (περίοδοι), are made by lyric poets not only in those meters that are not governed by the law of verse, but also in verses.

Here is one by Flaccus:

> It was night, and the moon shone in a cloudless sky  
> Among the lesser stars.  
> (*Nox erat, et caelo fulgebat luna sereno  
> Inter minora sidera.*)  
> (Horace, *Epodes* 15)

This is a two-member period, consisting of verses. These two verses cannot correspond to one another unless each is referred to six-foot measure. For the heroic measure does not harmonize with the iambic or trochaic measure, because the feet of the former divide their parts into equal amounts, while those of the latter divide them into double amounts.

Periods are therefore made either entirely from meters without verses, such as those discussed in the preceding book when we were treating the meters themselves; or entirely from verses, such as those just mentioned; or from a mixture of verses and other meters [Note: [Col. 1162] So manuscript A: “Or they are balanced by verses and other meters.” M.], as in this example:

> The snows have fled; now the grass returns to the fields,  
> And the foliage to the trees.  
> (*Diffugere nives, redeunt iam gramina campis,  
> Arboribusque comae.*)  
> (The same author, *Book 4 of the Odes*, Ode 7.)

As for the order in which verses are placed with other meters, or larger members with smaller ones, it makes no difference to the pleasure of the ears, provided that the period is neither shorter than a two-member period nor longer than a four-member period.

But now, if you have no objection, let this discussion come to an end, so that henceforth, concerning that part of music which lies in the durations of rhythms, we may advance from these sensible traces of it, with as much acumen as we possess, to its very inner chambers, where it is separate from every bodily thing.

# BOOK SIX

In this book the mind is raised from consideration of mutable numbers in lower things to immutable numbers, which exist in immutable truth itself.

[Col. 1161]

## CHAPTER I — The Purpose and Audience of the Earlier Books

[Col. 1161]

1. M. For almost five books—indeed, quite plainly, in a rather childish fashion—we have lingered over the traces of numbers that pertain to temporal durations. Our frivolous undertaking may perhaps readily be excused among kindly disposed people by the dutiful labor involved. We thought it ought to be undertaken for no other reason than that adolescents, or people of any age whom God has endowed with good intelligence, might not be torn away too hastily, but by certain stages and under the guidance of reason, from the senses of the flesh and from those carnal letters to which it is difficult for them not to cling; and that they might adhere through love of immutable truth to the one God and Lord of all things, who presides over human minds without any intervening nature.

Whoever reads those books will find that we have moved among grammatical and poetic minds, not by choice of dwelling but by necessity of travel. When he comes to this book, however, if—as I hope and humbly beseech—our God and Lord has guided my purpose and will and brought them to the goal toward which they are directed, he will understand that the road to a possession of great value is not itself contemptible. On that road we have now preferred to walk with the weaker, without pretending that we ourselves are especially strong, rather than cast those less winged headlong through freer air.

Thus, I think, he will judge that we have committed either no fault or not much fault, provided that he is one of the spiritual people. For if the rest of the crowd, emerging from schools of clamorous languages and rejoicing with vulgar frivolity at the noise of applause, should happen upon these writings, it will either despise them all or judge that the five books are sufficient for it. But this book, in which the fruit of those books is found, it will either cast aside as unnecessary or postpone as something necessary only later.

Those, however, who are not trained to understand these matters, if they are imbued with the sacraments of Christian purity [Note: [Col. 1163] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “imbued with truth”; but the manuscripts, with Ambrosius, have “imbued with purity.” M.], and, striving with the greatest love toward the one true God, have flown over all childish matters, I fraternally warn not to descend to these things and, once they begin to labor here, complain of their slowness. They do not know that by flying they can pass even over difficult and troublesome roads that would burden their feet, including roads they have not learned.

But if those are reading who can neither walk here with weak or untrained steps nor fly over these matters because they possess no wings of piety, let them not involve themselves in an unsuitable undertaking. Rather, let them nourish wings through the precepts of the most health-giving religion and in the nest of Christian faith, so that, borne aloft by them, they may escape the toil and dust of this journey, burning with love more for the homeland itself than for the winding roads.

For these writings are intended for those who, devoted to secular learning, are entangled in great errors and wear out good intelligence on trifles, not knowing what delights them there. If they noticed this, they would see how they might escape those nets and where the place of the most blessed security might be found.

## CHAPTER II — The Various Kinds of Numbers in Sound, and Whether Each Can Exist Without the Others. The First Kind of Numbers in the Sound Itself. The Second Kind in the Sense of the Hearer

2. M. You, then, with whom I am now reasoning, my friend, answer me, if you please. Since we are moving from bodily things to incorporeal ones, when we pronounce this verse, “God, creator of all” (*Deus creator omnium*), where do you think the four iambs of which it consists, and its twelve durations, exist? Are they only in the sound that is heard, or also in the sense of the hearer that pertains to the ears, or also in the action of the person pronouncing it, or, because it is a familiar verse, must we also acknowledge these numbers to be in our memory?

D. I think they are in all these things.

M. Nowhere else?

D. I do not see what else could remain, unless perhaps there is some inner and higher power from which these things proceed [Note: [Col. 1163] “There is,” according to manuscript A. M.].

M. I am not asking what one ought to conjecture. Therefore, if these four kinds appear to you to be such that you see no other equally evident kind, let us distinguish them from one another, if you please, and see whether each can exist without the others.

For I believe you will not deny that it can happen that somewhere there is a sound of this kind, striking the air with such intervals and durations, whether by dripping water or by some other impact of bodies, where no hearer is present. When this happens, apart from that first kind—in which the sound itself possesses these numbers—is any of the other four kinds found?

D. I see none.

3. M. What of the second, which is in the sense of the hearer? Can it exist if nothing sounds? I am not asking whether those ears possess the power of perceiving if something should sound—for they certainly do not lack it when there is no sound. For even in silence they differ in no respect from deaf ears. Rather, I am asking whether they possess the numbers themselves, even if nothing sounds.

For it is one thing to possess numbers and another to be able to perceive a sound that has rhythm. If you touch with your finger a bodily place that is capable of sensation, however many times it is touched, that many times the rhythm of the touch is perceived; and when it is perceived, the perceiving faculty does not lack that rhythm. But whether the number is present even when nothing touches it—that is what we are asking in the same way.

D. I would not easily say that the sense lacks such numbers established in itself, even before anything sounds. For otherwise it could not be either soothed by their harmony or offended by their discord. Whatever that is by which we assent or recoil, not by reason but by nature, when something sounds, I call the number of the sense itself. For this power of approving and disapproving does not arise in my ears at the moment when I hear a sound. Ears are equally open to good and bad sounds.

M. Consider rather whether these two should not be kept entirely distinct. If any verse is pronounced now more shortly and now more lengthily, the span of time it occupies must differ, even though the same arrangement of feet is preserved. Thus, for the ears to be soothed by its own kind, there is that power by which we accept harmonious things and reject discordant ones. But for it to be perceived in a shorter time when it is produced more quickly than when it is produced more slowly, nothing is relevant except how long the ears are touched by the sound.

This affection of the ears, therefore, when they are touched by a sound, is in no way the same as it would be if they were not touched. For just as hearing differs from not hearing, so hearing this sound differs from hearing another. This affection therefore neither extends beyond nor falls short of the sound, since it is the measure of the sound that produces it.

One affection is therefore present in an iamb and another in a tribrach; it is longer in a longer iamb and shorter in a shorter one; it is absent in silence. If it is produced by a rhythmic voice, it must itself also be rhythmic. Nor can it exist unless the sound that produces it is present. It resembles a footprint impressed in water, which is not formed before the body has pressed upon it and does not remain after the body has been removed.

But that natural power, as it were judicial, which is present to the ears, does not cease to exist in silence. The sound does not bring it to us; rather, the sound—whether it is to be approved or disapproved—is received by it. Therefore these two things, unless I am mistaken, must be distinguished. We must acknowledge that the numbers present in the very affection of the ears when something is heard are brought in by sound and removed by silence.

From this it follows that the numbers present in the sound itself can exist without those present in the act of hearing, whereas the latter cannot exist without the former.

## CHAPTER III — The Third Kind of Numbers in the Act of the Person Pronouncing; the Fourth Kind of Numbers in Memory
4. D. I agree. M. Attend, then, to this third kind, which is found in the very use [Note: [Col. 1164] *Nisu*, according to Manuscript A.] and activity of the person pronouncing; and see whether these numbers can exist without those that are in the memory. For even silently, within ourselves, we can perform certain numbers in thought, over the same duration of time in which they would be performed aloud. It is clear that these belong to a certain activity of the mind; and since this activity produces no sound and causes no affection in the ears, it shows that this kind can exist without the other two [Col. 1165]—one of which is in the sound, the other in the listener when he hears. But we ask whether it would exist without the assistance of memory.

Yet if the soul performs the numbers that we find in the pulse of the veins, the question is settled: for it is clear that these too belong to an activity, and memory contributes nothing to them. But if it is uncertain whether these numbers belong to the soul in activity, then with regard to those that we produce by alternate breathing there can certainly be no doubt that they consist of intervals of time, and that the soul performs them in such a way that, when the will is brought to bear, they can be varied in many ways; and nevertheless no memory is required for them to be performed.

D. It seems to me that this kind can exist without the other three. For although I do not doubt that, in accordance with the tempering of the body, different pulses of the veins and intervals of breathing occur, who would dare deny that they occur through the activity of the soul? Their course, even if faster in some bodies and slower in others because of bodily differences, does not exist at all unless the soul is there to produce it.

M. Consider, then, the fourth kind also—namely, the numbers that are in the memory. For if we draw them forth by recollection, and when we are carried away into other thoughts leave them again as though stored away in their own secret places, I think it is not hidden that they can exist without the others.

D. I do not doubt that they exist without the others; yet unless they had been heard or thought, they would not have been entrusted to memory. Therefore, although they remain when those others cease, they are nevertheless impressed by those others when they precede them.

## CHAPTER IV  
### The fifth kind of numbers, found in the natural judgment of perception; which of the five kinds is superior

5. M. I do not resist you, and I should already like to ask which of these four kinds you judge to be the most excellent—unless, while we were examining them, a fifth kind had somehow appeared to us: that found in the very natural judgment of perception, when we take pleasure in numerical equality or are offended when there is a fault in it. For I do not dismiss what seemed evident to you: that our sense could not operate at all without certain numbers concealed within it. Or do you perhaps think that this great power belongs to some one of these four kinds?

D. I think that this kind must be distinguished from all of them. For it is one thing to sound, which belongs to the body; another to hear, which is what the soul undergoes in the body from sounds; another to perform numbers, either at greater or lesser length; another to remember these things; and yet another to pass judgment upon all of them, whether by approving or recoiling, as though by a certain natural right.

6. M. Come, then, tell me now which of these five is the most excellent.

D. I think it is the fifth.

M. You think rightly: it could not judge the others unless it were superior to them. But I ask again which of the remaining four you approve most highly.

D. Surely that which is in the memory, because I see that the numbers there endure longer than when they sound, are heard, or are performed.

M. You therefore place things made above those who make them; for just now you said that the numbers in the memory are impressed by those other numbers.

D. I would not wish to place them above the others; but I do not see how I could fail to place what endures longer above what endures for less time.

[Col. 1166] M. Do not let that move you. For just as eternal things are not to be preferred to temporal things simply in that way, so neither are things that are effaced more slowly necessarily preferable to those that pass away more quickly. One day of health is certainly better than many days of weakness. And if we compare desirable things with desirable things, reading for one day is better than writing for several days, if the same matter is read in one day that is written over several days.

Likewise, although the numbers in the memory remain longer than those by which they are impressed, we ought not therefore to place them above the numbers that we perform—not in the body but in the soul. Both kinds pass away: the former through cessation, the latter through forgetfulness. But the numbers we perform seem to be taken away from us by the succession of those that follow even before we ourselves cease: the first yield their place to the second, the second to the third, and so on, as the earlier give way to the later, until cessation itself destroys the last.

Through forgetfulness, however, many numbers at once are gradually wiped away; for even they do not remain intact for any length of time. What is not found in the memory after a year, for example, is already less even after one day. The diminution is not perceived, but it is nevertheless rightly inferred from the fact that what has been retained does not suddenly fly away on the day before the year is complete. Thus it can be understood that it begins to slip away from the moment when it enters the memory. Hence we commonly say, “I remember faintly,” when after some time we recall and repeat something before it has completely fallen from memory.

Accordingly, both of these kinds of numbers are mortal. Nevertheless, those who make are rightly placed above what is made.

D. I accept and approve this.

7. M. Now consider the remaining three, and explain which of them is best and ought to be preferred to the others.

D. This is not easy. For according to the rule that those who make must be preferred to what is made, I am compelled to award the palm to the sounding numbers. We perceive these as listeners, and when we perceive them, we undergo them. Thus they produce the numbers that are in the affection of the ears when we hear; and these, in turn, produce other numbers in the memory, which are rightly preferred to them because they are made by them.

But here, since both perception and memory belong to the soul, I am not disturbed if I place something that occurs in the soul above something else that likewise occurs in the soul. What troubles me is how sounding numbers, which are certainly corporeal, or exist in some fashion in the body, should be more worthy of praise than those which, when we perceive them, are found to exist in the soul. But I am troubled again by the question why they should not be more worthy of praise, since these produce those, whereas those are produced by these.

M. Be more astonished that the body can produce anything in the soul. For perhaps it could not do so if, through the first sin, that body—which the soul had animated and governed without any distress and with the greatest ease—had not been changed for the worse and subjected to corruption and death. Yet it possesses a beauty of its own, and by that very fact sufficiently commends the dignity of the soul, whose wound and disease have not been without the honor of some adornment.

This wound the supreme Wisdom of God deigned to assume through a marvelous and ineffable sacrament, when he accepted a human being without sin, though not without the condition of the sinner. For he willed to be born as a human being, to suffer, and to die—not on account of any merit of his own, but through the most excellent goodness. He did this so that we might fear more the pride by which we most deservedly fell into this condition than the insults which one undeserving received; so that we might pay the death we owed with an even spirit, since, for our sake, he was able to endure even a death he did not owe; and so that we might understand whatever more secret and purer meaning can be grasped by holy and better minds in such a sacrament.

It is therefore not surprising that the soul, operating in mortal flesh, perceives the affections of bodies. Nor, because the soul itself is better than the body, should everything that occurs in it be considered better than everything that occurs in the body. I believe you think that the true should be preferred to the false.

D. Who could doubt it?

M. Is the tree that we see in a dream a real tree?

D. In no way.

M. Yet its form is produced in the soul, whereas the form of the tree we now see has been produced in the body. Therefore, since the true is better than the false and the soul is better than the body, the true in the body is better than the false in the soul. But just as the former is better insofar as it is true, not insofar as it occurs in the body, so the latter is perhaps worse insofar as it is false, not insofar as it occurs in the soul. Do you have anything to say to this?

D. Nothing at all.

M. Hear another point which, I think, is more proximate than “better” [Note: [Col. 1167] The printed editions read: “I think, more proximate.” For you will not deny it; omitting *than better*, we have restored the reading from the manuscripts.]. You will not deny that what is fitting ought to be better than what is unfitting.

D. Indeed, I admit it.

M. Yet who could doubt that the same garment in which a woman appears appropriately dressed could be indecent on a man?

D. That too is obvious.

M. What, then, if this form of numbers is fitting in sounds that flow into the ears but unfitting in the soul when the soul possesses them by perceiving and undergoing them? Is that greatly surprising?

D. I do not think so.

M. Why, then, do we hesitate to place the sounding and corporeal numbers above those that are produced by them, even though the latter occur in the soul, which is better than the body? We are placing numbers above numbers, and those that produce above what is produced [Note: [Col. 1167] According to Manuscript A: “And those who make above what is made.” M.]. We are not placing the body above the soul. Bodies are better in proportion as they are more numerically ordered according to such numbers.

The soul, however, becomes better by being without those things that it receives through the body, when it turns away from bodily senses and is reformed according to the divine numbers of wisdom. Thus it is said in the Holy Scriptures: “I went around, to know and examine and seek wisdom and number” (Ecclesiastes 7:26). This must in no way be understood as referring to the numbers with which even disgraceful theaters resound; rather, I believe it refers to those numbers which the soul does not receive from the body, but which, having received them from the supreme God, it impresses upon the body. What this means need not be considered here.

## CHAPTER V  
### Whether the soul suffers from the body, and how it perceives

8. Yet lest the thought arise that the life of a tree is better than ours because it does not receive numbers from the body by perception—for it has no sense—we must carefully consider whether hearing really means anything other than something being produced in the soul by the body. But it would be absurd to subject the soul in any way to the body that forms it. For the soul is never inferior to the body, and every material is inferior to the craftsman who forms it. Therefore the soul is in no way subject as material to the forming body [Col. 1168]. It would be so if the body produced any numbers in it.

Therefore, when we hear, numbers are not produced in the soul by those numbers that we recognize in sounds. Do you object to anything?

D. What, then, occurs in the one who hears?

M. Whatever it may be that we perhaps cannot discover or explain, can it serve as a reason for us to doubt that the soul is better than the body? Or, once we admit this, can we subject the soul to the body that operates and imposes numbers, so that the body is the craftsman and the soul the material out of which and in which something numerically ordered is fashioned? If we believe this, we must believe that the soul is inferior. What could be believed more wretched or more detestable than that?

Since this is so, I shall try, insofar as God deigns to help, to conjecture and discuss what is hidden there. But if, because of the weakness of either or both of us, this does not succeed according to our wishes, we shall either investigate it ourselves at another, clearer time, or leave it to those of greater understanding to investigate, or endure with equanimity that it remain hidden. Nevertheless, we must not for that reason lose from our grasp the things that are more certain.

D. I shall hold fast to that, if I can, and yet I hope that this hiding place is not impenetrable to us.

9. M. I shall quickly say what I think; but follow me—or even go ahead, if you can—whenever you notice me hesitating and wavering. For I do not think that the body is animated by the soul except through the intention of the one who acts. Nor do I think that the soul suffers anything from the body; rather, it acts upon and within the body as upon a subject divinely subjected to its authority. Sometimes it operates with ease, sometimes with difficulty, according as bodily nature yields to it more or less in proportion to its merits.

Whatever corporeal things, therefore, are introduced or brought against this body from outside do something not in the soul but in the body itself, either opposing or harmonizing with its work. Thus, when the soul resists what opposes it and has difficulty forcing the material subject to it into the paths of its own activity, it becomes more attentive because of the difficulty. Since this difficulty does not escape it on account of its attention, the soul is said to perceive it, and this is called pain or labor.

When what is introduced is harmonious or adjacent, the soul easily transfers the whole of it—or as much of it as is needed—into the paths of its own activity. This action by which it joins its body to a body compatible with it from outside does not escape notice, because it is carried out with greater attention on account of something adventitious; but because of the compatibility, it is perceived with pleasure.

When, however, the things by which the body’s losses are repaired are lacking, want ensues. When the soul becomes more attentive through the difficulty of this activity, and this mode of operating does not escape it, it is called hunger or thirst, or something of that kind.

When, on the other hand, what has been taken in is excessive, and the burden of it creates difficulty in operating, this too does not occur without attention; and when such an action does not escape notice, indigestion is perceived. The soul also operates attentively when it expels what is superfluous: gently, with pleasure; harshly, with pain.

It likewise acts attentively upon the body’s diseased disturbance, desiring to come to the aid of what is collapsing and dispersing; and when this action does not escape notice, it is said to perceive diseases and illnesses.

[Col. 1169] 10. To avoid making this lengthy, it seems to me that, when the soul perceives in the body, it does not suffer something from the body but acts more attentively in the body’s affections. These actions—easy because of harmony, or difficult because of disharmony—do not escape the soul; and this entire process is what is called perception.

This perception, which is present even when we perceive nothing, is nevertheless an instrument of the body. Through it the soul governs the body’s condition so that it is readier to deal attentively with the body’s affections, joining like things to like and repelling what is harmful.

The soul operates, I think, through something luminous in the eyes; something airy, exceedingly clear and mobile, in the ears; something dark in the nostrils; something moist in the mouth; and something earthy and almost muddy in touch. But whether these things are conjectured according to this distribution or another, the soul operates peacefully when the things present in the unity of health have yielded, as it were, through a kind of familiar concord [Note: [Col. 1169] So read all the manuscripts except the Vatican manuscript, which, together with the manuscripts of Amerbach and Erasmus, has *cohaeserint* (“have adhered”). Lovato, however, has *concesserint* (“have yielded”).].

When things are applied that affect the body with a certain, so to speak, otherness, it puts forth more attentive actions, adapted to their respective places and instruments. It is then said to see, hear, smell, taste, or perceive through touch. It willingly associates with what is harmonious to these actions and resists what is disharmonious with distress. I think that, when it perceives, the soul presents these operations to the body’s affections; it does not receive those affections themselves.

11. Since the present question concerns the numbers of sounds, and the sense of hearing is being called into doubt, we ought not wander any longer through other matters. Let us therefore return to the subject at hand and see whether sound does anything in the ears. Will you deny that?

D. Nothing could be further from my mind.

M. What, then? Do you not grant that the ears are an animated bodily member?

D. I grant it.

M. When, then, what in that member is similar to air is moved by air that has been struck, do we suppose that the soul—which, before this sound, was giving life to the body of the ears by its vital movement in silence—can either cease from the work of moving what it animates, or move the air of its own ear, now disturbed from outside, in the same way as it moved it before that sound entered?

D. It seems that it must move it differently.

M. Must we not therefore admit that this moving it differently [Note: [Col. 1169] The printed editions read: “It does not seem to me that it moves it differently. M. This kind, then, moves differently.” But our reading is found in the better manuscripts.] is an act of doing, not of suffering?

D. That is so.

M. We therefore do not believe absurdly that, when it perceives, the soul is not unaware of its own movements—or actions, or operations, or whatever other name may more suitably express them.

12. These operations are undertaken either in response to preceding affections of bodies—as when forms interrupt the light of our eyes, sound flows into the ears, exhalations enter the nostrils, flavors reach the palate, or solid and corporeal things are brought from outside against the rest of the body—or when something within the body moves or passes from one place to another, or when the entire body itself is moved by its own weight or by that of another body.

These are the operations that the soul undertakes in response to preceding affections of the body. They please it when it associates itself with them and offend it when it resists them. But when it suffers something from its own operations, it suffers from itself, not from the body; yet it does so plainly when it accommodates itself to the body. For that reason it is diminished in relation to itself, since the body is always less than the soul.

13. When, therefore, the soul turns from its Lord toward its servant, it necessarily declines. When it turns from its servant toward its Lord, it necessarily advances, and it provides that same servant with a life of the greatest ease, one that is therefore least laborious and troublesome, and toward which no attention is diverted because of its profound repose. Such is the bodily condition called health.

Health requires none of our attention—not because the soul then does nothing in the body, but because it does nothing more easily. For in all our actions, the more difficultly we work, the more attentively we work.

This health will be most firm and certain when, at its appointed time and in its proper order, this body has been restored to its original stability [Note: [Col. 1170] See *Retractions* 1.11.3.]. Its resurrection is beneficially believed before it is fully understood.

The soul must both be governed by what is above and govern what is below. What is above the soul is God alone; what is below it, if we consider the whole and entire soul, is the body alone. Therefore, just as the soul cannot be whole without its Lord, so it cannot excel without its servant. But just as its Lord is more than the soul, so its servant is less.

When the soul is intent upon the Lord, it understands his eternal things and becomes more; and through it the servant too becomes more in its own order. But when, neglecting its Lord, it is intent upon its servant through the carnal desire by which it is led [Note: [Col. 1170] Erasmus has *carnalem*; Lovato, *carnalis*; Amerbach, *carnali*, as do eight manuscripts above the Vatican manuscript, which alone continues: “through the carnal desire by which it is led.” [The reading *carnali quae dicitur concupiscentia* (“through the carnal desire that is called desire”) is also found.]], it perceives its own movements, which it presents to the servant, and it is diminished. Yet it is not diminished as much as the servant itself, even when the servant is most fully in its own nature.

By this fault of its mistress, the servant is much less excellent than it was when the soul was more excellent before the fault [Note: [Col. 1170] This seems to be the reading required by the manuscripts. Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovato have: “when it was more excellent before the fault.”].

14. Therefore, since the soul is now mortal and fragile, it governs with great difficulty and attention. Hence it falls into error, valuing bodily pleasure more highly because the material yields to its attention than it values health itself, which requires no attention. It is not surprising that it becomes entangled in troubles when it places care above security.

When it turns toward the Lord, a greater care arises: that it not turn away. This continues until the impetus of carnal affairs, driven onward by long habit and inserting itself amid tumultuous memories into the soul’s conversion, comes to rest. When the movements by which it was borne outward have thus been calmed, the soul conducts an inward freedom of leisure, signified by the Sabbath. It then recognizes that God alone is its Lord, and that he alone is served in supreme freedom.

Yet the soul does not extinguish those carnal movements at will, just as it brings them forth at will. For sin is in its power, but the punishment of sin is not likewise in its power. The soul is a great thing, but it does not remain sufficient to itself for suppressing its wanton movements. It sins when it is stronger, and after sin, having been made weaker by divine law, it is less able to remove what it has done.

“Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:24–25).

A movement of the soul that retains its impetus and has not yet been extinguished is therefore said to be in the memory. When the mind is directed toward something else, the earlier movement is as though no longer present in the mind, and in fact becomes weaker, unless, before it disappears, it is renewed through a certain proximity of similar things.

15. But I should like to know whether none of this troubles you.

D. You seem to me to be speaking plausibly, and I would not dare resist you.

M. Since perceiving is itself the moving of the body in opposition to the movement that has been produced in it, do you not think that we fail to perceive when bones, nails, and hair are cut—not because these things are entirely without life in us? For otherwise they could not be held together, nourished, or grow, nor could they display their power in the generation of offspring—but because they are penetrated less freely by air, the mobile element, than would be necessary for a movement to occur there through the soul as rapidly as the movement against which it occurs when perception is said to take place?

When a certain kind of life is understood to exist in trees and other plants, it is in no way appropriate to place it above not only our own life, which is also preeminent through reason, but even the life of animals. It is one thing to perceive nothing through the greatest stupidity, another to perceive nothing through the greatest bodily health. In the one case the instruments that move against the body’s affections are absent; in the other, the affections themselves are absent.

D. I approve and agree.

## CHAPTER VI  
### The order among the kinds of numbers, and their names

16. M. Return with me, then, to our subject, and answer concerning those three kinds of numbers: one in the memory, another in perception, and another in sound. Which of them seems to you to be superior?

D. I place sound below the two that exist in the soul and are alive, in a certain sense. But which of these two I should judge superior, I am uncertain—unless perhaps, since we said that the numbers in activity ought to be preferred to those in the memory for no other reason than that the former are producing and the latter are produced by them, the same reasoning requires us to place those that are in the soul while we hear above those that are produced by them in the memory, as seemed to me earlier.

M. I do not think your answer absurd. But since it has been argued that these numbers in perception are also operations of the soul, how do you distinguish them from those that we observed to be in activity, even when, in silence and without recollecting, the soul performs something numerically ordered through temporal intervals [Note: [Col. 1171] The printed editions read: “through temporal intervals of numbers.” We have restored *merosum*, on the authority of six manuscripts.]? Is it because the former are the movements of the soul directing itself toward its own body, whereas the latter are the movements of the soul, in hearing, against the affections of its body?

D. I accept that distinction.

M. What, then? Do you think we should maintain the view that those directed toward the body are superior to those directed against the body’s affections?

D. Those that exist in silence seem to me freer than those that are directed not only toward the body but also against the body’s affections.

M. We have distinguished and arranged according to certain degrees of merit five kinds of numbers [Col. 1172]. If you agree, let us give them suitable names, so that in the rest of our discussion we need not use more words than things.

D. I agree.

M. Let the first, then, be called *judicial*; the second, *progressive*; the third, *occurring*; the fourth, *recollective*; and the fifth, *sounding*.

D. I understand, and I shall use these names willingly.

## CHAPTER VII  
### Whether the judicial numbers are immortal

17. M. Attend, then, to what follows, and tell me which of these numbers seem to you immortal, or whether you think that all of them in their own times decline and perish.

D. I think only the judicial numbers are immortal. I see that the others either pass away as they are produced or are erased from the memory through forgetfulness.

M. Are you as certain of the immortality of these as of the destruction of the others? Or should we investigate more carefully whether these truly are immortal?

D. Let us certainly investigate.

M. Tell me, then: when I pronounce a verse with syllables somewhat shorter or longer, while observing the law of time according to which feet correspond from the simple to the double, do I offend your judgment of perception by any irregularity?

D. Not at all.

M. What, then? Can that sound which is produced in shorter and, as it were, swifter syllables occupy more time than the sound itself?

D. How could it?

M. If, then, those judicial numbers were held within the bond of time for as long a duration as these sounding numbers are distributed, could they extend their judgment to sounding numbers that are uttered somewhat more slowly according to the same iambic law?

D. In no way.

M. It is therefore evident that those numbers which preside in judgment are not held within the duration of time.

D. It is entirely evident.

18. M. You agree rightly. But if they were held within no limits, then however slowly I might produce legitimate iambic sounds at their proper intervals, they would still be employed for judgment. Yet if I were to produce one syllable over the time—not to say more—of three paces by a walking person, and another over twice that time, and were to arrange iambs of such lengths successively, the law of the simple and the double would nevertheless be preserved. Still, we could not employ that natural judgment to approve these measurements. Does this not seem so to you?

D. I cannot deny that it seems so; for in my judgment the matter is clear.

M. The judicial numbers, then, are also held within certain limits of temporal intervals, which they cannot exceed in judging; and whatever exceeds those intervals they cannot reach in order to judge. If they are thus held within limits, I do not see how they can be immortal.

D. Nor do I see what answer to make. Yet although I now presume less about their immortality, I do not understand how they are thereby proved mortal. For it may be that, however great the intervals they can judge, they can always judge them, since I cannot say that they are erased by forgetfulness as the others are, nor that they exist for as long or extend as far as sound lasts and the occurring numbers extend, nor as long or as far as the numbers we have called progressive are performed and prolonged. Both the latter kinds pass away together with the time of their operation.

But these judicial numbers—whether they also exist in the soul I do not know; certainly they remain in human nature itself, to judge what is presented to them. Although they vary from a certain brevity to a certain length, they approve what is numerically ordered in these intervals and condemn what is disordered.

[Col. 1173] 19. M. At least you grant that some people are offended more quickly by limping numbers, others more slowly, and that most judge defective numbers only by comparison with complete ones, after they have heard both the harmonious and the disharmonious.

D. I grant it.

M. From what source, then, do you think this difference arises, unless from nature, practice, or both?

D. That is my belief.

M. I ask, then, whether someone might at some time judge and approve longer intervals that another person could not.

D. I believe that this is possible.

M. What, then? Could the person who cannot do so acquire the ability through suitable practice, provided he is not excessively slow?

D. Certainly he could.

M. Could they advance so far in judging longer intervals that, even when interrupted by sleep, they could comprehend double and simple intervals of hours, days, or even months and years through that judicial sense, and approve them by a kind of nod corresponding to those iambs of movement?

D. They cannot.

M. Why can they not, unless because each living creature has been given, according to its own kind and in proportion to the universe, a sense of places and times, so that just as its body is of such a size in proportion to the whole body of the universe, of which it is a part, and its age is of such a length in proportion to the whole age of the world, of which it is a part, so its sense corresponds to the action it performs in proportion to the universal movement, of which this is a part?

By containing all things in this way, this great world—which is often called by the name of heaven and earth in the divine Scriptures—is great. If all its parts are reduced proportionally, it remains equally great; and if they are increased proportionally, it remains equally great. For nothing in the dimensions of places and times is great in itself, but only in relation to something shorter; and nothing in them is short in itself, but only in relation to something greater.

Therefore, if human nature has been given such a sense for the activities of mortal life that it cannot judge temporal intervals greater than those required for the use proper to such a life, then, since such human nature is mortal, I also think that such a sense is mortal. For it is not without reason that habit is called a second nature, as though nature fashioned anew.
