We see, moreover, certain new senses arise through habit in judging various bodily matters, and through a different habit perish.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### The other kinds of numbers are subjected to the examination of the judicial numbers

20. However these judicial numbers may stand, they are certainly superior in this respect: we are uncertain, or investigate only with difficulty, whether they are mortal. As for the other four kinds, there is no question that they are mortal. Although they do not comprehend some of them, because those extend beyond their proper limits, they nevertheless claim the kinds themselves for their own examination.

For when the progressive numbers desire some numerically ordered activity in the body, they are modified by the hidden nod of these judicial numbers. The fact that, when we walk, we are restrained from unequal steps; when we strike, from unequal intervals between blows; when we eat or drink, from unequal movements of the jaws; when we scratch, from unequal strokes of the fingernails; and, not to pass through many other activities, the fact that in any attentive action through the members of the body we are restrained and checked from unequal movements, and silently commanded to observe a certain equality—all this is that judicial something which reveals the Creator of the living creature: he whom we must certainly believe to be the author of all harmony and concord.

21. Those occurring numbers, which are certainly performed not according to their own will but according to the body’s affections, are offered to these judicial numbers for judgment, and judged by them, to the extent that the memory is able to preserve their intervals. For this number, which consists of intervals of time, cannot be judged by us in any way unless we are assisted by memory.

However short a syllable may be, since it both begins and ends, its beginning sounds at one time and its end at another. It is therefore extended through however small an interval of time, and from its beginning, through its middle, it extends toward its end. Reason thus discovers that both spatial and temporal intervals admit of infinite division; and for this reason the end of no syllable is heard together with its beginning.

In hearing even the shortest syllable, therefore, unless memory assists us—so that at the moment when not the beginning but the end of the syllable is sounding, the movement in the mind that occurred when the beginning itself sounded remains—we cannot say that we have heard anything.

Hence it often happens that, being occupied with another thought, we seem not to have heard people speaking in our presence. This is not because the occurring numbers are not then being performed by the soul, since without doubt the sound reaches the ears and the soul cannot cease from the affection of its body, nor can it move except differently from how it would move if that affection did not occur. Rather, because attention is directed elsewhere, the impetus of the movement is gradually extinguished; if it remained, it would certainly remain in the memory, so that we would both discover and perceive that we had heard.

If, in the case of a single short syllable, the slower mind does not follow what reason discovers, then certainly no one doubts that no soul can hear two syllables simultaneously. For the second does not sound until the first has ceased; and what cannot sound simultaneously, how can it be heard simultaneously?

Just as the spreading of rays assists us in grasping spatial intervals, when they flash out from small pupils into the open and belong so much to our body that, although they are directed toward distant objects that we see, they are animated by our soul—so, by their diffusion, we are assisted in grasping spatial intervals [Note: [Col. 1174] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have: “So they are assisted by the diffusion of light.”]—in the same way memory, which is as it were the light of temporal intervals, grasps as much of those intervals as can in some fashion be extended within its own kind.

When sound beats upon the ears for a longer time without being divided into distinct articulations, and another sound, joined to it at some final point, is produced over twice as long an interval—or even over an interval of equal length—the movement of the mind that was formed by attention to the earlier sound, as attention passed over to the sound that had already elapsed, is suppressed by attention to the sound that follows; that is, it does not remain in the memory to the same extent.

Therefore, those judicial numbers—which cannot judge numbers situated in temporal intervals, except for the progressive numbers whose very progression they also regulate, unless memory, as their servant, presents them to the judicial numbers [Col. 1175]—must they not themselves be considered to extend through a determinate interval of time?

The important question is over what temporal intervals what they judge either falls from our grasp or is retained in memory. For even in the bodily forms that pertain to the eyes, we cannot judge or altogether perceive anything round, square, or otherwise solid and determinate unless we keep it before our eyes [Note: [Col. 1175] Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovato read: “We could . . . unless we turned our eyes obliquely.” But the manuscript reading that we have adopted is more coherent.]. When another part is being observed, if what was seen in the other part slips away, the attention of the one judging is entirely frustrated. This too occurs over some duration of time, and memory must watch over the variation.

### 22. The Recollectable Numbers

It is much more evident that we judge the recollectable numbers by these judicial numbers, with memory itself presenting them. For if the occurrent numbers are judged to the extent that memory presents them, much more must those numbers be found to live in memory to which, as though stored away after other acts of attention, we are recalled by recollection. For what else do we do when we recall something to memory except, in a certain manner, seek what we have stored there?

A movement of the mind, not extinguished, returns to thought on the occasion of similar movements; and this is what is called recollection. Thus we perform numbers, either in thought alone or also through the movement of our limbs, which we have already performed at some earlier time. We know that they have not come but returned to thought because, when they were entrusted to memory, they were recalled with difficulty, and we needed some prior indication in order to follow them. Once that difficulty has been removed, however, when they offer themselves readily to the will, in their proper times and order, so easily that those which have taken firmer hold are carried out, even while we are thinking of something else, as though by their own impulse, we plainly perceive that they are not new.

There is also another reason, I think, why we perceive that a present movement of the mind has already occurred: namely, recognition. When we remember the recent movements of the activity in which we are engaged—which are certainly more vivid—we compare them with the recollectable numbers, now more subdued, by means of a certain inner light. Such apprehension is recognition and recollection.

The recollectable numbers, then, are also judged by the judicial numbers—never by them alone, but together with the active numbers, or the occurrent numbers, or both. These bring the recollectable numbers, as it were, out of their hiding places into the open and recall them again as though restored, although they were already fading away.

Thus, since the occurrent numbers are judged to the extent that memory brings them before those judging, the recollectable numbers, which are in memory, can in turn be judged when the occurrent numbers display them. The difference is that, when the occurrent numbers are judged, memory presents them as though they were the recent traces of things fleeing away; but when we judge the recollectable numbers by hearing them, those same traces seem to grow green again as the occurrent numbers pass by.

What need is there to say anything further about the sounding numbers, since they are judged among the occurrent numbers whenever they are heard? But if they sound where they are not heard, who could doubt that we cannot judge them? In sounds, then, through the instrument of the ears, and likewise in dances and other visible movements, insofar as temporal numbers are concerned, with the same assistance of memory we distinguish and judge by the same judicial numbers.

### Chapter IX — Other Numbers in the Soul Superior to the Judicial Numbers

**23.** Since this is so, let us attempt, if we can, to transcend these judicial numbers and inquire whether there are higher ones. For although in them we no longer see temporal intervals at all, they are nevertheless employed only to judge what takes place within a temporal interval—not even everything of that kind, but only what can be articulated in memory.

Unless perhaps you have something you wish to say against this.

**D.** The force and power of these judicial numbers greatly impresses me. For they seem to me to be the numbers to which the services of all the senses are referred. Therefore, I do not know whether anything superior to them can be found among numbers.

**M.** Nothing is lost when we inquire more carefully. Either we shall find superior numbers in the human soul, or we shall establish that these are the highest within it—provided, that is, that it becomes clear that there are none more excellent in it. For it is one thing for something not to exist, and another for it not to be discoverable, whether by anyone or by us.

But I think that, when the verse we have proposed is sung—“God, creator of all”—we hear it through those occurrent numbers, recognize it through the recollectable numbers, pronounce it through the progressive numbers, take delight in it through these judicial numbers, and assess it through I know not what other numbers. From that delight—which is, as it were, the judgment of these judicial numbers—we deliver another, more certain judgment according to numbers more hidden than these.

[Note: Col. 1176. Printed editions: “another judgment, more hidden but more certain according to these.” MSS: “according to these more hidden [numbers].” Supply “numbers.”]

Does it seem to you that taking delight through the senses and assessing by reason are one and the same thing?

**D.** I admit that they are different. But first, I am struck by the very term: why should those in which reason resides not rather be called *judicial*, instead of those in which delight resides? Further, I fear that this assessment by reason is nothing other than a somewhat more careful judgment of the numbers upon themselves. Thus the numbers in delight and those in reason would not be different; rather, the same numbers would at one time judge what takes place in the body, when memory presents them—as was demonstrated above—and at another time judge themselves, more remotely from the body and more purely.

**24. M.** Do not trouble yourself over terms. The matter is within our control; names are imposed by convention, not by nature.

But as for your supposition that they are the same, and your refusal to accept two kinds of numbers: if I am not mistaken, you are led astray because the same soul performs both activities. Yet you must observe that, in the progressive numbers, the same soul moves the body or is moved toward the body; in the occurrent numbers, this same soul goes to meet the affections produced in it; and in the recollectable numbers, this very soul, until those affections somehow subside, fluctuates, as it were, among the movements themselves.

When, therefore, we number and distinguish these kinds, we are discerning the movements and affections of one nature—that is, of the soul. Accordingly, just as it is one thing to move toward what the body undergoes, which occurs in sensation; another to move oneself toward the body, which occurs in activity; and another to retain what has been produced in the soul by these movements, which is remembering; so it is one thing to assent or refuse assent to these movements, whether when they are first produced or when they are revived by recollection. This takes place in delight at the appropriate and in displeasure at the absurdity of such movements or affections. It is another thing to assess whether these delights are right or wrong, and this takes place through reasoning.

We must therefore admit that these are two kinds, just as the others are three. And if our view is correct, then unless the very sense of delight had been imbued with certain numbers, it could in no way assent to equal intervals or reject disturbed ones. It may likewise rightly appear that reason, which is imposed upon this delight, could in no way judge the numbers beneath it without certain more vigorous numbers of its own.

If this is true, it becomes clear that five kinds of numbers have been found in the soul. When you add to them those bodily numbers which we called sounding numbers, you will recognize six kinds of numbers, arranged and ordered.

Now, if you approve, let those who had insinuated themselves among us in order to seize the chief position be called *sensory* numbers; and let these, which have been found to be superior, receive the name *judicial*, since that is the more honorable name. I also think that the name *sounding* should be changed, since, if they are called *bodily* numbers, they will more clearly signify also those found in dancing and in every other visible movement.

That is, if you approve what has been said.

**D.** I certainly approve, for these things seem to me both true and clear. I gladly accept this correction of the terms as well.

### Chapter X — The Power of Reason in Perceiving Matters Belonging to Music, Where Nothing Delights Except Equality

**25. M.** Come now, consider the force and power of reason, insofar as we can observe it from its works. For, to mention what especially concerns the undertaking of this work, reason first considered what good modulation itself is and perceived that it consists in a certain free movement directed toward the end of its own beauty.

Then it saw that, in the movements of bodies, one element varied through the shortening and lengthening of time, according as the movement lasted for a greater or lesser duration; while another varied through the striking of local intervals at certain degrees of swiftness and slowness.

[Note: Col. 1177. Seven MSS read *percussionem* (“striking”) rather than *percussione*.] Having made this division, it articulated into various numbers, through measured intervals suited to human perception, that which consisted in the duration of time; and it pursued their kinds and order all the way to the measures of verses.

Finally, it considered what the soul did in regulating, performing, sensing, and retaining these things, the soul being their governing principle.

[Note: Col. 1177. Most MSS, with the Am. edition, have this reading. The Lov. edition reads: “what the soul did in regulating, sensing, retaining, and delighting in these things.”] It separated all these animal numbers from the bodily numbers, and recognized that it could neither attend to, distinguish, nor correctly number all these things without certain numbers of its own. By a certain judicial assessment it therefore placed those numbers above the others, which belong to a lower order.

**26.** And now, when the soul acts through its own delight, weighing temporal moments and directing its impulses toward the regulation of such numbers, what is it that we love in sensible numerosity?

[Note: Col. 1177. Two MSS read *quam*; three others, *qua*. Shortly afterward, one of the Victorine codices reads *propendet*, “leans/weighs,” with “such numbers.”] Is it anything other than a certain parity and intervals measured equally?

Would the pyrrhic foot, or the spondee, or the anapest, or the dactyl, or the proceleusmatic, or the dispondee delight us in any other way than by assigning one part to another through equal division? What beauty do the iamb, trochee, and tribrach possess except that they divide their larger part into two equal parts by means of their smaller part?

Further, why do the feet of six times delight the ear more agreeably and pleasantly than for this reason:

[Note: Col. 1178. MS A reads: “They sound more pleasantly and festively for no other reason.”] that they are divided according to either of two laws—either into two equal parts, each containing three times, or into one simple part and another double part,

[Note: Col. 1178. Twelve MSS read: “from each part.”] that is, so that the greater part contains twice the lesser and is divided equally from it, with two times measuring and cutting four times into two equal portions?

And what of the feet of five and seven times? Why do they seem more suitable to prose, which is looser, than to verse, except that their smaller part does not divide the larger into equal parts? Yet how are these feet themselves admitted into the order of their kind among temporal numbers, unless because, in the five-time foot, the smaller part contains two portions equal to the three portions of the larger, and, in the seven-time foot, the smaller contains three portions equal to the larger’s four?

Thus, in every foot, there is no smallest part marked off by some measured division to which the remaining parts do not correspond with whatever equality they can possess.

**27.** Come now: whether this combination of connected feet is extended in unrestricted continuity, as in rhythms; or recalled from a definite ending, as in meters; or even assigned according to some rule to two mutually corresponding members, as in verses—in what other respect, except equality, is one foot a companion to another?

How can the middle syllable of the molossi and of the Ionic feet, which is long, be distributed—not by division, but by the very impulse of the person pronouncing and clapping—into two equal moments, so that the entire foot also corresponds to three times when it is joined to others divided in the same way? Is this not because the law of equality prevails—namely, because the long middle syllable is equal to its sides, which consist of two times each, since it too is of two times?

[Note: Col. 1178. The MSS read “by the very impulse” (*nutu*); earlier editions read “by movement” (*motu*). MS A has the same reading as the earlier editions. Am., Er., and Lov. read “equal sides”; several MSS more clearly read: “it is equal—that is, both the molossus and the Ionic foot—to its sides.”]

Why cannot the same thing happen in the amphibrach when it is joined to other four-time feet, except because there is not found in it an equality of this kind: a double middle part and simple sides?

Why is the sense not deceived in intervals of silence, except because the same law of equality is fulfilled—not in sound, but in the temporal interval that is owed?

Why, when silence follows, is a short syllable accepted in place of a long one—not by convention, but by the natural judgment itself that presides over the ears—unless because that same law of equality forbids us to confine a sound within the narrower limits of a longer temporal interval?

Thus nature’s faculty of hearing and silence permits a syllable to be extended beyond two times, so that what can be filled by silence may also be filled by sound. But for a syllable to occupy less than two times, while the remaining interval is supplied by silent gestures, is a kind of fraud against equality, because equality cannot exist in less than two times.

[Note: Col. 1178–79. Most MSS read “hearing and singing.” The editions read “the space of silence,” where the MSS’ “by silent gestures” has been adopted.]

Further, in the very equality of the members by which those structures are varied that the Greeks call *periodoi* (περίοδοι), and by which verses are formed, how is the return to that same equality made more subtly except in such a way that, in a period, the shorter member corresponds to the longer through equal feet for the sake of the clap, and that, in a verse, the unequal members that are joined are found, upon more hidden consideration of the numbers, to possess the force of equality?

**28.** Reason therefore questions the soul’s carnal delight, which had claimed for itself the judicial role. Since this delight is pleased by equality in temporal intervals, reason asks whether two short syllables, whatever they may be, which it hears are truly equal, or whether it is possible for one of them to be uttered somewhat more lengthily—not to the extent of a long syllable, but by any amount short of that—yet nevertheless to exceed its companion.

Can it be denied that this is possible, when the delight does not perceive the difference and rejoices in unequal things as though they were equal? What is more disgraceful than such error and inequality?

From this we are warned to turn our joy away from things that imitate equality when we cannot comprehend whether they fulfill it. Indeed, perhaps we do comprehend that they do not fulfill it; nevertheless, insofar as they imitate it, we cannot deny that they are beautiful in their own kind and order.

### Chapter XI — We Should Not Be Offended by Inferior Things but Take Delight in the Higher Numbers Alone. The Difference between *Phantasia* and *Phantasma*

**29.** Let us not therefore envy those things that are beneath us. With God and our Lord assisting us, let us place ourselves between what is beneath us and what is above us in such an order that we are not offended by inferior things but take delight in higher things alone.

For delight is, as it were, the soul’s weight. Delight therefore orders the soul. “For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matt. 6:21). Where there is delight, there is treasure; and where the heart is, there is either blessedness or misery.

What, then, are the higher things except those in which the highest, unshaken, unchangeable, eternal equality remains? There is no time there, because there is no change; and from it times are fashioned, ordered, and regulated in imitation of eternity, while the revolution of the heavens returns to the same point and brings the heavenly bodies back to the same point, obeying, in days, months, years, lustrums, and the other orbits of the stars, the laws of equality, unity, and order.

[Note: Col. 1179. Am., Er., and most MSS read “returns to the day” and, below, “brings back to the day.” The same MSS read “the orbits of the stars,” whereas the editions read “the orders and laws of the stars.”]

Thus earthly things, subjected to heavenly things, join the orbits of their times, through their numerically ordered succession, to the universal song.

**30.** In these things many features appear to us disordered and confused because we have been sewn into their order according to our merits, without knowing what beautiful work divine providence is accomplishing concerning us.

[Note: Col. 1179–80. Manuscripts and printed books read *assueti sumus* (“we have become accustomed”); *assuti sumus* (“we have been sewn into”) is unquestionably to be read, as in the Corbie codex before a second hand inserted *e* and made *assueti*. See *De vera religione*, ch. 22, §43, where Augustine presses the same point: “We have become parts of the ages by condemnation.”]

For if someone were placed like a statue in some corner of a very large and beautiful building, he could not perceive the beauty of the whole structure, although he himself would be part of it. Nor can a soldier in battle observe the order of the entire army.

Likewise, if the syllables in a poem lived and perceived for exactly as long as they sound, that numerical structure and beauty of the connected work—which they could not perceive and approve in its entirety—could in no way please them, although the whole had been fashioned and perfected from those individual syllables as they passed away.

Thus God ordered the sinful human being as something ugly, but not in an ugly manner. He became ugly by his will, losing the whole which he possessed while obeying God’s commands; and he was ordered within the universe so that, refusing to act according to the law, he might be acted upon by the law.

Whatever is done lawfully is, of course, done justly; and whatever is done justly is not necessarily done disgracefully, since even in our evil deeds God’s works are good. For insofar as a human being is a human being, he is some good; but adultery, insofar as it is adultery, is an evil deed. Yet a human being is often born from adultery—from the evil deed of a human being, certainly, but as God’s good work.

**31.** To return, then, to the purpose for which these things have been said: these numbers excel by the beauty of reason. If we were entirely cut off from them when we incline toward the body, the progressive numbers would not regulate the sensory numbers. The latter, in turn, produce the sensible beauties of time by moving bodies; and thus the occurrent numbers are formed as they meet the sounding numbers.

The same soul receives all these impulses into itself, as though multiplying them within itself, and makes them recollectable. This power of the soul is called memory, and it is a great aid in the extremely busy activities of this life.

**32.** Whatever memory retains of the movements of the soul that have been directed against the affections of the body is called in Greek *phantasia* (φαντασία). I do not know what I would rather call it in Latin. To regard these things as known and perceived is the way of life established at the very entrance of error.

[Note: Col. 1180. The Lov. edition reads: “it seemed to be certain opinions”; Am., Er., and several MSS read: “it is a life of opinion”; other MSS read “a way of opinion,” or “opining,” or “more opinionatedly.”]

But when these movements encounter one another and seethe as though under diverse and conflicting currents of attention, they produce other movements from one another—not now those retained as impressions from the encounters with bodily affections, received through the senses, but similar movements, as it were images of images, which it has pleased us to call *phantasmata*.

For I think of my father, whom I have often seen, in one way; and of my grandfather, whom I have never seen, in another. The first is *phantasia*; the second is *phantasma*. I find the former in memory; the latter in that movement of the soul which has arisen from the things retained in memory.

How these things arise is difficult both to discover and to explain. Yet I think that, if I had never seen human bodies, I could in no way represent them in thought under a visible form. What I construct from what I have seen, I construct through memory. Nevertheless, it is one thing to find a *phantasia* in memory and another to make a *phantasma* from memory.

All this lies within the power of the soul. But to regard even true *phantasmata* as known is the highest error. There is, nevertheless, something that we may reasonably say we know in both kinds: namely, that we have sensed such things or that we imagine such things.

I can say without rashness that I had a father and a grandfather. But to say that they are precisely those whom my mind retains in *phantasia* or *phantasma* would be utter madness.

Some people follow their *phantasmata* so recklessly that there is no other source of all false opinions than regarding *phantasiai* or *phantasmata* as known—things that are known through sensation.

[Note: Col. 1181. Most MSS omit: “than regarding *phantasiai* or *phantasmata* as known—things that are known through sensation.”] Let us therefore resist these above all, and let us not accommodate the mind to them in such a way that, while thought remains occupied with them, we imagine that they can be discerned by understanding.

**33.** But if these numbers, which are produced in the soul devoted to temporal things, possess a beauty of their own, although they exercise it only in passing, why should divine providence envy this beauty, which is formed from our penal mortality, a condition we deserved under the most just law of God?

Yet God did not abandon us in this condition so completely that we could not return, and, with his mercy extending a hand, be recalled from delight in carnal sensations. For such delight fixes deeply in memory what it draws from slippery sensations.

This habit of the soul, formed together with the flesh because of carnal affection, is called *flesh* in the divine Scriptures. It struggles against the mind, when that apostolic statement can already be made: “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25).

But when the mind is lifted toward spiritual things, fixed and remaining there, the force of this habit too is broken, and, gradually restrained, is extinguished. It was stronger when we followed it; yet it is not entirely absent. Certainly it is weaker when we restrain it. Thus, through definite returns from every wanton movement—which is a failure of the soul’s being—our delight is restored to the numbers of reason, and our whole life is turned toward God, giving the body the numbers of health rather than receiving pleasure from it.

This will occur when the outer person has been corrupted and changed for the better.

### Chapter XII — Spiritual and Eternal Numbers

**34.** Memory receives not only the carnal movements of the soul, about which we have already spoken in connection with numbers, but also spiritual movements, which I shall discuss briefly. The simpler these are, the fewer words they require, but the more they demand a serene mind.

We recognized that the equality which we did not find with certainty and permanence in sensible numbers, but nevertheless recognized there as shadowed and passing, could nowhere be desired by the mind unless it were known somewhere. But this “somewhere” is not in spatial or temporal intervals, for the former swell and the latter pass away.

Where, then, do you think it is? Answer, I beg you, if you can. You do not think it is in the forms of bodies, for you will never dare, with clear judgment, to call them equal. Nor do you think it is in temporal intervals, in which we are similarly unaware whether something may be extended or shortened somewhat beyond what it ought to be, escaping our perception.

I am asking where you think that equality exists which, when we contemplate it, leads us to desire certain bodies or bodily movements to be equal, while, on considering them more carefully, we do not dare to trust them.

**D.** I think it is in something superior to bodies; but whether in the soul itself or also above the soul, I do not know.

**35. M.** If, then, we inquire about that rhythmic or metric art used by those who compose verses, do they possess certain pure numbers according to which they construct verses?

**D.** I can imagine nothing else.

**M.** Whatever these numbers are, do they seem to you to pass away with the verses, or to remain?

**D.** Certainly to remain.

**M.** We must therefore agree that some passing numbers are constructed from certain numbers that remain?

**D.** Reason compels me to agree.

**M.** What? Do you think that this art is anything other than a certain affection of the soul of the artist?

**D.** I believe that it is.

**M.** Do you believe that this affection exists also in someone who is ignorant of the art?

**D.** Not at all.

**M.** What about someone who has forgotten it?

**D.** Not in him either, because he too is ignorant, even if he was once proficient.

**M.** What if someone reminds him of it by questioning him? Do you think that the numbers return to him from the questioner himself, or that he moves himself inwardly within his own mind toward something from which what he had lost is restored to him?

**D.** I think that he performs this action within himself.

**M.** Do you also think that, if he has completely forgotten which syllable is shortened and which is lengthened, he can be reminded of this by questioning, even though, by the ancient convention and usage of human beings, different durations have been assigned to different syllables—shorter to some and longer to others?

For surely, if nature or instruction had fixed this matter firmly and permanently, learned people of more recent times would not have lengthened some syllables that the ancients shortened, or shortened some that the ancients lengthened.

**D.** I think this too is possible, since whatever is forgotten, however completely, can return to memory when questioning recalls it.

**M.** You would be surprised if you thought that, no matter who questioned you, you could remember what you had eaten for dinner a year ago.

**D.** I admit that I cannot. Nor do I now think that he could be reminded by questioning of syllables whose durations he has completely forgotten.

**M.** Why is that, unless because in the name *Italia* the first syllable was shortened according to the will of some people and is now lengthened according to the will of others?

But that one and two should not make three, and that two should not correspond to one as a double, no dead person has been able to make so, no living person can, and no future person will be able to.

**D.** Nothing is clearer.

**M.** What, then, if in the same way that we asked most clearly about one and two, we questioned the person who is ignorant of all the other matters belonging to those numbers—not because he has forgotten them, but because he has never learned them? Do you not think that he could similarly come to know this art, apart from the syllables?

**D.** Who could doubt it?

**M.** In what way, then, do you think that this person too will move himself so that these numbers may be impressed upon his mind and produce in him that affection called art? Or will the questioner at least give the numbers to him?

**D.** I think that, in this case also, he acts within himself, so that he understands that the things being asked are true and answers accordingly.

**36. M.** Come now, tell me whether these numbers about which we are questioning seem to you changeable.

**D.** Not at all.

**M.** Then you do not deny that they are eternal?

**D.** On the contrary, I admit it.

**M.** What, then? Is there not a danger that some inequality among them may deceive us?

**D.** I am entirely more secure concerning the equality of these numbers than concerning anything else.

**M.** How, then, should we believe that what is eternal and unchangeable is bestowed upon the soul, unless by the one eternal and unchangeable God?

**D.** I do not see what else we ought to believe.

**M.** Finally, is this not clear: when someone, questioned by another, moves himself inwardly toward God in order to understand the unchangeable truth, he cannot be recalled to the contemplation of that truth by any external reminder unless his memory retains that same movement?

**D.** It is clear.

### Chapter XIII — How the Mind Is Turned Away from Unchangeable Truth

**37. M.** I ask, then, where this person departs from the contemplation of such things, so that memory must recall him to it. Or is it perhaps to be thought that, when the mind is intent upon something else, it needs such a return?

**D.** That is what I think.

**M.** Let us see, if you please, what that something might be upon which the mind can become so intent that it is turned away from the contemplation of unchangeable and supreme equality. For I see no more than three possibilities.

When the mind turns away from this equality, it either directs itself toward something equal and of the same kind, or toward something superior, or toward something inferior.

**D.** We must inquire about the other two possibilities, for I do not see what could be superior to eternal equality.

**M.** Do you see, I ask, what could be equal to it and yet different from it?

**D.** I do not see that either.

**M.** It remains, then, that we inquire what is inferior. But does not the soul itself first occur to you? Certainly it confesses that equality to be unchangeable, while it recognizes that it itself is changed by the very fact that at one time it contemplates this and at another something else. In this way, by following one thing and then another, it produces the variation of time, which does not exist in eternal and unchangeable things.

**D.** I agree.

**M.** Is not this affection or movement of the soul—by which it understands eternal things, and that temporal things are inferior to them, even within itself, and knows that the higher things ought to be desired rather than the lower—what you would call prudence?

**D.** It seems to be nothing else.

**38. M.** What of this? Do you think it deserves less consideration that the soul has not yet simultaneously clung to eternal things, although it already knows that it ought to cling to them?

**D.** On the contrary, I ask most earnestly that we consider this, and I want to know how it comes about.

**M.** You will see it easily if you observe the things toward which we are accustomed to direct our minds most intensely and to devote great care. For I think these are the things we love greatly. Or do you think otherwise?

**D.** I think there are no others.

**M.** Tell me, I beg you: can we love anything except what is beautiful? For although some people seem to love ugly things—those whom the Greeks commonly call *saprophiloi* (σαπροφίλοι), “lovers of rotten things”—nevertheless, consider how much less beautiful these things are than those pleasing to the majority.

It is clear that no one loves those things whose ugliness offends the senses.

**D.** It is as you say.

**M.** Beautiful things, then, please us through number, in which we have already shown that equality is desired. For this is found not only in the beauty that pertains to the ears and to bodily movement, but also in visible forms themselves, in which beauty is now more commonly said to reside.

What else do you think it is but numerical equality when paired members correspond to paired members, while those that are single occupy the middle position, so that equal intervals are preserved toward them from both sides?

**D.** I think it is nothing else.

**M.** What of visible light itself, which has primacy among all colors—for color too delights us in bodily forms? What else do we seek in light and colors except what agrees with our eyes?

We turn away from excessive brilliance and do not wish to see what is too dark. Similarly, in sounds we recoil from sounds that are too loud and do not love those that are almost whispers. This is not a matter of temporal intervals but of the sound itself, which is, as it were, the light of such numbers, and silence is opposed to it as darkness is opposed to colors.

When, then, we desire what is harmonious according to the measure of our nature and reject what is discordant, although we perceive that it may suit other animals, do we not here too take pleasure according to a certain law of equality, recognizing that in more hidden ways equals have been assigned to equals?

The same may be observed in odors, flavors, and the sense of touch. It would take too long to pursue these matters in greater detail, but it is very easy to investigate them. There is nothing among these sensible things that does not please us through equality or similarity.

Where there is equality or similarity, there is number; for nothing is so equal or similar as one and one.

Unless you have something to say against this.

**D.** I agree completely.

**39. M.** What, then? Did our earlier discussion not persuade us that the soul acts upon bodies rather than suffering action from bodies?

**D.** It certainly persuaded us.

**M.** The love of acting against the successive affections of its body therefore turns the soul away from the contemplation of eternal things, drawing its attention aside through concern for sensible pleasure. This is effected through the occurrent numbers.

The love of operating upon bodies also turns the soul away and makes it restless. This is effected through the progressive numbers.

*Phantasiai* and *phantasmata* turn it away, and these are produced through the recollectable numbers.

Finally, the love of a most empty knowledge of such things turns it away. This is effected through the sensory numbers, which contain, as it were, certain rules of an art that rejoice in imitation.

From these arises curiosity, which, by the very name of care, is hostile to security and, through vanity, an opponent of truth.

[Note: Col. 1184. The better MSS read: “and, through vanity, an opponent of truth.” Am. and Er. read: “and lacking health and truth”; Lov. reads: “and vanity opposed to truth.”]

**40.** The general love of activity that turns the soul away from truth proceeds from pride, through which vice the soul preferred to imitate God rather than serve God.

Rightly, then, it is written in the sacred books: “The beginning of man’s pride is apostasy from God,” and, “The beginning of every sin is pride.”

Nothing could better demonstrate what pride is than what is said there: “Why is earth and ashes proud, since in his life he cast away his inmost parts?” (Ecclus. 10:14–15, 9–10.)

For since the soul in itself is nothing—for otherwise it would not be changeable and would not suffer defect from being—since, then, it is nothing in itself, whatever being it possesses comes from God. Remaining in its proper order, it is enlivened by the presence of God himself in mind and consciousness.

Thus it possesses this good within itself. Pride, therefore, means swelling outward for the soul; and, so to speak, becoming empty, which is to become less and less.

But what is moving outward except casting away the inward things—that is, putting God far from oneself, not by spatial distance but by the soul’s affection?

**41.** This is the soul’s desire to have other souls beneath it—not animals, which divine law has granted us authority over, but rational beings, that is, its neighbors, companions and partners under the same law.

The proud soul desires to act upon these, and this action appears so much more excellent than action upon bodies as every soul is better than every body.

But to act upon rational souls, not through the body but by oneself, belongs to God alone. Yet, because of the condition of sinners, souls are permitted to act upon souls to some extent, moving them by means of one another’s bodies, either through natural signs, such as the face or a gesture, or through conventional signs, such as words.

For people act through signs both when commanding and when persuading, and also in anything else, beyond command and persuasion, by which souls act upon souls or together with souls.

It rightly follows that those who, through pride, desired to excel others cannot command even their own limbs and bodies without difficulty and pain, being partly foolish in themselves and partly weighed down by mortal members.

Through these numbers and movements, then, by which souls act upon souls, they are turned away from the pure and sincere vision of truth as they seek honors and praises.

For God alone honors the soul, making blessed in secret before himself the soul that lives justly and devoutly.

### 42

The movements, therefore, which the soul exercises upon the souls adhering to it and subject to it are like those that advance forward; for it acts as though upon its own body. But the movements which it exercises when it wishes to gather some souls to itself or subject them to itself are reckoned among those that encounter resistance. For it acts as though it were laboring upon the senses so that what is brought near from outside may become one with it, and what cannot be made one with it may be repelled. Memory receives both kinds of movement and makes them capable of recollection, boiling up tumultuously in phantasies and images of such actions in a similar way.

Nor are those evaluative numbers lacking, as it were, inspectors who perceive what in these actions moves suitably or unsuitably. We may also call them sensory, since the sensible signs are the means by which souls act upon souls in this manner. Since the soul is entangled in so many and such great impulses, what wonder is it if it is turned away from contemplation of the truth? And insofar as it draws breath, so to speak, from these things, it sees that truth; but because it has not yet overcome them, it is not allowed to remain in it. Hence the soul does not simultaneously possess knowledge of where it ought to remain and the ability to remain there. But perhaps you have some objection to this?

D. I dare not contradict anything.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### The soul is summoned to love God by the principle of number and order, which it loves in things

[Col. 1186]

### 43

M. What, then, remains? Is it that, since we have considered as best we could the defilement and burdening of the soul, we should see what action is divinely commanded to it, by which, once purified and relieved of its burden, it may fly back to rest and enter into the joy of its Lord?

D. Let it be so.

M. What more do you suppose I ought to say on this subject, when all the many volumes of divine Scripture, endowed with such authority and holiness, do nothing else with us than command us to love God and our Lord with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and to love our neighbor as ourselves? If, then, we refer all those movements and numbers of human action to this end, we shall unquestionably be cleansed. Do you think otherwise?

D. I certainly think nothing else. But as brief as this is to hear, so difficult and arduous is it to do.

### 44

M. What, then, is easy? Is it easy for the soul to love colors, sounds, pastries, roses, and gently soft bodies? Is it easy for it to love these things, in which it seeks nothing but equality and likeness, and, considering them somewhat more carefully, scarcely recognizes the outermost shadow and trace of those qualities; while it is difficult to love God, whom the soul, still wounded and filthy, conceiving him insofar as it can, suspects to contain nothing unequal, nothing unlike himself, nothing separated by place, nothing varied by time?

Or is it pleasing to construct massive buildings and to take delight in extending oneself through works of this kind? If numbers please us in them—for I find nothing else—what is said to be equal or similar in them [Note: [Col. 1186] Erasmus and Lovaniensis: “In which what pleases us, if not numbers? For I find nothing else that can be called equal and similar in them.” I have chosen the reading of the manuscripts.] that the reasoning of the discipline does not ridicule? But if this is so, why does the soul fall from that truest citadel of equality to these things and raise earthly structures through its own ruins? This was not promised by the one who does not know how to deceive. “For my yoke,” he says, “is easy” (Matthew 11:30).

The love of this world is more laborious. For what the soul seeks in it—namely, constancy and eternity—it does not find, since the lowest beauty is completed through the passing-away of things, and whatever in it imitates constancy is transmitted from the supreme God through the soul. For the form that is changeable only in time is prior to that which is changeable both in time and in place [Note: [Col. 1186] See Retractations, book 1, chapter 11, no. 4.].

Just as, therefore, the Lord has commanded souls what they should love, so through the apostle John he has commanded what they should not love. “Do not love the world,” he says, “because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of this age” (1 John 2:15–16).

### 45

But what sort of person do you think it is who refers all those numbers that arise from the body, and against the passions of the body, and that are retained in memory from these things, not to carnal pleasure but solely to the body’s health; and who reduces all those numbers that operate upon souls joined to him, or that are exercised in order to join souls to himself, and that from these things adhere to memory, not to his proud preeminence but to the benefit of those very souls?

And when those numbers that preside in both kinds as moderators and inspectors, as it were, of the other numbers passing through sensation, he uses not for superfluous or harmful curiosity but for necessary approval or disapproval—does he not exercise all these numbers while becoming entangled in the snares of none of them?

For he chooses the body’s health so that it may not hinder him, and he directs all those actions toward the benefit of his neighbor, whom he has been commanded to love as himself because of the natural bond of a common law.

D. You praise a great man, and one truly most humane.

### 46

M. It is not, then, the numbers that are beneath reason and beautiful in their own kind that defile the soul, but the love of inferior beauty. Although the soul loves in that beauty not only equality, about which enough has been said in accordance with the subject under discussion, but also order, it has itself lost its own order. Yet it has not departed from the order of things, since it is there, and is in such a place and such a condition, that its being there and being so is most orderly.

For it is one thing to maintain order, another to be maintained by order. The soul maintains order when, loving with its whole self what is above it—that is, God—and loving associated souls as itself, it orders what is below. Through this power of love it orders inferior things and is not defiled by them [Note: [Col. 1187] Thus eleven manuscripts. Am., Er., and Lov. have “is ordered.”].

What defiles it is not evil, since the body too is God’s creature and, although it is adorned with beauty of its own, it is despised in comparison with the dignity of the soul—just as the dignity of gold is sullied even by an admixture of the purest silver.

Therefore, whatever numbers have been formed from our penal mortality [Note: [Col. 1187] Lov. has “our equal mortality.” But Am. and Er., together with the manuscripts, are better in reading “penal,” as above, no. 33: “which is formed from our penal mortality.”—] we should not reject from the work of divine providence, since they are beautiful in their own kind. Nor should we love them as though we could become blessed by enjoying such things.

Since they are temporal, we shall be rid of them by using them well, like a person on a plank in the waves: neither casting them away as burdensome nor embracing them as though they were securely grounded. But from love of our neighbor, in the measure commanded, there is made for us a most certain step by which we cling to God. We are not merely held by his ordering, but also hold our own order firm and secure.

### 47

Or perhaps the soul does not love order, even when the sensory numbers bear witness to it? Why, then, is the first foot a pyrrhic, the second an iamb, the third a trochee, and the others thereafter? You would rightly say that reason, rather than sensation, has been followed here.

What, then, must be attributed to sensory numbers? Is it not that, although eight long syllables occupy as much time as sixteen short syllables, within the same span the short syllables nevertheless expect to be mixed with the long ones rather than the reverse? When reason judges this sensation and declares that proceleusmatic feet are equal to spondaic feet, it finds that nothing else has force here except the power of order. For long syllables are long only in comparison with short ones, and short syllables are short only in comparison with long ones.

Therefore, although an iambic verse is pronounced with any degree of prolongation, it does not lose its name so long as the rule of one-to-two is not lost. But a verse consisting of pyrrhic feet, when a delay in pronunciation is gradually added, suddenly becomes spondaic if one consults not grammar but music. If, however, it is dactylic or anapaestic, since its long syllables are perceived in comparison with the short syllables mixed with them, however slowly it is pronounced, it retains its name.

Why are additions of half-feet to be preserved according to one law at the beginning and another at the end, and why are not all such additions to be employed, even though they are fitted to the same beat? Why is the placement at the end sometimes of two short syllables preferred to that of one long syllable? Are these things not modified by sensation itself? In them we find not the number of equality, which loses nothing whether one form or another is present, but the bond of order.

It would take too long to review the other matters belonging to the same principle in the numbers of durations. But surely sensation itself also rejects visible forms that lean contrary to what is proper, or are upside down, and similar forms. In such cases what is disapproved is not inequality—since the equality of the parts remains—but perversity.

Finally, in all our sensations and activities, when we reconcile many unusual things, and therefore unpleasant to some, to our appetite by successive stages, and accept them first tolerably and then willingly, do we not weave pleasure through order? And unless the earlier things are harmoniously joined to the middle ones, and the middle ones to the final ones, do we not recoil?

### 48

Therefore let us place our joys neither in carnal pleasure, nor in human honors and praises, nor in examining those things that touch the body from outside, since we possess God in our inmost being, where everything that we love is certain and unchangeable.

Thus it comes about that, even when these temporal things are present, we are not entangled in them; and when things external to the body are absent, they are absent without our experiencing pain. The body itself is taken away either without pain or without serious pain, and by death is restored to its nature, to be reformed.

For the soul’s attention contracts restless occupations concerning a part of the body [Note: [Col. 1188] Several manuscripts read “concerning a part of time.”], and, neglecting the universal law, the love of a particular activity—although that activity itself cannot be separated from the universe governed by God—takes possession of it. Thus the person who does not love the laws is subjected to them.

## CHAPTER XV  
### After the resurrection the soul will exercise bodily numbers in tranquility. The four virtues by which the soul is perfected here

### 49

If, when we are thinking with the greatest concentration about incorporeal things that always remain in the same condition, the temporal numbers that we happen to exercise in any bodily movement pass by easily and in the most familiar manner—whether we are walking or singing—without our knowing it at all, although without our exercising them they would not exist;

and if, finally, when we are occupied with our own empty phantasies, these same things likewise pass by while we exercise them without perceiving them;

how much more easily and consistently will this happen when “this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:53)—that is, to express the same thing more plainly, when God has given life to our mortal bodies, as the Apostle says, “because of the Spirit dwelling in us” (Romans 8:11)?

How much more, then, will we be intent upon the one God and the clearly perceived truth—as has been said, face to face—and sense and rejoice in the numbers by which we exercise our bodies without any disturbance? Unless perhaps we must believe that, although the soul can rejoice in the things that are good through it, it cannot rejoice in the things through which it itself is good.

### 50

But this action by which the soul, with the help of God and its Lord, withdraws itself from the love of inferior beauty, conquering and destroying the habit that fights against it, and, through this victory, triumphing within itself over the powers of this air, while those powers envy it and seek to hinder it, flies toward its own stability and to God its foundation—does this action not seem to you to be the virtue called temperance?

D. I recognize and understand it.

M. What next? As it makes progress on this journey, already anticipating and almost grasping eternal joys, is it deterred by the loss of temporal things or by any death, when it is already able to say to its inferior companions: “It is good for me to depart and to be with Christ; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1:23–24)?

D. That is my view.

M. But what else should its disposition be called, by which it fears neither adversities nor death, except fortitude?

D. I recognize this also.

M. And now, what virtue does its ordering seem to you to be, by which it serves no one except the one God, wishes to be made equal to no one except the purest souls, and desires to rule over no nature except the bestial and bodily?

D. Who could fail to understand that this is justice?

M. You understand correctly.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### Whether and how the four virtues exist in the blessed

### 51

But now I ask this. Since we agreed above that prudence is that by which the soul understands where it ought to remain, and by which it raises itself through temperance—that is, through the conversion of love toward God, which is called charity—and through turning away from this world, accompanied also by fortitude and justice, do you think that, when it has reached the fruit of its love and effort through perfect sanctification, and through the perfect restoration of its body, and when the tumult of phantasies has been erased from its memory, it will begin to live with God himself by God alone, when what is divinely promised to us in these words has been fulfilled:

“Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2)?

I ask, then, whether you think that the virtues we have mentioned will exist there also.

D. I do not see how, once the adversities against which it struggles have passed away, prudence could exist there, since it chooses what to pursue only amid adversities; or temperance, since it turns love away only from adversities; or fortitude, since it endures only adversities; or justice, since it does not seek to be made equal to the most blessed souls and to rule over an inferior nature except amid adversities—that is, before it has attained the very thing it seeks.

### 52

M. Your answer is not altogether unreasonable, and I do not deny that this has seemed so to certain learned men. But when I consult the Books whose authority surpasses all others, I find the following words:

“Taste and see that the Lord is good” (Psalm 33:9).

The apostle Peter also inserted this in the following form: “If indeed you have tasted that the Lord is good” (1 Peter 2:3).

I think this is what is accomplished in those virtues by which the soul is purified through conversion itself. For the love of temporal things would not be conquered unless there were some sweetness of eternal things.

But when we have reached what is sung:

“The children of men will hope beneath the shelter of your wings; they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight; for with you is the fountain of life,”

the Psalm does not then say that the Lord will be good by being tasted. Rather, you see what flood and abundance of the eternal fountain are proclaimed. A kind of intoxication follows from it, and by this name I think the forgetting of worldly vanities and phantasies is wonderfully signified.

He then continues and says:

“In your light we shall see light. Extend your mercy to those who know you.”

“Light” is to be understood here as Christ, who is the Wisdom of God and is so often called light. Therefore, when it says, “We shall see,” and “those who know you,” it cannot be denied that prudence will exist there. Can the true good be seen and known by the soul where there is no prudence?

D. I understand now.

### 53

M. What of this? Can those who are upright in heart exist without justice?

D. I recognize that this word more frequently signifies justice.

M. What else, then, does the prophet immediately add when he sings: “And your justice to those who are upright in heart”?

D. It is clear.

M. Come, then: recall, if you please, that we discussed above how the soul, through pride, falls into certain activities of its own power and, neglecting the universal law, falls into carrying out certain private actions. This is called apostasy from God.

D. I remember.

M. When, therefore, it acts so that such a thing will no longer delight it, does it not seem to you to fix its love upon God and to live, with the utmost temperance, purity, and security, free from every defilement?

D. It certainly seems so.

M. Observe also how the prophet adds this, saying: “Let not the foot of pride come to me.” By calling it a foot, he signifies the very departure or fall from which the soul, restraining itself, lives eternally by clinging to God.

D. I accept this and follow you.

### 54

M. Fortitude, then, remains. But just as temperance is directed against the fall that occurs through free will, so fortitude is directed against force, by which a person can also be compelled, if he is not strong enough, into those things by which he is overturned and lies in the utmost misery.

This force is suitably and customarily signified in Scripture by the name “hand.” But who tries to inflict this force except sinners? When the soul is fortified against this very thing and guarded by the strength of God, so that it cannot in any way suffer this from any source, it possesses a certain stable and, so to speak, impassible power. Unless you object, this is rightly called fortitude, and I think it is what is meant when the text adds:

“Nor let the hand of sinners move me” (Psalm 35:8–12) [Note: [Col. 1190] Thus the editions and the better manuscripts. Some printed editions have: “But the soul is fortified against this very thing.”].

### 55

But whether this or something else is to be understood in these words, will you deny that in that perfection and blessedness the soul is established, beholds the truth, remains undefiled, is able to suffer no distress, and is subject to God alone while surpassing all other natures?

D. On the contrary, I do not see how it could be perfect and blessed in any other way.

M. These contemplation, sanctification, impassibility, and ordering of the soul, then, are either the four virtues perfected and brought to completion; or, so that we do not labor uselessly over names when the realities agree, instead of these virtues, which the soul uses when established amid labors, we must hope for certain powers of this kind in its eternal life.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### That the sinful soul exercises numbers and is governed by numbers. Conclusion of the work

### 56

Let us remember only what bears most directly upon the discussion we have undertaken: through the providence of God, by which he created and governs all things, even the sinful and wretched soul is governed by numbers and exercises numbers, all the way to the lowest corruption of the flesh. These numbers may be progressively less and less beautiful, but they cannot be wholly without beauty.

God, supremely good and supremely just, envies no beauty that is produced either by the soul’s condemnation, its return, or its continuance. Number begins from one; it is beautiful through equality and likeness; and it is joined together by order.

Therefore anyone who admits that there is no nature that does not, in order to be whatever it is, seek unity, and strive insofar as it can to be like itself, and preserve its proper order—whether in places, in times, or in some bodily equilibrium [Note: [Col. 1191] Erasmus and Lovaniensis have “in some incorporeal balance.” Several manuscripts have “in some corporeal balance.” Am. and most of the older codices, however, prefer “in some bodily balance,” which we consider the better reading.]—must admit that all things that exist, insofar as they exist, were made and established from one beginning, through a form equal and similar to that beginning, from the riches of its goodness, by which the one and the one from the one are joined together by the dearest love, so to speak [Note: [Col. 1191] This notable passage concerning the Trinity is corrupt in the editions of Erasmus and Lovaniensis and in several more recent manuscripts: “by which the one and the two, so to speak, are joined together by the dearest love.” In the edition of Am. it reads: “by which the one and the one from the one are joined together as a gift; and, so to speak.” We have restored the whole passage according to the best older books.], by the most beloved love.

### 57

Thus the verse we proposed, “God, creator of all,” is pleasing not only to the ears through its measured sound, but much more to the soul through the soundness and truth of its meaning.

Unless perhaps you are troubled by the slowness of those people—to put it more gently—who deny that anything can be made from nothing, although it is said that almighty God made it.

Can a craftsman, through the rational numbers that exist in his art, produce the sensory numbers that exist in his customary practice; and through sensory numbers produce those advancing numbers by which he moves his limbs in working, to which intervals of time already belong; and from these again fashion visible forms from wood, numerically ordered by intervals of place; while the nature of things, serving the commands of God, cannot make the wood itself from earth and the other elements?

And could those very lowest things themselves not be made from nothing [Note: [Col. 1192] The negative particle would seem to need to be deleted, unless it were preserved in the manuscripts. Yet since the following words—namely, “and could the ultimate elements themselves not be made from nothing?”—are absent from them, we admit that they should not be given such authority here, since the passage has been corrupted through scribal error.]?

Indeed, the local numbers of a tree must necessarily be preceded by temporal numbers. For there is no kind of plant that does not, according to the dimensions appropriate to its seed, grow together and germinate at fixed periods of time, emerge into the air, unfold its leaves, grow strong, and, whether through fruit or through the most hidden numbers of the wood itself, reproduce the power of its seed.

How much more is this true of animal bodies, in which the intervals of the limbs present a numerical equality much more clearly to the eyes?

Can these things be made from the elements while the elements themselves could not be made from nothing? As though there were anything in them more worthless and base than earth.

Earth first possesses the general form of a body, in which a certain unity, number, and order are demonstrably present. For any portion of it, however small, must necessarily extend from some indivisible mark into length, take on breadth as a third dimension, and receive height as a fourth dimension by which the body is filled.

Where, then, does this progression from the first to the fourth dimension come from? And where does the equality of the parts found in length, breadth, and height come from? Where does a certain proportionality come from—for I prefer to call analogy by this name—so that the relation of length to the indivisible mark is the same as that of breadth to length, and that of height to breadth?

Where, I ask, do these things come from except from that supreme and eternal dominion of number, likeness, equality, and order? Yet if you take these away from earth, nothing will remain. Therefore almighty God made the earth, and the earth was made from nothing.

### 58

What next? Does not the very form by which earth is distinguished from the other elements likewise show that it has received a certain unity; that no part of it is unlike the whole; and that, through the connection and harmony of its parts, it occupies, in its own kind, the lowest and most healthful place?

Upon it is poured the nature of water, itself striving toward unity, more beautiful and more transparent because of the greater likeness of its parts, and preserving the place of its order and its well-being.

What shall I say about the nature of air, striving toward unity with a much easier cohesion, and so much more beautiful than water as water is more beautiful than earth, and so much higher in relation to well-being [Note: [Col. 1192] Lov. has: “And so much more beautiful as the waters are more beautiful than earth, and so much higher in its striving toward superior well-being than the earth.”]?

What shall I say about the highest circuit of heaven, by which the entire universe of visible bodies is bounded, and which possesses the highest beauty in this order and the most healthful excellence of place?

All these things, certainly, which we count through the service of bodily sensation, and everything that exists in them, possess local numbers that appear in some fixed state. But unless these are preceded by inward and silent temporal numbers that exist in movement, they can neither receive nor possess those local numbers.

The vital movement, active through intervals of time, precedes and regulates those temporal numbers. It serves the Lord of all things, possessing not temporal intervals arranged as its own numbers, but possessing a power that supplies time. Above this, rational and intellectual numbers belonging to blessed and holy souls receive the very law of God—without which not even a leaf falls from a tree, and by which even the hairs of our head are numbered—without any intervening nature, and transmit it down to earthly and infernal laws [Note: [Col. 1193] See Retractations, book 1, chapter 1, no. 4.].

## CONCLUSION OF THE WORK

### 59

I have discussed with you, as much as I could and in the manner I could, matters so great with such small resources. Those who read this conversation of ours after it has been committed to writing should know that these things were written for people far weaker than those who, following the authority of the two Testaments, venerate and worship the consubstantial and unchangeable Trinity of the one supreme God—from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are—by believing, hoping, and loving.

For such people are purified not by human reasonings that merely sparkle, but by the strongest and most ardent fire of charity. We, however, because we do not think those should be neglected who are deceived by heretics through the deceptive promise of reason and knowledge, proceed more slowly, examining the roads themselves—roads that holy men do not deign to notice because they fly along them.

Yet we would not dare to do this if we had not seen many devout sons of the Catholic Church, our best mother, who had acquired through childish studies as much ability to speak and reason as was sufficient, doing the same thing out of the necessity of refuting heretics.

[Col. 1193]

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO  
## One Book of *The Teacher*

[Note: [Col. 1193] Written about the year 389 after Christ.]

[Note: [Col. 1193] This book was collated with the Fécamp, Saint Michael’s, Bec, three Victorine, two Navarrese, one manuscript of the church of Reims, and one manuscript of the Vatican Library; with the readings of three Belgian manuscripts published by the Louvain scholars; and with the editions of Badius, Amerbach, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis.]

[Note: [Col. 1193] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.]

(C)

# NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK, *THE TEACHER*

[Note: [Col. 1193] See also book 1, chapter 12, of the *Retractations*, col. 602, from the words “At that time” to the words “When we speak.” M.]

The date of the following little work is disclosed by its author himself in book 9, chapter 6, of the *Confessions*. There, after stating that Adeodatus was “about fifteen years old” when he joined Augustine and his companions as they were going to Milan to receive baptism, he testifies that this dialogue with him had subsequently been held “when he was sixteen years old”—that is, in the second year after their baptism, which certainly took place in the year of Christ 387.

Accordingly, after listing the books *On Genesis against the Manichaeans* and *On Music*, which had been completed about the year 389, Augustine added in book 1, chapter 12, of the *Retractations* that he had written *The Teacher* at about the same time.

## SAINT AUGUSTINE, BOOK 9 OF THE *CONFESSIONS*, CHAPTER 6

“We also joined to ourselves the boy Adeodatus, born carnally from me and from my sin. You had made him well. He was about fifteen years old, and in talent he surpassed many grave and learned men . . . . I confess to you your gifts . . . . There is our book entitled *The Teacher*: he himself speaks with me in it. You know that all the thoughts inserted there in the role of my interlocutor are his, when he was sixteen years old. I experienced many other things in him that were even more remarkable. That talent filled me with horror . . . .”

## [DISPUTATIONS]

In this work the force and function of words are discussed at length, and it is finally demonstrated that knowledge of things is obtained not through the words that a person utters outwardly, but through eternal truth teaching inwardly.

## CHAPTER I  
### For what purpose speech was instituted

[Col. 1193]

### 1

AUGUSTINE: What do we seem to you to want to accomplish when we speak?

ADEODATUS: As far as occurs to me at present, either to teach or to learn.

AUGUSTINE: I see and agree with one of these. For it is clear that by speaking we want to teach. But how do we want to learn?

ADEODATUS: What else do you think, except when we ask questions?

AUGUSTINE: Even then I understand us to want nothing other than to teach. For I ask you whether you ask for any other reason than to teach the person whom you question what you want.

ADEODATUS: You are right.

AUGUSTINE: You see, then, that by speaking we seek nothing except to teach.

ADEODATUS: I do not see that clearly. For if speaking is nothing other than bringing forth words, I see that we do this when we sing. Since we often do this alone, with no one present to learn, I do not think that we want to teach anything.

AUGUSTINE: But I think there is a certain kind of teaching through reminding—a very important kind—which the matter itself will indicate in this conversation of ours. But if you do not think that we learn when we remember, or that the person who reminds teaches, I do not resist you. I therefore now establish two purposes of speaking: either to teach, or to remind others or ourselves. We accomplish the latter also when we sing. Does this not seem so to you?

ADEODATUS: Not entirely. For it is extremely rare that I sing in order to remind myself; I sing merely for pleasure.

AUGUSTINE: I understand what you mean. But do you not notice that what delights you in singing is a certain modulation of sound? Since this can be added to or removed from words, speaking is one thing and singing another. For people sing with pipes and lyres, birds sing, and we sometimes produce something musical without words. That sound can be called singing, but it cannot be called speech. Do you have anything to say against this?

ADEODATUS: Nothing at all.

### 2

AUGUSTINE: It seems to you, then, that speech was instituted for no purpose except either teaching or reminding?

ADEODATUS: It would seem so, if I were not troubled by the fact that when we pray, we certainly speak, and yet we must not believe that God is either taught something by us or reminded of something.

AUGUSTINE: I think you do not know that we were commanded to pray in closed rooms (Matthew 6:6)—by which the inner chambers of the mind are signified—for no other reason than that God does not seek to have us remind or teach him through our speech in order to grant us what we desire.

For the person who speaks gives outwardly, through articulated sound, a sign of his will. But God must be sought and entreated in the very secrets of the rational soul, which is called the inner person; for he wished these to be his temples.

Have you not read in the Apostle: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:16), and: “That Christ may dwell in the inner person” (Ephesians 3:16–17)?

Have you not also noticed in the prophet: “Speak within your hearts, and be pierced in your chambers; sacrifice the sacrifice of righteousness, and hope in the Lord”? (Psalm 4:5–6.)

Where do you think the sacrifice of righteousness is offered except in the temple of the mind and in the chambers of the heart? But where sacrifice is to be offered, there too prayer is to be made.

Therefore speech is not necessary when we pray—that is, sounding words—unless perhaps, as priests do, we use it to signify our state of mind, not so that God but so that human beings may hear, and so that through a kind of common assent they may be lifted toward God by remembering. Or do you think otherwise?

ADEODATUS: I entirely agree.

AUGUSTINE: Then you are not troubled by the fact that the supreme Teacher, when he taught his disciples to pray, taught them certain words (Matthew 6:9), appearing to have done nothing other than teach them how they ought to speak when praying?

ADEODATUS: This does not trouble me at all. For he taught them through words not the words themselves but the things, so that they might remind themselves, as they prayed in the inner chambers of the mind, as has been said, from whom and what they ought to request.

AUGUSTINE: You understand correctly. I also believe that you notice that, even if someone insists that, although we utter no sound, we nevertheless speak inwardly within the mind because we think the words themselves, then by speech too we are doing nothing other than reminding. Memory, to which the words adhere, turns them over and brings into the mind the things themselves of which the words are signs.

ADEODATUS: I understand and agree.

## CHAPTER II  
### The meaning of words is shown by a person only through words

### 3

AUGUSTINE: We agree, then, that words are signs.

ADEODATUS: We agree.

AUGUSTINE: What do you say? Can a sign be a sign unless it signifies something?

ADEODATUS: It cannot.

AUGUSTINE: How many words are there in this verse,
“If it pleases the gods above that nothing be left from so great a city?” (*Aeneid*, Book 2, verse 659.)

Ad. Eight.

Aug. There are therefore eight signs.

Ad. That is so.

Aug. I believe you understand this verse.

Ad. I think I understand it sufficiently.

Aug. Tell me what each individual word signifies.

Ad. I do see what *si* signifies; but I cannot find any other word by which it could be explained.

Aug. At least, can you find where whatever is signified by this word is located?

Ad. It seems to me that *si* signifies doubt; and where can doubt be except in the mind?
