Aug. I accept that for the moment; proceed with the rest.

Ad. *Nihil* signifies what else but that which is not?

Aug. Perhaps you are right. But what prevents me from agreeing is the concession you made above, that something cannot be a sign unless it signifies something; and what is not cannot in any way be something. Therefore the second word in this verse is not a sign, because it signifies nothing; and our agreement that all words are signs, or that every sign signifies something, was false.

Ad. You press the point too hard. Yet when we have nothing to signify, we utter a word altogether foolishly. But now, when you speak with me, I believe you do not emit any sound in vain; rather, with everything that bursts from your mouth, you give me a sign so that I may understand something. Therefore, while you are speaking, you ought not to utter these two syllables if through them you signify nothing. But if you see that some utterance through them is necessary, and that we are taught or reminded when they strike our ears, then you certainly see what I mean, although I cannot explain it.

Aug. What, then, shall we do? Shall we say that this word signifies some affection of the mind which, although it does not see a thing, discovers—or thinks it has discovered—that it is not there, rather than the thing itself, which is nothing?

Ad. That is perhaps precisely what I was trying to explain.

Aug. Let us therefore pass on from this, whatever its status may be, lest something utterly absurd happen to us.

Ad. What, exactly?

Aug. That nothing should hold us and we should suffer delay.

Ad. This is indeed ridiculous, yet somehow I see that it could happen—or rather, I plainly see that it has happened.

**4.** Aug. In its proper place, if God permits, we shall understand this kind of contradiction more clearly. For now, return to that verse and try, as best you can, to unfold what its remaining words signify.

Ad. The third word is the preposition *ex*, for which, I think, we may say *de*.

Aug. I am not asking you to give, in place of one very familiar word, another equally familiar word that signifies the same thing—if indeed it does signify the same thing. But let us grant for the moment that it does. Certainly, if this poet had said not *ex tanta urbe* (“from so great a city”) but *de tanta urbe*, and I asked [Col. 1197] you what *de* signified, you would say *ex*, since these two words are signs, each signifying, as you think, one thing. But I am asking about that one thing—whatever it may be—which is signified by these two signs.

Ad. It seems to me to signify a kind of separation from the thing in which something had been, and from which it is said to be. That thing may no longer remain, as in this verse: while the city did not remain, some Trojans could have been from it; or it may remain, as when we say that merchants in Africa are from the city of Rome.

Aug. Even if I grant that this is so, and do not enumerate how many cases may perhaps be found beyond your rule, you can certainly observe that you have explained words by words—that is, signs by signs—and the most familiar by the most familiar. But I would like you, if you could, to show me the very things of which these are signs.

### CHAPTER III  
### Whether a thing can be shown without a sign

**5.** Ad. I am surprised that you do not know—or rather, pretend not to know—that my answer makes what you want entirely impossible. We are conversing, and in conversation we cannot answer except with words. Yet you are asking me about things which, whatever they may be, are certainly not words, and which you nevertheless ask me about through words. Therefore you first ask without words, so that I may then answer under that condition.

Aug. You are right, I admit. But if I asked what these three syllables signify when one says *paries* (“wall”), could you not point with your finger, so that I might see the thing itself, whose sign is this trisyllabic word, while you demonstrated it without uttering any words?

Ad. I grant that this can happen only with nouns by which bodies are signified, provided that the bodies themselves are present.

Aug. Do we call a color a body, or rather a certain quality of a body?

Ad. That is so.

Aug. Why, then, can it also be pointed out here? Or do you add the qualities of bodies to bodies, so that these too, when present, can be taught without words?

Ad. When I spoke of bodies, I meant all corporeal things—that is, everything perceived in bodies.

Aug. Consider, nevertheless, whether some things must be excepted from this as well.

Ad. You rightly remind me. I should not have said all corporeal things, but all visible things. For I admit that sound, smell, taste, weight, heat, and other things belonging to the remaining senses, although they cannot be perceived without bodies and are therefore corporeal, nevertheless cannot be shown with a finger.

Aug. Have you never seen people converse by gestures, as it were, with the deaf, while the deaf themselves use gestures no less to ask, answer, teach, indicate, or convey either everything they wish or at least very many things? When this happens, not only visible things are shown without words, but also sounds, tastes, and other things of this kind. Actors, too, often reveal and present entire plays in theaters by dancing without words.

Ad. I have nothing to object, except that *ex* could not be shown to you without words—not only by me, but not even by the actor-dancer himself.

**6.** Aug. Perhaps you are right. But let us suppose that he could. Surely, I think, you do not doubt that whatever bodily movement he might make in trying to demonstrate to me the thing signified by this word [*ex*], [Col. 1198] that movement itself would not be the thing, but a sign. Therefore here too he would indicate not, indeed, a word by a word, but nevertheless a sign by a sign: this monosyllable *ex* and that gesture would signify one thing. I would prefer that this thing be shown to me without being signified.

Ad. How can what you are asking be done, I beg you?

Aug. In the same way that the wall could be shown.

Ad. Not even the wall, so far as advancing reason has taught us, can be shown without a sign. The pointing of the finger is not the wall; rather, a sign is given through which the wall can be seen. I therefore see nothing that can be shown without signs.

Aug. What if I asked you what walking is, and you rose and performed it? Would you not teach me by the thing itself rather than by words or any other signs?

Ad. I admit that this is so, and I am ashamed not to have seen something so obvious. From this, too, thousands of things now occur to me that can be shown by themselves, not through signs: eating, drinking, sitting, standing, shouting, and countless others.

Aug. Come, then, tell me: if, entirely ignorant of the meaning of this word, I asked you while you were walking what walking is, how would you teach me?

Ad. I would do the same thing somewhat more quickly, so that after my question you might be reminded by some novelty; yet nothing else would happen except what ought to be shown.

Aug. Do you know that walking is one thing and hurrying another? Someone who walks does not immediately hurry, and someone who hurries does not necessarily walk; for we speak of hurrying in writing, reading, and countless other activities. Therefore, when you performed more quickly what you were doing after my question, I would think that walking was nothing other than hurrying, since you had added this new feature; and I would be deceived.

Ad. I admit that we cannot show a thing without a sign if we are questioned while we are doing it. For if we add nothing, the questioner will think that we do not want to show it and, despising him, continue with what we were doing. But if he asks about things we can do, and does not ask us at the very time we are doing them, then after his question we can demonstrate what he asks by doing it, through the thing itself rather than by a sign—unless, perhaps, he asks me while I am speaking what speaking is. Whatever I say, I must speak in order to teach him. From this it follows that I will continue teaching until I make clear to him what he wants, without departing from the very thing he wanted shown to him and without seeking signs by which to show it apart from the thing itself.

### CHAPTER IV  
### Whether signs are shown by signs

**7.** Aug. You have reasoned with complete acuity. Consider, then, whether we now agree that those things can be shown without signs which either we are not doing when questioned but can immediately do, or which perhaps are themselves signs. For when we speak, we make signs, as was indicated by the word *signify*.

Ad. We agree.

Aug. Therefore, when signs are being asked about, signs can be shown by signs; but when things that are not signs are asked about, they can be shown either by doing them after the inquiry, if they can be done, or by giving signs through which they can be perceived.

Ad. That is so.

Aug. In this threefold division, then, let us first consider, if you agree, the case in which signs are shown by signs. For are only words signs?

Ad. No.

Aug. [Col. 1199] It seems to me, then, that in speaking we either signify words themselves by words, or other signs—for example, a gesture when we say *gesture*, or a letter when we say *letter*. The things signified by these two words are themselves nevertheless signs. Or we signify something else that is not a sign, as when we say *stone*. This word is a sign, because it signifies something, but what it signifies is not necessarily a sign. That class, namely, cases in which things that are not signs are signified by words, does not belong to the part we have undertaken to examine. We have undertaken to consider the case in which signs are shown by signs, and within it we have found two divisions: either we teach or recall the same signs by signs, or different signs by signs. Do you not think so?

Ad. It is clear.

**8.** Aug. Tell me, then, to which sense signs that are words belong.

Ad. To hearing.

Aug. What about gestures?

Ad. To sight.

Aug. And when we encounter written words? Are they not words, or are they more properly understood as signs of words? Let a word be something uttered in an articulated voice with some signification; and since voice can be perceived by no sense other than hearing, it follows that when a word is written, it becomes a sign for the eyes, by which what belongs to the ears comes into the mind.

Ad. I entirely agree.

Aug. I believe you will also agree that when we say *noun*, we signify something.

Ad. That is true.

Aug. What, then?

Ad. That by which each thing is called: for example, Romulus, Rome, virtue, river, and countless others.

Aug. Do these four nouns signify no things?

Ad. On the contrary, they signify certain things.

Aug. Is there no difference between these nouns and the things signified by them?

Ad. On the contrary, there is a very great difference.

Aug. I would like to hear from you what that difference is.

Ad. First of all, these are signs, whereas those are not.

Aug. Shall we call those things which can be signified by signs but are not signs *significables*, just as we call things that can be seen *visibles*, so that we may discuss them more conveniently from now on?

Ad. Certainly.

Aug. What, then? Are those four signs you just pronounced not signified by any other sign?

Ad. I am surprised that you think I have already forgotten that we discovered that written things are signs of things uttered by the voice.

Aug. Tell me what difference there is between them.

Ad. The former are visible, the latter audible. For why should you not admit this term as well, if we have admitted *significables*?

Aug. I admit it completely, and gladly. But I ask again: can these four signs not be signified by some other audible sign, just as you recalled that they are visible?

Ad. I also remember this more recent point. I answered that *noun* signifies something, and I placed those four things under its signification. I recognize that both *noun* and those four, if they are uttered by the voice, are audible.

Aug. What, then, is the difference between an audible sign and audible significates which are themselves again signs?

Ad. I see this difference between what we say, *noun*, and the four things we placed under its signification: the former is an audible sign of audible signs, whereas the latter are indeed audible signs, but not signs of signs. Rather, they are signs partly of visible things, as Romulus, Rome, and river are; and partly of intelligible things, as virtue is.

[Col. 1200]

**9.** Aug. I accept and approve this. But do you know that everything uttered in an articulated voice with some signification is called a word?

Ad. I know it.

Aug. Therefore a noun is also a word, since we see it uttered in an articulated voice with some signification. When we say that an eloquent person uses good words, he certainly uses nouns as well. And when, in Terence, a servant reported to an old master, “Good words, please” (*Bona verba quaeso*, *Andria*, act 1, scene 2, verse 33), he had also spoken many nouns.

Ad. I agree.

Aug. You therefore grant that by those two syllables which we utter when we say *word*, a noun is also signified, and that for this reason *word* is a sign of *noun*.

Ad. I grant it.

Aug. I would like you to answer this as well. When a word is a sign of a noun, and a noun is a sign of a river, and a river is a sign of a thing which can now be seen, you said what difference there is between that thing and the river, that is, its sign, and between this sign and the noun, which is the sign of this sign. What difference do you think there is between the sign of a noun, which we have discovered to be a word, and the noun itself of which it is the sign?

Ad. I understand the difference to be that whatever is signified by a noun is also signified by a word. For just as a noun is a word, so a river is a word. But not everything signified by a word is also signified by a noun. For *si*, which stands at the beginning of the verse you proposed, and *ex*, about which we have been reasoning for a long time and through which our discussion has reached this point, are words but not nouns; and many such examples are found. Since all nouns are words, but not all words are nouns, I think it is clear what difference there is between a word and a noun: that is, between the sign of a sign of that which itself signifies no other signs, and the sign of a sign which in turn signifies other things.

Aug. Do you grant that every horse is an animal, but not every animal is a horse?

Ad. Who could doubt it?

Aug. This, then, is the difference between a noun and a word: the same as the difference between a horse and an animal. Unless perhaps what prevents you from agreeing is that we use *word* in another way, to mean those things which are inflected through tenses, such as *scribo*, *scripsi*, *lego*, *legi* (“I write,” “I wrote,” “I read,” “I have read”), which are plainly not nouns.

Ad. You have stated exactly what was causing me to doubt.

Aug. Do not let this trouble you. We also speak of signs universally, meaning everything that signifies something; and among these we find words. We also speak of military signs, which are properly called *signs*, and to which words do not belong. Yet if I said to you that, just as every horse is an animal but not every animal a horse, so every word is a sign but not every sign a word, you would, I think, have no doubts.

Ad. I now understand and entirely agree that the difference between that universal term *word* and *noun* is the same as the difference between animal and horse.

**10.** Aug. Do you also know that when we say *animal*, there is one thing—the trisyllabic noun uttered by the voice—and another thing—the thing signified?

Ad. Above I already granted this concerning all signs and significables.

Aug. Do all signs seem to you to signify something other than what they are themselves, as this trisyllabic word *animal*, when we say it, in no way signifies the same thing as what it itself is?

Ad. Not at all. For when we say *sign*, it signifies not only all the other [Col. 1201] signs that exist, but also itself. It is a word, and all words are certainly signs.

Aug. What about the disyllable *word*? Does something similar not occur there? For if everything uttered in an articulated voice with some signification is signified by this disyllable, then this very expression is also included in that class.

Ad. That is so.

Aug. What about *noun*? Does it not behave similarly? For it signifies nouns of every kind, and *noun* itself is a neuter noun. If I asked you what part of speech *noun* is, could you answer correctly with anything other than *noun*?

Ad. You are right.

Aug. There are therefore signs which, among the things they signify, signify themselves as well.

Ad. There are.

Aug. Does this four-syllable sign seem to you to be of that kind when we say *conjunction*?

Ad. Not at all. For the things it signifies are not nouns, whereas this expression is a noun.

### CHAPTER V  
### Mutual signs

**11.** Aug. You have paid close attention. Now consider whether there are signs which signify one another, so that just as this is signified by that, so that is signified by this. The four-syllable word *conjunction* and the things signified by it—*si* (“if”), *vel* (“or”), *nam* (“for”), *namque* (“for indeed”), *nisi* (“unless”), *ergo* (“therefore”), *quoniam* (“since”), and similar words—do not stand in this relation. Those expressions are signified by that one term, but that one four-syllable term is not signified by any one of them.

Ad. I see that. I wish to know what signs signify one another.

Aug. Do you not know that when we say *noun and word*, we are saying two words?

Ad. I know it.

Aug. And do you not know that when we say *noun and word*, we are saying two nouns?

Ad. I know that as well.

Aug. You therefore know that a noun is signified by a word, and a word by a noun.

Ad. I agree.

Aug. Can you say, apart from the fact that they are written and pronounced differently, how they differ from one another?

Ad. Perhaps I can. I see that it is what I said shortly before. When we say *words*, we signify everything uttered in an articulated voice with some signification. Hence every noun—and *noun* itself when we say it—is a word. But not every word is a noun, although *word* is a noun when we say it.

**12.** Aug. What if someone asserted and proved to you that, just as every noun is a word, so every word is a noun? Could you find any difference between them apart from the different sound of their letters?

Ad. I could not, nor do I think there would be any difference.

Aug. What if everything uttered in an articulated voice with some signification were both words and nouns, but were words for one reason and nouns for another? Would there be no difference between a noun and a word?

Ad. I do not understand how that could be.

Aug. You understand at least that everything colored is visible, and everything visible is colored, although these two words signify distinctly and differently.

Ad. I understand.

Aug. What if, then, every word were a noun and every noun a word, although these two nouns—or these two words—that is, *noun* and *word*—had different significations?

Ad. I now see that this could happen, but I await your explanation of how it does.

Aug. Everything that bursts forth in an articulated voice with some signification, as I think you observe, both strikes the ear [Col. 1202] and is thereby perceived, and is committed to memory so that it may be known.

Ad. I observe this.

Aug. Two things therefore occur when we utter something in such a voice.

Ad. That is so.

Aug. What if words received their name from one of these two things, and nouns from the other—words, evidently, from striking (*verberando*), but nouns from knowing (*nosciendo*)—so that the first deserved to be named from the ears, and the second from the mind?

**13.** Ad. I will grant this when you show how we can correctly call all words nouns.

Aug. It is easy. I believe you have learned and retained what is called a pronoun: a form that has the force of a noun, but marks a thing with less complete signification than a noun. For, as I think, the grammarian to whom you rendered an account defined it in this way: “A pronoun is a part of speech which, placed in the position of a noun, signifies the same thing, indeed less fully, but nevertheless the same.”

Ad. I remember this and approve it.

Aug. According to this definition, then, you see that pronouns serve only nouns and can be placed only in their position, as when we say *this man*, *that king himself*, *the same woman*, *this gold*, *that silver*. *This*, *himself*, *the same*, *this*, and *that* are pronouns; *man*, *king*, *woman*, *gold*, and *silver* are nouns, by which the things signified are signified more fully than by those pronouns.

Ad. I see and agree.

Aug. Now pronounce for me any few conjunctions you please.

Ad. *Et*, *-que*, *at*, *atque* (“and,” “and,” “but,” “and”).

Aug. Do all these things you have uttered seem to you to be nouns?

Ad. Not at all.

Aug. At least, did I seem to have spoken correctly when I said, “All these things you have uttered”?

Ad. Entirely correctly. I now understand how wonderfully you showed that I had uttered nouns. For otherwise it could not correctly have been said of them, “all these.” Yet I am still afraid that you seem to have spoken correctly for this reason: I do not deny that these four conjunctions are also words, so that it could correctly be said of them, “all these,” since one can correctly say, “all these words.” But if you ask me what part of speech *words* is, I will answer nothing other than *noun*. Therefore perhaps a pronoun was attached to this noun, so that your expression would be correct.

**14.** Aug. Your error is clever indeed, but attend more cleverly to what I shall say, if I am able to say it as I wish. To discuss words by means of words is as intricate as inserting and rubbing one finger against another: scarcely anyone can discern, except the person doing it, which finger itches and which helps the itching one.

Ad. I am present with my whole mind, for this comparison has made me extremely attentive.

Aug. Words certainly consist of sound and letters.

Ad. That is so.

Aug. Therefore, to use an authority especially dear to us, when the apostle Paul says, “There was not in Christ ‘Yes’ (*est*) and ‘No’ (*non*) [Note: [Col. 1202] Greek: Ναὶ καὶ οὔ (‘yes and no’)], but ‘Yes’ (*est*) was in him” (2 Cor. 1:19), I do not think we should suppose that the three letters which we utter when we say *est* were in Christ, but rather what is signified by those three letters.

Ad. You are right.

Aug. You understand, then, that the person who says, “ ‘Yes’ (*est*) was in him,” has said nothing other than “What was in him is called *est*”—just as if he had said, [Col. 1203] “Virtue was in him,” he would plainly be understood to have said nothing other than “What was in him is called virtue.” We should not suppose that the two syllables which we utter when we say *virtus* (“virtue”), rather than what those two syllables signify, were in him.

Ad. I understand and follow you.

Aug. What? Do you not also understand that it makes no difference whether someone says, “Virtue is called so,” or “Virtue is named”?

Ad. It is clear.

Aug. Then it is equally clear that it makes no difference whether someone says, “What was in him is called *est*,” or “What was in him is named *est*.”

Ad. I see that there is no difference here either.

Aug. Do you now see what I want to demonstrate?

Ad. Not yet, certainly.

Aug. Do you not see, then, that a noun is that by which something is named?

Ad. I see nothing more certain than this.

Aug. You see, therefore, that *est* is a noun, since what was in him is named *est*.

Ad. I cannot deny it.

Aug. But if I asked you what part of speech *est* is, I do not think you would say it was a noun, but a verb, although reason has also shown it to be a noun.

Ad. It is exactly as you say.

Aug. Do you still doubt that other parts of speech are nouns in the same way that we have demonstrated?

Ad. I do not doubt it, since I admit that they signify something. But if you ask what each thing they signify is called—that is, named—I cannot answer except with the very parts of speech which we do not call nouns, but which, as I see, we are compelled to call nouns.

**15.** Aug. Does it not trouble you that someone might arise to undermine this reasoning of ours by saying that authority should be attributed to the Apostle not for words but for things, and that therefore the foundation of this argument is not as firm as we think? It could happen that Paul, although he lived and taught with complete correctness [Note: [Col. 1203] The manuscripts read, “although he spoke and taught with complete correctness”], nevertheless spoke less correctly when he said, “ ‘Yes’ was in him,” especially since he himself admits that he was unskilled in speech (2 Cor. 11:6). How do you think such an objection should be refuted?

Ad. I have nothing to say against it, and I ask you to find someone among those to whom supreme knowledge of words is granted, whose authority you can use to accomplish what you want.

Aug. Does reason itself seem less adequate to you, once authorities have been set aside—the reason by which it is shown that all parts of speech signify something and are named from that; and if they are named, are called by a name? This can be judged very easily from different languages. Who would not see that, if you ask what the Greeks call what we call *quis* (“who”), the answer is *τίς*; what the Greeks call what we call *volo* (“I wish”), the answer is *θέλω*; what the Greeks call what we call *bene* (“well”), the answer is *καλῶς*; what the Greeks call what we call *scriptum* (“written”), the answer is *τὸ γεγραμμένον*; what the Greeks call what we call *et* (“and”), the answer is *καὶ*; what the Greeks call what we call *ab* (“from”), the answer is *ἀπό*; and what the Greeks call what we call *heu* (“alas”), the answer is *οἴ*? In all these parts of speech which I have now enumerated, the person who asks in this way speaks correctly. This could not happen unless they were nouns.

By this reasoning, then, we can establish that the apostle Paul spoke correctly, without relying on the authority of any eloquent persons. Why, then, should we seek whose person might support our judgment?

[Col. 1204]

**16.** But so that no one who is slower or more shameless may yet refuse to yield, and assert that without those authorities to whom, by common agreement, the laws of words are assigned, he will in no way submit—what can be found more excellent in the Latin language than Cicero? Yet in his most celebrated speeches, which are called the *Verrines*, he called *coram*—whether it is an adverb in that passage or a preposition—a noun.

Nevertheless, since it may happen that I understand that passage less well, and that it may be explained differently either by me or by someone else, there is one point to which I think no answer can be made. The most distinguished teachers of disputation state that a complete proposition, which can be affirmed or denied, consists of a noun and a verb. In one place Tullius calls this kind of expression a *pronouncement*. They also say that when the verb is in the third person, a nominative noun must accompany it; and they are right. If you consider this with me—for example, when we say, “A man sits,” “A horse runs”—you recognize, I think, that there are two pronouncements.

Ad. I recognize it.

Aug. Do you see that in each there is one noun—in one, *man*, and in the other, *horse*—and one verb—in one, *sits*, and in the other, *runs*?

Ad. I see it.

Aug. Therefore, if I said only “sits” or only “runs,” you would rightly ask me, “Who?” or “What?” so that I could answer “a man,” “a horse,” “an animal,” or anything else by which a noun could be supplied to complete the verb’s pronouncement—that is, the sentence which can be affirmed or denied.

Ad. I understand.

Aug. Attend to what follows. Imagine that we see something at a distance and are uncertain whether it is an animal or a stone, or something else, and that I say to you, “Because it is a man, it is an animal.” Would I not be speaking rashly?

Ad. Entirely rashly. But you would not be speaking rashly if you said, “If it is a man, it is an animal.”

Aug. You are right. Thus, in your expression, I approve *si* (“if”), and you approve it as well; but both of us disapprove *quia* (“because”) in mine.

Ad. I agree.

Aug. Now see whether these two sentences are complete pronouncements: “It pleases if”; “It displeases because.”

Ad. Entirely complete.

Aug. Come, then, tell me which words and which nouns are there.

Ad. I see the words *placet* (“it pleases”) and *displicet* (“it displeases”); but what else could the nouns be except *si* and *quia*?

Aug. It has therefore been sufficiently proved that these two conjunctions are also nouns.

Ad. Entirely sufficiently.

Aug. Can you yourself, on your own, demonstrate the same thing concerning the other parts of speech according to this same rule?

Ad. I can.

### CHAPTER VI  
### Signs signifying themselves

**17.** Aug. Let us pass on from here. Tell me now whether, just as we discovered that all words are nouns and all nouns are words, you also think that all nouns are appellations and all appellations are nouns.

Ad. I plainly see no difference between them apart from the different sound of their syllables.

Aug. For the moment I do not resist you, although there are some who distinguish them also by signification; it is not necessary now to consider their opinion. But surely you notice that we have now reached signs which signify one another, differing in nothing except sound, and which signify themselves along with all the other parts of speech.

Ad. I do not understand.

Aug. Then you do not understand that *appellation* is signified by *noun*, and *noun* by *appellation*, so that, apart from the sound of the letters, there is no difference between them as far as the general term [Col. 1205] is concerned. For we also speak of a specific noun, which among the eight parts of speech is such that it does not include the other seven.

Ad. I understand.

Aug. But this is what I said: *appellation* and *noun* signify one another.

**18.** Ad. I understand, but I ask what you meant by saying, “They also signify themselves along with the other parts of speech.”

Aug. Did the preceding reasoning not teach us that all parts of speech can be called nouns and appellations—that is, that they can be signified by *noun* and by *appellation*?

Ad. That is so.

Aug. What, then? If I ask you what you call this very noun—that is, this sound expressed in two syllables—will you not rightly answer, “Noun”?

Ad. Correctly.

Aug. Does the sign which we utter in four syllables when we say *conjunction* signify itself in this way? For this noun cannot be counted among the things it signifies.

Ad. I understand correctly.

Aug. This is what was meant by saying that *noun* signifies itself along with the other things it signifies. You can also understand the same thing for *appellation* by yourself.

Ad. It is now easy. But it occurs to me that *noun* is used both generally and specifically, whereas *appellation* is not counted among the eight parts of speech. For that reason, I think these two terms also differ from one another apart from their different sound.

Aug. What? Do you think *noun* and *ὄνομα* (“name”) differ from one another in anything except sound—the sound by which the Latin and Greek languages are also distinguished?

Ad. Here I understand nothing else.

Aug. We have therefore arrived at signs which signify themselves, in which one signifies the other mutually, and whatever is signified by one is also signified by the other, and which differ from one another in nothing except sound. For we have now discovered this fourth case; the preceding three are understood of *noun* and *word*.

Ad. We have arrived at it completely.

### CHAPTER VII  
### Summary of the preceding chapters

**19.** Aug. I would like you to review what we have discovered through our conversation.

Ad. I shall do so as best I can. First of all, I remember that we spent some time asking why we speak, and discovered that we speak for the sake of teaching or reminding, since even when we ask a question we are doing nothing else than ensuring that the person questioned learns what we wish to hear. In singing, which we seem to do for the sake of pleasure, there is nothing proper to speech. In praying to God, whom we cannot suppose to be taught or reminded, words serve either to remind ourselves or to enable others to be reminded or taught through us.

Next, once it had been sufficiently established that words are nothing other than signs, and that things which signify nothing cannot be signs, you proposed a verse whose individual words I was to try to explain. It was:

> “If it pleases the gods above that nothing be left from so great a city.”

Although the second word was very familiar and perfectly clear, we could not discover what it signified. Since it seemed to me that we did not insert it into our speech without purpose, but that through it we taught the hearer something—that this word perhaps indicated the mind’s affection when it discovers, or thinks it has discovered, that the thing it seeks is not there—you did indeed respond, but, avoiding by a joke I know not what depth of the question, postponed its illumination to another time. Do not suppose that I have forgotten your obligation as well.

Then, when I was trying to explain the third [Col. 1206] word in the verse, you pressed me to show not another word with the same value, but rather the very thing signified by the words. When I said that this could not be done in our conversation, we came to things which can be pointed out to those who ask. I thought that all these were corporeal things, but we discovered that they were only visible things.

From there, somehow, we came to the deaf and to actors, who signify by gestures without voice not only things that can be seen, but many additional things and nearly everything that we express in speech. Yet we discovered that these gestures themselves are signs.

Then we began again to ask how we might be able to show the things themselves that are signified by signs without any signs at all, since the wall, the color, and every visible thing shown by the pointing of a finger were proved to be shown by a certain sign.

Here, while I was mistaken in saying that nothing of this kind could be found, we finally agreed that those things can be demonstrated without a sign which we are not doing when they are asked about, but which we can do after the inquiry. Speech, however, does not belong to this class, since it became sufficiently clear that when we are speaking and are asked what speech is, it is easy to demonstrate it by speech itself.

20. From this we were reminded that either signs are indicated by signs, or things other than signs are indicated by signs, or things that we can do after being questioned are indicated without a sign. We therefore undertook to consider and examine more carefully the first of these three alternatives. In the course of that discussion it became clear that some signs could not in turn be signified by the signs that signified them—for example, when we say this four-syllable word *conjunction*; while others could be so signified, as when we say *sign*, by which we also signify a word, and when we say *word*, by which we also signify a sign. For *sign* and *word* are both two signs and two words.

In this class, in which signs signify one another, some were shown not to have equal scope, some to have equal scope, and some to have precisely the same meaning. Indeed, the disyllable that is sounded when we say *sign* signifies absolutely everything by which anything is signified. But when we say *word*, it is not a sign of every sign, but only of those signs that are uttered in articulate speech. Hence it is evident that, although both *word* is signified by *sign* and *sign* by *word*—that is, although these two syllables are signified by those and those by these—*sign* nevertheless has greater force than *word*, since those two syllables signify more than these do.

A general word has the same force as a general noun. For reason has taught that all the parts of speech are also nouns: pronouns can be added to them, it can be said of them all that they name something, and there is none of them whose utterance cannot be completed by the addition of a verb. Yet although noun and verb have the same scope, since everything that is a verb is also a noun, they do not have the same force. It has been argued with sufficient probability that they are called by different names for different reasons. One of them, it has been discovered, marks the striking of the ear, and the other the recalling of something to the mind. This can be understood even from the fact that in speaking we correctly say, “What is the name of this thing?” when we wish to commit the thing to memory; but we do not usually say, “What is the word for this thing?”

As for words that signify not only the same amount but precisely the same thing, between which nothing differs except the sound of their letters, we find *nomen* and ὄνομα (*onoma*). It had escaped me that, in this class in which signs signify one another, we had found no sign that did not also signify itself among the other things it signifies.

This is what I have been able to recall. You must now judge whether I have arranged these matters well and in proper order—you, whom I think to have said nothing in this discussion except knowingly and with certainty.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### That this discussion is not pointless; and that, after signs have been heard, the mind must be directed to the things signified in order to answer the questioner

**21. Augustine.** You have indeed recalled from memory everything I wished, and, to confess the truth, these matters now seem to me much more clearly distinguished than when, while investigating and discussing them, we both dragged them out from I know not what hidden recesses. But what I am trying to reach with you through such great winding paths is difficult to say at this point. You may perhaps think that we are merely playing, diverting our minds from serious matters with childish little questions; or that we are seeking some small or moderate benefit. Or, if you suspect that this discussion is bringing something important to birth, you may now be eager either to know it or at least to hear it.

But I would have you believe that I did not begin this conversation for the sake of trivial amusement, although we may perhaps be playing—and even that must not be judged in a childish spirit—nor am I thinking about small or moderate goods. Yet if I say that what I desire to reach, with God as our guide—that is, with Truth itself—is a kind of blessed and everlasting life, and that we are to be led to it by certain steps adapted to our feeble stride, I fear I may seem ridiculous for having begun so long a journey not by considering the things themselves that are signified, but by considering signs.

You will therefore forgive me if I make this preliminary excursion with you, not for the sake of playing, but for exercising the strength and sharpening the mind by which we may be able not merely to endure but even to love the warmth and light of that region where blessed life is found.

**Adeodatus.** Continue rather as you have begun. I shall never regard as contemptible anything you think ought to be said or done.

**22. Augustine.** Come, then, let us now consider that class in which signs signify not other signs, but what we call signifiable things. First tell me whether a human being is a human being.

**Adeodatus.** I do not know whether you are joking now.

**Augustine.** Why?

**Adeodatus.** Because you think you must ask me whether a human being is something other than a human being.

**Augustine.** I suppose you would think yourself mocked if I also asked whether the first syllable of this name is something other than *ho*, and whether the second is something other than *mo*.

**Adeodatus.** Entirely so.

**Augustine.** But when those two syllables are joined, they make *homo*—“human being.” Will you deny that?

**Adeodatus.** Who could deny it?

**Augustine.** Then I ask whether you are those two syllables joined together.

**Adeodatus.** Certainly not. But I see where you are heading.

**Augustine.** Say it, then, so that you do not think me insulting you.

**Adeodatus.** You think it has been proved that I am not a human being.

**Augustine.** Do you not think the same, since you admit that everything from which this conclusion was drawn is true?

**Adeodatus.** I shall not tell you what I think until I have first heard from you whether, when you asked whether a human being is a human being, you were asking me about those two syllables or about the thing itself that they signify.

**Augustine.** You should rather answer from which aspect you understood my question. For if it was ambiguous, you ought first to have guarded against that and not answered me before becoming certain in what sense I had asked.

**Adeodatus.** What would this ambiguity have prevented, since I answered with respect to both? A human being is entirely a human being: those two syllables are nothing other than those two syllables, and what they signify is nothing other than what it is.

**Augustine.** That is clever enough. But why did you take only the word *human being* that was spoken in both senses, and not the other things we said?

**Adeodatus.** How am I proved not to have taken the other things in the same way?

**Augustine.** To leave other matters aside, if you had taken my very first question entirely in the aspect in which the syllables sound, you would have answered me nothing. You might even have seemed to yourself not to have been asked anything. But since I uttered three words, one of which I repeated in the middle by saying, “Whether a human being is a human being,” it is evident from this alone that you understood the first and last words not according to the signs themselves, but according to what they signify: you immediately thought the question had to be answered with certainty and confidence.

**Adeodatus.** You are right.

**Augustine.** Why, then, did you choose to understand only what was placed in the middle both according to what it sounds like and according to what it signifies?

**Adeodatus.** Now I take the whole question only in the aspect of what is signified. I agree with you that we cannot speak at all unless, after hearing words, the mind is directed toward the things of which those words are signs. So show me how I was deceived by the reasoning through which it is concluded that I am not a human being.

**Augustine.** Rather, I shall ask the same questions again, so that you yourself may discover where you went astray.

**Adeodatus.** That is well done.

**23. Augustine.** Since you have already granted what I first asked, I shall not ask it again. Consider more carefully, then, whether the syllable *ho* is nothing other than *ho*, and whether *mo* is nothing other than *mo*.

**Adeodatus.** Here I see absolutely nothing else.

**Augustine.** Consider also whether, when these two are joined, *homo* results.

**Adeodatus.** I would by no means grant that. For it was agreed—and rightly agreed—that once a sign has been given, attention should be directed to what is signified, and that from consideration of it one should either grant or deny what is said. But those syllables, uttered separately, sounded without any signification; thus it was granted that they are what they sounded like.

**Augustine.** So you approve and firmly hold in mind that questions are not to be answered except from the things signified by the words.

**Adeodatus.** I do not understand why that should be objectionable, provided they are words.

**Augustine.** I should like to know how you would resist the man about whom we jokingly hear that he concluded, from the mouth of the person with whom he was arguing, that a lion had come forth. He had asked whether what we were saying came forth from our mouths, and the other could not deny it. This was easy enough. He then contrived that the man, while speaking, should mention a lion. When this had been done, he began mockingly to taunt and press him: since he had confessed that whatever we say comes out of our mouths, and could not deny that he had spoken of a lion, the poor man seemed to have vomited up so monstrous a beast.

**Adeodatus.** It would have been by no means difficult to resist this buffoon. I would not grant that whatever we say comes out of our mouths. For what we say, we signify; but it is not the thing signified that proceeds from the speaker’s mouth, but the sign by which it is signified—except when the signs themselves are being signified. We discussed that class a little earlier.

**24. Augustine.** You would indeed have been prepared to oppose him in this way. But what will you answer me when I ask whether *human being* is a noun?

**Adeodatus.** What else but that it is a noun?

**Augustine.** What? When I see you, do I see a noun?

**Adeodatus.** No.

**Augustine.** Shall I say what follows?

**Adeodatus.** Please do not. For I myself now declare that I am not a human being, since I answered that it was a noun when you asked whether *human being* was a noun. It had already been agreed that what is said must be affirmed or denied according to the thing signified.

**Augustine.** Yet it seems to me that you did not fall into this answer without reason. The very law of reason implanted in our minds has overcome your vigilance. If I asked what a human being was, you might answer “an animal”; but if I asked what part of speech *human being* was, you could answer correctly in no other way than “a noun.” Since *human being* is found to be both a noun and an animal, the first is said according to the aspect in which it is a sign, and the second according to the aspect of the thing it signifies.

Therefore, when someone asks whether *human being* is a noun, I answer nothing other than that it is. For the question itself sufficiently indicates that he wishes to hear the answer according to the aspect in which it is a sign. But if he asks whether it is an animal, I will assent much more readily. For if, while mentioning neither *noun* nor *animal*, he simply asked what a human being is, the accepted rule of speaking would direct the mind toward what is signified by those two syllables, and nothing would be answered except “an animal,” or the whole definition might even be given: “a rational mortal animal.” Does this not seem so to you?

**Adeodatus.** It certainly does. But once we have granted that it is a noun, how shall we avoid that excessively insulting conclusion by which it is established that we are not human beings?

**Augustine.** How do you think, except by showing that the conclusion was not drawn according to the aspect in which we were assenting to the question? Or, if he admits that he is drawing it according to that aspect, there is no reason to fear it at all. What should I fear in confessing that I am not a human being—that is, that I am not those three syllables?

**Adeodatus.** Nothing is truer.

**Augustine.** Why, then, does it offend the mind when it is said, “You are therefore not a human being,” when, according to what has been granted, nothing truer could have been said?

**Augustine.** Because, as soon as those words have sounded, I cannot help thinking that the conclusion refers to what is signified by those two syllables, in accordance with that rule which naturally has the greatest force: once signs have been heard, attention is directed toward the things signified.

**Adeodatus.** I accept what you say.

## CHAPTER IX  
### Whether a thing, or knowledge of it, ought to be valued more highly than its signs

**25. Augustine.** I want you now to understand that the things signified should be valued more highly than the signs. Whatever exists for the sake of something else must necessarily be less valuable than that for whose sake it exists—unless you think otherwise.

**Adeodatus.** It seems to me that we should not assent to this recklessly. For when we say *filth* (*coenum*), I consider this word far superior to the thing it signifies. What offends us when we hear it does not belong to the sound of the word itself: *coenum*, “mud,” becomes *coelum*, “heaven,” by changing one letter. Yet we see how great the difference is between the things signified by these names. I would therefore by no means attribute to this sign what we hate in the thing it signifies, and for that reason I rightly place the sign above the thing: we hear the word more willingly than we touch the thing with any sense.

**Augustine.** You are extraordinarily vigilant. Thus it is false that all things are to be valued more highly than their signs.

**Adeodatus.** So it seems.

**Augustine.** Tell me, then, what you think those people were pursuing who gave this name to such a foul and despicable thing; or whether you approve or disapprove of them.

**Adeodatus.** I dare neither approve nor disapprove of them, and I do not know what they were pursuing.

**Augustine.** Can you at least know what you are pursuing when you utter this name?

**Adeodatus.** I certainly can. I want to signify something, so that I may teach or remind the person with whom I am speaking about that thing, since I think he ought to be taught or reminded of it.

**Augustine.** What of the teaching or reminding itself—or being taught or reminded—which either you conveniently effect by means of this name or which is effected for you? Is it not to be valued more highly than the name itself?

**Adeodatus.** I grant that the knowledge produced through this sign should be placed above the sign itself; but for that reason I do not think that the thing itself should also be placed above it.

**26. Augustine.** In that proposition of ours, then, although it is false that all things ought to be placed above their signs, it is nevertheless not false that everything which exists for the sake of something else is inferior to that for whose sake it exists. Knowledge of mud, for whose sake this name was established, is to be valued more highly than the name itself; and we have found that it should be placed above the mud to which it refers. For knowledge has been placed above the sign we are discussing for no other reason than that the sign is proved to exist for the sake of knowledge, not knowledge for the sake of the sign.

Thus, when a certain glutton—and, as the Apostle says, a worshiper of his belly (Rom. 16:18)—said that he lived in order to eat, a temperate man who heard him could not endure it and said, “How much better it would be if you ate in order to live!” He was certainly speaking according to this same rule [Note: [Col. 1210] Thus in the manuscripts. But in the editions, “in order to live?” Both, however, spoke according to the same rule.]. The first man displeased his hearer for no other reason than that he valued his life so cheaply that he regarded it as less valuable than the pleasure of his throat, saying that he lived for the sake of meals. The second man is rightly praised for no other reason than that, understanding in those two matters what was for the sake of what—that is, what was subordinate to what—he reminded him that one should eat in order to live rather than live in order to eat.

Similarly, you and anyone who evaluates things with some discernment would perhaps answer a talkative lover of words who said, “I teach in order to speak”: “Human being, why do you not rather speak in order to teach?” If this is true, as you recognize that it is, you plainly see how much less valuable words should be considered than that for whose sake we use words, since the use of words itself must already be placed above words. Words exist so that we may use them; we use them in order to teach. How much better, then, it is to teach than to speak, so much better is speech than words. Doctrine, therefore, is much better than words. But I want to hear what you may think should be said in opposition.

**27. Adeodatus.** I agree that doctrine is better than words. But whether anything can be brought against the rule that everything which exists for the sake of something else is inferior to that for whose sake it exists, I do not know.

**Augustine.** We shall deal with that on another occasion, at a more suitable time and more carefully. For now, what you grant is sufficient for what I am trying to establish. You grant that knowledge of things is more valuable than signs of things. Therefore knowledge of the things that are signified ought to be preferred to knowledge of the signs. Does this not seem so to you?

**Adeodatus.** Did I grant that knowledge of things is superior to knowledge of signs, rather than superior to the signs themselves? Therefore I fear that I cannot agree with you here. For what if, just as the name *mud* is better than the thing it signifies, knowledge of this name is likewise to be preferred to knowledge of that thing, although the name itself is inferior to the knowledge of the thing? There are four things: the name, the thing, knowledge of the name, and knowledge of the thing. Just as the first surpasses the second, why should the third not also surpass the fourth? But even if it does not surpass it, must it therefore be subordinate to it?

**28. Augustine.** I see that you have both wonderfully retained what you granted and explained what you thought. But, as I believe, you understand that this trisyllabic name, which is sounded when we say *vice* (*vitium*), is better than what it signifies, whereas knowledge of the name itself is far inferior to knowledge of vices. You may therefore establish and consider these four things as well: the name and the thing, knowledge of the name and knowledge of the thing. We rightly place the first above the second. For this name, placed in a poem when Persius says, “But here he is stunned by vice” (*Sed stupet hic vitio*, Satire 3, verse 32), not only caused no defect in the verse but also supplied it with some ornament. Yet the thing itself signified by this name, wherever it is present, compels the person who possesses it to be vicious.

But the third does not similarly surpass the fourth; rather, we see the fourth surpassing the third. Knowledge of the name is worthless in comparison with knowledge of vices.

**Adeodatus.** Even when that knowledge makes people more miserable, do you think it should be preferred? For Persius places it above all punishments devised by the cruelty or imposed by the desire of tyrants: the punishment suffered by people who are compelled to recognize the vices they cannot avoid.

**Augustine.** By the same reasoning you could deny that knowledge of virtue itself ought to be preferred to knowledge of this name, since to see virtue without possessing it is a punishment—the punishment that the same satirist wished tyrants to suffer (ibid., verses 35–38).

**Adeodatus.** May God avert such madness! I now understand that it is not the kinds of knowledge with which the best of all disciplines enriches the mind that should be blamed. Rather, those people should be judged the most miserable—and I think Persius judged them so—who are afflicted with a disease that even so great a medicine cannot cure.

**Augustine.** You understand correctly. But whatever the Persius passage may mean, what does it have to do with us? We are not subject to the authority of these writers in such matters. Besides, if one kind of knowledge should be preferred to another, it is not easy to explain that here. I am satisfied with what has been established: knowledge of the things that are signified, although not superior to knowledge of the signs, is nevertheless superior to the signs themselves.

Let us therefore examine more and more closely what sort of things those are which, as we said, can be shown without signs by themselves—for example, walking, sitting, lying down, and other things of that kind.

**Adeodatus.** I now remember what you mean.

## CHAPTER X  
### Whether some things can be taught without signs; things are not learned through the words themselves

**29. Augustine.** Do all things seem to you that we can immediately do when questioned to be capable of being shown without a sign? Or do you make some exception?

**Adeodatus.** Considering this entire class again and again, I still find nothing that can be taught without a sign, except perhaps speech—and, if it is possible, the question of what it means to teach. For I see that when someone asks me what it means to walk, and I am idle or doing something else, if I immediately try to teach him what he has asked by walking, I cannot prevent him from thinking that walking consists in as much walking as I have done. If he thinks that, he will be deceived: whoever has walked more or less than I did, he will not consider to have walked.

What I have said about this one word applies to everything else that I had agreed could be shown without a sign, except for those two things that we excluded.

**30. Augustine.** I accept this. But do you not think that speaking is one thing and teaching another?

**Adeodatus.** Certainly. For if they were the same, no one would teach except by speaking. But since we teach many things through other signs besides words, who could doubt that they are different?

**Augustine.** What, then? Is there no difference between teaching and signifying? Or do they differ in some way?

**Adeodatus.** I think they are the same.

**Augustine.** Is the person not speaking correctly who says that we signify in order to teach?

**Adeodatus.** Entirely correctly.

**Augustine.** What if someone else says that we teach in order to signify? Would that not easily be refuted by the preceding statement?

**Adeodatus.** It would.

**Augustine.** Therefore, if we signify in order to teach, we do not teach in order to signify. Teaching is one thing, signifying another.

**Adeodatus.** You are right, and I was wrong to answer that they were the same.

**Augustine.** Now answer this: when someone teaches what it means to teach, does he do so by signifying it, or in some other way?

**Adeodatus.** I do not see how he could do so otherwise.

**Augustine.** Therefore what you said a little earlier was false: that a thing can be taught without signs when the question is what teaching itself means. For we do not even see that this can be done without signification, once you have granted that signifying is one thing and teaching another. If they are different, as is evident, and the one is shown only through the other, then it is certainly not shown by itself, as you had thought.

Thus nothing has yet been found that can be shown by itself except speech, which, among the other things it signifies, also signifies itself. Yet since speech itself is a sign, there still appears to be nothing that can be taught entirely without signs.

**Adeodatus.** I have no reason not to agree.

**31. Augustine.** It has therefore been established both that nothing can be taught without signs and that knowledge itself ought to be valued more highly by us than the signs through which we acquire knowledge, although not everything signified can be superior to its signs.

**Adeodatus.** So it seems.

**Augustine.** Do you remember, I ask, through how much wandering we have accomplished so small a matter? Ever since we have been hurling words at one another—which we have been doing for so long—we have labored to discover these three things: whether nothing can be taught without signs; whether some signs ought to be preferred to the things they signify; and whether knowledge of things itself is better than signs.

But there is a fourth matter on which I would like to hear from you briefly: do you think these conclusions have been established in such a way that you can no longer doubt them?

**Adeodatus.** I would certainly wish that such great winding paths and circuits had brought us to certainty. Yet your question somehow troubles me and deters me from assenting. It seems to me that you would not have asked me these questions unless you had something with which to oppose them. Moreover, the complexity of the matters prevents me from examining everything and answering confidently, since I fear that something may lie hidden amid so many entanglements which the sharpness of my mind cannot inspect.

**Augustine.** I accept your doubt willingly. It indicates a mind that is by no means rash, and that is the greatest safeguard of tranquility. For it is extremely difficult not to be disturbed when the things we held with ready and easy approval are shaken by opposing arguments and, as it were, torn from our hands. Just as it is right to yield when reasons have been carefully considered and understood, so it is dangerous to regard unknown things as known.

There is a danger that, when the things we confidently presumed would stand firm and endure are repeatedly undermined, we may fall into such hatred or fear of reason that we may think even clear truth itself unworthy of belief.

**32.** Come, then, let us now more freely reconsider whether you were right to think these matters doubtful. I ask you this: suppose that someone ignorant of the way birds are captured with reeds and birdlime happened to meet a fowler, equipped with his apparatus but not actually hunting, merely traveling. Seeing him, the passerby might slow his step and, as happens, wonder and ask himself what the man intended by such equipment.

Suppose the fowler, noticing that the man was watching him, unwound the reeds in his eagerness to display himself, and, having spotted a little bird nearby, struck it with his pipe and hawk, subdued it, and caught it [Note: [Col. 1214] In the Bad. edition and in our manuscripts, *sarabarae* is consistently written here and below with *r*, as Tertullian also wrote it in *On the Pallium* and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. The Greek text, however, at Daniel 3:94 has the neuter plural *ta sarabara*, a spelling followed by not a few writers. Jerome, in his commentary on Daniel 3:21, rejects this form and wishes *saraballa* to be read. In addition, the Fiscannensis and Michaelinus manuscripts have, instead of “certain coverings of the head,” “certain coverings of the feet,” and consistently prefer this reading below: “or what the feet are,” and so forth; “when we say feet, ears,” and so forth; “indicating feet,” and so forth. Finally, they omit “of the head” at the place where we read “those coverings, certainly, of the head.” This variation arose from the differing interpretation of the word: for some, as Isidore reports (*Etymologies* 19.23), it means coverings of the head; for others, as Isidore himself prefers in the same place, it means loose and flowing garments; for Vatablus and other interpreters of Scripture, it means cloaks; for some, footwear; and finally, for Jerome in the passage cited, trousers or leggings.]. Would he not teach that spectator, without any signification but by the thing itself, what the spectator wished to know?

**Adeodatus.** I fear that something similar may be involved here to what I said about the person who asks what walking is. For I do not see that the whole of that art of bird-catching has been shown in this way.

**Augustine.** It is easy to relieve you of this concern. Let me add that the spectator was so intelligent that, from what he saw, he recognized the whole class of that art. That is sufficient for our purpose: it is possible to teach certain things, though not all things, and certain people, without a sign.

**Adeodatus.** I can add this as well: if he were intelligent, after walking a few paces he would recognize what walking as a whole is.

**Augustine.** You may do so with my permission. I not only offer no resistance; I even approve. For you see that both of us have brought it about that certain things can be taught to certain people without signs, and that the proposition which shortly before seemed true to us—namely, that there is absolutely nothing that can be shown without signs—is false.

For now countless things come to mind, not merely one or two, that are shown by themselves without any sign being given. Why, I ask you, should we doubt this? To leave aside the innumerable spectacles presented by human beings in all the theaters without signs, does God and nature not exhibit and display to those who see them, by themselves, the sun and the light that floods and clothes all these things, the moon and the other stars, the earth and the seas, and the countless things generated in them?

**33.** But if we consider the matter more carefully, perhaps you will find that nothing is learned through its signs. When a sign is given to me, if it finds me ignorant of the thing of which it is a sign, it can teach me nothing; but if it finds me knowledgeable, what do I learn through the sign?

When I read, “And their *saraballae* were not altered” (Dan. 3:94) [Note: [Col. 1214] In the Bad. edition and in our manuscripts, *sarabarae* is consistently written here and below with *r*, as Tertullian also wrote it in *On the Pallium* and *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. The Greek text, however, at Daniel 3:94 has the neuter plural *ta sarabara*, a spelling followed by not a few writers. Jerome, in his commentary on Daniel 3:21, rejects this form and wishes *saraballa* to be read. In addition, the Fiscannensis and Michaelinus manuscripts have, instead of “certain coverings of the head,” “certain coverings of the feet,” and consistently prefer this reading below: “or what the feet are,” and so forth; “when we say feet, ears,” and so forth; “indicating feet,” and so forth. Finally, they omit “of the head” at the place where we read “those coverings, certainly, of the head.” This variation arose from the differing interpretation of the word: for some, as Isidore reports (*Etymologies* 19.23), it means coverings of the head; for others, as Isidore himself prefers in the same place, it means loose and flowing garments; for Vatablus and other interpreters of Scripture, it means cloaks; for some, footwear; and finally, for Jerome in the passage cited, trousers or leggings.], the word does not show me the thing it signifies. For if certain coverings of the head are called by this name, when I hear it, do I learn either what a head is or what coverings are? I already knew these things. Nor did I come to know them when they were named by others, but when I saw them.

Indeed, when those two syllables first struck my ears, when we say *caput*—“head”—I was as ignorant of what they signified as when I first heard or read *saraballae*. But when *caput* was repeatedly said, and I observed and attended to the occasions on which it was said, I discovered that the word was the name of a thing already well known to me through sight. Before I discovered this, the word was merely a sound to me. I learned that it was a sign when I discovered what thing it was a sign of; and that thing, as I have said, I had learned not through its signification but through seeing it.

Thus the thing itself is learned after the sign has been known, rather than the thing being learned through the sign.

**34.** To understand this more clearly, imagine that we are now hearing the word *caput* for the first time. Not knowing whether this utterance is merely a sound or also signifies something, we ask what a head is. Remember that we want to know not the thing signified but the sign itself, of which we are certainly ignorant so long as we do not know what it is a sign of.

If, then, while we are asking in this way, the thing itself is pointed out with a finger, once we have seen it we learn the sign that we had heard but did not yet know. Yet this sign contains two elements, sound and signification. We do not perceive the sound through the sign, but through the ear itself, which is struck by it; we perceive its signification through seeing the thing signified.

For the intention of the finger can signify nothing other than that toward which the finger is directed. But it is directed not toward the sign, but toward the bodily member called a head. Therefore through that gesture I cannot come to know either the thing that I already knew or the sign toward which the finger is not directed.

I am not especially concerned with the pointing of the finger, because it seems to me to be a sign of the pointing itself rather than of any things that are pointed out, just as when we say the adverb *ecce*—“behold.” We commonly point the finger along with this adverb as well, so that one sign of demonstration may not seem sufficient.

What I am chiefly trying to persuade you of, if I can, is that through the signs called words we learn nothing. Rather, as I have said, once we have learned the thing itself that is signified, we learn the force of the word—that is, the signification hidden in the sound—more readily than we apprehend the thing through that signification.

**35.** What I have said about the head may also be said about coverings and countless other things. Although I already know these things, I still do not know what those *saraballae* are. If someone signifies them to me by a gesture or paints them, or shows me something similar to them, I shall not say that he has not taught me—something I could easily establish if I wished to speak at greater length—but I say what is more immediate: he has not taught me through words.

If, while I am present and looking at them, he reminds me by saying, “Behold the *saraballae*,” I shall learn the thing I did not know, not through the words that were spoken but through seeing them, by which it came about that I also came to know and retain what that name meant. For when I learned the thing itself, I did not trust someone else’s words but my own eyes. I may perhaps have trusted his words in order to pay attention—that is, to seek through sight what I was seeing.

## CHAPTER XI  
### We learn not through words sounding outwardly, but through Truth teaching inwardly

**36.** Up to this point words have had their effect. To grant them the greatest possible role, they merely prompt us to seek things; they do not present them to us so that we may know them. The person who teaches me something is the one who presents to my eyes, or to any bodily sense, or even to the mind itself, the things I wish to know.

Through words, therefore, we learn only words—or rather, the sound and noise of words. For if things that are not signs cannot be words, then, although I have already heard a word, I do not know that it is a word until I know what it signifies.

Knowledge of words is therefore completed by knowledge of things; but words heard do not teach us words. We do not learn the words we already know, nor can we admit that we have learned words we do not know unless we have perceived their signification—and that perception occurs not through hearing the sounds uttered but through knowledge of the things signified.

For the truest reasoning, and a statement that is most truly made, is this: when words are uttered, either we know what they signify or we do not. If we know, we are being reminded rather than taught; but if we do not know, we are not even being reminded, though perhaps we are prompted to seek.

**37.** If you should say that those coverings of the head, whose name we possess only as a sound, cannot be known by us except through seeing them, and that we cannot know the name itself fully except after knowing the things, what shall we say of the story we learned about the three young men: how they overcame the king and the flames through faith and devotion; what praises they sang to God; and what honors they received even from the enemy himself? Did we learn these matters in any other way than through words?

I shall answer that everything signified by those words was already present in our knowledge. I already knew what three young men are, what a furnace is, what fire is, what a king is, what it means to be unharmed by fire, and all the other things signified by those words [Col. 1216]. But Ananias, Azariah, and Misael are as unknown to me as those *saraballae*; nor did those names help or could they now help me to know them.

As for everything reported in that story, I confess that I believe rather than know that it happened at that time in the manner in which it was written. Nor were the very people whom we believe unaware of this distinction. For the prophet says, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint). He certainly would not have said this if he had judged that there was no difference between the two.

What I understand, I also believe; but not everything I believe, I also understand. Everything I understand, however, I know; not everything I believe, I know. Nor do I therefore fail to recognize how useful it is to believe many things that I do not know. To this usefulness I add the story of the three young men: although I cannot know most things, I do know how greatly useful it is to believe them.

**38.** In regard to everything that we understand, we do not consult the speaker who makes a sound outwardly, but the Truth presiding within the mind itself—though words may have prompted us to consult it. The one whom we consult teaches: he is the one who is said to dwell in the inner person, Christ (Eph. 3:16–17), that is, the unchangeable Power of God and eternal Wisdom.

Every rational soul consults this Wisdom, but it is disclosed to each person only to the extent that he can receive it through his own will, whether good or evil. And whenever someone is deceived, the fault does not lie in the Truth consulted, just as it is not a fault of the light outside us that bodily eyes are often deceived. We acknowledge that this light is consulted concerning visible things, so that it may display them to us insofar as we are able to see them.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Christ, the Truth, teaches inwardly
39. But if, with respect to colors, we consult the light, and with respect to the other things that we perceive through the body, the elements of this world—and likewise the bodies that we perceive—and the senses themselves, which the mind uses as interpreters for knowing such things; whereas with respect to things that are understood, we consult the inner truth through reason: what can be said that would make clear that we learn anything through words apart from the sound itself, which strikes our ears? For everything that we perceive, we perceive either through bodily sense or through the mind. The former are sensible things, the latter intelligible; or, to speak according to the usage of our authors, we call the former corporeal and the latter spiritual.

When we are questioned about sensible things, we answer if the things we perceive are present—for example, when, as we look at the new moon, we are asked what it is like or where it is. Here, if the questioner does not see it, he believes the words, and often does not believe them; but he learns in no way unless he himself sees what is being said. At that point he learns not through the words that have sounded, but through the things themselves and his senses. The same words sound to one who sees as they sounded to one who does not see.

When, however, we are asked not about things that we presently perceive before us, but about things that we once perceived, we speak no longer of the things themselves, but of the images impressed by them and committed to memory. I do not know how we can call these wholly true when we are looking at false things, unless it is because we say not that we see and perceive them, but that we saw and perceived them. Thus we carry in the inner chambers of memory these images as a kind of testimony to things previously perceived; and when we contemplate them in the mind, we do not lie in good conscience when we speak, for they are testimonies to us. The one who hears us, if he perceived and witnessed those things, does not learn them from my words, but recognizes them by means of the images that he himself has brought away. But if he did not perceive them, [Col. 1217] who would fail to understand that he believes the words rather than learns?

40. When, however, the subject is things that we behold with the mind—that is, through understanding and reason—we certainly speak of things that we contemplate as present in that inner light of truth, by which the one called the inner man is himself illumined and enjoys the light. But even then our hearer, if he too sees those things with a secret and simple eye, knows what I say through his own contemplation, not through my words.

Therefore, even when I speak the truth to one who beholds the truth, I do not teach him. He is taught not by my words, but by the things themselves, which God reveals inwardly and makes manifest. Thus, questioned about these matters, he could also answer. For what could be more absurd than to think that someone is taught by my speech when, before I spoke, he could have explained the very things in question?

The fact that it often happens that, when questioned, someone denies something and is pressed by further questions to admit it, results from the weakness of the person who sees, who cannot consult that light concerning the whole matter. In order that he may do so piece by piece, he is prompted when he is questioned about those same parts of which the whole consists—a whole that he was unable to see in its entirety. If he is led to it by the words of the questioner, the words nevertheless do not teach him; they merely inquire in the manner by which the person questioned is capable of learning inwardly.

Suppose, for example, that I asked you about the very matter now under discussion—whether it is possible to learn nothing through words—and that at first it seemed absurd to you because you were unable to see the whole matter. I ought then to question you in accordance with your capacity to hear that inner teacher. I might say: “The things that, while I was speaking, you acknowledge to be true, and of which you are certain, affirming that you know them—where did you learn them?” You might perhaps answer, “You taught me.” Then I would continue: “What if I said that I had seen a flying human being? Would my words make you as certain as they would if you heard that wise people are better than fools?”

You would certainly deny it and answer that you did not believe the former—or that, even if you believed it, you did not know it—whereas you knew the latter with complete certainty. From this you would surely understand that, both in the case of the thing you did not know when I asserted it and in the case of the thing you knew very well, you had learned nothing from my words, since, when questioned about each separately, you would swear that the former was unknown to you and the latter known.

Then you would admit the whole proposition that you had denied, once you recognized that the elements of which it consists were clear and certain.
