In short, of everything we say, the hearer either does not know whether it is true, or knows that it is false, or knows that it is true. In the first case he either believes, supposes, or doubts; in the second he opposes and rejects; in the third he bears witness. Nowhere, therefore, does he learn. For the person who, after our words, remains ignorant of the matter; the person who knows that he has heard falsehoods; and the person who, if questioned, could give the same answers that were spoken—all are shown to have learned nothing from my words. [Col. 1218]

## CHAPTER XIII — Not even the speaker’s mind is disclosed by the force of words

41. For this reason, even in matters perceived by the mind, anyone who cannot perceive them hears the speech of one who perceives them to no purpose—unless, indeed, it is useful to believe such things so long as they are unknown. Whoever can perceive them is inwardly a disciple of truth and outwardly a judge of the speaker—or rather, of the speech itself. For often he knows what has been said while the speaker himself does not know what he has said.

For example, suppose someone who believes the Epicureans and thinks the soul mortal gives an account of the arguments that wiser people have advanced concerning its immortality, in the hearing of one who can contemplate spiritual realities. The latter judges that he is speaking the truth, while the speaker himself does not know whether he is speaking the truth and even considers it utterly false. Should he then be thought to teach what he does not know? Yet he uses the same words that he could use even if he did know.

42. Therefore not even this remains for words: that through them, at least, the speaker’s mind may be revealed, since it is uncertain whether he knows what he is saying. Add liars and deceivers, through whom you can easily understand that words not only fail to disclose the mind but even conceal it.

I do not doubt that the words of truthful people strive, in a certain way, to make the speaker’s mind apparent and to declare it; they would achieve this if everyone conceded that liars were not permitted to speak. Yet we have often experienced, both in ourselves and in others, that words are uttered which do not express the things being thought. I see that this can happen in two ways: either when speech committed to memory and frequently recited pours from the mouth while something else is being thought—as often happens to us when we sing a hymn—or when, through an error of the tongue itself, words for other words spring forth against our will. In this case too, what is heard is not the sign of the things we have in mind.

Liars, to be sure, also think about the things they are saying, so that, even though we do not know whether they speak the truth, we nevertheless know that they have in mind what they are saying, unless one of the two circumstances I have mentioned befalls them. If someone insists that these circumstances sometimes occur and that, when they do occur, they become apparent—although often they remain hidden, and have often deceived me as a hearer—I do not resist.

43. But there is another kind of occurrence, one that extends very widely and is the source of innumerable disagreements and disputes. The person speaking signifies, indeed, the same things that he is thinking, but generally only to himself and to certain others; to the person he is addressing, however, and to some others, he signifies something different.

Suppose someone says in our hearing that a human being is surpassed in virtue by certain animals. We immediately cannot endure this and vigorously refute so false and pernicious an opinion. Yet perhaps he calls physical strength “virtue” and expresses by that name what he has thought. He is not lying, nor is he mistaken about the facts, nor is he turning something else over in his mind while stringing together words committed to memory, nor does his tongue sound anything other than what he intended. He simply calls the thing he is thinking about by a name different from the one we use. We would immediately agree with him if we could look into his thought, which, by the words already spoken and the proposition he has explained, he has not yet been able to disclose to us. [Col. 1219]

They say that a definition can remedy this error: if, in such a question, he defined what virtue is, it would become clear, they say, that the dispute concerned not the thing but the word. Granting that this is so, how many good definers can be found? And yet much has been argued against the discipline of definition—matters that it is neither appropriate to treat here nor matters that I entirely approve.

44. I omit the fact that we often hear many things incorrectly and then argue at length and with great insistence about what we have heard. For example, recently, when I had spoken of “mercy,” you said that you had heard from those more familiar with that language that a certain Punic word signified “piety.” I, however, objected and asserted that you had completely forgotten what you had heard; for it seemed to me that you had said “faith,” although you were sitting very close beside me and the sound of these two names could in no way deceive the ear.

For a long time, nevertheless, I thought that you did not know what had been said to you, since I did not know what you had said. If I had heard you correctly, it would by no means have seemed absurd to me that “piety” and “mercy” should be expressed by one Punic word.

Such things happen frequently; but, as I said, let us omit them, lest I seem to bring an accusation against words based on the hearer’s negligence or even on human deafness. What troubles me more are the matters I listed above, where, although the words have been heard distinctly and are Latin, we are unable, despite sharing the same language, to know the thoughts of those speaking.

45. But now I concede and grant that, when a speaker’s words are received by a hearer who knows them, the hearer can know that the speaker was thinking about the things the words signify. Does he therefore learn what is now being asked—whether the speaker spoke the truth?

## CHAPTER XIV — Christ teaches inwardly; the human being admonishes outwardly through words

Do teachers claim that their thoughts are to be perceived and retained, rather than the disciplines themselves that they think they transmit by speaking? Who is so foolishly inquisitive as to send his son to school so that he may learn what the teacher is thinking?

But when teachers have explained in words all the disciplines they profess to teach, as well as matters of virtue and wisdom, those called students consider within themselves whether what has been said is true, contemplating, as far as they are able, that inner truth. Then they learn. When they have discovered inwardly that the things said are true, they praise them, not knowing that they are praising not so much their teachers as those who have been taught—provided, of course, that the teachers themselves also know what they are saying.

People are deceived into calling those who are not teachers “teachers,” because generally no interval intervenes between the time of speaking and the time of knowing. Since, after the speaker’s admonition, they quickly learn inwardly, they suppose that they have learned outwardly from the one who admonished them. [Col. 1220]

46. But concerning the whole usefulness of words—which, if properly considered, is by no means small—we shall inquire elsewhere, if God permits. For now I have admonished you so that we might not attribute more to words than is proper, and so that we might begin not merely to believe but also to understand how truly it is written by divine authority that we should not call anyone our teacher on earth, since one alone is the teacher of all in heaven (Matt. 23:8–10).

What “in heaven” means, he himself will teach, by whom we are also admonished outwardly through human beings by means of signs, so that, turning inward toward him, we may be instructed. To love and know him is the blessed life, which everyone proclaims himself to be seeking, but few rejoice in having truly found.

But now I should like you to tell me what you think of this whole speech of mine. For if you know that the things said are true, then, when questioned about each individual proposition, you would have said that you knew them. You therefore see from whom you learned them; for you would have answered everything when I questioned you, and not from me. If, on the other hand, you do not know that they are true, then neither I nor he has taught you: I, because I can never teach; he, because you are not yet able to learn.

**Student.** Indeed, I have learned through the admonition of your words that words do nothing more than admonish a person to learn, and that very little of the speaker’s thought appears through speech. But whether what is said is true, only that one teaches who, while speaking outwardly, admonished the person that he dwells inwardly. With his favor, I shall love him all the more fervently the further I advance in learning.

Nevertheless, I am especially grateful for this discourse of yours, which you have conducted throughout, because it anticipated and resolved everything I was prepared to object to; you have left nothing at all that made me doubtful about which that secret oracle did not answer me in the manner asserted by your words.

[Col. 1219]

# THREE BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON FREE WILL

[Note: [Col. 1221] Begun in the year of Christ 388, completed in 395.]

[Note: [Col. 1221] The following manuscripts assisted in correcting these works: Corbeiensis, Germanensis, Gemmeticensis, Pratellensis, Audoenensis, Sergiensis, Casalensis, Regio-Montensis, Regius, Arnuliensis, Thuaneus, Victorinus, two Sorbonici manuscripts, one of the Augustinians of the greater Paris convent, one of the Dominicans of the Rue Saint-Jacques, the manuscript of the church of Rera, Vedastinus, and Vaticanus; also the readings of four Belgian manuscripts at Louvain, as well as the editions of Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1221] In addition, we compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.]

(C)

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING THREE BOOKS ON FREE WILL

[Note: [Col. 1221] See also Book 1, chapter 9 of the *Retractations*, col. 595, beginning with the words “When I was still at Rome,” no. 1, through col. 599, no. 6, ending with the words “is not the author of evil.” M.]

Among the remaining books of this volume that concern the refutation of the errors of the Manichaeans, the first presented here, as in the works printed thus far, is the treatise entitled *On Free Will*. Augustine began it at Rome in the year of Christ 388, and we judge that he completed it in 395. It was not completed by him after the year in which he became bishop, since, as he says, he finished its second and third books after he had been ordained a presbyter (*Retractations*, Book 1, chapter 9, no. 1). Nor was it completed before that same year, since Augustine writes in Letter 27, no. 4, to Paulinus, bishop of Nola, that he did not know of any kind of writing he had published that Romanianus—who had departed for Italy at the beginning of that year—did not possess. Later, in Letter 31, no. 7, he offers this work to Paulinus himself in the following words:

> “I have sent three books to Your Holiness and Charity—if only they were as great in their explanation as the question is great—for their subject is Free Will. I know that our brother Romanianus does not possess them, or does not possess them all,” etc. [Col. 1221]

In the first book, Augustine explains the extremely difficult question that once greatly troubled him and drove him toward the Manichaeans: namely, where evil originated. He first explains what it is to do evil; then he proves that human evil deeds arise only from free choice of the will, since the mind is compelled by no one to serve the desire that dominates all evil deeds.

In the second book, since the difficulty arises that the freedom by which one sins was given by God, three questions are investigated: by what reasoning it is evident that God exists; whether all good things are from him; and whether free will is to be counted among good things.

In the third, the question is examined of where the movement arises by which the will itself turns away from the unchangeable good toward a changeable good; and whether God’s foreknowledge of human sins and human freedom in sinning are mutually opposed. It is then shown that what necessarily occurs in a creature in such a way that it comes about through the will of those who sin must by no means be attributed to the Creator; and that God must altogether be praised for the condition and punishment of the creature subject to sin. From there, the discussion proceeds to the defect of origin, and it is explained how this defect passed down to Adam’s descendants without injustice. Several related difficulties are then disentangled.

## SAINT AUGUSTINE, LETTER 143, TO MARCELLINUS

> “Your letter . . . contains a question proposed to me from books—not divine books, but my own—which I wrote on Free Will. In questions of this kind I do not labor greatly; for even if my opinion cannot be defended by clear reasoning, it is my opinion, not that of an author whose meaning it is not right to condemn . . .
>
> “Nevertheless, in the third book of *On Free Will*, when I was treating of rational substance, I wrote as follows: ‘Among the lower bodies, the soul, ordered after sin, governs its body, not wholly according to its own choice, but as the laws of the universe permit.’ Let those who think that I established and fixed something certain concerning the human soul carefully attend to this—something that either comes from parents through propagation or that sinned in the actions of a former and heavenly life and thereby deserved to be enclosed in corruptible flesh. Let them see that I weighed my words in such a way that, retaining what I hold to be certain—namely, that after the sin of the first human being, the other human beings were and are born in the flesh of sin, for whose healing the likeness of sinful flesh came in the Lord—all my words would be so framed as to prejudice none of the four opinions that I later set out and distinguished. I did not confirm any one of them, but, while setting aside their discussion for the time being, I determined the matter I was treating in such a way that, whichever of them might be true, God would undoubtedly be praised. For whether . . .,” etc.

# BOOK ONE

In this book, after raising the question “Where does evil come from?” Augustine explains what it is to do evil, and then shows that human evil deeds arise from free choice of the will, since the mind is compelled by no one to serve the desire that rules in every evil deed.

[Col. 1221]

## CHAPTER ONE — Whether God is the author of any evil

[Col. 1221]

**1. Evodius.** Tell me, please: is God not the author of evil?

**Augustine.** I shall answer, if you make clear what evil you are asking about. For we customarily call something evil in two ways: in one way, when we say that someone has done evil; in another, when someone has suffered some evil.

**E.** I want to know about both.

**A.** But if you know—or believe—that God is good, as indeed it is not lawful to think otherwise, he does not do evil. Again, if we acknowledge that God is just—for it is sacrilegious to deny this—then, just as he assigns rewards to the good, so he assigns punishments to the evil; and these punishments are certainly evils for those who suffer them.

Therefore, if no one suffers punishment unjustly—which we must believe, since we believe that the whole universe is governed by divine providence—God is in no way the author of evils of the first kind, but he is the author of those of the second kind.

**E.** Is there, then, another author of that evil whose author God is evidently not?

**A.** Certainly. For it could not occur without an author. But if you ask who this author is, it cannot be stated as one individual; for there is not one such author, but each wicked person is the author of his own evil deed. If you doubt this, consider what was said above: evil deeds are punished by the justice of God. They would not be punished justly unless they were committed voluntarily. [Note: [Col. 1223] See *Retractations*, Book 1, chapter 9, no. 3.]

## 2

**E.** I do not know whether anyone sins who has not learned to do so. If this is true, I ask from whom we learned to sin.

**A.** Do you think discipline is something good?

**E.** Who would dare say that discipline is evil?

**A.** What if it is neither good nor evil?

**E.** It seems good to me.

**A.** Very well. Since through it knowledge is given or awakened, and no one learns anything except through discipline—is that not your view?

**E.** I believe that through discipline only good things are learned.

**A.** See, then, whether evil things are not learned. For *discipline* takes its name from learning.

**E.** How, then, are evil deeds committed by human beings if they are not learned?

**A.** Perhaps because a person turns away and withdraws from discipline—that is, from learning. But whether this or something else is the case, one thing is certainly clear: since discipline is good and is named from learning, evil things cannot be learned at all. For if they are learned, they are contained within discipline, and then discipline will not be good. But it is good, as you yourself concede. Therefore evil things are not learned, and you are asking in vain for the person from whom we learn to do evil. Or, if evil things are learned, what is learned is to avoid them, not to commit them. Hence doing evil is nothing other than departing from discipline.

## 3

**E.** I think there are really two disciplines: one by which we learn to do good, and another by which we learn to do evil. But when you asked whether discipline was good, my love of the good carried my attention toward the discipline by which one learns to do good, and so I answered that it was good. Now, however, I am reminded that there is another discipline, which I unquestionably affirm to be evil, and I ask for its author.

**A.** At least, do you think understanding is good and nothing but good?

**E.** I certainly think it so good that I cannot see what could be superior in a human being; and I would in no way say that any understanding could be evil.

**A.** What, then? When someone is being taught, if he does not understand, can he seem learned to you?

**E.** Absolutely not.

**A.** If, then, all understanding is good, and no one who does not understand learns, everyone who learns does good. For everyone who learns understands, and everyone who understands does good. Therefore whoever seeks the author through whom we learn something is plainly seeking the author through whom we do good.

So stop wanting to investigate some unknown evil teacher. If he is evil, he is not a teacher; if he is a teacher, he is not evil.

## CHAPTER TWO — Before investigating where evil comes from, what should be believed about God

[Col. 1224]

## 4

**E.** Come, then. Since you compel me sufficiently to admit that we do not learn to do evil, tell me where we do evil.

**A.** You are raising the question that greatly exercised me when I was still quite young, and that, when I was exhausted, drove me into the heretics and cast me down among them. In that crisis I was so afflicted and buried beneath such heaps of empty fables that, unless my love of finding the truth had obtained divine assistance for me, I would not have been able to emerge from there and draw breath again in the very first freedom of inquiry.

And since I was carefully dealt with so that I might be freed from this question, I shall deal with you according to the course that I followed in escaping it. God will be present, and he will make us understand what we have believed. We are well aware that we must hold to the step prescribed through the prophet, who says, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

We believe that everything that exists comes from the one God, and yet that God is not the author of sins. But the mind is troubled by this: if sins come from the souls that God created, and those souls come from God, how can sins not, by a short interval, be referred back to God?

## 5

**E.** You have now stated precisely what torments me when I think about it, and what forced and drew me into this investigation.

**A.** Be strong in spirit, and believe what you believe. Nothing better can be believed, even if the reason why it is so remains hidden. For to think of God in the best possible way is the truest beginning of piety. No one thinks rightly of him unless he believes him omnipotent and wholly unchangeable in every respect; the creator also of all good things, while himself superior to them; the most just ruler of everything he created; and unaided by any nature in creating, as though he were insufficient for himself.

It follows that he created everything from nothing. But he did not create from himself; rather, he begot from himself one equal to himself, whom we call the only Son of God. When we try to express this more clearly, we call him the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, through whom he made all things that were made from nothing.

With these points established, let us strive, with God’s help, to understand the matter you are asking about in the following way.

## CHAPTER THREE — The nature of evil arising from desire

## 6

You certainly ask where we do evil. First, then, we must investigate what it is to do evil. State your view on this matter. If you cannot grasp the whole of it briefly in words all at once, at least make your opinion known to me by recalling particular evil deeds.

**E.** Adultery, murder, and sacrilege—to omit the rest, whose enumeration would exceed either our time or our memory—who is there who does not regard these as evil deeds?

**A.** Tell me first why you think adultery is evil. Is it because the law forbids it?

**E.** It is not evil because the law forbids it; rather, the law forbids it because it is evil.

**A.** What if someone attacks us, exaggerating the pleasures of adultery, and asks why we judge it evil and worthy of condemnation? Do you think we should appeal to the authority of the law before people who now desire not merely to believe but also to understand?

For I too believe with you—and I firmly believe, and proclaim that all peoples and nations ought to believe—that adultery is evil. But now we are attempting to know and hold with the greatest certainty, through understanding as well, what we have accepted by faith. Consider, therefore, as much as you can, and tell me by what reasoning you have recognized adultery to be evil.

**E.** I know that what I would not want to suffer myself from my wife is evil. Whoever does to another what he does not want done to himself certainly does evil.

**A.** What if someone’s desire were such that he willingly offered his wife to another and allowed her to be corrupted by him, while in return he desired equal permission with that man’s wife? Would you think that he was doing nothing evil?

**E.** On the contrary, he would be doing a very great evil.

**A.** But that man does not sin according to your rule, for he does not do what he is unwilling to suffer. You must therefore seek another basis by which to prove adultery evil.

## 7

**E.** It seems evil to me because I have often seen people condemned for this crime.

**A.** What? Have people not often been condemned for righteous deeds? Review history—so that I need not send you to other books—and review that history which surpasses all others in divine authority. You will then discover how badly we would think of the Apostles and all the martyrs if we considered condemnation a sure indication of wrongdoing, since all of them were judged worthy of condemnation because of their confession.

Therefore, if everything condemned is evil, then at that time it was evil to believe in Christ and to confess that faith. But if not everything condemned is evil, seek another way by which you can show that adultery is evil.

**E.** I do not know what to answer you.

## 8

**A.** Perhaps, then, desire is what is evil in adultery. But while you seek evil outwardly in the deed itself, which can already be seen, you are caught in difficulties. To understand that desire is evil in adultery, consider this: even if someone does not have the opportunity to lie with another’s spouse, it may nevertheless be clear in some way that he desires to do so and would do it if the opportunity were given. He is no less guilty than if he were caught in the act itself.

**E.** Nothing is clearer, and I now see that no lengthy discussion is needed to convince me about murder, sacrilege, and all sins generally. It is clear that nothing other than desire rules throughout the entire category of wrongdoing.

## CHAPTER FOUR — An objection concerning murder committed out of fear; what culpable desire is

## 9

**A.** Do you know that this desire is also called by another name, “cupidity” (*cupiditas*)?

**E.** I know.

**A.** What, then? Do you think there is no difference between this and fear, or do you think there is some difference?

**E.** On the contrary, I think they differ very greatly.

**A.** I believe you think this because desire seeks something, whereas fear flees something.

**E.** That is as you say.

**A.** What if someone killed another person not out of desire to obtain something, but because he feared that some evil would befall him? Would he not be a murderer?

**E.** He would indeed, but the deed would not for that reason be free from the rule of desire. For the person who kills another out of fear certainly desires to live without fear.

**A.** Does living without fear seem to you a small good?

**E.** It is a great good, but that good can in no way come to that murderer through his crime.

**A.** I am not asking what can come to him, but what he himself desires. Certainly the person who desires a life free from fear desires a good; and for that reason this desire is not to be blamed. Otherwise we would blame everyone who loves the good.

We are therefore forced to admit that there is a murder in which the domination of that evil desire cannot be found. Then the claim that desire rules in all sins so that they are evil will be false; or there will be some murder that can fail to be a sin.

[Note: [Col. 1226] In earlier editions the interlocutors were very often inserted in place of one another and placed where they did not belong. Thus here “E.” was omitted and later “E. I agree” was inserted. “Answer, then”: wherever the assistance of ancient manuscripts enables us to correct such matters, we shall not hesitate to note the corrections in their proper places. We have also removed the particle *tamen* (“nevertheless”), which appears in the printed editions in the phrase “it can nevertheless sometimes happen”; it is absent from the manuscripts. M.]

**E.** If murder means killing a human being, it can sometimes occur without sin. For a soldier who kills an enemy, a judge or his official who kills a guilty person, and someone from whose hand a weapon slips against his will and without his knowledge do not, in my opinion, sin when they kill a human being.

**A.** I agree; but such people are not usually called murderers. Answer this, then: do you think the person who kills a master from whom he feared severe torments should be counted among those who kill a human being in such a way that they are not even worthy of the name “murderers”?

**E.** I see that he differs greatly from them. They act either according to the laws or not against the laws; but no law approves this man’s crime.

## 10

**A.** Again you appeal to authority. But you must remember that we have now undertaken to understand what we believe; and we believe in the laws. We must therefore try, if we can in some way, to understand whether the law that punishes this deed does not punish it rightly.

**E.** It certainly does not punish it wrongly, since it punishes the person who knowingly and willingly kills his master—something none of those others does.

**A.** Do you remember saying shortly before that desire rules in every evil deed, and that this is what makes it evil?

**E.** I certainly remember.

**A.** Did you not also concede that the person who desires to live without fear does not have an evil desire?

**E.** I remember that as well.

**A.** Since, then, the master is killed by a slave with this desire, he is not killed by that culpable desire. We have therefore not yet discovered why this deed is evil. We agreed that all evil deeds are evil for no other reason than that they are committed through desire—that is, through a desire that ought to be rejected.

**E.** It now seems to me that this man is condemned unjustly. I would not dare say so if I had anything else to say.

**A.** Have you first persuaded yourself that so great a crime ought to go unpunished before considering whether that slave desired freedom from fear of his master in order to satisfy his own desires?

For the desire to live without fear belongs not only to good people but also to all evil people. The difference is that good people pursue this good by withdrawing their love from things that cannot be possessed without the danger of losing them, whereas evil people, so that they may cling securely to the enjoyment of such things, try to remove the obstacles. For this reason they lead a criminal and wicked life—a life that is more properly called death. [Col. 1227]

**E.** I recover my senses, and I am very glad that I now clearly understand what that culpable desire, which is called lust, is. It is evidently the love of things that anyone can lose against his will.

## CHAPTER FIVE — A second objection: whether, under human laws, killing a person who uses force is lawful

## 11

**A.** Come, then; let us ask, if you please, whether desire also rules in sacrileges, which we see committed in greater number because of superstition.

**A.** Take care that this is not too hasty. First, it seems to me that we must investigate whether an attacking enemy or an ambushing assassin can be killed without any desire—whether the killing is done for the sake of life, liberty, or chastity.

**E.** How can I think that such people are free from desire when they fight for things that they can lose against their will? Or, if they cannot lose them, what need is there to go so far as killing a human being for their sake?

**E.** [Note: [Col. 1227] The printed editions omit “A.” here and below insert it before “The law, indeed.” But both the sequence of the speech and the manuscripts indicate that what follows belongs to Evodius.]

Then the law is not just if it grants a traveler permission to kill a robber so that the robber does not kill him; or grants a man or woman permission, if possible, to kill before the act of rape a rapist violently attacking him or her. For the law also commands a soldier to kill the enemy; and if he refrains from that killing, he suffers punishment from his commander.

Shall we dare to call these laws unjust—or rather, not laws at all? For a law does not seem to me to be a law unless it is just.

### 12

**E.** I see clearly enough that the law is protected against an accusation of this kind: in the people whom it governs, it has granted permission for lesser wrongs, so that greater ones might not be committed. For it is much milder that a person who lies in wait for another’s life should be killed than that someone defending his own life should be killed. And it is much more savage that an unwilling person should suffer rape than that the person by whom the violence is inflicted should be killed by the one whom he attempts to assault.

Moreover, in killing an enemy the soldier is an instrument of the law; therefore he can readily fulfill his duty without any lust. And the law itself, enacted for the purpose of defending the people, cannot be accused of any lust. For if the one who enacted it did so at God’s command—that is, in accordance with what eternal justice prescribed—he could have done so entirely without lust. But if he established this with some lust, it does not follow that one must obey that law with lust, since a good law can also be enacted by someone who is not good.

For example, if someone who has acquired tyrannical power accepts payment from a person who benefits from it, in order to establish that no one may abduct a woman for marriage, the law is not thereby bad because it was enacted by an unjust and corrupt man. Thus one may obey without lust the law that commands hostile force to be repelled by the same force, for the sake of protecting citizens. The same may be said of all officers who are subject, lawfully and in due order, to whatever authorities they serve.

But how people who kill can themselves be without blame under a blameless law, I do not see. The law does not compel them to kill; it leaves the matter in their power. They are therefore free to kill no one for the sake of things which they can lose against their will [Col. 1228] and which, for that very reason, they ought not to love.

As for life, someone might perhaps doubt whether it can in no way be taken away from the soul when this body is destroyed. But if it can be taken away, it is something to be despised; if it cannot, there is nothing to fear. With regard to chastity, however, who could doubt that it resides in the soul itself, since it is a virtue? Consequently, even chastity itself cannot be snatched away by a violent rapist.

Whatever, then, the person who is killed would have taken away, all of it is not within our power. Therefore I do not understand how it should be called ours. For this reason I do not criticize the law, which permits such people to be killed; but I cannot find a way to defend those who kill them.

### 13

[Note: [Col. 1228] In the editions hitherto published, E. reads: “Much less”; shortly afterward A. reads: “Perhaps none”; and below, E. reads: “It seems to me, therefore.”]

**A.** I can find even less reason to seek a defense for people whom no law holds guilty.

**E.** Perhaps no law does—at least none of those laws which are visible and read by human beings. For I do not know whether they may not be held by some more powerful and most secret law, if nothing exists that divine providence does not administer. For how can those people be free from guilt before it, when they have been stained by human bloodshed for the sake of things that ought to be despised?

It seems to me, then, that the law written for governing the people rightly permits these acts, and that divine providence rightly punishes them. For this law of the people takes upon itself those matters that are sufficient to establish peace among inexperienced human beings and that can be governed by human authority. Those offenses, however, have other punishments appropriate to them, from which wisdom alone, as I see it, can set one free.

**A.** I praise and approve your distinction. It is still undeveloped and less than perfect, but it is confident and reaches toward lofty matters. For it seems to you that the law enacted for governing states grants many permissions and leaves many things unpunished, although they are nevertheless vindicated by divine providence—and rightly so. For the fact that it does not do everything is no reason to disapprove of what it does.

## CHAPTER VI  
### The eternal law as regulator of human affairs. The notion of the eternal law

But let us examine carefully, if you please, how far offenses should be punished under this law which restrains peoples in the present life; and then let us determine what remains to be punished more inevitably and secretly through divine providence.

**A.** Rather, attend with your whole mind, and, trusting in piety, enter upon the paths of reason. First answer me this: does the law promulgated in writing assist human beings who live this present life?

**E.** Clearly it does, for peoples and states are composed precisely of such human beings.

**E.** Who could doubt that this kind of thing is plainly changeable and subject to time? [Col. 1229]

**A.** Therefore, if a people is well ordered and serious, and a most diligent guardian of the common good—so that each person values private interests less than public ones—is it not right for a law to be enacted allowing that very people to elect magistrates for itself, through whom its affairs, that is, public affairs, may be administered?

**E.** Entirely right.

**A.** But if that same people gradually becomes corrupt, preferring private interests to the public good, selling its votes, and, corrupted by those who desire office, entrusting its government to disgraceful and criminal men, would it not likewise be right if a good man then arose, possessing great power, to take away from this people the authority to confer offices and reduce it to the judgment of a few good men, or even of one?

**E.** That too would be right.

**A.** Since, then, these two laws seem so opposed to one another that one grants the people the power to confer offices while the other takes it away—and since the second has been enacted in such a way that both cannot possibly exist together in one state—shall we say that either of them is unjust and ought never to have been enacted?

**E.** Not at all.

**A.** Let us therefore call this a temporal law, if you please. Although it is just, it can nevertheless be justly changed over time.

**E.** Let us call it that.

### 15

**A.** What, then, of the law called supreme reason, which must always be obeyed, through which the wicked deserve a miserable life and the good a blessed life, and through which, finally, the law we have decided to call temporal is rightly enacted and rightly changed? Can it appear anything other than unchangeable and eternal to anyone who understands? Or could it ever be unjust that the wicked should be miserable and the good blessed; or that a serious and disciplined people should create its own magistrates, while a dissolute and worthless people should lack that permission?

**E.** I see that this law is eternal and unchangeable.

**A.** At the same time, I believe you see that nothing is just and lawful in that temporal law which human beings have not derived from this eternal law. For if that people justly granted offices at one time and at another time justly did not grant them, this temporal alternation was just because it was drawn from that eternity in which it is always just for a serious people to grant offices and for a frivolous people not to grant them. Do you see it otherwise?

**E.** I agree.

**A.** Therefore, to explain briefly in words, as far as I am able, the notion of the eternal law that has been impressed upon us: it is the law by which it is just that all things should be arranged in the most orderly manner. If you think otherwise, state your view.

**E.** I have nothing with which to contradict you when you speak the truth.

**A.** Since, then, this is the one law from which all those temporal laws are varied for the governing of human beings, can it itself be varied in any way?

**E.** I understand completely that it cannot. No force, no chance, and no disorder in things could ever bring it about that it would not be just for all things to be arranged in the most orderly manner.

## CHAPTER VII  
### How the human being is most perfectly ordered according to the eternal law; and how, for this reason, it is shown to be better to know than to live

### 16

**A.** Come now, let us see how the human being himself is most perfectly ordered within himself. For a people consists of human beings joined together under one law, and that law, as has been said, is temporal.

Tell me: are you absolutely certain that you are alive?

**E.** What could I answer that is more certain than this?

**A.** What, then? Can you distinguish between being alive and knowing that one is alive?

**E.** I certainly know that no one knows himself to be alive unless he is alive; but whether every living being knows that it is alive, I do not know.

But since you say that you do not know, you are setting in motion a lengthy conversation. For this is not a matter which, if passed over, I can allow us to proceed to what we have in mind, given the close connection of reasoning that I consider necessary.

Tell me, then: since we have often seen beasts tamed by human beings—that is, not merely the bodies of beasts, but also their souls so subjected to human beings that they serve their will through a certain kind of perception and habituation—does it seem in any way possible to you that some beast, however savage in ferocity or body, or however keen in any kind of perception, might in turn attempt to subject a human being to itself, even though its body could be killed either by force or secretly by many human beings?

**E.** I agree that this is in no way possible.

**A.** Very well. But tell me this as well: since it is clear that in strength and in the other functions of the body a human being is easily surpassed by many beasts, what is the thing in which a human being excels, so that no beast can command him while he can command many beasts? Or is it perhaps the very thing usually called reason or intelligence?

**E.** I find nothing else. Since it is in the soul that we possess what makes us superior to animals, if they were lifeless I would say that we surpass them because we possess a soul. But since they too are living animals, and since that which is absent from their souls, so that they are subject to us, is present in ours, so that we are superior to them—and since it is obvious to everyone that this is neither nothing nor something insignificant—what could I more correctly call it than reason?

**A.** See how easily, with God’s help, what human beings consider most difficult can be accomplished. For I confess to you that I had thought this question—which, as I now understand, has been settled—would hold us for as long as perhaps everything that has been said from the very beginning of our discussion. So now accept what follows, so that the reasoning may proceed in its proper connection.

I believe you are not unaware that what we call knowing is nothing other than having grasped something through reason.

**E.** That is so.

**A.** Whoever, then, knows that he is alive is not without reason.

**E.** That follows.

**A.** But animals are alive and, as has already become clear, are without reason.

**E.** It is evident.

**A.** There you have now learned what you answered that you did not know: not everything that lives knows that it lives, although everything that knows that it lives necessarily lives.

### 17

**E.** I have no doubt about it now. Continue toward the point you had in mind. I have learned clearly that being alive is one thing and knowing that one is alive another.

**A.** Which of these two seems to you superior?

**E.** What do you think, except knowledge of life?

**A.** Does knowledge of life seem better to you than life itself? Or perhaps you understand that knowledge is a higher and purer kind of life, which no one can possess except one who understands? And what is understanding except living more brightly and perfectly by that very light of the mind? Therefore, unless I am mistaken, you have preferred to one kind of life another, better kind of life.

**A.** I think it cannot, except when, by a transferred use of the word, we call experience “knowledge.” For experience is not always good, as in experiencing punishments. But that which is properly and purely called knowledge, because it is acquired through reason and understanding—how could it be bad?

**E.** I grasp this distinction as well. Continue with the rest.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### The reason by which the human being excels beasts ought to rule within him

### 18

**A.** This is what I want to say: whatever it is by which the human being is placed above animals—whether it is more correctly called mind, spirit, or both, for we find both terms in the divine Books—if it rules and commands all the other elements of which the human being consists, then the human being is most perfectly ordered.

For we see that we have much in common not only with animals but also with shrubs and plants. We see that nourishment of the body, growth, generation, and vigor are also attributed to trees, which are contained within a certain lowest kind of life. We observe and acknowledge that animals can see and hear and perceive bodily things through smell, taste, and touch—and that most of them do so more keenly than we do.

Add to this their strength, vigor, bodily firmness, speed, and extremely easy bodily movements. In all these respects we surpass some of them, equal others, and are ourselves overcome by still others. Yet the very kind of things involved is certainly common to us and to animals. Again, pursuing bodily pleasures and avoiding discomforts is the activity of every animal life.

There are certain other things which do not seem to belong to beasts, and yet are not the highest things in the human being himself, such as playing and laughing. Whoever judges human nature with the greatest correctness considers these human, certainly, but the lowest aspects of the human being.

Then there are the love of praise and glory, and the desire to rule. Although these are not found in beasts, we should not suppose that we are superior to beasts because of our lust for such things. For this appetite too makes people miserable when it is not subject to reason. Yet no one has thought that anyone should place himself above another because of misery.

When reason rules these movements of the soul, the human being must be called ordered. For there is no right order—or indeed no order at all—when inferior things are subjected to superior things. Do you not agree?

**E.** It is clear.

**A.** This reason, then—or mind or spirit—when it governs the irrational movements of the soul, rules in the human being; and rule is owed to it by the law which we have discovered to be eternal.

**E.** I understand and follow you.

### The mind is justly punished when, by free will, it serves lust

**A.** It follows that you must think it just for the mind to pay the penalty for so great a sin.

**E.** I cannot deny it.

**A.** What, then? Should this very punishment be considered small: that lust rules the mind, strips it of the wealth of virtue, and drags it impoverished and needy through various directions—now approving false things as true, now even defending them, now disapproving what it had previously approved, and nevertheless rushing into other falsehoods; now suspending its assent, and often fearing clear lines of reasoning; now despairing of the discovery of truth as a whole and clinging utterly to the darkness of folly; now striving toward the light of understanding and again collapsing from weariness?

### By the will we live a blessed life; by the will we live a miserable one

**A.** It is therefore pleasing that a person should be blessed who loves his good will and, in preference to it, despises whatever other good is called good—something whose loss can occur even while the will to retain it remains.

**E.** Why should it not be pleasing, when the conclusions we have accepted above necessarily lead to it?

**A.** You understand well. But tell me, please: is not loving one’s good will and valuing it as highly as has been said itself a good will?

**E.** You speak truly.

**A.** But if we rightly judge this person blessed, do we not rightly judge the person of the contrary will miserable?

**E.** Most rightly.

**A.** What reason, then, is there for us to doubt that, even if we have never previously been wise, we nevertheless deserve and live a praiseworthy and blessed life by our will, and by our will a shameful and miserable one? [Note: See *Retractions*, Book 1, chapter 9, section 3.]

**E.** I admit that we have reached this conclusion through certain facts that cannot be denied.

### 29

**A.** Consider something else as well. For I believe you remember what we said a good will is. I think we said that it is the will by which we desire to live rightly and honorably.

**E.** I remember.

**A.** If, then, we love and embrace this will with a good will as well, and prefer it to all things which we cannot retain merely because we wish to retain them, the virtues which reason has taught us will consequently dwell in our soul. To possess these virtues is itself to live rightly and honorably.

From this it follows that whoever wants to live rightly and honorably, if he wants this more than fleeting goods, attains so great a thing with such ease that, in order to possess what he wanted, he needs nothing other than the very act of willing it. [Note: See *Retractions*, Book 1, chapter 9, section 3.]

**E.** I tell you truly: I can scarcely keep myself from crying out with joy, since such a great good has suddenly appeared to me, and one so readily attainable.

**A.** And yet this very joy, which arises from the acquisition of this good and which raises the soul calmly, peacefully, and steadfastly, is called the blessed life—unless you think that living blessedly means something other than rejoicing in true and certain goods.

**E.** That is my view.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Why, then, do few attain blessedness when everyone wants it?

### 30

**A.** Rightly so. But do you think that any human being does not want and desire a blessed life in every possible way?

**E.** Who doubts that every human being wants it?

**A.** Why, then, do not all attain it? For we had said, and had agreed among ourselves, that people deserve it by their will, and by their will also deserve a miserable life—in such a way that they receive what they deserve.

Now some contradiction arises, and unless we examine it carefully, it attempts to disturb the reasoning we established earlier so attentively and firmly. How does each person endure a miserable life by his will, when absolutely no one wants to live miserably? Or how does a human being attain a blessed life by his will, when so many are miserable and everyone wants to be blessed?

Does this happen because it is one thing to want something well or badly, and another to deserve something through a good or bad will? For those who are blessed—and who must also be good—are not blessed because they wanted to live blessedly, since the wicked want this too, but because they want what is right, which the wicked do not want.

It is therefore not surprising that miserable people do not attain what they want, namely, a blessed life. For they do not likewise want that which accompanies it and without which no one is worthy of it or attains it: namely, living rightly.

That eternal law, to whose consideration it is now time to return, established with unchangeable stability that merit lies in the will, while blessedness and misery are reward and punishment. [Note: See the same work.]

Thus, when we say that people are miserable by their will, we do not mean that they want to be miserable, but that they are in a will which misery must necessarily follow, even against their will. Therefore it does not conflict with the preceding reasoning that everyone wants to be blessed but cannot be so. For not everyone wants to live rightly, and the blessed life is owed to that one will alone—unless you have something to say against this.

**E.** I have nothing at all.

## CHAPTER XV
### To whom, and to what extent, the eternal law and the temporal law apply
31. But let us now see how these matters relate to that question proposed earlier concerning the two laws.

A. Let it be so; but first tell me whether the person who loves living rightly, and takes such delight in it that what is right is not merely right for him but also sweet and pleasant, loves this law and holds it most dear—the law by which he sees that a blessed life is assigned to the good will and a miserable one to the evil will.

E. He certainly loves it, and with great intensity; for by following that very law he lives in this way. [Col. 1238]

A. What then? When he loves this law, does he love something changeable and temporal, or something stable and eternal?

E. Clearly, something eternal and unchangeable.

A. What of those who persist in an evil will and nevertheless desire to be happy? Can they love this law, by which misery is deservedly repaid to such people?

E. I think they cannot at all.

A. Do they love nothing else?

E. On the contrary, very many things—namely, those things in whose pursuit or retention that evil will persists.

A. I suppose you mean wealth, honors, pleasures, bodily beauty, and all the other things which people may fail to obtain even when they desire them, and may lose against their will.

E. Those very things.

A. Do you think these things are eternal, when you see that they are subject to the revolving course of time?

E. Who, however insane, would think that?

A. Since it is therefore clear that some people are lovers of eternal things and others of temporal things, and since we have agreed that there are two laws, one eternal and the other temporal, if you have any understanding of justice, which of these people do you judge should be subject to the eternal law, and which to the temporal law?

E. I think the answer to your question is obvious. I believe that those happy people act under the eternal law because of their love for eternal things; but the temporal law is imposed upon the miserable.

A. You judge correctly, provided that you hold firmly what reason has now demonstrated most clearly: those who serve the temporal law cannot be free from the eternal law. From it, we said, all things that are just, and are justly changed, are derived. But you understand well enough, as is apparent, that those who cling to the eternal law through a good will have no need of the temporal law.

E. I hold what you say.

32. A. The eternal law therefore commands that love be turned away from temporal things and, once purified, directed toward eternal things.

E. It certainly commands this.

A. What else do you think the temporal law commands except that people possess those things which may for a time be called ours, when human beings cling to them through desire, in accordance with the right by which human peace and society are preserved, insofar as such peace can be preserved in these matters?

These things are, first, this body and what are called its goods: sound health, keenness of the senses, strength, beauty, and whatever else there may be—some of them necessary for good practices and therefore to be valued more highly, others of less worth. Then there is liberty, which is truly possessed only by the blessed and those who cling to the eternal law. But at present I am referring to the liberty by which those who have no human masters consider themselves free, and which is desired by those who wish to be manumitted by human masters.

Then there are parents, brothers, a spouse, children, relatives, relations by marriage, household members, and all who are joined to us by some relationship. Finally, there is the state itself, which is customarily regarded as standing in the place of a parent; also honors and praises, and what is called popular glory.

Lastly, there is money, a single name under which are included all the things of which we are legally owners and which we seem to have the power to sell or give away.

It would be difficult and lengthy to explain how that law distributes all these things to each person, and it is plainly unnecessary for the matter we have proposed. For it is enough to see that the power of this law in punishment does not extend farther than to deprive and take away from the person whom it punishes these things, or some of them. It therefore restrains by fear and bends and redirects toward what it wishes the minds of the miserable [Col. 1239], to govern whom it is suited. For while they fear losing these things, they maintain in using them a certain measure appropriate to the bond of civic society, such as can be formed from people of this kind.

But the law does not avenge sin when these things are loved; it avenges sin when they are wickedly taken away from others. Therefore see whether we have now reached what you thought was infinite. We had begun by asking how far the law by which earthly peoples and states are governed has the right to exact vengeance.

E. I see that we have reached it.

33. A. You see, then, that there would be no punishment—whether punishment inflicted through injustice or through such vengeance—if people did not love those things which can be taken away against their will?

E. I see that as well.

A. Since, then, one person uses the same things badly and another well—and the one who uses them badly clings to and becomes entangled in them through love, being made subject to things that ought to have been subject to him, and establishing as his goods those things which he himself ought to be good enough to order and manage well; whereas the one who uses them rightly shows indeed that they are goods, but not goods for himself—for they do not make him good or better; rather, they are made so by him—and therefore does not become glued to them by love or make them, as it were, parts of his soul, which is what happens through loving them, lest when they begin to be cut away they defile him with torment and corruption, but instead rises wholly above them, ready to possess and govern them when necessary, and readier still to lose and not possess them: since these things are so, do you think that silver and gold should be blamed because of misers, food because of gluttons, wine because of drunkards, or women’s beauty because of prostitutes and adulterers—and in the same way all the rest—especially when you see that a physician may use fire well and a poisoner bread wickedly?

E. It is entirely true: not the things themselves, but the people who use them badly, are to be blamed.

## CHAPTER XVI—Epilogue to the Question Discussed

34. A. Quite right. But since, as I think, we have already begun to see what force the eternal law possesses, and have discovered how far the temporal law can proceed in exacting punishment; and since two kinds of things—eternal and temporal—and likewise two kinds of people—those who pursue and value eternal things, and those who pursue and value temporal things—have been distinguished sufficiently and clearly; and since it has been established that what each person chooses to pursue and embrace is determined by the will [Note: [Col. 1239] See *Retractions*, Book 1, chapter 9, no. 3]; and that the mind is deposed from the citadel of dominion and from the right order by nothing except the will; and since it is clear [Col. 1240] that when anyone uses a thing badly, it is not the thing but the person who uses it badly who must be reproved—let us, if you please, return to the question proposed at the beginning of this discussion and see whether it has been resolved. For we had begun by asking what it is to do wrong, and it is for this reason that we have said everything that has been said.

Accordingly, we may now observe and consider whether doing wrong is anything other than, while neglecting eternal things—which the mind enjoys through itself and perceives through itself, and which it cannot lose if it loves them—pursuing as though they were great and wondrous things temporal objects, which are perceived through the body, the lowest part of the human being, and which can never be certain.

For it seems to me that all wrongdoing—that is, all sins—are included in this one kind. I await hearing what you think.

35. E. It is as you say, and I agree that all sins are contained in this one kind: whenever someone turns away from things that are divine and truly enduring and turns toward things that are changeable and uncertain. Although these things are rightly placed in their own order and complete a certain beauty of their own, it is nevertheless the mark of a perverse and disordered mind to subject oneself to things which, according to the divine order and law, one has been placed above in order to direct them according to one’s will.

At the same time, I seem already to see resolved and established that other matter which, after asking what it is to do wrong, we had next begun to ask: from where does wrongdoing arise? Unless I am mistaken, as the reasoning we have pursued has shown, we do it through the free choice of the will.

But I ask whether this very free choice, by which we are shown to have the capacity to sin, ought to have been given to us by the one who made us. For it seems that we would not have sinned if we lacked it; and there is a danger that, in this way, God might also be thought the author of our wrongdoings.

A. You should have no fear of that at all. But in order that the matter may be investigated more carefully, another time must be set aside. For this conversation now desires an end and a limit. I would have you believe that we have, as it were, knocked at the doors of great and hidden matters awaiting investigation. When, with God as our guide, we begin to enter their inner chambers, you will certainly judge how great the difference is between this discussion and those that follow, and how greatly the latter surpass this one [Note: [Col. 1240] In B: “illa praestent.” We have followed the reading of Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. M.]—not only in the acuity of their investigation but also in the majesty of their subject matter and the clearest light of truth. Let only piety be present, so that divine providence may permit us to keep to and complete the course we have begun.

E. I yield to your will, and most willingly join my own to it in judgment and desire.

# BOOK TWO

In this book, arising from the difficulty that the liberty by which one sins was given by God, three questions are investigated: how it is evident that God exists; whether all goods, insofar as they are goods, are from him; and whether free will is to be numbered among the goods.

[Col. 1239]

## CHAPTER I—Why the Liberty by Which One Sins Was Given by God

[Col. 1239]

1. E. Now, if possible, explain to me why God gave human beings free choice of the will—for [Col. 1240] certainly, if they had not received it, they could not sin.

A. Is it already certain and known to you that God gave human beings this thing which you do not think ought to have been given?

E. As far as I seemed to understand in the preceding book, we possess free choice of the will, and it is only through it [Col. 1241] that we sin.

A. I too remember that this was made clear to us. But now I asked whether you know that God gave us this thing which it is evident that we possess and through which we sin.

E. I think there is no other source. For we are from him; and whether we sin or act rightly, we deserve punishment or reward from him.

A. I wish to know whether you know this clearly, or whether, moved by authority, you gladly believe even what you do not know.

E. I acknowledge that I first believed this on the authority of others. But what is truer than that every good is from God, that everything just is good, and that punishment for sinners and reward for those who act rightly are just? From this it follows that God affects both those who sin with misery and those who act rightly with blessedness.

2. A. I offer no resistance; but I ask how you know that we are from him. For you have explained not this now, but that we deserve punishment or reward from him.

E. I see this also to be evident from no other source than the established fact that God punishes sins. For all justice is from him. For justice is not like a kind of goodness whose office is to bestow benefits on others: its office is to exact punishment from others. Hence it is evident that we belong to him, since he is not only supremely kind in bestowing benefits upon us but also supremely just in punishing us.

Moreover, from what I asserted and you conceded—that every good is from God—it can also be understood that human beings are from God. For a human being, insofar as he is a human being, is some good, because, when he wishes, he is able to live rightly [Note: [Col. 1241] See *Retractions*, Book 1, chapter 9, no. 3].

3. A. Clearly, if these things are so, the question you proposed has been resolved. For if a human being is some good, and could not act rightly except when he wished to do so, he ought to have free will, without which he could not act rightly.

It is not because sin is also committed through free will that we should believe God gave it for that purpose. There is therefore sufficient reason why it ought to have been given: without it, a human being cannot live rightly.

That it was given for this purpose can also be understood from the following consideration: if anyone uses it for sinning, divine punishment is imposed upon him. This would be unjust if free will had been given not only for living rightly but also for sinning. For how could the person who used his will for the purpose for which it was given be justly punished?

But when God punishes the sinner, what else does he seem to say than: “Why did you not use your free will for the purpose for which I gave it to you—that is, for doing what is right?”

Furthermore, how could that good exist by which justice is commended in condemning sins and honoring right actions, if a human being lacked free choice of the will? For neither sin nor a right action would exist if it were not done voluntarily.

Consequently, both punishment and reward would be unjust if a human being did not possess a free will. But justice ought to exist both in punishment and in reward, since this is one of the goods that come from God. Therefore God ought to have given human beings free will.

## CHAPTER II—Objection: If Free Will Was Given for Good, How Is It Capable of Turning toward Evil?

4. E. I now concede that God gave it. But please tell me: if it was given for doing what is right, does it not seem to you that it ought not to have been capable of turning toward sin? Consider justice itself, which was given to human beings for living well: surely no one can live badly through his justice. In the same way, no one could sin through the will if the will had been given for doing what is right.

A. May God grant—as I hope—that I may be able to answer you, or rather that you yourself may answer yourself through the same truth inwardly teaching you, that truth which is the supreme teacher of all. But tell me briefly: if you hold as certain and known what I asked you earlier—namely, that God gave us free will—should we say that what we confess God gave us ought not to have been given?

For if it is uncertain whether he gave it, we rightly ask whether it was well given; and when we discover that it was well given, we will also discover that it was given by the one from whom all goods have been given to human beings [Note: [Col. 1242] Fourteen manuscripts read, “from whom all goods have been given to the soul.”]

But if we discover that it was not well given, we will understand that it was not given by the one whom it would be impious to blame. If, however, it is certain that he himself gave it, we must confess that, however it was given, it ought neither not to have been given nor to have been given otherwise than it was given. For it was given by one whose work cannot rightly be criticized in any way.

5. E. Although I hold these things by unshaken faith, I do not yet hold them by knowledge. Let us therefore investigate as though everything were uncertain. For from this uncertainty—whether free will was given for doing what is right, since through it we can also sin—it follows that it is uncertain whether it ought to have been given.

If it is uncertain whether it was given for doing what is right, it is also uncertain whether it ought to have been given; and consequently it will also be uncertain whether God gave it, since, if it is uncertain whether it ought to have been given, it is uncertain whether it was given by the one whom it is impious to believe gave something that ought not to have been given.

A. At least, is it certain to you that God exists?

E. Even this I hold unshakably, not by contemplation but by faith.

A. If, then, one of those foolish people of whom it is written, “The fool has said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Psalm 52:1), were to say this to you, and did not wish to believe with you what you believe but wished to know whether you had believed the truth, would you abandon the man, or would you judge that somehow what you hold unshakably ought to be demonstrated to him—especially if he did not wish to resist obstinately but earnestly desired to acknowledge it?

E. The final point you made sufficiently reminds me what I ought to answer him. Certainly, however absurd he might be, he would grant me that one ought not to debate with a deceitful and obstinate person about anything at all, and especially not about so important a matter.

Once he had granted this, he would first deal with me so that I would believe that he was asking this in good faith and that no deceit or obstinacy concerning this matter was concealed within him. Then I would demonstrate what I think would be easy for anyone: how much fairer it would be for him, who wished another person to believe what he himself knew about the hidden matters of his own mind, to believe that God exists on the testimony of those great men who left written testimony that they had lived with the Son of God.

For they wrote that they had seen things that could in no way have happened if God did not exist. And he would be exceedingly foolish if he reproached me for believing those whom he wished me to believe. Moreover, since he would find no valid reason to criticize this, he could in no way discover why he should refuse to imitate me.

A. If, then, you think that the question whether God exists is sufficiently settled by our judgment that such great men ought not to be believed rashly, why, I ask you, do you not think that in those other matters which we have begun to investigate as uncertain and wholly unknown, we should likewise trust the authority of those same men, so that we need undertake no further labor in investigating them?

E. But we desire to know and understand what we believe.

6. A. You rightly remember what we also stated at the beginning of our earlier discussion and cannot deny (Book 1, chapter 2). For unless believing and understanding were different things, and unless one had first to believe what we desired to understand—something great and divine—the prophet would have said in vain, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

Our Lord himself also first urged those whom he called to salvation to believe, both by his words and by his deeds. But afterward, when he spoke of the gift he was going to give to believers, he did not say, “This is eternal life: that they may believe”; rather, he said, “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

Then he says to those who already believe, “Seek and you will find” (Matthew 7:7). For what is believed while still unknown cannot be called “found”; nor does anyone become fit to find God unless he has first believed what he is afterward going to know.

Therefore, obeying the Lord’s commands, let us seek persistently. What we seek at his urging, we will find through his demonstration, insofar as such things can be found by us in this life and by people of our condition. For it must be believed that even while they inhabit this earth these things are seen and attained more clearly and perfectly by those who are better; and certainly after this life they are seen and attained by all good and devout people. We must hope that this will also be the case for us, and, despising earthly and human things, we must desire and love these matters in every way.

## CHAPTER III—In Order That It May Become Evident That God Exists, It Is Investigated What Is Most Excellent in the Human Being

7. Let us investigate in the following order, if you please: first, how it is evident that God exists; next, whether all things that are goods in any degree are from him; lastly, whether free will is to be numbered among the goods. Once these matters have been established, it will be sufficiently apparent, I think, whether free will was rightly given to human beings.

Therefore I first ask you, so that we may begin with what is most evident: do you yourself exist? Or are you perhaps afraid that you might be deceived in this question, when, clearly, if you did not exist, you could not be deceived at all?

E. Go on to the other matters instead.

A. Since it is therefore evident that you exist—and it would not be evident to you in any other way unless you were alive—it is also evident that you are alive. Do you understand that these two things are entirely true?

E. I understand them completely.

A. Then this third thing is also evident: that you understand.

E. It is evident.

A. Which of these three seems to you to excel?

E. Understanding.

A. Why does this seem so to you?

E. Because there are these three things: existing, living, and understanding. A stone exists, and an animal lives, yet I do not think that a stone lives or that an animal understands. But it is absolutely certain that whatever understands both exists and lives. Therefore I do not hesitate to judge that what possesses all three is more excellent than what lacks either two or one.

For what lives certainly exists, but it does not follow that it also understands; such, I think, is the life of an animal. What exists does not necessarily also live and understand: I can admit that corpses exist, but no one would say that they live. And what does not live understands even less.

A. We therefore hold that of these three, two are lacking in a corpse, one in an animal, and none in a human being.

E. That is true.

A. We also hold that among these three the most excellent is what a human being possesses along with the other two—namely, understanding, which entails both existence and life in the one who possesses it.

E. Certainly we hold that.

8. A. Now tell me whether you know that you possess the five familiar bodily senses: sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

E. I know that I do.

A. What do you think belongs to the sense of sight? That is, what do you think we perceive by seeing?

E. Whatever is corporeal.

A. Do we also perceive hard and soft things by seeing?

E. No.

A. What, then, properly belongs to the eyes, which we perceive through them?

E. Color.

A. What belongs to the ears?

E. Sound.

A. What belongs to smell?

E. Odor.

A. What belongs to taste?

E. Flavor.

A. What belongs to touch?

E. Soft or hard, smooth or rough, and many things of that kind.

A. What then? Do we not perceive the shapes of bodies—large, short, square, round, and whatever is similar—both by touching and by seeing? And therefore can these shapes be attributed neither properly to sight nor properly to touch, but to both?

E. I understand.

A. Then you understand that certain things belong properly to each individual sense, about which it reports, while certain things are common to some or all of them?

E. I understand this as well.

A. Can we determine by any of these senses what belongs to each sense, and what all or some of them have in common with one another?

E. Not at all; these matters are determined by some more inward faculty.

A. Is that perhaps reason itself, which animals lack? For I think that we comprehend these matters by reason, and recognize that they are so.

E. I think that by reason we comprehend the existence of some more inward sense, to which everything is referred by these five most familiar senses.

For the faculty by which an animal sees is one thing, and the faculty by which it either avoids or pursues what it perceives by seeing is another. The former is in the eyes, but the latter is inward, in the soul itself. By it animals not only pursue and take in with pleasure what is seen, but also what is heard and what is apprehended through the other bodily senses; when offended, they avoid and reject these things.

This faculty cannot be called sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch, but is some other faculty that presides over all of them in common. Although, as I said, we comprehend it by reason, I nevertheless cannot call it reason itself, since it is plainly present in animals as well.

9. A. I acknowledge whatever this faculty is, and I do not hesitate to call it the inner sense. But unless what is brought to us by the bodily senses passes beyond this sense as well, it cannot arrive at knowledge. For whatever we know, we hold as having been comprehended by reason.

To say nothing of other matters, we know that colors cannot be perceived by hearing, nor sounds by sight. When we know this, we know it neither through the eyes nor through the ears, nor through that inner sense which animals also possess. For we must not believe that animals know that light cannot be perceived by the ears, or sound by the eyes, since we distinguish these things only by rational attention and thought.

E. I cannot say that I have grasped this. What if animals distinguish this also through that inner sense, which you concede they possess—namely, that colors cannot be perceived by hearing, nor sounds by sight?

A. Do you also think that they can distinguish from one another the color that is perceived, the sense located in the eye, that inner sense in the soul, and the reason by which these are separately defined and counted?

E. Not at all.

A. What then? Could reason distinguish these four from one another and delimit them by definitions unless the color were referred to it through the sense of the eyes, and the sense itself in turn through that inner sense which presides over it, and that inner sense through itself—if indeed nothing else intervenes?

E. I do not see how it could happen otherwise.

A. What then? Do you see that color is perceived by the sense of the eyes, but that this same sense is not perceived by that same sense? For you do not see the very act of seeing by the sense by which you see color.

E. Certainly not.

A. Try to distinguish this also. I believe you do not deny that color is one thing, seeing color another, and again something else: possessing, when color is absent, the sense by which it could be seen if it were present.

E. I distinguish these things as well, and I agree that they differ from one another.

A. Do you see any one of these three things with your eyes, apart from color?

E. Nothing else.

A. Tell me, then, from where you see the other two; for you could not distinguish what you had not seen.

E. I know that they exist, but I do not know what else they are.

A. Then you do not know whether this is reason itself, or the life that we call the inner sense, which is superior to the bodily senses, or something else?

E. I do not know.

A. You do know, however, that these things cannot be defined except by reason, and that reason cannot do this except with regard to things offered for its examination.

E. That is certain.
