A. Whatever else it is by which everything we know can be sensed is therefore an instrument of reason. It presents and reports to reason whatever it reaches, so that the things perceived may be distinguished within their proper limits and comprehended not only by perception but also by knowledge.

E. That is so.

A. What then? When reason itself distinguishes its instruments and the things they report from one another, and likewise recognizes the difference between these things and itself, and confirms that it is more powerful than they are, does it comprehend itself by anything other than itself—that is, by reason? Or would you know that you possess reason unless you perceived it by reason?

E. That is entirely true.

A. Since, therefore, when we perceive color, we do not likewise perceive by the very sense itself that we are perceiving; and when we hear a sound, we do not also hear our hearing; and when we smell a rose, the smell itself does not smell to us; and when we taste something, taste itself does not have a flavor in our mouth; and when we touch something, we cannot touch the sense of touch itself—it is evident that these five senses cannot be perceived by any one of them, although through them all corporeal things are perceived.

E. It is evident.

## CHAPTER IV—The Inner Sense Perceives the Act of Perceiving Itself: Does It Also Distinguish Itself?

10. A. I think it is also evident that the inner sense perceives not only what it receives from the five bodily senses but also the bodily senses themselves. For otherwise an animal could not move itself, either by pursuing something or by fleeing from it, unless it perceived that it was perceiving—not in order to know, for that belongs to reason, but merely in order to move, which it certainly does not perceive through any one of those five senses.

If this is still obscure, it will become clear if you observe what is sufficient as an example in one particular sense, such as sight. For an animal could in no way open its eye and direct it by looking toward what it desires to see unless, with its eye closed or not moved in the appropriate way, it perceived that it was not seeing that thing.

But if it perceives that it does not see when it does not see, it must also perceive that it sees when it sees. For when it sees, it does not move its eye with the same desire with which it moves it when it does not see; this shows that it perceives both states.

But whether this living faculty itself also perceives itself—the faculty that perceives that it perceives corporeal things—is not equally clear. One consideration is that, when each person questions himself inwardly, he finds that every living thing flees death. Since death is contrary to life, life must also perceive itself, because it flees what is contrary to it.

If this is still not clear, let us set it aside, so that we do not strive toward what we want unless we have certain and evident proofs. For it is evident that corporeal things are perceived by the bodily sense; that this same sense cannot be perceived by that same sense; that through the inner sense both corporeal things are perceived through the bodily sense and the bodily sense itself is perceived; and that by reason all these things become known, including reason itself, and are contained in knowledge. Does this not seem so to you?

E. It certainly does.

A. Come, then, answer now from what source the question arose whose solution we desire to reach, and for which we have been laboring along this path for so long.

## CHAPTER V—The Inner Sense Is Superior to the External Senses, of Which It Is the Governor and Judge

11. E. As far as I remember, we are now dealing with the first of those three questions which we proposed earlier in order to construct the order of this discussion: namely, how it can be made evident that God exists, although we must believe most firmly and tenaciously that he does exist.

A. You hold this correctly. But I also want you carefully to hold what became apparent to us when I asked whether you knew that you existed: namely, that you knew not only this but two other things as well.

E. I hold that also.

A. Now consider to which of these three you understand everything touched by the bodily senses to belong. That is, in which category of things do you think we should place whatever our sense reaches through the eyes or through any other bodily instrument: among things that merely exist, among things that also live, or among things that also understand?

E. Among things that merely exist.

A. What of the sense itself? To which of these three categories do you think it belongs?

E. To that which lives.

A. Which of these two do you judge to be better: the sense itself, or what the sense perceives?

E. The sense, obviously. [Col. 1247]

A. Why?

E. Because what also lives is better than what merely exists.

12. A. What then? Will you hesitate to place above this sense through which we reach the body that inner sense which we investigated earlier as below reason and still shared by us with animals—and which you have already said ought to be placed above the body itself?

E. I would not hesitate at all.

A. I want to hear from you why you do not hesitate. For you cannot say that this inner sense should already be placed in the category of the three things that also understand; it still belongs to what exists and lives, even though it lacks understanding. For this sense is present in animals as well, and animals do not possess understanding.

Since this is so, I ask why you place the inner sense above the sense by which corporeal things are perceived, when both belong to the category of what lives.

You placed the sense that reaches bodies above bodies because bodies belong to the category of what merely exists, while the sense belongs to what also lives. Since that inner sense is found in the same category, tell me why you think it is better.

If you say that it is because the inner sense perceives the bodily sense, I do not think you will find a rule by which we can establish that everything that perceives is better than what is perceived by it. Otherwise we might also be compelled to say that everything that understands is better than what is understood by it.

That is false, because a human being understands wisdom, and is not better than wisdom itself. Therefore consider for what reason it seemed to you that the inner sense should be preferred to the sense by which we perceive bodies.

E. Because I recognize that the inner sense is a kind of governor and judge of the bodily sense. If anything is deficient in the bodily sense in the performance of its function, the inner sense demands it as something owed by a servant, as we discussed earlier.

The sense of the eye does not see whether it sees or does not see; and because it does not see, it cannot judge what it lacks or what is sufficient for it. But the inner sense, by which the soul of the animal is admonished to open its closed eye and to supply what it perceives to be lacking, does this.

No one doubts that the one who judges is better than that about which he judges.

A. You see, then, that the bodily sense also judges bodies in a certain way. For pleasure and pain belong to it when it is touched by a body either gently or harshly.

Just as the inner sense judges what is lacking or sufficient in the sense of the eyes, so the sense of the eyes itself judges what is lacking or sufficient in colors.

Likewise, just as the inner sense judges whether our hearing is less or sufficiently attentive, so hearing itself judges sounds: what flows gently into it and what strikes it harshly.

There is no need to pursue the other bodily senses. By now, I think, you understand what I mean: that the inner sense judges these bodily senses when it approves their integrity and demands what is owed to them, just as the bodily senses themselves judge bodies, accepting in them what is gentle to the touch and rejecting what is contrary.

E. I see this clearly, and I agree that it is entirely true.

## CHAPTER VI—Reason Is Superior to the Other Faculties in Human Beings; If Anything Is Superior to Reason, It Is God

[Col. 1248]

13. A. Now consider whether reason also judges this inner sense. I am no longer asking whether you doubt that reason is better than it, because I do not doubt that you judge it to be so. Indeed, I do not think we even need to ask whether reason judges this sense.

For among the things that lie below reason—namely, bodies, bodily senses, and this inner sense—how one is better than another, and how much more excellent reason itself is than they are, can only be reported by reason itself. It certainly could not do this unless it judged these things itself.

E. It is evident.

A. Since, then, a nature that merely exists, neither living nor understanding, such as an inanimate body, is surpassed by a nature that not only exists but also lives, although it does not understand, such as the soul of animals; and since this latter nature is in turn surpassed by one that simultaneously exists, lives, and understands, such as the rational mind in a human being—do you think that in us, that is, in those faculties by which our nature is completed so that we are human beings, anything can be found more excellent than what we have placed third among these three?

It is evident that we possess a body, and also a certain life by which the body is animated and nourished; we recognize these two in animals as well. There is also a third thing, as it were the head or eye of our soul—or, if some more appropriate term can be found, the faculty of reason and understanding—which the nature of animals does not possess.

Therefore consider, I ask you, whether you can find anything in human nature more exalted than reason.

E. I see nothing at all that is better.

14. A. What if we should be able to find something which you do not merely doubt exists, but which is even superior to our reason itself? Would you hesitate to call whatever it is God?

E. I would not immediately call something God merely because I could find something better than what is best in my nature. For I do not approve of calling “God” that than which my reason is inferior, but that than which nothing is superior.

A. Quite so. For it was he himself who gave your reason the capacity to think this about him piously and truly. But, I ask you, if you should find that nothing exists above our reason except what is eternal and unchangeable, would you hesitate to call this God? You recognize that bodies are mutable; and it is evident that the very life by which the body is animated is not free from mutability through its various affections. Reason itself, moreover, is plainly shown to be mutable, since at one time it strives to reach the truth and at another does not, and sometimes reaches it and sometimes does not. If, without employing any bodily instrument—not through touch, taste, smell, ears, eyes, or any sense inferior to itself—but by itself, reason perceives something eternal and unchangeable, then it must at the same time acknowledge both that it is inferior to this thing and that this thing is its God.

E. I shall plainly acknowledge as God that than which nothing higher is shown to exist.

A. Good. For it will be enough for me to show that something of this kind exists: either you will acknowledge it to be God, or, if something exists above it, you will concede that the higher thing itself is God. Therefore, whether something exists above it or not, it will be evident that God exists, once, with his own assistance, I have shown that what I promised exists above reason. [Col. 1249]

E. Demonstrate, then, what you promise.

## CHAPTER VII — How the Same Thing Is Perceived by Many, and What Is Whole, What Is Not Whole, and What Is Perceived Simultaneously by Each

15. A. I shall. But first I ask whether my bodily sense is the same as yours, or whether mine is mine alone and yours yours alone; for if this were not so, I could not see with my eyes something that you did not see.

E. I fully grant that, although our senses are of the same kind, each of us has his own individual senses—of sight, hearing, and each of the others. For one person can not only see something that another does not see, but also hear something that another does not hear, and perceive through any other sense something that another does not perceive. Hence it is clear that your sense is yours alone, and mine mine alone.

A. Will you give the same answer concerning that interior sense, or something different?

E. Certainly nothing different. For that sense too is my sense, and it perceives my sensations; yours is yours, and perceives yours. That is why someone who sees something often asks me whether I also see it: I feel whether I see or do not see, whereas the person asking does not.

A. What of reason itself? Does not each of us have his own reason, since it can happen that I understand something while you do not understand it, and you cannot know whether I understand it, whereas I do know?

E. It is also evident that each of us has an individual rational mind.

16. A. Can you likewise say that each of us has an individual sun which we see, or an individual moon, or individual morning stars, or other things of this kind, although each person sees them through his own and private sense?

E. I could not say that at all.

A. We can therefore see one and the same thing simultaneously, although our senses are individual to each of us, through all of which we sense the one thing that we see together. Thus, although my sense is one thing and yours another, what we see need not be one thing belonging to me and another belonging to you; rather, the one thing is present to both of us and is seen simultaneously by both.

E. That is perfectly clear.

A. We can also hear one and the same voice simultaneously. Although my hearing is one thing and yours another, the voice we hear together is not one voice for me and another for you; nor is one part of it grasped by my hearing and another by yours. Whatever has sounded is present to both of us as one whole to be heard simultaneously.

E. This too is clear.

17. A. You may now observe the same point concerning the other bodily senses. In relation to the matter at hand, they are neither wholly like the senses of sight and hearing nor wholly unlike them. Both you and I can draw breath from the same air and perceive the air’s condition by its odor; likewise, from the same honey or any other food or drink, we can both taste and perceive its condition by its flavor. Although the air or food is one, our senses are individual—yours yours and mine mine. Thus, when we both perceive one odor or one flavor, you do not perceive it through my sense, nor I through yours, nor through some single sense that could belong commonly to both of us. My sense is entirely mine, and yours yours, even when one odor or flavor is perceived by both.

In this respect these senses are found to have something in common with the senses of sight and hearing. But, so far as our present discussion is concerned, they differ in that, although we both draw in the same air through our nostrils, I do not draw the same portion of air as you, nor do I take the same portion of food as you. I take one portion and you another. Thus, when I breathe, I draw from the whole air as much as is sufficient for me, and you likewise draw from the whole another portion, as much as is sufficient for you. Although the food is one and is consumed wholly by both of us, it cannot be wholly consumed both by me and wholly by you, as it can be that I hear the whole word and you hear the whole simultaneously, or that whatever extent of visible form I see, you also see to the same extent simultaneously. Rather, a different portion of the food or drink must pass into me and another into you. Do you understand this poorly?

E. On the contrary, I agree that it is entirely clear and certain. [Col. 1250]

18. A. Do you think the sense of touch should be compared with the senses of sight and hearing in the matter now under discussion? Not only can both of us perceive one body by touching it, but you can also touch the same part that I have touched, so that by touching we can both perceive not merely the same body but the same part of the body. For when we are both eating a food placed before us, we cannot each take the whole of it, yours wholly and mine wholly; but touching is not like that. What I have touched, one whole thing, you too can touch, so that we both touch it—not each in separate parts, but each the whole.

E. In this respect I admit that the sense of touch closely resembles those two higher senses. But I see that it differs in this respect: we can both see one whole thing and hear it simultaneously, that is, at one time; and we can indeed both touch an entire thing at one time, but each through separate parts. We cannot touch the same part except at separate times. For I cannot bring my touch to any part that you have grasped by touch unless you withdraw yours.

19. A. You have answered with great vigilance. But you must also see that, among all the things we perceive, some are perceived by both of us and others by each individually, while each of us individually perceives his own senses. Thus I do not perceive your sense, nor you mine. As regards the things perceived by us through the bodily senses—that is, bodily things—we cannot perceive them together, but each separately, except when they become ours in such a way that we can turn and transform them into ourselves, as happens with food and drink. No portion of what I have taken in can also be taken in by you.

For even if nurses return chewed food to infants, what the taste has seized from it and transformed into the entrails of the person chewing can in no way be brought back and returned as food to the infant. When the throat tastes something pleasant, it claims for itself even a small portion of it, yet an irrevocable portion, and compels this to happen [Col. 1251] in accordance with the body’s nature. If this were not so, no taste would remain in the mouth after the chewed food had been returned and spat out.

The same can properly be said of the portions of air that we draw through our nostrils. Even if you can draw in some of the air that I have expelled, you cannot also draw in what has thereby become my nourishment, since it cannot be expelled again. Physicians even teach that we take nourishment through the nostrils. I can perceive this nourishment simply by breathing in, but I cannot restore it by breathing out so that you too might perceive it drawn in through your nostrils.

Other sensible things, however, although we perceive them, are not thereby corrupted and transformed into our own bodies. We can both perceive them, either at the same time or at separate times in turn, so that either the whole thing or the very part that I perceive may also be perceived by you. Such things include light, sound, and bodies that we touch without damaging them.

E. I understand.

A. It is therefore evident that those things which we do not transform but nevertheless perceive through the bodily senses do not belong to the nature of our senses and are consequently more common to us, because they are not turned and transformed into something our own and, as it were, private.

E. I entirely agree.

A. What is proper and, as it were, private must therefore be understood as what belongs solely to each of us and what each alone perceives within himself, and which properly belongs to his own nature. What is common and, as it were, public is what is perceived by all perceivers without any corruption or transformation of itself.

E. That is so.

## CHAPTER VIII — The Rational Structure of Numbers Is Not Perceived by Any Bodily Sense; Once Perceived by Anyone Who Understands, It Is One and Unchangeable

20. A. Come now, pay attention and tell me whether there is something that all people who reason can see commonly, each through his own reason and mind, when the thing seen is present to everyone and is not altered for the use of those to whom it is present, as food or drink is, but remains uncorrupted and entire, whether they see it or do not see it—or do you perhaps think that nothing of this kind exists?

E. On the contrary, I see that many such things exist. It is enough to mention one: the rational structure and truth of number is present to everyone who reasons, so that every calculator attempts to grasp it through his own reason and understanding. One person may do so more easily, another with greater difficulty, and another may be entirely unable; nevertheless, it presents itself equally to all who are capable of grasping it. Nor, when each person perceives it, is it turned and changed into something like nourishment for the person perceiving it. Nor, when someone is mistaken about it, does it fail; rather, while it remains true and entire, the person is in error to the greater extent that he sees it less clearly.

21. A. Quite rightly. But I see that, as though you were not inexperienced in these matters, you quickly found something to say. Yet if someone were to tell you that these numbers were impressed upon our minds not from some nature of their own but from the things we touch through the bodily senses, like certain images of visible things, what would you answer? [Col. 1252] Do you perhaps think so yourself?

E. I would never think that. For even if I perceived numbers through the bodily sense, I could not for that reason have perceived through the bodily sense the rational structure of dividing or combining numbers. By this light of the mind I refute anyone who, while calculating either addition or subtraction, reports a false total.

Whatever I touch through the bodily sense—such as this sky, this earth, and all the other bodies I perceive in them—I do not know how long it will exist. But seven and three are ten, not only now but always. Nor was there ever a time when seven and three were not ten, nor will there ever be a time when seven and three are not ten. I therefore said that this incorruptible truth of number [Note: [Col. 1252] In the older editions and in nine manuscripts, “the nature of number”] is common to me and to anyone who reasons.

22. A. I do not resist you, since your answer is most true and certain. But you will easily see that the numbers themselves are not drawn in through the bodily senses if you consider that any number is called what it is as often as it contains one. For example, if it contains one twice, it is called two; if three times, three; and if it contains one ten times, it is called ten. Every number receives its name from how often it contains one and is called accordingly.

Anyone who thinks about one with complete truth finds that it cannot be perceived through the bodily senses. Whatever is grasped by such a sense is already proved to be not one but many. For it is a body, and therefore has innumerable parts. Without pursuing the smallest and least articulated parts, however small that little body may be, it certainly has one right part and another left; one upper part and another lower; one farther part and another nearer; or outermost parts and a middle part. We must admit that these features exist in any bodily dimension, however small. Therefore we concede that no body is truly and purely one, although such a multitude could not be numbered within it without knowledge of that one by which they are distinguished.

When I seek one in a body, and do not doubt that I fail to find it, I nevertheless know what I am seeking there, what I do not find there, and what cannot be found—or rather, what is wholly absent there. Since, then, I know that what is in the body is not one, I know what one is. For if I did not know one, I could not number the many things in a body.

Wherever, therefore, I know one, I do not know it through the bodily sense, since through the bodily sense I know only a body, which we have proved is not truly and purely one. Further, if we have not perceived one through the bodily sense, we have perceived no number through that sense—at least none of the numbers that the understanding perceives. For there is none of them that is not called what it is according to how often it contains one, and one is not perceived through the bodily sense.

Half of any little body, of which the whole consists as two parts, itself also has a half. Thus the two parts in a body are such that they themselves are not simply two. But the number called two, because it contains what is simply one twice, has as its half—that is, that very thing which is simply one—something that cannot again have a half, a third, or any fractional part, since it is simple and truly one. [Col. 1253]

23. Furthermore, as we follow the order of numbers, after one we see two, which, compared with one, is found to be its double. The double of two does not follow immediately, however; with three intervening, four follows, and four is the double of two. This reasoning continues through all the other numbers according to a most certain and unchangeable law.

After one—that is, after the first of all numbers—excluding one itself, the first number that has its double is two, for two follows. After the second, that is, after two, excluding two itself, the second number that has its double is four: after two, three is first and four second, and four is the double of the second. After the third, that is, three, excluding three itself, the third number that is its double is six: after three, four is first, five second, and six third, and six is the double of the third.

Likewise, after the fourth, excluding four itself, the fourth number has its double: after four, five is first, six second, seven third, and eight fourth, and eight is double the fourth. Thus, throughout all the remaining numbers, you will find what was discovered in the first pairing of numbers, one and two: whatever number each is from the beginning, the number occupying that same position after it is its double.

Where, then, do we see this fact—which we observe to be fixed, firm, and uncorrupted throughout all numbers? No one through any bodily sense apprehends all numbers, since they are innumerable. How, then, do we know that this holds throughout them all? By what image or phantasm could such a certain truth of number, extending through the innumerable, be so confidently perceived, unless it is seen in the inner light, which bodily sense does not know?

24. By these and many other such demonstrations, those to whom God has granted intelligence in debate, and whom obstinacy does not obscure with darkness, are compelled to acknowledge that the rational structure and truth of numbers do not belong to the bodily senses, that they stand unalterable and pure, and that they are common for all who reason to see.

Therefore, although many other things may present themselves which are present to those who reason commonly and, as it were, publicly, and which are seen by the mind and reason of each individual observer, while remaining inviolate and unchangeable, I nevertheless willingly accept that this rational structure and truth of number occurred to you above all when you wished to answer what I had asked. For it was not without reason that number was joined to wisdom in the sacred Books, where it is said: “I went about, and my heart” [Note: [Col. 1253] The printed editions have, “and I inclined my heart.” But “I inclined” is absent from the manuscripts and also from the Greek text of Scripture, according to which Augustine later customarily reads, “wisdom and number”; Ambrose likewise reads it in *On the Good of Death*, chapter 7], “that I might know, and consider, and seek wisdom and number” (*Ecclesiastes* 7:26).

## CHAPTER IX — What Wisdom Is, Without Which No One Is Blessed; Whether It Is One in All the Wise

25. Nevertheless, I ask you: what do you think should be understood about wisdom itself? Do you think that each individual has his own wisdom, or rather that one wisdom is commonly present to all, so that the more each person shares in it, the wiser he is?

E. I do not yet know what wisdom you mean. I see that people judge differently about what is wisely done or said. Those who serve in the military think they act wisely; those who reject military service and devote their care and effort to cultivating the land praise this course instead and attribute it to wisdom. Those who are clever at devising ways of acquiring money appear wise to themselves. Those who neglect or reject all these things and other temporal matters of this kind, and devote their entire effort to investigating truth so that they may know themselves and God, judge this to be the great work of wisdom. Those who do not wish to devote themselves to the leisure of seeking and contemplating truth, but instead act through the most burdensome cares and duties in order to serve human beings, and engage in the activity of justly ordering and governing human affairs, consider themselves wise. Those who do both—partly living in contemplation of truth and partly engaging in the dutiful labors which they think they owe to human society—seem to themselves to hold the palm of wisdom.

I omit the innumerable schools of thought, none of which does not prefer its own followers to the others and wish them alone to be wise. Since our present concern is not to answer what we believe but what we grasp through clear understanding, I will not be able to answer what you have asked unless I know, through believing, contemplating, and seeing by reason, what wisdom itself is.

26. A. Do you think wisdom is anything other than truth, in which the highest good is seen and grasped? All those whom you mentioned, although they pursue different ways, seek the good and flee evil. They pursue different ways because one thing appears good to one person and another thing to another. Whoever desires what ought not to be desired is therefore in error, although he desires it only because it appears good to him.

But neither the person who desires nothing nor the person who desires what he ought to desire can be in error. Insofar as all human beings desire the blessed life, they do not err. But insofar as someone does not follow the way of life that leads to blessedness, while admitting and professing that he wishes to reach blessedness and nothing else, he is in error to that extent. Error occurs when we follow something that does not lead to the destination we wish to reach. The more someone errs on the way of life, the less wise he is, for he is that much farther from the truth in which the highest good is seen and grasped.

Once the highest good has been attained and possessed, each person becomes blessed; and this is what we all want without dispute. Therefore, just as it is certain that we wish to be blessed, so it is certain that we wish to be wise, because no one is blessed without wisdom. No one is blessed except through the highest good, which is seen and grasped in that truth which we call wisdom.

Thus, before we are blessed, the notion of blessedness is nevertheless impressed upon our minds. Through it we know, and confidently and without any doubt say, that we wish to be blessed. Likewise, before we are wise, we have the notion of wisdom impressed upon our minds, through which each of us, if asked whether he wishes to be wise, answers without any obscurity of doubt that he does.

27. Therefore, if it is now established between us what wisdom is—something you perhaps could not explain in words—for if you did not in any way perceive it in your mind, you could in no way know that you wish to be wise and ought to wish to be wise, which I do not think you would deny—I now want you to tell me whether you also think that wisdom presents itself as common to all who reason, just as the rational structure and truth of number does; or, since there are as many human minds as there are human beings, and since neither I perceive anything of your mind nor you anything of mine, do you think there are as many wisdoms as there can be wise people?

E. If the highest good is one for all, then the truth in which it is seen and grasped—that is, wisdom—must also be one and common to all.

A. Do you doubt that the highest good, whatever it is, is one for all human beings?

E. I certainly do, because I see different people taking delight in different things as though these were their highest goods.

A. I should certainly wish no one to doubt about the highest good in the way no one doubts that, whatever it is, a person can become blessed only by attaining it. But since this is a major question and may require a long discussion, let us suppose that there are as many highest goods as there are different things that different people pursue as their highest goods. Does it therefore follow that wisdom itself is not one and common to all, because the goods which people see and choose within it are many and different?

If you think so, you might also doubt that sunlight is one because the things we see in it are many and different. From among these many things, each person chooses, according to his will, what he may enjoy through the sense of sight. One person gladly gazes at the height of a mountain and rejoices in the sight; another at the level expanse of a plain; another at the vaulted valleys; another at the greenness of groves; another at the shifting evenness of the sea; another at all these things, or at some of them, combining them together for the joy of seeing.

Therefore, just as the things that people see in sunlight and choose for enjoyment are many and different, the light itself is nevertheless one, and in it the sight of each observer sees and holds what he enjoys. So, even if goods are many and different, and each person chooses what he wishes and rightly and truly establishes it for himself as his highest good by seeing and grasping it for enjoyment, it can nevertheless be the case that the light of wisdom itself, in which these things can be seen and grasped, is one and common to all the wise.

E. I admit that this is possible, and that nothing prevents there being one wisdom common to all, even if the highest goods are many and different. But I should like to know whether this is actually so. To concede that it is possible does not immediately amount to conceding that it is so.

A. For the moment, we hold that wisdom exists. But whether it is one and common to all, or whether individual wise people have their own wisdom, just as they have their own souls or minds, we do not yet hold.

E. That is so.

## CHAPTER X — The Light of Wisdom Is One and Common to All the Wise

[Col. 1256]

28. A. What of this: where do we see what we hold, namely, that wisdom exists, that there are wise people, and that all human beings wish to be blessed? I would certainly have no doubt that you see this and that it is true. Do you see this truth in the same way as you see your own thought—which I entirely fail to know if you do not tell it to me—or in such a way that you understand that I too can see this truth, even though you do not tell it to me?

E. Rather, I see it in such a way that I have no doubt that you too can see it, even against my will.

A. Therefore, since we both see one and the same truth through our individual minds, is it not common to both of us?

E. Most certainly.

A. Likewise, I believe you do not deny that we ought to strive for wisdom, and you grant that this is true.

E. I have no doubt of it.

A. Can we deny that this truth is also one and common for all who know it to see, although each person perceives it not through my mind, nor yours, nor anyone else’s, but through his own, while what is perceived is commonly present to all who perceive it?

E. We cannot deny it at all.

A. Likewise, will you not admit that it is most true that inferior things ought to be subjected to superior things, equals compared with equals, and each person’s own things assigned to their proper owners, and that this is commonly present to me, to you, and to all who see it?

E. I agree.

A. Can you deny that the incorruptible is better than the corruptible, the eternal than the temporal, and the inviolable than the violable?

E. Who could?

A. Can anyone therefore call this truth his own and private, when it is present for all who are capable of contemplating it to contemplate unchangeably?

E. No one could truly call it his own and private, since it is as one and common to all as it is true.

A. Likewise, who denies that the mind ought to be turned away from corruption and turned toward incorruption—that is, that incorruption, not corruption, ought to be loved? Or who, while acknowledging this to be true, does not also understand it to be unchangeable and see that it is commonly present to all minds capable of contemplating it?

E. It is most true.

A. What of the life that is not moved from a certain and honorable judgment by any adversity? Will anyone doubt that it is better than a life that is easily broken and overthrown by temporal misfortunes?

E. Who would doubt it?

29. A. I shall not ask for more examples of this kind. It is enough that you see with me, and grant as most certain, that these things—like rules and certain lights of the virtues—are true and unchangeable, and that, whether taken individually or all together, they are commonly present for contemplation to those who are capable of seeing them, each through his own reason and mind.

But I do ask whether you think these things belong to wisdom. For I suppose you think that someone who has attained wisdom is wise.

E. Certainly.

A. Could someone live justly without seeing which inferior things he ought to subject to superior things, which equals he ought to join with their equals, and which things he ought to distribute to their proper owners?

E. He could not.

A. Then will you deny that someone who sees these things sees wisely?

E. I do not deny it.

A. What of someone who lives prudently? Does he not choose incorruption and decide that it ought to be preferred to corruption? [Col. 1257]

E. Most certainly.

A. When, therefore, he chooses that toward which to turn his mind—something no one doubts ought to be chosen—can it be denied that he chooses wisely?

E. I would deny it in no way.

A. When, therefore, he turns his mind toward what he wisely chooses, he certainly turns it wisely.

E. That is most certain.

A. And someone who is not driven away by any terrors or punishments from what he wisely chooses and toward which he wisely turns himself is without doubt acting wisely.

E. Without any doubt.

A. It is therefore perfectly evident that all these things which we have called rules and lights belong to wisdom. For the more each person uses them in conducting his life and lives according to them, the more wisely he lives and acts; and whatever is done wisely cannot rightly be said to be separate from wisdom.

E. That is entirely so.

A. Therefore, the rules of wisdom are as true and unchangeable as the rules of numbers, whose rational structure and truth you said are unchangeably and commonly present to all who see them. You have just now, when questioned individually about a few of these rules, answered that they are true and evident, and you grant that they are present for contemplation as common to all who are capable of observing them.

## CHAPTER XI — Whether Wisdom and Number Are the Same, or Whether One Exists from the Other or in the Other

30. E. I cannot doubt it. But I should very much like to know whether these two things—wisdom and number—are contained under some single genus, since you mentioned that they are also joined together in the sacred Scriptures; or whether one exists from the other, or one subsists in the other, as number exists from wisdom or in wisdom.

I would not dare to say that wisdom exists from number or subsists in number. For I do not know how this could be so. I know many people who are skilled at numbers or calculators—or whatever they should be called—who calculate supremely and wonderfully, but very few wise people, or perhaps none at all. Wisdom therefore presents itself to me as far more venerable than number.

A. You speak of something that I too am accustomed to marvel at. When I consider within myself the unchangeable truth of numbers, and its, as it were, dwelling, inner chamber, or some region—or whatever other suitable name can be found by which we might name a kind of habitation and seat of numbers—I am carried far away from the body. Perhaps I find something that I can think, but I do not find something that I am capable of expressing in words. I return, as though exhausted, to these things of ours, so that I can speak, and I describe what lies before my eyes in the way such things are usually described.

The same thing happens to me when I think as vigilantly and intently as I can about wisdom. And therefore I am greatly astonished: these two things exist in the most secret and certain truth, and Scripture also bears witness to their having been placed together, as I mentioned. Yet, as I said, I am greatly astonished that number is despised by the multitude of human beings while wisdom is dear to them.

But surely the reason is that there is one and the same thing. Nevertheless, since the divine Books also say of wisdom that it “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (*Wisdom* 8:1), perhaps it is called number in respect of the power by which it reaches mightily from end to end; while in respect of the power by which it orders all things sweetly, it is properly called wisdom, although both are of one and the same wisdom.

31. Yet wisdom gave numbers to all things, even the lowest and those placed at the end of the order of things. For all bodies, although they are at the lowest level among things, have their own numbers. But it did not give the capacity for wisdom to bodies, nor to all souls, but only to rational ones, as though it had established its seat in them, from which it might order even all those lowest things to which it gave numbers.

Since we judge bodies easily, as things ordered below us, and see that the numbers impressed upon them are below us, we consequently value them less. But when we begin, as it were, to retrace our way upward, we find that numbers also transcend our minds and remain unchangeable in truth itself.

And because few can be wise, while even fools are permitted to count, people marvel at wisdom and despise numbers. But educated and diligent people, the farther they are removed from earthly defilement, the more they contemplate both number and wisdom in truth itself, and hold both dear. In comparison with that truth, not only gold and silver and the other things over which people struggle, but even those people themselves, become cheap in their own eyes.

32. Do not be surprised that numbers are for this reason cheap to people while wisdom is dear, because they can count more easily than they can be wise. You see that they value gold more highly than the light of a lamp, although gold appears ridiculous when compared with the lamp. Yet a thing far inferior is honored more highly because even a beggar lights a lamp, whereas few possess gold.

It would be wrong, however, to suppose that wisdom is inferior to number, since they are the same. Rather, wisdom seeks the eye by which it may be seen [Note: [Col. 1258] The printed editions have: “If the eye by which it may be seen should seek it.” But the manuscripts read: “Yet it seeks the eye ...”].

Just as, in one fire, radiance and heat are perceived as, so to speak, consubstantial, and cannot be separated from one another, yet heat reaches those things brought near, while radiance is diffused farther and more widely, so the power of understanding which is present in wisdom warms what is nearer [Note: [Col. 1258] Four manuscripts read: “which are nearer to wisdom are warmed”], such as rational souls. But what is farther away, such as bodies, it does not reach with the heat of wisdom; rather, it drenches them with the light of numbers.

Perhaps this is obscure to you. No visible likeness can be adapted to an invisible reality in every respect. Attend only to what is sufficient for the question we have undertaken and is made clear even to minds as humble as ours: although it cannot be clear to us whether number is in wisdom or from wisdom, or wisdom itself is from number or in number, or whether the two names can be shown to belong to one thing, this much is certainly evident: both are true, and unchangeably true.

## CHAPTER XII — The Truth That Is One and Unchangeable in All Who Understand, and That Is Superior to Our Mind

[Col. 1259]

33. Therefore, you must in no way deny that there exists an immutable truth containing all these things that are immutably true. You cannot call it yours, or mine, or anyone’s; rather, it is present and offers itself in common to all who perceive immutable truths, like a light hidden and public in wondrous ways. But who would say that whatever is present in common to all who reason and understand belongs properly to the nature of any one of them? You remember, I think, what was discussed shortly before concerning the bodily senses: those things that we apprehend in common through the sense of sight or hearing—such as colors and sounds, which you and I see or hear together—do not belong to the nature of our eyes or ears, but are common to us for the purpose of sensation. In the same way, then, you must not say that those things which you and I each perceive together in our own minds belong to the nature of anyone’s mind. What the eyes of two people see together cannot be said to belong either to this person’s eyes or to that person’s, but to something third toward which the sight of both is directed.

E. It is utterly clear and entirely true.

34. A. Do you therefore think that this truth, about which we have been speaking for so long, and in which we perceive so many things as one, is superior to our mind, equal to our minds, or even inferior? But if it were inferior, we would judge according to it, not about it, just as we judge about bodies because they are beneath us. We commonly say of bodies not merely that they are or are not this way, but that they ought to be this way or that. Likewise, concerning our minds, we know not only that a mind is this way, but often also that it ought to be this way.

We judge in this manner about bodies when we say, “It is less white than it ought to be,” or “less square,” and so forth. Concerning minds, we say, “He is less capable than he ought to be,” or “less gentle,” or “less forceful,” as the standard of our conduct requires. We judge these things according to those inner rules of truth that we perceive in common; but no one judges those rules themselves in any way. When someone says that eternal things are better than temporal things, or that seven and three make ten, no one says that they ought to be so. Rather, recognizing simply that they are so, the examiner does not correct them but merely rejoices in having discovered them.

If this truth were equal to our minds, it too would be mutable. For our minds sometimes see it more clearly and sometimes less clearly, and by this they acknowledge themselves to be mutable. But truth, remaining in itself, neither increases when we see more of it nor diminishes when we see less. It remains whole and incorrupt, rejoicing those who turn toward it with its light and punishing those who turn away with blindness.

Moreover, we judge even our minds according to it, although we cannot in any way judge it. We say, “He understands less than he ought,” or “He understands as much as he ought.” But the mind ought to understand as much as it is able to approach and adhere more closely to immutable truth. Therefore, if truth is neither inferior nor equal, it remains [Col. 1260] that it is superior and more excellent.

## CHAPTER XIII — Exhortation to Embrace the Truth, Which Alone Makes Blessed

35. I had promised, if you remember, to show you something that is higher than our mind and reason. Behold, here it is: truth itself. Embrace it if you can, and enjoy it, and delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart (Psalm 36:4). For what more do you ask than to be blessed? And who is more blessed than one who enjoys truth that is steadfast, immutable, and supremely excellent?

Do people not loudly proclaim themselves blessed when they embrace beautiful bodies, desired with great longing, whether those of spouses or even of prostitutes? And shall we doubt that we are blessed in the embrace of truth? People proclaim themselves blessed when, with throats parched by heat, they reach a plentiful and wholesome spring, or when, hungry, they find an abundant and well-prepared lunch or dinner. Shall we deny that we are blessed when we are watered and nourished by truth?

We often hear people proclaiming themselves blessed when they lie among roses and other flowers [Note: [Col. 1260] In B., “when they lie among a rose and other flowers.” Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., “roses.” M.]. or enjoy the most fragrant perfumes. What is more fragrant, what more delightful, than the inspiration of truth? And shall we hesitate to call ourselves blessed when we are inspired by it?

Many establish their happy life in the singing of voices, strings, and flutes. When these are absent, they judge themselves wretched; when they are present, they are transported with joy. And when a kind of melodious and eloquent silence of truth, so to speak, flows into our minds without any noise, shall we seek another happy life and fail to enjoy one so certain and present?

People delighted by the radiance and beauty of gold and silver, gems and other colors—whether the light that reaches these eyes, or the light of earthly fires, stars, moon, and sun—consider themselves blessed when no annoyance or deprivation recalls them from that pleasure, and for its sake they always wish to live. Shall we be afraid to place the happy life in the light of truth?

36. Rather, since the highest good is known and held in truth, and since that truth is wisdom, let us perceive and hold the highest good in it, and enjoy it. For blessed is the one who enjoys the highest good. This truth displays all true goods, which understanding people choose, singly or in combination, according to their capacity, in order to enjoy them.

But just as those who are in sunlight choose what they are pleased to look at and rejoice in the sight, while those among them who happen to possess keener, healthier, and stronger eyes look at nothing more willingly than the sun itself—which also illuminates the other things in which weaker eyes take delight—so a strong and vigorous mind, when it has perceived many true and immutable things with sound reasoning, directs itself toward truth itself, through which all things are displayed. Adhering to it, it somehow forgets the rest and enjoys all things in it at once. [Col. 1261] For whatever is delightful in the other true things is delightful through truth itself.

37. This is our freedom when we submit to this truth; and it is our God who frees us from death, that is, from the condition of sin. Truth itself, speaking as a human being among human beings, said to those who believed in it: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32). For the soul enjoys nothing in freedom unless it enjoys it in security.

## CHAPTER XIV — Truth Is Possessed with Security

No one is secure in those goods that he can lose against his will. But no one loses truth and wisdom against his will. No one can be separated from them by a change of place; rather, what is called separation from truth and wisdom is a perverse will by which inferior things are loved. No one wants something unwillingly.

We therefore have something that all may enjoy equally and in common: there is no narrowness or deficiency in it. It receives all its lovers without any jealousy; it is common to all and chaste for each. No one says to another, “Step aside so that I too may approach; remove your hands so that I too may embrace.” All adhere to it; all touch the same thing [Note: [Col. 1261] The printed editions read, “they all touch it itself.” But the manuscripts read, “they all touch the same thing.”]. Its food is not torn apart in any part; you drink nothing from it that I cannot also drink. You do not make something from it your private possession by taking it for yourself; rather, what you take from it remains whole for me as well. I do not wait for what inspires you to be returned by you so that I may be inspired by it. Nothing belonging to it ever becomes the property of one person or of a few; it is wholly common to all at once.

38. The things we touch, taste, or smell are therefore less like this truth; things we hear and see are more like it. Every word that is heard is heard wholly by all who hear it, and wholly by each at the same time. Every visible appearance that lies before the eyes is seen by one in its entirety and simultaneously by another.

Yet these things are very imperfect likenesses. For no voice sounds wholly at once: it extends and unfolds through time, with one part sounding earlier and another later. Every visible appearance, as if swelling through space, is not wholly present everywhere. Moreover, all these things are taken away from us against our will, and various limitations prevent us from enjoying them as we might.

Suppose, for example, that someone’s beautiful song could be everlasting, and that its devoted admirers came eagerly to hear it. They would crowd together and struggle over places, the more numerous they were, so that each might be closer to the singer. Yet while hearing it they would possess nothing that could remain with them; they would merely be touched by all the sounds as they fled.

As for this sun, if I wished to look at it and could persist in doing so, it would abandon me at its setting, be hidden by clouds, and be withdrawn from me against my will by many other obstacles that would deprive me of the pleasure of seeing it. Finally, even if the pleasure of light for the one who sees and of sound for the one who hears were always present, what great thing would reach me, since I would share it with animals?

But the [Col. 1262] beauty of truth and wisdom is different. Provided that the will to enjoy it perseveres, it neither excludes those who come because of a crowd of hearers pressing in upon it, nor passes away in time, nor changes its place, nor is interrupted by night, nor blocked by shadow, nor subject to the bodily senses.

It is close to all who love it, wherever they may be in the whole world and turn toward it; it is eternal for all. It is in no place, yet it is absent nowhere. Outside, it admonishes; within, it teaches. It changes all who perceive it for the better, but it is changed for the worse by no one. No one judges it, and no one judges well without it. It is therefore clear that it is superior to our minds, which are made individually wise by that one truth and which judge about other things not from it but through it.

## CHAPTER XV — From the Reasoning Fully Expounded, It Is Now Certain That God Exists

39. You had granted that, if I showed you something above our minds, you would confess it to be God, provided that nothing higher still existed. Accepting your concession, I had said that it was enough for me to demonstrate this. If something more excellent exists, that is rather God; if nothing does, then truth itself is God. Therefore, whether that higher reality exists or not, you cannot deny that God exists. This was the question we had undertaken to discuss and examine.

If what troubles you is that, within the most sacred teaching of Christ, we have accepted on faith that the Father of Wisdom exists, remember that we have also accepted on faith that the Wisdom begotten by the eternal Father is equal to him. Nothing need be sought concerning this now; it must be held by steadfast faith.

God exists, and truly and supremely exists. We now hold this not only by faith, as I think, without doubt, but also attain it through a certain, though still very slight, form of knowledge. That is sufficient for the question we undertook, so that we may explain the other matters relevant to it—unless you have something to bring against these conclusions.

E. I receive these conclusions with an utterly incredible joy, which I cannot explain to you in words, and I proclaim them to be most certain. I proclaim this with an inner voice by which I desire to be heard by truth itself and to adhere to it. I acknowledge that this is not merely good but the highest good and that which makes one blessed.

40. A. Quite rightly; I too rejoice greatly. But tell me, please: are we already wise and blessed, or are we still striving toward becoming so?

E. I think that we are still striving toward it.

A. How then do you grasp these things, which you proclaim yourself to rejoice in as true and certain, and which you acknowledge to belong to wisdom? Can anyone foolish know wisdom?

E. As long as he is foolish, he cannot.

A. Then you are already wise, or you do not yet know wisdom.

E. I am not yet wise, certainly; but, insofar as I know wisdom, I would not call myself foolish either. For the things I know are certain, and I cannot deny that they belong to wisdom.

A. Tell me, please: will you not admit that one who is not just is unjust, one who is not prudent is imprudent, and one who is not temperate is intemperate? Can there be any doubt about these matters?

E. I admit that when a person [Col. 1263] is not just, he is unjust. I would answer the same concerning prudence and temperance.

A. Why then, when someone is not wise, should he not be foolish?

E. I admit this as well: whenever someone is not wise, he is foolish.

A. What, then, are you now?

E. Whatever of these names you may apply to me, I still do not dare to call myself wise. From what I have admitted, however, I see that I must not hesitate to call myself foolish.

A. Then a foolish person knows wisdom. For, as has already been said, he would not be certain that he wished to be wise, and that he ought to be wise, unless the knowledge of wisdom adhered to his mind—just as, concerning the matters you answered about individually when questioned, which belong to wisdom itself, you rejoiced in possessing knowledge.

E. It is as you say.

## CHAPTER XVI — Wisdom Shows Itself on the Way to Those Who Diligently Seek It, Namely through the Numbers Impressed upon Each Thing

41. A. What else are we doing, then, when we strive to be wise, except gathering our whole soul, with as much eagerness as we can, around that which we touch with the mind, placing it there and fixing it firmly, so that it may no longer rejoice in something private of its own, entangled in passing things, but, stripped of every attachment to times and places, may grasp that which is always one and the same?

For just as the soul is the whole life of the body, so God is the blessed life of the soul. While we are doing this, until we complete it, we are on the way.

Now consider whether the joy we are permitted to take in these true and certain goods, although they still flash before us in this dark journey, is what has been written about wisdom—what it does for those who love and seek it when they come to it. For it is said: “She will show herself to them cheerfully on the ways, and will meet them with every providence” (Wisdom 6:17).

Wherever you turn, wisdom speaks to you through certain traces that it has impressed upon its works. When you slip back into external things, it calls you inward again through the very forms of those external things, so that whatever delights you in the body and attracts you through bodily senses, you may see to be ordered by number. You then seek its source, return into yourself, and understand that you cannot approve or disapprove what you apprehend through the bodily senses unless you possess within yourself certain laws of beauty to which you refer whatever beautiful things you perceive externally.

42. Look upon heaven and earth and the sea, and all that in them either shines above, creeps below, flies, or swims. They have forms because they have numbers. Take these away from them, and they will be nothing. From whom, then, do they derive their being, if not from the one from whom number comes, since they exist precisely insofar as they are ordered by number?

Human craftsmen possess numbers in their art for all bodily forms, and according to them they fit their works together. They move their hands and tools in making something until the external object being formed, referred back to the inner light of numbers, obtains as much completion as it can and pleases, through the interpreting senses, the inner judge who contemplates the higher numbers.

Then ask what moves the craftsman’s own limbs. It will be number, for they too move according to number. If you remove from his hands the work and from his mind [Col. 1264] the intention of making, and refer that movement of the limbs to pleasure, it will be called dancing.

Ask, then, what delights us in dancing. Number will answer you: “Here I am.”

Now examine the beauty of a formed body: numbers are held in place. Examine the beauty of movement in a body: numbers operate in time. Enter into the art from which these things proceed, and seek time and place in it. They will never be there, nowhere will they be there; yet number lives in the art. Its region is not one of spaces, nor its age one of days.

Nevertheless, those who wish to become craftsmen accommodate themselves to the art by moving their bodies through places and times and their minds through times. Through the passage of time they become more skilled.

Go beyond the craftsman’s mind, then, so that you may see eternal number. Wisdom will already shine for you from its own inner seat and from the sanctuary of truth itself. If it still dazzles your weakened sight, direct the eye of your mind back toward that way where wisdom showed itself cheerfully. Remember that you have deferred the vision, so that you may return to it stronger and healthier.

43. Woe to those who abandon you as their guide and wander among your traces; who love your signs instead of you and forget what you signify, O wisdom, most sweet light of the purified mind! For you never cease signifying to us what and how great you are, and your signs are the whole beauty of creatures.

The craftsman too, in a certain way, signifies to the spectator of his work what he himself is through the beauty of the work, lest the spectator cling wholly to it, but pass with his eyes over the appearance of the crafted body in such a way that his affection returns to the one who made it.

Those who love the things you make instead of loving you are like people who hear an eloquent and wise speaker and, while greedily listening too closely to the sweetness of his voice and the structures of his well-ordered syllables, lose sight of the supremacy of the meanings, whose signs those words sounded forth.

Woe to those who turn away from your light and cling sweetly to their own darkness! Turning their backs upon you, as it were, they become fixed in carnal activity as in their own shadow. Yet even there, what delights them still comes from the radiance of your light [Note: [Col. 1264] Several manuscripts read, “it still has from the radiance of your light.”].

But when the shadow is loved, it makes the eye of the mind weaker and less able to endure your sight. Thus a person becomes more and more darkened while pursuing more eagerly whatever a weakened sight can tolerate more easily. From this he begins to be unable to see what is supreme, and to regard as evil whatever deceives the unwary, seduces the needy [Note: [Col. 1264] Quite a few manuscripts, together with the older editions, read, “or seduces one who is unworthy.”], or tortures the captive, although he suffers these things deservedly because of his turning away, and whatever is just cannot be evil.

44. If, then, you cannot apprehend anything mutable, whether through bodily sensation or through the mind’s reflection, unless it is held by some form of number, and, once that form is removed, falls into nothing, do not doubt that, so that mutable things may not be destroyed but may proceed through measured movements and a differentiated variety of forms, completing something like verses of time, there exists an eternal and immutable form. It is neither contained in and spread out [Col. 1265] through places, nor extended and varied through times. Through it all these things are able to be formed and, according to their kind, to fulfill and enact the numbers of places and times.

## CHAPTER XVII — Every Good and Every Perfection Is from God

45. Every mutable thing must also be formable. Just as we call mutable that which can be changed, so I would call formable that which can be formed. But no thing can form itself, because no thing can give itself what it does not have; and in order for it to have form, something must be formed.

Therefore, if a thing has any form, it does not need to receive what it already has. If it has no form, it cannot receive from itself what it does not have. No thing, then, can form itself, as we have said. What more need we say about the mutability of body and soul? Enough has already been said above.

It follows, therefore, that both body and soul are formed by some immutable and ever-abiding form. Concerning this form it is said: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years will not fail” (Psalm 102:27–28). Prophetic speech has put “years without failure” in place of eternity.

Concerning this form it is likewise said that, remaining in itself, it renews all things (Wisdom 7:27). From this it is also understood that all things are governed by providence. For if all existing things, once form had been entirely removed, would be nothing, then the immutable form through which all mutable things subsist, so that they may be filled out and enacted according to the numbers of their forms, is itself their providence. They would not exist if it did not exist.

Therefore, whoever looks upon and considers the whole of creation while journeying toward wisdom senses that wisdom shows itself cheerfully on the way and meets him with every providence. He burns with all the greater eagerness to complete this journey because the way itself is beautiful through wisdom, toward which he burns to arrive.

46. But if you discover any other kind of creature besides that which exists but does not live; that which exists and lives but does not understand; and that which exists, lives, and understands, then dare to say that there is some good that is not from God.

These three can also be expressed under two names, if they are called body and life. For that which merely lives and does not understand, such as animals, and that which understands, such as human beings, is rightly called life.

These two things—body and life—are indeed counted as creatures (for the life of the Creator himself is also spoken of, and it is the supreme life). Since these two creatures, body and life, are formable, as the foregoing arguments have shown, and since, when they entirely lose their form, they fall into nothing, they clearly show that they subsist from that form which is always of this kind.

Therefore, however great or small any goods may be, they cannot be except from God. For what can be greater among creatures than an understanding life, or what can be less than a body? However much these things may decline and tend toward nonexistence, some form still remains in them, so that they exist in some fashion. Whatever form remains in a declining thing comes from that form which does not know decline [Col. 1266] and does not permit even the movements of declining or advancing things to exceed the laws of their numbers.

Whatever, therefore, is perceived to be praiseworthy in the nature of things—whether it is judged worthy of slight or great praise—must be referred to the excellent and ineffable praise of the Creator, unless you have something to say against this.

## CHAPTER XVIII — Free Will, Although It Can Be Turned to Evil Use, Must Be Counted among Goods

47. E. I admit that I am sufficiently convinced, insofar as it can become clear in this life and among people such as we are, both that God exists and that all good things are from God. Everything that exists—whether things that understand, live, and exist; things that merely live and exist; or things that merely exist—is from God.

Let us now consider the third question: whether it can be established that free will is to be counted among goods. Once this has been demonstrated, I will without hesitation concede that God gave it to us and that it ought to have been given.

A. You remember our starting points well, and you have attentively observed that the second question has already been explained. But you should also have seen that this third question has already been resolved. You had said that it seemed to you that free choice of the will ought not to have been given, because through it people sin.

When I had responded to this opinion of yours by asserting that no one can act rightly except through that same free choice of the will [Note: [Col. 1266] See *Retractions* 1.9.3.] and that God gave it to us precisely for this purpose, you replied that free will ought to have been given to us in the way justice was given, so that no one could use it except rightly.

That response of yours compelled us to enter into such lengthy circuits of argument that we might prove to you that both greater and lesser goods are from God. This could not have been shown so clearly unless, against the opinions of impious folly—which says in its heart, “There is no God” (Psalm 14:1)—some form of reasoning about so great a matter, according to our limited ability and with God himself assisting us on so dangerous a journey, had been directed toward something manifest.

These two conclusions, nevertheless—that God exists and that all good things are from him—were already held beforehand by steadfast faith. Yet they have been treated in such a way that this third point too may become entirely clear: free will is to be counted among goods.

48. For the preceding discussion has already made it clear, and we agreed among ourselves, that the nature of body is on a lower level than the nature of soul and that, consequently, the soul is a greater good than the body.

If, then, among bodily goods we find some things that a person can use wrongly, yet we do not therefore say that they ought not to have been given, since we confess them to be good, why should it be surprising if there are also certain goods in the soul that we can use wrongly? Since they are good, they could have been given only by the one from whom all good things come.

You see how much good is lacking in a body without hands, and yet one who uses his hands to perform savage or shameful deeds uses them badly. If you saw someone without feet, you would admit that a great deal of good was lacking from the integrity of his body. Yet you would not deny that someone who used his feet to harm another or dishonor himself [Col. 1267] was using his feet badly.

With our eyes we see this light and distinguish the forms of bodies. This is also the most beautiful feature of our body, which is why these members have been placed at a kind of summit of dignity. The use of the eyes contributes to preserving health and to many other conveniences of life. Yet many people do many shameful things with their eyes and force them to serve lust.

You see how much good is lacking from a face if the eyes are absent. But when they are present, who gave them except God, the giver of all good things?

Therefore, just as you approve these things in the body and, without considering those who use them badly, praise the one who gave these good things, so you must acknowledge that free will, without which no one can live rightly, is both a good and divinely given. You must condemn those who use this good badly rather than admit that the one who gave it ought not to have given it.

49. E. I would first like you to prove to me that free will is some good, and then I would concede that God gave it to us, since I acknowledge that all good things are from God.

A. Have I not proved this to you, then, through the great labor of our preceding discussion, when you admitted that every form and shape of body subsists from the supreme form of all things, that is, from truth, and conceded that it is good? For Truth herself says in the Gospel that even the hairs of our head are numbered (Matthew 10:30).

Have you forgotten what we said about the supremacy of number and the power that extends from beginning to end? What sort of perversity is this, then: to count our hairs, although they belong among the smallest and most insignificant things, among goods, and to find no author to whom they can be attributed except God, the creator of all good things—for both the greatest and the smallest goods come from the one from whom every good comes—yet to doubt free will, without which even those who live most wickedly admit that one cannot live rightly?

Now answer me, please: what seems better to you in us—that without which one can live rightly, or that without which one cannot live rightly?

E. Spare me now, please; I am ashamed of my blindness. For who could doubt that the thing without which a right life is impossible is far more excellent?

A. Then will you deny that a one-eyed person can live rightly?

E. May such monstrous madness be far from me.

A. Since, then, you admit that in the body the eye is a good, even though losing it does not prevent someone from living rightly, will free will seem to you no good, when no one can live rightly without it?

50. Consider justice, which no one uses badly. It is counted among the highest goods that exist in a human being, along with all the virtues of the soul, through which the right and honorable life is constituted. No one uses prudence, courage, or temperance badly. In all these, as in justice itself, which you mentioned, right reason is active, and without it virtues cannot exist. But no one can use right reason badly.

## CHAPTER XIX — Great, Lesser, and Intermediate Goods. Freedom Is Counted among the Intermediate Goods

These, then, are great goods. But you must remember that not only great goods, but also lesser goods, can exist only from the one from whom all good things come—that is, from God [Col. 1268]. The preceding discussion persuaded you of this, and you assented to it so often and so gladly.

The virtues by which one lives rightly are therefore great goods. The forms of bodies, without which one can live rightly, are lesser goods. The powers of the soul, without which one cannot live rightly, are intermediate goods.

No one uses the virtues badly. But the other goods—that is, the intermediate and lesser goods—can be used not only well but also badly. The reason no one uses virtue badly is that the work of virtue consists in the good use of those things that we can also use wrongly. No one uses something badly by using it well.

Therefore, the abundance and greatness of God’s goodness has provided not only great goods but also intermediate and lesser goods. His goodness is more deserving of praise in great goods than in intermediate goods, and more in intermediate than in lesser goods; but it is more deserving of praise in all of them together than it would be if he had not bestowed them all.

51. E. I agree. But this troubles me: since the question concerns free will, and we see that free will itself uses the other things either well or badly, how can it itself be counted among the things we use?

A. In the same way that we know everything belonging to knowledge through reason, yet reason itself is also counted among the things that we know through reason. Have you forgotten that, when we were asking what things are known through reason, you admitted that reason too is known through reason?

Do not be surprised, then, if we use the other things through free will and can also use free will itself through free will. In this way, the will that uses other things somehow uses itself, just as reason, which knows other things, also knows itself.

Memory too not only contains all the other things that we remember; since we do not forget that we possess memory, memory itself somehow holds itself within us. It remembers not only other things but also itself—or rather, through memory we remember both other things and memory itself.

52. The will, then, which is an intermediate good, adheres to the immutable good, which is common rather than private—namely, that truth about which we have spoken so much and said nothing worthy of it—and thus a person possesses the blessed life.

This blessed life itself, that is, the soul’s disposition of adhering to the immutable good, is the proper and primary good of the human being. All the virtues, which no one can use badly, are also contained in it. Although these virtues are great and primary in a human being, it is sufficiently clear that they are proper to each individual, not common to all.

Through truth and wisdom, which are common to everyone, all become wise and blessed by adhering to them. But one person does not become blessed through another person’s blessedness. Even when someone imitates another person in order to become blessed, he seeks to become blessed from the source in which he sees that person made blessed—namely, from immutable and common truth.

Nor does anyone become prudent through another person’s prudence, courageous through another’s courage, temperate through another’s temperance, or just through another’s justice. Rather, one becomes so by fitting the soul to those immutable rules and lights of the virtues that live incorruptibly in truth and wisdom themselves, which are common to all. The person whom he set before himself for imitation as endowed with these virtues also fitted and fixed his soul to those rules and lights.

[Col. 1269] 53. The will, therefore, adhering to the common and immutable good, obtains the first and great goods of the human being, although it itself is a certain intermediate good.

But the will, turned away from the immutable and common good and turned toward a private, external, or inferior good, sins. It turns toward a private good when it wishes to belong to itself and be its own master; toward an external good when it strives to know what belongs to others or whatever does not pertain to it; toward an inferior good when it loves bodily pleasure.

Thus a person becomes proud, curious, and lustful, and is received into another life which, in comparison with the higher life, is death. Yet this life is governed by the administration of divine providence, which assigns everything to fitting places and distributes to each person according to his merits.

It follows that neither the goods desired by sinners are in any way evil, nor is free will itself evil, since we have discovered that it must be counted among certain intermediate goods. Rather, the evil is the will’s turning away from the immutable good and turning toward mutable goods. Since this turning away and turning toward are not compelled but voluntary, the just penalty of misery rightly follows them.
