## CHAPTER XX — That Movement by Which the Will Turns Away from the Immutable Good Is Not from God
54. But perhaps you will ask, since the will is moved when it turns away from the unchangeable good toward a changeable good, where this movement originates—for it is surely evil, even though the free will, since without it one cannot live rightly, must be counted among goods. For if this movement, that is, the turning of the will away from the Lord God, is undoubtedly sin, can we call God the author of sin? This movement, then, will not be from God. From where, then, will it be? If, when you ask this, I answer that I do not know, perhaps you will be more troubled; but I will nevertheless have given the true answer. For what is nothing cannot be known. Hold firmly to this unwavering piety: let no good present itself to you—whether perceived, understood, or in any way considered—that is not from God. For thus no nature presents itself that is not from God. Whenever you see measure, number, and order in anything, do not hesitate to attribute it to God the craftsman. But if you wholly remove these from anything, absolutely nothing will remain. For even if some beginning of a form should remain, where you find neither measure, nor number, nor order—since wherever these are present, the form is perfected—you must also remove that very beginning of form which seems to lie beneath the craftsman like material awaiting completion. For if the perfection of form is a good, then the beginning of form is already some good. Thus, when every good has been completely removed, not merely something insignificant but absolutely nothing will remain.

[Note: [Col. 1270] Most manuscripts and the older editions lack the words “not merely something but”; here we retain them from Lovaniensis.]

Every good, however, is from God; therefore no nature exists that is not from God. Consider, then, where that movement of turning away belongs—the movement which we acknowledge to be sin—for it is a deficient movement, and every deficiency is from nothing; and do not doubt that it does not belong to God.

[Note: [Col. 1270] Bad. and Er. omit the negation and read: “do not doubt that it belongs to God.” A gross error, refuted by the manuscripts and by the context of the passage itself.]

Yet because this deficiency is voluntary, it has been placed within our power. If you fear it, you must not will it; and if you do not will it, it will not occur. What, then, is safer than to be in that life where what you do not will cannot happen to you? But since, just as human beings fell voluntarily, they cannot likewise rise voluntarily, let us hold firmly by faith the hand of God extended to us from above—that is, our Lord Jesus Christ—and await him with certain hope and desire him with burning love.

If you still think that something more careful must be asked about the origin of sin—for I myself now think that there is no need at all—then, if you do think so, the matter must be postponed to another discussion.

E. I certainly follow your will, so that we may postpone to another time whatever has arisen from this discussion. But I will not grant you that you should consider the matter sufficiently investigated already.

# BOOK THREE

In this book the question is investigated whence that movement arises by which the will turns away from the unchangeable good; and whether God’s foreknowledge of human sins conflicts with human freedom in sinning. It is then shown that the Creator is in no way to be charged with whatever must occur in his creature in such a way that it occurs by the will of those who sin; and that God is wholly to be praised for creating and punishing a creature subject to sin. From this the discussion proceeds to the defects of origin, explaining how they justly descend upon Adam’s posterity, and how those who sin undeservedly on account of these very defects put forward an excuse. Thereafter several related difficulties are disentangled.

[Col. 1269]

# CHAPTER ONE

## Whence comes that movement by which the will turns away from the unchangeable good

1. E. Since it is sufficiently clear to me that free will must be counted among goods—and indeed among no small goods—from which we are also compelled to acknowledge that it was given by God and ought to have been given—if you think the time is right, I wish to learn from you whence that movement arises by which the will itself turns away from the common and unchangeable good and turns toward goods that are its own, or those of others, or the lowest goods—in short, toward all changeable goods.

[Note: [Col. 1270] Three manuscripts read: “and turns toward all wholly changeable goods.” This is correct.]

A. What need is there to know this?

E. Because if it was given in such a way that it has this movement by nature, then it turns toward these things by necessity; and no fault can be detected where nature and necessity rule.

A. Does this movement please you, or displease you?

E. It displeases me.

A. Then you condemn it.

E. Certainly I condemn it.

A. Then you condemn a movement of the soul that is without blame.

E. I do not condemn a blameless movement of the soul, but I do not know whether there is any fault in turning away from the unchangeable good toward changeable goods.

A. Then you condemn what you do not know.

E. Do not press me over a word. I said, “I do not know whether there is any fault,” intending it to be understood that there certainly is fault. By the word “I do not know,” I clearly mocked doubt about something evident.

A. Consider what the most certain truth is, which compelled you so quickly to forget what you said a little earlier. If this movement arises by nature or necessity, it cannot in any way be blameworthy; yet you hold so firmly that it is blameworthy that you considered doubt about so certain a matter worthy of ridicule. Why, then, did it seem necessary for you either to affirm or at least to state with some doubt what you yourself prove to be plainly false? You said: “If free will was given in such a way that it has this movement by nature, then it turns toward these things by necessity; and no fault can be detected where nature and necessity rule.” But you ought not to have doubted at all that it was not given in this way, since you do not doubt that this movement is blameworthy.

E. I said that the movement itself is blameworthy, and therefore I cannot doubt that it displeases me and must be condemned. But I deny that the soul which is dragged by this movement from the unchangeable good toward changeable goods is to be blamed, if its nature is such that it is necessarily moved by it.

2. A. Whose movement is this, which you certainly admit must be condemned?

E. I see it in the soul, but I do not know whose it is.

A. Do you deny that the soul is moved by this movement?

E. I do not deny it.

A. Then do you deny that the movement by which a stone is moved is the movement of the stone? I am not speaking of the movement by which we move it, or by which it is moved by some external force—as when it is thrown into the sky—but of the movement by which, by its own inclination, it tends toward the earth and falls.

E. I do not deny that the movement by which it inclines as you say and seeks the lowest place is the movement of the stone; but it is natural. If the soul likewise has this kind of movement, then that movement too is certainly natural, and it cannot rightly be blamed simply because it moves naturally—for even if it is moved toward destruction, it is nevertheless compelled by the necessity of its nature. Moreover, since we do not doubt that this movement is blameworthy, we must altogether deny that it is natural; and therefore it is unlike the movement by which a stone is moved naturally.

A. Did we accomplish anything in the two preceding discussions?

E. Certainly we did.

A. Then I believe you remember that in the first discussion it was established clearly enough that nothing makes the mind a slave of lust except its own will.

[Note: [Col. 1271] Above, Book 1, chapter 11, section 21.]

For neither can it be compelled to this disgrace by something superior or equal, since that would be unjust, nor by something inferior, since that is impossible. It remains, therefore, that this movement is its own—the movement by which it turns the will to enjoy away from the Creator toward the creature. If this movement is charged as fault—for you thought anyone who doubts this worthy of ridicule—it is certainly not natural but voluntary. In this respect it resembles the movement by which a stone is carried downward: just as the latter belongs to the stone, so the former belongs to the soul. Yet they differ in this, that the stone has no power to restrain the movement by which it is carried downward, whereas the soul, when it does not will to do so, is not moved in such a way that, having abandoned higher things, it chooses lower ones.

[Note: [Col. 1272] In eight manuscripts: “it loves the lower things.” Bad. has the same reading.]

Therefore that movement is natural to the stone, but this movement is voluntary in the soul. Hence, if someone says that a stone sins because by its own weight it tends toward the lowest place, he would be judged not merely more foolish than the stone itself but certainly insane. But we accuse the soul of sin when we convict it of abandoning higher things and preferring lower things for enjoyment. Why, then, should we ask where this movement originates, by which the will turns away from the unchangeable good toward a changeable good, when we acknowledge that it belongs only to the soul, is voluntary, and therefore blameworthy? All instruction on this subject is useful only insofar as, by condemning and restraining that movement, we turn our will away from the fall into temporal things toward enjoyment of the eternal good.

[Note: [Col. 1272] See Retractationes, Book 1, chapter 9, section 3.]

3. E. I see, and in a certain way touch and grasp, that what you say is true. For I feel nothing so firmly and intimately as that I possess a will and am moved by it toward enjoying something. But if the will by which I will and do not will is not mine, I cannot discover at all what I should call my own. Therefore, to whom should it be attributed if I do something evil through it, except to me? Since the good God made me, and I can do nothing good except through the will, it is sufficiently evident that the will was given for this purpose by the good God.

But unless the movement by which the will turns this way or that were voluntary and placed within our power, a person could neither be praised when he turns toward higher things nor blamed when he twists toward lower things, as though he were some kind of hinge of the will. Nor would he be admonished at all to neglect these things and desire to attain eternal things, or to refuse to live badly and instead will to live well. Whoever thinks that a human being should not be admonished in this way ought to be expelled from the human race.

# CHAPTER TWO

## How God’s foreknowledge does not deprive sinners of free will: a question that troubles many

4. Since these things are so, I am ineffably troubled by how it can be that God is foreknowing of all future events and yet we sin without necessity. For whoever says that something can occur otherwise than God foreknew attempts, with utterly impious madness, to destroy God’s foreknowledge.

Therefore, if God foreknew that the first human being would sin—as anyone who acknowledges with me that God foreknows all future events must grant—then, if this is so, I do not say that he should not have made him. God made him good, and the sin of one whom he himself made good could not harm God. Rather, in the act of making him, God had displayed his goodness; in punishing him he also displayed his justice, and in liberating him his mercy. I do not, then, say that he should not have made him. But I say this: since God foreknew that he would sin, it was necessary that what God foreknew would happen should happen. How, then, is the will free where such unavoidable necessity appears?

5. A. You have knocked forcefully. May God’s mercy be present and open to those who knock.

[Note: [Col. 1273] Seventeen manuscripts read: “You have knocked forcefully at God’s mercy. May it be present,” and so forth.]

Nevertheless, I believe that the greater part of humanity is tormented by this question for no other reason than that people do not ask it piously and are quicker to make excuses than to confess their sins. Some willingly suppose that no divine providence presides over human affairs. Entrusting both their minds and bodies to chance events, they surrender themselves to be struck and torn apart by lusts; they deny divine judgments, deceive human beings, and think that they can drive away those who accuse them under the protection of fortune. Yet they habitually fashion and paint fortune as blind, so that either they may be better than the thing by which they believe themselves governed, or may admit that they too, with the same blindness, both feel and express such opinions. Nor is it absurd to grant such people that chance directs everything they do, since in their actions they fall. Against this opinion, full of the most foolish and senseless error, enough has, I think, been said in our second discussion.

Others, although they do not dare deny that God’s providence presides over human life, nevertheless prefer, in their wicked error, to believe it weak, unjust, or evil rather than humbly and piously confess their own sins. If all these people could be persuaded, when they think about the supremely good, just, and powerful God, to believe that God’s goodness, justice, and power are far greater and higher than anything they can conceive in thought; and if, considering themselves, they understood that they owe thanks to God even if he had wished them to be something lower than they are; and if with all the bones and marrow of their conscience they cried out, “I said, Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Psalm 40:5)—then they would be led by sure paths of divine mercy into wisdom. They would neither be inflated by what they had found nor thrown into turmoil by what they had not found; through knowledge they would become better equipped to see, and through ignorance gentler in seeking.

But you, whom I do not doubt have already been persuaded of this, will see how easily I can answer so great a question, since you answered my earlier question with only a few words.

# CHAPTER THREE

## God’s foreknowledge does not cause us to sin without free will

6. Surely this is what troubles you and what you marvel at: how these two things are not contrary and opposed—that God is foreknowing of all future events, and that we sin not by necessity but by will. For, you say, if God foreknows that a human being will sin, that person must sin; but if it is necessary, then there is no freedom of will in sinning, but rather an unavoidable and fixed necessity. By this reasoning, you evidently fear that it may be concluded either that God is impiously denied to be foreknowing of all future events, or that, if we cannot deny this, we must admit that sin is committed not by will but by necessity. Or does something else trouble you?

E. Nothing else for the moment.

A. You therefore think that all things of which God is foreknowing occur not by will but by necessity.

E. That is exactly what I think.

[Col. 1274]

A. Wake up at last, look at yourself for a little while, and tell me, if you can, what sort of will you will have tomorrow: one inclined to sinning or one inclined to doing right.

E. I do not know.

A. What? Do you likewise think that God does not know?

E. I could never think that.

A. If, then, he knows your will tomorrow, and foresees the future wills of all human beings, both those who now exist and those who will exist, how much more does he foresee what he will do concerning the just and the wicked?

E. If I call God foreknowing of my actions, I would say with much greater confidence that he foreknows his own actions and most certainly foresees what he will do.

A. Are you not then careful lest someone say to you that he too will do whatever he is going to do not by will but by necessity, if everything of which God is foreknowing occurs by necessity and not by will?

E. When I said that everything God foreknew would occur occurs by necessity, I had in mind only what happens in his creature, not what happens in God himself; for those things do not happen but are eternal.

A. Then God does nothing in his creature.

E. He established once and for all how the order of the universe he created should proceed; for he does not administer anything by a new act of will.

A. Does he not make anyone blessed?

E. Indeed, he does.

A. He makes someone blessed, then, when that person becomes blessed.

E. That is so.

A. If, for example, you are going to be blessed after a year, he will make you blessed after a year.

E. Yes.

A. Then he already foreknows today what he will do after a year.

E. He has always foreknown this. I also agree that he now foreknows it, if it is going to happen in this way.

7. A. Tell me, please: are you not his creature, or will your blessedness not occur in you?

E. On the contrary, I am both his creature, and what will make me blessed will occur in me.

A. Then your blessedness will occur in you through God’s making you blessed, not by will but by necessity.

E. His will is necessity for me.

A. Then you will be blessed against your will.

E. If it were within my power to be blessed, I would certainly already be blessed; for I desire it even now, yet I am not blessed because it is not I but he who makes me blessed.

[Note: [Col. 1274] The passage is confused in the Lovaniensis edition as follows: “Your blessedness will occur in you through God’s making you blessed. E. Then are you blessed against your will? His will is necessity for me. For if it were within my power,” and so forth.]

A. Truth rightly cries out concerning you. For you could not think anything to be within our power except what we do when we will it. Therefore nothing is so much within our power as the will itself. For it is immediately present, without any interval, as soon as we will.

[Note: [Col. 1274] See Retractationes, Book 1, chapter 9, section 3.]

And so we can rightly say, “We grow old not by will but by necessity,” or “We die not by will but by necessity,” and anything else of this kind. But who, unless delirious, would dare say that we will not by will?

Therefore, although God foreknows our future wills, it does not follow that we will something not by will. As for what you said about blessedness—that you are not made blessed by yourself—you spoke as though I had denied this. But I say that when you are going to be blessed, you will become so not unwillingly but willingly.

Since, then, God is foreknowing of your future blessedness, and since nothing can occur otherwise than he foreknew—for otherwise there would be no foreknowledge—we are nevertheless not compelled to believe what is utterly absurd and entirely removed from truth: that you will become blessed unwillingly. Just as God’s foreknowledge, which is certain even today concerning your future blessedness, does not take away your will to be blessed when you begin to be blessed, so a blameworthy will, if one is going to exist in you, will not for that reason cease to be a will because God foreknew that it would exist.

8. Consider, please, with what blindness someone says: “If God foreknew my future will, and since nothing can occur otherwise than he foreknew, I must will what he foreknew. But if I must, then I must admit that I will it not by will but by necessity.”

What extraordinary foolishness! How, then, can something not occur otherwise than God foreknew if the will that God foreknew would exist will not exist? I pass over another equally monstrous point: a person says, as I mentioned earlier, “I must will in this way,” while attempting to remove the will by positing necessity.

[Note: [Col. 1275] The printed editions read: “who, by placing necessity above it, attempts to remove the will.” Eight manuscripts read: “who, by positing necessity, attempts to remove the will.”]

For if he must will, how will he will when there will be no will? But if he does not speak in this way, and instead says that, because he must will, he does not have the will itself within his power, he will be answered from what he himself said when I asked whether he would become blessed unwillingly. For you replied that you would already be blessed if the power were in you; you said that you desired it but could not yet do so.

I then added that truth had cried out concerning you. For we cannot deny that we have power except when what we want is not present to us. But when we want, if the will itself were absent from us, we would not be willing. Since it is impossible that, while we will, we should not will, the will is present to those who will. Nothing is within our power except what is present to those who will.

Our will, therefore, would not be will unless it were within our power. And because it is within our power, it is free for us. For what we do not have within our power is not free for us, nor can what we possess fail to exist.

Thus it follows both that we do not deny God’s foreknowledge of all future events and that we nevertheless will what we will. Since he is foreknowing of our will, the will of which he is foreknowing is what it will be. Therefore it will be a will, because he is foreknowing of a will. Nor could it be a will if it were not within our power. Therefore he is also foreknowing of our power.

His foreknowledge, then, does not take away my power; indeed, that power will be all the more certain for me because the one whose foreknowledge cannot be deceived foreknew that it would be present to me.

E. I now no longer deny that whatever God foreknew must occur, and that he foreknows our sins in such a way that our will nevertheless remains free and placed within our power.

# CHAPTER FOUR

## God’s foreknowledge does not compel anyone to sin, and therefore he justly punishes sins

9. A. What, then, troubles you? Have you perhaps forgotten what our first discussion established, and will you deny that we sin without being compelled by anything—whether superior, inferior, or equal—but by our own will?

E. I dare not deny any of this. Yet I confess that I still do not see how these two things do not conflict: God’s foreknowledge of our sins and our free will in sinning. For we must acknowledge God to be both just and foreknowing. But I should like to know by what justice he punishes sins that must occur, or how those things do not have to occur which he foreknew would occur, or how the Creator is not to be charged with whatever must occur in his creature.

10. A. Why does our free will seem to you to conflict with God’s foreknowledge? Is it because it is foreknowledge, or because it is God’s foreknowledge?

E. Because it is God’s foreknowledge.

A. What, then? If you foreknew that someone would sin, would it not be necessary for him to sin?

E. On the contrary, it would be necessary for him to sin; for my foreknowledge would not be foreknowledge unless I foreknew it with certainty.

A. Therefore it is not because it is God’s foreknowledge that what he foreknows must occur, but only because it is foreknowledge; and if it does not foreknow with certainty, it is no foreknowledge at all.

E. I agree. But what is the point of this?

A. Because, unless I am mistaken, you would not immediately compel someone to sin whom you foreknew would sin; nor would your foreknowledge itself compel him to sin, although he would certainly sin, since otherwise you would not foreknow that it would happen. Just as these two things do not conflict—that you know through your foreknowledge what another will do by his own will—so God, compelling no one to sin, nevertheless foresees those who will sin by their own will.

11. Why, then, should the just God not punish what he foreknows without compelling it to occur? For just as your memory does not compel past events to have happened, so God’s foreknowledge does not compel future events to happen. And just as you remember certain things that you did, although you did not do everything that you remember, so God foreknows everything of which he is the author, although he is not the author of everything that he foreknows. Of what he is not the evil author, he is the just avenger.

[Note: [Col. 1276] The word “evil” is absent from the Lovaniensis edition but is present in the older editions of Bad. and Er., as well as in seventeen manuscripts.]

From this, then, understand already with what justice God punishes sins: he foreknows what will happen but does not cause it. For if he ought not to assign punishment to sinners because he foresees that they will sin, then neither ought he to assign rewards to those who act rightly, because he likewise foresees that they will act rightly.

Rather, let us acknowledge both that it belongs to his foreknowledge that nothing future is hidden from him and that it belongs to his justice that sin, because it is committed by the will, should not remain unpunished in his judgment—just as foreknowledge does not compel it to occur.

# CHAPTER FIVE

## God is to be praised for creating even a creature subject to misery and sin

12. As for the third point you raised—how the Creator is not to be charged with whatever must occur in his creature—the rule of piety will easily remind us of the answer, a rule we ought to remember: we owe thanksgiving to our Creator.

[Note: [Col. 1276] Er. and Lov. read thus. But Bad. reads: “The rule of piety will easily remind us.” Five manuscripts read: “That rule of piety will not easily be removed”; three others, “will not be moved”; seven others, “that rule of piety will not easily move”; finally, the Corbie manuscript reads, “That rule of piety will not easily move.”]

His most abundant goodness would certainly deserve the highest praise even if he had created us at some lower level of the creaturely order. For although our soul has been corrupted by sins, it is nevertheless nobler and better than it would be if it were transformed into this visible light.

And you surely see how greatly souls, even when devoted to bodily senses, praise God for the excellence of this light. Therefore do not now be troubled by the fact that sinful souls are blamed, so that you say in your heart that it would have been better if they had not existed. They are blamed in comparison with themselves, when one considers what they would have been if they had not wished to sin.

Nevertheless, God, their maker, must be praised most gloriously, insofar as human ability permits—not only because he justly orders them when they sin, but also because he made them such that, even when stained by sins, they are in no way surpassed by the dignity of bodily light, for which too he is rightly praised.

13. I also warn you to take care lest you do not say that it would have been better if they had not existed, but instead say that they ought to have been made differently. Whatever appears better to you through true reasoning, know that God made it, as the creator of all good things.

But it is not true reasoning, rather envious weakness, when you imagine that something ought to have been made better and then wish that nothing inferior had been made—as though, after contemplating the heavens, you did not want the earth to have been made. That would be wholly unjust.

You would rightly criticize the matter if, with the heavens omitted, you saw that the earth had been made, since you would say that it ought to have been made in the way you could conceive the heavens. But once you saw that even the thing whose appearance you wished to give the earth had been made—not as the earth but as the heavens—I believe that, since you had not been deprived of the better reality, you should in no way begrudge the making of something inferior as well, so that it would be earth.

In the earth itself, again, there is such variety among its parts that nothing belonging to the appearance of the earth can occur to anyone’s thought that God, the creator of all things, has not made within its entire mass. For from the most fertile and delightful earth to the saltiest and most barren, one arrives by gradual steps through the intermediate forms, so that you would dare criticize none except in comparison with a better one. Thus you ascend through all the degrees of praise, yet when you have found the highest kind of earth, you would not wish it to be the only kind.

[Note: [Col. 1277] Bad. and Er. read: “you would not wish it to be heaven.”]

And how great is the distance between the whole earth and the heavens? For moist and airy nature is interposed between them. From these four elements innumerable kinds and forms of things are varied for us, though they are numbered by God.

Something, then, can exist in the nature of things that you do not conceive by your reasoning. But that what you conceive through true reasoning should not exist is impossible. For you cannot conceive something better in creation that escaped the creator of creation.

The human soul is naturally joined to the divine principles on which it depends. When it says, “This would be better made than that,” if it speaks truly and sees what it says, it sees it in those principles to which it is joined. Let it therefore believe that God made what it recognizes through true reasoning ought to have been made by him, even if it does not see this among created things.

For even if it could not see the heavens with its eyes, yet if it inferred by true reasoning that something of this kind ought to have been made, it should believe that it had been made, although it did not see it with its eyes. It would not see by thought that such a thing ought to have been made unless it saw it in those principles by which all things were made. What is not there, no one can see through truthful thought any more than what is not true.

[Col. 1278]

14. Most people go wrong in this respect: after perceiving better things with the mind, they seek them with the eyes in suitable settings. It is as if someone, having grasped perfect roundness through reason, became indignant because he did not find such roundness in a nut, if he had never seen any round body except fruits of this kind.

In the same way, some people see through very true reasoning that a better creature is one which, although it has free will, remains always fixed in God and never sins. Then, when they look upon human sins, instead of wanting human beings to cease sinning, they grieve that they were made, saying: “He should have made us such that we would always enjoy his unchangeable truth and never wish to sin.”

Let them not cry out or become angry. God did not compel them to sin merely because he made them and gave them the power to choose whether they would sin. And there are certain angels who have never sinned and never will sin.

Therefore, if you delight in a creature that does not sin through a most steadfast will, there is no doubt that you rightly prefer it to a creature that sins. But just as you prefer it in thought, so God the Creator has preferred it in his ordering. Believe that such a creature exists in the higher places and in the heights of heaven. For if the Creator bestowed the goodness of existence upon a creature whose future sins he foresaw, he would certainly not have failed to bestow that goodness in creating a creature whom he foreknew would not sin.

15. That exalted creature possesses its perpetual blessedness, forever enjoying its Creator, which it merits through its perpetual will to hold fast to righteousness. This sinful creature, too, has its own order: it has lost blessedness through sins, but has not been deprived of the capacity to recover blessedness.

It certainly surpasses the creature held by a perpetual will to sin.

[Note: [Col. 1278] Lov. reads: “held by perpetual pleasure.” But the older editions and the manuscripts consistently read “will.”]

Between this creature and the former one, which remains in the will to righteousness, it displays a kind of middle position; through the humility of repentance it recovers its former height.

For God did not refrain from the generosity of his goodness even toward the creature whom he foreknew would not merely sin but would remain in the will to sin, so as not to create it. Just as a wandering horse is better than a stone that does not wander precisely because it lacks its own movement and perception, so a creature that sins by free will is more excellent than one that does not sin because it lacks free will.

And just as I would praise wine that is good in its own kind, while blaming the person whom that wine had made drunk, and yet would place that same person, already blamed and still drunk, above the wine I had praised, the wine by which he became drunk—so bodily creation is rightly to be praised in its own rank, while those who are turned away from perceiving the truth by its immoderate use are to be blamed. Yet those same people, now perverted and in a certain sense intoxicated, are again placed above that same creation, praiseworthy in its own order, through desire for which they have become empty—not now on account of their vices, but because of the continuing dignity of their nature.

16. Since, therefore, every soul is better than every body, and since every sinful soul, wherever it may fall, does not become a body through any change, nor is what it is as a soul wholly taken away from it, it in no way loses its superiority to the body.

And since light holds the first place among bodies, it follows that even the lowest soul must be preferred to the first body. It can happen that one body is preferred to another body belonging to some soul, but it can in no way be preferred to the soul itself.

Why, then, should God not be praised—indeed, praised with ineffable proclamation—when, having made souls that would remain in the laws of righteousness, he also made other souls whom he foresaw would either sin or even persist in sins? For even such souls are still better than those which, because they have no rational and free judgment of the will, cannot sin.

Yet even those souls are themselves still better than the most splendid brilliance of any bodies, a brilliance which some people, although with great error, venerate as though it were the substance of the supreme God.

And if, within the order of bodily creatures, from the choirs of the stars all the way to the number of the hairs on our heads, the beauty of good things is woven together by such gradual steps that it would be exceedingly ignorant to say, “What is this? What purpose does this serve?”—for everything has been created in its order—

[Note: [Col. 1279] According to the manuscripts, the reading should be: “for everything has been created in its order.”]

how much more ignorant is it to say this of any soul which, no matter how far it has fallen into a diminution and defect of its own beauty, will nevertheless always surpass the dignity of all bodies without any doubt?

[Note: [Col. 1279] The printed editions read: “surpassed without any doubt.” But the manuscripts read: “will always surpass.”]

17. Reason evaluates one way, custom another. Reason evaluates by the light of truth, so that in sound judgment it subjects lesser things to greater. Custom, however, is usually inclined by familiarity and convenience to value more highly what truth proves to be lesser.

Since reason places heavenly bodies far above earthly bodies, with a great difference between them, which fleshly human being would nevertheless not prefer that more stars be missing from heaven than that a single little tree be missing from his field, or a cow from his herd?

But just as adults either entirely disregard the judgments of children, or at least patiently await their correction—children who, apart from certain individuals whose affection delights them, would rather see any other human being die than their own sparrow, and all the more so if that human being were terrifying while the sparrow were tuneful and beautiful—so those who have advanced in spirit and progressed toward wisdom, when they encounter inexperienced evaluators of things praising God in lesser creatures because they employ them in ways more suited to their bodily senses, but in the case of higher and better things either do not praise him or praise him less, or even attempt to blame or correct him, or do not believe that he is their creator, should become accustomed either to disregard such judgments entirely if they cannot correct them, or to tolerate and endure them with equanimity until they do correct them.

# CHAPTER SIX

## No one can truly say that he would rather not exist than be miserable
18. Since this is so, it is utterly contrary to the truth to suppose that the sins of a creature should be charged to the Creator [Col. 1280], even though what He foreknew would happen must necessarily happen, that when you say you cannot see how anything that must happen in His creature could not be charged to Him, I, on the contrary, cannot find—and affirm that it is impossible to find, and that there simply is no—way in which anything in His creature can be charged to Him if it must happen through the will of those who sin.

For if someone says, “I would rather not exist than be miserable,” I shall answer: “You are lying. For even now you are miserable, and you do not wish to die for any other reason than that you may exist. Thus, although you do not wish to be miserable, you nevertheless wish to exist. Give thanks, then, for the fact that you exist willingly, so that what you are unwillingly may be taken away. You exist willingly, and you are unwillingly miserable. But if you are ungrateful for what you wish to be, you are rightly compelled to be what you do not wish to be.”

Therefore, for the fact that even in your ingratitude you possess what you wish, I praise the goodness of the Creator; but for the fact that, in your ingratitude, you suffer what you do not wish, I praise the justice of the Ordainer.

19. If he says, “I do not wish to die for the reason that I would rather be miserable than not exist at all, but so that I may not be more miserable after death,” I shall answer: “If this is unjust, you will not be so; but if this is just, let us praise Him according to whose laws you will be so.”

If he says, “How may I presume that, if this is unjust, I shall not be so?” I shall answer: “Because, if you are in your own power, either you will not be miserable, or, by ruling yourself unjustly, you will justly be miserable; or, if you wish to rule yourself justly but cannot, you will not be in your own power, but either in no one’s power or in another’s.

“If you are in no one’s power, you will be so either unwillingly or willingly. But you can be unwillingly subject to nothing unless some force has overcome you; and no one who is in no one’s power can be overcome by any force. If, however, you are willingly in no one’s power, reasoning returns us to the conclusion that you are in your own power; and either, by ruling yourself unjustly, you will be justly miserable, or, since you will willingly possess whatever you possess, you will still have reason to give thanks for the goodness of your Creator.

“But if you are not in your own power, someone more powerful or less powerful than you will certainly have you in his power. If someone less powerful has you in his power, this will be through your fault, and your misery will be just; for, if you wish, you will be able to overcome one who is weaker. But if someone more powerful has you, who are weaker, in his power, you will in no way be able rightly to regard so orderly an arrangement as unjust.”

Therefore it was most truly said: “If this is unjust, you will not be so; but if it is just, let us praise Him according to whose laws you will be so.”

## CHAPTER VII — Existence is loved even by the miserable, because they derive their existence from Him who supremely is

20. If he says: “I would rather be miserable than not exist at all because I already exist; but if I could have been consulted before I existed, I would have chosen not to exist rather than to be miserable. For now, since I am miserable, the fact that I fear not existing belongs to misery itself, because I do not wish what I ought to wish; I ought rather to wish not to exist than to be miserable. Yet I admit that I would rather be miserable than nothing; but I desire this all the more foolishly the more miserable I am, and I am all the more miserable the more truly I see that I ought not to have wished this.”

I shall answer: “Take care lest you be mistaken precisely where you think you see the truth. For if you were blessed, you would certainly prefer to exist rather than not exist; and now, although you are miserable, you nevertheless prefer to exist—even miserably—rather than not exist at all, although you do not wish to be miserable.

“Consider, then, as far as you can, how great a good existence itself is, since both the blessed and the miserable desire it. For if you consider this carefully, you will see that you are miserable to the extent that you do not draw near to Him who supremely is; but that you think it better for someone not to exist than to be miserable to the extent that you do not see Him who supremely is. Yet you still wish to exist because you derive your existence from Him who supremely is.”

21. If, then, you wish to escape misery, love in yourself this very fact: that you wish to exist. For if you increasingly desire to exist, you will draw near to Him who supremely is; and now give thanks that you exist.

Although you are inferior to the blessed, you are nevertheless superior to those things that possess not even the desire for blessedness—though many of these too are praised by the miserable. Everything, however, is rightly to be praised precisely insofar as it exists, because precisely insofar as it exists, it is good.

For the more you love existence, the more you will desire eternal life, and the more earnestly you will wish to be so formed that your affections are not temporal, stamped and impressed by love of temporal things. Temporal things do not exist before they come to be; when they exist, they are passing away; and when they have passed away, they will no longer exist. Thus, when they are future, they do not yet exist; but when they are past, they no longer exist. How, then, can things be held fast so that they remain, when for them to begin to exist is the same as to proceed toward ceasing to exist?

But whoever loves existence approves these things insofar as they exist, and loves what always exists. And if he was wavering in his love of these things, he will be fortified in love of that one [Note: [Col. 1281] The Gemmeticensis manuscript reads, “And if he wavers in his love of these things”; immediately afterward, together with eleven other manuscripts, it has “he is fortified in love of that one.”]; and if he was dissipating himself in love of passing things, he will be made firm in love of what endures. He will stand and attain existence itself, which he wished for when he feared not existing, but could not stand because he was entangled in love of things that pass away.

Therefore, let it not displease you—but rather let it please you greatly—that you prefer to be miserable rather than, by not being miserable, to be nothing. If, to this beginning by which you wish to exist, you add an increasing desire to exist, you will rise and be built up toward Him who supremely is. In this way you will restrain yourself from every corruption by which what is lowest passes away into nonexistence and drags down with it the strength of those who love it.

Hence it will come about that the one who prefers not to exist lest he be miserable, because he cannot avoid existing, will remain miserable. But whoever loves existence more than he hates being miserable will, by adding to what he loves, exclude what he hates; for when he begins perfectly to exist in his own order, he will not be miserable.

## CHAPTER VIII — No one chooses not to exist, not even those who kill themselves

22. Consider how absurd and inappropriate it is to say: “I would rather not exist than be miserable.” For whoever says, “I would rather have this than that,” chooses something. But not to exist is not something; it is nothing. Therefore you cannot rightly choose it in any way, since what you choose does not exist.

You say that you do wish to exist, although you are miserable, but that you ought not to have wished this. What, then, ought you to have wished? “Not to exist,” you reply, “rather.” If you ought to have wished this, then this is better; but what does not exist cannot be better. Therefore you ought not to have wished it; and the feeling by which you do not wish it is more truthful than the opinion by which you suppose that you ought to have wished it.

Furthermore, whatever anyone rightly chooses as desirable must make him better when he reaches it; but one who will not exist cannot become better. Therefore no one can rightly choose not to exist.

Nor ought we to be moved by the judgment of those who, driven by misery, killed themselves. For either they fled to a place where they thought they would be better off—and this is not contrary to our reasoning, whatever they may have thought—or, if they believed that they would not exist at all, their false choice will move those who choose nothing still less. For how can I follow someone who chooses, when, if I ask him what he chooses, he will answer, “Nothing”? For whoever chooses not to exist is plainly convicted of choosing nothing, even if he does not wish to admit it.

23. Nevertheless, if I can, I shall say what I think about this entire matter: no one, when he kills himself or desires to die in any way, seems to possess in his feeling the belief that he will not exist after death, even though he may hold this to some extent as an opinion.

For opinion belongs either to the error or to the truth of one who reasons or believes; feeling, however, derives its force either from habit or from nature. That one thing may be present in opinion and another in feeling can easily be recognized from the fact that we often believe that one thing ought to be done, while we take pleasure in doing another.

Sometimes feeling is more truthful than opinion, if the opinion arises from error and the feeling from nature—as when a sick person usually takes pleasure in cold water because it is beneficial [Note: [Col. 1282] Erasmus reads: “as when a sick person usually takes sweet pleasure in cold water when it does no harm.”], although he believes that it will harm him if he drinks it.

Sometimes opinion is more truthful than feeling, if someone believes medical science that cold water is harmful when in fact it will harm him, while nevertheless taking pleasure in drinking it. Sometimes both are in accord with truth, when what is beneficial is not only believed to be so but is also desired. Sometimes both are in error, when what is harmful is believed to be beneficial and the person does not cease to drink it freely.

Right opinion also commonly corrects bad habit, and bad opinion corrupts sound nature: so great is the power exercised by the rule and authority of reason.

When, therefore, someone who believes that he will not exist after death is nevertheless driven by intolerable troubles toward a complete desire for death, and resolves upon and seizes death, he possesses in his opinion the error of total annihilation, but in his feeling a natural desire for rest.

Now what is at rest is not nothing; indeed, it exists more than what is restless. Restlessness varies the affections, so that one destroys another; but rest possesses constancy, in which the meaning of the statement “it is” is most clearly understood [Note: [Col. 1282] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “in which it is understood that what was said is.” But the word “is” is absent from the Badian edition and the manuscripts, although a few of them, instead of “what was said,” have “what is said, is”; this appears to be the true reading.].

Thus all that desire expressed in the will for death is directed not toward the nonexistence of the one who dies, but toward his being at rest. Therefore, although he mistakenly believes that he will not exist, he nevertheless desires by nature to be at rest—that is, to exist more fully.

Consequently, just as it is in no way possible for anyone to take pleasure in not existing, so it ought in no way to be possible for anyone to be ungrateful for the goodness of the Creator on account of the fact that he exists.

## CHAPTER IX — The misery of sinful souls contributes to the perfection of the universe

24. If he says: “It would nevertheless not have been difficult or burdensome for almighty God to arrange everything He made in such a way that no creature ever reached misery; for either the Almighty could not do this, or the Good One begrudged it,” I shall answer:

“The order of creatures descends from the highest to the lowest through just degrees in such a way that anyone who says, ‘This should not exist,’ is envious; and anyone who says, ‘This should be such,’ is also envious.

“For if he wishes it to be such as what is higher, then it already is that, and it is so great that nothing ought to be added to it, because it is perfect. Therefore, whoever says, ‘This too should be such,’ either wishes to add something to what is perfect and will be immoderate and unjust, or wishes to destroy this thing and will be wicked and envious.

“Whoever says, ‘This should not exist,’ will likewise be wicked and envious, since he does not want that to exist which he is still compelled to praise as inferior.

“It would be like someone saying, ‘There should be no moon,’ while admitting—or most foolishly and obstinately denying—that even the light of a lamp, though far inferior, is nevertheless beautiful in its own order and suited to earthly darkness and to the uses of night, and in all these respects worthy of praise in its own measure.

“How, then, will he dare rightly to say, ‘There should be no moon in the universe,’ when, if he said, ‘There should be no lamp,’ he would realize that he deserved ridicule? If he does not say, ‘There should be no moon,’ but says that the moon ought to be such as he sees the sun to be, he does not understand that he is saying nothing other than, ‘There should be no moon, but there should be two suns.’ In this he errs in two ways: he wishes to add something to the perfection of things by desiring another sun, and to diminish it by wishing the moon removed.”

25. Perhaps he will say that he makes no complaint about the moon because its splendor is so much less that it is not miserable, but that he grieves over souls not because of their obscurity but because of their misery.

Let him carefully consider that the moon’s splendor is not miserable, just as the sun’s splendor is not blessed. For although heavenly bodies are bodies, they are still bodies insofar as this light is concerned, which can be perceived through bodily eyes. No bodies, insofar as they themselves are concerned, can be either blessed or miserable, although there can be bodies belonging to the blessed or to the miserable.

But the comparison drawn from those lights teaches this: when contemplating differences among bodies, you see some brighter than others and unjustly demand that the darker ones you observe be removed or made equal to the brighter ones. Yet, when you refer everything to the perfection of the whole, the more or less bright things are in relation to one another, the more clearly you see that all things exist; and the perfection of the whole does not present itself to you unless greater things are present in such a way that lesser things are not absent.

So also consider the differences among souls. In them you will find this as well: the misery you grieve over contributes to the perfection of the universe, since even those souls are not absent which had to become miserable because they wished to be sinful.

It is therefore far from true that God ought not to have made such souls; indeed, He made even the other creatures, which are far inferior to miserable souls, in a praiseworthy manner.

26. Yet someone who understands less clearly what has been said may still seem to have an objection. For he says: “If our misery completes the perfection of the universe, something would have been lacking from this perfection if we had always been blessed. Therefore, if a soul reaches misery only by sinning, our sins too are necessary to the perfection of the universe that God created. How, then, does He justly punish sins which, if they were absent, would leave His creature incomplete and imperfect?”

The answer is that it is not the sins themselves, nor misery itself, that are necessary to the perfection of the universe, but souls insofar as they are souls—souls which, if they wish, sin, and which, if they sin, become miserable.

For if, once their sins have been removed, misery continues or even precedes sins, then the order and administration of the universe are rightly said to be disfigured. Again, if sins occur but misery is absent, iniquity nevertheless dishonors the order.

When blessedness is present with those who do not sin, the universe is perfect. When misery is present with those who sin, the universe is nevertheless perfect. The universe is always full and perfect with respect to all natures, since those souls are not absent whom misery follows when they sin, or blessedness follows when they act rightly.

For sin and the punishment of sin are not themselves certain natures, but affections of natures: the former voluntary, the latter penal. Yet the voluntary affection that occurs in sin is a shameful affection. For this reason a penalty is applied to it, so that it may place that affection in an order where it is not shameful to be such, and compel it to conform to the beauty of the universe, so that the punishment of sin may correct the disgrace of sin.

27. Hence it comes about that a sinful creature is punished by lower creatures, because those creatures are so low that they can even be adorned by shameful souls, and thus conform to the beauty of the universe.

For what is as great in a household as a human being? And what is as base and low as the household sewer? Yet a servant caught in such a sin that he is judged worthy of cleaning the sewer adorns it even by his own shame. Both of these—the servant’s shame and the cleaning of the sewer—once joined together and reduced to a certain unity of their own kind, are fitted and subordinated to the well-ordered household in such a way that they harmonize with its whole in the most orderly beauty.

Yet if that servant had not wished to sin, another provision of domestic discipline would not have been lacking, by which what needed cleaning would be cleaned.

What, then, is as low among created things as every earthly body? Yet a sinful soul adorns even this corruptible flesh in such a way that it gives it a most fitting appearance and vital movement.

Therefore such a soul does not suit a heavenly dwelling through sin, but it suits an earthly dwelling through punishment, so that whichever it has chosen, the universe may always be beautiful, ordered in parts of the greatest appropriateness. God is its Creator and Administrator.

For when the best souls dwell in the lowest creatures, they do not adorn them by their misery, which they do not possess, but by their beneficial use of them. If sinful souls were permitted to dwell in the higher places, this would be dishonorable, because they do not suit those places, since they can neither use them well nor contribute anything of adornment to them.

28. Therefore, although this earthly world has been assigned to corruptible things, it nevertheless continues, insofar as it can, to preserve an image of higher things and to display examples and certain indications to us.

For if, urged by the duty of honor, we see some good and great man being consumed by fire insofar as his body is concerned, we do not call this the punishment of sin, but a proof of courage and patience. We love him more when the most shameful bodily corruption consumes his limbs than if he suffered nothing of the kind; for we marvel that the nature of the soul is not changed by the mutability of the body.

But when we see the limbs of a most cruel bandit destroyed by such punishment, we approve the order of the laws. Thus both torments adorn, but the one by reason of virtue, the other by reason of sin.

If, after those fires—or even before them—we saw that excellent man transformed and raised to the stars, made suitable for a heavenly dwelling, we would certainly rejoice. But if we saw the wicked bandit, either before or after his punishment, raised into heaven to an eternal seat of honor while retaining the same evil will, who would not be offended?

Thus both of them could adorn the lower creatures, but only one of them could adorn the higher.

From this we are warned to observe that the mortality of this flesh adorned both the first man, so that punishment might correspond to sin, and our Lord, so that He might free us from sin by mercy.

But just as the just man could possess a mortal body while remaining in justice, so the wicked man, while he remains wicked, cannot attain the immortality of the saints—that is, the sublime and angelic immortality. These are not the angels of whom the Apostle says, “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (I Cor. VI, 3), but those of whom the Lord says, “And they will be equal to the angels of God” (Luke XX, 36).

For those who desire equality with the angels for the sake of empty glory do not thereby wish to be equal to the angels, but to have the angels equal to themselves. Therefore, persisting in such a desire, they will be made equal in punishment to the transgressing angels, since they love their own power rather than that of almighty God.

When such people are placed on the left, because they did not seek God through the gate of humility which the Lord Jesus Christ displayed in Himself, and because they lived without mercy and in pride, it will be said to them: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV, 41).

## CHAPTER X — By what right the devil possessed humanity, and by what right God set humanity free

29. Since there are two origins of sins—one arising from spontaneous thought, the other from the persuasion of another—I think this is what the Prophet refers to when he says: “Cleanse me, Lord, from my hidden faults, and spare Your servant from those of others” (Ps. XVIII, 13–14).

Both are voluntary. For just as someone does not sin by his own thought unwillingly, so, when he consents to one who gives evil advice, he consents only by his will. Nevertheless, it is more serious not merely to sin by one’s own thought without anyone’s prompting, but also to persuade another to sin through envy and deceit, than to be led into sin by another’s persuasion.

The justice of the Lord who punishes was therefore preserved in both sins. For the balance of equity also required that humanity not be denied to the power of the devil himself, since he had subjected it to himself by giving it evil counsel. For it was unjust that he should not rule the one whom he had captured.

Nor can it in any way happen that the perfect justice of the highest and true God, which extends everywhere, would abandon even the falls of sinners that must be ordered.

Yet because humanity had sinned less than the devil, the very fact that humanity was subjected to the ruler of this world—the ruler, that is, of this mortal and lowest part of creation, and therefore the ruler of all sinners [Note: [Col. 1286] Earlier editions read “the beginning of all sinners”; nineteen manuscripts here have “the ruler.”] and overseer of death—even unto the mortality of the flesh, served to restore humanity’s salvation.

For thus, fearful through awareness of mortality, dreading troubles and destruction even from the vilest and most contemptible beasts, or from the tiniest creatures, and uncertain about the future, humanity is accustomed to restrain unlawful enjoyments [Note: [Col. 1286] Thus the Badian edition and most manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis, however, read “to restrain delights.”], and especially to break pride—by whose persuasion it was cast down and by which alone the remedy of mercy is rejected.

For what has greater need of mercy than the miserable? And what is more unworthy of mercy than a proud miserable person?

30. From this it came about that the Word of God, through whom all things were made and whom all angelic blessedness enjoys, extended His clemency even to our misery: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 3, 14).

Thus a human being, not yet made equal to the angels, could eat the bread of angels, if that very bread of angels deigned to become equal to human beings.

He did not descend to us in such a way as to abandon them; rather, He remained whole among them and whole among us. He nourishes them inwardly by what He is as God, while outwardly admonishing us by what we are, making us fit through faith to be nourished equally by sight.

For rational creation is nourished by that Word as by its best food. The human soul, however, is rational, and it was held by the mortal bonds of the punishment of sin. It had been brought to such a diminished condition that it struggled toward understanding invisible things through conjectures drawn from visible things.

Therefore the food of rational creation became visible—not by changing its own nature, but by assuming the form of ours—in order to call back to Himself, the invisible one, those pursuing visible things.

Thus the soul found outside itself, in humility, the one whom it had proudly abandoned within; it would imitate His visible humility and return to invisible exaltation.

31. And the Word of God, the only Son of God, who always has held and will hold the devil under His laws, also subjected the devil to humanity by clothing Himself in humanity.

He extorted nothing from him by violent domination, but overcame him by the law of justice. For since the woman had been deceived, and the man had been cast down through the woman, the devil, through a malicious desire to harm but nevertheless by a most equitable right, claimed all the offspring of the first man as sinners under the laws of death.

His power would remain valid until he killed the Just One, in whom he could show nothing deserving death—not only because He was killed without guilt, but also because He was born without lust. The devil had subjected to that lust those whom he had captured, so that whatever was born from them, as the fruit of his own tree, he might retain through a perverse desire to possess, but nevertheless by a lawful right of possession.

Therefore he is most justly compelled to release those who believe in the One whom he most unjustly killed, so that they may pay what they owe by dying temporally, and may live forever in Him who paid on their behalf what He did not owe.

But those whom he had persuaded to persist in unbelief he would justly have as companions with him in perpetual damnation.

Thus humanity was not forcibly snatched from the devil, since the devil himself had captured humanity not by force but by persuasion. And humanity, which had been justly humbled all the more so that it might serve the one to whom it had consented for evil, was justly liberated by the One to whom it consented for good, because this one had sinned less in consenting than the devil had in giving evil counsel [Note: [Col. 1287] Printed editions read “more justly,” supported by a few manuscripts; twelve manuscripts of better quality have “justly more.”].

## CHAPTER XI — A creature, whether destined to remain in justice or to fall, contributes to the adornment of the universe

32. God therefore made all natures—not only those destined to remain in virtue and justice, but also those destined to sin—not so that they would sin, but so that they would adorn the universe, whether they wished to sin or not [Note: [Col. 1287] Several of the better manuscripts read “to adorn the perfection of the universe.”].

For if souls were absent that occupied the very summit of order in the whole of creation in such a way that, if they wished to sin, the universe would be weakened and shaken, something great would be lacking from creation: there would be lacking that whose removal would disturb the stability and coherence of things.

Such are the best, holy, and exalted creatures of the heavenly and superheavenly powers, over whom God alone rules, while the whole universe is subject to them. Without their just and perfect services the universe cannot exist.

Likewise, if those creatures were absent which, whether they sinned or did not sin, would cause nothing to be diminished from the order of the universe, even then much would be lacking. For they are rational souls, and although they are unequal to those higher beings in function, they are equal in nature. Below them are many others, and yet these too are praiseworthy levels of the things established by the highest God.

33. The nature, then, whose function is higher is one whose absence would diminish the order of the universe, and whose sin would also diminish it. This other nature has a lower function: the universe would be diminished if it were absent, but not if it sinned.

To the higher nature was given the power to contain all things through its proper function, which cannot be lacking from the order of things. It does not therefore remain in a good will because it received this function; rather, it received the function because it was foreseen by the One who gave it that it would remain.

Yet it does not contain all things by its own majesty, but by cleaving to His majesty and obeying most devotedly His commands—He from whom, through whom, and in whom all things were made.

To the other nature, if it did not sin, was indeed given the most powerful function of containing all things, but this was not its proper function; it was shared with the higher nature, since this other nature was foreknown as destined to sin.

All spiritual things possess among themselves both conjunction without accumulation and separation without diminution. Thus the higher nature would not be helped in the ease of its activity when this one was joined to it, nor would its activity become more difficult if this one abandoned its function by sinning.

For spiritual creatures are joined not by the places or masses of their bodies, but by similarity of affections, and separated by dissimilarity, although each possesses its own body.

34. Among the lower and mortal bodies [Col. 1288], once the soul has been ordered through sin, it rules its own body—not entirely according to its will, but as the laws of the universe permit.

Yet such a soul is not thereby inferior to the heavenly body, to which even earthly bodies are subject.

The ragged garment of a condemned servant is far inferior to the garment of one who has served well and stands in great honor with his master; but the servant himself is better than any costly garment, because he is a human being.

The higher soul, therefore, cleaves to God and, by angelic power in a heavenly body, adorns and rules even an earthly body, as the One whose will it ineffably contemplates commands.

The lower soul, burdened with mortal limbs, scarcely administers inwardly even that by which it is weighed down, and nevertheless adorns it as much as it can. As for the other things lying outside it, it affects them externally as best it can, though with a much weaker operation.

## CHAPTER XII — The governance of the universe would not be disturbed even if the entire angelic creation sinned

35. Hence it follows that the lowest bodily creation would have had a most fitting adornment even if this soul had not wished to sin.

For what can rule the whole can also rule a part; but what has less power cannot thereby rule greater things.

A perfect physician, for example, can effectively heal even a scab; but one who gives useful advice to a person afflicted with a scab cannot thereby heal the health of the entire human race.

And if a certain reason is clearly perceived, by which it is made evident that there ought to have been a creature that never sinned and never would sin, that same reason also declares that this creature abstains from sin by free will, not because it is compelled not to sin, but willingly.

Nevertheless, even if it had sinned—although it did not sin, just as God foreknew that it would not sin—even if it had sinned, the power of God, whose potency is ineffable, would have sufficed to govern this universe, rewarding all things suitably and deservedly, and permitting nothing disgraceful or unbecoming in His entire dominion.

For if, with no powers created for this very purpose, the entire angelic nature had fallen away from His commands by sinning, He would by His own majesty [Note: [Col. 1288] Four manuscripts read: “had fallen away, but by His majesty.” This is not a bad reading.] govern all things most fittingly and perfectly.

He did not begrudge the spiritual creature its existence, since He established even the bodily creature, which is far inferior to sinful spiritual creatures, with such abundant goodness that no one who rationally contemplates heaven and earth and all visible natures ordered and formed according to their kinds can either believe that anyone other than God is their maker or fail to confess that He is to be praised beyond expression.

Or if there is no better ordering of things unless angelic power, through excellence of nature and goodness of will, stands supreme in the disposition of the universe, even if all the angels had sinned, they would cause no lack to the Creator of angels in governing His dominion [Note: [Col. 1288] Lovaniensis has in the text, “whether there is any.” But the Badian and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts read “whether there is none” [Col. 1289]; this reading was wrongly relegated to the margin in the Lovaniensis edition, since the disjunctive particle *sive* indicates that this is the second member opposed to the preceding one: “whether by no powers created for this purpose.”].

For neither His goodness, as though wearied by some annoyance, nor His omnipotence, because of any difficulty, would fail to create others whom He could place in the seats that others had abandoned by sinning. Nor could a spiritual creature of however great a number [Note: [Col. 1289] Five old manuscripts of no inferior quality read “of whatever office.”], if it were condemned according to its merits, constrict the order that fittingly and appropriately receives all who are to be condemned [Note: [Col. 1289] Erasmus and Lovaniensis add “many” after “all who are to be condemned.” We have removed “many,” because it is redundant and absent from the Badian edition and fifteen manuscripts.].

Therefore, wherever our consideration turns, it finds God, the best Creator of all natures and the most just Administrator, worthy of ineffable praise.

36. Finally, let us leave the contemplation of the beauty of things to those who, by divine gift, are able to see it, and let us not attempt by words to lead those who cannot see it toward what cannot be expressed [Note: [Col. 1289] The printed editions and most manuscripts lack the words “those who cannot,” which we have restored here from another Sorbonne manuscript and two others.]. Yet, for the sake of those who are talkative, weak, or deceitful, let us bring so great a question to its conclusion in the briefest possible statement.

## CHAPTER XIII — The goodness of a nature is shown by its corruption and by the condemnation of its defect

Every nature that can become less good is good; and every nature, when it is corrupted, becomes less good.

For either corruption does not harm it, in which case it is not corrupted; or, if it is corrupted, corruption harms it. And if it harms it, it diminishes something of its goodness and makes it less good.

For if corruption deprived it completely of every good, whatever remained of it could no longer be corrupted, because there would be no good whose removal could cause corruption to harm it. But that which corruption cannot harm is not corrupted.

Moreover, a nature that is not corrupted is incorruptible. Therefore there would be an incorruptible nature produced by corruption—which is utterly absurd to say.

Accordingly, what is said most truly is that every nature, insofar as it is a nature, is good. For if it is incorruptible, it is better than one that is corruptible; but if it is corruptible, then, since it becomes less good as it is corrupted, it is unquestionably good.

Every nature, moreover, is either corruptible or incorruptible. Therefore every nature is good. By “nature” I mean what is also usually called substance.

Every substance, then, is either God or from God, because every good is either God or from God.

37. With these points established and secured, as though at the head of our reasoning, attend to what I say.

Every rational nature, created with the free choice of the will, is unquestionably worthy of praise if it remains in enjoyment of the highest and unchangeable good; and every nature that strives to remain there is itself also worthy of praise.

But every nature that does not remain in that good and does not wish to act so as to remain there is to be blamed, insofar as it is not there and insofar as it does not act so as to be there.

Therefore, if the rational nature that has been made is praised, no one doubts that the one who made it must be praised; and if it is blamed, no one doubts that its Creator is praised in that very blame.

For when we blame it because it does not wish to enjoy the highest and unchangeable good—that is, its Creator—we praise Him without any doubt.

How great, then, is God, the Creator of all things, and how ineffably He is to be proclaimed and honored by every tongue and every thought—for without His praise we can neither be praised nor blamed!

We can be blamed for not remaining in Him only because remaining in Him is our great, highest, and primary good. And from where does this come, except from the fact that He is the ineffable good?

What, then, can be found in our sins by which He might be blamed, when the blameworthiness of our sins is nothing unless He is praised?

38. What then? Even in the very things that are censured, is anything censured except vice? But no one’s vice is censured unless that person’s nature is praised. For either what you censure is according to nature—and then it is not vice, and you rather need correction, so that you may learn to censure rightly, than does the thing you censure wrongly—or, if it is vice, so that it can rightly be censured, it must also be contrary to nature. For every vice, precisely insofar as it is vice, is contrary to nature. If it does not harm nature, it is not vice; but if it is vice because it harms, it is vice because it is contrary to nature.

But if some nature is corrupted not by its own vice but by the vice of another, it is unjustly censured; and one must ask whether that other nature is not corrupted by its own vice, by whose vice another nature could be corrupted. But what else is it to be vitiated than to be corrupted by vice? Further, the nature that is not vitiated is without vice; but whatever nature corrupts another by its vice necessarily has vice. The former, then, is vicious, and is first corrupted by its own vice, by whose vice another nature also can be corrupted.

From this it follows that every vice is contrary to nature, even to the nature of the thing whose vice it is. Therefore, since in anything it is only vice that is censured, and since vice is vice because it is contrary to the nature of the thing whose vice it is, no thing’s vice is rightly censured unless the nature of that thing is praised. For vice does not rightly displease you except because it vitiates what pleases you in nature.

### CHAPTER XIV  
### Not every corruption deserves censure

39. We must also consider whether it is truly said that one nature is corrupted by the vice of another nature, with no vice of its own being involved. For if a nature approaches another in order to corrupt it, carrying its own vice, but finds in that other nothing corruptible, it does not corrupt it. If, however, it finds something corruptible, it effects its corruption with the vice of that other nature involved.

A more powerful nature, if it does not wish to be corrupted by a weaker one, is not corrupted; but if it does wish this, it begins to be corrupted by its own vice before being corrupted by the other. Likewise, an equal nature cannot be corrupted by an equal one if it does not wish to be corrupted. For any nature that approaches one without vice, carrying vice, in order to corrupt it, does not thereby approach as an equal, but as one made weaker by its own vice.

If a more powerful nature corrupts a weaker one, this happens either through the vice of both, if it results from the wrongful desire of both; or through the vice of the more powerful, if the superiority of its nature is so great that it surpasses the inferior nature it corrupts even while itself is vicious. For who would rightly censure the fruits of the earth because human beings do not use them well, but corrupt them by abusing them for luxury; [Col. 1291] when it would be madness to doubt that human nature, even when vicious, is superior and more powerful than any fruits of the earth?

40. It can also happen that a more powerful nature corrupts an inferior one, and that this occurs through the vice of neither. For we call vice what deserves censure. Who, then, would dare censure a frugal person who seeks from the fruits of the earth nothing other than the sustenance of nature [Note: [Col. 1291] Bad., Erasmus, and two manuscripts have “the alleviation of nature.”], or censure the same fruits because they are corrupted by being used as food?

Such a thing is not even ordinarily called corruption, since the name “corruption” usually belongs especially to vice. It can also easily be observed in other things that a more powerful nature often corrupts an inferior one for no use at all in satisfying its own need [Note: [Col. 1291] The printed editions have “for some uses”; but the manuscripts have “for no uses,” which we adopt.]: either in the order of justice, when it punishes guilt—for from this principle the Apostle’s statement was made, “If anyone corrupts the temple of God, God will corrupt him” (1 Cor. 3:17)—or according to the mutable order of things that yield to it, under laws most fittingly assigned to the universe in accordance with the power of each part.

For if the sun, by the measure of its own nature, corrupts someone’s eyes because they are too weak to endure its light, it should not be thought either that the sun changes them in order to satisfy its need for their light, or that it does this through any vice of its own. Nor should the eyes themselves necessarily be censured, because they yielded both to their master by opening against the light, and to the light by being corrupted.
