Of all corruptions, therefore, only vicious corruption is rightly censured. The others either should not even be called corruptions, or, since they are not vicious, cannot deserve censure. For censure itself is believed to have derived its name from being prepared, that is, suited and owed, only to vice—whence it is called *vituperatio*.

41. Vice, I began to say, is evil for no other reason than that it is opposed to the nature of the very thing whose vice it is. Hence it is clear that the same thing whose vice is censured is by nature praiseworthy, so that we must acknowledge that the very censure of vices is praise of the natures whose vices are censured.

Because vice opposes nature, the evil of vices increases in proportion as the integrity of natures diminishes. Thus, when you censure vice, you certainly praise that whose integrity you desire. And what do you praise except the integrity of nature? For a perfect nature deserves not only no censure but also praise, within its own kind.

Whatever, therefore, you perceive to be lacking from the perfection of nature, you call vice, thereby sufficiently declaring that the nature pleases you: by censuring its imperfection, you wish it to be perfect.

### CHAPTER XV  
### The defect of a creature is not always culpable

42. If, then, the censure of vices commends the beauty and dignity even of the natures whose vices they are, how much more must God, the creator of all natures, be praised even in their vices! For from him they have the fact that they are natures; and they are vicious precisely insofar as they depart from the art of him by whom they were made [Note: [Col. 1291] The printed editions read, “from him by whom they were made”; but the manuscripts read, “from the art by which they were made.”]; and they are rightly censured [Col. 1292] precisely insofar as the one who censures them sees the art by which they were made, so that he censures in them what he does not see there.

And if the art by which all things were made—that is, the supreme and immutable Wisdom of God—is truly and supremely what it is, consider where everything that departs from it is tending. Yet this defection would not deserve censure unless it were voluntary.

Consider, I ask, whether you rightly censure something that is as it ought to be. I do not think so; rather, you censure what is not as it ought to be. But no one ought to have what he has not received; and whoever owes something owes it to whom, except to the one from whom he received the obligation to owe? Even things returned by transfer are returned to the one who had transferred them. And what is returned to the rightful successors of creditors is returned, of course, to those whom they lawfully succeed. Otherwise it is not called repayment but cession, admission, or something of that kind.

Therefore, of all temporal things—which in this order of things have been placed so that, unless they fail, past things cannot give way to future things, and the whole beauty of time cannot be completed—it is utterly absurd to say that they ought not to fail. They act for as long as they have received to act, and they return to the one to whom they owe the fact that they are, insofar as they are.

Anyone who grieves that they fail ought to attend to his own speech. If he thinks that the very speech by which he complains of this is just and proceeds from wisdom, then, as far as its sound is concerned, if someone loved a single syllable of it and refused to let it give way by passing away to the other syllables from which, through their departing and succeeding, the whole speech is composed, he would rightly be judged astonishingly insane.

43. In those things, then, that fail because they were not given existence beyond a certain point, so that everything may be completed in its proper times, no one rightly censures their failure. For no one can say, “It ought to have remained,” when it could not pass beyond the limits it had received.

But in rational creatures, through whose sinning or not sinning universal beauty is brought to completion in the most fitting ways, one of four alternatives must hold. Either there are no sins—which is most absurd to say, since at least the one who condemns as sins those things that are not sins would then sin—or sins should not be censured, which is equally absurd. For then rightly performed acts would cease to be praised, the whole attention of the human mind would be thrown into confusion, and human life would be overturned. Or an act that was done as it ought to be would be censured, and execrable madness—or, to speak more mildly, a most wretched error—would arise. Or, if the most truthful reason compels us, as it does, both to censure sins and to say that whatever is rightly censured is censured because it is not as it ought to be, then ask what a sinful nature owes, and you will find that it is rightly done; ask to whom it owes it, and you will find God.

For from the one from whom it received the ability to act rightly when it wishes, it also received the condition of being miserable if it does not act rightly, and blessed if it does.

44. Since no one surpasses the laws of the omnipotent Creator, the soul is not permitted not to repay what it owes. Either it repays by using well what it received, or it repays by losing what it refused to use well. Thus, if it does not repay by doing justice, it will repay by suffering misery, because in both cases that word “debt” is present.

This could also have been said in the following way: “If it does not repay by doing what it ought, it will repay by suffering what it ought.” [Col. 1293] These two things are not separated by any interval of time, as though at one time it did not do what it ought and at another time suffered what it ought; otherwise the universal beauty would be disfigured even for a moment, so that within it there would be the ugliness of sin without the beauty of punishment.

Whatever is now being punished most secretly is reserved for the future judgment, for its manifestation and for the keenest experience of misery. For just as one who does not keep watch sleeps, so everyone who does not do what he ought suffers without interruption what he ought, since the blessedness of justice is so great that no one can depart from it except into misery.

In every failure, therefore, either the things that fail were not given existence beyond that point, and there is no fault—as likewise, while they exist, there is no fault in their not having been given more existence than they possess—or they do not wish to be what they received the ability to be if they wished; and since being what they ought to be is good, guilt attaches if they do not wish it.

[Note: [Col. 1293] Erasmus and Louvain have “they would receive the ability to be.” But the manuscripts, in strong agreement, have “they received the ability to be,” and this is better; for it answers, in contracted form, the words of the preceding argument: “From the one from whom it received the ability to act rightly when it wishes.” The edition of Basel supports this reading, preferring “they received the ability to be.”]

### CHAPTER XVI  
### Our sins cannot be referred back to God

45. God, however, owes nothing to anyone, because he bestows everything freely. And if someone says that something is owed to him on account of his merits, certainly existence was not owed to him. For there was no one to whom it could be owed.

And yet what merit is it to turn toward him from whom you exist [Note: [Col. 1293] Erasmus and Louvain read “turn” (*convertere*) rather than “to turn” (*converti*). Six manuscripts have *converte*; eleven others more aptly have *converti*.], so that you may also become better through the one from whom you have existence? What, then, do you offer him in advance, so as to demand it as a debt, when, if you did not wish to turn toward him, nothing would be lacking to him, whereas he himself would be lacking to you—he without whom you would be nothing, and from whom you are something in such a way that, unless by turning yourself toward him you return to him what you are from him, you will indeed not be nothing, but you will nevertheless be miserable?

Everything, therefore, owes him, first, whatever it is, insofar as it is a nature; then, whatever better thing it can be if it wishes, whatever it has received in order to wish; and whatever it ought to be. No one, therefore, is guilty for what he did not receive; but he is justly guilty for not doing what he ought. He ought to do it if he received both free will and fully sufficient ability.

46. Yet so far is the Creator from being at fault when someone does not do what he ought that he is even to be praised, since the person suffers what he ought; and even in the very fact that the person is censured for not doing what he ought, the one to whom he owes it is praised.

For if you are praised when you see what you ought to do—although you see it only in him who is immutable Truth—how much more is he to be praised who both commanded you to will and supplied the ability, and did not permit you to refuse with impunity?

If each person owes what he received, and a human being was made in such a way that he necessarily sins, then he owes it to sin. When he sins, therefore, he does what he owes. But if it is a crime to say this, then no one is compelled by his own nature to sin [Note: [Col. 1293] See *Retractations* 1.9.3.]. Nor is anyone compelled by another’s nature. [Col. 1294]

For whoever suffers what he does not wish does not thereby sin. If he suffers justly, he does not sin in suffering unwillingly what he suffers, but he sinned in willingly acting in such a way that he justly suffered what he did not wish. If he suffers unjustly, how does he sin? For it is not a sin to suffer something unjustly, but to do something unjustly.

If, then, no one is compelled to sin either by his own nature or by another’s, it remains that sin is committed by one’s own will. But if you wish to attribute this to the Creator, you will absolve the sinner, who has committed nothing other than what was established by his Creator; and if the sinner is rightly defended, he has not sinned. Therefore, there is no reason to attribute it to the Creator.

Let us praise the Creator, then, if the sinner can be defended; let us praise him if the sinner cannot. If the sinner is justly defended, he is not a sinner—so praise the Creator. But if he cannot be defended, he is a sinner insofar as he has turned away from the Creator—so praise the Creator.

I therefore find no way—and affirm that no way can be found, and indeed that none exists—for our sins to be attributed to our Creator God, since I find him praiseworthy even in those sins: not only because he punishes them, but also because they occur when one departs from his truth.

E. I gladly accept and approve all this, and I entirely agree that it is wholly true that our sins can in no way rightly be attributed to our Creator.

### CHAPTER XVII  
### The will is the first cause of sin

47. Yet I would like to know, if this could be done, why that nature does not sin which God foreknew would not sin, and why this nature sins which was foreseen by him as going to sin. For I no longer think that God’s foreknowledge compels either this nature to sin or that one not to sin.

Yet if there were no cause, rational creation would not be distributed in this way: one part would never sin, another would persist in sinning, and another, as though midway between the two, would sometimes sin and sometimes turn toward doing what is right. What cause distributes it into these three divisions?

But I do not want the answer “the will.” I am asking for the cause of the will itself. For it is not without a cause that one will never wishes to sin, another never wishes not to sin, while some wills sometimes wish and sometimes do not wish, although all are of the same kind. This alone I seem to see: that this threefold division of the will of rational creation is not without a cause; but what the cause is, I do not know.

48. A. Since the will is the cause of sin, while you are asking for the cause of the will itself, if I can discover it, will you not also ask for the cause of whatever cause is discovered? What limit will there be to asking, what end to questioning and discussion, when you ought not to seek beyond the root?

Take care, then, lest you think anything could have been said more truly than what was said: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10)—that is, wanting more than is enough. But what is enough is determined by the measure required by nature for its preservation within its own kind.

For avarice, called in Greek *philargyria* (φιλαργυρία), is not to be understood as pertaining only to silver or coins, from which the name seems especially to derive its sound—for among the ancients coins were more often made of silver or of silver alloy—but as pertaining to all things that are desired immoderately, wherever anyone wants more than is enough.

This avarice is desire; [Col. 1295] and desire is a wrongful will. Therefore a wrongful will is the cause of all evils. If it were according to nature, it would preserve nature and would not be harmful to it; and for that reason it would not be wrongful.

Hence it follows that the root of all evils is not according to nature; and this is sufficient against all who wish to accuse natures. But if you seek the cause of this root, how will it be the root of all evils? For that cause which produces it will itself be the root; and when you have found it, as I said, you will seek the cause of that cause as well, with no limit to your inquiry.

49. But what cause could there be of the will before the will? Either it too is a will, and one does not depart from this root of the will; or it is not a will, and it has no sin. Therefore either the will itself is the first cause of sin, or no sin is the first cause of sin.

Nor is there anyone to whom sin can rightly be attributed except the sinner. Therefore there is no one to whom it can rightly be attributed except the willing person [Note: [Col. 1295] See *Retractations* 1.9.3.]. But I do not know why you wish to seek anything else.

Moreover, whatever that cause of the will may be, it is certainly either just or unjust. If it is just, whoever obeys it will not sin; if it is unjust, let him not obey it, and he will not sin.

### CHAPTER XVIII  
### Whether anyone sins in what cannot be avoided

50. Or perhaps it is violent and compels someone against his will? Shall we repeat the same points so many times? Recall what we have said above at such length about sin and free will. But if it is burdensome to commit everything to memory, retain this very brief point:

Whatever that cause of the will may be, if it cannot be resisted, one yields to it without sin; but if it can be resisted, one should not yield to it, and one will not sin.

Or perhaps it deceives the unwary? Then let him take care not to be deceived. Or is the deception so great that it cannot be avoided at all? If that is so, there are no sins. For who sins in what cannot possibly be avoided [Note: [Col. 1295] See the same work.]? But sin is committed; therefore it can be avoided [Note: [Col. 1295] At this point Pelagius, using the statement wrongly, is refuted by Augustine in *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 67, §80: “Therefore that cause, whatever it is, can be resisted; it certainly can. For this is why we ask for help when we say, ‘Do not lead us into temptation’; and we would not ask for this help if we believed that resistance were in no way possible. Sin can be avoided, but with the assistance of him who cannot be deceived.”].

51. Nevertheless, certain acts done through ignorance are also disapproved and judged to require correction, as we read in the divine authorities. For the Apostle says, “I received mercy because I acted in ignorance” (1 Tim. 1:13); and the prophet says, “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. 24:7).

Acts done under necessity are also to be disapproved, when a person wishes to act rightly but cannot. For where else do those statements come from: “For I do not do the good that I want, but I do the evil that I do not want”; and, “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find”; and, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Rom. 7:19; Gal. 5:17)?

But all these conditions belong to human beings who come from that condemnation of death. For if this is not the punishment of a human being but his nature, then none of these things are sins. If he has not departed from the condition in which he was naturally made, so that he could not be better, then, when he does these things, he does what he ought.

But if he would be a good person were he otherwise [Note: [Col. 1296] The printed editions have: “But if he were a good person, he would be otherwise,” omitting the second *si* (“if”), which we have restored from the manuscripts.], then, since he is as he is, he is not good, nor does he have it within his power to be good—whether because he does not see what he ought to be, or because he sees it but is unable to be what he sees he ought to be. Who could doubt that this is a punishment?

Every punishment, however, if it is just, is punishment for sin and is called a penalty. But if the punishment is unjust—since no one doubts that it is a punishment—it was imposed on the human being by some unjust ruler. Yet since it is madness to doubt God’s omnipotence and justice, this punishment is just and is being paid for some sin.

For no unjust ruler could either seize the human being, as though God were unaware, or extort him from God against his will, as though God were the weaker party, by frightening or fighting him, so as to torment the human being with an unjust punishment. It remains, therefore, that this just punishment comes from the condemnation of the human being [Note: [Col. 1296] See *Retractations* 1.9.5.].

52. Nor is it surprising that a person, either through ignorance, does not have free choice of will for choosing what he should rightly do, or, because of the resistance of carnal habit—which has in a certain way naturally grown strong through the violence of mortal succession—sees what should rightly be done and wishes to do it, yet cannot carry it out.

For it is the most just punishment of sin that a person lose what he refused to use well, although he could have used it without any difficulty if he had wished. That is, the person who knowingly does not do what is right loses the knowledge of what is right; and the person who, when he could, refused to do what is right loses the ability to do it when he wishes.

There are truly these two punishments for every sinful soul: ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance comes the degradation of error; from difficulty comes the affliction of torment.

But to approve falsehoods as truths, so that one errs unwillingly, and, because of the resistance and torment of the pain of the carnal bond, to be unable to abstain from lustful deeds—this is not the nature in which human beings were established, but the punishment of the condemned.

When we speak of free will for doing what is right, we are speaking of that condition in which the human being was made [Note: [Col. 1296] See the same passage.].

### CHAPTER XIX  
### Let those who sin not excuse ignorance and difficulty, vices transmitted to them from Adam’s sin

53. Here arises that question which people customarily gnaw at among themselves while murmuring, people who are ready to accuse anything whatsoever rather than themselves for sinning. They say:

“If Adam and Eve sinned, what have we wretched people done, that we should be born with the blindness of ignorance and the torments of difficulty, first going astray because we do not know what we ought to do; and then, when the commandments of justice begin to be disclosed to us, wishing to do them, yet unable, through I know not what necessity of carnal desire, to do so?” [Col. 1297]

They should be answered briefly: let them be quiet and stop murmuring against God. They might perhaps complain with justification if no human being ever emerged victorious over error and desire. But since the one who is present everywhere calls back the one who has turned away in many ways through the creation serving its Lord, teaches the believer, consoles the hopeful, exhorts the loving, helps the one who strives, and hears the one who prays, it is not counted as guilt against you that you are unwillingly ignorant, but that you neglect to seek what you do not know.

Nor is it counted against you that you do not bind up wounded members, but that you despise the one who wishes to heal you. These are your own sins. For no human being has been deprived of the ability to know that what is uselessly unknown should be usefully sought [Note: [Col. 1297] Louvain has: “to know how to seek usefully what one ignorantly does not know.” The older editions of Basel and Erasmus, and four manuscripts, have: “to know usefully what is uselessly unknown.” Eleven other manuscripts—including the Royal Codex, Victorinus, two Sorbonnes manuscripts, the Germanensis, the Gemmeticensis, and others—have: “to know that what is uselessly unknown should be usefully sought.” We choose this reading.]. Nor has anyone been deprived of the knowledge that weakness must be confessed humbly, so that the one who seeks and confesses may be helped by him who neither errs when he helps nor grows weary.

54. For that which someone does not do rightly through ignorance, and that which someone wishing to do what is right cannot do, are called sins because they derive their origin from that sin of free will: the preceding sin merited these subsequent conditions.

Just as we call “tongue” not only the member we move in the mouth when we speak, but also what follows from the movement of this member—that is, the form and sequence of words, according to which one language is called Greek and another Latin—so we call “sin” not only that which is properly called sin, since it is committed by free will and by one who knows, but also that which necessarily follows from the punishment of that sin.

We likewise use the word “nature” in different ways. In the proper sense, we speak of human nature, in which the first human being was made blameless within his kind; in another sense, we speak of this nature in which, as a result of the punishment of that condemned person, we are born mortal, ignorant, and subject to the flesh. In this sense the Apostle says, “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

### CHAPTER XX  
### Punitive defects have not unjustly descended to Adam’s descendants, whatever the true view of the origin of souls may finally be

55. That we are born from that first marriage with ignorance, difficulty, and mortality was most justly pleasing to God, the supreme governor of things, since, after they had sinned, they were plunged into error, misery, and death. Thus justice in punishment would appear in the origin of the human being, and mercy in deliverance would appear in his development.

For blessedness was not taken away from the first human being after his condemnation in such a way that fertility was also removed. From his offspring, although carnal and mortal, some beauty and adornment of its own kind could indeed be produced for the earth. But it would not have been equitable for him to produce offspring better than he himself was.

Rather, for each person to overcome through turning toward God the punishment that his origin had deserved through turning away, it was necessary not only that the willing person not be prevented but also that he be helped. For in this way too the Creator of things showed how easily a human being could have retained, if he had wished, what he was made to be, since his offspring could even surpass what it was born as.

[Col. 1298] 56. Further, if one soul was made from which the souls of all human beings born thereafter are derived, who can say that he did not sin when that first person sinned?

But if souls are made individually in each person who is born, it is not perverse—indeed it appears most fitting and perfectly ordered—that the evil merit of the earlier person should become the nature of the later one, and that the good merit of the later one should become the nature of the earlier one.

For what is unworthy if the Creator also wished to show in this way that the dignity of souls so greatly surpasses bodily creatures that one soul’s origin could be from the very degree to which another’s fall had been brought?

When that sinful soul has reached ignorance and difficulty, these are rightly called punishment because it was better before this punishment. If another soul begins in such a condition not only before its own sin but before its whole life, in the condition in which another became after a culpable life, it nevertheless possesses no small good for which it should give thanks to its Creator: its very origin and beginning is better than any perfect body.

For these are no insignificant goods: not only that it is a soul, by which nature it already surpasses every body, but also that it has the capacity, with the Creator’s help, to cultivate itself and, through devoted effort, to acquire and grasp all the virtues by which it may be freed both from tormenting difficulty and from blinding ignorance.

If this is so, ignorance and difficulty in souls at birth will not be the punishment of sin, but an exhortation to progress and the beginning of perfection. For even before any merit from good works, it is no small gift to have received a natural judgment by which one prefers wisdom to error and rest to difficulty, so as to reach these things not by being born but by striving.

If it refuses to act, however, it will rightly be held guilty of sin, as one that has not used well the capacity it received. For although it was born in ignorance and difficulty, it is not constrained by any necessity to remain in what it was born as.

Nor could anyone except God almighty be the creator of such souls [Note: [Col. 1298] Louvain reads “were almighty”; Basel and Erasmus, supported by the manuscripts, read “to be almighty.” The words “and, loving them, restores them,” found in all printed editions, are absent from the manuscripts.]—of souls whom, when he is not loved, he himself makes; whom, loving them, he restores; and whom, when he is loved, he perfects; who grants existence to those who do not yet exist, and grants blessedness to those who love him from whom they are.

57. But if souls already existing somewhere in a divine secret are sent by the Lord God to inhabit and govern the bodies of those being born, they are sent for this purpose: that by managing well the body born from the punishment of sin—that is, from the mortality of the first human being—by disciplining it through the virtues and subjecting it to the most ordered and lawful service, they may themselves, in due order and at the appropriate time, prepare a place for heavenly incorruption.

When they enter this life and undertake mortal members to bear, they must also undergo both forgetfulness of their former life and the labor of the present one. Hence comes ignorance and difficulty, which in the first human being was the punishment of mortality for measuring out the misery of the soul [Note: [Col. 1298] Four manuscripts have “for relieving the misery of the soul.”]; [Col. 1299] but in these souls it is the gateway of service for restoring the body’s incorruption.

For in this way too these conditions are not called sins except because flesh descended from a sinner imposes this ignorance and difficulty upon the souls that come to it; neither of these conditions should be attributed as blame to the souls or to the Creator.

For he gave them both the ability to act well in laborious duties and the way of faith amid the blindness of forgetfulness. Above all, he gave them that judgment by which every soul acknowledges that what it uselessly does not know must be sought, that it must persevere in dutiful labors to overcome the difficulty of doing what is right, and that help must be implored from the Creator, so that he may assist the one who strives [Note: [Col. 1299] Basel reads, “especially that indication, because every soul”; this was also Louvain’s reading, with *because* changed to *that*. Erasmus and the manuscripts read, “that judgment … which every soul,” perhaps because scribes frequently wrote *which* for *that*.].

He commanded that one should strive either outwardly through the law or inwardly through an address to the heart, and he prepares the glory of the most blessed city for those who triumph over the one who, through wicked persuasion, first brought the human being into this misery—a misery they accept in order to conquer him through excellent faith.

For it is no small glory to wage war against the devil by undergoing the very punishment in which he boasts that he led the human being whom he conquered. But whoever, captivated by love of this life, neglects this will in no way justly attribute the disgrace of his desertion to the command of his king. Rather, under the Lord of all, he will be assigned a place among the devil’s forces, because he loved the shameful pay by which the devil induced him to desert his camp.

58. But if souls situated elsewhere are not sent by the Lord God, but come of their own accord to inhabit bodies, then it is already easy to see that whatever ignorance and difficulty follows is attributable to their own will, and that the Creator cannot in any way be blamed for it.

For even if he had sent them—since he did not take away from them, even in ignorance and difficulty, the free will to ask, seek, and strive, and since he is shown to give to those who ask, reveal to those who seek, and open to those who knock—he would be entirely free from blame.

He would have established that this ignorance and difficulty should be overcome by the diligent and well-disposed as a means to the crown of glory. But for the negligent, who wish to defend their sins on the basis of weakness, he would not charge ignorance and difficulty themselves as a crime; rather, because they preferred to remain in them instead of reaching truth and ease through diligent seeking and learning, and through humble confession and prayer, he would punish them with a just penalty.

### CHAPTER XXI  
### The error concerning this matter is harmful

59. Of these four opinions concerning the soul—whether souls come by descent from a parent soul, whether new souls are made individually for each person being born, or whether souls already existing somewhere are either divinely sent into the bodies of those being born or slip into them of their own accord—none should be rashly affirmed [Note: [Col. 1299] Augustine cites this passage in *Letter* 166.7, to Jerome, in these words: “Some years ago, when I was writing certain books on Free Will, which have come into the hands of many and are now possessed by very many people, I thought that the four opinions concerning the soul’s embodiment should be treated in such a way that, whichever of them were true, it would not impede my purpose at that time, by which I was striving with all the strength I could against those who attempt to introduce a nature of evil possessing its own principle against God—that is, against the Manichaeans. For at that time I had not yet heard anything about the Priscillianists … Therefore I did not add the fifth opinion, which you mentioned among the others in your letter.”].

[Col. 1300] Either this question has not yet been unfolded and clarified, in proportion to its obscurity and complexity, by Catholic interpreters of the divine Books; or, if this has already been done, writings of this kind have not yet come into our hands.

Let faith simply remain present that we think nothing false or unworthy concerning the substance of the Creator. For we are traveling toward him by the way of devotion. If, then, we think of him as other than he is, our purpose will compel us to go not toward blessedness but toward vanity.

But if we think something about the creature otherwise than it is, there is no danger, provided we do not hold it as something known and grasped. For we are not commanded to move toward the creature in order to become blessed, but toward the Creator himself. If we are persuaded to think of him as other than we ought and other than the reality is, we are deceived by a most pernicious error.

For by proceeding toward that which either does not exist or, if it exists, does not make people blessed, no one can arrive at the blessed life.

60. But in order to contemplate the eternity of truth, so that we may be able to enjoy and cleave to it, a way suited to our weakness has been provided through temporal things: insofar as is sufficient for those journeying toward eternal things, we are to believe what is past and what is future. This discipline of faith, so that it may prevail by authority, is governed by divine mercy. As far as the creature is concerned, the present is experienced as something passing away, because of the mutability and changeability of body and soul. Whatever we do not experience in these matters, we cannot grasp by any kind of knowledge.

Whatever, therefore, we are told by divine authority to believe concerning any creatures, whether past or future—although some of these things passed away before we could experience them, while others have not yet reached our senses—must nevertheless be believed without hesitation, because they are of great value in strengthening our hope and arousing our love, while they commend to us, through the most orderly succession of times, the fact that God does not neglect our liberation.

But whoever assumes the role of divine authority while teaching error is refuted most particularly if he is convicted either of believing or asserting that there exists, apart from God’s creation, some mutable form, or some mutable form within the substance of God, and if he maintains that God’s substance is either something more or something less than the Trinity. All Christian vigilance is devoted to understanding this Trinity piously and soberly, and all Christian progress is directed toward it. It is not appropriate here to discuss the unity and equality of this Trinity, or the particular distinctiveness of the individual Persons within it.

For to recall certain things concerning the Lord God, the author, fashioner, and ordering principle of all things—things pertaining to the most salutary faith, by which the purpose of the person who is still being nourished and is beginning to raise himself from earthly things toward heavenly things may be usefully assisted—is both very easy to do and has already been done by many. But to treat this entire question and handle it in such a way that every human understanding might be subjected to clear reasoning, insofar as that is granted in this life, does not appear to be an undertaking sufficiently manageable or easy for anyone—not merely in speech, but even in thought.

Now, therefore, let us carry out what we have undertaken, to the extent that we are helped and permitted to do so. Whatever, as far as the creature is concerned, is reported to us as having happened in the past or is announced as going to happen in the future, insofar as it is capable of commending the integrity of religion by stirring us to the most sincere love of God and neighbor, must be believed without hesitation. Against unbelievers, however, such things should be defended only to the extent that either the weight of authority crushes their unbelief, or it is shown to them, as far as possible, first, that it is not foolish to believe such things, and then, that it is foolish not to believe them.

Nevertheless, false doctrine ought to be refuted not so much concerning past and future things as concerning present things, and especially concerning things that are immutable; and, insofar as possible, it ought to be convicted by clear reasoning.

61. Certainly, within the succession of temporal things [Note: [Col. 1301] Bad. Er. and seven manuscripts read: “Certainly, in the misery of temporal things.”], expectation of the future is to be preferred to inquiry into the past. For even in the divine Books, the things narrated as past display either a foreshadowing of future things, or a promise, or a testimony.

Indeed, even in matters belonging to this life, whether prosperous or adverse, no one is especially concerned with what he has been; but all the turmoil of his concerns gathers around what he hopes will be in the future. By some deep and natural sense, the things that have happened to us, because they are past, are regarded in relation to happiness and misery as though they had never happened.

What harm, then, does it do me if I do not know when I began to exist, since I know that I exist and do not despair that I shall exist in the future? I do not dwell upon the past, fearing as though it were a most pernicious error that I might think of it otherwise than it was; rather, I direct my course toward what I shall be, guided by the mercy of my Creator.

With regard, then, to what I shall be and to the One with whom I shall be, I must be exceedingly wary of error if I believe or think otherwise than the truth requires and reality is. Otherwise, I may fail to prepare what is necessary for myself, or, while one thing appears to me to be another, I may be unable to arrive at the very end toward which I have resolved to strive.

Thus, just as it would do me no harm in procuring clothing if I had forgotten the past winter, but it would harm me if I did not believe that future cold was approaching, so it will do my soul no harm if it has forgotten what it may have endured, provided that it carefully considers and retains what it is warned to prepare for from now on.

And just as, for example, it would do someone sailing to Rome no harm if he had forgotten from which shore he had cast off, provided that he knew from his present location where to direct the prow; but it would be of no benefit to remember the shore from which he had begun his journey if, believing something false about the Roman harbor, he ran into the rocks—so neither will it harm me if I do not retain the beginning of the temporal course of my life, provided that I know at what end I shall find rest. Nor would any memory or conjecture concerning the beginning of my life benefit me if, thinking falsely about God himself, who alone is the end of the soul’s labors, I were to rush upon the rocks of error [Col. 1302].

62. Nor should this discussion be understood to mean that we wish to prevent anyone who is able from seeking, according to the divinely inspired Scriptures, whether the soul is propagated from another soul, whether individual souls are made in each living being at the moment of its animation, whether they are sent from elsewhere by divine command to govern and animate the body, or whether they enter it by their own will.

Such matters may properly be considered and examined either when the investigation of some necessary question demands it, or when leisure is granted for seeking and discussing them after matters of greater necessity have been addressed.

Rather, I have said these things so that no one, in such a matter, may rashly become angry with someone who does not yield to his opinion, perhaps because of a more humane doubt; or, even if someone has grasped something certain and clear concerning the matter, may not therefore suppose that another has lost hope of the future because he does not recall the beginning of the past.

## Chapter XXII — If ignorance and difficulty are natural to man, this does not deprive the Creator of praise

63. However this matter may stand—whether it should be omitted altogether, or postponed for now and considered elsewhere—the present question is not thereby prevented from making clear that souls pay the penalties for their sins under the utterly blameless, most just, unshaken, and immutable majesty and substance of the Creator. As we have discussed at length, these sins must be attributed solely to their own will, and no further cause of their sins should be sought [Note: [Col. 1302] This is the reading of the manuscripts and older editions. Lov. reads: “and no inner cause.”].

64. But if ignorance and difficulty are natural, the soul begins from them to make progress and to advance toward knowledge and rest, until the blessed life is perfected in it. If, by its own will, it neglects this progress in excellent studies and piety—the opportunity for which has not been denied to it—it is justly plunged into a more serious ignorance and difficulty, which are now penal, through a most fitting and appropriate ordering of things among inferior realities [Note: [Col. 1302] The printed editions read, “with the inferior things ordering”; fifteen manuscripts read, “ordered among inferior things.”].

For the soul is not charged with guilt because it naturally does not know or naturally cannot do something, but because it has not made the effort to know, and has not devoted appropriate diligence to acquiring the facility necessary for doing what is right.

For an infant, not knowing and not being able to speak is natural. This ignorance and difficulty of speech is not merely blameless according to the rules of grammarians; it is also pleasing and attractive to human affection. The infant has not neglected through any fault to acquire that ability, nor through any fault lost what it had acquired.

Therefore, if our happiness were established in eloquence, and if an error in the sounds of speech were regarded as a crime in the same way as an error in the actions of life, no one would be accused on the ground that he had begun as an infant in order to attain eloquence. But he would rightly be condemned if, through the perversity of his will, he either fell back into infancy or remained there.

So now, too, if ignorance of truth and difficulty in doing what is right are natural to man, and if from them he begins to rise toward the blessedness of wisdom and peace, no one rightly blames him for this natural beginning. But if he refuses to make progress, or wishes to fall backward from progress, he will justly and deservedly pay the penalty.

65. The Creator of the soul is praised everywhere: either because from its very beginnings he initiated it toward the capacity for the highest good, or because he assists its progress, or because he fills and perfects it as it progresses, or because he orders, by a most just judgment according to its merits, the soul that sins—that is, the soul that either refuses from its beginnings to raise itself toward perfection or falls back after making some progress.

He did not create it evil merely because it is not yet as great as it received the capacity to become through progress. All the perfections of bodies are far inferior to its beginning; nevertheless, anyone who judges soundly about things considers them praiseworthy in their own kind.

That the soul does not know what it ought to do is due to the fact that it has not yet received this knowledge. But it will also receive it if it makes good use of what it has received. It has received the ability to seek piously and diligently, if it wishes.

And when, recognizing what it ought to do, it is not immediately able to accomplish it, it has not yet received this ability either. For one part of it, the higher part, has gone ahead in perceiving the good that it ought to do; but another, slower and carnal part, does not follow at once into agreement with that judgment. Through this very difficulty the soul is admonished to implore the One who assists its perfection, just as it recognizes him as the author of its beginning.

Thus he becomes dearer to it, since it is not raised by its own powers, but by the mercy of the One whose goodness gave it existence. The dearer he is to it, the more firmly it rests in him, and the more abundantly it enjoys his eternity.

If we do not rightly call a young and undeveloped shoot of a tree sterile, even though it passes several summers without fruit until, at the appropriate time, it brings forth its fertility, why should we not praise the author of the soul with due piety if he grants it such a beginning that, by study and progress, it may reach the fruitfulness of wisdom and righteousness, and grants it such dignity that he places it even within its own power, if it wishes, to strive toward blessedness?

## Chapter XXIII — The uninstructed complain unjustly about the death of infants and the bodily tortures by which they are afflicted. What pain is

66. The uninstructed commonly bring a certain accusation against this discussion concerning the deaths of infants and certain bodily tortures by which we often see them afflicted.

They say: “What need was there for someone to be born who, before undertaking any merit in life, departed from life? Or what place will be assigned at the future judgment to someone who has no place among the righteous, since he did nothing rightly, nor among the wicked, since he committed no sin?”

The answer is that, in the encompassing unity of the universe and in the most orderly connection of the whole creation through places and times, no human being of any kind can have been created superfluously, when not even a leaf of a tree is created superfluously. But it is certainly superfluous to inquire about the merits of someone who has earned no merit [Col. 1304].

There is no need to fear that there may have been a kind of intermediate life between righteous action and sin, while there cannot be an intermediate judgment between reward and punishment.

67. In this connection people also commonly investigate what benefit the sacrament of Christ’s baptism provides to infants, since they usually die after receiving it, before they could have been able to understand anything concerning it.

In this matter it is rightly and piously believed that the faith of those by whom the infant is brought for consecration benefits the infant. The most salutary authority of the Church also commends this teaching, so that each person may perceive from it what benefit his own faith provides, since the faith of another can also be applied for the benefit of those who do not yet possess faith of their own.

For what benefit did the faith of the widow’s son provide him—a faith that, since he was dead, he certainly did not possess—when nevertheless his mother’s faith benefited him so that he might rise again? (Luke 7:12–15.) How much more, then, can another’s faith assist an infant whose own unbelief cannot be held against him?

68. As for the bodily tortures by which infants are afflicted, though they have no sins on account of their age: if the souls by which they are animated did not begin to exist before the human beings themselves began to exist, then people usually set aside their greater complaint and their supposedly compassionate objection when they say: “What evil have they done that they should suffer these things?”

This is as though innocence could be a merit before anyone is capable of doing harm. But when God accomplishes some good in correcting adults by chastising them through the pains and deaths of their little ones whom they love, why should such things not happen, since, once they have passed away, they will count as though they had not happened to those in whom they happened? As for those on whose account they happened, they will either become better, if, corrected by temporal troubles, they choose to live more rightly, or they will have no excuse at the punishment of the future judgment if they refuse to turn their desire toward eternal life through the anguish of this life.

Who knows what God reserves for the infants themselves, in the hiddenness of his judgments, as a good recompense? Their sufferings may break the hardness of adults, exercise faith, or test compassion; yet who knows what God reserves for the infants themselves, who, although they have done nothing rightly, nevertheless suffered these things without having committed any sin?

For it is not without reason that the Church commends those infants who were killed when the Lord Jesus Christ was being sought by Herod in order to be killed (Matt. 2:16), having received them into the honor of the martyrs [Note: [Col. 1304] See Letter 166 to Jerome, §18.].

69. These faultfinders, who are not the most diligent investigators but the most talkative disseminators of such questions, also commonly trouble the faith of the less instructed concerning the pains and labors of animals. They say: “What evil have even animals deserved, that they should suffer such troubles? Or what good do they hope for, since they are subjected to such troubles?”

They say or think this because they judge things most unjustly. Unable to contemplate what and how great the highest good is, they want everything to be such as they imagine the highest good to be. For they cannot conceive of the highest good except in terms of the highest bodies, which are heavenly and less subject to corruption. Therefore, they demand in the most disorderly way that the bodies of beasts should suffer neither death nor any corruption, as though, being the lowest things, they were not mortal—or as though they were evil because heavenly things are better [Col. 1305].

But the pain that animals feel commends a certain power of even animal souls that is wonderful and praiseworthy in its own kind. For this very fact makes sufficiently clear how eager they are for unity in governing and animating their bodies.

What else is pain than a certain sense that cannot tolerate division or corruption? Hence it becomes clearer than daylight how avid of unity and tenacious of it is the soul in the totality of its body. It is not directed toward the bodily affection that undermines its unity and integrity willingly or indifferently, but rather with resistance and struggle, and it is distressed by that affection.

The appetite for unity possessed by the lower animal creatures would not therefore be apparent without the pain of animals. And if it were not apparent, we would be less admonished than we ought to be that all these things have been established by the highest, sublime, and ineffable unity of the Creator.

70. Indeed, if you attend piously and diligently, every form and movement of creation that falls under human reflection speaks to our instruction. Through diverse movements and affections, as though through a variety of languages, everything cries out and admonishes us from every side that the Creator must be known.

There is no thing among those that experience neither pain nor pleasure that does not attain the beauty of its own kind, or at least some stability proper to its nature, through a certain unity.

Likewise, there is no thing among those that experience either the discomforts of pain or the attractions of pleasure that does not, by the very fact that it flees pain and seeks pleasure, confess that it flees separation and seeks unity.

And in rational souls themselves, every appetite for knowledge—a source of joy to that nature—refers everything it perceives to unity, and in error flees nothing other than being confused by incomprehensible ambiguity. But what makes every ambiguity troublesome except that it lacks a firm unity?

From this it is clear that all things—whether they give offense or are offended, whether they delight or are delighted—suggest and proclaim the unity of the Creator.

But if ignorance and difficulty, from which this life necessarily begins, are not natural to souls, it remains that they have either been undertaken as a duty or imposed as a punishment. I think enough has already been said about these matters.

## Chapter XXIV — The first man was not created foolish, but capable of wisdom. What foolishness is

71. Therefore, what sort of being the first man was made should be investigated more than how his posterity was propagated.

Those who say, “If the first man was made wise, why was he deceived? But if he was made foolish, how is God not the author of vices, since foolishness is the greatest vice?” seem to themselves to pose the question very cleverly.

It is as though human nature admitted no intermediate condition between foolishness and wisdom—some affection that could rightly be called neither foolishness nor wisdom.

A person begins to be either foolish or wise, so that he must necessarily be called one or the other, when he is already able, unless he neglects it, to possess wisdom, and thus his will becomes guilty of vicious foolishness.

No one is so foolish as to call an infant foolish, although it would be even more absurd if he wished to call the infant wise. Just as an infant, although already a human being, can be called neither foolish nor wise, and this shows that human nature admits something intermediate that one could rightly call neither foolishness nor wisdom, so if someone were animated by the kind of condition possessed by those who lack wisdom through negligence, no one would rightly call him foolish if he saw that he was such by nature rather than through fault.

For foolishness is not every kind of ignorance concerning things to be sought or avoided, but a vicious ignorance.

Thus we do not call an irrational animal foolish, because it has not received the capacity to become wise. Yet we often use names by analogy, without using them properly. For although blindness is the greatest defect of the eyes, it is not a defect in newborn puppies, nor can it properly be called blindness in them.

72. If, then, man was made in such a way that, although he was not yet wise, he could nevertheless receive a command—which he certainly ought to obey—then it is neither surprising that he could be deceived, nor unjust that he paid the penalty for disobeying the command. Nor is his Creator the author of vices, because not yet possessing wisdom was not yet a human vice, if he had not yet received what would enable him to possess it.

Nevertheless, he possessed something by which, if he wished to use it well, he could rise to what he did not possess. For it is one thing to be rational and another to be wise.

By reason a person becomes capable of receiving a command, to which he owes faith so that he may do what is commanded. Just as rational nature receives a command, so observance of the command produces wisdom.

What nature is in relation to receiving a command, the will is in relation to observing it. And just as rational nature is, as it were, the merit by which a command may be received, so observance of the command is the merit by which wisdom may be received.

From the moment a person becomes capable of receiving a command, he becomes capable of sinning. Before becoming wise, he sins in two ways: either by failing to prepare himself to receive the command, or, after receiving it, by failing to observe it.

A wise person sins if he turns away from wisdom. For just as the command does not come from the one to whom it is given but from the one who gives it, so wisdom does not come from the one who is illuminated but from the one who illuminates.

Why, then, should the Creator of man not be praised? Man is a good thing, and is better than cattle, because he is capable of receiving a command. He is better still when he has received the command; better again when he has obeyed it; and better than all these conditions when he is blessed by the eternal light of wisdom.

Sin, however, is evil, whether in neglecting to receive the command, in neglecting to observe it, or in neglecting to preserve the contemplation of wisdom.

From this it follows that even if the first man was created wise [Note: [Col. 1306] Lov. reads, “had been created.” Bad. Er. and most manuscripts more correctly read, “was created.” Of these, the Royal Codex adds after “could be deceived”: “and could sin.” Er. has in the margin “had been created,” as Lov., and “could sin” instead of “could be deceived.” M.], he could nevertheless be deceived. Since that sin lay within free will, punishment followed it under the just law of God [Note: [Col. 1306] Several manuscripts read: “a just punishment followed it under the divine law.”].

The apostle Paul says likewise: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” [Col. 1307]. Pride turned them away from wisdom, and foolishness followed that turning away. Foolishness is a kind of blindness, as he also says: “Their foolish heart was darkened” (Rom. 1:22, 21).

But from what did this darkening arise, if not from turning away from the light of wisdom? And from what did this turning away arise, if not from the fact that the one for whom God is the good wished to be his own good, just as God is his own good?

Thus he says: “My soul is troubled within me” (Ps. 41:7); and, “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5).

73. This troubles those who consider the matter and ask: “Did the first man depart from God because of foolishness? Or did he become foolish by departing?”

If you answer that he departed from wisdom through foolishness, he appears to have been foolish before he departed from wisdom, so that foolishness would have been the cause of his departure. Again, if you answer that he became foolish by departing, they ask whether he acted foolishly or wisely in departing.

If he acted wisely, he acted rightly and committed no sin; but if foolishly, they say, foolishness was already in him, and it caused him to depart. For he could not do something foolishly without foolishness.

From this it is clear that there is an intermediate condition by which one passes from wisdom to foolishness, and that this passage cannot be said to have been made either foolishly or wisely. This can be understood by contrast from human beings situated in this life.

No mortal becomes wise except by passing from foolishness to wisdom. But if this passage occurs foolishly, then it is certainly not made well—which would be utterly absurd to say. If it occurs wisely, then wisdom was already in the person before he passed into wisdom, which is equally absurd.

It follows that there is an intermediate condition that can be called neither one nor the other. Likewise, when the first man passed from the height of wisdom into foolishness, that passage was neither foolish nor wise.

It is like sleep and waking: falling asleep is not the same as sleeping, nor waking up the same as being awake, but each is a passage from one state to the other. The difference is that these things usually happen without the will, whereas the former passage never occurs except through the will; hence the most just recompenses follow it.

## Chapter XXV — What touches rational nature when it turns its attention toward evil

74. Since the will is not attracted to doing anything unless by something perceived, while what each person chooses or rejects lies within his power, but what perceived object touches him does not lie within his power, we must acknowledge, on the basis of what has been said above and below, that the soul is touched by perceived objects both from above and from below, so that the rational substance may choose from either what it wills, and that either misery or blessedness follows according to the merit of its choice.

In paradise, for example, the perceived object from above was God’s command; the perceived object from below was the serpent’s suggestion. Neither what the Lord commanded nor what the serpent suggested was within the man’s power.

How free and released from every constraint of difficulty a person is when established in the health of wisdom, and how he can refuse the attractions of lower things, may also be understood from this: even foolish people overcome such attractions when they are going to pass into wisdom, despite the distress involved in abandoning the diseased sweetness of destructive habits.

[Col. 1308] 75. At this point one may ask: if perceived objects were present to man from both sides—one from God’s command and the other from the serpent’s suggestion—whence was the devil himself prompted to the design of impiety that he might fall from the lofty seats? 

For if he had been touched by no perceived object, he would not have chosen to do what he did. If nothing had come into his mind, he could in no way have turned his attention toward wickedness.

From where, then, did there come into his mind whatever it was that came into his mind, so that he might devise the acts by which he would become a devil from a good angel? For whoever wills certainly wills something; and unless he is prompted either externally through bodily sensation or in hidden ways by something entering his mind, he cannot will.

We must therefore distinguish kinds of perceived objects. One kind proceeds from the will of someone offering persuasion, as in the devil’s case; by consenting to this, the man sinned. The other proceeds from things lying beneath either the soul’s attention or the bodily senses.

What lies beneath the soul’s attention is, apart from the immutability of the Trinity—which does not lie beneath it but rather towers above it—first, the soul itself, through which we also perceive that we live; then the body that it governs. Thus, whenever some action is to be performed, the soul moves the limb required for the action when it is needed.

Whatever is corporeal lies beneath the bodily senses.

76. For the soul to contemplate supreme wisdom—which is certainly not itself, since wisdom is immutable—and also to contemplate itself, even though it is changeable, so that it in some sense comes into its own mind, this occurs only through the difference by which it is not God, yet is something that can please after God.

It is better when, out of love for the immutable God, it forgets itself, or utterly despises itself in comparison with him. But if, as though confronted with itself, it pleases itself in order to imitate God perversely, wishing to enjoy its own power, it becomes smaller in proportion as it desires to be greater.

This is what is meant by: “The beginning of every sin is pride,” and “The beginning of man’s pride is apostasy from God” (Ecclus. 10:15, 14).

To the devil’s pride was added a most malevolent envy, by which he persuaded man to this pride, through which he perceived that he himself had been condemned.

Thus it happened that punishment came upon man as corrective rather than destructive, so that the Lord might offer himself to the one to whom the devil had offered himself as an example of pride, as an example of humility. Through him eternal life is promised to us.

When Christ’s blood has been bestowed on us, may we cleave to our liberator with such love after unutterable labors and miseries, and be borne away into him by such radiance of his, that no perceived object from below may turn us away from the higher vision. Even if something were suggested to our attention by the appetite for lower things, the eternal condemnation and torment of the devil would call us back.

77. So great is the beauty of righteousness, so great the delight of eternal light—that is, of immutable truth and wisdom—that even if we were not permitted to remain in it longer than the duration of a single day, then, for this reason alone, innumerable years of this life, filled with pleasures and overflowing temporal goods, would rightly and deservedly be despised [Col. 1309].

For it was not falsely or with little feeling that it was said: “For one day in your courts is better than thousands” (Ps. 83:11). This may also be understood in another sense, so that the thousands are understood as thousands of days in the mutability of time, while the name “one day” signifies the immutability of eternity.

I do not know that I have omitted anything which, insofar as the Lord has deigned to grant it, is lacking in my response to your questions. Yet even if something has occurred to you, the limits of the book now compel us to bring it to an end and at last to rest from this discussion.

[Col. 1309]

# The Two Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, On the Morals of the Catholic Church and On the Morals of the Manichaeans

[Note: [Col. 1309] Written toward the beginning of the year of Christ 388, and perhaps published in 389.]

[Note: [Col. 1313] The book On the Morals of the Catholic Church was collated against the Vatican and Royal manuscripts; three Sorbonic manuscripts; two Navarric manuscripts; two Victorine manuscripts; one from the larger community of the Augustinians of Paris; the Theoderican manuscript, of excellent quality; and the Gemmetic, Arnulfian, Cistercian, Royal-Mont, and Vedastine manuscripts; against the readings of five Belgian manuscripts published by Lov.; and against the editions of Bad., Er., Lov., and the more recent edition of Arnald.]

[Note: [Col. 1313] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the Retractations and the Confessions. M.]

(C)

## Notice Concerning the Two Following Books

[Note: [Col. 1309] Before these two books, the Benedictine edition places two books On Genesis against the Manichaeans. We have decided to transfer them in their entirety to volume 3, where Scripture is discussed. M.]

[Note: [Col. 1309] See Book 1, chapter 7, of the Retractations, col. 591, beginning with the words “Already baptized,” §1, through col. 594, §6, ending with the words “I think we have acted.” M.]

The two books On the Morals of the Catholic Church and On the Morals of the Manichaeans follow. Although Augustine places them, in the first book of his Retractations, before the other works he composed at Rome shortly after his baptism, someone might perhaps object that they were published in this order.

First, at the beginning of the first book, he says that in other books he had sufficiently dealt with how one might answer the impious and ignorant attacks of the Manichaeans against the Old Testament. The work On Genesis against the Manichaeans, placed before these books, is relevant here; for he plainly indicates that this work was first published against those same heretics after his return to Africa, as he states in Book 1, chapter 10, of the Retractations.

Moreover, near the end of the second book he speaks in a way that may suggest that he had already left the city of Rome. Finally, in chapter 12 of the same book he reports something that he had recently heard at Carthage.

Nevertheless, these considerations do not make Augustine’s statement doubtful when he says that, after he had already been baptized and while he was at Rome, he wrote the following books—thus toward the end of the year of Christ 387, when he withdrew to that city, or certainly at the beginning of the following year, a large part of which he spent there.

The matters can be reconciled in this way: the books may have been written at Rome, while their publication or completion was postponed for some time. Whatever the truth may be concerning this matter, an understanding of the errors of the Manichaeans, as set out in the preceding work, will assist in understanding these books.

In the first book, On the Morals of the Catholic Church, Augustine is going to teach that the highest good, to which our morals ought to be referred, is nothing other than God. We must strive toward him with the greatest love, as is taught in the Catholic Church by the authority of the Old Testament as well as the New.

He then briefly treats the duties of charity toward one’s neighbor, and finally recounts examples of continence and genuinely Christian conduct that shone forth among the members of the Catholic Church.

In the second book, which he entitled On the Morals of the Manichaeans, he first refutes the error of these heretics concerning the origin and nature of evil. He then examines the three seals of mouth, hands, and breast, as they called them, by which they concealed their impious morals. He rebukes their superstitious abstinence and finally recalls certain crimes discovered among them.

# Book One: On the Morals of the Catholic Church

Augustine begins by establishing that those morals by which a holy life is lived in the Church ought to be referred to the highest good of man, that is, God. We must strive toward him with the greatest love, and this doctrine is confirmed in the Catholic Church by the authority of both Testaments.

He shows that the four virtues are named from various forms of the soul’s love of God. He discusses the duties of charity toward one’s neighbor and finally recounts examples of continence and genuinely Christian conduct that shone forth among the members of the Catholic Church.

[Col. 1309]

## Chapter I — How he will expose the cosmetics of the Manichaeans. The two means by which the Manichaeans deceive

[Col. 1309]

1. In other books, I think, I have sufficiently dealt with how we may answer the attacks of the Manichaeans, by which they ignorantly and impiously assail the Law called the Old Testament and, amid the applause of the ignorant, display themselves in empty boasting. I can also mention the matter briefly here.

Who, if only moderately sane, would not easily understand that an interpretation of the Scriptures should be sought from those who profess to be their teachers? It can happen—indeed, it always happens—that many things seem absurd to the unlearned, but when they are explained by the more learned, they appear worthy of praise, and are received with greater sweetness precisely because they were opened with greater difficulty when closed.

This is generally what happens with the sacred books of the Old Testament, provided that the person offended by them seeks a pious teacher of those books rather than an impious mutilator of them, and is imbued first with the devotion of one who seeks than with the recklessness of one who condemns.

Nor should someone lose hope that knowledge of the truth exists merely because, while wishing to learn these things, he happens to encounter bishops, presbyters, or any other leaders and ministers of the Catholic Church who either habitually avoid laying bare the mysteries indiscriminately or, content with simple faith, have not taken care to investigate higher matters.

The truth is not absent wherever not everyone from whom it is sought is able to teach, nor where not everyone who seeks is worthy to learn. Both diligence and piety must therefore be applied: through the one we shall find those who know; through the other we shall become worthy to know.

2. But since there are two chief attractions of the Manichaeans by which the unwary are deceived into wishing to have them as teachers—the one, when they criticize the Scriptures, whether because they misunderstand them or because they want them to be misunderstood; the other, when they present the appearance of a chaste and remarkable continence of life—this book will contain our judgment concerning life and conduct, in agreement with Catholic teaching. In it, perhaps, it will become clear both how easy it is to feign virtue and how difficult it is to possess it.

I shall maintain this approach, if I can, so that I may not attack those diseases of theirs, which are very well known to me, as severely as they attack what they do not know; for I wish them to be healed, if possible, rather than assaulted. I shall also draw from Scripture those testimonies which they must believe—namely, from the New Testament—though I shall not produce any of the things they are accustomed to say were inserted when they are pressed by great difficulties; rather, I shall say those things which they are compelled both to approve and to praise. Nor shall I leave unintroduced any testimony drawn from apostolic teaching without matching it with a similar passage from the Old Testament. Thus, if at last they wish to awaken, laying aside the obstinacy of their dreams and breathing toward the light of Christian faith, they may perceive both how un-Christian is the life they display and how truly Christ’s is the Scripture they tear apart.

## CHAPTER II—He first argues by reasoning, accommodating himself to the vicious custom of the Manichaeans

3. Where, then, shall I begin—with authority or with reason? The order of nature is certainly such that, when we learn something, authority precedes reason. For reason may appear weak when, after it has been given, it then adopts authority by which it may be strengthened. But because the minds of human beings, darkened by the habit of the darkness with which they are veiled in the night of sins and vices, cannot direct a suitable gaze toward the clarity and sincerity of reason, it has most beneficially been arranged that authority should lead their wavering sight into the light of truth, as though shaded by the branches of humanity.

But since we are dealing with people who think, speak, and act contrary to all order, and who say nothing more emphatically than that a reason must first be given, I shall indulge them and undertake what, I admit, is faulty in debate. For I am pleased, as far as I can, to imitate the gentleness of my Lord Jesus Christ, who even clothed himself with the evil of death itself, in order to strip it from us.

## CHAPTER III—Blessed is the one who enjoys what is best for a human being. What is best for a human being. Two conditions of the highest good: first, that nothing is better than it; second, that it is such that one cannot lose it unwillingly

4. Let us therefore seek by reason how a human being ought to live. Certainly we all wish to live happily; nor is there anyone among the human race who does not assent to this proposition before it has even been fully stated.

But, as I understand it, one cannot be called happy who does not possess what he loves, whatever it may be; nor one who possesses what he loves, if it is harmful; nor one who does not love what he possesses, even if it is excellent. For the one who desires what he cannot attain is tormented; the one who has attained what ought not to be desired is deceived; and the one who does not desire what ought to be attained is sick. None of these conditions comes upon the soul without misery; and misery and happiness do not customarily dwell together in the same person. None of them, therefore, is happy.

A fourth possibility remains, as I see it, in which the happy life may be found: when what is best for a human being is both loved and possessed. For what else do we mean by “enjoy” than to have at hand what you love? No one is happy who does not enjoy what is best for a human being, and no one who enjoys it is unhappy. Our highest good, then, must be present to us if we intend to live happily.

5. It follows that we must seek what is best for a human being. This certainly cannot be worse than the human being himself. For whoever follows what is worse than himself becomes worse himself. Every human being ought to follow what is best. What is best for a human being, therefore, cannot be worse than a human being.

Perhaps it will be something like the human being himself. Let that indeed be so, if there is nothing better than a human being that he can enjoy. But if we find something that is both superior to a human being and capable of being present to a human being who loves it, who could doubt that a person must strive toward that, in order to be happy, which is manifestly more excellent than the one who strives toward it?

For if being happy means arriving at such a good that nothing greater is possible—and that is what we call the highest good—how could one who has not yet reached his highest good be included in that definition? Or how is it the highest good if there is something better to which we can attain?

If this, then, is the case, it must be such that one cannot lose it unwillingly. For no one can have confidence in a good that he perceives can be taken from him, even if he wishes to retain and embrace it. But whoever lacks confidence concerning the good he enjoys—how can he be happy amid so great a fear of losing it?

## CHAPTER IV—What is a human being?

[Col. 1313]

6. Let us therefore seek what is better than a human being. This is certainly difficult to discover unless we first consider and examine what the human being himself is. I do not think that I should now be asked for a definition of the human being. Rather, what seems to me to require investigation here is this: since nearly everyone agrees—or at least this much is agreed between me and those with whom I am now dealing—that we are composed of soul and body, what is the human being himself? Is it both of these which I have named, or merely the body, or merely the soul?

Although there are two things, soul and body, and neither would be called a human being if the other did not exist—for the body would not be a human being if there were no soul, nor again would the soul be a human being if it did not animate a body—it can nevertheless happen that one of these is both regarded as the human being and called the human being.

What, then, do we call the human being? Soul and body, like a team of horses or a centaur? Or merely the body, which is employed by the soul that governs it—like a lamp, which we call not both the fire and the vessel but the vessel alone, because of the fire? Or do we call nothing other than the soul a human being, but, on account of the body which it governs, call it a rider—not both horse and human being, but the human being alone—because it is adapted to governing the horse?

It is difficult to settle this controversy; or, if it is easy by reason, it is lengthy in exposition. There is no need to undertake and endure that labor and delay. For whether both together or the soul alone bears the name “human being,” what is best for the body is not what is best for the human being; rather, what is best either for body and soul together or for the soul alone is what is best for the human being.

## CHAPTER V—What is best for a human being is not what is best for the body alone, but what is best for the soul

7. If we ask what is best for the body, sound reasoning compels us to acknowledge that it is whatever enables the body to be in the best possible condition. Nothing among all the things that invigorate the body is better or more excellent than the soul. The highest good of the body, then, is not its pleasure, freedom from pain, strength, beauty, speed, or anything else customarily counted among bodily goods, but the soul altogether.

For the soul supplies the body with these things that have been mentioned by its presence, and, more importantly than all of them, with life. Therefore it does not seem to me that the soul is the highest good of the human being, whether we call both soul and body the human being or call the soul alone the human being.

For just as reason discovers that the highest good of the body is that which is better than the body and by which vigor and life are supplied to it, so—whether the human being is body and soul or the soul itself—we must find whether there is something that precedes the soul itself, and which, when the soul follows it, makes the soul as excellent as possible in its own kind. If we can discover this, it will certainly be what, once every ambiguity has been removed, ought rightly and deservedly to be called the highest good of the human being.

8. Or, if the body is the human being, I cannot deny that the soul itself is what is best for the human being.
