But certainly, when conduct is at issue, when we ask what way of life must be followed so that we may attain happiness, precepts are not given to the body, nor is the discipline of the body what must be investigated.

Finally, it is that part of us which investigates and learns that will perform good actions; and these are proper to the soul. Thus the question is not about the body when we are concerned to obtain virtue.

If it follows—as it does—that the body itself, when governed by the soul, which possesses virtue, is governed both much better and more honorably, and is in the best condition when that soul is at its best and rules it according to a just law, then what makes the soul best will be what is best for the human being, even if we call the body the human being.

If my charioteer obeys me and feeds and governs the horses under his command most suitably, and if he himself enjoys my generosity in proportion as he is more obedient to me, can anyone deny that not only the charioteer but also the horses being in the best condition is owed to me?

Thus, whether the human being is body alone, soul alone, or both together, I do not think that I should chiefly investigate anything except what makes the soul best. For once this has been obtained, the human being cannot fail either to be in the best condition or at least to be much better than if this one thing were lacking.

[Note: The printed editions read: “the horses under his command he drives and governs.” Twelve manuscripts read: “he feeds.”]

## CHAPTER VI—Virtue makes the soul best; the soul acquires virtue by following God; the attainment of God is the happy life

9. No one will doubt that virtue makes the soul best. But it may rightly be asked whether virtue exists through itself or whether it can exist only in a soul.

Again there arises a very profound question requiring a lengthy discussion. But perhaps I shall make good use of brevity here; I hope that God will be present, so that, insofar as our weakness permits, we may teach concerning such great matters not only clearly but also briefly.

Whichever of these alternatives is true—whether virtue can exist by itself without a soul or can exist only in a soul—the soul undoubtedly follows something in order to attain virtue. That something will be either the soul itself, virtue, or a third thing.

But if it follows itself in order to acquire virtue, it follows, I know not what foolish thing; for before acquiring virtue it is foolish. Yet the highest desire of those who follow something is to attain what each one follows. Therefore either the soul will wish not to attain what it follows—which is something no more absurd or perverse can be said—or, while following itself in its foolishness, it will attain the very foolishness it avoids.

But if it follows virtue, desiring to attain it, how does it follow what does not exist? Or how can it desire to attain what it already possesses?

Therefore either virtue exists apart from the soul, or, if we do not wish to call virtue anything except the very habit and, as it were, quality of the wise soul—which cannot exist except in a soul—the soul must follow something else so that virtue may be born in it. For, as far as my reason can discern, by following nothing or by following foolishness it cannot reach wisdom.

10. This other thing, then, by following which the soul becomes possessed of virtue and wisdom, is either a wise human being or God. But it was said above that it must be something which we cannot lose unwillingly.

Who, then, would hesitate to think that a wise human being, if we were to regard following him as sufficient, could be taken away from us even against our will, and not merely when we refuse but even when we resist? God, therefore, remains. If we follow him, we live well; if we attain him, we live not merely well but happily.

As for those who deny that he exists, what argument should I consider for persuading them, when I do not know whether one ought to converse with them at all? If that should seem appropriate, however, we would have to adopt a very different beginning, method, and point of entry from the one we have undertaken for the present.

For now I am dealing with those who do not deny that God exists. More than that, they also admit that human affairs are not neglected by him. For I do not think that anyone is held by any name of religion who does not at least believe that our souls are cared for by divine providence.

## CHAPTER VII—God must be sought through the authority of Scripture. The character and principal mysteries of the divine economy for our salvation. The sum of faith

11. But how do we follow one whom we do not see? Or how do we see him, when we are not only human beings but foolish human beings? Although he is perceived not by the eyes but by the mind, what mind can be found fit, when it is covered by the cloud of foolishness, either to absorb or even to attempt to absorb that light?

We must therefore have recourse to the teachings of those whom it is probable were wise. Reason could be carried only this far. Until now it had been moving through human affairs, made more secure not by truth but by habit. But when it reached divine things, it turned away. It cannot look; it trembles, burns, and longs with love; it is struck back by the light of truth; and it turns toward the familiarity of its own darkness, not by choice but through weariness.

How much fear and trembling are needed here, lest the soul conceive greater weakness precisely where, exhausted, it seeks rest! Therefore, for those wishing to flee into darkness, let that obscurity of authority meet us through the dispensation of ineffable Wisdom, and let it be gracious to us through the marvelous events and the words of the books—like gentler signs of the truth—and through shadows.

12. What more could have been done for our salvation? What could be said to be more beneficent or generous than divine providence, which did not entirely abandon the human being who had fallen from its laws and who, through desire for mortal things, was rightly and deservedly propagating a mortal offspring?

For that supremely just power possesses, through marvelous and incomprehensible means and through certain most secret successions of created things that serve it, both the severity with which it punishes and the mercy with which it liberates.

We will not be able to understand how beautiful, how great, how worthy of God this is—or, finally, how truly it is what is being sought—unless, beginning with human and near things, we do not abandon the path which God has fortified for us by the separation of the Patriarchs, the bond of the Law, the foretelling of the Prophets, the sacrament of the assumed Man, the testimony of the Apostles, the blood of the martyrs, and the incorporation of the nations, while maintaining the faith and commands of true religion.

Therefore, from this point onward let no one ask me for my opinion; rather, let us listen to the oracles and submit our little reasonings to the divine utterances.

## CHAPTER VIII—God is the highest good, toward which we are commanded to strive with the highest love

13. Let us see how the Lord himself commanded us in the Gospel to live, and how the Apostle Paul did so as well; for they do not dare to condemn these Scriptures.

Let us therefore hear what end of goods you prescribe for us, Christ. There is no doubt that it will be the end toward which you command us to strive with the highest love:

“You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God.”

Tell me also, I ask you, what degree of love is required; for I fear that I may be inflamed with desire and love for my Lord either more or less than I ought.

“With all your heart,” he says.

That is not enough.

“With all your soul.”

Even that is not enough.

“With all your mind” (Matt. 22:37).

What more do you want? Perhaps I would wish for more, if I could see what more there could be.

What does Paul say to this?

“We know,” he says, “that all things work together for good for those who love God.”

[Note: He seems to have read συγχωρεῖ (“permits”) for συνεργεῖ (“works together”).]

Let him himself also state the measure of love.

“Who, then,” he says, “will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?” (Rom. 8:28).

We have heard what we must love and how greatly we must love it. We must strive entirely toward this, and refer all our plans to it.

God is for us the sum of goods. God is for us the highest good. We must remain neither below it nor seek beyond it: the one is dangerous, and the other is nothing.

## CHAPTER IX—The agreement of the Old and New Testaments concerning the commandments of love

14. Come now, let us investigate—or rather, let us attend, since the matter is present and very easily seen—whether the authority of the Old Testament also agrees with these statements brought forward from the Gospel and the Apostle.

Why should I speak of the earlier statement, when it is obvious to everyone that it is drawn from the Law given through Moses? For there it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Deut. 6:5).

But what passage from the Old Testament could I compare with what was said by the Apostle? So that I would not have to search any longer, he himself supplied one. For when he had said that no tribulation, no distress, no persecution, no necessity arising from bodily want, no danger, and no sword could separate us from the love of Christ, he immediately added: “As it is written: Because of you we are afflicted all day long; we have been regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Rom. 8:38; Ps. 43:22).

They are accustomed to say that these words were inserted by the corrupters of Scripture. Yet they have so little with which to contradict them that the wretched men are compelled to answer with these very words. But who does not understand that the final utterance of defeated men could have been no other?

[Col. 1317]

15. Nevertheless, I ask them whether they deny that this statement is in the Old Testament, or whether they assert that it does not agree with the apostolic statement.

I shall establish the first point from the books. As for the second, I shall either call back these evasive men, fleeing over precipices, to peace, if they are willing to look back for a while and consider what has been said, or I shall pursue them with the understanding of the others who judge without desire.

For what could be more harmonious than these statements? Tribulation, distress, persecution, famine, nakedness, and danger grievously afflict a human being placed in this life. All these words, then, are summed up in that one testimony of the ancient Law which says, “Because of you we are afflicted.”

The sword remained, and it does not bring an anguished life but takes away the life it finds. To this, therefore, corresponds: “We have been regarded as sheep for slaughter.”

Love itself could not have been indicated more expressly than by the words, “Because of you.”

Suppose that this testimony were not found in the Apostle Paul but had been uttered by me. Is it necessary to demonstrate to you, heretic, anything except either that it is not written in the ancient Law or that it does not agree with the Apostle? If you dare to say neither—for you are pressed when the book is read and it is clear that the passage is written, and when people understand that nothing could agree more closely with what the Apostle said—why, then, do you think that anything is accomplished by daring to accuse the Scriptures of being corrupted?

Finally, what will you answer someone who says to you: “I understand it this way; I receive it this way; I believe it this way; and I read those books for no other reason than that I see everything there agreeing with the Christian faith”?

Rather say, if you dare and intend to speak against me, that we ought not to believe that the Apostles and martyrs are said to have suffered grievous hardships for Christ, or that they were regarded by their persecutors as sheep for slaughter.

If you cannot say this, why do you bring a false charge against the book in which I find what you confess that I ought to believe?

[Note: Several manuscripts read, “in which book I shall believe”; and some read, “in which book I shall believe that it is written.”]

[Note: See *Retractations* 1.7.2.]

## CHAPTER X—What the Church teaches about God. The two gods of the Manichaeans

16. Or do you say that you grant that God must be loved, but not the God worshiped by those who accept the authority of the Old Testament?

Then you do not say that the God who made heaven and earth must be worshiped. For this God is proclaimed throughout all the parts of those volumes. Yet you admit that this entire world, which is signified by the name “heaven and earth,” has God as its author and maker, and that God is good.

When “God” is mentioned, one must speak to you with a qualification. For you assert that there are two gods, one good and the other evil.

But if you say that you worship and consider worthy of worship the God by whom the world was made, but that he is not the one commended by the authority of the Old Testament, you act shamelessly when you attempt to interpret falsely the mind and judgment of another which we have received rightly and beneficially. It is wholly futile.

For your foolish and impious arguments cannot in any way be compared with the discourse of pious and learned people through whom those Scriptures are opened in the Catholic Church to those who wish and are worthy to understand them.

The Law and the Prophets are understood by us in a manner entirely different from what you suppose. Stop wandering in error. We do not worship a God who repents, or one who is envious, needy, cruel, or who seeks pleasure from the blood of human beings or animals; nor one who delights in shameful acts and crimes; nor one who confines his possession to a certain portion of the earth.

For you are accustomed to attack these and similar absurdities at length and with great vehemence. Therefore your attack does not touch us; rather, you tear apart certain old-womanish or even childish opinions with a speech all the more inept because it is vehement.

Anyone who is moved by this and passes over to you does not condemn the discipline of our Church but demonstrates that he is ignorant of it.

17. Therefore, if you retain anything human in your heart, if you care for yourselves, seek instead, diligently and piously, how those statements are to be understood.

Seek, wretched men. For we condemn more forcefully and abundantly a faith by which something inappropriate to God is believed. In the passages mentioned, when they are understood as the letter sounds, we correct simplicity and ridicule obstinacy.

Catholic teaching also forbids those who advance—not in years but in zeal and understanding—beyond a certain mental childhood and toward the gray hairs of wisdom to believe many other things which you cannot understand.

It is taught how foolish it is to believe that God is contained in some place, however infinite, within whatever expanses of quantity; and it is held impious to suppose that either God himself or some part of him moves and passes from place to place.

But if anyone supposes that any change or alteration of his substance and nature can occur in any way, he will be condemned as extraordinarily foolish and impious.

Thus among us there are found certain children who imagine God in human form and suppose him to be constituted in that way—an opinion more degraded than any other. But there are also many old men who, with the same mind, contemplate his majesty as remaining inviolate and unchangeable, not only above the human body but even above the mind itself.

It has already been said that these ages must be distinguished not by time but by virtue and prudence.

Among you, however, no one is found who describes God’s substance in the form of a human body. But, on the other hand, no one is found who separates him from the stain of human error.

[Note: Lovaniensis reads, “who separates himself from the stain of human error.” But *se* is absent from the manuscripts and ought to be absent from the other editions as well, because Augustine is there reproaching the Manichaeans for wishing to free God from the configuration of a human body, but not from the stain of human error, since they dogmatize that the human soul—which is certainly subject to error—is part of God himself. He presses this argument in Book II of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 8, section 11.]

Thus those whom the breasts of the Catholic Church support like crying infants, if they are not preyed upon by heretics,

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “corrupted.”]

are nourished according to each one’s capacity and strength. One is led in this way and another in that way, first to mature manhood, and then to the maturity and gray hairs of wisdom, so that they may live as much as they wish—and live most blessedly.

## CHAPTER XI—God alone must be loved, and therefore is the highest good. Nothing is better than God; no one loses God unwillingly: these are the two conditions of the highest good stated above in chapter 3

[Col. 1319]

18. The following of God, then, is the desire for blessedness; the attainment of God is blessedness itself.

We follow him by loving him, but we attain him not by becoming altogether what he is, but by drawing near to him and touching him in a wondrous and intelligible manner, and by being wholly illuminated and embraced by his truth and holiness.

For he himself is the light; we, however, are permitted to be illuminated by him.

The greatest and first commandment, therefore, which leads to the happy life is: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind.”

“For those who love God, all things work together for good.”

Therefore, shortly afterward Paul himself says: “I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor powers, nor things present nor things to come, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. 8:28, 38–39).

If, then, all things work together for good for those who love God; and if no one doubts that the highest good—which is also called the best good—must not merely be loved but loved in such a way that we ought to love nothing more; and if this is signified and expressed by the words “with all your soul,” “with all your heart,” and “with all your mind,” who, I ask, could doubt that, once all these things have been established and most firmly believed, there is nothing else best for us toward which we ought to hasten, setting aside everything else, than God?

Likewise, if no thing separates us from his love, what good could be not only better but also more certain than this?

19. But let us consider each point briefly.

No one separates us from him by threatening death. For that very thing by which we love God cannot die except when it does not love God; and not loving God is itself death, since it is nothing other than preferring something else to him in loving and following.

No one separates us from him by promising life. No one separates a person from the very source by promising water.

An angel does not separate us. For when we cling to God, no angel is more powerful than our mind.

Virtue does not separate us. For if “virtue” here means a power that possesses some authority in this world, the mind clinging to God is altogether higher than the whole world. But if “virtue” means the very right disposition of our soul: if it exists in another, it favors our union with God; if it exists in us, it itself unites us.

Present troubles do not separate us. For we feel them to be lighter in proportion as we cling more closely to him from whom they attempt to separate us.

The promise of future things does not separate us. Whatever good is to come, God promises more certainly; and nothing is better than God himself, who is already present to those who cling to him rightly.

Neither height nor depth separates us. For if these words perhaps signify the height or depth of knowledge, I will not be inquisitive, lest I be separated from God; nor will any teaching separate me from him, as though it were to drive away error, since no one could err at all except one who had been separated from him.

But if “height” and “depth” signify the upper and lower regions of this world, who could promise me heaven so as to separate me from the maker of heaven? Or who could frighten me with hell so that I would abandon God, whom, if I had never abandoned, I would not know as hell?

Finally, what place could tear me away from his love, who would not be wholly everywhere if he were contained in any place?

## CHAPTER XII—We are joined to God by love when we submit to him

20. “Nor any other creature,” he says.

O man of the highest mysteries! He was not content to say “creature,” but added “other creature,” reminding us that the very thing by which we love God and cling to God—that is, the soul and mind—is also a creature.

The other creature, therefore, is the body. And if the soul is an intelligible thing—that is, something known only through understanding—then every sensible thing is another creature: whatever presents some knowledge of itself through the eyes, ears, sense of smell, taste, or touch. This must necessarily be inferior to what is grasped by understanding alone.

Since God can become known to worthy souls only through understanding, although he is himself superior to the mind by which he is understood—for he is its creator and author—it was to be feared that the human soul, because it is numbered among invisible and intelligible things, might suppose itself to be of the same nature as the one who created it, and thus fall away from him through pride, when it ought to be joined to him by love.

The soul becomes like God insofar as this has been granted, when it submits itself to him in order to be enlightened by him and illuminated. And although it draws closest to him through this submission, by which it becomes like him, it must become far from him through the boldness by which it wishes to be more like him.

This is the boldness by which the soul refuses to obey God’s laws while wishing to be its own master, as God is.

[Note: Erasmus, Lovaniensis, and the Arnulfensis read, “This is what refuses.” But the manuscripts and Badius have *qua*, “by which,” and this is better: the passage explains what that boldness is by which the soul wishes to be more like God.]

21. The farther it departs from God—not in place but in disposition and desire—toward things lower than he is, the more it is filled with foolishness and misery.

It returns to God, therefore, by love, through which it seeks not to make itself equal to him but to place itself beneath him. The more earnestly and diligently it does this, the happier and more exalted it will be, and, with him alone ruling, the freer it will be.

It must therefore know that it is a creature. It ought to believe that its creator remains always as he is, in the inviolate and unchangeable nature of truth and wisdom; but it ought to confess that foolishness and deception can befall it because of the errors from which it desires to be stripped.

Yet again it must beware lest it be separated from the love of God, by which it is sanctified so that it may remain most blessed, through love of another creature—that is, this sensible world.

Therefore no other creature separates us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, since we ourselves are also creatures.

## CHAPTER XIII—Through Christ and his Spirit we are joined inseparably to God

22. Let the same Paul tell us who this Christ Jesus our Lord is:

“To those who are called,” he says, “we preach Christ, the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–24).

What? Does Christ himself not say, “I am the Truth”?

If, then, we ask what it means to live well—that is, to strive toward blessedness by living well—it will certainly mean loving Power, loving Wisdom, loving Truth, and loving with all the heart, all the soul, and all the mind: Power that is inviolate and unconquered; Wisdom to which foolishness does not succeed; Truth that does not know how to turn or to be otherwise than it always is.

Through this one the Father himself is seen. For it is said: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

We cling to him through sanctification. For once sanctified, we burn with a full and complete love, by which alone it comes about that we are not turned away from God but are conformed to him rather than to this world.

“For he predestined us,” says the same Apostle, “to be conformed to the image of his Son” (Rom. 8:29).

23. Through love, then, we are conformed to God; and once conformed and fashioned after him, and circumcised from this world, we are not confused with those things which ought to be subject to us.

This occurs through the Holy Spirit.

“For hope,” he says, “does not put us to shame, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (ibid. 5:5).

We could in no way be restored through the Holy Spirit unless he himself always remained whole and unchangeable. This certainly could not be the case unless he belonged to the nature and substance of God, to whom alone unchangeability and, so to speak, unturnability (*invertibilitas*) always belong.

[Note: Five manuscripts read *inconvertibilitas semper est* (“unconvertibility always belongs”); two others read *inconversibilitas*.]

For every creature is subject to vanity—not I but the same Paul declares this (ibid. 8:20). Nor can what is subject to vanity separate us from vanity and join us to truth.

The Holy Spirit grants this to us; therefore he is not a creature. For everything that exists is either God or a creature.

## CHAPTER XIV—By love we cling to the Trinity, the highest good

24. We must therefore love God as a certain triune unity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I shall say that this is nothing other than being itself.

For he truly and supremely is God, from whom all things are, through whom all things are, and in whom all things are. These are Paul’s words.

What does he add next? “To him be glory” (Rom. 11:36).

Entirely and most sincerely. For he does not say, “To them”; there is one God.

What, then, is “to him be glory” except the best, highest, and most widely spread renown belonging to him? For the more excellently and widely he is renowned, the more ardently he is loved and cherished.

When this happens, the human race advances by no other course than a sure and steady path toward the best and most blessed life.

I do not think that, when the question concerns conduct and life, anything further need be sought concerning what the highest good of the human being is, to which all things must be referred. It became clear both by reason, insofar as we were able, and by divine authority, which surpasses our reason, that it is nothing other than God himself.

For what else will be the best thing for a human being except that to which it is most blessed to cling?

That is God alone. We certainly cannot cling to him except by devotion, love, and charity.

## CHAPTER XV—He defines the four virtues in a Christian manner
25. And if virtue leads us to the blessed life, I would affirm that virtue is nothing other than the supreme love of God. For that which is called the fourfold virtue is, as I understand it, named from certain varied dispositions of this very love. Thus I would not hesitate to define those four virtues—whose names, I wish, may be as present in people’s minds as they are on everyone’s lips—in the following way: temperance is love offering itself whole and undivided to that which is loved; fortitude is love readily enduring all things for the sake of that which is loved; justice is love serving the beloved alone and therefore rightly ruling; prudence is love skillfully choosing between those things by which one is helped and those by which one is hindered.

[Note: [Col. 1322] The Theodoricus codex has: “So may this be the disposition of your minds.” Arnulfus: “So may this be the understanding in your minds.” The Cistercian codex finally has: “So may these effects be present in your minds.”]

But we have said that this love is not love of just anything, but love of God—that is, of the supreme good, supreme wisdom, and supreme harmony. Therefore it is also possible to define the virtues in this way: temperance is love preserving itself whole and undefiled for God; fortitude is love readily enduring all things for God; justice is love serving God alone and, for that reason, ruling well over all other things subject to human beings; prudence is love rightly distinguishing those things by which one may be aided toward God from those by which one may be hindered.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### The Harmony of the Old and New Testaments

26. I shall explain briefly what manner of life follows from each of these virtues, provided that I first compare with the testimonies of the New Testament, which I have been using for some time, corresponding passages from the Old Testament, as I promised [Note: See *Retractions* 1.7.2.].

Does Paul merely say that we ought to be subject to God [Note: Printed editions have *subjectos*, “subject.” But the better manuscripts have *subjunctos*, “joined to” or “subordinate to.”] in such a way that there is nothing between us and him that could separate us? Does not the prophet also express this most aptly and briefly when he says: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Psalm 72:28)? Is not what is expressed there at length concerning charity contained here in the single word “cling”? Likewise, when he adds, “it is good,” does this not refer to what is stated there: “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans 8:35, 28)? Thus, in a single brief statement and two words, the prophet shows both the power and the fruit of charity.

27. Since it is said there that the Son of God is “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), and since power is understood to pertain to action, while wisdom pertains to instruction—for which reason these two are themselves indicated in the Gospel when it says, “All things were made through him,” since this belongs to action and power, and then, with reference to instruction and the knowledge of truth, “and the life was the light of human beings” (John 1:3–4)—what could correspond more harmoniously with these testimonies of the New Testament than what is said in the Old concerning Wisdom: “She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly”?

For “reaching mightily” signifies power more particularly, while “ordering sweetly” signifies, as it were, the very art and rational principle. But if this seems [Col. 1323] obscure, consider what follows: “The Lord of all loved her, for she is the instructor of God’s discipline and the chooser of his works.” Here nothing else seems to be said about action; for choosing works is not the same as performing them. Therefore these words pertain to instruction. The work belongs to power, so that the statement we wish to demonstrate may be complete.

Read what follows. “If,” he says, “an honorable possession is desired in life, what is more honorable than Wisdom, which accomplishes all things?” Can anything more splendid, clearer, or more abundant be offered? Hear another passage, if you think this insufficient, expressing the same idea: “For Wisdom,” he says, “teaches sobriety and justice and virtue.” Sobriety seems to me to pertain to the knowledge of truth—that is, to instruction—while justice and virtue pertain to action and performance. I do not know what can be compared with these two gifts—that is, effectiveness in action and sober contemplation—which the Power of God and the Wisdom of God, namely the Son of God, grants to those who love him, since the same prophet immediately declares how highly they are to be valued: “For Wisdom teaches sobriety, and justice, and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life” [Note: See *Retractions* 1.7.3.].

28. Perhaps someone may think that these words were not spoken concerning the Son of God. What else, then, does the statement show: “She magnifies her nobility by dwelling with God” (Wisdom 8:3)? Does “nobility” ordinarily signify anything other than parentage? And does “dwelling together” not proclaim and affirm equality with the Father himself?

Moreover, since Paul says that the Son of God is the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), and the Lord himself says, “No one knows the Father except the only-begotten Son” (Matthew 11:27), what could the prophet have said more fittingly than this: “And with you is Wisdom, which knows your works, which was present when you made the world, and knew what would be pleasing in your sight” (Wisdom 9:9)?

And since Christ is the truth, as is likewise shown when he is called the splendor of the Father (Hebrews 1:3)—for there is nothing around the sun except the splendor it generates [Note: Erasmus, Venice, and Louvain read: “For is there anything around the sun except the splendor it generates?” The manuscript reading is as translated.]—what could agree more openly and clearly with this teaching from the Old Testament than the statement: “Your truth is round about you” (Psalm 88:9)?

Finally, Wisdom itself says in the Gospel, “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). The prophet says: “Who, then, knows your mind unless you give wisdom?” and shortly afterward: “People learned what pleases you, and through Wisdom they were saved” (Wisdom 9:17–19).

29. Paul says, “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). The prophet says, “For the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wisdom 1:5). For where there is deceit, there is no charity.

Paul says that we are “to be conformed to the image of the Son of God” (Romans 8:29). The prophet says, “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:7).

Paul shows that the Holy Spirit is God and therefore is not a creature. The prophet says, “And you will send the Holy Spirit from on high” (Wisdom 9:17). For God alone is the [Col. 1324] Most High, than whom nothing is higher.

Paul shows that this Trinity is one God when he says, “To him be glory” (Romans 11:36). In the Old Testament it is said: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deuteronomy 6:4).

## CHAPTER XVII  
### An Address to the Manichaeans, Urging Them to Come to Their Senses

30. What more do you want? Why do you rage so foolishly and impiously? Why do you corrupt unlearned souls through your pernicious persuasion? The God of both Testaments is one.

Just as the passages we have drawn from both Testaments agree with one another, so do the others also, if you are willing to attend to them carefully and with impartial judgment. But because many things are spoken in a humbler manner, more suited to minds that creep along the ground, so that through human things they may rise to divine things [Note: Thus in the better manuscripts. The editions have: “To minds humbled and creeping along the ground, so that they may rise more suitably through human things to divine things.”], and because many things are expressed figuratively so that the studious mind may be exercised more profitably by seeking and may rejoice more abundantly when it finds, you abuse these things through the wonderful arrangement of the Holy Spirit in order to deceive your hearers and entangle them.

Why divine providence permits you to do this, and how true the Apostle’s statement is that “there must be many heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Corinthians 11:19) [Note: The Vatican and Cistercian codices omit “many,” a word found in most of the other manuscripts and printed editions. We have already observed that the same sentence of the Apostle is cited in the manuscripts in Book 1 of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 1.], would take too long to discuss; and it is not for you to understand what must be said.

I know you rather well. You bring coarse minds, diseased by the poisonous nourishment of bodily images, to judge divine things that are far higher than you suppose.

31. Therefore this is how one must deal with you for the present—not so that you may already understand these things, which is impossible, but so that you may at some time desire to understand them. This is accomplished by the simple and pure love of God, which is especially evident in conduct and about which we have already said much. Inspired by the Holy Spirit, it leads to the Son, that is, to the Wisdom of God, through whom the Father himself is known.

For unless wisdom and truth are desired with the whole strength of the soul, they cannot be found at all. But if they are sought as they ought to be sought, they cannot withdraw and hide themselves from those who love them.

Hence comes the saying which you too are accustomed to have on your lips: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7). “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (ibid. 10:26). It is by love that one asks, by love that one seeks, by love that one knocks, by love that one receives revelation, and finally by love that one remains in what has been revealed.

The Old Testament does not deter us from this love and diligence in seeking wisdom, as you always falsely claim; rather, it urges us toward them with the greatest force.

32. Listen, then, at last, and pay attention, I ask you, without obstinacy, to what the prophet says: “Wisdom is radiant and unfading, and she is easily seen by those who love her and is found by those who seek her. She anticipates those who desire her, so that she may show herself to them. Whoever rises early for her will not labor, for he will find her sitting at his doors. To think about her is perfect understanding; and whoever keeps vigil for her will soon be secure, because she goes about seeking those worthy of herself, and she shows herself to them graciously on the paths, and meets them with all forethought.

“For the truest beginning of discipline is the desire for her. [Col. 1325] Care for discipline is love; love is the keeping of her laws; the keeping of her laws is the confirmation of incorruption; and incorruption brings one near to God. Therefore the desire for Wisdom leads to the kingdom” (Wisdom 6:13–21).

Will you still bark against these things? Do they not, stated in this way and not yet understood, signify to anyone that they contain something profound and ineffable? If only you could understand what has been said! You would immediately cast away all the foolishness of your fables and your most empty imaginings about bodies, and with great eagerness, sincere love, and the firmest faith you would place yourselves wholly in the most holy bosom of the Catholic Church.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### Perfect Truth Exists in the Catholic Church Alone through the Agreement of Both Testaments

33. Given my limited ability, I could examine each point and draw out and demonstrate what I have received—things whose excellence and profundity often leave words inadequate. But as long as you bark, this should not be done. For it was not said without reason: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matthew 7:6).

Do not be angry. I too barked and was a dog when I was being dealt with rightly—not with the food of instruction, but with clubs for refutation [Note: Five manuscripts have “with clubs for driving back.”].

But if you possessed the charity about which we are now speaking—or even if you should possess it at some time, to the extent that the greatness of knowing the truth requires—God would be present to show you that Christian faith, which leads to the highest summit of wisdom and truth, in the enjoyment of which consists nothing other than living blessedly, is found neither among the Manichaeans nor anywhere else except in Catholic teaching.

For what else does the Apostle Paul seem to desire when he says:

“For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his glory, to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inner person, and that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts; so that, rooted and founded in charity, you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the height and length and breadth and depth, and also to know the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge [Note: [Col. 1325] Most manuscripts have “the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge.” The editions read: “the knowledge of the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge.” Shortly afterward, two manuscripts have “into all the fullness of God.”], so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Ephesians 3:14–19).

Can anything be stated more clearly?

34. I beg you, keep watch for a little while. See the harmony of both Testaments, which sufficiently reveals and teaches what manner of life is required in conduct and toward what all things must be directed.

[Note: The editions read: “sufficiently revealing and teaching by the love of God.” Thirteen manuscripts prefer the present reading, although most of them punctuate the words differently.]

The Gospels urge us to love God when they say, “Ask, seek, knock” (Matthew 7:7). Paul urges us when he says, “That, rooted and founded in charity, you may be able to comprehend” (Ephesians 3:17). The prophet also urges us when he says that Wisdom can easily be known by those who love, [Col. 1326] seek, desire, keep watch for, think about, and care for her.

The salvation of the soul and the way of blessedness are displayed by the peaceful agreement of both Scriptures, yet you prefer to bark against these things rather than obey them.

I shall briefly say what I think: listen to the learned men of the Catholic Church with the same peace of mind and with the same desire with which I once listened to you, and there will be no need for the nine years during which you mocked me [Note: Augustine was a Manichaean for nine years, from the age of nineteen to twenty-eight. See below, Book 2, chapter 19, section 68, and *Confessions* 4.2.]. In a far shorter time—far shorter indeed—you will discern the difference between truth and vanity.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### The Duties of Temperance Described from the Holy Scriptures

35. But it is time to return to those four virtues and to draw out from each of them a manner of life. Let us first consider temperance, which promises us a certain integrity and incorruption of that love by which we are bound to God.

Its task is to restrain and calm the desires by which we hunger for those things that turn us away from God’s laws and from the fruit of his goodness—which, to explain it briefly, is the blessed life. For there is the seat of truth [Note: Bad., Am., Er., and Lov., as well as most manuscripts, have “faith in the truth.” Antonius Arnulfus prefers the reading found in the margin of certain editions, “the seat of truth,” which is supported by five manuscripts, in which “the seat of truth” is read.]. By contemplating and clinging wholly to it, we are undoubtedly blessed; but when we fall away from it, we become entangled in great errors and sufferings.

For, as the Apostle says, “For desire is the root of all evils; by following it, some have shipwrecked from the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:10). This sin of the soul is sufficiently and clearly signified, for those who understand rightly, in the transgression of the first human being who was in paradise.

“For in Adam,” as the same Apostle says, “we all die, and in Christ we shall all rise again” (1 Corinthians 15:22). O profound mysteries! But I shall restrain myself. For I have not undertaken at present to teach you what is right, but, if I can—if God favors my purpose concerning you—to unteach you what is wrong.

36. Paul therefore says that the root of all evils is desire, through which the old Law also signifies that the first human being fell. Paul urges us to “put off the old person and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9–10). By the old person he wishes Adam, who sinned, to be understood; by the new, the one whom the Son of God assumed in the mystery of God in order to free us.

For elsewhere he says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man is from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, so are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, so are the heavenly. Just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15:47–49). This means: put off the old and put on the new.

The whole duty of temperance, therefore, is to put off the old person and to be renewed in God—that is, to despise all bodily allurements and popular praise, and to direct the whole of one’s love toward invisible and divine things.

Hence follows that remarkable statement: “Though our outer person is being corrupted, our inner person is being renewed day by day” [Col. 1327] (2 Corinthians 4:16).

Hear also the prophet singing: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Psalm 50:12). What can be said against this agreement except by blind barkers?

## CHAPTER XX  
### We Are Commanded to Despise All Sensible Things and Love God Alone

37. The allurements of the body lie in all those things touched by bodily sensation, which some also call “sensibles.” Among these, ordinary light is especially prominent, because even among our own senses—which the soul uses through the body—nothing is preferable to the eyes. For this reason, in the Holy Scriptures all sensibles are signified under the name of visible things [Note: Eight manuscripts have “are assigned”; three others have “are condemned.”].

Thus in the New Testament we are forbidden to love these things: “We look not at the things that are seen,” it says, “but at the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

From this it can be understood how unchristian are those who think that the sun and moon are not only to be loved but also to be worshiped. For what do we see if we do not see the sun and moon? Yet we are forbidden to turn toward the things that are seen.

Therefore these things too are not to be loved by one who intends to offer that love, whole and incorrupt, to God. But there will be another place where these matters may be examined more carefully. For I have not now undertaken to speak about faith, but about the manner of life by which we become worthy to know what we believe.

God alone, then, is to be loved. This whole world, that is, all sensible things, is to be despised; yet they are to be used as needed for the necessities of this life.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### Popular Glory and Curiosity Condemned by the Holy Scriptures

38. Popular glory is rejected and despised in the New Testament in this way: “If I were seeking to please human beings,” it says, “I would not be a servant of Christ” (Galatians 1:10).

There is also another allurement: through certain imaginings [Note: The editions have “through images.” Most manuscripts have “through imaginings.”], the soul conceives ideas about bodies and calls this knowledge of things. For this reason, we are rightly also forbidden to be curious, which is an important duty of temperance.

Hence the saying: “Beware lest anyone deceive you through philosophy.” And because the very name “philosophy,” if considered, signifies something great and something to be sought with the whole mind [Note: [Col. 1327] The better manuscripts read *totamque* (“and the whole,” accusative feminine); other manuscripts and the editions read *totoque animo* (“and with the whole mind”).]—for philosophy is the love and pursuit of wisdom—the Apostle, taking great care not to seem to deter us from the love of wisdom, added: “and the elements of this world” (Colossians 2:8).

There are people who, having abandoned the virtues and not knowing what God is or how great is the majesty of a nature that always remains the same, think they are accomplishing something great if they investigate with the greatest curiosity and intensity the entire mass of bodies that we call the world.

From this also arises such great pride that they seem to themselves to dwell in the very heaven about which they often argue. Therefore, if the soul has resolved to preserve itself chaste for God, it must restrain itself from the desire for such vain knowledge [Note: Several manuscripts have “from the desire for such wandering thought.”].

For through this kind of love it is often deceived, so that it either thinks that [Col. 1328] nothing exists except body, or, even if moved by authority it confesses that something incorporeal exists, is nevertheless unable to think of it except through bodily images and believes it to be whatever the deceptive bodily sense presents.

The command to beware of images also serves this purpose.

39. To this authority of the New Testament, by which we are commanded to love nothing in this world (1 John 2:15), belongs above all the statement: “Do not be conformed to this world” (Romans 12:2). For it must be demonstrated at the same time that everyone is conformed to that thing which he loves.

If, then, I seek from the Old Testament what I can compare with this authority, I find many passages. But the one book of Solomon called Ecclesiastes leads all these matters most abundantly to the highest contempt. For it begins in this way: “Vanity of vanities,” says Ecclesiastes, “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What profit does a human being have from all his labor at which he labors under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes 1:2–3) [Note: See *Retractions* 1.7.3.].

If all these words are attended to, weighed, and examined, many things are found that are extremely necessary for those who desire to flee this world and take refuge in God. But that would be lengthy, and the discourse is hurrying toward another subject.

Having established such a beginning, Ecclesiastes goes on to show that those who are deceived by such things are vain, calling the very things by which they are deceived “vanity”—not because God did not create them, but because human beings, through sins, wish to subject themselves to those things which, through right conduct and by divine law, have been subjected to them.

For what else is it to be mocked and deceived by false goods than to regard things inferior to oneself as worthy of admiration and desire?

The temperate person therefore has, concerning such mortal and fleeting things, a rule of life confirmed by both Testaments: he loves none of them, considers none of them desirable for their own sake, but uses them as much as is sufficient for the necessities of this life and its duties, with the moderation of one who uses them, not the attachment of one who loves them.

Let this suffice concerning temperance—briefly in view of the greatness of the subject, though perhaps more fully than was necessary for the work undertaken.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### The Love of God Produces Fortitude

40. Not much needs to be said about fortitude. That love of which we are speaking, which ought to be wholly inflamed with holiness toward God, is called temperate in not desiring these things and strong in losing them.

But among all the things possessed in this life, the body is for human beings the heaviest bond, by the most just laws of God, because of the ancient sin—nothing is more obvious for proclaiming, yet nothing more hidden for understanding.

The fear of labor and pain shakes the soul lest this bond be disturbed and afflicted; the fear of death shakes it lest the bond be taken away and destroyed. For the soul loves the body through the force of habit, without understanding that, if it uses the body well and knowingly, its resurrection and restoration will, through the power and law of God, be subjected to its rightful claim without any distress.

But when the soul has turned this love wholly toward God [Note: Three manuscripts have: “But when he has turned this entire love toward God.”], once it has understood these things, it will not merely despise death [Col. 1329] but will even desire it.

41. Yet a great struggle with pain remains. Nevertheless, nothing is so hard and iron-like that it cannot be conquered by the fire of love. When the soul rushes toward God through this fire, it will fly free above every torture, on wondrous and most beautiful wings, wholly undefiled—the wings by which chaste love is supported in its embrace of God.

When God should allow lovers of gold, lovers of praise, and lovers of women to be stronger than those who love him, although what is called love in them should more properly be called desire or lust? Yet even in these cases it is evident how great is the soul’s impetus toward the things it loves, pressing onward without weariness through every kind of monstrous obstacle [Note: Fifteen manuscripts have “with a diverted course.”].

This shows us how much must be endured so that we do not abandon God, if people endure so much for those things that they abandon him to pursue.

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Exhortations and Examples of Fortitude from the Scriptures

42. Why should I gather here the authorities of the New Testament, where it is said, “Tribulation produces perseverance, perseverance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope” (Romans 5:3–4), and where this has been established and confirmed not only by words but also by the examples of those who spoke them? Rather, from the Old Testament, against which they rage so violently, I shall bring forward an example of perseverance.

I shall not mention that man who, amid great bodily torments and the terrible wasting of his limbs, not only endured human sufferings but also discussed divine matters. In each of his words it is sufficiently clear, if anyone attends with an impartial mind, how highly such things must be valued—things which people wish to possess by domination, yet by desire are themselves possessed by those very things, becoming slaves of mortal realities while foolishly wishing to be their masters.

That man lost all his wealth and suddenly became utterly poor, yet maintained a spirit so unshaken and fixed upon God that he clearly demonstrated that it was not those things that were great to him, but that he was great to them, while God was great to him (Job 1–2).

If people of our own time could possess such a spirit, we would not be strongly forbidden in the New Testament to possess these things, so that we might become perfect. For it is much more remarkable not to cling to possessions even when one possesses them than not to possess them at all.

43. But since we are now dealing with enduring bodily pain and torments, I shall leave that man aside—great and unconquered though he was, yet still a man. For those astonishing Scriptures offer me a woman of extraordinary fortitude, and compel me now to turn to her.

With seven sons, she first surrendered all her inward parts to the tyrant and executioner rather than utter a single sacrilegious word. While her sons were strengthened by her exhortation, she herself was tortured in their limbs, yet she was prepared to undergo personally what she had commanded them to endure (2 Maccabees 7).

What, I ask, could be added to such perseverance? Yet is it surprising that the love of God, conceived in all the marrow of her being, resisted the tyrant, the executioner, pain, the body, her sex, and natural affection?

Had she not heard: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115:15)? Had she not heard: “A patient man is better than the strongest [Col. 1330]” (Proverbs 16:32)? Had she not heard: “Accept whatever is brought upon you; endure in pain, and have patience in your humiliation, for gold and silver are tested in fire” (Sirach 2:4–5)? Had she not heard: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests righteous people” (Sirach 27:6)?

Indeed, she had received these and many other teachings, in which, by the one Holy Spirit of God, divine commands concerning fortitude were written in those books just as in these books of the New Testament; those former books alone then existed.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On Justice and Prudence

44. What shall we say of justice as it pertains to God? Does not the Lord say, “You cannot serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24), and does not the Apostle rebuke those who serve the creature rather than the Creator (Romans 1:25), while in the Old Testament it was first said: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone you shall serve” (Deuteronomy 6:13)?

But why say more about this, when everything there is filled with such statements?

Justice will therefore give the lover of whom we are speaking this rule of life: he should gladly serve the God whom he loves—that is, the supreme good, supreme wisdom, and supreme peace [Note: Four manuscripts have “supreme power.” Other codices have “peace.” Augustine repeatedly uses this word to designate the Holy Spirit, as again below in chapter 30.]—and should govern some other things as already subject to him, while undertaking to subject others.

This rule of living, as we have shown, is strengthened by the authority of both Testaments.

45. Nor need we discuss prudence at greater length. It concerns the discernment of what is to be desired and what is to be avoided. If it is absent, none of the things already mentioned can be accomplished.

Its duties are watchfulness and the most diligent vigilance, lest, as an evil persuasion gradually creeps in, we be deceived. Hence the Lord often cries, “Keep watch” (Matthew 24:42), and says, “Walk while you have the light, lest darkness overtake you” (John 12:35).

Likewise it is said: “Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?” (1 Corinthians 5:6).

What could be stated more clearly from the Old Testament against this drowsiness of the soul—through which we fail to notice destruction creeping along little by little—than the prophet’s statement: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall” (Sirach 19:1)? If time permitted and we were not hurrying, I could discuss this statement at great length [Note: Some manuscripts have *disputare*, “to dispute,” instead of *disputarem*, “I would dispute.”]. And if the task we have now undertaken required it, we might perhaps demonstrate how profound are the mysteries which the most ignorant and sacrilegious people mockingly ridicule. They are not merely gradually falling; they are rushing headlong in a great collapse.

## CHAPTER XXV  
### The Duties of the Four Virtues in Relation to the Love of God, Whose Reward Is Eternal Life and Knowledge of the Truth

46. What more should I discuss concerning conduct? For if God is the supreme good of human beings, which you cannot deny, it necessarily follows that, since desiring the supreme good is living well, living well is nothing other than loving God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind.

From this it follows that love is [Col. 1331] preserved incorrupt and whole in him—which belongs to temperance; that it is not broken by any adversities—which belongs to fortitude; that it serves no other—which belongs to justice; and that it remains watchful in discerning things, lest deceit or trickery gradually creep in—which belongs to prudence.

This is the one perfection of the human being, by which alone one obtains the enjoyment of the sincerity of truth. Both Testaments harmonize in teaching this to us; from both sides this is urged upon us.

Why do you continue to slander Scriptures that you do not understand? Do you not realize how foolishly you attack books that are criticized only by those who do not understand them, and can be understood only by those who do not criticize them? No enemy is permitted to know them, nor can anyone who knows them remain anything but a friend.

47. Let us therefore love God with our whole heart, our whole soul, and our whole mind, all of us who have resolved to attain eternal life. Eternal life is the entire reward for which we rejoice in hope; and the reward cannot precede merit or be given to a person before that person is worthy of it.

For what could be more unjust than this, and what could be more just in relation to God? We must not therefore demand the reward before we deserve to receive it.

Perhaps it is not inappropriate to ask what eternal life itself is. But let us rather listen to its giver: “This is eternal life,” he says, “that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

Eternal life, then, is the knowledge of truth itself.

Consider, therefore, how perverse and disorderly are those who think that they can transmit the knowledge of God so that we may become perfect, when knowledge of God is itself the reward of the perfect.

What, then, must be done? What, I ask, except that we first love with complete charity the very one whom we wish to know [Note: See *Retractions* 1.7.4.]?

Hence arises what we have been laboring toward from the beginning: that nothing more salutary can be done in the Catholic Church than for authority to precede reason.

## CHAPTER XXVI  
### Love of Oneself and of One’s Neighbor

48. But let us consider the remaining matters. It may seem that nothing has been done concerning the human being himself—that is, concerning the lover himself—but anyone who thinks this understands the matter only obscurely.

For it is impossible that one who loves God should not love himself. Indeed, only the person who loves God knows how to love himself.

A person loves himself sufficiently if he diligently acts so as to enjoy the supreme and true good. If this good is nothing other than God, as the preceding discussion has shown, who can hesitate to say that the lover of God loves himself?

What, then, is there no bond of love among human beings themselves? On the contrary, there must be one, so that no surer step toward the love of God can be believed possible than the charity of one human being toward another.

49. Let the Lord himself, when questioned about the commandments of life, bring forward for us the second commandment. He was not content with one commandment, since he knew that God is one thing and a human being another, and that the difference is as great as that between the one who created and that which was created in the likeness of the Creator.

He therefore says that the second commandment is: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22:39).

You love yourself beneficially if you love God more than yourself. Therefore what you do for yourself you must do for your neighbor: namely, that he too may [Col. 1332] love God with perfect love.

For you do not love him as yourself if you do not strive to lead him to the good toward which you yourself are striving [Note: Many manuscripts have: “if you do not lead him to the good toward which you yourself are striving.”].

That is the one good which does not become narrow for all who strive toward it with you.

From this commandment arise the duties of human fellowship, in which it is difficult not to go wrong. Above all, one must act so as to be benevolent—that is, to use no malice and no malicious deceit against another human being.

For what is closer to a human being than another human being?

50. Hear also what Paul says: “Love of one’s neighbor does no evil” (Romans 13:10).

I am using very brief testimonies, but, unless I am mistaken, they are suitable and sufficient for the matter undertaken. For who does not know how many words, and words of what weight, concerning love of one’s neighbor are spread everywhere throughout those books?

But since there are two ways in which one sins against another human being—one, by harming him; the other, by failing to help him when one can—and since these are precisely the things by which wicked people are said to be wicked, while the person who loves does neither of them, I think that the statement, “Love of one’s neighbor does no evil,” sufficiently demonstrates what we wish to show.

And if we cannot reach good things unless we cease doing evil, these are, as it were, the cradle of the love of God: through them we love our neighbor. Since love of one’s neighbor does no evil, from this we ascend to what is said: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (ibid. 8:28).

51. But I do not know in what manner these two things either rise together into fullness and perfection, or whether the love of God is begun first and the love of neighbor perfected first. For divine love perhaps seizes us more swiftly for the beginning, but we more easily perfect lesser things. However the matter may stand, this must be held above all: no one should think that, having despised his neighbor, he can arrive at blessedness and at God, whom he loves. And would that, just as it is easy for one rightly disposed and benevolent to love his neighbor, so it were easy either to benefit him or to do him no harm. For good will alone is not enough for these things; rather, a certain great reason and prudence is required, which no one can employ unless that God, the source of all good things, has granted it. Concerning this matter, which I judge to be exceedingly difficult, we shall attempt to say a few things in accordance with the work undertaken, placing all our hope in him whose gifts alone these are.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Beneficence toward the Body of One’s Neighbor

52. Man, then, as he appears to man, is a rational soul making use of a mortal and earthly body. Accordingly, the person who loves his neighbor benefits partly the body and partly the soul of man. What pertains to the body is called medicine; what pertains to the soul, instruction. By “medicine,” however, I now mean everything that either preserves or restores the body’s health. To this therefore belong not only the things supplied by the art of those who are properly called physicians, but also food and drink, clothing and shelter, and finally every defense and protection by which our body is preserved even against external blows and accidents. For hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and whatever else is inflicted from outside with harmful force [Col. 1333] do not allow the health now under discussion to remain intact.

53. Therefore those who dutifully and humanely provide all the things by which such evils and inconveniences are resisted are called merciful, even if they are so wise that they are no longer disturbed by any pain of soul [Note: [Col. 1333] See *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 7, no. 4.]. For who does not know that *mercy*—*misericordia*—is so called because it makes the heart of one who suffers with another’s evil “wretched” (*miserum*)? And who would not concede that the wise person ought to be free from every misery when he assists the needy, supplies food to the hungry and drink to the thirsty, clothes the naked, receives the stranger under his roof, frees the oppressed, and finally extends his humanity even to the burial of the dead? Even if he does this with a tranquil mind, moved by no goads of pain but led by the duty of goodness, he must nevertheless be called merciful. For the name does him no harm when misery is absent.

54. Fools, however, while avoiding mercy as though it were a vice, because they cannot be sufficiently moved by duty if they are not moved by disturbance as well, freeze rather in the hardness of inhumanity than find serenity in the tranquility of reason. Therefore God himself is called merciful with far greater wisdom. How he is so called remains to be understood by those who have shown themselves fit through devotion and religious commitment, lest, by using the words of teachers foolishly, we make the souls of the ignorant harden themselves by avoiding mercy before we soften them by seeking kindness. And just as mercy commands us to drive these hardships away from a human being, so innocence forbids us to inflict them.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Beneficence toward the Soul of One’s Neighbor. The Two Parts of Instruction: Restraint and Teaching. Through Good Conduct We Come to the Recognition of Truth

55. As for instruction, by which health is restored to the soul itself—and without it that bodily health is of no use for driving away misery—the matter is altogether exceedingly difficult. Just as, concerning the body, we said that curing diseases and wounds is one thing, something few people can do well, while relieving hunger and thirst and the other needs in which one human being is commonly and generally allowed to assist another is something else, so there are certain matters concerning the soul in which that exceptional and rare mastery is not especially needed: for example, when we exhort and admonish people to provide for the needy the very things which, as we said, ought to be provided for the body. When we do these things, we assist the body; but when we teach that they should be done, we assist the soul through instruction.

There are, however, other means by which the soul’s many and various diseases are healed through a certain great and altogether ineffable method. If this medicine were not sent divinely to the peoples, there would be no hope of salvation for those who sin with such unrestrained progression. Yet even bodily medicine, if one traces the origin of things more deeply, cannot be found to have flowed to human beings from anywhere except God, to whom the order and health of all things must be ascribed.

56. This instruction of which we are now speaking, then, which is medicine for the soul, is divided, insofar as it can be gathered from the divine Scriptures themselves, into two parts: restraint and teaching. Restraint is accomplished through fear, but teaching through love [Col. 1334]—I mean the love of the one who is assisted through instruction; for the person who assists possesses neither of these two things except love.

In these two matters God himself, by whose goodness and mercy it comes about that we are anything at all, has given us the rule of instruction in the two Testaments, the Old and the New. For although both elements are present in each Testament, fear nevertheless predominates in the Old, and love in the New. The apostles proclaim that there is slavery there [Note: [Col. 1334] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “because there is slavery there,” etc.], but freedom here.

To speak of the remarkable and divine harmony of these Testaments would take a very long time, and many devout and learned people have already done so. The matter demands many books if it is to be explained and proclaimed as fully as humanly possible. Accordingly, the person who loves his neighbor acts as far as he can so that his neighbor may be safe in body and safe in soul; but care for the body must be referred to the health of the soul. In this way, then, he acts with respect to the soul: first, so that the person may fear God, and afterward love him. These are the best dispositions, through which the recognition of truth itself also comes to us—the truth toward which we are driven with every effort.

57. In these two matters I agree with the Manichaeans: namely, that we should love God and our neighbor. But they deny that this is contained in the Old Testament. How greatly they are mistaken is sufficiently evident, I think, from the statements about both matters that we brought forward earlier.

Nevertheless, to say something brief, but something which only utter madness could resist: do they not notice that these very two commandments, which they are compelled to praise, they most perversely deny were proclaimed by the Lord in the Gospel as belonging to the Old Testament, where it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and also the other: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself”? (Deut. 6:5; Lev. 19:18; Matt. 22:37, 39.)

Or, if they do not dare to deny these things—for the light of truth presses them—let them dare to deny that these commandments are salutary; let them deny, if they can, that the best moral dispositions are contained in them, and say that God ought not to be loved, that one’s neighbor ought not to be loved, that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. 8:28), and that “love of neighbor does not work evil” (ibid. 13:10)—the two principles by which human life is ordered most healthfully and rightly.

If they say these things, they have no common ground not only with Christians, but not even with human beings. But if they do not dare to say them, and are compelled to confess that these teachings are divine, why do they not cease to assail and condemn with impious wickedness the Books from which such teachings have been brought forth?

58. Or will they say that it does not follow that everything in that place is good simply because we were able to find these things there? For this is what they usually say. I do not readily see what answer I should give to this evasion or how I should meet it. Shall I examine the individual words of the Old Testament in order to demonstrate to obstinate and ignorant people that in these matters there is complete agreement with the Gospel? But when will that be? When will I be sufficient for the task, or when will they endure it?

What, then, shall I do? Shall I abandon the case and allow them to hide themselves in an opinion that is indeed wicked and false, but difficult to [Col. 1335] dismantle? I shall not do so. God himself, to whom those commandments belong, will draw near; nor will he allow me, in such great straits, to be helpless and abandoned.

## CHAPTER XXIX — On the Authority of the Scriptures

59. Therefore, Manichaeans, attend with your minds, if perhaps you are held by that superstition in such a way that you may at last escape. Attend, I say, without obstinacy, without the desire to resist; for otherwise it is exceedingly harmful for you to judge.

Certainly no one is in doubt—and you are not so turned away from the truth that you fail to understand this—that if it is good to love God and one’s neighbor, which no one can deny, whatever depends upon these two commandments cannot rightly be blamed. What, then, depends upon them? It is ridiculous if you think that you should ask me. Hear Christ himself; hear, I say, Christ; hear the Wisdom of God: “On these two commandments,” he says, “hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40).

60. What can the most shameless obstinacy say at this point? That Christ did not say this? But these words of his are written in the Gospel. That what is written is false? What could be found more impious than such sacrilege? What more shameless than such a statement? What more audacious? What more wicked?

Even the worshipers of idols, who hate Christ’s name as well, have never dared to say this against those Scriptures. For the complete perversion of all writings and the abolition of all books committed to memory would follow if what has been strengthened by the religious observance of so many peoples and confirmed by the agreement of so many people and ages were brought into such doubt that it could not retain even the credibility and authority of ordinary history.

Finally, what can you produce from any writings where I may not use this same argument, if something is brought forward against my reasoning and purpose?

61. Who could tolerate this: that they forbid us to believe books that are universally known and already in everyone’s hands, while they command us to believe the things they themselves produce? If Scripture is to be doubted, what should be doubted more than writings that have not deserved to be made notorious, and that could have been wholly fabricated under another name?

If you thrust this upon me against my will and compel belief by exaggerating its authority [Note: [Col. 1335] The Theoderician codex: “And by the reason of its authority you compel [me] to demand it as credible.” Six others: “And you compel [me] to exaggerate the force of authority in order to bring it to an end.”], shall I, wretched man, doubt the writing that I see consistently and most widely disseminated and fortified by the testimony of Churches scattered throughout the world—and, more wretched still, doubt it on your authority?

Even if you were to produce alternative copies, I ought to accept only those commended by the agreement of the greater number. But now, when you produce nothing with which to compare it except an utterly empty assertion, full of rashness, do you think that the human race is so perverse and so abandoned by the help of divine providence that it would prefer your mere words to those Scriptures—not alternative writings produced by you with which they might be refuted, but merely your words?

You must produce another codex containing the same material, but uncorrupted and more reliable, in which only those passages are absent that you accuse this one of having had inserted. For example, if you contend that Paul’s Epistle written to the Romans [Col. 1336] has been corrupted, you must produce another uncorrupted copy—or rather, another codex in which the same Epistle of that apostle has been written in a genuine and uncorrupted form.

“You will not,” you say, “lest I myself be thought to have corrupted it.” For this is what you usually say, and you speak truly: if you did this, even moderately sensible people would suspect nothing else. Consider, then, what judgment you yourself have made concerning your authority, and understand whether people ought to believe your words against those Scriptures, if it is exceedingly rash to believe a codex merely because it is produced by you.

## CHAPTER XXX — An Address to the Church, Teacher of All Wisdom. The Teaching of the Catholic Church

62. But why say more about this? Who does not see that those who dare to say such things against the Christian Scriptures, whatever else they may be thought to be, are certainly not Christians?

For Christians have been given this rule of life: that we love the Lord our God with all our heart, and with all our soul, and with all our mind, and then our neighbor as ourselves. For “on these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Deut. 6:5; Matt. 22:37).

Rightly, therefore, the Catholic Church, the truest mother of Christians, proclaims that not only God himself—whose attainment is the most blessed life—is to be worshiped with the greatest purity and chastity, introducing no creature for us to worship and serve; and that from that incorruptible and inviolable eternity, to which alone man ought to be subject, to which alone the rational soul, by cleaving, is not miserable, it excludes everything that has been made, everything subject to change, everything subject to time; neither confusing what eternity, truth, and finally peace itself distinguish, nor again separating what a single majesty joins together.

But you also embrace love and charity toward one’s neighbor in such a way that with you every medicine for the various diseases by which souls are sick on account of their sins prevails.
