63. You train and teach children in a childlike manner, young men with strength, and old men quietly, according to the age not merely of each person’s body but also of his soul. You subject women to their husbands—not for the satisfaction of lust, but for the propagation of offspring and the partnership of household affairs—in chaste and faithful obedience. You place husbands over their wives, not to mock the weaker sex, but according to the laws of sincere love.

You join children to their parents in a kind of free servitude, and place parents before their children in devout authority. You bind brothers to brothers by the stronger and closer bond of religion than that of blood. You unite every relationship of kinship and affinity in mutual love, while preserving the bonds of nature and willing affection.

You teach servants to cling to their masters, not so much through the necessity of their condition as through the pleasure of duty. You make masters gracious toward their servants by consideration of the supreme God, their common Lord, and more inclined to provide for them than to restrain them.

You join citizens to citizens, nations to nations, and, in the fullest sense, human beings to one another through remembrance of their first parents—not merely in fellowship but also in a kind of brotherhood. You teach kings to look after their peoples; you admonish peoples to submit to their kings.

You carefully teach to whom honor is owed, to whom affection, to whom reverence, to whom fear, to whom consolation, to whom admonition, to whom encouragement, to whom discipline, and to whom reproof [Col. 1337] [Note: [Col. 1337] Some codices have *coertio*, or *coercitio*.]; showing how not everything is owed to everyone, while charity is owed to all and injustice to no one.

64. When this human love has nourished the soul clinging to your breasts and strengthened it, making it fit to follow God, then, when his majesty begins to reveal itself in such measure as is sufficient for a human being while he is an inhabitant of this earth, such a fire of charity is kindled within, and such a blaze of divine love rises, that, when all vices have been burned away and the human being purified and sanctified, it becomes sufficiently clear how divinely it was said: “I am a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24) [Note: [Col. 1337] See *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 7, no. 5.]; and, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49).

These two utterances of the one God, marked out in the two Testaments, declare the sanctification of the soul by harmonious testimony, so that what was also taken from the Old into the New Scripture may at last come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your sting? Where, O death, is your contention?” (1 Cor. 15:54–55).

If these heretics could understand this one thing, they would nowhere worship God except with you and in your embrace, without arrogance and in deep peace.

Rightly, therefore, the divine commandments are preserved broadly and extensively among you. Rightly, among you, it is understood how much graver it is to sin against a known law than against an unknown one. “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law” (ibid. 56): the conscience of a despised commandment strikes and kills with greater force [Note: [Col. 1337] Four manuscripts: “because the conscience strikes more gravely.” Three Sorbonic manuscripts and two others: “how gravely the conscience strikes.”].

Rightly, among you, it is seen how vain conduct under the law is, when lust ravages the soul and is restrained by fear of punishment rather than overwhelmed by love of virtue.

Rightly, so many among you are seen to be hospitable, dutiful, merciful, learned, chaste, holy, and so aflame with love of God that even solitude delights them in their supreme self-restraint and their astonishing contempt for this world.

## CHAPTER XXXI — Against the Manichaeans’ Continence, the Life of the Anchorites and Coenobites

65. What is it, I ask, that those people see who cannot refrain from loving a human being and yet can refrain from seeing a human being? Whatever it is, it is certainly superior to human affairs, since through contemplation of it a person can live without other people.

Now, Manichaeans, listen to the conduct and extraordinary continence of perfect Christians, for whom the highest chastity has seemed not merely worthy of praise but also worthy of pursuit. If you possess any sense of shame, do not dare to boast shamelessly before the minds of the ignorant as though abstinence from difficult things were your special achievement.

I shall not speak of things unknown to you, but of things you conceal from us. For who does not know that the multitude of Christians practicing the highest continence is spreading throughout the world more and more each day, especially in the East and in Egypt—something that cannot possibly be hidden from you?

66. I shall say nothing about those whom I mentioned shortly before, who are completely withdrawn and hidden from every human gaze, living in the most deserted regions, content with bread alone, brought to them at fixed intervals of time [Col. 1338], and with water; delighting in converse with God, to whom they have clung with pure minds, and blessed in contemplation of his beauty, which can be perceived only by the understanding of the holy.

I shall say nothing, I repeat, about them. To some they seem to have abandoned human affairs more than they ought, since they do not understand how much their spirit benefits us through their prayers, and their life through its example, although we are not permitted to see their bodies.

But I consider it lengthy and unnecessary to argue this point. For how can our speech make visible that lofty height of holiness which naturally appears wondrous and worthy of honor to anyone who sees it? These people need only be reminded that the temperance and continence of the most holy Christians of the Catholic faith have advanced so far that to some it seems they must be restrained and, as it were, brought back within human limits. Indeed, even those who disapprove of it judge that their minds have risen so far above human beings.

67. But if this exceeds the limits of our endurance, who would not admire and praise those who, having despised and abandoned the allurements of this world, have gathered together into a common life of the utmost chastity and holiness, spending their years together in prayers, readings, and discussions?

They are swollen with no pride, turbulent with no obstinacy, embittered by no envy. Rather, they are modest, reverent, peaceful, and offer to God himself, from whom they have merited the ability to do these things, a life of the greatest harmony and the most intense devotion to him as a most pleasing gift.

No one possesses anything as his own; no one is a burden to anyone else. They work with their hands at tasks by which the body can be nourished and the mind cannot be hindered from God. They hand over their work [Note: [Col. 1338] Lov. and Arn.: “They hand over their work together.” Thirteen manuscripts, Bad., and Er.: “They hand over their own work.”] to those whom they call deans, because they are placed over groups of ten, so that none of them need concern himself with the care of his body—neither with food, nor clothing, nor anything else required by daily necessity or by a change in health, as commonly happens.

The deans, however, arranging everything with great care and providing whatever that life requires because of bodily weakness, themselves nevertheless render an account [Note: [Col. 1338] Most codices have *traditionem* (“a handing over”); in its place, Latinus Latinius and Antonius Arnaldus thought *rationem* (“an account”) should be read. This is also what is found in the Vatican manuscript and in Bad.’s edition.] to one person whom they call “father.”

These fathers are not only most holy in conduct but also outstanding in divine teaching and excellent in every respect. They advise those whom they call their sons without any arrogance, exercising great authority in commanding and meeting with great willingness on the part of the others in obeying.

At the final hour of the day, while they are still fasting, they come from their respective dwellings to hear that father. At least three thousand people come to each father; indeed, many more live under one father.

They listen with incredible eagerness and profound silence, expressing the movements of their souls according as the speaker’s discourse affects them—by groaning, weeping, or a modest joy free from every outcry [Note: [Col. 1338] The printed editions have: “But expressing joy with modesty and without shouting.” The more harmonious reading of the manuscripts has been restored here.].

Afterward the body is restored with as much food as is sufficient for health and well-being [Col. 1339], each person restraining his appetite so that it does not plunge even into the meager and inexpensive things that are available.

Thus they abstain not only from meat and wine, as sufficient for the subduing of lusts, but also from those things that provoke the appetite of the belly and throat more vigorously because they seem cleaner to some. Under this pretext, the shameful desire for elaborate foods—which is unrelated to meat—is often defended both ridiculously and disgracefully.

Whatever exceeds what is necessary for food—for much is left over from the work of their hands and from the restriction of their meals—is distributed to the needy with greater care than it was acquired by those who distribute it. For they do not take pains in any way to ensure that these things abound for them; rather, they make every effort to ensure that what remains in excess does not remain with them, to such an extent that they even send loaded ships to regions inhabited by the poor.

There is no need to say more about a matter so well known.

68. This is also the life of women who serve God with devoted chastity. They live in dwellings separated from men and as remote from them as propriety requires, joined to them only by devout charity and the imitation of virtue.

No young men have access to them, nor even the most serious and reputable old men, except as far as the vestibule, for the necessary purpose of supplying what they need. They exercise and support their bodies by woolworking, and hand over the garments themselves to the brothers, receiving from them in turn what is necessary for food.

If I wished to praise these customs, this life, this order, and this institution, I would neither be able to do so worthily nor avoid seeming to judge that what is set forth plainly by itself could not please unless, in addition to the narrator’s simplicity, I added the grand style of a eulogist.

Manichaeans, criticize these things if you can. Do not point out our weeds to blind people who are unable to distinguish them.

## CHAPTER XXXII — Praise of the Clergy

69. Yet the excellent customs of the Catholic Church are not so narrowly confined that I would think only the life of those whom I have mentioned worthy of praise.

How many excellent and most holy bishops I have known; how many presbyters; how many deacons; and how many ministers of the divine Sacraments of every sort! Their virtue seems to me all the more remarkable and worthy of greater praise because it is more difficult to preserve amid the diversity of humanity and the greater turbulence of this life.

For they preside not over people who have already been healed, but over people who are still to be healed. The vices of the multitude must be endured in order that they may be cured, and the pestilence must first be tolerated before it can be calmed.

It is exceedingly difficult here to maintain the best way of life and a peaceful, tranquil mind. For, to explain briefly, these people live where one is learning to live, while the others live where life is already being lived.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — Another Class Living Together in the City. Three-Day Fasts

70. Nor for that reason would I despise the praiseworthy class of Christians who live in cities, though they are as far removed as possible from ordinary life.

I myself saw in Milan a lodging-house of holy people, not a small number, over whom one presbyter presided—a man of the highest goodness and learning.

In Rome, too, I came to know several such communities. In each, a person distinguished by gravity, prudence, and divine knowledge presides over the others living with him, who live in Christian charity, holiness, and freedom. They themselves are burdensome to no one, but, following the custom of the East and the authority of the apostle Paul, they support themselves by the work of their own hands.

I also learned that many practice fasts that are altogether extraordinary—not merely restoring the body once each day toward evening, which is entirely customary, but very often spending three continuous days or more without food or drink.

This occurs not only among men but also among women. Groups of widows and virgins likewise live together, and each group is presided over by women of the greatest seriousness and proven character, skilled and prepared not only for establishing and ordering conduct [Note: [Col. 1340] This phrase is absent from most manuscripts: “for establishing and ordering conduct.”], but also for instructing minds.

71. Amid all this, no one is forced into hardships that he cannot endure; no one is compelled to do what he refuses; nor is anyone condemned by the others because he admits that he is too weak to imitate them.

For they remember how strongly charity is commended throughout all the Scriptures. They remember: “To the pure all things are pure” (Tit. 1:15); and, “It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out” (Matt. 15:11).

Therefore all their diligence is directed not toward rejecting kinds of food as polluted, but toward conquering desire and preserving love for the brothers. They remember: “Food is for the stomach and the stomach for food, and God will destroy both one and the other” (1 Cor. 6:13); and elsewhere: “Neither, if we eat, will we abound; nor, if we do not eat, will we lack” (ibid. 8:8); and above all: “It is good, brothers, not to eat meat, nor to drink wine, nor to do anything by which your brother is offended.”

For this shows that all these things must be directed toward the goal of charity. “One believes he may eat everything, but the one who is weak eats vegetables,” he says. “Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he will stand, for God is able to make him stand.”

And shortly afterward: “The one who eats eats for the Lord and gives thanks to God; and the one who does not eat does not eat for the Lord and gives thanks to God.”

And again, later: “Therefore each of us shall give an account of himself. Let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that you do not place a stumbling block or an occasion of offense before your brother. I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; but to the one who considers something unclean, to that person it is unclean.”

Could he have shown more clearly that the power capable of defiling a person lies not in the very things by which we are nourished but in the mind? And for that reason, even those who are fit to despise such things and know with certainty that they are not polluted if they take some food with no shameful desire and with elevation of mind must nevertheless keep charity in view.

See what follows: “For if your brother is grieved because of food, you are no longer walking according to charity” (Rom. 14:2–21).

72. Read the rest, for it would take too long to include everything. You will find the command that those who are able to despise such things—that is, those who are stronger and more secure—must nevertheless exercise restraint, lest those who still need such restraint because of their weakness be offended.

The people of whom I was speaking know and observe these things. For they are Christians, not heretics; they understand the Scriptures according to apostolic discipline, not according to the proud and fictitious title of “Apostle” [Note: [Col. 1341] The printed editions have *Apostolatus* (“apostolate”). Some manuscripts have *Apostolus* (“apostle”). The Gemmeticensis codex has *Apostoli* (“of the apostle”). Augustine is evidently alluding to the letters of Manichaeus, all of which began: “Manichaeus, apostle of Jesus Christ,” etc., as is said in *Against Faustus*, book 13, chapter 4.].

No one despises the person who does not eat; no one judges the person who eats; the weak person eats vegetables. Many who are strong do the same for the sake of the weak. For many, however, the reason is not this, but that they prefer to live on cheaper food and to pass their lives in tranquility with the least expensive bodily nourishment.

“For all things are lawful for me,” he says, “but I will not be brought under the power of anything” (1 Cor. 6:12).

Thus many neither eat meat nor superstitiously consider it unclean. The very same people who abstain from it when healthy accept it without any fear when illness demands it.

Many do not drink wine, but they do not consider themselves defiled by it [Note: [Col. 1341] Eight manuscripts: “Nor do they consider those who drink to be defiled.”]. They ensure that it is provided with the greatest humanity and moderation both to certain people who are weaker and to all who cannot preserve bodily health without it.

They fraternally admonish some foolish people who refuse it, lest through empty superstition they become weak more quickly rather than holy more truly. They read to them the apostle’s instruction to his disciple that he should take a little wine on account of his frequent illnesses (1 Tim. 5:23) [Note: [Col. 1341] Eleven manuscripts: “On account of his various illnesses.”].

Thus they diligently practice piety; but they know that bodily exercise, as the same apostle says, is useful for a little while (ibid. 4:8).

73. Those who are able, then—and they are innumerable—abstain both from meat and from wine for two reasons: either because of the weakness of their brothers or because of their own freedom.

Charity is guarded above all. Food is adapted to charity, speech to charity, dress to charity, appearance to charity; they come together and conspire in one charity. To violate it is regarded as an offense against God. Whatever resists it [Note: [Col. 1341] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “if anyone resists”; shortly afterward, “if anyone offends.”] is conquered and expelled; whatever offends it is not allowed to last even one day.

They know that charity has been so commended by Christ and the apostles that, if it is absent, everything is empty, but if it is present, everything is full.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — The Church Is Not to Be Blamed for the Conduct of Wicked Christians. Worshipers of Tombs and Pictures

74. Manichaeans, resist these people if you can. Look at them, and, if you dare, name them without lying and with contempt. Compare your fasts with their fasts, your chastity with their chastity, your clothing with their clothing, your feasts with their feasts, your modesty with their modesty, and finally your charity with their charity—and, as the matter especially demands, compare commandments with commandments.

Then you will see what difference there is between display and sincerity, between the straight path and error, between faith and deceit, between strength and swelling pride, between blessedness and misery, between unity and dismemberment, and finally between the sirens of superstition and the harbor of religion.

75. Do not gather for me people who profess the Christian name without either knowing or displaying the force of their profession. Do not pursue crowds of ignorant people who are either superstitious even within the true religion or so devoted to lusts that they have forgotten what they promised God.

I know that there are many worshipers of tombs and pictures. I know that there are many who drink most extravagantly over the dead, and, offering feasts to corpses, bury themselves over the buried and count their gluttony and drunkenness as religion.

I know that there are many who have renounced this age in words and yet wish to be crushed by all the burdens of this age, rejoicing when they have been crushed.

Nor is it surprising that, amid such a vast multitude of peoples, there are not lacking people whose censured lives you use to deceive the unwary and turn them away from Catholic salvation, when in your small number [Note: [Col. 1342] The printed editions prefer *paupertate* (“poverty”), except Bad., who, with the manuscripts, has *paucitate* (“smallness of number”).] you suffer great straits because you are required to produce even one of those whom you call the Elect who observes those very commandments that you defend with irrational superstition.

I have also undertaken to show in another volume how empty, harmful, and sacrilegious those commandments are, and how they are not observed by a large part of you—indeed, almost by all of you.

76. For now I admonish you to stop at last cursing the Catholic Church by condemning the conduct of people whom the Church itself condemns and whom it strives daily to correct as though they were bad children.

But all those who are corrected by good will and God’s help recover through repentance what they had lost by sinning. Those who continue in their former vices through ill will, or even add worse things to their earlier offenses, are indeed allowed to remain in the Lord’s field and to grow together with the good seed; but the time will come when the weeds will be separated.

Or, if because of the Christian name itself they should be considered more like chaff than thorns, the one who cleanses the threshing floor will also come, separating the chaff from the grain and distributing to each part, according to its own merit, what is fitting with the utmost equity (Matt. 3:13 and 13:24–43).

## CHAPTER XXXV — Marriage and Possessions Also Granted to the Baptized by the Apostle
77. Meanwhile, why do you rage? Why are you blinded by partisan zeal? Why do you entangle yourselves in the prolonged defense of so great an error? Seek the crops in the field, the grain on the threshing floor: they will readily appear and offer themselves to those who seek them. Why do you fix your eyes so intently on the refuse? Why do you frighten inexperienced people away from the fertility of a rich garden by the harshness of its hedges? There is a sure entrance, though known to fewer people, by which one can enter—an entrance which you either do not believe exists or do not wish to find.

There are countless faithful people in the Catholic Church who do not use this world; there are those who use it “as though not using it,” [Note: [Col. 1343] Thus Bad. and most manuscripts. But Er., Lov., and Arn.: “pernicious.”] as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 7:31)—something already demonstrated in those times when Christians were compelled to worship idols. For how many wealthy men then, how many rural heads of households, how many merchants, how many soldiers, how many leading citizens of their cities, how many senators in the end, of both sexes, abandoned all these vain and temporal things—things which, although they used them, did not hold them captive—and underwent death for the sake of a saving faith and religion! Thus they showed unbelievers that they themselves rather possessed those things than were possessed by them.

**78.** Why do you falsely accuse the faithful, now renewed by Baptism, saying that they ought not to beget children or possess fields, houses, or any money? Paul permits this. For—and this cannot be denied—he wrote to the faithful, after listing many kinds of vicious people who will not possess the kingdom of God:

“And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God.”

No one will dare to understand “washed” and “sanctified” as referring to anyone other than the faithful, and those who have renounced this world. But since he has shown to whom he was writing, let us see whether he permits these things to such people. For he continues:

“All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient. All things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any. Foods are for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them. The body, however, is not for fornication but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. Now God has both raised up the Lord and will also raise us up by his power. Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Shall I therefore take the members of Christ and make them members of a prostitute? Certainly not. Do you not know that whoever joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, he says, ‘The two shall be one flesh.’ But whoever joins himself to the Lord is one spirit. Flee fornication. Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body. Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God, and that you are not your own? For you were bought at a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:11–20).

“And concerning the matters about which you wrote to me: ‘It is good for a man not to touch a woman.’ But because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband. Let the husband render to his wife her due, and likewise also the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise also the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does. Do not defraud one another, unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same relationship, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this by way of concession, not by command. I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (ibid. 7:1–7).

**79.** Does the Apostle not seem to you to have shown the highest way to the strong, while permitting the weaker what is next to it? For when he says, “I wish that all people were as I myself am,” he shows that not touching a woman is the highest way. Conjugal chastity is next to this highest way, so that a person may not be ruined by fornication.

Did he therefore say that these people were still not faithful because they make use of marriage? Indeed, by this chastity of marriage he said that the spouses themselves, if one of them should be an unbeliever, and the offspring born from them, are sanctified through one another:

“For the unbelieving husband is sanctified through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through the believing husband; otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (ibid. 14).

Why do you oppose such great truth with such obstinacy? Why do you try to obscure the light of the Scriptures with vain shadows?

**80.** Stop saying that catechumens may use marriage but the faithful may not; that catechumens may possess money but the faithful may not. For there are also many who use things “as though not using them.” In that most sacred washing the renewal of the new human being begins, so that it may be brought to completion by progress—more quickly in some, more slowly in others. Nevertheless, many advance into a new life, if only someone observes the matter carefully, not with hostility.

For, as the Apostle says, “although our outward person is being corrupted, the inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). The Apostle says that the inward person is renewed day by day so that he may be perfected, whereas you want people to begin with perfection. Would that you wanted this! But you seek rather not a means by which to raise up the weak, but a means by which to deceive the unsuspecting.

You ought not to have spoken with such boldness, even if it were established that you yourselves were perfect in those very frivolous commandments of yours. But your conscience knows that those whom you introduce into your sect, once they begin to associate more closely with you, will discover many things existing among you which no one suspected when you were accusing others. How great, then, is the shamelessness of seeking perfection in weaker Catholics in order to turn the inexperienced away from them, while in no way displaying that perfection among those whom you have turned away?

But lest we now seem to be pouring anything rashly upon you, let this be the limit of the present volume, so that at some point we may proceed to demonstrate the rules of your life and your celebrated conduct.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE MORALS OF THE MANICHAEANS

In this book, after their doctrine concerning the origin and nature of evil has been carefully refuted, those three things—of the mouth, hands, and bosom—which they proclaimed as seals in their impious way of life are examined, and their superstitious abstinence and wicked mysteries are mocked. Afterwards, certain crimes discovered among them are reported.

[Note: [Col. 1345] The book *On the Morals of the Manichaeans* was collated with three Sorbonne manuscripts, an equal number of Victorine manuscripts, and the Navarrese, Christinaean, Cistercian, Regiomontane, and Gembloux manuscripts, as well as one from the major convent of the Reverend Franciscan Fathers of Paris, with the readings of five Belgian manuscripts at Louvain, and finally with the editions of Erasmus and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1345] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.]

[Col. 1345]

# CHAPTER ONE. The highest good is that to which supreme being belongs

[Col. 1345]

**1.** I think no one can doubt that, when inquiry is made concerning good and evil, this kind of question belongs to moral discipline, in which we are engaged in this discussion. Therefore I would indeed wish people to bring such a clear-sighted mind to the investigation of these matters that they could see that highest good than which nothing is better or higher, to which a pure and perfect rational soul is subordinated.

Once this has been understood and perfected, they would at the same time see that this is rightly said to possess being supremely and first of all. For that must be said to possess being most fully which always remains in the same condition, which is in every respect like itself, which cannot be corrupted or changed in any way, which is not subject to time, and which cannot now be in a different condition from that in which it was before.

This is what is most truly said to possess being. For the meaning of a nature remaining in itself and existing unchangeably lies beneath this word. We can call this nothing other than God; and if you rightly seek what is contrary to him, there is absolutely nothing.

For the contrary of being is nothing other than not-being. Therefore no nature is contrary to God. But since we bring to the contemplation of these things a mind’s vision wounded and dulled by frivolous opinions and depraved will, let us try, as far as we can, to arrive gradually and cautiously at some knowledge of so great a matter—not as sighted people usually seek, but as those who grope with their hands.

# CHAPTER TWO. What evil is. The Manichaeans say most truly that evil is what is contrary to nature, but their heresy is overturned by this very statement

**2.** Often, and almost always, Manichaeans, you ask those whom you try to persuade of your heresy where evil comes from. Suppose that I have now encountered you for the first time. If you please, grant me this much: lay aside your opinion for a little while, the opinion by which you think you know these things, and try with me, as beginners, to investigate so great a matter.

You ask me where evil comes from; but I in turn ask you what evil is. Which inquiry is more reasonable: that of those who ask where something comes from while they do not know what it is, or that of someone who first thinks it necessary to ask what it is, so that the origin of an unknown thing—which would be utterly absurd—is not sought?

You speak most truly [Note: [Col. 1345] Thus in the editions published up to the present. But in seven manuscripts, “You speak most truly” is omitted; in four others it reads: “If you say that it is what is contrary to nature, you speak most truly.”]. For who is so blind in mind that he does not see that what is contrary to its nature is evil for each kind of thing?

But once this has been established, your heresy is overturned. For no nature is evil, if what is contrary to nature is evil. Yet you assert that a certain nature and substance is evil. Moreover, whatever is contrary to nature necessarily opposes nature and tries to destroy it. Therefore what exists tends to bring about its own nonexistence.

For nature itself is nothing other than that which is understood to possess being in its own kind. Thus, just as we now call “essence” by a new name what possesses being, and often also call it “substance,” so the ancients, who did not have these terms, called it “nature” in place of essence and substance.

Evil, then—if you are willing to attend to the matter rather than stubbornly resist—is to fall away from essence and tend toward nonexistence.

**3.** Accordingly, when it is said in the Catholic Church that God is the author of all natures and substances, those who are able to understand this simultaneously understand that God is not the author of evil. For how can the one who is the cause that all things which exist should exist also be the cause that they should not exist—that is, that they should fall away from essence and tend toward nonexistence? Sound reason loudly declares that this is general evil.

But that race of yours belonging to evil, which you wish to be the highest evil, how will it be contrary to nature—that is, contrary to substance—when you say that it is a nature and substance? For if it acts against itself, it deprives itself of being; and if it accomplishes this, it will then finally reach the highest evil.

Yet it will not accomplish this, because you wish it not only to exist but also to exist eternally. Therefore that which is said to be a substance cannot be the highest evil.

**4.** But what am I to do? I know that many among you are wholly unable to understand these things. I know also that there are some who, although they can perceive them to some extent by a good natural intelligence, nevertheless act stubbornly with the evil will by which they will lose even that intelligence. They seek rather something to say against these arguments that may easily be persuaded to the slow and weak, than to agree that they are true.

Still, I shall not regret having written this, whether someone among you may eventually consider it with a fair judgment and abandon your error, or whether intelligent people who are subject to God and still untouched by zeal for your cause may read it and be unable to be deceived by your arguments.

# CHAPTER THREE. If evil is defined as what harms, the Manichaeans are again refuted on this basis

**5.** Let us therefore investigate these matters more carefully and, as far as possible, more plainly. I ask you again: what is evil? If you say, “That which harms,” you will not be lying here either.

But, I beg you, pay attention; I beg you, stay alert; I beg you, lay aside partisan zeal and seek the truth—not for the sake of winning, but for the sake of finding it.

Whatever harms deprives the thing it harms of some good; for if it takes away no good at all, it harms absolutely nothing. What could be clearer, I ask you? What could be plainer? What is so evident to anyone of average understanding, provided he is not stubborn?

Once this has been established, what follows already seems clear, as I think. In that race which you suppose to be the highest evil, nothing can be harmed, since there is no good there. But if there are two natures, as you assert—the kingdom of light and the kingdom of darkness—then, since you confess that the kingdom of light is God, to whom you grant a certain simple nature, so that nothing there is worse than anything else, you must confess something strongly opposed to you but nevertheless necessary to confess: that this nature, which you not only do not deny to be the highest good but vigorously try to persuade us is so, is unchangeable, impenetrable, incorruptible, and inviolable.

For otherwise it would not be the highest good; the highest good is that than which nothing is better. But such a nature cannot be harmed in any way.

If, then, to harm is to deprive of good, as I have shown, the kingdom of darkness cannot be harmed because there is no good there; and the kingdom of light cannot be harmed because it is inviolable. Whom, then, will that which you call evil harm?

# CHAPTER FOUR. The distinction between good in itself and good by participation

**6.** Therefore, since you cannot extricate yourselves, see how straightforward is the position of Catholic teaching. It says that there is one good which is supremely and in itself good—not through participation in some other good, but by its own nature [Note: [Col. 1347] Many manuscripts omit the words: “not through participation in some other good, but by its own nature.”] and essence—and another good which is good by participating in and possessing the good. This latter has from that highest good the fact that it is good, while the highest good itself remains in being and loses nothing.

This latter good, which we have mentioned second, it calls a creature. A creature can be harmed through defect. God is not the author of its defect, because he is the author of its existence—or, so to speak, of its being.

Thus it is also shown how evil is spoken of: it is most truly spoken of not according to essence but according to privation. And a nature which can be harmed becomes apparent. For it is neither the highest evil, since good is taken away from it when it is harmed, nor the highest good, since it can fall away from good precisely because it is called good not by being good but by possessing good.

Nor is a thing naturally good when, since it is said to have been made, it necessarily received the fact of being good. Thus God is the highest good, and all the things he made are good, although they are not as good as the one who made them.

For who would be so insane as to demand that the works be equal to the craftsman and the created things equal to their creator? What more do you want? Do you also want something plainer?

# CHAPTER FIVE. If evil is defined as corruption, their heresy is also utterly overturned on this basis

**7.** Let me ask a third time, then, what evil is. Perhaps you will answer, “Corruption.” Who would deny that this too is general evil? For this is what is contrary to nature; this is what harms [Note: [Col. 1347] Here we have restored from the manuscripts the words “this is,” and below, after “is not evil,” we have added “is not,” which are absent from the editions.] [Col. 1348].

But corruption does not exist in itself; it exists in some substance which it corrupts. For corruption itself is not a substance. Therefore the thing which corruption corrupts is not corruption; it is not evil [Note: [Col. 1348] In the editions of Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, with the words “is not” omitted, the passage reads: “Therefore the thing which corruption corrupts is not evil. For what is corrupted …” M.].

For what is corrupted is deprived of integrity and purity. Therefore what has no purity of which it can be deprived cannot be corrupted; but what possesses purity is certainly good by participation in purity.

Likewise, what is corrupted is certainly perverted; but what is perverted is deprived of order, and order is a good. Therefore what is corrupted is not without good; indeed, it can be deprived, when it is corrupted, of that very thing by which it is not without good.

Therefore, if that race of darkness was without every good, as you say, it could not be corrupted. For it did not possess anything that corruption could take away from it; and if corruption takes nothing away, it does not corrupt.

Now dare to say, if you can, that God and God’s kingdom could have been corrupted, if you cannot discover how the kingdom of the devil, as you describe it, could be corrupted.

# CHAPTER SIX. What thing corruption affects, and what corruption is

**8.** What, then, does Catholic truth say at this point? What do you suppose, except what truth teaches: that a created substance can be corrupted; that the uncreated substance, which is the highest good, is incorruptible; and that corruption itself, which is the highest evil, cannot be corrupted, but is not a substance?

If you ask what corruption is, observe where it tries to lead the things it corrupts. For it affects the things corrupted from itself. Everything through corruption falls away from what it was and is compelled not to remain, compelled not to exist. For “to exist” refers to remaining.

Therefore what is said to exist supremely and most fully is said to do so by remaining in itself. But what is changed for the better is not changed because it remained; rather, it was being perverted for the worse—that is, falling away from essence. The author of essence is not the author of this falling away.

Some things, then, are changed for the better and therefore tend toward existence. They are not said to be perverted by this change, but to return and be converted. For perversion is contrary to ordering.

But those things which tend toward existence tend toward order. When they have attained it, they attain existence insofar as a creature can attain it. For order brings the thing it orders into a certain fittingness.

Existence is nothing other than being one. Therefore, to the extent that anything acquires unity, to that extent it exists. The activity of unity is fittingness and harmony, by which composite things exist insofar as they exist. Simple things exist through themselves because they are one; things that are not simple imitate unity through the harmony of their parts, and exist insofar as they attain it.

Consequently, ordering compels existence, whereas disorder compels nonexistence. Disorder is also called perversion and corruption. Whatever, then, is corrupted tends toward nonexistence.

It is now your task to consider where corruption compels things, so that you may discover the highest evil; for that is where corruption tries to lead them.

# CHAPTER SEVEN. God’s goodness does not allow anything to be brought by corruption to nonexistence. The difference between creating and establishing

[Col. 1349]

**9.** But God’s goodness does not allow a thing to be brought to that point. He orders all things that are falling away in such a way that they are placed where they can exist most fittingly, until through ordered movements they return to the place from which they fell [Note: [Col. 1349] See *Retractations* 1.7.6.].

Thus he also orders rational souls, in which free will is most powerful [Note: [Col. 1349] The editions read *potissimum* (“especially”); eleven manuscripts instead have *potentissimum* (“most powerful”).], when they fall away from him, among the lower levels of creation, where it is fitting for them to be such.

They therefore become miserable by divine judgment while being ordered suitably according to their merits. Hence that saying, which you especially try to attack, was most aptly spoken:

“I make good things and create evil things” (Isa. 45:7).

For “to create” is said of establishing and ordering. Accordingly, in many copies it is written: “I make good things and establish evil things.” To make is to produce what did not exist at all; to establish is to order what already existed in some fashion, so that it may be better and more fully what it is.

God establishes—that is, orders—the things that are falling away, things that tend toward nonexistence, when he says, “I establish evil things”; he does not establish those which have reached the goal toward which they tend.

For it has been said: Nothing is permitted by divine providence to reach the point of nonexistence.

**10.** These matters are treated more fully and extensively elsewhere, but while dealing with you this is sufficient. For the door which you despair of, and make the inexperienced despair of, had to be shown to you.

No one introduces you except good will, which divine mercy makes peaceful, as the Gospel sings:

“Glory to God in the highest, and peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

It is enough, I say, for you to see that there is no conclusion to a religious discussion of good and evil except that whatever exists, insofar as it exists, is from God; but insofar as it falls away from essence, it is not from God, although it is always ordered by divine providence in a manner fitting to the whole.

If you do not yet see this, I do not know what more I can do now except treat in still greater detail what has been said. For piety and purity alone lead the mind to greater things.

# CHAPTER EIGHT. Evil is not any substance, but an incompatibility hostile to substance

**11.** When I ask what evil is, what else will you answer except either that it is what is contrary to nature, or what harms, or corruption, or something of this kind? But in these answers I have shown your shipwrecks—unless, as you are accustomed to do when pressed, you answer childishly to children [Note: [Col. 1349] Seven manuscripts and the Chevallon edition read: “You are accustomed, when you have been pressed, to act childishly.” A little later, the editions read “that no substance is evil”; we have corrected this according to the manuscripts to “that evil is.”] and say that evil is fire, poison, a wild animal, and other things of this kind.

For when one of the leading members of this heresy, whom we used to hear more familiarly and more frequently, was speaking about someone who said that no substance is evil, he said: “I would like to place a scorpion in a person’s hand and see whether he would not withdraw his hand. If he did so, he would be convicted—not by words but by the fact itself—of there being some substance that is evil, since he would not deny that the animal is a substance.”

He did not say this in the presence of the person in question, but when, agitated, we reported to him what that person had said. Thus he responded, as I have said, childishly to children.

For who, if somewhat educated and instructed, does not see that such things harm through an incompatibility of bodily constitution, and again do not harm through compatibility, often even conferring considerable benefits? For if that poison were evil in itself, it would destroy the scorpion itself sooner and more thoroughly.

On the contrary, if something were entirely removed from it by some means, it would unquestionably die. Therefore it is evil for that creature’s body to lose what it is good for our body to receive; likewise, it is good for that creature to possess what it is good for us to lack.

Will the same thing, then, be both good and evil? By no means. Rather, evil is what is contrary to nature. For this is evil both for that animal and for us: the incompatibility itself, which is undoubtedly not a substance but, indeed, hostile to substance.

Where, then, does it come from? Observe where it compels things to go, and you will learn—provided that some inner light is still alive in you. For everything that destroys compels what it destroys toward nonexistence.

God, however, is the author of essence. No essence can be seen to be something which, wherever it exists, compels that thing to be nonexistent. Therefore one may say whence incompatibility does not arise; but nothing can be said as to whence it arises.

**12.** As history relates, a criminal woman of Athens gradually drank the poison which condemned people used to swallow in a fixed measure in order to die, and trained herself to drink it without any, even slight, harm to her health.

Accordingly, when she was eventually condemned, she received, like the others, the standard quantity of poison which she had overcome through habituation, but she did not die like the others. Since this was considered a great marvel, she was sent into exile.

What are we to think? If poison is evil, did she make it so that evil would not be evil for her? What could be more absurd? But because incompatibility is evil, she instead brought it about through moderate habituation that that substance became compatible with her body.

For when could she, by any cleverness, bring it about that incompatibility would not harm her? Why could she not? Because what is truly and generally evil always harms everyone.

Oil is beneficial to our bodies, but strongly hostile to many animals that have six feet. Is hellebore not food in one way, medicine in another, and poison in another? Who would not declare that salt taken in excessive quantity is poison? Yet who can count how many and how great bodily benefits come from it?

When seawater is drunk, it is harmful to land animals; but while many bodies are wetted by it, it is highly suitable and useful to them. For fish, in both respects, it is healthful and pleasurable.

Bread nourishes a human being but kills a hawk. Mud itself, which gravely offends and harms when drunk or smelled, does it not cool when touched in summer and serve as medicine for wounds caused by fire?

What is more contemptible than dung? What is more worthless than ash? Yet these bring such great benefits to fields that the Romans thought divine honors should be offered to their inventor, Stercutius, from whom even the word for dung is derived.

**13.** But why should I gather minor examples, when they are innumerable? Who would doubt that the four elements themselves, which are readily at hand, benefit through compatibility, but when applied incompatibly are strongly hostile to nature?

We, who live by air, are killed when buried beneath earth and water; yet countless animals crawl alive through sand and looser earth. Fish, on the other hand, die in this air.

Fire corrupts our bodies, but when suitably applied it restores heat lost through cold and drives away countless illnesses.

This sun to which you bend the knee—than which, among visible things, nothing more beautiful is truly found—strengthens the eyes of eagles, but wounds and darkens ours when we look at it. Yet through habituation we too come to fix our gaze upon it without harm.

Will you therefore allow us to compare it with that poison which habituation made harmless to the Athenian woman? Look back and pay attention at last: if any substance is evil because it harms someone, the light you worship cannot be defended from this charge.

Consider instead that this incompatibility is universal evil, through which the sun’s ray makes the eyes dark, although nothing is more delightful to them than light.

# CHAPTER NINE. The Manichaeans’ fables about good and evil cannot even stand

**14.** I have said this so that, if possible, you may finally stop saying that the earth is evil because it is immeasurably deep and long; that the mind wandering through the earth is evil; that the five caves of the elements are evil—one filled with darkness, another with waters, another with winds, another with fire, and another with smoke; and that the animals born in each of those elements are evil—those that crawl in darkness, swim in water, fly in winds, walk on four feet in fire, and walk on two feet in smoke.

For, as you describe them, these things cannot exist in any way, since whatever is such must, insofar as it exists, be from the highest God, because insofar as it exists it is certainly good.

If pain and weakness are evil, then those animals possessed such bodily strength that, after the world had been fashioned from them according to your sect, you say their aborted offspring fell from heaven to earth and could not die.

If blindness is evil, they saw; if deafness, they heard. If becoming speechless or being mute is evil, voices there were so marked and distinct that, as you assert, they were persuaded in an assembly by a single speaker to wage war against God.

If sterility is evil, there was there great fertility for begetting children. If exile is evil, they were in their own land and inhabited their own regions. If slavery is evil, there were also those who ruled there. If death is evil, they were alive—and they lived in such a way that you proclaim that the mind itself could never in any way die, not even after God’s victory.

**15.** Why, I ask, do I find in the highest evil so many goods opposed to the evils I have mentioned? Or if these things are not evils, will any substance, insofar as it is a substance, ultimately be evil?

If weakness is not evil, will a weak body be evil? If blindness is not evil, will darkness be evil? If deafness is not evil, will a deaf person be evil? If being mute is not evil, will a fish be evil? If sterility is not evil, how is a sterile animal evil? If exile is not evil, how is an animal in exile evil, or an animal sending someone into exile? If slavery is not evil, how is a serving animal evil, or one that compels someone to serve? [Note: [Col. 1352] The editions and most manuscripts do not contain “or one that compels someone to serve.” We have added these words from the Regiomontane manuscript and three Sorbonne manuscripts.]

If death is not evil, how is a mortal animal evil, or one that inflicts death? But if these things are evils, how can bodily strength, sight, hearing, persuasive speech, fertility, native soil, freedom, and life not be goods—all of which, you claim, existed in that kingdom of evil, which you dare to assert was the highest evil?

**16.** Finally, if—and no one has ever denied this—incompatibility is evil, what is more compatible than those elements with their respective animals: darkness with creatures that crawl, water with creatures that swim, winds with creatures that fly, fire with creatures that are more voracious, and smoke with creatures that are loftier?

For you describe such harmony in a race of discord and such order in the abode of perversion.

If what harms is evil, I shall pass over the powerful point stated above: nothing could have been harmed where there was no good. But if that is obscure, this certainly stands out and is apparent to everyone: since, as I said, and as everyone agrees, what harms is evil, smoke in that race did not harm the two-footed animals. It generated them, nourished them, and sustained them without blemish as they were born, grew, and ruled.

But now, after good has been mixed with evil, smoke has become more harmful, so that it cannot be endured by us, who are certainly two-footed; it blinds, oppresses, and kills us.

Has the mixture of good with the elements of evil added such monstrousness to them? Has such perversion arisen while God reigns?

**17.** Certainly, why do we see this compatibility in the other cases—the compatibility which deceived and enticed your author into composing his lies? Why, I ask, are darkness compatible with creatures that crawl, water with creatures that swim, and winds with creatures that fly, while fire burns the four-footed animal and smoke suffocates us?

What of the fact that serpents also see with extraordinary sharpness and rejoice in the presence of the sun, and are more abundant wherever the clear air more rarely and with greater difficulty gathers clouds? What could be more absurd than for the inhabitants and lovers of darkness to be better accommodated and more at home where the clarity of light is enjoyed?

If you say that they take pleasure in warmth rather than light, you would much more consistently say that serpents were born lively in fire than that the sluggish donkey was. Yet who would deny that the asp is friendly to this light, when its eyes are compared with those of an eagle?

But I shall deal with the beasts later. Let us consider ourselves, I beg you, without stubbornness, and finally strip our minds of vain and destructive fables.

For who could tolerate such an inversion as this: in the race of darkness, to which no light had been mixed, two-footed animals are said to have possessed such firm, vigorous—in short, such incredible—power in their eyesight that in their own darkness they saw the purest light of God’s kingdoms, which you praise, since you wish it to have been visible even to such beings; that they looked upon it, contemplated it, delighted in it, and desired it; while our eyes, through the mixture of light, the mixture of the highest good, and finally the mixture of God, were made so weak and feeble that we see nothing at all in darkness, cannot endure the sight of the sun in any way, and, turning away from it, even seek the things that had been visible to us?

**18.** These arguments can also be made if corruption is evil, which no one doubts either. For at that time smoke did not corrupt the species of animals which it now corrupts.

And, not to go through each matter individually, which would be lengthy and unnecessary, the animals you imagine to have existed there were so much less vulnerable to corruption that their aborted offspring, not yet fit to be born, were hurled from heaven to earth and were nevertheless able to live, beget offspring, and conspire again. They possessed their former strength, certainly, because they had already been conceived [Note: [Col. 1353] The editions read “because they had already been conceived in it.” Eleven manuscripts have “because,” perhaps correctly, instead of “in which.”] before the mixture of good and evil.

For after this amalgamation, you say that those born from them are the animals which we now see to be extremely weak and easily yielding to corruption. Who could tolerate this error any longer, except someone who either does not see these things or, through some incredible habit and familiarity with you, has become hardened against all the weight of reason?

# CHAPTER TEN. The three seals of conduct wrongly devised by the Manichaeans
19. But since I have shown, as I believe, in what great darkness and falsehood concerning general good and evil you are involved, let us now examine those three “seals” which you loudly extol and celebrate in your way of life. What, then, are these seals? Certainly those of the mouth, the hands, and the bosom. What does this mean? “A person,” he says, “must be chaste and innocent in mouth, hands, and bosom.” What if he sins with his eyes, ears, or nostrils? What if he assaults or even kills someone with his heels? How shall we hold him guilty, since he has not sinned with mouth, hands, or bosom? But, he says, when I mention the mouth, I want all the senses located in the head to be understood; by the hand, every action; by the bosom, every seminal lust.

Where, then, do you wish blasphemies to belong—to the mouth or to the hand? For this action is performed through the tongue. Thus, if you include every action under one category, why do you join the action of the feet to the hands but separate that of the tongue? Is it because the tongue signifies something by words, and you therefore wish to separate it from that action which is performed not for the sake of signifying—so that the seal of the hands is defined as restraint from an evil action that is not performed for the sake of signifying? But what will you do if someone sins by signifying something with his hands, as happens when we write or indicate by a gesture something that is understood? You cannot assign this to the mouth and tongue, since it is done with the hands. What could be more absurd than this: although three seals are named—of the mouth, hands, and bosom—certain sins discovered in the hands are attributed to the mouth?

But if the general category of action is assigned to the hands, what reason is there for adding the action of the feet to it and not adding that of the tongue? Do you see how the appetite for novelty, accompanied by error, is led into great difficulties? For with these three seals, which you proclaim under some new division, you cannot discover how to include the cleansing of all sins. [Col. 1354]

## CHAPTER XI — The nature of the seal of the mouth among the Manichaeans, who are proved guilty of blasphemy against God

20. But divide things as you wish and omit whatever you wish; let us discuss what you are especially accustomed to commend. You say that the seal of the mouth consists in refraining from every blasphemy. Blasphemy, however, occurs when evil things are said about good things. Thus, in ordinary usage, “blasphemy” is understood to mean nothing other than speaking evil words about God; for one may have doubts about human beings, but God is unquestionably good.

If, therefore, reason proves that no one speaks worse things about God than you do, where will your celebrated seal of the mouth be? Reason teaches—and not some hidden reason, but one situated openly and plainly before everyone’s understanding, unconquered and all the more unconquerable because no one is permitted to be ignorant of it—that God is incorruptible, unchangeable, inviolate, and incapable of being subject to any need, weakness, or misery. Indeed, every rational soul perceives these things in common, so that even you assent when they are stated.

21. But when you begin to recount your fables, you persuade those possessed by an extraordinary blindness—and, with an extraordinary blindness, those whom you persuade—that God is corruptible, changeable, violable, subject to need, capable of weakness, and not safe from misery. And this is not enough: you say not merely that God is corruptible, but that he has been corrupted; not merely changeable, but changed; not merely violable, but violated; not merely capable of suffering need, but needy; not merely that weakness could befall him, but that weakness has befallen him; not merely that he could be miserable, but that he is miserable.

For you say that the soul is God, or a part of God. Nor do I see how that which is called a part of God is not God. A part of gold is gold, a part of silver is silver, and a part of stone is stone; and, to come to greater examples, a part of earth is earth, a part of water is water, and a part of air is air. If you take something away from fire, you will not deny that it is fire; and whatever part of light is taken, it can be nothing other than light. Why, then, will a part of God not be God? Or does God have an articulated form, as a human being and other animals do? For a part of a human being is not a human being.

**Note:** The Royal Manuscript reads: “Or is the soul a particle of God, just as …”

22. But I will descend to either of these opinions and examine each separately. If you wish God to be like light, you cannot deny that some part of God is God. Therefore, when you say that the soul is a part of God—a soul which you do not deny to be corrupted when it is foolish, changed when it was wise, violated when it does not possess its proper perfection, needy when it asks for help, weak when it requires medicine, and miserable when it longs to be blessed—you ascribe all these things to God in a sacrilegious belief.

Or, if you do not concede these things concerning the soul, then the Spirit is not necessary to lead the soul into truth, since it is not foolish [Col. 1355]; the soul is not renewed through true religion, since it is not grown old; it is not perfected by your seals, since it is already perfect; God does not help it, since it has no need; Christ is not its physician, since it is healthy; and a blessed life is not rightly promised to it.

What of the fact that Jesus is called the liberator, and that he himself cries out in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36)? And the apostle Paul says: “You were called to freedom” (Galatians 5:13). The soul, therefore, which has not yet attained this freedom is enslaved.

Thus, with you as its authors, if indeed a part of God is God, God has been corrupted by folly, changed by falling, violated by the loss of perfection, made needy through lack of help, weakened by disease, oppressed by misery, and disgraced by slavery.

**Note:** Seven manuscripts read, “nor is the apostle necessary.” Other codices read, “nor is the Spirit necessary.” Perhaps both belong to the text. The Manichaean is being noted here: he claimed for himself the title of apostle, as is recorded in *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 33, §72; and he falsely claimed that the Holy Spirit was personally within him, as recorded in *Confessions* 5.5.8. A little later, the reading appears to be, “nor is the soul renewed through your religion”; and somewhat farther on most manuscripts read, “because it has not been changed,” where the printed editions have “grown old.”

23. But if God’s part is not God, then God cannot be incorruptible if there is corruption in one of his parts; he cannot be unchangeable if he has been changed in some part; he cannot be inviolate if he is not perfect in every part; he cannot be without need if he diligently acts to restore his part to himself; he cannot be wholly healthy if he is weak in some part; he cannot be supremely blessed if he has some part subject to misery; and he cannot be wholly free if some part of him is oppressed by slavery.

You are compelled to say all these things when you declare that the soul, which you see overwhelmed by such great calamities, is a part of God. If you can remove these and many similar things from your sect, then at last say that your mouth is free from blasphemies. Indeed, abandon that sect. For if you cease to believe and say what its founder wrote, you will certainly no longer be Manichaeans.

24. If we intend to think of God as free from blasphemies, God must be understood or believed to be the supreme good, than which nothing better can exist or be conceived. A relation of numbers cannot in any way be violated or changed; no nature, by whatever violence, could make the number following one fail to correspond to it as double. This cannot in any way be changed, yet you call God changeable!

That relation preserves its inviolate integrity, and you do not wish God to be at least equal to it! Let any nation of darkness cause the intelligible number three—within which one is so truly one that it has no parts—to be divided into two equal parts. Let that nation of darkness do so. Your mind surely sees that this cannot happen through anyone’s malice. That which could not violate the relation of number—could it violate God? If it could not, what necessity, I ask, was there for a part of him to be mixed with evil and thrust into such great miseries?

## CHAPTER XII — Refutation of the Manichaeans’ evasions

25. From this arose the difficulty which, even when we were listening to you attentively, pressed us with great anguish; and we found no way out as we asked what the nation of darkness would do to God if it did not wish to fight with it at the cost of such great calamity to a part of himself.

For if the nation of darkness was not going to harm God while he remained at rest, we complained that we had been cruelly treated, since we had been sent into these troubles. But if [Col. 1356] it was going to harm him, then his nature was not incorruptible, as God’s nature ought to be.

In this question someone was not lacking who said that God did not wish to be without evil, nor take precautions lest he be harmed, but that, because of his natural goodness, he wished to benefit an unruly and perverse nature by bringing it into order. The Manichaean books do not sound like this. They very frequently indicate, and very frequently say, that God took precautions lest he be invaded by enemies.

But let us grant that the Manichaean understood matters as that person said, since he could find nothing else to say. Is God thereby defended against cruelty or weakness? His goodness toward the hostile nation became a great disaster for his own people. Moreover, if that nature could not be corrupted or changed, neither would any plague change or corrupt us; and the order that had to be supplied for that alien nature could have been supplied without our perversity.

26. This, however, had not yet been said—something I recently heard at Carthage. When someone whom I especially desire to be freed from that error was being driven by this question into the same difficulties, he dared to say that, evidently, the kingdom had certain boundaries of its own which could be invaded by the opposing nation, whereas God himself could in no way be violated.

But he said what even your author would not in any way have been forced to say. Perhaps he saw that the consequences for his sect would follow much more easily from this position than from the other. And in fact the matter stands as follows: if a person of ordinary understanding hears that in that nature there was one thing violable and another inviolate, he will easily understand that there are no longer two natures but three—one inviolate, another violable, and a third that violates.

**Note:** Although the word “recently” can sometimes extend over several years, here we do not know whether it indicates a very recent time. He seems to suggest that this second answer was given on behalf of the Manichaeans to that question—which Nebridius used to raise in Italy “all the way from Carthage,” as we read in *Confessions* 7.2.3—not at the first time Nebridius proposed it, nor during the period when Augustine was listening attentively to the Manichaeans, but somewhat later, perhaps only after Augustine’s return from Italy. If this is so, Augustine added this passage to the book, which he wrote at Rome, with a second revision while delaying its publication.

## CHAPTER XIII — Actions are judged not by their objects but by their intention; hence the proper judgment of the Manichaeans’ abstinence

27. Since these blasphemies, proceeding from your hearts, dwell daily on your lips, stop at last proclaiming your seal of the mouth, as though it were something great, for the attraction of the ignorant. Unless perhaps you think that because you do not eat meat and do not drink wine, the seal of the mouth is something to be admired and praised.

I ask you: for what purpose do you do this? For the end toward which the things we do are directed—that is, the reason for which we do whatever we do—must first be not merely blameless but praiseworthy if our actions too are to deserve any praise. But if the one whom we regard and contemplate when engaged in some duty is rightly and deservedly blamed, no one will doubt that the duty itself should likewise be disapproved and condemned.

28. It has been handed down concerning Catiline that he could endure cold [Col. 1357], thirst, and hunger (Sallust, *Catiline*, prologue, chapter 3). These things were common to that filthy and sacrilegious man and to our apostles. By what, then, is this parricide distinguished from our apostles, except by the utterly different end that he pursued?

He endured these things in order to satisfy his immoderate and savage desires; they, by contrast, endured them in order to suppress such desires and compel them to serve reason as their ruler.

You too, when a multitude of Catholic virgins is praised to you, are accustomed to say: “A mule too is a virgin.” This is rash, indeed, because of your ignorance of Catholic discipline; nevertheless, by saying this you indicate that such continence is empty unless it is directed by a definite rational purpose toward some supremely righteous end.

Catholic Christians could likewise compare your abstinence from wine and meat with that of beasts of burden, many sparrows, and finally innumerable kinds of worms. But, lest I fall into your rashness, I will not do this hastily; I will first investigate the purpose for which you do these things.

For, as I think, we have already agreed among ourselves that nothing else is to be sought in practices of this kind. If, then, you abstain for the sake of frugality and restraining lust—the desire by which we are delighted and captivated by such foods and drink—I listen and approve. But that is not the case.

29. For I ask you: suppose there is someone—and this is possible—so frugal and temperate that, moderating his appetite for food and drink, he does not feast twice in a single day. Suppose that, when he dines, he is served some vegetables with a little bacon, greased and seasoned with that same bacon, as much as is sufficient to suppress hunger; and that, out of concern for his health, he quenches his thirst with two or three drinks of unmixed wine; and that this is his daily diet.

Suppose another person, on the other hand, tasting no meat and no wine, gladly eats at the ninth hour carefully selected and exotic grains, varied among many courses and sprinkled with abundant pepper, intending to dine on such things again at the beginning of the night. Let him drink honeyed wine, boiled must (*caroenum*), raisin wine (*passum*), and the expressed juices of various fruits, sufficiently resembling wine and even surpassing it in sweetness; let him drink not as much as he thirsts for, but as much as he wishes; let him arrange to have this provided for himself every day, and enjoy such food and luxuries without necessity but with great pleasure.

Which of these two, as far as eating and drinking are concerned, do you judge to lead the more abstinent life? I do not think you are so blind that you would not prefer the one who eats a little bacon and wine to this glutton.

30. Truth indeed compels this judgment, but your error sings a very different tune. If your Elect, celebrated for his three seals, lived every day like the man whom we described second, he could be reproved by one, and perhaps two, serious objections, but he could not be condemned at all as a violator of the seal.

But if he once dined with the first man, smeared his lips with a piece of ham or rancid meat, and moistened them with cheap wine, then, according to the judgment of your founder—and to your amazement, yet with your consent—[Col. 1358] he would be judged to have broken the seal and immediately destined for Gehenna.

Please abandon your error; please attend to reason; please resist custom for a little while. What is more perverse than this perversity? What is more delirious? What could be said or imagined more insane than that a man who, with his belly distended, belches in delight after eating mushrooms, rice, truffles, pastries, raisin wine, pepper, and laser, and who seeks such things every day, cannot be shown to have fallen away from the three seals—that is, from the rule of holiness; while another man, seasoning the cheapest grains with smoky meat, taking only as much as suffices to restore his body, sipping three cups of wine for the sake of maintaining his health, and moving from the former diet to this one, is being prepared for certain punishment?

## CHAPTER XIV — Three reasons for laudably abstaining from certain kinds of food

31. But the Apostle says: “It is good, brothers, not to eat meat and not to drink wine” (Romans 14:21). As though any one of us denied that this is good! But it is good either for the purpose I mentioned above, according to which it is said, “Do not provide for the flesh in its desires” (ibid., 13:14), or for the purposes that Paul himself again sets forth: either to restrain the appetite, which is accustomed to rush more fiercely and excessively toward these things; or so that a brother may not be offended; or so that the weak may not participate in food offered to idols.

At the time when the Apostle wrote these words, much sacrificial meat was being sold in the marketplace. And because wine too was offered in libations to the gods of the Gentiles, many weaker brothers who also made use of these goods preferred to abstain entirely from meat and wine rather than unknowingly fall into what they believed to be fellowship with idols.

For their sake, even those who were stronger, who judged that these things ought to be rejected with greater faith, knowing that nothing is unclean except through an evil conscience and holding to the Lord’s saying, “It is not what enters your mouth that defiles you, but what comes out” (Matthew 15:11), nevertheless had to abstain from these things so as not to offend the weaker.

This is not inferred merely from suspicion; it is plainly found in the Apostles’ own letters. You are accustomed to say only this to us: “It is good, brothers, not to eat meat and not to drink wine,” but you do not add what follows: “or anything by which your brother is offended, scandalized, or weakened.” From this it is clear for what purpose the Apostle gave these instructions.

32. The preceding and following passages make this still clearer. It would be lengthy to recall them, but for the sake of those who are lazy about reading and examining the divine Scriptures, we are compelled to set out the entire passage:

“Receive the one who is weak in faith, not for disputes about opinions. One believes that he may eat everything; but the one who is weak eats vegetables. Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat; and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats, for God has accepted him. Who are you to judge another’s servant? He stands or falls before his own master; and he will stand, for God is able to make him stand.

“One person judges one day to be above another; another judges every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind. The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord; and the one who eats [Col. 1359] eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God. The one who does not eat abstains for the Lord, and gives thanks to God.

“For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself. If we live, we live for the Lord; if we die, we die for the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s. For to this end Christ both lived, died, and rose again, that he might be Lord of the living and of the dead.

“But why do you judge your brother? Or why do you despise your brother? For we shall all stand before the tribunal of God. For it is written: ‘As I live, says the Lord, every knee shall bend before me, and every tongue shall confess to God’ (Isaiah 45:23–24). Therefore each of us shall give an account of himself to God.

“Let us no longer judge one another, but judge this rather: that no one place a stumbling block or scandal before his brother. I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean through him, except for the one who considers something unclean; for that person it is unclean.

“If your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking according to love. Do not destroy by your food the one for whom Christ died. Therefore let not our good be blasphemed. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. Whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by human beings.
