“Therefore let us pursue the things that make for peace and the things that build one another up. Do not destroy the work of God for the sake of food. All things indeed are clean, but it is evil for a person to eat through giving offense. It is good not to eat meat and not to drink wine, nor anything by which your brother is offended, scandalized, or weakened.

“You have faith within yourself; have it before God. Blessed is the one who does not condemn himself in what he approves. But the one who distinguishes, if he eats, is condemned, because he does not act from faith. Everything that is not from faith is sin.

“But we who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of the weak and not to please ourselves. Let each of us please his neighbor for good, for edification. For Christ too did not please himself” (Romans 14 and 15:1–3).

**Note:** Nine manuscripts read, “Let each of us please him for good edification.”

33. Is it sufficiently evident that the Apostle commanded those who were stronger not to eat meat or drink wine because they offended the weak by failing to accommodate them, and caused them to think that those who judged all things clean through faith were unwilling to abstain from such food and drink out of regard for idols?

He indicates the same thing when writing to the Corinthians in this way:

“Concerning food sacrificed to idols, we know that an idol is nothing in the world and that there is no God but one. For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we are in him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him.

“But not everyone possesses this knowledge. Some, accustomed until now to the idol, eat the food as something sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled. Food does not commend us to God. For neither, if we eat, do we abound; nor, if we do not eat, do we lack.

“But take care lest this freedom of yours become a stumbling block [Col. 1360] to the weak. For if someone sees the one who possesses knowledge reclining in an idol’s temple, will not his weak conscience be encouraged to eat food sacrificed to idols? And through your knowledge the weak brother for whom Christ died will perish.

“By sinning in this way against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, you sin against Christ. Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat, so that I may not cause my brother to stumble” (1 Corinthians 8:4 and following).

34. Again, in another place:

“What then? Do I say that something sacrificed to idols is anything, or that an idol is anything?

**Note:** Nine manuscripts read, “not that.” But the things that the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God. I do not want you to become partners with demons. You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons. Are we provoking the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?

“Everything is lawful for me, but not everything is beneficial. Everything is lawful for me, but not everything builds up. Let no one seek his own advantage, but that of the other.

“Eat everything sold in the marketplace, asking no questions for the sake of conscience. But if someone says, ‘This has been sacrificed to idols,’ do not eat it, for the sake of the one who indicated this and for the sake of conscience. I mean the conscience not of yourself but of the other.

“For why should my freedom be judged by another’s conscience? If I partake with thanksgiving, why am I blasphemed for that for which I give thanks? Therefore, whether you eat or drink or do anything else, do everything for the glory of God.

“Be without offense to Jews and Greeks and the church of God, just as I too please everyone in everything, not seeking my own advantage but that of the many, so that they may be saved. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:19–33 and 11:1).

35. It is clear, then, as I believe, for what purpose one should abstain from meat and wine. The purpose is threefold: to restrain the pleasure ordinarily found especially in these foods and which, through such drink, can proceed as far as drunkenness; to protect weakness because of the things that are sacrificed and offered in libation; and—and this is most worth commending—for the sake of love, so that the weakness of the weaker, who abstain from these things, may not be offended.

But you say that these foods are unclean, although the Apostle says that all things are clean, but that it is evil for the one who eats through giving offense. And I certainly believe that you are defiled by these meals precisely because you consider them unclean.

For he says: “I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean through him; but for the one who considers something unclean, for that person it is unclean.” Who could doubt that he called the one who considers something unclean unclean and defiled?

But it is foolish to argue Scripture with you, since you deceive people by promising reason while also claiming that the Books in which religious authority is so great have been corrupted by the insertion of false chapters. Convince me by reason, then, how eating meat defiles a person if it is consumed without any offense, without any weak opinion, and without any lust.

## CHAPTER XV — Why the Manichaeans prohibit the eating of meat

36. It is worthwhile to understand the entire rationale of this superstitious [Col. 1361] abstinence. It is stated as follows:

“Since,” he says, “a member of God has been mixed with the substance of evils in order to restrain it and suppress it from its utmost fury”—for this is what you say—“the world was fashioned from the mixture of both natures, that is, of good and evil.

“That divine part is daily cleansed from every part of the world and restored to its own realms. But as it exhales through the earth and rises toward heaven, it encounters plants, because they are fixed by their roots in the earth; and thus it fertilizes and nourishes all herbs and all trees.

“From these animals obtain food. If they mate, they bind that divine member in flesh and, turning it aside and hindering it from its appointed course, entangle it in errors and sufferings.

“Therefore, if foods prepared from grains and fruits come to the holy ones—that is, to the Manichaeans—whatever is luminous and divine in them is cleansed through their chastity, prayers, and psalms; that is, it is perfected in every respect so that it may be carried back to its own realms without any difficulty from impurities.”

This is why you forbid a beggar who is not a Manichaean to be given bread, any grain, or even water itself, which is despised by everyone: so that the member of God mixed into these things may not be soiled by his sins and prevented from returning.

**Note:** The printed editions read “the muddy part is cleansed.” Eight manuscripts read “whatever is luminous and divine,” as the following words require: “it is perfected so that it may return to the realms,” and so forth.

37. But you say that meats have already been formed from those very impurities. For, as you claim, some of that divine part escapes when grains and fruits are plucked; it escapes when they are crushed, ground, cooked, or even bitten and chewed. It also escapes in all the movements of animals—when they exult, exercise themselves, labor, or perform any action at all.

It escapes even in our very repose, while the process called digestion is completed in the body by interior heat. And thus, because the divine nature escapes through so many circumstances, something utterly filthy remains, from which flesh is formed through sexual intercourse—although the soul of the good kind remains, since, however much good escapes through those movements, it is not all of it.

Therefore, once the soul too has abandoned the flesh, you say that excessive impurities remain, and that for this reason the soul of those who eat meat is defiled.

**Note:** Erasmus and Louvain omit the preposition *cum* (“with”) and punctuate the text as follows: “flesh is formed. But the soul of the good …” The manuscript reading adopted here is somewhat more coherent.

## CHAPTER XVI — He discloses the Manichaeans’ monstrous mysteries

38. O obscurity of nature—what a covering for falsehood! Who, hearing these things, if he has not learned the causes of things, if he has not yet been touched by even the smallest light of truth and is deceived by bodily images, would not suppose them true precisely because they are not directly apparent, are conceived through certain representations of visible things, and can be expressed fluently?

Large crowds and herds of such people are summoned, whom religious fear makes safer from these deceptions than reason does. Therefore I will attempt to refute these claims, insofar as God deigns to help me, so that not only the judgment of the wise [Col. 1362]—who reject them as soon as they are stated—but even ordinary understanding may clearly see how false and absurd they are.

39. First I ask where you learn that this mysterious part of God exists in grains, legumes, vegetables, flowers, and fruits. “It is evident,” they say, “from the brightness of their color, the pleasantness of their smell, and the sweetness of their taste. When rotten things lack these qualities, they thereby show that they have been abandoned by the same good.”

Are you not ashamed to think that God is discovered by the nose and palate? But I will pass over this. I will speak to you in Latin—and, as the saying goes, this is very much to the point.

Rather, you ought to understand with whatever kind of mind you possess that, if the presence of the good in bodies is apparent through color, the dung of animals—which is itself the refuse of their flesh—shines in various colors: sometimes white, more often yellowish, and in other such hues, which you accept in fruits and flowers as witnesses to the God who is present and indwelling.

What, then, is the reason that you declare the redness of a rose to be a sign of abundant good, while condemning the same color in blood? Why do you embrace that same color in a violet, but reject it in bile, in the illness of jaundiced people, and finally in an infant’s dung?

Why do you suppose that the sheen and brilliance of oil proclaim an abundance of mixed-in good, while you prepare the throat and stomach to cleanse it, yet fear to let your lips touch drops dripping from fatty meat with exactly the same brilliance?

Why do you think that, because of God’s treasures, a melon is golden, while you do not think the rancid fat of ham—or the middle of an egg—is so? Why does whiteness proclaim God in lettuces but not in milk?

I am still speaking of colors. To leave everything else aside, you cannot compare any meadow clothed in flowers with the feathers and plumage of a single peacock—which certainly arise from sexual intercourse and flesh.

40. For if this good is also found through smell, ointments of wonderful fragrance are made from the flesh of certain animals. Finally, foods themselves, which are customarily digested more easily with better kinds of meat, smell much more pleasantly than they would if meat were absent from them.

In the end, if you judge the more fragrant things to be cleaner, you ought to have preferred eating a certain mud to drinking water from a cistern, because earth soaked by rain and then dried delights the nostrils with a wonderful smell, and such mud smells better than it would if it had merely collected purer rainwater.

But if taste must testify, so that we may know that something of God dwells in a body, then it dwells more in dates and honey than in pork, but more in pork than in beans. I concede that it dwells more in a fig than in fig-fed liver (*ficatum*); but concede also that it dwells more in fig-fed liver than in beet.

What is more, by this reasoning you are compelled to admit that certain plants—which you certainly all wish to be cleaner than meat—receive God from meat itself, if God is recognized as mixed in according to taste. For vegetables become tastier when cooked with meat; and we cannot taste the herbs on which cattle feed, whereas, when transformed into the juice of milk, we judge them superior in color [Col. 1363] and most agreeable in taste.

41. Or do you think that wherever three good qualities are present together—good color, smell, and taste—the greater part of the good is present? Then do not admire and praise flowers so greatly, since you cannot admit them to judgment before the tribunal of the palate.

At least, do not prefer purslane to meat, since cooked meat surpasses it in color, taste, and smell.

Roast pork—for you force us to debate with you about good and evil not with writers and copyists, but rather with cooks and pastry-makers—roast pork, then, is bright in color, pleasing in smell, and delightful in taste. You have a perfect indication of the indwelling divine substance: by its threefold testimony it invites you and desires to be cleansed by your holiness.

Attack it! Why do you hesitate? Why are you preparing to object?

In color alone, an infant’s dung surpasses a lentil; in smell alone, a roasted morsel surpasses a tender green fig; in taste alone, a slaughtered kid surpasses the grass on which it feeds while alive. Meat has even been found whose case is supported by all three witnesses together. What more are you looking for? What will you say?

Why should meat dishes make you unclean when you eat them, while these monstrous arguments do not make you unclean when you discuss them? Especially since the ray of the sun—which you certainly place above all meat and all grains—neither smells nor tastes, but merely stands out among other bodies through the excellence of its most brilliant color. It strongly urges you, indeed compels you against your will, to prefer nothing to the brilliance of color among the proofs of the good that has been mixed in.

42. You are therefore driven into this difficulty: you must admit that more of the divine part dwells in blood, and in the foulest but brightly colored materials discharged from animal flesh in the streets, than in the pale leaves of the olive.

But if you say—for you say this too—that olive leaves, when burned, give off fire in which the presence of light is apparent, whereas meat, when burned, does not do the same, what will you answer about fat, which lights almost all the lamps of Italy?

What will you say about cow dung, which is certainly dirtier than the flesh of the cow and which, when dried, country people use for the fire, since nothing is easier to burn or purer of smoke than its flame?

Moreover, if brightness and brilliance display a greater presence of the divine part, why do you not cleanse, seal, or liberate it? For it is found especially in flowers—to say nothing of blood—and in countless things that are in meat or closely resemble meat, yet you certainly cannot have flowers at your feasts.

Even if you did eat meat, you would surely not add to your dishes fish scales, or certain worms and flies, all of which sparkle with their own light even in darkness.

### 43

What, then, remains except that you cease saying that your eyes, noses, and palate are competent judges by which you approve the presence of the divine element in bodies? Once these have been removed, how will you demonstrate not only that a greater portion of God is in plants than in flesh, but that any part of him exists in plants at all?

Does beauty move you—not beauty consisting in the pleasantness of color, but in the harmonious proportion of the parts? If only that were so! For when would you dare to compare twisted pieces of wood with the bodies of animals, in whose form corresponding limbs answer to one another in symmetry? But if you delight in the testimony of bodily senses—which must be the case with those unable to see the force of essence with the mind—how do you prove, through the passage of time and through certain processes of rubbing and wearing down, that the substance of the good flees from bodies, unless because, as you assert, God departs from them and migrates from place to place? This is utterly insane.

Nevertheless, as far as I can judge, no signs or indications at all have led you to this opinion. For many things cut from trees or pulled from the earth are improved by the intervention of some interval of time before they reach our food: leeks and endives, lettuces, grapes, apples, figs, and certain pears. Many other things, moreover, acquire a better color when they are not consumed immediately after being plucked; they are taken into the body more healthfully and taste more delicately in the mouth. Such convenience and pleasantness ought not to exist in these things at all if, according to your opinion, they became increasingly deserted by the good the longer they were stored after being separated from the earth as from a mother.

Even meat from animals slaughtered the day before is certainly more agreeable and wholesome. But this ought not to be so if, as you assert, it contained more of the good on the day when the living creature had recently been killed than on the following day, when a greater flight of the divine substance had occurred.

### 44

Who does not know that wine becomes purer and better with age? Nor does it become more fragrant, as you suppose, in order to pervert the senses, but more useful for invigorating the body—provided only that moderation is present, as it ought to rule in everything. For with newer must, derangement of the senses usually occurs more quickly. Thus, if it has at some time remained in a vat and fermented somewhat, it drives those looking down into it headlong, as though their brains had been struck, and, unless help is provided in some way, kills them.

As for health, who denies that bodies are dangerously inflated and distended by it? Is it therefore because it contains more of the good that such serious inconveniences are present in it? And are these absent from old wine because a large part of the divine substance has departed? It is absurd to say this—especially for you, who judge the presence of God’s element by the eyes, nose, and palate when these senses are agreeably affected.

What perversity, then, is it to think wine the gall of the princes of darkness, while not sparing grapes when you eat them? Is that gall present in greater measure when the grapes are in the cask than when they are still on the clusters? If, when the good departs, evil remains behind as though more unmixed, and if this happens through the passage of time, the same grapes ought not to become, while hanging and being preserved, milder, sweeter, and more healthful. Nor ought the wine mentioned above—after its light has been lost, more fluid and more luminous, and, after the salutary substance has departed, more healthful—to become so.

*[Note: [Col. 1364] Several manuscripts read dolentius (“more painfully”) instead of redolentius (“more fragrant”).]*

### 45

What shall I say about wood and leaves, which dry out with time and yet cannot, on that account, be said by you to become worse? They lose that from which smoke is produced, but retain that from which the shining flame rises; and by that brightness, which you greatly prize, they testify that the good is purer in the drier than in the greener materials.

From this it follows either that you deny that a greater portion of God is in pure light than in smoky light, thereby throwing all your proofs into confusion; or you must admit that, from plants cut off or uprooted, if they are stored for a longer period, the nature of evil may flee more abundantly than that of the good. Once this is granted, we shall maintain that a greater amount of evil can depart from plucked crops, and thus that a greater amount of good can remain in flesh. Let this, then, have been said concerning time.

### 46

For if that divine nature finds an opportunity for flight through the agitation, kneading, and friction of these things, many similar examples refute you—things that become better through being moved.

Some people imitate wine with barley juice; it becomes excellent through agitation. Certainly—and this must not be passed over—this kind of drink intoxicates extremely quickly; yet you have never said that barley juice is the gall of the princes.

Flour is skillfully mixed with a smaller quantity of water, somewhat more stiffly, so that it becomes better through kneading—and, in a result against which nothing more perverse can be said, whiter as its light departs. The confectioner kneads honey for a long time so that it reaches that whiteness and becomes a milder, less harmful sweetness. Explain how this happens when the good departs.

If you are pleased to prove the presence of God not only by sight, smell, and taste, but also by hearing, flesh supplies the strings of lyres and the bones of flutes; when dried, rubbed, and bent, they produce sound. Thus musical sweetness, which you insist came from the divine kingdoms, is displayed to us through the filth of dead flesh—flesh dried by time, thinned by friction, and stretched by bending. Yet you proclaim that through these same afflictions the divine substance flees even from living things; and you say that this also happens through boiling them.

Why, then, do boiled cardoons cause no harm to health? Is it to be thought that, while they are being cooked in this way, God—or a part of God—departs from them?

*[Note: [Col. 1365] This is the reading of Erasmus, supported by three Sorbonne manuscripts and the Regiomontanus manuscript. Lovaniensis and other manuscripts have “or the pestilence departs.”]*

### 47

Why should I pursue the remaining examples, all of which it is neither easy nor necessary to enumerate? Who does not realize how many things are made more pleasant and healthful by cooking? They ought not to be so if, as you believe, they are abandoned by the good through such processes of agitation.

I think you can find absolutely nothing by which you can establish through these bodily senses that meats are unclean and pollute the souls of those who eat them on the ground that plucked crops, after many transformations, become flesh. This is especially so since you think even the age and corruption of vinegar purer than wine, while we see that the caroenum you drink is nothing other than cooked wine—which ought to be dirtier than wine if, through movements and cooking of bodily things, the divine members depart from them.

But if this is not so, there is no reason for you to think that, when crops are plucked, stored, handled, cooked, and digested, they are abandoned as the good flees, and therefore provide the most filthy material for the creation of bodies.

### 48

If you are not led by color, form, smell, and taste to judge that the good is present in these things, what else can you produce? Is it perhaps a certain firmness and strength which seems to be taken away from these things as they are separated from and handled apart from the earth?

But if this moved you—although one can quickly observe that it is false, since the firmness of some things increases after they have been removed from the earth, as has already been mentioned in the case of wine, which becomes stronger with age—still, if this firmness moved you, as I said, you would approve that a more abundant portion of God exists in no food more than in flesh. For athletes, who especially need strength and vigor, do not feed on vegetables and fruit rather than meat.

### 49

Or is it because flesh is nourished by trees, whereas trees are not nourished by flesh, that you therefore think their bodies better than ours? You do not consider a matter so obvious: orchards become more luxuriant and fertile, and crops richer, through nourishment from dung, even though, in accusing flesh, you seem unable to say anything more damning than that it is a dwelling-place of dung.

Thus the things that are clean to you are nourished by what you declare to be much more unclean in the thing that is unclean to you. And if you reject flesh for this reason—that it is born after intercourse—then let the flesh of worms delight you, since they are born in such great numbers and sizes in fruit, wood, and finally the earth itself, without any intercourse.

But I do not know what this pretense is. For if flesh displeased you because it is formed by the mingling of father and mother, you would not say that those princes of darkness were born from the fruits of their own trees—princes whom you certainly reject more thoroughly than the flesh you refuse to taste.

### 50

As for your belief that all the souls of animals come from the food of their parents, and that you boast of liberating from those prisons the divine substance held in your foods, this belief presses you exceedingly hard—and most urgently toward eating flesh.

Why do you not liberate by anticipating and eating the souls which those who feast on flesh are going to bind to a body?

“But,” he says, “nothing of the good part is bound to them from flesh, but from the crops which they consume together with flesh.”

What, then, should be said about the souls of lions, whose food is flesh alone?

“They drink,” he says, “and therefore that soul is drawn from water and entangled in flesh.”

What of countless birds? What can be said of the eagles themselves, which feed on nothing but flesh and require no drink? Here, certainly, you fail, and no answer can be found.

For if the soul comes from foods, and there are animals that produce offspring whose only food is flesh and which take no drink, then there is a soul in flesh, and according to your custom you ought to assist in purifying it by eating flesh. Unless perhaps you think that the pig, which is nourished both by crops and by water, possesses a soul of light, while you maintain that the eagle, to which the sun is especially congenial, contains a soul of darkness because it lives on flesh alone.

### 51

What straits, what incredible absurdities you would certainly not have fallen into if, free from utterly vain fables, you had followed in the restraint of food what truth approves: namely, that luxurious foods should be rejected for the sake of restraining desire, not in order to avoid an uncleanness that does not exist.

For even if someone, paying insufficient attention to the nature of things and to the power of the soul, should grant you that the soul is polluted by food, you nevertheless concede that it becomes much more unclean through desire. What reasoning is there—or rather, what madness—in expelling from the number of the elect a person who perhaps tasted meat for the sake of his health, without any desire, while, if he desired to devour peppered truffles greedily, you might perhaps reproach him only for immoderation, but not condemn him as a corrupter of the seal?

Thus, among your elect there cannot be one who has been denounced for having eaten some portion of a hen, not from desire but for medical treatment; yet there can be among them one who has shown himself to have craved intensely cumiphae [term uncertain] and other meatless cakes. Thus someone who is plunged into filth by desire is retained among your elect; but someone whom the food itself, as you suppose, defiles is not retained, even though you admit that pollution is produced far more by desire than by food.

*[Note: [Col. 1367] The manuscripts read medendo (“for medical treatment”); the printed editions have edendo (“by eating”).]* You nevertheless embrace the one who eagerly yearns for the most delicately seasoned crops and cannot control himself, while excluding the one who, for the purpose of suppressing hunger, is prepared to take any human food without desire and equally prepared to give it up.

Behold your strange customs! Behold your admirable discipline! Behold your memorable temperance!

### 52

Moreover, how full of shame and sometimes even crime is the practice by which you consider it unlawful for anyone other than the elect to touch at meals those things offered to you as though they required purification?

For often so much is given that a few people cannot easily consume it. And because it is considered sacrilege either to give the excess to others or, at any rate, to throw it away, you are driven into great digestive disorders, wishing to “purify” everything that has been given.

Then, when you are distended and almost bursting, you compel the children under your discipline, through cruel domination, to devour the leftovers. Thus it was charged against a certain person at Rome that, by forcing miserable children to eat in accordance with this superstition, he had killed them.

I would not believe this unless I knew how unlawful you consider it either to give these things to others who are not elect or, certainly, to arrange for them to be thrown away. Hence there remains that necessity of eating which almost daily leads to the most shameful digestive excess—and sometimes can even proceed as far as homicide.

*[Note: [Col. 1367] The printed editions have crudelitatem (“cruelty”); the manuscripts have cruditatem (“digestive excess”), which replaces it.]*

### 53

Since this is so, you even forbid giving bread to a beggar; yet you judge that money should be given out of compassion—or rather, out of envy.

What should I accuse first here: cruelty or folly? What if the matter takes place where no food is available for purchase? That needy man will die of hunger while you, a wise and benevolent man, show more pity for a cucumber than for a human being. This surely is—what could I say more fittingly and plainly?—false compassion and genuine cruelty.

Now let us consider the folly. What if he buys bread for himself with the money you give him? Will that portion of your divine element, which takes it from the seller, not suffer in him what it would have suffered if he had taken it from you as the giver?

Thus that beggar, a sinner, envelops in filth the part of God striving to fly away, aided to such an extent by your money; yet you, wisest of men, think there is a difference between refusing to give a man to someone about to commit murder, and knowingly giving money with which he can purchase the man to be killed.

What can be added to this madness? The result is either that the man dies if he cannot find food for sale, or that the food itself dies if he can find it. Of these, the former is genuine homicide; the latter is yours, yet must be attributed to you as though both were genuine homicide.

And since you do not forbid your hearers to eat meat, but do forbid them to kill animals, what could be more foolish and perverse? If such food does not defile, then eat it yourselves. If it does defile, what madness is it to consider it a greater crime to release a pig’s soul from its body than to stain a human soul with a pig’s body?

## Chapter XVII — The Nature of the Seal of the Hands among the Manichaeans Is Revealed

### 54

But let us now come to consider and discuss the seal of the hands. First of all, Christ showed how superstitious it is that you abstain from killing animals and from tearing up plants. Judging that we have no association of legal fellowship with beasts and trees, he both sent demons into a herd of pigs and caused a tree in which he had found no fruit to wither by a curse.

Certainly neither the pigs nor that tree had committed any sin. For we are not so insane as to think that a tree is fruitful or barren of its own accord. Nor need you say here that by these acts our Lord wished to signify something else; who does not know that?

But certainly the Son of God ought not to have been given a sign through homicide, if killing a tree—as you say—is homicide, or if killing animals is homicide. He also gave signs involving human beings, with whom we are certainly joined in a fellowship of law; but he did so by healing people, not by killing them.

He would have done the same with beasts and trees if he had judged that we were joined with them by the same fellowship that you imagine.

### 55

At this point I have thought it necessary to introduce authority, because it is impossible to debate subtly with you about the soul of livestock and about a certain life by which trees are said to live.

But since you protect yourselves by a kind of privilege, so that you cannot be overthrown by the Scriptures, claiming that they have been falsified—even though you have never said that the matters I mentioned concerning the tree and the herd of pigs were inserted by corruptors—still, lest you should eventually wish to say the same of these passages when you consider how much they oppose you, I shall maintain my purpose.

I ask you, great boasters of reason and truth, first what harm is done to a tree—not, I say, if you pluck a fruit or leaf from it, for among you anyone who knowingly does this, rather than through ignorance, will undoubtedly be condemned as a corrupter of the seal, but simply if you uproot it from its roots.

For that soul which you believe to be rationally present in trees is released from its bond when the tree is cut down. This is what you say—and released from a bond in which it was held in great misery and without any benefit.

It is also well known that you—or your own founder—are accustomed to threaten that a human being will be transformed into a tree as a very great punishment, though not the greatest. But can a soul become wiser in a tree than it was in a human being?

The most certain reason for not killing a human being is that one might kill either someone whose wisdom and virtue are of great benefit to others, or someone who might perhaps attain wisdom, whether instructed outwardly by another or divinely enlightened through inward thoughts.

Truth teaches that the more wisely a human soul has surpassed the body, the more beneficially it departs from it—both by the most subtle reasoning and by an authority spread most widely.

Therefore, whoever cuts down a tree releases from that body a soul that makes no progress in wisdom. Thus you holy men—you especially, I say—ought to cut down trees and lead their souls, freed from that bond, toward better things by prayers and psalms.

Or can this be done with those souls which you assist not with your minds, but receive into your bellies?

### 56

Indeed, your desperate straits compel you, as I think, to admit that the souls of trees make no progress toward wisdom so long as they are in trees, when you are asked why an apostolic teacher is not also sent to trees, or why the one sent to human beings does not preach the truth to trees as well.

Here you are forced to answer that those souls cannot receive divine instructions in such bodies. But you are pressed much more forcefully from another side, since you claim that they both hear our voices, understand our words, observe bodies and the movements of bodies, and finally even perceive thoughts themselves.

If these things are true, why can they learn nothing from the apostle of light? Or why can they not learn much more easily than we can, since they even see the inner things of the mind? For that teacher who, as you say, can scarcely teach you by speaking could instruct them by thinking, since they would perceive his propositions in their minds before speech.

But if these things are false, consider at last in what error you lie.

### 57

Moreover, although you yourselves do not pluck fruit or pull up herbs, you nevertheless order your hearers to pluck, pull up, and bring them to you—not so that you may benefit only those who bring them, but also the things that are brought—who, upon careful consideration, could tolerate this in any way?

First, because it makes no difference whether you yourself commit the crime or wish it to be committed by another for your sake. You say that you do not wish this. How, then, is that divine element which lies in lettuces and leeks assisted if no one pulls them up and brings them to the saints for purification?

Furthermore, if you yourself are passing through a field in which, by right of friendship, you are allowed to pluck whatever you wish, and you see a crow attacking a fig tree, what will you do? According to your belief, does not the fig tree itself seem to speak with you and miserably implore you to pluck it yourself, burying it to be purified and restored in the holy belly, rather than allowing that crow to devour it, mix it with its deadly body, and send it on to be bound and tormented in other forms?

What could be more cruel than you, if this is true? What more absurd, if it is false? What more contrary to your discipline, if you loosen the seal? What more hostile to a member of God, if you preserve it?

### 58

But this follows from your false and frivolous opinion. For a definite and obvious cruelty is proved to exist among you, arising from that same error.

Suppose someone, his body weakened by illness, exhausted from travel, and half-dead from disease, is lying on the road, able to do no more than utter a few words. Suppose that giving him a pear would help restore his body, and that, as you pass, he begs and implores you to help him by bringing a fruit from the nearest tree—a tree from which no human law, indeed no true law at all, forbids you to take it. The man will die shortly afterward if you do not do this.

Will you, a Christian and holy man, pass by instead and abandon a man in such condition who is begging and entreating you, lest the tree weep while its fruit is removed and you, as a dissolver of the seal, be consigned to Manichaean punishments?

*[Note: [Col. 1370] Lovaniensis reads “be consigned to punishments for the Manichaeans.” The manuscripts read manichaeias, meaning “the punishments which Manichaeus threatened”; see above, §55. “For the Manichaeans” follows Erasmus and the Venetian edition.]*

What customs! What singular innocence!

### 59

But let us now investigate what troubles me concerning the killing of animals; many things of this kind can also be said in this connection.

What harm will come to the soul of the wolf from someone who has killed a wolf, since, while it lives, that wolf will remain a wolf and obey no preacher who tells it to refrain somewhat from the blood of sheep? And, according to you, when the beast is killed, its rational soul will be released from that bodily bond.

You even prohibit your hearers from this killing, for it seems greater than the killing of trees. Here I do not greatly condemn your senses—your bodily senses, that is. For we see and perceive by their cries that animals die in pain, though a human being disregards this in a beast with which, since it does not possess a rational soul, he is joined by no fellowship of law.

But I ask you to apply those same senses when observing trees, and I find you utterly blind. To omit the fact that no movement in wood reveals any sensation of pain, what could be clearer than that a tree is in its best condition when it flourishes, puts forth leaves, rejoices in flowers, and is rich in fruit? Yet this condition is most often and most fully produced by pruning.

If iron felt pain in the way you wish it to, it would waste away after being afflicted by so many and such great wounds, rather than springing forth from those places and reviving with such unmistakable exuberance.

### 60

Nevertheless, why do you think it a greater crime to kill animals than to cut down plants, when the latter seem to you to possess a purer soul than flesh?

“There is,” he says, “a certain compensation, when some portion of what is taken from the fields is given to the elect and saints for purification.”

The argument has already been refuted above, and, as far as I judge, it has been sufficiently demonstrated that there is no rational basis for saying that a greater portion of that good element exists in crops than in flesh.

But if someone supports his livelihood by selling meat and spends all the profit from such commerce on purchasing food for your elect, bringing these saints more food than a farmer or peasant does, will he not loudly claim that, by the same compensation, he too is permitted to kill animals?

“There is,” he says, “another, wholly secret reason.”

A clever man is never without a refuge against the unlearned in the obscurity of nature. He says that the celestial princes, who were captured and bound from the nation of darkness and assigned by the Creator of the world to those places, each possess on earth animals that come from their own race and lineage. They hold their killers guilty, do not allow them to depart from this world, and wear them down with whatever punishments and torments they can inflict.

Who among the unlearned would not fear these things? And who, seeing nothing amid such darkness, would not think that matters are as they are described? But I shall not abandon my undertaking; God will assist me so that the obscure falsehoods may be refuted by the clearest truth.

### 61

For I ask: if the animals on land and in the waters come from that race of princes through the succession of offspring and the operation of intercourse—since the origin of those born is traced back even to aborted fetuses—if this is so, I ask whether it is not unlawful to kill bees, frogs, and many other creatures that are born without intercourse.

You say that it is unlawful. Therefore you do not prohibit your hearers from killing animals because of kinship with some princes or other.

Or, if you say that all bodies share a general kinship, then trees too will unquestionably belong to the same offense against the princes, yet your hearers have not been commanded to spare them.

*[Note: [Col. 1371] Lovaniensis reads auctoribus (“authors”); other manuscripts read auditoribus (“hearers”). The latter is the better reading, although Lovaniensis relegates it to the margin. There is much here and elsewhere about the Manichaean hearers.]*

We are therefore brought back to that weak argument: that the harms which hearers inflict upon plants are expiated by the fruits they bring to your church.

For it has been said that those who butcher animals in the market and sell meat, if they are your hearers and contribute their profits to you through the crops they purchase, may disregard the daily slaughter as permitted to them, and whatever sin it contains is erased by your banquets.

### 62

But if you say that, just as with fruit and vegetables, a contribution ought to be made so that the killing might obtain forgiveness—and that, since this cannot be done because the elect do not eat meat, hearers must abstain from killing animals—what will you answer about useless thorns and weeds, which farmers kill by pulling them up while clearing their fields, even though they cannot provide you with any food from them?

How will such destruction lead to forgiveness when it yields no food for the saints?

Or perhaps you dissolve whatever sin has been committed so that crops and fruit may flourish by eating some of those crops and fruits? What, then, if locusts, mice, or field-mice devastate the fields, as plainly often happens? Will they be killed with impunity by your farmer-hearer because he kills them so that the crops may flourish?

Here you are certainly trapped. Either you grant hearers permission to kill animals, which your founder refused to grant, or you must also prohibit them from farming, which he allowed.

Although you often even dare to say that a moneylender is more innocent than a farmer—you are so much more friendly to melons than to human beings. For you judge that it is better for a man to be slaughtered through usury so long as the melons are not harmed.

Is this a justice to be desired and proclaimed, or rather a deceit to be cursed and condemned? Is this a memorable compassion, or rather a brutality to be cursed?

### 63

What of the fact that you yourselves do not abstain from killing lice, fleas, and bedbugs? You think you have a strong defense for this in saying that these are the filth of our bodies.

First, this is plainly false when said of the flea and the bedbug. For whom is it not clear that these animals do not arise from our bodies?

Furthermore, if you detest intercourse so vehemently—as you wish to appear to do—why do you not consider cleaner those animals that arise without intercourse from our flesh? Although they later reproduce by mating, they do not initially arise from our bodies through our mating.

Moreover, if whatever is generated from living bodies is to be considered exceedingly filthy, then much more so whatever is generated from the dead. A shrew, a snake, or a scorpion, which we especially often hear you say are born from human corpses, may therefore be killed with greater impunity.

But I shall omit obscure and uncertain matters. It is certainly more widely reported that bees arise from the corpses of oxen. They may therefore be killed with impunity. But even if this too is doubtful, scarcely anyone doubts that beetles arise from dung rounded into a ball and buried by them.

*[Note: [Col. 1372] See *Retractationes*, Book 1, chapter 7, §6.]*

You ought therefore to consider these and other animals, whose enumeration would be tedious, filthier than your lice. Yet you think it unlawful to kill those animals and foolish to spare these—unless perhaps you despise them because they are small.

Certainly, if the rule is that the shorter an animal is, the more contemptible it ought to be, you must necessarily prefer a camel to a human being.

### 64

To this must be added that progression which, when I heard you, often disturbed us. There is no reason why a flea should be killed because of its small bodily size but not a fly that is born in a bean.

And if the fly may be killed, why not the creature somewhat larger than it, whose offspring is certainly smaller than that fly? It follows also that a bee may be killed without guilt, since its young is equal in size to this fly.

From there we proceed to the young of the locust and then the locust itself; from there to the young of the mouse and then the mouse. And, not to prolong the matter, do you not see that by these steps one arrives at the elephant, so that it cannot at all be denied that anyone who does not think the killing of a flea a sin may kill that enormous beast without guilt?

But I think enough has now been said about such trifles.

## Chapter XVIII — Concerning the Seal of the Bosom and the Unspeakable Mysteries of the Manichaeans

### 65

The seal of the bosom remains, and in it your chastity is highly uncertain. For you prohibit not intercourse but, as the Apostle said long ago, marriage itself, which is the one honorable defense against such an act.

Here I do not doubt that you will cry out and attempt to arouse resentment, saying that you strongly commend and praise perfect chastity, but do not prohibit marriage, since your hearers—the second rank among you—are not prohibited from marrying and having wives.

When you have said this loudly and indignantly, I shall question you more gently in this way: are you not the ones who consider the begetting of children, because souls are bound in flesh, a graver sin than intercourse itself?

Are you not the ones who used to advise us, as far as possible, to observe the time when a woman, after the cleansing of her reproductive organs, would be suited for conception, and at that time to abstain from intercourse, lest a soul be bound to flesh?

It follows from this that you think a wife should be kept not for the procreation of children but for the satisfaction of lust.

Marriage, however, as the marriage contracts themselves proclaim, joins male and female for the procreation of children. Therefore whoever says that procreating children is a graver sin than intercourse certainly prohibits marriage. He makes the woman not a wife but a prostitute, joined to a man for the satisfaction of his lust in exchange for the things granted to her.

For if she is a wife, there is a marriage. But there is no marriage where efforts are made to prevent her from being a mother; therefore she is not a wife.

Consequently, you prohibit marriage, and you cannot defend yourselves by any argument against this charge, which the Holy Spirit long ago foretold concerning you.

### 66

Moreover, when you make every effort to prevent the soul from being bound to flesh through intercourse, and strongly assert that the soul is released from seeds through the food of the saints, do you not, wretched men, confirm what people suspect about you?

For why should it be believed that, when you eat wheat, beans, lentils, and other seeds, you wish to liberate the soul from them, but not believed that you wish to liberate it from the seeds of animals?

You cannot say that the flesh of a dead animal is unclean because it has no soul, and say the same of the seed of a living animal, in which you believe the soul that will appear in the offspring to be bound—and in which you admit that the soul of Manichaeus himself was entangled.

And since such seeds cannot be brought to you by your hearers for purification, who would not suspect that such a purification is secretly carried out among you yourselves and concealed from them so that they will not leave you?

If you do not do these things—which, I wish, were indeed the case—you nevertheless see how greatly your superstition exposes itself to suspicion, and how people cannot fairly be reproached for thinking what follows from your profession, since you proclaim that you liberate souls from bodies and senses through food and drink.

I do not wish to linger here longer; you see how ample a field there would be for denunciation. But since the matter is such that speech should fear it rather than attack it, and since my purpose throughout this discourse can be discerned—I have resolved to exaggerate nothing, but to proceed, so to speak, by bare facts and arguments—let us pass on to something else.

## Chapter XIX — The Crimes of the Manichaeans

### 67

It is now sufficiently clear what your three seals are like. These are your customs; this is the outcome of your admirable precepts: nothing certain, nothing consistent, nothing rational, nothing blameless, but everything doubtful—or rather, without any doubt, utterly false; everything contradictory, abominable, and absurd.

Finally, so many grave sins are detected in these customs that if someone wished to accuse them all, a person of some ability could treat each one, at the very least, in a separate volume.

If you guarded these practices and fulfilled your profession, nothing would be more inept, more foolish, or more ignorant than you. But when you praise and teach these things while not practicing them, what could be said or found more deceitful, more treacherous, or more malicious than you?

### 68

For nine whole years I listened to you with great care and diligence. No one among the elect became known to me who, according to these precepts, was not either caught in sin or at least subject to suspicion.

Many were found drinking wine and eating meat; many were found bathing in public baths. But we merely heard these things.

Some were proved to have seduced other men’s women, so that on this point I can plainly have no doubt. But let even this be regarded as rumor rather than truth.

I myself saw—not alone, but together with men who had in part already been freed from that superstition and in part whom I still hope will be freed—indeed, we saw in the crossroads of Carthage, in a most crowded street, not one but more than three of the elect simultaneously neighing after some women who were passing by, with such wanton gestures that they surpassed the immodesty and shamelessness of every street-corner libertine.

It was sufficiently evident that this arose from a long-standing habit and that they lived among themselves in this way, since none of them showed any fear of his companions’ presence; all, or certainly almost all, indicated that they were held by the same plague.

For these men did not live in one household. They lived in entirely different places and had perhaps come down together from the place where the meeting of all had been held.

We were deeply disturbed and also lodged a serious complaint. Who, then, thought that this ought to be punished—not, I say, by separation from the church, but at least by severe reproach proportionate to the enormity of the offense?

69. And this was their entire excuse for impunity: because at that time their assemblies were prohibited by public law, it was feared that they might expose some wrong that had been done to them. Where, then, is the claim they proclaim that perpetual persecution will be theirs in this world, and by which they wish to make themselves more commendable—interpreting from this that the world hates them (John 15:18), and asserting that the truth must therefore be sought among them because it was said in the promise of the Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, that this world cannot receive him (John 14:17)? This is not the place to discuss that matter. But certainly, if perpetual persecution is to be yours until the end of the age, this dissolution and impunity for such great disgrace will also be perpetual, so long as you fear harming people of this sort.

70. We were also given this reply when we had reported to the leading members that a woman had complained to us that, while she was in a room with other women—secure, of course, in their holiness—several of the Elect had entered, and one of them had extinguished the lamp; then, in the darkness, one of them—she did not know which—had attempted to embrace her and forced her into a shameful act, unless she had escaped by calling for help. Since this crime is also well known to us, from what extensive practice should we suppose it to have arisen? [Col. 1375] This happened on the night when the festive vigils are celebrated among you. But in truth, even if there had been no fear of betrayal, who could have presented for condemnation a bishop who had taken such precautions not to be recognized? As though the crime did not implicate all those who had entered together! For when the lamp was extinguished, all of them had delighted in behaving wantonly.

71. How many doors were opened to suspicion when we found them envious, greedy, extremely eager for elaborate banquets, constantly involved in quarrels, and highly volatile over trivial matters! Certainly we did not think that they could abstain from what they professed to abstain from when they found hiding places and darkness.

There were two men of fairly good reputation, gifted in intellect, leaders in those debates of theirs, and more closely and familiarly connected with us than the others. One of them, who was even more closely attached to us because of his liberal studies, is now said to be a presbyter there. These two were intensely jealous of one another. One of them charged the other—not by an open accusation, but in conversation with whoever would listen and in whispers—with having violently attempted the wife of one of his auditors. The other, while clearing himself, meanwhile accused another Elect of the same crime. That man lived with the same auditor as though he were his most trusted friend. Because he had suddenly entered and caught him with a woman, he said that the woman and the adulterer had been advised by that enemy of his, driven by envy, to fabricate this accusation against him, so that, if he exposed anything, he would not be believed.

We were distressed and bore the matter with the greatest irritation. Even though it was uncertain whether the woman had actually been pursued, the most savage jealousy was nevertheless evident between those two men, among whom we found no better persons there; and it compelled us to draw further conclusions.

72. Finally, we very often found Elect members in the theaters—men serious in age and, as they appeared, in character—together with an elderly presbyter. I omit the young men, whom we were also accustomed to catch quarreling over theatrical performers and charioteers. This is no small indication of how capable they are of restraining themselves from hidden things, when they cannot overcome the desire that displays them before the eyes of their own hearers and betrays them as they blush and flee.

Or would even the wickedness of that holy man to whose debates we used to go in the street of the fig trees have been exposed, if he had been able to make a consecrated virgin a woman only, and not also pregnant? But the hidden and incredible evil was not allowed to remain concealed by the growing womb. When the mother revealed the matter to the young man’s brother, he was in the deepest grief; nevertheless, out of respect for religion, he was restrained from making a public accusation. He did, however, arrange for that man—for no one could endure this—to be expelled from that church. And, so that the affair might not be entirely unpunished, he devised a plan to join his friends in beating the man to pieces with fists and kicks.

But while he was being severely beaten, the man cried out that he should be spared on the authority of Mani, since Adam, the first hero, had sinned and had become holier after his sin.

73. Such, indeed, is your opinion concerning Adam and Eve. The story is long, but I shall touch on what is sufficient for the present. You say that Adam was begotten in this way by his parents, those abortive rulers of darkness: that he had the greatest part of the light in his soul [Note: [Col. 1376] Almost all manuscripts read *in animam*, “into the soul”; that is, in place of *pro anima*, “for the soul.”], and a very small part of the opposing race. While he was living holily because of the surpassing abundance of the good, that opposing part was nevertheless stirred within him so that he turned toward sexual intercourse. Thus he fell and sinned, but afterward lived more holily.

Here I am not so much complaining about the wicked man who, through an abominable sexual crime, brought another’s household to such disgrace and infamy under the guise of an Elect and holy man. I do not charge this against you. Let it have been the act of a thoroughly ruined individual rather than of your custom. I am not accusing you of such a great crime in yourselves, but him. Yet I do not know how this can be endured and tolerated in all of you: you say that the soul is a part of God, and yet you assert that even when a small amount of evil has been mixed into it, its greater abundance and fullness can be overcome. For who, once he has believed this and has been struck by lust, would not resort to such a defense rather than restraining and suppressing his lust?

## CHAPTER XX — The Crimes of These People Discovered at Rome

74. What more shall I say about your morals? I have related what I myself discovered when I was in that city where these things were committed. But what happened at Rome in my absence would take too long to explain in full. I shall nevertheless state it briefly.

The matter reached such a point that it could not remain hidden from those who were absent. When I was later at Rome, I confirmed that everything I had heard was true, although the report had been brought to me by a man so intimate with me and so trustworthy that I could not doubt it at all.

One of your auditors, equal to the Elect in that celebrated abstinence of yours, a man liberally educated and accustomed and willing to defend your sect at length, was deeply distressed because, whenever he argued with them, the utterly depraved morals of the Elect—men living scattered and behaving indiscriminately—were repeatedly thrown in his face.

He therefore wished, if possible, to gather into his house all who were prepared to live according to those precepts and to support them at his own expense. For he was both no ordinary despiser of money and no ordinary possessor of it. He complained that his great undertaking was being obstructed by the dissolution of the bishops, with whose assistance he was supposed to complete it.

Meanwhile there was a certain bishop of yours, a man plainly—as I myself discovered—rustic and uncultivated, but, somehow, that very harshness made him appear more severe in guarding good morals. The auditor seized this man, whom he had long desired and had finally found present, and explained his wish to him. The bishop praised and approved it, and agreed that he himself should first begin living in the auditor’s house.

When this had been done, all the Elect who could be in Rome gathered there. A rule of life was proposed from a letter of Mani. Many found it intolerable and departed; nevertheless, quite a few remained out of shame. They began to live as had been agreed and as so great an authority prescribed. Meanwhile, the auditor vigorously compelled everyone to observe everything, but no one to do anything that he himself had not first undertaken. [Col. 1377]

In the meantime, quarrels arose very frequently among the Elect. They brought accusations against one another, all of which the auditor heard with groans; he took care to make them betray themselves most incautiously in their quarrels. They exposed abominable and monstrous things. It became clear what sort of men they were, even though they had thought that, among the others, they ought to submit themselves to the force of those precepts.

What, then, was to be suspected—or rather judged—about the rest? What more is there to say? At length they were compelled to murmur that those commands could not be maintained, and from there they proceeded to revolt. The auditor stated his case in the briefest possible form: either all those commands had to be observed, or the man who had prescribed such things under such a condition—one that no one could fulfill—had to be considered utterly foolish.

Nevertheless, the unrestrained uproar of the majority overcame the judgment of the one man—for it could not have been otherwise. Later the bishop himself also withdrew and fled in great disgrace. It was reported that he had secretly taken food contrary to the rule and had often been discovered doing so, since abundant money was supplied to him from his own purse, which he carefully kept hidden.

75. If you say that these things are false, you are resisting matters too clear and too widely known. But would that you said so! For since these things are manifest and very easy to know for those who wish to learn them, it can be understood how truthful those people are accustomed to be who deny that these things are true.

But you employ other defenses, which I do not reject. Either you say that there are some who keep your precepts and that they ought not to be stained by the crimes of others; or you say that one ought not to inquire at all what sort of people those are who profess your sect, but what the profession itself is like.

Even if I grant both points—although you can neither demonstrate those who faithfully observe the commands nor cleanse the heresy itself of so many and such great absurdities and crimes—I shall nevertheless demand this of you above all: why do you attack Christians of the Catholic name with curses, looking at the ruined life of some of them, while, when an inquiry is raised concerning your people, you either shamelessly refuse it or, still more shamelessly, do not refuse it, wishing it to be understood that, amid your very small number, certain people whose own precepts they observe are hidden, while you do not wish the same to be understood amid the enormous multitude of Catholics?

## Rule of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, for the Servants of God

[Note: [Col. 1377] This Rule was compared with the oldest Rule manuscript of Corbie, more than a thousand years old; with the manuscripts of Sorbonne, Thuaneus, Albinus, Michaelinus, Medardus, Victorinus, three German manuscripts, and two Vatican manuscripts; with the readings of the Gembloux manuscript as printed by Louvain, together with Letter 211; and with the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, Louvain, and Desnos.]

[Note: [Col. 1377] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*. M.]

(C, G, S)

## Prefatory Notice Concerning the Following Rule of Saint Augustine for the Servants of God

This same Rule, whose diction, sentences, and precepts—ultimately composed with pious humanity—identify Augustine as its author, appears in Letter 211, which he wrote to consecrated women. That it was extracted from there and adapted for men has been observed, among others, by Bernard Winding and Prosper Stellartius, both members of the Augustinian family, and most recently by the learned Nicolaus Desnos of the order of the Augustinian Canons Regular.

Whether this is so or not, it has certainly long been employed in forming the morals of men. For it constitutes the principal part of the very ancient Rule of Tarnat; it is praised in the *Concordia Regularum* by Benedict, abbot of Aniane; and—what it is useful for us to note here—it is contained in the more than thousand-year-old Corbie manuscript, adapted for men and combined into a single body of rules with the work entitled *Rule for Clerics II*.

## [The Rule]

### On the Love of God and Neighbor, the Unity of Hearts, and the Common Ownership of Goods

1. Above all, dearest brothers, let God be loved, and then one’s neighbor, because these are the principal commandments given to us [Note: [Col. 1377] Winding and Stellartius do not regard this introductory passage as Augustine’s; it was taken from the Second Rule, which is included below in the appendix.].

These, then, are the things that we who have been established in the monastery command you to observe [Col. 1378]. First, the reason you have been gathered together is that you may live unanimously in the house [Note: [Col. 1377] Printed editions have “in the house of the Lord.” The word “Lord,” however, is absent from the manuscripts and from Letter 211.], and that you may have one soul and one heart in God.

Do not call anything your own; let everything be common to you. Let food and clothing be distributed to each of you by your superior [Note: [Col. 1378] The Albinus and Sorbonne manuscripts omit “by your superior.” Three others substitute “by your elder.”], not equally to all, since you are not all equally strong, but rather to each according to his need. For so you read in the Acts of the Apostles: “They had everything in common, and it was distributed to each according to each one’s need” (Acts 4:32, 35).

Those who possessed anything in the world when they entered the monastery should willingly wish it to be held in common among them. Those who possessed nothing should not seek in the monastery what they could not have possessed outside it. Nevertheless, what is necessary should be supplied to their weakness, even if, when they were outside, their poverty could not obtain even those necessities. But they should not therefore consider themselves fortunate merely because they have found food and clothing of a kind they could not find outside [Note: [Col. 1379] Three manuscripts here, and almost all copies of Letter 211, read “and not for this reason now.”].

### On Humility

2. They should not hold their heads high because they are associated with people whom they did not dare approach outside; rather, let them lift up their hearts and not seek earthly and empty things [Note: [Col. 1379] The Corbie manuscript and several others, as well as Letter 211, read: “and let them not seek earthly goods.”], lest monasteries begin to be useful to the rich and not to the poor—if the rich are humbled there while the poor are puffed up there.

Again, those who appeared to be something in the world should not despise their brothers who have come from poverty into that holy fellowship. Rather, let them strive to glory not in the dignity of wealthy parents but in the fellowship of poor brothers.

Nor should they become proud if they have contributed some of their possessions to the common life, lest they take greater pride in their wealth because they share it in the monastery than they would if they enjoyed it in the world. For every other iniquity is practiced in evil deeds so that they may be committed; but pride lies in wait even for good deeds so that they may perish. What good is it to scatter one’s goods by giving to the poor and to become poor, if the wretched soul becomes prouder by despising riches than it had been by possessing them?

Live, then, all of you with one mind and in concord, and honor in one another the God whose temples you have become.

### On Prayer and the Divine Office

3. Devote yourselves to prayer at the appointed hours and times. In the oratory, no one should do anything except that for which it was made and from which it received its name. Thus, if some should wish to pray even outside the appointed hours, when they have the opportunity, they will not be a hindrance to those who think that something must be done there.

When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let what is spoken be present in your heart; and do not sing anything except what you read is to be sung [Note: [Col. 1379] Nine manuscripts read “what you have read.”]. Anything that is not written to be sung should not be sung.

### On Fasting and Meals

4. Discipline your flesh with fasts and abstinence from food and drink, insofar as health permits. When someone cannot fast, nevertheless he should not take food outside the hour of the meal [Note: [Col. 1379] The Albinus and Michaelinus manuscripts omit “of the meal.” The word is found in the others and signifies a second meal permitted to the weak, as Father Stephen Rabache, reformer of the Augustinians in France, notes in the Gallican observances. For among the ancients it was customary to refresh the body only once daily, toward evening, as is stated in the work *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 33.] except when he is ill.

When you come to the table, listen without disturbance or contention to what is read to you according to custom until you rise from it. Let it not be only your throats that receive food; let your ears also hunger for the word of God [Note: [Col. 1380] Letter 211 reads “receive the word of God.”].

### On Indulgence toward the Sick

5. Those who are weak because of their former way of life, if they are treated differently in food, should not cause annoyance to others, nor should it seem unjust to those whom another custom has made stronger. They should not consider the others more fortunate because they receive what they themselves do not; rather, they should congratulate themselves because they possess the strength that the others lack.

If something is given to those who have come to the monastery from more delicate habits—food, clothing, bedding [Note: [Col. 1380] This word, omitted in most printed editions, has been restored from the Corbie manuscript; indeed, Desnos restored it before us. It is also found in Letter 211.], or coverings—that is not given to the stronger and therefore more fortunate, they should reflect on how far those who receive these things have descended from their worldly life into this one, even though they have not been able to reach the frugality of others whose bodies are stronger.

Nor should they wish everyone to receive what they see a few receiving in greater measure [Note: [Col. 1380] This is the reading of the manuscripts. Letter 211 has: “Nor should they be disturbed because they see them receiving more.”], not because they are honored, but because they are being tolerated. Otherwise the detestable perversity may arise that, in a monastery where the rich labor as much as they can, the poor become delicate.

Just as the sick necessarily need to receive less, lest they be burdened, so after illness they should be treated in such a way that they recover more quickly, even if they came from the deepest poverty of the world. It should be as though their recent illness had conferred on them what an earlier habit had conferred on the rich.

But when they have recovered their former strength, let them return to their more fortunate custom, which suits the servants of God all the better the less they need. Let pleasure not keep them vigorous where necessity had placed the sick [Note: [Col. 1380] Many books read: “Let the pleasure of food not keep them vigorous, whom necessity had raised up when they were sick.” But the reading of the Corbie manuscript, restored here, is more harmonious and is confirmed by Letter 211. It should be noted that Letter 211 has *voluntas*, “will,” in place of *voluptas*, “pleasure.” M.].

Let them consider those richer who have been stronger in enduring frugality. For it is better to need less than to have more.

### On Clothing and the Arrangement of the Exterior Person

6. Let your clothing not be conspicuous. Do not seek to please by your garments but by your conduct [Note: [Col. 1380] Letter 211 here inserts certain matters appropriate to women, not men, namely: “Let your head coverings not be so delicate that little nets are visible beneath them,” and so forth.].

When you go out, walk together; when you arrive where you are going, stand together. In your walking, standing, clothing, and all your movements, let nothing occur that offends anyone’s gaze, but only what befits your holiness.

Even if your eyes fall upon some women, let them settle upon none. You are not forbidden to see women when you go out; but it is criminal to desire them or to wish to be desired by them. Lust for women is both aroused and arouses, not only by touch and feeling but also by sight [Note: [Col. 1380] This is the reading of Louvain, the Corbie manuscript, and several others. Erasmus and five manuscripts have: “It is not only by silent feeling, but also by feeling and sight that the desire of women is sought and seeks.” Desnos: “It is not only by silent feeling, but also by sight.” Finally, Letter 211 reads: “It is not only by touch but also by feeling and sight that a woman is desired and desires,” where Winding would prefer *and someone desires* in the rule for men. The Rule of Tarnat rearranges the passage as follows: “But desire for women is also incurred by sight.”].

Do not say that you have chaste minds if you have immodest eyes, because an immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart. When, even while the tongue is silent, people reveal immodest hearts to one another by their mutual gaze and take pleasure in one another’s ardor according to the desire of the flesh, chastity itself flees from their conduct, even though their bodies have not been violated by touch.

A man who fixes his eyes on a woman and delights in her fixing hers upon him should not think that others do not see him when he does this. He is certainly seen, even by those whom he does not suppose to see him. But suppose he remains hidden and is seen by no human being: what will he do about the one above, from whom nothing can be hidden? Is he to be thought not to see because he sees with greater patience and wisdom?

Let the holy man therefore fear displeasing that one, lest he wish to please the woman wrongly. Let him think that God sees everything, lest he wish to look wrongly at the woman. For God’s fear is commended even in this matter, where it is written: “An abomination to the Lord is one who fixes his eye” [Note: [Col. 1381] Greek: *Edélugma Kuriô stêridzôn ophtalmon*, “An abomination to the Lord is one who fixes his eye.”] (Proverbs 27:20, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, when you are together in church, and wherever women are also present, guard one another’s chastity. For God, who dwells in you, will also guard you from yourselves in this way.

### On Fraternal Correction

7. If you notice in any of your number the wantonness of the eye of which I am speaking, warn him immediately, so that what has begun may not progress but may be corrected at once. If, after the warning, you see him do the same thing again, or on any other day, let whoever discovers it expose him as one wounded and in need of healing. But first let the matter be shown to another or a third person, so that he may be convicted by the testimony of two or three [the source gives only “16)”], and restrained with appropriate severity.

Do not think yourselves malicious when you report this. You are even less innocent if, by remaining silent, you allow brothers whom you could correct by reporting them to perish.

If your brother had a wound on his body that he wished to conceal because he feared surgery, would it not be cruel of you to remain silent, and merciful to report it? How much more, then, ought you to reveal him, lest the wound putrefy more seriously in his heart?

Before the matter is shown to those by whom he must be convicted if he denies it, it must first be shown to the superior [Note: [Col. 1381] Three manuscripts have “to the elder,” and shortly afterward the same three, together with another manuscript, add “according to the judgment of the brothers or even of the abbot to whose…”], if, after being warned, he has neglected correction, so that perhaps, having been rebuked privately, he may not become known to the others.

If he denies it, then others must be brought in against the denier, so that, before everyone, he may be accused not by a single witness but convicted by two or three. Once convicted, he must, according to the judgment of the superior or even of the presbyter to whose administration the matter belongs, undergo corrective punishment. If he refuses to endure it, he is to be expelled from your fellowship, even if he does not leave of his own accord. For this too is not done cruelly but mercifully, lest he destroy many through the contagion of a pestilential evil.

What I have said about not fixing the eyes must also be carefully and faithfully observed in discovering, preventing, reporting, proving, and punishing other sins—with love for persons and hatred of vices.

Whoever has progressed so far in evil that he secretly receives letters or any little gifts from a woman [Note: [Col. 1382] Most codices have: “from someone he receives a letter or any gift.” We have corrected the passage according to the Corbie manuscript, following also the conjecture of Stellartius and Winding, who think that this instruction concerns amorous gifts; therefore, just as the women’s Rule reads “from someone,” here it should read “from a woman.” Shortly afterward, after the words “or of the superior,” Letter 211 adds “or even of the bishop,” which is absent from all copies of the Rule adapted for men.], if he confesses this voluntarily, let him be spared and let prayers be offered for him. But if he is discovered and convicted, let him be corrected more severely according to the judgment of the presbyter or superior.

### On the Vice of Claiming a Particular Possession as One’s Own

8. Keep your garments together, under one keeper, or two, or as many as may suffice to shake them out so that they are not damaged by moths. Just as you are fed from one storeroom, so let your clothing come from one wardrobe.

If possible, it should not be your concern what garment is brought out for you as appropriate to the season—whether each person receives what he had taken off or something another had worn—provided that each is not denied what he needs.
