If quarrels and murmuring arise among you over this, when someone complains that he has received something worse than what he had before, or considers himself unworthy because he is not clothed as another brother was, then test how much you lack in that inner holy clothing of the heart, since you quarrel over bodily clothing.

Nevertheless, if your weakness is tolerated to the extent that you receive what you had taken off, keep what you put away in one place under common guardians. Let no one make anything for himself; let all your work be done in common [Note: [Col. 1382] Printed editions have “let all your work be done as one.” The better manuscripts have “in common.” Letter 211 likewise reads “in common,” and shortly before the word “works” adds: “whether it is for you to dress, or where you are to lie, or with what you are to gird or cover yourself, or cover your head.”], with greater dedication and more frequent eagerness than if you were making things for yourselves individually.

For love, of which it is written that it does not seek what is its own (1 Corinthians 13:5), is understood in this way: it places common things before private ones, not private things before common ones. Therefore, the more carefully you care for the common property than for your own, the more you should know that you have progressed, so that in everything used by passing necessity, enduring love may stand supreme.

It follows, then, that if someone gives a garment—or anything else counted among necessities—to his sons or to persons connected with him by some relationship who are living in the monastery, it should not be received secretly. Rather, it should be under the authority of the superior, so that, having been added to the common property, it may be given to whoever needs it.

If anyone conceals an item given to him, let him be condemned as a thief [Note: [Col. 1382] This sentence—“If anyone conceals an item,” and so forth—is absent from the Corbie manuscript and from most other manuscripts.].

### On Washing Clothes, Baths, and Other Ways of Caring for the Brothers’ Needs

9. Let your garments be washed according to the superior’s judgment, either by you or by launderers, lest an excessive desire for clean clothing produce inward stains in the soul.

Nor should bathing be denied to the body when the necessity of illness requires it [Note: [Col. 1383] Letter 211 reads: “The use of bathing and of baths should not be constant; rather, it should be provided at the customary interval, namely once a month. If the necessity of an illness compels the body to be washed, it should not be delayed longer. Let it be done without murmuring.”].

Let it be done without murmuring, on the advice of the physician, so that even if the sick man does not wish it, he will do what must be done for his health when the superior commands it. But if he wishes it and it is perhaps not beneficial, his desire should not be obeyed. For sometimes, even if something is harmful, what gives pleasure is nevertheless believed to be beneficial.

Finally, if there is a hidden pain in the body, let the servant of God be believed without hesitation when he says what hurts him. Nevertheless, if it is uncertain whether what gives pleasure is beneficial for curing that pain, let the physician be consulted.

Do not go to the baths, or wherever else it is necessary to go, with fewer than two or three people. Whoever has some necessity of going somewhere must go with those whom the superior orders [Note: [Col. 1383] Four manuscripts read: “Nor should one who has a need to go somewhere go with whomever he wishes, but with those whom the elder orders.”].

Care of the sick—or of those recovering after illness, or suffering from some weakness even without fever—should be assigned to one person, so that he himself may request from the storeroom whatever he sees each person needs.

Whether those placed in charge of the storeroom, clothing, or books, let them serve their brothers without murmuring. Books are to be requested at a fixed hour each day; whoever asks outside that hour should not receive one.

When clothing or shoes are needed by those who lack them, let those under whose custody the requested items are not delay in giving them.

### On Asking Forgiveness and Forgiving Offenses Out of Love

10. Have no quarrels, or settle them as quickly as possible, lest anger grow into hatred, make a beam out of a splinter, and make the soul murderous. For you read: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

Whoever has injured someone by insult, curse, or even accusation of a crime should remember to repair what he has done as quickly as possible by making satisfaction; and the one who has been injured should forgive without dispute.

If they have injured one another, they must mutually forgive one another’s debts, for the sake of your prayers. The more frequent your prayers are, the healthier they ought to be.

The better person is the one who, although often tempted by anger, nevertheless hastens to obtain forgiveness from the person whom he acknowledges having wronged, rather than the one who is slower to become angry but more reluctant to bend toward asking forgiveness [Note: [Col. 1383] Printed editions have “slower to bend.” The Corbie manuscript and others have “more reluctantly.”].

Whoever does not wish to forgive his brother should not hope to receive the effect of prayer. Whoever never wishes to ask forgiveness, or does not ask sincerely, is in the monastery without purpose, even if he is not expelled from it.

Therefore, refrain from harsh words toward one another. If such words escape your mouths, do not be reluctant to utter from those same mouths the remedies by which the wounds were made [Col. 1384].

When the necessity of discipline in correcting conduct compels you to speak harsh words, if you yourselves also realize that you have exceeded the proper measure, you are not required to ask forgiveness from your subordinates, lest, while humility is observed excessively before those who ought to be subject, the authority of governance be broken. Nevertheless, forgiveness must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with what goodwill you love even those whom you perhaps rebuke more severely than is just.

Your love for one another must not be carnal but spiritual.

### On Obedience to the Superior

11. Let the superior be obeyed as a father [Note: [Col. 1384] The old Corbie manuscript reads: “Let him be obeyed with honor preserved, lest God be offended in him.” Four other manuscripts likewise continue: “much more the abbot.”], and much more the presbyter who has charge of all of you.

Therefore, so that all these things may be observed, and so that anything insufficiently observed may not be passed over carelessly but may be corrected and amended, it will belong especially to the superior to refer to the presbyter, whose authority among you is greater, whatever exceeds his capacity or strength.

The one who presides over you should not consider himself fortunate because of ruling power, but because of serving in love. Let him be placed above you in honor before you, but let him be beneath your feet in fear before God. In all things, let him offer himself as an example of good works (Titus 2:7). Let him rebuke the restless, console the fainthearted, support the weak, and be patient with all (1 Thessalonians 5:14); let him gladly maintain discipline and impose it with fear [Note: [Col. 1384] Louvain reads “let him impose it as one to be feared.” But the following words require the reading “let him impose it with fear,” as four manuscripts have.].

Although both are necessary, let him nevertheless desire to be loved by you more than feared, always considering that he will have to render an account to God for you [Note: [Col. 1384] Four manuscripts read: “It is nevertheless fitting that he be loved by you more than feared, as he constantly considers.” The common reading is more correct, and Saint Benedict renders it in Rule 64 as follows: “Let him strive to be loved rather than feared.”].

Therefore, by obeying, show mercy not only to yourselves but also to him, because the higher his position among you, the greater the danger in which he stands.

### On the Generous Observance of the Rule and Frequent Reading

12. May the Lord grant that you observe all these things with love [Note: [Col. 1384] This is the reading of the Corbie manuscript and three others. The printed editions omit “with love.”], as lovers of spiritual beauty and fragrant with the good odor of Christ through good conduct, not as slaves under the law but as free persons established under grace.

So that you may look upon yourselves in this little book as in a mirror and not neglect anything through forgetfulness, let it be read to you once a week.

When any of you finds that he is doing what is written, let him give thanks to the Lord, the giver of all good things. When someone sees that he lacks something, let him grieve over the past, take care for the future, and pray that his debt may be forgiven and that he may not be led into temptation. Amen.

## Appendix to Volume One of the Works of Saint Augustine, Containing Certain Works Once Wrongly Attributed to Him

They are:

- *The Book on Grammar*
- *Principles of Dialectic*
- *The Ten Categories*
- *Principles of Rhetoric*
- *Fragment of the Rule Delivered to Clerics*
- *The Second Rule*
- *On the Eremitical Life, to a Sister*

[Col. 1385]

## Prefatory Notice Concerning the Book on Grammar and the Three Treatises That Immediately Follow

(C, G, S)

We reckon the *Book on Grammar*, formerly attributed to Augustine in the first printed editions, among the spurious works, chiefly for this reason: its method and purpose entirely differ from that work which Augustine himself, in *Retractions* 1.6, acknowledges that he composed at Milan, together with the other books on the disciplines, when he was already on the point of receiving baptism. For he had written those books in dialogue form, and with the intention—so he says there—of either reaching incorporeal realities through corporeal things by certain fixed steps, or leading others to them. Indeed, from the time of his conversion it was a religious duty for him thereafter to devote himself to letters only if they served Christ, as appears from *Confessions* 9.4.7.

The work before us, however, is neither cast in dialogue form nor does it advance the mind toward incorporeal realities. Moreover, it does not display the skill of any learned writer, much less of so great a man—a skill that appears especially remarkable and exalted when he applies himself to a subject humble and commonplace in itself. Compare the books *On Music*, and also that passage in Book 2 *On Order* where he briefly touches upon the order of the disciplines among themselves, as well as their occasion, nature, and properties. From this you will certainly understand that Augustine did not commit to writing some randomly encountered matter about grammar, or something trampled under everyone’s feet. These considerations apply no less strongly against the three other little works that we have placed here as well, entitled *Principles of Dialectic*, *The Ten Categories*, and *Principles of Rhetoric*. A difficulty was raised by the clause appended to chapter 7 of Book 1 of the *Retractions*, namely: “This work begins as follows: ‘All nouns end in thirteen [letters],’”—which is the beginning of the following book. But we detected the deception from manuscripts, both ancient and more recent, that do not contain it.

[Col. 1385]

# BOOK ON GRAMMAR

## CHAPTER I — The endings of nouns, and first those ending in vowels

All nouns end in thirteen letters: five vowels, *a, e, i, o, u*; six semivowels, *l, m, n, r, s, x*; and two mutes, *c, t*.

Nouns ending in *a* are masculine, such as *Seneca, Catilina, Sulla, Uva, Cinna, Pansa*; Greek names, *Sosia, Pareta*; and African names, *Jugurtha, Micipsa*. Feminine nouns include *femina, musa, regula, norma, forma*, and similar words. Neuter nouns ending in *a* are only Greek—*thema, schema*—and one Latin name of a river, *Turia*, as Sallust says: “the river Turia” (*Jugurthine War*). Common-gender nouns include *advena, convena, indigena, Trojugena*, and similar words. Epicene nouns include *vipera, aquila, musca, locusta, ulula*, and similar words.

We have spoken of the letter *a*; now let us speak of *e*. No Latin masculine noun is found ending in the vowel *e*, except when a preposition has been joined to it, as in *proconsule* and *propraetore*. Thus, when joined to a preposition, such forms become Latin, as I have said: *propraetore, proquaestore*. For the ancients used *proconsul* in the nominative, observing that no Latin masculine noun ends in *e* in the nominative. There is no Latin feminine noun ending in *e*, but only Greek ones, such as *Andromache, Niobe, Libye, Hecate, Euterpe*, whose genitives end in *-es*: *Andromaches, Niobes, Libyes, Hecates, Euterpes*. But we shall treat these among the Greek nouns.

Neuter nouns ending in *e* in the nominative include *monile, sedile, cubile*, and the other nouns that we shall shortly set out completely in the rule for the neuter gender. There is no common-gender noun ending in *e*, and likewise none that is epicene.

Now let us discuss which genders are contained in the letter *i* in the nominative. No masculine noun ends in *i*, nor any feminine noun. Among neuters there is *gummi*, which is **ἄπτωτον** (*áptōton*, indeclinable) [Note: [Col. 1386] Augustine would have said “indeclinable,” since in Latin speech he does not use Greek words without necessity, as appears from *On Music* 1.12.23]. There is no common-gender noun ending in *i*. Words of every gender include *frugi* and *nihili*. They are declined as follows: *hic vir frugi* (“this useful man”), *femina frugi* (“a useful woman”), *mancipium frugi* (“a useful slave”); the genitive is likewise *frugi*: *hujus viri frugi, hujus feminae frugi, hujus mancipii frugi*. We use *frugi* in all the cases. *Nihili* is declined similarly: *hic nihili vir* (“this worthless man”), *haec nihili mulier* (“this worthless woman”), *hoc nihili mancipium* (“this worthless slave”). In the same form as the nominative, all the cases are declined; likewise in the plural: *viri nihili, feminae nihili, mancipia nihili*. No epicene noun likewise ends in *i*.

A masculine common noun has a nominative ending in the vowel *o*, such as *ligo, ligonis*. Proper names include *Cato, Cicero, Maro, Nero, Tubero*, and similar names. Feminine common nouns include *vertigo, indago, ferrago, siligo*. Juvenal has the following:

> But a face that is coated and pampered with so many altered cosmetics,  
> and receives morsels of cooked fine wheat and damp [matter]—  
> will it be called a face or an ulcer?  
> (*Satire* 6, vv. 461–473)

Also *sartago, virago, lanugo, aurugo, aerugo, crepido*. Juvenal writes of the last:

> No curb is empty; nowhere is a bridge or a part of a mat [empty].  
> (*Satire* 5, v. 8)

And similar words.

A feminine proper name ending in *o* is *Carthago*. Foreign names include *Dido, Ino, Io, Alecto, Celeno, Clio, Manto*, whose genitives end in *-us*: *Didus, Inus, Ius, Alectus, Celenus, Clius, Mantus*. But we shall treat these among the Greek names.

No neuter nominative ends in *o*. Common-gender nouns include *fullo, latro, caupo*, and so forth. Epicene nouns include *struthio, hirundo, hirudo, gurgulio, bufo*, and similar words.

Of nouns ending in the vowel *u*, only neuters are found. In the singular they are indeclinable, but in the plural they are declined: *cornu, veru, genu, tonitru*. In the singular, all the cases are pronounced in this same form, as we have said; in the plural they are declined *cornua, verua, genua*; in the genitive, *horum cornuum, veruum, genuum*. The others are declined according to the rule of *versuum, fluctuum*.

## CHAPTER II — Nouns ending in semivowels and their genders

We have spoken of the five vowels with which the nominative ends; now let us speak of the semivowels.

A nominative ending in the letter *l* is masculine in common nouns, as *hic sal* (“salt”), and in proper names, *Sol*. Among feminine nouns there is only the name *Tanaquil*. Among neuters: *mel* (“honey”), *fel* (“gall”). Among common-gender nouns: *vigil* (“watchman”), *pugil* (“boxer”); hence Terence also says of a woman, “They say she is a boxer” (*Eunuchus* 2.3.24). There is no epicene noun ending in *l*.

No Latin masculine noun has a nominative ending in *m*. Feminine nouns include *Glycerium, Phanium, Dorcium, Philocomasium*. Neuter nouns include *templum, telum, tectum*, and others whose plurals are easy. No common-gender noun ends in *m*, nor does any epicene noun.

Let us now discuss the semivowel *n*. Masculine nominatives ending in *n* include *flamen, pecten, lien*, the latter meaning “spleen.” Feminines include *siren*, plural *sirenes*. Neuters include *carmen, germen, gramen*, and similar words, which we shall treat below under the rules for the neuter gender. Common-gender nouns ending in *n* include *tubicen, tibicen, fidicen, lyricen, cornicen*, the one who plays upon the *litui* [curved trumpets]. Epicene nouns include *oscen*, that is, a bird from which augurs obtain an omen, and *attagen*.

Now let us discuss the semivowel *r*. Masculine nominatives ending in *r* include *Caesar, Arar, Nar, victor, tutor, sopor, moeror*, and other words, whether common or proper, that are easy. Feminines include *arbor, soror*. Neuters include *marmor, aequor*, and others. Common-gender nouns include *pauper, acer, alacer, memor, auctor*. Epicenes include *passer, accipiter, anser*.

Now let us discuss the semivowel *s*. Masculine nominatives ending in *s* include *justus, doctus, pius*. Feminines include *dos, sors, mors*, and similar words. Neuters include *vulnus, pectus, pecus*, and the others whose rule will shortly be reviewed. Common-gender nouns include *sacerdos, impos, compos, similis, nobilis, agilis*. Words of every gender include *nugas*, and so forth. We shall discuss these more fully below. Epicene nouns include *tigris, mus, lepus*, and so forth.

Now let us discuss the semivowel *x*. A nominative ending in *x* is masculine in *vertex, cortex, pumex*, and in the proper name *Pollux*. Feminines include *nex, prex, fex, pax, fax*, and others. There is no neuter noun, unless it is joined to every gender, as *felix*.

## CHAPTER III — Nouns ending in mutes

Two mutes remain, the letters *c* and *t*. A nominative ending in *c* is masculine in *alec*, and neuter in *lac*. A nominative ending in *t* is neuter in *caput, sinciput, semicaput*.

## CHAPTER IV — The ending and declension of neuter nouns

Neuter nouns ending in the syllable *-um*, such as *templum*, are declined as follows:

Singular: nominative *hoc templum*; genitive *hujus templi*; dative *huic templo*; accusative *hoc templum*; vocative *o templum*; ablative *ab hoc templo*.

Plural: nominative *haec templa*; genitive *horum templorum*; dative *his templis*; accusative *haec templa*; vocative *o templa*; ablative *ab his templis*.

All the following proceed according to the same declension: *telum, tectum, scamnum, bellum, monstrum, portentum, oppidum, carpentum, venenum, donum, bonum, malum, magnum, pessimum, parvum, frumentum, medicamentum, membrum, forum, metrum, porrum, tignum, plaustrum, claustrum, instrumentum, olivetum, vinetum, palmetum, quercetum, esculetum, lauretum, argumentum, sacrum, testamentum, jugerum, vinum*, and *cicera*. At present, *vinum* is used only in the singular, for poets have used *vina*.

Likewise *oleum, hordeum, triticum, ferrum, viscum, aurum, argentum, plumbum, stamnum, vitrum, electrum*, and similar words that are reckoned by weight or measure belong to this form.

Neuter nouns ending in *-ium* are written with two *i*’s in the genitive: *hoc ingenium, hujus ingenii*; likewise *imperium, imperii; scrinium, scrinii; capitolium, capitolii; tentorium, tentorii; armarium, armarii; solarium, solarii; tectorium, tectorii; armamentarium, armamentarii; spatium, spatii; sacrarium, sacrarii; horarium, horarii; salarium, salarii; viridarium, viridarii; pomoerium, pomoerii; sacrificium, sacrificii; folium, folii; solium, solii; testimonium, testimonii; rosarium, rosarii; aviarium, aviarii; augurium, augurii; auspicium, auspicii; exitium, exitii; exsilium, exsilii; prodigium, prodigii; auxilium, auxilii; praesidium, praesidii; atrium, atrii; aucupium, aucupii; adjutorium, adjutorii; mancipium, mancipii; dolium, dolii*.

There is another neuter form ending in *-us*, namely *hoc pecus* (“cattle”):

Singular: nominative *hoc pecus*; genitive *hujus pecoris*; dative *huic pecori*; accusative *hoc pecus*; vocative *o pecus*; ablative *ab hoc pecore*.

Plural: nominative *haec pecora*; genitive *horum pecorum*; dative *his pecoribus*; accusative *haec pecora*; vocative *o pecora*; ablative *ab his pecoribus*.

According to this pattern we decline *ulcus, ulcera; facinus, facinora; vellus, vellera; viscus, viscera; rus, rura; jus, jura; nemus, nemora; tergus, tergora; pectus, pectora; genus, genera; pondus, pondera; corpus, corpora; decus, decora; funus, funera; fenus, fenora; olus, olera; littus, littora; opus, opera; rudus, rudera; tus, tura; tempus, tempora; foedus, foedera; stercus, stercora; onus, onera; latus, latera*.

There is another neuter species containing nouns ending in *-ur*, such as *hoc murmur*:

Singular: nominative *hoc murmur*; genitive *hujus murmuris*; dative *huic murmuri*; accusative *hoc murmur*; vocative *o murmur*; ablative *ab hoc murmure*.

Plural: nominative *haec murmura*; genitive *horum murmurum*; dative *his murmuribus*; accusative *haec murmura*; vocative *o murmura*; ablative *ab his murmuribus*.

According to this pattern you will decline *ebur, ebora; femur, femora; sulfur, sulfura; fulgur, fulgura*. Few nouns of this kind are found, since few neuters end in *-or*. One is *marmor*:

Singular: nominative *marmor*; genitive *marmoris*; dative *marmori*; accusative *marmor*; vocative *o marmor*; ablative *ab hoc marmore*.

Plural: nominative *marmora*; genitive *marmorum*; dative *marmoribus*; accusative *marmora*; vocative *o marmora*; ablative *ab his marmoribus*.

Likewise *aequor, aequora; cor, corda*.

Another neuter species contains nouns ending in the syllable *-ar*, such as *far*:

Singular: nominative *hoc far*; genitive *hujus farris*; dative *huic farri*; accusative *hoc far*; vocative *o far*; ablative *ab hoc farre*.

In the plural it has only three cases: nominative *haec farra*, accusative *haec farra*, and vocative *o farra*. Thus it has no genitive, dative, or ablative. For this reason such nouns are called **τρίπτωτα** (*tríptōta*, “three-case nouns”) in the plural. Thus, in the case of *jura*, we do not say *horum jurium* in the genitive or *his juribus* in the dative; nor *aerum, aeribus*; nor *mellum, mellibus*. There are few such words. Likewise we cannot say *horum farrum* in the genitive or *his farribus* in the dative.

This form is therefore declined only in the singular: *hoc nectar, nectaris; laser, laseris*; and *instar*, meaning “likeness.” The latter has only three cases—nominative, accusative, and vocative—and exists only in the singular.

Another neuter species contains all nouns ending in *-er*, but only in the singular:

*N. hoc piper; G. hujus piperis; D. huic piperi; A. hoc piper; V. o piper; A. ab hoc pipere.*

According to this form, and only in the singular, you will decline *ver*:

*N. hoc ver; G. hujus veris; D. huic veri; A. hoc ver; V. o ver; A. ab hoc vere.*

Likewise you will decline *siler*, as Virgil says:

> Tender siler  
> (*Georgics* 2.13)

You will also decline *juger*, but it has a plural, *juger, jugera*, according to the ancients, who used *jugerum*. Likewise *uber, ubera; tuber, tubera*. As I have said, there are few nouns of this kind.

Another species ends in *-os*, such as *os, ora* (“mouth”), from which comes *osculum* (“little mouth”). In the latter word the vowel is long; in *ossa* (“bones”) it is short. It is declined in the singular as follows:

*N. hoc os; G. hujus ossis; D. huic ossi; A. hoc os; V. o os; A. ab hoc osse.*

Plural:

*N. haec ossa; G. horum ossium; D. his ossibus; A. haec ossa; V. o ossa; A. ab his ossibus.*

Another neuter species contains nouns ending in *-e*, such as *monile*:

Singular: nominative *hoc monile*; genitive *hujus monilis*; dative *huic monili*; accusative *hoc monile*; vocative *o monile*; ablative *ab hoc monili*.

Plural: nominative *haec monilia*; genitive *horum monilium*; dative *his monilibus*; accusative *haec monilia*; vocative *o monilia*; ablative *ab his monilibus*.

Similarly decline *sedile, sedilia; praesepe, praesepia; collare, collaria; ducale, ducalia; molle, mollia; grave, gravia; vile, vilia; mite, mitia; suave, suavia; vitale, vitalia; morale, moralia; lene, lenia; leva, levia; ancile, ancilia*. Of the last Virgil says:

> And he carried the left-hand sacred shield  
> (*Aeneid* 7.188)

Also *facile, facilia; nobile, nobilia; agile, agilia; mare, maria*. But *mare* has only three plural cases: nominative, accusative, and vocative. It has no genitive, dative, or ablative; for we do not say *horum marium* in the genitive, *his maribus* in the dative, or *ab his maribus* in the ablative. Other similar nouns are declined according to this form.

In this rule the ablative ends in *-i*, not *-e*, because the neuter gender never has four identical cases. It does not therefore form *hoc monile* in the nominative, *hoc monile* in the accusative, *o monile* in the vocative, and *ab hoc monile* in the ablative, but rather *ab hoc monili*. Hence Virgil:

> From the stone-strewn couch  
> (*Georgics* 3.230)

That is, *ab hoc cubili*. Likewise:

> The sacred rite is performed upon the sea  
> (*Aeneid* 3.73)

And:

> The father urges him to go by sea  
> (*Aeneid* 3.144)

Likewise:

> From slender osier  
> (*Georgics* 3.166)

And:

> With cruel wound  
> (*Eclogue* 5.20)

And:

> With deadly wound  
> (*Aeneid* 9.580)

And:

> They flash from the sweet mouth  
> (*Aeneid* 12.802)

Similarly, when we say “born of noble stock,” we say *nobili genere natus*, not *nobile genere natus*. Thus, in a neuter noun whose singular nominative ends in *e*, you must observe as a perpetual rule that the ablative ends in *i*.

Another neuter species contains nouns ending in *-al*, such as *animal*:

*N. hoc animal; G. hujus animalis; D. huic animali; A. hoc animal; V. o animal; A. ab hoc animali.*

Plural:

*N. haec animalia; G. horum animalium; D. his animalibus; A. haec animalia; V. o animalia; A. ab his animalibus.*

According to this form you will decline *tribunal, tribunalia* and *lupercal, lupercalia*. These are sacred things belonging to the spirit called Pan. Thus Virgil speaks of the place itself:

> And he points out the Lupercal beneath the chilly rock  
> (*Aeneid* 8.343)

Another neuter species contains nouns ending in *-el*, such as *mel*:

*N. hoc mel; G. hujus mellis; D. huic melli; A. hoc mel; V. o mel; A. ab hoc melle.*

Likewise decline *fel*:

*N. hoc fel; G. hujus fellis; D. huic felli; A. hoc fel; V. o fel; A. ab hoc felle.*

But in the plural they proceed only through three cases: nominative, accusative, and vocative.

Another neuter species contains nouns ending in the syllable *-en*:

*N. hoc crimen; G. hujus criminis; D. huic crimini; A. hoc crimen; V. o crimen; A. ab hoc crimine.*

Plural:

*N. haec crimina; G. horum criminum; D. his criminibus; A. haec crimina; V. o crimina; A. ab his criminibus.*

According to this rule you will decline *carmen, carminis; numen, numinis; flamen, flaminis; agmen, agminis; acumen, acuminis; gramen, graminis; flumen, fluminis; stramen, straminis; lumen, luminis; semen, seminis; liquamen, liquaminis; fulmen, fulminis; rumen, ruminis; bitumen, bituminis; gluten, glutinis; legumen, leguminis; fundamen, fundaminis; tegimen, tegiminis; munimen, muniminis; levamen, levaminis; specimen, speciminis*. But *specimen* does not admit a plural. Likewise *subtegimen, subtegiminis*.

Another neuter species consists of **ἄπτωτα**, that is, indeclinable nouns, such as *genu*:

Singular: nominative *hoc genu*; genitive *hujus genu*; dative *huic genu*; accusative *hoc genu*; vocative *o genu*; ablative *ab hoc genu*.

Plural: nominative *haec genua*; genitive *horum genuum*; dative *his genibus*; accusative *haec genua*; vocative *o genua*; ablative *ab his genibus*.

According to this form also decline *cornu*: as stated above, *cornu, cornua*; and *veru, verua*, which are the iron spits of butchers. Virgil refers to them:

> And they fix the trembling spits  
> (*Aeneid* 1.212)

Also *tonitru, tonitrua*. The declension of such nouns is found very rarely.

There is another neuter species, discussed above, consisting of nouns ending in the two mutes *c* and *t*: *caput, sinciput, lac,* and *alec*. These two do not admit a plural.

The neuter gender also ends in *a*, but in Greek nouns: *thema, themata; toreuma, τορεύματα [toreumata]; schema, schemata; emblema, emblemata; theorema, theoremata; boethema, boethemata*, and others.

Let us also remember that individual letters, both Greek and Latin, are neuter. We say *unum alpha, unum beta, unum gamma* (“one alpha, one beta, one gamma”), and likewise of the other letters. In the plural: *duo alpha, duo beta, duo gamma*; likewise *tria alpha, tria beta, tria gamma*. Hence the expression **τρία κάππα κάκιστα** (*tría káppa kákista*), that is, “three very bad kappas,” referring to Cornelius Sulla, Cornelius Cinna, and Cornelius Lentulus. For these men are designated in the Sibylline Books by three letters.

There is also one neuter noun ending in *a*, namely the river *Turia*, as we said above.

## CHAPTER V — The ending and declension of common-gender nouns

Common gender ends in *-a*, as *advena*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec advena* (“this male or female newcomer”); genitive *hujus advenae*; dative *huic advenae*; accusative *hunc et hanc advenam*; vocative *o advena*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac advena*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae advenae*; genitive *horum et harum advenarum*; dative *his advenis*; accusative *hos et has advenas*; vocative *o advenae*; ablative *ab his advenis*.

According to this form you will decline *Trojugena, indigena, incola, agricola, convena, coelicola, sacricola, publicola, terricola, orbicola, plebicola, Numida, Dalmata, ruricola, lucifuga, Persa, Romulida*, and so forth.

In the nominative, *e* and *i* do not have common gender; but *o* does, as *latro*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec latro*; genitive *hujus latronis*; dative *huic latroni*; accusative *hunc et hanc latronem*; vocative *o latro*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac latrone*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae latrones*; genitive *horum et harum latronum*; dative *his latronibus*; accusative *hos et has latrones*; vocative *o latrones*; ablative *ab his latronibus*.

According to this form decline *homo, ganeo, degulo, caupo, fullo, nemo, helluo*, also called *gluto*, and others. It has no common-gender form ending in *u*.

In the nominative common gender also ends in the syllable *-es*, as *comes*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec comes*; genitive *hujus comitis*; dative *huic comiti*; accusative *hunc et hanc comitem*; vocative *o comes*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac comite*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae comites*; genitive *horum et harum comitum*; dative *his comitibus*; accusative *hos et has comites*; vocative *o comites*; ablative *ab his comitibus*.

Decline similar nouns according to this form: *sospes, locuples, hospes*—although Virgil used *hospitam*, “hospitable,” in *Hospita tellus* (“hospitable land,” *Aeneid* 3.539)—*miles, veles*, that is, a lightly armed soldier, *interpres, ales, praepes, praes*, that is, a guarantor, *satelles, deses, praeses, dives, haeres, coeles, coelites*, those who make their way to heaven, and *indiges, indigetis*, and so forth.

It ends in *-is*, as *similis*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec similis*; genitive *hujus similis*; dative *huic simili*; accusative *hunc et hanc similem*; vocative *o similis*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac simili*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae similes*; genitive *horum et harum similium*; dative *his similibus*; accusative *hos et has similes*; vocative *o similes*; ablative *ab his similibus*.

According to this form are declined *agilis, facilis, fragilis, viridis, mobilis, humilis, mitis, lenis, mollis, civis, testis, hostis, tristis, fortis, suavis, frugalis, crudelis, inanis, gracilis, immanis*, and so forth.

It ends in *-os*, as *sacerdos*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec sacerdos*; genitive *hujus sacerdotis*; dative *huic sacerdoti*; accusative *hunc et hanc sacerdotem*; vocative *o sacerdos*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac sacerdote*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae sacerdotes*; genitive *horum et harum sacerdotum*; dative *his sacerdotibus*; accusative *hos et has sacerdotes*; vocative *o sacerdotes*; ablative *ab his sacerdotibus*.

According to this form are declined *custos, impos, compos, nepos*.

It also ends in *-us*, as *sus*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec sus*; genitive *hujus suis*; dative *huic sui*; accusative *hunc et hanc suem*; vocative *o sus*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac sue*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae sues*; genitive *horum et harum suum*; dative *his suibus*; accusative *hos et has sues*; vocative *o sues*; ablative *ab his suibus*.

It also ends in *-er*, as *pauper*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec pauper*; genitive *hujus pauperis*; dative *huic pauperi*; accusative *hunc et hanc pauperem*; vocative *o pauper*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac paupere*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae pauperes*; genitive *horum et harum pauperum*; dative *his pauperibus*; accusative *hos et has pauperes*; vocative *o pauperes*; ablative *ab his pauperibus*.

According to this form are also declined *acer, alacer*, that is, “joyful.”

Common gender ends in *-ex*, as *opifex*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec opifex*; genitive *hujus opificis*; dative *huic opifici*; accusative *hunc et hanc opificem*; vocative *o opifex*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac opifice*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae opifices*; genitive *horum et harum opificum*; dative *his opificibus*; accusative *hos et has opifices*; vocative *o opifices*; ablative *ab his opificibus*.

According to this form decline *aurifex, artifex, judex, carnifex, index, vindex, auspex, aruspex, signifex*, and others.

Common gender ends in the syllable *-eps*, as *princeps*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec princeps*; genitive *hujus principis*; dative *huic principi*; accusative *hunc et hanc principem*; vocative *o princeps*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac principe*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae principes*; genitive *horum et harum principum*; dative *his principibus*; accusative *hos et has principes*; vocative *o principes*; ablative *ab his principibus*.

*Manceps, particeps, municeps* are declined in the same way.

But *anceps, biceps, triceps, quadriceps, multiceps,* and *praeceps*—these six nouns—contrary to the preceding rule, send the singular genitive into the syllable *-tis*, not *-pis*: *anceps, ancipitis; biceps, bicipitis; triceps, tricipitis; quadriceps, quadricipitis; multiceps, multicipitis; praeceps, praecipitis*. They end in *-tis*, rather than *-pis* as in *principis* and *mancipis*, because they derive from the meaning of *caput* (“head”), whereas the preceding words derive from the meaning of “taking.” *Princeps* means “one who takes first,” and *manceps* “one who takes with the hand.” *Anceps* means one whose head is doubtful or inclined in either direction.

Common gender ends in the syllable *-junx*, as *conjunx*: nominative *hic et haec conjunx*. It ends in *-ux*, as *hic et haec dux, redux*. It ends in *-eps*, which returns to every gender. It ends in *-ebs*, as *caelebs*.

A *caelebs* is a man who has no wife, or a woman who has no husband: such are the divinities in heaven who are without a spouse, if we do not take the *agapetae* (“beloved companions”) into account [Note: [Col. 1391] May this statement be far from Augustine].

Singular: nominative *hic et haec caelebs*; genitive *hujus caelibis*; dative *huic caelibi*; accusative *hunc et hanc caelibem*; vocative *o caelebs*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac caelibe*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae caelibes*; genitive *horum et harum caelibum*; dative *his caelibibus*; accusative *hos et has caelibes*; vocative *o caelibes*; ablative *ab his caelibibus*.

It also ends in *-yx*, as *Phryx*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec Phryx*; genitive *hujus Phrygis*; dative *huic Phrygi*; accusative *hunc et hanc Phrygem*; vocative *o Phryx*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac Phryge*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae Phryges*; genitive *horum et harum Phrygum*; dative *his Phrygibus*; accusative *hos et has Phryges*; vocative *o Phryges*; ablative *ab his Phrygibus*.

It also ends in *-us*, as *Ligus*. Like *Phryx*, this is a geographic name:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec Ligus*; genitive *hujus Liguris*; dative *huic Liguri*; accusative *hunc et hanc Ligurem*; vocative *o Ligus*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac Ligure*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae Ligures*; genitive *horum et harum Ligurum*; dative *his Liguribus*; accusative *hos et has Ligures*; vocative *o Ligures*; ablative *ab his Liguribus*.

Common gender ends in *-il*, as *vigil*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec vigil*; genitive *hujus vigilis*; dative *huic vigili*; accusative *hunc et hanc vigilem*; vocative *o vigil*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac vigile*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae vigiles*; genitive *horum et harum vigilum*; dative *his vigilibus*; accusative *hos et has vigiles*; vocative *o vigiles*; ablative *ab his vigilibus*.

According to this rule decline *hic et haec pugil*.

It ends in *-ul*, as *exsul*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec exsul*; genitive *hujus exsulis*; dative *huic exsuli*; accusative *hunc et hanc exsulem*; vocative *o exsul*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac exsule*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae exsules*; genitive *horum et harum exsulum*; dative *his exsulibus*; accusative *hos et has exsules*; vocative *o exsules*; ablative *ab his exsulibus*.

According to this form decline *praesul*: *hic et haec praesul*, for it is masculine, like *consul*.

It ends in *-ur*, as *fur*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec fur*; genitive *hujus furis*; dative *huic furi*; accusative *hunc et hanc furem*; vocative *o fur*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac fure*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae fures*; genitive *horum et harum furum*; dative *his furibus*; accusative *hos et has fures*; vocative *o fures*; ablative *ab his furibus*.

According to this form decline *augur*: *hic et haec augur*.

Common gender ends in *-or*, as *major, memor*. But *memor*, according to another rule, does not admit the neuter in *-jus*, whereas *major* admits the neuter *majus*.

Singular: nominative *hic et haec memor*; genitive *hujus memoris*; dative *huic memori*; accusative *hunc et hanc memorem*; vocative *o memor*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac memore*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae memores*; genitive *horum et harum memorum*; dative *his memoribus*; accusative *hos et has memores*; vocative *o memores*; ablative *ab his memoribus*.

It also admits a neuter, but not according to the rule of every gender, as *hoc memor*. Hence Virgil:

> Then, if some divinity holds lovers’ cares under an unequal covenant,  
> she prays to it as just and mindful.  
> (*Aeneid* 4.520–521)

It does not admit a plural, and therefore does not belong to every gender. For we do not say *memora* or *memoria numina* (“mindful divinities”).

Likewise decline *auctor* in the singular nominative, *hic et haec auctor*, as Juno says:

> I am the author of the attempt  
> (*Aeneid* 12.159)

Plural: *hi et hae auctores*.

## CHAPTER VI — The ending and declension of nouns of every gender

Every gender ends in *-ax, -ex, -ix, -ox, -ux, -ans, -ens, -ons, -ar* [Note: [Col. 1392] All the editions omit the word *ons*, although it seems necessary from the examples given below. They then print *ars* instead of *ar*, which we have restored as more suitable to the following examples. M.], *-ers, -ors, -us,* and *-es*.

In *-ax*, as *pertinax*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc pertinax*; genitive *hujus pertinacis*; dative *huic pertinaci*; accusative *hunc et hanc pertinacem*, and *hoc pertinax*; vocative *o pertinax*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc pertinaci*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae pertinaces*, and *haec pertinacia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum pertinacium*; dative *his pertinacibus*; accusative *hos et has pertinaces*, and *haec pertinacia*; vocative *o pertinaces*, and *o pertinacia*; ablative *ab his pertinacibus*.

According to this form decline *efficax, tenax, pervicax, dicax, sequax, rapax, mordax, capax, furax, emax, fallax, mendax, nugax, vivax*. All these and similar words send the singular ablative into *-i*.

Every gender also ends in *-ex*, according to the order of the rules set out above, as *simplex*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc simplex*; genitive *hujus simplicis*; dative *huic simplici*; accusative *hunc et hanc simplicem*, and *hoc simplex*; vocative *o simplex*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc simplici*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae simplices*, and *haec simplicia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum simplicium*; dative *his simplicibus*; accusative *hos et has simplices*, and *haec simplicia*; vocative *o simplices*, and *o simplicia*; ablative *ab his simplicibus*.

According to this form are declined *duplex, triplex, quadruplex, quintuplex, sextuplex, septuplex*, excluding the *m*, since *septemplex* is also Latin and is declined as above.

According to the rule in *-ix*, as *felix*, which is declined as follows:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc felix*; genitive *hujus felicis*; dative *huic felici*; accusative *hunc et hanc felicem*, and *hoc felix*; vocative *o felix*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc felici*. This is according to the sound of the neuter gender; with proper names, which end in *e*, one says *ab hoc felice*, and it is masculine.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae felices*, and *haec felicia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum felicium*; dative *his felicibus*; accusative *hos et has felices*, and *haec felicia*; vocative *o felices* and *o felicia*; ablative *ab his felicibus*.

According to this rule *pernix* is declined, meaning “swift.”

According to the rule in *-ox*, as *ferox*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc ferox*; genitive *hujus ferocis*; dative *huic feroci*; accusative *hunc et hanc ferocem*, and *hoc ferox*; vocative *o ferox*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc feroci*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae feroces*, and *haec ferocia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum ferocium*; dative *his ferocibus*; accusative *hos et has feroces*, and *haec ferocia*; vocative *o feroces*, and *o ferocia*; ablative *ab his ferocibus*.

According to this form *atrox* and *velox* are declined.

There is one noun according to the rule in *-ux*: *trux*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc trux*; genitive *hujus trucis*; dative *huic truci*; accusative *hunc et hanc trucem*, and *hoc trux*; vocative *o trux*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc truci*, according to the sound of the neuter gender.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae truces*, and *haec trucia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum trucium*; dative *his trucibus*; accusative *hos et has truces*, and *haec trucia*; vocative *o truces* and *o trucia*; ablative *ab his trucibus*.

According to the rule in *-ans*, as *praestans*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc praestans*; genitive *hujus praestantis*; dative *huic praestanti*; accusative *hunc et hanc praestantem*, and *hoc praestans*; vocative *o praestans*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc praestanti*, according to the sound of the neuter gender.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae praestantes*, and *haec praestantia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum praestantium*; dative *his praestantibus*; accusative *hos et has praestantes*, and *haec praestantia*; vocative *o praestantes*, and *o praestantia*; ablative *ab his praestantibus*.

According to this form are declined *amans, clamans, cantans, luctans, constans, prostans, regnans, pugnans, mirans, minans, miserans, aestuans, versans*, and similar words.

According to the rule in *-ens*, as *amens*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc amens*; genitive *hujus amentis*; dative *huic amenti*; accusative *hunc et hanc amentem*, and *hoc amens*; vocative *o amens*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc amenti*, likewise according to the sound of the neuter gender.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae amentes*, and *haec amentia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum amentium*; dative *his amentibus*; accusative *hos et has amentes*, and *haec amentia*; vocative *o amentes* and *o amentia*; ablative *ab his amentibus*.

According to this form are declined *demens, potens, impotens, praepotens, prudens, imprudens, pudens, impudens, frequens, infrequens, sedens, haerens, moriens, moerens, tenens, egens, ferens, cedens, saeviens, serviens, sapiens, incipiens, decipiens*, and similar words.

According to the rule in *-ons*, as *sons*, meaning “guilty”:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc sons*; genitive *hujus sontis*; dative *huic sonti*; accusative *hunc et hanc sontem*, and *hoc sons*; vocative *o sons*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc sonti*, according to the sound of the neuter gender.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae sontes*, and *haec sontia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum sontium*; dative *his sontibus*; accusative *hos et has sontes*, and *haec sontia*; vocative *o sontes* and *o sontia*; ablative *ab his sontibus*.

According to this rule *insons* is declined, that is, “innocent.” These two alone belong to every gender.

According to the rule in *-ar*, as *par*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc par*; genitive *hujus paris*; dative *huic pari*; accusative *hunc et hanc parem*, and *hoc par*; vocative *o par*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc pari*, according to the sound of the neuter gender.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae pares*, and *haec paria*; genitive *horum et harum et horum parium*; dative *his paribus*; accusative *hos et has pares*, and *haec paria*; vocative *o pares* and *o paria*; ablative *ab his paribus*.

According to this form are declined *impar* and *suppar*. These three alone belong to every gender.

According to the rule in *-ers*, as *iners*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc iners*; genitive *hujus inertis*; dative *huic inerti*; accusative *hunc et hanc inertem*, and *hoc iners*; vocative *o iners*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc inerti*.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae inertes*, and *haec inertia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum inertium*; dative *his inertibus*; accusative *hos et has inertes*, and *haec inertia*; vocative *o inertes* and *o inertia*; ablative *ab his inertibus*.

According to the rule in *-ors*, as *vecors*:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc vecors*; genitive *hujus vecordis*; dative *huic vecordi*; accusative *hunc et hanc vecordem*, and *hoc vecors*; vocative *o vecors*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc vecordi*, according to the neuter gender.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae vecordes*, and *haec vecordia*; genitive *horum et harum et horum vecordium*; dative *his vecordibus*; accusative *hos et has vecordes*, and *haec vecordia*; vocative *o vecordes* and *o vecordia*; ablative *ab his vecordibus*.

According to this rule are declined *excors, concors, discors, dissors*. But *consors* and *dissors*—that is, these two—have *-tis* in the singular genitive: *consortis, dissortis*. *Dissors* means “of a different lot.”

According to the rule in *-us*, as *vetus*, it is declined as follows:

Singular: nominative *hic et haec et hoc vetus*; genitive *hujus veteris*; dative *huic veteri*; accusative *hunc et hanc veterem*, and *hoc vetus*; vocative *o vetus*; ablative *ab hoc et ab hac et ab hoc veteri*, according to the sound of the neuter gender.

Plural: nominative *hi et hae veteres*, and *haec vetera*; genitive *horum et harum et horum veterum*; dative *his veteribus*; accusative *hos et has veteres*, and *haec vetera*; vocative *o veteres* and *o vetera*; ablative *ab his veteribus*.

This is the only noun ending in *-us* that belongs to every gender.

In *-es*, as *teres*, meaning “round”: it is declined *hic et haec et hoc teres*. *Teres* is said to derive from *terere* (“to rub smooth”).

According to the rule of the **ἄπτωτα** (*áptōta*, indeclinables) is *nequam*; for all its cases in every gender are declined with the same sound.

# CHAPTER VII—On Nouns of the Epicene Gender, and the Difference of This Gender from the Common Gender

The epicene gender is that in which sex is understood under a single article; for example, *hic passer* (“this sparrow”): although it is spoken with the single article *hic*, the female is also included. It is declined as follows:

N. *hic passer*; G. *huius passeris*; D. *huic passeri*; A. *hunc passerem*; V. *o passer*; A. *ab hoc passere*. In the plural: N. *hi passeres*; G. *horum passerum*; D. *his passeribus*; A. *hos passeres*; V. *o passeres*; A. *ab his passeribus*.

Likewise, *haec aquila* (“this eagle”), under the single article *haec*, also includes the male. So too with *haec tigris* (“this tiger”), under which the male is also understood. Likewise, with *haec hirundo* (“this swallow”), the male is also understood; with *hic struthio* (“this ostrich”), the female is understood; and similarly with *sorex* (“shrew”), *stellio* (“newt”), and *musca* (“fly”).

Thus the difference between the common and epicene genders is this: in the common gender there are both human beings and animals, whereas in the epicene there are animals only. In the common gender both articles—namely, *hic* and *haec*—are used with the noun, as in *hic et haec canis* (“this male dog” and “this female dog”). In the epicene, however, a feminine noun is joined to a single masculine article; for example, when I say *hic passer*, under the very article pronounced *hic*, the female is also understood.

The same applies to the neuter-gender article, as in *hoc pecus* (“this animal”): under the article pronounced *hoc*, the female is also understood, as Virgil says, *Lenta salix feto pecori* (“The pliant willow for the pregnant flock,” *Eclogue* 3.83). Although *pecus* is neuter, the feminine gender is also heard there when he says *feto pecori*, that is, “for the pregnant [female animal].”

# CHAPTER VIII—On Nouns Used Only in the Singular or Only in the Plural

We must now discuss nouns that are either used only in the singular number or only in the plural, such as *cancelli* (“latticework”), *manes* (“spirits of the dead”), and *penates* (“household gods”).

Those used only in the feminine plural include *thermae* (“baths”), *exsequiae* (“funeral rites”), *insidiae* (“ambush”), *divitiae* (“riches”), and *nundinae* (“market days”). Among names of cities are *Amyclae*, *Thenae*, *Athenae*, *Syracusae*, *Thebae*, *Tubunae*, *Saldae*, *Abiturae*, *Macomades*, *Cales*, *Carreasi*, *Relares*, and *Furnitum*—places which are called *turni*—and others of the same kind.

Those used only in the neuter singular include *aurum* (“gold”), *argentum* (“silver”), *plumbum* (“lead”), *stannum* (“tin”), *piper* (“pepper”), *triticum* (“wheat”), *oleum* (“oil”), *hordeum* (“barley”), and *vinum* (“wine”). Although Virgil used *vina* (“wines,” *Georgics* 2.97), and Cicero more rarely allowed the plural through poetic license, as in *Serite hordea campis* (“Sow barley in the fields,” *ibid.* 1.210), only the nominative is declined.

Those used only in the neuter plural include *castra* (“camp”), *moenia* (“walls”), *arma* (“arms”), and *exta*, that is, “entrails.” *Bactra* is also plural; it is a city of Parthia. Thus this city too is neuter in gender and plural only in number.

There are, moreover, nouns expressed in two parts, such as *tribunus militum* (“military tribune”), *praefectus urbis* (“prefect of the city”), *praefectus fundis* (“prefect of estates”), *praefectus annonae* (“prefect of the grain supply”), *praefectus vigilibus* (“prefect of the watch”), *plebiscitum* (“plebiscite”), and *senatus consultum* (“decree of the Senate”). In these expressions one part is declined and the other is not.

For example, in *praefectus vigilibus*, the nominative itself is inflected through the cases: *praefectus, praefecti, praefecto, praefectum, praefecte, a praefecto*. *Vigilibus* remains as it is and is not inflected.

Likewise, *senatus consultum*: *hoc consultum, huius consulti, huic consulto, hoc consultum, o consultum, ab hoc consulto*. *Senatus* is a genitive and is not inflected here.

We have explained the noun more fully than was appropriate for a beginner. We must now discuss the pronoun, which is the second of the eight parts of speech.

# CHAPTER IX—On the Pronoun

The pronoun is so called because it performs the function of a noun, as in *ille* (“that one”), *iste* (“that one of yours”), and *ipse* (“himself”). For just as, by speaking a noun, we identify a person—for example, *Virgilius* (“Virgil”)—so pronouns properly have the same force when, with the noun understood, we say, “This one did it” or “That one did it.”

Pronouns are either definite, indefinite, or less than definite.

Definite pronouns are those that identify a definite person, such as *ego* (“I”).

Indefinite pronouns include *quis* (“who”), *quisque* (“each”), *quicumque* (“whoever”), *quaecumque* (“whatever”), *qui* (“who”), *aliqui* (“some”), *quae* (“which”), and *aliquae* (“some,” feminine).

Pronouns are called less than definite when they do not identify a person so completely that they require no demonstrator, as happens when we say *ego* (“I”). For *tu* (“you”) itself is not fully definite unless you point your finger toward the person intended.

These, then, should be called less than definite. They have a certain indication, but not a complete signification, unlike *ego*. Suppose, for example, that there is a crowd. The word *tu* is not spoken with the same distinctness within the crowd as *ego* is spoken when one person among the crowd says it. Rather, when we wish to identify one person from among many, we either add a noun or point with a finger, so that it becomes clearer whom we are addressing.

Therefore *tu*, *ille*, *iste*, and the other pronouns that can define a person only to some extent should be called less than definite. [Col. 1395]

# CHAPTER X—On the Declension of the Pronouns of the First, Second, and Third Persons

The first person is *ego* (“I”). Both in the singular and in the plural, when we say *nos* (“we”), it has no vocative case, because no one calls himself: *o ego*, “O I,” or *o nos*, “O we.” It is therefore declined in the singular as follows:

N. *ego*; G. *mei*; D. *mihi*; A. *me*; A. *a me*.

In the plural:

N. *nos*; G. *nostrum*; D. *nobis*; A. *nos*; A. *a nobis*.

As I said, it has no vocative, either in the singular or in the plural.

The nominative *tu* (“you”) has the following forms: G. *tui*; D. *tibi*; A. *te*; V. *o tu*; A. *a te*.

In the plural: N. *vos*; G. *vestrum*; D. *vobis*; A. *vos*; V. *o vos*; A. *a vobis*.

The first and second persons—that is, *ego* and *tu*—belong to every gender. A man says *ego*, a woman says *ego*, and a slave says *ego*. The same applies to *tu*: we say *tu* to a man, to a woman, and to a slave. In the plural, too, they belong to every gender, as with *nos* and *vos*.

The declension of the third person is as follows.

In the masculine gender, singular number:

N. *ille*; G. *illius*; D. *illi*; A. *illum*; V. *o ille*; A. *ab illo*.

In the plural:

N. *illi*; G. *illorum*; D. *illis*; A. *illos*; V. *o illi*; A. *ab illis*.

In the feminine gender:

N. *illa*; G. *illius*; D. *illi*; A. *illam*; V. *o illa*; A. *ab illa*.

In the plural:

N. *illae*; G. *illarum*; D. *illis*; A. *illas*; V. *o illae*; A. *ab illis*.

In the neuter gender, singular number:

N. *illud*; G. *illius*; D. *illi*; A. *illud*; V. *o illud*; A. *ab illo*.

In the plural:

N. *illa*; G. *illorum*; D. *illis*; A. *illa*; V. *o illa*; A. *ab illis*.

You will decline *iste* (“that one”) and likewise *ipse* (“himself”) according to the preceding pattern, both with respect to genders and with respect to numbers.

There is, however, a question concerning the pronoun *ipse*: why, when in the neuter gender we say *istud* and *illud*, do we say *ipsum*, as Virgil says, *Atque ipsum corpus amici* (“And the very body of his friend,” *Aeneid* 1.490), rather than *ipsud*?

The question is resolved as follows. The ancients more often said *ipsus* in the masculine nominative singular than *ipse*. Attending to this ancient usage, the writers on grammar transferred this pronoun to the pattern of nouns. Thus, just as in nouns we say *justus, justa, justum* (“just,” masculine, feminine, neuter) and *perfectus, perfecta, perfectum* (“perfect”), so this pronoun too is pronounced *ipsus, ipsa, ipsum*, not *ipsud*, as with *istud* and *illud*.

# CHAPTER XI—On the Declension of the Indefinite Pronouns

Masculine:

N. *quis*; G. *cuius*; D. *cui*; A. *quem*; V. *o qui*; A. *a quo*.

In the plural: N. *qui*; G. *quorum*; D. *quis* or *quibus*—as Virgil has, *Quis ante ora patrum* (“To whom before the eyes of [his] fathers,” *ibid.* 99); A. *quos*; V. *o qui*; A. *a quibus*.

Feminine:

N. *quae*; G. *cuius*; D. *cui*; A. *quam*; V. *o quae*; A. *a qua*.

In the plural: N. *quae*; G. *quarum*; D. *quis*; A. *quas*; V. *o quae*; A. *a quibus*.

Neuter:

N. *quod*; G. *cuius*; D. *cui*; A. *quod*; V. *o quod*; A. *a quo*.

In the plural: N. *quae*; G. *quorum*; D. *quis*—although according to present usage we say *quibus*; A. *quae*; V. *o quae*; A. *a quibus*.

The ancients used *quis* as a common-gender form:

N. *hic et haec quis*; G. *huius quis*; D. *huic qui*; A. *hunc et hanc quem*; V. *o quis*; A. *ab hoc et ab hac qui*.

From this comes the ablative ending in *-bus*. The plural ablative *a quis* is derived from the ablative ending in *-o*, just as, in the rule governing ablatives, when the ablative ends in *-o*, it sends the plural dative into *-is*: *a justo, justis* (“from the just man, to the just”); *a docto, doctis* (“from the learned man, to the learned”); *a perfecto, perfectis* (“from the perfect man, to the perfect”); *a fortunato, fortunatis* (“from the fortunate man, to the fortunate”).

Thus, as I said above, the ancients said *hic et haec quis*, and just as in nouns we have *hic et haec similis* (“this similar one”), *hic et haec agilis* (“this agile one”), and *hic et haec facilis* (“this easy one”), so in pronouns we have *hic et haec quis*, *ab hoc et ab hac qui*.

Therefore, when Virgil was speaking of Camilla’s companion, he said, *Quicum partiri curas* (“With whom you share your cares,” *Aeneid* 11.822), that is, *cum qua partiri curas* (“with whom you share your cares”).

There are also other indefinite pronouns that are interrogative and are declined as follows:

Masculine:

N. *uter*; G. *utrius*; D. *utri*; A. *utrum*; V. *o uter*; A. *ab utro*.

In the plural: N. *utri*; G. *utrorum*; D. *utris*; A. *utros*; V. *o utri*; A. *ab utris*.

When the syllable *-que* is added in composition, it produces *uterque* (“each of the two,” “both”) and signifies both. It nevertheless has a singular form but a dual meaning. For when Virgil said:

> *Constitit in digitos extemplo arrectus uterque;*  
> (“At once each of the two stood erect on his toes,” *ibid.* 5.426),

two persons are signified by *uterque*. But when he used *arrectus* (“erect,” singular), he did not wish the plural to be expected, as though the form were the plural *utrique*.

The difference is this: although *uterque* signifies two, it signifies simply two; *utrique* also signifies two, but in such a way that within each of the two there may be many. If you say *utrique exercitus* (“both armies”), I signify two, but I wish a multitude to be understood within each one.

These forms are distinct, but they are also confused by authoritative usage. For when Virgil says, *Super utraque quassat tempora* (“He shakes both temples above,” *ibid.* 855), he confused them. He ought to have said *super utrumque tempus* (“above each of the two temples”), for he was speaking of only two temples, for which the accusative *utrumque tempus* was sufficient; he should have said, *utrumque quassat tempus* (“he shakes each temple”).

Just as we declined the masculine pronoun, so we will decline the feminine:

*utra mulier* (“which of the two women”); *utrius mulieris*; *utri mulieri*; *utram mulierem*; *o utra mulier*; *ab hac utra muliere*.

In the plural: N. *utrae mulieres*; G. *utrarum mulierum*; D. *utris mulieribus*; A. *utras mulieres*; V. *o utrae mulieres*; A. *ab his utris mulieribus*.

Likewise in the neuter: *utrum mancipium* (“which of the two slaves”); *utrius mancipii*; *utri mancipio*; *utrum mancipium*; *o utrum mancipium*; *ab hoc utro mancipio*.

In the plural: N. *utra mancipia*; G. *utrorum mancipiorum*; D. *utris mancipiis*; A. *utra mancipia*; V. *o utra mancipia*; A. *ab his utris mancipiis*.

We will decline its opposite, *neuter* (“neither of the two”), in the same way: masculine *neuter*, feminine *neutra*, and neuter *hoc neutrum mancipium*. Hence usage has now taken hold of the form *generis neutri* (“of the neuter gender”), although we ought to say *neutrius*, just as we say *utrius*.

When the conjunctional syllable *-que* is added, the pronoun itself is declined according to the rule stated above: masculine *uterque*, feminine *utraque*, neuter *utrumque*.

In the plural: masculine *utrique*; feminine *utraque*; neuter *utra mancipia*.

There is also another pronoun, *ullus* (“any,” “anyone”):

Masculine: *ullus, ullius, ulli, ullum, o ullus, ab ullo*; in the plural, *ulli, ullorum, ullis, ullos, o ulli, ab ullis*.

Feminine: *ulla, ullius, ulli, ullam, o ulla, ab ulla*; in the plural, *ullae, ullarum, ullis, ullas, o ullae, ab ullis*.

Neuter: *ullum, ullius, ulli, ullum, o ullum, ab ullo*; in the plural, *ulla, ullorum, ullis, ulla, o ulla, ab ullis*.

You will decline *nullus, nulla, nullum* (“no,” “none”) according to this pattern; likewise *alius* (“another”): *huius alius*, *huic alii*; *alter* (“the other of two”): *huius alterius*, *huic alteri*; *totus* (“whole”): *huius totius*, *huic toti*; *solus* (“alone,” “only”): *huius solius*, *huic soli*; and *unus* (“one”): *huius unius*, *huic uni*.

Hence Virgil says:

> *Forsitan huic uni potui succumbere culpae.*  
> (“Perhaps I alone could have yielded to this fault,” *ibid.* 4.19.)

# CHAPTER XII—Pronouns of Quality

There are also pronouns of quality: *hic et haec qualis* (“what sort of man or woman”), *huius qualis*, common in gender; and, in the neuter gender, *hoc quale*, *huius qualis*. In the plural: *haec qualia*, *horum qualium*.

There are also pronouns of quantity, such as *quantus* (“how great”) and *tantus* (“so great”); *quanti* and *tanti*. They are declined like *justus, justi*. In the feminine, *quanta* and *tanta* are declined like *justa*. In the neuter, *quantum* and *tantum* are declined like *justum*.

There is likewise the pronoun *quotus* (“which in number,” “what numbered”), *totus* (“so numbered,” “that many”) in the masculine; *quota*, *tota* in the feminine; and *quotum*, *totum* in the neuter.

In the plural: masculine *quoti, toti*; feminine *quotae, totae*; neuter *quota iugera, quotorum iugerum* (“how many acres, of how many acres”).

There are relative forms that refer back to a question, as in: “Who is he?”—the answer is: “He is that one.” They are declined in the masculine as follows:

*is, eius, ei, eum, o is, ab eo*.

In the plural: *ii, eorum, eis, eos, o ei, ab eis*.

In the feminine: *ea, eius, ei, eam, o ea, ab ea*.

In the neuter: *id, eius, ei, id, o id, ab eo*.

Therefore, when we speak of a journey, one must say *per id iter* (“through that journey”), not *per eum iter*, because *eum*, in the accusative case, is masculine. In the plural: *ea itinera* (“those journeys”), *ab eis itineribus* (“from those journeys”).

Likewise: *per id nostrum* (“through that possession of ours”), *per id tectum* (“through that roof”), *per id caput* (“through that head”), not *per eum*, except when the noun is masculine.

# CHAPTER XIII—On the Verb

We understand verbs in four ways.

First, we use *verba* (“words”) for deceits, when we say, “He gave him words,” that is, “He deceived him.” Hence Terence said, *Cui verba dare difficile est* (“It is difficult to deceive him,” *Andria*, act 1, scene 3, line 6).

Second, we use *verba* for an utterance, as when we say that Cicero “made speeches” (*verba fecisse*) in the Senate-house.

Third, we use *verba* for common sayings, which are called proverbs, as Terence said:

> *Verum illud verbum vulgo est quod dici solet.*  
> (“That saying is truly one commonly used,” *Terence, Andria*, act 2, scene 5, line 15.) [Col. 1397]

Fourth, we call *verba* the forms that proceed through tenses and persons, such as *clamo, clamas, clamat* (“I shout, you shout, he shouts”).

Here too there are three persons: *clamo* (“I shout”), *clamas* (“you shout”), *clamat* (“he shouts”); and the tense is present. Then in the plural: *clamamus* (“we shout”), *clamatis* (“you shout”), *clamant* (“they shout”).

In the imperfect past tense: *clamabam* (“I was shouting”), *clamabas* (“you were shouting”), *clamabat* (“he was shouting”); and in the plural, *clamabamus*, *clamabatis*, *clamabant*.

In the perfect past tense, singular number: *clamavi* (“I shouted”), *clamavisti* (“you shouted”), *clamavit* (“he shouted”).

In the pluperfect past tense, when we signify not only that we did something but also that we did it earlier, we say in the singular: *clamaveram* (“I had shouted”), *clamaveras* (“you had shouted”), *clamaverat* (“he had shouted”); and in the plural: *clamaveramus*, *clamaveratis*, *clamaverant*.

In the future tense, singular number: *clamabo* (“I shall shout”), *clamabis* (“you will shout”), *clamabit* (“he will shout”); *clamabimus* (“we shall shout”), *clamabitis* (“you will shout”), *clamabunt* (“they will shout”).

Up to this point, everything we have said belongs to the indicative mood, which indicates.

The imperative is so called because it has the sound of commanding. This mood does not have a first person, because no one commands himself; rather, one speaks to the second and third persons.

In the singular, to the second person: *clama* (“shout”); to the third: *clamet* (“let him shout”). In the plural, to the second: *clamate* (“shout”); to the third: *clament* (“let them shout”).

In the future tense, to the second person: *clamato* (“you shall shout”); to the third person likewise: *clamato* (“let him shout”). There is a reason why it has the same form in the second and third persons, but it must be passed over for now.

To return to the plural, to the second person: *clamatote* (“you shall shout”); to the third: *clamanto* (“let them shout”).

We call the optative what speaks in the manner of one expressing a wish. In the present tense, singular: *utinam clamarem* (“would that I might shout”), *utinam clamares* (“would that you might shout”), *utinam clamaret* (“would that he might shout”); and in the plural: *utinam clamaremus*, *utinam clamaretis*, *utinam clamarent*.

In the past tense, singular: *utinam clamassem ego* (“would that I had shouted”), *utinam clamasses tu* (“would that you had shouted”), *utinam clamasset ille* (“would that he had shouted”); and in the plural: *utinam clamassemus*, *utinam clamassetis*, *utinam clamassent*.

In the future tense: *utinam clamem ego* (“would that I may shout”), *utinam clames tu* (“would that you may shout”), *utinam clamet ille* (“would that he may shout”); and in the plural: *utinam clamemus*, *clametis*, *clament*.

The subjunctive is so called because it requires something else to complete its meaning. For example, when we say *cum clamem, clames, clamet* (“when I shout, you shout, he shouts”), the sense is suspended and needs something else to complete the statement, as if I should say, “When I shout, why do you tell me to be silent?”

It is therefore also called the conjunctive mood, because something is joined to it so that the meaning of the utterance may be complete.

Let us therefore decline this mood as we did the preceding ones. It is declined through three persons.

Present tense: first person, *cum clamem* (“when I shout”); second, *cum clames*; third, *cum clamet*; and in the plural, *cum clamemus*, *cum clametis*, *cum clament*.

Imperfect past tense: *cum clamarem*, *cum clamares*, *cum clamaret*; and in the plural, *cum clamaremus*, *cum clamaretis*, *cum clamarent*.

Perfect past tense: *cum clamaverim*, *cum clamaveris*, *cum clamaverit*; and in the plural, *cum clamaverimus*, *cum clamaveritis*, *cum clamaverint*.

Pluperfect tense: *cum clamavissem*, *cum clamavisses*, *cum clamavisset*; and in the plural, *cum clamavissemus*, *cum clamavissetis*, *cum clamavissent*.

Future tense: *cum clamavero*, *cum clamaveris*, *cum clamaverit*; and in the plural, *cum clamaverimus*, *cum clamaveritis*, *cum clamaverint*.

The infinitive is so called because the preceding moods define persons—the first, second, and third—whereas this mood is without persons and has only a defined tense: present, past, or future. For example, *clamare* (“to shout”) is present; *clamasse* (“to have shouted”) is past; *clamatum ire* (“to be going to shout”) is future.

You see that these forms designate only tenses, not persons. From *clamare*, *clamasse*, and *clamatum ire*, the person is unknown unless you join something to them and say, for example, *clamare debet ille* (“that one ought to shout”); then it becomes, in a sense, definite. But if you do not add *ille*, *ipse*, or *iste*, it is called the infinitive mood. It is also indefinite in both the singular and the plural number. When I say *clamare* or *clamasse*, it is not definite whether I am speaking of one or of two.

These, then, are the moods through which all verbs proceed.

# CHAPTER XIV—On the First Conjugation

Having proceeded through the pattern of one verb, let us run through the other verbs in the same way:

*clamo, clamas, clamat* (“I shout, you shout, he shouts”);  
*amo, amas, amat* (“I love, you love, he loves”);  
*canto, cantas, cantat* (“I sing, you sing, he sings”);  
*pulso, pulsas, pulsat* (“I strike, you strike, he strikes”);  
*freno, frenas, frenat* (“I bridle, you bridle, he bridles”);  
*armo, armas, armat* (“I arm, you arm, he arms”);  
*impugno, impugnas, impugnat* (“I attack”);  
*capto, captas, captat* (“I seize”);  
*paro, paras, parat* (“I prepare”);  
*separo, separas, separat* (“I separate”);  
*accuso, accusas, accusat* (“I accuse”);  
*mando, mandas, mandat* (“I entrust”);  
*gravo, gravas, gravat* (“I burden”);  
*lavo, lavas, lavat* (“I wash”);  
*genero, generas, generat* (“I beget”);  
*creo, creas, creat* (“I create”);  
*ligo, ligas, ligat* (“I bind”);  
*alligo, alligas, alligat* (“I fasten”);  
*sanctifico, sanctificas, sanctificat* (“I sanctify”);  
*cito, citas, citat* (“I summon”);  
*vulnero, vulneras, vulnerat* (“I wound”);  
*macero, maceras, macerat* (“I weaken”);  
*lacero, laceras, lacerat* (“I tear”);  
*aro, aras, arat* (“I plow”);  
*calco, calcas, calcat* (“I trample”);  
*lanio, lanias, laniat* (“I tear to pieces”);  
*memoro, memoras, memorat* (“I mention”);  
*calceo, calceas, calceat* (“I shoe”);  
*investigo, investigas, investigat* (“I investigate”);  
*vallo, vallas, vallat* (“I fortify with a rampart”);  
*domo, domas, domat* (“I tame”);  
*circumvallo, circumvallas, circumvallat* (“I surround with a rampart”);  
*curvo, curvas, curvat* (“I bend”);  
*medico, medicas, medicat* (“I treat”);  
*consulto, consultas, consultat* (“I consult”);  
*intimo, intimas, intimat* (“I make known”);  
*insinuo, insinuas, insinuat* (“I insinuate”);  
*frequento, frequentas, frequentat* (“I frequent”);  
*celebro, celebras, celebrat* (“I celebrate”);  
*ministro, ministras, ministrat* (“I serve”);  
*palpo, palpas, palpat* (“I touch”);  
*sono, sonas, sonat* (“I sound”);  
*socio, socias, sociat* (“I associate”);  
*muto, mutas, mutat* (“I change”);  
*postulo, postulas, postulat* (“I demand”);  
*quasso, quassas, quassat* (“I shake”);  
*eviscero, evisceras, eviscerat* (“I disembowel”);  
*denso, densas, densat* (“I thicken”);  
*enervo, enervas, enervat* (“I weaken”);  
*verbero, verberas, verberat* (“I beat”);  
*macto, mactas, mactat* (“I sacrifice”);  
*fugo, fugas, fugat* (“I put to flight”);  
*elimino, eliminas, eliminat* (“I remove”);  
*caelo, caelas, caelat* (“I engrave”);  
*signo, signas, signat* (“I mark”);  
*ventilo, ventilas, ventilat* (“I fan”);  
*contristo, contristas, contristat* (“I sadden”);  
*sereno, serenas, serenat* (“I clear”); and others of the same kind.

An *r* is added to all of these, and they become passive: *clamor, clamaris, clamatur* (“I am shouted for, you are shouted for, he is shouted for”); *amor, amaris, amatur* (“I am loved, you are loved, he is loved”); *pulsor, pulsaris, pulsatur* (“I am struck”); *secor, secaris, secatur* (“I am cut”); *curor, curaris, curatur* (“I am treated”).

You will run through all these according to the moods mentioned above: indicative, imperative, optative, subjunctive, and infinitive.

There are also, in the same sound-pattern in which we arranged the active verbs—that is, in which we signified that we perform an action—verbs of similar form that belong to the neuter category. But so that you are not disturbed by the reason they are called neuter, the explanation is this: they neither perform an action nor undergo one, as *sto* (“I stand”), *jaceo* (“I lie”), *cubo* (“I lie down”), and *sedeo* (“I sit”). These belong neither to any action nor to any passion.

Other verbs are called neuter by an abuse of terminology. They have an action but no passive form, as *certo* (“I contend”): it has an action, but we do not say *certor*; similarly *curro* (“I run”).

There are many verbs of this sound which, although they end in *-o*, do not admit *-or*, such as:

*pugno, pugnas, pugnat* (“I fight”);  
*bello, bellas, bellat* (“I wage war”);  
*coeno, coenas, coenat* (“I dine”);  
*nato, natas, natat* (“I swim”);  
*ambulo, ambulas, ambulat* (“I walk”);  
*navigo, navigas, navigat* (“I sail”);  
*commeo, commeas, commeat* (“I go back and forth”);  
*aestuo, aestuas, aestuat* (“I boil”);  
*regno, regnas, regnat* (“I reign”);  
*gelo, gelas, gelat* (“I freeze”);  
*dico, dicas, dicat* (“I say”);  
*exsulo, exsulas, exsulat* (“I live in exile”);  
*sacrifico, sacrificas, sacrificat* (“I sacrifice”);  
*cachinno, cachinnas, cachinnat* (“I laugh loudly”).

All these belong to the first conjugation. They send the second person of all these verbs into the syllable *-as*: *amo, amas*; *canto, cantas*; *pulso, pulsas*; *freno, frenas*; *armo, armas*; *impugno, impugnas*; *salto, saltas*; *curvo, curvas*; *pugno, pugnas*.

You have therefore heard what the first conjugation is, and you must know that the second person of its verbs ends in the syllable *-as*. It is called a conjugation because it joins many forms together in one sound. The Greeks call these conjugations *συζυγίαι* (*syzygiai*, “conjugations,” literally “yokings”). You will proceed in the same way through all similar forms discovered here.

# CHAPTER XV—On the Second Conjugation

The second conjugation is likewise recognized in the second person, and ends in *-es*, as:

*teneo, tenes* (“I hold, you hold”);  
*praebeo, praebes* (“I provide”);  
*moneo, mones* (“I warn”);  
*doleo, doles* (“I grieve”);  
*tergeo, terges* (“I wipe”);  
*arceo, arces* (“I ward off”);  
*egeo, eges* (“I lack”);  
*terreo, terres* (“I frighten”);  
*mulceo, mulces* (“I soothe”);  
*impleo, imples* (“I fill”);  
*compleo, comples* (“I complete”);  
*repleo, reples* (“I refill”);  
*supleo, supples* (“I supply”);  
*mordeo, mordes* (“I bite”);  
*spondeo, spondes* (“I promise”); and others of the same kind.

An *r* is added to these, and they become passive: *teneor, teneris* (“I am held, you are held”); *mordeor, morderis* (“I am bitten”); *arceor, arceris* (“I am warded off”); *mulceor, mulceris* (“I am soothed”); *impleor, impleris* (“I am filled”).

You will decline these passives through moods, tenses, and persons. Through moods, as I said, they are declined through the indicative, imperative, optative, subjunctive, and infinitive—that is what I meant by “through moods.” Through tenses, they are declined through past, present, and future. As for persons, I mentioned the first, second, and third: *teneor, teneris, tenetur* (“I am held, you are held, he is held”); and in the plural, *tenemur, tenemini, tenentur*. You will observe these forms as I have explained.

But just as I said above that the first conjugation, which ends in *-as*, as *amo, amas*, also includes neuter verbs such as *certo, certas* and *nato, natas*, in which the letter *r* is not admitted—for we do not say *certor* or *nator*—so in this second conjugation, which ends in *-eo, -es*, as *moneo, mones* and *doceo, doces*, there are many verbs that do not admit the letter *r* in the first person, such as *algeo, alges* (“I am cold, you are cold”) and *scateo, scates* (“I bubble, you bubble”). *Algeor* is not Latin.

Likewise, *ferveo, ferves* (“I boil, you boil”); *torpeo, torpes* (“I am numb”); *pendeo, pendes* (“I hang”); *invideo, invides* (“I envy”). Although the poet Horace used *invideor* (*Ars Poetica* 56), he did so as a new usage. Likewise, *emineo, emines* (“I project, you project”); we do not say *emineor*.

These two conjugations—the first and the second—which, as we have said, end in *-as* and *-es*, as *amo, amas* and *moneo, mones*, always put the future tense into the syllable *-bo*, as *amabo* (“I shall love”) and *monebo* (“I shall warn”).

# CHAPTER XVI—On the Third and Fourth Conjugations

You will observe this wherever you put the future tense into the syllable *-bo*, because there are two other conjugations that put the future tense into the syllable *-am*, not *-bo*. They are called the shortened third conjugation and the lengthened third conjugation.

The shortened third conjugation is the one that puts the imperative mood into a shortened *e*, as *scribe* (“write”), *tolle* (“take away”), *carpe* (“pluck”), *occide* (“kill”), *sere* (“sow”), and *lege* (“read”).

You have therefore seen that the imperative ends in this way. The shortened third conjugation always puts the future tense into *-am*, never into *-bo*: *scribam* (“I shall write”), *legam* (“I shall read”), *tollam* (“I shall take away”), *carpam* (“I shall pluck”). It is not Latin if someone says *scribebo*, *legebo*, *tollebo*, or *carpebo*.

The lengthened third conjugation is likewise recognized from the same imperative mood. When the imperative ends in the letter *-i*, the conjugation is the lengthened third: *audi* (“hear”), *nutri* (“nourish”), *senti* (“feel”), *muni* (“fortify”), *sarci* (“mend”), *leni* (“soothe”), and others of the same kind.

These likewise put the future tense into *-am*: *muniam* (“I shall fortify”), *leniam* (“I shall soothe”), *nutriam* (“I shall nourish”), *audiam* (“I shall hear”).
