The shortened third conjugation has a shortened *e* before the final syllable in the infinitive, as *scribere* (“to write”), *legere* (“to read”), *tollere* (“to take away”), and similar forms. The lengthened third conjugation, however, has an *i* in the penultimate syllable of the infinitive, and that *i* is long, as *munire* (“to fortify”), *lenire* (“to soothe”), *audire* (“to hear”), *sarcire* (“to mend”), *sentire* (“to feel”), and *venire* (“to come”).

Thus these conjugations are observed in all verbs. Those that end in *-as* and *-es* put the future tense into *-bo*, as I have often said. Those that end in *-is* put the future tense into *-am*, never into *-bo*, unless one relies on an assumed authority; grammar forbids it.

Let us give some verbs of the shortened third conjugation, from which you may derive others. They are:

*lego* (“I read”), *tollo* (“I take away”), *erigo* (“I raise”), *carpo* (“I pluck”), *cognosco* (“I learn”), *capio* (“I take”), *fugio* (“I flee”), *mergo* (“I submerge”), *sero* (“I sow”), *arguo* (“I accuse”), *accipio* (“I receive”), *pono* (“I place”), *sumo* (“I take”), *accendo* (“I kindle”), *expono* (“I explain”), *incipio* (“I begin”).

These take the letter *r* and form passive verbs: *legor* (“I am read”), *carpor* (“I am plucked”), *capior* (“I am taken”), and so forth.

Under this pattern are neuter verbs that do not take the letter *r*, such as *cado* (“I fall”); we do not say *cador*. Likewise *ruo* (“I rush”), for we do not say *ruor*; and *facio* (“I make”), for we do not say *facior*.

Likewise: *fulgesco* (“I begin to shine”), *nitesco* (“I begin to glitter”), *fervesco* (“I begin to boil”), *algesco* (“I begin to grow cold”), *torpesco* (“I begin to grow numb”), *compesco* (“I restrain”), and *nigresco* (“I grow black”).

None of these has the letter *r*. They are called neuter verbs because they end in *-sco*. Therefore remember that neuter verbs never admit the letter *r*.

# CHAPTER XVII—What the Common Verb Is Called and Its Conjugation

Two other types of verbs remain: those called common and those called deponent.

They are called common because, in a single form, they simultaneously contain the active and passive. Just as a noun is called common gender when it includes both masculine and feminine under one form—*sacerdos* (“priest”), *homo* (“human being”), *hic et haec sacerdos*, *hic et haec homo*—so verbs are also called common. They never lay aside the letter *r*, since otherwise they would not be Latin.

For example, *osculor* means “I kiss.” If you remove the *r* and say *osculo*, the form is not Latin. When we perform the action, we say *osculor te* (“I kiss you”); when we undergo it and are affected by another, we say *osculor a te* (“I am kissed by you”).

Similarly, when we signify an action, that is, when we bring an accusation, we say *criminor te* (“I accuse you”), not *crimino*. But when an accusation is brought against us, we say *criminor a te* (“I am accused by you”), that is, “I hear an accusation from you,” and the meaning is passive.

These verbs are declined through moods, tenses, and persons like the preceding verbs.

Present tense, singular:

*criminor, criminaris, criminatur* (“I accuse/am accused, you accuse/are accused, he accuses/is accused”).

Plural:

*criminamur, criminamini, criminantur*.

Imperfect past tense, singular:

*criminabar, criminabaris, criminabatur*.

Plural:

*criminabamur, criminabamini, criminabantur*.

Perfect past tense, singular:

*criminatus sum, criminatus es, criminatus est* (“I have accused/been accused, you have accused/been accused, he has accused/been accused”).

Plural:

*criminati sumus, criminati estis, criminati sunt*.

Pluperfect past tense, singular:

*criminatus eram, criminatus eras, criminatus erat*.

Plural:

*criminati eramus, criminati eratis, criminati erant*.

Future tense, singular:

*criminabor, criminaberis, criminabitur*.

Plural:

*criminabimur, criminabimini, criminabuntur*.

The imperative mood always ends in *-re* in these verbs, as when you say *criminare illum* (“accuse him”), that is, “bring an accusation against him.”

In the optative mood:

*utinam criminarer, criminareris, criminaretur* (“would that I might accuse/be accused, you might accuse/be accused, he might accuse/be accused”).

Plural:

*utinam criminaremur, criminaremini, criminarentur*.

Perfect past tense, singular:

*utinam criminatus essem, criminatus esses, criminatus esset*.

Plural:

*criminati essemus, criminati essetis, criminati essent*.

Future tense, singular:

*utinam criminer, crimineris, criminetur*.

Plural:

*utinam criminemur, criminemini, criminentur*.

In the subjunctive mood, singular:

*cum criminer, crimineris, criminetur*.

Imperfect past tense, singular:

*cum criminarer, criminareris, criminaretur*.

Perfect past tense, singular:

*cum criminatus sim, criminatus sis, criminatus sit*.

Plural:

*cum criminati simus, criminati sitis, criminati sint*.

Pluperfect past tense, singular:

*cum criminatus essem, criminatus esses, criminatus esset*.

Plural:

*cum criminati essemus, criminati essetis, criminati essent*.

Future tense, singular:

*cum criminatus ero, eris, erit*.

Plural:

*cum criminati erimus, eritis, erunt*.

In the infinitive mood, which, as we said, signifies no persons, the forms are: present, *criminari* (“to accuse/be accused”); past, *criminatum esse* (“to have accused/been accused”); future, *criminatum iri* (“to be going to accuse/be accused”).

You will decline common verbs according to this pattern: *hortor* (“I exhort”), *jaculor* (“I hurl”), *osculor* (“I kiss”), *nidificor* (“I build a nest”), *tutor* (“I protect”), *consolor* (“I console”), *scrutor* (“I examine”), *moror* (“I delay”), *feneror* (“I lend at interest”), *amplector* (“I embrace”), and *furor* (“I rage”), whence come *furor, furaris, furatur*.

Also: *comitor* (“I accompany”), *recordor* (“I remember”), *reminiscor* (“I remember”), *percunctor* (“I inquire”), *minor* (“I threaten”), *gestor* (“I conduct myself”), *piscor* (“I fish”), *odoror* (“I smell”), *aucupor* (“I hunt birds”), *venor* (“I hunt”), *contemplor* (“I contemplate”), *speculor* (“I observe”), *sector* (“I follow”), *veneror* (“I venerate”), *dignor* (“I deem worthy”), *precor* (“I pray”), *miseror* (“I pity”), *vador* (“I make a formal pledge”), that is, “I give my word,” *calumnior* (“I slander”), and others of the same kind, which never lay aside the letter *r*. For if they lay it aside, they are not Latin.

Who, for example, would say *reminisco*, *recordo*, *digno*, or *secto*? Therefore remember always to pronounce these with the letter *r*.

# CHAPTER XVIII—On the Deponent Verb

The deponent verb remains. It is so called because it lays aside something from the full range of the common verb.

The common verb has four participles: present, as *criminans* (“accusing”); future, *criminaturus* (“about to accuse”); past, *criminatus* (“having accused”); and future, *criminandus* (“to be accused”). A deponent verb does not have *criminandus* in the passive sense. It is therefore called deponent because it lays aside one future-tense participle of the passive verb, the one ending in the syllable *-dus*.

For example, *opinor* (“I think”) or *minor* (“I threaten”) are deponent verbs. It has the present participle *minans* (“threatening”); in the future it forms *minaturus* (“about to threaten”); in the past, *minatus* (“having threatened”). In the future passive sense it does not form *minandus* (“to be threatened”).

Likewise, it has *opinans* (“thinking”), *opinaturus* (“about to think”), and *opinatus* (“having thought”), but it does not form *opinandus*. Or if you say *moriens* (“dying”), *moriturus* (“about to die”), and *mortuus* (“dead”), it does not form *moriendus* (“to be dying”), because that is not Latin.

This deponent verb, then, proceeds through moods, tenses, and persons in the same way.

Just as it was said above that a common verb is Latin when its *r* is not removed, but is not Latin when the *r* is removed, so deponent verbs are not Latin when they lose the letter *r*.

I shall now list a few deponent verbs; Latin usage will teach the rest. They are:

*opinor* (“I think”), *minor* (“I threaten”), *grator* (“I congratulate”), *gratulor* (“I rejoice/congratulate”), *arbitror* (“I judge”), *gratificor* (“I oblige”), *auspicor* (“I take auspices”), *misereor* (“I pity”), *lenocinor* (“I entice”), *meditor* (“I meditate”), *luctor* (“I wrestle”), *conor* (“I attempt”), *suffragor* (“I support by vote”), *vescor* (“I feed”), *laetor* (“I rejoice”), *morior* (“I die”), *stomachor* (“I am angry”), *hariolor* (“I prophesy”), *lezor*, that is, “I am painted with color,” *argutor* (“I argue”), *paciscor* (“I make an agreement”), *complector* (“I embrace”), *adversor* (“I oppose”), *angor* (“I am distressed”), *queror* (“I complain”), in the sense of making a complaint, *macior* (“I am wasted away”), *ratiocinor* (“I reason”), *argumentor* (“I argue”), *blandior* (“I flatter”), *fabulor* (“I converse”), *nitor* (“I strive”), *labor*, in the sense of slipping or falling, *vagor* (“I wander”), *rusticor* (“I live in the country”), *concionor*, that is, “I address the people,” *mercor* (“I buy”), *vociferor* (“I cry out”), *nanciscor* (“I obtain,” “I find”), *suspicor* (“I suspect”), and others.

Remember, as I have already said, to pronounce them with the letter *r*. No one says *blandio* or *pacisco*. All these are declined according to the pattern of the common verb that I gave as *criminor*.

# CHAPTER XIX—On Neuter-Passive and Impersonal Verbs
We have therefore discussed active verbs, which are so called from *agere*, “to act”; we have discussed neuter verbs, which receive this name because they neither do anything nor suffer anything, as we said: *sto*, “I stand”; *jaceo*, “I lie”; *sedeo*, “I sit”; *cubo*, “I recline”; and others. We have also discussed other neuter verbs that do something but do not suffer anything, and are therefore called, as it were, semi-neuter: *nato*, “I swim”; *curro*, “I run.” There are others that suffer something and do not act, such as *vapulo*, “I am beaten”; *pendeo*, “I hang”; *sudo*, “I sweat”; *algeo*, “I am cold”; *aestuo*, “I am hot”; *ferveo*, “I boil”; *febrio*, “I have a fever”; *somnio*, “I dream”; *meridio*, “I rest at midday”; *rigeo*, “I am stiff”; *frigeo*, “I am cold”; *tumeo*, “I swell”; *langueo*, “I am weak”; *oleo*, “I smell”; *rubeo*, “I am red”; *fulgeo*, “I shine”; *stupeo*, “I am numb”; and others. In all these—both those that do absolutely nothing and suffer nothing, those that act but do not suffer, and those that suffer something but nevertheless do not act—the letter *r* is never added; for if it is added, they cease to be Latin. We likewise discussed common verbs and explained why they are called common: because they contain both action and passion within themselves. We discussed deponent verbs and explained why they are called deponent: because they lay aside the future participle with passive meaning, which ends in *-dus*. Thus we do not say *moriendus*, “about to die,” *gloriandus*, “about to be glorified,” *blandiendus*, “about to be flattered,” or the other forms derived from deponent verbs.

The writers on grammar have indeed added another species of verb, which they called neuter-passive; but this novel class of verb was discovered for the sake of euphony, and occurs in only a few verbs, such as *gaudeo*, “I rejoice.” Since it was harsh to say *gavisi* for the past tense, they altered the sound from the past tense of the passive verb: *gaudeo, gavisus sum*; likewise *audeo, ausus sum*; *soleo, solitus sum*; and *fido, fisus sum*. But there are very few verbs of this new class.

There are also a few other verbs called impersonal, ending in the syllables *-et* and *-tur*: *pudet*, “it shames”; *taedet*, “it wearies”; *decet*, “it is fitting”; *libet*, “it pleases”; *poenitet*, “it causes regret”; *patet*, “it is evident”; *piget*, “it displeases”; *miseret*, “it moves to pity”; *liquet*, “it is clear.” They are called impersonal because they lack two persons, the first and the second, and have only the third person. For we do not say *pudeo, pudes*; *deceo, deces*; *libeo, libes*; *pigeo, piges*; *misereo, miseres*; *poeniteo, poenites*; *pateo, pates*; or *liqueo, liques*.

You should know that *patet* and *liquet* mean what we express by “it is evident.” Thus, if you say, “And if it is evident that you said this, you have committed an injury,” this is also the meaning of *liquet*, that is, “it is evident.” *Taedet* signifies that there is weariness, just as *piget* signifies, as it were, displeasure or reluctance. For when we say, “I regret having done it” (*piget me fecisse*), this means: “My mind does not rise to approve what I have done.”

All these verbs are declined in the following way: *pudet me*, “I am ashamed”; *piget me*, “I am displeased”; *miseret me*, “I am an object of pity”; *poenitet me*, “I regret.” Besides these there are *libet* and *licet*, *patet* and *liquet*. With these we join the dative case: *libet mihi*, “it pleases me”; *licet mihi*, “it is permitted to me”; *patet mihi*, “it is evident to me”; *liquet mihi*, “it is clear to me.”

[Note: [Col. 1401] Augustine frequently joins the accusative.]

The other species, which ends in *-tur*, is also impersonal, as in *itur*, “there is going”; *curritur*, “there is running”; *certatur*, “there is contending”; *pugnatur*, “there is fighting.” These do not have a first or second person; for neither *eor, iris*, nor *curror, curreris*, nor *pugnor, pugnaris*, nor *certor, certaris* is said. These verbs are declined as follows: *itur a me, a te, ab illo*, “there is going by me, by you, by him”; *pugnatur a me, a te, ab illo*, “there is fighting by me, by you, by him.”

Thus, in the imperfect: *ibatur a me, a te, ab illo*, “there was going by me, by you, by him”; *pugnabatur a me, a te, ab illo*, “there was fighting by me, by you, by him”; *certabatur a me, a te, ab illo*, “there was contending by me, by you, by him.”

In the perfect: *itum est a me, a te, ab illo*, “there has been going by me, by you, by him”; *cursum est a me, a te, ab illo*, “there has been running by me, by you, by him”; *pugnatum est a me, a te, ab illo*, “there has been fighting by me, by you, by him”; *certatum est a me, a te, ab illo*, “there has been contending by me, by you, by him.”

In the pluperfect: *itum erat a me, a te, ab illo*, “there had been going by me, by you, by him”; *cursum erat a me, a te, ab illo*, “there had been running by me, by you, by him”; *pugnatum erat a me, a te, ab illo*, “there had been fighting by me, by you, by him”; *certatum erat a me, a te, ab illo*, “there had been contending by me, by you, by him.”

In the future: *ibitur a me, a te, ab illo*, “there will be going by me, by you, by him”; *curretur a me, a te, ab illo*, “there will be running by me, by you, by him”; *pugnabitur* [Col. 1402] *a me, a te, ab illo*, “there will be fighting by me, by you, by him”; *certabitur a me, a te, ab illo*, “there will be contending by me, by you, by him.” In the plural: *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the imperative: *eatur a me, a te, ab illo; a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “let there be going by me, by you, by him; by us, by you, by them.”

In the optative: *utinam iretur a me, a te, ab illo; a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “would that there were going by me, by you, by him; by us, by you, by them.”

In the perfect and pluperfect: *utinam itum esset a me, a te, ab illo*, “would that there had been going by me, by you, by him”; and in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the future: *utinam eatur a me, a te, ab illo*, “would that there be going by me, by you, by him”; in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the present subjunctive: *cum curratur a me, a te, ab illo*, “when there is running by me, by you, by him”; and in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the imperfect: *cum curreretur a me, a te, ab illo*, “when there was running by me, by you, by him”; in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the perfect: *cum cursum sit a me, a te, ab illo*, “when there has been running by me, by you, by him”; in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the pluperfect: *cum cursum esset a me, a te, ab illo*, “when there had been running by me, by you, by him”; in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the future: *cum cursum erit a me, a te, ab illo*, “when there will have been running by me, by you, by him”; in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the infinitive: *curri debet a me, a te, ab illo*, “there ought to be running by me, by you, by him”; in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the past: *cursum esse debuit a me, a te, ab illo*, “there ought to have been running by me, by you, by him”; in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

In the future: *cursum iri debet a me, a te, ab illo*, “there ought to be going to be running by me, by you, by him”; in the plural, *a nobis, a vobis, ab illis*, “by us, by you, by them.”

## CHAPTER XX — On inchoative, frequentative, and desiderative verbs

There are other verbs called inchoatives, which arise from a sudden affection and end in the syllable *-sco*: *ardeo, ardesco*, “I burn, I begin to burn”; *caleo, calesco*, “I am hot, I become hot”; *candeo, candesco*, “I shine white, I become white”; *labo, labasco*, “I totter, I begin to totter”; *tepeo, tepesco*, “I am warm, I become warm”; *ferveo, fervesco*, “I boil, I begin to boil”; *vireo, viresco*, “I am green, I become green”; *algeo, algesco*, “I am cold, I become cold”; *dormio, dormisco*, “I sleep, I fall asleep”; and the rest.

None of these has a past tense. For one may form *calui* and *fervi*, but one may not form *caluifecit* or *fervifecit* from *calesco* or *fervesco*. Rather, from *ferveo* comes *fervi*, from *caleo*, *calui*; for *calescui*, *fervescui*, and *virescui* are not Latin. They are therefore said not to have a past tense because things we begin are not yet complete.

All the verbs I have mentioned as ending in *-sco* are always neuter; they do not take the letter *r*. That is why I warned that they are neuter. Nor should certain verbs ending in *-scor* confuse you, although they admit a past tense, such as *obliviscor, oblitus sum*, “I forget, I forgot”; *paciscor, pactus sum*, “I make an agreement, I made an agreement”; *adipiscor, adeptus sum*, “I attain, I attained.” These too, while they are neuter, belong among the verbs in which, as we said, the past tenses are absent.

There are also other verbs called frequentatives, by which something is signified as being done more frequently: from *dicto*, *dictito*; from *lego*, *lectito*; from *scribo*, *scriptito*; from *clamo*, *clamito*; from *cio*, *cito*, which means “I call frequently.” Hence we now say of certain people *voce praeconis citatos*, “summoned by the herald’s voice,” that is, “called repeatedly,” and so forth.

There are also a very few verbs called desideratives: *esurio*, “I desire to eat”; *parturio*, “I desire to give birth”; and, as Cicero says of philosophers, *morituriunt*, “they desire to die.” But these, as I said, are few, having been introduced into the sound of Latin.

## CHAPTER XXI — On the adverb

The adverb is so called because it clings to the verb. The force of the verb cannot sound with sufficiently precise meaning unless an adverb is joined to it. For example, the verbs *dico*, “I speak”; *navigo*, “I sail”; *valeo*, “I am well”; *curro*, “I run”; and others do not have complete meaning unless adverbs are added: *bene*, “well”; *male*, “badly”; *docte*, “learnedly”; *feliciter*, “successfully.” Thus: *bene dicit*, “he speaks well”; *imperite dicit*, “he speaks incompetently”; *prospere navigat*, “he sails successfully”; *infeliciter navigat*, “he sails unsuccessfully”; *integre valet*, “he is wholly well”; *debiliter valet*, “he is weakly”; *agiliter currit*, “he runs nimbly”; *tardius currit*, “he runs more slowly.” You see that the meaning of verbs cannot be complete unless adverbs are joined to them.

Other adverbs are joined to complete the meaning of the verb, such as adverbs of place and adverbs of time: *hic dico*, “I speak here”; *hic habito*, “I live here”; *intro eo*, “I go inside”; *intus sum*, “I am inside”; *foras eo*, “I go outside”; *foris sum*, “I am outside”; *hinc navigo*, “I sail from here.” Likewise concerning time: *cras navigo*, “I sail tomorrow”; *hodie navigo*, “I sail today.” There are other matters treated in other disciplines and clear to the understanding, which I did not wish to set down here, because brevity is appropriate to avoid weariness in speaking.

In adverbs we must observe when they end in *-e* and when in the syllable *-ter*. The ablative case teaches this. When the ablative ends in *-o*, the adverb ends in *-e*: from *docto*, *docte*; from *justo*, *juste*; from *perfecto*, *perfecte*; from *pio*, *pie*; from *valido*, *valide*; from *fortunato*, *fortunate*; from *magno*, *magne*; [Col. 1403] from *amplo*, *ample*; from *minimo*, *minime*; and others.

When the adverb ends in the syllable *-ter*, the ablative likewise teaches us, as I said: from *agili*, *agiliter*; from *humili*, *humiliter*; from *acri*, *acriter*; from *forti*, *fortiter*; from *levi*, *leviter*; from *gravi*, *graviter*; from *jugi*, *jugiter*.

There are, however, certain forms which, because they would sound harsh, have been abandoned and should not be treated according to this rule. We do not say *mititer* from *miti*, nor *tristiter* from *tristi*. To prevent such forms from sounding harsh, they lost their final syllable: from *sapienti*, *sapienter*, not *sapientiter*; from *prudenti*, *prudenter*, not *prudentiter*; from *praestanti*, *praestanter*, not *praestantiter*.

Let us therefore observe this rule in such a way that we neither apply euphony indiscriminately to the rule nor reject euphony. Euphony—that is, pleasantness of sound—has been admitted into Latin speech to soften what is harsh; and in cases where harshness offended the ear, usage has departed from the rule according to reason. Thus Cicero says: “Reason has obtained permission to err for the sake of pleasantness.” Yet euphony has been admitted only in a few cases. For the rule is well supplied and supported by the most thoroughly Latin writers.

With respect to these rules, authority has indeed ventured to presume in a few cases. Thus Cicero says *humaniter* where he should have said *humane*; and Terence says, “He lived sparingly and harshly” (*Vitam parce ac duriter agebat*, *Andria*, act 1, scene 1, line 47), instead of *dure*. Yet these authors themselves presumed against the rule only modestly and with a certain restraint. They also said *falso* instead of *false*, *necessario* instead of *necessarie*, *sedulo* instead of *sedule*, *raro* instead of *rare*, *crebro* instead of *crebre*, and *tuto* instead of *tute*. Other such forms, though few, have likewise been used—not recklessly, but cautiously.

Some adverbs end in other syllables: from *fundus*, *funditus*; from *caelum*, *caelitus*; from *radix*, *radicitus*; from *penetralia loca*, *penitus*; from *stirps*, *stirpitus*. Others end in *-im*: from *vicus*, *vicatim*; from *ostium*, *ostiatim*; from *viri*, *viritim*. Likewise *nimis* from *nimium*, as in “Let nothing be excessive” (*Ne quid nimis*).

Some end in *-ens*, as *recens*, “recently,” that is, “at a recent time.” Virgil says: “With the sun having recently risen” (*Sole recens orto*, *Georgics* 3.156), that is, “at a recent time.” All these are therefore adverbs, without distinction.

There is also this difference between *intro* and *intus*: *intro* expresses motion, *intus* location. Thus: *intro eo*, “I go inside”; *intus sum*, “I am inside.” *Eo*, “I go,” expresses motion; *sum*, “I am,” expresses location.

There is also a certain obscurity concerning *secundo, tertio, quarto, quinto, sexto* and *secundum, tertium, quartum, quintum, sextum*. For example: *secundo factus est consul*, “he was made consul secondly,” and *secundum factus fuit consul*, “he was made the second consul.” *Secundo* pertains to order, while *secundum* pertains to number. Thus, when I say, “He was made consul secondly,” this pertains, as I said, to order: one person was made consul first, and another second. But when we say “the second consul,” or “the third,” “fourth,” “fifth,” or “sixth,” this pertains to number, meaning that he was consul six times. Thus Cicero says of Marius: “Sixth consul,” that is, one who earned six consulships; and “seventh consul,” meaning that he earned a seventh consulship. Varro distinguished this in his books *On Numbers*.

The remaining matters concerning adverbs are already clear and easy to understand from the various disciplines.

## CHAPTER XXII — Again on the adverb

The adverb is a part of speech which, added to a verb, explains and completes its meaning: *scribo bene*, “I write well”; *lego optime*, “I read very well.” The properties of the adverb are meaning, form, and degree.

Adverbs either arise independently, as *heri*, “yesterday,” and *nuper*, “recently,” or pass over from other words, as *docte*, “learnedly,” and *sapienter*, “wisely,” from *doctus*, “learned,” and *sapiens*, “wise.”

There are many meanings of adverbs. They may be adverbs of time, such as *heri*, “yesterday,” and *nuper*, “recently”; of person, such as *mecum*, “with me,” and *tecum*, “with you”; or of place, such as *hic*, “here,” and *isthic*, “there.”

Local adverbs may be interrogative, such as *unde*, “from where?”; *ubi*, “where?”; and *qua*, “by what route?” They may be responsive: *illinc*, “from there”; *hinc*, “from here”; *illo*, “to there.” Some have a double form, such as *intus* and *intro*, *foris* and *foras*.

Their usage is as follows. *Foris* and *intus* indicate location: *intus est*, “he is inside”; *intus fuit*, “he was inside”; *futurus est*, “he will be inside”; *intus erat*, “he was inside”; *futurus erat*, “he was going to be inside”; *foris erat*, “he was outside”; *fuerat*, “he had been outside”; *futurus erat*, “he was going to be outside.” Concerning movement from a place, one says *intus venio*, “I come from inside,” and *foris venio*, “I come from outside.” *Foras* and *intro* indicate movement to a place: *foras eo*, “I go outside”; *foras venio*, “I come outside”; *intro eo*, “I go inside”; *intro venio*, “I come inside”; *foras ieram*, “I had gone outside”; *intro ieram*, “I had gone inside.”

These are formed in four ways: through a place, to a place, in a place, and from a place.

Through a place:

> “This way lies our road to Elysium.”  
> (*Aeneid* 6.542)

To a place:

> “Come here, O Galatea.”  
> (*Eclogues* 9.39)

In a place:

[Col. 1404]

> “Here the Locrians of Naryx established their walls.”  
> (*Aeneid* 3.399)

From a place:

> “From here, as I departed, a god brought me to your shores.”  
> (*Aeneid* 3.715)

Some adverbs signify both location and movement from a place, such as *intus sum*, “I am inside,” and *intus venio*, “I come from inside.” Others signify location, movement to a place, and movement from a place, such as *penitus sum*, “I am deep within”; *penitus eo*, “I go deep within”; *penitus venio*, “I come from deep within.”

Some adverbs express number: *semel*, “once”; *bis*, “twice”; *ter*, “three times.” Some express demonstration: *en*, “behold”; *ecce*, “look.” Some express affirmation: *quidem*, “indeed”; *quippe*, “certainly.” Some express exhortation: *eia*, “come on.” Some express interrogation: *cur*, “why?”; *quare*, “for what reason?” Some express similarity: *sic*, “thus”; *quasi*, “as if.” Some express comparison or preference: *magis*, “more”; *potius*, “rather.” Some express doubt: *fortasse*, “perhaps.” Some express assent: *plane*, “clearly”; *sane*, “certainly.” Some express separation: *seorsum*, “apart”; *segregatim*, “separately.” Some express wishing: *utinam*, “would that.” Some express calling: *heus*, “hey!” Some express answering: *he*, “yes.” Some express rejection: *nequaquam*, “by no means”; *frustra*, “in vain.” Some express swearing: *Aedepol*, “by Pollux”; *Aecastor*, “by Castor.” Some express prohibition: *ne*, “lest.” Some express negation: *non*, “not”; *haud*, “not”; *minime*, “not at all.” Some express gathering: *una*, “together”; *simul*, “at the same time.” Some express ordering: *deinde*, “then”; *denique*, “finally.” Some express wonder: *papae*, “ah!” Some express praise: *euge*, “well done!” Some express exclamation: *proh*, “oh!” Some express grief: *heu*, “alas!” Some express choice: *vah*, “ah!” Some express groaning: *hei*, “alas!”

Since these signify an emotion of the mind, many call them interjections. They wish an interjection to be separated from the adverb and made a separate part of speech for this reason: it is characteristic of the adverb that it can be joined to a verb. The Greeks, however, do not separate the interjection from the adverb, because they assign it to the quality of emotional movement and believe that all these belong to the general category of quality among adverbs.

There are adverbs of quantity, such as *longe*, “far,” and *late*, “widely”; and of quality, such as *bene*, “well,” and *male*, “badly.”

Adverbs do not pass only from appellatives—that is, from common nouns, as *pulchre*, “beautifully,” from *pulcher*, “beautiful”—but also from proper names, as *Tulliane*, “in the manner of Tullius,” from *Tullius*. They also arise from pronouns: from *meus*, “my,” *meatim*; from *tuus*, “your,” *tuatim*. They are also found from verbs, as *cursim*, “at a run,” from *curro*, “I run.” Some are derived from both, such as *pedetentim*, “step by step,” from *pes*, “foot,” and *tento*, “I attempt”—that is, from a noun and a verb together.

There are also adverbs concerning which it is uncertain whether they pass from a noun or a verb, such as *furtim*, “secretly.” For it is uncertain whether it derives from *fur*, “a thief,” which is a noun, or from *furor, furaris*, “I steal,” which is a verb. Some do not wish adverbs to be derived from participles, but they are found nevertheless, as *decenter*, “becomingly,” from *decens*, “becoming.”

## CHAPTER XXIII — Adverbs derived from nouns have six endings. The common rule

Adverbs derived from nouns end in six ways: in *-e*, as *docte*, “learnedly”; *pulchre*, “beautifully”; *honeste*, “honorably”; in *-r*, as *velociter*, “quickly”; in *-im*, as *ubertim*, “abundantly,” and *singillatim*, “one by one”; in *-us*, as *radicitus*, “by the roots,” and *mordicus*, “with the teeth”; in *-u*, as *noctu*, “at night,” and *diu*, “for a long time”; or in *-i*, as *domi*, “at home”; *humi*, “on the ground”; *vesperi*, “in the evening.”

Adverbs of quality ending in the letter *e* ought to have a long *e*. There are, however, exceptions: forms that waver in the comparative or superlative, such as *bene*, “well,” and *male*, “badly”; or forms that do not pass from an appellative, such as *impune*, “with impunity,” and *saepe*, “often.” Moreover, *facile* and *difficile*, which are used as adverbs, are nouns from which these adverbs arise: *faciliter*, “easily,” and *difficiliter*, “with difficulty.” Usage, however, has claimed the former forms as adverbs.

All nouns of quality or quantity that end in *-o* in the singular dative send the adverb out with a long *e*: from *justo*, *juste*, “justly.” The ancients nevertheless used some forms indifferently, such as *humaniter*, “humanely,” and *duriter*, “harshly.”

Those that end in the letter *i* send the adverb out in the syllable *-ter*: from *agili*, *agiliter*; from *nobili*, *nobiliter*; from *audaci*, *audaciter*; from *difficili*, *difficiliter*. Some of these, however, are formed by syncope for the sake of euphony: *audacter*, “boldly”; *difficulter*, “with difficulty”; *sapienter*, “wisely”; and *constanter*, “steadfastly.”

Some adverbs are common with other parts of speech. They are common with nouns, as Sallust says:

> “The human race falsely complains about its nature.”  
> (*In the Jugurthine War*)

Here *falso* is used instead of *false*. Virgil says:

> “And repeatedly strikes the earth with his foot”  
> (*Georgics* 3.500)

and:

> “Having humbly prayed much to Jupiter with upturned hands.”  
> (*Aeneid* 4.205)

The conjunction *ut*, when it functions with an adverb, has several meanings.

It expresses similarity:

> “As once, it is said, the Labyrinth [was] in lofty Crete.”  
> (*Aeneid* 5.588)

It expresses time:

> “When [I saw] the king of like age,”  
> (*Aeneid* 2.561)

and:

[Col. 1405]

> “When I saw [you], when I perished, when a baneful error carried me away.”  
> (*Eclogues* 8.41)

It expresses quality:

> “How [the Greeks overthrew] the Trojan wealth and lamentable kingdom.”  
> (*Aeneid* 2.4)

It expresses quantity:

> “From what shores do you come, long-awaited Hector? How [long] after the many funerals of your people …”  
> (*Aeneid* 2.282–283)

It expresses conjunction:

> “As Cupid, having changed his face and features, [comes] in place of dear Ascanius.”  
> (*Aeneid* 1.662–663)

It can also function as a preposition, as *pro*.

The form of adverbs is either simple, as *docte*, “learnedly,” and *prudenter*, “prudently,” or compound, as *indocte*, “unlearnedly,” and *imprudenter*, “imprudently.”

Adverbs receive degrees whenever the appellations from which they pass are compared: *docte*, “learnedly”; *doctius*, “more learnedly”; *doctissime*, “most learnedly.” They also receive diminutives, as *meliuscule*, “rather better.” Even those that arise independently receive comparison and diminutive forms, as *nuper*, “recently,” and *nuperrime*, “most recently.”

A preposition should not be added separately to any adverb, although one finds *ab hinc* in Terence:

> “Meanwhile, a certain woman, three years from now …”  
> (*Andria*, act 1, scene 1, line 40)

And in Virgil:

> “From there we are sent through deep Elysium.”  
> (*Aeneid* 6.743–744)

Likewise *dehinc*, as in:

> “From then on he speaks thus.”  
> (*Aeneid* 1.256)

And *deinde*:

> “Then the fertile plants are set in.”  
> (*Georgics* 2.79–80)

All these, and any similar forms such as *proinde*, have had their accent placed contrary to the rule so that the prepositions would not appear to have been added separately to the adverbs.

## CHAPTER XXIV — On participles. The common rule

This part of speech receives one part from the verb and one from the noun; for this reason it is called a participle. In the present tense it ends in the syllables *-ens* and *-ans*, as *legens*, “reading,” and *amans*, “loving.” In the future it ends in *-rus*: *legens, lecturus*, “reading, about to read”; *amans, amaturus*, “loving, about to love.” In the past: *lectus*, “read”; *amatus*, “loved.” In the future passive: *legendus*, “to be read”; *amandus*, “to be loved.”

You see that this part of speech exists through tenses; all this it borrows from the verb. For tenses belong to the verb. But because it is declined through cases, it borrows this from the noun. For case-declension belongs to the noun: *hic legens*, “this reader”; *hujus legentis*, “of this reader”; *huic legenti*, “to this reader”; *hunc legentem*, “this reader” in the accusative; *o legens*, “O reader”; *ab hoc legente*, “from this reader.” Since this part of speech therefore proceeds either through tenses or through cases, it is called a participle, because it takes part in the noun and part in the verb.

It is not a difficult part of speech, but easy to understand. The present tense ends in *-ans* and *-ens*: *amans*, “loving”; *legens*, “reading.” The future with active meaning ends in *-rus*: *amaturus*, “about to love”; *lecturus*, “about to read.” With passive meaning it ends in *-tus* and *-dus*: *amatus*, “loved”; *legendus*, “to be read.”

The past tense itself ends in three syllables. In *-tus*: *lectus*, “read”; *scriptus*, “written.” In *-sus*: *occisus*, “killed”; *visus*, “seen.” In *-xus*: *fixus*, “fixed.” You will find no more. Thus, as we said, the present ends in *-ens* and *-ans*, the future in *-rus*, the past in *-tus*, and the future passive always in *-dus*.

There are certainly nouns which, by their sound, are thought to be participles, but they are nouns. Participles are those that come from verbs: from *lego*, “I read,” come *legens*, “reading”; *lecturus*, “about to read”; *lectus*, “read”; and *legendus*, “to be read.” *Tunicatus*, “clad in a tunic”; *galeatus*, “wearing a helmet”; *clypeatus*, “armed with a shield”; and *tropaeatus*, “adorned with a trophy,” are nouns, not participles, because they do not come from verbs.

There is one past-tense participle ending in *-uus*, which ought to end with one *u*, not two. For where the nominative has a doubled *u*, the word is a noun, not a participle: *fatuus*, “foolish”; *ingenuus*, “native” or “freeborn”; *arduus*, “steep”; *carduus*, “thistle”; *exiguus*, “small”; *belluus*, “beastly,” as Cicero said. Ending in *-us*, *mortuus*, “dead,” is thought to be a participle contrary to the rule concerning participles, but it has been converted to the force and rule of a noun.

## CHAPTER XXV — On the conjunction

The conjunction is a part of speech that connects and orders a sentence. The properties of the conjunction are form, order, and function.

Form appears in the simple form, but order also appears in the fact that some conjunctions can only be placed before what they govern, such as *nam*, “for”; some can only be placed after it, such as *-que*, “and”; and some can be placed either before or after it, such as *igitur*, “therefore.”

[Col. 1406]

The functions of conjunctions are divided into five classes. There are copulative conjunctions: *et*, *-que*, *ast*, *at*, *atque*, “and,” “but.” Disjunctive conjunctions: *aut*, *vel*, *-ve*, *nec*, *neque*, *neve*, *an*, *utrum*, “or,” “nor,” “whether.” Expletive conjunctions: *quidem*, *equidem*, *autem*, *tamen*, *porro*, *videlicet*, *proinde*, *denique*, *utique*, “indeed,” “however,” “nevertheless,” “moreover,” “evidently,” “therefore,” “finally,” “in any case.” Causal conjunctions: *si*, *etsi*, *tametsi*, *etiamsi*, *siquidem*, *quando*, *equidem*, *quin*, *quinetiam*, *sin*, *sinetiam*, *quanquam*, *quamvis*, *sinautem*, *seu*, *sive*, *namque*, *nisi*, *nisi si*, *enim*, *etenim*, *sed*, *ut*, *praeterea*, *interea*, *quamobrem*, *quare*, *praesertim*, *item*, *itemque*, *caeterum*, *alioquin*, “if,” “although,” “even if,” “since,” “but if,” “or,” “for,” “but,” “that,” “besides,” “meanwhile,” “for which reason,” “why,” “especially,” “likewise,” “otherwise,” and others. Rational conjunctions: *ita*, *itaque*, *enim*, *enimvero*, *quapropter*, *quippe*, *quoniam*, *quoniamquidem*, *ergo*, *igitur*, *ideo*, *idcirco*, *scilicet*, *praeterea*, “thus,” “therefore,” “for,” “indeed,” “for this reason,” “since,” “therefore,” “that is,” “besides.”

Among these, *et*, “and,” has many meanings. Often it passes into another functional class. Sometimes it is expletive, as:

> “And what such reason was there for you to see Rome?”  
> (*Eclogues* 1.27)

Sometimes it expresses quality or quantity:

> “I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts.”  
> (*Aeneid* 2.49)

Sometimes it is used as a disjunctive:

> “And would anyone worship the power of Juno, or, suppliant, place honor upon her altars?”  
> (*Aeneid* 1.52–53)

Sometimes it is causal:

> “Of whom Iphytus was already weighed down by age, and Pelias slow because of his wound to Ulysses”;  
> (*Aeneid* 2.435–436)

that is, “also slow because of his wound.”

Sometimes it is taken as an adverb of ordering:

> “They wash the body of the cold man and anoint it,”  
> (*Aeneid* 6.219)

instead of “then they anoint it.”

The conjunction *aut*, “or,” likewise has many meanings. Sometimes it is taken as an adverb of distinction:

> “Before the city the boys and youth in the first flower of life train their horses and tame chariots in the dust; or they bend strong bows, or hurl supple arrows with their arms.”  
> (*Aeneid* 7.163–165)

Sometimes it expresses time:

> “Or before the eyes of the gods he strolls among the rich altars and renews the feasts with gifts,”  
> (*Aeneid* 4.62–63)

that is, “now he strolls before the eyes of the gods among the altars.”

Likewise:

> “Or he tramples the columns with his chariot, or hurls spears snatched from the fleeing.”  
> (*Aeneid* 9.762–763)

The forms of conjunctions are twofold: simple, as *nam*, “for”; and compound, as *namque*, “for indeed.”

The order of conjunctions consists in this: some are prepositive, such as *at* and *ast*; some are postpositive, such as *-que*; and some are common, such as *et* and *igitur*. There are also expressions concerning which it is uncertain whether we should call them prepositions or adverbs, although they can all easily be distinguished. Conjunctions are also found placed in the position of other conjunctions, with their function altered.

## CHAPTER XXVI — On the preposition: prepositions governing the accusative, the ablative, or both

All prepositions are so called in general. Their species are these: some govern the accusative, some the ablative, and some both.

Accusative prepositions are expressed with the accusative case: *ad*, *apud*, *ante*, *adversus*, *cis*, *citra*, *circum*, *circa*, *contra*, *erga*, *extra*, *intra*, *infra*, *juxta*, *ob*, *penes*, *per*, *prope*, *propter*, *praeter*, *post*, *pone*, *secundum*, *supra*, *trans*, *ultra*. With these prepositions one must preserve the genders of nouns—that is, masculine, feminine, neuter, and common—and also preserve number.

Thus, masculine singular: *ad agrum*, “to the field”; plural: *ad agros*, “to the fields.” Feminine singular: *ad villam*, “to the farmhouse,” or *ad possessionem*, “to the estate”; plural: *ad villas*, “to the farmhouses,” or *ad possessiones*, “to the estates.” Neuter singular: *ad templum*, “to the temple,” *ad Capitolium*, “to the Capitol”; plural: *ad templa*, “to the temples,” *ad Capitolia*, “to the Capitols.” Common gender, singular: *ad civem*, “to the citizen”; *ad hostem*, “to the enemy”; *ad sacerdotem*, “to the priest.” Plural: *ad cives*, *ad hostes*, *ad sacerdotes*.

You should therefore observe all prepositions while preserving, as I said, gender and singular or plural number. Likewise preserve pronouns according to gender: masculine singular, *ad hunc*, “to this man”; plural, *ad hos*, “to these men”; feminine, *ad hanc*, “to this woman”; plural, *ad has*, “to these women.” Neuter: *ad* [Col. 1407] *hoc templum vado*, “I go to this temple”; plural, *ad haec templa*, “to these temples.” Common gender: *ad hunc et ad hanc sacerdotem*, “to this male and female priest”; plural, *ad hos et ad has sacerdotes*, “to these male and female priests”; likewise, *ad hos et ad has hostes*, “to these male and female enemies.”

The following prepositions govern the ablative in both singular and plural, with gender and number preserved: *a*, *ab*, *abs*, *cum*, *coram*, *clam*, *de*, *e*, *ex*, *pro*, *prae*, *palam*, *sine*, *absque*, *tenus*.

Masculine singular: *a fratre*, “from the brother”; plural: *a fratribus*, “from the brothers.” Feminine singular: *a sorore*, “from the sister”; plural: *a sororibus*, “from the sisters”; likewise *a civitate*, “from the city,” and *a civitatibus*, “from the cities.” Masculine singular with *ab*: *ab amico*, “from the friend”; plural: *ab amicis*, “from the friends”; *ab agro*, “from the field”; *ab agris*, “from the fields.” Feminine singular: *ab urbe*, “from the city”; plural: *ab urbibus*, “from the cities.” Neuter singular: *ab templo*, “from the temple”; plural: *ab templis*, “from the temples.” Common gender singular: *a cive*, “from the citizen”; plural: *a civibus*, “from the citizens”; *ab hoste*, “from the enemy”; plural: *ab hostibus*, “from the enemies.”

Observe this declension in all these ablative prepositions according to gender and number.

There remains a third class of prepositions, called prepositions of both cases, which govern both the accusative and the ablative.

## CHAPTER XXVII — The double class of prepositions called “of both cases”

Most people fail to understand the principle of these prepositions, and therefore their exposition does not appear clear. The distinction lies in motion and location. Some have thought that motion governs the accusative alone; it governs both cases, but according to a definite principle.

Motion governs the accusative when we signify that we move from one place to another, as *curro in forum*, “I run into the marketplace,” or *in campum*, “into the field.” If we say that we run from another place into the marketplace or into the field, we use the accusative.

But if the action takes place in one and the same place, we use the ablative: *curro in foro*, “I run in the marketplace”; *curro in campo*, “I run in the field.” Likewise: *ambulo in foro*, “I walk in the marketplace”; *ambulo in campo*, “I walk in the field.” If we walk from another place into the marketplace, we use the accusative; if we walk in the same place, we use the ablative: *ambulo in foro*, “I walk in the marketplace.” Likewise: *cadit in forum*, “he falls into the marketplace,” and *cadit in foro*, “he falls in the marketplace.”

Virgil says:

> “And he enters upon the ground and hides his head among the clouds.”  
> (*Aeneid* 4.177)

As in:

> “He walks more deeply through the fields,”  
> (*Georgics* 3.75–76)

that is, “he walks.” You see that there is motion, yet the ablative is claimed for it, because, as I said, the motion is in a place, not from one place to another.

Thus we say both *lapsum in piscinam*, “having fallen into the pool,” and *lapsum in piscina*, “having fallen in the pool.” If someone falls from another place into the pool, it is the accusative; but if he falls while already in that same pool, it is the ablative.

*Venio*, “I come,” always takes the accusative, because someone comes from one place to another. Once someone is already in a place, however, motion ceases.

Likewise, motion from one place to another is expressed by *volvo* or *evolvo*, “I roll” or “I roll out”:

> “To find a way by which he could roll the Xanthus out into the sea,”  
> (*Aeneid* 5.807–808)

that is, from its channel into the sea. But for rolling within the same place it takes the ablative:

> “They roll at the very bottom.”  
> (*Aeneid* 6.581)

Likewise *sub*, “under,” takes the accusative for motion from one place to another. Concerning a spear Virgil says: *sub pectus*, “under the breast,” and *sub illam rem*, “under that thing.” It also takes the ablative:

> “It happened to die beneath the high walls of Troy.”  
> (*Aeneid* 1.99–100)

that is, “to fall or lie beneath them.” “Beneath the high walls of Troy,” he says. Likewise, for motion from one place to another:

> “Or beneath uncertain shadows changed by the Zephyrs.”  
> (*Eclogues* 5.5)

And he added *succedimus*, “we advance,” where there is motion from one place to another.

*Super*, “over,” expresses motion in:

> “He will extend his rule over the Garamantes and Indians.”  
> (*Aeneid* 6.794–795)

But in a place:

> “The twin birds sit upon the tree.”  
> (*Aeneid* 6.203)

Likewise *subter*, “beneath,” expresses motion from one place to another:

> “He led huge Aeneas beneath the roof of the narrow dwelling.”  
> (*Aeneid* 8.366–367)

But in a place:

> “It is pleasing to endure all things beneath the dense shell.”  
> (*Aeneid* 9.513–514)

Thus *sub*, “under,” takes the accusative when motion is made from one place to another: *sub speluncam curro*, “I run under the cave.” But if you run while positioned beneath the cave itself, it takes the ablative: *sub spelunca curro*, “I run beneath the cave.”

Likewise *super*, “over,” takes the accusative when there is motion from one place to another: *super tectum curro*, “I run onto the roof.” But if someone [Col. 1408] runs while positioned on the roof, it takes the ablative: *super tecto curro*, “I run on the roof.”

Similarly, *subter fluctus mergo*, “I plunge beneath the waves,” takes the accusative if the motion of immersion is made from the shore. If someone is already among the waves, he is submerged *subter fluctibus*, “beneath the waves,” with the ablative.

Two local adverbs greatly assist this usage and distinction: *quo* and *ubi*. *Quo* indicates motion to a place; *ubi* indicates location in a place. Thus: “Where did the weapon come?”—“Into the enemy”; “Where did it stick?”—“In the enemy.” “Where did Catiline wish to direct the weapon?”—“Into the consul’s body”; “Where did he wish it to be fixed?”—“In the consul’s body.” Thus he says of the dagger: “So that you might think he fixed it in the consul’s body.”

Likewise, when we say, “Where are we fleeing?” the answer concerns a place to which we are going. “Where is he hiding?” concerns a place where he is. These two adverbs therefore assist, as we said, in distinguishing prepositions that govern both cases.

In this way they also clarify the passage in the *Verrines*: “What he had received on the head from the leader of the enemy.” He had therefore received a wound directed onto the head, but received in the head. Do we say, “To where do you receive a wound?” Certainly not, but “Where do you receive it?” And Virgil’s “Where do you order me to go?” signifies motion to a place. But for location: “Where should I place the seats?” (*Aeneid* 3.88). Location takes the ablative because it is contrary to motion.

The noun itself signifies a kind of sitting, as in: *sum in foro*, “I am in the marketplace”; *eram in foro*, “I was in the marketplace”; *fui in foro*, “I was in the marketplace”; *futurus sum in foro*, “I will be in the marketplace.” Likewise, simply: *sedeo*, “I sit”; *jaceo*, “I lie”; *cubo*, “I recline”; *sto*, “I stand”; *consisto*, “I remain”; *haereo*, “I stay.” All these pertain to location.

These matters must therefore be carefully considered and put into practice, so that in this system of prepositions we may show that we have diligently trained ourselves to speak correctly and without hesitation.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — On the interjection

The interjection is not a part of speech, but a sign of an emotion erupting from the mind into the voice. It signifies either joy, as *evax*, “hurrah!”; or bitterness, as *heu*, “alas!”; among the Greeks, *φεῦ* (*pheu*), “alas!”

Thus, as many as are the agitated movements of the mind, so many voices do they produce. They are called interjections because they interrupt speech, as in the following passage:

> “Here among the thick hazels she had just left the twin hopes of the flock—ah!—after bringing them forth upon the bare rock.”  
> (*Eclogues* 1.14–15)

The letter *a* is inserted in the middle of the speech.

## CHAPTER XXIX — Epilogue; and on the names of numbers

We have gone through all the parts of speech, enough for those who are occupied or negligent. What we omitted we supplied in the treatment of the noun.

We must know that the names of numbers from four up to one hundred are *ἄπτωτα* (*aptōta*), that is, indeclinable, and apply to every gender: *quatuor viri*, “four men”; *quatuor feminae*, “four women”; *quatuor mancipia*, “four slaves.” Thus we say *quatuor* in every case: *virorum quatuor*, “of four men”; *mulierum quatuor*, “of four women”; *mancipiorum quatuor*, “of four slaves.” In the dative: *viris quatuor*, *feminis quatuor*, *mancipiis quatuor*. In the accusative: *viros quatuor*, *feminas quatuor*, *mancipia quatuor*. In the vocative: *o viri quatuor*, *o feminae quatuor*, *o mancipia quatuor*. In the ablative: *a viris quatuor*, *a feminis quatuor*, *a mancipiis quatuor*.

I said that the numbers from four up to one hundred are indeclinable because *duo*, “two,” is declined: *duorum*, “of two”; *duobus*, “to or by two”; *duos* or *duo*, “two” in the accusative; *o duo*, “O two”; *ab his duobus*, “from these two.”

Three is likewise declined through the cases:

- Nominative: *hi et hae tres*, “these three men and women.”
- Genitive: *horum et harum trium*, “of these three men and women.”
- Dative: *his tribus*, “to or for these three.”
- Accusative: *hos et has tres*, “these three men and women.”
- Vocative: *o tres*, “O three.”
- Ablative: *ab his tribus*, “from these three.”

In the neuter gender: *haec tria*, “these three things”; *horum trium*, “of these three things”; *his tribus*, “to or by these three things”; *haec tria*, “these three things”; *o tria*, “O three”; *ab his tribus*, “from these three things.”

From this form we understand how to decline compounds. *Hic duumvir*, “this duumvir,” is as though one man among two men. Likewise *triumvir*, “triumvir,” means one man among three men. Thus this compound admits the genitive.

But when *quatuor*, “four,” is indeclinable, we say *quatuorviri*, “four men”; likewise *quinqueviri*, “five men,” and *sexviri*, “six men.” Hence Lucan says:

> “And the septemvir at the feasts,”

using *septem*, “seven,” in place of the genitive.

From two hundred up to nine hundred the names of numbers are declined: *hi ducenti*, “these two hundred men”; *hae ducentae*, “these two hundred women”; neuter *ducenta*, “these two hundred things.” *Mille*, “thousand,” is declinable.

[Col. 1409]

# PRINCIPLES OF DIALECTIC

[Note: [Col. 1409] This little work has recently been corrected from five manuscripts in which it is entitled *Treatise on Dialectic* and attributed to Augustine. But it was published under the name of Chirius Fortunatianus at Basel in the year 1558.]

*(C, G, S)*

## CHAPTER I — On simple words

Dialectic is the science of reasoning well. We reason through words. Words are therefore either simple or joined.

Simple words signify one thing: when we say *homo*, “man”; *equus*, “horse”; *disputat*, “he argues”; *currit*, “he runs.” You should not be surprised that *disputat*, although composed of two elements, is nevertheless numbered among simple words. For a matter is clarified by definition. It was said that a simple word is one that signifies one thing. Accordingly, we include *disputat* within this definition, but we do not include *loquor*, “I speak.”

Although *loquor* is one word, it nevertheless does not have a simple meaning, since it also signifies the person who speaks. It is therefore already subject to truth or falsity, for it can be denied or affirmed. Every first- and second-person verb, then, although uttered individually, will nevertheless be counted among joined words, which do not have a simple meaning.

For whoever says *ambulo*, “I walk,” makes both the walking and the person who walks understood. And whoever says *ambulas*, “you walk,” likewise signifies both the action that is performed and the person who performs it. But whoever says *ambulat*, “he walks,” signifies nothing other than the walking itself.

For this reason, the third person of a verb will always be counted among simple words. Yet it cannot as yet be affirmed or denied unless it is one of those words to which the meaning of a person is necessarily attached by the custom of speech, as when we say *pluit*, “it is raining,” or *ningit*, “it is snowing.” Even if we do not add who is raining or snowing, nevertheless, because this is understood, such a word cannot be numbered among simple words.

## CHAPTER II — Joined words
Conjoined words are those which, connected with one another, signify several things, as when we say, “A man walks,” or “A man hastening to the mountain walks,” and anything of that kind. But among conjoined words there are some which comprise a proposition, such as those just mentioned; others do not comprise one, but await something, as those same words we mentioned if you remove the verb *walks*, which has been supplied. For although the words “a man hastening to the mountain” are conjoined, the utterance still remains incomplete.

When, therefore, those words which do not complete a proposition have been separated out, what remain are conjoined words which do comprise a proposition. These likewise have two kinds. For either a proposition is comprised in such a way that it is subject to being true or false, as in “Every man walks,” or “No man walks,” and anything of this sort; or it is completed in such a way that, although it fulfills the mind’s intention, it cannot be affirmed or denied, as when we command, wish, curse, and in similar cases. For if someone says, “Proceed to the country house,” or “Would that he might proceed to the country house,” or “May the gods destroy him,” he cannot be accused of lying, nor can he be believed to be speaking the truth. He has affirmed or denied nothing. Consequently, propositions of this kind do not come under inquiry, nor do they require a disputant.

## CHAPTER III.—Which Propositions Are Simple and Which Conjoined

Those propositions which are subject to inquiry are either simple or conjoined. Simple propositions are uttered without any coupling with another proposition, as in what we say, “Every man walks.” Conjoined propositions are those whose coupling is judged, as in “If he walks, he moves.”

But when a judgment is made concerning the conjunction of propositions, this continues until one reaches the conclusion. The conclusion is what is established from the premises granted. What I mean is this: whoever says, “If he walks, he moves,” wishes to prove something, so that, once this has been granted, it remains for him to say that he walks; and the conclusion follows, which can no longer be denied—namely, that he moves—nor, likewise, can it be granted that he does not walk.

Again, if [Col. 1410] someone wishes to say in this way, “This man walks,” that is a simple proposition. If I grant it, and he adds another proposition which awaits something for the completion of the proposition—“Whoever walks moves”—and if I grant this also, then from this conjunction of propositions, although each has been separately uttered and granted, there follows that conclusion which must now necessarily be granted: “Therefore this man moves.”

## CHAPTER IV.—He Subdivides Conjoined Propositions

These points having been briefly established, let us consider the individual parts. There are two primary divisions: one concerning things that are spoken simply, where there is, as it were, the material of dialectic; the other concerning things that are spoken in conjunction, where the work itself already appears.

The part concerning simple expressions is called *On Speaking*. The part concerning conjoined expressions is divided into three sections. When the conjunction of words which does not complete a proposition has been set aside, that which completes a proposition in such a way that it does not yet produce an inquiry or require a disputant is called *On Expressing*. That which so completes the sense that simple propositions are judged is called *On Proposing*. That which so comprises a proposition that the conjunction itself is judged until one reaches the conclusion is called *On the Conclusion of Propositions*. Let us therefore explain each of these parts more carefully.

## CHAPTER V.—How Things, Words, the Sayable, and Expressions Are Treated in Logic. The Sayable and the Expression Differ

A word is the sign of any given thing, uttered by a speaker so that it can be understood by a hearer. A thing is whatever is understood, perceived, or hidden. [For corporeal things are known, spiritual things are understood; but God himself and formless matter are hidden. God is that which is neither a body, nor an animal, nor a sense, nor an intellect, nor anything that can be conceived. Formless matter is the mutability of mutable things, capable of receiving all forms. [Note: [Col. 1410] The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the Corbie and German manuscripts.]] A sign is also something which presents itself to the senses and displays something other than itself to the mind. To speak is to give a sign by means of articulated sound. By “articulated” I mean that which can be represented by letters.

Whether all these things that have been defined have been defined correctly, and whether the wording of the definitions should at this point have been followed by further definitions, will be determined by the place where the discipline of defining is treated. For now, listen attentively to what follows.

Every word produces a sound. For when it is in writing, it is not a word but the sign of a word. When the reader looks at the letters, what would burst forth in sound presents itself to the mind. For what else do written letters display to the eyes than themselves, and, beyond themselves, vocal sounds to the mind? Since shortly before we said that a sign is something which displays itself to the senses and something beyond itself to the mind, what we read are not words but signs of words.

But just as we misuse the term “letter”—although a letter is the smallest part of articulated speech—so that we call it a letter even when we see it written, although it is entirely silent and appears not as any part of speech but as the sign of a part of speech, so too a word is called a word when it is written, although the sign of the word’s signifying sound does not shine forth. Therefore, as I began to say, every word produces a sound.

But what produces a sound has nothing to do with dialectic. The sound of a word is at issue when one asks or observes by what arrangement of vowels it is softened or by what collision it gapes open; likewise, by what interposition of consonants it is knotted or by what congestion it is made harsh; and of how many or what kinds of syllables it consists. In such matters poetic rhythm and accent are treated by grammarians solely as matters of the ear.

Nevertheless, when these matters are discussed, the discussion is not outside dialectic, for dialectic is the science of disputation. But words are signs of things when they have force in respect of those things; whereas the things discussed here concern words. For since we cannot speak about words except by means of words, and since whenever we speak we speak about certain things, it occurs to the mind that words are signs of things in such a way that they do not cease to be things.

But when a word proceeds from the mouth, if it proceeds for its own sake—that is, so that something may be asked or disputed about the word itself—it is certainly a thing [Col. 1411] subject to disputation and inquiry. But the thing itself is called a word. Whatever the mind, not the ear, perceives from a word, and holds enclosed within the mind itself, is called the *sayable*. But when a word proceeds not for its own sake, but in order to signify something else, it is called an *expression*.

The thing itself, which is no longer a word, nor the conception of a word in the mind, whether it possesses a word by which it can already be signified or does not possess one, is called by its proper name simply a *thing*.

Thus these four must be distinctly held apart: word, sayable, expression, and thing.

What I called a word is both a word and signifies a word. What I called the sayable is a word, yet it does not signify a word; rather, it signifies what is understood in the word and contained in the mind. What I called an expression is a word, but one by which those two things together are signified: the word itself and what comes about in the mind through the word. What I called a thing is a word which signifies whatever remains beyond those three things just mentioned.

I see that these matters must be clarified by examples. Suppose, then, that a grammarian asks a boy the following question: “*Arms*—what part of speech is it?”

The word “*arms*” was uttered for its own sake—that is, the word was uttered for the sake of the word itself. But the rest of the question, “What part of speech is it?”, was uttered not for its own sake, but for the sake of the word “arms,” whether that word was perceived by the mind or uttered aloud.

When these words are perceived by the mind, before sound they are sayables; but when, on account of what I have said, they burst forth into sound, they become expressions.

The word “*arms*” itself, which here is a word, when pronounced by Virgil, was an expression. It was not uttered for its own sake, but so that by it there might be signified either the wars Aeneas waged, or his shield, or the other arms that Vulcan forged for Aeneas.

The wars or arms themselves—those waged or borne by Aeneas—which, when they were being conducted and existed, could be seen, and which, if they were present now, we could point to with a finger or touch; and even if they were not being thought of, this would not make them not to have existed—these, I say, are in themselves neither words, nor sayables, nor expressions. They are things, which are now called things by their proper name.

In this part of dialectic, therefore, we must treat words, expressions, sayables, and things. Since in all these, some words and some non-words are signified—for there is nothing about which it is not necessary to dispute by means of words—we first dispute about those means through which we are permitted to dispute about the rest.

Thus every word, apart from its sound, about which one may properly dispute, belongs to the capacity of dialectic, not to the discipline of dialectic. Cicero’s defenses, for example, certainly belong to the capacity of rhetoric, but rhetoric itself is not taught by means of those defenses.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the Origin of the Word. From What “Word” Is Derived. The Stoics’ Opinion Concerning the Origin of the Word

Every word, then, on account of the sound it produces, brings four matters necessarily into question: its origin, its force, its inflection, and its arrangement.

The origin of a word is investigated when one asks why it is called what it is called. In my opinion, this is an excessively curious matter and not very necessary. Nor did I say this merely because Cicero seems to think the same; for who needs authority in a matter so evident? If explaining the origin of a word were of much assistance, it would be foolish to undertake a task whose pursuit is plainly infinite. For who could discover what any word was called, or from what it received the name by which it is called?

Moreover, just as the interpretation of dreams is proclaimed according to each person’s ingenuity, so the origin of words is proclaimed according to each person’s ingenuity. For example, someone thinks that the words themselves were named from the fact that they seem to “strike” (*verberare*) the ear. “Rather,” says another, “because they strike the air.” But our disagreement is not great, since each derives the origin of this word from striking.

Then a third comes from the opposite direction—see what a quarrel he introduces. “Because it is necessary for us to speak what is true,” [Col. 1412] he says, “and because, by nature’s own judgment, lying is hateful, the word *verbum* is derived from *verum*, ‘true.’”

Nor was there a fourth theory lacking. Some think that *verbum* is indeed derived from *verum*, “true,” but maintain that, although attention has been paid to the first syllable, the second must not be neglected. For when we say *verbum*, they say, its first syllable signifies *verum*, “true,” and the second signifies a sound. They wish this sound to be a *bombus*, a boom. Hence Ennius said “the sound of feet,” *bombum pedum*; and the Greeks say *boan*, “to cry out”; and Virgil says, “The forests resound” (*Georgics* 3.223).

Thus, they say, *verbum* was named as though from “sounding forth the true”—that is, from “uttering the truth.” If this is so, the name indeed prescribes that, when we make a word, we should not lie; but I fear that those who say these things are themselves lying.

It is therefore for you to judge whether we should think that *verbum* was derived from striking, from *verum* alone, or from “sounding forth the true”—or whether we should rather not concern ourselves with where it was derived from, since we understand what it signifies.

Nevertheless, I want you briefly to accept this short discussion of the origin of words, so that we may not seem to have omitted any part of the work we have undertaken.

The Stoics maintain—and Cicero ridicules them on this point—that there is no word whose certain derivation cannot be explained. Since it was easy to suggest this by saying that the matter is infinite, they proposed that, when you have interpreted the origin of one word through other words, you must in turn investigate the origin of those words, until one reaches a point where the thing corresponds to the sound of the word by some resemblance, as when we speak of the ringing of bronze, the neighing of horses, the bleating of sheep, the blaring of trumpets, or the rattling of chains.

You see that these words sound in such a way as to resemble the things signified by them. But since there are things that do not produce sounds, they held that in such cases resemblance of touch is effective: if things touch the sense gently or harshly, then the gentleness or harshness of the letters, just as it touches the hearing, gave birth to their names.

Even the word *lene*, “gentle,” sounds gentle. Who, likewise, would not judge harshness to be harsh in the very name? It is gentle to the ears when we say *voluptas*, “pleasure”; it is harsh when we say *crux*, “cross.” Thus things themselves affect us in the manner in which words are perceived.

As sweetly as honey itself touches the taste, so sweetly does its name touch the hearing. *Acre*, “sharp,” is harsh in both respects. Wool and brambles affect the touch just as their words affect the hearing.

They believed these to be, as it were, the cradles of words: the senses of things corresponded with the sense of sounds. From there, the freedom of naming proceeded to the resemblance of things among themselves. Thus, for example, the *cross* (*crux*) was supposedly so called because the harshness of the word itself corresponds to the harshness of the pain produced by a cross.

But *crura*, “legs,” were not so called because of the harshness of pain; rather, because in length and hardness they are more similar than the other limbs to the wood of a cross, they received that name.

From there the process reached abuse of language, so that a word came to be used for something not so much similar as, so to speak, adjacent. For what similarity is there between the signification of “small” and “minced,” since something can be small without being at all minced, and may even have grown? Nevertheless, because of a certain proximity, we say *minutum* for “small.”

But this abusive use of a word lies within the speaker’s power: he has *parvum*, “small,” available so that it need not be called *minutum*.

What bears more directly on the point we wish to establish is that when *piscina*, “pool,” is spoken of in a bathhouse, although it contains no fish and has nothing resembling fish, it nevertheless seems to have been named from fish because of the water in which fish live. Thus the word was used not by a transfer based on resemblance, but because of a certain proximity.

If someone says that human beings become like fish by swimming, and that this is the origin of the name *piscina*, it is foolish to refute him, since neither explanation is contrary to the matter and both remain concealed.

Still, it is useful that by means of one example we can now make clear the difference between an origin of a word drawn from proximity and one derived from resemblance.

From this the progression reached even to contraries. For *lucus*, “grove,” is thought to have been named because it shines least; *bellum*, “war,” because the matter is not beautiful; and *foedus*, “treaty,” because the matter is not foul.

But if *foedus* was derived from the foulness of the pig, as some wish, then it returns to that proximity by which what is done is named from that through which it is done. For this kind of proximity is extremely broad and is divided into many parts:

Either by the agent, [Col. 1413] as in this case, from the foulness of the pig by which the treaty is made;

or by the effect, as *puteus*, “well,” is thought to have been so called because its effect is drinking;

or by what contains something, as they wish *urbs*, “city,” to have been named from *orbis*, “circle,” because a plow is customarily driven around the place auspiciously marked out. Virgil also recalls this when Aeneas marks out a city with a plow (*Aeneid* 5.755);

or by what is contained, as when someone maintains that *horreum*, “granary,” was named from *hordeum*, “barley,” with the letter *d* changed;

or by abuse of language, as when we say “barley” although wheat is stored there;

or from the part for the whole, as when the name *mucro*, “point,” which is the uppermost part of a sword, is used for the whole sword;

or from the whole for the part, as in *capillus*, “hair,” as though “the hair of the head.”

Why should I proceed further? You will see that whatever else can be counted is contained either under resemblance of things and sounds, or resemblance of things themselves, or proximity, or contrariety. Such is the origin of words. We cannot pursue it beyond resemblance of sound—though even that is not always possible.

For there are countless words whose derivation cannot be explained—either, as I think, because no derivation exists, or, as the Stoics maintain, because it is hidden.

Observe, however, briefly how they think one reaches the cradles of words—or rather their root and, indeed, their seed—beyond which they forbid further inquiry into the origin, and beyond which, even if someone wished to inquire, he could discover nothing.

No one doubts that syllables in which the letter *V* functions as a consonant, as in *venter*, “belly,” *vafer*, “cunning,” *velum*, “sail,” *vinum*, “wine,” *vomis*, “plowshare,” and *vulnus*, “wound,” produce a thick and, so to speak, forceful sound.

This is also confirmed by ordinary speech, when we remove those letters from certain words so that they do not burden the ear. Hence we say *amasti* rather than *amavisti*, “you loved,” and *abiit* rather than *abivit*, “he went away,” and countless examples of the same kind.

Therefore, when we say *vim*, “force,” the sound of the word, as has been said, corresponds, as it were, in its forcefulness to the thing signified.

Then, from that proximity based on what things produce—that is, because they are violent—*vincula*, “bonds,” may be thought to have been named, as well as *vimen*, “a flexible twig,” by which something is bound. From this come *vites*, “vines,” because they hang from supports by the ties with which they are bound.

From this, also by resemblance, Terence called a bent old man *vietus*, “withered” or “bent.”

From this comes *via*, “road,” because the earth, bent and worn by the feet of travelers, is called a road. But if *via*, the road worn by the force of feet, is believed to have been so called, the origin returns to that proximity.

Let us suppose, however, that it was named from the resemblance of a vine or flexible twig—that is, from its bending. Someone then asks me why it is called *via*. I answer: “From bending,” because the ancients called something bent or crooked *vietum*, “bent.” Hence they call the wooden parts of wheels *vieti*, because they are enclosed by the rim.

He continues to ask where *vietum*, “bent,” received this meaning. I answer: “From the resemblance of a vine.”

He presses and demands the origin of the name *vitis*, “vine.” I say: “Because it binds (*vincit*) whatever it has grasped.”

He examines where *vincire*, “to bind,” received its name. We say: “From *vis*, ‘force.’”

He asks why *vis* is so called. The explanation is given: “Because the word, with its strong and forceful sound, corresponds to the thing signified.” Beyond this he has nothing to ask.

It would be pointless to pursue the many ways in which the origin of words is altered through corruption of sounds. The discussion would be lengthy and less necessary than what has already been said.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the Force of the Word

Let us now consider briefly, insofar as the subject permits, the force of words. The force of a word is that by which one recognizes how much power it possesses. It possesses as much power as it can exert upon the hearer.

Moreover, it moves the hearer either according to itself, or according to what it signifies, or according to both together. When it moves him according to itself, this concerns either the sense alone, or an art, or both.

The sense is moved either by nature or by habit.

It is moved by nature when someone is offended if King Artaxerxes is named, or is pleased when he hears “Euryalus.” For who, even if he has heard nothing at all about the men whose names these are, would not nevertheless judge the former to possess the greatest harshness and the latter gentleness?

The sense is moved by habit when it is offended upon hearing something. For in this case the pleasantness or unpleasantness of the sound has no bearing; nevertheless, the innermost recesses of the ears are affected according to whether, as sounds pass through, they receive them as familiar guests or as strangers.

The hearer is moved by an art when, after a word has been uttered to him, he attends [Col. 1414] to what part of speech it is, or to anything else that he has learned in those disciplines which are taught concerning words.

But a word is judged according to both sense and art when reason observes what the ears measure and assigns the name accordingly, as in *optimus*, “best.” As soon as one long syllable and two short syllables of this word strike the ear, the mind immediately recognizes, through its knowledge of the art, a dactylic foot.

The word moves the sense not according to itself but according to what it signifies when, having received the sign through the word, the mind looks at nothing other than the thing itself of which it has received the sign. Thus, when “Augustine” is named, I myself alone am thought of by the person who knows me [Note: [Col. 1414] From this passage it clearly follows that the author of this little work is named Augustine. Which Augustine he is, however, is uncertain. Some have thought that he is the same person to whom the books *On the Wonders of Holy Scripture* are attributed, though they have been relegated to the appendix of volume 3. M.]; or any person comes to the mind if he happens to hear this name—whether someone who does not know me, or someone who knows another man called Augustine.

But when a word moves the hearer both according to itself and according to what it signifies, then both the word that has been uttered and what is uttered through it are perceived together.

For why is the chastity of the ears not offended when one hears, “With hand, belly, and penis he had torn apart his paternal estate,” while it would be offended if an obscene part of the body were called by a sordid and vulgar name? In this case, the ugliness of both would offend sense and mind unless the ugliness of the thing signified were covered by the beauty of the word signifying it, since the thing is the same though it has two names. It is like the same prostitute who appears one way in the dress in which she usually stands before a judge, and another way in the dress in which she lies in the chamber of a debauched man.
