Since, then, words evidently possess so great and so manifold a force, which we have briefly and summarily touched upon as the occasion permitted, a twofold consideration of sense arises here: partly for explaining truth, and partly for preserving decorum. The first belongs chiefly to the dialectician, the second to the orator.

For although an inept argument is unbecoming and eloquence ought not to be deceitful, nevertheless in disputation—and indeed almost always—the desire for learning disregards the pleasures of hearing; whereas in oratory the less educated crowd often thinks that what is said elegantly is also said truthfully.

Since, then, it is clear what belongs properly to each, it is evident that a disputant, if he has any concern for pleasing, should be sprinkled with rhetorical color; and that an orator, if he wishes to persuade people of the truth, must be strengthened by something like the sinews and bones of dialectic. Nature itself could neither remove these from the firmness of our bodies nor permit them to be exposed as an offense to the eyes.

Therefore, in order to judge the truth, which dialectic professes to do, let us examine what obstacles arise from this force of words, some seeds of which we have scattered here and there.

## CHAPTER VIII.—The Obscure and the Ambiguous. The Difference Between the Obscure and the Ambiguous. Three Kinds of Obscurity

In words, either obscurity or ambiguity prevents the hearer from seeing the truth.

The difference between the obscure and the ambiguous is this: in the ambiguous, several possibilities present themselves, but it is unknown which one ought rather to be accepted; in the obscure, nothing, or very little that can be attended to, appears.

But when little appears, the obscure resembles the ambiguous. For example, suppose someone traveling along a road is confronted by a place where there are two roads, or three, or even—as I may put it—a multitude of roads, but because of the density of the fog none of the roads is visible. At first, then, obscurity prevents him from proceeding.

When the fog begins to thin somewhat, something becomes visible, but it is uncertain whether it is a road or the brighter, more polished color peculiar to the ground. This is an obscure situation resembling an ambiguous one.

When the sky has cleared sufficiently for the eyes, the course of all the roads is now clear; but which road one should take is uncertain not because of obscurity, but because of ambiguity.

There are likewise three kinds of obscurity.

The first is something that is open to the senses but closed to the mind. For example, suppose someone sees a painted pomegranate but has never [Col. 1415] seen one before and has never heard what it is like. The problem lies not with the eyes but with the mind, which does not know what thing the picture represents.

The second kind occurs when the thing would be open to the mind if it were not closed to the senses, as with a painted man in darkness. For when he appears to the eyes, the mind will have no doubt that he is a painted man.

The third kind is that in which something is hidden even from the senses and, if it were shown, would still not stand out any more clearly to the mind. This is the most obscure kind of all: for example, if an ignorant person were compelled to recognize that painted pomegranate even in darkness.

Now turn your attention to words, to which these examples correspond.

Suppose a grammarian, having summoned his students and established silence, says in a subdued voice, “*Temetum*.” Those sitting nearby hear what he has said well; those farther away hear it imperfectly; those farthest away are not touched by any sound at all.

Some of these knew what *temetum* was—namely, those who by some chance were farther away—while the others were entirely unaware of it. All were hindered by obscurity.

Here you can now see all those kinds of obscurity. Those who heard the word without uncertainty suffered the first kind, corresponding to the pomegranate unknown to those who see it painted in the light.

Those who knew the word but received its sound only imperfectly or not at all through their ears suffered from the second kind, corresponding to the image of a man not in a visible place but in a wholly dark one.

Those who lacked not only the sound but also the meaning of the word were enveloped in the blindness of the third kind, which is altogether the worst.

What was said earlier—that a certain obscurity resembles ambiguity—can be seen in those who knew the word but had perceived either no sound at all or no definite sound.

The person who uses a voice clear enough, with an unobstructed mouth, and words that are thoroughly familiar will avoid all kinds of obscurity in speaking.

Now observe in the same example of the grammarian how much more extensively ambiguity obstructs understanding than the obscurity of a word.

Suppose that those who were present had heard the teacher’s voice clearly and through their senses, and that he had uttered a word familiar to everyone. Let us suppose, for example, that he said “*Magnus*” and then fell silent.

Consider what uncertainty they experience upon hearing this word.

What if he is about to ask, “What part of speech is it?”

What if he is going to ask, concerning meters, what kind of foot it is?

What if he is going to ask a historical question, such as how many wars Magnus Pompey fought?

What if, in order to praise poems, he is going to say, “Magnus, and almost the only poet, is Virgil”?

What if, to rebuke the students’ negligence, he should continue with these words: “A great sluggishness has seized you in your zeal for study and discipline”?

Do you see that, once the fog of obscurity has been removed, what was said above has emerged as though it were a place with many roads?

For this one utterance, *magnus*, is a noun, a choreic foot, Pompey, Virgil, and a great torpor of negligence. And there are other possibilities—indeed innumerably many—not mentioned here, which nevertheless can be understood through this utterance of the word.

## CHAPTER IX.—Two Kinds of Ambiguity

The dialecticians were therefore entirely correct in saying that every word is ambiguous.

Nor should one be disturbed by what Hortensius, in Cicero, reproachfully says in the following manner: “They claim that they hear ambiguities sharply and explain them clearly. They also say that every word is ambiguous. How, then, will they explain ambiguities by means of ambiguities? For this is to bring extinguished light into darkness.”

It is certainly a facile and clever remark. But this is what Antonius says to Scaevola in that same Cicero: “In short, so that you may seem to speak eloquently to the wise and truthfully even to fools.”

For what else does Hortensius do in that passage except, through keenness of intellect and charm of speech, pour darkness over the inexperienced as though with a pure and pleasant drink?

When it is said that every word is ambiguous, this is said of individual words. Ambiguities are explained through disputation, and no one disputes by means of single words. Therefore no one will explain ambiguous words by ambiguous words.

Nevertheless, although every word is ambiguous, no one will explain an ambiguous word except by words—though by conjoined words, which are no longer ambiguous.

For if it were said, “Every soldier is two-footed,” it would not follow from this that an entire cohort [Col. 1416] consisted of two-footed soldiers. Likewise, when I say that every word is ambiguous, I am not speaking of a proposition or of a disputation, although these things are woven together out of words.

Every ambiguous word, therefore, will be explained by a non-ambiguous disputation.

Let us now examine the kinds of ambiguity. There are two primary kinds: one occurs even in things that are spoken; the other creates uncertainty only in things that are written.

For if someone hears *acies*, or if someone reads it, he may remain uncertain—unless the proposition makes the meaning clear—whether the word refers to a line of soldiers, the edge of a weapon, or the sharpness of the eyes.

But if someone finds written, for example, *leporem*, and it is not apparent in what sense it has been used, he will certainly wonder whether the penultimate syllable of this word should be lengthened, from *lepos*, “charm,” or shortened, from *lepus*, “hare.”

He would of course not experience this ambiguity if he received the accusative case of the noun from a speaker’s voice.

If someone says that the speaker could have pronounced it incorrectly, the hearer would then be obstructed not by ambiguity but by obscurity. Yet it belongs to that kind which resembles ambiguity, because a word badly pronounced in Latin does not draw the thinker toward different interpretations, but drives him toward the one that appears.

Although these two kinds differ greatly from one another, the first kind is again divided into two. Whatever is said can be understood in several ways, and these several meanings are held either by one word and one interpretation, or by one word alone but are explained through different interpretations.

Those which can be included under one definition are called *univocal*. But those which must be defined differently under one name are called *equivocal*.

Let us therefore first consider univocal terms, so that this already-disclosed category may be illuminated by examples.

When we say “man,” we include a boy, a young man, and an old man; a foolish man and a wise man; a great man and a small man; a citizen and a foreigner; a city-dweller and a rustic; one who has already lived and one who lives now; one who is sitting and one who is standing; a rich man and a poor man; one who is doing something and one who is idle; one who is rejoicing and one who is grieving—or one who is doing neither.

But among all these expressions there is nothing which, just as it receives the name “man,” is not also enclosed by the definition of man. For the definition of man is “a rational mortal animal.”

No one can therefore say that “rational mortal animal” means only a young man, and not also an old man or a boy; or only a wise man, and not also a foolish one. On the contrary, all these and the other cases listed are contained both by the name “man” and by the definition.

For whether someone is a boy, a fool, a poor man, or even asleep, if he is not a rational mortal animal, he is not a man. But he is a man; therefore he must be contained by that definition.

There is no ambiguity concerning the other cases. But regarding a small boy, a fool, or one who is completely stupid, or someone asleep, drunk, or raving, it may be questioned how they can be rational animals, even if this could be defended. But that would take us too far while we are hurrying toward other matters.

For the present, it is enough that this definition of man is not correct unless every man is contained by it and nothing besides man is.

These, then, are univocal terms: they are enclosed not only under one name but also under one definition of that same name, although they can be distinguished from one another by their proper names and definitions.

For the different names—boy, adolescent, rich man and poor man, free man and slave, and whatever other differences there may be—will each have their own proper definitions. But just as they have one common name, “man,” so they also have one common definition, “rational mortal animal.”

## CHAPTER X.—The Various Forms of Ambiguity Arising from Equivocal Terms

[The supplied source ends here.]

Now let us examine equivocal terms, in which the tangle of ambiguities grows almost without limit. I shall nevertheless try to classify them into definite kinds. Whether my effort is matched by my ability, you will judge.

There are, then, three primary kinds of ambiguity arising from equivocal terms: one arising from technical usage, another from ordinary usage, and a third from both. By “technical usage” I now mean the names imposed upon words in the disciplines concerning language. For the same thing that I call *Tullius* is defined one way among grammarians and another among dialecticians; yet this one item—*Tullius*, as I call it—is both a name, a dactylic foot, and an equivocal term.

Thus, if someone demanded that I define what *Tullius* is, I could answer by explaining any one of its meanings. I could properly say: “*Tullius* is the name by which a certain supreme orator is signified, the man who, as consul, suppressed Catiline’s conspiracy.” Pay close attention to the fact that I have defined the name itself. For if I had to define Tullius himself—the man who, if he were alive, could be pointed out with a finger—I would not say, “Tullius is the name by which a man is signified,” but rather, “Tullius is a man,” and I would add the rest in the same way.

I could likewise answer: “This name *Tullius* is a dactyl, consisting of these letters”; for it is necessary to indicate that it possesses those letters. One may even say: “*Tullius* is a word by which all the things mentioned above, together with anything else that can be found, are made equivocal with one another.”

But I say: since this name that I have mentioned, *Tullius*, may properly be defined in so many ways according to the terminology of the disciplines, why should we hesitate to recognize a kind of ambiguity arising from equivocal terms that may rightly be said to arise from technical usage? For we have said that equivocal terms are those which cannot be held together by one definition any more than by one name.

Hence there is a second kind, which, as we have recalled, arises from ordinary usage in speech. By “usage” I now mean that verbal expression through which we recognize words. For who would seek out and gather words merely for the sake of words? Let us therefore suppose someone listening in such a way that he knows that no question is being raised about the parts of speech, about meters, or about any discipline concerning words. Even so, when the word *Tullius* is uttered, he may still be obstructed by the ambiguity of equivocal terms.

For by this name one may signify the man himself who was the supreme orator, his painted likeness or statue, the book containing his writings, or whatever remains of his corpse in his tomb. We speak in different senses when we say: “Tullius freed his country from destruction”; “Gilded Tullius stands in the Capitol”; “Tullius must be read by you in its entirety”; and “Tullius is buried in this place.” There is one name, but all these expressions must be explained by different definitions.

This, then, is the kind of equivocal term in which no ambiguity arises from the discipline of words, but from the very things that are signified. If, however, both kinds confuse the listener or reader—whether what is said arises from technical usage or from ordinary usage in speech—should we not rightly count a third kind? Its example appears more clearly in a sentence, as when someone says: “Many have written in dactylic meter, such as Tullius.” Here it is uncertain whether *Tullius* is given as an example of a dactylic foot or of a poet who wrote in dactylic meter: the former meaning is taken from technical usage, the latter from ordinary usage in speech.

But this also occurs in simple words, even if a grammarian merely pronounces the sound of this word before his pupils, as we showed above. Since these three kinds therefore differ from one another according to clear distinctions, the first kind is again divided into two.

Whatever, through technical usage, creates ambiguity in words may either itself serve as an example or may not. When I define what the noun signifies, I can use the very thing I call a noun as an example: it is certainly a noun, for according to this rule it is inflected through the cases when we say *nomen, nominis, nomini*, and so on. Likewise, when I define what *dactyl* signifies, the word itself can serve as an example; for when we say *dactylus*, we utter one long syllable followed by two short ones.

But when what an adverb signifies is defined, the word itself cannot be given as an example. For when we say *adverbium*, that utterance itself is a noun. According to one meaning, therefore, *adverbium* is indeed an adverb; according to another, it is not an adverb, because it is a noun.

Likewise, when the meaning of a Cretic foot is defined, the word itself cannot serve as an example. For when we say *creticus*, the utterance consists of a first long syllable followed by two short ones; but what the word signifies is a long syllable, a short syllable, and a long syllable. Thus, according to one meaning, *creticus* is nothing other than a Cretic foot and is not a dactyl; according to another, *creticus* is not a Cretic foot, because it is a dactyl.

The second kind—already said to belong to ordinary usage because of the disciplines concerning words—has two forms. For equivocal terms arise either from the same origin or from different origins.

I call them “from the same origin” when, although they are held together by one name and not by one definition, they nevertheless flow, as it were, from a single source. Such is the case when *Tullius* can be understood as a man, a statue, a book, or a corpse. These cannot indeed be enclosed within one definition, but they have one source: the actual man Tullius, whose statue, book, and corpse they are.

They arise from different origins when, for example, the word *nepos* signifies, from entirely different origins, a son’s son and a dissolute man.

Let us keep these distinctions in view. The kind that I call “from the same origin” is itself divided again, for it is divided into two forms, one arising through transference and the other through inflection.

I call it “transference” when one name is applied to many things either on account of resemblance—as when *Tullius* is said both of the man in whom there was great eloquence and of his statue—or from the whole to the part, as when his corpse can be called *Tullius*; or from the part to the whole, as when we call the roofs entire houses.

It may also arise from a genus to a species. For the Romans call all the expressions with which we speak *verba* (“words”); yet *verba* properly names those expressions that we inflect through moods and tenses. Or it may arise from a species to a genus: for although *scholastici* properly and originally denotes those who are still in school, all who live devoted to letters nevertheless use this name.

It may arise from the agent to the effect, as when Cicero is called a book of Cicero; or from the effect to the agent, as with *terror*, because it produced terror. It may arise from the container to what it contains, as when the house is also said of those who are in the house; or in the reverse direction, as when *chestnut tree* is said both of the tree and of its fruit. Or it may arise in any other way that can be found, when something receives a transferred name from the same origin.

You see, I think, what produces ambiguity in words. What we call ambiguous through the condition of inflection, when it belongs to the same origin, is of the following sort.

Suppose, for example, that someone has said *pluit* (“it is raining”). This must certainly be defined in different ways. Likewise, when someone says *scribere* (“to write”), it is uncertain whether it has been pronounced as the active infinitive or as the passive imperative. Although *homo* is one name and one utterance, it becomes one thing when taken as a nominative and another when taken as a vocative.

[Note: In B., *quid*; Er., *quin*. M.]

The utterance of the words *doctius* (“more learned” or “more learnedly”) and *docte* (“learnedly”) is likewise different. It is one thing when we say *doctius mancipium* (“a more learned slave”), and another when we say *doctius illo disputavit* (“he argued more learnedly than that man”).

The ambiguity has therefore arisen through inflection. By “inflection” I now mean whatever happens when words are bent, whether through their sounds or through their meanings. In *doctus* and *docte*, the inflection occurs only through the sounds; in *homo* and *homo*, according to their meanings alone.

To divide up and pursue this kind of ambiguity in detail would be almost endless. It will therefore be enough to have indicated the matter itself thus far, especially in view of your intelligence.

Now consider those that arise from different origins. These are themselves divided into two primary forms. One occurs through the diversity of languages: for example, when we say *iste*, this single sound signifies one thing among the Greeks and another among us. Not everyone knows this kind, however; it is not evident to anyone except one who knows languages or who is discussing languages.

The other form creates ambiguity within one language, although the things signified by one word have different origins. Such is the example of *nepos* that we gave above. This is again divided into two: either the meanings belong under the same part of speech, as *nepos* is a noun both when it signifies a son’s son and when it signifies a dissolute man; or they belong under different parts of speech, as in the line quoted from Terence:

> “Who, then, could know that, unless you had made the experiment?”  
> (*Terence, Andria* 3.3.33)

Here *istuc* is both a pronoun and an adverb.

Thus, from both sources together—that is, from the technical and ordinary uses of words—the third kind that we had placed among equivocal terms can produce as many forms of ambiguity as we had placed in the two preceding kinds.

There remains that kind of ambiguity which is found only in writing. It has three species: ambiguity may arise from the quantity of the syllables, from accent, or from both.

It arises from quantity when *venit* is written: it is uncertain whether the word refers to the present or the past, because the quantity of the first syllable is concealed.

It arises from accent when *pone* is written: it is uncertain whether it comes from *pono* (“I place”) or is used as in the following line:

> “Following behind, for Proserpina had imposed this law.”  
> (*Georgics* 4.487)

The uncertainty arises because the position of the accent is hidden.

It arises from both quantity and accent, as in the example concerning *lepore* that we gave above. For the penultimate syllable of this word must not only be lengthened but also accented if it is inflected from *lepos* (“charm”), rather than from *lepus* (“hare”).

## TEN CATEGORIES EXCERPTED FROM ARISTOTLE  
*(C, G, S)*

### Editorial Notice Concerning the Following Little Work

We have again corrected the little work *On the Ten Categories* against seven manuscripts. Of these, the very ancient Germanensis manuscript places the following at its front:

> Prologue of Alcuin to Charles Augustus on Augustine’s *Categories*.
>
> This little book contains ten words of nature,
>
> Words which now hold the meanings of things,
> In a manner astonishing to reason,
>
> Everything that could flow into our understanding.
>
> Whoever reads it should praise the marvelous genius of the ancients,
>
> And strive to exercise his own through such labor,
>
> Adorning the times allotted to life with honorable titles.
>
> Augustine the teacher was pleased to translate this work,
>
> With a Latin key from the treasures of the ancient Greeks.
>
> This work I now send for you to read,
> Great King, seeker and lover of wisdom,
>
> You who rejoice in such a gift.

[Col. 1419] Aristotle’s *Categories* translated from Greek into Latin by Augustine. The same verses are found in the Michaelinus manuscript and in the Amerbach edition, but without the superscription “Prologue of Alcuin,” and so forth.

We think that this very work is designated in Book 1 of the life of Odo, abbot of Cluny, by these words:

> “In those days Odo went to Paris, and there read through Augustine’s *Dialectic*, sent to Augustine’s son Adeodatus, and frequently studied Martianus in the liberal arts; for in all these matters he had Remigius as his teacher.”

[Note: Through an error arising from a gloss in the manuscripts, of which Michael has the following in the margin: “He sent these *Categories* to his son named Adeodatus.”]

Thus in former times the author of this little work was believed to be Augustine, to whom many other works were falsely attributed by the ancients, as no one is unaware. Certainly Augustine himself nowhere mentions that he dealt with the *Categories*. Nor, as we observed above, are the same features found here as in the book on *Dialectic* mentioned in Book 1 of the *Retractions*, chapter 6. That work he had written in dialogue form, with the purpose of reaching or leading to incorporeal things through corporeal things.

Moreover, observe how highly the author of this little work values Aristotle’s categories, which he professes to have acquired through unremitting labor and under the instruction of the philosopher Themistius. Augustine, by contrast, in Book 5 of *Against Julian*, chapter 14, reproaches that adversary of his for possessing a foolish knowledge of Aristotle’s categories; and in Book 4 of the *Confessions*, chapter 16, he declares that he understood them without difficulty and without the assistance of his teacher.

Furthermore, Augustine preferred Plato to Aristotle, as can be seen in Book 8 of *The City of God*, chapter 12. The other author, without doubt, prefers Aristotle to the rest, calling him simply “the Philosopher” by antonomasia.

Finally, the name Adeodatus, which appears in the printed editions at the beginning after the words “O son,” should not be passed over in silence. It is not found in the manuscripts, except perhaps written by a second hand in the margin or between the lines.

## THE TEN CATEGORIES

### CHAPTER ONE — On Speech, and How Broadly the Signification of οὐσία Extends

Although every science and discipline of the various arts is treated only through speech, no one distinguished in any field has yet been found who wished to discuss the origin or beginning of speech itself. Aristotle the philosopher’s diligence is therefore worthy of wonder: eager to reason about everything, he began with an examination of speech itself, knowing that it had been neglected by everyone and was necessary to everyone.

He therefore taught us that, of the eight parts of speech which grammarians call such, only that one is properly called a part of speech which indicates something and signifies it by a word. Accordingly, on Aristotle’s authority, we ought to accept only the noun and the verb as parts of speech; the rest should rather be called combinations of speech than its parts. For a noun indicates a person, while a verb indicates what someone does or undergoes.

From this teaching we must also observe how, through a process of gradual compression, speech has progressively enclosed within a single word everything that exists. Although the names of mortals are diverse and innumerable, and such a wide variety of names could not be comprehended, nevertheless, once you have said “man,” you recognize them all. The same is true of other things: that horse is *ξανθός* (*xanthos*, “yellow-haired”), or *αἴθριος* (*aithrios*, “bright”), or *δῖος* (*dios*, “divine”), or this one and that one.

Although the range of these names is also infinite, when someone says “horse,” he indicates them all. If someone gives names, as is customary, to individual lions or oxen, knowledge of each one extends without limit and the mind’s vision is blunted. But when you say “lion” or “bull,” all those existing everywhere fall under one name of nature.

Yet the power of speech, which had gathered the infinite kinds produced by the variety of generation into individual words, seemed to have accomplished too little unless it also compressed them and enclosed them under one universal designation. Thus it called man, beast, and horse “animal,” giving all of them a name that possessed everything.

Nor did it deal less efficiently with things without souls, marking them out briefly from an immense range of examples. For although there are trees of walnut, chestnut, oak, apple, and other inexplicable kinds of shrubs, it bound them all together under the single common word “shoot.” Likewise, it called the various stones used for ornaments “gems.”

Finally, although it had adequately provided for the scattered kinds by joining them under a special designation, it nevertheless embraced everything that exists under one immense name, capable of extending to infinity: it called it *οὐσία* (*ousia*, “substance”), beyond which nothing can be found or conceived.

This is one of the ten categories. It is clear that they were called “categories” because they cannot be recognized except from things that underlie them: *ὡς κατὰ τινῶν λεχθεῖσαι* (“as being spoken of certain things”). For who could recognize what man is unless he placed some man before his eyes as the subject of the term “man”?

But lest, as the discussion proceeds—where many examples are needed—the same names have to be repeated for instruction, and lest the frequent use of examples such as Hortensius, a taller man, a higher animal, or a more elevated *ousia* become wearisome, he adapted other terms that philosophers would use in argument. Thus he called Hortensius, the walnut tree, the horse Xanthus, and similar things *αἰσθητά* (*aisthēta*, “perceptible”), *ἄτομα* (*atoma*, “indivisible”), *ἑνάριθμα* (*henarithma*, “numbered as one”), and *καθ᾽ ἕκαστα* (*kath’ hekastā*, “particulars”).

He called them *αἰσθητά* because they are perceived by touch; *ἄτομα* because they cannot be divided or cut. For who could believe that Hortensius could be cut into parts? If that happened, Hortensius would no longer exist. He called them *ἑνάριθμα* because they are numerically one; and *καθ᾽ ἕκαστα* because they are particulars. For these cannot be multiplied within any one individual.

Next, he called the higher entities—that is, man, horse, lion, and tree—*εἴδεα* or *ἰδέαι* (*eidea* or *ideai*, “forms” or “ideas”), as though they were parts of a genus and forms of things.

Then he called the higher entities—that is, animals, plants, gems, and stones—genera, from which the parts or forms arise. Yet these same entities may also be called genera, species, or ideas, because they possess something higher, namely *ousia*, from which they appear to arise and be generated. They wished *ousia* itself, above which nothing exists, to be called a genus.

### CHAPTER TWO — On Equivocal and Multivocal Terms

With these matters arranged, Aristotle proceeded to what can be marked and indicated by the mind, while for the moment omitting what concerns the nature of words, since in the use of language it has happened that many things are called by one name and one thing by many names.

For the things comprehended by one name, technical language supplied two terms, calling some *homonyma* and others *synonyma*. Homonymous terms occur when several things receive a common name but are separated in the interpretation of that name, as with a painted man and a real man. The name is the same in both cases; but if you return to the definition or interpretation of “man,” you find that the two are different.

When you say that a real man is an animal capable of laughter and receptive of rational power, while you cannot say the same of a painted man, it necessarily follows that they are different.

As a rule, we should understand every name, even a proper name, which can be shared with others to be called homonymous—for example, Cicero, since there is not one Cicero but several. If, however, instead of using the name, you wish to indicate by signs which Cicero is meant—this Cicero, another, or a third—you must relate different signs for each: you might call one thick and another thin, one tall and another short, one fair in complexion and another dark.

Since these therefore differ from one another while being joined only by the name, they are called homonymous: joined in word, but differing in the interpretation of the thing.

Synonymous terms, by contrast, are things joined both in name and in the interpretation of themselves, as with “animal.” For “animal” can be said of man, horse, beast, and birds. An animal is something that takes nourishment, is mortal, and is moved by sensation.

Let us now come to those things which are customarily signified by several names each. Although Aristotle, as was said above, passed over this part because he thought that one ought to discuss the things signified rather than the things that signify, in this matter the question concerns not things but names.

These are likewise divided into two parts: some are *πολυώνυμα* (*polyonoma*, “many-named”), others *ἑτερώνυμα* (*heteronyma*, “differently named”).

They are *polyonoma* when many names signify one thing and no account of the difference between the names is given—for example, *ensis*, *mucro*, and *gladius* (“sword,” “point,” and “blade”). For one cannot distinguish or define why these many names signify one thing.

Next, *heteronyma* are names which hold individual things under several equally valid names. In these, however, the diversity of the names has a rationale, as in *homo*, *terrenus*, *mortalis* (“man,” “earthly,” “mortal”): *homo* comes from humanity; *terrenus* from earth, in which all things are generated; and *mortalis* from the necessity of death.

It is therefore clear that in these cases the origin of the names is being sought, whereas in the preceding cases the origin of the things is being sought. Aristotle therefore preferred to omit the former and discuss the latter.

Let us therefore return to homonymous terms, which are divided into two parts: they arise either by chance or by human choice. They arise by chance when, through some accident, one person receives a name like another’s; they arise by choice when the similarity of the name is attached deliberately by the person imposing it.

Of those that arise through design or choice, there are four kinds: *εἰκών* (*eikōn*, “likeness”), *κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν* (*kat’ analogian*, “by proportion”), *ἀφ᾽ ἑνός* (*aph’ henos*, “from one”), and *πρὸς ἕν* (*pros hen*, “toward one”). Latin speech expresses the same distinctions as “likeness,” “proportion,” “from one,” and “toward one.”

Likeness occurs when a painted man and a real man are joined solely by resemblance.

Proportion is what the Greeks call *κατ᾽ ἀναλογίαν*: just as we call the heart the beginning of an animal, so we call a spring the beginning of water. A proportional similarity of the names appears to have been added.

“From one” occurs when we speak of a medical instrument, medical knowledge, medical practice, and a medical prescription: all descend from one source.

“Toward one” occurs when we say that a potion is health-giving, that a physician is health-giving, and that an instrument is health-giving. All these seem to touch upon one thing, namely health.

### CHAPTER THREE — What Aristotle Does in the Categories

Many people are accustomed to raise the question of what Aristotle wished to take as the starting point of his discussion. First, he deals with things that exist; second, with things that are perceived; third, with things that are spoken.

The first are all the things produced by nature. The second are those whose images we form by seeing them with the mind and store within it. The third are those by which what has been impressed upon the mind is brought forth. For whatever someone conceives in the mind, he declares through the accompanying activity of the tongue.

But, as Themistius, the learned philosopher of our age, holds, Aristotle begins by treating what is perceived, which he calls by the Greek terms *σημαινόμενα* or *φαντασίαι* (*sēmainomena* or *phantasiai*), that is, images of things residing in the mind. Yet when he proposes to discuss perceived things, he will necessarily speak both of things that exist and of things that are spoken.

For perceptions arise from things that exist, which we perceive by seeing; and there can be no demonstration of perceptions unless they have been demonstrated with the assistance of things that are spoken. Therefore, although he will later define separately the things that exist, we must understand his discussion as mingled among all three. For whoever speaks of perceptions derives their origin from things and calls upon the aid of speech.

The question is therefore superfluous when someone says that one ought to investigate why Aristotle at the beginning of his work either stated or disclosed the law of homonymous terms, if he was going to discuss things perceived. It is evident that nothing can be said unless it has first been perceived, and that nothing can be perceived unless there is a thing from which an image may be apprehended by seeing.

### CHAPTER FOUR — On Denominative Terms: How Paronyms Differ from Homonyms

Having learned these matters, let us examine paronyms. They stand between homonymous and synonymous terms, and they cannot be called paronyms unless they contain within themselves something drawn from both: that is, unless they appear to have the name in common with homonyms and the thing signified in common with synonyms.

Thus from *sapientia* (“wisdom”) we say *sapiens* (“wise”), or from *medicina* (“medicine”) we say *medicus* (“medical” or “physician”). In *medicus* there appears to be the same similarity of activity and of name that exists in *medicina*. It was therefore rightly called a paronym, because it received its name from elsewhere.

But lest paronyms and homonyms—those said to be “from one,” that is, *ὁμοῦ* (“together”)—appear to be the same, we must recognize this distinction: the paronyms themselves are homonymous with one another because of the similarity of their names, but they are called paronyms in relation to the name from which they received their names.

For example, from *sapientia* we say *sapiens homo* (“a wise man”) and *sapiens consilium* (“a wise decision”). These are homonymous with one another, but they are paronyms of *sapientia* itself.

It must nevertheless be observed that they undergo a change in their final syllable. Paronyms do not end in the same way as the terms from which they derive their origin: *medicina* and *medicus* end with different letters.

Unless paronyms possess this difference, and unless they are joined to synonyms in function and to homonyms in name, they are called homonyms rather than paronyms. Thus, if from *malitia* (“wickedness”) we say *vitiosus* (“vicious”), it agrees with synonyms in the thing signified but differs from homonyms in name. For *vitiosus* and *malitia* are not similar in form, although they are understood with the same meaning.

If, however, from *malitia* we say *malus* (“bad”), both requirements are properly met.

But they do not change in their final syllable when we say, for example, from *sapientia* the words *sapientia*. Since no syllable has been changed here, the designation “paronym” is excluded. It is therefore clear that such terms and those like them ought rather to be joined with homonyms.

We must also know that expressions are either simple or, at any rate, compound. They are compound, as in *equus currit* (“the horse runs”); they are simple when these are separated and said individually, as *equus* and *currit*.

But I think enough has now been said about the things that are signified.

### CHAPTER FIVE — Substance and Accident

What remains is for us to explain how Aristotle treated the things that exist. These are the things that we apprehend either through the senses or by gathering them through the mind and thought.

We grasp through the senses whatever we know by seeing, touching, hearing, tasting, or smelling.

We grasp through the mind when, for example, someone has seen a horse, a man, or any animal. Although he replies that it is one body, he nevertheless understands that it is composed of many parts. One part is the head, another the feet, and others the remaining limbs. Within the head itself, the ears have their own parts, and the tongue has its own proper structure.

The individual parts themselves also contain many things that can be divided and separated: flesh is one thing, skin another, veins another, nerves another, and hair another. We therefore gather these matters through the mind or intellect, to which our senses cannot penetrate.

We also consider and know through the mind’s attention that a man or another animal grows and grows old; that it now stands and now moves its steps; that at one moment it is troubled by cares and at another rests with an untroubled mind; that at one time it enjoys health and at another suffers pain; that it changes from black to white and from white to black; that it becomes skilled from unskilled and learned from ignorant; that it becomes wild from tame and tame from wild.

Since, then, among the things that exist some are gathered by the senses and others by the mind, learned men preferred to distinguish them by proper names. They wished to call what is recognized by the senses *οὐσία* (*ousia*, “substance”), and what is gathered through the mind’s activity and often undergoes change *συμβεβηκός* (*symbebēkos*), that is, an accident.

And because accidents are recognized as existing in a permanent *ousia*, they wished to call the *ousia* itself *ὑποκείμενον* (*hypokeimenon*), that is, “underlying,” and “not in a subject”; but they called the things that occur *ἐν ὑποκειμένῳ* (*en hypokeimenō*), that is, “in an underlying subject.”

Nevertheless, we must undoubtedly recognize this point: just as we call *ousia* superior to accidents, so we should judge an *ἄτομον* or *καθ᾽ ἕκαστον*—that is, this man or this lion—to be superior to things that are common or are called by the common name “animals.”

### CHAPTER SIX — What Is Said of a Subject and What Is in a Subject

Aristotle returned again to the things that are signified, intending to show in how many ways the things that exist are customarily signified.

Among the things that exist, some are signified of a subject but are not in a subject, as “man.” “Man” is signified of some man; for “man” could not be said unless there were someone of whom it was said. But it is not in a subject, since it is itself an *ousia*, which we said above is never in an underlying subject, especially since it is itself the subject of other things.

Others are neither in a subject nor signified of a subject, as Cicero. He is not in a subject because he is an *ousia*; nor is he signified of some subject, since he possesses a name originating from himself and cannot be understood as deriving from something else.

Two things pertaining to *ousia* have now been discussed, namely how they are signified. The higher is called *κοινόν* (*koinon*, “common”); the lower is called *καθ᾽ ἕκαστον* (*kath’ hekaston*, “singular”).

We must now explain how the things that belong to accidents are signified. Among these, some are both in a subject and signified of a subject, such as knowledge or color.

They are in some subject, that is, in a mind or body. For knowledge cannot exist unless there is a soul as the subject containing it; nor could knowledge be signified unless it were said of some subject, such as grammar. Nor could any color exist unless it were in a bodily subject; nor could it be signified unless it were said of some subject by means of a color. Thus they are both in a subject and signified of a subject.

Others among the same *συμβεβηκότα* (*symbebēkota*), that is, accidents, are in a subject but are not at all signified of a subject, such as this grammar or this white color. They are indeed in a subject, whether mind or body, but they are not signified of a subject. Their name does not depend on something else; rather, they are designated by their own particular name.

In these cases also we call the higher accident “common”; the lower, when it is already a definite thing in its particularity, is called *καθ᾽ ἕκαστον* (“particular”).

But lest Aristotle appear to pass over anything unclear and thereby provide an occasion for questions to arise, he wished to discuss more carefully what it means for something to be in a subject and to define it, so as to close the way to those who might raise objections.

He therefore defines being in a subject as being in something else, not as a part of it, and as something that can never exist without that in which it is.

This definition was added because someone might say that a finger or foot is in a subject, namely in the body. He excluded this by a careful definition, saying that something is in a subject when it is not a part of that in which it is; but it is clear that a finger or foot is a part of the body.

Someone might then say that water or wine is in a jar as in a subject. But the learned definition prevents this as well, adding that something is in a subject when it cannot exist without its subject. It cannot be doubted that wine or water can exist elsewhere without the jar in which it happened to be.

Meanwhile, we must observe here by what art a definition is arranged. First, it must extend broadly, beginning from the genus; then, proceeding gradually through its parts, it must arrive at that in which alone the thing being defined is found.

Thus those who fashion statues first select a huge stone; then, by gradually reducing it and cutting away what is superfluous, they arrive at the formation of faces and limbs. In the same way, a definition begins from a genus, gradually casting off the generality of its words, and tends to approach the proper dwelling place of the thing to be demonstrated.

But let us return to the matter at hand. The discussion concerned how the things that exist are signified. Since much has already been said about them, we must retain this rule: all *καθ᾽ ἕκαστα*, *ἑνάριθμα*, *ἄτομα*, or *αἰσθητά*—that is, this man, this horse, or this tree—cannot be signified of a subject.

If, however, these same terms belong to accidents—such as this color or this discipline—they can be in a subject. For, as was demonstrated above, no accident can exist without a subject.

We have therefore learned how to recognize either a subject or something in a subject.

### CHAPTER SEVEN — What Is a Genus and What Is a Species
From this point Aristotle teaches us how we may recognize those things that are signified of a subject. In these matters there is a particular point: the same things found in the subject are also found in that which is signified of the subject. For just as “animal” is signified of a subject, namely a human being or a horse, so “human being” must likewise be signified of some subject, namely an individual human being. Cicero, however, is both a human being and an animal. Whatever, therefore, can be predicated of animal is likewise predicated of human being and of Cicero. Consequently, whatever is found in that which is signified of a subject must necessarily also be found in that which is the subject. Thus, if you say that an animal is something that takes food, is mortal, and is moved by sensation—and animal is signified of the subject human being—it is nevertheless necessary that the same things said of animal also be said of human being. Next, whatever has been said of human being is likewise said of Socrates. It is certain, however, that Socrates is subject to human being, and human being to animal. Whatever, therefore, is said of things signified of a subject will likewise be predicated of those things that we call subjects.

As a general rule, those things are signified of a subject that cannot be known by themselves: animal cannot be understood except in relation to a subject such as human being, and human being cannot be apprehended unless it is recognized in relation to some individual human being.

Now, since he is about to discuss the genera, species, and differentia of all the categories, it seems necessary first to examine what genus, species, and differentia are. Genus, then, is that through which what a thing is is shown and signified according to many things that differ in species, as in the case of *usia*—that is, substance. In general we speak of “substance”; but this common name is divided according to species when we say “animal” or “stone.” Thus things joined together, as it were, under a single word are separated according to species.

Differentia, on the other hand, is that which is predicated according to many things that differ in species, not to show what a thing is, but what sort of thing it is—for example, an animal that walks, flies, lives in water, is two-footed, or is four-footed. Genus and differentia, therefore, are signified according to species. Yet genus can be recognized as what a thing is, whereas differentia can be recognized as what sort of thing it is.

Species—called by some “form”—is that which is predicated and recognized according to many things differing in number, showing what a thing is. [Col. 1425] Such is “human being.” This name embraces all human beings and appears to perform the function of a species, which is predicated of some individual human being containing number in itself: for example, this one as first, that one as second, and another as third.

To illustrate these three by a single example: genus is “animal”; differentiae are “two-footed” and “four-footed”; species are “human being” and “horse.”

But just as there is no genus that does not have a differentia, so we must not understand a differentia that does not have a species. “Black” and “white,” for example, do not have a differentia, because they do not produce species from themselves. For what other species of white or black can be found?

Since, then, what genus, differentia, and species are has been distinguished, let us now turn to Aristotle’s statements. From his teaching we have learned that among genera differing from one another there can be neither the same differentiae nor the same species. The differentia and species are one thing when we ask what something is, another when we ask what sort of thing it is, and another when we ask how much it is. Thus, if you wish to state the differentiae of animal, you may say “flying,” “two-footed,” or “walking”; if you wish to state its species, you may say “human being,” “bird,” or “horse.”

Can the same differentia or species be predicated of discipline, since the genera are different—animal and discipline? Animal belongs to the category of substance, whereas discipline belongs to the category of quality.

Finally, those genera that are joined to one another in an alternating relationship (*epallēla*, ἐπάλληλα) have the same differentiae and the same species. Such is substance, whose species is animal. But animal is itself a genus in relation to other things; hence it is called both species and genus.

Since these two genera, then, hold one another in reciprocal relation—and Aristotle also called them *epallēla*—they have the same differentiae. Thus, if you say that substance is a mortal animal, two-footed and capable of laughter, you can say the same of animal: animal is a mortal human being, two-footed and capable of laughter. The same can also be said of human being. It is therefore certain that genera joined to one another reciprocally have the same differentiae and species. This cannot occur, however, among different genera.

## CHAPTER VIII — On the Categories in General

Again Aristotle returns to those things that are said, although we stated above that one cannot be treated without the other. For whoever says something says it of something that is; and what is cannot be understood through something else unless it is said.

Among things that are spoken without any combination with one another, whatever individual expression is uttered signifies either substance (*usia*), quantity, quality, relation, position, action, passion, place, time, or possession. These are the ten categories. The first is substance, which supports the remaining nine. The other nine are *symbebēkota* (συμβεβηκότα), that is, accidents.

Of these nine, some are in substance itself, some outside substance, and some both within and outside it. Quality, quantity, and position are in substance itself. For as soon as we have said “substance,” “human being,” or “horse,” we must attend to whether it is two-footed or four-footed, white or black, standing or lying down. These things are in substance itself and cannot exist without it.

Other categories are outside substance: place, time, and possession. Place does not belong to substance, nor does time, nor being clothed or armed; these are separated from substance.

Others are common—that is, they are both within and outside substance: relation, action, and passion. Relation includes “greater” and “less,” since neither can be said unless the other is joined to it, namely that in relation to which something is greater or less. Thus one of these is contained within the thing itself, while the other lies outside it.

Action is likewise both outside and within. No one can be said to strike unless he strikes another; nor can anyone be said to read unless the reader himself is one thing and what he reads another. Thus action is both in substance and outside substance.

Passion is similar. No one can be struck or burned unless he undergoes this from another. Therefore passion too is both in substance and outside substance.

When these expressions are singular, they affirm nothing. When combined, however, they produce from themselves a kind of discourse, whether *proσταktikon* (προστακτικόν), imperative; *euktikon* (εὐκτικόν), optative; *erōtēmatikon* (ἐρωτηματικόν), interrogative; or *klētikon* (κλητικόν), vocative. To express these in Latin terms, they are commands, wishes, questions, and calls.

These four kinds of discourse are, as it were, suspended and for the moment simple, and therefore incomplete. For it is not yet understood what is imperative, optative, interrogative, or vocative unless there is added the genus called *apophantikon* (ἀποφαντικόν), that is, declarative discourse. This contains a certain judgment of affirmation that either adds something or removes something. Aristotle called this *kataphasis* (κατάφασις), affirmation, and *apophasis* (ἀπόφασις), negation. Examples are: “This heaven is revolving” and “This heaven is not revolving.”

The declarative expression itself, which we have called *apophantikon*, is either false or true. For this reason Aristotle passed over the four forms that belong more properly to grammarians and rhetoricians, and discussed this apophantic form, which concerns philosophers.

## CHAPTER IX — On *Usia*, or Substance. Substance Properly So Called. What Are Called Second Substances

After setting out everything that seemed necessary for the discussion to follow, it was appropriate to define the individual categories. But since substance could not be defined according to the proper method—which requires that a definition, in order to extend more broadly, begin from a genus, whereas substance itself has no genus, since it supports everything—Aristotle wished to define it by its parts, so that what it is might be known not only from its definition but also through knowledge of its parts.

Substance, properly and principally so called, is that which is neither in a subject nor signified of a subject, such as this particular human being or this particular horse.

“Second substances” are called genus and species, that is, animal and human being. He says that these are called second substances because that substance is superior which is neither in a subject nor predicated of a subject. Genus and species are called second substances because they alone indicate the first substance.

Thus, if someone does not wish or does not know how to name Socrates, let him say “animal” or “human being”—that is, genus or species—and from these expressions what Socrates is can be recognized. But if he says something else, such as “he runs” or “he walks,” nothing can be recognized.

It is clear that those things signified of a subject share both a name and the account of the name with the things that are subjects. Thus “human being” is signified of some individual human being as its subject; and in the subject one will find not only the same name but also the same account that can be found in that which is signified of the subject.

Among the second substances themselves, species is superior to genus, for species is closer to first substance than genus is. If someone wishes to show what first substance is, he will demonstrate it more easily by naming the species than by naming the genus. Thus, if someone wishes to identify Socrates while omitting his name, he identifies him more precisely by saying “human being” than by saying “animal.” For “animal” could identify both a horse and an eagle.

Again, just as first substances are subject to all things and all things are supported by them, so species is subject to genus. For this reason species is more substantially a substance than the other categories.

We must also consider whether something that we think is only a species may also be a genus. If someone says “animal,” he has named a genus. If he then says “human being,” “horse,” “fish,” or “bird,” should we declare all of these to be only species? Since human being and horse are clearly species, whereas fish and bird are both genera and species—for birds and fish do not each have a single form—they are therefore called both species and genera.

Those that are species alone, such as human being, horse, eagle, and bull, are substances in equal measure. For just as human being is a substance, so horse, eagle, and bull are substances within their own genera.

Having proceeded through the parts by which substance has been defined, Aristotle wished to define it in another way as well, by showing what things must naturally be found in it. For whatever is present in anything is either in it alone and in every instance, or in it alone but not in every instance, or in every instance but not in it alone, or neither in it alone nor in every instance.

The Greeks call these conditions: *en monō kai en panti* (ἐν μόνῳ καὶ ἐν παντί), “in it alone and in every instance”; *en monō kai ouk en panti* (ἐν μόνῳ καὶ οὐκ ἐν παντί), “in it alone and not in every instance”; *en panti kai ouk en monō* (ἐν παντὶ καὶ οὐκ ἐν μόνῳ), “in every instance and not in it alone”; and *ouk en monō kai ouk en panti* (οὐκ ἐν μόνῳ καὶ οὐκ ἐν παντί), “neither in it alone nor in every instance.”

Thus, if someone wishing to define human being says that it is capable of laughter, this is both in human being alone and in every human being. For only a human being laughs, and it is natural for every human being to laugh.

Second, something may be in human being alone but not in every human being. Thus, if someone defining human being says that it is capable of learning, this can indeed be found in human beings alone, but not in every human being, since not everyone has learned some discipline.

Third, something may be in every human being but not in human being alone. Thus, if someone defining human being says that a human being is something that walks and takes food, this is found in every human being but not in human beings alone, since cattle also take food and wild animals also run.

Fourth, something may be neither in human being alone nor in every human being. Thus, if someone says in defining human being that to be human is to be white, this is neither in human beings alone nor in every human being. A human being is not the only white creature, since an ox or horse may also be white, nor is every human being white.

There are therefore two conditions that indicate a path for investigating something, and two that cannot signify anything certain. From what is neither in the thing alone nor in every instance, we can recognize nothing, since it is general. The other condition, being in every instance but not in the thing alone, has no differentia and must therefore likewise be rejected.

The two remaining conditions can demonstrate by certain signs the thing in which they are found: namely, being in the thing alone and in every instance. For there can be no doubt that, when you have found this condition, you may state what the thing is in which it is recognized to be present.

The other condition—being in the thing alone but not in every instance—is not of equal strength, yet it must necessarily be sought in defining a thing if the first condition cannot be found.

Now, in order to designate substance, Aristotle begins by arguing from what is in every instance but not in the thing alone. He shows that there are second substances, which he calls second because what is found in the first substances can also be found in them.

Finally, he says that this is common to every substance: it is not in a subject. Since neither genus nor species is found in a subject, it is clear that these must be called second substances.

Next, he shows from this also that genus and species are second substances: things that are in a subject sometimes share only their name with the things subject to them, but not the account of the name. Genus and species, however, share with their subjects—that is, with some individual human being—both the name and its account in a definite way.

After second substances, namely genus and species, have been demonstrated, only differentia remained. Upon closer consideration, differentia appears to be almost an accident. For when “two-footed,” “mortal,” or “rational” is predicated of animal, it demonstrates not what a thing is but rather what sort of thing it is, and therefore seems to possess the force of quality.

Yet since the first differentia arises from the genus and species follows from it, differentia ought not to be counted among the accidents. Consequently Aristotle said that it is mixed in signification, but decided that in its force it should be reckoned among substances. For he declares that the same things are found in it as are found in the other substances: namely, that it can have both a name and an account corresponding to the subject.

When we say “walking human being,” for example, we can find in the subject both the same designation and the same account. Socrates is a human being and is also walking.

He proceeds similarly through the remaining arguments, varying their form and demonstrating that some things inhere in substance alone and in every instance, some in substance alone but not in every instance, some in every instance but not in substance alone, and some neither in substance alone nor in every instance.

Since these matters are evident in Aristotle himself, it seemed superfluous to explain them further, especially since this work has decided not to translate everything written by the Philosopher, but to expound more plainly those matters that seemed obscure to beginners.

## CHAPTER X — On Quantity. Nothing Is Contrary to Quantity. What Are Called Contraries

Once substance had been described—since it could not be defined for the reasons mentioned above—the necessary order required the definition of the accidents. The first of these is quantity, and not without reason. For whenever we see something, we must determine how much it is.

What its quantity is cannot be discovered unless it has been gathered by applying a measure. If, therefore, someone wishes to measure only length while omitting breadth, length subjected to measurement without breadth is called a *grammē* (γραμμή), a line. This does not mean that there is some length lacking breadth; rather, someone who measures only length is said to measure a *grammē*.

When breadth has been measured together with length, the result is called *epiphaneia* (ἐπιφάνεια), a surface. If height is also added to the measurement, the whole constitutes a body. We do not understand this, however, in the way we ordinarily understand a natural body, lest we seem to return to substance.

We also measure the place in which something has been established. Time too is subjected to measurement. For when something moves, it must necessarily possess a measure of time through that movement, as when we say that it arrived in the first, second, or third year, or in a month, a day, an hour, or a moment. In this way, therefore, the quantity of each thing is determined.

Of quantity itself, one kind is continuous and another separated. The continuous kinds are the line, surface, body, place, and time. In these, the boundaries of the individual parts cannot have separate measures. For as soon as you place a point in the middle of a line and thereby provide what seems to be a definite boundary of measurement, that boundary becomes common to both parts into which the line has been divided, so that it is uncertain to which part the boundary appears to belong. Each part is so continuous and joined to the other.

A surface is likewise called connected and continuous for the same reason. If someone wishes to divide it, he must place a line in its middle. When this line dividing the surface has made two parts from it, that line itself begins to be the common boundary of the two parts. The parts are so joined to one another that it is not apparent to which of them the boundary seems to be fixed.

Similarly, if someone wishes to cut a body, the boundary of the body being divided must be a line or a surface. The cut made by the line together with the surface must extend into the body. Therefore it is uncertain whether the line or the surface has given a boundary to either part, since once the body has been divided, the surface must be found in both parts. A body is therefore continuous because the boundary for making its two parts is common.

The same reasoning applies to time. If we wish to give it a boundary when dividing it, we say “now.” But “now,” lying between past and future time, is so confused with both that it is uncertain where it ought to divide them.

Place, since it surrounds every body and is occupied by the parts of the body, is divided by a common boundary in the same way as the body. Therefore it must likewise be called continuous, like the other kinds.

Separated quantities are number and speech. Who does not perceive that one is separated from two by its own boundary, and two from three? In speech, too, the individual syllables are separated. They are distinguished by nature and number when we say that one is short and another long, or that there is one syllable or two. It is plainly evident that the things we have mentioned belong to quantity and ought to be called separated.

There is another difference among quantities. Some have parts that possess position, so that it can be recognized which part is joined to which; others have parts that cannot possess position.

By “position” I mean that we see the right and left, upper and lower, front and back, far and near of a thing. The quantities whose parts are joined by a manifest position are the line, surface, body, and place.

Whether one divides a line, a surface, or any of these other things by placing boundaries in them, although the parts appear continuous and joined, it is nevertheless possible to observe physically where each part is, which part is near another, and to which it is joined.

The quantities whose parts do not possess position are time, number, and speech. When we say “one,” naming the number by itself rather than counting some physical object, we do not see its right or left. Since it exists only in the word, in sound, and in no body, it cannot display the position of its parts—unless perhaps we call sequence a position, on the ground that two follows one. But position cannot properly be found in these things.

The same applies to time and speech, especially since these seem to slip away as soon as they appear. Time runs on when you say that it does; and speech, before it has been uttered, does not exist, while once it has been uttered, it is no longer apparent. It is therefore clear that these three do not have the position of distinct parts.

Strictly speaking, only the things mentioned above are called quantities. If anything else besides these can be found, it ought to be classified as an accident. Some things happen to the accidents themselves. Thus we may say “much white.” “Much white” is not said because the white itself is immense, but because the surface in which the white occurs is seen to be large.

It is therefore clear that when we say “much white,” the white—which is an accident of the surface—is assessed from the quantity of the surface. Similarly, when we say “long actions,” the actions are not called long because they are immense; rather, the quantity of the actions is estimated from the measure of the time in which they are contained.

We must recognize as a special property of quantity that nothing is contrary to it. Nothing is contrary to a surface, a line, two cubits, or three cubits.

Unless perhaps, through some error, we think that “much” and “little” are contraries, failing to notice that these must be transferred into the class of things said in relation to something. For nothing is called much or little unless it has been compared with something else.

When we call a mountain short, we indicate that something else, with which it is compared, is larger. Or when we call a grain of millet large, we show by comparison with its own kind—among which something smaller is found—that it is larger. It is therefore clear that “much” and “little,” “large” and “short,” receive their names when compared with something else.

Nor is the person who thinks that “much” and “little” belong to quantity mistaken only in this respect; he is also mistaken if he believes them to be contraries. That is entirely impossible. For if, deceived by this error, we call them contraries, it will follow that contraries can occur in one and the same thing at one and the same time.

For one and the same thing could at the same time be called larger than something smaller and shorter than something larger. Neither the nature of things nor reason itself permits this. Therefore the opinion of those who believe these to be contraries must be rejected.

Contrariety can no more be seen in quantity than in a circle. The ancients said that above and below were contrary because of the distance between heaven and earth, asserting that everywhere the earth is below and heaven above.

When we contemplate the nature of things, the earth, which appears to be in the middle, is below everywhere. For even our antipodes, who are said to plant their feet opposite ours, have the heaven above them. It is therefore clear that the earth is always situated below.

Physicists add another argument: because of the diversity of places, earth is contrary to heaven—heaven always being above, earth below—since everything heavy by weight is naturally carried toward the earth, whereas what appears lighter must be lifted toward heaven.

For this reason they said that heaven and earth are contrary to one another: natural necessity has placed the one below and the other above.

From this reasoning the definition of all contraries seems to have been established. Those things are called contraries which, although they belong to one and the same genus, are separated from one another by a considerable distance.

But those who assert this must recognize that these expressions ought rather to be joined with things said in relation to something. “Above” cannot be said unless “below” has also been designated.

If someone wishes to dispute this, “above” and “below” may perhaps be seen as belonging more properly to the category in which “where” is spoken. For when we say “above” and “below,” we recognize where something is occurring.

But these, as we have said, are the arguments of chatterers. We must not believe that contrariety is admitted in quantity.

Meanwhile, on the occasion of this discussion, we may observe that natural “above” and “below” are one thing, while what is so called in relation to us is another. The natural arrangement cannot be changed, but what concerns us is changed by the movement of human beings.

Thus, if someone who has been below climbs to a higher place, or wishes to descend from a higher place to a lower one, everything is changed for him. When he descends, the things that had previously been below are seen by him as above.

It also belongs to quantity, being in every instance but not in it alone, that it does not admit of more and less, which is expressed in Greek as *mallon kai hēsson* (μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον), “more and less.”

When we say “two-footed,” we cannot say that one thing is more or less two-footed than another. A second two-footed thing is two-footed in the same way as the first. If one thing should be greater than another, it no longer receives the name “two-footed,” but the name of another measure.

Nor does number admit of more and less, since it would be madness to call three more or less three. Time likewise cannot be more or less time than another time. It is therefore clear from what has been explained that more and less cannot be found in quantity.

The proper characteristic of quantity, which is found in every instance and in the thing alone, is that all its instances are called equal or unequal. Thus number is called even or odd; an even number is not called equal, nor an odd number unequal.

Similarly, all other quantities are called not even or odd, but equal or unequal. Things that do not belong to quantity, however, are called similar or dissimilar rather than equal or unequal: for example, white is called similar or dissimilar to white. This word seems to be specially attached to things belonging to quantity.

## CHAPTER XI — On Relation. When Something Is Said Relatively. Opposites
The third of the Categories is that which in Latin is called *ad aliquid*, and in Greek *πρός τι*. Indeed, this third category was established not by the order of the work but by the necessities of the discussion: for after quantity, quality would have followed. But since, at the end of the treatment of quantity, certain things of the same kind seemed capable of being transferred to *ad aliquid*, he necessarily wished to place this category third, so that, after everything appropriate to each category had been examined and demonstrated, the frequent confusion that had arisen might be resolved.

Aristotle does not begin with his own definitions, but with the terms of those who, before him, attempted improperly to define *ad aliquid*. We must nevertheless listen to this as necessary to the discussion. For the philosopher both skillfully gives them assistance and seeks a remedy for their wrongly stated terms, intending later, by expressing his own judgment concerning *πρός τι*, to reject everything that had been improperly defined.

We therefore call *ad aliquid* that category in which what a thing is is said from reference to something else, without whose association it cannot exist, and whose entire force proceeds from conjunction with another: for example, the double is called double in relation to the single, the greater is called greater in relation to the lesser, and the like is called like in relation to the like. It is therefore clear that *ad aliquid* subsists not through its own force but through conjunction with something else.

The other things recognized as belonging to the same category are to be understood in the same way: possession, affection, knowledge, position, and perception. Aristotle called these *ἕξις*, *διάθεσις*, *ἐπιστήμη*, *θέσις*, and *αἴσθησις*. These too depend upon something else. A possession is called the possession of something; an affection is the affection of something; and knowledge, position, and perception are recognized by the same reasoning.

We should not, however, be disturbed by the fact that some things are said to belong to this category which also seem to be connected with quality. Possession, affection, knowledge, and the other things just mentioned seem especially appropriate to quality. But we must attend to the distinction by which these two categories—quality and *ad aliquid*, or *πρός τι καὶ ποιότης*—are separated from one another.

Whenever knowledge is called knowledge of something that can be known, and perception is called perception of something perceptible, we must understand them as *ad aliquid*. But when knowledge or learning is spoken of not as knowledge of some particular thing, but as belonging to a person, we must recognize quality.

This is the distinction for the present, although, if we wish to define properly the category called *ad aliquid*, so that it may be separated from the others—for it seems to run into all of them—we must define it in another way, lest error continually arise among those who give the matter too little consideration.

Something is then truly and properly called *ad aliquid* when, under one and the same origin and disappearance, both that which is joined and that to which it is joined are found together. Thus slave and master either exist simultaneously or do not exist simultaneously. For when you have posited a master, a slave necessarily exists; but when you have removed the master, the slave no longer appears.

Likewise, the double and the single either destroy or reveal one another. When the double appears, the single comes into being; when the double disappears, the single cannot remain. Similarly, if there is no single, there is no double; but if there is a single, the double necessarily appears.

More specifically and regularly, so that this category may be recognized more clearly, we must observe that something is not properly called *ad aliquid* unless *καθ’ ἕκαστον πρὸς καθ’ ἕκαστον ἀναφέρεται*, that is, unless one singular thing is referred to another singular thing. For when we say “double,” we undoubtedly mean not a general but a particular double, and we call it the double of this particular single.

Therefore the category is truly *ad aliquid* whenever, for example, we say that [Col. 1431] Socrates resembles Chrysippus in appearance. For how could we demonstrate either who resembles or whom he resembles unless we indicate personally both who the resembling person is and the person whom he resembles?

Some, however, wish to raise an unnecessary objection to this definition, asserting that something described as *ad aliquid* may exist first, while that which is later to be named in relation to it comes into being afterward. Thus these two would seem not to be joined either in origin or in disappearance. They give as examples the knowable and knowledge, asserting that the knowable existed first and that knowledge followed afterward.

For example, among geometricians, a line (*γραμμή*) or a circle existed first, but knowledge of them was later grasped by learned men. Therefore, they say, the knowable existed beforehand, as something in which knowledge could subsequently be found. By this argument they show that there are many things in this category for which origin and disappearance do not seem to be shared.

They argue similarly from the example of the perceptible and perception, since perceptible things existed beforehand. The elements of which every body consists existed before any body was born in which perception could exist.

By these arguments, then, they attempt to show that the definition of the category called *ad aliquid* has not been correctly established. Such claims are usually made by those who observe the nature of things insufficiently carefully.
