Everything that exists is said to exist either by natural power or by an operation of making—what the Greeks call *δύναμις* and *ἐνέργεια*. If someone wishes to separate these and not confuse them through any association, he will understand that what is called *ad aliquid* cannot exist without the other thing in relation to which it is said to exist.

For knowledge is associated with the knowable line or circle at the very origin of its nature. As soon as it began to be knowable, it possessed knowledge of itself, although this knowledge had not yet been demonstrated *ἐνεργείᾳ*, that is, through operation. Its knowledge did not therefore begin to exist when it began to operate; rather, it arose together with the knowable, while the operation followed afterward.

We must distinguish the beginning of operation. We can then recognize that knowledge was generated together with the knowable, while its operation appeared later through the investigation of the wise.

Once these objections have been removed, the best definition of things related to one another is that they are always destroyed or born together.

We must also retain in memory that not everything called *ad aliquid* is related to the things with which it is joined by the same grammatical cases. Some are joined by the genitive, others by the dative, and many by the ablative.

By the genitive: “the slave of the master,” “the double of the single.”

By the dative: “like to the like,” “equal to the equal.”

By the ablative: “the perceptible is perceptible by perception,” “the knowable is knowable by knowledge,” and other such expressions, in which things are bound to one another through the association of another by various cases.

There is also in this category—and in it alone and in every instance belonging to it—the feature that, between two associated things which depend upon one another, there is reciprocal conversion, called in Greek *ἀντιστροφή*. Thus the double is said to be the double of the single, and the single the single of the double; the slave is the slave of the master, and the master the master of the slave.

It is therefore apparent that these coupled terms are converted into one another through reciprocal repetition, provided that the conversion is made knowingly and intelligently. For if these terms are converted incompetently, great confusion arises. If someone were to say incompetently, “a bird’s feather,” that would be a foolish conversion. Not every feather belongs to a bird, since there are certain feathers that do not belong to birds, such as those of cicadas, flies, and other animals that nature has similarly formed.

But if someone were to say, “the feather of the feathered thing,” this would seem to be a valid conversion.

At this point I have wished to dispel certain obscurities that usually arise from the similarity of the Categories. When we say “the feather of the feathered thing” and “the head of the headed thing,” we seem to place parts of substance among accidents. For a feather is undoubtedly a part of substance, as are a head or a hand. If these are referred to *ad aliquid*, there would seem to be no distinction between substances and *ad aliquid*.

To remove all confusion, therefore, we must observe in what way *ad aliquid* has been defined both truly and properly. Its definition is as follows: something is called *ad aliquid* when what it is depends upon another, and when it is necessary for it, as an individual—that is, *καθ’ ἕκαστον*—to be converted reciprocally through a change into one another.

When this is considered, one will discover that neither “the feather of the feathered thing” nor “the head of the headed thing” can properly be called *ad aliquid*. For just as we say “the feather of the feathered thing,” we cannot say “the feathered thing of the [Col. 1432] feather” or “the headed thing of the head.” Anyone who said this would be mocked.

Being feathered does not derive from a feather, nor does a feather consist of being feathered. Similarly, being headed does not consist of a head, nor does the head seem to subsist from being headed.

But what is truly called *ad aliquid* can be converted reciprocally, as we said above: “the master of the slave” and “the slave of the master.” Again, when the slave is removed, there is no master; when the master is removed, the slave no longer appears.

A thing can be feathered even when the feather has perished; and, conversely, the feather can exist when the feathered thing has perished. Once the definition of this category has been considered, the distinction arising from their similarity can therefore also be found.

In the same way, we can separate this category from the similarity of opposites. Aristotle calls opposites *ἀντικείμενα*, and they present a certain similarity to this category. Hot and cold seem to be joined by a relation of opposition. Yet we do not say “hot of the cold,” but “hot opposed to cold”; nor do we call the just “the just of the unjust,” but “the just contrary to the unjust.”

As we said at the beginning of this category, Aristotle proposes many examples that do not seem to belong to it in any definite form. His purpose is to criticize, by what follows, the errors of those who attempted to define this category differently.

Finally, he placed virtue and vice, and knowledge and ignorance, as though they belonged to *ad aliquid*, and said that they could receive a contrary—not because the nature of the matter required this, but so that he might expose the errors of those arguing unlearnedly. For, as we explained above, these should be judged opposites rather than things called *ad aliquid*.

In my view, as Aristotle himself also holds, this category seems capable of receiving more and less—not in every instance, and not in this category alone. For we can say that something is like anyone, more like, or less like. But this cannot be found in everything that belongs to *ad aliquid*, as I have said. One cannot say “more father” or “less father,” “less son” or “more son,” “less double” or “more double.”

Nor should we be deceived into thinking that something is *ad aliquid* whenever, for example, we say “whose horse,” “whose wood,” or “whose estate.” These expressions, since they indicate a master or an owner, should not be considered expressions of *ad aliquid*.

We have explained as much as we could about this category, although its intermixture with the others seems so extensive that Aristotle himself also found it difficult to identify its boundaries. A long and sustained reconsideration of the matter is therefore not inappropriate.

## CHAPTER XII — On Quality. The Four Species of Quality. Possession. Affection. Natural Power. Passive Qualities

Let us now discuss quality, according to which existing things are called “such-and-such.” Many ask what quality is and what “such” means, but the distinction between them is easy.

We call sweetness, astringency, whiteness, and blackness qualities. “Such” is understood whenever we say that something is white, sweet, astringent, or black. Although Aristotle used “such” indifferently for quality and “quality” for “such,” and we have therefore followed him in understanding them similarly, this category is considered more difficult than the others because it seems to run into all of them more readily.

Thus it is found in substance when we say “a grammatical man”; in quantity, “a white or black surface”; in *ad aliquid*, “a prudent father” or “an excellent son”; in doing, “he dances vigorously”; in undergoing, “he bears wounds courageously”; in place, “a dark place”; in time, “a hot month” or “a cold month”; in position, “he lies face down or on his back”; and in having, “he is suitably armed.”

It will therefore require no small degree of discernment to separate quality, which is almost confused with the others, through the liveliness of the mind.

There are four species of quality. Aristotle set them forth as genera, because each of them in turn has its own species. When this occurs, they are called subordinate genera, which the Greeks called *ὑπάλληλα*.

The first genus is possession and affection; the second, natural power; the third, passive qualities or passions; the fourth, forms and figures. Aristotle [Col. 1433] called these *ἕξις καὶ διάθεσις*, *φυσικὴ δύναμις*, *παθητικαὶ ποιότητες καὶ πάθη*, and *σχήματα καὶ μορφαί*.

Possession is an affection of the mind that persists for a long time, such as virtue and learning, which are evaluated by their persistence and duration, unless some bodily weakness or an accidental debility cuts them short.

Affection, by contrast, is a changeable impulse of the mind, or a light desire, which is erased within a short time.

Possession, therefore, can be seen to arise from affection: it begins from affection, and if the affection persists, possession is born. Affection, however, cannot be regarded as possession; for if it reaches the level of possession, it will no longer retain its proper name.

Here it is not inappropriate to resolve briefly a question that has often been raised and to explain what distinguishes virtue from learning.

Learning is confined to that part of the soul which is called rational. Virtue, however, embraces every part of the soul and governs and directs the whole soul by its authority. Thus it subdues anger and removes desires from the mind—something that learning is by no means able to do.

Natural power exists whenever someone seems, by nature, either able or unable to do something. For example, after observing the bodies and limbs of boys, we often make predictions about the future and say that they will become either boxers or runners—not because they already possess the art or practice, but because their bodily configuration seems likely to enable them to accomplish these things more easily.

Similarly, we call people healthy or weak according as they easily or with difficulty contract illness. Natural power is recognized in these cases as well, since it makes them either more frequently subject to weakness or able to retain lasting health.

The terms “hard” and “soft” also indicate natural power. Something is hard if, because of the firmness of its nature, it does not easily admit its own corruption; something is soft if its nature is more yielding and insufficient to repel contrary forces.

The third genus or species of quality is passive qualities and passions, such as astringency, heating, and cooling. Thus it is appropriate to speak of *θερμότης* and *ψυχρότης*, as well as whiteness and blackness.

They are not called passive qualities because they themselves undergo something, but because they cause a passion. Honey, for example, has not undergone something from sweetness in order to be sweet; rather, it produces a sweet sensation in those who taste it.

Whiteness and blackness, and the intermediate colors—that is, redness and pallor—are more properly called passive qualities, since they arise only from a passion of the soul or body.

For someone to become black is a bodily passion; to become pale or red is a passion of the soul. When the soul cannot bear the shame of disgrace, as though to conceal itself, it pours an abundance of blood into the outer parts of the body, and thus we become red from excessive shame.

Pallor likewise results from a similar passion of the soul. When the soul is struck by excessive fear, it flees toward the innermost parts of the heart, and the blood follows it, so that the body visible to us, deprived of blood, becomes pale.

Philosophers affirm that this is truly a passion of the soul, to such an extent that even if pallor or redness remains continually in the body, they maintain that it has arisen from a similar passion.

If these qualities persist in the body, then, because we are called “such” according to them, they themselves are also judged passive qualities. If they exist only briefly and quickly depart, we call them passions instead.

For if someone is angry, blushes, becomes hot, or becomes cold only for a time, and soon returns to the condition of nature, he cannot be called red, angry, hot, or cold merely because he has temporarily undergone something.

The distinction between passive qualities and passions is therefore this: passions arise temporarily and are easily changed, whereas passive qualities, according to which we are called “such,” persist permanently.

We must now revisit the fourth species of quality, which includes forms and figures. Figures are attributed to inanimate things, forms to animals.

We indicate figures when we speak of a triangle, quadrilateral, cone, cylinder, or sphere; [Col. 1434] we speak of forms when we declare certain people handsome or deformed.

Curvature and straightness belong to the same genus of quality. We may translate *εὐθύτητα καὶ καμπυλότητα* in this way. Something is called straight or curved according to them.

Smoothness, roughness, sparseness, and density are also numbered among qualities, since from them we designate things as sparse, dense, smooth, or rough; but they have another interpretation of their meaning.

Density seems to indicate an excessive compression of adjoining parts; sparseness, by contrast, indicates a looser joining of parts with frequent intervals. Smoothness properly indicates something in which the arrangement of the parts has been ordered so suitably and evenly that none of them projects beyond the measure of another. Roughness, by contrast, is produced by the irregularity of joined parts: roughness arises only from inequality among the parts, so that one is longer and another lower.

For this reason some wish to associate these qualities with another category, called by the Greeks *κεῖσθαι* and by us “to lie,” or, as Augurius [Note: [Col. 1434] Other editions have *Augurius*. M.]—whom I consider among the most learned—preferred, “position.”

It is clear that each of the parts composing a body exists through its position. Nevertheless, when we call something smooth, rough, dense, or sparse, we indicate what sort of thing it is; and all that was explained above about these terms seems to pertain not so much to the interpretation of the word as to the nature of the thing. For this reason reason requires us to number these also among qualities.

From the qualities we have enumerated, things are called “such” *παρωνύμως*, that is, by a derivative name: smooth from smoothness, dense from density, and the rest in the same way.

It sometimes happens, although rarely, that “such” things do not descend *παρωνύμως* from their quality. Thus from virtue one cannot say “virtuous” in this sense, but rather “moderate” or “industrious.” Nor in Greek is *ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς*—“from virtue”—expressed as *ἀρετός*, but as *σπουδαῖος*. It is therefore clear that things called “such” can exist even when the derivation from their qualities by paronymy is disregarded.

So much for this. Let us now examine the consequences and the property of this quality whose various species we have explained.

There is no doubt that qualities admit contrariety. Who doubts that weakness is contrary to health, injustice to justice, heat to cold, good to evil, and the unlearned to the educated?

But this will not be found in every quality. Nothing can be contrary to pale, brown, square, or triangular.

It will therefore not be inappropriate to offer a rule by which we may recognize which qualities do not admit contrariety. Learned persons will know that those qualities which lie between contraries, and those which arise from forms and figures, entirely exclude contrariety [Note: The old manuscripts read *excusare*. The printed editions have *recusare*.].

By qualities lying between contraries I mean brown and pale. These arise from whiteness and blackness and lie between them; whiteness and blackness themselves are contrary to one another, but nothing is contrary to brown or pale.

It is therefore clear that what lies between contraries has no contrary.

Likewise, a quality that consists in form or figure is ignorant of contrariety. What could anyone set against a square or a triangle, a circle, a cone, or a cylinder as its contrary?

Let us therefore hold as a rule that the quality which admits contrariety is neither every quality nor quality alone.

Nor should we omit the fact that, among contrary qualities, one falls under the same category as the other. Injustice is contrary to justice; justice is a quality; therefore injustice is also a quality.

Similarly, whiteness is a quality; therefore blackness must also be a quality. Thus contrary qualities are always joined under the same category.

Since admitting contrariety is neither the property of quality alone nor of all quality, let us investigate something else in seeking the proper feature of quality.

I see that quality admits more and less—that is, *μᾶλλον καὶ ἧττον*. We can say “whiter,” “blacker,” “more musical,” or “less musical.”

But this too will [Col. 1435] be found neither in every quality nor in quality alone. Who could say that one prudence is more prudent than another, or one whiteness whiter than another whiteness, or one learning more learned than another learning, or one triangle more triangular than another triangle, or one square more square than another?

If something is a triangle, it cannot be more a triangle than it is; and if it is more or less than a triangle, it will no longer be a triangle.

It is nevertheless useful to separate and distinguish those qualities that admit more and less from those that exclude this degree of comparison [Note: [Col. 1435] The old manuscripts read *excusent*. The printed editions have *recusent*.].

Let this therefore be the rule: qualities themselves cannot admit more and less. Things formed from qualities, however, can, when compared, admit more or less. No one can say that eloquence itself is more eloquence or less eloquence; but we can say that someone called eloquent is more or less eloquent than others.

It is therefore clear that more and less can be found in things called “such,” but can never fall upon qualities themselves.

Figures likewise do not admit more and less, as was explained above. If you add or subtract anything from a circle, it will no longer retain the name “circle” and will pass into the name of another figure.

It has therefore been clearly established which qualities accept this kind of degree of comparison and which seem foreign to it.

It remains for us to investigate the proper feature of quality, which in Greek is called *ἴδιον*.

Substance has this proper feature: as one individual and numerically one, it can receive contraries within itself. I said that it can receive them, not that it possesses contraries.

We must remember that, when we discussed substance, we said that nothing is contrary to substance.

Thus, just as it is the property of substance to receive contraries—that is, now health and now illness; and of quantity, or *τοῦ πόσου*, to be called even or odd; and of *τοῦ δὲ πρός τι*, or *ad aliquid*, to have reciprocal conversions, that is, to be converted into one another and joined together by nature—so it is the property of quality that all things called “such” are called similar or dissimilar.

Sweet things are properly called similar or dissimilar to sweet things; white things to white things; foolish things to foolish things; smooth things to smooth things; and hot things to hot things. If they are spoken of in another way, they will not have their proper designation.

So that certain readers may not be confused when they find that affection, possession, and learning, which are placed among things called *ad aliquid*, that is, *ἐν τοῖς πρός τι*, are also connected with this same quality, we offer the following distinction.

They are joined to the category *ad aliquid* when they are genera; when they are species, they belong to quality.

For example, if you speak of learning as the genus of the other kinds, it must be referred to *ad aliquid*. Learning is called learning of something that can be learned.

But if you speak of music, music is a species of learning, not its genus; it must be joined to quality. We cannot say “the music of a musical person,” but we can say “the learning of a musical person.”

Affection and possession are similarly joined now to *ad aliquid*, now to quality, according to whether they are genera or species.

If you speak of affection or possession—that is, *διάθεσις* and *ἕξις*—in the sense of a genus, namely learning, they are referred to *ad aliquid*. But if you call affection or possession a species, namely of music or grammar, we must recognize them as qualities.

Although Aristotle himself, a man of great intelligence, conceded almost this entire intermixture, he said that it could happen that something belonging to quality might also be referred to *ad aliquid*, and that it was not improper for one thing to be enclosed under the name of two categories.

## CHAPTER XIII — On Doing and Undergoing

Everything belonging to the four greatest and most difficult categories has now been stated. The order of the discussion now requires that, after quality, we treat of doing and undergoing.

These two seem to descend from the source of quality. For that which makes something hot must itself be hot; and we know that hot is a quality.

Similarly, that which becomes hot receives a quality through its undergoing. The person who teaches is a teacher while teaching and makes another a student; yet both the teacher and the student are “such.” Consideration of other similar examples demonstrates that these two categories are rightly treated after quality.

[Col. 1436] Many have said that doing and undergoing can arise only in things that are contrary. Something sweet makes sweet only what was not sweet. For if what undergoes were already sweet, by its own nature it would have no capacity to receive another sweetness. Therefore what undergoes must not be sweet in order to receive a foreign sweetness. Consequently, since what acts is sweet and what undergoes is not sweet, they necessarily seem to be contraries.

Others have thought differently, asserting that these things can be found only in things that are similar and established under the same genus. Nothing, they say, can undergo or act unless it acts upon something similar or undergoes something from something similar.

Although sweet and bitter, or hot and cold, seem to be contrary, they nevertheless affirm that, when they fall under the same sense, they are similar.

Finally, they say that the process of undergoing or acting cannot exist between things that are wholly alien and distinct. What, for example, could number do to bitterness, or what could whiteness undergo from number?

But let this be the dispute of others. For us, the following rule is sufficient: doing and undergoing are joined in genus but distinguished in quality.

Hot, which bestows its heat upon cold, belongs to the same genus as cold; but it differs in quality because it is hot. The learned person who teaches an unlearned person belongs to the same genus as the unlearned person, but they are distinguished in quality.

It is therefore clear that doing and undergoing are similar in genus and contrary in quality.

These two categories, as we said above, seem to be joined to quality not only in order but also in reasoning, so that they receive the same features that we said quality receives.

They do not reject contrariety, which quality receives; they also admit more and less, of which we likewise said that quality is receptive.

As for the proper feature of these categories, which in Greek is called *ἴδιον*, Aristotle himself omitted it; nor should the reader seek it from us.

## CHAPTER XIV — On Lying, or Position

It follows that we should speak of “lying,” or of position, as some think. This category already seems to have been treated among things related to one another.

For whatever lies, lies in a position; position belongs to what is positioned, and what is positioned belongs to position. For this reason, as Aristotle himself, whom we follow, did, let us pass on to other matters.

## CHAPTER XV — On Where and When

“Where” and “when” seem to be place and time, although they are not; rather, things are in place and time: for example, “at Rome,” “in the senate,” “before the third hour,” “after the month of March.”

These things, as we said, are in place and time, but they are not place and time.

Finally, in order to make these categories clear and to avoid a discussion requiring further treatment, Aristotle also passed over them; we shall do the same.

For among the highest philosophers there is an ancient and important dispute concerning time and place: some wish them to be corporeal, while others judge them to exist without bodies.

## CHAPTER XVI — On Having

We are said to have something in more than one way. As far as we have gathered through our discussion, there are, under this verb, almost eight species.

The first is whenever we have something in the mind, such as justice, chastity, injustice, or lust.

The second is whenever we are said to have something in the body, such as whiteness, blackness, variegation, or the other things that belong to the body through quality.

The third descends from quantity, whenever we are said to have a length of four or five feet.

The fourth is when we are affirmed to have something not in the whole body but in a part of the body, such as a ring on a finger or shoes or boots on a foot.

The fifth species is when we are said to have something not on the body but around the body, such as clothing and all garments.

The sixth is whenever we are said to have the parts of the body themselves, such as hands, feet, a head, or the other things belonging to the structure of the limbs.

The seventh place is whenever grain or wine is said to have some vessel.

The eighth degree of having is that which seems to indicate our possession or ownership, when someone is said to have a house, a farm, or the tombs of his ancestors.

These are the modes of having, which we have comprehended under a stated number. If someone is able to discover another [Col. 1437] beyond them, this will not be due to any fault of our laziness, since the Philosopher himself has left freedom of inquiry to those who investigate.

Many learned men reject the word “to have” in another usage and maintain that it is improperly spoken when a woman is said to have a husband, a man a wife, a father a son, or a son a parent. They assert that something cannot be had if it itself has the one who has it.

They therefore consider it more correct to say that a woman has a husband in the sense that a husband exists for a woman, that a wife exists for a man, a father for a son, and a master for servants.

They maintain that the force of this verb is such that it cannot signify both having someone and being had by someone.

## CHAPTER XVII — On the Post-Predicaments

At last, as though we had crossed the straits of a great sea, we have completed the number of the Categories—so I think, not unpersuasively for the learned, and sufficiently clearly for those who wish to learn.

But certain matters remain which prevent us from touching the end of this book. For each individual category has included a treatment of contrariety, since we said which things receive a contrary and which reject one.

Yet no discussion has so far shown what contrariety itself is, and some terms remain whose force and proper meaning must be explained.

For this reason, let us proceed to the necessary treatment of opposites.

## CHAPTER XVIII — On Opposites. Three Species of Contraries.

There are four kinds of opposites: one thing is opposed to another, first, in the manner of the form of the category called relative; second, in the manner of contraries; third, in the manner of things whose possession (*habitus*) or privation is said to be in us; fourth, when we affirm or deny something. Here *habitus* must be understood from *having*, not as we defined it above, namely, as a certain permanent affection of the mind.

As an example of things called relative, let us posit the following. The first apparent opposite is double and simple, or father and son. As an example of contraries, let bad and good serve. Of those expressed through condition and privation, an example is blindness and sight. Of those in which there are negation and affirmation, an example is “he is running” and “he is not running.”

The distinction between contraries and things called relative is evident to those who consider it. Things called relative are named in relation to their opposites: simple is opposed to double, and double to simple. Contraries, however, possess what they are called from themselves and do not require the other. For who would call evil the evil of good, or good the good of evil? This, then, is the clear and evident distinction between these two kinds arising from opposites.

Contraries themselves are divided into three kinds. They are either intermediate—that is, they have something intermediate between them—or without an intermediate—or, as reason discovers in certain cases, they do have an intermediate, but its name is not apparent except insofar as it consists in the negation of both opposites.

Intermediate opposites are, for example, white and black, between which pallid or dark-brown may arise; these are called intermediate opposites. In the case of intermediate opposites, it is not necessary for one of the two opposites to be found in the body. If black is absent, there may be dark brown; or if white is lacking, pallid may be found.

But among those opposites that are not intermediate, one of the two must necessarily occur, as with health and illness. There is nothing intermediate between these, because human bodies must necessarily retain either health or illness.

Those opposites that have an intermediate but lack a name unless it is formed by negating the opposites are such as “just” and “unjust.” There is something intermediate, but it has no name; therefore the negation of both opposites creates its designation, so that we call what is intermediate “neither just nor unjust.”

Let us now reconsider more carefully those opposites that arise through condition and privation. In these cases, it must be observed that both apply to the same matter, the same place, and the appropriate time.

Blindness and sight belong to the same matter, for they consist in seeing and not seeing. They are also in the same place, since both blindness and sight have their location in the eyes.

Above all, however, the appropriateness of the time is sought in these cases. No one is rightly called bald except at the time when, if he ought to have hair, he does not have it. Nor can anyone call toothless an infant—whom the Greeks call *nōdon* (νωδὸν)—when his young age has still denied him teeth. For privation, which in Greek is called *stērēsis* (στέρησις), has this force: it shows that someone has been endowed by nature with something and does not have it.

Here we ought to remember that sight and blindness are one thing, and having sight or being deprived of it another; otherwise, if we judged these to be the same, the reasoning would appear confused.

If anyone considers this doubtful or insufficiently certain, let him observe what follows from each thing. For if “blind” and “blindness” were the same, both would be said of one thing. We do say “a blind man,” but a man cannot be called “blindness.” It is therefore clear that being blind is one thing and blindness another.

Affirmation and negation are likewise not the same as the things that fall under affirmation and negation. Affirmation or negation is a word affirming or denying something; the other things are those found under them, such as “Socrates is discussing” and “Socrates is not discussing.” Nevertheless, all these are held to be opposites of one another.

Sometimes evils are opposed to evils, whenever the intermediates of the contraries are good, as with deficiency and excess, which the Greeks call *endeia* and *hyperbolē* (ἐνδείαν καὶ ὑπερβολὴν). Between these two evils, opposed to one another, moderation is found as the intermediate.

Following this reasoning, the Peripatetics said that virtues are intermediates. Thus they called excess beyond what is just *pleonexia* (πλεονεξίαν), and deficiency below what is just *meionexia* (μειονεξίαν); between these evils they placed justice as the mean. Similarly, they placed prudence between cunning and dullness; temperance between lust and insensibility, which the Greeks call *anaisthēsia* (ἀναισθησίαν); and courage between timidity and rashness.

Thus, careful investigation discovered a certain hidden kind of opposites, so that sometimes evils are found to be contrary to evils.

Aristotle, however, explained more fully and in many ways the properties and differences of these four kinds arising from opposites. For us, it is enough to have set out the genus and the species, lest, occupied with finer details, we cause the necessary matters to become tedious.

# Chapter XIX — On the Prior

One thing is said to be prior to another in five ways.

The first is when we say that someone is older in time.

The second is when something arises from what is prior, but when the prior perishes, the subsequent also perishes, whereas when the subsequent perishes, the prior remains unharmed. Thus one is naturally prior to two: for two arise from one, but without one there cannot be two; without two, the existence of one remains. When two exist, one must exist; but when one alone appears, nothing compels the existence of two.

In the third way, a certain order makes one thing prior to another, as we find in disciplines and the liberal arts. In grammar, for example, it is prior to learn the forms and names of the individual letters, then to recognize the combinations of syllables, and thereafter to acquire an understanding of words. Finally, the use of speech must be taken up, for whose sake we recognize all its parts as though they had preceded it.

The order of priority is similarly arranged in rhetoric. We first speak the prologue, then the narration, after that the refutation, then the proof; the epilogue is placed last. These examples sufficiently demonstrate the third mode of priority.

The fourth mode is not very credible, and Aristotle himself explains it as rejected: for example, when the common people customarily call those who are better by fortune or more illustrious “prior.” In my judgment, the force of this kind of priority has been dismissed.

These are the four modes of what is called “prior.” But a more obscure fifth is added whenever, of two things that are convertible into one another, that one is preferred which causes the other to be what it is.

For example, if a human being exists, we rightly say that he is a rational, mortal animal, capable of laughter. And if this is the true definition of a human being, it is true that he is a human being. Thus each is convertible with the other: both that the definition of a human being is true and that the definition truly describes a human being.

But since the definition could not be true unless the nature of the human being appeared first, among these two things—which we have said are convertible into one another—the human being holds the place of priority, since his existence expresses the truth of his definition.

[Col. 1439]

# Chapter XX — On Things Existing Simultaneously

It remains for us to express the property of the word by which we say that certain things exist simultaneously. Reason seems to require that, after treating the prior, we discuss those things that are established as simultaneous.

Things are said to be simultaneous in three ways.

First, when any things exist or appear at the same time, so that neither of the two is prior or follows the other, but the origin of both appears to be common, as with heat and radiance in the sun.

The second applies to things that are naturally simultaneous, although neither gives precedence to the other. For example, if we posit simple and double, they must naturally exist simultaneously; but double does not cause simple to exist, nor does simple cause double.

Here we must not allow ourselves to become confused. When we were discussing things called relative, we said that something is relative because it depends upon another; now we might seem to be arguing against what was defined above. We argued that all things called relative are said from another, not that they exist from another. There is no error in this, if anyone examines the force of our words more carefully.

The third case occurs whenever things flowing from the same genus appear naturally to be simultaneous but are distinguished in species. They do not provide anything to one another in what they are called, as with animal: it is one genus, but its species are widely different. No flying creature contributes anything to a walking creature so that it may exist, nor a walking creature to a flying one; nor does one provide any substance whatsoever to the other in respect of its being. None is prior to another; rather, all arise and come into existence simultaneously from animal, that is, from one genus.

# Chapter XXI — On Change

Every alteration—which in Greek is called *metabolē* (μεταβολή)—takes place in three ways: either from a non-subject into a subject, as in origin or birth, which the Greeks call *genesis* (γένεσιν); or from a subject into a non-subject, as in destruction or corruption, which the Greeks call *phthora* (φθοράν); or from a subject into a subject, as in motion, which in Greek is called *kinēsis* (κίνησις).

Motion itself also has three species: increase, decrease, and alteration of quality or place. These are called by the Greeks *auxēsis*, *meiōsis*, *alloiōsis*, or *phora* (αὔξησις, μείωσις, ἀλλοίωσις, φορά). They wished alteration concerning place to be called *phora*; following the teachers, we too have preferred to call it transgression.

This order, which we have presently arranged with careful examination, as though differing from the book called the *Categories*, Aristotle himself also explained in his books on nature. In the *Categories*, however, following the brevity required for teaching, he did not hesitate to take the species for the genus—that is, motion for alteration—and to say that six species are subordinate to motion as to a genus: *genesis*, *phthora*, *auxēsis*, *meiōsis*, *alloiōsis poiotētos* (γένεσιν, φθοράν, αὔξησιν, μείωσιν, ἀλλοίωσιν ποιότητος), and alteration according to place.

> [Note: [Col. 1439] Aristotle does not have the word *poiōtētos*. M.]

[Col. 1440]

We have rendered these in Latin as origin, destruction, increase, decrease, alteration of quality, and transgression of place.

These six species are distinguished from one another in every respect—unless, perhaps, someone insufficiently educated might think that alteration of quality, that is, *alloiōsis*, also occurs whenever the other kinds exist, so that whenever something is born, perishes, grows, or diminishes, alteration would also be said to have occurred.

Reason shows this to be false. Things that grow or diminish are altered in quantity, not changed in quality. For alteration properly concerns quality.

We must also remember that alteration in general is one thing and change in a particular respect another. Alteration is the genus; particular change is the species subordinate to motion, which we have called a species of alteration.

Finally, to make their distinction clear, let us give a geometrical example. If you divide a larger square, depicted within by lines running through its middle, into small squares, and then remove one small square from it, you have diminished the larger square. But if, in place of what was removed, you add a gnomon, which is set out in the form of a semicircle, you have restored to the larger square more than you had taken away. This concerns quantity, not quality, and belongs more properly to alteration than to change in quality; hence the two differ greatly from one another.

Difference among all things arises in three ways: by material, by workmanship, or by both. It arises by material if there are two similar rings, one gold and the other silver; by workmanship if dissimilar rings are made from gold; and by both if the ring is gold but its stylus is silver.

It is therefore clear that these species of alteration are not joined to one another by material, workmanship, or both. They are so separate that some of them even appear to be contrary to one another.

Who, for example, would doubt that *genesis* and *phthora*—that is, origin and destruction—are contrary, or increase and decrease? Alteration itself, whether of quality or of place, although not belonging to the same number of species, nevertheless has something that appears contrary to it.

Alteration of quality occurs when something changes from white to black, or from black to white; these are manifestly contrary to one another. Alteration of place, which we have called transgression, likewise undergoes the contrariety of higher and lower positions, and therefore appears also to have contraries.

# Chapter XXII — Conclusion of the Work

These are the matters, dearest son, that we have attained through unremitting labor, with the instruction of Themistius, an outstanding philosopher in our memory, not lacking to us. For your benefit we have translated them from Greek into Latin, so that you too may receive from us the good fruit of study, if, not unlike us, desire for other things—slippery and empty things—has held you back.

For in this book we have omitted nothing that could either delight those already learned or teach the unlearned more clearly.

[Col. 1439]

# PRINCIPLES OF RHETORIC

(C, G, S)

> [Note: [Col. 1439] We have found no manuscript copy of this little work. The author uses Greek words without necessity, contrary to Augustine’s practice. M.]

# Chapter I — The Orator’s Function

The function of the orator, once a civil question has been proposed, is first to understand the question itself: whether it is general or particular, simple or composed of several parts, absolute or comparative.

After understanding it, he must discover within it the topics appropriate to its division and adapt moral or natural propositions to them. He must then judge what he has discovered and reject whatever has arisen insufficiently well. Finally, he must give a fixed order to what he has examined by judgment.

For although many relevant matters may have been discovered, unless they are placed according to their quality and magnitude in certain and, as it were, legitimate positions, they will either do harm or provide little benefit.

Next, the rhetorician must supply an explanation of the matters according to their arrangement.

[Col. 1440]

This consists of two parts: the quality of the structure and the quantity of the words.

Memory receives all these matters. Most Greeks, and especially Marcus Tullius, affirm that memory is necessary to the orator, in the following manner, as I think:

> “I now come to the treasury of all things, memory. Unless it is employed as guardian of the things discovered and arranged, we understand that everything, even if most excellent, will perish in the orator.”

Delivery follows memory. According to Demosthenes, it is among the orator’s functions either first or alone. It consists of two things: bodily movement and the sound of the voice.

It is enough to have touched on these matters only in summary, since they are the functions of the orator. It remains to see what the end is.

# Chapter II — What the Orator’s End Is

The end, as I think, is that toward which everything in all matters is referred and for whose sake all other things are done. The Greeks call it *telos* (τέλος).

This is also sought in nearly all philosophical discussions: what is the end of living well—virtue or pleasure?

Different people have approved different accounts of the proper end of the orator’s function. Some have thought that the whole function of the orator consists in speaking well; others, in speaking correctly; others, in persuading.

Moreover, those who thought that speaking well or speaking truthfully was the end of the orator’s function nevertheless do not deny that the end of these very things is persuasion. Thus the end of the orator’s function is speaking well, and the end of speaking well is persuading.

Therefore, by something like universal agreement, the end of the orator’s function is persuasion.

Because this seemed open to criticism—for the orator does not always persuade, and if at some time he cannot persuade, he does not thereby lose either the ability or the name of orator—Hermagoras added, to escape this criticism, that the end of the orator’s function is persuasion insofar as the condition of circumstances and persons permits.

A further criticism arose from the same word “persuasion.” It was devised by Plato and treated extensively in the *Gorgias*, but later, and much more shamelessly, was repeatedly employed by certain technical writers who attacked Hermagoras.

> [Note: [Col. 1441] The Benedictines add the word “are,” which we have found nowhere in the editions. M.]

They deny that persuasion is the proper end of the orator’s function, but say that it is almost common to everyone. Mathematicians, they argue, persuade others about matters that have come within their knowledge; physicians persuade others about matters contained within their art; craftsmen, shopkeepers, smiths, and others of this kind can also plausibly persuade anyone about what they do, as though they acted according to reason.

Therefore, they say, an end is not complete if it possesses only commonality and lacks particularity. The act of persuading is common to many, and therefore persuasion is not the proper end of the orator’s function.

Hermagoras very suitably resists this criticism as well. He says that the function of the orator is to persuade insofar as the condition of circumstances and persons permits, but only in civil questions. For the questions of physicians, philosophers, and others of this kind lie outside the civil rule, which the Greeks call *politikē* (πολιτική).

# Chapter III — Civil Questions and the Difference between General and Particular Questions

Civil questions are those whose consideration can fall within the common conception of the mind, which the Greeks call *ennoia* (ἔννοια).

To make this condition—which we wish to have been demonstrated—easier for you to understand, consider all matters of this kind: matters of which it would be shameful to be ignorant, and which, even when we do not know them, we nevertheless present ourselves as though we knew them, with a show of confidence. Whenever such matters are called into doubt, they produce a civil question.

What I mean is this. If the weight of something is asked, and you do not appear to know how many pounds it weighs, there is no need for shame. If its length is asked, and you do not appear to know how many feet it measures, there is no need for shame. The same applies to other matters of this kind, which it would take too long to pursue. Whenever such matters come into doubt, they may indeed produce a question, but they cannot produce a civil question.

But when the question is whether something is just or unjust, honorable or dishonorable, worthy of praise or blame, deserving of reward or punishment, useful or useless, and so forth, no one, even if entirely outside every art and science, fails to feel shame if he appears ignorant of such matters.

Hence everyone is convinced—or at least does not hesitate to persuade others—that he can conceive in his mind the distinction between just and unjust, honorable and dishonorable, and the other things mentioned above. Therefore the doubts that arise in such matters are called civil questions, as though they were not the property of a few but common to everyone.

Since this is so, and since such matters can be perceived through common conception of the mind, questions that can be grasped *dia tēs ennoias* (διὰ τῆς ἐννοίας), “through conception,” are called civil questions. These are the questions in which the orator must operate and persevere.

There are two primary and, as it were, general kinds of civil questions. The Greeks call one *thesis* (θέσις) and the other *hypothesis* (ὑπόθεσις).

We cannot give the former any name except its Greek one, nor can we give the latter any other name than one that may appear already to have been supplied. We have supplied it, since we call it a “controversy,” a name that can apply both to *thesis* and to *hypothesis*. In both cases there is a question—that is, a controversy.

The meaning of *hypothesis* is disclosed both by the compound word itself and by the fact that it is something *hypo tēn thesin* (ὑπὸ τὴν θέσιν), “under the thesis,” as it were a species under that genus.

A thesis is a matter that admits rational consideration without the specification of a person. A hypothesis—or controversy, if we use the term improperly—is a matter that admits rational dispute with the specification of a person.

This will be better explained by examples. A thesis is a question such as whether one ought to sail or philosophize. A hypothesis is a question such as whether a battle by single combat ought to be decreed.

Some also bring accusations against Hermagoras on this point, especially Apollodorus, who denies that a hypothesis is anything other than a thesis and says that the distinction made by persons is of no importance, although Hermagoras appears to have distinguished both kinds of question. For he says that the question of the hypothesis is no less unlimited and undetermined than that of the thesis.

When the question is whether Orestes ought to be punished, they argue, it is not the person who creates the question but the act. It makes no difference whether the question is framed as whether a matricide ought to be punished. If this is so, there would be no difference between hypothesis and thesis.

To this our writers reply, first, that the qualities of persons introduce a difference into questions, and that even in hypotheses—that is, controversies—it often happens that some matters appear to be punishable or unpunishable, honorable or dishonorable, not so much because of the quality of the acts as because of the quality of the person.

Second, these two kinds of question also differ in that in a thesis the consideration concerns what a matter is like, whereas in a hypothesis there is contention. As much as consideration differs from contention, so much does thesis differ from hypothesis.

Further, a thesis asks what everyone ought to do; a hypothesis asks what one person, two persons, or a few more—in any case, a defined number of people—ought to do.

Another difference also occurs: in a thesis we ask, as though ignorant, what is best to do; in a hypothesis we defend our position as though we knew.

There is also this distinction: every thesis concerns the future, whereas a hypothesis rarely—and indeed never, except concerning the past or something already in progress—raises a question about the future. No one can become a defendant unless he has done something or is said to have done it; nor can anyone seek a reward or anything of that kind unless he has already deserved it or claims that he deserves it.

At this point they bring forward defendants accused of tyranny and treason, and of ordered poisoning, along with any other examples that can be devised in the same manner. In their eagerness to accuse, however, they are mistaken.

Even when someone is accused of treason, the question is not about a future matter—that is, about the treason itself—but whether he formed the plan of treason, which plainly preceded the act. The same applies to tyranny: the question is whether he contemplated tyranny; and to parricide, whether it was committed; and likewise to poisoning.

Therefore, in a hypothesis the question always arises either about the past or about the present; in a thesis, by contrast, it arises only about the future. If this is so, the difference between the two has been sufficiently demonstrated.

# Chapter IV — The Circumstances That Produce a Controversy

Since enough has now been said about the difference between general and particular questions, and since thesis has been separated from hypothesis so that they differ in reality as well as in name, it seems appropriate to say what produces a hypothesis—that is, a controversy.

There is therefore a circumstance of matters, which Hermagoras calls *peristasis* (περίστασις), without which no controversy whatever can exist.

What *peristasis* is can be discovered more easily by division than by definition. The parts of circumstance, that is, of *peristasis*, are seven. Hermagoras calls them *moria peristaseōs* (μόρια περιστάσεως), “parts of circumstance”; Theodorus calls them *stoicheia pragmatōn* (στοιχεῖα πραγμάτων), “elements of matters,” because questions arise from their combination just as we see names and words arise from the combination of letters.

But whether *stoicheia* or *moria* is the more correct term, let us set aside the controversy over the name and state what the things themselves are.

They are: who, what, when, where, why, how, and by what aids. The Greeks call these the *aphormai tēs peristaseōs* (ἀφορμαὶ περιστάσεως), “the starting points of circumstance.”

A rational or legal combination of all or most of these forms a question. But the particular property of each must be expressed.

“Who” signifies the person under consideration, which is viewed in two ways: by name and by quality.

By name:

> Who? Camillus, Gaius Marius, Lucius Sulla.

By quality:

> Who? A rich man, a poor man, a commander.

Consideration of persons is definite in names and indefinite in qualities. In the former case, nothing beyond the name falls under the designation; in the latter, fortune, age, condition, education, and other things whose number is unlimited are included.

“What” signifies the matter that has been done, said, or thought by someone—or that appears to be about to be done, said, or thought—whether good or bad, honorable or dishonorable, just or unjust, useful or the contrary, necessary or trivial, great or little-used, or new.

“When” signifies time: for example, by day or by night, on a sacred or an irreligious day. It also includes circumstances that sometimes give time its quality, such as in wartime or peacetime, during sedition or concord, under freedom or under domination, and any matters that fall into the same category.

“Where” signifies place: for example, in the city or outside it, in a sacred or profane place, at sea or on land.

“Why” signifies the cause of doing, saying, or thinking something. In my opinion, this is especially necessary for establishing a question.

“How” signifies the manner, as shown by the act, by what is being done, or by what is going to happen: secretly, openly, by force, by deceit, and anything similar that falls into the same category.

The *aphormai*, which we call “aids,” signify the things through which something is said to have been done: a noose, a sword, poison, letters, a messenger, orders, a slave, an accomplice, an assassin.

As I said above, the rational concurrence of all or most of these elements produces a civil question.

# Chapter V — Rational Questions Arise in Four Ways

Rational questions are what Hermagoras calls *logikai* (λογικαί). I think it better to call them “rational” than “verbal,” because the technical writers derive *logikai* not from the meaning of a word but from the meaning of reason, although *logos* (λόγος) can sometimes mean “word” and sometimes “reason.”

Rational—or *logikai*—questions therefore arise in four ways. The question concerns whether something exists, what it is, what sort of thing it is, or whether it ought to be brought before a court.

When the question is whether something exists, Hermagoras calls this kind of question *stochasmos* (σοχασμός); we may call it “conjecture.” Theodorus calls it *peri tēs ousias* (περὶ τῆς οὐσίας), “concerning substance.” For nothing can appear to have been done unless it has had substance, nor can anything be about to happen unless it will have substance. Some have called this kind of question by the expression through which it asks whether something exists.

The second rational question is what Hermagoras calls “definition” (*finis*); Theodorus calls it *peri tēs idiotētos* (περὶ τῆς ἰδιότητος), “concerning particularity” or “property.” Some call it “what it is”; others call it *peri tou autou kai heterou* (περὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ καὶ ἑτέρου), “concerning the same and the other.”

Everyone calls the third rational question by one name: quality.

There is great controversy concerning the fourth, which we said above concerns bringing a matter before a court. Most deny that it is a question, since they act so as to prevent the matter from entering the sphere of questions. But among all authorities Hermagoras is preeminent. He considers it a question, and a particularly necessary one; he says that it is much debated in court and must also be introduced at once in the other kinds of issue, at the very first encounter, if the condition of the case permits.

For nothing matters so much to those against whom judgment is sought as avoiding judgment. Moreover, the avoidance of judgment itself possesses a certain kind of judicial character.

If matters were arranged so that whenever someone did not want a case to be judged, this lay entirely within his power, there would be no question. But since there are always people who obstruct, the very contention by which one person summons another to judgment while the other refuses judgment produces a question.

Hermagoras calls this kind of controversy *asystaton* (ἀσύστατον), “unconstituted.” Among our writers, a few have called it “reprehension,” while most have called it “transfer,” both following a rationale.

Those who called it “reprehension” did so because, when the matter is especially brought before judgment, the case is challenged and, as it were, dragged back. Those who called it “transfer” did so because the defendant does not entirely exclude the action but excuses himself from the action under its present conditions and transfers it to another kind of judgment, whether one already established or one yet to come.

# Chapter VI — The Four Legal Questions

There are also four other questions, which their inventors call *nomikai* (νομικαί), and which we call “legal.”

The legal questions are the written word and the intention, which they call *rhēton kai dianoian* (ῥητὸν καὶ διάνοιαν); *antinomia* (ἀντινομία), which we call a conflict of contrary laws; ambiguity, which they call *amphibolia* (ἀμφιβολίαν); and collection, which they call *syllogē* (συλλογήν).

We shall treat these a little later with greater care, so that the meaning of each may be expressed more clearly and the species may be added to the genera.

For the moment, it seems to me that we should say by what elements every question is linked and by what kinds of knots it is successively bound until it reaches its complete form.

# Chapter VII — By What Elements a Question Is Bound
There is a certain statement which the Greeks call *phasis* (φάσις, “assertion”). It is divided into two parts: one is *apophasis* (ἀπόφασις), and the other *kataphasis* (κατάφασις). We may call *kataphasis* an assertion made in words—that is, the statement by which a charge is brought: “You struck him,” “You betrayed him,” “You killed him.” What they call *apophasis*, we call the denial of the crime which the accuser has asserted in words: “I did not strike him,” “I did not betray him,” “I did not kill him.”

From these two—assertion and response, or accusation and denial—the question arises between them, in this way: the assertion is, “You killed him”; the denial, “I did not kill him”; the question, “Did he kill him?” But let us now move away from the conjectural form: the assertion is, “You killed him unjustly”; the denial, “I did not kill him unjustly”; the question, “Did he kill him unjustly?” Or, in some legal status, the assertion is, “The law did not permit you to do this”; the denial is, “The law permitted me to do it”; the question is, “Did the law permit him to do this?”

Some have called this a *question*, as we have hitherto called it; others have called it a *status*, evidently because in it both the beginning and the substance of the question stand. At first, as though from a distance, when one side says that something happened and the other says that it did not happen, there is no struggle, but rather a preparation for a future struggle. Then, when the opponents have drawn nearer and have, as it were, come to blows, the intervening question—whether the act occurred or not—enters into their mutual dispute and contention; each party takes his stand upon it, abandoning what he had said before. Hence the name *status* was given to this question.

Theodorus calls the same thing *kephalaion* (κεφάλαιον, “main point”), using a metaphor drawn from the principal part of the body: for in this combination of the two statements made on either side, it becomes, as it were, the head of the whole controversy.

The topic that follows this is either equally necessary or even more so: it demonstrates what the cause is, what the containing matter is, and what is being disputed. Hermagoras calls the cause *aition* (αἴτιον); the containing matter *synechon* (συνέχον); and what is being disputed *to krinomenon* (τὸ κρινόμενον).

The cause, then, is that without which the controversy cannot arise. My meaning is as follows: a son is disowned by his father. There is no controversy for this reason, because no cause has preceded that would explain why he was disowned by his father. Let us add a cause, and at once a controversy has been created: “He swore that he would not marry, and he is disowned.” The fact that he swore has become the *aition*, that is, the cause for which he deserved disownment.

The *synechon*, or containing matter, is what appears to be brought forward in order to refute the *aition*, that is, in order to rebut the cause. Thus, in this case: “The commander killed a soldier who had sworn that he would desert, and is accused of murder.” Here the *aition*, that is, the cause of the trial, is that he killed him; for he would not be accused unless he had killed him. The *synechon*, that is, the containing matter, is the reason on account of which he says that he killed him—namely, the soldier’s oath, by which he had sworn that he would desert.

Hermagoras sometimes calls this *synechon*, that is, “the containing matter,” because the whole defense of the case is contained in it; at other times he calls it the *aition of the aition*, as though it were “the cause of the cause.” For just as the cause of the charge is that he killed the soldier, so [Col. 1445] the cause of the killing is that the soldier had sworn that he would desert.

Now that we know what the cause and the containing matter are, let us also see what is being disputed—that is, what *to krinomenon* is. It is nothing other than an examination of the containing matter, *tou synechontos* (τοῦ συνέχοντος).

My meaning is as follows—for I think we should remain with the same controversy, so that what we are teaching may be clearer. The *aition* is the fact that the commander killed the soldier. The *synechon* is what the accused relies upon, that is, the reason on account of which he says that he killed him: namely, that the soldier had sworn that he would desert. The *krinomenon* is the examination of this very matter which the accused has brought forward in his defense.

The question is therefore whether the commander had some other reason for killing the soldier; and this is alleged as a pretext, so that he may appear to have killed him not because the soldier had sworn to desert, but for some reason of hostility or jealousy. This point may also be handled in the following way: whether, even if the soldier had sworn, that was nevertheless insufficient as a just cause for which he ought to have been killed. The complete determination of the whole *synechon* brought forward against the *aition* is called the *krinomenon*.

Sometimes, however, it happens that in one controversy the *aition*, *synechon*, and *krinomenon* are not all treated together, but that the same elements are repeatedly turned over and examined in succession. Thus, in this controversy: “Ulysses is accused under the law of the state because he killed the suitors.”

Here the *aition* is that he killed them; the *synechon* is that he killed those who were plundering his property and plotting against his wife’s chastity; the *krinomenon* is whether, although this circumstance preceded, he nevertheless killed them for some other reason than the one he alleges—or whether, even if they had acted most wickedly against him, he ought to have killed them without trial.

Ulysses then brings forward another *synechon* for this *krinomenon*: he says that he killed them at Minerva’s command. The *synechon* itself then becomes a *krinomenon*, as the question is raised whether he killed them because of Minerva’s command, and whether, in such a matter, he ought not to have obeyed even Minerva. The *aition* is the proper topic of the accuser; the *synechon*, of the defender; the *krinomenon*, common to both.

## CHAPTER VIII — The Forms of Asystatic Controversies

I think it should next be explained how, and in how many ways, a controversy becomes *asystatos* (ἀσύστατος, “without a basis”). Indeed, controversies that have no status ought not even to be called controversies, but irrational *plegmata* (πλέγματα), that is, “irrational entanglements.”

They become *asystata* in four ways.

The first is when something is missing from the circumstances. We have explained above what force the circumstances possess: namely, when one of the questions, or the cause, the person, the place, or something else among those elements by which we said that a circumstance is constituted, is missing. This type of *asystatos* cannot occur in scholastic material, because no theme can exist when a circumstance is lacking. In actual cases, however, it sometimes happens that one of these elements is missing, and that the case comes before the judge already ruined through the advocate’s lack of foresight.

The second mode of *asystatos* is what they call *kat’ isotēta* (κατ’ ἰσότητα, “according to equality”). Even if we cannot give it a Latin name, we should understand its force. For when the same things are said on both sides, and the parties are distinguished by nothing—not even by the smallest point—nevertheless such a *plegma*, because of the equality of the two sides, entangles the issue.

For example, two neighboring young men, who had handsome wives, met one another at night. Each accuses the other of adultery. Whatever one side says, the other must necessarily say as well:

“It is probable that you intended to commit adultery, because you are a young man.”

“It is equally probable that you intended to commit adultery, because you are a young man.”

“It is probable because I have a handsome wife.”

“It is equally probable in your case, because I too have a handsome wife.”

“Your being my neighbor gave you the opportunity.”

“Your being my neighbor gave you the same opportunity.”

“Why were you out at night against me?”

“Why did you come upon me?”

There is nothing by which the two cases can be distinguished. Therefore, whichever of them accuses the other accuses himself; and whichever clears himself defends the man whom he appears to accuse.

The third kind of *asystatos* is what the Greeks call *kath’ heteromerian* (καθ’ ἑτερομέρειαν), that is, “according to the other side.” This occurs when the accused has no defense, and either no appearance of justification can be found in the act, or the appearance that is found is scarcely credible.

For this reason my teacher Democrates used to say that even those controversies in which a justification is sought for a long time have no status. He stated the matter more strictly; we admit a defense if something at least moderately [Col. 1446] plausible is offered. But if the case is plainly confessed, we reject it as belonging to *heteromeria*, as is proper.

Sometimes questions arise, especially in actual cases, which grant the accuser the fullest opportunity and the accused none at all. We do not call these controversies, however, but commonplaces, since in them the task is not to prove the crime, but to portray it as an unmistakable and evident offense.

The fourth mode of *asystatos* is the most obscure of all, so much so that it sometimes deceives even learned men. It has some appearance of plausible and coherent material. It is the kind in which the judge cannot discover a basis for reaching a decision. The Greeks call this *aporon* (ἄπορον, “insoluble” or “without a way through”).

Let us add an example. One man claimed interest from another as though on money lent. The other admitted that he had received the money, but said that it had been deposited with him; therefore he wished to return the principal without interest. Meanwhile, while the case was pending, a law concerning the cancellation of debts was passed. The claimant demanded the money as though it had been deposited; the other retained it as though it had been lent.

I do not see what the judge could follow here in delivering a decision, since the claimant sometimes says that he lent the money and sometimes that he deposited it, while the other sometimes says that he received it as a deposit and sometimes as a loan. Neither man relies on his own earlier position; each relies on the other’s previous statement.

## CHAPTER IX — The Figures of Controversies

It also seems relevant to know the figures of controversies and how they differ from one another, so that it may be more evident how each is to be treated.

There are therefore four themes, that is, figures of controversies: *eudoxon* (εὔδοξον), which we may call “of good repute”; *amphidoxon* (ἀμφίδοξον), which we may call “of mixed repute,” both good and bad; *paradoxon* (παράδοξον), which we may call “of bad repute.” Some people, speaking Greek rather carelessly, take *paradoxon* to mean things of good repute. Hence they commonly call Olympic victors and the other winners of sacred contests *paradoxoi*, being guided more by custom than by reason. For, as I think, *paradoxon* is what is *para tēn doxan* (παρὰ τὴν δόξαν), that is, contrary to good repute.

Finally, although we may prefer to approve other common meanings of this word, here we should understand it—as many new terms are named by technical writers, mathematicians, and philosophers—not according to ordinary customary usage, but according to the character of the rule.

The fourth kind of controversy is called in Greek *adoxos* (ἄδοξος). We do not understand this, as it is commonly understood, as “of bad repute,” but as “of no repute,” that is, humble and sordid. The following examples will make these distinctions clear.

An *eudoxos* controversy is one in which both the person and the matter are honorable. For example, Scipio, after conquering the Carthaginians, asks as a reward to watch the games wearing a crown of laurel. Scipio’s person is honorable, and what he requests is not shameful.

An *amphidoxos* controversy is one in which either the honor of the person is stained by the shamefulness of the matter, or the reverse. For example, suppose that the same Scipio asks, as his reward, the death of Tiberius Asellus. The person of the petitioner is honorable, but what he requests is dishonorable.

Conversely, suppose that a man who has been disowned has performed some brave deed and asks, as his reward, to return to his father’s household. The person making the request—the disowned man—is dishonorable, but the matter he requests, his return to his father’s home, is honorable.

A *paradoxon* is the kind of controversy which I defined above as one in which both elements are dishonorable, both the matter and the person. For example, a man accused of unchastity performs a brave deed and asks, as his reward, the death of his accuser. The person of the petitioner is dishonorable, since he was accused of unchastity, although the fact that he acted bravely has somewhat reduced the shame attaching to him; and the matter he requests is also wrong.

An *adoxon* is a kind of controversy without repute on either side, humble and sordid. A poor man was selling clothing. Another poor man appeared and claimed the clothes, saying that they had been stolen from him. The seller said that he had stripped the clothes from an adulterer whom he had caught. They accuse each other: one of adultery, the other of theft.

Here both the persons—the poor men—and the matters that appear to constitute the question are low and contemptible: the claim to and recognition of the clothing. Although the charge of adultery, which is not itself contemptible, has entered the case, nevertheless, because most of the elements preceding the *peristasis* (περίστασις, “circumstantial setting”) are humble and sordid, they [Col. 1447] determine the appearance of the entire controversy.

## CHAPTER X — The Usefulness of Recognizing Such Figures

Recognizing these figures of controversies is useful for many purposes, but especially for enabling us to find a suitable manner of introduction—that is, of delivering the opening—corresponding to the character of the material. The opening should not have the same form in an *eudoxos*, an *amphidoxos*, and a *paradoxos* theme; each must be given its own form.

First, in material of the *eudoxos* kind, Hermagoras denies that an introduction should be made. If, he says, we ordinarily use an opening to gain goodwill, what need is there of such an opening in a theme of good repute, such as that of Scipio? Those before whom we are going to speak are already favorably disposed; there is no point in preparing what is already prepared.

But I think the matter is quite different, if I may say so with due respect to so great a man. Authority should not always be followed, especially when reason defeats it. I therefore judge that nothing prevents us from making an introduction in material of the *eudoxos* kind. There is nothing wrong, in my opinion, in making kind judges still kinder through an opening, just as, when we see judges offended by our opponents, we try through our words to increase that offense.

Finally, we see that flute players, lyre players, and other artists of this kind, although they do not promise a speech, nevertheless say something before their performance. In general, a speech is stunted and headless if it begins with the facts themselves without an introduction.

We shall therefore also use introductions in controversies of good repute, but somewhat shorter and more direct, confident and full of dignity, provided that there is no boasting, lest the matter produce resentment. Thus Marcus Tullius, speaking against the assembly of Metellus, appears to exult when he says:

> “For so, I think, I shall pursue him in his flight, since I may not engage with him while he resists.”

He would certainly never have begun an exordium by speaking so magnificently at once unless both the person of the advocate himself had been honorable and the matter on which he was about to speak had not been disreputable.

Likewise, elsewhere, when speaking of the punishment of the conspirators, he says:

> “I see, Conscript Fathers, that the faces and eyes of all of you are turned toward me,”

and continues in the same vein. All of these expressions are such that the speaker appears to rely, with good reason, both on his own distinction and on the matters about which he is going to speak, as though they were altogether honorable.

There are many such openings in Quintus Gracchus. His spirit was so much nobler that no one would tolerate them from a Merucius, or from someone out of the band of Cannae.

In material of the *amphidoxos* kind, some moderation should be used when we begin, so that we may diminish the shamefulness that is present and increase the dignity belonging to the matter or the person by illuminating it, or so combine the two in varied ways that the honor of one side covers the shamefulness of the other.

Even then, however, we should not speak with the degree of self-display used in the preceding type of material, but rather with a certain confident modesty. If the shamefulness lies in the matter, we shall divert the judge, as far as possible, toward the dignity of the person. If it lies in the person, we shall flee toward the dignity of the matter, as though from a dangerous place to a safer one. We shall yield briefly and lightly, however, so that we may appear to disdain the suspicion rather than fear it.

We shall strive to make it appear that, although the dignity of both matter and person is confused together, we have more confidence in the honorable element than fear of the dishonorable one.

To make this manner of beginning clearer, I shall give the example used by Marcus Tullius when he spoke in defense of Marcus Scaurus. The controversy was *amphidoxos*, since he relied on the dignity of Marcus Scaurus’s person but was weighed down by the shamefulness of the charge involving extortion. The orator immediately combined both elements in his opening, so that he covered the shamefulness of the charge with the dignity of the person, yet not too generously or triumphantly, but in such a way as to reveal some suspicion of fear as well:

> “It would have been especially desirable for Marcus Scaurus, judges, that without having incurred anyone’s hatred, without offense or annoyance…”

[Note: [Col. 1447] “We diminish it by concealing it.” Something of this sort appears to be missing.]

In a *paradoxon*, that is, a theme of bad repute, where both the person and the dignity are equally in difficulty, longer openings should be used. Effort must be devoted to clearing away suspicions, and one must speak humbly, both in one’s thoughts and in one’s words, with language approaching flattery, and with a complaint as though a false charge had been brought against us and a false disgrace contrived against us through envy. The whole body should be shaped in a posture of modesty, with lowered face and eyes directed toward the ground. The expressions should not be delivered sharply, but, if possible, with fear also simulated.

In an *adoxon*, that is, in humble material, the openings should be close to ordinary conversation: neither employing lofty thoughts nor words ornamented beyond measure, nor a weightier structure, but appearing relaxed and simple.

The force of all the thoughts that we apply in such openings should be directed toward bringing the matter back from its particular circumstances to the common interest, and toward saying that everyone has an interest in seeing it vindicated. For the smaller things are, the more frequently and widely they can occur among people.

The magnitude of the matters and persons should not be considered so much as the principles of justice and injustice, truth and falsehood. The force of these principles is the same in small matters as in great ones.

There are many such openings in Demosthenes, in the books entitled *Idiotic*; still more in Lysias; and in some of our own earlier writers. Certainly, when Marcus Tullius spoke in defense of Archias, he began in no other way.

[Col. 1447]
