# FRAGMENT OF RULES HANDED DOWN TO CLERICS (C, G, S)

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING OPUSCULE

By the unanimous judgment of all learned men, this little work is rejected as Augustine’s. In Lucas Holstenius’s *Book of Rules*, part two, it is entitled *The Agreement of Monks*, a more suitable title. Nevertheless, it did not seem appropriate to alter the title long received in this Appendix, especially since the authority of ancient books is lacking; for we have found no manuscript copy of this little work.

[Col. 1447] We have established among ourselves by common definition a rule which no one thereafter may violate. While residing in the monastery in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, we have all agreed, according to apostolic tradition, to have one mind in the Lord and to possess everything in common. As it is written: “Be of one mind in the Lord” (Wis. I, 1). Let no one claim anything as his own, but let it be as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They held everything in common; no one said that anything was his own” (Acts II, 44; IV, 32).

This has been written by us. Let us therefore hold to it in the Lord by the right of [Col. 1448] observance, and remain in it to the end, because it is written in the law: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

If anyone wishes to come to the community of the brothers who appear to be united as one, let him not be unaware of the saying of the Gospel, which says: “Let him sell all that he has and distribute it to the needy and the poor” (ibid. XIX, 21). And again: “Let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke IX, 23).

Let him not deliberate in his heart about food or clothing, or about the other things necessary for the body, since the Lord himself gives warning in the Gospel and [Col. 1449] says: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles think about these things. Your Father knows that you need all these things. Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be given to you” (Matt. VI, 31–33).

Nevertheless, before he decides to remain in the monastery, let him test the purpose and example of the brothers; and let him himself be tested in his entire way of life by the Prior, with the agreement of the others, because Scripture teaches and warns, saying: “Do not quickly approve a friend.”

But if it should happen that someone is taken away from the monastery for any necessary reason, let him not even conceive in his mind the intention of carrying away with him anything of all that was in the monastery—whether something he had once brought with him, or something he had acquired together with the brothers. For it is certain that the brothers ought neither to have, possess, give, nor receive anything without the permission of their superior.

If a relative, friend, or any of the brothers wishes to offer something, it must first be reported to the Prior, and then accepted if he orders it. Nothing else, however, is to be done with it except what pleases or is permitted by the Prior, since one must greatly fear that what is written may happen to him: “A man changeable in speech falls into evil” (Prov. XIII, 3).

And again, no one at all should entice one of the brothers to leave with him, lest he appear more a destroyer than a builder of the monastery, because it is written: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. XII, 30).

Whoever is enticed by someone and wishes to leave the monastery should either rebuke the one who entices him or report the matter beforehand to the Superior [Note: [Col. 1449] Holstenius: “to the Abbot”]. I do not think that anything of what we have decreed in common should be withheld from him, because it is written: “Let many be at peace with you, but let one among a thousand be your counselor” (Ecclus. VI, 6).

Therefore, the things written here must be observed with the greatest care by the Superior down to [Col. 1450] all the brothers. If anyone hears instruction from someone other than the one to whom he entrusted himself in the monastery, he should receive it and not withhold it from his teacher, because it is written: “Everything that is made manifest is light” (Eph. V, 13). If the instruction is good, it should be praised together with him; if it is bad, it should be rejected.

If one of the brothers who stand in unity suddenly quarrels with the Superior, it is permitted to admonish him not only once but a second and a third time, as the Gospel teaches (Matt. XVIII, 15–17). If he refuses to amend himself, the person who has been injured, after the first or second correction, if he has not brought the obstinate offender back, should report this also to the Superior, lest through silence both he and his brother be endangered, as Solomon says: “He who conceals hostility contrives deceit.”

If, as often happens, a sudden attack or hostile incursion occurs, so that the brothers cannot flee together because of the pursuit of enemies, and afterward, by God’s favor, they escape and are able to reach a place where they know the Superior to be, they must hasten to him like sons to their father. Those whom divine love has joined cannot in any way be separated, because it is written: “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John IV, 18).

If anyone is detained for a necessary reason, as we said above, he must carry what he took with him from the monastery to the place where his Superior is. He will not be able to keep for himself what by agreement belongs to all and has been consecrated to God. But if he plans to retain any of these things, he appears to act against the Apostle’s saying: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Rom. XIII, 8).

Therefore, all the brothers must observe everything contained in this book, and those who desire to be good must subscribe to it. These provisions have been made—that is, written—for those who are known to be steadfast in all things.

[Col. 1449]

# SECOND RULE (C, G, S)

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING OPUSCULE

[Col. 1449] We compared this little work with a Corbie exemplar apparently written a thousand years ago. In that copy, from the place beginning “Psalms III, LXII, etc.” (where Lucas Holstenius, in the second part of his *Book of Rules*, agrees sufficiently with the printed editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain), the text varies as follows:

“Three psalms: the sixty-second, the fifth, and the eighty-ninth.”

[There is a small lacuna here, apparently caused by the deletion of a word of about six letters; immediately afterward the text continues:]

“At the third hour, a psalm shall be said responsively; then two antiphons, a reading, and Compline. Likewise at the sixth and ninth hours. At the lighting of the lamps, one responsorial psalm, four antiphons, likewise one responsorial psalm, a reading, and Compline. At the proper time after the lighting of the lamps, with everyone seated, readings shall be read.”

[One word has been erased here, and the text immediately continues:]

“After this, the customary psalms before sleep shall be said; at night, prayers; in November, etc.”

Where the phrase “and Compline” is said once and again, it seems to have the same meaning as the formula used twice by our father Benedict when arranging the office of Matins, “and it is completed”—that is, the office will then be performed or completed; alternatively, a final prayer such as the one called *Ad complendum* (“For completion”) in ancient missals will be added.

Moreover, in the same manuscript the little work begins without a title: “Above all things, etc.” But at the words “for your salvation. Amen,” the Rule of Saint Augustine adapted for men follows continuously and on the very same line, as we have already observed, ending with these words: “Here ends the Rule of Saint Augustine, bishop.”

1. Above all things, dearest brothers, let God be loved, and then one’s neighbor, because these commandments have been given to us as the principal ones. We describe how we ought to pray and sing the psalms: namely, at Matins Psalms III, LXII, VI, and LXXXVIII shall be said, with their appointed antiphons, verses, and responsories.

At Prime and Terce, their appointed psalms shall be said, with two antiphons and two readings. Likewise at Sext and None, their appointed psalms shall be said, with the appropriate responsories and antiphons. The same arrangement shall be observed at Vespers and Compline.

At the lighting of the lamps, one psalm, one responsory, three antiphons, and three readings shall be given. At the proper time after the lighting of the lamps, with everyone seated, readings shall be read.

At the night offices in November, December, January, and February: twelve antiphons, six psalms, [Col. 1450] and three readings. In March, April, September, and October: ten antiphons, five psalms, and three readings. In May, June, July, and August: eight antiphons, four psalms, and two readings.

2. Let them work from morning until Sext; from Sext until None let them devote themselves to reading; and at None let them return the books. After they have refreshed themselves, whether in the garden or wherever necessary, let them work until the hour of the lighting of the lamps.

Let no one claim anything as his own, whether in clothing or in any other matter. For we desire to live the apostolic life (Acts XI, 43). Let no one do anything with murmuring, lest he perish under a similar judgment with the murmurers. Let them obey faithfully; after God, let them honor their father; let them show the respect due to holy men toward their Superior. Let them sit [Col. 1451] silently at table, listening to the reading. If anything is needed, let their Superior take care of it.

On Saturday and Sunday, as is customary [Note: [Col. 1451] The Corbie manuscript reads: “as has been established”], those who wish may receive wine.

If it is necessary to send anyone on some business of the monastery, let two go. No one may eat or drink outside the monastery without an order, for this does not belong to the discipline of the monastery.

If brothers are sent to sell the monastery’s goods, let them carefully ensure that they do nothing contrary to the command, knowing that they provoke God in his servants. If they buy anything needed by the monastery, let them act carefully and faithfully as servants of God.

There must be no idle word among them. From morning [Col. 1452] let them sit down to their work; after the prayer of Terce, let them likewise go to their work. Let them not stand weaving stories, unless something concerns the benefit of the soul; but while sitting at their work, let them remain silent, unless the needs of the work require someone to speak.

If anyone does not strive with all his strength, aided by the mercy of God, to fulfill these things, but contemptuously disregards them, then, after being warned once and again, if he does not amend himself, he should know that he is subject to the discipline of the monastery, as is proper. If his age permits, let him even be beaten.

If you faithfully and devoutly observe these things in the name of Christ, you will make progress, and our joy in your salvation will be no small one. Amen.

These are the things which, having been established in the monastery, we command you to observe. First, etc.

[Col. 1451]

# A BOOK ON THE EREMITIC LIFE, TO HIS SISTER (G, S)*

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOK

That this book is not Augustine’s is clear from many other arguments, and especially from the fact that the rule of Blessed Benedict is cited in chapters 14 and 19. Lucas Holstenius says that he knows for certain, in the second part of his *Book of Rules*, that it belongs to Blessed Aelred of Rievaulx, abbot in England, who was writing in the middle of the twelfth century. Indeed, in the catalogue of the works of Saint Aelred, *Centuria II of British Writers*, no. 99, it is listed under the title: *One Book on the Institution of Recluses*. For many years you have been asking this of me. You have approximately the third part of this same book among the works published under the name of Saint Anselm, namely *Meditations* XV, XVI, and XVII.

## PROLOGUE

For many years, sister, you have been asking me to give you, according to the manner of life which you have undertaken, a definite rule, according to which you may direct your conduct and order both the life of religion and the exercises of the religious life, which you have undertaken for Christ. Would that you had asked this of, and obtained it from, someone wiser, who had learned through experience—not through some conjecture—what he should teach others.

For my part, since I am your brother in flesh and spirit and cannot refuse whatever you command, I shall do what you urge. Selecting from the various institutions of the Fathers certain things that seem necessary to you, I shall endeavor to give you a definite rule for arranging the condition of the external person, adding certain provisions according to place and time, and inserting spiritual matters among bodily ones wherever that seems useful.

## CHAPTER I — How the Hermit Life Was Established

First, you ought to know for what reason and in what manner this life was either established or adopted by the ancients.

There are some for whom living among many people is harmful. There are others for whom, even if it is not harmful, it is nevertheless costly. There are also some for whom neither of these dangers need be feared, but who judge solitary life more fruitful.

Thus the ancients chose to live alone either to avoid danger, to escape loss, or to breathe and sigh more freely for the embrace of Christ. This is why many sat alone in the desert, supporting their lives by the work of their hands.

Those, however, who did not consider even this safe for themselves amid the freedom of solitude and the opportunity to wander about thought it safer to be enclosed and kept within a cell whose exit had been closed.

## CHAPTER II — The Mere Enclosure of the Body Is of No Benefit

What did you have in mind when you devoted yourself to this institution? Many people, either ignorant of the purpose of this order or unconcerned about it, think it sufficient merely to restrain their limbs within walls, although the mind is not only loosened by wandering and scattered by cares and anxieties, and agitated by filthy and unlawful desires, but the tongue also runs idly all day through villages and cities, across marketplaces and fairs.

## CHAPTER III — Conversations of Recluses with Women from Outside

You will scarcely find one of the recluses of this time who is alone, before whose window there does not sit some talkative old woman or some woman full of foolish chatter, occupying her with stories, feeding her on rumors or slanders, and describing the appearance, face, and habits of this or that monk, cleric, or man of any other order.

She also introduces seductive matters: she portrays the wantonness of young girls, the freedom of widows, to whom whatever they desire is permitted, and the cleverness of wives in deceiving their husbands and satisfying their pleasures. Meanwhile the mouth dissolves into laughter and bursts of merriment, and poison, drunk with sweetness, spreads through the [Col. 1452] entrails and limbs.

## CHAPTER IV — The Destruction Caused by Conversations with Women from Outside

When the hour compels them to part, the recluse, filled with pleasures, withdraws, while the old woman departs loaded with food.

Restored to quiet, the wretched woman turns over in her heart the images that hearing has introduced. She kindles more fiercely by her own thoughts the fire conceived through the preceding conversation. Like a drunkard, she stumbles through the psalm, falls in the reading, and is tossed about in prayer.

When the light of day returns, the little women come again, adding new tales to the old ones. They do not stop until they expose their captive more freely to the mockery of demons. For now the conversation proceeds openly, no longer about kindling pleasure but about satisfying it: they discuss together where, when, and through whom she might accomplish what she is thinking about.

The cell is turned into a brothel, and, through some delicate device or other, either she goes out or the adulterer enters. This misery, as is often demonstrated, is a common cause of the ruin of many men in our age.

## CHAPTER V — The Avarice of Certain Recluses
Others, although they avoid shameful conduct, are nevertheless talkative and constantly associate with talkative women, devoting their tongues and ears all day long, in idleness and gossip, to excessive curiosity. Others, caring little about such things—which is a vice that spreads through nearly all the enclosed women of our time—yearn to accumulate money or multiply flocks. They extend themselves so far in this concern that you would take them for mothers or heads of households, not anchorites. They seek out pastures and shepherds to manage and guard the flocks; they demand from the keepers the produce, price, weight, or number. Buying and selling follows, so that money may heap up money and kindle the thirst of avarice. For the evil spirit deceives such women by persuading them that this is useful and necessary for distributing alms, supporting orphans, showing charity to visiting relatives or friends, and receiving religious women. This is not your concern; it belongs rather to you to receive alms as a poor woman among the poor than, after abandoning everything of your own for Christ, to seek what belongs to others in order to distribute it. It is a sign of great faithlessness if [Col. 1453] an enclosed woman is anxious about tomorrow, when the Lord says: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33). Therefore care must be taken that the mind be stripped of every concern for temporal things and relieved of anxiety.

## CHAPTER VI — An enclosed woman should not wish to possess resources under the pretext of helping the poor or receiving guests; she should use a proven servant and should not teach girls.

For this to happen, let the enclosed woman see to it that, if possible, she lives by the work of her hands. For this is perfection. But if either illness or physical delicacy does not permit it, before she is enclosed let her seek out reliable persons from whom she may humbly receive each day what is sufficient for one day, and let her add nothing under the pretext of the poor or of guests. Let no poor people cry out around her cell, no orphans weep, and no widow lament.

“But who,” you will say, “can prevent this?” You sit, you keep silent, you endure. As soon as they know that you have nothing and that they will receive nothing, they will depart, even if wearied by waiting. You may call this inhuman. But if you have anything beyond necessary food and clothing, you are not a nun. What, then, will you distribute? Nevertheless, the enclosed woman is instructed to send whatever remains from the work of her hands after providing for her sustenance to some faithful person, who may distribute it to the poor.

I do not want some old woman who lies in wait for chastity to approach mixed in with the poor, bringing eulogiae—blessed gifts—from one of the monks or clergy; let her not whisper flattering words into the ear, lest, kissing the hand in return for the alms received, she whisper into the ear. Moreover, care must be taken that, even in order to receive religious women, the enclosed woman should not undertake any burden of hospitality. For among the good there often come even the very worst, who sit down before the enclosed woman’s window and, after beginning with very little religious conversation, turn to worldly subjects, then weave amorous matters into them, and spend nearly the whole night sleepless.

You should certainly avoid such a woman, lest you be forced to hear what you would shudder to see. For things may perhaps seem bitter when they are heard or seen, but sweet when they are imagined. If you fear scandal because you do not distribute even to the poor and do not receive guests, once everyone has learned of your poverty there will be no one to reproach you. But if I do not want you to be wealthy even for the sake of the poor or of guests, still less do I want this on account of a larger household.

Therefore choose for yourself some old woman who is not talkative, not wandering, not quarrelsome, and not frivolous, but one who has cultivated good morals and has received from everyone a testimony of truth. Let her guard the door of the cell and admit or retain whatever ought to be admitted or retained. Under her care let there be a stronger girl, capable of bearing burdens, who will carry water and wood and cook beans or vegetables; or, if illness requires it, prepare more nourishing foods. Let this girl be kept under the discipline of the rod, lest her wantonness pollute your holy dwelling and your profession be blasphemed.

Do not allow boys or girls any access to you. There are some enclosed women who occupy themselves with teaching girls and turn their cell into a school. One sits at the window, another sits in the portico. The former watches each one and, amid the movements of girls, now becomes angry, now laughs, now threatens, now strikes, now caresses, now kisses; she calls the girl weeping from a beating closer, strokes her face, clasps her neck, and, rushing into an embrace, calls her now “daughter,” now “friend.” How, amid these things, can the memory of God remain, unless worldly and carnal matters—though they are not carried out—are nevertheless stirred and pictured as if before one’s eyes? Those two women should certainly be sufficient for you, for conversation and service.

## CHAPTER VII — Let her devote herself to silence and speak rarely and modestly.

We especially urge the enclosed woman to preserve the gravity of silence. For in it there is great rest and abundant fruit. “The cultivation of justice is silence.” As Jeremiah says: “It is good to wait in silence for the salvation of God.” And again: “It is good for a man when he has borne the yoke” (Lam. 3:26–27), so that he should sit alone and be silent.

Hence it is written: “Hear, Israel, and be silent.” Do therefore what the prophet says: “I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue. I have set a guard over my mouth” (Ps. 38: [Col. 1454] 1–2). Thus, fearing a fall of the tongue, which according to the Apostle James no human being can tame (James 3:8), let the enclosed woman set a guard over her mouth, sit alone, and be silent with her lips; let her speak in spirit, and believe that she is not alone when she is alone. For then she is with Christ, who does not deign to be with her amid crowds.

Let her therefore sit alone, be silent while listening to Christ and speaking with Christ, and set a guard over her mouth. First, let her speak rarely; then let her consider what she says, to whom she says it, and how she says it. Let her speak rarely—that is, at fixed and appointed hours, about which we shall speak later. [Note: The Louvain edition, as the Benedictine Fathers report, reads “What.” There is doubtless a lacuna here; for the author does not explain all the parts of the preceding enumeration—namely, what, to whom, and how—but omits one, namely, what. M.] To whom she should speak—that is, to particular persons, and to those who have been designated for her. How she should speak—that is, humbly, moderately, not in a loud voice, neither harshly nor flatteringly, and without laughter. For if this is inappropriate toward any honorable man, how much more so toward a woman? How much more toward a virgin? How much more toward an enclosed woman?

Sit therefore, my sister, and be silent. If you are compelled to speak, speak little, humbly and modestly, whether the subject is the need of bodily matters or the salvation of the soul.

## CHAPTER VIII — With which persons it is fitting for an enclosed woman to speak.

Now let us designate the persons with whom she ought to speak. Blessed is the woman who neither admitted a husband nor wished to see or address any man. But which of the enclosed women now follows this example? Those who exist today do enough if they preserve this bodily chastity, if they are not brought out with a burdened belly, and if infamous weeping has not produced offspring.

We cannot impose perpetual silence upon them so that they never speak with men; let us see, then, with whom they may speak more honorably. Therefore, if possible, let some elderly priest, mature in conduct, be provided in a large monastery or church. Let her speak with him rarely, except concerning confession and the edification of the soul; let her receive counsel from him in doubts and consolation in tribulations.

But because that evil enclosed within the body, which we fear, often rouses itself and softens even withered old age, let her not offer him her hand to touch or caress. Let none of you be concerned about thinness of face, slenderness of arms, or roughness of skin.

## CHAPTER IX — At his sister’s request, he writes a rule of life for enclosed women.

These things, sister—thanks be to God—would not have needed to be said to you. But because you wished this rule to be handed to you not only for your own sake, but also for the sake of younger women who eagerly desire to undertake a similar life on your advice, I thought these matters should be inserted: if any person of great reputation or good standing—an abbot, for example, or a prior—wishes to speak with the enclosed woman, let him speak in the presence of someone else.

## CHAPTER X — Conversation with various persons: what an enclosed woman must observe in this matter.

Certainly, I would not want any person to visit you frequently, nor would I want you to maintain a familiar private relationship with anyone who visits you repeatedly. For the reputation of a virgin is endangered by the frequent greeting of any particular person, and her conscience is endangered as well. For the more often you see the same face or hear the same voice, the more distinctly that person’s image will be impressed upon your memory.

Therefore an enclosed woman ought to speak with a man even with her face veiled and to avoid his gaze; she should grant him only her hearing, and that with fear. I have no doubt that for some women it is dangerous to admit the same man’s voice frequently. Avoid conversation with young men and with persons under suspicion. Never speak with anyone unless you yourself have granted an audience to the person who is to speak with you—and even then only if definite necessity demands it.

Therefore speak with none of those who come to you, except a bishop, an abbot, or a prior of great reputation, without the permission or instruction of the priest himself, so that the difficulty of speaking with you may bring you peace. Never let messengers pass between you and any man under the pretext of showing charity, fostering affection, seeking familiarity, or cultivating spiritual friendship. [Col. 1455] Do not accept their little gifts or letters, and do not send them yours, as is customary—for example, belts and purses decorated with different warp and weft, and other things of this sort that monks send to younger women through clerics. This is fuel for illicit love and material for great evil.

## CHAPTER XI — Let her work with her hands and be adorned with modesty.

Therefore work at whatever necessity demands or usefulness prescribes, and let the price of these things be applied to your own needs. If you do not require it, give it, as we have said, either to the necessities of the church or to the poor.

Let modesty adorn every movement and every word of the enclosed woman—modesty that restrains the tongue, moderates anger, and avoids quarrels. For how fitting it is that a woman should be ashamed to speak what is honorably honorable; how great is the shamelessness of speaking dishonorably, even when provoked by insults or goaded by fury?

## CHAPTER XII — How an enclosed woman should conduct herself when provoked by words.

Therefore let the enclosed woman not answer one who quarrels, not reproach one who slanders, and not contradict one who provokes her. But in everything that is brought against her or whispered, whether publicly or secretly, let her disregard it from the citadel of a serene conscience, saying with the Apostle: “But to me it is a very small matter that I should be judged by you” (1 Cor. 4:3).

Above all, the enclosed woman must strive to retain continually tranquility of spirit and peace of heart, so that she may have as the eternal inhabitant of her breast the one of whom it is written: “His place has been made in peace” (Ps. 75:3). And elsewhere the Lord says through the prophet: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet person who fears my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Not only foolish talk overturns this most sacred state of mind; it also perverts it. I consider that you should pursue nothing so much as silence.

## CHAPTER XIII — Concerning the time for speaking and the time for silence.

Now let us distinguish the time for speaking from the time for silence. Therefore, from the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until Lent, let her observe silence after Compline until dawn. Then, after Prime has been said, if she wishes to communicate anything else concerning the day’s needs to her servant, let her do so in a few words; afterward let her speak to no one until Terce.

Between Terce and None, if those who have arrived are to be admitted, let her answer them appropriately first, and let her assign to the servants whatever she wishes. After None, once food has been taken, let her avoid all conversation and every occasion of levity, lest what is written about her be fulfilled: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32:6).

After Vespers has been completed, let her discuss necessities with her servant until the time of the collation. During Lent, the enclosed woman ought always to keep silence; but because this is thought harsh and impossible, let her speak with her confessor and servant less often than at other times, and with no one else, unless perhaps some venerable person from another province should arrive.

After Easter, until the time mentioned above, let silence be observed from Compline until sunrise. Once she has celebrated Prime in the daily offices, let her speak with her servants if necessary; with visitors, between None and Vespers. When Vespers is finished, let her arrange with her servants whatever is necessary until the collation.

## CHAPTER XIV — What exercises she should practice from the Kalends of November to Lent.

With these matters considered, let fixed times be assigned to manual work, reading, and prayer. Idleness is indeed the enemy of the soul, and the enclosed woman must avoid it above all. For it is the parent of every evil, the craftsman of lust, the nurse of wandering, the fosterer of vices, the fuel of weariness, and the stimulus of sadness. It sows the worst thoughts, seeks illicit affections, and arouses desires. It produces disgust with rest and instills horror of the cell.

Never let the spirit find you unprepared; never let it find you idle. But since our mind, subjected to vanity in this life, never remains in the same condition, idleness must be driven away by a variety of exercises, and [Col. 1456] our rest supported by a certain alternation of tasks.

Therefore, from the Kalends of November until Lent, let her rest, according to her own judgment, for more than half the night. Rising in this way, let her celebrate the nocturnal vigils with whatever devotion she can, according to the form of the Rule of blessed Benedict. Let prayer immediately follow them; according as the Holy Spirit assists her, she should either prolong it or shorten it. Let her beware, however, lest prolonged prayer produce weariness. For it is more useful to pray briefly more often than once at excessive length—unless perhaps devotion inspired by prayer prolongs it without the one praying being aware of it.

After prayer, let her discharge the office owed in honor of the Virgin, adding commemorations of the saints. But beware of imposing any rule upon yourself concerning the number of Psalms or commemorations; use the Psalms as long as they delight you. If they begin to burden you, pass to reading; if reading brings weariness, rise to prayer; then pass to manual work when wearied by these, so that you may refresh your spirit by a healthful alternation and drive away spiritual torpor.

When the commemorations are finished—and let their number be dictated not by necessity forcing an obligation upon your intention or voice, but by inspired devotion—let the remaining time until dawn be devoted to manual work accompanied by the chanting of Psalms. At dawn, let her complete the morning praises with the hymns of the prayers of Prime. Then, alternating readings and Psalms according as her devotion varies, let her await Terce; after Terce has been said, let her be occupied with manual work until None.

After taking food and offering thanks to God, let her return to the prescribed gentleness, interrupting bodily work for spiritual exercises until Vespers. After a short interval, let her read privately some account from the Lives, teachings, or miracles of the Fathers, so that, when compunction has arisen from these things, she may say Compline in a certain fervor of spirit and, with her breast full of devotion, lay her limbs upon her bed.

The woman who does not understand letters should apply herself more diligently to manual work. Thus, when she has gradually become tired, let her rise, bend her knees, briefly pray to her Lord, and immediately resume the work she had interrupted. Let her do this at both times, namely during reading and during labor, repeating the Lord’s Prayer more frequently amid these same tasks and inserting whatever Psalms she wishes.

## CHAPTER XV — Concerning the exercises from Easter to the Kalends of November.

From Easter until the aforementioned Kalends, let her rise for the vigils in such a way that, when the nocturnal hymns and prayers have been completed, she begins Matins after a very brief interval. When these are finished, let her devote herself to prayers and Psalms until full sunrise; then, after Prime has been said, let her begin the daily work of sacrifice until Terce. Let her occupy her spirit with reading and prayer until Sext.

After taking food at Sext, let her rest in her little bed until None; then let her work with her hands until Vespers. After Vespers, let her devote herself to prayers and Psalms, regulating the time of the collation so that her bed receives her limbs before sunset.

For at all times care must be taken lest night cover the entire daylight with its darkness before she goes to sleep and she be compelled to sleep when she ought to be awake.

## CHAPTER XVI — Concerning the Lenten fast.

As we are about to speak of the Lenten season, we believe that its excellence should first be commended. Although Christians have many fasts, the Lenten fast surpasses them all, for by divine authority it is imposed not upon just any particular persons, nor upon people of this or that order, but upon all Christians.

It has testimony to its excellence from the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. For Moses, the servant of God, fasted forty days and forty nights so that he might deserve to receive the law of the Lord. The prophet Elijah, after he had eaten bread baked under the ashes and drunk the water that the angel had supplied to him, fasted forty days and forty nights, and then merited hearing the voice of the Lord. When our Lord and Savior [Col. 1457] fasted forty days and forty nights, he overcame the tempter, and angels approached and ministered to him.

## CHAPTER XVII — He continues concerning the virtue of fasting.

Fasting, therefore, is directed against every temptation and sinful condition. In every tribulation it is a useful refuge and an unassailable support for all our needs. Christ himself did not conceal how great a virtue fasting possesses when asked why they had not been able to cast out the demon that had possessed the epileptic. “This kind of demon,” he said, “cannot be cast out except by prayer and fasting” (Mark 9:28).

## CHAPTER XVIII — Concerning the meaning of Lent.

Although fasting ought always to be the companion of religion, without which chastity cannot be safe, this Lenten observance nevertheless contains a great mystery within itself.

The first place of our habitation was paradise. The second is this world, full of afflictions. The third is in heaven with the angels and spirits. These forty days signify the whole period from the time Adam was driven from paradise until the last day, on which we will be fully liberated from this exile.

Here we exist in fear, labor, and sorrow, cast away from the sight of God’s eyes, excluded from the joys of paradise, fasting from heavenly nourishment. We must always consider and lament this misery of ours and show by our works that we are resident aliens and pilgrims in the world.

But because human weakness cannot easily do this, the Holy Spirit established a third period in which we might perform it and ordained that certain observances be carried out in the Church, by which we may perceive the reason for this period itself.

When ashes are sprinkled upon us, we are told, “You are dust, and to dust you shall return” (Gen. 3:19), showing that we have been driven out and sentenced to death because of the word the Lord spoke to Adam when he expelled him from paradise. We are also shown that, in this exile, the vision of God is denied us: a veil is hung between us and the Holy of Holies.

But to recall that we are far from the company of those of whom it is written, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5), we interrupt the customary word of praise. And the fact that we are constrained by this more profound fast reminds us that in this life we are not satisfied with heavenly bread.

Therefore, in this period every Christian is said to add something to his customary observances and to occupy himself more diligently and more frequently with guarding the heart and mouth. But the enclosed woman understands the purpose of this season’s discipline much better, insofar as she recognizes it more distinctly expressed in her own life.

Accordingly, in these sacred prayers by which she especially desires to please Christ, let her devote and sanctify herself entirely to God. Let her reject every delicacy and renounce every conversation; and, considering this period as though it were the days of a wedding, let her sigh with every desire for Christ’s embrace.

Let her apply herself to prayer more frequently than usual, fall more often at Jesus’ feet, stir up compunction by frequent repetition of his name, provoke tears, and restrain her heart from every wandering. When the sacred vigils are finished, let the interval dividing the nocturnal praises from Matins be devoted to prayer and meditation. After Matins, and after Prime has been said, let her devote herself to Psalms and readings until Terce in full. When the praise of Terce has been completed, let her devote herself earnestly to manual work until None, inserting brief prayers at intervals. After None has been said, she will refresh her body, and then, singing Psalms, await the time of Compline.

## CHAPTER XIX — Concerning the quality and quantity of food and drink.

Now, concerning the quality and quantity of food and drink: it would indeed be excessive for me to impose a rule upon you, sister, who from infancy to old age—the age that now weakens your limbs—have barely sustained your body on very little food. For the sake of others, whom I judge this to be useful for, I shall attempt to prescribe a definite rule concerning these matters.

Blessed Benedict grants a monk a pound of bread and a hemina of drink. We do not deny this to more delicate enclosed women; nevertheless, for young women strong in body, it is most useful [Col. 1458] to abstain from everything capable of causing intoxication. Let them avoid bright white bread and delicate foods as though they were the poison of immodesty. Let them provide for necessity in such a way that they repel hunger without satisfying appetite.

Therefore, those who cannot advance to more perfect abstinence should be content with a pound of bread and a hemina of better-quality drink, whether they eat twice or once. Let them have one dish of vegetables or legumes, or at least one made from grain. Adding a little oil, butter, or milk, let them use this seasoning to dispel disgust. If she is going to dine that day, this should be enough for her.

At dinner let her add a little milk, a small amount of fish, or something of this sort, if it is available. Content with one kind of food, she may add fruit and raw herbs, if she has any; if she eats these only once in the day, they may be added after she has tasted the dish.

At the vigils of the saints, however, and on the fasts of the Four Seasons, and also on every Wednesday and Friday outside Quinquagesima, let her fast with Lenten food. During Lent, one dish each day should be sufficient for her. Unless illness prevents it, let her fast on Friday on bread and water.

From the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until Lent, let her refresh herself once a day at None. During Lent, let her break her fast after Vespers has been said. From Easter until Pentecost, let her eat lunch at Sext and keep silence at lunch. She should do the same throughout the summer, except on Wednesdays and Fridays and on solemn fast days.

On the days when she fasts, during the summer let her be permitted to grant her little body a short rest in place of the midday sleep and between Matins and Prime.

## CHAPTER XX — Concerning clothing and footwear.

Let such clothing suffice for her as repels the cold. Let her use thicker pelts and furs for winter; for summer, let her have one tunic. In both seasons, however, let her have two shirts or linen garments of coarse material. Her head covering should not be of fine or costly cloth, but of ordinary black cloth, lest she seem to seek adornment through varied color.

Let her have footwear, foot-wraps, and leggings in whatever quantity is sufficient. Let the guardian of her poverty carefully consider that she should have even somewhat less than what just necessity might permit her to indulge in.

These things, dearest sister, concerning the conduct of the outer person I have written because the span of our present age compels you to them, not out of zeal for antiquity. I propose a certain tempered way of life for the weak, while leaving the stronger free to advance toward more perfect things.

## CHAPTER XXI — Solitude is to be preferred to human companionship for the preservation of virginity.

But now let any woman who, renouncing the world, has chosen this solitary life hear and understand my words—any woman who desires to be hidden, not seen, and, as one dead to the world, to be buried with Christ in a cave.

First, pay careful attention to this: you ought to prefer solitude to human companionship. “The virgin,” says the Apostle, “thinks about the things of God, how she may please God, so that she may be holy in body and spirit” (1 Cor. 7:34). This is a voluntary sacrifice, a spontaneous offering, to which no law compels her. But necessity urges her; a command does not force her. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let the one who is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. 19:12).

Who is able? Certainly the one to whom the Lord has inspired this will and granted the capacity. Therefore, first of all, as a virgin, commend your good purpose with the greatest devotion of heart to the one who inspired it, asking with the most earnest prayer that what is impossible through merit may be experienced as easy through grace.

Always consider what a precious treasure you carry in what a fragile vessel, and what reward, glory, and crown preserved virginity bestows. Constantly turn over in your mind what punishment, shame, and condemnation the loss of it brings.

What is more precious than this treasure? By it heaven is purchased; by it the angel rejoices; Christ himself longs for it. Through it he is enticed to love and provoked to bestow—what shall I dare to say?—himself and all that is his.

Therefore, the nard of your virginity, giving forth its fragrance even in heavenly places, causes the king to desire [Col. 1459] your beauty, and he himself is your Lord and God. See what kind of bridegroom you have chosen, what kind of friend you have brought to yourself. He is beautiful beyond the sons of men, more beautiful even than the sun and beyond all the beauty of the stars. His spirit is sweeter than honey, and his inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Length is in his right hand, and in his left hand riches and glory.

He has already chosen you as his bride. But he will crown only one whom he has tested. Scripture says: “One who has not been tested is not approved” (Ecclus. 34:9).

Virginity is gold; the cell is the furnace; the devil is the refiner; temptation is the fire; the virgin’s flesh is the clay vessel in which the gold is stored, and once damaged the vessel cannot be repaired by any craftsman.

## CHAPTER XXII — How the commitment to virginity must be religiously guarded.

Thinking continually about the most precious treasure of virginity, which is possessed with such benefit but lost so irretrievably, let the virgin guard it with the utmost diligence and the utmost fear. Let her think without ceasing for whose bridal chamber she is being prepared and for whose embrace; let her set before herself the Lamb whom she must follow wherever he goes.

Let her contemplate the most blessed Mary, who goes before the choirs of virgins and leads that sweet song with the virginal tambourine, which no one can sing except virgins of either sex. Of them it is written: “These are they who have not been defiled with women; for they are virgins” (Rev. 14:4).

Do not understand this saying as though a man without a woman, or a woman without a man, could not be defiled. Let that detestable crime be condemned as more disgraceful than every other offense, by which a man engages with a man or a woman with a woman. Yet even without the company of another’s flesh, virginity is often corrupted and chastity violated.

If more violent heat, shaking the flesh, subdues the will and seizes the limbs, let the virgin think that all her members are sanctified to God, undefiled for Christ, and dedicated to the Holy Spirit. Let her judge it unworthy to hand over what belongs to Christ to Satan, and let her be ashamed that his virginal members should be stained even by a simple movement.

## CHAPTER XXIII — The loss of chastity must be feared at table and in conversation.

Therefore let her direct her whole mind toward guarding her virginity. Let her weigh her thoughts so that, hungering for the perfection of this virtue, she considers hunger a delicacy and riches poverty.

In food, drink, sleep, and speech, let her always fear the loss of chastity, lest, if she gives the flesh more than is due, she provide strength to the adversary and secretly nourish the enemy. Sitting at table, let her turn over in her mind the beauty of modesty, and, sighing for its perfection, let her disdain food and shudder at drink. Even what necessity judges should be taken, or reason dictates, let her sometimes consume with sorrow or shame, sometimes with tears.

If she speaks with anyone, let her always fear hearing something that might in the least cloud the serenity of chastity. Let her have no doubt that grace will abandon her if she utters even one word contrary to decency.

## CHAPTER XXIV — Before sleep the conscience must be examined, and sins must be mourned.

Having prostrated yourself upon your bed, commend your chastity to God. Then, armed with the sign of the cross, consider in your mind how you lived that day: whether by word, deed, or affection you offended the eyes of your Lord; whether you were more frivolous, more idle, or more negligent than you ought to have been; whether, being too gross in food or too unrestrained in drink, you exceeded the limits of necessity.

If you discover that any of these things has stealthily come upon you, sigh and strike your breast. Then may the Bridegroom receive you, reconciled to your Bridegroom by this evening sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XXV — In unchaste temptations the story of the virgin Agnes should be recalled.

If, while you are awake, during quiet sleep, or through the tempter’s art, bodily heat is suddenly aroused, and the cunning enemy brings it into your sleep and disturbs the rest of chastity with various thoughts; if he sets delicacies before you and instills horror of a harsher life, let the blessed virgin come to your mind, she who, in tender youth, so frequently carried off triumph over the most impious enemy.

Think [Col. 1460] of the most blessed Agnes, for whom gold, silver, the most precious garments, precious stones, and the whole pomp of worldly glory were regarded as a kind of dung. Called to the tribunal, she did not stay away. The judge flattered her; she despised him. He threatened her; she mocked him, fearing more that he might spare her than that he might punish her. She turned a foul brothel into an oratory. When the angel entered with the virgin, he poured light into the darkness and punished the persecutor of chastity with death.

Therefore, if you too pray and raise the weapons of your tears against the inciter of lust, the angel will certainly not be absent from your chaste chamber, he who was not absent from the brothel.

It was fitting that this material fire could not burn blessed Agnes, whose fleshly flame had grown cold—the flame that the fire of charity had kindled. Whenever the wicked spirit suggests unlawful things and more violent heat presses upon you, know that the one who searches hearts and kidneys is present, and that whatever you do or think is beneath his eyes.

Therefore have reverence for the Lord, whom you should not doubt is standing beside you, and answer the plunderer: “I have an angel who loves me and guards my body with excessive zeal.” Let discreet abstinence aid your effort in such a necessity. For where there is much affliction of the flesh, there can be either no pleasure or only a small amount.

## CHAPTER XXVI — In youth chastity does not remain intact without great mortification of heart and body.

Let no one flatter herself, let no one indulge herself, let no one deceive herself. Chastity is never acquired or preserved by young people without great contrition of heart and affliction of the flesh; it is often endangered even among the sick or the aged.

For although continence is a gift of God, and no one can be continent unless God grants it, and although this gift must be attributed not to any merits of ours but to his gratuitous grace, he nevertheless judges those unworthy of so great a gift who refuse to undertake any labor for it, wishing to be chaste amid delicacies, continent amid feasts; to associate with boys and girls and not be tempted; to be swollen with foul humors amid banquets and drunkenness and not be defiled; to bind their eyes together with flames and not be burned.

Whether this is difficult or impossible, you may judge.

## CHAPTER XXVII — Concerning a monk who scarcely restrained the stimulus of the flesh through harsh mortifications, without extinguishing it completely.

I knew a monk who, at the beginning of his conversion, was so tempted by natural impulses, by the violence of vicious habit, and by the suggestions of the cunning enemy that he feared for his chastity. He rose up against himself and, conceiving the sweetest hatred toward his own flesh, sought nothing more eagerly than whatever would afflict it.

Thus he tormented his body with starvation, and by withholding even what was due to it, he suppressed its ordinary movements. But when excessive weakness again compelled him to indulge himself somewhat more, behold, the flesh once more raised its head and assailed the peace it thought it had acquired.

Often plunging himself into cold water, he would tremble for a while as he sang Psalms and prayed. Often, too, when he felt illicit movements, he rubbed his body with nettles; laying bare his naked flesh, he overcame burning with burning. And when all this was still not enough and the spirit of fornication nevertheless pressed him, then, as the only thing left, he prostrated himself before the feet of Jesus and prayed, wept, sighed, asked, implored, and entreated him either to kill or to heal him.

He cried out repeatedly: “I will not leave; I will not be still; nor will I let you go unless you bless me.” Relief was granted for an hour, but security was denied. For when the stimuli of the flesh had rested briefly, illicit affections invaded his breast again.

My God! What crosses and torments that wretched man endured then, until such love of chastity was poured into him that all pleasures that can be felt or imagined, however many might be brought to bear [the surviving reading is defective]; and then it too departed from him. But only for a time; and now old age has also brought its illness, yet even so he does not flatter himself with security.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Against old men who do not wish to do without the company of concubines.

Therefore, it is no small cause for shame that certain men, having grown old in their filth, still refuse to do without the company of suspect persons; and—what is unspeakable—while lying in the same bed amid embraces and kisses, they claim to be secure in their chastity, though, when the body grows cold, their limbs grow warm only to fail them. These men are wretched and more miserable than all other mortals: although they lack the ability to commit the crime, they still retain the capacity for that very foulness. Shameful desire does not rest, even though bodily coldness denies it fulfillment. Let him see, however, whether he is speaking the truth, or whether iniquity is deceiving itself; while striving to conceal one disgrace, let him reveal a double one: for nocturnal emissions sometimes deceive even the nearly decrepit, and this inward evil frequently troubles lifeless old age.

## CHAPTER XXIX  
### The ever-fearful virgin should fortify herself through meditation on God’s word

I never want you, sister, to be secure; rather, you should fear, always regard your frailty with suspicion, frequent the streams of water like a timid dove, and, as in a mirror, perceive the image of a hawk flying overhead—and beware.

The streams of water are the sayings of Scripture. Flowing from the clearest fountain of wisdom, they expose the image and meaning of demonic suggestions, so that these may be avoided and defeated. For nothing more effectively excludes useless thoughts or restrains lust than meditation on God’s word. A virgin should become so accustomed to it in her mind that, unwilling to meditate on anything else, she cannot meditate on anything else.

When she is thinking about Scripture, let sleep come upon her. When she wakes, let something from Scripture first present itself to her. Let some saying from Scripture season the dreams of the sleeping woman’s memory.

## CHAPTER XXX  
### Against those who do not embrace the rigor of abstinence lest they incur bodily weakness

Some are held back from salutary exercises by fear that, through excessive abstinence or immoderate vigils, they may fall into weakness and thus become a burden to others and a cause of pain to themselves. This is our excuse in our sins.

How few there are today whom such fervor has kindled! We are all wise, all prudent, all discerning. We hate war from afar, and so fear bodily illness before we feel it, so that, terrified, we neglect the sickness of the soul that we do feel—as though it were more bearable to endure the flame of lust than the rumbling of the belly, or as though it were much better to avoid lust through continual bodily weakness than, while sound and healthy, to be reduced to its slavery.

For what difference does it make whether the proud flesh is restrained by abstinence or by weakness, so long as chastity is preserved?

“But,” someone says, “relaxation must be avoided, lest perhaps, under the pretext of infirmity, we fall into the allurements of pleasure.”

Certainly, if he is weak, if he is ill, if his bowels are tortured, if his stomach withers, any delicacies will be more of a burden than a pleasure.

## CHAPTER XXXI  
### On a young man who came to his senses and saw Christ at the hour of death

I saw a man who, although overcome by the force of habit despite his repentance, was unable to remain continent. At last, coming to his senses, he was excessively ashamed; immediately his heart grew warm within him, and in his meditation a fire blazed up.

Then, healthily angry with himself, he attacked himself with the gravest reproaches; declaring war on his body, he deprived it even of what seemed necessary. Gravity took the place of levity, and silence of loquacity. No one afterward saw him joking; no one saw him laughing; no one heard an idle word from his mouth.

He so despised and abhorred temporal consolations and everything thought pleasant by the flesh that he permitted himself no rest and no consolation in food or drink. He was so watchful and scrupulous concerning his thoughts that in this one respect alone he seemed excessive.

He stood and sat with his face lowered and his eyes cast down, so that he appeared to be standing before the divine tribunals in fear and trembling. With such weapons he won a glorious triumph over the tyrant.

For after contracting a grave disorder of the stomach and enduring a prolonged illness, when the hour of his death was already approaching, he said: “Let it be; look, Jesus is coming.”

## CHAPTER XXXII  
### True discretion: to place the soul before the flesh

[Col. 1462]

I say this in order to disclose discretion, which is both the mother and the nurse of all virtues. Let us restrain the sources of vices—gluttony, bodily ease, and the companionship and intimacy of women and effeminate men—within necessary limits, because we often conceal an affair of pleasure beneath the false name of discretion.

True discretion is to place the soul before the flesh; and where both are in danger, and the salvation of the one cannot be maintained without such harm to the other, to neglect the latter for the benefit of the former.

I have said these things so that you may recognize how great your concern ought to be in guarding chastity. Although chastity is the flower and ornament of all virtues, without humility it withers and fades.

## CHAPTER XXXIII  
### On pride and its forms

This is the sure, though by no means safe, foundation of all sins: whatever you build upon it is exposed to ruin. Pride is the beginning of every sin; it drove the angel from heaven and the human being from paradise.

Although this worst of evils has many branches, they are all divided into two forms: carnal and spiritual. Carnal pride is pride in carnal things; spiritual pride is pride in spiritual things.

Carnal pride is further divided into two kinds: boasting and vanity. Vanity exists when a handmaid of Christ inwardly boasts in her heart that she was born of noble parents; when she takes pleasure in having preferred poverty to riches for Christ’s sake; when she tries to place herself above the poor and lowly; or when she admires, as though it were something great, the fact that she rejected the marriages of the rich.

## CHAPTER XXXIV  
### On a certain form of vanity in the adornment of the cell and oratory

There is also a form of vanity in taking pleasure in some contrived beauty, even within one’s cell: adorning the walls with various paintings and carvings, and decorating the oratory with a variety of cloths and images. Beware of all these things as contrary, so to speak, to your profession.

## CHAPTER XXXV  
### Again, on a certain empty glory

With what face do you glory in riches or ancestry, when you wish to appear the bride of him who, though he was rich, became poor, and chose a poor mother, a poor family, a poor little house, and the lowliness of a manger?

Are you to glory in having preferred the Son of God to the sons of men; in having rejected foul flesh for the sake of the beauty of virginity; in having exchanged the eternal riches and delights of heaven for the martyrdoms of the saints?

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
### On preferring the ornaments of the virtues

If you glory in the Lord, serve him with fear. But do not pursue that glory, as though under the guise of devotion, in paintings or sculptures, in feathers of birds, or in varied images of beasts or different flowers.

Let these things belong to those who, having nothing within in which to glory, acquire outwardly things in which they may take pleasure.

“All the glory of the king’s daughter is within; clothed round about with golden borders and varied adornments” (Ps. XLIV, 14–15, 11).

But if you are already the king’s daughter, being the bride of the King’s Son, and have heard the Father’s voice saying, “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear” (Ps. XLIV, 11), let all your glory be within. See to it that your glory is the testimony of your conscience.

There let the most beautiful variety of virtues be found. There let different colors so meet and join together that one may increase the beauty of another, and that what shines less in its own nature may appear brighter through comparison with another.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### He continues concerning the ornaments of the virtues

Let humility be joined to chastity, and nothing will be more radiant. Let simplicity be associated with prudence, and nothing will be clearer. Let mercy be coupled with justice, and nothing will be sweeter. Add modesty to courage, and nothing will be more useful.

Occupy the eyes of your mind with this variety. Shape it with every effort in your soul. If you add to it golden borders, you will have woven a many-colored garment in which your bridegroom may behold you with the greatest love.

The border is the outermost part, as though the end, of a garment. “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith” [Col. 1463] (1 Tim. I, 5).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### From consideration of the linen with which the altar is adorned: how one’s conduct should be formed

Glory in these things; take pleasure in these things: inwardly, not outwardly; in true virtues, not in paintings and images.

Let white linen cloths adorn your altar, commending chastity by their whiteness and foreshadowing simplicity. Consider through what labor and what strippings the earthly-colored linen, in which it grew, cast off its color and reached such whiteness that the altar is adorned with it and Christ’s body is veiled by it.

We are all born with an earthly color, since “I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L, 7).

First, therefore, dearest daughter, the linen is immersed in water. We are buried with Christ in the waters of Baptism. There iniquity is erased, but weakness is not yet healed. We receive some whiteness in the remission of sins, but we are not yet entirely stripped of the earthly color because of the corruption of nature that remains.

After the water, the linen is dried. For after the waters of Baptism, the body must necessarily be worn down through abstinence and emptied of unlawful honors.

Then the linen is beaten with mallets, and our flesh is wearied by many temptations.

After this the linen is torn with iron hooks so that it may lay aside what is superfluous; and we, scraped by the claws of discipline, scarcely retain what is necessary.

After this a gentler and lighter cleansing by means of the instruments is applied to the linen; and we, having overcome the worst passions with great labor, are cleansed from lighter and daily sins by simple confession and satisfaction.

Then the linen is drawn out lengthwise by the spinners; and we are extended toward what lies ahead through steadfastness.

Moreover, so that a more complete perfection and beauty may be added to it, fire and water are applied. We too must pass through the fire of tribulation and the water of compunction, so that we may reach the refreshment of chastity.

Let the ornaments of your oratory represent these things to you; let them not feed your eyes with the mind’s varieties.

## CHAPTER XXXIX  
### The image of the Crucified One, with Mary and John standing on either side, should suffice in the oratory of religious women

Let the image of the Savior hanging upon the cross suffice for you on your altar. Let it represent his passion to you, so that you may imitate it; with arms outstretched, let it invite you to his embraces, in which you may delight; with exposed breasts, let it pour forth the milk of sweetness, by which you may be consoled.

And if you wish, in order to commend to yourself the excellence of virginity, let the virgin mother bend in her own image and the virgin disciple in his beside the cross. Thus you may consider how pleasing to Christ is the virginity of both sexes, which he consecrated in his mother and in the disciple whom he loved above the others.

Hence, while hanging on the cross, he joined them by so great a bond that he assigned her as mother to the disciple and him as son to the mother.

O most blessed John, to whom, by the authority of the testament, he entrusted the honor of the whole human race, the riches of the world, the glory of heaven, the refuge of the wretched, the consolation of the afflicted, the comfort of the poor, the raising up of the despairing, the reconciliation of sinners—and, finally, the mistress of the world and queen of heaven!

Let these things provide you with an incentive to charity, not a spectacle of vanity. For it is necessary that you strive toward all these things as toward one thing, since “one thing is necessary.” That one thing is found only in the One, with the One, and before the One, with whom there is no change or shadow of alteration.

Whoever clings to him becomes one spirit with him, passing into that one thing which is always the same and whose years do not fail. This attachment of charity is, as it were, the special ornament’s end and border.

## CHAPTER XL  
### On love of God and neighbor, and first on its exercise toward one’s neighbor by religious women

The nuptial garment, woven from the variety of virtues, ought to be surrounded by golden borders—that is, by the splendors of charity—which contains all the virtues and binds them together as one. By imparting its own singular brightness, charity makes one out of many and joins the many to the One, so that all are no longer many but one.

Charity is divided into two parts: love of God and love of neighbor. Love of neighbor, in turn, is subdivided into innocence and benevolence: namely, that you harm no one and do good to those whom you can.

For it is written, “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tob. IV, 16); this is innocence. And the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do also to them” (Matt. VII, 12); this is benevolence.

Carefully consider how these two things concern you. First, that you harm no one; then, that you wish to harm no one.

The first is easy for you, since you can scarcely do so except perhaps by striking someone with your tongue. The second will not be difficult if you attend to your resolve and love the nakedness you have professed.

For there can be no material for ill will toward anyone where there is no desire, where nothing is loved that can be taken away; nothing is removed that ought to be loved.

Finally, wish well to everyone and benefit those whom you can.

“But how?” you ask. “Since I am not permitted to possess even a little something that I might give to those in need?”

## CHAPTER XLI  
### On the example of Mary and Martha, and on the active and contemplative life

Recognize your condition, dearest daughter. Martha and Mary were two sisters: the one labored, the other was free; the one distributed, the other asked; the one rendered service, the other nourished affection.

Finally, Mary did not walk about or hurry here and there; she was not concerned with receiving guests, distracted by the care of household affairs, or attentive to the cries of the poor. She sat at Jesus’ feet and listened to his word.

This is your portion, dearest daughter. Since you are dead and buried to the world, you must be deaf to all the world’s flatteries that might be heard and mute in speaking. You must not be distracted, but extended; filled, not emptied.

Let Martha carry out her own portion. Although it is not denied that hers is good, Mary is nevertheless proclaimed better.

Did Mary envy Martha? Rather, Martha envied her. So too, let those things that seem best in the world emulate your life; do not emulate theirs.

The distribution of alms belongs to those who possess earthly property or who have been entrusted with the administration of ecclesiastical goods.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### On the administration of ecclesiastical goods

Whatever the faithful have contributed to the holy churches, bishops, priests, and clerics receive for distribution, not for storage; not for possession, but for giving away.

Whatever they have belongs to the poor, widows, and orphans, and to those who serve at the altar, so that they may live from the altar.

But those things contributed to monasteries for the use of Christ’s servants ought to be distributed by designated persons, so that what remains beyond the brothers’ needs may not be shut up in purses but distributed to guests, travelers, and the poor.

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### Those living in enclosure ought not to be distracted by concern for the poor and guests

This too is the concern of those to whom Martha’s portion has been entrusted, not of those who, with Mary, devote themselves to salutary leisure.

Thus those living in enclosure should have no concern for the poor and no distraction over receiving guests. They should have no care for tomorrow and no provision of food or drink. Rather, let them be nourished in saffron-colored garments and fed with spiritual things.

But those appointed to judge contemptible things embrace dung more deeply. For they are the oxen whose dung pelts the sluggard.

## CHAPTER XLIV  
### The administration of temporal goods is not fitting for those in monasteries, and much less for a virgin in reclusion

There are some who, sluggish and lazy concerning spiritual things like the sinful people, grow nauseated at the heavenly manna. Seeing others occupied with temporal matters, they envy, slander, and murmur; and, in place of the dung with which they themselves are defiled, they bring forth goads of zeal and bitterness.

If such people should happen to obtain some administration of temporal goods, it may aptly be said of them: “Those who were nourished in saffron-colored garments have embraced dung” (Lam. IV, 5).

Since even those living in monasteries—who have a considerable share in Martha’s portion—are not permitted to be occupied with many things, how much less are you, who have stripped yourself entirely of the world, and to whom it is not only forbidden to possess but even to see or hear what belongs to the world?

## CHAPTER XLV  
### How a religious woman should distribute whatever remains to her

If no one gives you anything to distribute, where will you obtain what you may distribute? But if you have something from your own labor, give it through another’s hand, not your own, if your food comes to you in abundance.

How can you distribute what belongs to others when you are not permitted to appropriate anything beyond what is necessary?

What benefit, then, will you bestow upon your neighbor?

“Nothing is richer than good will,” as a certain saint says: give this generously. What is more humane than compassion? Offer this. What is more useful than prayer? Give this generously.

## CHAPTER XLVI  
### What kind of almsgiving it is fitting for nuns to offer

Therefore embrace the whole world in one embrace of love. There consider together all who are good and rejoice with them; where there are wicked people, look upon them and mourn.

Let the misery of the poor, the groaning of orphans, the desolation of widows, the sorrow of the grieving, the needs of travelers, the dangers of those at sea, the vows of virgins, the temptations of monks, the anxieties of prelates, and the labor of soldiers come before your mind.

Open the breast of your love to all. Spend your tears on them; pour out your prayers for them.

This almsgiving is more pleasing to God, more acceptable to Christ, more suited to your profession, and more fruitful for those to whom it is offered. This gift of benevolence assists your purpose and does not disturb your love of neighbor; it increases it and does not diminish it; it preserves the mind’s peace and does not impede it.

Nothing should be desired in order to have something to give, since having nothing is perfection.

Why should we say more about this? The saints, so that they might love their neighbors perfectly, took care in this world to possess nothing and to hold nothing, even without desire.

You recognize the words of blessed Gregory. See how many think the opposite: in order to fulfill the law of charity, they seek to have something to distribute, although he ascribes its perfection precisely to those who consider that nothing should be possessed or held, even without desire.

## CHAPTER XLVII  
### On stirring up love of God through meditation on the mysteries of Christ

Having prefaced these remarks on love of neighbor, I shall add a few things about love of God [Note: [Col. 1465] The remaining part of this book is found among the works of St. Anselm as Meditation XV–XVII.].

Although each sister loved God and neighbor, Martha was especially occupied with serving her neighbors, while Mary drew from the fountain of divine reading.

Two things pertain to love of God: the mind’s affection and the work’s effect. The work consists in the exercise of the virtues; the mind’s affection consists in the sweetness of spiritual taste.

The exercise of the virtues is commended in a fixed manner of life, in fasts, vigils, labor, love, prayer, poverty, and other such things. The mind’s affection is nourished by salutary meditation.

Therefore, so that that most sweet love of Jesus may grow in your affection, you need a threefold meditation: on past, present, and future things—that is, on the recollection of the past, the experience of the present, and the consideration of the future.

When your mind has been cleansed from every stain of thought through the exercise of the virtues [Note: [Col. 1465] In Anselm: “has been free from the tumult of thoughts.”], turn your purified eyes back toward the things behind.

First, enter the chamber with blessed Mary and unfold the books in which the Virgin’s childbirth is foretold together with Christ’s coming. There await the arrival of the angel, so that you may see him enter and hear him greet her. And, filled with amazement and ecstasy, greet your sweetest Lady together with the greeting angel, crying out:

“Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women” (Luke I, 28).

Repeating this more fully, consider what this fullness of grace is, from which the whole world borrowed grace, since “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, full of grace and truth” (John I, 14).

Contemplate and marvel at the Lord who fills earth and heaven, enclosed within the womb of one girl [Col. 1466], whom the Father sanctified, the Son made fruitful, and the Holy Spirit overshadowed.

O sweet Lady, with what sweetness were you intoxicated, with what fire of love were you kindled, when you felt the presence of such majesty in your mind and womb; when he took flesh for himself from your flesh and fashioned from your members the limbs in which the fullness of divinity would bodily dwell!

All these things happened for your sake, virgin, so that you might love the Virgin whom you have resolved to imitate and the fruit of the Virgin [Note: [Col. 1466] In Anselm: “the Son of the Virgin.”], to whom you have been wedded.

Now ascend with your sweetest Lady into the hill country, and look upon the tender embrace of the barren woman and the virgin. Consider the service of the greeting in which the servant recognized the Lord, the herald the Judge, and the voice the Word—though he was enclosed within an old woman’s womb—who was shut within the virgin’s womb, and greeted him with unspeakable joy.

Blessed are the wombs in which the salvation of the whole world arises and in which, when the darkness of sorrow has been driven away, everlasting joy is foretold.

What are you doing, O virgin? Hurry, I beg you, hurry, and mingle with such great joys. Prostrate yourself at the feet of both women; in one woman’s womb embrace your bridegroom, and in the other’s womb venerate his friend.

Follow him with all devotion as he goes to Bethlehem. When he turns aside into the lodging, stand beside her and assist her in childbirth. When the little child has been placed in the manger, burst forth in a voice of exultation, crying out with Isaiah:

“A little child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. IX, 6).

Embrace that sweet manger. Let love conquer modesty and affection drive away fear, so that you may press your lips to his most sacred feet and multiply your kisses [Note: [Col. 1466] In Anselm: “and kisses upon his knees.” A little later he adds: “insert your prayers.”].

Then consider in your mind the shepherds’ watch. Marvel at the army of angels. Add your own part to the heavenly melody; sing with heart and mouth:

“Glory to God in the highest” (Luke II, 14).

## CHAPTER XLVIII  
### On the Magi’s adoration, Christ’s flight into Egypt, and the thief crucified at Christ’s right hand

Do not pass over the gifts of the Magi in your meditation, nor leave him unaccompanied as he flees into Egypt [Note: [Col. 1466] In Anselm, approximately sixteen lines are inserted at this point.].

Consider true what is said: that he was caught on the road by robbers and rescued through the kindness of a certain young man.

That young man, they say, was the son of the leader of the robbers. Having obtained his booty, he found the little child in his mother’s lap. Such a majestic splendor appeared to him in the child’s most beautiful face that, without doubting that he was more than human, he grew warm with love and embraced him.

“And O,” he said, “most blessed of little ones! If ever an opportunity should present itself for mercy to be shown me, then remember me and do not forget this time.”

They say that this was the thief who was crucified at Christ’s right hand. When he rebuked the other thief for blaspheming, saying, “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive the punishment deserved by our deeds; but this man has done nothing wrong,” he turned to the Lord, looking upon him with the majesty that had appeared in the child, and, mindful of his promise, said:

“Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke XXIII, 40–42).
