Therefore, as an incentive to love, I do not think it useless to adopt this opinion, provided all rashness of assertion is removed.

## CHAPTER XLIX  
### On the contemplation of Christ as a child

Moreover, do you think no sweetness will come to you if you contemplate him as a child among children at Nazareth? If you look upon him obeying his mother and assisting his foster father at his work?

What if you seek him for three days with his mother, when at twelve years old he went up to Jerusalem with his parents and, as they returned without knowing it, remained in the city?

O how abundant the tears that will flow when you hear the mother striking her son with a kind of sweet reproach:

“Son, why have you dealt with us in this way? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you in sorrow” (Luke II, 48).

## CHAPTER L  
### On consideration of Christ’s baptism, fasting, and temptation

But if you wish to follow the virgin [Note: [Col. 1466] In Anselm: “the virgin bridegroom.”] wherever he goes, let it delight you to search out his higher and more secret things [Col. 1467], so that in the river Jordan you may hear the Father in the voice, the Son in the flesh, and see the Holy Spirit in the dove.

There, initiated [Note: [Col. 1467] In Anselm: “invited.”] into spiritual marriage, you receive the bridegroom given by the Father, purification from the Son, and the pledge of love from the Holy Spirit.

After this he enriched for you the secrets of solitude and sanctified fasting, teaching there that you must enter into conflict with the crafty enemy.

Attend carefully to these things done by him, done for you, and to how they were done. Love the one by whom they were done, and imitate what was done.

## CHAPTER LI  
### On the woman caught in adultery

Now the memory of that woman caught in adultery comes to mind. Recall what Jesus did and what he said when he was asked for his judgment.

When, writing on the ground and exposing them as earthly rather than heavenly, he had revealed them, he said: “Let the one among you who is without sin first cast a stone at her.”

When his judgment had held them all [Note: [Col. 1467] In Anselm: “O the wondrous and unquenchable kindness of Christ! Observe how mercifully and cautiously he freed the woman whom he could justly have condemned.”] and driven them from the temple, imagine how gently he raised his eyes to her and how sweetly, in his voice, he pronounced the sentence of her absolution.

Suppose that he sighed and wept when he said:

“Woman, has no one condemned you?”

“Neither will I condemn you.”

Happy, so to speak, is this woman who was caught in adultery: she is absolved from the past and made secure concerning the future.

Good Jesus, when you say, “I will not condemn you,” who will condemn? “God is the one who justifies; who is he that condemns?”

Let your voice be heard thereafter:

“Go, and now sin no more” (John VIII, 7).

## CHAPTER LII  
### On the woman wetting his feet with her tears

Now enter the house of the Pharisee, and observe your Lord reclining there. Approach with that most blessed sinner to his feet. Wash them with tears, wipe them with your hair, caress them with kisses, and cherish them with ointments.

Are you not already drenched in the fragrance of that sacred liquid? If he still refuses you his feet, persist, pray, and lift your tear-filled eyes. With deep sighs and unspeakable cries, wrest from him what you seek.

Struggle with God like Jacob, so that he may rejoice at being overcome by you. At times it may seem to you that he turns his eyes away, closes his ears, and hides the feet you desire.

Nevertheless, persist at a suitable and unsuitable time; cry out:

“How long will you turn your face away from me? How long shall I cry out, and you will not hear?” (Ps. XII, 1).

“Restore to me, good Jesus, the joy of your salvation, for my heart has said to you: ‘I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will seek’” (Ps. XXVI, 8).

Certainly he will not deny his feet to a virgin, when he offered them to a sinner to kiss.

## CHAPTER LIII  
### On the paralytic brought in through the tiles and healed bodily and spiritually

You will not pass by that house either, where the paralytic is lowered through the tiles before his feet, where compassion and power meet one another.

“Son,” he says, “your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. IX, 2).

O wondrous clemency! O unspeakable mercy! The blessed man received forgiveness of sins, though confession had not preceded it, satisfaction had not earned it, and contrition had not demanded it.

He had asked for bodily health, not the soul’s; and he received health of body and soul.

Truly, Lord, life is in your will. If you have decided to save us, no one dares say, “Why do you act in this way?”

Pharisee, why do you murmur? Is your eye evil because he is good? Certainly, he has mercy on whomever he wishes. Let us weep and pray that he may wish it.

Let prayer grow rich in good works, devotion increase, and love be stirred up. Let pure hands be raised in prayer—hands unstained by the blood of impurity, undefiled by illicit touch, and not embittered by greed.

Let the heart also be raised, free from anger and dispute: a heart calmed by tranquility, composed by peace, and enlivened by purity of conscience.

Yet this paralytic is not read to have done any of these things beforehand; nevertheless, he is read to have merited forgiveness of sins.

This is the ineffable power of Christ’s mercy. Just as it is blasphemous to detract from it, so it is exceedingly foolish to presume it for oneself.

He can effectively say to anyone he wishes the very words he said to that paralytic: “Your sins are forgiven.”

But whoever expects these words to be said to him without his own labor, contrition, confession, or even prayer will never have his sins forgiven [Col. 1468].

## CHAPTER LIV  
### On Christ’s reception in the house of Martha and Mary

But we must leave this place and come to Bethany, where the most sacred bonds of friendship are consecrated by the authority of the Lord.

For no one doubts that Jesus loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus, since he was held by the hospitable friendship with which they clung to him in a more intimate affection [Note: [Col. 1468] In Anselm: “since no one doubts that he was held by the special privilege of friendship with which they …”].

Those sweet tears are witnesses: he wept with those who wept, and the whole people interpret them as a sign of love.

“See how he loved him,” they said. And they prepared a supper for him there, while Martha served. Lazarus was one of those reclining at table. Mary took an alabaster jar of ointment, broke the jar, and poured it over Jesus’ head (John XI, 36; XII, 2–3).

Rejoice, I beg you, to be present at this banquet; distinguish the duties of each person. Martha serves, Lazarus reclines at table, Mary anoints.

This last is your part. Therefore break the alabaster jar of your heart, and whatever devotion, whatever love, whatever desire, whatever affection you possess, pour it all over the head of your bridegroom, worshiping the human being in God and God in the human being.

If someone rages, murmurs, envies, or, as a traitor, calls devotion destruction, do not be concerned.

“Why,” he says, “this waste? This ointment could have been sold for much and given to the poor!”

The Pharisee murmurs, envying the penitent; Judas murmurs, envying the outpouring of the ointment. But the judge does not accept the accusation; he acquits the accused woman.

“Let her alone,” he says. “She has performed a good work upon me” (Mark XIV, 4–6).

Let Martha labor, serve, and prepare hospitality for the traveler, food for the hungry, and clothing for the cold.

I belong to Mary alone, and she to me. Let her offer everything she has; let her expect from me whatever she desires.

What then? Would you advise Mary to abandon the feet she kisses so sweetly; to turn her eyes away from that most beautiful face upon which she gazes; to withdraw her hearing from his sweet discourse by which she is refreshed?

## CHAPTER LV  
### On Christ’s entry into Jerusalem, with the children shouting “Hosanna,” and so forth

But now let us rise and go from here.

“Where?” you ask.

Certainly, so that you may accompany the Lord of heaven and earth as he sits upon a donkey. Marveling at the great things done for you, add your own voice to the children’s praises, crying out:

“Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. XXI, 9).

Now ascend with him into the large upper room prepared for the feast, and rejoice to share in the delights of the saving supper.

## CHAPTER LVI  
### On the Lord’s Supper and the events that took place there

Let love conquer modesty and affection drive away fear, so that he may at least offer alms to the beggar from the crumbs of his table.

Or stand at a distance and, like a poor person gazing at a rich one, stretch out your hand to receive something; reveal your hunger through tears.

When, rising from supper, he girded himself with a linen cloth and poured water into a basin, consider what majesty and power it was that washed and wiped human feet; what kindness it was that touched the traitor’s footprints with sacred hands.

Watch and wait, and offer him your own feet to wash last of all, because the one whom he does not wash will have no share with him.

Why are you hurrying out now? Wait a little.

Do you see, I ask you, who that person is who reclines upon his breast and rests his head in his bosom? Blessed is whoever he is.

O, I see: his name is John.

O John, tell me what sweetness, grace and delight, light and devotion I may draw from that fountain. There are surely all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge; there is the fountain of mercy, the dwelling place of compassion, and the honeycomb of eternal sweetness.

How have you come by all these things, O John? Are you higher than Peter, holier than Andrew, more pleasing than all the other Apostles?

This is the special privilege of virginity: because you were chosen by the Lord as a virgin, you were loved before you went with your mother and loved more than the others [Note: [Col. 1469] In Anselm: “and loved more than the others.”].

Rejoice now in mercy, virgin; draw nearer, and do not delay to claim for yourself some portion of this sweetness.

If you cannot reach what is higher, leave John his breast, where the wine of joy may intoxicate him in the knowledge of divinity. Run to the breasts of his humanity and draw out the milk by which you may be nourished.

Amid these things, let him commend the disciples to the Father in that most sacred prayer and say:

“Father, keep them in your name.”

Incline your head, so that you too may deserve to hear:

“I will that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 11, 24).

## CHAPTER LVII  
### On Christ’s agony on the Mount of Olives
It is good for you to be here. But you must go out; he himself goes ahead to the Mount of Olives—follow him. And although, taking Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he withdrew into solitude, observe from a distance how he transferred our necessity onto himself. See how he, to whom all things belong, begins to be afraid and distressed, saying, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26:38). From where does this come, my God? You show yourself compassionate toward me by presenting the human being, so that in a certain way you seem not to know that you are God. Prostrate on his face, he prays, and “his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the ground” (Luke 22:44). Why are you standing still? Hasten forward, lick those sweetest drops, and lick the dust from his feet. Do not sleep with Peter, lest you deserve to hear: “So, could you not watch one hour with me?” (Matt. 26:40).

## CHAPTER LVIII—Christ’s Betrayal

But look: the crowd of wicked men is already following the traitor as he goes before them, and when Judas offers the kiss, they lay hands on your Lord, seize him, bind him, and fasten those sweet hands with chains. Who could endure it? I know that piety now seizes your heart and zeal inflames all your inward parts. Allow him, I beg you, to suffer who suffers for you. Why do you desire a sword? Why are you angry? Why are you indignant? If, like Peter, you cut off someone’s ear; if with the sword you take away an arm; if you sever a foot—he himself will restore everything. Even if you kill someone, he will undoubtedly raise him up.

## CHAPTER LIX—The Injuries Inflicted on Christ before the High Priest and Pilate

Rather, follow him as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and wash with your tears his most beautiful face, which they smear with spittle. Observe with what devout eyes, how mercifully, how effectively he looked upon Peter when he denied him for the third time, and when Peter, turning and coming to himself, wept bitterly. Would that your sweet eye, good Jesus, might look upon me—me who have denied you so many times at the voice of the insolent maidservant, through the worst deeds and desires of my flesh.

But now, when morning has come, he is handed over to Pilate. There he is accused and remains silent, because “like a sheep he is led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth” (Isa. 53:7; Acts 8:32). Look; attend to how he stands before the governor: head bowed, eyes lowered, countenance calm, speech restrained, prepared for insults and ready even for blows.

I know that you can no longer bear to see his sweetest back worn down by lashes, his face struck with blows, that venerable head crowned with thorns, or his right hand—which contains heaven and earth—dishonored with a reed. Behold, he is led out after being scourged, carrying a crown of thorns and wearing a purple garment. And Pilate says, “Behold the man” (John 19:5). Truly he is a man—who could doubt it? The witnesses are the stripes of the rods, the lividness of the wounds, and the foulness of the spittle.

“Now I acknowledge, O Devil, that he is a man.” “Truly he is a man,” you say. But what is this: amid so many injuries he does not become angry as a man, is not moved as a man, and is not indignant at his torturers as a man? Therefore he is more than a man. But who recognizes him? He is certainly recognized as a man enduring the judgments of the wicked; but he will be recognized as God when he executes judgment.

## CHAPTER LX—Christ’s Passion and the Devil’s Deception

You noticed it too late, O Devil. What did you intend to accomplish through the woman [Col. 1470], so that he might be released? You spoke too late. The judge sits on the tribunal; the sentence has been pronounced; he now carries his own cross and is led to death.

O spectacle! Do you see? “Behold, the principality is upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9:6). This is the rod of his justice, the rod of his kingdom. He is given wine mixed with gall. He is stripped of his garments, and they are divided among the soldiers. His tunic is not torn but passes by lot to one man. His sweet hands and feet are pierced with nails, and, stretched out on the cross, he is suspended between thieves.

## CHAPTER LXI—Christ upon the Cross

The Mediator of God and human beings, hanging midway between heaven and earth, unites the lowest with the highest and joins earthly things to heavenly things. Heaven is astonished, and earth marvels. What of you? It is no wonder that, when the sun is darkened, you are saddened; when the earth trembles, you tremble; when the rocks are split, your heart is split; when the women weep beside the cross, you weep with them.

## CHAPTER LXII—Christ’s Wondrous Patience upon the Cross

Yet amid all these things, consider that sweetest heart: what tranquility it preserved and what compassion it possessed. He does not attend to his own injury, does not reckon the punishment, and does not feel the insults. Rather, he pities those by whom he suffers; he heals those by whom he is wounded; he procures life for those by whom he is killed. With what sweetness of mind, with what devotion of spirit, with what fullness of charity he cries, “Father, forgive them!” (Luke 23:34).

## CHAPTER LXIII—The Virgin Stands Nearer to the Cross

Behold me, Lord: an adorer of your majesty, not the slayer of your body; a worshiper of your death, not a mocker of your passion; a contemplator of your mercy, not a despiser of your weakness. Therefore may your sweet humanity intercede for me; may your ineffable compassion commend me to the Father. Say, then, sweet Lord, “Father, forgive him.”

But you, virgin, who have greater confidence with the Son of the Virgin than the women who stand far away, approach the cross with the virgin Mother and the virgin disciple, and gaze closely upon his face, drenched in pallor. What then? Will you see the tears of that most loving Lady without tears of your own? Will you remain with dry eyes while a sword of sorrow has pierced her soul? Without a sob will you hear him say to his mother, “Woman, behold your son,” and to John, “Behold your mother” (John 19:26–27)?

While he entrusted his mother to the disciple and promised paradise to the thief, one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and blood and water came out (ibid. 34). Hasten; do not delay. Eat the honeycomb with your honey. Drink your wine with your milk. The blood becomes wine for you, so that you may be intoxicated; the water is changed into milk, so that you may be nourished.

For you, rivers have been made in the rock: wounds in his limbs, and caves in the wall of his body, in which, like a dove, you may hide and kiss each one. From his blood let your lips become like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech sweet.

## CHAPTER LXIV—The Decurion

But wait still until that noble decurion comes and, removing the nails, releases his hands and feet. See how he embraces the body with his most blessed arms and presses it to his breast. Then that most holy man could have said: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh; he will abide between my breasts” (Song 1:12).

Follow that most precious treasure of heaven and earth: either carry his feet, or support his hands and arms, or at least gather with the greatest care the drops of his most precious blood as they trickle down one by one, and lick the dust from his feet.

Observe also how blessed Nicodemus tenderly handled his most sacred wounds with his fingers, anointed them with ointments, and, together with holy Joseph, wrapped him in a shroud and laid him in the tomb.

## CHAPTER LXV—Magdalene Visiting the Tomb

Do not, moreover, abandon the company of Magdalene. Prepare spices and remember to visit the tomb of your Lord with her. O that you might be worthy to perceive in spirit what she saw with her eyes: now the angel sitting upon the stone rolled away from the entrance of the tomb; now, inside the tomb, one at the head and another at the feet, proclaiming the glory of the resurrection; now Jesus himself, looking upon the weeping and sorrowful Mary [Col. 1471] with so sweet an eye and saying in so gentle a voice, “Mary.”

What is sweeter than this voice, what more gentle, what more pleasing—“Mary”? At this voice all the floodgates of the head are broken open; tears are drawn from the very marrow; sobs and sighs are dragged up from the deepest inward parts.

“Mary.” O blessed woman! What did you have in return for your merits, what was your state of mind, when at this voice you prostrated yourself and, returning a voice to him who greeted you, cried out, “Rabboni”?

With what emotion, I ask, with what longing and ardor of mind did you cry, “Rabboni”? For the tears prevent you from saying more, since emotion closes your voice and excessive ardor absorbs every sense of soul and body.

But, sweet Jesus, why do you thus drive away the woman who loves you from your most sacred and most desired feet? O hard word! “Do not touch me,” he says (John 20:16–17).

Why, Lord? Why should I not touch those desired footprints of yours, pierced with nails for my sake and drenched in blood? Shall I not touch them, shall I not kiss them? Or are you more hostile because you are more glorious?

Behold, I will not let you go; I will not withdraw from you; I will not spare my tears. My breast will be torn apart by sobs and sighs unless I touch you.

And he says, “Do not touch me.” Do not fear; this good is not being taken away from you but postponed. Go, however, and tell my brothers that I have risen.

She runs quickly, wishing to return. She returns with the other women. When Jesus meets them with a gracious greeting, he raises up those who have fallen and consoles those who are sorrowful. Pay attention. Then what had previously been postponed was granted. For they approached and took hold of his feet.

Here, virgin, remain as long as you can. Let no sleep interrupt these delights of yours; let no external tumult interfere.

## CHAPTER LXVI—Contempt for the World and Present Things

Yet because in this wretched life nothing is stable and nothing eternal, and a human being never remains in the same condition, it is necessary that while we live our soul be nourished by a certain variety. Therefore let us pass from remembrance of the past to experience of the present, so that from these things also we may all understand how greatly God ought to be loved by us.

Turn all these matters over in your mind, so that your entire affection may be dissolved into him. Let the world become worthless to you; let every carnal love become filthy. Do not regard yourself as being in this world, since you have transferred your love to those who are in heaven and live for God.

“Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” Do not enclose your soul, together with silver idols, in a wretched purse—a soul that will never be able to fly up to heaven with the weight of coins. Consider yourself to be dying every day, and do not think about tomorrow.

Let neither the barrenness of the future frighten you nor fear of future hunger cast down your mind. Rather, let all your confidence depend upon him who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies. Let he himself be your granary, he himself your storeroom, he himself your purse, he himself your riches; let him alone be everything to you in all things.

For now, let this suffice concerning present things.

## CHAPTER LXVII—The Saints Desire Death

But if he grants his own people so much in the present, how much is he reserving for them in the future? Death is the beginning of future things and the end of present things. Whose nature does not recoil from it? Whose affection does not dread it? For beasts avoid death by flight, by hiding places, and by a thousand other means, and cling to life.

Now attend carefully to what your conscience answers you, what your faith presumes, what your hope promises, and what your affection expects. If your life is a burden to you, if the world is wearisome, if the flesh is painful, then death is certainly your desire: it lays down the yoke of this burden, removes weariness, and absorbs bodily pains.

This one thing I say surpasses all the delights, honors, and riches of this world: that, because of the serenity of conscience, the firmness of faith, and the certainty of hope, you do not fear death. He will be able to experience this above all who, sighing for some time under this servitude, have escaped into the air of a freer conscience.

These are the healing firstfruits of your future blessedness: when death comes, faith overcomes natural dread, hope moderates it, and a secure conscience drives it away.

## CHAPTER LXVIII—For the Just, Death Is the Beginning of Happiness

And see how death is the beginning of blessedness [Col. 1472], the goal of labors, and the destruction of vices. For it is written: “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord. From now on, says the Spirit, let them rest from their labors” (Rev. 14:13).

Therefore the prophet, distinguishing the death of the rejected from that of the elect, says: “All the kings will sleep in glory, each in his own house; but you have been cast out from your tomb, like a useless shoot, polluted and wrapped up” (Isa. 14:18–19).

## CHAPTER LXIX—The Rest or Punishment of the Soul Departing from the Body

Those whose good conscience commends their death sleep in glory, because “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.” He truly sleeps in glory whose repose is attended by angels, whose fellow saints and fellow citizens come to meet him, offering their help and granting consolation. They oppose his enemies, repel those who resist, and refute his accusers; thus they accompany the holy soul as far as Abraham’s bosom and place it in a place of peace and rest.

It is not so with the wicked. Evil spirits, as though drawing them from a stinking tomb, drag them from the body with infernal instruments; polluted by lust and wrapped in greed, they thrust them into fires to be burned, hand them over to worms to be torn apart, and consign them to eternal foulness to be suffocated.

“Truly, the expectation of the righteous is joy, but the hope of the wicked will perish” (Prov. 10:28).

## CHAPTER LXX—The Eternal Rest and Glory of the Saints

What that rest is like, what that peace and joy are like, what is promised and awaited there by those resting in Abraham’s bosom—because experience has not taught us, no style of writing can explain. The blessed wait until the number of their brothers is complete, so that on the day of resurrection, clothed in a double garment, they may enjoy perpetual happiness of both body and soul.

## CHAPTER LXXI—The Day of the Last Judgment

Now contemplate the terror of that day, when the powers of heaven will be shaken, the elements will be dissolved by the heat of fire, hell will be opened, and all hidden things will be exposed. From above will come the angry judge; his fury will burn, and his chariots will be like a storm, so that in wrath he may repay vengeance and destruction in a flame of fire.

Blessed is the one who is prepared to meet him. What will then become of the wretched souls? How wretched will those be whom luxury now stains, greed scatters, and pride exalts?

The angels will go out and separate the wicked from the midst of the righteous, placing some on the right and others on the left. Imagine yourself now standing before the tribunal between these two communities, not yet separated into one side or the other. Turn your eyes now toward the Judge’s left and look upon that miserable multitude.

## CHAPTER LXXII—The Shame and Punishment of the Wicked

What horror is there! What fear! What foulness! What pain! The wretched stand there, gnashing their teeth, trembling with their sides exposed, horrifying in appearance, deformed in countenance, cast down through shame. Confounded by the ugliness and nakedness of their bodies, they wish to hide, but are not allowed to; they try to flee, but are not permitted.

If they raise their eyes, the Judge’s fury hangs over them from above; if they lower them, the horror of the infernal pit is thrust upon them. No excuse for their crimes is available, nor can there be any complaint about an unjust judgment, since their own conscience will not fail to know that whatever has been decreed is just.

## CHAPTER LXXIII—Love Owed to God for the Grace of Predestination

See now how greatly he must be loved who, by predestining you, distinguished you from that condemned company; by calling you, separated you; and by justifying you, purified you. Turn your eyes now to the right and observe into which company he will insert you by glorifying you.

## CHAPTER LXXIV—The Glory of the Good

What beauty is there! What honor! What happiness! What security! Some are exalted by the judicial seat; others shine with the crown of martyrdom; others are radiant with the white flower of virginity; others are fruitful in the generosity of almsgiving; others are distinguished by teaching and learning. They are joined together by one bond of charity.

The face of Jesus Christ shines upon them—not terrifying but lovable; not bitter but sweet; not frightening but encouraging.

## CHAPTER LXXV—We Are Counted among Those Saved by the Grace of God Alone

[Col. 1473]

Stand now in the midst, not knowing to which side the Judge’s sentence will assign you. O harsh expectation! “Fear and trembling have come upon me, and darkness has covered me” (Ps. 54:6).

If he joins me to those on the left, I will not call it unjust. If he enrolls me among those on the right, this must be attributed to his grace, not to my merits. Truly, Lord, “life is in your will.”

You see, therefore, how greatly your soul ought to be extended in love of him who, although he could justly have turned against you as well the sentence pronounced upon the wicked, preferred to insert you among the righteous and those who are to be saved.

Now imagine yourself joined to that holy company and hearing the decree of that voice: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.”

The wretched will hear a harsh word, full of wrath and fury: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” “And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:34, 41, 46).

O harsh separation! O miserable condition!

## CHAPTER LXXVI—The Kingdom of God after the Judgment

When the wicked have been removed so that they may not see the glory of God, and each of the righteous has been inserted according to his rank and merit into the angelic orders, that glorious procession will take place: Christ our head going before, and all his members following. The kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, so that he himself may reign in them and they may reign with him, receiving that kingdom which was prepared for them from the foundation of the world.

## CHAPTER LXXVII—The Happiness of God’s Kingdom

The condition of that kingdom cannot even be imagined by us, much less spoken or written. This must be known: nothing at all will be absent that you would wish to be present, and nothing will be present that you would wish to be absent.

Therefore there will be no mourning, no weeping, no fear, no pain, no distrust, no envy, no tribulation, no temptation, no change or corruption of the atmosphere, no suspicion, no ambition, no flattery, no slander, no sickness, no old age, no death, no poverty, and no darkness. There will be no necessity of eating, drinking, or sleeping, no weariness, and no exhaustion.

What good, then, is there where there is neither mourning nor weeping, neither pain nor sadness? What can there be except perfect joy, where there is no tribulation, no temptation, no change of seasons, no corruption of the atmosphere, no excessive heat, and no harsher winter?

What can there be except a supreme harmony of all things and true, perfect tranquility of mind and flesh? Where there is nothing to fear, what can there be except supreme security? Where there is no discord, envy, suspicion, ambition, flattery, or slander, what can there be except supreme and true love?

Where there is no poverty and no greed, what can there be except the fullness of all good things? Where there is no deformity, what can there be except true beauty? Where there is no labor or exhaustion, what will there be except perfect rest and strength? Where there is nothing that weighs down or burdens, what is there except complete ease?

Where old age is neither awaited nor illness feared, what can there be except true health? Where there is neither night nor darkness, what will there be except perfect light? When death and all mortality have been swallowed up, what will there be except eternal life?

What more is there for us to seek? Certainly that which surpasses all these things: the vision, knowledge, and love of the Creator.

He will be seen in himself and seen in his creatures, governing all things without anxiety, sustaining all things without labor, imparting himself and, in a certain way, distributing himself to each according to its capacity, without diminution or division of himself.

That lovable and desirable face will be seen upon which the angels long to gaze. What can be said of its fullness, its light, its sweetness? The Father will be seen in the Son, the Son in the Father, and the Holy Spirit in both. He will be seen not through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face.

For he will be seen as he is, when that promise has been fulfilled in which he says: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

From this vision proceeds the knowledge of which he himself says: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the one God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (ibid. 17:3).

From these arises such great love, such ardor of fatherly love, such sweetness of charity, such abundance of fervor, and such intensity of desire that neither satiety diminishes desire nor desire prevents satiety.

What is this? Certainly it is what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man—the things God has prepared for those who love him.”

[Note: [Col. 1474] In Anselm, “pious love”; and shortly afterward, “such abundance of enjoyment.”]

## CHAPTER LXXVIII—Epilogue of the Work

These things I have taken care to sow beforehand for you, sister, as certain seeds of spiritual meditation: the remembrance of Christ’s past benefits, experience of present things, and expectation of future things. From them may the richer fruit of divine love arise and grow, so that meditation may exercise affection, affection may produce desire, and desire may stir tears; so that your tears may be your bread day and night until you appear in his presence, are received into his embraces, and say what is written in the Song of Songs: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 1:12).

You now have, as you requested, bodily regulations by which, enclosed within them, you may order the conduct of the outward person. You have the prescribed form by which you may either cleanse the inward person from vices or adorn it with virtues. You have, in the threefold meditation, the means by which you may arouse, nourish, and kindle love within yourself.

### Notable Verses

“Sweet are the consolations of the soul which I entrust to you.”

For they are of no benefit unless you preserve them by putting them into practice. Therefore, if anyone has made progress through the wording of this little book [Note: Thus in B. and Lov.; perhaps *lectione* (“reading”) would be better. M.], let him render this service in return for my labor or study: let him intercede for my sins before my Savior, whom I love; before my rewarder, whom I await; and before my judge, whom I fear.

Augustine asks him for some time in which, in retreat, he may prepare himself for the duties of the presbyterate through prayer and the study of the sacred Scriptures. 5. Valerius appears to grant this. 6. At Valerius’ command, Augustine the presbyter expounds the word of God to the people, even with the bishop himself present. 168 **V.** 1. He establishes a monastery at Hippo. 2. On his disciples. 3. Several of them are elevated to the episcopate. 4. Monastic life is spread throughout Africa through Augustine’s efforts. 5. How deeply he grieved at the fall of certain monks from his own number. 6. He demonstrates that a monastic profession cannot be made to contain no bad people mixed with the good. 7. He orders people of the lowest rank to be admitted to it, and says that less gratitude should not be shown to the rich who wish to enter, whether they have given their possessions to needy people elsewhere or to the monastery. 8. On the community of life professed by the consecrated women of Hippo in the monastery he established. 174 **VI.** 1. Aurelius is made bishop of Carthage, from which immense benefits flow to the African Churches. 2. Augustine writes to him so that he may remove from the churches banquets and other indecencies. 3. He laments that contention and the desire for empty praise are found even among the clergy themselves. 183 **VII.** 1. He writes the book *On the Usefulness of Believing* to Honoratus, who was devoted to the Manichaeans. 2. Then the book *On Two Souls* against the same Manichaeans. 3. He convicts Fortunatus the Manichaean presbyter in a public disputation. 4. He refutes Adimantus, a disciple of the Manichaeans. 185 **VIII.** 1. A general council of all Africa is held at Hippo, at which Augustine explains the creed. 2. He writes to Jerome. 3. He publishes the unfinished book *On Genesis Literally*. 4. Later, the books *On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*. 5. He writes on the Epistle to the Romans. 6. Also on the Epistle to the Galatians. 7. The short work *On Lying*. 189 **IX.** 1. An epitome of the history of the Donatists. 2. How powerful they were in numbers in Africa when Augustine reached the presbyterate, and how immediately he attacked them. [Col. 1478] 3. The Donatists do not dare to engage him. 4. He composes an alphabetical psalm against them. 5. He refutes Donatus’ letter. 6. He writes to Maximinus, the Donatist bishop of Siniti, concerning a deacon whom Maximinus was said to have rebaptized. 192 **X.** 1. Through his own nocturnal studies and Alypius’ report, Augustine becomes known to Paulinus. 2. The latter sends separate letters to Alypius and Augustine. 3. Licentius sends a poem to Augustine. 4. Augustine replies to Paulinus’ letter. 5. Since he did not receive Augustine’s reply, Paulinus writes him a second letter. 199 **XI.** 1. He preaches to the people of Hippo against the very bad custom of holding banquets in church. 2. The next day he attacks the same custom more forcefully. 3. On the following day he abolishes it completely. 4. He puts the finishing touch to the work *On Free Choice*. 5. The Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians claimed that certain points in that work supported them. 203 **BOOK FOUR.**—In it is shown how Augustine lived as a bishop and what he published from his ordination through the following fifth year. 209–210 **CHAPTER ONE.** 1. Valerius asks Augustine to become his colleague. 2. Megalius, primate of Numidia, opposes his ordination on the charge of a false accusation, but soon regrets this. 3. Augustine finally consents to his own ordination and sits as co-bishop with Valerius. 4. His ordination took place at the end of the year of the Lord 395. 5. Writing to Paulinus, he informs him of his ordination. 6. The latter writes to Romanianus about the same matter, adding a poem to Licentius. Ibid. **II.** 1. What Augustine’s state of soul and character were when he was already bishop. 2. He is forbidden by God to flee into solitude; his delights are the Scriptures of God and being free for God. 3. What bodily adornment he preferred in clothing and footwear. 4. What his table was like. 5. He would have liked to work with his hands every day, if health and duties had allowed it. 6. His poor health and responsibilities. 7. He establishes a monastery for clergy in the bishop’s house. A letter to Laetus, perhaps a member of this monastery. 8. In that monastery he lives with his clergy according to a rule and in strict simplicity. 9. How he conducted himself toward women: he did not allow any woman, not even a relative, to live in his house. 215 **III.** 1. Augustine was always free in spirit in administering the goods of his Church. 2. When given the opportunity to increase them, he was wholly removed from every form of greed. 3. He approves and accepts pious offerings. 4. The very different opinions of himself and Alypius concerning the inheritance of the presbyter Honoratus. 5. He arranges for basilicas and a hospice to be built. 225 **IV.** 1. He devotes himself to relieving the poor. 2. He writes to the people of Hippo on behalf of Fascius, who was burdened with debt. 3. In recommending others and interceding for them before the authorities, he conducts himself modestly. 4. He writes to Romulus on behalf of the country people. 230 **V.** 1. Augustine’s rule and prudence in visitations and in other services he rendered. 2. He writes to Pancharius on behalf of the parish of Germanicianum. 3. He does everything within his share and ability for the universal Church. 4. He complains that he is occupied with settling disputes. 233 **VI.** 1. The holy bishop diligently devotes himself to preaching the divine word. 2. Firmus the Manichaean is converted to the faith of Christ after hearing him preach. 3. Certain noteworthy features of his sermons. 4. He preached in Latin at Hippo. 5. He preferred hearing the word of God while seated to the African Churches’ custom of hearing it while standing. 236 **VII.** 1. He inveighs against vices. 2. His prudence and charity in correcting sinners. 3. He abstains from the company of disreputable Christians more than from that of pagans. 4. He does not approve of excommunicating an entire household because of one person’s sin. 5. He admits a certain astrologer among the penitents. 6. He instructs Lampadius, who was entangled in the question of the fate determined by the stars. 241 **VIII.** 1. He inflames Christinus with devotion. 2. He strengthens Sebastian against scandals. 3. And Restitutus. 4. He recalls Chrisimus from despair. 5. He reproves Ecdicia, a pious woman, for acting without counsel. 6. He presses upon Cornelius’ hardened mind. 7. He does not refuse to instruct Florentina by letter. 8. He warns Fabiola that the presence of the saints bodily is not greatly to be desired. 9. He takes care of an orphan girl. 245 **IX.** 1. He endeavors to lead the people of Madaura to the Christian religion. [Col. 1479] 2. He corresponds with Longinianus, a pagan priest, so that he may embrace it. 3. He consoles and strengthens Maxima, disturbed by errors that had arisen in her province. 4. He enters into conflict with various heretics; against a certain Novatian he writes to Seleuciana. 5. The heresy of the Tertullianists is destroyed in his presence. 6. The Abelonians, or Abeloites, are likewise eliminated from the region of Hippo through his ministry and labor. 249 **X.** 1. He attempts to converse with Proculeianus, the Donatist bishop of Hippo. 2. He writes to Eusebius about this matter. 3. He complains to the same man that Proculeianus received a young man who had assaulted his mother and had him rebaptized in Proculeianus’ party. 4. He also protests concerning Primus, a subdeacon from Spain and a disreputable man, who was rebaptized by the Donatists. 5. The death of Bishop Valerius. 6. Augustine replies to Casulanus concerning the Saturday fast. 253 **XI.** 1. On the books written to Simplicianus, in whose work the truth of predestination is revealed to him by God. 2. When those books were published. 3. Augustine refutes the Manichaean letter that they called *The Foundation*. 4. He publishes the book *On Christian Combat*. 258 **XII.** 1. Augustine labors over the four books *On Christian Doctrine*. 2. Then the book against the Donatist party and the thirteen books of the *Confessions*. 3. The work against Faustus is published at about the same time. 4. What seemed worth observing in assigning certain short works to their proper place. 5. Augustine writes a book of songs for the altar. 6. *Questions on the Gospels*. 7. Notes on Job. 8. The book *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*. 9. And fifteen books *On the Trinity*. 262 **XIII.** 1. Possidius’ ordination as bishop of Calama. 2. In writing to Augustine, Jerome honors him with the title “pope.” 3. The letter to Jerome, sent for delivery by Paul, reaches him only after a delay. 4. Two letters from Augustine to Paulinus requesting a reply. 268 **XIV.** 1. Augustine, traveling with Alypius to Cirta to ordain Fortunatus bishop, enters into a conversation with Fortunius, the Donatist bishop of Tubursicum. 2. At what time this conversation took place. 3. Letters written after the conversation to Glorius and certain other Donatists. 4. Another conversation held with the same men before the encounter with Fortunius. 5. He begins a written disputation with Fortunatus, the Donatist bishop. 6. On the Caelicolists. 270 **XV.** 1. Augustine writes to Eudoxius the abbot. 2. He preaches against Christians who join pagans in their festivals. 3. The statue of Hercules at Carthage is treated disgracefully. 4. Publicola’s questions are answered. 276 **XVI.** 1. Pagan superstition is then overthrown everywhere, when it was about to be restored through the oracles of demons. 2. In the East it is prohibited and abolished by the authority of Arcadius. 3. In the West also, by the authority of Honorius. 4. Jovius and Gaudentius see to the execution of the law that Honorius issued on this matter. 5. The temple of the heavenly goddess at Carthage is dedicated to Christ by Aurelius. 6. Certain traces of idolatry remain in some places. 7. The martyrs of Suffecte. Augustine writes to the leading men of the colony of Suffecte. 8. A rescript granted by Julian to the flattering petitions of the Donatists is ordered to be posted in public places. 280 **BOOK FIVE.**—On Augustine’s deeds from the year of Christ 400 to the year 405. 285–286 **CHAPTER ONE.** 1. He demonstrates the harmony of the four Evangelists against unbelievers. 2. He answers Januarius’ inquiries about the sacraments and various customs of the Church. 3. He writes *On the Work of Monks* for the benefit of those who supported themselves by the labor of their hands. Ibid. **II.** 1. He presses Crispinus, the Donatist bishop of Calama, to have the question of the cause of the schism discussed in writings exchanged between them. 2. Alypius and Augustine deal by letter with the same question with Clarentius, writing to Naucelius. 3. Augustine strives to rescue his relative Severinus from the schism. 4. He writes to Generosus so that he may not allow himself to be deceived by a certain Donatist presbyter. 289 **III.** 1. Who Petilianus, a bishop of Donatus’ party, was. 2. On his letter against the Catholic Church. 3. Augustine refutes its first part. 4. At what time he undertook this. 5. He refutes Parmenianus’ letter against Tichonius, written in support of the schism. 6. He publishes the books *On Baptism against the Donatists*. 7. On the book *Against What Centurius Brought Forward* [the title is uncertain], from the Donatists. 8. On the letter to Celer. 292 **IV.** 1. The book *On the Good of Marriage*, published on the occasion of the Jovinianist heresy. 2. Also the book *On Holy Virginity*. 3. Commentaries on Genesis literally. 298 **V.** 1. The council held at Carthage on June 16 decrees that bishops should be sent as legates to the overseas sees, so that Donatists returning to unity might be admitted into the clergy; and that certain requests should be made of the Emperor through the same legates. 2. Another council of Carthage in the same year, held on September 13, deals with recalling the same schismatics to the Church and decides that their clergy should be received with their honors. 3. The method and procedure for admitting Donatists by the Church. 4. Certain provisions of the Council of Carthage are noted. 300 **VI.** 1. Victorinus and Xanthippus contend over primacy. 2. Pammachius recalls his tenants who adhered to Donatus’ party to the Church. 3. Donatus leaves Augustine’s monastery with his brother. 4. Augustine replies to the presbyter Quintianus, who had a case before Aurelius. 5. The latter’s complaint over Privation, who had been received into Augustine’s monastery. 6. Augustine removes Abundantius, a presbyter of his diocese, from office. 7. At the end of this year, 401, Crispinus rebaptizes the country people of the Mappalian district. 307 **VII.** 1. A dispute arises between Augustine and Severus of Milevis on account of Timothy. 2. Augustine sends Timothy to Severus, who persistently demanded him. 3. A highly ornate encomium is delivered to Augustine by Severus. 4. Augustine’s reply to the praise given him by his friend. 5. How close Augustine was to Severus, and certain episodes from the latter’s history. 313 **VIII.** 1. The second book against Petilianus is composed in the year of Christ 402. 2. In this book Augustine refutes Petilianus’ entire letter. 3. He writes a letter to the Catholics, which is not called *On the Unity of the Church* from the beginning. 4. Petilianus responds by heaping insults and curses upon Augustine. 5. Augustine’s remarkable reply to Petilianus’ abuse and insults. 6. While explaining Psalm 36 to the people of Carthage, Augustine argues against the Donatists. 318 **IX.** 1. On certain decrees of the First Council of Milevis. 2. Maximianus of Bagai voluntarily resigns the episcopate for the peace and benefit of the Church; Castorius is pressed to succeed him as his brother. 3. Toward the end of this year Augustine and Jerome exchange letters with one another. 4. Also other letters in the following year. 327 **X.** 1. Provoked by the preaching of the truth, the Donatists undertake many violent actions. 2. Augustine is rescued from danger after losing his way on the road. 3. Because they endured violence inflicted by these men, some acquire the name “confessors.” 4. The Catholic bishops publicly invite the Donatist bishops to hold a conference. 5. They refuse arrogantly; Augustine writes to their laypeople. 330 **XI.** 1. When invited to a conference, Crispinus replies with bitter and abusive words. 2. The Donatists attack Possidius. 3. Then the defender of the Church has Crispinus condemned to the gold fine imposed on heretics; Possidius subsequently also declares him a heretic. 4. Nevertheless, the Catholics later obtain a remission of this punishment for him. 5. A delegation from the Council of Carthage goes to request from the Emperor laws against the schismatics, but moderate ones. 6. This delegation is entrusted to Theasius and Evasius. 7. The Donatists’ savagery toward Maximianus. 8. They also attack Bishop Servus. 334 **XII.** 1. A scandal arises at Hippo concerning the presbyter Boniface and Spes. 2. Augustine writes to the people of Hippo about this to strengthen them. 3. He convicts Felix the Manichaean and recalls him from error. 4. He writes the book *On the Nature of the Good* against the Manichaean heresy. 5. He completely overturns this heresy especially in the book published against Secundinus. 6. He calms Jerome’s anger by his humility. 7. Their letters are exchanged. 342 **BOOK SIX.**—In it are related the things Augustine did from the time when new laws were issued against the Donatists in 405 until the Carthaginian Conference with those same schismatics. 347–348 **CHAPTER ONE.** 1. A severe law is issued by Honorius against the Donatists. 2. Other laws are issued against them. 3. Augustine’s letters to Paulinus. 4. How great a benefit the Church derives from the laws of Honorius. 5. A council is held at Carthage after unity has begun to be restored there. Ibid. **II.** 1. The savagery of the Donatists at Hippo. 2. Augustine appeals for the protection of Caecilianus. [Col. 1481] 3. The fury of the schismatics throughout the rest of Africa. 4. The Church flourishes with their blood poured out by their own hands. 5. The Donatists send legates to the Emperor. 6. The clergy of Hippo complain to Januarius about their injuries. 353 **III.** 1. Augustine writes against Cresconius. 2. He tries unsuccessfully to bring Paulus Cataquensis back to a way of life worthy of a bishop. 3. He writes to Emeritus, grieving that he is entangled in the schism. 4. Three short works perhaps published at that time against the Donatists. 5. The book *On the Divination of Demons*. 6. Six questions explained against the pagans, addressed to the presbyter Deogratias. 7. An exposition of the Epistle of James to the twelve tribes. 8. The book *On One Baptism*, addressed to Constantius. 359 **IV.** 1. The decree of the Council of Carthage in 407 concerning appointing a bishop over peoples converted from the schism of Donatus. 2. Laws are granted to the same council’s delegation to the Emperor. 3. The schism of the Rogatists is confined to the town of Cartenna and neighboring places. 4. Augustine refutes the letter of Vincentius, the leading bishop among the Rogatists. 365 **V.** 1. The elder Melania comes to Africa. 2. Augustine writes to Paulinus, from whom he in turn receives letters. 3. The insolence and ferocity of the idolaters of Calama. 4. Nectarius pleads with Augustine on behalf of his fellow citizens of Calama who are defendants. 5. Because of their crime, Possidius goes to the imperial court. 6. Augustine replies to Paulinus. 7. Also to Bishop Memorius, to whom he sends the sixth of his books on music. 368 **VI.** 1. Olympius succeeds to Stilicho’s authority. 2. Augustine sends him a letter concerning the case of Boniface, bishop of Cataqua. 3. Augustine explains the questions of Bishop Boniface. 4. After Stilicho’s death, the Church is disturbed by pagans and heretics rioting. 5. New laws against them are obtained from the Emperor. 6. Augustine asks Donatus, remembering Christian gentleness, to restrain the Donatists with the authority granted him, but not to kill them. 7. He writes to Italica. 374 **VII.** 1. Honorius confirms the laws enacted against pagans and heretics; Nectarius again asks Augustine on behalf of the people of Calama. 2. Honorius grants freedom to heretics and pagans. 3. Augustine writes to the Donatists. 4. Also to Festus. 5. He insists most earnestly that Macrobius not rebaptize Rusticianus, the apostate subdeacon. 6. He writes letters to various people on behalf of Faventius. 7. He strengthens Victorianus, whose spirit has been broken by the intolerable disasters of the world. 381 **VIII.** 1. In the year 410, after the City was captured, he delivers various sermons to the people on this subject. 2. He excuses his absence to the people of Hippo and urges them to consider clothing the poor according to their custom. 3. Recovering from illness in the countryside, he replies to Dioscorus concerning the questions sent by him. 4. He corrects Consentium, who was mistaken with simplicity and without arrogance, and imbues him with sounder doctrine. 5. Honorius removes the freedom granted to each person to practice the religion he chooses. 6. He also orders the Catholics to enter into conference with the Donatists. 7. Marcellinus is appointed to arrange the procedure and order of the forthcoming Conference. 389 **IX.** 1. Pinianus and Melania arrive at Tagaste with Melania’s mother, Albina. 2. Augustine is not permitted to visit them there. 3. Pinianus comes to Hippo. 4. The people of Hippo demand him as their presbyter. 5. Pinianus calms the resulting tumult, promising under oath that he will remain at Hippo. 6. Albina and Alypius complain about what had happened to them or to Pinianus. 7. Augustine clears himself before them. 8. Later the people of Hippo undoubtedly grant Pinianus permission to depart wherever he wished. 9. Augustine urges Armentarius and Paulina to despise the world and fulfill their vow of continence. 397 **X.** 1. On the Conference held at Carthage between the Catholic and Donatist bishops: Marcellinus calls it. 2. As the Conference approaches, Augustine preaches near Carthage. 3. The Donatists’ insolent entry into that city and their number. 4. Marcellinus prescribes the entire procedure of the Conference by edict. 5. The Donatists wish all their people who have come to participate at the place of the Conference, but refuse to give their signatures to the records. 6. The Catholics offer them this condition: if the Church wins the case, they may either retain their episcopates by returning to unity or, together with the Catholics, lay them down themselves. 7. Another of Augustine’s sermons before the Conference, on peace. 8. The Catholics designate the bishops who are to dispute with the schismatics and provide them with an excellent mandate. 405 **XI.** 1. The opening of the Conference held on the first day of June. 2. The Donatists demand that all the Catholics be summoned so that they may be informed about the signatures to their mandate. 3. The Donatists do not accept the offered opportunity to sit together; instead, they declare that selected representatives will argue on their behalf. 4. They are shown to have made several errors in the signatures to the mandate given to their disputants. 5. They are also shown to have admitted a lie concerning Bishop Quodvultdeus. 6. On the day agreed for the second Conference, only seven Donatist bishops who are disputants attend, whereas eighteen Catholic delegates are present. 7. The Donatists are granted a postponement. 413 **XII.** 1. At the third Conference, held on June 8, the Donatists insist that it be determined who should be regarded as the petitioners and that the Catholics’ mandates concerning requesting a Conference be examined. 2. They acknowledge that the Catholic Church is the one spread throughout the whole world. 3. To determine which side consists of the petitioners, various records are read aloud, and thus the central issue is reached despite the Donatists’ opposition. 4. The Donatists produce a little book on the “purity,” as they call it, of the Church. 5. Augustine refutes it and resolves the controversy concerning that most serious issue. 6. The question concerning Caecilianus and the schism is taken up. 7. Disturbed and overwhelmed by the history of the Maximianists, the Donatists admit that neither the cause of one matter should prejudice another cause nor one person another person. 8. They raise a controversy concerning the truth of the Council of Cirta. 9. They wish to examine the passage of Optatus by which they are refuted. 10. When documents demonstrating the innocence of Caecilianus and Felix are produced, they cut through all the knots of the difficulties. 11. Finally, the Judge awards the case to the Catholics. 419 **XIII.** 1. How prominently Augustine stood out at the Conference. 2. The Donatists’ many evasions and tergiversations. 3. How prudently Marcellinus conducted himself. 4. The Donatists appeal to the Emperor. 5. Marcellinus publishes the records of the Conference in a written edict against the schismatics. 6. Augustine reduces them to a summary. 7. After the Conference, large numbers of Donatists return to the Church. 8. Among them are specifically Gabinus and the virgin Felicia. 432 **BOOK SEVEN.**—It covers the eight years beginning in 411, from which year Augustine began to deal with the enemies of God’s grace. 439–446 **CHAPTER ONE.** 1. Pelagius begins to set forth his heresy.
begins to put forward. 2 His disciple Coelestius is condemned by the Council of Carthage. 3 Augustine attacks the Pelagians and writes two books to Marcellinus on the baptism of infants. 4 He adds to them a third work against the Pelagians, addressed to the same man, or rather a book. 5 A book dedicated to the same Marcellinus, *On the Spirit and the Letter*. 6 At Carthage he delivers a sermon to the people against the Pelagian error. 7 He writes back to Pelagius. 8 In a letter to Anastasius he proves the necessity of grace for fulfilling the law. 9 In reply to Honoratus he discusses the grace of the New Testament. Ibid.

II. 1 After the Conference Augustine writes to the lay Donatists. 2 The Donatists are condemned by an imperial rescript of Honorius. 3 Their frenzy. 4 Restitutus is beaten by them. 5 How vigorously Augustine acts to prevent those charged with the killings from being punished capitally. 6 He takes care that the violence of the schismatics in the diocese of Hippo and throughout the rest of Numidia be restrained. 7 He writes various short works. 446

III. 1 Augustine and Marcellinus strive to bring Volusianus from the worship of idols to the Christian faith. 2 Augustine’s celebrated letter to Volusianus. 3 The Council of Zerta. 4 Certain Donatist presbyters and clerics, and also citizens of Cirta, return to the Catholic Church. 5 Where Augustine wishes his writings to be placed, and where he wishes them to be placed by his friends. 453

IV. 1 Augustine publishes the book *On Faith and Works*. 2 He writes to Paulina *On Seeing God*, and also to Fortunatianus, through whose assistance he wishes to be restored to friendship with a certain bishop who had taken offense at his statements against an erroneous opinion. 3 Paulinus and Augustine send various letters to one another. 4 Augustine then turns his attention to writing his work *On the City of God*. 456

V. 1 Marinus, conqueror of Heraclianus, loses the reputation he had gained by the killing of Marcellinus. 2 That this was the very man whose death is related in the letter to Caecilianus. 3 Marcellinus is held in custody with his brother by order of Marinus. 4 In order to impose upon the Church, he persuades them to send men to the Emperor to petition for pardon on their behalf. 5 Marcellinus and his brother are condemned, and he is struck down with the sword. 6 Marinus falls from the Emperor’s favor; Marcellinus is distinguished by a reputation for integrity and innocence and by the crown of martyrdom. 7 Augustine secretly leaves Carthage, deeply grieving Marcellinus’ death. 461

[Col. 1483]

VI. 1 Demetrias travels from Rome, captured by the Goths, to Africa together with her mother and grandmother. 2 Augustine instructs Proba, Demetrias’ grandmother, by letter, and gives her precepts concerning prayer to God. 3 At her urging Demetrias embraces virginal chastity. 4 Augustine rejoices with the whole Church at Demetrias’ veiling. 5 He writes the book *On the Good of Widowhood* to Juliana, her mother. 6 On the pretext of instructing the virgin Demetrias, Pelagius publishes a letter steeped in the poison of his heresy. 467

VII. 1 A harsher law of Honorius against obstinate Donatists. 2 Donatus of Mutugenna and another presbyter with him, from the party of Donatus, are placed in custody. 3 Augustine writes to Macedonius concerning bishops’ intercessions on behalf of accused persons. 4 How prudently and modestly Augustine conducted himself in these intercessions, according to the testimony of Macedonius, to whom he imparts instruction concerning the duties of a Christian magistrate and true virtues. 5 He replies to the questions sent from Sicily by Hilary against the Pelagians. 471

VIII. 1 Several psalms are explained, both in the year of Christ 415 and earlier. 2 Orosius, a presbyter from the farthest part of Spain, comes to Augustine. 3 To satisfy his inquiries Augustine composes a book against the Priscillianists and Origenists. 4 He sends Orosius, together with some of his writings, to Jerome, from whom he wishes especially to learn about the origin of the soul. 5 He recalls Timasius and Jacobus from Pelagius’ error, against whom he publishes a short work *On Nature and Grace*. 6 He replies in several letters to certain questions of Evodius, especially important ones. 7 He composes the book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*. 475

IX. 1 Jerome attacks Pelagius’ heresy in Palestine, and the same matter is discussed in the assembly at Jerusalem. 2 Pelagius, accused by Heros and Lazarus, is brought before the episcopal tribunal held at Diospolis, where Pelagius’ heresy is condemned, although Pelagius himself is acquitted. 3 Violent actions are taken against Jerome and the virgin Eustochium by the Pelagians after that synod’s judgment. 4 After the same Synod of Diospolis, Pelagius publishes various writings. 480

X. 1 Jerome’s letters, together with other letters of Heros and Lazarus, are brought to Africa by Orosius. 2 The Council of Carthage, and, following its example, the Council of Milevis, write to Pope Innocent against Pelagius. 3 Five African bishops jointly do the same. 4 Augustine makes the African decrees against the Pelagian errors known to Hilary of Narbonne. 5 He writes to John of Jerusalem concerning the same errors detected in Pelagius. 6 A letter is sent by him to Oceanus. 7 The task of investigating more deeply the Church’s teaching in Scripture is entrusted to Augustine by two councils. 483

XI. 1 At Augustine’s urging Orosius writes his history. 2 In his reply to the Africans, Pope Innocent anathematizes Pelagius and Coelestius, condemning the doctrine of both. 3 Augustine publishes for general circulation a book *On the Proceedings of the Palestinian Synod*. 4 The outstanding qualities of Count Boniface, and his mind inclined to devote himself exclusively to God after renouncing all other things. 5 Augustine writes for him the book *On Correcting the Donatists*. 6 A book by the same author to Dardanus *On the Presence of God*. 7 Augustine writes a letter to Paulinus, in his own name and that of Alypius, against the Pelagians. 486–487

XII. 1 Coelestius comes to Rome; Zosimus treats him with great leniency and writes on his behalf to the African bishops. 2 Pelagius’ letter to Innocent is delivered to Zosimus, who is also deceived by its ambiguous wording and, through his favor toward Pelagius, writes to Africa. 3 The Council of Carthage, consisting of 214 bishops, replies to Zosimus and defends the judgment pronounced by Innocent against the aforementioned heretics. 4 Zosimus writes back to the Africans, saying that he had changed nothing after receiving their letters. The plenary Council of Africa publishes eight or nine canons against the Pelagians. 5 The same council enacts certain measures concerning matters relating to the Donatists. 6 The Pelagians are condemned both by Pope Zosimus and by the Emperor Honorius. 7 All the bishops confirm their condemnation with their signatures, except eighteen, who appeal to a plenary synod. 8 The Pelagians are defeated by the Church, not without much labor on Augustine’s part. 9 He writes two books against Pelagius to Pinianus. 492

XIII. 1 Augustine travels to Caesarea on Church business. 2 Emeritus comes to that city to dispute with him; in Emeritus’ presence, and while Emeritus remains silent, Augustine preaches. 3 On the following day, when Emeritus has been placed inside the church and persists in his silence, the holy bishop turns this conveniently to the advantage of his case. [Col. 1484] 4 Here, in a sermon delivered to the people, he abolishes a depraved custom of the citizens of Caesarea. 5 He writes back to Optatus concerning the question of the soul’s origin. 6 He likewise replies to Mercator. 7 Also to Coelestinus and Sixtus. 8 Against Aptus, he writes to Asellicus concerning avoidance of Judaism. 497–498

XIV. 1 In the year 419 Honorius sends an instruction to Aurelius and also to Augustine, requiring every bishop to give his signature against the Pelagian heresy. 2 Augustine recounts in a sermon at Carthage prodigies recently seen at Jerusalem and elsewhere. 3 Jerome is inflamed with love for Augustine, especially because through Augustine’s aid the Coelestian heresy had been cut down. 4 Augustine writes to Hesychius of Salona concerning the end of the world. 5 He publishes the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. 6 *Questions and Expressions in the Heptateuch*. 7 Augustine refutes Vincentius Victor in books *On the Origin of the Soul*. 8 Two books *On Adulterous Marriages* are written to Pollentius. 9 *The Adversary of the Law and the Prophets* is refuted. 504–505

# BOOK EIGHT

It encompasses the remaining acts of Augustine, from the year of Christ 420 to the year 430. 511–512

## CHAPTER ONE

1. The Donatists, driven by their own madness, kill and burn themselves. 2. Dulcitius, tribune and notary, strives to dissuade Gaudentius, a bishop of the party of Donatus, from his plan to burn himself, and receives two letters from him. 3. At Dulcitius’ request Augustine replies to Gaudentius. 4. He writes to Consent(i)us the book *Against Lying*, arguing that Catholics may not use lying even to investigate the Priscillianists. 5. He explains the same Consent(i)us’ questions, especially whether the Lord’s body now has bones and blood and the remaining features of flesh. 6. He writes to Ceretius against the Priscillianists. Ibid.

II. 1. Julianus writes four books against Augustine and several letters on behalf of the Pelagians. 2. Augustine refutes excerpts from Julianus’ first books in a book addressed to Valerius, the second book; and he writes four books to Boniface against two letters of the Pelagians. 3. Alypius carries all these books of Augustine to Italy. 4. Augustine publishes six other books against Julianus. 5. A rescript of the Emperor Constantius is promulgated against the Pelagians; and the temple of the goddess Caelestis is razed to the ground. 518

III. 1. Certain Manichaeans are discovered at Carthage. 2. Augustine expels Victorinus the Manichaean. 3. He composes the *Enchiridion* for the benefit of Laurentius. 4. To Paulinus, who consults him, he writes the book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*. 5. He replies to eight questions of Dulcitius. 523

IV. 1. Augustine arranges for Antonius to be ordained bishop of Fussala. 2. He is compelled to remove from him the administration of that Church. 3. Antonius deceives the primate of Numidia and Pope Boniface in order to be restored completely. 4. Augustine entreats Coelestinus to allow the sentence passed against him to remain in force and to cooperate with him for the peace of the Church of Fussala. 5. Otherwise the holy man considers laying down his own dignity because he had imprudently supported Antonius’ ordination. 528

V. 1. The relics of the martyr Stephen are found at Hippo around the year of Christ 424. 2. Januarius, a presbyter of Hippo, dies, leaving to the Church money that he had retained contrary to the rule of common life. 3. Augustine delivers a sermon to the people on this matter; he rejects Januarius’ inheritance and leaves it to his sons, and declares that he permits clerics who wish to possess something of their own to preserve the honor of their rank by living outside the episcopal residence. 4. In a later sermon he testifies that he wishes all his clerics to remain faithful to the rule of common life and to shun private property, and that those who retained anything for themselves should be removed from the clerical register; he also clears before the same people those who were said to be rich and wealthy. 5. The dreadful punishment of ten children against whom their mother had pronounced a curse. 6. Of those ten, Paul is divinely healed near Hippo. 7. On the following day Palladia is likewise healed there. 8. Augustine commends Galla and Simpliciola to Quintilianus. 532

VI. 1. The death of Severus, bishop of Milevis. 2. Concerning Heraclius the presbyter. 3. Augustine transfers the administration of affairs to him, having designated him as his successor. 4. Disputes among the monks of Hadrumetum concerning grace and free will. 5. Defenders of free will against grace come to Augustine; he instructs them and gives them, together with two letters, the book *On Grace and Free Will*, addressed to Valentinus and the monks with him. 6. The holy Teacher sends them another book, *On Correction and Grace*. 541

VII. 1. Augustine fights against the remnants of the Pelagian error detected in Vitalis, and puts forward twelve propositions concerning grace. 2. He advises Palatinus to seek from God the help of grace for perseverance in the good. 3. Leporius’ errors in Gaul against the faith of the Incarnation and grace are condemned. 4. Leporius is recalled to sound faith through Augustine’s work. 5. Augustine then applies himself to reviewing his own short works. 6. He compiles a *Speculum* from passages of the whole of Scripture suitable for shaping or correcting conduct. 547

VIII. 1. Boniface takes a second wife and afterward suffers great calamities. 2. War is waged against him, after he has been declared an enemy of the Empire, with Mavortius and other commanders sent against him. 3. Augustine exhorts Boniface by letter to return to his duty. 4. Segisvultus takes charge of the war begun against Boniface. 5. By God’s will the Vandals pour into Africa, so that some may be punished and others crowned. 6. A savage and dreadful devastation of Africa by the Vandals. 7. Whether bishops may provide for their own safety by flight in calamities of this kind. 554

IX. 1. The holy Teacher undertakes his final work against Julianus. 2. He enters into a conference with Maximinus, an Arian bishop, whom he also refutes in published books. 3. He exhorts Maximus, converted from the Arian heresy, to strive to bring his own people and others entangled in the same error to the Catholic faith. 4. He refutes the *Sermon of the Arians*. 5. He publishes a written account of his conference with Pascentius, likewise devoted to the Arian heresy, in letters addressed to him. 6. He writes back to Elpidius, who is mistaken concerning the faith of the Trinity. 561

X. 1. The men of Massilia and certain others in Gaul, not wholly alien to the Pelagians, rise up against the doctrine of predestination and grace explained by Augustine in his earlier books. 2. At the urging of Prosper and Hilary, Augustine defends the Catholic faith against them in books *On the Predestination of the Saints*. 3. Quodvultdeus asks the holy Teacher to write about heresies. 4. Pressed by Quodvultdeus, Augustine undertakes a work *On Heresies*, which he is compelled to leave unfinished. 5. In a letter to the aged Alypius he recounts the conversion of Dioscorus, full of miraculous events. 566

XI. 1. Boniface is reconciled with Placidia, apparently through the agency, among others, of Count Darius; Augustine seeks Darius’ friendship. 2. Defeated by the Vandals, Boniface withdraws to Hippo Regius; the Vandals advance there to besiege him; meanwhile Augustine is seized by illness. 3. Healings are divinely effected at Augustine’s prayers; he devotes himself entirely to tears and repentance in order to prepare himself for his departure; he dies; and, after the sacrifice has been offered for the commendation of his deposition, he is buried. 4. The year of Augustine’s death: in that very year he was summoned by Theodosius to the Synod of Ephesus. 5. Although the city of Hippo Regius was devastated by fire some time afterward, his writings were nevertheless preserved there; Possidius appended an index of them to the Life of Augustine, which he committed to writing. 572–573

# NOTICE CONCERNING THE BOOKS OF THE *CONFESSIONS*

657–658

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: THE THIRTEEN BOOKS OF THE *CONFESSIONS*

659–660

# BOOK ONE

After prefacing an invocation of God, he recalls the beginnings of his life up to his fifteenth year. He acknowledges the sins of infancy and childhood, and confesses that at this age he was more inclined toward play and every childish amusement than toward the study of letters. Ibid.

## CHAPTER ONE

He wishes to praise God, stirred up by God himself. Ibid.

II. God, whom he invokes, is within him, and he himself is in God. 661

III. God is wholly everywhere, in such a way that no thing contains him wholly. 662

IV. God’s majesty and perfections are beyond explanation. Ibid.

V. He asks for God’s love and forgiveness of sins. 663

VI. He describes his infancy and praises God’s providence and eternity. Ibid.

VII. Infancy too is subject to sins. 665

VIII. How the child learned to speak. 666

IX. Children’s hatred of letters, love of play, and fear of being beaten. 667

X. Love of play and spectacles distracts him from the study of letters. 668

XI. Afflicted by illness, he urgently requests baptism, which his mother deliberately postpones. Ibid.

XII. He was compelled to study letters, which God nevertheless used for good. 669

XIII. In which studies he took the greatest pleasure. 670

XIV. He hated Greek letters. 671

XV. A prayer to God. Ibid.

XVI. He disapproves of the way in which youth is educated. 672

XVII. He continues his criticism of the way youth is trained in literary studies. 673

XVIII. People take care to observe the laws of grammarians but not the divine commandments. Ibid.

XIX. The faults of childhood that pass into later ages. 674

XX. He gives thanks to God for the benefits bestowed on him in childhood. 675

# BOOK TWO

He advances to another period of life and recalls, with great sorrow, the first year of his adolescence—that is, his sixteenth year—which he had spent in his father’s house, after interrupting his studies, indulging in his temperament and lusts. He is especially severe in judging the theft he had committed at that time with his companions. 675–676

## CHAPTER ONE

He recalls the period and vices of adolescence. Ibid.

II. His sixteenth year spent in the heat of lust. Ibid.

III. Concerning his departure for study and his parents’ plans. 677

IV. The theft committed with his companions. 678

V. No one sins without a cause. 679

VI. Everything that invites people to vices under the appearance of good is true and perfect in God alone. 680

VII. He gives thanks to God for the remission of sins and for having preserved him from many dangers. 681

VIII. He loved the companionship of those who sinned together in the theft. Ibid.

IX. Evil companions are a contagious influence. 682

# BOOK THREE

He recalls the years spent at Carthage—his seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth years—where, while completing the course of literary studies, he remembers having been ensnared in the trap of lustful love and having fallen into the heresy of the Manichaeans. He argues eloquently against their errors and absurdities. He relates his mother’s pious tears and the response divinely given to her concerning his conversion. 683–684

## CHAPTER ONE

He is captured by the love he was pursuing. Ibid.

II. He loved tragic spectacles. Ibid.

III. In the school of the rhetorician he recoiled from the deeds of the *Eversores*. 685

IV. Cicero’s *Hortensius* awakened in him a passion for philosophy. Ibid.

V. He found the sacred writings distasteful because of the simplicity of their style. 668

[Col. 1488]

VI. How he was captured by the Manichaeans. 686

VII. The absurd doctrine of the Manichaeans, to which he gave his support. 688

VIII. Against the Manichaeans he states which vices must always be detested and which crimes must be condemned. 689

IX. The distinction between sins, and between God’s judgment and that of human beings. 690

X. The Manichaeans’ foolish notions concerning the fruits of the earth. 691

XI. The mother’s mourning and dream concerning her son. Ibid.

XII. What answer Augustine’s mother received from a certain bishop concerning his conversion. 692

# BOOK FOUR

Augustine is ashamed that he had been devoted to the Manichaean sect for nine years and had drawn others with him into the same error. He had also consulted astrologers; meanwhile a friend was taken from him by death, and he mourned him with a grief more bitter than was fitting. On this occasion he says much about empty and solid friendship. He mentions the books *On the Beautiful and the Fitting*, written by him in his twenty-seventh year, and also how, with little difficulty, he had understood for himself the books on the liberal arts and Aristotle’s *Categories*, when he was about twenty years old. 693–694

## CHAPTER ONE

How long and in what way he led others astray. Ibid.

II. He teaches rhetoric, keeps a concubine, and dismisses a diviner who promised him victory. Ibid.

III. He is recalled from astrology, to which he had been devoted, by an old man skilled in medicine and other matters. Ibid.

IV. He recounts his friend’s illness and baptism; he had also involved him in his own errors, and when death took him away he grieved most bitterly. The wondrous efficacy of the sacrament of Baptism. 696
