# BOOK FIVE

He presents his twenty-ninth year, in which, after discovering the incompetence of Faustus the Manichaean, he abandoned his intention of making progress in that sect. In the same year, having been sent from Rome, where he was then teaching rhetoric, to Milan to teach the same art, he began, after hearing Ambrose, to recover his senses and to decide to renounce Manichaeism and resume the status of a catechumen. 705–706

Now that Monnica, his mother, had arrived at Milan, and he himself was about to enter his thirtieth year, he understood more and more clearly, admonished by Ambrose’s sermons, the truth of Catholic doctrine, which the Manichaeans falsely accused. He continues with the character of his friend Alypius. He was drawn in different directions while deliberating about reforming his life, and, struck also by fear of death and judgment, he was daily more strongly impelled toward conversion of life. 717–718

He brings before the eyes of his mind the beginning of his youth—that is, his thirty-first year. He relates that at that age he was still enveloped in denser darkness of ignorance, wandering concerning the nature of God and the origin of evil. He reaches the most celebrated part of his life, his thirty-second year, when, after consulting Simplicianus and learning from him about Victorinus’ conversion, and after learning from Pontitianus’ account about the life of Antony the Egyptian monk, he inspected the Apostle’s book after a heavenly admonition, following a violent struggle between flesh and spirit; immediately after reading it he was wholly changed for the better and completely converted to God. 747–748

XIII. He prays for his deceased mother. 778

# BOOK TEN

He next examines himself and openly declares not what he had been before but what he is now. He strives to make known the God whom he loves; and, leading the discussion through each category of things, he explains at length the utterly astonishing power of memory and rejoices that God has a place in his memory. He examines his acts, senses, and affections in relation to the threefold temptation of pleasure, curiosity, and pride. He confesses the Lord Christ as the one mediator between God and human beings, and trusts that through Christ’s aid all the weaknesses of his soul must be healed. 779–780

## CHAPTER ONE

In God alone are hope and joy. Ibid.

II. Since hidden things are known to God, what does it mean to confess to him? Ibid.

## BOOK ELEVEN

He next undertakes to praise God on the basis of his own confession, whether of ignorance or knowledge of the Holy Scriptures, or of the zeal with which, by divine gift, he burned for them. He begins by explaining the opening of the Book of Genesis and first elucidates these words: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” He answers those who objected: What was God doing before he made heaven and earth, and what finally induced him to make them, since previously he had not made them? While he persists in refuting them, he composes an extensive discussion of time. 809–810

## BOOK TWELVE

He continues his interpretation of this verse: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” By the name “heaven” he understands that spiritual or intellectual creation which always contemplates the face of God; by the term “earth,” however, he understands formless matter, from which the forms of corporeal things were afterward fashioned. Yet he acknowledges that other modes of interpretation are by no means to be rejected; indeed, from the depth of divine Scripture many meanings may be drawn. 825–826

## BOOK THIRTEEN

He shows that God’s truth shines forth in the production and perfection of things, and that the Trinity, and the distinctive nature of the Holy Spirit, are also intimated in the first words of Genesis. He then transfers the entire history of the created world, by allegorical interpretation, to those things which God works in the Church for the holiness and glory of human beings. 845–846

## BOOK ONE

Augustine himself undertakes to pursue knowledge of God and of the soul. First he implores divine assistance; then, having recognized the excellence of the knowledge he desires, he converses with himself about advancing the health of his soul, so that at last he may safely rise to contemplate God. At the end of the book he concludes that those things which truly are are immortal. 869–870

## NOTICE ON THE THREE BOOKS AGAINST THE ACADEMICS

## THREE BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST THE ACADEMICS

905–906

## BOOK ONE

Romanianus is encouraged toward philosophy in the preface to this book, in which his son Licentius engages Trygetius in three discussions. The former maintains, on behalf of the Academics, that the happy life consists in the investigation itself of truth; the latter argues against them that it consists only in the apprehension of truth. The definition of error becomes a matter of dispute, as does the definition of wisdom, which is lucidly explained. Ibid.

### CHAPTER ONE

He exhorts Romanianus to true philosophy. Ibid. II. Whether apprehension of truth or its investigation alone is necessary for the happy life. 908 III. The position is defended, on behalf of the Academics, that happiness lies in the investigation of truth. 909 IV. What error is. 911 V. What wisdom is. 913 VI. A definition of wisdom is given and challenged. The divinations of Albicerius. 914 VII. The proposed definition of wisdom is defended. 915 VIII. Whether a soothsayer is wise, and what a wise person is. A description of wisdom suited to defending the Academic position. 916 IX. Epilogue. Ibid.

## BOOK TWO

Once again, with an expression of gratitude, he urges his patron Romanianus to embrace philosophy, and describes for him three Conferences, in the first of which the doctrines of the Academics are explained. In the second, the differences between the New and the Old Academy are related, and the opinion of those philosophers is rejected who, although they thought that truth could not be apprehended, nevertheless professed to follow what was probable or likely. In the third, he explains what they called the likely or probable. 919–920

### CHAPTER ONE

Against the Academic arguments, the help of God is necessary. Ibid. II. He offers Romanianus the service of a grateful mind and urges him toward philosophy. Ibid. III. Philocalia and philosophy. Whether the Academics concealed that they knew the truth. 933

## BOOK THREE

He presents two discussions. At their beginning it is established that fortune is neither a help nor a hindrance to the wise person. Soon afterward Augustine, with Alypius opposing him in accordance with the position he has undertaken, proves that the wise person knows something, since at least he knows wisdom. He then examines Zeno’s definition and refutes those two Academic doctrines: “Nothing can be apprehended,” and “One ought to assent to no thing.” Finally, he says that it seems to him that the Academics did not think as they are commonly believed to have thought. 933–934

## BOOK ONE

It presents two discussions. The first teaches that absolutely all things, both good and evil, are contained within the order of divine providence. The second touches somewhat upon the excellence and meaning of order. On this occasion Augustine severely censures the disordered movements of the soul and the quarrels among his students undertaken for the sake of childish little honors; he also says that Monnica should by no means be excluded from philosophical discussion on account of her sex. Ibid.

### CHAPTER ONE

Order is the guide to God. 990 X. What order is. How the impulses of rivalry and empty boasting are to be restrained in young people devoted to learning. Ibid. XI. Monnica should not be excluded from philosophical discussion on account of her sex. 992

## BOOK TWO

This book contains two discussions. While the interlocutors examine the definition of order, they encounter various questions: How does the wise person remain unmoved with God? Are even the things done wrongly by human beings carried out according to God’s order? Was God just before the origin of evil? Did evil arise from God’s order? Finally, they deal more fully with the proper order of study, which requires that, once character has been rightly formed and human disciplines acquired, the mind advance to the apprehension of higher and divine things. 993–994

## NOTICE ON THE BOOK ON THE QUANTITY OF THE SOUL

## THE ONE BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE QUANTITY OF THE SOUL

That is, a dialogue in which the interlocutor proposes six questions about the soul to Augustine. In treating the third question—namely, how great the soul is—he first distinguishes two kinds of quantity: one named from bulk and spatial extension, the other from power and capacity. He teaches that the former, which is proper to the body, is excluded from the soul, which is entirely incorporeal; the latter, however, is found in the soul. He then assigns seven grades of this greatness, to which he refers whatever the human soul is capable of, whether in the body, in itself, or finally with God. 1035–1036

The objection is raised that the soul grows with age. 1049 XVI. The objection is answered, and it is shown that the soul progresses without bodily increase. 1050 XVII. The soul is said metaphorically to grow over a period of time. 1051 XVIII. The faculty of speech, which a child gradually acquires, is not to be attributed to an increase of the soul. 1052 XIX. How the soul is said to grow or diminish. 1054 XX. Whether the soul knows anything from itself. Ibid. XXI. Although the soul senses throughout the entire body, it is not therefore extended together with the body. What sensation is, and how vision occurs. 1058 XXIV. The definition of sensation is examined. 1060 XXV. How a definition should be examined. 1062 XXVI. Whether knowledge and reason exist in animals. 1063 XXVII. Reason and reasoning. 1065 XXVIII. **BOOK THREE**, in which the origin of that movement is sought by which the will turns aside from the unchangeable good; and whether God’s foreknowledge of human sins conflicts with the freedom of human beings themselves in sinning. It is then shown that what must occur in a creature through the will of those who sin cannot in any way be attributed to the Creator; and that God must altogether be praised for creating and punishing a creature subject to sin. From this the discussion proceeds to the faults of origin, and it is explained how they are not unjustly transmitted to Adam’s descendants, and how those who sin on account of them cannot rightly plead an excuse; thereafter several related difficulties are resolved. 1269–1270

**OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE MORALS OF THE CATHOLIC CHURCH AND ON THE MORALS OF THE MANICHAEANS.** Ibid.

**BOOK ONE.** Augustine first establishes that those morals by which one lives holily in the Church ought to be referred to the supreme good of the human being, that is, to God. Then he shows that one must strive toward him with the greatest love, and that this doctrine is confirmed in the Catholic Church by the authority of both Testaments. He demonstrates that the four virtues are named from various forms of love for God. He discusses the duties of charity toward one’s neighbor, and finally relates examples of continence and truly Christian conduct that have shone forth among the members of the Catholic Church. Ibid.
